**(Sūrat al-Baqarah)**
It is Madani, except for verse 281, which was revealed at Mina during the Farewell Pilgrimage. Its verses number two hundred and eighty-six.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ Concerning it there are two issues.

**The first issue:**

Know that the words by which the letters are spelled out are names whose referents are the letters themselves. For example, *ḍād* is a single word that signifies, by convention (*tawāṭu'*, mutual agreement), a meaning that stands on its own, without indicating any particular time for that meaning. That meaning is the first letter of *ḍaraba* (he struck). It is thus established that they are names. Moreover, they are subject to inflection (*taṣarruf*) through *imālah* (vowel-raising), *tafkhīm* (emphasis), definiteness, indefiniteness, pluralization, diminutive formation, description, predication, and annexation. Therefore they are necessarily names.

If it is objected: Abū ʿĪsā al-Tirmidhī narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever recites a letter from the Book of Allah the Exalted, for him is a good deed, and a good deed is multiplied tenfold. I do not say that *Alif Lām Mīm* is one letter; rather, *alif* is a letter, *lām* is a letter, and *mīm* is a letter." The hadith is then cited, and using it as evidence contradicts what you have said.

We reply: He called it a letter metaphorically, because the name is that of the letter. Applying the name of one of two mutually implying things to the other is a well-known metaphor.

**Branches:**

The first: They observed this naming for subtle meanings. Since the things named are words like their names, and the names are single letters, and names tend to reach three letters in their count, a way opened for them to indicate the referent within the name. So they made the referent the initial element of each name, except for *alif*, for which they borrowed the *hamzah* in place of its referent, since the *alif* can only be unvowelled.

The second: Its ruling, so long as no governing particles precede it, is that its final part is unvowelled, like number-names. Thus one says *alif lām mīm*, just as you say *wāḥid, ithnān, thalāthah* (one, two, three). When governing particles precede them, inflection (*iʿrāb*) takes hold of them, as in your saying: *hādhihi alifun* (this is an *alif*), *katabtu alifan* (I wrote an *alif*), and *naẓartu ilā alifin* (I looked at an *alif*). The same applies to every name you use merely to convey its referent, because the substance of a word is assigned to the substance of the meaning, while the vowels of a word indicate the states of the meaning. When one wants to convey the substance of the meaning, the word must be free of vowels.

The third: These names are inflected, and they are unvowelled as all other names are unvowelled where inflection does not touch them, due to the absence of the cause that requires it. The evidence that their unvowelled state is a pause (*waqf*) and not a fixed indeclinability (*binā'*) is that, had they been indeclinable, they would have been treated like *kayfa* (how), *ayna* (where), and *hā'ulā'* (these), and one would not say *ṣād qāf nūn* with the two unvowelled consonants joined together.

**The second issue:** Regarding His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ and what resembles it of the opening letters, there are two opinions:

The first: that this is a hidden knowledge and a concealed secret which Allah, blessed and exalted, has reserved for Himself. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "For Allah there is a secret in every book, and His secret in the Qur'an is the openings of the chapters." ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Every book has an essence, and the essence of this Book is the letters of spelling out." Some of the knowers (*ʿārifīn*) said: Knowledge is like the sea. From it a valley is channeled; then from the valley a river is channeled; then from the river a rivulet is channeled; then from the rivulet a small irrigation channel is channeled. If that valley were channeled into the rivulet, it would drown and ruin it, and if the sea flowed into the valley, it would ruin it. This is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17]. So the oceans of knowledge are with Allah, Exalted is He. He gives the Messengers of them valleys; then the Messengers give from their valleys rivers to the scholars; then the scholars give to the common people small rivulets according to their capacity; then the common people channel irrigation channels to their families according to their capacity.

Accordingly is what has been related in a report: "The scholars have a secret, the rulers have a secret, the prophets have a secret, the angels have a secret, and Allah has, beyond all of that, a secret. If the ignorant were to learn the secret of the scholars, they would destroy them; if the scholars were to learn the secret of the rulers, they would oppose them; if the rulers were to learn the secret of the prophets, they would contradict them; if the prophets were to learn the secret of the angels, they would accuse them; and if the angels were to learn the secret of Allah, the Exalted, they would stray bewildered and perish in ruin."

The reason for this is that weak intellects cannot bear powerful secrets, just as the eyes of bats cannot bear the light of the sun. When the prophets were given increased intellects, they were able to bear the secrets of prophethood. When the scholars were given increased intellects, they were able to bear secrets which the common people could not. Likewise, the scholars of the inner (*bāṭin*), who are the sages (*ḥukamāʾ*), had their intellects increased, so they were able to bear what the scholars of the outer (*ẓāhir*) could not.

Al-Shaʿbī was asked about these letters and said: "It is Allah's secret, so do not seek it." Abū Ẓabyān narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The scholars were unable to comprehend them." Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl said: "It is of the *mutashābih* (the ambiguous)."

Know that the theologians (*mutakallimūn*) rejected this view. They said: It is not permissible for the Book of Allah, Exalted is He, to contain what is not understood by created beings. They argued for this with verses, reports, and rational arguments.

As for the verses, there are fourteen:

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they not ponder the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muḥammad: 24]. He commanded them to ponder the Qur'an. Had it been incomprehensible, how could He command them to ponder it?

The second: His saying: ﴿Do they not ponder the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisā': 82]. How, then, does He command them to ponder it in order to know the absence of contradiction and discrepancy, while it is incomprehensible to created beings?

The third: His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shuʿarā': 192–195]. Had it not been comprehensible, the Messenger's being a warner by it would be void. Also, His saying "in a clear Arabic tongue" indicates that it was sent down in the language of the Arabs, and if that is so, it must be comprehensible.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿Those among them who derive it would have known it﴾ [al-Nisā': 83]. Deriving from it is impossible except with comprehension of its meaning.

The fifth: His saying: ﴿An elucidation of all things﴾ [al-Naḥl: 89], and His saying: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-Anʿām: 38].

The sixth: His saying: ﴿A guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. What is not known cannot be a guidance.

The seventh: His saying: ﴿Far-reaching wisdom﴾ [al-Qamar: 5], and His saying: ﴿a healing for what is in the breasts, and a guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [Yūnus: 57]. All these attributes are not realized in what is not known.

The eighth: His saying: ﴿There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 15].

The ninth: His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 51]. How can the Book be sufficient, and how can it be a reminder, if it is incomprehensible?

The tenth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is a message for mankind, that they may be warned by it﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 52]. How can it be a message, and how can warning occur by it, if it is not known? And He said at the end of the verse: ﴿and that people of understanding may take heed﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 52], and that would only be so if it were known.

The eleventh: His saying: ﴿There has come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [al-Nisā': 174]. How can it be a proof and a manifest light if it is not known?

The twelfth: His saying: ﴿Whoever follows My guidance will not go astray nor be distressed. And whoever turns away from My remembrance, for him is a constricted life﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 123–124]. How is it possible to follow it, and to turn away from it, if it is not known?

The thirteenth: ﴿Indeed this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isrā': 9]. How can it be a guide if it is not known?

The fourteenth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Messenger believes in what was sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers … they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285]. Obedience is not possible except after understanding, so it is necessary that the Qur'an be comprehensible.

As for the reports: His saying, peace be upon him: "I have left among you that which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah and my Sunnah." How is it possible to hold fast to it if it is not known?

And from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Upon you is the Book of Allah. In it is the news of what came before you, the report of what will come after you, and the judgment of what is among you. It is the decisive word, not a jest. Whoever abandons it from among the tyrants, Allah will break him. Whoever seeks guidance elsewhere, Allah will lead him astray. It is the firm rope of Allah, the wise remembrance, and the straight path. It is that by which desires do not deviate, by which the scholars are not sated, which does not wear out through much repetition, and whose wonders do not end. Whoever speaks by it speaks truly, whoever judges by it acts justly, whoever argues by it prevails, and whoever calls to it is guided to a straight path."

As for rational arguments, they are of several aspects:

The first: If something were revealed for which there was no way to knowledge, then addressing with it would be like addressing an Arab in the Zanj language, and since that is not permissible, neither is this.

The second: The purpose of speech is communication. If it were not understood, addressing with it would be pointless and foolish, and that is not fitting for the Wise.

The third: The challenge (*taḥaddī*) was issued with the Qur'an, and a challenge cannot be issued with what is not known.

That is the sum of the theologians' argument. Their opponents argued with the verse, the report, and rational argument.

As for the verse: it is that the *mutashābih* (ambiguous) part of the Qur'an is not known, on the basis of His saying: ﴿and none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 7]. The pause here is obligatory, for several reasons:

The first: If His saying ﴿and those firm in knowledge﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 7] were conjoined to ﴿except Allah﴾, then ﴿they say, "We believe in it"﴾ would be cut off from it, and that is impermissible, because it would not convey meaning on its own. It cannot be said that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), because we would say that then it returns to everything before it, and it would follow that Allah, Exalted is He, is saying, "We believe in it, all of it is from our Lord," and that is disbelief.

The second: If those firm in knowledge knew its interpretation, there would be no point in singling them out for belief in it, since once they knew it by evidence, believing in it would be no different from believing in the clear (*muḥkam*) verses, and so there would be no added praise in believing in it.

The third: If its interpretation were something that must be known, then seeking that interpretation would not be blameworthy. But Allah has made it blameworthy, saying: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 7].

As for the report: we have already related at the beginning of this issue a report that supports our view. It has also been related that he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, among knowledge is something like a hidden treasure, which none knows except the scholars of Allah. When they speak of it, those heedless of Allah deny it." Moreover, the view that these openings are not known has been related from the great Companions, so it must be true, in light of his saying, peace be upon him: "My Companions are like the stars: whichever of them you follow, you will be guided."

As for rational argument: the actions we are obligated to perform are of two kinds. Among them are those whose wisdom we know in general by our intellects, such as prayer, zakāh, and fasting. Prayer is pure humility and submission to the Creator; zakāh is striving to meet the needs of the poor; and fasting is striving to break desire.

Among them are matters whose wisdom we do not know, such as the rites of the Hajj: by our intellects we do not know the wisdom in stoning the pillars (al-jamarat), in the running between Safa and Marwa, in the ramal (hastening the pace in the first circuits of the tawaf), or in the idtiba' (baring the right shoulder). The verifying scholars have agreed that just as it is fitting for God, exalted is He, to command His servants with the first type, so too is it fitting for Him to command them with the second type. This is because obedience in the first type does not show complete submission, since it is possible that the one commanded performed it only because his intellect understood the benefit in it. Obedience in the second type, however, does show complete submission and the utmost surrender, because when he does not know at all any benefit in it, his performing it can only be for pure submission and surrender. If this is the case with actions, why should it not also be the case with utterances? That is, God, exalted is He, may command us at times to speak things whose meaning we understand, and at other times things whose meaning we do not understand. The purpose of this is to show the submission and surrender of the commanded to the Commander. Moreover, there is another benefit in it: when a person understands the meaning and grasps it fully, its impact on the heart fades; but when he does not reach the intended meaning, while being certain that the speaker is the most wise of judges, his heart remains turned toward it forever and continually reflects upon it. The essence of obligation is occupying the inner self with the remembrance of God, exalted is He, and reflecting upon His speech. Thus it is not far-fetched that God, exalted is He, knows that the servant remaining with a mind turned toward it and a heart continually occupied with it holds a great benefit for him, so He worships Him with this in order to achieve that benefit. This is the summary of the words of both groups on this matter.

The second opinion: the view of those who claim that the meaning of these opening letters is known, though they differed regarding it and mentioned several aspects:

The first: they are the names of the surahs. This is the view of most of the scholars of kalam, and it is the choice of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. Al-Qaffal said: "The Arabs have named things with these letters. They named the father of Haritha ibn Lam al-Ta'i 'Lam,' and they say 'sad' for brass, 'ayn' for money, and 'ghayn' for a cloud. They also said 'Mount Qaf,' and they named the fish 'nun.'"

The second: they are names of God, exalted is He. It was narrated from Ali, peace be upon him, that he used to say: "Ya Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad, ya Ha-Mim-'Ayn-Sin-Qaf."

The third: they are fragments of the names of God, exalted is He. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "His saying (Alif-Lam-Ra, Ha-Mim, Nun), all of them together form the name al-Rahman, but we cannot determine how the rest of them are composed."

The fourth: they are names of the Qur'an. This is the view of al-Kalbi, al-Suddi, and Qatada.

The fifth: each of them indicates one of the names of God, exalted is He, and one of His attributes. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said regarding (Alif-Lam-Mim): the Alif indicates that He is One (Ahad), the First (Awwal), the Last (Akhir), the Eternal (Azali), the Everlasting (Abadi); the Lam indicates that He is Subtle (Latif); and the Mim indicates that He is King (Malik), Glorious (Majid), and Bestower (Mannan). He said regarding (Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad) that it is praise from God upon Himself: the Kaf indicates that He is Sufficient (Kafi), the Ha indicates that He is Guide (Hadi), the 'Ayn indicates that He is Knowing ('Alim), and the Sad indicates that He is Truthful (Sadiq). Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he interpreted the Kaf as the Great (Kabir) and the Generous (Karim), the Ya as the One who grants protection (Yujir), and the 'Ayn as the Mighty ('Aziz) and the Just ('Adl). The difference between these two aspects is that in the first, each letter was specified with a particular name, whereas in the second it is not so.

The sixth: some of them indicate names of the Essence, and some indicate names of the Attributes. Ibn 'Abbas said regarding (Alif-Lam-Mim): "I am God, the All-Knowing (A'lam)." Regarding (Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad) he said: "I am God, the Distinguisher (Afsil)." Regarding (Alif-Lam-Ra) he said: "I am God, the One who sees (Ara)." This is the narration of Abu Salih and Sa'id ibn Jubayr from him.

The seventh: each of them indicates attributes of action. The Alif is His blessings (ala'), the Lam His kindness (lutf), and the Mim His glory (majd). This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "There is no letter among them except that it is mentioned in relation to His blessings and favors."

The eighth: some of them indicate names of God, exalted is He, and some indicate names other than God. Al-Dahhak said: "The Alif is from Allah, the Lam is from Jibril, and the Mim is from Muhammad," meaning that God sent down the Book through the tongue of Jibril to Muhammad (ﷺ).

[p. 7]

The ninth: each of these letters indicates one of the acts. The Alif means "Allah made Muhammad (ﷺ) (alafa) and sent him as a prophet"; the Lam means "those who deny (lamahu al-jahidun) him"; and the Mim means "the unbelievers (mim al-kafirun) were enraged and humiliated by the manifestation of the truth." Some of the Sufis said: "The Alif means 'ana' (I), the Lam means 'li' (to me), and the Mim means 'minni' (from me)."

The tenth: this is what al-Mubarrad said, and a great group of the verifying scholars chose it: God mentioned them as an argument against the unbelievers. When the Messenger (ﷺ) challenged them to bring the like of the Qur'an, or ten surahs, or a single surah, and they were unable to do so, these letters were revealed as an alert that the Qur'an is nothing but made of these letters, which you are capable of and know the rules of eloquence for. So you should have been able to bring the like of this Qur'an. When you were unable to do so, that showed that it is from God and not from man.

The eleventh: 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya said: God mentioned them because, in the estimation, it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Listen to them separated, so that when they come to you joined together, you will already have known them beforehand, just as children learn these letters first, individually, and then learn compound words."

The twelfth: this is the view of Ibn Rawq and Qutrub: when the unbelievers said, "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you will prevail," and they urged one another to turn away from it, God, exalted is He, desiring their good and benefit, wanted to present to them what they did not understand, so that this would be a cause for their silence and for their listening to what the Qur'an brings to them. God revealed these letters to them, and whenever they heard them they would say, as if amazed, "Listen to what Muhammad, peace be upon him, brings!" When they gave their attention, the Qur'an would overwhelm them, and this became a cause for their listening and a path to their benefit.

The thirteenth: the view of Abu al-'Aliya, that each letter of them is within the term of certain peoples and the lifespans of others. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said: "Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab passed by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while he was reciting the Surah of al-Baqara, (Alif-Lam-Mim) (That is the Book). Then his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf came and asked him about (Alif-Lam-Mim) and said: 'We adjure you by God, besides whom there is no god, is it true that these came to you from heaven?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Yes, thus it was revealed.' Huyayy said: 'If you are truthful, I know the term of this community in years.' Then he said: 'How shall we enter the religion of a man whose letters, by the reckoning of the abjad, indicate that the end of his community's term is seventy-one years?' The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed, and Huyayy said: 'Is there anything other than this?' He said: 'Yes, (Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad).' Huyayy said: 'This is more than the first; this is a hundred and sixty-one years. Is there anything other than this?' He said: 'Yes, (Alif-Lam-Ra).' Huyayy said: 'This is more than the first and the second. We testify, if you are truthful, that your community has ruled only two hundred and thirty-one years. Is there anything other than this?' He said: 'Yes, (Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra).' Huyayy said: 'We testify that we are among those who do not believe, and we do not know which of your sayings to take.' Abu Yasir said: 'As for me, I testify that our prophets informed us about the dominion of this community but did not explain how long it would be. If Muhammad is truthful in what he says, I see that all of this is gathered for him.' Then the Jews stood and said: 'Your affair has become confused for us entirely; we do not know whether to take the little or the much.'" That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He it is who has sent down to you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7].

The fourteenth: these letters indicate the cutting off of one speech and the beginning of another. Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Tha'lab said: "When the Arabs begin a new speech, it is their habit to bring something other than the speech they wish to begin, making it an alert to the addressees to cut off the first speech and begin the new one."

The fifteenth: Ibn al-Jawzi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that these letters are a praise which God, mighty and majestic is He, praised Himself with.

The sixteenth: al-Akhfash said: "God, exalted is He, swore by the disjointed letters because of their nobility and excellence, and because they are the building blocks of His revealed books in the various tongues, the building blocks of the Most Beautiful Names of God and His Sublime Attributes, and the foundations of the speech of the nations, through which they recognize one another and mention God and affirm His oneness. Then He, exalted is He, confined Himself to mentioning a part, though the whole is intended, just as you say, 'I recited al-Hamd' while meaning the entire surah. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: 'I swear by these letters that this Book is that Book inscribed in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).'"

The seventeenth: although speaking these letters is familiar to everyone, that they are called by these names is known only to those who have occupied themselves with learning and acquiring knowledge. When the Messenger, peace be upon him, informed about them without any prior learning or acquisition, that was an informing about the unseen. For this reason God, exalted is He, placed their mention first, so that the first thing heard from this surah would be a miracle indicating his truthfulness.

The eighteenth: Abu Bakr al-Tibrizi said: "God, exalted is He, knew that a group from this community would say that the Qur'an is eternal (qadim), so He mentioned these letters as an alert that His speech is composed of these letters, and therefore it must not be eternal."

The nineteenth: al-Qadi al-Mawardi said: "The meaning of (Alif-Lam-Mim) is that this Book has visited you (alamma bikum), that is, it descended upon you. Al-ilmam is a visit. God, exalted is He, said that because Jibril, peace be upon him, descended with it as a visitor descends."

The twentieth: the Alif indicates the uprightness that is indispensable at the beginning of the matter, which is observing the Shari'ah. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain upright﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. The Lam indicates the bending (inhina') that occurs during the struggles (mujahadat), which is observing the path (tariqa). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 69]. The Mim indicates that the servant comes to the station of love, like a circle whose end is the very same as its beginning and whose beginning is the very same as its end. This happens only through annihilation in God, exalted is He, completely, and this is the station of reality (haqiqa). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say, "God." Then leave them in their plunging, playing﴾ [al-An'am: 91].

The twenty-first: the Alif comes from the farthest part of the throat, which is the first of the places of articulation of the letters; the Lam comes from the tip of the tongue, which is the middle of the places of articulation; and the Mim comes from the lips, which is the last of the places of articulation. These are an indication that the beginning of the servant's mention, its middle, and its end must be none other than God, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿So flee to God﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 50].

The preferred view among most of the verifying scholars, out of these sayings, is that they are the names of the surahs. The evidence for this is that these expressions are either not understood, or they are understood. The first is invalid. As for the first point, if that were permissible, it would be permissible to speak with an Arab in the language of the Zanj. As for the second point, God, exalted is He, described the entire Qur'an as guidance, and that contradicts its being unknown.

[p. 8]

[Page 8]

As for the second division, we say: either God, exalted is He, intends by them that they be names of epithets (*alqab*), or names of meanings. The second is invalid, because these letters are not assigned in the language of the Arabs to the meanings that the exegetes have mentioned, so it is impossible to interpret them according to those meanings. For the Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, so it is not permissible to interpret them in a way that does not exist in the language of the Arabs. Furthermore, the exegetes have mentioned various different views, and the indication of these letters for some of what they mentioned is no more preferable than their indication for the rest. So either they are interpreted as all of them, which is impossible by *ijma'* (scholarly consensus), because each of the exegetes interpreted these letters only as one of these mentioned meanings, and none of them interpreted them as all of them; or they are not interpreted as any of them, and this is the remaining option. Since this division is invalid, it is necessary to judge that they are among the names of epithets.

If it is said: Why is it not permissible to say that these letters are not known? [Your] statement, "If that were permissible, it would be permissible to speak with an Arab in the language of the Zanj," [we answer:] Why would that not be permissible? Its explanation is that God, exalted is He, spoke [the word] *mishkat* (niche), and it is in the tongue of Abyssinia; and *sijjil* and *istabraq* are Persian. [Your] statement, "The description of the Qur'an as a whole as guidance and clarification," [we answer:] There is no dispute that the Qur'an includes *mujmal* (general, unspecified) and *mutashabihat* (ambiguous) elements. So if that does not detract from its being guidance and clarification, then likewise here. Even if we grant that these letters are understandable, your statement, "They are either among the names of epithets or among the names of meanings," is only valid if it is established that they are assigned to convey a specific matter, and that is disputed. Perhaps God, exalted is He, spoke with them for another wisdom, like what Qutrub said: that when they agreed at the beginning

[Page 9]

not to pay attention to the Qur'an, God, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger to speak these letters at the beginning, so that they would be astonished upon hearing them and fall silent; then the Qur'an would overwhelm their ears. Even if we grant that they are assigned to a specific matter, why would it not be permissible to say that they are among the names of meanings? [Your] statement, "They are, in the language, not assigned to anything whatsoever," [we answer:] There is no dispute that they, by themselves, are not assigned to anything. But why would it not be permissible to say that, together with a particular indicator, they convey a specific meaning? Its explanation is in several respects:

(First): He, peace be upon him, used to challenge them with the Qur'an time and again. When he mentioned these letters, the context indicated that God's purpose in mentioning them was to say to them: This Qur'an is composed only of these letters which you are able to use. So if this were the work of humans, you would be able to produce something like it.

(Second): Interpreting these letters according to *hisab al-jummal* (the numerical value of letters, abjad reckoning) is a well-known custom among people.

(Third): Since these letters are the foundations of speech, they are noble and precious, so God, exalted is He, swore by them just as He swore by other things.

(Fourth): Using a single letter of a name in place of the whole name is a well-known custom among the Arabs, so God, exalted is He, mentioned these letters as an allusion to His names, exalted is He.

Even if we grant your proof, it is opposed by several respects:

(First): We find that many surahs share [the openings] *Alif-Lam-Mim* and *Ha-Mim*, so confusion arises among them, and the purpose of a proper name is to remove confusion.

If it is said: This is objected to by the many people named Muhammad, since sharing a name does not negate being a proper name. We say: The statement "Alif-Lam-Mim" conveys no meaning whatsoever, so if we made it a proper name, there would be no benefit in it except specification and the removal of confusion. When this aim is not achieved, it is impossible to make it a proper name. This is unlike naming someone Muhammad, for in naming someone with it there are other purposes beyond specification, namely seeking blessing through it because it is the name of the Messenger, and because it indicates an attribute of nobility. So it is permissible to intend naming someone with it for another purpose among these purposes besides specification. This is unlike our statement "Alif-Lam-Mim," for there is no benefit in it except specification. So when it does not yield this benefit, naming with it is pure futility.

(Second): If these expressions were names of the surahs, it would have to be known by *tawatur* (mass transmission), because these names are not according to the patterns of Arabic names, and remarkable matters are such that the motives to transmit them are strong, especially in what does not relate to concealing it out of desire or fear. If the motives to transmit them were strong, that would be known by *tawatur* and the disagreement about it would be removed. Since the matter is not like that, we know that they are not among the names of the surahs.

(Third): The Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and they did not exceed in naming with a compound of two names, such as *Ma'd Yakrib* and *Ba'labakk*. None of them named anything with a compound of three, four, or five names. So the claim that these are names of the surahs is a departure from the language of the Arabs, and that is not permissible.

(Fourth): If these were the names of these surahs, these surahs would have to be well known by them and not by the rest of the names. But they became known by the rest of the names, as in their saying "Surat al-Baqarah" and "Surat Al 'Imran."

(Fifth): These expressions are included within the surah and are a part of it. The part of a thing precedes the thing in rank, while the name of a thing comes after the thing in rank. So if we made them a name for the surah, precedence and subsequence would occur together, which is impossible. If it is said: The compound of our statement "Sad" is a name for its first letter. So if a compound may be a name for some of its individual elements, why would it not be permissible for some of the individual elements of that compound to be a name for that compound? We say: The difference is clear, because the compound comes after the individual element, and the name comes after the named. So if we made the compound a name for the individual element, there would be no necessary consequence except that the compound comes after that individual element in two respects, and that is not impossible. But if we made the individual element a name for the compound, it would follow that insofar as it is an individual element it precedes, and insofar as it is a name it comes after, and that is impossible.

(Sixth): If it were so, it would necessarily follow that no surah of the Qur'an would be without a name in this manner, and it is known that this does not occur.

[Page 10]

The answer: [Your] statement, "*Mishkat* and *sijjil* are not from the language of the Arabs." We say: There are two answers to this:

The first: All of that is Arabic, but it coincides with other languages, and such a thing may happen in two languages.

The second: The thing named by these names did not first exist in the lands of the Arabs. When they came to know it, they came to know its names from it, so they spoke those names, and those expressions became Arabic as well.

[Your] statement, "It is found that the *mujmal* in the Book of God does not detract from its being clarification." We say: Every *mujmal* found in the Book of God has had its clarification found either in reason, in the Book, or in the Sunnah, and at that point it ceases to be non-beneficial. Clarification is only lacking in what it is not possible to know the intention of God from.

As for [your] statement, "Why would it not be permissible for the purpose of mentioning these expressions to be to silence them from clamor?" We say: If mentioning these expressions were permissible for this purpose, then mentioning all sorts of nonsense would be permissible for a similar purpose, and that is by *ijma'* invalid.

As for the rest of the aspects they mentioned, we have shown that the statement "﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾" is not assigned in the language of the Arabs to convey those meanings, so it is not permissible to use it for them, because the Qur'an was revealed only in the language of the Arabs. Furthermore, they conflict, so interpreting the expression according to some of them is no more preferable than according to others. Also, if we opened this door, the doors of the interpretations of the Batiniyya (esoteric sects) and all sorts of nonsense would open, and that is not a path that can be taken.

As for the answer to the first opposition: it is not unlikely that there is a hidden wisdom in naming many surahs with one name, and then distinguishing each of them from the others by another sign.

As for the second: naming a surah with a specific expression is not among the great matters, so it may not reach the level of fame that amounts to *tawatur*.

As for the third: naming with three names is a departure from the speech of the Arabs if it is made a single name in the manner of "Hadramawt." But as for names that are not compounded, but rather a form of listing the names of numbers, that is permissible. Sibawayh explicitly stated the permissibility of naming with a sentence, with a line of poetry, and with a group of names of the letters of the alphabet.

As for the fourth: it is not unlikely that an epithet (*laqab*) becomes more famous than a proper name, so likewise here.

As for the fifth: a name is an expression that indicates a matter standing independently by itself without indicating its specific time, and the expression "name" is like that, so the name is a name for itself. If that is permissible, why would it not be permissible for a part of a thing to be a name for it?

As for the sixth: the assignment of a name is only according to what wisdom requires, and it is not unlikely that wisdom requires assigning a name to some surahs and not others. Moreover, the true position is that He, exalted is He, does what He wills. This is the end of the discussion in support of this method.

Know that after this position which we have supported with the arguments we have related, there is the view of Qutrub: that the polytheists said to one another, "﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it﴾" (41:26). So whenever the Messenger of God (ﷺ) spoke at the beginning of this surah with these expressions, they understood nothing from them, and a person is eager for what he is forbidden. So they would listen to the Qur'an, reflect, and ponder its openings and closings, hoping that perhaps a statement would come that explains that ambiguity and clarifies that difficulty. This became a means for them to become listeners to the Qur'an and contemplators of its beginnings and endings. Two things confirm this view:

The first: these letters only came at the beginnings of surahs, and that gives the impression that the purpose is what we have mentioned.

The second: [Page 11]

the scholars have said that the wisdom in revealing the *mutashabihat* is that the one who reasons, when he knows that the Qur'an includes *mutashabihat*, will examine the Qur'an and strive in reflecting on it, hoping that he may find something that strengthens his position and supports his school of thought. This becomes a cause for him to come to the *muhkamat* (clear verses) that save him from misguidance. So if it is permissible to reveal the *mutashabihat* that give the impression of misguidance for such a purpose, then it is all the more permissible to reveal these letters, which give no impression of any error or misguidance, for such a purpose; this is more fitting. The most that can be said is: if that is permissible, then it would be permissible to speak Zanji with an Arab, and to speak nonsense for this purpose. Moreover, this would detract from the Qur'an being guidance and clarification. But we say: why would it not be permissible to say that when God, exalted is He, speaks Zanji with an Arab, and that includes such a benefit, then that is permissible? Its verification is that speech is one of the acts, and its motive may be communication, and it may be other than that. [Your] statement, "It would be nonsense," we say: If by nonsense you mean an act entirely devoid of benefit, then that is not the case. And if you mean by it expressions devoid of communication, then why do you say that this detracts from wisdom when it has other aspects of benefit besides this one? As for describing the Qur'an as guidance and clarification, that does not contradict what we have said, for if the purpose is what we have mentioned, then listening to them is among the greatest aspects of clarification and guidance. And God knows best.

(Branches on the view that they are names of surahs):

The first point: these names fall into two categories. One category admits i'rab (grammatical inflection, the system of case endings). This is either a single letter-name such as Sad, Qaf, and Nun, or a group of names whose combined form matches the pattern of a single word, such as Ha Mim, Ta Sin, and Ya Sin. For they are of the same weight as Qabil and Habil. As for Ta Sin Mim, although it is composed of three names, it is like Darabjird, and it belongs to the category of what does not take tanwin (the nunation that marks indefinite nouns), because two causes of non-declension combine in it: being a proper name (ʿalamiyyah) and being feminine (taʾnith).

The second category is what does not admit i'rab, such as Kaf Ha Ya ʿAyn Sad and Alif Lam Mim Ra. Having understood this, we say: as for the single letters, there are two readings.

The first is the reading of those who read Sad, Qaf, and Nun with a fatha. This vowel may be the accusative case governed by a hidden verb, such as "udhkur" (mention). It is not accompanied by tanwin because of the prohibition of declension, as its explanation has already preceded. Sibawayh permitted the same for Ha Mim, Ta Sin, and Ya Sin if they were recited that way. Al-Sirafi reported that some people read "Ya Sin" with a fatha on the Nun. The fatha may also indicate the genitive case, by assuming that the letter is governed by an elided oath particle "ba" (the particle of swearing), as has come from them: "Allah, I will certainly do it." Yet it was given a fatha in the genitive position because it does not take declension. This is reinforced by what we have transmitted from some of them, that "God Most High swore by these letters."

The second is the reading of some who read Sad with a kasra, and its cause is the vowelling to resolve the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). As for the second category, which does not admit i'rab, it must be treated as quoted speech (mahkiyy), meaning that the utterance is produced after being transmitted, preserving its original form, as in your saying: "Leave me alone with Tamratan."

The second point: God Most High has included in these openings half the names of the letters of the alphabet, fourteen in total, namely: Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad, Ra, Kaf, Ha, Ya, ʿAyn, Ta, Sin, Ha, Qaf, and Nun, across twenty-nine surahs.

The third point: these openings come in differing numbers of letters. "Sad," "Qaf," and "Nun" appear as one letter; "Ta Ha," "Ta Sin," "Ya Sin," and "Ha Mim" as two letters; "Alif Lam Mim," "Alif Lam Ra," and "Ta Sin Mim" as three letters; "Alif Lam Mim Sad" and "Alif Lam Mim Ra" as four letters; and "Kaf Ha Ya ʿAyn Sad" and "Ha Mim ʿAyn Sin Qaf" as five letters. The reason is that the patterns of their words consist of one, two, up to five letters only, and so it is here.

The fourth point: do these openings have a place in i'rab or not? We say: if we take them as names of the surahs, then yes, and they may take the three cases. The nominative is by being the subject of a sentence (ibtida'). The accusative and genitive are because of what has passed concerning the validity of swearing by them. Whoever does not take them as names of the surahs cannot conceive that they have a place in i'rab according to his view, just as there is no place in i'rab for independent sentences or for enumerated single words.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 2 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is the Book﴾. On this there are several issues.

The first issue: One may say: the thing being pointed to here is present, and "dhalika" (that) is a vague demonstrative used for what is distant. The answer to this is in two respects. The first: We do not concede that the thing pointed to is present. Its explanation is from several aspects.

One of them: what al-Asamm (Abu Bakr al-Asamm) said, namely that God, exalted is He, sent down the Book piece by piece, so before the Surah al-Baqarah there descended many surahs, which are everything revealed in Mecca that contains the proof of divine unity, the corruption of polytheism, the establishment of prophethood, and the establishment of the return (to God). So His saying "That" refers to those surahs that were revealed before this surah. Some of the Qur'an may be called Qur'an. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it﴾ [al-A'raf: 204], and He said, relating from the jinn: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30]. They had heard only a part, which was what had been revealed up to that time.

The second: that God promised His Messenger, at the time of his mission, that He would send down upon him a Book that the eraser cannot erase. He, peace be upon him, informed his community of this, and the community related that from him. It is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon you a weighty word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5]. This is in Surah al-Muzzammil, which was revealed at the beginning of the mission.

The third: that God addressed the Children of Israel, because Surah al-Baqarah is Medinan, and most of it is an argument against the Children of Israel. The Children of Israel had been told by Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, that God would send Muhammad ﷺ and reveal to him a Book. So He said: ﴿That is the Book﴾, meaning the Book that the earlier prophets had announced God would send down upon the prophet raised from the descendants of Isma'il.

The fourth: that when God informed about the Qur'an that it is in the Preserved Tablet, by His saying: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 4], and he, peace be upon him, had informed his community of this, it is not impossible that He says: ﴿That is the Book﴾, to make known that this revealed Book is that Book recorded in the Preserved Tablet.

The fifth: that the pointing with "that" occurred to "Alif Lam Mim" after its utterance had passed and ended, and what has passed is in the status of what is distant.

The sixth: that when it reached from the sender to the one sent to, it fell into the realm of distance, as you say to your companion, when you have given him something: "Keep that safe."

The seventh: that since the Qur'an contains great wisdoms and many sciences, of which the human faculty finds it difficult to grasp all of them, and the Qur'an, although present as to its form, is absent as to its secrets and realities, it is permissible to point to it as one points to the distant absent.

The second respect: Suppose that the thing pointed to is present. Still, we do not concede that the word "dhalika" is only used to point to the distant. Its explanation: "dha" and "dhalika" are two demonstrative particles, and their root is "dha," because it is a particle of pointing. God said: ﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245]. The meaning of "ha" is alerting. So when a thing is near, it is pointed to and it is said: "hadha," meaning: be alert, O addressee, to what I point to, for it is present for you in a place where you see it.

Page 13

The kaf may be attached to "dha" for addressing, and the lam to emphasize the meaning of pointing, so it is said "dhalika." It is as if the speaker is exaggerating in alerting, because the thing pointed to is delayed from him. This indicates that the word "dhalika" does not, in its original coinage, convey distance. Rather, by convention it became specific to pointing at the distant, owing to the indication we mentioned. It became like the word "dabbah" (beast), which is in convention specific to the horse, although in its original coinage it applies to everything that crawls upon the earth. Once this is established, we say: we interpret it here according to the linguistic original coinage, not according to the conventional coinage, and then it does not convey distance. For this closeness, each of the two words is used in place of the other. God said: ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham and Isaac...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and all of them are among the chosen ones﴾ [Sad: 45-48]. Then He said: ﴿This is a reminder﴾ [Sad: 49]. And He said: ﴿And with them are those restraining their gaze, equal in age. This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾ [Sad: 52-53]. And He said: ﴿And the agony of death came with truth. That is what you were trying to avoid﴾ [Qaf: 19]. And He said: ﴿So God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first. Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 25-26]. And He said: ﴿And We had written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105], then He said: ﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship﴾ [al-Anbiya': 106]. And He said: ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it." Thus God brings the dead to life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 73], meaning: thus God brings the dead to life. And He said: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17], meaning: what is this that is in your right hand. And God knows best.

The second issue: One may say: why is the demonstrative masculine when the thing pointed to is feminine, namely the surah? The answer: We do not concede that the thing pointed to is feminine, because the feminine is either the named thing or the name. The first is invalid, because the named thing is that portion of the Qur'an, and it is not feminine. As for the name, it is "Alif Lam Mim," and it is not feminine. Yes, that named thing has another name, which is "surah," and that is feminine. But the earlier mentioned item is the name which is not feminine, which is "Alif Lam Mim," not the one which is feminine, which is "surah."

* * *

The third issue: Know that the names of the Qur'an are many. One of them: al-Kitab (the Book), which is a verbal noun like al-qiyam and al-siyam. It has been said that it is fi'al in the sense of maf'ul, like al-libas in the sense of al-malbus (what is worn). They agreed that what is meant by al-Kitab is the Qur'an. He said: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you﴾ [Sad: 29]. The word al-Kitab occurs in the Qur'an in several senses:

One: obligation: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183], ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times﴾ [al-Nisa': 103].

Two: proof and evidence: ﴿So bring your proof, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Saffat: 157], meaning your proof.

Three: term: ﴿And We did not destroy any city but that it had a known term﴾ [al-Hijr: 4], meaning a term.

Four: in the sense of a master's contract with his slave: ﴿And those who seek a writing [of emancipation] from among those whom your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. This verbal noun is fi'al in the sense of mufa'alah, like al-jidal, al-khisam and al-qital in the sense of mujadalah, mukhasamah and muqatalah. The derivation of kutub is from "kataba al-shay'" when you gather it, and the battalion (katibah) was named for its gathering. So the Book was named kitab because it is like a battalion arrayed against the armies of doubts, or because all the sciences are gathered in it, or because God imposed the obligations upon creation through it.

Second: al-Qur'an: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an...﴾ [al-Isra': 88], ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3], ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra': 9]. Regarding it, the commentators have two opinions:

One of them: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas that the Qur'an and the recitation (qira'ah) are one, just as al-khusran and al-khasarah are one. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18], meaning its recitation; that is, when We recite it to you, follow its recitation.

Page 14

The second, which is the saying of Qatadah: it is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "I qara'tu al-ma' fi al-hawd" when you gather it. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: The Qur'an was named Qur'an because the letters were gathered and became words, the words were gathered and became verses, the verses were gathered and became surahs, and the surahs were gathered and became Qur'an, and then in it were gathered the sciences of the first and the last. The conclusion is that the derivation of the word Qur'an is either from recitation (tilawah) or from collectedness (jam'iyyah).

Third: al-Furqan: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan: 1], ﴿And clear proofs of guidance and the Criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. They differed in its interpretation. It has been said: it was so named because its descent was scattered; He sent it down over twenty-some years. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿And a Qur'an We have separated so that you may recite it to the people over a period, and We have sent it down progressively﴾ [al-Isra': 106]. The other Books descended all at once. The wisdom in this we mentioned in Surah al-Furqan in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once?" Thus, that We may strengthen your heart with it﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. It has also been said: it was so named because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood, the lawful and the unlawful, the general and the specified, the decisive and the interpretable. It has also been said: al-Furqan is salvation, which is the saying of 'Ikrimah and al-Suddi, because creation was in the darkness of misguidance, and through the Qur'an they found salvation. The commentators interpreted His saying accordingly: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion that you might be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 53].

Fourth: al-Dhikr, al-Tadhkirah, and al-Dhikra. As for al-Dhikr: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya': 50], ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. Regarding it there are two aspects:

One: that it is a reminder from God, by which He reminded His servants, informing them of His obligations and commands.

The second: that it is a reminder, honor and pride for whoever believes in it, and that it is an honor for Muhammad ﷺ and his community. As for al-Tadhkirah, it is His saying: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Haqqah: 48]. As for al-Dhikra, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 55].

Fifth: al-Tanzil: ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192-193].

Sixth: al-Hadith: ﴿God has sent down the best statement as a Book﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. He named it hadith because its arrival to you is a hadith, and because He, exalted is He, likened it to what is spoken of, for God addressed the responsible ones through it.

Seventh: al-Mawi'zah (admonition): ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ [Yunus: 57]. In reality it is an admonition, because the speaker is God, exalted is He, the one who receives it is Jibril, and the one who conveys it is Muhammad ﷺ, so how would the admonition not take effect through it?

Eighth: al-Hukm, al-Hikmah, al-Hakim, and al-Muhkam. As for al-Hukm: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 37]. As for al-Hikmah: ﴿Far-reaching wisdom﴾ [al-Qamar: 5], ﴿And remember what is recited in your homes of the signs of God and the wisdom﴾ [al-Ahzab: 34]. As for al-Hakim: ﴿Ya Sin. By the wise Qur'an﴾ [Ya Sin: 1-2]. As for al-Muhkam: ﴿A Book whose verses have been made precise﴾ [Hud: 1]. They differed about the meaning of hikmah. Al-Khalil said: it is derived from ihkam (making firm) and ilzam (binding). Al-Mu'arrij said: it is derived from the hikmah of the bridle, because it controls the beast, and wisdom restrains from foolishness.

Ninth: al-Shifa' (healing): ﴿And We send down from the Qur'an that which is a healing and mercy for the believers﴾ [al-Isra': 82], and His saying: ﴿And a healing for what is in the chests﴾ [Yunus: 57]. Regarding it there are two aspects:

One: that it is a healing from diseases.

The second: that it is a healing from the sickness of disbelief, because God described disbelief and doubt as a sickness, saying: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10], and through the Qur'an every doubt is removed from the heart, so its description as a healing is correct.

Tenth: al-Huda (guidance) and al-Hadi (the Guide). As for al-Huda: His saying: ﴿A guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], ﴿A guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], ﴿And a healing for what is in the chests, and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [Yunus: 57]. As for al-Hadi: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra': 9], and the jinn said: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an, which guides to right conduct﴾ [al-Jinn: 1-2].

Eleventh: al-Sirat al-Mustaqim (the Straight Path). Ibn 'Abbas said in its interpretation that it is the Qur'an, and He said: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153].

The Second Name: the Rope (al-Habl). In the exegesis, it is said that it is the Qur'an. It was named so because whoever holds fast to it in the affairs of his religion is delivered by it from the punishment of the Hereafter and the chastisement of this world, just as one who grasps a rope is saved from drowning and ruin. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) also called it a protection (ʿiṣmah), saying: "Indeed this Qur'an is a protection for whoever holds fast to it," because it protects people from acts of disobedience.

The Thirteenth Name: Mercy. ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers﴾ [al-Isra' 17:82]. And what mercy is greater than deliverance from ignorance and misguidance?

The Fourteenth Name: The Spirit (al-Ruh). ﴿And thus have We revealed to you a Spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura 42:52]. ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command﴾ [al-Nahl 16:2]. It was named so because it is the cause of the life of hearts. Gabriel is also called the Spirit: ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ [Maryam 19:17], and Jesus is called a Spirit: ﴿He cast it to Mary, and a Spirit from Him﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:171].

The Fifteenth Name: Narratives (al-Qasas). ﴿We relate to you the best of narratives﴾ [Yusuf 12:3]. It was named so because it must be followed. ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow his track"﴾ [al-Qasas 28:11], meaning: follow his trail. Or because the Qur'an traces the narratives of earlier peoples. From this is the saying of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:62].

The Sixteenth Name: Clarification (al-Bayan), Explanation (al-Tibyan), and the Clear (al-Mubin). As for al-Bayan, it is His saying: ﴿This is a clarification for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:138]. As for al-Tibyan, it is His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl 16:89]. As for al-Mubin, it is His saying: ﴿These are the verses of the clear Book﴾ [Yusuf 12:1].

The Seventeenth Name: Insights (al-Basa'ir). ﴿This is insights from your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf 7:203], meaning: these are proofs by which the truth is seen, likened to the sight that perceives the path of deliverance.

The Eighteenth Name: The Decisive (al-Fasl). ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word, and it is not a jest﴾ [al-Tariq 86:13-14]. Scholars differed regarding it. It was said that its meaning is judgment, because Allah the Exalted judges among people by it with truth. It was said that it is because it separates people on the Day of Resurrection, guiding some to Paradise and driving others to the Fire. Whoever made it his leader in this world, it leads him to Paradise, and whoever put it behind him, it drives him to the Fire.

[p. 16]

The Nineteenth Name: The Stars (al-Nujum). ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:75], and ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm 53:1]. It was named so because it was sent down star by star.

The Twentieth Name: The Oft-Repeated (al-Mathani). ﴿Oft-repeated, at which the skins shudder of those who fear their Lord﴾ [al-Zumar 39:23]. It was said that it is because it repeats in it the narratives and reports.

The Twenty-First Name: Blessing (al-Ni'mah). ﴿But as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [al-Duha 93:11]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the Qur'an.

The Twenty-Second Name: Proof (al-Burhan). ﴿There has come to you a proof from your Lord﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:174]. And how could it not be a proof, when the eloquent have been unable to produce its like?

The Twenty-Third Name: Bearer of Good News and Warner (al-Bashir wal-Nadhir). It is with this name that the Qur'an shares a common designation with the prophets. The Most High said concerning the messengers: ﴿Bearers of good news and warners﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213]. And He said concerning Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, and a warner﴾ [al-Fath 48:8]. And He said concerning the Qur'an in Ha Mim al-Sajdah: ﴿A bringer of good news and a warner, but most of them turned away﴾ [Fussilat 41:4], meaning: a bringer of good news of Paradise for whoever obeys, and a warner of the Fire for whoever disobeys. Here we mention the names shared between Allah the Exalted and the Qur'an.

The Twenty-Fourth Name: The Upright (al-Qayyim). ﴿An upright book, to warn of severe punishment﴾ [al-Kahf 18:2]. The religion is also called upright: ﴿That is the upright religion﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:36]. And Allah the Glorified is al-Qayyum: ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Living, the Self-Sustaining﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255]. It was named qayyim because it subsists by its own essence in clarification and benefit.

The Twenty-Fifth Name: The Guardian (al-Muhaymin). ﴿And We have revealed to you the Book in truth, confirming that which preceded it of the Book and as a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:48]. It is derived from al-Amin (the trustworthy). It is described by this because whoever holds fast to the Qur'an is safe from harm in this world and the Hereafter. The Lord, the Guardian, sent down the Guardian Book upon the Trustworthy Prophet, for the sake of a people who are the trustees of Allah the Exalted over His creation, as He said: ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143].

The Twenty-Sixth Name: The Guide (al-Hadi). ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra' 17:9]. And He said: ﴿It guides to righteousness﴾ [al-Jinn 72:2]. Allah the Exalted is the Guide, because it has come in the report: "The Guiding Light."

The Twenty-Seventh Name: Light (al-Nur). ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nur 24:35]. In the Qur'an: ﴿And they followed the light that was sent down with him﴾ [al-A'raf 7:157], meaning the Qur'an. The Messenger was also called light: ﴿There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:15], meaning Muhammad. His religion was called light: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾ [al-Saff 61:8]. His clarification was called light: ﴿So is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam and he is upon light from his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar 39:22]. The Torah was called light: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:44]. The Gospel was called light: ﴿And We gave him the Gospel, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:46]. And faith was called light: ﴿Their light running before them﴾ [al-Hadid 57:12].

The Twenty-Eighth Name: The Truth (al-Haqq). It occurs among the names: "the Awakener, the Witness, the Truth." The Qur'an is the truth: ﴿And indeed it is the certain truth﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:51]. Allah named it truth because it is the opposite of falsehood, and so it removes falsehood, as He said: ﴿Rather, We cast the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:18], meaning: it departs and disappears.

[p. 17]

The Twenty-Ninth Name: The Mighty (al-'Aziz). ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:9]. Concerning the description of the Qur'an: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty Book﴾ [Fussilat 41:41]. The Prophet is mighty: ﴿There has certainly come to you a messenger from yourselves; it grieves him that you suffer﴾, and the community is mighty: ﴿And might belongs to Allah and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:8]. So many a mighty one has sent down a mighty Book upon a mighty Prophet for a mighty community. The word al-'Aziz has two meanings:
The first: the Subduer, and the Qur'an is likewise, for it is what subdued the enemies and resisted whoever sought to oppose it.
The second: that there is no one like it.

The Thirtieth Name: The Noble (al-Karim). ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:77], ﴿in a protected Book﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:78]. Know that the Most High named seven things "noble." ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Noble?﴾ [al-Infitar 82:6], since there is no one more generous than Him. The Qur'an is called noble because no book yields from wisdom and knowledge what can be derived from it. He called Moses noble: ﴿And there came to them a noble messenger﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:17]. He called the reward of deeds noble: ﴿So give him good news of forgiveness and a noble reward﴾ [Ya Sin 36:11]. He called His Throne noble: ﴿There is no deity except Him, the Lord of the Noble Throne﴾ [al-Naml 27:26], because it is the place of descent of mercy. He called Gabriel noble: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:40], and its meaning is that he is mighty. He called the letter of Solomon noble: ﴿Indeed, it has been delivered to me, a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml 27:29]. So it is a noble Book from a noble Lord, sent down by a noble angel upon a noble Prophet for the sake of a noble community. When they hold fast to it, they gain a noble reward.

The Thirty-First Name: The Great (al-'Azim). ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the great Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr 15:87]. Know that the Most High named Himself great: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Great﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255]. He named His Throne great: ﴿And He is the Lord of the Great Throne﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:129]. He named His Book great: ﴿And the great Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr 15:87]. He named the Day of Resurrection great: ﴿For a great day﴾, ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 83:5-6]. He named the earthquake great: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a great thing﴾ [al-Hajj 22:1]. He named the character of the Messenger great: ﴿And indeed you are of a great character﴾ [al-Qalam 68:4]. He named knowledge great, and the grace of Allah upon you great: ﴿And the grace of Allah upon you has been great﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:113]. He named the guile of women great: ﴿Indeed, your guile is great﴾ [Yusuf 12:28]. He named the sorcery of Pharaoh's magicians great: ﴿And they came with great magic﴾ [al-A'raf 7:116]. He named the reward itself great: ﴿Allah has promised those who believed and did righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Fath 48:29]. He named the punishment of the hypocrites great: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:176].

The Thirty-Second Name: The Blessed (al-Mubarak). ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:50]. Allah the Exalted named things with this name. He named the place where Moses, peace be upon him, was spoken to "blessed": ﴿From the blessed ground, from the tree﴾ [al-Qasas 28:30]. He named the olive tree blessed: ﴿Lit from a blessed tree, an olive﴾ [al-Nur 24:35], because of its many benefits. He named Jesus blessed: ﴿And He made me blessed﴾ [Maryam 19:31]. He named rain blessed: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water﴾ [Qaf 50:9], because of the benefits in it. He named the Night of Decree blessed: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:3]. So the Qur'an is a blessed reminder, sent down by a blessed angel, in a blessed night, upon a blessed Prophet, for a blessed community.

* * *

The Fourth Issue: On explaining the connection of His saying "Alif Lam Mim" with His saying "That is the Book." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: If you make "Alif Lam Mim" the name of the sura, then there are several possibilities in the construction:

The first: that "Alif Lam Mim" is the subject, and "That" is a second subject, and "the Book" is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the first subject. Its meaning: that is the complete Book, as though the other books, in comparison to it, are deficient, and it is the one worthy of being called a Book. As you say, "He is the man," meaning the perfect one in manhood, who combines what is desirable in qualities found among men. Or "the Book" is an attribute, and its meaning is: that is the promised Book. Or "Alif Lam Mim" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this is "Alif Lam Mim," and "That is the Book" is a second predicate, or an appositive on the basis that "the Book" is an attribute, and its meaning is: that is it. Or these "Alif Lam Mim" are a sentence, and "That is the Book" is another sentence. If "Alif Lam Mim" is treated as a mere sound, then "That" is the subject and "the Book" its predicate, meaning: that revealed Book is the complete Book; or "the Book" is an attribute and the predicate is what follows it; or an omitted subject is assumed, meaning: it, that is, what is composed of these letters, is that Book. Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: "Alif Lam Mim. The sending down of the Book, there is no doubt in it" [al-Sajdah 32:2]. The construction of this is clear.

* *

The Most High's saying: "There is no doubt in it." Concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: doubt (al-rayb) is close to suspicion (al-shakk), but with an added element, as though it were an evil assumption. You say, "The matter of so-and-so troubled me (rabani)," when you assume evil about him. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Leave what troubles you for what does not trouble you." If it is objected that doubt is also used in the phrase "the vicissitudes of time" (rayb al-dahr) and "the vicissitudes of the age" (rayb al-zaman), meaning its calamities, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We await for him the misfortunes of death﴾ [al-Tur 52:30], and it is also used to mean what stirs in the heart of causes of anger, as in the poet's words:
"We have settled from Tihama every doubt, and Khaybar, then we gathered the swords."
We reply: these may return to the meaning of doubt, because what is feared from the misfortunes of death is a possibility, so it is like something doubted; and likewise what stirs in the heart is not certain. So the Most High's saying "There is no doubt in it" means the negation of its being a cause for doubt in any respect. The intended meaning is that there is no uncertainty about its authenticity, nor about its being from Allah, nor about its being miraculous. If you say that the intended meaning is that there is no doubt about its being miraculous in particular, that would be closer to supporting this interpretation, with His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:23].

Here there are questions:

The first question: Some of the heretics (al-mulhidah) criticized it, saying: If it means that there is no doubt in it according to us, then we do doubt it; and if it means that there is no doubt in it according to Him, then there is no benefit in it. The answer: the intended meaning is that it has reached such clarity that no one who doubts should doubt it. And the matter is as such, because the Arabs, despite their attainment of the utmost eloquence, were unable to match even the shortest sura of the Qur'an, and this testifies that this proof has reached such manifestness that it is not permissible for a rational person to doubt it.

**Second question: Why did He say here, ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾, while in another place He said, ﴿No ghoul is in them﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]?**

The answer is that they put the more important first, and the more important here is the total negation of doubt from the Book. If you said, "There is doubt in it," it would suggest that there is another book in which doubt does occur, but not this one. In His words, ﴿No ghoul is in them﴾, He intended to show the superiority of the wine of Paradise over the wine of this world, since it does not confound the intellects as the wine of this world does.

**Third question: From where does His saying, ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾, indicate the total negation of doubt?**

Abu al-Sha'tha' read ﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ with a *raf'* (nominative ending) on *rayb*. Know that the well-known reading necessitates the complete removal of doubt. The proof is that His saying ﴿لا رَيْبَ﴾ is a negation of the *mahiyyah* (quiddity, the essence) of doubt, and the negation of the quiddity requires the negation of every individual instance of that quiddity. For if one instance of the quiddity were established, the quiddity would be established, and that contradicts the negation of the quiddity. For this very reason, our saying "There is no god but God" is a negation of all gods besides God, the Exalted. As for our saying "There is no doubt in it" with *raf'*, it is the contradictory of our saying "There is doubt in it," which conveys the establishment of a single instance. Thus that negation necessitates the absence of all instances, so that the contradiction is realized.

**The Pause on "فِيهِ" (fihi):**

**The second issue:** Stopping on ﴿فِيهِ﴾ (fihi) is the well-known practice. However, from Nafi' and 'Asim it is reported that they paused on ﴿لا رَيْبَ﴾. The one who pauses must intend a predicate (*khabar*), and a parallel to this is His saying: ﴿They said, "No harm"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 50], and the Arabs' saying "la ba's" (no harm), which is frequent in the speech of the people of the Hijaz. The intended sense is: "There is no doubt in it; in it is guidance" (*la rayba fihi, fihi hudan*). Know that the first reading is preferable, because on the first reading the Book itself is guidance, whereas on the second reading the Book itself is not guidance, but rather there is guidance in it. The first is preferable because of what is repeated in the Qur'an, that the Qur'an is light and guidance. And God knows best.

* * *

**﴿Guidance for those who are mindful of God﴾**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Guidance for those who are mindful of God﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue: On the reality of guidance (huda).** Guidance is an expression for indication (*dalalah*). The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: guidance is the indication that leads to the desired goal. Others said: guidance is the being guided (*ihtida'*) and knowledge. What shows the soundness of the first view and the unsoundness of the second and third is that if the condition that the indication leads to the desired goal were part of the meaning of guidance, the occurrence of guidance would be impossible when there is no being guided. For an indication that leads to being guided while there is no being guided is impossible. But it is not impossible, as shown by His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17]; He affirmed guidance together with the absence of being guided. Also, in the Arabic language it is correct to say, "I guided him, but he was not guided," and that supports our view. Al-Zamakhshari argued with three matters:

First: The opposite of guidance is misguidance. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those are the ones who bought misguidance in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16], and He said: ﴿Indeed, we or you are upon guidance or in clear misguidance﴾ [Saba': 24].

Second: The one who is guided (*mahdi*) is called praiseworthy, as is the "guided one" (*muhtadi*). If it were not a condition of guidance that the indication lead to the desired goal, then describing someone as guided would not be praise, since it would be possible that he was guided but did not follow the guidance.

Third: *Ihtada* is the reflexive (*mutawa'ah*) of *hada*. It is said: "I guided him, so he was guided," just as it is said: "I broke it, so it broke," and "I cut it, so it was cut." Just as breaking and cutting are necessary consequences of breaking and cutting, so being guided must be a necessary consequence of guidance.

The answer to the first is that the difference between guidance and being guided is known necessarily. The opposite of guidance is misguidance, and the opposite of being guided is leading astray. So making guidance the opposite of misguidance is impossible.

The answer to the second is that the one who benefits from guidance is called guided, and one who does not benefit from it is not called guided. Furthermore, when a means does not lead to its aim, it is treated as if it were non-existent.

The answer to the third is that *i'timar* is the reflexive of *amr* (command). It is said: "I commanded him, so he complied" (*fa-'tamara*). But it does not follow that obeying is a condition of being a commander. Likewise, it does not follow from its being guidance that it must lead to being guided. Moreover, the argument is countered by the saying: "I guided him, but he was not guided."

Among what shows the falsity of the view of those who say that guidance is knowledge alone is that God, the Exalted, described the Qur'an as guidance, and there is no doubt that in itself it is not knowledge. This shows that guidance is indication, not being guided and knowledge.

**The second issue: On the meaning of *al-muttaqi* (one who is mindful of God).** In language, *al-muttaqi* is the active participle from the phrase "waqahu, fa-ittaqa," and *al-wiqayah* is extreme protection. Knowing this, we say: God, the Exalted, mentioned the mindful one here in the context of praise, and one who is like this is more deserving of being mindful in worldly affairs, and even more so in matters connected with religion. This means performing the acts of worship and abstaining from what is forbidden.

They differed over whether avoiding minor sins enters into *taqwa* (God-consciousness). Some said: it enters, just as minor sins enter into the threat of punishment. Others said: it does not enter. There is no dispute about the obligation to repent from all sins. The dispute is only about whether, if one does not guard against minor sins, he deserves this title. It is reported from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "A servant does not reach the rank of the mindful until he abandons what is not harmful out of fear of what is harmful."

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that they are those who fear God's punishment by abandoning what the desire inclines them to, and hope for His mercy by affirming what came from Him.

Know that *taqwa* is fear (*khashyah*). He said at the beginning of al-Nisa': ﴿O people, be mindful of your Lord﴾ [al-Nisa': 1], and a similar phrase appears at the beginning of al-Hajj.
