In al-Shu'ara': ﴿When their brother Nuh said to them, "Will you not be mindful?"﴾ [Hud: 106], meaning: "Will you not fear God?" Likewise Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb said to their peoples. In al-'Ankabut, Ibrahim said to his people: ﴿Worship God and be mindful of Him﴾ [Nuh: 3], meaning: fear Him. Similarly His saying: ﴿Be mindful of God with the mindfulness due to Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102]; ﴿Take provision, for the best provision is taqwa﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]; ﴿Guard against a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48].

Know that although the real meaning of *taqwa* is what we have mentioned, it has come in the Qur'an with the principal aim of it being faith at one time, repentance at another, obedience a third time, abstention from disobedience a fourth time, and sincerity a fifth time.

As for faith, it is His saying: ﴿And He made them hold to the word of *taqwa*﴾ [al-Fath: 26], i.e., monotheism; ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God has tested for *taqwa*﴾ [al-Hujurat: 3]; and in al-Shu'ara': ﴿the people of Pharaoh. Will they not be mindful?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 11], i.e., will they not believe?

As for repentance, it is His saying: ﴿Had the people of the towns believed and been mindful﴾ [al-A'raf: 96], i.e., repented.

As for obedience, it is His saying in al-Nahl: ﴿that there is no god but Me, so be mindful of Me﴾ [al-Nahl: 2]; and in it also: ﴿Do you then fear other than God?﴾ [al-Nahl: 52]; and in al-Mu'minun: ﴿And I am your Lord, so be mindful of Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52].

As for abstaining from disobedience, it is His saying: ﴿Enter houses by their doors, and be mindful of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], i.e., do not disobey Him.

As for sincerity, it is His saying in al-Hajj: ﴿For it is from the *taqwa* of the hearts﴾ [al-Hajj: 32], i.e., from the sincerity of hearts. Likewise His saying: ﴿And fear Me alone﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41].

Know that the station of *taqwa* is a noble station. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, God is with those who are mindful and those who do good﴾ [al-Nahl: 128]; and He said: ﴿Indeed, the most honorable of you with God is the most mindful of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13].

From Ibn 'Abbas, he (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever wishes to be the most honorable of people, let him be mindful of God; whoever wishes to be the strongest of people, let him rely upon God; and whoever wishes to be the richest of people, let him be more confident in what is in God's hand than in what is in his own hand."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: *Taqwa* is abandoning persistence in disobedience and abandoning being deceived by obedience. Al-Hasan said: *Taqwa* is that you do not choose anything besides God over God, and that you know all matters are in God's hand. Ibrahim ibn Adham said: *Taqwa* is that creation finds no fault in your tongue, nor the angels any fault in your deeds, nor the King of the Throne any fault in your inner self. Al-Waqidi said: *Taqwa* is that you adorn your inner self for the Truth as you adorn your outer self for creation. It is also said: *Taqwa* is that your Master does not see you where He has forbidden you. It is also said: the mindful one is the one who takes the path of the Chosen One, casts the world behind his back, obliges himself to sincerity and fidelity, and avoids the forbidden and harshness. And if the mindful one had no virtue except what is in His saying, ﴿Guidance for those who are mindful of God﴾, it would suffice him, because He, the Exalted, made clear that the Qur'an is guidance for mankind in His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down, a guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Then He said here, concerning the Qur'an, that it is guidance for those who are mindful. This shows that the mindful are all of mankind, and whoever is not mindful is as if he were not a human being.

**The third issue: Questions.**

**First question:** That a thing is guidance and an indicator does not differ according to one person and not another. So why did He make the Qur'an guidance for the mindful only? Also, the mindful one is already guided, and the guided one does not get guided a second time, so the Qur'an cannot be guidance for the mindful.

*Answer:* The Qur'an is, just as it is guidance for the mindful and an indication for them of the existence of the Creator, of His religion, and of the truthfulness of His Messenger, also an indication for the disbelievers. However, God, the Exalted, mentioned the mindful in praise, to make clear that they are the ones who were guided and benefited from it, as He said: ﴿You are only a warner to the one who fears it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], and He said: ﴿You can only warn the one who follows the Reminder﴾ [Ya Sin: 11]. The Prophet, peace be upon him, was a warner to all people, but He mentioned these people because they are the ones who benefited from his warning. As for one who interprets guidance as the indication that leads to the desired goal, this question does not arise for him, because the Qur'an leading to the desired goal is only for the mindful.

**Second question:** How can the whole Qur'an be described as guidance when it contains much that is general (*mujmal*) and ambiguous (*mutashabih*)? Without the indication of reason, the clear (*muhkam*) could not be distinguished from the ambiguous. So guidance in reality would be the rational indication, not the Qur'an. From this, it is reported of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, that he said to Ibn 'Abbas when he sent him as a messenger to the Kharijites: "Do not argue against them with the Qur'an, for it is a two-faced adversary." And if it were guidance, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib would not have said this about it. Also, we see that all the sects of Islam argue with it, and we see the Qur'an filled with verses, some of which are explicit in determinism (*jabr*) and some explicit in free will (*qadar*), so reconciling them is impossible except by extreme forcing. How then can it be guidance?

*Answer:* Because that ambiguous and general material, since it does not escape from what is the intended meaning specifically, which is either the indication of reason or the indication of revelation (*sam'*), the whole of it becomes guidance.

**Third question:** Whatever the soundness of the Qur'an as a proof depends upon, the Qur'an cannot be guidance in it. Therefore it is impossible for the Qur'an to be guidance regarding the essence of God, the Exalted, and His attributes, and regarding prophethood. There is no doubt that these subjects are the most noble of subjects. If the Qur'an is not guidance in them, how did God, the Exalted, make it guidance absolutely?

*Answer:* It is not a condition of its being guidance that it be guidance in everything. It suffices that it be guidance in some things, namely by clarifying the laws (*shara'i*), or by confirming what is in the intellects. This verse is among the strongest proofs that the unrestricted (*mutlaq*) does not imply generality. For God, the Exalted, described it as guidance without any restriction in the wording, although it is impossible that it be guidance in establishing the Creator and His attributes and establishing prophethood. Thus it is established that the unrestricted does not convey generality.

Fourth question: Guidance (al-huda) is that which has reached such a degree of clarity and explicitness that it makes other things clear. The Qur'an is not like this, for the commentators do not mention a single verse without mentioning in it many conflicting opinions, and what is like this is not itself clear, let alone able to make other things clear. How then can it be guidance? We say: whoever speaks on tafsir in such a way that he presents conflicting opinions without preferring any one of them over the rest is subject to this very question. As for us, we have preferred one of them over the rest on the basis of evidence, so this question does not apply to us.

Fourth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The position (mahall) of ﴿hudan lil-muttaqin﴾ is nominative (raf'), because it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), or a predicate together with ﴿la rayba fihi﴾ for ﴿dhalika﴾, or a subject (mubtada') if the preceding adverbial phrase is made its predicate. It is also permissible that it be put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the element governing it is the demonstrative (al-isharah) or the adverbial phrase (al-zarf). But what is more deeply rooted in eloquence (al-balaghah) is to turn away from this field entirely and to say: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ is a complete sentence in itself, or a group of letters of the alphabet standing independently by itself; ﴿dhalika al-kitab﴾ is a second sentence; ﴿la rayba fihi﴾ is a third; and ﴿hudan lil-muttaqin﴾ is a fourth. The essence of eloquence and the reason for the excellence of the composition have been attained by their arrangement, in that they have been brought together harmoniously in this way without a conjunction particle, because they come in close connection, each one taking hold of the neck of the other, the second being united with the first, and so on to the third and the fourth.

Its explanation: First, attention is drawn to the fact that it is the speech with which challenge is made; then it is indicated that it is the Book described with the utmost perfection. Thus the aspect of the challenge is established. Then doubt is negated from it, so that this is a testimony to its perfection. Then it is informed that it is guidance for the muttaqun, thereby establishing that it is a certainty around which doubt does not hover. Then each one of these four, after being arranged in this elegant order, is not without a subtle point: in the first, there is omission and allusion to the purpose in the most delicate manner; in the second, there is the majesty found in the definite form; in the third, there is what is found in placing "doubt" before the adverbial phrase; and in the fourth, there is the omission, and the placing of the verbal noun (masdar), which is "huda", in the position of the attributive participle (wasf), which is "hadin", and its being indefinite.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 3 (part 1 of 3):

God Most High says: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen, and establish the prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them.﴾

Know that in this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: ﴿Those who believe﴾ may be a relative clause (mawsul) attached to "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqin), in which case it is a genitive attributive (sifah majrurah); or it is in the accusative, or it is a laudatory (madh) construction in the nominative by the implied verb "I mean" (a'ni), i.e. "those who believe," or "they are those who"; or it is disjoined from "the God-fearing" and is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿They are upon guidance﴾. So, if it is a relative clause, the pause at "the God-fearing" is acceptable but not complete (hasan ghayr tamm); and if it is disjoined, the pause is complete (waqf tamm).

* * *

The second issue: Some have said: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen, and establish the prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them﴾ may be an explanation of their being God-fearing (muttaqin). This is because the God-fearing person is one who does good deeds and abstains from evil deeds. As for action, it is either an action of the heart, which is the phrase ﴿those who believe﴾; or an action of the limbs, whose foundation is prayer (salah), almsgiving (zakah) and charity (sadaqah), because worship is either bodily, the most excellent of which is prayer, or financial, the most excellent of which is zakah. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ called prayer "the pillar of the religion, and zakah the bridge of Islam." As for abstention, it is included in prayer, because of His saying: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45]. However, the more likely view is that these things are not an explanation of their being God-fearing; because the perfection of happiness is only attained by abandoning what is not fitting and doing what is fitting. So abstention is God-fearing, and action is either an action of the heart, which is faith, or an action of the limbs, which is prayer and zakah. The reason He placed God-fearing, which is abstention, before action, which is faith, prayer and zakah, is that the heart is like a tablet receptive to the imprinting of sound beliefs and virtuous morals, and the tablet must first be purified of corrupt imprints so that good imprints can be established in it. The same applies to morals. For this reason He placed God-fearing, which is abstention from what is not fitting, first, and then mentioned after it the doing of what is fitting.

* * *

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: faith (iman) is of the form af'ala, from security (amn). Then it is said: "amanahu" when one confirms him (saddaqahu), and its literal meaning is that he gave him security from denial and opposition. As for its being transitive with the preposition bi, this is because it includes the meaning of "I acknowledge and I admit." As for what Abu Zayd related: "ma amintu an ajida sahabatan," meaning "I did not trust that I would find a companion," its literal meaning is "I became one with security," i.e. one with tranquility and calm. Both meanings are fine in ﴿believe in the unseen﴾, i.e. they acknowledge it, or they trust that it is true.

I say: The People of the Qiblah have differed over the designation of faith in the terminology of the Shari'ah, and they fall into four groups.

The first group: Those who said: faith is a term for actions of the heart and the limbs and verbal affirmation by the tongue. These are the Mu'tazilah, the Khawarij, the Zaydiyyah, and the People of Hadith. As for the Khawarij, they agreed that faith in God includes knowledge of God and of everything for which God has placed a rational or transmitted proof from the Book and the Sunnah, and includes obedience to God in all that He has commanded of actions and abstentions, small or great. They said: the totality of these things is faith, and abandoning any one of these traits is disbelief. As for the Mu'tazilah, they agreed that when faith is transitive with bi, what is meant is affirmation (tasdiq), which is why it is said: "So-and-so believed in God and His Messenger," and what is meant is affirmation, since faith in the sense of performing obligations cannot take this transitivity; so one does not say "So-and-so believed in such-and-such when he prayed and fasted," but rather "So-and-so believed in God," just as one says "He fasted and prayed for God." Thus faith with bi follows the usage of the linguists. As for when it is mentioned absolutely and not transitive, they agreed that it has been transferred from its linguistic designation, which is affirmation, to another meaning. Then they differed concerning it in several ways:

The first: that faith is an expression for performing all acts of obedience, whether obligatory or recommended, whether they belong to the category of statements, actions, or beliefs. This is the view of Wasil ibn 'Ata', Abu al-Hudhayl and the qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar ibn Ahmad.

The second: that it is an expression for performing obligations only, not supererogatory acts. This is the view of Abu 'Ali and Abu Hashim.

The third: that faith is an expression for avoiding everything for which a threat (wa'id) has been stated. So the believer in God's sight is everyone who avoids all major sins, and the believer in our view is everyone who avoids everything for which a threat has come. This is the view of al-Nazzam. Some of his companions said: the condition for being a believer, both in our view and in God's, is avoiding all major sins.

As for the People of Hadith, they mentioned two views:

The first: that knowledge (ma'rifah) is complete faith and is the foundation; then after that every act of obedience is a faith of its own, and none of these acts is faith unless it is ordered upon the foundation, which is knowledge. They claimed that denial and rejection of the heart is disbelief, and then every act of disobedience after it is a disbelief of its own. They did not make any of the acts of obedience faith unless knowledge and affirmation exist, nor any of the acts of disobedience disbelief unless denial and rejection exist, because a branch does not arise without what is its root. This is the view of 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id ibn Kullab.

The second: they claimed that faith is a term for all acts of obedience, and it is one single faith; and they made the obligations and the supererogatory acts all part of faith. Whoever abandons any of the obligations has diminished his faith, and whoever abandons the supererogatory acts does not diminish his faith. Among them are those who said: faith is a term for the obligations only, not the supererogatory acts.

The second group: Those who said: faith is by the heart and the tongue together. These differed into several positions. The first: that faith is affirmation by the tongue and knowledge in the heart. This is the view of Abu Hanifah and most jurists. These then differed on two points. The first: they differed on the reality of this knowledge. Some explained it as firm belief (i'tiqad jazim), whether it is imitative belief (i'tiqad taqlidi) or knowledge arising from proof; and they are the majority, who rule that the one who follows another in belief is a Muslim. Others explained it as knowledge arising from reasoning (istidlal). The second: they differed concerning what knowledge is required for the realization of faith; knowledge of what? Some of the theologians said: it is knowledge of God and His attributes in complete and perfect manner. Then, since the disagreement of creation about the attributes of God became great, each sect inevitably proceeded to declare the other sects disbelievers. The People of Equity (Ahl al-Insaf) said: what is required is knowledge of everything known necessarily to be from the religion of Muhammad ﷺ. According to this view, knowledge that God is knowing by knowledge or knowing by His essence, and that He is seen or not seen, does not fall within the designation of faith. The second view: that faith is affirmation by the heart and the tongue together. This is the view of Bishr ibn 'Ataf al-Marisi and Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, and what is meant by affirmation of the heart is the speech subsisting in the self. The third view: the view of a group of Sufis: faith is verbal affirmation and sincerity of the heart.

The third group: Those who said: faith is an expression for the action of the heart only. These differed into two views. One: that faith is an expression for knowledge of God by the heart, so that whoever knows God with his heart, then denies with his tongue and dies before professing it, is a believer of complete faith. This is the view of Jahm ibn Safwan. He claimed that knowledge of the Books, the Messengers, and the Last Day is not included in the definition of faith. Al-Ka'bi related from him that faith is knowledge of God together with knowledge of everything known necessarily to be from the religion of Muhammad ﷺ. The second: that faith is mere affirmation by the heart. This is the view of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Bajali.

The fourth group: Those who said: faith is verbal affirmation alone. These are of two kinds. The first: that verbal affirmation alone is faith, but the condition for it being faith is the presence of knowledge in the heart; so knowledge is a condition for verbal affirmation to be faith, not something included in the designation of faith. This is the view of Ghaylan ibn Muslim al-Dimashqi and al-Fadl al-Raqashi, although al-Ka'bi denied that this was a view of Ghaylan. The second: that faith is merely verbal affirmation. This is the view of the Karramiyyah, who claimed that the hypocrite is a believer outwardly and a disbeliever inwardly, so he holds the rulings of believers in this world and the rulings of disbelievers in the Hereafter.

This is the totality of what people have said concerning the designation of faith in the terminology of the Shari'ah. What we hold is that faith is an expression for affirmation by the heart. Here we need to explain the reality of affirmation by the heart, so we say: when someone says "the world is originated," the meaning of these words is not that the world is described as having originated, but rather the judgment of that speaker that the world is originated. The judgment that origination is established for the world is different from origination itself being established for the world. This mental judgment of affirmation or negation is something expressed in every language by a particular word, and the difference of forms and expressions while the mental judgment is one thing indicates that the mental judgment is something different from these forms and expressions; and because these forms indicate that judgment, and the indicator is other than the indicated. Then we say: this mental judgment is other than knowledge, because the ignorant person may judge something. So we know that this mental judgment is different from knowledge. Therefore what is meant by affirmation by the heart is this mental judgment. There remains a lexical question here: whether what is named "affirmation" in linguistic usage is that mental judgment or the expression that indicates that mental judgment. The verification of this view has been mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

* * *

Having understood this introduction, we say: faith is an expression for affirmation of everything known necessarily to be from the religion of Muhammad ﷺ together with conviction (i'tiqad). In establishing this position, we need to establish four conditions.

The first condition: that faith is an expression for affirmation (tasdiq). This is indicated by several considerations:

The first: that it was in original linguistic usage for affirmation. If in the terminology of the Shari'ah it became for something other than affirmation, it would follow that the one speaking it would be speaking other than the language of the Arabs, and that contradicts the description of the Qur'an as being in Arabic.

The second: that faith is among the most frequently recurring words on the tongues of Muslims. If it had been transferred to something other than its original meaning, the motives to know that designation would have been abundant, it would have become well known, and reached the level of mass transmission (tawatur). Since this is not the case, we know that it remained on its original linguistic meaning.

The third: we agreed that faith transitive with the preposition bi is retained on the original linguistic usage, so it is necessary that the non-transitive form likewise be so.

The fourth: that God Most High, whenever He mentions faith in the Qur'an, attributes it to the heart. He says: ﴿Among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths, but their hearts have not believed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41]; and His saying: ﴿while his heart is at rest with faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106]; ﴿He has written faith into their hearts﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22]; ﴿But say, "We have submitted," for faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14].

The fifth: that wherever God mentions faith, He pairs it with righteous deeds; and if righteous deeds were included within faith, that would be repetition.

The sixth: that He Most High often mentions faith and pairs it with sins. He says: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ [al-An'am: 82]; ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of God﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9]. Ibn 'Abbas argued for this with His saying: ﴿O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], from three aspects:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 3 (part 2 of 3):

First: qisas (retaliation) is due only upon the intentional killer. Then He addressed him with His words: ﴿O you who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], which indicates that he is a believer.

Second: His words: ﴿But if he is pardoned by his brother [i.e., the victim's heir] something﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]. This brotherhood is none other than the brotherhood of faith, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10].

Third: His words: ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]. This is fitting only for a believer. Among what indicates the point sought is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who believed but did not emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. Here He kept the name of faith for the one who did not emigrate, despite the severity of the threat for abandoning emigration in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 28], and His saying: ﴿You have no obligation of guardianship toward them until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. Despite this, He made them believers. It is also indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], and He said: ﴿O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger or betray your trusts﴾ [al-Anfal: 27], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, repent to Allah with sincere repentance﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8]. The command to repent is absurd for one who has no sin. And His saying: ﴿And repent to Allah all of you, O believers﴾ [al-Nur: 31]. It may be said that this implies every believer is a sinner, and it is not so. Our reply: suppose that it is specific to those other than the sinner; the proof then remains regarding them.

The second condition: faith is not an expression of verbal affirmation alone. The evidence for this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. He negated their being believers, and if faith in Allah were an expression of verbal affirmation alone, this negation would not be valid.

The third condition: faith is not an expression of mere affirmation (taṣdīq), because one who affirms the idols (jibt) and false deities (ṭāghūt) is not called a believer.

The fourth condition: it is not a requirement of faith to affirm all of Allah's attributes, Mighty and Majestic is He, because the Messenger, peace be upon him, used to judge the faith of one who had not considered that God is knowing by His essence or by knowledge. Had this condition and its like been a considered requirement for the realization of faith, it would not have been permissible for the Messenger to judge his faith before testing him as to whether he knows that or not. This is the explanation of the statement on the realization of faith. If someone says: here there are two cases.

The first case: one who knew God through proof and demonstration, and when his knowledge was complete he died without finding the time or moment in which to pronounce the words of testimony (shahada). Here, if you judge that he is a believer, you have judged that verbal confession is not considered in the realization of faith, and this is a breach of the consensus (ijma'), which is the scholarly agreement of the community. And if you judge that he is not a believer, that is false, because of the Prophet's, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever has in his heart the weight of an atom's worth of faith will come out of the Fire." This is a heart overflowing with faith, so how can he not be a believer?

The second case: one who knew God through proof and found the time in which he could pronounce the words of testimony, but did not pronounce them. If you say he is a believer, that is a breach of the consensus; and if you say he is not a believer, that is false, because of the Prophet's, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever has in his heart the weight of an atom's worth of faith will come out of the Fire." Faith is not removed from the heart by silence from speech.

The answer: al-Ghazali rejected this consensus in both cases, judged them both to be believers, and held that refraining from speech is treated like the sins that are committed alongside faith.

The fourth issue: it has been said that "al-ghayb" (the unseen) is a verbal noun used in place of the active participle, like al-ṣawm meaning "the fasting one" and al-zawr meaning "the visitor." Then regarding His saying, ﴿they believe in the unseen﴾, there are two opinions.

The first, which is the choice of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, is that His saying ﴿in the unseen﴾ is an attribute of the believers, meaning that they believe in Allah when He is unseen just as they believe in Him when He is present, unlike the hypocrites who, when they meet those who believe, say, "We believe," and when they are alone with their devils, say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿That is so he may know that I did not betray him in the unseen﴾ [Yusuf: 52]. A man may say to another, "So-and-so is an excellent friend to you in his absence." All of this is praise for the believers in that their outward conduct conforms to their inward state and in that they differ from the hypocrites who say with their mouths what is not in their hearts.

The second, which is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun), is that the unseen is that which is absent from the senses. This unseen is divided into that for which there is a proof and that for which there is no proof. So the meaning of this verse is praise for the pious: that they believe in the unseen for which a proof exists, by reflecting, reasoning and thereby believing in it. On this view, it includes knowledge of Allah, His attributes, knowledge of the Hereafter, knowledge of prophethood and knowledge of the rulings and laws, for in acquiring these sciences through reasoning there is hardship, so it is fitting to be a cause for deserving great praise.

Abu Muslim argued for his view with several points. First: His saying, ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4], is faith in unseen things. So if what is meant by His saying, ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾, were faith in unseen things, then the conjoined would be the very same as the conjoined-to, and that is impermissible. Second: if we take it to mean belief in the unseen, it would entail the statement that man knows the unseen, which contradicts His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. But if we interpret the verse as we have said, this prohibited consequence does not follow. Third: the word "unseen" may only be applied to that which is possible to be present. Accordingly, the word "unseen" may not be applied to the essence of Allah and His attributes. So His saying, ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾, if it meant faith in the unseen, would not include belief in the essence of Allah and His attributes, and nothing would remain in it except belief in the Hereafter. That is impermissible, because the great pillar of faith is belief in the essence of Allah and His attributes, so how is it permissible to interpret the word with a meaning that entails the exclusion of the foundation? But if we take it according to the interpretation we have chosen, this prohibited consequence does not follow.

The answer to the first: His saying, ﴿they believe in the unseen﴾, encompasses belief in unseen things in general; then after that, His saying: ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4], encompasses belief in some of the unseen things. So this is of the type of detailing after a general statement, which is permissible, as in His saying: ﴿His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98].

The answer to the second: there is no dispute that we believe in things unseen by us, so that specification is necessary under both interpretations.

If it is said: do you say that the servant knows the unseen or not? We say: we have explained that the unseen is divided into that for which a proof exists and that for which no proof exists. As for that for which no proof exists, it is known only to Him, Glorified and Exalted, and no other. As for that for which a proof exists, there is no impediment to saying: we know of the unseen what we have a proof for, and the statement is clear and not ambiguous. On this basis the scholars said: inferring the absent from the present is one of the categories of evidence.

The answer to the third: we do not accept that the word "unseen" is used only for what may be present. The proof for this is that the theologians (mutakallimun) say, "This is of the category of attaching the absent to the present," and by "the absent" they mean the essence of Allah and His attributes. And Allah knows best.

* * *

(Fifth issue): Some of the Shi'a (a Muslim sect) said: the intended meaning of "the unseen" is the awaited Mahdi, whom Allah promised in the Qur'an and in reports. As for the Qur'an, it is His saying: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe among you and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth, just as He granted succession to those before them﴾ [al-Nur: 55]. As for the report, it is his saying, peace be upon him: "Were there to remain of the world but one day, Allah would prolong that day until a man from my household emerges, whose name matches my name and whose kunya (patronymic) matches my kunya; he will fill the earth with justice and equity just as it had been filled with injustice and oppression." Know that specifying the general term without evidence is invalid.

* * *

(Sixth issue): They mentioned several interpretations of the expression "establishing the prayer" (iqamat al-salah):

First: its establishment means perfecting its pillars and preserving it from any defect in its obligatory parts, its sunnahs and its etiquettes, from the phrase "aqama al-'ud," meaning he straightened the stick when he made it straight.

Second: it is an expression for persistence in it, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who are attentive to their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 34], and He said: ﴿Those who are constant in their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 23]. From "qamat al-suq," meaning the market became brisk when goods sold well. Its establishment is its being in demand, because when it is preserved, it is like a commodity in demand toward which desires are directed, and when it is neglected, it is like a stagnant commodity that is not desired.

Third: it is an expression for devoting oneself to performing it and that there be no lethargy in the one who performs it, from the expressions "qama bil-amr" (he took up the matter) and "qamat al-harb 'ala saqihā" (the war stood on its leg). Its opposite is "qa'ada 'an al-amr" (he sat back from the matter) and "taqa'ada 'anhu" (he hung back from it) when he shirked and held back.

Fourth: its establishment is an expression for its performance. The performance was expressed by "establishment" because standing is one of its pillars, just as it was expressed by "qunut" (devout standing), "ruku'" (bowing) and "sujud" (prostration). They said "sabbaha" (he glorified) meaning he prayed, because of the glorifying (tasbih) that is in it, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So had he not been of those who glorify [Allah]﴾ [al-Saffat: 143].

Know that the better course is to interpret the statement by what great praise is obtained through it, and that is not obtained unless we take "establishment" to mean continuous performance of it without defect in its pillars and conditions. For this reason, the one in charge of the soldiers' provisions is described as "qayyim" (custodian) only when he gives the rights without diminishing or withholding. For this reason also Allah, Exalted is He, is described as "Qa'im" and "Qayyum" (the Self-Subsisting), because His existence must perpetually continue, and because He perpetually sends down provision upon His servants.

* * *

(Seventh issue): They mentioned several meanings of the word "salah" in its original linguistic sense:

First: it is supplication (du'a'). The poet said:
"The wind met it in its jar, and he prayed over its jar and crossed himself."

Second: al-Kharazanji said: its derivation is from "al-ṣalā," which is fire, from their saying, "ṣallaytu al-'aṣā" when I straightened the stick with the fire. So the worshipper seems to strive to correct his inner and outer self, like one who tries to straighten a piece of wood by holding it over the fire.

Third: prayer is an expression for constant attachment, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Burning in a scorching fire﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 4], ﴿He will burn in a fire of blazing flame﴾ [al-Masad: 3]. The second horse in a race is also named "musalli" (one who follows closely).

Fourth: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "salah" is a form (fa'lah) from "ṣallā," like "zakah" from "zakkā." It is written with a waw according to the pronunciation of the emphatic form. The literal meaning of ṣallā is "he moved the two ṣalawān" (the two sides of the back/hip), because the worshipper does that in his bowing and prostration. It was also said that the supplicator is called "musalli" by way of comparing him in his humility to one who bows and prostrates. I say: here there are two discussions:

**First:** This derivation (*ishtiqaq*, deriving a word from a root) that the author of *al-Kashshaf* mentions leads to a grave objection against the Qur'an being a proof. The word *al-salah* (prayer) is among the most widely known words and the most frequently used on the tongues of Muslims, and its derivation from the movement of the two *salawayn* (the two bones at the back of the thigh, or the two sides of the spine) is among the least known things among the transmitters. Suppose we allowed that the referent of *al-salah* originally was what he mentioned, and then it became obscure and lost, until only a few individuals knew it. Then the same would be permissible for all other words. And if we allowed that, we could not be certain that what God Most High intends by these words is what our understandings immediately grasp from their meanings in our time, since it is possible that these words were, in the time of the Messenger, coined for other meanings, and God Most High intended those meanings, but those meanings became obscure and lost in our time, as has happened with this very word. Since that is invalid by the consensus of the Muslims, we know that the derivation he mentions is rejected and false.

**Second:** In the Sharia, *al-salah* is an expression for specific actions that follow one another, beginning with the *tahrim* (the opening takbir) and concluding with the *tahlil* (the closing salam). This term applies to both the obligatory (*fard*) and the voluntary (*nafl*) prayer. However, what is meant in this verse is specifically the obligatory, because it is the one on which success depends. This is because when the Prophet ﷺ explained to a Bedouin the description of the obligatory prayer, the man said: "By God, I will not add anything to it or subtract anything from it." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "He will be successful if he is truthful."

\* \* \*

**(Eighth issue):** *Al-rizq* (provision) in the speech of the Arabs means *al-hazz* (portion, share). God Most High said: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82], meaning your portion of this matter. *Al-hazz* is a man's share and what is specific to him to the exclusion of others. Then some said: *al-rizq* is everything that is eaten or used. This is false, because God Most High commanded us to spend from what He has provided us, saying: ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. If *al-rizq* were what is eaten, it would not be possible to spend it. Others said: *al-rizq* is what is owned. This too is false, because a person may say: "O God, provide me with a righteous child, or a righteous wife," and he does not own the child or the wife. He says: "O God, provide me with intellect by which I may live," and intellect is not owned. Also, an animal has a provision, yet it does not own anything.

As for the usage in the terminology of the Sharia, they have differed about it. Abu al-Husayn al-Basri said: *al-rizq* is enabling a living being to benefit from a thing and prohibiting others from preventing it from benefiting from it. So when we say, "God Most High has provided us with wealth," the meaning is that He has enabled us to benefit from it. When we ask God Most High to provide us with wealth, we intend by that that He make us more specially connected to the wealth. When we ask Him to provide an animal, we intend that He make it more specially connected to it. It becomes more specially connected to it when He enables it to benefit from it and no one has the right to prevent it from benefiting from it.

Know that the Mu'tazilah, since they defined *al-rizq* this way, necessarily said: what is unlawful cannot be a provision. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: what is unlawful may be a provision. The argument of our companions is from two aspects.

The first: *al-rizq* in the original language is *al-hazz* and *al-nasib* (share and portion), as we have explained. So whoever benefits from the unlawful, that unlawful thing becomes a share and portion for him, and therefore it must be a provision for him.

The second: God Most High said: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth except that its provision is upon God﴾ [Hud: 6]. A man may live his whole life eating only from theft, so it must be said that throughout his life he did not eat from his provision at all.

As for the Mu'tazilah, they argued from the Book, the Sunnah, and reason. As for the Book, there are several points:

The first is His saying: ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾. He praised them for spending from what God provided them. So if the unlawful were a provision, they would deserve praise when they spend from the unlawful, and that is false by consensus.

The second: If the unlawful were a provision, it would be permissible for a usurper to spend from it, due to His saying: ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. The Muslims agree that it is not permissible for the usurper to spend from what he took; rather, it is obligatory for him to return it. This shows that the unlawful is not a provision.

The third is His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision, and you made from it the unlawful and the lawful? Say: Did God permit you?﴾ [Yunus: 59]. He made clear that whoever forbids the provision of God is one who fabricates against God. Thus it is established that the unlawful is not a provision.

As for the Sunnah, there is what Abu al-Husayn narrated in his book *Kitab al-Gharar* with his chain: "From Safwan ibn Umayyah, who said: We were with the Messenger of God ﷺ when Amr ibn Qurrah came to him and said: 'O Messenger of God, God has decreed misery upon me, so I do not see myself being provided for except from my drum with my hand. So permit me to sing without indecency.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'No permission for you, and no honour, and no blessing. You lied, O enemy of God. God has indeed provided you with good provision, but you chose what God has forbidden you from His provision in place of what God has permitted you from His lawful. Indeed, if you say anything after this introduction, I will strike you a painful blow.'"

As for reason: God Most High prevented the responsible person from benefiting from the unlawful and commanded others to prevent him from benefiting from it. Whoever prevents someone from taking a thing and benefiting from it is not said to have provided it to him. Do you not see that it is not said: "The sultan has provided his soldiers with money which he has prevented them from taking"? Rather, it is said: "He provided them with what he enabled them to take, and did not prevent them from it, nor commanded that they be prevented from it."

Our companions answered the argument from the verses by saying: although everything is from God, it is like saying: "O Creator of created things, of the Throne and the Chair," and one does not say: "O Creator of dogs and pigs." And He said: ﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6], so He restricted the name "servants" to the righteous, although the disbelievers are also among the servants. Likewise here, He restricted the name *rizq* to the lawful as a mark of honour, although the unlawful is also a provision.

They answered the argument from the Hadith by saying: it is evidence for us, because his saying ﷺ: "You chose what God has forbidden you from His provision" is explicit that a provision may be unlawful. They answered the argument from reason by saying: this question is purely a matter of language, namely whether the unlawful is called a provision or not. Rational proofs have no place in words. And God knows best.

\* \* \*

**(Ninth issue):** The origin of *al-infaq* (spending) is taking wealth out of the hand. From it comes *nafaqa al-mabi'* (the goods sold well) when many buyers come for it, and *nafaqat al-dabbah* (the animal died), meaning its soul departed. And *nafiqa'* of the mouse, because it exits through it. And from it is *al-nafaq* in His saying: ﴿that you seek a tunnel in the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 35].

**(Tenth issue):** In His saying ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ there are several benefits:

First: He used *min* (from), which is partitive, to protect them and to restrain them from extravagance and wastefulness, which are forbidden.

Second: He placed the object of the verb first, indicating that it is more important, as if He said: "They specify some of their wealth for giving in charity."

Third: The spending mentioned in the verse includes obligatory spending and recommended spending. Obligatory spending has categories:

The first is *zakah* (obligatory almsgiving), which is His saying in the verse about hoarding: ﴿and do not spend it in the way of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34].

The second is spending on oneself and on those whose maintenance is obligatory upon him.

The third is spending in *jihad* (struggle in the way of God).

As for recommended spending, it is also spending, due to His saying: ﴿And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. He meant by it charity, due to His saying after it: ﴿and I would give charity and be among the righteous﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. So all these kinds of spending fall under the verse, because all of them are a cause for deserving praise.

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verse 4:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you, and what was revealed before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ is general, encompassing everyone who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), whether before that he had been a believer in Musa and Isa, peace be upon them both, or had not been a believer in them. The indication of a general expression regarding some of what it includes is weaker than the indication of a specific expression regarding that same part, because the general expression admits of specification (takhsis), whereas the specific expression does not admit of it. Since this surah is Medinan, and Allah Exalted has honored the Muslims with His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾, He then mentioned, after that, the People of the Book who believed in the Messenger, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like, with His saying ﴿and those who believe in what has been revealed to you, and what was revealed before you﴾. This is because there is in this specific mention an added honor for them, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. Then, singling out Abdullah ibn Salam and his like with this honor is an encouragement for their likes toward the religion. This is the reason for mentioning this specific after that general. Then we say: as for His saying ﴿and those who believe in what has been revealed to you﴾, there are several issues in it:

(First issue): There is no dispute between our companions (the Ash'arites) and the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) that when faith (iman) is followed by the preposition bi (in), what is meant by it is affirmation (tasdiq). So when we say, "So-and-so believed in such-and-such," what is meant is that he affirmed it, and what is not meant is that he fasted and prayed. Thus the meaning of faith here is, by consensus, affirmation. However, knowledge (ma'rifah) must accompany it, because faith here came in the mode of praise, and one who affirms with doubt cannot be secure from being a liar, so he is closer to blame.

* * *

(Second issue): What is meant by the sending down of revelation, and by the Qur'an being "sent down," "causing to descend," and "conveyed" is that Jibril, peace be upon him, heard the speech of Allah Exalted in the heaven, and then descended to the Messenger with it. This is like when one says, "The message of the ruler descended from the palace," though a message does not descend; rather, the listener hears the message from on high, then descends and delivers it below. The ruler's speech does not separate from his essence, but the hearer listens, then descends and conveys it in his own words. It is also said, "So-and-so conveys the speech" when he hears it in one place and delivers it in another. If it is asked: how did Jibril hear the speech of Allah Exalted, when His speech, according to you, is not of letters and sounds? We say: it is possible that Allah creates for him a hearing for His speech, then empowers him to an expression by which he conveys that eternal speech. It is also possible that Allah created in the Preserved Tablet a writing in this particular arrangement, and Jibril, peace be upon him, read it and memorized it. It is also possible that Allah creates sounds, separated, in this particular arrangement in a particular body, and Jibril, peace be upon him, receives them, and Allah creates in him necessary knowledge that this is the expression conveying the meaning of that eternal speech.

* * *

(Third issue): His saying ﴿and those who believe in what has been revealed to you﴾: this faith is obligatory, because He said at its end: ﴿and those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. Thus it is established that whoever does not have this faith, it is necessary that he not be successful. And when it is established that it is obligatory, it is necessary to acquire knowledge of what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) in detail, because a person cannot fulfill what Allah has obligated upon him in knowledge and action unless he knows it in detail, for if he does not know it thus, it is impossible for him to carry it out. However, acquiring this knowledge is obligatory as a collective duty (fard al-kifayah), for acquiring knowledge of the laws revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) in detail is not obligatory upon the common people. As for His saying ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾, what is meant by it is what was revealed to the prophets who were before Muhammad, and faith in it is obligatory in general, because Allah Exalted has not obligated us now to worship by it, so as to require us to know it in detail. Rather, if we know some of its details, then at that point it becomes obligatory upon us to believe in those details.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾, there are issues in it:

(First issue): The Hereafter (al-akhirah) is an attribute of the Abode of the Hereafter, and it was so named because it comes after the world. It was also said that the world was called "dunya" because it is nearer (adna) than the Hereafter.

(Second issue): Certainty (yaqin) is knowledge of a thing after its possessor had been in doubt about it. For this reason, one does not say, "I am certain of the existence of myself," or "I am certain that the sky is above me," since knowledge of these is not something acquired anew. It is said of newly acquired knowledge of matters, whether that knowledge is necessary (daruri) or inferential (istidlali). So one says, "I am certain of what I meant by this statement," even if he knew its meaning by necessity, and he says, "I am certain that God is one," even if he knew it by acquisition. For this reason, Allah Exalted is not described as being certain of things.

(Third issue): Allah Exalted praised them for being certain of the Hereafter, and it is known that a person is not praised merely for being certain of the existence of the Hereafter. Rather, he deserves praise only if he is certain of the existence of the Hereafter together with what is in it of reckoning, questioning, the admission of believers into Paradise, and the disbelievers into the Fire. It has been related from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "How strange, utterly strange, is the one who doubts Allah while he sees His creation! How strange is the one who knows the first creation, then denies the later creation! How strange is the one who denies resurrection and rising while he dies and lives every day and night, meaning sleep and waking! How strange is the one who believes in Paradise and what is in it of bliss, then strives for the abode of delusion! How strange is the arrogant boaster, while he knows that his beginning is a drop of semen, and his end is a foul carcass!"

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 5:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord, and it is they who are the successful.﴾ Know that there are several issues concerning this verse.

**The First Issue:** Regarding how this verse relates to what precedes it, there are three views.

The first: one intends to begin with "those who believe in the unseen." This is because when it was said, ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾, singling out the God-fearing as those for whom the Book is guidance, a questioner could ask: "What is the reason for restricting this to the God-fearing?" So the words ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ up to ﴿and it is they who are the successful﴾ came as an answer to this question, as if it were said: whoever is occupied with faith, establishing the prayer, paying the zakat, and attaining success and salvation, must be upon guidance from his Lord.

The second: one does not intend to begin with it, but makes it a continuation of ﴿for the God-fearing﴾, and then the new beginning is from His saying ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾. As if it were said: what is the cause that those described by these attributes are singled out for guidance? It is answered that it is not unlikely that these described people should attain, above others, guidance in this world and success in the next.

The third: the first relative pronoun is made a description of "the God-fearing," and the second is put in the nominative as a new beginning, with ﴿They are﴾ as its predicate. The purpose is to make their exclusive possession of success and guidance an indirect reference to the People of the Book, who did not believe in the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while they supposed themselves to be upon guidance and hoped that they would attain success with God, may He be exalted.

[p. 32]

**The Second Issue:** The sense of elevation in His saying ﴿upon guidance﴾ indicates their firm establishment upon guidance and their steadfastness in it, since their state is likened to one who mounts a thing and rides it. A parallel is "So-and-so is upon the truth, or upon falsehood," and they have stated it explicitly in their saying: "He made error a mount and bestrode ignorance." The fuller explanation of their being upon guidance is their adherence to what the proof requires, because the duty of one who adheres to proof is to remain constant in it and to guard it against objections and doubts. Thus God praised them for believing in what was sent down to him first, and praised them secondly for persisting in that and remaining steadfast in guarding it against doubts. This is obligatory upon the responsible person, because if he is strict in religion, fearful and anxious, he must call himself to account regarding his knowledge and his action, and examine his state in both. When he guards himself against failing, he is praised as being upon guidance and insight. The word ﴿guidance﴾ is indefinite to convey a kind of vagueness that cannot be fully grasped nor its measure determined, as one says: "If you saw so-and-so, you would see a man." ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allah said: "The guidance from God is abundant, and only one with insight sees it, and only a few act upon it. Do you not see that the stars of the sky are seen by those with sight, but only the scholars are guided by them?"

**The Third Issue:** The repetition of ﴿They﴾ is a reminder that, just as they are singled out for guidance, they are also singled out for success. Thus they are distinguished from others by these two distinctions. If it is asked: why did it come with a conjunction, and what is the difference between this and His saying ﴿They are like cattle, nay, they are further astray; they are the heedless﴾ [al-A'raf: 179]? We answer: the two predications here differ, which is why the conjunction is present, unlike the two predications there, which are identical, since recording heedlessness against them and likening them to beasts are one and the same thing, and the second sentence was confirming what was in the first, so it is entirely free of conjunction.

**The Fourth Issue:** ﴿Hum﴾ is a separating pronoun (fasl), and it has two benefits. The first: indicating that what follows it is a predicate and not a description. The second: restricting the predicate to the subject. For if you say, "Man is laughing," this does not indicate that the capacity to laugh occurs only in man. But if you say, "Man is the one who laughs," this indicates that the capacity to laugh occurs only in man.

**The Fifth Issue:** The meaning of the definiteness in ﴿the successful﴾ is an indication that the God-fearing are the people of whom you have been informed that they will succeed in the Hereafter, as when you have heard that a man among the people of your city has repented, and you inquire: "Who is he?" and it is said: "Zayd the penitent," meaning he is the one whose repentance you were told of. Or it means that they are those who, if the attribute of ﴿the successful﴾ occurs, then they are they, as you say to your companion: "Have you known the lion and what it is created with of excessive boldness?" Indeed Zayd is he, he is he.

**The Sixth Issue:** The *muflih* (successful one) is the one who attains the sought-after goal, as if he is one for whom the faces of victory have been opened, and it has not been locked against him. The *muflij* with a *jim* is similar, and the root indicates the meaning of splitting and opening. For this reason the farmer was called *fallah* (tiller), and one whose lower lip is split is called *aflah*. In the proverb: "Iron is opened by iron." Its verification is that when God described them as performing what is incumbent upon them in knowledge and action, He clarified the result of that, which is attaining the sought-after goal, namely lasting bliss without any impurity, in the manner of reverence and magnification, because that is the reward sought for acts of worship.

**The Seventh Issue:** These verses are used by the Wa'idiyya (the adherents of the threat doctrine) in one respect, and by the Murji'a (the postponers) in another respect. As for the Wa'idiyya, it is from two angles. The first: His saying ﴿and it is they who are the successful﴾ implies restriction, so it is necessary that whoever neglects the prayer and zakat should not be successful, and this requires certainty regarding the threat against the one who abandons prayer and zakat. The second: the arrangement of the judgment upon the attribute suggests that this attribute is the cause of that judgment, so it follows that the cause of success is the performance of faith, prayer and zakat. Whoever neglects these things does not possess the cause of success, so success must not be attained. As for the Murji'a, they argued that God judged success upon those described by the attributes mentioned in this verse, so whoever is described by these things must be successful even if he commits adultery, steals, and drinks wine. And if the realization of pardon is established for this group, it is necessarily established for others, since no one distinguishes between them. The answer: each of the two arguments is countered by the other, so they cancel each other out. Then the answer to the Wa'idiyya's claim that His saying ﴿and it is they who are the successful﴾ indicates that they are the perfect ones in success, so it follows that the perpetrator of a grave sin is not perfect in success. We say in accordance with this: how can he be perfect in success when he is not certain of deliverance from punishment, but it is permissible for him to be fearful of it? As for the second: the negation of a single cause does not entail the negation of the effect, since for us among the causes of success is God's pardon. The answer to the Murji'a's claim: their being described as God-fearing suffices for attaining the reward, because it includes avoiding sins and avoiding the abandonment of obligations. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 6 (part 1 of 5):**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾

Know that this verse raises grammatical issues (masa'il nahwiyya, questions of grammar) and legal-theoretical issues (masa'il usuliyya, questions of the principles of jurisprudence). We shall address them, God willing. As for His words, "inna" (indeed, verily), there are several issues:

**First issue:** Know that *inna* is a particle (harf), and a particle has no inherent capacity to govern (amal) in the sentence. However, this particle resembles the verb (fi'l) in form and in meaning, and this resemblance requires that it govern. There are preliminaries to this:

**First preliminary:** On explaining the resemblance. Know that this resemblance exists in both wording and meaning. As for wording, it is because it is composed of three letters, its last letter is vowelled with fatha, and it attaches to nouns just as verbs do. It also takes the protective nun (nun al-wiqaya), as in *innani* and *ka'annani*, just as it attaches to verbs, as in *a'taani* and *akramani*. As for meaning, it conveys a meaning in the noun, namely the affirmation of the predicate's ascription to the subject, just as when you say "Zayd stood (qama Zaydun)," the word "qama" conveyed a meaning in the noun.

**Second preliminary:** Since it resembles verbs, it must resemble them in governing, and this is evident by the principle of concomitance (al-dawaran).

**Third preliminary:** Why did it put the noun in the accusative and raise the predicate? Its explanation is that one may say: since it has become a governing particle, it either raises both the subject and the predicate, or puts both in the accusative, or raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative, or the reverse. The first is invalid, because the subject and predicate were both in the nominative before *inna* entered upon them; if they remained so after its entry, it would have no effect at all. Moreover, it has been given the governing capacity of the verb, and a verb does not raise two nouns, so there would be no point in sharing. A branch (far') cannot be stronger than its root (asl). The second option is also invalid, because this too contradicts the governing of the verb, since a verb does not put something in the accusative while leaving unmarked what would raise it. The third option is also invalid, because it leads to equating the root and the branch: the verb's governing first affects the subject in the nominative and then the object in the accusative, so if the particle were so, the root and the branch would be equal. When the three options are refuted, the fourth is determined: that it puts the noun in the accusative and raises the predicate.

[Page 34]

This indicates that these particles govern by an added (dakhila) and not an original (asliyya) capacity, because placing the accusative before the nominative in verbal construction is a departure from the original order. So this indicates here that the governing of these particles is not established by way of原 origin, but by way of an incidental mechanism.

* * *

**Second issue:** The Basran grammarians said: this particle puts the noun in the accusative and raises the predicate. The Kufan grammarians said: it has no effect on raising the predicate; rather, the predicate remains raised by what raised it before. The argument of the Basrans: these particles resemble the verb with a complete resemblance, as already explained, and the verb has an effect in raising and putting in the accusative, so these particles must be the same. The argument of the Kufans is in two parts:

The first: the sense of predicativeness (al-khabariyya) remains in the predicate of the subject, and it is more appropriate to require raising, so predicativeness is the raising factor. Since predicativeness is raising, it is impossible for it to be raised by these particles. This comprises three premises:

The first of them is our statement "predicativeness remains," which is evident, because by predicativeness is meant the predicate being attributed to the subject, and after the particle *inna* enters upon it, that attribution remains.

The second is our statement "predicativeness here requires raising." This is because predicativeness before the entry of *inna* required raising, and the absence of the particle was not part of the requirement, since absence cannot be part of a cause. So after these particles enter, predicativeness requires raising, because if the full requirement is present and does not take effect, that would be due to an impediment, and that contradicts the default.

The third is our statement "predicativeness is more appropriate for requiring," and its explanation is in two parts:

The first: its being a predicate is a real attribute subsisting in itself, while that particle is a foreign element separate from it. As it is separate from it, it is not adjacent to it, because the noun intervenes between them.

The second: the predicate resembles the verb with a real, meaningful resemblance, namely that each of them is attributed to another. As for the particle, it does not resemble the verb in a real, meaningful attribute, since there is no attribution in it. So the resemblance of the predicate to the verb is stronger than the resemblance of this particle to the verb. When this is established, predicativeness requiring raising, for the sake of its resemblance to the verb, is more appropriate than the particle, by virtue of its resemblance to the verb.

Fourth: since predicativeness is stronger in requiring raising, it is impossible for this particle to be the raiser, because predicativeness is more appropriate in relation to this particle. If this is so, the judgment of predicativeness has already been established before this particle exists, so after the particle exists, attributing this judgment to it would be establishing what is already established, and that is impossible.

The second part of the argument: Sibawayh agreed that the particle is not original in governing, so its operation is contrary to the evidence, and what is established contrary to evidence is limited to the extent of necessity. The necessity is met by its operating on the noun, so it is required that it not operate on the predicate.

* * *

**Third issue:** Al-Anbari narrated that al-Kindi, the philosopher-minded man, went to al-Mubarrad and said: "I find redundancy (hashw) in the speech of the Arabs. I find the Arabs say, 'Abd Allah is standing (qa'im),' then they say, 'Indeed, Abd Allah is standing (inna Abd Allah qa'im),' then they say, 'Indeed, Abd Allah is certainly standing (inna Abd Allah la-qa'im).'" Al-Mubarrad said: "Rather, the meanings differ according to the difference in the words. Their saying, 'Abd Allah is standing,' is an informing about his standing; their saying, 'Indeed, Abd Allah is standing,' is an answer to a questioner's question; and their saying, 'Indeed, Abd Allah is certainly standing,' is an answer to the denial of a denier of his standing." Abd al-Qahir argued in support of this view that they are only mentioned as an answer to a questioner's question, saying: "We have seen that they make the sentence of subject and predicate obligatory when it is an answer to an oath, as in: 'By God, indeed Zayd is departing (wallahi inna Zaydan muntaliq).'" Evidence for this from the Revelation is His words: ﴿And they ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn. Say: I will recite to you from him a mention.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾ [al-Kahf 18:83–84]; and His words at the beginning of the surah: ﴿We relate to you their story in truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 18:13]; and His words: ﴿And if they disobey you, then say: Indeed, I am free of what you do﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:216]; and His words: ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those you invoke besides Allah﴾ [al-An'am 6:56]; and His words: ﴿And say: Indeed, I am the clear warner﴾ [al-Hajj 22:89]; and similar verses, which show that it indicates the command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to answer the disbelievers with it in some of what they argued and deliberated about. Likewise His words: ﴿So come to Pharaoh and say: Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:16]; and His words: ﴿Moses said: O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-A'raf 7:104]; and in the story of the magicians: ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we are returning﴾ [al-A'raf 7:125], since it is evident that it was an answer to Pharaoh's words: ﴿He said: Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:71].

Abd al-Qahir said: "The verification is that it is for emphasis (li-l-ta'kid). When the statement concerns a matter about which the addressee has no contrary suspicion, there is no need there for *inna*. It is needed only when the listener suspects the contrary. For this reason you find it becomes more elegant when the statement concerns something whose like is unlikely, as in the verse of Abu Nuwas:

*So resort to despair from people, for indeed the wealth of your soul is in despair.*

Its position is fine only because most people do not compel themselves to despair. As for placing it with the *lam* as an answer to the one who denies, as in your saying, 'Indeed Zayd is certainly standing (inna Zaydan la-qa'im),' it is good, because when the speech is addressed to a denier, the need for emphasis is greater. Just as the denial may come from the listener, it may also come from those present."

Know that it may also come when the speaker suspects in what he has found that it is not found, as in your saying: "Indeed, there was from me to him a kindness, and he treated me with evil." It is as if you are refuting your own suspicion that you had supposed, and clarifying the error in what you imagined. Upon this is His words, exalted, quoting the mother of Mary: ﴿She said: My Lord, indeed I have given birth to her as a female, and Allah knows best what she bore﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:36]. Likewise the words of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿He said: My Lord, indeed my people have denied me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:117].

* * *

As for His words, exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾, there are issues:

**First issue:** Know that it is difficult for the theologians (al-mutakallimun) to state the definition of disbelief (kufr). The verified statement on it is: whatever is transmitted from Muhammad (ﷺ) that he held and said, its authenticity is either known by necessity (bi-l-darura), or by reasoning (bi-l-istidlal), or by a single report (khabar al-wahid). As for the first category, which is that whose coming from the Messenger (peace be upon him) is known by necessity, whoever affirms him in all of that is a believer. Whoever does not affirm him in that, either by not affirming all of it, or by affirming some and not others, that is the disbeliever. So disbelief is the non-affirmation of the Messenger in anything that is known by necessity to have come from him. An example: whoever denies the existence of the Creator, or that He is knowing, powerful, choosing, or that He is one, or that He is exalted above deficiencies and defects, or denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), or the soundness of the noble Qur'an, or denies the legal commands that we know by necessity to be from the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), such as the obligation of prayer, zakat, fasting and pilgrimage, and the prohibition of usury and wine, that person is a disbeliever, because he has abandoned affirming the Messenger in what is known by necessity to be from his religion.

As for what is known by proof to be from his religion, such as his being knowing by knowledge or by his essence, whether he is seen or not seen, and whether he creates the actions of servants or not: since the coming of the Messenger (peace be upon him) with one of the two positions over the other has not been transmitted by decisive mass transmission (tawatur), rather the soundness of one of the two positions and the falsity of the other is known only by reasoning, therefore neither denying it nor affirming it is part of the essence of faith, and so it does not necessitate disbelief. The proof of this is that if that were a part of the essence of faith, it would be obligatory for the Messenger (ﷺ) not to judge anyone as a believer until he knew whether that person recognized the truth in that question. If that were so, his statement on that question would have become famous among the whole community and transmitted by mass transmission. Since that has not been transmitted, it shows that he (peace be upon him) did not make faith dependent upon it. If that is so, then knowing it cannot be part of faith, nor denying it a cause of disbelief. On account of this principle, no one from this community is declared a disbeliever, and we do not declare the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) to be disbelievers.

[Page 36]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 6 (part 2 of 5):

As for what can be known only through single-transmitter reports (ahad), it is clear that faith and disbelief cannot depend on it. This is our position on the reality of disbelief (kufr). If it is said: what you have stated is refuted by the reverse case, namely wearing the ghiyar (the distinguishing belt or garment imposed on non-Muslims) and tying the zunnar (the sacred cord worn by some non-Muslim communities), and similar acts, for a person who does these becomes a disbeliever, although these acts are something other than failing to affirm the Messenger (ﷺ) in what is known by necessity that he brought. We reply: these acts are, in reality, not disbelief, because affirmation (tasdiq) and its absence are an inner matter that creatures have no access to. It is the custom of the Sacred Law (shar') that it does not base rulings in such matters on the inner meaning itself, since there is no way to know it. Rather, it sets up apparent markers and signs for them, and it makes those apparent indications the basis for the legal rulings. The ghiyar and the tying of the zunnar do not belong to this category. For the apparent indication is that whoever affirms the Messenger (peace be upon him) does not do these acts. So when a person does them, this indicates the absence of affirmation. Therefore the Sacred Law builds its rulings upon them, not because they are in themselves disbelief. This is the summary of the discussion on this point, and Allah knows best.
* * *
The second issue: his saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ is a report about their disbelief in the past tense. A report about something in the past tense requires that what is reported about be prior to that report. Once you have understood this, we say: the Mu'tazilah argued from every report by God about something past, such as His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, or ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardian﴾ [15:9], ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [97:1], and ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah﴾ [71:1], to establish that the speech of God is originated (muhdath), whether that speech is these letters and sounds or something else. They said: a report in this form is not true unless it is preceded by what it reports about, and the eternal (qadim) cannot be preceded by anything other than itself. Therefore this report cannot be eternal, so it must be originated. Those who hold that speech is eternal answered this in two ways. The first: God, exalted is He, was in pre-eternity knowing that the world would come into existence. When He brought it into existence, the knowledge that it will exist in the future changed into knowledge that it has come into existence in the past, and this did not entail that God's knowledge became originated. So why is it not permissible to say that God's report in pre-eternity was a report that they will disbelieve, and when their disbelief occurred, that report became a report that they have disbelieved, without entailing that God's report became originated? The second: God, exalted is He, said ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [48:27]. When they entered the Mosque, that report necessarily changed into the statement that they had entered the Sacred Mosque, without the original report changing. If that is permissible, why is the same not permissible in our issue? The one raising the argument answered the first objection first, saying: according to Abu al-Husayn al-Basri and his companions, knowledge changes when the objects of knowledge change. How could it be otherwise? The knowledge that the world does not exist, and that it will exist if it remained in the state of its existence, would be ignorance rather than knowledge. If that is so, that knowledge must change, and by this the objection is dropped. As for the second: God's report and speech are particular sounds. So His saying ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ means that God spoke this speech at a time prior to entering the Mosque, not that He spoke it after entering the Mosque. The parallel in our issue would be to say that God, exalted is He, spoke His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ after the disbelief had proceeded from them, not before it. Yet when this is said, it is an acknowledgment that His speaking of that did not exist in pre-eternity, and this is precisely the point at issue. The advocates of eternity answered: if we said that knowledge changes with the change of the object of knowledge, then we would have to say either that the existence of the world, which will come into being, was present in pre-eternity or that it was not. If it was not present in pre-eternity, that would be an explicit declaration of ignorance, and that is disbelief.
