As for their speech with their brethren, they were saying it from conviction, and they knew that the listeners would accept it from them; therefore emphasis was fitting for it.

As for His words, ﴿we were only mocking﴾, there are two questions. The first question: what is mockery (istihza')? The answer: the root of the matter is lightness from "hazw," which is quick running; "hazi'a yahza'u" means he died on the spot; and "his she-camel tahza'u bihi" means she hastens. Its definition is that it is an expression for displaying agreement while concealing what amounts to evil, by way of ridicule. Accordingly, their saying "we were only mocking" means: we show them agreement with their religion so that we may be safe from their evil, learn their secrets, and take from their charities and spoils.

The second question: how is His words "we were only mocking" connected to His words "Indeed we are with you"?

The answer: It is an emphasis of it, because His words "Indeed we are with you" mean persistence in disbelief, and His words "we were only mocking" are a rejection of Islam; and rejecting the opposite of a thing is an affirmation of its firmness. Or it is a substitute for it, because whoever belittles Islam has magnified disbelief. Or it is a resumed statement, as if they had been objected to when they said "Indeed we are with you," so they said: if that is true, how do you agree with the people of Islam? So they said: "we were only mocking."

Know that when the Glorified and Exalted related this of them, He answered them with several things.

The first of these is His words: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, and concerning it there are questions.

The first question: how is it permissible to describe Allah the Exalted as mocking, when it is established that mockery cannot be free of deception, which is impossible for Allah; and because it cannot be free of ignorance, as in His words: "They said, 'Do you take us in mockery?' He said, 'I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant'" [al-Baqara: 67], and ignorance is impossible for Allah.

The answer: They mentioned five interpretations regarding this.

The first: what Allah does to them is recompense for their mockery, which He called by the name of mockery, because a part of a thing is named by the name of that thing. The Exalted said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]; ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqara: 194]; ﴿They deceive Allah, but He is their deceiver﴾ [al-Nisa': 142]; ﴿And they plotted, and Allah plotted﴾ [Al ʿImran: 54]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, so-and-so has satirized me, and he knows that I am not a poet; so satirize him. O Allah, curse him as many times as he satirized me," meaning: repay him the recompense of his satire. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Take upon yourselves of deeds what you are able to bear, for Allah does not tire until you tire."

The second: the harm of their mockery of the believers returns upon them and does not harm the believers, so it becomes as if Allah had mocked them.

The third: among the effects of mockery is the occurrence of humiliation and abasement; so mockery is mentioned while what is meant is the occurrence of humiliation for them, expressing the cause to denote the effect.

The fourth: Allah's mockery of them is that He shows them, in this world, rulings whose outcome for them with Allah in the Hereafter is the opposite, just as they showed the Prophet and the believers a matter while what was in their secret was the opposite of it. This interpretation is weak, because when He showed them the rulings of this world, He had already shown the clear proofs of how they would be treated in the Hereafter, of evil outcome and great punishment; so there is no contradiction in that with what He showed in this world.

The fifth: Allah the Exalted treats them as one who mocks, in this world and in the Hereafter. In this world, because He informed the Messenger of their secrets even though they were exerting great effort to conceal them from him. In the Hereafter, Ibn ʿAbbas said: when the believers enter Paradise and the disbelievers the Fire, Allah opens a door from Paradise onto the Hellfire at the place where the hypocrites dwell. When the hypocrites see the door open, they begin to come out of the Hellfire and head toward Paradise, while the people of Paradise look at them. When they reach the door of Paradise, the door is shut against them there. This is His words: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed... So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29–34]. This is the mockery of them.

The second question: how did He begin His words "Allah mocks them" without conjoining it to the statement before it?

The answer: It is a resumption of supreme eloquence and grandeur, and in it is that Allah is the one who mocks them with a great mockery, in comparison with which their mockery becomes as nothing. And in it also is that Allah is the one who undertakes mocking them in retribution for the believers, and does not require the believers to oppose them with a mockery like it.

The third question: was it said that Allah mocks them so as to correspond with His words "we were only mocking"?

The answer: Because "yastahzi'u" indicates the occurrence and renewal of mockery time after time. And this was the case with Allah's afflictions upon them: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested every year once or twice?﴾ [al-Tawba: 126]. Also, they were not, for most of their time, free from the tearing of veils, the exposure of secrets, and the sense of fear lest a verse be revealed concerning them: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down concerning them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say: Mock on; indeed Allah will bring out what you fear﴾ [al-Tawba: 64].

The second answer: His words ﴿and He leaves them to continue in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqara: 15]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it is from "madda al-jaysh" and "amadda-hu," when he increases it and adds to it what strengthens and multiplies it; likewise "madda al-dawāt" and "amaddaha," when he increases the inkwell with what sustains it; and "maddatu al-sirāj" and "al-ard," when I improve them with oil and manure; and "maddahu al-shaytan fi al-ghayy," and "amadda-hu," when he joins him with whisperings. "Madda" and "amadda" have one meaning.

Some of them said: "madda" is used for evil, and "amadda" for good, as He said: ﴿Do they reckon that We extend to them with wealth and children?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55]. Among the people is one who claimed that it is from extending the lifespan, granting respite and delaying; and this is an error for two reasons. The first: the reading of Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin, "wa-numiddu-hum," and the reading of Nafi' "(wa-ikhwanuhum yamiddunahum fi al-ghayy)" [al-A'raf: 202], indicate that it is from "madad" and not "madd."

The second: what means "amhala-hu" (granted him respite) is only "madda lahu," like "amla lahu." The Mu'tazila said: this verse cannot be taken according to its apparent meaning, for several reasons:

The first: His words ﴿and their brethren extend them in error﴾ attribute that error to their brethren; how then can it be attributed to Allah the Exalted?

The second: Allah the Exalted blamed them for this transgression; if it were an act of Allah the Exalted, how could He blame them for it?

The third: if it were an act of Allah the Exalted, prophethood would be void and the Qur'an would be void, and occupation with its exegesis would be futile.

The fourth: He the Exalted attributed the transgression to them with His words "in their transgression"; and if it were from Allah, He would not have attributed it to them. So it becomes clear that He attributed it to them only so that it would be known that He the Exalted is not its creator. The proof of this is that when He attributed the extension to the devils, He left the error unrestricted by attribution in His words: ﴿and their brethren extend them in error﴾ [al-A'raf: 202]. Having established this, we say: the interpretation has several aspects.

The first, which is the interpretation of al-Ka'bi and Abu Muslim ibn Yahya al-Isfahani: when Allah granted them His kindnesses which He grants to the believers, but abandoned them because of their disbelief and their persistence in it, their hearts remained dark through the increase of darkness in them, while the light in the hearts of the Muslims increased. So He called that increase "madad" and attributed it to Allah the Exalted, since it is caused by His act toward them.

The second: that it be taken to mean the prevention of compulsion and coercion, as it is said: when the fool is not restrained, he is commanded.

The third: that the act of the devil be attributed to Allah the Exalted, since it is through His enabling and empowering and leaving between him and the misleading of His servants.

Fourth: what al-Jubba'i said. He said: "wa-yamudduhum" means "He extends their lifespan," and then, despite that, they remain in their transgression, wandering blindly. This is weak for two reasons. The first: as we have shown, it is not permissible in the language to interpret "wa-yamuddu-hum" as extending the lifespan. The second: grant that it is valid, yet it implies that He extends their lifespan for the purpose that they remain in their transgression, wandering blindly, and that implies the problem.

The judge (al-Qadi) answered this by saying: what is meant is not that He extends their lifespan for the purpose that they remain in transgression; rather, what is meant is that He keeps them alive and shows them kindness in obedience, but they refuse except to wander blindly.

Know that the discussion on this subject has already passed in His words: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts﴾, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

Know that *ṭughyān* (overweening rebellion, transgression) means excessive persistence in disbelief and exceeding the limit in defiance. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 11], meaning it exceeded its measure, and He said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 24], meaning he went to excess and exceeded the limit.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī recited (*fī ṭighyānihim*) with a kasra, and both are dialectal forms, like *luqyān* and *liqyān*. And *al-ʿamah* (bewilderment) is like *al-ʿamā* (blindness), except that *al-ʿamā* is general, applying to sight and to judgment, whereas *al-ʿamah* is specifically in judgment; it is hesitation and perplexity, not knowing where to turn.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance, so their trade has not profited them, nor were they guided.﴾

Know that "buying misguidance in exchange for guidance" means choosing misguidance over guidance and substituting it for guidance. If it is said: how did they buy misguidance in exchange for guidance when they were not upon guidance? We say: they were treated as though they possessed it, because they had secure hold of it, as if it were in their hands. So when they abandoned it and inclined toward misguidance, they had substituted misguidance for it.

Page 66
Misguidance (ḍalāla) means deviation, departing from the right course, and the loss of being guided. It is used figuratively for going astray from what is correct in religion. As for His saying, ﴿so their trade has not profited them﴾, the meaning is that they did not gain in their trade. Here there are two questions.

The first question: how is loss attributed to trade, when it belongs to its owners?
The answer: this is figurative attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī), which is when a verb is ascribed to a thing that is connected to the one to whom it truly belongs, just as trade is connected to the buyer.

The second question: granted that buying misguidance in exchange for guidance is used figuratively in the sense of substitution, what is the point of mentioning profit and trade when there was no actual sale? The answer: this strengthens the figurative usage and beautifies it, as the poet said:

When I saw the eagle (nasr) had overcome the son of Da'ya, and nested in its two nests, my chest was stirred for him.

Having likened gray hair to the eagle and jet-black hair to the crow, he followed it with mention of nesting and the nest. Likewise here, when He, glorified is He, mentioned buying, He followed it with what is compatible with it and akin to it, as an illustration of their loss and a depiction of its reality. As for His saying, ﴿nor were they guided﴾, the meaning is that what merchants seek in their dealings is two things: the safety of their capital and profit. These people have lost both, because their capital is the intellect free of any obstacle. When they adopted these misguided beliefs, those corrupt acquired beliefs became an obstacle preventing them from occupying themselves with seeking sound beliefs.

Qatada said: they moved from guidance to misguidance, from obedience to disobedience, from unity to division, from security to fear, and from the Sunnah to innovation. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their parable is like that of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see.﴾

Know that before we enter into explaining the words of this verse, we speak about two matters. The first: the purpose of coining parables (amthal) is that they make an impression on hearts that the description of a thing in itself does not make. This is because the aim of a parable (mathal) is to liken the hidden to the manifest and the unseen to the witnessed, so that grasping its reality is firmly established, and sense perception agrees with reason, and this is the utmost in clarification. Do you not see that when encouragement toward faith occurs without a parable being coined for it, its settling in the heart is not as firm as when it is likened to light? And when one is made to renounce disbelief merely by mention, its ugliness does not become as firmly fixed in the intellects as when it is likened to darkness? And when one reports the weakness of a matter and coins for it the parable of a spider's web, this is more eloquent in establishing its image than reporting its weakness alone. For this reason Allah the Exalted has multiplied parables in His Clear Book and in all His other books. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And these parables We strike for the people﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. Among the surahs of the Injil is the Surah of Parables. There are issues in the verse:

The first issue: the word mathal in the origin of their speech means "like" (mithl), which is its counterpart. It is said mathal, mithl and mathil, like shabah, shibh and shabih. Then the saying that is widely circulated, whose range of application is drawn from its source, was called a mathal. Its condition is that it be a saying which has some strangeness from certain aspects.

[Page 67]

The second issue: when Allah the Exalted had explained the reality of the attributes of the hypocrites, He followed them with the coining of two parables for further disclosure and explanation. One of them is this parable, and in it there are difficulties. The first: it may be asked, what is the basis of likening them to one who was given light and then that light was taken away from him, when the hypocrite has no light at all?

The second: it may be said that one who kindled a fire which lit up only a little has benefited from it and from its light, and then was deprived of it. But the hypocrites have no benefit whatsoever from faith, so what is the basis of the comparison?

The third: the one who kindled the fire acquired the light for himself, and Allah took away his light and left him in darkness, whereas the hypocrite has acquired no good, and what befell him of loss and bewilderment came from himself. So what is the basis of the comparison?

The answer: the scholars have mentioned several aspects regarding the manner of the comparison:

The first: al-Suddi said: some people entered Islam when he (peace be upon him) arrived at Madinah, then they became hypocrites. The comparison here is most accurate, because by their faith initially they acquired light, then by their hypocrisy afterward they extinguished that light and fell into a tremendous bewilderment. There is no bewilderment greater than the bewilderment of religion, because one who is bewildered on his path due to darkness loses only a little of the world, but one who is bewildered in religion loses himself in the Hereafter forever and ever.

The second: if what al-Suddi said is not sound, but rather they were hypocrites from the beginning of their affair, then there is another interpretation mentioned by al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him. It is that when they displayed Islam, they gained the protection of their blood, the safety of their property from plunder, and of their children from captivity, and they gained a share of the spoils of jihad and other rulings of the Muslims. This was counted as a light from the lights of faith. And since this was, in comparison with the everlasting punishment, a little, you may consider their likeness to the one who kindled a fire from whose light he benefited a little, then that was taken from him, so his bewilderment and regret remained because of the darkness that came upon him after the light. Thus their small benefit in this world resembles the light, and their great harm in the Hereafter resembles the darkness.

The third: we may say that the basis of the comparison is not that the hypocrite has a light, but rather the basis of the comparison with this kindler of fire is that when the light departed from him, he became bewildered. And the bewilderment of one who was in light and then it departed from him is greater than the bewilderment of a traveller on a path in constant darkness. However, He mentioned the light in the kindler of the fire so that it would be correct to describe him with this intense darkness, not that the basis of the comparison is a combination of light and darkness.

The fourth: what they displayed gives the impression that it is of the kind of light by which one benefits, and the departure of the light is what manifests to its companions of disbelief and hypocrisy. Whoever says this says that the parable was joined as a continuation of His saying: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; and when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed we are with you"﴾. So the fire is a parable for their saying "We believe", and its going away is a parable for their saying to the disbelievers "Indeed we are with you". If it is said: how did what the hypocrite displays of the word of faith become a parable of light, when at the time he uttered it he concealed its opposite? We say: if he had added to the utterance belief in it and action according to it, he would have completed the light for himself. But since he did not do so, his light was not completed. And he was called the mere utterance a light only because it is a true statement in itself.

The fifth: it is possible that the kindling of the fire is an expression for the hypocrite's display of the word of faith, and he was called a light because his outward appearance is adorned by it among them and he becomes praised because of it among them. Then Allah the Exalted takes away that light by exposing the hypocrite's concealment, through making known to His Prophet and the believers the reality of his affair. So the name of hypocrisy appears to him in place of the name of faith that appeared from him. Thus he remains in darkness, not seeing, since the light that he had before has been removed, as Allah has exposed his affair and it has vanished.

The sixth: when they were described as having purchased error in exchange for guidance, He followed that with this parable, to liken their guidance which they sold to the blazing fire that illuminated what was around the kindler, and the error which they purchased and which was sealed upon their hearts to Allah's taking away their light and leaving them in the darkness.

The seventh: it is possible that the kindler here is a kindler of a fire which Allah the Exalted does not approve, and the purpose is to liken the strife which the hypocrites attempted to stir up to this fire, for the strife they were stirring was short-lived. Do you not see His saying the Exalted: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64].

The eighth: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed concerning the Jews

[Page 68]

and their awaiting the emergence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and their seeking victory through him over the polytheists of the Arabs. When he emerged, they disbelieved in him. So their waiting for Muhammad (ﷺ) was like the kindling of the fire, and their disbelief in him after his manifestation was like the removal of that light.

The third issue: as for the likening of faith to light and disbelief to darkness, it is abundant in the Book of Allah the Exalted. The aspect of this is that light has reached the utmost in being a guide to the right path and to the road of benefit and in removing bewilderment, and this is the state of faith in the matter of religion. So He likened what is the utmost in removing bewilderment and finding benefit in the matter of religion to what is the ultimate in the matter of the world. Similarly, the statement regarding likening disbelief to darkness: the one who has strayed from the path and needs to travel it encounters no greater causes of deprivation and bewilderment than darkness, and nothing in the matter of religion is greater than disbelief. So Allah the Exalted likened one of them to the other. This is what is said concerning the overall aim of this verse. There remain here questions and answers connected with the details:

The first question: His saying the Exalted: ﴿Their parable is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ requires likening their parable to the parable of the kindler. So what is the parable of the hypocrites and what is the parable of the kindler, such that one is likened to the other?

The answer: the word mathal is borrowed for a story or a description when it has a matter of importance and strangeness in it. As if it were said: their astonishing story is like the story of the one who kindled a fire. Likewise His saying: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the righteous have been promised﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], meaning: among the marvels We have related to you is the story of the astonishing Garden. ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾ [al-Nahl: 60], meaning the attribute which has a matter of majesty and grandeur. ﴿Their description in the Torah﴾ [al-Fath: 29], meaning their description and their wondrous state. And because of the sense of strangeness in mathal, they said: "So-and-so's mathal is in good and evil", and they derived from it an adjective for one of wondrous state.

The second question: how is a group likened to a single person?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: it is permissible in the language to place alladhi (the one who) in the position of alladhina (those who), as in His saying: ﴿And you plunged as those who plunged did﴾ [al-Tawbah: 69]. This is permissible because alladhi, being a link to describing every general definite noun, and due to its frequent occurrence in their speech, and because it is elongated by its relative clause, it deserves lightening. For this reason they made it defective by deletion, so they deleted its ya', then they kasrated it, then they restricted themselves to the lam alone in the forms of the active and passive participles.

The second: that the intended meaning is the genus of kindlers, or the plural is intended, or the group who kindled a fire.

The third, and it is the strongest: that the hypocrites and their persons were not likened to the person of the kindler, such that it would necessitate likening a group to an individual. Rather, their story was likened to the story of the kindler. A similar example is His saying: ﴿The parable of those who were entrusted with the Torah, then did not carry it, is like the parable of a donkey﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 5], and His saying: ﴿They look at you with eyes rolling like one fainting from death﴾ [Muhammad: 20].

The fourth: the meaning is: and the parable of each one of them is like His saying: ﴿He brings you forth as a child﴾ [Ghafir: 67], meaning He brings forth each one of you.

The third question: what is al-wuqud (the blazing)? What is the fire? What is al-idha'ah (the illumination)? What is the light? What is the darkness?

The answer: as for the blazing of the fire, it is its flaring up and the rise of its flame. As for the fire (nar), it is a subtle, luminous, hot, burning substance. Its derivation is from nara yanur, meaning it fled, because in it there is movement and agitation. The light (nur) is derived from it and is its illumination. Al-manar is a sign, and al-manarah is the thing upon which the call to prayer is given. It is also said of the thing on which a lamp is placed. From it comes al-nurah (depilatory), because it purifies the body. Al-idha'ah is the excess of illumination, and the evidence for this is His saying the Exalted: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾ [Yunus: 5]. The verb adha' occurs both intransitive and transitive. You say: adha'a al-qamar al-zulmah (the moon lit up the darkness), and adha'a al-qamar meaning istadha' (it became illuminated). The poet said:

Their lineages and their faces lit up for them the darkness of the night, until the piercer of the jiz' (onyx/stone) strung it.

As for what is around a thing (hawla), it is that which is connected to it. You say: dara hawlahu and hawaliyhi (it turned around him). Al-haul (year) is so called because it revolves (tahul). Hala 'an al-'ahd means it changed; hala lawnuhu means its color changed. Al-hawalah is the transfer of a right from one person to another. Al-muhawalah is seeking to do an act after one was not seeking it. Al-hawal is the turning of the eye, and al-hiwal is the turning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will not desire any change from it﴾ [al-Kahf: 108]. Darkness (zulmah) is the absence of light from that which by nature should be illuminated. In the original language, zulm is an expression for deficiency. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short (lam tazlim) of it in anything﴾ [al-Kahf: 33], meaning it did not diminish. And in the proverb: "Whoever resembles his father has not wronged (fa ma zalam)", meaning he has not diminished the right of resemblance. Al-zulm also means snow, because it diminishes quickly. And al-zulm is the water of the tooth and its freshness and whiteness, likening it to snow.

The fourth question: is adha'at transitive or not?

The answer: both are permissible. It is said: the fire lit up by itself (adha'at al-nar binafsiha), and it lit up other than itself (wa-adha'at ghayraha). Likewise al-shay' was darkened by itself and darkened another, meaning made it dark. Here the closer view is that it is transitive, though it may be intransitive, ascribed to what is around it. Its feminine marking is for agreement according to meaning, because what is around the kindler are places and things. The reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah, "da'a", supports this.

The fifth question: why was it not said: "Allah took away their illumination (diya')", in accordance with His saying: ﴿when it lit up (fa-lamma adha'at)﴾?

[Page 69]

Answer: the mention of "light" is more eloquent, because light carries the implication of increase. Had it been said, "God took away their brightness," it would have suggested the loss of perfection while something still called light remained. The purpose is the complete removal of light from them. Do you not see how He mentioned right after it: ﴿and left them in darkness, they do not see﴾? Darkness is an expression for the absence of light. And how did He make it plural, how did He make it indefinite, and how did He follow it with what indicates that it is pure darkness, namely His saying: ﴿they do not see﴾?

The Seventh Question: Why did He say ﴿dhahaba Allahu bi-nurihim﴾ and not "adhhaba Allahu nurahum"?

The answer: the difference between adhhaba and dhahaba bihi is that the meaning of adhhabahu is "he removed it and made it go away," while it is said dhahaba bihi when one takes it along with him (bi-hi meaning "with him"), and "the ruler dhahaba with his wealth" means he took it. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿fa-lamma dhahabu bihi﴾ [Yusuf: 15] and ﴿idhan la-dhahaba kullu ilahin bi-ma khalaqa﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91]. The meaning is that God took their light and held it back: ﴿wa-ma yumsik fa-la mursila lahu﴾ [Fatir: 2]. So it is more eloquent than removal. Al-Yamani recited "adhhaba Allahu nurahum."

The Eighth Question: What is the meaning of [wa-taraka hum]? The answer: taraka, when connected to one object, means "to cast aside" (taraha), and when connected to two objects, it means "to make/render" (sayyara), so it works like the verbs of the heart. From this is His saying: ﴿wa-taraka hum fi zulumatin﴾. Its origin is "hum fi zulumatin," then "taraka" entered and made both parts accusative.

The Ninth Question: Why was one of the two objects omitted from ﴿la yubsirun﴾?

The answer: it belongs to the category of what is left unstated, to which the mind does not turn for consideration, not to the category of what is implied and intended. As if the verb were intransitive in the first place.

﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾

Page 70

Know that since what was known of their condition was that they used to hear, speak and see, it was impossible to take that literally. Nothing remained but to liken their condition, because of the intensity of their clinging to obstinacy and their turning away from what reached their hearing of the Qur'an, and the proofs and signs the Messenger displayed, to one who is truly deaf and does not hear. And when one does not hear, he cannot respond, so He made him like one who is mute. And when one does not benefit from proofs and does not see the path of guidance, he is like the blind. As for His saying: ﴿so they do not return﴾, there are several aspects:

First: they do not return from what was mentioned before, namely clinging to hypocrisy. Because of their clinging to it, God described them with these attributes, so this indicates that they persist in their hypocrisy forever.

Second: they do not return to guidance after having sold it, nor to misguidance after having purchased it.

Third: he meant that they are like the bewildered who remain motionless in their place, not moving, not knowing whether to advance or retreat. And how can they return to the place from which they started?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their parable is like that of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see.﴾

Know that before we enter into explaining the words of this verse, we speak about two matters. The first: the purpose of coining parables (amthal) is that they make an impression on hearts that the description of a thing in itself does not make. This is because the aim of a parable (mathal) is to liken the hidden to the manifest and the unseen to the witnessed, so that grasping its reality is firmly established, and sense perception agrees with reason, and this is the utmost in clarification. Do you not see that when encouragement toward faith occurs without a parable being coined for it, its settling in the heart is not as firm as when it is likened to light? And when one is made to renounce disbelief merely by mention, its ugliness does not become as firmly fixed in the intellects as when it is likened to darkness? And when one reports the weakness of a matter and coins for it the parable of a spider's web, this is more eloquent in establishing its image than reporting its weakness alone. For this reason Allah the Exalted has multiplied parables in His Clear Book and in all His other books. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And these parables We strike for the people﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. Among the surahs of the Injil is the Surah of Parables. There are issues in the verse:

The first issue: the word mathal in the origin of their speech means "like" (mithl), which is its counterpart. It is said mathal, mithl and mathil, like shabah, shibh and shabih. Then the saying that is widely circulated, whose range of application is drawn from its source, was called a mathal. Its condition is that it be a saying which has some strangeness from certain aspects.

[Page 67]

The second issue: when Allah the Exalted had explained the reality of the attributes of the hypocrites, He followed them with the coining of two parables for further disclosure and explanation. One of them is this parable, and in it there are difficulties. The first: it may be asked, what is the basis of likening them to one who was given light and then that light was taken away from him, when the hypocrite has no light at all?

The second: it may be said that one who kindled a fire which lit up only a little has benefited from it and from its light, and then was deprived of it. But the hypocrites have no benefit whatsoever from faith, so what is the basis of the comparison?

The third: the one who kindled the fire acquired the light for himself, and Allah took away his light and left him in darkness, whereas the hypocrite has acquired no good, and what befell him of loss and bewilderment came from himself. So what is the basis of the comparison?

The answer: the scholars have mentioned several aspects regarding the manner of the comparison:

The first: al-Suddi said: some people entered Islam when he (peace be upon him) arrived at Madinah, then they became hypocrites. The comparison here is most accurate, because by their faith initially they acquired light, then by their hypocrisy afterward they extinguished that light and fell into a tremendous bewilderment. There is no bewilderment greater than the bewilderment of religion, because one who is bewildered on his path due to darkness loses only a little of the world, but one who is bewildered in religion loses himself in the Hereafter forever and ever.

The second: if what al-Suddi said is not sound, but rather they were hypocrites from the beginning of their affair, then there is another interpretation mentioned by al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him. It is that when they displayed Islam, they gained the protection of their blood, the safety of their property from plunder, and of their children from captivity, and they gained a share of the spoils of jihad and other rulings of the Muslims. This was counted as a light from the lights of faith. And since this was, in comparison with the everlasting punishment, a little, you may consider their likeness to the one who kindled a fire from whose light he benefited a little, then that was taken from him, so his bewilderment and regret remained because of the darkness that came upon him after the light. Thus their small benefit in this world resembles the light, and their great harm in the Hereafter resembles the darkness.

The third: we may say that the basis of the comparison is not that the hypocrite has a light, but rather the basis of the comparison with this kindler of fire is that when the light departed from him, he became bewildered. And the bewilderment of one who was in light and then it departed from him is greater than the bewilderment of a traveller on a path in constant darkness. However, He mentioned the light in the kindler of the fire so that it would be correct to describe him with this intense darkness, not that the basis of the comparison is a combination of light and darkness.

The fourth: what they displayed gives the impression that it is of the kind of light by which one benefits, and the departure of the light is what manifests to its companions of disbelief and hypocrisy. Whoever says this says that the parable was joined as a continuation of His saying: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; and when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed we are with you"﴾. So the fire is a parable for their saying "We believe", and its going away is a parable for their saying to the disbelievers "Indeed we are with you". If it is said: how did what the hypocrite displays of the word of faith become a parable of light, when at the time he uttered it he concealed its opposite? We say: if he had added to the utterance belief in it and action according to it, he would have completed the light for himself. But since he did not do so, his light was not completed. And he was called the mere utterance a light only because it is a true statement in itself.

The fifth: it is possible that the kindling of the fire is an expression for the hypocrite's display of the word of faith, and he was called a light because his outward appearance is adorned by it among them and he becomes praised because of it among them. Then Allah the Exalted takes away that light by exposing the hypocrite's concealment, through making known to His Prophet and the believers the reality of his affair. So the name of hypocrisy appears to him in place of the name of faith that appeared from him. Thus he remains in darkness, not seeing, since the light that he had before has been removed, as Allah has exposed his affair and it has vanished.

The sixth: when they were described as having purchased error in exchange for guidance, He followed that with this parable, to liken their guidance which they sold to the blazing fire that illuminated what was around the kindler, and the error which they purchased and which was sealed upon their hearts to Allah's taking away their light and leaving them in the darkness.

The seventh: it is possible that the kindler here is a kindler of a fire which Allah the Exalted does not approve, and the purpose is to liken the strife which the hypocrites attempted to stir up to this fire, for the strife they were stirring was short-lived. Do you not see His saying the Exalted: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64].

The eighth: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed concerning the Jews

[Page 68]

and their awaiting the emergence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and their seeking victory through him over the polytheists of the Arabs. When he emerged, they disbelieved in him. So their waiting for Muhammad (ﷺ) was like the kindling of the fire, and their disbelief in him after his manifestation was like the removal of that light.

The third issue: as for the likening of faith to light and disbelief to darkness, it is abundant in the Book of Allah the Exalted. The aspect of this is that light has reached the utmost in being a guide to the right path and to the road of benefit and in removing bewilderment, and this is the state of faith in the matter of religion. So He likened what is the utmost in removing bewilderment and finding benefit in the matter of religion to what is the ultimate in the matter of the world. Similarly, the statement regarding likening disbelief to darkness: the one who has strayed from the path and needs to travel it encounters no greater causes of deprivation and bewilderment than darkness, and nothing in the matter of religion is greater than disbelief. So Allah the Exalted likened one of them to the other. This is what is said concerning the overall aim of this verse. There remain here questions and answers connected with the details:

The first question: His saying the Exalted: ﴿Their parable is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ requires likening their parable to the parable of the kindler. So what is the parable of the hypocrites and what is the parable of the kindler, such that one is likened to the other?

The answer: the word mathal is borrowed for a story or a description when it has a matter of importance and strangeness in it. As if it were said: their astonishing story is like the story of the one who kindled a fire. Likewise His saying: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the righteous have been promised﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], meaning: among the marvels We have related to you is the story of the astonishing Garden. ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾ [al-Nahl: 60], meaning the attribute which has a matter of majesty and grandeur. ﴿Their description in the Torah﴾ [al-Fath: 29], meaning their description and their wondrous state. And because of the sense of strangeness in mathal, they said: "So-and-so's mathal is in good and evil", and they derived from it an adjective for one of wondrous state.

The second question: how is a group likened to a single person?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: it is permissible in the language to place alladhi (the one who) in the position of alladhina (those who), as in His saying: ﴿And you plunged as those who plunged did﴾ [al-Tawbah: 69]. This is permissible because alladhi, being a link to describing every general definite noun, and due to its frequent occurrence in their speech, and because it is elongated by its relative clause, it deserves lightening. For this reason they made it defective by deletion, so they deleted its ya', then they kasrated it, then they restricted themselves to the lam alone in the forms of the active and passive participles.

The second: that the intended meaning is the genus of kindlers, or the plural is intended, or the group who kindled a fire.

The third, and it is the strongest: that the hypocrites and their persons were not likened to the person of the kindler, such that it would necessitate likening a group to an individual. Rather, their story was likened to the story of the kindler. A similar example is His saying: ﴿The parable of those who were entrusted with the Torah, then did not carry it, is like the parable of a donkey﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 5], and His saying: ﴿They look at you with eyes rolling like one fainting from death﴾ [Muhammad: 20].

The fourth: the meaning is: and the parable of each one of them is like His saying: ﴿He brings you forth as a child﴾ [Ghafir: 67], meaning He brings forth each one of you.

The third question: what is al-wuqud (the blazing)? What is the fire? What is al-idha'ah (the illumination)? What is the light? What is the darkness?

The answer: as for the blazing of the fire, it is its flaring up and the rise of its flame. As for the fire (nar), it is a subtle, luminous, hot, burning substance. Its derivation is from nara yanur, meaning it fled, because in it there is movement and agitation. The light (nur) is derived from it and is its illumination. Al-manar is a sign, and al-manarah is the thing upon which the call to prayer is given. It is also said of the thing on which a lamp is placed. From it comes al-nurah (depilatory), because it purifies the body. Al-idha'ah is the excess of illumination, and the evidence for this is His saying the Exalted: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾ [Yunus: 5]. The verb adha' occurs both intransitive and transitive. You say: adha'a al-qamar al-zulmah (the moon lit up the darkness), and adha'a al-qamar meaning istadha' (it became illuminated). The poet said:

Their lineages and their faces lit up for them the darkness of the night, until the piercer of the jiz' (onyx/stone) strung it.

As for what is around a thing (hawla), it is that which is connected to it. You say: dara hawlahu and hawaliyhi (it turned around him). Al-haul (year) is so called because it revolves (tahul). Hala 'an al-'ahd means it changed; hala lawnuhu means its color changed. Al-hawalah is the transfer of a right from one person to another. Al-muhawalah is seeking to do an act after one was not seeking it. Al-hawal is the turning of the eye, and al-hiwal is the turning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will not desire any change from it﴾ [al-Kahf: 108]. Darkness (zulmah) is the absence of light from that which by nature should be illuminated. In the original language, zulm is an expression for deficiency. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short (lam tazlim) of it in anything﴾ [al-Kahf: 33], meaning it did not diminish. And in the proverb: "Whoever resembles his father has not wronged (fa ma zalam)", meaning he has not diminished the right of resemblance. Al-zulm also means snow, because it diminishes quickly. And al-zulm is the water of the tooth and its freshness and whiteness, likening it to snow.

The fourth question: is adha'at transitive or not?

The answer: both are permissible. It is said: the fire lit up by itself (adha'at al-nar binafsiha), and it lit up other than itself (wa-adha'at ghayraha). Likewise al-shay' was darkened by itself and darkened another, meaning made it dark. Here the closer view is that it is transitive, though it may be intransitive, ascribed to what is around it. Its feminine marking is for agreement according to meaning, because what is around the kindler are places and things. The reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah, "da'a", supports this.

The fifth question: why was it not said: "Allah took away their illumination (diya')", in accordance with His saying: ﴿when it lit up (fa-lamma adha'at)﴾?

[Page 69]

Answer: the mention of "light" is more eloquent, because light carries the implication of increase. Had it been said, "God took away their brightness," it would have suggested the loss of perfection while something still called light remained. The purpose is the complete removal of light from them. Do you not see how He mentioned right after it: ﴿and left them in darkness, they do not see﴾? Darkness is an expression for the absence of light. And how did He make it plural, how did He make it indefinite, and how did He follow it with what indicates that it is pure darkness, namely His saying: ﴿they do not see﴾?

The Seventh Question: Why did He say ﴿dhahaba Allahu bi-nurihim﴾ and not "adhhaba Allahu nurahum"?

The answer: the difference between adhhaba and dhahaba bihi is that the meaning of adhhabahu is "he removed it and made it go away," while it is said dhahaba bihi when one takes it along with him (bi-hi meaning "with him"), and "the ruler dhahaba with his wealth" means he took it. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿fa-lamma dhahabu bihi﴾ [Yusuf: 15] and ﴿idhan la-dhahaba kullu ilahin bi-ma khalaqa﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91]. The meaning is that God took their light and held it back: ﴿wa-ma yumsik fa-la mursila lahu﴾ [Fatir: 2]. So it is more eloquent than removal. Al-Yamani recited "adhhaba Allahu nurahum."

The Eighth Question: What is the meaning of [wa-taraka hum]? The answer: taraka, when connected to one object, means "to cast aside" (taraha), and when connected to two objects, it means "to make/render" (sayyara), so it works like the verbs of the heart. From this is His saying: ﴿wa-taraka hum fi zulumatin﴾. Its origin is "hum fi zulumatin," then "taraka" entered and made both parts accusative.

The Ninth Question: Why was one of the two objects omitted from ﴿la yubsirun﴾?

The answer: it belongs to the category of what is left unstated, to which the mind does not turn for consideration, not to the category of what is implied and intended. As if the verb were intransitive in the first place.

﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾

Page 70

Know that since what was known of their condition was that they used to hear, speak and see, it was impossible to take that literally. Nothing remained but to liken their condition, because of the intensity of their clinging to obstinacy and their turning away from what reached their hearing of the Qur'an, and the proofs and signs the Messenger displayed, to one who is truly deaf and does not hear. And when one does not hear, he cannot respond, so He made him like one who is mute. And when one does not benefit from proofs and does not see the path of guidance, he is like the blind. As for His saying: ﴿so they do not return﴾, there are several aspects:

First: they do not return from what was mentioned before, namely clinging to hypocrisy. Because of their clinging to it, God described them with these attributes, so this indicates that they persist in their hypocrisy forever.

Second: they do not return to guidance after having sold it, nor to misguidance after having purchased it.

Third: he meant that they are like the bewildered who remain motionless in their place, not moving, not knowing whether to advance or retreat. And how can they return to the place from which they started?

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 19–20 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky, in which are darknesses, thunder and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts, for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it, and when darkness falls over them, they stand still. If Allah willed, He would surely take away their hearing and their sight. Indeed Allah is over all things capable.﴾

Know that this is the second parable of the hypocrites. The manner of the resemblance is in several respects:

The first: when the cloud that contains the darknesses, thunder and lightning forms, the darkness of the cloud combines with the darkness of the night and the darkness of the rain. When the thunderbolts strike them, they put their fingers in their ears for fear of death, and the lightning nearly snatches away their sight. When it lights up for them, they walk in it, and when it goes away they remain in a great darkness and stand bewildered. For whoever is struck by lightning amid these three darknesses and then it leaves him, his bewilderment becomes intense, the darkness grows greater in his eyes, and he has an advantage over one who has never ceased to be in darkness. Thus He likened the hypocrites in their bewilderment and their ignorance of the religion to these people He described, since they see no path and are not guided.

The second: although rain is beneficial, when it comes in this form and with these harmful circumstances, its benefit disappears. Likewise, the outward profession of faith is beneficial to the hypocrite if his inner self agrees with it. But when sincerity is lacking and hypocrisy accompanies it, it becomes a harm to the religion.

The third: whoever is struck by these matters together with the thunderbolts thinks that his escape from them lies in putting his fingers in his ears, but this does not save him from what Allah, exalted is He, intends for him of destruction and death. Since this is established in customary experience, Allah, exalted is He, likened the state of the hypocrites, in their supposition that their outward display of faith before the believers benefits them, while in reality the matter is not as they think, to this.

The fourth: the habit of the hypocrites was to hold back from jihad, fleeing from death and killing. So Allah likened their state in this to the state of one whom these matters befall, who wants to ward them off by putting his two fingers in his ears.

The fifth: those who put their fingers in their ears, even if they escape death at that moment, death and destruction are behind them and there is no escape for them from it. Likewise, the state of the hypocrites is that what they plunge into does not save them from the punishment of the Fire.

The sixth: whoever is in this state has reached the extreme of bewilderment, because of the gathering of kinds of darkness and the occurrence of kinds of fear. The hypocrites have reached the extreme of bewilderment in the matter of religion and the extreme of fear in this world, because the hypocrite imagines at every moment that if his inner state were discovered, he would be killed. So fear and dread scarcely leave his heart while he is a hypocrite.

The seventh: what is meant by the rainstorm (ṣayyib) is faith and the Qur'an, and the darknesses, thunder and lightning are the things that are burdensome to the hypocrites, namely the heavy obligations of prayer, fasting, abandoning leadership and jihad, leaving the ancient religions, and submitting to Muhammad (ﷺ), together with their great aversion to submitting to him. Just as a person takes great care to avoid a heavy rain, which is among the most beneficial of things, because of these accompanying matters, so the hypocrites guard against faith and the Qur'an because of these accompanying matters. What is meant by His saying ﴿whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ is that whenever they obtain some of the benefits, namely the protection of their property and their blood and the acquisition of spoils, they are eager for the religion. ﴿And when darkness falls over them, they stand still﴾ means that whenever they find none of those benefits, then they dislike faith and are not eager for it. These aspects are evident in the comparison, and there remain questions and answers concerning the verse.

The first question: which of the two similitudes is more eloquent? The answer: the second similitude, because it is more indicative of the extreme of bewilderment and the intensity of hardship. That is why you see them proceeding in such matters from the easier to the more severe.

The second question: why has one of the two similitudes been joined to the other with the particle of doubt (aw)?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: because *aw* (or) originally signifies two or more things in doubt, and then its use was extended so that it is employed to denote equivalence in something other than doubt, as in your saying: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," meaning that the two of them are equal in the desirability of sitting with whichever of them you wish. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey from among them any sinner or disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24], meaning that the sinner and the disbeliever are equal in the obligation of disobeying both. Likewise His saying ﴿or like a rainstorm﴾ means that the state of the hypocrites resembles the states of these two stories; so whichever of them you liken it to, you are correct, and if you liken it to both of them, it is likewise.

The second: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned it that way because the hypocrites are of two kinds: some resemble the people of the Fire, and some resemble the people of the rain. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], and His saying: ﴿And how many a town We destroyed, so Our punishment came upon it by night or while they were napping at midday﴾ [al-A'raf: 4].

The third: *aw* here means *bal* (rather). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat: 147].

The fourth: *aw* here means *wa* (and), as if He had said: "and like a rainstorm from the sky." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you eat from your houses or the houses of your fathers or the houses of your mothers﴾ [al-Nur: 61]. And the poet said:

*Laylā has claimed that I am wicked, for my soul is either its piety or its wickedness.*

These aspects apply consistently to His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones or even harder in hardness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74].

The third question: what are the things compared to the rainstorm, the darknesses, the thunder, the lightning and the thunderbolts?

The answer: the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamāʾ al-bayān) have two opinions here:

The first: this is a *tashbīh mufarraq* (differentiated comparison), meaning that the similitude is composed of several elements and the thing compared is likewise composed of several elements, and each element of the similitude resembles each element of the thing compared. Here, the religion of Islam is likened to the rainstorm, because hearts come alive through it as the earth comes alive through rain; what is connected to it of the doubts of the disbelievers is likened to the darknesses; what it contains of promise and threat is likened to the lightning and thunder; and what befalls the disbelievers of trials from the people of Islam is likened to the thunderbolts. The meaning is: "or like the case of people who were overtaken by the sky in this state." The meaning is like the case of a people whom the sky overtook in this description.

The second opinion: it is a *tashbīh murakkab* (composite comparison), which is that in which one of the two sentences is likened to the other in some respect, even if the individual parts of one sentence do not resemble the individual parts of the other sentence. Here the intended meaning is to liken the bewilderment of the hypocrites in this world and in religion to the bewilderment of one whose fire has gone out after it was kindled, and to the bewilderment of one whom the sky overtook on a dark night with thunder and lightning. If it is said: does what you were estimating in the differentiated comparison, namely the omission of the modifier in your saying "or like the case of people of a rainstorm," also need to be estimated in the composite one? We say: were it not for the demand for a returning pronoun in His saying ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾, to which it refers, there would be no need for us to estimate it.

The fourth question: what is the *ṣayyib*?

The answer: it is the rain that is poured down (yuṣawwabu), that is, descends, from *ṣāba yaṣūbu* when it descends; and from it comes *ṣawwaba raʾsahu* when he lowered his head. It was said that it is from *ṣāba yaṣūbu* meaning "to aim" (qaṣada). And *ṣayyib* is said only of abundant rain. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "O Allah, make it an abundant, wholesome rain" (ṣayyiban hanī'an), meaning abundant rain. Also, the cloud is called *ṣayyib*. Al-Shammakh said:

*And a dark, low, true-promised, rain-laden cloud.*

The indefiniteness of *ṣayyib* is because a kind of rain that is intense and terrifying is intended, just as fire was made indefinite in the first similitude. It was also read as *aw kaṣā'ib*. But *ṣayyib* is more eloquent. As for "the sky," this is the canopy.

The fifth question: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿from the sky﴾, since the *ṣayyib* is only from the sky?

The answer has two aspects. The first: had He said "or like a rainstorm in which are darknesses," it would have been possible that that rainstorm descended from some sides of the sky and not others. But when He said "from the sky," it indicates that it is general, all-enveloping, seizing the horizons of the sky. So just as the word *ṣayyib* contains intensifications through its structure and its indefiniteness, He reinforced this by making it all-enveloping.

The second: some people said that rain only results from the rising of moist vapours from the earth into the air, where they condense because of the intense cold of the air, and then they descend again; that is the rain. Allah, exalted and glorified is He, refuted that view here by making clear that this rainstorm descended from the sky. Likewise His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ [al-Furqan: 48], and His saying: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail in them﴾ [al-Nur: 43].

The sixth question: what are thunder and lightning? The answer: thunder is the sound heard from the cloud, as if the bodies of the cloud tremble, break apart and quake when the wind takes them, so a sound arises from that quaking. And lightning is what flashes from the cloud, from *baraqa al-shayʾu bariqan* when a thing gleams.

The seventh question: the *ṣayyib* is the rain and the cloud, so whichever of them is meant, what are its darknesses?

The answer: as for the darkness of the cloud, if it is black and covering, its darkness is its blackness, and its covering combined with them is the darkness of the night. As for the darkness of the rain, its darkness is its density and its continuous pouring with the successive drops, and its darkness is the shading of the cloud together with the darkness of the night.

The eighth question: how can the rain be a place for thunder and lightning, when their place is only the cloud?

The answer: since the connection between the cloud and the rain is strong, it is permissible to treat one of them as the other in rulings.

The ninth question: why was it not said *ruʿūd* and *burūq* (plural thunders and lightnings) as it was said *ẓulumāt* (darknesses)?

The answer: the difference is that various kinds of darknesses came together, so the plural form was needed. As for thunder, it is one kind, and likewise lightning, and it is not possible for the kinds of thunder and lightning to gather in a single cloud, so the plural form was not mentioned for them.

The tenth question: why did these things come in indefinite form?

The answer: because what is meant is kinds of them, as if it were said: in it are dense darknesses, a crashing thunder and a snatching lightning.

The eleventh question: to what does the pronoun in *yajʿalūna* ("they put") refer?

The answer: to the people of the rainstorm. Although it is omitted in wording, it remains in meaning. And *yajʿalūna* has no grammatical position (maḥall) because it is a new sentence (mustaʾnaf), since when He mentioned the thunder and lightning in a manner that indicates intensity and terror, it is as if a questioner asked: "What is their condition with such thunder?" So it was said: "they put their fingers in their ears." Then, as if asking: "What is their condition with such lightning?" He said: ﴿the lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾.

The twelfth question: it is the tips of the fingers that are put in the ears, so why was it not said *anāmilahum* ("their fingertips")?

The answer: although what is mentioned is the finger (*uṣbuʿ*), what is meant is part of it, as in His saying: ﴿So cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38], where what is meant is part of both of them.

The thirteenth question: what is the thunderbolt (ṣāʿiqah)? The answer: it is a crash of thunder from which a flame of fire is hurled down. It is a subtle, powerful fire that does not pass over anything without consuming it, except that despite its strength it is quick to die out.

The fourteenth question: what is the encompassing of Allah over the disbelievers? The answer: it is figurative (majāz), and the meaning is that they cannot escape Him, just as the one encompassed cannot escape the one who encompasses him literally. Then there are three opinions concerning it:

The first: that He knows them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Talaq: 12].

The second: His power prevails over them, as in ﴿and Allah is encompassing them from behind﴾ [al-Buruj: 20].

The third: He will destroy them, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿unless you are encompassed﴾ [Yusuf: 66].

**Question Fifteen: What is al-khatf (snatching)?** The answer: it is seizing something swiftly. Mujahid read *yakhtifu* with a kasra on the ṭāʾ (يَخْطِفُ), but the fatḥa is more eloquent. From Ibn Masʿud it is reported as *yakhtatifu* (يَخْتَطِفُ). From al-Hasan it is reported as *yakhtafu* (يَخْطَفُ) with fatḥa on the yāʾ and the khāʾ, its original form being *yakhtatifu*. Also from him: *yakhtifu* with kasra on both, making the yāʾ take the kasra of the khāʾ. From Zayd ibn ʿAli: *yakhtifu*, from *khatafa*. From Ubayy: *yatakhattafu*, from His saying: ﴿And mankind are snatched away from around them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 67].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Every time it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20], this is a third new sentence, as if it were an answer to someone who asks: how do they behave in the two states of the lightning's appearing and its disappearing? The purpose is to depict the severity of the situation for the hypocrites by its severity for the people of the downpour, and their extreme bewilderment and ignorance about what they should do or leave undone. When they encounter a flash of lightning, with fear that it will snatch away their sight, they seize that flash as an opportunity and take a few short steps. When it fades and its gleam weakens, they remain standing, bound and unable to move.

Had God willed, He would have increased the crash of the thunder and made them deaf, and the light of the lightning and made them blind. *Aḍāʾa* (أضاءَ) may be transitive, meaning "whenever it illuminates a path for them, they take it," in which case the object is omitted. Or it may be intransitive, meaning "whenever it flashes for them, they walk in the place of its light." The reading of Ibn Abi ʿAbla, *kullamā ḍāʾa* (كُلَّما ضاءَ), supports this.

If it is asked: why did He say *kullamā* (كُلَّما, "whenever") with illumination, but *idhā* (إذا, "when") with darkness?

We say: because they are eager for the possibility of walking, so whenever they encounter an opportunity from it, they seize it. Stopping is not like that. The more likely reading for *aẓlama* (أظْلَمَ, "it became dark") is that it is intransitive, and this is the apparent meaning. The meaning of *qāmū* (قامُوا) is that they stopped, halted, and remained in their place. From this comes *qāmati al-sūq* (the market stood still), and *qāma al-māʾ* (the water stood still, i.e., froze).

The object of *shāʾa* (شاءَ, "willed") is omitted, because the answer indicates it. The meaning is: "Had God willed that He take away their hearing and their sight, He would have taken them away."

Here there is a question. It is well known that *law* (لَوْ, "if/had") indicates the negation of one thing because of the negation of another. Some have denied this and claimed that it indicates only a conditional linkage. They argued for this from the Qur'an and from a report.

From the Qur'an: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being opposed﴾ [al-Anfal: 23]. If the particle *law* indicated the negation of one thing but not the negation of another, this would lead to contradiction. His saying "And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear" implies that He did not know any good in them and did not make them hear. And His saying "And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away" indicates that God did not make them hear and they did not turn away. But not turning away is good, so it follows that He knew good in them, while He did not know good in them.

From a report: the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "What a fine man Suhayb is! If he did not fear God, he would not disobey Him." According to their reasoning, it would follow that he feared God and disobeyed Him, and that is contradictory. Thus we know that the word *law* indicates only conditional linkage. And God knows best.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, God is over all things competent﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Some have used it as evidence that the nonexistent is a "thing." They said: God affirmed power over a thing, and an existent does not fall under power, because it is impossible to bring into being what already exists. So the one over which power is exercised is nonexistent, and it is a thing; therefore the nonexistent is a thing.

The answer: if this argument were valid, it would follow that what God does not have power over is not a thing. Then the existent, since God has no power over it, must not be a thing.

**The second issue:** Jahm (ibn Safwan) used this verse to argue that God, exalted is He, is not a thing. He said: it indicates that every thing is within God's power, and God is not within His own power; therefore He must not be a thing. He also argued for this from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. He said: if He, exalted is He, were a thing, then He would be like His own self, and that would contradict His saying "There is nothing like unto Him." So He must not be a thing, so that this verse does not contradict itself.

Know that this disagreement concerns the name, because there is no intermediate between the existent and the nonexistent. Our companions (the Ashʿarites) argued with two points. The first is His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "God"﴾ [al-Anʿam: 19]. The second is His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. The exception is included in what is excepted from, so it must be a thing.

**The third issue:** Our companions used this verse as evidence that the creature's capacity is within God's power, contrary to Abu ʿAli (al-Jubba'i) and Abu Hashim (al-Jubba'i). The method of argument is: the creature's capacity is a thing, and every thing is within God's power by this verse, so the creature's capacity must be within God's power.

**The fourth issue:** Our companions used this verse as evidence that a created thing, at the moment of its coming into being, is within God's power, contrary to the Mu'tazilah. They say: capability before the act is impossible, so a thing is within power only before it comes into being. The explanation of the companions' argument is: a created thing at the time of its existence is a thing, and every thing is within power. This argument requires that what remains be within power. That was left unapplied, but it remains applied in the point of dispute, because at the time of its continuance it is within His power, in the sense that He is able to annihilate it. As for the moment of its coming into being, it is impossible for God to annihilate it, because it is impossible for it to become nonexistent at the very first instant of its existence. So there remains only that He is capable of bringing it into being.

**The fifth issue:** The specification of a general term is permissible in general. Also, the specification of a general term by rational proof is permissible. This is because His saying: ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾ requires that He be capable of Himself, and then this is specified by rational proof. If it is said: when a word is set for the whole, and then it becomes clear that it is not true of the whole, this would be a lie, and that would entail a criticism of the Qur'an. We say: the word "all" (*kull*), just as it is used for the totality, may also be used figuratively for the majority. And when that is a well-known figurative usage in the language, using the word in this way is not a lie. And God knows best.
