The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 19–20 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky, in which are darknesses, thunder and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts, for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it, and when darkness falls over them, they stand still. If Allah willed, He would surely take away their hearing and their sight. Indeed Allah is over all things capable.﴾

Know that this is the second parable of the hypocrites. The manner of the resemblance is in several respects:

The first: when the cloud that contains the darknesses, thunder and lightning forms, the darkness of the cloud combines with the darkness of the night and the darkness of the rain. When the thunderbolts strike them, they put their fingers in their ears for fear of death, and the lightning nearly snatches away their sight. When it lights up for them, they walk in it, and when it goes away they remain in a great darkness and stand bewildered. For whoever is struck by lightning amid these three darknesses and then it leaves him, his bewilderment becomes intense, the darkness grows greater in his eyes, and he has an advantage over one who has never ceased to be in darkness. Thus He likened the hypocrites in their bewilderment and their ignorance of the religion to these people He described, since they see no path and are not guided.

The second: although rain is beneficial, when it comes in this form and with these harmful circumstances, its benefit disappears. Likewise, the outward profession of faith is beneficial to the hypocrite if his inner self agrees with it. But when sincerity is lacking and hypocrisy accompanies it, it becomes a harm to the religion.

The third: whoever is struck by these matters together with the thunderbolts thinks that his escape from them lies in putting his fingers in his ears, but this does not save him from what Allah, exalted is He, intends for him of destruction and death. Since this is established in customary experience, Allah, exalted is He, likened the state of the hypocrites, in their supposition that their outward display of faith before the believers benefits them, while in reality the matter is not as they think, to this.

The fourth: the habit of the hypocrites was to hold back from jihad, fleeing from death and killing. So Allah likened their state in this to the state of one whom these matters befall, who wants to ward them off by putting his two fingers in his ears.

The fifth: those who put their fingers in their ears, even if they escape death at that moment, death and destruction are behind them and there is no escape for them from it. Likewise, the state of the hypocrites is that what they plunge into does not save them from the punishment of the Fire.

The sixth: whoever is in this state has reached the extreme of bewilderment, because of the gathering of kinds of darkness and the occurrence of kinds of fear. The hypocrites have reached the extreme of bewilderment in the matter of religion and the extreme of fear in this world, because the hypocrite imagines at every moment that if his inner state were discovered, he would be killed. So fear and dread scarcely leave his heart while he is a hypocrite.

The seventh: what is meant by the rainstorm (ṣayyib) is faith and the Qur'an, and the darknesses, thunder and lightning are the things that are burdensome to the hypocrites, namely the heavy obligations of prayer, fasting, abandoning leadership and jihad, leaving the ancient religions, and submitting to Muhammad (ﷺ), together with their great aversion to submitting to him. Just as a person takes great care to avoid a heavy rain, which is among the most beneficial of things, because of these accompanying matters, so the hypocrites guard against faith and the Qur'an because of these accompanying matters. What is meant by His saying ﴿whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ is that whenever they obtain some of the benefits, namely the protection of their property and their blood and the acquisition of spoils, they are eager for the religion. ﴿And when darkness falls over them, they stand still﴾ means that whenever they find none of those benefits, then they dislike faith and are not eager for it. These aspects are evident in the comparison, and there remain questions and answers concerning the verse.

The first question: which of the two similitudes is more eloquent? The answer: the second similitude, because it is more indicative of the extreme of bewilderment and the intensity of hardship. That is why you see them proceeding in such matters from the easier to the more severe.

The second question: why has one of the two similitudes been joined to the other with the particle of doubt (aw)?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: because *aw* (or) originally signifies two or more things in doubt, and then its use was extended so that it is employed to denote equivalence in something other than doubt, as in your saying: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," meaning that the two of them are equal in the desirability of sitting with whichever of them you wish. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey from among them any sinner or disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24], meaning that the sinner and the disbeliever are equal in the obligation of disobeying both. Likewise His saying ﴿or like a rainstorm﴾ means that the state of the hypocrites resembles the states of these two stories; so whichever of them you liken it to, you are correct, and if you liken it to both of them, it is likewise.

The second: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned it that way because the hypocrites are of two kinds: some resemble the people of the Fire, and some resemble the people of the rain. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], and His saying: ﴿And how many a town We destroyed, so Our punishment came upon it by night or while they were napping at midday﴾ [al-A'raf: 4].

The third: *aw* here means *bal* (rather). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat: 147].

The fourth: *aw* here means *wa* (and), as if He had said: "and like a rainstorm from the sky." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you eat from your houses or the houses of your fathers or the houses of your mothers﴾ [al-Nur: 61]. And the poet said:

*Laylā has claimed that I am wicked, for my soul is either its piety or its wickedness.*

These aspects apply consistently to His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones or even harder in hardness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74].

The third question: what are the things compared to the rainstorm, the darknesses, the thunder, the lightning and the thunderbolts?

The answer: the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamāʾ al-bayān) have two opinions here:

The first: this is a *tashbīh mufarraq* (differentiated comparison), meaning that the similitude is composed of several elements and the thing compared is likewise composed of several elements, and each element of the similitude resembles each element of the thing compared. Here, the religion of Islam is likened to the rainstorm, because hearts come alive through it as the earth comes alive through rain; what is connected to it of the doubts of the disbelievers is likened to the darknesses; what it contains of promise and threat is likened to the lightning and thunder; and what befalls the disbelievers of trials from the people of Islam is likened to the thunderbolts. The meaning is: "or like the case of people who were overtaken by the sky in this state." The meaning is like the case of a people whom the sky overtook in this description.

The second opinion: it is a *tashbīh murakkab* (composite comparison), which is that in which one of the two sentences is likened to the other in some respect, even if the individual parts of one sentence do not resemble the individual parts of the other sentence. Here the intended meaning is to liken the bewilderment of the hypocrites in this world and in religion to the bewilderment of one whose fire has gone out after it was kindled, and to the bewilderment of one whom the sky overtook on a dark night with thunder and lightning. If it is said: does what you were estimating in the differentiated comparison, namely the omission of the modifier in your saying "or like the case of people of a rainstorm," also need to be estimated in the composite one? We say: were it not for the demand for a returning pronoun in His saying ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾, to which it refers, there would be no need for us to estimate it.

The fourth question: what is the *ṣayyib*?

The answer: it is the rain that is poured down (yuṣawwabu), that is, descends, from *ṣāba yaṣūbu* when it descends; and from it comes *ṣawwaba raʾsahu* when he lowered his head. It was said that it is from *ṣāba yaṣūbu* meaning "to aim" (qaṣada). And *ṣayyib* is said only of abundant rain. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "O Allah, make it an abundant, wholesome rain" (ṣayyiban hanī'an), meaning abundant rain. Also, the cloud is called *ṣayyib*. Al-Shammakh said:

*And a dark, low, true-promised, rain-laden cloud.*

The indefiniteness of *ṣayyib* is because a kind of rain that is intense and terrifying is intended, just as fire was made indefinite in the first similitude. It was also read as *aw kaṣā'ib*. But *ṣayyib* is more eloquent. As for "the sky," this is the canopy.

The fifth question: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿from the sky﴾, since the *ṣayyib* is only from the sky?

The answer has two aspects. The first: had He said "or like a rainstorm in which are darknesses," it would have been possible that that rainstorm descended from some sides of the sky and not others. But when He said "from the sky," it indicates that it is general, all-enveloping, seizing the horizons of the sky. So just as the word *ṣayyib* contains intensifications through its structure and its indefiniteness, He reinforced this by making it all-enveloping.

The second: some people said that rain only results from the rising of moist vapours from the earth into the air, where they condense because of the intense cold of the air, and then they descend again; that is the rain. Allah, exalted and glorified is He, refuted that view here by making clear that this rainstorm descended from the sky. Likewise His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ [al-Furqan: 48], and His saying: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail in them﴾ [al-Nur: 43].

The sixth question: what are thunder and lightning? The answer: thunder is the sound heard from the cloud, as if the bodies of the cloud tremble, break apart and quake when the wind takes them, so a sound arises from that quaking. And lightning is what flashes from the cloud, from *baraqa al-shayʾu bariqan* when a thing gleams.

The seventh question: the *ṣayyib* is the rain and the cloud, so whichever of them is meant, what are its darknesses?

The answer: as for the darkness of the cloud, if it is black and covering, its darkness is its blackness, and its covering combined with them is the darkness of the night. As for the darkness of the rain, its darkness is its density and its continuous pouring with the successive drops, and its darkness is the shading of the cloud together with the darkness of the night.

The eighth question: how can the rain be a place for thunder and lightning, when their place is only the cloud?

The answer: since the connection between the cloud and the rain is strong, it is permissible to treat one of them as the other in rulings.

The ninth question: why was it not said *ruʿūd* and *burūq* (plural thunders and lightnings) as it was said *ẓulumāt* (darknesses)?

The answer: the difference is that various kinds of darknesses came together, so the plural form was needed. As for thunder, it is one kind, and likewise lightning, and it is not possible for the kinds of thunder and lightning to gather in a single cloud, so the plural form was not mentioned for them.

The tenth question: why did these things come in indefinite form?

The answer: because what is meant is kinds of them, as if it were said: in it are dense darknesses, a crashing thunder and a snatching lightning.

The eleventh question: to what does the pronoun in *yajʿalūna* ("they put") refer?

The answer: to the people of the rainstorm. Although it is omitted in wording, it remains in meaning. And *yajʿalūna* has no grammatical position (maḥall) because it is a new sentence (mustaʾnaf), since when He mentioned the thunder and lightning in a manner that indicates intensity and terror, it is as if a questioner asked: "What is their condition with such thunder?" So it was said: "they put their fingers in their ears." Then, as if asking: "What is their condition with such lightning?" He said: ﴿the lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾.

The twelfth question: it is the tips of the fingers that are put in the ears, so why was it not said *anāmilahum* ("their fingertips")?

The answer: although what is mentioned is the finger (*uṣbuʿ*), what is meant is part of it, as in His saying: ﴿So cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38], where what is meant is part of both of them.

The second: His power prevails over them, as in ﴿and Allah is encompassing them from behind﴾ [al-Buruj: 20].

The third: He will destroy them, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿unless you are encompassed﴾ [Yusuf: 66].

The explanation of the companions' argument is: a created thing at the time of its existence is a thing, and every thing is within power. This argument requires that what remains be within power. That was left unapplied, but it remains applied in the point of dispute, because at the time of its continuance it is within His power, in the sense that He is able to annihilate it. As for the moment of its coming into being, it is impossible for God to annihilate it, because it is impossible for it to become nonexistent at the very first instant of its existence. So there remains only that He is capable of bringing it into being.

**The fifth issue:** The specification of a general term is permissible in general. Also, the specification of a general term by rational proof is permissible. This is because His saying: ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾ requires that He be capable of Himself, and then this is specified by rational proof. If it is said: when a word is set for the whole, and then it becomes clear that it is not true of the whole, this would be a lie, and that would entail a criticism of the Qur'an. We say: the word "all" (*kull*), just as it is used for the totality, may also be used figuratively for the majority. And when that is a well-known figurative usage in the language, using the word in this way is not a lie. And God knows best.

[p. 75]

The Discussion on Establishing the Proofs for Monotheism, Prophethood and the Resurrection

As for monotheism (tawhid), there is the words of the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ ﴿Who made for you the earth as a bed and the sky as a canopy, and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. So do not set up rivals to Allah while you know [better]﴾.

Know that in these verses there are several issues:

The first issue: When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the rulings concerning the three groups, namely the believers, the disbelievers and the hypocrites, He turned to them with direct address. This is of the type of iltifat (shift of grammatical person) mentioned in the words of the Exalted: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4]. And in it there are benefits:

The first of them: it contains greater stirring and arousal of the hearer, just as when you say to your companion, speaking about a third person: "So-and-so, his story is such and such," and then you address that third person, saying: "O so-and-so, it is your duty to follow the praiseworthy way in the course of your affairs." This transition from the third person to the second person causes greater stirring of that third person.

The second: It is as if He, glorified and exalted, is saying: "I made the Messenger an intermediary between Me and you first; now I increase in honouring you and bringing you near, so I address you without an intermediary, so that, together with the alerting to the proofs, you may attain the honour of being spoken to and conversed with."

The third: It indicates that when a servant is occupied with servitude, he is always ascending, as evidenced by the fact that in this verse he moved from the third person to the second person.

The fourth: The preceding verses were narrating their states, whereas these verses are a command and an obligation, and so there is in them hardship and difficulty; therefore there must be a relief that counterbalances this hardship, and that relief is that the King of kings removes the intermediary from between them and addresses them Himself, just as when a servant is charged with a difficult duty, if the master speaks to him directly and says, "I want you to do such and such," that difficult task becomes sweet because of that address.

* * *

The second issue: It is related from 'Alqamah and al-Hasan that he said: "Everything in the Qur'an that begins with ﴿O mankind﴾ is Meccan, and whatever begins with ﴿O you who believe﴾ is Medinan." Al-Qadi said: "What they have mentioned, if the reference in it is to transmission, then it is accepted; but if the reason for it is that the believers in Medina were more numerous than in Mecca, then this is weak, because it is possible to address the believers sometimes by their attribute and sometimes by the name of their category, and one who is not a believer may be commanded to worship, just as the believer is commanded to persist in worship and increase in it. So the address is possible in all cases."

* * *

The third issue: Know that words are, for the most part, expressions indicating things, which are either words or other than words. As for words, they are such as the noun, the verb and the particle, for each of these three indicates something, while being itself a particular word. Other than words are such as a stone, the sky and the earth. The vocative particle has not been made to indicate anything else; rather it is a word that functions as an action performed by an agent for the purpose of alerting.

As for those who explained our saying "Ya Zayd" as "I call Zayd" or "I address Zayd," this is wrong for several reasons:

The first: our saying "I call Zayd" is a statement that may be true or false, whereas our saying "Ya Zayd" does not admit of that.

The second: our saying "Ya Zayd" implies that Zayd becomes one being called at the moment, whereas our saying "I call Zayd" does not imply that.

The third: our saying "Ya Zayd" implies that Zayd becomes addressed by this address, whereas our saying "I call Zayd" does not imply that, because it is not impossible that one informs another person that "I am calling Zayd."

The fourth: our saying "I call Zayd" is a report about the calling, and a report about the calling is other than the calling, and the calling is our saying "Ya Zayd"; therefore our saying "I call Zayd" is other than our saying "Ya Zayd." Thus through these considerations the falsity of this view is established. Then here there is a subtle point that we will mention: the highest of ranks is the noun and the lowest is the particle, so some people thought that the noun does not combine with the particle. Likewise, the greatest of existents is the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, and the weakest is the human being: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [al-Nisa': 28]. The angels said: "What correspondence is there between them? ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾" [al-Baqarah: 30]. It was said: the noun does combine with the particle in the case of the vocative, so likewise the human being is fit to serve the Lord in the state of calling and humble supplication: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23], ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60].

* * *

The fourth issue: "Ya" is a particle originally laid down for calling the distant, and although it is used for calling the near, that is for a matter of great importance. As for calling the near, it has "ay" and the hamzah. Then it was used for calling one who is heedless and forgetful even if near, treating him as if he were distant. If it is said: why does the supplicant say "Ya Rabbi, ya Allah," when He is ﴿nearer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16]?

We say: it is a self-depreciation, a diminishing of oneself from the places of nearness and that which brings one close to the stations of those brought near, humbling oneself and acknowledging deficiency, until the answer is realized in accordance with His saying: "I am with those whose hearts are broken for My sake." Or because answering supplication is among the most important of matters for the supplicant.

* * *

The fifth issue: "Ay" is a link to the calling of what has the definite article "al-" (alif-lam), just as "dhu" and "alladhi" are links to the description by names of kinds and the description of definites by clauses. It is an ambiguous noun that requires something to remove its ambiguity, so it must be followed by a common noun or what takes its place, which it is described by, so that the intended purpose of the calling is attained. Thus the word that the vocative particle governs is "ay," and the noun following it is an attribute, as in your saying "Ya Zayd the witty," except that "ay" does not stand independently as Zayd does, so it is never separated from the attribute and what it qualifies. As for the interjection of attention inserted between the attribute and what it qualifies, it has two benefits: the first is the reinforcement of the vocative particle by stressing its meaning; the second is that it stands as a substitute for what "ay" deserves of annexation. The reason that the calling in this manner is frequent in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, is that it is independent with these emphases and intensifications, for everything that Allah, the Exalted, has called His servants to, of commands and prohibitions, promise and warning, and the relating of the reports of earlier peoples with great matters and things that the listeners must be alert to although they are heedless of them, therefore it was necessary that they be called in the most eloquent and emphatic manner.

* * *

The sixth issue: Know that His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ requires that Allah, exalted is He, has commanded all people
page 77
to worship; so if some were excluded from this address, that would be a specification of the general. Here there are discussions:

The first discussion: The plural noun defined by the definite article indicates generality. There is disagreement on this with al-Ash'ari, al-Qadi Abu Bakr and Abu Hashim. Our proof is that it is valid to emphasize it with something that indicates generality, as in His saying: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾ [al-Hijr: 30]. Had the word not originally been for generality, "kulluhum" would not be an emphasis but an explanation. Also, it is valid to make an exception of each one of the people from it, and an exception removes what would have been included without it, so it must indicate generality. Its full establishment is in the books of usul al-fiqh.

The second discussion: Since it has been established that His saying: ﴿O mankind﴾ encompasses all people who existed in that era, does it also encompass those who will exist afterward or not? The closer view is that it does not encompass them, because "O mankind" is a direct address, and direct address to one who does not exist is not permissible. Also, those who will exist after that were not existing in that state, and what does not exist is not a human being, and what is not a human being does not fall under His saying: ﴿O mankind﴾. If it is said: then none of these addresses should include those who came into existence after that time, and that is definitely false, we say: were there no separate evidence, the matter would be as stated; but we know by mass transmission from the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) that these addresses hold good for whoever will exist after that until the Hour arises. So by this separate evidence we have judged that it is general.

The third discussion: His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ is a command to all to worship. Does it then indicate the command to all to every act of worship? The truth is no; because His saying "worship" means "bring this reality into existence," so when they perform one individual instance of the reality in existence, they have brought the reality into existence, since an individual instance of the reality includes the reality, for this worship is worship together with the qualification of being this; and whenever the compound exists, both its components exist. So one who performs an individual instance of worship has performed worship, and one who has performed worship has performed the full content of what His saying "worship" required; and if that is so, he is discharged of the obligation. If we wish to make it indicate generality, we say: the command to worship must be for the sake of its being worship, since the connection of a ruling to an attribute indicates that the attribute is the cause, especially when the attribute is appropriate to the ruling; and here, that worship is worship is appropriate to the command to it, because worship is an expression for exalting Allah, the Exalted, and manifesting submission to Him, and all of that is fitting to reason. And since it is established that its being worship is the cause of the command to it, it must be that every act of worship is commanded, for wherever the cause is present, the ruling necessarily follows.

The fourth discussion: One may say: His saying "O mankind, worship" does not include the disbelievers at all, because disbelievers cannot be commanded with faith, and if that is impossible, then they cannot be commanded with worship. As for its being impossible that they be commanded with faith: the command to know Allah, the Exalted, either encompasses him while he is not knowing Allah, the Exalted, or while he is knowing Allah, the Exalted. If it encompasses him while he is not knowing Allah, then it is impossible that he should be knowing the command of Allah, the Exalted, because knowledge of an attribute together with ignorance of the essence is impossible; so if the command encompasses him in this state, it has encompassed him in a state in which it is impossible for him to know that he is commanded by that command, and that is the charging of what cannot be borne. And if the command to knowledge encompasses him while he is knowing Allah, the Exalted, that is impossible, because it is a command to obtain what is already obtained, and that is not possible. Thus it is established that the disbeliever is impossible to be commanded to attain knowledge, and if that is impossible, then it is impossible that he be commanded to worship, because he is either commanded to worship before

page 78

...the knowledge (ma'rifa, knowledge of God), and that is impossible. For the worship of one who has no knowledge is impossible, or else he would be commanded to worship after gaining knowledge. Yet on this assumption the command to worship depends on the command to gain knowledge. Since the command to gain knowledge is impossible, the command to worship is also impossible. Furthermore, it is impossible that this address be directed to the believers, because they already worship God, so commanding them to worship would be a command to obtain what is already obtained, which is impossible.

The answer: Some people said that the command to worship is conditional upon the attainment of knowledge, just as the command to pay zakat (obligatory alms) is conditional upon possessing the nisab (the minimum amount liable to zakat). These are the ones who hold that cognitions are necessary (daruri). As for those who do not hold this view, they cited this verse to show that cognitions are not necessary. They said: The command to worship is established, and worship is not possible except through knowledge, and a command to something is a command to what is among its necessary prerequisites. Just as ritual purity cannot be valid except by bringing water, so bringing water becomes obligatory. The materialist (dahri) cannot validly affirm the Messenger except by first knowing God the Exalted, so this is obligatory. The one in a state of ritual impurity cannot validly pray except by first purifying himself, so this is obligatory. The one holding a deposit cannot return it except by going to it, so going to it is obligatory. Likewise here, it is valid for the unbeliever to be addressed with the command to worship, and the condition for performing it is that he first perform faith (iman), and then perform worship after that. There remains for them: the command to attain knowledge is impossible. We say: This question is treated at length in the books of usul (the principles of jurisprudence). What we say here is: Although this argument holds for everything on which knowledge depends, with God commanding the knowledge of it, it does not apply to the other attributes. So why would it not be permissible for a command concerning that to come? Even if we grant that, why could it not be said that this command includes the believers?

[Regarding] his saying: "because that would become a command to obtain what is already obtained, which is impossible." We say: Since that is impossible, we interpret it either as a command to persist in worship or as a command to increase in it. It is known that increase in worship is itself worship, so interpreting His saying ﴿Worship﴾ as increasing in worship is valid.

**The Fifth Issue:** Those who deny obligation (taklif) said: It is not permissible for God the Exalted to send down a command of taklif, for several reasons:

The first: Taklif either falls upon the servant in a state where his motives toward doing and not doing are equal, or in a state where one of them is preponderant over the other. If it is the first, it is impossible, because in a state of equality, preponderance cannot occur, since equality contradicts preponderance, so combining them is impossible. And obligating the act while the two motives are equal is obligating what cannot be borne. If it is the second, then the preponderant option must necessarily occur, because the less preponderant option, while it is equal to the preponderant one, is impossible to occur; otherwise a possibility would occur without a determining cause. And if the state of equality is impossible to occur, then the state of being less preponderant is even more impossible. And when the less preponderant option is impossible to occur, the preponderant option must necessarily occur, since there is no escape from the two contradictories. Given this, if taklif falls upon the preponderant option, then taklif is an obligation to bring about what must necessarily occur. And if it falls upon the less preponderant option, then taklif is an obligation to do what is impossible to occur. Both are obligations to do what cannot be borne.

Second: What taklif is directed at either God has known in eternity that it will occur, or He has known that it will not occur, or He has not known either of these. If the first, then what must occur cannot not occur, so there is no benefit in a command to it. If it is known that it will not occur, then what is impossible to occur must necessarily not occur, so a command to bring it about is a command to bring about the impossible. If it is not known either way, then that is ascribing ignorance to God the Exalted, which is impossible. Furthermore, if the matter were such, the obedient could not be distinguished from the disobedient, and then there would be no benefit in obedience.

Third: The sending down of commands of taklif is either for a benefit or not for a benefit. If it is for a benefit, that benefit either returns to the One worshipped or to the worshipper. As for returning to the One worshipped, it is impossible, because He is perfect in His essence, and one who is perfect in His essence cannot be made perfect by another. Moreover, we know by necessity that the God who is exalted above time and eternity cannot benefit from the bowing and prostration of His servant. As for returning to the worshipper, it is impossible, because all benefits are confined to attaining pleasure and removing pain, and He, glory be to Him, is able to bring all of that to the servant from the beginning without the mediation of these hardships. So the mediation of these hardships would be pointless, and pointlessness is not permissible for the Wise.

Fourth: The servant does not bring his acts into existence, because he does not know their details, and one who does not know the details of a thing does not bring it into existence. And if the servant does not bring about his own acts, then if He commands him to that act at the time He creates it in him, He has commanded him to obtain what is already obtained; and if He commands him to it at a time when He has not created it in him, He has commanded him to the impossible. And all of that is false.

Fifth: The purpose of taklif is only the purification of the heart, as the apparent meanings of the Qur'an indicate. So if we suppose a person whose heart is constantly occupied with God the Exalted, such that if he were to engage in these outward acts it would become an obstacle preventing him from being absorbed in knowledge of God the Exalted, then these outward obligations must fall away from him. For the jurists and the analogists (qiyasiyyun) said: When the purpose and wisdom behind obligations becomes evident, it is obligatory to follow the rational rulings, not to follow the apparent meanings.

As for the answer to the first three doubts, it is in two respects. The first: These proponents of these doubts, by what they have stated, have made it obligatory to believe in the absence of obligations, so this is an obligation that negates obligation, and this is self-contradictory. The second: According to us, everything is permissible for God the Exalted, whether that is obligating what cannot be borne or something else, because He is the Creator and the Owner, and there is no objection to the Owner regarding His act.

**The Sixth Issue:** They said: The command to worship, although it is general for all people, is restricted in the case of those who do not understand, such as the child, the insane, the heedless and the forgetful, and in the case of one who is unable, according to His saying: ﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [2:286].

Some said: It is restricted in the case of slaves, because God the Exalted made it obligatory for them to obey their masters, and their occupation with obeying their masters prevents them from occupying themselves with worship. And the command indicating the obligation to obey the master is more specific than the command indicating the obligation to worship, and the specific takes precedence over the general. The discussion of this principle is mentioned in the books of usul al-fiqh.

* * *

**The Seventh Issue:** The qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: The verse indicates that the cause of the existence of worship is what He has shown of His creating us and His bestowing favor upon us. Know that our companions (the Ash'aris) argue with this verse that the servant does not deserve reward by his act, because since His creating us and His bestowing favor upon us was the cause of the obligation of worship, then our occupation with worship is the performance of an obligation, and a person does not deserve anything by performing an obligation, so it is necessary that the servant does not deserve a reward from God the Exalted for worship.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾, there are several issues in it.

**The First Issue:** Know that when He, glory be to Him, commanded the worship of the Lord, He followed it with what indicates the existence of the Maker, namely the creation of the responsible persons and the creation of those before them. This indicates that there is no path to knowledge of God the Exalted except through reflection (nazar) and reasoning (istidlal). Some of the Hashwiyya (literalists) criticized this method and said: Occupation with this science is an innovation (bid'a). For us, there are rational and transmitted arguments for establishing our position, and here there are three stations:

**The First Station:** On explaining the excellence of this science, and it is in several respects:

The first: The nobility of a science is according to the nobility of its object. Whenever the object is more noble, the knowledge attained through it is more noble. Since the most noble of objects of knowledge is the essence of God the Exalted and His attributes, the knowledge concerned with Him must be the most noble of sciences.

Second: Knowledge is either religious or non-religious, and there is no doubt that religious knowledge is more noble than non-religious knowledge. As for religious knowledge, it is either the science of the fundamentals (usul), or other than it. As for other than it, its soundness depends on the science of the fundamentals, because the exegete (mufassir) only investigates the meanings of the speech of God the Exalted, and that is subordinate to the existence of the Maker who chooses and speaks. And the hadith scholar (muhaddith) only investigates the speech of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and that is subordinate to the establishment of his prophethood (ﷺ). And the jurist (faqih) only investigates the rulings of God, and that is subordinate to tawhid (the oneness of God) and prophethood. So it is established that these sciences depend on the science of the fundamentals, and it is evident that the science of the fundamentals does not depend on them, so the science of the fundamentals must be the most noble of sciences.

Third: The nobility of a thing may appear through the baseness of its opposite. The more base its opposite, the more noble it is. The opposite of the science of the fundamentals is disbelief (kufr) and innovation, and these two are among the basest of things, so the science of the fundamentals must be the most noble of things.

Fourth: The nobility of a thing may be due to the nobility of its subject, or to the intensity of need for it, or to the strength of its proofs. The science of the fundamentals comprises all of these. For the science of astronomy (hay'a) is more noble than the science of medicine, in view of the fact that the subject of astronomy is more noble than the subject of medicine, even though medicine is more noble than it in view of the fact that the need for medicine is greater than the need for astronomy. And the science of arithmetic (hisab) is more noble than both of them, in view of the fact that the proofs of arithmetic are stronger. As for the science of the fundamentals, what is sought from it is knowledge of the essence of God the Exalted, His attributes and His acts, and knowledge of the categories of knowables, existent and non-existent. There is no doubt that this is the most noble of matters. As for the need for it, it is intense, because the need is either in religion or in worldly life. As for religion, it is intense, because whoever knows these things merits a great reward and joins the angels, and whoever is ignorant of them merits a great punishment and joins the devils. As for worldly life, it is because the affairs of the world are only put in order by belief in the Maker, the Resurrection and the Gathering, for if this belief did not occur, chaos and disorder would befall the world. As for the strength of proofs, the proofs of this science must necessarily be composed of certain premises, in a certain composition, and this is the ultimate in strength. Thus it is established that this science comprises all aspects of nobility and excellence, so it must be the most noble of sciences.

Fifth: This science is not subject to abrogation (naskh) or alteration, and does not vary according to the differences of nations and regions, unlike other sciences, so it must be the most noble of sciences.

Sixth: The verses containing the subjects of this science and its proofs are more noble than the verses containing legal (fiqhi) subjects, as evidenced by the fact that for the merit of ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ [112:1], and ﴿The Messenger believes﴾ [2:285], and the Verse of the Throne, there is reported what has not been reported similarly for the merit of His saying: ﴿They ask you about menstruation﴾ [2:222], and His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt﴾ [2:282]. And this indicates that this science is superior.

[Page 81]

Seventh: The verses that contain legal rulings (al-ahkam al-shar'iyyah) are fewer than six hundred. As for the rest, they explain monotheism (tawhid) and prophethood (nubuwwah), and refute the worshippers of idols and the various kinds of polytheists. As for the verses that recount stories (al-qasas), their purpose is to make known God's wisdom and power, as He said: ﴿There is certainly in their stories a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 12:111]. This indicates that this science (kalam, speculative theology) is the most excellent. We shall now point to the foundations of the proofs.

As for what proves the existence of the Creator, the Qur'an is full of it.

The first is what is mentioned here of the five proofs: the creation of those who are responsible (al-mukallafin) and the creation of those before them, the creation of the heaven, the creation of the earth, and the bringing forth of fruits from the water that descends from the sky to the earth. Whatever wonders of the heavens and the earth occur in the Qur'an, their purpose is this.

As for what proves the attributes:

As for knowledge, it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from God on the earth or in the heaven﴾, followed by His saying: ﴿It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:5-6]. This is exactly the proof of the mutakallimun (theologians), for they argue from the perfection of acts and their precision to the knowledge of the Creator. Here, the Glorified Creator argues from the forming of images in the wombs to His being knowing of things. He said: ﴿Does He not know who created, while He is the Subtle, the All-Aware?﴾ [al-Mulk 67:14], which is the very same proof. He also said: ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ [al-An'am 6:59], which is a reminder that He, exalted is He, knows all that is known, because He informs about the unseen, and those things occur in accordance with that report. Were He not knowing of the unseen, they would not occur as He said.

As for the attribute of power: all that He, Glorified is He, mentioned of the arising of diverse fruits and diverse animals, while all share the same four natures (al-taba'i' al-arba'), indicates that He, Glorified is He, is Powerful and Choosing, not one who acts by necessity in His essence.

As for transcendence (al-tanzih), what proves that He is not a body nor in a place is His saying: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas 112:1]. For the composite requires its parts, and the one who requires is originated. If He is One (ahad), it is necessary that He not be a body, and if He is not a body, He is not in a place.

As for unity (tawhid), what proves it is His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than God, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:22]; His saying: ﴿Then they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Isra' 17:42]; and His saying: ﴿Some of them would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:91].

As for prophethood, what proves it is His saying here: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:23].

As for the resurrection (al-ma'ad), it is His saying: ﴿Say: He will bring them to life who produced them the first time﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:79].

Indeed, if you examine the science of kalam, you will find in it nothing but the establishment of these proofs, defending them, and repelling the objections and doubts that undermine them. Do you think that kalam is blamed for including these proofs that God mentioned, or for including the repelling of objections and defects against these proofs? I do not think any sensible Muslim would say that or be content with it.

Second: God related the argument with these proofs from the angels and most of the prophets. As for the angels: when they said: ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:30], the meaning was that creating such a thing is ugly, and the Wise does not do what is ugly. So God answered them with His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾, meaning: since I know all that is known, I have known in their creation and formation a wisdom that you do not know. There is no doubt that this is the argumentation. As for God's debate with Iblis, it is also clear.

As for the prophets, peace be upon them: the first of them is Adam, peace be upon him. God displayed His proof of his superiority by showing his knowledge to the angels, and that is pure argumentation.

As for Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him: God related the words of the disbelievers: ﴿They said: O Nuh, you have disputed with us and multiplied our disputation﴾ [Hud 11:32]. It is known that this dispute was not about the details of the legal rulings, but about monotheism and prophethood. So disputing in defense of the truth in this science is the craft of the prophets.

As for Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him: a thorough account of his circumstances in this domain would be lengthy, and he had several stations.

The first: with himself, which is His saying: ﴿When the night covered him, he saw a star and said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love the setting ones"﴾ [al-An'am 6:76]. This is the method of the mutakallimun in proving the origination of things from their change. Then God praised him for that, saying: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Ibrahim against his people﴾ [al-An'am 6:83].

The second: his circumstance with his father, which is His saying: ﴿O father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees nor avails you at all?﴾ [Maryam 19:42].

The third: his circumstance with his people, at times by speech and at others by action. As for speech, His saying: ﴿What are these images to which you are devoted?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:52]. As for action, His saying: ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except for a large one among them, that they might return to it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:58].

The fourth: his circumstance with the king of his time, in His saying: ﴿My Lord is the one who gives life and causes death. He said, "I give life and cause death"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:258], to the end of the account. Anyone whose nature is sound knows that the science of kalam is nothing but the establishment of these proofs and the repelling of questions and objections against them. All of this is Ibrahim's inquiry into the origin (al-mabda'). As for his inquiry into the resurrection, he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:260], to the end.

As for Musa (Moses), peace be upon him: look at his debate with Pharaoh regarding monotheism and prophethood. As for monotheism, know that Musa, peace be upon him, relied for the most part on the proofs of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. This is because God related in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿He said, "Then who is your Lord, O Musa?" He said, "Our Lord is the one who gave everything its creation, then guided it"﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:49-50]. This is the proof that Ibrahim mentioned in His saying: ﴿The One who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:78]. And in Surah al-Shu'ara' He said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:26]. This is what Ibrahim said: ﴿My Lord is the one who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:258]. When Pharaoh was not satisfied with that and demanded something else, Musa said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:28]. This alerts you that adhering to these proofs is the craft of these infallible ones (al-ma'sumin), and that just as they derived them from their intellects, they also inherited them from their pure ancestors.

As for Musa's proof of prophethood through the miracle, it is in His saying: ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:30]. This is the argument from miracle (al-mu'jizah) to truthfulness.

As for Muhammad (ﷺ), his occupation with the proofs of monotheism, prophethood, and resurrection is too evident to require lengthy elaboration, for the Qur'an is full of it. He (ﷺ) was tested by all the groups of disbelievers.

The first: the materialists (al-dahriyyah), who used to say: ﴿Nothing destroys us except time﴾ [al-Jathiyah 45:24]. God nullified their claim with various kinds of proofs.

The second: those who deny the Powerful and Choosing Agent. God nullified their claim by the origination of kinds of plants and varieties of animals, while all share the same natures and the influences of the celestial spheres. This indicates the existence of a Powerful Agent.

The third: those who affirmed a partner with God. That partner is either celestial or terrestrial. As for the celestial partner, it is like one who made the stars influential in this world, and God nullified it by the argument of the Friend (Khalil, Ibrahim) in His saying: ﴿When the night covered him﴾ [al-An'am 6:76]. As for the terrestrial partner, the Christians affirmed the divinity of the Messiah, and the idol-worshippers affirmed the divinity of idols. God gave many proofs against the falsity of their claims.

The fourth: those who disputed prophethood, and they are of two kinds.

One: those who disputed the very principle of prophethood, and they are the ones whom God related as saying: ﴿Has God sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra' 17:94].

Two: those who accepted the principle of prophethood but disputed the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they are the Jews and the Christians. The Qur'an is full of refutation of them. Their disputes took various forms: at times by attacking the Qur'an, and God answered with His saying: ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to strike an example, even of a mosquito﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:26]; at other times by demanding the rest of the miracles, as in His saying: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring"﴾ [al-Isra' 17:90]; and at other times by saying that this Qur'an was sent down piecemeal, which makes it susceptible to accusation. God answered this with His saying: ﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [al-Furqan 25:32].

The fifth: those who disputed the gathering and the resurrection. God presented many kinds of proofs for the validity of that and against the claim of those who deny it.

The sixth: those who attacked legal responsibility (al-taklif), at times by saying that it has no benefit. God answered this with His saying: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is against them﴾ [al-Isra' 17:7]. At other times they said that the truth is determinism (al-jabr), and that it contradicts the validity of legal responsibility. God answered this with His saying that He ﴿is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:23].

We have been content in this place with these brief indications, because the thorough treatment of them is recorded in the body of this book. Since it is established that this craft is the craft of all the prophets and messengers, we know that whoever disparages it is either a disbeliever or ignorant.

* * *

The second station: on demonstrating that acquiring this science is obligatory, which is established by both reason and transmitted texts.

As for reason: there is no preference in following the taqlid (blind acceptance) of some over others. If it is permitted to follow the taqlid of all, we would be obliged to follow the disbelievers. If it is required to follow the taqlid of some but not others, it follows that a person would be obligated to follow some and not others without any way to know why he followed one and not the other. And if taqlid is not permitted at all, which is what is sought, then once taqlid is invalidated, nothing remains but this rational method.

As for transmitted texts, the verses and reports establish it. As for the verses, the first of them is His saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl 16:125]. There is no doubt that by "wisdom" is meant proof and argument; so calling to God through argument and proof is what has been commanded. As for His saying: ﴿and argue with them in the best manner﴾, it does not mean disputation over the branches of the Shari'ah, for whoever denies his prophethood, there is no benefit in discussing with him the details of the Shari'ah, and whoever affirms his prophethood does not oppose him in them. So we know that this argument was about monotheism and prophethood, and that argument concerning them is commanded. Furthermore, we are commanded to follow him (ﷺ), as He said: ﴿Follow me, and God will love you﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:31], and He said: ﴿Certainly there has been for you in the Messenger of God an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:21]. Therefore it is obligatory for us to be commanded with that argument.

Second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the people is one who disputes about God without knowledge﴾ [al-Hajj 22:3, 8; Luqman 31:20]. This is a censure of one who disputes about God without knowledge, and this implies that one who disputes with knowledge is not blameworthy but praiseworthy. Also, God related this from Nuh in His saying: ﴿They said, "O Nuh, you have disputed with us and multiplied our disputation"﴾ [Hud 11:32].

**Fourth Part**

Third: God, exalted is He, commanded reflection, saying: ﴿Do they not then ponder the Qur'an?﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]; ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17]; ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves﴾ [Fussilat: 53]; ﴿Have they not seen that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41]; ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yunus: 101]; ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185].

Fourth: God, exalted is He, mentioned reflection in the context of praise, saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]; ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for those of vision﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13]; ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those of intellect﴾ [Ta-Ha: 54, 128]. He also censured those who turn away, saying: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, while they turn away from it﴾ [Yusuf: 105]; ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾ [al-A'raf: 179].

Fifth: God, exalted is He, censured imitation (taqlid, blind acceptance of authority without examination). He related the words of the disbelievers: ﴿And thus We did not send before you any warner to a town except that its affluent said: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23]. He said: ﴿Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon﴾ [Luqman: 21]; He said: ﴿Rather, we found our fathers doing thus﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 74]; He said: ﴿He had nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast to them﴾ [al-Furqan: 42]; and He said concerning the father of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me for a long time﴾ [Maryam: 46]. All of this indicates the obligation of speculative inquiry (nazar), reasoning (istidlal) and reflection, and the censure of imitation. Whoever calls to speculation and reasoning is in accordance with the Qur'an and the religion of the prophets, and whoever calls to imitation is contrary to the Qur'an and in agreement with the religion of the disbelievers.

As for the reports (akhbar), there are many of them, and we shall mention some aspects of them:

The first: what al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "A man from the Banu Fazarah came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'My wife has given birth to a black boy.' He said to him: 'Do you have camels?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What are their colours?' He said: 'Red.' He said: 'Is there among them any grey?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'How is that?' He said: 'Perhaps a vein has drawn it out.' He said: 'And perhaps this one too has been drawn out by a vein.'" Know that this is the holding to argument by analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy).

The second: from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'God, exalted is He, said: The son of Adam has denied Me, and he had no right to deny Me; and the son of Adam has reviled Me, and he had no right to revile Me. As for his denial of Me, it is his saying: He will not bring me back as He originated me, and the first creation is not easier for Me than its re-creation. As for his reviling of Me, it is his saying: God has taken a son, while I am God, the One, the Eternal Refuge; I begot not, nor was I begotten, and there is none comparable to Me.'" Observe how God, exalted is He, in the first case argued from the power over origination to the power over re-creation, and in the second case argued from His oneness (ahadiyyah) to the negation of corporeality (jismiyyah), parenthood and being born.

The third: 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit narrated that he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him, and whoever dislikes to meet God, God dislikes to meet him." Then 'A'ishah said: "O Messenger of God, we dislike death, is that our dislike of meeting God?" He, peace be upon him, said: "No; but the believer loves to meet God, so God loves to meet him, and the disbeliever dislikes to meet God, so God dislikes to meet him." All of this indicates that speculation and reflection upon the proofs are commanded.

* * *

Know that the opponent (al-khasm) has positions:

The first: that speculation does not produce knowledge. The second: that speculation which produces knowledge is not within our power. The third: that it is not permissible to undertake it. The fourth: that the Messenger did not command it. The fifth: that it is an innovation (bid'ah).

As for the first position, the opponent argued for it with several matters:

The first: when we reflect and there arises in us, following our reflection, a belief, and we then know that this belief is knowledge, this knowledge is either necessary (daruri) or acquired (nazari). The first is false, because when a person examines his belief that this belief is knowledge, and his belief that one is half of two, that the sun gives light, and that fire burns, he finds the first to be weaker than the second. This indicates that the admission of weakness into the first and the second is false, because the discussion about that second reflection is like the discussion about the first, so there follows an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible.

The second: we have seen a multitude of people who reflected and strove, and there arose in them, following their reflection, a belief, and they were certain that it was knowledge; then it became clear to them, or to others, that this was ignorance, so they retracted it and abandoned it. When we observe this in the first instance, it is possible that the belief arising the second time is also like this. By this method it is not possible to be certain of the correctness of any of the beliefs derived from reflection and speculation.

The third: if the sought object (al-matlub) is perceived, then seeking it is impossible, because obtaining what is already obtained is impossible; and if it is not perceived, the mind is heedless of it, and it is impossible for seeking to be directed toward what one is heedless of.

The fourth: knowledge that speculation produces knowledge is either necessary or acquired. If it is necessary, it must be shared by all rational people, and it is not so. If it is acquired, it entails proving the nature of a thing by one of its individual instances, and that is impossible, because when the dispute arose concerning the quiddity, it also arose concerning that instance, so there follows proving a thing by itself, which is impossible; for insofar as it is a means of proof it must be known beforehand, and insofar as it is something sought it must not be known beforehand, so there follows the conjunction of negation and affirmation, which is impossible.

The fifth: a single premise does not produce a conclusion; rather, what produces it is the combination of two premises. But the presence of two premises together in the mind at one time is impossible, because we have tested ourselves and found that whenever we direct the mind toward one known object, it is impossible at that time to direct it toward another known object.

Perhaps some of them concede that speculation in general produces knowledge, but they say: speculation concerning divine matters (ilahiyyat) does not produce it. They argued for this with two aspects:

The first: the reality of God (haqiqat al-Ilah) is not conceivable, and when the reality is not conceivable, assent (tasdiq) becomes impossible, whether to His existence or to the existence of any of His attributes.

The explanation of the first: what is known to human beings is that the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud) is transcendent above place (hayyiz) and direction (jihah), and that He is characterised by knowledge and power. As for necessity and transcendence, they are a negative qualifier, and their reality is not the very negation itself; so knowledge of this negation is not knowledge of His reality. As for being characterised by knowledge and power, it is an expression of the attribution of His essence to these attributes, and His essence is not the very attribution; so knowledge of this attribution is not knowledge of His essence.

The explanation of the second: assent depends upon conception, so when conception is absent, assent is impossible. It cannot be said: His essence, even if it is not conceived according to the particular reality that belongs to Him, is nevertheless conceived according to its necessary properties; that is, we know that He is a thing which necessarily has necessity, transcendence and permanence, so judgement is made upon this conceived thing. We say: these known matters, either it is said that they are the essence itself, which is impossible, or they are matters external to the essence. Since we do not know the essence, it is not possible for us to know that it is characterised by these attributes. If the conception which is the condition for ascribing these attributes to His essence is itself a conception according to other attributes, then the discussion concerning it is as in the first, and there follows an infinite regress, which is impossible.

The second aspect: the most evident thing to us is our own essence and reality, to which we point by our saying: "I." Then people have been perplexed about the quiddity of the thing indicated by the word "I." Among them is one who says: it is this structure (bunyah); among them is one who says: it is the temperament (mizaj); among them is one who says: it is some of the parts entering into this structure; and among them is one who says: it is a thing which is neither inside this body nor outside it. If the situation is thus with the most evident of things, then what is your opinion of the things most remote from us and from our states?

As for the second position, namely that speculation which produces knowledge is not within our power, they argued for it with several aspects:

The first: the acquisition of conceptions is not within our power, so self-evident assents are not within our power, and therefore all assents are not within our power. We say that conceptions are not within our power because the one seeking their acquisition, if he is aware of them, it is impossible for him to seek them, since obtaining what is already obtained is impossible; and if he is heedless of them, it is impossible that he be seeking them, since the one heedless of a thing is not seeking it.

If it is said: why is it not permissible that it be known in one respect and unknown in another? We reply: because the aspect in which it is known is other than the aspect in which it is not known; otherwise negation and affirmation would both apply to one thing, which is impossible. Then we say: the aspect that is known, its seeking is impossible because of the impossibility of obtaining what is obtained; and the aspect that is not known, its seeking is impossible because what one is heedless of cannot be sought. We have said that since conceptions are not acquired, it is impossible for self-evident assents to be acquired, and that is because when the two terms of the subject and predicate of a self-evident proposition are present in the mind, either the mere presence of the two entails the mind's certainty of ascribing one to the other by negation or affirmation, or it does not entail it. If it does not entail it, the proposition is not self-evident but doubtful. If it does entail it, then assent is necessarily obtained upon the presence of those two conceptions and impossible to obtain upon their absence. Whatever is necessarily concomitant in negation and affirmation with what is not within our power in negation and affirmation must also be so; so it is established that self-evident assents are not acquired. We have said that since these assents are not acquired, no assent is acquired, because an assent which is not self-evident must be theoretical (nazari), and it is either necessarily entailed upon the presence of those self-evident assents or not. If it is not necessarily entailed by them, then from the truth of those premises the truth of that conclusion does not follow, and it is not a certain inference, but rather either conjecture or imitative belief. If it is necessarily entailed, then those theoretical matters are necessarily concomitant in negation and affirmation with those necessary propositions, so it follows that none of those theoretical matters is within the servant's power at all.

The second: a human being is only able to bring a thing into existence if he is able to distinguish that sought object from other things. Knowledge is distinguished from ignorance by its being in conformity with the known object, and not by ignorance. This is known only if the known object is known as it is. Therefore he cannot produce knowledge of that thing unless he already knows that thing; but that is impossible because of the impossibility of obtaining what is obtained. So it follows that the servant is not able to produce knowledge, nor to seek it.

The third: what necessitates speculation is either the necessity of reason (darurat al-'aql), or speculation itself, or revelation (al-sam'). The first is false, because a necessary matter (darurah) does not require reason as a condition, whereas the obligation of reflection and speculation is not like that, rather many rational people regard it as ugly and say: in most cases it leads its practitioner to ignorance, so it is obligatory to guard against it. The second is also false, because if knowledge of its obligation is theoretical, then he cannot know the obligation of speculation before speculating; so imposing it upon him would be imposing what cannot be borne. As for after speculating, he cannot speculate, because there is no benefit in it.

The third is false, because before reflection one cannot be in a position to know that reflection is obligatory, and after reflection it is also impossible to make it obligatory, since it would then serve no purpose. When all the divisions are invalid, the negation of obligation is established.

* * *

The fourth position: even granting that reflection is in itself not ugly, we establish the proof that God and His Messenger did not command it. The evidence for this is that these inquiries either have knowledge of their proofs as something necessary and self-evident, needing no learning or acquisition, or they do not. They are not of the first kind, for otherwise this knowledge would be attained by everyone, and that is obstinate denial. Moreover, we test the most intelligent people in this science, and they cannot attain it over long years even with the help of a teacher and books. If it is of the second kind, then this knowledge could be attained by a person only after intense practice and extensive discussion. If religion were based on it, the Messenger would not have judged the Islam of a man to be valid until he had questioned him about these issues and tested him thoroughly in knowledge of these proofs. Had the Messenger done that, it would have become well known. Since it did not become well known, but rather what is widely transmitted from him is that he used to judge the Islam of those whom one knows by necessity had no such thought come to their minds, we know that this is not a condition for the validity of religion.

If it is said: knowledge of the basic proofs is attained by most rational people; what requires precision is repelling objections and answering doubts, and that is not a condition for the validity of the basic religion. We reply: this is weak. For a proof does not admit of increase or decrease at all. If a proof is built upon ten premises, and a man is certain of the validity of those premises, then he has knowledge of the proof that cannot be increased. For if additional matters were a condition for establishing that proof, then our statement that the proof is composed of only ten would be void; and if they were not a condition, then knowledge of them would not be knowledge of an added element in the proof, but a separate knowledge. Thus it is established that a proof admits neither increase nor decrease. Moreover, if nine of them were certain but the tenth premise were conjectural, it would be impossible for the conclusion to be certain, because what is built upon the conjectural is more fitting to be conjectural. Thus it is established that a proof admits neither increase nor decrease, and with the refutation of that, the objection is also refuted.

Example: when a person sees rain, thunder and lightning occur after the air had been clear, he says, "Glory be to God." Some people say that his saying "Glory be to God" indicates that he knew God through a proof. This is false, because he is only a knower of God if he knows by proof that this occurrence must have an agent, and then knows by proof that it is impossible for the agent to be other than God, the Exalted. This second premise holds only if he knows by proof that it is impossible to attribute this occurrence to the spheres, the stars, nature, or the causative efficient cause. For if he did not know the falsity of that by proof, he would be believing this second premise without evidence, so the premise would be imitative (taqlidi), and what is built upon it would be imitation, not certainty. Thus the corruption of what you have asserted is established.

* * *

The fifth position: we say that engaging in the science of kalam is an innovation (bid'ah), and the evidence for this is the Qur'an, the report (khabar), consensus (ijma'), the statements of the earlier generations (salaf), and the ruling.

As for the Qur'an, it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They have not put this to you except as a dispute. Rather, they are a quarrelsome people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58]. He condemned disputation. He also said: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different discourse﴾ [al-An'am: 68]. They said: He commanded turning away from them when they immerse themselves in the verses of God, the Exalted.

As for the report, it is his saying (peace be upon him): "Reflect upon creation, but do not reflect upon the Creator." And his saying (peace be upon him): "Hold fast to the religion of the old women." And his saying: "When predestination is mentioned, then refrain."

As for consensus, it is that this is a science in which the Companions did not speak, so it is an innovation and therefore forbidden. That the Companions did not speak about it is evident, because it is not reported from any one of them that he set himself up to argue about these matters. Rather, they were among the most vehement of people in rejecting those who delved into it. Once this is established, it is established that it is an innovation, and every innovation is forbidden by consensus.

As for the athar (report from the early authorities): Malik ibn Anas said: "Beware of innovations." It was asked: "And what are innovations, O Abu Abd Allah?" He said: "The people of innovation are those who speak about the names of God, His attributes and His speech, and do not keep silent about what the Companions and the Successors kept silent about." Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna was asked about kalam and he said: "Follow the Sunnah and leave innovation." Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "For God to test a servant with every sin except shirk is better for him than that he meet God with anything of kalam." He also said: "If a man bequeaths his scholarly books to another, and among them are books of kalam, those books do not enter the bequest."

As for the ruling: if one bequeaths to "the scholars," the one who engages in kalam is not included among them. And God knows best.

This is the totality of the statements of those who criticize reasoning and inference.

The answer: as for the doubts they relied upon to claim that reasoning does not yield knowledge, they are corrupt, because the doubts they mentioned are not self-evident but theoretical. They invalidated all reasoning by means of some of its types, and that is self-contradictory. As for the doubts they relied upon to claim that reasoning is not within one's power, they are corrupt, because they themselves choose to extract those doubts, so their claim that they are not voluntary is refuted. As for the doubts they relied upon to claim that relying on reasoning is ugly, they are self-contradictory, because it would follow for them that their own presentation of these doubts is ugly. As for the doubts they relied upon to claim that the Messenger did not command this, that is false, because we have shown that all the prophets came only with commanding reasoning and inference.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿They have not put this to you except as a dispute﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58], it is to be understood as disputation based on falsehood, in harmony with His saying: ﴿And argue with them in the way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. As for His saying: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 68], its answer is that engaging in vain talk is not reasoning; rather, engaging in vain talk about a thing is obstinate contention (lajaj). As for his saying (peace be upon him): "Reflect upon creation," he only commanded it so that knowledge of the Creator might be derived from it, and that is what is sought. As for his saying (peace be upon him): "Hold fast to the religion of the old women," the intended meaning is nothing but entrusting all affairs to God, the Exalted, and relying upon God in all matters, as we have said. As for his saying (peace be upon him): "When predestination is mentioned, then refrain," it is weak, because a prohibition on a particular does not imply a general prohibition.

As for consensus, we say: if you mean that the Companions did not use the terms of the speculative theologians (mutakallimun), this is granted, but it does not follow from it that kalam is to be disparaged, just as they did not use the terms of the jurists (fuqaha'), and that does not at all entail disparaging jurisprudence (fiqh). If you mean that they did not know God and His Messenger through proof, then what you have said is wretched. As for the severity of the early authorities against kalam, it is to be understood as directed at the people of innovation. As for the question of the bequest, it is countered by the fact that if one bequeathed to whoever is knowledgeable of the essence of God, His attributes, His acts, His prophets and His messengers, the jurist would not be included in it. Moreover, the basis of bequests is custom (urf). This completes the discussion of this question. And God knows best.

* * *

The second question: as for the reality of worship ('ibadah), we have discussed it in His saying: ﴿You alone do we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4]. As for creation (khalq), al-Azhari, the author of "al-Tahdhib," reported from Ibn al-Anbari that it means determination (taqdir) and leveling (taswiyah). They argued for this with the verse, with poetry, and with usage. As for the verse, it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the best of the creators (al-khaliqin)﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], that is, the determiners; ﴿and you create falsehood (takhluqna ifkan)﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 17], that is, you determine a lie; ﴿and when you create (takhluqu) from clay﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110], that is, you determine.

As for poetry, there is the verse of Zuhayr:

"Indeed you measure what you fashion, while some of the people fashion without measuring."

And another said:

"Nor does it squeak under the hands of those who fashion, nor the hands of the cutters, except the fine leather."

As for usage: it is said "khalaqa al-na'l" (he fashioned the sandal) when he determined and leveled it by measure. From this is the Arabs' saying of stories that are not believed: "ahadith al-khuluq" (tales of invention). From this is His saying: ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients (khuluq al-awwalin)﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 137]. Khalaq means a portion of good, and he is khaliq, that is, worthy, as if he were one from whom the portion is derived. A "khalqa' rock" is a smooth one, because in smoothness there is evenness, while in roughness there is irregularity (ikhtilaq). From this comes "akhlaqa al-thawb" (the garment became worn), because when it wears out it becomes smooth and its protrusions and crookedness level out. Thus it is established that creation is an expression for determination and leveling.

The Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar said: creation is an act meaning determination. Language does not require that this be possible only from God, the Exalted. Rather, the Book speaks otherwise in His saying: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], and ﴿and when you create from clay the likeness of a bird﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. But since He, Exalted, performs acts with knowledge of their consequences and the manner of their benefit, and He has no act except in this manner, He is therefore specifically described by this name.
