حملُ اللفظ عليهما معًا؟ وبتقدير التعذر فأيهما أولى؟ قلنا: أما الأول فممكن، لأن الشهداء جمع شهيد بمعنى الحاضر أو القائم بالشهادة، فيمكن جعله مجازًا (المجاز: استعمال اللفظ في غير معناه الأصلي لعلاقة) عن المعين والناصر، وأوثانهم وأكابرهم مشتركة في أنهم كانوا يعتقدون فيهم كونهم أنصارًا لهم وأعوانًا، وإذا حملنا اللفظ على هذا المفهوم المشترك دخل الكل فيه. وأما الثاني فنقول: الأولى حمله على الأكابر، وذلك لأن لفظ الشهداء لا يُطلق ظاهرًا إلا على من يصح أن يُشاهِد ويَشهَد، فيتحمل بالمشاهدة ويؤدي الشهادة، وذلك لا يتحقق إلا في حق رؤسائهم. أما إذا حملناه على الأوثان لزم المجاز في إطلاق لفظ الشهداء على الأوثان، أو يُقال: المراد: وادعوا من تزعمون أنهم شهداؤكم، والإضمار خلاف الأصل. أما إذا حملنا على الوجه الأول صح الكلام، لأنه يصير كأنه قال: وادعوا من يشهد بعضكم لبعض لاتفاقكم على هذا الإنكار. فإن المتفقين على المذهب يشهد بعضهم لبعض لمكان الموافقة، فصحت الإضافة في قوله: ﴿شهداءكم﴾ (شهداءكم: أي شهداءكم)، ولأنه كان في العرب أكابر يشهدون على المتنازعين في الفصاحة بأن أيهما أعلى درجة من الآخر، وإذا ثبت ذلك ظهر أن حمل الكلام على الحقيقة أولى من حمله على المجاز.

**المسألة الثامنة:** أما [دُونَ]، فهو أدنى مكان من الشيء، ومنه الشيءُ الدُّون، وهو الحقير الدنيّ. ودوَّن الكتب: إذا جمعها، لأن جمع الشيء أدناه بعضَه من بعض. ويُقال: هذا دُونَ ذاك: إذا كان أحطَّ منه قليلًا. ودونَك هذا، أصله: خذه من دونك، أي من أدنى مكان منك، فاختُصر، ثم استُعير هذا اللفظ للتفاوت في الأحوال، فقيل: زيد دونَ عمرو في الشرف والعلم، ثم اتُّسع فيه فاستُعمل في كل ما يجاوز حدًّا إلى حدٍّ. قال الله تعالى: ﴿لا يتخذ المؤمنون الكافرين أولياء من دون المؤمنين﴾ [آل عمران: ٢٨] (لا يتخذ المؤمنون الكافرين أولياء من دون المؤمنين)، أي لا يتجاوزون ولاية المؤمنين إلى ولاية الكافرين.

فإن قيل: فما متعلِّق (مِن دونِ اللهِ)؟ قلنا: فيه وجهان:

أحدهما: أن متعلقه ﴿شهداءكم﴾، وهذا فيه احتمالان: الأول: المعنى: ادعوا الذين اتخذتموهم آلهةً من دون الله، وزعمتم أنهم يشهدون لكم يوم القيامة أنكم على الحق، وفي أمرهم أن يستظهروا بالجماد الذي لا ينطق في معارضة القرآن المعجز بفصاحته غايةُ التهكم بهم. والثاني: ادعوا شهداءكم من دون الله، أي من دون أوليائه ومن غير المؤمنين ليشهدوا لكم أنكم أتيتم بمثله، وهذا من المساهلة والإشعار بأن شهداءهم وهم فرسان الفصاحة تأبى عليهم الطبائع السليمة أن يرضوا لأنفسهم بالشهادة الكاذبة.

وثانيهما: أن متعلقه هو الدعاء، والمعنى: ادعوا من دون الله شهداءكم، يعني لا تستشهدوا بالله ولا تقولوا: الله يشهد أن ما ندَّعيه حق، كما يقول العاجز عن إقامة البينة على صحة دعواه. وادعوا الشهداء من الناس الذين شهادتهم بينة تُصحَّح بها الدعاوى عند الحكام. وهذا تعجيز لهم وبيان لانقطاعهم، وأنه لم يبق لهم متشبَّث عن قولهم: الله يشهد إنا لصادقون.

**The ninth issue:** The Qadi said: This challenge refutes the doctrine of compulsion (jabr) in several respects:

First: It is based on the impossibility of producing its like from one who is capable of performing the act. Whoever denies that the servant is an agent cannot affirm the challenge at all, and in this lies the nullification of the argument from the miraculous (al-mu'jiz).

Second: On their view, its impossibility would be due to the lack of the determining power (al-qudrah al-mujibah), and in that respect what is miraculous and what is not are equal. Thus the meaning of the challenge does not hold on their view.

[Page 111]

Third: Whatever is attributed to the servant, God Most High is its Creator. So His challenge to them ultimately amounts to His challenging Himself, while He is undoubtedly capable of its like. Therefore, on this view, the miraculous cannot be established.

Fourth: The miraculous only indicates (the prophethood) through its breaking of habit (naqd al-'adah). If their claim is accepted, that the habitual is also not an act, then this distinction is not established, and so the argument from the miraculous does not hold.

Fifth: The Messenger ﷺ argues that God specially granted him this as confirmation of what he claimed. Had it not come from God Most High, it would not be included in the miracle. But on their doctrine of compulsion this distinction does not hold, since both the habitual and the unhabitual come only from Him.

The answer: What is required by the challenge is either that the opponent brings the challenged thing intentionally, or that it occurs from him by chance. The second is invalid, since chance events are not within his power. Thus the first is established. And if that is so, it is established that his bringing about the challenge depends on a purpose arising in his heart toward it. If that purpose is from him, an infinite regress (tasalsul) follows, which is impossible. If it is from God Most High, then compulsion returns, and everything he raised against us applies to him, so everything he said is nullified.

As for the words of God Most High: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do﴾, know that this verse indicates the miraculous in four respects:

First: We know by mass transmission (tawatur) that the Arabs were in extreme enmity toward the Messenger of God ﷺ and in extreme eagerness to nullify his affair, for leaving homelands and tribes and sacrificing lives and souls is among the strongest indications of this. When such a rebuke is added to it, namely His saying ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do﴾, then if it had been within their power and capacity to bring the like of the Qur'an, or the like of a single sura of it, they would have brought it. Since they did not bring it, the miracle is manifest.

Second: He ﷺ, although he was suspected by them in matters related to prophethood, was known to be of great intellect, excellence, and knowledge of consequences. If doubt had entered into his claim of prophethood, he would not have permitted himself to challenge them and push the challenge to its limit. Rather he would have been fearful and anxious about the disgrace whose consequences would return upon all his affairs. Far be that from him ﷺ. So had he not known by necessity from their condition that they were unable to contend, he would not have allowed himself to drive them to contend by the most eloquent means.

Third: Had he ﷺ not been certain of the truth of his prophethood, he would not have asserted categorically in the statement that they would never bring the like of it. For if he were not certain of the truth of his prophethood, its opposite would be possible, and if its opposite occurred, his lie would be exposed. A liar and a fabricator would never assert a statement definitively or affirm it with certainty. Since he affirmed it, this shows that he ﷺ was certain about his affair.

Fourth: The content of this statement was verified in this manner, for from his time ﷺ until our present age no period has passed without someone opposing the religion and Islam, whose motives were strong in disparaging it. Yet despite this intense eagerness, no contention ever occurred.

These four aspects in the indication of the miraculous are included in this verse, and this shows the corruption of the view of the ignorant who claim that the Book of God does not contain proof and argumentation.

And here are some questions:

**First question:** The non-occurrence of their bringing a sura is certain, so why was ﴿idhā﴾ (when), which denotes certainty, not used instead of ﴿in﴾ (if), which denotes doubt?

The answer: There are two aspects. One: the statement is framed in accordance with their own assumption, for they were still not certain of their inability to contend, relying on their eloquence and their capacity for speech. Two: he is mocking them, as one endowed with strength and confident of his superiority over his opponent says: "If I defeat you," while he knows that he will defeat him, as a form of mockery.

**Second question:** Why did He say ﴿But if you do not﴾ and not "But if you do not bring it"?

The answer: Because this is more concise than saying: "But if you do not bring a sura like it, and you will never bring a sura like it."

**Third question:** What is the grammatical position of ﴿and you will never do﴾?

The answer: It has no grammatical position, because it is a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah).

**Fourth question:** What is the reality of (lan) in the context of negation?

The answer: Lā and lan are siblings in negating the future, except that in lan there is emphasis and intensification. You say to your companion: "Lā uqimu ghadan 'indaka" (I will not stay with you tomorrow). If he objects to you, you say: "Lan uqima ghadan" (I will certainly not stay tomorrow). There are three opinions about it:

One: its origin is lā plus an (an), and this is the view of al-Khalil.

Second: it is lā, whose alif was replaced by a nun, and this is the view of al-Farra'.

Third: it is a particle of naṣb (accusative) for emphasizing the negation of the future, and this is the view of Sibawayh and one of the two reports from al-Khalil.

**Fifth question:** What is the meaning of making the avoidance of the Fire conditional on their not bringing a sura like it?

The answer: When their inability to contend becomes manifest, the truth of the Messenger of God ﷺ is established for them. And when this is established, then if they persist in obstinacy, they deserve punishment by the Fire. Thus avoiding the Fire necessitates abandoning obstinacy. So the effect (the cause) is put in place of the result, and His saying ﴿so fear the Fire﴾ is made to stand in place of His saying: "so abandon obstinacy." This is the conciseness (al-ijaz) which is one of the gates of eloquence. It also contains a terrifying emphasis on the gravity of obstinacy, by substituting the avoidance of the Fire in its place, and then following it with a terrifying description of the Fire.

**Sixth question:** What is al-waqud (fuel)?

The answer: It is that with which the fire is kindled. As for the verbal noun (masdar), it is pronounced with a ḍamma (waqūd), though a fatḥa has also been reported in it. Sibawayh said: "We have heard from the Arabs one who says: waqadna al-nāra wuqūdan 'āliyan" (we kindled the fire with a high kindling). Then he said: "And al-waqūd is more common." Al-waqūd means firewood. 'Īsā ibn 'Umar recited it with a ḍamma, naming it by the verbal noun, just as one says: "Fulān fakhr qawmihi wa zayn baladihi" (So-and-so is the pride of his people and the adornment of his land).

**Seventh question:** The relative clause (ṣilah) of ﴿alladhī﴾ must be a known matter, so how did those people know that the Fire of the Hereafter is kindled with people and stones?

The answer: It is not impossible that they had heard this beforehand from the People of the Book, or they heard it from the Messenger of God ﷺ, or they heard before this verse his saying in Sura al-Tahrim: ﴿a fire whose fuel is people and stones﴾.

**Eighth question:** Why did the Fire described by this sentence come indefinite (nakirah) in Sura al-Tahrim, while here it is definite (ma'rifah)?

The answer: That verse was revealed in Mecca, so they came to know from it a fire described with this attribute. Then this verse was revealed in Medina, referring back to what they had already come to know.

**Ninth question:** What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿whose fuel is people and stones﴾?

The answer: It is a fire distinguished from other fires in that it is kindled only with people and stones. This indicates its intensity in two respects. The first: when other fires are used to burn people or heat stones, they are first kindled with fuel, and then what is to be burned or heated is thrown into them. But that Fire, may God protect us from it by His vast mercy, is kindled by the very things it burns. The second: because of the extreme intensity of its heat, it ignites within the stone itself.

**Tenth question:** Why are people paired with stones, and why are the stones made fuel along with them?

The answer: Because in this world they paired themselves with stones, when they carved them into idols, made them rivals to God, and worshipped them besides Him. God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. This verse explains it. So His saying ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98] has the same meaning as "the people and the stones," and "the fuel of Hell" has the same meaning as "its fuel."

[Page 113]

Since the disbelievers believed that their stone gods, worshipped besides God, were intercessors and witnesses whom they sought to intercede for them and to ward off harms from themselves, clinging to them, God made them their punishment. So He paired them with those disbelievers, heated in the Fire of Hell, as an intensification and as a means of making their regret more severe. Similar to this is what He does to the disbelievers who made their gold and silver a provision and a store, withholding them and refusing their dues, when they will be heated in the Fire of Hell, and their foreheads, sides, and backs will be branded with them.

It has also been said: they are stones of sulphur (kibrīt). This is a restriction without evidence. Rather, there is in it what indicates its corruption, because the purpose here is to magnify the attribute of this Fire, and kindling with sulphur stones is a common matter, so kindling with them does not indicate the intensity of the Fire. But if we interpret it as referring to all stones, that indicates the magnitude of the Fire's affair, for all stones are used to extinguish fires. So it is as if He said: those fires have reached, in their intensity, the point of taking hold, from their very beginning, of the stones which extinguish the fires of this world. As for His saying ﴿it has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, it indicates that this described Fire is prepared for the disbelievers, and there is nothing in it indicating that there are other fires, not described by these attributes, prepared for the sinful people of prayer.

**The Discourse on the Return**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with a fruit therefrom, they will say, "This is what we were provided with before," and it will be given to them in likeness; and for them therein are purified spouses, and they will abide therein eternally.﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, spoke about Divine Oneness (tawhid) and prophethood (nubuwwah), He spoke after them about the Return (al-ma'ad), explaining the punishment of the disbeliever and the reward of the obedient. It is a custom of God, exalted is He, that when He mentions a verse of threat, He follows it with a verse of promise. Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that the question of the gathering and resurrection (al-hashr wa al-nashr) is among the matters on which the soundness of the religion depends. Discussion of this question either concerns its possibility (imkan) or its actual occurrence (wuqu'). As for its possibility, it may be established sometimes by reason ('aql) and sometimes by transmitted evidence (naql). As for its occurrence, there is no way to it except by transmitted evidence. God has mentioned these two questions in His Book and clarified the truth concerning them in several ways:

**The first way:** He often relates the denial of the gathering and resurrection by the deniers, and then He decrees that it is certain to occur, without mentioning proof for it. This is permissible because everything upon which the validity of the Messenger's prophethood (ﷺ) does not depend can be established by transmitted proof, and this question is of that kind; so it may be established by transmission. An example of this is what He decrees here regarding the Fire for the disbelievers and the Garden for the righteous, without establishing proof for it, relying only on assertion. But regarding the establishment of the Creator and the establishment of prophethood, He did not rely on assertion alone but mentioned proof. The reason for the difference is what we have mentioned. And He said in Surat al-Nahl:

[Page 114]

﴿And they swear by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not resurrect those who die. Yes! It is a promise binding upon Him, but most of mankind do not know.﴾ [al-Nahl: 38]

And He said in Surat al-Taghabun: ﴿Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be resurrected. Say, "Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected; then you will surely be informed of what you did."﴾ [al-Taghabun: 7]

**The second way:** He established the possibility of the gathering and resurrection on the basis that He is capable of matters similar to the gathering and resurrection. God has established this method in several ways, and the most comprehensive of them is what comes in Surat al-Waqi'ah, where He relates, quoting the companions of the left, that they used to say: ﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers of old?"﴾ Then God answered them by His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the former and the latter will surely be gathered for the appointment of a known Day."﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 50]

Then He argued for its possibility with four matters. The first is His saying: ﴿Have you considered that which you emit? Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58]. The manner of inference from this is that semen (al-mani) arises only from the residue of the fourth digestion (fadlat al-hadm al-rabi'), which is like a mist spread throughout the extremities of the limbs. For this reason the limbs share in the pleasure of intercourse, through the dissolution that occurs from all of them. Then God empowered the force of desire over the remainder so that it gathers those misty particles. The sum is that those particles were at first extremely scattered throughout the regions of the world; then God gathered them in the body of that living being; then they were scattered again in the extremities of that body, and God, glorified and exalted, gathered them into the vessels of semen; then He brought them forth as a gushing fluid into the womb's resting place. So if these parts were scattered and He gathered them and formed from them that person, then when they separate by death a second time, how could it be impossible for Him to gather them again? This is the formulation of this argument. God mentioned it in several places in His Book, among them in Surat al-Hajj: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, indeed We created you from dust...﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], up to His saying: ﴿and you see the earth lifeless﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]; then He said: ﴿That is because God is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things competent. And [because] the Hour is coming, there is no doubt concerning it, and God will resurrect those who are in the graves.﴾ [al-Hajj: 6–7]. He also said in Surat Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun, after mentioning the stages of creation: ﴿Then indeed, after that, you will surely die. Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be resurrected.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15–16]. And He said in Surat al-Tariq: ﴿So let man observe from what he was created. He was created from a fluid, ejected, emerging...﴾ [al-Tariq: 5–6], up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is Able to return him [to life].﴾ [al-Tariq: 8]

The second is His saying: ﴿Have you considered that which you plant? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the grower?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63–64], up to His saying: ﴿Rather, we are deprived.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 67]. The manner of inference from this is that grain and its kinds, long and split, or unsplit like rice and barley, and round, triangular, square, and other forms in their varying shapes, when it falls into moist earth and water and dust overcomes it, then rational consideration requires that it rot and decay, because either one of these is sufficient to cause decay, so both together are even more so. Yet it does not decay; rather it remains preserved. Then when moisture increases, the seed splits into two halves, and two leaves emerge from it. As for the long one, a hole appears at its top and the long leaf appears, as in cereal crops. As for the date stone, the great hardness it possesses, by which most people are unable to split it, splits when it falls into moist earth by God's permission. A date pit splits from a notch on its back, and the whole pit becomes two halves; from one half emerges the ascending part, and from the other the descending part. The ascending part rises, and the descending part sinks into the depths of the earth. The sum is that from the small pit two trees emerge: one light and ascending, the other heavy and descending, with the element being one, the nature of the pit, water, air, and soil being one. Does this not indicate complete power and comprehensive wisdom? How then could He who is so capable be unable to gather the parts and assemble the limbs? A parallel to this is His saying in al-Hajj: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless; then when We send down upon it water, it stirs and swells.﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]

The third is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Is it you who bring it down from the cloud, or are We the sender-down?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 68–69]. Its basis is that water is a heavy body by nature, and raising a heavy thing is contrary to its nature. Therefore there must be a Capable, Dominant Agent who overpowers the nature, nullifies the property, and raises what by its essence tends to descend and fall.

[Page 115]

Also: those water particles gathered after they had dispersed; and their being moved by winds; and their being sent down to where they are needed, and to dead land. All of this indicates the permissibility of the gathering (al-hashr). As for the rising of the heavy, it is a reversal of nature; so if this is permissible, why should it not be permissible for Him to bring forth life and moisture from the dryness of dust and water?

Second: since He was able to gather those water particles after their dispersal, why would it not be permissible to gather the earthly parts after their dispersal?

Third: the movement of the winds. If He is able to move the winds that gather some of those homogeneous parts together, why would it not be permissible here?

Fourth: He created the clouds for people's need of them; so the need for recreating the responsible beings a second time, so that they may receive what they deserve of reward and punishment, is more fitting.

Know that God expressed this indication in another place in His Book, when, in al-A'raf, mentioning the indication of Divine Oneness, He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth...﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], up to His saying: ﴿near to the doers of good.﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]. Then He mentioned the proof of the gathering, saying: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy...﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], up to His saying: ﴿Thus We bring forth the dead, that you may remember.﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]

The fourth is His saying: ﴿Have you considered the fire which you kindle? Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the producer?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 71–72]. The manner of inference is that fire ascends, while the tree descends; also, fire is subtle while the tree is dense; also, fire is luminous while the tree is dark; and fire is hot and dry while the tree is cold and moist. So when God holds within the interior of that tree the luminous, fiery particles, He has by His power joined these disparate things together. If He is not incapable of that, how could He be incapable of composing and assembling living beings?

God mentioned this indication in Surat Ya Sin, saying: ﴿He who has made for you from the green tree fire.﴾ [Ya Sin: 80]

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah the matter of water and fire, and He mentioned in al-Naml the matter of air, in His saying: ﴿Is He who guides you through the darknesses of the land and the sea...﴾ [al-Naml: 63], up to His saying: ﴿Is He who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ [al-Naml: 64]; and He mentioned earth in al-Hajj in His saying: ﴿and you see the earth lifeless﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. It is as though He, glorified and exalted, showed that the four elements, in all their states, bear witness to the possibility of the gathering and resurrection.

**The second type of proof for the possibility of the gathering:** He, exalted is He, says: since I was capable of originating creation at first, then I am even more capable of restoring it. The rational explanation of this proof is evident, and He mentioned it in several places in His Book, among them in al-Baqarah: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then give you life, then to Him you will be returned.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. Among them is His saying in Surat Subhan (al-Isra'): ﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled remains, will we indeed be resurrected as a new creation?" Say, "Be stones or iron"...﴾ [al-Isra': 49–50], up to His saying: ﴿Say, "He who created you the first time."﴾ [al-Isra': 51]. Among them is His saying in al-'Ankabut: ﴿Have they not considered how God originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 19]. Among them is His saying in al-Rum: ﴿And it is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him. To Him belongs the highest description.﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. Among them in Ya Sin: ﴿Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time."﴾ [Ya Sin: 79]

**The third type of proof:** the inference from His power over the heavens to His power over the gathering. This occurs in several verses, among them in Surat Subhan (al-Isra'): ﴿Have they not considered that God, who created the heavens and the earth, is Able to create the likes of them?﴾ [al-Isra': 99]. He said in Ya Sin: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, and He is the Creator, the Knowing.﴾ [Ya Sin: 81]. He said in al-Ahqaf: ﴿Have they not considered that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is Able to give life to the dead? Yes, indeed He is over all things competent.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33]. Among them in Surat Qaf: ﴿When we have died and become dust?...﴾ [Qaf: 3], up to His saying:

[Page 116]

﴿as provision for the servants; and We give life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the Emergence.﴾ [Qaf: 11]. Then He said: ﴿Were We incapable with the first creation? Rather, they are in confusion about a new creation.﴾ [Qaf: 15]

**The fourth type of proof**, for the occurrence of the gathering: it is necessary that the doer of good be rewarded, the disobedient be punished, and the one from the other be distinguished. Among the verses for this, in Surat Yunus: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you, as a promise of God, true. Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it, that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice.﴾ [Yunus: 4]. Among them in Ta Ha: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives.﴾ [Ta Ha: 15]. Among them in Sad: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ [Sad: 27] ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like corrupters on the earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28]

**Type 5:** Arguing from the revival of the dead in this world for the soundness of the Resurrection and the Gathering (al-hashr wa'l-nashr). Among these examples is God's creation of Adam, upon him be peace, from the beginning. Another is the story of the cow, which is His saying: ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it. Thus God brings the dead to life"﴾ (al-Baqarah: 73). Another is the story of Abraham, upon him be peace: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ (al-Baqarah: 260). Another is His saying: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town that lay in ruins upon its roofs﴾ (al-Baqarah: 259). Another is the story of Yahya and Isa, upon them both be peace, for God argued for their possibility by the very same argument He used to establish the possibility of the Gathering, when He said: ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾ (Maryam: 9). Another is the story of the People of the Cave, and for this reason He said: ﴿so that they might know that the promise of God is true and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾ (al-Kahf: 21). Another is the story of Ayyub, upon him be peace, which is His saying: ﴿And We gave him his family﴾ (al-Anbiya': 84), which indicates that God revived them after they had died. Another is what God manifested through the hand of Isa, upon him be peace, of reviving the dead, such that He said: ﴿who brings the dead to life﴾ (al-Hajj: 6), and He said: ﴿And when you shaped from clay the likeness of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 110). Another is His saying: ﴿Does not man consider that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ (Maryam: 67). This, then, is the indication of the foundations of the proofs which God mentioned in His Book for the soundness of the doctrine of the Gathering. The full discussion of each of these verses will come, God willing, when we reach them.

Then, God explicitly stated in the Qur'an that the one who denies the Gathering and the Resurrection is a disbeliever. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish. And I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a return."﴾ ﴿His companion said to him while he was arguing with him, "Have you disbelieved in He who created you from dust?"﴾ (al-Kahf: 35). The way in which disbelief is established is that the existence of this thing (the Resurrection) is possible in itself. For if it were impossible in existence, it would not have existed the first time. Since it existed the first time, we know that it is possible in its essence. So if God were not able to do it, that would indicate either His incapacity, because He would not be able to bring into existence what is possible in its own nature, or His ignorance, because it would be impossible for Him to distinguish the parts of the body of each one of the accountable from the parts of the body of another accountable. And with the assertion of incapacity and ignorance, the establishing of prophethood is not valid. So this necessarily entails disbelief with certainty. And God knows best.

**Second issue:** These verses are explicit that Paradise and Hell are created. As for Hell, God said describing it: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 24). This is explicit that it is created. As for Paradise, God said in another verse: ﴿It has been prepared for the righteous﴾ (Al 'Imran: 133). And because God said here: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. This is information about the occurrence and realization of this possession, and the realization of possession in the present requires the existence of the possessed in the present. So this indicates that Paradise and Hell are created.

**Third issue:** Know that the greatest pleasures are gathered in one of three things: the dwelling, the food, or the spouse. God described the dwelling by His saying: ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, the food by His saying: ﴿Every time they are provided with a provision of its fruit, they say, "This is what we were provided with before"﴾, and the spouse by His saying: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses﴾. Then, when these things are attained and the fear of their loss accompanies them, the enjoyment becomes disturbed. So God explained that this fear is removed from them, and He said: ﴿And they therein will abide eternally﴾. Thus the verse indicates the completeness of enjoyment and joy. Now let us discuss the wording of the verse.

As for His saying: ﴿And give good tidings﴾, there are questions about it.

**First question:** To what is this command coordinated? The answer has several aspects.

One: The thing that is coordinated is not the command itself, such that one would seek for it a counterpart of a command or prohibition to be coordinated with it. What is coordinated is rather the sentence describing the reward of the believers, which is coordinated with the sentence describing the punishment of the disbelievers, as you say: "Zayd is punished with shackles and beating, and give 'Amr good news of pardon and release."

Two: It is coordinated with His saying: ﴿So fear﴾ (al-Baqarah: 24), as you say: "O Banu Tamim, beware the punishment of what you have committed, and give good news, O so-and-so, to Banu Asad of my kindness toward them."

Three: Zayd ibn 'Ali read (*wa-Bushshira*) in the passive form, coordinated with *u'iddat* (it has been prepared).

**Second question:** Who is the one addressed by His saying: *wa-bashshir*? The answer: It is permissible that it be the Messenger of God ﷺ, and it is permissible that it be everyone, as he, upon him be peace, said: "Give good news to those who walk to the mosques in darkness of the complete light on the Day of Resurrection." He did not command this of one specific person, but rather everyone is commanded with it. This aspect is better and more eloquent, because it indicates that this matter, because of its greatness and magnificence, deserves that everyone who is able to give good news of it should do so.

**Third question:** What is *bishara* (good news)? The answer: It is the report that shows happiness. For this reason the jurists said: If a man says to his slaves, "Whichever of you gives me good news of the arrival of so-and-so, he is free," and they give him the news individually, the first of them is freed, because he is the one whose report brought him joy. But if he said instead of "gave me good news" (*bashsharani*), "informed me" (*akhbarani*), then all of them are freed, because they all informed him. From the same root come *al-bashara* (the outer skin) and *tabashir al-subh* (the first light of dawn), which is what appears of the first of its light. As for His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ (Al 'Imran: 21), this is from the kind of speech intended as sarcastic mockery that increases the anger of the one mocked, as a man says to his enemy: "Rejoice at the killing of your offspring and the plundering of your wealth."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, there are issues:

**(First issue):** This verse indicates that deeds are not included in the definition of faith, because when He mentioned faith and then coordinated with it righteous deeds, difference becomes necessary; otherwise repetition would follow, and repetition is contrary to the original principle.

**(Second issue):** Some people apply this verse to its apparent meaning and say: Everyone who brings faith and righteous deeds has Paradise. When it is said to them: What is your view of one who brought faith and righteous deeds and then disbelieved? They say: This is impossible, because performing faith and obedience necessitates deserving an everlasting reward, and performing disbelief necessitates deserving an everlasting punishment, and combining the two is impossible, and the claim of cancellation (*tahabut*) is also impossible. So nothing remains except to say: This supposition you have posited is impossible. We say that the claim of cancellation is impossible for several reasons:

*[Page 118]*

One: The two entitlements either oppose one another or do not oppose one another. If they oppose one another, the occurrence of the newer one is conditioned upon the removal of the remaining one. If the removal of the remaining one were caused by the occurrence of the newer one, a circularity (*dawr*) would follow, and that is impossible.

Two: The mutual exclusion exists from both sides, so the removal of the remaining by the newer is no more preferable than the cancellation of the newer by the remaining. Then either both exist together, which is impossible, or they repel one another, and in that case the doctrine of cancellation is refuted.

Three: The two entitlements either are equal, or the earlier is greater or lesser. If they are equal, as when it is said: The entitlement to ten parts of reward has occurred, and then the entitlement to ten parts of punishment occurs, we say: The entitlement to each part of the punishment is independently sufficient to remove each part of the entitlement to reward. And if that is so, then the effect of this part in removing that part is no more preferable than its effect in removing another part, or the effect of another part in removing it. So either each of these newer parts is an effective cause in removing each of the earlier parts, and then it would follow that each cause has many effects, and each effect has many independent causes, and all of that is impossible; or each of the newer parts is specifically assigned to one of the remaining parts without any specifier, and that is impossible because it is impossible for one of the two sides of a possible thing to be preferred over the other without a preponderant cause. As for when the earlier is greater, the newer removes only some parts of the remaining, so no part of the remaining is more suitable to be removed by it than the others. Then either all of it is removed, which is impossible because what is removed is not removed except by what is less; or some part is determined for removal without a specifier, which is impossible; or none of it is removed, which is what is sought. Moreover, when this newer removes some parts of the remaining, either the newer remains or it is removed. As for the claim that the newer remains, no sane person has held it. As for the claim that it is removed, that is false, because either the effect of each of them in removing the other is simultaneous or in sequence. The first is false, because the remover must necessarily exist at the time of removal; so if both removals occurred together, both removers would have occurred together, and it would follow that they both exist at the time they are nonexistent, which is impossible. If it is in sequence, then the defeated cannot become victorious. As for when the earlier is lesser, either the cause of its removal is some parts of the newer, and that is impossible because all its parts are suitable for removal, and the specifying of some by this is a preponderance without a preponderant cause, which is impossible; or the whole becomes an effective cause in removal, and then it would follow that several independent causes converge upon one single effect, and that is impossible. Thus, through these rational aspects, the invalidity of the doctrine of cancellation (*al-ihbat*) has been established. At this point, two answers become determined:

The first: the view of those who take into account *al-muwafah* (the condition that one dies in faith), which is that the condition for faith to be valid is that one not die upon disbelief. So if he dies upon disbelief, we know that what he did first was disbelief. This view is clearly untenable.

The second: that the servant does not deserve reward for obedience nor punishment for disobedience by necessary rational entitlement. This is the view of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) and our chosen position, and through it deliverance from these darknesses is achieved.

* * *

**(Third issue):** The Mu'tazilah argued that obedience necessitates reward. For at the time when He gave them good news that for them are gardens, this had not come about for them in actual occurrence. And since it is not possible to interpret the verse as such, it must be interpreted as the deserving of occurrence, because it is permissible to express occurrence metaphorically by the deserving of occurrence.

**Fourth issue:** *Al-jannah* (the garden) is an orchard of palm trees and dense trees whose branches intertwine to cast shade. The root has the meaning of covering. Perhaps because of their density and shading, it was named *al-jannah*, which is the single form of the verbal noun of *janna*, meaning he covered it, as if it were one cover because of the extreme intertwining of its branches. And the abode of reward was named *jannah* because of the hidden things (*al-jinan*) within it. If it is asked: Why are the gardens indefinite while the rivers are definite? The answer: As for the first, it is because *al-jannah* is the name of the whole abode of reward, and it contains many gardens arranged in ranks according to the entitlements of those who did deeds, so for each class of them there are gardens from among those gardens. As for the definiteness of the rivers, what is intended by it is the genus, as one says: "So-and-so has an orchard in which there is running water, figs, and grapes," indicating the kinds known to the addressee; or it is indicated by the definite article to the rivers mentioned in His saying: ﴿therein are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change﴾ (Muhammad: 15).

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Every time they are provided﴾, this either is a second attribute of *jannat* (gardens), or the predicate of a deleted subject, or a resumed sentence. For when it was said, "that for them are gardens," the listener's heart could not avoid wondering whether the fruits of those gardens are like the fruits of this world or not. And here there are questions:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 25 (part 3 of 3):

The First Question: What is the grammatical position of "min thamarah" (from fruit)? The answer: There are two views.

The first: It is like your saying: "Whenever I eat some pomegranates from your orchard, I praise you." So the position of "min thamarah" is the position of your saying "min al-rumman" (of the pomegranates). The first "min" and the second "min" are both for the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah, "the point of origin"), because the provision began from the gardens, and the provision from the gardens began from a fruit. On this interpretation, "thamarah" does not mean a single apple or a single pomegranate; rather it means a kind of fruit.

The second: That "min thamarah" be an explanatory (bayan) phrase, following the pattern of your saying: "I saw from you a lion," meaning "you are a lion." On this view, "thamarah" may mean a kind of fruit or a single berry.

The Second Question: How is it valid for them to say: "This is what we were provided with before"?

The answer: Since the two share the same quiddity (mahiyyah) even though they differ in number, it is valid to say "this is that," that is, in terms of the quiddity. For the unity of kind is not negated by plurality of individuals. For this reason, when the resemblance of a son to his father is very strong, people say: "He is the father."

The Third Question: The verse indicates that they likened the provision that comes to them in Paradise to another provision that came to them before. So is the compared-to (al-mushabbah bihi) from the provisions of this world or from the provisions of Paradise? The answer has two views.

The first: That it is from the provisions of this world. This is indicated by two arguments:

The first: A person is more at ease with the familiar and more inclined to the known. When he sees what he is not accustomed to, his nature shrinks from it. Then, when he obtains something of the same kind he once knew, and finds it more noble than what he first knew, his joy and delight in it become great. So when the people of Paradise see a pomegranate in this world, and then see it in the Hereafter and find the pomegranate of Paradise more pleasant and more noble than the pomegranate of this world, their joy in it is greater than their joy in anything they witnessed in this world.

The second argument: His saying "whenever they are provided with from it" (kullama ruziqu minha) encompasses all occasions. Thus it includes the first occasion. So for them, on the first occasion, there is some provision of Paradise, and they must say: "This is what we were provided with before." But before the first occasion there was no provision of Paradise to which this could be compared. Therefore it is necessary to interpret it as referring to the provisions of this world.

The second view: The compared-to is also the provision of Paradise, and what is meant is the resemblance of their provisions. Then they differed about the respect in which the resemblance occurs, on two points:

The first: What is meant is the equality of their reward at all times in measure and rank, so that it neither increases nor decreases.

The second: What is meant is the resemblance in appearance, so that the second is as if it were the first, as is reported from al-Hasan. Then these are of differing opinions: Some say that the confusion of resemblance that occurs in appearance also occurs in taste, for when a man takes delight in something and is pleased by it, his soul is attached only to its like; so when there comes something resembling the first in every respect, that is the height of pleasure. Others say that although the resemblance occurs in color, they differ in taste. Al-Hasan said: One of them is brought a dish, he eats from it, then another is brought, and he says: "This is what was brought to us before." The angel says: "Eat, for the color is one and the taste is different."

[Page 120]

There is a third view in the verse, on the authority of the people of gnosis (ahl al-ma'rifah), which is that the perfection of happiness lies only in knowing the Essence of God, the Most High, knowing His attributes, and knowing His acts, [including] the Cherubic angels, the spiritual angels, the levels of spirits, and the world of the heavens. In sum, the soul of a human must become like a mirror facing the world of holiness (alam al-qudus). Then these knowledges are attained in this world, but the complete delight and joy are not attained through them, because bodily attachments obstruct the manifestation of those happinesses and pleasures. When this obstacle is removed, great happiness and supreme bliss are attained. The upshot is that every spiritual happiness a person finds after death, he says: "This is what was attained by me when I was in this world." This is an indication that the psychic perfections attained in the Hereafter are those that were attained in this world, except that in this world they did not produce delight, gladness, and joy, whereas in the Hereafter they produced these things because the obstacle has been removed.

As for His saying "and they were brought it resembling" (wa utu bihi mutashabihan), there are two questions:

The First Question: To what does the pronoun in "wa utu bihi" refer? The answer: If we say the compared-to is the provision of this world, then it refers to the thing provided in this world and in the Hereafter, meaning: they were brought that kind resembling, so that what they obtain in the Hereafter resembles what they obtained in this world. If we say the compared-to is also the provision of Paradise, then it refers to the thing provided in Paradise, meaning: they were brought that kind in Paradise, such that some of it resembles some other.

The Second Question: What is the position of His saying "and they were brought it resembling" within the structure of the discourse? The answer: When God, the Most High, related of the people of Paradise their claim of the resemblance of provisions in His saying "They said: This is what we were provided with before," God, the Most High, confirmed them in that claim by His saying "and they were brought it resembling."

* * *

As for His saying "and for them therein are purified spouses" (wa lahum fiha azwajun mutahharatun), what is meant is the purity of their bodies from menstruation, istihadah, and all filth, and the purity of their husbands from all blameworthy qualities, especially those that pertain to women. We have applied the wording to the whole because the two categories share a common measure. The people of allusion (ahl al-isharah) said: This indicates that one must be alert to several issues:

One: When a woman menstruates, God, the Most High, prohibits you from intimacy with her, as God, the Most High, said: "Say: It is an injury, so keep away from women during menstruation" [al-Baqarah: 222]. If He forbids you from approaching them because of the impurity upon them, which they are excused for, then if the spouses in Paradise are purified, it is more fitting that He would forbid you from them while you are defiled with the impurities of sins, when you are not excused in them.

Two: Whoever satisfies his desire through what is lawful is prevented from entering the mosque, which every pious and wicked person enters. So whoever satisfies his desire through what is unlawful, how could he be enabled to enter Paradise, which none inhabits except the purified? For this reason, when Adam committed the lapse, he was expelled from it.

Three: Whoever has upon his garment a speck of impurity, his prayer is not valid according to al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him. So whoever has upon his heart impurities of sins greater than this world, how could his prayer be accepted? Here there are two questions. The First: Why did the adjective not come in the plural like the noun it modifies? The answer: Both are eloquent dialects: it is said "al-nisa' fa'alna" and "al-nisa' fa'alat." From this is the verse of the Hamasah:

"And when the virgins were veiled with smoke, and they worked at the cooking-pots and grew weary."

[Page 121]

The meaning is "a group of purified spouses." Zayd ibn 'Ali read "mutahharat" (purified, plural), and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read "mutattahirah" (purifying herself), meaning "making herself pure."

The Second Question: Why was it not said "tahirah" (pure)? The answer: In "mutahharah" there is an indication that a purifier purified them, and that is none other than God, the Most High. This conveys the grandeur of the matter of the people of reward, as if it were said: God, the Most High, is the One who adorned them for the people of reward.

As for His saying "and they therein are abiding" (wa hum fiha khalidun), the Mu'tazilah said: Khuld here is the enduring permanence and the everlasting duration that does not end. They argued for this with the verse and with poetry. As for the verse, it is His saying: "And We did not grant to any human before you immortality. Then if you die, will they be immortal?" [al-Anbiya': 34]. He negated immortality from humans, although He gave some of them long life, and what is negated is other than what is affirmed. So khuld is everlasting permanence. As for the poetry, it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Is there any delight except for a happy one made immortal, little troubled by cares, who does not spend the night in distress?"

Our companions (ashabuna) said: Khuld is long-lasting permanence, whether or not it endures. They argued for this with the verse and with custom. As for the verse, it is His saying, the Most High: "Abiding therein forever" [al-Nisa': 169]. If perpetuity were included in the concept of khuld, that would be repetition. As for custom, one says: "So-and-so imprisoned so-and-so with a khuld imprisonment," and because it is written in endowment deeds: "So-and-so endowed an endowment khuld." This is the discussion of whether this term indicates the perpetuity of reward or not. Others said: Reason indicates its perpetuity, because if its perpetuity were not obligatory, they would permit its cessation, and the fear of cessation would embitter that blessing for them, since the greater a blessing is, the greater the impact of fear of its loss on the heart. That requires that the people of reward never be free from grief and regret. And God, the Most High, knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 26 (part 1 of 6):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to strike an example, even of a gnat or what is above it. As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. But as for those who disbelieve, they say, "What did God intend by this as an example?" He misleads many by it and guides many by it, and He misleads by it only the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin), ﴿those who break the covenant of God after its ratification, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth. Those are the losers.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, demonstrated by proof that the Qur'an is inimitable (i'jaz), He raised here an objection (shubha) that the disbelievers had raised to discredit it, and He answered it. The statement of the objection is this: the Qur'an mentions the bee, the fly, the spider and the ant, and these things are not fitting to be mentioned in the speech of eloquent people. So the inclusion of these in the Qur'an detracts from its eloquence, let alone from its being inimitable. God, exalted is He, answered this by saying that [p. 122] the smallness of these things does not detract from eloquence when their mention includes profound wisdoms. This is the indication of how this verse is connected to what precedes it. Then, there are several issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that when the verse ﴿O people, an example has been struck, so listen to it﴾ [al-Hajj: 73] was revealed, he (Ibn 'Abbas) criticised their idols and then likened their worship to the spider's web. The Jews said, "What value do the fly and the spider have that God should strike an example with them?" So this verse was revealed.

The second view is that the hypocrites (munafiqun) criticised the striking of examples with fire, darkness, thunder and lightning, in His saying: ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17].

The third view is that this criticism came from the polytheists. Al-Qaffal said: "All of these are possible here. As for the Jews, it is because it was said at the end of the verse: ﴿and He misleads by it only the defiantly disobedient, those who break the covenant of God after its ratification,﴾ and this is the attribute of the Jews, because the address concerning fulfilment and covenant in what follows is only to the Children of Israel. As for the disbelievers and the hypocrites, they are mentioned in Surah al-Muddaththir: ﴿and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, 'What did God intend by this as an example?' Thus God misleads whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31], to the end of the verse. So those in whose hearts is a disease are the hypocrites, and those who disbelieved may include the polytheists, because the surah is Meccan. Thus both groups are brought together here. Once this is established, we say: all of these possibilities are valid here, because the disbelievers, the hypocrites and the Jews were united in harming the Messenger of God (ﷺ). From the beginning of the surah up to this point, the Jews, the hypocrites and the polytheists have been mentioned, and all of them are among those who disbelieved." Then al-Qaffal said: "It is also possible that this was revealed without a specific cause, because its meaning in itself is beneficial."

\* \* \*

**The second issue:** Know that modesty (haya') is a change and breaking that befalls a person out of fear of being blamed or censured. Its derivation is from life (hayah). It is said: "al-rajul hayiya" (the man was shy), just as it is said "nasiya" (he forgot) and "khashiya" (he feared), and "shadhiya al-faras" (the horse's limbs were affected) when these limbs become ailing. The shy person, because of the breaking and change that overtakes him, is made one whose strength is broken and whose life is troubled. Just as they say: "So-and-so perished out of shame at such-and-such," "he died of shame," "I saw ruin in his face from the intensity of shame," and "he melted with shame." Once this is established, modesty is impossible for God, exalted is He, because it is a change that affects the body, and this is only conceivable with respect to a body. However, it appears in the traditions. Salman reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed God is Living, Generous; He is shy when His servant raises his hands to Him that He should return them empty, until He places good in them." Since this is so, it must be interpreted, and there are two ways to do so:

The first, which is the general principle (qanun) regarding such matters: every attribute established for the servant that pertains to bodies, when God is described with it, is to be understood as referring to the final outcomes of the accidents (nihayat al-a'rad), not their initial stages (bidayat al-a'rad). An example of this is that modesty is a state that occurs in a human being, but it has a beginning and an end. Its beginning is the bodily change that affects a person out of fear of being attributed to something ugly, and its end is that the person abandons that act. So when modesty is attributed to God, exalted is He, what is meant is not that fear which is its beginning and preface, but the abandoning of the act, which is its end and final purpose. Similarly, anger has a sign and a preface, which is the boiling of the blood of the heart and the desire for retaliation, and it has an aim, which is the infliction of punishment on the one who is angered against. So when we describe God, exalted is He, with anger, what is meant is not that beginning, namely the desire for retaliation and the boiling of the blood of the heart, but rather that end, which is the infliction of punishment. This is the universal principle in this matter.

The second: it is possible that this expression occurred in the speech of the disbelievers, who said: "Is the Lord of Muhammad not ashamed to strike an example with the fly and the spider?" So this speech came as a manner of answering the question in a comprehensive way (itbaq al-jawab 'ala al-su'al), and this is a wondrous kind of speech. Then [p. 123] al-Qadi said: "Whatever is impermissible for God of this kind, in affirmation, must also not be applied to Him in negation. Rather, it should be said that He is not described with it. But to say, 'He is not ashamed,' and to apply that to Him, is impossible, because it implies negating what is permissible for Him. What God has mentioned in His Book in His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying: ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3], is in the form of a negation but is not a negation in actual reality. Likewise His saying: ﴿God has not taken any son﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91], and likewise His saying: ﴿He feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'am: 14]. And not everything that occurs in the Qur'an in its general form is permissible to be used in ordinary address. So it is not permissible to apply that except with a clarification that it is impossible."

It may be said: there is no doubt that these attributes are negated of God, glorified is He, so reporting their negation is truthful, and therefore it must be permissible. It remains to be said that reporting their negation indicates their validity concerning Him. We say: this implication is disputed, because singling out this negation for mention does not indicate the establishment of its opposite. Indeed, if the wording were accompanied by something that indicates the negation of validity as well, that would be better, as it would be an intensification in clarity. And that something else is better does not make the first one ugly.

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** Know that striking examples is among the things considered good by the intellects, and this is indicated by several considerations:

The first: the consensus of the Arabs and the non-Arabs (al-'ajam) upon it. As for the Arabs, this is well known among them, and they have used the most insignificant things as examples. They said, in illustrating with the dhurra (ant or small particle): "more gathered than a dhurra," "more precise than a dhurra," and "more hidden than the dhurra." In illustrating with the fly: "bolder than the fly," "more mistaken than the fly," "more flighty than the fly," "more similar to the fly than the fly is to the fly," and "more persistent than the fly." In illustrating with the tick (qurad): "more attentive than a tick," "smaller than a tick," "more clinging than a tick," "more troubled than a tick," and "more persistent than a tick." They said of the locust: "more flying than a locust," "more destructive than a locust," "more corrupting than a locust," and "purer than the saliva of the locust." Of the butterfly (farasha): "weaker than a butterfly," "more flighty than a butterfly," and "more ignorant than a butterfly." Of the gnat (ba'ud): "weaker than a gnat," "more precious than the brain of a gnat," and "he burdened me with the brain of a gnat," in the manner of burdening with what cannot be borne. As for the non-Arabs, this is shown by the book *Kalila wa Dimna* and similar works, and in some of them: the gnat, having landed on a tall palm tree and wishing to fly off it, said: "O you, hold firm, for I want to fly." The palm tree said: "By God, I did not notice your landing, so how would I notice your flying away?"

The second: He (God) struck examples in the Gospel of Jesus, peace be upon him, with lowly things. He said: "The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good, pure wheat in his field. When people slept, his enemy came and sowed darnel (zuwan) among the wheat. When the crop grew and the ears bore fruit, the darnel overcame it. The servants of the sower said: 'Our master, did you not sow good, pure wheat in your field? From where then is this darnel?' He said: 'It was an enemy who did this.' They said: 'Shall we go and pull up the darnel?' He said: 'Lest, in pulling up the darnel, you also uproot the wheat. Leave them both to grow together until the harvest.' He then ordered the reapers to gather the darnel from the wheat, to bind it in bundles, then burn it with fire, and to gather the wheat into the storehouses."

And I will explain to you: that man who sowed the good wheat is the father of humanity, the field is the world, the good, pure wheat is us, the sons of the kingdom who act by obedience to God, exalted is He. The enemy who sowed the darnel is Iblis, the darnel is the sins that Iblis and his companions sow, and the reapers are the angels, who leave people until their terms draw near, then they harvest the people of good to the kingdom of God, and the people of evil to the abyss (al-hawiyah). And just as the darnel is gathered and burned with fire, so too the messengers of God and His angels gather from His kingdom the lazy and all the workers of sin, and cast them into the furnace of the abyss, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, and the righteous will be there in the kingdom of their Lord. Whoever has an ear to hear, let him hear.

I will strike for you another example resembling the kingdom of heaven: if a man took a grain of mustard, which is the smallest of seeds, and sowed it in his field, and when it sprouted it grew until it became like the greatest of the herbs (buqul), and a bird from the sky came and nested in its branches, so too is guidance: whoever calls to it, God multiplies his reward, magnifies him, raises his name, and saves whoever follows him."

He also said: "Do not be like a sieve, which lets out the good flour and retains the bran. Likewise, you let wisdom come out of your mouths while you keep rancour in your hearts." And he said: "Your hearts are like the pebble which fire does not ripen, water does not soften, and winds do not scatter." He also said: "Do not store your treasures where moths and worms destroy them, nor in the wilderness where the scorching winds and thieves are, so that the winds burn them and thieves steal them. Rather, store your treasures with God." He said: "We dig and find creatures that have their clothing, and there is their provision, and they neither sow nor reap. Among them are some that are in the heart of the solid rock or in the core of wood. Who brings them their clothing and their provisions except God? Do you not understand?" He also said: "Do not stir up the wasps, lest they sting you, and do not argue with fools, lest they insult you."

Thus it becomes clear that God struck examples with these lowly things. As for reason, it is because the nature of imagination (khayal) is imitation and resemblance. When the meaning is mentioned alone, the intellect grasps it, but with the imagination resisting. When a likeness is mentioned along with it, the intellect grasps it with the assistance of the imagination. There is no doubt that the second is more complete. Also, we observe that a person may mention a meaning but it does not become clear to him as it should. When he mentions the example, it becomes clear, explicit and uncovered. And since the illustration gives additional clarity and explicitness, it is necessary to mention it in a book whose sole purpose is elucidation and explanation.

Issue Four: Al-Asamm said that "ma" in His words "a parable, ma" (*mathalan ma*) is an extra, superfluous particle (*silah za'idah*), as in His words ﴿So by a mercy from Allah﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 159]. Abu Muslim said: "God forbid that there should be superfluity and meaningless words in the Qur'an." The more correct view is that of Abu Muslim, because Allah, exalted is He, described the Qur'an as guidance and clarification (*huda* and *bayan*), and its being meaningless contradicts that.

As for *ba'udatan* (a gnat), there are two readings. One is the accusative (*nasb*). On this reading, the word *ma* has two possible analyses:

The first: it is indeclinable (*mabniyyah*), and it is the kind that, when attached to an indefinite noun, makes that noun vague and increases its generality and remoteness from specificity.

Its explanation: if a man says to his companion, "Give me a book so I may look into it," and he gives him some book, he may later say, "I wanted another book and did not want this one." But if he had said it with *ma* ("Give me a book, ma"), he could not say that, because the sense of the sentence is: "Give me a book, any book whatever."

The second: it is an indefinite noun whose explanation is supplied by the generic noun (*ism al-jins*) standing in the place of a qualifier (*sifah*). As for the reading in the nominative (*raf'*), there are two views on it:

The first: it is a relative pronoun (*ma mawsulah*) whose complement is the clause, because the implied meaning is "it is a gnat," so the subject has been omitted, as it is omitted in ﴿Completion [of Our favour] upon him who did good﴾ [Surah Al-An'am: 154].

The second: it is an interrogative (*istifhamiyyah*). When He said, ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even of a gnat or what is above it]﴾, it is as if He then said: "What is a gnat, and what is above it?" so that He would give the example of it. Rather, He is free to give as an example something much less than that, as one says: "So-and-so is not concerned with what he gives away: what is a dinar or two dinars?" meaning, he gives away much more than that.

Issue Five: The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *darb al-mathal* (striking an example) means to adopt it and form it, from *darb al-labin* (shaping bricks) and *darb al-khatam* (striking a seal).

Issue Six: *Ba'udatan* is in the accusative either as an apposition (*'atf bayan*) to *mathalan*, or as the object of *yadriba* (strike). *Mathalan* is then a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) placed before its indefinite noun. Alternatively, it is the second of two objects of *yadriba*, given the meaning of *yaj'alu* (make). This applies when *ma* is a complement or vague. If *ma* is explained by *ba'udatan*, then it follows what it explains, and the explained and the explainer together form either an apposition or an object, with *mathalan* as a preceding circumstantial qualifier.

As for its nominative reading, it is the predicate (*khabar*) of a subject. If *ma* is a relative, a qualifier, or an interrogative, its case is clear. If it is vague, then it is in the form of an answer, as if someone had said: "What is it?" and it was answered: "A gnat."

Issue Seven: The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: The derivation of *al-ba'ud* (gnat) is from *al-ba'd*, which means cutting, like *al-bad'* and *al-'adb*. It is said: *ba'adahu al-ba'ud* (the gnat bit him). From it comes *ba'd al-shay'* (a part of a thing), because it is a piece of it. *Al-ba'ud* in its origin is an adjective on the pattern *fa'ul*, like *qatul*, but its nominal usage became dominant. It is reported from some scholars that its derivation is from *ba'd al-shay'* (a part of a thing), and it was named so because of its small body and its tiny size, and because a part of a thing is small in comparison to its whole. But the strong view is the first. He said: It is among the wonders of Allah's creation, for it is very small, and its proboscis is extremely tiny, and yet it is hollow. That proboscis, despite its extreme smallness and hollowness, pierces the hide of the elephant and the buffalo despite its thickness, as a man dips his finger into honey. This is because Allah placed poison in the tip of its proboscis.

Issue Eight: Concerning His words ﴿and what is above it﴾ there are two views:

One: it means what is larger than it in body, such as the fly, the spider, the donkey, and the dog, since the people denied that Allah would give as an example all of these things.

The second: it means what is above it in smallness, that is, what is smaller than it. The verifiers (*al-muhaqqiqun*) inclined to this view for several reasons:

First: the purpose of this illustration is to belittle the idols, and the more insignificant the thing compared, the more fully the aim is achieved in this matter.

Second: the point here is to show that Allah is not averse to giving as an example a lowly thing. In such a context the second mentioned thing must be even more insignificant than the first. It is said: "So-and-so endures humiliation to earn a dinar, and what is above it," meaning in lowness, because enduring humiliation to earn something less than a dinar is greater than enduring it to earn a dinar.

Third: the smaller a thing is, the harder it is to grasp its secrets. When it is at the extreme of smallness, none encompasses it except the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. So giving it as an example is stronger in indicating the perfection of wisdom than giving a large thing as an example.

The first group argued with two points:

First: the word *fawq* (above) indicates elevation. When it is said, "This is above that," its meaning is that it is larger than it. It is related that a man praised Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, while the man was suspected of insincerity in it, and Ali said: "I am less than what you say and above what is in your heart," meaning: "I am higher than what is in your heart."

Second: how can an example be given with what is below the gnat, when it is the extreme of smallness?

The answer to the first: whenever the presence of a quality in one thing is stronger than its presence in another thing, that stronger one is "above" the weaker in that quality. It is said: "So-and-so is above so-and-so in baseness and meanness," meaning he is more base and mean than him. Likewise, when it is said: "This is above that in smallness," it must be smaller than it.

The answer to the second: the wing of the gnat is smaller than it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ struck it as an example for this world.

* * *

Issue Nine: *Amma* is a particle carrying the meaning of a condition, and for this reason it is answered with *fa* (then). This conveys emphasis. You say, "Zayd is going," and if you intend to stress that he is definitely going, you say, "As for Zayd, he is going." Having established this, we say: The bringing of the two sentences introduced by it is a great commendation of the affair of the believers, and a great reliance on their knowledge that it is the truth, and a great censure of the disbelievers for what they said and mentioned.

Issue Ten: *Al-haqq* (the truth) is that which is established and cannot rightly be denied. It is said: *haqqa al-amr* when the matter is established and binding; ﴿and the word of your Lord has come into effect﴾; and *thawb muhaqqaq* (a well-woven garment), meaning one with firm weave.

Issue Eleven: As for *madha* (what), there are two possibilities. Either *dha* is a relative noun meaning "the one who," in which case it is two words; or *dha* is combined with *ma* and the two are treated as one noun, in which case it is one word. On both views: in the first, it is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is *dha* together with its complement. In the second, it is in the accusative position, in the judgment of *ma* alone, as when you say, "What did Allah intend?"

* * *

Issue Twelve: Will (*iradah*) is a reality (*mahiyyah*) that the rational person finds within himself, and he perceives the obvious distinction between it and his knowledge, his power, his pain, and his pleasure. Since this is so, grasping its reality does not need definition. The theologians (*al-mutakallimun*) said: It is an attribute that requires the preference of one of two possible sides over the other, not in its occurrence but in its bringing about. We added this last restriction to exclude power (*qudrah*).

They differed on whether Allah, exalted is He, has will, although the Muslims agree on applying this word to Allah, exalted is He. The Najjariyya said: it is a negative attribute, and its meaning is that He is not overpowered and not compelled. Some of them said it is an affirmative attribute. Those who held this differed. Al-Jahiz, al-Ka'bi, and Abu al-Hasan al-Basri said: its meaning is His knowledge, exalted is He, that the act includes benefit or harm. They call this knowledge "the motivation" (*al-da'i*) or "the deterrent" (*al-sarif*).

Our companions (the Ash'arites), Abu 'Ali, Abu Hashim, and their followers said: it is an attribute added to knowledge. Then the division concerning that attribute is: either it is essential (*dhatiyyah*), which is the second view of the Najjariyya; or it is a meaningful attribute (*ma'nawiyyah*). That meaning is either eternal, which is the view of the Ash'ariyya, or originated. That originated meaning is either subsisting in Allah, exalted is He, which is the view of the Karramiyya, or subsisting in another body, and no one has held this view; or it exists not in a substratum, which is the view of Abu 'Ali, Abu Hashim, and their followers.

Issue Thirteen: The pronoun in ﴿that it is the truth﴾ refers either to the example or to *an yadriba* (that He strikes). In their saying, "What did Allah intend by this?" there is contempt, as 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said about 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: "How strange is this son of 'Amr!"

* * *

Issue Fourteen: *Mathalan* is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*), as when you say to someone who gave a poor answer, "What did you intend by this answer?" or to someone who carried a poor weapon, "How will you benefit from this weapon?" Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), as in His words ﴿This is Allah's she-camel, a sign for you﴾ [Surah Al-A'raf: 73].

Issue Fifteen: Know that when Allah, glorified and exalted is He, related their disbelief and their belittling of the words of Allah by saying ﴿What did Allah intend by this as an example?﴾, He answered them with His words ﴿He leads many astray by it and He guides many by it﴾. We want to speak here about guidance and misguidance, so that this place may serve as a foundation to which every verse on this theme may be referred. So we first speak about *al-idlal* (leading astray), and we say: the hamzah (*alif* of causation) sometimes comes to transfer a verb from the intransitive to the transitive, as when you say *kharaja* (he went out), which is intransitive, and when you say *akhraja* (he took out), you have made it transitive. It also sometimes comes to transfer a verb from the transitive to the intransitive, as when you say *kababtuhu fa-akabba* (I overturned him, so he fell face down). It also sometimes comes to mean simply finding something. It is reported from 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib that he said to Bani Sulaym: "We fought you and did not find you cowardly; we satirized you and did not find you silenced; we asked you and did not find you stingy." That is, we did not find you cowardly, nor silenced, nor stingy.

It is said: "I came to the land of so-and-so and found it cultivated" (*a'marturaha*), meaning I found it cultivated. Al-Mukhabbal said:

*Husayn desired to rule over Khuza'a, but Husayn became humbled and subdued.*

That is, he was found humiliated and subdued.

Someone may say: why is it not permissible to say that the hamzah only conveys the transfer of a verb from intransitive to transitive? As for his saying "I overturned him, so he fell," perhaps it means "I overturned him, so he fell on his face," and so the verb is mentioned with its two objects omitted, and this is not rare. As for his saying, "We fought you and did not find you cowardly," the meaning is that our fighting did not make you cowards, and our satire did not make you silenced. The same applies to the rest. This view we have stated is preferable, to avoid homonymy (*li-daf' al-ishtirak*). Having established this, we say: our saying "Allah misguided him" (*adallahu Allah*) cannot be interpreted except in two ways:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 26 (part 3 of 6):

One of them: that He made him go astray; the second: that He found him astray. As for the first interpretation, namely that He made him go astray, the wording gives no indication of what He made him go astray from, and there are two possibilities. The first: that He made him go astray from the religion (al-din). The second: that He made him go astray from Paradise. As for the first, namely that God Most High made him go astray from the religion, know that the meaning of "leading astray from the religion" (al-ida' 'an al-din) linguistically is calling to abandoning the religion and making it appear ugly in its essence, and this is the misguidance that God Most High attributed to Iblis, when He said: ﴿Indeed, he is an enemy, a clear misleader﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], and He said: ﴿And I will mislead them and I will arouse in them desires﴾ [al-Nisa': 119], ﴿And those who disbelieved say, "Our Lord, show us the two who misled us from among the jinn and mankind; we will put them under our feet﴾ [Fussilat: 29], and He said: ﴿And Satan made their deeds appealing to them and barred them from the way﴾ [al-Naml: 24], ﴿And Satan said﴾ [Ibrahim: 22], up to His saying: ﴿And I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. Also, God Most High attributed this misguidance to Pharaoh, when He said: ﴿And Pharaoh misled his people and did not guide them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 79].

Know that the community (ummah) is unanimously agreed that misguidance in this sense is not permissible for God Most High, because He did not call to disbelief nor encourage it; rather He forbade it, warned against it, and threatened punishment for it.
