And since the original linguistic meaning of misguidance (al-idlal) is nothing but this, and this meaning is negated by consensus, it is established that there is consensus that this expression may not be taken according to its apparent meaning.

At this point, the people of compulsion (Jabriyyah) and the people of qadar (Qadariyyah) were compelled to interpretation. As for the Jabriyyah, they understood it to mean that God Most High created misguidance and disbelief in them, barred them from faith, and placed a barrier between them and Him; and they sometimes said: this is the literal meaning of the word in its original linguistic usage, since idlal is an expression for making a thing astray, just as ikhraj and idkhal are expressions for making a thing go out and go in. The Mu'tazilah said: this interpretation is not permissible, neither according to linguistic conventions nor according to rational proofs.

* * *

As for linguistic conventions, its clarification is from several aspects:

First: it is not correct, in the language, to say of one who prevents another from taking a path by compulsion and force that he misled him; rather it is said: he prevented him from it and turned him away from it. They only say "he misled him from the path" when he confuses him and presents doubts that obscure the path for him so that he does not find it.

Second: God Most High described Iblis and Pharaoh as misleaders, although Pharaoh and Iblis were not, by agreement, the creators of misguidance in the hearts of those who responded to them. As for the Jabriyyah, it is because the servant has no power to originate; and as for the Qadariyyah, it is because the servant has no power over this kind of origination. So when the name "misleader" is truly applied despite the negation of being a creator, by agreement, we know that the name "misleader" is not established in the language for the Creator of misguidance.

Third: that idlal stands in opposition to guidance; just as it is correct to say, "I guided him, but he was not guided," it must be correct to say, "I misled him, but he was not led astray." And if that is so, it is impossible to interpret idlal as the creation of misguidance.

As for rational proofs, they are of several aspects:

First: if God Most High created misguidance in the servant and then obligated him to believe, He would have obligated him to combine opposites, and that is folly and injustice. God Most High said: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], and He said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and He said: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].

Second: if God Most High were the creator of ignorance and one who confused the obligated, He would not be a clarifier of what the servant is obligated to; yet the community has unanimously agreed that He is a clarifier.

Third: if God Most High had created misguidance in them and barred them from faith, there would be no benefit in sending down books upon them and sending messengers to them; for the thing that is not possible to attain, striving to attain it is futile and foolish.

Fourth: it is in great contradiction with verses such as His saying: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 20], ﴿So what is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49], ﴿And what prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, "Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra': 94]. Thus He made clear that there is absolutely no barrier preventing them from faith, and that they refrained only on account of their denial that messengers would be sent from among humans. And He said: ﴿And what prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them and from seeking forgiveness from their Lord?﴾ [al-Kahf: 55]; and He said: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]; and He said: ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ [Yunus: 32]; and He said: ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ [al-An'am: 95]. So if God Most High had misled them from the religion and turned them away from faith, these verses would be false.

Fifth: God Most High censured Iblis, his party, and whoever follows his way in misleading people from the religion and turning them away from the truth, and He commanded His servants and His Messenger to seek refuge from them, by His saying: ﴿Say, "I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 1] up to His saying: ﴿from the evil of the whisperer﴾ [al-Nas: 4], and ﴿Say, "I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak﴾ [al-Falaq: 1], ﴿And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils﴾, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾. So if God Most High were to mislead His servants from the religion as the devils mislead, He would deserve the same blame they deserve, and it would be obligatory to seek refuge from Him as it is obligatory from them, and it would be obligatory to take Him as an enemy because He misled most of His creation, just as it is obligatory to take Iblis as an enemy for that reason. They (the opponents) say: rather, God's distinction in this is greater; for Iblis's misleading, whether he exists or not, makes no difference regarding the occurrence of misguidance, whereas God's misleading is what truly produces misguidance. From this it follows that Iblis is absolved of all evil and that all of it is attributed to God Most High; so the blame would be cut off entirely from Iblis and return to God, exalted is He above the saying of the wrongdoers.

Sixth: God Most High attributed the misleading from the religion to others and blamed them for it, saying: ﴿And Pharaoh misled his people and did not guide them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 79], ﴿And the Samiri misled them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 85], ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 116], ﴿Indeed, those who go astray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Account﴾ [Sad: 26], and His saying, relating from Iblis: ﴿And I will mislead them and I will arouse in them desires and I will command them﴾ [al-Nisa': 119]. These either misled others from the religion in reality, or God is the One who misled them, or the misleading occurred by God and by them jointly. If God Most High misled them from the religion apart from these, then He has falsely accused them, having charged them with His own deed and reproached them for what they did not do, and God is exalted above that. And if God Most High were a partner with them in that, how could He blame them for an act in which He is a partner and equal with them? And when both possibilities are invalid, it is correct that the creation of misguidance not be attributed to God Most High.

Seventh: God Most High mentioned most of the verses in which misguidance is mentioned as attributed to sinners, as in His saying: ﴿And He does not mislead thereby except the defiantly disobedient﴾, ﴿And Allah misleads the wrongdoers﴾ [Ibrahim: 27], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67], ﴿Thus does Allah mislead whoever is excessive and doubtful﴾ [Ghafir: 34], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is excessive and a liar﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. So if the misguidance attributed to God Most High meant what they are in, that would be establishing the already established, and this is absurd.

Eighth: God Most High negated the divinity of the things they worshipped on the ground that they do not guide to the truth. He said: ﴿Is one who guides to the truth more worthy of being followed or one who does not guide unless he is guided?﴾ [Yunus: 35]. So He negated the lordship of those things on the ground that they do not guide, and affirmed His own lordship on the ground that He, glory be to Him, guides. So if He, glory be to Him, misled from the truth, He would have equaled them in misguidance and in that for which He forbade following them; rather He would have surpassed them, since idols, just as they do not guide, do not mislead, whereas He, glory be to Him, though He is God, guides and also misleads.

Ninth: God Most High mentions this misguidance as a recompense for them for their evil conduct and as a punishment for it. So if what was meant were the misguidance they are already in, that would be punishment and threat with a matter they are already engaged in, inclined toward, delighting in, and content with; and if that were permissible, then punishment for fornication would be fornication, and punishment for drinking wine would be drinking wine, and this is not permissible.

Tenth: the saying of God Most High: ﴿And He does not mislead thereby except the defiantly disobedient﴾ ﴿who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾ is explicit that God only does this misleading to them after they have become, by their own choice, among the defiant ones who break the covenant of Allah. This indicates that this misleading which occurs after they become defiant and covenant-breakers is distinct from their defiance and their breaking.

Eleventh: God Most High explained the misleading attributed to Himself in His Book either as being a trial and test, or as being a punishment and chastisement. As for the trial, He said: ﴿And We have not made the keepers of the Fire except angels, and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31], that is, a test, up to His saying: ﴿Thus does Allah mislead whom He wills and guide whom He wills﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. So He made clear that His misleading of the servant in this way is by sending down a verse that is ambiguous or an act that is ambiguous, whose true purpose is not known; and the one misled thereby is the one who does not stop at the intended meaning and does not reflect on the wisdom in it, but clings to doubts in establishing a false ambiguity, as God Most High said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is unspecific, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. As for punishment and chastisement, it is like His saying: ﴿When the shackles are around their necks and the chains, they will be dragged﴾ [Ghafir: 71], up to His saying: ﴿Thus does Allah mislead the disbelievers﴾ [Ghafir: 74]. So He made clear that His misleading does not exceed one of these two aspects; and when misleading is explained by one of these two aspects, it must not be explained by anything else, to avoid ambiguity. Thus it is established that it is not permissible to interpret misleading as the creation of disbelief and misguidance. And when that is established, we say: we have explained that idlal in the original language is calling to falsehood, encouraging it, and striving to conceal its ugliness, and that is not permissible for God Most High; so it is necessary to resort to interpretation. The interpretation the Jabriyyah adopted we have refuted, so it is necessary to turn to other aspects of interpretation:

First: that when a man goes astray by his own choice upon the occurrence of something, without that thing having had an effect in

صفحة ١٣٠

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 26 (part 4 of 6):

*[Passage continues mid-argument.]* ...the meaning of misguidance (ḍalāl) being attributed to something: it is said of that thing that it "misled" (aḍallahu). Concerning the idols, God, exalted is He, says: ﴿My Lord, they have indeed led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], meaning: they went astray because of them. And He says: ﴿And they have said, "Do not leave your gods, and do not leave Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, or Nasr." And they have certainly led many astray﴾ [Nuh: 23, 24], meaning: many people went astray because of them. And He says: ﴿But what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]. And He says: ﴿But my calling them has only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh: 6], meaning: my calling them did not increase them, for their part, in anything but flight. And He says: ﴿So you took them in mockery until they made you forget My remembrance﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 110]. They did not, in reality, cause them to forget; rather they were reminding them of God and calling them to Him. But since their preoccupation with mockery of them was a cause of their forgetting, the causing of forgetting was attributed to them. And He says in Bara'ah: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, there are among them those who say, "Which of you has this increased in faith?"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124]; ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124]; ﴿And as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has increased them in filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

So God, glorified is He, informs that the descent of a surah containing the laws reveals their states: among them are those who are made upright by it and thereby increase in faith, and among them are those who are corrupted by it and thereby increase in disbelief. Therefore, the increase in faith and the increase in disbelief are attributed to the surah, since they were made upright when it descended and were likewise corrupted. Thus guidance and misguidance are also attributed to God, exalted is He, when their occurrence is at the time of His setting forth parables for them.

And He says in Surah al-Muddaththir: ﴿And We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain and those who believed may increase in faith﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. So God, exalted is He, informs that the mention of the number of the guardians of the Fire is a test from Him for His servants, so that the sincere may be distinguished from the doubter. The outcome was that the believers were made upright by it and the disbelievers were corrupted by it. He attributed the increase in faith and its opposite to those being tested, saying: (so that they may increase) and (so that they may say). Then, after His saying ﴿What did God intend by this as an example?﴾, He said: ﴿Thus God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. So He attributed their misguidance and their guidance to Himself after having attributed both to them together. Thus He made clear that misguidance is explained by this test.

It is also said in common usage: "Love made me ill" (amradani al-ḥubb), meaning: I became ill with it. And it is said: "So-and-so corrupted so-and-so," while she did not know of it. And the poet said:

*Leave off blaming me, for blame is an incitement*

meaning: it incites the one blamed by blaming.

Misguidance (iḍlāl) in this sense may be attributed to God, exalted is He, in the sense that the disbelievers went astray because of the verses containing the trials. So in this verse, when the disbelievers said, "What is the need for parables, and what is their benefit?" and this trial became severe for them, this attribution was apt.

Second: that misguidance (iḍlāl) is naming someone as astray (tasmiyah bi'l-ḍalāl). It is said: "He misled him," i.e., he named him astray and judged him to be so. And "So-and-so declared so-and-so a disbeliever (akfara)" when he named him a disbeliever. They cited the verse of al-Kumayt:

*And a group has declared me a disbeliever for loving you,*
*and a group said: "He is a wrongdoer and a sinner."*

And Tarafah said:

*My drinking of wine never ceased until my friend misled me,*
*and until some of that displeased me.*

He meant: named me astray.

This view was held by Qutrub and many of the Mu'tazilah. Some of the lexicographers denied it and said: one only says "dallaltuhu tadlīlan" when one names him astray; likewise "fassaqtuhu" and "fajjartuhu" when one names him a wrongdoer or a sinner. It was answered that whenever he makes him astray in his own self, it necessarily follows that he becomes one judged to be astray; this judgment is a necessary consequence of that making, and naming the necessitating thing by the necessitated is a well-known and established metaphor. Also, when one man says of another, "So-and-so is astray," it is permissible to say to him, "Why did you make him astray?" and the meaning is: why did you name him so, and why did you judge him to be so? On this view they interpreted misguidance as judgment and naming.

Third: that misguidance (iḍlāl) is leaving alone and abandoning prevention by force and compulsion. It is said, "He misled him" when he left him and his going astray. They said: among its figurative uses is the saying: "So-and-so corrupted his son and destroyed him and ruined him," when he did not oversee his discipline. Similar is the saying of al-'Arji:

*They abandoned me, and what a youth they abandoned,*
*for a day of distress and for sealing a breach.*

And one says of someone who left his sword on wet ground until it rusted and decayed: "You corrupted your sword and rusted it."

Fourth: misguidance and misguiding (ḍalāl and iḍlāl) mean punishment and chastisement, by the proof of His saying: ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness, the Day they are dragged into the Fire on their faces: "Taste the touch of Saqar"﴾ [al-Qamar: 47, 48]. So He described them as being, on the Day of Resurrection, in misguidance, and that is only their punishment. And He says: ﴿When the shackles are around their necks and the chains; they are dragged, in scalding water, then in the Fire they are burned. Then it will be said to them, "Where is that which you used to associate, besides God?" They will say, "They have departed from us; rather, we had not been calling upon anything before." Thus God misleads the disbelievers﴾ [Ghafir: 71–74]. That misguidance was explained as punishment.

Fifth: misguidance (iḍlāl) may be interpreted as destruction and annulment, as in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved and averted [others] from the way of God—He has caused their deeds to be lost﴾ [Muhammad: 1]. It was said: He nullified them and destroyed them. Among its figurative uses is the saying: "The water went astray in the milk," when it became absorbed in it. And one says: "I misled it," when you do that to it, destroying it and making it like the non-existent. From this one says: "The people misled their dead," when they buried him in his grave and concealed him until he was not seen. The poet al-Nabigha said:

*His misleaders returned with a clear sign,*
*and Hazm and Na'il were left at al-Jawlan.*

And God says: ﴿And they say, "When we have gone astray in the earth, will we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10], meaning: when we have been buried in it and our persons have become hidden. On this meaning, it is possible to say: God misleads a person, i.e., destroys him and annihilates him, and so the attribution of misleading to Him, exalted is He, is permissible in this way. These five aspects are when we interpret misleading as misleading from the religion.

Sixth: misleading may be interpreted as misleading from Paradise. The Mu'tazilah said: this is in reality not an interpretation but keeping the word on its apparent meaning, for the verse indicates that He misleads them, and there is no indication in it as to from what He misleads them; so we take it to mean that He misleads them from the path to Paradise. Then they interpreted every instance of this kind in the Qur'an according to this sense; this was the view chosen by al-Jubba'i. God says: ﴿It is decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [al-Hajj: 4]; meaning: He misleads him from Paradise and its reward. All of this applies if we take the hamzah in iḍlāl as making transitive.

Seventh: that we take the hamzah not as making transitive but as indicating finding (al-wujdān), in the sense already explained at the beginning of this issue. It is said: "So-and-so found his camel astray" (aḍalla fulān ba'īrahu), i.e., it went astray from him. Thus the meaning of God's misleading them is that He found them astray.

Eighth: that His saying, ﴿He misleads by it many and guides by it many﴾, is part of the speech of the disbelievers. For they said: "What did God intend by this parable, whose benefit is not apparent?" Then they said: "He misleads by it many and guides by it many," mentioning it in mockery. This is the speech of the disbelievers. Then God, exalted is He, answered them: ﴿And He misleads by it none except the defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning: He has not misled by it except the defiantly disobedient. This is the summary of the Mu'tazilah's discourse.

* * *

The Jabriyyah said: We have heard your speech and acknowledge to you the excellence of your argument, the beauty of its order, and the strength of your discourse. But what can we do, when you have three enemies who confuse these fine aspects and subtle proofs for you?

The first of them: the question of the motive (al-dā'ī): namely, the One Able over knowledge and ignorance, guidance and misguidance—why did He do one of the two and not the other?

*[Page 132]*

The second: the question of knowledge, as its exposition has already preceded in His saying: ﴿God has set a seal upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7]. We have not seen from you, in refuting these two statements, any strong and sound reply; and we certainly know that it is not hidden from you, with your intelligence, that you are weak in respect of those answers which you have spoken. Just as we have been fair and acknowledged to you the excellence of the speech you mentioned, so be fair and acknowledge also that you have no way out of these two aspects, for blindness and heedlessness do not befit the intelligent.

The third: that the act of the servant, if it were by his own origination, would not have resulted except in what he intended to originate. But no one wills except to attain knowledge and guidance, and guards with all caution against ignorance and error. How, then, does ignorance and misguidance come about for the servant, when he intended nothing but attaining knowledge and guidance? If it is said: "He became confused, so that disbelief was confused for him with faith and knowledge with ignorance, and he thought ignorance to be knowledge, so he intended to bring it about, and therefore ignorance came to him"—we reply: his thinking ignorance to be knowledge is a mistaken thought. If he chose it first, then he chose ignorance and error for himself, which is not possible. And if we say that this was confused for him because of another earlier thought, it would follow that before every thought there would be a thought, without end, which is impossible.

The fourth: that conceptions are not acquired, and self-evident assents are not acquired, and all assents are not acquired. These are three premises:

First premise: the demonstration that conceptions are not acquired. For whoever attempts to acquire them: either he is conceiving of them, or he is not conceiving of them. If he is conceiving of them, it is impossible for him to seek to acquire their conception, because acquiring what is already acquired is impossible. If he is not conceiving of them, his mind is heedless of them, and the one heedless of a thing cannot be seeking it.

Second premise: the demonstration that self-evident assents are not acquired, because the obtaining of the two terms of an assent either suffices to make the mind firmly assent to that assent or does not suffice. If the first, then that assent revolves with those two conceptions necessarily, in affirmation and negation, and what is so is not within one's power. If the second, then the assent is not self-evident but depends on something else.

Third premise: the demonstration that all assents are not acquired. For these theoretical propositions, if their necessary consequence from those self-evident premises (which are not within one's power) is necessary, then those theoretical propositions are also not within one's power. And if they are not necessarily consequent from those self-evident premises, then it is impossible to infer those theoretical propositions from those self-evident premises, and so those beliefs obtained in those theoretical propositions are not knowledge, but only a belief held by the one who imitates, and our discussion is not about that. Thus it is established that your claim that guidance and misguidance are not attributed to God, exalted is He, is opposed by these decisive rational aspects, for which there is no answer.

Now let us discuss what they have mentioned of interpretations.

As for the first interpretation, it falls: for the sending down of these ambiguous verses—does it have an effect in moving the motives, or does it have no effect in that? If the first, then according to you it must be deemed defective for two reasons. The first: we have demonstrated in the explanation of His saying ﴿God has set a seal upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7] that whenever preponderance occurs, necessity must occur, and that there is no intermediary between equality and the necessity that excludes the opposite. So when the sending down of these ambiguous verses has an effect in tipping the balance, and it is established that whenever preponderance occurs, necessity has occurred, then compulsion comes in, and what you have said is nullified.

The second: suppose that it does not reach the limit of necessity; still, the responsible person ought to be left without excuse or pretext, and the sending down of these ambiguous verses upon him, despite that...

*[Page 133]*

لَها أثَرًا في تَرْجِيحِ جانِبِ الضَّلالِ عَلى جانِبِ الِاهْتِداءِ كالعُذْرِ لِلْمُكَلَّفِ في عَدَمِ الإقْدامِ عَلى الطّاعَةِ، فَوَجَبَ أنْ يُقَبَّحَ ذَلِكَ مِنَ اللَّهِ تَعالى، وأمّا إنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ لِذَلِكَ أثَرٌ في إقْدامِهِمْ عَلى تَرْجِيحِ جانِبِ الضَّلالِ عَلى جانِبِ الِاهْتِداءِ كانَتْ نِسْبَةُ هَذِهِ المُتَشابِهاتِ إلى ضَلالِهِمْ كَصَرِيرِ البابِ ونَعِيقِ الغُرابِ، فَكَما أنَّ ضَلالَهم لا يُنْسَبُ إلى هَذِهِ الأُمُورِ الأجْنَبِيَّةِ كَذَلِكَ وجَبَ أنْ لا يُنْسَبَ إلى هَذِهِ المُتَشابِهاتِ بِوَجْهٍ ما، وحِينَئِذٍ يَبْطُلُ تَأْوِيلُهم.

As for the second interpretation, namely naming and judgment (التَّسْمِيَةُ والحُكْمُ), although it is extremely far-fetched, the problem remains with it. For if God names him by that and judges him by it, then, should the responsible person not do it, God's report would turn from truth into falsehood and His knowledge into ignorance, and all of that is impossible. Therefore the non-performance of the act by the responsible person is impossible, and his performance of it is necessary. This is precisely the compulsion (الجَبْرُ) from which you flee, and it "will certainly meet you" (﴿وأنَّهُ مُلاقِيكم لا مَحالَةَ﴾). Here the discussion arrives at the two well-known answers to this point, and every intelligent person knows by the immediate judgment of his reason that both are invalid.

As for the third interpretation, namely leaving alone and not preventing, this is called misguidance only if it would have been better and more fitting for the father to prevent his son from that act. But if the son is such that, were his father to prevent him from it, he would fall into a corruption greater than that first corruption, then no one would say that he corrupted his son and misguided him. Here the matter is not like that, for if God were to prevent the responsible person from this corruption by compulsion, a different corruption greater than the first would follow. So how can it be said that God corrupted the responsible person and misguided him, in the sense that He did not prevent him from error, while if He had prevented him that corruption would have been greater?

As for the fourth interpretation, al-Qaffal (d. 1 AH/ca. 9th century, the commentator) objected to it, saying: "We do not accept that *ḍalāl* (error) came with the meaning of punishment. As for His saying, ﴿Indeed the criminals are in error and burning torment﴾ [al-Qamar 54:47], it is possible that what is meant is: in error from the truth in this world, and in burning torment, that is, in the torment of Hell in the Hereafter, and His saying ﴿The Day they are dragged﴾ [al-Qamar 54:48] is a complement of *su'ur* (burning torment). As for His saying, ﴿When the shackles are around their necks﴾ [Ghafir 40:71] up to His saying, ﴿Thus does God misguide the disbelievers﴾ [Ghafir 40:74], the meaning of His saying *ḍallū 'annā* ('they have gone astray from us') is: they perished, so we did not benefit from them on this day, when we were hoping for their intercession. Then His saying, ﴿Thus does God misguide the disbelievers﴾ may mean: thus does God misguide their deeds, that is, He nullifies them on the Day of Resurrection. It may also be understood as: thus does God forsake them in this world, so He does not grant them success to accept the truth, since they have become accustomed to falsehood and turned away from reflection. When God forsakes them and they come on the Day of Resurrection, their deeds, which they were hoping would benefit them in this world, have been nullified."

As for the fifth interpretation, namely destruction (الإهْلاكُ), it is unfitting for this context, because His saying ﴿and He guides many by it﴾ prevents taking *iḍlāl* (misguidance) to mean destruction.

As for the sixth interpretation, namely that He misguides him from the path to Paradise, it is weak, because He said ﴿He misguides by it﴾, that is, He misguides by means of hearing these verses, whereas misguidance from the path to Paradise is not caused by hearing these verses but by his engaging in vile deeds. How then is it permissible to interpret it that way?

As for the seventh interpretation, namely that His saying ﴿He misguides him﴾ [al-An'am 6:125] means "He finds him astray" — we have already shown that there is no proof for the existence of this usage. Furthermore, it has transitively governed *iḍlāl* with the preposition *bā'* (ب) by saying ﴿He misguides by it﴾, and *iḍlāl* in the sense of "finding" is not transitive with the preposition *bā'*.

Page 134

As for the eighth interpretation, in this verse it requires breaking the structure of the discourse, because up to His saying "(He misguides by it many and He guides by it many)" it is the speech of the disbelievers, then His saying ﴿and none misguides by it except the defiantly disobedient﴾ is the speech of God, without any separation between them, rather with the conjunctive particle *wāw* (و). Then, granting that here it is like that, in Surah al-Muddaththir it is His saying ﴿Thus does God misguide whom He wills and guide whom He wills﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], which is undoubtedly the speech of God. This is what is to be said about misguidance.

* * *

As for guidance (الهُدى), it has come in several aspects:

First: indication and clarification. He said, ﴿Did it not guide them how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:26]. And He said, ﴿If guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38]. This holds only if guidance is an expression for clarification. And He said, ﴿They follow only assumption and what their souls desire, though guidance has already come to them from their Lord﴾ [al-Najm 53:23]. And He said, ﴿Indeed We guided him to the way, whether he is grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan 76:3], meaning: whether he gives thanks or disbelieves, guidance has come to him in both states. And He said, ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 41:17]. And He said, ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book, complete for the one who did good, and detailing everything, and guidance and mercy, that perhaps they would believe in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [al-An'am 6:154]; this is not said of a believer. And God said, quoting the adversaries of David, peace be upon him: ﴿And do not be unjust, and guide us to the even path﴾ [Sad 38:22], meaning: show us the way. And He said, ﴿Indeed those who turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them, Satan has beguiled them and given them false hope﴾ [Muhammad 47:25]. And He said, ﴿lest a soul say, "Oh my regret over what I neglected in regard to God"﴾ [al-Zumar 39:56], up to His saying ﴿or say, "If God had guided me, I would have been among the righteous"﴾ [al-Zumar 39:57], up to His saying ﴿Yes, My verses did come to you, but you denied them and were arrogant﴾ [al-Zumar 39:59]. He informs that He had guided the disbeliever by the verses that came to him. And He said, ﴿Or you say, "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them." Clear proof has now come to you from your Lord, and guidance﴾ [al-An'am 6:157]. This address is to the disbelievers.

Second: they said regarding His saying ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura 42:52], meaning: you call (to it). And His saying ﴿and for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:7], meaning: a caller who calls them to error or to guidance.

Third: success from God through favours conditioned upon faith, which He bestows upon the believers as a reward for their faith, and as help for it and for increasing in His obedience. This is a reward for them. Its opposite for the disbelievers is that He deprives them of that, so that, although God has not guided them, He has in effect misguided them. The evidence for this aspect is His saying, ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad 47:17], ﴿and God increases in guidance those who are guided﴾ [Maryam 19:76], ﴿and God does not guide the unjust people﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:258], ﴿God makes firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the Hereafter, and God misguides the wrongdoers﴾ [Ibrahim 14:27], ﴿How will God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, and had testified that the Messenger is true and clear proofs had come to them? And God does not guide the unjust people﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:86]. Thus He informs that He does not guide them, and that clear proofs had come to them; so this guidance is undoubtedly other than clarification. And God said, ﴿And whoever believes in God, He guides his heart﴾ [al-Taghabun 64:11], and ﴿Those, He has written faith into their hearts and strengthened them with a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Mujadila 58:22].

Fourth: guidance to the path to Paradise. God said, ﴿As for those who believed in God and held fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty, and guide them to Himself on a straight path﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:175]. And He said, ﴿There has come to you from God a light and a clear Book, by which God guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace, and brings them out of darknesses into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:15-16]. And He said, ﴿And those who are killed in the cause of God, He will not let their deeds go astray. He will guide them and set their minds at ease, and admit them into Paradise﴾ [Muhammad 47:4-6]. Guidance after killing can only be to Paradise. And God said, ﴿Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith; rivers will flow beneath them﴾ [Yunus 10:9]. This is the interpretation of al-Jubba'i (d. 303 AH, a leading Mu'tazili scholar).

Fifth: guidance in the sense of preceding. It is said, "Such-and-such guided such-and-such," meaning he preceded him in front of him. The origin of *hadā* is from guiding the road, because the guide precedes the one guided. The Arabs say, "The *hawādī* of the horses came forward," meaning their front parts. The neck is called *hādī*, and the *hawādī* of the horses are their necks, because they go in front.

Sixth: *yahdī*, meaning that He judges the believer to be guided, and its being so named is because the reality of the speaker's saying "*hadāhu*" (he guided him) is: he made him guided. This word may be applied to judgment and naming. God said, ﴿God did not appoint any bahira (slit-eared she-camel)﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:103], meaning: He did not judge or legislate. And He said, ﴿Indeed guidance is the guidance of God﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:73], meaning that guidance is what God has judged to be guidance. And He said, ﴿Whom God guides, he is the one guided﴾ [al-Kahf 18:17], meaning: whomever God judges to be guided, he is the one deserving to be named "guided." These are the aspects mentioned by the Mu'tazilah (the Rationalist school), and we have discussed them previously in the section on misguidance.

The Jabriyyah (determinist school) said: Here there is another aspect, namely that guidance means the creation of the guidance and knowledge. God said, ﴿And God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus 10:25]. The Qadariyyah (the school upholding human free will) said: This is not permissible, for several reasons.

First: it is not valid in the language to say of one who compels another to take a path by force and coercion that "he guided him to it." One says only that he returned him to the straight path, or drove him to it, or dragged him to it. But to say, "He guided him to it," is not valid.

Second: if that occurred by the creation of God, Most High, then commanding, forbidding, praise, blame, reward, and punishment would all be void. If it is said, "Grant that it is God's creation, but it is the servant's acquisition (*kasb*)," we reply that this acquisition is refuted in two respects.

The first: the occurrence of this movement is either by God's creating it or not by His creating it. If by His creating it, then whenever God creates it, it becomes impossible for the servant to refrain from it, and whenever He does not create it, it becomes impossible for the servant to perform it, and then the aforementioned problems arise. If it is not by God's creating it, but from the servant, then this is the doctrine of Mu'tazilism.

The second: if it were God's creation and the servant's acquisition, it could not be free of one of three aspects: either God creates it first and then the servant acquires it, or the servant acquires it first and then God creates it, or both occur together. If God creates it, the servant is compelled in acquiring it, and the objection recurs. If the servant acquires it first, then God is compelled in creating it. If both occur together, then this matter must not occur except after their agreement; but this agreement is not known to us, so it must be that this agreement does not occur. Furthermore, this agreement must not occur except through another agreement, since it is from His acquisition and act, and that leads to an infinite regress of agreements, which is impossible. This is the summary of the Mu'tazilah's speech.

The Jabriyyah said: We have demonstrated by rational proofs that admit of no doubt or figurative interpretation that the creator of these acts is God, Most High, either through an intermediary or without an intermediary. The aspects you have relied upon are transmitted textual aspects that admit of possibility, and the definitive is not opposed by the probable. Therefore it is necessary to adopt what we have said. And success is from God.

* * *

Question sixteen: One may ask: Why were the guided described as many, when fewness is their attribute, as in His saying, ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba' 34:13], ﴿and few are they﴾ [Sad 38:24], and the hadith: "People are like a hundred camels, among which you will not find a single riding-camel," and the hadith: "People: test them and you will despise them"? The answer: The people of guidance are many in themselves, and where they are described as few, they are described as few only in comparison with the people of error. Furthermore, the few among the guided are in reality many, even if they are few in outward form, so they are called "many" by reference to the reality.

Question Seventeen: al-Farra' said: the word fasiq (ṣinful, one who transgresses; lit. "defiant") is originally derived from their saying: "fasaqat al-rutbah min qishriha," meaning it came out of its skin. So the fasiq is one who goes out of obedience. The mouse is called fuwaysiqah because it comes out (of its hole) to cause harm. The people of the qiblah (i.e., the Muslims) differed over whether the fasiq is a believer or a disbeliever. According to our companions (the Ash'ariyyah), he is a believer; according to the Khawarij, he is a disbeliever; and according to the Mu'tazilah, he is neither a believer nor a disbeliever. The opponent argued with the words of the Exalted: ﴿How evil is the name of defiance after faith﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and He said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], and He said: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you the faith and made it pleasing in your hearts, and He has made hateful to you disbelief, defiance, and disobedience﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. This question is lengthy and is discussed in the science of kalam (theology).

**The Seventeenth Issue** (al-mas'alah al-thaminah 'ashrah)... 

Let me correct the numbering: this passage begins with the eighteenth issue.

**The Eighteenth Issue:** The scholars differed over the meaning of the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾, and they mentioned several views.

The first: The "covenant" here refers to His proofs established upon His servants, which indicate to them the soundness of His Oneness and the truthfulness of His messengers. These proofs thus constitute a covenant and a pledge to hold fast to the Oneness of God, since by these proofs it becomes binding to hold fast to Oneness and other things we have mentioned. For this reason His words are valid: ﴿Fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40].

The second: It may mean what is indicated by His words: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a warner came to them, they would be better guided than any of the nations. But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾ [Fatir: 42]. When they did not do what they had sworn to do, He described them as breakers of His covenant and pledge. The first interpretation allows the verse to be general, applying to everyone who goes astray and disbelieves, whereas the second can apply only to those bound by this oath. If this is established, the superiority of the first interpretation over the second appears in two respects:

First: On the first interpretation the verse can be taken in its general sense, whereas on the second it requires restriction (takhsis).

Second: On the first interpretation, blame is due to them because they broke a covenant that Allah had confirmed and made firm through the evidences He sent down, which He repeated to them in themselves and in the horizons, which He made clear, removing confusion from them, and through the proofs He deposited in their intellects, and by sending prophets and revealing books confirming them. As for the second interpretation, blame is due to them because they abandoned something they had themselves committed to. It is well known that ordering the blame on the first basis is more fitting.

The third: al-Qaffal said: It is possible that the intended people in the verse are a group from the People of the Book, upon whom a covenant and pledge were taken in the Books revealed to their prophets, to confirm Muhammad (ﷺ), and to explain to them his affair and the affair of his community. They broke that, turned away from it, and denied his prophethood.

The fourth: Some said that He meant by it a covenant He took from people while they were in the form of atoms, and brought them forth from the loins of Adam in that manner. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. The theologians said: This is invalid, because He, exalted is He, does not hold His servants to account for a covenant and pledge of which they are unaware, just as He does not punish them for what has left their hearts through forgetfulness and neglect. How, then, could it be permissible for Him to reproach them for that?

The fifth: Allah's covenant with His creation is of three kinds. The first covenant is the one He took from all the descendants of Adam, which is the acknowledgment of His lordship, as in His words: ﴿And when your Lord took...﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. The second is a covenant He specifically took from the prophets, that they should convey the message, establish the religion, and not divide over it, as in His words: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7]. The third is a covenant He specifically took from the scholars, as in His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book: "You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: The pronoun in "covenant" (mithaqihi) refers to the pledge, which is what they bound themselves by when accepting the covenant of Allah. It may also mean "its binding" (tawthiq), just as al-mi'ad and al-milad mean al-wa'd and al-wiladah. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to Allah, exalted is He, meaning after He had confirmed His covenant through His signs, His books and His messengers.

* * *

**The Nineteenth Issue:** The scholars differed over the meaning of the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾, and they mentioned several views:

The first: It refers to severing the ties of kinship and the rights of relatives which Allah commanded to be maintained. This is like His words: ﴿Then would you, if you turned away, cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Muhammad: 22]. It also points to the fact that they severed the kinship between them and the Prophet (ﷺ). On this interpretation, the verse is specific.

The second: Allah commanded them to join their rope with the rope of the believers, but they severed themselves from the believers and allied with the disbelievers. That is what is meant by His words: ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾.

The third: They were forbidden from strife and stirring up discord, and they were occupied with exactly that.

**The Twentieth Issue:** As for His words: ﴿And they cause corruption on the earth﴾, the more apparent view is that it refers to corruption that extends beyond themselves. The more apparent view is that it means barring people from obedience to the Messenger (peace be upon him), because the complete righteousness on earth lies in obedience; for by adhering to the laws a person fulfils all that is incumbent upon him and refrains from transgressing against others. From this comes the removal of oppression, and in its removal is the justice upon which the heavens and the earth stand. Allah related of Pharaoh that he said: ﴿Indeed I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾ [Ghafir: 26]. Then He, glorified and exalted, informed that whoever does these deeds is a loser, saying: ﴿Those are the losers.﴾ There are several aspects to this loss:

First: They lost the bliss of Paradise, for there is no one who does not have in Paradise a dwelling and a place. If he obeys Allah, he finds it; if he disobeys Him, the believers inherit it. That is His words: ﴿Those are the inheritors, who will inherit al-Firdaws; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10–11], and He said: ﴿Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Shura: 45].

Second: They lost their good deeds which they had done, because they nullified them by their disbelief, so no good or reward reached them from them. The verse concerns the Jews, who had deeds under their own law, and the hypocrites, who in outward appearance do what the sincere do; all of that was nullified.

Third: They persisted in disbelief only out of fear that worldly pleasures would escape them, yet those pleasures escape them anyway, either when the Messenger (ﷺ) is permitted to wage jihad or at their death. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In sum, "loser" is a general term applied to everyone who performs an action for which he receives no recompense, so he is called a loser, like the man who exerts himself and acts in a matter but gains no benefit from it; it is said of him: "he failed and lost," because he is like one who gave something and received nothing in return to take its place. Thus He called the disbelievers who commit acts of disobedience to Allah "losers." He said: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Asr: 2–3], and He said: ﴿Say: "Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is wasted in the life of this world"﴾ [al-Kahf: 103–104]. And Allah knows best.

[Page 137 onward, as the passage begins]

Know that He, glory be to Him and exalted, when He spoke about the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood and the resurrection up to this point, then from this point up to His saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 40), spoke about explaining the blessings that encompass all accountable people, and they are four.

The first of them is the blessing of life, which is mentioned in this verse. Know that His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾ is, although in the form of a question, intended as a rebuke and reproach, because the greatness of a blessing necessitates the greatness of disobedience toward the Benefactor. This is shown by the fact that the more a father's favour to his child is great, by raising him, teaching him, educating him, providing for him and placing him in good circumstances, the greater his child's disobedience toward him becomes. Thus God, glory be to Him and exalted, showed by this the greatness of what they had undertaken of disbelief, by reminding them of His great blessings upon them, so that He might deter them by this from what they had undertaken of clinging to disbelief, and prompt them to acquire faith. He mentioned among His blessings that which is the foundation of all blessings, which is life. This is the overall aim.

If it is said: Why was the first conjunction with fā' (فَ, "then/so") and the rest with thumma (ثُمَّ, "then, after an interval")? We say: because the first life may be followed by death without delay, whereas death is separated from life by an interval, and the second life is likewise separated from death by a clear interval, if by it is meant the resurrection. Here there are several issues.

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates that disbelief originates from the servants, in several respects.

One of them: If He were the Creator of disbelief in them, it would not be permissible for Him to say, rebuking them: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾, just as it is not permissible to say: "How do you become black, become white, become healthy, or become sick?" since all of that is created in them by Him.

The second: If He created them first for wretchedness and the Fire, and He did not intend their creation except for disbelief and the intention that they fall into the Fire, how can it be sound for Him to say to them, rebuking them: "How can you disbelieve?"

The third: How can it be conceived from the All-Wise that He says to them: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾ at the very time He creates disbelief in them, and says: ﴿And what prevented people from believing?﴾ (Al-Isra: 94) at the very time He prevents them from faith, and says: ﴿Why do they not believe?﴾ (Al-Inshiqaq: 20), ﴿Why are they turning away from the reminder?﴾ (Al-Muddaththir: 49), while He creates in them turning away; and He says: ﴿Then where are you deluded?﴾ (Al-An'am: 95), ﴿Then where are you turned away?﴾ (Yunus: 32), while He creates in them delusion and turning away? Such speech, by which it would be regarded as mockery, is more fitting than that it be mentioned in the context of establishing the proof against the servants.

The fourth: When God says to the servants: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾, has He mentioned this speech to direct the proof against the servant and to demand an answer from him, or not? If He did not intend this meaning, there would be no benefit in mentioning it, and this address would be futile. And if He mentioned it to direct the proof against the servant, then the servant may say: many matters have occurred in my case that necessitate disbelief.

The first is that You knew of disbelief from me, and knowledge of disbelief necessitates disbelief. The second is that You willed disbelief from me, and this will necessitates it. The third is that You created disbelief in me, and I am not able to remove Your act. The fourth is that You created in me a power that necessitates disbelief. The fifth is that You created in me a will that necessitates disbelief. The sixth is that You created in me a power that necessitates the will that necessitates disbelief. Then, when these six causes are present in the occurrence of disbelief and faith, the six causes are determined in the case of faith, and all of them were absent. So there are twelve causes for the absence of faith, each one of which independently prevents faith. And with the presence of these many causes, how can it be conceived that it be said: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾

The fifth: He said to His Messenger: Say to them: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God, who has bestowed upon you this great blessing?﴾, meaning the blessing of life. According to the view of the Jabriyyah (determinists), God has no blessing upon the disbeliever, because in their view everything God does to the disbeliever He does only to lead him gradually into disbelief and to burn him in the Fire. So what blessing would God have upon the servant on this assumption? Would that not be like one who presents to another a dish of poisoned halwa? Its outward appearance is delicious and is regarded as a blessing, but since its inward part is deadly, no one regards it as a blessing. And it is known that everlasting punishment is more harmful than that poison. So God has no blessing upon the disbeliever. How then does He command His Messenger to say to them: "How can you disbelieve in Him who has bestowed upon you these great blessings?"

The answer: These aspects, upon investigation, return in their conclusion to adherence to the method of praise and blame, command and prohibition, reward and punishment. So we too confront them with the reasoning relied upon in this doubt, which is that God, glory be to Him and exalted, knew that it would not occur. If it were to occur, His knowledge would turn into ignorance, and that is impossible; and what necessitates the impossible is impossible. So its occurrence is impossible, while He said: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ Furthermore, if the power to disbelieve is capable of faith, it is impossible for it to be the source of faith specifically unless there is a determining factor. If that determining factor comes from the servant, the question returns; and if it comes from God, then as long as that determining factor has not come from God, the occurrence of disbelief is impossible; and when that determining factor occurs, it becomes necessary. On this basis, how is His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾ not conceivable?

Know that when a Mu'tazilite lengthens his speech and multiplies his arguments concerning praise and blame, then it is incumbent upon you to confront them with these two aspects, for they demolish all his speech and confuse all his doubts. And success is from God.

* * *

The second issue: They agreed that His saying: ﴿and you were dead﴾ means: you were dust and drops of semen, because the beginning of Adam's creation was from dust, and all accountable people among his descendants were created from drops of semen, except for Jesus, upon him be peace. However, they differed as to whether the application of the term "dead" to what is inanimate is literal or metaphorical. Most of them held that it is metaphorical, because it likens the lifeless to the dead, and neither of the two is part of the other in any way, since the dead is that to which death occurs, and it must have the characteristics of one who is customarily capable of being alive, such as flesh and moisture. The earlier scholars said it is literal, and this is narrated from Qatadah, who said: "They were dead in their fathers' loins, so God gave them life, then brought them forth, then caused them the death that is unavoidable, then gave them life after death. So there are two lives and two deaths." They argued with His saying: ﴿He created death and life﴾ (Al-Mulk: 2), and the death that precedes life is their being lifeless, which indicates that applying the term "dead" to the lifeless is established literally. The first view is closer to the truth, because it is said of the inanimate that it is lifeless (mawat), and not dead (mayyit), so it is likely that the use of one for the other is by way of likeness. Al-Qaffal said: This is like His saying: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ (Al-Insan: 1). God made clear that man was not a thing worth mentioning, then God made him living, and made him hearing and seeing. Its metaphorical use is from the expressions: "So-and-so is dead in remembrance" (mayyit al-dhikr), "This matter is dead," and "This commodity is dead" when it has no seeker and no one mentions it. Al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di said:

"You revived my remembrance, though I was not obscure; yet some remembrance is more distinguished than other."

So likewise the meaning of the verse: ﴿and you were dead﴾, that is, obscure, with no mention of you, because you were not a thing; ﴿then He gave you life﴾, that is, then He made you a created being, hearing and seeing.

* * *

The third issue: Some people used this verse to refute the punishment of the grave. They said: God has explained that He gives them life once in this world and once in the Hereafter, and did not mention life in the grave. This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿Then indeed you, after that, will surely die﴾ and ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised up﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 15-16), and He did not mention life between these two states. They said: It is not permissible to use as evidence His saying: ﴿They will say: Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice and given us life twice﴾ (Ghafir: 11), because this is the saying of the disbelievers. And because many people have affirmed a life of the seeds of descendants in the loins of Adam, upon him be peace, when He brought them forth and said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ (Al-A'raf: 172). On this assumption, two lives and two deaths occur without any need to affirm a life in the grave. The answer: The absence of mention in this verse does not necessitate that it does not occur.

Also, one may say: God has mentioned the life of the grave in this verse, because His saying: ﴿Then He gives you life﴾ is not the everlasting life, since otherwise it would not be correct for Him to say: ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾, because the particle thumma (ثُمَّ) requires an interval, while the return to God occurs immediately after everlasting life without any interval. So if we take the verse from this angle as evidence for the life of the grave, it is close to correct.

* * *

The fourth issue: Al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, said: His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾ refers to the general people. As for some people, He caused them to die three times, as in what He related in His saying: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town which was in ruins with its roofs fallen in﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 259), up to His saying: ﴿So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 259); and like His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who left their homes in their thousands, fearing death? God said to them: Die, then He gave them life﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 243); and like His saying: ﴿Then the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on﴾ and ﴿Then We raised you after your death﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 55); and like His saying: ﴿So We said: Strike him with part of it; thus God gives life to the dead﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 73); and like His saying: ﴿And thus We made them known, so that they might know that the promise of God is true and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾ (Al-Kahf: 21); and like His saying in the story of Job, upon him be peace: ﴿And We gave him his family and with them the like of them﴾ (Al-Anbiya: 84), for God returned to him his family after He had caused them to die.

* * *

The fifth issue: The Mujassimah (anthropomorphists) held to His saying: ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾ as proof that He is in a place. This is weak. What is meant is that they will be returned to His judgment, because He raises up those in the graves and gathers them in the place of assembly, and that is the return to God, the Exalted. It is described thus only because it is a return to a place where no one else administers judgment, like the saying: "His affair was returned to the amir," meaning to a place where no one else judges.

* * *

The sixth issue: This verse indicates several matters. First: it indicates that no one is able to give life and cause death except God, the Exalted. By this the view of the naturalists (ahl al-taba'i') is refuted, that the one who affects life and death is such-and-such from the spheres, the stars, the elements and the temperaments, as God related about a people in His saying: ﴿And they say: There is only our life of this world; we die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time﴾ (Al-Jathiyah: 24).

Second: it indicates the truth of the resurrection and the gathering, along with an alert to the rational proof that indicates it, because He explained that He gave life to these things after their death the first time, so it is necessary that this be possible the second time.

Third: it indicates obligation, encouragement and warning.

Fourth: it indicates predestination and divine decree (al-jabr wa-al-qadar), as its explanation has already passed.

Fifth: it indicates that worldly asceticism (zuhd) is obligatory, because He said: ﴿Then He gave you life, then He causes you to die, then He will give you life again﴾. He made clear that death is unavoidable. Then He made clear that a person is not left in this state of death, but must return to Him. As for the fact that death is unavoidable, Glorified and Exalted is He has made clear that after a person was a drop of semen, God gave him life, formed him in the best form, made him a complete human being, perfected his intellect, and made him discerning of the kinds of benefit and harm. He granted him wealth, children, houses and palaces. Then the Exalted removes all of that from him by causing him to die and bringing him to a state in which he owns nothing, and no news or trace of him remains in this world. He remains in the grave for a long period, as the Exalted said: ﴿And behind them is a barrier (barzakh)﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100]. He is called and does not answer, he is questioned and does not speak. Then his close relatives do not visit him, and his family and children forget him, as Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi said:

"My relatives pass by the place of my grave,
as though my relatives did not know me."

He also said: "My God, it is as if I see my soul when they have laid it in its pit, and the mourners have turned away from its burial, and the stranger wept over it because of its strangeness, and the one who loved it called to it from the edge of the grave, and the enemies had mercy on it at its distress, and the helplessness of its state was not hidden from those who looked on. My only hope is that You will say what My angels say: 'Look at one who is alone, whom the closest have abandoned, and one whom his loved ones have rejected. He was near to Me, and in the grave he is a stranger. He had in the world one who called him and one who answered him, and he hoped for My kindness at his arrival at this house. So be kind to me there, O Ancient of kindness, and fulfill my hope in You, O Vast in forgiveness.'"

As for the fact that return to God is unavoidable: He, Glorified is He, commands that the trumpet be blown, ﴿and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. He said: ﴿They will emerge from the graves rushing, as if they were hastening to a shrine﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43]. Then they will be presented to God, as He said: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ [al-Kahf: 48]. They will stand humbled and submissive, as He said: ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 108].

Some of them said: "Our God, when we rise from the dust of the graves, our heads will be dust-covered, our faces pale from the intensity of fear, our heads bowed from the terror of the Resurrection, our bellies hungry from the length of the Day of Judgment, our private parts exposed to the people of the place of standing, and our backs burdened by the weight of sins. We will remain bewildered about our affairs, regretful for our sins. So do not let the calamities grow heavier by Your turning away from us, and expand Your mercy and forgiveness for us, O Greatly Merciful, O Vast in forgiveness."

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 29 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He it is who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven and fashioned them as seven heavens. And He is Knowing of all things.﴾

Know that this is the second blessing, which encompasses all the responsible (mukallafin) without exception. How excellent is the order that God, glorified and exalted, has arranged here. The benefit of the earth and the heaven only comes after life has been established. Therefore God mentioned the matter of life first, then followed it with the mention of the heaven and the earth.

As for His saying ﴿created﴾, its explanation has already passed in His saying: ﴿Worship your Lord, who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. As for His saying ﴿for you﴾, it indicates that what is mentioned after ﴿created﴾ is for our benefit in both religion and worldly life. In worldly life it is so that our bodies may be made right and so that we may be strengthened by it for acts of obedience. In religion it is for deriving proofs from these things and taking lessons from them.

By His saying ﴿all that is on the earth﴾ He gathered all the benefits. Some of them relate to animals, plants, minerals and mountains, and some relate to the various crafts and the matters that intelligent people have devised. God explained that He created all of these so that they may be benefited from, as He said: ﴿And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 13]. It is as if God, glorified and exalted, were saying: How do you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life? And how do you disbelieve in God when He has created for you all that is in the heavens and on the earth? Or it may be said: How do you disbelieve in God's power to restore you, when He has given you life after your death? And since He created for you all that is on the earth, how could He be unable to restore you?

Then He mentioned the details of these benefits in different surahs, as He said: ﴿That We poured down the water in torrents﴾ [Abasa: 25], and in the beginning of the surah "When God's command comes" He said: ﴿And the cattle, He created them for you﴾ [al-Nahl: 5], to the end of the verse. Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: God, glorified and exalted, does not act for a purpose (gharad). For if He did, He would be perfected by that purpose, and whoever is perfected by another is deficient in his essence, and that is impossible for God, exalted is He. If it is said: His act is caused by a purpose that does not return to Him but to another, we say: Does the return of that purpose to that other party benefit God more than its not returning to Him, or not? If it is more beneficial to Him, then He has benefited from that act, and the forbidden matter mentioned returns. If it is the second case, then achieving that purpose for that other party is not a purpose for God, exalted is He, and so it does not affect Him.

The second: Whoever does an act for a purpose is unable to achieve that purpose except through that act, and inability is impossible for God.

The third: If God acted for a purpose, that purpose would either be eternal, which would require the eternity of the act, or it would be originated, in which case His act for that purpose would be for another purpose, and this leads to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible.

The fourth: If God acted for a purpose, that purpose would be the preservation of the interest of the responsible persons. And if His capacity to act depended on that, He would not have done what is harmful to them. But He has done that, in that He imposed obligations on one whom He knew would not believe.

Then they (the scholars) spoke about the lam (the particle "for") in His saying ﴿He created for you all that is on the earth﴾ and in His saying ﴿except that they worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. They said: When God does something which, if another did it, would be done for that thing for the sake of a purpose, God has therefore applied the word "purpose" to Him because of this resemblance.

* * *

**The second issue:** The people of permissiveness (Ahl al-Ibahah) argued by His saying ﴿He created for you all that is on the earth﴾ that God created everything for everyone, so no one has any exclusive right to anything at all. This argument is weak, because God set the whole against the whole, which requires setting the individual against the individual, and specification is derived from a separate proof. The jurists, may God have mercy on them, used this verse to establish that the original ruling on benefits is permissibility (ibahah), and we have explained this in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

**The third issue:** It has been said that the verse indicates the prohibition of eating clay, because God created for us what is on the earth and not the earth itself. It may be replied that the whole earth includes what can be said to be "in the earth," so it is a gathering of both meanings. There is no doubt that minerals are included in this, and likewise the roots of the earth and what is similar to some of them. Also, specifying a thing by mention does not indicate the negation of the ruling for other than it.

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿He created for you all that is on the earth﴾ implies that need cannot be attributed to God, for otherwise He would have created these things for Himself too, not only for others.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿then He turned to the heaven﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Istiwa' (turning, rising straight) in the language of the Arabs may mean standing upright, whose opposite is crookedness. Since that is one of the attributes of bodies, God must be exalted above it. Also, there is in the verse something that shows its corruption, because His saying ﴿then﴾ requires a gap in time. If the meaning of this istiwa' were elevation in place, that elevation would have been present first, and if it had been present first, it would not have come after the creation of what is on the earth.

But His saying ﴿then﴾ requires a temporal gap, and since this is established, interpretation (ta'wil) becomes obligatory. Its explanation is that istiwa' is straightness. It is said: "The stick became straight" when it stood up and was level. Then it was said: "He turned to it" like an arrow that is released when it aims directly at its target, without turning to anything else. From this the phrase ﴿then He turned to the heaven﴾ is borrowed, meaning: He created the heaven after the earth, without placing any time between them, and without intending anything else after His creation of the earth.

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿He it is who created for you all that is on the earth, then He turned to the heaven﴾ is explained by His saying: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds. And He placed on it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance in four days, equally for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat: 9-10]. This means the measuring of the earth in two days and the measuring of its provisions in two other days, just as one says: "From Kufa to Medina is twenty days, and to Mecca thirty days," meaning that all of that is this amount. Then He turned to the heaven in two other days, and the total of all this is six days, as He said: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ [al-A'raf: 54].

* * *

**The third issue:** Some of the heretics (al-mulhidah) said: This verse indicates that the creation of the earth was before the creation of the heaven. Likewise His saying ﴿Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 9], up to His saying ﴿then He turned to the heaven﴾. And He said in the surah al-Nazi'at: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He built it. He raised its height and made it level. He darkened its night and brought forth its morning. And the earth, after that, He spread it out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27-30]. This indicates that the creation of the earth was after the heaven. The scholars mentioned several answers to this:

The first: It is possible that the earth was created before the heaven, but He did not spread it out until He had created the heaven, because spreading (tadhiyah) is extension. It may be said: This matter is problematic in two respects:

First: The earth is a massive body, so it is impossible for its creation to be separated from its spreading. If its spreading is after the creation of the heaven, then its creation is also necessarily after the creation of the heaven.

Second: His saying ﴿He created for you all that is on the earth, then He turned to the heaven﴾ indicates that the creation of the earth and the creation of everything in it is before the creation of the heaven. But the creation of things in the earth is not possible unless it has been spread out. So this verse requires that its being spread out precede the creation of the heaven, and then a contradiction is established.

The answer: His saying ﴿And the earth, after that, He spread it out﴾ requires that the creation of the heaven precede the earth, and does not require that the levelling of the heaven precede the creation of the earth. On this assumption the contradiction disappears. It may be said: His saying ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He built it. He raised its height and made it level﴾ requires that the creation of the heaven and its levelling precede the spreading of the earth. But the spreading of the earth is inseparable from the creation of the earth's very substance, for the substance of the heaven and its levelling precede the substance of the earth. In that case the question returns.

The third, and this is the correct answer: His saying "then" (thumma) here is not for sequence, but is by way of enumerating blessings. An example of this is a man saying to another: "Did I not give you great blessings, then raise your rank, then repel the adversaries from you?" Some of what he delayed in mention may have happened earlier. So it is likewise here, and God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** The pronoun in ﴿fashioned them﴾ (fasawwahunna) is an ambiguous pronoun, and "seven heavens" is its explanation, like His saying "his Lord, a man" (rabbahu rajulan). Its benefit is that when the ambiguous is made clear, it is more majestic and grander than if it were stated first, because when it is left ambiguous, souls become eager to learn about it, and after the explanation there is a cure for that eagerness. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the heaven, and "the heaven" is in the sense of a genus. It has also been said that it is the plural of "sima'ah." The Arabic reading preferred is the first. The meaning of "fashioning them" is making their creation balanced, freeing it from crookedness and flaws, and completing their creation.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** Know that the Qur'an here has indicated the existence of seven heavens. The astronomers (ashab al-hay'ah) said: The nearest of them to us is the sphere of the moon, above it the sphere of Mercury, then the sphere of Venus, then the sphere of the sun, then the sphere of Mars, then the sphere of Jupiter, then the sphere of Saturn. They said: There is no way to know this order except by two means:

The first: Occultation. When a lower star passes between our sight and a higher star, they appear as one star, and the occulting body is distinguished from the occulted by its being the dominant one, like the redness of Mars, the yellowness of Mercury, the whiteness of Venus, the blueness of Jupiter, and the dimness of Saturn. Likewise the ancients found that the moon eclipses the six planets, and Mercury eclipses Venus, and Venus eclipses Mars. This order by this method indicates that the sun is above the moon, since the sun is eclipsed by it. But it does not indicate that the sun is below or above the rest of the planets, because it is not eclipsed by any of them, since the other planets vanish when it rises. At this point they mentioned two methods:

One of them: Some of them said that he saw Venus like a mole on the face of the sun. This is weak, because some of them claimed that there is a mole on the face of the sun, just as there is a blemish (mahw) on the face of the moon.

Second point: the difference in viewing position (ikhtilaf al-manzar). This is perceptible for the Moon, Mercury and Venus, but not perceptible for Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. As for the Sun, it is very slight. Therefore the Sun must be intermediate between the two categories. This is what most (scholars) have said. However, Abu al-Rayhan said in his summary of al-Farghani's Fusul: "The difference in viewing position is perceived only for the Moon." Thus these considerations are invalidated, and the position of the Sun remains uncertain.

Know that the astronomers (ashab al-arsad) and the masters of cosmology (arbab al-hay'a) claim that the spheres are nine. The seven are these that we have mentioned. The eighth sphere is that in which the fixed stars are situated. As for the ninth sphere, it is the Greatest Sphere (al-falak al-a'zam), which rotates once approximately every day and night. They argued for the existence of the eighth sphere by saying: We have found that these fixed stars have slow movements, and it is established that stars move only by the movement of their sphere, and the spheres carrying these wandering bodies move with rapid movements. So there must be another body moving with a slow movement, which is the carrier of these fixed stars. This proof is weak in several respects:

First: Why is it not permissible to say: the stars move by themselves, without being fixed in another body? This possibility does not fail except by invalidating the one who chooses (al-mukhtar), and short of that is hard labour (kharṭ al-qatad).
