Second: Granting that, why is it not permissible to say: these stars are fixed in the representative bodies of the wandering planets (mumaththilat al-sayyarat), and the wandering planets are fixed in their carriers? In that case there is no need to establish the eighth sphere.

Third: Why is it not permissible that this sphere is beneath the sphere of the Moon, so that it is beneath the spheres of the planets rather than above them? If it is said: We see these wandering planets eclipse these fixed stars, and the eclipsing body is necessarily beneath the eclipsed one. We reply: These wandering planets only eclipse the fixed stars near the zodiac belt (al-mintaqa), but not those near the two poles. So why is it not permissible to say: these fixed stars near the zodiac belt are fixed in the eighth sphere which is above the sphere of Saturn, and these fixed stars near the two poles, which cannot be eclipsed by the planets, are fixed in another sphere beneath the sphere of the Moon? This possibility has no refutation. Then we say: Suppose you have established these nine spheres, what has shown you the negation of a tenth sphere? The most that can be said is that observation has indicated only this much
Page 145
but the absence of evidence does not prove the absence of what is evidenced. What confirms this is that one of the investigating scholars among them said: "It has not become clear to me until now whether the sphere of the fixed stars is one sphere or spheres enfolded one within another." I say: This possibility is real, because what is used to prove the unity of the sphere of the fixed stars is nothing more than saying: their movements are similar, and whenever this is the case they are fixed in one sphere. Both premises are not certain.

As for the first: their movements, although they are one in perception, may in reality not be one. For if we assume that one of them completes its circuit in thirty-six thousand years, and another completes the circuit in a similar period less one year, then when we distribute that deficit over these years, the share of one year would be thirteen thousand two hundred parts out of one thousand... (in a unit), and this amount is not perceptible. Rather, ten years and a hundred and a thousand are not perceptible at all.

And if that is possible, certainty about the uniformity of the movements of the fixed stars is entirely dropped.

As for the second: the uniformity of the fixed stars in the measures of their movements does not necessitate that they are all fixed in one sphere, because they may be fixed in different spheres, even if they share the measures of their movements. This is as they say concerning the representative bodies of most of the planets, which in their movements are equal to the sphere of the fixed stars; so it is the same here.

I say: This possibility which this speaker mentioned is not specific to the sphere of the fixed stars. Perhaps the body moving with the daily motion is not one body but many bodies, either of differing movements but with slight variation that our lifetimes and observations cannot grasp, or equal absolutely, but their equality does not necessitate their unity. Among the astronomers, some have definitively affirmed other spheres besides these nine. For among people there is one who established a sphere above the sphere of the fixed stars and below the greatest sphere, and he argued for it in several ways:

The first: The observers of the greatest obliquity (al-mayl al-a'zam) found it to vary in magnitude; whoever's observation was earlier found the magnitude of the obliquity greater. Ptolemy found it to be "lah ya" (a numerical notation), then in the time of al-Ma'mun it was found to be "kah lah," then after al-Ma'mun it was found to have decreased by a minute. This indicates that it is in the nature of the two zones that their inclination sometimes decreases and sometimes increases. This is only possible if between the sphere of the whole and the sphere of the fixed stars there is another sphere whose poles revolve around the poles of the sphere of the whole, while the sphere of the fixed stars has its poles revolving around the poles of that sphere. Thus its pole sometimes comes to the northern side, lowered, and sometimes to the southern side, raised. It follows from this that the equator of the day coincides with the zodiac belt, and at another time it separates from it toward the south when the pole of the sphere of the fixed stars rises toward the south, and at another time toward the north, as it is now.

The second: The astronomers greatly disagreed concerning the measure of the sun's course, as is explained in the "Books of the Stars," to the extent that Ptolemy related from Abrakhis that he was doubtful whether this return occurs in equal or unequal times, and that in some of his statements he said they are unequal, and in others that they are equal. Then people mentioned two reasons for its difference:

One of them: the view of those who make the apogee of the sun moving. He claimed that the difference which affects the motion of the sun from this direction varies at the point of equinox according to its differing distance from the apogee, so the time of the sun's course varies on account of it.

The second: the view of the people of India, China, Babylon, most of the ancient Romans, Egypt and Syria: that the cause of it is the displacement of the sphere of the zodiac, the rising and lowering of its pole. It is related of Abrakhis that he held this opinion, and Baria' the Alexandrian mentioned that the practitioners of talismans held this belief, and that the point of the zodiac sphere advances from its place and recedes by eight degrees. They said: the beginning of the motion is from one degree of Pisces to the first point of Aries. Know that this confusion indicates to you that there is no path for human intellects to grasp these matters, and that none encompasses them except the knowledge of their Originator and Creator; therefore it is necessary to restrict oneself in this to the revealed evidences.

If someone says: Does the explicit mention of seven heavens indicate the negation of a greater number? We say: The truth is that specifying a number by mention does not indicate the negation of what exceeds it.

The sixth issue: The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And He is Knower of all things﴾ indicate that He, glory be to Him and exalted, cannot be the creator of the earth and what is in it, and of the heavens and what is in them of wonders and marvels, unless He is knowing of them, encompassing their particulars and universals. This indicates several matters:

The first: the corruption of the view of the philosophers who said that He does not know particulars, and the soundness of the view of the theologians (mutakallimun). This is because the theologians proved God's knowledge of particulars by saying: God the Exalted is the agent of these bodies in the manner of perfection and precision, and every agent in this manner must necessarily know what he has done. This very proof is what God the Exalted mentioned in this place, for He mentioned the creation of the heavens and the earth and then based upon it His being Knower. Thus it is established by this that the theologians' position in this doctrine and in this argument agrees with the Qur'an.

The second: the corruption of the view of the Mu'tazila. This is because He, glory be to Him and exalted, made clear that the one who creates a thing by way of measure and determination must necessarily know it and its details, because its creator has specified it with a measure rather than another, and specification with a definite measure must be by will, otherwise preponderance would occur without a preponderant. And will is conditioned upon knowledge. Thus it is established that the creator of a thing must necessarily know it in detail.

So if the servant were the originator of his own acts, he would know them and their details in number, quantity and quality. Since this knowledge does not occur, we know that he is not the originator of himself.

The third: The Mu'tazila said: When you combine this verse with His words: ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one Knowing﴾ [Yusuf: 76], it becomes apparent that He, the Exalted, is knowing by His essence. The answer: His words ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one Knowing﴾ are general, and His words ﴿He sent it down with His knowledge﴾ [al-Nisa: 166] are specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 1 of 6):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am placing upon the earth a khalifah (successor)." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" He said, "Indeed I know that which you do not know."﴾

Know that this verse indicates the manner in which Adam, peace be upon him, was created and the manner in which Allah, exalted is He, honored him. This is therefore a general favor upon all the descendants of Adam. It is the third of those general favors that He mentioned in this passage. Then in it are several issues:

[p. 147]

The first issue: concerning *idh* (when), there are two opinions:
One of them: it is an extra connective particle, except that the Arabs are accustomed to speaking with it, and the Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs.
The second, and it is the correct view: there is nothing in the Qur'an that has no meaning. It is in the accusative by an implied *udhkur* (remember), and the meaning is: "Remember for them when your Lord said to the angels." This was implied for two reasons:
One of them: the meaning is well known.
The second: Allah, exalted is He, has made this explicit in many places, such as His saying: ﴿And remember the brother of ʿAd, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21], and He said: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud﴾ [Sad: 17], and ﴿And present to them a parable: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it﴾, ﴿when We sent to them two﴾ [Ya-Sin: 13, 14]. The entire Qur'an is like a single word. It is not far-fetched that these explicit places were revealed before this surah, so this was rightly omitted here, being sufficient with that explicit mention. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: It is permissible for *idh* to be in the accusative governed by *qalu* (they said).

* * *

The second issue: *al-malak* (the angel) is originally from *al-risalah* (message). It is said: *alakani ilayhi*, meaning he sent me to him. *Al-ma'lakah* and *al-ulukah* mean a message. Its origin is the hamzah from *mal'akah*, the hamzah was dropped and its vowel was transferred onto the letter before it, seeking lightness because of its frequent use. The author of al-Kashshaf said: *al-mala'ik* is the plural of *mal'ak* according to the original form, like *al-shimal* being the plural of *sham'al*, and the addition of the *ta'* is for the feminine plural.

The third issue: Some people said: discussion of the angels should precede discussion of the prophets, for two reasons:
The first: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned belief in the angels before belief in the messengers in His saying: ﴿And the believers, each one believed in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285]. And indeed he (ﷺ) said: "Begin with what Allah began with."
The second: the angel is an intermediary between Allah and the Messenger in conveying the revelation and the law, so it is prior to the Messenger. Others said: discussion of prophethood precedes discussion of the angels, because there is no way for us to know the existence of the angels by reason, but only by revelation (sam'). So discussion of prophethood is the foundation for discussion of the angels, and therefore it is necessary to give precedence to discussion of prophethood. The better view is that the angel is before the Prophet in rank and eminence, and after him in our minds and understandings, according to the extent of our arrival at them through our thinking.

Know that there is no disagreement among rational people that the nobility of rank of the higher world lies in the existence of the angels in it, just as the nobility of rank of the lower world lies in the existence of man in it. However, people differed concerning the reality (*mahiyyah*) and nature of the angels.

The method of organizing the positions is to say: the angels must be essences subsisting in themselves. Then those essences are either spatially located (*mutahayyizah*) or not. As for the first, that the angels are spatially located essences, then there are opinions here:
One of them: they are subtle aerial bodies, able to take on different forms, their dwelling is the heavens. This is the view of most Muslims.
Second: the view of groups of idol-worshippers, that the angels are the reality of those stars described as bringing good fortune and misfortune. For they claim they are living rational beings, and that the ones that bring good fortune among them are angels of mercy, and the ones that bring misfortune among them are angels of punishment.
Third: the view of most of the Magians and the Dualists, that this world is composed of two eternal principles, which are light and darkness. In reality they are two transparent, willing, capable substances, opposed in essence and form, differing in action and management. The substance of light is virtuous, good, pure, of pleasant fragrance, noble in essence; it gives joy and does not harm, benefits and does not withhold, gives life and does not destroy. The substance of darkness is the opposite of that. Then the substance of light has continually generated the allies, who are the angels, not by way of marriage, but by way of the generation of wisdom from the wise and of light from the luminous. And the substance of darkness has continually generated the enemies, who are the devils, by way of the generation of foolishness from the foolish, not by way of marriage. These are the opinions of those who made the angels spatial, corporeal things.

The second opinion: that the angels are essences subsisting in themselves, not spatially located and not bodies. Here there are two views:
One of them: the view of groups of Christians, that the angels in reality are the rational souls separated from their bodies in the manner of purity and goodness. For these separated souls, if they are pure and sincere, they are the angels, and if they are wicked and turbid, they are the devils.
The second of them: the view of the philosophers, that they are substances subsisting in themselves, not spatially located at all, and that they are essentially different from the species of human rational souls, and that they are more complete in power and more knowing than them, and that for the human souls they stand like the sun in relation to lights. Then these substances are of two kinds: some of them are, in relation to the bodies of the spheres and stars, like our rational souls in relation to our bodies, and others are not in the management of the spheres at all, but are absorbed in knowledge of Allah and His love, and occupied with His obedience. This kind are the angels brought near (*al-muqarrabun*), and their relation to the angels who manage the heavens is like the relation of those managers to our rational souls.

These two kinds the philosophers have agreed upon establishing. Some of them established other kinds of angels, namely the earthly angels who manage the conditions of this lower world. Then if the managers of this world are good, they are the angels, and if they are evil, they are the devils. This is the detailed account of the positions of people concerning the angels.

The scholars differed as to whether it is possible to judge their existence by reason, or whether there is no way to establish them except by revelation. As for the philosophers, they agreed that reason contains proofs indicating the existence of the angels, and we have with them in those proofs subtle and profound investigations. Some people have mentioned in this regard rational, persuasive arguments, and let us point to them.

The first: that what is meant by the angel is a living, speaking being that is not dead. We say: rational division requires the existence of three categories. The living being is either speaking and dead together, which is man; or dead and not speaking, which is the beasts; or speaking and not dead, which is the angel. Without doubt the lowest rank is the dead non-speaking, and the middle is the speaking dead, and the highest is the speaking non-dead. So if divine wisdom requires the creation of the lowest and middle ranks, then requiring the creation of the highest and most exalted rank is more fitting.

The second: that natural disposition (*fitrah*) bears witness that the world of the heavens is nobler than this lower world, and bears witness that life, reason and speech are nobler than their opposites and counterparts. So in reason it is remote that life, reason and speech should occur in this turbid, dark world, and not occur at all in that world, which is the world of light and radiance and nobility.

The third: that the people of spiritual struggle (*mujahadat*) established them through witnessing and unveiling, and the people of needs and necessities established them from another direction, which is what is observed of the wonders of their effects in guiding to rare and strange treatments, the composition of compounds, and the extraction of the craft of antidotes. Among what indicates this is the state of the true dream. These are persuasive arguments with respect to one who has heard them but has not practiced them, and conclusive with respect to one who has tested them, witnessed them, and become acquainted with their secrets. As for the transmitted proofs, there is absolutely no dispute among the prophets, peace be upon them, in establishing the angels. Rather, that is like a matter agreed upon among them. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: concerning explaining their multitude. He (ﷺ) said: "The heaven has creaked, and it has a right to creak. There is not a place the width of a foot in it except that there is an angel prostrating or bowing." It is also related that the descendants of Adam are one-tenth of the jinn, and the jinn and the descendants of Adam are one-tenth of the land animals, and all of these are one-tenth of the birds, and all of these are one-tenth of the sea animals, and all of these are one-tenth of the angels of the earth who are assigned to it, and all of these are one-tenth of the angels of the first heaven, and all of these are one-tenth of the angels of the third heaven, and in this order up to the angels of the seventh heaven. Then all of these, in comparison with the angels of the Kursi (Footstool), are a tiny handful. Then all of these are one-tenth of the angels of one pavilion of the pavilions of the Throne, whose number is six hundred thousand. The length, breadth and thickness of each pavilion, if compared with it the heavens and the earths and what is in them and between them, would all be a small thing and a little measure. There is not a place the width of a foot except that in it there is an angel prostrating, bowing or standing, for them is a loud sound of glorifying and sanctifying. Then all of these, in comparison with the angels who circle around the Throne, are like a drop in the sea, and none knows their number except Allah. Then along with these are the angels of the Tablet, who are the followers of Israfil, peace be upon him, and the angels who are the soldiers of Jibril, peace be upon him. All of them are hearing and obedient, never slackening, occupied with the worship of Him, glorified be He, with tongues moist with His remembrance and exaltation, competing in that since He created them, not disdaining His worship by night and day, and not growing weary. None enumerates their kinds, nor the length of their lives, nor the manner of their worship, except Allah, exalted is He. This is the realization of the reality of His dominion, majestic is His majesty, as He said: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. I say: I saw in some books of admonition that "when he (ﷺ) was taken up on the night journey, he saw angels in a place like a marketplace, some of them walking facing others. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked: Where are they going? Jibril, peace be upon him, said: I do not know, except that I see them since I was created, and I do not see one of them whom I had seen before that. Then they asked one of them, and it was said to him: Since when were you created? He said: I do not know, except that Allah, exalted is He, creates a star every four hundred thousand years, and He has created the like of that star since He created me four hundred thousand times." Glory be to a God whose power is so great and whose perfection is so majestic.

Know that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned in the Qur'an their categories and their attributes. As for the categories:

The first of them: the bearers of the Throne, as in His saying: ﴿And above them on that day eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17].
The second: those surrounding the Throne, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And you see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying the praise of their Lord﴾ [az-Zumar: 75].

[Page 150]

Third: the chief angels. Among them are Jibril (Gabriel) and Mika'il (Michael), may the blessings of Allah be upon them both, based on His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. Then, Glorified and Exalted is He, described Jibril, peace be upon him, with several attributes:

The first: he is the bearer of revelation to the prophets. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down ﴿upon your heart﴾﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193-194].

The second: Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned him before the rest of the angels in the Qur'an: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]. Also, Jibril is the bearer of revelation and knowledge, while Mika'il is the bearer of provisions and sustenance. Knowledge, which is the spiritual nourishment, is more noble than physical nourishment. Therefore, Jibril, peace be upon him, must be more noble than Mika'il.

The third: Allah, Exalted is He, made him the second of His own self: ﴿Indeed, Allah is his protector, and Jibril and the righteous of the believers﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].

The fourth: He named him the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus). Concerning 'Isa, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿When I supported you with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110].

The fifth: He supports the friends of Allah and overpowers His enemies, together with a thousand angels, marked (for battle).

The sixth: Allah, Exalted is He, praised him with six attributes in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, ﴿one of power, with rank before the Owner of the Throne, obeyed and trustworthy﴾﴾ [al-Takwir: 19-21]. So his message is that he is the messenger of Allah ﷺ to all the prophets, and all the prophets and messengers are his community. His generosity toward his Lord is that He made him an intermediary between Him and the most noble of His servants, who are the prophets. His strength is that he lifted the cities of the people of Lut into the sky and overturned them. His standing with Allah is that He made him the second of His own self in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is his protector, and Jibril and the righteous of the believers﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. That he is obeyed means that he is the leader and exemplar of the angels. As for his being trustworthy, it is His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down ﴿upon your heart, that you may be among the warners﴾﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193-194].

Among the chief angels are Israfil and 'Izra'il, may the blessings of Allah be upon them both. Their existence is established by reports, and it is established by a report that 'Izra'il is the Angel of Death, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11]. As for His saying: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him﴾ [al-An'am: 61], this indicates the existence of angels assigned to seize souls. It is possible that the Angel of Death is the chief of a group who have been assigned to seize souls. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿If only you could see when the angels take those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50]. As for Israfil, peace be upon him, the reports indicate that he is the bearer of the Trumpet, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown again, and immediately they will be standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68].

Fourth: the angels of Paradise. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate. ﴿Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final home﴾﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23-24].

Fifth: the angels of the Fire. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30]. And His saying: ﴿We have not made the companions of the Fire but angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. Their chief is Malik, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 77]. The name for all of them is the Zabaniyah, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Then let him call his assembly. We will call the Zabaniyah﴾ [al-'Alaq: 17-18].

Sixth: those assigned to the children of Adam, based on His saying: ﴿One sitting on the right and one on the left. Not a word does he utter except that with him is an observer, ready﴾ [Qaf: 17-18]. And His saying: ﴿For him are successive (angels) before him and behind him, protecting him by the command of Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11]. And His saying: ﴿He is the Subjugator over His servants, and He sends over you guardians﴾ [al-An'am: 61].

Seventh: the recorders of deeds, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, over you are guardians, noble and recording, who know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 10-12].

Eighth: those assigned to the affairs of this world, who are the ones meant by His saying: ﴿By those ranged in ranks﴾ [al-Saffat: 1], and by His saying: ﴿By those that scatter (dust) dispersing﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 1], up to His saying: ﴿And those that distribute by command﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 4], and by His saying: ﴿By those who extract with violence﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 1]. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Indeed, Allah has angels other than the guardians who write down what falls from the leaves of the trees. So when one of you is lost in a barren desert, let him call out: 'Help, servants of Allah, may Allah have mercy on you.'"

* * *

As for the attributes of the angels, they are of several aspects:

The first: the angels are the messengers of Allah. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir: 1]. As for His saying: ﴿Allah chooses messengers from among the angels﴾ [al-Hajj: 75], this indicates that only some of the angels are the messengers. The answer is that "min" (from) here is for explanation, not for partition.

The second: their nearness to Allah, Exalted is He. This is impossible to be by place and direction. Therefore, that nearness can only be nearness by rank, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain from His worship﴾ [al-Anbiya: 19], and His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 26], and His saying: ﴿They exalt the night and the day; they do not slacken﴾.

The third: the description of their acts of obedience, which is in several aspects:

The first: His saying, Exalted is He, quoting them: ﴿While we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾, and He said in another place: ﴿And indeed, we are those who stand in ranks. And indeed, we are those who glorify﴾ [al-Saffat: 165-166]. Allah did not deny them in that, and thus their constancy in worship is established.

The second: their eagerness to carry out Allah's command, out of exaltation for Him, as in His saying: ﴿So all the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾ [al-Hijr: 30].

The third: that they do nothing except by His revelation and command, as in His saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya: 27].

The fourth: the description of their power, which is in several aspects. The first: the bearers of the Throne, who are eight, carry the Throne and the Kursi. Then the Kursi, which is smaller than the Throne, is greater than all the seven heavens, as indicated by His saying: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. So consider the extent of their power and strength.

The second: the loftiness of the Throne is something the imagination cannot encompass, as indicated by His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day the measure of which is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. Then, because of the intensity of their power, they descend from it in a single moment.

The third: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown again, and immediately they will be standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. The bearer of the Trumpet reaches such strength that with a single blast from him, whoever is in the heavens and the earth will be struck unconscious, and with a second blast from him, they will return to life. So understand from this the greatness of this power.

The fourth: Jibril, peace be upon him, reached such strength that he uprooted the mountains of the family of Lut and their lands in a single thrust.

The fifth: the description of their fear, which is indicated by several aspects:

The first: despite the abundance of their worship and their absolute avoidance of lapses, they are fearful and anxious, to the point that it is as if their worship were sins. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 50], and He said: ﴿And they are fearful of His awe﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28].

The second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Until, when terror is removed from their hearts, they say, "What has your Lord said?" They say, "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great"﴾ [Saba': 23]. It is related in the tafsir that when Allah speaks with the revelation, the people of the heavens hear it like the sound of a chain on smooth rock, and they are terrified. When the revelation is over, some of them say to others: "What has your Lord said?" They say: "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great."

The third: al-Bayhaqi related in Shu'ab al-Iman from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in a certain region with Jibril, the horizon of the sky split open, and Jibril began to shrink, entering part of himself into another part, and drawing near to the earth. Then there was an angel who appeared before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: 'O Muhammad, indeed your Lord sends you greetings of peace and gives you the choice between being a prophet-king and being a prophet-servant.' He, peace be upon him, said: Jibril gestured to me with his hand, meaning 'be humble.' So I knew he was giving me sincere counsel, and I said: 'A prophet-servant.' Then that angel ascended to the sky. I said: 'O Jibril, I had wanted to ask you about this, but I saw your condition, which occupied me from asking. Who is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is Israfil, whom Allah created on the day He created him, placed before Him, standing with his feet together, not raising his gaze. Between the Lord and him are seventy lights, none of which draws near to him without being burned. Before him is the Preserved Tablet. When Allah permits him regarding something in the heaven or on the earth, that tablet is raised near his forehead, and he looks into it. If it is of my deeds, he commands me concerning it; if it is of Mika'il's deeds, he commands him concerning it; and if it is of the Angel of Death's deeds, he commands him concerning it.'" I said: "O Jibril, over what are you?" He said: "Over the winds and the hosts." I said: "Over what is Mika'il?" He said: "Over the plants." I said: "Over what is the Angel of Death?" He said: "Over the seizing of souls." I did not think he had descended except for the Hour being established, and what you saw in me was nothing but fear of the Hour being established."

Know that after the words of Allah and the words of His Messenger, there is no statement on the description of the angels more lofty and more sublime than the words of the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali, peace be upon him. He said in one of his sermons: "Then He filled the gap between the lofty heavens and gave them shape with various orders of angels. Among them are those who prostrate and never bow, and those who bow and never stand upright, those who stand in ranks and never move apart, and those who glorify and never tire. Sleep does not overcome them, nor forgetfulness of the intellect, nor weakness of the bodies, nor heedlessness of forgetfulness. Among them are the trustees of His revelation and the tongues to His messengers, and those who differ by His decree and command. Among them are the guardians of His servants and the keepers of the gates of His Gardens. Among them are those whose feet are firmly fixed in the lowest earths, and whose necks pass beyond the highest heaven, and whose sides are outside the regions, and whose shoulders support the pillars of the Throne, with their gazes lowered below it, wrapped in their wings. Between them and those beneath them are placed veils of majesty and curtains of power. They do not imagine their Lord by form, nor ascribe to Him the attributes of created things, nor limit Him by places, nor point to Him by likenesses."

* * *

The fifth issue: scholars differed over whether the intended meaning of His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a khalifah (successor)"﴾ is all the angels or some of them. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas that He, Glorified and Exalted is He, said this only to the angels who were fighting alongside Iblis. This is because when Allah settled the jinn on the earth, they corrupted it, shed blood, and killed one another. So Allah sent Iblis with a host of angels, and Iblis killed them with his soldiers until they drove them out of the earth and confined them to the islands of the sea. Then He said to them: ﴿Indeed, I will make upon the earth a khalifah.﴾ But most of the Companions and the Successors said that He said this to the whole group of angels without specification, because the word "angels" indicates generality, so specification would be contrary to the original meaning.

The sixth issue: "Ja'il" (making) is derived from "ja'ala," which takes two objects. It entered upon the subject and predicate, which are His saying: ﴿upon the earth, khalifah﴾, so they became two objects. Its meaning is: "one who will place upon the earth a khalifah."

The seventh issue: the apparent meaning of "the earth" in the verse is the entire earth from east to west. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The earth was spread out from Makkah, and the angels used to circumambulate the House, and they were the first to circle it. It is in the earth which Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned: 'Indeed, I will make upon the earth a khalifah.'" But the first (view) is closer to the apparent meaning.

Eighth issue: the khalifah (caliph, successor) is one who succeeds another and takes his place. God Most High said: ﴿Then We appointed you as successors (khala'if) in the earth﴾ [Yunus: 14]. ﴿And remember when He made you successors (khulafa')﴾ [al-A'raf: 69]. As to who is meant by the khalifah, there are two opinions:

The first: it is Adam, peace be upon him. And His saying: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein?﴾ means his descendants, not himself.

The second: it is the offspring of Adam. As for those who said that Adam is meant, they differed about why God called him a khalifah, and they mentioned two explanations. The first: when God removed the jinn from the earth and settled Adam in the earth, Adam, peace be upon him, was a khalifah to those jinn who preceded him. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: God named him a khalifah only because he succeeds God in judging among the accountable beings of His creation. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi, and this view is reinforced by His saying: ﴿Indeed We have made you a khalifah on the earth, so judge between the people with truth﴾ [Sad: 26]. As for those who said that the offspring of Adam is meant, they said: He named them khalifah only because some of them succeed others, and this is the view of al-Hasan. It is reinforced by His saying: ﴿And it is He who made you successors (khala'if) of the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 165]. The word khalifah is a term that applies to the singular and the plural, as it applies to the masculine and the feminine. It was also read khaliqah with a qaf.

If it is asked: what is the benefit in God saying to the angels: ﴿Indeed, I will make on earth a khalifah﴾, given that He is exempt from need for consultation? The answer has two aspects. The first: God knew that when they were informed of this secret they would raise that question, so the interest required that they be made aware of that answer. He therefore informed them of this event so that they would raise that question and hear that answer.

The second aspect: God taught His servants consultation.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿They said: Will You place therein...﴾ to the end of the verse, there are issues in it:

The first issue: the great majority of the scholars of religion agree on the infallibility (ismah) of all the angels from all sins, and among the Hashwiyya there is one who disagreed on this. Our proofs are several:

[page 153]

The first: His saying: ﴿They do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. However, this verse is specific to the angels of Hell. When we want the general indication, we rely on His saying: ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Nahl: 50]. His saying: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾ encompasses the performance of all commanded acts and the abandonment of all prohibited acts, because one who is prohibited from something is commanded to abandon it. If it is asked: what is the evidence that His saying: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾ conveys generality? We say: because there is nothing among the commanded matters except that an exception (istithna') can validly be made from it, and exception removes from the speech what would otherwise have been included, as we have explained in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

The second: His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26-27]. This is explicit in their freedom from disobedience, and that they are dependent in all matters except in accordance with command and revelation.

The third: God related of them that they criticized the children of Adam for disobedience. Had they been among the disobedient, that criticism would not have been fitting from them.

The fourth: God related of them that they glorify Him night and day without slackening. One who is like this cannot commit disobedience.

The opponent argued with several proofs:

The first: God related of them that they said: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood, while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You?﴾ This indicates that sin proceeded from them, and several things indicate this:

One: their saying "Will You place therein" is an objection against God Most High, and that is among the greatest sins.

Second: they criticized the children of Adam for corruption and bloodshed, and that is backbiting (ghibah), and backbiting is among the major sins.

Third: after criticizing the children of Adam, they praised themselves by saying: ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾, and they said: ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks (al-saffunah)﴾ and ﴿indeed, we are those who glorify﴾ [al-Saffat: 165-166]. This is restrictive, as though they denied that others were like this, and this resembles self-admiration (ujb) and backbiting, which are among the destructive sins. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Three things destroy, and among them is a man's admiration of himself." And God said: ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾ [al-Najm: 32].

Fourth: their saying "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us" resembles an excuse, and had there not been a prior sin, they would not have occupied themselves with excuse.

Fifth: His saying: ﴿Inform me of the names of these, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31] indicates that they were lying in what they had said first.

Sixth: His saying: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33] indicates that the angels did not know this before this event, and that they were doubtful about God being knowing of all knowable things.

Seventh: their knowledge that [the children of Adam] would cause corruption and shed blood either came by revelation to them concerning it or they said it by inference. The first is far-fetched, because if God had revealed that to them, there would be no benefit in repeating that statement. Thus it is established that they said it from inference and assumption, and disparaging others on the basis of assumption is not permissible, because of His saying: ﴿And do not pursue what you have no knowledge of﴾ [al-Isra': 36], and He said: ﴿Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all﴾ [al-Najm: 28].

Eighth: it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, that he said: God, glorified and exalted, said to the angels who were the army of Iblis in fighting the jinn: ﴿Indeed, I will make on earth a khalifah﴾, and the angels replied to Him, glorified be He:

[page 154]

﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein?﴾ Then they realized God's anger against them, and they said: ﴿Glory be to You, we have no knowledge﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32]. It is related from al-Jinn and Qatadah that when God began creating Adam, the angels whispered among themselves and said: Let our Lord create whatever He wills; He will not create any creation except that we are greater than it and more honored before Him. Then when He created Adam, peace be upon him, and preferred him over them, ﴿and He taught Adam the names, all of them, then presented them to the angels and said: Inform me of the names of these, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], [meaning]: that I do not create any creation except that you are better than it. At that, the people panicked and turned to repentance, and ﴿they said: Glory be to You, we have no knowledge﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32]. In some narrations, when they said "Will You place therein," God sent fire upon them and it burned them.

The second doubt: they held to the story of Harut and Marut, and claimed that they were two of the angels, and that when they looked at what the people of the earth did of sins, they denounced that and considered it great, and they invoked curses upon the people of the earth. So God revealed to them: "If I tested you with what I tested the children of Adam with of desires, you would disobey Me." They said: "O Lord, if You had tested us we would not have done so; so test us." He sent them down to the earth and God tested them with the desires of the children of Adam. They remained on the earth, and God commanded the star called Venus (al-Zuhrah) and its angel assigned to it, and they descended to the earth. Venus was made into the form of a woman and the angel into the form of a man. Then Venus took a dwelling and adorned herself and invited them to herself. The angel set himself up in her dwelling in the likeness of an idol. They came to her dwelling and invited her to indecency, but she refused them unless they drank wine. They said: "We do not drink wine." Then desire overcame them and they drank. Then they invited her again, and she said: "There remains one matter; I will not allow you to have me until you do it." They said: "And what is it?" She said: "You must prostrate to this idol." They said: "We do not associate anything with God." Then desire overcame them again and they said: "We will do it, then seek forgiveness." So they prostrated to the idol, and Venus and her angel rose up to their place in the sky. Then they knew that this had befallen them only because of their disparagement of the children of Adam. In another narration, Venus was a wicked woman of the people of the earth, and they had intercourse with her only after they had drunk wine, killed a soul, and prostrated to the idol, and they taught her the Greatest Name by which they used to ascend to the sky. The woman spoke that Name and ascended to the sky, so God transformed her and made her this star called Venus. Then God made Harut and Marut aware of the ugliness of what they had done, and gave them the choice between the punishment of the Hereafter, deferred, and the punishment of this world, immediate. They chose the punishment of this world, so He placed them at Babylon, hung upside down in a well until the Day of Resurrection. They teach people magic and call them to it, and no one sees them except one who goes to that place specifically to learn magic. They relied on His saying: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102].

The third doubt: Iblis was among the honored angels, then he disobeyed God and disbelieved, and this indicates that disobedience proceeds from the kind of the angels.

The fourth doubt: His saying: ﴿And We did not make the companions of the Fire except angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. They said: This indicates that the angels are punished, because the companions of the Fire are only those who are punished therein, as He said: ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾.

The answer to the first doubt: as for the first aspect, their saying that they objected to God Most High, which is among the greatest sins, we say: their purpose in that question was not to alert God to something He was unaware of, for whoever believes that about God is a disbeliever, nor was it an objection against God for an act He performed. Rather, the intended purpose of that question was several matters:

[page 155]

One: when a person is certain of the wisdom of another, and then sees that other do an act whose wisdom he cannot grasp, he says to him: "Do you do this?", as if marveling at the perfection of his wisdom and knowledge, saying: granting these blessings to one who causes corruption is among matters whose wisdom minds cannot discern; yet you do it, and I know that you do it only for a subtle reason and a hidden secret that you are aware of. How great is your wisdom and how sublime your knowledge! The gist is that their saying "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein?" was as though marveling at the perfection of God's knowledge and the comprehensiveness of His wisdom regarding what is hidden from all the intellects.

Second: raising a difficulty in order to seek an answer is not prohibited. It is as though they said: "Our God, You are the Wise who never does what is foolish at all. We see in custom that enabling a fool to be foolish is foolishness. So if You create a people who will corrupt and kill, and You, with Your knowledge that their state is such, create them and empower them and do not prevent them from it, this suggests foolishness, while You are the absolutely Wise. How can the two matters be reconciled?" So the angels raised this question seeking an answer. This is the answer of the Mu'tazilah, who said: This indicates that the angels did not permit the commission of an ugly act by God Most High, and they held the doctrine of the people of justice ('adl). They said: What confirms this answer are two aspects:

One: they attributed corruption and bloodshed to created beings, not to the Creator.

Second: they said: ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾, because glorification (tasbih) is declaring His essence free from the attributes of bodies, and sanctification (taqdis) is declaring His acts free from the attribute of blame and the description of foolishness.

Thirdly: although evils exist within the composition of this lower world, they are among the necessary consequences of the goods present in it, and its goods outweigh its evils. Forgoing a great good for the sake of a small evil is itself a great evil. The angels mentioned those evils, so God answered them with His words: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾. That is, the goods that arise from the arrangements of the lower world are more numerous than the evils that arise within them, and wisdom requires bringing into existence what is of this nature, not abandoning it. This is the answer of the philosophers (ḥukamāʾ).

Fourthly: their question was made in exaggerated reverence of God, for a sincere servant, out of intense love for his Master, dislikes that there should be a servant who disobeys Him.

Fifthly: the angels' statement ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ was a request from them that God make the earth, or part of it, theirs, if that were good. It was as though they said: "O our God, make the earth ours, not theirs," just as Moses (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:155], meaning: "Do not destroy us." God said: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾ concerning your welfare and the welfare of those whom I place on earth. Thereby He made clear that He had chosen the heavens specifically for them and the earth specifically for these, knowing what was good for each in their religions, so that every group would be content with what God had chosen for it.

Sixthly: they sought the wisdom for which He created them despite this corruption and bloodshed.

Seventhly: al-Qaffāl said: it is possible that when God informed them that He would place a successor (khalīfah) on earth, they said ﴿Will You place?﴾, meaning, "You will do that." It is an affirmation in the form of a question, as Jarīr said:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts,
and the most generous of all people in filling the bellies of the wine-cups?"

That is, "You are indeed like that." Had it been a genuine question, it would not have been praise. Then the angels said: "Indeed You will do that, and yet we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You," because we know that You do only what is right and wise. When they said this, God said to them: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾, as though He said, and God knows best: "How excellent is what you did, in that you did not make this a flaw in My wisdom. For I know what you do not know. You knew their outward aspect, which is corruption and bloodshed, but you did not know their inward aspect, while I know both their outward and inward aspects."

[Page 156]

So I know from their inner selves hidden secrets and profound wisdoms that require their creation and bringing into existence.

As for the second objection, namely that they spoke of the children of Adam in a manner that is not fitting, which is backbiting (ghībah): the answer is that the locus of the difficulty regarding the creation of the children of Adam is their committing corruption and murder. Whoever raises an objection must address the locus of the difficulty and not something else. For this reason they mentioned these two attributes of the children of Adam, and they did not mention their worship and monotheism, because that is not the locus of the difficulty.

As for the third objection, namely that they praised themselves, and this entails self-admiration (ʿujb) and self-purification: the answer is that praising oneself is not prohibited absolutely, based on His saying: ﴿As for the favour of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā 93:11]. Furthermore, it is possible that their saying ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ does not intend praise of themselves. Rather, it intends to explain that they did not raise this question to find fault with Your wisdom, O Lord, for we glorify You with Your praise and acknowledge You as God and as wise. The purpose of this, then, is to explain that they did not raise the question to attack wisdom and divinity, but to seek the reason for wisdom in detail.

As for the fourth objection, namely that their saying ﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:32] resembles an excuse, and an excuse presupposes a prior sin: we say that we concede that it would have been better for the angels not to raise that question. When they abandoned this better course, that statement was an excuse for abandoning the better course. If it is said: Did not He say ﴿they do not precede Him in speech﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:27]? Then this question must have been by God's permission, and if they were permitted to ask it, how then did they make an excuse for it? We say: a general ruling may admit of specification.

As for the fifth objection, namely that the angels' report of corruption and the shedding of blood either came from revelation or they said it by inference and conjecture: we say that the scholars differed on this. Some of them said that they stated it as a conjecture, and then they gave two explanations:

The first, which is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Kalbī, is that they analogized it to the state of the jinn who were on earth before Adam (peace be upon him).

The second is that they knew his creation and knew that he was composed of these four humours, so the appetite and anger must be inherent in him, so corruption arises from appetite and bloodshed from anger.

Others said that they spoke of it with certainty. This is related from Ibn Masʿūd and some of the Companions. Then they mentioned several explanations:

The first: when God said to the angels ﴿Indeed, I am placing in the earth a successor﴾, they said: "Our Lord, what will that successor be?" He said: "He will have offspring who will cause corruption on earth, envy one another, and kill one another." At that they said: "Our Lord, will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?"

The second: God had informed the angels that when there is a great created kind on earth, they will cause corruption and shed blood.

The third: Ibn Zayd said: when God created the Fire, the angels were terribly frightened and said: "Our Lord, for whom have You created this Fire?" He said: "For whoever disobeys Me among My creation." At that time God had no creation except the angels, and there was no creation on earth at all. So when He said ﴿Indeed, I am placing in the earth a successor﴾, they understood that disobedience would appear among them.

The fourth: when the Pen wrote on the Preserved Tablet what would occur until the Day of Resurrection, perhaps they looked into the Tablet and so knew that.

The fifth: if the meaning of khalīfah is one who acts as God's deputy in judgment and governance, and the need for a ruler and judge arises only at the time of dispute and oppression, then announcing the existence of a successor was an announcement, by implication, of the occurrence of corruption and evil. The people of verification (ahl al-taḥqīq) said: the claim that this announcement was merely a conjecture is false, because it is a slander against others about which one cannot be sure it is untrue, and that contradicts infallibility and purity.

As for the sixth objection: the reports they cited belong to the category of solitary reports (akhbār al-āḥād), so they do not oppose the proofs we have mentioned.

As for the second doubt, namely the story of Hārūt and Mārūt, the answer regarding it is that the story they cited is false in several respects:

First: they mentioned in the story that God said to them: "If I had tested you with what I tested the children of Adam with, you would have disobeyed Me." They said: "If You did that to us, our Lord, we would not disobey You." This statement from them is a denial of God and an attribution of ignorance to Him, and that is manifest disbelief. The literalists (Ḥashawiyyah) concede that the two were infallible before their descent to earth.

Second: the story says that they were given the choice between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. This is corrupt. Rather, the better course would have been that they be given the choice between repentance and punishment. Yet God gave the choice between these two to one who associated partners with Him throughout his life and went to great lengths to harm His prophets.

Third: the story says that they teach magic while being punished, and they invite to it while being punished for disobedience.

Fourth: how is it conceivable that a dissolute woman, when she committed immorality, ascended to heaven, and God made her a shining star and magnified its rank to the point that He swore by it, saying: ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the running, the hiding﴾ [al-Takwīr 81:15–16]? This story is a feeble story, and every sound mind testifies to its utter feebleness. As for the discussion of teaching magic, it will come in the explanation of that verse in its proper place, God willing.

As for the third doubt: we will speak to explain that Iblīs was not of the angels.

As for the fourth doubt, namely His saying ﴿And We have made the companions of the Fire none but angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31]: this does not indicate that they are punished in the Fire. And His saying ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [Yūnus 10:27] also does not indicate by this verse alone that they are punished by the Fire. Rather, that is known from another proof. So His saying ﴿And We have made the companions of the Fire none but angels﴾ means the guardians of the Fire, those who manage it and direct its affairs. And God knows best.

* * *

The second issue: scholars differed over whether the angels are capable of sins and evils or not. The majority of the philosophers and many of the Jabriyyah (determinists) said: they are pure goodness, and they have absolutely no capacity for evils and corruption. The majority of the Muʿtazilah and many of the jurists said: they are capable of both, and they argued for this with several arguments:

First: their saying ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ is either a sin or an abandonment of the better course, and under either supposition the intended point is achieved.

Second: God's saying ﴿Whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him," We will recompense him with Hell﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:29]. This requires that they be restrained and prevented. He also said ﴿they do not disdain from His worship﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:206], and praise for not being arrogant is only permissible if they were capable of being arrogant.

Third: if they were not capable of abandoning good deeds, they would not be praised for performing them, because one who is compelled toward a thing, and who cannot refrain from it, is not praised for doing that thing. Some Muʿtazilah argued with this, and I said to him: Is it not the case that reward and recompense are obligatory upon God, the Exalted? The meaning of its being obligatory for Him is that if He abandoned it, then from His abandoning it would follow either ignorance or need, and both are impossible, and what leads to the impossible is impossible. So His abandoning it would be impossible for God, and if abandoning it is impossible, then doing it is obligatory. So God is the doer of reward, and recompense is obligatory, and its abandonment is impossible, yet God is praised for doing that. Thus it is established that the impossibility of abandoning does not prevent the attainment of praise. He was silenced and could not answer.

* * *

The third issue: the waw in ﴿while we﴾ is for the circumstantial state (ḥāl), as when you say: "Do you do good to so-and-so while I am more deserving of kindness?" Tasbīḥ (glorification) is placing God far from evil, and likewise taqdīs (sanctification), from sabaḥa in water and qaddasa in the land, when one goes into it and goes far. Know that if by placing far is meant placing far from evil, that is tasbīḥ, and if by it is meant placing far from good, that is cursing (laʿn). So we say: placing far from evil includes placing far from evil in essence, attributes, and actions. As for essence, it means that He is not a locus of possibility, for the prevention of evil and its possibility is nonexistence, and negating possibility entails negating multiplicity, and negating multiplicity entails negating corporeality and accidentality, and negating opposite and equal, and the attainment of absolute unity and necessary existence. As for attributes, it means that He is exempt from ignorance, so that He encompasses all knowable things and is capable of all possible things, and His attributes are exempt from change. As for actions, it means that His actions are not for bringing benefits or repelling harms, and that He is not perfected by any of them, nor diminished by the nonexistence of any of them, so that He is independent of all existent and nonexistent things, exercising dominion through annihilation and origination over all existent and nonexistent things.

The people of admonition (ahl al-tadhkīr) said: tasbīḥ in the Qur'an has come sometimes with the meaning of exaltation above imperfection, and sometimes with the meaning of wonder.

As for the first meaning, it has come in several ways:

(a) "I am the One exalted above peer and partner; He is God, the One, the Subduer."

(b) "I am the Manager of the heavens and the earth: Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth."

(c) "I am the Manager of all worlds: Glory be to God, the Lord of the worlds."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 5 of 6):

(d) I am the One exempt from the utterance of the wrongdoers: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe."
(h) I am the One independent of all: "Glory be to Him, the Self-Sufficient."
(w) I am the Sovereign, to whom everything other than Me is subject to My domination and control. "So glory be to the One in whose hand is the dominion of everything."
(z) I am the Knower of everything. "Glory be to God above what they describe, the Knower of the unseen."
(h) I am exempt from consort and offspring. "Glory be to Him; how could He have a son?"
(t) I am exempt from their description and their saying. "Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate, above what they say, above what they describe."

As for wonder, it is similar:

(a) I am the One who subjected the strong beasts to frail humankind. "Glory be to the One who subjected this to us."
(b) I am the One who created the world, and I am exempt from fatigue and exhaustion. "Glory be to Him when He decrees a matter."
(j) I am the One who knows without the teaching of teachers or the guidance of guides. "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us."
(d) I am the One who removes the disobedience of seventy years by one hour of repentance. So glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun. Then He says: If you want God's good pleasure, then glorify Him, and glorify Him morning and evening. If you want deliverance from affliction, then glorify Him: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I was among the wrongdoers." If you want the pleasure of the Truth, then glorify Him: "And glorify Him during part of the night and at the ends of the day, that you may be pleased." If you want escape from the Fire, then glorify Him: "Glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire." O servant, be constant in My glorification. So glorify God, and glorify Him. If you do not glorify Me, the harm returns to you, because I have those who glorify Me. Among them are the bearers of the Throne: "But if they are arrogant, then those who are with your Lord glorify Him" [Fussilat: 38]. Among them are those brought near: "They say: Glory be to You; You are our Protector" [Saba': 41]. Among them are all the angels: "They say: Glory be to You; it was not for us to take any protector besides You" [al-Furqan: 18]. Among them are the prophets, as Dhu al-Nun said: "There is no god but You; glory be to You" [al-Anbiya': 87], and Moses said: "Glory be to You; I have turned to You in repentance" [al-A'raf: 143]. The Companions glorify Him in His saying: "Glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire" [Al 'Imran: 191]. All glorify Him, including insects, animals, and atoms: "There is not a thing but glorifies His praise" [al-Isra': 44]. Likewise the stone, the clay, the sands, the mountains, the night, the day, the darknesses, the lights, Paradise, the Fire, time, place, the elements, the pillars, the spirits, and the bodies, as He said: "Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God" [al-Hadid: 1]. Then He says:

[p. 159]

O servant: I am exempt from the glorification of these things, and these things are not living beings, so they have no need of the reward of this glorification. The reward of these glorifications would then be wasted, and that is not fitting for Me: "We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain" [Sad: 27]. But I convey the reward of these things to you, so that everyone may know that whoever strives in My service, I make the whole world serve him.

The other point: Remember Me with servitude so that you benefit from it, not that I benefit. "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might" [al-Saffat: 180]. When you remember Me with glorification, I purify you from sins: "And glorify Him morning and evening" [al-Ahzab: 42]. Lend to Me: "And lend God a goodly loan" [al-Hadid: 18]. Although I am the Self-Sufficient, I return one to you as tenfold: "Who is it that will lend God a goodly loan, so He will multiply it for him?" [al-Hadid: 11]. Be a helper to Me, although I am independent of your help: "And to God belong the armies of the heavens and the earth" [al-Fath: 4]. Also, I have no need of an army: "If God had willed, He would have taken vengeance on them" [Muhammad: 4]. But if you help Me, I will help you: "If you help God, He will help you" [Muhammad: 7]. Be constant in remembering Me: "And remember God during numbered days" [al-Baqarah: 203]. I have no need of your remembrance, because all remember Me: "If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: God" [Luqman: 25]. But when you remember Me, I remember you: "So remember Me, and I will remember you" [al-Baqarah: 152]. Serve Me: "O mankind, worship your Lord" [al-Baqarah: 21], not because I need your service, for I am the King: "And to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth" [Al 'Imran: 189]. "And to God prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth" [al-Ra'd: 15]. But turn to My service in these few days, so that you may attain many comforts: "Say: God. Then leave them" [al-An'am: 91].

* * *

The fourth question: His saying "bi-hamdika" (with Your praise). The author of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary) said: "bi-hamdika" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: we glorify You while praising You, and clothed in Your praise. As for the meaning, there are two views. The first: when we glorify You, we also praise You, "Glory be to You," meaning our glorification is not glorification without entitlement; rather, by Your praise and majesty You deserve this glorification. The second: we glorify You with Your praise, for without Your bounty upon us in granting success, we would not be able to do so, as Dawud, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, how can I thank You, when I cannot reach the thanks of Your blessing except through Your blessing?" God revealed to him: "Now you have thanked Me, since you have recognized that all of that is from Me." The scholars differed about the intended meaning of this glorification. It is related that Abu Dharr entered upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at dawn, or the reverse, and said: "O Messenger of God, may my father and mother be ransomed for you, which speech is most beloved to God?" He said: "What God chose for His angels: 'Glory be to God and praise be to Him.'" Narrated by Muslim.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated, saying: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was praying, and a man from the Muslims passed by a man from the hypocrites and said to him: 'The Messenger of God is praying while you are sitting and not praying.' He said to him: 'Go about your work, if you have work.' He said: 'I think only that someone will pass by you who will object to you.' Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab passed by him and said: 'O so-and-so, the Messenger of God is praying while you are sitting.' He said to him the same thing, so he (Umar) leapt upon him and struck him, and said: 'This is from my work.' Then he entered the mosque and prayed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When the Messenger of God finished his prayer, 'Umar came to him and said: 'O Prophet of God, a while ago I passed by so-and-so while you were praying and he was sitting, so I said to him: The Prophet of God is praying while you are sitting, and he said to me: Go about your work.' He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Why did you not strike his neck?' 'Umar rose hastily to catch him and kill him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'O 'Umar, return, for your anger is might and your pleasure is judgment. Indeed, God has angels in the heavens who have sufficiency in their prayer from the prayer of so-and-so.' 'Umar said: 'O Messenger of God, and what is their prayer?' He gave him no answer. Then Jibril came to him and said: 'O Prophet of God, did 'Umar ask you about the prayer of the people of heaven?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Convey my greetings to him and inform him that the people of the lowest heaven are in prostration until the Day of Resurrection, saying: Glory be to the Lord of dominion and sovereignty. The people of the second heaven are standing until the Day of Resurrection, saying: Glory be to the Lord of might and majesty. The people of the third heaven are bowing until the Day of Resurrection, saying: Glory be to the Living who does not die. This is the glorification of the angels.'"

The second view: the intended meaning of His saying "nusabbih" (we glorify) is "nusalli" (we pray), and tasbih (glorification) is salah (prayer). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

* * *

The fifth question: taqdis (sanctification) is purification, and from it comes "the sacred land." The scholars differed on several views:

First: "nuqaddisu-ka" means we describe You with what befits You of exaltation and might.
Second: the view of Mujahid: we purify our souls from our sins and errors, seeking Your good pleasure.
Third: the view of Abu Muslim: we purify our deeds from our sins, so that they may be purely for You.
Fourth: we purify our hearts from turning to other than You, until they become absorbed in the lights of Your knowledge.

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: this verse indicates divine justice in several respects:

First: their saying "And we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You" attributes these acts to themselves. If they were acts of God Most High, praising oneself for them would not be good, nor would it be any merit over shedding blood, since all of that is from the act of God Most High.

Second: if corruption and killing were an act of God Most High, the answer should have been: "I am the Owner; I do what I will."

Third: His saying "I know what you do not know" requires disassociation from corruption and killing, but disassociation from one's own act is impossible.

Fourth: if there is no indecency, no ugliness, no injustice, no wrongdoing, and no corruption except by His making, His creation, and His will, how can exaltation and sanctification be valid?

Fifth: His saying "I know what you do not know" indicates the doctrine of justice, for if He were the creator of disbelief, He would have created them for that disbelief. Then the answer should have been: "Yes, I created them so that they would corrupt and kill." Since He did not accept this answer, this doctrine is refuted.

Sixth: if corruption and killing were from the act of God Most High, they would be like their colors and their bodies, and just as it is not valid to marvel at these things, so too it would not be valid to marvel at corruption and killing. The answer to these objections is by the question of the motive and knowledge. And God knows best.

* * *

The sixth question: If it is said: How is His saying "Indeed I know what you do not know" a valid answer to the question they raised? We say: We have mentioned that the question may have several aspects:

First: that it was an expression of wonder, so His saying "I know what you do not know" is an answer to it, in that He, Most High, said: Do not wonder that among them there are those who corrupt and kill, for I know, in spite of this, that among them there is a group of the righteous and the God-fearing, and you do not know.

Second: that it was an expression of grief, so the answer is: Do not grieve over the existence of corrupters, for I also know that among them there is a group of the God-fearing, and whoever, if he swore by Me, I would fulfill his oath.

Third: that it was a request for wisdom, so its answer is that your benefit in it is that you know the wisdom in it in general terms, not in detail, for perhaps that detail would be a harm to you.

Fourth: that it was a petition that He leave them on the earth, and its answer: "Indeed I know that your benefit is that you be in the heaven, not on the earth."

A fifth aspect: when they said "We glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You," He, Most High, said: "Indeed I know what you do not know," namely that with you is Iblis, and that in his heart there is envy, arrogance, and hypocrisy.

A sixth aspect: I know what you do not know, for when you described yourselves with these praises, you magnified yourselves. It is as if you, with this speech, were glorifying yourselves, not glorifying Me. But be patient until mankind appears, and they will humble themselves before God, saying: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves" [al-A'raf: 23], and His saying: "And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive my sin" [al-Shu'ara': 82], and His saying: "And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants" [al-Naml: 19].

[p. 161]

"And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He presented them to the angels and said: Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful."

His saying, Most High: "And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He presented them to the angels and said: Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful." He informs us that when the angels asked about the wisdom in the creation of Adam and his descendants, and God's placing them on the earth, God, Most High, informed them about the wisdom in that in general terms by His saying: "Indeed I know what you do not know." He, Most High, wished to increase them in clarification and to explain that general matter to them. So He, Most High, made clear to them the excellence of Adam, peace be upon him, which had not been known to them, by teaching Adam all the names, then presenting them to the angels, to manifest by this the perfection of his excellence and their deficiency in knowledge, so that this general answer would be confirmed by this detailed answer. Here there are questions:

The first issue: al-Ash'ari, al-Jubba'i and al-Ka'bi said: all languages are tawqifiyya (divinely revealed/ taught), in the sense that God Most High created in people a necessary knowledge of those words and those meanings, and that those words were laid down for those meanings. They argued for this by His saying, ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾, and the discussion of relying on this verse, in questions and answers, we have mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

Abu Hashim said: it is necessary that there be a prior conventional language (lughahistilahiyyah), and he argued that the assignment (al-wad') must be preceded by convention (al-istilah) by several matters:

The first: if the necessary knowledge arose that God Most High assigned this word to this meaning, then that knowledge would either arise for a rational being or for a non-rational being. It is not possible that it arise for a rational being, because if necessary knowledge arose that God Most High assigned that word to that meaning, then the attribute of God Most High would become known by necessity, while His essence is known by inference, and that is impossible. Nor is it possible that it arise for a non-rational being, because it is far-fetched in the minds that knowledge of these languages, with what they contain of wondrous wisdoms, would arise for a non-rational being. Thus it is established that the view of tawqif is corrupt.

The second: that He Most High addressed the angels, and that requires a language prior to that speech.

The third: that His saying, ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾, requires the attribution of the teaching to the names, and that requires that those names were names before that teaching; and if that is so, then languages were present before that teaching.

The fourth: that when Adam, peace be upon him, challenged the angels with knowledge of the names, the angels must have known his truthfulness in designating those names to those named things, otherwise knowledge of his truthfulness would not have been attained; and that requires that the assignment of those names to those named things was prior to that teaching.

As for the answer to the first: why is it not permissible to say that the necessary knowledge was created that some assigner assigned these names to these named things, without specifying whether that assigner was God Most High or people? On this view it does not follow that the attribute becomes known by necessity while the essence is known by proof. Granting that He Most High did not create this knowledge in a rational being, why is it not permissible to say that He created it in a non-rational being? Relying on the notion of being taught (al-istibad) in this context is far-fetched.

As for the second: why is it not permissible to say that He addressed the angels by another means, by writing and other than it?

As for the third: there is no doubt that God Most High's will to assign those words to those meanings preceded the teaching, so that suffices for attributing the teaching to the names.

As for the fourth: its explanation will come, God willing. And God Most High knows best.

**Second issue:** Some people said: His saying, ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾, means that He taught him the attributes of things, their descriptions and their properties.
