The evidence for this is that the derivation of *ism* (name) is either from *simah* (mark) or from *sumuw* (elevation). If it is from *simah*, then the *ism* is a sign, and the attributes, descriptions and properties of things indicate their realities (*mahiyyat*). So it is valid that the meaning of "names" is "attributes." If it is from *sumuw*, the same holds, because the indicator of a thing is like something elevated above that thing, since knowledge of the indicator is acquired before knowledge of what it indicates. Thus the indicator is, in reality, more elevated. It is established, then, that there is no linguistic impediment to taking *ism* to mean "attribute." Afterwards, the grammarians (*ahl al-nahw*) restricted the term *ism* to specific kinds of words, but that is a newly coined convention that carries no weight. When it is established that this interpretation is linguistically possible, it must be the intended meaning and no other, for several reasons:

The first: the excellence of knowing the realities of things is greater than the excellence of knowing their names. Interpreting the passage, which is meant to display excellence, as referring to what entails greater excellence is preferable to interpreting it as referring to something that does not.

The second: a challenge (*tahaddi*) is only valid and appropriate when the listener is able, in some measure, to match it. Someone who knows the language and eloquence may fittingly say to another, as a challenge: "Produce speech like my speech in eloquence." But an Arab may not fittingly say to a Zanj (an African) in the context of a challenge: "Speak in my language." This is because reason has no path to knowing languages at all; that knowledge is acquired only through instruction. If instruction takes place, knowledge is acquired; otherwise it is not. Knowledge of the realities of things, however, is something reason is able to acquire, so the challenge is valid in that domain.

The second opinion, which is the well-known one, is that the intended meaning is the names of every created kind among all the different languages that the children of Adam speak today, Arabic, Persian, Greek and others. The children of Adam (peace be upon him) used to speak these languages. When Adam died and his descendants scattered across the regions of the world, each of them spoke one specific language among those, and that tongue came to dominate him. When time lengthened and generation after generation died, they forgot the rest of the languages. This is the reason for the change of tongues among the children of Adam (peace be upon him).

The scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: The words of the Exalted, ﴿And He taught Adam the names﴾, necessarily require an implied element. It may be that the intended meaning is "He taught Adam the names of the named things," or it may be that the intended meaning is "He taught Adam the named things of the names." They said: But the first is preferable, because of His saying, ﴿Tell Me the names of these﴾, and His saying, ﴿So when he informed them of their names﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 33], and He did not say "Tell Me about these" or "He informed them about them." If it is asked: Since God taught him the kinds of all the named things, and among the named things there are some that are not rational, why did He say "He presented them" (*'aradahum*) and not "He presented them" in the feminine (*'aradaha*)? We answer: Because among them were the angels, humans and jinn, who are rational, the more excellent category was given precedence. This is because it is the custom of the Arabs to give precedence to the complete over the deficient whenever they give precedence.

* * *

**Third issue:** Some people held to the words of the Exalted, ﴿Tell Me the names of these﴾, as evidence for the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne (*taklif ma la yutaq*). This is weak, because He only asked them to inform Him while knowing their incapacity, as a form of rebuke (*tabkit*). What confirms this is His saying, ﴿if you are truthful﴾.

Page 163

**Fourth issue:** The Mu'tazila (a theological school) said: What appeared from Adam (peace be upon him) of his knowledge of the names is a miracle (*mu'jizah*) indicating his prophethood (peace be upon him) at that time. The most likely view is that he was sent to Hawwa (Eve). It is also not far-fetched that he was sent to those to whom the challenge was directed among the angels, because although they were all messengers, it is permissible to send a messenger to another messenger, like the mission of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to Lut (peace be upon him). They argued for this by saying that the acquisition of that knowledge by him breaks the normal course of things, so it must be a miracle. And if it is established that it is a miracle, it is established that he was a messenger at that time.

One may say: We do not grant that this knowledge breaks the normal course, because the acquisition of knowledge of a language by one whom God taught, and its non-acquisition by one whom God did not teach, does not break the normal course. Moreover, either it is said that the angels knew that those names were assigned to those named things, or they did not know that. If they knew it, then they were capable of mentioning the names of those named things, and then opposition (*mu'aradah*) would arise and no distinction or excellence would appear. If they did not know it, then how did they know that Adam (peace be upon him) was correct in what he mentioned, namely that each of those words is a name for each of those named things?

Know that this question can be answered in two ways:

The first: It may be that each category of angels had a language among these languages, and each category was ignorant of the language of the other category. Then all categories of angels were present, and Adam (peace be upon him) enumerated for them all those languages in their entirety, so each category recognised his correctness in its own particular language. In this way they recognised his truthfulness, though all of them together were unable to know all those languages in their entirety, and that was the miracle.

The second: It is not impossible to say that God made them know, before they heard those names from Adam (peace be upon him), the thing by which they could infer Adam's truthfulness. Then, when they heard those names from him (peace be upon him), they recognised his truthfulness in them, and so they recognised that it was a miracle. Suppose we grant that a supernatural act appeared through him; why could that not be among the *karamat* (wondrous gifts granted to the righteous) or among the *irhas* (preparatory signs before prophethood)? Both are permissible in our view. In that case, the discussion of this question becomes a branch of the discussion of those two.

Those who asserted with certainty that he (peace be upon him) was not a prophet at that time argued with several points:

The first: If he had been a prophet at that time, then sin would have proceeded from him after prophethood, and that is impermissible. Therefore it must be that he was not a prophet at that time. As for the necessary connection (*mulazamah*), it is that the slip which proceeded from him occurred after this event by agreement, and that slip was among the major sins, as will be explained if God wills. Committing a major sin entails deserving expulsion, contempt and cursing, and all of this is impermissible for prophets. Hence it must be said that this event occurred before prophethood.

The second: If he were a messenger at that time, then he would either have been sent to someone or not. If he was sent to someone, then he was sent either to the angels, to humans or to the jinn. The first is invalid, because according to the Mu'tazila the angels are more excellent than humans, and it is not permissible to make the lesser a messenger to the more excellent, since the messenger is a leader (*qa'id*) and the community is a follower, and making the lesser the one followed by the more excellent contradicts the basic principle. Also, a person is more inclined to accept speech from one of his own kind. For this reason the Exalted said, ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [Al-An'am: 9]. It is also impermissible that he was sent to humans, because there was no human there except Hawwa (Eve), and Hawwa came to know the obligation not through the mediation of Adam, as shown by the words of the Exalted, ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 35], where He addressed them directly with this obligation and did not make Adam an intermediary. It is also impermissible that he was sent to the jinn, because there was no jinn in the heaven. It is also impermissible that he was sent to anyone at all, because the purpose of making him a messenger is conveyance (*tabligh*), so where there is no one to whom to convey, there is no benefit in making him a messenger.

Page 164

This argument is not of the strongest kind.

The third: The words of the Exalted, ﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]. This verse shows that He chose him only after the slip, so it must be said that before the slip he was not one chosen. And if he was not chosen at that time, it must be that he was not a messenger, because messengership and being chosen are mutually entailing. This is because being chosen has no meaning except being singled out with various kinds of honours, and everyone whom God made a messenger has been singled out with this, by the words of the Exalted, ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am: 124].

**Fifth issue:** They mentioned several interpretations of the words of the Exalted, ﴿if you are truthful﴾:

The first: its meaning is "Inform me of the names of these, if you know that you will be truthful in that informing."

The second: its meaning is "Tell me, and say nothing but what is true and right." The purpose of this is to emphasise what He had alerted them to, namely their deficiency and incapacity. For once the knowledge becomes firmly fixed in their souls that if they informed Him they would not be truthful, and they have no way to do so, they would know that this is beyond them.

The third: "If you are truthful in your claim that no creature is worshipped with anything except that you are fit for it and perform it." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

The fourth: "If you are truthful in your claim that I have created no creature except that you would know more about it than it. So inform Me of the names of these."

**Sixth issue:** This verse indicates the excellence of knowledge. He, glory be to Him, did not manifest the perfection of His wisdom in creating Adam (peace be upon him) except by manifesting his knowledge. So if it were possible for something more noble than knowledge to exist, it would have been obligatory to manifest his excellence through that thing rather than through knowledge. Know that the excellence of knowledge is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah and transmitted reports. As for the Book, there are several points:

The first: The Exalted named knowledge "wisdom" (*hikmah*), and then He magnified the matter of wisdom, which indicates the great station of knowledge.

The explanation that the Exalted named knowledge "wisdom" is what is related from Muqatil, who said: The interpretation of *hikmah* in the Qur'an has four aspects:

One: the admonitions of the Qur'an. He said in Al-Baqarah: ﴿And what He sent down to you of the Book and wisdom﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 231], meaning the admonitions of the Qur'an. In An-Nisa: ﴿And God sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾ [An-Nisa: 113], meaning the admonitions, and similarly in Al 'Imran.

Two: *hikmah* in the sense of understanding and knowledge, as in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We gave him judgement while a child﴾ [Maryam: 12]. In Luqman: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman: 12], meaning understanding and knowledge. In Al-An'am: ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book and judgement﴾ [Al-An'am: 89].

Three: *hikmah* in the sense of prophethood. In An-Nisa: ﴿Then We had given the family of Ibrahim the Book and wisdom﴾ [An-Nisa: 54], meaning prophethood. In Sad: ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾ [Sad: 20], meaning prophethood. In Al-Baqarah: ﴿And God gave him dominion and wisdom﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 251].

Four: the Qur'an. In An-Nahl: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾ [An-Nahl: 125]. In Al-Baqarah: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 269]. All of these aspects, on careful examination, return to knowledge. Then reflect: God did not give of knowledge except a little. He said: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [Al-Isra: 85], and He called the whole of this world little: ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little﴾ [An-Nisa: 77]. So if He called what is little something whose quantity we cannot grasp, what then do you think of what He called much? Moreover, the rational proof of the scarcity of this world and the abundance of wisdom is that this world is limited in extent, limited in number and limited in duration, whereas knowledge has no limit to its extent, its number or its duration, nor to the happiness that results from it. This alerts you to the excellence of knowledge.

The second: the words of the Exalted, ﴿Say: Are those who know and those who do not know equal?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 9]. He has distinguished between seven groups

in His Book. He distinguished between the wicked and the good, saying: ﴿Say, "The wicked and the good are not equal"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100], meaning the lawful and the unlawful. He distinguished between the blind and the seeing, saying: ﴿Say, "Are the blind and the seeing equal?"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16]. He distinguished between light and darkness, saying: ﴿Or are the darknesses and the light equal?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16]. He distinguished between Paradise and the Fire, and between the shade and the scorching heat. If you reflect, you will find that all of this is derived from the distinction between the knowing and the ignorant.

Third: His saying: ﴿Obey God, and obey the Messenger, and those in authority among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. The intended meaning of "those in authority" (ulu al-amr) is, according to the most sound opinions, the scholars, because rulers are obligated to obey the scholars, and not the reverse. Then consider this rank: God, exalted is He, mentioned the scholars in two places in His Book, in the second rank. He said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but Him, and the angels and those of knowledge [bear witness]﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], and He said: ﴿Obey God, and obey the Messenger, and those in authority among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. Then, glorified and exalted is He, He increased in honour by placing them in the first rank in two verses. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿None knows its interpretation except God, and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], and He said: ﴿Say, "God is sufficient as a witness between me and you, and [so is] whoever has knowledge of the Book"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

Fourth: ﴿God will raise those who have believed among you, and those who were given knowledge, by degrees﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 11]. Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned degrees for four categories. The first of them: for the believers among the people of Badr. He said: ﴿The believers are only those who, when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾ [al-Anfal: 2], up to His saying: ﴿For them are degrees with their Lord﴾ [al-Anfal: 4].

The second: for those who strive (in the way of God). He said: ﴿God has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their selves over those who sit [at home] by a degree﴾ [al-Nisa': 95].

The third: for the righteous. He said: ﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds, for them are the high degrees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 75].

The fourth: for the scholars. He said: ﴿And those who were given knowledge [will be raised] by degrees﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 11]. God preferred the people of Badr over other believers by degrees, preferred those who strive over those who sit by degrees, preferred the righteous over these by degrees, and then preferred the scholars over all of the categories by degrees. Therefore it is necessary that the scholars be the most excellent of people.

Fifth: His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28]. God, exalted is He, described the scholars in His Book with five virtues. The first of them is faith: ﴿And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, "We believe in it"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7].

The second: monotheism and testimony: ﴿God bears witness﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], up to His saying: ﴿and those of knowledge﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18].

The third: weeping: ﴿And they fall upon their faces weeping﴾ [al-Isra': 109].

The fourth: humility: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ [al-Isra': 107], the verse.

The fifth: fear: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28].

As for the reports (akhbar), there are several aspects:

First: Thabit narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to look at the freed ones of God from the Fire, let him look at the seekers of knowledge. By the One in whose hand is my soul, there is no seeker of knowledge who goes to the door of a scholar except that God records for him the worship of a year for every step, builds for him a city in Paradise for every step, and he walks on the earth while the earth seeks forgiveness for him, and he becomes forgiven in the morning and the evening, and the angels bear witness for them that they are the freed ones of God from the Fire."

Second: From Anas, who said: He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever seeks knowledge for other than God, he will not leave this world until knowledge comes to him and it becomes for God. Whoever seeks knowledge for God is like one who fasts by day and stands in prayer by night. Indeed, a chapter of knowledge that a man learns is better for him than to have Abu Qubays [a mountain] in gold and spend it in the way of God."

Third: From al-Hasan, marfu' (traced back to the Prophet): "Whoever death comes to while he is seeking knowledge to revive Islam, between him and the prophets there will be one degree in Paradise."

Fourth: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, marfu': "God will raise the servants on the Day of Resurrection, then He will single out the scholars and say: 'O assembly of scholars, I did not place My light in you except because of My knowledge of you, and I did not place My knowledge in you to punish you. Go, for I have forgiven you.'"

Fifth: He, peace be upon him, said: "The teacher of good, when he dies, the birds of the sky, the beasts of the earth, and the fish of the seas weep over him."

Sixth: Abu Hurayrah, marfu': "Whoever prays behind a scholar of the scholars, it is as if he prayed behind one of the prophets."

Seventh: Ibn 'Umar, marfu': "The scholar is preferred over the worshipper by seventy degrees, between each degree is the pace of a horse for seventy years. That is because Satan introduces innovation to the people, and the scholar sees it and removes it, while the worshipper turns to his worship, not paying attention to it and not recognizing it."

Eighth: al-Hasan, marfu', he, peace be upon him, said: "May God have mercy on my successors." It was said: "Who are your successors, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Those who revive my sunnah and teach it to the servants of God."

Ninth: He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever goes out seeking a chapter of knowledge to return falsehood to truth or misguidance to guidance, his deed is like the worship of forty years."

Tenth: He, peace be upon him, said to 'Ali when he sent him to Yemen: "For God to guide one man through you is better for you than what the sun rises upon or sets upon."

Eleventh: Ibn Mas'ud, marfu': "Whoever seeks knowledge to narrate it to the people, seeking the face of God, He will give him the reward of seventy prophets."

Twelfth: 'Amir al-Juhani, marfu': "On the Day of Resurrection the ink of the seeker of knowledge and the blood of the martyr will be brought, and neither of them will be preferred over the other." In another narration: "Then the ink of the scholars will be weighed [and found heavier]."

Thirteenth: Abu Waqid al-Laythi: "While he, peace be upon him, was sitting with the people around him, three men came. One of them saw a gap in the circle and sat in it. The second sat behind them. As for the third, he turned back and fled. When he, peace be upon him, finished his speech, he said: 'Shall I tell you about the three men? As for the first, he sought refuge with God, so God sheltered him. As for the second, he was shy before God, so God was shy of him. As for the third, he turned away from God, so God turned away from him.'" Related by Muslim.

As for the reports from the companions and the successors (athar), there are several aspects:

(a) The scholar is more compassionate to the student than the father and mother, because parents protect him from the fire of this world and its afflictions, while scholars protect him from the fire of the Hereafter and its hardships.

(b) It was said to Ibn Mas'ud: "How did you acquire this knowledge?" He said: "With an inquiring tongue and an understanding heart."

(c) Some of them said: "Ask the question of the ignorant, and memorize as the wise memorize."

(d) Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr said to his son: "O my son, learn knowledge, for if you have wealth, knowledge will be a beauty for you, and if you do not have wealth, knowledge will be wealth for you."

(e) 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "There is no good in silence about knowledge, just as there is no good in speech about ignorance."

(f) Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: "Scholars are of three kinds: a scholar of God who is not a scholar of the command of God; a scholar of the command of God who is not a scholar of God; and a scholar of God and of the command of God."

As for the first: he is a servant over whom divine knowledge has taken control of his heart, so he becomes absorbed in witnessing the light of majesty and the pages of grandeur, and so he does not devote himself to learning the knowledge of rulings except what is necessary.

The second: he is the one who is a scholar of the command of God and not a scholar of God. He is the one who knows the lawful and the unlawful and the realities of the rulings, but he does not know the secrets of God's majesty.

As for the scholar of God and of the rulings of God: he sits on the shared boundary between the world of intelligibles and the world of sensibles. At times he is with God through love for Him, and at times he is with creation through compassion and mercy. When he returns from his Lord to creation, he is with them like one of them, as if he did not know God. And when he is alone with his Lord, occupied with His remembrance and service, it is as if he did not know creation. This is the way of the messengers and the truthful ones (siddiqun). This is what is meant by his, peace be upon him, saying: "Ask the scholars, mix with the wise, and sit with the great." So what is meant by his, peace be upon him, saying "Ask the scholars" is the scholars of the command of God who are not scholars of God, and he commanded asking them when there is need, seeking a fatwa from them. As for the wise, they are the scholars of God who do not know the commands of God, and he commanded associating with them. As for the great, they are the scholars of God and of the rulings of God, and he commanded sitting with them, because in that sitting are benefits of this world and the Hereafter.

Then Shaqiq al-Balkhi said: "Each of these three has three signs. As for the scholar of the command of God, he has three signs: that he is remembering with the tongue but not the heart, that he fears creatures but not the Lord, and that he is shy before people outwardly but is not shy before God in secret. As for the scholar of God, he is remembering, fearing, and shy."

As for remembrance, it is remembrance of the heart, not remembrance of the tongue. As for fear, it is fear of showing off, not fear of disobedience. As for shyness, it is shyness of what passes through the heart, not outward shyness. As for the scholar of God and of the command of God, he has six things: the three we mentioned for the scholar of God alone, together with three others: that he sits on the shared boundary between the world of the unseen and the world of the witnessed, that he is a teacher to the first two categories, and that he is in a position where the first two groups need him while he is independent of them.

Then he said: "The likeness of the scholar of God and of the command of God is like the sun, which neither increases nor decreases. The likeness of the scholar of God alone is like the moon, which at times becomes full and at other times wanes. The likeness of the scholar of the command of God alone is like a lamp, which burns itself and gives light to others."

(g) Fath al-Mawsili said: "Is it not the case that when a patient is deprived of food, drink, and medicine, he dies? Likewise, when the heart is deprived of knowledge, thought, and wisdom, it dies."

(h) Shaqiq al-Balkhi said: "People rise from my assembly in three categories: a pure disbeliever, a pure hypocrite, and a pure believer. That is because I interpret the Qur'an and I say on behalf of God and His Messenger. Whoever does not believe me is a pure disbeliever; whoever his heart is constricted by it is a pure hypocrite; and whoever regrets what he did and resolves not to sin is a pure believer."

He also said: "There are three kinds of sleep that God dislikes, and three kinds of laughter: sleeping after the Fajr prayer and before the 'Atamah prayer, sleeping during prayer, and sleeping at the gathering of remembrance. And laughing behind a funeral bier, laughing in graveyards, and laughing in a gathering of remembrance."

(i) Some of them said regarding His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So the torrent carries a rising foam﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17]: "The torrent here is knowledge. God likened it to water in five respects. The first: just as rain descends from the sky, so knowledge descends from the sky. The second: just as the land is restored by rain, so creation is restored by knowledge. The third: just as crops and plants do not grow without rain, so deeds and acts of worship do not come forth without knowledge. The fourth: just as rain is accompanied by thunder and lightning, so knowledge is accompanied by promise and threat. The fifth: just as rain is both beneficial and harmful, so knowledge is beneficial and harmful: beneficial to whoever acts by it, harmful to whoever does not act by it."

(j) How many a reminder of God is forgetful of God; how many one who fears God is bold against God; how many one brought near to God is far from God; how many a caller to God flees from God; and how many a reciter of the Book of God has stripped himself of the signs of God.

(k) The world is a garden adorned with five things: the knowledge of scholars, the justice of rulers, the worship of worshippers, the trustworthiness of merchants, and the sincere counsel of craftsmen.

Then Iblis came with five banners and planted them beside these five. He brought envy and planted it beside knowledge; he brought oppression and planted it beside justice; he brought showing-off (riya') and planted it beside worship; he brought betrayal and planted it beside trustworthiness; and he brought deceit and planted it beside sincere counsel.

(يب) Al-Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) was preferred over the Successors (al-tabi'un) in five things. The first: he did not command anyone to do something until he had done it himself.
The second: he did not forbid anyone from something until he had refrained from it himself.
The third: whoever asked him for anything that Allah Most High had provided him with, whether knowledge or wealth, he did not withhold it.
The fourth: he was self-sufficient through his knowledge, independent of people.
The fifth: his inner state and outward conduct were the same.

(يج) If you wish to know whether your knowledge benefits you or not, then ask yourself about five traits: love of poverty for the sake of having few needs; love of obedience seeking reward; love of asceticism in this world seeking freedom from distraction; love of wisdom seeking the soundness of the heart; and love of solitude seeking intimate conversation with the Lord.

(يد) Seek five things in five: First, seek honour in humility, not in wealth and kinship.
Second, seek richness in contentment, not in abundance.
Third, seek security in Paradise, not in this world.
Fourth, seek rest in having little, not in having much.
Fifth, seek the benefit of knowledge in action, not in the abundance of narration.

(يه) Ibn al-Mubarak said: The corruption of this community has come only from its elite, and they are five: the scholars, the warriors, the ascetics, the merchants, and the rulers.
As for the scholars, they are the heirs of the Prophets; as for the ascetics, they are the pillars of the people of the earth; as for the warriors, they are the soldiers of Allah on earth; as for the merchants, they are the trustees of Allah on His earth; and as for the rulers, they are the shepherds. So if the scholar is lowly in religion and elevated by wealth, whom will the ignorant follow? And if the ascetic in this world is covetous, whom will the penitent follow? And if the warrior is greedy and showing-off, how will he prevail over the enemy? And if the merchant is a traitor, how will trustworthiness be realised? And if the shepherd is a wolf, how will care be achieved?

(يو) Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Knowledge is better than wealth in seven respects. The first: knowledge is the inheritance of the Prophets, while wealth is the inheritance of Pharaohs.
The second: knowledge does not diminish by being spent, whereas wealth diminishes.
The third: wealth needs a guardian, while knowledge guards its possessor.
The fourth: when a man dies, his wealth remains behind, while knowledge enters the grave with its possessor.
The fifth: wealth is attained by both the believer and the unbeliever, while knowledge is attained only by the believer.
The sixth: all people need the one who has knowledge in matters of their religion, and they do not need the one who has wealth.
The seventh: knowledge strengthens a man to cross the Sirat, while wealth hinders him.

(يز) The jurist Abu al-Layth said: Whoever sits with a scholar and is unable to memorise anything of that knowledge has seven honours:
The first: he attains the merit of the learners.
The second: as long as he is sitting with him, he is restrained from sins.
The third: when he leaves his home seeking knowledge, mercy descends upon him.
The fourth: when he sits in a circle of knowledge and mercy descends upon them, he obtains a share of it.
The fifth: as long as he is in the state of listening, an act of obedience is recorded for him.
The sixth: if he listens and does not understand, his heart is constricted by his deprivation of grasping knowledge, and that grief becomes a means for him to the presence of Allah Most High, by His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: "I am with those whose hearts are broken for My sake."
The seventh: he sees the Muslims honouring the scholar and humiliating the sinners, so his heart is turned away from sin and his nature inclines towards knowledge; for this reason, the Prophet (peace be upon him) commanded us to sit with the righteous.

(يح) It has been said: Among the scholars is one who withholds his knowledge and does not like it to be found with anyone else; he is in the first level of the Fire. Among the scholars is one who in his knowledge is like a ruler: if anything of his right is refused, he becomes angry; he is in the second level of the Fire. Among the scholars is one who makes his speech and rare points of knowledge only for the people of rank and wealth, and does not regard the poor as worthy of it; he is in the third level of the Fire. Among the scholars is one who is self-admiring: if he admonishes, he browbeats; and if he is admonished, he is offended; he is in the fourth level of the Fire.
Among the scholars is one who sets himself up for issuing legal rulings and issues them in error; he is in the fifth level of the Fire. Among the scholars is one who learns the speech of the falsifiers and mixes it with religion; he is in the sixth level of the Fire. Among the scholars is one who seeks knowledge for the sake of people's faces; he is in the seventh level of the Fire.

(يط) The jurist Abu al-Layth said: Whoever sits with eight categories of people, Allah will increase him by eight things. Whoever sits with the rich, Allah will increase him in love of this world and desire for it. Whoever sits with the poor, Allah will grant him gratitude and contentment with Allah's allotment. Whoever sits with the ruler, Allah will increase him in harshness and pride. Whoever sits with women, Allah will increase him in ignorance and desire. Whoever sits with children, he will increase in play and joking. Whoever sits with the wicked, he will increase in boldness regarding sins and in postponing repentance. Whoever sits with the righteous, he will increase in eagerness for acts of obedience. Whoever sits with the scholars, he will increase in knowledge and scrupulousness.

(يي) Allah taught seven persons seven things: (أ) He taught Adam the names: "And He taught Adam the names, all of them."
(ب) He taught Khidr insight: "And We taught him knowledge from Our presence" [al-Kahf: 65].
(ج) He taught Yusuf the science of interpretation: "My Lord, You have given me of sovereignty and taught me of the interpretation of events" [Yusuf: 101].
(د) He taught Dawud the craft of making coats of mail: "And We taught him the making of armour for you" [al-Anbiya': 80].
(ه) He taught Sulayman the speech of birds: "O mankind, we have been taught the speech of birds" [al-Naml: 16].
(و) He taught Isa, peace be upon him, the knowledge of the Torah and the Gospel: "And He will teach him the Book and wisdom, and the Torah and the Gospel" [Al 'Imran: 48].
(ز) He taught Muhammad (ﷺ) the Law and monotheism: "And He taught you what you did not know" [al-Nisa': 113]; "and teaches them the Book and wisdom" [al-Baqarah: 129]; "The Most Merciful, taught the Qur'an" [al-Rahman: 1-2].

The knowledge of Adam was the cause of his obtaining prostration and honour; the knowledge of Khidr was the cause of his finding a student like Musa and Yusha', peace be upon them both; the knowledge of Yusuf was the cause of his gaining family and kingdom; the knowledge of Dawud was the cause of his gaining leadership and rank; the knowledge of Sulayman was the cause of his gaining Bilqis and dominion; the knowledge of Isa was the cause of the removal of accusation from his mother; and the knowledge of Muhammad (ﷺ) was the cause of the existence of intercession.
Then we say: whoever knows the names of created things finds greeting from the angels; so whoever knows the Creator's essence and attributes, will he not find the greeting of the angels? Rather, he finds the greeting of the Lord: "Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful" [Ya-Sin: 58]. Khidr, through the knowledge of insight, found the companionship of Musa; so O community of the Beloved, through knowledge of the reality, how would you not find the companionship of Muhammad (ﷺ)? "Those are with those whom Allah has blessed of the prophets" [al-Nisa': 69]. Yusuf, through interpreting the dream, was delivered from the prison of this world; so whoever is knowledgeable of the interpretation of Allah's Book, how would he not be delivered from the prison of desires? "And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path" [Yunus: 25]. Also, Yusuf, peace be upon him, mentioned Allah's favour upon himself when he said: "and You taught me of the interpretation of events" [Yusuf: 101].

So you, O scholar, do you not remember Allah's favour upon yourself, that He taught you the interpretation of His Book? What greater blessing is there than what Allah has given you? He made you an interpreter of His speech, a namesake of Himself, an heir of His Prophet, a caller to His creation, an admonisher of His servants, a lamp for the people of His lands, and a leader of creation to His Paradise and His reward, and a deterrent for them from His Fire and His punishment, as has come in the hadith: "The scholars are lords, the jurists are leaders, and sitting with them is an increase."

(كا) The believer does not desire to seek knowledge until he sees six traits in himself. One of them: that he says, "Allah has commanded me to perform the obligations, and I cannot perform them except by knowledge."
The second: that he says, "He has forbidden me from sins, and I cannot avoid them except by knowledge."
The third: that He, Most High, has made it obligatory upon me to thank Him for His blessings, and I cannot do that except by knowledge.
The fourth: He commanded me to be just to creation, and I cannot be just to them except by knowledge.
The fifth: that Allah commanded me to be patient under His trial, and I cannot do that except by knowledge.
The sixth: that Allah commanded me to be hostile to Satan, and I cannot be so except by knowledge.

(كب) The path to Paradise is in the hands of four: the scholar, the ascetic, the worshipper, and the fighter for the cause of Allah. If the ascetic is truthful in his claim, Allah grants him security; if the worshipper is truthful in his claim, Allah grants him fear; if the fighter is truthful in his claim, Allah grants him praise and commendation; if the scholar is truthful in his claim, Allah grants him wisdom.

(كج) Seek four things from four: from the place, safety; from the companion, honour; from wealth, freedom from want; from knowledge, benefit. If you do not find safety from the place, then prison is better than it; if you do not find honour from your companion, then a dog is better than him; if you do not find freedom from want from your wealth, then clay is better than it; and if you do not find benefit from knowledge, then death is better than it.

(كد) Four things are not completed except by four things: religion is not completed except by piety; speech is not completed except by action; manliness is not completed except by humility; and knowledge is not completed except by action. So religion without piety is in peril; speech without action is like nothing; manliness without humility is like a tree without fruit; and knowledge without action is like rain without a downpour.

(كه) Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Jabir ibn Abdullah al-Ansari: The affairs of the world stand on four: a scholar who acts on his knowledge; an ignorant person who does not disdain to learn; a rich person who does not withhold his wealth; and a poor person who does not sell his Hereafter for his worldly life. When the scholar does not act on his knowledge, the ignorant person disdains to learn; and when the rich person withholds his kindness, the poor person sells his Hereafter for his worldly life. So woe to them, and destruction seventy times over.

(كو) Al-Khalil said: Men are of four kinds: a man who knows and knows that he knows; he is a scholar, so follow him. A man who knows but does not know that he knows; he is asleep, so wake him. A man who does not know but knows that he does not know; he is seeking guidance, so guide him. And a man who does not know and does not know that he does not know; he is a devil, so avoid him.

(كز) There are four things that a noble person should not be too proud to do, even if he is a commander: rising from his seat for his father; serving his guest; serving the scholar from whom he learns; and asking about what he does not know from one who knows more than him.

(كح) When scholars busy themselves with gathering the lawful, the common people become eaters of doubtful things; and when the scholar becomes an eater of doubtful things, the common person becomes an eater of the unlawful; and when the scholar becomes an eater of the unlawful, the common person becomes a disbeliever, meaning if they deem it permissible.

As for the rational aspects: there are several matters. One of them: affairs are of four categories. One category is what reason approves of but desire does not; a second is what desire approves of but reason does not; a third is what both reason and desire approve of together; and a fourth is what neither reason nor desire approves of.
As for the first: it is illnesses and hardships in this world.
As for the second: it is sins in their entirety.
As for the third: it is knowledge.

Now, as for the fourth: it is ignorance. Knowledge stands in relation to ignorance as Paradise stands in relation to Hell. Just as the intellect and desire do not accept the Fire, so they do not accept ignorance; and just as they desire Paradise, so they desire knowledge. Whoever is content with ignorance has become content with a Fire that is present, and whoever occupies himself with knowledge has plunged into a Paradise that is present. So everyone who chooses knowledge is told: "You have accustomed yourself to dwelling in Paradise, so enter Paradise," and whoever is satisfied with ignorance is told: "You have accustomed yourself to the Fire, so enter the Fire."

What shows that knowledge is Paradise and ignorance is Fire is that the perfection of pleasure lies in attaining the beloved, and the perfection of pain lies in distance from the beloved. A wound causes pain only because it separates one part of the body from another part that is loved, namely their connection. Since the wound necessitates the removal of that connection, it necessitates the removal and distance of the beloved, and so it is necessarily painful. Burning by fire is more painful than a wound, because a wound only produces the separation of a specific part from a specific part, whereas fire penetrates all the parts and necessitates the separation of all the parts from one another. Since the dissociations in burning are greater, the pain there is more severe. As for pleasure, it is the attainment of the beloved: the pleasure of eating is the attainment of those tastes because they agree with the body; likewise the pleasure of seeing arises because the faculty of sight longs to perceive visible things, so that perception is a pleasure to it. Thus it has become clear that pleasure is the attainment of the beloved and pain is the attainment of the disliked. Knowing this, we say: whenever the perception is deeper and stronger, the perceiver more noble and perfect, and the perceived purer and more lasting, the pleasure must be more noble and perfect.

There is no doubt that the bearer of knowledge is the soul, and it is nobler than the body. There is no doubt that intellectual perception is deeper and nobler, as will be explained in the commentary on His words: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [An-Nur: 35]. As for the known, there is no doubt that it is the noblest, for it is Allah, Lord of the worlds, and all His creation: the angels, the spheres, the elements, the inanimate, the plants and the animals, and all His rulings, commands and obligations. What known object is nobler than that? Thus it is established that there is no perfection and no pleasure above the perfection and pleasures of knowledge, and no wretchedness and no deficiency above the wretchedness and deficiency of ignorance.

Among what supports what we have said: when one of us is asked a question of knowledge, if he knows it and is able to answer correctly, he rejoices and is delighted by it; and if he does not know it, he lowers his head out of shame. This shows that the pleasure gained from knowledge is the most perfect of pleasures, and the misery gained from ignorance is the most perfect kind of misery.

* * *

Know that there are other textual proofs showing the virtue of knowledge, which we forgot to mention earlier, so there is no harm in mentioning them here.

The first proof: the first thing revealed was His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾ ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿who taught by the pen﴾ ﴿taught man that which he did not know﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 1-5]. It has been said concerning this: there must be observance of coherence between the verses, so what is the connection between His saying ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾ and His saying ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous who taught by the pen﴾? It is answered that the aspect of connection is that He mentioned the first state of man, which is that he was a clinging substance, though that is the lowliest of things, and his last state, which is becoming a knower, which is the most exalted rank. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "You were, in your first state, in that degree which is the extreme of lowliness, and you became, in your last state, in that degree which is the extreme of nobility." This is only complete if knowledge is the noblest of ranks, for if something else were nobler, mentioning that thing in this context would be more fitting.

The second: He said: ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous who taught by the pen﴾. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that the arrangement of a ruling upon a description indicates that the description is the cause. So this shows that He, glorified and exalted is He, deserved the description of being Most Generous because He gave knowledge. Had knowledge not been nobler than other things, its bestowal would not be nobler than the bestowal of other things.

The third: His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾. This verse contains several proofs of the virtue of knowledge.

The first of them: that it indicates a group among the people of Paradise. This is because the scholars are among the people of fear, and whoever is among the people of fear is among the people of Paradise; therefore the scholars are among the people of Paradise. The proof that the scholars are among the people of fear is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. The proof that the people of fear are among the people of Paradise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their reward with their Lord is gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 8], up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is for whoever fears his Lord﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 8]. Also indicating this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for he who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 46]. Also indicating this is the hadith: "By My might and My majesty, I will not combine for My servant two fears, nor will I combine for him two securities. If he feels secure from Me in the world, I will make him fearful on the Day of Resurrection, and if he fears Me in the world, I will make him secure on the Day of Resurrection."

Know that it is possible to establish the two premises of this argument by reason. As for showing that one who knows Allah must fear Him: whoever does not know a thing cannot possibly be afraid of it. Furthermore, knowledge of the essence alone is not sufficient for fear; rather, it requires knowledge of three matters. Among them: knowledge of power, for a king knows that his subjects are aware of his evil deeds, yet he does not fear them because he knows they are unable to repel them. Among them: knowledge that He is knowing, for a thief stealing from the sultan's wealth knows the sultan's power, but he knows the sultan does not know of his theft, so he does not fear him. Among them: knowledge that He is wise, for the courtier of the sultan knows that the sultan is able to prevent him, and knows his evil deeds, but he knows that the sultan may be pleased with what is not fitting, so fear does not arise. But if he knows the sultan's awareness of his evil deeds, knows his power to prevent them, and knows that he is wise and will not be pleased with his wrongdoing, then these three knowledges become necessary for fear to arise in his heart. Thus it is established that the servant's fear of Allah does not arise unless he knows that He, exalted is He, is knowing of all that is known, powerful over all that is within power, and not pleased with the abominable and the forbidden. Thus it is established that fear is a necessary consequence of knowledge of Allah. We have said that fear is the cause of attaining Paradise, because when a immediate pleasure presents itself to the servant, and that pleasure is contrary to the command of Allah, and the doing of that thing involves both benefit and harm, then clear reason judges that the preponderant side should be preferred over the outweighed side. So when he knows by the light of faith that the immediate pleasure is trifling in comparison with the deferred pain, that faith becomes the cause of his flight from that immediate pleasure, and that is fear. When he abstains from what is prohibited and performs what is obligatory, he becomes among the people of reward. Thus it has been established, by textual and rational evidence, that the knower of Allah is fearful, and the fearful is among the people of Paradise.

The second of them: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that there are no people of Paradise except the scholars, for the particle (innama) denotes restriction. So this shows that the fear of Allah does not arise except in the scholars. The second verse, His saying: ﴿That is for whoever fears his Lord﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 8], indicates that Paradise is for the people of fear, and its being for the people of fear excludes its being for others. Thus the two verses together indicate that there are no people of Paradise except the scholars. Know that this verse contains a severe warning, for it has been established that fear of Allah is a necessary consequence of knowledge of Allah; so when fear is absent, knowledge of Allah is absent. This subtlety alerts you that the knowledge which is the cause of nearness to Allah is that which produces fear, and that kinds of disputation, however subtle and obscure, if they are devoid of producing fear, belong to blameworthy knowledge.

The third of them: it has been recited ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28] with the first word in the nominative and the second in the accusative (Allah in the accusative, ulama in the nominative). The meaning of this reading is: if fear were permissible for Him, the scholars would not fear, because they are the ones who distinguish between what is permissible and what is not; as for the ignorant one who does not distinguish between these two categories, what concern is he, and what regard is paid to him? So in this reading there is the utmost elevation of station and honour for the scholars.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. In it is the strongest proof of the preciousness of knowledge and the loftiness of its rank, and of Allah's exceeding love for it, in that He commanded His Prophet to seek increase from it specifically, and not from anything else. Qatadah said: "If anyone could be satisfied with knowledge, the Prophet of Allah Musa, peace be upon him, would have been satisfied, and he would not have said: ﴿May I follow you on the condition that you teach me of what you have been taught as guidance?﴾ [Al-Kahf: 66]."

The fifth: Sulayman, peace be upon him, possessed worldly dominion to such a degree that ﴿he said: My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me﴾ [Sad: 35]. Yet he did not boast of the kingdom, but boasted of knowledge when he said: ﴿And he said: O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of all things﴾ [An-Naml: 16]. So he boasted of being knowing of the speech of birds. If it is fitting for Sulayman to boast of that knowledge, then it is all the more fitting for the believer to boast of knowing the Lord of the worlds. Moreover, he placed that before His saying: ﴿and we have been given of all things﴾ [An-Naml: 16]. Also, when He mentioned the perfection of their state, He placed knowledge first, saying: ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the field﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 78], up to His saying: ﴿And to each We gave judgement and knowledge﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 79]. Then He mentioned after that what relates to worldly affairs, which indicates that knowledge is nobler.

The sixth: some have said: the hoopoe, despite being in the utmost weakness, and despite being in a position of rebuke, said to Sulayman: ﴿I have encompassed that which you have not encompassed﴾ [An-Naml: 22]. Had knowledge not been the noblest of things, from where would the hoopoe have obtained the ability to speak in Sulayman's assembly with such words? That is why a man of low standing, when he acquires knowledge, becomes one whose word is effective before sultans, and this is nothing but by the blessing of knowledge.

The seventh: the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "An hour of reflection is better than sixty years of worship." Regarding its preference there are two aspects. The first: reflection leads you to Allah, exalted is He, and worship leads you to the reward of Allah, exalted is He, and that which leads you to Allah is better than that which leads you to other than Allah. The second: reflection is an act of the heart, and obedience is an act of the limbs, and the heart is nobler than the limbs, so the act of the heart is nobler than the act of the limbs. What confirms this aspect is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]; He made the prayer a means to remembrance of the heart, and the purpose is nobler than the means. This shows that knowledge is nobler than other things.

The eighth: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know﴾ [An-Nisa: 113], and ﴿And the bounty of Allah upon you has been great﴾ [An-Nisa: 113]. So He called knowledge "great," and called wisdom "much good." Wisdom is knowledge. He also said: ﴿The Most Merciful, taught the Qur'an﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 1-2], thereby placing this blessing ahead of all blessings. This shows that it is superior to other things.

[Page 174]

Ninth: All the other Books of God speak of the excellence of knowledge. In the Torah, God Most High said to Moses, peace be upon him: "Magnify wisdom, for I do not place wisdom in the heart of a servant except that I intend to forgive him. So learn it, then act by it, then give it away, so that through it you may attain My honour in this world and the next." In the Psalms (Zabur), the Glorified and Exalted said: "O David, tell the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Children of Israel and their monks (ruhbān): Keep company with the God-fearing (al-atqiyā') among the people. If you do not find a God-fearing person among them, then keep company with the scholars ('ulamā'). If you do not find a scholar, then keep company with the intelligent ('uqalā'). For God-consciousness (taqwā), knowledge, and intellect are three ranks, and I have not placed any one of them in any of My creatures while intending to destroy him."

I say: God Most High placed God-consciousness before knowledge because God-consciousness cannot exist without knowledge, as we have explained that awe (khashyah) is not attained except with knowledge. The one who possesses both qualities is more noble than the one who possesses only one. For this same reason, He placed the scholar before the intelligent person, because the scholar must necessarily be intelligent, whereas the intelligent person may not be a scholar. Thus intellect is like the seed, knowledge is like the tree, and God-consciousness is like the fruit.

As for the Gospel (Injīl), God Most High said in its seventeenth chapter: "Woe to the one who hears of knowledge and does not seek it! How will he be gathered with the ignorant to the Fire? Seek knowledge and learn it, for knowledge, if it does not make you happy, will not make you miserable; if it does not raise you, it will not lower you; if it does not enrich you, it will not impoverish you; if it does not benefit you, it will not harm you. And do not say, 'We fear that we will know and not act.' Rather, say, 'We hope that we will know and then act.'" Knowledge is an intercessor for its possessor, and it is a right upon God Most High that He not disgrace him. God Most High says on the Day of Resurrection: "O assembly of scholars, what is your opinion of your Lord?" They say: "Our opinion is that He will have mercy on us and forgive us." He says: "Indeed, I have done so. I have entrusted you with My wisdom, not for an evil I intended for you, but for a good I intended for you. So enter the Garden of My righteous servants by My mercy."

Muqātil ibn Sulaymān said: "I found in the Gospel that God Most High said to Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon them both: 'O Jesus, magnify the scholars and recognise their excellence, for I have preferred them over all My creation except the prophets and messengers, as the excellence of the sun over the stars, and as the excellence of the Hereafter over this world, and as My excellence over everything.'"

* * *

As for the reports (akhbār):

(a) From 'Abdullāh ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God Most High says to the scholars: 'I did not place My knowledge in you while intending to punish you. Enter the Garden, in accordance with what was in you.'"

(b) Abū Hurayrah and Ibn 'Abbās said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) delivered to us an eloquent sermon before his death, and it was the last sermon he delivered in Medina. He said: "Whoever learns knowledge, and is humble in knowledge, and teaches it to the servants of God, seeking what is with God, there will be no greater reward in the Garden than his, and no greater station. There is no lofty, precious rank or degree in the Garden except that he will have in it the fullest portion and the most noble abodes."

(c) Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet (marfū'): "On the Day of Resurrection, pulpits of gold will be arranged, upon which are domes of silver, set with pearls, rubies, and emeralds, their coverings of green silk and brocade. Then the caller of the Most Merciful will call out: 'Where are those who carried knowledge to the community of Muḥammad, seeking by it the face of God? Sit upon these pulpits; there is no fear upon you until you enter the Garden.'"

(d) From Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon them both: The community of Muḥammad, peace be upon him, are scholars and wise men, as if they were prophets in understanding. They are content with little provision from God, and God is content with little action from them. They will enter the Garden by "There is no god but God."

(e) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever has his feet covered in dust in the pursuit of knowledge, God will forbid his body to the Fire, and his two angels will seek forgiveness for him. If he dies in its pursuit, he dies a martyr. His grave will be a garden of the gardens of Paradise, and his grave will be widened as far as his sight extends, and he will illuminate forty graves of his neighbours on his right, forty on his left, forty behind him, and forty in front of him. The sleep of the scholar is worship, his study is glorification (tasbīḥ), his soul is charity. Every drop that falls from his eyes extinguishes a sea of Hellfire. Whoever humiliates a scholar has humiliated knowledge; whoever humiliates knowledge has humiliated the Prophet; whoever humiliates the Prophet has humiliated Gabriel; whoever humiliates Gabriel has humiliated God; and whoever humiliates God, God will humiliate him on the Day of Resurrection."

(f) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Shall I not inform you of the most generous of the generous?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "God Most High is the most generous of the generous, and I am the most generous of the children of Adam. And the most generous after me is a scholar who spreads his knowledge, and he will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a community unto himself; and a man who strives in the way of God until he is killed."

(g) From Abū Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet: "Whoever relieves a believer of one of the distresses of this world, God will relieve him of one of the distresses of the Hereafter. Whoever eases the lot of one in difficulty, God will ease his lot in this world and the next. God is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother. Whoever treads a path seeking knowledge, God will make easy for him a path to the Garden. No people gather in one of the mosques of God, reciting the Book of God and studying it among themselves, except that tranquillity descends upon them, mercy envelops them, the angels surround them, and God mentions them among those who are with Him." Narrated by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

(h) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Three will intercede on the Day of Resurrection: the prophets, then the scholars, then the martyrs."

The narrator said: The highest rank is the intermediate station between prophethood and martyrdom.

(i) Mu'ādh ibn Jabal: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Learn knowledge, for learning it for the sake of God is fear (khashyah), seeking it is worship, studying it is glorification, searching for it is jihad, teaching it is charity, and giving it to its people is a means of drawing near to God." Because it is the markers of the lawful and the unlawful, the beacon of the paths to the Garden, the companion in loneliness, the confidant in solitude, the guide in ease and hardship, the weapon against enemies. Religion, when there is disagreement, God raises by it peoples and makes them leaders and guides in goodness, by whom one is guided, and imams in goodness whose traces are followed, whose deeds are emulated, and whose opinions are adopted. The angels desire their creation and wipe them with their wings, and in their prayers they seek forgiveness for them, until every moist and dry thing, the fish of the sea, its creeping creatures, the beasts of the land and its livestock, the sky and its stars [seek forgiveness for them]. For knowledge is the life of hearts from blindness, the light of sights from darkness, and the strength of bodies from weakness. By it one reaches, though distant, the stations of the free, the assemblies of kings, and the high ranks in this world and the next. Reflecting upon it is equal to fasting, and studying it is equal to standing in prayer by night. By it God is obeyed and worshipped, by it He is glorified and declared one, by it kinship ties are maintained, and by it the lawful and the unlawful are known.

(j) Abū Hurayrah: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: ongoing charity (ṣadaqah jāriyah), knowledge from which people benefit, or a righteous child who prays for him."

(k) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "When you ask for your needs, ask people for them." It was said: "O Messenger of God, who are the people?" He said: "The people of the Qur'an." It was said: "Then who?" He said: "The people of knowledge." It was said: "Then who?" He said: "Those with bright faces."

The narrator said: By "the people of the Qur'an" is meant one who memorises its meanings.

(l) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever enjoins what is good and forbids what is evil is the vicegerent (khalīfah) of God on His earth, the vicegerent of His Book, and the vicegerent of His Messenger. And this world is the deadly poison of God for His servants, so take from it an amount equal to the poison in medicines, so that perhaps you may be saved."

The narrator said: The scholars are included in this, because they say: "This is unlawful, so avoid it," and "This is lawful, so take it."

(m) In a report: The scholar is a prophet to whom revelation has not come.

(n) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Be a scholar, or a learner, or a listener, or a lover, and do not be the fifth, lest you perish."

* * *

The narrator said: The way to reconcile this report with another report, namely his saying, peace be upon him: "People are of two kinds: a scholar and a learner. The rest of the people are rabble with no good in them," is that the listener and the lover are in the position of the learner. How excellent is the saying of a certain Bedouin to his son: "Be a lion that seizes, or a wolf that stealthily takes, or a guarding dog, and beware of being an incomplete human being."

(o) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever leans upon the hand of a scholar, God writes for him the freeing of a slave with every step. Whoever kisses the head of a scholar, God writes for him a good deed for every hair."

(p) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said, in a report from Abū Hurayrah: "The seven heavens and whoever is in them and upon them, and the seven earths and whoever is in them and upon them, weep for a mighty one who was humiliated, a rich one who became poor, and a scholar with whom the ignorant play."

(q) He, peace be upon him, said: "The bearers of the Qur'an are the foremost (fuqarā') of the people of Paradise, the martyrs are the commanders of the people of Paradise, and the prophets are the lords of the people of Paradise."

(r) He, peace be upon him, said: "The scholars are the keys to Paradise and the successors of the prophets."

The narrator said: A human being cannot be a key; the meaning is that they possess the knowledge that is the key to the Gardens. The evidence for this is that whoever sees in a dream that he holds the keys of Paradise will be granted knowledge of religion.

(s) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, God Most High has in every day and night a thousand mercies for all His creatures, the heedless and the mature, and those who are not mature. Of these, nine hundred and ninety-nine mercies are for the scholars, the seekers of knowledge, and the Muslims, and the one remaining mercy is for the rest of the people."

(t) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "I said: 'O Gabriel, which deeds are most excellent for my community?' He said: 'Knowledge.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'Looking at the scholar.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'Visiting the scholar.' Then he said: 'And whoever acquires knowledge for the sake of God, intending by it the good of himself and the good of the Muslims, and does not intend by it any worldly gain, I am its guarantor for Paradise.'"

(u) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Ten are those whose supplication is answered: the scholar, the learner, the one of good character, the sick, the orphan, the warrior, the pilgrim, the one who gives sincere advice to the Muslims, the child who obeys his parents, and the wife who obeys her husband."

(v) "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: What is knowledge? He said: The guide to action. It was said: What is intellect? He said: The leader to good. It was said: What is desire? He said: The vehicle of sins. It was said: What is wealth? He said: The cloak of the arrogant. It was said: What is this world? He said: The marketplace of the Hereafter."

(w) That the Prophet, peace be upon him, was speaking with a man, when God revealed to him that only an hour of the life of this man to whom he was speaking remained. This was at the time of 'Aṣr. The Messenger informed him of this, and the man became agitated and said: "O Messenger of God, direct me to the most suitable action for me in this hour." He said: "Occupy yourself with learning." So he occupied himself with learning, and he died before Maghrib.

The narrator said: If anything had been more excellent than knowledge, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have commanded him to do it at that time.

(x) The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "All people are dead except the scholars." This report is well known.

(y) From Anas, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Seven things continue for the servant after his death: one who taught knowledge, or who channelled a river, or who dug a well, or who built a mosque, or who bequeathed a copy of the Qur'an, or who left a righteous child who prays for him, or a charity that flows for him after his death." The Prophet, peace be upon him, therefore placed teaching above all forms of benefit, because it is spiritual, and the spiritual is more enduring than corporeal things.

(كو) The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not sit with the scholars except when they call you from five to five: from doubt to certainty, from arrogance to humility, from enmity to sincere counsel, from showing off to sincerity, and from desire to asceticism."

(كز) "The Prophet (ﷺ) entrusted ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: O ʿAlī, preserve the tawḥīd (affirmation of Allah's oneness), for it is the capital of my wealth. Hold fast to action, for it is my craft. Establish the prayer, for it is the coolness of my eyes. Remember the Lord, for He is the insight of my heart. And put knowledge into practice, for it is my inheritance."

(كح) Abū Kabsha al-Anṣārī said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck for us a parable of this world as the parable of four men. A man whom Allah gave knowledge and also gave wealth, and he acts upon his knowledge with his wealth. A man whom Allah gave knowledge but did not give wealth, and he says: 'If Allah had given me the like of what was given to so-and-so, I would do with it what so-and-so does.' These two are equal in reward. A man whom Allah gave wealth but did not give knowledge, so he withholds it from what is right and spends it in falsehood. And a man whom Allah gave neither knowledge nor wealth, and he says: 'If Allah had given me the like of what was given to so-and-so, I would do with it what so-and-so does.' These two are equal in sin."

**Transmitted reports (al-Āthār):**

(a) Kumayl ibn Ziyād said: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) took my hand and brought me out to the jabbāna (open burial ground). When he came out into the open, he let out a long sigh, then said: "O Kumayl ibn Ziyād, these hearts are vessels, and the best of them is the one that holds the most. So preserve what I say to you. People are of three kinds: a rabbānī scholar (one who lives by knowledge of the Lord), a learner on the path of salvation, and worthless rabble, followers of every caller, swaying with every wind. They have not been illuminated by the light of knowledge, nor have they taken refuge in a firm pillar. O Kumayl, knowledge is better than wealth. Knowledge guards you while you guard wealth. Wealth diminishes by spending, while knowledge grows by being spent. The works of wealth vanish with its passing. O Kumayl, the recognition of knowledge is an adornment by which a person gains obedience in his life and a good reputation after his death. Knowledge is the judge, and wealth is the thing judged."

(b) On the authority of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him): "A man leaves his home with sins upon him like the mountain of Tihāma. Then when he hears knowledge, fears, and repents for his sins, he returns to his home with no sin upon him. So do not part from the gatherings of the scholars, for Allah has not created on the face of the earth a soil more noble than the gatherings of the scholars."

(c) On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Sulaymān was given a choice between kingship and wealth on one hand and knowledge on the other, and he chose knowledge. So he was given knowledge and kingship together."

(d) Sulaymān did not need the hoopoe except for its knowledge, as narrated from Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq, who said to Ibn ʿAbbās: "How did Sulaymān choose the hoopoe to search for water?" Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Because the earth is like a glass, its inside visible from its outside." Nāfiʿ said: "Then what about the times of the trap, when it is covered for it with a finger's depth of dust, and it does not see it, but falls into it?" Ibn ʿAbbās said: "When the decree comes, sight goes blind."

(e) Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said: "Paradise is divided into ten thousand parts. Nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine of them are for those who understood Allah's command. This is their reward, according to the measure of the intellects Allah apportioned to them, and they divide among themselves the dwellings in it. And one part is for the believing weak, the poor, and the righteous."

(f) Ibn ʿAbbās said to his son: "My son, cling to adab (refined conduct), for it is a sign of manliness, a companion in loneliness, a friend in estrangement, a comrade at home, a seat of honor in the assembly, a means when all means have ended, wealth in poverty, elevation for the lowly, perfection for the noble, and majesty for the king."

(g) On the authority of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: "The scratching of the scholars' pens is glorification (tasbīḥ). Writing knowledge and studying it is worship. If some of that ink touches a man's garment, it is as if the blood of martyrs has touched it. If it drips onto the ground, its light shines. And when he rises from his grave, the people of the gathering will look at him and say: 'This is a servant of Allah's servants whom Allah honored and who was gathered with the prophets (peace be upon them).'"

(h) In the book Kalīla wa Dimna: "The most deserving of not being belittled in their rights are three: the scholar, the ruler, and the brothers. For whoever belittles the scholar destroys his religion, whoever belittles the ruler destroys his worldly life, and whoever belittles his brothers destroys his manliness."

(i) Socrates said: "Among the virtues of knowledge is that you cannot have anyone serve you in it as you find someone serving you in all other things. Rather, you must serve it yourself, and no one can take it away from you."

(j) It was said to one of the wise men: "Do not look." So he closed his eyes. It was said: "Do not listen." So he plugged his ears. It was said: "Do not speak." So he put his hand over his mouth. It was said to him: "Do not know." He said: "I cannot do that."

(k) If a thief is a learned man, his hand is not cut off, because he says: "The money was a deposit with me." Likewise a drinker says: "I thought it was vinegar." And likewise an adulterer says: "I married her." So he is not subjected to the ḥadd (the prescribed punishment).

(l) Some of them said: "Revive the hearts of your brothers with the insights of your explanation, just as you revive dead land with plants and seeds. For a soul that keeps far from desires and doubts is better than land fit for planting." The poet said:

"In ignorance, before death, there is death for its people, and their bodies are graves before the graves.
And a man who has not been revived by knowledge is dead, and for him there is no resurrection even at the resurrection."
