**Subtle points (al-Nukat):**

(a) Sin committed out of ignorance is not hoped to be removed, whereas sin committed out of desire is hoped to be removed. Consider the slip of Ādam: through his knowledge he sought forgiveness, while Satan went astray and remained in his error forever, because his was caused by ignorance.

(b) When Yūsuf (peace be upon him) became a king, he needed a vizier. He asked his Lord about this, and Jibrīl said to him: "Your Lord says: choose none but so-and-so." Yūsuf saw him in the worst of conditions and said to Jibrīl: "How can he be fit for this task given his bad state?" Jibrīl said: "Your Lord has designated him for this, because he defended you when he said: ﴿And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful﴾ [Yūsuf 12:27]." The point is that the one who defended Yūsuf (peace be upon him) deserved a share in his kingdom. So how would one who defends the upright religion with clear proof not deserve kindness and beautification from Allah?

(c) A man wished to serve a king, and the king said: "Go and learn until you are fit for my service." When he began learning and tasted the sweetness of knowledge, the king sent for him and said: "Stop learning, for you have become fit for my service." He said: "I was fit for your service when you did not see me as fit for it. And when you saw me as fit for it, I saw myself as fit for the service of Allah, the Exalted. For I used to think the door was your door out of my ignorance, but now I know the door is the door of the Lord."

(d) Acquiring knowledge is difficult for you only because of your excessive love of this world. For He, the Exalted, gave you the blackness of the eye (sawād al-ʿayn) and the little black of the heart (suwaydāʾ al-qalb). There is no doubt that sawād is greater than suwaydāʾ in word, since suwaydāʾ is the diminutive of sawād. Now, if you place on the blackness of your eye a part of this world, you see nothing. So how will you see with your heart if you place upon the suwaydāʾ the whole world?

(e) A sage said: "The heart is dead, and its life is through knowledge. Knowledge is dead, and its life is through seeking. Seeking is weak, and its strength is through study. When it grows strong through study, it is hidden, and its manifestation is through debate. When it manifests through debate, it is barren, and its offspring is through action. So when knowledge is wed to action, it begets and multiplies, a kingdom everlasting with no end."

(f) ﴿An ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings"﴾ [al-Naml 27:18] up to His words: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ [al-Naml 27:18]. That ant's leadership over the others was only due to the fact that she knew one single matter, namely His saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾. It was as if she said: "Sulaymān is infallible, and the infallible may not harm the innocent of wrongdoing. But if he crushes you, that will only come from him by way of inadvertence, because he does not know your state." So His saying ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ points to the exoneration of the prophets (peace be upon them) from disobedience. When that ant knew this one matter, she deserved complete leadership. So how would one who knows the realities of things, both existent and non-existent, not deserve leadership in this world and in religion?

(g) A dog, when trained and released by its owner in the name of Allah, the Exalted, makes its impure game pure. The point is that knowledge joined the dog, so the impure became pure through the blessing of knowledge. Likewise, the soul and the spirit are pure in their original nature, except that they have been soiled by the filth of disobedience. Then knowledge of Allah and His attributes joined them. So we hope, from His abundant kindness, that He will turn the impure pure here and the rejected accepted.

(h) The heart is the chief of the organs. Yet this leadership is not due to strength, for bone is stronger than it. Nor is it due to size, for the thigh is larger than it. Nor is it due to sharpness, for the fingernail is sharper than it. Rather, that leadership is due to knowledge. This shows that knowledge is the most noble of attributes.

**Anecdotes (al-Ḥikāyāt):**

(a) It is related that Hārūn al-Rashīd had jurists with him, and among them was Abū Yūsuf. A man was brought before him, and another man claimed against him that he had taken money from his house at night. The taker admitted this in the assembly. The jurists agreed that his hand should be cut off. Abū Yūsuf said: "There is no amputation for him." They asked: "Why?" He said: "Because he confessed to taking, and taking does not necessitate amputation. Rather, a confession of theft is required." They all accepted his statement. Then they said to the taker: "Did you steal it?" He said: "Yes." So they all agreed that the amputation was due, since he had confessed to theft. Abū Yūsuf said: "There is no amputation, because although he confessed to theft, it came after liability had already become due upon him by his confession to taking. So when he then confesses to theft, he removes liability from himself by this confession, and his confession is not heard." Everyone marvelled at this.

(b) On the authority of al-Shaʿbī: "I was with al-Ḥajjāj when Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, the jurist of Khurāsān and Balkh, was brought in, shackled in iron. Al-Ḥajjāj said to him: 'Did you claim that al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn are descendants of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' He said: 'Yes.' Al-Ḥajjāj said: 'You will bring me proof of it, clear and manifest, from the Book of Allah, or I will cut you limb from limb.' He said: 'I will bring it to you clear and manifest from the Book of Allah, O Ḥajjāj.' I marvelled at his boldness in saying 'O Ḥajjāj.' Al-Ḥajjāj said: 'And do not bring me this verse: ﴿We call our sons and your sons﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:61].' He said: 'I will bring it to you clear from the Book of Allah, namely His saying: ﴿And Nūḥ We guided before, and of his descendants Dāwūd and Sulaymān﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:84], up to His saying: ﴿and Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:85]. So who was the father of ʿĪsā, when he has been attached to the descendants of Nūḥ?' He lowered his head for a while, then raised it and said: 'It is as if I had never read this verse of the Book of Allah. Untie his bonds and give him such-and-such of the money.'"

(c) It is said that a group of people of Madīna came to Abū Ḥanīfa to debate him about reciting behind the imam, and to humiliate and disgrace him. He said to them: "I cannot debate all of you. So entrust the debate to the most knowledgeable of you, so that I may debate him." They pointed to one man. He said: "This is your most knowledgeable?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Is debating with him the same as debating with you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "And is an argument against him the same as an argument against you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "And if I debate him and establish the proof against him, will the proof then be established against you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "How?" They said: "Because we accepted him as imam, so his speech became our speech." Abū Ḥanīfa said: "Likewise, when we chose the imam in prayer, his recitation became our recitation, and he stands in for us." So they acknowledged to him the force of the argument.

(d) al-Farazdaq satirized a man, and said:

My poetry was lost at your door, as a pearl is lost upon Khalisa.

(h) Al-Mansur summoned Abu Hanifa one day. Al-Rabi', who was hostile to him, said: "O Commander of the Believers, this man (meaning Abu Hanifa) contradicts your grandfather, for he says that the detached exception (istithna' munfasil) is permissible, while Abu Hanifa denies it." Abu Hanifa said: "This al-Rabi' says: 'You have no pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) on the necks of the people.'" He asked: "How?" Abu Hanifa said: "They pledge allegiance to you, then they return to their homes and make an exception, and so their pledge becomes void." Al-Mansur laughed and said: "Beware of al-Rabi' and Abu Hanifa!" When Abu Hanifa left, al-Rabi' said: "O Abu Hanifa, you sought my blood!" Abu Hanifa said: "You were the aggressor, and I was the defender."

It is related that a Muslim killed a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection) intentionally. Abu Yusuf ruled that the Muslim should be executed for him. This reached Zubayda, and she sent to Abu Yusuf, saying: "Beware of executing the Muslim!" She took great care regarding the affairs of Muslims. When Abu Yusuf arrived, along with the jurists, and the guardians of the dhimmi and of the Muslim were brought, al-Rashid said to him: "Rule for his execution." He said: "O Commander of the Believers, that is my school of thought, but I will not execute the Muslim for him unless a just proof is established that the dhimmi, on the day the Muslim killed him, was one of those who pay the jizya (poll tax on non-Muslim subjects). But they could not establish this, so his blood was voided."

(z) Al-Ghadban entered upon al-Hajjaj after he had said to his enemy Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath: "Have your lunch with al-Hajjaj before he has his dinner with you." Al-Hajjaj said to him: "What is the response to 'Peace be upon you'?" He replied: "And upon you be peace." Then al-Hajjaj perceived the trick and said: "May God fight you, O Ghadban! You secured safety for yourself by my returning your greeting. By God, were it not for loyalty and generosity, you would not drink cold water after this hour of yours."

Consider the benefit of knowledge in this scene. How excellent is knowledge and whoever is saved by it, and woe to ignorance and whoever falls into its valleys.

(ḥ) The words of the poet reached Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan:

"Among us are Suwayd, al-Batin, and Qa'nab, ∗∗∗ and among us is the Commander of the Believers, Shabib."

He said: "Yes, I said it, but it was about a vineyard of such-and-such when I saw the unripe grapes." He admired his statement and pardoned him.

(y) A man said to Abu Hanifa: "I have sworn that I will not speak to my wife until she speaks to me, and she has sworn, by the charity of all that she owns, that she will not speak to me or I will speak to her." The jurists were perplexed by this. Sufyan said: "Whoever speaks to his companion breaks the oath."

Abu Hanifa said: "Go and speak to her, and there is no breach of oath upon you both." The man went to Sufyan and informed him of what Abu Hanifa had said. Sufyan went to Abu Hanifa in anger and said: "You make lawful the private parts!" Abu Hanifa said: "And what is that?" Sufyan said: "Repeat the question to Abu Hanifa." They repeated it, and Abu Hanifa repeated his ruling. He said: "From where did you derive this?" He replied: "When she addressed him with the oath after he had sworn, she became one who speaks, so his oath fell. If he speaks to her, then there is no breach upon him or upon her, because he spoke to her after the oath, so the oath fell from both of them." Sufyan said: "Indeed, knowledge is revealed to you about something of which we are all unaware."

(yā) Thieves entered upon a man, took his goods, and made him swear by divorce three times that he would not inform anyone. The man woke up and saw the thieves selling his goods, and he could not speak because of his oath. The man came to consult Abu Hanifa. He said: "Bring me the imam of your mosque and the people of your quarter." They brought them to him. Abu Hanifa said to them: "Would you like God to return this man's goods to him?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Gather them all together, put them in a house, then bring them out one by one, and say: 'Is this your thief?' If he is not his thief, he will say: 'No.' If he is his thief, let him be silent. When he is silent, seize him." They did what Abu Hanifa had instructed, and God returned to him everything that had been stolen from him.

﴿They said: "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾ ﴿He said: "O Adam, inform them of their names." So when he had informed them of their names, He said: "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and that I know what you disclose and what you have been concealing?"﴾

[p. 192]

Know that those who hold that the angels committed a sin in their saying, ﴿Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein?﴾ said: when they recognized their error in this question, they returned, repented, and apologized for their mistake by saying, ﴿Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.﴾ As for those who deny that they committed a sin, they mentioned two explanations for this:

The first: they only said that by way of acknowledging their incapacity and submitting that they do not know what they were asked about. That is because they said: "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. So if You have not taught us that, how can we know it?"

The second: the angels only said, ﴿Will You place in it...﴾ because God, exalted is He, had informed them of that. So it is as if they said: "You informed us that they will cause corruption on the earth and shed blood, so we said to You, 'Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein?'" As for these names, You did not inform us of their nature, so how could we know them?

Here there are several issues:

**First issue:** Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued from His saying, ﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us,﴾ that cognitions are created by God, exalted is He. The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a theological school) said: the meaning is that we have no knowledge except from Him, either through teaching or through establishing the proof. The answer is that *ta'lim* (teaching) is an expression for bringing about knowledge in another, like *tasweed* (blackening), which is an expression for bringing about blackness in another. It cannot be said that teaching is an expression for conveying the matter which knowledge follows if the condition is met and the impediment is absent; that is why one says, "I taught him, but he did not learn." The matter which knowledge follows is the establishing of the proof, and God, exalted is He, has indeed done that. We say: the agent in bringing about knowledge is not the very essence of the proof, but rather the reflection upon the proof, and that reflection is the act of the servant. Therefore the acquisition of that knowledge was not by God's teaching, and this would contradict His saying, ﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.﴾

* * *

**Second issue:** The People of Islam (Ahl al-Islam) have used this verse to show that there is no way to know the unseen except through God's teaching, and that it is not possible to reach it by astrology, soothsaying, or fortune-telling. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him﴾ [al-An'am 6:59], and His saying, ﴿The Knower of the unseen; He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ [al-Jinn 72:26–27]. An astrologer may say to the Mu'tazili: if you interpret teaching as the placing of indications, then in my view the movements of the stars are indications which God created to indicate the states of this world. When I infer these states from them, that too is by God's teaching. It may also be said that since the angels were unable to know the unseen, it is more fitting that one of us would be unable to know it.

**Third issue:** *al-'Alim* (the All-Knowing) is an intensive form denoting complete abundance of knowledge, and complete abundance is not realized except by encompassing all that is known, and none has this but Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He. Therefore the All-Knowing in the absolute sense is none other than Him. For this reason He said, ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise,﴾ in the manner of restriction (*hasr*).

**Fourth issue:** *al-Hakim* (the All-Wise) is used in two ways:

One: in the sense of *al-'Alim* (the All-Knowing), and so it is one of the attributes of the essence (*sifat al-dhat*). According to this interpretation we say that He is All-Wise from eternity.

The other: He is the one who does what no one has any objection to. So it is one of the attributes of action (*sifat al-fi'l*), and we do not say that He is All-Wise from eternity.

Here the closer view is that the intended meaning is the second, otherwise there would be repetition. It is as if the angels said: "You are the Knower of all that is known, so You were able to teach Adam; and You are the All-Wise in this action, correct in it." It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the angels' intended meaning by *al-Hakim* was that He is the One who decreed the appointment of Adam as a vicegerent (khalifah) on the earth.

(Fifth issue): When God, exalted is He, commanded Adam, peace be upon him, to inform them of the names of things, and he, peace be upon him, informed them of them, God, glorified and exalted, said to them at that time: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾

Page 193
﴿of the heavens and the earth﴾. What is meant by this unseen is that He, exalted is He, was knowing of the circumstances of Adam, peace be upon him, before He created him. This indicates that He, glorified and exalted, knows things before they occur, and that proves the falsity of the doctrine of Hisham ibn al-Hakam, that He knows things only when they occur. If it is said: faith is knowledge, so His saying, exalted is He: ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] indicates that the servant knows the unseen; how then does He say here: ﴿I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾? The implication is that knowledge of the unseen belongs only to Me, and that everyone other than Me is devoid of knowledge of the unseen. Its answer is what has preceded in His saying: ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. As for His saying: ﴿and I know what you disclose and what you were concealing﴾, there are several aspects to it:

The first: what al-Sha'bi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them, that His saying: ﴿and I know what you disclose﴾ refers to their saying: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein?﴾, and His saying: ﴿and what you were concealing﴾ refers to what Iblis concealed within himself of arrogance and of not prostrating.

The second: ﴿I know that which you do not know﴾ of the hidden matters and the secret realities, which in appearance seem to have no benefit in them, but I, through My knowledge of the hidden secrets, know that the benefit lies in their creation.

The third: when God, exalted is He, created Adam, the angels saw a wondrous creation, and they said: Let it be whatever He wills; our Lord will not create any creation except that we will be more honored by Him than it. This is what they concealed. It is possible that this statement was a secret they kept among themselves, so some of them revealed it to others while concealing it from others; thus in this single act there was both disclosure and concealment.

The fourth: which is the saying of the sages, that the divisions are five, because a thing is either pure good, or pure evil, or mixed; and in the case of mixture, either the matter is balanced, or good predominates, or evil predominates. As for pure good, wisdom requires its existence; and as for that in which good predominates, wisdom requires its existence, because abandoning much good for the sake of little evil is great evil. The angels mentioned corruption and bloodshed, which is a small evil relative to the good that comes from them. So His saying: ﴿I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ means: I know that their good predominates over these evils, so wisdom required their existence and their creation.

(Sixth issue): Know that in this verse there is great fear and great joy. As for the fear: nothing of the circumstances of hearts is hidden from Him, so a person must strive to purify his inner self, and not be such that he abandons sin because creatures see it, while not abandoning it when the Creator sees it. And the reports affirm this.

The first: 'Adi ibn Hatim narrated that he, peace be upon him, said: "People will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and commanded toward Paradise. When they approach it and smell its fragrance and look at its palaces and at what Allah has prepared for its people, they will be called: 'Turn them away from it; they have no share in it.' So they will return from it with a regret such that no one has returned with its like, and they will say: 'O our Lord, if You had caused us to enter the Fire before You showed us what You showed us of Your reward and what You prepared therein for Your friends, it would have been easier for us.'

Then it will be said to them: 'That is what I wanted for you. When you were alone you defied Me with great sins, and when you met people you met them with love, humble, showing people what is contrary to what you conceal in your hearts. You feared people and did not fear Me; you revered people and did not revere Me; you abandoned sins for people and did not abandon them for My sake. I was the least of those who looked upon you. So today I will make you taste My painful punishment, along with what I have deprived you of of bliss.'"

The second: Sulayman ibn 'Ali said to Humayd al-Tawil: "Advise me." He said: "If, when you disobey Allah in private, you think that He sees you, then you have dared a great matter; and if you think that He does not see you, then you have disbelieved."

The third: Hatim al-Asamm said: "Purify yourself in three states: when you are acting with the limbs, remember God's gaze upon you; when you are speaking, remember God's hearing of you; and when you are silent while acting in the heart, remember God's knowledge of you, for He says:

Page 194
﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]."

The fourth: know that no one has access to the secrets of the wisdom of God, exalted is He. The angels' gaze fell upon corruption and bloodshed, so they belittled humankind; and their gaze fell upon the obedience of Iblis, so they magnified him. As for the Knower of the unseen, He was knowing that they, though they commit corruption and bloodshed, would afterward say: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23], and that Iblis, though he performs acts of obedience, would afterward say: ﴿I am better than him﴾. It is part of the nature of the intellect not to rely on what it sees, and to always be in fear and dread. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ means: I am the One who knows the outward and the inward, the actual and the expected; and I know that the one you see as a worshipper and obedient will disbelieve and be distanced from My presence, and the one you see as a wicked and far-off one will draw near to My service. Creatures cannot emerge from the veil of ignorance, nor can they easily tear the curtains of incapacity, for they do not encompass any of His knowledge. Then He, glorified is He, verified through the unseen knowledge and the incapacity of the angels that He would show from among humankind the perfection of servitude, and from among the most devoted inhabitants of the heavens the perfection of disbelief; lest anyone be deceived by his deed, and so that they would entrust the knowledge of things to the wisdom of the Creator, and remove objection from the heart and tongue concerning His creatures and His originations.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 34 (part 1 of 7):**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers.﴾

Know that this is the fourth of the general blessings granted to all of mankind, namely that He, glorified and exalted, made our father the one before whom the angels prostrate. This is because He, exalted is He, first mentioned Adam's being singled out for the caliphate (khilafah), then his being singled out for abundant knowledge, then his attaining in knowledge to the point where the angels were unable to reach his level of knowledge. Now He mentions his being prostrated to by the angels. There are several issues here:

**The first issue:** The command to prostrate occurred before God, exalted is He, perfected Adam's creation, as is shown by His words: ﴿Indeed, I am creating a human from clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down to him in prostration﴾ [Sad: 71-72]. The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that when he (peace be upon him) became alive, he became the one before whom the angels prostrate, because the particle *fa* (فَ) in His words *(faqa'u)* ("fall down") indicates sequence (ta'qib). According to this interpretation, the teaching of the names and his debate with the angels concerning it occurred after he had become the one before whom the angels prostrate.

* * *

**The second issue:** The Muslims are unanimous that this prostration was not an act of worship, because prostrating in worship to other than God is disbelief, and a command is not issued to commit disbelief. Then they differed on three views:

*The first view:* That prostration was for God, exalted is He, and Adam (peace be upon him) was like a qiblah (the direction of prayer). Some people objected to this view on two grounds:

*The first:* It is not said "I prayed *to* the qiblah" (*sallaytu lil-qiblah*); rather it is said "I prayed *toward* the qiblah" (*sallaytu ila al-qiblah*). So if Adam (peace be upon him) had been a qiblah for that prostration, it would have been necessary to say "prostrate *toward* Adam" (*usjudu ila Adam*). Since the command did not come in this form, but rather "prostrate *to* Adam" (*usjudu li-Adam*), we know that Adam (peace be upon him) was not a qiblah.

*The second:* Iblis said: ﴿Have You seen this one whom You have honored over me?﴾ [al-Isra: 62]. That is, the fact that he was prostrated to indicates that he was of greater status than the one who prostrated. If he had been a qiblah, this rank would not have been achieved, as evidenced by the fact that Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) used to pray toward the Ka'bah, yet it did not follow that the Ka'bah was superior to Muhammad (ﷺ).

The answer to the first objection is that just as it is not permissible to say "I prayed toward the qiblah," it is permissible to say "I prayed *to* the qiblah." The evidence for this is the Qur'an and poetry. As for the Qur'an, there is His words: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra: 78]. Prayer is for God, not for the decline of the sun. If that is permissible, why is it not permissible to say "I prayed to the qiblah," even though prayer is for God, exalted is He, and not for the qiblah? As for poetry, there is the verse of Hassan:

*I did not know that the matter had turned away from Hashim,*
*and then from her, away from Abu Hasan.*
*Was he not the first to pray toward your qiblah,*
*and the most knowledgeable of people in the Qur'an and the Sunnah?*

His statement "pray to your qiblah" (*sallaa li-qiblatikum*) is a clear text on the intended meaning.

The answer to the second objection is that Iblis complained of his (Adam's) honor, and we do not accept that this honor was achieved merely by that being prostrated to. Rather, it may have been achieved by that together with other matters.

This is what is in the first view. As for the second view, it is that the prostration was to Adam (peace be upon him) as a means of glorifying him and as a greeting to him, like the greeting of peace from them to him. Previous nations used to do this, just as Muslims greet one another with peace. Qatadah said, regarding His words: ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾ [Yusuf: 100], "The greeting of the people on that day was the prostration of some of them to others."

From Suhayb: "When Mu'adh came from Yemen, he prostrated to the Prophet (ﷺ). He said, 'O Mu'adh, what is this?' He said, 'The Jews prostrate to their great ones and their scholars, and I saw the Christians prostrate to their priests and their patriarchs.' I said, 'What is this?' They said, 'It is the greeting of the prophets.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'They lied about their prophets.'"

From al-Thawri, from Simak ibn Harb, who said: "The Jathaliq (a Christian patriarch) entered upon Ali ibn Abi Talib and wanted to prostrate to him. Ali said to him, 'Prostrate to God, and do not prostrate to me.'"

He (peace be upon him) also said: "If I were to command anyone to prostrate to other than God, I would command the woman to prostrate to her husband, because of the greatness of his right over her."

*The third view:* That prostration in the original sense of the language means submission and humility. The poet said:

*You see the hills in it prostrating to the hooves [of horses],*

That is, those small hills were subdued to the hooves of horses. From this is His words: ﴿And the stars and the trees prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6].

Know that the first view is weak, because the purpose of this story is to explain the glorification of Adam (peace be upon him), and making him merely a qiblah does not convey the glorification of his state. As for the third view, it is also weak, because there is no doubt that prostration in the terminology of the sacred law (shar') is a reference to placing the forehead upon the ground. It must therefore be the same in the original sense of the language, because the basic principle is the absence of change. If it is said: "Prostration is worship, and worship to other than God is not permissible," we say: We do not accept that it is worship. The explanation is that an action may come to convey meaning through convention, like speech. This is shown by the fact that one of us standing up for another conveys the same honor as speech does, and this is only because of custom. Once this is established, it is not impossible that at some times a person's falling to the ground and pressing his forehead to it conveys a kind of glorification, even if it is not worship. If this is the case, it is not impossible that God made the angels prostrate in this manner, to show his elevated rank and dignity.

* * *

**The third issue:** They differed over whether Iblis was among the angels. Some theologians (mutakallimun), especially the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school), said he was not among them, while many jurists (fuqaha') said he was among them. The first group argued with several points:

*The first:* He was from the jinn, so he could not have been from the angels. We say he was from the jinn based on His words in Surah al-Kahf: ﴿except Iblis; he was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]. Know that some people thought that since it is established that he was from the jinn, he could not be from the angels, because the jinn are a species distinct from the angel. This is weak, because "jinn" (jinn) is derived from *al-ijtinan*, which means concealment. For this reason the fetus is called *janin* because it is hidden, and from it comes *al-junnah* (shield), because it conceals, and *al-jannah* (garden), because it is concealed by its branches, and from it comes *al-junun* (madness), because the intellect is concealed in it. Since this is established, and the angels are hidden from the eyes, it is necessary by linguistic usage to apply the term "jinn" to them. Thus it is established that this alone does not prove the intended point. So we say: since it is established that Iblis was of the jinn, he must not be of the angels, because of His words: ﴿And the Day He will gather them all, then He will say to the angels, "Did these worship you?" They will say, "Exalted are You; You are our protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn"﴾ [Saba: 40-41]. This verse is explicit in distinguishing between the jinn and the angel.

If it is said: "We do not accept that he was of the jinn. As for His words ﴿was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], why could it not be that the meaning is 'he was of the garden (jannah)'? This is as reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said, 'He was of the jinn,' meaning he was the keeper of the garden." Suppose we accept that. But why could it not be that His words "of the jinn" mean "he became of the jinn," just as His words ﴿and he was of the disbelievers﴾ mean "he became of the disbelievers"? Suppose we accept that what you mentioned indicates he was of the jinn; why do you say that his being of the jinn contradicts his being of the angels? And what you cited from the verse is opposed by another verse, His words: ﴿And they made between Him and the jinn a relationship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. This is because the Quraysh said, "The angels are the daughters of God." So this verse indicates that the angel is called a jinn?

The answer: It is not permissible that the meaning of His words ﴿was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50] be that he was the keeper of the garden, because His words "except Iblis, he was of the jinn" imply that the reason for his refusal to prostrate was that he was a jinni, and it is not possible to explain his refusal to prostrate by his being the keeper of the garden. Therefore this nullifies the claim that "he was of the jinn" means "he became of the jinn."

We say: This is contrary to the apparent meaning, so one should not resort to it except in cases of necessity. As for His words ﴿And they made between Him and the jinn a relationship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158], we say it is possible that some disbelievers affirmed that relationship with the jinn just as they affirmed it with the angels. Also, we have shown that the angel is called a jinn according to the original linguistic meaning, but the term "jinn" by conventional usage became restricted to others, just as the term *dabbah* (creature that crawls), though in its original linguistic meaning it covers everything that crawls, became by convention restricted to some of what crawls. So this verse is to be understood according to the original linguistic meaning, while the verse we cited is understood according to the newer convention.

*The second:* Iblis has offspring (dhurriyyah), and the angels have no offspring. We say Iblis has offspring based on His words describing him: ﴿Will you then take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me?﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]. This is explicit in affirming offspring for him. And we say the angels have no offspring because offspring come only from a male and a female, and the angels have no females in them, based on His words: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. He denounced those who judged them to be female. When femaleness is negated, procreation is necessarily negated, and thus offspring are negated.

*The third:* The angels are infallible (ma'sumun), as has been explained before, and Iblis was not like that, so he must not be of the angels.

*The fourth:* Iblis was created from fire, and the angels were not. We say Iblis was created from fire based on his own statement quoted in the Qur'an: ﴿You created me from fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. Also, he was of the jinn based on His words ﴿was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and the jinn were created from fire, based on His words: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the scorching wind﴾ [al-Hijr: 27], and He said: ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ and ﴿He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ [al-Rahman: 14-15]. As for the claim that the angels were not created from fire but from light, this is based on what al-Zuhri reported from Urwah, from Aisha, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "The angels were created from light, and the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire." Also, it is well known that the angels are spiritual beings (ruhaniyyun), and it has been said they were named this because they were created from wind (rih) or spirit (rawh).

*The fifth:* The angels are messengers (rusul), based on His words: ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir: 1], and God's messengers are infallible, based on His words: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. Since Iblis was not like that, he must not be of the angels. Those who argued that he was of the angels relied on two matters:

The first point: God excepted him (Iblis) from the angels, and istithna' (exception) indicates the exclusion of something which, were it not for the exception, would have been included, or whose inclusion would have been valid. This requires that he was of the angels. It may be said: the munqati' (disjunctive) exception is well known in the speech of the Arabs. God says: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾ ﴿except He who created me﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 27]. And He says: ﴿They will not hear therein any vain speech or sin﴾ ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 25]. And He says: ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade by mutual consent﴾ [An-Nisa': 29]. And He says: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by error﴾ [An-Nisa': 92]. Also, he was a single jinni among thousands of angels, so they were given precedence in his case in the phrase "so they prostrated," and then he was excepted from them as an exception of one from among them.

We say: each of these two aspects is contrary to the original principle, so resorting to them is only done under necessity. The proofs you have cited for denying that he was among the angels contain nothing but reliance on general expressions. So if we make him one of the angels, it would necessitate specifying what you have relied upon of the general expressions. And if we say he is not one of the angels, it would necessitate that we interpret the exception as a disjunctive exception. It is known that the specification of general expressions is more frequent in the Book of God, Exalted is He, than interpreting the exception as a disjunctive exception, so our view is preferable.

Also, istithna' is derived from thanny (turning back) and sarf (diverting). The meaning of diverting is realized only where, without the diverting, it would have entered. A thing does not enter into other than its genus, so the realization of the meaning of istithna' in it is impossible. As for his saying that he was a single jinni among the angels, we say: applying the ruling of the many to the few is permissible only when the few is of no account and is not taken into consideration. When the bulk of the discourse concerns only that one individual, it is not permissible to apply to him the ruling of others.

The second argument: they said, if Iblis were not of the angels, then God's saying ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ would not include him. And if it did not include him, it would be impossible for his refusing to prostrate to be disobedience, arrogance and sin, and he would not deserve blame and punishment. Since these matters occurred, we know that this address includes him, and that address includes him only if he is of the angels. It cannot be said that although he was not of the angels, he grew up with them, his association with them was long, and he was joined to them, so that address necessarily includes him. Also, why is it not permissible to say that although he did not enter into this command, God commanded him to prostrate with another expression which is not related in the Qur'an, as is shown by His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 12]?

We say: As for the first, its answer is that association does not necessitate what you have mentioned. For this reason we say in the principles of jurisprudence that the address to males does not include females, and vice versa, despite the great intermingling between the two categories. Also, the great intermingling between the angels and Iblis did not prevent the curse from being confined to Iblis; so how would it prevent this obligation from being confined to the angels? As for the second, its answer is that the connection of a ruling to a description indicates causation. So when He mentioned His saying ﴿he refused and was arrogant﴾ immediately after His saying ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, this immediate sequence indicates that this refusal occurred because of opposing this command, not because of opposing another command. This is what I hold on both sides, and God knows best the realities of matters.

The fourth issue: Know that a group of our companions argue from God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, that Adam is superior to the angels. So we have seen fit to mention this issue here, and we say: Most of the People of the Sunnah said: the prophets are superior to the angels. The Mu'tazilah said: rather, the angels are superior to the prophets, and this is the view of the majority of the Shi'ah. This view was chosen by Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani among our theologians, and Abu 'Abd Allah al-Halimi among our jurists. We will mention the essence of the discussion from both sides. As for those who hold that the angels are superior to humans, they have argued with several matters.

One of them: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And those who are with Him are not too proud to worship Him﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 19], to His saying ﴿They exalt [Him] night and day; they do not slacken﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 20]. The argument with this verse is from two aspects:

The first: the intended meaning of this "withness" is not withness of place and direction, for that is impossible for God, Exalted is He; rather it is withness of nearness and honour. Since this verse was revealed describing the angels, we know that this kind of nearness and honour is possessed by them and not by others. And one may say: He, Exalted is He, affirmed this withness in the Hereafter for individual believers, saying ﴿in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent﴾ [Al-Qamar: 55]. As for in this world, He, Exalted is He, related through the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, ''I am with those whose hearts are broken for My sake''. And this is more indicative of exaltation, because this hadith shows that He, Exalted is He, is with those whose hearts are broken, whereas what they argued from the verse shows that the angels are with God, Exalted is He. There is no doubt that God, Exalted is He, being with the servant is more emphatic in exaltation than the servant being with God, Exalted is He.

The second aspect in the argument from the verse: God, Exalted is He, argued from their not being arrogant that others must not be arrogant either. Had humans been superior to them, this argument would not be complete. For if a sultan wishes to establish upon his subjects the obligation of obeying him, he says: Kings do not refuse to obey me; so who are these wretches that they should rebel against my obedience! In sum, it is known that this argument is only complete by [citing] the stronger over the weaker.

One may say: there is no dispute that the angels are stronger and more capable than humans, and this degree of difference suffices for the soundness of the argument. For He, Exalted is He, says that the angels, despite their great strength and their dominion over the bodies of the heavens and the earth, and their safety from decrepitude and sickness and their long lives, do not abandon servitude for a single moment; and humans, despite their extreme weakness and their falling into the most rapid states of sickness, decrepitude and kinds of calamities, are more deserving of not rebelling. This degree of difference is therefore sufficient for the soundness of this argument. There is no dispute about the occurrence of difference in this meaning; the dispute is only about superiority in the sense of abundance of reward. Why do you say that this argument is not sound unless the king has more reward than humans, and there must be evidence for that, besides the fact that what is most immediately understood is what we have mentioned?

The second: they said: the worship of the angels is more arduous than the worship of humans, so it is more rewarding than the worship of humans. We say it is more arduous for several reasons:

The first: their inclination to rebellion is stronger, so their obedience is more arduous. And we say their inclination to rebellion is stronger because the servant who is free from afflictions and independent of seeking needs is more inclined to pleasures and delights than one immersed in needs; he is like one who is distressed in returning to the worship of his Master and turning to Him. Hence God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion; but when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate others with Him﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 65]. It is known that the angels are the dwellers of the heavens, which are gardens and orchards, places of leisure and comfort, and they are safe

from sickness and poverty. Then, despite the completeness of the causes of luxury for them, they have been continuously, since they were created, occupied with worship, humble, fearful, anxious, fearing, as though they were prisoners, not turning to the bliss of the gardens and pleasures, but rather devoted to arduous acts of obedience, described by intense fear and great terror. It seems that none of the sons of Adam could remain thus for a single day, let alone those lengthy ages. This is confirmed by the story of Adam, peace be upon him, for He released him to all the places of the Garden by His saying ﴿And eat from it freely wherever you will﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 35], then he was forbidden one tree, and he did not master himself until he fell into evil. This indicates that their obedience is more arduous than the obedience of humans.

The second: the transition of the responsible person from one kind of worship to another is like moving from one garden to another; whereas remaining upon one kind produces hardship and weariness. For this reason, writings are divided into chapters and sections, and God's Book is divided into suras, sections, tenths and fifths. Now each of the angels is constantly engaged in one work from which he does not turn to another, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿They exalt [Him] night and day; they do not slacken﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 20], and He said: ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks [in worship]﴾ ﴿And indeed, we are the glorifiers﴾ [As-Saffat: 165–166]. When that is so, their worship is at the utmost degree of hardship. If this is established, their worship must be more excellent, because of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, ''The best of deeds is the most arduous'', i.e., the hardest, and his saying to 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, ''Your reward is in proportion to your fatigue''. Analogy also requires this, for the more a servant bears hardships for the sake of his Master's pleasure, the more he deserves exaltation and precedence.

One may say on both aspects: Grant that their hardship is greater; why do you say their reward must be greater? For we see some Sufis in our time who bear in the path of striving such hardships and toils that it is certain the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not bear some of that. Then we are certain that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is more excellent than him and his like. Indeed, it is related of the worshippers, ascetics and monks of India that they bear, in humility before God, Exalted is He, hardships the like of which has not been related of any of the prophets or saints, yet we are certain of their disbelief. So we know that the abundance of hardship in worship does not necessitate an increase in reward. The verification of this is that abundance of reward is only obtained based on intentions and aims. It may be that one act is performed by two obligated persons alike as regards outward actions, and one of them merits great reward by it while the other merits little reward, because the sincerity of the one is stronger and greater than the sincerity of the second. Therefore, the abundance of worships and their hardship do not necessitate a difference in excellence. Then we say: we do not concede that the worship of the angels is more arduous.

As for his statement in the first aspect, that the heavens are like pleasant gardens, we say: granted; but why do you say that performing worship in good places is more arduous than performing it in bad places?

At most it may be said: the causes of luxury are prepared for him, so his abstaining from them while they are prepared for him is more arduous. But this is countered by the fact that the causes of affliction are gathered upon humans; yet even with these gathered upon them, they are content with God's decree, and those trials and calamities do not divert them from humility before Him and persistence in His worship, and that is more fitting for worship. For servants and slaves have their hearts content with service while they enjoy blessings and comfort, and none of them endures service in hardship except one who is at the utmost sincerity. So their claim is the reverse, and is more fitting.

As for his statement, that persistence in one kind of worship is arduous, we say this is countered by another aspect, namely that when they...

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 34 (part 3 of 7):**

They accustomed themselves to one type of worship, and so they became like those compelled toward a thing they cannot oppose. This is according to what is said: "Habit is a fifth nature," so that type of worship becomes extremely easy for them. For this reason, the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade continuous fasting (*wisal*) and said: "The best fasting is the fasting of Dawud (peace be upon him)," which is to fast one day and break the fast the next day.

The third argument: They said: The worship of the angels is more constant, so it is superior. The proof that it is more constant is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They glorify (Him) night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya': 20]. Based on this, if their lifespans were equal to the lifespans of humans, their acts of obedience would be more constant and more numerous. So how much more so, since there is no comparison between the lifespan of all humanity and the lifespan of the angels, as was previously explained in the chapter on the attributes of the angels. Regarding this verse, there is an objection. It was narrated in *Shu'ab al-Iman* from Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, who said: I said to Ka'b: "What do you say about God's saying ﴿They glorify (Him) night and day, never tiring﴾, and then His saying ﴿who makes the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir: 1]? Would not being messengers prevent them from this glorification?" And also, He said: ﴿Upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161]. So how can they be occupied with cursing while they are occupied with glorifying? Ka'b al-Ahbar answered and said: Glorification for them is like breathing for us. Just as our being occupied with breathing does not prevent us from speaking, similarly our being occupied with glorification does not prevent them from all other deeds.

I say: One may say: Being occupied with breathing does not prevent speech only because the instrument of breathing is other than the instrument of speech. But cursing and glorifying are of the same kind (genus) as speech, so their combination in a single verse is impossible. The first answer: What is so improbable about God creating for them many tongues, with which they glorify God, the Exalted, using some of them, and curse the enemies of God, the Exalted, using others?

The second answer: Cursing is driving away and distancing, and glorifying is engaging in the praise of God, the Exalted. There is no doubt that praising God necessitates distancing whoever believes about God what is not befitting. Thus that cursing is among its necessary consequences.

The third answer: His saying ﴿they never tire﴾ [al-Anbiya': 20] means that they never tire of the resolve to perform it at its fitting times. Just as it is said: "So-and-so is persistent in the congregational prayers and never tires of them," it is not meant that he is constantly occupied with them, but that he is persistent in the resolve always to perform them at their times. When it is established that their worship is more constant, it must be that it is superior.

As for the first point: The more constant is more difficult, so it is superior, according to what was previously established in the second argument. As for the second point: His (peace be upon him) saying: "The best of servants is the one whose life is long and whose deeds are good." The angels (may the blessings of God be upon them) have the longest lives among the servants and the best deeds, so they must be the best of servants. Also, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "An elder among his people is like a prophet among his community." This implies that they, among humanity, are like the Prophet among the community, and this requires their superiority over humanity.

One may say: Noah (peace be upon him), and likewise Luqman and likewise al-Khadir, had longer lives than Muhammad (ﷺ), so they must be superior to Muhammad (ﷺ). That is false by consensus (*ijma'*), so what they said is refuted. Indeed, we find in this community someone who has a longer life and is more diligent in striving than the Prophet (ﷺ), yet he is further from him in rank than the Throne is from what lies beneath the earth.

The verification of this is what we have explained: that abundance of reward is only obtained through a matter that relates to motives and intentions. So it is possible that a small act of obedience may be performed by a person in a manner that merits a great reward, and that many acts of obedience may be performed in a manner that merits only a small reward.

The fourth argument: They are the foremost of the foremost in all acts of worship. There is no characteristic of religion except that they are leaders who precede in it. Rather, they are the originators and the ones who populate the paths of religion. Precedence in worship is a basis for preference and honor. As for the first point, it is by consensus. As for the second point, it is His saying: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost; those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10–11]. As for the third point, it is His (peace be upon him) saying: "Whoever establishes a good practice, for him is its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." This implies that the angels have obtained all the reward that the prophets obtained, together with additional reward that they merited by their deeds which they performed before the creation of humanity.

One may say: This implies that Adam (peace be upon him) is superior to Muhammad (ﷺ), because he was the first of humanity to establish the worship of God, the Exalted, and the first to establish calling the disbelievers to God, the Exalted. Since that is false by consensus, what they mentioned is refuted. The verification of this is what we presented earlier: that abundance of reward occurs through a matter that relates to intention. So it is possible that the intention of the later one is purer, and thus he deserves more reward than the earlier one deserves.

The fifth argument: The angels are the messengers of the prophets, and the messenger is superior to the community. Therefore the angels are superior to the prophets. As for the angels being messengers to the prophets, it is based on His saying: ﴿He has been taught by one mighty in power﴾ [an-Najm: 5], and His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 193–194]. As for the messenger being superior to the community, it is by analogy: prophets from among humanity are superior to their nations, so likewise here.

If it is said: By custom, when a ruler sends one person to a great assembly to be a judge over them and to manage their affairs, that messenger is more noble than that assembly. But if he sends one person to one person, the messenger may not be more noble than the one to whom he is sent. For example, if he sends one of his slaves to his vizier regarding an important matter, it does not follow that the slave is more noble than the vizier. We say: But Gabriel (peace be upon him) is sent to all the prophets and messengers from among humanity. So according to this rule which the questioner has mentioned, it follows that Gabriel (peace be upon him) is superior to them.

Know that this argument can be established in another way, namely that the angels are messengers, based on His saying: ﴿who makes the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir: 1]. Then the situation must be one of two matters: either the angel is a messenger to another angel, or to one of the prophets who are from humanity. In either case, the angel is a messenger and his community are messengers. As for the human messenger, he is a messenger, but his community are not messengers. The messenger all of whose community are messengers is superior to the messenger who is not like that. So the superiority of the angel over humanity is established from this aspect. Also, Abraham (peace be upon him) was a messenger to Lot (peace be upon him), so he was superior to him. And Moses (peace be upon him) was a messenger to the prophets who were in his army, and he was superior to them. So likewise here.

One may say: When a king sends a messenger to some region, that may be because he has made that messenger a ruler over them, a manager of their affairs, and one who disposes of their conditions. And it may not be so, because he sends him to them only to inform them of some matters, without making him a ruler over them or manager of their affairs. So the messenger in the first case must be superior to the one to whom he is sent. As for the second case, it is clear that he need not be superior to the one to whom he is sent. So the prophets sent to their nations belong to the first case, and therefore they were necessarily superior to their nations. Why do you say that the sending of the angels to the prophets is of the first case, so that it would follow that they must be superior to the prophets?

* * *

The sixth argument: The angels are more God-fearing (*taqwa*) than humanity, so they must be superior to humanity. As for their being more God-fearing, it is because they are free from errors and from inclination toward them, for their fear is constant and their apprehension is constant, as in His saying: ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾ [an-Nahl: 50], and His saying: ﴿and they are apprehensive out of fear of Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. Fear and apprehension are incompatible with the resolve to disobey. As for the prophets (peace be upon them), although they are the best of humanity, each of them is free of some kind of slip. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "There is none of us except that he has disobeyed or intended disobedience, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya (peace be upon them both)." So it is established that the God-fearing of the angels is more intense, and therefore they must be superior to humanity, according to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most God-conscious of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. If it is said: His saying ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most God-conscious of you﴾ is addressed to the children of Adam, so it does not encompass the angels. Also, taqwa is derived from *wiqaya* (protection), and there is no desire (*shahwa*) in the case of the angels, so realizing taqwa in their case is impossible.

As for the answer to the first: The linking of honor to taqwa indicates that honor is caused by taqwa. Wherever taqwa is greater, honor is greater. As for the answer to the second: We do not concede that there is no desire in their case. Rather, they have no desire for eating and intercourse, but the lack of a particular desire does not necessitate the lack of desire in general. Rather, they have the desire for advancement and elevation. For this reason they said: ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾ And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever among them should say, "Indeed, I am a deity other than Him," - then We would recompense him with Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 29].

One may say: The hadith you mentioned indicates that Yahya (peace be upon him) was more God-fearing than the rest of the prophets, so he must be superior to Muhammad (ﷺ). That is false by consensus. So we know that increase in taqwa does not necessitate increase in excellence. The verification of this is what we presented earlier: it is possible that a person never committed disobedience, yet performed acts of obedience that merit a hundred units of reward; and another person committed a disobedience, and then performed an act of obedience that merits a thousand units of reward. Then a hundred units of reward are set against a hundred units of punishment, leaving him nine hundred units of reward. This person, despite having committed disobedience, is superior to the person who never committed disobedience at all. Also, we do not concede that the taqwa of the angels is more intense, because taqwa is derived from protection, and the factors leading to disobedience are more numerous in the children of Adam, so the taqwa of the God-fearing among them is greater.

As for his saying: The angels have the desire for leadership, we say: This does not harm us, because this desire is present in humanity as well, and other types of desire have also been present in them, namely the desire of the belly and of the private parts. Since that is so, the desires that divert from acts of obedience are more numerous in the children of Adam, and therefore the taqwa of the God-fearing among them must be more intense.

The seventh argument: His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels who are near [to Him]﴾ [an-Nisa': 172]. The way of inference is that His saying ﴿nor will the angels who are near [to Him]﴾ comes as an emphasis on the first part. Such emphasis is only made by mentioning the more excellent. It is said: "This piece of wood cannot be carried by ten, nor by a hundred," and it is not said: "It cannot be carried by ten, nor by one." And it is said: "This scholar does not disdain to serve him, nor does the vizier or the king," and it is not said: "The vizier does not disdain to serve him, nor does the doorkeeper."

Someone might say: if this verse indicates anything, it indicates the superiority of the angels brought near over the Messiah. But it does not follow from this that the angels brought near are superior to one who is greater than the Messiah, namely Muhammad, Moses and Abraham, peace be upon them. In sum, if it were established that the Messiah is superior to all the prophets, their aim would be achieved; but since they have not established proof of that, their aim is not achieved, especially since the Muslims have agreed that Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to the Messiah, peace be upon him, and we have not seen any Muslim assert with certainty the superiority of the Messiah over Moses and Abraham, peace be upon them both.

Then we say: His saying ﴿nor the angels brought near﴾ contains nothing but the conjunctive waw, and the waw denotes general conjunction. It therefore indicates that the Messiah does not disdain, and the angels do not disdain. As for whether it indicates that the angels are superior to the Messiah, it does not.

As for the examples they mentioned, we say: an example is not sufficient to establish a universal claim. Moreover, the example is countered by other examples, such as his saying, "Zayd and 'Amr did not help me in this matter," which does not indicate that 'Amr is superior to Zayd. Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor the sacrificial animals, nor the garlands, nor those making for the Sacred House﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. Since the examples differ, relying on them is impossible.

Then the verification is that when one says, "This piece of wood cannot be lifted by one person or by ten," we know by our intellects that ten are stronger than one, and so we know for certain that the purpose of mentioning the second is to exaggerate. This exaggeration we have come to know only through this route, not from the bare wording. Here in the verse, we can know that the meaning of His saying ﴿nor the angels brought near﴾ [an-Nisa': 172] is to express exaggeration only if we already knew beforehand that the angels brought near are superior to the Messiah. In that case, the soundness of using this verse as evidence would depend on the claim being established before this proof, while the establishment of the claim would depend on this verse's indication of it, so circularity arises, and that is invalid.

Suppose we grant that it indicates a difference, but it does not indicate a difference in every respect, only in some and not others. Its explanation: when it is said, "This scholar does not disdain to serve the judge or the sultan," this indicates only that the sultan is more complete than the judge in some matters, namely power, strength, dominance and authority, and does not indicate that he is superior to the judge in knowledge, asceticism and humility before God, exalted is He. If this is established, we say in accordance with its implication. That is because the angel is superior to the human in power and might: Gabriel, peace be upon him, uprooted the cities of Lot, and humans cannot do anything of that kind. So why do you say that the angel is superior to the human in the abundance of reward obtained through greater submission and servitude? The full verification of this is that the difference disputed in this question is abundance of reward, and abundance of reward is obtained only through servitude, and servitude is an expression for the utmost humility and submission. For a servant described by utmost humility before God, exalted is He, it is not fitting to disdain the servitude of God; rather it contradicts it and is incompatible with it. Since this statement is manifest and clear, interpreting the words of God, exalted is He, in accordance with it would remove them from their benefit. As for a person being characterized by great power and immense dominance, that is suitable for rebellion and abandoning servitude. When the Christians witnessed from the Messiah, peace be upon him, the raising of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper, they took him out of servitude because of this degree of power. So God, exalted is He, said: Jesus does not disdain, because of this degree of power, to be His servant; nor do the angels brought near, who are above him in power, might, strength and dominance over the worlds of the heavens and the earths. On this understanding, the way the verse indicates that the angel is superior to the human in strength and might is coherent; but it does not at all indicate that he is superior to the human in abundance of reward. Or it may be said: they only claimed his divinity because he came into being without a father. It was said to them: the angel did not come into being from a father or a mother, and yet they were more amazed at Jesus in this respect, while they do not disdain servitude.

If it is said: the verse contains what indicates that the intended difference is between the Messiah and the angels in servitude, not in power, might and strength. This is because He described them as "brought near," and nearness to God, exalted is He, is not by place or direction, but by rank and station. So when He described them here as "brought near," we know that the intended difference between them and the Messiah is in degrees of excellence, not in strength and might.

We reply: if your purpose in this question is that He described the angels as brought near, therefore the Messiah must not be so described, this is invalid, because specifying a thing by mention does not indicate the negation of it for other things. If your purpose is that since He described them as brought near, the difference must lie in that, this too is invalid, because it is possible that the Messiah and the brought-near ones, although they share the attribute of nearness in obedience, differ in other respects, so the intended meaning is the explanation of the difference in those other respects.

* * *

Another objection: we say in accordance with the verse's implication, and grant that Jesus, peace be upon him, is inferior to the totality of the angels in excellence. Why do you say that he is inferior to each one of the angels in excellence?

Another objection: perhaps He, exalted is He, mentioned this address with peoples who believed that the angel is superior to the human, so He framed the speech according to their belief, as in His saying: ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ [ar-Rum: 27].

Eighth: His saying, exalted is He, relating from Iblis: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become two angels or become of the immortal﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]. Had it not been established with Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, that the angel is superior to the human, Iblis would not have been able to deceive them with it, nor would Adam and Eve have been deceived by it.

Someone may say: this is the statement of Iblis, so it is not a proof. It may not be said that Adam believed it to be correct, for otherwise he would not have been deceived; and Adam's belief is a proof. We reply: perhaps Adam, peace be upon him, erred in this, either because error is permissible for prophets, or because he was not yet a prophet at that time. Moreover, grant that it is a proof; yet Adam, peace be upon him, was not a prophet before the lapse, so the angel's superiority over him at that time does not entail the angel's superiority over him once he became a prophet. Furthermore, grant that the verse indicates that the angel is superior to the human in some desirable matters; why do you say that it indicates the angel's superiority over the human in the domain of reward? For there is no dispute that the angel is superior to the human in power and strength, in beauty and comeliness, and in purity and freedom from the turbidities caused by compound constitution. The angels were created from light, while Adam was created from earth. So perhaps Adam, peace be upon him, although he was superior to them in abundance of reward, nonetheless desired to be equal to them in those matters we have enumerated, and so the deception was achieved from this direction. Also, His saying ﴿unless you become two angels﴾ [al-A'raf: 20] may mean: unless you are transformed into two angels; in that case your inference is sound. It may also mean that the prohibition is specific to the angels and the immortals and not to you two. This is like one of us saying to another: "You did not forbid this except that you be so-and-so," meaning that the one forbidden is so-and-so and not you, without intending anything beyond that he should be transformed and become so-and-so. Since Iblis's aim was to cast doubt upon them, among the strongest forms of doubt is to suggest that they were not forbidden, and that the one forbidden is someone else. Also, grant that the verse indicates that the angel is superior to Adam; why do you say that it indicates the angel is superior to Muhammad? For the Muslims have agreed that Muhammad is superior to Adam, peace be upon them both, and it does not follow from the angel's being superior to the inferior that he is superior to the superior.

Ninth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not say to you that with me are the treasuries of God, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say to you that I am an angel﴾ [al-An'am: 50]. Someone may say: it is possible that the intended meaning is "nor do I say to you that I am an angel" in the abundance of knowledge and the intensity of power. What indicates the soundness of this possibility are several considerations.

The first: the disbelievers demanded of him great things, such as ascending to the sky, moving mountains, and bringing great wealth, and these things cannot be achieved except with abundant knowledge and great power.

The second: His saying ﴿I do not say to you that with me are the treasuries of God﴾ indicates his acknowledgment that he is not capable of all things; and His saying ﴿nor do I know the unseen﴾ indicates his acknowledgment that he does not know all known things. Then His saying ﴿nor do I say to you that I am an angel﴾ means, and God knows best: just as I do not claim power over all things and knowledge of all things, so I do not claim a power like the power of the angel, nor knowledge like their knowledge.

The third: His saying ﴿nor do I say to you that I am an angel﴾ does not intend the negation of form, since that would not serve the purpose; rather it negates that he has what they have of attributes. For its truth it suffices that he does not have what they have, and that his attributes are not equal to theirs in every respect. There is no indication in it of a difference in all attributes, for lack of equality in everything is one thing, and occurrence of difference in everything is another.

Tenth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is not a human; this is only a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. If it is said: why could the intended meaning not be a resemblance in form and beauty? We reply: it is better that the resemblance be in conduct and not in form, because He said ﴿this is only a noble angel﴾, so he likened him to a noble angel, and the angel is noble only through his pleasing conduct, not merely through his form. Thus it is established that the intended meaning is his likeness to the angel in the negation of human drives toward lust and eager pursuit of desired things, and the affirmation of the opposite of these, namely the state of the angel, which is lowering the gaze and restraining the inclination toward forbidden things. So this verse indicates the consensus of intelligent people, men and women, believer and disbeliever, that the angels are specially distinguished by a rank far above the ranks of humans.

Someone may say: the woman's words, ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾, are almost explicit that the women's intention in their saying ﴿this is only a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31] was to magnify Joseph's state in beauty and comeliness, not in conduct; for the manifestation of her excuse in the intensity of her passion arises only from Joseph's surpassing beauty, not from his surpassing asceticism and piety, since that would not suit the intensity of her love for him. Grant that the intended meaning is the likening of Joseph, peace be upon him, to the angel in turning away from desired things; it still does not follow that Joseph, peace be upon him, had less reward than the angels. For there is no dispute that the human's not being drawn to food and marriage is less than the angels' not being drawn to these things; but why do you say that this necessitates greater excellence in the sense of abundance of reward? If they hold that whoever has fewer sins must be more excellent, the discussion of that has already passed.

The Eleventh Argument: the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We have preferred them above many of those whom We have created with a (marked) preference﴾ [al-Isra' 17:70]. The creatures of God Exalted are either the mukallafun (those charged with religious obligation) or others than them. There is no doubt that the mukallafun are superior to others. As for the mukallafun, they are of four kinds: the angels, mankind, the jinn, and the devils.

There is no doubt that mankind is superior to the jinn and the devils. So if mankind were also superior to the angels, it would follow that humanity is superior to all creatures, and then the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We have preferred them above many of those whom We have created with a (marked) preference﴾ [al-Isra' 17:70], would serve no purpose. Rather, it should have been said: "And We have preferred them above all whom We have created with a (marked) preference." Since it was not said this, we know that the angel is superior to the human.

One may say: the essence of this statement is an reliance on dalil al-khitab (the argument from the implication of speech), because the explicit statement that He preferred them above many creatures does not indicate that He did not prefer them above the rest, except through dalil al-khitab. Moreover, suppose that the class of angels is superior to the class of the children of Adam. Still, it does not follow that because one of two groups is superior to the second group, each individual of the first group is superior to the second group. For we may suppose ten slaves, each of whom is worth one hundred dinars, and ten others among whom there is one slave worth two hundred dinars, while the remaining nine are each worth one dinar.

Then the first group is superior to the second group, yet in the second group there is one who is superior to each single member of the first group. So it is likewise here. Furthermore, the words ﴿And We have preferred them﴾ [al-Isra' 17:70] may mean: We have preferred them in the honour mentioned at the beginning of the verse, which is the words ﴿And We have honoured the children of Adam﴾ [al-Isra' 17:70]. The honour here may mean beauty of form, abundance of intelligence, the capacity for wondrous deeds, and great attention to cleanliness and purity. If that is so, we concede that the angel exceeds the human in these matters; but why do you say that the angel has greater reward than the human?

Furthermore, the words ﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [Luqman 31:10] do not imply that there are invisible pillars. Likewise, the words of the Exalted ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with God, for which he has no proof﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:117] do not imply that there is another god for whom there is a proof; so it is likewise here.

* * *

The Twelfth Argument: the prophets, peace be upon them, never sought forgiveness for anyone without beginning with seeking forgiveness for themselves, and only after that for others among the believers. Adam said: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf 7:23]. Noah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house as a believer﴾ [Nuh 71:28]. Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾ [Ibrahim 14:41]. He said: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:83]. Moses said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my brother﴾ [al-A'raf 7:151]. God Exalted said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad 47:19], and said: ﴿That God may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what follows﴾ [al-Fath 48:2]. As for the angels, they did not seek forgiveness for themselves, but they sought forgiveness for the believers among mankind. This is indicated by the words of the Exalted, quoting them: ﴿So forgive those who have repented and followed Your way, and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾ [Ghafir 40:7], and He said: ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir 40:7].
