Had they needed seeking forgiveness, they would have begun with themselves, because averting harm from oneself takes precedence over averting harm from others. And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Begin with yourself, then with those whom you support." This indicates that the angel is superior to the human.

One may say: this argument does not show that the angels never committed any slip while humans have committed slips. But we have already demonstrated above that difference in this matter does not necessitate difference in excellence. Some people have said that their seeking forgiveness for mankind is like an excuse for those who criticised them when they said ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾

The Thirteenth Argument: the words of the Exalted ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and recording﴾ [al-Infitar 82:10-11]. This is general concerning all the mukallafun of the children of Adam, so the prophets and others are included. This requires that they are superior to mankind for two reasons:

The first: He made them guardians over the children of Adam, and the guardian of a mukallaf against disobedience must be further from error and slip than the one guarded. That requires that they are further from sins and closer to acts of obedience than mankind, and that requires greater excellence.

The second: He, glorified and exalted, made their recording a proof for mankind in acts of obedience and against them in acts of disobedience. That requires that their word be more worthy of acceptance than the word of mankind. Had mankind been of greater rank than them, the matter would be reversed.

One may say: as for your statement that the guardian must be more noble than the guarded, this is far-fetched, for a king may appoint some of his servants over his child without it being necessary that the guardian be nobler than the guarded there. As for your statement that He made their testimony binding upon mankind, this is weak, for the witness may be of lower standing than the one witnessed against.

The Fourteenth Argument: the words of the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none shall speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and who speaks what is correct﴾ [al-Naba' 78:38]. The purpose of mentioning their conditions is to emphasise the greatness and majesty of God Exalted. Had there been among creation another group whose standing and supplication were more powerful in declaring the greatness and pride of God than their standing, their mention would have been more fitting in this context. Then, just as He, glorified, showed the greatness of His essence in the Hereafter by mentioning the angels, so He showed His greatness in this world by mentioning the angels, in His words ﴿And you see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying with praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Zumar 39:75]. One may say: all of this indicates that they are of greater state than mankind in some matters, so why should it not be that this state is their strength, might and force? This is like saying that when the sultan sat, the kings of the regions of the world stood around his throne, humbled and submissive, for the greatness of the sultan is indeed explained by that. Yet this does not show that they are more honoured in the sultan's sight than his own son; so it is likewise here.

The Fifteenth Argument: the words of the Exalted ﴿And the believers, each believed in God, His angels, His books and His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:285].

He, Exalted, made clear that the correctness of faith requires these things, then began with Himself, then mentioned the angels second, the books third, and the messengers fourth. Likewise in His words ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:18], and He said ﴿Indeed, God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:56]. Precedence in mention indicates precedence in rank. This is indicated also by the fact that placing the lower before the higher in mention is ugly by custom, and so it must be ugly by the Law.

As for its being ugly by custom: a poet said:

"Umayrah, bid farewell if you have prepared to depart in the morning; grey hair and Islam suffice a man as a restrainer."

'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "If you had put the greeting first, I would have granted you (the verse)." Also, when they wrote the treaty of truce between the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the polytheists, a dispute arose over placing the name first; likewise in the treaty between 'Ali and Mu'awiyah. This indicates that precedence in mention indicates greater nobility. And since this is established in custom, it must be so in the Law, by his saying, peace be upon him: "What the Muslims see as good is good in the sight of God." Thus it is established that placing the angels before the messengers in mention indicates their precedence in excellence.

One may say: this argument is weak, for if the reliance is on the conjunction waw, then waw does not indicate order; and if the reliance is on precedence in mention, it is refuted by the placing of the Surah Tabbat before the Surah Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad.

The Sixteenth Argument: the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:56]. He made the blessings of the angels a form of honouring the Prophet (ﷺ), and this indicates that the angels are more noble than the Prophet (ﷺ).

One may say: this is refuted by His words: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:56]. He commanded the believers to send blessings upon the Prophet, and it did not follow that the believers are more excellent than the Prophet, peace be upon him; so likewise with the angels.

The Seventeenth Argument: let us speak concerning Gabriel and Muhammad (ﷺ). We say: Gabriel, peace be upon him, is superior to Muhammad. The proof for this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne, obeyed and trustworthy. And your companion is not a madman﴾ [al-Takwir 81:19-22]. God Exalted described Gabriel, peace be upon him, with six attributes of perfection. The first: that he is a messenger of God. The second: that he is noble with God Exalted. The third: that he is possessor of power with God, and his power with God is nothing other than his power in acts of obedience, such that no other can prevail in them. The fourth: that he is esteemed with God. The fifth: that he is obeyed in the world of the heavens. The sixth: that he is trustworthy in all acts of obedience, free from every kind of betrayal.

Then, after describing Gabriel, peace be upon him, with these lofty attributes, He, glorified and exalted, described Muhammad (ﷺ) by saying: ﴿And your companion is not a madman﴾ [al-Takwir 81:22]. Had Muhammad been equal to Gabriel, peace be upon him, in attributes of excellence, or near to him, then describing Muhammad with this attribute after describing Gabriel with those attributes would have been a diminution of the station of Muhammad (ﷺ), a belittling of his standing, and an annulling of his right; and that is not permissible for God. Therefore this verse indicates that Muhammad (ﷺ) has with God no rank beyond the measure of being said to be not a madman, and that indicates there is no comparison between Gabriel and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, in excellence and rank.

If it is said: why should it not be that His words ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Takwir 81:19] are a description of Muhammad rather than of Gabriel, peace be upon them both? We say: because His words ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾ [al-Takwir 81:23] nullify that.

One may say: we are all agreed that Muhammad (ﷺ) had other virtues besides not being a madman, and that God Exalted did not mention any of those virtues in this passage. So the fact that God did not mention those virtues here does not indicate their absence, by consensus. Or if it is established that Muhammad, peace be upon him, had virtues beyond those mentioned here, why should it not be said that Muhammad, peace be upon him, because of those virtues not mentioned here, is superior to Gabriel, peace be upon him? For just as He described Gabriel here with these six attributes, He also described Muhammad (ﷺ) with six attributes, namely His words: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and as one calling to God by His permission, and as a lamp giving light﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:45-46]. The first attribute is that he is a prophet; the second, that he is a messenger; the third, that he is a witness; the fourth, that he is a bringer of good tidings; the fifth, that he is a warner; the sixth, that he is one calling to God Exalted by His permission; the seventh, that he is a lamp; and the eighth, that he is a giver of light. In sum, singling out one of two persons with an attribute does not at all indicate the negation of those attributes from the other.

* * *

**The eighteenth argument:** The angel is more knowledgeable than the human, and the more knowledgeable is more excellent, so the angel is more excellent. We say that the angel is more knowledgeable than the human because Jibril (peace be upon him) was a teacher to Muhammad (peace be upon him), as is shown by His saying: ﴿One mighty in power taught him﴾ [An-Najm: 5]. A teacher must necessarily be more knowledgeable than the one taught. Furthermore, knowledge is of two kinds:

The first: knowledge that is reached by the intellects, such as knowledge of the essence of Allah the Exalted and His attributes. Deficiency in this cannot be attributed to Jibril (peace be upon him) or to Muhammad (ﷺ), because deficiency in that is ignorance, and it is damaging to the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. As for knowledge of the reality of Allah's creation and the wonders within it, knowledge of the states of the Throne, the Footstool, the Preserved Tablet, the Pen, Paradise and Hell, the layers of the heavens, the categories of angels, and the kinds of animals in caves, mountains and seas, there is no doubt that Jibril (peace be upon him) knows these better, because he (peace be upon him) is longer-lived and has witnessed them more, so his knowledge of them is greater and more complete.

The second: knowledge that is not reached except through revelation. Muhammad (ﷺ) and all the other prophets (peace be upon them) had it only through Jibril (peace be upon him). It is therefore impossible that Muhammad (peace be upon him) should have any superiority over Jibril (peace be upon him) in this. As for Jibril (peace be upon him), he was the intermediary between Allah the Exalted and all the prophets, so he knew all the past and present laws, and he also knows the laws and obligations of the angels. Muhammad (peace be upon him) did not know this. Thus it is established that Jibril (peace be upon him) had more knowledge than Muhammad (peace be upon him). When this is established, it is necessary that he be more excellent than him, because of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 9].

Someone may say: We do not concede that they are more knowledgeable than humans. The evidence for this is that they acknowledged that Adam (peace be upon him) had more knowledge than them, as shown by His saying the Exalted: ﴿He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names."﴾ Then, even if we concede their greater knowledge, that does not necessitate greater reward. We see a person who is an innovator (mubtadi') encompassing many subtle points of knowledge, yet he does not deserve any reward, let alone that his reward be greater. The cause of this, which we have pointed out repeatedly, is that greater reward is obtained only according to sincerity (ikhlas) in actions, and we do not know that the sincerity of the angels is greater.

**The nineteenth argument:** The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever of them should say, "Indeed, I am a deity other than Him," - We would recompense him with Hell﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 29].

[Page 209]

This verse indicates that they reached such a height of elevation and loftiness of rank that if they were to disobey the command of Allah the Exalted, they would not disobey except by claiming divinity, and not by anything else, such as following desires. This indicates the extreme of their majesty.

Someone may say: There is no dispute about the extreme of their majesty. As for his saying that they reached such elevation and loftiness of rank that if they disobeyed the command of Allah the Exalted, they would only disobey in claiming divinity, this is conceded, because their knowledge is abundant, their powers are strong, and they are free of desire for the belly and the private parts. Whoever is like this, if he disobeys the command of Allah, does not disobey except in this matter that you mentioned. But why did you say that this indicates that they have greater reward than humans? The point of dispute is nothing other than that.

**The twentieth argument:** The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), narrated from Allah the Exalted: "And if My servant remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than his gathering." This indicates that the Higher Assembly is more noble.

Someone may say: This is a single report (khabar wahid). Furthermore, this indicates that the assembly of angels is more excellent than the assembly of humans, but the assembly of humans refers to the common people, not to the prophets. So it does not follow from the angel being more excellent than the common people that they are more excellent than the prophets.

This is the end of the discussion of the transmitted proofs. Know that the philosophers agreed that the celestial spirits called angels are more excellent than the rational human souls, and they relied in this matter on rational considerations which we will mention, if Allah the Exalted wills.

**The first argument:** They said: The angels' essences are simple, free from multiplicity. Humans are composed of soul and body. The soul is composed of many powers, and the body is composed of many parts. The simple is better than the composite, because the causes of non-existence for the composite are more numerous than for the simple. This is why the oneness of Allah the Exalted is among the attributes of His majesty and the qualities of His grandeur.

Objection to this: We do not concede that the simple is more noble than the composite. This is because the spiritual aspect is one thing, while the corporeal aspect is two things: its soul and its body. So from the standpoint of the soul it belongs to the world of spiritual realities and lights, and from the standpoint of the body it belongs to the world of bodies. Since it combines the spiritual and the corporeal, it must be more excellent than the purely spiritual and the purely corporeal. This is the secret of why Allah made the first human the one to whom the angels prostrated. And from another aspect: the angelic spirits are detached, separated from corporeal ties, so their absorption in their luminous stations prevents them from managing this corporeal world. As for the prophetic human souls, they are strong enough to combine the two worlds: the constant ascent of their progress in the ladders of knowledge and the worlds of holiness does not prevent them from managing the lower world, and their attention to the arrangement of the world of bodies does not prevent them from perfecting themselves in the world of spirits. So their power is sufficient to manage both worlds, encompassing the control of both kinds. Therefore it is necessary that they be more noble and greater.

**The second argument:** The spiritual substances are free from the desire that is the source of the shedding of blood, while human spirits are joined with it. The one who is free from the source of evil is more noble than the one afflicted with it.

Objection: There is no doubt that persevering in service with many obstacles and hindrances is a stronger indication of sincerity than persevering in it without any obstacles or hindrances. This indicates that the human station in love is higher and more complete. Also, since the spiritual beings obeyed their Creator, their obedience did not necessitate the subduing of the devils, who are the enemies of Allah. But as for human spirits, when they obeyed their Creator, that obedience necessarily involved subduing the appetitive and irascible powers, which are the devils of mankind. So their acts of obedience are more perfect. Also, it is evident that the ranks of the spiritual beings when they said: ﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾ are more perfect than their ranks when they said: ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ And this is only because of the humility resulting from error, and this is more perfect in humans. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) said, relating from his Lord the Exalted: "Indeed, the groaning of sinners is more beloved to Me than the chanting of those who glorify (Me)."

[Page 210]

**The third argument:** The spiritual beings are free from the nature of potentiality. For everything that was possible for them according to their kinds that are in their individuals has come out into actuality. The prophets are not like this. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I seek forgiveness from Allah a hundred times in a day and a night, and I do not know what will be done with me or with you." ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [Ash-Shura: 52]. And there is no doubt that what is in complete actuality is more noble than what is in potentiality.

Objection: We do not concede that they are in complete actuality. Perhaps they are in potentiality in some matters. This is why it has been said that their movements of the spheres are for the purpose of extracting intellections from potentiality into actuality, and these movements in relation to them are like the movements that occur to the spirits carrying the faculties of thought and imagination when attempting to extract intellections that are in potentiality into actuality.

**The fourth argument:** The spiritual beings are eternal in existence, free from the nature of change. Potentiality and the human rational souls are not like this.

Objection: Both premises are disputed. Is it not the case that spiritual beings are possible in existence in themselves and necessary in existence through their substrate? So they are created. Let us concede that. We do not concede that human spirits are created. Rather, according to some of them they are eternal. These said: These spirits were eternally existing like shadows beneath the Throne, glorifying their Lord. But the First Originator commanded them until they descended into the world of bodies and the dwellings of matters. When they became attached to these bodies, they fell in love with them, and their familiarity with them became firmly established. So He sent from those shadows the most perfect and noblest of them to this world, to devise a means for rescuing those spirits from those dwellings. This is what is meant by the story of the ringdove with the collar mentioned in the book *Kalilah wa Dimnah*.

* * *

**The fifth argument:** The spiritual beings are luminous, high and subtle, while the corporeal beings are dark, low and dense. Primary intellect bears witness that light is more noble than darkness, the high is better than the low, and the subtle is more perfect than the dense.

Objection: All of this is an indication toward matter. For us, the cause of nobility is submission to the command of the Lord of the worlds, as He said: ﴿Say: The soul is of the command of my Lord﴾ [Al-Isra': 85]. And claiming nobility on account of the nobility of matter is the argument of the first accursed one, and he was told what was told.

**The sixth argument:** The celestial spiritual beings surpass the corporeal beings in the powers of knowledge and action. As for knowledge: there is agreement among the sages that the celestial spiritual beings encompass the unseen and are aware of future matters. Also, their knowledge is active, innate, universal and permanent, whereas the knowledge of humans is the opposite in all of this. As for action: they persevere in service constantly, glorifying night and day without slackening. Sleep does not overtake their eyes, nor heedlessness their intellects, nor negligence their bodies. Their food is glorification, their drink is sanctification, praise and declaring the oneness of God, their breathing is remembrance of Allah, and their joy is in serving Allah. They are detached from bodily ties, not veiled by any of the appetitive or irascible powers. So where is one of the two categories relative to the other?

Objection: There is no dispute about all that you have mentioned, except that there is a subtle point here: the one who constantly partakes of subtle foods does not take pleasure in them as one afflicted with hunger takes pleasure in them after many days. So the angels, because of their constant persistence in those lofty ranks, do not find pleasure like that which humans find, who are for most of the time veiled by corporeal ties and dark veils. This advantage of pleasure is something specific to humans. Perhaps this is what is meant by His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it, and mankind bore it﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 72]. For the perception of what is agreeable after being tested with what is contrary is more pleasurable than the perception of what is agreeable on a continuous basis. This is why physicians said: the heat in consumptive fever (ḥummā al-diqq, i.e. a wasting fever) is more intense than in intermittent fever (ḥummā al-ghibb). But the heat of fever in consumption, if it persists and becomes settled, the sensation of it ceases. This state did not occur for the angels, because their perfections are constant, and it did not occur for the other bodies, because they were devoid of the power prepared to perceive the immaterial beings. So there remained no one who is able to bear this trust except humans.

**The seventh argument:** Spiritual beings (al-Ruhaniyyat) have the power to direct bodies and turn celestial matter over. This power is not of the kind that belongs to temperaments, so it is not subject to fatigue or weariness. Moreover, you see the tender shoot of crops at the start of its growth splitting stone and cleaving rock. This is due only to a vegetative power that has flowed into it from the essences of the celestial powers. So consider what those celestial powers must be like. The spiritual beings are the ones who act upon lower bodies, turning and directing them without difficulty. They do not find it heavy to carry great loads, nor hard to move mountains. Thus the winds blow by their motions, and clouds form and disperse by their direction. Likewise earthquakes occur in mountains through their agency. The revealed law speaks of this, as the Exalted said: ﴿And those who apportion, by command﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 4]. The intellects also indicate this. The lower spirits are not like this. So where is one of the two categories in relation to the other?

What is said, that the devils, who are the evil spirits, have the power to do this, is disputed. Even if it is granted, there is no dispute that the power of the angels to do this is stronger and more complete. Also, the good, angelic spirits direct their powers toward the order and welfare of this lower world, while the evil spirits direct their powers toward evils. So where is one of these in relation to the other?

**The objection:** It is not far-fetched that among human rational souls there may arise a strong, perfect soul, exalted over elemental bodies, able to turn and direct them. So what is the proof that such a soul is impossible?

**The eighth argument:** Spiritual beings have choices that flow from the lights of the majesty of God, the Mighty and Majestic, directed toward goods, confined to the order of this world, and never mixed with any trace of evil or corruption. Human choices, by contrast, waver between the directions of height and lowness and between the two extremes of good. Their inclination toward goods arises only through the assistance of angels, as reported in the traditions that every person has an angel who guides and directs him.

**The objection:** This shows that the angels are like those compelled to their obedience, while the prophets waver between the two extremes. The one who chooses is superior to the one who is compelled. This is weak, because as long as wavering remains, the act cannot occur. When a preponderance arises, it joins the necessitating cause. So the prophets have goods in potential, and through the angels these become goods in actuality. As for the angels, they are goods in actuality. So where is this in relation to that?

**The ninth argument:** The spiritual beings are specifically attached to vehicles, which are the seven wandering planets and the rest of the fixed stars. The spheres are like bodies, the stars are like hearts, and the angels are like spirits. Thus the relation of spirits to spirits is like the relation of bodies to bodies. Furthermore, we know that differences in the states of the spheres are the sources of differences in the states of this world. The motions of the stars produce various conjunctions: sextile, trine, square, opposition, and close approach. Likewise the zones of the spheres sometimes become coincident, one upon another, and this is the "closing" (al-Ratq), whereupon the order of the world is annulled. At other times some of them separate from others, and the order shifts from one side of the upper world to govern the bodies of the lower world. So likewise the spirits of the lower world, especially since the philosophical inquiries and the sciences of wisdom have shown that the spirits of this world are effects of the spirits of the upper world, and their perfections are effects of the perfections of those spirits. The relation of these spirits to those is like a small flame relative to the disc of the sun, and like a small drop relative to the great sea. These are the effects, and there is a principle and a return. So how is it fitting to claim equality, let alone superiority?

**The objection:** All that you have mentioned is disputed. But even granting it, the discussion still stands. For we have shown that reaching a pleasure after deprivation is more delightful than reaching it in a continuous manner. This state is not attained except by humans.

**The tenth argument:** They said: the celestial spiritual beings are the principles of the spiritual beings of this world and their counterparts. The principle is more noble than what proceeds from it. For every perfection that belongs to what proceeds from the principle is derived from the principle, and what derives is of lesser rank than the necessary source. Likewise the return must be more noble. So the world of spiritual beings is the world of perfection. Its principle is from them, its return is to them, its origin is from them, and its destination is to them. Also, the spirits descended from their world until they became attached to bodies, and were defiled by the filth of bodies. Then they were purified of these through pure morals and pleasing deeds, until they separated from them and returned to their first world. Thus descent is the first creation, and ascent is the second creation. It is therefore known that spiritual beings are more noble than human persons.

**The objection:** These words are built upon the denial of the resurrection and the denial of the gathering of bodies, and without these two, it is like scraping at thorns.

**The eleventh argument:** Is it not the case that the prophets, may God's blessings be upon them, agreed that they do not speak any knowledge or sciences except after revelation? This is an acknowledgment that their knowledge is derived from others. Is it not also the case that they agreed that the angels are those who help them against their enemies, as in the destruction of the cities of the people of Lot and on the day of Badr, and that they are those who guide them to their welfare, as in the story of Noah and the shaping of the ark? When they agreed upon this, how did it come to you to prefer them over the angels, given that they admit their need for them in all matters?

[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]

(The seventh issue): His saying, ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾. There is no doubt that it is a prohibition, but there are two discussions concerning it.

(The first): Is this a prohibition of unlawfulness (nahy tahrim) or a prohibition of disapproval (nahy tanzih)? There is disagreement. Some scholars said: This form is for the prohibition of disapproval, because this form occurs sometimes for disapproval and sometimes for unlawfulness, and the basic principle is that a word is not shared (between meanings). Therefore, the word must be taken as a literal meaning for the common element between the two categories, and that is nothing other than making it literally signify the preference of abstaining over acting, without indicating a prohibition of the act or an absolute permission regarding it. However, permission regarding it was already established by the basic rule, for the basic rule concerning benefits is permissibility. So when we combine the meaning of the word with this basic rule, the whole becomes evidence for disapproval. They said: This is the more fitting view in this context, because according to this assumption, the outcome of Adam's disobedience (peace be upon him) returns to leaving what is better (tark al-awla). It is well known that every doctrine that leads more to the infallibility (ismah) of the Prophets (peace be upon them) is more deserving of acceptance. Others said: Rather, this prohibition is a prohibition of unlawfulness (nahy tahrim), and they argued for it with several points.

(The first of them): His exalted saying, ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾, is like His saying, ﴿And do not approach them until they are pure﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], and His saying, ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ [al-An'am: 152]. Just as this (the latter) is for unlawfulness, so too the first.

(The second): He said, ﴿And you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]. Its meaning is: If you eat from it, then you have wronged yourselves. Do you not see that when they ate, they said, ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]?

(The third): If this prohibition were a prohibition of disapproval, Adam would not have deserved expulsion from Paradise by his act, and repentance would not have been obligatory upon him. As for the answer to the first (argument), we say: Although the prohibition is originally for disapproval, it may be understood as unlawfulness due to a separate indication. As for the answer to the second: His saying, ﴿And you would be among the wrongdoers﴾, means: "you would wrong yourselves by doing what it is better for you to leave," because if you did that, you would be expelled from the Garden in which you neither thirst, nor hunger, nor are exposed to the sun, nor are naked, to a place where you have none of these things. As for the answer to the third: We do not concede that the expulsion from Paradise was for this reason, and its explanation will come, God willing.

(The second discussion): Some said that His saying, ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾, indicates by its implication a prohibition of eating. This is weak, because a prohibition of approaching does not indicate a prohibition of eating, since perhaps the benefit lies in not approaching it, even though if it were brought to him, it would be permissible for him to eat it. Rather, the apparent meaning of the statement covers only the prohibition of approaching.

As for the prohibition of eating, it is known from other indications, namely His saying in another place: ﴿And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 22]. Also, He introduced the statement in the context of permission with eating, saying: ﴿And eat from it in abundance wherever you wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]. This became like an indication that He forbade them from eating the fruit of that tree. However, the prohibition on that by this statement includes eating and all other uses, and if He had specified eating, it would not have included all of that, so there is additional benefit in it.

* * *

(The eighth issue): They differed concerning what the tree was. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was wheat and the ear of grain. It is also narrated that "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the tree, and he said: It is the blessed tree, the ear of grain." Al-Suddi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud that it was the grapevine, and from Mujahid and Qatadah that it was the fig. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: It was a tree whoever ate from it would have his bodily waste released, and it is not fitting that there be such discharge in Paradise. Know that there is nothing in the apparent wording that indicates a specific identification, so there is no need to explain it either, because the purpose of this statement is not to inform us of the exact identity of that tree. What is not intended in the speech is not obligatory for the Wise One to explain; rather, explaining it might be pointless. For if one of us wished to give another person an excuse for being late and said: "I was busy disciplining my servants because they had misbehaved," this general statement would be better than mentioning the exact identity of this servant, his name, and his description. So no one should think that there was a shortcoming in the explanation here.

Then some said: The closest meaning of the word "tree" (shajarah) is that it includes whatever has a trunk and branches. It was said: There is no need for that, because of His exalted saying: ﴿And We caused a gourd plant to grow over him﴾ [al-Saffat: 146], although it is like crops and watermelon, and its lying flat on the ground did not prevent it from being called a tree. Al-Mubarrad said: I think that everything that has branches and stems is called a tree by the Arabs when it spreads out, and the origin of this is that it is whatever "shajara," meaning it took to the right and left. It is said: I saw so-and-so, the spears had struck him on both sides (shajarathu al-rimah). And He said, exalted is He: ﴿Until they make you judge in what has become disputed among them﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], and two men disputed (tashajara al-rajulan) over such-and-such a matter.

(The ninth issue): They agreed that what is meant by His exalted saying, ﴿And you would be among the wrongdoers﴾, is that if you both eat, then you have wronged yourselves, because eating from the tree is wronging another (i.e., Allah's command), and a person may be a wrongdoer by wronging himself or by wronging others, and the wronging of oneself is more general and greater. Then people differed here into three opinions:

The first: The view of the Hashawiyya, who said: He committed a major sin, so his act was necessarily an act of wrongdoing.

The second: The view of the Mu'tazila, who said: He committed a minor sin. Then, for these there are two views:

One of them: The view of Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, which is that he wronged himself by imposing upon it what is burdensome of repentance and making amends.

The second of them: The view of Abu Hashim, which is that he wronged himself in that he nullified some of his accumulated reward, so that became a deficiency in what he had earned.

The third: The view of those who deny that sin ever proceeds from them (the Prophets) absolutely, and they interpreted this wronging as meaning that he did what it was better for him not to do. An example of this: a person who sought a ministerial post, then abandoned it and occupied himself with weaving, so it is said to him: "O wronger of your own self, why did you do that?" If it is asked: Is it permissible to describe the Prophets (peace be upon them) as wrongdoers, or as wronging themselves? The answer is that it is better not to use that expression, because it gives an impression of blame.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, Verse 36 (Part 1 of 4)**

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip from it, and removed them from that in which they were, and We said: "Go down, some of you enemies to others, and for you on earth is a settlement and provision for a time."﴾

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: The meaning of ﴿Satan caused them to slip from it﴾ is that Satan brought about their slip from it. The word *ʿan* ("from") in this verse is like its use in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾ [al-Kahf: 82].

Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: It is from *al-zallal* (slipping). A person stands firm on something and then slips away from it, becoming displaced from that place. As for the one who reads *fa-azallahumā* (with the verb in the form that means to cause to move), it is from *al-zawāl* (departing from a place). It is related from Abu Muʿadh that he said: It is said, "I removed you from such-and-such until you departed from it," and "I made you slip until you slipped," and both have the same meaning, namely: I turned you away from it.

Some scholars said: *Azallahumā al-shayṭān* means *istazallahumā* (Satan made them slip). It derives from your saying, "He slipped in his religion" when he erred, and "another caused him to slip" when he caused him something by which he slipped in his religion or his worldly affairs.

Know that there are several issues (*masāʾil*) in this verse.

**The first issue:** People have differed concerning the infallibility (*ʿiṣmah*, freedom from sin) of the prophets, peace be upon them. The proper way to state the position on this matter is to say: Disagreement on this topic falls under four categories.

The first: what occurs in the domain of belief (*iʿtiqād*).
The second: what occurs in the domain of conveying the message (*tablīgh*).
The third: what occurs in the domain of rulings and legal opinions (*aḥkām wa-l-fatyā*).
The fourth: what occurs in their actions and conduct (*afʿāl wa-sīrah*).

As for their holding disbelief or misguidance as belief, this is not permitted according to the majority of the community. The Fudayliyyah among the Khawarij said that sins had indeed occurred from them, and that sin, in their view, is disbelief and polytheism; therefore they inevitably said that disbelief had occurred from them. The Imamiyyah permitted that they might display disbelief as a matter of *taqiyyah* (dissimulation).

As for the second category, that which relates to conveying the message: the community has agreed that they are protected from lying and distortion in what they convey, otherwise trust in the transmission would be lost. They agreed that this cannot occur from them deliberately, and likewise it is not permitted by inadvertence (*sahw*). Some people permitted it by inadvertence, saying: because avoiding it is not possible.

As for the third category, that which relates to legal opinions: they agreed that their error in it is not permitted deliberately. As for error by inadvertence, some permitted it and others rejected it.

*Page 8*

As for the fourth category, which is what occurs in their actions, the community differed about it in five positions.

The first: the view of those who permitted major sins (*kabāʾir*) from them deliberately, which is the view of the Hashawiyyah.

The second: the view of those who do not permit major sins from them, but permit minor sins (*ṣaghāʾir*) deliberately, except those that cause repulsion, such as lying and cheating in measure. This is the view of most of the Muʿtazilah.

The third view: that it is not permitted for them to commit a minor or a major sin deliberately at all, but only by way of interpretation (*taʾwīl*). This is the view of al-Jubbaʾi.

The fourth view: that sin does not occur from them except through inadvertence and error, but they are held accountable for what occurs from them in this manner, even though this is lifted from their communities. This is because their knowledge is stronger, their proofs are more numerous, and they are able to guard against what others cannot.

The fifth view: that sin does not occur from them, neither major nor minor, neither deliberately nor by inadvertence, nor by interpretation or error. This is the doctrine of the Rafidah.

People differed about the time of infallibility according to three views.

The first: the view of those who held that they are infallible from the time of their birth. This is the view of the Rafidah.

The second: the view of those who held that the time of their infallibility is the time of their reaching maturity, and they did not permit them to commit disbelief or a major sin before prophethood. This is the view of many of the Muʿtazilah.

The third: the view of those who held that this is not permitted during prophethood, but before prophethood it is permitted. This is the view of most of our companions (the Ashʿarites), and the view of Abu al-Hudhayl and Abu ʿAli among the Muʿtazilah.

The position we choose is that sin has not issued from them at all during prophethood, neither major nor minor. Several arguments support this:

**The first:** If sin had issued from them, they would have been of lower rank than the sinners of the community, and this is not permitted. The reasoning for the necessary connection is that the rank of the prophets is in the utmost grandeur and nobility, and whoever is like this, the sin issuing from him is more heinous. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear indecency, the punishment will be doubled for her, twofold﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]. The married person is stoned, while others are lashed, and the punishment of a slave is half that of a free person. As for the impermissibility of the prophet being in a lesser state than the community, that is agreed upon.

**The second:** If he were to engage in wickedness (*fisq*), it would necessarily follow that his testimony would not be accepted, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If a wicked person comes to you with news, investigate﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6]. But his testimony is accepted; otherwise he would be in a lesser state than the just (*ʿudul*) of the community. And how can we not say this, when there is no meaning to prophethood and messengership except that he bears witness before God that He legislated this ruling and that? Moreover, on the Day of Resurrection he is a witness over all, as in His saying: ﴿That you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

**The third:** If he were to commit a major sin, it would be obligatory to restrain him from it, and therefore harming him would not be forbidden. But harming him is forbidden, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who harm God and His Messenger, God has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57].

**The fourth:** If Muhammad ﷺ had committed disobedience, it would be obligatory for us to follow him in it, because of His saying: ﴿Follow me﴾. This would lead to combining prohibition and obligation, which is impossible. And if this is established regarding Muhammad ﷺ, it is also established regarding all the prophets, since no one makes a distinction.

**The fifth:** We know by the immediate judgment of reason that there is nothing more hideous than a prophet whom God has raised in rank, entrusted with His revelation, and made a successor over His servants and lands, who hears his Lord calling him: "Do not do such-and-such," and then he proceeds to it, preferring his pleasure, paying no heed to his Lord's prohibition, and not restrained by His threat. This is known to be hideous by necessity.

**The sixth:** If disobedience had issued from the prophets, they would deserve punishment, because of His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn: 23]. And they would deserve the curse, because of His saying: ﴿Surely the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 18]. The community has agreed that none of the prophets deserved the curse or punishment. Thus it is established that disobedience did not issue from them.

*Page 9*

**The seventh:** They used to command the people to obey God. If they had not obeyed Him, they would have fallen under His saying: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves, while you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44]. And He said: ﴿I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you﴾ [Hud: 88]. So what does not befit one of the preachers of the community, how can it be attributed to the prophets, peace be upon them?

**The eighth:** His saying: ﴿Indeed, they used to hasten in good works﴾ [al-Anbiya: 90]. The word *al-khayrāt* (good works) is general, encompassing everything, and it includes doing what is fitting and abandoning what is not fitting. Thus it is established that the prophets did every fitting deed and abandoned every unfitting one, and this contradicts the issuing of sin from them.

**The ninth:** His saying: ﴿And indeed, they are with Us among the chosen and the good﴾ [Sad: 47]. This includes all actions and abstentions, as evidenced by the permissibility of exception: one says, "So-and-so is among the chosen and the good, except in such-and-such an act," and exception removes from the statement what would otherwise be included. Thus it is established that they were good in all matters, and this contradicts the issuing of sin from them. And He said: ﴿God chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind﴾ [al-Hajj: 75]; ﴿Indeed God chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran above all peoples﴾ [Al ʿImran: 33]. He said about Abraham: ﴿And We indeed chose him in this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130]. He said about Moses: ﴿I have chosen you above the people by My messages and My speech﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 144]. And He said: ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, possessors of strength and insight﴾, ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: remembrance of the abode﴾, ﴿And indeed, they are with Us among the chosen and the good﴾ [Sad: 45–47]. All these verses indicate that they are described as chosen and good, and this contradicts the issuing of sin from them.

**The tenth:** He, exalted is He, related the words of Iblis: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾, ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [Sad: 82–83]. So he excepted from those he would mislead the sincere ones (*al-mukhlaṣīn*), and they are the prophets, peace be upon them. He said, exalted is He, describing Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: remembrance of the abode﴾ [Sad: 46]. And He said about Joseph: ﴿Indeed, he was among Our sincere servants﴾ [Yusuf: 24]. And when the necessity of infallibility is established for some, it is established for all, since no one makes a distinction.

**The eleventh:** His saying: ﴿And Iblis had indeed proven true his assumption about them, so they followed him, except a group of the believers﴾ [Saba: 20]. Those who did not follow him must be said not to have committed sin, otherwise they would have been followers of him. And if it is established regarding that group that they did not sin, then that group is either the prophets or others. If they are the prophets, then it is established regarding the prophet that he does not sin. If they are other than the prophets, then if it were established that the prophets had sinned, they would be of lower rank with God than that group, and so a non-prophet would be superior to a prophet, and that is false by consensus. Thus it is established that sin did not issue from them.

**The twelfth:** He, exalted is He, divided creation into two groups. He said: ﴿Those are the party of Satan. Indeed, the party of Satan are the losers﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 19], and He said about the other group: ﴿Those are the party of God. Indeed, the party of God are the successful﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22]. There is no doubt that the party of Satan are those who do what Satan approves, and what Satan approves is disobedience. So everyone who disobeys God is of the party of Satan. If disobedience had issued from the Messenger, it would be true of him that he is of the party of Satan, and true of him that he is among the losers, and true of the ascetics of the community that they are of the party of God and among the successful. Then that one person from the community would be far superior with God than that Messenger, and no Muslim would say this.

*Page 10*

**The thirteenth:** The Messenger is superior to the angel, so sin must not issue from the Messenger. We say he is superior because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, God chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran above all peoples﴾ [Al ʿImran: 33]. The way of deriving proof from it has been mentioned in the question of the superiority of the angel over humans. And we say: when it is so, sin must not issue from the Messenger, because He described the angels as abstaining from sin, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ [al-Anbiya: 27], and He said: ﴿They do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. So if disobedience had issued from the Messenger, his being superior to the angel would be impossible, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like corrupters on the earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28].

**The fourteenth:** It is related that "Khuzaymah ibn Thabit bore witness for the Messenger of God ﷺ in support of his claim. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'How did you bear witness for me?' He said: 'O Messenger of God, I affirm you concerning the revelation sent down upon you from above the seven heavens; should I not affirm you in this matter?' So the Messenger of God ﷺ affirmed him and named him Dhu al-Shahadatayn (the one of the two testimonies)." And if disobedience were permissible for the prophets, that testimony would not have been permissible.

**[Page 11]**

Fifteenth: God said concerning Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader (imam) for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. An imam is one who is followed, so He made it obligatory upon all people to follow him. Had sin proceeded from him, it would have been obligatory upon them to follow him in that sin, and that leads to contradiction.

Sixteenth: God, the Exalted, said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. The intended covenant is either the covenant of prophethood or the covenant of leadership (imamah). If the intended covenant is the covenant of prophethood, then prophethood must not be established for wrongdoers. If the intended covenant is the covenant of leadership, then leadership must not be established for wrongdoers. And if leadership is not established for wrongdoers, then prophethood must not be established for wrongdoers either, because every prophet must necessarily be an imam who is followed and emulated.

* * *

The verse, under all these interpretations, indicates that a prophet is not sinful. As for the opponent, he has held fast, in each of the four positions we mentioned, to verses. We will point to their core arguments, and we will refer the thorough treatment to what will come later in this commentary, God willing.

As for the verses they relied upon in the domain of belief ('aqidah), there are three:

The first: They impugned the belief of Adam, peace be upon him, citing His saying: ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul and made from it its mate that he might find tranquility in her﴾ [al-A'raf: 189], to the end of the verse. They said: There is no doubt that the single soul is Adam, and his mate created from him is Eve. So all these pronouns refer to the two of them. Then His saying: ﴿They made for Him partners in what He gave them. Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 190] requires that association (shirk) proceeded from the two of them.

The answer: We do not concede that the single soul is Adam, and there is nothing in the verse that indicates it. Rather, we say: the address is to the Quraysh, who are the family of Qusayy, and the meaning is: He created you from the soul of Qusayy and made from its kind an Arab wife that he might find tranquility in her. Then, when He gave them the righteous offspring they had asked for, they named their four children ʿAbd Manaf, ʿAbd al-ʿUzza, ʿAbd al-Dar, and ʿAbd Qusayy. The pronoun in "they associate" refers to the two of them and to their descendants. This answer is the one relied upon.

Second: They said: Abraham was not knowing of Allah, nor of the Last Day.

As for the first, it is because he said about the stars: ﴿This is my lord﴾ [al-An'am: 77]. As for the second, it is His saying: ﴿Show me how You give life to the dead. He said: Have you not believed? He said: Yes, but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

The answer: As for his saying ﴿This is my lord﴾, it is an interrogative in the manner of denial. As for his saying ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾, the intended meaning is that hearsay is not like direct witnessing.

Third: They held fast to His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who read the Book before you. Certainly the truth has come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾ [Yunus: 94]. The verse, they said, indicates that Muhammad ﷺ was in doubt about what was revealed to him.

The answer: The heart in this worldly abode is never free of thoughts that lead to doubts, but he, peace and blessings be upon him, would remove them through proofs.

As for the verses they held fast to in the domain of conveying (tabligh), there are three:

One of them: His saying: ﴿We will make you recite, so you will not forget, except what Allah wills﴾ [al-A'la: 6–7]. This exception, they said, indicates that forgetting occurred in the revelation.

The answer: The prohibition is not against forgetting in the sense opposite to remembrance, since that is not within one's capacity. Rather it is against forgetting in the sense of abandonment (tark), so we interpret it as abandoning what is better (tark al-awla).

Second: His saying: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish﴾ [al-Hajj: 52]. The discussion of it is mentioned in Surat al-Hajj in detail.

Third: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Knower of the unseen, and He does not reveal His unseen to anyone, except to one whom He has approved of as a messenger. Indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ [al-Jinn: 26–27], ﴿that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾ [al-Jinn: 28]. They said: Were it not for the fear of corruption entering the conveyance of revelation from the side of the prophets, there would be no benefit in sending guards along with them for reinforcement. The answer: Why could it not be that the benefit is that this guarding repels the devils from casting whispers?

As for the verses they held fast to in the matter of legal rulings (fatwa), there are three:

One of them: His saying: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the tilth﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78]. We have discussed it in Surat al-Anbiya'.

Second: His saying concerning the captives of Badr, when the Prophet ﷺ accepted ransom from them: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives until he has inflicted slaughter upon the land﴾ [al-Anfal: 67]. Had he not erred in this judgment, he would not have been rebuked.

Third: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿May Allah pardon you. Why did you give them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43].

The answer concerning all of them: We interpret it as abandoning what is better.

As for the verses they held fast to concerning actions, they are numerous. The first of them is the story of Adam, peace be upon him. They held fast to it in seven aspects:

The first: that he was disobedient, and the disobedient must be one who commits a major sin (kabirah). We said he was disobedient because of God's saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]. And we said that the disobedient is one who commits a major sin for two reasons:

The first: that the text requires that he be punished, because of His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed, for him is the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 23]. There is no meaning for "one who commits a major sin" except that.

The second: that "disobedient" is a term of blame, so it must apply only to one who commits a major sin.

The second aspect in holding fast to the story of Adam: that he was erring (ghawi), because of His saying: ﴿so he erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]. Error (ghayy) is the opposite of right guidance (rushd), because of His saying: ﴿The right course has become clear from error﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256], so He made error the counterpart of rushd.

The third aspect: that he was a penitent (ta'ib), and the penitent is a sinner. We said he was a penitent because of His saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37], and He said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, and accepted his repentance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]. And we said: the penitent is a sinner, because the penitent

**[Page 12]**

is one who regrets committing a sin, and one who regrets committing a sin is informing of his having committed the sin. If he lied in that report, he is a sinner through the lie; and if he was truthful in it, then that is what is sought.

The fourth aspect: that he committed what was forbidden, in His saying: ﴿Did I not forbid you from that tree?﴾ [al-A'raf: 22], and ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ [al-A'raf: 19]. And committing what is forbidden is itself the sin.

The fifth aspect: He called him a wrongdoer (zalim) in His saying: ﴿So you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], and he called himself a wrongdoer in his saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. And the wrongdoer is cursed, because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 18]. And whoever deserves the curse is one who commits a major sin.

The sixth aspect: that he acknowledged that were it not for Allah's forgiveness of him, he would have been among the losers, in His saying: ﴿And if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. This requires that he was one who committed a major sin.

The seventh: that he was expelled from the Garden because of the whispering and misleading of Satan, as a punishment for what he undertook of obeying Satan. This indicates that he was one who committed a major sin.

Then they said: Even if each one of these aspects does not indicate that he committed a major sin, the collection of them is undoubtedly decisive in indicating it. It is possible that each one of these aspects, though it does not indicate the matter, yet the collection of those aspects does indicate it.

The answer that we rely upon concerning the seven aspects is this: Your argument is only complete if you bring proof that this occurred while he was a prophet, and that is disputed. So why is it not permissible to say: Adam, peace be upon him, at the time when this slip proceeded from him, was not yet a prophet, and then after that he became a prophet? We have already shown that there is no proof for this position.

As for the thorough answer to each of the detailed aspects, it will come, God willing, when we discuss the interpretation of each of these verses.

Let us mention here the manner of that slip, so that the intent of God, the Exalted, from His saying ﴿so Satan caused them to slip﴾ may become clear. We say: Let us assume that this act proceeded from Adam, peace be upon him, after prophethood. His undertaking of that act is either while he was forgetful or while he was mindful. As for the first, that he did it forgetfully, this is the view of a group of theologians (mutakallimun), and they argued for it with His saying: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115], and they illustrated it with the fasting person who occupies himself with a matter that absorbs him and overwhelms him, so that he becomes heedless of the fast and eats during that heedlessness, not deliberately.

It is said: This is false for two reasons:

The first: that His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortal﴾ [al-A'raf: 20], and His saying: ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you of the advisers"﴾ [al-A'raf: 21], indicates that he did not forget the prohibition at the time of the act. And it has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbas what indicates that Adam acted deliberately, for he said: When they ate from it, their private parts became apparent to them, and Adam fled, and a tree from the trees of the Garden seized him and held him back. Then Allah, the Exalted, called out to him: "Are you fleeing from Me?" He said: "No, but out of shame before You." He said to him: "Was there not, among what I granted you of the Garden, ample provision apart from what I forbade you?" He said: "Yes, my Lord, but by Your might, I did not think that anyone would swear by You falsely." He said: "By My might, I will surely cause you to descend from it, and then you will not attain life except with hardship."

The second: that if he had been forgetful, he would not have been rebuked for that act. As for the rational side, it is because the forgetful one is not capable of the act, so he is not obligated to it, because of His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. As for the transmitted side, it is because of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The pen has been lifted from three [categories]..." So when he was rebuked for it, this indicates that it was not in the manner of

**[Page 13]**

Part of the commentary, the answer to the first objection: We say that as for the reply to the first, it is that we do not concede that Adam and Eve accepted that statement from Iblis, nor did they believe him in it. For if they had believed him, their disobedience in this belief would have been greater than eating from the tree, because when Iblis said to them: ﴿"Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree, lest you become angels or become of the eternal"﴾ [al-A'raf: 20], he had cast into them evil suspicion about God and invited them to abandon submission to His command and contentment with His judgment, and to believe in Him that Iblis was a sincere advisor to them and that the Lord, exalted is He, had deceived them. There is no doubt that these matters are greater than eating from the tree, so the reproach for that would have been more severe. Also, Adam, peace be upon him, knew of Iblis's refusal to prostrate, of his being hateful toward him, and of his envy of what God had bestowed upon him of blessings. How, then, is it permissible for a rational person to accept the word of his enemy given these indications? The verse does not state that they committed that act at the time of that speech or after it, and it indicates that Adam knew of his enmity, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not expel you from the Garden, lest you suffer"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117]. As for what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, it is a report transmitted through individual narrators (ahad), so how could it contradict the Qur'an?

As for the reply to the second: the reproach arose only from not guarding against the causes of forgetfulness. This type of lapse (sahw) is lifted from the Muslims, although it was possible for them to be held accountable for it, and it is not lifted from the prophets because of the greatness of their station. He illustrated this by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any of the women"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32], then He said: ﴿"Whoever of you commits a clear immorality, the punishment will be doubled for her, double"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]. The Prophet, peace be upon him, also said: "The people most severely tested are the prophets, then the righteous, then the next best, and then the next best." He also said: "Indeed I am feverish as two men of you are feverish." If it is said: how is it permissible that the greatness of their condition and the loftiness of their rank should affect the fulfilment of a condition in their obligations, but not the obligations of others? We say: Have you not heard, "The good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of the near ones (muqarrabun)"? The Prophet, peace be upon him, had stricter obligations than others. This, then, is the explanation that this occurred from Adam, peace be upon him, by way of inadvertence and forgetfulness.

I have seen in some tafsir books that Eve gave him wine until he became intoxicated, and then in the midst of his intoxication he did that. They said: this is not far-fetched, for he, peace be upon him, was permitted to take all things except that tree. So if we interpret the tree as wheat, he would have been permitted to take wine. One may say: the wine of Paradise does not intoxicate, as He, exalted is He, said describing the wine of Paradise: ﴿"Neither in it is any intoxication"﴾ [al-Saffat: 47].

As for the second view, that he, peace be upon him, did it deliberately, there are four opinions here:

The first opinion: that the prohibition was a prohibition of disapproval (tanzih), not a prohibition of unlawfulness (tahrim), and the discussion of this view and its rationale has already preceded.

The second opinion: that it was deliberate on Adam's part, and that this was a major sin (kabirah), even though Adam, peace be upon him, was a prophet at that time. I have already explained the corruption of this view.

The third opinion: that he, peace be upon him, did it deliberately, but with him was such trepidation, fear and apprehension that it placed it in the category of a minor sin (saghirah). This view is also invalid by the evidences previously mentioned, because one who deliberately abandons an obligation or commits a forbidden act, even if he does it with fear, is nonetheless a disobedient person deserving of curse, blame, and eternal abiding in the Fire, and it is not valid to describe the prophets, peace be upon them, with that. Moreover, He, exalted is He, described him with forgetfulness in His saying: ﴿"So he forgot, and We did not find in him determination"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115], and that contradicts deliberateness.

The fourth opinion, which is the choice of most of the Mu'tazilah: that he, peace be upon him, undertook the eating on the basis of an ijtihad (independent reasoning) in which he erred, and this does not necessitate that the sin be a major sin. The explanation of the erroneous ijtihad is that when it was said to him: ﴿"And do not approach this tree"﴾, the word ﴿"this"﴾ may refer to an individual, and it may refer to a kind. It is related that he, peace be upon him, took silk and gold in his hand and said: "These two are lawful for the females of my community and forbidden for their males," and he intended by it their kind. It is also related that he, peace be upon him, performed ablution once and said: "This is ablution, with which God does not accept prayer except by it," and he intended its kind. So when Adam, peace be upon him, heard His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And do not approach this tree"﴾, he thought the prohibition applied only to that specific tree, so he left it and took from another tree of that kind. However, he was mistaken in that ijtihad, because the intention of God, exalted is He, by the word ﴿"this"﴾ was the kind and not the individual. And ijtihad in the branches, if it is erroneous, does not necessitate deserving punishment or curse, since it may be a minor sin that is forgiven, as in our law. If it is said: there are several objections to this opinion:

One: the word "this" (hadha) in the original language is for pointing at a present thing, and a present thing is only a specific thing, so the word "hadha" in its original usage points to a specific thing. As for its being intended to point to a kind, that is contrary to the original usage. Also, because pointing is impossible with respect to Him, exalted is He, it is necessary that He commanded some of the angels to point at that individual, so whatever else is outside the prohibition, necessarily. Once this is established, we say: the mujtahid is obligated to take the word in its literal meaning, so Adam, peace be upon him, when he took the word "this" as referring to the specific one, had done what was obligatory, and it was not permissible for him to take it as referring to the kind. Know that this objection is reinforced by two other matters:

The first: His saying: ﴿"And eat from it freely wherever you wish"﴾ conveyed permission to take anything in the Garden except what the evidence specified.

The second: reason requires the permissibility of benefiting from all benefits except what the evidence specified, and the specifying evidence indicated only that specific one. Thus it is established that Adam, peace be upon him, was permitted to benefit from all the other trees, and once this is established, it is impossible that he deserved reproach because of this, or that he be judged as having erred. Thus it is established that interpreting the narrative in this way necessitates judging him to have been correct rather than mistaken, and if that is so, the corruption of this interpretation is established.

The second objection to this interpretation: Grant that the word "hadha" is ambiguous between the individual and the kind, but did God join to this word anything that indicates that the intended meaning is the kind and not the individual, or did He not do so? If the first, then either it is said that Adam, peace be upon him, was negligent in understanding that clarification, and then he committed the sin; or, if he was not negligent in understanding it but knew it, then he knew at that point that the intended meaning was the kind, and his proceeding to eat from a tree of that kind would be a deliberate sin.

The third objection: prophets, peace be upon them, may not undertake ijtihad, because ijtihad is proceeding to act on the basis of conjecture, and this is permissible only for one who cannot attain knowledge. As for the prophets, they are able to attain certainty, so it is necessary that ijtihad not be permissible for them, because relying on conjecture while able to attain certainty is impermissible both by reason and by law. Once this is established, it is established that proceeding to ijtihad is disobedience.

The fourth objection: this question is either among the definitive matters or among the speculative matters. If it is among the definitive matters, the error in it would be great, and then the difficulty returns. If it is among the speculative matters, then if we say that every mujtahid is correct, no error is realized in it at all; and if we say that the correct one in it is one and the incorrect one is excused by consensus, then how did this degree of error become a cause for Adam, peace be upon him, being stripped of his garment, expelled from the Garden, and sent down to the earth?

The answer to the first: that the word "this," although in origin it points to an individual, may be used to point to a kind, as its explanation has preceded, and that God, glory be to Him and exalted is He, had joined to it what indicates that the intended meaning is the kind.

The answer to the second: Adam, peace be upon him, perhaps was negligent in knowing that indication, because he thought that it did not bind him at the present time; or it may be said: he knew that indication at the time when God forbade him the very tree, but when the period lengthened, he became heedless of it, because the report says that Adam, peace be upon him, remained in the Garden for a long time before he was brought out.

The answer to the third: there is no need here to establish that the prophets, peace be upon them, relied on ijtihad, for we have shown that he, peace be upon him, was negligent in knowing that indication, or that he had known it but had forgotten it, and that is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"So he forgot, and We did not find in him determination"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115].

The answer to the fourth: it may be said that the indication was definitive, but when he, peace be upon him, forgot it, forgetfulness became an excuse so that the sin would not become a major one; or it may be said that it was speculative, but there followed from it stricter consequences than follow from the error of other mujtahids, because that may differ according to the persons involved, and just as the Messenger, peace be upon him, was singled out in many matters in the domain of stricter and lighter rulings that are not established for his community, so too here.

Know that it may be said regarding this question another point, namely that when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿"And do not approach this tree"﴾ and forbade them both together, Adam, peace be upon him, thought that each of them individually was permitted to approach the tree and to take from it, because His saying ﴿"and do not approach"﴾ is a prohibition addressed to them in the plural, and the occurrence of the prohibition when they are together does not necessitate its occurrence when they are alone. Perhaps the error in this ijtihad occurred from this aspect. This is the sum of what is said in this chapter, and God knows best.

* * *

The second issue: they differed over how Iblis was able to whisper to Adam, peace be upon him, when Iblis was outside the Garden and Adam was inside the Garden, and they mentioned for this several views:

The first: the statement of the storytellers (qussas), which they related from Wahb ibn Munabbih al-Yamani and al-Suddi, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, and others: that when Iblis wished to enter the Garden, the guardians (khazanah) prevented him, so he came to the serpent, which was a creature with four legs like a Bactrian camel, and it was the most beautiful of animals, after he had presented himself to all the other animals and none of them accepted him. The serpent swallowed him and brought him into the Garden secretly from the guardians. When the serpent entered the Garden, Iblis came out of its mouth and busied himself with whispering. Therefore the serpent was cursed, its legs fell off, it began to walk on its belly, its provision was placed in the dust, and it became an enemy to the children of Adam. Know that this and similar accounts are things that must not be paid attention to, because if Iblis was able to enter the mouth of the serpent, why was he not able to make himself a serpent and then enter the Garden? And because when he did that with the serpent, why was the serpent punished, although it is neither rational nor accountable?

The second: that Iblis entered the Garden in the form of an animal. This view is less corrupt than the first.

The third: some of the scholars of the principles (usul) said: perhaps Adam and Eve, peace be upon them both, used to go out to the gate of the Garden, and Iblis was near the gate, whispering to them.

Fourthly: this is the view of al-Hasan that Iblis was on the earth and conveyed the whispering (waswasa) to the two of them in the Garden. Some scholars said: this is far-fetched, because whispering is a hidden speech, and hidden speech cannot be conveyed from the earth to the heavens. They also disagreed on another point: did Iblis address them directly, or is it said that he conveyed the whispering to them through some of his followers?

The argument of the first view is God's words: ﴿And he swore to them, "I am surely to you one of the sincere advisers"﴾ [al-A'raf: 21], which requires direct address, and likewise His words: ﴿So he brought them down by deception﴾ [al-A'raf: 22].

The argument of the second view is that Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, knew him and knew the envy and enmity he harboured, so it would be unthinkable in the normal course of things that they would accept his words or pay attention to him. Therefore the one who directly performed the whispering must have been one of Iblis's followers.

Two questions remain:

First question: God attributed this slipping to Iblis, so why did He rebuke them for that act? We say: the meaning of His words ﴿so he caused them to slip﴾ is that they, at his whispering, performed that act, and so it was attributed to Iblis, just as in His words ﴿but my call only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh: 6]. And God, quoting Iblis, said: ﴿And I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. This is what the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said. The correct explanation of this attribution, which we have established repeatedly, is that a human being is able to do or to abstain, and where the two options are equal, it is impossible for him to become the source of either of them except when a motive (da'i) is joined to it. In the case of a servant, a motive means knowledge, or assumption, or belief that the act contains some benefit. When that knowledge or assumption arises through a reminder that prompted it, the act is attributed to that which brought about the agent's readiness to act. For this reason, the act is here attributed to the whispering. How well one of the knowers (al-'arifin) said: even if Adam's slip was due to the whispering of Iblis, then Iblis's disobedience came about by a whispering from us. This shows you that if the motive does not arise, the act does not arise, and that motives, although some follow others, must ultimately terminate in what God creates initially. This is what Moses, peace be upon him, stated in His words: ﴿It is none but Your trial; You send astray thereby whom You will and You guide whom You will﴾ [al-A'raf: 155].

Second question: what was that whispering like? The answer: it is the one God related in His words: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortals﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]. They did not accept this from him. When he despaired of that, he turned to swearing an oath, as He said: ﴿And he swore to them, "I am surely to you one of the sincere advisers"﴾ [al-A'raf: 21]. They did not believe him either. The apparent view is that after that he turned to something else: he occupied them with enjoying permissible pleasures until they became absorbed in them, and through this absorption they forgot the prohibition. At that point what happened, happened. God knows best the realities of matters, however they were.

As for His words ﴿And We said: "Go down"﴾, there are several issues:
