Second question: The person who is given good tidings of in these books either had his time of emergence and place of emergence and all the related details mentioned in these books, or none of that was mentioned. If that text was a clear text, transmitted in books to the people of knowledge through mass transmission (tawatur), then it would be impossible for them to conceal it, and it would have to be known necessarily from the religion of the earlier prophets. If the second case holds, then that text does not indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they could say that this promised one will come after that, as is the view of the majority of the Jews.

The answer: those who understood His words: ﴿And fulfill My covenant; I will fulfill your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:40] as an command to reflect on the evidences indicating divine oneness (tawhid) and prophethood, as we explained in the first opinion, adopted it only because of the strength of this question. As for one who wishes to support the second opinion, he answers it by saying that the specification of the time and place was not stated in a clear text that everyone would know; rather, it was stated in a hidden text. Therefore, it did not necessarily follow that it would be known necessarily from the religion of the earlier prophets, peace be upon them.

Let us now mention some of what came in the books of the earlier prophets concerning the good tidings of the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ):

The first: It is stated in the ninth chapter of the first book of the Torah that when Hagar was angry at Sarah, an angel appeared to her from [before] God and said to her: "O Hagar, where are you going, and where have you come from?" She said: "I am fleeing from my mistress Sarah." He said to her: "Return to your mistress and submit to her, for God will multiply your offspring and you will conceive and bear a son whom you will name Isma'il, because God has heard your devotion and humility. He will be the eye of the people, his hand will be above all, and all hands will be extended to him in submission, and he will be thankful in spite of all his brothers."

Know that the argument from this text is that this statement came in the form of good tidings. It is not permissible for an angel to bring good tidings from God of injustice and tyranny, or of a matter that could only be accomplished through lying about God, the Exalted. It is known that Isma'il and his offspring did not control everything, meaning most of the world and most of the nations, nor did they mix with all of them by way of domination, except through Islam. Before Islam they were confined to the desert and did not dare to enter the outskirts of Iraq and the outskirts of Syria except in the greatest fear. When Islam came, they gained dominion over East and West through Islam, mingled with the nations, and trod their lands. The nations also mingled with them, made pilgrimage to their House, and entered their deserts because of their proximity to the Ka'bah. So if the Prophet (ﷺ) had not been truthful, this mixing of theirs with the nations and of the nations with them would have been disobedience to God and a departure from His obedience into the obedience of Satan, and God, the Exalted, is far above giving good tidings of something of this nature.

The second: It is stated in the eleventh chapter of the fifth book: "Indeed, the Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you and from your brothers." In this chapter, the Lord, the Exalted, said to Moses: "I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and whoever does not hear My words that he conveys from Me in My name, I will take vengeance upon him." This statement indicates that the prophet whom God raises up is not from the Children of Israel, just as one who said to the Banu Hashim: "There will be an imam from among your brothers," would understand that he would not be from the Banu Hashim. Furthermore, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, is Israel, and he had no brother except Esau, and none of Esau's descendants were prophets except Job, who lived before Moses, peace be upon him. So it is not permissible for Moses, peace be upon him, to be the one given good tidings of. As for Isma'il, he was the brother of Isaac, the father of Ya'qub. Furthermore, every prophet sent after Moses was from the Children of Israel, so the Prophet, peace be upon him, was not from them, but was from their brothers, since he was from the descendants of Isma'il, who was the brother of Isaac, peace be upon them.

If it is said: his words "from among you" prevent the meaning from being Muhammad (ﷺ), because he did not arise from among the Children of Israel. We say: rather, he did arise from among them, because he, peace be upon him, appeared in the Hijaz, was sent as a prophet in Makkah, emigrated to Madinah, and his affair was completed there. Around Madinah were the lands of the Jews, such as Khaybar, Banu Qaynuqa', al-Nadir, and others. Also, the Hijaz is close to Syria, and the majority of the Jews were in Syria at that time. So when Muhammad arose in the Hijaz, he arose from among them. Also, since he was from their brothers, he arose from among them, for he was not far from them.

The third: It is stated in the twentieth chapter of this book: "Indeed, the Lord, the Exalted, came at Mount Sinai, rose up for us from Seir, appeared from the mountains of Paran, and arranged on His right hand the host of the holy ones. He gave them honor and made them beloved to the peoples, and He invoked blessing upon all His holy ones." The basis of the argument: the mountain of Paran is in the Hijaz, because in the Torah it is stated that Isma'il learned archery in the wilderness of Paran, and it is known that he settled only in Makkah. Having established this, we say: His words "He gave them honor" cannot mean Isma'il, peace be upon him, because no honor came about after Isma'il settled there, nor did the holy ones gather there. Therefore it must be applied to Muhammad, peace be upon him.

The Jews said: the meaning is that when the fire appeared from Mount Sinai, fire also appeared from Seir and from Mount Paran, and it spread in these places. We say: this is not valid, because if God created fire in a place, it is not said that God came from it when that event is not followed by a revelation descending in that place or a punishment or the like. According to you, no revelation or speech followed the appearance of the fire except from Mount Sinai. So it should have been said only: "He appeared from Seir and from Mount Paran," and it is not permissible to say otherwise, just as one does not say "God came from the cloud" when fire and burning appear in the cloud, as happens in the days of spring. Also, the Book of Habakkuk clarifies what we have said, which reads: "God came from Mount Sinai, and the Holy One from the mountain of Paran. The heavens were uncovered by the splendor of Muhammad, and the earth was filled with his praise. The ray of his appearance will be like light, guarding his land by his might. Deaths march before him, and birds of prey accompany his soldiers. He arose, measured the earth, considered the nations and searched them out, so the ancient mountains were shattered, the hills and the eternal ones were made low, and the curtains of the people of Midian were shaken. You rode upon horses and mounted chariots of submission and aid. You will draw your bows to the full, and your arrows will be drunk by your command, O Muhammad, to the full, and the earth will flow with rivers. The mountains saw you and were terrified, the torrent of rain turned away from you, the camels fled in dismay and terror, they raised their hands in trembling and fear, the sun and moon stood still in their courses, and the armies marched in the lightning of your arrows and the gleam of your eloquence, trampling the earth in anger and crushing the nations with rebuke, because you appeared for the deliverance of your people and the rescue of the land of your fathers." Thus it was transmitted from Ibn Razin al-Tabari.

As for the Christians, Abu al-Husayn, may God have mercy on him, said in the book al-Gharar: "I have seen in their transmissions: 'And He appeared from the mountains of Paran. The heavens were rent by the splendor of the praised Muhammad, and the arrows drink by your praised command, because you appeared for the deliverance of [Page 36] your people and the rescue of your Messiah.'" From what we have mentioned, it becomes clear that His words in the Torah, "The Lord appeared from the mountains of Paran," do not mean the appearance of fire from Him, but mean the appearance of a person described by these attributes, and that is none other than our Messenger, Muhammad (ﷺ). If they say: the meaning is the coming of God, the Exalted, and that is why at the end of the statement it says "and the rescue of your Messiah," we say: it is not permissible to describe God, the Exalted, as riding horses, or as having a ray of appearance like light, or as having passed the ancient sanctuaries. As for the words "and the rescue of your Messiah," Muhammad, peace be upon him, rescued the Messiah from the lies of the Jews and the Christians.

[Page 37]

The fourth: what came in the book of Isaiah, in its twenty-second chapter: "Arise, shine your lamp" (he means Mecca), "for your time has drawn near, and the honor of God, exalted is He, has risen over you. Darkness has covered the earth, and fog has overspread the nations. The Lord shines upon you with a shining, and manifests His honor upon you. The nations will walk toward your light, and the kings toward the brightness of your rising. Lift up your eyes to what is around you and consider, for they are gathered before you. They will make pilgrimage to you, and your son will come to you from a distant land, because you are the mother of the cities. The children of all the lands will be as if they were the children of Mecca. Your garments will be adorned upon the couches and the beds. When you see this, you will rejoice and be glad, because the treasures of the sea will incline toward you, the armies of the nations will make pilgrimage to you, the rams of Midian will be driven to you, the people of Sheba will come to you and will speak of the blessings of God and glorify Him, the flocks of Faran will travel to you, and what pleases Me will be offered upon My altar. Then I will bring forth praise for the House of My praise." The argument from this is that all these attributes are present in Mecca: the armies of the nations have made pilgrimage to it, and the treasures of the sea have inclined toward it. His words "I will bring forth praise for the House of My praise" mean that the Arabs, before Islam, used to recite the talbiyah, saying: "Here I am, O God, You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You; You possess him and what he possesses." Then in Islam it became: "Here I am, O God, here I am; You have no partner, here I am." This is the praise that God renewed for the House of His praise. If it is said that what is meant is the Temple of Jerusalem and that this will happen later, we say: it is not permissible for a wise one to say "your time has drawn near" when it has not drawn near, but rather what has drawn near is a matter that does not accord with His good pleasure, and yet He does not warn against it. Furthermore, the book of Isaiah is full of mention of the desert and its description, and that refutes their claim.

The fifth: al-Sammān related in his tafsir, in the first book of the Torah, that God, exalted is He, revealed to Abraham, peace be upon him, saying: "I have answered your supplication concerning Ishmael, and I have blessed him, and I have made him great, exceedingly, exceedingly. He will beget twelve great ones, and I will make him into a great nation." The argument from this is that among the descendants of Ishmael there was no one who was for a great nation other than our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). As for the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him, and Ishmael, it was for our Messenger, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, when they finished building the Ka'bah. It is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, and teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. For this reason he (ﷺ) used to say: "I am the supplication of my father Abraham and the glad tidings of Jesus." And this is His saying: ﴿and a bringer of good tidings of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6]. For it is derived from praise (hamd), and the name derived from praise belongs to none but our Prophet, for his names are Muhammad, Ahmad, and Mahmud. It has been said that his description in the Torah is that his birth is in Mecca, his dwelling in Taybah, his dominion in Syria, and his community are the praisers (al-hammadun).

The sixth: the Messiah said to the disciples: "I am going, and there will come to you the Farqalit, the Spirit of Truth, who does not speak from himself, but says only what is said to him." Confirmation of this is His saying: ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9], and His saying: ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord; I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ [Yunus: 15]. As for "Farqalit" (Paraclete), there are two interpretations in its explanation:

The first: that it is the intercessor who is granted intercession, and this is also his attribute, peace be upon him.

The second: some Christians said: the Farqalit is the one who distinguishes between truth and falsehood. Originally it was "faruq," just as "rawuq" is said of that by which something is strained. As for "lit," it is the verification of the matter, just as one says "shaybun ashyab, dhu shaybin" (a gray-haired man with gray hair). This too is an attribute of our law, because it is the one who distinguishes between truth and falsehood.

The seventh: Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar, when he asked him about the dream that he had seen without having related it to him: "You saw, O king, a fearsome sight: its head was of pure gold, its arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, its shins of iron, and some of it of clay. And you saw a stone, which was cut without a cutter, and it struck the foot of that idol and crushed it severely, so the whole idol was pulverized: its iron, its bronze, its silver, and its gold, and they became dust, and the winds scattered them, and no trace of them was found. And that stone that struck that foot of that idol became a high mountain that filled the earth. This is your dream, O king. As for its interpretation: you are the head that you saw of gold. After you there will arise another kingdom inferior to you. The third kingdom, which resembles bronze, will spread over all the earth. The fourth kingdom will have strength like iron. As for the feet, some of which were of clay, some of the kingdom will be strong and some of it weak, and the word of kingship will be divided. In those days the God of heaven will establish a kingdom that is everlasting, which will not change nor pass away, and it will remove all kingdoms, and its authority will nullify all rulers, and it will endure to the eternal age. This is the interpretation of the stone that you saw being cut from a mountain without a cutter, until it crushed the iron, the bronze, and the clay. And God knows best what will be at the end of time." These are the glad tidings found in the earlier books concerning the sending of our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ).

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fulfill My covenant﴾. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that holds God is bound by rational necessities such as rewarding the obedient) said: that covenant is what reason indicates, namely that God, exalted is He, is obligated to bestow reward upon the obedient. The attribution of that obligation to a covenant is valid, because it is such that fulfilling it is obligatory, so that is more binding than a covenant established by vows and oaths. Our companions (the Ash'aris, followers of Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari) said: nothing is obligatory for the servant upon God, and this verse contains what indicates that. For when He, exalted is He, mentioned the blessings first and then ordered the fulfillment of the covenant upon them, it indicates that those past blessings necessitate the covenant of servanthood. If that is so, then performing the acts of worship is fulfilling what became obligatory because of the past blessings, and the performance of an obligation does not become a cause of another obligation. Thus it is established that the performance of obligations does not necessitate reward, and the Mu'tazilite claim is refuted. Rather, the true interpretation is in two respects:

The first: when He, exalted is He, promised reward, and whatever He promised is impossible not to occur, for if it did not occur, His true report would become false, and falsehood regarding Him is impossible, and what leads to the impossible is impossible. So it is necessarily to occur, and that is more binding than what is established by oath and vow.

The second: it may be said that "covenant" means command, and the servant may be commanded, but God, exalted is He, cannot be commanded. Rather, He, glorified and exalted, proceeds in that according to conformity of wording, as in His saying: ﴿They deceive God, but He is their Deceiver﴾ [al-Nisa: 142], and ﴿They schemed, and God schemed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54]. As for His saying: ﴿And fear Me alone﴾, know that fear (rahbah) is dread. The speakers of kalam (theological discourse) said: fear of Him, exalted is He, is fear of His punishment. And it may be said of the responsible person that he is fearful in two ways:

The first: with knowledge, and the second: with supposition. As for knowledge: when one is certain that he has done all that he was commanded and has refrained from all that he was forbidden, then his fear is only concerning the future. On this basis we describe the angels and the prophets, peace be upon them, as fearful and dreading. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They fear their Lord from above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 50]. As for supposition: when he is not certain that he has performed the commanded acts and refrained from the forbidden ones, then he fears that he may not be among the people of reward. Know that whoever's fear in this world is greater, his security on the Day of Resurrection will be greater, and vice versa. It has been narrated: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: By My might and My majesty, I do not combine for My servant two fears or two securities. Whoever felt secure from Me in the world, I will make him fearful on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever feared Me in the world, I will make him secure on the Day of Resurrection." The Gnostics (al-'arifun, mystics) said: fear is of two kinds: fear of punishment and fear of majesty (jalal). The first is the portion of the people of the outward, and the second is the portion of the people of the heart. The first passes away, and the second does not pass away. Know that in the verse there is an indication that the abundance of blessings magnifies disobedience, and an indication that the covenant magnifies opposition, and an indication that the Messenger, just as he was sent to the Arabs, was also sent to the Children of Israel.

His saying: ﴿And fear Me alone﴾ indicates that a person must not fear anyone except God, exalted is He. And just as this is required regarding fear, so too regarding hope and aspiration. This indicates that everything is by the decree and destiny of God, for if the servant were independent in action, it would be necessary to fear him as one fears God, exalted is He, and then the restriction indicated by His saying ﴿And fear Me alone﴾ would be nullified. Rather, he would have to fear only himself, because the keys of reward and punishment are in his hand and not in the hand of God, exalted is He. So he would have to fear only himself and never fear God at all. And in it there is an indication that the responsible person must perform the acts of obedience out of fear and hope, and that this is indispensable for their validity. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it, and do not exchange My signs for a small price, and fear Me alone, so be mindful of Me﴾.

Know that those addressed by His saying ﴿And believe﴾ are the Children of Israel, and two aspects indicate this:

The first: it is coordinated with His saying ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾, as if it were said: Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, fulfil My covenant, and believe in what I have sent down.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿confirming what is with you﴾ indicates this.

As for His saying ﴿what I have sent down﴾, there are two opinions, the stronger being that it is the Qur'an, and on this there are two proofs:

One of them: He described it as being sent down, and that is the Qur'an, for He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth, confirming what is before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3].

The second: describing it as confirming what is with them of the books, and that is the Qur'an. Qatadah said: the intended meaning of ﴿And believe in what I have sent down﴾ is a book and a messenger that you find written in the Torah and the Gospel.

As for His saying ﴿confirming what is with you﴾, there are two explanations:

One of them: that in the Qur'an it is affirmed that Moses and Jesus are true, that the Torah and the Gospel are true, that the Torah was sent down to Moses and the Gospel to Jesus, peace be upon them both. So belief in the Qur'an confirms belief in the Torah and the Gospel. It is as if it were said to them: If you want to affirm belief in the Torah and the Gospel to the fullest, then believe in the Qur'an, for belief in it confirms belief in the Torah and the Gospel.

The second: that the good tidings of Muhammad ﷺ and of the Qur'an occur in the Torah and the Gospel, so belief in Muhammad and in the Qur'an is as if it were confirmation of the Torah and the Gospel, and denial of Muhammad and the Qur'an is denial of the Torah and the Gospel.

Page 39

and this explanation is preferable, because on the first explanation belief in Muhammad, peace be upon him, is not necessarily required, for merely by his being one who reports that the Torah and the Gospel are true, belief in his prophethood is not made obligatory. But on the second explanation belief in him is required, because if the Torah and the Gospel contain the affirmation that Muhammad ﷺ is truthful, then belief in the Torah and the Gospel necessarily entails belief that Muhammad is truthful. It is known that God, exalted is He, only mentioned this statement so that it would be a proof against them regarding the obligation to believe in Muhammad ﷺ, so it is established that this explanation is preferable.

Know that this second explanation indicates the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ in two respects:

The first: that the testimony of the books of the prophets, peace be upon them, cannot be anything but true.

The second: that he, peace be upon him, reported about their books, and he had no knowledge of that except through revelation.

As for His saying ﴿and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾, its meaning is: the first who disbelieved in it, or the first group or company disbelieving in it, or: let not each one of you be the first disbeliever in it. Then there are two questions:

The first question: how were they made the first to disbelieve in it, when the idolaters of the Arabs had preceded them in disbelief in it? The answer is from several aspects:

One of them: that this is a description that they ought to have been the first to believe in it, because of their knowledge of it and its attributes; and because they were the ones who gave good tidings of the time of Muhammad ﷺ and sought victory through him over those who disbelieved, so when he was sent, their situation became the reverse; this is by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89].

The second: it is permissible that it be meant: do not be like the first disbeliever in it, that is, those among the people of Makkah who associated partners with God; that is, do not be—while you know him mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel—like one who does not know him and is a polytheist without a book.

The third: do not be the first disbeliever in it from among the People of the Book, for these were the first among the Children of Israel to disbelieve in the Qur'an, even though the Quraysh had disbelieved in it before that.

The fourth: do not be the first disbeliever in it, that is, in your book; He says this to their scholars: that is, do not be the first of your nation to do the same with your book, for your denial of Muhammad ﷺ necessitates your denial of your book.

The fifth: that what is meant by it is clarifying the gravity of their disbelief; for when they witnessed the miracles indicating his truthfulness, they recognised the good tidings in the Torah and the Gospel of his coming, so their disbelief was more severe than the disbelief of one who knew only one kind of proof; and the one who is first to disbelieve is greater in sin than the one who comes after him, by His saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever establishes a bad practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it." So when their disbelief was great and the disbelief of him who was first in disbelief was great, they shared in this respect, and so it is correct to apply the name of one of them to the other by way of metaphor.

The sixth: the meaning is: do not be the first to deny while knowing; for the disbelief of Quraysh was with ignorance, not with knowledge.

The seventh: the first disbeliever in it from among the Jews; for when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah, Qurayzah and al-Nadir were there, and they disbelieved in him, then the rest of the Jews followed them in that disbelief; so it is as if it were said: the first of the People of the Book to disbelieve in it. It is like His saying: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 47], meaning over the worlds of their time.

The eighth: do not be the first disbeliever in it upon hearing its mention; rather, be steadfast regarding it and reflect upon your minds concerning it.

The ninth: that the word "first" is superfluous, and the meaning is: do not be disbelievers in it; but this is weak.

The second question: it would have been permissible for them to disbelieve if they were not the first. The answer is from several aspects:

One of them: that there is no indication in mentioning that particular thing that what is other than it is different.

The second: that in His saying ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾ there is an indication that their disbelief, whether first or last, is forbidden.

The third: that His saying ﴿He raised the heavens without pillars that you see﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2] does not indicate the existence of pillars that they do not see; and His saying ﴿and their killing of the prophets without right﴾ [al-Nisa': 155] does not indicate that the killing of prophets occurred with right.

And His saying, after this verse: ﴿and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ does not indicate the permissibility of that for a large price; likewise here. Rather, the purpose of this context is to magnify the occurrence of denial and rejection by one who has read in the books the description and attributes of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Page 40

The fourth: al-Mubarrad said: this speech is addressed to a people who were addressed before others, and it was said to them: Do not disbelieve in Muhammad, for after you there will be disbelievers, so do not be you the first of the disbelievers; for this being first necessitates greater sin, because if they precede others into disbelief, then either others will follow them in that disbelief or they will not. If others follow them in that disbelief, they will bear the burden of that disbelief and the burden of everyone who disbelieves until the Day of Resurrection; and if others do not follow them, two matters gather upon them:

One of them: precedence in disbelief.

The second: being alone in it; and there is no doubt that this is a great defect. So His saying ﴿do not be the first disbeliever in it﴾ is an indication of this meaning.

As for His saying ﴿and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾, we have explained in His saying ﴿those are the ones who bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] that "bought" is used in place of "exchanged," and likewise "price" is used in place of "substitute" and "equivalent" for a thing; so when some worldly thing is chosen over God's reward, that thing has been made a price in the eyes of its doer. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: The chiefs of the Jews, such as Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab and their likes, used to take gifts from the poor Jews, and they knew that if they followed Muhammad those gifts would cease for them, so they persisted in disbelief lest that meagre amount be cut off from them; this is because the whole world in relation to religion is very small, so its relation to it is the relation of the finite to the infinite; then those gifts were at the utmost smallness in relation to the world, so what ratio does the very small of the very small have to the abundance that is without end?

Know that this prohibition is valid whether or not there were among them those who did that; indeed, even if it were established that their scholars used to take bribes for concealing the matter of the Messenger ﷺ and distorting what indicates it in the Torah, the speech would be clearer. As for His saying ﴿and fear Me alone, so be mindful of Me﴾, its meaning is close to what preceded from His saying ﴿and fear Me alone, so be in awe of Me﴾; and the difference is that awe is an expression for fear, whereas taqwa (mindfulness) is only needed when there is certainty of the occurrence of what is to be guarded against. So it is as if He, may He be exalted, commanded them to have awe because the possibility of punishment exists, then commanded them to have taqwa because the certainty of punishment is established.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know [it]﴾

Know that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And believe in what I have sent down﴾ is a command to abandon disbelief and misguidance, and His saying ﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood﴾ is a command to abandon incitement (al-ighra') and leading astray (al-idlal). Know that leading another person astray cannot occur except by two means. That is because, if that other person has heard the proofs of the truth, then leading him astray is not possible except by confusing those proofs for him; and if he has not heard them, then leading him astray is only possible by concealing those proofs from him and preventing him from reaching them. So His saying ﴿do not mix up the truth with falsehood﴾ is a reference to the first category, which is confusing the proofs for him, and His saying ﴿nor conceal the truth﴾ is a reference to the second category, which is preventing him from reaching the proofs.

Know that the most apparent reading of the bā' in His saying ﴿with falsehood﴾ is that it is the bā' of instrumentality (bā' al-isti'āna), like in your saying: "I wrote with the pen." The meaning is: do not mix up the truth by means of the doubts (shubuhat) that you present to the listeners. That is because the texts in the Torah and the Gospel concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) were hidden texts whose knowledge required inference. Then they used to dispute concerning them and obscure the direction of the indication for those who reflected upon them, by means of casting doubts. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿do not mix up the truth with falsehood﴾, and it is what is mentioned in His saying: ﴿and they disputed with falsehood in order to refute the truth by it﴾ [Ghafir: 5]. As for His saying ﴿while you know﴾, that is, you know the great harm that comes back upon you on the Day of Resurrection from misleading creation; because that confusion becomes a barrier turning people away from accepting the truth until the Day of Resurrection, and a call for them to persist in falsehood until the Day of Resurrection. There is no doubt that its sin is great. And although this address was directed at them, it is a warning to all of creation and a caution against the like of it. Thus the address, though specific in form, is general in meaning.

Then here are two discussions:

The first discussion: His saying ﴿and conceal the truth﴾ is a jussive (majzum) falling under the rule of the prohibition, meaning "and do not conceal," or it is in the accusative (mansub) by the implied particle an (bi-idmar an).

The second discussion: The prohibition against confusion and concealment, even though it is restricted by knowledge, does not indicate their permissibility when knowledge is absent. That is because when the state of a thing is not known, it is not known whether that confusion and concealment is truth or falsehood, and what is not known to be truth or falsehood may not be undertaken either by negation or by affirmation; rather, one must refrain from it. The reason for this restriction is that undertaking a harmful act while knowing it is harmful is more heinous than undertaking it while ignorant of its harm. Since they were knowing of the corruptions in confusion, their undertaking it was more abominable. The verse indicates that one who knows the truth is obligated to manifest it and it is forbidden for him to conceal it. And Allah knows best.

And so it is in His words, the Exalted: ﴿Establish the prayer, give the zakah, and bow with those who bow﴾.

Know that when Allah, glorified and exalted, first commanded them to believe, and then secondly forbade them from mixing truth with falsehood and from concealing the proofs of prophethood, He then mentioned the explanation of the legal obligations (shara'i') that were binding upon them. Among the legal obligations He mentioned those that were foremost, namely the salah (ritual prayer), which is the greatest of the bodily acts of worship, and the zakah (obligatory almsgiving), which is the greatest of the financial acts of worship. Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Those who hold that it is not permissible to delay the clarification of a mujmal (a general, unspecified term) beyond the time of address said: The address in His words ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ came after the Prophet ﷺ had already described to them the pillars and conditions of the prayer. So it is as if He, the Exalted, said: "Establish the prayer that you have come to know." Those who hold that delay is permissible said: It is possible that what is meant is the command to pray, even if they did not know what the prayer is, and the purpose is that the listener should prepare himself to comply, even if he does not know what is commanded. Just as there is no dispute that it is fitting for a master to say to his servant: "I will command you tomorrow to do something, so you must do it," and his purpose is that the servant should resolve immediately to carry it out at the second time.

* * *

**The second issue:** The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: The word salah is among the shar'i (religious-legal) terms. They said: Because it is a matter that came into existence in the Shari'ah, it is impossible that the word assigned to it had already existed before the Shari'ah. Then they differed concerning the basis of the figurative comparison. Some of them said: Its original meaning in the lexicon is supplication (du'a'). Al-A'sha said:

*"Upon you is like what you prayed (salleiti), so hold fast; a man's side will certainly lie down (in the grave)."*

Another said:

*"The wind touched her jar, and she prayed over her jar and was marked (with its sign)."*

Others said: The original basis is adherence (luzum). A poet said:

*"I was not among its gardens, Allah knows, and today I am burning in its sea."*

That is, one who keeps close to it (mulazim). Others said: Rather, it is derived from al-musalli, which is the horse that follows another. The closest view, however, is that it is derived from supplication, since there is no salah without supplication occurring within it, or something that takes its place. And there may be a salah in which following another does not occur. When the basis of comparison is something that covers all forms, it is more appropriate to make the basis of comparison something specific to some forms.

Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) said: Among the well-known figurative usages in the language is applying the name of a part to the whole. Since the legal salah includes supplication, the name of supplication was applied to it by way of figurative usage. So if what the Mu'tazila mean by it being a shar'i term is this, then that is correct. But if they mean that the Shari'ah coined this word initially for this designated meaning, then that is invalid, because otherwise this word would not be Arabic, and that contradicts His words: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ (Yusuf 12:2).

As for zakah, it linguistically denotes growth, as one says: "The crop grew (zaka)" when it increased, and it also denotes purification. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you killed a pure soul?﴾ (al-Kahf 18:74), meaning pure. And He said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾ (al-A'la 87:14), meaning he purified himself. And He said: ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would have been purified (zaka) ever﴾ (al-Nur 24:21). And He said: ﴿And whoever purifies himself, purifies himself only for his own soul﴾ (Fatir 35:18), meaning he purified himself through obedience to Allah. Perhaps giving out half a dinar from twenty dinars was named zakah by analogy with these two meanings, because giving out that amount causes the remainder to grow in terms of blessing, since Allah removes calamity from that wealth by means of the purification of that gift. Thus that giving becomes growth in meaning, even if it is a decrease in form. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "Upon you is charity, for in it are six qualities, three in this world and three in the Hereafter. As for those in this world, it increases provision, multiplies wealth, and makes dwellings prosper. As for those in the Hereafter, it covers nakedness, becomes a shade above the head, and becomes a screen from the Fire."

It is also permissible to name zakah by the second meaning, in that it purifies the one who pays zakah from all sins. For this reason the Exalted said to His Prophet: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow (tuzakkihim) through it﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:103).

* * *

**The third issue:** His words, the Exalted: ﴿Establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾ are addressed to the Jews, and this indicates that the disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the legal obligations. As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾, there are several views concerning it:

First: The Jews had no ruku' (bowing) in their prayer, so Allah singled out the ruku' for mention, to urge them to adopt the prayer of the Muslims.

Second: The intended meaning is "pray with those who pray." On this view the repetition disappears, because in the first part He commanded them to perfect it, and in the second He commanded them to perform it in congregation.

Third: The intended meaning of the command to bow is the command to humble oneself, because ruku' and khudu' (submission, humility) are the same in the language. It is then a prohibition of blameworthy arrogance and a command to lowliness, as He said concerning the believers: ﴿Allah will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty over the disbelievers﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:54). And like His words, disciplining His Messenger, peace be upon him: ﴿Lower your wing to those who follow you among the believers﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:215). And like His praise of him: ﴿It is by a mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them; and had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:159). And so in His words, the Exalted: ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger and those who believe — those who establish the prayer, give zakah, and they are bowing (raki'un)﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:55). It is as if He, the Exalted, when He commanded them with prayer and zakah, then commanded them after that with submission, compliance, and abandoning rebellion.

Al-Asamm (a Mu'tazili scholar) related from some of them that Allah, the Exalted, only commanded the Children of Israel with zakah because they were not paying zakah. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿and their consuming of the forbidden (al-suht)﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:62), and by His words: "and their consuming of usury (al-riba)," and ﴿their consuming people's wealth falsely﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:161). So Allah, the Exalted, revealed in this place what had been concealed, so that they would beware lest He expose them regarding the rest of their secrets and sins. Thus this becomes like information about the unseen, which is one of the proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, though you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?﴾

Know that the hamzah (the interrogative particle *alif-hamzah*) in *a-ta'murūna al-nāsa bil-birr* is for *taqrīr* (affirmation, compelling the listener to admit a fact) together with *taqrī'* (rebuke) and wonder at their condition. As for *al-birr*, it is a comprehensive term for acts of goodness. From it comes *birr al-wālidayn*, which is obeying one's parents. From it also comes *ʿamalun mabrūr*, meaning a deed that Allah the Exalted has accepted. It can also mean truthfulness, as one says *barra fī yamīnihi*, meaning he was truthful in his oath and did not break it, and it is said *ṣadaqta wa-barirta* (you spoke truly and were righteous). The Almighty said: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], so He informed that *birr* includes *taqwā* (God-consciousness).

Know that when the Glorified and Exalted commanded faith and the laws, based on the blessings He had bestowed upon them, and encouraged them to that, He built it upon another basis. That basis is that neglecting the deeds of righteousness while urging people toward them is considered repugnant by reason, since the purpose of commanding people to it is either sincere counsel (*naṣīḥah*) or compassion (*shafqah*). It is not reasonable for a person to show compassion to another, or to give counsel to another, while neglecting himself. So Allah the Exalted warned them against this by rebuking them with this statement.

The scholars differed about what is meant by *al-birr* in this place, in several respects:

First: this is the view of al-Suddī, that they used to command people to obey Allah and forbid them from disobeying Allah, while they themselves abandoned obedience and committed disobedience.

Second: the view of Ibn Jurayj, that they used to command people to pray and to give *zakāt*, while they themselves did not do these.

Third: that when someone came to them secretly to inquire about the affair of Muḥammad (ﷺ), they would say: "He is truthful in what he says, and his command is true, so follow him." Yet they did not follow him, out of their greed for the gifts and gratuities that reached them from their followers.

Fourth: that a group of Jews, before the Messenger (ﷺ) was sent, used to inform the polytheists of the Arabs that a messenger would arise from among them and call to the truth, and they used to command following him before his appearance. When he appeared, they abandoned him and turned away from his religion. This is the choice of Abū Muslim.

Fifth: the view of al-Zajjāj, that they used to command people to give charity while they themselves were stingy with it, because Allah the Exalted described them with hardness of hearts, eating usury and illicit gain (*suḥt*).

Sixth: perhaps the hypocrites among the Jews used to command following Muḥammad (ﷺ) outwardly, while in their hearts they denied him, so Allah the Exalted rebuked them for this.

Seventh: that the Jews used to command others to follow the Torah, then they themselves opposed it, because they found in it what indicates the truthfulness of Muḥammad (ﷺ), yet they did not believe in him.

As for His saying ﴿and forget yourselves﴾: *al-nisyān* (forgetting) is an expression for a lapse of attention that occurs after knowledge has been attained, and the forgetful person is not accountable, and whoever is not accountable cannot be blamed by Allah the Exalted for what proceeds from him. Therefore, the meaning of ﴿and forget yourselves﴾ is that you are heedless of the right of your own selves and you neglect what benefit they have in it. As for His saying ﴿though you recite the Book﴾, its meaning is that you read the Torah, study it, and know what is in it of exhortation to deeds of righteousness and turning away from deeds of sin.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾, it is an expression of wonder, directed at the intelligent, concerning their actions. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Uff to you and to what you worship besides Allah! Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 67]. The causes of this wonder are several:

The first: the purpose of enjoining good and forbidding evil is to guide others toward attaining benefit and to warn them against what leads them into harm. Doing good to oneself takes priority over doing good to others, and this is known from the evidences of reason and transmission. Whoever admonishes but does not heed admonition has, as it were, committed an act contradictory that reason does not accept. Therefore He said: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾.

The second: whoever admonishes people and displays his knowledge to creation, then does not heed it, that admonition becomes a cause for people's desire for disobedience. For people say: "He, with this knowledge, would not have committed disobedience unless he knew that there is no basis for these warnings. Then he has done an act which necessitates boldness in disobedience." So he has combined two contradictories, and that does not befit the conduct of the intelligent. Therefore He said: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾.

The third: whoever admonishes must strive that his admonition become effective in hearts, while whoever disobeys has as his aim that his admonition not become effective in hearts. The combination of the two is contradictory and unfitting for the intelligent. For this reason ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Two men broke my back: a scholar who flaunts his sin, and an ignorant man who is excessively devout."

Some issues remain here:

The first issue: some said: it is not permissible for a sinner to enjoin good and forbid evil. They argued with the verse and with reason. As for the verse, it is His saying ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves﴾, and there is no doubt that He mentioned this in the context of blame. He also said: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do? Greatly hateful is it in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Ṣaff: 2–3]. As for reason, it is that if this were permissible, it would be permissible for someone committing adultery with a woman to object to her, during the act of fornication, to her uncovering her face, and it is known that this is abhorrent. The answer: the accountable person is commanded with two things: one is abandoning disobedience, and the second is preventing others from committing disobedience. Failing in one of the two obligations does not necessitate failing in the other. As for His saying ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves﴾, it is a prohibition against combining the two, and a prohibition against combining two things can be understood in two ways:

One: that what is meant is the prohibition against forgetting oneself absolutely.

The other: that what is meant is the prohibition against encouraging people to righteousness while in a state of forgetting oneself.

In our view, the meaning of the verse is the first and not the second. On this basis, the argument of this opponent falls away. As for the rational argument they cited, it applies to them.

The second issue: the Muʿtazilah (a rationalist theological school) argued with this verse that the act of the servant is not created by Allah the Mighty and Majestic. They said: His saying ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves﴾ is valid and appropriate only if that act is from them. But if it is created in them by way of compulsion, it would not be appropriate, just as it is not permissible to say to the black person: "Why do you not become white?" since blackness was created in him. The answer: since His power is suited to both opposites, if one of the two opposites occurs without a determining cause, that is pure chance, and a chance occurrence cannot be the object of reproach. If it occurs, then if that determining factor is from him, the inquiry returns concerning it. If it occurs from Allah the Exalted, then at the moment of its occurrence that side becomes preponderant and the other becomes subordinate, and the subordinate is impossible to occur. For when there is equal balance it is impossible to occur, so the state of being subordinate is more fitting to be impossible to occur. And when one of two contradictories is impossible, the other becomes necessary. At that point everything you have raised against us returns against you. Then the true answer to all of this is: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾.

The third issue: (a) On the authority of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I passed by a people whose lips were being cut with scissors of fire. I said: 'O my brother, O Jibrīl, who are these?' He said: 'These are preachers from among the people of the world who used to command people to righteousness and forget themselves.'"

(b) The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "Indeed, in the Fire there is a man whose odor pains the people of the Fire. It was said: 'Who is he, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'A scholar who does not benefit from his knowledge.'"

(c) The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "The example of one who teaches people good but does not act upon it is like a lamp that gives light to people while burning itself."

(d) On the authority of al-Shaʿbī: a people from among the people of Paradise will look down upon a people in the Fire, and they will say: "Why did you enter the Fire when we only entered Paradise through your teaching?" They will say: "We used to command good and not do it."

As it has been said: whoever admonishes with his speech, his words are lost, and whoever admonishes with his deeds, his arrows strike home. And the poet said:

O you who teach others,
would that you had taught yourself first!

You prescribe the medicine for the sick and the ailing,
so that they may be healed by it, while you yourself are ill.

Begin with yourself and restrain it from its error,
and when it refrains from it, then you are wise.

Then your admonition will be accepted, and your opinion will be followed,
and the teaching will benefit.

It has been said: the action of one man among a thousand men is more eloquent than the speech of a thousand men about one man. As for one who admonishes and is himself admonished, his station with Allah is great.

It is narrated that Yazīd ibn Hārūn died, and he was a preacher and ascetic. He was seen in a dream, and it was said to him: "What did Allah do with you?" He said: "He forgave me. The first thing that Munkar and Nakīr asked me was: 'Who is your Lord?' I said: 'Are you not ashamed before an elder who called to Allah the Exalted for so many years, that you ask him: Who is your Lord?'"

It was said to al-Shiblī at the time of death: "Say: there is no god but Allah." He said:

Indeed, a house that you inhabit
does not need lamps.

(And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is burdensome except for the humble, who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that to Him they will return.)

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 45–46 (part 1 of 2):

His, glorified and exalted be He, saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer; and indeed it is hard, except for the humble (khashi'un)﴾ ﴿Who are certain that they will meet their Lord, and that they are to return to Him﴾.

The first issue: The scholars differed regarding the addressees of His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾. Some said: they are the believers in the Messenger. He said: because one who denies prayer altogether and patience in the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) would hardly be told: seek help through patience and prayer. Therefore it is necessary to restrict it to those who affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ). It is not impossible that the address was first to the Children of Israel and then after that became an address to the believers in Muhammad (ﷺ). The closer view is that the addressees are the Children of Israel, because diverting the address to others would break the coherence of the discourse (nazm). If it is said: how are they commanded to be patient and to pray while they deny them? We say: we do not grant that they deny them. This is because everyone knows that patience in what one must be patient about is good, and that prayer, which is humility before the Creator and occupation with the remembrance of God, the Exalted, consoles one for the trials and calamities of the world. The disagreement is only about the manner: the prayer of the Jews is performed in one manner, and the prayer of the Muslims in another manner. When the object of the command is the reality (mahiyyah) which is the common element, the mentioned difficulty disappears. Based on this we say: when He, the Exalted, commanded them to faith, to abandoning misguidance, and to adherence to the laws, which are prayer and zakat, and this was burdensome for them because it involved giving up leadership and turning away from wealth and status, God, the Exalted, therefore treated this illness, saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

* * *

The second issue: They mentioned several aspects regarding patience and prayer:

The first: It is as if it were said: seek help in abandoning what you love of the world and in entering into what your natures find heavy, namely accepting the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), through patience, that is, by restraining the self from pleasures. For when you impose that upon yourselves, you become accustomed to it and it becomes light for you. Then, when you add prayer to that, the matter is complete, because one who is occupied with prayer must be occupied with the remembrance of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and the remembrance of His majesty and subjugation, and the remembrance of His mercy and grace. When he remembers His mercy, he inclines to obey Him, and when he remembers His punishment, he abandons disobeying Him. Thus his occupation with obedience becomes easy and his leaving off disobedience becomes easy.

The second: The intended meaning of patience here is fasting, because the one who fasts is patient regarding food and drink, and whoever restrains himself from fulfilling the desires of the belly and the private parts, the turbidities of love of the world are removed from him. When prayer is added to it, the heart is illuminated with the lights of the knowledge of God, the Exalted. He mentioned fasting before prayer because the effect of fasting is in removing what is not fitting, and the effect of prayer is in attaining what is fitting, and negation precedes affirmation. Also, the peace and blessings of God be upon him said: "Fasting is a shield from the Fire," and God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45], because prayer prevents one from being occupied with the world, humbles the heart, and through it comes the recitation of the Book and the understanding of what it contains of promise and threat, admonitions and fine manners, and the mention of the final destination of creatures to the abode of reward or the abode of punishment, out of desire for the Hereafter and aversion from the world. Thus it becomes easy for a person then to abandon leadership, and he is cut off from created beings toward the direction of service to the Creator. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted be He:
Page 47
﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer; indeed God is with the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153].

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed it﴾, there are several views regarding this pronoun:

The first: The pronoun refers to prayer, meaning: it is a heavy prayer, except for the humble.

The second: The pronoun refers to the seeking of help which is indicated by His saying: ﴿And seek help﴾.

The third: It refers to all the matters which the Children of Israel were commanded and forbidden, from His saying: ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ to His saying: ﴿And seek help﴾. The Arabs sometimes omit a thing for brevity, or confine themselves to an allusion when they are confident in the addressee's knowledge. A speaker says: "There is no one better than so-and-so upon it," meaning the earth; and they say: "Nothing between its two lava-plains is more noble than so-and-so," meaning Medina. And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if God were to take mankind to account for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it any creature﴾ [al-Nahl: 61], and there is no mention of the earth. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed it is hard﴾, meaning: it is burdensome and heavy upon these, but easy upon the humble. Therefore their reward must be greater and the reward of the humble lesser, and that is an objectionable statement. We say: the intended meaning is not that the fatigue which befalls them is greater than that which befalls the humble. How could that be, when the humble person in prayer employs his limbs, heart, hearing and sight, and does not neglect pondering what he brings of remembrance, humility and submission? And when he remembers the threat, he is not free from grief and sorrow, and when he mentions the promise, it is similar to that. Since this is the act of the humble, the burden upon him in performing prayer is greater. The intended meaning of His saying "and indeed it is heavy upon those who are not humble" is that, since they do not believe in a reward for performing it nor in a punishment for abandoning it, it is difficult for them to perform it.

The conclusion: when the unbeliever does not believe that there is any benefit in performing it, it becomes heavy upon him to perform it, because occupation with what has no benefit is heavy upon the nature. As for the monotheist, since he believes that performing it brings the greatest benefits and abandoning it the greatest harms, that does not weigh upon him, because of what he believes about its reward, the great success of eternal bliss, and deliverance from painful punishment. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾, meaning: they expect to attain His reward and deliverance from His punishment. An example: if a sick person is told: eat this bitter thing, if he believes that there is healing in it, it is easy for him, and if he does not believe that, the matter is hard for him. Upon this is to be understood his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer." He described prayer thus for the aspects we have mentioned, not because it was not heavy upon him; and how could it be, when he, peace and blessings be upon him, would pray until his feet swelled. As for khushu', it is humbling oneself and submission. As for His saying: ﴿Who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾, the exegetes have two views regarding it:

The first view: that "ẓann" here means "'ilm" (knowledge). They said: because ẓann, which is a belief accompanied by the possibility of the opposite, requires that its holder not be firm regarding the Day of Resurrection, and that is disbelief, while God, the Exalted, praised them for this ẓann, and praise for disbelief is not permissible; therefore the intended meaning of ẓann here must be 'ilm. The cause of this metaphor is that 'ilm and ẓann share in that each of them is a preponderant belief, except that 'ilm is preponderant and prevents the opposite, while ẓann is preponderant but does not prevent the opposite. When they resembled each other in this respect, it became valid to apply the name of one to the other. Aws ibn Hajar said:

So he released it, certain in his ẓann that it would penetrate between the ribs, piercing through.

And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾ [al-Haqqah: 20], and He said: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 4]. God mentioned that as a rebuke against them and an urging toward ẓann, and it is not permissible that He would urge them toward a belief which allows the opposite. Thus it is established that the intended meaning of ẓann here is 'ilm.

Page 48

The second view: that the word be taken in its apparent sense, which is true ẓann. Then there are several aspects here:

The first: that meeting the Lord be taken as a metaphor for death, because meeting the Lord is caused by death, so the cause is mentioned and the effect is intended, and this is a well-known metaphor; for it is said of one who has died: he has met his Lord. Having established this, we say: "And indeed it is heavy except upon the humble who expect death at every moment." This is because whoever is expecting death at every moment, the humility does not leave his heart; so they hasten to repentance, since fear of death, along with humility, strengthens the motives for repentance. In every state, one must not feel secure from some shortcoming that has occurred from him, which obliges him to make amends. When his condition is as we have mentioned, this becomes a motive for him to hasten to repentance.

The second: that meeting the Lord be explained as meeting the reward of the Lord, and that is something supposed, not known, for the ascetic worshipper does not assert that he will meet God's reward; rather he supposes it, but that supposition is something that leads him to perfect humility.

The third: the meaning is "those who suppose that they will meet their Lord with their sins," for the humble person may think badly of himself and his deeds, so it prevails upon his supposition that he will meet God, the Exalted, with his sins. At that point he hastens to repentance, and that is among the praiseworthy attributes.

Two questions remain here:

The first question: Some of our companions used His saying: ﴿who will meet their Lord﴾ as evidence for the permissibility of seeing God, the Exalted. The Mu'tazilah said: the word liqa' does not indicate seeing. The proof for this is the verse, the report, and custom. As for the verse, it is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 77], and the hypocrite does not see his Lord. And He said: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. And God, the Exalted, said in a context of threat: ﴿And fear God, and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], and this encompasses the unbeliever and the believer, and seeing is not established for the unbeliever, so we know that liqa' is not an expression for seeing. As for the report, it is his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever swears an oath in order to seize by it the property of a Muslim man will meet God while He is angry with him," and the intended meaning is not "sees God," because that is a description of the people of the Fire. As for custom, it is the saying of Muslims about one who has died: "he met God," and they do not mean that he saw God, the Mighty and Majestic. Moreover, liqa' is meant to denote nearness to the one met, in a manner whereby the veil between them is removed. That is why a man, when he is barred from the commander, says: "I have not met him yet," even if he has seen him; and when he is permitted to enter upon him, he says: "I have met him," even if he is blind. It is said: "So-and-so met great hardship," "I met a calamity from so-and-so," "So-and-so met his end." All of this indicates that liqa' is not an expression for seeing. And His saying, exalted be He, also indicates this: ﴿Then the waters met for a matter already decreed﴾ [al-Qamar: 12], and this is valid only of a body and is not valid of God, the Exalted.

The Companions said: liqa' in the original language is an expression for one of two bodies reaching the other such that it touches it with a flat surface. It is said: "This met that" when it touched it and was joined to it. Since meeting between the two perceiving kinds was a cause of perception, wherever applying the word to contact is impossible, it must be taken to mean perception, because applying the name of the cause to the effect is among the strongest forms of metaphor. Thus it is established that the word liqa' must be taken to mean perception. At most, this meaning has been set aside in some instances due to a specific indication, so it must be applied to perception in the remaining cases. On this explanation, the questions disappear.

As for His saying: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 77], and the hypocrite does not see his Lord, we say: for this necessity, the intended meaning is "until the Day they meet His reckoning and His judgment." However, this implicit meaning goes against the apparent evidence, and one resorts to it only when necessary; so in this place, since we are compelled to it, we take it into account. But in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿that they are to meet their Lord﴾, there is no necessity to divert the word from its apparent meaning, nor to supply this additional element, and therefore it is required to link the liqa' to God.
