Part 2 of the commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 45–46:

...Exalted is He, not by the judgment of God. If they occupy themselves with mentioning the rational proofs which prevent the permissibility of seeing God, we have already demonstrated their weakness, and at that point, relying on the apparent meaning from this aspect becomes sound.

The second issue: What is meant by "return to God" (al-ruju' ila Allah, the return to God) is a return to a state in which no one other than Him owns them, and in which no one else possesses benefit or harm for them except Him, just as they were in that condition at the beginning of creation. Thus their final state, being like the state they were in at first, is called a "return to God," in contrast with their condition during all the days of their lives, when another may hold authority over them and may harm and benefit them, even though God, Exalted is He, is the owner of them in all their circumstances. Two groups of the misguided (mubtilun) have argued from this verse:

The first: the Mujassimah (anthropomorphists, those who attribute a body to God). They said: "Return to something that is not a body is impossible. Since the return to God is established, it is necessary that God be a body."

The second: the Tanasukhiyyah (metempsychosists, believers in the transmigration of souls). They said: "Return to a thing is preceded by existence with it. This verse therefore indicates that souls are eternal and that they existed in the world of spiritual beings (ʿalam al-ruhaniyyat)." The answer to them has already been given on the basis of what was stated earlier.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 45–46 (part 1 of 2):

His, glorified and exalted be He, saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer; and indeed it is hard, except for the humble (khashi'un)﴾ ﴿Who are certain that they will meet their Lord, and that they are to return to Him﴾.

The first issue: The scholars differed regarding the addressees of His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾. Some said: they are the believers in the Messenger. He said: because one who denies prayer altogether and patience in the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) would hardly be told: seek help through patience and prayer. Therefore it is necessary to restrict it to those who affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ). It is not impossible that the address was first to the Children of Israel and then after that became an address to the believers in Muhammad (ﷺ). The closer view is that the addressees are the Children of Israel, because diverting the address to others would break the coherence of the discourse (nazm). If it is said: how are they commanded to be patient and to pray while they deny them? We say: we do not grant that they deny them. This is because everyone knows that patience in what one must be patient about is good, and that prayer, which is humility before the Creator and occupation with the remembrance of God, the Exalted, consoles one for the trials and calamities of the world. The disagreement is only about the manner: the prayer of the Jews is performed in one manner, and the prayer of the Muslims in another manner. When the object of the command is the reality (mahiyyah) which is the common element, the mentioned difficulty disappears. Based on this we say: when He, the Exalted, commanded them to faith, to abandoning misguidance, and to adherence to the laws, which are prayer and zakat, and this was burdensome for them because it involved giving up leadership and turning away from wealth and status, God, the Exalted, therefore treated this illness, saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

* * *

The second issue: They mentioned several aspects regarding patience and prayer:

The first: It is as if it were said: seek help in abandoning what you love of the world and in entering into what your natures find heavy, namely accepting the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), through patience, that is, by restraining the self from pleasures. For when you impose that upon yourselves, you become accustomed to it and it becomes light for you. Then, when you add prayer to that, the matter is complete, because one who is occupied with prayer must be occupied with the remembrance of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and the remembrance of His majesty and subjugation, and the remembrance of His mercy and grace. When he remembers His mercy, he inclines to obey Him, and when he remembers His punishment, he abandons disobeying Him. Thus his occupation with obedience becomes easy and his leaving off disobedience becomes easy.

The second: The intended meaning of patience here is fasting, because the one who fasts is patient regarding food and drink, and whoever restrains himself from fulfilling the desires of the belly and the private parts, the turbidities of love of the world are removed from him. When prayer is added to it, the heart is illuminated with the lights of the knowledge of God, the Exalted. He mentioned fasting before prayer because the effect of fasting is in removing what is not fitting, and the effect of prayer is in attaining what is fitting, and negation precedes affirmation. Also, the peace and blessings of God be upon him said: "Fasting is a shield from the Fire," and God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45], because prayer prevents one from being occupied with the world, humbles the heart, and through it comes the recitation of the Book and the understanding of what it contains of promise and threat, admonitions and fine manners, and the mention of the final destination of creatures to the abode of reward or the abode of punishment, out of desire for the Hereafter and aversion from the world. Thus it becomes easy for a person then to abandon leadership, and he is cut off from created beings toward the direction of service to the Creator. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted be He:
Page 47
﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer; indeed God is with the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153].

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed it﴾, there are several views regarding this pronoun:

The first: The pronoun refers to prayer, meaning: it is a heavy prayer, except for the humble.

The second: The pronoun refers to the seeking of help which is indicated by His saying: ﴿And seek help﴾.

The third: It refers to all the matters which the Children of Israel were commanded and forbidden, from His saying: ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ to His saying: ﴿And seek help﴾. The Arabs sometimes omit a thing for brevity, or confine themselves to an allusion when they are confident in the addressee's knowledge. A speaker says: "There is no one better than so-and-so upon it," meaning the earth; and they say: "Nothing between its two lava-plains is more noble than so-and-so," meaning Medina. And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if God were to take mankind to account for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it any creature﴾ [al-Nahl: 61], and there is no mention of the earth. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed it is hard﴾, meaning: it is burdensome and heavy upon these, but easy upon the humble. Therefore their reward must be greater and the reward of the humble lesser, and that is an objectionable statement. We say: the intended meaning is not that the fatigue which befalls them is greater than that which befalls the humble. How could that be, when the humble person in prayer employs his limbs, heart, hearing and sight, and does not neglect pondering what he brings of remembrance, humility and submission? And when he remembers the threat, he is not free from grief and sorrow, and when he mentions the promise, it is similar to that. Since this is the act of the humble, the burden upon him in performing prayer is greater. The intended meaning of His saying "and indeed it is heavy upon those who are not humble" is that, since they do not believe in a reward for performing it nor in a punishment for abandoning it, it is difficult for them to perform it.

The conclusion: when the unbeliever does not believe that there is any benefit in performing it, it becomes heavy upon him to perform it, because occupation with what has no benefit is heavy upon the nature. As for the monotheist, since he believes that performing it brings the greatest benefits and abandoning it the greatest harms, that does not weigh upon him, because of what he believes about its reward, the great success of eternal bliss, and deliverance from painful punishment. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾, meaning: they expect to attain His reward and deliverance from His punishment. An example: if a sick person is told: eat this bitter thing, if he believes that there is healing in it, it is easy for him, and if he does not believe that, the matter is hard for him. Upon this is to be understood his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer." He described prayer thus for the aspects we have mentioned, not because it was not heavy upon him; and how could it be, when he, peace and blessings be upon him, would pray until his feet swelled. As for khushu', it is humbling oneself and submission. As for His saying: ﴿Who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾, the exegetes have two views regarding it:

The first view: that "ẓann" here means "'ilm" (knowledge). They said: because ẓann, which is a belief accompanied by the possibility of the opposite, requires that its holder not be firm regarding the Day of Resurrection, and that is disbelief, while God, the Exalted, praised them for this ẓann, and praise for disbelief is not permissible; therefore the intended meaning of ẓann here must be 'ilm. The cause of this metaphor is that 'ilm and ẓann share in that each of them is a preponderant belief, except that 'ilm is preponderant and prevents the opposite, while ẓann is preponderant but does not prevent the opposite. When they resembled each other in this respect, it became valid to apply the name of one to the other. Aws ibn Hajar said:

So he released it, certain in his ẓann that it would penetrate between the ribs, piercing through.

And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾ [al-Haqqah: 20], and He said: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 4]. God mentioned that as a rebuke against them and an urging toward ẓann, and it is not permissible that He would urge them toward a belief which allows the opposite. Thus it is established that the intended meaning of ẓann here is 'ilm.

Page 48

The second view: that the word be taken in its apparent sense, which is true ẓann. Then there are several aspects here:

The first: that meeting the Lord be taken as a metaphor for death, because meeting the Lord is caused by death, so the cause is mentioned and the effect is intended, and this is a well-known metaphor; for it is said of one who has died: he has met his Lord. Having established this, we say: "And indeed it is heavy except upon the humble who expect death at every moment." This is because whoever is expecting death at every moment, the humility does not leave his heart; so they hasten to repentance, since fear of death, along with humility, strengthens the motives for repentance. In every state, one must not feel secure from some shortcoming that has occurred from him, which obliges him to make amends. When his condition is as we have mentioned, this becomes a motive for him to hasten to repentance.

The second: that meeting the Lord be explained as meeting the reward of the Lord, and that is something supposed, not known, for the ascetic worshipper does not assert that he will meet God's reward; rather he supposes it, but that supposition is something that leads him to perfect humility.

The third: the meaning is "those who suppose that they will meet their Lord with their sins," for the humble person may think badly of himself and his deeds, so it prevails upon his supposition that he will meet God, the Exalted, with his sins. At that point he hastens to repentance, and that is among the praiseworthy attributes.

Two questions remain here:

The first question: Some of our companions used His saying: ﴿who will meet their Lord﴾ as evidence for the permissibility of seeing God, the Exalted. The Mu'tazilah said: the word liqa' does not indicate seeing. The proof for this is the verse, the report, and custom. As for the verse, it is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 77], and the hypocrite does not see his Lord. And He said: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. And God, the Exalted, said in a context of threat: ﴿And fear God, and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], and this encompasses the unbeliever and the believer, and seeing is not established for the unbeliever, so we know that liqa' is not an expression for seeing. As for the report, it is his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever swears an oath in order to seize by it the property of a Muslim man will meet God while He is angry with him," and the intended meaning is not "sees God," because that is a description of the people of the Fire. As for custom, it is the saying of Muslims about one who has died: "he met God," and they do not mean that he saw God, the Mighty and Majestic. Moreover, liqa' is meant to denote nearness to the one met, in a manner whereby the veil between them is removed. That is why a man, when he is barred from the commander, says: "I have not met him yet," even if he has seen him; and when he is permitted to enter upon him, he says: "I have met him," even if he is blind. It is said: "So-and-so met great hardship," "I met a calamity from so-and-so," "So-and-so met his end." All of this indicates that liqa' is not an expression for seeing. And His saying, exalted be He, also indicates this: ﴿Then the waters met for a matter already decreed﴾ [al-Qamar: 12], and this is valid only of a body and is not valid of God, the Exalted.

The Companions said: liqa' in the original language is an expression for one of two bodies reaching the other such that it touches it with a flat surface. It is said: "This met that" when it touched it and was joined to it. Since meeting between the two perceiving kinds was a cause of perception, wherever applying the word to contact is impossible, it must be taken to mean perception, because applying the name of the cause to the effect is among the strongest forms of metaphor. Thus it is established that the word liqa' must be taken to mean perception. At most, this meaning has been set aside in some instances due to a specific indication, so it must be applied to perception in the remaining cases. On this explanation, the questions disappear.

As for His saying: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 77], and the hypocrite does not see his Lord, we say: for this necessity, the intended meaning is "until the Day they meet His reckoning and His judgment." However, this implicit meaning goes against the apparent evidence, and one resorts to it only when necessary; so in this place, since we are compelled to it, we take it into account. But in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿that they are to meet their Lord﴾, there is no necessity to divert the word from its apparent meaning, nor to supply this additional element, and therefore it is required to link the liqa' to God.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 47:**

His statement, may He be blessed and exalted: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾.

Know that He, exalted is He, repeated this statement a second time in order to emphasise the proof against them and to warn them against abandoning the following of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then He joined it to the threat, which is His statement: ﴿And fear a Day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48]. It is as if He said: "If you do not obey Me for the sake of the favours I bestowed upon you in the past, then obey Me out of fear of My punishment in the future."

As for His statement: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾, there is a question about it, namely that it would necessarily follow that they are better than Muhammad, peace be upon him, and that is false by consensus. The answer to it comes in several aspects:

First: Some people said: *al-'alam* (the world, the worlds) is an expression for a large group of people, as in your saying, "I saw a world (*'alaman*) of people," and what is meant by it is the many, not the whole. This view is weak, because the word *'alam* is derived from *'alam* (a sign), which is an indicator. Everything that is an indicator of God, exalted is He, is an *'alam*, and so it is one of the *'alam*. This is the verification of the statement of the theologians (*mutakallimun*): "The world is every existent other than God." According to this, it is not possible to restrict the word to some of the created things.

Second: What is meant is that He preferred you over the worlds of your times. This is because the person who will exist after that, and who does not exist now, was not among the worlds during his non-existence, since the condition for being a world is that it be existent, and a thing during its non-existence is not existent. So a thing during its non-existence is not among the worlds. Muhammad, peace be upon him, did not exist at that time, so that time was not among the worlds. Therefore, the fact that the Children of Israel were the best of the worlds at that time does not necessarily mean that they were better than Muhammad (ﷺ) at that time. This is also the answer to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿when He made among you prophets, and made you kings, and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20], and His statement: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ [al-Dukhan: 32]. By it He meant the worlds of that time. They were better than others only because of what they were given of kingship, prophethood, and divine books.

Third: His statement: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ is general in terms of the worlds, but it is unrestricted in terms of the preference (*fadl*), and an unrestricted statement is satisfied in its truth by a single instance. So the verse indicates that the Children of Israel were preferred over the worlds in a particular matter. This does not require that they be better than all the worlds in all matters. Rather, perhaps they were better than others in one matter, while others are better than them in matters other than that one. At this point it becomes clear that it is not valid to use His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of Imran over the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran: 33] as evidence that the prophets are better than the angels.

There remain some discussions:

**The first discussion:** Ibn Zayd said: By it He meant: the believers among them, because their disobedient ones were transformed into apes and swine, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and made of them apes and swine﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], and He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 78].

**The second discussion:** All that God, exalted is He, addressed to the Children of Israel is an admonition for the Arabs, because the virtue through the Prophet has reached them as well, and all the stories of the prophets are an admonition and guidance. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ [al-Zumar: 18], and He said: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 55], and He said: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf: 111]. For this reason Qatadah narrated, saying: It was mentioned to us that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say: "By God, the Children of Israel have passed away, and what you hear does not benefit you beyond others."

**The third discussion:** al-Qaffal said: *al-ni'mah* (favour) with a kasrah on the nun means the kindness (*minnah*) and what a man bestows upon his companion. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And this is a favour (*ni'mah*) which you bestow upon me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 22]. As for *al-na'mah* with a fatha on the nun, it is what one enjoys in life. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and luxury (*na'mah*) in which they had delighted﴾ [al-Dukhan: 27].

**The fourth discussion:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ indicates that the upkeep of what is most beneficial (*ri'ayat al-aslah*) is not obligatory upon God, exalted is He, neither in this world nor in religion. This is because His statement: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ includes all the favours of this world and religion. That preference is either obligatory or not obligatory. If it were obligatory, it would not be valid to make it a kindness upon them, because whoever performs an obligation has no kindness upon anyone. If it is not obligatory, and He specified some with it over others, then this indicates that the upkeep of what is most beneficial is not obligatory, neither in this world nor in religion. If it is said: Since He singled them out with great favours in this world, this would suit Him to single them out also with great favours in the Hereafter, as it is said: "Completing a kindness is better than beginning it." Why then did He follow that with the severe warning in His statement: ﴿And fear a Day﴾? The answer: Because disobedience, together with the greatness of the favour, is more ugly and more shameful, and for this reason He warned them against it.

**The fifth discussion:** In explaining which of the groups of the world is the best, that is, which of them is most endowed with the qualities of goodness. Know that this is among the matters over which there has been severe dispute among the inhabitants of the regions. Each group claims that it is the best and most endowed with the attributes of perfection. We will point to the central points of discussion in this chapter, by God's guidance and help.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 48 (part 1 of 5):**

The words of the Most High: ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will any intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾

Know that guarding oneself against the Day means guarding oneself against the punishment and hardships that occur on that Day, because the Day itself is not something one guards against, and both the people of Paradise and the people of Hell will certainly arrive at it. So the intended meaning is what we have mentioned. Then the Most High described the Day with the most severe and most terrifying attributes. This is because when an Arab is pushed into a calamity and his helpers try to defend him from it, they expend what is in their proud souls of zeal, and they defend him as a father defends his child with the utmost of his strength. If he sees that the one he is defending against has more power than they, he resorts to supplication and various kinds of intercession, and he tries by gentleness what he failed to achieve by harshness. If neither harshness nor gentleness avails him, nothing remains after that except ransoming one thing with its equivalent, whether wealth or something else. If these three do not avail him, he finds excuse in the help he hopes for from friends and brothers. So God, glory be to Him, informed that none of these matters will avail the guilty in the Hereafter. Two questions remain on this arrangement:

The first question: The benefit of His words ﴿no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ is the same as the benefit of His words ﴿nor will they be helped﴾. So what is the purpose of this repetition? The answer: What is meant by ﴿no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ is that no one will bear on his behalf the requital that is due to him. As for help, it is that one tries to free him from the ruling of the one being punished. We will mention another difference, God willing.

The second question: God, the Exalted, in this verse placed the acceptance of intercession before the taking of ransom, and He mentioned this verse in this surah after the one hundred and twentieth verse, and He placed the acceptance of ransom before the mention of intercession. What is the wisdom in this? The answer: Whoever's inclination is toward love of wealth more than toward elevation of the soul will put holding on to intercessors before giving ransom, and whoever is the opposite will put ransom before intercession. So the benefit of changing the order is to indicate these two types.

Now let us mention the explanation of the words. As for His words ﴿no soul will avail another soul at all﴾, al-Qaffal said: The basic meaning of *jaza* (to avail) among the people of language is *qada* (to settle, to suffice). From this is the hadith that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Abu Burda ibn Yasar: "*Tajzika wa la tajzi ahadan ba'daka*" ("It will suffice for you, and it will not suffice anyone after you"). The people of Arabic grammar narrate it as *tajzika* with an open *ta* and without hamza, meaning: it will settle on your behalf (for your sacrifice) and will substitute. The meaning of the verse is that on the Day of Resurrection no soul will substitute for another soul in anything, nor will it bear for it anything of what has befallen it. Rather, a person will flee on that Day from his brother, his mother, and his father. The meaning of this substitution is that the obedience of the obedient will not settle what was obligatory upon the disobedient. This substitution may occur in this world, as when a man settles his relative's or friend's debt and bears it on his behalf. But on the Day of Resurrection, the settling of rights occurs only through good deeds. Abu Hurayrah narrated that he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May God have mercy on a servant who had an injustice against his brother in his honor, his wealth, or his standing, and he sought his pardon before it is taken from him, when there is no dinar or dirham. If he has good deeds, some of his good deeds will be taken from him, and if he has no good deeds, some of his evil deeds will be placed upon him."

The author of al-Kashshaf said:

[p. 52]

"Shay'an" (anything) is the direct object, and it may also be in the position of a verbal noun, meaning "a little of the requital," like His words ﴿and they will not be wronged in anything﴾ [Maryam: 60]. And whoever reads *la yajzi* (from *ajza'a 'anhu*, meaning "it sufficed for him" or "it replaced him") does not, in his recitation, have the meaning except of "anything" from the sense of sufficing. This sentence is in the accusative position as a describing clause of *yawman* (a Day). If it is said: where is the returning pronoun from it to the described noun? We say: it is omitted, its estimate being *la tajzi fihi* (in which no soul will avail). The indefiniteness of the phrase means that any soul among souls will not avail on behalf of the soul of another anything of things, and this is the complete cutting off that severs all hopes.

As for His words ﴿nor will any intercession be accepted from it﴾, intercession (*shafa'ah*) is that one seeks for another a gift or requests a need on his behalf. Its origin is from *shaf'* (even number), which is the opposite of *witr* (odd number). It is as if the one in need was a single unit, and then the intercessor became a pair with him, meaning they became two as a couple. Know that the pronoun in His words ﴿nor will any intercession be accepted from it﴾ refers to the second soul, the disobedient one, from which no compensation is taken. The meaning of "no intercession will be accepted from it" is that if it brings the intercession of an intercessor, it will not be accepted from it. It is also permissible that it refers to the first soul, on the basis that if it were to intercede for itself, its intercession would not be accepted, just as it does not avail it anything.

As for His words ﴿nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾, that is ransom (*fidyah*). The root of the word comes from equating one thing with another. You say: "I do not equate anyone with so-and-so," meaning "I do not see anyone as his equal." The Most High said: ﴿then those who disbelieve, in their Lord, equate (others with Him)﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. Its counterpart in this verse is His words: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, even if they had all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 36]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth's fullness of gold, even if he ransomed himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91]. And He said: ﴿And if he offers every compensation, it will not be taken from him﴾ [al-An'am: 70].

As for His words ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, know that help occurs in this world through companionship and kinship, and God, the Exalted, has informed that on that Day there is no intimate friendship nor intercession, and that there are no lineages among them. A person flees from his brother, his mother, his father, and his relatives. Al-Qaffal said: By "help" (*nasr*) is meant aid, as in His words (ﷺ): "Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed." From it is the meaning of relief: the Arabs say "a land that is *mansurah*," meaning "rained upon," and the rain "helps" the lands when it makes them grow, as if it relieved its people. It was also said regarding His words ﴿whoever thinks that God will not help him﴾ [al-Hajj: 15] that it means "that God will not provide for him as the rain provides for the lands." Retribution is also called *nusrah* and *intisar* (victory/vindication). The Most High said: ﴿And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77]. They said its meaning is: "We took vengeance for him." So His words ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ may contain all these meanings: on the Day of Resurrection they will not be relieved, and it may also mean that when they are punished they will find no one who takes vengeance on their behalf against God. In general, it seems that help is the warding off of hardships, so the Most High informed that there is no one there to ward off His punishment. Two issues remain in the verse:

The first issue: In the verse there is the greatest warning against sins and the strongest encouragement to make up for what a person has committed of sin through repentance. This is because when he conceives that after death there is no making up, no intercession, no help, and no ransom, he knows that he has no escape except through obedience. Since he cannot be safe at any moment from shortcoming in worship, and whoever loses repentance, given that he has no certainty of remaining alive, becomes cautious and fearful in every state. Although the verse was addressed to the Children of Israel, in meaning it addresses everyone, because the attribute mentioned in it is an attribute of the Day, and that encompasses everyone who attends that Day.

The second issue: The community has agreed that Muhammad (ﷺ) has intercession in the Hereafter, and His words ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra': 79] and His words ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 5] are interpreted as referring to that. Then they differed after this regarding for whom his intercession (peace be upon him) is: is it for the believers who deserve reward, or is it for the people of major sins who deserve punishment? The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) held that it is for those who deserve reward, and its effect is that an increase in benefits beyond what they deserved is obtained. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: its effect is in dropping punishment from those who deserve punishment, either by his interceding for them in the place of Resurrection so that they do not enter the Fire, or if they have entered the Fire, he intercedes for them until they come out of it and enter Paradise. They agreed that it is not for the disbelievers. The Mu'tazilah used several arguments to deny intercession for the people of major sins:

The first of them: this verse. They said it indicates the negation of intercession in three respects:

The first: His words ﴿no soul will avail another soul at all﴾. If intercession had an effect in dropping punishment, then a soul would have availed another soul in something.

The second: His words ﴿nor will any intercession be accepted from it﴾. This is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it encompasses all types of intercession.

The third: His words ﴿nor will they be helped﴾. If Muhammad were an intercessor for any of the disobedient, he would be a helper for him, and that is contrary to the verse.

It may be said that there are two responses to the verse:

The first: The Jews used to claim that their forefathers would intercede for them, so they were despaired of that, and the verse was revealed concerning them.

The second: The apparent meaning of the verse requires the negation of intercession absolutely, but we have agreed that specification applies to it regarding increase of reward for the people of obedience. So we too specify it regarding the Muslim who has committed a major sin, by the proofs we will mention. For we answer the first point that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation. As for the second point, it is not permissible that the meaning of the verse be the negation of intercession for an increase of benefits, because God warned about that Day by saying that no intercession will benefit in it, and the warning does not arise if the negation of intercession is taken to refer to obtaining an increase of benefit, because the non-attainment of an increase of benefit carries no danger or harm. This is clarified by the fact that if He had said: "Guard yourselves against a Day in which I will not increase the benefits of the one deserving reward through anyone's intercession," no restraint from sins would have been achieved by that. But if He had said: "Guard yourselves against a Day in which I will not drop the punishment of the one deserving punishment through an intercessor's intercession," that would have been a restraint from sins. Thus it is established that the intended meaning of the verse is the negation of the effect of intercession in dropping punishment, not the negation of its effect in increasing benefits.

The second: His words ﴿They have no friend nor intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. The wrongdoer is the one who commits injustice, and that includes the disbeliever and others. It cannot be said that He negated that there be for the wrongdoers an intercessor who is obeyed, and did not negate an intercessor who is answered. We say that its implication is in accord with this: there will not be in the Hereafter an intercessor who is obeyed, because the one who is obeyed is above the one who obeys, and there is no one above Him, the Most High, whom God obeys. We say: it is not permissible to interpret the verse in the way you have stated, for two reasons:

The first: The knowledge that there is no one above Him, the Most High, whom He obeys is agreed upon among rational people. As for the one who affirms Him, glory be to Him, he has acknowledged that He obeys no one. And as for the one who denies Him, while holding the denial, it is impossible for him to believe that He is obedient to another. If this is established, then interpreting the verse in the way you have mentioned is interpreting it with a meaning that conveys nothing.

The second: He, the Most High, negated an intercessor who is obeyed, and an intercessor is only below the one interceded with, because the one above would be an commander over him and a judge over him, and such a one is not called an intercessor. So His words "intercessor" (*shafi'*) indicate that He is below God, the Most High, so it is not possible to interpret His words "who is obeyed" (*yuta'*) as referring to one above Him. Therefore it is necessary to interpret it as meaning that they have no intercessor who is answered.

The third: His words ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trading, nor intimate friendship, nor intercession﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254]. The apparent meaning of the verse requires the negation of all intercessions.

The fourth: His words ﴿And the wrongdoers have no helpers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 270]. If the Messenger were interceding for the sinful among his community, they would be described as "helped," because if he delivers someone from punishment through the intercession of the Messenger, then the Messenger has reached the utmost in helping him.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 48 (part 2 of 5):**

Fifth: the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:28]. Allah, the Exalted, informs about His angels that they do not intercede for anyone except one whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, approves. The sinner is not approved by Allah, the Exalted. If the angels do not intercede for him, then likewise the prophets, peace be upon them, do not, because no one holds a distinction between them.

Sixth: the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:48]. If intercession were effective in removing punishment, then intercession would benefit them, and that contradicts the verse.

Seventh: the Ummah is in agreement that we should desire from Allah, the Exalted, that He make us among the people of His intercession, peace be upon him. In the course of their supplications they say: "And make us among the people of his intercession." So if the one deserving intercession were the one who left this world persisting in major sins, they would be desiring from Allah, the Exalted, that He end their lives for them while persisting in major sins. It cannot be said: why is it not permissible to say that they desire from Allah, the Exalted, that He make them among the people of His intercession if they leave [this world] persisting [in sin], and not that they desire that He end their lives for them while persisting? Just as they say in their supplication: "Make us among the repentant," and they do not desire that they commit sins and then repent. Rather, they desire that He grant them success in repentance when they are sinners. Both desires are conditioned by a condition, namely the prior occurrence of persistence and the prior occurrence of sin. We say: the answer to this is from two aspects:

(The first): It is not necessary, when we stipulate a condition in our saying "O Allah, make us among the repentant," that we add a condition to our saying "make us among the people of intercession."

(The second): In both desires towards Allah, the Exalted, the Ummah asks of Him, the Exalted, that He do to them what brings them to the desired end. So in their saying "make us among the repentant," they desire that He grant them success in repentance from sins. And in the second, they desire that He do to them what makes them worthy of his intercession, peace be upon him. So if the worthiness for intercession were attained only by leaving this world persisting in major sins, then asking for worthiness for intercession would be asking for death in the state of persistence in major sins, and that is impermissible by consensus. But according to our view, that worthiness for intercession is attained only by leaving this world deserving reward. Then asking for worthiness for intercession is good, and thus the distinction becomes clear.

Eighth: the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire﴾ ﴿They will burn therein on the Day of Recompense﴾ ﴿And they will not be absent from it﴾ [al-Infitar 82:13–16] indicate that all the wicked enter the Fire and that they are not absent from it. And when it is established that they are not absent from it, it is established that they do not leave it. And if that is the case, then intercession has no effect, neither in pardoning punishment nor in bringing [them] out of the Fire after entering it.

Ninth: the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He arranges the affair. No intercessor [can intercede] except after His permission﴾ [Yunus 10:3]. So intercession for one for whom He has not given permission for intercession [is not valid]. Likewise His words: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255]. Likewise the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and he speaks what is correct﴾ [Saba' 34:38]. And He, the Exalted, has not given permission for intercession on behalf of the people of major sins. For this permission, if it were known, would be known either by reason or by transmission. As for reason, there is no room for it in this matter. As for transmission, it is either by mass transmission (tawatur) or by solitary reports (ahad). Solitary reports have no room in this matter, because a solitary report yields only conjecture, and the question is one of certain knowledge (ilmiyyah), and relying on conjectural evidence in matters of certain knowledge is impermissible. As for mass transmission, it is false, because if such [permission] had occurred, the majority of Muslims would have known it, and if that were so, they would not have denied this intercession. So since the majority agreed in denying it, we know that this permission does not exist.

Tenth: the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believed: "Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way"﴾ [Ghafir 40:7]. If intercession were attainable for the sinner, then its restriction to repentance and following the way would have no meaning.

Eleventh: the reports indicating that intercession does not exist for the people of major sins, and they are four:

The first: what al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah: "that he, peace and blessings be upon him, entered the graveyard and said: 'Peace be upon you, abode of a believing people. Indeed, we, if Allah wills, will join you. I wished that I had seen our brothers.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, are we not your brothers?' He said: 'Rather, you are my companions, and our brothers are those who have not yet come.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how will you know those of your Ummah who come after you?' He said: 'Do you see, if a man had horses, bright-faced and white-legged, among dark horses, would he not recognize his horses?' They said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'They will come on the Day of Resurrection bright-faced and white-legged from the ablution. And I will be their forerunner at the Basin. Indeed, men will be driven away from my Basin as a stray camel is driven away. I will call to them: Come, come! Then it will be said: Indeed, they changed after you. So I will say: Away, away!'" The inference from this report for the negation of intercession is that if he were an intercessor for them, he would not have said "Away, away!" for an intercessor does not say that. And how could he be an intercessor for them in deliverance from eternal punishment while he prevents them from a sip of water?

The second: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabat narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that "the Prophet ﷺ said to Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah: 'O Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, I seek refuge for you in Allah from the rule of the foolish. There will be rulers; whoever enters upon them and aids them in their oppression and believes their lies, he is not of me and I am not of him, and he will not come to me at the Basin. And whoever does not enter upon them, nor aids them in their oppression, nor believes their lies, he is of me and I am of him, and he will come to me at the Basin. O Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, prayer is a sacrifice, fasting is a shield, and charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire. O Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, no flesh that grew from unlawful gain will enter Paradise.'" The inference from this report is in three aspects:

One of them: that if he is not of the Prophet and the Prophet is not of him, how could he intercede for him?

The second: his words "he will not come to me at the Basin" are evidence for the negation of intercession, because if he is prevented from reaching the Messenger so that he does not come to the Basin, then it is more fitting that the Messenger would be prevented from delivering him from punishment.

(The third): his words "no flesh that grew from unlawful gain will enter Paradise" are explicit that there is no effect of intercession regarding the person who committed a major sin.

The third: from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "I will not find any one of you on the Day of Resurrection with a sheep on his neck, which bleats, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, help me!' And I will say: 'I possess nothing for you against Allah. I have indeed conveyed [the message] to you.'" This is explicit in the matter sought, because if he does not possess anything for him from Allah, then he has no share in intercession.

The fourth: from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Three [persons], I will be their adversary on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever I am his adversary, I will defeat him: a man who gave [a pledge] in My name and then betrayed; a man who sold a free person and consumed his price; and a man who hired a laborer, took full work from him, and did not pay him his wage." The inference from it is that when he, peace be upon him, is the adversary of these, it is impossible for him to be their intercessor. This is the totality of the Mu'tazilah's arguments in this chapter. As for our companions (the Ash'arites), they held to it with the following arguments:

(Ash'arites' Arguments)

One of them: the words of the Glorified and Exalted, relating about 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:118]. The inference: this intercession by 'Isa, peace be upon him, is either said to be for the disbelievers, or for the obedient Muslim, or for the Muslim who committed a minor sin, or for the Muslim who committed a major sin after repentance, or for the Muslim who committed a major sin before repentance. The first part is false, because the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:118] are not fitting for disbelievers. The second, third and fourth parts are false, because the obedient Muslim, the Muslim with a minor sin, and the Muslim with a major sin after repentance may not, by reason according to the opponent, be punished. And if that is so, then the words ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:118] would not be fitting for them. And if that is false, nothing remains except to say that this intercession was only for the Muslim who committed a major sin before repentance. And if the validity of this intercession for 'Isa, peace be upon him, is established, then its validity for Muhammad ﷺ is established, by necessity, since no one distinguishes between them.

Second: the words of Allah, the Exalted, relating about Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim 14:36]. His words "whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful" cannot be taken to refer to the disbeliever, because he is not, by consensus, deserving of forgiveness. Nor can it be taken to refer to one who committed a minor sin, nor to one who committed a major sin after repentance, because His forgiving them is, according to the opponent, obligatory by reason, so there is no need for intercession for them. Nothing remains except to take it as referring to the one who committed a major sin before repentance. And among what reinforces the indication of these two verses for what we have said is what al-Bayhaqi narrated in the book Shu'ab al-Iman: "that he, peace be upon him, recited the words of Allah, the Exalted, concerning Ibrahim: ﴿Whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim 14:36], and the words of 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:118], the verse, then he raised his hands and said: 'O Allah, my Ummah, my Ummah!' and he wept. Then Allah, the Exalted, said: 'O Jibril, go to Muhammad—and your Lord knows best—and ask him what makes him weep.' Jibril came to him and asked him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed him of what he had said. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'O Jibril, go to Muhammad and say to him: Indeed, We will please you concerning your Ummah, and We will not grieve you.'" Narrated by Muslim in the Sahih.

Third: the words of Allah, the Exalted, in Surah Maryam: ﴿The Day We will gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾ ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ ﴿They will not possess intercession, except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam 19:85–87]. We say: the apparent meaning of the verse does not establish that the intended meaning is that the criminals do not possess intercession for others, or that they do not possess the intercession of others for them, because the verbal noun (masdar), just as its addition to the agent is permissible and good, its addition to the object is also permissible and good. However, we say that interpreting the verse according to the second meaning is preferable, because interpreting it according to the first meaning would be like clarifying the obvious, for everyone knows that the criminals who are driven to Hell as a thirsty herd do not possess intercession for others. So it is determined that it must be interpreted according to the second meaning. Having established this, we say: the verse indicates the occurrence of intercession for the people of major sins, because He said after it: ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam 19:87]. The meaning is that the criminals do not deserve that others intercede for them except if they have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful. So whoever has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful must be included in it. And the person of major sin has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, namely tawhid and Islam, so he must be included under it. The most that can be said is: the Jew has also taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, namely belief in Allah, so he must be included under it. But we say: the application of this (verse) to him was set aside by the necessity of consensus, so it must be acted upon in regard to what lies beyond him.

Fourth: the words of Allah, the Exalted, describing the angels: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:28]. The inference

...that the one who commits a grave sin is approved by Allah, the Exalted, and whoever is approved by Allah, the Exalted, must be among the people of intercession. We say that the one who commits a grave sin is approved by Allah, the Exalted, because he is approved by Allah according to his faith and his monotheism. Whoever is truly described as approved by Allah according to this attribute is truly described as approved by Allah, the Exalted, because being approved by Allah is part of the meaning of our statement "approved by Allah according to his faith." When the compound proposition is true, the simple one is true. Thus it is established that the one who commits a grave sin is approved by Allah. Once this is established, he must be among the people of intercession, because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. This is a negation of intercession except for one who is approved, and the exception from the negation is an affirmation. So it is necessary that the approved one is eligible for their intercession. When it is established that the one who commits a grave sin is included in the intercession of the angels, it is necessary that he is included in the intercession of the prophets and the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ), since there is no one who distinguishes between them.

If it is said: the discussion of this argument proceeds in two respects.

The first: the grave sinner (fasiq) is not approved, so he must not be eligible for the intercession of the angels. If he is not eligible for the intercession of the angels, he must not be eligible for the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ). We say he is not approved because he is not approved according to his wickedness and immorality. Whoever is truly described as not approved according to his wickedness is truly described as not approved by exactly the proof you have mentioned. When it is established that he is not approved, it is necessary that he is not eligible for the intercession of the angels, because His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ indicates the negation of intercession for everyone except the one who is approved. So if the one who commits a grave sin is not approved, he must be included in the negation.

The second respect: the argument from the verse is only complete if His saying ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ is understood to mean "except for one whom Allah approves," that is, whom Allah has chosen. But if we understand it to mean "except for one for whom Allah approves His intercession," then the verse does not indicate anything unless it is established that Allah, the Exalted, approved the intercession of the one who commits a grave sin, and this is the very question at issue.

As for the answer to the first: it is established in logic that the particular propositions (al-muhmalatan, the indefinite ones) do not contradict each other. Our statement "Zayd is learned" and "Zayd is not learned" do not contradict, because it is possible that what is meant is "Zayd is learned in jurisprudence" and "Zayd is not learned in theology." When this is established, the same applies to our statement "the one who commits a grave sin is approved" and "the one who commits a grave sin is not approved." They do not contradict, because it is possible to say: he is approved according to his religion, and not approved according to his wickedness. Also, whenever it is established that he is approved according to his Islam, the name of being approved is established for him. Since what is excepted is merely being approved, and merely being approved is present when he is approved according to his faith, it is necessary that he enter under the exception and be excluded from the excepted negation. When this is so, it is established that he is among the people of intercession.

As for the second question, its answer is that understanding the verse to mean "except for one whom Allah has approved" is more appropriate than understanding it to mean "except for one for whom Allah approves intercession," because on the first interpretation the verse conveys encouragement and incitement to seek the pleasure of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to refrain from His disobedience. On the second interpretation the verse does not convey that. There is no doubt that interpreting the speech of Allah, the Exalted, in the way that yields more benefit is more appropriate.

Fifth: His saying, the Exalted, describing the disbelievers: ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48]. He specified them with this, so it is necessary that the state of the Muslim is the opposite, based on the question of the proof from the implication of speech (dalil al-khitab, the argument from what is implied by the opposite of the stated).

Sixth: His saying, the Exalted, to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad: 19]. The verse indicates that He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to ask forgiveness for all believing men and believing women. We have explained in the commentary on His saying, the Exalted, ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] that the one who commits a grave sin is a believer. When this is so, it is established that Muhammad (ﷺ) asked forgiveness for them. When this is so, it is established that Allah, the Exalted, forgave them. Otherwise, Allah, the Exalted, would have commanded him to supplicate only for His rejecting his supplication, and that would be mere humiliation and harm, which is unfitting for Allah, the Exalted, and for Muhammad (ﷺ). This indicates that when Allah, the Exalted, commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to ask forgiveness for all the sinners, He answered his supplication. This is only complete if He forgave them, and there is no meaning to intercession except this.

Seventh: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it﴾ [al-Nisa': 86]. Allah, the Exalted, commanded all that when someone greets them with a greeting, they should respond with a better greeting or return it. Then He commanded us to greet Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: ﴿O you who have believed, invoke blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56]. The prayer (salah) from Allah is mercy, and there is no doubt that this is a greeting. When we ask Allah for mercy for Muhammad (ﷺ), upon whom be prayers and peace, it becomes necessary, by the requirement of His saying ﴿greet with better than it or return it﴾ [al-Nisa': 86], that Muhammad (ﷺ) do the like, which is to ask Allah, the Exalted, for mercy for all Muslims. This is the meaning of intercession. Then we agree that his supplication, upon him be prayers and peace, is not rejected. So it is necessary that Allah accept his intercession for all, and this is what was to be proven.

Eighth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they, when they had wronged themselves, had come to you and asked forgiveness of Allah, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa': 64]. There is no mention of repentance in the verse, and the verse indicates that whenever the Messenger asks forgiveness for the sinners and wrongdoers, Allah forgives them. This indicates that the Messenger's intercession on behalf of the people of grave sins is accepted in this world, so it is necessary that it be accepted in the Hereafter, because there is no one who distinguishes.

Ninth: We are agreed on the obligation of intercession for Muhammad (ﷺ). Its effect is either an increase in benefits or the removal of harms. The first is false, for otherwise we would be interceding for the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, whenever we ask Allah, the Exalted, to increase his favour when we say: "O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad." When the first part is false, the second is determined, and this is what was to be proven. If it is said: we are not called intercessors for Muhammad (ﷺ) for two reasons:

The first: the intercessor must necessarily be higher in rank than the one for whom he intercedes. We, although we seek good for him, upon him be prayers and peace, but since we are of lower rank than him, upon him be prayers and peace, it is not correct to describe us as intercessors for him.

The second: Abu al-Husayn (al-Basri) said: asking benefits for another is only intercession if the performance of those benefits is for the sake of his request, and without it they would not have been done, or his request has an effect on their performance. But if they would be done whether he asks for them or not, and the purpose of the asker is to draw near to the one asked by this, even if the one asked does not deserve an additional benefit by this request, then this is not intercession for him. Do you not see that if a sultan intends to appoint his son to a position, and some of his supporters urge him to do so while he would do it in any case, whether they urged him or not, and they intend by that to draw near to the sultan so as to gain a standing with him, it is not said that they intercede for the sultan's son? Our situation regarding the Messenger (ﷺ) is the same in what we ask for him from Allah, the Exalted. So it is not correct that we are intercessors.

The answer to the first: we do not concede that rank is a condition in intercession. The evidence for this is that the intercessor (shafi') is so named as derived from "shaf'" (pair, joining), and this meaning does not require rank. So their claim falls. By this same consideration the second question also falls.

Moreover, we say in answer to the second question: although we are certain that Allah, the Exalted, honours His Messenger and exalts him, whether the community asks for it or not, we do not know with certainty that it is impossible that He increases his honour because of the community's request, in such a way that without the community's request this increase would not have occurred. Since this possibility is permissible, it must remain permissible that we are intercessors for the Messenger (ﷺ). And since this has been refuted by the consensus of the community, their claim is refuted.

Tenth: His saying, the Exalted, describing the angels: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. The grave sinner is among the believers, so he must be included among those for whom the angels ask forgiveness. At most, what follows this is His saying: ﴿So forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. However, this does not require restricting that general statement, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that when a general term is followed by mention of some of its categories, this does not necessitate restricting that general term to that particular category.

Eleventh: the reports indicating that intercession is attained by the people of grave sins. We mention from them three aspects.

The first: his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "My intercession is for the people of grave sins from among my community." The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) said: the objection to it is from three aspects.

One of them: it is a single report (khabar al-wahid, a report transmitted by one or few narrators, not reaching the level of certainty) which came in opposition to the Qur'an. We have shown that many verses indicate the negation of this intercession, and a single report which comes in opposition to the Qur'an must be rejected.

The second: it indicates that his intercession is only for the people of grave sins, and this is not permissible, because his intercession is a great station, so restricting it to the people of grave sins alone implies depriving the people of reward of it, and that is not permissible, since at least equality is required.

The third: this question is not among the practical matters (al-masa'il al-'amaliyyah), so it is not permissible to rely in it on conjecture, and a single report only yields conjecture, so it is not permissible to hold to this report in this question. Then, even if we grant the authenticity of the report, it would have possibilities:

One of them: that what is meant by it is interrogation in the sense of denial, meaning: "Is my intercession for the people of grave sins from my community?" just as what is meant by His saying: ﴿This is my Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 77] is "Is this my Lord?"

The second: the word "grave sin" (kabirah) is not specific, neither in its original linguistic usage nor in the usage of the Sharia, to disobedience. Rather, just as it covers disobedience, it also covers obedience. He, the Exalted, said about the prayer: ﴿And indeed it is burdensome except for the humble﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45]. When this is so, his saying "for the people of grave sins" does not necessarily mean the people of grave acts of disobedience, but perhaps it means the people of great acts of obedience. If it is said: grant that the word "grave" covers both acts of obedience and acts of disobedience, but his saying "people of grave sins" is a plural form with the definite article, so it implies generality, and therefore the report must indicate the establishment of intercession for everyone who is among the people of grave sins, whether among the people of great acts of obedience or great acts of disobedience. We say: although the word "grave sins" is general, the word "people" (ahl) is singular in form, so it does not imply generality. It suffices for the truth of the report that one person among the people of grave sins is meant, so we interpret it as referring to the person who performs all acts of obedience, for it suffices in acting upon the content of the hadith to interpret it in this way.

**Thirdly:** Grant that it is necessary to restrict "the people of major sins" to "the people of major sins" who have not repented. Still, the people of major sins are more general than the people of major sins after repentance or before repentance. So we restrict the report to the people of major sins after repentance, and the effect of intercession will be that God bestows on him, by grace, the reward of his earlier acts of obedience that had been nullified by his immorality. We grant that the report indicates what you say, but it is contradicted by what is reported from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Is my intercession for the people of major sins from my Community?" He mentioned it with the interrogative particle *hamzah*, in the manner of denial.

Al-Hasan reported from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "I have reserved my intercession only for the people of major sins from my Community."

Know that, in fairness, it is not possible to rely on this report alone in a matter such as this, but rather on the totality of the reports concerning intercession. Indeed, the other reports indicate the invalidity of all these interpretations.

**Second:** Abu Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Every prophet has a granted supplication, and every prophet hastened to make his supplication. But I have kept my supplication as an intercession for my Community on the Day of Resurrection. It will reach whoever of my Community dies without associating anything with God, God willing." Muslim narrated it in the *Sahih*. The argument from it is that the hadith is explicit that his intercession, peace be upon him, attains everyone of his Community who dies without associating anything with God, and the person who committed a major sin is likewise, so it is obligatory that intercession attain him.

**Third:** From Abu Hurayrah, who said: "One day meat was brought to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and a foreleg was lifted to him, which he liked. He took a bite from it and then said: 'I am the master of mankind on the Day of Resurrection. Do you know why?' They said: 'No, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'God will gather the first and the last in one plain. The caller will make them hear, and the sight will reach them, and the sun will draw near. People will feel such distress and anguish that they cannot bear it. Some people will say to others: "Do you not see what you are in? Do you not see what has reached you? Will you not go to one who will intercede for you with your Lord?" Some will say to others: "Your father is Adam." So they will come to Adam and say: "O Adam, you are the father of mankind. God created you with His hand, breathed into you of His spirit, commanded the angels and they prostrated to you. Intercede for us with your Lord. Do you not see what we are in? Do you not see what has befallen us?" He will say to them: "My Lord has become angry today with an anger like which He has never been angry before, and will never be angry after it like it. He forbade me from the tree, and I disobeyed Him. Myself, myself! Go to someone other than me. Go to Noah." They will come to Noah and say: "O Noah, you are the first of the messengers to the people of the earth, and God named you a grateful servant. Intercede for us with your Lord. Do you not see what we are in?" He will say to them: "My Lord has become angry today with an anger like which He has never been angry before, and will never be angry after it like it. I had a supplication which I made against my people. Myself, myself! Go to someone other than me. Go to Abraham." They will come to Abraham, peace be upon him, and say: "You are Abraham, the prophet of God and His intimate friend from among the people of the earth. Intercede for us with your Lord. Do you not see what we are in?" Abraham will say to them: "My Lord has become angry today with an anger like which He has never been angry before, and will never be angry after it like it." And he mentioned his lies. "Myself, myself! Go to someone other than me. Go to Moses." They will come to Moses and say: "O Moses, you are the Messenger of God. God preferred you over people with His message and His speech. Intercede for us with your Lord. Do you not see what we are in?" Moses will say to them: "My Lord has become angry today with an anger like which He has never been angry before, and will never be angry after it like it. I killed a soul which I had not been commanded to kill. Myself, myself! Go to someone other than me. Go to Jesus, son of Mary." They will come to Jesus and say: "You are the Messenger of God and His word which He cast to Mary, and a spirit from Him, and you spoke to people in the cradle. Intercede for us with your Lord. Do you not see what we are in?" Jesus will say to them: "My Lord has become angry today with an anger like which He has never been angry before, and will never be angry after it like it." He did not mention any sin of his own. "Myself, myself! Go to someone other than me. Go to Muhammad." They will come to me and say: "O Muhammad, you are the Messenger of God and the seal of the prophets. God has forgiven you what preceded of your sin and what followed. Intercede for us with your Lord. Do you not see what we are in?" So I will set out and seek permission to come before my Lord, and permission will be granted to me. When I see my Lord, I will fall prostrate, and He will leave me as long as He wills to leave me. Then He will say: "O Muhammad, raise your head, speak and you will be heard, ask and you will be given, and intercede and your intercession will be accepted." So I will praise my Lord with praises which He taught me. Then I will intercede, and He will set a limit for me, and I will admit them into Paradise. Then I will return, and when I see my Lord, the Blessed and Exalted, I will fall prostrate before Him, and He will leave me as long as God wills to leave me. Then He will say: "Raise your head, speak and you will be heard, ask and you will be given, and intercede and your intercession will be accepted." So I will praise my Lord with praises which He taught me. Then I will intercede, and He will set a limit for me, and I will admit them into Paradise. Then I will return, and when I see my Lord I will fall prostrate before Him, and He will leave me as long as God wills to leave me. Then He will say: "O Muhammad, raise your head, speak and you will be heard, ask and you will be given, and intercede and your intercession will be accepted." So I will praise my Lord with praises which He taught me. Then I will intercede, and He will set a limit for me, and I will admit them into Paradise. Then I will return and say: "O Lord, there remains in the Fire only those whom the Qur'an has detained," meaning: those upon whom eternal abiding has become obligatory.'"

Most of this hadith is narrated in its wording in the two *Sahihs*.

The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites) said: The discussion of this hadith and its like takes several aspects:

First: These reports are lengthy, so it is not possible that their wording be preserved as the words of the Messenger ﷺ. The apparent meaning is that the narrator related them in his own words, and on this supposition none of them is a proof.

Second: They report one single event, and they were transmitted in different forms with additions and omissions, and this too exposes them to suspicion.

Third: They contain anthropomorphism, which is also false and exposes them to suspicion.

Fourth: They contradict the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, which also exposes them to suspicion.

Fifth: They report a great event whose transmission would be strongly motivated. Had it been sound, it would have had to reach the level of *tawatur* (mass transmission). Since it did not, suspicion has entered them.

Sixth: Relying on a single-transmitted report (*khabar al-wahid*), which yields only probable knowledge, in matters that are definitive is not permissible.

Our companions (the Ash'aris) answered these objections: Although each of these reports is transmitted by single chains, they are very numerous, and among them there is one common element, namely that people deserving punishment will come out of the Fire through intercession. This meaning thus becomes transmitted by way of *tawatur*, and so it is a proof. And God knows best.

The answer to all the Mu'tazilite proofs, in one word, is this: their proofs for negating intercession establish the negation of all kinds of intercession, while our proofs for establishing intercession establish a specific intercession. When the general and the specific conflict, the specific is given precedence over the general. So our proofs take precedence over theirs. Then we address each of the aspects they mentioned with a separate answer:

As for the first aspect, which is their reliance on God's saying: ﴿and no intercession will be accepted from it﴾: Grant that what matters is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the occasion of revelation. Still, restricting such a general statement to that particular occasion requires only the slightest evidence. When the proofs establishing the existence of intercession are present, it becomes necessary to resort to restricting it.

As for the second aspect, which is God's saying: ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Ghafir 18]: The answer is that His saying ﴿The wrongdoers have no intimate friend nor intercessor﴾ is the contradictory of our statement, "The wrongdoers have an intimate friend and an intercessor." But our statement "The wrongdoers have an intimate friend and an intercessor" is a universal affirmative, and the contradictory of a universal affirmative is a particular negative. For a particular negative to be true, it suffices that the negation be realized in some cases, and it is not required that the negation be realized in all cases. On this basis, we say what it implies, because in our view there is for some of the wrongdoers neither an intimate friend nor an intercessor who is answered, namely the disbelievers. But to judge that each one of them has no intimate friend and no intercessor is not the case.

As for the third aspect, which is His saying: ﴿before a day comes in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾ [al-Baqarah 254]: The answer to it is what preceded in the first aspect.

As for the fourth aspect, which is His saying: ﴿and the wrongdoers have no helpers﴾ [al-Baqarah 270]: The answer to it is that it is the contradictory of our statement, "The wrongdoers have helpers," and this is a universal affirmative. So His saying ﴿and the wrongdoers have no helpers﴾ is a particular negative, and its meaning is the negation of generality, and the negation of generality does not establish a general negation.

As for the fifth aspect, which is His saying: ﴿so the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir 48]: This is directed at the disbelievers, and by means of restriction it indicates the opposite of this ruling with respect to the believers.

As for the sixth aspect, which is His saying: ﴿and they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 28]: The discussion of it has already preceded.

As for the seventh aspect, which is the saying of the Muslims: "O God, make us among the people of the intercession of Muhammad ﷺ": The answer to it is that in our view intercession has an effect in bringing about a desired matter, and by this I mean the common element between bringing benefits beyond what is deserved and removing harms that are merited by sins. This common element does not depend on the servant being disobedient, so the objection is dispelled.

As for the eighth aspect, which is their reliance on His saying: ﴿And indeed the wicked are in Hellfire﴾ [al-Infitar 14]: The discussion of it will come, God willing, in the question of threat (*al-wa'id*).

As for the ninth aspect, which is their saying that there is no evidence indicating God's permission for intercession for the people of major sins: The answer is that this is disputed, and the proof against it is what we have cited of the proofs indicating the occurrence of this intercession.

As for the tenth aspect, which is His saying concerning the angels: ﴿So forgive those who repent﴾ [Ghafir 7]: The answer to it is what we have explained, that the particularity of the last part of this verse does not undermine the generality of its first part.

As for the hadiths, they indicate that Muhammad ﷺ does not intercede for some people, nor is he interceded for in some stations of the Resurrection. That does not indicate that he does not intercede at all for anyone among the people of major sins, nor that he is prevented from intercession in all stations.

What we affirm is that God has made clear that none of the interceders is granted intercession except by God's permission. Perhaps the Messenger was not permitted in some places and some times, so he is not granted intercession in that place or at that time. Then he will be permitted in another place and at another time for intercession, and he will intercede there. And God knows best.

The philosophers, in interpreting intercession (shafa'ah), said: the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud) is universal in overflow (ʿamm al-fayd) and complete in bounty (tamm al-jud). Therefore, wherever [the overflow] does not occur, it does not occur only because the recipient is not disposed (musta'idd) [to receive it]. It is possible that a thing is not disposed to receive the overflow from the Necessary Existent, except that it is disposed to receive that overflow from something before it that comes from the Necessary Existent. That thing is then like an intermediary between the Necessary Existent and that first thing. An example of this in the sensible world: the sun shines only upon what faces it, and since the ceiling of a house does not face the body of the sun, it has no disposition to receive light from the sun. However, if a basin full of clear water is placed and the light of the sun falls upon it, that light is reflected from that water onto the ceiling.
