Thus that clear water becomes an intermediary in the arrival of light from the disc of the sun to the ceiling, which does not face the sun. Likewise, the spirits of the prophets are like intermediaries between the Necessary Existent and the spirits of the common folk in the arrival of the Necessary Existent's overflow to the spirits of the common folk. This is what they said about intercession, as a derivation from their principles.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 49 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted on you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, first mentioned His blessings upon the Children of Israel in summary, He then explained the categories of those blessings in detail, so that the reminder would be more effective and the proof more compelling. It is as if He said: Remember My blessing; remember when We delivered you; remember when We divided the sea for you. These are favours, and what is mentioned in this verse is the first favour.

As for His saying, ﴿And when We delivered you﴾, it is also read as anjaynakum and najjaytukum. Al-Qaffal said: The root of al-injaʾ and at-tanjiyah is deliverance, and the separation of one thing from another so that they do not connect. They are two dialects: najja and anjā, and najā by itself (intransitive). They called an elevated place najwah, because whoever reaches it is saved (najā), that is, delivered; and because an elevated place is separated from what lies below it, so it is as if it is delivered from it.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: The origin of āl is ahl (people), which is why it is diminutized as uhayl; its hāʾ was changed into an alif, and its usage was restricted to people of high status and rank, such as kings and their like. One does not say āl al-ḥajjām (the cupper's people) or āl al-iskāf (the cobbler's people). ʿĪsā said: ahl is more general than āl. One says ahl al-Kūfah, ahl al-balad, and ahl al-ʿilm, but one does not say āl al-Kūfah, āl al-balad, or āl al-ʿilm. So it is as if he said: the ahl of a thing are its particular members by way of their predominance over it, while the āl of a man are his particular members by way of kinship or companionship. It is reported from Abū ʿUbaydah that he heard an eloquent speaker say: the people of Makkah are the āl of God.

As for Pharaoh (Fir'awn), it is a title for whoever ruled Egypt from the Amalekites, just as Caesar (Qayṣar) is for the ruler of the Romans, Heraclius (Hiraql) for the ruler of the Romans, Khosrow (Kisrā) for the ruler of the Persians, Tubbaʿ for the ruler of Yemen, and Khaqan for the ruler of the Turks. Scholars differed concerning Pharaoh in two respects:

The first: they differed about his name. Ibn Juraij transmitted from a people that they said: Muṣʿab ibn Rayyān. Ibn Ishaq said: he was al-Walid ibn Muṣʿab, and none of the Pharaohs was more severe in harshness or harder of heart than him. Wahb ibn Munabbih mentioned that the People of the Two Books said that the name of Pharaoh was Qābūs, and that he was from the Copts.

The second: Ibn Wahb said that the Pharaoh of Joseph, peace be upon him, is the Pharaoh of Moses. This is not correct, for between Joseph's entry into Egypt and Moses's entry into it there were more than four hundred years. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: he is other than the Pharaoh of Joseph, and that the Pharaoh of Joseph was named al-Rayyān ibn al-Walid.

As for "the people of Pharaoh", there is no doubt that what is meant here is those who were among Pharaoh's people, namely those who resolved to destroy the Children of Israel, so that He, exalted is He, would be their deliverer from them through the favours He bestowed, which entailed their survival and the destruction of Pharaoh and his people.

As for His saying, ﴿yasūmūnakum﴾, it comes from sāmahu khasfan, meaning he inflicted injustice upon him. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said:
When the king inflicts humiliation upon the people, we refuse to accept humiliation among us.

Its root is from sāma al-silʿah, meaning he sought it. It is as if it means: they desire for you the worst torment and intend it for you. The word sūʾ is the verbal noun of sāʾa in the sense of the bad (al-sayyiʾ). One says: I seek refuge in God from the evil of character (sūʾ al-khulq) and evil conduct (sūʾ al-fiʿl), meaning their ugliness. The meaning of sūʾ al-ʿadhāb (the worst torment), and torment is all of it bad, the most severe and most difficult of it being its worst, as if its ugliness increased by its being attributed to sāʾa.

The exegetes differed about what is meant by "the worst torment". Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: he made them slaves and servants to himself, and divided them into categories of labour: one group built for him, another group ploughed for him, another group planted for him. They were engaged in his works, and whoever was not in some kind of his work was ordered to have a poll tax imposed upon him, which he would pay. As-Suddi said: he assigned them to the filthy and arduous labours, such as cleaning latrines, working with clay, and carving mountains. God, exalted is He, related of the Children of Israel that they said to Moses: ﴿We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 129]. Moses said to Pharaoh: ﴿And this is a favour you claim to bestow upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Shuʿaraʾ: 22].

Know that a person being under the hand of another, such that he disposes of him as he wishes, especially when he employs him in arduous, difficult and filthy labours, is among the most severe kinds of torment, to the point that one in such a state may sometimes wish for death. So God, exalted is He, explained His great blessings upon them by delivering them from that. Then He followed that with another blessing greater than it, saying: ﴿slaughtering your sons﴾, meaning they killed the male children and spared the females.

Here there are discussions.

First discussion: slaying the males but not the females is harmful in several respects:

One: slaying the sons entails the annihilation of men, and that entails the cutting off of offspring, for when women are alone they have no effect whatsoever in this, and that ultimately leads to the destruction of both men and women.

Two: the destruction of men entails the corruption of women's interests in matters of livelihood, for a woman may wish for death, once the care and support of men has ceased for her, because of the hardship of life that falls upon her when alone. So this trait becomes a great affliction, and deliverance from it is in proportion to its greatness.

Three: killing a child after a long pregnancy, the bearing of toil, and strong hope of benefiting from the newborn, is among the greatest torments, for killing him in such a state is more severe than killing one who has remained for a long period enjoying life and delighted by his circumstances. So God's blessing in delivering them from that is according to the severity of the trial in it.

Four: sons are more beloved to parents than daughters, which is why most people find daughters burdensome and dislike them even if their males are many. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when one of them is given tidings of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief. He hides himself from the people because of the evil of what he has been given tidings of﴾ [al-Nahl: 58], and so on. For this reason He forbade the Arabs from burying daughters alive by His saying: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra: 31]. They used to bury only females, not males.

Five: the survival of women without men entails that they become the bedfellows of enemies, and that is the utmost of humiliation and disgrace.

Second discussion: in this surah He mentioned ﴿yudhabbihūna﴾ without a waw, whereas in the surah of Ibrahim He mentioned it with a waw. The reason is that if His saying ﴿yasūmūnakum sūʾ al-ʿadhāb﴾ is taken as explained by His saying ﴿yudhabbihūna abnāʾakum﴾, no waw is needed. But if His saying ﴿yasūmūnakum sūʾ al-ʿadhāb﴾ is taken as explained by the other burdensome tasks apart from slaughter, and slaughter is taken as something other than the worst torment, a waw is needed. In both places the reading admits both possibilities. However, the benefit that may be the intended one in the mention of the conjunctive particle in the surah of Ibrahim is that He said before that verse: ﴿And We had already sent Moses with Our signs, saying: Bring your people out of darkness into light, and remind them of the days of God﴾ [Ibrahim: 5]. Reminding them of the days of God is only achieved by enumerating God's blessings. Therefore it was necessary that what is meant by His saying ﴿yasūmūnakum sūʾ al-ʿadhāb﴾ be one kind of torment, and what is meant by His saying ﴿wa-yudhabbihūna abnāʾakum﴾ be another kind, so that deliverance from both would be two kinds of blessing. Hence the conjunctive was required there. As for this verse, the command was only to remind of the genus of blessing, which is His saying: ﴿Remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]. So whether what is meant by sūʾ al-ʿadhāb is slaughter or something else, the reminder of the genus of blessing is achieved. Thus the difference is clear.

Third discussion: some said that by His saying ﴿yudhabbihūna abnāʾakum﴾ He meant the men, not the children, so that it would stand in contrast to the women, since the women are the adult females. Likewise, by "sons" is meant the adult men. They said: he used to order the killing of men whom he feared would rebel against him and gather to corrupt his affairs. But most exegetes hold that the verse refers to children, not adults, and this is preferable for several reasons:

First: taking the word "sons" in its apparent sense.

Second: it would have been impossible to kill all the men given their great number.

Third: they needed them for employment in arduous crafts.

Fourth: if it were so, there would be no meaning to the casting of Moses, peace be upon him, into the chest while still a small child.

As for the claim that it must be understood as men in order to stand in contrast to the women, there are two answers:

First: when the sons were killed while still in childhood, they did not become men, so it was not permissible to apply the name "men" to them. As for the daughters, since they were not killed but reached the stage of womanhood, it was permissible to apply the name "women" to them.

Second: some said: by His saying ﴿and spare your women﴾ is meant that they searched the modesty of the woman, that is, her private part, to see whether she was pregnant or not. This was refuted on the ground that what is in their wombs, if it is not apparent to the eyes, is not known by searching, nor can it be reached and extracted by hand.

Fourth discussion: concerning the cause of the killing of the sons, they mentioned several views:

One: the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, that there reached Pharaoh and his circle what God had promised Abraham, that He would place among his offspring prophets and kings. They feared that, and their word agreed to prepare men with them carrying knives who would roam among the Children of Israel, and whenever they found a male newborn they would slaughter him. When they saw their elders dying and their young being slaughtered, they feared annihilation, for then they would not find anyone to perform the arduous tasks. So they began to kill in one year and spare in the next.

Two: the statement of as-Suddi: Pharaoh saw a fire coming from Jerusalem until it enveloped the houses of Egypt, burning the Copts and sparing the Children of Israel. Pharaoh summoned the priests and asked them about that. They said: there will come out of Jerusalem one at whose hand the destruction of the Copts will be.

Three: the astrologers informed Pharaoh of that and specified the year for him, and so he used to kill their sons in that year. The closest of these is the first, because what is derived from the science of interpretation and the science of the stars is not a detailed matter; otherwise that would detract from the foretelling of the unseen being a miracle, but rather it would be a general matter. And it is not the apparent condition of a rational person to undertake such a great action on its basis. If it is said: Pharaoh was an unbeliever in God, so he would be even more an unbeliever in the messengers; and if that is so, how could he undertake this great action on the basis of Abraham's report about him? We say: perhaps Pharaoh was a knower of God and of the truthfulness of the prophets, but he was an unbeliever of denial and obstinacy. Or it may be said: he was doubtful and perplexed in his religion, and he considered that Abraham might be truthful, so he took that action as a precaution.

Fifth discussion: know that the benefit in mentioning this blessing is in several respects:

One: since these matters which God mentioned are among the greatest trials by which people are tested at the hands of kings and oppressors, God's deliverance of them from these trials became among the greatest blessings. That is because they witnessed the destruction of the one who sought to destroy them, and they saw the humiliation of the one who went to extremes in their abasement. There is no doubt that this is among the greatest blessings, and magnifying a blessing requires submission and obedience, and entails the utmost ugliness of disobedience and obstinacy. For this reason God, exalted is He, mentioned this great blessing, as an exaggeration in establishing the proof against them and cutting off their excuse.

Secondly: When they knew that they were in the utmost humiliation while their adversary was in the utmost power, yet they were in the right and their adversary was in the wrong, the humiliation of the righteous inevitably ceased and the power of the wrongdoers came to nothing. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Do not be deceived by Muhammad's poverty and the scarcity of his helpers at present, for he is in the right, and power will inevitably turn to his side and humiliation to the side of his enemies."

Thirdly: By this, Allah, exalted is He, drew attention to the fact that sovereignty is in the hand of Allah, who gives it to whomever He wills. So a person should not be deceived by the power of this world; rather, he must strive to seek the power of the Hereafter.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord﴾, al-Qaffal said: The root of the word is from ibtila' (trial), which means testing and examination. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35], and He said: ﴿And We tested them with good deeds and bad deeds﴾ [al-A'raf 168]. The word bala' (trial) applies to both types, so it is said of a blessing that it is a bala', and of a severe ordeal that it is a bala'. Most often, it is said of good (i.e., blessing) ibla' and of evil bala', though one may sometimes be used in place of the other. Zuhayr said:

"May Allah reward with goodness what the two of them did with you,
and what tested them, the best of tests, is that which tests (i.e., gives blessing)."

Having understood this, we say: bala' here means an ordeal if the word "dhalikum" ("that") refers to the deed of Pharaoh, and it means a blessing if it refers to the deliverance. Taking it as a blessing is preferable, because it is that which proceeded from the Lord, exalted is He, and because the point of argument against the Jews is Allah's bounty upon their forefathers.

This is the second blessing. His saying ﴿and We divided﴾ means We separated parts of it from one another until paths were made in it for you. The word is also read ﴿faraqna﴾ with a shadda, meaning "We made distinct" (faṣṣalna). One says faraqa bayna al-shay'ayn and faraqa bayna al-ashya'. The paths were twelve, according to the number of the tribes (asbāṭ).

If you ask: what is the meaning of "for you" (bikum)? We answer: there are two interpretations.

The first: they travelled along it, and the water parted as they passed, so it was as if He had divided it by means of them, just as two things are divided by what lies between them.

The second: We divided it on account of you and on account of your deliverance.

Next, there are several investigations.

**First investigation:** It is related that when God, exalted is He, wanted to drown Pharaoh and the Copts, and matters reached the point where, in God's knowledge, none of them would believe, He commanded Moses, peace be upon him, that the Children of Israel should borrow the jewellery of the Copts. This was for two purposes. The first was that they would go out after them for the sake of the wealth. The second was that their wealth would remain in their hands.

Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended in the evening and said to Moses: "Take your people out by night." This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: Travel by night with My servants﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 52]. They numbered six hundred thousand souls, for they were twelve tribes, each tribe of fifty thousand.

When Moses, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel, the news reached Pharaoh, and he said: "Do not follow them until the rooster crows." The narrator said: "By God, no rooster crowed that night." When morning came, Pharaoh called for a sheep, which was slaughtered, and then he said: "I will not finish taking the liver of this sheep until six hundred thousand of the Copts have gathered to me." Qatādah said: "There gathered to him a thousand thousand and two hundred thousand souls, each one of them on a noble horse, and they followed them in the daytime." This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 60], that is, after the sun had risen.

﴿When the two groups came in sight of each other, the companions of Moses said: "We are certainly going to be overtaken."﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 61] Moses said: ﴿"No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 62]

[Page 67]

When Moses travelled with them and came to the sea, Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn said to him: "Where has your Lord commanded you?" Moses said: "Straight ahead of you," and he pointed to the sea. Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn then urged his horse into the sea, and it walked in the water until it reached the depth. The horse swam with him on it, then returned and said to him: "O Moses, where has your Lord commanded you?" He said: "The sea." He said: "By God, you have not lied." He did this three times. Then God revealed to him: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff,﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 63] and ﴿it parted, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 63]. The sea split into twelve mountains, and in each one there was a path. He said to them: "Enter." There was mud in it, so the east wind blew and the sea dried, and every path in it became dry land, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So strike for them a dry path through the sea﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 77]. Each tribe took a path and entered it. They said to Moses: "Some of us cannot see the others." So Moses struck the sea with his staff, and openings and windows appeared between the paths, and they could see one another.

Then Pharaoh followed them. When he reached the shore of the sea, he saw Iblīs standing there, and Iblīs forbade him from entering. Pharaoh resolved not to enter the sea. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came upon a female horse (ḥajrah) and went ahead of Pharaoh, who was on a stallion (faḥl), and Pharaoh's horse followed it and entered the sea. When Pharaoh entered the sea, Michael cried out to them: "Join your last to your first." When they had all entered the sea, God commanded the water, and it came down upon them. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were watching﴾.

It was also said that this day was the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, and Moses, peace be upon him, fasted on that day in thanks to God, exalted is He.

**Second investigation:** Know that this event included many blessings, in both religion and worldly life. As for the worldly blessings in regard to Moses, peace be upon him, they are of several kinds:

First: when they found themselves in that narrow place, with Pharaoh and his armies behind them and the sea before them, if they stopped, the enemy would overtake them and destroy them with the severest punishment, and if they went forward, they would drown. No fear could be greater than this. Then God delivered them by splitting the sea, and no relief could be greater than that.

Second: God singled them out with this great blessing and this dazzling miracle, and this was a cause of the manifestation of their honour before God, exalted is He.

Third: they witnessed that God destroyed their enemies. It is known that deliverance from such a trial is among the greatest blessings, how much more so when there is also this great honour and the destruction of the enemy.

Fourth: He made them inherit their land, their homes, their bounties and their wealth.

Fifth: when God drowned the family of Pharaoh, He freed the Children of Israel from them. This is a great blessing, for they had been afraid of them. Had God delivered Moses and his people from that predicament without destroying Pharaoh and his people, the fear would have remained, since they might have regrouped, contrived some scheme and intended to harm Moses, peace be upon him, and his people. But when God drowned them, He completely cut off the source of fear.

Sixth: this drowning took place in the presence of the Children of Israel, and this is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while you were watching﴾.

As for the religious blessings in regard to Moses, peace be upon him, they are of several kinds:

First: when the people of Moses witnessed that dazzling miracle, doubts and suspicions were removed from their hearts. The indication of such a miracle of the existence of the wise Creator and of the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him, approaches necessary knowledge. It is as if God lifted from them the burden of careful reflection and of arduous reasoning.

Second: when they saw that, it became a motive for them to remain steadfast in confirming Moses and submitting to him, and it became a motive for the people of Pharaoh to abandon denying Moses, peace be upon him, and to proceed to deny Pharaoh.

Third: they came to know that affairs are in the hand of God, for there is no greater honour in the world than what Pharaoh had, and no harder hardship than what the Children of Israel had. Then God, in a single moment, made the mighty humble and the humble mighty. This necessitates the heart's detachment from the attachments of this world and its complete turning to the service of the Creator and reliance upon Him in all affairs.

As for the blessings that accrue to the community of Muḥammad ﷺ from the mention of this story, they are many:

First: it serves as a proof for Muḥammad ﷺ against the People of the Book, for it was known of Muḥammad, peace be upon him, that he was unlettered: he neither read nor wrote, nor did he mix with the People of the Book. When he presented to them detailed accounts of their history that can only be known from books, they knew that he was reporting from revelation and that he was truthful. This became a proof for him, peace be upon him, against the Jews, and a proof for us in confirming him.

Second: when we picture what happened to them and against them through these momentous events, we know that whoever opposes God is wretched in this world and the next, and whoever obeys Him is happy in this world and the next. This becomes an encouragement for us to obedience and a deterrent from disobedience.

Third: the community of Moses, peace be upon him, although they were singled out with these manifest miracles and dazzling proofs, opposed Moses, peace be upon him, in matters, to the point that they said: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'rāf: 138]. As for the community of Muḥammad ﷺ, although his miracle is the Qur'an, whose miraculous nature is only recognised through subtle proofs, they submitted to Muḥammad ﷺ and did not oppose him in any matter whatsoever. This indicates that the community of Muḥammad ﷺ is superior to the community of Moses, peace be upon him.

There remain two questions regarding the verse.

**First question:** The splitting of the sea, as a proof of the existence of the powerful Creator and as a proof of the truthfulness of Moses, is like a matter of necessary knowledge. How, then, is its occurrence permissible during the time of obligation (taklīf)?

The answer: as for our position, it is clear. As for the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), al-Ka'bī gave a general answer: among the obligated there are those who are far from perceptiveness and intelligence and are characterised by dullness, and the general body of the Children of Israel were like this. So they needed, for awakening, to witness great signs such as the splitting of the sea, the lifting of Mount Sinai, and the raising of the dead. Do you not see that after this they passed by a people devoted to idols of their own, and they said: ﴿O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'rāf: 138]? As for the Arabs, their condition was different, for they were at the height of perfection in intellect. Therefore God, exalted is He, dealt with them only through subtle proofs and delicate miracles.

**Second question:** When Pharaoh witnessed the splitting of the sea, and he was rational, he must have known that this was not his own doing, but that there must be a powerful, knowing Agent unlike all other powerful beings. How, then, did he remain in disbelief despite that? If you say: he was a knower of his Lord, but he was a disbeliever out of obstinacy and denial. I say: if he knew this in his heart, how could he resolve to throw himself into destruction and enter the sea, when at that moment he was like one compelled to know the existence of the Creator and the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him?

The answer: love of a thing makes one blind and deaf. His love of rank and deception drove him to plunge into that destruction.

\* \* \*

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while you were watching﴾, there are several interpretations:

First: you were seeing the waves of the sea dash upon Pharaoh and his people.

Second: the people of Moses, peace be upon him, asked him to show them what God would do to them, so Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to show them them. The sea then cast them out, one thousand thousand and two hundred thousand souls, together with Pharaoh. They looked at them floating, and the sea did not accept any one of them because of the wickedness of their disbelief. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today We will save your body, that you may be a sign to those after you﴾ [Yūnus: 92], that is, We will bring you out from the narrowness of the sea into the wide expanse, so that people may see you and you may be a lesson to them.

Third: the meaning is "while you were close to them," where you were facing and confronting them, even though they could not see them with their eyes. Al-Farrā' said: this is like your saying: "I struck you while your family were looking at you, yet they did not come to your aid." One says this when his family is near him even though they do not see him, and its meaning returns to knowledge.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 51–52 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful﴾.

Know that this is the third favour. As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿وإذ واعدنا (wa-idh wā'adnā)﴾, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read "وإذ وعدنا موسى" (wa-idh wa'adnā Mūsā) without an alif in this surah, in al-A'raf and in Ta-Ha, while the rest read "واعدنا" (wā'adnā) with an alif in the three places. As for the reading without an alif, its basis is clear, because the promise came from God, Exalted is He, and al-muwā'adah (mutual promising) is a form of mufā'alah which requires two parties. As for the reading with an alif, it has several explanations:

The first: although the promise came from God, Exalted is He, its acceptance came from Moses, peace be upon him, and the acceptance of a promise resembles the promise itself, because the one who accepts a promise must say, "I will do that."

The second: al-Qaffal said: It is not far-fetched that a human promises God, and its meaning is that he covenants with God.

The third: it is a matter that took place between two parties, so it is permissible to say "wā'adnā."

The fourth, and it is the strongest: God, Exalted is He, promised him revelation, and he promised God that he would come to the appointed place at Mount Tur. As for Moses, there are several points concerning him:

The first: his measure is fu'lā, and the mīm in it is original, derived from māsa yamīsu when he swaggered in his walk, and Moses, peace be upon him, was such.

The second: his measure is mufil, so the mīm in it is additional, and it is from awsaytu al-shajarah, when I took off the leaves that were on the tree; it is as if he was named thus because of his baldness.

The third: it is a compound word from two words in Hebrew: "mū" is water in their language, and "sā" is tree. He was named thus because his mother placed him in the chest when she feared for him from Pharaoh, and cast him into the sea. The waves of the sea pushed him until they brought him between trees near Pharaoh's house. Then the maidservants of Asiyah, Pharaoh's wife, came out to bathe, found the chest, and took it. So he was named after the place where he was found, which is water and tree.

Know that the first two explanations are utterly corrupt. As for the first, the Children of Israel and the Copts did not speak the language of the Arabs, so it is not permissible that this is what they meant. As for the second, this word is a proper name, and a proper name conveys no meaning in its essence. The closest is the third explanation, and it is a matter customary among people. As for his lineage, peace be upon him, he is Moses son of 'Imran son of Yashhar son of Qahath son of Lawi son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿forty nights﴾, there are several discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: Moses, peace be upon him, had said to the Children of Israel: "If we come out of the sea safe, I will bring you a clear book from God containing what is obligatory for you of doing and abstaining." When Moses crossed the sea with the Children of Israel, and God drowned Pharaoh, they said, "O Moses, bring us that promised book." So he went to his Lord and promised them forty nights. This is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]. He appointed Harun as successor over them, and he remained on Tur for forty nights. God sent down the Torah upon him in tablets, and the tablets were of emerald. The Lord brought him near in private conversation, spoke to him without an intermediary, and made him hear the scratching of the pen. Abu al-Aliyah said: "We have been told that he did not commit any offence during the forty nights until he came down from Tur."

The second discussion: He said "forty nights" only because months begin with nights.

[Page 70]

The third discussion: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾ means: We appointed for Moses the completion of forty nights, like their saying: "Today is forty days since so-and-so left," meaning the completion of the forty. The sum is that He omitted the mudaf (the governing noun) and placed the mudaf ilayh (the governed noun) in its position, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. Also, the intended meaning is not the completion of any forty whatsoever, but specific forty, namely the thirty of Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, because Moses, peace be upon him, knew that this was the intended forty. Also, His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾ may mean that He had promised, before these forty nights, that he would come to the mountain for these forty nights until the Torah descended upon him; and it may mean that he was commanded to come to the mountain for these forty nights, and He promised that the Torah would descend upon him after that. This second possibility is the one supported by the reports.

The fourth discussion: His saying here, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾, indicates that the appointment was from the beginning for forty, while His saying in al-A'raf, ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten﴾ [al-A'raf: 142], indicates that the appointment was at the beginning for thirty. So how is the reconciliation between them? Al-Hasan al-Basri answered, saying: "It is not meant that his promise was thirty nights, and after that He promised him ten more. Rather, He promised him forty nights all together." It is like His saying: ﴿Three days in the pilgrimage and seven when you return; those are ten complete﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Then you took the calf after him﴾, there are several discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: He mentioned the particle "thumma" (then) because He had promised Moses the presence at the appointed time for the sending down of the Torah upon him in the presence of the seventy. He thereby showed the rank of Moses, peace be upon him, and the excellence of the Children of Israel, so that this would be an alert to those present regarding the height of their rank and an informing to those absent, and a completion of the religion. This was among the greatest of favours. So when they came after that with the worst kinds of ignorance and disbelief, it was a matter of astonishment. It is like one who says: "I have done good to you and done such and such, then you intend me with evil and harm."

The second discussion: The people of the histories said that when God, may He be exalted, drowned Pharaoh and promised Moses, peace be upon him, the sending down of the Torah upon him, Moses said to his brother Harun: ﴿Take my place among my people, act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]. When Moses went to Tur, and there remained with the Children of Israel the clothes and jewellery which they had borrowed from the Copts, Harun said to them: "These clothes and jewellery are not lawful for you, so burn them." They gathered a fire and burned them. Now al-Samiri, during his journey with Moses, peace be upon him, in the sea, had seen the hoofprint of Jibril's mount when he advanced before Pharaoh into the sea. So he took a handful of dust from the hoofprint of that mount. Then al-Samiri took what he had of gold and silver, fashioned from it a calf, and cast that dust into it. A sound came out of it as if it were a lowing. He said to the people: ﴿This is your god and the god of Moses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88], and the people took it as a god for themselves. This is what is in the report. One may say: a great multitude of intelligent people cannot agree upon what is known to be false by the immediate judgement of reason, and this account is of that kind, for several reasons:

The first: every intelligent person knows by the immediate judgement of his reason that an idol made of gold, which does not move, does not sense, and does not understand, is impossible to be the god of the heavens and the earth. Grant that it produced a lowing; yet this degree of matter is not fit to be a doubt in the heart of any intelligent person as to its being a god.

The second: the people had already witnessed, before that, overwhelming miracles, which were close to the limit of compulsion, in pointing to the Maker and to the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him. So with the strength of this proof and its reaching the level of necessity, and with the fact that the emission of a lowing from that golden calf is impossible to give rise to doubt that that sounding body is a god.

The answer: this event cannot be rectified except in one way, namely that it is said: al-Samiri suggested to the people that Moses, peace be upon him, was able to do what he did only because he used talismans linked to celestial powers, and through them he was able to perform these miracles. So al-Samiri said to the people: "I too will make for you a talisman like his," and he made it appear to them by fashioning it so that a wondrous sound came out of it, and so he enticed them into hoping to become like Moses, peace be upon him, in performing extraordinary acts. Or perhaps the people were anthropomorphists and incarnationists, so they permitted the indwelling of God in some bodies, and therefore fell into that doubt.

The third discussion: this story contains several benefits:

The first: it indicates that the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of communities, because those Jews, although they witnessed those overwhelming proofs, were deceived by this exceedingly feeble doubt. As for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), although they need subtle proofs to know that the Qur'an is a miracle, they were not deceived by the strong and great doubts. This indicates that this community is better than those, more perfect in intellect, and purer in insight than them.

The second: that he, peace be upon him, related this account although he had learned no knowledge, and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, took it from the one who revealed it.

The third: it contains a great warning against blind imitation and ignorance of the proofs, for if those peoples had known God through proof with complete knowledge, they would not have fallen into the doubt of al-Samiri.

The fourth: it is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he witnessed from the polytheists of the Arabs, the Jews and the Christians in opposition to him. It is as if God, may He be exalted, commanded him to be patient in this, just as Moses, peace be upon him and his family, was patient in this distressing event. For after God had delivered them from Pharaoh and shown them astonishing miracles from the first appearance of Moses until that time, they were deceived by that feeble doubt. Then Moses, peace be upon him, was patient in this. So it is more fitting that Muhammad, peace be upon him, be patient with the harm of his people.

The fifth: the most contentious of people towards the Messenger (ﷺ) and the most hostile to him are the Jews. So it is as if God, may He be exalted, said: "These people only boast of their forefathers, yet their forefathers were in such dullness, ignorance and obstinacy to this degree. So how about these descendants?"

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾, there are several discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: concerning the explanation of injustice (zulm), and it has two views:

The first: Abu Muslim said: Injustice, in the original language, is deficiency. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fall short in anything thereof﴾ [al-Kahf: 33]. The meaning is that when they abandoned the worship of the Creator, the Giver of life and death, and occupied themselves with worshipping the calf, they became deficient in the good of religion and of the world.

The second: in the usage of the Sharia, injustice is an expression for harm that is free of any benefit exceeding it, or for the repelling of a greater harm, and for taking what is due from another in one's knowledge or assumption. When an act is with this attribute, its doer is a wrongdoer. Then, if a man does what leads him to punishment and the Fire, he is said to be a wrongdoer to himself, even if it brings him benefit and pleasure at present, as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a tremendous injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13], and He said: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ [Fatir: 32]. And since their worship of other than God was polytheism [and polytheism leads to the Fire, it was named injustice].

The second discussion: the Mu'tazilah (a theological school) argued from His saying, ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾, that sins are not created by God, may He be exalted, in several respects:

The first: He blamed them for it, and if it had been created by God, may He be exalted, one would deserve blame only for the one who performed it.

The second: if it had been by the will of God, may He be exalted, they would have been obedient to God, may He be exalted, by performing it, because obedience is an expression for doing what is willed.

The third point: if disobedience were created by God Most High, then blaming someone for it would be like blaming them for being black or white, tall or short.

The answer: this is an argument from the praise and blame of human acts, and it is countered by the two issues of the motive (al-dā'ī) and of divine knowledge, which we have already addressed many times [we have mentioned this].

Third issue: the verse indicates that the harm of disbelief returns only to them, because they gained nothing by it except that they wronged themselves. This shows that the majesty of God is exalted above being made complete by the obedience of the pious or diminished by the disobedience of the wretched.

As for His saying, ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾, the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school of theology) said: the meaning is, "Then We pardoned you because of your repentance, which was killing one another." This is weak for two reasons:

First: accepting repentance is obligatory by reason. If that were the meaning, it would not be proper to count it among the favours, because performing an obligation is not considered an act of bounty, whereas the purpose of these verses is to enumerate God's blessings upon them.

Second: pardon (al-'afw) is the name for dropping a deserved punishment. Dropping what must be dropped is not called pardon. Do you not see that when a wrongdoer may not punish the wronged, the abstaining from that punishment is not called pardon? So it is here. Once this is established, we say there is no doubt that repentance occurred in this case, by His saying, ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54]. If that is so, this verse indicates that accepting repentance is not obligatory by reason. And once that is established, it also follows that God has dropped the punishment of one who may rightfully be punished by reason and by law, and this too contradicts the position of the Mu'tazila. Since it is established that He pardoned the disbelievers of the people of Moses, then pardoning the sinners of the community of Muhammad ﷺ is all the more fitting, given that they are ﴿the best community brought forth for mankind﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 110].

As for His saying, ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾, know that the discussion of the meaning of "la'alla" (perhaps, so that) has already preceded in His saying, ﴿so that you may be mindful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. As for the discussion of the reality and quiddity of gratitude (al-shukr), it is lengthy and will come, God willing. Then the Mu'tazila said: God Most High has made clear that He pardoned them and did not hold them to account only so that they would be grateful, and this indicates that He did not desire from them anything except gratitude.

The answer: If God Most High desired gratitude from them, He would have desired it either on the condition that the grateful person first acquires the motive to be grateful, or without it. The first is invalid. For if He desired it on this condition, then if this condition comes from the servant, the motive would require another motive, and if it comes from God, then whenever God creates the motive, gratitude necessarily occurs, and whenever He does not create the motive, gratitude becomes impossible. That is the opposite of the Mu'tazila's position. And if He desired gratitude from them without this motive, then He desired something impossible, because an act without a motive is impossible. Thus it is established that the difficulty applies to them as well. And God knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful﴾.
