As for the reading with an alif, it has several explanations:

The first: although the promise came from God, Exalted is He, its acceptance came from Moses, peace be upon him, and the acceptance of a promise resembles the promise itself, because the one who accepts a promise must say, "I will do that."

The second: al-Qaffal said: It is not far-fetched that a human promises God, and its meaning is that he covenants with God.

The third: it is a matter that took place between two parties, so it is permissible to say "wā'adnā."

The fourth, and it is the strongest: God, Exalted is He, promised him revelation, and he promised God that he would come to the appointed place at Mount Tur. As for Moses, there are several points concerning him:

The first: his measure is fu'lā, and the mīm in it is original, derived from māsa yamīsu when he swaggered in his walk, and Moses, peace be upon him, was such.

The second: his measure is mufil, so the mīm in it is additional, and it is from awsaytu al-shajarah, when I took off the leaves that were on the tree; it is as if he was named thus because of his baldness.

The third: it is a compound word from two words in Hebrew: "mū" is water in their language, and "sā" is tree. He was named thus because his mother placed him in the chest when she feared for him from Pharaoh, and cast him into the sea. The waves of the sea pushed him until they brought him between trees near Pharaoh's house. Then the maidservants of Asiyah, Pharaoh's wife, came out to bathe, found the chest, and took it. So he was named after the place where he was found, which is water and tree.

Know that the first two explanations are utterly corrupt. As for the first, the Children of Israel and the Copts did not speak the language of the Arabs, so it is not permissible that this is what they meant. As for the second, this word is a proper name, and a proper name conveys no meaning in its essence. The closest is the third explanation, and it is a matter customary among people. As for his lineage, peace be upon him, he is Moses son of 'Imran son of Yashhar son of Qahath son of Lawi son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿forty nights﴾, there are several discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: Moses, peace be upon him, had said to the Children of Israel: "If we come out of the sea safe, I will bring you a clear book from God containing what is obligatory for you of doing and abstaining." When Moses crossed the sea with the Children of Israel, and God drowned Pharaoh, they said, "O Moses, bring us that promised book." So he went to his Lord and promised them forty nights. This is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]. He appointed Harun as successor over them, and he remained on Tur for forty nights. God sent down the Torah upon him in tablets, and the tablets were of emerald. The Lord brought him near in private conversation, spoke to him without an intermediary, and made him hear the scratching of the pen. Abu al-Aliyah said: "We have been told that he did not commit any offence during the forty nights until he came down from Tur."

The second discussion: He said "forty nights" only because months begin with nights.

[Page 70]

The third discussion: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾ means: We appointed for Moses the completion of forty nights, like their saying: "Today is forty days since so-and-so left," meaning the completion of the forty. The sum is that He omitted the mudaf (the governing noun) and placed the mudaf ilayh (the governed noun) in its position, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. Also, the intended meaning is not the completion of any forty whatsoever, but specific forty, namely the thirty of Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, because Moses, peace be upon him, knew that this was the intended forty. Also, His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾ may mean that He had promised, before these forty nights, that he would come to the mountain for these forty nights until the Torah descended upon him; and it may mean that he was commanded to come to the mountain for these forty nights, and He promised that the Torah would descend upon him after that. This second possibility is the one supported by the reports.

The fourth discussion: His saying here, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾, indicates that the appointment was from the beginning for forty, while His saying in al-A'raf, ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten﴾ [al-A'raf: 142], indicates that the appointment was at the beginning for thirty. So how is the reconciliation between them? Al-Hasan al-Basri answered, saying: "It is not meant that his promise was thirty nights, and after that He promised him ten more. Rather, He promised him forty nights all together." It is like His saying: ﴿Three days in the pilgrimage and seven when you return; those are ten complete﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Then you took the calf after him﴾, there are several discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: He mentioned the particle "thumma" (then) because He had promised Moses the presence at the appointed time for the sending down of the Torah upon him in the presence of the seventy. He thereby showed the rank of Moses, peace be upon him, and the excellence of the Children of Israel, so that this would be an alert to those present regarding the height of their rank and an informing to those absent, and a completion of the religion. This was among the greatest of favours. So when they came after that with the worst kinds of ignorance and disbelief, it was a matter of astonishment. It is like one who says: "I have done good to you and done such and such, then you intend me with evil and harm."

The second discussion: The people of the histories said that when God, may He be exalted, drowned Pharaoh and promised Moses, peace be upon him, the sending down of the Torah upon him, Moses said to his brother Harun: ﴿Take my place among my people, act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]. When Moses went to Tur, and there remained with the Children of Israel the clothes and jewellery which they had borrowed from the Copts, Harun said to them: "These clothes and jewellery are not lawful for you, so burn them." They gathered a fire and burned them. Now al-Samiri, during his journey with Moses, peace be upon him, in the sea, had seen the hoofprint of Jibril's mount when he advanced before Pharaoh into the sea. So he took a handful of dust from the hoofprint of that mount. Then al-Samiri took what he had of gold and silver, fashioned from it a calf, and cast that dust into it. A sound came out of it as if it were a lowing. He said to the people: ﴿This is your god and the god of Moses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88], and the people took it as a god for themselves. This is what is in the report. One may say: a great multitude of intelligent people cannot agree upon what is known to be false by the immediate judgement of reason, and this account is of that kind, for several reasons:

The first: every intelligent person knows by the immediate judgement of his reason that an idol made of gold, which does not move, does not sense, and does not understand, is impossible to be the god of the heavens and the earth. Grant that it produced a lowing; yet this degree of matter is not fit to be a doubt in the heart of any intelligent person as to its being a god.

The second: the people had already witnessed, before that, overwhelming miracles, which were close to the limit of compulsion, in pointing to the Maker and to the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him. So with the strength of this proof and its reaching the level of necessity, and with the fact that the emission of a lowing from that golden calf is impossible to give rise to doubt that that sounding body is a god.

The answer: this event cannot be rectified except in one way, namely that it is said: al-Samiri suggested to the people that Moses, peace be upon him, was able to do what he did only because he used talismans linked to celestial powers, and through them he was able to perform these miracles. So al-Samiri said to the people: "I too will make for you a talisman like his," and he made it appear to them by fashioning it so that a wondrous sound came out of it, and so he enticed them into hoping to become like Moses, peace be upon him, in performing extraordinary acts. Or perhaps the people were anthropomorphists and incarnationists, so they permitted the indwelling of God in some bodies, and therefore fell into that doubt.

The third discussion: this story contains several benefits:

The first: it indicates that the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of communities, because those Jews, although they witnessed those overwhelming proofs, were deceived by this exceedingly feeble doubt. As for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), although they need subtle proofs to know that the Qur'an is a miracle, they were not deceived by the strong and great doubts. This indicates that this community is better than those, more perfect in intellect, and purer in insight than them.

The second: that he, peace be upon him, related this account although he had learned no knowledge, and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, took it from the one who revealed it.

The third: it contains a great warning against blind imitation and ignorance of the proofs, for if those peoples had known God through proof with complete knowledge, they would not have fallen into the doubt of al-Samiri.

The fourth: it is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he witnessed from the polytheists of the Arabs, the Jews and the Christians in opposition to him. It is as if God, may He be exalted, commanded him to be patient in this, just as Moses, peace be upon him and his family, was patient in this distressing event. For after God had delivered them from Pharaoh and shown them astonishing miracles from the first appearance of Moses until that time, they were deceived by that feeble doubt. Then Moses, peace be upon him, was patient in this. So it is more fitting that Muhammad, peace be upon him, be patient with the harm of his people.

The fifth: the most contentious of people towards the Messenger (ﷺ) and the most hostile to him are the Jews. So it is as if God, may He be exalted, said: "These people only boast of their forefathers, yet their forefathers were in such dullness, ignorance and obstinacy to this degree. So how about these descendants?"

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾, there are several discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: concerning the explanation of injustice (zulm), and it has two views:

The first: Abu Muslim said: Injustice, in the original language, is deficiency. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fall short in anything thereof﴾ [al-Kahf: 33]. The meaning is that when they abandoned the worship of the Creator, the Giver of life and death, and occupied themselves with worshipping the calf, they became deficient in the good of religion and of the world.

The second: in the usage of the Sharia, injustice is an expression for harm that is free of any benefit exceeding it, or for the repelling of a greater harm, and for taking what is due from another in one's knowledge or assumption. When an act is with this attribute, its doer is a wrongdoer. Then, if a man does what leads him to punishment and the Fire, he is said to be a wrongdoer to himself, even if it brings him benefit and pleasure at present, as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a tremendous injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13], and He said: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ [Fatir: 32]. And since their worship of other than God was polytheism [and polytheism leads to the Fire, it was named injustice].

The second discussion: the Mu'tazilah (a theological school) argued from His saying, ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾, that sins are not created by God, may He be exalted, in several respects:

The first: He blamed them for it, and if it had been created by God, may He be exalted, one would deserve blame only for the one who performed it.

The second: if it had been by the will of God, may He be exalted, they would have been obedient to God, may He be exalted, by performing it, because obedience is an expression for doing what is willed.

The third point: if disobedience were created by God Most High, then blaming someone for it would be like blaming them for being black or white, tall or short.

The answer: this is an argument from the praise and blame of human acts, and it is countered by the two issues of the motive (al-dā'ī) and of divine knowledge, which we have already addressed many times [we have mentioned this].

Third issue: the verse indicates that the harm of disbelief returns only to them, because they gained nothing by it except that they wronged themselves. This shows that the majesty of God is exalted above being made complete by the obedience of the pious or diminished by the disobedience of the wretched.

As for His saying, ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾, the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school of theology) said: the meaning is, "Then We pardoned you because of your repentance, which was killing one another." This is weak for two reasons:

First: accepting repentance is obligatory by reason. If that were the meaning, it would not be proper to count it among the favours, because performing an obligation is not considered an act of bounty, whereas the purpose of these verses is to enumerate God's blessings upon them.

Second: pardon (al-'afw) is the name for dropping a deserved punishment. Dropping what must be dropped is not called pardon. Do you not see that when a wrongdoer may not punish the wronged, the abstaining from that punishment is not called pardon? So it is here. Once this is established, we say there is no doubt that repentance occurred in this case, by His saying, ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54]. If that is so, this verse indicates that accepting repentance is not obligatory by reason. And once that is established, it also follows that God has dropped the punishment of one who may rightfully be punished by reason and by law, and this too contradicts the position of the Mu'tazila. Since it is established that He pardoned the disbelievers of the people of Moses, then pardoning the sinners of the community of Muhammad ﷺ is all the more fitting, given that they are ﴿the best community brought forth for mankind﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 110].

As for His saying, ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾, know that the discussion of the meaning of "la'alla" (perhaps, so that) has already preceded in His saying, ﴿so that you may be mindful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. As for the discussion of the reality and quiddity of gratitude (al-shukr), it is lengthy and will come, God willing. Then the Mu'tazila said: God Most High has made clear that He pardoned them and did not hold them to account only so that they would be grateful, and this indicates that He did not desire from them anything except gratitude.

The answer: If God Most High desired gratitude from them, He would have desired it either on the condition that the grateful person first acquires the motive to be grateful, or without it. The first is invalid. For if He desired it on this condition, then if this condition comes from the servant, the motive would require another motive, and if it comes from God, then whenever God creates the motive, gratitude necessarily occurs, and whenever He does not create the motive, gratitude becomes impossible. That is the opposite of the Mu'tazila's position. And if He desired gratitude from them without this motive, then He desired something impossible, because an act without a motive is impossible. Thus it is established that the difficulty applies to them as well. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 53:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, that perhaps you would be guided﴾.

Know that this is the fourth blessing, and the intended meaning of al-Furqan (the Criterion) may be one of three things: it may be the Torah itself, or something included within the Torah, or something outside the Torah. These are three divisions with no further addition beyond them. The explanation of the first possibility is that the Torah has two attributes: being a revealed Book, and being a Criterion that distinguishes between truth and falsehood. So it is like your saying: "I saw the rain-cloud and the lion," meaning a man who combines generosity and courage. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light and a reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya候: 48]. As for the explanation of the second possibility, it is that the intended meaning of al-Furqan is what is in the Torah of the clarification of the religion, because when something is made clear, the truth appears distinct from falsehood. Thus the intended meaning of al-Furqan is a part of what is in the Torah, namely the explanation of the roots and branches of the religion. As for the explanation of the third possibility, it comes in several aspects:

The first: that the intended meaning of al-Furqan is what he, peace be upon him, was given of the hand and the staff and the rest of the signs, and they were called al-Furqan because they distinguished between truth and falsehood.

The second: that the intended meaning of al-Furqan is the victory and deliverance that God granted the Children of Israel over the people of Pharaoh. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not send down upon Our servant on the Day of the Criterion, the day the two hosts met﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]. The intended meaning is the victory God granted on the Day of Badr. This is because before victory appears, each of the two adversaries expects that he will be the dominant one and his companion the vanquished; when victory appears, the superior is distinguished from the inferior, and genuine hope is separated from false hope.

The third: Qutrub said: al-Furqan is the parting of the sea for Moses, peace be upon him. If you say: this has already been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾, and moreover His saying, exalted is He, after that: ﴿that perhaps you would be guided﴾ is fitting only for the Book, because that is mentioned only following guidance.

I say: The answer to the first is that He, exalted is He, did not specify in His saying ﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾ that this was for the sake of Moses, peace be upon him; in this verse He clarified that specification explicitly. As for the second, the parting of the sea was among the proofs, so perhaps the meaning is that when We gave Moses the Criterion of the sea, they inferred from that the existence of the Creator and the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him, and that is guidance. Also, guidance may be intended to mean success and salvation just as it may mean indication; so it is as if He, exalted is He, clarified that He gave them the Book as a blessing in religion, and the Criterion by which their deliverance from the adversary was achieved as an immediate blessing. Know that some people erred and thought that al-Furqan is the Qur'an and that it was sent down to Moses, peace be upon him; this is false, because al-Furqan is that which distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and every proof is like that, so there is no basis for restricting this term to the Qur'an. Others said: the meaning is: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book﴾, meaning the Torah, and We gave Muhammad (ﷺ) the Criterion so that you, People of the Book, might be guided by it. Among the grammarians, al-Farra', Tha'lab and Qutrub inclined to this view, but this is extreme far-fetching without any necessity whatsoever.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that perhaps you would be guided﴾, the explanation of la'alla (perhaps) and the explanation of guidance have already been given. The Mu'tazilah used His saying ﴿that perhaps you would be guided﴾ as evidence that God, exalted is He, intended guidance from all, and this refutes the view of those who say He intended disbelief from the disbeliever. Also, if according to them He, exalted is He, creates guidance for whoever is guided and creates misguidance for whoever goes astray, then what is the benefit in sending down the Book and the Criterion and saying ﴿that perhaps you would be guided﴾? It is known that if guidance is something He creates, then sending down Books has no effect on it: if guidance were created, it would occur even without a Book; and if He sent down a thousand books in place of one book but did not create guidance in them, guidance would not occur. So how is it permissible to say: "I sent down the Book so that you might be guided"? Know that this argument has been mentioned countless times before, together with its answer. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 54 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking the calf [for worship], so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator." And He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

Know that this is the fifth blessing. Some of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: this verse and what follows it are disconnected from what came before of the reminder of blessings, because it is a command to kill, which would not be a blessing. This view is weak for several reasons:

First: God, exalted is He, alerted them to the magnitude of their sin, then alerted them to that by which they could be freed from that great sin, and that is among the greatest blessings in religion. Since God enumerated the worldly blessings upon them, it is more fitting that He enumerate this religious blessing. Moreover, this blessing, namely the manner of this repentance, could not be described except with a preface mentioning the disobedience, so mentioning it is also part of the completion of the blessing. Thus everything this verse contains is counted among God's blessings, and so it is permissible to remind them of it.

Second: when God commanded them to kill, He lifted that command from them before they were completely annihilated, and that was a blessing for those who remained. It was also a blessing with regard to those who existed in the time of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, because had God not lifted killing from their fathers, those sons would not have come into existence. So it is fitting to mention it in the context of favour upon those present in the time of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

Third: when God explained that the repentance of those people was not completed except by killing, although Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, used to tell them: "There is no need for you now, in repentance, for killing; rather, if you turn back from your disbelief and believe, God accepts your faith from you." So the explanation of the severity in that repentance is an alert to the great favour of accepting such an easy, light repentance.

Fourth: it contains a strong encouragement for the community of Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, toward repentance. For when the people of Moses, peace be upon him, were eager for that repentance despite its extreme hardship upon the self, it is more fitting that one of us should be eager for repentance, which is merely regret. It is well known that encouraging a person toward what is an important benefit is among the greatest blessings.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾, meaning: remember when Moses said to his people, after he returned from the appointed meeting which his Lord had promised him, and found them having taken the calf: ﴿O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves﴾. Regarding "wronging" (zulm), the exegetes have two views:

One: that you deprived yourselves of the reward that was obligatory through remaining upon the covenant of Moses, peace be upon him.

The second: that wronging (zulm) is persistence in what is not deserved and in which there is no benefit nor averting of harm, neither in knowledge nor in medicine. When they worshipped the calf, they had harmed themselves, because what leads to eternal harm is among the greatest wrongs. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, association [of others with God] is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. However, this wronging ought to be qualified so that its unqualified use does not give the impression that it is wronging others, since the basic meaning of wronging is that which transgresses onto others. Therefore He said: ﴿you have wronged yourselves﴾.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿by your taking the calf﴾, there is an ellipsis (hadhf) in it, because they did not wrong themselves merely by this amount, for if they had taken it but did not make it a god, their act would not have been wronging. So the meaning of "your taking the calf" is taking it as a god; but since the preceding part of the verse indicates this omitted element, the ellipsis is fitting.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾, there are questions concerning it.

The first question: the saying of God, exalted is He, ﴿so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ implies that repentance is explained by killing oneself, just as His saying, peace be upon him: "God does not accept the prayer of any one of you until he places the purification (tahur) in its proper places, so he washes his face and then his hands" implies that placing the purification in its proper places is by washing the face and the hands. But that is invalid, because repentance is an expression of regret over the past ugly act and resolve not to commit its like thereafter, and that differs from killing oneself and does not entail it, so how can it be permissible to explain it by that?

The answer: the intent is not to explain repentance as killing oneself, but to state that their repentance is not completed nor attained except by killing oneself. That was so because God, exalted is He, revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, that the condition of their repentance was the killing of the self, just as for one who has killed intentionally, his repentance is not completed except by surrendering himself, until the heirs of the victim are pleased or they kill him. So there is no impossibility that it was part of the law of Moses, peace be upon him, that the repentance of an apostate is not completed except by killing. Once this is established, we say: the condition of a thing is sometimes called by the name of that thing figuratively, as one says to the usurper who intends repentance: "Your repentance is the return of what you usurped," meaning that your repentance is not completed except by it. So it is here too.

The second question: what is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so turn in repentance to your Creator﴾, since repentance is only to the Creator?

The answer: what is intended is a prohibition of showing off (riya') in repentance, as if He said to them: if you show repentance not from the heart, then you have not repented to God, who is aware of your inner selves, but you have repented to people, and that is of no benefit. For if you sinned against God...

The third question: why was this place specifically mentioned with the mention of the Creator (al-Bari')?

The answer: al-Bari' is He who created creation free from disparity: ﴿You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any disparity﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], and who distinguishes some of it from others by its differing forms and varying images. So this was an alert that whoever is so is more deserving of worship than the cow, which is proverbial for dullness.

The fourth question: what is the difference between the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-tubu﴾ ("so turn in repentance") and the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-uqtulu﴾ ("so kill")?

The answer: the first fa' indicates causation, because wronging is the cause of repentance; the second indicates sequence, because killing is part of the completion of repentance. So the meaning of His saying ﴿fa-tubu﴾ is: then follow the repentance with killing as a completion of your repentance.

The fifth question: what is meant by His saying ﴿fa-uqtulu anfusakum﴾ ("so kill yourselves")? Is it what its apparent meaning requires, that each one kills himself, or is something else intended?

The answer: people differed regarding this. A group of the exegetes said: it is not permissible that what is meant is the command for each of the repentant to kill himself. This is the choice of the judge Abd al-Jabbar, and they argued for it with two arguments:

The first, on which the exegetes relied: the exegetes agreed that they did not kill themselves with their own hands, and if they had been commanded to do so, they would have become disobedient by abandoning it.

The second, on which the judge Abd al-Jabbar relied: killing is the dismantling of the structure upon which life must depart; whatever else leads to death, sooner or later, is only called killing figuratively.

Having understood the true nature of killing, we say: it is not permissible for God, exalted is He, to command it, because legislated acts of worship are good only because they are benefits for that obligated person, and they are benefits only regarding future matters, and after killing there is no state of obligation in which killing would be a benefit. This differs from what God does of causing death, because that is an act of God, so it is good that He does it when it is beneficial for another obligated person, and He compensates that person with a great reward. And it differs from God commanding that one wound himself or cut off a limb without death resulting immediately, for since he remains alive after that act, it is not impossible that that act could be beneficial for future acts.

One may say: we do not grant that killing is the name of the act that immediately removes the soul. Rather, it is an expression for the act that leads to departure, either immediately or after. The proof of this is that if one swears not to kill a person, and wounds him with a grievous wound, and he remains alive for a single moment after that wound and then dies, he breaks his oath, and all the people of this language call him a killer; and usage is originally literal. This shows that the name of killing is the name of the act that leads to departure, whether it leads to it immediately or after. And you have granted the permissibility of the occurrence of a command to a wound that does not immediately lead to departure. If that is so, it is established that it is permissible for the command to be that a person kills himself. Even if we grant that killing is the name of the act that immediately removes the soul, why is the occurrence of a command to it not permissible? As for his saying that a future benefit must be present in the command to it, we say: first, we do not grant that a benefit must be present in it. The proof is that He commanded one who knows his disbelief to believe, and there is no benefit in that, since the only outcome of that obligation is the occurrence of punishment. Even if we grant that a benefit must be present, why do you say that the benefit must return to him? Why is it not permissible that his killing himself is a benefit for another, so God commands him to do it so that other person benefits from it, and then God conveys the great reward to him? Even if we grant that the benefit must return to him, why is it not permissible to say that his knowledge that he is commanded to perform that act is itself a benefit for him, like that when He commanded him to kill himself tomorrow, his knowledge of this becomes a motive for him to abandon ugly deeds from now until tomorrow arrives? And if these possibilities are feasible, what the judge said falls away. Rather, the first view on which the exegetes relied is stronger, and on this basis the verse must be turned from its apparent meaning. Then in it there are two views:

The first view: it is said that He commanded each of those repentant ones to kill some of them by others. So His saying ﴿kill yourselves﴾ means: let some of you kill others. This is like His saying elsewhere: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [an-Nisa': 29], meaning: let not some of you kill others. Its verification is that the believers are like a single self. It was said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not defame yourselves﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], meaning your brothers among the believers; and regarding His saying: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of their own kind?﴾ [an-Nur: 12], meaning of their likes among the Muslims; and like His saying: ﴿then greet one another﴾ [an-Nur: 61], meaning let some of you greet others. Then the exegetes said: those repentant ones lined up in two rows, and some of them struck others until nightfall.

The second view: God commanded others than those repentant ones to kill those repentant ones. So the meaning of His saying ﴿kill yourselves﴾ is: submit yourselves to being killed. This second view is closer, because in the first view the hardship increases, since when a group shares in a sin, some of them feel stronger compassion toward one another than toward others; so when they are obligated to kill one another, the hardship is greatly magnified.

Then the reports differed:

The first: that He commanded those who had not worshipped the calf among the seventy chosen for attendance at the appointed time to kill those among them who had worshipped the calf. The ones killed were seventy thousand, and they did not move until they were killed over three

**Second:** When Moses, peace be upon him, commanded them to kill one another, they complied. He took covenants from them to be steadfast in the killing. They gathered, each tribe separately, and Aaron came to them with twelve thousand men, those who had not worshipped the calf at all, and with swords in their hands. The repentant ones said: "These are your brothers. They have come to you with drawn swords. So fear God and be steadfast." God curses any man who rises from his seat, or directs his gaze at them, or wards them off with a hand or a foot. They would say, "Amen." So they began killing them until evening. Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them, stood up, supplicating God and saying, "The remnant, the remnant, O our God!" God revealed to them both: "I have forgiven those who were killed, and I have turned in forgiveness toward those who remain." He said: The number of those killed was seventy thousand. This is the narration of al-Kalbi.

**Third:** The Children of Israel were of two groups. Some of them worshipped the calf, and some did not worship it, but they did not denounce those who did. So He commanded those who did not busy themselves with denunciation to kill those who busied themselves with the worship. Then the exegetes said: A man would see his father, his son, and his neighbour, and he could not bring himself to carry out God's command. So God sent a black cloud, and then He commanded the killing. They killed until evening, until Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them, supplicated and said: "O Lord, the Children of Israel are being destroyed! The remnant, the remnant!" Then the cloud dispersed, the Torah was sent down, and the blades fell from their hands.

**Question Six:** How did they deserve to be killed when they had repented of apostasy (*ridda*), and one who repents of apostasy is not killed?

**Answer:** This varies according to the sacred laws (*shara'i'*, the divine legislations). Perhaps the law of Moses, peace be upon him, required the killing of one who repented of apostasy, either as a general ruling binding on everyone, or as a ruling specific to that people.

**Question Seven:** Is it sound what is reported, that some of them were not killed, though God had accepted their repentance?

**Answer:** That is not impossible, because the words of God, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed you have wronged yourselves﴾, are a direct address (*khitab mushafaha*), so perhaps it was addressed to some of them, or it was general, and a general statement may admit of specification (*takhsis*).

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿That is better for you with your Creator﴾, it contains an indication of the reason why this hardship could be borne. Their situation was caught between the harm of this world and the harm of the Hereafter, and the former is more deserving of endurance because it is finite, while the harm of the Hereafter is infinite. Moreover, death is inevitable, so enduring the killing amounts only to bringing it forward or delaying it. As for deliverance from punishment and success in reward, that is the supreme aim.

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Then He turned to you﴾, there is an ellipsis in it, and there are two possibilities:

The first: that it be understood as part of Moses' speech, as if he had said: "If you do this, then He has turned to you."

The second: that it be an address from God to them, in the manner of *iltifat* (shift of address), so the implied meaning is: "You did what Moses commanded you, and so your Creator turned to you."

As for the meaning of His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Then He turned to you; indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾, it has already been discussed in His words: ﴿Then He turned to him; indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37].

**The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verses 55–56 (Part 1 of 2)**

The Exalted said: ﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly," the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ ﴿Then We revived you after your death, that you might be grateful.﴾

Know that this is the sixth of the blessings, and its explanation is in several aspects:

First: It is as if He, the Exalted, said: Remember My blessing when you said to Musa, "We will never believe you until we see Allah openly," and the thunderbolt seized you. Then I revived you so that you might repent of your rebellion, escape the punishment, and attain the reward.

Second: In it is a warning to those who lived in the time of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) against doing that which would make them deserving of what was done to those people.

Third: It is a comparison of their denial of the miracles of the Prophet (ﷺ) with their ancestors' denial of the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him), despite their witnessing the greatness of those manifest signs. It is also an alert that Allah, the Exalted, only withholds from the Prophet (ﷺ) miracles like them because He knows that if He manifested them, they would deny them, and if they denied them, they would deserve the punishment that their ancestors deserved.

Fourth: In it is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he encountered from them, and strengthening of his heart to be patient, as the Messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-azm) were patient.

Fifth: In it is the removal of the doubt of one who says: If the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) were true, the people most deserving to believe in him would be the People of the Book, because they know his report. This is because He, the Exalted, explained that their ancestors, despite witnessing those dazzling signs for the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him), would apostatize at every moment, would dictate to him, and would oppose him. So their opposition to Muhammad (peace be upon him) is not to be wondered at, even if they find reports about his prophethood in their books.

Sixth: When Muhammad (peace be upon him) reported these stories, although he was unlettered (ummi) and had never occupied himself with learning at all, it became necessary that this be from revelation.

**The second discussion:** Among the exegetes (mufassirun) there are two opinions regarding this event:

**The first opinion:** This event occurred after Allah had commanded the worshippers of the calf to be killed. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: When Musa (peace be upon him) returned from the Mount (al-Tur) to his people, he saw what they were doing of worshipping the calf, and he said what he said to his brother and to al-Samiri. He burned the calf and threw it into the sea. He chose from his people seventy men of their best. When they went out to the Mount, they said to Musa: "Ask your Lord that He let us hear His speech." So he (peace be upon him) asked that, and Allah granted his request. When he drew near the mountain, a column of cloud descended upon him, and the whole mountain was covered. That cloud came close to Musa until it entered into it, and he said to the people: "Enter and listen." Whenever his Lord spoke to Musa (peace be upon him), a shining light would fall upon his forehead, which no son of Adam could look at. The people heard the speech of Allah with Musa, (as He) saying to him: "Do" and "Do not." When the speech was complete, the cloud which had entered became uncovered from Musa. Then the people said: "We will never believe you until we see Allah openly." So the thunderbolt seized them, and they all died. Musa stood, raising his hands to the sky, supplicating and saying: "O my God, I chose from the Children of Israel seventy men so that they would be my witnesses to the acceptance of their repentance. I will return to them, and none of them will be with me. What will they say about me?" Musa continued occupied with supplication until Allah returned their souls to them, and He requested the repentance of the Children of Israel from worshipping the calf. He said: "No, unless they kill themselves."

[Page 79]

**The second opinion:** This event occurred after the killing. Al-Suddi said: When the Children of Israel repented of worshipping the calf by killing themselves, Allah, the Exalted, commanded that Musa come to them with some men of the Children of Israel, who would apologize to Him for their worship of the calf. Musa chose seventy men. When they came to the Mount, they said: "We will never believe you until we see Allah openly." So the thunderbolt seized them, and they died. Musa stood weeping and saying: "O Lord, what shall I say to the Children of Israel? For I commanded them to kill, then I chose these from the remainder of them. When I return to them and none of them is with me, what shall I say to them?" Then Allah revealed to Musa that these seventy were among those who had taken the calf as a god. Musa said: ﴿It is none but Your trial﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 156]. Then He, the Exalted, revived them, and they stood up, and each one of them looked at the other, (wondering) how Allah, the Exalted, would revive him. They said: "O Musa, you do not ask Allah for anything except that He gives it to you. So call upon Him to make us prophets." So he supplicated Him with that, and Allah answered his supplication.

Know that there is nothing in the verse that indicates the preference of one of the two opinions over the other. Likewise, there is nothing in it that indicates whether those who asked to see Allah were the ones who worshipped the calf or others.

As for His saying: ﴿We will never believe you﴾, its meaning is: We will not confirm you, nor acknowledge your prophethood, until we see Allah openly, that is, with (our own) eyes. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Jihratan" is a verbal noun (masdar) from your saying: "I recited aloud (jahartu) with the recitation and with the supplication," as if the one who sees with the eye is one who makes the seeing manifest, and the one who sees with the heart is one who makes it inaudible. Its accusative case is because it is a type of seeing, so it is put in the accusative by its verb, just as "al-qurfusa'" (squatting) is put in the accusative by the verb of sitting. Or it is in the accusative of circumstance, meaning "possessors of openness." It has also been read as "jahratan" with a fatha on the ha', and it is either a verbal noun like "ghalabah," or the plural of "jahir."

Al-Qaffal said: The root of "jahrah" is from manifestation. One says: "I uncovered (jahartu) the thing" when you uncover it, and "I cleared (jahartu) the well" when its water was covered with mud and you cleaned it until its water appeared. One says: "a loud voice (sawt jahir)," and "a man with a powerful voice (jahwari al-sawt)" when his voice is high. One says: "a conspicuous face (wajh jahir)" when it is clearly radiant. They only said "jahratan" as emphasis, lest someone suppose that the meaning of seeing is knowledge or imagination, like what the sleeper sees.

As for His saying: ﴿The thunderbolt seized you﴾, there are discussions concerning it:

**The first discussion:** The Mu'tazilah (the Rationalist theologians) used this to prove that seeing Allah is impossible. Al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: If it were permissible, they would have been asking for a permissible matter, and so the punishment should not have descended upon them, just as the punishment did not descend upon them when they asked for a change from one food to another, from a meal to a meal, in His saying: ﴿We will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord to bring forth for us of what the earth grows﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. Abu al-Husayn said in the book al-Tasaffuh: Allah, the Exalted, only mentioned asking to see Him in order to make it appear greatly serious, and that is in several verses. (The first of them) is this verse. If seeing were permissible, their saying ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾ would be like the saying of nations to their prophets, "We will never believe unless you bring the dead to life," in that it is not considered grave, and the thunderbolt would not seize them.

The second: His saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from the heaven. Indeed they asked Musa for something greater than that, when they said: "Show us Allah openly," so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Nisa': 153]. So He called that wrongdoing and punished them immediately. If seeing were permissible, their asking for it would be like one who asks for an additional miracle.

If you say: Did He not, glory be to Him and exalted, make the sending down of a book from the heaven like seeing, in that each of them is a transgression (utuww)? Just as the sending down of a book is not impossible in itself, so too the asking for seeing. I say: The apparent meaning requires that each of them be impossible, so the abandonment of acting by it regarding the sending down of the book leaves it acted upon regarding seeing.

The third: His saying: ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or [why] do we not see our Lord?" Indeed they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

[Page 80]

So if seeing were permissible, and it is among the greatest benefits according to those who permit it, asking for it would not be transgression, because whoever asks Allah for a blessing in religion or in the world is not a transgressor. This is like what is said: "We will never believe you until Allah brings this dead man to life by your supplication."

Know that these aspects share one common point: that if seeing were permissible, asking for it would not be transgression and reprehensible, and that is denied. As for the claim that requesting all other benefits, such as moving from one food to another, was possible, so the one who requested it was not a transgressor, and the same applies to requesting all other miracles: We say, why did you say that since the requester of that possible thing is not a transgressor, every requester of every possibility must not be a transgressor? Reliance in such a matter upon various examples is not appropriate for people of knowledge. How is it, since Allah, the Exalted, only mentioned seeing and mentioned with it something possible, which we have judged to be permissible by consensus, namely the sending down of a book from the sky or the sending down of angels? He attributed the attribute of transgression to both matters together, and that is like decisive evidence that the attribute of transgression did not arise because the sought thing was impossible.

As for the statement of Abu al-Husayn: "The apparent meaning requires that all of them be impossible, and abandoning acting by it regarding some leaves it acted upon regarding the rest": We say: You have not established any proof that the sense of greatness is only realized if the sought thing is impossible; rather you relied upon various examples, and an example is not useful in this matter. Thus your statement "the apparent meaning requires that all be impossible" is void. By what we have said, the argument of the Mu'tazilah is refuted.

If someone says: What is the reason for the gravity of asking to see? The answer to that has several aspects:

First: The seeing of Allah, the Exalted, is only realized in the Hereafter, so seeking it in this world is considered unacceptable.

Second: The judgment of Allah, the Exalted, is that He removes obligation (taklif) from the servant at the time he sees Allah. So asking for seeing would be asking for the removal of obligation. This is more fitting according to the opinion of the Mu'tazilah, because seeing includes necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri), and necessary knowledge contradicts obligation.

Third: When the proofs for the truth of the claim were complete, seeking additional proofs was obstinacy (ta'annut), and the obstinate deserve reproach.

Fourth: It is not impossible that Allah, the Exalted, knows that in preventing creation from seeing Him, glory be to Him, in this world, there is a kind of important benefit. Therefore He considered seeking to see Him in this world unacceptable, just as He knows that in the sending down of a book from the sky and the sending down of angels from the sky there is a great harm. Therefore He considered seeking those unacceptable. And Allah knows best.

**The second discussion:** Regarding the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah), the exegetes have two opinions:

The first: It is death itself. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah, and they argued for it with His saying: ﴿And the trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious, except whom Allah wills﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. This is weak for several reasons:

First: His saying: ﴿The thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on﴾. If the thunderbolt were death, it would be impossible for them to be looking at the thunderbolt.

Second: He, the Exalted, said regarding Musa: ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], affirming the thunderbolt concerning him, though he was not dead, because He said: ﴿So when he regained consciousness﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. Regaining consciousness is not from death but from a swoon.

Third: The thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah) is that which strikes (tasi'u), and that points to the cause of death.

Fourth: Its coming upon them while they were witnessing it is greater in the matter of punishment than if it came suddenly while they did not know. For this reason He said: ﴿while you were looking on﴾, alerting to the greatness of the punishment.

The second opinion, which is the view of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun), is that the thunderbolt is the cause of death. For this reason He said in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿So the earthquake (al-rajfah) seized them﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. They differed about what that cause was, in three ways:

First: It was a fire that fell from the sky and burned them.

Second: A cry (sayhah) that came from the sky.

Third: Allah, the Exalted, sent armies who heard its sound, so they fell down unconscious, dead, for a day and a night.

[Page 81]

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We resurrected you after your death﴾, because resurrection may only occur after death, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We sealed their ears in the cave for a number of years, then We woke them, that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing what they had remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 11]. If you ask: Is Moses, peace be upon him, included in this statement? I say: No, for two reasons.

The first: it is a direct address (khitab mushafahah), so it does not necessarily include Moses, peace be upon him.

The second: if it did include Moses, it would necessarily be restricted by His saying, exalted is He, concerning Moses: ﴿When he regained consciousness﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], even though the term "regaining consciousness" (al-ifaqah) is not used for death. Ibn Qutaybah said that Moses, peace be upon him, had died, and this is an error for the reason we have explained.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, the meaning is that He resurrected them after death in the world of this life only so that He might impose obligations upon them, and so that they might be able to have faith and to make up for the sins that proceeded from them. As for His having imposed obligations upon them, it is based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, and the word "gratitude" (shukr) encompasses all acts of obedience, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba': 13]. If it is said: How is it permissible for Him to impose obligations upon them when He had caused them to die? And if that is permissible, why is it not permissible for Him to impose obligations upon the people of the Hereafter when He resurrects them after death? We say: What prevents imposing obligations upon them in the Hereafter is not the causing of death and then of life. Rather, what prevents that is that on the Day of Resurrection He has compelled them to know Him, and to know the pleasures of Paradise and the pains of Hell, and after necessary knowledge there is no obligation. So if this is the barrier, it is not impossible for these whom God caused to die by the thunderbolt that He had not compelled them, and if that is so, it is correct that they be obligated afterward, and their death and then their revival would be like sleep or like fainting.

It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that God terminated their lifespans by this causing of death and then restored them, just as He revived the one who passed by a village that was fallen upon its roofs, and He revived those who died after they had left their homes, who were thousands, fleeing from death. This is weak, because when He caused them to die by the thunderbolt, He had already decreed and informed of that, so that moment became the term (ajal) of their first death, and then the other moment became the term of their life.

As for the Mu'tazilah's argument from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, that He wills faith from all, our answer to it has been given many times before, so there is no need to repeat it.

The third: His saying: ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or [why] do we not see our Lord?" Indeed they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

[Page 80]

So if seeing were permissible, and it is among the greatest benefits according to those who permit it, asking for it would not be transgression, because whoever asks Allah for a blessing in religion or in the world is not a transgressor. This is like what is said: "We will never believe you until Allah brings this dead man to life by your supplication."

Know that these aspects share one common point: that if seeing were permissible, asking for it would not be transgression and reprehensible, and that is denied. As for the claim that requesting all other benefits, such as moving from one food to another, was possible, so the one who requested it was not a transgressor, and the same applies to requesting all other miracles: We say, why did you say that since the requester of that possible thing is not a transgressor, every requester of every possibility must not be a transgressor? Reliance in such a matter upon various examples is not appropriate for people of knowledge. How is it, since Allah, the Exalted, only mentioned seeing and mentioned with it something possible, which we have judged to be permissible by consensus, namely the sending down of a book from the sky or the sending down of angels? He attributed the attribute of transgression to both matters together, and that is like decisive evidence that the attribute of transgression did not arise because the sought thing was impossible.

As for the statement of Abu al-Husayn: "The apparent meaning requires that all of them be impossible, and abandoning acting by it regarding some leaves it acted upon regarding the rest": We say: You have not established any proof that the sense of greatness is only realized if the sought thing is impossible; rather you relied upon various examples, and an example is not useful in this matter. Thus your statement "the apparent meaning requires that all be impossible" is void. By what we have said, the argument of the Mu'tazilah is refuted.

If someone says: What is the reason for the gravity of asking to see? The answer to that has several aspects:

First: The seeing of Allah, the Exalted, is only realized in the Hereafter, so seeking it in this world is considered unacceptable.

Second: The judgment of Allah, the Exalted, is that He removes obligation (taklif) from the servant at the time he sees Allah. So asking for seeing would be asking for the removal of obligation. This is more fitting according to the opinion of the Mu'tazilah, because seeing includes necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri), and necessary knowledge contradicts obligation.

Third: When the proofs for the truth of the claim were complete, seeking additional proofs was obstinacy (ta'annut), and the obstinate deserve reproach.

Fourth: It is not impossible that Allah, the Exalted, knows that in preventing creation from seeing Him, glory be to Him, in this world, there is a kind of important benefit. Therefore He considered seeking to see Him in this world unacceptable, just as He knows that in the sending down of a book from the sky and the sending down of angels from the sky there is a great harm. Therefore He considered seeking those unacceptable. And Allah knows best.

**The second discussion:** Regarding the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah), the exegetes have two opinions:

The first: It is death itself. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah, and they argued for it with His saying: ﴿And the trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious, except whom Allah wills﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. This is weak for several reasons:

First: His saying: ﴿The thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on﴾. If the thunderbolt were death, it would be impossible for them to be looking at the thunderbolt.

Second: He, the Exalted, said regarding Musa: ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], affirming the thunderbolt concerning him, though he was not dead, because He said: ﴿So when he regained consciousness﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. Regaining consciousness is not from death but from a swoon.

Third: The thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah) is that which strikes (tasi'u), and that points to the cause of death.

Fourth: Its coming upon them while they were witnessing it is greater in the matter of punishment than if it came suddenly while they did not know. For this reason He said: ﴿while you were looking on﴾, alerting to the greatness of the punishment.

The second opinion, which is the view of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun), is that the thunderbolt is the cause of death. For this reason He said in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿So the earthquake (al-rajfah) seized them﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. They differed about what that cause was, in three ways:

First: It was a fire that fell from the sky and burned them.

Second: A cry (sayhah) that came from the sky.

Third: Allah, the Exalted, sent armies who heard its sound, so they fell down unconscious, dead, for a day and a night.

[Page 81]

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We resurrected you after your death﴾, because resurrection may only occur after death, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We sealed their ears in the cave for a number of years, then We woke them, that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing what they had remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 11]. If you ask: Is Moses, peace be upon him, included in this statement? I say: No, for two reasons.

The first: it is a direct address (khitab mushafahah), so it does not necessarily include Moses, peace be upon him.

The second: if it did include Moses, it would necessarily be restricted by His saying, exalted is He, concerning Moses: ﴿When he regained consciousness﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], even though the term "regaining consciousness" (al-ifaqah) is not used for death. Ibn Qutaybah said that Moses, peace be upon him, had died, and this is an error for the reason we have explained.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, the meaning is that He resurrected them after death in the world of this life only so that He might impose obligations upon them, and so that they might be able to have faith and to make up for the sins that proceeded from them. As for His having imposed obligations upon them, it is based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, and the word "gratitude" (shukr) encompasses all acts of obedience, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba': 13]. If it is said: How is it permissible for Him to impose obligations upon them when He had caused them to die? And if that is permissible, why is it not permissible for Him to impose obligations upon the people of the Hereafter when He resurrects them after death? We say: What prevents imposing obligations upon them in the Hereafter is not the causing of death and then of life. Rather, what prevents that is that on the Day of Resurrection He has compelled them to know Him, and to know the pleasures of Paradise and the pains of Hell, and after necessary knowledge there is no obligation. So if this is the barrier, it is not impossible for these whom God caused to die by the thunderbolt that He had not compelled them, and if that is so, it is correct that they be obligated afterward, and their death and then their revival would be like sleep or like fainting.

It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that God terminated their lifespans by this causing of death and then restored them, just as He revived the one who passed by a village that was fallen upon its roofs, and He revived those who died after they had left their homes, who were thousands, fleeing from death. This is weak, because when He caused them to die by the thunderbolt, He had already decreed and informed of that, so that moment became the term (ajal) of their first death, and then the other moment became the term of their life.

As for the Mu'tazilah's argument from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, that He wills faith from all, our answer to it has been given many times before, so there is no need to repeat it.

[Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 57–58]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down upon you manna and quail. Eat of the good things with which We have provided you. They did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

Know that this is the seventh favour that God, may He be exalted, mentioned. God, may He be exalted, mentioned this verse in these same words in Surat al-A'raf. The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that this shading occurred after He revived them, because He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then We revived you after your death, so that you might be grateful. And We shaded you with the clouds﴾. Some parts are conjoined to others, although it is not impossible that the order is otherwise, because the purpose is to enumerate the blessings with which God, may He be exalted, distinguished them.

[p. 82]

The exegetes said: ﴿And We shaded﴾ means We made the clouds shade you. This was in the wilderness of al-Tih (the desert in which the Children of Israel wandered). God subjected to them a cloud that moved with their movement, shading them from the sun. He sent down upon them the manna, which is the taranjabin (a sweet, gum-like substance), like snow, from the break of dawn until sunrise, a sa' (a measure of volume) for each person. God sent them the quail, which is the sumani (quail), and a man would slaughter from it what sufficed him. ﴿Eat﴾ is said with the implied meaning of "We said." ﴿They did not wrong Us﴾, meaning: they wronged themselves by rejecting these blessings, or by taking more than what was permitted to them to take, or by asking for something other than that kind. The speech was abbreviated by omitting that clause, because of the indication of ﴿They did not wrong Us﴾ upon it.

[Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 57–58]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, Verse 59 (Part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating and say, 'Hittah (a request for the removal of sins),' and We will forgive you your wrongs and increase the reward of the good-doers."﴾ ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them, so We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they were defiantly disobeying.﴾

Know that this is the eighth blessing, and this verse is joined to the blessings mentioned earlier. Just as He, exalted is He, explained His blessings upon them by shading them with the clouds and sending down upon them the manna and the quail, which are immediate blessings, He followed that with His blessings upon them in the matter of religion, when He commanded them with what would erase their sins and explained to them the way of deliverance from the punishment they had deserved.

Know that discussion of this verse is of two kinds.

The first kind concerns the explanation (tafsir, the science of interpreting the Qur'an). We say: as for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town"﴾, know that it is a command of obligation (taklif), and two points indicate this:

The first: He, exalted is He, commanded entering the gate prostrating, and that is a difficult act, so the command to it was an obligation. Entering the gate prostrating is conditional upon entering the town, and whatever a required act cannot be completed without is itself required. Thus it is established that the command to enter the town is a command of obligation, not a command of permissibility.

The second: His saying, ﴿Enter the holy land which Allah has prescribed for you and do not turn back on your heels﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 21) is evidence for what we have mentioned. As for the town, the apparent meaning of the Qur'an does not indicate its specific identity, and it is referred back to reports (akhbar). Concerning this there are several views:

The first, which is the choice of Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, is that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). They argued for this with His saying in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿Enter the holy land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 21), and there is no doubt that the intended meaning of "the town" in the two verses is one and the same.

The second: it is Egypt itself.

The third, which is the saying of Ibn Abbas and Abu Zayd, is that it is Ariha (Jericho), which is near Bayt al-Maqdis. Those who held this argued that the town cannot be Bayt al-Maqdis, because the particle "fa" (then) in His saying, ﴿So those who did wrong substituted﴾, requires immediate sequence, so that substitution must have occurred immediately after this command during the lifetime of Musa. But Musa died in the wilderness of al-Tih and did not enter Bayt al-Maqdis. Thus it is established that the intended town is not Bayt al-Maqdis.

The first group answered that this verse does not say that We said "enter this town" through the tongue of Musa or through the tongue of Yusha'. If we take it as through the tongue of Yusha', the difficulty disappears.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance﴾, its explanation has already passed in the story of Adam, peace be upon him, and it is a command of permissibility.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾, there are two discussions concerning it:

The first: they differed about "the gate" in two ways:

One of them, which is the saying of Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Qatadah, is that it is a gate in Bayt al-Maqdis called the Gate of Hittah.

The second: al-Asamm reported from some of them that by "the gate" is meant one of the directions of the town and an entrance to it.

The second discussion: they differed about what is meant by prostration. Al-Hasan said that it means prostration itself, which is pressing the face to the ground. This is far-fetched, because the apparent meaning requires entering while prostrating, and if we took prostration in its apparent sense, that would be impossible. Others took it to mean something other than prostration, and they mentioned two views:

The first: the report of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas that what is meant is bowing (ruku'), because the gate was small and narrow, so the one entering needed to bend. This is far-fetched, because if it were narrow, they would have been compelled to enter bowing, and then there would have been no need for a command concerning it.

The second: it means humility (khudu'), and this is the closest view, because when literal prostration was impossible, it was necessary to take it to mean humbleness. When they undertook repentance, the one who repents from sin must be humble and submissive.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And say, "Hittah"﴾, there are several views:

The first, which is the saying of the qadi (al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar): the meaning is that after He commanded them to enter the gate in a state of humility, He commanded them to say what indicates repentance. This is because repentance is a quality of the heart, which others do not perceive. So when someone becomes known for a sin and then repents after it, it is incumbent upon him to convey his repentance to those who witnessed his sin, because repentance is not complete without that. For a mute person's repentance is valid even if no speech comes from him, but it is for the sake of making others aware of his turning away from sin to repentance and for removing suspicion from himself. Likewise, one who was known for a mistaken doctrine and then the truth became clear to him must make known to his brethren, who knew him for the error, his turning away from it, so that suspicion of his persistence in falsehood may be removed and they may return to his allegiance after their enmity. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, obligated the Children of Israel, together with the humility which is a quality of the heart, to say the utterance that indicates that repentance, which is His saying: ﴿And say, "Hittah"﴾. So the summary is that He commanded the people to enter the gate in a state of humility and to voice with their tongues a request for the removal of sins, so that they would combine regret of the heart, humility of the limbs, and seeking forgiveness with the tongue. This view is the best of the views and the closest to verification.

The second: the saying of al-Asamm: this word is from the vocabulary of the People of the Book, meaning that its meaning is not known in Arabic.

The third: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "Hittah" is a form (fi'lah) from the verb "hatta" (to remove), like "jilsah" and "rikbah", and it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "our request is hittah" or "your command is hittah." The original form is the accusative, in the sense of "remove from us our sins, a removal," but it was made nominative to give the meaning of permanence, as in his saying:

*Patience is beautiful, for each of us is tested.*

The original is "patience" (sabran) under the supposition of "be patient, patience." Ibn Abi Ablah read it in the accusative.

The fourth: the saying of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani: its meaning is "our matter is hittah," that is, that we should descend in this town and settle in it. The qadi rejected this, saying: if that were the meaning, the forgiveness of their wrongs would not be connected to it. But His saying, ﴿And say "Hittah" and We will forgive you your wrongs﴾, indicates that the forgiveness of wrongs was on account of their saying "hittah." It may be answered that when they descended into that town, humbly, to enter prostrating, the forgiveness was connected to it.

The fifth: the saying of al-Qaffal: its meaning is, "O Allah, remove from us our sins, for we have only lowered ourselves for Your sake and out of desire to humble ourselves before You, so remove our sins from us." If someone asks: was the obligation to use this exact word, or not? We say: it was narrated from Ibn Abbas that they were commanded with this exact word, and this is possible, but the closer view is the opposite, for two reasons:

One: this word is Arabic, and they did not speak Arabic.

Two, and this is the closer: they were commanded to say a statement indicating repentance, regret and humility, so that if they had said, in place of their saying "hittah," "O Allah, we seek Your forgiveness and turn to You," the intended purpose would have been achieved. This is because the purpose of repentance is either the heart or the tongue. As for the heart, it is regret; as for the tongue, it is mentioning a word that indicates the presence of regret in the heart, and that does not depend upon mentioning one specific word.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will forgive you﴾, the discussion of forgiveness has already preceded. Here there are two discussions:

The first: His saying, ﴿We will forgive you﴾, was mentioned by Allah, exalted is He, in the context of granting favour. Had acceptance of repentance been obligatory by reason, as the Mu'tazilah (a theological school) say, the matter would not be so, but rather it would be the discharge of an obligation, and the discharge of an obligation may not be mentioned in the context of granting favour.

The second: here there are readings (qira'at):

The first: Abu 'Amr and Ibn al-Munadi read "naghfir" with the nun and a kasrah on the fa'.

The second: Nafi' read it with the ya' and a fathah on the fa'.

The third: the rest of the people of Madinah, and Jabalah from al-Mufaddal, read it with the ta' and a dammah on it, and a fathah on the fa'.

The fourth: al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Haywah and al-Ju'dari read it with the ya', a dammah on it, and a fathah on the fa'.

Al-Qaffal said: the meaning in all these readings is one, because when Allah, exalted is He, forgives a wrong, it has been forgiven, and when it has been forgiven, it is only Allah who forgives it. A verb may precede a feminine noun, and when something intervenes between it and its agent, both masculine and feminine forms are permitted, as in His saying: ﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾ (Hud: 67). The intended meaning of "wrong" (khati'ah) here is the genus, not a single wrong in number.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿your wrongs (khataya)﴾, there are readings concerning it:

The first: al-Ju'dari read "khati'atukum" with a long vowel, a hamzah, and a ta' with a dammah after the hamzah, in the singular.

The second: al-A'mash read "khati'atikum" with a long vowel, a hamzah, and an alif after the hamzah before the ta', with a kasrah on the ta'.

The third: al-Hasan likewise, except that he read the ta' with a dammah.

The fourth: al-Kisa'i read "khataya-kum" with a silent hamzah after the ta' before the ya'.

The fifth: Ibn Kathir read it with a silent hamzah after the ya' and before the kaf.

The sixth: al-Kisa'i read it with a kasrah on the ta' and the ya', while the rest read it with only the ya' inclined (imalah).

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We will increase the good-doers﴾, what is meant by "the good-doer" is either the one who was a good-doer through obedience in this obligation, or the one who was a good-doer through other acts of obedience in all the obligations.

According to the first possibility, the promised increase may be from the benefits of this world or from the benefits of religion.

As for the first possibility, that it is from the benefits of this world: the meaning is that whoever was a good-doer by this act of obedience, We will increase him in provision in this world and open for him other towns besides this town. As for the second possibility, that it is from the benefits of the Hereafter: the meaning is that whoever was a good-doer by this act of obedience and repentance, We will forgive him his wrongs and increase him, beyond the forgiveness of sins, the giving of abundant reward, as He said: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾ (Yunus: 26), meaning, We will recompense them for good with good and more, just as He made the reward for one good deed ten times or more. And if what is meant by "the good-doers" is one who was a good-doer through other acts of obedience after this repentance, then the meaning is that We make your entering the gate prostrating and your saying "hittah" effective in the forgiveness of sins, and then, when you afterwards perform other acts of obedience, We will give you the reward for those additional acts of obedience.

There is another interpretation of the verse, which is that the meaning is: whoever was a wrongdoer, We forgave him his sin by this act, and whoever was not a wrongdoer but a good-doer, We increased his goodness, that is, We recorded that obedience in his good deeds and increased him from Us in it. So forgiveness is for the believers and increase is for the obedient.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So those who did wrong substituted﴾, there are two views:

The first: Abu Muslim said: His saying, ﴿substituted﴾, indicates that they did not do what they were commanded, not that they brought a substitute for it. The evidence for this is that the substitution of a saying may be used to mean opposition, as He said: ﴿The stay-behinds among the Bedouins will say to you﴾ (Al-Fath: 11), up to His saying: ﴿They want to change the words of Allah﴾ (Al-Fath: 15). Their substitution was only opposition in action, not in speech. So it is the same here. The meaning is that when they were commanded to humility and to asking forgiveness, they did not comply with the command of Allah and did not pay attention to it.

[Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 59 (part 2 of 2)]
