The second view, which is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun), is that "substitution" (tabdil) means that they brought in a replacement for what had been said. This is because tabdil is derived from badal (replacement), so there must be a replacement. This is like saying, "So-and-so changed (baddala) his religion," which indicates that he moved from one religion to another. This is confirmed by His saying, ﴿a word other than what had been said to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59]. Then they differed over what that word and action were. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they entered through the gate they had been commanded to enter in prostration, dragging themselves on their buttocks, saying, "Hintah min sha'irah" (a grain of wheat in a barley-corn). From Mujahid, they entered on their backs and said "hintah" in mockery. Ibn Zayd said it was mockery of Musa, and they said, "Musa has done nothing but play with us, saying 'hittah hittah' (a dropping of burden), what kind of thing is hittah?"

As for His saying, ﴿those who did wrong﴾, Allah described them thus either because they strove to diminish their own good, both in this world and in religion, or because they harmed themselves, and that is wrongdoing (zulm), as has been explained earlier.

As for His saying, ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment (rijz) from the heaven﴾, there are two discussions here:

The first: the repetition of ﴿those who did wrong﴾ adds to the condemnation of their affair and signals that the sending down of the punishment upon them was because of their wrongdoing.

The second: rijz means punishment ('adhab). The evidence for this is His saying, ﴿And when the punishment (rijz) fell upon them﴾, meaning the retribution ('uqubah), and likewise His saying, ﴿If you remove from us the punishment (rijz)﴾ [al-A'raf: 134]. Al-Zajjaj mentioned that rijz and rijs have the same meaning, which is punishment.

As for His saying, ﴿and that He may remove from you the defilement (rijz) of Satan﴾ [al-Anfal: 11], its meaning is the soiling of the heart and what calls to disbelief (kufr). Then, as for what that punishment was, the verse gives no indication of it. Ibn 'Abbas said that twenty-four thousand of them died suddenly in a single hour. Ibn Zayd said that Allah sent the plague (ta'un) upon them, so that from morning until evening twenty-five thousand died, and none of them remained.

As for His saying, ﴿because they used to defy (yafsuqun)﴾, fisq derives from "going out" in a harmful way. It is said, "fasaqat al-rutbah" when the date-fruit came out of its skin. In the sacred law (shar'), it is an expression for going out from obedience to Allah into disobedience. Abu Muslim said: this fisq is the same wrongdoing (zulm) mentioned in His saying, ﴿upon those who did wrong﴾, and the purpose of the repetition is emphasis. The truth, however, is that it is not a repetition, for two reasons:

The first: wrongdoing (zulm) may be of minor sins (saghair) and may be of major sins (kaba'ir). For this reason Allah described the prophets with wrongdoing in His saying, ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. If zulm were only great, mentioning the great would be a repetition. Fisq must be of the major sins. So when Allah described them with zulm first, He described them with fisq second, so that it would be known that their wrongdoing was of the major sins and not of the minor.

The second: it is possible that they deserved the name of wrongdoers (zalimun) because of that substitution, so the punishment was sent down upon them from heaven because of that substitution. Or it was because of the defiance they had committed before that substitution. On this view, the repetition disappears.

The second topic concerning this verse: know that Allah mentioned this verse in surah al-A'raf, in His saying: ﴿And when it was said to them, "Dwell in this town and eat from it wherever you wish, and say 'hittah' (a dropping of burden), and enter the gate in prostration, We will forgive you your sins, and We will increase the good-doers."﴾ ﴿But those who did wrong among them substituted a word other than what had been said to them, so We sent upon them a punishment from the heaven because they had been defying (yazlimun)﴾ [al-A'raf: 161]. Know that some people argue from His saying, ﴿But those who did wrong substituted﴾, that whatever has been revealed as tawqif (a fixed, divinely prescribed form, such as certain remembrances) is not permissible to alter or to replace with something else. Perhaps the companions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued from it that it is not permissible to begin the prayer (tahrim) with the words of glorification and exaltation (ta'zim and tasbih), and that the recitation may not be in Persian. Abu Bakr al-Razi answered that they only deserved blame for changing the word to another word whose meaning is contrary to the meaning of the first. Therefore they rightly deserved blame. But whoever changes the wording while the meaning remains the same is not in that case.

The answer is that the apparent meaning of His saying, ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a word other than what had been said to them﴾, covers everyone who substitutes one word for another, whether or not the two words agree in meaning. Here there are several questions:

The first question: Why did He say in surah al-Baqarah, ﴿And when We said﴾, and in al-A'raf, ﴿And when it was said to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 160]?

The answer: Allah stated at the beginning of the Qur'an that the speaker of this statement is Allah, to remove ambiguity. Also, He mentioned at the beginning of the discourse, ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 47], and then began enumerating His blessings one by one. So the fitting thing in this context is to say, ﴿And when We said﴾. As for surah al-A'raf, after the clear statement in surah al-Baqarah, there remains no ambiguity in His saying, ﴿And when it was said to them﴾.

The second question: Why did He say in al-Baqarah, ﴿We said: enter﴾, and in al-A'raf, ﴿Dwell﴾ [al-A'raf: 161]?

The answer: entering precedes dwelling, and both are necessary. Therefore He mentioned entering in the earlier surah and dwelling in the later surah.

The third question: Why did He say in al-Baqarah, ﴿then eat﴾ with fa', and in al-A'raf, ﴿and eat﴾ [al-A'raf: 31] with wa'?

The answer here is the same as what we mentioned concerning His saying in surah al-Baqarah, ﴿and eat from it in abundance (raghadan)﴾, and in al-A'raf, ﴿so eat﴾ [al-A'raf: 19].

The fourth question: Why did He say in al-Baqarah, ﴿We will forgive you your sins (khataya)﴾, and in al-A'raf, ﴿We will forgive you your sins (khati'at)﴾ [al-A'raf: 161]?

The answer: khataya is the plural of abundance, and khati'at is the sound plural, which is for fewness. In surah al-Baqarah, since He attributed that statement to Himself, saying, ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town"﴾, He therefore joined to it what befits His generosity and bounty, namely the forgiveness of many sins. So He mentioned it with the plural form indicating abundance. In al-A'raf, since He did not attribute that statement to Himself but said, ﴿And when it was said to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 161], He therefore mentioned it with the plural of fewness. The conclusion is that when He mentioned the agent, He mentioned what befits His generosity, namely the forgiveness of [many] sins. In al-A'raf, since the agent was not named, He did not mention the word that indicates abundance.

The fifth question: Why did He mention ﴿raghadan﴾ in al-Baqarah and omit it in al-A'raf?

The answer to this question is like the answer concerning khataya and khati'at. Since He attributed the act to Himself, He therefore mentioned with it the greatest favour, which is that they should eat in abundance (raghadan). In al-A'raf, since He did not attribute the act to Himself, He did not mention the greatest favour in it.

The sixth question: Why did He mention in al-Baqarah, ﴿and enter the gate in prostration and say "hittah"﴾, while in al-A'raf He put the latter before the former?

The answer: the wa' indicates general joining (al-jam' al-mutlaq). Also, those addressed by His saying, ﴿and enter the gate in prostration and say "hittah"﴾, may be understood thus: some of them were sinners and others were not sinners. For the sinner, his occupation with removing sins must necessarily precede his occupation with worship, because repentance from sin necessarily precedes occupation with future acts of worship. Therefore the obligation for these people was to say "hittah" first and then enter the gate in prostration. As for the one who is not a sinner, it is better for him to occupy himself first with worship and then mention repentance second, as a way of humbling the self and removing vanity regarding that act of worship. Those people must enter the gate in prostration first and then say "hittah" second. Since it was possible that those addressed were divided into these two categories, Allah mentioned the ruling for each of them in a different surah.

The seventh question: Why did He say, ﴿and We will increase the good-doers﴾, with wa' in al-Baqarah, and in al-A'raf, ﴿We will increase the good-doers﴾ without wa' [al-A'raf: 161]?

The answer: In al-A'raf He mentioned two matters. One is saying "hittah," which is an indication of repentance. The second is entering the gate in prostration, which is an indication of worship. Then He mentioned two parts. One is His saying, ﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾, which corresponds to the saying of "hittah." The other is His saying, ﴿We will increase the good-doers﴾, which corresponds to entering the gate in prostration. So omitting the wa' indicates that each of the two parts is distributed over each of the two conditions. As for surah al-Baqarah, it indicates that the forgiveness and the increase together form one reward for the combined two actions, namely entering the gate and saying "hittah."

The eighth question: Allah said in surah al-Baqarah, ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a word﴾, and in al-A'raf, ﴿But those who did wrong among them substituted a word﴾ [al-A'raf: 162]. What is the benefit of adding the word "among them" in al-A'raf?

The answer: The reason for adding this word in surah al-A'raf is that the beginning of the story here is based on particularization with the particle "min" (among), because He said, ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice﴾ [al-A'raf: 159]. So He mentioned that among them are those who do this. Then He enumerated the kinds of His blessings upon them and His commands to them. When the story ended, Allah said, ﴿But those who did wrong among them﴾ [al-A'raf: 162]. So He mentioned the word "among them" at the end of the story just as He mentioned it at the beginning, so that the end of the discourse corresponds to its beginning. The wrongdoers among the people of Musa are thus in contrast to those among them who guide. There He mentioned a just community, and here He mentioned an oppressive community, and both are from the people of Musa. This is the reason for mentioning this word in surah al-A'raf. As for surah al-Baqarah, He did not mention, in the verses before His saying, ﴿But those who did wrong﴾, any distinction or particularization, so that at the end of the story it would be necessary to mention that particularization. Thus the difference is clear.

The ninth question: Why did He say in al-Baqarah, ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment (rijz)﴾, and in al-A'raf, ﴿So We sent﴾ [al-A'raf: 162]?

The answer: inzal (sending down) indicates its occurrence at the beginning of the matter, while irsal (sending) indicates its domination over them and its total eradication of them, and that only happens at the end.

The tenth question: Why did He say in al-Baqarah, ﴿because they used to defy (yafsuqun)﴾, and in al-A'raf, ﴿because they used to do wrong (yazlimun)﴾ [al-A'raf: 161]?

The answer: Since Allah, in surah al-Baqarah, explained that this wrongdoing was defiance (fisq), He was satisfied in surah al-A'raf with the word "wrongdoing," because of the explanation that had already preceded in surah al-Baqarah. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 60 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said: "Strike the rock with your staff." And there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew their own drinking place. "Eat and drink from the provision of Allah, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief."﴾

The reading of the common reciters is ithnatā ʿashrata with the shīn sukūn (ith-na-ʿashrah, pronounced with a light form). The reading of Abū Jaʿfar is with a kasra on the shīn, and it is reported from some of them with a fatḥa on the shīn. The first is the preferred form, because it is lighter, and most reciters follow it. Know that this is the ninth of the enumerated blessings bestowed upon the Children of Israel, and it encompasses the blessings of this world and the religion. As for this world, Allah removed from them the severe need for water; had it not been for this, they would have perished in the wilderness (al-tīh), just as, had it not been for His sending down the manna and the quail, they would have perished. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not make them bodies that do not eat food﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 8], and He said: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 30]. Indeed, the blessing of water in the wilderness is greater than the blessing of ordinary water, because when a person's need for water becomes intense in the desert, and the doors of hope are closed to him because he is in a place with no water and no vegetation, then when Allah provides him with water from a rock struck by a staff, which splits and yields water for him to drink, he knows that this blessing is hardly matched by any other blessing. As for its being a blessing of the religion, it is because it is among the clearest proofs of the existence of the Creator, His power and His knowledge, and among the most truthful proofs of the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him. Here are some issues:

The first issue: The majority of the exegetes agree that this request for water took place in the wilderness (al-tīh), because when Allah shaded them with the clouds, sent down upon them the manna and the quail, and made their garments such that they would neither wear out nor become soiled, they feared thirst, so Allah gave them water from that rock. Abū Muslim denied that this miracle should be attributed to the days of their journey into the wilderness, and said: Rather, it is a separate statement on its own. The meaning of istisqāʾ is seeking watering from rain, in the customary way of people when they suffer drought, and what Allah did by making water gush from the rock would be beyond the answering with watering and sending down of rain. The truth is that there is nothing in the verse indicating that this or that is the correct view, although the closer view is that this occurred in the wilderness, and two things indicate it:
One of them: It is customary in towns to be free from seeking water except rarely.
The second: What is narrated, that they used to carry the rock with themselves, since it had become prepared for this purpose. Just as the manna and quail descended upon them every morning, so the water gushed forth for them at every time; and this is not fitting except during their days in the wilderness.

* * *

The second issue: They differed concerning the staff. Al-Ḥasan said: It was a staff which he took from one of the trees. It was said: It was of the myrtle (ās) of Paradise, its length was ten cubits by the height of Moses, and it had two branches which glowed in the darkness. What the Qur'an indicates is that its size was such that he could lean upon it and that it could turn into a great serpent; and it is not so unless it has a certain length and thickness, and anything beyond that has no indication.
Page 89
Know that abstaining from discussing such matters is obligatory, because there is no definite, mutually transmitted (mutawātir) text in them, and no action depends on them such that one would be content with the conjecture derived from solitary reports (akhbār al-āḥād). Therefore, it is better to leave them aside.

The third issue: The alif-lām in "al-ḥajar" (the rock) is either for prior reference, pointing to a known rock. It is reported that it was a Ṭūrī (Sinai) stone which he carried with him; it was square, having four faces, and from each face three springs gushed forth, one for each tribe, flowing in a channel to that tribe. They numbered six hundred thousand, and the width of the camp was twelve miles. It was also said that it was sent down with Adam from Paradise, and they inherited it until it came to Shuʿayb, who gave it to him together with the staff. It was also said: It is the stone upon which he placed his garment when he washed, when they accused him of having a swollen testicle (udra), and he fled with it. Gabriel said to him: "Allah, exalted is He, says: Lift this stone, for I have power in it and it is a miracle for you." So he carried it in his bag. Or it is for the genus, meaning: strike the thing called a rock. Al-Ḥasan reported: They were not commanded to strike a specific rock. He said: This is more evident as a proof and clearer as an indication of power. It is also reported that they said: "What will become of us if we arrive at a land with no stones?" So he carried a stone in his bag, and whenever they halted he would set it down. It was said: He would strike it with his staff and it would gush forth, and he would strike it with it and it would dry up. They said: "If Moses loses his staff, we will die of thirst." So Allah revealed to him: "Do not knock the stones; speak to them, and they will obey you." They differed concerning the description of the rock. It was said: It was of marble, a cubit by a cubit. It was said: Like the head of a man. Our preferred view is to entrust its knowledge to Allah, exalted is He.

The fourth issue: The fāʾ in His saying ﴿fa-infajarat﴾ ("and there gushed forth") is connected to an elided element, meaning: so he struck, and it gushed forth; or: if you strike, then it has gushed forth. Remaining here are questions:

The first question: Is it permissible for Allah to command him to strike the rock with his staff so that it gushes forth without striking, so as to dispense with this elided element?
The answer: There is no impossibility in power that Allah command him to strike the rock with his staff, and that before he strikes it gushes forth in the measure of need, for that, if it were said, would be more eloquent in miraculousness and closer to it. However, the correct view is that he struck and it gushed forth, because if Allah commanded His messenger with something and then the messenger did not do it, the messenger would become disobedient; and because if it gushed forth without striking, the command to strike with the staff would become pointless, as though it had no meaning; and because what is transmitted in reports is that its implied form is: "So he struck and it gushed forth," as in His saying: ﴿fa-infalaq﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 63], where the intended meaning is: "So he struck and it split."

The second question: Here He mentioned ﴿fa-infajarat﴾, and in al-Aʿrāf: ﴿fa-inbajasat﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 160]. Between them there is a contradiction, because infijār is the outpouring of water in abundance, and inbijās is its outpouring in small amounts.
The answer has three aspects:
One: al-fajr originally means splitting, and infijār means bursting open; from it comes fājir (the wicked one), because he splits the staff of the Muslims by his going out into wickedness. Inbijās is a name for a narrow, small split. So they differ as general and particular, and therefore they do not contradict.
Two: Perhaps it first welled up (inbajasa), then gushed forth (infajara) afterward; likewise with springs: water appears from them in small amounts, then increases because its flow continues.
Three: It is not impossible that their need for water was intense, so it gushed forth, meaning water came out abundantly; then their need diminished, so the water welled up, meaning it came out in small amounts.

The third question: How can it be understood that great waters come out of a small rock?
The answer: This questioner either grants the existence of a choosing agent or denies it. If he grants it, the question is resolved, because He is able to create a body however He wills, just as He created the seas and other things. If he disputes it, there is no benefit in his inquiry into the meaning of the Qur'an and the consideration of its exegesis. This is the answer to everything they deem improbable among the miracles which Allah, exalted is He, has related in the Qur'an, such as the raising of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper.
Page 90
Furthermore, the philosophers cannot definitively rule out the impossibility of this, because the four elements, according to them, share a common prime matter (hayūlā), and they said: generation and corruption are valid upon it, and it is valid for air to turn into water and vice versa. They also said: when air is placed in a silver cup, it congeals, for droplets of water gather on the cup's rim; they said: those droplets came into being only because the air turned into water. Thus it is established that this is possible in general, and the sublunary events obey celestial conjunctions, so it is not improbable that a celestial conjunction might occur that requires this strange event to happen in this world. Thus it is established that the philosophers cannot definitively judge the impossibility of this.
As for the Mu'tazilites, since they hold that the servant is the originator of his own acts, we say to them: Why is it not possible for the servant to be able to create a body? They mention two arguments in this regard, both extremely weak, which we will mention, if Allah wills, in the exegesis of the verse on magic, and we will mention the reason for their weakness and their collapse. Given this, they cannot definitively assert that this is from the act of Allah, exalted is He, and so the doors of miracles and prophethood are closed to them. As for our companions, since they hold that there is no originator except Allah, exalted is He, they definitively affirm that the one who brings about these extraordinary acts that break customary patterns is Allah, exalted is He. Therefore, they are able to argue, by their manifestation at the hand of a claimant, that he is truthful.

The fifth question (the fourth in some numbering): Is the miracle of Moses in this respect greater, or the miracle of Muhammad, peace be upon him?
The answer: Each of them is a dazzling and overpowering miracle, but the one given to Muhammad ﷺ is stronger, because the gushing of water from a rock is known in general, but its gushing from between the fingers is not customary at all, so that is stronger.

The sixth question: What is the wisdom in making the water into twelve springs?
The answer: The people of Moses were numerous, and when many people are in severe need of water and then find it, disputes and quarrels arise among them, and perhaps that leads to great strife. So Allah completed this blessing by designating for each tribe a specific water that does not mix with anything else, and it is customary that among a single clan there is not the kind of quarrel that arises among people who differ.

The seventh question: In how many respects does this gushing indicate the miracle?
The answer: In several respects:
One: The very appearance of water is a miracle.
Two: The great quantity of water from a small rock.
Three: The water coming out in proportion to their need.
Four: The water coming out when the rock is struck with the staff.
Five: The water ceasing when they no longer need it.
These five aspects cannot be achieved except by complete power that is executed over all possibilities, knowledge that encompasses all knowables, and lofty wisdom over the ages and times, and that is only for the Truth, glory be to Him.
Page 91

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Every people knew their drinking place﴾, we say: They only knew it because He commanded each person not to drink except from a specific channel, lest they dispute at the time of need for water. As for attributing the drinking place to them, it is because when Allah permitted each tribe of the tribes that water which emerged from the crack adjacent to it, it became as if it were their possession, and it was permissible to attribute it to them.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Eat and drink from the provision of Allah﴾, there is an ellipsis in it, and the meaning is: So We said to them, or Moses said to them: "Eat and drink." He said "eat" for two reasons:
One of them: because of what preceded regarding the mention of the manna and the quail, as if he said: "Eat of the manna and quail which Allah has provided you without toil or hardship, and drink of this water."

Secondly: food cannot exist without water, so when He gave them water, it is as if He, exalted is He, gave them food and drink.

The Mu'tazilah cited this verse as evidence that provision (rizq) is what is lawful (halal). They said: the least degree of His saying, ﴿Eat and drink﴾, is permissibility (ibahah), and this requires that provision be permissible. So if an unlawful provision were found, that provision would be both permissible and impermissible, and that is not valid.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾, al-'Athi is the most severe corruption. It was said to them: do not persist in corruption while you are engaged in corrupting, because they were persisting in it. What is intended by it is what is customary among people of quarrelling and disputing over water when the need for it becomes intense. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: if a dispute arises because of that water, then do not go to excess in the dispute. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions." He said, "Would you exchange what is lower for what is better? Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you asked for." And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger from Allah. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾

Know that the well-known recitation is "yakhruju lana" (with a damma on the yaa' and a kasra on the raa'), and "tunbitu" (with a damma on the taa' and a kasra on the baa'). Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "yakhruju" with a fatha on the yaa' and a damma on the raa', and "tanbutu" with a fatha on the taa' and a damma on the baa'.

Then know that most of the exoteric commentators (al-Zahiriyyun, those who adhere to the apparent meaning of the text) claimed that this request was an act of disobedience. Our view, however, is that the matter is not so. The evidence for this is that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Eat and drink﴾, which comes before this verse at the sending down of the manna and the quails, is not an obligation but a permission (ibahah). If that is the case, then their saying ﴿we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord for us﴾ was not disobedience, because one who is permitted a type of food may properly ask for something other than it, either by himself or through the Messenger. Since they believed that if they asked Moses to ask this of his Lord, the supplication would be closer to being answered, it was permissible for them, and there was no disobedience in it.

Know also that the request for the other kinds of food may be for several purposes:

First: when they had eaten that one kind for forty years, they grew tired of it and desired something else.

Second: perhaps by their original nature they were not accustomed to that kind, and were only accustomed to the other kinds. A person's desire for what he has become accustomed to in his upbringing, even if it is base, exceeds his desire for what he is not accustomed to, even if it is noble.

Third: perhaps they tired of remaining in the tih (the wilderness), so they asked for these foods which are found only in cities, their aim being to reach the cities, not the foods themselves.

Fourth: constant reliance on one food is a cause of diminished appetite, weakness of digestion, and lack of desire, whereas having many kinds strengthens appetite and increases enjoyment. Thus it is established that exchanging one kind for another may be the aim of rational people, and it is established that there is nothing in the Qur'an indicating that they were forbidden from it. Therefore this degree of request cannot be disobedience. What confirms this is that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you asked for﴾ is like an answer to what they requested. If they had been disobedient in that request, then granting it would have been disobedience, and that is impermissible for the prophets.

It may not be said: when they refused something that Allah had chosen for them, He gave them the immediate portion of what they asked for, as He said: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him from it﴾ [al-Shura: 20]. This is because we say that this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Those who argued that this request was disobedience cited several arguments:

First: their saying ﴿we will not endure one kind of food﴾ indicates that they disliked the sending down of the manna and the quails, and that dislike is disobedience.

Second: Moses's saying, peace be upon him, ﴿Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ is a question in the manner of denunciation, and that indicates that it was disobedience.

Third: Moses, peace be upon him, described what they asked for as lower (adna) and what they were upon as better, and that indicates what we have said.

As for the answer to the first: there is no indication in their saying ﴿we will not endure one kind of food﴾ that they were merely dissatisfied with it, but rather they desired something else. Moreover, their saying ﴿we will not endure﴾ refers to the future, since the particle lan denotes negation in the future, so it does not indicate that they were angry at the present reality.

As for the answer to the second: the interrogation in the manner of denunciation may be because of the loss of what is more beneficial in this world, and it may be because of the loss of what is more beneficial in the Hereafter.

As for the answer to the third: it is similar to that. A thing may be described as better from the perspective that its benefit is present and certain, and from the perspective that it comes effortlessly without hardship, as is said of what is present. Likewise, a distant thing that is uncertain may be described as lower from the perspective that it is not certain, and from the perspective that it cannot be reached except through hardship. Therefore there is no objection to the meaning of His saying ﴿Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ being this meaning or part of it. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that this request was not disobedience, but a permissible request. If that is so, then His saying ﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger from Allah﴾ cannot be due to what preceded, but rather to what Allah mentioned after it, namely His saying ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right﴾. Thus He made clear that He only stamped humiliation and poverty upon them, and made them the object of wrath and punishment, because they disbelieved, not because they made that request.

The second issue: His saying ﴿we will not endure one kind of food﴾ does not mean that it is one in kind, but rather that it is one in manner (nahj), as is said: "the food of so-and-so at his table is one food" when it does not change from its manner.

The third issue: the well-known recitation is ﴿wa-qith-tha'iha﴾ with a kasra on the qaf, while al-A'mash and Talhah recited "wa-qutha'iha" with a damma on the qaf. The well-known recitation is ﴿wa-fumiha﴾ with a fa', while on the authority of 'Alqamah, from Ibn Mas'ud, it is recited "wa-thumiha" with a tha', and this is the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas. They said: this is more fitting with the mention of the onion. They differed concerning the fum. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, it is wheat; and also on his authority, the fum is bread, which is also related from Mujahid, 'Ata', and Ibn Zayd. It is related from some Arabs: "fawwimu lana," meaning "bake for us." It was also said that it is garlic (thum), which is also related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, and this was the preference of al-Kisa'i. They argued for this with several points:

First: it is in the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud as "wa-thumiha."

Second: if the meaning were wheat, it would not be permissible to say ﴿Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾, because wheat is the noblest of foods.

Third: garlic is more suited alongside lentils and onions than wheat is.

The fourth issue: the well-known recitation is ﴿a-tastabdiluna﴾ ("Would you exchange"), while in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "a-tubdiluna" with the baa' sukun. On the authority of Zuhayr al-Furqubi, it is "adna'" with a hamzah, from al-dana'ah (baseness). They differed concerning the meaning of "adna" (lower), and the summary of the view on it is that the meaning is either that it is lower in benefit for religion, or lower in benefit for this world. The first is not intended, because if what they were upon were more beneficial in religious matters than what they asked for, it would not have been permissible for Him to grant them it. But He did grant it to them by His saying ﴿Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you asked for﴾. So what remains is that the intended meaning is benefit in this world. Then it is not permissible that the meaning be that this kind which you are upon is superior to what you seek, because we have explained that the food which is most delicious to one people may be the basest to another. Rather, the intended meaning is what we have explained: that the manna and quails were certain to be obtained, while what they sought was uncertain to be obtained, and what is certain is better than what is uncertain, or because this comes without effort or toil, whereas that is only obtained with effort and toil, so the former is preferable.

If it is said: they could have said, "This which comes effortlessly and purely, when we dislike it by our natures, eating it is more difficult than that which is obtained only with effort, when our natures desire it."

We say: suppose a conflict arose from this aspect, yet the preference is decided by the fact that the present and certain is weightier than the absent and uncertain.

The fifth issue: the well-known recitation is ﴿ihbitu﴾ with a kasra on the baa'; it is also recited with a damma on the baa'. The well-known recitation is ﴿misran﴾ with tanwin. The reason it takes tanwin, despite the two causes of diptotic inflection being present in it (definiteness and feminine form), is that its middle letter is quiescent, like His saying ﴿and Noah, We guided﴾ [al-An'am: 84] and ﴿and Lot﴾ [al-An'am: 86]. In these two there is also 'ujmah (foreign origin) and definiteness. If it is intended as a city, then there is only one cause in it. In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), and as recited by al-A'mash, it is ﴿ihbitu misran﴾ without tanwin, like His saying ﴿Enter Egypt (Misr)﴾ [Yusuf: 99]. The commentators differed concerning His saying ﴿ihbitu misran﴾. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the tanwin is omitted. Al-Hasan said: the alif in (misran) is an addition by the scribe, and therefore it is definite, so it must be taken to refer to what is specifically this name, namely the city in which Pharaoh was. This is related from Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Rabi'. As for those who recited with tanwin, which is the well-known recitation, they differed. Some of them said: the intended meaning is the city in which Pharaoh was, and the entry of tanwin into it is like its entry into Noah and Lot. Others said: the intended meaning is the command to enter any city whatsoever, as if it were said to them, "Enter a city, any city, so that you may find these things in it." In sum, the commentators differed as to whether the intended meaning of Misr is the city in which they were at first or another city.

Many of the commentators said: it cannot be the city in which they were with Pharaoh, and they argued for this with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Enter the holy land which Allah has written for you, and do not turn back on your heels﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21]. The inference from this verse is from three aspects:

First: His saying ﴿Enter the holy land﴾ is an obligation to enter that land, and that requires the prohibition of entering another land.

Second: His saying ﴿which Allah has written﴾ requires the permanence of their being in it.

Third: His saying ﴿and do not turn back on your heels﴾ is explicit in prohibiting their returning from Bayt al-Maqdis.

Fourth: after He commanded them to enter the holy land, He said ﴿It is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 26]. When this command came first, and then He made clear that they were prevented from entering it for this period, then when the excuse was removed it became obligatory for them to enter it. If that is so, it is not permissible that the intended meaning of Misr be anything other than it.

If it is said: these aspects are weak.

As for the first: His saying ﴿Enter the holy land﴾ is a command, and a command is for recommendation (nadb). Perhaps they were only recommended to enter the holy land, even though they were not prevented from entering Egypt.

As for the second: it is like His saying ﴿which Allah has written for you﴾, and that indicates the permanence of that recommendation.

As for the third, His saying ﴿and do not turn back on your heels﴾: we do not concede that its meaning is "do not return to Egypt." Rather, there are two other meanings in it:

First: the intended meaning is "do not disobey in what you have been commanded," since the Arabs say of one who disobeys in what he has been commanded: "he turned back on his heels." The intended meaning of this disobedience is that one denies that entering the holy land is preferable.

Second: that this prohibition be restricted to a specific time only.

We say: it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, so our argument is completed on the basis of this principle. Furthermore, even if we grant that it is for recommendation, the permission to leave it would be permission to abandon what is recommended, and that is not becoming for the prophets.

His saying: "We do not concede that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿and do not turn back﴾ is 'do not return.'" We say: the evidence for this is that when He commanded entry into the holy land, and then said after it, ﴿and do not turn back on your heels﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21], it comes readily to understanding that this prohibition refers to what that command was related to.

His saying: "that this prohibition be restricted to a specific time." We say: restriction (takhsis) is contrary to the apparent meaning.

As for Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, he permitted that the intended meaning be the Misr of Pharaoh, and he argued for this with two aspects:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 2 of 2):

The first aspect: If we read "ihbitu Misr" without tanwin (nunation), it is necessarily a proper name for a specific city, and there is no city in the world bearing this title other than this specific city. Therefore the word must be understood as referring to it. Also, when a word can be either a proper name or a descriptive adjective, reading it as a proper name is preferable to reading it as an adjective, like *zalim* and *hadith*, since when they came as proper names, it is preferable to read them as proper names. But if we read it with tanwin, then either we make it a proper name nonetheless and say that tanwin entered it because its middle letter is sukun (vowelless), as in *Nuh* and *Lut*, so the argument is the same as what preceded. Or, if we make it a common noun (ism jins), then His saying, ﴿Go down to a city﴾, implies choice, just as if He said, "Free a slave," which implies a choice among all the slaves of the world.

The second aspect: God made the Children of Israel inherit the land of Egypt, and if it was inherited by them, it is impossible that He would forbid them to enter it. The proof that it was inherited by them is His saying: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs and treasures and a noble station. Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 57–59]. And since it is established that it was inherited by them, it must be that they were not prevented from entering it, because inheritance confers ownership, and ownership is unrestricted in its disposal. If it is said: A man may own a house while being prevented from entering it for another reason, like the case of someone who has vowed to make i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque) for several days; his house is his property, yet it is forbidden for him to enter it. So why could it not be said that God gave them Egypt as an inheritance in the sense of authority and disposal over it, and then He forbade them to enter it insofar as He obligated them to dwell in the holy land by His saying: ﴿Enter the holy land﴾ [al-Ma'idah 21]? We say: The principle is that ownership is unrestricted in its disposal, and preventing disposal contradicts the evidence.

The first group answered these two arguments that Abu Muslim raised, and they said:

As for the first argument, our answer is that we hold to the well-known reading, which is the one with tanwin. As for his claim that this reading implies choice, we say: Yes, but we restrict the generality in regard to this specific city by the evidence we have mentioned.

As for the second argument, our answer is that we do not dispute that ownership is unrestricted in its disposal, but this principle may be set aside due to an external factor, as with the pledged property and the rented property. So we have set aside this principle on account of the proof we have presented.

As for His saying: ﴿And humiliation and misery were struck upon them﴾, the meaning is that humiliation was made to surround them completely, encompassing them, so they were within it like one who is inside a tent that has been pitched, or it was attached to them so that it clung to them, like a plaster that is applied to a wall and adheres to it. In regard to *dhillah* (humiliation), the closer view is that what is meant by it is what functions as a due consequence, like His saying concerning those who wage war and cause corruption: ﴿That is their disgrace in this world﴾ [al-Ma'idah 33]. As for those who say that what is meant is specifically the jizyah (poll tax), based on His saying: ﴿until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled﴾ [al-Tawbah 29], that view is far-fetched, because the jizyah was not imposed upon them from the very beginning.

As for His saying: ﴿And misery (maskanah)﴾, what is meant by it is poverty, destitution, and the intensification of hardship. This type may be like a punishment. Some scholars counted this among the miracles, because he (peace be upon him) reported that humiliation and misery would be struck upon them, and the matter happened exactly so, and so this was a report of the unseen, and therefore it is a miracle.

As for His saying: ﴿And they returned (ba'u)﴾, there are several opinions:

The first: *al-bawʾ* means return, so His saying "ba'u" means they returned and departed with that. And *ba'a* is not said except with regard to evil.

The second: *al-bawʾ* means equalization, so His saying "ba'u" means the anger of God became equal upon them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: "ba'u" means they deserved, and from this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I wish that you would bear my sin and your sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah 29], meaning you would deserve both sins together. As for the anger of God, it is the will to take vengeance.

As for His saying: ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God﴾, it is a reason for what was mentioned before, namely the striking of humiliation and misery upon them and the bringing of anger upon them. The Mu'tazilites said: If disbelief occurred in them by the creation of God, just as humiliation and misery occurred in them by His creation, then making one of them a recompense for the other would not be more appropriate than the reverse. The answer to this is a counter-argument based on knowledge and motive. As for the reality of disbelief, the discussion of it has already preceded.

As for His saying: ﴿And they killed the prophets without right﴾, the meaning is that they deserve what has been mentioned before because of these deeds as well, and there are questions about this.

The first question: His saying ﴿they disbelieve﴾ includes the killing of the prophets, so why did He mention it again?

The answer: What is mentioned here is disbelief in the signs of God, and that is ignorance of and denial of His signs, so the killing of the prophets does not fall under it.

The second question: Why did He say ﴿without right﴾, when the killing of prophets can only be in this way?

The answer has two parts:

The first: Acting with falsehood may be right, because the one who does it believes it to be true due to a doubt that has entered his heart, and he may do it while knowing that it is false. There is no doubt that the second is more ugly. So His saying ﴿and they killed the prophets without right﴾ means that they killed them without that killing being right in their belief and imagination; rather, they knew its ugliness, and despite that they did it.

The second: This repetition is for the sake of emphasis, like His saying: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with God, for which he has no proof﴾ [al-Mu'minun 117], and it is impossible that the one claiming a second god would have proof.

The third: If God had blamed them merely for killing, they would have said: Is it not the case that God kills them? But He, exalted is He, said: The killing that proceeds from God is killing with right, and the killing that proceeds from other than God is killing without right.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾, it is an emphasis through repeating the matter with words other than the first. It is like a man saying to his slave, who has committed several sins before, and who he punishes at the end of them: "This is because you disobeyed me and opposed my command, this is because you dared against me and were deceived by my forbearance, and this is because of such-and-such." He enumerates his sins in different terms as a rebuke.

As for His saying: ﴿and they used to transgress (ya'tadun)﴾, what is meant by it is injustice, that is, they went beyond the truth into falsehood.

Know that when He mentioned the sending down of punishment upon them, He explained its cause. He began first with what they did regarding the right of God, which is their ignorance of Him and their denial of His blessings. Then He followed it with what comes next in gravity, which is the killing of the prophets. Then He made it three with the sins that are specific to them. Then He made it four with the sins that extend to others, like transgression and injustice, and this is in the utmost excellence of ordering.

If it is said: Here He said ﴿and they killed the prophets without right﴾, mentioning *al-haqq* (the truth) with the definite article as a definite noun, while in Al 'Imran He said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right﴾ [Al 'Imran 21] with an indefinite noun. Likewise in this surah: ﴿and they kill the prophets without right, that is because they disobeyed and used to transgress. They are not equal﴾ [Al 'Imran 112]. So what is the difference?

The answer: *al-haqq* (the truth) known among the Muslims is that which makes killing obligatory. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The blood of a Muslim man may not be shed except in one of three cases: disbelief after faith, adultery after marriage, or killing a soul without right." So the definite *al-haqq* mentioned here is a reference to this. As for the indefinite negated *haqq*, what is meant by it is the emphasis of generality, that is, there was no right at all there, neither this one that Muslims know nor any other whatsoever.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians, whoever believed in God and the Last Day and did righteous deeds, they will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.﴾

Know that the well-known reading of ﴿هادُوا﴾ is with a ḍammah on the dāl. It is also reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid with a fatḥah on the dāl and a sukūn on the wāw. The well-known reading of الصّابِئِينَ and الصّابِئُونَ is with a hamzah in both, wherever they occur. It is reported from Nāfi', Shaybah, and al-Zuhrī as الصّابِّينَ, with a silent yā' and no hamzah, and الصّابُونَ with a ḍammah on the bā' and the hamzah omitted. It is reported from al-ʿUmarī with the hamzah in both places, and from Abū Jaʿfar with two pure yā's, which replace the hamzah. As for omitting the hamzah, it has two possible explanations:

The first: that it derives from ṣabā, yaṣbū, meaning he inclined toward a thing and so loved it.

The second: that the hamzah has been changed, so we say الصّابِيِينَ and الصّابِيُونَ. The preferred reading is with the hamzah, because it is the reading of most people, and it is closer to the sense of the exegesis, since the scholars said: he is one who leaves one religion for another. Know that it is God's practice that when He mentions a promise or a threat, He follows it with its opposite, so that the speech is complete. Here, when He mentioned the judgment on the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the punishment that befell them, He informed of the great reward and noble recompense for the believers, indicating that He, glory be to Him and exalted, rewards the good-doer for his goodness and the evildoer for his evil, as He said: ﴿That He may reward those who did evil according to what they did, and reward those who did good with the best [reward]﴾ [al-Najm: 31]. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾. The exegetes differed concerning what is meant by this, and the cause of this difference is His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿whoever believed in God and the Last Day﴾. This requires that the meaning of "belief" in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ be different from its meaning in His saying ﴿whoever believed in God﴾. A parallel to this difficulty is His saying: ﴿O you who believed, believe﴾ [al-Nisā': 136]. Because of this difficulty, they mentioned several explanations:

The first, which is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās: what is meant is those who believed before the mission of Muḥammad, in the time of ʿĪsā, peace be upon them both, while being free of the falsehoods of the Jews and Christians, such as Quss ibn Sāʿidah, Baḥīrā the monk, Ḥabīb the carpenter, Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, Salmān al-Fārisī, Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, and the delegation of the Negus. It is as if He, exalted, said: Indeed, those who believed before the mission of Muḥammad, and those who were upon the false religion of the Jews, and those who were upon the false religion of the Christians, all of those among them who believed after the mission of Muḥammad, peace be upon him, in God and the Last Day and in Muḥammad, they will have their reward with their Lord.

The second: He, exalted, mentioned at the beginning of this sūrah the way of the hypocrites, then the way of the Jews. So what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ are those who believe with the tongue but not with the heart, and they are the hypocrites. Then He mentioned the hypocrites, then the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians. It is as if He, exalted, said: These people are falsifiers; whoever among them comes with true faith becomes one of the believers before God. This is the saying of Sufyān al-Thawrī.

The third: what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ are those who truly believe in Muḥammad, peace be upon him. This refers to the past. Then His saying ﴿whoever believed in God﴾ implies the future. So what is meant is those who believed in the past, remained steadfast upon that, and persisted in it in the future. This is the saying of the theologians.

As for His saying ﴿and those who were Jews﴾, they differed concerning its derivation in several ways:

The first: they were named so when they repented from worshipping the calf, and said: ﴿Indeed we have turned back to You﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 156], meaning we repented and returned. This is from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: they were named so because they were attributed to Yahūdhā, the eldest son of Yaʿqūb. The Arabs used the dāl for Arabization, since when the Arabs take names from the non-Arabic languages into their language, they change some of their letters.

The third: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: they were named so because they "yatahawwadūn," meaning they move when reciting the Torah.

As for the Christians, there are several explanations for the derivation of this name:

The first: the village where ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, used to dwell was called Nāṣirah, so they were attributed to it. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: because they helped one another among themselves, meaning they supported one another.

The third: because ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, said to the disciples: "Who are my helpers to God?" The author of al-Kashshāf said: al-Naṣārā is the plural of naṣrān; one says a man is naṣrān, and a woman is naṣrānah, and the yā' in naṣrānī is for intensification, like the one in aḥmarī, because they supported the Messiah.

As for His saying ﴿and the Sabians﴾, it is from ṣabaʾa, meaning he left his religion for another religion. In this way the Arabs used to call the Prophet, peace be upon him, a Sabian, because he manifested a religion contrary to their religions. And the stars "ṣabaʾat" when they emerge from their rising point, and "ṣabaʾnā bihi" when we went forth with it. The exegetes have several sayings about their creed:

The first: Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan said: they are a group among the Magians and the Jews whose slaughtered animals may not be eaten and whose women may not be married.

The second: Qatādah said: they are a people who worship the angels and pray toward the sun five prayers every day. He also said: the religions are five, of which four belong to Satan and one to the Merciful: the Sabians, who worship the angels; the Magians, who worship fire; those who associate partners with God, who worship idols; and the Jews and Christians.

The third, which is the closest: they are a people who worship the stars. For them there are two sayings:

The first: that the Creator of the world is God, glory be to Him, but He commanded that these stars be venerated and taken as a qiblah for prayer, supplication, and veneration.

The second: that God, glory be to Him, created the spheres and the stars, and the stars are what govern what is in this world of good and evil, health and sickness, and they are the ones who create these things. Therefore it is obligatory for humans to venerate them, because they are the governing gods of this world, and they in turn worship God, glory be to Him. This doctrine is the view attributed to the Chaldeans, to whom Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, came, refuting them and nullifying their saying.

Then, glory be to Him, He explained among these four groups that if they believe in God, they have the reward in the Hereafter, so that it may be known that all the lords of misguidance, when they return from their misguidance and believe in the true religion, God, glory be to Him and exalted, accepts their faith and their obedience and never turns them away from His presence. Know that belief in God includes belief in what He has made obligatory, namely belief in His messengers, and belief in the Last Day includes all the rulings of the Hereafter. Thus these two sayings encompass everything connected with religions, both in the state of obligation and in the state of the Hereafter, of reward and punishment.

As for His saying ﴿with their Lord﴾, the intended meaning is not spatial nearness, since that is impossible with respect to God, exalted, nor is it a matter of safekeeping like deposits. Rather, what is meant is that their reward is certain, as though it were already obtained with their Lord.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted: ﴿and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾, it has been said: He means the removal of fear and grief from them in this world. Some said it means in the Hereafter, in the state of reward. This second view is more sound, because His saying ﴿and no fear will be upon them﴾ is general in negation, and likewise ﴿nor will they grieve﴾. This attribute does not occur in this world, especially for those who are morally responsible, because at every time they are never free of fear and grief, either concerning the affairs of this world or the affairs of the Hereafter. So it is as if He, glory be to Him, promised them in the Hereafter the reward, and then explained that among the attributes of that reward is that it is free of fear and grief, and this necessarily means that their bliss is everlasting, because if they allowed for it to be cut off, great grief would overtake them.

If someone says: God, exalted, mentioned this verse in Sūrat al-Mā'idah in this way: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians and the Christians, whoever believed in God and the Last Day and did righteous deeds, then no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 69]. And in Sūrat al-Ḥajj: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated partners, indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed God is over all things a witness﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 17]. Is there, in the variation of these verses by the order of the groups being placed earlier or later, and the raising of "al-Ṣābiʾīn" in one verse and its putting in the accusative in another, a benefit that requires this?

The answer: since the Speaker is the most wise of the wise, these changes must have wisdoms and benefits. If we perceive those wisdoms, we have attained perfection; and if we are unable, we attribute the deficiency to our own minds, not to the speech of the All-Wise. And God knows best.

[Page 100]

The Most High says: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful."﴾ ﴿Then you turned away after that. Had it not been for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy, you would surely have been among the losers.﴾

Know that this is the tenth blessing. That is because Allah, exalted is He, took their covenant only for their benefit, so it became one of His favours upon them.

As for the Most High's words, ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾, there are two discussions.

The first: Know that a covenant (mithaq) is only made through the performance of matters that necessitate submission and obedience. The exegetes have mentioned several interpretations of the covenant:

One of them: it is what Allah deposited in the intellects of the proofs that indicate the existence of the Creator and His wisdom, and the proofs that indicate the truthfulness of His prophets and messengers. This kind of covenant is the strongest of covenants and pacts, because it admits of no breach or alteration in any way whatsoever. This is the view of al-Asamm.

The second: what is related from Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, that when Musa, peace be upon him, returned from his Lord with the tablets, he told them: "In them is the Book of Allah." They said: "We will not accept your word until we see Allah openly, and He says: 'This is My Book, so take it.'" Then the thunderbolt seized them and they died. Then He brought them back to life, and afterwards said to them: "Take the Book of Allah." They refused, so the mountain was raised above them, and it was said to them: "Take the Book, or else We will cast it upon you." So they took it. Thus the raising of the mountain was the covenant, because the raising of the mountain was a stunning and wondrous sign, which dazzles the intellects and returns the disbeliever to belief and the doubter to certainty. When they saw that, and knew that it came from Him, exalted is He, as a sign for Musa, peace be upon him, added to the other signs, they acknowledged to him the truthfulness of what he had brought, showed repentance, and gave the pledge and covenant that they would not return to what they had done of worshipping the calf, and that they would uphold the Torah. This was a firm pledge which they made to Allah against themselves. This is the view chosen by Abu Muslim.

The third: Allah has two covenants. The first is when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam and made them bear witness against themselves. The second is that He obligated people to follow the prophets, and the intended meaning here is this second covenant. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, and it is weak.

The second discussion: al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He said ﴿your covenant﴾ and did not say "your covenants" for two reasons:

One of them: He intended by it to indicate that each one of them had taken it, as He said: ﴿Then He brings you forth as a child﴾ [Ghafir: 67], meaning each one of you.

The second: that it was one single thing, taken from each one of them, just as it was taken from others. Therefore all of it was one single covenant. Had it said "covenants," it would have suggested that there were multiple covenants taken from them, not one single covenant. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for the Most High's words, ﴿and We raised the mountain above you﴾, its parallel is the Most High's words: ﴿And when We shook the mountain above them as though it were a canopy﴾ [al-A'raf: 171]. There are discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: The "wa" (and) in His words ﴿and We raised﴾ is a conjunctive "wa" according to the interpretation of Ibn Abbas, meaning that the taking of the covenant happened earlier, and when they broke it by refusing to accept the Book, the mountain was raised over them. But according to the interpretation of Abu Muslim, it is not a conjunctive "wa" but the "wa" of circumstance (wa al-hal), as one says: "I did that while the time was such-and-such." So it is as if He said: "And when We took your covenant at the time of Our raising the mountain above you."

The second discussion: It has been said that the Tur (ṭūr) is any mountain. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*He brought his two wings near to the Tur, so he passed*
*the swooping of the falcon, when the falcon dives*

As for al-Khalil, he said in his book that al-Tur is the name of a known mountain. This is closer to the truth, because the definite article in it requires that it be taken to refer to a specific, known mountain, whose name is recognized. The known one is the mountain upon which the communion (munajat) took place. It is possible that Allah, exalted is He, moved it to where they were and made it above them, even though it was far from them, because the One who is able to keep a mountain suspended in the air is also able to uproot it and move it to them from a distant place. Ibn Abbas said: "The Most High commanded a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, and it was uprooted from its base until it stood above them like a canopy. The encampment was a farsakh by a farsakh. Allah revealed to them: 'Accept the Torah, or else I will throw the mountain upon you.' When they saw there was no escape, they accepted the Torah with what is in it, and they prostrated out of fear, watching the mountain. For this reason the Jews prostrate with the halves of their faces."

The third discussion: Among the heretics (al-malahida) are those who deny the possibility of a heavy object standing in the air without support. As for the earth, they say it stays only because by its nature it seeks the center, so it stands at the center. Our proof against their view is that He, glorified is He, is capable of all possibilities, and the standing of a heavy object in the air is one of the possibilities. Therefore it is necessary that Allah be capable of it. The complete establishment of these two premises is known in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (kutub al-usul; here, the foundational theological works).

The fourth: Some have said: the shading of the mountain is not permissible, because if it were to happen it would function as compulsion (ilja') to faith, and that contradicts moral responsibility (taklif).

Al-Qadi replied that it does not compel, because the most that is in it is the fear of its falling upon them. So when it remains in its place for a period, and they have witnessed the heavens raised above them without support, it is possible in this case that the fear is removed from them, so the compulsion is removed and moral responsibility remains.

As for the Most High's words, ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you, with strength﴾, meaning with earnestness, complete resolve, and turning away from negligence and laziness. Al-Ju'ba'i said: This indicates that the capacity (istita'a) exists before the act, because it is not permissible to say, "Take this with strength" when no strength is present, just as one does not say, "Write with the pen" when there is no pen. Our companions replied that what is meant is: "Take what We have given you with earnestness and resolve," and in our view resolve may precede the act.

* * *

As for the Most High's words, ﴿and remember what is in it﴾, meaning: preserve what is in the Book, study it, do not forget it, and do not neglect it. If it is asked: "Why did you not interpret it as remembrance itself?" We reply: Because remembrance, which is the opposite of forgetting, is an act of Allah, the Most High, so how is it permissible to command it? But when we interpret it as studying, there is no difficulty.

As for the Most High's words, ﴿that you may be mindful﴾, meaning: so that you may be mindful. Al-Ju'ba'i used this as evidence that He, the Most High, intended the performance of obedience from all of them. His answer is what has preceded.

Know that what is understood from the Most High's words, ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, with strength"﴾, is that they [did] what was commanded; otherwise that would not have been a taking of covenant, and His later words ﴿Then you turned away﴾ would not be valid. This indicates from them acceptance and commitment.

[Page 101]

As for the Most High's words, ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾, meaning: then you turned away from the covenant and from fulfilling it. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is generally known that after accepting the Torah and the raising of the mountain, they turned away from the Torah in many matters. They distorted the Torah, abandoned acting upon it, killed the prophets, disbelieved in them, and disobeyed their command. Perhaps among these matters some were peculiar to some of them and not others; some were done by their earlier generations and some by their later ones. They continued in the wandering (tih) while witnessing wonders night and day, opposing Musa, contending with him, inflicting every kind of harm upon him, and openly committing sins in their encampment. To the extent that some of them were swallowed by the earth, fire burned some of them, and they were punished with plague. All of this is mentioned in the Torah's texts which they acknowledge. Then their later generations did what is not hidden, to the extent that they were punished with the destruction of the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis), disbelieved in the Messiah, and intended to kill him. Although the Qur'an does not give a full account of what they turned away from in the Torah, the matter is well known, and that is a report from Allah, the Most High, concerning the obstinacy of their forefathers. Thus it is not strange that they denied what Muhammad, peace be upon him, brought of the Book, and rejected his truth, given their condition in their own Book and with their own prophet as has been mentioned. And Allah knows best.

As for the Most High's words, ﴿Had it not been for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy, you would surely have been among the losers﴾, there are two discussions:

The first: al-Qaffal mentioned two interpretations in his commentary:

The first: "Had it not been for what Allah bestowed upon you of granting you respite and delaying punishment from you, you would surely have been among the losers," meaning among the perishing ones who sold their souls for the fire of Hell. This statement indicates that they only came out of this loss because Allah, the Most High, showed grace to them by granting respite until they repented.

The second: that the narrative ends at His words ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾, and then it is said ﴿Had it not been for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy﴾ as a return of the discourse to its beginning, meaning: "Had it not been for Allah's kindness toward you by raising the mountain above you, you would have persisted in rejecting the Book. But He showed you grace and mercy, and was gentle with you in this way until you repented."

The second discussion: One might say: the word ﴿fa-lawla﴾ indicates the negation of one thing because of the affirmation of another. This would require that the negation of loss is a necessary consequence of the occurrence of Allah's grace. Therefore, wherever loss occurs, Allah's kindness must not be present there. This requires that Allah did not do any of the religious kindnesses (al-alṭaf al-diniyya) for the disbeliever, and that contradicts the view of the Mu'tazila (a theological school holding that Allah is bound by justice and benefit to humans). Al-Ka'bi replied that He equalized everyone in the grace, but some benefited from it and others did not, so it is correct to say this, just as a man says to someone who has distributed gifts equally among his children, and some of them benefited: "Had your father not favoured you, you would have been poor." This reply is weak, because the people of the language have stated that "lawla" indicates the negation of one thing because of the affirmation of another. And once this premise is established, al-Ka'bi's statement collapses entirely.

[Page 100]

The Most High says: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful."﴾ ﴿Then you turned away after that. Had it not been for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy, you would surely have been among the losers.﴾

Know that this is the tenth blessing. That is because Allah, exalted is He, took their covenant only for their benefit, so it became one of His favours upon them.

As for the Most High's words, ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾, there are two discussions.

The first: Know that a covenant (mithaq) is only made through the performance of matters that necessitate submission and obedience. The exegetes have mentioned several interpretations of the covenant:

One of them: it is what Allah deposited in the intellects of the proofs that indicate the existence of the Creator and His wisdom, and the proofs that indicate the truthfulness of His prophets and messengers. This kind of covenant is the strongest of covenants and pacts, because it admits of no breach or alteration in any way whatsoever. This is the view of al-Asamm.

The second: what is related from Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, that when Musa, peace be upon him, returned from his Lord with the tablets, he told them: "In them is the Book of Allah." They said: "We will not accept your word until we see Allah openly, and He says: 'This is My Book, so take it.'" Then the thunderbolt seized them and they died. Then He brought them back to life, and afterwards said to them: "Take the Book of Allah." They refused, so the mountain was raised above them, and it was said to them: "Take the Book, or else We will cast it upon you." So they took it. Thus the raising of the mountain was the covenant, because the raising of the mountain was a stunning and wondrous sign, which dazzles the intellects and returns the disbeliever to belief and the doubter to certainty. When they saw that, and knew that it came from Him, exalted is He, as a sign for Musa, peace be upon him, added to the other signs, they acknowledged to him the truthfulness of what he had brought, showed repentance, and gave the pledge and covenant that they would not return to what they had done of worshipping the calf, and that they would uphold the Torah. This was a firm pledge which they made to Allah against themselves. This is the view chosen by Abu Muslim.

The third: Allah has two covenants. The first is when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam and made them bear witness against themselves. The second is that He obligated people to follow the prophets, and the intended meaning here is this second covenant. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, and it is weak.

The second discussion: al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He said ﴿your covenant﴾ and did not say "your covenants" for two reasons:

One of them: He intended by it to indicate that each one of them had taken it, as He said: ﴿Then He brings you forth as a child﴾ [Ghafir: 67], meaning each one of you.

The second: that it was one single thing, taken from each one of them, just as it was taken from others. Therefore all of it was one single covenant. Had it said "covenants," it would have suggested that there were multiple covenants taken from them, not one single covenant. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for the Most High's words, ﴿and We raised the mountain above you﴾, its parallel is the Most High's words: ﴿And when We shook the mountain above them as though it were a canopy﴾ [al-A'raf: 171]. There are discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: The "wa" (and) in His words ﴿and We raised﴾ is a conjunctive "wa" according to the interpretation of Ibn Abbas, meaning that the taking of the covenant happened earlier, and when they broke it by refusing to accept the Book, the mountain was raised over them. But according to the interpretation of Abu Muslim, it is not a conjunctive "wa" but the "wa" of circumstance (wa al-hal), as one says: "I did that while the time was such-and-such." So it is as if He said: "And when We took your covenant at the time of Our raising the mountain above you."

The second discussion: It has been said that the Tur (ṭūr) is any mountain. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*He brought his two wings near to the Tur, so he passed*
*the swooping of the falcon, when the falcon dives*

As for al-Khalil, he said in his book that al-Tur is the name of a known mountain. This is closer to the truth, because the definite article in it requires that it be taken to refer to a specific, known mountain, whose name is recognized. The known one is the mountain upon which the communion (munajat) took place. It is possible that Allah, exalted is He, moved it to where they were and made it above them, even though it was far from them, because the One who is able to keep a mountain suspended in the air is also able to uproot it and move it to them from a distant place. Ibn Abbas said: "The Most High commanded a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, and it was uprooted from its base until it stood above them like a canopy. The encampment was a farsakh by a farsakh. Allah revealed to them: 'Accept the Torah, or else I will throw the mountain upon you.' When they saw there was no escape, they accepted the Torah with what is in it, and they prostrated out of fear, watching the mountain. For this reason the Jews prostrate with the halves of their faces."

The third discussion: Among the heretics (al-malahida) are those who deny the possibility of a heavy object standing in the air without support. As for the earth, they say it stays only because by its nature it seeks the center, so it stands at the center. Our proof against their view is that He, glorified is He, is capable of all possibilities, and the standing of a heavy object in the air is one of the possibilities. Therefore it is necessary that Allah be capable of it. The complete establishment of these two premises is known in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (kutub al-usul; here, the foundational theological works).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 65–66 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾ ﴿So We made it a deterrent for those present and those to follow, and an admonition to the God-fearing.﴾

[Page 102]

Know that when He, may He be exalted, enumerated the aspects of His favour upon them first, He concluded that by explaining some of the severe measures He imposed on them. This is the first type, and in it there are several issues.

The first issue: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that these people lived in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him) at Ayla, on the seashore between Madina and Syria. It is a place on the sea to which fish gather from every land during one month of the year, so much so that the water cannot be seen because of their abundance, and in other months they gathered especially on every Saturday. This is the town mentioned in His saying: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. They dug pools by the sea and channelled canals to them, so the fish would enter them, and they would catch them on Sunday. That confinement of the fish in the pools was their transgression. Then they took the fish and became wealthy by it, while fearing punishment. When the time passed, the sons followed the custom of their fathers and acquired wealth. Groups from the people of the town who disliked hunting on Saturday came to them and forbade them, but they did not desist and said: "We have been in this work for a long time, and Allah has increased us in it only in goodness." So it was said to them: "Do not be deceived, for perhaps punishment and destruction will descend upon you." Then the people woke up as apes, rejected, and they remained so for three days, then they perished.
