The second issue: The purpose of mentioning this story is twofold.

The first: to demonstrate the miracle of Muhammad (peace be upon him). His saying: ﴿And you certainly knew﴾ is like an address to the Jews who were in the time of Muhammad (peace be upon him). When Muhammad (peace be upon him) informed them of this event, although he was unlettered, who neither read nor wrote, nor mixed with these people, this shows that he (peace be upon him) knew it only through revelation.

The second: When He, may He be exalted, informed them of what He did to the people of the Sabbath, it is as if He were saying to them: "Do you not fear that there will descend upon you, because of your rebellion, what descended upon them of punishment? So do not be deceived by the extended respite granted to you." A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces and turn them back on their backs﴾ [al-Nisa': 47].

The third issue: The speech contains an ellipsis, as if He had said: "And you certainly knew the transgression of those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so that what was mentioned of punishment would be a recompense for that." The word transgression (i'tida') indicates that what they did on the Sabbath was forbidden to them. The details of this are not mentioned in this verse, but they are mentioned in His saying: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. Then it may be said that they transgressed only in that hunting, and it may be said that they transgressed because they hunted while they considered that hunting lawful.

The fourth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Sabt (Sabbath) is a verbal noun from 'sabatat al-yahud,' when the Jews glorified the day of Sabbath." If it is asked: Since Allah had forbidden them to hunt on the Sabbath, what is the wisdom in the fact that most of the fish came on the Sabbath and not on the other days, as He said: ﴿Their fish come to them on their Sabbath day, appearing openly, and on the day they do not keep Sabbath, they do not come. Thus We test them﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]? Is this not an incitement to temptation and a desire to lead astray? We say: As for the position of the People of the Sunna, the desire to lead astray is permissible from Allah, the Exalted. As for the position of the Mu'tazila, severity in the obligations is good for the purpose of increasing reward.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾ there are several issues in it.

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿apes, despised and rejected﴾ is a predicate, meaning: "Be combining apehood and rejection, which is humiliation and expulsion."

[Page 103]

The second issue: His saying: ﴿Be apes, despised and rejected﴾ is not a command, because they were not able to transform themselves into the form of apes. Rather, what is meant is the swiftness of the bringing into being, like His saying: ﴿Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40], and like His saying: ﴿They said, "We come willingly"﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. The meaning is that He, may He be exalted, was not unable to do what He willed of punishment for these people, but when He said to them: ﴿Be apes, despised and rejected,﴾ they became so, that is, when He willed that for them, they became as He willed. This is like His saying: ﴿As We cursed the people of the Sabbath, and the command of Allah was carried out﴾ [al-Nisa': 47]. It is also not impossible that Allah speaks with that at this bringing into being, except that the effective cause in this bringing into being is power and will. If it is asked: Since this utterance has no effect on the bringing into being, what is its benefit? We say: As for us, the rulings and acts of Allah, the Exalted, do not depend upon the observance of benefits at all. As for the Mu'tazila, perhaps this utterance is a word for some angels or others.

The third issue: It is narrated from Mujahid that He, glory be to Him, transformed their hearts in the sense of sealing and imprinting, not that He transformed their forms. This is like His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah and then did not carry it is like the likeness of a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 5]. A parallel to this is that a teacher might say to a dull student whose instruction does not succeed: "Be a donkey." The impossibility of this was argued by two matters:

The first: A human being is this visible frame and the perceptible structure. So if He annuls it and creates in those bodies the composition and shape of an ape, that would be annihilating the human and creating an ape. The outcome of the transformation on this view returns to His annihilating the accidents by which those bodies were a human, and creating in them the accidents by which they were an ape. This would then be annihilation and creation, not transformation.

The second: If we permit that, we would not be secure, regarding everything we see as an ape or a dog, that it was not a rational human being, and that leads to doubt about what is observed.

It is answered regarding the first: The human being is not the whole of this frame. This is because this person may become fat after having been thin, and conversely. So the parts are changing, and the specific human is the one who existed, and the remaining is not the vanishing. So the human is a matter beyond this perceptible frame, and that matter is either a body pervading the body, or a part in some sides of the body like a heart or brain, or an existent abstract, as the philosophers say. On all estimates, there is no impossibility in the persistence of that thing while change befalls this frame. This is the transformation (maskh). By this estimate, it is possible for an angel whose body is extremely large to enter the chamber of the Messenger (peace be upon him).

As for the second: Security is achieved by the consensus of the community. And since the permissibility of transformation has been established by what we have established, it became possible to apply the verse to its apparent meaning, and we had no need for the interpretation mentioned by Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him, although what he mentioned is not very far-fetched. This is because when a person persists in his ignorance after the signs have appeared and the clear proofs have become manifest, it may be said in common usage that he is a donkey and an ape. And since this metaphor is among the widely known and prominent metaphors, there is absolutely no objection to resorting to it.

Two questions remain here:

The first question: After he becomes an ape, no understanding, reason, or knowledge remains for him, so he does not know the punishment that befell him, and mere apehood is not painful, as evidenced by the fact that apes in their sound state are not in pain. So from where does punishment arise because of it?

The answer: Why would it not be permissible to say that the matter by which the human is a rational, understanding human remained, except that when the creation and form changed, they were certainly not able to speak or perform human acts? Yet they knew what had befallen them of change of creation due to the ill omen of disobedience, and they were in the utmost fear and shame. Perhaps they were in pain because of the change of those limbs. And it does not follow that the non-pain of the original apes in that form entails the non-pain of the human in that strange, accidental form.

[Page 104]

The second question: Did those apes remain, or did Allah destroy them? If we say they remained, are these apes that exist in our time permitted to be said to be from the offspring of those transformed people, or not?

The answer: All of that is rationally permissible, except that the narration from Ibn 'Abbas is that they did not remain except three days, then they perished.

The fourth issue: The people of language said: al-khasi' is the humbled, the distanced, the expelled, like a dog when it approaches people, it is said to it: "Ikhsa'" (begone), that is, keep away and be expelled humbled, "this place is not one of your places." Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Your sight will return to you humbled and it is exhausted﴾ [al-Mulk: 4]. It may mean humbled, abased, prevented from repeating the look, because He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Look again; do you see any flaw?﴾ ﴿Then look again, twice; your sight will return to you humbled and it is exhausted﴾. So it is as if He said: "Repeat your gaze in the sky, repeating like one who seeks a flaw. For even if you increase that, you will not find a flaw, and your glance will return to you abased, just as the disappointed one returns after long striving in seeking something and does not achieve it. He returns disappointed, humbled, expelled from where he intended to repeat."

As for His saying: ﴿So We made it﴾, the scholars differed about what this pronoun refers to, in several ways:

One: al-Farra' said: "Ja'alnaha" means the transformation (al-mis-kha) by which they were transformed.

Second: al-Akhfash said: That is, We made the apes a deterrent.

Third: We made the town of the people of the Sabbath a deterrent.

Fourthly: We made this nation an example of deterrence (nakal) because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And you certainly know those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ refers to the nation and the group or something similar. The two first views are closer, because when a pronoun can be returned to a previously mentioned referent, there is no reason to return it to something else. In the preceding verse there is nothing but mention of them and mention of their punishment. As for nakal, al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: it is a severe punishment that deters people from committing the like of that disobedience. Its root meaning is prevention and confinement, and from it comes nukul (refusal) regarding an oath, which is abstaining from it. A shackle is called nikl, and a heavy bridle is also called nikl, because both involve prevention and confinement. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles and a blazing fire﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 12]. And God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is stronger in might and stronger in punishment﴾ [An-Nisa: 84]. The meaning is: We made what befell these people a deterrent punishment for others. That is, we did not intend by it what human beings intend, which is satisfying anger, because that only belongs to one whom sins harm, whose dominion they diminish, and whom they affect. As for us, we only punish for the benefit of the servants, so our punishment is a restraint and an admonition. The judge (al-Qadi) said: a little blame is not described as nakal; only when it becomes great, abundant and well known is it described as such. On this basis, God, exalted is He, required amputation for the persistent thief as a recompense and a nakal, and He intended by it that it be carried out in a manner of humiliation and contempt. It is like disgrace (khizy), which is hardly used except for great blame. So when He, exalted is He, explained what He sent down upon these people who transgressed in the Sabbath and who made lawful, from the hunting of fish and other things, what He had forbidden them for the sake of worldly gain, and who broke the covenants they had made, He explained that He, exalted is He, sent upon them a punishment not for the sake of benefit. For it was not impossible for Him to reduce the extent of their transformation and to change their forms, like the illnesses that befall the accountable and alter their appearance, which would be a trial and not a punishment. So He explained by His saying ﴿So We made it a deterrent﴾ that He, exalted is He, did it as a punishment for what they had done.

As for His saying ﴿for what was before it and what was after it﴾, there are several views:
First: it means for what preceded it, accompanied it and followed it of nations and generations, because their transformation was mentioned in the books of the earlier peoples, so they took heed from it, and whoever among the later peoples received news of this event also took heed from it.
Second: what is before it means the generations and nations present at it.
Third: the meaning is that He, exalted is He, made it a punishment for all that they committed of this act and what followed it, and this is the view of al-Hasan.

As for His saying ﴿and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾, there are two views:
One: whoever learns of the matter that befell them is admonished by it, and fears that if he does the like of their deed, there may befall him the like of what befell them. And if it does not befall him immediately, he must fear the deferred punishment, which is greater and more lasting. As for singling out the God-fearing for mention, it is like what we explained at the beginning of the surah at His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾. For when they are singled out for being admonished, restrained and benefited by this, it is fitting that they be singled out for it, since it is not a benefit to others.
Second: the meaning of His saying ﴿and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ is that the God-fearing admonish one another. That is, We made it a deterrent, and some of the God-fearing admonish others by it. The admonition is then attributed to the God-fearing in the sense that they are the ones who take heed from it, and this is specific to them and not to others. And God knows best.

[Page 105]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 65–66 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾ ﴿So We made it a deterrent for those present and those to follow, and an admonition to the God-fearing.﴾

[Page 102]

Know that when He, may He be exalted, enumerated the aspects of His favour upon them first, He concluded that by explaining some of the severe measures He imposed on them. This is the first type, and in it there are several issues.

The first issue: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that these people lived in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him) at Ayla, on the seashore between Madina and Syria. It is a place on the sea to which fish gather from every land during one month of the year, so much so that the water cannot be seen because of their abundance, and in other months they gathered especially on every Saturday. This is the town mentioned in His saying: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. They dug pools by the sea and channelled canals to them, so the fish would enter them, and they would catch them on Sunday. That confinement of the fish in the pools was their transgression. Then they took the fish and became wealthy by it, while fearing punishment. When the time passed, the sons followed the custom of their fathers and acquired wealth. Groups from the people of the town who disliked hunting on Saturday came to them and forbade them, but they did not desist and said: "We have been in this work for a long time, and Allah has increased us in it only in goodness." So it was said to them: "Do not be deceived, for perhaps punishment and destruction will descend upon you." Then the people woke up as apes, rejected, and they remained so for three days, then they perished.

The second issue: The purpose of mentioning this story is twofold.

The first: to demonstrate the miracle of Muhammad (peace be upon him). His saying: ﴿And you certainly knew﴾ is like an address to the Jews who were in the time of Muhammad (peace be upon him). When Muhammad (peace be upon him) informed them of this event, although he was unlettered, who neither read nor wrote, nor mixed with these people, this shows that he (peace be upon him) knew it only through revelation.

The second: When He, may He be exalted, informed them of what He did to the people of the Sabbath, it is as if He were saying to them: "Do you not fear that there will descend upon you, because of your rebellion, what descended upon them of punishment? So do not be deceived by the extended respite granted to you." A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces and turn them back on their backs﴾ [al-Nisa': 47].

The third issue: The speech contains an ellipsis, as if He had said: "And you certainly knew the transgression of those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so that what was mentioned of punishment would be a recompense for that." The word transgression (i'tida') indicates that what they did on the Sabbath was forbidden to them. The details of this are not mentioned in this verse, but they are mentioned in His saying: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. Then it may be said that they transgressed only in that hunting, and it may be said that they transgressed because they hunted while they considered that hunting lawful.

The fourth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Sabt (Sabbath) is a verbal noun from 'sabatat al-yahud,' when the Jews glorified the day of Sabbath." If it is asked: Since Allah had forbidden them to hunt on the Sabbath, what is the wisdom in the fact that most of the fish came on the Sabbath and not on the other days, as He said: ﴿Their fish come to them on their Sabbath day, appearing openly, and on the day they do not keep Sabbath, they do not come. Thus We test them﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]? Is this not an incitement to temptation and a desire to lead astray? We say: As for the position of the People of the Sunna, the desire to lead astray is permissible from Allah, the Exalted. As for the position of the Mu'tazila, severity in the obligations is good for the purpose of increasing reward.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾ there are several issues in it.

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿apes, despised and rejected﴾ is a predicate, meaning: "Be combining apehood and rejection, which is humiliation and expulsion."

[Page 103]

The second issue: His saying: ﴿Be apes, despised and rejected﴾ is not a command, because they were not able to transform themselves into the form of apes. Rather, what is meant is the swiftness of the bringing into being, like His saying: ﴿Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40], and like His saying: ﴿They said, "We come willingly"﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. The meaning is that He, may He be exalted, was not unable to do what He willed of punishment for these people, but when He said to them: ﴿Be apes, despised and rejected,﴾ they became so, that is, when He willed that for them, they became as He willed. This is like His saying: ﴿As We cursed the people of the Sabbath, and the command of Allah was carried out﴾ [al-Nisa': 47]. It is also not impossible that Allah speaks with that at this bringing into being, except that the effective cause in this bringing into being is power and will. If it is asked: Since this utterance has no effect on the bringing into being, what is its benefit? We say: As for us, the rulings and acts of Allah, the Exalted, do not depend upon the observance of benefits at all. As for the Mu'tazila, perhaps this utterance is a word for some angels or others.

The third issue: It is narrated from Mujahid that He, glory be to Him, transformed their hearts in the sense of sealing and imprinting, not that He transformed their forms. This is like His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah and then did not carry it is like the likeness of a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 5]. A parallel to this is that a teacher might say to a dull student whose instruction does not succeed: "Be a donkey." The impossibility of this was argued by two matters:

The first: A human being is this visible frame and the perceptible structure. So if He annuls it and creates in those bodies the composition and shape of an ape, that would be annihilating the human and creating an ape. The outcome of the transformation on this view returns to His annihilating the accidents by which those bodies were a human, and creating in them the accidents by which they were an ape. This would then be annihilation and creation, not transformation.

The second: If we permit that, we would not be secure, regarding everything we see as an ape or a dog, that it was not a rational human being, and that leads to doubt about what is observed.

It is answered regarding the first: The human being is not the whole of this frame. This is because this person may become fat after having been thin, and conversely. So the parts are changing, and the specific human is the one who existed, and the remaining is not the vanishing. So the human is a matter beyond this perceptible frame, and that matter is either a body pervading the body, or a part in some sides of the body like a heart or brain, or an existent abstract, as the philosophers say. On all estimates, there is no impossibility in the persistence of that thing while change befalls this frame. This is the transformation (maskh). By this estimate, it is possible for an angel whose body is extremely large to enter the chamber of the Messenger (peace be upon him).

As for the second: Security is achieved by the consensus of the community. And since the permissibility of transformation has been established by what we have established, it became possible to apply the verse to its apparent meaning, and we had no need for the interpretation mentioned by Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him, although what he mentioned is not very far-fetched. This is because when a person persists in his ignorance after the signs have appeared and the clear proofs have become manifest, it may be said in common usage that he is a donkey and an ape. And since this metaphor is among the widely known and prominent metaphors, there is absolutely no objection to resorting to it.

Two questions remain here:

The first question: After he becomes an ape, no understanding, reason, or knowledge remains for him, so he does not know the punishment that befell him, and mere apehood is not painful, as evidenced by the fact that apes in their sound state are not in pain. So from where does punishment arise because of it?

The answer: Why would it not be permissible to say that the matter by which the human is a rational, understanding human remained, except that when the creation and form changed, they were certainly not able to speak or perform human acts? Yet they knew what had befallen them of change of creation due to the ill omen of disobedience, and they were in the utmost fear and shame. Perhaps they were in pain because of the change of those limbs. And it does not follow that the non-pain of the original apes in that form entails the non-pain of the human in that strange, accidental form.

[Page 104]

The second question: Did those apes remain, or did Allah destroy them? If we say they remained, are these apes that exist in our time permitted to be said to be from the offspring of those transformed people, or not?

The answer: All of that is rationally permissible, except that the narration from Ibn 'Abbas is that they did not remain except three days, then they perished.

The fourth issue: The people of language said: al-khasi' is the humbled, the distanced, the expelled, like a dog when it approaches people, it is said to it: "Ikhsa'" (begone), that is, keep away and be expelled humbled, "this place is not one of your places." Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Your sight will return to you humbled and it is exhausted﴾ [al-Mulk: 4]. It may mean humbled, abased, prevented from repeating the look, because He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Look again; do you see any flaw?﴾ ﴿Then look again, twice; your sight will return to you humbled and it is exhausted﴾. So it is as if He said: "Repeat your gaze in the sky, repeating like one who seeks a flaw. For even if you increase that, you will not find a flaw, and your glance will return to you abased, just as the disappointed one returns after long striving in seeking something and does not achieve it. He returns disappointed, humbled, expelled from where he intended to repeat."

As for His saying: ﴿So We made it﴾, the scholars differed about what this pronoun refers to, in several ways:

One: al-Farra' said: "Ja'alnaha" means the transformation (al-mis-kha) by which they were transformed.

Second: al-Akhfash said: That is, We made the apes a deterrent.

Third: We made the town of the people of the Sabbath a deterrent.

Fourthly: We made this nation an example of deterrence (nakal) because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And you certainly know those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ refers to the nation and the group or something similar. The two first views are closer, because when a pronoun can be returned to a previously mentioned referent, there is no reason to return it to something else. In the preceding verse there is nothing but mention of them and mention of their punishment. As for nakal, al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: it is a severe punishment that deters people from committing the like of that disobedience. Its root meaning is prevention and confinement, and from it comes nukul (refusal) regarding an oath, which is abstaining from it. A shackle is called nikl, and a heavy bridle is also called nikl, because both involve prevention and confinement. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles and a blazing fire﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 12]. And God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is stronger in might and stronger in punishment﴾ [An-Nisa: 84]. The meaning is: We made what befell these people a deterrent punishment for others. That is, we did not intend by it what human beings intend, which is satisfying anger, because that only belongs to one whom sins harm, whose dominion they diminish, and whom they affect. As for us, we only punish for the benefit of the servants, so our punishment is a restraint and an admonition. The judge (al-Qadi) said: a little blame is not described as nakal; only when it becomes great, abundant and well known is it described as such. On this basis, God, exalted is He, required amputation for the persistent thief as a recompense and a nakal, and He intended by it that it be carried out in a manner of humiliation and contempt. It is like disgrace (khizy), which is hardly used except for great blame. So when He, exalted is He, explained what He sent down upon these people who transgressed in the Sabbath and who made lawful, from the hunting of fish and other things, what He had forbidden them for the sake of worldly gain, and who broke the covenants they had made, He explained that He, exalted is He, sent upon them a punishment not for the sake of benefit. For it was not impossible for Him to reduce the extent of their transformation and to change their forms, like the illnesses that befall the accountable and alter their appearance, which would be a trial and not a punishment. So He explained by His saying ﴿So We made it a deterrent﴾ that He, exalted is He, did it as a punishment for what they had done.

As for His saying ﴿for what was before it and what was after it﴾, there are several views:
First: it means for what preceded it, accompanied it and followed it of nations and generations, because their transformation was mentioned in the books of the earlier peoples, so they took heed from it, and whoever among the later peoples received news of this event also took heed from it.
Second: what is before it means the generations and nations present at it.
Third: the meaning is that He, exalted is He, made it a punishment for all that they committed of this act and what followed it, and this is the view of al-Hasan.

As for His saying ﴿and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾, there are two views:
One: whoever learns of the matter that befell them is admonished by it, and fears that if he does the like of their deed, there may befall him the like of what befell them. And if it does not befall him immediately, he must fear the deferred punishment, which is greater and more lasting. As for singling out the God-fearing for mention, it is like what we explained at the beginning of the surah at His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾. For when they are singled out for being admonished, restrained and benefited by this, it is fitting that they be singled out for it, since it is not a benefit to others.
Second: the meaning of His saying ﴿and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ is that the God-fearing admonish one another. That is, We made it a deterrent, and some of the God-fearing admonish others by it. The admonition is then attributed to the God-fearing in the sense that they are the ones who take heed from it, and this is specific to them and not to others. And God knows best.

[Page 105]

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verses 67–68 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow neither old nor virgin, but median between that, so do what you are commanded."﴾ ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow bright yellow in color, pleasing to the observers."﴾ ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is. Indeed, cows have become confused to us, and indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow not trained to plow the earth or water the field, sound and without blemish." They said, "Now you have brought the truth." So they slaughtered it, though they nearly did not.﴾ ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it, but Allah was to bring out that which you were concealing.﴾ ﴿So We said, "Strike the dead body with part of it." Thus Allah brings the dead to life and shows you His signs that you may reason.﴾

Know that this is the second type of the "tashdid" (the making of things harder). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and the rest of the exegetes that a man from the Children of Israel killed a relative in order to inherit from him, then threw him at a crossroads, and then complained of that to Moses, peace be upon him. Moses strove to identify the killer, but when it did not become clear, they said to him, "Ask your Lord for us so that He may make it clear." So he asked, and Allah revealed to him: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾. They were astonished at that, and then made things hard upon themselves by questioning, step after step, and they pressed for the description. When it was determined, they did not find it with that description except with a particular person, and he did not sell it except for many times its price. They bought it, slaughtered it, and Moses commanded them to take a part of it and strike the victim with it. They did so, and the one who had been killed became alive, and he named to them his killer, who was the one who had initiated the complaint, and they killed him in retaliation (qawad). Then here there are issues:

The first issue: the inflicting of pain and the slaughtering are good, otherwise Allah would not have commanded them. Then, according to us, the aspect of their goodness is that He, exalted is He, is the Owner of the dominion, so no one has any objection against Him. According to the Mu'tazilah, it is good only for the sake of compensations ('iwad).

The second issue: He, exalted is He, commanded the slaughter of a cow from among the cows of this world, and this is the "wajib mukhayyar" (obligation with choice among options), so this indicates the soundness of our view regarding the wajib mukhayyar.

The third issue: Those who hold that words are general (al-qa'ilun bil-'umum) agree that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ means: slaughter whatever cow you wish. So this form (sigha) conveys this generality. But those who deny generality (munkiru al-'umum) said: this does not indicate generality, and they argued for it with several arguments:

The first: What is understood from the speaker's saying "slaughter a cow" can be divided into two parts, for it is correct to say: "Slaughter a specific cow having such-and-such characteristics," and it is also correct to say: "Slaughter a cow, whatever cow you wish." So what is understood from your saying "slaughter" is a meaning shared between these two parts, and what is shared between two parts does not necessitate either of them. Therefore His saying "slaughter a cow" does not necessitate the meaning of His saying "slaughter a cow, whatever cow you wish." Thus it is established that it does not indicate generality, because if it indicated generality, then His saying "slaughter a cow, whatever cow you wish" would be a repetition, and His saying "slaughter a specific cow" would be a contradiction. Since this is not so, we know the invalidity of this view.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿slaughter a cow﴾ is like the negation of our saying "do not slaughter a cow," and our saying "do not slaughter a cow" indicates general negation. So it is necessary that our saying "slaughter a cow" removes the generality of the negation, and the particularity of affirmation in one way suffices to remove the generality of negation. Therefore His saying "slaughter a cow" indicates the command to slaughter one cow only. As for the unrestricted permission to slaughter whichever cow they wished, there is no need for it in removing that negation, so it must not be derived from the utterance.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a cow﴾ is a singular indefinite word (lafzah mufradah munakkarah), and the singular indefinite only indicates an individual that is specific in itself, though unspecified by the wording that signifies it, and it is not permissible that it indicates any individual whatsoever. The proof is that when someone says, "I saw a man," it indicates nothing except what we have mentioned. When it is established that this is so in the report, it must be so in the command. Those who hold generality argued that if he slaughtered any cow whatsoever, he would be discharged from the obligation, so it must indicate generality.

The answer: This is begging the question (musadarah 'ala al-matlub al-awwal), for this would be established only if it were established that His saying "slaughter a cow" means "slaughter whatever cow you wish," and this is the very point in dispute. This is the discussion of this issue. Having understood this, we say: people have differed as to whether His saying, exalted is He, ﴿slaughter a cow﴾ is a command to slaughter a specific, defined cow, or a command to slaughter any cow whatsoever. Those who permit the delay of clarification (ta'khir al-bayan) from the time of address say: it was a command to slaughter a specific cow, but it had not been defined. Those who prohibit it said: although it was a command to slaughter any cow whatsoever,

[Page 107]

when the people asked for a change of the obligation at that point, because the first obligation was sufficient had they obeyed, and the choice within the genus of cows was then the good. When they disobeyed, did not comply, and returned to questioning, a change in the benefit was not impossible, and this is known in observation, for the one who manages his child may command him with the easy by choice, and when the child refuses it, he may see the benefit in commanding him with the difficult. So it is here too. The first party argued with several arguments:

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is﴾, and ﴿what its color is﴾, and the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He says it is a cow neither old﴾, ﴿Indeed, it is a cow bright yellow﴾, ﴿Indeed, it is a cow not trained to plow the earth﴾, refer to what they had been commanded to slaughter before. These pronominal references (kinayat) indicate that what was commanded was not the slaughter of any cow whatsoever, but rather the slaughter of a specific cow.

The second: The attributes mentioned in the answer to the second question: either it is said that they are the attributes of the cow they were commanded to slaughter first, or they are the attributes of a cow that became obligatory upon them at that questioning, and what had been obligatory upon them before that was abrogated. The first is what is sought, and the second entails that they would be satisfied with the attributes mentioned last, and that it would not be obligatory to have the attributes mentioned before that. Since the Muslims have unanimously agreed that all those attributes were considered binding, we know the invalidity of this division. If it is said: as for the pronominal references, we do not concede that they return to the cow, so why is it not permissible to say that they are pronouns referring to the matter and the affair (al-qissah wal-sha'n), and this is a well-known method among the Arabs? We say: This is false, for several reasons:

One: If these pronominal references referred to the matter and the affair, then what follows these pronouns would remain without benefit, for there would be no benefit in His saying, "a cow bright yellow." Rather, something else would have to be supplied, and that contradicts the default principle. But if we make the pronominal references refer to what was commanded first, this problem does not arise.

Two: The ruling that the pronoun refers to the matter and the affair contradicts the default principle, for a pronoun must refer to something whose mention has preceded, and the matter and the affair have not been mentioned, so it is not permissible for the pronoun to refer to them. However, we have departed from this principle out of necessity in some places, and what is other than that remains on the default principle.

Three: The pronoun in His saying, ﴿what its color is﴾ and ﴿what it is﴾ undoubtedly refers to the cow commanded, so the pronoun in His saying, ﴿indeed, it is a cow bright yellow﴾ must refer to that same cow, otherwise the answer would not correspond to the question.

The third: If they had been questioners who were stubborn, the amount of what Moses commanded them would not have removed the possibility, for the amount that Moses mentioned is that it be a yellow cow, middle-aged, and complete in strength, and this amount is open to many possibilities. When they were silent here and were satisfied with it, we know that they were not stubborn. The second party argued with several arguments:

One: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ means: He commands you to slaughter a cow, whatever cow it may be, and that indicates generality, and that requires that the consideration of the attribute after that be a new obligation.

Two: If the intended meaning were the slaughter of a specific cow, they would not have deserved reproach for asking for clarification, but rather they would have deserved praise for it. Since Allah reproached them in His saying, ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, and in His saying, ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they nearly did not﴾, we know their shortcoming in carrying out what they had been commanded first, and that would only be the case if what they had been commanded first was the slaughter of a specific cow.

Three: What has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Had they slaughtered whatever cow they wished, it would have sufficed for them, but they made things hard upon themselves, so Allah made things hard upon them."

Four: At the time in which they were commanded to slaughter the cow, they were in need of slaughtering it. So if what was commanded was the slaughter of a specific cow while Allah had not clarified it, that would be a delay of the clarification beyond the time of need, and that is impermissible.

The answer: As for the first, we have explained at the beginning of the issue that His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ does not indicate that what is commanded is the slaughter of a cow, any cow whatsoever. As for the second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they nearly did not do it﴾ does not contain any indication that they were negligent at the beginning of the story, and that they nearly were negligent after the completion of the clarification. Rather, the wording admits of each of them, so we interpret it according to the latter, namely that when they came to the completion of the clarification, they hesitated at that point and nearly did not do it. As for the third: this narration from Ibn 'Abbas is of the category of single reports (akhbar al-ahad), and even if it is authentic, it cannot stand in opposition to the Book of Allah, exalted is He. As for the fourth: delaying the clarification beyond the time of need only follows if the command indicates immediacy (al-fawr), and that is prohibited according to us.

Know that when we build upon the view that what is commanded is "a cow, any cow whatsoever," it is necessary that we say: the obligations are distinct. So they were first obligated to slaughter any cow whatsoever, and second, that it be neither old nor virgin but median. When they did not do that, they were obligated that it be yellow. When they did not do that, they were obligated that it be, in addition to that, not trained to plow the earth nor to water the field. Then those who hold this view differed. Some said: the obligation that came last must include every attribute that preceded it, so that the cow, together with the last attribute, is neither old nor virgin, and bright yellow. Others say: it is only necessary that it have the last attribute alone, and this resembles the apparent meaning of the speech if it is one obligation after another. Though the first view resembles the narrations more, and the method of making things hard upon them when compliance was in doubt. When it is established that clarification does not come late, it must be one obligation after another, and that indicates that the easier may be abrogated by the more difficult (al-aslah yunsakh bil-ashaqq), and it indicates the permissibility of abrogation before the act is performed, but it does not indicate the permissibility of abrogation before the time of performance. It also indicates the occurrence of abrogation in the Law of Moses, peace be upon him. It also has a connection to the question of whether an addition to a text is abrogation or not. And it indicates the goodness of an obligation being imposed a second time upon one who disobeyed and did not do what he was obligated to do first.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Do you take us in mockery?"﴾, there are issues concerning it:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 67–68 (part 2 of 2):

The first issue: it is read "huzuwan" (هُزُوًا) with a damma, and "huzu'an" (هُزْءًا) with the letter zay sukun, like "kufu'an" and "kufan" (كُفُؤًا وكُفْءً). Hafs read (هُزُوًا) with two dammas and a waw, and likewise "kufuwan" (كُفُوًا).

The second issue: al-Qaffal said that God's words ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾ (أتَتَّخِذُنا) are an interrogative in the sense of denial. The word "huzu" (هُزْء, mockery) may carry the sense of the object of mockery, as one says, "this was in God's knowledge" (كان هذا في علم الله), meaning in what is known to Him, and "God is our hope" (الله رجاؤنا), meaning our object of hope. A parallel is God's words ﴿so you took them in mockery (سِخْرِيًّا)﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 110]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Do you take us as a mockery (أتَتَّخِذُنا هُزُءًا)" means: do you make us a place of mockery, or people of mockery, or ones mocked; and the mockery itself is extreme derision.

The third issue: the people only said this because, when they asked Musa (peace be upon him) to identify the killer, Musa said: "Slaughter a cow." They did not see any connection between this answer and that question, so they thought he was joking with them. It is possible that Musa (peace be upon him) commanded them to slaughter the cow without informing them that when they slaughtered the cow and struck the slain man with part of it, he would come to life; therefore this statement was taken by them as mockery. It is also possible that Musa (peace be upon him), although he had explained the state of affairs to them, they were amazed that the slain man could come to life by being struck with some part of the cow, so they thought this was in the manner of mockery.

صفحة ١٠٩

The fourth issue: some said that those people became unbelievers by their saying to Musa (peace be upon him): "Do you take us in mockery?" For if they said that and doubted God's power to revive the dead, then it is disbelief; and if they doubted whether what Musa (peace be upon him) commanded them was by God's command, then they permitted treachery in Musa's (peace be upon him) conveying of revelation, and that too is disbelief. Others among people said: it does not necessitate disbelief, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: jesting with the prophets is permissible, so perhaps they thought of him (peace be upon him) that he was jesting with them in a permissible jest, and that does not necessitate disbelief.

The second: the meaning of God's words ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾ (أتَتَّخِذُنا هُزُوًا) is: how strange this answer is, as if you were mocking us, not that they affirmed mockery against Musa.

As for God's words ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾, there are several aspects:

One: engaging in mockery occurs only from ignorance, and the station of prophethood does not admit undertaking mockery; so Musa (peace be upon him) did not seek refuge from the very thing they attributed to him, but sought refuge from the cause that necessitates it, as a man may say in such a situation: "I seek refuge in God from lack of reason and the dominance of desire." The sum is that he applied the name of the cause to the effect metaphorically. This is the strongest aspect.

Second: "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant of what mockery entails in matters of religion of severe punishment and great threat, for whenever I know that, my undertaking mockery is precluded."

Third: some said: the very act of mockery is sometimes called ignorance and folly, for it was narrated from some lexicographers that ignorance (الجهل) is the opposite of forbearance (الحلم), just as some said it is the opposite of knowledge (العلم).

Know that this statement of Musa (peace be upon him) indicates that mockery is among the grave major sins, and the full discussion of it has already passed in God's words ﴿They say: We are only with you, we are only mocking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15].

Know that the people asked Musa (peace be upon him) about three matters concerning the cow:

The first question: as God related of them, they said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is﴾. Musa (peace be upon him) answered with his words: ﴿He says it is a cow, neither old nor virgin, but between that; so do what you are commanded﴾. Know that there are discussions in this verse:

The first: if we say that God's words ﴿God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ indicate a command to slaughter a specific cow in itself, without its specification being clarified, then their question is fitting, since the commanded thing was general, and inquiry and seeking information are appropriate. As for those who say that it is in original usage for generality, it is necessary to explain what prompted them to this inquiry? And there are several aspects:

One: when Musa (peace be upon him) informed them that if they slaughtered the cow and struck the slain man with part of it, he would become alive, they were amazed at the matter of that cow, and thought that a cow with such a property could only be a specific cow, so they thoroughly inquired about its description, like Musa's staff which was specific among other staffs with those properties. However, the people were mistaken in that, because this wondrous sign was not a property of the cow; rather it was a miracle that God manifested at the hand of Musa (peace be upon him).

Second: perhaps the people intended a cow, any cow whatsoever, but the killer feared exposure, so he cast doubt into the specification and said the commanded thing is a specific cow, not just any cow. When the time of dispute over it arrived, they returned at that point to Musa.

Third: although the first address conveyed generality, the people wanted to take precaution in it, so they asked seeking further clarification and to remove all other possibilities; but the benefit changed and required the command to slaughter the specific cow.

صفحة ١١٠

The second discussion: the question "what is it (ما هِيَ)" is a request for defining the quiddity and reality; for "ma" is an interrogative and "hiya" refers to the reality, so "ma hiya" must be a request for the reality, and defining the quiddity and reality occurs only by mentioning its parts and preliminaries, not by mentioning its attributes that lie outside its quiddity. It is known that the attribute of age is among matters external to the quiddity, so this answer ought not to correspond to this question.

The reply to this: although the matter is as you mentioned, the circumstantial indication shows that their intent in saying "what is the cow" was not seeking its quiddity and explaining its reality, but rather their intent was seeking the attributes by which some cows are distinguished from others; therefore it was fitting to mention external attributes as an answer to this question.

The third discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "al-Fariḍ" is the aged one, and she was named fariḍ because she has finished her age, that is, she cut it off and reached its end. "Al-Bikr" is the young one, and "al-'Awān" is the middle one.

The judge said: as for al-bikr, it is said she is the small one; it is said she is the one who has not given birth; and it is said she is the one who gave birth once. Al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Salamah [al-Ḍabbi] said: he mentioned for al-fariḍ that she is the aged one, and for al-bikr that she is the young one, and she is among women the one not yet having intercourse, and among camels the one that has borne one offspring. Al-Qaffal said: al-bikr indicates the first, and from it comes "al-bakūrah" for the first of the fruit, and from it "bukrat al-nahar" (the early part of the day); and it is said: "bakkartu 'alayhima al-barihah" when he came at the beginning of the night. And it seems the more apparent is that she is the one who has not given birth, because the known sense of "bikr" among female humans is the one on whom the stallion has not mounted. Some said: al-'awān is the one that has given birth more than once. "Harb 'awān" (a war of attrition) is when a war has been fought in it time after time, and "hajah 'awān" (a repeated need) is when it has been fulfilled time after time.

The fourth discussion: the scholars argued from God's words ﴿neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent reasoning) and acting upon predominant opinion (ghalib al-zann) in rulings, since it cannot be known that she is between the aged and the virgin except through ijtihad. Here are two questions:

The first: the word "bayn" (between) requires two things or more, so from where is its use permitted with "dhalika"?

The answer: because it carries the sense of two things, since it occurred referring to what was mentioned, the aged and the virgin.

The second question: how is it permitted to refer with the word "dhalika" to two feminine things, while it is for pointing at a single masculine thing?

The answer: mentioning "dhalika" is permitted under the interpretation of "what was mentioned" or "what preceded," for brevity in speech.

As for God's words ﴿so do what you are commanded﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: do what you are commanded to do, from your saying: "I commanded you to good (amartuka al-khayr)."

The second: that the intended meaning is "do your command," in the sense of "your commanded thing," calling the object by the verbal noun, like "the beating of the amir (ḍarb al-amīr)."

Know that the original intended purpose of this answer is that the cow be in its most perfect condition, for the young one is deficient because she has not yet reached the state of perfection, and the aged one is as if she has become deficient and gone beyond the limit of perfection; but the middle one is the one in the state of perfection.

Then God related their second question, which is His words: ﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is﴾. Know that when they knew the state of age, they proceeded after it to learn the state of color, and God answered them that it is ﴿yellow, its color is bright (fāqi')﴾. Fuqūʿ (brightness) is the most intense and purest degree of yellow, and it is said for emphasis: "aṣfar fāqi'" (intensely yellow), "aswad ḥālik" (intensely black), "abyaḍ yaqaq" (intensely white), "aḥmar qānin" (intensely red), and "akhḍar nāḍir" (intensely green). Here there are two questions:

The first question: "fāqi'" here is in the position of a predicate about the color, so how can it come as an emphasis for "ṣafrā'"?

The answer: it did not come as a predicate about the color; it came as an emphasis for "ṣafrā'," except that the color was raised by it in the manner of a subject, and the color is its cause and is joined with it, so there was no difference between your saying "ṣafrā' fāqi'a" and "ṣafrā' fāqi'un lawnuhā."

صفحة ١١١

The second question: why was it not said "ṣafrā' fāqi'a," and what is the benefit in mentioning the color?

The answer: the benefit in it is emphasis, because color is a name for the form, and that is the yellowness; so it is as if it were said: "intensely yellow, its yellowness is," and it is from your saying: "the true diligence of his diligence" (jiddu jiddihi) and "the madness of a madman" (junūnu majnūn). It is narrated from Wahb: when you look at it, it appears to you as if the rays of the sun come out of its skin.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verses 67–68 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow neither old nor virgin, but median between that, so do what you are commanded."﴾ ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow bright yellow in color, pleasing to the observers."﴾ ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is. Indeed, cows have become confused to us, and indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow not trained to plow the earth or water the field, sound and without blemish." They said, "Now you have brought the truth." So they slaughtered it, though they nearly did not.﴾ ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it, but Allah was to bring out that which you were concealing.﴾ ﴿So We said, "Strike the dead body with part of it." Thus Allah brings the dead to life and shows you His signs that you may reason.﴾

Know that this is the second type of the "tashdid" (the making of things harder). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and the rest of the exegetes that a man from the Children of Israel killed a relative in order to inherit from him, then threw him at a crossroads, and then complained of that to Moses, peace be upon him. Moses strove to identify the killer, but when it did not become clear, they said to him, "Ask your Lord for us so that He may make it clear." So he asked, and Allah revealed to him: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾. They were astonished at that, and then made things hard upon themselves by questioning, step after step, and they pressed for the description. When it was determined, they did not find it with that description except with a particular person, and he did not sell it except for many times its price. They bought it, slaughtered it, and Moses commanded them to take a part of it and strike the victim with it. They did so, and the one who had been killed became alive, and he named to them his killer, who was the one who had initiated the complaint, and they killed him in retaliation (qawad). Then here there are issues:

The first issue: the inflicting of pain and the slaughtering are good, otherwise Allah would not have commanded them. Then, according to us, the aspect of their goodness is that He, exalted is He, is the Owner of the dominion, so no one has any objection against Him. According to the Mu'tazilah, it is good only for the sake of compensations ('iwad).

The second issue: He, exalted is He, commanded the slaughter of a cow from among the cows of this world, and this is the "wajib mukhayyar" (obligation with choice among options), so this indicates the soundness of our view regarding the wajib mukhayyar.

The third issue: Those who hold that words are general (al-qa'ilun bil-'umum) agree that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ means: slaughter whatever cow you wish. So this form (sigha) conveys this generality. But those who deny generality (munkiru al-'umum) said: this does not indicate generality, and they argued for it with several arguments:

The first: What is understood from the speaker's saying "slaughter a cow" can be divided into two parts, for it is correct to say: "Slaughter a specific cow having such-and-such characteristics," and it is also correct to say: "Slaughter a cow, whatever cow you wish." So what is understood from your saying "slaughter" is a meaning shared between these two parts, and what is shared between two parts does not necessitate either of them. Therefore His saying "slaughter a cow" does not necessitate the meaning of His saying "slaughter a cow, whatever cow you wish." Thus it is established that it does not indicate generality, because if it indicated generality, then His saying "slaughter a cow, whatever cow you wish" would be a repetition, and His saying "slaughter a specific cow" would be a contradiction. Since this is not so, we know the invalidity of this view.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿slaughter a cow﴾ is like the negation of our saying "do not slaughter a cow," and our saying "do not slaughter a cow" indicates general negation. So it is necessary that our saying "slaughter a cow" removes the generality of the negation, and the particularity of affirmation in one way suffices to remove the generality of negation. Therefore His saying "slaughter a cow" indicates the command to slaughter one cow only. As for the unrestricted permission to slaughter whichever cow they wished, there is no need for it in removing that negation, so it must not be derived from the utterance.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a cow﴾ is a singular indefinite word (lafzah mufradah munakkarah), and the singular indefinite only indicates an individual that is specific in itself, though unspecified by the wording that signifies it, and it is not permissible that it indicates any individual whatsoever. The proof is that when someone says, "I saw a man," it indicates nothing except what we have mentioned. When it is established that this is so in the report, it must be so in the command. Those who hold generality argued that if he slaughtered any cow whatsoever, he would be discharged from the obligation, so it must indicate generality.

The answer: This is begging the question (musadarah 'ala al-matlub al-awwal), for this would be established only if it were established that His saying "slaughter a cow" means "slaughter whatever cow you wish," and this is the very point in dispute. This is the discussion of this issue. Having understood this, we say: people have differed as to whether His saying, exalted is He, ﴿slaughter a cow﴾ is a command to slaughter a specific, defined cow, or a command to slaughter any cow whatsoever. Those who permit the delay of clarification (ta'khir al-bayan) from the time of address say: it was a command to slaughter a specific cow, but it had not been defined. Those who prohibit it said: although it was a command to slaughter any cow whatsoever,

[Page 107]

when the people asked for a change of the obligation at that point, because the first obligation was sufficient had they obeyed, and the choice within the genus of cows was then the good. When they disobeyed, did not comply, and returned to questioning, a change in the benefit was not impossible, and this is known in observation, for the one who manages his child may command him with the easy by choice, and when the child refuses it, he may see the benefit in commanding him with the difficult. So it is here too. The first party argued with several arguments:

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is﴾, and ﴿what its color is﴾, and the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He says it is a cow neither old﴾, ﴿Indeed, it is a cow bright yellow﴾, ﴿Indeed, it is a cow not trained to plow the earth﴾, refer to what they had been commanded to slaughter before. These pronominal references (kinayat) indicate that what was commanded was not the slaughter of any cow whatsoever, but rather the slaughter of a specific cow.

The second: The attributes mentioned in the answer to the second question: either it is said that they are the attributes of the cow they were commanded to slaughter first, or they are the attributes of a cow that became obligatory upon them at that questioning, and what had been obligatory upon them before that was abrogated. The first is what is sought, and the second entails that they would be satisfied with the attributes mentioned last, and that it would not be obligatory to have the attributes mentioned before that. Since the Muslims have unanimously agreed that all those attributes were considered binding, we know the invalidity of this division. If it is said: as for the pronominal references, we do not concede that they return to the cow, so why is it not permissible to say that they are pronouns referring to the matter and the affair (al-qissah wal-sha'n), and this is a well-known method among the Arabs? We say: This is false, for several reasons:

One: If these pronominal references referred to the matter and the affair, then what follows these pronouns would remain without benefit, for there would be no benefit in His saying, "a cow bright yellow." Rather, something else would have to be supplied, and that contradicts the default principle. But if we make the pronominal references refer to what was commanded first, this problem does not arise.

Two: The ruling that the pronoun refers to the matter and the affair contradicts the default principle, for a pronoun must refer to something whose mention has preceded, and the matter and the affair have not been mentioned, so it is not permissible for the pronoun to refer to them. However, we have departed from this principle out of necessity in some places, and what is other than that remains on the default principle.

Three: The pronoun in His saying, ﴿what its color is﴾ and ﴿what it is﴾ undoubtedly refers to the cow commanded, so the pronoun in His saying, ﴿indeed, it is a cow bright yellow﴾ must refer to that same cow, otherwise the answer would not correspond to the question.

The third: If they had been questioners who were stubborn, the amount of what Moses commanded them would not have removed the possibility, for the amount that Moses mentioned is that it be a yellow cow, middle-aged, and complete in strength, and this amount is open to many possibilities. When they were silent here and were satisfied with it, we know that they were not stubborn. The second party argued with several arguments:

One: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ means: He commands you to slaughter a cow, whatever cow it may be, and that indicates generality, and that requires that the consideration of the attribute after that be a new obligation.

Two: If the intended meaning were the slaughter of a specific cow, they would not have deserved reproach for asking for clarification, but rather they would have deserved praise for it. Since Allah reproached them in His saying, ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, and in His saying, ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they nearly did not﴾, we know their shortcoming in carrying out what they had been commanded first, and that would only be the case if what they had been commanded first was the slaughter of a specific cow.

Three: What has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Had they slaughtered whatever cow they wished, it would have sufficed for them, but they made things hard upon themselves, so Allah made things hard upon them."

Four: At the time in which they were commanded to slaughter the cow, they were in need of slaughtering it. So if what was commanded was the slaughter of a specific cow while Allah had not clarified it, that would be a delay of the clarification beyond the time of need, and that is impermissible.

The answer: As for the first, we have explained at the beginning of the issue that His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ does not indicate that what is commanded is the slaughter of a cow, any cow whatsoever. As for the second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they nearly did not do it﴾ does not contain any indication that they were negligent at the beginning of the story, and that they nearly were negligent after the completion of the clarification. Rather, the wording admits of each of them, so we interpret it according to the latter, namely that when they came to the completion of the clarification, they hesitated at that point and nearly did not do it. As for the third: this narration from Ibn 'Abbas is of the category of single reports (akhbar al-ahad), and even if it is authentic, it cannot stand in opposition to the Book of Allah, exalted is He. As for the fourth: delaying the clarification beyond the time of need only follows if the command indicates immediacy (al-fawr), and that is prohibited according to us.

Know that when we build upon the view that what is commanded is "a cow, any cow whatsoever," it is necessary that we say: the obligations are distinct. So they were first obligated to slaughter any cow whatsoever, and second, that it be neither old nor virgin but median. When they did not do that, they were obligated that it be yellow. When they did not do that, they were obligated that it be, in addition to that, not trained to plow the earth nor to water the field. Then those who hold this view differed. Some said: the obligation that came last must include every attribute that preceded it, so that the cow, together with the last attribute, is neither old nor virgin, and bright yellow. Others say: it is only necessary that it have the last attribute alone, and this resembles the apparent meaning of the speech if it is one obligation after another. Though the first view resembles the narrations more, and the method of making things hard upon them when compliance was in doubt. When it is established that clarification does not come late, it must be one obligation after another, and that indicates that the easier may be abrogated by the more difficult (al-aslah yunsakh bil-ashaqq), and it indicates the permissibility of abrogation before the act is performed, but it does not indicate the permissibility of abrogation before the time of performance. It also indicates the occurrence of abrogation in the Law of Moses, peace be upon him. It also has a connection to the question of whether an addition to a text is abrogation or not. And it indicates the goodness of an obligation being imposed a second time upon one who disobeyed and did not do what he was obligated to do first.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Do you take us in mockery?"﴾, there are issues concerning it:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 67–68 (part 2 of 2):

The first issue: it is read "huzuwan" (هُزُوًا) with a damma, and "huzu'an" (هُزْءًا) with the letter zay sukun, like "kufu'an" and "kufan" (كُفُؤًا وكُفْءً). Hafs read (هُزُوًا) with two dammas and a waw, and likewise "kufuwan" (كُفُوًا).

The second issue: al-Qaffal said that God's words ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾ (أتَتَّخِذُنا) are an interrogative in the sense of denial. The word "huzu" (هُزْء, mockery) may carry the sense of the object of mockery, as one says, "this was in God's knowledge" (كان هذا في علم الله), meaning in what is known to Him, and "God is our hope" (الله رجاؤنا), meaning our object of hope. A parallel is God's words ﴿so you took them in mockery (سِخْرِيًّا)﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 110]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Do you take us as a mockery (أتَتَّخِذُنا هُزُءًا)" means: do you make us a place of mockery, or people of mockery, or ones mocked; and the mockery itself is extreme derision.

The third issue: the people only said this because, when they asked Musa (peace be upon him) to identify the killer, Musa said: "Slaughter a cow." They did not see any connection between this answer and that question, so they thought he was joking with them. It is possible that Musa (peace be upon him) commanded them to slaughter the cow without informing them that when they slaughtered the cow and struck the slain man with part of it, he would come to life; therefore this statement was taken by them as mockery. It is also possible that Musa (peace be upon him), although he had explained the state of affairs to them, they were amazed that the slain man could come to life by being struck with some part of the cow, so they thought this was in the manner of mockery.

صفحة ١٠٩

The fourth issue: some said that those people became unbelievers by their saying to Musa (peace be upon him): "Do you take us in mockery?" For if they said that and doubted God's power to revive the dead, then it is disbelief; and if they doubted whether what Musa (peace be upon him) commanded them was by God's command, then they permitted treachery in Musa's (peace be upon him) conveying of revelation, and that too is disbelief. Others among people said: it does not necessitate disbelief, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: jesting with the prophets is permissible, so perhaps they thought of him (peace be upon him) that he was jesting with them in a permissible jest, and that does not necessitate disbelief.

The second: the meaning of God's words ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾ (أتَتَّخِذُنا هُزُوًا) is: how strange this answer is, as if you were mocking us, not that they affirmed mockery against Musa.

As for God's words ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾, there are several aspects:

One: engaging in mockery occurs only from ignorance, and the station of prophethood does not admit undertaking mockery; so Musa (peace be upon him) did not seek refuge from the very thing they attributed to him, but sought refuge from the cause that necessitates it, as a man may say in such a situation: "I seek refuge in God from lack of reason and the dominance of desire." The sum is that he applied the name of the cause to the effect metaphorically. This is the strongest aspect.

Second: "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant of what mockery entails in matters of religion of severe punishment and great threat, for whenever I know that, my undertaking mockery is precluded."

Third: some said: the very act of mockery is sometimes called ignorance and folly, for it was narrated from some lexicographers that ignorance (الجهل) is the opposite of forbearance (الحلم), just as some said it is the opposite of knowledge (العلم).

Know that this statement of Musa (peace be upon him) indicates that mockery is among the grave major sins, and the full discussion of it has already passed in God's words ﴿They say: We are only with you, we are only mocking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15].

Know that the people asked Musa (peace be upon him) about three matters concerning the cow:

The first question: as God related of them, they said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is﴾. Musa (peace be upon him) answered with his words: ﴿He says it is a cow, neither old nor virgin, but between that; so do what you are commanded﴾. Know that there are discussions in this verse:

The first: if we say that God's words ﴿God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ indicate a command to slaughter a specific cow in itself, without its specification being clarified, then their question is fitting, since the commanded thing was general, and inquiry and seeking information are appropriate. As for those who say that it is in original usage for generality, it is necessary to explain what prompted them to this inquiry? And there are several aspects:

One: when Musa (peace be upon him) informed them that if they slaughtered the cow and struck the slain man with part of it, he would become alive, they were amazed at the matter of that cow, and thought that a cow with such a property could only be a specific cow, so they thoroughly inquired about its description, like Musa's staff which was specific among other staffs with those properties. However, the people were mistaken in that, because this wondrous sign was not a property of the cow; rather it was a miracle that God manifested at the hand of Musa (peace be upon him).

Second: perhaps the people intended a cow, any cow whatsoever, but the killer feared exposure, so he cast doubt into the specification and said the commanded thing is a specific cow, not just any cow. When the time of dispute over it arrived, they returned at that point to Musa.

Third: although the first address conveyed generality, the people wanted to take precaution in it, so they asked seeking further clarification and to remove all other possibilities; but the benefit changed and required the command to slaughter the specific cow.

صفحة ١١٠

The second discussion: the question "what is it (ما هِيَ)" is a request for defining the quiddity and reality; for "ma" is an interrogative and "hiya" refers to the reality, so "ma hiya" must be a request for the reality, and defining the quiddity and reality occurs only by mentioning its parts and preliminaries, not by mentioning its attributes that lie outside its quiddity. It is known that the attribute of age is among matters external to the quiddity, so this answer ought not to correspond to this question.

The reply to this: although the matter is as you mentioned, the circumstantial indication shows that their intent in saying "what is the cow" was not seeking its quiddity and explaining its reality, but rather their intent was seeking the attributes by which some cows are distinguished from others; therefore it was fitting to mention external attributes as an answer to this question.

The third discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "al-Fariḍ" is the aged one, and she was named fariḍ because she has finished her age, that is, she cut it off and reached its end. "Al-Bikr" is the young one, and "al-'Awān" is the middle one.

The judge said: as for al-bikr, it is said she is the small one; it is said she is the one who has not given birth; and it is said she is the one who gave birth once. Al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Salamah [al-Ḍabbi] said: he mentioned for al-fariḍ that she is the aged one, and for al-bikr that she is the young one, and she is among women the one not yet having intercourse, and among camels the one that has borne one offspring. Al-Qaffal said: al-bikr indicates the first, and from it comes "al-bakūrah" for the first of the fruit, and from it "bukrat al-nahar" (the early part of the day); and it is said: "bakkartu 'alayhima al-barihah" when he came at the beginning of the night. And it seems the more apparent is that she is the one who has not given birth, because the known sense of "bikr" among female humans is the one on whom the stallion has not mounted. Some said: al-'awān is the one that has given birth more than once. "Harb 'awān" (a war of attrition) is when a war has been fought in it time after time, and "hajah 'awān" (a repeated need) is when it has been fulfilled time after time.

The fourth discussion: the scholars argued from God's words ﴿neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent reasoning) and acting upon predominant opinion (ghalib al-zann) in rulings, since it cannot be known that she is between the aged and the virgin except through ijtihad. Here are two questions:

The first: the word "bayn" (between) requires two things or more, so from where is its use permitted with "dhalika"?

The answer: because it carries the sense of two things, since it occurred referring to what was mentioned, the aged and the virgin.

The second question: how is it permitted to refer with the word "dhalika" to two feminine things, while it is for pointing at a single masculine thing?

The answer: mentioning "dhalika" is permitted under the interpretation of "what was mentioned" or "what preceded," for brevity in speech.

As for God's words ﴿so do what you are commanded﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: do what you are commanded to do, from your saying: "I commanded you to good (amartuka al-khayr)."

The second: that the intended meaning is "do your command," in the sense of "your commanded thing," calling the object by the verbal noun, like "the beating of the amir (ḍarb al-amīr)."

Know that the original intended purpose of this answer is that the cow be in its most perfect condition, for the young one is deficient because she has not yet reached the state of perfection, and the aged one is as if she has become deficient and gone beyond the limit of perfection; but the middle one is the one in the state of perfection.

Then God related their second question, which is His words: ﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is﴾. Know that when they knew the state of age, they proceeded after it to learn the state of color, and God answered them that it is ﴿yellow, its color is bright (fāqi')﴾. Fuqūʿ (brightness) is the most intense and purest degree of yellow, and it is said for emphasis: "aṣfar fāqi'" (intensely yellow), "aswad ḥālik" (intensely black), "abyaḍ yaqaq" (intensely white), "aḥmar qānin" (intensely red), and "akhḍar nāḍir" (intensely green). Here there are two questions:

The first question: "fāqi'" here is in the position of a predicate about the color, so how can it come as an emphasis for "ṣafrā'"?

The answer: it did not come as a predicate about the color; it came as an emphasis for "ṣafrā'," except that the color was raised by it in the manner of a subject, and the color is its cause and is joined with it, so there was no difference between your saying "ṣafrā' fāqi'a" and "ṣafrā' fāqi'un lawnuhā."

صفحة ١١١
