The second question: why was it not said "ṣafrā' fāqi'a," and what is the benefit in mentioning the color?

The answer: the benefit in it is emphasis, because color is a name for the form, and that is the yellowness; so it is as if it were said: "intensely yellow, its yellowness is," and it is from your saying: "the true diligence of his diligence" (jiddu jiddihi) and "the madness of a madman" (junūnu majnūn). It is narrated from Wahb: when you look at it, it appears to you as if the rays of the sun come out of its skin.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 69–70:

As for His saying, ﴿pleasing to the onlookers﴾, the meaning is that this cow, because of the beauty of its color, pleases whoever looks at it. Al-Hasan said: "Al-asfar (yellow) here means al-aswad (black), because the Arabs call black 'yellow' (asfar). Its parallel is His saying about the smoke: ﴿as if they were yellow camels﴾ [al-Mursalat 77:33], meaning black." They objected to this interpretation, saying that yellow is never understood to mean black at all, so it is not a true meaning of the word. Moreover, black is not described as intensely bright (fuqu'), since one says "intensely yellow" (asfar faqi') and "deeply black" (aswad halik). And Allah knows best. As for delight (surur), it is an inner state that arises when one believes, knows, or thinks that something pleasant or beneficial has been obtained.

Then Allah related their third question, His saying: ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is, for cows have become confused for us, and indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided."﴾ Here there are several issues.

The first issue: Al-Hasan reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, had they not said 'if Allah wills,' they would never have been granted it." Know that this indicates that uttering this phrase is recommended in every action one intends to accomplish. For this reason Allah said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," ﴿unless Allah wills﴾﴾ [al-Kahf 18:23–24]. It involves seeking Allah's help, entrusting the matter to Him, and acknowledging His power and the effectiveness of His will.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) used this as evidence that all events are willed by Allah. According to the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), when Allah commanded them to do this, He necessarily willed their guidance, and so there would be no point in their saying "if Allah wills." But according to our companions, Allah may command something He does not will, and so there remains a point to our saying "if Allah wills."

The third issue: The Mu'tazilah argued that the will of Allah is created (muhdath), from His saying ﴿if Allah wills﴾, on two grounds:

The first: the entry of the particle "in" (if) into it requires that it be contingent (hudut).

The second: He made the attainment of guidance dependent upon the attainment of the will to be guided. Since the attainment of guidance is not eternal, the will to be guided must also not be eternal.

Let us return to the commentary. As for His saying ﴿make clear to us what it is﴾, the question concerns the one already mentioned: our saying "what is it?" seeks clarification of the reality (haqiqah), while what is mentioned in the answer are accidental, separable attributes. So how can this answer correspond to the question? Its answer has already been given.

As for His saying ﴿for cows have become confused for us﴾, the meaning is that many cows are described as having a yellow color and similar features, so it became confused for us which of them we should slaughter. It was also read as tashabaha (with the ta' dropped and assimilated into the shin), meaning tatashabaha, and it was read as tashabahat, mutashabihah, and mutashabih.

As for His saying ﴿and indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided﴾, there are several interpretations mentioned by al-Qaffal:

One of them: and indeed we, by Allah's will, will be guided to the cow commanded to be slaughtered, once we acquire its attributes by which it is distinguished from others.

The second: and indeed we, if Allah wills His description of it to us, by adding to our clarification, will be guided to it.

The third: and indeed we, if Allah wills, are upon guidance in our thorough questioning about the attributes of the cow; that is, we hope that we are not in error in what we are doing in this inquiry.

The fourth: indeed we, by Allah's will, will be guided to the killer if you describe this cow to us by that which distinguishes it from others.

Then Allah answered their question with His saying: ﴿He says, "It is a cow neither trained to plow the earth"﴾. His saying ﴿neither trained﴾ is an attribute of "cow," meaning: a cow that is not trained, that has not been made submissive for riding or for plowing the earth, ﴿nor is it one that irrigates the field﴾. The first "la" (not) is for negation, and the second is additional, for emphasis of the first. The meaning is: "not trained, plowing and irrigating," as though it were said: "not a trained one that plows and irrigates." The summary is that a cow made docile through work must necessarily be deficient, so Allah clarified that it does not plow the earth nor irrigate the field, because these two works reveal deficiency.

As for His saying ﴿sound (musallamah)﴾, there are several interpretations:

One of them: free from defects in general.

The second: free from the effects of the work mentioned.

The third: musallamah, meaning wild, released from confinement.

The fourth: musallamah from the shiyah, which is the opposite of its color; that is, its yellowness is pure, unmixed with other colors. This fourth interpretation is weak, since otherwise His saying ﴿there is no blemish in it﴾ would be a repetition without benefit. Rather, it is better to understand it as freedom from defects, and the wording requires this, because it indicates complete soundness from ailments and faults. The scholars used this as evidence for the permissibility of relying on the outward appearance while allowing that the inner reality may be different. For when we interpret ﴿sound﴾ as "free from defects," we do not know this through certainty but only through the outward appearance.

As for His saying ﴿there is no blemish in it﴾, the meaning is that its yellowness is pure, not mixed with other colors. For a yellow cow may be described as such when yellowness appears in most of it, so Allah wished to clarify the generality of this with His saying ﴿there is no blemish in it﴾. It was narrated that it was yellow in its hooves and yellow in its horns. Al-washy means mixing one color with another.

Then Allah informed them that they stopped at this explanation and limited themselves to it, saying: ﴿"Now you have brought the truth."﴾ That is: now this cow has been distinguished from others, because it is a middle-aged yellow cow, not made docile by work. The Qadi said: Their saying ﴿"Now you have brought the truth"﴾ is undoubtedly disbelief on their part, because it indicates that they believed in the previous commands that they were not true. This is weak, since it is possible that the meaning is: now the reality of what we were commanded has become manifest, until it was distinguished from others, and so it is not disbelief.

[Page 113]

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done so﴾, the meaning is: they slaughtered the cow, and they did not almost slaughter it. Here there is a discussion. The grammarians mention two explanations of *kāda* (كادَ, "to be about to / to almost").

The first: they said that its negation is affirmation and its affirmation is negation. Thus our saying *kāda yafʿalu kadhā* (كادَ يَفْعَلُ كَذا) means "he came close to doing such-and-such but did not do it," and our saying *mā kāda yafʿalu kadhā* (ما كادَ يَفْعَلُ كَذا) means "he came close to not doing it [but] he did it."

The second, which is the choice of the grammarian Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī, is that *kāda* means proximity (al-muqāraba). Thus our saying *kāda yafʿalu* means "he came close to the act," and our saying *mā kāda yafʿalu* means "he did not come close to it." The first group may argue against the invalidity of this second view with this verse, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they almost did not do it﴾ means "and they did not come close to doing it," and negating proximity to the act contradicts the affirmation that the act occurred. So if *kāda* signified proximity, a contradiction would arise in this verse. Here there are several discussions:

The first discussion: It is related that among the Children of Israel there was a righteous old man who had a calf. He brought it to the thicket and said: "O God, I entrust it to You for my son until it grows up." He was dutiful to his parents. The calf grew up and became one of the finest and fattest of cows. They haggled over it with the orphan and his mother until they bought it by filling its hide with gold. At that time the cow was worth three dinars. They had been seeking the described cow for forty years.

Page 114

The second discussion: It is related from al-Ḥasan that the cow is slaughtered (tudhbaḥ, تُذْبَحُ) and not sacrificed by cutting the throat (tunḥar, تُنْحَرُ). From ʿAṭāʾ it is related that it is slaughtered by nahr. He said: "I recited the verse to him, and he said: 'Dhabḥ (ذبح) and naḥr (نحر) are the same.'" It is related from Qatāda and al-Zuhrī that: "If you wish, you may perform nahr, and if you wish, you may perform dhabḥ." The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that they were commanded to perform dhabḥ, and that they did what is called dhabḥ. Although naḥr may suffice in place of dhabḥ, its form differs from the form of dhabḥ. The apparent meaning therefore requires what we have said, such that even if they had performed naḥr without any evidence that it stands in place of dhabḥ, it would not be valid.

The third discussion: They differed about the reason for which they "almost did not slaughter." Some said it was because of the high price of the cow, and others said they feared fame and public disgrace. On both views, refraining from what one has been commanded is not permissible.

As for the first: when they were commanded to slaughter that specific cow, and that act could not be completed except with a large price, it became obligatory for them to pay it, because what is necessary for an obligation to be fulfilled is itself obligatory, unless evidence indicates otherwise. Indeed, the worshipper is not obliged to perform purification with water if he finds it only at a high price, by the ruling of the Sharia; but were it not for this exemption, it would be obligatory whenever purification is obligatory in absolute terms.

As for the second, which is the fear of disgrace: that does not remove the obligation. If retaliation (qawad, قَوَد) is obligatory upon him, he is bound to surrender himself to the blood-avenger (walī al-dam) if the latter demands it. It may also be obligatory for him to make the matter known so that evil and strife may be removed, and it may be obligatory for him to do so so that the suspicion of murder may be lifted from the people near whom the victim was dumped, because he is the one who exposed them to suspicion, so it is incumbent upon him to remove it. How then is it permissible to make it a cause for hesitation in this act?

The fourth discussion: Those who hold that a command indicates obligation have argued from this verse, because in this case nothing was present except the bare command. Then God, exalted is He, censured hesitation in it and laziness in engaging with its requirement, and that indicates that a command means obligation. The Qadi said: When the purpose of the commanded act is the removal of evil and strife, this indicates its obligation. God, exalted is He, commanded its slaughter only so that the killer would be revealed, and the strife and the harmful evil feared among them would be removed. Guarding against this kind of harm is obligatory. Since the remedy is its removal by this act, the act becomes obligatory. It is not impossible that in that law, the worship through offering (qurbān, قُرْبان) was only a way of obligation, and since they already knew this, the bare command sufficed for them.

I say: The gist of these two objections returns to one point, namely that although we do not say that a command requires obligation, we also do not say that it negates obligation. Perhaps they understood the obligation here through another cause besides the command. That separate cause is either an external circumstantial indicator, which is the knowledge that averting harms is obligatory, or a verbal indicator, which is what was explained earlier: that offering (qurbān) is only legislated as an obligation.

The answer: What was mentioned is merely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾. When censure and rebuke were mentioned for abandoning the slaughter that was commanded, we knew that the source of this is merely the arrival of the command for it, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh, أصول الفقه, the foundations of Islamic legal theory) that linking a ruling to an attribute indicates that the attribute is the cause (ʿilla, عِلَّة) of that ruling.

The fifth discussion: Those who hold that a command conveys immediacy (al-fawr, الفَوْر) have argued from this verse, saying: because censure was directed at abandoning the commanded act upon the arrival of a bare command, this indicates that it is for immediacy.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾: know that the occurrence of that killing must have preceded His command to slaughter. As for the report about the occurrence of that killing, and that the victim must be struck with part of that cow, it does not necessarily have to precede the report about the story of the cow. So the claim of one who says that this story must come earlier in the recitation than the first is an error, because this story in itself must come before the first in existence. But precedence in mention is not obligatory, since sometimes the mention of the cause precedes the mention of the ruling, and at other times the reverse occurs. It is as if, when that incident befell them, God commanded them to slaughter the cow; then when they had slaughtered it, He said: "And when you killed a soul before, and you differed and disputed, I will reveal to you the killer whom you concealed, by striking the victim with part of this slaughtered cow." This is consistent. If it is said: Grant that there is no flaw in this arrangement, but the other arrangement was preferable; what is the benefit of preferring this arrangement? We say: The story of the command to slaughter the cow was placed before the mention of the victim because, had it been arranged in reverse, it would have been a single story, and if it were a single story, the purpose of the intervening (bayniyya, بَيْنِيَّة) connective sequence would be lost.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿disputed about it﴾ (*idārra'tum fīhā*, فادّارَأْتُمْ فِيها), there are several interpretations:

One of them: You differed and contended concerning its matter, because disputants push one another away (*yadra'u*), that is, they repel and crowd one another.

The second: "*Idārra'tum*" means that each of you denies the killing from himself and attributes it to another.

The third: each of you pushes the others away from innocence and from the accusation. The gist of the matter is that *dar'* (الدَّرْء) is repelling. When disputants argue, each one of them repels from himself that accusation, and each one repels his opponent's argument regarding that deed, and each one repels his opponent's argument in attributing that accusation to someone else and his opponent's argument for clearing himself of it. Al-Qaffāl said: The pronoun in *fīhā* refers to the soul (nafs), that is, you differed concerning the soul. It may also refer to the killing, because His saying "*qatal-tum*" (you killed) indicates the verbal noun.

The commentary, on the words of God, "And God will bring out what you were hiding" (2:72), says that God will bring to light, without doubt, what you concealed concerning the matter of the killing. If it is asked, "How can *mukhrijun* (bringing out) be given grammatical force when it has the sense of the past tense?", we answer: it narrates what was future at the time of the dispute, just as the present tense is used in His words, "stretching out his forelegs" (Al-Kahf 18:18). This sentence is a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, which are "you disputed about it" and "so We said." Then there are several issues:

**First issue:** The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that holds God is bound by justice and wisdom) say that His words, "And God will bring out what you were hiding," mean that He must certainly do this. The reason it is judged that He must do this is that disagreement and contention in matters of killing would be a cause of strife and corruption, and God does not love corruption. For this reason He said that He must remove this concealment so that the corruption would disappear. This shows that He, glorified is He, does not will corruption, does not approve of it, and does not create it.

**Second issue:** The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, knows all that is knowable, for otherwise He would not be able to reveal what they had concealed.

**Third issue:** The verse indicates that whatever good or evil a servant keeps secret, if he persists in it, God will reveal it. He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "If a servant were to obey God from behind seventy veils, God would make that known through the tongues of people." The same applies to disobedience. It is also narrated that God, exalted is He, revealed to Musa (Moses), peace be upon him: "Tell the Children of Israel: they conceal their deeds from Me, but it is upon Me to make them manifest to them."

**Fourth issue:** The verse indicates that it is permissible for a general expression to be used while a specific meaning is intended, because His words, "what you were hiding," encompass all things concealed, and then God, exalted is He, intended this particular incident.

Page 115

As for His saying, ﴿So We said: Strike him with part of it﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the owner of the cow of the Children of Israel searched for it for forty years until he found it, and then it was slaughtered. However, this report contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, because the particle *fa* (فَ) in His saying, ﴿So We said: Strike him with part of it﴾, indicates sequence (*ta'qib*, immediate succession). That implies that His saying, ﴿Strike him with part of it﴾, occurred immediately after His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾.

Page 115

The second issue: The pronoun in His saying, ﴿Strike him﴾ (اضْرِبُوهُ) is a pronoun, and it may refer either to the soul (*nafs*), in which case the masculine form is used with the interpretation of "the person" or "the human being," or it may refer to the slain man, which is what is indicated by His saying, ﴿what you were concealing﴾.

The third issue: It is possible that Allah, exalted is He, commanded the slaughter of the cow only because a benefit was bound to its slaughter that could not be attained except by slaughtering it. It is also possible that the situation regarding it and regarding other than it was equal. The first is closer to the truth, because if something else could have taken its place, it would not have been obligatory specifically, but rather optional, between it and something else. Here there are two questions:

The first question: What is the benefit in striking the slain man with part of the cow, given that Allah, exalted is He, is able to bring him back to life directly?

The answer: The benefit is that the proof becomes more confirmed and further from any trickery. It would have been possible for a heretic to suggest that Musa (peace be upon him) revived him through some kind of magic and trickery. But when he came to life upon being struck with a piece of the slaughtered cow, the doubt that he had come to life through something transferred to him from the body with which he was struck is removed, since it was by an act performed by them. This indicates that the informing of the prophets comes from Allah and not by deception from the servants. Also, offering the sacrifice is something that magnifies the matter of the sacrifice.

The second question: Why did He not command the slaughter of something other than the cow? They answered that the discussion about other than it would be the same as the discussion about it, had they been commanded with it. Then they mentioned benefits in it: among them, drawing near to Allah through the sacrifice, which was a customary practice; and because this sacrifice was among the greatest sacrifices in their view; and because of the greater reward for bearing the hardship of obtaining this cow despite its high price; and because of the great wealth it brought to the owner of the cow.

The fourth issue: They differed about what that part was with which they struck the slain man. The closer view is that they had the choice among the parts of the cow, because they were commanded to strike the slain man with part of the cow, and whichever part of the cow's parts they struck him with, they were obeying what His saying required: ﴿Strike him with part of it﴾. Carrying out what is commanded indicates discharge from the obligation, as is established in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence), and that requires choice. They differed about the part with which the slain man was struck. It was said: its tongue. It was said: its right thigh. It was said: its tail. It was said: the bone adjoining the cartilage (*ghudrūf*), which is the root of the ears. It was said: the piece between the two shoulders. There is no doubt that the Qur'an does not indicate any of these. If a sound report comes, it is accepted; otherwise, silence about it is obligatory.

The fifth issue: There is an omitted element in the speech, and the implied meaning is: "So We said: Strike him with part of it, so they struck him with part of it, and he came to life." However, that was omitted because of the indication of His saying, ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾. On this view, it is like His saying, ﴿Strike the rock with your staff, and it gushed forth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 60], meaning: "So he struck, and it gushed forth." It is narrated that when they struck him, he rose by the permission of Allah, while his veins were gushing blood, and he said: "So-and-so and so-and-so killed me," naming his two paternal cousins; then he fell dead. And the two were killed.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: In this verse there are two views:

One is that it refers to the very same dead man.

The second is that it is an argument for the possibility of resurrection. Then, is this argument directed at the polytheists or at others? There are two views on this:

The first: al-Asamm said: It is directed at the polytheists, because if it became known to them through widespread transmission (*tawatur*) that this revival happened in this manner, they would know the possibility of resurrection; and if it did not become known through widespread transmission, it would still be a motive for them to reflect. Al-Qadi said: This is the closer view, because Allah, exalted is He, had previously mentioned the command to strike and that it was the cause of the revival of that dead man, and then He said: ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾, using the plural ﴿the dead﴾. Had the intended meaning been that slain man alone, He would not have used the plural in the statement. It is as if He said: "By this He indicated that resurrection is like initial creation in His power."

The second: al-Qaffal said: The apparent meaning of the speech indicates that Allah, exalted is He, said to the Children of Israel: "Allah's bringing back all the other dead will be like this revival that you have witnessed." For although they believed in that, they only believed in it through reasoning, and they had not witnessed any of it. So when they witnessed it, their hearts were reassured and the doubt that the one who reasons cannot escape was removed from them. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260], up to His saying: ﴿so that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. So Allah, exalted is He, brought the slain man back to life before the Children of Israel's eyes, and then He said to them: ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾, meaning: as He brought him to life in this world, He will bring them to life in the Hereafter, without that creation requiring any material, duration, model, or instrument.

The second issue: Some people have used His saying, ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾ to argue that the slain man was dead, but this is weak, because He, exalted is He, drew an analogy between the revival of that slain man and the revival of the dead, so it does not follow from this that the slain man was dead.

As for His saying, ﴿and shows you His signs﴾, someone may say: If that was one sign, why were they called "signs" (*ayat*, plural)?

The answer: They indicate the existence of the Creator, who is capable of all things that can be done, knowing of all that can be known, and who chooses in creation and origination; and they indicate the truthfulness of Musa (peace be upon him); and they indicate the innocence of one who was not the killer; and they indicate that the accusation is specifically directed at the one who perpetrated that killing. So although it was one sign, since it indicated these many implications, it therefore took the place of many signs.

As for His saying, ﴿so that you may understand﴾ (*la'allakum ta'qilun*), there are two discussions:

The first: The word *la'alla* (لَعَلَّ) has already had its explanation given in His saying: ﴿so that you may be mindful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21].

The second: The people were rational before these signs were presented to them. When reason is already present, it is impossible to say: "I presented to you such-and-such a sign so that you would become rational." Therefore it is not possible to take the verse in its apparent sense; rather, interpretation is necessary, namely that the intended meaning is "so that you may act according to the dictates of your reason," and that whoever is able to bring one soul back to life is able to bring all souls back to life, since there is no restriction, so that they do not deny resurrection. This is the end of the discussion about the interpretation of the verse.

Know that many of the earlier scholars mentioned that among the rulings of this verse is the question of whether the killer inherits or not. They said: No; because it has been narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah al-Salmani that the man who was the killer in this incident was deprived of inheritance because he was a killer. Al-Qadi said: It is not permissible to make this question one of the rulings of this verse, because it is not apparent from the verse whether the killer was an heir of his victim or not, and even if he was an heir, was he deprived of the inheritance or not? And it is not necessary, if it is narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah that the killer was deprived of inheritance because of his killing, that this be counted among the rulings of the Qur'an when the Qur'an does not indicate it, neither in summary nor in detail. And since it has not been established that their law is like our law, and that it is not obligatory to follow them, then including this discussion among the rulings of the Qur'an is forced.

Know that what al-Qadi said is correct. Nevertheless, let us mention this question, so we say: The jurists differed on whether the killer inherits or not. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, he does not inherit, whether the killing was unjustified, whether intentional or by mistake, or justified, such as when a just person kills a rebel. According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, he does not inherit in cases of intentional or accidental killing, except that a just person who kills a rebel does inherit from him. Likewise, a killer who is a minor or insane inherits, but not from the blood money (*diyah*) nor from the rest of his property. This is the view of 'Ali, 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. 'Uthman al-Batti said: The killer by mistake inherits, and the intentional killer does not inherit. Malik said: He does not inherit from the blood money, but he inherits from the rest of the property. This is also the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Zuhri, and al-Awza'i.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued with the general wording of the well-known, widely transmitted report that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The killer has no share in the inheritance." However, the argument with this report is valid only if we permit specifying the general wording of the Book by a solitary report (*khabar al-wahid*), and the discussion of that is mentioned in *usul al-fiqh*. Then there is a subtle point here: that the admission of specification into a general text introduces a kind of weakness. So if we specify this report with some cases, then weaknesses accumulate upon it: the fact that it is a solitary report causes weakness; its being in conflict with the Book is another cause; and its being specified is another cause. So if we specify the general wording of the Book by it, we would have preferred something extremely weak over something extremely strong. But if this report is not specified at all, some causes of weakness are removed from it, and then it is not far-fetched to specify the general wording of the Book by it.

Abu Bakr al-Razi argued that a just person who kills a rebel does not become deprived of inheritance, because we know of no disagreement that whoever is owed retaliation (*qawad*) from a person, and then kills him by way of retaliation, is not deprived of inheritance. And know that the Shafi'is reject this case. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 74 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they were like stones, or even harder. And indeed, of stones there are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed there are those that split open so water comes out of them, and indeed there are those that fall down out of fear of Allah. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾

Know that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that﴾ contains several issues.

The first issue: That which by its very nature is capable of receiving an impression from something else, but then something befalls that receptive thing by which it becomes such that it no longer receives an impression, is described as having become hard, dense and unyielding. Thus a body, insofar as it is a body, receives an impression from others, but when the quality of stoniness befalls the body, the substance of the stone becomes unreceptive. Likewise, the heart by its nature is affected by contemplating the proofs, signs and lessons, and its being affected is expressed as abandoning rebelliousness, arrogance and pride, and showing obedience, submission, and fear of Allah, the Exalted. When something befalls the heart that removes it from this quality, it becomes like a stone in its non-receptiveness, and it is said: the heart has hardened and become coarse. For this reason, Allah, the Exalted, described the believers with tenderness, saying: ﴿a Book consistent, repeating; the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it﴾ [al-Zumar: 23].

The second issue: al-Qaffal said: It is possible that those addressed by His saying ﴿your hearts﴾ are the People of the Book who were in the time of Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: your hearts became hard, unyielding and stiff after the clear proofs that came to your forefathers, the events that befell them, the punishment that descended upon those among them who persisted in disobedience, the signs that their prophets brought them, the covenants they took upon themselves and upon everyone who adhered to the Torah from among others. Thus He informs about their transgression and harshness, despite their knowledge of the signs of Allah by which hearts are softened. This is more apt, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then your hearts hardened﴾ is direct address, so applying it to those present is more appropriate. It is also possible that what is meant are those specific Jews who were in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, and it is possible that He means those before them among their predecessors.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿after that﴾ may mean after what Allah, exalted is He, showed of the reviving of that slain man when he was struck with part of the slaughtered cow until the killer was identified. It is related that when that slain man identified the killer, the killer denied it and did not abandon denial, rather he sought strife and a group supported him in it. At that point, Allah, exalted is He, said describing them: after the appearance of such a sign, their hearts hardened, meaning their hearts after the appearance of such a sign became like stones in hardness. It is also possible that His saying ﴿after that﴾ refers to all the great blessings and striking signs that Allah, glorified is He, enumerated which He manifested through the hand of Moses, peace be upon him, for those Jews, after their witnessing of them became abundant, were not free of obstinacy and objection toward Moses, peace be upon him. This is clear in their accounts in the wilderness for whoever considers them.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿or even harder﴾, there are issues.

The first issue: The word ﴿or﴾ (aw) denotes choice, and it is not fitting for the Knower of the unseen, so an interpretation is necessary, and there are several:

One: It has the meaning of waw (and), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat: 147], meaning and more; and as in His saying: ﴿and they should not reveal their adornment except to their husbands or their fathers﴾ [al-Nur: 31], meaning and their fathers; and as in His saying: ﴿that you eat from your houses or the houses of your fathers﴾ [al-Nur: 61], meaning and the houses of your fathers. Among its parallels is His saying: ﴿perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], and ﴿those that bring reminder, as excuse or warning﴾ [al-Mursalat: 5–6].

Two: He, exalted is He, intended to keep it vague for the servants, so He said that as a person says to another: "I ate bread or dates," while he has no doubt that he ate one of them, when he intends not to specify it to his companion.

Three: The meaning is: they are like stones, and among them is what is, or is even harder than stones.

Four: That when humans look into the states of their hearts they say: they are like stones, or they are even harder than stones, and this is what is meant in His saying: ﴿and he was at a distance of two bows or nearer﴾ [al-Najm: 9], meaning in your view and your belief.

Five: That the word ﴿or﴾ means "rather" (bal), and they recited:
"By Allah, I do not know whether Salma has been seized by a ghoul, or the people, or all are beloved to me."
They said: he meant "rather all."

Six: That it is in the manner of your saying: "I eat nothing but sweet or sour," meaning my food does not go beyond these two, rather it moves between them. In sum, the purpose is not to create uncertainty between them, but to negate other than them.

Seven: That "or" is a particle of permission, as if it were said: by whichever of these two you liken their hearts, it would be true, as in your saying: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," meaning: whichever of them you sit with, you are correct, and if you sit with both together, you are also correct.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿ashaddu﴾ is conjoined to the kaf (in "like"), either by way of the meaning "or like" with an omitted noun: "or like a harder thing," so the annexed word is removed and the annexed-to word is put in its place; or by way of "or they themselves are harder in hardness."

The third issue: Why He described them as harder in hardness: for several reasons:

One: If stones were rational and this verse reached them, they would accept it, as He said: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled, split apart out of fear of Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 21].

Two: Stones have no resistance to what occurs in them by the command of Allah, even if they are hard; rather they are directed according to the will of Allah and do not refuse His subjugation. Yet these people, despite what we have described of their states regarding the continuous signs with them and the successive blessings from Allah upon them, refuse obedience to Him, and their hearts do not soften to recognize His right. This is like His saying: ﴿There is no creature on the earth nor a bird that flies with its wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38], up to His saying: ﴿And those who denied Our signs are deaf and dumb in darkness﴾ [al-An'am: 39]. It is as if the meaning is that animals other than the children of Adam are nations, each one of which is subjugated to something and is compliant with what is required of it, whereas these disbelievers refuse what Allah wants from them.

Three: ﴿or even harder﴾, because stones may benefit in some respects, and water may appear from them in some states, but the hearts of these people have no benefit in them whatsoever and do not soften to obey Allah in any way.

The fourth issue: The Qadi said: If Allah, exalted is He, is the Creator who makes them persist in the disbelief they are upon, how is it right to blame them in this manner? If Moses, peace be upon him, addressed them, they would have said to him: "The One who created hardness in stones is the One who created hardness in our hearts, and the One who created the gushing of rivers from stones is the One able to transfer us from the disbelief we are upon by creating faith in us. So if He does not do so, our excuse is evident, and their argument against Him would be firmer than His argument against them." This kind of speech has been established in detail and in branches many times and in various ways.

The fifth issue: He said ﴿harder in hardness﴾ and did not say ﴿more hard﴾ (aqsa), because that is more indicative of the excess of hardness. Another reason is that He did not intend the meaning of "harder" (aqsa), but intended to describe hardness with intensity, as if it were said: the hardness of stones has intensified and their hearts are harder in hardness. It was also recited as "qasawa" (qasāwah). The object of comparison was omitted to avoid ambiguity, as in your saying: "Zayd is generous and 'Amr is more generous." Then, glorified and exalted is He, preferred the stones over their hearts by explaining that from stones three kinds of benefits may come forth, while none of these benefits is found in the hearts of these people.

The first of them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, of stones there are those from which rivers gush forth﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: It was recited "wa-in" with the light (mukhaffafa) form, which is the lightened form of the heavy "inna," which is followed by the distinguishing lam, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, all of them, when brought together, are present before Us﴾ [Ya-Sin: 32].

The second issue: Tafajjur (gushing) is opening with breadth and abundance. It is said: the sore of so-and-so burst, meaning it split open with pus; and from it come al-fajr (dawn) and al-fujur (dissoluteness). Malik ibn Dinar recited "yanfajir" in the sense of: "and indeed of stones there is that which splits, so water comes out of it, which flows until rivers come from it." The philosophers said: rivers are only generated from vapors that gather in the interior of the earth. If the surface of the earth is loose, those vapors break through and separate; if the surface of the earth is solid and stony, those vapors gather, and their successive accumulations continue to join their predecessors until they become very abundant, and then, from their abundance and the frequency of their flow, it happens that the earth splits and those waters flow as valleys and rivers.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, of them there are those that split open so water comes out of them﴾, meaning: of stones there are those that crack open so water comes out of them, so it becomes a spring, not a flowing river. That is, stones may be moistened with much water or with little water, and this indicates the variation of moisture in them, and that they may abound in some state until there comes out of them what forms rivers, and they may be scarce. These people's hearts are in extreme hardness; they are not moistened by accepting any of the admonitions, nor do they open up to them, nor do they turn toward guidance. His saying ﴿yashsha'aqqaq﴾ means yatashaqqaq, so the taa' was assimilated, as in His saying ﴿yadhdhakkaru﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269], meaning yatadhakkaru, and His saying: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1], ﴿O you who are covered﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1].

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, of them there are those that fall down out of fear of Allah.﴾

Know that there is a difficulty in it, which is that falling down out of fear of Allah is a quality of rational living beings, whereas a stone is inanimate, so this cannot be realized in it. Because of this difficulty, they mentioned several interpretations of this verse:

The saying of Abu Muslim specifically: that the pronoun in His saying ﴿And indeed of them﴾ refers to the hearts, since fear cannot be attributed to hearts, nor to stones. The hearts were mentioned earlier just as the stones were mentioned. At most, the stones are the nearer of the two mentioned, but since this attribute is fitting for hearts and not for stones, it is obligatory that this pronoun refer to the hearts and not the stones. They raised two objections against this:

The first: that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So they are like stones, or even harder﴾ is a complete sentence; then He began and mentioned the state of stones with His saying ﴿And indeed, of stones there are those from which rivers gush forth﴾, so it is necessary that His saying ﴿And indeed, of them there are those that fall down out of fear of Allah﴾ refers back to them.

The second: that falling down is fitting for stones and not for hearts, so interpreting "falling down" is no better than interpreting "fear."

Second: the view of a number of the exegetes that the pronoun refers to the stones. But we do not concede that stones are not living and rational. The explanation is that what is meant is the mountain of Musa (peace be upon him) when it was broken apart and his Lord manifested Himself to it. This is because Allah, glorified and exalted is He, created in it life, reason, and perception, and this is not far-fetched in the power of Allah. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?" They will say, "Allah has made us speak, the One who made everything speak."﴾ [Fussilat: 21]. Just as the skin was made to speak, hear, and understand, so likewise the mountain: He described it with fear. He also said: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled, split apart out of fear of Allah.﴾ [al-Hashr: 21]. The meaning is that if He had placed reason and understanding in it, it would have become so. It is also narrated that the trunk of the palm tree moaned when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ascended the pulpit. It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when the revelation came to him at the beginning of the mission and the Prophet (ﷺ) returned to his home, the stones and trees greeted him, and all of them were saying: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah." They said: it is not impossible that reason and understanding be created in some stones so that fear arises in them. The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology) rejected this interpretation, because they hold that a specific structure and balanced temperament are a condition for the acceptance of life and reason. They have no proof for the requirement of structure except mere improbability, so it is necessary that they not be given consideration.

Third: the view of most of the exegetes, namely that the pronoun refers to the stones, and that stones do not reason or understand. On this view they mentioned several kinds of interpretation:

The first: some stones roll down from a high place where they were, and descend to a lower place. These disbelievers are persistent in obstinacy and arrogance, so descending from height is made an example of submission. His saying, ﴿out of fear of Allah﴾, means: that descent, if it had come from a rational, choosing being, would have been fearful of Allah. This is like His saying: ﴿They found in it a wall about to collapse, so he set it up straight.﴾ [al-Kahf: 77], meaning a wall in which there had appeared such inclination and nearness to falling that if the like of it had appeared in a choosing living being, it would have been intending to fall. Something similar is the saying of one of them:

A miser, whose courtyards the dappled horses lose their way in; you see the hills prostrating before their hooves.

And the saying of Jarir:

When news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Madina trembled, and the humbled mountains.

So the first poet made the traces of hooves visible on the hillocks, while they did not resist removing them from themselves, like prostration of them before the hooves; and likewise the second made the signs of anxiety visible among the people of Madina like humility. On this manner the scholars of inquiry interpreted His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them exalt Him; and there is not a thing but exalts His praise.﴾ [al-Isra': 44], His saying: ﴿To Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Nahl: 49] to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate.﴾ [al-Rahman: 6].

The second interpretation: His saying, ﴿out of fear of Allah﴾, means: and among the stones are those that fall, split, and separate from one another, during earthquakes, because of what Allah wills by it of the fear of His servants of Him and their turning to Him in supplication and repentance. Its verification is that since the primary purpose of the stones' descent in severe earthquakes is that the fear of Allah, exalted is He, arise in the hearts of the servants, that fear became like the effective cause of the occurrence of that descent. So the word "min" (from) is for denoting the starting point, and His saying, ﴿out of fear of Allah﴾, means: because of the arising of the fear of Allah in the hearts.

The third interpretation: what al-Jubba'i mentioned, namely that he interpreted the stones as hail that descends from the clouds, as a warning from Allah, exalted is He, to His servants so that He may deter them by it. He said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿out of fear of Allah﴾ means: out of the fear of Allah, that is, it descends as intimidation to the servants, or by what necessitates fear of Allah, just as it is said: the Qur'an descended with the prohibition of such-and-such and the permission of such-and-such, meaning by making that obligatory upon people. Al-Qadi said: this interpretation abandons the apparent meaning without necessity, because hail is not described as stones, for although it hardens upon descent, it is in reality water, and because that name does not suit it.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾, the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, is watchful over these whose hearts are hard, and guards their deeds, counting them. He will recompense them for them in this world and the Hereafter. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord was not forgetful.﴾ [Maryam: 64]. In this is a great threat and intimidation to them, so that they may desist. If it is said: is it correct to describe Allah as "not unaware"? We say: al-Qadi said: it is not correct, because it gives the impression of the possibility of unawareness applying to Him. The matter is not so, because negating an attribute from a thing does not entail the establishment of its soundness upon it, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and ﴿He feeds but is not fed.﴾ [al-An'am: 14]. And Allah knows best.

[p. 121]

[p. 122]

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you, when a group of them used to hear the words of Allah and then distort them after they had understood them, while they knew?﴾**

Know that when He, glory be to Him, had mentioned the ugly deeds of the forefathers of the Jews up to this point, He then explained the ugly deeds of the Jews who were in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: In what Allah, the Exalted, has mentioned in this surah of the stories of the Children of Israel there are several aims:

The first: to use them as evidence for the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), because he reported them without having learned them, and that cannot be except through revelation. Both the People of the Book and the Arabs share in benefiting from this evidence. As for the People of the Book, they used to know these stories, so when they heard them from Muhammad without any discrepancy at all, they knew for certain that he had taken them only from revelation. As for the Arabs, they saw that the People of the Book confirm Muhammad in these reports.

The second: enumerating the blessings bestowed upon the Children of Israel and the kinds of honour and favour which Allah conferred upon their forefathers, such as rescuing them from the family of Pharaoh after they had been subdued and enslaved; His giving them victory and making them prophets and kings; His establishing them in the land; His parting the sea for them; His destroying their enemy; His sending down the light and clear guidance upon them through the revelation of the Torah; His pardoning the sins they committed, such as worshipping the calf, breaking covenants, and asking to see Allah openly; then what He brought forth for them in the wilderness of water from the rock; His sending down upon them the manna and the quail; and His protecting them from the heat of the sun by shading them with clouds. So Allah reminded them of these ancient and recent blessings.

The third: the Prophet (peace be upon him) being informed of their earlier disbelief, opposition, defiance and obstinacy towards the prophets, and their opposition to them, and their reaching in this what no other nation before them had reached. This is because, after witnessing the manifest signs, they worshipped the calf shortly after Moses (peace be upon him) had left them. This shows their dullness. Then, when they were commanded to enter the gate prostrating and to say "Hittah" (remission), and He promised to forgive their sins and increase the reward of their good-doers, they changed the word and transgressed. Then they asked for garlic and onions instead of the manna and quail. Then they refused to accept the Torah after they had believed in Moses and pledged to him by covenants that they would believe in him and submit to what he brought, until the mountain was lifted above them. Then they made hunting lawful on the Sabbath and transgressed. Then, when they were commanded to slaughter a cow, they said to Moses (peace be upon him) to his face: ﴿Do you make us a mockery?﴾ Then, when they witnessed the raising of the dead, they increased in hardness. It is as if Allah, the Exalted, is saying: If these are their deeds among themselves and in their dealings with their prophet, through whom Allah honoured them and delivered them from slavery and calamity, then it is no wonder that their descendants treat Muhammad (peace be upon him) as they do. So, O Prophet and believers, let not what you see of their obstinacy and turning away from the truth trouble you.

The fourth: warning the People of the Book who were present in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) against the descent of punishment upon them as it descended upon their forefathers in those recorded events.

The fifth: warning the polytheists of the Arabs that punishment may descend upon them as it descended upon those Jews.

The sixth: that it is an argument against the polytheists of the Arabs who denied the resurrection while acknowledging the initial creation. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾.

Having understood this, we say: He (peace be upon him) was extremely eager to call to the truth and for them to accept faith from him, and his chest would constrict because of their obstinacy and rebelliousness. So Allah related to him the reports of the Children of Israel in their great obstinacy despite witnessing the manifest signs, as a consolation to His Messenger regarding what appears from the People of the Book in his time of little acceptance and response. So He said: ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you?﴾ Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** In His saying ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you?﴾ there are two views:

The first: this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, that it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, because he is the caller and he is the one intended for the response. Although the wording is general, we have taken it as specific due to this context. It is narrated that when he (peace be upon him) entered Medina and called the Jews to the Book of Allah, they denied him, so Allah revealed this verse.

The second: this is the view of al-Hasan, that it is addressed to the Messenger and the believers. Al-Qadi said: This is closer to the apparent meaning, because although the call was primarily his, there were among the Companions those who called others to faith, showed them the proofs and alerted them to them. Therefore it is correct that He says ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you?﴾ and means by it the Messenger and those among his companions in such a state. If this is correct, there is no reason to abandon the apparent meaning.

**The second issue:** What is meant by His saying ﴿that they will believe you﴾ is the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger (peace be upon him), because they are the ones for whom it is valid to hope that they will believe, or not. This is because hope is valid only regarding the future, not regarding the present.

**The third issue:** They mentioned several reasons for the improbability:

One: ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you,﴾ although they did not believe in Moses (peace be upon him), who was the cause of Allah rescuing them from humiliation and preferring them over all, and despite the successive miracles at his hand and the appearance of various kinds of punishment upon the rebellious?

Two: ﴿Do you hope that they will believe and show acceptance,﴾ when whoever among them knows the truth does not acknowledge it, but changes and alters it?

Three: ﴿Do you hope that these will believe you through reflection and reasoning?﴾ How could they, when a group of their forefathers used to hear the words of Allah and know that it was true, and then opposed it?

**The fourth issue:** Someone may say: The people are obligated to believe in Allah. What is the benefit of His saying ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you?﴾

The answer: It is an acknowledgment on their part of what they were called to. Even if faith were for Allah, as He said: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 26], when he acknowledged his prophethood and confirmed it. And it is permissible that it means: that they believe for your sake and for the sake of your insistence in calling them to it. This is the meaning of the attribution.

As for His saying ﴿And a group of them had indeed﴾, the scholars differed regarding that group. Some said: The intended group is those who were in the time of Moses (peace be upon him), because He described this group as those who used to hear the words of Allah, and those who heard the words of Allah were the people of the appointed time (al-Miqat). Others said: Rather, the intended group is those who were in the time of Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is closer, because the pronoun in His saying ﴿And a group of them had indeed﴾ refers back to what preceded, namely those whom Allah meant by His saying ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you?﴾ We have already explained that those whose belief one hopes for are those who were in the time of Muhammad (peace be upon him). If it is said: Those who heard the words of Allah were those who attended the appointed time, we say: We do not accept that. Rather, it is permissible for one who heard the Torah to be described as having heard the words of Allah, just as it is said of one of us that he heard the words of Allah when the Qur'an was recited to him.

\* \* \*

As for His saying ﴿then distort it﴾, there are issues:

**The first issue:** Al-Qaffal said: Tahrif (distortion) means alteration and substitution, and its root is deviation from a thing and bending away from it. He said: ﴿unless he is one who swerves for battle or joins a company﴾ [al-Anfal: 16]. Tahrif is turning a thing away from its right. It is said: "a pen is muharraf (bent)" if its tip is inclined and not straight.

**The second issue:** Al-Qadi said: Tahrif is either in the wording or in the meaning. Interpreting tahrif as alteration of the wording is preferable to interpreting it as alteration of the meaning, because when the speech of Allah remains in its original form and they change its interpretation, they are only altering its meaning, not the heard speech itself. If it is possible to understand it in that sense, as is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, that they added to it and subtracted from it, then that is preferable. If that is not possible, then it must be understood as altering its interpretation, even if the revelation remains intact. This is only impossible when the speech of Allah has been manifested in a mass-transmitted way, as the Qur'an has. As for before it reached that state, altering the text itself is not impossible. However, one must examine this: if their alteration affects the establishment of the proof through it, then Allah must prevent it; but if it does not affect that, then its occurrence is valid. So the tahrif that is valid in speech must be divided as we have mentioned. As for altering meaning, it may be valid in some way where the Messenger's intention is not known with certainty; for when it is known, alteration by them is impossible, because of their prior knowledge to the contrary, just as it is impossible now for an interpreter to interpret the prohibition of the flesh of swine, carrion, and blood as referring to something else.

**The third issue:** Know that if we say that those who distorted were those who were in the time of Moses (peace be upon him), then it is most likely that they distorted what was not related to the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is narrated that some of the seventy chosen men heard the words of Allah when He spoke to Moses at Mount Tur, and what Moses was commanded and what he was forbidden. Then they said: We heard Allah say at the end of it: If you are able to do these things, then do them, and if you wish not to do them, then there is no harm. But if we say that those who distorted were those who were in the time of Muhammad (peace be upon him), then it is most likely that what is meant is the distortion of the matter of Muhammad (peace be upon him). That is either because they distorted the description and attributes of the Messenger, or because they distorted the laws, as they distorted the verse of stoning. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an does not indicate what exactly they distorted.

**The fourth issue:** Someone may say: How does the despair of the faith of the remaining ones follow from the initiative of some in distortion, since the obstinacy of some does not negate the acknowledgment of the rest?

Al-Qaffal answered this, saying: It is possible that the meaning is: How will these believe, when they take their religion and learn it only from people who deliberately distort it out of obstinacy? Those people teach them only what they have distorted and altered from its proper form, and the followers accept nothing but that and do not turn to the words of the people of truth. It is like your saying to a man: How will you prosper when your teacher is so-and-so! Meaning: you take only from him and do not take from anyone else.

**The fifth issue:** They differed regarding His saying ﴿Do you hope﴾. Some said: Allah has despaired them of the faith of this group, who are specific individuals. Others said: He has not despaired them of it except in terms of its improbability given their distortion, alteration and obstinacy. They said: It is like how we do not hope that our slaves and servants will possess our lands. Yet we do not definitively assert that they will never possess them; rather we consider it improbable. Someone may say: His saying ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you?﴾ is a question in the mode of denial, and so it constitutes a definite judgment that they will never believe at all. The faith of one whom Allah has informed will not believe is impossible. Then the considerations establishing the report return to what has preceded.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 75 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, ﴿after they had understood it﴾, the meaning is that they knew its soundness and the corruption of what they had altered, and so they were obstinate, deliberately proceeding with that on purpose. For this reason the statement must be taken to mean that they were among the scholars (ʿulamaʾ) of them, and that they did this for a kind of worldly aim, as Allah the Exalted explained later in His saying: ﴿and sold it for a small price﴾ [Al ʿImran: 187], and His saying: ﴿They recognize it as they recognize their own sons﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. And it must be that their number was small, because it is not permissible for a great multitude to conceal what they believe, for if we permitted that, the true would not be distinguished from the false, however great the number.

As for His saying, ﴿while they know﴾, one might say: His saying ﴿after they had understood it, while they know﴾ is a repetition with no benefit in it. Al-Qaffal answered this in two ways:

The first: after they had understood Allah's intended meaning, they interpreted it with a corrupt interpretation, knowing that it was not the intended meaning of Allah the Exalted.

The second: they understood the intended meaning of Allah the Exalted, and they knew that the corrupt interpretation would earn them sin and punishment from Allah the Exalted. When they deliberately distorted it while knowing the sin in it, their hardness was greater and their boldness more immense. Since the purpose of this was to console the Messenger, peace be upon him, and to make him patient with their obstinacy, the more their obstinacy was great, the more this served as a stronger consolation. There are two issues in the verse:

The first issue: al-Qadi said: His saying, ﴿Do you hope that they will believe for you?﴾, as its interpretation has preceded, indicates that their belief comes from themselves, because if it were by Allah's creation in them, the hope concerning them would not change by the attribute of the group mentioned earlier, and it would not be valid that this is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, because according to this view their affair regarding faith depends on Allah's creating it, and its removal depends on His not creating it in them. Another aspect is Allah's magnifying of their sin in distorting it, since they did it while they knew its soundness; and if it were by His creation, then whether they knew or did not know, that would not change. His attributing the distortion to them in the manner of censure indicates this. Know that the discussion of this has preceded many times and in various ways, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

The second issue: Abu Bakr al-Razi said: the verse indicates that the knowledgeable obstinate person is farther from right guidance and nearer to despair than the ignorant one, because His saying, ﴿Do you hope that they will believe for you?﴾ implies the loss of hope in their guidance, due to their stubbornness toward the truth after knowing it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 76–77:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with one another, they say, "Do you talk to them about what Allah has disclosed to you, so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord? Do you not then use your reason?"﴾ ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾

Know that this is the second type of the vile deeds of the Jews who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the hypocrites among the People of the Book, when they met the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), would say to them: "We believe in what you believe, and we testify that your companion is truthful, and that his saying is true, and we find him by his description and attributes in our Book." Then, when they were alone with one another, their leaders would say to them: "Do you talk to them about what Allah has disclosed to you in His Book of his description and attributes, so that they may argue with you by it? For when the opponent acknowledges the soundness of the Torah and acknowledges the Torah's testimony to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), there is no stronger argument than that. Therefore, some of them would prevent others from acknowledging this before Muhammad (ﷺ) and his Companions." Al-Qaffal said: His saying, ﴿disclosed to you﴾, is derived from their saying, "It has been opened to so-and-so in the knowledge of such-and-such," meaning he was granted that and its pursuit was made easy for him.

As for His saying, ﴿before your Lord﴾, there are several views:

The first: They made their argument with it, and their saying "it is in your Book thus" is an argument before Allah, for you say "it is in the Book of Allah thus" and "it is before Allah thus," with one meaning.

The second: Al-Hasan said: that is, so that they may argue with you concerning your Lord, because argument concerning what Allah has obligated, namely following the Messengers, may rightly be described as an argument concerning Him, since it is an argument concerning His religion.

The third: Al-Asamm said: the meaning is that they will argue with you on the Day of Resurrection and at the time of questioning, and this will add to your reproach and to the manifestation of your disgrace before all creatures on the Plain of Standing, for there is no acknowledgment of the truth followed by concealment like one who persists in denial. The people believed that the manifestation of this would increase the exposure of their disgrace in the Hereafter.

The fourth: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr said: One who argues with a thing may argue with it while his aim in displaying that argument is the joy that comes from the opponent's defeat, and he may have as his aim only piety and sincere counsel, to cut off his opponent's excuse and to establish the proof of Allah against him. So the people said in private: "You have told them what Allah has disclosed to you of their argument from the Torah," and so they became able to argue with it in the manner of piety and sincere counsel, for one who mentions an argument in this manner may say to his companion: "I have made you responsible before Allah and established the proof against you between me and my Lord. If you accept, you have done good to yourself; if you deny, you are the loser and the failed."

The fifth: Al-Qaffal said: It is said, "So-and-so is knowledgeable in my view," meaning in my belief and judgment. And this is lawful according to al-Shafiʿi and unlawful according to Abu Hanifa, meaning in their judgment. And His saying, ﴿that they may argue with you by it before your Lord﴾, means that you would become those argued against by those proofs in the judgment of Allah. Some scholars interpreted His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then, since they did not bring witnesses, those are, in the sight of Allah, the liars﴾ [al-Nur: 13] as meaning in the judgment and decree of Allah, because the slanderer who does not bring witnesses is bound by the ruling of liars, even if he is truthful in himself.

As for His saying, ﴿Do you not then use your reason?﴾, there are several views:

The first: It refers to the believers, as if Allah, exalted is He, said: "Do you not use your reason regarding what I have mentioned to you of their description, that there is no hope for you in their belief?" This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: It refers back to them, as if when they were alone with one another they said to them: "Do you talk to them about what will bring its harm back upon you, and you will become those argued against by it? Do you not use your reason to see that this is not fitting for what you are upon?" This view is more apparent, because it is part of the continuing report about them, so there is no reason to turn it away from them to others.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾, there are two opinions:

The first, which is the view of most scholars: The Jews knew Allah and knew that He, exalted is He, knows the secret and the open, so Allah frightened them with it.

The second: They did not know this, so He encouraged them with this statement to reflect, so that they would come to know that they have a Lord who knows their secret and their open, and that they cannot feel safe from the descent of punishment because of their hypocrisy. On both opinions, this statement is a rebuke to them for hypocrisy and for one of them charging another to conceal the proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). The closer view is that the Jews addressed by this were aware of it, for it is hardly said in the manner of rebuke, "Do they not know such-and-such?" except that the speaker knows that thing, and that thing serves as a deterrent from that act. Some said: How can these Jews permit themselves to privately instruct their brethren to forbid revealing the proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), when they are not like the hypocrites who do not know Allah and do not know that He knows the secret and the open? Their condition in this respect is the more astonishing.

Al-Qadi said: The verse indicates several matters:

The first: If He, exalted is He, is the Creator of the deeds of the servants, how is it valid that He rebukes them for those sayings and deeds?

The second: It indicates the validity of argument and reasoning, and that this was the practice of the Companions and the believers, and that this was evident to the Jews, so that some of them said to others what they said.

The third: It indicates that argument may be binding, for when they acknowledged the soundness of the Torah and its containing what points to the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him), acknowledging prophethood became necessarily binding upon them; and if they had denied either of those two premises, the proof would not have been complete.

The fourth: It indicates that one who commits disobedience while knowing it to be disobedience is greater in sin and burden. And Allah knows best.
