Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 78–79:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book, except for wishful fancies, and they do nothing but conjecture.﴾ ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands and then say, "This is from Allah," to trade it for a small price. So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾

Know that what is meant by His words ﴿And among them are unlettered people﴾ is the Jews. This is because, when He described them with obstinacy and removed any hope of their faith, He divided them into groups. The first group is the misguided group that misleads others, and they are the ones who distort the words from their places. The second group is the hypocrites. The third group is those who argue with the hypocrites. The fourth group is those mentioned in this verse, namely the common unlettered people who have no knowledge of reading or writing, and whose way is imitation (taqlid, blind following) and acceptance of what is said to them. So Allah the Exalted made clear that those who refuse to accept faith do not all have one cause for this refusal, but each category among them has a different cause. Whoever reflects on what Allah the Exalted mentioned in this verse, describing the groups of the Jews, will find exactly the same in the groups of this community. Among them are those who obstinately oppose the truth and strive to lead others astray, among them are those who are moderate, and among them are those who are purely common and imitators. Here there are several issues:

The first issue: They differed about the meaning of "unlettered" (ummi). Some said it is one who does not acknowledge a Book or a Messenger. Others said it is one who does not write or read well. The second view is more correct, because the verse concerns the Jews, and they acknowledged the Book and the Messenger. Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We are an unlettered nation; we do not write and we do not calculate," and this supports the second view. Also, His words ﴿do not know the Book﴾ fit only this meaning.

The second issue: "Amani" (wishful fancies) is the plural of umniyya, and it has several meanings that share one root:

One of them: what a person imagines, so he supposes in his soul that it happens and speaks to himself about it as if it were so. From this is the saying: "So-and-so promises so-and-so and gives him false hopes (yumanniyuhu)." And from this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿He promises them and gives them false hopes, but Satan promises them nothing but delusion﴾ [al-Nisa: 120]. If we interpret amani with this meaning, then His words ﴿except wishful fancies﴾ mean: except what they hold of their wishful fancies, that Allah will not punish them for their sins, that their forefathers, the prophets, will intercede for them, and what their rabbis give them false hope about, that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of days.

Second: ﴿except wishful fancies﴾ means except various falsehoods they heard from their scholars and accepted through imitation. A Bedouin said to Ibn Da'b about something he narrated: "Is this something you narrated, or wished for, or fabricated?"

Third: ﴿except wishful fancies﴾ means except what they recite of the saying: "He wished (tamanna) the Book of Allah at the first night." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The derivation is from mana, meaning to estimate, because the one who wishes estimates in his soul and imagines what he wishes for; likewise the fabricator and the reciter estimate that such-and-such a word comes after such-and-such. Abu Muslim said: Interpreting it as the wish of the heart is better, as evidenced by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise unless he is a Jew or a Christian." Those are their wishful fancies﴾ [al-Baqara: 111], meaning their wishes. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is not by your wishful fancies, nor the wishful fancies of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa: 123]. And He said: ﴿Those are their wishful fancies. Say, "Produce your proof"﴾ [al-Baqara: 111]. And the Exalted said: ﴿And they say, "There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live, and nothing destroys us but time." And they have no knowledge of that; they only conjecture﴾ [al-Jathiya: 24], meaning they estimate and guess. Most scholars said: Interpreting it as recitation is better, as in His words: ﴿When he wishes, Satan casts into his wish﴾ [al-Hajj: 52]. Also, interpreting it as recitation fits the manner of the exception better, because if we interpret it that way, it has a connection to what precedes. It is as if He said: "They do not know the Book except to the extent that it is recited to them and they hear it, and to the extent that it is mentioned to them and they accept it." Then they are not able to ponder and reflect. But if it is interpreted as meaning tales and falsehoods, or conjecture, estimation, and inner speech, the exception would be rare in it.

The third issue: His words ﴿except wishful fancies﴾ are an exception of the discontinuous type (al-istithna' al-munqati', where the excluded item is not of the same kind as what precedes). Al-Nabigha said:

*I swore an oath, not one with reservation, and I have no knowledge except a good opinion of an absent one.*

It was also read as "illa amanīya" with the lightened pronunciation. As for His words ﴿and they only conjecture﴾, it confirms what we have said, because if amani is meant as estimation and thought about matters that have no reality, then it is conjecture, and this would be a repetition. One might say: inner speech is different from conjecture, so there is no repetition. And if we interpret it as recitation to them, its meaning is sound. It is as if He said: "And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book except by its being recited to them so they hear it, and except by its being explained to them so they suppose it, as is intended, and so they conjecture it." And Allah the Exalted made clear that this method does not lead to the truth. In the verse there are several issues:

The first: Knowledge is acquired (kasbiyya), not necessary (darurri, innate and self-evident), and therefore He blamed the one who does not know and only conjectures.

The second: The absolute invalidity of taqlid. This is problematic, because taqlid in the branches of law is permissible according to us.

The third: Although the one who misleads is blameworthy, the one deceived by the misleader is also blameworthy, because He blamed them even though they had this quality.

The fourth: Relying on conjecture in the foundations of religion is not permissible. And Allah knows best.

As for His words ﴿So woe﴾: they said, "Woe (wayl) is a word that every distressed person says." Ibn Abbas said: It is the painful punishment. From Sufyan al-Thawri: It is the flow of the pus of the people of Hell. And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "It is a valley in Hell into which the disbeliever falls for forty autumns before reaching its bottom." The Qadi (Qadi Abd al-Jabbar) said: "Woe" includes the utmost threat and warning, so this much is beyond doubt, whether woe is an expression for a valley in Hell or for great punishment.

As for His words ﴿who write the Book with their own hands﴾, there are two views:

The first: A man may say "I wrote" when he ordered it to be written, so the benefit of His words ﴿with their own hands﴾ is that it was done by them only in this manner.

The second: It is an emphasis, and this is a place where emphasis is appropriate, as when you say to one who denies knowing what he wrote: "Sir, you wrote it with your right hand."

As for His words ﴿then say, "This is from Allah"﴾, what is meant is that one who writes this writing and earns this earning is in the utmost wickedness, because they strayed from the religion and led others astray, and they sold their Hereafter for their worldly life. So their sin is greater than the sin of others, for it is known that lying against others in a way that harms them is greatly sinful, so how much more so for one who lies against Allah, adds misguidance to the lie, adds to these the love of this world and scheming to obtain it, and adds to these that he paved a path of misguidance lasting until the end of time. For this reason, Allah the Exalted magnified what they did. If it is said: He the Exalted attributed two matters to them: one, the writers of the Book, and the other, attributing it to Allah the Exalted as a lie. Is this threat connected to the writing, or to attributing what is written to Allah, or to both together? We say: There is no doubt that the writers of false things with the intent of misleading, from among the evils and lies against Allah the Exalted, are likewise, and combining the two is a very great evil.

As for His words ﴿to trade it for a small price﴾, it is an alert to two matters:

The first: It is an alert to the extreme of their wretchedness, because the sensible person must not be content with a small burden in the Hereafter for the sake of a great reward in this world. How then could it be fitting for him to be content with a great punishment in the Hereafter for the sake of a petty benefit in this world?

The second: It indicates that they did not do this distortion out of religious conviction, but only to seek wealth and status. This shows that taking money for falsehood, even if by mutual consent, is forbidden, because those who gave them money did so out of affection and approval. Yet Allah the Exalted alerted to its prohibition regardless.

As for His words ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾, what is meant is that their writing of what they wrote is a great sin in itself, and likewise their taking money for it. For this reason He repeated the mention of woe with the earnings. Had He not repeated it, it would have been possible to say that their combination entails the great threat, but not each one of them separately. So Allah the Exalted removed this doubt. They differed about His words ﴿for what they earn﴾: is what is meant only what they took for this writing and distortion, or is what is meant all their other sins? The closer reading in the structure of the speech is that it refers to what was mentioned, namely the money taken in this way. Although in terms of generality the closer reading is that it includes everything, what favors the first view is that if their earning is not restricted by this condition, the threat would not be fitting for it, because earning includes lawful and unlawful. So it must be restricted, and the most appropriate restriction is what was mentioned earlier.

The Qadi said: The verse indicates that their writing is not a creation of Allah the Exalted, because if it were a creation of Allah the Exalted, then attributing it to Him through their saying ﴿this is from Allah﴾ would be true, for when He the Exalted creates it in them, even if the servant acquires it, the attribution of the act to the Creator is stronger than its attribution to the one who acquires it. So attributing that writing to Allah the Exalted would be more fitting than attributing it to the servant. Therefore they should deserve praise for their saying about it that it is from Allah. But since that is not the case, we know that that writing is not created by Allah the Exalted.

The answer: The motive that causes it is from Allah the Exalted's creation, by the evidences mentioned, so it too is like that. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 80:**

﴿And they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days." Say, "Have you taken a covenant from Allah, so that Allah will not break His covenant? Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?"﴾

Know that this is the third category of their ugly sayings and deeds, namely their certainty that Allah, exalted is He, will punish them only for a few days. This certainty has no basis in reason whatsoever. As for our position (the Ash'aris), Allah does what He wills and decrees what He desires, and no one can object to His actions. Therefore there is no way to know this except through the transmitted evidence (al-dalil al-sam'i). As for the position of the Mu'tazilites, reason indicates to them that sins make one deserving of Allah's everlasting punishment. Once reason indicates this, one needs transmitted evidence to specify the duration of the punishment and its cessation after that. Thus it is established that on both positions there is no way to know this except through transmitted evidence. Where transmitted evidence is found, it is not permissible to be certain about it. Here there are two issues.

**The first issue:** They have mentioned two explanations of the phrase "counted days" (ayyaman ma'dudatan).

The first: the word *ayyam* (days) is only attributed to numbers up to ten and what is below them, and is not attributed to what is above them. One says *ayyam khamsah* (five days) and *ayyam 'ashrah* (ten days), but one does not say *ayyam ahada 'ashar* (eleven days). However, this is problematic in light of His words: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous, [for] a number of days (ayyaman ma'dudat)﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:183), which are the days of the entire month, and they are more than ten.

Then al-Qadi said: Since it is established that *ayyam* is restricted to ten and what is below it, the more fitting view is that it refers either to the least or to the most. For whoever says "three" says: I take it to its minimal sense, and that has a basis. And whoever says "ten" says: I take it to its maximal sense, and that too has a basis. But to take it to an intermediate number, namely a number that is less than ten and more than three, has no basis, because no one number is more deserving than another, except when a sound report has come concerning its specification, in which case it must be affirmed.

A group of exegetes specified them as seven days. Mujahid said: The Jews used to say, "The world is seven thousand years, and Allah punishes them for one day in place of every thousand years," so they would say, "Allah punishes us for seven days." Al-Asamm related from some Jews that they worshipped the calf for seven days, so they would say, "Allah punishes us for seven days." These two explanations are weak.

As for the first: there is no connection or necessary correspondence whatsoever between the world being seven thousand years and the punishment being seven days.

As for the second: it does not follow from the sin being fixed at seven days that its punishment is likewise.

As for our position, it is because everything is good from Allah by the judgment of His sovereignty (al-malikiyyah). As for the Mu'tazilites, the disobedient one deserves everlasting punishment for his disobedience, as long as repentance or pardon does not occur. If it is said: Did He not prohibit exceeding the requital, when He said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (al-Shura 42:40)? So the punishment must not exceed the sin. We say: The sin increases in proportion to the blessing. Since Allah's blessings upon His servants are beyond limit and measure, their disobedience is necessarily exceedingly great.

The second explanation: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he interpreted these days as forty, which is the number of days during which they worshipped the calf. The discussion of it is also like the discussion of the seven.

The third explanation: It was said that the meaning of *ma'dudah* (counted) is "few," as in His words: ﴿And they sold him for a low price, a few dirhams (darahima ma'dudah)﴾ (Yusuf 12:20). And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** The Hanafis held that the minimum period of menstruation (*hayd*) is three days and its maximum is ten. They argued with the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Leave the prayer during the days of your menses (ayyam aqra'ik)." So the duration of menstruation is what is called "days," the least number that is called "days" is three, and its maximum is ten, as we have explained. Therefore the minimum menstruation must be three and its maximum ten. The objection to this is what has preceded.

**The third issue:** Here He said: ﴿And they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days"﴾, and in Al 'Imran: ﴿except for a few counted days (ayyaman ma'dudat)﴾. Someone may ask: Why was the first *ma'dudah* (singular feminine form) and the second *ma'dudat* (plural feminine sound form), when the described noun in both places is one and the same, namely *ayyaman*?

The answer: If the noun is masculine, the basic form of the plural adjective is with the *ta'* (feminine ending), as one says *kuzun* (a jug, masculine) and *kiyzan* (jugs), *makswrah* (broken, feminine singular)... and *thiyab maqtu'ah* (cut garments). If the noun is feminine, the basic form of its plural adjective is with *alif* and *ta'*, as one says *jarrah* (a jar, feminine) and *jirar* (jars), *maksurat* (broken, feminine plural), and *khabiyah* (a jug) and *khawabi maksurat* (broken jugs). However, the plural with *alif* and *ta'* is sometimes found for a singular that is masculine in some forms, rarely, such as *hammam* (bath) and *hammamat*, and *jamal sibatr* (a large camel) and *sibatrat*. Based on this, the words of Allah occur: ﴿in days counted (ayyamin ma'dudat)﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:203), and ﴿in known days (ayyamin ma'lumat)﴾ (al-Hajj 22:28). So Allah, in Surat al-Baqarah, spoke in the original form, which is His words "ayyaman ma'dudah," and in Al 'Imran in the derived form.

\* \* \*

As for His words: ﴿Say, "Have you taken a covenant from Allah, so that Allah will not break His covenant?"﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** The word *'ahd* (covenant) here functions as a promise and a report. His report, glorified is He, is called a covenant because His report is more binding than the solemn covenants we make with oaths and vows. Thus a covenant from Allah occurs only in this manner.

**Second issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf said: "*fa-lan yukhlifa Allah*" (then Allah will not break) is connected to an omitted element, and its estimate is: "If you have taken a covenant with Allah, then Allah will not break His covenant."

**Third issue:** His words ﴿Have you taken?﴾ (ittakhadtum) are not an interrogative, but a denial. It is not permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to make the interrogation of His messenger the proof in refuting their claim. Rather, the purpose is to draw attention to the method of inference, which is that there is no way to know this estimate except through transmitted evidence. Since no transmitted evidence has been found, it is obligatory that one not be certain of this estimate.

**Fourth issue:** His words ﴿so Allah will not break His covenant﴾ indicate that He, glorified and exalted is He, is free from lying in His promise and His threat. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: Because lying is a characteristic of deficiency, and deficiency is impossible for Allah. The Mu'tazilites said: Because He, glorified is He, knows the ugliness of the ugly and knows that He is free of it, and lying is ugly because it is a lie. The one who knows the ugliness of the ugly and knows that he is free of it is impossible to do it. Thus it indicates that lying is impossible for Him. This is why He said: ﴿so Allah will not break His covenant﴾. If it is said: The covenant is the promise, and specifying something by mention indicates the negation of what is other than it. Since He specified the promise by saying He will not break it, we know that breaking a threat is permissible. Then reason corresponds to this, because breaking a promise is baseness, while breaking a threat is generosity. We say: The stated indication applies to all kinds of lying.

**Fifth issue:** Al-Jubba'i said: The verse indicates that Allah had not promised Moses, nor any of the prophets after him, that He would bring out the people of sins and major sins from the Fire after punishment. For if He had promised them this, it would not be permissible for Him to deny this statement to the Jews. And since it is established that He did not guide them to that, and it is established that He guided them to the threat against the sinners, which serves to deter them from sins, then it must be that their punishment is everlasting, according to the statement of the Wa'idiyyah (those who hold the everlasting punishment of sinners). And if this is established for the rest of the nations, it must be established for this nation, because His judgment concerning promise and threat cannot differ among the nations, since the measure of sin is not different among all of them. Know that this argument is in extreme artificiality. So we say: We do not concede that He did not promise Moses that He would bring out the people of major sins from the Fire. As for his saying: If He had promised them this, He would not have denied the Jews' statement, we say: Why did you say that if He had promised them that, He would not have denied it to the Jews? What is the evidence for this necessary connection? Then we demonstrate, by revealed law, that this is not necessary, from several aspects:

First: Perhaps Allah denied it to them only because they minimized the days of punishment, for their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days﴾ indicates very few days. So Allah denied to them their certainty about this fewness, not that He denied to them the cessation of punishment.

Second: The Murji'ah (those who deferred judgment) are certain in general of pardon, but regarding a specific individual there is no way to certainty. So when they judged in regard to themselves with lightening (of punishment) with certainty, Allah indeed denied this to them.

Third: They were disbelievers, and according to us, the punishment of the disbeliever is everlasting and does not end. Suppose we concede that He did not promise Moses, peace be upon him, that He would bring out the people of major sins from the Fire, why do you say that He will not bring them out of the Fire? Its explanation: There is a difference between saying that He did not promise him their removal from the Fire, and saying that He informed him that He would not remove them from the Fire. The first has no harm in it, for He may not have said that to Moses except that He would do it on the Day of Resurrection. He refuted the Jews only because they were certain of it without evidence, so it would have been incumbent upon them to suspend judgment and neither to deny nor affirm it definitively. Suppose we concede that He does not bring out the disobedient of the people of Moses from the Fire, why do you say that He does not bring out the disobedient of this nation from the Fire? As for al-Jubba'i's statement: "because His judgment concerning promise and threat cannot differ among the nations," this is pure arbitrariness, for punishment is the right of Allah, exalted is He. So He may show favor to some by remission and not show such favor to the rest. Thus it is established that this argument is weak.

As for His words: ﴿Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾, this is an explanation of the completion of the stated argument. For when there is no way to the stated estimate except through revelation, and it is established that no revelation has been found, then to be certain of that estimate would be speaking about Allah, exalted is He, with what is not necessarily known. This verse indicates several benefits:

One: When He blamed them for a statement they made without evidence, we know that speaking without evidence is false.

Two: Whatever is possible in existence and non-existence by reason, it is not permissible to resort to affirmation or negation except by transmitted evidence.

Three: The deniers of analogy (qiyas) and of solitary reports (khabar al-wahid) hold fast to this verse. They say: Because analogy and solitary reports do not yield knowledge, it is obligatory that relying on them is not permissible, based on His words: ﴿Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾, which He mentioned in the context of denial.

The answer: When evidence has indicated the obligation to act upon a conjecture (zann) arising from analogy or from a solitary report, the obligation to act becomes known. Thus speaking by it is speaking by what is known, not by what is unknown.

God says: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him — those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Bala" (بلى, "yes/on the contrary") is an affirmation of what follows the negative particle, namely God's words ﴿The Fire will not touch us﴾; that is, "Yes, you will be touched by it forever," as evidenced by His words ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾. As for "sayyi'ah" (evil deed), it encompasses all sins. God said: ﴿The recompense for an evil deed is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123]. Since it is possible to think that every evil deed, whether small or great, has the same status in that its doer will be eternally in the Fire, God therefore made clear that what merits eternal abiding is an evil deed that encompasses him. It is known that the word "ihatah" (encompassing) is literally used for one body encompassing another, like the wall encompassing a town or the pitcher encompassing water, and that is impossible here, so we interpret it as the case where the evil deed is a major sin, for two reasons:

First: the encompassing thing covers what it encompasses, and a major sin, by encompassing the rewards of acts of obedience, is like something that covers those acts, so the resemblance exists from this aspect.

Second: when a major sin cancels the reward of acts of obedience, it is as if it has taken control of those acts and encircled them, as an enemy army encircles a person so that he cannot free himself from it. It is as if God said: "Yes, whoever earns a major sin and his major sin encompasses his acts of obedience, those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever." If it is said: this verse was revealed concerning the Jews, we reply: the lesson is in the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation. This is the argument with which the Mu'tazilah proved the threat (wa'id) against the people of major sins.

Know that this question is among the greatest questions, and we shall mention it here. We say: the people of the qiblah (Muslims) differed concerning the threat against the people of major sins. Among people are those who affirmed with certainty that they are threatened, and they are of two groups: some affirmed a perpetual threat, and this is the view of the majority of the Mu'tazilah and the Kharijites; and some affirmed a finite threat, and this is the view of Bishr al-Marisi and al-Khalid. Among people are those who affirmed with certainty that there is no threat for them, and this is an odd view attributed to Muqatil ibn Sulayman the exegete.

The third view: we affirm with certainty that God, glorified and exalted, pardons some sins, but we suspend judgment concerning each specific individual as to whether He will pardon him or not; and we affirm with certainty that if God punishes any of them for a period, He will not punish him forever, but will end his punishment. This is the view of most of the Companions and the Successors, the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah, and most of the Imamiyyah. So this discussion comprises two issues:

The first: concerning the certainty of the threat.

The second: whether, if the threat is established, it is of the nature of permanence or not?

* * *

The first issue: concerning the threat. Let us first mention the proofs of the Mu'tazilah, then the pure proofs of the Murji'ah, then the proofs of our companions, may God have mercy on them. As for the Mu'tazilah, they relied on the general texts in this regard, and these generalities are of two kinds: some are expressed with the word "man" (whoever) in conditional form, and some are expressed with the plural. As for the first kind, there are verses:

The first: God's words in the verse of inheritance: ﴿These are the limits of God﴾ [al-Nisa': 13], up to His words: ﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein﴾ [al-Nisa': 14]. We know that whoever abandons prayer, zakah, fasting, and hajj, and jihad, and commits drinking wine, fornication, and the killing of a forbidden soul, transgresses the limits of God, so he must be among those deserving punishment. This is because the word "man" in conditional form conveys generality, as established in the principles of jurisprudence. So whenever the opponent restricts this verse to the disbeliever and not the believer, that is contrary to the evidence. Then what refutes his view are two aspects:

First: God clarified His limits in the matter of inheritance, then promised reward to whoever obeys Him in those limits and threatened whoever disobeys Him in them. Whoever holds to faith and affirmation of Him, exalted is He, is closer to obedience in them than one who denies His lordship and rejects His messengers and laws. So encouraging him to obey in them is more specific to one who is closer to obedience in them, namely the believer. And when the believer is intended in the beginning of the verse, so is he in its end.

Second: He said: ﴿These are the limits of God﴾ [al-Nisa': 13], and there is no doubt that what is meant is the limits mentioned. Then He linked the promise to obedience in them and the threat to disobedience in them. The context of the verse requires that the threat is tied to disobedience in these limits only, not adding to that the transgression of other limits. For this reason he is restrained by this threat only regarding transgressing these limits; had the threat not been intended for him, he would not be restrained by it. And since it is established that the believer is intended by it just as the disbeliever is, the view of one who restricts it to the disbeliever is refuted. If it is said: God's words ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾ [al-Nisa': 14] is a plural in construct form, and the plural in construct form, according to you, conveys generality, just as if one said "I beat my slaves," it includes all his slaves. And if that is established, this verse is restricted to one who transgresses all the limits of God, and that is necessarily the disbeliever and not the believer. We reply: although the matter is as you have mentioned, considering the wording, there are indications showing that what is meant here is not transgression of all the limits:

First: God placed before His words ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾ His words ﴿These are the limits of God﴾, so His words ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾ refer to those limits.

Second: the community agrees that the believer is restrained by this verse from sins, and if what you said were correct, the believer would not be restrained by it.

Third: if we took the verse to mean transgression of all the limits, the threat in it would have no benefit, because none of the responsible persons transgresses all the limits of God, since among the limits are some whose combined transgression is impossible due to their contradiction, for no one can at one time hold the doctrine of the Dualists and the Christians; and there is none among the responsible who disobeys God in all sins.

Fourth: God's words concerning the one who kills a believer intentionally: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein﴾ [al-Nisa': 93]; the verse shows that this is his recompense, so this recompense must befall him, by God's words ﴿whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123].

Fifth: God's words: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Anfal: 15], up to His words: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, except one who withdraws for battle or joins a company, has earned anger from God, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾ [al-Anfal: 16].

Sixth: God's words: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7-8].

Seventh: God's words: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], up to His words: ﴿And whoever does that in aggression and injustice, We will drive him into a Fire﴾ [al-Nisa': 30].

Eighth: God's words: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live﴾. ﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74-75]. So God clarified that the disbeliever and the sinner are among the people of enduring punishment, just as the believer is among the people of reward.

Ninth: God's words: ﴿And he has failed who carries injustice﴾ [Ta-Ha: 111]; this requires that the wrongdoer among the people of prayer falls under this threat.

Tenth: God's words after enumerating sins: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾. ﴿His punishment will be doubled on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein humiliated﴾ [al-Furqan: 68-69]. He clarified that the sinner is like the disbeliever in that he is among those who abide forever, except one who repents of the sinners or believes from among the disbelievers.

Eleventh: God's words: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it, and they will be safe from terror that Day. And whoever brings an evil deed﴾ [al-Naml: 89-90], and so on; this shows that all sins are threatened, just as all acts of obedience are promised.

Twelfth: God's words: ﴿As for one who transgressed﴾. ﴿And preferred the worldly life﴾. ﴿Then indeed Hellfire will be the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 37-39].

Thirteenth: God's words: ﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the Fire of Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 23], and it does not distinguish between the disbeliever and the sinner.

Fourteenth: God's words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him﴾, and so on. In the beginning of this verse He related the view of the Murji'ah among the Jews, saying: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾, then God refuted them in it, then said: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him, those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾ These are the verses by which they held to the matter, since they contain the conditional form "man", and they argued that this word conveys generality in several ways:

First: if it were not established for generality, it would be either established for specificity or shared between the two, and both divisions are invalid, so it must be established for generality. As for its not being established for specificity: if it were so, it would not be proper for the speaker to give the recompense to everyone who fulfills the condition, because on that assumption the recompense would not be attached to that condition. But they agreed that if one says "Whoever enters my house, I will honor him," it is proper to honor everyone who enters his house, so we know this word is not for specificity. As for its not being established for sharing (ishtirak): firstly, sharing is contrary to the default; secondly, if it were so, the manner in which the recompense is attached to the condition would not be known except after asking about all the possible divisions, as when he says "Whoever enters my house, I will honor him," one asks him: "Do you mean men or women?" When he says "Men," one asks: "Do you mean Arabs or non-Arabs?" When he says "Arabs," one asks: "Do you mean Rabi'ah or Mudar?" and so on, until all the possible divisions are covered. Since we know by necessity from the custom of the people of the language that this is ugly, we know that the claim of sharing is false.

Second: if he says "Whoever enters my house, I will honor him," it is proper to except each one of the rational beings from it, and exception removes from the speech what would otherwise necessarily be included in it, since there is no dispute that the excepted item of a genus must be such that it is proper for it to be included under the item excepted from. Either this propriety is taken together with necessity, or it is not taken; and the first is false.

As for the first point: it would necessitate that there be no difference between exception from an indefinite plural, as in "The jurists came to me except Zayd," and exception from a definite plural, as in "The jurists came to me except Zayd," in the propriety of Zayd's inclusion in both sentences; yet the difference between them is known by necessity.

As for the second point: exception from a number removes what would otherwise necessarily be included under it, so this must be the purpose of exception in all places, because no one among the people of the language has distinguished between exception applied to a number and exception applied to other words. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that exception removes from speech what would otherwise necessarily be included in it, and this shows that the conditional form "man" is for generality.

**Third**: When God revealed His words, ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:98], Ibn al-Zib'ara said, "I will dispute with Muhammad." Then he said, "O Muhammad, have the angels not been worshipped? Has 'Isa son of Maryam not been worshipped?" He held to the generality of the wording (ʿumum al-lafz), and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not deny him this. This indicates that this form conveys generality (ʿumum).

* * *

**The second type** of the Mu'tazilite evidences: they rely, regarding the threat (wa'id), on the definite plural form marked by *al-* (the definite article). It occurs in several verses. The first is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the wicked are in Hellfire﴾ [al-Infitar 82:14]. Know that al-Qadi, al-Jubba'i and Abu al-Hasan say that this form conveys generality, whereas Abu Hashim says that it does not convey generality. We say: the evidences that it is for generality are several:

The first: When the Ansar asked for the imamate, Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him) argued against them with the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "The imams are from Quraysh." The Ansar accepted this argument. Had the plural defined by the *lam* of genus (lam al-jins) not indicated comprehensiveness (istighraq), this inference would not have been valid, because our saying "some of the imams are from Quraysh" does not contradict the existence of an imam from other tribes. But the claim that all the imams are from Quraysh contradicts the claim that some imams are from other than them. It is also related that when Abu Bakr intended to fight those who withheld zakat, ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) said to him: "Did the Prophet (ﷺ) not say: 'I have been commanded to fight the people until they say, there is no god but God'?" He argued against Abu Bakr by the generality of the wording. Then neither Abu Bakr nor any of the Companions said, "The wording does not convey this." Rather, he turned to the exception, saying: "He (ﷺ) said: 'except for its right,'" and zakat is among its rights.

The second: This plural is emphasized by what implies comprehensiveness, so it must convey comprehensiveness. That it is emphasized is shown by His saying: ﴿So the angels all prostrated together﴾ [al-Hijr 15:30]. That after emphasis it implies comprehensiveness is by consensus. And that whenever this is the case, the emphasized term must originally be comprehensive, because these words are, by consensus, named emphasis (ta'kid), and emphasis is the strengthening of a ruling that was already established in the original. So if comprehensiveness were not present originally, and was only produced by these words from the start, then the effect of these words would not be strengthening the ruling but giving a new ruling, and they would be clarifying an ambiguous term (mujmal), not emphasizing. Since they agreed that they are emphasis, we know that the implication of comprehensiveness was present originally.

The third: When the *alif* and *lam* enter a noun, the noun becomes definite (maʿrifa). This is what is reported from the lexicographers. So it must be interpreted as referring to that which yields definiteness. Definiteness is achieved upon its unqualified use by interpreting it as referring to the whole, since this is known to the addressee. But interpreting it as referring to less than the whole does not yield definiteness, because no part of the plural is preferable to another, so it would remain unknown. If you say: when it conveys a specific plural from that genus, it has conveyed the definiteness of that genus; we reply: this benefit was already present without the *alif* and *lam*, because if he said "I saw men (rijal)," this would convey the definiteness of that genus and its distinction from others. Thus it shows that the *alif* and *lam* have an additional benefit, and that benefit is none other than comprehensiveness.

The fourth: The exception of any one of them is valid, and this conveys generality.

The fifth: The definite plural, in implying multiplicity, exceeds the indefinite, because it is valid to extract the indefinite from the definite, but not the reverse. It is permissible to say, "I saw men (rijal) from among the men," but one cannot say, "I saw the men from among men." It is known by necessity that what is extracted from the definite is more than what is extracted. Given this, we say: what is understood from the definite plural is either the whole or less than the whole. The second is invalid, because for any number less than the whole, it is valid to extract it from the definite plural, and you know that what is extracted from it is more. Therefore the definite plural must convey the whole. And God knows best.

As for the method of Abu Hashim, namely that the definite plural does not convey generality, the verse can be used as evidence in two other ways:

The first: The arrangement of a ruling upon an attribute indicates causation (ʿilliyya). So His saying, ﴿Indeed, the wicked are in Hellfire﴾ [al-Infitar 82:14], implies that wickedness (fujur) is the cause. If this is established, the generality of the ruling follows from the generality of its cause, which is what is sought.

There is a third method on this matter, which the grammarians mention: the *lam* in His saying, ﴿Indeed, the wicked (al-fujjar)﴾, is not the *lam* of definiteness but means "those who" (alladhi). Two things indicate this:

One: it is answered by *fa'* (the consequent particle), as in His saying: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:38], and as you say, "Whoever meets me, then for him is a dirham."

The second: It is valid to conjoin a verb to the thing that this *lam* precedes. He said: ﴿Indeed, the male charity-givers and the female charity-givers (al-mussaddiqin wal-mussaddiqat), and those who lend to God a goodly loan﴾ [al-Hadid 57:18]. Had His saying "Indeed, the male charity-givers" not meant "indeed, those who gave charity," it would not be valid to conjoin to it His saying "and those who lend to God." Given that this is established, His saying, ﴿Indeed, the wicked are in Hellfire﴾ [al-Infitar 82:14], means: "Indeed, those who committed wickedness are in Hellfire," and this implies generality.

The second verse in this category is His saying: ﴿On the day We gather the God-fearing to the All-Merciful as a delegation, and drive the criminals to Hell as a herd﴾ [Maryam 19:85]. The word "the criminals" (al-mujrimin) is a definite plural with *al-*.

The third: His saying: ﴿And We will leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees﴾ [Maryam 19:72].

The fourth: His saying: ﴿Had God taken people to task for what they earned, He would not have left upon it (the earth) a single creature, but He defers them﴾ [Fatir 35:45]. He made clear that He defers their punishment to another day, and this is only true if their punishment were to take place on that day.

* * *

**The third type** of generalities: plural forms accompanied by the relative particle *alladhi* (who/those who):

The first: His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders (al-mutaffifin), who, when they take measure from people, take their full share﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 83:1–2].

The second: His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:10].

The third: His saying: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wrongdoers to themselves﴾ [al-Nahl 16:28]. Here He explains what is deserved for abandoning emigration and abandoning support, even if one acknowledges God and His Messenger.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿And those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent, and humiliation will cover them﴾ [Yunus 10:27]. He did not distinguish in the threat between the disbeliever and others.

The fifth: His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of God﴾ [al-Tawba 9:34].

The sixth: His saying: ﴿And repentance is not for those who commit evil deeds﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:18]. Had the sinner (fasiq) not been among those subject to threat and punishment, this saying would have no meaning, and there would be no need for repentance mentioned in it.

The seventh: His saying: ﴿The recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is that they be killed or crucified﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:33]. Here He explains the punishment for the sinner in this world and the Hereafter.

The eighth: His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price, those will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:77].

* * *

**The fourth type** of generalities: His saying: ﴿They will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:180]. This is a threat against withholding zakat.

**The fifth type** of generalities: the word "kull" (every/all). This is His saying: ﴿And if every soul that wronged had all that is on the earth, it would ransom itself with it﴾ [Yunus 10:54]. Here He explains what the wrongdoer deserves for his wrongdoing.

**The sixth type**: what indicates that He, glorified is He, will surely carry out the threat He made to them. This is His saying: ﴿He said: Do not dispute before Me, for I had already sent forward to you the threat. The word is not changed before Me, and I am not unjust to the servants﴾ [Qaf 50:28–29]. He made clear that His word concerning the threat is not changed. The argument from the verse is in two ways:

The first: He made the cause for removing excuse the sending forward of the threat. That is, once the threat has been sent forward, no one has any excuse or means of escape from His punishment.

The second: His saying: ﴿The word is not changed before Me﴾ [Qaf 50:29]. This is explicit that He, exalted is He, must surely do what the wording indicates.

This is the totality of what they relied upon from the generalities of the Qur'an.

* * *

As for the generalities of the reports (akhbar), they are numerous.

**The first type**: that which is mentioned with the form "man" (whoever):

The first: What Waqqas ibn Rabi'a related from al-Miswar ibn Shaddad, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever eats by means of his brother a meal, God will feed him from the fire of Hell; whoever takes by means of his brother a garment, God will clothe him from the fire of Hell; and whoever stands in a station of show and reputation, God will set him up on the Day of Resurrection in a station of show and reputation." This is an explicit text on the threat against the sinner, and the meaning of "aqamahu" (set him up) is: He will recompense him for that.

The second: He (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has two tongues and two faces will be in the Fire with two tongues and two faces." He did not distinguish between the hypocrite and others in this matter.

The third: From Sa'id ibn Zayd, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever usurps a span of land will have it hung around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."

The fourth: From Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The believer is one from whom people feel safe, the Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe, the emigrant is one who emigrates from evil, and by Him in whose hand is my soul, a servant whose neighbour does not feel safe from his harm will not enter Paradise." This report indicates the threat against the wicked wrongdoer, and indicates that he is neither a believer nor a Muslim, according to what the Mu'tazila say about the intermediate position between the two positions (al-manzila bayn al-manzilatayn).

The fifth: From Thawban, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever comes on the Day of Resurrection free from three things will enter Paradise: pride, embezzlement, and debt." This indicates that the possessor of these three does not enter Paradise, otherwise this statement would have no meaning. The intended meaning of "debt" is one who died disobedient and refusing, not intending repentance and not repenting from it.

The sixth: From Abu Hurayra (may God be pleased with him), from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever treads a path seeking knowledge, God will make easy for him a path among the paths of Paradise; and whoever his deeds delay, his lineage will not hasten him." This is an explicit text that reward comes only through obedience, and deliverance from the Fire comes only through righteous deeds.

The seventh: From Ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is khamr, and every khamr is forbidden, and whoever drinks khamr in this world and does not repent from it will not drink it in the Hereafter." This is explicit about the threat against the sinner and that he is among the people of eternal abode, because if he does not drink it, he does not enter Paradise, for in it is what souls desire and eyes delight in.

The eighth: From Umm Salama, who said: He (ﷺ) said: "I am only a human like you, and you bring your disputes to me, and perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than another. So whomever I decide in his favour concerning the right of his brother, I have only cut for him a piece of the Fire."

The ninth: From Thabit ibn al-Dahhak, who said: He (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears by a religion other than Islam, lying and deliberately, will be as he said; and whoever kills himself with something, he will be punished with it in the Fire of Hell."

The tenth: From ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the prayer: "Whoever observes it, it will be for him a light, a proof, and a salvation on the Day of Resurrection; and whoever does not observe it, it will not be for him a light, nor a proof, nor a salvation, nor a reward, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be with Qarun, Haman, Pharaoh, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf." This is an explicit text that abandoning prayer nullifies deeds and entails the threat of eternal abode.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 81 (part 3 of 6):**

Eleventh: From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet, peace be upon him (ﷺ), said: "Whoever meets Allah as one who persists in drinking wine, will meet Him like one who worships an idol." Since it is established that such a person does not disbelieve, we know that what is meant is the nullification of the deed (ihbat al-'amal).

Twelfth: From Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever kills himself with an iron implement, his iron implement will be in his hand, with which he will stab his own belly in the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever and ever. And whoever throws himself from a mountain deliberately, killing himself, he will be thrown down into the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever and ever."

Thirteenth: From Abu Dharr, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Three people, Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at them, nor purify them, and for them there is a painful punishment." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are they? They have failed and lost." He said: "The one who lets his garment trail (al-musbil), the one who reminds of his favours (al-mannan), and the one who sells his merchandise by swearing falsely." By "al-musbil" is meant the arrogant one who lets his lower garment trail. And it is known that whoever Allah does not speak to, and does not show mercy to, and for whom there is a painful punishment, is among the people of the Fire. Its application to the sinner (al-fasiq) is an explicit text on the matter.

Fourteenth: From Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever learns a branch of knowledge of those by which the countenance of Allah is sought, but does not learn it except to obtain a worldly good, will not smell the fragrance of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection." And whoever does not smell the fragrance of Paradise, there is no doubt that he is in the Fire, because the responsible person (al-mukallaf) must be either in Paradise or in the Fire.

Fifteenth: From Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever conceals knowledge will be bridled with a bridle of fire on the Day of Resurrection."

Sixteenth: From Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath falsely in order to cut off by it the property of his brother, will meet Allah while He is angry with him." This is because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, those who exchange the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77], to the end of the verse. This is an explicit text regarding the threat, and an explicit text that the verse applies to the sinners just as it applies to the disbelievers.

Seventeenth: From Abu Umamah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath of a wicked nature in order to cut off by it the property of a Muslim man, without right, Allah will forbid Paradise to him and make the Fire obligatory for him." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, even if it is something trivial?" He said: "Even if it is a twig of the arak tree."

Eighteenth: From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "I was with Ibn 'Abbas when a man came to him and said: 'I am a man whose livelihood is from these images (pictures).' Ibn 'Abbas said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever makes an image, Allah will punish him until he breathes the spirit into it, and he will not be able to breathe it. And whoever listens to the talk of people who flee from him, molten lead will be poured into his ears. And whoever claims in a dream to have seen what he has not seen, he will be commanded to tie two barley grains together."'"

Nineteenth: From Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "There is no servant whom Allah has entrusted with a flock, and who dies on the day he dies while he is deceiving his flock, except that Allah forbids Paradise to him."

Twentieth: From Ibn 'Umar, in his debate with 'Uthman when he wanted to appoint him as judge (qadi), he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever is a judge who judges with ignorance is among the people of the Fire, and whoever is a judge who judges with injustice is among the people of the Fire."

Twenty-first: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever claims a father in Islam while he knows that he is not his father, then Paradise is forbidden to him."

Twenty-second: From al-Hasan, from Abu Bakrah, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever kills a person under a covenant (mu'ahad), will not smell the fragrance of Paradise." And if this is the case regarding the killing of disbelievers, then what is your opinion regarding the killing of the children of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?

Twenty-third: From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter." And if he does not wear it in the Hereafter, it is necessary that he not be among the people of Paradise, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And therein is what the souls desire﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71].

* * *

The second type: from the general statements (al-'umumat al-ikhbariyyah) which come not in the form of "man" (whoever), and which are very numerous:

First: From Nafi', the freedman of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "No poor arrogant person will enter Paradise, nor an old fornicator, nor one who reminds of his good deeds before Allah." And whoever among the responsible persons does not enter Paradise is among the people of the Fire, by consensus (ijma').

Second: From Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Three will enter Paradise: the martyr, a servant who advises his master and worships his Lord well, and a chaste person who abstains. And three will enter the Fire: a ruler who is domineering, a wealthy person with property who does not pay the right of Allah, and a poor boastful person."

Third: From Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Allah created the womb (rahim). When He finished creating, the womb stood up and said: 'This is the station of one who seeks refuge from severing ties.' He said: 'Yes. Are you not pleased that I join with whoever joins with you, and sever from whoever severs you?' It said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then that is for you.'" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿Then would you, if you were given authority, cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He deafened them and blinded their eyes﴾ [Muhammad: 22, 23]." This is an explicit text regarding the threat against the severer of ties of kinship and an interpretation of the verse. And in the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf: "Allah, exalted is He, said: 'I am the Most Merciful. I created the womb and derived for it a name from My name. Whoever joins it, I will join him, and whoever severs it, I will sever him.'" And in the hadith of Abu Bakrah, that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "There is no sin more deserving that Allah hastens its punishment for its doer in this world, in addition to what He stores up for him in the Hereafter, than rebellion (al-baghy) and severing the ties of kinship."

Fourth: From Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said to some of those present: "What is the right of Allah upon the servants?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "That they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him." He said: "What is their right upon Allah when they do that?" [They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best."] He said: "That He forgives them and does not punish them." And it is known that what is conditioned upon a condition is absent when the condition is absent, so it follows that He will not forgive them if they do not worship Him.

Fifth: From Abu Bakrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If two Muslims fight with their swords and one of them kills his companion, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, so what about the one killed?" He said: "Indeed, he was eager to kill his companion." Related by Muslim.

Sixth: From Umm Salamah, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "He who drinks in vessels of gold and silver is only swallowing the fire of Hell into his belly."

Seventh: From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, no man hates the People of the House (ahl al-bayt) except that Allah will cause him to enter the Fire." And if they deserve the Fire by hating them, then it is all the more fitting that they deserve it by killing them.

Eighth: In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the year of Khaybar, until we were at Wadi al-Qura. While a man was attending to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), an arrow came and killed him. The people said: "Congratulations to him for Paradise!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No! By He in whose hand is my soul, the cloak which he took on the Day of Hunayn from the spoils, which had not yet been distributed, will blaze against him with fire." When the people heard that, a man came with one sandal or two sandals to the Messenger of Allah, and he (peace be upon him) said: "A sandal of fire, or two sandals of fire."

Ninth: From Abu Burdah, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three will not enter Paradise: the habitual drinker of wine, the severer of ties of kinship, and the one who believes in magic."

Tenth: From Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "There is no servant who has property and does not pay its zakat, except that Allah will gather for him on the Day of Resurrection plates of fire from the Fire of Hell, with which his forehead and back will be branded, until Allah judges between His servants on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years of what you count."

* * *

This is the sum of the Mu'tazilah's argument from the general statements of the Qur'an and the reports. Our companions (the Ash'arites) answered them in several ways.

The first of them: We do not concede that the form "man" in the context of a condition is for generality, nor do we concede that the plural form when defined by the article (al-) is for generality. What indicates this are several matters:

First: It is valid to attach the words "all" (kull) and "some" (ba'd) to these two expressions: "All who enter my house I honour him," and "Some who enter my house I honour him." It is also said: "All people are such," and "Some people are such." If the word "man" in the conditional sense conveyed comprehensiveness, then attaching the word "all" to it would be redundant, and attaching the word "some" to it would be contradictory. The same applies to the defined plural. Thus it is established that these forms do not convey generality.

Second: These forms came in the Book of Allah, and what is meant by them is sometimes comprehensiveness and sometimes a part. For most of the generalities of the Qur'an are specified (makhsus), and metaphor (majaz) and homonymy (ishtirak) are contrary to the basic principle. It is necessary to make the word literally (haqiqah) applicable to the common measure between generality and particularity, which is that it be understood to convey the majority without an explanation that it conveys comprehensiveness or does not.

Third: If these forms conveyed generality with certainty, then attaching an emphasizing word to them would be impossible, because achieving what is already achieved is impossible. Since it is proper to attach these words to them, we know that they do not, without doubt, convey the meaning of generality. Suppose we concede that they convey the meaning of [generality], but is it with a definite or a speculative conveyance? The first is prohibited and absolutely false, because it is known by necessity that people often express the majority by the word "all" and "the entirety" as a form of exaggeration, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And she was given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 23]. So if these words convey the meaning of generality speculatively, and this question is not one of speculative matters, it is not permissible to rely on these generalities in it. Suppose we concede that they convey the meaning of generality with certainty, but it is necessary to stipulate that none of the specifying elements (mukhassisat) exists. For there is no dispute over the permissibility of specification entering the general term. So why do you say that none of the specifying elements exists? At most, one could say: we searched and did not find any specifying element. But you know that failure to find does not indicate non-existence. And if the conveyance of these words to the meaning of comprehensiveness depends on the negation of specifying elements, and this condition is not known, then the indication depends on an unknown condition, so the indication must not be achieved. What confirms this position is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. He judged concerning all those who disbelieved that they would not believe. Then we witnessed some of them who believed, so we know that one of two matters must be the case: either this form is not established for the meaning of inclusiveness, or it is established for this meaning, but there was an indicator in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) by which they knew that the intended meaning of Allah, exalted is He, from this generality was the particular. And what was there is not permissible here like it.

Suppose we concede that it is necessary to explain the specifying element, but the verses of pardon (al-'afw) specify them. And the preponderance is with us, because the verses of pardon, in relation to the verses of threat, are specific in relation to the general, and the specific takes precedence over the general without doubt. Suppose we concede that no specifying element exists, but the general statements of threat are opposed by the general statements of promise, and preference is necessary. And preference is with us in several respects:

First: Fulfilling a promise is more part of generosity (karam) than fulfilling a threat.

Second: It is well known in the reports that the mercy of Allah precedes His wrath and overcomes it, so preferring the general statements of promise is more fitting.

Third: The threat (al-wa'id, the promise of punishment) is a right of God Most High, while the promise (al-wa'd, the promise of reward) is a right of the servant, and the right of the servant is more deserving of being fulfilled than the right of God Most High. Even granting that no contrary evidence exists, these general expressions were revealed concerning the disbelievers, so they are not decisive in their generality. If it is said that the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the occasion of revelation (sabab), we reply: suppose it is so. Nevertheless, since we have seen that many general expressions came in connection with particular occasions, and only those particular occasions were intended, we know that their indication of generality is not strong. And God knows best.

As for those who definitively asserted the negation of punishment for the people of grave sins (al-kaba'ir), they argued with several points:

The first: God Most High says: ﴿Indeed, today disgrace and evil are upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Nahl: 27], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon him who denies and turns away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 48]. These verses indicate that the reality of disgrace, evil and punishment is specific to the disbeliever. Therefore no individual instance of this reality may befall anyone other than the disbelievers.

The second: God Most High says: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed, God forgives all sins"﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. He decreed that He forgives all sins and did not stipulate repentance or anything else. This indicates definitively the forgiveness of all sins.

The third: God Most High says: ﴿And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6]. The word "ʿalā" (despite/upon) indicates a state, as in your saying: "I saw the king while he was eating (ʿalā aklihi)," meaning you saw him while he was occupied with eating. Likewise here: God must forgive them while they are occupied with wrongdoing. The state of being occupied with wrongdoing precludes their repenting. Thus we know that forgiveness occurs without repentance. The implication of this verse would be that He forgives the disbeliever too, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a tremendous wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. However, He left off acting upon it there, so it remains operative in the rest. The distinction is that disbelief is graver in status than disobedience.

The fourth: God Most High says: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes, none will enter it but the most wretched, who denied and turned away﴾ [al-Layl: 14–16]. Every fire is necessarily blazing, so it is as if He said: the Fire will not be entered except by the most wretched, who is the denier who turns away.

The fifth: God Most High says: ﴿Every time a company is thrown into it, its keepers ask them, "Did no warner come to you?" They say, "Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied him and said, 'God has not sent down anything. You are only in great error.'"﴾ [al-Mulk: 8–9]. The verse indicates that all the people of the Fire are deniers. It cannot be said that this verse is specific to the disbelievers. Do you not see that He says before it: ﴿For those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and wretched is the destination. When they are thrown into it, they hear its roaring while it boils, almost bursting with fury﴾ [al-Mulk: 6–8]?

This indicates that it is specific to some of the disbelievers, namely those who said: "Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied him and said, 'God has not sent down anything.'" This is not the saying of all the disbelievers. We reply: the indication of what precedes this verse upon the disbelievers does not prevent the generality of what follows it.

As for his saying that this is not the saying of the disbelievers, we reply: we do not concede that. The Jews and Christians used to say: "God has not sent down anything upon Muhammad." If that is so, then it is true of them that they were saying "God has not sent down anything."

The sixth: God Most High says: ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾ [Saba': 17]. This is an intensive form (bina' al-mubalagha), so it must be specific to original disbelief (al-kufr al-asli).

The seventh: After He informed that people are of two kinds, those whose faces are white and those whose faces are black, He said: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 106]. He mentioned that they are the disbelievers.

The eighth: After He made people three categories, the foremost (al-sabiqun), the companions of the right (ashab al-maymana), and the companions of the left (ashab al-mash'ama), He explained that the foremost and the companions of the right are in Paradise, and the companions of the left are in the Fire. Then He clarified that they are disbelievers by His saying: ﴿And they used to say, "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 47].

The ninth: The person of grave sin is not disgraced, and everyone who is admitted to the Fire is disgraced. Therefore the person of grave sin does not enter the Fire. We said that the person of grave sin is not disgraced because the person of grave sin is a believer, and the believer is not disgraced. We said that he is a believer on account of what has already been explained in the commentary on His saying: ﴿Who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqara: 3], that the person of grave sin is a believer. We said that the believer is not disgraced for several reasons:

[Page 142]

The first: His saying: ﴿On the Day when God will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8].

The second: His saying: ﴿Indeed, disgrace and evil today are upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Nahl: 27].

The third: His saying: ﴿Those who remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 191], up to where He reports of them that they said: ﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 194]. Then He said: ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 195]. It is known that those who remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth, include the disobedient, the adulterer, and the drinker of wine. When God reports that they said: "And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection," and then clarifies that He responded to them in that, it is established that He does not disgrace them. Thus, from what we have mentioned, it is established that He does not disgrace the disobedient among the people of the Qibla (ahl al-qibla, i.e., Muslims). We said that everyone who is admitted to the Fire is disgraced on account of His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 192]. Thus, by these two premises together, it is established that the person of grave sin does not enter the Fire.

The tenth: The numerous general expressions in the promise, such as His saying: ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and of the Hereafter they are certain. Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqara: 4–5]. He decreed success for everyone who believed. And He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, Christians, and Sabians, whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqara: 62]. His saying: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqara: 62] is indefinite in affirmative form, so affirmation by a single deed suffices. And He said: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise﴾ [al-Nisa': 124]. These are very numerous, and we have a separate treatise on this. Whoever wishes it should consult that treatise.

The reply to these points: they are opposed by the general expressions of the threat, and the discussion of the interpretation of each of these verses will come in its proper place, God willing.

* * *

As for our companions who definitively asserted pardon regarding some and suspended judgment regarding others, they argued from the Qur'an with verses:

The first argument: the verses indicating that God Most High is Pardoning (ʿAfuw) and Forgiving (Ghafur), such as His saying: ﴿And He is the One who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons evil deeds, and He knows what you do﴾ [al-Shura: 25], and His saying: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 30], and His saying: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains﴾ [al-Shura: 32], up to His saying: ﴿Or He would wreck them for what they have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 34]. Also, the Ummah has agreed that God pardons His servants, and they agreed that among His names is al-ʿAfuw. So we say: pardon (al-ʿafw) is either an expression for dropping punishment from one whose punishment is good, or from one whose punishment is not good. The second part is false, because punishing one whose punishment is not good is ugly, and one who abstains from such an act is not described as having pardoned. Do you not see that when a person has not wronged anyone, it is not said that he pardoned him? It is said of someone that he pardoned only when it was within his power to punish him and he left it. This is why He said: ﴿And that you pardon is closer to piety﴾ [al-Baqara: 237]. Also, since He said: ﴿And He is the One who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons evil deeds﴾ [al-Shura: 25], if pardon meant dropping punishment from the penitent, that would be repetition without benefit. So we know that pardon is an expression for dropping punishment from one whose punishment is good, and that is our doctrine.

The second argument: the verses indicating that He is Forgiving (Ghafir), Forgiver (Ghafur) and Much-Forgiving (Ghaffar). He said: ﴿Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance﴾ [Ghafir: 3], and He said: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-Kahf: 58], and He said: ﴿And indeed I am Much-Forgiving to those who repent﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82], and He said: ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return﴾ [al-Baqara: 285]. Forgiveness is not an expression for dropping punishment from one whose punishment is not good, so it must be an expression for dropping punishment from one whose punishment is good. We said that the first aspect is false because He mentions the attribute of forgiveness in the context of bestowing favor upon the servants. If we interpreted it according to the first meaning, this sense would not remain, because abstaining from ugliness is not a favor upon the servant. Rather, it is as if He benefited Himself, for if He did it He would deserve blame, reproach, and to be outside the bounds of divinity. So by abstaining from ugliness He does not deserve thanks from the servant. Since that is invalid, it is necessarily to be interpreted according to the second aspect, which is what is sought.

If it is said: why may pardon and forgiveness not be interpreted as deferring punishment from this world to the Hereafter? The evidence that pardon is used for deferring punishment from this world is His saying in the story of the Jews: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾ [al-Baqara: 52]. What is meant is not dropping punishment, but deferring it to the Hereafter. Likewise His saying: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 30], meaning: whatever calamities of His punishment God hastens, whether as a trial or as a hastened punishment, are because of your sins, and He does not hasten trial or punishment for much of them. Similarly His saying: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains﴾ [al-Shura: 32], up to His saying: ﴿Or He would wreck them for what they have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 34], meaning: if He willed to destroy them, He would destroy them, but He does not destroy for much of the sins.

The reply: the root of pardon (al-ʿafw) is from ʿafa al-athar, meaning he removed it. Since this is so, what is meant by pardon must be removal. This is why He said: ﴿But whoever is pardoned something by his brother﴾ [al-Baqara: 178]. What is meant is not deferment but removal. Likewise His saying: ﴿And that you pardon is closer to piety﴾ [al-Baqara: 237]. What is meant is not deferment until a known time, but absolute remission. Among what indicates that pardon does not encompass deferment is that when a creditor postpones the demand, it is not said that he pardoned him, but if he remitted it, it is said that he pardoned him. Thus it is established that pardon cannot be explained as deferment.

Third proof: the verses showing that He, exalted is He, is Most Merciful (Rahman, Rahim). The argument from them is that His mercy, glorified is He, either appears toward the obedient who deserve reward, or toward the disobedient who deserve punishment. The first is invalid, because His mercy toward the obedient either arises because He gave them the reward which is their due, or because He bestowed on them more than their due. The first is invalid because the performance of an obligation is not called mercy.
