Do you not see that if someone is owed one hundred dinars by a man and takes them from him by compulsion and obligation, it is not said of the one who paid that he gave the taker that amount out of mercy? The second is invalid because the one under obligation, by what he took of the reward which is his due, has become like one excluded from that bounty, so that extra is called an increase in favour and is never at all called mercy. Do you not see that if a great sultan has in his service an amir who has great wealth and a complete realm, and then the sultan adds to his kingdom another realm, it is not said that the sultan showed him mercy, but rather that he increased his favour toward him. So it is here.

As for the second division, namely that His mercy appears only toward the one who deserves punishment: either His mercy is because He, exalted is He, left off the punishment in excess of the punishment deserved. This is invalid, because leaving that off is obligatory, and what is obligatory is not called mercy. Also, it would follow that every disbeliever and wrongdoer would be merciful to us because he did not wrong us. It remains that He is merciful only because He left off the punishment that was deserved, and this is not realised toward the one who commits a minor sin, nor toward the one who commits a major sin after repentance, because leaving off their punishment is obligatory. This shows that His mercy arises because He left off the punishment of the one who commits a major sin before repentance.

If it is said: why may His mercy not be because creation, obligation and provision are all bounty, and because He lightens the punishment of the one who commits a major sin? We say: as for the first, it indicates that He is merciful in this world, so where is His mercy in the Hereafter, when the community is agreed that His mercy in the Hereafter is greater than His mercy in this world? As for the second: you hold that lightening the punishment is not permissible, in the view of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) of the Wa'idiyya (those who insist on the binding character of the threat of punishment). If the occurrence of lightening is established by the requirement of this verse, then the permissibility of pardon is established, because whoever holds one of the two holds the other.

Fourth proof: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa: 48]. We say: "for whom He wills" cannot include the one who commits a minor sin, nor the one who commits a major sin after repentance. So it is necessary that what is meant is the one who commits a major sin before repentance. We say that it is not permissible to apply it to the minor sinner or to the major sinner after repentance, for several reasons:

The first: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but forgives what is less than that﴾, means that He does not forgive it as bounty, not that He does not forgive it by entitlement, as reason and revelation indicate. If that is so, then the meaning of His saying ﴿and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ must be: and He bestows forgiveness of what is less than that association, so that the negation and the affirmation are directed to one thing. Do you not see that if one said: "So-and-so does not bestow a hundred dinars, but gives what is less than it to whoever is entitled," it would not be a coherent statement? And since the forgiveness of the minor sinner and of the major sinner after repentance is due by entitlement, it is impossible that they be what is meant by the verse.

The second: if His saying ﴿and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ meant that He forgives those who are entitled, such as the penitent and the minor sinners, there would remain no meaning in distinguishing association from what is less than association. For just as He forgives what is less than association when entitlement exists and does not forgive it when entitlement is absent, so He would forgive association when entitlement exists and not forgive it when entitlement is absent, and then the distinction would serve no purpose.

The third: the forgiveness of penitents and minor sinners is obligatory, and what is obligatory is not made contingent on will, because what is contingent on will is that which, if its doer wills to do it, he does it, and if he wills to leave it, he leaves it. The obligatory is that which must be done, whether he wills it or refuses. The forgiveness mentioned in the verse is contingent on will, so it is not permissible that the forgiveness mentioned in the verse be the forgiveness of penitents and minor sinners.

Know that all these arguments are built upon the view of the Mu'tazila that it is obligatory to forgive the minor sinner and the major sinner after repentance. As for us, we do not say that.

The fourth: His saying, ﴿and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾, indicates with certainty that He forgives everything other than association, and this includes minor sins and major sins both after and before repentance. However, the forgiveness of each of these three may be of two kinds, because it is possible that He forgives all of them for everyone, and possible that He forgives all of them for some and not others. So His saying ﴿and forgives what is less than that﴾ indicates that He forgives all three, and then His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾ indicates that He forgives all of those things not for everyone but for some. This is the argument most fitting to our principles.

If it is said: we do not concede that forgiveness indicates that He, exalted is He, does not punish disobedient people in the Hereafter. Its explanation is that forgiveness is the removal of punishment, and the removal of punishment is more general than removal of punishment permanently or not permanently, and a word laid down for the shared meaning has no indication of either of those two conditions. Therefore the word forgiveness has no indication of permanent removal. Given this, we say: why may it not be that what is meant is that God, exalted is He, does not defer the punishment of association beyond this world, and defers the punishment of what is less than association beyond this world for whom He wills? It cannot be said: how is this valid, when we do not see any increase for the unbelievers in worldly punishment over the believers? We say: the sense of the verse is that God does not defer the punishment of association in this world for whom He wills, and defers the punishment of what is less than association in this world for whom He wills. Thus both groups are frightened, by the hastening of punishment for the disbelievers and the wicked, since each of these may suppose that his punishment will be hastened, even though He does not do that to many of them. We grant that forgiveness is an expression for removal in the manner of permanence. Why do you say that it is impossible to take it as the forgiveness of the penitent and the forgiveness of the one who commits a minor sin? As for the first three arguments, they are based on principles which they (the Mu'tazila) do not hold, namely the obligation of forgiving the minor sinner and the major sinner after repentance.

As for the fourth argument: we do not concede that His saying ﴿what is less than that﴾ indicates generality. The evidence for this is that it is valid to substitute the words "all" and "some" for it, as when one says: "and forgives all of what is less than that," and "and forgives some of what is less than that." If His saying ﴿what is less than that﴾ indicated generality, this would not be valid. We grant that it is for generality, but we specify it as applying to the minor sinner and to the major sinner after repentance. That is because the verses of threat, each of which is specific to one kind of major sin, such as killing and fornication, and this verse encompasses all sins, and the specific takes precedence over the general. So the verses of threat must take precedence over this verse.

As for the answer to the first point: when we take forgiveness to mean deferral of punishment, it becomes necessary, by the ruling of the verse, that the punishment of polytheists in this world be greater than the punishment of believers; otherwise there would be no benefit in this distinction. It is known that this is not so, by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And were it not that people would become one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 33], and so on.

As for his saying: why do you say that His saying ﴿what is less than that﴾ indicates generality? We say: because the word "ma" indicates a reference to the essence described as being less than association, and this essence is a single essence, and He has judged with certainty that He forgives it. So in every instance in which this essence is realised, forgiveness must be realised. Thus it is established that it is for generality. Also, it is valid to make an exception of any disobedience whatsoever, and according to the Wa'idiyya, the validity of the exception indicates generality. As for his saying that the verses of threat are more specific than this verse, we say: rather, this verse is more specific than them, because it indicates pardon for some and not for others, whereas what you cite indicates threat for all. Also, the preference for verses of pardon is more appropriate because of the great number of reports in the Qur'an and the traditions that encourage pardon.

Fifth proof: that we hold fast to the general promises, which are numerous in the Qur'an. Then we say: when a conflict occurs, there must be either preference or reconciliation, and preference has several aspects.

The first: the general promises are more numerous, and preference by the greater number of evidences is a matter recognised in the Law, and we have demonstrated its soundness in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh, the foundations of Islamic law).

The second: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [Hud: 114], indicates that a good deed removes an evil deed only because it is a good deed, as established in the principles of jurisprudence. So by the requirement of this allusion, every good deed must remove every evil deed, and the good deeds issuing from disbelievers are an exception, since they do not remove their evil deeds. So the rule remains acted upon in the rest.

The third: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever comes with an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160]. Then He increased beyond the ten, saying ﴿like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261], then He increased beyond that, saying ﴿and Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. As for the side of the evil deed, He said ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160]. This is most clearly indicative that the side of the good deed outweighs the side of the evil deed in the sight of Allah, exalted is He.

The fourth: He, exalted is He, said in the verse of promise in the chapter of an-Nisa: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; the promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ [an-Nisa: 122]. His saying ﴿the promise of Allah is true﴾ is mentioned only for emphasis, and He did not say in any place "the threat of Allah is true."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The word is not changed in My presence﴾ [Qaf: 29], and so on, it encompasses both the promise and the threat.

The fifth: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness of Allah, will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ and ﴿And whoever earns sin, he earns it only against himself, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [an-Nisa: 110, 111]. Seeking forgiveness (istighfar) is the request for forgiveness, and it is other than repentance. So here He declared that whether he repents or does not repent, if he seeks forgiveness, Allah forgives him. And He did not say "whoever earns sin, indeed he will find Allah punishing and retributive," but rather said ﴿he earns it only against himself﴾ [an-Nisa: 111]. This indicates that the side of the good deed outweighs. A parallel is His saying: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own selves, and if you do evil, it is against them﴾ [al-Isra: 7]. He did not say "if you do evil, you do evil against them," so it is as if He, exalted is He, displayed His good by repeating it twice, and concealed His evil by mentioning it only once. All of this indicates that the side of the good deed outweighs.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 81 (part 6 of 6):

Sixth: We have already shown that His saying, ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ [al-Nisa: 48], does not cover anything except pardon for the one who commits a major sin. Moreover, He repeated this verse twice in the same surah, and repetition is only good for emphasis. He did not mention any verse of threat in the form of repetition with the same wording, neither in one surah nor in two surahs. This shows that God's concern for the side of promise, that is, for good deeds and pardon for evil deeds, is more complete.

Seventh: When the general statements of promise and threat conflict, the interpretation must be directed to one of the two sides. Directing the interpretation to the threat is better than directing it to the promise, because pardoning a threat is considered praiseworthy by custom, while neglecting a promise is considered blameworthy by custom. So directing the interpretation to the threat is more fitting than directing it to the promise.

Eighth: The Qur'an is full of God being Forgiving, Very Forgiving, and Oft-Forgiving, and that He possesses forgiveness and pardon, and that He is Merciful and Generous, and that He possesses pardon, kindness, grace, and bounty. The reports that indicate these attributes have reached the level of tawatur (mass transmission). All of this strengthens the side of promise, and there is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates that He is far from mercy, generosity, and pardon. All of this makes the side of promise preponderant over the side of threat.

Ninth: This person has performed what is the best of good deeds, which is faith, and has not performed what is the worst of abominations, which is disbelief. Rather, he has committed an evil that belongs to the category of abominations but is not at its extreme. A master who has a servant, and the servant performs the greatest acts of obedience and commits a moderate act of disobedience, if the master preferred that moderate act of disobedience over the great obedience, that master would be considered mean and harmful. So likewise here. Since that is not permissible for God, it is established that the preponderance is for the side of promise.

Tenth: Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi said: "My God, if the tawhid (monotheism) of one hour destroys the disbelief of fifty years, how would the tawhid of fifty years not destroy the disobedience of one hour! My God, since disbelief is not benefited by any act of obedience, it is required by justice that faith is not harmed by any act of disobedience; otherwise disbelief would be greater than faith! So if that is the case, there is at least hope for pardon." This is a good statement.

Eleventh: We have already shown by proof that His saying, ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ [al-Nisa: 48], cannot be applied to minor sins, nor to major sins after repentance. So if we do not apply it to major sins before repentance, it would lead to nullifying the verse. As for specifying the general statements of threat to those who consider them permissible, this only entails specifying a general statement, and it is known that specification is easier than nullification.

The Mu'tazilah said: Preferring the side of threat is better, for several reasons:

First: The community (ummah) agreed that the wrongdoer (fasiq) is cursed and is punished with a hadd (prescribed penalty) as a deterrent and punishment, and that he is among the people of disgrace. This shows that he deserves punishment, and if he deserves punishment, it is impossible for him to simultaneously deserve reward. Once this is established, the side of threat is preponderant over the side of promise.

As for the proof that he is cursed, it is from the Qur'an and consensus. From the Qur'an is His saying about the killer of a believer: ﴿And Allah is angry with him and has cursed him﴾ [al-Nisa: 93]. Likewise His saying: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 18]. As for consensus, it is clear.

As for the proof that he is subjected to hadd as a deterrent, it is His saying: ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, a deterrent from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. As for the proof that he is punished by hadd, it is His saying about the adulterer: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. As for the proof that they are among the people of disgrace, it is His saying about the highway robbers: ﴿The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger is only that...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33], up to His saying: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33]. Once it is established that the wrongdoer is characterized by these attributes, it is established that he deserves punishment and blame. Whoever deserves both of them permanently, and whenever he deserves them permanently, it is impossible for him to remain deserving reward, because reward and punishment are mutually contradictory. So combining the deserving of both is impossible. And when he no longer deserves reward, it is established that the side of threat is preponderant over the side of promise.

Second: The verses of promise are general, while the verses of threat are specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

Third: People were created with a disposition toward corruption and injustice, so the need for restraint is greater, and therefore the side of threat is more appropriate.

We say: The answer to the first argument has several aspects:

The first: Just as there are verses indicating that they are cursed and punished in this world because of their sins, there are also verses indicating that they are honored and respected in this world because of their faith. God Most High says: ﴿When those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 54]. So preferring the verses of threat concerning the Hereafter over the verses indicating that they are honored and punished in this world is no better than preferring the verses of promise concerning the Hereafter over the verses indicating that they are honored in this world because of their faith.

The second: Just as the verses of promise conflict with the verses of threat concerning the Hereafter, they also conflict with the verses of threat and deterrence in this world. So why is preferring the verses of the threat of this world over the verses of the threat of the Hereafter more appropriate than the reverse?

The third: We agree that a thief, even if he repents, still has his hand cut off, not as a deterrent but as a trial. So it is established that His saying, ﴿as a recompense for what they earned, a deterrent from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38], is conditioned on the absence of repentance. Why then is it not also permissible that it is conditioned on the absence of pardon?

The fourth: Recompense (jaza') is that which suffices and is enough. If it is sufficient, it must not be permissible to punish in the Hereafter, otherwise that would undermine its being sufficient and adequate. So it is established that this contradicts punishment in the Hereafter. And once the corruption of their claim regarding preference of the side of threat is established, we say: The two verses, one indicating promise and the other threat, both exist, so reconciliation between them is necessary. Either it is said: the servant first receives reward and then is transferred to the abode of punishment, which is a false statement by consensus of the community; or it is said: the servant first receives punishment and then is transferred to the abode of reward and remains there forever. This is what is sought.

As for the second preference, it is weak, because His saying, ﴿And He forgives what is less than that﴾ [al-Nisa: 48], does not cover disbelief, while His saying, ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa: 14], covers everything. So our statement is the specific one, and God knows best.

The sixth argument: We have already shown that the intercession (shafa'ah) of Muhammad (ﷺ) is effective in removing punishment, and this indicates our position on this issue.

The seventh argument: His saying, ﴿Indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], which is explicit on the matter. If it is said: If this verse indicates something, it either indicates certainty of forgiveness for all sinners, and you do not hold this doctrine, so what the verse indicates you do not hold, and what you hold the verse does not indicate? We grant that, but what is meant by it is that He forgives all sins with repentance, and interpreting the verse this way is preferable for two reasons:

One: If we interpret it this way, we have interpreted it as covering all sins without specification.

Two: He Most High mentioned after this verse His saying: ﴿And turn back in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you﴾ [al-Zumar: 54]. And turning back (inabah) is repentance. This indicates that repentance is a condition for it.

The answer to the first: His saying, ﴿Indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾, is a promise from Him that He will remove them in the future. We are certain that He will do so in the future, for we are certain that He will bring believers out of the Fire without fail. So this is certainty of forgiveness without fail. By this it is established that there is no need to apply the verse to its apparent meaning with the condition of repentance. This is the complete discussion of this issue, and success is from God.

Let us return to the explanation of the verse. The Mu'tazilah interpreted the sin "encompassing" (ihatah) as being a major sin that nullifies the reward of its doer. The objection to this is on several grounds:

Page 148

The first: Just as one of the conditions for a sin to encompass a person is that it be a major sin, the condition for this encompassing is the absence of pardon. If pardon were realized, the sin would not encompass the person. So the sin cannot be established as encompassing the person unless the absence of pardon is established. This is the very point in question, and the argument from this verse to prove the desired conclusion depends on it, which is invalid.

The second: We do not interpret the encompassing of sin as being a major sin. Rather, we interpret it as meaning that his outward and inward self is characterized by disobedience. This is realized only with the disbeliever who disobeys God with his heart, tongue, and limbs. As for the Muslim who obeys God with his heart and tongue, but disobeys God with some of his limbs and not others, the encompassing of sin is not realized for him. There is no doubt that interpreting encompassing in the way we have mentioned is better, because when a body touches some parts of another body but not others, it is not said to encompass it. At this point it becomes clear that the encompassing of sin is not realized for the servant except when he is a disbeliever. Once this is established, we say: His saying, ﴿then those are the companions of the Fire﴾, implies that the companions of the Fire are none other than they, and this implies that the person with a major sin is not among the people of the Fire.

The third: His saying, ﴿then those are the companions of the Fire﴾, implies that they are in the Fire at present, and that is false, so it must be understood to mean that they deserve the Fire. We say in accordance with this: but there is no dispute about whether He pardons this right, and this is the very point in question. Let us conclude the discussion of this verse with a juristic principle: The condition here consists of two matters:

One: the acquisition of an evil deed.

Two: the encompassing of that evil deed around the servant. The consequence conditioned on the existence of both conditions is not realized when only one of them is present. This indicates that whoever makes an oath on two conditions regarding divorce or manumission does not break the oath by the existence of only one of them. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 82:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾

Know that He, glorified and exalted, has not mentioned in the Qur'an any verse concerning threat (wa'id) without mentioning beside it a verse concerning promise (wa'd), and that is for several benefits:

The first of them: that by this He manifests His justice, glorified is He, because when He decreed the everlasting punishment upon those who persist in disbelief, it was necessary that He decree the everlasting bliss upon those who persist in belief.

The second: that the believer must balance his fear and his hope, as the Prayer and Peace be upon him said: "If the fear of the believer and his hope were weighed, they would balance." And that balance is not attained except by this path.

The third: that by His promise He manifests the perfection of His mercy, and by His threat the perfection of His wisdom, and this becomes a means to recognition (irfan). Here there are several issues:

The first issue: good deeds lie outside the designation (musamma) of faith, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. So if faith indicated righteous deeds, mentioning righteous deeds after faith would be repetition. The judge (al-Qadi) replied that although all righteous deeds enter into faith, the statement "he believed" (amana) only indicates that he performed one single act of the acts of faith; therefore it is good to say: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾.

The answer: the past tense verb indicates the occurrence of the verbal noun (masdar) in a past time, and faith is the masdar; so if that indicated all righteous deeds, the saying "he believed" would be evidence of the issuing from him of all those righteous deeds. And God knows best.

Page 149

The second issue: this verse indicates that the person who commits a major sin may enter the Garden, because we are speaking of one who brought faith and righteous deeds, then afterward committed a major sin and did not repent from it. This person, before committing the major sin, was truly described as having believed and done righteous deeds at that time, and whoever is truly described as such is truly described as having believed and done righteous deeds; and when that is true of him, it is necessary that he be included under His saying: ﴿They are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾ If it is said that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and done righteous deeds﴾ is not true of him unless he has performed all righteous deeds, and among the righteous deeds is repentance, so when he has not performed it, he has not performed the righteous deeds, and so he is not included under the verse. We say: we have already shown that before committing the major sin he was truly described as having believed and done righteous deeds at that time, and when that is true of him, it is true of him that he believed and did righteous deeds; for whenever a compound statement is true, the truth of its component is necessary. Rather, when he commits the major sin, it is not true of him that he believed and did righteous deeds at all times; but our saying "he believed and did righteous deeds" is more general than our saying "he is so at all times or at some times," and what is considered in the verse is the common element, so it is established that he is included under the ruling of the promise. There remains their claim that the wicked person's punishment for his disobedience nullifies the reward for his obedience, so the weighting would be toward the threat; but the discussion of that has already preceded.

The third issue: al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) argued by this verse that whoever enters the Garden does not enter it by grace (tafaddul), because His saying: ﴿They are the companions of the Garden﴾ is for restriction (hasr), so it indicates that there are no companions of the Garden except those who believed and did righteous deeds. We say: why is it not permissible that what is meant is that they are the ones who deserve it, so whoever is given the Garden by grace has not entered under this ruling? And God knows best.

**[Page 150]**

The words of the Most High: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: Worship none but Allah, and be good to parents, and to kindred, and orphans, and the needy, and speak kindly to people, and establish prayer, and give zakah. Then you turned away, except for a few of you, and you were averse.﴾

Know that this is another kind of the blessings with which Allah favoured them. That is because the imposition of these duties leads to the greatest blessing, which is Paradise, and that which leads to a blessing is itself a blessing. Therefore this imposition is without doubt among the blessings. Then, the Most High has explained here that He imposed upon them several things.

The first imposition: the words of the Most High, ﴿Worship none but Allah.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues.

The first issue: Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *ya'budūna* with the *yā'* (third person), while the rest read it with the *tā'* (second person). The reading with *yā'* is because they are an absent group about whom He informs; the reading with *tā'* is because they were addressed. The preferred reading is with *tā'*. Abu 'Amr said: Do you not see that He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿and speak kindly to people﴾? Thus the address supports the *tā'*.

The second issue: They differed about the grammatical position (*i'rāb*) of *ya'budūna*, in five opinions.

**[Page 150]**

The first opinion: al-Kisa'i said: It is in the nominative, on the basis that it means "that they not worship," as if it were said: "We took their covenant that they should not worship except Allah." But when *an* (that) was dropped, the verb became nominative, as Tarafah said:

*Unquestioningly, O you who blame me, to attend the battles,*
*and to witness the pleasures: will you make me immortal?*

He meant *an aḥḍura* (that I attend), and for this reason he coordinated *an* with it. This view was permitted by al-Akhfash, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, Qutrub, 'Ali ibn 'Isa and Abu Muslim.

The second opinion: Its position is nominative on the basis that it is the answer to an oath, as if it were said: "And when We swore to them that they would not worship..." This view was permitted by al-Mubarrad, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, and it is one of the two opinions of al-Akhfash.

The third opinion: the view of Qutrub: that it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), so its position is accusative, as if he said: "We took your covenant as those not worshipping except Allah."

The fourth opinion: the view of al-Farra': that the position of *lā ta'budūna* is in the mode of prohibition, but it came in the form of an informative statement, like His saying: ﴿A mother shall not be harmed through her child﴾ (al-Baqarah: 233), with the nominative, while the meaning is prohibition. What confirms that it is a prohibition are several matters:

First: His saying: "Establish" (*aqīmū*).

Second: that the reading of 'Abd Allah and Ubayy supports it: "*Lā ta'budū*" (do not worship).

Third: that informing in the sense of command and prohibition is more emphatic and more eloquent than the explicit command and prohibition, because it is as if one has hastened to comply and to desist, so it reports about it.

The fifth opinion: the estimate is that "*an lā ta'budū*" (that you not worship), with *an* together with the verb, is a substitute for the covenant, as if it were said: "We took the covenant of the Children of Israel regarding their monotheism."

The third issue: This covenant indicates the completeness of what is indispensable in religion. This is because, when He commanded the worship of Allah, the Most High, and forbade the worship of other than Him, there is no doubt that the command to worship Him and the prohibition of worshipping other than Him is preceded by knowledge of His essence, may He be glorified, and of everything that is necessary, permissible and impossible for Him; and by knowledge of His unity (*tawḥīd*), His freedom from opposites and equals, and His freedom from consort and offspring. It is also preceded by knowledge of the manner of that worship, which cannot be known except through revelation and prophethood. Therefore His saying ﴿Worship none but Allah﴾ includes all that is contained in the science of theology (*'ilm al-kalām*) and the science of jurisprudence and rulings (*'ilm al-fiqh*), because worship cannot be realised without them.

The second imposition: the words of the Most High, ﴿and be good to parents﴾. Concerning this there are several issues.

The first issue: It is said: With what is the *bā'* in the words of the Most High, ﴿and be good to parents﴾ connected, and what is it governed by in its accusative position? We say: There are three opinions:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: It is accusative on the meaning of "do good to the parents, a good deed."

The second: It was said: on the meaning of "We enjoined them regarding the parents, a goodness," because the connection of the *bā'* to it is better on this view. Had it been according to the first, it would have been "*wa ilā al-wālidayn*" (and toward the parents), as if it were said: "And do good toward the parents."

The third: It was said: Rather, it is in the informative mode, coordinated with the first meaning, i.e., that you worship and do good.

The second issue: The reason why the worship of Allah is followed by goodness to parents is for several reasons:

First: The blessing of Allah upon the servant is greater, so His thanks must be given precedence over the thanks of others. Then, after the blessing of Allah, the blessing of parents is the most general of blessings. That is because the parents are the origin and the cause of the child's being and existence, just as they bestow blessings upon him through rearing. As for anyone other than the parents, bestowal does not proceed from them regarding the very existence, but only regarding rearing. Thus it is established that their bestowal is the greatest aspect of bestowal after the bestowal of Allah, the Most High.

Second: Allah, glorified is He, is in reality the one who effects the existence of man, while the parents are the ones who effect his existence according to the apparent custom. So when He mentioned the real effector, He followed it with the effector according to the apparent custom.

Third: Allah, the Most High, does not seek any compensation at all for His bestowal upon the servant; rather the purpose is pure bestowal. The parents are likewise: they do not seek a material compensation or reward for bestowing upon the child. Indeed, whoever denies the promised return still does good to his child and raises him. Thus, from this aspect, their bestowal resembles the bestowal of Allah, the Most High.

Fourth: Allah, the Most High, never tires of bestowing upon the servant, even if the servant commits the greatest crimes; He does not cut off from him the sources of His blessings and the following of His generosity. Likewise, parents do not tire of the child and do not cut off from him the sources of their giving and generosity, even if the child is wrongdoing toward his parents.

Fifth: Just as the affectionate parent manages his child's property seeking profit and increase, and guards it from loss and diminution, so likewise the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, manages the servant's obedience, guarding it from being lost. Then, He, glorified is He, makes his deeds, which do not last, like something that remains forever, as He said: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains﴾ (al-Baqarah: 261).

Sixth: Although the blessing of Allah is greater than the blessing of the parents, the blessing of Allah is known by reasoning, while the blessing of the parents is known by necessity. Yet the latter is few in comparison with the blessings of Allah. Thus they are balanced in this respect, and the preponderance belongs to the blessings of Allah. Therefore, we have made the blessings of the parents as following upon the blessings of Allah, the Most High.

The third issue: Most scholars agree that honouring the parents is obligatory even if they are both disbelievers. Several things prove it:

First: His saying in this verse ﴿and be good to parents﴾ is not restricted by their being believers or not. Also, it has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (*uṣūl al-fiqh*) that a ruling connected to an attribute indicates that the attribute is its cause. So this verse indicates that the command to honour the parents is due purely to their being parents, and this requires generality. Similarly the argument from His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and be good to parents﴾ (al-Isra': 23).

Second: His saying: ﴿So do not say to them "Uff", nor scold them﴾ (al-Isra': 23), up to the verse, and this is the utmost emphasis in forbidding harming them. Then, at the end of the verse He said: ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small﴾ (al-Isra': 24), thus explicitly stating the reason for the obligation of this honour.

Third: Allah, the Most High, related that Abraham, peace be upon him, how gently he called his father from disbelief to faith, in His saying: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees, nor benefits you at all?﴾ (Maryam: 42). Then his father used to harm him and utter harsh replies, and he, peace be upon him, used to bear that. If this is established regarding Abraham, peace be upon him, then the like of it is established regarding this community, due to His saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ (al-Nahl: 123).

The fourth issue: Know that goodness toward them is that one never harms them at all, and conveys to them from benefits as much as they need. Therefore it includes calling them to faith if they are disbelievers, and enjoining them to good in a gentle manner if they are sinners.

The third imposition: the words of the Most High, ﴿and to kindred﴾. Concerning this there are several issues.

The first issue: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: If someone bequeaths to the relatives of Zayd, the heir who is a mahram and the one who is not a mahram both enter it, but the father and the son do not enter it, because they are not known as "relatives" (*qarīb*). Grandchildren and grandparents enter it. It was also said: the ancestors (*uṣūl*) and descendants (*furū'*) do not enter it; and it was said that all enter it. Here there is a subtle point: the Arabs preserve the distant ancestors, so their offspring spread and they are all relatives. If we ascend to a distant grandfather and count his children, they become many. For this reason al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: One ascends to the nearest grandfather to whom he traces his lineage and by whom he is known, even if he is a disbeliever. The companions (*al-aṣḥāb*) mentioned as an example: if someone bequeaths to the relatives of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, we direct it to the Banu Shafi', not to the Banu al-Muttalib or the Banu 'Abd Manaf, even if they are relatives, because al-Shafi'i is, according to the well-known account, traced to Shafi', not to 'Abd Manaf. Al-Shaykh al-Ghazali said: This is in the time of al-Shafi'i. As for our time, it is directed only to the children of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and it does not ascend to the Banu Shafi', because in our time the nearest whom his relatives are known by is himself. As for maternal kinship, it enters the bequest of non-Arabs, but it does not enter the bequest of Arabs according to the more apparent view, because they do not count that as kinship. However, if he says "for the womb (*arḥām*) of so-and-so," then both paternal and maternal kinship enter it.

The second issue: Know that the right of the kindred is subsidiary to the right of the parents, because a person is connected to his relatives only through their connection to the parents, and connection to the parents takes precedence over connection to kindred. Therefore Allah delayed its mention after the parents. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed the womb is a branch (*shijnah*) from the Most Merciful. When the Day of Resurrection comes, it will say: 'O Lord, I was wronged, I was mistreated, I was severed.' Its Lord will answer it: 'Are you not pleased that I join with whoever joins with you, and sever whoever severs you?'" Then he recited: ﴿Would you perhaps, if you turned away, cause corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ The rational reason for emphasising the observance of this right is that kinship is the likely cause of unity, affection, care and support. If none of that were present, it would be harder on the heart and more painful, causing greater hurt, estrangement and need. And the stronger the bond, the more obligatory its preservation. Therefore the observance of the rights of relatives became obligatory.

The fourth imposition: the words of the Most High, ﴿and orphans﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

The first issue: The orphan is one whose father has died before he reaches puberty. Its plural is *aytām* and *yatāmā*, like *nadīm* and *nadāmā* (companion and companions). One does not call one whose mother has died an orphan. Al-Zajjaj said: This is regarding humans; but regarding non-humans, its orphanhood is from the side of its mother.

The second issue: The orphan is mentioned alongside the observance of the rights of relatives, because, being small, he does not benefit anyone, and because of his orphanhood and being devoid of one who looks after him, he needs someone who will benefit him, and a person rarely desires the company of such a one. Since this imposition is difficult for the soul, its rank in religion is therefore great.

The fifth imposition: the words of the Most High, ﴿and the needy﴾. Concerning this there are several issues.

**[Page 152]**

**First issue:** *al-masakin* (the needy) is the plural of *miskin*, derived from *sukun* (stillness), as though poverty has settled upon him. According to most lexicographers, the *miskin* is worse off than the *faqir* (the poor). This is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, and they cite the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿or a needy person in misery﴾ [al-Balad: 16]. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, the *faqir* is worse off, because the *faqir* is derived from *fiqar al-zahr* (the vertebrae of the back), as though his spine has been broken by the severity of his need. This is the view of Ibn al-Anbari. They cite as evidence the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to needy people who worked on the sea﴾ [al-Kahf: 79]. He called them *masakin* although the boat was their property.

**Second issue:** Their rank is mentioned after the orphans only because the *miskin* may be such that he can be put to use in service, so there is greater inclination to associate with him than with orphans. Also, the *miskin* is able to occupy himself with looking after himself and the affairs of his livelihood, whereas the orphan is not like that. Therefore Allah, undoubtedly, mentioned the orphan before the *miskin*.

**Third issue:** Kindness to the near of kin and to orphans must necessarily be distinct from *zakah* (obligatory almsgiving), because conjunction (*'atf*) requires difference.

**The sixth obligation:** the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And speak to people with goodness (husnan)﴾. On this there are several issues:

**First issue:** Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *hasanan* with a fatha on the *ha'* and the *sin*, in the sense of a description of the speech, as though He said: "Speak to people a good speech." The rest read *husnan* with a damma on the *ha'* and a sukun on the *sin*. They cited the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We enjoined upon man goodness to his parents (husnan)﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 8], and His words: ﴿Then He changed evil to good (husnan) after evil﴾ [al-Naml: 11]. On this there are several views:

First: al-Akhfash said its meaning is "speech that has goodness (husn)."

Second: It is permissible that *husnan* stands in place of *hasanan*, as you say "a just man" (*rajulun 'adl*).

Third: The meaning of His words "And speak to people with goodness" is so that your speech may be good; it is put in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*) of the verb indicated by the preceding statement.

Fourth: *husnan* means a speech which is good in itself, due to its extreme goodness.

**Second issue:** It is said: Why were they addressed with *qulu* (speak) after the report? The answer has three aspects:

One: It is by way of *iltifat* (shift of address), as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Until, when you are in ships and they sail with them﴾ [Yunus: 22].

Second: There is an ellipsis, meaning: We said to them, "Speak."

Third: A covenant is not made except by speech, as though it was said: "I said: Do not worship except Allah, and speak [to people with goodness]."

**Third issue:** They differed about who is addressed by His words, "And speak to people with goodness." It may be said that He took the covenant from them not to worship except Allah and to speak to people with goodness. It may also be said that He took the covenant from them not to worship except Allah, then He said to Moses and his community: "Speak to people with goodness." All of this is possible according to the wording, although the first is closer, so that the account is one unified narrative comprising the noblest customs and the highest moral qualities from every aspect.

**Fourth issue:** Some said: good speech is obligatory only with believers; with disbelievers and wrongdoers it is not. The evidence for this is two-fold:

First: It is obligatory to curse them, to censure them, and to fight them. How then can speech with them be good?

Second: The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged﴾ [al-Nisa': 148]. So He permitted public mention of evil to the one who has been wronged. Then, those who hold this view: some claim this ruling was abrogated (*mansukh*) by the verse of fighting, and some said it has been specified (*takhsis*). On this assumption, two possibilities arise here:

One of them: the specification is with respect to the addressee, meaning: "Speak good to the believers."

The second: the specification is with respect to the address, meaning: "Speak good in calling to Allah, the Exalted, and in enjoining good."

On the first view, specification applies to the addressee and not to the address; on the second, it applies to the address and not to the addressee. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir claimed that this generality remains on its apparent meaning and there is no need for specification, and this is the stronger view. The evidence for it is that Moses and Aaron, despite the greatness of their station, were commanded to be gentle and lenient with Pharaoh. Likewise, Muhammad ﷺ is commanded to be gentle and to avoid harshness. Likewise is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not revile those whom they call upon besides Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge﴾ [al-An'am: 108]; and His words: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]; and His words: ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199].

As for what they held onto first, that it is obligatory to curse them and censure them, so good speech with them is not possible: we say, first, we do not concede that it is obligatory to curse them and revile them, and the evidence for this is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not revile those whom they call upon besides Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 108]. Even if we concede that it is obligatory to curse them, yet we do not concede that cursing is not good speech.

Its explanation: good speech is not an expression for the speech they desire and love; rather, good speech is that from which they benefit. When we curse them and censure them so that they refrain from the evil deed, that meaning is beneficial for them, so that cursing is good and beneficial speech, just as a father's harshness of speech toward his child may be good and beneficial, in that the child refrains from the evil deed. Even if we concede that cursing them is not good speech, yet we do not concede that its obligation contradicts the obligation of good speech. Its explanation: there is no contradiction between a person deserving honour because of his kindness to us and deserving contempt because of his disbelief. Given this, why could the obligation of good speech with them not be possible?

As for what they held onto second, which is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged﴾ [al-Nisa': 148], the answer is: why could it not be that its intended meaning is exposing the state of the wrongdoer, so that people may guard against him? This is what is meant by the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Mention the wrongdoer for what is in him, so that people may beware of him."

**Fifth issue:** The people of verification (*ahl al-tahqiq*) said: Speech between people is either about religious matters or worldly matters. If it concerns religious matters, it is either in calling to faith, which is with disbelievers, or in calling to obedience, which is with the wrongdoer. As for calling to faith, it must be with good speech, as Allah, the Exalted, said to Moses and Aaron: ﴿Speak to him gently, perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]. Allah, the Exalted, commanded them to be gentle with Pharaoh despite their exalted rank and the extreme of Pharaoh's disbelief, rebellion, and arrogance against Allah, the Exalted. And He said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], and so on. As for calling the wrongdoers, good speech is considered therein. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition﴾ [al-Nahl: 125], and He said: ﴿Repel with that which is better, and then the one between you and him who has enmity will be as if he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. As for worldly matters, it is known by necessity that when the goal can be reached through gentle speech, nothing else is good. Thus it is established that all the etiquette of religion and worldly life falls under the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And speak to people with goodness﴾.

**Sixth issue:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that kindness to the near of kin, orphans and the needy was obligatory for them in their religion, and likewise good speech to people was obligatory for them, because taking the covenant indicates obligation. This is because the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, and because He censured them for turning away from it, and that indicates obligation. The command in our law also is likewise in some respects. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Zakah abrogated every right." This is weak, because there is no disagreement that whoever is in dire need, and we witness him in this state, it is obligatory upon us to give charity to him, even if zakah is not obligatory upon us; indeed, if his need is not met by zakah, then charity becomes obligatory. And there is no doubt about the obligation of speaking with people in a manner by which they are not harmed.

**The seventh and eighth obligations:** the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾, and their explanation has already preceded.

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, explained that He took the covenant from them in these eight obligations, He made clear that, despite His bounty to them in taking the covenant from them in all of that so that they would accept, and thus attain the supreme station with their Lord, they turned away and harmed themselves, and did not receive the blessings of their Lord with acceptance, despite the emphasis of the proofs and covenants upon them. This increases the ugliness of their state of turning away and aversion, because undertaking to oppose Allah, the Exalted, after the matter has been made fully clear and firmly established, is greater than opposition in ignorance. Commentators differed about who is meant by the words, "Then you turned away," on three views:

One of them: it refers to those who preceded from the Children of Israel.

Second: it is an address to those among the Jews in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: you turned away after the appearance of the miracles, like the turning away of your forefathers.

Third: what is meant by "Then you turned away" includes those who preceded with His words "and you are turning away," and those who came later.

As for the justification of the first view: if the first statement concerns those who preceded among them, then the apparent sense of the address requires that its end also concerns them, unless there is evidence requiring departure from this apparent sense. This is shown by the fact that He presented the first statement in the manner of displaying blessings by establishing proofs against them. Then He clarified afterwards that they turned away, except for a few of them, who remained upon what they had entered into.

As for the justification of the second view: the words "Then you turned away" are a direct address, which is more fitting for those present, whereas what preceded is a report, which is more fitting for their absent predecessors. So it is as though He, the Exalted, made clear that just as those covenants and pacts bound them to hold fast to them, that same obligation binds you, because you know what is in the Torah concerning Muhammad ﷺ and the truth of his prophethood. Thus the same proof that bound them binds you, yet you have turned away and aversion from it, except for a few of you, who are those who believed and submitted. This is a possibility.

As for the justification of the third view: when He, the Exalted, explained that He bestowed those blessings upon them, and then they turned away from them, this indicates the extreme ugliness of their deeds. The words "and you are turning away" are specific to those in the time of Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: you are in the position of the earlier people who turned away after these covenants were taken. For after you were informed of the proofs of the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ, you turned away from him and disbelieved in him. Thus, in this aversion you are in the same position as those earlier people in that turning away. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The Exalted's statement: ﴿And when We took your covenant: that you would not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes; then you acknowledged it, while you were witnesses.﴾

Know that this verse points to another kind of the favours of Allah upon them: that He imposed this obligation upon them, that they acknowledged its soundness, and then they broke the covenant concerning it.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: it is addressed to the scholars of the Jews in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: it is addressed to their predecessors, and its implied meaning is: "And when We took the covenant of your fathers."

The third: it is addressed to the predecessors and is a rebuke to the successors. The meaning of ﴿We took your covenant﴾ is: We commanded you, emphasised the command, and you accepted and acknowledged its binding obligation and its necessity.

* * *

As for the Exalted's statement: ﴿that you would not shed your blood﴾, there is a difficulty in it, namely that a human being is naturally inclined not to kill himself, and if that is so, there is no benefit in forbidding it.

The answer to this is given in several ways:

The first: this natural inclination may change, as is established among the people of India (Ahl al-Hind), who consider that by killing oneself they are freed from the world of corruption and join the world of light and goodness. Or many a person for whom life has become hard and some matter has become burdensome, so he kills himself. When the condition that a human being is naturally compelled not to kill himself no longer holds, it is valid for him to be obligated concerning it.

The second: the meaning is that some of you should not kill others of you, and the man treats the one who is connected to him by lineage and religion as himself. This is like the Exalted's saying: ﴿So kill yourselves﴾ (al-Baqarah: 54).

The third: when he kills another, it is as if he has killed himself, because he will be retaliated against (qisas).

[Page 156]

The fourth: do not expose yourselves to fighting those who kill you, for then you would have killed yourselves.

The fifth: do not shed the blood of those upon whom your worldly interests depend, for then you would be destroying yourselves.

As for the Exalted's statement: ﴿nor expel yourselves﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: do not do what would make you deserve to be expelled from your homes.

The second: the meaning is a prohibition against expelling some of them from their homes by others, because that is among the things in which the trial and hardship are great, to the point of nearing destruction.

As for the Exalted's statement: ﴿then you acknowledged it, while you were witnesses﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first, which is the strongest: that is, then you acknowledged the covenant and admitted against yourselves its binding obligation, while you were bearing witness against yourselves to it. This is like your saying: "So-and-so acknowledges against himself such-and-such," meaning he is a witness against himself.

The second: you admitted its acceptance, and some of you bore witness against others concerning it, because it was widespread and well known among them.

The third: and you are witnesses today, O assembly of Jews, to the acknowledgment of your predecessors of this covenant.

The fourth: the acknowledgment in the sense of consent to the matter and endurance upon it, as when it is said: "So-and-so does not accept injustice." The meaning then is that He, the Exalted, commands you with this, and you consented to it, so you persisted in it and bore witness to its obligation and soundness.

If it is asked: why did He say ﴿you acknowledged, while you were witnesses﴾ when the meaning is one? We answer that there are three opinions concerning it:

The first: "you acknowledged" refers to your predecessors, and "you are witnesses" now refers to their acknowledgment.

The second: "you acknowledged" at the time of the covenant that has passed, and "you are witnesses" after that.

The third: that it is for emphasis.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 85:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you are these people, killing yourselves and expelling a group of you from their homes, backing one another against them in sin and enmity. And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion was forbidden to you. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part? So what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the life of this world; and on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the severest punishment. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you are these people﴾, there is a difficulty here, because His saying "you" (antum) is for those present and "these people" (ha'ulaa') is for those absent, so how can the present be the same as the absent? Its answer comes in several ways:

The first: its estimated form is "Then you, O these people" (ya ha'ulaa').

The second: its estimated form is "Then you, I mean these present ones."

The third: that it has the meaning of "alladhi" (who), and its relative clause is "killing" (taqtuluna), and the position of taqtuluna is nominative if it is the predicate, and has no position if it is a relative clause. Al-Zajjaj said: similar to it in the relative clause is His saying: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17], meaning "And what is that which is in your right hand?"

The fourth: "these people" (ha'ulaa') is an emphasis for "you" (antum), and the predicate is "killing" (taqtuluna). As for His saying ﴿killing﴾?

Page 157
﴿yourselves﴾: we have mentioned the views on it, and the most correct is that the meaning is that some of you kill others among you, and the killing of some by others may be called killing of the self, since all are like a single self. We have also explained what is meant by expulsion from homes.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿backing one another against them in sin and enmity﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: ʿĀsim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "taẓāharūna" with the ẓāʾ lightened, while the rest read it with the ẓāʾ doubled. The reading with lightening is by deleting one of the two tāʾs, as in His saying: ﴿And do not cooperate﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. The reading with doubling is by assimilating the tāʾ into the ẓāʾ, as in His saying: ﴿You clung heavily﴾. Deletion is lighter and assimilation is more indicative of the original form.

The second issue: know that tazāhur (backing one another) is cooperation. Since expulsion from homes and killing some by others are among things by which strife is magnified, and which require power and dominance, Allah the Exalted explained that they did it by seeking the help of those who back them in wrongdoing and enmity.

The third issue: the verse indicates that just as wrongdoing is forbidden, so too is aiding the wrongdoer in his wrongdoing forbidden. If it is said: Did not Allah, when He empowered the wrongdoer to wrong and removed the obstacles and barriers and imposed upon him the desire that calls to wrongdoing, thereby assist him in wrongdoing? So if aiding the wrongdoer in his wrongdoing were ugly, it would necessarily follow that this should not occur from Allah the Exalted. The answer: although He, exalted is He, enabled the wrongdoer to do that, He has restrained him from wrongdoing by threat and reproof, unlike the one who helps the wrongdoer in his wrongdoing, for he encourages him to it, makes it appealing in his eyes, and calls him to it. Thus the difference is clear.

The fourth issue: the verse does not indicate that the sin of the helper is equal in degree to the sin of the one who directly commits the act; rather the evidence indicates that it is less than it, because if assistance occurred without direct commission, it would not have an effect in bringing about the wrongdoing, and if direct commission occurred without assistance, the harm and wrongdoing would still occur. So we know that direct commission is more weighty in prohibition than assistance.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Nāfiʿ, ʿĀsim and al-Kisāʾī read "ʾusārā tufādūhum" with the alif in both; Ḥamzah alone read both without alif; and the rest read "ʾusārā" with the alif and "tufdūhum" without alif. "Al-Asrā" is the plural of asīr, like jarīḥ and jarḥā. Regarding ʾusārā there are two views:

One: that it is the plural of asrā, like sakrā and sukārā.

The second: that it is the plural of asīr. Abū ʿAmr distinguished between al-Asrā and al-Usārā, and said: al-Usārā are those who are in bonds, and al-Asrā are those who are in the hand, as if he went to the view that ʾusārā is more intensive. Thaʿlab denied that, and ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā said: the preferred reading is ʾusārā with the alif, because most of the imams hold it, and because it indicates the meaning of plurality more, since it is said in abundance, while it is rare in the singular, like shukāʿā; and because it is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

The second issue: tufdūhum and tufādūhum are two well-known dialects. Tufdūhum is from al-fidāʾ, which is the compensation for a thing in order to safeguard it; one says: fadāhu fidyatan. Tufādūhum is from al-mufādāh.

The third issue: the majority of the exegetes said: what is meant by His saying ﴿you ransom them﴾ is a description of them as doing what is obedience, namely the release from captivity by paying wealth or otherwise, so that they return to their disbelief. Abū Muslim mentioned that it is the opposite of that, and the meaning is that you, along with killing and expulsion, when a captive falls into your hands, you are not satisfied with him except by taking wealth, even though that is forbidden to you; then at that point you bring him out of captivity. Abū Muslim and the exegetes said: they were only led to this by His saying: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾. This is weak, because this statement refers back to what preceded concerning the Prophet ﷺ and what was revealed to them, and the meaning is that if in the Book which is with you there is the account of Muhammad and you denied it, then you have believed in part of the Book and disbelieved in part. Both views allow the word mufādāh, because the one who pays for the captive is described as having ransomed him, and the one who takes from him for release is also described as such. However, what the exegetes have agreed upon is closer, because the return of His saying ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ to what was mentioned earlier in this verse is more preferable than its return to matters mentioned after several verses.

The fourth issue: some said: those who were expelled and those who were ransomed are one group, because Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr were two brothers like al-Aws and al-Khazraj; they split, so al-Naḍīr were with al-Khazraj and Qurayẓah were with al-Aws. Each group fought alongside its allies, and when they prevailed they destroyed their homes and expelled them; and when a man from either of the two groups was captured, they gathered for him until they ransomed him. The Arabs reproached them and said: How do you fight them and then ransom them? They would say: We were commanded to ransom them, and fighting them was forbidden to us; but we are ashamed to humiliate our allies. Others said: those whom they expelled were not the ones ransomed; rather they were another people, and Allah reproached them for it.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their expulsion was forbidden to you﴾, in His saying ﴿and it﴾ there are two views:

The first: that it is the pronoun of the matter and situation, as if it were said: the matter is that their expulsion is forbidden to you.

The second: that it is a reference back to the expulsion, repeated for emphasis, because it has been separated from it by speech; so its position on this view is nominative, as if it were said: and their expulsion is forbidden to you; then the mention of their expulsion is repeated, clarifying the first.

As for His saying: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾, the scholars differed concerning it in two ways:

One of them: their expulsion is disbelief, and their ransoming is belief. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Qatādah and Ibn Jurayj. He did not blame them for the ransoming; rather He blamed them for the contradiction, since they did part of what was obligatory and left out part. Contradiction may be more deserving of blame. It is not said: suppose that expulsion was a disobedience; why then did He call it disbelief, when it is established that the disobedient does not disbelieve? We say: perhaps they explicitly stated that the expulsion was not obligatory, although the explicit text of the Torah indicated its obligation.

The second: what is meant by it is to alert to the fact that in their adherence to the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him, while denying Muhammad ﷺ, although the proof concerning both is equal, is a course like the way of their predecessors, in believing in part and disbelieving in part, while all are equal in the covenant.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you are these people, killing yourselves﴾, the root of khizy is humiliation and abhorrence. One says: Allah has disgraced him (akhzāhu Allāh), when He abhors him and removes him far away. It is said: its root is shame; so when it is said: Allah has disgraced him, it is as if it were said: He placed him in a position that is shameful. In sum, what is meant by it is great reproach. They differed concerning this disgrace in several ways:

The first: al-Ḥasan said: what is meant is the jizyah (poll tax) and humiliation. This is weak, because there is no indication that the jizyah was established in their law; rather, if we take the verse as referring to those in the time of Muhammad ﷺ, this view is sound, because among the disgrace that befalls the dhimmis is taking the jizyah from them.

The second: the expulsion of the Banū al-Naḍīr from their homes, and the killing of the Banū Qurayẓah and the taking of their offspring as captives. This is valid only if we take the verse as referring to those present in the time of Muhammad ﷺ.

The third, and it is the preferred: that what is meant is great reproach and extreme abasement, without restricting that to some aspects rather than others. The indefinite form in His saying "khizy" indicates that the reproach is at its greatest extent.

As for His saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the severest punishment﴾, there is a question: the punishment of the materialists who deny the Creator must be more severe than the punishment of the Jews, so how did He say concerning the Jews: ﴿they will be returned to the severest punishment﴾? The answer: what is meant is that it is more severe than the disgrace occurring in this world. The word "al-ashadd" (severest), although absolute, is intended to be severer from this aspect.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ and ʿĀsim read with the tāʾ of address, while the rest read with the yāʾ of the third person. The reasoning of the first: building on the beginning of the speech, "Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?" The reasoning of the second: building on it being the end of the speech; and the choice of address is because most hold it, and because it indicates the meaning more, by giving precedence to address over the third person when they are combined.

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a severe threat and a great deterrent from disobedience, and a great glad tidings for obedience, because if heedlessness is impossible for Him, glorified is He, despite being the most capable of the capable, then rights will inevitably reach their rightful owners.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 86:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter. So their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be helped.﴾

Know that combining the attainment of the pleasures of this world and the pleasures of the Hereafter is impossible and not feasible. God, glorified is He, enabled the responsible person (al-mukallaf) to attain whichever of the two he wills and desires. When he occupies himself with attaining one of them, he has thereby forfeited the other for himself. God made what the Jews turned away from, namely faith in what is in their books, and what they obtained in their hands of disbelief and the pleasures of this world, such as buying and selling, [a matter of] exchange. This is from God, exalted is He, in the utmost censure of them, because the one who is cheated in buying and selling in this world is blameworthy, to the point that he is described as having deranged his mind; so the one who buys the goods of this world with the Hereafter is more deserving of blame.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So their punishment will not be lightened﴾, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: concerning the entry of the particle fa' (فَ, "so") in His saying ﴿so it will not be lightened﴾, there are two opinions:

One of them: it is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon ﴿have bought﴾. The other opinion: it carries the meaning of a response to a command (jawab al-amr), like your saying: "Those are the misguided ones, pay attention, so there is no good in them." The first is more likely (awjah), because it does not require any supposition (idmar).

The second issue: some interpreted the lightening (takhfif) as meaning that it will not cease but will endure, because if it ceased, it would have been lightened. Others interpreted it as referring to its severity, not to its perpetuity. The preferable view is to say: the punishment may be lightened by its cessation, and it may be lightened by being lessened at every time or at some times. So when He, exalted is He, describes their punishment as not being lightened, that necessitates the negation of all that we have mentioned.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, there are two possibilities in it:

Most of them interpreted it as the negation of help in the Hereafter, meaning that no one will repel this punishment from them, nor will they be helped against one who wishes to punish them. Among them are those who interpreted it as the negation of help in this world. The first is preferable, because He, exalted is He, made that a recompense for their conduct, and for this reason He said: ﴿So their punishment will not be lightened﴾. This description befits only the Hereafter, because the punishment of this world, even if it occurs, becomes like the prescribed legal penalties (hudud) imposed upon the negligent; and because the disbelievers may become dominant over the believers at some times.

The Exalted said: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and followed him up with messengers after him. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. So is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you grew arrogant? Some you denied, and some you killed.﴾

Know that this is another kind of the blessings which Allah poured out upon them, and yet they met it with disbelief and vile deeds. This is because He, exalted is He, when He described the condition of the Jews earlier, saying that they opposed the command of Allah in killing their own selves and in expelling some of them from their homes, and clarified that by this conduct they had bought the worldly life in exchange for the Hereafter, He added to their rebuke with what He mentioned in this verse. As for "the Book," it is the Torah, which Allah gave to him all at once. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that when the Torah was revealed, Allah commanded Moses to carry it, but he was not able to do so. Then Allah sent for each letter of it an angel, but they were not able to carry it either, so Allah lightened it for Moses and he carried it.

* * *

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We followed him up with messengers﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: "qaffaynā" means "We caused to follow," derived from the saying that something comes behind another thing at its back (qafā), i.e., after the tail of something from its tail. Its parallel is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 44].

The second issue: It is reported that after Moses, peace be upon him, until the days of Jesus, peace be upon him, messengers kept coming in succession, and some of them appeared one after another, while the sharia remained one until the days of Jesus, peace be upon him, for he, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, came with a renewed sharia. They argued for the soundness of this from the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We followed him up with messengers﴾, for it requires that they were on one standard in the sharia, following one another in it. The Qadi said: The second messenger cannot be upon the sharia of the first, so as not to lead to that same sharia without addition or subtraction, especially since that sharia is preserved and its knowledge is attainable through mass transmission from the earlier ones. For if the messenger were in this condition, he could not know from any source except what had already been known or could be known beforehand. Just as it is not permissible for Allah to send a messenger with no sharia at all, which clarifies the rational matters for this reason, so too is the case in our issue. Thus it is established that the messengers who came after Moses, peace be upon him, must have brought a new sharia, if the first one was preserved, or one that revived some of what had been effaced of the first sharia. The response: Why is it not permissible that the purpose of sending these messengers was to implement that earlier sharia upon the community, or another kind of divine kindness that only Allah knows? In sum, the Qadi did not produce in this proof anything but a restatement of the claim. So why did he say that it is not permissible to send these messengers except for a new sharia or for reviving a sharia that had been effaced? Was the dispute about anything but this?

The third issue: These messengers are: Joshua, Samuel, Simeon, David, Solomon, Shaʿyaʾ (Isaiah), Armiyaʾ (Jeremiah), ʿUzayr (Ezra), Ezekiel (Ḥizqīl), Elijah (Ilyās), Elisha (al-Yasaʿ), Jonah (Yūnus), Zechariah (Zakariyyā), John (Yaḥyā), and others.

* * *

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear proofs﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: The reason Allah mentioned the messengers in general and then detailed the mention of Jesus is that those messengers before him came with the sharia of Moses and were therefore followers of him, but Jesus was not like that, for his law abrogated most of the law of Moses, peace be upon him.
