The second issue: It is said that Jesus in Syriac is Ishuʿ, and Mary means "servant." It is also said that Mary in Hebrew means a woman, like zīr means a man, and it was on this basis that the verse of Ruʾbah was explained:

I said to a zīr whose mariyyah did not reach him.

The third issue: Regarding "the clear proofs" there are several views:
First: the miracles, such as the raising of the dead and the like, reported from Ibn ʿAbbas.
Second: that they are the Gospel (al-Injīl).
Third, and it is the strongest: that all of these enter into it, because the miracle demonstrates the soundness of his prophethood, just as the Gospel demonstrates the manner of his sharia, so there is no sense in restricting it.

* * *

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: It was read "wa-ayyadnāhu." Ibn Kathir read "al-Qudsi" with lightening (takhfīf), and the rest read it with emphasis (tathqīl), and both are dialects, like ruʿb and ruʿb.

The second issue: They differed about "the Spirit" in several ways:

First: that it is Gabriel, peace be upon him. It was called that for several reasons:

The first: that what is meant by "the Holy Spirit" is the holy spirit, as one says "the generosity of Ḥātim" and "a man of truth" (ṣidq); so Gabriel was described with this as an honour for him and a declaration of the loftiness of his rank with Allah, exalted is He.

The second: Gabriel, peace be upon him, was named so because religion lives through him just as the body lives through the spirit, for he is the one entrusted with bringing down revelation to the prophets, and those charged with it live in their religion through it.

The third: that the predominant quality of his is spirituality, and so too all the angels, except that his spirituality is more complete and perfect.

The fourth: Gabriel, peace be upon him, was called a spirit because he was not contained by the loins of stallions nor the wombs of mothers.

Second: What is meant by "the Holy Spirit" is the Gospel, as He said in the Qur'an: ﴿a spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52], and it was so called because religion lives by it and the affairs of the world are organized on its account.

Third: that it is the Name by which he, peace be upon him, used to give life to the dead, reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Fourth: that it is the spirit which was breathed into him, and the "Qudus" is Allah, exalted is He, so He attributed the spirit of Jesus, peace be upon him, to Himself, honouring and glorifying him, as one says "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah," reported from al-Rabiʿ. According to this, what is meant is the spirit by which a human lives.

Know that applying the name "spirit" to Gabriel, to the Gospel, and to the Greatest Name is figurative, because the spirit is the wind moving through the human passages and openings, and it is known that these three were not like that; rather, each of these three was called "spirit" by way of analogy, in that just as the spirit is the cause of a man's life, so Gabriel, peace be upon him, is the cause of the life of hearts through knowledge; the Gospel is the cause of the manifestation and life of the laws; and the Greatest Name is the cause of being approached through it to attain aims. However, the resemblance between the referent of "spirit" and Gabriel is more complete, for several reasons:

First: because Gabriel, peace be upon him, was created from subtle luminous air, so the resemblance is more complete, and therefore applying the name "spirit" to Gabriel is more fitting.

Second: this naming is more evident in him than in others.

Third: that the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾, mean "We strengthened him," and the intended strengthening is assistance; attributing assistance to Gabriel, peace be upon him, is literal, while attributing it to the Gospel and the Greatest Name is figurative, so that is more fitting.

Fourth: that the particular connection of Jesus with Gabriel, peace be upon them both, is among the most emphatic forms of special connection, such that none of the prophets, peace be upon them, had the like of it, for he is the one who gave Mary the good news of her child, and Jesus, peace be upon him, was born from the breath of Gabriel, peace be upon him; he is the one who nurtured him in all circumstances, and he would travel with him wherever he went, and he was with him when he ascended to heaven.

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿So is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you grew arrogant?﴾, this is the utmost of blame against them, for the Jews of the Children of Israel, whenever a messenger came to them with something contrary to their desires, they denied him, and if they were able to kill him, they killed him. They were like this only because they desired elevation in this world, sought its pleasures, wanted leadership over their common people, and took their wealth unjustly; and the messengers would nullify this for them, so they denied them on account of that, and deceived their common folk into thinking they were liars, and argued for this through distortion and bad interpretation. Among them were those who acted arrogantly toward the prophets, as Iblis acted arrogantly toward Adam.

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿Some you denied, and some you kill﴾, one might ask: Why was it not said "and some you killed"? The answer to this is in two ways:

One: that the present tense is intended, because the matter is grave, so it is meant to bring it to mind and picture it in the hearts.

The second: that it is meant "some you will kill afterward," because you attempted to kill Muhammad (ﷺ), had I not protected him from you; and for that reason you bewitched him and poisoned a sheep for him. And when he (ﷺ) was dying he said: "The morsel of Khaybar has not ceased to trouble me; now is the time of the cutting of my aorta." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 88:

Allah's words: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are wrapped up." Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is it that they believe.﴾

As for "ghulf" (wrapped up), there are three interpretations:

First: it is the plural of aghlaf, and aghlaf means that which is in a covering (ghilaf), meaning: "Our hearts are veiled by coverings that prevent the effect of your call from reaching them."

Second: al-Asamm reported from some of them that their hearts are "ghulf" in the sense of being filled with knowledge and brimming with wisdom, so there is no need for them, with it, for the law of Muhammad, upon him be peace.

Third: "ghulf" means like an empty sheath, with nothing in it that indicates the truth of your statement.

As for the Mu'tazilah, they chose the first interpretation. Then they said: this verse indicates that there is nothing in the hearts of the disbelievers that prevents them from faith, neither a wrapping, nor a covering, nor a barrier, as the Mujbirah (determinists) claim. For if it were so, these Jews would have been truthful in this statement, and Allah would not have refuted them with His words: ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾, because He, exalted is He, only blames the liar who is in falsehood, not the truthful one who is rightly guided and excused. They said: and this indicates that the meaning of His words: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears is deafness﴾ [al-Kahf: 57], and His words: ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles upon their necks﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8], and His words: ﴿And We have put before them a barrier﴾ [Ya-Sin: 9], is not that they are prevented from faith; rather, what is meant is either the withholding of divine favours (al-altaf), or the likening of their state, in their persistence in disbelief, to the state of one compelled to disbelieve. They said: and the parallel to Allah's blaming of the Jews for this statement is His blaming of the disbelievers for a similar statement, which is His words: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you there is a barrier"﴾ [Fussilat: 5]. Had the matter been as the Mujbirah claim, these people would have been truthful in that, and had they been truthful, He would not have blamed them; rather, what He related from them would be a manifestation of their excuse and a removal of blame from them.

Know that we have explained three interpretations of "ghulf", so it is not obligatory to be certain of any one of them without evidence. Even if we grant that the intended meaning is that interpretation, why do you say that the verse indicates that this statement is blameworthy?

As for His words: ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾, there are several answers:

First: this indicates that He cursed them because of their disbelief. As for your claim that He cursed them only because of this statement, perhaps He related a statement from them and then clarified that among their condition is that they are cursed because of their disbelief.

Second: what is meant by His words: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are wrapped up"﴾ is that they mentioned it by way of a question in the sense of denial, meaning: "Our hearts are not in wrappings or coverings; rather, they are strong, and our perceptions are luminous. Then, with these perceptions and understandings, we have reflected upon your proofs, O Muhammad, and we found nothing strong in them." When they stated this false boasting, Allah indeed cursed them for their disbelief that resulted from this statement.

Third: perhaps their hearts were not in coverings; rather, they were knowing of the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, as He said: ﴿They recognise it as they recognise their own sons﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. Yet they denied that recognition and claimed that their hearts were wrapped up and not aware of that. So their disbelief was disbelief born of obstinacy, and therefore Allah cursed them for that disbelief.

As for His words: ﴿so little is it that they believe﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: regarding its interpretation there are three views:

First: that "qalilan" (little) is an attribute of the believers, meaning: only a few of them believe. This is related from Qatadah, al-Asamm, and Abu Muslim.

Second: that it is an attribute of faith, meaning: they believe only in a little of what they were charged with, because they used to believe in Allah, but they used to disbelieve in the messengers.

Third: its meaning is that they do not believe at all, neither a little nor a lot, as it is said: "qalilan ma yaf'alu" meaning "he does not do at all." Al-Kisa'i said: the Arabs say, "We passed by a land, little does it grow [anything]," meaning it grows nothing. The first view is preferable, because it is parallel to His words: ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe, except a few﴾ [al-Nisa': 155], and because when the preceding clause explicitly mentions a people, the exception must apply to some of those people.

The second issue: regarding the accusative case of "qalilan" there are several views:

First: the sense is "imanan qalilan ma yu'minun," where "ma" is superfluous, and it refers to their belief in part of the Book.

Second: it is accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning "bi-qalilin yu'minun" (they believe in a little).

Third: "fa-sarru qalilan ma yu'minun" (so they became few who believe).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, Verse 89:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God, confirming what they possessed, and before that they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved; but when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of God is upon the disbelievers.﴾

Know that this is a kind of the abominable deeds of the Jews. As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿a Book﴾, the scholars agree that this Book is the Qur'an, because His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿confirming what is with them﴾ indicates that this Book is other than what is with them, and that is none but the Qur'an. As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿confirming what is with them﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: there is no doubt that the Qur'an confirms what is with them in a matter that relates to their obligation to affirm Muhammad (ﷺ) as a prophet. What is fitting for this is that it agrees with what is with them regarding the evidence of his prophethood, since they knew that it does not agree with what is with them in the rest of the laws. We also know that agreement was not intended in the domain of the proofs of the Qur'an, because all the Books of God are like that. And since the whole [of that alternative] is ruled out, it is established that what is meant is its agreement with their Books concerning what is specific to prophethood and what points to it of signs, descriptions and attributes.

The second issue: it has been read as *muṣaddiqan* (confirming) in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, a state clause). If it is asked: how is it permissible for it to be in the accusative from an indefinite noun (*nakirah*)? We reply: when an indefinite noun is qualified, it becomes specified, so it is valid for a *ḥāl* to take the accusative from it. And ﴿a Book﴾ has been qualified by His saying: ﴿from God﴾.

The third issue: concerning the answer to *lammā* (when/since), there are three possibilities.

The first: it is omitted, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which the mountains were moved...﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 31], where its answer is omitted, and it is: "this Qur'an would be..." This is from al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj.

The second: it is a repetition because of the length of the speech, and the answer is ﴿they disbelieved in it﴾, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Does he promise you that you...﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 35] up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 35]. This is from al-Mubarrad.

The third: the *fa'* (then) is the answer to the first *lammā*, and ﴿they disbelieved in it﴾ is the answer to the second *lammā*. This is like His saying: ﴿And if guidance comes to you from Me, then whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear upon them...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38], to the end of the verse. This is from al-Farra'.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And before that they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved﴾, there are several views concerning the occasion of revelation:

The first: the Jews, before the mission of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the descent of the Qur'an, used to seek victory, that is, they asked for triumph and support, and they used to say: "O God, grant us victory and support us through the unlettered Prophet."

The second: they used to say to their opponents at the time of fighting: "This is a prophet whose time has drawn near; he will support us against you." This is from Ibn Abbas.

The third: they used to ask the Arabs about his birth and describe him, saying that the prophet has such-and-such attributes, and they would search for him. ﴿Against those who disbelieved﴾ means against the polytheists of the Arabs. This is from Abu Muslim.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning the Banu Qurayza and an-Nadir. They used to seek victory against al-Aws and al-Khazraj through the Messenger of God before the mission. This is from Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and as-Suddi.

The fifth: it was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews. Whenever they read and mentioned Muhammad in the Torah, and that he was a sent one, and that he was from the Arabs, they would ask the polytheists of the Arabs about those attributes, to know whether there had been born among them someone whose condition matched the condition of this sent one.

* * *

[Page 165]

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: the verse indicates that they were acquainted with his prophethood. And there is an objection concerning this: the Torah was transmitted by mass transmission (*tawātur*, a report so widely transmitted that its falsehood cannot be conceived). Either it is said that the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) occurred in it in detail, meaning a statement that the person described with such-and-such form and such-and-such conduct will appear in such-and-such year, in such-and-such place; or this description did not exist in this manner. If it was the first, the people would have been compelled to know the Torah's testimony to the truthfulness of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him). How then is it permissible for a mass-transmitted group to agree upon lying? And if the description was not in this quality, then it would not follow from the attributes mentioned in the Torah that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a messenger. So how did God, Exalted is He, say: ﴿But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾? The answer: the description mentioned in the Torah was a general description, and when they did not recognize his prophethood merely by those attributes, but rather by the appearance of miracles, those attributes became as confirmation. Therefore God, Exalted is He, censured them for denial.

The second issue: it may be said that they disbelieved in him for several reasons:

The first: they were thinking that the one sent would be from the Children of Israel, because of the great number of prophets who had come from the Children of Israel. They used to encourage people toward their religion and call them to it. So when God, Exalted is He, sent Muhammad from the Arabs, from the offspring of Ishmael (may the blessings of God be upon him), this weighed heavily upon them, so they openly denied and opposed their former path.

The second: their acknowledgment of his prophethood would have required the loss of their leadership and their wealth, so they refused and persisted in denial.

The third: perhaps they thought that he was sent only to the Arabs, and therefore they undoubtedly disbelieved in him.

The third issue: He, Exalted is He, declared them disbelievers after He had shown that they knew of his prophethood, and this indicates that disbelief is not merely ignorance of God, Exalted is He.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the curse of God is upon the disbelievers﴾, what is meant is distance from the good things of the Hereafter, because one who is distanced from the good things of this world is not necessarily cursed. If it is asked: did He not mention in the preceding verse: ﴿And speak kindly to people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83], and say: ﴿And do not revile those whom they call upon besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge﴾ [al-An'am: 108]? We reply: a general statement may be subject to specification. Moreover, we have already explained earlier that cursing one who deserves to be cursed is part of good speech. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 90:**

[Page 166]

Know that the investigation into the reality of بِئْسَما (*bi'sama*, "how evil is that which") occurs only in several issues:

**The first issue:** The origin of نِعْمَ (*ni'ma*, "how good") and بِئْسَ (*bi'sa*, "how evil") is with a fatha on the first letter and a kasra on the second, like our saying عَلِمَ (*'alima*, "he knew"). However, when the second letter is a guttural letter (ḥarf ḥalq) and is kasra, four dialectal forms are permissible:

The first: according to the origin, meaning with a fatha on the first letter and a kasra on the second.

The second: assimilating the first to the second, which is with a kasra on the nūn and on the ʿayn, and similarly it is said فِخِذٌ (*fikhidh*, "thigh") with a kasra on the fā' and the khā'. Although they flee from combining two kasras, they permitted it here because the guttural letter is followed by what is adjacent to it.

The third: making the kasra-marked guttural letter sukūn and leaving what precedes it as it was, so it is said نَعْمَ وبَئْسَ with a fatha on the first letter and sukūn on the second, just as it is said فَخْذٌ (*fakhdh*) with a fatha on the fā' and sukūn on the khā'.

The fourth: that the guttural letter be made sukūn and its kasra transferred to the letter before it, so it is said نِعْمَ with a kasra on the nūn and sukūn on the ʿayn, just as it is said فِخْذٌ with a kasra on the fā' and sukūn on the khā'.

Know that this last change, although it is permissible when these two words are used without qualification, they have made it obligatory for both of them, because they have departed from what the past verbs are designed for, namely reporting the existence of the verbal noun in past time, and have become words of praise and blame, and the intention is emphasis in praise and blame. So this obligatory change in the wording indicates the change from the original in meaning. Thus they say نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ (*ni'ma al-rajulu Zaydun*, "Zayd is an excellent man"), and they do not mention it in the original form except in poetic necessity, as al-Mubarrad recited:

*Then ransom for the Banu Qays, for what has befallen the people of evil and harm,*

*What my two feet have carried—indeed they are the best of those who strive in the grave matter.*

**The second issue:** They are two verbs from نَعِمَ يَنْعَمُ (*na'ima ya'manu*) and بَئِسَ يَبْأَسُ (*ba'isa ya'va's*). The evidence for this is the entry of the tā' which is the sign of the feminine into them, so it is said نِعْمَتْ and بِئْسَتْ. Al-Farrā' treats them as if they were nouns, and he argues with the words of Ḥassān ibn Thābit, may Allah be pleased with him:

*Are we not the excellent neighbour, whose house is frequented, among people, both the one with much wealth and the one in poverty?*

And with what is narrated: a Bedouin was given the good news of a daughter, and it was said to him, "How excellent is your newborn, your daughter," and he said, "By Allah, she is not an excellent newborn!" The Basrians answer him that this is by way of quotation (ḥikāya).

**The third issue:** Know that نِعْمَ وبِئْسَ are two roots for goodness and badness, and their agent (fā'il) is a noun that encompasses the whole class (jins), either explicit or implicit, and the explicit one is in two forms:

The first: like your saying نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ, you do not mean a man other than the man, but you intend the man in an absolute sense.

The second: like your saying نِعْمَ غُلامُ الرَّجُلِ زَيْدٌ. As for his saying:

*So excellent is the companion of a people who have no weapons, and the companion of the caravan is ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.*

This is rare, and it was said that this was because his saying "and the companion of the caravan" may indicate the intended meaning, since the referent is one; so when he brought the definite article in "the caravan," it is as if he had brought it in "the people."

As for the implicit, it is like your saying نِعْمَ رَجُلًا زَيْدٌ. The original is نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ رَجُلًا زَيْدٌ, then the mention of the first was omitted because the indefinite accusative noun indicates it. رَجُلًا is put in the accusative as a specifier (tamyīz, "specification"), like its use in your saying عِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا (*ʿishrūna rajulan*, "twenty men"), and the specifier can only be indefinite. Do you not see that no one says عِشْرُونَ الدِّرْهَمَ? If they had introduced the definite article into this and said نِعْمَ الرَّجُلَ in the accusative, it would have defeated the purpose, since if they wished to bring the definite article they would have put it in the nominative and said نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ, and spared themselves the burden of the implicit. They implied the agent only for the sake of brevity, since نِعْمَ رَجُلًا indicates the class over which it is preferred.

[Page 167]

**The fourth issue:** If you say نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ, it is of two possibilities:

One of them: that it is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), as if it were said: زَيْدٌ نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ (*Zaydun ni'ma al-rajul*, "Zayd, how excellent the man is"). You have postponed Zayd while the intention is to put him first, as you say مَرَرْتُ بِهِ المِسْكِينُ (*marartu bihi al-miskīn*, "I passed by him, the poor man"), meaning: "the poor man, I passed by him." As for the pronoun that refers back to the subject, since الرَّجُلُ, being common, encompasses the class, Zayd is included under it, so he takes the place of the mention that refers back to it.

The other possibility: that Zayd in your saying نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ is the predicate of an omitted subject, as if, when it was said نِعْمَ الرَّجُلُ, it was asked, "Who is this one who is praised?" and it was answered, "Zayd," meaning "he is Zayd."

**The fifth issue:** The one specified by praise or blame must only be of the same class as what is mentioned after نِعْمَ وبِئْسَ, like زَيْدٌ مِنَ الرِّجالِ (*Zaydun min al-rijāl*, "Zayd among men"). When that is so, the genitive construction referring to the people in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ساءَ مَثَلًا القَوْمُ الَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا﴾ ("Evil is the example of the people who denied Our signs," Q. 7:177) is omitted, and its estimate is ساءَ مَثَلًا مَثَلُ القَوْمِ الَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا ("Evil is the example of the example of the people who denied Our signs"). Now that we have summarized these issues, let us return to the exegesis.

\* \* \*

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهم أنْ يَكْفُرُوا﴾ ("How evil is that for which they sold their souls: that they disbelieve..."), there are two issues in it:

**The first issue:** ما (*ma*) is an indefinite accusative noun that explains the agent of بِئْسَ, in the sense of "how evil a thing is the thing for which they sold their souls," and the one specified by blame is أَنْ يَكْفُرُوا ("that they disbelieve").

**The second issue:** Regarding the purchase (*shirā'*) here there are two opinions:

One of them: that it means selling (*bay'*). Its explanation is that when Allah, exalted is He, enabled the responsible person (mukallaf) to have faith, which leads him to Paradise, and disbelief, which leads him to the Fire, his choosing one of them over the other becomes like choosing to acquire one commodity over another commodity. When he chooses faith, in which lies his success and salvation, it is said: "How excellent is what he bought!" Since the purpose of sale and purchase is the exchange of ownership of a possessed thing, each of the two may be described as a seller and a buyer, because this meaning occurs from each of them. Thus the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ is valid, namely that the meaning is: "They sold their souls with their disbelief," because what they obtained in exchange for the benefits of their souls was disbelief, so they became sellers of their souls through it.

The second opinion, which is more correct in my view: when the responsible person fears for himself from the punishment of Allah, he performs deeds that he thinks will save him from punishment, so it is as if he had bought his soul with those deeds. These Jews, since they believed that what they did would save them from punishment and bring them to reward, thought that they had bought their souls with them. So Allah, exalted is He, censured them, saying: ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾. This opinion is closer to the meaning and the wording than the first. Then He, exalted is He, explained what they bought their souls with, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿أنْ يَكْفُرُوا بِما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down"). There is no doubt that what is meant by this is their disbelief in the Qur'an, because the address is to the Jews, and they were believers in other than it. Then He explained the reason for which they chose this disbelief in what Allah has sent down, saying: ﴿بَغْيًا﴾ ("out of envy"), and by this He indicated their aim in disbelief, as one says "so-and-so is hostile to so-and-so out of envy," thereby drawing attention to his aim. Had it not been for this statement, we would have allowed that they disbelieved out of ignorance and not out of envy.

Know that this verse indicates that envy (ḥasad) is forbidden. Since rebellion (baghy) may have many causes, Allah, exalted is He, explained their aim from this rebellion in His saying: ﴿أنْ يُنَزِّلَ اللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ عَلى مَن يَشاءُ مِن عِبادِهِ﴾ ("that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants"). The story suits only what we have related, that they thought this great favour, the awaited prophethood, would be found among their own people; when they found it among the Arabs, this led them to rebellion and envy.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ عَلى غَضَبٍ﴾ ("So they returned with anger upon anger"), there are issues in it:

\* \* \*

[Page 168]

**The first issue:** Regarding the interpretation of the two angers, there are several opinions:

The first: it is necessary to establish two causes for the two angers:

One of them: what has preceded, namely their denial of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, and what was revealed to him. The other: their denial of Muḥammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, and what was revealed to him. Thus it became entering into anger after anger and wrath after wrath from Him, exalted is He, because they entered into one cause after another. This is the saying of al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, ʿIkrima, Abū al-ʿĀliya and Qatāda.

The second: the intention is not merely to establish two angers, but to establish kinds of anger, successive, for successive matters that proceeded from them, such as their saying: ﴿عُزَيْرٌ ابْنُ اللَّهِ﴾ ("ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," Q. 9:30), ﴿يَدُ اللَّهِ مَغْلُولَةٌ﴾ ("the hand of Allah is chained," Q. 5:64), ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ فَقِيرٌ ونَحْنُ أغْنِياءُ﴾ ("Allah is poor and we are rich," Q. 3:181), and other kinds of their disbelief. This is the saying of ʿAṭā' and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr.

The third: that what is meant is the emphasis and multiplication of anger, because this disbelief, although it is one, is great. This is the saying of Abū Muslim.

The fourth: the first is by their worship of the calf, and the second by their concealing the description of Muḥammad and denying his prophethood. This is from al-Suddī.

**The second issue:** Anger (*ghaḍab*) is an expression for the change that occurs to a human being in his temperament when the blood of his heart boils because of witnessing a hateful matter. This is impossible with regard to Allah, exalted is He, so it is understood as His will to harm the one who disobeys Him by cursing and by ordering that.

**The third issue:** It is valid to describe Him, exalted is He, with anger, and that His anger increases and multiplies, and this is valid of Him just as it is valid regarding punishment. So His anger toward the one who disbelieves in one characteristic is not like His anger toward the one who disbelieves in many characteristics.

\* \* \*

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ولِلْكافِرِينَ عَذابٌ مُهِينٌ﴾ ("and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment"), there are issues in it:

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿ولِلْكافِرِينَ عَذابٌ مُهِينٌ﴾ has a distinction over His saying ولَهم عَذابٌ مُهِينٌ (*wa lahum ʿadhābun muhīn*, "and for them is a humiliating punishment"), because in the first expression those disbelievers and others are included, while in the second only they are included.

**The second issue:** Punishment in reality is not humiliating, because the meaning of that is that He humiliated someone else, and that cannot be done except to one who understands. So Allah, exalted is He, is the One who humiliates those punished with great punishment. However, since humiliation occurred together with punishment, it is permissible to make that one of His attributes. If it is said: "Punishment is only with humiliation, so what is the benefit of this description?" We say: that punishment is accompanied by humiliation is a matter that requires evidence, so Allah, exalted is He, mentioned it so that it would be evidence for it.

**The third issue:** Some people said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿ولِلْكافِرِينَ عَذابٌ مُهِينٌ﴾ indicates that there is no punishment except for the disbelievers. Then, after establishing this premise, two groups argued with this verse:

One of them: the Khawārij said: It is established by other verses that the sinner (fāsiq) is punished, and it is established by this verse that none is punished except the disbeliever, so it follows that the sinner is a disbeliever.

The second of them: the Murji'a said: It is established by this verse that none is punished except the disbeliever, and it is established that the sinner is not a disbeliever, so it is necessary to affirm definitively that he is not punished. The corruption of these two opinions is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 91:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and they reject what is beyond it, while it is the truth confirming what is with them. Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were believers?"﴾

Know that this type also is among their foul deeds. ﴿And when it is said to them﴾ means the Jews. ﴿"Believe in what Allah has sent down," they say﴾ meaning: in all that Allah has sent down. Those who hold that generality is indicated have used this verse as evidence that the word "mā" (what), in the sense of "alladhī" (that which), conveys generality. They said: Because Allah commanded them to believe in what Allah has sent down, and when they believed in some and not others, He censured them for that. Had the word "mā" not conveyed generality, this censure would not be apt. Then, Exalted is He, reports of them that when they were commanded to this, ﴿they said, "We believe in what was sent down to us"﴾, meaning the Torah and the books of the rest of the prophets who came to affirm the law of Moses, peace be upon him. Then Allah, Exalted is He, informs about them that they reject what is beyond it, which is the Gospel and the Qur'an. He related this account of them by way of censure of them, because it is not permissible to say to them "Believe in what Allah has sent down" unless they have a way to know that it was sent down from Allah; otherwise that would be imposing what cannot be borne. And when evidence indicates that it was sent down from Allah, belief in it becomes obligatory. Thus it is established that believing in some of what Allah has sent down and not others is a contradiction.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and it is the truth confirming what is with them﴾, it is like an indication of what proves the obligation of believing in Muhammad ﷺ, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: what is indicated by His saying: ﴿and it is the truth﴾, that when the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ was established by the miracles that appeared at his hands, he, peace be upon him, reported that this Qur'an is sent down from Allah Exalted, and that He commanded the responsible persons to believe in it, and belief in it was necessarily obligatory. At this point it becomes clear that believing in some prophets and some books while disbelieving in some prophets and some books is impossible.

The second: what is indicated by His saying: ﴿confirming what is with them﴾, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: that Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, did not learn any knowledge nor benefit from a teacher. So when he brought accounts and stories agreeing with what is in the Torah without any discrepancy at all, we know that he, peace be upon him, took them only from revelation and sending down.

The second: that the Qur'an indicates the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. So when Allah, Exalted is He, reported about it that it confirms the Torah, it became necessary that the Torah include information about his prophethood; otherwise the Qur'an would not be confirming the Torah but contradicting it. And since the Torah includes the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and they have acknowledged the obligation of believing in the Torah, it follows for them from this aspect the obligation of believing in the Qur'an and in the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Exalted and Glorified is He has shown, from another aspect, that their claim to be believers in the Torah is self-contradictory in several respects. This is because the Torah indicates that a miracle is a proof of truthfulness, and it indicates that whoever is truthful in claiming prophethood, killing him is disbelief. If that is the case, then striving to kill Yahya, Zakariyya and Isa, peace be upon them, is disbelief. So why did you strive in that, if you are truthful in your claim to be believers in the Torah?

The second issue: this verse indicates that disputation in religion is a practice of the prophets, peace be upon them, and that presenting a contradiction to an opponent is permissible.

The third issue: His saying ﴿Why do you kill﴾, although it is addressed in the second person, the intended meaning is those who preceded from their forefathers. This is indicated by several aspects:

The first: that the prophets were not present in that time.

The second: that they did not undertake that themselves.

The third: that the present tense cannot apply to it with "min qablu" (before).

As for the meaning being the past, it is evident, because the context indicates it. If it is said: His saying "Believe" is addressed to those present, and "Why do you kill" is a report of the deed of their forefathers, so how is the combination of the two construed? We say its meaning is: by this denial you have come out of the belief in what you claim to believe, just as your forefathers came out of belief in the rest by killing some of the prophets.

The fourth issue: It may be asked how it is permissible to say "Why do you kill ... before" when it is not permissible to say "I strike you yesterday"? The answer to this has two opinions:

One of them: that this is permissible in what has the status of a necessary attribute, like your saying to one whom you know for his past ugly deed: "Woe to you, why do you lie?" as if you said: "This was not of your nature." Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and they followed what the devils recited﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102], and did not say "what they recited", because He intended their habitual recitation.

The second: as if He said: Why do you approve of the killing of the prophets before, if you believed in the Torah? And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 92:

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf [for worship] after him while you were wrongdoers.﴾

Know that the repetition of this verse makes its explanation unnecessary. The reason for its repetition is that when God, exalted is He, related the way of the Jews in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), described them with obstinacy and denial, and compared them with their predecessors in killing the prophets, which suits their denial of him and even exceeds it, He repeated the mention of Moses (peace be upon him) and the clear proofs he brought, and that they, despite the clarity of that, permitted themselves to take the calf as a god. Yet Moses remained patient and steadfast in calling to his Lord and in adhering to His religion and law. The same applies to my situation with you, even if you exaggerate in denial and rejection.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you: "Take what We have given you with strength and listen." They said: "We have heard and we have disobeyed." And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief. Say: "Wretched is what your faith enjoins upon you, if you are believers."﴾

Page 171
Know that in the repetition there are several aspects:

The first: that repetition in this and similar cases is for emphasis and for establishing the proof against the opponent, according to the custom of the Arabs.

The second: that He mentioned it only with an addition, which is His saying: ﴿We have heard and we have disobeyed﴾, and this indicates the extreme of their obstinacy.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 93:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We have heard and we disobey"﴾, there are several issues in it.

The first issue: There is no doubt that the overshadowing of the mountain is among the most frightening of things, and yet they persisted in their disbelief and declared with their words, ﴿"We have heard and we disobey"﴾. This indicates that fear, however great, does not necessarily compel obedience.

The second issue: Most of the exegetes acknowledged that they said this statement. Abu Muslim said: It is possible that the meaning is that they heard it and received it with disobedience, and so this was expressed as speech even though they did not actually say it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117], and as in His saying: ﴿They said, "We come willingly"﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. The first (interpretation) is preferable, because diverting the speech from its apparent meaning without evidence is not permissible.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they were made to drink into their hearts the calf﴾, there are several issues in it.

The first issue: "And they were made to drink into their hearts the love of the calf." Regarding the aspect of this metaphor, there are two views:

The first: Its meaning is that its love and eagerness to worship it permeated them, as dye permeates cloth. His saying, ﴿in their hearts﴾, specifies the place of the "drinking", as in His saying: ﴿Those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire in their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa: 10].

The second: Just as drinking is the matter by which what the earth produces is given life, so that love was the matter for all the actions that proceeded from them.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿And they were made to drink﴾, indicates that another agent other than them did this to them, and it is known that none is capable of this except God. The Mu'tazilah answered this in two ways:

The first: God did not intend that another did this to them, but rather, because of their excessive attachment and familiarity with worshipping it, they made their hearts drink its love. So this was expressed in the passive form, as one says: "So-and-so is self-admiring."

The second: The intended meaning of "ashraba" is that he (the Samiri, Iblis, and the devils of mankind and jinn) made it appealing to them and invited them to it.

The Companions (the Ash'arites) answered both views by saying that both views divert the wording from its apparent meaning, and such diversion is not permissible except with a separate evidence. And since we have established by definitive rational proofs that the originator of all things is God, there is no need for us to abandon this apparent meaning.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿because of their disbelief﴾, the intended meaning is their belief in anthropomorphism regarding God, and their permitting worship of other than Him, glorified and exalted is He.

As for His saying: ﴿Say: "Wretched is what your faith commands you"﴾, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: The intended meaning of "Wretched is what your faith commands you" is your faith in the Torah, because there is no worship of the calf in the Torah. Attributing the command to their faith is mockery, as He said in the story of Shu'ayb: ﴿Does your prayer command you﴾ [Hud: 87], and likewise the attribution of faith to them.

The second issue: Faith is an accident (ʿaraḍ), and command and prohibition cannot proceed from it; but the one who calls to an action may be likened to one who commands, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 45].

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿if you are believers﴾, the intended meaning is to cast doubt on their faith and to impugn the soundness of their claim.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 94–95 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is yours exclusively, to the exclusion of other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.﴾ ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forward. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾

Know that this is another of their ugly qualities, namely their claim that the Last Abode is exclusively theirs, to the exclusion of other people. Several considerations indicate this:

The first: it is not permissible to say, by way of argument against an opponent, "If such-and-such is the case, then do such-and-such," unless the first party holds that view, so that the second party's argument against him is valid.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 94–95 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is yours exclusively, to the exclusion of other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.﴾ ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forward. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾

Know that this is another of their ugly qualities, namely their claim that the Last Abode is exclusively theirs, to the exclusion of other people. Several considerations indicate this:

The first: it is not permissible to say, by way of argument against an opponent, "If such-and-such is the case, then do such-and-such," unless the first party holds that view, so that the second party's argument against him is valid.

The second: what Allah relates of them in His saying: ﴿They say: None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and in His saying: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and in His saying: ﴿They say: The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80].

The third: their belief about themselves that they are the ones upholding the truth, because abrogation (naskh) is not permissible in their law, and that all other sects are false.

The fourth: their belief that their lineage to the great prophets, peace be upon them, namely Ya'qub, Ishaq and Ibrahim, will deliver them from the punishment of Allah and bring them to His reward. Then, because of these things, they exalted their own status, so that they would boast over the Arabs. Sometimes they used this as an argument that the awaited prophet, who was foretold in the Torah, would be from among them and not from the Arabs, and by this doubt they would turn people away from following Muhammad (ﷺ). Then Allah argued against the corruption of their view by His saying: ﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is yours exclusively, to the exclusion of other people, then wish for death⁠…﴾. The explanation of this implication is that the blessings of this world are few and insignificant in comparison with the blessings of the Hereafter. Moreover, the blessings of this world, despite their scarcity, were made bitter for them by the appearance of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his contending with them through debate and fighting. Whoever is in few and embittered blessings, and then becomes certain that after death he must transfer to those great blessings, must necessarily desire death, because those great blessings are sought and there is no way to them except through death; and what a sought-after thing depends upon must itself be sought. So this person must be content with death and wish for it. Thus it is established that if the Last Abode were exclusively theirs, they would have to wish for death. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that they did not wish for death, but rather "they will never wish for it," and then it necessarily follows with certainty that their claim, that the Last Abode is exclusively theirs to the exclusion of other people, is false.

If it is objected: we do not concede that if the Last Abode were exclusively theirs they would have to wish for death, since the blessing of the Hereafter is sought, there is no way to it except through death, and whatever the sought thing depends upon must be sought. We reply: what the sought thing depends upon may be sought in view of its being a means to that sought thing, but it is disliked in view of its own essence; and death is something that cannot occur except with great pains, which they could not bear. Therefore they did not wish for death.

Question two: they could have turned this argument back against Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: "You claim that the Last Abode is exclusively yours and your community's, to the exclusion of whoever contends with you in the matter. If the matter is so, then consent that we kill you and your community, for we see you and your community in severe harm and great affliction because of debate and fighting, and after death you will attain the bliss of Paradise. So you must be content with your own killing!"

Question three: perhaps they were saying that the Last Abode is exclusively for whoever holds their religion, but on condition of avoiding the major sins; as for the one who commits a major sin, he will remain forever in the Fire, because they were Wa'idiyya, or because they permitted that the one who commits a major sin would become punished. Because of this they did not wish for death. Nor can anyone answer this question by saying that their view is that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of days, because each day of the Day of Resurrection is like a thousand years of what you count. Thus these days, although few in number, were long in duration; therefore they did not wish for death because of this fear.

Question four: he, upon him be prayers and peace, forbade wishing for death, saying: "Let none of you wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him, but let him say: O Allah, keep me alive if life is good for me, and take me if death is good for me." Also Allah, exalted is He, said in His Book: ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it, while those who believe are apprehensive of it﴾ [al-Shura: 18]. How then is it permissible that he forbids seeking to hasten, and then challenges the people with it?

Question five: the word tamanni (wishing) is shared between the tamanni that is the meaning standing in the heart, and the word expressing that meaning, which is the speaker's saying: "Would that I had died." So the Jews could say: "You asked us to wish, and wishing is an ambiguous term." If we mention it by tongue, he may say: "I did not intend this word; I only intended the meaning in the heart." And if we do that meaning standing in the heart, he may say: "You lie, you did not bring that in your hearts." When the Jews knew that he had brought a shared term against which no objection could be raised, they therefore paid no attention to him.

Question six: suppose that if the Last Abode were theirs they would have had to wish for death; why do you say that they did not wish for death? The argument by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾ is weak, because the argument by this only holds if the Qur'an is established as true, and the dispute is only about that.

(The answer): His saying [first], that the existence of death involving pain acts as a deterrent from wishing for it: we reply, just as the pain occurring during cupping does not deter from cupping, because of the knowledge that the benefit obtained through cupping is great, so the matter here must be likewise.

His saying second: if they turned the speech back upon Muhammad (ﷺ), it would necessitate that he consent to being killed. We reply: the difference between Muhammad (peace be upon him) and them is that Muhammad used to say, "I was sent to convey the laws to the people of tawatur (mass transmission)," and this aim has not yet been achieved; for this reason I do not consent to being killed. As for you, you are not like that, so the difference is clear.

His saying third: they were afraid of the punishment for major sins. We reply: the people claimed that the Hereafter is exclusively theirs, and that would secure them from the mixing of its reward with punishment.

His saying fourth: he was forbidden from wishing for death. We reply: this prohibition is the method of the Law, so the situation may differ regarding it according to differences of time. It is narrated that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, used to walk between the two lines wearing a light tunic, and his son al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: "This is not the dress of those who fight." He said: "O my son, your father does not care whether he falls upon death or death falls upon him." And Ammar, may Allah be pleased with him, said at Siffin:
Now I shall meet the beloved, Muhammad and his party.
And wishing for death has appeared from the prophets at many times. This prohibition is specific to a particular cause: he, upon him be prayers and peace, forbade a person to wish for death at times of hardship, because that is like impatience and departure from contentment with what Allah has decreed. So where is this from the wishing that indicates the soundness of prophethood?

His saying fifth: they did not know whether the intended wishing was by tongue or by heart. We reply: in the language of the Arabs, tamanni is only recognized as what appears of it, just as khabar (report) is only recognized as what appears through speech; and what is in the heart of that is not called by this name. Moreover, it is absurd that the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, would say to them, "Wish for death," while intending something that cannot be ascertained, especially since the purpose of that would not be achieved except by its appearing.

His saying sixth: what is the proof that the wishing did not occur? We reply, in several ways:

The first: if it had occurred, it would have been transmitted by mass transmission, because it is a great matter. For if it did not occur, the claim that Muhammad's prophethood is true would stand, and if this wishing had occurred, the claim of his prophethood would be void. Whatever is like this is among the great events, so it must be transmitted by mass transmission. Since it was not transmitted, we know that it did not occur.

The second: he, upon him be prayers and peace, together with his foresight and resolve, his good judgment regarding the outcome, and his arrival at the position he reached in this world and religion, and his attainment of the great leadership to which the opponent submitted by force and the supporter submitted willingly, could not have been without being sure, through the revelation sent down to him from his Lord, that he would not challenge them with a matter whose outcome he could not be sure of, nor be sure that his opponent would not overcome him with proof and argument. For a sensible person who has not tested affairs would hardly accept this; how then of the most intelligent of the intelligent? It is thus established that he, upon him be prayers and peace, did not undertake to set down these proofs except that God Most High had revealed to him that they would not wish for it.

The third: what is narrated, that he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "If the Jews had wished for death, they would have died and seen their seats in the Fire. And if those who challenged to mutual imprecation (mubahala) had come out, they would have returned finding neither family nor property." Ibn Abbas said: "If they had wished for death, they would have choked on it and died." In sum, the reports that they did not wish for it reached the level of mass transmission, so the proof is established. This is the end of the discussion of establishing this argument. Let us return to the exegesis.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If the Last Abode⁠…﴾, what is meant is Paradise, because it is what is sought from the Abode of the Hereafter, not the Fire, since they used to claim that Paradise was theirs.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with Allah﴾, what is meant is not place but rank. There is also no remoteness in taking it to mean place; perhaps the Jews were anthropomorphists (mushabbiha) and believed in nearness of place, so Allah refuted all of that with the proof He mentioned.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿exclusively﴾, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of "the Last Abode," meaning: safe for you, specifically yours, with no one other than you having any right in it; that is, if your saying holds, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians." And "people" (al-nas) is for the genus; it was said it refers to a specific group, namely the Muslims, but the genus is preferable because of His saying, "except those who are Jews or Christians," and because no specific referent is found here.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿to the exclusion of other people﴾, what is meant by it is "other than," not the meaning of place, as one says to someone who has been granted a kingdom: "This is yours to the exclusion of people."

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then wish for death, if you are truthful﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: this is a command conditioned upon a condition that is absent, namely their being truthful; so the command does not exist, and its purpose is challenge and the manifestation of their lie in their claim.

The second issue: concerning this wishing there are two views:

One: the saying of Ibn Abbas, that they would challenge one another by calling down death upon whichever party was the liar.

The second: that they would say, "Would that we die." This second is preferable, because it is closer to conforming with the wording.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾, it is a definitive report that this will not occur in the future. This is a report about the unseen, because despite the strong motives to deny Muhammad (ﷺ) and the ease of uttering this word, He informed that they would not bring it. This is a firm report about a matter against which the signs point to the opposite, and it cannot be reached except through revelation.

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 94–95 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿forever﴾, it is another unseen matter, because He informed that it will not exist, nor in any of the future times to come. There is no doubt that the report of its non-existence with respect to all times is two unseen matters.
* * *
As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿because of what their hands have sent forward﴾, it is an explanation of the cause for which they do not wish for death. When they know the badness of their way and the abundance of their sins, this calls them to not wish for death.
* * *
As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, it is like a warning and a threat, because when He is Knowing of the secret and the private conversation, and nothing can be concealed from Him, the accountable person's awareness of this is among the greatest deterrents from sins. He mentioned "the wrongdoers" because every disbeliever is a wrongdoer, but not every wrongdoer is a disbeliever. Since that is more general, it was more fitting to mention.

If it is said: He, Exalted is He, said here, ﴿and they will never wish for it﴾, and in Surat al-Jumu'ah He said, ﴿and they will not wish for it, ever﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 7]. Why did He mention "lan" (never) here, and "lā" (not) in Surat al-Jumu'ah? We say: In this surah they claimed that the Last Abode is exclusively theirs, to the exclusion of people, and in Surat al-Jumu'ah they claimed that they are the friends (awliya') of Allah to the exclusion of people. Allah, Exalted is He, refuted these two matters by saying that if it were so, they would necessarily wish for death. The first claim is greater than the second, since the supreme happiness is attaining the abode of reward. As for the rank of friendship, although it is noble, it is only desired as a means to reach Paradise. So, since the first claim is greater, Exalted is He, rightly refuted their statement with the word "lan," because it is the strongest of the negating particles. And since the second claim is not at the utmost level of greatness, He sufficed in refuting it with the word "lā," because it is not at the highest degree of strength in conveying the meaning of negation. And Allah knows best.

The first: if it had occurred, it would have been transmitted by mass transmission, because it is a great matter. For if it did not occur, the claim that Muhammad's prophethood is true would stand, and if this wishing had occurred, the claim of his prophethood would be void. Whatever is like this is among the great events, so it must be transmitted by mass transmission. Since it was not transmitted, we know that it did not occur.

The second: he, upon him be prayers and peace, together with his foresight and resolve, his good judgment regarding the outcome, and his arrival at the position he reached in this world and religion, and his attainment of the great leadership to which the opponent submitted by force and the supporter submitted willingly, could not have been without being sure, through the revelation sent down to him from his Lord, that he would not challenge them with a matter whose outcome he could not be sure of, nor be sure that his opponent would not overcome him with proof and argument. For a sensible person who has not tested affairs would hardly accept this; how then of the most intelligent of the intelligent? It is thus established that he, upon him be prayers and peace, did not undertake to set down these proofs except that God Most High had revealed to him that they would not wish for it.

The third: what is narrated, that he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "If the Jews had wished for death, they would have died and seen their seats in the Fire. And if those who challenged to mutual imprecation (mubahala) had come out, they would have returned finding neither family nor property." Ibn Abbas said: "If they had wished for death, they would have choked on it and died." In sum, the reports that they did not wish for it reached the level of mass transmission, so the proof is established. This is the end of the discussion of establishing this argument. Let us return to the exegesis.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If the Last Abode⁠…﴾, what is meant is Paradise, because it is what is sought from the Abode of the Hereafter, not the Fire, since they used to claim that Paradise was theirs.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with Allah﴾, what is meant is not place but rank. There is also no remoteness in taking it to mean place; perhaps the Jews were anthropomorphists (mushabbiha) and believed in nearness of place, so Allah refuted all of that with the proof He mentioned.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿exclusively﴾, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of "the Last Abode," meaning: safe for you, specifically yours, with no one other than you having any right in it; that is, if your saying holds, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians." And "people" (al-nas) is for the genus; it was said it refers to a specific group, namely the Muslims, but the genus is preferable because of His saying, "except those who are Jews or Christians," and because no specific referent is found here.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿to the exclusion of other people﴾, what is meant by it is "other than," not the meaning of place, as one says to someone who has been granted a kingdom: "This is yours to the exclusion of people."

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then wish for death, if you are truthful﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: this is a command conditioned upon a condition that is absent, namely their being truthful; so the command does not exist, and its purpose is challenge and the manifestation of their lie in their claim.

The second issue: concerning this wishing there are two views:

One: the saying of Ibn Abbas, that they would challenge one another by calling down death upon whichever party was the liar.

The second: that they would say, "Would that we die." This second is preferable, because it is closer to conforming with the wording.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾, it is a definitive report that this will not occur in the future. This is a report about the unseen, because despite the strong motives to deny Muhammad (ﷺ) and the ease of uttering this word, He informed that they would not bring it. This is a firm report about a matter against which the signs point to the opposite, and it cannot be reached except through revelation.

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 94–95 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿forever﴾, it is another unseen matter, because He informed that it will not exist, nor in any of the future times to come. There is no doubt that the report of its non-existence with respect to all times is two unseen matters.
* * *
As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿because of what their hands have sent forward﴾, it is an explanation of the cause for which they do not wish for death. When they know the badness of their way and the abundance of their sins, this calls them to not wish for death.
* * *
As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, it is like a warning and a threat, because when He is Knowing of the secret and the private conversation, and nothing can be concealed from Him, the accountable person's awareness of this is among the greatest deterrents from sins. He mentioned "the wrongdoers" because every disbeliever is a wrongdoer, but not every wrongdoer is a disbeliever. Since that is more general, it was more fitting to mention.

If it is said: He, Exalted is He, said here, ﴿and they will never wish for it﴾, and in Surat al-Jumu'ah He said, ﴿and they will not wish for it, ever﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 7]. Why did He mention "lan" (never) here, and "lā" (not) in Surat al-Jumu'ah? We say: In this surah they claimed that the Last Abode is exclusively theirs, to the exclusion of people, and in Surat al-Jumu'ah they claimed that they are the friends (awliya') of Allah to the exclusion of people. Allah, Exalted is He, refuted these two matters by saying that if it were so, they would necessarily wish for death. The first claim is greater than the second, since the supreme happiness is attaining the abode of reward. As for the rank of friendship, although it is noble, it is only desired as a means to reach Paradise. So, since the first claim is greater, Exalted is He, rightly refuted their statement with the word "lan," because it is the strongest of the negating particles. And since the second claim is not at the utmost level of greatness, He sufficed in refuting it with the word "lā," because it is not at the highest degree of strength in conveying the meaning of negation. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 96:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you will surely find them the most avid of people for life, and [more avid] than those who associate others with God. Each one of them wishes he could be granted a life of a thousand years, but granting him a long life will not remove him from the punishment. And God is Seeing of what they do.﴾

Know that when the Glorified and Exalted informed, in the previous verse, that they do not wish for death, He informed in this verse that they are at the utmost eagerness for life, because here there is a third category, namely that a person is in a state in which he neither wishes for death nor wishes for

Page 176

life. So He said: ﴿And you will surely find them the most avid of people for life﴾.

As for His saying, ﴿and you will surely find them﴾, it is from wajada in the sense of "knew" (ʿalima), which is transitive to two objects, as in "I found Zayd a man of great memory" (wajadtu Zaydan dhā ḥifāẓ). Its two objects are "them" (hum) and "most avid" (aḥraṣa). He said ﴿for life﴾ in indefinite form because it is a specific life, namely the long-drawn-out life, and for this reason the reading with it is more forceful than the reading of Ubayy, "for the life" (ʿalā al-ḥayāh). As for the waw in His saying, ﴿and [more avid] than those who associate others with God﴾, there are three opinions concerning it:

The first: it is a conjunctive waw (wāw ʿaṭf), and the meaning is that the Jews are the most avid of people for life, and more avid than those who associate others with God, as when you say: "He is the most generous of people, and [more generous] than Ḥātim." This is the view of al-Farrāʾ and al-Aṣamm. If it is said: Are not those who associate others with God included among "people"? We say: Yes, but they are singled out for mention because their eagerness is intense, and there is in it a great rebuke, because those who associate others with God do not believe in the Return, and they know only the life of this world, so their eagerness for it is not surprising, since it is their paradise. Then, if one who has a Scripture, and who acknowledges recompense, exceeds them in eagerness, he deserves the greatest rebuke. If it is said: Why did their eagerness exceed the eagerness of the polytheists? We say: Because they know that they are bound for the Fire without doubt, whereas the polytheists do not know this.

The second opinion: this waw is a waw of resumption (wāw istiʾnāf), and the sentence is complete at His saying "for life." Its implicit reading is: and among those who associate others with God are people, each one of whom wishes, with the qualified noun omitted, as in His saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 164].

The third opinion: there is in it an inversion (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr), and its implicit reading is: "And you will surely find them, and a group of those who associate others with God, the most avid of people for life." Then He explained this love by His saying: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be granted a life of a thousand years﴾. This is the view of Abū Muslim. The first opinion is preferable, because if the account concerns the Jews specifically, then the more fitting meaning by the apparent sense is: "And you will surely find the Jews the most avid for life of all people, and [more avid] than those who associate others with God," so that this is more emphatic in refuting their claim and in showing the falsehood of their saying: "The Last Abode is ours alone, not for others." And God knows best.

The second issue: they differed concerning the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿and [more avid] than those who associate others with God﴾, according to three opinions. It was said: the Magians, because they used to say to their king: "Live a thousand Nowruz and a thousand Mihrajan." It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is the saying of the non-Arabs: "Zī-i Hazārsāl" (may you live a thousand years). It was also said: the intended are the polytheists of the Arabs. And it was said: every polytheist who does not believe in the Return, because we have shown that the eagerness of these people for the world should be greater. The intention behind mentioning "a thousand years" is not the saying of the non-Arabs, "Live a thousand years," but rather it is for amplification, which is well known in the speech of the Arabs.

As for His saying, ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be granted a life of a thousand years﴾, the meaning is that He, may He be exalted, showed their remoteness from wishing for death, in that they wish for this continuance and are eager for it with this intense eagerness; and one whose condition is this, how can wishing for death be conceived of him?

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿and granting him a long life will not remove him from the punishment﴾, there are two issues:
The first issue: concerning what the pronoun in His saying ﴿and it is not﴾ refers back to. There are three opinions:

The first: it refers back to "one of them" (aḥadahum) which has been mentioned, i.e., "and none of them is one whose long life would remove him from the Fire."

The second: it is a pronoun for what is indicated by "be granted a long life" (yuʿammar) from its verbal noun, and "that he be granted a long life" (an yuʿammar) is a substitute for it.

The third: that it is ambiguous, and "that he be granted a long life" (an yuʿammar) clarifies it.

Page 177

The second issue: zaḥzaḥa (zaḥzaḥah) means to distance and to rescue. The judge (al-Qāḍī) said: the meaning is that it does not have the least effect in removing the punishment; and if He had said, "and it is not what distances him or saves him," it would not indicate the slightness of the effect in the way this statement does.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿And God is Seeing of what they do﴾, know that "baṣar" (sight) may be intended to mean knowledge; it is said: "So-and-so has baṣar in this matter," meaning knowledge. It may also be intended that He has an attribute such that, if visible things existed, He would see them. Both attributes are valid for Him, may He be glorified; however, whoever says that among deeds there are things that cannot be seen takes this seeing necessarily to mean knowledge. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verses 97–98 (part 1 of 2)**

**His saying, exalted is He:** ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel – indeed, he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah, confirming what came before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers.﴾ ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael – indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.﴾

Know that this type is also one of the types of the abominable deeds of the Jews and their objectionable statements and actions. In it are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾必 necessarily has a cause and a matter that appeared from the Jews, for which he was commanded to address them with this, because it proceeds in the manner of a debate. So if no such matter has been established from them, it is not permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to command him with this. The exegetes (mufassirun) have mentioned several matters. One of them: "When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, arrived in Medina, Abdullah ibn Suriya came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, how is your sleep? For we have been told about the sleep of the Prophet who will come at the end of time.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'My eyes sleep but my heart does not sleep.' He said: 'You have spoken truly, O Muhammad. So tell me about the child: is it from the man or from the woman?' He said: 'As for the bones, the sinews and the veins, they are from the man; and as for the flesh, the blood, the nails and the hair, they are from the woman.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' He said: 'Then what is the matter with a man who resembles his paternal uncles but not his maternal uncles, or resembles his maternal uncles but not his paternal uncles?' He said: 'Whichever of the two waters overcomes the water of the other, the resemblance is to it.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he said: 'Tell me, which food did Israel (Jacob) forbid to himself, and in the Torah it is stated that the unlettered Prophet informs about it?' He, peace be upon him, said: 'I adjure you by Allah, who sent down the Torah to Moses: do you know that Israel fell severely ill, and his sickness lasted long, so he vowed to Allah that if Allah cured him of his sickness, he would forbid to himself the food and drink he loved most, which were the meat and milk of camels?' They said: 'Yes.' He said to him: 'One characteristic remains; if you say it, I will believe in you. Which angel comes to you with what you say from Allah?' Gabriel said: 'He says that Gabriel is our enemy; he descends with war and hardship, while our messenger is Michael, who brings good news and ease. So if it were he who came to you, we would believe in you.' Umar said: 'And what is the origin of this enmity?' Ibn Suriya said: 'The origin of this enmity is that Allah, exalted is He, sent down to our Prophet that the Temple of Jerusalem would be destroyed in the time of a man called Bukhtunassar, and He described him to us. We sought him, and when we found him we sent men to kill him, but Gabriel repelled them from him and said: "If Allah empowers you over killing him, then this is not the one whom Allah informed about, who would destroy the Temple of Jerusalem, so there is no benefit in killing him." Then he grew old, became strong, ruled, invaded us, destroyed the Temple of Jerusalem and killed us. Therefore we take him as an enemy. As for Michael—' [p. 178] '—he is the enemy of Gabriel.' Umar said: 'Then I bear witness that whoever is an enemy to Gabriel is an enemy to Michael, and they are both enemies to whoever opposes them.' So this was rejected from Umar, and Allah, exalted is He, sent down these two verses."

**The second:** It is narrated that Umar had land on the upper part of Medina, and his route passed by the Jewish study house (midras), and he would sit with them and listen to their speech. They said: "O Umar, we have come to love you, and we hope for you." He said: "By Allah, I do not come to you out of your love, nor do I ask you because I am in doubt about my religion; rather I enter upon you only to increase my insight into the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, and I see his traces in your Book." Then he asked them about Gabriel. They said: "That one is our enemy; he informs Muhammad of our secrets, and he is the one in charge of every earthquake and punishment, whereas Michael comes with fertility and peace." He said to them: "And what is their status with Allah?" They said: "The closest in rank: Gabriel is on his right and Michael on his left, and Michael is an enemy to Gabriel." Umar said: "If it is as you say, then they are not enemies, and you are more disbelieving than donkeys. Whoever is an enemy to one of them is an enemy to the other, and whoever is an enemy to both of them is an enemy to Allah." Then Umar returned and found that Gabriel, peace be upon him, had preceded him with the revelation. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Your Lord has agreed with you, O Umar." Umar said: "After that I found myself in my religion firmer than a rock."

**The third:** Muqatil said: "The Jews claimed that Gabriel, peace be upon him, is our enemy. He was commanded to place prophethood among us, but he placed it among others. So Allah sent down these verses."

Know that the closer view is that the cause of their enmity toward him was that he used to bring the Qur'an down upon Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is because His saying, ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel – indeed, he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah﴾, indicates that this descent should not be a cause of enmity, since he only did it by the command of Allah; so it should not be a cause of enmity.
