This is established in several ways:

First: What Gabriel brought down of the Qur'an was the good tidings of reward for the obedient, the warning of punishment for the disobedient, and the command to fight and battle. Since he did not do this by his own choice, but by the command of Allah, which they acknowledge there is no escape from and no way to oppose, then enmity toward one whose situation is this entails enmity toward Allah, and enmity toward Allah is disbelief; so it follows that enmity toward one of this kind is disbelief.

Second: If Allah had commanded Michael to bring down such a Book, then either it would be said that he would rebel or refuse to accept the command of Allah, and that is not fitting for the infallible angels; or he would accept it and bring it in accordance with the command of Allah. In that case, what they said about Gabriel would apply to Michael, peace be upon them both. So what is the reason for singling out Gabriel for enmity?

Third: The descent of the Qur'an upon Muhammad was as burdensome to the Jews as the descent of the Torah upon Moses was burdensome to other people. If the aversion of some people to the descent of the Qur'an necessitated its ugliness, then the aversion of those earlier people to the descent of the Torah upon Moses, peace be upon him, would necessitate its ugliness. It is known that all of this is false. Thus, by these considerations, the corruption of what they said is established.

**The second issue:** Some people have found it unlikely that a people of the Jews would say that Gabriel is their enemy. They said: "We see the Jews in our time unanimous in denying this, insisting that none of their predecessors said so." Know that this is false, because Allah's report is more truthful, and because their ignorance was severe; and they are the ones who said, ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138].

**The third issue:** Ibn Kathir read "Jibril" (جَبْرِيلَ) with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the ra, without a hamza. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from Asim read it with a fatha on the jim and the ra, with a hamza. The rest read it with a kasra on the jim and the ra, without a hamza, on the pattern of qindil. In it there are seven dialects; three of them we have mentioned. Jibra'il (جِبْرائِلُ) is on the pattern of jibra'il, Jibra'il is on the pattern of jibra'il, Jibra'il is on the pattern of jibra'il, and Jibrin with a nun. It is not declined (diptote) because of definiteness and foreignness.

**The fourth issue:** Some said: Jibril means "servant of God": "jabar" means "servant" and "il" means "God." Mika'il means "servant of God." This is the view of Ibn Abbas and a group of scholars. Abu Ali al-Susi said: "This is not correct, for two reasons: first, 'il' is not known among the names of Allah; and second, if it were so, the last part of the name would be in the genitive case."

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then indeed he has brought it down upon your heart﴾, there are questions:

**The first question:** To what do the pronouns in His saying "fa-innahu" (فَإنَّهُ) and in "nazzalahu" (نَزَّلَهُ) refer? The answer has two views:

One: The first pronoun refers to Gabriel and the second to the Qur'an, even though it has not been mentioned, because it is understood, like His saying, ﴿He left upon its back no creature﴾ [Fatir: 45], meaning upon the earth. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and most scholars. That is, if their enmity is because Gabriel brings down the Qur'an, then he only brings it down by the permission of Allah. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Referring to something not previously mentioned carries grandeur for its owner, since because of his great fame it is as if it indicates him by himself, and one dispenses with his explicit name by mentioning some of his attributes."

The second: The meaning is that Allah sent down Gabriel, peace be upon him, not that he sent down himself.

**The second question:** The Qur'an was only sent down upon Muhammad ﷺ, so what is the reason for His saying, "he sent it down upon your heart"? The answer: We have discussed this matter in Surat al-Shu'ara' in His saying, ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193]. Most of the community holds that He sent the Qur'an down upon him, not upon his heart; but He specifically mentioned the heart because what was brought down was firmly established in his heart by memorization until he conveyed it to his community. Since the cause of his ability to convey it was its firm establishment in his heart by memorization, it became permissible to say "He sent it down upon your heart," even though in reality He sent it down upon him, not upon his heart.

**The third question:** The proper wording would have been "upon my heart." The answer: It came in the form of quoting Allah's speech as He spoke it, as if it were said: "Say what I have spoken, as my word: whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, indeed he has brought it down upon your heart."

**The fourth question:** How is His saying "fa-innahu nazzalahu" (فَإنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ) acceptable as the response (jaza') to the condition (shart)? The answer has two aspects:

The first: He, glorified and exalted, made clear that this enmity is corrupt, because he did nothing except that he was commanded to bring down a Book containing guidance and good tidings, so he brought it down. Insofar as he is commanded, he must be excused; and insofar as he brought guidance and good tidings, he must be thanked. So how does enmity befit him?

The second: He, exalted is He, made clear that if the Jews are hostile to him, that is their right, because he brought down the Book to you as proof of your prophethood and confirmation of your truthfulness, and they dislike that. So how would they not hate the one who confirmed upon them the matter they dislike?

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, the more apparent meaning is "by the command of Allah," and this is preferable to interpreting it as "by the knowledge of Allah," for several reasons:

First: "idhn" (إذْن) is literally "command" and metaphorically "knowledge," and a word must be taken in its literal sense wherever possible.

Second: His bringing it down was obligatory, and obligation is derived from command, not from knowledge.

Third: When that descent is by a binding command, it is more emphatic as a proof.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿confirming what came before it﴾, it is taken to mean what most exegetes have agreed upon: that what is intended is the books of the prophets that came before it, and there is no sense in restricting it to one book. Among them are those who restricted it to the Torah, and claimed that it indicates that [p. 180] the Qur'an agrees with the Torah in pointing to the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. If it is said: Are not the laws of the Qur'an different from the laws of all the other books? Why, then, is it considered confirming of them, because they agree in pointing to monotheism, while the prophethood of Muhammad would be even more appropriate for not confirming them? We say: The laws contained in the other books were limited to those times and ended in this time, on the basis that abrogation (naskh) is a clarification of the end of the period of worship. In that case, there is no difference between the Qur'an and the other books regarding the laws.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and guidance﴾, what is meant is that the Qur'an contains two matters:

One: The clarification of what obligations have been imposed, concerning actions of the heart and actions of the limbs; from this aspect it is guidance.

The second: The clarification of how the reward of the one who performs those actions will be; from this aspect it is good tidings. Since the first precedes the second in existence, God therefore placed the word "guidance" before the word "good tidings." If it is said: Why did He specify that it is guidance and good tidings for the believers, when it is so for everyone in relation to all? The answer has two aspects:

The first: He, exalted is He, specified them with it only because they are the ones who were guided by the Book; so it is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

The second reason: it is only good news (bushra) for the believers, because bushra is a report indicating the attainment of a great good, and this only applies to the believers. For this reason God singled them out for it.

As for the second verse, which is His saying, ﴿Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels﴾, know that when He, exalted is He, had explained in the first verse, ﴿whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾, because he sent down the Qur'an upon the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), it was necessary that such a person be an enemy to God, the Exalted, He explained in this verse that whoever is an enemy to God, God is his enemy. Thus He explained that, in exchange for their enmity, there is something that magnifies the harm that comes upon them, which is God's enmity toward them, because their enmity does not affect, benefit, or harm Him, whereas His enmity leads to everlasting, painful punishment, beyond which there is no greater harm. Here there are some questions.

The first question: How is it permissible that they be enemies of God, when the essence of enmity is to harm the enemy, and that is impossible for God, the Exalted? The answer: The literal meaning of enmity (ʿadawah) applies only to us, because the enemy of another is one who wishes to inflict harm upon him, and that is impossible for God, the Exalted. Rather, what is meant by it is one of two things. Either they are hostile to the friends of God, and this constitutes enmity toward God, like His saying, ﴿Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:33], and His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who abuse God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:57], because the intended meaning of the two verses is the friends of God, not God Himself, since war and harm are impossible for Him. Or what is meant is their aversion to carrying out His obedience and worship and their remoteness from adhering to it. Since an enemy hardly agrees with his enemy or submits to him, their way in this respect is likened to enmity. As for their enmity toward Gabriel and the messengers, it is genuine, because harm is possible for them; but their enmity does not affect them, since they are incapable of the things that would affect them. Their enmity does affect the Jews, because in the present it entails humiliation and wretchedness, and in the future it entails everlasting punishment.

The second question: Since He mentioned the angels, why did He repeat the mention of Gabriel and Michael, given that they are included among the angels? The answer has two aspects:

First: He singled them out for mention because of their excellence, as if, owing to their perfect excellence, they had become a kind distinct from the kind of angels.

Second: What had passed between the Messenger and the Jews was the mention of these two, and the verse was revealed on account of them, so there is no doubt that He explicitly named them both. Know that this implies that they are more excellent than all the angels; otherwise this interpretation would not be valid. Having established this, we say: Gabriel, peace be upon him, must be more excellent than Michael, for several reasons:

One: He, exalted is He, mentioned Gabriel, peace be upon him, first, and mentioning the lesser before the greater is considered reprehensible by custom, so it must be reprehensible by the law, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "What the Muslims see as good is good in the sight of God."

[Page 181]

Two: Gabriel, peace be upon him, descends with the Qur'an, revelation, and knowledge, which are the sustenance of the souls, while Michael descends with fertility and rain, which are the sustenance of the bodies. Since knowledge is more noble than foods, it must be that Gabriel is more excellent than Michael.

Three: His saying, exalted is He, describing Gabriel: ﴿obeyed there, trustworthy﴾ [al-Takwir 81:21]. He described him with the attribute of "obeyed" in an absolute sense, and its apparent meaning implies that he is obeyed in relation to Michael, so he must be more excellent than him.

The second issue: Abu ʿAmr and Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, recited "Mikal" on the pattern of "Qintar," while Nafiʿ recited "Mikail" with the vowel elided (mukhtalasah), there being no yaʾ after the hamzah, on the pattern of "Mikaʿil." The rest recited "Mikaʾil" on the pattern of "Mikaʿil." There is also another dialect, "Mikaʾil" on the pattern of "Mikayʿil," and "Mikaʾil" like "Mikaʿil." Ibn Jinni said: when the Arabs pronounce a non-Arabic word, they mix up its forms.

The third issue: The waw in "Jibril" and "Mikal" — it is said that it is the waw of conjunction, and it is said that it means "or," that is: whoever is an enemy to any one of these, then indeed God is an enemy to all the disbelievers.

The fourth issue: ﴿an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. He intended "an enemy to them," but He used the apparent noun to indicate that God, the Exalted, opposed them only because of their disbelief, and that enmity toward the angels is disbelief.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verses 97–98 (part 1 of 2)**

**His saying, exalted is He:** ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel – indeed, he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah, confirming what came before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers.﴾ ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael – indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.﴾

Know that this type is also one of the types of the abominable deeds of the Jews and their objectionable statements and actions. In it are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾必 necessarily has a cause and a matter that appeared from the Jews, for which he was commanded to address them with this, because it proceeds in the manner of a debate. So if no such matter has been established from them, it is not permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to command him with this. The exegetes (mufassirun) have mentioned several matters. One of them: "When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, arrived in Medina, Abdullah ibn Suriya came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, how is your sleep? For we have been told about the sleep of the Prophet who will come at the end of time.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'My eyes sleep but my heart does not sleep.' He said: 'You have spoken truly, O Muhammad. So tell me about the child: is it from the man or from the woman?' He said: 'As for the bones, the sinews and the veins, they are from the man; and as for the flesh, the blood, the nails and the hair, they are from the woman.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' He said: 'Then what is the matter with a man who resembles his paternal uncles but not his maternal uncles, or resembles his maternal uncles but not his paternal uncles?' He said: 'Whichever of the two waters overcomes the water of the other, the resemblance is to it.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he said: 'Tell me, which food did Israel (Jacob) forbid to himself, and in the Torah it is stated that the unlettered Prophet informs about it?' He, peace be upon him, said: 'I adjure you by Allah, who sent down the Torah to Moses: do you know that Israel fell severely ill, and his sickness lasted long, so he vowed to Allah that if Allah cured him of his sickness, he would forbid to himself the food and drink he loved most, which were the meat and milk of camels?' They said: 'Yes.' He said to him: 'One characteristic remains; if you say it, I will believe in you. Which angel comes to you with what you say from Allah?' Gabriel said: 'He says that Gabriel is our enemy; he descends with war and hardship, while our messenger is Michael, who brings good news and ease. So if it were he who came to you, we would believe in you.' Umar said: 'And what is the origin of this enmity?' Ibn Suriya said: 'The origin of this enmity is that Allah, exalted is He, sent down to our Prophet that the Temple of Jerusalem would be destroyed in the time of a man called Bukhtunassar, and He described him to us. We sought him, and when we found him we sent men to kill him, but Gabriel repelled them from him and said: "If Allah empowers you over killing him, then this is not the one whom Allah informed about, who would destroy the Temple of Jerusalem, so there is no benefit in killing him." Then he grew old, became strong, ruled, invaded us, destroyed the Temple of Jerusalem and killed us. Therefore we take him as an enemy. As for Michael—' [p. 178] '—he is the enemy of Gabriel.' Umar said: 'Then I bear witness that whoever is an enemy to Gabriel is an enemy to Michael, and they are both enemies to whoever opposes them.' So this was rejected from Umar, and Allah, exalted is He, sent down these two verses."

**The second:** It is narrated that Umar had land on the upper part of Medina, and his route passed by the Jewish study house (midras), and he would sit with them and listen to their speech. They said: "O Umar, we have come to love you, and we hope for you." He said: "By Allah, I do not come to you out of your love, nor do I ask you because I am in doubt about my religion; rather I enter upon you only to increase my insight into the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, and I see his traces in your Book." Then he asked them about Gabriel. They said: "That one is our enemy; he informs Muhammad of our secrets, and he is the one in charge of every earthquake and punishment, whereas Michael comes with fertility and peace." He said to them: "And what is their status with Allah?" They said: "The closest in rank: Gabriel is on his right and Michael on his left, and Michael is an enemy to Gabriel." Umar said: "If it is as you say, then they are not enemies, and you are more disbelieving than donkeys. Whoever is an enemy to one of them is an enemy to the other, and whoever is an enemy to both of them is an enemy to Allah." Then Umar returned and found that Gabriel, peace be upon him, had preceded him with the revelation. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Your Lord has agreed with you, O Umar." Umar said: "After that I found myself in my religion firmer than a rock."

**The third:** Muqatil said: "The Jews claimed that Gabriel, peace be upon him, is our enemy. He was commanded to place prophethood among us, but he placed it among others. So Allah sent down these verses."

Know that the closer view is that the cause of their enmity toward him was that he used to bring the Qur'an down upon Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is because His saying, ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel – indeed, he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah﴾, indicates that this descent should not be a cause of enmity, since he only did it by the command of Allah; so it should not be a cause of enmity. This is established in several ways:

First: What Gabriel brought down of the Qur'an was the good tidings of reward for the obedient, the warning of punishment for the disobedient, and the command to fight and battle. Since he did not do this by his own choice, but by the command of Allah, which they acknowledge there is no escape from and no way to oppose, then enmity toward one whose situation is this entails enmity toward Allah, and enmity toward Allah is disbelief; so it follows that enmity toward one of this kind is disbelief.

Second: If Allah had commanded Michael to bring down such a Book, then either it would be said that he would rebel or refuse to accept the command of Allah, and that is not fitting for the infallible angels; or he would accept it and bring it in accordance with the command of Allah. In that case, what they said about Gabriel would apply to Michael, peace be upon them both. So what is the reason for singling out Gabriel for enmity?

Third: The descent of the Qur'an upon Muhammad was as burdensome to the Jews as the descent of the Torah upon Moses was burdensome to other people. If the aversion of some people to the descent of the Qur'an necessitated its ugliness, then the aversion of those earlier people to the descent of the Torah upon Moses, peace be upon him, would necessitate its ugliness. It is known that all of this is false. Thus, by these considerations, the corruption of what they said is established.

**The second issue:** Some people have found it unlikely that a people of the Jews would say that Gabriel is their enemy. They said: "We see the Jews in our time unanimous in denying this, insisting that none of their predecessors said so." Know that this is false, because Allah's report is more truthful, and because their ignorance was severe; and they are the ones who said, ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138].

**The third issue:** Ibn Kathir read "Jibril" (جَبْرِيلَ) with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the ra, without a hamza. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from Asim read it with a fatha on the jim and the ra, with a hamza. The rest read it with a kasra on the jim and the ra, without a hamza, on the pattern of qindil. In it there are seven dialects; three of them we have mentioned. Jibra'il (جِبْرائِلُ) is on the pattern of jibra'il, Jibra'il is on the pattern of jibra'il, Jibra'il is on the pattern of jibra'il, and Jibrin with a nun. It is not declined (diptote) because of definiteness and foreignness.

**The fourth issue:** Some said: Jibril means "servant of God": "jabar" means "servant" and "il" means "God." Mika'il means "servant of God." This is the view of Ibn Abbas and a group of scholars. Abu Ali al-Susi said: "This is not correct, for two reasons: first, 'il' is not known among the names of Allah; and second, if it were so, the last part of the name would be in the genitive case."

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then indeed he has brought it down upon your heart﴾, there are questions:

**The first question:** To what do the pronouns in His saying "fa-innahu" (فَإنَّهُ) and in "nazzalahu" (نَزَّلَهُ) refer? The answer has two views:

One: The first pronoun refers to Gabriel and the second to the Qur'an, even though it has not been mentioned, because it is understood, like His saying, ﴿He left upon its back no creature﴾ [Fatir: 45], meaning upon the earth. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and most scholars. That is, if their enmity is because Gabriel brings down the Qur'an, then he only brings it down by the permission of Allah. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Referring to something not previously mentioned carries grandeur for its owner, since because of his great fame it is as if it indicates him by himself, and one dispenses with his explicit name by mentioning some of his attributes."

The second: The meaning is that Allah sent down Gabriel, peace be upon him, not that he sent down himself.

**The second question:** The Qur'an was only sent down upon Muhammad ﷺ, so what is the reason for His saying, "he sent it down upon your heart"? The answer: We have discussed this matter in Surat al-Shu'ara' in His saying, ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193]. Most of the community holds that He sent the Qur'an down upon him, not upon his heart; but He specifically mentioned the heart because what was brought down was firmly established in his heart by memorization until he conveyed it to his community. Since the cause of his ability to convey it was its firm establishment in his heart by memorization, it became permissible to say "He sent it down upon your heart," even though in reality He sent it down upon him, not upon his heart.

**The third question:** The proper wording would have been "upon my heart." The answer: It came in the form of quoting Allah's speech as He spoke it, as if it were said: "Say what I have spoken, as my word: whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, indeed he has brought it down upon your heart."

**The fourth question:** How is His saying "fa-innahu nazzalahu" (فَإنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ) acceptable as the response (jaza') to the condition (shart)? The answer has two aspects:

The first: He, glorified and exalted, made clear that this enmity is corrupt, because he did nothing except that he was commanded to bring down a Book containing guidance and good tidings, so he brought it down. Insofar as he is commanded, he must be excused; and insofar as he brought guidance and good tidings, he must be thanked. So how does enmity befit him?

The second: He, exalted is He, made clear that if the Jews are hostile to him, that is their right, because he brought down the Book to you as proof of your prophethood and confirmation of your truthfulness, and they dislike that. So how would they not hate the one who confirmed upon them the matter they dislike?

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, the more apparent meaning is "by the command of Allah," and this is preferable to interpreting it as "by the knowledge of Allah," for several reasons:

First: "idhn" (إذْن) is literally "command" and metaphorically "knowledge," and a word must be taken in its literal sense wherever possible.

Second: His bringing it down was obligatory, and obligation is derived from command, not from knowledge.

Third: When that descent is by a binding command, it is more emphatic as a proof.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿confirming what came before it﴾, it is taken to mean what most exegetes have agreed upon: that what is intended is the books of the prophets that came before it, and there is no sense in restricting it to one book. Among them are those who restricted it to the Torah, and claimed that it indicates that [p. 180] the Qur'an agrees with the Torah in pointing to the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. If it is said: Are not the laws of the Qur'an different from the laws of all the other books? Why, then, is it considered confirming of them, because they agree in pointing to monotheism, while the prophethood of Muhammad would be even more appropriate for not confirming them? We say: The laws contained in the other books were limited to those times and ended in this time, on the basis that abrogation (naskh) is a clarification of the end of the period of worship. In that case, there is no difference between the Qur'an and the other books regarding the laws.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and guidance﴾, what is meant is that the Qur'an contains two matters:

One: The clarification of what obligations have been imposed, concerning actions of the heart and actions of the limbs; from this aspect it is guidance.

The second: The clarification of how the reward of the one who performs those actions will be; from this aspect it is good tidings. Since the first precedes the second in existence, God therefore placed the word "guidance" before the word "good tidings." If it is said: Why did He specify that it is guidance and good tidings for the believers, when it is so for everyone in relation to all? The answer has two aspects:

The first: He, exalted is He, specified them with it only because they are the ones who were guided by the Book; so it is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

The second reason: it is only good news (bushra) for the believers, because bushra is a report indicating the attainment of a great good, and this only applies to the believers. For this reason God singled them out for it.

As for the second verse, which is His saying, ﴿Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels﴾, know that when He, exalted is He, had explained in the first verse, ﴿whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾, because he sent down the Qur'an upon the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), it was necessary that such a person be an enemy to God, the Exalted, He explained in this verse that whoever is an enemy to God, God is his enemy. Thus He explained that, in exchange for their enmity, there is something that magnifies the harm that comes upon them, which is God's enmity toward them, because their enmity does not affect, benefit, or harm Him, whereas His enmity leads to everlasting, painful punishment, beyond which there is no greater harm. Here there are some questions.

The first question: How is it permissible that they be enemies of God, when the essence of enmity is to harm the enemy, and that is impossible for God, the Exalted? The answer: The literal meaning of enmity (ʿadawah) applies only to us, because the enemy of another is one who wishes to inflict harm upon him, and that is impossible for God, the Exalted. Rather, what is meant by it is one of two things. Either they are hostile to the friends of God, and this constitutes enmity toward God, like His saying, ﴿Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:33], and His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who abuse God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:57], because the intended meaning of the two verses is the friends of God, not God Himself, since war and harm are impossible for Him. Or what is meant is their aversion to carrying out His obedience and worship and their remoteness from adhering to it. Since an enemy hardly agrees with his enemy or submits to him, their way in this respect is likened to enmity. As for their enmity toward Gabriel and the messengers, it is genuine, because harm is possible for them; but their enmity does not affect them, since they are incapable of the things that would affect them. Their enmity does affect the Jews, because in the present it entails humiliation and wretchedness, and in the future it entails everlasting punishment.

The second question: Since He mentioned the angels, why did He repeat the mention of Gabriel and Michael, given that they are included among the angels? The answer has two aspects:

First: He singled them out for mention because of their excellence, as if, owing to their perfect excellence, they had become a kind distinct from the kind of angels.

Second: What had passed between the Messenger and the Jews was the mention of these two, and the verse was revealed on account of them, so there is no doubt that He explicitly named them both. Know that this implies that they are more excellent than all the angels; otherwise this interpretation would not be valid. Having established this, we say: Gabriel, peace be upon him, must be more excellent than Michael, for several reasons:

One: He, exalted is He, mentioned Gabriel, peace be upon him, first, and mentioning the lesser before the greater is considered reprehensible by custom, so it must be reprehensible by the law, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "What the Muslims see as good is good in the sight of God."

[Page 181]

Two: Gabriel, peace be upon him, descends with the Qur'an, revelation, and knowledge, which are the sustenance of the souls, while Michael descends with fertility and rain, which are the sustenance of the bodies. Since knowledge is more noble than foods, it must be that Gabriel is more excellent than Michael.

Three: His saying, exalted is He, describing Gabriel: ﴿obeyed there, trustworthy﴾ [al-Takwir 81:21]. He described him with the attribute of "obeyed" in an absolute sense, and its apparent meaning implies that he is obeyed in relation to Michael, so he must be more excellent than him.

The second issue: Abu ʿAmr and Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, recited "Mikal" on the pattern of "Qintar," while Nafiʿ recited "Mikail" with the vowel elided (mukhtalasah), there being no yaʾ after the hamzah, on the pattern of "Mikaʿil." The rest recited "Mikaʾil" on the pattern of "Mikaʿil." There is also another dialect, "Mikaʾil" on the pattern of "Mikayʿil," and "Mikaʾil" like "Mikaʿil." Ibn Jinni said: when the Arabs pronounce a non-Arabic word, they mix up its forms.

The third issue: The waw in "Jibril" and "Mikal" — it is said that it is the waw of conjunction, and it is said that it means "or," that is: whoever is an enemy to any one of these, then indeed God is an enemy to all the disbelievers.

The fourth issue: ﴿an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. He intended "an enemy to them," but He used the apparent noun to indicate that God, the Exalted, opposed them only because of their disbelief, and that enmity toward the angels is disbelief.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 99:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient.﴾

Know that this is another kind of their ugly deeds and disgraces. Ibn Abbas said: The Jews used to seek victory over the Aws and the Khazraj through the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before his mission. But when he was sent from among the Arabs, they disbelieved in him and denied what they had been saying about him. Mu'adh ibn Jabal said to them: "O assembly of Jews, fear Allah and submit. You used to seek victory over us through Muhammad, and we were people of polytheism, and you informed us that he would be sent and described his attributes to us." Some of them said: "He has not brought us anything of the clear signs, and he is not the one we used to mention to you." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Here there are several issues.

First issue: The more evident view is that the intended meaning of "the clear signs" (al-ayat al-bayyinat) is the verses of the Qur'an, the like of which neither jinn nor humans could produce, even if they were to back one another up. Others said: It is not impossible that what is meant by "the clear signs" is the Qur'an together with the rest of the proofs, such as their refusal to engage in mubahalah (mutual invocation of divine curse) and to wish for death, and all the other miracles, such as feeding a great multitude with a little food, water gushing from between his fingers, and the splitting of the moon. Al-Qadi said: It is preferable to restrict this to the Qur'an, because when "signs" (ayat) is joined to "revelation" (tanzil), it is more specific to the Qur'an. And Allah knows best.

Second issue: The reason for calling the Qur'an "signs" has several aspects.

The first: an ayah (sign, verse) is that which indicates. When parts of the Qur'an indicate, by their eloquence, the truthfulness of the one who makes the claim, they are signs.

The second: some of it indicates reports of the unseen, so it indicates those unseen matters.

The third: it indicates the proofs of divine unity (tawhid), prophethood (nubuwwa), and the laws (shara'i), so from this aspect it is signs. If it is said: A proof is only clear, so what is the meaning of describing the signs as being clear? No one may say that what is meant is that some of them are clearer than others, because that would be valid only if it were possible for some sciences to be stronger than others, and that is impossible. This is because the one who knows something either has, together with that knowledge, the possibility of the opposite of what he believes, or he does not. If that possibility accompanies it, then that belief is not knowledge; and if it does not, it is impossible for something else to be more firmly established than it. We say: The difference does not occur in the essence of knowledge itself, but in its path. The sciences are divided into those whose path of acquisition and the proof indicating them have more premises, so reaching them is more difficult, and those with fewer premises, so reaching them is nearer. This is what is meant by the clear sign.

Third issue: Revelation (inzal) is an expression for moving a thing from above to below, and that cannot be realized except in a corporeal body. Therefore, according to this discourse, it is impossible. But when Gabriel descended from above to below and reported it, that was called revelation.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾, there are issues in it.

The first issue: Disbelief (kufr) in them is of two kinds:

One: denying them while knowing their truth.

The second: denying them out of ignorance, neglecting to reflect on them, and turning away from their proofs. There is no specification in the apparent wording, so everyone is included in it.

The second issue: Fisq (defiant disobedience) in the linguistic sense is a person's going beyond what is prescribed for him. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Except Iblis, who was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]. The Arabs say of a date pit: when it comes out of the ripe date upon its falling, the pit has fasaqat (went out). Its meaning is close to fujur (wickedness), because it is derived from the fujur of the dam, which prevents water from reaching the place where it would cause corruption [if it reaches it]; so the transgression of a person beyond what is prescribed for him toward corruption is likened to one who breaches the dam until it reaches the place where it causes corruption. If it is said: Is it not the case that the one who commits a minor sin has transgressed Allah's command, yet he is not described as fasiq or fajir? We say: These two terms are applied only to a matter that is great from the category we have mentioned, because whoever opens a small breach in a river is not described as having burst that river. Likewise, fisq is only said when the transgression is great.

Having established this, we say that regarding His saying ﴿the fasiqun﴾ there are two aspects:

One: every disbeliever is fasiq, but not conversely. So the mention of the fasiq comes to include the disbeliever and others, and therefore it is more appropriate.

The second: that what is meant is: none disbelieve in them except the disbeliever who exceeds every limit in his disbelief. The meaning is that since these verses are clear and manifest, none disbelieve in them except the disbeliever who reaches the utmost extreme in disbelief and exceeds every limit that is considered good by reason and by the Sharia.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 100:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Is it not that every time they make a covenant, a party of them casts it aside? Nay, most of them do not believe.﴾

Know that this is another type of their ugly conduct, and in it there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿Is it not that every time they make a covenant﴾, the wa (waw) is a conjunction (waw al-'atf) which the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham) has entered upon. It has been said that the waw is superfluous (za'idah), but this is not sound, because, even though its meaning is correct, it is not permissible to rule that it is superfluous.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: the waw is for coordination (li al-'atf) upon an omitted element whose meaning is: "Did they disbelieve in the signs and the clear proofs, and every time they make a covenant..." Abu al-Sammak read the waw with sukun, on the basis that al-fasiqun (the defiant ones) is in the sense of alladhina fasaqu (those who defied), as if it were said: "None disbelieves in them except those who defied, or who broke the covenant of God many times." It is also read ʿawahadu and ʿuhidu.

صفحة ١٨٣
The third issue: The purpose of this interrogation is denunciation and magnifying the enormity of what they undertake, because when something of this kind is stated in this form, it is more forceful in rebuke and reproach. By His saying, ﴿every time they make a covenant﴾, He indicates a covenant after a covenant which they broke and cast aside. Indeed, it indicates that this is customary among them. So the Exalted intended to console the Messenger, at their disbelief in what was sent down to him of the signs, that this is no novelty from them; rather it is their disposition and their custom, and the custom of their predecessors, as He explained in the preceding verses concerning their breaking of covenants and pacts state after state, because one who habitually follows this way does not find it difficult to violate it, unlike one whose custom has not been so.

The fourth issue: Regarding the covenant there are several views:

First: when God, the Exalted, manifested the proofs indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the soundness of his law, that was like a covenant from Him, glory be to Him, and their acceptance of those proofs was like a pledge from them to God, glory be to Him and exalted.

Second: the covenant is what they used to say before his mission, peace be upon him: "If the Prophet emerges, we will surely believe in him and surely drive the polytheists out of their homes."

Third: they used to make covenants with God often and then break them.

Fourth: the Jews had made a covenant with Him not to aid anyone of the disbelievers against him, but they broke that and aided Quraysh against him on the day of the Trench. The judge (al-Qadi) said: if this report is sound, there is no impediment to its inclusion under the verse, but it is not permissible to restrict the verse to it. Rather, the closer view is that what is meant is what is connected with what was mentioned before, of their disbelief in the signs of God. And if that is so, then interpreting it as breaking the covenant regarding what the earlier scriptures and the rational proofs contain, of the soundness of the statement and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), is stronger.

The fifth issue: He only said, ﴿a party of them casts it aside﴾, because among those who made the covenant there were those who believed, or who could come to believe. Since that was not the attribute of all of them, He singled out a party for mention. Then, since it could be supposed that that party were the fewer, He clarified that they were the majority, saying, ﴿Nay, most of them do not believe﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: most of those defiant ones do not believe in you ever, out of their envy and insolence.

The second: "do not believe" means they do not affirm their own Book, because they were among their people like hypocrites with the Messenger, showing them faith in their Book and their messenger, and then not acting upon its requirement and its demand.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 101:**

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from God, confirming what was with them, a party of those who had been given the Book threw the Book of God behind their backs, as if they did not know.﴾

Know that the meaning of the Messenger being one who confirms what is with them is that he acknowledged the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him) and the authenticity of the Torah (al-Tawrah). Alternatively, [it means he confirms what is with them] in the sense that the Torah gave good tidings of the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ). So when Muhammad came, his mere coming was a confirmation of the Torah.

Page 184

As for God's words, ﴿threw﴾, it is a metaphor for their abandoning and turning away from it, like something thrown behind the back, out of self-sufficiency with it and little attention paid to it.

As for God's words, ﴿of those who had been given the Book﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: What is meant is those who were given the knowledge of the Book, namely those who study it and memorize it. The one who said this stated: The evidence for this is that God described this party with knowledge in His words, ﴿they do not know﴾.

The second: What is meant is those who claim to hold fast to the Book, whether or not they know it. This is like describing the Muslims as "people of the Qur'an," which does not mean those who specialize in knowing its sciences; rather, it means those who believe in it and adhere to its requirements.

As for God's words, ﴿the Book of God behind their backs﴾, it has been said that it is the Torah, and it has been said that it is the Qur'an. This second view is the closer one, for two reasons:

The first: Throwing away is only conceivable regarding what they had previously held fast to. As for what they never paid attention to, it is not said that they threw it away.

The second: He said, ﴿a party of those who had been given the Book threw [it away]﴾. If what is meant were the Qur'an, singling out a party would have no meaning, because all of them do not believe in the Qur'an. If it is asked: How is it valid for them to cast aside the Torah when they hold fast to it? We answer: When it indicates the prophethood of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, through its description and attributes, and it obligates belief in him, and then they deviated from it, they became casters-off of the Torah.

As for God's words, ﴿as if they did not know﴾, this is evidence that they threw it away knowingly and with awareness, for this is only said of one who knows. Thus the verse indicates from this angle that this party had knowledge of the validity of his prophethood, but they denied what they knew. It has been established that a great multitude cannot be held to have denied, so it is necessary to affirm with certainty that those deniers were few enough that obstinacy could be attributed to them.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, Verse 102 (Part 1 of 7)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic, and what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. Yet they taught no one until they had said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." And they learned from them that by which they cause division between a man and his wife. But they could not harm anyone thereby except by Allah's permission. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them. And they certainly knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter. How wretched is that for which they sold their souls, if only they knew.﴾

[Page 185]

Know that this is another kind of their ugly deeds, namely their occupation with magic, their devotion to it, and their calling people to it.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And they followed﴾, is a report about those previously mentioned, who are the Jews. There are then several opinions:

The first: they are the Jews who were in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second: they are the Jews who came before them.

The third: they are those among the magicians in the time of Solomon (peace be upon him), because most Jews deny Solomon's prophethood and regard him as one of the kings of this world. Therefore, those among them in his time may well have believed that this great kingdom came into being only through magic.

The fourth: it encompasses all of them, and this is the more preferable view, because there is no reason to restrict the wording to some of them rather than others, as there is no evidence for specification. As-Suddi said: When Muhammad (ﷺ) came to them, they opposed him with the Torah and argued with him by it. The Torah and the Qur'an agreed, so they discarded the Torah and took up the Book of Asaf and the magic of Harut and Marut, which did not agree with the Qur'an. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah, confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Book threw the Book of Allah behind their backs﴾. Then He informed about them that they followed the books of magic.

**The second issue:** They mentioned several interpretations of ﴿recited﴾:

The first: what is meant by it is recitation and reporting.

The second: Abu Muslim said: (tatlu) means "they lie concerning the kingdom of Solomon." It is said: "talā ʿalayhi" when one lies, and "talā ʿanhu" when one tells the truth, and when the object is left unspecified, both usages are permissible. But the closer view is the first, because recitation is literally applied to reporting. However, when a reporter's report is false, it is said that so-and-so "recited," and that he "recited against so-and-so," in order to distinguish it from true reporting, for which one does not say "rawā ʿalā fulān" (narrated against so-and-so), but rather "rawā ʿan fulān," "akhbara ʿan fulān," and "talā ʿan fulān." That usage is appropriate only to reports and recitation. And there is nothing to prevent what they reported about Solomon from being something recited and read, so that all these attributes are combined in it.

* * *

**The third issue:** They differed concerning the devils (ash-shayāṭīn). It is said that what is meant is the devils of the jinn, and this is the view of most scholars. It is said that they are the devils of mankind, and this is the view of the theologians among the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazila, the rationalist school). And it is said that they are both the devils of mankind and of the jinn together.

As for those who understood it as the devils of the jinn, they said: The devils used to eavesdrop on the heavens, then add to what they heard fabrications which they invented and conveyed to the soothsayers (kahana). They wrote these down in books which they read and taught to people. This spread in the time of Solomon (peace be upon him), to the point that people said the jinn know the unseen. They used to say: "This is the knowledge of Solomon, and his kingdom was complete only through this knowledge, and by it he subjected the jinn, mankind, and the wind which runs by his command."

As for those who understood it as the devils of mankind, they said: It has been reported in a khabar (report) that Solomon (peace be upon him) had buried many of the sciences which Allah had specially granted him beneath the throne of his kingdom, out of concern that if the apparent part of them perished, the buried part would remain. When a period had passed, some hypocrites managed, in the midst of that, to write things of magic which resembled those sciences in some respects. Then, after his death, when people came upon those books, they gave people the impression that it was the work of Solomon, and that he had attained what he attained only through these things. This is the meaning of: ﴿what the devils recited﴾.

Those who held this view argued against the first view: if the devils of the jinn were able to alter the books of the prophets and their laws in such a way that the alteration remained among people, then trust in all the laws would be lost, and that would lead to disparaging all religions. If it is said: If you permit this from the devils of mankind, why not allow the same from the devils of the jinn? We say: The difference is that what a human does must in some respects become apparent. But if we allowed the jinn such fabrication, namely adding to the books of Solomon in a hand like Solomon's handwriting, that would not become apparent and would remain hidden, and that would lead to disparaging all religions.

**The fourth issue:** As for His saying, ﴿during the reign of Solomon﴾, it was said: "concerning the kingdom of Solomon," reported from Ibn Juraij. It was also said: "during the era of the reign of Solomon." The closer view is that what is meant is: "they followed what the devils recited, fabricating against the kingdom of Solomon," because they used to read from the books of magic and say that Solomon attained that kingdom only through this knowledge. Thus their reciting those books was like fabrication against the kingdom of Solomon.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** They differed about what is meant by the kingdom of Solomon. The judge (al-Qadi) said: The kingdom of Solomon is prophethood, or prophethood is included in it, and under prophethood is the Book revealed to him and the sharia (law). If this is established, then when these people brought out a scroll containing kinds of magic, which they had buried beneath the throne of his kingdom, and brought it out after his death, giving the impression that it came from him, that became from them a false attribution against his kingdom in reality. The more correct view in my opinion is that it is said: When these people claimed that Solomon attained that realm only through that knowledge, that claim was like fabrication against the kingdom of Solomon.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** The reasons why they attributed magic to Solomon (peace be upon him) are several:

The first: they attributed magic to Solomon in order to magnify his station and exalt his affair, and to encourage the people to accept it from them.

The second: the Jews did not acknowledge the prophethood of Solomon, but used to say that he attained that kingdom only through magic.

The third: when Allah subjected the jinn to Solomon, he would mix with them and benefit from them in wondrous secrets, so it became prevalent in people's assumptions that he (peace be upon him) had acquired magic from them.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Solomon did not disbelieve﴾, this is a declaration of his innocence (peace be upon him) from disbelief, and this indicates that the people had attributed to him both disbelief and magic. Several things have been said about it:

The first: what has been reported from some of the rabbis of the Jews, that they said: "Do you not marvel at Muhammad, who claims that Solomon was a prophet, when he was nothing but a magician?" So Allah revealed this verse.

The second: the magicians among the Jews claimed that they had learned magic from Solomon, so Allah, exalted is He, cleared him of it.

The third: some people claimed that the foundation of his kingdom was through magic, so Allah cleared him of it, because being a prophet is incompatible with being a magician and a disbeliever. Then He, exalted is He, explained that what He cleared him of is attached to others, so He said: ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾. By this He refers to those already mentioned who took magic as a trade for themselves and attributed it to Solomon. Then He, exalted is He, explained what they disbelieved in, since it could have been assumed that they had not disbelieved at first by magic. So He said: ﴿teaching people magic﴾.

Know that discussion of magic occurs from several aspects:

**The first issue:** Concerning its study according to the language. We say: The people of the language have mentioned that it originally means that which is subtle and whose cause is hidden. "As-saḥr" (with a fatḥah) is nourishment, because of its concealment and the subtlety of its pathways. Labid said:

*"And we are bewitched by food and by drink."*

Two meanings have been stated for it:

One: we are deceived and tricked like one who is bewitched and deceived.

The other: we are nourished. Whichever of the two views is correct, its meaning is concealment. And he said:

*"So if you ask us what we are about, indeed we are sparrows of this bewitched (musaḥḥar) humankind."*

This line may bear the same meaning as the first, and it may also mean by "musaḥḥar" one who has a sahr, and "sahr" is the lung and what is attached to the throat. This too returns to the sense of concealment. From this is the saying of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died between my sahr and my nahr (chest)." And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are only one of the bewitched﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 153], meaning one of the created beings who eats and drinks. This is indicated by their saying: ﴿You are only a human like us﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 154]. It may also be understood as "one who has a sahr like us." And Allah, exalted is He, related about Moses (peace be upon him) that he said to the magicians: ﴿What you have brought is magic; indeed Allah will nullify it﴾ [Yūnus: 81]. And He said: ﴿When they cast, they bewitched the eyes of the people and terrified them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 116]. This is the meaning of magic in its original linguistic sense.

**The second issue:** Know that the term "sihr" in the usage of the Sharia is specific to every matter whose cause is hidden, which is imagined to be other than its reality, and which operates as deception and trickery. When it is used without qualification, it conveys the blame of its practitioner. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾, meaning they deceived them until they thought their ropes and staffs were moving. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It was imagined to him by their magic that they were moving﴾ [Ṭāhā: 66]. It may also be used qualified, in what is praised and commended. It is reported that "az-Zibriqan ibn Badr and ʿAmr ibn al-Ahtam came before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said to ʿAmr: 'Inform me about az-Zibriqan.' He said: 'He is obeyed in his assembly, strong in his eloquence, and withholds what is behind his back.' Az-Zibriqan said: 'By Allah, he knows that I am better than him.' ʿAmr said: 'He is in a time of manliness, narrow in his tent, foolish in his father, and base in his maternal uncle. O Messenger of Allah, you have spoken truly about both. He pleased me so I said the best I know, and he angered me so I said the worst I know.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, there is magic in eloquence.'" So the Prophet (ﷺ) called some eloquence "magic," because its speaker clarifies a difficult matter and reveals its reality through the beauty of his explanation and the eloquence of his expression.

If it is said: How is it permissible to call what clarifies the truth and reveals it "magic," when this speaker intended only to make the hidden manifest, not to conceal the apparent, and the term "sihr" conveys only the concealment of the apparent? We say: He called it magic for two reasons:

The first: that measure, because of its subtlety and beauty, attracted hearts, so it resembled the magic which attracts hearts. For this aspect it was called magic, not from the aspect you supposed.

The second: the one capable of eloquence is able to beautify what is ugly and make ugly what is beautiful, and in this respect it resembles magic.

* * *

**The third issue:** Concerning the categories of magic. Know that magic is of several categories:

The first: the magic of the Chaldeans (al-Kaldāniyyīn) and Kasdānīyyīn (Kasdanites), who existed in ancient times. They were a people who worshipped the stars and claimed that they were the ones governing this world, and from them proceed good and evil, happiness and misfortune. They were the people whom Allah sent Abraham (peace be upon him) to refute their doctrine and to counter them in their creed. As for the Mu'tazilah, they have agreed that other than Allah, exalted is He, is unable to create bodies, life, color, or taste. They argued with several arguments mentioned by al-Qadi, which he summarized in his tafsir and in his other books, and we will transmit those arguments and examine them.

[p. 188]

First: the rational principle on which they rely is that everything other than God is either spatially located (mutahayyiz) or subsists in something spatially located. So if anything other than God were the agent of body and life, that other thing would be spatially located, and whatever is spatially located must be capable through a power (qudra), for if it were capable in its own essence, then every body would be capable in the same way, on the premise that bodies are alike. But a being capable through a power cannot be the agent of body and life.

[p. 188 continues]

And two arguments support this:

The first: It is known by necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-darurI) that one of us cannot create body and life ex nihilo. Our power is shared in its inability to do this, and this inability is a shared judgment, so it must have a shared cause. Nothing is shared here except that we are capable through a power. Once this is established, it follows that whoever is capable through a power is incapable of producing body and life.

The second: This power we have certainly differs among its instances. If we posited a power suited to creating body and life, its opposition to this power would not be greater than the opposition of some of these powers to others. So if that degree of opposition sufficed for its suitability to create body and life, then this power would have to be such that some of its parts oppose others and that it is suitable to create body and life. Since this is not the case, we know that one capable through a power cannot create body and life.

Second: If we allowed this, the proof of prophethood through miracles would be impossible. For if we allowed the production of extraordinary events through the combination of heavenly forces with earthly forces, we could not be certain that the extraordinary events which appeared at the hands of the prophets, peace be upon them, came from God, Exalted. Rather, it would be possible that they performed them by means of magic, and then the doctrine of prophethood would be entirely invalid.

Third: If we allowed that among people there could be one who is able to create body, life and colours, that person would be able to acquire great wealth without effort. But we see that the one who claims magic only reaches the acquisition of petty wealth through great exertion. So we know his claim is false. By this method we know the invalidity of what some people claim about alchemy (al-kimya'). For we say: if they could, by some medicines, turn non-gold into gold, then either they could do this with a small amount of wealth, in which case they should have freed themselves from hardship and humiliation, or they could only do it with great instruments and valuable wealth, in which case they should have shown this to the kings who have the means for it. Indeed, kings should have become aware of it, for it would be more beneficial to them than conquering lands, which cannot be accomplished without spending wealth and treasures. Our knowledge that souls and aspirations do not turn towards this is evidence of the invalidity of this claim. The Qadi (al-Qadi) said: Thus it is established by this whole account that the sorcerer cannot be the agent of any of this.

Know that these proofs are very weak.

As for the first argument: we say, what is the evidence that everything other than God is either spatially located or subsists in what is spatially located? Do you not know that the philosophers insist on affirming intellects, celestial souls and rational souls, and claim that these in themselves are neither spatially located nor subsisting in what is spatially located? What is the evidence against this view? If they say: if such an existent were posited, it would follow that it is like God, Exalted, we reply: we do not grant that, because sharing a mode does not entail sharing the quiddity. Granting it, why could it not be that some bodies are capable of this by their own essence? Your statement: "Bodies are alike; so if one body were like this, every body would be like this." We reply: what is the evidence for the likeness of bodies? If they say: there is no meaning of "body" except that which extends in directions and occupies spaces, and there is no difference between them in this meaning, we reply: extension in directions and occupation of spaces are attributes of it and necessary consequences of its nature, and it is not improbable that things differing in quiddity share some necessary consequences. Granting that it must be capable through a power, why do you say that one capable through a power cannot create body and life? Your statement: "Because the power we have is shared in this inability, and this inability is a shared judgment, so it must have a shared cause, and nothing is shared except our being capable through a power." We reply: all these premises are disputed. We do not grant that the inability is a caused judgment, for the inability is a negative matter (adami), and a negative matter is not caused. Granting that it is an existential matter, according to their own doctrine many judgments are not caused, so why could it not be so here? Granting that it is caused, why do you say that a shared judgment must have a shared cause? Is it not the case that ugliness in injustice arises as caused by its being injustice, in lying by its being lying, and in ignorance by its being ignorance? Granting that there must be a shared cause, we do not grant that nothing is shared except our being capable through a power. Why could it not be that this power we have is shared in some specific attribute, while that power which is suited to create body lies outside that attribute? What is the evidence that the matter is not so?

As for the first argument, namely that the opposition of that power to some powers is not greater than the opposition of some of these powers to others, we say: this is weak, for we do not explain its suitability to create body by its being opposed to these powers, but by its specific particularity for which it opposes the rest of the powers, and it is known that this particularity is not present in the rest of the powers. A parallel to what they have mentioned would be to say: the opposition of sound to whiteness is not greater than the opposition of blackness to whiteness; so if that opposition were preventing sound from being capable of being seen, then blackness's opposition to whiteness would have to make its being seen impossible. Since this speech is corrupt, so is what they have said.

It is strange of the Qadi that when he related these arguments from the Ash'ariyya in the question of the vision (of God) and refuted them with these objections, he himself then relied upon them in this question, which is the foundation for establishing prophethood and for refuting those who posit an intermediary between God and us.

As for the second argument, namely that the doctrine of the validity of prophethood cannot survive the allowance of this principle: we say, either the doctrine of the validity of prophethood is derived from the invalidity of this principle or it is not. If it is the former, then the invalidity of this principle is precluded by building on the validity of prophethood, otherwise a circularity (dawr) arises. If it is the latter, then this argument falls away entirely.

As for the third argument: one may say that the discussion concerns possibility, which is a different matter. We do not claim that this state is present in every person; rather, this state does not occur among humans except in widely separated eras, so how does what you mention apply to us?

That is the discussion regarding the first type of magic.

The second type of magic: the magic of people with powerful imaginations and souls. They said: People have differed over what each person indicates by his saying "ana" (I). Some people say: it is this structure (bunya). Others say: it is a body that has come to be in this structure. Others say: it is an existent which is neither a body nor corporeal. As for when we say that the human being is this structure, there is no doubt that this structure is composed of the four humours. Why could it not happen in some cold eras that its temperament becomes one of the temperaments in some region, one which entails the capacity to create body and knowledge of matters hidden and inaccessible to us? The same applies when we say the human being is a body that has come to be in this structure. As for when we say the human being is the soul (nafs), why could it not be said that souls differ, so that in some souls, if they are by their essence capable of these strange events and aware of hidden secrets, it occurs? This possibility is one for which no proof of its invalidity has been established besides the aforementioned arguments, and their invalidity has become clear. Then, several things confirm this possibility:

The first: a plank on which a person can walk if it is placed on the ground cannot be walked upon if it is like a bridge over an abyss beneath it. This is only because the imagination of falling, when it grows strong, causes it.

The second: the physicians agreed to forbid the one afflicted with vertigo (al-mar'uf) from looking at red things, and the one afflicted with seizure (al-mas'ur) from looking at things with strong shine and rotation. This is only because souls were created obedient to imaginations.

The third: the author of al-Shifa' (The Healing) related from Aristotle that in the nature of animals: when a hen greatly resembles roosters in voice and in fighting with roosters, something like what grows on the leg of a rooster grows on her leg. Then the author of al-Shifa' said: this indicates that bodily states follow psychic states.

The fourth: all nations agree that supplication by the tongue, devoid of inner striving, is of little effect and has no impact. This shows that aspirations and souls have effects. This agreement is not specific to one particular matter or one specific wisdom.

The fifth: if you were fair, you would know that the proximate principles of animal actions are nothing but psychic representations (tasawwurat nafsaniyya), because the motive power fixed in the muscles is suitable for the act, for its abandonment, or for its opposite. Neither of the two sides is preferred over the other except by a preponderant factor, and that factor is nothing but the representation of the act as beautiful or pleasant, or the representation of it as ugly or painful. These representations are the principles for the muscular powers becoming principles for the act, once the acts have come into existence after having been so only potentially. If these representations are principles for the principles of these acts, then what is strange about their being the principles of the acts themselves, and eliminating the intermediary from consideration?

The sixth: experience and direct observation bear witness that these representations are proximate principles for the occurrence of qualities in bodies. The angry person's temperament becomes hot to the point that it gives him a strong heat.

It is related that one of the kings was afflicted with paralysis (falij), and the physicians were unable to treat him. One of the skilled ones entered upon him at a moment of his heedlessness and insulted him openly and disparaged his honour. The king's anger intensified, and he leapt from his bed in an involuntary leap because of the intensity of that speech, and that chronic illness and deadly sickness were removed. If it is permissible that representations be principles for the occurrence of events within the body, then what is strange about their being principles for the occurrence of events outside the body?

Seventh: The affliction caused by the evil eye (al-ʿayn) is something on which rational people agree, and this also confirms the possibility of what we have said. Once you understand this, we say: the souls that perform these acts may be very strong, so that they dispense with the aid of instruments and tools in these acts, and they may be weak, so that they need these instruments. The explanation is that when the soul is elevated above the body and strongly drawn toward the world of [the heavens], it is as though it were one of the celestial spirits, and so it is powerful in influencing the matter of this world. But if it is weak and strongly attached to these bodily pleasures, then it has no effect at all except upon this body. If this person wants to make it such that its influence passes from its own body to another body, he takes an image of that other person and places it before the senses, and the senses occupy themselves with it, so the imagination follows it upon it, and the rational soul turns toward it, and the psychic influences and spiritual actions grow strong. For this reason the nations have agreed that the practice of these works requires abandoning habitual and desired things, reducing food, and withdrawing from mixing with people. Whenever these matters are more complete, that influence is stronger. If it happens that the soul is suited to this matter, considering its essence and its special nature, the influence becomes great. The determined cause in this is that when the soul occupies itself with the first aspect, it devotes all its power to that act, but when it occupies itself with many acts, its power is scattered and distributed among those acts, so that each act receives only a branch of that power and a rivulet of that river. For this reason we see that two people are equal in quickness of mind when one occupies himself with a single craft and the other with two crafts; the one of a single craft is stronger than the one of two. Whoever tries to grasp the reality of a question among questions, while he reflects upon it he must empty his mind of other things, for when the mind is emptied it turns fully toward it, and the act becomes easier and better. Since this is so, when a person's concern and aspiration are occupied with seeking pleasures and attaining desires, the psychic power is occupied with them and absorbed in them, so its inclination toward achieving the strange act that he attempts is not strong, especially since there is another calamity here, namely that such a soul has become accustomed to occupying itself with pleasures from the beginning of its life to its end, and has never occupied itself with inventing these strange acts. So it is by nature inclined toward the first and averse to the second. When it finds what it seeks of the first kind, how would it turn toward the other side? It has become clear from this that the practice of these works can only be achieved with detachment from bodily states, abandoning mixing with people, and turning entirely toward the world of purity and spirits.

As for incantations (al-ruqā), if they are known, the matter regarding them is evident, because their purpose is that just as we occupy the sense of sight with things suited to that purpose, we also occupy the sense of hearing with things suited to that purpose, for when the senses agree upon directing themselves to one purpose, the soul's turning toward it is then stronger. But if they are with words that are not known, a state resembling bewilderment and astonishment arises in the soul there, for when a person believes that these words are recited for seeking aid from some spiritual things, and does not know the manner of that aid, a state resembling bewilderment and astonishment arises in the soul, and in the course of that a cutting-off from sensible things occurs in the soul, along with turning toward that act and great zeal, so the psychic influence grows strong and the purpose is attained. The same is said regarding fumigation (al-dukhn). They said: it has thus been established that this amount of psychic power is occupied with influence, and if the first kind of magic is combined with it, namely seeking aid from the stars and their influences, the influence becomes great. Indeed, there are two other kinds here.

The first: souls that have departed from bodies may include some that are very similar to these souls in their power and in their influences. When those souls become pure, it is not far-fetched that there may be drawn to them souls similar to them among the departed souls, and some kind of attachment to this body arises in those souls, so many souls support one another in that act, and when the power is complete and increases, the influence becomes strong.

The second: when these rational souls become pure of bodily defilements, they become receptive to the lights that overflow from the celestial spirits and the heavenly souls, so these souls are strengthened by the lights of those spirits, and they become capable of strange matters that break customary habit. This is the explanation of the magic of those with illusions and incantations.

The third kind of magic: seeking aid from earthly spirits. Know that the affirmation of jinn is something that some later philosophers and Muʿtazila denied. As for the eminent philosophers, they did not deny the belief in them except that they named them "earthly spirits," and these are different in themselves: some are good and some are evil. The good ones are the believing jinn, and the evil ones are the disbelieving jinn and their devils. Then the later ones among them said: these spirits are substances subsisting by themselves, neither spatially extended nor inhering in what is spatially extended; they are capable, knowing, perceiving particulars. The connection of rational souls with them is easier than their connection with the celestial spirits, but the power that rational souls acquire by their connection with these earthly spirits is weaker than the power acquired by their connection with those celestial spirits. As for the connection being easier, that is because the affinity between our souls and these earthly spirits is easier, and because the similarity and resemblance between them is more complete and stronger than the resemblance between our souls and the celestial spirits. As for the power by connection with the celestial spirits being greater, that is because the celestial spirits are, in relation to the earthly spirits, like the sun in relation to a spark, the sea in relation to a drop, and the sultan in relation to his subjects.

They said: although no compelling proof has been established for the existence of these things, there is at least the possibility of their being conceivable. Moreover, practitioners of the craft and people of experience have witnessed that connection with these earthly spirits is achieved by easy and few acts of incantation, fumigation, and abstraction. This kind is what is called "ʿazāʾim" (formulas of compulsion) and the work of subjugating the jinn.

The fourth kind of magic: imaginings and the seizing of eyes (al-akhdh bil-ʿuyūn). This seizing is based on premises:

The first: errors of sight are many. The passenger on a ship, when he looks at the shore, sees the ship standing still and the shore moving. This indicates that the still is seen as moving and the moving is seen as still. A falling drop is seen as a straight line; a wick spun rapidly is seen as a circle; a grape is seen in water as large like a plum; a small person is seen in fog as huge; and like the earth's vapor which shows you the disc of the sun at its rising as large, and when it leaves it and rises above it, it becomes small. As for seeing a large thing from afar as small, that is evident. These things have guided minds to the understanding that the faculty of sight may perceive a thing contrary to what it is in general, due to some accidental causes.

The second: the faculty of sight only stands fully upon sensible things when it perceives the sensible within a period of time having some measure. But when it perceives a sensible thing in a very short time and then perceives another sensible thing after it, and so on, some of them become mixed with others, and some sensible things cannot be distinguished from others. This is because if you draw from the center of a wheel to its circumference many lines of different colors and then it is rotated, the sense perceives one color as if it were composed of all those colors.

The third: when the soul is occupied with something, something else may be present before the sense and the sense does not perceive it at all, just as a person, upon entering before the sultan, may meet another person and speak with him, yet he does not recognize him nor understand his speech, because his heart is occupied with something else.
