Likewise the one looking into a mirror: he may intend to see a speck in his eye and see it, and not see what is larger than it, if there is a mark on his face or on his forehead or on other limbs facing the mirror; and he may intend to see whether the surface of the mirror is level or not, and then he sees nothing of what is in the mirror. Once you know these premises, the manner of this kind of magic becomes easy to conceive. A skilled conjuror displays the performance of something that occupies the minds of the spectators and draws their eyes to it, until, when their preoccupation with that thing and their fixed gaze upon it has absorbed them, he performs something else very swiftly, and that act remains hidden because of the difference between the two things: first, their preoccupation with the first matter; second, the swiftness of carrying out this second act. Then something appears to them other than what they had awaited, and they marvel at it greatly. Had he remained silent and not spoken with what diverts the thoughts away from what he intends to do, and had the souls and imaginations not been moved toward other than what he intends to bring about, the spectators would have noticed everything he does. This is what is meant by their saying that the conjuror "seizes the eyes," for in reality he draws the eyes to other than the direction in which he is tricking, and whenever his seizing of the eyes and thoughts and his drawing of them to other than his intended aim is stronger, he is more skilled in his work. And whenever the conditions that affect the sense of sight in some kind of disorder are more intense, this work is better: for example, if the conjuror sits in a very bright place, for brightness causes the sight weariness and disorder; likewise intense darkness; and likewise bright, strong colors cause the sight weariness and disorder, while dark colors rarely allow the faculty of sight to fix upon their states. This is the sum of what is said regarding this kind of magic.

The fifth kind of magic: the wondrous acts that appear from the assembling of machines arranged according to geometric proportions, and at other times from kinds of imaginary contrivance. Examples: two horsemen fighting, and one kills the other; and a horseman on a horse with a trumpet in his hand, who, each time an hour of the day passes, sounds the trumpet without anyone touching him. Among them are the statues which the Romans and the Indians make, so that the observer cannot distinguish them from a human being, to the extent that they make them laughing and weeping, so that one can distinguish in them the laughter of joy, the laughter of shame, and the laughter of one gloating. These aspects are among the subtle matters of appearances. The magic of Pharaoh's magicians was of this type. From this category is the construction of the clock-box. Within this category falls the science of moving heavy weights, which is to move a great heavy thing by a light, easy instrument. In reality, this should not be counted as a kind of magic, because for it there are causes

[p. 193]

**[Page 193 continued]**

...a precious knowledge. Whoever gains access to it is able to use it. However, since gaining access to it is extremely difficult, and no one reaches it except one individual after another, the literalists (ahl al-zahir) have therefore counted this among the kinds of magic. Of this type is the work of Arjaʿyanus the musician in the old Temple of Jerusalem at the time of its renovation. The story is that he happened to be passing through a desert land, where he found a chick of the baraasil. The baraasil is a tender bird. This chick used to whistle a sorrowful whistle, unlike the whistling of other baraasil. The baraasil used to bring it choice olives and drop them before it. It would eat some of them when it needed to, and some would be left over. This musician stopped there and reflected on the condition of that chick. He realized that in its whistle, which differed from the whistling of the baraasil, there was a kind of pleading and appeal for pity, so much so that the birds were moved and brought it food. He then cleverly made an instrument resembling a whistle which, when it faced the wind, produced that same whistling sound. He kept testing it until he was confident in it. The baraasil came to him with olives, just as they used to come to that chick, because they thought there was a chick of their kind there. When his aim was achieved, he displayed asceticism and went to the Temple of Jerusalem. He asked about the night in which Ustarkhus, the ascetic who was in charge of the upkeep of that Temple, had died. He was told that he had died on the first night of Ab. He then made a figure of hollow glass in the shape of a barsala (a kind of bird-shaped vessel), set it above that Temple, and placed a dome above that figure. He ordered them to open it on the first of Ab. The sound of the barsala would be heard because of the wind passing through that figure. The baraasil kept bringing olives, until that dome was filled with that olive every day. People believed that this was one of the miracles (karamat) of that buried man. Many kinds fall under this category, and their explanation is not appropriate in this place.

**The sixth kind of magic:** seeking help from the special properties of medicines, such as putting some numbing medicines that remove the intellect, or intoxicating fumes, into a person's food, like the brain of a donkey. If a person consumes it, his intellect becomes dulled and his intelligence diminishes. Know that there is no way to deny the existence of special properties, for the effect of the magnet is observable. However, people have exaggerated about it and mixed truth with falsehood and falsehood with truth.

**The seventh kind of magic:** the binding of the heart (taʿlīq al-qalb). This is when the sorcerer claims that he knows the Greatest Name (al-ism al-aʿzam), and that the jinn obey him and submit to him in most matters. If it happens that the listener to this is weak-minded and has little discernment, he believes it to be true, his heart becomes attached to it, and a kind of terror and fear arises in his soul. When fear arises, the sensitive faculties weaken. At that point the sorcerer is able to do whatever he wishes. Whoever has tested affairs and known the conditions of the people of knowledge knows that the attachment of the heart has a great effect on carrying out deeds and concealing secrets.

**The eighth kind of magic:** spreading gossip and sowing discord (al-tadrib) by subtle and gentle means. This is common among people. This is the summary of the discussion on the categories of magic and the explanation of its types and kinds. And God knows best.

* * *

**Question Four:** On the views of the Muslims as to whether these types are possible or not.

As for the Mu'tazila, they agreed on denying them, except for the type attributed to imagination, the type attributed to giving people certain numbing medicines, and the type attributed to sowing discord and gossip. As for the first five types, they denied them outright, and it is likely that they declared disbelief (takfir) of whoever affirmed them and held them to be possible.

As for the Sunni scholars (ahl al-sunna), they permitted that a sorcerer might be able to fly in the air and turn a man into a donkey and a donkey into a man. However, they said that God Almighty is the Creator of these things when the sorcerer recites particular incantations (ruqa) and specific words. As for the claim that the cause of this is the sphere (falak) and the stars, that is not so.

As for the philosophers, the astrologers, and the Sabians, their view is as previously established.

**[Page 194]**

Our companions argued against the view of the Sabians as follows: It has been established that the world is originated (muhdath). Therefore, its Originator must be capable. Whatever reason judges to be capable of being done can only be capable of being done because it is possible. Possibility is a common attribute shared by all possible things. Therefore, all possible things are within God's power. If any of those things came to exist through another cause, that cause would necessarily have to remove the relation of God's power to that object, and the originated thing would become a cause of God's incapacity, which is impossible. Thus it is established that the occurrence of any possible thing is impossible except by God's power. With this, everything the Sabians said is refuted. They said: "If this is established, then we claim that these extraordinary events cannot occur through the normal course of custom by the magic of sorcerers." They argued for the occurrence of this type of magic from the Qur'an and from reports.

As for the Qur'an, it is His saying in this verse: ﴿They could not harm anyone with it except by the permission of God﴾. The exception indicates that the effects occur through it.

As for the reports, they have come from the Prophet ﷺ both as mutawatir (widely transmitted) and as ahad (solitary reports):

The first of them: it is narrated that he (peace be upon him) was bewitched, and that the magic took effect on him until he said: "It seems to me that I say a thing and do it, and I had not said it nor done it." It is also narrated that a Jewish woman bewitched him and placed that magic beneath the stone at the bottom of the well. When that was removed, that affliction left the Prophet ﷺ, and the two Mu'awwidhat (Surahs 113 and 114) were revealed on account of it.

The second: a woman came to ʿĀʾisha, may God be pleased with her, and said to her: "I am a sorceress; is there any repentance for me?" She said: "What is your sorcery?" She said: "I went to the place where Harut and Marut are at Babylon to seek the knowledge of magic. They said to me: 'O servant of God, do not choose the punishment of the Hereafter for the affairs of this world.' I refused. They said to me: 'Go and urinate on that ash.' I went to urinate on it, but I reflected within myself and said: 'I will not do it.' I came back to them and said: 'I have done it.' They said to me: 'What did you see when you did it?' I said: 'I saw nothing.' They said to me: 'You are on the verge of a matter; fear God and do not do it.' I refused. They said to me: 'Go and do it.' So I went and did it, and I saw as if a horseman clad in iron had come out of my private part, ascended to the sky. I went back to them and informed them, and they said: 'Your faith has left you, and you have mastered sorcery.' I said: 'And what is it?' They said: 'You do not desire anything and picture it in your imagination but it comes to be.' So I pictured in my soul a grain of wheat, and behold, there was a grain. I said: 'Be sown!' It was sown and immediately came out as an ear of grain. I said: 'Be ground!' It was ground at once. I said: 'Be baked!' It was baked. I do not desire anything that I picture in my soul but that it comes about." ʿĀʾisha said: "There is no repentance for you."

The third: the many stories that people relate on this subject, which are well known.

As for the Mu'tazila, they argued for the denial of this with several points:

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The sorcerer does not succeed wherever he comes﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:69).

The second: His saying, Exalted is He, describing Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿The wrongdoers say, "You are only following a man bewitched"﴾ (al-Furqan 25:8). If he (peace be upon him) had actually become bewitched, they would not have deserved blame for this statement.

The third: if such a thing were possible through magic, how could a miracle (muʿjiz) be distinguished from magic? Then they said: "These proofs are certain, whereas the reports you have cited are of the category of solitary reports (ahad), and they cannot stand against these proofs."

* * *

**Question Five:** On the fact that knowledge of magic is neither ugly nor forbidden. The verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) agreed on this, because knowledge in itself is noble. Also, because of the general meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ (al-Zumar 39:9). Also, because if magic were not knowable, it would not be possible to distinguish it from a miracle, and knowledge that a miracle is a miracle is obligatory, and whatever an obligatory thing depends upon is itself obligatory. This implies that acquiring knowledge of magic is obligatory. And how can what is obligatory be forbidden or ugly?

* * *

**Question Six:** On whether a sorcerer may be declared a disbeliever (yukaffar) or not. The jurists differed as to whether a sorcerer is to be declared a disbeliever or not. It has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever goes to a soothsayer (kahin) or a fortune-teller (ʿarraf) and believes what they say has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad." Know that there is no dispute among the Ummah that whoever believes that the stars are the governing agents of this world, and the creators of the events, goods, and evils in it, is a disbeliever absolutely. This is the first type of magic.

As for the second type, which is that one believes a human soul can reach such purity and power that by it he can create bodies, life, and power, and change structure and form, then there is also a near-consensus of the Ummah on declaring him a disbeliever.

As for the third type, which is that the sorcerer believes he can reach such a level of purification, reciting incantations, and burning certain medicines, that God Almighty creates, following his actions by way of custom, bodies, life, intellect, and changes in structure and form. Here the Mu'tazila agreed on declaring disbelief for whoever holds this permissible. They said: "Because with this belief he cannot recognize the truthfulness of the prophets and messengers." This is a weak argument. For one may say: if a person claims prophethood and is lying in his claim, God Almighty would not permit these things to appear at his hands, so as to avoid deception. But if he does not claim prophethood and these things appear at his hands, this does not lead to deception, for the true one is distinguished from the false one by the fact that the true one has these things together with the claim of prophethood, while the false one does not have these things together with the claim of prophethood.

As for the other kinds of magic that we have enumerated, there is no doubt that they are not disbelief.

If it is said: When the Jews attributed magic to Solomon, God Almighty said, declaring him free of it: ﴿Solomon did not disbelieve﴾. This indicates that magic is disbelief absolutely. Also, He said: ﴿But the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic﴾ (al-Baqara 2:102). This too implies that magic is disbelief absolutely. Also, He relates about the two angels that they would not teach anyone magic until they said: ﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾ (al-Baqara 2:102). This indicates that magic is disbelief absolutely.

We reply: a narrative account of a situation needs only one instance to be true, so we interpret it as referring to the magic of one who believes in the divinity of the stars.

* * *

**Question Seven:** On whether it is obligatory to kill them or not.

As for the first type, which is to believe that the stars are gods that govern.

And the second type, which is to believe that the sorcerer may come to be described as having the power to create bodies, create life, power, and intellect, and compose shapes. There is no doubt of the disbelief of both. Thus a Muslim who holds this belief is like an apostate, who is asked to repent; if he persists, he is killed. It is narrated from Malik and Abu Hanifa that his repentance is not accepted. Our argument is that he has embraced Islam, so his Islam is accepted, based on the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "We judge by what is apparent."

**Type 3:** This is the belief that God has established a custom whereby, upon the recitation of certain incantations (ruqa) and the fumigation of certain medicines, He creates bodies, grants life, and alters forms and shapes. The sorcerer believes that by this means it is possible to reach the bringing into existence of bodies and life, and the alteration of creation. We have already mentioned that the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held that human reason can establish moral truths and that the Qur'an was created) regarded this as disbelief. They said: "Because with this belief, one cannot use the miracle as evidence for the truthfulness of the Prophets." This is weak, because it is said: the distinction is that the one who claims prophethood, if he is truthful in his claim, is able to bring about these things, and if he is lying, that is impossible for him. Thus the distinction becomes clear. Once it is established that this type is not disbelief, and that it is possible to occur, then if the sorcerer performs something of this kind, if he believes that doing so is permissible, he has disbelieved, because he has judged what is forbidden to be permissible. If he believes it to be forbidden, then according to al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him), his ruling is the ruling of a criminal offence: if he says, "I bewitched him, and my sorcery kills in most cases," then retaliation (qawad) is obligatory upon him. If he says, "I bewitched him, and my sorcery may kill and may not kill," then it is quasi-intentional killing (shibh 'amd). If he says, "I bewitched someone else, and it happened to coincide with his name," then it is a mistaken killing, for which blood money (diyah) is due, lightened and payable from his own property, because it was established by his own confession, unless the 'aqilah (his paternal kin who bear such liability) confirm him, in which case the 'aqilah becomes liable. This is the detailed account of the school of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him). Al-Hasan ibn Ziyad narrated from Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him) that he said: the sorcerer is killed if it is known that he is a sorcerer, and he is not given a chance to repent, and his statement, "I will abandon sorcery and repent from it," is not accepted. If he confesses that he is a sorcerer, his blood has become lawful. If two witnesses testify that he is a sorcerer, or describe him with a description by which it is known that he is a sorcerer, he is killed and not given a chance to repent. If he confesses, "I used to practise sorcery once, and I abandoned that a long time ago," it is accepted from him and he is not killed. Muhammad ibn Shuja' related from 'Ali al-Razi, who said: I asked Abu Yusuf about the statement of Abu Hanifah regarding the sorcerer: "He is killed and not given a chance to repent," and whether this was not in the position of the apostate. He said: "The sorcerer has combined with his disbelief the striving for corruption on the earth, and whoever is like that, if he kills, he is killed."

Our companions (the Hanafi/Shafi'i scholars of the school) argued: since it has been established that this type is not disbelief, it is a sin (fisq). If it is not an offence against the right of another, then the correct position is the detailed account that we have mentioned.

**The second issue:** The sorcery of the Jews is not punished by death. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) was bewitched by a man from the Jews called Labid ibn al-A'sam, and by a woman from the Jews of Khaybar called Zaynab, and he did not kill them. Therefore it is necessary that a Muslim be likewise, based on his (ﷺ) saying: "They have what the Muslims have, and they have upon them what is upon the Muslims."

Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him) argued for his position with reports:

The first of them: what Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar, that a slave-girl of Hafsah had bewitched her. They seized her and she confessed to that. So Hafsah ordered 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd to kill her, and he killed her. The matter reached 'Uthman, and he disapproved of it. Ibn 'Umar came to him and informed him of her affair. It seems that 'Uthman disapproved only because she was killed without his permission.

The second: what 'Amr ibn Dinar narrated, that the letter of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) arrived: "Kill every sorcerer, male and female." So we killed three sorceresses.

The third: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "These soothsayers (al-'arrafin) are the diviners of the non-Arabs. Whoever comes to a diviner and believes in what he says has disowned what Allah has sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ)."

The answer: Perhaps the sorcerers who were killed were of the disbelievers, for a report of a case suffices for its authenticity with one instance. As for the rest of the types of sorcery, I mean performing varieties of sleight of hand (sha'badhah) and wondrous devices based on kinds of illusion and upon geometric ratios, and likewise the matter regarding one who creates various kinds of frightening and admonishment until the one afflicted with melancholy becomes firmly convinced of him, and one who moves about by inciting discord and tale-bearing and devises separation after union, and claims that this is by a writing he composes from the Greatest Name (ism al-a'zam), all of that is not disbelief. Likewise the matter regarding burying filthy things in people's houses, and likewise the matter regarding giving the impression that jinn are doing it, and likewise the matter regarding one who slips numbing drugs into food. None of these reaches the level of disbelief, nor does any of them necessitate death at all. This is the general discussion about sorcery. Allah is the Sufficient and the Protector. Let us return to the exegesis.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery﴾. The apparent meaning of the verse requires that they disbelieved only because they were teaching people sorcery, since linking a ruling to a description indicates causation, and teaching what is not disbelief does not necessitate disbelief. So the verse indicates that teaching sorcery is disbelief, and that sorcery itself is also disbelief. Whoever disputes this may say: "We do not accept that linking a ruling to a description indicates causation. Rather, the meaning is that they disbelieved, and yet at the same time they were teaching people sorcery." If it is said: "This is problematic, because Allah, exalted is He, informed at the end of the verse that the two angels teach people sorcery. If teaching sorcery were disbelief, it would follow that the two angels are disbelievers, and that is impermissible, since it has been established that all the angels are infallible (ma'sum). Also, you have shown that not everything called sorcery is disbelief." We say: a shared (mushtarak) term does not apply generally to all its referents. So we take this sorcery that is disbelief to be the first type of what is called sorcery, which is the belief in the divinity of the stars and seeking their aid in producing miracles and supernatural feats. This sorcery is disbelief, and the devils disbelieved only because of their practice of this sorcery, not because of the other categories.

As for the two angels, we do not accept that they taught this type of sorcery. Rather, perhaps they taught the other types, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they learn from the two what they use to cause division between a man and his wife﴾. Also, even if it were said that they taught this type, the teaching of this type is only disbelief if the teacher intends that it be believed in as real and correct. But if he teaches it so that one may be wary of it, that teaching is not disbelief. The teaching of the angels was for the purpose that the person under obligation would be wary of it, as He, exalted is He, said quoting them: ﴿And they do not teach anyone until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve."﴾ As for the devils who taught people sorcery, their intention was to have people believe in the reality of these things, and thus the distinction becomes clear.

**The eighth issue:** Nafi', Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read ﴿lakinna﴾ with a shadda (doubled nun) and ﴿ash-shayatina﴾ with a fatha, treating it as the subject of lakinna. The rest read ﴿lakin﴾ without the shadda and ﴿ash-shayatinu﴾ with a damma. The meaning is the same. Likewise in al-Anfal: ﴿but Allah threw﴾ [Al-Anfal: 17] and ﴿but Allah killed them﴾ [Al-Anfal: 17]. The preferred view is that when it is preceded by a waw, the doubled form is better, and when it is without a waw, the light form is better. The reasoning is that lakin without the shadda functions as a conjunction, so it does not need a waw to connect the speech, whereas the doubled form does not function as a conjunction, because it operates in the manner of inna.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The word "ma" in His saying ﴿and what was sent down﴾ has two possibilities:

The first: it means "alladhi" (that which). Then these scholars differed about it in three positions:

The first position: it is conjoined to "sihr" (sorcery), meaning: they teach people sorcery, and they also teach them what was sent down to the two angels.

The second: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿what the devils recited﴾, meaning: they followed what the devils recited, falsely attributing it to the kingdom of Sulayman, and what was sent down to the two angels, because sorcery includes that which is disbelief, which is what the devils recited, and that which has the effect of separating a man from his wife, which is what was sent down to the two angels. So it is as if He, exalted is He, informed about the Jews that they followed both matters and did not limit themselves to one of them.

The third: its position is in the genitive case, conjoined to ﴿the kingdom of Sulayman﴾. Its implied meaning: what the devils recited falsely attributing it to the kingdom of Sulayman, and to what was sent down to the two angels. This is the view chosen by Abu Muslim (may Allah have mercy on him). He denied that sorcery was sent down upon the two angels, and argued for this with several points:

First: if sorcery were sent down upon them, its sender would be Allah, exalted is He, and that is impermissible, because sorcery is disbelief and vanity, and it is not fitting for Allah to send such a thing down.

Second: His saying ﴿But the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery﴾ indicates that teaching sorcery is disbelief. So if it were established that the angels teach sorcery, disbelief would be necessary for them, and that is false.

Third: just as it is not permissible for the Prophets to be sent to teach sorcery, likewise for the angels, all the more so.

Fourth: sorcery is attributed only to disbelievers, sinners, and rebellious devils. How could Allah be attributed with what He forbids and threatens punishment for? Is sorcery anything other than falsehood disguised? The custom of Allah, exalted is He, is to nullify it, as He said in the story of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿What you have brought is sorcery; surely Allah will nullify it﴾ [Yunus: 81].

Then he (may Allah have mercy on him) took in the interpretation of the verse a method different from the opinion of most exegetes. He said: just as the devils attributed sorcery to the kingdom of Sulayman, though the kingdom of Sulayman was free of it, likewise they attributed what was sent down to the two angels to sorcery, though what was sent down to them was free of sorcery. This is because what was sent down to them was the Law (shar'), the religion, and the call to good. They taught people this, saying: ﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾, as an emphasis to urge them to accept and hold fast to it. One group adhered to it, while another group opposed it and turned away from it, and they learned from the two (i.e., from the trial and disbelief) the amount by which they could cause division between a man and his wife. This is the presentation of the position of Abu Muslim.

The second possibility: "ma" means negation, and it is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Sulayman did not disbelieve﴾. As if He said: Sulayman did not disbelieve, and no sorcery was sent down to the two angels, because the sorcerers used to attribute sorcery to Sulayman, claiming that it was among what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. So Allah refuted them on both claims. His saying ﴿And they do not teach anyone﴾ is also a negation, meaning: they do not teach anyone; rather they forbid it in the strongest terms.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until they say, "We are only a trial"﴾, i.e., a test and an examination, ﴿so do not disbelieve﴾. It is like your saying: "I did not order so-and-so to do such-and-such until I said to him: if you do such-and-such, such-and-such will befall you," meaning: I did not order him to it; rather I warned him against it.

Know that although these positions are good, the first position is better than them. This is because conjoining His saying ﴿and what was sent down﴾ to what immediately precedes it is preferable to conjoining it to what is further removed, unless there is a separate proof. As for their claim that "if sorcery had been sent down upon them, the one who sent down that sorcery would be Allah, exalted is He," we say: describing the nature of a thing may be for the purpose of encouraging its entry into existence, and it may be for the purpose of being wary of it, as the poet said:

*I came to know evil, not for the sake of evil, but in order to guard against it.*

**The second view:** that teaching magic is disbelief (kufr), based on His saying: ﴿But the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic﴾. The answer is that we have explained that this is a description of a situation (waqi'at hal), so its truth requires only one instance. That instance is when someone occupies himself with teaching the magic of those who believe in the divinity of the stars, and his purpose in that teaching is to establish that this doctrine is true.

**The third view:** it is not permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, to be sent to teach magic, so the angels likewise should not be. We reply: we do not concede that it is impermissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, to be sent to teach it, in a manner where the purpose of that teaching is to alert people to its falsehood.

**The fourth view:** magic is only attributed to disbelievers and rebellious beings, so how could God be credited with something He forbids? We reply: there is a difference between practicing (al-'amal) and teaching (al-ta'lim). Why should it not be that the practice is forbidden? As for His teaching it for the purpose of alerting people to its corruption, it is commanded.

**Second issue:** al-Hasan read ﴿malakayn﴾ with a kasra on the lam (مَلِكَيْنِ), and this is also reported from al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas. Then they differed. Al-Hasan said: they were two uncircumcised non-Arab men (‘ilajayn aqlafayn) in Babylon who taught people magic. It was also said: they were two righteous men among the kings. The well-known recitation (al-qira'a al-mashhurah) is with a fatha on the lam, and they were two angels who descended from heaven. Harut and Marut are their names. It was said: they were Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them. It was also said: they were others. As for those who read with a kasra on the lam, they argued with several points:

First: it is not fitting for angels to teach magic.

Second: how can two angels be sent down, given His saying: ﴿And if We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not be reprieved﴾ [al-An'am: 8]?

Third: if He sent down the two angels, either He would make them in the form of two men or not. If He made them in the form of two men, although they are not two men, that would be deception and misleading people, which is impermissible. And if that were permissible, why should it not be permissible that each of the people we see is not in reality a human but an angel? If He did not make them in the form of two men, that would contradict His saying: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9].

The answer to the first is that we will explain the wisdom in sending angels to teach magic. As for the second, this verse is general (‘amm), whereas the reading of ﴿malakayn﴾ with a fatha is mutawatir (transmitted through multiple unbroken chains, so it is certain), and it is specific (khass). The specific takes precedence over the general. As for the third, God sent them down in the form of two men, and it was obligatory upon those responsible in the time of the prophets not to assert about one whose form is that of a human that he is a human, just as in the time of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, it was obligatory upon anyone who saw Dihya al-Kalbi not to assert that he was of mankind. Rather, the obligation is to suspend judgment about him.

**Third issue:** if we say that they were from among the angels, then they differed about the cause of their descent. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that when God informed the angels about Adam, they said: ﴿Will You place upon it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾ God answered them with His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. Then God appointed over them a group of angels, namely the Noble Recorders (al-Kiraman al-Katibun), and they used to ascend with their evil deeds. The angels were astonished at them and at God's leaving them alone despite the vile things that had appeared from them. Then they added to that the practice of magic, so the angels' astonishment increased. God wished to test the angels, so He said to them: "Choose two angels from among the greatest of the angels in knowledge, asceticism, and piety, so that I may send them down to earth and test them." They chose Harut and Marut. He placed in them the desire of human beings, sent them down, and forbade them from associating partners with God, killing, adultery, and drinking. So they descended, and a woman of the most beautiful women, who was Zuhara, came to them. They solicited her, but she refused to obey them unless they worshipped an idol, and unless they drank wine. They refused at first, then desire overcame them, and they obeyed her in all of that. When they proceeded to drink and worship the idol, a questioner came in upon them. She said: "If this questioner reveals to the people what he saw of us, our affair will be ruined. So if you wish to reach me, kill this man." They refused at first, then they occupied themselves with killing him. When they finished the killing and sought the woman, they did not find her. Then the two angels, at that point, regretted, grieved, and humbled themselves before God. He gave them the choice between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, and they chose the punishment of this world. They are being punished in Babylon, suspended between heaven and earth, teaching people magic. Then, regarding Zuhara, there are two views:

The first view: when God tested the two angels with the desire of the children of Adam, God commanded the star called Zuhara and its orbit: "Descend to the earth," and so on until what happened happened. Then Zuhara and its orbit rose up to their place in the heavens, rebuking them for what they had witnessed from them.

The second view: the woman was a sinful woman from the people of the earth. They had intercourse with her after drinking wine, killing a soul, and worshipping an idol. Then they taught her the name by which they ascended to the heavens, so she spoke it and ascended to the heavens. Her name was "Bidakht." So God transformed her and made her the Zuhara. Know that this report is corrupt and rejected, not acceptable, because there is nothing in the Book of God that indicates this. Rather, there is in it what refutes it in several ways:

The first: what preceded regarding the evidence indicating the infallibility of the angels from all disobedience.

The second: their saying that they were given the choice between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter is corrupt. Rather, it would have been more fitting for them to be given the choice between repentance and punishment, because God gave that choice to whoever associated partners with Him for his whole life. So how would He be stingy with them in that?

The third: among the most astonishing matters is their saying that they teach magic while they are being punished, and call people to it while they themselves are being punished. Since the corruption of this view has become apparent, we say: the reason for their descent has several aspects:

First: magicians proliferated in that era, devised strange branches of magic, and claimed prophethood and challenged people with it. So God sent these two angels in order to teach people the branches of magic, so that they could oppose those who falsely claimed prophethood. There is no doubt that this is among the best purposes and aims.

Second: knowing that a miracle differs from magic depends on knowing the reality (mahiyyah) of the miracle and the reality of magic. The people were ignorant of the reality of magic, so knowing the true nature of the miracle was impossible for them. Therefore God sent these two angels to define the reality of magic for this purpose.

Third: it is not impossible to say that the magic which brings about separation between God's enemies and affection among God's friends was permissible or even recommended in their view. So God sent the two angels to teach magic for this purpose. Then the people learned it from them and used it for evil, to cause separation among God's friends and affection among God's enemies.

Fourth: acquiring knowledge of everything is good, and since magic was forbidden, it must be conceivable and known, because what is not conceivable cannot be forbidden.

Fifth: perhaps the jinn had kinds of magic that humans could not match, so God sent angels to teach humans matters by which they could oppose the jinn.

Sixth: it is possible that this was an added burden in the obligation, in that when he is taught what enables him to reach fleeting pleasures and then is forbidden from using them, that is the utmost hardship, and so he merits greater reward. Just as the people of Talut were tested with the river, as He said: ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249]. Thus it has been established by these aspects that it is not far from God to send down the two angels to teach magic, and God knows best.

**Fourth issue:** some said: this event occurred in the time of Idris, peace be upon him, because if they were two angels who descended in human form for this purpose, there must be a messenger in their time so that this would be a miracle for him. It is not permissible for them to be messengers, because it has been established that God does not send an angel as a messenger to mankind.

**Fifth issue:** "Harut and Marut" is an explicative apposition (‘atf al-bayan) to the two angels. They are proper names for them, and they are non-Arabic names, as evidenced by their being diptote (not taking tanwin). Had they been derived from al-hart and al-mart, which means breaking, as some claimed, they would have been declinable. Al-Zuhri read "Harutu wa Marutu" with a damma, as: "They are Harutu and Marutu."

As for His saying: ﴿And they teach no one until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾. Know that He explained their condition: these two angels do not teach magic except after a severe warning against acting upon it, and that is their saying: ﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.﴾ The meaning of "trial" (fitnah) here is the test by which the obedient is distinguished from the disobedient, like their saying: "I tested the gold with fire," when it is exposed to fire so that the pure is distinguished from the impure. We have explained the aspects of how it is fitting for two angels to be sent to teach magic. So the meaning is that they do not teach anyone magic, nor describe it to anyone, nor reveal to him the methods of deception, until they give him sincere advice, saying to him: ﴿We are only a trial﴾, that is, this which we describe to you. Although its purpose is that by it one may distinguish between magic and the miraculous, nonetheless it enables you to use it to reach corruptions and sins. So beware, after you have come to know it, of using it for what you have been forbidden, or of using it to attain any fleeting worldly benefit.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿So they learn from them that by which they cause separation between a man and his wife﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** they mentioned two aspects in interpreting this separation:

The first: this separation occurs when he believes that this magic has an effect on this separation, so he becomes a disbeliever, and when he becomes a disbeliever his wife is separated from him, so a separation between them occurs.

The second: he causes separation between them through deception, tricks, and striking (al-tadrib), and the other aspects mentioned.

**Second issue:** God did not mention that, because what they learn from them is nothing beyond this measure. But He mentioned this form as a reminder of other forms, because a man's dependence on his wife and his reliance upon her is known to be beyond all affection. So God, by mentioning that, alerted that if magic can accomplish this matter in its severity, then it is more fitting that it can accomplish other things.

As for His saying: ﴿And they could not harm anyone thereby﴾, it indicates what we have mentioned, because He stated harm in general and did not restrict it to separation between a man and his wife. This shows that He mentioned it only because it is among its highest levels.

As for His saying: ﴿except by permission of God﴾, know that permission (al-idhn) is in reality a command, and God does not command magic. Also, because He intended to disparage and blame them, and if He had commanded them to it, it would not be permissible for Him to blame them for it. So an interpretation is necessary, and there are several aspects:

The first: al-Hasan said: what is meant is "leaving free" (al-takhliyah), meaning: when magic affects a person, if God wills, He prevents it from him, and if He wills, He leaves him between himself and the harm of magic.

Second, al-Asamm said: the meaning is "except by the knowledge of Allah." The adhan is called adhan because it is an announcement to the people of the time of prayer, and the idhn (permission) is called idhn because permission is perceived by the faculty of hearing that is present in the one addressed. Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater pilgrimage﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3], meaning a notification; and His saying: ﴿Then be informed of war from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279], meaning: know; and His saying: ﴿I have announced to you on equal terms﴾ [al-Anbiya: 109].

Third: the harm that occurs when magic is performed comes about only by the creation of Allah, His bringing it into existence and His originating it. Whatever is of this kind may rightly be attributed to the permission of Allah, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40].

Fourth: the meaning of "permission" may be command. This interpretation is only fitting if the separation between a man and his wife is explained as his becoming a disbeliever, since disbelief necessitates separation; for this is a legal ruling, and that can only occur by the command of Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they learned what harmed them and did not benefit them. And they had certainly known that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: He mentioned the word "purchase" by way of metaphor, for several reasons:
One: when they cast the Book of Allah behind their backs and turned to adhering to what the devils recited, it is as though they had bought that magic with the Book of Allah.
Two: the two angels taught magic only with the aim of guarding against it, so that through that guarding they would reach the benefits of the Hereafter. When he used magic, it is as though he bought worldly benefits with the benefits of the Hereafter.
Three: when he used magic, we know that he bore hardship only so that he could enable himself to use it; so it is as though he bought, with the trials he endured, his capability for that use.

Second issue: Most of the scholars said: "al-khalaq" means share (nasib). al-Qaffal said: it seems the root of the word is from "khalq" (creation/measure), meaning measuring out, as in "khalaqa al-adim" (the hide was cut to measure), and from it one says: he assigned to the man so-and-so dirhams as provision in exchange for such-and-such work. Others said: al-khalaq means deliverance (khalas). From it is the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

They cry out "Woe" therein; they have no khalaq, except garments of tar and shackles.

A question remains concerning the verse: how did He first affirm knowledge for them in His saying ﴿And they had certainly known﴾ and then negate it from them in His saying ﴿if only they had known﴾? The answer has several aspects:

One: those who knew are other than those who did not know. Those who knew are those who knew magic and called people to learn it, and they are the ones about whom Allah said: ﴿A party of those who were given the Scripture cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know﴾. As for the ignorant who desire to learn magic, they are the ones who do not know. This is the answer of al-Akhfash and Qutrub.

Two: even if we grant that the people were one group, they knew some things and were ignorant of others: they knew that they had no share in the Hereafter, but they were ignorant of the extent of the benefits of the Hereafter that they had missed, and of the harms and punishments that they had incurred.

Three: even if we grant that the people were one group and the object of knowledge was one, they did not benefit from their knowledge; rather they turned away from it, so that knowledge became like non-existence, just as Allah named the disbelievers "deaf, dumb and blind" since they did not benefit from these senses. And it is said of a man who does something but does not place it in its proper place: "You did it, yet you did not do it."

The words of Allah Most High: ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, a reward from Allah would have been better, if only they knew.﴾

Know that the pronoun refers to the Jews already mentioned. When He Most High set out the threat (wa'īd) concerning them with His words ﴿And wretched is that for which they sold themselves,﴾ He followed it with a promise, combining intimidation (tarhīb) and encouragement (targhīb), because combining the two is more conducive to obedience and to turning away from disobedience.

As for His words ﴿they believed,﴾ know that when He Most High said ﴿a party of those given the Scripture threw the Book of Allah behind their backs,﴾ and then described them as following what the devils recited and as clinging to magic, He said after that: ﴿And if they had believed,﴾ meaning: in what they had cast away of the Book of Allah. If you take that to mean the Qur'an, it is permissible. If you take it to mean their own Scripture, which confirms the Qur'an, it is permissible. And if you take it to mean both, it is permissible. By taqwa (fear of Allah, God-consciousness) is meant refraining from what is forbidden and abandoning what is not commanded.

As for His words ﴿a reward from Allah is better,﴾ there are several aspects:

First: the answer (jawāb) is omitted, and its implied form is: "And if they had believed and feared Allah, they would have been rewarded." However, the verbal sentence was replaced by this nominal one because of what the nominal sentence indicates of the stability and permanence of the reward. If it is asked, "Why was it not said, 'the reward of Allah is better'?" we say: because the meaning is, "some of the reward of Allah is better for them."

Second: His words ﴿And if they had believed﴾ may be a wish (tamannī) for their belief, used figuratively (majāz) to express Allah's will for their belief, as if it were said, "Would that they had believed," and then He began, "a reward from Allah is better."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna" and listen. And for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, had explained the ugly deeds of the people before the mission of Muhammad, peace be upon him, He intended from here to explain their ugly deeds at the time of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ, and their zeal and effort in disparaging him and attacking his religion. This is the first type of this topic. Here there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that God, exalted is He, addressed the believers with His saying ﴿O you who believe﴾ in eighty-eight places in the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: "In the Torah He addressed them with the words: 'O you who are poor (al-masakin)'." So it is as if He, glorified and exalted is He, when He addressed them first with 'the poor,' established poverty for them at the end, where He said: ﴿Humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61].

This indicates that when God, exalted is He, addressed this Community first with faith, then He gives them security from the punishment of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. Also, the name "believer" is among the most noble of names and attributes. So if He addresses us in this world with the most noble of names and attributes, we hope from His bounty that He will deal with us in the Hereafter with the best of dealings.

The second issue: It is not far-fetched that of two synonymous words God forbids one of them and permits the other. For this reason, according to al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, prayer is not valid with a translation of al-Fatihah, whether it is in Hebrew or Persian. So it is not far-fetched that God forbids the saying ﴿ra'ina﴾ and permits the saying ﴿unzurna﴾, even if the two are synonymous. But the majority of exegetes hold that God forbade the saying ﴿ra'ina﴾ only because it includes a kind of corruption. Then they mentioned several aspects regarding it:

The first: The Muslims used to say to the Messenger of God ﷺ when he recited something of knowledge to them: "Ra'ina, O Messenger of God." The Jews had a Hebrew word they used to revile one another with, resembling this word, which is "ra'ina," and its meaning is: "Listen, may you not hear." When they heard the believers saying "Ra'ina," they seized upon it and addressed the Prophet with it, meaning that insult. So the believers were forbidden from it and were commanded to use another expression, which is His saying ﴿unzurna﴾. What supports the soundness of this interpretation is His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿And they say, "We hear and disobey," and "Hear, may you not be heard," and "Ra'ina," distorting with their tongues and slandering the religion﴾ [al-Nisa': 46]. It is also related that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh heard it from them and said: "O enemies of God, upon you be the curse of God! By Him in whose hand is my soul, if I hear it from any man of you saying it to the Messenger of God, I will surely strike his neck." They said: "Do you not say it yourselves?" So this verse was revealed.

The second: Qutrub said: Although this word is sound in meaning, the people of the Hijaz used to say it only at times of mockery and derision, so God therefore forbade it.

The third: The Jews used to say "ra'ina," meaning: "You are our shepherd (ra'i ghanamina)," so God forbade them from it.

The fourth: The saying "ra'ina" is a form of mutual action (mufa'alah) from "ra'y" (pasturing) between two parties, so this expression suggested equality between the addressees, as if they said: "Make your hearing graze for us so that we may make our hearing graze for you." So God, exalted is He, forbade them from it and made clear that there must be the honoring of the Messenger, peace be upon him, in address, as He said: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of some of you to others﴾ [al-Nur: 63].

The fifth: The saying "ra'ina" is an address with superiority, as if he says: "Attend to my speech and do not be negligent of it, and do not occupy yourself with anything else," whereas "unzurna" contains only a request for waiting, as if they said to him: "Pause in your speech and explanation for as long as we need to reach understanding of it."

The sixth: The saying "ra'ina" is on the pattern of "'atina," from "mu'ata" (giving), and "rámina," from "muramah" (throwing). Then they changed this nun into the original nun, and made it a word derived from "ru'una," which is foolishness. So "al-ra'in" is an active participle from "ru'una," and it is possible that they meant by it the verbal noun, like their saying "'iyadhan bika" (I seek refuge in You), meaning: "I seek refuge with You in refuge." So their saying "ra'inan" means: "You have done foolishness." It is also possible that they meant by it: "You have become ra'in," meaning: "You have become one possessing foolishness." When they intended these corrupt aspects, God, exalted is He, therefore forbade this expression.

The seventh: The intended meaning is: "Do not say a saying that is ra'in," meaning a saying attributed to foolishness, in the sense of ra'in, like "tamir" and "laban."

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And say "Unzurna"﴾, there are several aspects regarding it:

The first: It is from "nazarahu," meaning: "intazarahu" (wait for him). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Wait for us that we may borrow from your light﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. So He commanded them to ask him for respite so that they might transmit from him, and then they would not need to ask for repetition. If it is said: "Did the Prophet ﷺ hasten against them so that they would say this?" The answer is in two respects:

One: This expression may be said in the course of speech even when there is no haste requiring it, like a man's saying in the midst of his talk: "Listen" or "You heard."

The second: They explained His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16], that he, peace be upon him, used to hasten the recitation of what Gabriel, peace be upon him, delivered to him, out of eagerness to acquire the revelation and take the Qur'an. So it was said to him: "Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it." So it is not far-fetched that he would hasten in what he related to his companions of matters of religion, out of eagerness to speed their understanding, so they would ask him in this situation to give them respite in what he addressed them with until they understood all that speech.

The second: "Unzurna" means: "Look at us" (unzur ilayna), except that the particle "ila" (to) was omitted, as in His saying: ﴿And Moses chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], meaning: "from among his people." What is intended by it is that when the teacher looks at the student, his addressing of speech in the manner of making understanding and clarification is more evident and stronger.

The third: Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "Anzirna," from "al-nazirah," meaning: "Give us respite."

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And listen﴾, the occurrence of hearing when the sense is sound is a necessary matter beyond human capacity, so it is not permissible for a command to be directed to it. Therefore the intended meaning is one of three matters:

The first: Empty your ears for what the Prophet, peace be upon him, says, so that you do not need to ask for repetition.

The second: Listen with the hearing of acceptance and obedience, and let your hearing not be the hearing of the Jews, when they said: "We hear and disobey."

The third: Listen to what you are commanded so that you do not return to what you are forbidden from, as an emphasis upon them. Then God, exalted is He, explained the painful punishment for the disbelievers if they do not follow with the Messenger this manner of exalting, honoring, listening to what he says, and reflecting upon what he says. The meaning of "painful punishment" has already been explained.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 105–106 (part 1 of 3)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, and the polytheists, do not wish that any good should be sent down upon you from your Lord. But Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, described the condition of the Jews and the disbelievers in enmity and obstinacy, He warned the believers against them. So He said: ﴿Those who disbelieve do not wish﴾, thereby negating from their hearts affection and love for everything through which the superiority of the believers becomes apparent. Here there are two issues:

**The first issue:** The first "min" (from) is for specification (bayan), because "those who disbelieve" is a genus, under which are two types: the People of the Book and the polytheists. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not [going to desist]﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1]. The second "min" is added for the sake of covering all good (istighraq), and the third "min" is for the starting point of the action (ibtida' al-ghayah).

**The second issue:** "Good" (khayr) here means revelation, and likewise "mercy" (rahmah). This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32]. The meaning is that they consider themselves more deserving that revelation be sent down to them, so they envy you, and they do not wish that any part of revelation be sent down upon you. Then Allah, glorified is He, clarified that this envy does not affect the continuation of that [favour], for He, glorified is He, singles out for His mercy and beneficence whom He wills.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it. Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾

Know that this is the second type of the Jews' criticism of Islam. They said: "Do you not see Muhammad ordering his companions to do something, then forbidding them from it, and ordering them to do the opposite, and saying one thing today and retracting it tomorrow?" So this verse was revealed. The discussion of this verse is arranged in several issues:

**The first issue:** Naskh (abrogation, lit. annulment of a thing) in its original linguistic sense means the annulment of something. Al-Qaffal said that it means transfer and conveyance. Our evidence is that it is said: "The wind effaced (nasakhat) the traces of the people" when they are gone, and "the sun effaced (nasakhat) the shade" when it disappears, because the shade may not appear in another place until one thinks it has moved there. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿except when he wishes, Satan casts [something] into his wish; then Allah abolishes what Satan casts﴾ [al-Hajj: 52], i.e., removes and annuls it. The basic principle in speech is that a word is used in its literal meaning. When it is established that the word is literally used for annulment, it is necessary that it not be literally used for transfer, to avoid homonymy (al-ishtirak).

If it is said: Their describing the wind as "abrogating" traces and the sun as "abrogating" the shade is a figurative usage, because the one who removes traces and shade is Allah, exalted is He. If that is figurative, it is impossible to use it as evidence that the word is literal in its meaning. We then counter what you have mentioned and say: Rather, naskh is transfer and conveyance, and from it comes "nasakha the book into another book," as if he conveys it to it or conveys its content. From it comes the transmigration of souls (tanasukh al-arwah) and the succession of generations, one generation after another (tanasukh al-qurun), and the transmission of inheritances (tanasukh al-mawarith), which is nothing but the shift from one to another in place of the first. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿This is Our record; it speaks against you with truth. Indeed, We were having copied what you used to do﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29]. So it is necessary that the word be literal in transfer, and it follows that it is not literal in annulment, to avoid homonymy.

As for the answer to the first objection, it is in two respects:

First: It is not impossible that Allah be the one who abrogates that, insofar as it is the act of the sun and the wind, which are the influential agents in that removal. They are also abrogators, because they are specifically related to that influence.

Second: The people of the language erred only in attributing naskh to the sun and the wind. Suppose that is so; but our reliance is their use of the word naskh for removal, since they attribute this action to the wind and the sun.

As for the answer to the second objection: transfer is more specific than annulment, because wherever transfer exists, a attribute has ceased and another attribute has come into being after it. Pure non-existence is more comprehensive than a non-existence after which something else comes into being. When a word is ambiguous between the specific and the general, making it literal for the general is preferable. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** Ibn 'Amir recited (mā nunsikh) with a ḍammah on the nūn and a kasrah on the sīn, while the others recited both with a fatḥah. As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir, there are two possibilities:

One: that *nasakha* and *ansakha* have the same meaning.

The second: *ansakhtuhu* means "I made him one who has naskh," as some people said to al-Hajjaj when he had crucified a man: "Bury so-and-so," i.e., make him one who has a grave. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then He caused him to die and assigned him a grave﴾ [‘Abasa: 21].

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited (nanסאhā) with a fatḥah on the nūn and the hamzah, and it is a jussive by the conditional. Abu 'Amr does not drop the hamzah in such a case, because its sukūn is a sign of the jussive. It is from *al-nas'* (postponement). From it: ﴿The postponement [of months] is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37]. From it the sale on credit is called *nasī'ah*. The people of the language said: "Allah postponed his term" (anṣa'a Allāh ajalahu) and "he postponed in his term" (nasa'a fī ajalih), i.e., he delayed and increased. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would like his provision increased and his life extended, let him maintain his ties of kinship."

The others recited it with a ḍammah on the nūn and a kasrah on the sīn, and it is from *al-nisyān* (forgetting). Then most scholars took it to mean forgetting, which is the opposite of remembering. Some took *nisyān* to mean abandonment, in the sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so he forgot, and We found in him no determination﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 115], i.e., he abandoned. And He said: ﴿Today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their day﴾ [al-A'raf: 51], i.e., We will abandon them as they abandoned. The more apparent view is that taking *nisyān* to mean abandonment is figurative, because what is forgotten is abandoned. Since abandonment is a necessary consequence of forgetting, they used the name of the necessitated thing for the necessitating thing.

It was also recited *nunsihā* and *nunassihā* (with shaddah), *tunsahā* and *tansahā* addressing the Messenger. 'Abdullah recited: "mā nunsik min āyatin aw nansakhhā," and Hudhayfah recited: "mā nansakh min āyatin aw nunsikhhā."

**[Page 206]**

**The third issue:** *mā* in this verse is conditional, like your saying: *mā taṣna' aṣna'* ("whatever you do, I do"). Its function is to apply the jussive to the condition and the consequent when both are imperfect verbs. So His saying *nansakh* is the condition, and His saying *na'ti* is the consequent, and both are jussive.

**The fourth issue:** Know that *tanāsukh* (transmigration) in the technical usage of the scholars is an expression for a legal ruling (ṭarīq shar'ī) indicating that a ruling which was established by a legal ruling is no longer found after that, despite its being delayed from it, in a manner that, were it not for it, the ruling would have remained established. So our statement "a legal ruling" means by it the common element between the speech issuing from Allah, exalted is He, and from His Messenger, and the act transmitted from them both. Excluded from it is the consensus of the community (ijma') on one of two opinions, because that is not a legal ruling according to this definition. It is not necessary that the Shari'ah abrogate the ruling of reason, because reason is not a legal ruling. And it is not necessary that a miracle abrogate a legal ruling, because a miracle is not a legal ruling. And it is not necessary that the restriction of a ruling by a limit, a condition or an exception be considered abrogation, because that is not delayed. And it is not necessary to include the case where Allah commands us to do one act and then forbids us from its like, because if such a prohibition were not abrogating, the ruling of the command would not remain established.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** According to us, abrogation is rationally possible and actually occurs by revelation, in contrast to the Jews. Some of them rejected it rationally, and some of them allowed it rationally but prohibited it by revelation. Some Muslims are reported to have denied abrogation. The majority of Muslims argued for the permissibility and occurrence of abrogation: the proofs have established the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and his prophethood is not valid except with the affirmation of the abrogation of the law of those before him. Therefore, abrogation must be affirmed with certainty.

Also, we said: There are two arguments against the Jews:

The first: It is found in the Torah that Allah, exalted is He, said to Noah, peace be upon him, when he came out of the ark: "I have made every moving thing a food for you and your offspring, and I have permitted this to you like the green herbs, except the blood, so do not eat it." Then He, exalted is He, forbade Moses and the Children of Israel many animals.

The second: Adam, peace be upon him, used to marry a sister to a brother, and this was later forbidden by Moses, peace be upon him.

Those who deny abrogation say: We do not concede that the prophethood of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, is not valid except with the affirmation of abrogation, because it is possible to say that Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, were commanded that people follow their law until the time when the law of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, appeared; then after that people were commanded to follow Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. So with the appearance of the law of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, the obligation of their law ceased, and the obligation of the law of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, came into effect. But this would not be abrogation; rather it operates like His saying: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. Those Muslims who denied the occurrence of abrogation at all based their position on this point, and they said: It has been established in the Qur'an that Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, gave good news in the Torah and the Gospel of the advent of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and that upon his appearance it is obligatory to return to his law. If this is the case, then with the existence of this possibility, it is impossible to affirm with certainty the occurrence of abrogation. This is the objection to the two arguments mentioned.

The deniers of abrogation argued by saying: When Allah, exalted is He, clarified the law of Jesus, peace be upon him, the wording indicating that law either indicates its permanence, or does not indicate its permanence, or there is nothing in it indicating either permanence or non-permanence. If it clarified its establishment as permanent, and then it became clear that it did not last, then the first report would be false, and that is impossible for the law. Moreover, if we allowed this, we would have no way to know that our law will not become abrogated, because at most the law would say: "This law is permanent and will never become abrogated at all." But when we see a statement of this kind present in the law of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, although it did not last, trust in it is removed in all cases.

If it is said: Why is it not permissible to say that He mentioned the wording indicating permanence, and then joined to it what indicates that it will be abrogated; or that He joined to it something that does not indicate it, but He explicitly stated that, though it was not transmitted to us in general? We say: This is weak for several reasons:

**[Page 207]**

The first: Explicitly stating the wording indicating permanence together with explicitly stating that it will not last is a combination of two contradictory statements, and that is folly and futility.

The second: On this assumption, Allah, exalted is He, has clarified that their law will become abrogated. If the law itself was transmitted, it is necessary that this manner also be transmitted, because if the original law could be transmitted without this manner, then the same would be permissible for our law as well. In that case, we would have no way to be certain that our law is not abrogated, because that is among the great events for which the motives to transmit it are abundant. Whatever is like that must be widely known and reach the level of mass transmission (tawatur). Otherwise, perhaps the Qur'an was opposed and its opposition was not transmitted, and perhaps Muhammad (ﷺ) changed this law from this state and it was not transmitted. When it is established that this manner must be transmitted through mass transmission, we say: If Allah, exalted is He, had explicitly stated in the time of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, that their two laws would become abrogated, that would have been well known to those who transmit en masse and known to them necessarily. And if that were so, it would be impossible for a great multitude to dispute it. Since we see the Jews and Christians unanimously denying that, we know that there was no explicit statement that their two laws would become abrogated.

The second kind: it is said that God Most High explicitly stated the law of Moses, peace be upon him, and attached to it something indicating that it was limited and not perpetual. This is false, because if it were so, it would have to be known necessarily to the people of tawatur (mass transmission). Moreover, even if it were sound, that would not be naskh (abrogation); rather it would be the ending of a stated term.

The third kind: God Most High explicitly stated the law of Moses, peace be upon him, but did not specify in it whether it was perpetual or not perpetual. We say: it has been established in usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) that a bare command does not indicate repetition; it indicates only a single occurrence. So when the responsible person (mukallaf) performs the single occurrence, he has discharged the obligation of the command. Therefore, the arrival of another command after that is not an abrogation of the first command. By this division it is established that the claim of naskh is impossible.

Know that after we had established this whole matter in our book al-Mahsul fi Usul al-Fiqh, we relied, for the occurrence of naskh, on God's words: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one than it or its like﴾. But the argument from it is also weak, because "ma" here conveys the sense of a condition and a consequence. Just as your saying, "Whoever comes to you, honour him," does not indicate that the coming has taken place, but rather that whenever he comes, honouring him becomes obligatory, so this verse does not indicate that naskh has occurred, but rather that whenever naskh occurs, a better or similar one must come. So the stronger course is to rely, for proof, on God's words: ﴿And when We substitute one verse for another﴾ [al-Nahl: 101], and His words: ﴿God erases what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39]. And God knows best.

* * *

Question Six: The scholars agreed that naskh occurred in the Qur'an, in several ways.

The first of these is this verse, namely His words: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one than it or its like﴾. Abu Muslim answered it in several ways:

The first: the abrogated verses intended are the laws in the earlier books, the Torah and the Gospel, such as the Sabbath and prayer toward east and west, which God Most High set aside for us and commanded us to observe differently. For the Jews and Christians used to say, "Do not believe except in one who follows your religion," so God refuted this claim through this verse.

The second way: the intended meaning of naskh is copying it from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) and transferring it from there to the other books, as one says "I copied the book" (nasakhtu al-kitab).

The third way: we have shown that this verse does not indicate the occurrence of naskh, but rather that if naskh were to occur, it would occur in favour of something better. Some people answered the first objection by saying that when verses (ayat) are mentioned without qualification, what is meant by them is the verses of the Qur'an, since that is what is familiar to us.

As for the second objection: the copying of the Qur'an from the Preserved Tablet is not specific to some part of the Qur'an, whereas this naskh is specific to some part of it. The objector may say, on the first answer: we do not concede that the wording of the verse is specific to the Qur'an; rather it is general to all proofs (dala'il). And on the second answer: we do not concede that the naskh mentioned in the verse is specific to some part of the Qur'an; rather the meaning, and God knows best, is: "Whatever We copy from the Preserved Tablet, We bring after it something better."

The second proof for those who hold that naskh occurred in the Qur'an: God Most High commanded the widow whose husband had died to observe a waiting period of a full year, in His words: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, let them make a bequest for their wives, a provision for a year without expulsion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240]. Then this was abrogated by four months and ten days, as He said: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, let them wait for themselves four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]. Abu Muslim said: the observance of a year has not been removed entirely, because if she were pregnant and the period of her pregnancy were a full year, her waiting period would be a full year. And since this ruling remains in some cases, that is a specification (takhsis), not an abrogation. The answer: the waiting period of pregnancy ends with the delivery of the child, whether the delivery occurs after a year, or less, or more. So making the year the waiting period is entirely removed.

The third proof: God commanded that charity be given before private consultation with the Messenger, in His words: ﴿O you who believe, when you consult the Messenger privately, offer a charity before your consultation﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 12]. Then this was abrogated. Abu Muslim said: it was removed only because its cause was removed. For the cause of worshipping by it was that the hypocrites might be distinguished from the believers by their not giving charity. When this purpose was achieved, the obligation lapsed. The answer: if it were so, then whoever did not give charity would be a hypocrite, and that is false, because it is reported that none gave charity except Ali, may God be pleased with him. And this is indicated by God's words: ﴿Since you did not do it and God has relented toward you﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 13].

The fourth proof: God commanded that one man should stand firm against ten, in His words: ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 65]. Then He abrogated this with His words: ﴿Now God has lightened your burden, and He knows that among you there is weakness; so if there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 66].

The fifth proof: God's words: ﴿The foolish among the people will say, "What has turned them away from the qibla they used to face?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142]. Then God turned them away from it by His words: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. Abu Muslim said: the ruling of that qibla has been removed entirely, because it is permissible to face it when there is doubt, or with knowledge when there is an excuse. The answer: according to what you have mentioned, there is no difference between Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and the other directions. So the distinction by which Bayt al-Maqdis was set apart from the other directions has been entirely removed, and so that was naskh.

The sixth proof: God's words: ﴿And when We substitute one verse for another—and God knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are only a fabricator"﴾ [al-Nahl: 101]. Substitution (tabdil) involves removal and establishment. What is removed is either the recitation (tilawa) or the ruling (hukm). In whichever way it occurs, it is removal and naskh. We have elaborated these proofs because each of them indicates the occurrence of naskh in general.

Abu Muslim argued that God Most High described His Book as one to which falsehood does not come from before it or from behind it. So if it were abrogated, falsehood would have come to it. The answer: what is meant is that no book of God that preceded this Book refutes it, and nor will anything after it refute it.

* * *

Question Seven: The abrogated item is either the ruling alone, or the recitation alone, or both together. As for the case where the abrogated item is the ruling without the recitation, it is like the verses we have enumerated. As for the case where the abrogated item is the recitation alone, it is like what is reported from Umar, who said: "We used to recite the verse of stoning: 'The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as a punishment from God, and God is Mighty and Wise.'" And it is reported: "If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third; and nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust; and God relents toward whoever repents." As for the case where both the ruling and the recitation are abrogated, it is what 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, reported: that the Qur'an had been revealed concerning suckling with ten known sucklings, then they were abrogated by five known sucklings. So the ten are abrogated in both recitation and ruling, while the five are abrogated in recitation, with the ruling remaining.
