It is also reported that Surat al-Ahzab was equal to the seven long surahs or longer, and then deficiency entered into it.

* * *

Question Eight: The exegetes differed concerning God's words: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾. Some of them interpreted naskh as removal (izala), and some interpreted it as naskh in the sense of "I copied the book." This is the view of Ata' and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. Those who take the first view have mentioned several meanings:

The first: "Whatever verse We abrogate while you are reciting it, or cause to be forgotten," meaning: of the Qur'an, what was recited among you and then you were made to forget it. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Asamm, and most of the theologians (mutakallimun). They took the abrogation to refer to the ruling without the recitation, and the "causing to be forgotten" to refer to the abrogation of both ruling and recitation together. If it is said: the occurrence of this forgetting is impossible both rationally and by the Law. As for reason: the Qur'an must be conveyed to the people of tawatur, and forgetting on the part of all the people of tawatur together is impossible. As for the Law: God's words: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]. The answer to the first is in two ways:

The first: forgetting is possible if God commands that it be cast out of the Qur'an and removed from what is recited and brought forth in prayer or used as evidence. Then when the obligation of worship with it has been removed and a long time has passed, it is forgotten; or if it is mentioned, it is mentioned in the manner of a report of a single transmitter (khabar al-wahid), so for this reason it becomes forgotten from the breasts.

The second answer: that would be a miracle (mu'jiza) for the Messenger, peace be upon him. And a report is transmitted on this: that they would recite a surah, then in the morning they had forgotten it.

The answer to the second: it is contradicted by God's words: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget, except what God wills﴾ [al-A'la: 6], and by His words: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ [al-Kahf: 24].

The second view: "Whatever verse We abrogate," meaning: We change it, either by changing its ruling alone, or its recitation alone, or changing both. As for His words: "or cause to be forgotten," the meaning is: We leave it as it was, so We do not change it. We have shown that forgetting in the sense of leaving has occurred, so the meaning of the verse becomes: what We change, We bring something better than it or its like.

The third view: "Whatever verse We abrogate," that is: We lift it after its revelation, or "nansa'ha" according to the reading with the hamza, meaning: We delay its sending down from the Preserved Tablet; or the intended meaning is: We delay its abrogation, so We do not abrogate it at present, for We send down in its place something that serves the same purpose.

The fourth view: "Whatever verse We abrogate," which is the verse that has become abrogated in both ruling and recitation together; "or cause to be forgotten," that is, leave it, which is the verse that has become abrogated in ruling but is not abrogated in recitation; rather it remains in recitation. As for those who hold the second view, "Whatever verse We abrogate," that is: We abrogate it from the Preserved Tablet, or We delay it. And as for the reading "nunsiha," the meaning is: We leave it, that is, We leave its abrogation, so We do not abrogate it.

* * *

As for His words: ﴿from a verse﴾, all the exegetes took it to mean a verse of the Qur'an, except Abu Muslim, who took it to mean the Torah and the Gospel. This has already been discussed.

* * *

[Page 210]

As for His words: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, there are two views:

One of them: that it is the lighter.

The second: that it is the more beneficial (aslah). This is the stronger, because God directs the responsible person toward his benefits, not toward what is lighter for his natural disposition. If it is said: if the second is more beneficial than the first, then the first would be deficient in benefit, so how did God command it? We say: the first is more beneficial than the second with respect to its own time, and the second is the reverse of that, so the objection is removed.

Know that people have derived from this verse most of the questions of naskh.

The first question: Some people said: naskh of a ruling is permissible only to a substitute (badal). They argued that this verse indicates that when God abrogates, He must bring after it something better than it, or something like it, and that is explicit in the obligation of a substitute. The answer: why should it not be said that the intended meaning is that the removal of that ruling and the lapse of worship by it are better than its being established at that time? Moreover, what indicates the occurrence of naskh without a substitute is that the sending of charity before the private consultation with the Messenger, peace be upon him, was abrogated without a substitute.

**Page 211** (marker in source)

**Second issue:** Some people said: it is not permissible to abrogate (*naskh*) a ruling with one that is heavier than it. They argued that His saying, ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, contradicts the abrogating ruling being heavier, since what is heavier cannot be "better than it" or "like it." The response is: why should it not be permissible for "better" to mean that which yields greater reward in the Hereafter? Moreover, what proves that it has occurred is that Allah, glory be to Him, abrogated the confinement of adulterers to their houses with flogging and stoning, abrogated the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ with the fast of Ramadan, and, according to some, the prayer, which was two rakʿahs, was abrogated with four in the state of residence. Having understood this, we say: abrogation to something heavier has occurred in the cases mentioned. As for abrogation to something lighter, it is like the abrogation of the waiting period from a year to four months and ten days, and like the abrogation of the night prayer to optional performance. As for abrogation to something of equal weight, it is like the change of the direction of prayer from Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) to the Kaʿbah.

**Third issue:** al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Book (the Qur'an) is not abrogated by the widely-attested Sunnah (*mutawātir*), and he argued for this from this verse in several ways:

The first: He, may He be exalted, informed that what He abrogates of the verses, He brings something better than it, and this indicates that He brings something of the same kind, just as when a person says: "Whatever garment I take from you, I will bring you a better one," it indicates that he will bring him a garment of the same kind but better. And when it is established that it must be of the same kind, then the kind of the Qur'an is Qur'an.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾ indicates that it is the Qur'an, which is the speech of Allah, and not the Sunnah which the Messenger, peace be upon him, brings.

The third: His saying ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾ indicates that what is brought is better than the verse, and the Sunnah is not better than the Qur'an.

The fourth: He said ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾, which indicates that the one who brings that better thing is the one exclusively characterized by power over all good things, and that is Allah, may He be exalted.

The answer to all four points together is: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾ does not state that this better thing must be the abrogating one. Rather, it is not impossible that this better thing is something other than the abrogating ruling, which comes about after the abrogation has taken place. What proves the realization of this possibility is that this verse is explicit that bringing that better thing is consequent upon the abrogation of the first verse. So if the abrogation of that verse were consequent upon bringing this better thing, it would lead to circularity (*dawr*), which is invalid.

Then the majority (*al-Jumhūr*) argued for the occurrence of the abrogation of the Book by the Sunnah, because the verse on bequest to the closest relatives has been abrogated by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Verily, there is no bequest for an heir." And because the verse of flogging became abrogated by the report of stoning.

Al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: As for the first, it is weak, because the inheritance being a right of the heir prevents it from being diverted to bequest. Thus it is established that the verse of inheritance prevents bequest. As for the second, it is also weak, because ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, related that his saying: "The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely" was part of the Qur'an. So perhaps the abrogation occurred by means of it. The full discussion of this is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (*uṣūl al-fiqh*). And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾, it is an admonition to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and to others, regarding His power to direct the responsible person (*mukallaf*) under His will, His judgment and His wisdom, and that there is no repeller of what He wills and no preventer of what He chooses.

**Ninth issue:** The Muʿtazilah (a theological school that held the Qur'an to be created) used this verse to prove that the Qur'an is created, in several ways:

The first: If the speech of Allah, may He be exalted, were eternal, then the abrogating and the abrogated would both be eternal. But this is impossible, because the abrogating must necessarily be later than the abrogated, and what is later than something cannot be eternal. As for the abrogated, it is because it must cease and be removed, and what is established to cease is, by agreement, impossible to be eternal.

The second: The verse indicates that some of the Qur'an is better than some of it, and what is like that cannot be eternal.

The third: His saying ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ indicates that what is meant is that He, may He be exalted, is the One capable of abrogating some of it and bringing something else in its place. And what falls under power and is an act is originated (*muḥdath*). The Ashʿarī scholars (*al-Aṣḥāb*) answered this: the fact that it is abrogating and abrogated is only among the accidents of words, expressions and languages, and there is no dispute about their being originated. So why do you claim that the real meaning, which is the signified content of expressions and terms, is originated? The Muʿtazilah said: That meaning which is the signified content of expressions and languages, there is no doubt that its first relation has ceased and a different relation has come into being for it. So the first relation is originated because it ceased, and the eternal does not cease; and the second relation is originated because it came about after it had not been. The real speech cannot be separated from these relations, and what cannot be separated from these relations is originated, and the speech to which they are attached must be originated.

The Ashʿarī scholars answered: The power of Allah was, from eternity, related to bringing the world into existence. Then, when the world came into existence, did that relation remain or not? If it remained, it would follow that the Capable would be capable of bringing into existence what already exists, which is impossible. And if it did not remain, then that relation has ceased; so it follows for you that the power of Allah is originated in the manner you have described. Likewise, the knowledge of Allah was related to the world's being going to exist. Then, when the world came into existence, if the first relation remained, it would be ignorance; and if it did not remain, it follows for you that the first relation is originated, because if it were eternal it would not have ceased, and the relation that came about after that would be originated. Therefore Allah's being Knowing cannot be separated from originated relations, and what cannot be separated from the originated is originated; so Allah's knowing is originated. So whatever you give as an answer regarding the attribute of knowing and the attribute of power is our answer regarding speech.

**Tenth issue:** They argued from His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Verily Allah is over all things competent﴾, that the non-existent is a "thing." Its manner of argument has already been mentioned, so we will not repeat it. The word *qadīr* is of the pattern *faʿīl* in the sense of *fāʿil* (agent), and it is the form of intensification (*binā' al-mubālaghah*).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 105–106 (part 1 of 3)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, and the polytheists, do not wish that any good should be sent down upon you from your Lord. But Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, described the condition of the Jews and the disbelievers in enmity and obstinacy, He warned the believers against them. So He said: ﴿Those who disbelieve do not wish﴾, thereby negating from their hearts affection and love for everything through which the superiority of the believers becomes apparent. Here there are two issues:

**The first issue:** The first "min" (from) is for specification (bayan), because "those who disbelieve" is a genus, under which are two types: the People of the Book and the polytheists. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not [going to desist]﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1]. The second "min" is added for the sake of covering all good (istighraq), and the third "min" is for the starting point of the action (ibtida' al-ghayah).

**The second issue:** "Good" (khayr) here means revelation, and likewise "mercy" (rahmah). This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32]. The meaning is that they consider themselves more deserving that revelation be sent down to them, so they envy you, and they do not wish that any part of revelation be sent down upon you. Then Allah, glorified is He, clarified that this envy does not affect the continuation of that [favour], for He, glorified is He, singles out for His mercy and beneficence whom He wills.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it. Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾

Know that this is the second type of the Jews' criticism of Islam. They said: "Do you not see Muhammad ordering his companions to do something, then forbidding them from it, and ordering them to do the opposite, and saying one thing today and retracting it tomorrow?" So this verse was revealed. The discussion of this verse is arranged in several issues:

**The first issue:** Naskh (abrogation, lit. annulment of a thing) in its original linguistic sense means the annulment of something. Al-Qaffal said that it means transfer and conveyance. Our evidence is that it is said: "The wind effaced (nasakhat) the traces of the people" when they are gone, and "the sun effaced (nasakhat) the shade" when it disappears, because the shade may not appear in another place until one thinks it has moved there. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿except when he wishes, Satan casts [something] into his wish; then Allah abolishes what Satan casts﴾ [al-Hajj: 52], i.e., removes and annuls it. The basic principle in speech is that a word is used in its literal meaning. When it is established that the word is literally used for annulment, it is necessary that it not be literally used for transfer, to avoid homonymy (al-ishtirak).

If it is said: Their describing the wind as "abrogating" traces and the sun as "abrogating" the shade is a figurative usage, because the one who removes traces and shade is Allah, exalted is He. If that is figurative, it is impossible to use it as evidence that the word is literal in its meaning. We then counter what you have mentioned and say: Rather, naskh is transfer and conveyance, and from it comes "nasakha the book into another book," as if he conveys it to it or conveys its content. From it comes the transmigration of souls (tanasukh al-arwah) and the succession of generations, one generation after another (tanasukh al-qurun), and the transmission of inheritances (tanasukh al-mawarith), which is nothing but the shift from one to another in place of the first. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿This is Our record; it speaks against you with truth. Indeed, We were having copied what you used to do﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29]. So it is necessary that the word be literal in transfer, and it follows that it is not literal in annulment, to avoid homonymy.

As for the answer to the first objection, it is in two respects:

First: It is not impossible that Allah be the one who abrogates that, insofar as it is the act of the sun and the wind, which are the influential agents in that removal. They are also abrogators, because they are specifically related to that influence.

Second: The people of the language erred only in attributing naskh to the sun and the wind. Suppose that is so; but our reliance is their use of the word naskh for removal, since they attribute this action to the wind and the sun.

As for the answer to the second objection: transfer is more specific than annulment, because wherever transfer exists, a attribute has ceased and another attribute has come into being after it. Pure non-existence is more comprehensive than a non-existence after which something else comes into being. When a word is ambiguous between the specific and the general, making it literal for the general is preferable. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** Ibn 'Amir recited (mā nunsikh) with a ḍammah on the nūn and a kasrah on the sīn, while the others recited both with a fatḥah. As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir, there are two possibilities:

One: that *nasakha* and *ansakha* have the same meaning.

The second: *ansakhtuhu* means "I made him one who has naskh," as some people said to al-Hajjaj when he had crucified a man: "Bury so-and-so," i.e., make him one who has a grave. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then He caused him to die and assigned him a grave﴾ [‘Abasa: 21].

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited (nanסאhā) with a fatḥah on the nūn and the hamzah, and it is a jussive by the conditional. Abu 'Amr does not drop the hamzah in such a case, because its sukūn is a sign of the jussive. It is from *al-nas'* (postponement). From it: ﴿The postponement [of months] is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37]. From it the sale on credit is called *nasī'ah*. The people of the language said: "Allah postponed his term" (anṣa'a Allāh ajalahu) and "he postponed in his term" (nasa'a fī ajalih), i.e., he delayed and increased. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would like his provision increased and his life extended, let him maintain his ties of kinship."

The others recited it with a ḍammah on the nūn and a kasrah on the sīn, and it is from *al-nisyān* (forgetting). Then most scholars took it to mean forgetting, which is the opposite of remembering. Some took *nisyān* to mean abandonment, in the sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so he forgot, and We found in him no determination﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 115], i.e., he abandoned. And He said: ﴿Today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their day﴾ [al-A'raf: 51], i.e., We will abandon them as they abandoned. The more apparent view is that taking *nisyān* to mean abandonment is figurative, because what is forgotten is abandoned. Since abandonment is a necessary consequence of forgetting, they used the name of the necessitated thing for the necessitating thing.

It was also recited *nunsihā* and *nunassihā* (with shaddah), *tunsahā* and *tansahā* addressing the Messenger. 'Abdullah recited: "mā nunsik min āyatin aw nansakhhā," and Hudhayfah recited: "mā nansakh min āyatin aw nunsikhhā."

**[Page 206]**

**The third issue:** *mā* in this verse is conditional, like your saying: *mā taṣna' aṣna'* ("whatever you do, I do"). Its function is to apply the jussive to the condition and the consequent when both are imperfect verbs. So His saying *nansakh* is the condition, and His saying *na'ti* is the consequent, and both are jussive.

**The fourth issue:** Know that *tanāsukh* (transmigration) in the technical usage of the scholars is an expression for a legal ruling (ṭarīq shar'ī) indicating that a ruling which was established by a legal ruling is no longer found after that, despite its being delayed from it, in a manner that, were it not for it, the ruling would have remained established. So our statement "a legal ruling" means by it the common element between the speech issuing from Allah, exalted is He, and from His Messenger, and the act transmitted from them both. Excluded from it is the consensus of the community (ijma') on one of two opinions, because that is not a legal ruling according to this definition. It is not necessary that the Shari'ah abrogate the ruling of reason, because reason is not a legal ruling. And it is not necessary that a miracle abrogate a legal ruling, because a miracle is not a legal ruling. And it is not necessary that the restriction of a ruling by a limit, a condition or an exception be considered abrogation, because that is not delayed. And it is not necessary to include the case where Allah commands us to do one act and then forbids us from its like, because if such a prohibition were not abrogating, the ruling of the command would not remain established.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** According to us, abrogation is rationally possible and actually occurs by revelation, in contrast to the Jews. Some of them rejected it rationally, and some of them allowed it rationally but prohibited it by revelation. Some Muslims are reported to have denied abrogation. The majority of Muslims argued for the permissibility and occurrence of abrogation: the proofs have established the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and his prophethood is not valid except with the affirmation of the abrogation of the law of those before him. Therefore, abrogation must be affirmed with certainty.

Also, we said: There are two arguments against the Jews:

The first: It is found in the Torah that Allah, exalted is He, said to Noah, peace be upon him, when he came out of the ark: "I have made every moving thing a food for you and your offspring, and I have permitted this to you like the green herbs, except the blood, so do not eat it." Then He, exalted is He, forbade Moses and the Children of Israel many animals.

The second: Adam, peace be upon him, used to marry a sister to a brother, and this was later forbidden by Moses, peace be upon him.

Those who deny abrogation say: We do not concede that the prophethood of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, is not valid except with the affirmation of abrogation, because it is possible to say that Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, were commanded that people follow their law until the time when the law of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, appeared; then after that people were commanded to follow Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. So with the appearance of the law of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, the obligation of their law ceased, and the obligation of the law of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, came into effect. But this would not be abrogation; rather it operates like His saying: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. Those Muslims who denied the occurrence of abrogation at all based their position on this point, and they said: It has been established in the Qur'an that Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, gave good news in the Torah and the Gospel of the advent of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and that upon his appearance it is obligatory to return to his law. If this is the case, then with the existence of this possibility, it is impossible to affirm with certainty the occurrence of abrogation. This is the objection to the two arguments mentioned.

The deniers of abrogation argued by saying: When Allah, exalted is He, clarified the law of Jesus, peace be upon him, the wording indicating that law either indicates its permanence, or does not indicate its permanence, or there is nothing in it indicating either permanence or non-permanence. If it clarified its establishment as permanent, and then it became clear that it did not last, then the first report would be false, and that is impossible for the law. Moreover, if we allowed this, we would have no way to know that our law will not become abrogated, because at most the law would say: "This law is permanent and will never become abrogated at all." But when we see a statement of this kind present in the law of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, although it did not last, trust in it is removed in all cases.

If it is said: Why is it not permissible to say that He mentioned the wording indicating permanence, and then joined to it what indicates that it will be abrogated; or that He joined to it something that does not indicate it, but He explicitly stated that, though it was not transmitted to us in general? We say: This is weak for several reasons:

**[Page 207]**

The first: Explicitly stating the wording indicating permanence together with explicitly stating that it will not last is a combination of two contradictory statements, and that is folly and futility.

The second: On this assumption, Allah, exalted is He, has clarified that their law will become abrogated. If the law itself was transmitted, it is necessary that this manner also be transmitted, because if the original law could be transmitted without this manner, then the same would be permissible for our law as well. In that case, we would have no way to be certain that our law is not abrogated, because that is among the great events for which the motives to transmit it are abundant. Whatever is like that must be widely known and reach the level of mass transmission (tawatur). Otherwise, perhaps the Qur'an was opposed and its opposition was not transmitted, and perhaps Muhammad (ﷺ) changed this law from this state and it was not transmitted. When it is established that this manner must be transmitted through mass transmission, we say: If Allah, exalted is He, had explicitly stated in the time of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, that their two laws would become abrogated, that would have been well known to those who transmit en masse and known to them necessarily. And if that were so, it would be impossible for a great multitude to dispute it. Since we see the Jews and Christians unanimously denying that, we know that there was no explicit statement that their two laws would become abrogated.

The second kind: it is said that God Most High explicitly stated the law of Moses, peace be upon him, and attached to it something indicating that it was limited and not perpetual. This is false, because if it were so, it would have to be known necessarily to the people of tawatur (mass transmission). Moreover, even if it were sound, that would not be naskh (abrogation); rather it would be the ending of a stated term.

The third kind: God Most High explicitly stated the law of Moses, peace be upon him, but did not specify in it whether it was perpetual or not perpetual. We say: it has been established in usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) that a bare command does not indicate repetition; it indicates only a single occurrence. So when the responsible person (mukallaf) performs the single occurrence, he has discharged the obligation of the command. Therefore, the arrival of another command after that is not an abrogation of the first command. By this division it is established that the claim of naskh is impossible.

Know that after we had established this whole matter in our book al-Mahsul fi Usul al-Fiqh, we relied, for the occurrence of naskh, on God's words: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one than it or its like﴾. But the argument from it is also weak, because "ma" here conveys the sense of a condition and a consequence. Just as your saying, "Whoever comes to you, honour him," does not indicate that the coming has taken place, but rather that whenever he comes, honouring him becomes obligatory, so this verse does not indicate that naskh has occurred, but rather that whenever naskh occurs, a better or similar one must come. So the stronger course is to rely, for proof, on God's words: ﴿And when We substitute one verse for another﴾ [al-Nahl: 101], and His words: ﴿God erases what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39]. And God knows best.

* * *

Question Six: The scholars agreed that naskh occurred in the Qur'an, in several ways.

The first of these is this verse, namely His words: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one than it or its like﴾. Abu Muslim answered it in several ways:

The first: the abrogated verses intended are the laws in the earlier books, the Torah and the Gospel, such as the Sabbath and prayer toward east and west, which God Most High set aside for us and commanded us to observe differently. For the Jews and Christians used to say, "Do not believe except in one who follows your religion," so God refuted this claim through this verse.

The second way: the intended meaning of naskh is copying it from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) and transferring it from there to the other books, as one says "I copied the book" (nasakhtu al-kitab).

The third way: we have shown that this verse does not indicate the occurrence of naskh, but rather that if naskh were to occur, it would occur in favour of something better. Some people answered the first objection by saying that when verses (ayat) are mentioned without qualification, what is meant by them is the verses of the Qur'an, since that is what is familiar to us.

As for the second objection: the copying of the Qur'an from the Preserved Tablet is not specific to some part of the Qur'an, whereas this naskh is specific to some part of it. The objector may say, on the first answer: we do not concede that the wording of the verse is specific to the Qur'an; rather it is general to all proofs (dala'il). And on the second answer: we do not concede that the naskh mentioned in the verse is specific to some part of the Qur'an; rather the meaning, and God knows best, is: "Whatever We copy from the Preserved Tablet, We bring after it something better."

The second proof for those who hold that naskh occurred in the Qur'an: God Most High commanded the widow whose husband had died to observe a waiting period of a full year, in His words: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, let them make a bequest for their wives, a provision for a year without expulsion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240]. Then this was abrogated by four months and ten days, as He said: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, let them wait for themselves four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]. Abu Muslim said: the observance of a year has not been removed entirely, because if she were pregnant and the period of her pregnancy were a full year, her waiting period would be a full year. And since this ruling remains in some cases, that is a specification (takhsis), not an abrogation. The answer: the waiting period of pregnancy ends with the delivery of the child, whether the delivery occurs after a year, or less, or more. So making the year the waiting period is entirely removed.

The third proof: God commanded that charity be given before private consultation with the Messenger, in His words: ﴿O you who believe, when you consult the Messenger privately, offer a charity before your consultation﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 12]. Then this was abrogated. Abu Muslim said: it was removed only because its cause was removed. For the cause of worshipping by it was that the hypocrites might be distinguished from the believers by their not giving charity. When this purpose was achieved, the obligation lapsed. The answer: if it were so, then whoever did not give charity would be a hypocrite, and that is false, because it is reported that none gave charity except Ali, may God be pleased with him. And this is indicated by God's words: ﴿Since you did not do it and God has relented toward you﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 13].

The fourth proof: God commanded that one man should stand firm against ten, in His words: ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 65]. Then He abrogated this with His words: ﴿Now God has lightened your burden, and He knows that among you there is weakness; so if there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 66].

The fifth proof: God's words: ﴿The foolish among the people will say, "What has turned them away from the qibla they used to face?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142]. Then God turned them away from it by His words: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. Abu Muslim said: the ruling of that qibla has been removed entirely, because it is permissible to face it when there is doubt, or with knowledge when there is an excuse. The answer: according to what you have mentioned, there is no difference between Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and the other directions. So the distinction by which Bayt al-Maqdis was set apart from the other directions has been entirely removed, and so that was naskh.

The sixth proof: God's words: ﴿And when We substitute one verse for another—and God knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are only a fabricator"﴾ [al-Nahl: 101]. Substitution (tabdil) involves removal and establishment. What is removed is either the recitation (tilawa) or the ruling (hukm). In whichever way it occurs, it is removal and naskh. We have elaborated these proofs because each of them indicates the occurrence of naskh in general.

Abu Muslim argued that God Most High described His Book as one to which falsehood does not come from before it or from behind it. So if it were abrogated, falsehood would have come to it. The answer: what is meant is that no book of God that preceded this Book refutes it, and nor will anything after it refute it.

* * *

Question Seven: The abrogated item is either the ruling alone, or the recitation alone, or both together. As for the case where the abrogated item is the ruling without the recitation, it is like the verses we have enumerated. As for the case where the abrogated item is the recitation alone, it is like what is reported from Umar, who said: "We used to recite the verse of stoning: 'The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as a punishment from God, and God is Mighty and Wise.'" And it is reported: "If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third; and nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust; and God relents toward whoever repents." As for the case where both the ruling and the recitation are abrogated, it is what 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, reported: that the Qur'an had been revealed concerning suckling with ten known sucklings, then they were abrogated by five known sucklings. So the ten are abrogated in both recitation and ruling, while the five are abrogated in recitation, with the ruling remaining. It is also reported that Surat al-Ahzab was equal to the seven long surahs or longer, and then deficiency entered into it.

* * *

Question Eight: The exegetes differed concerning God's words: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾. Some of them interpreted naskh as removal (izala), and some interpreted it as naskh in the sense of "I copied the book." This is the view of Ata' and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. Those who take the first view have mentioned several meanings:

The first: "Whatever verse We abrogate while you are reciting it, or cause to be forgotten," meaning: of the Qur'an, what was recited among you and then you were made to forget it. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Asamm, and most of the theologians (mutakallimun). They took the abrogation to refer to the ruling without the recitation, and the "causing to be forgotten" to refer to the abrogation of both ruling and recitation together. If it is said: the occurrence of this forgetting is impossible both rationally and by the Law. As for reason: the Qur'an must be conveyed to the people of tawatur, and forgetting on the part of all the people of tawatur together is impossible. As for the Law: God's words: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]. The answer to the first is in two ways:

The first: forgetting is possible if God commands that it be cast out of the Qur'an and removed from what is recited and brought forth in prayer or used as evidence. Then when the obligation of worship with it has been removed and a long time has passed, it is forgotten; or if it is mentioned, it is mentioned in the manner of a report of a single transmitter (khabar al-wahid), so for this reason it becomes forgotten from the breasts.

The second answer: that would be a miracle (mu'jiza) for the Messenger, peace be upon him. And a report is transmitted on this: that they would recite a surah, then in the morning they had forgotten it.

The answer to the second: it is contradicted by God's words: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget, except what God wills﴾ [al-A'la: 6], and by His words: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ [al-Kahf: 24].

The second view: "Whatever verse We abrogate," meaning: We change it, either by changing its ruling alone, or its recitation alone, or changing both. As for His words: "or cause to be forgotten," the meaning is: We leave it as it was, so We do not change it. We have shown that forgetting in the sense of leaving has occurred, so the meaning of the verse becomes: what We change, We bring something better than it or its like.

The third view: "Whatever verse We abrogate," that is: We lift it after its revelation, or "nansa'ha" according to the reading with the hamza, meaning: We delay its sending down from the Preserved Tablet; or the intended meaning is: We delay its abrogation, so We do not abrogate it at present, for We send down in its place something that serves the same purpose.

The fourth view: "Whatever verse We abrogate," which is the verse that has become abrogated in both ruling and recitation together; "or cause to be forgotten," that is, leave it, which is the verse that has become abrogated in ruling but is not abrogated in recitation; rather it remains in recitation. As for those who hold the second view, "Whatever verse We abrogate," that is: We abrogate it from the Preserved Tablet, or We delay it. And as for the reading "nunsiha," the meaning is: We leave it, that is, We leave its abrogation, so We do not abrogate it.

* * *

As for His words: ﴿from a verse﴾, all the exegetes took it to mean a verse of the Qur'an, except Abu Muslim, who took it to mean the Torah and the Gospel. This has already been discussed.

* * *

[Page 210]

As for His words: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, there are two views:

One of them: that it is the lighter.

The second: that it is the more beneficial (aslah). This is the stronger, because God directs the responsible person toward his benefits, not toward what is lighter for his natural disposition. If it is said: if the second is more beneficial than the first, then the first would be deficient in benefit, so how did God command it? We say: the first is more beneficial than the second with respect to its own time, and the second is the reverse of that, so the objection is removed.

Know that people have derived from this verse most of the questions of naskh.

The first question: Some people said: naskh of a ruling is permissible only to a substitute (badal). They argued that this verse indicates that when God abrogates, He must bring after it something better than it, or something like it, and that is explicit in the obligation of a substitute. The answer: why should it not be said that the intended meaning is that the removal of that ruling and the lapse of worship by it are better than its being established at that time? Moreover, what indicates the occurrence of naskh without a substitute is that the sending of charity before the private consultation with the Messenger, peace be upon him, was abrogated without a substitute.

**Page 211** (marker in source)

**Second issue:** Some people said: it is not permissible to abrogate (*naskh*) a ruling with one that is heavier than it. They argued that His saying, ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, contradicts the abrogating ruling being heavier, since what is heavier cannot be "better than it" or "like it." The response is: why should it not be permissible for "better" to mean that which yields greater reward in the Hereafter? Moreover, what proves that it has occurred is that Allah, glory be to Him, abrogated the confinement of adulterers to their houses with flogging and stoning, abrogated the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ with the fast of Ramadan, and, according to some, the prayer, which was two rakʿahs, was abrogated with four in the state of residence. Having understood this, we say: abrogation to something heavier has occurred in the cases mentioned. As for abrogation to something lighter, it is like the abrogation of the waiting period from a year to four months and ten days, and like the abrogation of the night prayer to optional performance. As for abrogation to something of equal weight, it is like the change of the direction of prayer from Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) to the Kaʿbah.

**Third issue:** al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Book (the Qur'an) is not abrogated by the widely-attested Sunnah (*mutawātir*), and he argued for this from this verse in several ways:

The first: He, may He be exalted, informed that what He abrogates of the verses, He brings something better than it, and this indicates that He brings something of the same kind, just as when a person says: "Whatever garment I take from you, I will bring you a better one," it indicates that he will bring him a garment of the same kind but better. And when it is established that it must be of the same kind, then the kind of the Qur'an is Qur'an.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾ indicates that it is the Qur'an, which is the speech of Allah, and not the Sunnah which the Messenger, peace be upon him, brings.

The third: His saying ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾ indicates that what is brought is better than the verse, and the Sunnah is not better than the Qur'an.

The fourth: He said ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾, which indicates that the one who brings that better thing is the one exclusively characterized by power over all good things, and that is Allah, may He be exalted.

The answer to all four points together is: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾ does not state that this better thing must be the abrogating one. Rather, it is not impossible that this better thing is something other than the abrogating ruling, which comes about after the abrogation has taken place. What proves the realization of this possibility is that this verse is explicit that bringing that better thing is consequent upon the abrogation of the first verse. So if the abrogation of that verse were consequent upon bringing this better thing, it would lead to circularity (*dawr*), which is invalid.

Then the majority (*al-Jumhūr*) argued for the occurrence of the abrogation of the Book by the Sunnah, because the verse on bequest to the closest relatives has been abrogated by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Verily, there is no bequest for an heir." And because the verse of flogging became abrogated by the report of stoning.

Al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: As for the first, it is weak, because the inheritance being a right of the heir prevents it from being diverted to bequest. Thus it is established that the verse of inheritance prevents bequest. As for the second, it is also weak, because ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, related that his saying: "The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely" was part of the Qur'an. So perhaps the abrogation occurred by means of it. The full discussion of this is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (*uṣūl al-fiqh*). And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾, it is an admonition to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and to others, regarding His power to direct the responsible person (*mukallaf*) under His will, His judgment and His wisdom, and that there is no repeller of what He wills and no preventer of what He chooses.

**Ninth issue:** The Muʿtazilah (a theological school that held the Qur'an to be created) used this verse to prove that the Qur'an is created, in several ways:

The first: If the speech of Allah, may He be exalted, were eternal, then the abrogating and the abrogated would both be eternal. But this is impossible, because the abrogating must necessarily be later than the abrogated, and what is later than something cannot be eternal. As for the abrogated, it is because it must cease and be removed, and what is established to cease is, by agreement, impossible to be eternal.

The second: The verse indicates that some of the Qur'an is better than some of it, and what is like that cannot be eternal.

The third: His saying ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ indicates that what is meant is that He, may He be exalted, is the One capable of abrogating some of it and bringing something else in its place. And what falls under power and is an act is originated (*muḥdath*). The Ashʿarī scholars (*al-Aṣḥāb*) answered this: the fact that it is abrogating and abrogated is only among the accidents of words, expressions and languages, and there is no dispute about their being originated. So why do you claim that the real meaning, which is the signified content of expressions and terms, is originated? The Muʿtazilah said: That meaning which is the signified content of expressions and languages, there is no doubt that its first relation has ceased and a different relation has come into being for it. So the first relation is originated because it ceased, and the eternal does not cease; and the second relation is originated because it came about after it had not been. The real speech cannot be separated from these relations, and what cannot be separated from these relations is originated, and the speech to which they are attached must be originated.

The Ashʿarī scholars answered: The power of Allah was, from eternity, related to bringing the world into existence. Then, when the world came into existence, did that relation remain or not? If it remained, it would follow that the Capable would be capable of bringing into existence what already exists, which is impossible. And if it did not remain, then that relation has ceased; so it follows for you that the power of Allah is originated in the manner you have described. Likewise, the knowledge of Allah was related to the world's being going to exist. Then, when the world came into existence, if the first relation remained, it would be ignorance; and if it did not remain, it follows for you that the first relation is originated, because if it were eternal it would not have ceased, and the relation that came about after that would be originated. Therefore Allah's being Knowing cannot be separated from originated relations, and what cannot be separated from the originated is originated; so Allah's knowing is originated. So whatever you give as an answer regarding the attribute of knowing and the attribute of power is our answer regarding speech.

**Tenth issue:** They argued from His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Verily Allah is over all things competent﴾, that the non-existent is a "thing." Its manner of argument has already been mentioned, so we will not repeat it. The word *qadīr* is of the pattern *faʿīl* in the sense of *fāʿil* (agent), and it is the form of intensification (*binā' al-mubālaghah*).

**The Qur'anic text:** ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that besides Allah you have neither any guardian nor any helper?﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted is He, ruled that abrogation (naskh) is permissible, He followed this with a statement that the dominion (mulk) of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him and not to anyone else.

Page 212

This is an alert that He, glorified and exalted is He, is only entitled to command and prohibit because He is the Owner of creation. This is the position of our companions (the Ash'ari scholars), who hold that imposing obligations (taklif) on people is good from Him solely because He owns creation and has authority over them, not for a reward that will be gained or a punishment that will be averted.

Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that this is a reference to the matter of the qiblah. He, exalted is He, informed them that He is the Owner of the heavens and the earth, that all places and directions belong to Him, and that no direction is greater in sanctity than another except insofar as He, exalted is He, makes it so. Given this, and given that the command to face the qiblah is purely a specification for the sake of honour, there is nothing to prevent it from being changed from one direction to another.

As for *al-Waliyy* (the guardian) and *al-Nasir* (the helper), both are of the form *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* (active agent), in an intensive form.

Some people have used this verse to argue that dominion (mulk) is other than power (qudrah). They said: He, exalted is He, first said: ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ and then after it said: ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ So if mulk were an expression for qudrah, this would be repetition without benefit. The discussion of the reality of mulk and qudrah has already passed in His words: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 108:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before? And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the straight way.﴾ Know that there are several issues here.

The first issue: "am" (أم) is of two kinds: connective (muttasilah) and disconnective (munqati'ah). The connective "am" is the equivalent of the alif (of interrogation), and it separates what "ayy" (أي) has combined, just as "aw" (أو) separates what it has combined. You say: "Strike whichever of them you wish, Zayd or 'Amr" (اضْرِبْ أيَّهم شِئْتَ زَيْدًا أمْ عَمْرًا). When you say "Strike one of them," you say "Strike Zayd or 'Amr" (اضْرِبْ زَيْدًا أوْ عَمْرًا). The disconnective "am" occurs only after a complete statement, because it has the meaning of "bal" (بل, "rather") together with the alif, as in the saying of the Arabs: "Is it camels or sheep?" (إنَّها الإبِلُ أمْ شاءٌ), as if he said: "Rather, it is sheep." From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 3], meaning: "Rather, do they say...?" Al-Akhtal said:

"Your eye has deceived you, or did you see at Wasit
a phantom of the darkness' remnant from the Rabab?" (كَذَبَتْكَ عَيْنُكَ أمْ رَأيْتَ بِواسِطٍ غَلَسَ الظَّلامِ مِنَ الرَّبابِ خَيالًا)

The second issue: They differed about who is addressed by it, in several views.

The first of them: they are the Muslims. This is the view of al-Asamm, al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim, and they argued for it with several points:

The first: He said at the end of the verse: ﴿and whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾, and this statement is valid only with regard to the believers.

The second: His saying ﴿Or do you wish﴾ requires something to be coordinated with it, which is His saying: ﴿Do not say "Ra'ina"﴾ (لا تَقُولُوا راعِنا). So it is as if He said: "And say: 'Unzurna' (انْظُرْنا) and 'isma'u' (واسْمَعُوا). Will you do that as you were commanded, or do you wish to question your Messenger?"

The third: The Muslims used to question Muhammad (ﷺ) about matters in which there was no good for them in searching into them, in order to know them, just as the Jews asked Moses (peace be upon him) about what held no good for them in searching into it.

The fourth: A group of Muslims asked that a *dhat anwat* (ذات أنواط) be made for them, just as the polytheists had a *dhat anwat*. It was a tree they used to worship, hanging food and drink upon it, just as they (the Israelites) asked Moses to make for them a god just as they had gods.

The second view: It is addressed to the people of Makkah. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. He said: 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah al-Makhzumi came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a group of Quraysh and said: "O Muhammad, by God, I will not believe in you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth, or you have a garden of palms and grapes, or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky by climbing. And we will not believe in your ascent even after that until you send down to us a book from God to 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, so follow him."

The rest of the group said to him: "If you cannot do that, then bring us a book from the presence of God all at once, containing the lawful and the unlawful, the prescribed punishments and the obligations, just as Moses came to his people with the tablets from God containing all of that. Then we will believe in you." So God, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger Muhammad, as you asked for the signs from God, as the seventy asked, when they said: "Show us God openly"?﴾

And from Mujahid: Quraysh asked Muhammad (peace be upon him) to make Safa gold and silver for them. He said: "Yes, it will be yours, like the table for the Children of Israel." But they refused and turned back.

The third view: What is meant is the Jews. This view is more correct, because this surah, from His saying ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour﴾ [al-Baqarah: 47] onward, is a narration about them and a debate with them; and because this verse is Madani; and because the mention of the Jews has preceded and the mention of others has not; and because one who believes in the Messenger hardly asks him, and if he asks him, he is one who exchanges disbelief for faith.

The third issue: There is nothing in the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before﴾ that they actually brought the question, let alone how the question was put. Rather, the reference for that is the narrations we have mentioned that they asked, and God knows best.

The fourth issue: Know that if the question they mentioned was a request for miracles, then from where does it come that it is disbelief? It is well known that seeking evidence for a thing is not disbelief. And if it was a request for the wisdom behind the detailed rulings in the abrogation of rulings, then this too is not disbelief; for the angels asked about the detailed wisdom in the creation of man, and that was not disbelief. So perhaps the better reading of the verse is that they asked him to make for them a god just as they have gods. And even if they asked for miracles, they were asking them by way of obstinacy and contentiousness, and for this reason they disbelieved because of this question.

The fifth issue: They mentioned several views regarding the connection of this verse with what precedes it:

The first: When He ruled that abrogation is permissible in the laws, perhaps they were demanding from Him the details of that ruling, so God, may He be exalted, forbade them from that and made clear that it is not for them to occupy themselves with these questions, just as it was not for the people of Moses to mention their corrupt questions.

The second: Since the commands and prohibitions had preceded, He said to them: If you do not accept what I have commanded you and rebel against obedience, you will be like the one who asked Moses what it was not his right to ask; this is from Abu Muslim.

The third: When He commanded and forbade, He said: Will you do what you are commanded, or will you do as those before you did, the people of Moses?

The sixth issue: ﴿sawa' al-sabil﴾ means its middle. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So he looked down and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire (sawa' al-jahim)﴾ [al-Saffat: 55], meaning the middle of the Blazing Fire. The purpose is comparison, not the literal reality itself. The aspect of comparison in this is that whoever follows the path of faith is proceeding on the uprightness that leads to success and attaining the sought-after reward and bliss. So whoever exchanges that for disbelief has deviated from uprightness, and so it is said of him that he has strayed from the straight way (sawa' al-sabil).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 109–110 (part 1 of 3)**

God's words: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and overlook, until God brings His command. Indeed, God is over all things competent.﴾

Know that this is the third type of the scheming (*kayd*) of the Jews against the Muslims. The reason is that it was narrated that Finhas ibn Azura, Zayd ibn Qays, and a group of Jews said to Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman and Ammar ibn Yasir after the Battle of Uhud: "Did you not see what befell you? Had you been upon the truth, you would not have been defeated. So return to our religion, for it is better and more excellent for you, and we are more rightly guided than you on the path." Ammar said: "How would breaking the covenant be among you?" They said: "It is grave." He said: "Then I have covenanted that I will not disbelieve in Muhammad as long as I live." The Jews said: "As for this one, he has apostatized." Hudhayfa said: "As for me, I am content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, with the Qur'an as leader, with the Ka'bah as qibla, and with the believers as brothers." Then they both came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: "You have done well and prospered." Then this verse was revealed. Know that we will first speak about envy (*hasad*, the wish for another's blessing to be removed), and then return to the tafsir.

**The first issue: on the censure of envy, which is indicated by many reports.**

The first: the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Envy devours good deeds just as fire devours firewood."

The second: Anas said: "We were one day sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Now there will appear to you from this pass a man of the people of Paradise.' A man of the Ansar appeared, his beard dripping with water from his ablution, having hung his two sandals on his left side. He greeted (the Prophet). On the next day he (ﷺ) said the same, and that man appeared. On the third day he said the same, and that man appeared. When the Prophet (peace be upon him) rose, Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As followed him and said: 'I have been troubled by my father, and I swore I would not enter upon him for three days. If you see fit that I may stay at your house, you may do so.' He said: 'Yes.' So he spent three nights with him, and he did not see him rise at night for anything, except that when he turned over on his bed he remembered God, and he did not rise until he rose for the Fajr prayer. But I never heard him say anything except good. When the three days passed, and I was almost belittling his deed, I said: 'O servant of God, there was no anger or estrangement between me and my father, but I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say such-and-such, so I wanted to know your deed. I have not seen you do a great deal of action; what then has brought you to that station?' He said: 'It is nothing but what you have seen.' When I turned to leave, he called me back and said: 'It is nothing but what you have seen, except that I do not find in myself any defect or envy toward any Muslim for a good thing God has given him.' Abdullah said: 'It is this which has brought you to it, and it is the very thing that cannot be borne.'"

The third: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The disease of the nations before you has crept upon you: envy and hatred. Hatred is the shaver, I do not mean the shaver of hair, but the shaver of religion."

The fourth: He said: "There will befall my Ummah the disease of the nations." They said: "What is the disease of the nations?" He said: "Arrogance, insolence, excessive pursuit of worldly increase, rivalry in the world, estrangement, and mutual envy, until there is oppression and then bloodshed."

The fifth: When Musa (peace be upon him) went to his Lord, he saw in the shade of the Throne a man who was envied for his station. He said: "Surely this man is honored by his Lord." So he asked his Lord to inform him of his name, but He did not inform him of his name. He said: "I will tell you about his deeds in three: he did not envy people for what God had given them of His bounty, he did not disobey his parents, and he did not walk about spreading gossip."

The sixth: He (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, the blessings of God have enemies." It was said: "And who are they?" He said: "Those who envy people for what God has given them of His bounty."

The seventh: He (peace be upon him) said: "Six will enter the Fire before the Reckoning: rulers through tyranny, Arabs through tribalism, landowners through arrogance, merchants through treachery, villagers through ignorance, and scholars through envy."

As for the reports from the companions and successors:

The first: It is related that Awf ibn Abdullah entered upon al-Fadl ibn al-Muhallab, who was at that time governor of Wasit, and said: "I want to advise you with something: beware of pride, for it was the first sin with which Iblis disobeyed God." Then he recited: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused and was arrogant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 34]. "And beware of greed, for it expelled Adam from the Garden. God settled him in a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth, but he ate from it, so God expelled him." Then he recited: ﴿Go down from it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123]. "And beware of envy, for it caused the son of Adam to kill his brother when he envied him." Then he recited: ﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 27].

The second: Ibn al-Zubayr said: "I have never envied anyone over a matter of this world, for if he is among the people of Paradise, how could I envy him over the world, which is insignificant in Paradise? And if he is among the people of the Fire, how could I envy him over a matter of the world when he is going to the Fire?"

The third: A man said to al-Hasan: "Does the believer envy?" He said: "What has made you forget the sons of Ya'qub? However, it does not harm you so long as you do not prepare a hand or tongue for it."

The fourth: Mu'awiyah said: "All people are more capable of pleasing than the envious, for nothing satisfies him except the removal of the blessing."

The fifth: It was said: "The envious gains from gatherings nothing but blame and humiliation, from the angels nothing but curse and hatred, from creation nothing but distress and grief, at the time of terror nothing but severity and dread, and at the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment) nothing but disgrace and punishment."

* * *

**The second issue: on the reality of envy.** If God bestows a blessing upon your brother, and you wish for its removal, this is envy (*hasad*). If you desire a similar one for yourself, this is *ghibta* (wishing to attain the same blessing without wishing its removal from the other) and *munafasah* (rivalry). The first is forbidden in every case, except a blessing obtained by a wicked or disbelieving person who uses it for evil and corruption; in that case your love for its removal does no harm, since you do not love its removal as a blessing, but as something through which evil, corruption, and harm are facilitated.

The verses that show that envy is what we have mentioned are:

The first: this verse, namely His words: ﴿They wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed, out of envy from themselves﴾. So He informed that their wish for the removal of the blessing of faith is envy.

The second: His words: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be equal﴾ [al-Nisa': 89].

The third: His words: ﴿If good touches you, it distresses them; and if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 120]. This rejoicing is malicious glee, and envy and malicious glee are inseparable.

The fourth: God mentioned the envy of the brothers of Yusuf and expressed what was in their hearts by His words: ﴿They said, "Yusuf and his brother are more beloved to our father than we, though we are a group. Indeed, our father is in clear error." ... "Kill Yusuf or cast him into some land, and the face of your father will be clear for you"﴾ [Yusuf: 8–9]. Thus He clarified that their envy of him was an expression of their dislike of that blessing reaching him.

The fifth: His words: ﴿And they find in their breasts no need for what they have been given﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], meaning their breasts are not constricted by it, and they do not grieve. Thus God praised them for not envying.

The sixth: He said, in the context of denunciation: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what God has given them of His bounty?﴾ [al-Nisa': 54].

The seventh: God said: ﴿The people were one nation, so God sent the prophets﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], up to His words: ﴿except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213]. It was said in the tafsir that the "rebellion" here is envy.

The eighth: His words: ﴿They did not divide except after knowledge had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 14]. God sent down knowledge to unite them upon His obedience, but they envied one another and differed, since each one wanted to be alone in leadership and in acceptance of his word.

The ninth: Ibn Abbas said: "Before the mission of the Prophet (peace be upon him), the Jews, when they fought a people, would say: 'We ask you by the Prophet whom You promised to send, and by the Book You will send down, that You help us.' So they were helped. But when the Prophet (peace be upon him) came from the descendants of Isma'il, they recognized him and disbelieved in him after knowing him." God said: ﴿And previously they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89], up to His words: ﴿that they disbelieve in what God has sent down, out of rebellion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90], meaning out of envy. "And Safiyyah bint Huyayy said to the Prophet (peace be upon him): 'My father and my uncle came from your presence. My father said to my uncle: "What do you say about him?" He said: "I say he is the Prophet whom Musa (peace be upon him) foretold." He said: "What do you think?" He said: "I think we should oppose him as long as we live."'" This is the ruling on envy.

As for rivalry (*munafasah*), it is not forbidden. It is derived from *nafasah* (preciousness), and what indicates that it is not forbidden are several points:

The first: His words: ﴿And for this let those who compete compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 26].

The second: His words: ﴿Race toward forgiveness from your Lord﴾. Racing occurs only out of fear of missing out. It is like two servants competing to serve their master, each fearing that the other will precede him, so that one gains a rank with his master that the other does not attain.

The third: The saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "There is no envy except in two: a man whom God has given wealth and who spends it in the way of God, and a man whom God has given knowledge, who acts upon it and teaches it to people."

This hadith indicates that the word *hasad* may be applied to rivalry. Then we say: rivalry may be obligatory, recommended, or permissible. The obligatory is like when that blessing is an obligatory religious blessing, such as faith, prayer, and zakat. In that case he must have a similar one, for if he does not love to have it, he is content with disobedience, and that is forbidden. As for when that blessing is among the recommended virtues, such as spending in the way of God and striving to teach people, rivalry in it is recommended. And if that blessing is among the permissible things, rivalry in it is permissible. In sum, what is blameworthy is to love the removal of the blessing from another. As for loving that it be attained for oneself and that one's deficiency be removed, this is not blameworthy. But there is a subtlety here: removing one's deficiency relative to another has two paths:

The first: that he obtains what the other has obtained.

The second: that the other loses what he has not obtained.

When despair arises regarding one of the two paths, the heart nearly cannot be free of longing for the other path. Here, if he finds his heart such that if he were able to remove that virtue from that person, he would remove it, then he is the one with blameworthy envy. But if he finds his heart such that piety restrains him from removing that blessing from another, then it is hoped from God, exalted is He, that He will pardon him for that. Perhaps this is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Three things a believer cannot be free of: envy, suspicion, and omens. But there is a way out of them: if you envy, do not act upon it." That is, if you find something in your heart, do not act upon it. This is the discourse on the reality of envy, and all of it is from the words of Shaykh al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him.

* * *

**The third issue: on the degrees of envy.** Al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, said there are four:

The first: that he loves the removal of that blessing, even if it does not come to him. This is the utmost degree of envy.

The second: that he loves the removal of that blessing from the other and its transfer to himself. This is like his desire for a beautiful house, a beautiful woman, or an effective authority that another has attained, and he loves that it be his. What is sought in essence is its attainment for himself; as for its removal from another, that is sought incidentally.

The third: that he does not desire the thing itself, but desires a similar one for himself. If he is unable to obtain a similar one, he loves its removal so that the disparity between them does not appear.

The fourth [condition]: that one wishes for oneself something similar to it. If one does not obtain it, one does not love its disappearance. This last is what is pardoned if it concerns worldly matters, and what is recommended if it concerns religion. The third of these is blameworthy in some cases and not blameworthy in others, and the second is lighter than the third, while the first is purely blameworthy. God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not wish for that by which God has favoured some of you over others﴾ [al-Nisa': 32]. So wishing for something similar to it is not blameworthy, but wishing for that very thing is blameworthy.

* * *

The fourth issue: Shaykh al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, mentioned seven causes of ḥasad (envy):

The first cause: enmity and hatred. When a person harms another, the heart hates him and becomes angry with him. That anger generates resentment, and resentment demands revenge and retaliation. If the one who hates is unable to take revenge himself, he wishes that time would take revenge on him for him. So whenever a calamity or affliction befalls his enemy, he rejoices, and whenever a blessing befalls him, it grieves him, because that is contrary to what he wants. Envy is thus a necessary consequence of hatred and enmity and never separates from them. The most that can be done in this regard is not to display that enmity from oneself and to dislike that state within oneself. But for a person to hate another and yet for his joy and his sorrow to be equal to him is impossible. This type of envy is what God described the unbelievers as having, when He said: ﴿And when they meet you, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage. Say, "Die in your rage. Indeed, God is Knowing of what is in the breasts." If good touches you, it distresses them; and if an affliction strikes you, they rejoice at it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119–120]. Likewise He said: ﴿They wish you would suffer. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]. Know that envy may lead to dispute and fighting.

Page 217

The second cause: the desire for superiority. When one of one's peers attains a high rank and rises above him, he cannot bear that, so he wishes that rank to be taken away from him. His aim is not to be arrogant, but to ward off his own humiliation, for he may accept being equal to him, but he does not accept being elevated above him.

The third cause: that it is in one's nature to make others serve him. He therefore wishes the blessing to be removed from that other person so that he can be able to achieve that aim. From this category was the envy of most of the unbelievers toward the Messenger, peace be upon him, when they said: "How can a young orphan take precedence over us, and how can we lower our heads before him?" They said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. And God the Exalted, describing the words of the Quraysh, said: ﴿Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour from among us?﴾ [al-An'am: 53], expressing contempt for them and disdain of them.

The fourth cause: astonishment, as God reported of the earlier nations, when they said: ﴿You are only a human being like us﴾ [Ya Sin: 15]; and they said: ﴿Shall we believe two humans like us, while their people are our worshippers?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 47]; and they said in astonishment: ﴿Has God sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra': 94]; and they said: ﴿Why have angels not been sent down to us?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21]; and He said: ﴿Are you astonished that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 63].

The fifth cause: fear of losing one's objectives. This applies specifically to those competing for one single objective, for each of them envies the other for every blessing that would help him to be alone in achieving his aim. From this category is the envy of co-wives in competing for the aims of marriage, and the envy of brothers in competing to gain a position in the hearts of their parents, in order to reach the aims of wealth and honour. Likewise is the envy of preachers competing over the people of one town, since the aim of each of them is to gain wealth and acceptance among them.

The sixth cause: love of leadership and the pursuit of status for its own sake, without using it as a means to another aim. This is like the man who wishes to be unrivalled in one of the arts. If he hears of a rival to him at the farthest end of the world, that displeases him, and he wishes for that person's death and for the removal of the blessing by which he shares the same standing with him, whether it be courage, knowledge, asceticism, or wealth, and he rejoices at being unique.

The seventh cause: stinginess of the soul with good toward God's servants. You will find someone who is not occupied with leadership, arrogance, or the pursuit of wealth, yet when he is told of the good condition of one of God's servants, it pains him; and when he is told of the disorder of people's affairs, their adversity, and the embitterment of their lives, he rejoices. He always loves others' misfortune and is stingy with God's blessing toward His servants, as though they were taking it from his own possession and treasury. It is said: "The miser is one who is stingy with someone else's wealth." This person is stingy with God's blessing toward His servants, between whom and himself there is neither enmity nor connection. This has no apparent cause except the corruption of the soul and the baseness of its natural disposition. For all other kinds of envy are hoped to be removed by removing their cause, but this is a corruption of the innate character, not from an incidental cause, so its removal is difficult. These, then, are the causes of envy. Some of these causes, or most of them, or all of them, may be combined in one person, so that envy grows greatly within him and becomes so strong that its bearer can no longer conceal it or behave courteously, but tears away the veil of courtesy and reveals his enmity openly. Most cases of envy combine a number of these causes, and rarely is one of them free of all the others.

* * *

The fifth issue: concerning the cause of the abundance or scarcity of envy, and its strength or weakness.

Know that envy occurs most often among people in whom the causes we have mentioned are abundant, for an individual may envy because he refuses the speech of the arrogant person, or because he is arrogant himself, or because he is an enemy for some other of these reasons. And these causes are most common among a group of people bound together by ties, by which they gather in assemblies of discourse and converge on the same objectives. Rivalry is a source of discord, and discord leads to envy. Where there is no association, there is no envying. Since no tie exists between two persons in two different cities, naturally there is no envy between them. That is why you see a scholar envying a scholar but not a worshipper, and a worshipper envying a worshipper but not a scholar, and a merchant envying a merchant, indeed a cobbler envying a cobbler, but not a cloth-seller. A man envies his brother and his paternal cousin more than he envies strangers, and a woman envies her co-wife and her husband's concubine more than she envies her mother-in-law and her husband's daughter. This is because the aim of the cloth-seller is not the aim of the cobbler, so they do not compete for the same objectives. Moreover, the competition of a cloth-seller with the neighbouring cloth-seller is greater than the competition with one far away at the other end of the market. In sum, the root of envy is enmity, and the root of enmity is competition for one objective. A single objective does not unite those who are far apart; rather, it unites only those who are similar. Therefore envy is abundant among them. Yes, whoever is intensely eager for broad status and fame throughout the world will envy everyone in the world who shares with him the quality in which he takes pride.
