I say: the true cause of this is that perfection is loved in itself, and the opposite of what is loved is hated. Among the kinds of perfection is being unique in perfection, so inevitably a partner in perfection is hated, because he contests the uniqueness which is among the greatest gateways to perfection. However, since this kind of perfection cannot be attained except by God the Glorified, and despair of it has set in, envy has become restricted to worldly matters. This is because the world cannot accommodate those who compete for it, whereas the Hereafter has no constriction. The example of the Hereafter is the blessing of knowledge. Therefore whoever loves to know God the Exalted, His attributes, and His angels will not envy others once he knows, for knowledge does not constrict those who possess it. Rather, one single known object may be known by a thousand thousand people, and each rejoices in knowing it and takes pleasure in it, and no one's pleasure diminishes because of another. Indeed, with the multiplication of those who know, the intimacy increases. Therefore there is no envy among the scholars of religion, for their aim is knowledge of God, which is a vast ocean with no constriction, and their goal is nearness to God, which has no constriction. Yes, if scholars seek knowledge for the sake of wealth and status, they envy one another, because wealth consists of tangible items: when they fall into one person's hand, they leave another's hand empty. The meaning of status is filling hearts, and whenever one person's heart is filled with the veneration of one scholar, it turns away from venerating another. But when a heart is filled with joy at knowing God, that does not prevent the heart of another from being filled with it too and rejoicing in it. Therefore God the Exalted described them as free of envy when He said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; [they will be] brothers on couches, facing one another﴾ [al-Hijr: 47].

* * *

The sixth issue: concerning the remedy that removes envy. It consists of two things: knowledge and action.

As for knowledge, it has two levels: general and detailed. The general level is that one knows that whatever comes into existence has occurred as a necessary consequence of God's decree and destiny, for a possible thing does not stop until it reaches the Necessary Being. Once this is the case, there is no benefit in recoiling from it. When contentment with the decree is achieved, envy disappears.

The detailed level is that you know that envy is harmful to you in religion and in worldly life, and that it does not harm the envied person in religion or in worldly life, but rather he benefits from it in religion and in worldly life.

As for it being harmful to you in religion, that is in several respects:

The first: by envying, you have disliked God's judgment and disputed His allotment, which He apportioned to His servants, and His justice, which He established in His creation through His hidden wisdom. This is an offence against the pupil of monotheism and a speck in the eye of faith.

The second: if you deceive one of the believers, you have departed from the friends of God in their love of good for God's servants, and you have shared with Iblis and all the unbelievers in their love of afflictions for the believers.

The third: the great punishment that is ordained for it in the Hereafter.

As for it being harmful to you in this world, it is that because of envy you will never cease to be in grief and sorrow, while God does not leave your enemies without various blessings. So you will continue to be tormented by every blessing you see them receiving and pained by every calamity that passes them by. Thus you will remain forever sad and distressed. You have obtained for yourself what you wanted for your enemies, and what your enemies wanted for you. You wanted trial for your enemy, so you strove to bring trial upon yourself.

Furthermore, if that grief takes control of you, it sickens your body, removes your health, leads you into obsessive thoughts, and spoils for you the pleasure of food and drink.

As for the fact that the envied person suffers no harm in his religion or his worldly life, that is clear, for the blessing does not leave him because of your envy. Rather, whatever ascent and blessing God has decreed for him must endure until a term that God has set, for everything with Him is by measure, and for every term there is a Book. As long as the blessing is not removed through envy, the envied person suffers no harm in this world, and no sin is upon him in the Hereafter.

Perhaps you will say: "I wish the blessing were mine, and that it would be removed from the envied person through my envy." But this is utmost ignorance, for it is a trial that you would first desire for yourself, since you too are not free of an enemy who envies you. If blessings were removed through envy, no blessing from God would remain upon you, neither in religion nor in worldly life. And if you desire that blessings be removed from creatures through your envy, but not removed from you through the envy of others, that too is ignorance, for every one of the foolish envious people desires to be the exclusive possessor of this quality, and you are no more entitled to it than anyone else. So God's blessing upon you, in that He has not removed the blessing from you through envy, is among the things that must be thanked for, yet in your ignorance you dislike it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 109–110 (part 3 of 3):

As for the envied person benefiting from envy in religion and in this world, that is clear. His benefit in religion is that he is wronged by you, especially when you bring envy out into speech and action, through backbiting, disparaging him, exposing his concealed faults, and mentioning his shortcomings. These are gifts that Allah bestows on him, meaning that you give him your good deeds. Whenever you speak ill of him, your good deeds are transferred to his record and your sins increase. It is as if you desired the removal of Allah's blessings from him and onto you, so Allah's blessings are removed from you and given to him, and you continue at every moment and time to grow in wretchedness.

As for his benefit in this world, it is in several respects.

The first: The most important aim of people is to grieve their enemies and see them distressed and tormented, and there is no torment greater than what you are in, the pain of envy. Indeed, the intelligent person does not wish for the death of his enemy but wishes for him a long life, so that he may remain in the torment of envy, looking at every moment and time at Allah's blessings upon him, so that his heart is torn apart by that. For this reason it was said:

"May your enemies not die, but be made to live forever,
until they see from you what burns them.
May you never cease to be envied for a blessing,
for only the perfect one is envied."

The second: People know that the envied person must have a blessing, so they infer from the envy of the envier that he has been singled out by Allah with various kinds of virtues and excellences. The greatest virtues are those that cannot be repelled, and they are what produce envy. Thus envy becomes one of the strongest indications that the envied person is characterized by various kinds of virtues and excellences.

The third: The envier becomes blameworthy among creation and cursed in the sight of the Creator, and this is among the greatest aims of the envied person.

The fourth: It is a cause of increasing the joy of Iblis (Satan). This is because the envier, having lacked the virtues that the envied person has been singled out with, if he were content with that, would deserve a great reward. Iblis feared that he would be content with it and thereby deserve that reward. When he was not content with it but showed envy, he lost that reward and deserved punishment. This becomes a cause of Iblis's joy and the anger of Allah, exalted is He.

The fifth: You may envy a man of knowledge and love that he err in the religion of Allah, that you expose his error so that he is disgraced, and that his tongue be silenced so that he cannot speak, or that he fall ill so that he can neither teach nor learn. What sin could be greater than this, and what rank could be lower than this?

It has become clear from these aspects, O envier, that you are like one who throws a stone at his enemy to strike his vital spot, but it does not hit him. Rather, it returns to his right eye and plucks it out, so his anger increases and he returns and throws it a second time, harder than the first. The stone returns to his other eye and blinds it, so his rage increases and he returns a third time, and it comes back upon his head and splits it open, while his enemy remains unharmed in every state, and the ruin returns to him always. [p. 220]

And his enemies around him rejoice at him and laugh at him. Indeed, the state of the envier is worse than this, because the returning stone only destroyed the eye, and if it had remained, it would have been lost through death. As for his envy, it drives him to the anger of Allah and to the Fire. So it is better for him that his eye be lost in this world than that he keep an eye and enter the Fire with it. Observe how Allah has taken vengeance on the envier who wishes the blessing removed from the envied person: He did not remove it from him, but then removed the blessing from the envier, confirming the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And the evil scheming encompasses none but its own people.﴾ [Fatir: 43]

These are the scientific remedies. Whenever a person reflects on them with a clear mind and a present heart, the fire of envy is extinguished from his heart. As for the beneficial action, it is that he performs deeds opposed to what envy demands. If envy moves him to disparage the envied person, he compels his tongue to praise him. If it moves him to be arrogant toward him, he compels himself to humility toward him. If it moves him to cut off the means of good from him, he compels himself to strive to convey good things to him. Whenever the envied person comes to know this, his heart becomes content and he loves the envier. This ultimately leads to the removal of envy in two ways:

The first: When the envied person loves the envier, he does what the envier loves, so the envier then becomes a lover of the envied person, and envy is removed at that point.

The second: When the envier performs the opposite of what envy requires by way of deliberate effort, that eventually becomes a natural disposition in him, and envy is removed from him.

* * *

The seventh issue: Know that the aversion present in the heart of the envier toward the envied person is a matter not within his capacity, so how can he be punished for it? What is within his capacity is two things:

One: that he be content with that aversion (i.e., that he not act on it, or accept it as settled).

The second: showing the effects of that aversion, through disparagement of him, the aim of removing that blessing from him, and drawing the means of love toward him. This is what falls under the obligation. Let us now return to the exegesis.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back to disbelief after you have believed﴾, the meaning is that they were wanting the believers to turn back from faith after it had become clear to them that faith is correct and true. One who knows that another is upon the truth cannot wish to turn him away from it except by a doubt he casts to him, because one who is rightly guided does not deviate from the truth except by a doubt. Doubts are of two kinds:

One: that which relates to this world, which is to say to them: "You know what has befallen you of expulsion from your homes, the straitening of your affairs, and the continuing fear upon you. So abandon the faith that has brought you to these things."

The second: in matters of religion, by casting doubts about the miracles or distorting what is in the Torah.

* * *

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿out of envy from their own selves﴾, there are issues here:

The first issue: He, exalted is He, has made clear that their love for their turning back from faith was only for the sake of envy. Al-Jubba'i said: By His saying ﴿disbelievers out of envy from their own selves﴾ He meant that they were not given this by Him, and that their disbelief is their own action, not something Allah created in them. The answer is that His saying ﴿from their own selves﴾ has two possible meanings:

One: that it relates to "wish," meaning that they loved that after it had become clear to them that you are upon the truth. How, then, could their wishing be from seeking the truth?

Two: that it relates to "envy," meaning great envy arising from their own selves.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾, this indicates that the Jews, after they wished to turn the believers away from faith and resorted to casting doubts as we have explained, it is not permissible that He commands them to pardon and overlook in a way that implies approval of what they did, because that would be disbelief. Therefore it must be interpreted in one of two ways:

The first: that the intended meaning is to abandon retaliation and turn away from responding, because that is closer to calming the uprising at that time. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, commanded the Messenger to pardon and overlook the Jews, and likewise commanded him to pardon and overlook the idolaters of the Arabs, by His saying: ﴿Say to those who believe: forgive those who do not expect the Days of Allah﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14], and His saying: ﴿and forsake them with a graceful forsaking﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10]. For this reason He did not command this permanently but limited it by an endpoint, saying: ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾. Commentators have mentioned several interpretations of this:

One of them: that it is the requital on the Day of Resurrection, related from al-Hasan [al-Basri].

The second: that it is the strength of the Messenger and the increase of his community.

The third, which is the view of most of the Companions and the Successors: that it is the command to fight, because at that point one of two things becomes necessary: either Islam, or submission to paying the jizya (poll tax) and bearing humiliation and lowliness. For this reason the scholars said that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah nor in the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. It is related from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not commanded to fight until Jibril, peace be upon him, came down with the words: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39], and he girded him with a sword. The first fighting engaged in by the companions of Abdullah ibn Jahsh at Batn Nakhl was before it, and after it the expedition of Badr.

Here there are two questions:

The first question: How can it be abrogated when it is limited by an endpoint, like His saying: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]? And if the arrival of the night is not an abrogator, then likewise here. The answer: when the endpoint to which the command is tied is known only by revelation, the revealed text does not cease to be abrogating merely because it is revealed with a limit. It takes the place of His saying ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾ until He abrogates it for you.

The second question: How could they pardon and overlook when the disbelievers held power and strength, and forgiving is only possible from a position of power? The answer: a man among the Muslims would be harmed, and in that state, before the enemies had gathered, he was able to repel his enemy from himself and seek help from his companions. So Allah, exalted is He, at that point commanded pardon and overlooking, so that they would not provoke evil and fighting.

The second opinion regarding the interpretation: His saying ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾ is a call that is good, and what is required in it of advice, compassion and firmness is employed. According to this interpretation, it is not permissible for it to be abrogated; it is permissible to abrogate it only according to the first interpretation.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾, it is a warning to them with the threat of punishment, whether it is taken as a command to fight or to something else.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 109–110 (part 1 of 3)**

God's words: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and overlook, until God brings His command. Indeed, God is over all things competent.﴾

Know that this is the third type of the scheming (*kayd*) of the Jews against the Muslims. The reason is that it was narrated that Finhas ibn Azura, Zayd ibn Qays, and a group of Jews said to Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman and Ammar ibn Yasir after the Battle of Uhud: "Did you not see what befell you? Had you been upon the truth, you would not have been defeated. So return to our religion, for it is better and more excellent for you, and we are more rightly guided than you on the path." Ammar said: "How would breaking the covenant be among you?" They said: "It is grave." He said: "Then I have covenanted that I will not disbelieve in Muhammad as long as I live." The Jews said: "As for this one, he has apostatized." Hudhayfa said: "As for me, I am content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, with the Qur'an as leader, with the Ka'bah as qibla, and with the believers as brothers." Then they both came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: "You have done well and prospered." Then this verse was revealed. Know that we will first speak about envy (*hasad*, the wish for another's blessing to be removed), and then return to the tafsir.

**The first issue: on the censure of envy, which is indicated by many reports.**

The first: the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Envy devours good deeds just as fire devours firewood."

The second: Anas said: "We were one day sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Now there will appear to you from this pass a man of the people of Paradise.' A man of the Ansar appeared, his beard dripping with water from his ablution, having hung his two sandals on his left side. He greeted (the Prophet). On the next day he (ﷺ) said the same, and that man appeared. On the third day he said the same, and that man appeared. When the Prophet (peace be upon him) rose, Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As followed him and said: 'I have been troubled by my father, and I swore I would not enter upon him for three days. If you see fit that I may stay at your house, you may do so.' He said: 'Yes.' So he spent three nights with him, and he did not see him rise at night for anything, except that when he turned over on his bed he remembered God, and he did not rise until he rose for the Fajr prayer. But I never heard him say anything except good. When the three days passed, and I was almost belittling his deed, I said: 'O servant of God, there was no anger or estrangement between me and my father, but I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say such-and-such, so I wanted to know your deed. I have not seen you do a great deal of action; what then has brought you to that station?' He said: 'It is nothing but what you have seen.' When I turned to leave, he called me back and said: 'It is nothing but what you have seen, except that I do not find in myself any defect or envy toward any Muslim for a good thing God has given him.' Abdullah said: 'It is this which has brought you to it, and it is the very thing that cannot be borne.'"

The third: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The disease of the nations before you has crept upon you: envy and hatred. Hatred is the shaver, I do not mean the shaver of hair, but the shaver of religion."

The fourth: He said: "There will befall my Ummah the disease of the nations." They said: "What is the disease of the nations?" He said: "Arrogance, insolence, excessive pursuit of worldly increase, rivalry in the world, estrangement, and mutual envy, until there is oppression and then bloodshed."

The fifth: When Musa (peace be upon him) went to his Lord, he saw in the shade of the Throne a man who was envied for his station. He said: "Surely this man is honored by his Lord." So he asked his Lord to inform him of his name, but He did not inform him of his name. He said: "I will tell you about his deeds in three: he did not envy people for what God had given them of His bounty, he did not disobey his parents, and he did not walk about spreading gossip."

The sixth: He (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, the blessings of God have enemies." It was said: "And who are they?" He said: "Those who envy people for what God has given them of His bounty."

The seventh: He (peace be upon him) said: "Six will enter the Fire before the Reckoning: rulers through tyranny, Arabs through tribalism, landowners through arrogance, merchants through treachery, villagers through ignorance, and scholars through envy."

As for the reports from the companions and successors:

The first: It is related that Awf ibn Abdullah entered upon al-Fadl ibn al-Muhallab, who was at that time governor of Wasit, and said: "I want to advise you with something: beware of pride, for it was the first sin with which Iblis disobeyed God." Then he recited: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused and was arrogant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 34]. "And beware of greed, for it expelled Adam from the Garden. God settled him in a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth, but he ate from it, so God expelled him." Then he recited: ﴿Go down from it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123]. "And beware of envy, for it caused the son of Adam to kill his brother when he envied him." Then he recited: ﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 27].

The second: Ibn al-Zubayr said: "I have never envied anyone over a matter of this world, for if he is among the people of Paradise, how could I envy him over the world, which is insignificant in Paradise? And if he is among the people of the Fire, how could I envy him over a matter of the world when he is going to the Fire?"

The third: A man said to al-Hasan: "Does the believer envy?" He said: "What has made you forget the sons of Ya'qub? However, it does not harm you so long as you do not prepare a hand or tongue for it."

The fourth: Mu'awiyah said: "All people are more capable of pleasing than the envious, for nothing satisfies him except the removal of the blessing."

The fifth: It was said: "The envious gains from gatherings nothing but blame and humiliation, from the angels nothing but curse and hatred, from creation nothing but distress and grief, at the time of terror nothing but severity and dread, and at the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment) nothing but disgrace and punishment."

* * *

**The second issue: on the reality of envy.** If God bestows a blessing upon your brother, and you wish for its removal, this is envy (*hasad*). If you desire a similar one for yourself, this is *ghibta* (wishing to attain the same blessing without wishing its removal from the other) and *munafasah* (rivalry). The first is forbidden in every case, except a blessing obtained by a wicked or disbelieving person who uses it for evil and corruption; in that case your love for its removal does no harm, since you do not love its removal as a blessing, but as something through which evil, corruption, and harm are facilitated.

The verses that show that envy is what we have mentioned are:

The first: this verse, namely His words: ﴿They wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed, out of envy from themselves﴾. So He informed that their wish for the removal of the blessing of faith is envy.

The second: His words: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be equal﴾ [al-Nisa': 89].

The third: His words: ﴿If good touches you, it distresses them; and if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 120]. This rejoicing is malicious glee, and envy and malicious glee are inseparable.

The fourth: God mentioned the envy of the brothers of Yusuf and expressed what was in their hearts by His words: ﴿They said, "Yusuf and his brother are more beloved to our father than we, though we are a group. Indeed, our father is in clear error." ... "Kill Yusuf or cast him into some land, and the face of your father will be clear for you"﴾ [Yusuf: 8–9]. Thus He clarified that their envy of him was an expression of their dislike of that blessing reaching him.

The fifth: His words: ﴿And they find in their breasts no need for what they have been given﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], meaning their breasts are not constricted by it, and they do not grieve. Thus God praised them for not envying.

The sixth: He said, in the context of denunciation: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what God has given them of His bounty?﴾ [al-Nisa': 54].

The seventh: God said: ﴿The people were one nation, so God sent the prophets﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], up to His words: ﴿except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213]. It was said in the tafsir that the "rebellion" here is envy.

The eighth: His words: ﴿They did not divide except after knowledge had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 14]. God sent down knowledge to unite them upon His obedience, but they envied one another and differed, since each one wanted to be alone in leadership and in acceptance of his word.

The ninth: Ibn Abbas said: "Before the mission of the Prophet (peace be upon him), the Jews, when they fought a people, would say: 'We ask you by the Prophet whom You promised to send, and by the Book You will send down, that You help us.' So they were helped. But when the Prophet (peace be upon him) came from the descendants of Isma'il, they recognized him and disbelieved in him after knowing him." God said: ﴿And previously they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89], up to His words: ﴿that they disbelieve in what God has sent down, out of rebellion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90], meaning out of envy. "And Safiyyah bint Huyayy said to the Prophet (peace be upon him): 'My father and my uncle came from your presence. My father said to my uncle: "What do you say about him?" He said: "I say he is the Prophet whom Musa (peace be upon him) foretold." He said: "What do you think?" He said: "I think we should oppose him as long as we live."'" This is the ruling on envy.

As for rivalry (*munafasah*), it is not forbidden. It is derived from *nafasah* (preciousness), and what indicates that it is not forbidden are several points:

The first: His words: ﴿And for this let those who compete compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 26].

The second: His words: ﴿Race toward forgiveness from your Lord﴾. Racing occurs only out of fear of missing out. It is like two servants competing to serve their master, each fearing that the other will precede him, so that one gains a rank with his master that the other does not attain.

The third: The saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "There is no envy except in two: a man whom God has given wealth and who spends it in the way of God, and a man whom God has given knowledge, who acts upon it and teaches it to people."

This hadith indicates that the word *hasad* may be applied to rivalry. Then we say: rivalry may be obligatory, recommended, or permissible. The obligatory is like when that blessing is an obligatory religious blessing, such as faith, prayer, and zakat. In that case he must have a similar one, for if he does not love to have it, he is content with disobedience, and that is forbidden. As for when that blessing is among the recommended virtues, such as spending in the way of God and striving to teach people, rivalry in it is recommended. And if that blessing is among the permissible things, rivalry in it is permissible. In sum, what is blameworthy is to love the removal of the blessing from another. As for loving that it be attained for oneself and that one's deficiency be removed, this is not blameworthy. But there is a subtlety here: removing one's deficiency relative to another has two paths:

The first: that he obtains what the other has obtained.

The second: that the other loses what he has not obtained.

When despair arises regarding one of the two paths, the heart nearly cannot be free of longing for the other path. Here, if he finds his heart such that if he were able to remove that virtue from that person, he would remove it, then he is the one with blameworthy envy. But if he finds his heart such that piety restrains him from removing that blessing from another, then it is hoped from God, exalted is He, that He will pardon him for that. Perhaps this is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Three things a believer cannot be free of: envy, suspicion, and omens. But there is a way out of them: if you envy, do not act upon it." That is, if you find something in your heart, do not act upon it. This is the discourse on the reality of envy, and all of it is from the words of Shaykh al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him.

* * *

**The third issue: on the degrees of envy.** Al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, said there are four:

The first: that he loves the removal of that blessing, even if it does not come to him. This is the utmost degree of envy.

The second: that he loves the removal of that blessing from the other and its transfer to himself. This is like his desire for a beautiful house, a beautiful woman, or an effective authority that another has attained, and he loves that it be his. What is sought in essence is its attainment for himself; as for its removal from another, that is sought incidentally.

The third: that he does not desire the thing itself, but desires a similar one for himself. If he is unable to obtain a similar one, he loves its removal so that the disparity between them does not appear.

The fourth [condition]: that one wishes for oneself something similar to it. If one does not obtain it, one does not love its disappearance. This last is what is pardoned if it concerns worldly matters, and what is recommended if it concerns religion. The third of these is blameworthy in some cases and not blameworthy in others, and the second is lighter than the third, while the first is purely blameworthy. God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not wish for that by which God has favoured some of you over others﴾ [al-Nisa': 32]. So wishing for something similar to it is not blameworthy, but wishing for that very thing is blameworthy.

* * *

The fourth issue: Shaykh al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, mentioned seven causes of ḥasad (envy):

The first cause: enmity and hatred. When a person harms another, the heart hates him and becomes angry with him. That anger generates resentment, and resentment demands revenge and retaliation. If the one who hates is unable to take revenge himself, he wishes that time would take revenge on him for him. So whenever a calamity or affliction befalls his enemy, he rejoices, and whenever a blessing befalls him, it grieves him, because that is contrary to what he wants. Envy is thus a necessary consequence of hatred and enmity and never separates from them. The most that can be done in this regard is not to display that enmity from oneself and to dislike that state within oneself. But for a person to hate another and yet for his joy and his sorrow to be equal to him is impossible. This type of envy is what God described the unbelievers as having, when He said: ﴿And when they meet you, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage. Say, "Die in your rage. Indeed, God is Knowing of what is in the breasts." If good touches you, it distresses them; and if an affliction strikes you, they rejoice at it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119–120]. Likewise He said: ﴿They wish you would suffer. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]. Know that envy may lead to dispute and fighting.

Page 217

The second cause: the desire for superiority. When one of one's peers attains a high rank and rises above him, he cannot bear that, so he wishes that rank to be taken away from him. His aim is not to be arrogant, but to ward off his own humiliation, for he may accept being equal to him, but he does not accept being elevated above him.

The third cause: that it is in one's nature to make others serve him. He therefore wishes the blessing to be removed from that other person so that he can be able to achieve that aim. From this category was the envy of most of the unbelievers toward the Messenger, peace be upon him, when they said: "How can a young orphan take precedence over us, and how can we lower our heads before him?" They said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. And God the Exalted, describing the words of the Quraysh, said: ﴿Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour from among us?﴾ [al-An'am: 53], expressing contempt for them and disdain of them.

The fourth cause: astonishment, as God reported of the earlier nations, when they said: ﴿You are only a human being like us﴾ [Ya Sin: 15]; and they said: ﴿Shall we believe two humans like us, while their people are our worshippers?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 47]; and they said in astonishment: ﴿Has God sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra': 94]; and they said: ﴿Why have angels not been sent down to us?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21]; and He said: ﴿Are you astonished that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 63].

The fifth cause: fear of losing one's objectives. This applies specifically to those competing for one single objective, for each of them envies the other for every blessing that would help him to be alone in achieving his aim. From this category is the envy of co-wives in competing for the aims of marriage, and the envy of brothers in competing to gain a position in the hearts of their parents, in order to reach the aims of wealth and honour. Likewise is the envy of preachers competing over the people of one town, since the aim of each of them is to gain wealth and acceptance among them.

The sixth cause: love of leadership and the pursuit of status for its own sake, without using it as a means to another aim. This is like the man who wishes to be unrivalled in one of the arts. If he hears of a rival to him at the farthest end of the world, that displeases him, and he wishes for that person's death and for the removal of the blessing by which he shares the same standing with him, whether it be courage, knowledge, asceticism, or wealth, and he rejoices at being unique.

The seventh cause: stinginess of the soul with good toward God's servants. You will find someone who is not occupied with leadership, arrogance, or the pursuit of wealth, yet when he is told of the good condition of one of God's servants, it pains him; and when he is told of the disorder of people's affairs, their adversity, and the embitterment of their lives, he rejoices. He always loves others' misfortune and is stingy with God's blessing toward His servants, as though they were taking it from his own possession and treasury. It is said: "The miser is one who is stingy with someone else's wealth." This person is stingy with God's blessing toward His servants, between whom and himself there is neither enmity nor connection. This has no apparent cause except the corruption of the soul and the baseness of its natural disposition. For all other kinds of envy are hoped to be removed by removing their cause, but this is a corruption of the innate character, not from an incidental cause, so its removal is difficult. These, then, are the causes of envy. Some of these causes, or most of them, or all of them, may be combined in one person, so that envy grows greatly within him and becomes so strong that its bearer can no longer conceal it or behave courteously, but tears away the veil of courtesy and reveals his enmity openly. Most cases of envy combine a number of these causes, and rarely is one of them free of all the others.

* * *

The fifth issue: concerning the cause of the abundance or scarcity of envy, and its strength or weakness.

Know that envy occurs most often among people in whom the causes we have mentioned are abundant, for an individual may envy because he refuses the speech of the arrogant person, or because he is arrogant himself, or because he is an enemy for some other of these reasons. And these causes are most common among a group of people bound together by ties, by which they gather in assemblies of discourse and converge on the same objectives. Rivalry is a source of discord, and discord leads to envy. Where there is no association, there is no envying. Since no tie exists between two persons in two different cities, naturally there is no envy between them. That is why you see a scholar envying a scholar but not a worshipper, and a worshipper envying a worshipper but not a scholar, and a merchant envying a merchant, indeed a cobbler envying a cobbler, but not a cloth-seller. A man envies his brother and his paternal cousin more than he envies strangers, and a woman envies her co-wife and her husband's concubine more than she envies her mother-in-law and her husband's daughter. This is because the aim of the cloth-seller is not the aim of the cobbler, so they do not compete for the same objectives. Moreover, the competition of a cloth-seller with the neighbouring cloth-seller is greater than the competition with one far away at the other end of the market. In sum, the root of envy is enmity, and the root of enmity is competition for one objective. A single objective does not unite those who are far apart; rather, it unites only those who are similar. Therefore envy is abundant among them. Yes, whoever is intensely eager for broad status and fame throughout the world will envy everyone in the world who shares with him the quality in which he takes pride.

I say: the true cause of this is that perfection is loved in itself, and the opposite of what is loved is hated. Among the kinds of perfection is being unique in perfection, so inevitably a partner in perfection is hated, because he contests the uniqueness which is among the greatest gateways to perfection. However, since this kind of perfection cannot be attained except by God the Glorified, and despair of it has set in, envy has become restricted to worldly matters. This is because the world cannot accommodate those who compete for it, whereas the Hereafter has no constriction. The example of the Hereafter is the blessing of knowledge. Therefore whoever loves to know God the Exalted, His attributes, and His angels will not envy others once he knows, for knowledge does not constrict those who possess it. Rather, one single known object may be known by a thousand thousand people, and each rejoices in knowing it and takes pleasure in it, and no one's pleasure diminishes because of another. Indeed, with the multiplication of those who know, the intimacy increases. Therefore there is no envy among the scholars of religion, for their aim is knowledge of God, which is a vast ocean with no constriction, and their goal is nearness to God, which has no constriction. Yes, if scholars seek knowledge for the sake of wealth and status, they envy one another, because wealth consists of tangible items: when they fall into one person's hand, they leave another's hand empty. The meaning of status is filling hearts, and whenever one person's heart is filled with the veneration of one scholar, it turns away from venerating another. But when a heart is filled with joy at knowing God, that does not prevent the heart of another from being filled with it too and rejoicing in it. Therefore God the Exalted described them as free of envy when He said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; [they will be] brothers on couches, facing one another﴾ [al-Hijr: 47].

* * *

The sixth issue: concerning the remedy that removes envy. It consists of two things: knowledge and action.

As for knowledge, it has two levels: general and detailed. The general level is that one knows that whatever comes into existence has occurred as a necessary consequence of God's decree and destiny, for a possible thing does not stop until it reaches the Necessary Being. Once this is the case, there is no benefit in recoiling from it. When contentment with the decree is achieved, envy disappears.

The detailed level is that you know that envy is harmful to you in religion and in worldly life, and that it does not harm the envied person in religion or in worldly life, but rather he benefits from it in religion and in worldly life.

As for it being harmful to you in religion, that is in several respects:

The first: by envying, you have disliked God's judgment and disputed His allotment, which He apportioned to His servants, and His justice, which He established in His creation through His hidden wisdom. This is an offence against the pupil of monotheism and a speck in the eye of faith.

The second: if you deceive one of the believers, you have departed from the friends of God in their love of good for God's servants, and you have shared with Iblis and all the unbelievers in their love of afflictions for the believers.

The third: the great punishment that is ordained for it in the Hereafter.

As for it being harmful to you in this world, it is that because of envy you will never cease to be in grief and sorrow, while God does not leave your enemies without various blessings. So you will continue to be tormented by every blessing you see them receiving and pained by every calamity that passes them by. Thus you will remain forever sad and distressed. You have obtained for yourself what you wanted for your enemies, and what your enemies wanted for you. You wanted trial for your enemy, so you strove to bring trial upon yourself.

Furthermore, if that grief takes control of you, it sickens your body, removes your health, leads you into obsessive thoughts, and spoils for you the pleasure of food and drink.

As for the fact that the envied person suffers no harm in his religion or his worldly life, that is clear, for the blessing does not leave him because of your envy. Rather, whatever ascent and blessing God has decreed for him must endure until a term that God has set, for everything with Him is by measure, and for every term there is a Book. As long as the blessing is not removed through envy, the envied person suffers no harm in this world, and no sin is upon him in the Hereafter.

Perhaps you will say: "I wish the blessing were mine, and that it would be removed from the envied person through my envy." But this is utmost ignorance, for it is a trial that you would first desire for yourself, since you too are not free of an enemy who envies you. If blessings were removed through envy, no blessing from God would remain upon you, neither in religion nor in worldly life. And if you desire that blessings be removed from creatures through your envy, but not removed from you through the envy of others, that too is ignorance, for every one of the foolish envious people desires to be the exclusive possessor of this quality, and you are no more entitled to it than anyone else. So God's blessing upon you, in that He has not removed the blessing from you through envy, is among the things that must be thanked for, yet in your ignorance you dislike it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 109–110 (part 3 of 3):

As for the envied person benefiting from envy in religion and in this world, that is clear. His benefit in religion is that he is wronged by you, especially when you bring envy out into speech and action, through backbiting, disparaging him, exposing his concealed faults, and mentioning his shortcomings. These are gifts that Allah bestows on him, meaning that you give him your good deeds. Whenever you speak ill of him, your good deeds are transferred to his record and your sins increase. It is as if you desired the removal of Allah's blessings from him and onto you, so Allah's blessings are removed from you and given to him, and you continue at every moment and time to grow in wretchedness.

As for his benefit in this world, it is in several respects.

The first: The most important aim of people is to grieve their enemies and see them distressed and tormented, and there is no torment greater than what you are in, the pain of envy. Indeed, the intelligent person does not wish for the death of his enemy but wishes for him a long life, so that he may remain in the torment of envy, looking at every moment and time at Allah's blessings upon him, so that his heart is torn apart by that. For this reason it was said:

"May your enemies not die, but be made to live forever,
until they see from you what burns them.
May you never cease to be envied for a blessing,
for only the perfect one is envied."

The second: People know that the envied person must have a blessing, so they infer from the envy of the envier that he has been singled out by Allah with various kinds of virtues and excellences. The greatest virtues are those that cannot be repelled, and they are what produce envy. Thus envy becomes one of the strongest indications that the envied person is characterized by various kinds of virtues and excellences.

The third: The envier becomes blameworthy among creation and cursed in the sight of the Creator, and this is among the greatest aims of the envied person.

The fourth: It is a cause of increasing the joy of Iblis (Satan). This is because the envier, having lacked the virtues that the envied person has been singled out with, if he were content with that, would deserve a great reward. Iblis feared that he would be content with it and thereby deserve that reward. When he was not content with it but showed envy, he lost that reward and deserved punishment. This becomes a cause of Iblis's joy and the anger of Allah, exalted is He.

The fifth: You may envy a man of knowledge and love that he err in the religion of Allah, that you expose his error so that he is disgraced, and that his tongue be silenced so that he cannot speak, or that he fall ill so that he can neither teach nor learn. What sin could be greater than this, and what rank could be lower than this?

It has become clear from these aspects, O envier, that you are like one who throws a stone at his enemy to strike his vital spot, but it does not hit him. Rather, it returns to his right eye and plucks it out, so his anger increases and he returns and throws it a second time, harder than the first. The stone returns to his other eye and blinds it, so his rage increases and he returns a third time, and it comes back upon his head and splits it open, while his enemy remains unharmed in every state, and the ruin returns to him always. [p. 220]

And his enemies around him rejoice at him and laugh at him. Indeed, the state of the envier is worse than this, because the returning stone only destroyed the eye, and if it had remained, it would have been lost through death. As for his envy, it drives him to the anger of Allah and to the Fire. So it is better for him that his eye be lost in this world than that he keep an eye and enter the Fire with it. Observe how Allah has taken vengeance on the envier who wishes the blessing removed from the envied person: He did not remove it from him, but then removed the blessing from the envier, confirming the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And the evil scheming encompasses none but its own people.﴾ [Fatir: 43]

These are the scientific remedies. Whenever a person reflects on them with a clear mind and a present heart, the fire of envy is extinguished from his heart. As for the beneficial action, it is that he performs deeds opposed to what envy demands. If envy moves him to disparage the envied person, he compels his tongue to praise him. If it moves him to be arrogant toward him, he compels himself to humility toward him. If it moves him to cut off the means of good from him, he compels himself to strive to convey good things to him. Whenever the envied person comes to know this, his heart becomes content and he loves the envier. This ultimately leads to the removal of envy in two ways:

The first: When the envied person loves the envier, he does what the envier loves, so the envier then becomes a lover of the envied person, and envy is removed at that point.

The second: When the envier performs the opposite of what envy requires by way of deliberate effort, that eventually becomes a natural disposition in him, and envy is removed from him.

* * *

The seventh issue: Know that the aversion present in the heart of the envier toward the envied person is a matter not within his capacity, so how can he be punished for it? What is within his capacity is two things:

One: that he be content with that aversion (i.e., that he not act on it, or accept it as settled).

The second: showing the effects of that aversion, through disparagement of him, the aim of removing that blessing from him, and drawing the means of love toward him. This is what falls under the obligation. Let us now return to the exegesis.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back to disbelief after you have believed﴾, the meaning is that they were wanting the believers to turn back from faith after it had become clear to them that faith is correct and true. One who knows that another is upon the truth cannot wish to turn him away from it except by a doubt he casts to him, because one who is rightly guided does not deviate from the truth except by a doubt. Doubts are of two kinds:

One: that which relates to this world, which is to say to them: "You know what has befallen you of expulsion from your homes, the straitening of your affairs, and the continuing fear upon you. So abandon the faith that has brought you to these things."

The second: in matters of religion, by casting doubts about the miracles or distorting what is in the Torah.

* * *

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿out of envy from their own selves﴾, there are issues here:

The first issue: He, exalted is He, has made clear that their love for their turning back from faith was only for the sake of envy. Al-Jubba'i said: By His saying ﴿disbelievers out of envy from their own selves﴾ He meant that they were not given this by Him, and that their disbelief is their own action, not something Allah created in them. The answer is that His saying ﴿from their own selves﴾ has two possible meanings:

One: that it relates to "wish," meaning that they loved that after it had become clear to them that you are upon the truth. How, then, could their wishing be from seeking the truth?

Two: that it relates to "envy," meaning great envy arising from their own selves.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾, this indicates that the Jews, after they wished to turn the believers away from faith and resorted to casting doubts as we have explained, it is not permissible that He commands them to pardon and overlook in a way that implies approval of what they did, because that would be disbelief. Therefore it must be interpreted in one of two ways:

The first: that the intended meaning is to abandon retaliation and turn away from responding, because that is closer to calming the uprising at that time. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, commanded the Messenger to pardon and overlook the Jews, and likewise commanded him to pardon and overlook the idolaters of the Arabs, by His saying: ﴿Say to those who believe: forgive those who do not expect the Days of Allah﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14], and His saying: ﴿and forsake them with a graceful forsaking﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10]. For this reason He did not command this permanently but limited it by an endpoint, saying: ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾. Commentators have mentioned several interpretations of this:

One of them: that it is the requital on the Day of Resurrection, related from al-Hasan [al-Basri].

The second: that it is the strength of the Messenger and the increase of his community.

The third, which is the view of most of the Companions and the Successors: that it is the command to fight, because at that point one of two things becomes necessary: either Islam, or submission to paying the jizya (poll tax) and bearing humiliation and lowliness. For this reason the scholars said that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah nor in the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. It is related from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not commanded to fight until Jibril, peace be upon him, came down with the words: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39], and he girded him with a sword. The first fighting engaged in by the companions of Abdullah ibn Jahsh at Batn Nakhl was before it, and after it the expedition of Badr.

Here there are two questions:

The first question: How can it be abrogated when it is limited by an endpoint, like His saying: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]? And if the arrival of the night is not an abrogator, then likewise here. The answer: when the endpoint to which the command is tied is known only by revelation, the revealed text does not cease to be abrogating merely because it is revealed with a limit. It takes the place of His saying ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾ until He abrogates it for you.

The second question: How could they pardon and overlook when the disbelievers held power and strength, and forgiving is only possible from a position of power? The answer: a man among the Muslims would be harmed, and in that state, before the enemies had gathered, he was able to repel his enemy from himself and seek help from his companions. So Allah, exalted is He, at that point commanded pardon and overlooking, so that they would not provoke evil and fighting.

The second opinion regarding the interpretation: His saying ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾ is a call that is good, and what is required in it of advice, compassion and firmness is employed. According to this interpretation, it is not permissible for it to be abrogated; it is permissible to abrogate it only according to the first interpretation.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾, it is a warning to them with the threat of punishment, whether it is taken as a command to fight or to something else.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 111–112 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat. And whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, commanded pardon and forgiveness toward the Jews, then followed it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾, as an alert that just as He obligated them to pardon and forgiveness for the sake of others' welfare, so likewise He obligated them, for the sake of their own welfare, to perform the obligatory prayer and zakat, and by these two He alerted to the other obligations besides them. Then He said after it: ﴿And whatever good you send forth for yourselves﴾. The most apparent meaning is that it refers to voluntary acts of prayer and zakat. Allah, exalted is He, explained that they will find it, and the meaning is not that they will find the very same deeds, because those do not endure, and because finding the very same things is not something desired. So it remains that the meaning is finding its reward and recompense. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, meaning: nothing of the deeds, whether small or great, is hidden from Him. This is an encouragement, in that it indicates that He rewards the small as He rewards the great, and a warning against the opposite, which is evil. As for good (khayr), it is beneficial benefit and that which leads to it. Since what a person does of obedience leads by it to great benefits, it is right that it be described as such. In this sense He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do good that you may succeed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77].

﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians." That is their wishful thinking. Say, "Produce your proof, if you should be truthful."﴾ ﴿Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while being a doer of good, will have his reward with his Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾

Know that this is the fourth type of the Jews' confusion and casting of doubts into the hearts of the Muslims. Know that the Jews do not say of the Christians that they will enter Paradise, nor do the Christians say it of the Jews, so there must be a detail in the speech. It is as if He said:
[p. 4] The Jews said: "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews," and the Christians said: "None will enter Paradise except those who are Christians," and nothing other than this is valid in the speech, along with our knowledge that each of the two groups declares the other to be unbeliever. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And they say, "Be Jews or Christians"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135]. "Hud" is the plural of "ha'id," like "a'idh" and "'uudh," and "baazil" and "buzl." If it is said: how is it said "kana hudan," with the subject singular and the predicate plural? We say: the subject was taken according to the wording of "man," and the predicate according to its meaning, like the reading of al-Hasan: (illa man huwa salu al-jahim), and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: (illa man kana yahudiyyan aw nasraniyyan). As for His saying: ﴿That is their wishful thinking﴾, the meaning is that this is their wishes. Then, because of the intensity of their wishing for it, they regarded it as true in itself. If it is said: why did He say "that is their wishful thinking" when their saying "none will enter Paradise" is a single wish? We say: it refers to the wishes mentioned, and they are: their wish that no good from their Lord descend upon the believers, their wish that they return them as unbelievers, and their wish that no one other than them enter Paradise. That is, those false wishes are their wishes. His saying: ﴿Say, "Produce your proof"﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾, and ﴿That is their wishful thinking﴾ is a parenthetical interjection. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The wise one is he who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, and the incapable one is he who follows his desires and wishes upon Allah." And Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Do not rely on wishes, for they are the merchandise of the bankrupt."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Say, "Produce your proof"﴾, there are issues:
The first issue: "hat" is a sound in the position of "ha" meaning "bring here."
The second issue: the verse indicates that the claimant, whether he claims a negation or an affirmation, must have a proof and evidence, and this is among the most truthful indications of the invalidity of the view of blind conformity (taqlid). A poet said:
Whoever claims something without a witness, his claim must be nullified.

As for His saying: ﴿Yes (bala)﴾, there are several aspects:
The first: it is an affirmation of what they denied concerning others entering Paradise.
The second: since He negated that they had any proof, He affirmed that for whoever submits himself to Allah there is a proof.
The third: as if it were said to them: "You, in your present state, will not attain Paradise. Yes, if you change your way, submit yourselves to Allah, and do good, then you will have Paradise," so this is an encouragement to them toward Islam, and a clarification of the difference between their state and the state of one who enters Paradise, so that they may desist from what they are upon and turn to this way. As for the meaning of ﴿whoever submits himself to Allah﴾, it is the submission of the self to obedience to Allah. He specified the face (wajh) for mention for several reasons:
One: because it is the most noble of the organs, being the seat of the senses, thought and imagination; when the most noble humbles itself, others are more fitting.
Two: the face is sometimes used as a metonym for the self, as Allah said: ﴿Everything will perish except His face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Layl: 20].
Three: the greatest of acts of worship is prostration, which is accomplished only by the face, and therefore the face was specifically mentioned. For this reason Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said:
I have submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy rocks,
I have submitted my face to Him to whom the cloud submits, bearing sweet clear water.
Thus the person is giving his self to this matter by humbling it, and he mentioned the face and meant by it the self of the thing. That does not occur except through compliance, submission, and humbling of the self in His obedience and avoidance of His disobediences. The meaning of "for Allah" is: sincerely for Allah, not mixed with association (shirk), so that he does not worship another alongside Allah, nor hang his hope on another,
[p. 5] and in this is an indication that a person does not benefit from his deed unless he performs it as worship, in sincerity and seeking nearness.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿while he is a doer of good (muhsin)﴾: that is, it is necessary that his humbling before Allah be by a good deed, not by an evil deed, for the Hindus humble themselves before Allah but by evil deeds. The position of His saying ﴿while he is a doer of good﴾ is the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), like your saying: "So-and-so came while riding," meaning "So-and-so came riding." Then He clarified that whoever combines these two, for him is his reward with his Lord, meaning the great reward. Then, along with this blessing, no fear and no grief will reach him. As for fear, it occurs only regarding the future, and as for grief, it may occur regarding what has happened and the past just as it may occur regarding the future. So He alerted, by both matters, to the utmost of happiness, because a great blessing, when it lasts, multiplies, and is free of fear and grief, then one does not grieve over a matter that has escaped him, nor over a matter he attains, nor fear the cessation of what he is in or its change; so he has reached the ultimate. In this there is an encouragement toward this way and a warning against its opposite, which is the way of the unbelievers mentioned earlier.

Know that He, exalted is He, first used the singular and then the plural, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿And how many an angel in the heavens﴾ [al-Najm: 26], then He said: ﴿whose intercession﴾ [al-Najm: 26], and His saying: ﴿And among them is one who listens to you﴾ [al-An'am: 25], and in another place He said: ﴿They listen to you﴾ [Yunus: 42], and He said: ﴿And among them is one who listens to you until, when they leave from your presence﴾ [Muhammad: 16], and He did not say "he left."

Know that since we have interpreted His saying ﴿whoever submits himself to Allah﴾ as sincerity, we shall mention here the reality of sincerity, and this cannot be explained except in several issues:

The first issue: on the virtue of intention. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Actions are only by intentions," and he said: "Indeed Allah does not look at your forms nor at your deeds, but He looks at your hearts and your intentions." And in the Israelite narrations: a man passed by heaps of sand in a time of famine and said to himself: "If only this sand were food, I would distribute it among the people." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed to their prophet: "Tell him: Indeed Allah has accepted your charity, and thanked you for the goodness of your intention, and given you the reward of what would have been, had it been food, which you gave in charity."

The second issue: when a person knows, or thinks, or believes that in a certain act there is for him the bringing of benefit or the averting of harm, there arises in his heart an inclination and a seeking, and this is an attribute that requires the preponderance of the existence of that thing over its non-existence, and it is volition (irada). This volition is the intention, and what motivates him to that intention is that knowledge, belief, or opinion. Knowing this, we say: the motive for an act is either a single thing, or two things. In the second case, either each of them is independently motivating, or neither of them is independently motivating, or one of them is independently motivating without the other. So these are four divisions:
The first: that the motive is single, as when a beast attacks a person, and when he sees it he gets up from his place. This act has no motive except his belief that there is benefit in fleeing and harm in not fleeing. This intention is called pure (khalisah), and acting according to its requirement is called sincerity (ikhlas).
The second: that two independent motives converge on the act, as when a poor companion asks him for a need and he fulfills it, because he is a companion to him and because he is poor, each of the two attributes being such that if it stood alone it would independently motivate the fulfilling. The name of this is agreement of motives (muwafaqat al-ba'ith).
The third: that neither of them would be independent if alone, but the combination is independent. The name of this is participation (musharakah).
The fourth: that one of them is independent, and the other is supporting, such as when a person has a regular set of acts of obedience and it happens that a group of people is present at the time of performing it, so the act becomes lighter for him because of their presence. The name of this is assistance (mu'awanah).

[p. 6]

The third issue: on the interpretation of his saying, peace be upon him: "The intention of the believer is better than his deed." They mentioned several aspects regarding it:
One: that intention is secret and the deed is public, and the secret obedience is better than public obedience. This is nothing, because it would imply that the intention of prayer is better than the prayer itself.
Two: intention lasts until the end of the deed, and deeds do not last, and the lasting is better than the ceasing. This is nothing, because its meaning returns to the claim that a great deed is better than a small deed; and also the intention of the act of prayer may only occur in a few moments, while the acts endure.
Three: that intention by itself is better than deed by itself. This is weak, since a deed without intention has no good in it, and it is clearly preferable that the two share in the basic quality of goodness.
Four: that the intended meaning of "good" is not to establish superiority, but rather that the intention is a good among the goods that come through his deed. This is weak, because applying the hadith to this only conveys the clarifying of the obvious. Rather, the good way of interpreting it is to say: intention, so long as it is not free of all kinds of weakness, is not a firm intention; and when it is free of all aspects of weakness, it becomes necessary that the act follow from it if no obstacle exists. Since this is so, it is established that intention is never separated from the act, so it is claimed that this intention is better than that deed. Its explanation is from several aspects:
First: the aim of all deeds is the illumination of the heart with the knowledge of Allah, and its purification from everything other than Allah. Intention is a quality of the heart, and the act is not a quality of the heart, and the influence of a quality of the heart is stronger than the influence of a quality of the limbs upon the heart. Therefore, the intention of the believer is indeed better than his deed.
Second: there is no meaning to intention except the aim toward performing those deeds as obedience to the One worshipped and submission to Him; and the deeds are only brought forth so that remembrance is preserved through repetition. So the remembrance and the aim that is in the heart, in relation to the deed, is like the aim in relation to the means, and there is no doubt that the aim is nobler than the means.

Third: the heart is nobler than the body, so its act is nobler than the act of the body. Therefore intention (niyyah) is better than action.

The fourth issue: know that actions are of three kinds: acts of obedience, acts of disobedience, and permissible acts.

As for acts of disobedience, intention does not change them from what they are. So the ignorant person should not think that the Prophet's saying, ﷺ, "Actions are only by intentions" ("إنَّما الأعْمالُ بِالنِّيّاتِ"), implies that disobedience is turned into obedience by intention, like someone who feeds a poor man with another person's money, or builds a mosque with unlawful wealth.

Second: acts of obedience. These are connected to intentions in their basic validity and in their merit. As for their basic validity, it is that one intends by them the worship of God, Exalted. If one intends showing off (riya'), the act becomes disobedience. As for their merit, the good deed multiplies with the multiplication of intentions. An example is the one who sits in the mosque and makes many intentions in it:

The first: that he believes it is the House of God, and intends by it visiting his Master, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever sits in the mosque has visited God, and it is a right upon the one visited to honor his visitor."

The second: that he waits for prayer after prayer, so that during the waiting he is like one who is in prayer.

The third: lowering the hearing, the sight and the rest of the limbs from what is not fitting, for i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque) is restraint, and it has the meaning of fasting, and it is a kind of asceticism (tarahhub). For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "The monasticism (rahbaniyyah) of my community is sitting in the mosques."

The fourth: turning the heart and the inner self entirely to God, Exalted.

The fifth: removing from the heart everything other than God.

The sixth: intending to convey knowledge, or to enjoin good, or to forbid evil.

The seventh: intending to gain a brother in God, for that is the spoil of the people of religion.

The eighth: abandoning sins out of modesty before God. This is the way of multiplying intentions, and by analogy apply it to all other acts of obedience.

The third kind: all the permissible acts. There is none of them except that it admits an intention or intentions, by which it becomes one of the finest acts of drawing near to God. How great is the loss of the one who is heedless of them and does not direct them toward acts of drawing near.

In a report: "Whoever perfumes himself for God will come on the Day of Resurrection with a fragrance better than the scent of musk, and whoever perfumes himself for other than God will come on the Day of Resurrection with a smell more foul than a carrion."

If you say: explain to me how this intention is formed. Know that if the purpose of perfuming is enjoyment of the pleasures of this world, or displaying boastfulness with abundance of wealth, or showing off before people, or to make himself beloved to the hearts of women, then all of that makes perfuming a disobedience. But if the purpose is to establish the Sunnah, to repel offensive odours from the servants of God, and to honour the mosque, then it is itself obedience. When you know this, apply it by analogy to all permissible acts. The governing principle is that whatever you do for the call of truth is the true deed, and whatever you do for other than God, its lawful part is a reckoning and its unlawful part is punishment.

The fifth issue: know that when the ignorant person hears the rational and transmitted arguments that intention is necessary, he says to himself while teaching or trading: "I intend to teach for God, and to trade for God," thinking that this is intention. But far from it! That is a movement of the soul or a movement of the tongue, while intention is entirely apart from all of that. Intention is only the stirring of the soul and its inclination toward what appears to it as containing its aim, either immediately or in the future. When the inclination does not arise, a person cannot acquire it by will. It is like the words of one who is full: "I intend to desire food," or like the words of one who is idle: "I intend to fall in love." Indeed, there is no way to acquire the inclination toward a thing except by acquiring its causes, and these are nothing but the attainment of knowledge of the benefits in it. Then this knowledge does not necessitate this inclination except when the heart is free from all other preoccupations. So when the desire for intercourse overcomes, and one does not believe in the child any sound aim, neither immediate nor future, he cannot engage in intercourse with the intention of having a child. Indeed, he cannot do it except with the intention of satisfying desire, since intention is the response to the motive, and there is no motive except desire. So how can he intend a child? Thus it is established that intention is not an expression of speech by the tongue or by the heart, but rather it is an expression of the arising of this inclination, and that is a matter dependent on the unseen. It may be easy at some times and difficult at others.

The sixth issue: know that people's intentions in acts of obedience are of kinds. Among them are those whose action is a response to the motive of fear, for he guards against the Fire. Among them are those who act from the motive of hope, which is the desire for Paradise. The one who acts for the sake of Paradise is one who acts for his belly and his private parts, like the evil hireling, and his rank is the rank of the simple-minded. As for the worship of people of understanding, it does not go beyond the remembrance of God and reflection upon Him out of love for His majesty, and the rest of the deeds are reinforcements of it. These are the ones who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. The rewards of people are according to the measure of their intentions. Therefore the near ones (al-muqarrabun) became those who take delight in gazing upon His noble Face, and the relation of the nobility of delight in the bliss of Paradise to the nobility of delight in this station is like the relation of the bliss of Paradise to His noble Face.

[Page 7]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 111–112 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat. And whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, commanded pardon and forgiveness toward the Jews, then followed it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾, as an alert that just as He obligated them to pardon and forgiveness for the sake of others' welfare, so likewise He obligated them, for the sake of their own welfare, to perform the obligatory prayer and zakat, and by these two He alerted to the other obligations besides them. Then He said after it: ﴿And whatever good you send forth for yourselves﴾. The most apparent meaning is that it refers to voluntary acts of prayer and zakat. Allah, exalted is He, explained that they will find it, and the meaning is not that they will find the very same deeds, because those do not endure, and because finding the very same things is not something desired. So it remains that the meaning is finding its reward and recompense. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, meaning: nothing of the deeds, whether small or great, is hidden from Him. This is an encouragement, in that it indicates that He rewards the small as He rewards the great, and a warning against the opposite, which is evil. As for good (khayr), it is beneficial benefit and that which leads to it. Since what a person does of obedience leads by it to great benefits, it is right that it be described as such. In this sense He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do good that you may succeed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77].

﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians." That is their wishful thinking. Say, "Produce your proof, if you should be truthful."﴾ ﴿Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while being a doer of good, will have his reward with his Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾

Know that this is the fourth type of the Jews' confusion and casting of doubts into the hearts of the Muslims. Know that the Jews do not say of the Christians that they will enter Paradise, nor do the Christians say it of the Jews, so there must be a detail in the speech. It is as if He said:
[p. 4] The Jews said: "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews," and the Christians said: "None will enter Paradise except those who are Christians," and nothing other than this is valid in the speech, along with our knowledge that each of the two groups declares the other to be unbeliever. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And they say, "Be Jews or Christians"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135]. "Hud" is the plural of "ha'id," like "a'idh" and "'uudh," and "baazil" and "buzl." If it is said: how is it said "kana hudan," with the subject singular and the predicate plural? We say: the subject was taken according to the wording of "man," and the predicate according to its meaning, like the reading of al-Hasan: (illa man huwa salu al-jahim), and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: (illa man kana yahudiyyan aw nasraniyyan). As for His saying: ﴿That is their wishful thinking﴾, the meaning is that this is their wishes. Then, because of the intensity of their wishing for it, they regarded it as true in itself. If it is said: why did He say "that is their wishful thinking" when their saying "none will enter Paradise" is a single wish? We say: it refers to the wishes mentioned, and they are: their wish that no good from their Lord descend upon the believers, their wish that they return them as unbelievers, and their wish that no one other than them enter Paradise. That is, those false wishes are their wishes. His saying: ﴿Say, "Produce your proof"﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾, and ﴿That is their wishful thinking﴾ is a parenthetical interjection. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The wise one is he who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, and the incapable one is he who follows his desires and wishes upon Allah." And Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Do not rely on wishes, for they are the merchandise of the bankrupt."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Say, "Produce your proof"﴾, there are issues:
The first issue: "hat" is a sound in the position of "ha" meaning "bring here."
