The second issue: the verse indicates that the claimant, whether he claims a negation or an affirmation, must have a proof and evidence, and this is among the most truthful indications of the invalidity of the view of blind conformity (taqlid). A poet said:
Whoever claims something without a witness, his claim must be nullified.

As for His saying: ﴿Yes (bala)﴾, there are several aspects:
The first: it is an affirmation of what they denied concerning others entering Paradise.
The second: since He negated that they had any proof, He affirmed that for whoever submits himself to Allah there is a proof.
The third: as if it were said to them: "You, in your present state, will not attain Paradise. Yes, if you change your way, submit yourselves to Allah, and do good, then you will have Paradise," so this is an encouragement to them toward Islam, and a clarification of the difference between their state and the state of one who enters Paradise, so that they may desist from what they are upon and turn to this way. As for the meaning of ﴿whoever submits himself to Allah﴾, it is the submission of the self to obedience to Allah. He specified the face (wajh) for mention for several reasons:
One: because it is the most noble of the organs, being the seat of the senses, thought and imagination; when the most noble humbles itself, others are more fitting.
Two: the face is sometimes used as a metonym for the self, as Allah said: ﴿Everything will perish except His face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Layl: 20].
Three: the greatest of acts of worship is prostration, which is accomplished only by the face, and therefore the face was specifically mentioned. For this reason Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said:
I have submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy rocks,
I have submitted my face to Him to whom the cloud submits, bearing sweet clear water.
Thus the person is giving his self to this matter by humbling it, and he mentioned the face and meant by it the self of the thing. That does not occur except through compliance, submission, and humbling of the self in His obedience and avoidance of His disobediences. The meaning of "for Allah" is: sincerely for Allah, not mixed with association (shirk), so that he does not worship another alongside Allah, nor hang his hope on another,
[p. 5] and in this is an indication that a person does not benefit from his deed unless he performs it as worship, in sincerity and seeking nearness.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿while he is a doer of good (muhsin)﴾: that is, it is necessary that his humbling before Allah be by a good deed, not by an evil deed, for the Hindus humble themselves before Allah but by evil deeds. The position of His saying ﴿while he is a doer of good﴾ is the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), like your saying: "So-and-so came while riding," meaning "So-and-so came riding." Then He clarified that whoever combines these two, for him is his reward with his Lord, meaning the great reward. Then, along with this blessing, no fear and no grief will reach him. As for fear, it occurs only regarding the future, and as for grief, it may occur regarding what has happened and the past just as it may occur regarding the future. So He alerted, by both matters, to the utmost of happiness, because a great blessing, when it lasts, multiplies, and is free of fear and grief, then one does not grieve over a matter that has escaped him, nor over a matter he attains, nor fear the cessation of what he is in or its change; so he has reached the ultimate. In this there is an encouragement toward this way and a warning against its opposite, which is the way of the unbelievers mentioned earlier.

Know that He, exalted is He, first used the singular and then the plural, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿And how many an angel in the heavens﴾ [al-Najm: 26], then He said: ﴿whose intercession﴾ [al-Najm: 26], and His saying: ﴿And among them is one who listens to you﴾ [al-An'am: 25], and in another place He said: ﴿They listen to you﴾ [Yunus: 42], and He said: ﴿And among them is one who listens to you until, when they leave from your presence﴾ [Muhammad: 16], and He did not say "he left."

Know that since we have interpreted His saying ﴿whoever submits himself to Allah﴾ as sincerity, we shall mention here the reality of sincerity, and this cannot be explained except in several issues:

The first issue: on the virtue of intention. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Actions are only by intentions," and he said: "Indeed Allah does not look at your forms nor at your deeds, but He looks at your hearts and your intentions." And in the Israelite narrations: a man passed by heaps of sand in a time of famine and said to himself: "If only this sand were food, I would distribute it among the people." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed to their prophet: "Tell him: Indeed Allah has accepted your charity, and thanked you for the goodness of your intention, and given you the reward of what would have been, had it been food, which you gave in charity."

The second issue: when a person knows, or thinks, or believes that in a certain act there is for him the bringing of benefit or the averting of harm, there arises in his heart an inclination and a seeking, and this is an attribute that requires the preponderance of the existence of that thing over its non-existence, and it is volition (irada). This volition is the intention, and what motivates him to that intention is that knowledge, belief, or opinion. Knowing this, we say: the motive for an act is either a single thing, or two things. In the second case, either each of them is independently motivating, or neither of them is independently motivating, or one of them is independently motivating without the other. So these are four divisions:
The first: that the motive is single, as when a beast attacks a person, and when he sees it he gets up from his place. This act has no motive except his belief that there is benefit in fleeing and harm in not fleeing. This intention is called pure (khalisah), and acting according to its requirement is called sincerity (ikhlas).
The second: that two independent motives converge on the act, as when a poor companion asks him for a need and he fulfills it, because he is a companion to him and because he is poor, each of the two attributes being such that if it stood alone it would independently motivate the fulfilling. The name of this is agreement of motives (muwafaqat al-ba'ith).
The third: that neither of them would be independent if alone, but the combination is independent. The name of this is participation (musharakah).
The fourth: that one of them is independent, and the other is supporting, such as when a person has a regular set of acts of obedience and it happens that a group of people is present at the time of performing it, so the act becomes lighter for him because of their presence. The name of this is assistance (mu'awanah).

[p. 6]

The third issue: on the interpretation of his saying, peace be upon him: "The intention of the believer is better than his deed." They mentioned several aspects regarding it:
One: that intention is secret and the deed is public, and the secret obedience is better than public obedience. This is nothing, because it would imply that the intention of prayer is better than the prayer itself.
Two: intention lasts until the end of the deed, and deeds do not last, and the lasting is better than the ceasing. This is nothing, because its meaning returns to the claim that a great deed is better than a small deed; and also the intention of the act of prayer may only occur in a few moments, while the acts endure.
Three: that intention by itself is better than deed by itself. This is weak, since a deed without intention has no good in it, and it is clearly preferable that the two share in the basic quality of goodness.
Four: that the intended meaning of "good" is not to establish superiority, but rather that the intention is a good among the goods that come through his deed. This is weak, because applying the hadith to this only conveys the clarifying of the obvious. Rather, the good way of interpreting it is to say: intention, so long as it is not free of all kinds of weakness, is not a firm intention; and when it is free of all aspects of weakness, it becomes necessary that the act follow from it if no obstacle exists. Since this is so, it is established that intention is never separated from the act, so it is claimed that this intention is better than that deed. Its explanation is from several aspects:
First: the aim of all deeds is the illumination of the heart with the knowledge of Allah, and its purification from everything other than Allah. Intention is a quality of the heart, and the act is not a quality of the heart, and the influence of a quality of the heart is stronger than the influence of a quality of the limbs upon the heart. Therefore, the intention of the believer is indeed better than his deed.
Second: there is no meaning to intention except the aim toward performing those deeds as obedience to the One worshipped and submission to Him; and the deeds are only brought forth so that remembrance is preserved through repetition. So the remembrance and the aim that is in the heart, in relation to the deed, is like the aim in relation to the means, and there is no doubt that the aim is nobler than the means.

Third: the heart is nobler than the body, so its act is nobler than the act of the body. Therefore intention (niyyah) is better than action.

The fourth issue: know that actions are of three kinds: acts of obedience, acts of disobedience, and permissible acts.

As for acts of disobedience, intention does not change them from what they are. So the ignorant person should not think that the Prophet's saying, ﷺ, "Actions are only by intentions" ("إنَّما الأعْمالُ بِالنِّيّاتِ"), implies that disobedience is turned into obedience by intention, like someone who feeds a poor man with another person's money, or builds a mosque with unlawful wealth.

Second: acts of obedience. These are connected to intentions in their basic validity and in their merit. As for their basic validity, it is that one intends by them the worship of God, Exalted. If one intends showing off (riya'), the act becomes disobedience. As for their merit, the good deed multiplies with the multiplication of intentions. An example is the one who sits in the mosque and makes many intentions in it:

The first: that he believes it is the House of God, and intends by it visiting his Master, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever sits in the mosque has visited God, and it is a right upon the one visited to honor his visitor."

The second: that he waits for prayer after prayer, so that during the waiting he is like one who is in prayer.

The third: lowering the hearing, the sight and the rest of the limbs from what is not fitting, for i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque) is restraint, and it has the meaning of fasting, and it is a kind of asceticism (tarahhub). For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "The monasticism (rahbaniyyah) of my community is sitting in the mosques."

The fourth: turning the heart and the inner self entirely to God, Exalted.

The fifth: removing from the heart everything other than God.

The sixth: intending to convey knowledge, or to enjoin good, or to forbid evil.

The seventh: intending to gain a brother in God, for that is the spoil of the people of religion.

The eighth: abandoning sins out of modesty before God. This is the way of multiplying intentions, and by analogy apply it to all other acts of obedience.

The third kind: all the permissible acts. There is none of them except that it admits an intention or intentions, by which it becomes one of the finest acts of drawing near to God. How great is the loss of the one who is heedless of them and does not direct them toward acts of drawing near.

In a report: "Whoever perfumes himself for God will come on the Day of Resurrection with a fragrance better than the scent of musk, and whoever perfumes himself for other than God will come on the Day of Resurrection with a smell more foul than a carrion."

If you say: explain to me how this intention is formed. Know that if the purpose of perfuming is enjoyment of the pleasures of this world, or displaying boastfulness with abundance of wealth, or showing off before people, or to make himself beloved to the hearts of women, then all of that makes perfuming a disobedience. But if the purpose is to establish the Sunnah, to repel offensive odours from the servants of God, and to honour the mosque, then it is itself obedience. When you know this, apply it by analogy to all permissible acts. The governing principle is that whatever you do for the call of truth is the true deed, and whatever you do for other than God, its lawful part is a reckoning and its unlawful part is punishment.

The fifth issue: know that when the ignorant person hears the rational and transmitted arguments that intention is necessary, he says to himself while teaching or trading: "I intend to teach for God, and to trade for God," thinking that this is intention. But far from it! That is a movement of the soul or a movement of the tongue, while intention is entirely apart from all of that. Intention is only the stirring of the soul and its inclination toward what appears to it as containing its aim, either immediately or in the future. When the inclination does not arise, a person cannot acquire it by will. It is like the words of one who is full: "I intend to desire food," or like the words of one who is idle: "I intend to fall in love." Indeed, there is no way to acquire the inclination toward a thing except by acquiring its causes, and these are nothing but the attainment of knowledge of the benefits in it. Then this knowledge does not necessitate this inclination except when the heart is free from all other preoccupations. So when the desire for intercourse overcomes, and one does not believe in the child any sound aim, neither immediate nor future, he cannot engage in intercourse with the intention of having a child. Indeed, he cannot do it except with the intention of satisfying desire, since intention is the response to the motive, and there is no motive except desire. So how can he intend a child? Thus it is established that intention is not an expression of speech by the tongue or by the heart, but rather it is an expression of the arising of this inclination, and that is a matter dependent on the unseen. It may be easy at some times and difficult at others.

The sixth issue: know that people's intentions in acts of obedience are of kinds. Among them are those whose action is a response to the motive of fear, for he guards against the Fire. Among them are those who act from the motive of hope, which is the desire for Paradise. The one who acts for the sake of Paradise is one who acts for his belly and his private parts, like the evil hireling, and his rank is the rank of the simple-minded. As for the worship of people of understanding, it does not go beyond the remembrance of God and reflection upon Him out of love for His majesty, and the rest of the deeds are reinforcements of it. These are the ones who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. The rewards of people are according to the measure of their intentions. Therefore the near ones (al-muqarrabun) became those who take delight in gazing upon His noble Face, and the relation of the nobility of delight in the bliss of Paradise to the nobility of delight in this station is like the relation of the bliss of Paradise to His noble Face.

[Page 7]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 113:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Jews say: "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say: "The Jews are not upon anything," and they recite the Book. Thus say those who have no knowledge, the like of their saying. So Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, when He gathered them together in the first report, distinguished them in this verse, and clarified the saying of each group among them regarding the other, and how each sect denies the religion of the other. Here are some issues:

Issue one: His saying, ﴿The Christians are not upon anything﴾, meaning: upon anything that is valid and counts. This is a great exaggeration, and it is like their saying: "less than nothing." Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, you are not upon anything until you establish the Torah"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68]. If it is said: How did they say that, when both groups affirmed the Creator and His attributes, may He be glorified and exalted, and that is a statement with benefit? We say: The answer is from two aspects:

The first: that when they joined to that good statement a false statement that nullifies the reward of the first, it is as if they had not brought that truth at all.

The second: that this general statement be restricted to the matters in which they differed, which are those connected with the chapter of prophethoods.

Issue two: It is narrated that when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the rabbis of the Jews came to them and they debated until their voices rose. The Jews said: "You are not upon anything of the religion," and they disbelieved in Jesus, peace be upon him, and the Gospel. The Christians said the like of it to them, and they disbelieved in Moses, peace be upon him, and the Torah.

Issue three: They differed concerning who are those whom Allah, exalted is He, meant: are they those who existed from the time of the mission of Jesus, peace be upon him, or in the time of Muhammad, peace be upon him? The apparent truth is that there is no evidence in the apparent wording concerning this. Although it is more fitting that it be applied to all the Jews and all the Christians after the mission of Jesus, peace be upon him, and it is not necessary, because of what is related about the occasion of revelation, that a Jew addressed the Christians with that and Allah revealed this verse, that the verse not be meant to include anything else, when it is possible to take it according to its apparent meaning. And His saying: ﴿The Jews say: "The Christians are not upon anything"﴾ conveys generality, so what is the basis for taking it as restricted? It is known from the way of the Jews and the Christians that since they existed, this has been the saying of each group about the other.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they recite the Book﴾, the waw here is for the circumstantial state (hal), and "the Book" is generic. That is, they said that while their condition was that they were among the people of knowledge and the recitation of the books. Whoever carries the Torah or the Gospel or other books of Allah and believes in it has the right not to disbelieve in the rest, because each of the two Books confirms the other and testifies to its truth: the Torah confirms Jesus, peace be upon him, and the Gospel confirms Moses, peace be upon him.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus say those who have no knowledge﴾, it requires that whoever was previously mentioned must be knowledgeable for this distinction to be valid. So He, exalted is He, made clear that they, despite knowledge and recitation, when they differ with this difference, then what of the condition of one who has no knowledge? Know that this very incident has occurred in the community of Muhammad ﷺ, for each sect declares the other to be unbelievers despite their agreement on the recitation of the Qur'an. Then they differed concerning who are "those who have no knowledge," in several ways:

The first of them: they are the disbelieving Arabs who said that the Muslims are not upon anything. So He, exalted is He, made clear that if the statement of the Jews and Christians, while they read the Books, should not be accepted and paid heed to, then the statement of the disbelieving Arabs is more deserving of not being paid heed to.

The second of them: that if we take His saying ﴿The Jews say: "The Christians are not upon anything"﴾ to refer to those who were present in the time of Muhammad ﷺ, we take His saying ﴿Thus say those who have no knowledge﴾ to refer to their common folk, distinguishing between their elite and their common folk. The first is closer, because all the Jews and Christians entered into the verse, so whoever is distinguished from them by His saying ﴿Thus say those who have no knowledge﴾ must be other than them.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Allah will judge between them﴾, there are four aspects to it:

One of them: al-Hasan said: He will declare them all liars and cause them to enter the Fire.

The second: the judgment of retribution from the oppressor who denied the one oppressed who was denied.

The third: He will show them, plainly, who enters Paradise and who enters the Fire. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: He will judge between the one in the right and the one in the wrong regarding what they differed about. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 114 (part 1 of 3):**

[Page 9]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them and strives for their ruin? Those would not have entered them except in fear. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾

Know that this verse contains several issues.

**The first issue:** The exegetes (mufassirun) agree that the purpose of this verse is not merely to state a conditional and its consequence, meaning merely that whoever does such and such, Allah will do such and such to him. Rather, its purpose is to show that some of them prevented the maintenance of the mosques and strove for their ruin. Then Allah, exalted is He, repaid them with what is mentioned in the verse. However, they differed about who these people were who prevented the maintenance of the mosque and strove for its ruin. They mentioned four views:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: The king of the Christians attacked Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), destroyed it, threw carrion into it, besieged its people and killed them, took the rest captive, and burned the Torah. Bayt al-Maqdis remained in ruins until the people of Islam rebuilt it in the time of 'Umar.

The second: al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi said: It was revealed concerning Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar), when he destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis, and some of the Christians helped him in that out of hatred for the Jews.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said in *Ahkam al-Qur'an*: These two views are mistaken, because there is no disagreement among the scholars of history that the era of Bukhtansar was long before the birth of the Messiah, peace be upon him, and the Christians came after the Messiah. So how could they have been with Bukhtansar in the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis? Also, the Christians believe in the veneration of Bayt al-Maqdis just as the Jews do, and even more, so how would they have helped in its destruction?

The third: It was revealed concerning the polytheists of the Arabs who prevented the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, from calling to Allah in Makkah and compelled him to emigrate. They became those who prevented him and his companions from mentioning Allah in the Sacred Mosque. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, had built a mosque near his house, but he was prevented, and among those who harmed him were the children and women of Quraysh. It was also said that the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer, nor be silent therein﴾ [al-Isra: 110] was revealed concerning that, so he was prevented from praying aloud lest he be harmed. Abu Jahl threw filth upon the back of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. So it was said: And who is more unjust than these polytheists who prevent the Muslims, who affirm the oneness of Allah and do not associate anything with Him, and who pray to Him in humility and submission, occupying their hearts with reflection upon Him, their tongues with His remembrance, and their whole bodies with humbling themselves before His greatness and sovereignty.

The fourth: Abu Muslim said: The meaning is those who barred him from the Sacred Mosque when he went to it from Madinah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. He cited the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 25], and His saying: ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them while they bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque?﴾ [al-Anfal: 34]. He interpreted His saying: ﴿except in fear﴾ as referring to what Allah makes prevail of His power and manifests of His word, just as He said concerning the hypocrites: ﴿If the hypocrites... would not remain your neighbors in it except for a little, cursed wherever they are found; they will be seized and slain with [repeated] slaughter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60]. I have a fifth view, which is closer to the coherence of the text: it is that when the qibla was changed to the Ka'bah, this grieved the Jews, so they used to prevent people from praying when they faced the Ka'bah.

[Page 10]

Perhaps they also strove to destroy the Ka'bah by inciting some disbelievers to demolish it, and they also strove to destroy the mosque of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, so that people would not pray in it facing the qibla. So Allah blamed them for that and made clear the evil of their conduct in it. This interpretation is better than what came before it, because Allah, exalted is He, mentions in the verses preceding this verse only the ugly deeds of the Jews and Christians, and He also mentions after it their ugly deeds. So how would it be fitting for this single verse to refer to the ugly deeds of the polytheists in barring the Messenger from the Sacred Mosque? As for interpreting the verse as referring to the striving of the Christians in destroying Bayt al-Maqdis, it is also weak according to what Abu Bakr al-Razi explained. So nothing remains except what we have said.

**The second issue:** Concerning how this verse connects with what precedes it, there are several views.

As for the one who interprets it as referring to the Christians and the ruin of Bayt al-Maqdis, he says: It connects with what precedes it in that the Christians claimed that they alone are the people of Paradise, so it was said to them: How can you be like that when your treatment of the mosques is such, striving for their ruin?

As for the one who interprets it as referring to the Sacred Mosque and all other mosques, he says: The mention of the polytheists of the Arabs came in the saying of Allah: ﴿Thus said those who do not know, the like of their statement﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113]. It was also said: the mention of all the disbelievers and their blame came, so at one time the blame was directed at the Jews and Christians, and at another time at the polytheists.

**The third issue:** The saying ﴿mosques of Allah﴾ is general. Some said: its meaning is all mosques. Others interpreted it as referring to what we mentioned, namely the Sacred Mosque and other mosques of Makkah. They said: Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, had a mosque in Makkah where he would call upon Allah, and they destroyed it before the Hijrah. Others interpreted it as referring only to the Sacred Mosque, and this is the view of Abu Muslim, since he explained "preventing" as barring the Messenger from the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyah.

If it is asked: How is it permissible to take the word "mosques" as referring to one mosque? We say: There are several answers.

The first: This is like one who says to someone who harmed a single righteous person: And who is more unjust than one who harmed the righteous?

The second: A mosque is the place of prostration, so the Sacred Mosque in reality is not one mosque but many mosques.

**The fourth issue:** The saying ﴿from having His name mentioned in them﴾ is in the accusative position (mahall al-nasb). They differed about the governing element (al-'amil) in it, with several views:

The first: It is the second object of *manaʿa* (to prevent), because you say: *manaʿtuhu kadha* (I prevented him from such-and-such). A similar usage is His saying: ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs﴾ [al-Isra: 59] and ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing﴾ [al-Isra: 94].

The second: al-Akhfash said: It is permissible that it is by omitting *min* (from), as if it were said: He prevented the mosques of Allah from [the matter of] having His name mentioned in them.

The third: That it is in apposition (badal) to "mosques of Allah."

The fourth: al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that it means: out of aversion to His name being mentioned in them, and the governing element is *manaʿa* (prevented).

**The fifth issue:** Striving for the ruin of a mosque may take two forms:

One: preventing those who pray, worship, and maintain it from entering it, and this constitutes ruin.

The second: by demolition and destruction. No one should say: How is it valid to interpret this as referring to the Sacred House of Allah, when no destruction appeared in it? Because preventing people from establishing the rites of worship in it is itself a ruin of it. It was also said that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, had a place of prayer, and Quraysh destroyed it when he emigrated.

**The sixth issue:** The apparent meaning of the verse requires that this act is the greatest type of injustice, and there is a difficulty in this, because associating partners with Allah (shirk) is injustice, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, association [with Him] is great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13], and yet shirk is greater than this act. Likewise adultery, and the killing of a soul are greater than this act. The answer to this: At most, it is a general expression that has been subjected to specification, so it does not undermine the argument.

\* \* \*

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear﴾, know that the verse contains several issues.

[Page 11]

**The first issue:** The apparent meaning of the speech is that those who strove for the ruin of the mosque are the ones for whom it is forbidden to enter it except in fear. As for the one who takes it as general for all, they mentioned several views for the interpretation of this fear:

The first: It was not fitting for them to enter the mosques of Allah except in a state of awe, with trembling, out of fear that the believers would seize them, let alone that they would dominate them and prevent the believers from them. The meaning is: this was not the right and proper state for them, were it not for the oppression and tyranny of the disbelievers.

The second: This is a glad tidings from Allah to the Muslims that He would give them victory over the Sacred Mosque and all other mosques, and that He would humiliate the polytheists before them, so that not one of them would enter the Sacred Mosque except in fear, fearing that he would be seized and punished, or killed if he did not embrace Islam. Allah fulfilled the truth of this promise: He prevented them from entering the Sacred Mosque, and in the year Abu Bakr performed Hajj, he proclaimed among them: "Let no polytheist perform Hajj after this year." And the Prophet, peace be upon him, ordered the expulsion of the Jews from the Arabian Peninsula. So from the second year onward, no polytheist dared to perform Hajj or enter the Sacred Mosque openly. This is the interpretation of Abu Muslim in taking the prevention from the mosques as referring to their barring the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, from the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. This fear may also be understood as the manifestation of the Messenger's affair and his dominance over them, to the extent that they become fearful of him and his community.

The third: This fear may be understood as the humiliation and abasement they suffer through the jizya (poll tax) and degradation.

The fourth: It is forbidden for them to enter the Sacred Mosque except for a matter that involves fear, such as entering for dispute, litigation, or argument, since all of that involves fear. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while testifying against themselves with disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17].

The fifth: Qatada and al-Suddi said: The saying ﴿except in fear﴾ means that the Christians do not enter Bayt al-Maqdis except in fear, and no Christian is found in it except that he is struck painfully. This interpretation is rejected, because Bayt al-Maqdis remained for more than a hundred years in the hands of the Christians, such that none of the Muslims could enter it except in fear, until the king Salah al-Din, may Allah have mercy on him, liberated it in our time.

The sixth: The saying ﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear﴾, although its wording is that of a report, the intended meaning is a prohibition against enabling them to enter and granting them access to it. Like His saying: ﴿And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53].

\* \* \*

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾, they differed about the disgrace (khizy). Some said: It is the humiliation that befalls them through being barred from the mosques. Others said: It is the jizya for the protected non-Muslims (ahl al-dhimmah), and killing for the people of war (ahl al-harb). Know that all of this is possible, for disgrace is only what functions as a punishment, such as humiliation and abasement. So whatever has this description falls under it. That is a deterrent from Allah, exalted is He, against their steadfastness in disbelief, because present disgrace turns one away from adhering to what necessitates and requires it. As for the great punishment, Allah, exalted is He, described it with what amounts to the utmost degree of intensification, because those He mentioned earlier were described with the greatest injustice, so He made clear that they deserve the great punishment. In the verse there are two issues:

**The first issue:** Concerning the rulings on mosques, and there are several points:

The first: Concerning the excellence of mosques. This is indicated by the Qur'an, the reports, and reason. As for the Qur'an, there are verses:

One: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone along with Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. He attributed the mosques to His own essence by the lam of exclusivity (lam al-ikhtisas), then emphasized that exclusivity by His saying: ﴿so do not invoke anyone along with Allah﴾.

Two: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the mosques of Allah are maintained only by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 18]. He made the maintenance of the mosque a proof of faith. Indeed, the verse by its apparent meaning indicates that faith is restricted to them, because the word *innama* (only/indeed-only) is for restriction (hasr). (*Innama*: an Arabic particle that restricts a predication to what follows it.)

Three: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; glorifying Him therein in the mornings and the evenings﴾ [al-Nur: 36].

Fourth: this verse we are explaining, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mention of God's name in His mosques⦆ The apparent meaning of it requires that the one who strives to ruin mosques is in a worse state than the polytheist, because His saying "who is more unjust" encompasses the polytheist, since He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, association [with God] is a great injustice﴾. So if the one who strives to ruin it is in the highest degree of wickedness, it must be that the one who strives to build it is in the highest degree of faith.

As for the reports:

The first: what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related in their Sahihs, that ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may God be pleased with him, wanted to build the mosque, and the people disliked that and preferred that he leave it. ʿUthman, may God be pleased with him, said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Whoever builds a mosque for God, God will build for him a like of it in Paradise." In another narration: "God will build for him a house in Paradise."

The second: what Abu Hurayrah related, that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The dearest of lands to God, Exalted is He, are its mosques, and the most hateful of lands to God are its markets." Know that this report is an alert to the rational secret in the glorification of mosques, and its explanation is that places and times are only ennobled by the remembrance of God, Exalted is He. So when the mosque is a place for the remembrance of God, Exalted is He, to the extent that the one heedless of God's remembrance, when he enters the mosque, occupies himself with the remembrance of God, while the market is the opposite of that, because it is the place of buying and selling and turning toward worldly life, and that produces heedlessness of God and turning away from reflecting on the path of God, to the extent that one who remembers God, when he enters the market, becomes heedless of the remembrance of God. Hence, undoubtedly, mosques are the noblest places and markets the basest places.

The third: on the virtue of walking to the mosques:

(a) From Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever purifies himself in his house, then walks to one of the houses of God to fulfill one of the obligations of God, one of his steps erases a sin and the other raises a degree." Related by Muslim.

(b) Abu Hurayrah said: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever goes out in the morning or in the evening to the mosque, God prepares for him in Paradise a dwelling every time he goes out or comes back." Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related it in the Sahih.

(c) Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: "There was a man, I do not know of anyone from the people of Madinah who prayed toward the qiblah, who was farther from the mosque than he was, and prayers never escaped him along with the Messenger, peace be upon him. It was said to him: If only you would buy a donkey to ride in the dust and the darkness. He said: By God, I do not want my home to be beside the mosque. The Messenger of God ﷺ was informed of that and asked him about it, and he said: O Messenger of God, so that my footprints, my steps, my returning to my family, and my coming and going may be recorded. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'All of that is yours, as you intended.'" Related by Muslim.

(d) Jabir said: "The open land around the mosque became empty, so the Banu Salamah wanted to move closer to the mosque. This reached the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he said to them: 'It has reached me that you intend to move closer to the mosque.' They said: 'Yes, we have indeed intended that.' He said: 'O Banu Salamah, stay in your dwellings; your footprints are recorded.'" Related by Muslim. And from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: that this verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life and record what they have sent forth and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12].

(e) From Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may God be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Indeed, the people with the greatest reward in prayer are those who walk the farthest to the mosque, and the one who waits for the prayer until he prays it with the imam in congregation has greater reward than one who prays it and then sleeps." Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related it in the Sahih.

(f) ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir al-Juhani: that he, peace be upon him, said: "When a man purifies himself and then goes to the mosque seeking the prayer, his recording angel or two recording angels write for him ten good deeds for every step he takes toward the mosque, and the one who sits waiting for the prayer is like one devoutly standing in prayer, and he is recorded among those who pray from the time he leaves his house until he returns."

(g) From Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib who said: A man from the Ansar was near death, and he said to his family: Who is in the house? They said: Your family. As for your brothers and companions, they are in the mosque. He said: Lift me up. A man among them propped him up, and he opened his eyes and greeted the people, and they returned his greeting and said to him: May you be well. He said: Indeed, I will pass on to you today a narration which I have not related to anyone since I heard it from the Messenger of God ﷺ, seeking reward. And I am only relating it to you today seeking reward. I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Whoever performs ablution in his house, doing it well, then goes out to the mosque to pray in the congregation of the Muslims, he does not raise his right foot except that God records for him a good deed by it, and he does not place his left foot except that God removes from him a sin by it, until he reaches the mosque. When he prays with the imam, he departs forgiven. If he catches part of the prayer and misses part of it, it is the same."

(h) From Abu Hurayrah that he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever performs ablution and does it well, then goes out and finds the people have already prayed, God gives him the like of the reward of those who prayed and attended it, and that does not diminish their reward in any way."

(i) Abu Hurayrah said, peace be upon him: "Shall I not guide you to that by which God erases sins and raises degrees? They said: Yes, O Messenger of God. He said: Perfecting the ablution in difficult conditions, multiplying steps to the mosques, and waiting for the prayer after the prayer. That is the ribat (frontier-guarding), that is the ribat." Related by Muslim.

(j) Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman said to Dawud ibn Salih: "Do you know concerning what this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, be patient, endure, and remain stationed⦆ [Al ʿImran: 200]? He said: I said: No, O nephew. He said: I heard Abu Hurayrah say: There was no military campaign in the time of the Prophet ﷺ in which one would remain stationed, but rather it is waiting for the prayer after the prayer."

(k) Buraydah, peace be upon him, said: "Give glad tidings to those who walk in darkness to the mosque with complete light on the Day of Resurrection." Al-Nakha'i said: They used to regard walking to the mosque on a dark night as a meritorious act that necessitates reward.

(l) Al-Awza'i said: It used to be said: There are five things upon which the companions of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the Followers who followed them in goodness were: adhering to the congregation, following the Sunnah, maintaining the mosque, reciting the Qur'an, and jihad in the way of God.

(m) Abu Hurayrah said, peace be upon him: "Whoever builds a house for God in which God is worshipped, from lawful wealth, God builds for him a house in Paradise of pearls and rubies."

(n) Abu Dharr said, peace be upon him: "Whoever builds a mosque for God, even if it be as small as a nest of a sandgrouse, God builds for him a house in Paradise."

(o) Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said, peace be upon him: "When you see a man who frequents the mosque, bear witness to him of faith, for God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, only those maintain the mosques of God who believe in God and the Last Day⦆" [al-Tawbah: 18].

(p) From some of the companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ that they said: Indeed, mosques are the houses of God, and it is truly incumbent upon God to honor whoever visits Him in them.

(q) Anas said, peace be upon him: "Indeed, the maintainers of God's houses are the people of God's houses."

(r) Anas said: "God, Exalted is He, says: It is as if I were about to bring punishment upon the people of the earth, but when I look at the maintainers of My houses and those who love one another for My sake, and those who seek forgiveness at dawn, I turn it away from them."

(s) From Anas: he, peace be upon him, said: "When a calamity is sent down from the sky, it is turned away from the maintainers of the mosques."

(t) Salman wrote to Abu al-Darda': O my brother, let your house be the mosques, for I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "The mosque is the house of every pious person, and God has guaranteed for those whose houses are the mosques ease, mercy, and passage over the Sirat to the pleasure of God, Exalted is He."

(u) Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said, regarding ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam: Indeed, the mosques have pegs made of people, and they have companions among the angels. If they are absent, the angels ask about them; if they are sick, they visit them; and if they are in need, they help them.

(v) Al-Hasan said, peace be upon him: "A time will come upon the people when their talk in their mosques will be about the affairs of their worldly life; do not sit with them, for God has no need of them."

(w) Abu Hurayrah said, peace be upon him: "Indeed, the hypocrites have signs by which they are recognized: their greeting is a curse, their food is plunder, their booty is embezzlement. They do not approach the mosques except rarely, and they do not pray except late. They do not befriend or get befriended; they are like stumps at night and wanderers by day."

(x) Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah: He, peace be upon him, said: "Seven will be shaded by God in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His: a just ruler; a youth who grew up in the worship of God; a man whose heart is attached to the mosque when he leaves it until he returns to it; two men who loved each other for God's sake, gathered for that and separated; a man who remembered God in solitude and his eyes overflowed; a man who was called by a woman of beauty and loveliness and said: Indeed, I fear God; and a man who gave charity and concealed it until his left hand does not know what his right hand gives." This is a hadith related by the two Shaykhs in the Sahihs.

(y) ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever leaves his house for the mosque, his recording angel writes for him ten good deeds for every step he takes, and the one who sits in the mosque waiting for the prayer is like one devoutly standing in prayer, and he is recorded among those who pray until he returns to his house."

(z) ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak related from Hakim ibn Zurayq ibn al-Hakam, who said: I heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and my father asked him: Is attending a funeral more beloved to you or sitting in the mosque? He said: Whoever prays over a funeral has a qirat, and whoever follows it until it is buried has two qirats. Sitting in the mosque is more beloved to me; you glorify God, declare His oneness, and seek forgiveness, while the angels say: Amen, O God forgive him, O God have mercy on him. When you do that, say: O God, forgive Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

The fifth: on the adornment of mosques:

(a) Ibn ʿAbbas: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "I have not been commanded to decorate the mosques." By tashyid (elaborate construction) is meant raising and lengthening the building, from which is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in towers built high﴾ [al-Nisa': 78], which are those whose building is lengthened.

(b) ʿUmar ordered the building of a mosque and said to the builders: Shelter the people from the rain, and beware of reddening or yellowing it, lest you tempt the people.

(c) It is related that ʿUthman saw a plaster citron hanging in the mosque, so he ordered it cut down.

(d) Abu al-Darda' said: If you adorn your copies of the Qur'an and decorate your mosques, then destruction is upon you.

(e) Abu Qilabah said: We went out with Anas ibn Malik to the zawiyah, and the dawn prayer became due. We passed by a mosque, and Anas said: If only we prayed in this mosque? Some of the people said: Let us go until we reach the other mosque. Anas said: Which mosque? They said: A mosque that has just been built. Anas said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "There will come upon my community a time when they will boast about mosques, but they will maintain them only a little."

Fourth: on the greeting of the mosque. In the Sahihs, from Abu Qatadah al-Sulami, that he, peace be upon him, said: "When one of you enters the mosque, let him pray two rak'ahs before he sits." Know that this view is the position of al-Hasan al-Basri and Makhul, and the saying of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq. Others held that he sits and does not pray, and this was the view of Ibn Sirin, ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Nakha'i, and Qatadah, and Malik, al-Thawri, and the people of opinion also said so.

Fifth: on what one says when entering the mosque. Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ, related from her father, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ entered the mosque, he would send blessings upon Muhammad and greet him, and say: My Lord, forgive me my sins, and open for me the gates of Your mercy. And when he left, he would send blessings upon Muhammad and greet him, and say: My Lord, forgive me my sins, and open for me the gates of Your bounty."

Sixth: on the virtue of sitting in the mosque to wait for the prayer.

(a) Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The angels continue to pray for one of you as long as he remains in the place where he prayed, saying: 'O Allah, forgive him; O Allah, have mercy on him,' so long as he does not break wind." It is also narrated that Uthman ibn Maz'un came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Permit me to castrate myself." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He is not of us who castrates or has himself castrated. The castration of my community is fasting." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, permit me to travel (siyahah)." He said: "The travel of my community is jihad in the way of Allah." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, permit me to take up monasticism (tarahhub)." He said: "The monasticism of my community is sitting in the mosques awaiting the prayer."

The Seventh: On the disapproval of buying and selling in the mosque. From Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that he (upon him be peace) "forbade the recitation of poetry in mosques, buying and selling in them, and people forming circles in the mosques on Friday before the prayer."

Know that some of the scholars (Ahl al-'Ilm) disliked buying and selling in the mosque, and Ahmad, Ishaq and Ata ibn Yasar held this view. Whenever someone selling in the mosque passed by him, he would say: "Go to the market of this world; this is the market of the Hereafter." Salim ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with them, had an open courtyard beside the mosque which he called al-Batha'. He said: "Whoever wishes to make noise, recite poetry or raise his voice, let him go out to this courtyard." Know that the hadith we have narrated indicates the disapproval of forming circles and gathering on Friday before the prayer for the purpose of studying knowledge. Rather, one should occupy oneself with remembrance (dhikr), prayer and listening to the khutbah. Then there is no harm in gathering and forming circles after the prayer. As for seeking a lost item in the mosque and raising the voice for anything other than remembrance, this is disliked. From Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Whoever hears a man announcing a lost item in the mosque, let him say: 'May Allah not return it to you, for mosques were not built for this.'" Also from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (upon him be peace) said: "When you see someone selling or buying in the mosque, say: 'May Allah not make your trade profitable.'" Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Included in this is every matter for which the mosque was not built, from the transactions of people and the collection of their rights. Some of the early generations (salaf) disliked asking for charity in the mosque, and some of them held that one should not give to a beggar who solicits in the mosque. A prohibition has been reported against carrying out the prescribed punishments (hudud) in mosques. Umar said concerning one who was liable to a hadd punishment: 'Take him out of the mosque.' It is reported from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, something similar. Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: 'The mosques have been purified from five things: from having the hudud carried out in them, from collecting taxes in them, from reciting poetry in them, from announcing lost items in them, or from being made into a market.'" Some did not see any harm in judging in the mosque, because the Prophet (upon him be peace) performed li'an between al-Ajlani and his wife in the mosque; Umar performed li'an near the pulpit of the Prophet (ﷺ); and Shurayh, al-Sha'bi and Yahya ibn Ya'mar judged in the mosque. Al-Hasan and Zurarah ibn Awfa used to judge in the courtyard outside the mosque.

The Eighth: On sleeping in the mosque. In the two Sahihs, from Abbad ibn Tamim, from his uncle, that he "saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lying on his back in the mosque, with one of his legs placed over the other." Ibn Shihab said: "That was done by Umar and Uthman." In this there is evidence for the permissibility of reclining, lying down and various kinds of resting in the mosque, just as it is permitted in the house, except lying face down (inbitah), which the Prophet (upon him be peace) forbade, saying: "It is a lying-down that Allah dislikes." From Nafi' that Abd Allah was a young unmarried man with no family, so he would sleep in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). A number of the scholars permitted sleeping in the mosque. Ibn Abbas said: "Do not make it a place for spending the night or for midday rest."

The Ninth: On the disapproval of spitting in the mosque. From Anas, from the Prophet (upon him be peace), who said: "Spitting in the mosque is a sin, and its expiation is burying it." In the Sahih, from Abu Dharr, the Prophet (upon him be peace) said: "The deeds of my community were displayed to me, both their good and their bad. I found among the good deeds of my community the removal of harm from the road, and I found among their bad deeds phlegm in the mosque that is not buried." In a hadith: "The mosque shrinks from phlegm just as skin shrinks in the fire." That is, it contracts and draws itself together. Some said: the meaning is that being a mosque requires glorification, while throwing phlegm requires belittling, and between these there is a contradiction. So the Prophet (upon him be peace) expressed that contradiction by his saying "shrinks." Others said that he meant its people, namely the angels. In the two Sahihs, from Hammam ibn Munabbih, who said: "This is what Abu Hurayrah narrated to us from Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: 'When one of you stands for the prayer, let him not spit in front of him, for he is conversing with Allah as long as he is in his place of prayer; nor to his right, for there is an angel on his right; rather let him spit to his left or under his feet and bury it.'" From Anas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) saw phlegm in the qiblah, and this upset him until it showed on his face. He stood up and scraped it off with his hand, and said: 'When one of you stands in his prayer, he is conversing with his Lord; so let none of you spit toward his qiblah, but rather to his left or under his foot.' Then he took the edge of his garment, spat into it, folded part of it over another part, and said: 'Do it like this.'" Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih.

The Tenth: On garlic and onions. In the two Sahihs, from Anas, Ibn Umar and Jabir, the Prophet (upon him be peace) said: "Whoever eats from this foul-smelling plant, let him not come near our mosque, for the angels are harmed by what harms the people." From Jabir, that the Prophet (upon him be peace) said: "Whoever eats garlic or onion, let him keep away from our mosque." And that the Prophet (upon him be peace) was brought a pot containing greens, and he noticed their smell. He asked and was informed of the herbs in it. He said: "Bring it near to one of those present," and said to him: "Eat, for I converse with one with whom you do not converse." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The Eleventh: On mosques in residential quarters. From Hisham ibn Urwah, from his father, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that mosques be built in residential quarters, and that they be cleaned and perfumed." Anas ibn Malik said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in the mosque with his companions when a Bedouin came and urinated in the mosque. The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Stop, stop!' The Prophet (upon him be peace) said: 'Do not interrupt him.' Then he called him and said: 'These mosques are not fit for any filth, urine or excrement; they are only for reciting the Qur'an, remembering Allah and prayer.'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called for a bucket of water and they poured it over the spot.

[p. 15]

The Second Issue: The jurists (fuqaha) differed concerning the entry of a disbeliever into the mosque. Abu Hanifah permitted it absolutely, Malik forbade it absolutely, and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said that he is prevented from entering the Haram and the Masjid al-Haram. Al-Shafi'i argued with several points:

The first is the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are unclean, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this year of theirs﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. Al-Shafi'i said: "The Masjid al-Haram may refer to the Haram, because of the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ [al-Isra': 1], and he was taken by night from the house of Khadijah." So the verse indicates either the mosque alone or the entire Haram, and on either interpretation the purpose is achieved, since the prohibition applies to both. If it is said: "It means the Hajj, which is why He said 'after this year of theirs,' since the Hajj is performed only once a year," we say: this is weak for several reasons. The first is that it abandons the apparent meaning without any valid reason.

The second is that it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that attaching a ruling to a description indicates that the description is its cause (illah). This implies that the barrier to their approaching the Masjid al-Haram is their impurity, and that means that as long as they are polytheists they are prevented from the Masjid al-Haram.

The third is that if He had intended the Hajj, He would have mentioned the place where most of the pillars of the Hajj take place, which is Arafah.

The fourth is the evidence that the intended meaning is entry into the Haram, not the Hajj alone: the saying of Allah: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], where He meant entering for the purpose of trade.

The second is the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿It was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾. This implies that they should be prevented from entering the mosque, and that whenever they enter, they are in fear of being expelled, unless evidence indicates otherwise. If it is said: "This verse is restricted to those who destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis, or to those who prevented the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from worshipping in the Ka'bah. Also, the saying ﴿It was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾ does not mean the fear of expulsion, but the fear of the jizyah and of expulsion." We say: As for the first objection, the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾ is apparent in its generality, so restricting it to some cases goes against the apparent meaning. As for the second: the apparent meaning of ﴿It was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾ is that this fear arises from entering. On their view, the fear does not arise from entering but from something else, so their argument falls.

The third is the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while bearing witness against themselves of disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17]. Maintaining them (ʿimarah) occurs in two ways: the first is building and repairing them; the second is attending and frequenting them, as you say: "So-and-so maintains the mosque of so-and-so," meaning he attends it and is constant in it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you see a man who frequents the mosques, testify to his faith." This is based on the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿Indeed, those who maintain the mosques of Allah are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 18], so He made attending the mosques to be maintaining them.

The fourth is that the Haram is deserving of honour, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication: "O Allah, increase this House in honour, dignity and reverence," and awe. So protecting it from whatever would lead to its being belittled is obligatory, and allowing the disbelievers to enter it exposes the House to being belittled, since because of their corrupt beliefs about it, they may treat it lightly and proceed to defile and make it impure.

The fifth is that Allah commanded the purification of the House in His saying: ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], and the polytheist is impure because of the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are unclean﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. Purifying what is impure is obligatory, so keeping the disbelievers away from it is obligatory.

The sixth is that we agree that a person in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) is prevented from it, so the disbeliever is more deserving of being prevented. However, this is what the school of Malik requires, namely that he be prevented from all mosques.

Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, argued with several points:

The first: it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a delegation from Yathrib came to him and he housed them in the mosque.

The second: the saying of the Prophet (upon him be peace): "Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe, and whoever enters the Ka'bah is safe," which implies the permissibility of entering.

The third: a disbeliever is permitted to enter all the other mosques, so the Masjid al-Haram is likewise, just like a Muslim.

As for the answer to the first two hadiths: they belonged to the early period of Islam, and that ruling was then abrogated (naskh) by the verse. As for the analogy: the Masjid al-Haram is greater in rank than all other mosques, so the difference is clear. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, Verse 115 (Part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ Know that in this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** They differed concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse. The governing principle is that the majority claimed it was revealed concerning a matter related to prayer (salat), while some claimed it was revealed concerning a matter unrelated to prayer. As for the first view, it is stronger, for two reasons:

First: it is what has been transmitted from all of the Companions and the Successors (tabi'un), and their statement is a proof (hujjah).

Second: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿wherever you turn﴾ conveys turning toward the qiblah (direction of prayer) in prayer. For this reason, from His saying ﴿turn your faces﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], nothing is understood except this meaning. Having established this, we say: those who hold this view differed in several ways.

The first: He, exalted is He, intended by it the transfer of the believers from facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to the Ka'bah. So He, exalted is He, made clear that the east and the west, and all directions and sides, are entirely owned by Him, glorified is He, and created by Him. So wherever Allah commands you to face, that is the qiblah, because the qiblah is not a qiblah in itself, but rather because Allah, exalted is He, made it a qiblah. If He made the Ka'bah the qiblah, then do not deny that, for He, exalted is He, manages His servants as He wills, and He is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing of their interests. Thus it is as if He, exalted is He, mentioned this to explain the permissibility of abrogating the qiblah from one direction to another, and this becomes a preface to what He, exalted is He, intended of abrogating the qiblah.

The second: when the qiblah was changed from Bayt al-Maqdis, the Jews denied that, so the verse was revealed in refutation of them. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is similar to His saying: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142].

The third: the view of Abu Muslim, namely that the Jews and the Christians each said: Paradise belongs to him alone and not to anyone else. So Allah refuted them with this verse. The Jews faced Bayt al-Maqdis because they believed that Allah, exalted is He, ascended to the heaven from the rock, and the Christians faced the east because 'Isa (peace be upon him) was born there, as Allah related in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place﴾ [Maryam: 16]. So each of these two groups described its object of worship as dwelling in places, and whoever is like this is a created being, not a Creator. How then can Paradise be exclusively theirs, when they do not distinguish between the created and the Creator?

The fourth: some of them said: Allah, exalted is He, abrogated Bayt al-Maqdis by giving choice to face any direction He wished, by this verse. So it was permissible for the Muslims to turn toward wherever they wished in prayer. However, the Prophet (ﷺ) used to choose to face Bayt al-Maqdis, although it was permissible for him to turn wherever he wished. Then Allah, exalted is He, abrogated that by specifying the Ka'bah. This is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: the meaning of the verse is one who is witnessing the Ka'bah (i.e., directly before it), for he may face it from any direction he wishes and intends.

The sixth: what 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah narrated, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a military expedition, on a dark, pitch-black night, and we did not know the qiblah. So each man among us made his place of prostration (masjid) a stone placed before him, then we prayed. When we woke in the morning, we found ourselves not facing the qiblah. We mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse." This hadith indicates that they had by then been directed to the Ka'bah, because fighting was obligated after the Hijrah, after the abrogation of the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis.

The seventh: the verse was revealed concerning the traveler who performs voluntary prayers (nawafil) in whatever direction his mount turns him. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Umar, that he said: "This verse was only revealed concerning the man who prays toward wherever his mount turns him during travel." And "when he (peace be upon him) returned from Makkah, he would pray voluntarily upon his mount, indicating with his head toward Madinah." So the meaning of the verse: ﴿wherever you turn﴾ your faces for your voluntary prayers during your journeys, ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾, meaning you have reached the Sought One. ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Encompassing﴾ in bounty, Self-Sufficient. Out of the vastness of His bounty and self-sufficiency, He granted you leniency in this matter, for if He had obligated you to face the qiblah in such a situation, one of two harms would follow: either abandoning the voluntary prayers, or dismounting from the mount and falling behind the traveling company. This differs from the obligatory prayers (fara'id), for they are numbered and limited, so requiring dismounting from the mount at the time of performing them and facing the qiblah during them does not lead to hardship. Voluntary prayers, however, are not limited, so requiring facing the qiblah for them leads to hardship.

If it is said: which of these sayings is closest to the correct view? We say: His saying ﴿wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ indicates choice (takhyir), and choice is established only in two situations:

One of them: in voluntary prayer upon the mount.

The second: during travel when ijtihad (independent determination of the direction) is impossible due to darkness or other reasons, for in these two cases the one praying has a choice, whereas outside of these two cases there is no choice. As for the statement of one who says that Allah, exalted is He, gave the obligated persons the choice to face whichever direction they wished by this verse, while they used to choose Bayt al-Maqdis, not because it was obligatory but because it was superior and more fitting, this is far-fetched. For there is no disagreement that Bayt al-Maqdis had a special status in the Shari'ah before the change to the Ka'bah, and if the matter were as they claimed, that special status would not have been established. Also, it would have been necessary to say that Bayt al-Maqdis became abrogated by the Ka'bah. This indication requires that the verse be interpreted according to the third and fourth views. As for those who interpreted the verse according to the first view, they may say: when the qiblah was changed, the Jews spoke about the prayer of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the prayer of the believers toward Bayt al-Maqdis, so Allah, exalted is He, made clear by this verse that facing that former qiblah was correct at that time, and facing the Ka'bah is correct at this time, and He made clear that wherever they turn toward either of these two qiblahs in what is permitted, there is the Face of Allah. They said: interpreting the statement according to this view is preferable, because it encompasses every person praying. Whereas if it is interpreted according to the first view, it does not encompass all, because it would become restricted to voluntary prayer rather than obligatory prayer, and to travel in a specific situation rather than residence. When it is possible to apply a general expression in its generality, that is preferable to specification. The most that can be said is that under this interpretation there must also be a restrictive qualification, namely that it is said: ﴿wherever you turn﴾ among the directions commanded, ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾. However, this implicit supposition is necessary in every case, for it would be absurd for Him, exalted is He, to say: ﴿wherever you turn﴾ according to the inclination of your souls, ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾. Rather, the implicit supposition we mentioned is necessary. Given this, the idea of choice disappears. An analogy: if one of us turns to his son, having commanded him with many ordered matters, and says to him: "However you acted, you have followed my pleasure," that statement is understood as referring to what he commanded, in the manner he commanded, whether restricted or optional, and it is not understood as absolute choice. So likewise here.

**The second view:** This is the view of one who claimed that this verse was revealed concerning a matter other than prayer. They also have several interpretations:

The first: the meaning is that those who wronged by preventing My mosques from having My name mentioned in them and strove to ruin them, for them is such-and-such. Then wherever they turn fleeing from Me and from My authority, My authority will overtake them, My power will precede them, and I am All-Knowing of them; their location is not hidden from Me. In this there is a warning against sins and a deterrent from committing them. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ is similar to His saying: ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass through except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman: 33]. Accordingly, its meaning is breadth of knowledge, and it is similar to: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4], and His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation among three but that He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7], and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾ [Ghafir: 7], and His saying: ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]; that is, He has encompassed all things by His knowledge and His management, His encompassing of them, and His being above them.

The second: Qatadah said: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Your brother al-Najashi has died, so pray over him." They said: "Shall we pray over a man who is not a Muslim?" So the verse was revealed: ﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and what was revealed to you and what was revealed to them, humbly submitting to Allah, not exchanging the verses of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed Allah is swift in account﴾ [Al 'Imran: 199]. They then said: "He used to pray toward other than the qiblah," so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.﴾ Its meaning: the directions toward which the people of the religions pray, east and west and what lies between them, are all Mine. Whoever turns his face toward any of them, seeking My pleasure and desiring My obedience, will find Me there, meaning he will find My reward. In this there was an excuse for al-Najashi and his companions who died facing the east, and it is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah would never make your faith be lost﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

The third: when His saying, exalted is He, was revealed: ﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60], they said: "Where shall we call upon Him?" So this verse was revealed. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

The fourth: that it is addressed to the Muslims, meaning: let not the destruction by those who destroyed the mosques of Allah prevent you from remembering Him wherever you are in His land. To Allah belong the east and the west and all directions. This is the view of 'Ali ibn 'Isa.

The fifth: some people claim that it was revealed concerning the mujtahids (scholars exercising ijtihad) who fully meet the conditions of ijtihad, whether in prayer or in other matters. The meaning is that when a mujtahid reaches a judgment by the conditions of ijtihad, he is correct.

**The second issue:** If we interpret the verse as indicating the permissibility of facing any direction desired, then the verse is abrogated (mansukh). If we interpret it as indicating the abrogation of the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah, then the verse is abrogating (nasikh). If we interpret it according to the other views, then it is neither abrogating nor abrogated.

**The third issue:** The lam in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ is the lam of exclusive possession (lam al-ikhtisas), meaning: He is their Creator and their Owner. It is like His saying: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman: 17], and His saying: ﴿By the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 40], and ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9]. Then He, glorified is He, by mentioning the two directions, pointed to the mention of what lies between them of created beings, as He said: ﴿Then He rose to the heaven when it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly, obedient"﴾ [Fussilat: 11].

* * *

**The fourth issue:** The verse is among the strongest proofs for negating anthropomorphism (tajsim) and affirming transcendence (tanzih), and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾, thereby making clear that these two directions are owned by Him. This is so because a direction is something extended in imagination in length, breadth and depth, and everything that is like this is divisible, and everything divisible is composed and compound, and everything that is like this must have a creator and originator. This proof is general across all directions, I mean above and below. Thus it is established by this that He, exalted is He, is the Creator of all directions, and the Creator is necessarily prior to the created. Hence the Originator, exalted is He, before the creation of the world, was transcendent above directions and spaces, and it is necessary that He remain so after the creation of the world, since the inversion of realities and quiddities is impossible.

Second Aspect: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.﴾ If Allah were a body, and had a bodily face, then His face would be specific to a particular side and a particular direction, and His saying ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ would not be true. Since Allah, exalted is He, has affirmed this, we know that He is exalted above corporeality. The opponent argued with the verse in two ways:

The first: The verse indicates the affirmation of a Face for Allah, exalted is He, and a face only belongs to one who is a body.

The second: He, exalted is He, described Himself as being Vast (Wāsi‘), and vastness is an attribute of bodies.

The answer to the first: Although the word "wajh" (face) in its original linguistic usage refers to the specific organ, we have explained that if we took it here to mean the organ, then His saying ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ would be false, because if the face were facing the East, it would be impossible at that same time for it to face the West as well. Therefore, there must be an interpretation (ta'wil), and it is of several kinds:

The first: The attribution of "the Face of Allah" is like the attribution of "the House of Allah" and "the She-camel of Allah," and what is meant by it is attribution by creation and origination, as a mark of honour. So His saying ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾ means: there is His Face which He turned you towards, because the East and the West belong to Him with both their sides, and the purpose of the qibla is only a qibla because He appointed it. Thus, whichever of the faces of the world, attributed to Him by creation and origination, He appointed and specified, that is the qibla.

The second: The intended meaning of "wajh" is intention and purpose. The poet said:

*I seek the forgiveness of Allah for a sin I cannot count, Lord of the servants, to Him is the face and the deed.*

Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An‘am: 79].

The third: The intended meaning is: there is the good pleasure of Allah. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿We only feed you for the sake of Allah's Face﴾ [al-Insan: 9], meaning for the pleasure of Allah, and His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], meaning: whatever was for the pleasure of Allah. The basis of the metaphor is that whoever wishes to go to a person keeps approaching his face and front; likewise, whoever seeks the good pleasure of someone keeps approaching his pleasure. Therefore, seeking the good pleasure was called seeking his face.
