The fourth: "Wajh" is a filler (ṣilah), like His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾, and people say: "This is the face of the matter" — they do not mean by it anything other than it; they mean that from this direction this matter should be approached. Know that this explanation is correct in the language, but the discussion remains, for it may be said to this speaker: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾, given that place is not permissible for Him? So it must be interpreted as meaning: there is His qibla by which He is worshipped, or there is His mercy, His blessing, the path to His reward, and the seeking of His good pleasure.

As for the answer to the second: He described Himself as being Vast. There is no doubt that it cannot be taken in its apparent sense, otherwise He would be divisible and partible, and would then require a creator. Rather, it must be understood as vastness in power and dominion, or as being vast in giving and mercy, or as being vast in bestowing favour by clarifying what is beneficial for the servants so that they may reach His good pleasure. Perhaps this last meaning is the most fitting to the context. It is not permissible to take it as vastness in knowledge, for otherwise mentioning "the All-Knowing" after it would be repetition. As for His saying ﴿All-Knowing﴾ in this place, it is like a warning, so that the one praying may be cautious of negligence, since he imagines that He knows what is concealed and what is made apparent, and nothing is hidden from Allah of anything; thus he is wary of laxity. It is also possible that His saying ﴿Vast, All-Knowing﴾ means that He is vast in power to fully reward those who perform the prayer according to its conditions, and to fully requite those who are lax in it.

Fifth Issue: "Walla" means to turn toward (when it is intransitive, to face), and "walla" also means to turn away (to retreat); it is one of the words with opposite meanings (addad). Its meaning here is facing. Al-Hasan read: "fa-ainamā tawallaw" with a fatha on the ta', from the tawallī, meaning: wherever you turn — toward the qibla.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 116–117 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They say, "Allah has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾

Know that this is the tenth category of the abominable deeds of the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists. Know that the apparent meaning of His words, ﴿They say, "Allah has taken a son,"﴾ is that it refers back to His words, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:114]. We have already mentioned that some exegetes interpreted it as referring to the Christians, some as referring to the polytheists of the Arabs, and we have interpreted it as referring to the Jews. All of these groups attributed a son to Allah, the Exalted, because the Jews said, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and the polytheists of the Arabs said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Therefore this report is valid under all these interpretations. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it was revealed

[Page 22]

concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ka'b ibn Asad and Wahb ibn Yahudha, for they made Uzayr the son of Allah.

As for His words, ﴿Glory be to Him,﴾ it is a word of declaring Allah free from imperfection (tanzih), by which He declares Himself free from what they said, just as He said in another place, ﴿Glory be to Him that He should have a son﴾ [al-Nisa 4:171]. Sometimes He stated it explicitly and sometimes He limited Himself to it, because the context indicates it. He argued for this declaration of His freedom from imperfection with His words, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:116]. The argument from this verse against their doctrine is in several ways:

The first: every existent other than the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud) is possible in its own essence (mumkin li-dhatihi), and every possible in its essence is originated (muhdath), and every originated thing is a creation of the Necessary Existent, and a creation cannot be a son. As for the proof that everything other than the Necessary Existent is possible in its essence: if two necessary existents in their essences were found, they would share necessity of existence, and each one of them would be distinguished from the other by that by which it is individuated. What makes them share is other than what makes them distinct, and each of them would be composed of two qualifications. Every composite depends on each of its parts, and each of its parts is other than it. So every composite depends on something other than itself, and everything that depends on something other than itself is possible in its essence. Therefore each of the two necessary existents in their essences would be possible in its essence. This is a contradiction. Then we say: if each of those two components were necessary, the aforementioned division would recur and would lead to its being composed of infinitely many parts, and that is impossible. Even if we grant that it is not impossible, the intended conclusion is still established, because every plurality must have a one in it. If those units are necessary in their essences, they would be composite, as has been established, so the simple would be composite. This is a contradiction. If they are possible, then the composite that depends on them is more fitting to be possible. Thus this proof establishes that everything other than the Necessary Existent is possible in its essence, and everything possible in its essence requires an effecting cause (mu'aththir). The effect of that cause on it is either in the state of its non-existence or in the state of its existence. If it is the former, then that possible thing is originated. If it is the latter, then the need of that existent for the cause is either in the state of its persistence or in the state of its origination. The first is impossible, because it would entail the bringing into existence of existence, so the second is determined. That entails that the possible thing is originated. Thus it is established that everything other than Allah is originated, preceded by non-existence, and that its existence came about only by the creation, bringing into being and origination of Allah, the Exalted. It is therefore established that everything other than Him is His servant and His possession, so it is impossible that anything other than Him should be His son. We derived this proof only from His words, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, that is: to Him belongs everything other than Him by way of ownership, creation, bringing into existence and origination.

The second: this which is attributed to Him as a son is either eternal and without beginning, or originated. If it is eternal without beginning, then our judgment that one of them is the son and the other the father is no more fitting than the reverse, so that judgment would be a bare judgment without any proof. If the son is originated, then he is a creation of that eternal being and His servant, and so he cannot be His son.

The third: the son must be of the same kind as the father. If we supposed Him to have a son, that son would share with Him in some respects and be distinct from Him in another respect. That would entail that each of them is composite and originated, and that is impossible. Therefore sharing the same kind is impossible, and so being a son is impossible.

The fourth: a son is only taken for the need of him in old age and in hope of benefiting from his help when the father is unable to manage his own affairs. Accordingly, bringing a son into existence is only valid for one to whom poverty, incapacity and need can apply. If all of that is impossible, then bringing a son into existence for Him, glorified and exalted be He, is impossible. Know that in many places He related the sayings of those who attribute sons to Him and argued against them with this proof, namely that everyone in the heavens and the earth is His servant, and that when He decrees a matter He only says to it, "Be," and it is. He said concerning Maryam: ﴿That is Isa, son of Maryam, the word of truth about which they dispute﴾

[Page 23]

﴿It is not for Allah to take a son; Glory be to Him! When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Maryam 19:35]. He also said at the end of that surah: ﴿They say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ [Maryam 19:88] ﴿You have certainly brought a monstrous thing.﴾ ﴿The heavens almost burst apart from it, the earth splits open and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ ﴿that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son.﴾ ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 19:89–93].

If it is said: what is the wisdom in His arguing in this verse by His being the owner of what is in the heavens and the earth, while in the surah of Maryam He argued by His being the owner of those who are in the heavens and the earth, as in His words, ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 19:93]? We say: His words in this surah, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, are more complete, because the word "mā" encompasses all things.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, there are several issues in it:

The first issue: the root meaning of qunut (devout obedience and constancy) is constancy and perpetuity. It is then used in four senses:

Obedience, as in His words, ﴿O Maryam, be devoutly obedient to your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:43]. Prolonged standing, as in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, when he was asked, "Which prayer is best?" He said, "Prolonged qunut." Silence, as Zayd ibn Arqam said: "We used to speak during the prayer until His words were revealed, ﴿And stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:238], so we refrained from speaking." And it may mean perpetuity. Having understood this, we say: some exegetes said, ﴿all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, meaning: everything in the heavens and the earth is obedient and submissive. The tanwin in "kullun" is a substitute for the omitted genitive that follows it. This is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Abbas. It was said to them: the disbelievers are not obedient. At this point others said: the meaning is that they obey on the Day of Resurrection, and this is the view of al-Suddi. It was said to them: this is the attribute of those who are responsible (mukallaf), while His words, ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, include those who are not responsible. At this point they interpreted qunut in other ways:

The first: that they are evidence of the existence of the Creator, glorified be He, through the traces of craftsmanship in them, the signs of having been originated, and their indication of His lordship.

The second: that all of them are in His dominion and power, and He disposes of them as He wills. This is the view of Abu Muslim. According to these two interpretations the verse is general.

The third: He meant by it the angels, Uzayr and the Messiah, that is, each of those whom they judged to have a son is devoutly obedient to Him. It is reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said to one of the Christians: "Were it not for Isa's rebellion against the worship of Allah, I would have followed his religion." The Christian said: "How can that be attributed to Isa when he was so diligent in obeying Allah?" Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If Isa were a god, how could a god worship another? The servant is the one to whom worship is fitting." The Christian was silenced.

The second issue: since qunut in the original language is an expression for perpetuity, the meaning of the verse is that the perpetuity and continuance of contingent beings is through Him, glorified be He, and for His sake. This implies that the world, during its persistence and continuance, is in need of Him, glorified and exalted be He. It is thus established that a contingent being requires that its need of the effecting cause not be cut off, neither in the state of its origination nor in the state of its persistence.

The third issue: it is asked how He used "mā," which is for non-rational beings, together with His words, ﴿devoutly obedient﴾. The answer: it is as if He used "mā" rather than "man" to belittle their status.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, there are several issues in it:

The first issue: "badi'" (originator) and "mubdi'" (one who originates) have the same meaning. Al-Qaffal said: it is like "alim" meaning "mu'lim" (painful) and "hakim" meaning "muhkam" (firmly made), except that in "badi'" there is an intensification because of its form, and it indicates that the attribute is deserved outside the moment of the act, on the assumption that it is his nature to originate. In that respect it is like "sami'" (hearing) and "sami'" (hearer). "Badi'" may also come in the sense of "mubdi'". Ibda' (origination) means creating, and its opposite, ikhtira' (invention) on a model. For this reason people call one who says or does something that did not exist before a "mubtadi'" (innovator).

[Page 24]

The second issue: know that this is part of the first statement, because He, exalted be He, said, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, thereby showing that He owns what is in the heavens and the earth. Then He showed after that that He is also the owner of the heavens and the earth. Then He explained how He originates a thing, saying, ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ There are issues in it:

Second issue: the word qaḍāʾ (قَضاء, "decree/judgment") is a verbal noun in origin, named as such, which is why its plural is aqḍiyah like ghiṭāʾ and aghṭiyah. Its synonym is al-qaḍiyyah, whose plural is al-qaḍāyā. Its measure is faʿāl, from the root q-ḍ-y, and its original form was qaḍāyun. Because the yāʾ came at the end after the added alif, it underwent weak-letter change and became an alif; then, when that alif met the alif of faʿāl, it was changed to a hamzah, since two alifs cannot be pronounced together. Similar examples are al-maḍāʾ and al-atāʾ, from maḍaytu and ataytu, and al-siqāʾ and al-shifāʾ, from saqaytu and shafaytu. The evidence that the yāʾ is original rather than the hamzah is that it remains in most inflections of the word: you say qaḍaytu, qaḍaynā, qaḍayta… qaḍaytunna, qaḍayā, qaḍayna, huma yaqḍiyān, hiya wa-anta taqḍī, al-mar'atān wa-antumā taqḍiyān, hunna yaqḍīna. As for antī taqḍīna, the yāʾ in it is the pronoun of the feminine addressee. As for its meaning, the basic notion that its root indicates is cutting. From this is the saying: qaḍā al-qāḍī li-fulānin ʿalā fulānin bi-kadhā qaḍāʾan, meaning he ruled, because it separates the claim. For this reason it is said ḥākimun fayṣal when a judge puts an end to disputes. Ibn al-Anbārī related from the lexicographers that they said: al-qāḍī means one who cuts matters and makes them firm. Their saying: inqaḍā al-shayʾ means it was completed and ended; their saying: qaḍā ḥājatahu means he cut it off from the one in need and removed it from him; qaḍā daynahu means he paid it to him, as if he cut off the demanding and the claiming from himself, or each of the two was cut off from the other. Their saying: qaḍā al-amr means he completed and perfected it, and from it is the words of the Exalted: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 12], and it is from this, since completing a work involves cutting it off and finishing with it. From it also: dir'un qaḍḍāʾ, from qaḍāhā, meaning he made it firm and perfected its craft. As for their saying: qaḍā al-marīḍ, and qaḍā naḥbahu meaning he died, and qaḍā ʿalayhi meaning he killed him, these are metaphorical extensions of what has been mentioned, and the common element between them is clear. As for taqaḍḍī al-bāzī (the falcon's swooping), it is not from this root. Among what supports this is the evidence of what is used from reversing the arrangement of this root, namely qayḍ and ḍayq. As for the first, it is said qāḍahu fa-inqāḍ, meaning he split it and it split; from it is qayḍ al-bayḍ for what has cracked open from its upper shell, and inqāḍa al-ḥāʾiṭ when the wall collapsed without being demolished. Cutting, splitting, cleaving and demolishing are close in meaning. As for ḍayq and what is derived from it, its indication of the meaning of cutting is clear, because when a thing is cut it becomes narrow, or the reverse. Among what confirms this is that what is close to this root also indicates the meaning of cutting:
The first: qaḍaba, meaning he cut it; from it is al-qaḍbah al-muraṭṭabah (fresh green fodder), because it is qudiba, that is, cut, by way of naming by the verbal noun. And al-qaḍīb is a branch, a faʿīl in the sense of maf ʿūl. And al-miqḍab is what is cut with, like a sickle.
The second: al-qaḍm, which is eating with the tips of the teeth, since there is cutting of what is eaten. A sword that is qaḍīm has breakage and chipping at its edge.
The third: al-qaḍaf, which is thinness. One says rajulun qaḍīf, meaning lean, because scarcity is among the effects of cutting.
The fourth: al-quḍʾah, on the pattern fuʿlah, which is corruption. One says qaḍiʾat al-qirbah when the water-skin becomes worn out and spoiled, and fī ḥasabihi quḍʾah meaning a defect. All of this is among the causes or effects of cutting. This is the discussion of its original meaning according to the lexicon.

Third issue: concerning the senses of the word qaḍāʾ in the Qur'an. They said it is used in several ways:
First: in the sense of creation, the words of the Exalted: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 12], meaning He created them.
Second: in the sense of command, as the Exalted said: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 23].
Third: in the sense of judgment, for which reason the judge is called al-qāḍī.
Page 25
Fourth: in the sense of informing, as the Exalted said: ﴿And We conveyed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 4], meaning We informed them, and this comes accompanied by "ilā" (to).
Fifth: in the sense of finishing a thing, as the Exalted said: ﴿When it was finished, they returned to their people as warners﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 29], meaning when that was finished. And the Exalted said: ﴿And the matter was decided, and it settled upon al-Jūdī﴾ [Hūd: 44], meaning the destruction of the disbelievers was finished. And He said: ﴿let them complete their rites﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 29], in the sense of letting them finish with it. Having understood this, we say: as for His words: ﴿When He decrees a matter﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 47], it has been said: when He creates a thing; it has been said: He judges that He will do something; it has been said: He makes a matter firm. The poet said:
"And upon the two of them are interwoven coats of mail, which Dāwūd decreed, or which Tubbaʿ made as flowing coats."

Fourth issue: The scholars agreed that the word amr is literally applied to the specific speech, and is it literally applied to the act and the true affair? Yes, and that is what is meant by amr here, and the full discussion of it is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence.

Fifth issue: Ibn ʿĀmir read kun fa-yakūna with a fatḥah throughout the Qur'an, except in two places: at the beginning of Āl ʿImrān: ﴿kun fa-yakūn, al-ḥaqq﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 60], and in al-Anʿām: ﴿kun fa-yakūnu qawluhu al-ḥaqq﴾ [al-Anʿām: 73], where he read both with ḍammah. From al-Kisāʾī, with a fatḥah in al-Naḥl and Yā-Sīn, and with ḍammah in the rest of the Qur'an. The rest read with ḍammah throughout the Qur'an. As for the fatḥah, it is on the pattern of an answer to a command; it has been said that this is remote. The ḍammah is on the basis of resumption, meaning: so it comes to be.

Sixth issue: Know that the meaning of the Exalted's words: ﴿then He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 47] is not that God says to it "Be," whereupon that thing comes into being. That is false. What indicates the correct view are several arguments:
First: the words ﴿kun fa-yakūn﴾ are either eternal or created, and both are invalid. Therefore the view that the coming into being of things depends on "kun" is refuted. As for our saying that it cannot be eternal, this is for several reasons:
First: the word "kun" is a compound of the kāf and the nūn, on condition that the kāf precedes the nūn. The nūn, being preceded by the kāf, must be created; and the kāf, being prior to the created by a single moment of time, must also be created.
Second: the word "idhā" enters only with reference to the future, so that decree must be created, since the particle "idhā" has entered upon it; and the word "kun" is ordered after the decree by the fāʾ of consequence, since He said: ﴿then He only says to it, "Be"﴾. What comes after the created is created, so it is impossible for "kun" to be eternal.
Third: He ordered the existence of the created thing upon His word "kun" by the fāʾ of consequence, so His word "kun" is prior to the existence of the created thing by a single moment. What is prior to the created by a single moment must itself be created. Therefore His word "kun" cannot be eternal, and it is also not permissible that His word "kun" be created; for if every created thing depended on His word "kun", and His word "kun" were also created, then "kun" would depend on another "kun", which entails either infinite regress or circularity, and both are impossible. Thus by this proof it is established that the occurrence of created events cannot depend on His word "kun".
Second argument: He either addresses the created thing with "kun" before it enters existence, or while it is entering existence. The first is false, because addressing the non-existent while it is non-existent is folly. The second is also false, because its upshot returns to His commanding the existent to become existent, and that too has no benefit.
Third argument: the created thing may be inanimate, and commanding the inanimate is pointless and unbecoming to the All-Wise.
Fourth argument: the capable one is the one from whom the act and its omission are possible according to his volitions. If we suppose the capable, willing one separated from his word "kun", then either he is able to bring about existence and origination, or he is not able. If he is able, then bringing into being is not dependent on "kun". If he is not able, then it follows that the capable one is capable of the act only at the moment of uttering "kun", and the upshot returns to saying that you have heard capacity through "kun", which is a dispute over wording.
Fifth argument: if "kun" had an effect in bringing things into being, then whenever we uttered this word, that effect would have to follow; and since we know by necessity that this is false, we know that this word has no effect.
Sixth argument: "kun" is a compound of the kāf and the nūn, on condition that the kāf precedes the nūn. The agent is either one of these two letters or their combination. If it is the first, then "kun" has no effect at all, and the effect belongs to one of these two letters. If it is the second, it is impossible, because this combination has no existence at all: when the first letter occurs, the second is not yet present, and when the second comes, the first has passed. And if the combination has no existence at all, it is impossible for it to have any effect at all.
Seventh argument: the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of ʿĪsā before God is as the likeness of Ādam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he is﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 59] show that His word "kun" comes after His creating him; and what comes after a thing cannot be an influence on what precedes it. So we know that His word "kun" has no influence on the existence of the thing. Having shown the invalidity of this view by these arguments, we say: an interpretation is necessary, and it is of several kinds:
First, and the strongest: that the intended meaning of this word is the swiftness with which God's power takes effect in bringing things into being, and that the Exalted creates things without thought, toil or trial. Its parallel is the words of the Exalted when describing the creation of the heavens and the earth: ﴿He said to them and to the earth, "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 11], without any speech actually taking place between them, but by way of the swiftness with which His power takes effect in bringing them into being without obstruction or resistance. Its parallel is the saying of the Arabs: the wall said to the peg, "Why do you split me?" He said, "Ask him who strikes me, for he who is behind me has not left me behind." Its parallel is also the Exalted's words: ﴿And there is nothing that does not glorify Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 44].
Second: that it is a sign which God makes for the angels, so that when they hear it they know He has brought a new matter into being; this is related from Abū al-Hudhayl.
Third: that it is specific to the existent beings to whom He said: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65] and those who are like them; this is the view of al-Aṣamm.
Fourth: that it is a command to the living to die and to the dead to live. All of these are weak, and the strongest is the first.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 116–117 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They say, "Allah has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾

Know that this is the tenth category of the abominable deeds of the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists. Know that the apparent meaning of His words, ﴿They say, "Allah has taken a son,"﴾ is that it refers back to His words, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:114]. We have already mentioned that some exegetes interpreted it as referring to the Christians, some as referring to the polytheists of the Arabs, and we have interpreted it as referring to the Jews. All of these groups attributed a son to Allah, the Exalted, because the Jews said, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and the polytheists of the Arabs said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Therefore this report is valid under all these interpretations. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it was revealed

[Page 22]

concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ka'b ibn Asad and Wahb ibn Yahudha, for they made Uzayr the son of Allah.

As for His words, ﴿Glory be to Him,﴾ it is a word of declaring Allah free from imperfection (tanzih), by which He declares Himself free from what they said, just as He said in another place, ﴿Glory be to Him that He should have a son﴾ [al-Nisa 4:171]. Sometimes He stated it explicitly and sometimes He limited Himself to it, because the context indicates it. He argued for this declaration of His freedom from imperfection with His words, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:116]. The argument from this verse against their doctrine is in several ways:

The first: every existent other than the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud) is possible in its own essence (mumkin li-dhatihi), and every possible in its essence is originated (muhdath), and every originated thing is a creation of the Necessary Existent, and a creation cannot be a son. As for the proof that everything other than the Necessary Existent is possible in its essence: if two necessary existents in their essences were found, they would share necessity of existence, and each one of them would be distinguished from the other by that by which it is individuated. What makes them share is other than what makes them distinct, and each of them would be composed of two qualifications. Every composite depends on each of its parts, and each of its parts is other than it. So every composite depends on something other than itself, and everything that depends on something other than itself is possible in its essence. Therefore each of the two necessary existents in their essences would be possible in its essence. This is a contradiction. Then we say: if each of those two components were necessary, the aforementioned division would recur and would lead to its being composed of infinitely many parts, and that is impossible. Even if we grant that it is not impossible, the intended conclusion is still established, because every plurality must have a one in it. If those units are necessary in their essences, they would be composite, as has been established, so the simple would be composite. This is a contradiction. If they are possible, then the composite that depends on them is more fitting to be possible. Thus this proof establishes that everything other than the Necessary Existent is possible in its essence, and everything possible in its essence requires an effecting cause (mu'aththir). The effect of that cause on it is either in the state of its non-existence or in the state of its existence. If it is the former, then that possible thing is originated. If it is the latter, then the need of that existent for the cause is either in the state of its persistence or in the state of its origination. The first is impossible, because it would entail the bringing into existence of existence, so the second is determined. That entails that the possible thing is originated. Thus it is established that everything other than Allah is originated, preceded by non-existence, and that its existence came about only by the creation, bringing into being and origination of Allah, the Exalted. It is therefore established that everything other than Him is His servant and His possession, so it is impossible that anything other than Him should be His son. We derived this proof only from His words, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, that is: to Him belongs everything other than Him by way of ownership, creation, bringing into existence and origination.

The second: this which is attributed to Him as a son is either eternal and without beginning, or originated. If it is eternal without beginning, then our judgment that one of them is the son and the other the father is no more fitting than the reverse, so that judgment would be a bare judgment without any proof. If the son is originated, then he is a creation of that eternal being and His servant, and so he cannot be His son.

The third: the son must be of the same kind as the father. If we supposed Him to have a son, that son would share with Him in some respects and be distinct from Him in another respect. That would entail that each of them is composite and originated, and that is impossible. Therefore sharing the same kind is impossible, and so being a son is impossible.

The fourth: a son is only taken for the need of him in old age and in hope of benefiting from his help when the father is unable to manage his own affairs. Accordingly, bringing a son into existence is only valid for one to whom poverty, incapacity and need can apply. If all of that is impossible, then bringing a son into existence for Him, glorified and exalted be He, is impossible. Know that in many places He related the sayings of those who attribute sons to Him and argued against them with this proof, namely that everyone in the heavens and the earth is His servant, and that when He decrees a matter He only says to it, "Be," and it is. He said concerning Maryam: ﴿That is Isa, son of Maryam, the word of truth about which they dispute﴾

[Page 23]

﴿It is not for Allah to take a son; Glory be to Him! When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Maryam 19:35]. He also said at the end of that surah: ﴿They say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ [Maryam 19:88] ﴿You have certainly brought a monstrous thing.﴾ ﴿The heavens almost burst apart from it, the earth splits open and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ ﴿that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son.﴾ ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 19:89–93].

If it is said: what is the wisdom in His arguing in this verse by His being the owner of what is in the heavens and the earth, while in the surah of Maryam He argued by His being the owner of those who are in the heavens and the earth, as in His words, ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 19:93]? We say: His words in this surah, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, are more complete, because the word "mā" encompasses all things.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, there are several issues in it:

The first issue: the root meaning of qunut (devout obedience and constancy) is constancy and perpetuity. It is then used in four senses:

Obedience, as in His words, ﴿O Maryam, be devoutly obedient to your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:43]. Prolonged standing, as in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, when he was asked, "Which prayer is best?" He said, "Prolonged qunut." Silence, as Zayd ibn Arqam said: "We used to speak during the prayer until His words were revealed, ﴿And stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:238], so we refrained from speaking." And it may mean perpetuity. Having understood this, we say: some exegetes said, ﴿all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, meaning: everything in the heavens and the earth is obedient and submissive. The tanwin in "kullun" is a substitute for the omitted genitive that follows it. This is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Abbas. It was said to them: the disbelievers are not obedient. At this point others said: the meaning is that they obey on the Day of Resurrection, and this is the view of al-Suddi. It was said to them: this is the attribute of those who are responsible (mukallaf), while His words, ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, include those who are not responsible. At this point they interpreted qunut in other ways:

The first: that they are evidence of the existence of the Creator, glorified be He, through the traces of craftsmanship in them, the signs of having been originated, and their indication of His lordship.

The second: that all of them are in His dominion and power, and He disposes of them as He wills. This is the view of Abu Muslim. According to these two interpretations the verse is general.

The third: He meant by it the angels, Uzayr and the Messiah, that is, each of those whom they judged to have a son is devoutly obedient to Him. It is reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said to one of the Christians: "Were it not for Isa's rebellion against the worship of Allah, I would have followed his religion." The Christian said: "How can that be attributed to Isa when he was so diligent in obeying Allah?" Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If Isa were a god, how could a god worship another? The servant is the one to whom worship is fitting." The Christian was silenced.

The second issue: since qunut in the original language is an expression for perpetuity, the meaning of the verse is that the perpetuity and continuance of contingent beings is through Him, glorified be He, and for His sake. This implies that the world, during its persistence and continuance, is in need of Him, glorified and exalted be He. It is thus established that a contingent being requires that its need of the effecting cause not be cut off, neither in the state of its origination nor in the state of its persistence.

The third issue: it is asked how He used "mā," which is for non-rational beings, together with His words, ﴿devoutly obedient﴾. The answer: it is as if He used "mā" rather than "man" to belittle their status.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, there are several issues in it:

The first issue: "badi'" (originator) and "mubdi'" (one who originates) have the same meaning. Al-Qaffal said: it is like "alim" meaning "mu'lim" (painful) and "hakim" meaning "muhkam" (firmly made), except that in "badi'" there is an intensification because of its form, and it indicates that the attribute is deserved outside the moment of the act, on the assumption that it is his nature to originate. In that respect it is like "sami'" (hearing) and "sami'" (hearer). "Badi'" may also come in the sense of "mubdi'". Ibda' (origination) means creating, and its opposite, ikhtira' (invention) on a model. For this reason people call one who says or does something that did not exist before a "mubtadi'" (innovator).

[Page 24]

The second issue: know that this is part of the first statement, because He, exalted be He, said, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, thereby showing that He owns what is in the heavens and the earth. Then He showed after that that He is also the owner of the heavens and the earth. Then He explained how He originates a thing, saying, ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ There are issues in it:

Second issue: the word qaḍāʾ (قَضاء, "decree/judgment") is a verbal noun in origin, named as such, which is why its plural is aqḍiyah like ghiṭāʾ and aghṭiyah. Its synonym is al-qaḍiyyah, whose plural is al-qaḍāyā. Its measure is faʿāl, from the root q-ḍ-y, and its original form was qaḍāyun. Because the yāʾ came at the end after the added alif, it underwent weak-letter change and became an alif; then, when that alif met the alif of faʿāl, it was changed to a hamzah, since two alifs cannot be pronounced together. Similar examples are al-maḍāʾ and al-atāʾ, from maḍaytu and ataytu, and al-siqāʾ and al-shifāʾ, from saqaytu and shafaytu. The evidence that the yāʾ is original rather than the hamzah is that it remains in most inflections of the word: you say qaḍaytu, qaḍaynā, qaḍayta… qaḍaytunna, qaḍayā, qaḍayna, huma yaqḍiyān, hiya wa-anta taqḍī, al-mar'atān wa-antumā taqḍiyān, hunna yaqḍīna. As for antī taqḍīna, the yāʾ in it is the pronoun of the feminine addressee. As for its meaning, the basic notion that its root indicates is cutting. From this is the saying: qaḍā al-qāḍī li-fulānin ʿalā fulānin bi-kadhā qaḍāʾan, meaning he ruled, because it separates the claim. For this reason it is said ḥākimun fayṣal when a judge puts an end to disputes. Ibn al-Anbārī related from the lexicographers that they said: al-qāḍī means one who cuts matters and makes them firm. Their saying: inqaḍā al-shayʾ means it was completed and ended; their saying: qaḍā ḥājatahu means he cut it off from the one in need and removed it from him; qaḍā daynahu means he paid it to him, as if he cut off the demanding and the claiming from himself, or each of the two was cut off from the other. Their saying: qaḍā al-amr means he completed and perfected it, and from it is the words of the Exalted: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 12], and it is from this, since completing a work involves cutting it off and finishing with it. From it also: dir'un qaḍḍāʾ, from qaḍāhā, meaning he made it firm and perfected its craft. As for their saying: qaḍā al-marīḍ, and qaḍā naḥbahu meaning he died, and qaḍā ʿalayhi meaning he killed him, these are metaphorical extensions of what has been mentioned, and the common element between them is clear. As for taqaḍḍī al-bāzī (the falcon's swooping), it is not from this root. Among what supports this is the evidence of what is used from reversing the arrangement of this root, namely qayḍ and ḍayq. As for the first, it is said qāḍahu fa-inqāḍ, meaning he split it and it split; from it is qayḍ al-bayḍ for what has cracked open from its upper shell, and inqāḍa al-ḥāʾiṭ when the wall collapsed without being demolished. Cutting, splitting, cleaving and demolishing are close in meaning. As for ḍayq and what is derived from it, its indication of the meaning of cutting is clear, because when a thing is cut it becomes narrow, or the reverse. Among what confirms this is that what is close to this root also indicates the meaning of cutting:
The first: qaḍaba, meaning he cut it; from it is al-qaḍbah al-muraṭṭabah (fresh green fodder), because it is qudiba, that is, cut, by way of naming by the verbal noun. And al-qaḍīb is a branch, a faʿīl in the sense of maf ʿūl. And al-miqḍab is what is cut with, like a sickle.
The second: al-qaḍm, which is eating with the tips of the teeth, since there is cutting of what is eaten. A sword that is qaḍīm has breakage and chipping at its edge.
The third: al-qaḍaf, which is thinness. One says rajulun qaḍīf, meaning lean, because scarcity is among the effects of cutting.
The fourth: al-quḍʾah, on the pattern fuʿlah, which is corruption. One says qaḍiʾat al-qirbah when the water-skin becomes worn out and spoiled, and fī ḥasabihi quḍʾah meaning a defect. All of this is among the causes or effects of cutting. This is the discussion of its original meaning according to the lexicon.

Third issue: concerning the senses of the word qaḍāʾ in the Qur'an. They said it is used in several ways:
First: in the sense of creation, the words of the Exalted: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 12], meaning He created them.
Second: in the sense of command, as the Exalted said: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 23].
Third: in the sense of judgment, for which reason the judge is called al-qāḍī.
Page 25
Fourth: in the sense of informing, as the Exalted said: ﴿And We conveyed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 4], meaning We informed them, and this comes accompanied by "ilā" (to).
Fifth: in the sense of finishing a thing, as the Exalted said: ﴿When it was finished, they returned to their people as warners﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 29], meaning when that was finished. And the Exalted said: ﴿And the matter was decided, and it settled upon al-Jūdī﴾ [Hūd: 44], meaning the destruction of the disbelievers was finished. And He said: ﴿let them complete their rites﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 29], in the sense of letting them finish with it. Having understood this, we say: as for His words: ﴿When He decrees a matter﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 47], it has been said: when He creates a thing; it has been said: He judges that He will do something; it has been said: He makes a matter firm. The poet said:
"And upon the two of them are interwoven coats of mail, which Dāwūd decreed, or which Tubbaʿ made as flowing coats."

Fourth issue: The scholars agreed that the word amr is literally applied to the specific speech, and is it literally applied to the act and the true affair? Yes, and that is what is meant by amr here, and the full discussion of it is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence.

Fifth issue: Ibn ʿĀmir read kun fa-yakūna with a fatḥah throughout the Qur'an, except in two places: at the beginning of Āl ʿImrān: ﴿kun fa-yakūn, al-ḥaqq﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 60], and in al-Anʿām: ﴿kun fa-yakūnu qawluhu al-ḥaqq﴾ [al-Anʿām: 73], where he read both with ḍammah. From al-Kisāʾī, with a fatḥah in al-Naḥl and Yā-Sīn, and with ḍammah in the rest of the Qur'an. The rest read with ḍammah throughout the Qur'an. As for the fatḥah, it is on the pattern of an answer to a command; it has been said that this is remote. The ḍammah is on the basis of resumption, meaning: so it comes to be.

Sixth issue: Know that the meaning of the Exalted's words: ﴿then He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 47] is not that God says to it "Be," whereupon that thing comes into being. That is false. What indicates the correct view are several arguments:
First: the words ﴿kun fa-yakūn﴾ are either eternal or created, and both are invalid. Therefore the view that the coming into being of things depends on "kun" is refuted. As for our saying that it cannot be eternal, this is for several reasons:
First: the word "kun" is a compound of the kāf and the nūn, on condition that the kāf precedes the nūn. The nūn, being preceded by the kāf, must be created; and the kāf, being prior to the created by a single moment of time, must also be created.
Second: the word "idhā" enters only with reference to the future, so that decree must be created, since the particle "idhā" has entered upon it; and the word "kun" is ordered after the decree by the fāʾ of consequence, since He said: ﴿then He only says to it, "Be"﴾. What comes after the created is created, so it is impossible for "kun" to be eternal.
Third: He ordered the existence of the created thing upon His word "kun" by the fāʾ of consequence, so His word "kun" is prior to the existence of the created thing by a single moment. What is prior to the created by a single moment must itself be created. Therefore His word "kun" cannot be eternal, and it is also not permissible that His word "kun" be created; for if every created thing depended on His word "kun", and His word "kun" were also created, then "kun" would depend on another "kun", which entails either infinite regress or circularity, and both are impossible. Thus by this proof it is established that the occurrence of created events cannot depend on His word "kun".
Second argument: He either addresses the created thing with "kun" before it enters existence, or while it is entering existence. The first is false, because addressing the non-existent while it is non-existent is folly. The second is also false, because its upshot returns to His commanding the existent to become existent, and that too has no benefit.
Third argument: the created thing may be inanimate, and commanding the inanimate is pointless and unbecoming to the All-Wise.
Fourth argument: the capable one is the one from whom the act and its omission are possible according to his volitions. If we suppose the capable, willing one separated from his word "kun", then either he is able to bring about existence and origination, or he is not able. If he is able, then bringing into being is not dependent on "kun". If he is not able, then it follows that the capable one is capable of the act only at the moment of uttering "kun", and the upshot returns to saying that you have heard capacity through "kun", which is a dispute over wording.
Fifth argument: if "kun" had an effect in bringing things into being, then whenever we uttered this word, that effect would have to follow; and since we know by necessity that this is false, we know that this word has no effect.
Sixth argument: "kun" is a compound of the kāf and the nūn, on condition that the kāf precedes the nūn. The agent is either one of these two letters or their combination. If it is the first, then "kun" has no effect at all, and the effect belongs to one of these two letters. If it is the second, it is impossible, because this combination has no existence at all: when the first letter occurs, the second is not yet present, and when the second comes, the first has passed. And if the combination has no existence at all, it is impossible for it to have any effect at all.
Seventh argument: the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of ʿĪsā before God is as the likeness of Ādam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he is﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 59] show that His word "kun" comes after His creating him; and what comes after a thing cannot be an influence on what precedes it. So we know that His word "kun" has no influence on the existence of the thing. Having shown the invalidity of this view by these arguments, we say: an interpretation is necessary, and it is of several kinds:
First, and the strongest: that the intended meaning of this word is the swiftness with which God's power takes effect in bringing things into being, and that the Exalted creates things without thought, toil or trial. Its parallel is the words of the Exalted when describing the creation of the heavens and the earth: ﴿He said to them and to the earth, "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 11], without any speech actually taking place between them, but by way of the swiftness with which His power takes effect in bringing them into being without obstruction or resistance. Its parallel is the saying of the Arabs: the wall said to the peg, "Why do you split me?" He said, "Ask him who strikes me, for he who is behind me has not left me behind." Its parallel is also the Exalted's words: ﴿And there is nothing that does not glorify Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 44].
Second: that it is a sign which God makes for the angels, so that when they hear it they know He has brought a new matter into being; this is related from Abū al-Hudhayl.
Third: that it is specific to the existent beings to whom He said: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65] and those who are like them; this is the view of al-Aṣamm.
Fourth: that it is a command to the living to die and to the dead to live. All of these are weak, and the strongest is the first.

[p. 27]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us directly, or why does no sign come to us?" Likewise said those before them, a similar saying. Their hearts are alike. We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain.﴾

Know that this is the eleventh type of the ugly deeds of the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists. On it there are several issues:

The first issue: When Allah the Exalted related what the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists said that damages monotheism (al-tawhid, the affirmation of God's oneness), namely that He took a son, He now relates what they say that damages prophethood (al-nubuwwah). Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: these are the polytheists of the Arabs. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They said: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth"﴾ [al-Isra' 90], and they said: ﴿So let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent [with signs]﴾, and they said: ﴿Why were angels not sent down to us, or do we see our Lord?﴾. This is the saying of most of the exegetes. However, it is established that the People of the Book also asked for this. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven. They had asked Moses for greater than that﴾ [al-Nisa' 153]. If it is said: "The evidence that the intended people are the polytheists of the Arabs is that He described them as ones who do not know, whereas the People of the Book are people of knowledge," we say: the meaning is that they do not know tawhid and prophethood as they should, and the People of the Book were like that.

The second issue: The statement of the doubt they held on to is that when a wise one wants to achieve something, he must choose the closest ways leading to it and the furthest from doubts and suspicions. When this is established, we say: Allah the Exalted speaks to the angels and He spoke to Moses, and you say: "O Muhammad, He spoke to you." The evidence for this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm 10]. So why does He not speak to us face to face, and why does He not explicitly specify your prophethood, so that belief is confirmed and doubt is removed? Also, if He does not do that, why does He not single you out with a sign and a miracle? This from them is a criticism of the Qur'an being a sign and a miracle, for if they acknowledged it to be a miracle, it would be impossible for them to say: "Why does He not bring us a sign?" Then He answered this doubt by His saying: ﴿Likewise said those before them, a similar saying. Their hearts are alike. We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain.﴾ The essence of this answer is that We have supported the word of Muhammad (ﷺ) with miracles, and We have shown the truth of his word by the signs, which are the Qur'an and the rest of the miracles. Therefore, the demand for these additions is a form of obstinacy (ta'annut). When this is so, answering them is not obligatory, for several reasons:

The first: When one proof is present, the one who is accountable has become able to reach the sought truth. If his aim were seeking the truth, he would have been satisfied with that proof. Since he was not satisfied with it and demanded something beyond it, we know that this demand is of the kind of stubbornness and contentiousness, so answering it is not obligatory. A parallel to this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They say: "Why were no signs sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner." Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 50-51]. So He rebuked them with the sufficient proof that is in the Qur'an.

The second: Had it been within Allah's knowledge that they would believe upon the sending down of this sign, He would have done it. But He knew that if He gave them what they asked for, they would only increase in obstinacy. Therefore, He did not do it. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And had He made them hear, they would have turned away while refusing﴾ [al-Anfal 23].

The third: In those signs there arise various kinds of corruption, and perhaps their occurrence would bring about their destruction and annihilation if they persisted in denial after that. Perhaps some of them would reach the degree of compulsion that nullifies accountability (al-taklif). Perhaps their multiplicity and their succession would undermine their being a miracle, for when extraordinary events follow one another, the breaking of habit becomes a habit, and then it no longer remains a miracle. All of these are matters that none knows except Allah, the Knower of the unseen. Thus it is established that not granting them these signs does not undermine prophethood.

As for His saying: ﴿Their hearts are alike﴾, the meaning is that the deniers of the messengers have similar sayings and actions. Just as the people of Moses were always in obstinacy and proposing falsehoods, such as their saying: ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾ [al-Baqarah 61], and their saying: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf 138], and His saying: ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾ [al-Baqarah 67], and their saying: ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾

[p. 28]
[al-Nisa' 153], so likewise these polytheists are always in stubbornness, contentiousness and seeking falsehood.

As for His saying: ﴿We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain﴾, the meaning is that the Qur'an and the other miracles, such as the coming of the tree, the speech of the wolf, and the feeding of a large number of people with little food, are overpowering signs and dazzling miracles for those who seek certainty.

This is the commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

Know that when the people persisted in obstinacy and vain contentiousness, and demanded miracles in a spirit of willful stubbornness, God Most High showed His Messenger (ﷺ) that there is nothing more to add to what He had done regarding the interests of their religion, namely the manifestation of proofs. Just as He made this clear, He also made clear that there is nothing more to add to what the Messenger had done in the matter of conveying and warning, so that his grief would not increase because of their insistence upon their disbelief. As for His saying ﴿with the truth﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: it relates to the sending, meaning: We sent you with a sending in truth.

The second: it relates to "bringer of good tidings" and "warner," meaning: you bring good tidings of the truth and warn with it.

The third: that by "the truth" is meant the religion and the Qur'an, meaning: We sent you with the Qur'an, being a bringer of good tidings to those who obey God with reward, and a warner to those who disbelieve with punishment. It is preferable that "bringer of good tidings" and "warner" be attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ), so it is as if He, the Exalted, said: Indeed We have sent you, O Muhammad, with the truth, so that you would be a bringer of good tidings to whoever follows you and is guided by your religion, and a warner to whoever disbelieves in you and strays from your religion.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, there are two readings concerning it:

The majority read with a raised ta' and lam, as a statement. As for Nafi', it is with a jussive and a fatha on the ta', as a prohibition.

As for the first reading, there are several interpretations:

The first: their destination is the Blazing Fire, so their disobedience does not harm you, and you are not accountable for that. This is like His saying: ﴿Your duty is only to convey, and Ours is the reckoning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 40], and His saying: ﴿Upon him is what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾ [al-Nur: 54].

The second: you are a guide, and you have no part in the affair, so do not grieve or be overly concerned at their disbelief and their destination to punishment. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿So let not your soul go out in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8].

The third: do not look at the obedient and the disobedient in the present time, for the state may change, and it is unseen, so do not ask about it. The verse indicates that no one is questioned about the sin of another, nor is anyone held accountable for what another has committed, whether that other is near or far.

As for the second reading, it has two aspects:

The first: it is related that he said: "I wish I knew what my parents did!" So he was forbidden to ask about the disbelievers. This narration is far-fetched, because he (peace and blessings be upon him) knew of their disbelief, and knew that the disbeliever is punished; so with this knowledge, how could he possibly say: "I wish I knew what my parents did?"

The second: the meaning of this prohibition is to magnify what the disbelievers fell into of punishment, just as when you ask about a person who is in a calamity and you are told: "Do not ask about him." The reason for the magnification is that the one being asked would be distressed that what he is in should pass over his tongue, due to its awfulness, so do not ask him and do not burden him with what would vex him; or you are one who inquires but cannot bear to hear his news, because it would distress and vex the listener, so do not ask. The first reading is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "and you will not be asked" and the reading of Abdullah: "and you will never be asked."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 120–121:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion. Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [only] guidance." And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have from Allah no protector and no helper.﴾ Know that when Allah, exalted is He, consoled His Messenger with what preceded in the verse, and made clear that the obstacle had been removed on his side, not on theirs, and that they had no excuse for persisting in denying him, He followed this by [showing] that the people, in their obstinacy in falsehood and their steadfastness in their disbelief, had reached the point where they wanted, despite all this, that he follow their religion, and they would not be satisfied with him [merely] having the Book, but wanted him to agree with them in what they were upon. Thereby He made clear the intensity of their enmity toward the Messenger, and explained what makes despair of their agreement necessary. The *millah* (religion) is the *din* (religion). Then He said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [only] guidance."﴾ The meaning is that the guidance of Allah is what leads to Islam, and it is the true guidance; and what can rightly be called guidance is entirely this guidance, there being no guidance beyond it. What they call to following is not guidance at all; it is merely desire. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾, meaning their sayings, which are desires and innovations, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, meaning from the religion whose soundness is known through decisive proofs, ﴿you would have from Allah no protector and no helper﴾, meaning no one to aid you, to protect you and to defend you; rather, Allah protects you from the people if you remain in obedience and hold fast to His rope.

They said: The verse indicates several matters, among them that one whom Allah knows will not do a thing may nonetheless be threatened for doing it. In this case Allah knew that he would not follow their desires, and yet He threatened him for it. A parallel is His saying: ﴿If you were to associate [others with Allah], your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. This threat is good only because it is possible that the threat itself is what deters him from that act, or that this threat is one of its deterrents.

Second: His saying, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, indicates that a threat is not permissible except after the establishment of proofs. And if this is so, then it follows all the more that a threat is not permissible except after capability. Thereby the view of those who permit *taklif ma la yutaq* (imposing what cannot be borne) is refuted.

Third: In it is an indication that following desire is never anything but falsehood, and from this aspect it indicates the invalidity of *taqlid* (blind imitation).

Fourth: In it is an indication that there is no intercessor for one who deserves punishment. For if anyone other than the Messenger were to follow his desire, were he to find an intercessor and helper, the Messenger would be more entitled to that. But this is weak, because following their desires is disbelief, and according to us there is no intercession for disbelief.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it as it should be recited. Those believe in it. And whoever disbelieves in it – it is those who are the losers.﴾ Know that in the verse there are issues:

The first issue: ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who) is in the nominative case by being the subject of a nominal sentence; ﴿ula'ika﴾ (those) is a second subject; and ﴿yu'minuna bihi﴾ (they believe in it) is its predicate.

The second issue: What is meant by His saying, ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾? Who are they? There are two views.

The first view: They are the believers to whom Allah gave the Qur'an. They argued for this from several aspects:

One: His saying, ﴿they recite it as it should be recited﴾, is an exhortation and encouragement to recite this Book, and praise for that recitation. The Book of which this is the character is the Qur'an, not the Torah or the Gospel, since reciting them is not permissible.

Two: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those believe in it﴾, indicates that faith is restricted to them. Had the intended meaning been the People of the Book (*Ahl al-Kitab*), it would not be so.

Three: His saying, ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it – it is those who are the losers﴾. The Book to which this description is fitting is the Qur'an.

The second view: What is meant by ﴿those to whom We have given the Book﴾ is those among the Jews who believed in the Messenger. The evidence for this is that those previously mentioned are the People of the Book. When He censured their path and related their evil deeds, He followed this with praise for those who abandoned their path; indeed, they studied the Torah, abandoned its distortion, and recognized from it the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they recite it as it should be recited﴾: *al-tilawa* (recitation) has two meanings:

One: reading (*al-qira'a*).

The second: following in action (*al-ittiba'*), because one who follows another is said to "recite" him in action. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And by the moon when it follows it﴾ [al-Shams: 2]. The apparent meaning is that it applies to both together, and *mubalagha* (emphasis, intensification) is valid for both together, because one who follows another may fulfill the right of following so that he omits nothing of it, and likewise the reciter fulfills the right of his recitation so that he neglects nothing that is required of it. Those who interpreted it as recitation (*qira'a*) differed on several points:

The first of these: They reflected upon it and acted in accordance with its requirement, until they adhered to its rulings concerning the lawful and the unlawful and other matters.

The second: They humbled themselves at its recitation, and were humbly submissive when they recited the Qur'an in their prayers and in their private moments.

The third: They acted upon its clear (*muhkam*) verses, believed in its ambiguous (*mutashabih*) verses, paused regarding what was unclear to them, and entrusted it to Allah, glorified is He.

The fourth: They read it as Allah revealed it, and did not distort words from their places, nor interpret it in a manner contrary to the truth.

The fifth: The verse should be understood as encompassing all these aspects, because they share a single concept, which is glorifying it and submitting to it in wording and meaning. Therefore it is necessary to carry the wording upon this common element, multiplying the benefits of the speech of Allah, exalted is He. And Allah knows best.
