**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 124 (part 1 of 4):**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them. He said, "Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people." He said, "And from my descendants?" He said, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, had extensively explained the forms of His blessings upon the Children of Israel, and then their ugly deeds in their religions and actions, and concluded this section with what He had begun it with, which is His statement, ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor﴾, up to His statement, ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, He, glorified is He, began here another type of explanation. He mentioned the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, and the manner of his circumstances. The wisdom in this is that Abraham, peace be upon him, is a figure whose virtue is acknowledged by all the sects and religions. The polytheists acknowledged his virtue and took pride in being his descendants, residents of his Sacred Precinct (haram), and servants of his House. The People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab), from among the Jews and Christians, also acknowledged his virtue and took pride in being his descendants. So God, glorified and exalted, related from Abraham matters that obligate the polytheists and the Jews and Christians to accept the words of Muhammad ﷺ, to acknowledge his religion, and to submit to his law. Its explanation comes in several aspects:

The first: When He, exalted is He, commanded him with some obligations, and he fulfilled them and discharged his duty, he indeed attained prophethood and leadership. This alerts the Jews, Christians, and polytheists that good in this world and the Hereafter is attained only by abandoning rebellion, obstinacy, and submitting to the judgment and obligations of God, exalted is He.

The second: He, exalted is He, related of him that he requested leadership for his descendants, and God, exalted is He, said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.﴾ This shows that the office of leadership and authority in religion does not reach the wrongdoers. Thus, whenever these people wish to obtain this office, they are obliged to abandon contention and partisanship for falsehood.

The third: The Hajj is among the distinctive features of the religion of Muhammad ﷺ. God, exalted is He, related this from Abraham so that it would serve as a proof against the Jews and Christians regarding the obligation to submit to it.

The fourth: When the qiblah was changed to the Ka'bah, this was difficult for the Jews and Christians. So God, exalted is He, clarified that this House is the qiblah of Abraham, whose greatness they acknowledge and whose example they are obliged to follow. This was something that would necessitate the removal of that anger from their hearts.

The fifth: Some exegetes (mufassirun) interpreted the words with which God, exalted is He, tested Abraham as matters whose outcome returns to the cleansing of the body. This is something that obligates the polytheists to choose this path, because they acknowledged the virtue of Abraham, peace be upon him, and it obligates them to abandon what they were upon of being stained with blood and abandoning cleanliness. Other exegetes interpreted those words as that Abraham, peace be upon him, endured what he was tested with in the religion of God, exalted is He, which was his contemplation of the stars, the moon, and the sun, and his debating with the worshippers of idols, then his submission to the commands of God, exalted is He, regarding the slaughter of his son and being cast into the fire. This obligates these Jews, Christians, and polytheists, who acknowledge his virtue, to imitate him in this and to follow his way in

— page 32 —

abandoning envy and zealotry and disliking submission to Muhammad ﷺ. These are the aspects for the sake of which God, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Abraham, peace be upon him.

Know that He, exalted is He, related from Abraham, peace be upon him, matters some of which return to the arduous duties with which He charged him, and some of which return to the great honors with which God specially favored him. We will come to their explanation, God willing, and this verse indicates a duty after which came an honor.

* * *

As for the duty, it is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾. Regarding this there are issues:

The first issue: The author of the Kashshaf said: The governing element of "idh" (when) is either an implied verb, as in "And remember when Abraham was tested," or "when He tested him, such and such occurred"; or it is ﴿He said, "Indeed, I will make you﴾.

The second issue: He, exalted is He, described His imposing of duty upon him as a trial (bala') by way of extension (tawassu'), because such a thing among us takes the form of trial, testing, and affliction, since one who is commanded does not know what will come of it. Since this usage became common among us, it is permissible for God, exalted is He, to describe His command and prohibition with this, metaphorically. This is because testing and examination are not permissible for Him, since He, exalted is He, has knowledge of all knowable things, which have no end, in detail, from eternity to eternity.

Hisham ibn al-Hakam said: He had knowledge in eternity only of the realities of things and their quiddities. As for the occurrence of those quiddities and their entry into existence, He does not know them except at the time of their occurrence. He argued for this with the verse and with reason. As for the verse, it is this verse. He said: He, exalted is He, stated explicitly that He tests His servants and examines them, and He mentioned its parallels in other verses, such as His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know the strivers among you and the patient﴾ [Muhammad: 31]; and He said: ﴿to test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7]; and He said in this surah after that: ﴿and We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155]. He also mentioned what confirms this doctrine, such as His statement: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech; perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], and the word "perhaps" (la'alla) is for hope; and He said: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, so that you may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. These verses and their like indicate that He, glorified is He, does not know the occurrence of existing things before they occur. As for reason, it indicates several aspects:

The first: If He were knowing of the occurrence of things before their occurrence, it would necessitate denying power from the Creator and from the creatures, and that is impossible. So whatever leads to something like it is impossible. The proof of the implication: What God, exalted is He, knows to occur, it is impossible that it not occur, because knowledge of the occurrence of a thing and the non-occurrence of that thing are contradictory, and combining two contradictories is impossible. Likewise, what God knows will not occur, its occurrence is impossible, for the very same reason. So if the Creator, exalted is He, were knowing of all particular things before their occurrence, some of them would be necessary to occur and some impossible to occur, and there would be no power at all over the necessary or over the impossible. Thus it would follow the denial of power over these things from the Creator, exalted is He, and from the creatures. We say that this is impossible: as for the Creator, it is because it has been established that the world is originated and has an agent, and that agent must be capable, for if it were necessitating by its essence, its eternity would necessitate the eternity of the world, or the origination of the world would necessitate its origination. As for the creatures, it is because we find within ourselves a necessary awareness that we are able to act and to refrain, in the sense that if we wish to act, we have power over it, and if we wish to refrain, we have power over refraining. So if one of these were necessary and the other impossible, this ability, whose existence is known by necessity, would not be realized.

The second: The attachment of knowledge to one of two known things is different from its attachment to the other known thing. That is why we can conceive of one of the two attachments while being oblivious to the other attachment. If the two attachments were a single attachment, this would be impossible, because a single thing cannot be known and unknown at the same time. Having established this, we say: If He, exalted is He, were knowing of all these particulars, then He would have infinite knowledges, or His knowledge would have infinite attachments. On either assumption, it would follow that infinite existents come into being at once, and that is impossible, because the totality of those things is greater than that same totality when ten of them are subtracted. So the diminished totality is finite, and the greater exceeds the finite by those ten. And when a finite thing is added to an infinite thing, the whole is finite. Therefore the existence of infinite things is impossible. If it is said: What exists is knowledge, and as for those attachments, they are relational matters that have no existence in external reality, we reply: Knowledge is only knowledge if it is attached to the known. So if that attachment were not present in reality, it would follow that knowledge would not be knowledge in reality, and that is impossible.

The third: These infinite knowables, does God know their number or does He not know it? If He knows their number, then they are finite, because whatever has a determinate number is finite. And if God, exalted is He, does not know their number, then He is not knowing of them in detail, and our discussion concerns only detailed knowledge.

The fourth: Every known thing is distinguished in the mind from what is other than it, and everything distinguished from what is other than it, what is other than it is external to it, and whatever is external to it is finite. Therefore every known thing is finite. Hence whatever is infinite is impossible to be known.

The fifth: A thing is only known if knowledge has an attachment to it and a relation to it, and the relation of one thing to another is conditioned upon its being realized in itself. For when a thing has no determinate reality in itself, it is impossible for it to have a relation to something else as such. A particularized thing before its entry into existence was not particularized at all, so it is impossible for it to be an object of knowledge. If it is said: This is refuted by impossibilities and compounds before their entry into existence, for we know them even though they have no determinations at all, we reply: What you have raised is an objection to our argument, not an answer to our argument, and this does not remove doubt and suspicion. Hisham said: These rational aspects indicate that there is no need to turn these verses away from their apparent meanings.

Know that Hisham was the leader of the Rafidah (Rafidites, a name for some Shi'a), and for this reason the early Rafidah adopted the doctrine of al-bada' (the notion of divine change of decree or manifestation of what was not previously known). As for the majority of Muslims, they agreed that He, glorified and exalted, knows particular things before their occurrence. They argued for this by saying that before their occurrence they are valid to be known by God, exalted is He. We say they are valid to be known because we know them before their occurrence, for we know that the sun will rise from its east tomorrow, and occurrence indicates possibility. And we say: Since it is valid for them to be known, it is necessary that they be known to God, exalted is He, because the attachment of God's knowledge to the known is a matter established for Him by His essence. So its attachment to some of what is valid to be known is not more fitting than its attachment to others. If specification occurred, it would require a specifier, and that is impossible. Therefore it is necessary that it not be attached to any of the knowables at all. But if it is attached to some, then it is attached to all of them, and this is what was sought.

As for the first objection, the answer to it is that knowledge of occurrence follows occurrence, and occurrence follows power. So the follower does not contradict the one followed. Knowledge is a necessary consequence and does not dispense with power.

As for the second objection, the answer to it is that it is refuted by the levels of numbers, which have no end.

As for the third objection, the answer to it is that God, exalted is He, does not know their number, and this does not necessitate attributing ignorance to Him, because ignorance is for them to have a determinate number and for God, exalted is He, not to know their number. But when they have no number in themselves, then our saying that God, exalted is He, does not know their number does not necessitate attributing ignorance.

As for the fourth objection, the answer to it is that it is not a condition of the known that knowledge know its distinction from other things, because knowledge of its distinction from other things depends on knowledge of that other thing. So if the dependence of knowledge of a thing upon knowledge of its distinction from other things were the case, and it is established that knowledge of its distinction from others depends on knowledge of others, it would follow that a human being could not know a single thing unless he knew infinite things.

Sure. Here is the translation.

And as for the fifth doubt, its answer is by the refutation we have mentioned. When the doubt is refuted, it falls away, and what we have mentioned of the proof of the all-encompassing knowledge of God Most High remains intact, free from any counter-argument. And success is from God.
* * *
The third issue: Know that the pronoun must refer back to something mentioned earlier. The pronoun is either (1) preceding its referent both verbally and in meaning, or (2) following it both verbally and in meaning, or (3) preceding it verbally but following it in meaning, or (4) the reverse of this.

As for the first type, namely a pronoun preceding its referent both verbally and in meaning, the well-known view among the grammarians is that it is not permissible. Ibn Jinni held that it is permissible, and he argued for this with poetry and with reason. As for poetry, there is his saying:

"May his Lord reward ʿAdiyy ibn Ḥātim on my behalf, a reward like that of the snarling dogs, and indeed he has done so."

As for reason: the agent is influential and the object is receptive, and the connection of the verb to both is strong, so there is nothing far-fetched in placing either of them before the other verbally. Furthermore, we all agree that if the object is placed before the subject verbally, it is permissible; so likewise when it is not placed before, while that placement is permissible.

The second type: the pronoun follows its referent both verbally and in meaning. There is no dispute about its validity, as in your saying: "Zayd struck his slave."

The third type: the pronoun precedes verbally but follows in meaning, as in your saying: "His slave struck Zayd." Here the pronoun, although it precedes verbally, follows in meaning, because the object is, in the underlying structure, after the subject. It becomes as if you had said: "Zayd struck his slave." Therefore it is necessarily permissible.

The fourth type: the pronoun precedes in meaning but follows verbally, as in God's saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord﴾. Here the subject is, in meaning, before the object, so the sense is: "And when his Lord tested Abraham." However, although this is so in meaning, since the pronoun does not precede verbally but rather follows, it is necessarily permissible and good.

The fourth issue: Ibn ʿĀmir read "Ibrāhām" with an alif between the hā᾽ and the mīm, while the rest read "Ibrāhīm," and both are dialectal variants. Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Ḥaywa (may God be pleased with him) read "Ibrāhīmu rabbahu" with Ibrāhīm in the nominative and rabbahu in the accusative. The meaning is that he supplicated Him with words of supplication, acting as one who tests whether God Most High would answer him with them or not.

The fifth issue: The exegetes differed as to whether the apparent wording indicates those words or not. Some said: The wording indicates them, and they are what God mentioned: the imamate, purifying the House, raising its foundations, and the supplication for the sending of Muhammad ﷺ. These are arduous matters. As for the imamate, what is meant here is prophethood, and this duty entails great hardships, for the Prophet ﷺ must bear all the hardships and toils in conveying the message, must not betray any part of it, and even if death is incurred because of that. There is no doubt that this is among the greatest hardships. For this reason we say that the reward of a prophet is greater than the reward of others. As for building the House, purifying it, and raising its foundations, whoever considers what is narrated about how it was built will recognize the severity of the trial in it. Moreover, it includes establishing the rites, and God tested the Friend (al-Khalīl), upon him be peace, with Satan at the site for stoning the pillars and other matters. As for his occupation with supplication that God send Muhammad ﷺ at the end of time, this requires sincerity of action toward God and the complete removal of envy from the heart. Thus it is established that the matters mentioned after this verse are arduous, severe duties, and it is possible that what is meant by God's testing him with the words is that. Then, what indicates that this is the intended meaning is that He followed it by mentioning it without any conjunctive particle, and he (Abraham) did not accept, and said: ﴿Indeed I am making you an imam for the people﴾, rather He said: ﴿Indeed I am making you﴾. This indicates that the testing is nothing but the imposition of these mentioned matters. The judge (al-Qāḍī) objected to this view, saying: This would only be permissible if God had said: "And when his Lord tested Abraham with words, and Abraham fulfilled them, then He said to him after that: 'Indeed I am making you an imam for the people.'" But this is not the case; rather He mentioned His saying: ﴿Indeed I am making you an imam for the people﴾ after His saying: ﴿fulfilled them﴾, and this indicates that God tested him with the words and Abraham fulfilled them, and then God said to him after that: ﴿Indeed I am making you an imam for the people﴾. It may be answered that what is meant by the words is not the imamate alone, but the imamate, building the House, purifying it, and the supplication for the sending of Muhammad ﷺ; as if God tested him with the totality of these matters. God informed about him that He tested him with matters in summary, then informed that he fulfilled them, then followed that with detail and explanation. This is not far-fetched.

The second view: The apparent wording gives no indication of what these words are. This view allows two possibilities:

The first possibility: words with which God obligated him, namely His commands and prohibitions, so it is as if He said: "And when his Lord tested Abraham with words," with whatever He willed of obligating him to act upon them.

The second possibility: words that are from Abraham, which he speaks to his people, i.e., he conveys them to them. Those who held the first possibility differed as to what that obligation was, with several views.

The first: Ibn ʿAbbās said: They are ten characteristics which were obligatory in his law and are sunnah in our law: five on the head and five on the body. Those on the head: rinsing the mouth, sniffing water into the nose, parting the hair, trimming the moustache, and the siwak. Those on the body: circumcision, shaving the pubic area, plucking the armpit hair, clipping the nails, and cleansing with water.

The second: Some said: He was tested with thirty characteristics of Islam, ten of them in Sūrat Barāʾa: ﴿The repentant, the worshippers﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:112] to the end of the verse; ten of them in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb: ﴿Indeed the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:35] to the end of the verse; and ten of them in al-Mu'minūn: ﴿The believers have succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minūn 23:1] to His saying: ﴿those are the inheritors﴾ [al-Mu'minūn 23:10]. Ten were also narrated in: ﴿A questioner asked﴾ [al-Maʿārij 70:1] to His saying: ﴿and those who are upon their prayers maintain them﴾ [al-Maʿārij 70:34]. Thus he made them forty portions, according to Ibn ʿAbbās.

The third: He commanded him with the rites of the Hajj, such as circumambulation, running between Ṣafā and Marwah, stoning, and the state of ihrām. This is the view of Qatādah and Ibn ʿAbbās.

The fourth: He tested him with seven things: with the sun, the moon, the stars, circumcision in old age, the fire, the sacrifice of the son, and the emigration; and he fulfilled all of them. For this reason God said: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled﴾ [al-Najm 53:37]. This is from al-Ḥasan.

The fifth: That what is meant is what He mentioned in His saying: ﴿When his Lord said to him: "Submit," he said: "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:131].

The sixth: The numerous debates about monotheism with his father and his people and with Nimrod; the prayer, zakāh, fasting, the division of spoils, hospitality, and patience in these. Al-Qaffāl (may God have mercy on him) said: The gist is that testing encompasses the imposition of everything in whose performance there is burden, severity and hardship. So the wording includes the totality of these matters and includes each one of them. If the narration is established for all of them, it is necessary to affirm all of them. If the narration is established for some and not others, then conflict arises among these narrations, and so suspension of judgment is obligatory. God knows best.

The sixth issue: The judge said: This testing occurred before prophethood, because God indicated that his standing by these words was like a cause for God to make him an imam, and the cause precedes the effect; therefore this testing must be existentially prior to his becoming an imam. This also accords with the dictates of reason, for fulfillment is among the conditions of prophethood, and it is not attained except by turning away from all the pleasures and desires of this world, abandoning flattery toward creation, denouncing the false religions and corrupt beliefs they hold, and bearing harm from every kind of people. There is no doubt that this meaning is among the greatest hardships and the most weighty toils. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ has a greater reward than his community. Since this is so, God tested him with arduous duties, and when he fulfilled them, peace be upon him, He certainly granted him the robe of prophethood and messengership.

Others said: It was after prophethood, because he, peace be upon him, would not know that he was obligated with those duties except through revelation, so revelation must precede his knowledge of being so obligated. The judge answered this by saying: It is possible that God revealed to him, through Gabriel, peace be upon him, these arduous duties, and when he completed them, He made him a prophet sent to creation.

Now that you know this issue, we say: The judge said: It is permissible that what is meant by the words is what al-Ḥasan mentioned concerning the star, the sun and the moon, for God tested him with that before prophethood. As for the sacrifice of the son, the emigration, and the fire, all of these were after prophethood; and likewise circumcision, for it is narrated that he circumcised himself and he was one hundred and twenty years old. Then he said: If a decisive revelatory proof establishes that what is meant by the words is these matters, then what is meant by His saying "fulfilled them" is that He, glory be to Him, knew from his state that he would fulfill them and stand by them after prophethood, and therefore He granted him the robe of imamate and prophethood.

The seventh issue: The pronoun concealed in ﴿fulfilled them﴾ in one of the two readings refers to Ibrāhīm, meaning he stood by them as they should be stood by, and performed them in the best performance, without neglect or laxity. Similar to it is: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled﴾ [al-Najm 53:37]. In the other reading it refers to God Most High, meaning: He gave him what he asked for, not diminishing anything of it.

* * *
As for God's saying: ﴿Indeed I am making you an imam for the people﴾, the imam is the name of one who is followed, like the waistwrap is for what one wraps around oneself with, i.e., they follow you in your religion. On this there are issues:

The first issue: The people of verification said: What is meant by the imam here is the prophet, and this is indicated by several points:

The first: His saying: ﴿an imam for the people﴾ indicates that God made him an imam for all people, and whoever is so must be a messenger from God, independently holding the law, for if he were a follower of another messenger he would be one who is led by that messenger, not an imam for him; in that case the generality would be void.

The second: The wording indicates that he is an imam in every matter, and whoever is so must be a prophet.

[Page 37]

Third: The prophets, peace be upon them, are imams in the sense that the creation is obligated to follow them. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We made them leaders, guiding by Our command﴾ [al-Anbiya: 73]. The caliphs are also imams, because they are placed in the position that obligates people to follow them, to accept their word and their rulings. Judges and jurists are likewise imams in this sense. The one who leads the people in prayer is also called an imam, because whoever enters into his prayer is bound to follow him (iqtida'). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The imam is appointed only to be followed. So when he bows, bow; when he prostrates, prostrate; and do not differ with your imam." Thus it is established that the name imam applies to one who deserves to be followed in religion. It may also be applied to one who is followed in falsehood. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas: 41]. However, the name imam is not applied to such a person without restriction; it is used of him only with a qualifier. When He mentioned the imams of misguidance, He qualified the word with His saying: ﴿calling to the Fire﴾. This is like the name god (ilah), which applies only to the true object of worship. As for a false object of worship, the name god is applied to it only with a qualifier. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So their gods, which they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them anything﴾ [Hud: 101], and He says: ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted﴾ [Ta-Ha: 97]. Since it is established that the name imam covers what we have mentioned, and since it is established that the prophets are at the highest rank of imamate, it is necessary to interpret the word here in that sense. This is because Allah the Exalted mentioned the word imam here in the context of bestowing favour, so that blessing must be among the greatest blessings, for the attribution of favour to be fitting. Therefore this imamate must be interpreted as prophethood.

The second issue: When Allah promised him that He would make him an imam for the people, He fulfilled that promise until the Hour. Followers of the religions, despite the severity of their differences and the extremity of their opposition, honour Abraham, peace be upon him, and take pride in being linked to him, either by lineage or by religion and law. Even idol-worshippers used to honour Abraham, peace be upon him. Allah the Exalted says in His Book: ﴿Then We revealed to you, follow the religion of Abraham, upright﴾ [al-Nahl: 123], and He says: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130]. He says at the end of Surah al-Hajj: ﴿The religion of your father Abraham. He named you Muslims before﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. And all of the community of Muhammad, peace be upon him, say at the end of the prayer: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Abraham and the family of Abraham, and show mercy to Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You showed mercy to Abraham and the family of Abraham."

The third issue: Those who hold that the imam does not become imam except through explicit designation (nass) cling to this verse. They say that Allah the Exalted made clear that he became imam only because of an explicit designation of his imamate. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Indeed I will make on earth a successor (khalifah)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. Thus He made clear that the office of caliphate is not attained except through explicit designation. This argument is weak, because we have shown that the imamate here means prophethood. Even if we grant that it means general imamate, the verse indicates that explicit designation is a way to imamate, and there is no dispute about that. The dispute is whether imamate may be established without explicit designation, and this verse does not address that question, either by negation or by affirmation.

The fourth issue: His saying: ﴿Indeed I will make you an imam for the people﴾ indicates that he, peace be upon him, was protected (ma'sum) from all sins. This is because the imam is the one who is followed and emulated. If sin proceeded from him, it would be obligatory for us to emulate him in it, and so it would follow that it is obligatory for us to commit sin. That is impossible, because being a sin means being prohibited from doing it, and being obligatory means being prohibited from abandoning it, and both together are impossible.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And of my offspring﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: "Dhurriyyah" (offspring) means children and grandchildren of a man. It derives from "dhara'a Allahu al-khalq" (Allah created creation), and they dropped the hamzah for lightness, as they did in "al-barriyyah." There is another view, that it is derived from "dharr" (ants/particles).

The second issue: His saying "and of my offspring" is conjoined to the kaf (you) in "I will make you." It is as if he said: "and making some of my offspring [imams]." This is like someone saying to you: "I will honour you," and you reply: "and Zayd."

The third issue: Some said: Allah informed him that among his offspring there would be prophets. He wished to know whether this would apply to all of them or to some, and whether all of them were suited to this matter. Allah informed him that among them there is a wrongdoer who is not suited to it. Others said: He, peace be upon him, mentioned that by way of inquiry, and since he did not know its precise scope, Allah answered him explicitly that prophethood does not reach the wrongdoers among them. If it is asked: Was Abraham, peace be upon him, permitted to say: "and of my offspring," or was he not permitted? If Allah permitted this supplication, why did He reject his supplication? And if He did not permit him, then that would be a sin. We answer: His saying "and of my offspring" indicates that he, peace be upon him, asked that some of his offspring be imams for the people. Allah the Exalted fulfilled the answer to his supplication among the believers of his offspring, such as Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Yusuf, Musa, Harun, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yunus, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa, and He made their last Muhammad (ﷺ) from among his offspring, who is the most excellent of the prophets and imams, peace be upon them.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: Hamzah and Hafs, from 'Asim, read "'ahdi" (my covenant) with a sukun on the ya', while the rest read it with a fatha. Some read: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: whoever among your offspring is a wrongdoer, indeed My covenant does not reach him.

The second issue: They mentioned several views about the covenant:
First: that this covenant is the imamate mentioned previously. If the imamate meant there is prophethood, then the covenant is also prophethood; otherwise it is not.
Second: "My covenant" means My mercy, according to 'Ata'.
Third: My obedience, according to al-Dahhak.
Fourth: My security, according to Abu 'Ubayd.
The first view is preferable, because his saying "and of my offspring" is a request for that imamate which He had promised him with His saying: ﴿Indeed I will make you an imam for the people﴾. Therefore His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ can only be an answer to that question if by this covenant is meant that imamate.

The third issue: The verse indicates that Allah will give some of his descendants what he asked for. Had that not been so, the answer would have been "No," or He would have said: "My covenant does not reach your offspring." If it is asked: Did Abraham, peace be upon him, not know that prophethood is not fitting for wrongdoers? We answer: Yes, he did know. But he did not know the condition of his descendants, so Allah made clear that some of them have this condition, and that prophethood is granted only to one who is not a wrongdoer.

The fourth issue: The Rafidah (Rawafid) used this verse to discredit the imamate of Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, in three ways:
The first: Abu Bakr and Umar were disbelievers, and while in disbelief they were wrongdoers. It is therefore necessary that it be true of them in that state that they do not attain the covenant of imamate at all. And if it is true of them at that time that they never attain the covenant of imamate, nor at any other time, it is established that they are not suited for imamate.
The second: Whoever is sinful inwardly is among the wrongdoers. So, unless one knows that Abu Bakr and Umar were not among the wrongdoers, sinful outwardly and inwardly, one must not judge them to be imams. This holds only for one whose infallibility is established, and since they were not infallible by consensus, their imamate cannot be established at all.
The third: They said: They were polytheists, and every polytheist is a wrongdoer, and a wrongdoer does not attain the covenant of imamate; so it follows that the covenant of imamate does not reach them. That they were polytheists is agreed upon. That the polytheist is a wrongdoer is based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, association is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. That the wrongdoer does not attain the covenant of imamate is based on this verse. It cannot be said that they were wrongdoers while in disbelief, so after the disbelief is removed the name no longer applies. We say: The wrongdoer is one in whom wrongdoing has been found, and our saying "wrongdoing has been found in him" is more general than our saying "wrongdoing has been found in him in the past or in the present." This is shown by the fact that this concept can be divided into these two categories. The subject of a division into two categories is common to both categories, and whatever is common to both categories must be negated when one category is negated. Therefore, from the negation of his being a wrongdoer in the present it does not follow that he is not a wrongdoer. What indicates this, considering the legal evidences, is that the one asleep is called a believer, and faith is assent, and assent is not present while one is asleep. This shows that he is called a believer because faith was present before. Once this is established, it is necessary that he be a wrongdoer because of a wrong that existed before. Also, speech is a succession of letters, and walking is a succession of states in successive places. The totality of those things does not exist at any single moment. Therefore, if the presence of the derivative's root were a condition for the derived name to be literally true, then the names "speaker," "walker," and similar would not be literally true of anything at all, and that is definitively false. This shows that the presence of the root is not a condition for the derived name to be literally true.

The response: All that you have mentioned is countered by the following: If someone swears not to greet a disbeliever, and then greets a person who is now a believer but was a disbeliever many years before, he does not break his oath. This shows what we have said. Also, one who repents from disbelief is not called a disbeliever, and one who repents from sin is not called a sinner. The same applies to its parallels. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And do not incline toward those who wronged﴾ [Hud: 113]? He forbade inclining toward them while they persist in wrongdoing. And His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91] means: upon those who persist in good. Moreover, we have shown that the imamate in this verse means prophethood, and whoever disbelieves in Allah even for the blink of an eye is not fit for prophethood.

* * *

The fifth issue: The majority of jurists and theologians said: A corrupt person (fasiq), while in his corruption, may not be appointed as imam. They differed over whether corruption that arises after appointment invalidates the imamate. The majority argued that a corrupt person is not fit to be appointed imam, using this verse, and the argument from it is in two ways:
The first: We have shown that His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ is an answer to His saying: ﴿And of my offspring﴾, and His saying: ﴿And of my offspring﴾ is a request for the imamate that Allah mentioned. Therefore this covenant must mean the imamate, so that the answer corresponds to the question. The verse thus becomes as if He said: "The imamate does not reach the wrongdoers," and every disobedient person is a wrongdoer to himself. So the verse indicates what we have said. If it is objected: The apparent meaning of the verse requires that they not be wrongdoers outwardly and inwardly, and this does not hold for imams and judges, we answer: As for the Shi'ah, they use this verse to support their view that infallibility, outwardly and inwardly, is obligatory. As for us, we say: The verse's implication is that, but we have set aside consideration of the inward state, so outward uprightness (al-'adalah al-zahirah) remains a requirement. If it is objected: Did not Yunus, peace be upon him, say: ﴿Glory be to You; indeed I was of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87], and did not Adam say: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]? We answer: What is mentioned in the verse is absolute wrongdoing, and this is not present in Adam and Yunus, peace be upon them both.

**Page 40**

The second aspect: the covenant (*'ahd*) may be used in God's Book to mean a command. God the Exalted said: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 60], meaning: did I not command you of this? And God the Exalted said: ﴿They say: God has enjoined (*'ahida*) upon us﴾ [Al 'Imran: 183], meaning: He commanded us. From this is the usage of the caliphs' written instructions (*'uhud*) to their governors and judges. Since it is established that the covenant of God is His command, we say: His statement ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ can only mean one of two things. Either it means that wrongdoers are not commanded, or it means that wrongdoers cannot occupy a position from which God's commands would be accepted from them. Since the first meaning is invalid, by the consensus (*ijma'*) of the Muslims that God's commands bind wrongdoers just as they bind others, the second meaning is established: that they are not trusted with God's commands and are not to be followed in them, and therefore they cannot be leaders (*a'imma*) in religion. Thus the indication of the verse establishes the invalidity of the leadership of a sinner (*fasiq*). The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "There is no obedience to any creature in disobedience to the Creator." The verse also indicates that a sinner cannot be a judge, that his rulings are not enforced if he holds the office of judgeship, that his testimony is not accepted, nor his report from the Prophet (ﷺ), nor his legal opinion (*fatwa*) if he issues one, and that he is not to be put forward to lead the prayer, even if the prayer behind him would not be invalidated. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: Some people think that the doctrine of Abu Hanifa is that a sinner may be an imam and caliph, but may not be a judge. He said: This is an error. Abu Hanifa did not distinguish between the caliph and the judge in that the condition for each of them is uprightness ('adala). How could he be a caliph while his narration is not accepted and his rulings are not enforceable? How could anyone claim this of Abu Hanifa when Ibn Hubayra compelled him to accept judgeship during the days of the Banu Umayya, and beat him, and he refused, so he was imprisoned? Ibn Hubayra persisted and began beating him with whips every day. When he was feared for, the jurists said to him: Take up for him some task of his work, whatever it may be, until the beating stops from you. So he undertook for him to count the bundles of straw that entered, and he was released. Then al-Mansur summoned him to something similar, until he counted for him the bricks that were being made for the wall of the city of al-Mansur. His story concerning the matter of Zayd ibn 'Ali is well known, as is his carrying of money to him and his issuing of legal opinions to people in secret on the obligation of supporting him and fighting alongside him. Likewise was his position regarding Muhammad and Ibrahim, the two sons of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan. He said: Whoever erred regarding this report erred because the statement of Abu Hanifa is that if a judge is upright in himself, and he assumed the judgeship from an unjust ruler, his rulings are enforceable and prayer behind him is valid. This is because if a judge is upright in himself and it is possible for him to enforce rulings, his rulings are enforceable. No consideration is given in this to the one who appointed him, because the one who appointed him is in the position of all his assistants, and it is not a condition for a judge's assistants that they be upright. Do you not see that if the people of a town that has no ruler agreed, being content, to appoint a just man from among them as judge, so that they would be his helpers against whoever refused to accept his rulings, his judgment would be enforceable, even if he had no authority from an imam or ruler? And God knows best.

**The sixth issue:** The verse indicates the infallibility (*'ismat*) of the prophets in two respects:

The first: It has been established that what is meant by this covenant is the imamate (leadership). There is no doubt that every prophet is an imam, for the imam is the one who is followed, and the prophet is the most worthy of people to be followed. If the verse indicates that an imam cannot be a sinner, then it indicates all the more that the Messenger cannot be a sinner, committing sin and disobedience.

The second: He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. If this covenant is prophethood, then none of the wrongdoers may attain it. If it is the imamate, then likewise, because every prophet must be an imam who is followed, and every sinner is a wrongdoer to himself. Therefore prophethood must not be attained by any of the sinners. And God knows best.

**The seventh issue:** Know that He, glorified is He, has explained that He has a covenant with you and you have a covenant with Him. He explained that whenever you fulfill your covenant, He too fulfills His covenant. He said: ﴿Fulfill My covenant, I will fulfill your covenant﴾ [Al-Baqara: 40]. Then, in the rest of the verses, He mentions your covenant separately and mentions His own covenant separately. As for your covenant, He said of it: ﴿And those who fulfill their covenant when they make one﴾ [Al-Baqara: 177], and He said: ﴿And those who are keepers of their trusts and their covenant﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 8], and He said: ﴿O you who believe, fulfill the contracts﴾ [Al-Ma'ida: 1], and He said: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do? Greatly hateful is it in the sight of God that you say what you do not do﴾ [As-Saff: 2–3]. As for His covenant, glorified and exalted is He, He said of it: ﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than God?﴾ [At-Tawba: 111]. Then He explained the manner of His covenant with our father Adam, saying: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no determination﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115]. Then He explained the manner of His covenant with us, saying:

**Page 41**

﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam﴾ [Ya-Sin: 60]. Then He explained the manner of His covenant with the Children of Israel, saying: ﴿God has enjoined upon us that we not believe in any messenger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 183]. Then He explained the manner of His covenant with the prophets, peace be upon them, saying: ﴿And We charged Abraham and Ishmael﴾ [Al-Baqara: 125]. Then He explained in this verse that His covenant does not reach the wrongdoers, saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. This great emphasis in this mutual covenant requires investigating the reality of this covenant. So we say: The covenant taken upon you is nothing but the covenant of service and servitude, and the covenant that God, exalted is He, has undertaken on His part is nothing but the covenant of mercy and lordship. Then, if the intelligent person reflects on the state of this mutual covenant, he will find nothing from himself but breaking this covenant, and from his Lord nothing but fulfilling the covenant. So let us begin to explore the foundations of this topic. We say: The first of His bounties upon you is the bounty of creation, bringing into existence, giving life, and bestowing intellect and faculties. The purpose of all of that is your occupation with obedience, service, and servitude, as He said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 56]. He declared Himself far above creating in this manner in vain, saying: ﴿We did not create the heaven and earth and what is between them in play﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 16]. He also said: ﴿We did not create the heaven and earth and what is between them without purpose. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾ [Sad: 27]. And He said: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 115]. Then He explained in detail what the wisdom is in the creation and bringing into existence, saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 56]. So He, glorified is He, has fulfilled the covenant of lordship, in that He created you, gave you life, bestowed upon you the various kinds of blessings, and made you rational and discerning. So if you do not occupy yourself with His service, obedience, and worship, then you have broken the covenant of your servitude, while God, exalted is He, has fulfilled the covenant of His lordship.

The second: The covenant of lordship requires giving success (*tawfiq*) and guidance, and the covenant of servitude from you requires striving and diligence in action. Then He fulfilled the covenant of lordship, for He did not leave a single atom of atoms except that He made it a guide for you to the path of truth: ﴿There is not a thing except that it exalts Him with praise﴾ [Al-Isra: 44]. Yet you have not at all fulfilled the covenant of obedience and servitude.

The third: God's blessing of faith is the greatest of blessings. The proof of this is that if this blessing were lost to you, you would be the most wretched of the wretched forever and ever. Then this blessing is from God, as He said: ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from God﴾ [An-Nahl: 53]. Then, although this blessing is from Him, He thanks you for it, and He said: ﴿And those, their effort is appreciated﴾ [Al-Isra: 19]. If God, exalted is He, thanks you for this blessing, then it is all the more fitting that you thank Him for what He has given of success and guidance. Yet you have brought nothing but ingratitude, as He said: ﴿Destroyed is man; how ungrateful he is!﴾ [Abasa: 17]. So He has fulfilled His covenant, and you have broken your covenant.

The fourth: That His blessings be spent in the way of His pleasure. His covenant with you is that He gives you the kinds of blessings, and He has done so. Your covenant with Him is that you spend His blessings in the way of His pleasure, and you have not done that: ﴿No! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 6–7].

The fifth: He has bestowed upon you various kinds of blessings so that you would be a benefactor to the poor: ﴿And do good; indeed God loves the doers of good﴾ [Al-Baqara: 195]. Then you have used Him as a means to harm people and make them feel estranged: ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin upon people stinginess﴾ [An-Nisa: 37].

The sixth: He has given you great blessings so that you would be turned toward His praise, while you praise other than Him. Consider a great sultan who bestows upon you a precious robe of honor, and then in his presence you turn away from him and remain occupied with serving some worthless people. How do you deserve reproach and loathing? So it is likewise here. Know that if we occupied ourselves with explaining the manner of His fulfillment of the covenant of benevolence and lordship,

**Page 42**

and the manner of our breaking of the covenant of sincerity and servitude, we would not be able to do so. For from the beginning of life to its end, we have not been free for a single moment from the kinds of His blessings upon our outward and inward selves. Each of those blessings demands a separate thanks and a separate service. Then we have not brought them, rather we have not even become aware of them, nor known their manner or their quantity. Then He, glorified is He, despite the increase of our heedlessness and negligence, increases the kinds of blessings, mercy, and generosity. So from the beginning of our lives to their end, we keep increasing in degrees of deficiency, shortcoming, and deserving blame, while He, glorified is He, keeps increasing in benevolence, kindness, generosity, and deserving praise and commendation. For whenever our shortcoming is greater, His bestowal upon us afterward is of greater effect, and whenever His bestowal upon us is greater in effect, our shortcoming in thanking Him is more ugly and more evil. So our actions continue to increase in ugliness, and His beautiful acts continue perpetually, in a way that does not lead to cessation. Then He said in this verse: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, and this is a severe warning. We say: Our God, from You has proceeded what befits You of generosity, pardon, mercy, and benevolence, and from us has proceeded what befits us of ignorance, treachery, shortcoming, and laziness. So we ask You, by Yourself and by Your abundant grace, to overlook us, O Most Merciful of the merciful.

**[Page 43]**

God Most High says: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, and [said], "Take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer." And We charged Abraham and Ishmael, [saying], "Purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stay in it, and those who bow and prostrate."﴾

Know that God Most High explained the state of Abraham, peace be upon him, when He assigned him the office of imamate. This is an explanation of the second charge, which is the charge to purify the House. Next, we say: as for "the House" (al-bayt), it means the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram). He suffices with mentioning "the House" without qualification because of the definite article (al-) attached to it, since the article is used to define either a known referent (al-ma'hud) or a whole category (al-jins). The addressees knew that it was not meant as the category, so it was understood as the known referent for them, namely the Ka'ba. Next, we say: the intended meaning is not the Ka'ba itself, because God described it as "a sanctuary" (amnan), and this is a attribute of the entire Haram, not of the Ka'ba alone. The evidence that the term "House" may be used while meaning the whole Haram is God's words: ﴿as an offering to reach the Ka'ba﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 95]. What is meant there is the entire Haram, not the Ka'ba itself, because animals are not slaughtered inside the Ka'ba or in the Masjid al-Haram. Likewise is His words: ﴿so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾ [al-Tawba: 28]. What is meant, God knows best, is preventing them from attending the places of the rites of pilgrimage. In another verse He said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67]. God also said in another verse, reporting about Abraham: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. This shows that He described the House with security, and this implies the entire Haram. The reason that God used the word "House" and meant the whole Haram is that the sanctity of the Haram was due to the House, so it was permissible to refer to it by the name of the House.

* * *

As for God's words ﴿a place of return for the people﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: The lexicographers said: its root is from thāba, yathūbu, mathāba and thawban, meaning "to return." It is said: "The water returned (thāba)," when it came back to the river after it had stopped. And "his intellect returned to so-and-so," meaning it came back, and the people dispersed from him; then "they returned (thābū)," meaning they came back gathered together. The word thawāb (reward) is derived from this, as if what a person gives out of wealth or other things returns to him. Al-mathāb from the well is the gathering place of water at its bottom. Al-Qaffal said: it is said that mathāban and mathāba are two dialects, like maqām and maqāma, and this is the view of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It is also said that the "ha'" (tā' marbūṭa) was added to mathāba for emphasis, as in their saying nassāba (genealogist) and 'allāma (very knowledgeable). The original form of mathāba is mathūba, on the pattern mafʿula.

Second issue: al-Hasan said: its meaning is that they return to it every year. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid that no one departs from it without wishing to return to it. God Most High said: ﴿So make hearts among the people incline toward them﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. It is also said: mathāba means that they come to it for pilgrimage and thus are rewarded for it. If it is asked: the House being a place of return happens merely by their returning to it, and that occurs by their own action, not by the action of God Most High; so what is the meaning of His words ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people﴾? We reply: as for our view, the act of the servant is created by God Most High, so this verse is evidence for our position on this issue. As for the view of the Mu'tazila, its meaning is that God placed its glorification in hearts so that this would be a motive for them to return to it time after time. God did this because of the benefits it contains for this world and the Hereafter. As for the benefits of this world: the people of the East and West gather there, so there arise trade and various kinds of livelihood that bring great benefit. Also, by means of travel for pilgrimage, roads and lands are developed, and the diverse conditions of the world are witnessed.

As for the benefits of religion: whoever sets out for the House, desiring worship and drawing near to God Most High, and showing servitude to Him, and persevering in the 'umra and circumambulation, and establishing prayer in that honored mosque, and seclusion (i'tikaf) in it, merits by that a great reward with God Most High.

Second issue: Some of our companions relied on God's words ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people﴾ as evidence for the obligation of 'umra (the lesser pilgrimage). The way of inference from it is that His words ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people﴾ inform us that He made it characterized by being a place of return for the people. But it is not possible to apply the verse to this meaning, because being a place of return for the people is an attribute that depends on the choice of the people, and what depends on the choice of the people cannot be achieved by compulsion or coercion. When it is established that the verse cannot be applied to its apparent meaning, it becomes necessary to interpret the verse as an obligation, because when we interpret it as an obligation, that is more likely to make it so than if we interpret it as recommendation. Thus it is established that God obligated us to return to it time after time. It has been agreed that this obligation is not fulfilled in anything other than circumambulation (tawaf), so it is required that it be fulfilled in circumambulation. This is the way of inference from this verse. Most of those who have spoken about the rulings of the Qur'an have criticized the indication of this verse for this ruling, but we have shown its indication for it in this way that we have explained.

As for God's words ﴿and a sanctuary﴾, meaning a place of security. There is no doubt that His words ﴿We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary﴾ are a statement (khabar). Sometimes we leave it on its apparent meaning and say it is a statement; and sometimes we turn it away from its apparent meaning and say it is a command.

As for the first view: the meaning is that God made the people of the Haram safe from famine and drought, as He said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67] and His words: ﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary to which the fruits of everything are brought?﴾ [al-Qasas: 57]. It is not possible that what is meant by it is a report that killing does not occur in the Haram, because we observe that unlawful killing does sometimes occur in it. Also, lawful killing may occur in it. God Most High said: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you in it; but if they fight you, then kill them﴾ [al-Baqara: 191]. So He informed of the occurrence of killing in it.

The second view: we interpret it as a command by way of ta'wil (interpretation). The meaning is that God commanded people to make that place a safe place from raids and killing. Thus the House was honored by the judgment of God Most High. The people of the pre-Islamic era (jahiliyya) adhered to its sanctity; they would not attack anyone who took refuge in it, and they used to call the Quraysh "the People of God" in glorification of it. Then the matter of hunting was also taken into account, to the extent that a dog would chase a gazelle outside the Haram, the gazelle would flee, and the dog would pursue it; but when the gazelle entered the Haram, the dog would not pursue it. Reports were also transmitted about the sanctity of Mecca. He, peace be upon him, said: "God made Mecca sacred, and it is not lawful for anyone before me, and it is not lawful for anyone after me; it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day, and its sanctity has returned as it was." Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, held that the meaning is that it was not made lawful for anyone to wage war upon it, and that this was made lawful for the Messenger of God ﷺ. As for one who enters the House from among those who are liable to legal punishments (hudud), al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: the imam orders that he be pressed in a way that leads to his leaving the Haram; when he leaves, the legal punishment is carried out on him outside the Haram. If he does not leave until he is killed in the Haram, it is permissible. Likewise, whoever fights in the Haram may be killed there. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: it is not permissible. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, argued that when 'Asim ibn Thabit ibn al-Aflah was killed, and Khubayb (was killed), the Prophet ﷺ ordered the killing of Abu Sufyan in his house in Mecca by treachery, if he could be reached. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: this was at the time when Mecca was sacred, and so this shows that it does not protect anyone from something that is obligatory upon him, and that it is only protected from having war waged upon it, just as war is waged upon other places. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, argued with this verse. The answer to him is that His words ﴿and a sanctuary﴾ do not state what He made it a sanctuary from; so it is possible that it is a sanctuary from famine, and that it is a sanctuary from waging war, and that it is a sanctuary from carrying out legal punishments. The expression is not of a general form that would require it to be applied to all of these; rather, interpreting it as security from famine and calamities is more preferable, because on this explanation we do not need to take the form of the statement to mean a command, whereas in all the other views we need to do that. Therefore al-Shafi'i's view, may God have mercy on him, is more preferable.

* * *

As for God's words ﴿And take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read ﴿and take﴾ (wa-ittakhidhū) with a kasra on the kha', in the form of a command. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the kha' (wa-ittakhadhū), in the form of a statement.

As for the first reading: the words ﴿and take﴾ are coordinated with something, and there are several views on this.

The first: that it is coordinated with His words ﴿Remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾, and ﴿and take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾.

The second: that it is coordinated with His words ﴿Indeed I will make you an imam for the people﴾. The meaning is that when He tested him with words and he fulfilled them, He said to him, as a reward for what he had done of that: ﴿Indeed I will make you an imam for the people﴾, and He said: ﴿and take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾. It is also possible that He commanded this to his son, except that God Most High omitted His saying "and He said." A parallel to this is His words: ﴿And they thought that it would befall them: "Take what We have given you with strength"﴾ [al-A'raf: 171].

The third: this is a command from God Most High to the community of Muhammad ﷺ that they take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer. It is a statement that has been inserted in the midst of the account of Abraham, peace be upon him. Its structure seems to be: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, and [you], take [it]﴾; the meaning being that since We honored it and described it as a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, then take it yourselves as a qibla for yourselves. The conjunction "wa" (and) and the particle "fa" (then) are each sometimes mentioned in this position, although "fa" is clearer. As for the one who reads ﴿wa-ittakhadhū﴾ with a fatha, it is a statement about the children of Abraham, that they took from his station a place of prayer. So this is coordinated with "We made the House," and they took it as a place of prayer. It is also possible that it is coordinated with "And when We made the House," and "and when they took it as a place of prayer."

Second issue: They mentioned several views on what the station of Abraham, peace be upon him, is:

The first view: it is the place of the stone on which Abraham, peace be upon him, stood. Then these scholars mentioned two aspects:

One of them:
