It is the stone which the wife of Ishmael placed under the foot of Abraham, peace be upon him, when she washed his head. Abraham, peace be upon him, placed his foot on it while he was riding, and she washed one side of his head. Then she lifted it from under him, and his foot had sunk into the stone; so she placed it under the other foot, and his foot also sank into it. God Most High made this one of his miracles. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The second: what was reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that Abraham, peace be upon him, was building the House while Ishmael was handing him the stones, and they were saying: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us; indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [al-Baqara: 127]. When the building rose high and Abraham, peace be upon him, became weak from placing the stones, he stood upon a stone, and it was the station of Abraham, peace be upon him.

The second view: the station of Abraham is the entire Haram. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: it is 'Arafa, Muzdalifa and the jamarat. This is the view of 'Ata'.

The fourth: the entire Hajj is the station of Abraham. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The verifying scholars agreed that the first view is more preferable, and there are several reasons that indicate it.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 125 (part 2 of 3):**

The first: Jabir narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) finished the circumambulation (tawaf), he came to the Station (maqam) and recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And take, from the Station of Ibrahim, a place of prayer﴾. The recitation of this expression at that location shows that what is meant by this expression is that very place, which is evident.

Second: In custom, this name is specific to that place. The proof of this is that if a questioner asked a Meccan in Mecca about the Station of Ibrahim, he would not answer him and would understand nothing from it except this place.

Third: It was narrated that "he (ﷺ) passed by the Station with Umar, and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is this not the station of our father Ibrahim?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Shall we not take it as a place of prayer?' He said: 'I have not been commanded to do that.' Then the sun had not set on that day before the verse was revealed."

Fourth: The stone came under his two feet in the moisture of the clay until the feet of Ibrahim (ﷺ... peace be upon him) sank into it. This is among the clearest proofs of the Oneness of Allah the Exalted and of the miracle of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Therefore its being specifically associated with Ibrahim is more fitting than its being associated with anyone else, so applying this name to it is more fitting.

Fifth: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And take, from the Station of Ibrahim, a place of prayer﴾. Prayer has no connection with the Sacred Precinct (haram) or with any other places except this place. Therefore the Station of Ibrahim must be this place.

Sixth: The Station of Ibrahim is the place of his standing. It is established by reports that he stood on this stone at the washing place, and it is not established that he stood on anything else. So interpreting this expression, namely "the Station of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)", as referring to the stone is more fitting.

Al-Qaffal said: Whoever interprets "the Station of Ibrahim" as the stone takes His saying, ﴿And take, from the Station of Ibrahim, a place of prayer﴾, as a metaphorical usage, like the saying of a man: "I have taken a friend from so-and-so," and "Allah has given me from so-and-so a righteous brother," and "Allah has granted me from you a compassionate protector." The particle "min" (from) is used only to specify the thing taken and to distinguish it, in that meaning, from others. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** Scholars have mentioned several meanings for His saying: ﴿a place of prayer﴾:

First: "a place of prayer" is taken from the prayer that means supplication, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56]. This is the view of Mujahid, and he went to this interpretation only so that his statement that the whole Sacred Precinct is the Station of Ibrahim would be complete.

Second: Al-Hasan said: He meant by it the qiblah (direction of prayer).

Third: Qatadah and al-Suddi said: They were commanded to pray at it. The people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: This view is more fitting, because when the word "prayer" (salat) is used without qualification, what is understood from it is the prayer performed with bowing and prostration. Do you not see that the "musalla" of a city is the place where the Eid prayer is performed? And he (ﷺ) said to Usamah ibn Zayd: "The musalla is ahead of you," meaning by it the place of the prayer performed. This is also indicated by the Prophet's (ﷺ) praying at it after reciting the verse. Also, interpreting it as the known prayer is more fitting, because it encompasses all the meanings by which the scholars explained the verse.

Here there is a jurisprudential discussion: Are the two rak'ahs of the tawaf obligatory (fard) or recommended (sunnah)? If the tawaf is obligatory, then al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, has two opinions on this:

One: They are obligatory, because of His saying: ﴿And take, from the Station of Ibrahim, a place of prayer﴾, and the command indicates obligation.

The second: They are sunnah, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to the Bedouin when he asked: "Is there anything else incumbent upon me?" He said: "No, unless you perform voluntary prayer." And if the tawaf is voluntary, like the tawaf of arrival (tawaf al-qudum), then its two rak'ahs are sunnah. The narration from Abu Hanifa is also divergent on this issue. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** On the virtues of the House: Shaykh Ahmad al-Bayhaqi narrated in the book Shu'ab al-Iman from Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which mosque was placed on the earth first?' He said: 'The Sacred Mosque.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'Then the Farthest Mosque.' I said: 'How much time is between them?' He said: 'Forty years. Wherever prayer overtakes you, pray, for it is a mosque.'" Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it in the two Sahihs.

And from Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The House was created two thousand years before the earth, and then the earth was spread out from it." And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The first patch placed on the earth was the place of the House, then the earth was spread out from it. The first mountain that Allah the Exalted placed on the face of the earth was Abu Qubays, then the mountains were spread out from it."

And from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "When Adam (peace be upon him) was sent down to the earth, he felt lonely in it because of its vastness and because he saw no one in it besides himself. He said: 'O Lord, does not Your earth have anyone inhabiting it who glorifies You and sanctifies You besides me?' Allah the Exalted said: 'I will indeed place in it from your offspring those who glorify with My praise and sanctify for Me. And I will place in it houses that are raised for My remembrance, and My creatures will glorify Me in them. And I will settle you in it in a house that I have chosen for Myself, and I will single it out with My honor and prefer it over all the houses of the earth by My name, and I will name it My House. I will magnify it with My greatness, and I will surround it with My sanctity, and I will make it the most worthy of all houses and the most deserving of My remembrance. And I will place it in the spot that I have chosen for Myself, for I chose its place on the day I created the heavens and the earth. I will make that House, for you and for those after you, a secure sanctuary (haram), by whose sanctity I make sacred what is above it, below it, and around it. Whoever honors its sanctity honors My sanctity, and whoever makes it lawful has made My sanctity lawful. Whoever grants security to its people earns through that My security, and whoever frightens them has frightened Me. Whoever magnifies its affair has become great in My eyes, and whoever treats it lightly has become small in My eyes. Its residents are My neighbors, its inhabitants are My delegation, and its visitors are My guests. I will make it the first house placed for mankind, and I will populate it with the people of heaven and earth, who will come to it in groups, disheveled and dusty: ﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep mountain pass﴾ [al-Hajj: 27]. They will call out with takbir in a loud cry to Me, and they will pour out talbiyah in a flood. Whoever performs 'umrah to it, seeking none but Me, has visited Me, been a guest of Me, alighted with Me, and come as a delegation to Me. It is right for Me to honor him with My esteem, and it is right for the Generous that He honor His delegation, His guests, and His visitors, and that He meet each of them in his need. You, O Adam, will populate it as long as you are alive, then the nations, the generations, and the prophets from your offspring will populate it after you, one nation after another, one generation after another, and one prophet after another, until it ends with a prophet from your offspring called Muhammad (peace be upon him), who is the Seal of the Prophets. So make him among its residents, its populators, its guardians, and its custodians, and he will be My trustee over it as long as he lives. When he returns to Me, he will find that I have stored up for him from his reward what will enable him to draw near to Me through the means (wasilah) with Me. And I will make the name of that House, its remembrance, its honor, its glory, its brilliance, and its nobility for a prophet from your offspring who will come before this prophet, and he is his father, called Ibrahim. I will raise its foundations for him, and I will decree its rebuilding by his hands, and I will teach him its sacred sites (mashaʿir) and its rites (manasik). I will make him a community unto himself, devoutly obedient, standing by My command, calling to My way. I will choose him and guide him to a straight path. I will test him, and he will be patient; I will grant him well-being, and he will be grateful. I will command him and he will obey; he will vow to Me and fulfill it; he will call upon Me and I will answer his supplication concerning his offspring and his descendants after him. I will make him an intercessor for them, and I will make them the people of that House, its guardians, its custodians, its water-carriers, its servants, its keepers, and its doorkeepers, until they alter or change. And I will make Ibrahim the leader of that House and of that Law, whom everyone present at those sites among all jinn and mankind will follow."

And from Ata', who said: "Adam was sent down in India. He said: 'O Lord, why do I not hear the voice of the angels as I used to hear it in Paradise?' He said: 'Because of your sin, O Adam. Go to Mecca and build a house there, and circumambulate it as you saw them circumambulating.' So he set out for Mecca and built the House. The place of Adam's two feet became villages, rivers, and settlements, and the distance between his steps became deserts. Adam performed the Hajj to the House from India forty times."

And Umar asked Ka'b, and said: "Tell me about this House." He said: "Indeed, Allah the Exalted sent this House down from the sky as a hollow ruby with Adam (peace be upon him). He said: 'O Adam, this is My House, so circumambulate around it and pray around it as you saw My angels circumambulating around My Throne and praying.' The angels descended with him and raised its foundations from stones, and the House was placed upon the foundations. When Allah drowned the people of Noah, Allah lifted it up, but its foundations remained."

And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) is a house in the heaven called al-Durah. It is directly opposite the Ka'bah from above it. Its sanctity in the heaven is like the sanctity of the House on the earth. Seventy thousand angels pray in it every day, and they never return to it again." Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, also mentioned that after the building of Ibrahim, time passed and it collapsed, and the Amalekites rebuilt it. Time passed again and it collapsed, and Jurhum rebuilt it. Time passed again and it collapsed, and Quraysh rebuilt it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was then a young man. When they wanted to lift the Black Stone, they disputed about it, and they said: "Let the first man who comes out of this alley judge between us." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the first to come out to them, and he judged between them that they should place the stone in a cloth, and then all the tribes should lift it. They all lifted it, and then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took it and placed it.

And from al-Zuhri, who said: "It reached me that they found in the Station of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) three sheets, and in each sheet there was a writing. In the first sheet: 'I am Allah, Lord of Bakkah. I made it on the day I made the sun and the moon, and I encircled it with seven angels encircling it, and I blessed its people in meat and milk.'

In the second sheet: 'I am Allah, Lord of Bakkah. I created the womb (rahim) and I derived for it a name from My name. Whoever keeps it connected, I keep connected to him, and whoever severs it, I sever from him.'

In the third: 'I am Allah, Lord of Bakkah. I created good and evil. Blessed is the one at whose hands good occurs, and woe to the one at whose hands evil occurs.'"

**The fifth issue:** On the virtues of the Stone and the Station: From Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The Corner (rukn) and the Station are two rubies from the rubies of Paradise. Allah extinguished their light, and were it not so, they would have illuminated what is between the east and the west. No one with an ailment or a sickness touches them except that he is cured." And in the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "It was whiter than snow, but the sins of the people of polytheism blackened it." And from Ibn Abbas, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "This Stone will come on the Day of Resurrection with two eyes by which it sees, and a tongue by which it speaks, and it will testify for whoever touched it with truth." And it was narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he came to the Black Stone and said: "I indeed kiss you, and I know that you are a stone that neither harms nor benefits. Had I not seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kissing you, I would not have kissed you." Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it in the Sahih.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾, the more apt meaning is that We obligated them to that and commanded them with a command by which We bound them. The meaning of covenant (ʿahd) and pledge (mithaq) has already been mentioned previously.

As for His saying: ﴿that purify My House﴾, it must be understood as purification from everything unfitting for the House. So if the place of the House and its surroundings is a place of prayer, it is obligatory to purify it from impurities and filth. And if it is a place of worship and sincerity to Allah the Exalted, it is obligatory to purify it from polytheism and the worship of other than Allah. All of this falls within the meaning of the statement. Then the commentators mentioned several views:

First: The meaning of ﴿purify My House﴾ is: build it, purify it from polytheism, and found it upon piety, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who founded his building upon piety from Allah better, or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling bank?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 109].

Secondly: "Inform the people that My House is a place of purification for them whenever they perform the Hajj, visit it, and stay in it." The figurative sense is: "Make it pure in their eyes," just as one says: "Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) purifies this, while Abu Hanifa defiles it."

Thirdly: "Build it, and do not allow anyone from among the people of doubt and polytheism to crowd those who circumambulate it. Rather, keep it pure from the people of disbelief and doubt," just as one says: "Allah purified the earth from so-and-so." These interpretations are based on the premise that there was nothing requiring the purification of the House from idols and polytheism. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25]. It is known that they were not purified from any impurity; rather they were created pure. Likewise, the House commanded to be purified was created pure. And Allah knows best.

Fourthly: its meaning is: "Cleanse My House of idols, polytheism, and sins, so that the people may follow you both in that."

Fifthly: some have said: the site of the House, before it was built, was a place where carrion and filth were dumped, so Allah commanded Ibrahim to remove those filths and build the House there. This view is weak, because before the building the House did not exist, so cleansing that plot would not be cleansing the House. It may be answered that He called it a house because He knew that its eventual outcome would be to become a house, but this is a metaphor.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for those who circumambulate, and those who devote themselves to worship, and those who bow and prostrate﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: "al-'Akf" is a verbal noun of "'akafa" (with the vowel on the kaf either damma or kasra), meaning 'akfan, when one remains attached to a thing and stays upon it; one is then called 'akif. It is also said: when one turns toward it and does not turn one's face away from it.

The second issue: regarding these three descriptions there are two views:

The first, which is the closer one: that these are to be understood as three groups, because it is required that the conjoined be other than that to which it is conjoined. Therefore the circumambulators must be other than the devotees, and the devotees other than those who bow and prostrate, so that the benefit of the conjunction is realized. Thus "those who circumambulate" refers to whoever intends the House for pilgrimage or umrah and circumambulates it; "those who devote themselves to worship" refers to whoever stays there and resides; and "those who bow and prostrate" refers to whoever prays there.

The second view, which is the view of 'Ata': that if a person is circumambulating, he is among the circumambulators; if he is sitting, he is among the devotees; and if he is praying, he is among those who bow and prostrate.

The third issue: this verse indicates several matters:

One: if we interpret "those who circumambulate" as strangers, then the verse indicates that circumambulation is superior for strangers to prayer, because just as He singled them out for circumambulation, this shows that they have a special closeness to it. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata' that circumambulation is superior for the people of the cities, and prayer is superior for the people of Makkah.

Two: the verse indicates the permissibility of i'tikaf (retreat) in the House.

Three: it indicates the permissibility of prayer in the House, whether obligatory or voluntary, since the verse does not distinguish between any two of them. This is contrary to the view of Malik, who prohibited performing the obligatory prayer in the House. If it is said: "We do not accept that the verse indicates this, because He did not say 'those who bow and prostrate in the House,' and just as the verse does not indicate the permissibility of performing circumambulation inside the House, but only performing it outside it, likewise its indication is limited to the permissibility of performing prayer facing toward the House," we reply: the apparent meaning of the verse encompasses bowing and prostrating toward the House, whether that is inside it or outside it. We only required that circumambulation take place outside the House because circumambulating the House means going around the House, and one who goes around inside it is not called one who circumambulates the House. Allah, exalted is He, only commanded circumambulation "of" the House, not circumambulation "within" it, as in His saying: ﴿and let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj: 29]. Moreover, if the intended meaning were facing it for prayer, there would be no point in the command to purify the House for those who bow and prostrate, since those present at the House and those absent from it would be equal in the command to face it. Malik argued with His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], and whoever is inside the Sacred Mosque is not facing the Mosque but a part of its parts.

(The answer): a single one facing is impossible to be facing the whole Mosque; rather he must be facing a part of its parts. Whoever is inside the House is likewise, so it is necessary that he be included under the verse.

Four: His saying ﴿for those who circumambulate﴾ encompasses circumambulation in general, whether it is explicitly mentioned in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, as in His saying: ﴿and let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj: 29], or its ruling is established by the Sunnah, or it is among the recommended acts.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, make this a secure land and provide its people with fruits—whoever of them believes in Allah and the Last Day." He said, "And whoever disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little while; then I will force him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination."﴾

Know that this is the third type of the circumstances of Abraham, peace be upon him, which Allah, exalted is He, relates here. The Qadi (al-Qadi) said: In these verses there is an inversion of order (taqdim wa ta'khir), because His saying, ﴿My Lord, make this a secure land﴾ is not possible except after the land has come into existence, and what is mentioned later, namely His saying, ﴿And when Abraham raised the foundations of the House﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127], although it comes later in recitation, is earlier in meaning. Here there are several issues:

The first issue: The intended meaning of the verse is Abraham's supplication for the believers among the inhabitants of Makkah for security and abundance, through what is brought to Makkah, because it is a land with no crops and no plantations. Were it not for security, provisions would not be brought to it from the regions, and living there would be impossible. Then Allah, exalted is He, answered his supplication and made it secure from calamities, so that no tyrant reached it without Allah destroying him, as He did with the people of the Elephant. Here there are two questions:

The first question: Is it not the case that al-Hajjaj fought Ibn al-Zubayr, destroyed the Ka'bah, and intended to harm its people with every evil, and that this was accomplished for him?

The answer: His aim was not the destruction of the Ka'bah for its own sake; rather, his aim was something else.

The second question: What is sought from Allah, exalted is He, is that He make the land secure and abundant in fertility, and this belongs to the benefits of this world, so how is it fitting for the exalted Messenger to ask for it?

The answer to this is given in several respects:

The first of them: When the world is sought in order to be strengthened thereby for the religion, that is among the greatest pillars of the religion. So when the land is secure and fertile, its people are free to obey Allah, exalted is He, and when the land is the opposite of that, its people are the opposite of that.

The second: He, exalted is He, made it a place of return (mathabah) for people, and people can only go to it if the roads are safe and the provisions there are cheap.

The third: It is not far-fetched that security and fertility may be among the things that call a person to travel to that town, so then he witnesses the great sacred sites and the honoured standing-places, and security and fertility become the cause of his connection to that obedience.

Page 50
The second issue: ﴿baladan aminan﴾ may bear two meanings:
One of them: safe in it (ma'mun fihi), like His saying: ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 7], meaning pleasing (mardiyyah).

The second: that the intended meaning is the people of the town, like His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning its people, and this is a metaphor (majaz), because security and fear do not attach to the town itself.

* * *
The third issue: The scholars differed regarding the security that was requested in this verse, in several respects:
The first: He asked for security from famine, because He settled his family in a valley without crops or cattle.

The second: He asked for security from being swallowed up by the earth and from transformation (into animals).

The third: He asked for security from killing; this is the view of Abu Bakr al-Razi, and he argued for it by saying that he, peace be upon him, asked for security first and then asked for provision second, and if the security sought were security from famine, then asking for provision after it would be a repetition. So He said in this verse: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure land and provide its people with fruits﴾, and He said in another verse: ﴿My Lord, make this town secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], then He said at the end of the story: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without crops﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], up to His saying: ﴿and provide them with fruits﴾. Know that this argument is weak, for one may say: Perhaps the security sought is security from being swallowed up or transformed, or perhaps it is security from famine, and security from famine may come through the availability of what is needed of food, or it may come through abundance in it; so by the first request he sought the removal of famine, and by the second request he sought great abundance.

The fourth issue: The scholars differed as to whether Makkah was secure and sacred before the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him, or whether it only became so through his supplication. Some said: It was so forever, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "Indeed Allah made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth." And also Abraham said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without crops, by Your Sacred House﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], and this implies that it was sacred before that; then Abraham, peace be upon him, reaffirmed it with this supplication.

Others said: It only became a secure sanctuary through the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him, and before that it was like the other lands. The evidence for this is his saying, peace be upon him: "O Allah, I have made Madinah sacred as Abraham made Makkah sacred."

The third view: It was sacred before the supplication by a means other than the means by which it became sacred after the supplication. The first was by Allah's prevention of total destruction (al-isti'sal) and by the reverence He placed in souls; the second was by command upon the tongues of the Messengers.

The fifth issue: In this surah He said ﴿baladan aminan﴾ in indefinite form, while in the surah of Ibrahim He said ﴿hadha al-balada aminan﴾ [Ibrahim: 35] in definite form, for two reasons:

The first: The first supplication occurred when the place had not yet been made a town, as if He said: Make this valley a secure town, because He related of him that he said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without crops﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], so He said here: make this valley a secure town. The second supplication occurred after it had been made a town, so it is as if he said: Make this place, which You have made a town, one of security and safety, as when you say: "Make this man secure." 

The second: That both supplications occurred after the place had become a town. So His saying ﴿make this a town, secure﴾ means: make this the town which is a town, secure; this is only mentioned for emphasis in describing it with heat, because indefiniteness indicates emphasis. So His saying ﴿My Lord, make this a secure town﴾ means: make it among the towns perfect in security. As for His saying ﴿My Lord, make this town secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], there is nothing in it but a request for security, not a request for emphasis. As for His saying ﴿and provide its people with fruits﴾, the meaning is that he, peace be upon him, asked that the sustenance of the dwellers of Makkah be made to flow abundantly, and Allah, exalted is He, answered him, so that to Makkah are brought the fruits of every thing.

As for His saying ﴿whoever of them believes﴾, it is a substitution (badal) for His saying ﴿its people﴾, meaning: provide the believers among its people specifically; and it is like His saying: ﴿And to Allah is owed by mankind the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to make his way there﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. Know that when Allah, exalted is He, informed him that among them were people who were disbelievers, by His saying ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, he therefore specified his supplication for the believers, not the disbelievers. The basis for this specification is the text and analogy. As for the text, it is His saying: ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68]. As for analogy, it is in two respects:

The first respect: When he asked Allah, exalted is He, to place leadership (imamah) among his descendants, Allah said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, and this became a form of correction in the request. When Allah, exalted is He, distinguished the believers from the disbelievers in the matter of leadership, He therefore specified the believers in this supplication, not the disbelievers. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed him by His saying ﴿then I will grant him enjoyment for a little while﴾ of the difference between prophethood and worldly provision, because the rank of prophethood and leadership is not fitting for the corrupt, since leadership and prophethood require firmness of resolve and patience through all kinds of trial, until one conveys Allah's command and prohibition and is not deterred in religion by the blame of any blamer nor the might of any tyrant. As for provision, it is not ugly to deliver it to the obedient and the disbeliever, the truthful and the hypocrite; so whoever believes, the Garden is his dwelling and abode, and whoever disbelieves, the Fire is his resting-place and refuge.

The second respect: It is possible that Abraham, peace be upon him, strongly supposed that if he supplicated for everyone, the disbelievers would multiply in the town, and that in their dominance and multiplicity there would be a corruption and harm from people's going to the Hajj; so he specified the believers in the supplication for this reason.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little while﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Amir read ﴿fa-umni'uhu﴾ with the mim sukun and lightened, from amta'tu, while the rest read with the mim fathah and doubled, from matta'tu; and doubling indicates multiplication, unlike lightening.

The second issue: ﴿Umatti'uhu﴾ — it is said: with provision; it is said: with remaining in the world; it is said: with both, until the emergence of Muhammad ﷺ, who will kill him or expel him from these abodes if he persists in disbelief. The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, as if said: Although you have specified your supplication to the believers, I will grant the disbeliever among them the enjoyment of the immediate world, and I will not prevent him from that, what I bestow upon the believers, until his life is complete, then I will take him, then I will force him in the Hereafter to the punishment of the Fire. So He made what the disbeliever is provided in the abode of this world a little, since it occurs within the span of his life, and that span occurs between the eternal past and the everlasting future, and compared to both it is very little indeed. The summary is that Allah, exalted is He, made clear that the blessing of the believer in this world is connected to the blessing in the Hereafter, unlike the disbeliever, whose blessing in this world ends at death and is cut off from him in the Hereafter.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Then I will force him to the punishment of the Fire﴾, know that in the meaning of idtirar there are two views:
One of them: that He will do to him what makes his escape from it impossible, and here it is so, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the day they are pushed into the fire of Hell with a violent push﴾ [al-Tur: 13] and ﴿They are dragged in the Fire on their faces﴾ [al-Qamar: 48]. It is said: "I compelled him to the matter", meaning I forced him and drove him to it while he was averse to it; and they said: its origin is from harm (darr), which is bringing one thing near another, and from it comes "darrah" (co-wife) of a woman, because of their nearness and closeness.

The second: that idtirar is for the agent, through intimidation and threat, to come to perform that act by choice, like His saying: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173], where He described him as compelled to eat carrion, though that eating was done by him. So the meaning is: Allah, exalted is He, drives him to choose the Fire and to abide in it, by informing him that if he sought escape he would be prevented from it, because one in such a state is driven to fall into the Fire. Then He, exalted is He, explained that this is "wretched is the destination," because "excellent is the destination" is that in which bliss and joy are attained, and "wretched is the destination" is its opposite.

**Al-Razi's Commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, Verses 127–129 (Part 1 of 4)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House, [they said], "Our Lord, accept this from us. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, and make us Muslims [in submission] to You, and of our descendants a Muslim nation [in submission] to You. And show us our rites and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom and purify them. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise."﴾

Know that this is the fourth of the matters that Allah, exalted is He, related about Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them. When they were building the House, they mentioned three supplications. Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And when [Abraham] was raising﴾, is a narration of a past state. *Al-qawaʿid* (the foundations) is the plural of *qaʿidah*, which means the base, and the base is originally that which is beneath what is above it. It is a predominant attribute, and its meaning is "that which is firm." From it comes *aqʿadaka Allah*, meaning "I ask Allah to make you sit (qaʿada)," i.e., to make you firm. To "raise the foundations" means that the builder raises them by building upon them, because when something is built upon them they are moved from the state of lowness to the state of height, and they extend after having been short. It is also possible that what is meant is the courses (*sawafat*) of the building, because every course is a foundation for what is built upon it and placed above it. The meaning of raising the foundations is raising them by building, because when one places a course above a course, one has raised the courses. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** Most of the historians (*ahl al-akhbar*) hold that this House existed before Abraham, peace be upon him, according to the hadiths we have related concerning it. They argued with His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾, for this is explicit that those foundations already existed in a state of ruin, and Abraham, peace be upon him, raised them and rebuilt them.

**The third issue:** They differed as to whether Ishmael, peace be upon him, was a partner of Abraham, peace be upon him, in raising the foundations of the House and building it. Most said: he was a partner with him in that, and the sense is: "And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House." The evidence for this is that He, exalted is He, joined Ishmael to Abraham [in the verb], so this conjunction must be in an action from the actions previously mentioned, and nothing was mentioned before except the raising of the foundations of the House. Therefore Ishmael must be understood as conjoined with Abraham in that. Then their partnership in it may bear two possibilities:

The first: that they both share in the construction and the raising of the walls.

The second: that one of them builds the House while the other carries the stones and clay to him and prepares the tools and implements for him. On both possibilities, attributing the raising to both of them is correct, although the first possibility is more literal.

Among the people there are those who said: Ishmael at that time was a small child. This meaning was also related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that when [Abraham] built the House, he left and left Ishmael behind and [Hagar] migrated, and they said: "To whom do You entrust us?" Abraham said: "To Allah." Ishmael became thirsty and did not see any water. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, called to them and scraped the ground with his finger, and Zamzam gushed forth. These people placed the pause at His saying: ﴿from the House﴾, then began: "And Ishmael: Our Lord, accept from us our obedience in building this House." On this interpretation, Ishmael is a partner in the supplication, not in the building.

This interpretation is weak, because His saying: ﴿accept from us﴾ contains nothing that indicates what He accepts, so it must be directed to the previously mentioned matter, which is the raising of the House. If that was not his action, how could he supplicate Allah that He accept it from him? Therefore this view is contrary to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and must be rejected. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** He said: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations from the House﴾, and did not say: "raising the foundations of the House." This is because the indefiniteness of "the foundations" and then clarifying them after the indefiniteness contains an exaltation of the matter that the other expression does not have. Know that Allah, exalted is He, related after that three kinds of supplication from the two of them.

**The first kind:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Accept from us. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing.﴾ On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** They differed in explaining His saying: ﴿accept from us﴾. The theologians (*al-mutakallimun*) said: every act that Allah, exalted is He, accepts, He rewards its doer and is pleased with it from him, and whatever He does not reward and is not pleased with is rejected. Here he expressed one of two mutually concomitant things by the name of the other: he mentioned the word "acceptance" and intended by it the reward and pleasure, because *taqabbul* is that a person receives what is given to him. So he likened the act of the servant to a gift, and the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, to acceptance, by way of extension.

The mystics (*al-ʿarifun*) said: there is a difference between *qabul* (acceptance) and *taqabbul* (receiving/accepting with effort), because *taqabbul* is an expression of a person exerting himself in accepting, and that happens only where the deed is deficient and does not deserve to be accepted. So this is a confession from them both of shortcoming in the deed, and a confession of helplessness and brokenness. Also, the aim was not to be given a reward for it, because for the wise servant, that the act falls in the position of acceptance from the one served is more pleasing than being given a reward for it. The full verification of this will come in the explanation of love in His saying: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** After they performed that worship sincerely, they humbled themselves before Allah, exalted is He, to accept it and sought reward for it, according to what the theologians said. Had the arrangement of reward upon the act accompanied by sincerity been obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, there would be no benefit in this supplication and humbling. It would be like a person humbling himself before Allah and saying: "O my God, make fire hot and ice cold!" Rather, that supplication is better, because for the theologian there is no improbability in the fire, while remaining in its form of brightness and burning, becoming cold, or in the ice, while remaining in its form of solidity and whiteness, becoming hot. And it is impossible for the Mu'tazilah that reward not be arranged upon such an act; therefore the supplication here would be the most objectionable. Since it is not so, we know that nothing at all is obligatory for the servant upon Allah. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue (another):** He followed this supplication with His saying: ﴿Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing﴾, as if he were saying: "You hear our supplication and our humbling, and You know what is in our hearts of sincerity and of turning away from attention to anyone other than You." If it is said: His saying ﴿Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ implies exclusivity (*hasr*), and the matter is not so, for others may also be hearing. We say: because of His perfection in this attribute, He is as if He alone is specified with it, to the exclusion of others.

**The second kind:** of supplication is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and make us Muslims [in submission] to You﴾. On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued in the question of the creation of acts with His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and make us Muslims to You﴾. Islam either means the religion and belief, or submission and compliance. Whichever it is, they desired that He make them with this attribute. Making them with this attribute has no meaning except creating that in them, for *jaʿl* (making) is an expression of creation. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-Anʿam: 1]. This indicates that Islam is created by Allah, exalted is He.

If it is said: this verse has an apparent meaning that is abandoned, because it implies that at the time of the request they were not Muslims. For if they were Muslims, then asking that He make them Muslims would be asking for the obtaining of what is already obtained, and that is invalid. But the Muslims agreed that they were Muslims at that time, and because the utterance of this supplication from them is not appropriate unless they were already Muslims. And if it is established that the verse has an abandoned apparent meaning, it is not permissible to cite it as evidence. Even if we grant that it does not have an abandoned apparent meaning, we do not grant that *jaʿl* is an expression of creation and bringing into existence; rather it has other meanings besides creation:

First: *jaʿala* meaning *ṣayyara* (to turn/make into), as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And it is He who made the night for you as a garment and sleep as rest, and made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan: 47].

Second: *jaʿala* meaning *wahaba* (to give), as we say: "I made this estate for you, and this slave, and this horse."

Third: *jaʿala* meaning to describe a thing and to judge it with something, as in His saying: ﴿And they made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19], and He said: ﴿And they made for Allah partners, the jinn﴾ [al-Anʿam: 100].

Fourth: *jaʿala* meaning to command, as in His saying: ﴿And We made them leaders﴾ [al-Anbiya': 73], meaning: We commanded them to be followed. And He said: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], so it is by command.

Fifth: that it means teaching, as in the saying: "I made him a writer or a poet," when you teach him that.

Sixth: explanation and indication. You say: "I made so-and-so's speech false," when you present from the proof what shows its falsehood. If this is established, we say: why is it not permissible that what is meant is describing them with Islam and judging them to be so, just as one says: "So-and-so made me a thief," or "made me a learned, refined person," when he describes him with that. Even if we grant that what is meant by *jaʿl* is creation, why is it not permissible that what is meant is the creation of the inducements (*alṭaf*) that call them to Islam and the enabling of them for it? So whoever Allah enables for these matters until he does them, has made him Muslim to Him. Its example: one who disciplines his son until he becomes refined, so it is permissible to say: "I made you refined" and "I made you refined (*jaʿaltuka adīban*)." In the opposite case it is said: "He made his son a crafty thief."

Even if we grant that the apparent meaning of the verse requires that He, exalted is He, be the creator of Islam, it is contrary to the rational proofs, so it is obligatory to abandon saying so. We say it is contrary to rational proofs because if the act of the servant were a creation of Allah, exalted is He, the servant would not deserve praise or blame by it, nor reward or punishment, and it would be necessary that Allah, exalted is He, be the one who is Muslim and obedient, not the servant.

The answer: as for his saying that the verse has an abandoned apparent meaning, we say: we do not grant that. Its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: that Islam is an accident subsisting in the heart, and that it does not persist for two times. So His saying: ﴿and make us Muslims to You﴾ means: "Create this accident in us in the future time continuously." Seeking its acquisition in the future time does not contradict its occurrence in the present.

The second: that what is meant by it is an increase in Islam, as in His saying: ﴿That they may increase in faith along with their faith﴾ [al-Fath: 4], and ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17]. Abraham said: ﴿But [I ask] so that my heart may be assured﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. So it is as if they both asked for an increase in certainty and assent. Seeking an increase does not contradict the existence of the root in the present.

The third: that when Islam is mentioned absolutely, it denotes faith and belief. But when it is joined with the particle *lam*, as in His saying: ﴿Muslims to You﴾, what is meant is submission to Him, compliance, contentment with everything He decrees, and abandoning dispute with the decisions and judgments of Allah, exalted is He. Certainly they were both knowers and Muslims, but perhaps some kind of dispute arising from human nature remained in their hearts, so they wished that Allah remove that from them entirely, so that the station of contentment with the decree might be attained by them in perfection. Thus it is established by these aspects that the verse does not have an abandoned apparent meaning.

His saying: "*Jaʿl* is understood as judgment with that." We say: this is rebutted in several respects:

The first: when the described thing already possesses the attribute, there is no benefit in the attribute. And if what is sought by the supplication is not merely the description, it must be understood as the acquisition of the attribute. One cannot say: describing Him with that is praise and glorification, and that is desirable. We say: yes, but the desire for the acquisition of the thing itself is greater than the desire for the acquisition of the description of it and judgment with it, so understanding it in the first sense is preferable.

**Second:** Once Islam is realized in the two of them, they deserve the designation by it, and God, exalted is He, cannot be described as lying. So that attribute is already present, and what is the point of asking for it in supplication?

**Third:** If what is meant by it were merely naming, then everyone who names Abraham a Muslim would be permitted to say, "He made him a Muslim." As for the claim that it is to be understood as the bestowal of *lutf* (divine favours that facilitate obedience), we say that this too is refuted in several respects:

*First:* The word *ja'l* ("make") is connected to "Islam," so turning it away from that to something else abandons the apparent meaning.

*Second:* According to the Mu'tazilites, God has already performed those *lutf* and brought them into existence and into being, so asking for them would be asking for the attainment of what is already attained, and that is not permissible.

*Third:* Those *lutf* either have an effect in favouring the performance of the act over its omission, or they do not. If they have no effect in this favouring, then they are not *lutf*. If they do have an effect in favouring, then we say: once that preponderance is realized, the act has become necessary. This is because, with the realization of that degree of preponderance, the act either becomes necessary, or becomes impossible, or is neither necessary nor impossible. If it becomes necessary, then that is what is sought. If it becomes impossible, then it is a preventer, not a preponderant cause. If it is neither necessary nor impossible, then it is possible for the act to occur with it at one time and not occur at another time. The specification of the time of occurrence for occurring is either due to the addition of something to it, by which that time is distinguished for occurrence, or it is not so. If the former, then the preponderant cause is the whole of the *lutf* together with this added addition, and so this *lutf* has no effect in preponderance at all, though we had stipulated that it does. This is a contradiction. If the latter, then it follows that one of the two equal sides of a possibility is preferred over the other without a preponderant cause, and this is impossible. Thus it is established that the doctrine of this *lutf* is not intelligible.

As for the claim that rational proofs establish the impossibility of the occurrence of the servant's act by God's creation, and that this is the distinction of praise and blame: we say that this is opposed by the question of knowledge and the question of the one who supplicates, as has been established repeatedly and in various ways. And God knows best.

Know that the well-known question regarding this verse, namely that since the two of them were already Muslims, how could they ask for Islam? We have incorporated it into this issue, and we have mentioned concerning it answers that are sufficient and conclusive, and praise be to God for that. Then, what indicates by way of reason that their becoming Muslims is from Him alone, glorified is He, is what we mentioned: whether the capacity suitable for Islam is capable of abandoning it or not. If it is not capable of abandoning it, then that capacity is determinative, and the creation of that determinative capacity in them made them Muslims. If it is capable of abandoning it, then that is false; and even granting its possibility, the intended purpose is still attained. As for its falsity: abandonment is the remaining of a thing in its non-existence, and non-existence is pure negation, so it is impossible for capacity to have an effect upon it. Moreover, it is a continuing non-existence, and what continues is not an object of capacity. Thus it is established by this that there is no capacity over that enduring non-existence. Therefore there is no capacity except over existence, and so capacity is suitable only for existence. As for granting that capacity is suitable for both existence and non-existence, the intended purpose is still attained, because that suitable capacity is not specified to the side of existence except by a preponderant cause, and the preponderant causes must terminate in the act of God, exalted is He, to cut off infinite regress (*tasalsul*). When the preponderant cause from God is realized, the act must occur. Thus it is established that His saying, ﴿Our Lord, and make us Muslims submitting to You﴾, is what is valid according to the principles of rational proofs.

**Second issue:** His saying, ﴿Our Lord, and make us Muslims submitting to You﴾, conveys restriction, meaning: we would be Muslims to You, not to other than You. This indicates that the perfect happiness of the servant lies in his being a Muslim to the rulings of God, His decree and His predestination, and in his heart not turning toward anything other than Him. This is what is meant by the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him, in another place: ﴿For they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:77]. Here there are two opinions:

One: ﴿Our Lord, and make us Muslims submitting to You﴾, meaning: monotheists, sincere, who worship none but You.

The second: standing in full observance of all the laws of Islam. This is the more apt, because of its generality.

**Third issue:** Indeed, the servant does not address God, exalted is He, at the time of supplication except by saying, "Our Lord." Its explanation will come, God willing, in the commentary on His saying, ﴿And your Lord said, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you"﴾ [Ghafir 40:60], in the conditions of supplication.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And from our descendants a Muslim nation submitting to You﴾, the meaning is: make from our offspring [a Muslim nation]. The word "from" (*min*) is partitive, and He specified some of them, because He, exalted is He, informed them that among their descendants there would be the wrongdoer, by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. Some people said: by it He meant the Arabs, because they are of their descendants. As for "a nation," it was said they are the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), by the evidence of His saying, ﴿And send among them a messenger from themselves﴾. Here there are questions:

**First question:** We have explained that His saying, ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, indicates that among his descendants there are those who are wrongdoers, and similarly there are among them those who are not wrongdoers. Therefore, that some of his descendants are a Muslim nation has become known from that verse. So what is the benefit of asking for it again by supplication?

*Answer:* That indication was not conclusive, and one who is compassionate is inclined toward a bad opinion.

**Second question:** Why did he specify their descendants in the supplication? Is this not akin to stinginess in supplication?

*Answer:* Descendants are more deserving of compassion and of concern for their welfare. God, exalted is He, said, ﴿Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:6]. Moreover, when the children of prophets are righteous, others are made righteous through them and follow them in good deeds. Do you not see that when the earlier scholars and elders are upright, how they become causes of uprightness for those who come after them?

**Third question:** The apparent meaning is that if God had rejected this supplication, He would have stated that rejection explicitly. Since He did not state a rejection, we know that He answered it. And then the difficulty arises: in the time of the forefathers of Muhammad (ﷺ), not one of the Arabs was a Muslim, and no one besides the Arabs was among the descendants of Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them both.

*Answer:* Al-Qaffal said: among their descendants there never ceased to be those who worshipped God alone and did not associate anything with Him, and the messengers never ceased to come from the descendants of Abraham. In the pre-Islamic era there were Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Qass ibn Sa'idah, and it is said 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, grandfather of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and 'Amir ibn al-Zarib, who were upon the religion of Islam: they affirmed the origination and the return, reward and punishment, they affirmed the unity of God, exalted is He, they did not eat carrion, and they did not worship idols.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And show us our rites﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Regarding "show us" (*arina*), there are two opinions:

The first: its meaning is, "Teach us the laws of our pilgrimage, since You commanded us to build the House so that we may perform its pilgrimage and call the people to its pilgrimage. So teach us its laws and what befits us to do in it of act and utterance." The figurative use of this is from the sight of knowledge. God, exalted is He, said, ﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade?﴾ [al-Furqan 25:45], and ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [al-Fil 105:1].

The second: "Make them appear to our eyes so that we may see them."

al-Hasan said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, showed Abraham all the rites, until he reached 'Arafat, and said, "O Abraham, have you understood what I have shown you of the rites?" He said, "Yes." Therefore it was named 'Arafat (from *ma'rifah*, knowledge). When the Day of Sacrifice came, he wished to visit the House, and Iblis appeared to him and blocked the path. Gabriel, peace be upon him, commanded him to throw seven pebbles at him, and he did so, and the devil departed. Then he appeared to him on the second day, the third day and the fourth day, and each time Gabriel, peace be upon him, commanded him to throw the pebbles.

Here there is a third opinion, which is that what is meant is both knowledge and sight together. This is the view of al-Qadi, because the Hajj is not complete except by matters some of which are known but not seen, and some of which the purpose is not fulfilled except by seeing. So it is obligatory to take the word as encompassing both. This is weak, because it requires taking the word in both its literal and figurative senses at once, and that is not permissible. So the valid opinion remains, which are the first two. Whoever holds the second opinion says: the rites are the places and sites where the laws of the Hajj are performed, such as Mina, 'Arafat, Muzdalifah and the like. Whoever holds the first says: the rites are the acts of the Hajj, such as circumambulation, the running between Safa and Marwah, and standing.

**Second issue:** *Nusuk* means worship. A worshipper is called *nasik*. Then sacrifice was called *nusuk* and the sacrificial animal *nasikah*, and the acts of the Hajj were called *manasik*. He, peace be upon him, said: "Take from me your rites, for perhaps I will not meet you after this year of mine." The places where the laws of the Hajj are performed are also called *manasik*. It is said: *al-mansak* with a fatha on the *sin* means the act, and with a kasra on the *sin* means the place, like *al-masjid*, *al-mashriq* and *al-maghrib*. God, exalted is He, said, ﴿For every nation We have appointed rites which they perform﴾ [al-Hajj 22:67]. It has been read with fatha and with kasra. The apparent sense of the statement indicates the act. Likewise His saying, peace be upon him: "Take from me your rites" — he commanded them to learn his actions in the Hajj, not that he meant: "Take from me the places of your rites."

Knowing this, we say: if we take *manasik* as the rites of the Hajj, then if we take them as acts, the showing is to make known those acts; and if we take them as places, the showing is to make known the locations. Some of the commentators took *manasik* to mean only the sacrificial animal, and this is an error, because the sacrificial animal is called *nusuk* only because it falls under worship. For this reason they do not call what is slaughtered for eating by that name. The reason why the sacrificial animal is called *nusuk* — that it is an act of the Hajj — exists in all the other acts, so it is necessary that all of them be included in it. And if we take *manasik* as referring to what the root of this word returns to, namely worship and drawing near to God, and adhering to what pleases Him, and we make this general for everything God prescribed for Abraham, peace be upon him, then His saying, ﴿And show us our rites﴾ means: teach us how to worship You, where to worship You, and with what to draw near to You, so that we may serve You as a servant serves his master.

**Third issue:** Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, in some transmissions, read *arna* with a sukun on the *ra'* throughout the Qur'an. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir agreed with them in one instance, in Ha Mim al-Sajdah: ﴿Show us those who led us astray﴾ [Fussilat 41:29]. Abu 'Amr, in some of the well-known transmissions from him, read with *ikhtilas* (a rapid, reduced vowel) of the kasra of the *ra'* without prolonging it, throughout the Qur'an. The rest read with a fully prolonged kasra. Its origin is *ar'ina* with a kasra on the hamza: the kasra of the hamza was transferred to the *ra'* and the hamza was deleted. This is the preferred reading, because most of the reciters follow it. Also, because the hamza has been dropped, the *ra'* should not be made quiescent, lest the word be weakened and the indication of the hamza be lost. As for the sukun, it is based on deleting the hamza along with its vowel and on analogy with what has quiescence, as in their saying *fakhdh* and *kabd*. As for *ikhtilas*, it is for seeking lightness while preserving the indication of the deleted hamza.

As for His saying, ﴿And turn to us in repentance﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Those who permit sin upon the prophets have argued with this verse, saying: because repentance is conditioned upon the prior occurrence of sin, if there were no prior sin, the request for repentance would be a request for the impossible. As for the Mu'tazilites, they said: we permit minor sins upon the prophets, so this repentance was repentance from a minor sin. And one may say: minor sins have already been expiated by the reward of the one who commits them, and once they are expiated, repentance from them is impossible, because the effect of repentance is in removing them, and removing what has already been removed is impossible.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 127–129 (part 3 of 4):

Here there are other answers, suitable both for those who permit minor sins and for those who do not permit them, and they are of several aspects:

The first of them: it is possible that he (Abraham) adopted the form of repentance as a means of being firmly resolved in turning away from disobedience, because whoever imagines himself in the form of one who regrets and resolves on great caution, is closer to abandoning sins, so that this becomes a kindness (lutf) that calls to the abandoning of sins.

The second: that the servant, however much he strives in obedience to his Lord, does not escape shortcoming in some respects, either by way of forgetfulness (sahw) or by way of leaving what is better (tark al-awla); so this supplication was for the sake of that.

The third: that when God (exalted is He) informed Abraham, peace be upon him, that among his offspring there would be one who is a wrongdoer and a disobedient, he therefore asked here that He make some of his offspring a Muslim community, then he asked of Him that He grant those disobedient sinners success in repentance, saying: ﴿And accept our repentance﴾, meaning, for the sinners among our offspring. A father who is compassionate toward his son, when his son commits a sin and the father makes excuses for him, may say: "I have committed a crime, disobeyed and sinned, so accept my excuse," and his intention is: "My son has sinned, so accept his excuse, for a person's child is in the position of himself." What strengthens this interpretation are several aspects:

The first: what God (exalted is He) related in Surah Ibrahim, that he said: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols. My Lord, they have led many people astray. Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 35–36]. So it is possible that the meaning is: "and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are capable of turning to him in repentance if he repents, and forgiving him what preceded of his sins."

The second: it is mentioned that in the recitation of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "and show them their rites, and turn to them in repentance."

The third: that he said, in continuation of this: ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them﴾.

The fourth: they interpreted the saying of God (exalted is He): ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾ [al-A'raf: 11] by considering His creating of him as creating for them, since they were from him; so likewise it is not far-fetched that His saying: ﴿And show us our rites﴾ means: show us our offspring.

* * *

The second issue: The companions (the Ash'aris) used the saying ﴿and accept our repentance﴾ as evidence that the act of the servant is the creation of God (exalted is He). They said: because he (peace be upon him) asked God (exalted is He) to accept his repentance; if repentance were created by the servant, then asking it from God (exalted is He) would be absurd and ignorant. The Mu'tazilah said: this is countered by the fact that God (exalted is He) asked repentance from us, saying: ﴿O you who believe, turn to God in sincere repentance﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8]; and if it were an act of God (exalted is He), then asking it from the servant would be absurd and ignorant. Once that is established, His saying ﴿and accept our repentance﴾ is understood as referring to granting success (tawfiq) and performing kindnesses (lutf), or to accepting repentance from the servant. The companions said: the preference is with us, because rational proof supports our view in several aspects:

The first: that whenever God (exalted is He) does not create a motive (da'iyah) that necessitates repentance, the occurrence of repentance is impossible; so repentance is from God (exalted is He) and not from the servant. The exposition of the argument of the motive has been presented more than once.

The second: that repentance, as summarized by Shaykh al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, is a term for a combination of three ordered matters: knowledge, a state, and action. Knowledge is first, the state is second and it is what knowledge necessitates, and action is third and it is what the state necessitates. As for knowledge, it is recognition of the greatness of the harm of sins; from this recognition there arises the heart's pain because of the loss of benefit and the occurrence of harm, and this pain is what is called regret (nadam). Then from this regret there arises an attribute called will (irada), which relates to the present, the past, and the future. Its relation to the present is abandoning the sin that was clinging to him; its relation to the future is by resolving to abandon that act which causes the loss of the beloved until the end of life; and its relation in the past is by making up for what was lost through restitution and settlement, if it is capable of restitution. Knowledge is the first, and it is the dawn of these goods, and by this knowledge I mean faith and certainty, for faith is a term for affirming that sins are deadly poisons, and certainty is a term for the firmness of this affirmation, the absence of doubt about it, and its dominance over the heart. Then, whenever this certainty dominates the heart, the fire of regret blazes, and the heart is pained by it, as it perceives, by the light of faith shining, that it has become veiled from its beloved, like one upon whom the sunlight shines, having been in darkness, and who sees his beloved has come near to destruction, so the fires of love ignite in his heart, and from that state there arises his will to rise up to make amends.

Having known this, we say: the following of the act upon the will is necessary, because a firm will free of any opposing factor must be followed by the act; and the following of the will upon the pain of the heart is also necessary, for whoever's heart is pained by witnessing something disliked must have in his heart the will to repel it; and the following of that pain upon knowledge that this thing brings harms, and the repelling of benefits, is also a necessary matter. So all these stages are necessary, so how could they occur under testing and effort?

There remains to be said: what falls under obligation is knowledge, but there is also a difficulty in this, because that knowledge is either necessary (daruri) or acquired by reflection (nazari). If it is necessary, it does not fall under testing and obligation either; and if it is acquired by reflection, then it is inferred from necessary knowledges. So the totality of those necessary knowledges which produce the first acquired knowledge either is sufficient for that production or is not sufficient. If it is sufficient, then the acquired knowledge inferred from them being the first to follow from those necessary knowledges is obligatory, and what must follow from what is outside of choice is also outside of choice. And if it is not sufficient, then something else is needed; that other thing, if it is from the necessary knowledges, then if it is present, what we supposed was not sufficient, yet it was sufficient—this is a contradiction; and if it is from the acquired knowledges, then the first of the acquired knowledges requires another acquired knowledge before it, so the first of the acquired knowledges would not be first for the acquired knowledges, and this is a contradiction.

Then the discussion about that first is like what came before it, so it leads to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. Thus it is established by what we mentioned last that His saying ﴿and accept our repentance﴾ is to be taken in its apparent sense, which is the truth consistent with rational proofs, and that the other verses opposing this verse are more deserving of interpretation.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed You are the Ever-Accepting of Repentance, the Most Merciful﴾, it has already been mentioned.

The third type: His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them﴾. Know that there is no doubt that His saying ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger﴾ means those whom he intended by His saying ﴿and from our offspring a Muslim community submissive to You﴾, because that is what was mentioned before, and describing his offspring with that is not fitting except for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). So it is joined to it by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them﴾. This supplication conveys the perfection of the condition of his offspring in two respects:

One of them: that there be among them a messenger who perfects for them the religion and the law and calls them to that by which they will remain firm in Islam.

The second: that this raised one be from among them and not from others, for several reasons:

One of them: so that their station and rank in honour and religion would be greater, because when the messenger and the one sent to are both from his offspring, it is more noble for his request when it is granted.

The second: that when he is from among them, they know his birth and upbringing, so it is easier for them to recognize his truthfulness and trustworthiness.

The third: that when he is from among them, he is the most eager of people for their good and the most compassionate toward them, more than a stranger would be if sent to them.

When this is established, we say: if Abraham (peace be upon him) intended the establishment of the religion in the present and in the future, and it was predominant in his thought that this would be completed and perfected only if the people were from his offspring, it was good of him to intend that, so that the ultimate aim in religion would be gathered for him, and there is added to it great joy that this matter should be among his offspring, for there is no honour or nobility higher than this rank.

As for the fact that the messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), several aspects indicate it:

The first: the consensus of the exegetes, and that is a proof.

The second: what is narrated from him (peace be upon him) that he said: "I am the answered supplication of Abraham and the good news of Jesus." By "supplication" he meant this verse, and the good news of Jesus (peace be upon him) is what is mentioned in Surah al-Saff in His saying: ﴿and a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6].

The third: that Abraham (peace be upon him) made this supplication only in Mecca, for his offspring who would be there and in its surroundings, and God (exalted is He) did not send to those in Mecca and its surroundings except Muhammad (ﷺ).

Here there is a question: it is said, what is the wisdom in mentioning Abraham (peace be upon him) together with Muhammad (ﷺ) in the matter of prayer, where it is said: "O God, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Abraham and upon the family of Abraham"?

They answered it in several ways:

The first of them: that Abraham (peace be upon him) supplicated for Muhammad (peace be upon him) when he said: ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them who will recite to them Your verses﴾; so when the right of the supplication of the Friend (Khalil) upon the Beloved (Habib) became due, God (exalted is He) discharged His right to him by causing his mention to continue on the tongues of his community until the Day of Resurrection.

The second: that Abraham (peace be upon him) asked that from his Lord by saying: ﴿and grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 84], meaning: preserve for me a good praise in the community of Muhammad (ﷺ); so God (exalted is He) answered him and joined his mention to the mention of His beloved, to preserve the good praise of him among his community.

The third: that Abraham was the father of the religious community, according to His saying: ﴿the religion of your father Abraham﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and Muhammad was the father of mercy; and in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and he is a father to them," and in his story He said: ﴿compassionate and merciful toward the believers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], and he (peace be upon him) said: "I am to you only like a father," meaning in tenderness and mercy. So when each of them had the right of fatherhood in some respect, He brought their mentions close together in the context of praise and blessing.

The fourth: that Abraham (peace be upon him) was the herald of the law in the Hajj: ﴿and proclaim to the people the Hajj﴾ [al-Hajj: 27], and Muhammad (peace be upon him) was the herald of the religion: ﴿We have heard a caller calling to faith﴾ [Al 'Imran: 193]; so God (exalted is He) joined the two of them in the beautiful remembrance.

Know that when He (exalted is He) requested the sending of a messenger from among them to them, He mentioned attributes of that messenger.

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿who will recite to them Your verses﴾, and in it there are two aspects:

The first: that they are the Furqan which was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ), because what he used to recite to them was none other than that, so it is necessary to take it as such.

The second: it is permissible that the verses be the signs indicating the existence of the Creator and His attributes (exalted is He), and the meaning of his reciting them to them is that he would remind them of them, call them to them, and lead them to belief in them.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and teach them the Book﴾, and what is meant is that he would order them to recite the Book and teach them the meanings and realities of the Book, and that is because recitation is desired for several reasons:

Among them: the preservation of its wording on the tongues of the people of mass transmission (tawatur), so that it remains protected from distortion.

and the purity of the text, and it has among its features that its wording and arrangement are a miracle for Muhammad (ﷺ), and that its recitation is a kind of worship and obedience, and that its recitation in the prayers and in all other acts of worship is a kind of worship. This is the ruling on recitation. However, the great wisdom and the most noble purpose is teaching what it contains of proofs and rulings, for Allah the Exalted described the Qur'an as being guidance and light because of the meanings, wisdoms and secrets within it. So when Allah the Exalted first mentioned the matter of recitation, He then mentioned after it the teaching of its realities and secrets, and said: ﴿and teaches them the Book﴾.

The third attribute of the Messenger (ﷺ) is His saying: ﴿and the wisdom﴾, meaning: and teaches them the wisdom. Know that wisdom is: correctness in speech and action, and no one is called wise unless both matters are combined in him. It was also said: its origin is from "ahkamtu al-shay'" meaning I returned it, so wisdom is what turns away from ignorance and error, and that occurs only by what we mentioned of correctness in speech and action, and placing everything in its proper place.

Al-Qaffal said: Some philosophers described wisdom as "assimilation to God to the extent of human capacity."

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of wisdom here, in several ways:

First: Ibn Wahb said: I asked Malik: What is wisdom? He said: knowledge of the religion, understanding of it, and following it.

Second: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Wisdom is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is also the view of Qatadah. The companions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The evidence for this is that He mentioned the recitation of the Book first and its teaching second, then He joined wisdom to it by conjunction, so wisdom must be something outside the Book, and that is none other than the Sunnah of the Messenger, peace be upon him. If it is said: why can it not be taken to mean teaching the rational proofs for the Oneness of God, justice and prophethood? We say: because the intellects are receptive to that, so applying this expression to what is not derived from the Sharia is more appropriate.

Third: Wisdom is the distinguishing between truth and falsehood, and it is a verbal noun in the sense of judgment, like "al-qi'dah" and "al-jilsah." The meaning: He teaches them Your Book which You send down to them, and the distinction of Your decisions and rulings which You teach them. Examples of this: "al-khubr" and "al-khibrah," "al-'udhr" and "al-'idhrah," "al-ghull" and "al-ghillah," "al-dhull" and "al-dhillah."

Fourth: "and teaches them the Book" refers to the clear verses (muhkamat), and "and the wisdom" refers to the ambiguous verses (mutashabihat).

Fifth: "and teaches them the Book" means He teaches them what it contains of rulings.
