The first: its meaning is, "Teach us the laws of our pilgrimage, since You commanded us to build the House so that we may perform its pilgrimage and call the people to its pilgrimage. So teach us its laws and what befits us to do in it of act and utterance." The figurative use of this is from the sight of knowledge. God, exalted is He, said, ﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shade?﴾ [al-Furqan 25:45], and ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [al-Fil 105:1].

The second: "Make them appear to our eyes so that we may see them."

al-Hasan said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, showed Abraham all the rites, until he reached 'Arafat, and said, "O Abraham, have you understood what I have shown you of the rites?" He said, "Yes." Therefore it was named 'Arafat (from *ma'rifah*, knowledge). When the Day of Sacrifice came, he wished to visit the House, and Iblis appeared to him and blocked the path. Gabriel, peace be upon him, commanded him to throw seven pebbles at him, and he did so, and the devil departed. Then he appeared to him on the second day, the third day and the fourth day, and each time Gabriel, peace be upon him, commanded him to throw the pebbles.

Here there is a third opinion, which is that what is meant is both knowledge and sight together. This is the view of al-Qadi, because the Hajj is not complete except by matters some of which are known but not seen, and some of which the purpose is not fulfilled except by seeing. So it is obligatory to take the word as encompassing both. This is weak, because it requires taking the word in both its literal and figurative senses at once, and that is not permissible. So the valid opinion remains, which are the first two. Whoever holds the second opinion says: the rites are the places and sites where the laws of the Hajj are performed, such as Mina, 'Arafat, Muzdalifah and the like. Whoever holds the first says: the rites are the acts of the Hajj, such as circumambulation, the running between Safa and Marwah, and standing.

**Second issue:** *Nusuk* means worship. A worshipper is called *nasik*. Then sacrifice was called *nusuk* and the sacrificial animal *nasikah*, and the acts of the Hajj were called *manasik*. He, peace be upon him, said: "Take from me your rites, for perhaps I will not meet you after this year of mine." The places where the laws of the Hajj are performed are also called *manasik*. It is said: *al-mansak* with a fatha on the *sin* means the act, and with a kasra on the *sin* means the place, like *al-masjid*, *al-mashriq* and *al-maghrib*. God, exalted is He, said, ﴿For every nation We have appointed rites which they perform﴾ [al-Hajj 22:67]. It has been read with fatha and with kasra. The apparent sense of the statement indicates the act. Likewise His saying, peace be upon him: "Take from me your rites" — he commanded them to learn his actions in the Hajj, not that he meant: "Take from me the places of your rites."

Knowing this, we say: if we take *manasik* as the rites of the Hajj, then if we take them as acts, the showing is to make known those acts; and if we take them as places, the showing is to make known the locations. Some of the commentators took *manasik* to mean only the sacrificial animal, and this is an error, because the sacrificial animal is called *nusuk* only because it falls under worship. For this reason they do not call what is slaughtered for eating by that name. The reason why the sacrificial animal is called *nusuk* — that it is an act of the Hajj — exists in all the other acts, so it is necessary that all of them be included in it. And if we take *manasik* as referring to what the root of this word returns to, namely worship and drawing near to God, and adhering to what pleases Him, and we make this general for everything God prescribed for Abraham, peace be upon him, then His saying, ﴿And show us our rites﴾ means: teach us how to worship You, where to worship You, and with what to draw near to You, so that we may serve You as a servant serves his master.

**Third issue:** Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, in some transmissions, read *arna* with a sukun on the *ra'* throughout the Qur'an. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir agreed with them in one instance, in Ha Mim al-Sajdah: ﴿Show us those who led us astray﴾ [Fussilat 41:29]. Abu 'Amr, in some of the well-known transmissions from him, read with *ikhtilas* (a rapid, reduced vowel) of the kasra of the *ra'* without prolonging it, throughout the Qur'an. The rest read with a fully prolonged kasra. Its origin is *ar'ina* with a kasra on the hamza: the kasra of the hamza was transferred to the *ra'* and the hamza was deleted. This is the preferred reading, because most of the reciters follow it. Also, because the hamza has been dropped, the *ra'* should not be made quiescent, lest the word be weakened and the indication of the hamza be lost. As for the sukun, it is based on deleting the hamza along with its vowel and on analogy with what has quiescence, as in their saying *fakhdh* and *kabd*. As for *ikhtilas*, it is for seeking lightness while preserving the indication of the deleted hamza.

\* \* \*

As for His saying, ﴿And turn to us in repentance﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Those who permit sin upon the prophets have argued with this verse, saying: because repentance is conditioned upon the prior occurrence of sin, if there were no prior sin, the request for repentance would be a request for the impossible. As for the Mu'tazilites, they said: we permit minor sins upon the prophets, so this repentance was repentance from a minor sin. And one may say: minor sins have already been expiated by the reward of the one who commits them, and once they are expiated, repentance from them is impossible, because the effect of repentance is in removing them, and removing what has already been removed is impossible.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 127–129 (part 3 of 4):

Here there are other answers, suitable both for those who permit minor sins and for those who do not permit them, and they are of several aspects:

The first of them: it is possible that he (Abraham) adopted the form of repentance as a means of being firmly resolved in turning away from disobedience, because whoever imagines himself in the form of one who regrets and resolves on great caution, is closer to abandoning sins, so that this becomes a kindness (lutf) that calls to the abandoning of sins.

The second: that the servant, however much he strives in obedience to his Lord, does not escape shortcoming in some respects, either by way of forgetfulness (sahw) or by way of leaving what is better (tark al-awla); so this supplication was for the sake of that.

The third: that when God (exalted is He) informed Abraham, peace be upon him, that among his offspring there would be one who is a wrongdoer and a disobedient, he therefore asked here that He make some of his offspring a Muslim community, then he asked of Him that He grant those disobedient sinners success in repentance, saying: ﴿And accept our repentance﴾, meaning, for the sinners among our offspring. A father who is compassionate toward his son, when his son commits a sin and the father makes excuses for him, may say: "I have committed a crime, disobeyed and sinned, so accept my excuse," and his intention is: "My son has sinned, so accept his excuse, for a person's child is in the position of himself." What strengthens this interpretation are several aspects:

The first: what God (exalted is He) related in Surah Ibrahim, that he said: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols. My Lord, they have led many people astray. Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 35–36]. So it is possible that the meaning is: "and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are capable of turning to him in repentance if he repents, and forgiving him what preceded of his sins."

The second: it is mentioned that in the recitation of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "and show them their rites, and turn to them in repentance."

The third: that he said, in continuation of this: ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them﴾.

The fourth: they interpreted the saying of God (exalted is He): ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾ [al-A'raf: 11] by considering His creating of him as creating for them, since they were from him; so likewise it is not far-fetched that His saying: ﴿And show us our rites﴾ means: show us our offspring.

* * *

The second issue: The companions (the Ash'aris) used the saying ﴿and accept our repentance﴾ as evidence that the act of the servant is the creation of God (exalted is He). They said: because he (peace be upon him) asked God (exalted is He) to accept his repentance; if repentance were created by the servant, then asking it from God (exalted is He) would be absurd and ignorant. The Mu'tazilah said: this is countered by the fact that God (exalted is He) asked repentance from us, saying: ﴿O you who believe, turn to God in sincere repentance﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8]; and if it were an act of God (exalted is He), then asking it from the servant would be absurd and ignorant. Once that is established, His saying ﴿and accept our repentance﴾ is understood as referring to granting success (tawfiq) and performing kindnesses (lutf), or to accepting repentance from the servant. The companions said: the preference is with us, because rational proof supports our view in several aspects:

The first: that whenever God (exalted is He) does not create a motive (da'iyah) that necessitates repentance, the occurrence of repentance is impossible; so repentance is from God (exalted is He) and not from the servant. The exposition of the argument of the motive has been presented more than once.

The second: that repentance, as summarized by Shaykh al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, is a term for a combination of three ordered matters: knowledge, a state, and action. Knowledge is first, the state is second and it is what knowledge necessitates, and action is third and it is what the state necessitates. As for knowledge, it is recognition of the greatness of the harm of sins; from this recognition there arises the heart's pain because of the loss of benefit and the occurrence of harm, and this pain is what is called regret (nadam). Then from this regret there arises an attribute called will (irada), which relates to the present, the past, and the future. Its relation to the present is abandoning the sin that was clinging to him; its relation to the future is by resolving to abandon that act which causes the loss of the beloved until the end of life; and its relation in the past is by making up for what was lost through restitution and settlement, if it is capable of restitution. Knowledge is the first, and it is the dawn of these goods, and by this knowledge I mean faith and certainty, for faith is a term for affirming that sins are deadly poisons, and certainty is a term for the firmness of this affirmation, the absence of doubt about it, and its dominance over the heart. Then, whenever this certainty dominates the heart, the fire of regret blazes, and the heart is pained by it, as it perceives, by the light of faith shining, that it has become veiled from its beloved, like one upon whom the sunlight shines, having been in darkness, and who sees his beloved has come near to destruction, so the fires of love ignite in his heart, and from that state there arises his will to rise up to make amends.

Having known this, we say: the following of the act upon the will is necessary, because a firm will free of any opposing factor must be followed by the act; and the following of the will upon the pain of the heart is also necessary, for whoever's heart is pained by witnessing something disliked must have in his heart the will to repel it; and the following of that pain upon knowledge that this thing brings harms, and the repelling of benefits, is also a necessary matter. So all these stages are necessary, so how could they occur under testing and effort?

There remains to be said: what falls under obligation is knowledge, but there is also a difficulty in this, because that knowledge is either necessary (daruri) or acquired by reflection (nazari). If it is necessary, it does not fall under testing and obligation either; and if it is acquired by reflection, then it is inferred from necessary knowledges. So the totality of those necessary knowledges which produce the first acquired knowledge either is sufficient for that production or is not sufficient. If it is sufficient, then the acquired knowledge inferred from them being the first to follow from those necessary knowledges is obligatory, and what must follow from what is outside of choice is also outside of choice. And if it is not sufficient, then something else is needed; that other thing, if it is from the necessary knowledges, then if it is present, what we supposed was not sufficient, yet it was sufficient—this is a contradiction; and if it is from the acquired knowledges, then the first of the acquired knowledges requires another acquired knowledge before it, so the first of the acquired knowledges would not be first for the acquired knowledges, and this is a contradiction.

Then the discussion about that first is like what came before it, so it leads to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. Thus it is established by what we mentioned last that His saying ﴿and accept our repentance﴾ is to be taken in its apparent sense, which is the truth consistent with rational proofs, and that the other verses opposing this verse are more deserving of interpretation.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed You are the Ever-Accepting of Repentance, the Most Merciful﴾, it has already been mentioned.

The third type: His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them﴾. Know that there is no doubt that His saying ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger﴾ means those whom he intended by His saying ﴿and from our offspring a Muslim community submissive to You﴾, because that is what was mentioned before, and describing his offspring with that is not fitting except for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). So it is joined to it by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them﴾. This supplication conveys the perfection of the condition of his offspring in two respects:

One of them: that there be among them a messenger who perfects for them the religion and the law and calls them to that by which they will remain firm in Islam.

The second: that this raised one be from among them and not from others, for several reasons:

One of them: so that their station and rank in honour and religion would be greater, because when the messenger and the one sent to are both from his offspring, it is more noble for his request when it is granted.

The second: that when he is from among them, they know his birth and upbringing, so it is easier for them to recognize his truthfulness and trustworthiness.

The third: that when he is from among them, he is the most eager of people for their good and the most compassionate toward them, more than a stranger would be if sent to them.

When this is established, we say: if Abraham (peace be upon him) intended the establishment of the religion in the present and in the future, and it was predominant in his thought that this would be completed and perfected only if the people were from his offspring, it was good of him to intend that, so that the ultimate aim in religion would be gathered for him, and there is added to it great joy that this matter should be among his offspring, for there is no honour or nobility higher than this rank.

As for the fact that the messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), several aspects indicate it:

The first: the consensus of the exegetes, and that is a proof.

The second: what is narrated from him (peace be upon him) that he said: "I am the answered supplication of Abraham and the good news of Jesus." By "supplication" he meant this verse, and the good news of Jesus (peace be upon him) is what is mentioned in Surah al-Saff in His saying: ﴿and a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6].

The third: that Abraham (peace be upon him) made this supplication only in Mecca, for his offspring who would be there and in its surroundings, and God (exalted is He) did not send to those in Mecca and its surroundings except Muhammad (ﷺ).

Here there is a question: it is said, what is the wisdom in mentioning Abraham (peace be upon him) together with Muhammad (ﷺ) in the matter of prayer, where it is said: "O God, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Abraham and upon the family of Abraham"?

They answered it in several ways:

The first of them: that Abraham (peace be upon him) supplicated for Muhammad (peace be upon him) when he said: ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them who will recite to them Your verses﴾; so when the right of the supplication of the Friend (Khalil) upon the Beloved (Habib) became due, God (exalted is He) discharged His right to him by causing his mention to continue on the tongues of his community until the Day of Resurrection.

The second: that Abraham (peace be upon him) asked that from his Lord by saying: ﴿and grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 84], meaning: preserve for me a good praise in the community of Muhammad (ﷺ); so God (exalted is He) answered him and joined his mention to the mention of His beloved, to preserve the good praise of him among his community.

The third: that Abraham was the father of the religious community, according to His saying: ﴿the religion of your father Abraham﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and Muhammad was the father of mercy; and in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and he is a father to them," and in his story He said: ﴿compassionate and merciful toward the believers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], and he (peace be upon him) said: "I am to you only like a father," meaning in tenderness and mercy. So when each of them had the right of fatherhood in some respect, He brought their mentions close together in the context of praise and blessing.

The fourth: that Abraham (peace be upon him) was the herald of the law in the Hajj: ﴿and proclaim to the people the Hajj﴾ [al-Hajj: 27], and Muhammad (peace be upon him) was the herald of the religion: ﴿We have heard a caller calling to faith﴾ [Al 'Imran: 193]; so God (exalted is He) joined the two of them in the beautiful remembrance.

Know that when He (exalted is He) requested the sending of a messenger from among them to them, He mentioned attributes of that messenger.

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿who will recite to them Your verses﴾, and in it there are two aspects:

The first: that they are the Furqan which was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ), because what he used to recite to them was none other than that, so it is necessary to take it as such.

The second: it is permissible that the verses be the signs indicating the existence of the Creator and His attributes (exalted is He), and the meaning of his reciting them to them is that he would remind them of them, call them to them, and lead them to belief in them.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and teach them the Book﴾, and what is meant is that he would order them to recite the Book and teach them the meanings and realities of the Book, and that is because recitation is desired for several reasons:

Among them: the preservation of its wording on the tongues of the people of mass transmission (tawatur), so that it remains protected from distortion.

and the purity of the text, and it has among its features that its wording and arrangement are a miracle for Muhammad (ﷺ), and that its recitation is a kind of worship and obedience, and that its recitation in the prayers and in all other acts of worship is a kind of worship. This is the ruling on recitation. However, the great wisdom and the most noble purpose is teaching what it contains of proofs and rulings, for Allah the Exalted described the Qur'an as being guidance and light because of the meanings, wisdoms and secrets within it. So when Allah the Exalted first mentioned the matter of recitation, He then mentioned after it the teaching of its realities and secrets, and said: ﴿and teaches them the Book﴾.

The third attribute of the Messenger (ﷺ) is His saying: ﴿and the wisdom﴾, meaning: and teaches them the wisdom. Know that wisdom is: correctness in speech and action, and no one is called wise unless both matters are combined in him. It was also said: its origin is from "ahkamtu al-shay'" meaning I returned it, so wisdom is what turns away from ignorance and error, and that occurs only by what we mentioned of correctness in speech and action, and placing everything in its proper place.

Al-Qaffal said: Some philosophers described wisdom as "assimilation to God to the extent of human capacity."

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of wisdom here, in several ways:

First: Ibn Wahb said: I asked Malik: What is wisdom? He said: knowledge of the religion, understanding of it, and following it.

Second: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Wisdom is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is also the view of Qatadah. The companions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The evidence for this is that He mentioned the recitation of the Book first and its teaching second, then He joined wisdom to it by conjunction, so wisdom must be something outside the Book, and that is none other than the Sunnah of the Messenger, peace be upon him. If it is said: why can it not be taken to mean teaching the rational proofs for the Oneness of God, justice and prophethood? We say: because the intellects are receptive to that, so applying this expression to what is not derived from the Sharia is more appropriate.

Third: Wisdom is the distinguishing between truth and falsehood, and it is a verbal noun in the sense of judgment, like "al-qi'dah" and "al-jilsah." The meaning: He teaches them Your Book which You send down to them, and the distinction of Your decisions and rulings which You teach them. Examples of this: "al-khubr" and "al-khibrah," "al-'udhr" and "al-'idhrah," "al-ghull" and "al-ghillah," "al-dhull" and "al-dhillah."

Fourth: "and teaches them the Book" refers to the clear verses (muhkamat), and "and the wisdom" refers to the ambiguous verses (mutashabihat).

Fifth: "and teaches them the Book" means He teaches them what it contains of rulings. "And the wisdom" means that He teaches them the wisdom of those laws and what they contain of aspects of benefit and advantage. Some people said: all of these are attributes of the Book, as if He described it as being verses, as being a Book, and as being wisdom.

The fourth attribute of the Messenger (ﷺ) is His saying: ﴿and purifies them﴾. Know that the perfection of a human's state lies in two matters:

One of them: that he knows the truth for its own sake.

The second: that he knows the good for the sake of acting upon it. If he falls short in either of these two matters, he is not pure from vices and deficiencies, nor is he purified from them. So when He mentioned the attributes of excellence and perfection, He followed them with mention of purification from vices and deficiencies, saying: ﴿and purifies them﴾. Know that the Messenger has no power to act upon the inner states of the accountable, and even assuming he had such power, he does not exercise it, for otherwise that purification would be present in them by way of compulsion, not by way of choice. So this purification has two explanations:

The first: what he does besides the recitation and teaching of the Book and wisdom, so that this acts as a cause for their purity. Those matters were what he, peace be upon him, did of promise and warning, admonition and reminder, repeating that to them, and of attachment to worldly affairs until they believe and reform. He, peace be upon him, did many things of this kind to strengthen by them their motives toward faith and righteous action. For this reason Allah praised him, saying that he was upon a great character, and that he was given the noble qualities of character.

The second: "and purifies them" means He testifies for them that they are pure on the Day of Resurrection, when He bears witness against every soul for what it earned, like the purification of the witness by the one who vouches for witnesses. The first is better, because it is more in keeping with the intent of his supplication, for his intent is that this offspring attain completely the success of Paradise, and that is not achieved except by teaching the Book and wisdom, then by strong encouragement to action and warning against neglecting action, which is purification. This is the summarized discussion of this verse, and the exegetes have expressions concerning it:

First: al-Hasan said: He purifies them from their polytheism. So the verse indicates that there will be among the descendants of Isma'il ignorant people with no wisdom and no Book, and that polytheism defiles them, and that Allah the Exalted will send among them a Messenger from among them who will purify them and make them the wise of the earth after their ignorance.

Second: Purification is obedience to Allah and sincerity, from Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: "and purifies them" means from polytheism and all filth, like His saying: ﴿and makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the evil things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. Know that when he, peace be upon him, mentioned these supplications, he concluded them with praise of Allah the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾. The Mighty is the Capable who cannot be overcome, and the Wise is the Knowing who does not lack knowledge of anything. When He is knowing and capable, what He does is correct and free from futility and foolishness, and were He not so, it would not be valid for Him to answer supplication, nor to send messengers, nor to send down the Book.

Know that "the Mighty," as one of the essential attributes, when its meaning is His power over things and His being immune from humiliation and subjugation, since if He is exalted above needs, the humiliation of the needy does not befall Him, and it is not permissible that He be prevented from His will so that He suffers abasement; so He is Mighty without doubt. As for "the Wise," if it is meant in the sense of "the Knowing," it is one of the essential attributes. But if "might" is meant as perfection of might, which is being immune from others' domination over Him, and "wisdom" is meant as the performance of wise acts, then "the Mighty" and "the Wise" are not essential attributes but attributes of act. The difference between these two kinds of attributes lies in several aspects:

First: essential attributes are eternal, and attributes of act are not so.

Second: essential attributes cannot have their opposites true at any time, and attributes of act are not so.

Third: attributes of act are relational matters, whose realization requires the issuing of effects from the agent, while essential attributes are not so. An-Nazzam argued that He, exalted is He, is not capable of the ugly by saying: The God must necessarily be wise by His essence, and if He is wise by His essence, the ugly is not within His power, and wisdom by its nature contradicts the doing of the ugly; so it is impossible for God to do the ugly, and what is impossible is not within power. We only said: God must necessarily be wise because if that were not necessary, it would be permissible for Him to change into its opposite, and then it would follow that God would be God with the absence of wisdom, and that is impossible by consensus. As for wisdom contradicting the doing of folly, that too is known by necessity; and that what entails a contradiction is contradictory is known by necessity; so divinity cannot be established together with the doing of folly. And that the impossible is not within power is clear. Thus it is established that God is not capable of doing the ugly.

The answer to this: As for our school, none of the acts is folly from Him, so the objection falls away. And Allah knows best.

[Page 63]

Know that after God, exalted is He, had mentioned the matter of Abraham (peace be upon him) and what He had brought about through him of the noble laws with which He tested him, and of the building of the House and His command to the servants of God to make pilgrimage to it, and what God, exalted is He, had instilled in him of eagerness for the welfare of His servants and his supplication for good for them, and other matters that preceded in the previous verse, He amazed the people, saying: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham?﴾ Belief in what came of his laws was implied, and this constituted a rebuke to the Jews, the Christians, and the idolaters of the Arabs. The Jews only boast of him and claim kinship through the connection between them and him through the lineage of Israel. The Christians' boasting is not through Jesus, who is connected to Israel only through his mother. As for the Quraysh, they only attained every good in the pre-Islamic era through the House that he built, so they were thereby called to the Book of God. As for the rest of the Arabs, who are the 'Adnanites, their lineage returns to Isma'il, and they boast over the Qahtanites through Isma'il, because of the prophethood God, exalted is He, gave him. Thus, upon examination, the boasting of all of them returns to Abraham (peace be upon him). Since it is established that Abraham (peace be upon him) is the one who asked God, exalted is He, to send this Messenger at the end of time, and he is the one who humbly pleaded to God, exalted is He, to achieve this goal, it is strange that one whose greatest glories and virtues are affiliation with Abraham (peace be upon him) would then not believe in the Messenger who is the fulfilment of Abraham's supplication and the object of his humble request. Undoubtedly, this is something that deserves to be wondered at.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham, except one who makes a fool of himself﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: It is said: "raghibtu min al-amr" means I disliked it, and "raghibtu fīhi" means I desired it. The first "man" (who) is interrogative in meaning of denial, and the second is in the meaning of "alladhī" (the one who). The author of al-Kashshāf said: "man safiha" is in the nominative position as a *badal* (substitution, apposition) for the pronoun in *yarghab*, and the *badal* is valid because "man yarghab" is in a non-affirmative context, like your saying: "Has anyone come to you except Zayd?"

Second issue: One might ask here: the intended "religion of Abraham" is the religion brought by Muhammad (peace be upon him), because the purpose of the speech is to encourage people to accept this religion. So either it is said that this religion is identical to the religion of Abraham in its foundations and branches, or it is said that this religion is that religion in its foundations, namely monotheism, prophethood, and maintaining noble morals, but they differ in the branches of the laws and the manner of the acts. As for the first, it is false, because he (peace be upon him) claimed that his law abrogated (*naskh*, i.e., the annulling of earlier rulings by later revelation) all laws, so how can it be said that this law is identical to that law? As for the second, it does not yield the desired result, because acknowledging the foundations, namely monotheism, justice, noble morals, and the afterlife, does not entail acknowledging the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him), so how can this speech be relied upon for this goal?

Another question: Muhammad (peace be upon him), when he acknowledged that Abraham's law is abrogated, and the word "religion" includes foundations and branches, it follows that Muhammad (peace be upon him) would also be turning away from the religion of Abraham, and thus the same objection would apply to them.

The answer: When He, exalted is He, related about Abraham (peace be upon him) that he humbly pleaded to God, exalted is He, and asked Him to send this Messenger, to support him, strengthen him, and spread his law, He expressed this meaning as "the religion of Abraham." So when the Jews, Christians, and Arabs granted that Abraham (peace be upon him) was right in his statement, it became obligatory upon them to acknowledge the prophethood of this person who is the object of Abraham's (peace be upon him) request.

[Page 64]

The questioner says: The claim is not that they conceded that Abraham asked God, exalted is He, for such a Messenger; rather, Muhammad (peace be upon him) narrated this report from Abraham (peace be upon him) in order to build upon this narration the argument that they are obliged to acknowledge the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him). Therefore, his prophethood is not established unless this narration is established, and this narration is not established unless his prophethood is established, which leads to circular reasoning (*dawr*), and that is invalid. Suppose we grant that they conceded the soundness of this narration. Yet in this narration there is nothing but that Abraham asked God, exalted is He, to send a Messenger from his offspring and the offspring of Isma'il. So how can one be certain that this Messenger is this particular person? Perhaps he is another person who will come after that. And if it is permissible for the answer to this supplication to be delayed by a period of two thousand years, which is the time between Abraham and Muhammad (peace be upon both of them), why would it not be permissible for it to be delayed by three thousand years, so that the one sought by this supplication is a person other than this specific individual?

The answer to the first question: Perhaps the Torah and the Gospel are witnesses to the soundness of this narration. Were it not so, the Jews and the Christians would have been among the most eager of people to deny him in this claim.

As for the second: The reliance in establishing his prophethood (peace be upon him) is the manifestation of a miracle at his hand, which is the Qur'an, and his reporting of unseen matters that none knows except a prophet, and the like of these accounts. Moreover, this proof serves as a confirmation of the intended object and goal. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

Third issue: Regarding the grammatical status of "nafsahu" there are two views:

The first: that it is an object (*maf'ūl*). Al-Mubarrad said: *safiha* is intransitive, and *safaha* is transitive. On this view there are several explanations:

The first: he degraded it and treated it lightly. The root meaning of *safah* is lightness, and from it comes "a *zimām safīh*" (a loose, unruly rein). The evidence for this is what came in the hadith: "Arrogance is to belittle the truth and to despise people." This is because whoever turns away from what no intelligent person ever turns away from has gone to great lengths in corrupting his soul and rendering it incapable, since he has opposed with it every intelligent soul.

The second: al-Hasan said: "except one who ignores himself and ruins himself." The reality of it is that no one turns away from the religion of Abraham except one who is ignorant and does not reflect upon it, so that he would not derive from what he finds in it of signs of creation evidence for the oneness of God, exalted is He, and His wisdom, and thus derive from that evidence for the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him).

The third: he destroyed his soul and ruined it, according to Abu 'Ubayda.

The fourth: he misguided his soul.

The second view: that *nafsahu* is not an object. They mentioned several explanations on this view:

The first: that *nafsahu* is in the accusative by the omission of the preposition, its estimated sense being: "he was foolish in his soul."

The second: that it is in the accusative as a specification (*tafsīr*), according to al-Farra', and its meaning is: "he was foolish as to soul," then it was made an annexed construction; its estimated form being: "except the foolish one." The mention of "soul" is an emphasis, as one says: "this matter itself," and the intended purpose is to intensify his foolishness.

The third: it was read as "*man saffaha nafsahu*" with the letter *fā'* doubled. Then, when He, exalted is He, judged the one who turns away from the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him) to be foolish, He explained the reason, saying: ﴿And We indeed chose him in this world﴾. The meaning is that when We chose him for the messengership above all other creatures, and made known to him the religion that comprises monotheism, justice, laws, and an enduring leadership until the Hour, and then attributed to him the judgment of God, exalted is He, He honored him with this title, which carries the utmost grandeur for whoever attains it among the kings of mankind. How much more so for one who attains it from the King of kings and of laws. So let every person of understanding and intellect realize that whoever turns away from his religion is indeed foolish. Then He explained that he is of great rank in the Hereafter, so that one would desire a path like his to attain a similar rank. It has been said that in the verse there is a transposition, and its estimated form is: "And We indeed chose him in this world and the Hereafter, and he is indeed among the righteous." But when the speech is sound without transposition, it is preferable. Al-Hasan said: "[He is] among those who merit honor and good reward through the generosity of God, exalted is He."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 131:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."﴾

Know that this is the fifth of the matters which Allah related about Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and in it there are several issues:

The first issue: the position of "idh" (when) is in the accusative, and concerning its governing element (ʿamil) there are two opinions.

The first opinion: it is in the accusative governed by "isţafaynāhu" (We chose him), meaning: We chose him at the time when his Lord said to him, "Submit." It is as if He, exalted is He, mentioned the choosing and then followed it with mention of the cause of the choosing: when he surrendered himself to the worship of Allah, exalted is He, and submitted to it and obeyed it, Allah, exalted is He, knew from his state that he would not change over time and that he remained steadfast upon this path, and he was, in addition to that, purified from all sins. At that point He chose him for prophethood and singled him out with it, for Allah, exalted is He, does not choose for prophethood except one whose state is such at the beginning and at the end. So his submission to Allah, exalted is He, and the goodness of his response are stated explicitly. If it is said: His saying, ﴿And We certainly chose him﴾ is a report in the first person, and His saying, ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit"﴾ is a report in the third person, so how can it be understood that this composition is one? We say: this is from the type of shift (iltifat) that we have mentioned many times.

The second opinion: it is in the accusative governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember), as if it were said: Remember that time, so that it is known that he is the chosen righteous one, whose creed no one would turn away from the like of.

The second issue: they differed as to when Allah, exalted is He, said to him, "Submit"? The source of the difficulty is that "Submit" is said only at a time when one is not already a Muslim. So was Ibrahim, peace be upon him, not a Muslim at some time, so that he could be told at that time, "Submit"? The majority hold that Allah, exalted is He, said this before prophethood and before puberty, at the time of his reflection upon the star, the moon and the sun, and his perception of the signs of createdness in them, and his awareness of their need for a manager who differs from them in corporeality and the signs of createdness. So when he recognized his Lord, Allah, exalted is He, said to him: ﴿Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.﴾ For it is not permissible that He say this to him before he knew his Lord. It is also possible that His saying, "Submit," was before the reflection, so that what is meant by this saying is not the speech itself but the indication of the proof upon it, according to the customs of the Arabs in this, like the saying of the poet:

The basin filled and said, "Enough, my belly, gently, gently, you have filled my belly."

And the most truthful indication of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾ [al-Rum: 35], so He made the indication of the proof a speech. Some people said: this matter occurred after prophethood, and His saying, "Submit," does not mean Islam and faith, but other matters.

One of them: submission to the commands of Allah, exalted is He, hastening to receive them with acceptance, and abandoning opposition with the heart and the tongue; and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and make us both submitting to You﴾.

The second: al-Asamm said: "Submit" means: make your worship sincere and make it free from association and from regarding others.

The third: remain steadfast upon Islam and be firm upon monotheism, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾ [Muhammad: 19].

The fourth: faith is a quality of the heart and Islam is a quality of the limbs, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, in his heart, and then Allah, exalted is He, obligated him with the action of the limbs and the body parts by His saying: "Submit."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 132:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons, and so did Jacob: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims."﴾

Know that this is the sixth of the praiseworthy matters which Allah related about Abraham, and in it are several issues.

The first issue: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "wa-awsa" (ووصى) with an alif, and it is so in the codices of Medina and Syria. The rest read it without an alif, with the shadda (wa-şşā, وصّى), and it is so in their codices too. The meaning is one, except that in "wa-şşā" there is an indication of emphasis and intensification.

The second issue: To what does the pronoun in "bihā" (بِها, "with it") refer? There are two opinions:

The first: It refers to His saying, ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾, by way of interpreting it as the word and the sentence. A parallel to this is the return of the pronoun in His saying, ﴿and He made it a word that remains﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 28] to His saying, ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who originated me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 26–27]. And His saying, ﴿a word that remains﴾ is evidence that the feminine form is by way of interpreting it as the word.

The second opinion: It refers to the religion (millah, مِلَّة) in His saying, ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham?﴾ The judge (al-Qadi) said: This opinion is better than the first for two reasons.

The first: That [religion] is not explicitly mentioned, and returning a pronoun to something explicitly mentioned, when possible, is preferable to returning it to what is implied and understood.

The second: The religion (millah) is more comprehensive than that word, and it is known that he did not enjoin his children except with what gathers for them success and triumph in the Hereafter, and the testimony of faith alone does not entail that.

The third issue: Know that this narration contains subtle points that encourage acceptance of the religion.

One of them: He, Exalted is He, did not say "Abraham commanded his sons," but rather "instructed them" (waṣṣāhum, وصّاهم), and the word waṣiyyah (وصية, "instruction/bequest") is more emphatic than command, because a bequest is made at the fear of death, and at that time a person's care for his religion is most intense and complete. When one knows that he, peace be upon him, was at that time concerned with this matter and strict about it, the inclination to accept it is closer.

The second: He, peace be upon him, specified his sons with this, because a man's compassion for his sons is greater than his compassion for others. When he specified them with it at the end of his life, we know that his concern with it was greater than his concern with anything else.

The third: He generalized this instruction to all his sons and did not single out any one of them with it, and this too indicates intensity of concern.

The fourth: He, peace be upon him, stated this instruction without restricting it to a specific time or specific place, and then he warned them in the strongest terms against dying other than as Muslims, and this too indicates intensity of concern with this matter.

The fifth: He, peace be upon him, did not combine with this instruction any other instruction. This too indicates intensity of concern with this matter. And since Abraham, peace be upon him, was the man attested to for excellence, good conduct, and perfection of character, and it became known that he was at the utmost concern with this matter, it became known then that this matter is the most worthy of concern and the most deserving of care. This is the reason he specified his family and sons with this instruction. Otherwise, it is known from the state of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he always called everyone to Islam and the religion.

As for His saying, ﴿and Jacob﴾, there are two opinions:

The first, which is the most well known: it is coordinated (ma'tuf, مَعْطُوف) upon Abraham, and the meaning is that he (Jacob) instructed as Abraham's instruction was.

The second: "wa-Ya'qūba" (ويَعْقُوبَ) was read in the accusative, coordinated upon "banīhi" (بَنِيهِ, "his sons"), and its meaning: Abraham instructed his sons and his grandson Jacob.

As for His saying, ﴿O my sons﴾, it is by way of an implied verb of saying (idmar al-qawl) according to the Basrians; according to the Kufans, it is connected to "wa-şşā," because it carries the sense of saying. And in the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud, it is "an yā banīy" (أن يا بَنِيَّ).

As for His saying, ﴿He has chosen for you the religion﴾, the meaning is that He, Exalted is He, singled it out by establishing upon it clear and manifest proofs, calling you to it, and preventing you from other than it.

As for His saying, ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾, the meaning is urging them toward Islam. This is because a man who does not feel secure from death in every moment of his life, and who is commanded to bring about a thing before death, becomes commanded with it in every state, for it is feared that if he does not hasten to it, death may overtake him, so he misses the success of salvation and fears destruction, and thus he places himself in danger and deception.

The Lord's words: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death came to Ya'qub? When he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we are submitting."﴾ ﴿That is a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earned. You will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, related about Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that he exerted himself in enjoining his sons in the religion and in Islam, He mentioned right after it that Ya'qub also enjoined his sons with the same, to reinforce the proof against the Jews and the Christians, and to intensify the clarification. In this there are issues:

The first issue: Know that "am" (أمْ) has the meaning of an interrogative particle or a conjunctive particle. It resembles the conjunction "aw" (أوْ, "or") and it comes in two ways: connected (muttasila) to what precedes it, and disconnected (munqati'a) from it. As for the connected one, know that when you say, "Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?", you do not know whether one of them is with him, so you ask: "Is one of these two with you?" Therefore his answer is necessarily "no" or "yes." But if you know that one of these two men is with him, yet you do not know whether the one with him is Zayd or 'Amr, and you ask him to specify, you say: "Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?" That is, know that one of them is with you, but is it this one or that one? As for the disconnected one, they said that it has the meaning of "bal" (بَلْ, "rather") together with the interrogative hamza. Its example: if one says, "Indeed, they are camels, or sheep?", the speaker's sight fell upon the figures and he assumed that they were camels, so he reported according to what his assumption required, that they were camels. Then doubt came to him, and he wanted to retract that report and to ask whether they are sheep or not. So the retraction from the first is the meaning of "bal," and the question about whether they are sheep is what is intended by the interrogative hamza. Thus your saying, "Indeed, they are camels, or sheep?" runs in the manner of your saying, "Indeed, they are camels. Are they sheep?" So your saying, "Are they sheep?" is a resumed statement, not connected to your saying, "Indeed, they are camels." How could it not be, when the retraction from it has occurred? This is unlike the connected one, for your saying, "Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?" means "which of them is with you?" And "ma" (what) after "am" is not disconnected from what precedes it, by the evidence that 'Amr is the companion of Zayd. Sufficient as evidence of this is that you express it with a singular noun, saying, "Which of them is with you?" Both types occur abundantly in the Book of Allah, exalted is He. As for the connected type, the Lord's words: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is the sky? He raised its height﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 28], meaning, "Which of you is more difficult?" As for the disconnected type, the Lord's words: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, is from the Lord of the worlds. Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [al-Sajda: 1–3], and Allah knows best, the meaning is "rather, they say, 'He has invented it'," which indicates the retraction from the first and the questioning about what follows, since there is no meaning in the statement otherwise, just as in your saying, "Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?" Some exegetes who do not verify say that "am" here is equivalent to the hamza, and that is not correct, for what we mentioned: this disconnected "am" includes the meaning of "bal." Once you know this introduction, we say: is "am" in this verse disjunctive or connective? There are two opinions:

The first: it is disconnected from what precedes it, and the meaning of the hamza in it is denial, that is: "Rather, you were not witnesses." "Shuhada'" (witnesses) is the plural of "shahid" in the sense of "present," that is, you were not present when death came to Ya'qub. The address is to the People of the Book, as if Allah, exalted is He, said to them concerning what they claimed, that the religion they adhered to was the religion of the messengers: "How can you say that, when you witness the testaments of the prophets concerning the religion? Had you witnessed that, you would have abandoned what you are upon of religion and would have desired the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the very same that Ibrahim (peace be upon him), Ya'qub, and all the other prophets after him (peace be upon them) were upon."

If it is said: interrogation in the manner of denial is directed only at a false statement, and what is related of Ya'qub in this verse is not a false statement but a true one, so how can the interrogation in the manner of denial be directed at it? We say: the interrogation in the manner of denial relates only to their mere claim of being present at his death, and this is what Allah, exalted is He, denied. As for His subsequent mention of Ya'qub's words, "What will you worship after me?", it is a detailed statement. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, when He denied their presence at that time, then explained after that the manner of that testament.

The second opinion: that "am" in this verse is connective, and the way to explain this is that something omitted is supposed before it, as if it was said: "Do you claim against the prophets Judaism, or were you witnesses when death came to Ya'qub?" That is, your forefathers from the Children of Israel were present for him when he called his sons to the community of Islam and monotheism, and you know that, so why do you claim against the prophets what they are innocent of?

* * *

As for His words: ﴿when he said to his sons﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Qaffal said: His words, ﴿when death came to Ya'qub, when he said to his sons﴾, the first "idh" (when) is the time of the witnessing, and the second is the time of the presence.

The second issue: the verse indicates that the compassion of the prophets (peace be upon them) toward their children was within the matter of religion, and their concern was directed to it alone, and not to anything else.

* * *

As for His words: ﴿What will you worship after me?﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: the word "ma" (what) is for non-rational beings, so how did he use it for the true God?
Its answer is in two respects:
The first: "ma" is general for everything, and the meaning is "What thing will you worship?"
The second: His words, ﴿What you worship﴾, are like your saying, when asking for a definition or description, "What is man?"

[p. 69]

The second issue: His words, ﴿after me﴾. As for His words: ﴿They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq"﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: this verse has been held to by two groups of the ignorant:
The first: the imitators (al-muqallida) said: the sons of Ya'qub were satisfied with imitation (taqlid, blindly following others), and he (peace be upon him) did not denounce this from them, which indicates that imitation is sufficient.
The second: the Ta'limiyya (those who hold that knowledge of God is only through instruction). They said: there is no way to know Allah except through the teaching of the messenger and the imam, and the proof of this is this verse, for they did not say, "We will worship the God whom reason indicates," but rather they said, "We will worship the God whom you worship, and whom your fathers worshipped," and this indicates that the way of knowledge is learning.
The answer: just as there is no indication in the verse that they knew God through rational proof, there is likewise no indication in it that they only acknowledged God by way of imitation and instruction. Then, since the doctrine of imitation and instruction has been refuted by proof, we know that the faith of those people was not upon this way, but was attained through reasoning. At most one can say: then why did they not mention the way of reasoning?
The answer to this is in several respects:
The first: that is more concise in speech than explaining the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, in His oneness, knowledge, power, and justice.
The second: it is closer to calming the soul of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), as if they said: "We only proceed upon the same path as yours, so there is no disagreement from us against you regarding what we worship and what we sincerely devote worship to Him."
The third: perhaps this is an allusion to the mention of the proof of the existence of the Creator, as Allah, exalted is He, mentioned at the beginning of this surah in His words: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqara: 21]. Here, their intention in their words, ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾, means: we will worship the God whose existence is indicated by your existence and the existence of your fathers, and in this way that is an allusion to reasoning, not to imitation.

The second issue: al-Qaffal said: In some tafsirs it is related that when Ya'qub (peace be upon him) entered Egypt, he saw its people worshipping fires and idols, so he feared for his sons after his death, and so he said this statement to them, as an exhortation for them to hold fast to the worship of Allah, exalted is He.

And al-Qadi related from Ibn 'Abbas that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) gathered them to him at the time of his death, and they used to worship idols and fires, so he said: "O my sons, what will you worship after me?" They said: "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers." Then al-Qadi said: this is far-fetched for two reasons:
The first: they hastened to acknowledge monotheism in the manner of one from whom knowledge and certainty had already preceded.
The second: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in the Book the condition of the Asbat (the tribes) among the sons of Ya'qub, and that they were a righteous people, and that is not fitting for their state.

The third issue: His words, ﴿Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾, are an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) for "your fathers." So said al-Qaffal. It has also been said that He mentioned Isma'il before Ishaq because Isma'il was older than Ishaq.

The fourth issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: full brothers and full sisters, or paternal brothers and sisters, are not excluded by the paternal grandfather. This is also the view of 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them, and it is the view of Malik, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad.

Abu Hanifa said: they are excluded by the paternal grandfather. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them. Among the Followers, it is the view of al-Hasan, Tawus and 'Ata'. As for the first group, those who say that they are not excluded by the grandfather, they have two opinions:
One of them: the grandfather is given the choice between two matters: either sharing (al-muqasama) with them, or a third of the entire estate, and then the remainder is divided among the brothers and sisters, the male receiving the equivalent of the share of two females. This is the school of Zayd ibn Thabit and the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him.
The second: he is in the position of one of the brothers, as long as the sharing does not reduce him below a sixth. If the sharing reduces him below a sixth, he is given a sixth, and nothing is reduced from it. Abu Hanifa argued for his view that the grandfather is a father, and the father excludes the sisters and brothers, so it follows that the grandfather excludes them. We say the grandfather is a father based on the Qur'an and the report. As for the Qur'an, there are two verses: this verse, the Lord's words: ﴿They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq"﴾, where the word "father" is applied to the grandfather.

If it is said: it has also been applied to the paternal uncle, Isma'il, although by consensus he is not a father.
We say: usage is evidence of the literal meaning in the apparent sense; it was abandoned in the case of the uncle because of a proof that applied to him, so the proof of the verse remains valid for the rest. The second verse is the Lord's words, relating of Yusuf (peace be upon him): ﴿And I followed the religion of my fathers, Ibrahim and Ishaq and Ya'qub﴾ [Yusuf: 38].

As for the report, 'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Whoever wishes, I will curse him at the Black Stone: the grandfather is a father." And he also said: "Does Zayd ibn Thabit not fear Allah? He makes the son's son a son, but does not make the father's father a father." And when it is established that the grandfather is a father, it is necessary that he falls under the Lord's words: ﴿And his parents inherit from him, so his mother has a third﴾ [al-Nisa': 11], in that the grandfather is entitled to two-thirds to the exclusion of the brothers, just as the father is entitled to it to their exclusion when he is alive.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: We do not concede that the grandfather is a father, and the evidence for this is several points:
The first: just as you argued with these verses that the grandfather is a father, we argue that he is not a father, by the Lord's words: ﴿And Ibrahim enjoined it upon his sons, and so did Ya'qub﴾ [al-Baqara: 132]. For Allah, exalted is He, did not include Ya'qub among his sons, because He distinguished him from them. Had the one ascending in fatherhood been a father, then the one descending in sonship would in reality be a son. Since that is not the case, it is established that the grandfather is not a father.
The second: if the grandfather were a father in the literal sense, it would not be valid for one whose father has died while his grandfather is alive to deny that he has a father, just as it is not valid with the nearer father. And since that is valid, we know that he is not a father in the literal sense.

If it is said: the name of fatherhood applies to all of them, but the rank of the nearer is closer than the rank of the more remote, and therefore the negation is valid regarding it.

We said: If *al-ism* (the term "father") were literally applied to both of them together, then the sequence in existence would not be a reason for denying the name of father to him.

Third: If the grandfather were a father in the literal sense, it would be correct to say that a man died and left behind a mother and many fathers. No jurist, lexicographer, or exegete has ever used such a phrase.

Fourth: If the grandfather were a father, and there is no doubt that the Companions knew the language, they would not have disagreed about the inheritance of the grandfather. And if the grandfather were a father, the grandmother would be a mother. Had that been the case, doubt would not have arisen concerning the inheritance of the grandmother, so that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) would need to ask about it. These proofs indicate that the grandfather is not a father.

Fifth: The words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. If the grandfather were a father, then the son's son would necessarily be a son, and by the requirement of this verse, the son's son would inherit alongside the (existing) son. Since this is not the case, we know that the grandfather is not a father.

As for the verses you cite to establish that the grandfather is a father, the answer concerning the basis of your argument from them is in several respects:

First: Ubayy (ibn Ka'b) recited ﴿وإلَهَ إبْراهِيمَ﴾ with the omission of ﴿آبائِكَ﴾ (i.e., "the God of Ibrahim" without "your fathers"). However, this does not undermine the point, because a deviant (shadhdh) recitation does not override the widely transmitted (mutawatir) recitation. Rather, the answer is to say: he (the Prophet) used the word "father" for the grandfather and for the paternal uncle. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said about al-'Abbas: "This is the remainder of my fathers," and said: "Return my father to me." This indicates that he used it in a metaphorical sense. The evidence for this is what we previously stated, that it is correct to deny the name "father" of the grandfather, and if it were literal, this would not be so. As for the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, he applied the term to him only with regard to the ruling, not with regard to the linguistic term, because languages are not subject to disagreement among the people of the tongue. And Allah knows best.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿One God﴾, it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the God of your fathers﴾, like His saying: ﴿by the forelock, a lying, sinning forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq: 15–16]. Or it is in the mode of specification (ikhtisas), meaning: you intend by "the God of your fathers" one God.

As for His saying: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, there are several possibilities:

One: It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of *na'budu* ("we worship") or from its object, because the pronoun returns to it in *lahu* ("to Him").

Two: It may be a clause conjoined (ma'tufah) to *na'budu*.

Three: It may be a parenthetical emphatic clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah mu'akkidah), meaning: and it is our state that we are submitting to Him, sincere in monotheism or submissive.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾, it refers to those whom Allah the Exalted mentioned in the preceding verse: Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, and his sons, the monotheists. "Ummah" means a category. "Khalat" means passed on, departed, and perished. The meaning is that I have related to you their accounts and what they were upon of Islam and calling to Islam. So there is no benefit for you in their conduct unless you do what they did. If you do that, you will benefit; and if you refuse, you will not benefit from their deeds. The verse indicates several issues:

The first issue: The verse indicates the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation), because His saying: ﴿For it is what it has earned﴾ indicates that each person's earning belongs specifically to him, and no one else benefits from it. If taqlid were permissible, the earning of the one followed would benefit the follower. It is as if He said: I did not mention the narrative of their conditions seeking from you that you imitate them, but so that you may be alerted to what is incumbent upon you, so that you reflect and know that the religion they held was the truth.

The second issue: The verse indicates an encouragement to them to believe and to follow Muhammad (peace be upon him), and a warning to them against opposing him.

* * *

The third issue: The verse indicates that children are not rewarded for the obedience of their fathers, unlike the claim of the Jews that the righteousness of their fathers benefits them. The confirmation of this is what has been narrated from him (peace be upon him), that he said: "O Safiyyah, aunt of Muhammad, O Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, bring to me on the Day of Resurrection your deeds, not your lineages, for I cannot avail you anything against Allah." And he said: "Whoever his deed delays, his lineage will not hasten him." And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So there will be no lineages between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101]. And the Exalted said: ﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123]. Likewise His saying: ﴿And no soul earns except against itself﴾ [al-An'am: 164], and ﴿no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. And He said: ﴿But if they turn away, then upon him is only what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾ [al-Nur: 54].

* * *

The fourth issue: The verse indicates the invalidity of the view of those who say: children are punished for the disbelief of their fathers. The Jews used to say that they would be punished in the Fire for the disbelief of their fathers in taking the calf (as a deity). This is His saying: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and those were the days of worshipping the calf. So Allah the Exalted explained the invalidity of that.

* * *

The fifth issue: The verse indicates that the servant is an acquirer (muktasib). The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) and the Mu'tazilah differed in interpreting *kasb* (acquisition). As for the People of the Sunnah, they agreed that the meaning of the servant being an acquirer is not that some accident enters existence from non-existence by his power. After their agreement on this principle, they mentioned three interpretations of this acquisition.

The first, which is the view of al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him), is that power is an attribute related to the object of power, without power having any effect on the object of power. Rather, the power and the object of power both come into being by the creation of Allah the Exalted, just as knowledge and the known both come into being by the creation of Allah the Exalted. But the thing that comes into being by the creation of Allah the Exalted, which is the object related to the created power, is the acquisition.

The second: That the essence of the act comes into existence by the power of Allah the Exalted, and then that act acquires the attribute of being obedience or disobedience. This attribute is attained by created power. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Baqillani.

The third: That created power and eternal power, when they are related to one and the same object of power, the object comes to be by both of them, and as if the servant's act occurred with the assistance of Allah. This is acquisition, and this is attributed to Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, because it is narrated from him that he said: acquisition and the act that occurs by the one who assists.

As for those who hold that created power is effective, they are of two groups:

The first: Those who say that power together with motive (da'i) necessitates the act. Thus Allah the Exalted is the Creator of all in the sense that He, glorified and exalted, is the One who established the causes leading to these acts coming into existence, and the servant is the acquirer in the sense that the effective factor in the occurrence of his act is the power and the motive residing in him. This is the position of Imam al-Haramayn (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him), which he adopted in the book he named *al-Nizamiyyah*. The view of Abu al-Husayn al-Basri comes close to it, though he does not state it explicitly.

The second group of the Mu'tazilah: They are those who say: power together with motive does not necessitate the act; rather, the servant is able to do and to leave, empowered to do either, if he wills he does, and if he wills he leaves. As for this act and acquisition, the Mu'tazilah said to al-Ash'ari: If the object of the servant's power occurs by the creation of Allah the Exalted, then when He creates it in him, it is impossible for the servant not to be characterized by that act at that time; and if He does not create it in him, it is impossible for him to be characterized by it at that time.

If that is the case, he is never able to do or to leave, and there is no meaning to "capable" except that. Thus the servant is never capable. Also, this thing which is the acquisition of the servant is either occurring by the power of Allah, or not occurring at all by the power of Allah, or occurring by both powers together. If it occurs by the power of Allah the Exalted, the servant has no effect in it, so how can he be an acquirer of it? And if it occurs by the power of the servant, this is what is sought.

If it occurs by both powers together, this is impossible, because the power of Allah the Exalted is independent in bringing about. When the power of Allah the Exalted relates to it, how can any effect of the servant's power remain in it? As for the statement of al-Baqillani, it is weak, because the forbidden act of sitting in the usurped house is nothing but occupying those spaces. If this occupying occurs by the act of Allah the Exalted, then the forbidden thing itself has been created in it by Allah the Exalted, and this is exactly the imposition of what cannot be borne. And if it occurs by the power of the servant, then that is what is sought.

As for the statement of al-Isfara'ini, it is weak, because we have shown that the power of Allah the Exalted is independent in effecting, so no effect of the servant's power remains alongside it at all. The People of the Sunnah said: That the servant be independent in bringing into being and creating is impossible, for several reasons:

The first: If the servant were the originator of his acts, he would know the details of his act, but he does not know those details, so he is not their originator.

The second: If the servant were the originator of his own act, nothing would occur except what the servant intended. But this is not the case, because the disbeliever intends to acquire knowledge but acquires only ignorance.

The third: If the servant were the originator of his own act, then his being the originator of that act would be additional to the essence of that act and the essence of the power, because it is possible for us to conceive the essence of the act and the essence of the power while being unaware of the servant being its originator. But the conceived is not the same as the unnoticed. Then that originatorship is created. If its coming into being is by the servant, then it necessitates its dependence on another originatorship, and an infinite regress follows, which is impossible. And if it is by Allah the Exalted, and the effect is necessarily realized upon the realization of originatorship, then it follows that the act is attributed to Allah the Exalted. This does not apply to the originatorship of Allah the Exalted, because He is eternal, so His originatorship is eternal, and therefore it does not necessitate that this existentness depends on another existentness.

This is the summary of the discourse from both sides, and the disputes between the two groups concerning the wordings and meanings are many. And Allah is the Guide.

The Lord's words: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death came to Ya'qub? When he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we are submitting."﴾ ﴿That is a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earned. You will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, related about Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that he exerted himself in enjoining his sons in the religion and in Islam, He mentioned right after it that Ya'qub also enjoined his sons with the same, to reinforce the proof against the Jews and the Christians, and to intensify the clarification. In this there are issues:

The first issue: Know that "am" (أمْ) has the meaning of an interrogative particle or a conjunctive particle. It resembles the conjunction "aw" (أوْ, "or") and it comes in two ways: connected (muttasila) to what precedes it, and disconnected (munqati'a) from it. As for the connected one, know that when you say, "Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?", you do not know whether one of them is with him, so you ask: "Is one of these two with you?" Therefore his answer is necessarily "no" or "yes." But if you know that one of these two men is with him, yet you do not know whether the one with him is Zayd or 'Amr, and you ask him to specify, you say: "Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?" That is, know that one of them is with you, but is it this one or that one? As for the disconnected one, they said that it has the meaning of "bal" (بَلْ, "rather") together with the interrogative hamza. Its example: if one says, "Indeed, they are camels, or sheep?", the speaker's sight fell upon the figures and he assumed that they were camels, so he reported according to what his assumption required, that they were camels. Then doubt came to him, and he wanted to retract that report and to ask whether they are sheep or not. So the retraction from the first is the meaning of "bal," and the question about whether they are sheep is what is intended by the interrogative hamza. Thus your saying, "Indeed, they are camels, or sheep?" runs in the manner of your saying, "Indeed, they are camels. Are they sheep?" So your saying, "Are they sheep?" is a resumed statement, not connected to your saying, "Indeed, they are camels." How could it not be, when the retraction from it has occurred? This is unlike the connected one, for your saying, "Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?" means "which of them is with you?" And "ma" (what) after "am" is not disconnected from what precedes it, by the evidence that 'Amr is the companion of Zayd. Sufficient as evidence of this is that you express it with a singular noun, saying, "Which of them is with you?" Both types occur abundantly in the Book of Allah, exalted is He. As for the connected type, the Lord's words: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is the sky? He raised its height﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 28], meaning, "Which of you is more difficult?" As for the disconnected type, the Lord's words: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, is from the Lord of the worlds. Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [al-Sajda: 1–3], and Allah knows best, the meaning is "rather, they say, 'He has invented it'," which indicates the retraction from the first and the questioning about what follows, since there is no meaning in the statement otherwise, just as in your saying, "Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?" Some exegetes who do not verify say that "am" here is equivalent to the hamza, and that is not correct, for what we mentioned: this disconnected "am" includes the meaning of "bal." Once you know this introduction, we say: is "am" in this verse disjunctive or connective? There are two opinions:

The first: it is disconnected from what precedes it, and the meaning of the hamza in it is denial, that is: "Rather, you were not witnesses." "Shuhada'" (witnesses) is the plural of "shahid" in the sense of "present," that is, you were not present when death came to Ya'qub. The address is to the People of the Book, as if Allah, exalted is He, said to them concerning what they claimed, that the religion they adhered to was the religion of the messengers: "How can you say that, when you witness the testaments of the prophets concerning the religion? Had you witnessed that, you would have abandoned what you are upon of religion and would have desired the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the very same that Ibrahim (peace be upon him), Ya'qub, and all the other prophets after him (peace be upon them) were upon."

If it is said: interrogation in the manner of denial is directed only at a false statement, and what is related of Ya'qub in this verse is not a false statement but a true one, so how can the interrogation in the manner of denial be directed at it? We say: the interrogation in the manner of denial relates only to their mere claim of being present at his death, and this is what Allah, exalted is He, denied. As for His subsequent mention of Ya'qub's words, "What will you worship after me?", it is a detailed statement. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, when He denied their presence at that time, then explained after that the manner of that testament.

The second opinion: that "am" in this verse is connective, and the way to explain this is that something omitted is supposed before it, as if it was said: "Do you claim against the prophets Judaism, or were you witnesses when death came to Ya'qub?" That is, your forefathers from the Children of Israel were present for him when he called his sons to the community of Islam and monotheism, and you know that, so why do you claim against the prophets what they are innocent of?

* * *
