As for His words: ﴿when he said to his sons﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Qaffal said: His words, ﴿when death came to Ya'qub, when he said to his sons﴾, the first "idh" (when) is the time of the witnessing, and the second is the time of the presence.

The second issue: the verse indicates that the compassion of the prophets (peace be upon them) toward their children was within the matter of religion, and their concern was directed to it alone, and not to anything else.

* * *

As for His words: ﴿What will you worship after me?﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: the word "ma" (what) is for non-rational beings, so how did he use it for the true God?
Its answer is in two respects:
The first: "ma" is general for everything, and the meaning is "What thing will you worship?"
The second: His words, ﴿What you worship﴾, are like your saying, when asking for a definition or description, "What is man?"

[p. 69]

The second issue: His words, ﴿after me﴾. As for His words: ﴿They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq"﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: this verse has been held to by two groups of the ignorant:
The first: the imitators (al-muqallida) said: the sons of Ya'qub were satisfied with imitation (taqlid, blindly following others), and he (peace be upon him) did not denounce this from them, which indicates that imitation is sufficient.
The second: the Ta'limiyya (those who hold that knowledge of God is only through instruction). They said: there is no way to know Allah except through the teaching of the messenger and the imam, and the proof of this is this verse, for they did not say, "We will worship the God whom reason indicates," but rather they said, "We will worship the God whom you worship, and whom your fathers worshipped," and this indicates that the way of knowledge is learning.
The answer: just as there is no indication in the verse that they knew God through rational proof, there is likewise no indication in it that they only acknowledged God by way of imitation and instruction. Then, since the doctrine of imitation and instruction has been refuted by proof, we know that the faith of those people was not upon this way, but was attained through reasoning. At most one can say: then why did they not mention the way of reasoning?
The answer to this is in several respects:
The first: that is more concise in speech than explaining the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, in His oneness, knowledge, power, and justice.
The second: it is closer to calming the soul of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), as if they said: "We only proceed upon the same path as yours, so there is no disagreement from us against you regarding what we worship and what we sincerely devote worship to Him."
The third: perhaps this is an allusion to the mention of the proof of the existence of the Creator, as Allah, exalted is He, mentioned at the beginning of this surah in His words: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqara: 21]. Here, their intention in their words, ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾, means: we will worship the God whose existence is indicated by your existence and the existence of your fathers, and in this way that is an allusion to reasoning, not to imitation.

The second issue: al-Qaffal said: In some tafsirs it is related that when Ya'qub (peace be upon him) entered Egypt, he saw its people worshipping fires and idols, so he feared for his sons after his death, and so he said this statement to them, as an exhortation for them to hold fast to the worship of Allah, exalted is He.

And al-Qadi related from Ibn 'Abbas that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) gathered them to him at the time of his death, and they used to worship idols and fires, so he said: "O my sons, what will you worship after me?" They said: "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers." Then al-Qadi said: this is far-fetched for two reasons:
The first: they hastened to acknowledge monotheism in the manner of one from whom knowledge and certainty had already preceded.
The second: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in the Book the condition of the Asbat (the tribes) among the sons of Ya'qub, and that they were a righteous people, and that is not fitting for their state.

The third issue: His words, ﴿Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾, are an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) for "your fathers." So said al-Qaffal. It has also been said that He mentioned Isma'il before Ishaq because Isma'il was older than Ishaq.

The fourth issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: full brothers and full sisters, or paternal brothers and sisters, are not excluded by the paternal grandfather. This is also the view of 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them, and it is the view of Malik, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad.

Abu Hanifa said: they are excluded by the paternal grandfather. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them. Among the Followers, it is the view of al-Hasan, Tawus and 'Ata'. As for the first group, those who say that they are not excluded by the grandfather, they have two opinions:
One of them: the grandfather is given the choice between two matters: either sharing (al-muqasama) with them, or a third of the entire estate, and then the remainder is divided among the brothers and sisters, the male receiving the equivalent of the share of two females. This is the school of Zayd ibn Thabit and the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him.
The second: he is in the position of one of the brothers, as long as the sharing does not reduce him below a sixth. If the sharing reduces him below a sixth, he is given a sixth, and nothing is reduced from it. Abu Hanifa argued for his view that the grandfather is a father, and the father excludes the sisters and brothers, so it follows that the grandfather excludes them. We say the grandfather is a father based on the Qur'an and the report. As for the Qur'an, there are two verses: this verse, the Lord's words: ﴿They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq"﴾, where the word "father" is applied to the grandfather.

If it is said: it has also been applied to the paternal uncle, Isma'il, although by consensus he is not a father.
We say: usage is evidence of the literal meaning in the apparent sense; it was abandoned in the case of the uncle because of a proof that applied to him, so the proof of the verse remains valid for the rest. The second verse is the Lord's words, relating of Yusuf (peace be upon him): ﴿And I followed the religion of my fathers, Ibrahim and Ishaq and Ya'qub﴾ [Yusuf: 38].

As for the report, 'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Whoever wishes, I will curse him at the Black Stone: the grandfather is a father." And he also said: "Does Zayd ibn Thabit not fear Allah? He makes the son's son a son, but does not make the father's father a father." And when it is established that the grandfather is a father, it is necessary that he falls under the Lord's words: ﴿And his parents inherit from him, so his mother has a third﴾ [al-Nisa': 11], in that the grandfather is entitled to two-thirds to the exclusion of the brothers, just as the father is entitled to it to their exclusion when he is alive.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: We do not concede that the grandfather is a father, and the evidence for this is several points:
The first: just as you argued with these verses that the grandfather is a father, we argue that he is not a father, by the Lord's words: ﴿And Ibrahim enjoined it upon his sons, and so did Ya'qub﴾ [al-Baqara: 132]. For Allah, exalted is He, did not include Ya'qub among his sons, because He distinguished him from them. Had the one ascending in fatherhood been a father, then the one descending in sonship would in reality be a son. Since that is not the case, it is established that the grandfather is not a father.
The second: if the grandfather were a father in the literal sense, it would not be valid for one whose father has died while his grandfather is alive to deny that he has a father, just as it is not valid with the nearer father. And since that is valid, we know that he is not a father in the literal sense.

If it is said: the name of fatherhood applies to all of them, but the rank of the nearer is closer than the rank of the more remote, and therefore the negation is valid regarding it.

We said: If *al-ism* (the term "father") were literally applied to both of them together, then the sequence in existence would not be a reason for denying the name of father to him.

Third: If the grandfather were a father in the literal sense, it would be correct to say that a man died and left behind a mother and many fathers. No jurist, lexicographer, or exegete has ever used such a phrase.

Fourth: If the grandfather were a father, and there is no doubt that the Companions knew the language, they would not have disagreed about the inheritance of the grandfather. And if the grandfather were a father, the grandmother would be a mother. Had that been the case, doubt would not have arisen concerning the inheritance of the grandmother, so that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) would need to ask about it. These proofs indicate that the grandfather is not a father.

Fifth: The words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. If the grandfather were a father, then the son's son would necessarily be a son, and by the requirement of this verse, the son's son would inherit alongside the (existing) son. Since this is not the case, we know that the grandfather is not a father.

As for the verses you cite to establish that the grandfather is a father, the answer concerning the basis of your argument from them is in several respects:

First: Ubayy (ibn Ka'b) recited ﴿وإلَهَ إبْراهِيمَ﴾ with the omission of ﴿آبائِكَ﴾ (i.e., "the God of Ibrahim" without "your fathers"). However, this does not undermine the point, because a deviant (shadhdh) recitation does not override the widely transmitted (mutawatir) recitation. Rather, the answer is to say: he (the Prophet) used the word "father" for the grandfather and for the paternal uncle. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said about al-'Abbas: "This is the remainder of my fathers," and said: "Return my father to me." This indicates that he used it in a metaphorical sense. The evidence for this is what we previously stated, that it is correct to deny the name "father" of the grandfather, and if it were literal, this would not be so. As for the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, he applied the term to him only with regard to the ruling, not with regard to the linguistic term, because languages are not subject to disagreement among the people of the tongue. And Allah knows best.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿One God﴾, it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the God of your fathers﴾, like His saying: ﴿by the forelock, a lying, sinning forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq: 15–16]. Or it is in the mode of specification (ikhtisas), meaning: you intend by "the God of your fathers" one God.

As for His saying: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, there are several possibilities:

One: It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of *na'budu* ("we worship") or from its object, because the pronoun returns to it in *lahu* ("to Him").

Two: It may be a clause conjoined (ma'tufah) to *na'budu*.

Three: It may be a parenthetical emphatic clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah mu'akkidah), meaning: and it is our state that we are submitting to Him, sincere in monotheism or submissive.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾, it refers to those whom Allah the Exalted mentioned in the preceding verse: Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, and his sons, the monotheists. "Ummah" means a category. "Khalat" means passed on, departed, and perished. The meaning is that I have related to you their accounts and what they were upon of Islam and calling to Islam. So there is no benefit for you in their conduct unless you do what they did. If you do that, you will benefit; and if you refuse, you will not benefit from their deeds. The verse indicates several issues:

The first issue: The verse indicates the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation), because His saying: ﴿For it is what it has earned﴾ indicates that each person's earning belongs specifically to him, and no one else benefits from it. If taqlid were permissible, the earning of the one followed would benefit the follower. It is as if He said: I did not mention the narrative of their conditions seeking from you that you imitate them, but so that you may be alerted to what is incumbent upon you, so that you reflect and know that the religion they held was the truth.

The second issue: The verse indicates an encouragement to them to believe and to follow Muhammad (peace be upon him), and a warning to them against opposing him.

* * *

The third issue: The verse indicates that children are not rewarded for the obedience of their fathers, unlike the claim of the Jews that the righteousness of their fathers benefits them. The confirmation of this is what has been narrated from him (peace be upon him), that he said: "O Safiyyah, aunt of Muhammad, O Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, bring to me on the Day of Resurrection your deeds, not your lineages, for I cannot avail you anything against Allah." And he said: "Whoever his deed delays, his lineage will not hasten him." And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So there will be no lineages between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101]. And the Exalted said: ﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123]. Likewise His saying: ﴿And no soul earns except against itself﴾ [al-An'am: 164], and ﴿no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. And He said: ﴿But if they turn away, then upon him is only what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾ [al-Nur: 54].

* * *

The fourth issue: The verse indicates the invalidity of the view of those who say: children are punished for the disbelief of their fathers. The Jews used to say that they would be punished in the Fire for the disbelief of their fathers in taking the calf (as a deity). This is His saying: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and those were the days of worshipping the calf. So Allah the Exalted explained the invalidity of that.

* * *

The fifth issue: The verse indicates that the servant is an acquirer (muktasib). The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) and the Mu'tazilah differed in interpreting *kasb* (acquisition). As for the People of the Sunnah, they agreed that the meaning of the servant being an acquirer is not that some accident enters existence from non-existence by his power. After their agreement on this principle, they mentioned three interpretations of this acquisition.

The first, which is the view of al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him), is that power is an attribute related to the object of power, without power having any effect on the object of power. Rather, the power and the object of power both come into being by the creation of Allah the Exalted, just as knowledge and the known both come into being by the creation of Allah the Exalted. But the thing that comes into being by the creation of Allah the Exalted, which is the object related to the created power, is the acquisition.

The second: That the essence of the act comes into existence by the power of Allah the Exalted, and then that act acquires the attribute of being obedience or disobedience. This attribute is attained by created power. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Baqillani.

The third: That created power and eternal power, when they are related to one and the same object of power, the object comes to be by both of them, and as if the servant's act occurred with the assistance of Allah. This is acquisition, and this is attributed to Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, because it is narrated from him that he said: acquisition and the act that occurs by the one who assists.

As for those who hold that created power is effective, they are of two groups:

The first: Those who say that power together with motive (da'i) necessitates the act. Thus Allah the Exalted is the Creator of all in the sense that He, glorified and exalted, is the One who established the causes leading to these acts coming into existence, and the servant is the acquirer in the sense that the effective factor in the occurrence of his act is the power and the motive residing in him. This is the position of Imam al-Haramayn (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him), which he adopted in the book he named *al-Nizamiyyah*. The view of Abu al-Husayn al-Basri comes close to it, though he does not state it explicitly.

The second group of the Mu'tazilah: They are those who say: power together with motive does not necessitate the act; rather, the servant is able to do and to leave, empowered to do either, if he wills he does, and if he wills he leaves. As for this act and acquisition, the Mu'tazilah said to al-Ash'ari: If the object of the servant's power occurs by the creation of Allah the Exalted, then when He creates it in him, it is impossible for the servant not to be characterized by that act at that time; and if He does not create it in him, it is impossible for him to be characterized by it at that time.

If that is the case, he is never able to do or to leave, and there is no meaning to "capable" except that. Thus the servant is never capable. Also, this thing which is the acquisition of the servant is either occurring by the power of Allah, or not occurring at all by the power of Allah, or occurring by both powers together. If it occurs by the power of Allah the Exalted, the servant has no effect in it, so how can he be an acquirer of it? And if it occurs by the power of the servant, this is what is sought.

If it occurs by both powers together, this is impossible, because the power of Allah the Exalted is independent in bringing about. When the power of Allah the Exalted relates to it, how can any effect of the servant's power remain in it? As for the statement of al-Baqillani, it is weak, because the forbidden act of sitting in the usurped house is nothing but occupying those spaces. If this occupying occurs by the act of Allah the Exalted, then the forbidden thing itself has been created in it by Allah the Exalted, and this is exactly the imposition of what cannot be borne. And if it occurs by the power of the servant, then that is what is sought.

As for the statement of al-Isfara'ini, it is weak, because we have shown that the power of Allah the Exalted is independent in effecting, so no effect of the servant's power remains alongside it at all. The People of the Sunnah said: That the servant be independent in bringing into being and creating is impossible, for several reasons:

The first: If the servant were the originator of his acts, he would know the details of his act, but he does not know those details, so he is not their originator.

The second: If the servant were the originator of his own act, nothing would occur except what the servant intended. But this is not the case, because the disbeliever intends to acquire knowledge but acquires only ignorance.

The third: If the servant were the originator of his own act, then his being the originator of that act would be additional to the essence of that act and the essence of the power, because it is possible for us to conceive the essence of the act and the essence of the power while being unaware of the servant being its originator. But the conceived is not the same as the unnoticed. Then that originatorship is created. If its coming into being is by the servant, then it necessitates its dependence on another originatorship, and an infinite regress follows, which is impossible. And if it is by Allah the Exalted, and the effect is necessarily realized upon the realization of originatorship, then it follows that the act is attributed to Allah the Exalted. This does not apply to the originatorship of Allah the Exalted, because He is eternal, so His originatorship is eternal, and therefore it does not necessitate that this existentness depends on another existentness.

This is the summary of the discourse from both sides, and the disputes between the two groups concerning the wordings and meanings are many. And Allah is the Guide.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 135:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided." Say: "Nay, [we follow] the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the polytheists."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had clarified by the proofs that preceded the soundness of the religion of Islam, He then related types of the doubts of the opponents who disparaged Islam.

The first doubt: He related of them that they said: ﴿Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided,﴾ and they did not mention any argument in support of this, but insisted upon imitation (taqlid). So God, exalted is He, answered them concerning this doubt in several ways:

The first: He gave an ilzami (argumentum ad hominem) answer, which is His saying: ﴿Say: "Nay, [we follow] the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf."﴾ The explanation of this answer is that if the way of religion is imitation, then it is more fitting to follow the religion of Abraham, because these disputants have agreed upon the soundness of the religion of Abraham, and adhering to what is agreed upon is better than adhering to what is disputed. If reliance in religion is upon imitation, it is as if He, glorified is He, said: If reliance in religion is upon reasoning and inquiry, then we have already presented the proofs; and if reliance is upon imitation, then returning to the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, and abandoning Judaism and Christianity is better.

If it is said: Does not each of the Jews and the Christians claim that they are upon the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him?

We say: Since it is established that Abraham was a proponent of monotheism, and it is established that the Christians say in favor of trinity, and the Jews say in favor of anthropomorphism, it is thereby established that they are not upon the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him; and that Muhammad, peace be upon him, when he called to monotheism, was upon the religion of Abraham.

Let us return to the explanation of the words. As for His saying: ﴿And they say: "Be Jews or Christians,"﴾ it is not permissible that the intended meaning be choice, since it is known from the state of the Jews that they do not permit choosing Christianity over Judaism, but rather they claim it is disbelief. And it is known from the state of the Christians likewise. Rather, the intended meaning is that the Jews call to Judaism and the Christians call to Christianity, so each group calls to its religion and claims that it is the guidance. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿you will be guided,﴾ i.e., that if you do so, you will be guided and will be on the path of uprightness.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Nay, [we follow] the religion of Abraham,﴾ there are four opinions regarding the accusative case of "millata" (religion):

The first: it is conjoined in meaning to His saying: ﴿Be Jews or Christians,﴾ and its estimated sense is: They said: Follow Judaism. Say: Nay, follow the religion of Abraham.

The second: it is by ellipsis, its estimated sense being: Nay, we follow the religion of Abraham.

The third: its estimated sense is: Nay, we shall be people of the religion of Abraham, so the first noun (the annexed noun) is omitted and the annexed-to noun is put in its place, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning, ask its people.

The fourth: the estimate is: Nay, follow the religion of Abraham. And al-A'raj read "millatu Ibrāhīma" with a nominative ending, meaning: its religion is our religion, or our religion is the religion of Abraham. In sum, you have the choice of making it a subject (mubtada') or a predicate (khabar).

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿ḥanīfan,﴾ there are two issues:

The first issue: the lexicographers have two views concerning the ḥanīf:

The first: that the ḥanīf is the one who is upright, and from this it was said of the one with a bent foot: aḥnaf (one who has a crooked foot), as an optimistic omen of safety, just as they said to the one stung by a scorpion: salīm (safe), and to a deadly desert: mafāzah (a place of escape). They said: Every person who submits to God and does not deviate from Him in anything is a ḥanīf. This is related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

The second: that the ḥanīf is one who inclines, because the aḥnaf is one who turns each of his two feet toward the other with their toes, and taḥannafa means he inclined. So the meaning is that Abraham, peace be upon him, inclined (ḥanafa) to the religion of God, i.e., turned toward it. Thus His saying: ﴿the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf,﴾ i.e., differing from the Jews and Christians, turning away from both. As for the exegetes, they related several expressions:

One of them: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid: that ḥanīfiyyah is the pilgrimage to the House.

The second: that it is following the truth, from Mujahid.

The third: following Abraham in his laws, which are the laws of Islam.

The fourth: sincerity of practice, and its estimated sense is: Nay, we follow the religion of Abraham, which is monotheism, from al-Asamm. Al-Qaffal said: In sum, ḥanīf is a title for one who adheres to Islam, like the other titles of religions, and its origin is from Abraham, peace be upon him.

The second issue: concerning the accusative of ḥanīfan there are two views:

One of them: the saying of al-Zajjaj that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from Abraham, like your saying: I saw the face of Hind, standing (qā'imatan).

The second: that it is in the accusative as a detached qualifier (qaṭ'), meaning: Nay, the religion of Abraham, the ḥanīf. When the alif and lam were dropped, the indefinite did not follow the definite, so it was detached from it and took the accusative case; this was said by the grammarians of Kufa.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists,﴾ there are several aspects:

The first: it is an alert that in the doctrine of the Jews and Christians there are associates (partners), as we have explained, since He, exalted is He, related of some Jews their saying: "Uzayr is the son of God," and the Christians said: the Messiah is the son of God, and that is association.

The second: the ḥanīf is a name for one who adheres to the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, and it is known that he, peace be upon him, brought specific laws, including the pilgrimage to the House, circumcision, and others. Whoever adheres to these is a ḥanīf, and the Arabs used to adhere to these things, then they would associate others with God. So it was said for this reason: ﴿ḥanīfan and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ A parallel is His saying: ﴿ḥunafā' for God, not associating anything with Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], and His saying: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except that they are polytheists﴾ [Yusuf: 106]. The Qadi said: The verse indicates that one of us may argue against another with what operates as a counter-argument to his statement, to silence him, even if that is not in itself a proof. For it is known that he, peace be upon him, did not argue for his prophethood with such words, but rather with the manifest miracles that appeared at his hands. But when he, peace be upon him, had established the proof with them and removed the excuse, and then found them stubborn and persisting in their falsehood, at that point he presented against them an argument resembling what they held, and said: If religion is by following, then what is agreed upon, which is the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, is more worthy of following.

One may say: If the Jews and Christians acknowledge the merit of Abraham and affirm that Abraham was not among those who held to anthropomorphism and trinity, it is impossible for them to say that; rather they must be holders of transcendence (tanzih) and monotheism. And if they are holders of that, there is no benefit in calling them to it. And if they deny the merit of Abraham, or affirm it but deny that he denied anthropomorphism and trinity, then that is not agreed upon, and so it is not sound to impose the claim that this is agreed upon; hence adhering to it is more fitting.

The answer: It was known by mass transmission (tawatur) that Abraham, peace be upon him, did not attribute a son to God, exalted is He. So when it was established from the Jews and Christians that they said this, it became established that their way differs from the way of Abraham, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been revealed to us, and in what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, first answered with a dialectical (jadali) reply, He afterwards mentioned a demonstrative (burhani) reply in this verse. It is this: the way to knowing the prophethood of the prophets, peace be upon them, is the appearance of a miracle (mu'jiz) at their hands. When a miracle appeared at the hands of Muhammad (ﷺ), it became obligatory to acknowledge his prophethood and to believe in his message. For singling out some for acceptance and singling out others for rejection entails contradiction in the proof, and that is impossible by reason. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been revealed to us"﴾ to the end of the verse, and this is the principal purpose of mentioning this verse.

If it is said: How is it permissible to believe in Abraham, Moses and Jesus while holding that their laws have been abrogated? We reply: We believe that each of those laws was true in its own time, so no contradiction arises for us. As for the Jews and Christians, since they acknowledged the prophethood of some to whom a miracle appeared, yet denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) despite the miracle that appeared at his hand, then contradiction necessarily binds them, and the difference becomes clear. Then we say, concerning the verse, several issues:

The first issue: When God, exalted is He, related of them that they said: ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾, they mentioned, in opposition to the Messenger, peace be upon him: ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham﴾. Then He said to his community: ﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾. This is the view of al-Hasan. But al-Qadi said: His saying ﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾ encompasses all the responsible persons, namely the Prophet, peace be upon him, and his community. The evidence for this is two-fold:

One: His saying ﴿Say﴾ is a general address, so it encompasses all.

Two: His saying ﴿and in what has been revealed to us﴾ suits none but him (ﷺ), so at least he is included in it.

Al-Hasan argued for his view with two points:

The first: He, peace be upon him, had earlier been commanded with His saying: ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham﴾.

The second: He is at the peak of nobility, and the apparent sense is that the address is singled out for him.

The reply: Although these indications are possible, they are not strong enough to require restricting the generality of His saying ﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾. As for His saying ﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾, He placed it first because belief in God is the root of belief in the laws. Whoever does not know God cannot know a prophet or a book. This shows the invalidity of the doctrine of the Ta'limiyya (the Ismaili-type teachers who stress authoritative instruction) and the Muqallida (the blind followers) who say that the way to knowing God, exalted is He, is the Book and the Sunnah.

As for His saying ﴿and the Tribes﴾: al-Khalil said: the sibt (tribe) among the Children of Israel is like the qabilah (clan) among the Arabs. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the sibt is the grandson, and al-Hasan and al-Husayn were the two grandsons (sibtan) of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The asbat are the grandsons, and they are Jacob, peace be upon him, and the descendants of his twelve sons.

* * *

[Page 76]

As for His saying ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾, there are two views:

The first: We do not believe in some and disbelieve in others, for if we did so, contradiction would be necessary in the proof, and that is not permissible.

The second: We do not make a distinction between any of them, that is, we do not say that they differ in the fundamentals of the religions. Rather, they are united on the fundamentals which are Islam, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He has ordained for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you, and that which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus: "Establish the religion and do not be divided therein."﴾ [al-Shura: 13]. The first view is more fitting to the context of the verse.

As for His saying ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, the meaning is that our submission (Islam) is for the sake of obedience to God, exalted is He, not for the sake of desire. Since this is so, it requires that whenever a miracle appears, belief in it becomes obligatory. As for singling out some of the bearers of miracles for acceptance and others for rejection, that shows that the aim of such belief is not obedience to God and submission to Him, but rather the following of desire and inclination.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 137:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you have believed in, then they are [rightly] guided. But if they turn away, then they are only in dissension, and Allah will suffice you against them. And He is the Hearing, the Knowing.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had explained the clear path in religion, which is that a person acknowledges the prophethood of the one for whom the proof of prophethood has been established, and that he guards in this against contradiction, He encouraged them to adopt this kind of faith, saying: ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you have believed in, then they are [rightly] guided.﴾

On this there are several aspects:

The first: the purpose of it is affirmation (tathbit), and the meaning is: if they adopt a religion other than yours that is like your religion and equal to it in soundness and rectitude, then they are [rightly] guided. Since it is impossible that there should exist another religion equal to this religion in rectitude, guidance through anything else is impossible. A parallel to this is your saying to a man whom you advise: "This is the opinion and the correct one. If you have an opinion more correct than it, then act upon it." You know that there is no more correct opinion than your opinion, but you wish to affirm your companion and to make him stop at the point that the opinion you hold has no opinion beyond it. As for our saying that it is impossible that there should exist another religion equal to this religion in rectitude, that is because this religion is founded on the principle that whoever is shown a miracle (mu'jiz) must be acknowledged as a prophet, and every religion that differs from this religion must necessarily include contradiction, and that which contradicts is impossible to be equal to that which does not contradict in rectitude and soundness.

The second: the particle "like" (mithl) is an extra word (silah) in speech. Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11], meaning "there is nothing like Him" (laysa kahuwa shay'). The poet says:

"Like the stones (that) are set around (the cooking pot)..."

And Umm al-Ahnaf used to dance him and say:

"By Allah, were it not for Hanaf in his leg,
and thinness in his shin from his leanness..., there would be none of you like him."

Page 77

The third: you believed in the Furqan without alteration or distortion, so if they believe in the like of that, which is the Torah without alteration or distortion, then they are [rightly] guided, because they would be connected through it to knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

The fourth: the saying ﴿If they believe in the like of what you have believed in﴾ may mean: if they become believers in the like of that by which you became believers, then they are [rightly] guided. Thus the comparison in the verse is between the two faiths and the two affirmations. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari narrated that Ibn Abbas said: "Do not say, 'If they believe in the like of what you have believed in,' for there is no like of Allah; rather say, 'If they believe in that which you have believed in.'" The judge (al-Qadi) said: There is no justification for abandoning the mutawatir recitation on the ground that the meaning becomes problematic and confusing, because if one were to take this as a principle, one would be obliged to change the recitation of all the ambiguous verses, and that is prohibited. The first answer is the one relied upon.

As for His saying ﴿then they are [rightly] guided﴾, the meaning is: they have then acted upon what they were guided to and accepted it, and one in this condition becomes a friend of Allah and enters among the people of His pleasure. The verse indicates that guidance existed before this being-guided, and that guidance cannot be understood except as the proofs which Allah established, disclosed, and explained the aspects of their indication.

* * *

Then He explained, by way of warning, what will befall them if they turn away, saying: ﴿But if they turn away, then they are only in dissension﴾. And concerning "dissension" (shiqaq) there are two discussions:

The first discussion: Some of the lexicographers said: shiqaq is derived from shiqq (split, side), as if one has come to be on a side other than the side of his companion because of enmity; and one has split the staff of the Muslims when he divides their community and separates from it. A parallel to it is "muhadda" (opposition), which is that this one is in one limit and that one in another limit; and "ta'adi" (hostility) is similar, because this one is on one slope and that one on another slope; and "mujanaba" (avoidance) is that this one is on one side and that one on another side. Others said: it is from "mashaqqa" (hardship), because each of the two covets what burdens the other and harms him. Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And if you fear a breach (shiqaq) between the two of them﴾ [al-Nisa: 35], meaning a separation between them in disagreement, to the point that one of them burdens the other.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿But if they turn away, then they are only in dissension﴾ means: if they abandon such a faith, then they have committed themselves to contradiction, and the rational person never commits himself to contradiction at all. Since they have committed to it, we know that their aim is not the seeking of religion and submission, but rather their aim is contention and the display of enmity.

Then there are expressions of the exegetes:

First: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: ﴿they are only in dissension﴾ means in opposition, since they parted from the truth and clung to falsehood, so they became opposers of Allah.

Second: Abu Ubayda and Muqatil said: "in shiqaq" means: in misguidance (dalal).

Third: Ibn Zayd said: in contention and warfare.

Fourth: al-Hasan said: in enmity. The judge said: It is hardly said of opposing in the manner of the truth, or of disagreement which is not disobedience, that it is shiqaq; rather that is said only of a grave opposition which brings its doer into the enmity, anger, curse of Allah, and the deserving of the Fire. Thus this statement is a threat from Him, may He be exalted, against them, and their being described by it is a proof that these people are enemies of the Messenger, harboring evil towards him and lying in wait to bring him into trials. At this point Allah, may He be exalted, assured him against their plotting and assured the believers against their evil and deceit, and so He said: ﴿Allah will suffice you against them﴾, a strengthening of his heart and the hearts of the believers, because when He, may He be exalted, undertakes sufficiency in a matter, confidence in Him is achieved. The speakers (mutakallimun) said: This is an informing about the unseen, and so it is a miracle (mu'jiz) indicating his truthfulness. We say it is an informing about the unseen because we found that the one who gave this statement was as he reported, for Allah sufficed him the evil of the Jews and the Christians and granted him victory over them until the Muslims overcame them and took their homes and their wealth, so they became humbled in their hands, paying them the kharaj and the jizya, or being completely unable to free themselves from their hands.

Page 78

And we say it is a miracle because the one who guesses (mutakhris) does not hit upon such a matter in detail. The atheists said: We do not grant that this is a miracle, because a miracle is that which breaks the customary course, and it has been the custom that whoever is afflicted by the harming of others is told: "Be patient, for Allah will suffice you his evil," and then that happens sometimes and does not happen at other times. Since this is customary, how can it be said that it is a miracle? Moreover, perhaps he reached that through a dream he saw, and that cannot be refuted, for the astrologers say: whoever has the Lot of Fortune in his ascendant comes with such reports even if he is not a prophet.

The answer: our purpose in saying that it is a miracle is not that this informing alone is a miracle; rather our purpose is that the Qur'an contains much of this kind, and informing about many things in detail is something that cannot come from a lying guesser.

Then, when He had promised him support and aid, He followed it with what indicates that what they conceal and what they disclose of this matter is not hidden from Him, may He be exalted, so He said: ﴿And He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾. In it there are two aspects:

The first: it is a warning to them, and the meaning is that He perceives what they conceal and say, and He is Knowing of everything, so it is not permitted for them that any matter should come from them except that He is able to suffice him against it.

The second: it is a promise to the Messenger, peace be upon him, meaning: He hears your supplication and knows your intention, and He responds to you and brings you to your aim. The Ashab (Ash'ari theologians) argued by His saying ﴿And He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ that His hearing, may He be exalted, is an attribute additional to His knowledge of the heard things, because His saying "Knowing" (alim) is an intensive form (bina' mubalagha), so it encompasses His being Knowing of all the known things; so if His being Hearing were an expression of His knowledge of the heard things, it would entail repetition, which is impermissible; therefore the attribute of His being Hearing must be an additional matter beyond His being described as Knowing. And Allah knows best what is correct.

As for His saying ﴿with the like of what you have believed in﴾, there is in it a difficulty, namely that what the believers believed in has no like; and its answer is:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 138:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The baptism of Allah. And who is better than Allah at baptism? And we are worshippers of Him.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned the second answer, which is that He mentioned what indicates the soundness of this religion, He then mentioned after it what indicates that the proofs of this religion are clear and manifest, so He said: ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾. Then in the verse there are issues:

The first issue: al-ṣibgh (dye) is that with which garments are coloured. It is said: ṣabagha al-thawb yaṣbughuhu, with the vowel of the ba' being fatha, kasra and damma, three dialects; ṣabgan, with the ṣad being fatha or kasra, two dialects.

Al-ṣibgha (baptism/dye) is a form (fi'la) from ṣabagha, like al-jilsa from jalasa, and it is the state in which dyeing occurs. Then they differed about the meaning of "the baptism of Allah" into several opinions:

The first: that it is the religion of Allah. They mentioned several reasons why it was called the religion of Allah:

One of them: some Christians used to immerse their children in yellow water which they called the baptism (al-ma'mudiyya), and they would say: it is a purification for them. And when one did that to his child, he would say: Now he has become a Christian. So Allah, may He be exalted, said: Seek the baptism of Allah, which is the religion, and Islam, not their baptism. The reason for applying the word ṣibgha to religion is the figure of speech called al-mushākala (matching/correspondence), as when you say to one who plants trees while you want to order him to be generous: plant as so-and-so plants, meaning a man who is persistent in generosity. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿We are only mockers﴾ ﴿Allah mocks at them﴾ [al-Baqara: 14, 15], ﴿They deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them﴾ [al-Nisa: 142], ﴿And they plotted, and Allah plotted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], ﴿And the recompense of an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], ﴿If you mock us, we will mock you﴾ [Hud: 38].

Second: the Jews dye their children as Jews, and the Christians dye their children as Christians, meaning they immerse them in that, because of what they instil into their hearts. From Qatada. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is said: so-and-so dyes so-and-so in a thing, that is, he makes him enter into it and binds him to it, just as dye is made to adhere to cloth. Tha'lab recited:

Leave evil and take refuge in safety, out of caution, if you do not have a dyer who dyes you in evil.

Third: the religion was called a dye because its form becomes manifest to observation through the traces of purification and prayer. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Their mark is on their faces, from the trace of prostration﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

Fourth: al-Qadi said: His saying ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And we are Muslims to Him﴾. So He described this faith of theirs as the baptism of Allah, to make clear that the distinction between this religion which Allah has chosen and the religion which the falsifier has chosen is manifest and clear, just as the distinction between colours and dyes is manifest to one with sound sense.

The second opinion: that the baptism of Allah is His fitra (natural disposition). It is like His saying: ﴿The fitra of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no alteration in the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. The meaning of this view is that man is marked, in his composition and structure, with weakness and need, and the signs that testify to his being created and his need of the Creator; these signs are like a dye for him and a lasting mark.

Al-Qadi said: Whoever takes His saying ﴿the baptism of Allah﴾ to mean the fitra is close in meaning to the one who says it is the religion of Allah, because the fitra which they were commanded to follow is what the proofs of intellect and revelation require, and that is also the religion. But religion is more apparent, because what is meant, as we have explained, is what they described themselves with in His saying ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾. So it is as if He, may He be exalted, said: The religion of Allah which has obliged you to hold fast to it, its benefit will become manifest, in this world and the next, just as the beauty of a dye becomes manifest. And when the speech is understood according to what we have mentioned, there is no meaning in the saying of those who say that He only said that because of a custom practised by the Jews and Christians with a dye they used on their children, since when the speech is correct in its best sense without it, there is no benefit in it. Now let us mention the rest of the opinions of the exegetes:

The third opinion: that the baptism of Allah is circumcision, which is a purification, meaning: just as the particular rite of the Christians is a purification for them, so circumcision is a purification for the Muslims. From Abu al-'Aliya.

The fourth opinion: that it is the proof of Allah. From al-Asamm. It was also said: it is the sunna of Allah. From Abu 'Ubayda. The good opinion is the first, and Allah knows best.

The second issue: concerning the case-ending of ﴿ṣibgha﴾ there are opinions:

One: that it is a substitute (badal) for "millata" and an explanation of it.

Second: "Follow the baptism of Allah."

Third: Sibawayh said: it is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid), so it is in the accusative governed by His saying ﴿We believe in Allah﴾, just as the promise of Allah is in the accusative governed by what precedes it.

As for His saying: ﴿And who is better than Allah at baptism﴾, the meaning is that He dyes His servants with faith and purifies them by it from the filth of disbelief; so there is no baptism better than His baptism.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And we are worshippers of Him﴾, the author of the Kashshaf said: it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "We believe in Allah". This refutes the view of those who claim that "the baptism of Allah" is a substitute for "the religion of Ibrahim", or that it is in the accusative as a warning (al-ighra'), meaning "upon you is the baptism of Allah", because of what that involves of disjoining the composition; and its being in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun is what Sibawayh mentioned. And the saying is what Hidhām said.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 139:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Do you dispute with us concerning Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him.﴾ Know that in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: They differed concerning that disputation, and they mentioned several aspects:

One of them: that it was their saying that they were more deserving of the truth and prophethood, due to prophethood having come earlier among them. The meaning: Do you argue with us that Allah chose a messenger from the Arabs and not from you, and you say: "If Allah were to send down [revelation] to anyone, He would have sent it down to you," and you consider yourselves more deserving of prophethood than us?

Second: their saying: "We are more deserving of faith than the Arabs who worshipped idols."

Third: their saying ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and their saying: ﴿Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided﴾, related from al-Hasan.

Fourth: ﴿Do you dispute with us concerning Allah?﴾ i.e., do you dispute with us concerning the religion of Allah?

The second issue: With whom was this disputation? They mentioned several aspects regarding it:

One of them: that it is an address to the Jews and Christians.

Second: that it is an address to the polytheists of the Arabs, when they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from one of the two towns?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], and the Arabs used to acknowledge the Creator.

Third: that it is an address to all of them, and the first view is more fitting to the composition of the verse.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿while He is our Lord and your Lord﴾, in it there are two aspects:

The first: that He is most knowing of the management of His creation and of who is fit for messengership and who is not. So do not object against your Lord, for the servant has no right to object against his Lord; rather, it is obligatory upon him to entrust the matter entirely to Him.

The second: that you have no relation to Allah, may He be exalted, except through servitude, and this relation is shared between us and you. So why do you prefer yourselves over us? Rather, the preference is from our side, because we are sincere to Him in servitude, and you are not like that. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and we are sincere to Him﴾, and this interpretation is closer.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾, what is meant by it is sincere advice in religion, as if He, may He be exalted, said to His Prophet: Say to them this statement in a manner of compassion and sincere advice, i.e., no harm from your evil deeds returns to me, such that the purpose of this statement would be to repel that harm. Rather, what is meant is your counsel and guidance to what is more righteous. In sum, a person's words are only accepted when he is free of worldly motives; if he has some of those motives, his speech will not take effect in the heart at all. So this is what is meant, and in it there is deterrence and reproach that stirs reflection and moves natural dispositions toward inference and acceptance of the truth. As for the meaning of sincerity (ikhlas), it has already been discussed.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 140–141:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians? Say: "Are you more knowing, or is God?" And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God? God is not unaware of what you do.﴾

Know that there are two issues in this verse.

The first issue: Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs on the authority of ʿAsim recited ﴿Am taqūlūna﴾ with the taʾ (second person), addressing them, as if He said: "Do you dispute with us, or do you say...?" The rest read it with the yāʾ (third person), as a report about the Jews and the Christians. On the first reading, ʾam (or) may be connected (muttasilah), and its implied sense is: "By which of the two proofs do you hold on to your cause: by monotheism, for we are monotheists, or by following the religion of the prophets, for we are followers?" It may also be disconnected (munqatiʿah), in the sense of "Rather, do you say...", with the hamzah also being for denunciation. On the second reading, it is disconnected because its meaning has moved on to a different argument from the first, as if it was said: "Do you say that the prophets were, before the revelation of the Torah and the Gospel, Jews or Christians?"

The second issue: God denounced this statement against them for several reasons:

First: Muhammad (ﷺ) had his prophethood established by all kinds of miracles, and he reported their lying in this matter; thus their lying in it is necessarily established.

Second: the testimony of the Torah and the Gospel that the prophets were upon monotheism and the ḥanīfiyyah (pure monotheism).

Third: the Torah and the Gospel were revealed after them.

Fourth: they claimed this without evidence, so God rebuked them by speaking in the form of a question, as a denunciation, and the purpose of it is reproach and rebuke, and that God establish in their souls that they know they were lying in what they say.

As for His saying: ﴿Say: "Are you more knowing, or is God?"﴾, its meaning is that God is more knowing and His report is more truthful, and He has reported in the Torah, the Gospel and in the Qur'an, upon the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ), that they were Muslims, free of Judaism and Christianity. If it is said: this is said only of one who does not know, whereas they knew it and concealed it, so how is the statement valid? We say: whoever says they were upon supposition and conjecture, the statement is clear; and whoever says they knew and denied, its meaning is that your standing is the standing of those who object to what he knows God has reported, so that will not benefit him given his acknowledgment that God is more knowing.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?﴾, there are three aspects to it.

First: in the verse there is inversion (taqdim and taʾkhir), and the implied sense is: "And who is more unjust in the sight of God than one who conceals a testimony that came to him", just as you say: "And who is more unjust than Zayd among the group of those who conceal testimony?" The meaning: if Abraham and his sons were Jews or Christians, and then God concealed this testimony, none of those who conceal testimony would be more unjust than Him. But since that is impossible with His justice and His being free of lying, we know that the matter is not so.

Second: "And who is more unjust among you, O company of Jews and Christians, if you conceal this testimony from God?" Here "min" in His saying ﴿from God﴾ relates to the concealer according to the first view, and to the one concealed from according to the second view, as if He said: "And who is more unjust than one who has a testimony with God, and so does not establish it before God, but rather conceals and hides it?"

Third: "min" in His saying ﴿from God﴾ is a complement of "testimony", and the meaning is: "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony that came to him from God, and denies it?" Like a man saying to another: "I have a testimony from you", meaning a testimony I heard from you, and a testimony that came to me from your side and from your presence.

As for His saying: ﴿God is not unaware of what you do﴾, it is the comprehensive statement of every threat. Whoever imagines that He, may He be exalted, knows their secret and their openness, and nothing is hidden from Him, that behind His recompense, if good then good and if evil then evil, will not pass over him a blink of an eye without his being wary and fearful. Do you not see that if one of us had a watchman from a ruler's side counting his breaths, he would be in constant caution and dread, even though that watchman knows only the outward? So how much more so with the Lord, the Watcher, who knows the secret and what is more hidden, when He threatens and warns with this kind of speech.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 142 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn. And you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾ Know that when He, exalted is He, argued against the Jews concerning these prophets, He followed it with this verse for several reasons:

First: that it be an admonition and a deterrent for them, so that they do not argue about the merit of their forefathers, since each person is taken to account for his own deeds.

Second: that He, exalted is He, showed that just as it is not objectionable that your obligation should differ from theirs because of the difference in interests, so too it is not objectionable that interests should differ, so that Muhammad ﷺ transfers you from one religious community (millah) to another.

Third: that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the excellent way of the prophets whom He mentioned in these verses, He made clear that proof is not completed by that alone, but rather every person is answerable for his own deeds, and he has no excuse for abandoning the truth by imagining that he adheres to the way of those who came before, because whether they were right or wrong, it neither benefits these nor harms them. This is so that it is not supposed that the way of religion is imitation (taqlid). If it is asked, why was the verse repeated? We say that there are two opinions on this:

One of them: that by the first verse He meant Abraham and those mentioned with him, and by the second the predecessors of the Jews.

Al-Jubba'i said, al-Qadi said: this is far-fetched, because the predecessors of the Jews and Christians have not been mentioned explicitly. The point of confusion in this view is that the people, when they said of Abraham and his sons that they were Jews, it was as if they said: they were upon the same way as our forefathers among the Jews, so their predecessors became included in the ruling of those mentioned, and so it is permissible for Him to say: ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾ and specify them. But that is like forced interpretation. Rather, the one mentioned earlier is Abraham and his sons, so His saying: ﴿That is a community﴾ must refer back to them.

The second opinion: that when the times, circumstances and places differ, repetition is not in vain. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: this is nothing but a human being. The description of these prophets, in respect of the religion you are upon, does not justify imitation in this matter. So leave off speaking about that community, for ﴿for them is what they earned﴾, and look into what Muhammad ﷺ has called you to, for that is more beneficial for you and more returning to your benefit. And you will not be questioned except about your own deeds.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The foolish among the people will say: What has turned them away from their qiblah which they were upon? Say: To Allah belong the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾

Know that this is the second doubt among the doubts which the Jews and Christians raised, attacking Islam. They said: abrogation (naskh) necessarily implies either ignorance or causing ignorance, and both are unbefitting for the Wise. That is because a command is either free of any condition, or restricted without permanence, or restricted by the condition of permanence. If it is free of any condition, it requires the act only once, so a subsequent command contrary to it is not an abrogation. If it is restricted by the condition of non-permanence, then it is clear that what comes after it contrary to it is not an abrogation of it. If it is restricted by the condition of permanence, then if the command is believed to remain forever, while He has stated a word indicating that it remains forever, and then He lifted it afterward, here He was ignorant and then it became apparent to Him (bada' lahu). And if He was knowing that it would not remain forever, while He had stated a word indicating that it would remain forever, that would be causing ignorance. Thus it is established that abrogation necessarily implies either ignorance or causing ignorance, and both are impossible for Allah, exalted is He. So abrogation from Him is impossible, and whoever brings abrogation in the rulings of Allah, exalted is He, must be a falsifier. By this route they reached, through impugning the abrogation of the qiblah, an attack on Islam. Then they specified this case with further doubt, saying: when we permit abrogation, we permit it only where interests differ, and here the directions are equal in that they belong to Allah, exalted is He, and are created by Him. So changing the qiblah from one direction to another is an act devoid of interest, and so it is futile, and futility is unbefitting for the Wise. This indicates that this change is not from Allah, exalted is He. Thus by this means they reached an attack on Islam.

Now let us discuss the explanation of the words, and then mention the answer to this doubt in the manner which Allah, exalted is He, established in His noble Book.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿The foolish will say﴾, there are two opinions:

The first, which is the choice of al-Qaffal: although this expression is apparently for the future, it may also be used for the past, like a man who does an act and some of his enemies criticize it, so he says: I know that they will criticize me for what I did. The meaning of this is that the speech concerns what is repeated and recurs; when they have said it once, they will say it again after that. So on this interpretation it is correct to say: the foolish among the people will say that, and reports have come that when they said it, the verse was revealed.

The second opinion: that Allah, exalted is He, informed about them before they uttered this speech that they would say it. In this there are benefits:

First: when he, peace and blessings be upon him, is informed of that before it occurred, this is information of the unseen, and therefore it is a miracle (mu'jiz).

Second: when Allah, exalted is He, informs him of it first and then he hears it from them, his distress from this speech is less than if he had heard it from them first.

Third: when Allah, exalted is He, makes him hear it first and then mentions its answer along with it, then when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, hears it from them, the answer is ready at hand, and that is better than if he heard it without the answer being ready.

As for the basic linguistic meaning of sufah (foolishness), we explained it in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: Shall we believe as the foolish believed?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 13]. In sum, whoever does not distinguish between what benefits him and what harms him, and turns away from the path of his benefits to what harms him, is described as frivolous and foolish. There is no doubt that error in matters of religion is far more harmful than in matters of this world. So if one who turns away from clear judgment in the affairs of his worldly life is considered foolish, then whoever is like that in the affairs of his religion is more deserving of this name. Thus there is no disbeliever except that he is foolish. This expression can be applied to the Jews, to the polytheists, to the hypocrites, and to all of them together, and some of the exegetes have adopted each of these interpretations:

The first of them: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: they are the Jews, because they used to take comfort in the Messenger's agreement with them regarding the qiblah. They thought that his agreement with them on the qiblah might lead him to become entirely in agreement with them. So when he turned away from that qiblah, they felt estranged by this and grieved, and said: he has returned to the way of his forefathers, and has longed for their religion. Had he remained upon our qiblah, we would have known that he is the awaited Messenger, announced in the Torah. So they said what Allah related of them in this verse.

The second: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, al-Hasan and al-Asamm said they are the polytheists of the Arabs. That is because he, peace be upon him, used to face Bayt al-Maqdis while he was in Mecca, and the polytheists were harmed by him because of that. When he came to Medina and turned toward the Ka'bah, they said: he refused except to return to agreement with us; had he persisted in it, it would have been better for him.

The third: that they are the hypocrites, and this is the view of al-Suddi. These said it mockingly, since no distinguishing characteristic of reason distinguishes one direction from another so as to require turning the qiblah toward it; thus this turning was merely futility and acting by opinion and desire. We interpreted the word "foolish" as referring to the hypocrites because this designation is specific to them. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Surely they are the foolish, but they do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 13].

The fourth: that it includes all of them, because the word "foolish" is a general term with the definite article, and we have explained its suitability for all disbelievers according to rational proof, and the text also indicates this, namely His saying: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130]. So it must encompass all of them. Al-Qadi said: the purpose of the verse is to show that this speech did occur from them in general, and when that is so, claiming that it is general is not far-fetched. We say: this degree does not contradict generality, nor does it require restricting it. Rather, the closer view is that all of them said it, because enemies are naturally inclined to attack and criticize, and when they find an opportunity, they leave no statement unsaid at all.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What has turned them away from their qiblah which they were upon﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: wallaahu 'anhu means he turned him away from it, and wallaa ilayhi means he turned him toward it, unlike wallaa 'anhu. From this is His saying: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ [al-Anfal: 16]. And His saying: ﴿What has turned them away?﴾ is an interrogative used in the manner of mockery and astonishment.

The second issue: regarding this turning there are two views:

The first view, which is the well-known and agreed-upon view among the exegetes: when the qiblah was changed from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah, the disbelievers reproached the Muslims and said: what has turned them away from their qiblah which they were upon? So the pronoun in His saying ﴿what has turned them away﴾ refers to the Messenger and the believers, and the qiblah which they were upon is Bayt al-Maqdis. The reports differ as to when, after his migration to Medina, he, peace and blessings be upon him, changed the qiblah. From Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, [it is said] after nine or ten months; from Mu'adh, after thirteen months; from Qatadah, after sixteen months; and from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, after seventeen months. This view is more established in our estimation than all the other views. Some have said eighteen months from his arrival. Al-Waqidi said: the qiblah was changed on Monday, the middle of Rajab, at the end of seventeen months. Others said: rather, two years.

The second view: the statement of Abu Muslim, which is that when the report was sound that Allah, exalted is He, changed it from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah, it became obligatory to hold this view. Otherwise, the wording of the verse might allow that by His saying "which they were upon" it is meant that the foolish were upon it, for they knew no qiblah except the qiblah of the Jews and the qiblah of the Christians; the former is toward the west, and the latter toward the east. They had no custom of praying until they faced one of the directions. So when they saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ facing toward the Ka'bah, this was considered objectionable by them, and they said: how can anyone face these two well-known directions? Then Allah, exalted is He, answered them: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west.﴾ Know that Abu Muslim was right, for were it not for the apparent reports, this statement would be open to possibility. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: al-Qaffal said: the qiblah is the direction which a person faces, and it derives from facing one another. The qiblah is so named because the one praying faces it and it faces him. Qutrub said: they say in their speech, "Fulan has no qiblah," meaning he has no direction to which he resorts; this too is derived from facing. Others said: when two men face each other, each of them is a qiblah for the other. Some of the muhaddithun said:

"I made your dwelling mine as a resting place and a qiblah, wherever I take refuge."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 142 (part 2 of 3):

As for His saying, ﴿To God belong the east and the west﴾, know that this is the first answer to that objection. Its explanation is that all directions belong to God, both in ownership (milk) and in dominion (mulk). Therefore none of them deserves, in itself, to be a qibla. Rather, it becomes a qibla only because God made it a qibla. Since this is the case, there is no objection to Him changing the direction from one to another.

If it is said: What is the wisdom, first, in appointing a qibla? And then what is the wisdom in changing the qibla from one direction to another? We say: As for the first question, there is strong disagreement between the People of the Sunnah and the Mu'tazilah. The People of the Sunnah say: The rulings of God Most High are not at all required to have a reason (ta'lil). They argued for this with several points:

The first: Whoever does an act for a purpose, either the existence of that purpose is preferable for him over its non-existence, or it is not so, but existence and non-existence are equal with respect to him. If the first, then he is deficient in himself and completed by another, and that is impossible for God. If the second, then it is impossible for it to be a purpose, an aim, or a determining factor. If it is said: although its existence and non-existence are equal with respect to Him, its existence is more beneficial to others than its non-existence, so the Wise does it so that the benefit returns to others. We say: Does the return of benefit to others, and its not returning to Him, stand equal with respect to God Most High, or is the matter not so? Then the division returns.

The second: Whoever does an act for a purpose either is able to achieve that purpose without that intermediary, or is not able to. If the first, then the intermediary is pointless; if the second, then it is incapacity, and that is impossible for God.

The third: If God Most High does an act for a purpose, then that purpose, if it is eternal, entails that the act is eternal, and that is impossible; and if it is originated, its origination depends on another purpose, and it entails either circularity or an infinite regress, and that is impossible.

The fourth: The specification of the creation of the world to a particular time rather than what precedes it and what follows it, if it is for a wisdom that is peculiar to that time rather than what precedes and follows it, then seeking the cause of why that wisdom occurred at that time rather than other times is like seeking the cause of why the world occurred at that time rather than other times. If one of them is independent of a determinant, so is the other; if one requires it, so does the other. And if that does not depend on wisdom, then the claim that God's agency depends on wisdom and purpose has been refuted.

The fifth: the previous proofs that all existing things, of good and evil, of disbelief and faith, of obedience and disobedience, occur by the power and will of God Most High. This refutes the claim of purpose, because it is impossible that God should have a purpose that returns to the servant in creating disbelief in him and punishing him for it forever and ever.

The sixth: The connection of God Most High's power and will to bringing about a specific act in pre-eternity is either permissible or necessary. If it is permissible, it requires another effective cause, and this entails an infinite regress; and also it entails the possibility of non-existence for the Eternal. If it is necessary, then what is necessary is not caused. Thus it has been established for us by these points that giving a cause to God's acts and rulings by motives and purposes is impossible. Since this is so, His agency is by pure divinity, power, effectiveness and dominion. This is what the explicit words of His saying, Most High, ﴿To God belong the east and the west﴾ indicate, for He gave as the reason for the permissibility of abrogation His being the owner of the east and the west, and ownership ultimately returns to power. He did not give a reason for this in terms of wisdom, as the Mu'tazilah say. Thus it is established that this verse, by its explicit wording, indicates our view and our school.

As for the Mu'tazilah, they said: Since the proofs have shown that God is Wise, and the Wise cannot have acts devoid of purposes, we know that He, glorified is He, has wisdoms and purposes in all His acts and rulings. These are sometimes manifest and clear to us, and sometimes hidden and concealed from us. Changing the qibla from one direction to another may be for hidden benefits and concealed secrets from us. Since this is the case, it is impossible to object to the religion of Islam on the basis of this change.

Question Four: Discussion of those wisdoms in detail. Know that such discussions are not definitive; their best outcome is to be matters of probability. As for the appointment of the qibla in prayer, they have mentioned wisdoms for it:

The first: God Most High created in man a rational faculty that perceives abstract and intelligible things, and an imaginative faculty that operates in the world of bodies. The rational faculty is rarely free from the accompaniment and companionship of the imaginative faculty. So when a person wants to bring to mind an abstract intellectual matter, he must assign to it an imaginative form that he can picture, so that this imaginative form helps him grasp those intellectual meanings. That is why the geometer, when he wants to grasp a rule of magnitudes, assigns to it a specific form and a specific shape so that sense and imagination assist the intellect in grasping that universal rule. Since the weak servant, when he arrives at the assembly of a great king, must face him with his face, must not turn away from him, must praise him greatly with his tongue, and must exert himself in service and humble supplication to him, then facing the qibla in prayer takes the place of being turned toward the King and not turned away from Him; recitation and glorifications take the place of praise of Him; and bowing and prostration take the place of service.

The second: The purpose of prayer is the presence of the heart, and this presence is not achieved except with stillness and abandoning turning and movement. This cannot be done except if one remains in all of one's prayer facing one specific direction. So when some directions are singled out with greater honour in people's imaginations, facing that direction is more fitting.

The third: God Most High loves harmony and affection among the believers, and He mentioned the favour of it upon them, when He said: ﴿And remember God's favour upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231] up to His saying: ﴿brothers﴾. If each one turned in his prayer toward a different side, that would give the appearance of clear discord. So God Most High appointed for them a known direction and commanded them all to turn toward it, so that harmony would be achieved among them through this. And in it there is an indication that God Most High loves harmony among His servants in works of goodness.

The fourth: God Most High specially attributed the Ka'bah to Himself in His saying: ﴿My House﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125], and specially attributed the believers to Himself with the description of servanthood. Both attributions are for specification and honour. It is as if He, Most High, said: O believer, you are My servant, the Ka'bah is My House, and the prayer is My service; so turn your face in My service toward My House, and your heart toward Me.

The fifth: Some shaykhs said: The Jews faced the qibla because the call to Moses, upon him be peace, came from that direction, as in His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ [al-Qasas: 44] and so on. The Christians faced the west, because Gabriel, upon him be peace, went to Mary, upon her be peace, from the east side, according to His saying, Most High: ﴿And mention in the Book Mary, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place﴾ [Maryam: 16].
