The believers faced the Ka'bah because it is the qibla of the Friend of God, the birthplace of the Beloved of God, and the place of the sanctuary of God. Some of them used to say: The Christians faced the rising place of lights, and we have faced the rising place of the lord of lights, who is Muhammad (ﷺ); from his light all lights were created.

The sixth: They said: The Ka'bah is the navel of the earth and its centre, so God Most High commanded all His creation to turn toward the middle of the earth in their prayers. This is an indication that justice is required in everything, and for its sake He made the middle of the earth a qibla for creation.

The seventh: God Most High manifested His love for Muhammad, upon him be the blessings and peace, through the command to face the Ka'bah. This is because he, upon him be blessings and peace, used to wish for that for a period, for the sake of opposing the Jews. So God Most High sent down: ﴿We see the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], and so on. In the observable world, when one of people is described as loving another, they say: "So-and-so changes the qibla for the sake of so-and-so," by way of illustration. God Most High has changed the qibla for the sake of His beloved Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, in the way of reality. He said: ﴿So We shall surely turn you to a qibla that pleases you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], and He did not say "a qibla that I please." The indication in it is as if He, Most High, said: O Muhammad, everyone seeks My pleasure, and I seek your pleasure in both abodes. In this world, this is what we have mentioned; and in the Hereafter, His saying, Most High: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be pleased﴾ [al-Duha: 5]. There is also in it an indication of the honour of the poor: ﴿So that you would drive them away and be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-An'am: 52]. And He said regarding turning away from the qibla: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then you would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾. It is as if He, Most High, said: The Ka'bah is the qibla of your face, and the poor are the qibla of My mercy; so your turning away from the qibla of your face makes you a wrongdoer, so how could turning away from the qibla of My mercy be?

The eighth: The Throne is the qibla of the bearers, the Footstool is the qibla of the righteous, the House frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) is the qibla of the scribes, the Ka'bah is the qibla of the believers, and the Truth is the qibla of the bewildered among the believers. God Most High said: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115]. It is established that the Throne is created from light, the Footstool from pearls, the House frequented from rubies, and the Ka'bah from five mountains: Mount Sinai, Mount Zaytah, al-Judi, Lebanon, and Hira'. The indication in it is as if God Most High says: If you have sins as heavy as these mountains, and you come to the Ka'bah on pilgrimage, or turn toward it in prayer, I shall expiate them from you and forgive them for you. This is the sum of the aspects mentioned in this chapter, and the verified view is the first.

* * *

Question Five: On the wisdom of changing the qibla from one direction to another. We have mentioned the objection of those people to denying this change, which is that since the directions are equal in all attributes, changing the qibla from one direction to another is mere pointlessness, and so it is not the act of the Wise.

The answer to this: As for the view of the People of the Sunnah, that the rulings of God Most High are not required to have wisdoms, the matter is clear. As for the view of the Mu'tazilah, they have two approaches:

The first: It is not impossible for benefits to differ according to differences in directions. Its explanation is in several aspects:

One: When it becomes firmly rooted in the imaginations of some people that these directions are more noble than others because this House was built by the Friend (Abraham) and he honoured it, this person, when facing it, is more reverent and humble, and that is a sought-after benefit.

Two: Since the building of this House was a cause for the rise of the state of the Arabs, their desire to honour it was greater.

Three: When the Jews used to reproach the Muslims, at the time of facing Bayt al-Maqdis, by saying: "Were it not that we guided you to the qibla, you would not know the qibla," this became a cause of disturbing the thoughts, and that impairs humility and reverence. So this calls for turning away from that qibla.

Fourthly: the Kaaba is the birthplace of Muhammad (ﷺ), so venerating the Kaaba entails venerating Muhammad, peace be upon him, and that is something desired, because once his veneration becomes firmly rooted in their hearts, their acceptance of his commands and prohibitions in religion and the Sharia becomes quicker and easier. And whatever leads to a desired end is itself desired. Therefore, changing the qibla was fitting.

Fifthly: Allah the Exalted explained this in His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you were upon except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. So Allah the Exalted commanded them, when they were in Mecca, to face Bayt al-Maqdis, in order to distinguish themselves from the polytheists. Then, when they emigrated to Medina, where the Jews were, they were commanded to turn toward the Kaaba, in order to distinguish themselves from the Jews.

As for His saying: ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾, guidance has already been discussed. The Mu'tazilah said: it is only the guidance that conveys (al-dalala al-mūṣila), and the meaning is that He indicates what is most suitable for worship, and the straight path is that which, if they hold to it, leads them to Paradise. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: this guidance, either its intended meaning is the call (al-da'wa), or the indication (al-dalala), or the attainment of knowledge (taḥṣīl al-'ilm) of it. The first two are invalid, because they are general to all the responsible persons (mukallafun), so it must be understood in the third sense, and this requires that guidance and misguidance are from Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾.

Know that this verse raises several questions.

**The first question:** The *kaf* in *kadhalika* ("thus") is the *kaf* of comparison. What is the thing compared to? There are several opinions.

First: it refers back to the meaning of *yahdi* ("guides"). That is, just as We bestowed upon you guidance, so too We bestowed upon you by making you a middle nation.

Second: the view of Abu Muslim, whose explanation is: "Just as We guided you to a direction that is the most central of directions, so too We have made you a middle nation."

Third: it refers back to what came earlier concerning Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿And indeed We chose him in this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130]. That is, just as We chose him in this world, so too We have made you a middle nation.

Fourth: in my view, the sentence may be understood as: ﴿To God belong the east and the west﴾. These directions, although they are equal in being God's dominion and property, He singled out some of them for added honour and esteem by making one of them a *qiblah* (direction of prayer), as an act of grace and kindness. Likewise, all servants share in servitude, but He singled out this community for additional favour and worship, as an act of kindness and not as an obligation.

Fifth: the pronoun of a thing may be mentioned even when the thing it refers to has not been mentioned, provided the referent is well known and recognised. An example is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. Now, it is well known and recognised by everyone that He, glorified is He, is the one who grants honour to whomever He wills and humiliates whomever He wills. So His saying ﴿And thus We have made you﴾ means: and in the likeness of that wondrous making, which none other than Him is capable of, We have made you a middle nation.

**The second question:** When *wasat* is used as a noun, the *sin* is vocalised with a *fatha* (*wasat*), as in His saying ﴿a middle nation﴾. When it is used as an adverb of place, it is written with the *sin* sukun (*wasṭ*). You say: "I sat in the middle (*wasṭ*) of the people." The scholars differed in interpreting *wasat* and mentioned several matters.

First: *wasat* means justice (*'adl*). The evidence for this is the verse, the report, poetry, transmission, and meaning.

As for the verse, it is His saying: ﴿The most moderate of them said﴾ [al-Qalam: 28], meaning the most just of them.

As for the report, al-Qaffal narrated from al-Thawri, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding ﴿a middle nation﴾ that he said: "Just." The Prophet (peace be upon him) also said: "The best of matters is their middle (*awsatuha*)," meaning the most just of them. It is also said that the Prophet (ﷺ) was the most central of the Quraysh in lineage. And the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Keep to the middle *namat* (type of cloth or way)."

As for poetry, there is the verse of Zuhayr:

*They are a middle that mankind is content with in their judgment, when the great nights descend.*

As for transmission, al-Jawhari said in *al-Sihah*: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾, meaning just. This is what al-Akhfash, al-Khalil, and Qutrub said.

As for meaning, there are several points:

First: *wasat* is literally distance from the two extremes. Without doubt, the two extremes of excess and deficiency are both bad. Thus the one who is moderate in character is distant from both extremes, and so he is balanced and virtuous.

Second: justice is called *wasat* because it does not lean towards either of the two disputants. The just person is the balanced one who does not lean towards either extreme.

Third: there is no doubt that the purpose of His saying ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ is praise for them, because it is not permissible for God, exalted is He, to mention an attribute and make it like the cause for appointing them as witnesses to Him, and then to join to this the testimony of the Messenger, unless it is praise. Thus it is established that the meaning of His saying ﴿middle﴾ is that which relates to praise in matters of religion. It is not permissible for God to praise witnesses at the time of His judgment concerning them, by describing them as witnesses, except by their being just. Therefore, the meaning of *wasat* must be justice.

Fourth: the most just part of a thing is its middle, because its judgment with all its other parts is equal and balanced, while the extremities are quickly subject to defect and corruption, whereas the middles are protected and guarded. When this holds true for the middle, it becomes like an expression for the one who is balanced and does not lean towards one side over another.

The second view: *wasat* in everything means its best. They said: this interpretation is preferable to the first for several reasons.

The first reason: the word *wasat* is used for inanimate things. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "I hired a camel in Mecca for the pilgrimage from a Bedouin, and he said: 'Give me from the *wasat* of the *tahnah* (a type of coin),'" meaning from the best of the dinars. Justice, however, is not found in inanimate things. Therefore this interpretation is preferable.

The second reason: it corresponds to His saying: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

The third view: when a man says, "So-and-so is our *awsat* in lineage," the meaning is that he is the most excellent. He is in the middle of them like the middle of a necklace. The origin of this is that followers surround their leader, so he is in their midst and they are around him, and therefore he is called *wasat* in this sense.

The fourth view: it is permissible that they are *wasat* in the sense that they are moderate in religion, between the one who neglects and the one who exceeds, and between the extremist and the one who falls short in matters. This is because they did not exaggerate as the Christians exaggerated, who made Him a son and a god, nor did they fall short as the Jews fell short by killing the prophets, altering the scriptures, and other things in which they fell short.

Know that these views are closely related and not contradictory. And God knows best.

* * *

**The third question:** The Ash'ari theologians (*al-Ashab*) used this verse to argue that the act of the servant is created by God, because this verse indicates that the justice of this community and its being the best are by God's making and creating. This is explicit in their school of thought. The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist Mu'tazilites) said: the meaning of this making is the bestowing of favours (*al-alṭaf*) which God, exalted is He, knew that if He bestowed them upon this community, they would choose what is right in speech and action. The Ash'aris answered them in several ways.

The first: this is abandoning the apparent meaning, and that is not to be resorted to except when there is evidence that the verse cannot be taken in its apparent sense. But we have already shown that the clear rational proofs are only on our side. The most the Mu'tazilah can do in this matter is to cling to the distinction between praise and blame and reward and punishment. We have shown many times that this approach is refuted by their own principles, through the issue of knowledge and the issue of the motive. A refuted argument is not to be paid any attention at all.

The second: He, exalted is He, said before this verse: ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. We have shown the indication of this verse in our view, that He, exalted is He, singles out some for guidance and not others. Thus this verse must be understood in that way, so that each of the two verses confirms the content of the other.

The third: whatever favours God, exalted is He, can bestow upon all, He has bestowed. If that is the case, singling out believers for this meaning serves no purpose.

The fourth: God, exalted is He, mentioned this in the context of bestowing favour upon this community. Bestowing favour (*al-luṭf*) is obligatory, and what is obligatory may not be mentioned in the context of bestowing favour.

* * *

**The fourth question:** The majority of Ash'aris and the majority of Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that the consensus (*ijma'*) of the community (*ummah*) is a proof (*hujjah*). They said: God, exalted is He, informed about the justice of this community and its being the best. If they persisted in anything forbidden, they would not be described as the best. And since it is established that they do not commit anything forbidden, their statement must be a proof.

If it is said: the verse does not have its apparent meaning, because describing the community as just requires that each one of them be described as just, and the contrary of that is known by necessity. Therefore it must be restricted to part of them, and we restrict it to the infallible Imams. Even if we grant that the verse does not lose its apparent meaning, we do not grant that *wasat* means the best of everything. And the arguments you have mentioned are opposed by two points:

The first: the justice of a man is the carrying out of obligations and avoiding of prohibitions, and this is the act of the servant. God, exalted is He, has informed that He made them *wasat*. This requires that their being *wasat* is the act of God, exalted is He. This requires that their being *wasat* is different from their being just; otherwise, it would entail one created thing being brought about by two agents, which is impossible.

The second: *wasat* is a name for what is intermediate between two things. Making it literally refer to justice and being the best requires a shared meaning (*al-ishtirak*), which is contrary to the basic principle. Even if we grant that they are described as the best, why would it not suffice for obtaining this attribute merely to avoid major sins? In that case, it is possible that what they agreed upon, even if it was an error, was a minor sin, and so it does not harm their being the best. What strengthens this possibility is that He, exalted is He, ruled that they are just so that they may be witnesses over mankind, and committing minor sins does not prevent testimony. Even if we grant that they avoid both minor and major sins, God, exalted is He, has made clear that their being described in this way was because they are witnesses over mankind. It is known that this testimony is realised only in the Hereafter, so it is necessary that their justice must be realised there, because the justice of witnesses is considered at the time of giving testimony, not at the time of receiving it. This is not disputed. But why do you say that they are like that in this world? The community becomes infallible in the Hereafter. Even if we grant that they must be just in this world, the addressees of this address are those who were present at the time this verse was revealed, because addressing someone who does not exist is impossible. If that is the case, this verse indicates the justice of those who were present at that time, and does not indicate the justice of others. Therefore this verse shows that the consensus of those people is true. So we must not rely on consensus unless we know that the opinion of each of those people is included in it. But that is not possible unless we know each one of those groups individually, and know that each of them lived on until after the death of Muhammad (ﷺ), and know that the views of all of them were included in that consensus. Since this is almost impossible, it is impossible to rely on consensus.

[Page 91]

The answer to your statement that the verse does not have its apparent meaning: we say we do not grant this. His saying ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ implies that He made each one of them, when they are together with others, to have this attribute. In our view, in every matter on which they agree, each one of them is just in that matter. Indeed, when they disagree, at that point they may commit wrong. We have said that this is an address to them in the state of their agreement, because His saying ﴿We have made you﴾ is addressed to them collectively, not to each one of them alone. Furthermore, even if we grant that this implies that each one of them is just, we still say: the application of this to some of them was set aside because of evidence that was established, so it must remain in force with regard to the rest. This is the meaning of what the scholars said: the verse does not mean that all of them are like that, but rather that there must exist among them those who have this attribute. Since we do not know them individually, we need the collective agreement of their group in word and deed, so that those whose view counts are included among them. An example: if the Messenger (peace be upon him) said that one of the sons of so-and-so must be correct in opinion and judgment, and we do not know him individually, but we find his sons unanimous on an opinion, we know it to be true, because the one who is right must exist among them. But if they agree apart from one individual on an opinion, we do not judge that it is true, since it is possible that the correct view lies with that one individual who disagreed. For this reason, many scholars said: if we could distinguish within the community those who are correct from those who are wrong, the proof would rest on the view of the correct ones, and we would not at all consider the view of the one who is wrong.

His statement: if the meaning of their being *wasat* were the meaning of their justice, it would follow that the act of the servant is created by God, exalted is He. We say: this is our doctrine, as has already been explained.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 2 of 4):**

His statement: "Why do you say that God's report of their justice and excellence requires that they abstain from minor sins?" We reply: God's report is true, and a true report requires that what it reports about occurs. Committing a minor sin is not excellence, so combining the two is contradictory. But an opponent may say: reporting that a person is good is more general than reporting that he is good in all matters or in some matters. This is why the report can be divided into these two categories, so that one says: "The good is either good in some matters but not others, or good in all matters." The subject of the division is common to both categories. Whoever is good in some respects but not others is truly described as good. Therefore God's report about the excellence of the community does not require His report that they are excellent in all matters. It is established that this does not preclude their committing major sins, let alone minor ones. We have supported this proof in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence), but this objection applies to it. As for the other objection, it has been answered by saying that His words, *"And thus We have made you a middle community"* [2:143], are addressed to the whole community, its first and last members, whoever was present at the time this verse was revealed and whoever came after them until the Hour. Just as His words, *"Retaliation is prescribed for you"* [2:178] and *"Fasting is prescribed for you"* [2:183] encompass everyone and are not restricted to those present at that time, so too all of God's obligations, commands and prohibitions are addressed to the entire community. If it is said: "If that were the case, this would be an address to everyone who exists until the Hour. But the justice was ascribed only to their collective; so from where do you derive that the people of every age are just, to the extent that you make them a proof against those who come after them?" We reply: Because He, exalted is He, made them witnesses over mankind, if we considered the first and last of the community together as a collective being a proof against others, the benefit would vanish, since after its end there would be no one against whom the community could be a proof. So we know that what is meant is the people of each age. It is permissible to call the people of a single age a "community" (*ummah*), since *ummah* is a term for a group that heads toward one direction, and there is no doubt that the people of each age are like this. Also, He, exalted is He, said *"a middle community"* [2:143], expressing it with an indefinite noun, and there is no doubt that this encompasses the people of every age.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** People differ over whether the testimony mentioned in His words, *"that you may be witnesses over mankind"* [2:143],

[Page 92]

takes place in the Hereafter or in this world.

The first opinion is that it occurs in the Hereafter. Those who hold this view have two arguments. The first, which most of them adopt, is that this community will bear witness for the prophets against their peoples who denied them. It is related that the nations will deny the prophets' delivery of the message, so God will demand of the prophets proof that they had delivered it, though He knows best. Then the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought forward and will testify. The nations will say: "How do you know?" They will reply: "We knew this through God's report in His explicit Book, upon the tongue of His truthful Prophet." Then Muhammad, peace be upon him, will be brought and questioned about the condition of his community, and he will vouch for them and testify to their justice. This is His words: *"How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these?"* [4:41]. The Qadi has criticized this report in several respects:

The first is that the basis of this report is that the nations deny their prophets, and this is based on the premise that the people of the Resurrection may lie. This is false according to the Qadi. However, we will discuss this issue in surah al-An'am, in the interpretation of His words: *"Then their temptation was only that they said, 'By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.' Look how they lied against themselves"* [6:23–24].

The second is that the testimony of the community and the testimony of the Messenger in the Hereafter are based on God's testimony to the truthfulness of the prophets. If that is so, why does God not testify to this for them from the outset?

Its answer: The wisdom in that is to distinguish the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) in excellence from all other nations, by their hastening to affirm God's truth and the truth of all the prophets, and by believing in all of them. Thus, relative to the other nations, they are like the just person relative to the wicked. Therefore God accepts their testimony against the other nations and does not accept the testimony of the other nations against them, to manifest their justice and reveal their merit and nobility.

The third is that such reports are not called testimony. This is weak, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "If you know something like the sun, then testify." What God has reported about is known like the sun, so testimony about it is permissible.

The second argument is that they said: the meaning of the verse is "that you may testify against people concerning their deeds in which they opposed the truth." Ibn Zayd said: the witnesses are four.

The first are the angels appointed to record the deeds of the servants. He, exalted is He, said: *"And every soul will come with it a driver and a witness"* [50:21], and He said: *"Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer ready"* [50:18], and He said: *"Indeed, over you are guardians, noble and recording, who know what you do"* [82:10–12].

The second is the testimony of the prophets, which is what is meant by His words, quoting Jesus, peace be upon him: *"And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are, over all things, Witness"* [5:117]. And concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community He said in this verse: *"that you may be witnesses over mankind and the Messenger may be a witness over you"* [2:143], and He said: *"How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these?"* [4:41].

The third is the testimony of the community of Muhammad specifically. He, exalted is He, said: *"And the prophets and the witnesses will be brought"* [39:69], and He said: *"The day the witnesses will stand"* [40:51].

The fourth is the testimony of the limbs, which is like confession, indeed more remarkable than it. He, exalted is He, said: *"The day their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them"* [24:24], and He said: *"That Day We will seal over their mouths"* [36:65].

The second opinion: the discharge of this testimony takes place in this world. Its explanation is that witnessing (*shahadah*), observing (*mushahadah*) and seeing (*shuhud*) are all sight. One says: "I witnessed such-and-such" when one saw and perceived it. Since there is a strong affinity between seeing with the eye and knowing with the heart, knowledge in the heart is indeed called *mushahadah* and *shuhud*, and one who knows a thing is called *shahid* and *mushahid*. Then indication of a thing was called "witness to a thing," because it is by it that the witness becomes a witness. Since the one who reports about a thing and clarifies its state functions as evidence for it, he too was called a witness. Then, in the usage of the Sharia, this term became specifically applied to one who reports about people's rights in specific words and in specific ways. Having understood this, we say: everyone who knows the state of a thing and uncovers it is a witness to it. God described this community as witnesses. This testimony is either in the Hereafter or in this world. It cannot be in the Hereafter, because God made them just in this world so that they would be witnesses, and that requires that they be witnesses in this world. We say that God made them just in this world because He said: *"And thus We have made you a community"* [2:143], and this is a report about the past, so it has at least occurred at present. We say that this requires their becoming witnesses in this world because He said: *"And thus We have made you a middle community, that you may be witnesses over mankind"* [2:143]. He linked their being witnesses to their becoming middle, the link of consequence to condition. So when the attribute of being middle occurs in this world, the attribute of being witnesses must occur in this world.

If it is said: bearing testimony (*tahammul*) occurs only in this world, and one who bears testimony may be called a witness even though the delivery (*ada'*) occurs only at the Resurrection. We reply: The testimony that is considered in the verse is not bearing but delivery. The evidence is that He made justice a condition for this testimony, and the testimony for which justice is a condition is the delivery, not the bearing. Thus it is established that the verse requires that the community deliver testimony in the abode of this world. This requires that the consensus (*ijma'*) of the community, when it reports something, be a proof, and there is no meaning to our saying "consensus is a proof" except this. Thus it is established that the verse indicates that consensus is a proof from this aspect as well.

Know that the argument we mentioned for the soundness of this view does not refute the first two opinions, because by this reasoning we have shown that the community must be witnesses in this world, and this does not preclude their also being witnesses in the Resurrection in the manner in which the reports have come. The conclusion is that His words, *"that you may be witnesses over mankind,"* indicate that their statement, when there is consensus, is a proof, insofar as their statement when there is consensus makes the truth clear to mankind. This is confirmed by His words: *"and the Messenger may be a witness over you,"* meaning: a deliverer and clarifier. Then there is no impediment to their also obtaining testimony in the Hereafter, so that what they did in this world is treated as bearing testimony, because when they established the truth, they came to know who accepted it and who rejected it, and then they testify to that on the Day of Resurrection, just as the witness to contracts knows what was completed and what was not, then testifies to that before the judge.

The sixth issue: The verse indicates that whoever's disbelief or wickedness is evident, such as the Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists), the Khawarij and the Rafidah, is not counted in the consensus. This is because God only made witnesses those whom He described with justice and excellence, and the ruling does not differ regarding one who commits wickedness or disbelief by a statement or an act, or one who disbelieves by rejecting an explicit text or by interpretation.

The seventh issue: He said *"witnesses over mankind"* and did not say *"witnesses for mankind,"* because their statement requires obligation, either by speech or by action, and that is incumbent upon them, not for them, in the present. If it is asked: why was the complement of the testimony postponed the first time and placed first the second time? We reply: because the purpose in the first is to establish their testimony over the nations, and in the second is to single out the Messenger as a witness over them.

* *

His words, exalted is He: *"And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels. And indeed, it was difficult except for those whom God guided. And God would not have allowed your faith to be lost. Indeed, God is to the people Kind and Merciful"* [2:143].

Know that His words *"And We did not make"* mean "We did not legislate and did not decree," like His words: *"God did not establish any bahirah"* [5:103], meaning He did not prescribe it or make it a religion. His words *"which you used to face"* mean "which you used to hold as the direction to face." It is like a speaker's saying: "So-and-so had a debt upon such-and-such." His words *"which you used to face"* are not a description of the qiblah; rather, they are the second object of *ja'ala* (made), meaning: *"And We did not make the qiblah"* the direction *"which you used to face."*

There are two views here.

The first: this statement explains the wisdom in establishing the qiblah. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray in Makkah toward the Ka'bah, then after the Hijrah he was commanded to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis, to win over the Jews. Then he was turned back to the Ka'bah. So we say: *"And We did not make the qiblah,"* the direction, *"which you used to face"* at first, meaning: "We did not return you to it except as a test and trial for people."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 3 of 4):**

The second view: His saying ﴿the direction you used to face﴾ may be understood as a statement of the wisdom behind making Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) the qiblah. That is, the original command for you was to face the Ka'bah, and your facing Bayt al-Maqdis was an incidental matter for a purpose. We made the qiblah the direction you were facing before this time, which was Bayt al-Maqdis, in order to test the people and to see who follows the Messenger and who does not, and who turns away from him.

There is a third view, mentioned by Abu Muslim, who said: Were it not for the narrations, the verse would not indicate that the Messenger (peace be upon him) had any particular qiblah. This is because it may be said that "kuntu" means "sirtu" (I became), as in His saying: ﴿You are the best nation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. It may also be said that "kana" means "lam yazal" (he has always been), as in His saying: ﴿And Allah has always been Mighty and Wise﴾ [An-Nisa': 158]. So there is nothing to prevent the meaning of ﴿We did not make the qiblah that you used to face﴾ from being: the one you have always faced, which is the Ka'bah, except for such and such.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The lam in ﴿except that We might know﴾ is the lam of purpose (lam al-gharad). The discussion is whether purpose can be ascribed to God or not. If it cannot, then how is this statement to be interpreted? This has already been covered.

**The second issue:** "We did not make such-and-such, except that We might know," seems to imply that knowledge of that thing had not yet been attained; that He did the act in order that this knowledge might be obtained. This implies that God did not know those things before they occurred. A similar difficulty arises in His saying: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those who strive among you and the patient﴾ [Muhammad: 31]; His saying: ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden and knows that there is weakness in you﴾ [al-Anfal: 66]; His saying: ﴿Perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾ [Taha: 44]; His saying: ﴿So Allah will surely know those who are truthful﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3]; His saying: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while Allah does not yet know those of you who have striven and known the patient?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142]; and His saying: ﴿And he had no authority over them, except that We might know who believes in the Hereafter﴾ [Saba': 21]. The discussion of this issue has already been fully treated under His saying: ﴿And when He tried﴾. The exegetes have answered it in several ways:

[p. 95]

The first: His saying ﴿except that We might know﴾ means: except that Our party among the prophets and believers might know. This is like a king saying, "We conquered such-and-such a town," meaning that his agents conquered it. From this comes the saying that "Umar conquered al-Sawad." Also from this is the Prophet's (peace be upon him) account of what God says: "I lent to My servant and he did not repay Me. He reviled Me, though it was not fitting for him to revile Me. He says, 'Woe to me, O Time!' but I am Time." In a hadith also: "Whoever humiliates a friend of Mine, he has humiliated Me."

The second: its meaning is: so that what was non-existent might come into existence and become existent. Thus His saying ﴿except that We might know﴾ means: except that We might know it as existent. If it is said that this implies the createdness of knowledge, we respond: the scholars have differed on whether knowledge that a thing will exist is the same as knowing it when it exists. The disagreement on this is well known.

The third: except that We might distinguish these from those by the disclosure of what is in their hearts of sincerity and hypocrisy, so that the believers would know whom among them to befriend and whom to oppose. Thus distinction was called knowledge, because it is one of the benefits and fruits of knowledge.

The fourth: ﴿except that We might know﴾ means: except that We might see. The figurative sense of this is that the Arabs use "knowledge" in place of "seeing" and "seeing" in place of "knowledge," as in His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how﴾ (ألم تر كيف), and in the expressions "ra'aytu," "'alimtu," and "shahidtu," which are interchangeable words.

The fifth: what al-Farra' held, which is that the occurrence of knowledge in this verse refers to the addressees. An example of this is when an ignorant person and a wise person meet. The ignorant one says, "Wood burns fire," and the wise one says, "Rather, fire burns wood. We will bring them together so that we know which of them burns the other." The meaning is: so that we know which of us is the ignorant one. Likewise His saying ﴿except that We might know﴾ means: except that you might know. The purpose of this kind of speech is to win over and to soften the address, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance﴾ [Saba': 24], where the statement that suggests doubt is attributed to the speaker himself, in order to soften the address and to be gentle with the addressee. Similarly His saying ﴿except that We might know﴾.

The sixth: We treat you as one who is being tested, as if He did not know, since justice requires this.

The seventh: knowledge here is an additional connective element. So His saying ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾ means: except that the following of those who follow and the turning back of those who turn back might come to pass. A parallel is your saying about something you deny of yourself: "Allah did not know this from me," meaning: "This did not come from me." The meaning is: if it had been from me, Allah would have known it.

**The third issue:** The scholars have differed on whether this trial occurred because of the designation of the qiblah itself, or because of its change. Some people said that it occurred because of the designation of the qiblah: the Prophet (peace be upon him) used to pray toward the Ka'bah, but when he came to Medina he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and this was hard on the Arabs because he had abandoned their qiblah. Then when he turned it back again to the Ka'bah, this was hard on the Jews because he had abandoned their qiblah. The majority of the people of scholarly verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: this trial occurred only because of the change. They said: if Muhammad (ﷺ) had been certain of his matter, his opinion would not have changed. Al-Qaffal narrated from Ibn Jurayj that he said: "It has reached me that some people who had embraced Islam turned back, saying, 'Once here and once there.'" Al-Suddi said: When the Prophet (peace be upon him) turned toward the Masjid al-Haram, people differed. The hypocrites said: "What is wrong with them? They were on a qiblah and then abandoned it." The Muslims said: "We do not know the state of our brothers who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis." Others said: "He longed for the land of his father and birth." The polytheists said: "He has become confused in his religion."

[p. 96]

Know that this last view is more correct, because the doubt concerning abrogation (naskh) is greater than the doubt arising from the designation of the qiblah. God has described it as weighty, saying: ﴿And indeed, it was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided﴾. So interpreting it this way is more appropriate.

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿who turns back on his heels﴾ is a metaphor (isti'arah). Its meaning is: who disbelieves in Allah and His Messenger. The basis of the metaphor is that one who turns back on his heels has left what is before him and turned away from it. When they abandoned faith and the proofs, they became like one who turns his back on what lies before him, so they were described with this, as He said: ﴿Then he turned his back and was arrogant﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 23], and as He said: ﴿He denied and turned away﴾ [Taha: 48]. All of this is a comparison.

* * *

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, it was﴾ (wa-in kanat), there are several issues:

**The first issue:** "In" (إنْ) with a kasrah and light pronunciation has four meanings: conditional (jaza'), lightened from the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), negation (jahd), and superfluous (za'idah). As for the conditional, it establishes a connection between one clause and another; the implying element is the condition, and the implied element is the consequence, as in your saying: "If you come to me, I will honour you." As for the second, the lightened form of the heavy, it confirms the meaning of the clause in the sense of "inna" (indeed) with shaddah, as in your saying: "Indeed Zayd is standing." God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4], and He said: ﴿Indeed, the promise of our Lord was fulfilled﴾ [al-Isra': 108]. Similar examples are numerous in the Qur'an. The purpose of lightening it is that it is followed by what could not properly follow it of verbs. The lam is necessarily attached to this lightened form as a compensation for what has been omitted from it. The difference between it and the negating "in" in His saying ﴿The disbelievers are only in delusion﴾ [al-Mulk: 20] and His saying ﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [al-An'am: 50] is that each of these is followed by both a noun and a verb, as we have described. As for the third, the negating "in," as in His saying ﴿The judgement is only for Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 57], and He said: ﴿They follow only assumption﴾ [al-An'am: 148], and He said: ﴿And if they should cease, none could hold them after Him﴾ [Fatir: 41], meaning: none holds them. As for the fourth, the superfluous one, as in your saying: "Not (ma) if (in) you saw Zayd."

Having understood this, we say: "in" in His saying ﴿And indeed, it was a great matter﴾ is the lightened form to which the lam is attached, and its purpose is to confirm the meaning of the clause.

**The second issue:** To what does the pronoun in ﴿it was﴾ (kanat) refer? There are two views:

The first: it refers to the qiblah, because there must be an antecedent mentioned, and the only one is the qiblah in His saying: ﴿We did not make the qiblah that you used to face﴾.

The second: it refers to what is indicated by the preceding discourse, namely the abandonment of the qiblah. The feminine form is due to "tawliyah" (turning away), because He said: ﴿What turned them away from their qiblah that they had been facing?﴾ Then He said, in coordination with this: ﴿And indeed, it was a great matter﴾, meaning: "and indeed, the turning away was a great matter," because His saying ﴿what turned them away﴾ indicates the turning away. This is like what has been said about His saying: ﴿And do not eat from that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed, it is defiance﴾ [al-An'am: 121]. It is also possible that the meaning is: "and indeed, this act was great," similar to His saying "fa-bihā wa-ni'mat" (and so good it was).

Know that this discussion is a branch of the earlier issue, namely whether the trial and testing occurred by the qiblah itself or by the change of the qiblah. We have shown that the second is more correct, because the difficulty arising from abrogation is stronger than the difficulty arising from those directions. For this reason God described it as "great" in His saying: ﴿And indeed, it was a great matter﴾.

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿a great matter (la-kabirah)﴾, the meaning is: truly heavy, burdensome, and objectionable, like His saying: ﴿Great is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾ [al-Kahf: 5], meaning: the slander is grievous because of it. God the Exalted said: ﴿Glory be to You! This is a great slander﴾ [al-Nur: 16], and He said: ﴿Indeed, that was in the sight of Allah an enormity﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53].

Now, if we say that the trial occurred through the qiblah itself, then leaving it is heavy for them, because this requires abandoning familiarity and habit, and turning away from the way of the fathers and ancestors. If we say that the trial occurred through the alteration of the qiblah, then it is heavy in that a person cannot recognise that this is the truth except after he has understood the question of abrogation and freed himself from the objections it raises. That is a heavy and difficult matter, except for one whom Allah the Exalted has guided, until he knows that he should not find it strange that the qiblah is shifted from one direction to another, just as he should not find it strange that God moves them from one state to another, in health and sickness, wealth and poverty. Whoever is guided to this reflection, his insight increases; whoever is foolish and follows his desires and the surface appearances of matters, this question is burdensome for him.

As for His saying: ﴿except for those whom Allah has guided﴾, the companions (al-Ashab) cited this verse in the question of the creation of actions (khalq al-a'mal). They said: the meaning of guidance is either the call (da'wah), or the placing of proofs (wad' al-dalalah), or the creation of knowledge (khalq al-ma'rifah). The first two are invalid here, because He has judged it to be heavy for all except those whom Allah has guided. Therefore it must be said that the one whom Allah has guided does not find it heavy. If guidance meant the call, and the placing of proofs is general for all, then it would not be heavy for any of the disbelievers. Since it was heavy for them, we know that the meaning of guidance here is the creation of knowledge and understanding, which is what is sought.

The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) replied to this in three ways:

The first: Allah the Exalted mentioned them in a manner of praise, singling them out for this.

The second: He intended by it the taking of guidance (al-ihtida').

The third: they are the ones who benefited from Allah's guidance, while others were, as it were, not counted.

The answer to all of these is: this abandons the apparent sense, so it is contrary to the default understanding. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And Allah would not have caused your faith to be lost﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Some Muslim men, such as Abu Umamah, Sa'd ibn Zurarah, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, and others, died while facing the first qiblah (Jerusalem). Their tribes said, "O Messenger of Allah, our brothers died facing the first qiblah; what is their state?" So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

You should know that this occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is necessary, for otherwise some parts of the speech would not connect with others. The way the difficulty is stated is this: those who did not permit abrogation (naskh) except with a change of divine decision (bada') say: when the ruling changed, it must have been that the ruling was corrupt and void. So, based on this question, it occurred to their hearts that the prayers they had performed facing Jerusalem were lost. Then Allah the Exalted answered this difficulty and explained that abrogation is a transfer from one benefit to another benefit, and from one obligation to another obligation. The first is like the second in that the one who performs it is holding fast to the religion, and whoever is in this state, his reward is not lost. A parallel to this is what they asked after the prohibition of wine concerning one who had died while drinking it. Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 93]. So Allah informed them that there is no blame upon them for what had passed, since that was by Allah's permission.

If it is said: if the doubt arose only from permitting bada' regarding Allah the Exalted, how is such a thing fitting for the Companions? We say: the answer has several aspects.

First: that doubt arose from a hypocrite, and Allah the Exalted mentioned it so that the Muslims would mention it as an answer to the question of that hypocrite.

Second: perhaps they believed that prayer toward the Ka'bah was superior, so they said, "Would that our brothers who died had attained that." So Allah the Exalted mentioned this speech as an answer to that.

Third: perhaps He, the Exalted, mentioned this speech so that it would serve as a rebuttal to that question, should it occur to their minds.

**The second view:** This is the view of Ibn Zayd: when Allah the Exalted knows that the benefit lies in your transfer from Jerusalem to the Ka'bah, then if He left you upon prayer toward Jerusalem, that would be a waste of your prayer, because in this case it would be devoid of benefits, and so it would be lost. Allah the Exalted does not do that.

**The third view:** When He, the Exalted, mentioned the hardship upon them in this change, He followed it by mentioning the reward they have with Him, and that He does not waste what they have done. This is the view of al-Hasan.

**The fourth view:** It is as if He, the Exalted, said: I granted you success in accepting this obligation so that your faith would not be lost, for if they had rejected this obligation they would have disbelieved, and if they had disbelieved their faith would have been lost. So He said: ﴿And Allah would never waste your faith﴾. Therefore He granted you success in accepting this obligation and helped you to it.

**Second issue:** They differed about whom the words ﴿And Allah would never waste your faith﴾ are addressed to, on two views.

**The first view:** They are addressed to the believers. Al-Qaffal mentioned four aspects on this view:

The first: Allah addressed with it the believers who were present at that time, and this is an answer to what they had asked before.

The second: They asked about one who died before the change of the qiblah, and Allah answered them with His words: ﴿And Allah would never waste your faith﴾. That is: if your past faith before the abrogation is not wasted by Allah, then likewise the faith of one who died before the abrogation.

The third: It is possible that the living had imagined that when that was abrogated, it became void, and that what they now did after the abrogation, praying toward the Ka'bah, was an expiation for what had passed. They were thus content, regarding their own affairs, with this kind of interpretation, so they asked about their brothers who died and did not do anything that would expiate what had passed. So it was said: ﴿And Allah would never waste your faith﴾, and the intended meaning is the people of your religion, just as He said to the Jews present in the time of Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], and ﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50].

The fourth: It is possible that the question concerned both the living and the dead together, for they were apprehensive that their prayers' reward would be nullified, and this apprehension applied to both groups. So it was said: "Your faith" refers to the living and the dead, since it is the custom of the Arabs, when they report about one present and one absent, to give precedence to address, saying: "You and so-and-so, the absent one, did such and such." And Allah knows best.

**The second view:** This is the view of Abu Muslim, that it is possible that this is addressed to the People of the Book, and the intended meaning of "faith" is their prayer and obedience before the mission (ba'thah), which was then abrogated. Abu Muslim chose this view only so that it would not entail the occurrence of abrogation in our law.

* * *

**Third issue:** The Mu'tazilah cited His words ﴿And Allah would never waste your faith﴾ as proof that faith (iman) is a name for performing acts of obedience, since He, the Exalted, intended by "faith" here the prayer. (The answer): We do not concede that the intended meaning of "faith" here is the prayer. Rather, the intended meaning is affirmation (tasdiq) and acknowledgment (iqrar). It is as if He, the Exalted, said: He does not waste your affirmation of the obligation of that prayer. Even if we concede that the intended meaning of "faith" here is the prayer, prayer is nonetheless the greatest part of faith and the most noble of its fruits and benefits, so it is permissible to apply the name of faith to prayer by way of metaphor (isti'arah) on this account.

**Fourth issue:** His words ﴿And Allah would never waste your faith﴾ mean: He does not waste the reward of your faith, because faith has come to an end and perished. Since it is such, its preservation or waste is impossible in itself; yet the entitlement to reward remains after its end, so its preservation and waste are valid. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I will not waste the work of any worker among you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 195].

* * *

As for His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is, to the people, Kind and Merciful﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The difference between ra'fah and rahmah is that ra'fah is an intensification of a specific mercy, namely the averting of harm and the removal of injury, like His saying: ﴿And let not pity for them overtake you in the religion of Allah﴾ [al-Nur: 2], meaning: do not show them pity so that you lift the lashing from them. As for rahmah, it is a comprehensive name that includes that meaning and also includes bounty and favor. Allah the Exalted has called rain "mercy," saying: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], because it is a bounty and favor from Allah. So Allah the Exalted mentioned ra'fah first, in the sense that He does not waste their deeds and lightens their trials for them; then He mentioned rahmah so that it would be more general and inclusive. His mercy is not restricted to that type alone; rather, He is Merciful in that He both averts the harms, which is ra'fah, and brings benefits together.

**Second issue:** They mentioned several aspects regarding the connection of these two names to what precedes them:

First: When He, the Exalted, informed that He does not waste their faith, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is, to the people, Kind and Merciful﴾. How can such waste be conceived of from the Kind and Merciful?

Second: He is Kind and Merciful, and therefore He transfers you from one law to another law, which is more beneficial and useful for you in religion and in worldly life.

Third: He said: ﴿And indeed, it was difficult except for those whom Allah guided﴾. It is as if He, the Exalted, said: Allah guided them only because He is Kind and Merciful.

**Third issue:** 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited (ra'ufun rahim) with hamz, without elongation (ishba'), in the pattern of ra'fun (raʾufun → ra'fun). The rest recited (ra'ufun), with the vowel emphasized, hamzated, and elongated, in the pattern of ra'uf. There are four dialects in it: ra'if as well, like ḥazir; and ra'fun in the pattern of fa'l.

* * *

**Fourth issue:** The Mu'tazilah cited this verse as proof that He, the Exalted, does not create disbelief or corruption. They said: Since He, the Exalted, has declared that He is Kind and Merciful to the people, and the disbelievers are among the people, it is necessary that He be Kind and Merciful to them. He would only be so if He did not create in them the disbelief that drags them to eternal punishment and everlasting torment, and did not charge them with what they cannot bear. For if He, the Exalted, were Kind and Merciful despite such harm, then in what manner could it be conceived that He would not be Kind and Merciful? And know that the discussion of this has preceded many times. And Allah knows best.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 144 (part 1 of 5):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven. So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. And indeed, those who were given the Scripture well know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what they do.﴾

Page 100

Know that His saying, ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾, has two opinions:

The first opinion, which is the well-known one held by most of the exegetes, is that this was in anticipation of the change of the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to the Ka'bah. Those who hold this opinion have mentioned several aspects:

One of them: he used to dislike facing Bayt al-Maqdis and loved to face the Ka'bah, but he did not speak of that, so he would turn his face toward the heaven for this meaning. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "'O Jibril, I wish that Allah Exalted would turn me away from the qiblah of the Jews to another, for I dislike it.' Jibril said to him: 'I am a servant like you, so ask your Lord for that.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept looking constantly toward the heaven, hoping for Jibril's coming with what he had asked, and Allah Exalted revealed this verse." Those who hold this have mentioned several matters regarding the cause of this trial.

The first: the Jews used to say, "He opposes us, yet he follows our qiblah; had it not been for us, he would not have known where to face." So at that point he disliked to face their qiblah.

The second: the Ka'bah was the qiblah of Ibrahim.

The third: he, peace be upon him, was able to make this a means of attracting the Arabs and their entry into Islam.

The fourth: he, peace be upon him, loved that this honor would belong to the mosque in his city and place of origin, not to another mosque. The judge (al-Qadi) objected to this aspect and said: it is not becoming of him, peace be upon him, to dislike a qiblah he was commanded to pray toward, and to love that his Lord change it away from it to a qiblah that he desires by his nature and inclines to according to his appetite, because he, peace be upon him, knew and taught that righteousness lies in opposing nature and inclination. Know that this interpretation is of little substance, because what is objectionable from the Messenger is that he turn away from what Allah Exalted commanded him and occupy himself with what his nature calls him to. As for his heart inclining to something and wishing in his heart that Allah would permit him to it, there is no objection to that, especially if he did not utter it, i.e., there is no improbability that the Messenger's nature inclines to something and he wishes in his heart that Allah would permit him to it, and this is not improbable in any way whatsoever.

The second aspect: he, peace be upon him, had asked Jibril, peace be upon him, to ask Allah Exalted for that, and Jibril informed him that Allah had permitted him in this supplication. This is because the prophets do not ask Allah Exalted for anything except with His permission, lest they ask for what holds no good, so it is not granted and that leads to belittling their status. When Allah Exalted permitted him to be answered, he knew that it would be granted to him, so he kept turning his face toward the heaven awaiting Jibril's coming with the revelation of the answer.

The third aspect: al-Hasan said: Jibril, peace be upon him, came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informing him that Allah Exalted would change the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to another qiblah, but did not specify to him to what place He would change it. No qiblah was more beloved to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ than the Ka'bah, so the Messenger of Allah kept turning his face toward the heaven awaiting revelation, because he, peace be upon him, knew that Allah Exalted would not leave him without a prayer. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and commanded him to pray toward the Ka'bah. Those who hold this aspect differed: some said that he, peace be upon him, was prohibited from facing Bayt al-Maqdis and the qiblah had not been specified for him, so he feared that the time of prayer would come while the qiblah had not become clear and his prayer would be delayed; therefore he kept turning his face. This is from al-Asamm. Others said: rather, he was promised this, and the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis remained such that prayer toward it was permissible, but because of the promise he was anticipating it, and because he hoped at the change from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah for many religious benefits, such as: the desire of the Arabs for Islam, distinction from the Jews, and distinguishing the believer from the hypocrite. For this reason he kept turning his face. This aspect is preferable, for otherwise the second qiblah would not have been abrogating the first, but rather would have been an initial legislation; and the exegetes unanimously agree that it abrogated the first. Also, it is not permissible that he be commanded to pray except with the explanation of the place of facing.

The fourth: the turning of his face toward the heaven is supplication.

The second opinion, which is the opinion of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani: they said: were it not for the reports that point to this opinion, the wording of the verse could bear another meaning, namely that it may be that he, peace be upon him, was turning his face only at the beginning of his arrival in Medina. It is narrated that when he prayed in Mecca he would place the Ka'bah between himself and Bayt al-Maqdis, and this was a prayer toward the Ka'bah. When he emigrated, he did not know where to face, so he awaited the command of Allah Exalted until the saying came down: ﴿So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾.

Issue two: they differed regarding his prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis. Some people said: he was in Mecca praying toward the Ka'bah, then when he came to Medina he was commanded to face Bayt al-Maqdis for seventeen months. Others said: rather, he was in Mecca praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis, but he would place the Ka'bah between himself and it. Others said: rather, he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis only, and in Medina at first for seventeen months; then Allah Exalted commanded him to face the Ka'bah because of the good in it.

Issue three: they differed regarding the Prophet's ﷺ facing Bayt al-Maqdis: was it an obligation with no alternative, or was the Prophet ﷺ free to face it and other than it? Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: he had the choice in that. Ibn 'Abbas said: facing it was a definite obligation without choice.

Know that whichever of the two views applies, it has become abrogated. Those who held the first opinion argued with the Qur'an and the report. As for the Qur'an, it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115], and that requires that he had the choice to face whatever direction he wished. As for the report, what Abu Bakr al-Razi related in his book Ahkam al-Qur'an: "A group of men came to the Messenger ﷺ from Medina to Mecca for the pledge before the Hijrah, and among them was al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, who directed his prayer toward the Ka'bah on his way, while the others refused and said: he, peace be upon him, faces Bayt al-Maqdis. When they came to Mecca they asked the Prophet ﷺ, and he said to him: you were upon a qiblah—meaning Bayt al-Maqdis—had you remained upon it, it would have sufficed you, and he did not command him to repeat the prayer." This indicates that they had been given the choice. Those who held the second opinion argued that He said: ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾, which indicates that he, peace be upon him, was not pleased with the first qiblah; so had he been free between it and the Ka'bah, he would not have faced it. Since he faced it while he was not pleased with it, we know that he was not free between it and the Ka'bah.

Issue four: the well-known view is that facing Bayt al-Maqdis became abrogated only by the command to face the Ka'bah. Among people there are those who said: facing Bayt al-Maqdis was abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115], and then that was abrogated by His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾. They argued for this with the Qur'an and a report. As for the Qur'an, He, Exalted, first mentioned: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾, then after it mentioned: ﴿The foolish among the people will say: what has turned them from their qiblah which they were upon?﴾, then after it mentioned: ﴿So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾. This order requires the correctness of the view we have stated, that facing Bayt al-Maqdis was abrogated by His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾. It follows that His saying: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ is later in revelation and rank than His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, so its placement before it in the order is contrary to the original arrangement; thus what we have said is established. As for the report, it is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the matter of the qiblah was the first thing abrogated in the Qur'an, and the command to face Bayt al-Maqdis is not mentioned in the Qur'an; what is mentioned in the Qur'an is: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾.

Page 101

Therefore it is necessary that His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ be the abrogating text for that, not for the command to face Bayt al-Maqdis.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: ﴿falanuwalliyannaka﴾ means: We will surely give you and enable you to face it. It derives from your saying "wallaytuhu kadha" (I made him in charge of such-and-such) when you make him a governor; or it means: We will surely make you face its direction rather than the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿tardaha﴾ (that you will be pleased with) has several aspects:

One of them: ﴿tardaha﴾ means you love it and incline toward it, because the Ka'bah was more beloved to him than others according to the inclination of nature. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this is not permissible, for it is absurd that Allah Exalted should say: "We will surely turn you to a qiblah toward which your nature inclines," because that would detract from His wisdom in what He imposes, and would detract from the state of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in what he wills during the state of obligation. This objection is weak, because the criticism would apply only if Allah Exalted said: "We have turned you to the qiblah toward which your nature inclined merely because your nature inclined to it." But if He said: "We have turned you to the qiblah toward which your nature inclined because wisdom and benefit coincided with the inclination of your nature," then what harm would follow from that! The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "And the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer," so his nature inclined to prayer, although the benefit was consistent with that.

The second: ﴿qiblatan tardaha﴾ means: you love it because of what it includes of religious benefits. The third: al-Asamm said: meaning, any direction Allah turned you toward, it is for you a pleasure that you may not be displeased with, as those among the Arabs who had embraced Islam did when they turned back on their heels; when the qiblah changed they apostatized. The fourth: ﴿tardaha﴾ means: you are pleased with its outcome, because by it you recognize who follows you into Islam, and who follows you for other than that, for worldly gain he obtains or wealth he acquires.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: the intended meaning of "face" here is the whole body of the human being, because what is obligatory upon a person is that he face the qiblah with his whole body, not with his face alone. The word "face" is mentioned and intended to mean the essence of the thing, because the face is the most noble of the limbs, and because by the face some people are distinguished from others; for this reason the whole self is sometimes expressed by the face.

The second issue: the lexicographers said: "shatr" is a homonymous term that applies to two meanings:

One of them: half. It is said: "shatartu al-shay'" meaning I made it into two halves, and it is said in a proverb: "ajlib jalban laka shatruhu," meaning its half.

The second meaning: "nahwahu" (toward it), "tilqa'ahu" (facing it), "wijhatahu" (its direction). Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, cited in his book "al-Risala" four verses as evidence for this, saying: Khufaf ibn Nudba said:
"Is there anyone to convey a message to Amr, though a message does not benefit the side of Amr?"
Sa'ida ibn Ju'ayya said:
"I say to Umm Zinbaa': Turn the chests of the camels toward the side of the Banu Tamim."
Laqit al-Iyadi said:
"Calamity has overshadowed you from the side of your poetry, a dread whose darkness covers you in pieces."
Another said:
Page 103
"Indeed, a disease that clings to her is the difficult one, so her side is a bewitched sight of the two eyes."
Al-Shafi'i said: he means, "her facing (tilqa'ha) is a bewitched sight of the two eyes." Having understood this, we say: there are two opinions regarding the verse.

The first, which is the view of the majority of the commentators from among the Companions, the Successors and later scholars, and the choice of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, in his book al-Risala, is that what is meant is: the direction of the Sacred Mosque, its facing and its side. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "tilqa'a al-Masjid al-Haram" (facing the Sacred Mosque).

The second opinion, which is the view of al-Jubba'i and the choice of al-Qadi, is that what is meant by "shatr" here is: the middle of the Mosque and its center, because "shatr" means "half," and the Ka'ba lies within the Mosque at its midpoint on all sides. Since the obligation is to face the Ka'ba, and the Ka'ba lies at the midpoint of the Mosque, it is fitting for Him, exalted is He, to say: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning the half from every direction, and it is as if it were an expression for the spot of the Ka'ba. Al-Qadi said: What indicates that the intended meaning is what we have mentioned are two points.

First: if a worshipper outside the Mosque stands in a position where he faces the Mosque but does not face the midpoint of the Mosque, which is the place of the Ka'ba, his prayer is not valid.

Second: if we interpret "shatr" as "side," there would be no additional benefit in mentioning "shatr," because if you say, "So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque," the desired benefit is already achieved. But if we interpret "shatr" as what we have mentioned, its mention has an additional benefit, for if it were said, "So turn your face to the Sacred Mosque," it would not be understood from it that one must face its midpoint, which is the place of the Ka'ba. But when it is said, ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾, this additional benefit is obtained, so it is better to take this word in this sense. If it is said: if we take "shatr" as "side," there remains an additional benefit to mentioning "shatr," namely that if He had said, "So turn your face to the Sacred Mosque," it would impose what cannot be borne, because whoever is at the farthest east or west cannot turn his face to the Mosque itself; but when He says ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾, that is, the side of the Mosque, both those present and those absent are included. We reply: this benefit is derived from His saying ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾, so there remains no additional benefit in His saying "toward the Sacred Mosque." This is the statement of this view, and it has a problem, for the meaning becomes: "So turn your face toward half of the Mosque," and this is far-fetched, because this obligation has no connection with a half, and there is a difference between a half and a place which is capable of being divided in halves. The speech would only be correct if it were taken in the second sense, but the wording does not indicate it. They differed concerning what is meant by the Sacred Mosque. It is related in the book "Sharh al-Sunna" from Ibn Abbas that he said: the House is the qibla for the people of the Mosque, the Mosque is the qibla for the people of the Haram, and the Haram is the qibla for the people of the east and west; and this is the view of Malik. Others said: the qibla is the Ka'ba, and the evidence for this is what was recorded in the two Sahihs from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', from Ibn Abbas, who said: Usama ibn Zayd informed me, saying: "When the Prophet ﷺ entered the House, he supplicated in all its corners and did not pray until he came out of it; when he came out he prayed two rak'as in front of the Ka'ba and said: 'This is the qibla.'" Al-Qaffal said: Many reports have come concerning the turning of the qibla to the Ka'ba, and in the report of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib: "Then it was turned to the Ka'ba, and he used to love to face the Ka'ba," and in the report of Ibn Umar concerning the prayer of the people of Quba': "A comer came to them and said: 'Indeed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has been turned to the Ka'ba,'" and in the narration of Thumama ibn 'Abdullah ibn Anas: "The caller of the Messenger of Allah came and called out: 'Indeed the qibla has been turned to the Ka'ba,'" and so are the generality of the narrations. Others said: rather, what is meant is the entire Sacred Mosque. They said: because speech must be carried out according to its apparent wording unless some impediment prevents it. Others said: what is meant by the Sacred Mosque is the entire Haram, and the evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1], and he, upon whom be blessings and peace, was taken on the Night Journey outside the Mosque, so this shows that the whole Haram is named the Sacred Mosque.

* * *

The third issue: the author of al-Tahdhib said: when a congregation prays in the Sacred Mosque, it is recommended that the imam stand behind the Maqam, and the people stand in a circle around the House. If some of them are closer to the House than the imam, it is permissible. If the row extends in the Mosque, the prayer of whoever moves out of alignment with the Ka'ba is not valid; but according to Abu Hanifa it is valid, because for him the direction is sufficient. This is the choice of Shaykh al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, in his book Ihya'. The argument of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: the Qur'an, the report, and analogy. As for the Qur'an, it is the apparent meaning of this verse, because we have shown that what is meant by "shatr al-Masjid al-Haram" is its side, and the side of a thing is that which is opposite it and in line with it. The proof is that one says: Zayd turned his face toward the side of 'Amr, and if he faced his face toward him, making it opposite to him, so that if each of the two faced east, yet the face of one was not opposite the face of the other, one would not say he turned his face toward the side of 'Amr. Thus it is established that the indication of the verse is that facing the very Ka'ba is obligatory.

As for the report, it is what we have related: that when he, upon whom be blessings and peace, came out of the Ka'ba, he prayed two rak'as in the direction of the Ka'ba and said, "This is the qibla," and this statement implies restriction, so it is established that there is no qibla except the very Ka'ba, and likewise all the reports which we have related that the qibla is the Ka'ba. As for analogy, it is that the Messenger's ﷺ emphasis on the glorification of the Ka'ba is a matter that reached the level of mass transmission, and prayer is among the greatest rites of the religion, and making the validity of prayer depend on facing the very Ka'ba brings about additional honor for the Ka'ba, so it must be legislated. Also, that the Ka'ba being the qibla is a known matter, while the other being the qibla is a doubtful matter, and it is preferable to observe caution in prayer, so it is obligatory to make the validity of prayer depend on facing the Ka'ba. Abu Hanifa argued with several matters.

The first: the apparent meaning of this verse, because He, exalted is He, obligated the responsible person to turn his face to its side. Whoever turns his face toward the side in which the Ka'ba lies has done what he was commanded, whether he is facing the Ka'ba or not, so he must be discharged of the obligation. As for the report, what Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, related: that he, upon whom be blessings and peace, said: "Between the east and the west is a qibla." The companions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: what is meant by this hadith is not that everything that is truly between an east and a west is a qibla, since the region of the North Pole is truly between them, and by agreement it is not a qibla; rather what is meant is that the thing which lies between a specific east and a specific west is a qibla. We interpret that as the thing lying between the winter sunrise and the summer sunset, for that is a qibla, because the winter sunrise is southern, distant from the equator by the amount of the inclination, and the summer sunset is northern, distant from the equator by the amount of the inclination, and what lies between them is the line of Makkah's direction. They said: this hadith is more fitting to support our view than to support yours. As for the action of the Companions, it is from two aspects:

First: the people of the Quba' mosque were praying the dawn prayer in Medina facing Bayt al-Maqdis, turning their backs to the Ka'ba, because Medina lies between them.
