It was said to them: "Beware, the qibla has been turned to the Ka'ba," and they turned around in the middle of the prayer without seeking any evidence, and the Prophet ﷺ did not object to them, and their mosque was called "the mosque of the two qiblas." The alignment of the exact point from Medina to Makkah is not known except through geometric proofs which require lengthy consideration, so how did they grasp it instantly in the middle of the prayer and in the darkness of the night?

Second: from the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ people built mosques in all the lands of Islam, and they never brought an engineer when arranging the mihrab, and the exact alignment of a point is not attained except through the precise examination of geometry.

As for analogy, it is from several aspects:

The first: If facing the very point of the Ka'bah were obligatory, either by certain knowledge or by probable opinion, then no one's prayer would ever be valid. This is because, if the alignment with the Ka'bah is about twenty-odd cubits, it is known that the people of the East and the West cannot possibly stand within the alignment of that amount. Rather, what is known is that those among them who fall within the alignment of that small amount are few in comparison to the many. It is also known that the legal rulings of the Shari'ah are based on what is most common, and the rare is attached to it. Therefore, the prayer of none of them would be valid, especially since the one who falls in alignment with the Ka'bah cannot know that he falls in its alignment. Since the community has agreed on the validity of everyone's prayer, we know that alignment is not regarded.

If it is said: Although the circle is great, all the points drawn on it are aligned with the center of the circle. Thus the rows spread across the world are, as it were, a circle around the Ka'bah, and the Ka'bah is, as it were, the point of that circle. However, when a circle is small, its curvature is small throughout, and when it is large and vast, the curvature does not appear in each of its two halves; rather, we see each piece of it resembling a straight line. Therefore the congregation is validly formed in a long row in the East and the West, whose length exceeds many times the length of the House, and all of them are called as facing the very point of the Ka'bah.

We reply: Grant that the matter is as you have described. Yet a segment of a great circle, although it resembles a straight line to the senses, must nonetheless be curved in itself. For if it were straight in itself, and likewise with all the segments of that circle, then the circle would be composed of straight lines joined to one another, and it would follow that the circle is either a polygon or a straight line, and all of this is impossible. So we know that every segment of the great circle is curved in itself. Thus the rows connected at the ends of the world, each one of them faces the very point of the Ka'bah only if those rows do not lie on a straight line. Rather, when that slight curvature occurs in them, which the senses are absolutely unable to perceive, it cannot be the locus of obligation. If that is the case, then each of these rows is ignorant of whether he is facing the very point of the Ka'bah or not. So if facing the very point of the Ka'bah were a condition, the fulfilment of this condition would be unknown to him. Doubt about the fulfilment of a condition entails doubt about the fulfilment of the conditioned act, so each person in these rows would remain in doubt about the validity of his prayer, and that would mean he never gets out of his obligation at all. Since the community has agreed that this is not the case, we know that facing the very point is not a condition, either by knowledge or by opinion. This is a clear argument.

The second: If facing the very point of the Ka'bah were obligatory, and there is no way to it except by geometric indications (al-dalalah al-handasiyyah), and whatever the obligation cannot be fulfilled without is itself obligatory, then learning geometric indications would be obligatory upon everyone. Since it is not so, we know that facing the very point of the Ka'bah is not obligatory.

If it is said: According to us, facing the direction of the Ka'bah (the general direction) is obligatory by opinion, not by certainty, and what requires geometric indications is facing by certainty, not by opinion. We reply: If facing the very point of the Ka'bah were obligatory, then one who is able to attain certainty would not be permitted to be content with opinion. A man is able to attain that certainty through learning the geometric indications, so learning those indications would be obligatory upon him. Since that is not obligatory, we know that facing the very point of the Ka'bah is obligatory.

[p. 106]

The third: If facing the very point were obligatory, either by knowledge or by opinion, and it is known that there is no way to that opinion except through some kind of signs (amarat), and whatever the obligation cannot be fulfilled without is itself obligatory, then learning those signs would be an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) upon every one of the responsible persons. Since it is not so, we know that facing the very point is not obligatory.

* * *

Question Four: On the indications of the qiblah. Know that the indications are either earthly, such as using mountains, settlements and rivers; or aerial, such as using winds; or celestial, such as the stars.

As for the earthly and aerial indications, they are not governed by a universal rule. Many a road has a high mountain of which one cannot know whether it is on the right or left of the one facing it, or in front of him or behind him. Likewise the winds may indicate in some lands, and we cannot survey all of that, since each land has a different ruling in this.

As for the celestial indications, some of them are approximate and some are precise. As for the approximate ones, they have said: These indications are either diurnal or nocturnal. As for the diurnal, it is the sun. Before leaving the town, one must observe whether at midday the sun is between the eyebrows, or on the right eye, or on the left, or inclines toward the temple more than that. For in the northern lands the sun does not go beyond these positions. Likewise one observes the position of the sun at the time of 'Asr. As for the time of Maghrib, it is known by the place of sunset, namely that one knows the sun sets to the right of the one facing, or that it is inclined toward his face or his back. Likewise the time of 'Isha' is known by the place of the twilight (shafaq), and the time of Subh is known by the rising of the sun. Thus the sun indicates the qiblah in the five prayers. However, the ruling on this differs between winter and summer, for the risings and settings are many. Likewise the ruling in this matter differs according to the difference of lands.

As for the nocturnal, one uses as an indication the star called the Pole Star (al-Jady), for it is a star that seems fixed, whose movement is not apparent from its place. It is either at the back of the one facing, or at his right shoulder from behind, or his left shoulder, in the northern lands relative to Makkah; and in the southern lands relative to it, such as Yemen and beyond, it lies directly opposite the one facing. So let him know this, and whatever he has learned in his own land, let him rely on it along the whole road. However, if the journey is long, then as the distance grows, the position of the sun, the position of the region, and the position of the risings and settings differ, until he reaches a town during his journey. Then he should ask the people of insight or observe these stars while facing the mihrab of the town's congregational mosque until it becomes clear to him. Whenever he has learned these indications, he may rely upon them.

As for the certain method, which is the modes mentioned in the books of astronomy (al-hay'ah), they have said: The direction of the qiblah (samt al-qiblah) is the point of intersection between the circle of the horizon and a great circle passing through the zenith of our heads and the zenith of the people of Makkah. The deviation of the qiblah is an arc of the circle of the horizon between the direction of the qiblah and the meridian circle of our land; and the entire deviation is what lies between the direction of the qiblah and the western point of the equinox. They have said: Knowing the direction of the qiblah requires knowing the longitude and latitude of Makkah. If the longitude of the town equals the longitude of Makkah, but its latitude differs from that of Makkah, the direction of its qiblah lies on the meridian line; if the town is northern, then the qiblah is to the south, and if it is southern, then to the north. As for when the latitude of the town equals the latitude of Makkah and its longitude differs from it, one may suppose that the direction of the qiblah of that town is on the line of the equinox, and that is a mistaken supposition. It is also possible, in towns whose longitudes and latitudes differ from the longitude and latitude of Makkah, that the direction of their qiblah is the rising and setting of the equinox. If that is so, then it is necessary to derive the amount of deviation. For this there are methods, the easiest of which is to know the degree of the zodiac that is directly above the heads of the people of Makkah, from the ecliptic, which is (zayh) of Gemini and (kaj h) of Cancer. One places that degree on the line of the middle of the sky on the astrolabe made for the latitude of the town, and marks a sign on what is visible. Then one turns the spider (al-'ankabut) toward the west if the town is east of Makkah, as in the lands of Khurasan and Iraq, by the amount between the two longitudes in degrees of the equator. Then one observes where that degree falls among the altitude arcs, and whatever altitude that is, it is the altitude at which that degree is directly over the heads of the people of Makkah. Then one watches for the sun to come directly over that degree. When the sun's altitude reaches that altitude, the sun has come directly over the heads of the people of Makkah. Then one sets up a gnomon (miqyas) and draws on the shadow of the gnomon a line from the center of the pillar to the tip of the shadow. That line is the line of the shadow, and upon it one builds the mihrab. This is the discussion on the indications of the qiblah.

Question Five: Is knowing the indications of the qiblah an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) or a collective obligation (fard kifayah)? On this there are two views, the more correct of which is that it is an individual obligation, because every responsible person is commanded to face the qiblah, and he cannot face it except by means of knowing the indications of the qiblah. Whatever the obligation cannot be fulfilled without is itself obligatory.

* * *

Question Six: Know that the words of the Most High: ﴿Wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:144 and 2:150] are general as to persons and circumstances. However, we have agreed that facing the qiblah outside the prayer is not obligatory; rather, it is an act of obedience, according to his saying, peace be upon him: "The best of gatherings is that in which the qiblah is faced." So what remains is that the obligation of facing the qiblah is specific to the prayer. Then we say: A person is either watching the qiblah directly or absent from it. As for the one who sees it directly, they have agreed that facing it is obligatory for him. As for the absent one, he is either able to attain certainty or not able to attain it, but able to attain opinion, or unable to attain either certainty or opinion. These are three categories:

The first category: One who is able to attain knowledge. On this there are two discussions.

First discussion: You already know that the one absent from the qiblah has no way to attain certainty about the direction of the qiblah except through geometric indications, and whatever there is no way to fulfil the obligation without is itself obligatory. From this it follows that learning the geometric indications is an individual obligation upon everyone. However, the jurists have said that learning them is not obligatory, and some have even said that learning them is disliked or forbidden. I do not know what excuse they have for this.

Second discussion: If the one praying is in the land of Makkah, with a barrier between him and the Ka'bah, and it is unclear to him, may he make ijtihad (exert his judgment)? The author of al-Tahdhib said: If the barrier is original, such as mountains, then he may make ijtihad. If it is not original, such as buildings, then there are two views.

One of them: He may make ijtihad, because there is a barrier between him and it that prevents direct sight, as in the case of an original barrier.

The second: He may not make ijtihad, because his duty is to return to certainty, and he is able to attain certainty, so he must not be content with opinion in it. This view is the one most fitting to the context of the verse, because when it indicated the obligation of turning toward the Ka'bah, and the responsible person is able to attain knowledge, it is not permitted for him to be content with opinion, so it is obligatory upon him to seek certainty.

The second category: One who is able to attain opinion but not certainty. Know that there are several ways to attain this opinion:

The first way: ijtihad. The apparent meaning of the words of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, indicates that ijtihad takes precedence over relying on the statement of another, and this is the truth. What indicates this are several considerations:

One of them: the saying of the Most High: ﴿So take warning, O you with vision﴾ [al-Hashr 59:2]

[p. 108]

Third argument: the Prophet's saying (peace be upon him): "If I order you to do something, do of it what you are able." Here he is commanded to face the qiblah, and he is able to exert effort in seeking it, so it is obligatory for him to do so.

It may be objected: Does not the author of al-Tahdhib (al-Tahdhib, a work of Shafi'i jurisprudence) mention that if one is in a large town in which mihrabs are set up facing a single direction, or if one finds a mihrab or a sign of the qiblah on a road that is a thoroughfare for the Muslims, it is obligatory for him to turn toward it and it is not permissible for him to exert ijtihad regarding the direction; he said: because these signs are like certainty. But regarding deviation to the right or left, it is permissible for him to perform ijtihad alongside these signs. 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak used to say after returning from Hajj: "Veer to the right, O people of Marw." Likewise, if a Muslim informs him, saying: "I have seen the majority of Muslims or a group of Muslims agreeing on this direction," then he must accept it, and this is not taqlid (imitation); rather it is accepting the report from its people, as in the case of the time, namely if a trustworthy person informs him: "I have seen the dawn has risen" or "the sun has passed its zenith," then his statement must be accepted. This is the whole wording of the author of al-Tahdhib. Know that this discourse is problematic in several respects:

First: There is no meaning of taqlid except accepting the statement of another without proof or doubt. So if we accept the statement or action of another in determining the qiblah without proof or doubt, this is taqlid, and we have already mentioned the evidence that one who is able to perform ijtihad must be commanded to perform ijtihad.

Second: He permitted deviation to the right and left on the basis of ijtihad. We say: he is able to obtain a probable opinion on the basis of the ijtihad that he undertakes himself, so deviation should be permissible for him as in the case of right and left.

Third: Either he is prohibited from ijtihad, or from acting according to the requirement of ijtihad. The first is invalid, because when Mu'adh said, "I exert ijtihad with my own opinion," the Messenger (peace be upon him) praised him for that, which shows that ijtihad is not prohibited for him. The second is also invalid, because when he knows or thinks that the qiblah is not in the direction in which the mihrabs are, if it were obligatory upon him to turn toward that mihrab, that would be giving preference to taqlid over reasoning, and that is an error.

Fourth: The school of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) holds that it is not permissible for a mujtahid to imitate another mujtahid. So how is it permissible for one who is able to determine the direction of the qiblah by indicators to imitate the mihrabs of the lands? Those who argue for preferring the mihrabs of the major cities over the lands have offered several arguments:

The first: they are like mass-transmission (tawatur) together with ijtihad, so it is obligatory to prefer them over it.

The second: when a man sees that the muezzin has finished the adhan and the iqamah and the imam has already advanced, he does not need to ascertain the time; similarly here.

The third: the people of the town are content with it, and it is apparent that if it were an error they would have noticed it, and if they had noticed it they would not have been content with it. This is what can be said on both sides.

The second way: returning to the statement of another, such as when a trustworthy person informs him about the qiblah being in this direction; this yields a probable opinion that the qiblah is there. They agreed that two conditions must be met: Islam and sanity; so the statement of a disbeliever or a madman, and their knowledge, carry no weight in this matter. They differed concerning three conditions.

The first: puberty. Al-Khaydari transmitted an explicit text from al-Shafi'i that the statement of a child is not accepted, while Abu Zayd also transmitted from al-Shafi'i that it is accepted.

The second: uprightness ('adalah). They said: the report of a wicked person is not accepted, because it is like testimony; and it was said: it is accepted.

The third: number. Some of them required it as in testimony, especially those who required number in transmission as well, and some did not require number. From what we have said, several rulings follow:

The first: whoever's statement, if acted upon, yields a stronger probable opinion, his statement takes precedence over the statement of one who yields a weaker opinion. For example, imitating one who is certain takes precedence over imitating one who is merely probably right through ijtihad, and imitating a mujtahid who is probably right is better than imitating one who imitated another, and so on.

The second: if he knows that ijtihad cannot be completed except after the time has passed, then it is better for him to exert ijtihad so that the prayer becomes a qada' (make-up prayer), or to imitate another so that the prayer remains an ada' (prayer in its time). On this there is hesitation. The third: one who does not know the indicators of the qiblah may return to the statement of another at the time of prayer; indeed, it is obligatory.

The third way: if he witnesses in the abode of Islam a mihrab set up, it is permissible for him to turn toward it according to the detail mentioned earlier. But if he sees the qiblah set up on a road where few people pass, or on a road where Muslims and polytheists pass and he does not know who set it up, or he sees a mihrab in a village and does not know whether the Muslims or the polytheists built it, or it is a small village of Muslims where it is not predominantly probable that its people are acquainted with the indicators of the qiblah, then ijtihad is obligatory upon him.

The fourth way: that which is composed of ijtihad and the statement of another, namely that a person informs him of the positions of the stars, and he himself knows how to use them to determine the qiblah; here it is obligatory for him to reason from what he hears if he is unable to see them himself.

The third category: one who is unable to attain knowledge or probable opinion, namely one who is in darkness in which all indicators are entirely hidden from him, or a blind man who finds no one to inform him, or whose indicators conflict before him and he is unable to prefer one over another. Regarding this there are several discussions:

First discussion: it is impossible that this person be commanded to perform ijtihad, because ijtihad without any indication or sign is the imposition of what cannot be borne, and that is negated. So there remains only one of three matters: either it is said that the obligation of prayer is conditional upon facing the qiblah, and the impossibility of the condition entails the falling of the obligation of the conditioned act, so here the prayer is not obligatory upon him; or it is said that the condition of facing the qiblah has fallen from the obligated person for an excuse lesser than this, namely the situation of fighting in battle, so it falls here as well, and he must perform the prayer toward whatever direction he wishes, and the condition of facing the qiblah falls from him; or it is said that he performs that prayer toward all directions in order to discharge the obligation with certainty. These are the possible positions. As for the falling of the prayer from him, that is invalid by consensus. Also, we see in the Shari'ah in general that prayer is valid without facing the qiblah, as in the case of fighting and in voluntary prayer. As for requiring the prayer toward all directions, that too is invalid, since there is evidence that the obligation upon him is one prayer. Someone may say: Is it not the case that whoever forgets one prayer among the prayers of a day and night and does not know which it is, is obligated to make up all those prayers in order to discharge the obligation with certainty? Why then should it not be the same here? They said: Since the two divisions have been refuted, the third is determined, namely the option among all directions.

Second discussion: if his heart inclines to the view that this direction is more likely to be the qiblah than the other directions, without that preference being based on reasoning, but arising merely from whim and the inclination of the heart toward it, is this considered ijtihad, and is the obligated person required to rely upon it or not? The better view is that this is taken into account, because of his saying (peace be upon him): "The believer looks with the light of Allah." And because when all other ways of preference are closed, it is sufficient to rely upon this degree.

Third discussion: if he prays this prayer, the apparent ruling is that repetition is not obligatory, because he has fulfilled the duty of the time and it was valid for him, so repetition should not be obligatory for him. The apparent position of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) is that repetition is obligatory whether his correctness or his error becomes evident.

* * *

Seventh issue: Prayer inside the Ka'bah is permitted according to the majority of scholars, and one may face any side he wishes. Malik said: it is disliked to perform the obligatory prayer inside the Ka'bah, because one who is inside the Ka'bah is not facing the whole Ka'bah, but facing some of its parts and turning his back to some of its parts; and if that is so, he is not facing the whole Ka'bah, so his prayer should not be valid, because Allah Most High commanded facing the House. He said: As for voluntary prayer, it is permissible, because facing the qiblah is not obligatory in it. The argument of the majority is what al-Shaykhan recorded in the Two Sahihs, and al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) also narrated it from Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that the Prophet (peace be upon him) entered the Ka'bah with Usamah ibn Zayd, 'Uthman ibn Abi Talhah, and Bilal, and he closed it upon himself and remained inside. Abd Allah ibn Umar said: I asked Bilal when he came out: "What did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ do?" He said: "He made one pillar on his left, two pillars on his right, and three pillars behind him, and the House at that time was on six pillars; then he prayed." Know that the use of this report as evidence is weak in several respects:

First: a single-transmitted report (khabar al-wahid) does not oppose the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

Second: perhaps that prayer was voluntary, and that is permissible according to Malik.

Third: Malik himself opposed this report, and the opposition of a narrator, although it does not necessarily discredit the report, does yield a kind of lower standing relative to a single-transmitted report free of this criticism, so how much more so relative to the Qur'an.

Fourth: al-Shaykhan recorded in the Two Sahihs, from Ibn Juraij, from 'Ata': I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: "When the Prophet ﷺ entered the House, he supplicated in all its corners and did not pray until he came out of it. When he came out, he prayed two rak'ahs facing the Ka'bah and said: 'This is the qiblah.'" The contradiction arises in two respects:

The first: negation and affirmation contradict each other.

The second: his saying ﷺ, "This is the qiblah," indicates that it is necessary to face that place, whereas whoever permits prayer inside the House does not require facing that place, but permits turning one's back to it.

As for the answer to Malik's argument, we say: his saying, "Wherever you are" (Qur'an 2:144: "wa haythu ma kuntum"), either is a word of general scope or is not. If it is a word of general scope, then it encompasses the person who is inside the House, as if Allah Most High commanded the one who is in the House to face it, so the one who does so is discharged of the obligation. If it is not a word of general scope, then the verse does not address this issue at all, and it does not indicate its ruling either by negation or by affirmation. Then, the reliance in the matter is that a single person cannot face the entire House; he is only able to face a part of its parts, and the one who is inside the House faces a part of its parts, so he has been doing what he was commanded, and therefore he must be discharged of the obligation.

* * *

[p. 111]

**Issue eight:** Know that the Ka'bah refers to particular bodies: the roof, the walls, and the structure. There is no doubt that these bodies exist in particular spaces. The *qiblah* (the direction of prayer) must then be one of three things: only those spaces, or only those bodies, or those bodies on condition that they are situated in those spaces.

It is not valid to say that it is only those bodies, because we all agree that if the soil of the Ka'bah and the stones and wood in its structure were moved to another place and a building was constructed from them, and someone faced it in prayer, that would not be permitted. Nor is it valid to say that it is those bodies on condition that they are in those spaces, because if the Ka'bah were demolished, God forbid, and those stones and wood were removed from those spaces, leaving the open area empty, then the people of the East and the West would have valid prayers if they faced that place, and they would be facing the *qiblah*. What remains is to say that the *qiblah* is that empty space in which those bodies were situated. This meaning, as established by the rational proof we mentioned, also agrees with the verse, because the Sacred Mosque is the name of that composite building of roof and walls, while the measure and direction of the Sacred Mosque are the spaces in which those bodies are situated. So when God Most High commands facing the direction of the Sacred Mosque, the *qiblah* is that measure of empty space.

Having established this, we say: Our companions (the Shafi'is) said: If the Ka'bah were demolished, God forbid, then whoever stands in its open area does not have a valid prayer, because he is not considered to be facing the *qiblah*. Ibn Surayj mentioned that it is valid, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa. This is my preferred view. The evidence for it is what we have shown: that the *qiblah* is that specific measure of empty space, and whoever stands in the open area is facing a part of that empty space, and so he is facing the *qiblah*. Therefore his prayer must be valid.

They also said: Whoever stands on the roof of the Ka'bah without having a wall opposite him does not have a valid prayer, except according to the view of Ibn Surayj, which is my preferred view, because he is facing that empty space and open area which is the *qiblah*, so his prayer must be valid.

* * *

**Issue nine:** Since the verse indicates the obligation of facing the *qiblah*, and reason establishes that there is no way to face the directions except through *ijtihad* (independent reasoned effort), and reason also establishes that what the obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory, it follows that *ijtihad* is definitively obligatory. *Ijtihad* must necessarily be based on conjecture (*zann*), so the verse indicates the obligation to act on conjecture. Thus it is established that the obligation to act on conjecture applies in general. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) used this to argue that analogy (*qiyas*) is a valid proof in the Sharia. This argument is weak, because it establishes analogy by means of analogy, and that is not a valid way. And God knows best.

**Issue ten:** Apparently, it is not obligatory to intend facing the *qiblah*, because the verse indicates the obligation of facing it, and the one who does so has done what the verse indicates. Therefore no further intention should be obligatory for him, just as with covering the private parts and the purity of the place and clothing.

**Issue eleven:** Facing the *qiblah* is dropped when there is a valid excuse, such as during sword fighting. Similar to this is fear for one's life from an enemy, a wild animal, or an attacking camel, or an error in the *qiblah* due to turning right or left, or during voluntary (*nafl*) prayers. This implies that whoever is unable to obtain knowledge or conjecture about the *qiblah* and prays, the obligation to make up the prayer is dropped from him. Likewise for the *mujtahid* (one who exercises *ijtihad*) when the error becomes clear to him.

**Issue twelve:** If someone faces one direction and then his *ijtihad* changes while he is praying, he must turn, shift his direction, and continue his prayer, because a subsequent *ijtihad* does not invalidate an earlier one. Likewise for one who trusted an informant and then another came, whose soul is more at ease with him, and told him the opposite. This is what relates to the issues derived from this verse concerning the ruling on facing the *qiblah*. And God knows best.

* * *

God Most High says: ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾. This includes two issues.

**First issue:** This is not a repetition, and its explanation is from two aspects. The first: God's statement ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ is addressed to the Messenger (peace be upon him) and not to the community, while His statement ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ is addressed to everyone. The second: the first address was intended specifically for those who were in Medina, and had the address been limited to them, one might have thought that this *qiblah* was only for the people of Medina. So God Most High made clear that wherever they are on earth, they must face this *qiblah*.

**Second issue:** His statement ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ means: "And wherever you are." The position of ﴿you are﴾ in terms of *i'rab* (grammatical analysis) is a jussive after the conditional particle, as if it were said: "Wherever you may be," and the *fa'* (the particle introducing the response) is the answer to the condition.

* * *

As for God Most High's statement: ﴿And indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾, this includes two issues.

**First issue:** What is meant by ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾ is specifically the Jews. The Scripture refers to the Torah, according to al-Suddi. It was also said that what is meant is the rabbis of the Jews and the scholars of the Christians, and this is the correct view because of the generality of the wording. The earlier Scriptures are the Torah and the Gospel. There must have been a small number of them, because a large group could not conspire to conceal the truth.

**Second issue:** The pronoun in ﴿that it is the truth﴾ refers back to something previously mentioned. The Messenger was mentioned earlier, as was the *qiblah*. So it is possible that what is meant is that the people know that the Messenger, with his law and his prophethood, is true, and this would include the matter of the *qiblah* and other things. It is also possible that it refers to this specific obligation regarding the *qiblah*, and that they know it is the truth. This last possibility is closer to the meaning, because it fits the context better, since the purpose of the verse is that specifically and not anything else. Then they differed about how they knew this, and they mentioned several views:

First: Some scholars among the Jews had recognized in the books of their prophets the report about the Messenger and the report about the *qiblah*, and that he would pray toward both *qiblahs*.

Second: They knew that the Ka'bah is the Ancient House which God Most High made the *qiblah* for Abraham and Ishmael (peace be upon them both).

Third: They knew the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) from the miracles that appeared through him, and once they knew his prophethood, they inevitably knew that everything he brought was true, so this change of *qiblah* was true.

* * *

As for His statement: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾, this includes two issues.

**First issue:** Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿ta'malūn﴾ (you do) with a *ta'* (second person), addressing the Muslims. The rest read it with a *ya'* (third person), referring it to the Jews.

**Second issue:** If we take it as addressing the Muslims, it is a promise and good news for them, meaning: "Your striving and effort in accepting the religion are not hidden from me, so I will not diminish your reward." If we take it as speech addressed to the Jews, it is a warning and threat to them. It is also possible that it means He is not unaware of recompensing and requiting them, even if He does not hasten it for them, as in His statement: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only delays them for a Day when eyes will stare in horror﴾ [Ibrahim: 42].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 145 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah, nor are you one who follows their qiblah, nor are some of them followers of the qiblah of others. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained in the first verse that those who were given the Book know that this qiblah is the truth, He then explained that their attribute does not change in persisting in obstinacy. In the verse there are several issues:

Page 113

The first issue: they differed concerning His saying: ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book﴾. Al-Asamm said: What is meant is their scholars, whom God, may He be exalted, described in the preceding verse with His saying: ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾. He argued for this with several points:

The first: His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾. He described them as following desire, and whoever believes falsehood to be truth is not one who follows the desires of the self; rather, he thinks himself to be following guidance. As for those who know in their hearts and then deny with their tongues, they are the ones who follow desire.

The second: what precedes this verse, namely His saying: ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book know that it is the truth﴾, does not encompass their common folk but is specific to the scholars. What follows it, namely His saying: ﴿Those whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their own sons﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146], is also specific to the scholars, since if it were general to all, concealment would be impossible, because a great multitude cannot conceal together. Since what precedes and what follows it are specific, so too is this intervening verse.

The third: that God, may He be exalted, informed about them that they persist in their statement and continue in their falsehood, and that they do not return from that doctrine because of any proofs or signs. This is the condition of the obstinate and contentious, not the condition of the obstinate who is perplexed.

The fourth: that if we were to take it as general, the verse would become false, because many of the People of the Book believed in Muhammad ﷺ and followed his qiblah.

Others said: Rather, what is meant is all the People of the Book, Jews and Christians. They argued for this by saying that His saying: ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ is a general form, so it encompasses all. Then they answered the first argument by saying that the one holding the doubt is in reality a person of desire, because he did not complete the reflection and inference; for if he had completed reflection and inference he would have reached the truth. Since he did not reach it, we know that he abandoned complete reflection merely out of desire. They answered the second argument by saying that it is not impossible that in the first verse some of them are meant, and in the second verse all of them. They answered the third argument by saying that since the scholars were persisting in doubts, and the common folk were persisting in following those scholars, the persistence was present in all. They answered the fourth argument by saying that God, may He be exalted, informed about them that they, in their totality, do not believe, and our saying "all the Jews do not believe" is different from our saying "none of them believes."

The second issue: Al-Ka'bi argued by this verse for the permissibility that there might not be, within what is within God's power, any grace (lutf) for some of them. He said: for if there were within what is within God's power for these people a grace, then among the signs there would be something which, if He brought it to them, they would believe; and so this report would not be valid as a categorical statement.

The third issue: Abu Muslim argued by this verse that God's knowledge of His servants and what they do is not a proof for them regarding what they commit, for they are able to do the good that they were commanded and to leave its opposite that they were forbidden. Our companions argued by it for the view of imposing what cannot be borne (taklif ma la yutaq), namely that He, may He be exalted, informed about them that they do not follow His qiblah; so if they were to follow His qiblah, it would entail the reversal of God's true report into falsehood and His knowledge into ignorance, and this is impossible, and what entails the impossible is impossible; so that would be impossible, and they were commanded with it, so they were commanded with the impossible. The complete discussion of this is mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6].

The fourth issue: God, may He be exalted, judged regarding them that they do not return from their falsehoods because of demonstration, and that is because their turning away from accepting this religion is not due to a doubt which the bringing of proof would remove; rather it is pure arrogance, obstinacy and envy, and that does not disappear by the bringing of proofs.

The fifth issue: They differed concerning His saying: ﴿they would not follow your qiblah﴾. Al-Hasan and al-Jubba'i said: He meant all of them, as if He said: they do not unite upon following your qiblah, in the manner of His saying: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 35]. Al-Asamm and others said: Rather, what is meant is that none of them believes.

Page 114

Al-Qadi said: If by the People of the Book is meant all of them, both scholars and common folk, then the interpretation of al-Hasan is necessary. If by it is meant the scholars, we look: if among the scholars addressed by this verse there are some who have believed, then that interpretation is also necessary; but if there are none among them who have believed, then it is valid to apply it to its apparent meaning, with the negation returning to each one of them, because that is more fitting to the apparent sense, since there is no difference between His saying: ﴿they would not follow your qiblah﴾ and His saying: "not one of them would follow your qiblah."

The sixth issue: (la'in) is with the meaning of (law) ("if"), and it is answered with the answer of (law); and the scholars differed concerning this. It was said: since the two have come close in meaning, each of them is used in place of the other and is answered with its answer. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We sent a wind﴾ [al-Rum: 51], then He said: (they would remain) in answer to (law); and He said: ﴿And if they had believed and feared God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 103], then He said: ﴿a reward would surely be﴾ in answer to (la'in). That is because the original of (law) is for the past, and (la'in) is for the future; this is the view of al-Akhfash. Sibawayh said: each of them is in its own place, and the truth in the answer is that this interchange is due to the indication of the lam of oath, so the answer came like the answer of an oath.

The seventh issue: The word "ayah" (sign): its measure is fa'lah, and its original is ayyah; they found the doubling heavy in "ayah," so they replaced the first yā' with an alif because what precedes it is open. "Ayah" means proof and sign; "ayat al-rajul" means his person; and "kharaja al-qawm bi-ayatihim" means they went out in their entirety. The verse of the Qur'an was named thus because it is a group of letters. It was said: because it is a sign of the cessation of the speech that follows it. It was said: because it indicates its separation from created beings, and that it is nothing but the speech of God, may He be exalted.

The eighth issue: It is related that the Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran said to the Messenger ﷺ: "Bring us a sign as the prophets before you brought," so God, may He be exalted, revealed this verse. The more likely view is that this verse was not revealed in an independent incident; rather it is part of the rulings concerning the change of the qiblah.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿nor are you one who follows their qiblah﴾, there are several views:

The first: that it is a rebuttal of the permissibility of abrogation, and a clarification that this qiblah will not become abrogated.

The second: to cut off the hopes of the People of the Book, for they said: "If he remained upon our qiblah, we would hope that he is the one we are awaiting," and they hoped for his return to their qiblah.

The third: it is a contrast, meaning: they will not abandon their falsehood, and you will not abandon your truth.

The fourth: He meant that it is not obligatory upon you to reform them by following their qiblah, because that would be disobedience.

The fifth: and you are not one who follows the qiblah of all the People of the Book, Jews and Christians; for the qiblah of the Jews differs from the qiblah of the Christians: the Jews have Bayt al-Maqdis, while the Christians have the east. So hold to your qiblah and leave off their sayings.

As for His saying: ﴿nor are some of them followers of the qiblah of others﴾, al-Qaffal said: this can be taken as referring to the present and to the future. As for the present, it is on several grounds:

The first: that they are not gathered upon a single qiblah, so that it would be possible to satisfy them by following it.

The second: that the Jews and the Christians, despite their agreement in denying you, differ in qiblah; so how would they call you to abandon your qiblah while they disagree among themselves?

The third: that this is a refutation of their saying that it is not permissible to oppose the People of the Book; for if it is permissible that their two qiblahs differ for the sake of a benefit, it is permissible that the benefit lies in a third.

As for taking the verse as referring to the future, there is a difficulty, namely that His saying: ﴿nor are some of them followers of the qiblah of others﴾ negates that any one of them has followed the qiblah of another, but that has in fact occurred, which leads to contradiction. Its answer is that if we take the People of the Book as their scholars who were in that era, then it has not been established for us that any one of them follows the qiblah of another, so there is no contradiction; and if we take it as all of them, we say it is general and has been subject to specification.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: the maqsur hawa (desire, with a short vowel) is that to which the nature inclines, and the mamdud hawa' (air) is well known.

The second issue: they differed concerning who is addressed by this address. Some said: the Messenger. Others said: the Messenger and others. And others said: rather, other than him; for God knew that the Messenger would not do that, so it is not permissible that He single him out with this address. This third view is an error; for everything which, if it occurred from the Messenger, would be ugly, and the compulsion regarding him is removed, is forbidden, even if it is known that he will not do it. The following points prove this:

The first: if whatever God knows He will not do must not be forbidden by Him, then whatever He knows He will do must not be commanded by Him; and that would require that the Prophet not be commanded with anything nor forbidden from anything, and that is by consensus false.

The second: were it not for the prior prohibition and warning, the Prophet ﷺ would not have guarded against it; so since that guarding is conditioned upon that prohibition and warning, how can that guarding be made to contradict the prohibition and warning?

The third: that the purpose of the prohibition and the threat is to emphasize the ugliness of that in the intellect, so its purpose is emphasis. Since it was fitting for God to draw attention to the kinds of proofs that indicate tawhid after He had established them in the intellects, with the purpose of reinforcing intellect through transmission, what distance is there in such a purpose here?

Fourth: His saying, may He be exalted, regarding the angels: ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed I am a god besides Him," that We will recompense with Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 29], although He informed of their infallibility in His saying: ﴿They fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Nahl: 50]; and He said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿If you were to associate partners with God, your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and they have agreed that he, upon whom be blessings and peace, did not associate and did not incline towards it; and He said: ﴿O Prophet, fear God and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1]; and He said: ﴿They wish you would soften, so they would soften﴾ [al-Qalam: 9]; and He said: ﴿Convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord, and if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]; and His saying: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 14]. So it is established by what we have mentioned that he, upon whom be blessings and peace, is forbidden from that, and that others too are forbidden from it; for the prohibition concerning these matters is not among the special attributes of the Messenger, upon whom be blessings and peace. It remains to be asked: why did He single him out with the prohibition rather than others? We say concerning this several points:

The first: that whoever has more of God's blessings upon him, the occurrence of sin from him is more ugly; and there is no doubt that God's blessings upon the Messenger, upon whom be blessings and peace, are greater; so the occurrence of sin from him is uglier, and so it is more deserving of specification.

The second: that excess of love requires specification by excess of warning.

Third: when a wise man turns to his eldest and most virtuous son and rebukes him for a matter in the presence of all his children, he thereby alerts them to the gravity of that act should they choose and commit it. It is the custom of people to direct their commands and prohibitions at the one who is of greater rank, for the sake of alerting others or for emphasis. This is an established principle regarding verses of this kind.

The second view: the words ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ do not mean that he followed their desires in all matters. Perhaps he, upon him be blessings and peace, did follow their desires in some matters, such as refraining from harshness in speech and roughness in discourse, out of his hope to win them over. So God the Exalted forbade him from that degree as well, and despaired him of them entirely, as He said: ﴿And had We not strengthened you, you would have almost inclined to them a little﴾ [al-Isra: 74].

The third view: although the apparent address is to the Messenger, what is meant is someone other than him. This is like when you rebuke a person whose slave has wronged your slave, and you say to him: "If you do this deed again, I will punish you for it severely." The purpose is that none of the Ummah should incline to addressing or following them.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: He, the Exalted, did not mean by this that knowledge itself came to you; rather, what is meant is the proofs, the signs and the miracles, since these are among the means of knowledge. This is therefore a case of applying the name of the effect to the cause. Know that the purpose of metaphor is exaggeration and magnification. It is as though He, glorified and exalted, magnified the matter of prophethood and miracles by naming them with the name of knowledge, and this alerts you to the fact that knowledge is the most exalted of created things in nobility and rank.

* * *

The second issue: the verse indicates that the threat directed at the scholars is more severe than that directed at others, because His saying ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ indicates this.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you would then be of the wrongdoers﴾, the meaning is that if you did that, you would be in the position of the people in their disbelief and their wronging of themselves. The purpose of it is threat and admonition. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 146–148 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognise him as they recognise their own sons. Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth.﴾ ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾

Know that there are several issues (masa'il) in this verse.

**The first issue:** His words ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ are general in wording, but they are specific to the scholars among them. The evidence for this is that He described them as recognising him as they recognise their sons. Also, a large group that knows something would, by custom, be incapable of agreeing to conceal it. Do you not see that if a single person entered a city and asked about its congregational mosque, it would not be possible for no one to meet him except with lies and concealment? Yet such concealment is possible among a small group. And God knows best.

**The second issue:** To what does the pronoun in His words ﴿recognise him﴾ refer? Scholars have mentioned several possibilities.

The first is that it refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning they recognise him with a clear recognition, distinguishing him from others, as they recognise their sons, so that he is not confused for the sons of others. It is related from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he asked Abdullah ibn Salam about the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he replied: "I know him better than I know my own son." He asked: "Why?" He said: "Because I am not in doubt about Muhammad, that he is a prophet. As for my son, perhaps his mother was unfaithful." Then Umar kissed his head.

The pronoun may be used even if no prior mention has been made, because the context indicates it and it is not ambiguous to the listener. Such a pronoun carries an emphasis and conveys that, because of his fame, he is known without needing to be introduced. There are questions regarding this view.

**First question:** This statement has no connection to what came before it, concerning the matter of the qiblah.

**Answer:** In the preceding verse, when He warned the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) against following the Jews and Christians by His words ﴿If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be among the wrongdoers﴾, He informed the believers about the condition of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in this verse, saying: "Know, O company of believers, that the scholars of the People of the Book recognise Muhammad, what he has brought, his truthfulness, his call and his qiblah. They have no doubt about him, just as they have no doubt about their sons."

**Second question:** A similar statement is His words ﴿They find him written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], and His words ﴿and a bringer of good news of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6]. However, we say: it is impossible that they recognise him as they recognise their sons. This is because his description in the Torah and the Gospel either came in full detail, and that would require specifying the time, place, attributes, physical form, lineage and tribe, or this description did not come with this kind of detail. If it was the first, then he would necessarily have been known, at the specified time, in the specified city, from the specified direction, with the specified attributes, to the people of the East and the West, because the Torah and the Gospel were well known among the people of the East and the West. If this were so, no Christian or Jew would have been able to deny it.

As for the second division, it does not produce certainty of the truthfulness of the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him). For we say: suppose the Torah contained that a man from the Arabs would be a prophet. Yet since that description was not detailed to the point of certainty, acknowledging it would not necessarily entail acknowledging the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The answer to this objection arises only if we say that knowledge of his prophethood came solely from the Torah and the Gospel containing his description. We do not say this. Rather, we say that he claimed prophethood and a miracle appeared at his hand, and whoever is like this is a truthful prophet. This is a proof, and a proof yields certainty. Therefore knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) was stronger and more manifest than knowledge of the sonship of sons and the fatherhood of fathers.

**Third question:** According to this aspect which you have established, knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a demonstrative knowledge that does not admit error. But knowledge that this is my son is not certain knowledge; rather it is an assumption that admits error. So why is certainty compared with assumption?

**Answer:** The intention is not that knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) resembles knowledge of the sonship of sons. Rather, the intention is to compare the knowledge with the persons and individuals of the sons. Just as a father knows the person of his son with a knowledge in which he is not confused with anyone else, so it is here. At this point the comparison is sound, because this knowledge is necessary (daruri) and that knowledge is acquired through reasoning (nazari). Comparing the acquired with the necessary conveys exaggeration and the beauty of metaphor.

**Fourth question:** Why did He specify sons, the males?

**Answer:** Because males are better known and more prominent, and they are more constantly in the company of their fathers and more closely attached to their hearts.

**The second view:** The pronoun in His words ﴿recognise him﴾ refers to the matter of the qiblah. That is: the scholars of the People of the Book recognise the matter of the qiblah to which you have been turned as they recognise their sons. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

Know that the first view is preferable for several reasons.

The first: a pronoun refers to a previously mentioned item, and the closest item mentioned is "knowledge" in His words ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾. The intended meaning of that knowledge is prophethood. So it is as if He said: they recognise that knowledge as they recognise their sons. As for the matter of the qiblah, it has not been mentioned at all before this.

The second: Allah did not state in the Qur'an that the matter of changing the qiblah is mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, but He stated that the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel. Therefore directing this recognition to the matter of prophethood is more appropriate.

The third: miracles do not, at first, indicate anything except the truthfulness of Muhammad (peace be upon him). As for the matter of the qiblah, it is established only because it is one of the things Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. Therefore directing this recognition to the matter of prophethood is more appropriate.

As for His words ﴿Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth﴾: know that those who were given the Book and recognised the Messenger, among them were some who believed in him, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his followers, and among them were some who remained in their disbelief. Whoever believed is not described as concealing the truth. Only those who remained in their disbelief are described by this. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth﴾. He thus described a portion of them with this, and by His words ﴿conceal the truth﴾ He indicated, by way of blame, that concealing the truth in religion is forbidden when it is possible to make it known. They differed about what was concealed. It was said: the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: the matter of the qiblah. We have thoroughly investigated this question.

\* \* \*

As for His words ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** It is possible that "the truth" (al-haqq) is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: "it is the truth." His words ﴿from your Lord﴾ may be a predicate without a further predicate, or a circumstantial phrase (hal). It is also permissible that it be a subject whose predicate is ﴿from your Lord﴾. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "al-haqqa min Rabbika," as an apposition (badal) of the first term, meaning: "they conceal the truth from your Lord."

**The second issue:** The "al-" in His words ﴿the truth﴾ has two possibilities. The first is that it is for a specific known thing (al-'ahd), referring to the truth which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) holds, or to the truth mentioned in His words ﴿they conceal the truth﴾. That is: what they are concealing is the truth from your Lord. The second is that it is for the genus, meaning: "the truth is from Allah and not from anyone else." That is, what is established as coming from Allah, exalted is He, is the truth, like what you hold; and what is not established as coming from Allah, like what the People of the Book hold, is falsehood.

\* \* \*

As for His words ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾ concerning what? They differed on this in several views.

The first: "So do not be among the doubters" concerning the fact that those previously mentioned knew the validity of your prophethood, and that some of them were obstinate and concealed it. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: it refers instead to the matter of the qiblah.

The third: it refers to the validity of his prophethood and his law. This is the closest view, because the closest item mentioned to it is His words ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾. Since its apparent meaning demands prophethood and what it contains of the Qur'an, revelation and law, His words ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾ must refer back to it.

**The second issue:** Even though God forbade him from doubting, this does not show that he was in doubt about it. This question has already been explained earlier. And God knows best.

\* \* \*

[Page 119]

﴿For each there is a direction toward which it turns. So race to good deeds. Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together. Indeed God has power over all things.﴾

His words, exalted is He, ﴿For each there is a direction toward which it turns. So race to good deeds. Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together. Indeed God has power over all things.﴾

Know that they differed about the intended meaning of His words ﴿For each﴾, and there are two issues.

**The first issue:** He said ﴿For each﴾ and did not say "for every people or community," because the meaning is known to them, so omitting the mention of what is added to it does no harm. This is common in their speech, as in His words ﴿For each We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48].

**The second issue:** They mentioned four aspects.

The first: it encompasses all groups, meaning the Muslims, the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists. This is the view of al-Asamm, who said: because among the polytheists there were those who worshipped idols and drew near to God by that, as God related of them in His words ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18].

The second, which is the view of most of the scholars of the Followers (tabi'un), is that the intended meaning is the People of the Book, who are the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians, and the polytheists are not included in it.

The third: some said the intended meaning is that for each group of Muslims there is a direction (jihah), that is, a side of the Ka'bah toward which they pray: southern, northern, eastern or western. They argued for this view with two points.

The first: His words ﴿He is the one who turns it﴾, meaning: Allah turns it. And Allah's turning was realised only toward the Ka'bah, because anything else is the turning of Satan.

The second: Allah, exalted is He, followed it with His words ﴿So race to good deeds﴾, and it is apparent that the intended meaning of these good deeds is what belongs to each person from a direction, and the directions described as good are none other than the directions of the Ka'bah.

The fourth: others said: "For each there is a direction" means that for each of the messengers and the possessors of laws there is a direction of qiblah. So the qiblah of the most exalted (muqarrabun) is the Throne, the qiblah of the spiritual beings (ruhaniyyun) is the Footstool, the qiblah of the cherubim (karubiyyun) is the Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur), the qiblah of the prophets before you is Jerusalem, and your qiblah is the Ka'bah.

\* \* \*

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿direction (wijhah)﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** It was recited "wa-li-kulli wijhatin" with an idafah (construction of genitive), and the meaning is: "and every direction is one he turns to." The lam was added because the object was placed first, as in your saying: "To Zayd you struck," and "To Zayd his father is a striker."

**The second issue:** Al-Farra' said: wijhah, jihah and wajh have one meaning. They differed about what is intended. Al-Hasan said: the intended meaning is the method (minhaj) and the law (shar'). This is like His words ﴿For every community We have appointed a rite﴾ [al-Hajj: 67], and ﴿For each We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. The meaning is that the laws have benefits, and therefore laws differ according to the differences of persons. Just as they differ according to the differences of persons, it is also not far-fetched that they differ according to the differences of time with respect to a single person. For this reason the doctrine of abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one) and change is valid. The rest said: the intended meaning is the matter of the qiblah, because His words, exalted is He, ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ came earlier, so this direction must be understood as referring to that.

[Page 120]

As for His words, ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾, there are two interpretations.

The first: the pronoun refers to everyone. That is, for each person there is a direction (*wijhah*) toward which he turns his face (*muwalli wajhahu*) [see note: this is the meaning]
[Page 120]
toward it. The sense of the statement on the first interpretation is: for each of you there is a direction, that is, a side of the qibla, toward which he turns, meaning he faces it, and turns toward it for his prayer, through which he draws near to his Lord. Each one rejoices in what he is upon and does not leave it. So there is no way for you to be united on one qibla, given that the religions are different. ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾: that is, hold fast, O community of Muslims, to your qibla, for you are upon goods from it in this world and the Hereafter. As for this world, it is because of your honour in the qibla of Ibrahim. As for the Hereafter, it is because of the great reward you will receive for submitting to His commands. ﴿For to Allah is your return﴾, and wherever you are in the directions of the earth, Allah will bring you all together ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and He will separate the righteous among you from the wrongdoer, until it becomes clear who among you is obedient and who is disobedient, and who among you is correct and who is mistaken. ﴿Indeed, He is competent over all things.﴾

Whoever holds this interpretation says: the meaning is that each of the people of the religions has a direction that they have chosen, either by a law (*shari'ah*) or by desire. So you will not be held accountable for the deeds of others. ﴿For them is what they have earned and for you is what you have earned.﴾

As for the explanation of the statement on the second interpretation, namely that the pronoun in His words ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾ refers to Allah, there are two views here.

The first: Allah has informed us that each of these two qiblas, which are the Bayt al-Maqdis and the Ka'bah, is a direction that Allah turns His servants toward. If He wills, He does so according to what He knows to be beneficial. So both directions are from Allah, and it is He who turned the faces of His servants toward them. Therefore, race to the good deeds by submitting to the command of Allah in both situations, for your submission is good for you. Do not pay attention to the criticisms of those who say: ﴿What has turned them away from their qibla?﴾ For Allah will gather you and these foolish ones together on the plain of Resurrection, and He will judge between you.

The second: if we interpret His words ﴿and for each there is a direction﴾ as referring to the sides and directions of the Ka'bah, the meaning is: for each group among you, O community of Muslims, there is a direction, that is, a side of the Ka'bah. ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾ by facing it from all the sides. For although they differ, once they all lead to the Ka'bah, they are like one direction. Allah's knowledge of their intentions is not hidden, and He will gather them all and reward them for their deeds.

As for His words, ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾, meaning: he is the one who turns his face toward it, so the mention of "face" is dispensed with. Al-Farra' said: that is, he faces it. Abu Mu'adh said: ﴿muwalliha﴾ carries the sense of *mutawalliha*, as it is said: "He has taken it up, been pleased with it, and followed it." In the reading of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir al-Nakha'i it is read *(huwa mawlaha)*, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Ja'far, and Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir. In the reading of the rest it is *(muwalliha)*. Ibn 'Amir's reading has two meanings. The first: what you have made to turn toward you has made you turn toward it, because the meaning of "you turned it" is that you made it such that it faces you; and when this faces that, that also faces this. So each of the two has turned toward the other, like His words: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37] and ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾, meaning: that direction has been beautified for him and made beloved to him, so that he loves it and is pleased with it.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾, its meaning is a command to hasten to obedience at its time. Know that performing the prayer at the beginning of its time is more excellent according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, contrary to Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafi'i argued with several points:

The first: prayer is good, based on his saying ﷺ: "Prayer is the best thing to be established" [*khayr mawdu'*]. Since this is so, it must be that hastening to it is more excellent, based on His words: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾. The apparent meaning of a command is obligation. If that is not established, then at least it is recommendation.

The second: His words: ﴿Race to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [al-Hadid: 21]. Its meaning is: toward what necessitates forgiveness. Prayer is among what necessitates forgiveness, so racing to it must be recommended.

[Page 121]
The third: His words: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost, those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10–11]. There is no doubt that what is meant is the foremost in acts of obedience, and there is no doubt that prayer is among acts of obedience. His words ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ indicate restriction: its meaning is that none are brought near to Allah except the foremost. That indicates that the perfection of virtue is tied to racing.

The fourth: His words: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]. The meaning: hasten to what necessitates forgiveness. There is no doubt that prayer is like this, so hastening to it is commanded.

The fifth: He praised the prophets before us with His words: ﴿Indeed, they used to race to the good deeds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 90]. There is no doubt that prayer is among the good deeds, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "The best of your deeds is prayer."

The sixth: He blamed Iblis for not hastening, saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. This indicates that abandoning hastening necessitates blame.

The seventh: His words: ﴿Guard over the prayers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. Guarding cannot be achieved except by hastening, so that one is safe from missing it through forgetfulness and other preoccupations.

The eighth: His words, recounting Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84]. So it is established that hastening is better.

The ninth: His words: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and fought. They are greater in rank than those who spent afterwards and fought﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. He explained that racing is a cause of greater excellence, so it is likewise in this case.

The tenth: what 'Umar, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, Anas, and Abu Mahdhurah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Prayer at the beginning of its time is the pleasure of Allah, and at its end is the pardon of Allah." Al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The pleasure of Allah is more beloved to us than His pardon."

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The pleasure of Allah is only for the doers of good, while pardon is likely to be for the negligent. If it is said that this is an argument out of place, because it implies that one would be sinful by delaying, and we agree that he is not sinful, then nothing remains except that its meaning is that performing the act at the end of the time necessitates pardon for past misdeeds; and whatever is like that undoubtedly necessitates the pleasure of Allah. So delay necessitates pardon and pleasure, while early performance necessitates pleasure without pardon, so delay is better. We say: this is weak in several respects:

The first: if it were so, then delaying the Maghrib would be more excellent, and no one has said that.

The second: failure to hasten to compliance resembles failure to turn to it, and that would call for punishment, except that when he performs the act afterward, that requirement falls away.

The third: the explanation of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, invalidates this interpretation they have mentioned.

The eleventh: it was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "O 'Ali, do not delay three things: the prayer when it comes, the funeral when it is present, and the unmarried woman when you find a suitable match for her."

The twelfth: "From Ibn Mas'ud, that he asked the Messenger ﷺ, saying: Which deeds are best? He said: Prayer at its first appointed time."

The thirteenth: Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "A man may perform a prayer, though he has missed from its first time [something] better for him than his family and his wealth."

[Page 122]
The fourteenth: he said, peace be upon him: "Whoever establishes a good practice, for him is its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." So whoever is earlier in obedience is the one who establishes the act of obedience at that time, so his reward must be greater than the reward of the one who is later.

The fifteenth: we agree that one of the causes of excellence among the Companions is precedence in accepting Islam, to the extent that a sharp dispute arose between the People of the Sunnah and others as to whether Abu Bakr or 'Ali was earlier in Islam. That dispute arose only because they agree that precedence in obedience necessitates greater excellence, and that indicates our view.

The sixteenth: his words, peace be upon him, in a sermon of his: "Hasten to the righteous deeds before you are occupied." There is no doubt that prayer is among the righteous deeds.

The seventeenth: that hastening the rights of human beings is better than delaying them, so the situation must be the same regarding the rights of Allah, the Exalted. What joins them is observing the meaning of honouring.

The eighteenth: that hastening and racing to prayer is a display of eagerness for obedience, devotion to it, and desire for it, while delay is a sign of laziness regarding it, so the first is more fitting.

The nineteenth: that caution lies in hastening the prayer, for if he performs it at the beginning of its time, his obligation is discharged. If he delays, something may occur to preoccupy him and prevent him from performing it, and the obligation will remain upon him. So the course by which caution is achieved is undoubtedly better.

The twentieth: we agree regarding the fast of Ramadan that hastening it is better than delaying it. That is because the sick person may break his fast and postpone the fast, and he may also hasten and fast immediately. Then we agree that hastening in fasting is more excellent, as He said: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. So it is also necessary that hastening in prayer is more fitting. If it is said: these analogical proofs are refuted by the noon prayer in the intense heat, or by the case where he hopes to catch the congregation, or the availability of water, we say: delay is established in these situations due to incidental matters, whereas our discussion concerns the principle of what is required.

The twenty-first: hastening to compliance is better in custom than not hastening, so it must be the same in the law, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "What the Muslims see as good is good in the sight of Allah."

The twenty-second: a prayer whose conditions are complete must be performed at the beginning of its time, like the Maghrib. This excludes the noon prayer in intense heat, because delay is only recommended when he intends to pray it in the mosque, since walking to the mosque in intense heat is like an obstacle. But if he prays it in his house, hastening is better. This also excludes one who is holding back the two evacuations, or whose food is present while he is hungry, for the same reason. Likewise the one performing tayammum who is confident of finding water, and likewise when he expects the congregation to gather, for perfection is not achieved in these cases. These are the proofs indicating that hastening is more excellent. Let us mention each of the prayers:

As for the Dawn prayer, Muhammad [al-Shaybani] said: it is recommended to begin it in the dark (*taghlis*) and to finish it in the light (*isfar*). If one intends to limit himself to one of the two times, then *isfar* is better. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: *taghlis* is better, and this is the view of Abu [Page 123] Bakr and 'Umar, and Malik and Ahmad also said so. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued, after the preceding proofs, with several points:

First, the narrations on the side of performing the dawn prayer in the darkness:

The first: what is recorded in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) on the authority of ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would pray the Subh (dawn) prayer, and then turn away while the women, wrapped in their cloaks (mutalaffi‘at bi-muruṭihinna), could not be recognized because of the ghalas (the darkness)."

Muhyi al-Sunnah said in his book *Sharh al-Sunnah*: "Mutalaffi‘at bi-muruṭihinna" means covered in their wraps. At-talaffuʿ by a garment is the wrapping of oneself in it. Al-muruṭ are the wide outer garments; its singular is mirṭ. Al-ghalas is the darkness of the last part of the night.

If it is said: this was at the beginning of Islam, when women attended the congregational prayers, so the Prophet (ﷺ) would pray in the ghalas so that they would not be recognized. Likewise ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, would pray in the ghalas. Then, when women were forbidden to attend the congregations, he (ʿUmar) left this practice.

We say: the principle to which one returns in establishing all rulings is the absence of abrogation (naskh). Were it not for this principle, it would not be permissible to derive proof from any of the legal evidences.
