The second: what is recorded in the two Sahihs from Qatadah, from Anas, from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "We took the suhur (pre-dawn meal) with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then we stood up for the prayer." I (Anas) said: "How long was the gap between them?" He said: "About fifty verses." This also indicates the taghlis (praying at the earliest, dark part of dawn).

The third: what is reported from Abu Masʿud al-Ansari that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed the dawn prayer in the ghalas, then once he performed it in the isfar (when the light had spread), and after that he did not return to the isfar until Allah took him."

The fourth: Allah Most High praised those who seek forgiveness at dawn, saying: ﴿And those who seek forgiveness in the hours before dawn﴾ (Al ʿImran 3:17), and He praised those who forsake sleep, saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds; they call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾ (As-Sajdah 32:16). If this is established, then forsaking sleep for the performance of obligatory acts must be better, due to His words (ﷺ), relating from Allah: "Those who draw near to Me will not draw near with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon them." And if this is the case, then taghlis must be better.

The fifth: sleep at that time is more pleasant, so forsaking it is harder, and therefore its reward must be greater, due to his words (ﷺ): "The best of acts of worship are the most arduous," meaning the most difficult.

Abu Hanifah argued with several points:

The first: his (ﷺ) words: "Perform the dawn prayer when it is bright (asfirū bil-fajr), for it is greater in reward."

The second: ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud narrated that he prayed the dawn prayer at Muzdalifah in the darkness, then Ibn Masʿud said: "I have not seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pray any prayer except at its appointed time, except the dawn prayer, for he prayed it that day at other than its appointed time."

The third: from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "I have not seen the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) be more careful about anything than about performing the dawn prayer when it is illuminated (at-tanwīr)."

The fourth: from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he prayed the dawn prayer and recited Al ʿImran, and they said: "The sun nearly rose!" He said: "Had it risen, it would not have found us heedless." And from ʿUmar that he recited al-Baqarah, and they looked toward the sunrise, and he said: "Had it risen, it would not have found us heedless."

The fifth: delaying the prayer includes the virtue of waiting for it, and he (ﷺ) said: "The one who waits for the prayer is as if he is in the prayer." So whoever delays the prayer from the beginning of its time has first waited for the prayer and then performed it, while whoever prays at the very beginning of the time has missed the virtue of waiting.

The sixth: delaying leads to a larger congregation, so it must be preferable in order to obtain the virtue of congregational prayer.

The seventh: taghlis causes hardship for people, because if the prayer is performed at the time of taghlis, a person needs to make wudu' at night so that he is free to pray after dawn breaks, and hardship is negated in the Shariah.

The eighth: the prayer is disliked after the dawn prayer, so if one prays at the time of isfar, the time of disliked prayer becomes shorter, and if one prays with taghlis, the time of disliked prayer becomes longer.

As for the answer to the first point: al-fajr is the name for the light by which the darkness of the eastern horizon is dispelled. Thus it is dawn only if darkness is still present in the air. But when the darkness has completely disappeared and the air is fully lit, that is not dawn. As for al-isfar, it means becoming apparent. It is said: "The woman unveiled (asfarat) her face" when she uncovered it. Having established this, we say: the appearance of dawn occurs while darkness remains in the air, for the more intense the darkness, the stronger the light that appears within that darkness. So his saying: "Perform the dawn prayer when it is bright" must be understood as referring to taghlis, meaning: whenever your prayer is performed when the dawn is most apparent and most brilliant, its reward is greater. We have explained that this occurs only at the beginning of dawn. This is the meaning of the words of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, that the isfar mentioned in the hadith is to be understood as certainty of the emergence of dawn and removal of doubt about it. What indicates our view is that performing the prayer at that time is harder, so it must carry greater reward. As for delaying the prayer until the time of tanwir, it is the habit of the lazy. How could the Lawgiver say that laziness is better than striving in obedience?

As for the answer to the second point, which is the saying of Ibn Masʿud: "Be careful about the illumination of dawn," its answer is what we have established, because tanwir at dawn occurs only at the beginning of the time. As for when the world is filled with light, that is not called dawn. As for the remaining points, they are countered by some of what we have already mentioned. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together﴾. This is a promise to those who obey and a warning to those who disobey, as if He, Exalted, said: "Compete in good, O you who are truly aware and knowledgeable of prophethood and the Shariah, and bear hardships for it, so that on the Day of Resurrection you may reach what you have with Allah of the various kinds of honor and nearness." Then, He, glorified is He, confirmed this with His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things capable﴾. This is because resurrection in itself is possible, and He is capable of all possible things, so He must be capable of resurrection. As for the issues derived from this verse, we have already mentioned them in His words: ﴿And if Allah willed, He could take away their hearing and their sight. Indeed, Allah is over all things capable﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:20).

[p. 124]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 146–148 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognise him as they recognise their own sons. Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth.﴾ ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾

Know that there are several issues (masa'il) in this verse.

**The first issue:** His words ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ are general in wording, but they are specific to the scholars among them. The evidence for this is that He described them as recognising him as they recognise their sons. Also, a large group that knows something would, by custom, be incapable of agreeing to conceal it. Do you not see that if a single person entered a city and asked about its congregational mosque, it would not be possible for no one to meet him except with lies and concealment? Yet such concealment is possible among a small group. And God knows best.

**The second issue:** To what does the pronoun in His words ﴿recognise him﴾ refer? Scholars have mentioned several possibilities.

The first is that it refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning they recognise him with a clear recognition, distinguishing him from others, as they recognise their sons, so that he is not confused for the sons of others. It is related from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he asked Abdullah ibn Salam about the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he replied: "I know him better than I know my own son." He asked: "Why?" He said: "Because I am not in doubt about Muhammad, that he is a prophet. As for my son, perhaps his mother was unfaithful." Then Umar kissed his head.

The pronoun may be used even if no prior mention has been made, because the context indicates it and it is not ambiguous to the listener. Such a pronoun carries an emphasis and conveys that, because of his fame, he is known without needing to be introduced. There are questions regarding this view.

**First question:** This statement has no connection to what came before it, concerning the matter of the qiblah.

**Answer:** In the preceding verse, when He warned the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) against following the Jews and Christians by His words ﴿If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be among the wrongdoers﴾, He informed the believers about the condition of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in this verse, saying: "Know, O company of believers, that the scholars of the People of the Book recognise Muhammad, what he has brought, his truthfulness, his call and his qiblah. They have no doubt about him, just as they have no doubt about their sons."

**Second question:** A similar statement is His words ﴿They find him written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], and His words ﴿and a bringer of good news of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6]. However, we say: it is impossible that they recognise him as they recognise their sons. This is because his description in the Torah and the Gospel either came in full detail, and that would require specifying the time, place, attributes, physical form, lineage and tribe, or this description did not come with this kind of detail. If it was the first, then he would necessarily have been known, at the specified time, in the specified city, from the specified direction, with the specified attributes, to the people of the East and the West, because the Torah and the Gospel were well known among the people of the East and the West. If this were so, no Christian or Jew would have been able to deny it.

As for the second division, it does not produce certainty of the truthfulness of the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him). For we say: suppose the Torah contained that a man from the Arabs would be a prophet. Yet since that description was not detailed to the point of certainty, acknowledging it would not necessarily entail acknowledging the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The answer to this objection arises only if we say that knowledge of his prophethood came solely from the Torah and the Gospel containing his description. We do not say this. Rather, we say that he claimed prophethood and a miracle appeared at his hand, and whoever is like this is a truthful prophet. This is a proof, and a proof yields certainty. Therefore knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) was stronger and more manifest than knowledge of the sonship of sons and the fatherhood of fathers.

**Third question:** According to this aspect which you have established, knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a demonstrative knowledge that does not admit error. But knowledge that this is my son is not certain knowledge; rather it is an assumption that admits error. So why is certainty compared with assumption?

**Answer:** The intention is not that knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) resembles knowledge of the sonship of sons. Rather, the intention is to compare the knowledge with the persons and individuals of the sons. Just as a father knows the person of his son with a knowledge in which he is not confused with anyone else, so it is here. At this point the comparison is sound, because this knowledge is necessary (daruri) and that knowledge is acquired through reasoning (nazari). Comparing the acquired with the necessary conveys exaggeration and the beauty of metaphor.

**Fourth question:** Why did He specify sons, the males?

**Answer:** Because males are better known and more prominent, and they are more constantly in the company of their fathers and more closely attached to their hearts.

**The second view:** The pronoun in His words ﴿recognise him﴾ refers to the matter of the qiblah. That is: the scholars of the People of the Book recognise the matter of the qiblah to which you have been turned as they recognise their sons. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

Know that the first view is preferable for several reasons.

The first: a pronoun refers to a previously mentioned item, and the closest item mentioned is "knowledge" in His words ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾. The intended meaning of that knowledge is prophethood. So it is as if He said: they recognise that knowledge as they recognise their sons. As for the matter of the qiblah, it has not been mentioned at all before this.

The second: Allah did not state in the Qur'an that the matter of changing the qiblah is mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, but He stated that the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel. Therefore directing this recognition to the matter of prophethood is more appropriate.

The third: miracles do not, at first, indicate anything except the truthfulness of Muhammad (peace be upon him). As for the matter of the qiblah, it is established only because it is one of the things Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. Therefore directing this recognition to the matter of prophethood is more appropriate.

As for His words ﴿Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth﴾: know that those who were given the Book and recognised the Messenger, among them were some who believed in him, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his followers, and among them were some who remained in their disbelief. Whoever believed is not described as concealing the truth. Only those who remained in their disbelief are described by this. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth﴾. He thus described a portion of them with this, and by His words ﴿conceal the truth﴾ He indicated, by way of blame, that concealing the truth in religion is forbidden when it is possible to make it known. They differed about what was concealed. It was said: the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: the matter of the qiblah. We have thoroughly investigated this question.

\* \* \*

As for His words ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** It is possible that "the truth" (al-haqq) is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: "it is the truth." His words ﴿from your Lord﴾ may be a predicate without a further predicate, or a circumstantial phrase (hal). It is also permissible that it be a subject whose predicate is ﴿from your Lord﴾. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "al-haqqa min Rabbika," as an apposition (badal) of the first term, meaning: "they conceal the truth from your Lord."

**The second issue:** The "al-" in His words ﴿the truth﴾ has two possibilities. The first is that it is for a specific known thing (al-'ahd), referring to the truth which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) holds, or to the truth mentioned in His words ﴿they conceal the truth﴾. That is: what they are concealing is the truth from your Lord. The second is that it is for the genus, meaning: "the truth is from Allah and not from anyone else." That is, what is established as coming from Allah, exalted is He, is the truth, like what you hold; and what is not established as coming from Allah, like what the People of the Book hold, is falsehood.

\* \* \*

As for His words ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾ concerning what? They differed on this in several views.

The first: "So do not be among the doubters" concerning the fact that those previously mentioned knew the validity of your prophethood, and that some of them were obstinate and concealed it. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: it refers instead to the matter of the qiblah.

The third: it refers to the validity of his prophethood and his law. This is the closest view, because the closest item mentioned to it is His words ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾. Since its apparent meaning demands prophethood and what it contains of the Qur'an, revelation and law, His words ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾ must refer back to it.

**The second issue:** Even though God forbade him from doubting, this does not show that he was in doubt about it. This question has already been explained earlier. And God knows best.

\* \* \*

[Page 119]

﴿For each there is a direction toward which it turns. So race to good deeds. Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together. Indeed God has power over all things.﴾

His words, exalted is He, ﴿For each there is a direction toward which it turns. So race to good deeds. Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together. Indeed God has power over all things.﴾

Know that they differed about the intended meaning of His words ﴿For each﴾, and there are two issues.

**The first issue:** He said ﴿For each﴾ and did not say "for every people or community," because the meaning is known to them, so omitting the mention of what is added to it does no harm. This is common in their speech, as in His words ﴿For each We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48].

**The second issue:** They mentioned four aspects.

The first: it encompasses all groups, meaning the Muslims, the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists. This is the view of al-Asamm, who said: because among the polytheists there were those who worshipped idols and drew near to God by that, as God related of them in His words ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18].

The second, which is the view of most of the scholars of the Followers (tabi'un), is that the intended meaning is the People of the Book, who are the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians, and the polytheists are not included in it.

The third: some said the intended meaning is that for each group of Muslims there is a direction (jihah), that is, a side of the Ka'bah toward which they pray: southern, northern, eastern or western. They argued for this view with two points.

The first: His words ﴿He is the one who turns it﴾, meaning: Allah turns it. And Allah's turning was realised only toward the Ka'bah, because anything else is the turning of Satan.

The second: Allah, exalted is He, followed it with His words ﴿So race to good deeds﴾, and it is apparent that the intended meaning of these good deeds is what belongs to each person from a direction, and the directions described as good are none other than the directions of the Ka'bah.

The fourth: others said: "For each there is a direction" means that for each of the messengers and the possessors of laws there is a direction of qiblah. So the qiblah of the most exalted (muqarrabun) is the Throne, the qiblah of the spiritual beings (ruhaniyyun) is the Footstool, the qiblah of the cherubim (karubiyyun) is the Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur), the qiblah of the prophets before you is Jerusalem, and your qiblah is the Ka'bah.

\* \* \*

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿direction (wijhah)﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** It was recited "wa-li-kulli wijhatin" with an idafah (construction of genitive), and the meaning is: "and every direction is one he turns to." The lam was added because the object was placed first, as in your saying: "To Zayd you struck," and "To Zayd his father is a striker."

**The second issue:** Al-Farra' said: wijhah, jihah and wajh have one meaning. They differed about what is intended. Al-Hasan said: the intended meaning is the method (minhaj) and the law (shar'). This is like His words ﴿For every community We have appointed a rite﴾ [al-Hajj: 67], and ﴿For each We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. The meaning is that the laws have benefits, and therefore laws differ according to the differences of persons. Just as they differ according to the differences of persons, it is also not far-fetched that they differ according to the differences of time with respect to a single person. For this reason the doctrine of abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one) and change is valid. The rest said: the intended meaning is the matter of the qiblah, because His words, exalted is He, ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ came earlier, so this direction must be understood as referring to that.

[Page 120]

As for His words, ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾, there are two interpretations.

The first: the pronoun refers to everyone. That is, for each person there is a direction (*wijhah*) toward which he turns his face (*muwalli wajhahu*) [see note: this is the meaning]
[Page 120]
toward it. The sense of the statement on the first interpretation is: for each of you there is a direction, that is, a side of the qibla, toward which he turns, meaning he faces it, and turns toward it for his prayer, through which he draws near to his Lord. Each one rejoices in what he is upon and does not leave it. So there is no way for you to be united on one qibla, given that the religions are different. ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾: that is, hold fast, O community of Muslims, to your qibla, for you are upon goods from it in this world and the Hereafter. As for this world, it is because of your honour in the qibla of Ibrahim. As for the Hereafter, it is because of the great reward you will receive for submitting to His commands. ﴿For to Allah is your return﴾, and wherever you are in the directions of the earth, Allah will bring you all together ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and He will separate the righteous among you from the wrongdoer, until it becomes clear who among you is obedient and who is disobedient, and who among you is correct and who is mistaken. ﴿Indeed, He is competent over all things.﴾

Whoever holds this interpretation says: the meaning is that each of the people of the religions has a direction that they have chosen, either by a law (*shari'ah*) or by desire. So you will not be held accountable for the deeds of others. ﴿For them is what they have earned and for you is what you have earned.﴾

As for the explanation of the statement on the second interpretation, namely that the pronoun in His words ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾ refers to Allah, there are two views here.

The first: Allah has informed us that each of these two qiblas, which are the Bayt al-Maqdis and the Ka'bah, is a direction that Allah turns His servants toward. If He wills, He does so according to what He knows to be beneficial. So both directions are from Allah, and it is He who turned the faces of His servants toward them. Therefore, race to the good deeds by submitting to the command of Allah in both situations, for your submission is good for you. Do not pay attention to the criticisms of those who say: ﴿What has turned them away from their qibla?﴾ For Allah will gather you and these foolish ones together on the plain of Resurrection, and He will judge between you.

The second: if we interpret His words ﴿and for each there is a direction﴾ as referring to the sides and directions of the Ka'bah, the meaning is: for each group among you, O community of Muslims, there is a direction, that is, a side of the Ka'bah. ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾ by facing it from all the sides. For although they differ, once they all lead to the Ka'bah, they are like one direction. Allah's knowledge of their intentions is not hidden, and He will gather them all and reward them for their deeds.

As for His words, ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾, meaning: he is the one who turns his face toward it, so the mention of "face" is dispensed with. Al-Farra' said: that is, he faces it. Abu Mu'adh said: ﴿muwalliha﴾ carries the sense of *mutawalliha*, as it is said: "He has taken it up, been pleased with it, and followed it." In the reading of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir al-Nakha'i it is read *(huwa mawlaha)*, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Ja'far, and Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir. In the reading of the rest it is *(muwalliha)*. Ibn 'Amir's reading has two meanings. The first: what you have made to turn toward you has made you turn toward it, because the meaning of "you turned it" is that you made it such that it faces you; and when this faces that, that also faces this. So each of the two has turned toward the other, like His words: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37] and ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾, meaning: that direction has been beautified for him and made beloved to him, so that he loves it and is pleased with it.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾, its meaning is a command to hasten to obedience at its time. Know that performing the prayer at the beginning of its time is more excellent according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, contrary to Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafi'i argued with several points:

The first: prayer is good, based on his saying ﷺ: "Prayer is the best thing to be established" [*khayr mawdu'*]. Since this is so, it must be that hastening to it is more excellent, based on His words: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾. The apparent meaning of a command is obligation. If that is not established, then at least it is recommendation.

The second: His words: ﴿Race to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [al-Hadid: 21]. Its meaning is: toward what necessitates forgiveness. Prayer is among what necessitates forgiveness, so racing to it must be recommended.

[Page 121]
The third: His words: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost, those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10–11]. There is no doubt that what is meant is the foremost in acts of obedience, and there is no doubt that prayer is among acts of obedience. His words ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ indicate restriction: its meaning is that none are brought near to Allah except the foremost. That indicates that the perfection of virtue is tied to racing.

The fourth: His words: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]. The meaning: hasten to what necessitates forgiveness. There is no doubt that prayer is like this, so hastening to it is commanded.

The fifth: He praised the prophets before us with His words: ﴿Indeed, they used to race to the good deeds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 90]. There is no doubt that prayer is among the good deeds, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "The best of your deeds is prayer."

The sixth: He blamed Iblis for not hastening, saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. This indicates that abandoning hastening necessitates blame.

The seventh: His words: ﴿Guard over the prayers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. Guarding cannot be achieved except by hastening, so that one is safe from missing it through forgetfulness and other preoccupations.

The eighth: His words, recounting Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84]. So it is established that hastening is better.

The ninth: His words: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and fought. They are greater in rank than those who spent afterwards and fought﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. He explained that racing is a cause of greater excellence, so it is likewise in this case.

The tenth: what 'Umar, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, Anas, and Abu Mahdhurah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Prayer at the beginning of its time is the pleasure of Allah, and at its end is the pardon of Allah." Al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The pleasure of Allah is more beloved to us than His pardon."

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The pleasure of Allah is only for the doers of good, while pardon is likely to be for the negligent. If it is said that this is an argument out of place, because it implies that one would be sinful by delaying, and we agree that he is not sinful, then nothing remains except that its meaning is that performing the act at the end of the time necessitates pardon for past misdeeds; and whatever is like that undoubtedly necessitates the pleasure of Allah. So delay necessitates pardon and pleasure, while early performance necessitates pleasure without pardon, so delay is better. We say: this is weak in several respects:

The first: if it were so, then delaying the Maghrib would be more excellent, and no one has said that.

The second: failure to hasten to compliance resembles failure to turn to it, and that would call for punishment, except that when he performs the act afterward, that requirement falls away.

The third: the explanation of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, invalidates this interpretation they have mentioned.

The eleventh: it was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "O 'Ali, do not delay three things: the prayer when it comes, the funeral when it is present, and the unmarried woman when you find a suitable match for her."

The twelfth: "From Ibn Mas'ud, that he asked the Messenger ﷺ, saying: Which deeds are best? He said: Prayer at its first appointed time."

The thirteenth: Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "A man may perform a prayer, though he has missed from its first time [something] better for him than his family and his wealth."

[Page 122]
The fourteenth: he said, peace be upon him: "Whoever establishes a good practice, for him is its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." So whoever is earlier in obedience is the one who establishes the act of obedience at that time, so his reward must be greater than the reward of the one who is later.

The fifteenth: we agree that one of the causes of excellence among the Companions is precedence in accepting Islam, to the extent that a sharp dispute arose between the People of the Sunnah and others as to whether Abu Bakr or 'Ali was earlier in Islam. That dispute arose only because they agree that precedence in obedience necessitates greater excellence, and that indicates our view.

The sixteenth: his words, peace be upon him, in a sermon of his: "Hasten to the righteous deeds before you are occupied." There is no doubt that prayer is among the righteous deeds.

The seventeenth: that hastening the rights of human beings is better than delaying them, so the situation must be the same regarding the rights of Allah, the Exalted. What joins them is observing the meaning of honouring.

The eighteenth: that hastening and racing to prayer is a display of eagerness for obedience, devotion to it, and desire for it, while delay is a sign of laziness regarding it, so the first is more fitting.

The nineteenth: that caution lies in hastening the prayer, for if he performs it at the beginning of its time, his obligation is discharged. If he delays, something may occur to preoccupy him and prevent him from performing it, and the obligation will remain upon him. So the course by which caution is achieved is undoubtedly better.

The twentieth: we agree regarding the fast of Ramadan that hastening it is better than delaying it. That is because the sick person may break his fast and postpone the fast, and he may also hasten and fast immediately. Then we agree that hastening in fasting is more excellent, as He said: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. So it is also necessary that hastening in prayer is more fitting. If it is said: these analogical proofs are refuted by the noon prayer in the intense heat, or by the case where he hopes to catch the congregation, or the availability of water, we say: delay is established in these situations due to incidental matters, whereas our discussion concerns the principle of what is required.

The twenty-first: hastening to compliance is better in custom than not hastening, so it must be the same in the law, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "What the Muslims see as good is good in the sight of Allah."

The twenty-second: a prayer whose conditions are complete must be performed at the beginning of its time, like the Maghrib. This excludes the noon prayer in intense heat, because delay is only recommended when he intends to pray it in the mosque, since walking to the mosque in intense heat is like an obstacle. But if he prays it in his house, hastening is better. This also excludes one who is holding back the two evacuations, or whose food is present while he is hungry, for the same reason. Likewise the one performing tayammum who is confident of finding water, and likewise when he expects the congregation to gather, for perfection is not achieved in these cases. These are the proofs indicating that hastening is more excellent. Let us mention each of the prayers:

As for the Dawn prayer, Muhammad [al-Shaybani] said: it is recommended to begin it in the dark (*taghlis*) and to finish it in the light (*isfar*). If one intends to limit himself to one of the two times, then *isfar* is better. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: *taghlis* is better, and this is the view of Abu [Page 123] Bakr and 'Umar, and Malik and Ahmad also said so. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued, after the preceding proofs, with several points:

First, the narrations on the side of performing the dawn prayer in the darkness:

The first: what is recorded in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) on the authority of ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would pray the Subh (dawn) prayer, and then turn away while the women, wrapped in their cloaks (mutalaffi‘at bi-muruṭihinna), could not be recognized because of the ghalas (the darkness)."

Muhyi al-Sunnah said in his book *Sharh al-Sunnah*: "Mutalaffi‘at bi-muruṭihinna" means covered in their wraps. At-talaffuʿ by a garment is the wrapping of oneself in it. Al-muruṭ are the wide outer garments; its singular is mirṭ. Al-ghalas is the darkness of the last part of the night.

If it is said: this was at the beginning of Islam, when women attended the congregational prayers, so the Prophet (ﷺ) would pray in the ghalas so that they would not be recognized. Likewise ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, would pray in the ghalas. Then, when women were forbidden to attend the congregations, he (ʿUmar) left this practice.

We say: the principle to which one returns in establishing all rulings is the absence of abrogation (naskh). Were it not for this principle, it would not be permissible to derive proof from any of the legal evidences.

The second: what is recorded in the two Sahihs from Qatadah, from Anas, from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "We took the suhur (pre-dawn meal) with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then we stood up for the prayer." I (Anas) said: "How long was the gap between them?" He said: "About fifty verses." This also indicates the taghlis (praying at the earliest, dark part of dawn).

The third: what is reported from Abu Masʿud al-Ansari that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed the dawn prayer in the ghalas, then once he performed it in the isfar (when the light had spread), and after that he did not return to the isfar until Allah took him."

The fourth: Allah Most High praised those who seek forgiveness at dawn, saying: ﴿And those who seek forgiveness in the hours before dawn﴾ (Al ʿImran 3:17), and He praised those who forsake sleep, saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds; they call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾ (As-Sajdah 32:16). If this is established, then forsaking sleep for the performance of obligatory acts must be better, due to His words (ﷺ), relating from Allah: "Those who draw near to Me will not draw near with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon them." And if this is the case, then taghlis must be better.

The fifth: sleep at that time is more pleasant, so forsaking it is harder, and therefore its reward must be greater, due to his words (ﷺ): "The best of acts of worship are the most arduous," meaning the most difficult.

Abu Hanifah argued with several points:

The first: his (ﷺ) words: "Perform the dawn prayer when it is bright (asfirū bil-fajr), for it is greater in reward."

The second: ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud narrated that he prayed the dawn prayer at Muzdalifah in the darkness, then Ibn Masʿud said: "I have not seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pray any prayer except at its appointed time, except the dawn prayer, for he prayed it that day at other than its appointed time."

The third: from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "I have not seen the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) be more careful about anything than about performing the dawn prayer when it is illuminated (at-tanwīr)."

The fourth: from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he prayed the dawn prayer and recited Al ʿImran, and they said: "The sun nearly rose!" He said: "Had it risen, it would not have found us heedless." And from ʿUmar that he recited al-Baqarah, and they looked toward the sunrise, and he said: "Had it risen, it would not have found us heedless."

The fifth: delaying the prayer includes the virtue of waiting for it, and he (ﷺ) said: "The one who waits for the prayer is as if he is in the prayer." So whoever delays the prayer from the beginning of its time has first waited for the prayer and then performed it, while whoever prays at the very beginning of the time has missed the virtue of waiting.

The sixth: delaying leads to a larger congregation, so it must be preferable in order to obtain the virtue of congregational prayer.

The seventh: taghlis causes hardship for people, because if the prayer is performed at the time of taghlis, a person needs to make wudu' at night so that he is free to pray after dawn breaks, and hardship is negated in the Shariah.

The eighth: the prayer is disliked after the dawn prayer, so if one prays at the time of isfar, the time of disliked prayer becomes shorter, and if one prays with taghlis, the time of disliked prayer becomes longer.

As for the answer to the first point: al-fajr is the name for the light by which the darkness of the eastern horizon is dispelled. Thus it is dawn only if darkness is still present in the air. But when the darkness has completely disappeared and the air is fully lit, that is not dawn. As for al-isfar, it means becoming apparent. It is said: "The woman unveiled (asfarat) her face" when she uncovered it. Having established this, we say: the appearance of dawn occurs while darkness remains in the air, for the more intense the darkness, the stronger the light that appears within that darkness. So his saying: "Perform the dawn prayer when it is bright" must be understood as referring to taghlis, meaning: whenever your prayer is performed when the dawn is most apparent and most brilliant, its reward is greater. We have explained that this occurs only at the beginning of dawn. This is the meaning of the words of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, that the isfar mentioned in the hadith is to be understood as certainty of the emergence of dawn and removal of doubt about it. What indicates our view is that performing the prayer at that time is harder, so it must carry greater reward. As for delaying the prayer until the time of tanwir, it is the habit of the lazy. How could the Lawgiver say that laziness is better than striving in obedience?

As for the answer to the second point, which is the saying of Ibn Masʿud: "Be careful about the illumination of dawn," its answer is what we have established, because tanwir at dawn occurs only at the beginning of the time. As for when the world is filled with light, that is not called dawn. As for the remaining points, they are countered by some of what we have already mentioned. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together﴾. This is a promise to those who obey and a warning to those who disobey, as if He, Exalted, said: "Compete in good, O you who are truly aware and knowledgeable of prophethood and the Shariah, and bear hardships for it, so that on the Day of Resurrection you may reach what you have with Allah of the various kinds of honor and nearness." Then, He, glorified is He, confirmed this with His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things capable﴾. This is because resurrection in itself is possible, and He is capable of all possible things, so He must be capable of resurrection. As for the issues derived from this verse, we have already mentioned them in His words: ﴿And if Allah willed, He could take away their hearing and their sight. Indeed, Allah is over all things capable﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:20).

[p. 124]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 146–148 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognise him as they recognise their own sons. Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth.﴾ ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾

Know that there are several issues (masa'il) in this verse.

**The first issue:** His words ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ are general in wording, but they are specific to the scholars among them. The evidence for this is that He described them as recognising him as they recognise their sons. Also, a large group that knows something would, by custom, be incapable of agreeing to conceal it. Do you not see that if a single person entered a city and asked about its congregational mosque, it would not be possible for no one to meet him except with lies and concealment? Yet such concealment is possible among a small group. And God knows best.

**The second issue:** To what does the pronoun in His words ﴿recognise him﴾ refer? Scholars have mentioned several possibilities.

The first is that it refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning they recognise him with a clear recognition, distinguishing him from others, as they recognise their sons, so that he is not confused for the sons of others. It is related from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he asked Abdullah ibn Salam about the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he replied: "I know him better than I know my own son." He asked: "Why?" He said: "Because I am not in doubt about Muhammad, that he is a prophet. As for my son, perhaps his mother was unfaithful." Then Umar kissed his head.

The pronoun may be used even if no prior mention has been made, because the context indicates it and it is not ambiguous to the listener. Such a pronoun carries an emphasis and conveys that, because of his fame, he is known without needing to be introduced. There are questions regarding this view.

**First question:** This statement has no connection to what came before it, concerning the matter of the qiblah.

**Answer:** In the preceding verse, when He warned the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) against following the Jews and Christians by His words ﴿If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be among the wrongdoers﴾, He informed the believers about the condition of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in this verse, saying: "Know, O company of believers, that the scholars of the People of the Book recognise Muhammad, what he has brought, his truthfulness, his call and his qiblah. They have no doubt about him, just as they have no doubt about their sons."

**Second question:** A similar statement is His words ﴿They find him written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], and His words ﴿and a bringer of good news of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6]. However, we say: it is impossible that they recognise him as they recognise their sons. This is because his description in the Torah and the Gospel either came in full detail, and that would require specifying the time, place, attributes, physical form, lineage and tribe, or this description did not come with this kind of detail. If it was the first, then he would necessarily have been known, at the specified time, in the specified city, from the specified direction, with the specified attributes, to the people of the East and the West, because the Torah and the Gospel were well known among the people of the East and the West. If this were so, no Christian or Jew would have been able to deny it.

As for the second division, it does not produce certainty of the truthfulness of the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him). For we say: suppose the Torah contained that a man from the Arabs would be a prophet. Yet since that description was not detailed to the point of certainty, acknowledging it would not necessarily entail acknowledging the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The answer to this objection arises only if we say that knowledge of his prophethood came solely from the Torah and the Gospel containing his description. We do not say this. Rather, we say that he claimed prophethood and a miracle appeared at his hand, and whoever is like this is a truthful prophet. This is a proof, and a proof yields certainty. Therefore knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) was stronger and more manifest than knowledge of the sonship of sons and the fatherhood of fathers.

**Third question:** According to this aspect which you have established, knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a demonstrative knowledge that does not admit error. But knowledge that this is my son is not certain knowledge; rather it is an assumption that admits error. So why is certainty compared with assumption?

**Answer:** The intention is not that knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) resembles knowledge of the sonship of sons. Rather, the intention is to compare the knowledge with the persons and individuals of the sons. Just as a father knows the person of his son with a knowledge in which he is not confused with anyone else, so it is here. At this point the comparison is sound, because this knowledge is necessary (daruri) and that knowledge is acquired through reasoning (nazari). Comparing the acquired with the necessary conveys exaggeration and the beauty of metaphor.

**Fourth question:** Why did He specify sons, the males?

**Answer:** Because males are better known and more prominent, and they are more constantly in the company of their fathers and more closely attached to their hearts.

**The second view:** The pronoun in His words ﴿recognise him﴾ refers to the matter of the qiblah. That is: the scholars of the People of the Book recognise the matter of the qiblah to which you have been turned as they recognise their sons. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

Know that the first view is preferable for several reasons.

The first: a pronoun refers to a previously mentioned item, and the closest item mentioned is "knowledge" in His words ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾. The intended meaning of that knowledge is prophethood. So it is as if He said: they recognise that knowledge as they recognise their sons. As for the matter of the qiblah, it has not been mentioned at all before this.

The second: Allah did not state in the Qur'an that the matter of changing the qiblah is mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, but He stated that the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel. Therefore directing this recognition to the matter of prophethood is more appropriate.

The third: miracles do not, at first, indicate anything except the truthfulness of Muhammad (peace be upon him). As for the matter of the qiblah, it is established only because it is one of the things Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. Therefore directing this recognition to the matter of prophethood is more appropriate.

As for His words ﴿Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth﴾: know that those who were given the Book and recognised the Messenger, among them were some who believed in him, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his followers, and among them were some who remained in their disbelief. Whoever believed is not described as concealing the truth. Only those who remained in their disbelief are described by this. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth﴾. He thus described a portion of them with this, and by His words ﴿conceal the truth﴾ He indicated, by way of blame, that concealing the truth in religion is forbidden when it is possible to make it known. They differed about what was concealed. It was said: the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: the matter of the qiblah. We have thoroughly investigated this question.

\* \* \*

As for His words ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** It is possible that "the truth" (al-haqq) is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: "it is the truth." His words ﴿from your Lord﴾ may be a predicate without a further predicate, or a circumstantial phrase (hal). It is also permissible that it be a subject whose predicate is ﴿from your Lord﴾. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "al-haqqa min Rabbika," as an apposition (badal) of the first term, meaning: "they conceal the truth from your Lord."

**The second issue:** The "al-" in His words ﴿the truth﴾ has two possibilities. The first is that it is for a specific known thing (al-'ahd), referring to the truth which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) holds, or to the truth mentioned in His words ﴿they conceal the truth﴾. That is: what they are concealing is the truth from your Lord. The second is that it is for the genus, meaning: "the truth is from Allah and not from anyone else." That is, what is established as coming from Allah, exalted is He, is the truth, like what you hold; and what is not established as coming from Allah, like what the People of the Book hold, is falsehood.

\* \* \*

As for His words ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾ concerning what? They differed on this in several views.

The first: "So do not be among the doubters" concerning the fact that those previously mentioned knew the validity of your prophethood, and that some of them were obstinate and concealed it. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: it refers instead to the matter of the qiblah.

The third: it refers to the validity of his prophethood and his law. This is the closest view, because the closest item mentioned to it is His words ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾. Since its apparent meaning demands prophethood and what it contains of the Qur'an, revelation and law, His words ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾ must refer back to it.

**The second issue:** Even though God forbade him from doubting, this does not show that he was in doubt about it. This question has already been explained earlier. And God knows best.

\* \* \*

[Page 119]

﴿For each there is a direction toward which it turns. So race to good deeds. Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together. Indeed God has power over all things.﴾

His words, exalted is He, ﴿For each there is a direction toward which it turns. So race to good deeds. Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together. Indeed God has power over all things.﴾

Know that they differed about the intended meaning of His words ﴿For each﴾, and there are two issues.

**The first issue:** He said ﴿For each﴾ and did not say "for every people or community," because the meaning is known to them, so omitting the mention of what is added to it does no harm. This is common in their speech, as in His words ﴿For each We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48].

**The second issue:** They mentioned four aspects.

The first: it encompasses all groups, meaning the Muslims, the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists. This is the view of al-Asamm, who said: because among the polytheists there were those who worshipped idols and drew near to God by that, as God related of them in His words ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18].

The second, which is the view of most of the scholars of the Followers (tabi'un), is that the intended meaning is the People of the Book, who are the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians, and the polytheists are not included in it.

The third: some said the intended meaning is that for each group of Muslims there is a direction (jihah), that is, a side of the Ka'bah toward which they pray: southern, northern, eastern or western. They argued for this view with two points.

The first: His words ﴿He is the one who turns it﴾, meaning: Allah turns it. And Allah's turning was realised only toward the Ka'bah, because anything else is the turning of Satan.

The second: Allah, exalted is He, followed it with His words ﴿So race to good deeds﴾, and it is apparent that the intended meaning of these good deeds is what belongs to each person from a direction, and the directions described as good are none other than the directions of the Ka'bah.

The fourth: others said: "For each there is a direction" means that for each of the messengers and the possessors of laws there is a direction of qiblah. So the qiblah of the most exalted (muqarrabun) is the Throne, the qiblah of the spiritual beings (ruhaniyyun) is the Footstool, the qiblah of the cherubim (karubiyyun) is the Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur), the qiblah of the prophets before you is Jerusalem, and your qiblah is the Ka'bah.

\* \* \*

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿direction (wijhah)﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** It was recited "wa-li-kulli wijhatin" with an idafah (construction of genitive), and the meaning is: "and every direction is one he turns to." The lam was added because the object was placed first, as in your saying: "To Zayd you struck," and "To Zayd his father is a striker."

**The second issue:** Al-Farra' said: wijhah, jihah and wajh have one meaning. They differed about what is intended. Al-Hasan said: the intended meaning is the method (minhaj) and the law (shar'). This is like His words ﴿For every community We have appointed a rite﴾ [al-Hajj: 67], and ﴿For each We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. The meaning is that the laws have benefits, and therefore laws differ according to the differences of persons. Just as they differ according to the differences of persons, it is also not far-fetched that they differ according to the differences of time with respect to a single person. For this reason the doctrine of abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one) and change is valid. The rest said: the intended meaning is the matter of the qiblah, because His words, exalted is He, ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ came earlier, so this direction must be understood as referring to that.

[Page 120]

As for His words, ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾, there are two interpretations.

The first: the pronoun refers to everyone. That is, for each person there is a direction (*wijhah*) toward which he turns his face (*muwalli wajhahu*) [see note: this is the meaning]
[Page 120]
toward it. The sense of the statement on the first interpretation is: for each of you there is a direction, that is, a side of the qibla, toward which he turns, meaning he faces it, and turns toward it for his prayer, through which he draws near to his Lord. Each one rejoices in what he is upon and does not leave it. So there is no way for you to be united on one qibla, given that the religions are different. ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾: that is, hold fast, O community of Muslims, to your qibla, for you are upon goods from it in this world and the Hereafter. As for this world, it is because of your honour in the qibla of Ibrahim. As for the Hereafter, it is because of the great reward you will receive for submitting to His commands. ﴿For to Allah is your return﴾, and wherever you are in the directions of the earth, Allah will bring you all together ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and He will separate the righteous among you from the wrongdoer, until it becomes clear who among you is obedient and who is disobedient, and who among you is correct and who is mistaken. ﴿Indeed, He is competent over all things.﴾

Whoever holds this interpretation says: the meaning is that each of the people of the religions has a direction that they have chosen, either by a law (*shari'ah*) or by desire. So you will not be held accountable for the deeds of others. ﴿For them is what they have earned and for you is what you have earned.﴾

As for the explanation of the statement on the second interpretation, namely that the pronoun in His words ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾ refers to Allah, there are two views here.

The first: Allah has informed us that each of these two qiblas, which are the Bayt al-Maqdis and the Ka'bah, is a direction that Allah turns His servants toward. If He wills, He does so according to what He knows to be beneficial. So both directions are from Allah, and it is He who turned the faces of His servants toward them. Therefore, race to the good deeds by submitting to the command of Allah in both situations, for your submission is good for you. Do not pay attention to the criticisms of those who say: ﴿What has turned them away from their qibla?﴾ For Allah will gather you and these foolish ones together on the plain of Resurrection, and He will judge between you.

The second: if we interpret His words ﴿and for each there is a direction﴾ as referring to the sides and directions of the Ka'bah, the meaning is: for each group among you, O community of Muslims, there is a direction, that is, a side of the Ka'bah. ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾ by facing it from all the sides. For although they differ, once they all lead to the Ka'bah, they are like one direction. Allah's knowledge of their intentions is not hidden, and He will gather them all and reward them for their deeds.

As for His words, ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾, meaning: he is the one who turns his face toward it, so the mention of "face" is dispensed with. Al-Farra' said: that is, he faces it. Abu Mu'adh said: ﴿muwalliha﴾ carries the sense of *mutawalliha*, as it is said: "He has taken it up, been pleased with it, and followed it." In the reading of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir al-Nakha'i it is read *(huwa mawlaha)*, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Ja'far, and Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir. In the reading of the rest it is *(muwalliha)*. Ibn 'Amir's reading has two meanings. The first: what you have made to turn toward you has made you turn toward it, because the meaning of "you turned it" is that you made it such that it faces you; and when this faces that, that also faces this. So each of the two has turned toward the other, like His words: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37] and ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: ﴿He is its one toward which he turns﴾, meaning: that direction has been beautified for him and made beloved to him, so that he loves it and is pleased with it.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾, its meaning is a command to hasten to obedience at its time. Know that performing the prayer at the beginning of its time is more excellent according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, contrary to Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafi'i argued with several points:

The first: prayer is good, based on his saying ﷺ: "Prayer is the best thing to be established" [*khayr mawdu'*]. Since this is so, it must be that hastening to it is more excellent, based on His words: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾. The apparent meaning of a command is obligation. If that is not established, then at least it is recommendation.

The second: His words: ﴿Race to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [al-Hadid: 21]. Its meaning is: toward what necessitates forgiveness. Prayer is among what necessitates forgiveness, so racing to it must be recommended.

[Page 121]
The third: His words: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost, those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10–11]. There is no doubt that what is meant is the foremost in acts of obedience, and there is no doubt that prayer is among acts of obedience. His words ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ indicate restriction: its meaning is that none are brought near to Allah except the foremost. That indicates that the perfection of virtue is tied to racing.

The fourth: His words: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]. The meaning: hasten to what necessitates forgiveness. There is no doubt that prayer is like this, so hastening to it is commanded.

The fifth: He praised the prophets before us with His words: ﴿Indeed, they used to race to the good deeds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 90]. There is no doubt that prayer is among the good deeds, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "The best of your deeds is prayer."

The sixth: He blamed Iblis for not hastening, saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. This indicates that abandoning hastening necessitates blame.

The seventh: His words: ﴿Guard over the prayers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. Guarding cannot be achieved except by hastening, so that one is safe from missing it through forgetfulness and other preoccupations.

The eighth: His words, recounting Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84]. So it is established that hastening is better.

The ninth: His words: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and fought. They are greater in rank than those who spent afterwards and fought﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. He explained that racing is a cause of greater excellence, so it is likewise in this case.

The tenth: what 'Umar, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, Anas, and Abu Mahdhurah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Prayer at the beginning of its time is the pleasure of Allah, and at its end is the pardon of Allah." Al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The pleasure of Allah is more beloved to us than His pardon."

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The pleasure of Allah is only for the doers of good, while pardon is likely to be for the negligent. If it is said that this is an argument out of place, because it implies that one would be sinful by delaying, and we agree that he is not sinful, then nothing remains except that its meaning is that performing the act at the end of the time necessitates pardon for past misdeeds; and whatever is like that undoubtedly necessitates the pleasure of Allah. So delay necessitates pardon and pleasure, while early performance necessitates pleasure without pardon, so delay is better. We say: this is weak in several respects:

The first: if it were so, then delaying the Maghrib would be more excellent, and no one has said that.

The second: failure to hasten to compliance resembles failure to turn to it, and that would call for punishment, except that when he performs the act afterward, that requirement falls away.

The third: the explanation of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, invalidates this interpretation they have mentioned.

The eleventh: it was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "O 'Ali, do not delay three things: the prayer when it comes, the funeral when it is present, and the unmarried woman when you find a suitable match for her."

The twelfth: "From Ibn Mas'ud, that he asked the Messenger ﷺ, saying: Which deeds are best? He said: Prayer at its first appointed time."

The thirteenth: Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "A man may perform a prayer, though he has missed from its first time [something] better for him than his family and his wealth."

[Page 122]
The fourteenth: he said, peace be upon him: "Whoever establishes a good practice, for him is its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." So whoever is earlier in obedience is the one who establishes the act of obedience at that time, so his reward must be greater than the reward of the one who is later.

The fifteenth: we agree that one of the causes of excellence among the Companions is precedence in accepting Islam, to the extent that a sharp dispute arose between the People of the Sunnah and others as to whether Abu Bakr or 'Ali was earlier in Islam. That dispute arose only because they agree that precedence in obedience necessitates greater excellence, and that indicates our view.

The sixteenth: his words, peace be upon him, in a sermon of his: "Hasten to the righteous deeds before you are occupied." There is no doubt that prayer is among the righteous deeds.

The seventeenth: that hastening the rights of human beings is better than delaying them, so the situation must be the same regarding the rights of Allah, the Exalted. What joins them is observing the meaning of honouring.

The eighteenth: that hastening and racing to prayer is a display of eagerness for obedience, devotion to it, and desire for it, while delay is a sign of laziness regarding it, so the first is more fitting.

The nineteenth: that caution lies in hastening the prayer, for if he performs it at the beginning of its time, his obligation is discharged. If he delays, something may occur to preoccupy him and prevent him from performing it, and the obligation will remain upon him. So the course by which caution is achieved is undoubtedly better.

The twentieth: we agree regarding the fast of Ramadan that hastening it is better than delaying it. That is because the sick person may break his fast and postpone the fast, and he may also hasten and fast immediately. Then we agree that hastening in fasting is more excellent, as He said: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. So it is also necessary that hastening in prayer is more fitting. If it is said: these analogical proofs are refuted by the noon prayer in the intense heat, or by the case where he hopes to catch the congregation, or the availability of water, we say: delay is established in these situations due to incidental matters, whereas our discussion concerns the principle of what is required.

The twenty-first: hastening to compliance is better in custom than not hastening, so it must be the same in the law, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "What the Muslims see as good is good in the sight of Allah."

The twenty-second: a prayer whose conditions are complete must be performed at the beginning of its time, like the Maghrib. This excludes the noon prayer in intense heat, because delay is only recommended when he intends to pray it in the mosque, since walking to the mosque in intense heat is like an obstacle. But if he prays it in his house, hastening is better. This also excludes one who is holding back the two evacuations, or whose food is present while he is hungry, for the same reason. Likewise the one performing tayammum who is confident of finding water, and likewise when he expects the congregation to gather, for perfection is not achieved in these cases. These are the proofs indicating that hastening is more excellent. Let us mention each of the prayers:

As for the Dawn prayer, Muhammad [al-Shaybani] said: it is recommended to begin it in the dark (*taghlis*) and to finish it in the light (*isfar*). If one intends to limit himself to one of the two times, then *isfar* is better. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: *taghlis* is better, and this is the view of Abu [Page 123] Bakr and 'Umar, and Malik and Ahmad also said so. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued, after the preceding proofs, with several points:

First, the narrations on the side of performing the dawn prayer in the darkness:

The first: what is recorded in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) on the authority of ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would pray the Subh (dawn) prayer, and then turn away while the women, wrapped in their cloaks (mutalaffi‘at bi-muruṭihinna), could not be recognized because of the ghalas (the darkness)."

Muhyi al-Sunnah said in his book *Sharh al-Sunnah*: "Mutalaffi‘at bi-muruṭihinna" means covered in their wraps. At-talaffuʿ by a garment is the wrapping of oneself in it. Al-muruṭ are the wide outer garments; its singular is mirṭ. Al-ghalas is the darkness of the last part of the night.

If it is said: this was at the beginning of Islam, when women attended the congregational prayers, so the Prophet (ﷺ) would pray in the ghalas so that they would not be recognized. Likewise ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, would pray in the ghalas. Then, when women were forbidden to attend the congregations, he (ʿUmar) left this practice.

We say: the principle to which one returns in establishing all rulings is the absence of abrogation (naskh). Were it not for this principle, it would not be permissible to derive proof from any of the legal evidences.

The second: what is recorded in the two Sahihs from Qatadah, from Anas, from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "We took the suhur (pre-dawn meal) with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then we stood up for the prayer." I (Anas) said: "How long was the gap between them?" He said: "About fifty verses." This also indicates the taghlis (praying at the earliest, dark part of dawn).

The third: what is reported from Abu Masʿud al-Ansari that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed the dawn prayer in the ghalas, then once he performed it in the isfar (when the light had spread), and after that he did not return to the isfar until Allah took him."

The fourth: Allah Most High praised those who seek forgiveness at dawn, saying: ﴿And those who seek forgiveness in the hours before dawn﴾ (Al ʿImran 3:17), and He praised those who forsake sleep, saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds; they call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾ (As-Sajdah 32:16). If this is established, then forsaking sleep for the performance of obligatory acts must be better, due to His words (ﷺ), relating from Allah: "Those who draw near to Me will not draw near with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon them." And if this is the case, then taghlis must be better.

The fifth: sleep at that time is more pleasant, so forsaking it is harder, and therefore its reward must be greater, due to his words (ﷺ): "The best of acts of worship are the most arduous," meaning the most difficult.

Abu Hanifah argued with several points:

The first: his (ﷺ) words: "Perform the dawn prayer when it is bright (asfirū bil-fajr), for it is greater in reward."

The second: ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud narrated that he prayed the dawn prayer at Muzdalifah in the darkness, then Ibn Masʿud said: "I have not seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pray any prayer except at its appointed time, except the dawn prayer, for he prayed it that day at other than its appointed time."

The third: from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "I have not seen the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) be more careful about anything than about performing the dawn prayer when it is illuminated (at-tanwīr)."

The fourth: from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he prayed the dawn prayer and recited Al ʿImran, and they said: "The sun nearly rose!" He said: "Had it risen, it would not have found us heedless." And from ʿUmar that he recited al-Baqarah, and they looked toward the sunrise, and he said: "Had it risen, it would not have found us heedless."

The fifth: delaying the prayer includes the virtue of waiting for it, and he (ﷺ) said: "The one who waits for the prayer is as if he is in the prayer." So whoever delays the prayer from the beginning of its time has first waited for the prayer and then performed it, while whoever prays at the very beginning of the time has missed the virtue of waiting.

The sixth: delaying leads to a larger congregation, so it must be preferable in order to obtain the virtue of congregational prayer.

The seventh: taghlis causes hardship for people, because if the prayer is performed at the time of taghlis, a person needs to make wudu' at night so that he is free to pray after dawn breaks, and hardship is negated in the Shariah.

The eighth: the prayer is disliked after the dawn prayer, so if one prays at the time of isfar, the time of disliked prayer becomes shorter, and if one prays with taghlis, the time of disliked prayer becomes longer.

As for the answer to the first point: al-fajr is the name for the light by which the darkness of the eastern horizon is dispelled. Thus it is dawn only if darkness is still present in the air. But when the darkness has completely disappeared and the air is fully lit, that is not dawn. As for al-isfar, it means becoming apparent. It is said: "The woman unveiled (asfarat) her face" when she uncovered it. Having established this, we say: the appearance of dawn occurs while darkness remains in the air, for the more intense the darkness, the stronger the light that appears within that darkness. So his saying: "Perform the dawn prayer when it is bright" must be understood as referring to taghlis, meaning: whenever your prayer is performed when the dawn is most apparent and most brilliant, its reward is greater. We have explained that this occurs only at the beginning of dawn. This is the meaning of the words of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, that the isfar mentioned in the hadith is to be understood as certainty of the emergence of dawn and removal of doubt about it. What indicates our view is that performing the prayer at that time is harder, so it must carry greater reward. As for delaying the prayer until the time of tanwir, it is the habit of the lazy. How could the Lawgiver say that laziness is better than striving in obedience?

As for the answer to the second point, which is the saying of Ibn Masʿud: "Be careful about the illumination of dawn," its answer is what we have established, because tanwir at dawn occurs only at the beginning of the time. As for when the world is filled with light, that is not called dawn. As for the remaining points, they are countered by some of what we have already mentioned. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together﴾. This is a promise to those who obey and a warning to those who disobey, as if He, Exalted, said: "Compete in good, O you who are truly aware and knowledgeable of prophethood and the Shariah, and bear hardships for it, so that on the Day of Resurrection you may reach what you have with Allah of the various kinds of honor and nearness." Then, He, glorified is He, confirmed this with His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things capable﴾. This is because resurrection in itself is possible, and He is capable of all possible things, so He must be capable of resurrection. As for the issues derived from this verse, we have already mentioned them in His words: ﴿And if Allah willed, He could take away their hearing and their sight. Indeed, Allah is over all things capable﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:20).

[p. 124]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 149–150 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who commit wrong. So do not fear them, but fear Me, and so that I may complete My favor upon you and that you may be guided.﴾

Know that the first matter of inquiry in this verse is that Allah, exalted is He, said before these verses: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, so We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. And indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what they do.﴾ And He mentioned here, secondly, His saying, may He be exalted:
Page 125
﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ Then He mentioned, thirdly, His saying: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that people will have no argument against you⁠﴾. So is there any benefit in this repetition or not? The scholars have various opinions regarding it.

The first: The states are three. The first is that a person is in the Sacred Mosque. The second is that he leaves the Sacred Mosque and is in the city. The third is that he leaves the city for the regions of the earth. So the first verse is applied to the first state, the second to the second, and the third to the third; for it had been supposed that proximity has a sanctity that does not apply to the servant, so to remove this illusion Allah, exalted is He, repeated these verses.

The second answer: He, glorified is He, repeated that three times because He attached to each time an additional benefit. As for the first time, He made clear that the People of the Book know that the matter of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and the matter of this qiblah are true, because they witnessed that in the Torah and the Gospel. As for the second time, He made clear that He Himself bears witness that this is true, and the testimony of Allah to its being true is distinct from the knowledge of the People of the Book that it is true. As for the third time, He made clear that He only did that so that people would have no argument against you. Since these benefits differ, their repetition is fitting, so that in each repetition one of these benefits is established. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah," to exchange it for a small price. So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79].

The third answer: He, exalted is He, said in the first verse: ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. So it may have occurred to an ignorant person that He did that only seeking the pleasure of Muhammad ﷺ, because He said: ﴿a qiblah that you will be pleased with⁠﴾. So Allah, exalted is He, removed this corrupt illusion by His saying: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord⁠﴾, meaning: We did not turn you to this qiblah merely by your pleasure, but because this turning is the truth from which there is no escape. So facing it is not for the sake of desire and inclination, like the qiblah of the Jews, which was abrogated, and which they maintain only by mere desire and inclination. Then He, exalted is He, said thirdly: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it⁠﴾. The meaning is: persist upon this qiblah at all times and moments, and do not turn away, lest that turning become a cause for criticism of your religion. The conclusion is that the earlier verse is a command to persist in all places, the second is a command to persist in all times and places, and the third is a command to persist in all times and it signals that this will never be abrogated.

The fourth answer: The first command was accompanied by His honoring them with the qiblah they loved, which was the qiblah of their father Ibrahim, peace be upon him.
The second was accompanied by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For each there is a direction toward which he turns⁠﴾, meaning: for every possessor of a call and a religion there is a qiblah he faces.
