So turn yourselves toward the most noble of directions, which Allah, exalted is He, knows to be the truth, and that is His saying: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord⁠﴾. The third was accompanied by Allah, exalted is He, cutting off the argument of those Jews who disputed with him about the matter of the qiblah. So these were three causes, each of which was accompanied by a command to adhere to the qiblah. A parallel to this is to say: Adhere to this qiblah, for it is the qiblah you used to desire. Then it is said: Adhere to this qiblah, for it is the truth, not the qiblah of desire, and that is His saying: ﴿And indeed it is the truth from your Lord⁠﴾. Then it is said: Adhere to this qiblah, for in your adherence to it the arguments of the Jews against you are cut off. And this repetition in this place is like the repetition in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?⁠﴾ [al-Rahman: 13], and likewise what is repeated in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers⁠﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 121].

The fifth answer: This event is the first of the events in which abrogation appeared in our law, so the need called for repetition for the sake of emphasis, establishing, removing doubt, and clarifying the proofs.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do⁠﴾, it means what these obstinate people do, those who conceal the truth while knowing it, and who cast doubt upon the common people by their saying: ﴿What has turned them away from their qiblah which they were upon?⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142], and by saying that he has longed for his birthplace and the religion of his fathers. Allah knows this, so He sent down what nullifies it and uncovers its weakness and feebleness.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you⁠﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: Know that this statement implies disputation and speech that came earlier from the people regarding the matter of the qiblah, so Allah, exalted is He, wished to make clear that this argument is now removed by facing the Ka'bah. Regarding the nature of that argument there are reports.

The first: The Jews said: "He opposes us in our religion and follows our qiblah."
The second: They said: "Did Muhammad not know where to face in his prayer until we guided him?"
The third: The Arabs said: "He used to say: I am upon the religion of Ibrahim, and now he has abandoned facing the Ka'bah, and whoever abandons facing the Ka'bah has abandoned the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him." So these matters became means for them to criticize his legislation, peace and blessings be upon him. However, when Allah, exalted is He, knew that the good in that was that He obligate them to face Bayt al-Maqdis, because of the benefit in religion it contained, since their saying does not affect benefits—and we have already explained earlier that benefit—it was to distinguish those who followed him in Mecca from those who persisted in denying him, for that distinction would only appear through this kind (of test). When he, peace and blessings be upon him, moved to Madinah, the benefit changed, so wisdom required turning the qiblah to the Ka'bah. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you⁠﴾, meaning: that doubt which they mentioned is removed by means of this turning. And since it was known among them that his condition at this turning is that he would cling to another doubt, namely the saying of some Arabs: "Muhammad has returned to our religion regarding the Ka'bah and will return to our religion entirely," adhering to this doubt and persisting upon it was a cause for remaining in ignorance and disbelief, and that is an injustice to oneself, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, association is a tremendous injustice⁠﴾ [Luqman: 13]. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿except those of them who committed injustice⁠﴾.

The second issue: Nafi' read (لِيَلّا) [liyalla], dropping the hamzah, and every open hamzah preceded by a kasrah he changes into a yā'; the rest read with the hamzah, which is the original form.

The third issue: ﴿li'alla⁠﴾ is in the accusative position, and its governing element is (wallū), meaning: turn, so that. Al-Zajjaj said the estimate is: "I informed you of that so that people will have no argument against you."

The fourth issue: It is said: "the people" are the People of the Book, according to Qatadah and al-Rabi'; and it is said: it is general.

The fifth issue: Here there is a question, namely that the doubt of those who wronged themselves is not an argument, so how is it permissible to make an exception from the argument? People have differed on this in several opinions. The first: It is an exception that is connected (istithna' muttasil). On this view the question can be answered in several ways:

The first way: Just as an argument may be sound, it may also be false. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their argument is futile with their Lord⁠﴾ [al-Shura: 16], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever argues with you about it after knowledge has come to you⁠﴾ [Al 'Imran: 61]. Mujadalah (argument) is that each of them presents an argument against the other, and this requires that what the one presenting falsehood is called an argument. Also, "hujjah" is derived from "hajjahu," meaning he overcame him, so every speech intended to overpower another is a hujjah. Some have said it is derived from "mahajjat al-tariq" (the road); so every speech a person takes as a path for himself in establishing or refuting is a hujjah. Since it is established that a doubt may be called a hujjah, the exception is connected.

The second way, in establishing that it is a connected exception: the intended "people" are the People of the Book, for they found in their Book that he, peace be upon him, would change the qiblah; when it was changed, their argument was nullified, except for those who wronged themselves by concealing what they knew; on the authority of Abu Rawq.

The third way: When they presented that doubt believing it to be an argument, Allah named it "argument" according to their belief; or perhaps He named it "argument" in mockery of them.

The fourth way: By "argument" is meant disputation and contention, so He said: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who committed injustice⁠﴾, for they argue against you with falsehood.

The second view: It is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), and its meaning is: "But those of them who wronged cling to the doubt and place it in the position of argument." This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption⁠﴾ [al-Nisa': 157]. Al-Nabighah said:

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of the battalions."

Its meaning: "But their swords have notches, and that is not a fault." It is said: "He has no right over me except transgression," meaning: "But he transgresses and oppresses." A parallel to this is also His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who wrongs⁠﴾ [al-Naml: 10–11], and He said: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah except him upon whom He has mercy⁠﴾ [Hud: 43]. This type of speech is a well-known custom of the Arabs.

The third view: Abu 'Ubaydah claimed that (illa) here means (wa), as if He, exalted is He, said: "so that people will have no argument against you, and [none] for those who wronged," and he recited:

"And every brother separated from his brother — by the life of your father — except the two Farqads."

Meaning: "and the two Farqads."

The fourth view: Qutrub said: the position of (alladhina) is genitive, because it is a substitute (badal) for the kaf and mim in ʿalaykum, as if it were said: "so that there will be no argument against you, except those who wronged; for it will be an argument against them, and they are the disbelievers." 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: these two views are far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 149–150 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾, the meaning is: do not fear those mentioned earlier who harass, dispute and argue, and do not be afraid of their jabs at your qibla, for they cannot harm you. "But fear Me" means: beware of My punishment if you deviate from what I have obligated upon you and enjoined on you. This verse indicates that it is obligatory for a person, in all his actions and abstentions, to keep before his eyes the fear of God's punishment, to know that there is absolutely nothing in the hand of creation, and not to have his heart preoccupied with them nor his thoughts turned toward them.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾, the scholars have differed regarding what the lam (the particle of purpose, "so that") is connected to, in several ways:

The first: it refers to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That people will not have any argument against you﴾ and ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾. God, the Exalted, explained that He turned them to this Ka'bah for these two wisdoms: one, that their argument against Him would be cut off; and the second, the completion of the favor. Abu Muslim ibn Bahr al-Isfahani has explained what favor is in this, namely that the people used to take pride in following Abraham in all that they did. When he (ﷺ) was turned to Bayt al-Maqdis, a weakness of heart afflicted them, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to love the turning to the Ka'bah because of the honor of that place. This is the locus of the favor.

The second: the object of the lam is omitted, meaning: "And for the completion of My favor upon you and My desire for your guidance, I commanded you with that."

The third: it is coordinated with an implied cause, as if it were said: "And fear Me, so that I may grant you success and so that I may complete My favor upon you." The first opinion is closer to the truth.

If it is said: God revealed, near the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed upon you My favor﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], thereby showing that the completion of the favor took place on that day; how then did He say in this verse, many years before that day: ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾? We say: the completion of the favor appropriate to every time is that which He bestowed specifically at that time. And in a hadith: "The completion of the favor is entry into Paradise." And from Ali, may God be pleased with him: the completion of the favor is death upon Islam.

Know that what we have related from Abu Muslim, may God have mercy on him, of doubt regarding the prayer of the Messenger and the prayer of his community toward Bayt al-Maqdis: if his intention is that the wording of the Qur'an does not indicate this, then he is correct, because none of the words of the Qur'an contains any indication of this whatsoever, as we have explained. If he means by it the outright denial of it, then that is far-fetched, because the reports on this are close to being mutawatir (widely transmitted). Abu Muslim, may God have mercy on him, may contest mutawatir; and in that case he says: it is not valid to rely on a solitary report (khabar al-wahid) for the certainty of the occurrence of abrogation (naskh) in our law. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 149–150 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who commit wrong. So do not fear them, but fear Me, and so that I may complete My favor upon you and that you may be guided.﴾

Know that the first matter of inquiry in this verse is that Allah, exalted is He, said before these verses: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, so We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. And indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what they do.﴾ And He mentioned here, secondly, His saying, may He be exalted:
Page 125
﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ Then He mentioned, thirdly, His saying: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that people will have no argument against you⁠﴾. So is there any benefit in this repetition or not? The scholars have various opinions regarding it.

The first: The states are three. The first is that a person is in the Sacred Mosque. The second is that he leaves the Sacred Mosque and is in the city. The third is that he leaves the city for the regions of the earth. So the first verse is applied to the first state, the second to the second, and the third to the third; for it had been supposed that proximity has a sanctity that does not apply to the servant, so to remove this illusion Allah, exalted is He, repeated these verses.

The second answer: He, glorified is He, repeated that three times because He attached to each time an additional benefit. As for the first time, He made clear that the People of the Book know that the matter of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and the matter of this qiblah are true, because they witnessed that in the Torah and the Gospel. As for the second time, He made clear that He Himself bears witness that this is true, and the testimony of Allah to its being true is distinct from the knowledge of the People of the Book that it is true. As for the third time, He made clear that He only did that so that people would have no argument against you. Since these benefits differ, their repetition is fitting, so that in each repetition one of these benefits is established. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah," to exchange it for a small price. So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79].

The third answer: He, exalted is He, said in the first verse: ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. So it may have occurred to an ignorant person that He did that only seeking the pleasure of Muhammad ﷺ, because He said: ﴿a qiblah that you will be pleased with⁠﴾. So Allah, exalted is He, removed this corrupt illusion by His saying: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord⁠﴾, meaning: We did not turn you to this qiblah merely by your pleasure, but because this turning is the truth from which there is no escape. So facing it is not for the sake of desire and inclination, like the qiblah of the Jews, which was abrogated, and which they maintain only by mere desire and inclination. Then He, exalted is He, said thirdly: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it⁠﴾. The meaning is: persist upon this qiblah at all times and moments, and do not turn away, lest that turning become a cause for criticism of your religion. The conclusion is that the earlier verse is a command to persist in all places, the second is a command to persist in all times and places, and the third is a command to persist in all times and it signals that this will never be abrogated.

The fourth answer: The first command was accompanied by His honoring them with the qiblah they loved, which was the qiblah of their father Ibrahim, peace be upon him.
The second was accompanied by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For each there is a direction toward which he turns⁠﴾, meaning: for every possessor of a call and a religion there is a qiblah he faces. So turn yourselves toward the most noble of directions, which Allah, exalted is He, knows to be the truth, and that is His saying: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord⁠﴾. The third was accompanied by Allah, exalted is He, cutting off the argument of those Jews who disputed with him about the matter of the qiblah. So these were three causes, each of which was accompanied by a command to adhere to the qiblah. A parallel to this is to say: Adhere to this qiblah, for it is the qiblah you used to desire. Then it is said: Adhere to this qiblah, for it is the truth, not the qiblah of desire, and that is His saying: ﴿And indeed it is the truth from your Lord⁠﴾. Then it is said: Adhere to this qiblah, for in your adherence to it the arguments of the Jews against you are cut off. And this repetition in this place is like the repetition in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?⁠﴾ [al-Rahman: 13], and likewise what is repeated in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers⁠﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 121].

The fifth answer: This event is the first of the events in which abrogation appeared in our law, so the need called for repetition for the sake of emphasis, establishing, removing doubt, and clarifying the proofs.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do⁠﴾, it means what these obstinate people do, those who conceal the truth while knowing it, and who cast doubt upon the common people by their saying: ﴿What has turned them away from their qiblah which they were upon?⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142], and by saying that he has longed for his birthplace and the religion of his fathers. Allah knows this, so He sent down what nullifies it and uncovers its weakness and feebleness.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you⁠﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: Know that this statement implies disputation and speech that came earlier from the people regarding the matter of the qiblah, so Allah, exalted is He, wished to make clear that this argument is now removed by facing the Ka'bah. Regarding the nature of that argument there are reports.

The first: The Jews said: "He opposes us in our religion and follows our qiblah."
The second: They said: "Did Muhammad not know where to face in his prayer until we guided him?"
The third: The Arabs said: "He used to say: I am upon the religion of Ibrahim, and now he has abandoned facing the Ka'bah, and whoever abandons facing the Ka'bah has abandoned the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him." So these matters became means for them to criticize his legislation, peace and blessings be upon him. However, when Allah, exalted is He, knew that the good in that was that He obligate them to face Bayt al-Maqdis, because of the benefit in religion it contained, since their saying does not affect benefits—and we have already explained earlier that benefit—it was to distinguish those who followed him in Mecca from those who persisted in denying him, for that distinction would only appear through this kind (of test). When he, peace and blessings be upon him, moved to Madinah, the benefit changed, so wisdom required turning the qiblah to the Ka'bah. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you⁠﴾, meaning: that doubt which they mentioned is removed by means of this turning. And since it was known among them that his condition at this turning is that he would cling to another doubt, namely the saying of some Arabs: "Muhammad has returned to our religion regarding the Ka'bah and will return to our religion entirely," adhering to this doubt and persisting upon it was a cause for remaining in ignorance and disbelief, and that is an injustice to oneself, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, association is a tremendous injustice⁠﴾ [Luqman: 13]. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿except those of them who committed injustice⁠﴾.

The second issue: Nafi' read (لِيَلّا) [liyalla], dropping the hamzah, and every open hamzah preceded by a kasrah he changes into a yā'; the rest read with the hamzah, which is the original form.

The third issue: ﴿li'alla⁠﴾ is in the accusative position, and its governing element is (wallū), meaning: turn, so that. Al-Zajjaj said the estimate is: "I informed you of that so that people will have no argument against you."

The fourth issue: It is said: "the people" are the People of the Book, according to Qatadah and al-Rabi'; and it is said: it is general.

The fifth issue: Here there is a question, namely that the doubt of those who wronged themselves is not an argument, so how is it permissible to make an exception from the argument? People have differed on this in several opinions. The first: It is an exception that is connected (istithna' muttasil). On this view the question can be answered in several ways:

The first way: Just as an argument may be sound, it may also be false. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their argument is futile with their Lord⁠﴾ [al-Shura: 16], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever argues with you about it after knowledge has come to you⁠﴾ [Al 'Imran: 61]. Mujadalah (argument) is that each of them presents an argument against the other, and this requires that what the one presenting falsehood is called an argument. Also, "hujjah" is derived from "hajjahu," meaning he overcame him, so every speech intended to overpower another is a hujjah. Some have said it is derived from "mahajjat al-tariq" (the road); so every speech a person takes as a path for himself in establishing or refuting is a hujjah. Since it is established that a doubt may be called a hujjah, the exception is connected.

The second way, in establishing that it is a connected exception: the intended "people" are the People of the Book, for they found in their Book that he, peace be upon him, would change the qiblah; when it was changed, their argument was nullified, except for those who wronged themselves by concealing what they knew; on the authority of Abu Rawq.

The third way: When they presented that doubt believing it to be an argument, Allah named it "argument" according to their belief; or perhaps He named it "argument" in mockery of them.

The fourth way: By "argument" is meant disputation and contention, so He said: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who committed injustice⁠﴾, for they argue against you with falsehood.

The second view: It is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), and its meaning is: "But those of them who wronged cling to the doubt and place it in the position of argument." This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption⁠﴾ [al-Nisa': 157]. Al-Nabighah said:

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of the battalions."

Its meaning: "But their swords have notches, and that is not a fault." It is said: "He has no right over me except transgression," meaning: "But he transgresses and oppresses." A parallel to this is also His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who wrongs⁠﴾ [al-Naml: 10–11], and He said: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah except him upon whom He has mercy⁠﴾ [Hud: 43]. This type of speech is a well-known custom of the Arabs.

The third view: Abu 'Ubaydah claimed that (illa) here means (wa), as if He, exalted is He, said: "so that people will have no argument against you, and [none] for those who wronged," and he recited:

"And every brother separated from his brother — by the life of your father — except the two Farqads."

Meaning: "and the two Farqads."

The fourth view: Qutrub said: the position of (alladhina) is genitive, because it is a substitute (badal) for the kaf and mim in ʿalaykum, as if it were said: "so that there will be no argument against you, except those who wronged; for it will be an argument against them, and they are the disbelievers." 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: these two views are far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 149–150 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾, the meaning is: do not fear those mentioned earlier who harass, dispute and argue, and do not be afraid of their jabs at your qibla, for they cannot harm you. "But fear Me" means: beware of My punishment if you deviate from what I have obligated upon you and enjoined on you. This verse indicates that it is obligatory for a person, in all his actions and abstentions, to keep before his eyes the fear of God's punishment, to know that there is absolutely nothing in the hand of creation, and not to have his heart preoccupied with them nor his thoughts turned toward them.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾, the scholars have differed regarding what the lam (the particle of purpose, "so that") is connected to, in several ways:

The first: it refers to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That people will not have any argument against you﴾ and ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾. God, the Exalted, explained that He turned them to this Ka'bah for these two wisdoms: one, that their argument against Him would be cut off; and the second, the completion of the favor. Abu Muslim ibn Bahr al-Isfahani has explained what favor is in this, namely that the people used to take pride in following Abraham in all that they did. When he (ﷺ) was turned to Bayt al-Maqdis, a weakness of heart afflicted them, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to love the turning to the Ka'bah because of the honor of that place. This is the locus of the favor.

The second: the object of the lam is omitted, meaning: "And for the completion of My favor upon you and My desire for your guidance, I commanded you with that."

The third: it is coordinated with an implied cause, as if it were said: "And fear Me, so that I may grant you success and so that I may complete My favor upon you." The first opinion is closer to the truth.

If it is said: God revealed, near the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed upon you My favor﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], thereby showing that the completion of the favor took place on that day; how then did He say in this verse, many years before that day: ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾? We say: the completion of the favor appropriate to every time is that which He bestowed specifically at that time. And in a hadith: "The completion of the favor is entry into Paradise." And from Ali, may God be pleased with him: the completion of the favor is death upon Islam.

Know that what we have related from Abu Muslim, may God have mercy on him, of doubt regarding the prayer of the Messenger and the prayer of his community toward Bayt al-Maqdis: if his intention is that the wording of the Qur'an does not indicate this, then he is correct, because none of the words of the Qur'an contains any indication of this whatsoever, as we have explained. If he means by it the outright denial of it, then that is far-fetched, because the reports on this are close to being mutawatir (widely transmitted). Abu Muslim, may God have mercy on him, may contest mutawatir; and in that case he says: it is not valid to rely on a solitary report (khabar al-wahid) for the certainty of the occurrence of abrogation (naskh) in our law. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 151:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Just as We have sent among you a Messenger from among yourselves, who recites to you Our verses, purifies you, teaches you the Book and wisdom, and teaches you what you did not know﴾.

Know that we have already explained that Allah, exalted is He, argued for the validity of the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) by several means. Some of them are ad hominem arguments (ilzamiyya), namely that this religion is the religion of Abraham, so it is obligatory to accept it. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And who would turn away from the creed of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ [2:130]. Others are demonstrative arguments (burhaniyya), namely His saying: ﴿Say: We believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes﴾ [2:136]. Then, exalted is He, followed this argument by reporting two doubts raised by them. The first is His saying: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided﴾ [2:135]. The second is their argument, by denying abrogation (naskh), that this sacred law (shari'a) is discredited, which is His saying: ﴿The foolish among the people will say: What has turned them away from the qibla they used to face?﴾ [2:142]. Allah, exalted is He, was lengthy in answering this doubt, and He was right to do so, because the greatest doubt of the Jews in denying the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is their denial of abrogation. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, was indeed lengthy in answering this doubt, and He concluded that answer with His saying: ﴿And that I may complete My favour upon you﴾. Thus this statement, together with the answer to the doubt it contains, is an alert to the great blessings of Allah, exalted is He. Without doubt, this is more compelling for attaining honour and nobility in this world, and escaping humiliation and disgrace is something desired. When both matters come together, it has reached the utmost in this respect.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Just as We have sent﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: this kaf (the word "just as") either relates to what precedes it or to what follows it. If we say it relates to what precedes it, then there are several views:

The first: it refers to His saying: ﴿And that I may complete My favour upon you﴾, meaning: and that I may complete My favour upon you in this world by sending the Messenger.

The second: Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a Messenger from among them who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom and purify them﴾ [2:129], and he also said: ﴿And from our descendants raise a nation submitting to You, and show us our rites﴾ [2:128]. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "And that I may complete My favour upon you by explaining the laws, and guide you to the religion, in response to the supplication of Abraham, just as We have sent among you a Messenger in response to his supplication." This is reported from Ibn Jarir.

The third: the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, which is that the implied meaning is: "And thus We have made you a middle nation, just as We have sent among you a Messenger," meaning: just as We have sent among you a Messenger whose nature and attributes are such and such, so likewise We have made you a middle nation. As for if we say it relates to what follows it, then the implied meaning is: "Just as We have sent among you a Messenger from among you who teaches you the religion and the law, so remember Me and I will remember you." This is the choice of al-Asamm, and its explanation is: You were in a state in which you did not recite a book and did not know a messenger, and Muhammad (ﷺ) is a man from among you, not a possessor of a book. Then he brought you the most wondrous of verses, reciting them to you in your own tongue, and in it is what is in the books of the prophets, and in it is information about their conditions, and in it is an alert to the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God) and ma'ad (the return and the afterlife), and in it is an alert to noble character and a prohibition against the character of fools. In that is the greatest proof of his truthfulness. So He says: "Just as I have bestowed this blessing upon you and made it a proof for you, so remember Me with gratitude for it, and I will remember you with My mercy and reward." What confirms this is His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly conferred favour upon the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves﴾ [3:164]. So when He reminded them of this blessing and kindness, He commanded them, in return for it, to remember and be grateful.

If it is asked: can "kama" (just as) be the answer (jawab) of the imperative? We say: al-Farra' permitted this, and he made the imperative ﴿remember Me﴾ have two answers. One of them is "kama" (just as). The second is ﴿I will remember you﴾. The reasoning for this is that He obligated them to remember so that Allah would remember them with His mercy and for the blessing He had previously bestowed. Al-Qadi said: The first view is more preferable, because when what completes the statement is found before it without separation, then relating it to it is preferable.

Second issue: regarding the aspect of comparison, there are two views. If we say that the kaf relates to His saying ﴿and that I may complete My favour﴾, the meaning is that the blessing in the matter of the qibla is like the blessing of the messengership, because He, exalted is He, does what is best. If we say it relates to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so remember Me﴾, this indicates that the blessing of remembrance runs in the same manner as the blessing of the messengership.

Third issue: the ma in His saying ﴿Just as We have sent﴾ is masdariyya (verbal-noun forming), as if it were said: "like Our sending among you." It may also be kaffa (a particle that restricts the governing word).

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿among you﴾, what is meant is the Arabs. Likewise His saying ﴿from among you﴾. In sending him among them and from among them there are great blessings for them, because of the nobility they have in it, and because it is well known of the condition of the Arabs that they have a fierce aversion to submitting to others. So Allah, exalted is He, sent him from among them, so that they would be closer to acceptance.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿who recites to you Our verses﴾, know that it is among the greatest blessings, because it is a lasting miracle, and because it is recited, through which acts of worship are performed, and because it is recited, from which all the sciences are derived, and because it is recited, from which the comprehensive noble characters are derived. So it is as if all the good of this world and the next is obtained through its recitation.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and purifies you﴾, there are several views:

One of them: that he (ﷺ) teaches them what, if they adhere to it, they become pure; this is reported from al-Hasan.

The second: He purifies them by praise and commendation, meaning He knows the good characters you have and describes you with them, just as it is said: "The one who testifies to the witness, purified him," meaning he described him as being of good standing.

The third: purification is an expression for growth, as if He said: "He will increase you," as He said: ﴿And remember when you were few and He increased you﴾ [7:86]. This is by gathering them upon the truth, so that they unite and increase. This is reported from Abu Muslim. Al-Qadi said: These aspects are not mutually exclusive, so perhaps He, exalted is He, does all of that for the obedient.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and teaches you the Book﴾, it is not a repetition, because reciting the Qur'an to them is other than teaching it to them. As for "wisdom" (al-hikma), it is knowledge of the entire sacred law which the Qur'an contains the details of. For this reason al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Wisdom is the Sunna (practice) of the Messenger, peace be upon him."

As for His saying: ﴿and teaches you what you did not know﴾, this is an alert that He sent him at a time of a gap (fatra) between the messengers and ignorance among the nations. The creation were bewildered and astray regarding their religions, so Allah, exalted is He, sent Muhammad with the truth until he taught them what they needed in their religion, and that is among the greatest kinds of blessings.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 152:

God's words: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you. Give thanks to Me and do not be ungrateful to Me.﴾

Know that God Most High has charged us in this verse with two matters: remembrance (dhikr) and gratitude (shukr). As for remembrance, it may be by the tongue, by the heart, or by the limbs. Remembering Him by the tongue means praising Him, glorifying Him, extolling Him, and reciting His Book. Remembering Him by the heart has three kinds:

The first: that they reflect on the proofs that point to His essence and attributes, and reflect on the answer to the doubts that undermine those proofs.

The second: that they reflect on the proofs that point to the manner of His obligations, rulings, commands, prohibitions, promise and threat. When they know the manner of the obligation, and know what reward is in doing an act and what punishment is in abandoning it, its performance becomes easy for them.

The third: that they reflect on the secrets of God Most High's creation, until every atom of created things becomes like a polished mirror facing the realm of holiness (ʿalam al-qudus). When the servant looks at it, the ray of his sight is reflected from it to the realm of majesty (ʿalam al-jalal). This station has no end.

As for remembering Him by the limbs, it means that their limbs are wholly occupied with the acts they were commanded to perform, and free from the acts they were forbidden to do. In this sense God Most High named the prayer remembrance, in His words: ﴿So hasten to the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Jumuʿah: 9]. Thus the command ﴿So remember Me﴾ includes all acts of obedience. For this reason it is narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: "Remember Me through your obedience to Me," thereby summarizing it so that everything enters into it.

As for His words ﴿I will remember you﴾, it must be understood in a way that suits the context, and what is related to that is reward, praise, the manifestation of approval and honour, and the granting of a high rank. All of this falls under His words ﴿I will remember you﴾.

Then, people have various expressions regarding this verse:

The first: "Remember Me through your obedience, I will remember you with My mercy."

The second: "Remember Me through supplication, I will remember you with response and kindness," and this is equivalent to His words: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. This is the view of Abu Muslim, who said: "He commanded creation to remember Him, desiring and fearing, and hoping and dreading, and to make the remembrance sincerely for Him, free from partners. So when they remember Him by sincerity in His worship and His lordship, He remembers them with kindness, mercy and blessing in this world and the next."

The third: "Remember Me through praise and obedience, I will remember you with praise and blessing."

The fourth: "Remember Me in this world, I will remember you in the Hereafter."

The fifth: "Remember Me in solitude, I will remember you in the wastelands."

The sixth: "Remember Me in ease, I will remember you in affliction."

The seventh: "Remember Me through obedience to Me, I will remember you with My help."

The eighth: "Remember Me through striving against yourselves for My sake, I will remember you with My guidance."

The ninth: "Remember Me with truthfulness and sincerity, I will remember you with deliverance and increased closeness."

The tenth: "Remember Me by My lordship at the opening (al-Fatihah), I will remember you by mercy and servanthood at the close."

[Page 131]

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.﴾**

Know that when He, may He be exalted, made obligatory all acts of worship by His saying ﴿so remember Me﴾, and what pertains to gratitude by His saying ﴿and be grateful to Me﴾, He followed this with an explanation of what helps one to fulfil them, saying ﴿seek help through patience and prayer﴾. He singled out these two because of the assistance they give in acts of worship.

As for patience (ṣabr), it is the restraint of the self in enduring hardships for the sake of Allah, may He be exalted, and accustoming it to bear difficulties and to avoid impatience (jaza'). Whoever trains his self and heart in this discipline finds it easy to perform acts of obedience, to bear the hardships of worship, and to avoid what is forbidden. Some people understood patience as fasting, and others as jihad, because He, may He be exalted, mentioned after it: ﴿and do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 154]. Also, He commanded steadfastness in jihad, saying: ﴿when you meet a company, then stand firm﴾ [al-Anfal: 45], and steadfastness in prayer, that is, in supplication, saying: ﴿And their words were only that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ [Al ʿImran: 147]. However, the view we have chosen is preferable because of the generality of the wording and its not being restricted.

As for seeking help through prayer (ṣalāh), it must be performed with humility and submission to the One worshipped and with sincerity toward Him. One must devote his concern and heart to it and to what is recited in it, so that he reflects upon the promise and the threat, and the encouragement and the warning. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 45]. For this reason we see the people of goodness, at times of calamity, agreed in resorting to prayer. It is narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, "whenever a matter distressed him, he would turn to prayer."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾, meaning in giving them victory, as He said: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137]. It is as if He guaranteed them that if they seek help in His obedience through patience and prayer, He would increase them in success (tawfīq), firmness (tasdīd), and subtle kindnesses (alṭāf), as He said: ﴿And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance﴾ [Maryam: 76].

[Page 132]

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive.﴾**

Know that this verse is similar to His saying in Al 'Imran: ﴿Rather, they are alive, with their Lord, being provided for.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169]. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is as if it were said: "Seek help through patience and prayer in establishing My religion. If, in that establishment, you need to strive against My enemy with your wealth and your bodies, and you do so, and your souls perish, then do not think that you have wasted your souls. Rather, know that your slain are alive with Me." There are several issues here.

**First issue:** Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The verse was revealed concerning the slain of Badr. On that day fourteen men from the Muslims were killed: six from the Muhajirun and eight from the Ansar. From the Muhajirun were: 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Umar ibn Abi Waqqas, Dhu al-Shimalayn, 'Amr ibn Nufaylah, 'Amir ibn Bakr, and Mihja' ibn 'Abd Allah. From the Ansar were: Sa'id ibn Khaythamah, Qays ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir, Zayd ibn al-Harith, Tamim ibn al-Hammam, Rafi' ibn al-Mu'alla, Harithah ibn Suraqah, Mu'awwidh ibn 'Afra', and 'Awf ibn 'Afra'. They used to say, "So-and-so has died, and so-and-so has died," so Allah, exalted is He, forbade that it be said of them that they had died. And it was narrated from others that the disbelievers and the hypocrites said: "People kill themselves seeking the pleasure of Muhammad for no benefit," so this verse was revealed.

**Second issue:** "Dead" (*amwat*) is in the nominative case because it is the predicate of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), whose full form is: "Do not say: they are dead."

**Third issue:** Concerning the verse there are several opinions.

*The first opinion:* They are alive at this very time, as if Allah, exalted is He, had made them alive in order to deliver the reward to them. This is the view of most of the commentators. It is a proof that the obedient receive their reward while they are in their graves. If it is said: "We see their bodies dead in the graves, so how can what you have claimed be valid?" We answer: As for us, the bodily structure is not a condition for life, and there is no impossibility in Allah restoring life to each of those particles and tiny parts without any need for composition and assembly. As for the Mu'tazilah, it is not far-fetched that Allah restores life to the parts that are necessary for the essence of a living being, and that the extremities are not taken into account. It is also possible that He makes them alive without their being observed.

*The second opinion:* Al-Asamm said: It means: do not call them "the dead," but say to them "the martyrs who are alive." It is also possible that the polytheists said that they were "dead in religion," as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life?﴾ [Al An'am: 122]. So He said: Do not say to the martyrs what the polytheists said, but say: they are alive in religion, but you do not perceive, meaning the polytheists do not know that whoever is killed upon the religion of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, is alive in religion, and upon guidance from his Lord and light. As has been related in some anecdotes, a man said to another: "No man has died who left behind someone like you." And it is reported from Buqrat (Hippocrates) that he used to say to his students: "Die by the will, and you will live by nature," that is, by the spirit.

*The third opinion:* The polytheists used to say: The companions of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, kill themselves and lose their lives, so they leave this world for nothing, and waste their lives for no purpose. Those who said this may have been materialists (*dahriyyah*) who denied the Return, or they may have believed in the Return but denied the prophethood of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and therefore said this statement. So Allah, exalted is He, said: Do not say, as the polytheists said, that they are dead who will not be raised up and will not benefit from what they bore of hardships in this world. Rather, know that they are alive, that is, they will live, and they will be rewarded and made to enjoy bliss in Paradise. And the interpretation of His saying "alive" as "they will live" is not far-fetched. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous are in bliss﴾ ﴿and indeed, the wicked are in Hellfire﴾ [Al Infitar: 13-14], and He said: ﴿Its enclosure surrounds them﴾ [Al Kahf: 29], and He said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾ [An Nisa': 145], and He said: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in gardens of bliss﴾ [Al Hajj: 56], in the sense that they will become like that. This opinion was chosen by al-Ka'bi and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani. Know that most scholars favor the first opinion, and there are several proofs for it:

*First:* The verses that indicate the punishment of the grave, such as His saying: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice"﴾ [Ghafir: 11]. The two deaths are not realized except when life exists in the grave. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They were drowned, then they were made to enter a Fire﴾ [Nuh: 25], and the "fa'" (then) indicates sequence. And He said: ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the day the Hour is established: "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the severest punishment"﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. When the punishment of the grave is established, it is also necessary to affirm the reward of the grave, because punishment is Allah's right over the servant, and reward is the servant's right over Allah, exalted is He. Thus, if He removes the punishment until the Day of Resurrection, or rather establishes it in the grave, then it is more fitting that He does so for the reward.

*Second:* If the meaning were as was said in the second and third opinions, then His saying ﴿but you do not perceive﴾ would have no meaning, because the address is to the believers, and they did not know that they would live on the Day of Resurrection, and that they had died upon guidance and light. So it is known that the matter is as we have said: that Allah, exalted is He, made them alive in their graves.

*Third:* His saying: ﴿and they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 170] is evidence for the occurrence of life in the barzakh (intermediate realm) before the resurrection.

*Fourth:* His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise, or a pit from the pits of the Fires." And the reports concerning the reward and punishment of the grave are almost mutawatir (widely transmitted). And he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say at the end of his prayer: "And I seek refuge in You from the punishment of the grave."

*Fifth:* If what is meant by His saying "they are alive" were that they will live, then singling them out with this would have no benefit. Abu Muslim answered this by saying that He singled them out for mention only because their rank in Paradise is higher, and their station is loftier and more noble, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger—those will be with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets, the steadfast of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [An Nisa': 69], so He mentioned them to honor them.

But know that this answer is weak, because the station of the prophets and the steadfast of truth is greater, and yet Allah, exalted is He, did not single them out for mention.

*Sixth:* People visit the graves of the martyrs and venerate them, and this indicates, in some respects, what we have mentioned. Abu Muslim argued in favor of his opinion by saying that He, exalted is He, mentioned this verse in Al 'Imran, saying: ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord﴾, and this "with" (*'indiyyah*) is not one of place, but of being in Paradise. And it is known that the people of reward do not enter Paradise except after the Resurrection.

The response: We do not concede that this "with" means only being in Paradise; rather it means the elevation of ranks and the delivery of glad tidings to them while they are in the grave or in another place.

Know that there is another opinion regarding the verse, namely that the reward and punishment of the grave are for the spirit, not the body. This view is based on knowledge of the spirit, and we shall present a summary of the essence of the argument of these people. They said: A human being cannot be identified with this perceptible bodily frame. As for why he cannot be identified with this frame, there are two reasons:

*The first reason:* The parts of this frame are always in growth, decay, increase, decrease, maturation, and dissolution. There is no doubt that the human being, in and of himself, is something that remains from the beginning of his life, and what remains is not what does not remain. The one referred to by everyone with the words "I" must be different from this frame.

*The second reason:* I know that I am I while I am unaware of all my parts and limbs, and what is known is not what is unknown. So the one I refer to with my words "I" is different from these organs and limbs. As for the claim that the human being is not perceptible, this is because what is perceptible is only the surface and the color, and there is no doubt that the human being is not merely color and surface.

Then they differed about what it is that everyone refers to with the word "I." The opinions on this are many, but the most concise and comprehensive are two.

One of them: Bodily parts that flow through this frame like fire flowing through charcoal, oil through sesame, or rosewater through the rose. Those who hold this view are of two groups. One group believes in the similarity of bodies and says: those bodies are similar to the rest of the parts of which this frame is composed, except that the Capable, the Chooser, glorified is He, preserves some of the parts from the beginning of life to its end. Those parts are what everyone refers to with the word "I." Those parts are then living by a life which Allah, exalted is He, creates in them, and when life departs they die. This is the view of most of the theologians (*mutakallimun*). The second group believes in the difference of bodies, and they assert that the bodies that remain from the beginning of life to the end of life are different in essence and reality from the bodies of which this frame is composed. Those bodies are living by their own essence and perceiving by their own essence. When they mix with this body and become flowing through this frame, like fire flowing through charcoal, this frame becomes illuminated by the light of that spirit and moves by its movement. Then this frame is always in dissolution, disintegration, and transformation, but those parts remain in their state, and disintegration does not befall them because they are different in essence from these perishable bodies. When this vessel perishes, those subtle, luminous bodies separate and depart to the realm of the heavens, holiness, and purity if they are among the blessed, and to Hell and the realm of calamities if they are among the wretched.

The second opinion: That which everyone refers to with the words "I am existent" is neither spatially located nor subsisting in a spatially located thing, and it is neither inside the world nor outside the world. It does not follow from its being so that it must be like Allah, exalted is He, because sharing in attributes of negation does not entail sharing in essence. They argued for this by saying that among the known things there is something that is truly singular (*fard*), so the knowledge of it must be truly singular, and therefore the one characterized by that knowledge must be truly singular. Every body, and every accident in a body, is not truly singular. So that which is truly said of us, that it knows these singular things, must be neither a body nor corporeal. As for the claim that among known things there is something truly singular, this is because there is no doubt that something exists. If this existent is truly singular, then it is the desired conclusion. If it is composite, then the composite is composed upon a singular, so a singular must exist in every case. As for the claim that if among known things there is something singular, then among the knowable there is something singular, this is because the knowledge related to that singular, if it is divisible, then each of its parts, or some of its

They say: the knowledge of that object is either its parts' knowledge of it, which is impossible, because it would follow that a part equals the whole, which is impossible. Or none of its parts is knowledge of that object. Then, when those parts combine, either a new addition arises, which is the knowledge of that individual object, and in that case the knowledge of that object is this newly arising state and not those things we supposed before it. Then, if this state is divisible, the discussion returns to it; and if it is not divisible, that is what was sought. As for the claim that if there is knowledge in the object that does not accept division, then the thing described by it is also like that, the reason is this: if the thing described by it accepted division, then each of those parts, or some of them, would be described by it in its entirety. In that case, one accident (ʿaraḍ) would inhere in many things, which is impossible. Or the parts of the inhering thing would be distributed over the parts of the locus (maḥall), so the inhering thing would be divided, though we have assumed it is not divisible. Or no part of the locus would be described by it except through the whole inhering thing, and none of the parts of that inhering thing would be, in which case that locus would be empty of that inhering thing, though we have supposed it is described by it. This is a contradiction (khulf). As for the claim that every spatially extended thing (mutaḥayyiz) is divisible, it is established by the proofs mentioned in negating the indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard). They said: It is thus established that what each person points to with his saying, "I exist," is neither spatially extended nor subsisting in something spatially extended.

Then we say: this existent must necessarily perceive particulars, for I cannot judge of this indicated person that he is a human and not a horse, and the one who judges something concerning something must bring before himself both the subject and the predicate. So this thing perceives this particular and also the universal human, so that it can judge by this universal concerning this particular. The perceiver of universals is the soul (nafs), and the perceiver of particulars is also the soul. Therefore, whoever perceives particulars is not precluded from experiencing pleasure and pain.

They said: When this is established, we say: these spirits, after separation, experience pain and pleasure until God Most High returns them to the bodies on the Day of Resurrection, and there pleasure and pain occur for the bodies. This is a view held by a group of people. They said: Suppose there is no conclusive proof for this view, yet there is no proof for its invalidity either; and it is something that supports the Law (sharʿ), upholds the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and removes doubts and misgivings about what has come in the Book of God concerning the reward and punishment of the grave. Therefore it is necessary to turn to it. This is the brief indication in explaining this view, and God is the One who knows the realities of matters.

They said: What further confirms this view is that the reward and punishment of the grave either reach this structured body or reach a part of its parts. The first is plain denial, because we find this body scattered and torn apart, so how can it be said that reward and punishment reach it? Nothing remains but to say that God Most High revives some of those small parts and conveys reward and punishment to them. And if that is permissible, why should it not be said that the human being is the spirit, for it is not subject to dispersal and tearing apart, so pain and pleasure certainly reach it. Then He, glory be to Him and exalted, returns the spirit to the body on the Great Day of Resurrection, so that bodily states are joined to spiritual states.

[Page 136]

Know that al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is connected to His words, ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾ (2:45). That is, seek help through patience and prayer, for We test you with fear and with such-and-such. There are several issues in this.

The first issue: It may be asked, He said, ﴿Be grateful to Me and do not deny Me﴾ (2:152), and gratitude calls for increase, as He said, ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ (14:7). So how does He follow this with, ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear﴾? The answer has two aspects:

The first: He informed that the completion of the laws is the completion of the blessing, and this calls for gratitude. Then He informed that carrying out those laws is not possible except by enduring trials, so He commanded patience in them.

The second: He first bestowed blessings and commanded gratitude, then He tested and commanded patience, so that a person may attain the rank of those who are both grateful and patient, and thus his faith is perfected. As he (peace be upon him) said: "Faith is of two halves: half patience and half gratitude."

The second issue: It is narrated from ʿAṭāʾ and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas that the address here is to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) after the Hijrah.

* * *

The third issue: As for how testing can be attributed to Allah, the Most Blessed and Exalted, this has already been explained in the commentary on His words, ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord﴾ (2:124). As for the wisdom in mentioning this testing beforehand, there are several aspects:

One: So that they may prepare themselves to endure patiently when these come upon them, which will keep them further from despair and make it easier for them after they occur.

Two: When they know that these trials will reach them, their fear will intensify, and that fear becomes an early experience of the trial, so they deserve greater reward because of it.

Three: When the unbelievers see Muhammad and his Companions remaining steadfast in their religion, firmly upon it, despite the extreme harm, trial and hunger they endure, they will know that these people chose this religion because they are certain of its truth. This will prompt them to reflect more on its proofs. It is clear and known that when followers know that their leader is in the greatest trials because of the doctrine he supports, and then they see him remaining insistent upon that doctrine, this is more likely to make them follow him than if they saw him living in comfort, without hardship in that doctrine.

Four: He informed of the occurrence of this trial before it happened, and then the one who gave this information was found to be exactly as he had said. This was news of the unseen, and so it was a miracle.

Five: Among the hypocrites were those who showed following the Messenger out of greed for wealth and abundant provision. When Allah tests them with these trials, the hypocrite is distinguished from the sincere one, because when the hypocrite hears of such things he flees from it and abandons his religion. So this test had this benefit.

Six: A person's sincerity during affliction, and his returning to the door of Allah, the Most High, is greater than his sincerity when the world turns towards him. So the wisdom of this trial is that.

The fourth issue: He said bi-shayʾin ("with something") in the singular and did not say bi-ashyāʾ ("with things") in the plural, for two reasons.

The first: So that it does not give the impression of things from each category, which would indicate all kinds of fear. The implied meaning is: with something of such-and-such, and something of such-and-such.

The second: Its meaning is with a small amount of these things.

* * *

The fifth issue: Know that everything that meets you, whether disliked or loved, falls into what exists in the present, what existed in the past, and what will exist in the future. If something that existed in the past comes to your mind, it is called remembrance (dhikr) and recollection (tadhakkur). If it exists in the present, it is called taste (dhawq) and experience (wajd). It is called wajd because it is a state you find in yourself. If it comes to your mind that something will exist in the future, and this overwhelms your heart, it is called expectation (intiẓār) and anticipation (tawaqquʿ). If the awaited thing is disliked, a pain arises in the heart which is called fear (khawf) and apprehension (ishfāq). If it is loved, this is called elation (irtiyāḥ), and elation is hope (rajāʾ). So fear is the heart's contemplation while awaiting what is disliked by it, and hope is the heart's elation while awaiting what is loved by it.

As for hunger (jūʿ), it refers to drought and the difficulty of obtaining food. Al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: As for intense fear, it occurred to them when they confronted the Arabs because of the religion. They were not safe from the Arabs' intention to attack them and gather against them. There was much fear during the Battle of the Confederates, as Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking﴾ (33:11). As for hunger, it afflicted them at the beginning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration to Medina because of the scarcity of their wealth, to the extent that he (peace be upon him) would tie a stone to his stomach. Abū al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihān narrated that when he (peace be upon him) went out, he met Abū Bakr, and he said: "What brought you out?" He said: "Hunger." He said: "What brought you out is what brought me out."

As for loss of wealth and lives, this occurs during warfare with the enemy, when a person spends his wealth in preparation for jihad and may be killed. Then there occurs a loss of wealth and life. Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿Strive with your wealth and your lives﴾ (9:41). Hunger may also occur during the journey of jihad when provisions run out. Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿That is because they are not afflicted by thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of Allah﴾ (9:120). The loss of lives may also occur through the death of some brethren and relatives, according to the interpretation of His words: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ (4:29). As for the loss of fruits, it may occur through drought, or through neglect of cultivating lands due to occupation with fighting the enemies, and it may also occur through spending on those who came as delegations to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the end of al-Qaffal's words (may Allah have mercy on him).

Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The fear is the fear of Allah; the hunger is the fast of the month of Ramadan; the loss of wealth is zakat and voluntary charity; the loss of lives is illness; and the loss of fruits is the death of children.

* * *

Then, when He, the Most High, mentioned these things, He explained the category of those who are patient in these matters, by His words: ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾. There are several issues in this:

The first issue: Know that patience is obligatory in these matters when they come from Him, the Most High, because He knows that all of that is justice and wisdom. As for one who is not firmly established in faith, he is like the one of whom He said: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is reassured by it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face; he has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾ (22:11). As for what comes from the side of wrongdoers, patience is not obligatory regarding it. An example: an adolescent is obligated to be patient with what his father does to him in the way of discipline, but if someone else did it to him, he would have the right to resist, even to fight. Similarly with a slave and his master. What Allah, the Most High, arranges for His servants in this regard is nothing but wisdom and righteousness, unlike what the servants do of injustice.

The second issue: The address in (wa-bashshir, "and give good tidings") is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone from whom good tidings can come.

The third issue: Shaykh al-Ghazālī (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Know that patience is among the special qualities of man, and it cannot be conceived in animals or angels. As for animals, it is because of their deficiency; as for angels, it is because of their perfection. Its explanation: animals are subjected to desires, and their desires have no intellect that opposes them, so the steadfastness of that force against the demand of desire is not called patience. As for the angels, they were created solely for longing for the presence of Lordship and for delight in the rank of nearness to it. No desire was imposed upon them to turn them away from it, so that they would need to clash with what diverts them from the presence of majesty by means of another army. As for man, he was created in early childhood deficient, like an animal, and only the desire for nourishment that he needs was created in him. Then the desire for play appears in him, then the desire for marriage. He has absolutely no power of patience, since patience is an expression of the steadfastness of one army against another army, when fighting takes place between them due to the opposition of their aims. As for the adult, he has a desire that calls him to pursue immediate pleasures and turn away from the Hereafter, and he has an intellect that calls him to turn away from them and to seek lasting spiritual pleasures. When the intellect realizes that occupation with pursuing these immediate pleasures [prevents him] from reaching those lasting pleasures, the call of the intellect becomes that which repels and prevents the call of desire from acting. This repelling and prevention is called patience.

Know further that patience is of two kinds. The first is physical, such as bearing hardships with the body and remaining steadfast in them, and this is either actual, such as undertaking laborious work, or potential, such as patience under severe beating and great pain.

The second is the patience of the soul, which is restraining the soul from the demands of desire and the cravings of nature. This kind, if it is patience regarding the desire of the stomach and the private parts, is called chastity (ʿiffah). If it is enduring something disliked, its names differ among people according to the disliked thing one is patient with. If it is in a calamity, it is called patience only, and its opposite is a state called anxiety (jazaʿ) and panic (halaʿ), which is the release of the call of passion in raising the voice, striking the cheek, tearing the collar, and other things. If it is in a state of wealth, it is called self-control, and its opposite is a state called insolence (baṭar). If it is in war and fighting, it is called courage (shajaʿah), and its opposite is cowardice (jubn). If it is in restraining anger and rage, it is called forbearance (ḥilm), and its opposite is hastiness (nazaq). If it is in one of the afflictions of time that is distressing, it is called breadth of chest (saʿat al-ṣadr), and its opposite is distress, regret, and constriction of the chest. If it is in concealing speech, it is called keeping one's secret (kitmān al-nafs), and its possessor is called secretive (katūm). If it is about the superfluities of life, it is called asceticism (zuhd), and its opposite is greed (ḥirṣ). If it is about a small amount of wealth, it is called contentment (qanaʿah), and its opposite is avarice (sharah). Allah, the Most High, has gathered all these categories and called them all patience, when He said: ﴿And the patient in misfortune﴾ (2:177), that is, calamity; ﴿and adversity﴾, that is, poverty; ﴿and at the time of battle﴾ (2:177), that is, fighting; ﴿Those are the ones who are true, and those are the God-fearing﴾ (2:177).

Al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Patience is not that a person does not feel the pain of the disliked thing, nor that he does not dislike it, because that is impossible. Rather, patience is restraining the soul from showing anxiety. If he suppresses grief and restrains his soul from displaying its effects, the one who does so is patient, even if a tear appears in his eye or his color changes. He (peace be upon him) said: "Patience is at the first shock." This is so, because one who at the beginning showed what would not count him among the patient, and then became patient, this is called consolation (salw), and it is something unavoidable. Al-Ḥasan said: If people were commanded to continue in anxiety, they would not be able to bear it. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**Fourth issue: on the virtue of patience.** God Most High has described the patient with various attributes and mentioned patience in the Qur'an in about seventy places. He attributed most of the good things to it. He said: ﴿And We made among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24]. He said: ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience﴾ [al-A'raf: 137]. He said: ﴿And We will surely reward those who were patient with the best of what they used to do﴾. He said: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice because of their patience﴾ [al-Qasas: 54]. He said: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [al-Zumar: 10]. Every act of obedience has a measured reward, except patience. Because fasting is a form of patience, He said: (Fasting is Mine), attributing it to Himself. He promised the patient that He is with them, saying: ﴿And be patient; indeed, God is with the patient﴾ [al-Anfal: 46]. He made victory conditional upon patience, saying: ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear God, and they come at you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels﴾ [Al 'Imran: 125]. He gathered for the patient things He did not gather for others, saying: ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and it is they who are guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 157].

As for the reports, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Patience is half of faith." Its explanation is that faith is not complete except after abandoning what is not fitting of statements, actions and beliefs, and after achieving what is fitting. So persistence in abandoning what is not fitting is patience, and it is the other half. According to the implication of this statement, all of faith should be patience. However, abandoning what is unfitting and doing what is fitting may coincide with one's desire, in which case it does not require patience, or it may oppose one's desire, in which case it requires patience. Therefore, he made patience half of faith. He (ﷺ) also said: "Among the best of what you have been given is certainty and steadfast patience. Whoever is given his share of these two does not mind what he misses of night prayer and day fasting." He (ﷺ) also said: "Faith is patience." This resembles his saying (ﷺ): "Hajj is Arafah."

**Fifth issue: whether patience is superior to gratitude.** Shaykh al-Ghazali (may God have mercy on him) said: The indications of the reports regarding the virtue of patience are stronger. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Among the best of what you have been given is certainty and steadfast patience." He also said: "The most grateful people of the earth will be brought forward, and God will reward them with the reward of the grateful. The most patient people of the earth will be brought forward, and it will be said to him: 'Are you content that We reward you as We rewarded this grateful one?' He will say: 'Yes, my Lord.' God Most High will say: 'I bestowed favors upon you and you were grateful, and I tested you and you were patient. I will surely multiply the reward for you,' and he will be given multiples of the reward of the grateful." As for his (ﷺ) saying: "The one who eats and is grateful is like the one who fasts and is patient," it is evidence of the virtue of patience, because this is mentioned in the context of exaggeration, and exaggeration is only achieved when the one compared to is greater in rank than the one compared, as in his (ﷺ) saying: "The drinker of wine is like the worshipper of an idol." Also, it is related that Sulayman (peace be upon him) enters Paradise forty autumns after the prophets because of his kingdom, and the last of the Companions to enter Paradise is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf because of his wealth. In a report: "All the gates of Paradise are double-leaved except the gate of patience, which is single-leaved, and the first to enter it will be the people of trials, led by Ayyub (peace be upon him)."

**Sixth issue: this verse indicates several matters.**
First: these trials need not be punishments, because God promised them to the believers among the Messenger and his Companions.
Second: when these trials are accompanied by patience, they yield a high rank in religion.
Third: all these trials come from God Most High, contrary to the view of the Dualists who attribute diseases and other things to something else, and contrary to the view of the astrologers who attribute them to the fortunate or unfortunate positions of the stars.
Fourth: they indicate that food does not itself produce satiety, and drinking water does not itself produce quenching of thirst; rather, all of that occurs through what God has established as customary with these causes. This is because His saying ﴿And We will surely test you﴾ is explicit in attributing these matters to God Most High. The statement of whoever says that since God created their causes, this statement is valid, is weak, because it is a metaphor, and resorting to metaphor is not permissible except after the literal meaning is impossible.

[Page 139]

[Page 140]

Its Exalted Word: ﴿Those who, when a calamity strikes them, say: "Indeed we belong to God, and indeed to Him we return."﴾ ﴿They are the ones upon whom are blessings from their Lord, and mercy. And they are the ones who are guided.﴾

Know that when the Exalted said, ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾, He explained in this verse how a person becomes patient, and what that good tidings is. Then there are several issues in the verse.

**First issue:** Know that these calamities may come from the act of God, the Exalted, and may come from the act of the servant. As for the fear that comes from God, it is like fear of drowning, burning, lightning, and other such things. As for that which comes from the act of the servant, it is that the Arabs were united in enmity against the Prophet (ﷺ). As for hunger, it is due to poverty, and poverty may come from God by destroying their wealth, and it may come from the servant by their being overpowered and having their property destroyed. The loss of wealth from God, the Exalted, occurs only through the calamities that strike wealth and crops. From the enemy, it occurs because the people, being occupied, cannot devote themselves to cultivating the lands. The loss of lives from God is through causing death, and from the servants is through killing.

**Second issue:** The Qadi (judge) said: He, the Exalted, did not attribute this calamity to Himself but generalized, saying: ﴿Those who, when a calamity strikes them﴾. The apparent meaning is that it includes every harm that befalls a person from God, the Exalted, and that befalls them from people. This is because in both cases there is a duty upon him. If he turns away from it to its opposite, he has abandoned adherence to its fulfillment. So what befalls him from the side of God, the Exalted, he must believe that it is wisdom, rightness, justice, goodness, and righteousness; and that what is obligatory upon him is to be content with it and to abandon impatience. All of this is included in His saying: ﴿Indeed we belong to God﴾, because in their affirmation of servitude there is the entrusting of affairs to Him and contentment with His decree regarding what He tests them with, since He does not decree except with truth, as the Exalted said: ﴿And God judges with truth, while those they call upon besides Him judge nothing﴾ [Ghafir: 20].
