As for when a calamity befalls him from someone else, his duty is to return to God, the Exalted, for vindication from him, and to restrain his anger and rage, so that he does not transgress beyond what is lawful for him in the way of retaliation for his anger. It is also included in His saying: ﴿Indeed we belong to God﴾, because it is He who obligated him to follow this way so that he does not exceed His command. It is as if he says at first: "Indeed we belong to God; He manages us as He wills," and in the second he says: "Indeed we belong to God; He will vindicate us as He wills."

**Third issue:** Al-Kisa'i inclined the vowel in some transmissions in (innā) and in the lam of (lillāh), while the others used the full (non-inclined) pronunciation. The inclination (imalah, pronouncing the alif toward an i-sound) of this alif was permissible because of the kasrah and the frequency of use, until it became like a single word. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: it is not permissible to incline (innā) with anything other than the name of God, the Exalted. It is necessary for this reason because the original principle for particles and what is treated like them is the prohibition of inclination. Likewise, it is not permissible to incline (ḥattā) and (lākinna).

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed we belong to God, and indeed to Him we return﴾, there are issues in it:

**First issue:** Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: ﴿Indeed we belong to God﴾ is our affirmation to Him of dominion; ﴿and indeed to Him we return﴾ is our affirmation against ourselves of perishing. Know that returning to Him is not an expression for moving to a place or direction, for that is impossible for God. Rather, what is meant is that one comes to a state in which no one else holds the judgment over him, and that is the Last Abode, because at that time no one owns benefit or harm for them. While they are in this world, someone other than God may apparently possess benefit and harm for them. So God, the Exalted, made this a return to Him, the Exalted, just as it is said: dominion and rule return to Him, not in the sense of moving, but in the sense of power and abandoning dispute.

**Second issue:** This indicates that this is an affirmation of resurrection and rising again, and an acknowledgment that He, glorified is He, will recompense the patient according to the measure of their deserving, and that the reward of the good-doers is not lost with Him.

**Third issue:** His saying ﴿Indeed we belong to God﴾ indicates that he is content with all the kinds of trial that have befallen him at present. His saying ﴿and indeed to Him we return﴾ indicates that he is, at present, content with everything that will befall him afterward: from His rewarding him for what he has done, and from the entrusting of the matter to Him regarding what has befallen him, and from vindication against one who wronged him. Thus he becomes one who humbles himself, content with what God has promised him of reward in the Hereafter.

**Fourth issue:** The reports on this subject are many.

The first of them: from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever says the words of return at a calamity, God will mend his calamity, make its outcome good for him, and give him a good successor whom he is pleased with."

The second: "It is narrated that the lamp of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out, and he said: 'Indeed we belong to God, and indeed to Him we return.' It was said: 'Is it a calamity?' He said: 'Yes, everything that harms the believer is a calamity for him.'"

The third: Umm Salamah said: Abu Salamah narrated to me that he (peace be upon him) said: "No Muslim who is afflicted with a calamity and then turns to what God commanded him, [saying]: ﴿Indeed we belong to God, and indeed to Him we return﴾, O God, with You I seek reward for my calamity, so reward me for it and compensate me with something better than it, but God will reward him for it and compensate him with something better than it." She said: When Abu Salamah died, I recalled this hadith and said this statement, and God the Exalted compensated me with Muhammad (peace be upon him).

The fourth: Ibn 'Abbas said: God informed that when the believer submits to the command of God, the Exalted, and returns and says the words of return at his calamity, God, the Exalted, records for him three qualities: the blessings (ṣalawāt) from God, mercy, and the realization of the path of guidance.

The fifth: From 'Umar (may God be pleased with him), he said: "What excellent two supports these are: ﴿They are the ones upon whom are blessings from their Lord, and mercy﴾; and what an excellent addition is His saying: ﴿And they are the ones who are guided.﴾" And Ibn Mas'ud said: "To fall from the sky is dearer to me than to say about something that God has decreed: 'I wish it had not been.'"

As for His saying: ﴿They are the ones upon whom are blessings from their Lord, and mercy﴾, know that the blessings (ṣalāh) from God are: praise, commendation, and exaltation. As for His mercy, it is: the favors He sends down upon them, first in this world and then in the next.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And they are the ones who are guided﴾, there are several aspects to it:

The first: They are the ones guided to this way, which brings its follower to every good.

The second: They are the ones guided to Paradise, who attain the reward.

The third: They are guided to all that has become obligatory upon them. The closer view on this is what becomes included in the promise, so that its conjunction with what He mentioned of blessings and mercy is correct. It cannot be so unless what is meant is that they are the ones who attain the reward, Paradise, and the path to it; for all of that is included in guidance. Yet it is not impossible that what is meant is that they are those who observe its etiquette and adhere to what He has obligated and commanded.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: The verse includes two rulings: obligatory (fard) and voluntary (nafl). As for the obligatory, it is submission to the command of God, the Exalted, and contentment with His decree, and patience in performing His obligations, which the calamities of this world do not divert one from. As for the voluntary, it is the open declaration of His saying: ﴿Indeed we belong to God, and indeed to Him we return﴾, for in declaring it there are great benefits. Among them: others follow his example when they hear it; and among them: it enrages the disbelievers and makes them aware of his earnestness, striving in the religion of God, steadfastness upon it, and upon obedience to Him.

It is related from Da'ud al-Ta'i, who said: Asceticism in this world is not to love remaining in it, the best of deeds is contentment with God, and it is not fitting for the Muslim to grieve, because he knows that for every calamity there is a reward.

Let us conclude the interpretation of this verse by explaining contentment with the decree. We say: The servant only remains patient, content with the decree of God, the Exalted, by two paths: either by the path of disposition (taṣarruf), or by the path of attraction (jadhb). As for the path of disposition, it is by several aspects:

The first: Whenever his heart inclines to something and his thought turns to something, he makes that thing a source of afflictions. Then the face of the heart turns away from the world of origination toward the side of holiness. For when Adam (peace be upon him) had his heart attached to Paradise, He made it a trial for him until Paradise departed; so Adam remained with the remembrance of God. And when Ya'qub (Jacob) became attached to Yusuf (Joseph), peace be upon them both, He caused separation between them until Ya'qub remained with the remembrance of the Truth. And when Muhammad (peace be upon him) hoped from the people of Makkah for support and help, they became among the most hostile people toward him until

[Page 142]

he said: "No prophet has been harmed as I have been harmed."

The second: That he does not make that thing a trial, but removes it from the midst so that neither the trial nor the mercy remains. Then the servant returns to God, the Exalted.

The third: Whenever the servant expects something from a direction, God, the Exalted, gives him, without an intermediary, better than what he expected. So the servant is ashamed and returns to the door of God's mercy.

As for the path of attraction, it is as he (peace be upon him) said: "A pull from the pulls of the Truth equals the deeds of both humans and jinn." Whoever the Truth draws to Himself becomes overcome, for the Truth is the Victor, not the vanquished. The attribute of the Lord is lordship, and the attribute of the servant is servanthood, and lordship prevails over servanthood, not by opposition. The attribute of the Truth is reality, and the attribute of the servant is metaphor, and reality prevails over metaphor, not by opposition. The victor transforms the vanquished from one attribute to another attribute suitable to him. When the servant enters into the presence of a mighty king, he forgets himself and becomes, with all his heart, thought, and perception, turned toward him, occupied with him, and heedless of anything else. How much more so for one whose sight has gazed upon the presence of the King, before whom everything other than Him is contemptible. There, the servant becomes like one annihilated from himself and from the portions of his own self, and thus becomes content with the decrees of the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, and His rulings, without any trace of disputation remaining in his obedience.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 158 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever performs the Hajj to the House or the 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going around between them. And whoever volunteers good, indeed Allah is Shakir (Appreciative), Knowing.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is in several respects.

The first: Allah the Exalted explained that He only turned the qiblah toward the Ka'bah in order to complete His favour upon Muhammad (ﷺ) and his ummah by reviving the laws and religion of Ibrahim, as He said: ﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾. The sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah was among the rites of Ibrahim, as mentioned in the story of the building of the Ka'bah and the sa'y of Hajar between the two hills. Since this was the case, Allah the Exalted mentioned this ruling right after that verse.

The second: When Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ up to His words: ﴿and give good tidings to the patient﴾, He then said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah.﴾ He made them so because they are among the traces of Hajar and Isma'il, of what befell them of trial. From this they inferred that whoever is patient in trial must surely reach the highest ranks and the loftiest stations.

The third: The divisions of Allah's obligations are three:

The first: what the intellect judges to be good at the outset. He mentioned this category first, which is His words: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you; and be grateful to Me and do not deny Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152]. For every intelligent person knows that remembering the Benefactor with praise and thanks, and persistence in gratitude to Him, is something the intellects find commendable.

The second: what the intellect judges to be ugly at the outset, but because the Shari'ah has come with it, one accepts its goodness. This is like sending down pains, poverty and afflictions, for these are almost regarded as ugly by the intellects, since Allah the Exalted gains no benefit from them and the servant suffers pain from them. So it was almost regarded as ugly, but when the Shari'ah came with it and explained its wisdom, which is trial and examination, as He said: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾, then the Muslim believes in its goodness and that it is wisdom and correctness.

The third: the matter which one is not guided either to its goodness or its ugliness, but sees it as mere futility devoid of benefit or harm, such as the acts of Hajj, including the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah. Allah the Exalted mentioned this category after the first two, so that He would have alerted to all categories of His obligations and mentioned all of them by way of completeness and thoroughness. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The second issue: Know that al-Safa and al-Marwah are proper names for the two specific hills. However, people have discussed the root derivation of both. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is said that al-Safa is singular and its plural is Sifiyy and Asfa', as one says 'asa and 'isiyy, and raha and arha'. The rajiz (poet) said:

As if his two sides, from the tuff, were the places where birds alight upon the rocks (sifiyy).

It may also be used as a collective noun whose singular is safah. Jarir said:

When the enemy strikes our rocks (safat), they meet for us a hard, unyielding stone.

In the Kitab of al-Khalil: al-Safa is a large, hard, smooth stone. When they describe a rock they say: safah safwa'; and when they make it masculine they say: safa, safwan. So he treated al-Safa and al-Safah as if they had one meaning. Al-Mubarrad said: al-Safa is every stone not mixed with anything else, such as mud or dust attached to it, and its derivation is from safa, yasfu, when it becomes pure. As for al-Marwah, al-Khalil said: among stones it is that which is white, smooth, hard, and very firm. Others said: it is small stones; its plural for few is marawat and for many is marw. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

Until I am, for the calamities, like a marwah (stone) against the safa of the mash'ar, striking every day.

As for ﴿symbols of Allah﴾ (sha'a'ir Allah), they are the signs of His obedience, and everything made a sign of the signs of Allah's obedience is among the symbols of Allah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the camels We have made for you among the symbols of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 36], meaning a sign of nearness (to Allah). And He said: ﴿That, and whoever honours the symbols of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 32]. The symbols of Hajj are the landmarks of its rites, and from this is al-Mash'ar al-Haram. From it also is ish'ar of the hump, which is marking it with a knife, so that this becomes a sign of the pilgrim's ihram and that he has made it an offering to the House of Allah. From it also are the shi'ar in war, which is the sign by which one of the two groups is distinguished from the other. The word sha'a'ir is the plural of sha'irah, which is derived from ish'ar, which is informing, and from it your saying: sha'artu bi-kadha, meaning I knew.

The third issue: The symbols may be interpreted either as acts of worship or as rites, or as places of worship and rites. If we take the first, then there is an ellipsis in the speech, because the two hills themselves cannot be described as religion and rites; rather the meaning is that going around between them and the sa'y is from the religion of Allah the Exalted. If we take the second, the apparent meaning of the speech holds, because these two hills may be places for acts of worship and rites. However it is, the sa'y between these two hills is among the symbols of Allah and among the signs of His religion. Allah the Exalted prescribed it for the ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) and for Ibrahim (peace be upon him) before that. It is among the rites concerning which Allah the Exalted related that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And show us our rites﴾. Know that the sa'y is not in itself a complete act of worship; rather it becomes worship only when it becomes one of the parts of Hajj. For this reason Allah the Exalted specified the place where the sa'y becomes worship, saying: ﴿So whoever performs the Hajj to the House or the 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going around between them.﴾

* * *

The fourth issue: The wisdom in prescribing this sa'y is the well-known narration, that Hajar, the mother of Isma'il, when the matter became straitened for her, in her thirst and the thirst of her son Isma'il (peace be upon him), Allah the Exalted relieved her with the water which He caused to gush forth for her and her son from Zamzam, so that creation would know that He, glorified is He, though He does not leave His friends in the world free from various kinds of trials, His relief is near to whoever calls upon Him, for He is the Helper of those who seek help. Look at the state of Hajar and Isma'il, how He relieved them and answered their supplication. Then He made their actions an act of obedience for all the obligated until the Day of Resurrection, and their traces an example for all creation, so that it would be known that Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers. All of this is a confirmation of what He had informed before, that He tests His servants with something of fear and hunger and loss of wealth, lives and fruits; but whoever is patient in that attains happiness in both abodes and achieves the highest goal in both stations.

* * *

The fifth issue: Al-Qaffal mentioned several views regarding the word Hajj:

The first: Hajj in the language means frequently going to something and returning to it. Whoever visits the House for Hajj first comes to it to know it, then returns to it for the tawaf, then departs to Mina, then returns to it for the tawaf of ziyarah, then returns to it for the tawaf of departure.

The second: Qutrub said: Hajj is shaving. It is said: uhjuj shajjataka, meaning cut the hair around the wound so that the pilgrims may enter the wound; so the meaning is: "such a one hajja," i.e. shaved. Al-Qaffal said: this is possible in light of His words: ﴿You will surely enter al-Masjid al-Haram, if Allah wills, secure, shaving your heads and cutting short (your hair)﴾ [al-Fath: 27], meaning as pilgrims and visitors. He expressed that by shaving, so it is not far that Hajj is named by this name in the sense of shaving.

The third: Some people said Hajj is intention. It is said: a man is mahjuj, and a place is mahjuj when it is intended; and from this is mahajjat al-tariq (the road one follows). So when the House was intended by this kind of worship, that act was called hajj. Al-Qaffal said: The first view is closer to correct, because the saying "rajul mahjuj" refers only to one who is frequented again and again, and likewise mahajjat al-tariq is that road on which travel has frequently occurred.

As for 'umrah, the people of language said: al-i'timar is intention and visiting. Al-A'sha said:

And the soul was stirred when their host came, and a rider came from Taltheeth, a visitor (mu'tamir).

Qutrub said: 'Umrah in the speech of the tribe of 'Abd al-Qays means the mosque, the church, and the synagogue. Al-Qaffal said: There is no doubt that 'umrah, when attached to the House, means visiting, because the one performing 'umrah goes around the House and between al-Safa and al-Marwah, then departs like a visitor. As for al-junah, it comes from their saying: janaha ila kadha, meaning he inclined toward it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [al-Anfal: 61]. And the ship "janahat" when it stuck to the water and did not proceed; and a man "janaha" in a matter when he leans toward it with his chest. The ribs are called jawanih because of their bending, and the wing of a bird comes from this, because it inclines on one of its two sides and does not fly on the level of its natural form. Thus it is established that its origin is inclination. Then some people said: it remained so in the usage of the Qur'an as well, so the meaning of "there is no blame upon him" wherever it is mentioned in the Qur'an is: there is no inclination toward anyone to demand anything of anything. Others said: rather, it is specific to inclining toward falsehood and toward what incurs sin.

His words: ﴿to go around between them﴾ means: to make tawaf (yatatawwafa), so the ta' was assimilated into the ta' (tatawwafa becoming yattawwafa), as He said: ﴿O you who are wrapped up (al-Muddathir)﴾ [al-Muddathir: 1], ﴿O you who are wrapped up (al-Muzzammil)﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1], meaning al-mutadaththir and al-mutazammil. It is said: tafa and atafa with one meaning.

* * *

The sixth issue: The apparent meaning of His words: ﴿there is no blame upon him﴾ is that there is no sin upon him. Whatever truly means there is no sin in doing it includes the obligatory, the recommended and the permissible. Then each of these three is distinguished from the other by an additional condition. Thus the apparent meaning of this verse does not indicate whether the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah is obligatory or not obligatory, because a word indicating the common element among the categories has no indication whatsoever of a specific category without returning to another proof. Knowing this, we say: the school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that this sa'y is a pillar, and blood (sacrifice) cannot substitute for it. According to Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, it is not a pillar, and blood can substitute for it. It is narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and 'Ata' that whoever leaves it, there is nothing upon him. The argument of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is from several aspects:

The first: What is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed Allah has prescribed for you the sa'y, so perform sa'y." If it is said: this hadith has an apparent meaning that is abandoned, because it requires the obligation of sa'y, which is running, and that is not obligatory. We say: we do not accept that sa'y is a term for running, by the evidence of His words: ﴿then hasten (fas'aw) to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], and running in it is not obligatory. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and that man has only what he strives for (sa'a)﴾ [al-Najm: 39], and what is meant by it is not running, but striving and effort in intention and purpose. Even if we grant that it indicates running, running includes an attribute that is left unpracticed in respect of this attribute, so the basic walking remains obligatory.

The second: It is established that he (peace be upon him) performed sa'y when he approached al-Safa during his Hajj, and said: "Indeed al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah; begin with what Allah began with." So he began with al-Safa, climbed upon it until he saw the House. When it is established that he (peace be upon him) performed sa'y, it becomes obligatory upon us to perform sa'y, by the Qur'an and by the report. As for the Qur'an: His words: ﴿and follow him﴾, His words: ﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31], and His words: ﴿Indeed in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21]. As for the report: his words (peace be upon him): "Take your rites from me," and the command implies obligation.

The third: It is a series of circuits prescribed within a part of the sanctuary (Haram), or it is performed in a complete state of ihram, so its genus is a pillar, like the tawaf al-ziyarah. The tawaf al-sadr is not required, because the discussion concerns the genus, due to its being obligatory once. Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, argued with two aspects:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 158 (part 2 of 2):

One of them: this verse, which is His saying: ﴿there is no sin upon him for going around them﴾, and this is not said of obligatory acts (wajibat). Then He, exalted is He, emphasised this with His saying: ﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾, so He made clear that it is a voluntary act (tatawwu') and not an obligation.

The second: His saying: "The Hajj is 'Arafah" (al-Hajj 'Arafah). Whoever reaches 'Arafah has completed his Hajj. This requires completion in all respects, and it was set aside in some matters, so it remains in force regarding the sa'y (running between al-Safa and al-Marwah).

The answer to the first has several aspects:

The first: As we have explained, His saying ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ contains only that there is no sin upon the one who does it, and this bare meaning is shared between the obligatory and other than the obligatory. So it contains no proof for negating obligation. What confirms this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no sin upon you if you shorten the prayer if you fear﴾ [al-Nisa': 101]. Shortening (qasr) of the prayer is obligatory according to Abu Hanifah, yet He said in it ﴿there is no sin upon you﴾. So it is the same here.

The second: He removed the sin from going around them (bihima), not from going between them (baynahuma). According to us, the first is not obligatory, and only the second is obligatory.

The third: Ibn 'Abbas said: "There was an idol upon al-Safa and an idol upon al-Marwah, and the people of the Jahiliyyah used to go around them and rub themselves against them. When Islam came, the Muslims disliked going around them because of the two idols, so Allah sent down this verse." When you know this, we say: the permission turned to the existence of the two idols at the time of going around, not to the going around itself, just as if there were a small amount of impurity (najasah) on the garment according to you, or the blood of fleas according to us, and it was said: "There is no sin upon you if you pray in it," for the removal of sin turns to the place of the impurity, not to the prayer itself.

The fourth: It is narrated from 'Urwah that he said to 'A'ishah: "I think there is no harm upon me if I do not go around them." She said: "Evil is what you said. If it were so, it would have said: 'that he should not go around them'." Then she related what had preceded about the two idols. The interpretation of 'A'ishah is preferred over the interpretation of the Successors (tabi'un). If they say: Ibn Mas'ud recited: (﴿there is no sin upon him that he should not go around them﴾), and the wording also admits this, like His saying ﴿Allah makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], meaning: lest you go astray, and like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿lest you say on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], meaning: lest you say. We say: an irregular recitation (qira'ah shadhdhah) cannot be considered in the Qur'an, because affirming it would undermine the Qur'an being mutawatir (transmitted by an unbroken mass of narrators, making it certain).

The fifth: Just as His saying ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ is not applied to the obligatory, so also it is not applied to the recommended (mandub). There is no doubt that the sa'y is recommended. So the verse has become one whose apparent meaning is not acted upon.

As for relying on His saying ﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾, it is weak. This is because it does not require that the intended meaning of this volunteering be the going around mentioned first. Rather, it is possible that what is intended by it is something else. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor person﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. Then He said: ﴿And whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾. So He obligated the feeding of food upon them, then He encouraged them to volunteer good. The meaning is: whoever volunteers and adds to the feeding of one poor person, it is good. Likewise here, this volunteering may be directed to something else, and that is in two respects:

One of them: that he adds to the going around, so he goes around more than the obligatory circuits, such as going around eight times or more.

The second: that after the obligatory Hajj and 'Umrah, he volunteers a second Hajj and 'Umrah, until he goes around al-Safa and al-Marwah voluntarily.

As for the hadith they relied upon, we say: that hadith is general ('amm), and our hadith is specific (khass), and the specific takes precedence over the general. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: the recitation of Hamzah, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i is (yatawwa') with the yā' and the 'ayn vowelless (jazm). Its underlying form is yatatawwa', but the tā' was assimilated into the ṭā' because they are close in articulation. This is better, because the meaning is in the future tense, and the conditional and its response are best in the future. Although it is permissible to say: "Whoever comes to me, I honour him", placing the past tense in the position of the future in the response, nonetheless when the wording agrees with the meaning, it is better. As for the rest of the reciters, they read (tatawwa'a) in the form tafa"ala as a past tense verb. This reading admits two possibilities:

One of them: that the position of (tatawwa'a) is jazm (in a conditional sense).

The second: that (man) is not made a conditional particle, but is in the sense of (alladhī) and is a subject (mubtada'), and the fā' with what follows it is in the position of raf' (nominative) because it is the predicate of the relative subject. The meaning here is the meaning of a subject with a predicate, except that when this fā' enters the predicate of a relative pronoun or of an indefinite qualified noun, it indicates that the second is obligatory only because the first is obligatory, as in His saying: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 53]. Here (ma) is a relative subject, and the fā' with what follows it is its predicate. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Those who spend their wealth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 274] up to His saying: ﴿then for them is their reward﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believers﴾ [al-Buruj: 10] up to His saying: ﴿then for them is the punishment of Hell﴾, and His saying: ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], and His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, I will let him enjoy briefly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126], and His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed, for him is ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160], and His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. We will mention this issue, if Allah wills, at His saying: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 274].

The second issue: Abu Muslim said: (tatawwa'a) is tafa''ala from ṭā'ah (obedience), and the saying of one who says ṭā'a and the saying of one who says tatawwa'a are equal, just as it is said ḥāla and taḥawwala, qāla and taqawwala, ṭāfa and tatawwafa, and tafa''ala is used in the sense of fa'ala frequently. Ṭau' is submission, and ṭau' is what you desire from your own self of what is not obligatory upon you.

The third issue: Those who said the sa'y is obligatory interpreted this volunteering as the sa'y beyond the measure of what is obligatory, [p. 147] and among them are those who interpreted it as the sa'y in the second Hajj, which is not obligatory. Al-Hasan said: what is meant by it is all acts of obedience. This is better, because it is more in accord with the generality of the wording.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is Grateful, All-Knowing﴾. Know that the shākir (grateful one) in the language is the one who manifests the favour bestowed upon him, and this is impossible with regard to Allah, exalted is He. So the shākir with respect to Him is metaphorical, and its meaning is the one who rewards the obedience. The reason that the reward for obedience was called shukr (gratitude) is for several reasons:

The first: the wording came out in a gentle manner toward the servants, as an exaggeration in kindness to them, just as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who is it that would lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], and He does not borrow from any need, but it is a gentle form of solicitation, as if it were said: "Who is it that does the deed of a lender, by advancing (something) and receiving many times what he advanced?"

The second: since gratitude corresponds to a favour or to the reward for it, everything that is a reward was called gratitude by way of likeness.

The third: as if He says: "I, although I am independent of your obedience, nevertheless place it in such a position that if it were possible for me to benefit from it, its effect would not increase beyond what has occurred." In sum, the purpose is to explain that the servant's obedience is accepted by Allah, exalted is He, and occupies the highest rank of acceptance.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿All-Knowing﴾, the meaning is that He knows the measure of the reward, so He does not diminish what is due to the one who deserves it, because He, exalted is He, knows its measure and knows what exceeds it of bounty. This is more fitting to the speech, so that His saying ﴿All-Knowing﴾ has a connection with (Grateful). It may also be that He means that He knows what the servant does, so that he fulfils its right of worship and sincerity, and what he does not do to this limit. This is an encouragement to perform what is obligatory according to its conditions, and a warning against opposing that.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 159:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance after We have made it clear for the people in the Scripture — those are cursed by Allah and cursed by those who curse﴾, and in it there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾, there are two opinions.

One of them: that it is a new, independent statement that encompasses everyone who conceals anything of the religion.

The second: that it does not apply to its apparent generality. Among those who held this, some claimed that it refers specifically to the Jews. Ibn ʿAbbas said: A group of the Ansar asked some of the Jews about what was in the Torah concerning the attributes of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the rulings, and they concealed it, so the verse was revealed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi and al-Asamm. The first opinion is closer to the truth, for several reasons:

The first: the wording is general, and the particular circumstance present, namely its revelation on account of a specific cause, does not restrict it, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that what counts is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause.

The second: it is also established in the principles of jurisprudence that linking a ruling to a descriptive attribute indicates that the attribute is the cause (ʿillah) of that ruling, especially when the attribute is suitable to the ruling. There is no doubt that concealing the religion is suitable for deserving the curse of Allah, Exalted. If this attribute is the cause of this ruling, the ruling must be general whenever the attribute is general.

The third: a group of the Companions understood this wording in its generality. ʿA'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: Whoever claims that Muhammad (ﷺ) concealed anything of the revelation has greatly slandered Allah, and Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance﴾, so the verse was understood in its generality. And from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Were it not for two verses in the Book of Allah, I would not narrate a single hadith after people have said: Abu Hurayrah has narrated too much. And he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance﴾.

Those who restricted the verse to the People of the Book argued that concealment is only valid from them in the era of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), since the Qur'an is mass-transmitted (mutawatir), so its concealment is not possible. We reply: the Qur'an, before it became mass-transmitted, could be concealed; and a mujmal (general or ambiguous) matter of the Qur'an whose clarification is with a single reporter could be concealed; and likewise regarding the rational proofs that the responsible person needs.

The second issue: The judge (al-Qadi) said: Concealment is leaving off making something manifest when there is a need for it and a motive to make it manifest; for when this is not the case it is not counted as concealment. Since what Allah sent down of clear proofs and guidance is among the most needed matters in the religion, He described the one who knows it and does not make it manifest as a concealer, just as one of us is described as concealing in worldly affairs when they are of the kind that motives strongly urge one to disclose. In this sense, one who is able to keep a secret is praised, because concealment is burdensome to the soul.

* * *

The third issue: This verse indicates that what relates to the religion and what the responsible person needs must not be concealed, and whoever conceals it has greatly erred. Similar to this verse is His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: you must make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾ [Al ʿImran: 187]. And close to these two is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book and sell it for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah: 174]. All of this verse is a binding obligation to make the sciences of the religion manifest as a reminder to the people, and a deterrent from concealing them. A parallel to it regarding the transmission of knowledge, though without mention of a threat for the one who conceals, is His saying: ﴿Why should not a group from every division of them go forth, that they may gain understanding in the religion and warn their people when they return to them, that they may beware﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. Hajjaj narrated from ʿAta', from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Whoever conceals knowledge that he knows will come on the Day of Resurrection bridled with a bridle of fire."

As for His saying ﴿what We have sent down of clear proofs﴾, it means everything He sent down to the prophets as Book and revelation, apart from the proofs of reason. His saying ﴿and guidance﴾ includes both rational and transmitted proofs, since we explained in the commentary on His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] that guidance is an expression for proofs, so it encompasses all of them. If it is said: He has said ﴿and guidance after We have made it clear for the people in the Scripture﴾, which returns to the first meaning, we reply: the first is the revelation itself, and the second is what the revelation necessitates of benefits.

Know that since the Book indicates that the report of a single narrator, consensus and analogy are proofs, whatever is indicated by any of these matters has been indicated by the Book; so its concealment falls under the verse. Thus it is established that He threatened the concealment of both the transmitted and the rational proofs and combined the two in the threat. This verse indicates that whoever is able to explain the principles of the religion through rational proofs to one who needs them, and then abandons this or conceals some of the rulings of the Sharia despite the great need for it, has incurred a great threat.

The fourth issue: This making manifest is an obligation of sufficiency (fard kifayah), not an individual obligation, because when some make it manifest, it becomes such that everyone can reach it, so it is no longer hidden; and once it has left the bounds of concealment, it is not obligatory on the rest to make it manifest again.

The fifth issue: Some people argue from these verses for the acceptance of the report of a single narrator, saying: These verses indicate that making these rulings manifest is obligatory; and if acting upon them were not obligatory, making them manifest would not be obligatory. The full argument is in His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿except those who repent, amend and make clear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160], so He judged that clarification occurs by their report. If it is said: Why could it not be that each one is forbidden to conceal and commanded to clarify, so that the reporters increase and the report becomes mass-transmitted?
We reply: this is an error, because they were only forbidden to conceal while being of those among whom concealment is possible; and whoever among them could collude in concealment could also collude in fabrication and falsehood, so their report would not necessarily produce knowledge.

* * *

The sixth issue: They argued from this verse that it is not permissible to take payment for teaching, because since the verse indicates the obligation of that teaching, taking payment for it is taking payment for performing an obligation, which is impermissible. This is also indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book and sell it for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah: 174]. Its apparent meaning forbids taking payment both for making it manifest and for concealing it, since His saying ﴿and sell it for a small price﴾ prohibits taking any exchange for it in all respects.

As for His saying ﴿after We have made it clear for the people in the Scripture﴾: before this, in the Torah and the Gospel, there was clarification of the attributes of Muhammad (ﷺ) and of the rulings. It was said: the first revelation refers to what is in the books of earlier peoples, and the second to what is in the Qur'an.

As for His saying ﴿those — Allah curses them﴾: the curse (al-la'nah) in the original linguistic usage is distancing, and in the usage of the Sharia it is distancing from reward.

As for His saying ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾: it must be understood as referring to those for whom cursing has an effect. The scholars agreed that the angels, the prophets and the righteous are like this, so they are necessarily included in this generality. It is reinforced by His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers — upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of the people all together﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161]. People have mentioned other aspects:

One: that the ones who curse are the beasts of the earth and its creeping things, for they say: We have been withheld rain because of the sins of the children of Adam. This is from Mujahid and ʿIkrimah. He said ﴿those who curse﴾ and did not say "those who curse" in the feminine because He described them with the attribute of those who reason, so He gave them the plural of rational beings, as in His saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon, I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4], and ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml: 18], ﴿And they will say to their skins: why did you testify against us?﴾ [Fussilat: 21], and ﴿and each in an orbit they swim﴾ [Ya Sin: 40].

Two: that everything other than the two weighty ones, the jinn and mankind, curses them. If it is said: how can cursing be valid from animals and inanimate things? We reply in two ways:

The first: as an exaggeration, meaning that if they were rational they would curse them.

The second: that in the Hereafter, when they are restored and made among the rational beings, they will curse whoever did this in the world and died upon it.

Three: that the people of the Fire also curse them, since they concealed the religion from them; so it is general.

Four: Ibn Masʿud said: When two people mutually curse one another, the curse falls upon the one who deserves it; and if there is no one who deserves it, it returns upon the Jews who concealed what Allah, Glorified and Exalted, had sent down.

Five: from Ibn ʿAbbas: they have two curses: the curse of Allah and the curse of the creation. He said: That is when a man is placed in his grave and is asked: What is your religion? Who is your prophet? Who is your Lord? He says: I do not know. Then he is struck with a blow that everything hears except the two weighty ones, mankind and the jinn; so nothing hears his voice except that it curses him, and the angel says to him: You neither knew nor recited; thus were you in the world.

Six: Abu Muslim said: "those who curse" are those who believe in Him, and the meaning of cursing from them is distancing the one cursed, opposing him and being at odds with him, together with anger toward him and disavowal of him. The judge said: The verse indicates that this concealment is one of the major sins, since He, Exalted, made cursing obligatory for it. It also indicates that none of the prophets concealed what they were entrusted with of the message, for otherwise they would fall under the verse.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 160:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except for those who repent, make amends, and make clear (the truth). Those — I will turn to them in forgiveness, and I am the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained the great severity of the threat against those who conceal what Allah has sent down, it could be imagined that the threat applies to them in every circumstance. So Allah, exalted is He, clarified that if they repent, their ruling changes and they enter among the people of promise (of reward). We have already mentioned that repentance (tawbah) is an expression for regret over committing a wrong, not for any purpose other than that. For whoever neglects returning a deposit and then regrets it because people blamed him, or because the judge rejected his testimony, is not a repentant person. Likewise, if he resolves to return every deposit and fulfil every obligation so that his testimony will be accepted, or so that he will be praised and commended, he is not a repentant person. This is the meaning of sincerity in repentance. Then Allah, exalted is He, clarified that after repentance it is necessary for him to make amends for what he has corrupted. For example, if he corrupted another's religion by casting doubt upon him, it is incumbent on him to remove that doubt. Thirdly, He clarified that after this it is obligatory for him to do the opposite of concealment, which is making clear, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and make clear﴾. So this verse indicates that repentance is not attained except by abandoning everything that is not fitting and performing everything that is fitting.

The Mu'tazilah said: the verse indicates that repentance from some sins while persisting in others is not valid, because His saying ﴿and make amends﴾ is general over all. The answer to this is that an unrestricted expression is satisfied in its truth by the occurrence of a single one of its instances.

Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: the verse indicates that accepting repentance is not obligatory by reason, because He mentioned it in the context of praising and commending Himself, and had it been obligatory, this praise would not have been fitting. The meaning of ﴿I turn to them﴾ is: I accept their repentance. Accepting repentance includes the removal of the punishment for what one repented of. If it is said: why do you not say that the meaning of ﴿Those — I will turn to them﴾ is the acceptance of repentance in the sense of recompense and reward, as you say regarding the acceptance of obedience? We say: the acceptance of obedience only benefits in establishing entitlement to reward, because nothing other than that is deserved by it, and that is the purpose of performing it. This is not the case with repentance, because it is set for the removal of punishment, and that is the purpose of performing it, though it is necessary that one deserves reward by it if one was not mistaken. The meaning of His saying ﴿and I am the Accepting of repentance﴾ is: the one who accepts the repentance of every penitent, so it is an intensification in this matter. The meaning of "the Merciful" following that is an alert that, out of His mercy toward His accountable servants, He accepts their repentance after their great neglect.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 161–162:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved﴾. Know that in the verse there are several issues:

Page 151

The first issue: The apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾ is general concerning everyone who is in that state, so there is no basis for restricting it to some of those who are in that state. Abu Muslim said: It is necessary to restrict it to those previously mentioned, who are those who conceal the verses. He argued for this by saying that when Allah mentioned the condition of those who conceal, then mentioned the condition of those among them who repent, He also mentioned the condition of whoever among them dies without repenting. And also, when He mentioned that those who conceal are cursed during their life, He clarified in this verse that they are also cursed after death. The answer to this: This would only be valid if those who die without repentance were not included under the first verse. But if they are included under the first, then mentioning them is unnecessary, so the speech must be understood as referring to a new matter.

The second issue: When it is stated in the speech that whoever dies upon his disbelief, the threat becomes binding without any condition, and since what is dependent upon a condition is nonexistent when the condition is absent, we know that if the disbeliever repents before death, his state is not like that.

The third issue: If it is said: How can all of mankind curse him when the people of his own religion do not curse him? We say: The answer to this is from several aspects:

The first of them: The people of his religion will curse him in the Hereafter, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and curse one another﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25].

The second of them: Qatada and al-Rabi' said: By "mankind, all together" He intended the believers, as if He did not count anyone else, and He judged that the believers are mankind and no others.

The third of them: Everyone curses the ignorant and the wrongdoer, because the ugliness of that is established in the intellects. So if he himself is ignorant or a wrongdoer, even if he does not know from himself that he is such, his curse upon the ignorant and the wrongdoer includes himself. This is from al-Suddi.

The fourth of them: The occurrence of the curse may be understood as the deserving of the curse, and in that case it becomes general.

* * *

The fourth issue: Abu Bakr al-Razi said: In the verse there is evidence that it is obligatory upon the Muslims to curse whoever dies a disbeliever, and that the removal of legal responsibility from him by death does not drop from us the obligation of cursing him and disassociating from him. For His saying, ﴿and mankind, all together﴾ has required our command to curse him after his death. This indicates that if a disbeliever became insane, the removal of legal responsibility from him by insanity would not drop the obligation of cursing him and disassociating from him. The same applies to what necessitates praise and allegiance from faith and righteousness: the death or insanity of one who is such does not change his ruling from what it was before the condition arose in him.

The fifth issue: Those who hold the doctrine of muwafat (the coincidence of the outcome with one's state at death) argued with this verse, saying: Allah linked the obligation of His curse to his dying upon his disbelief. So if he deserved that before death, it would not be valid. Therefore we know that disbelief only produces the deserving of the curse if its bearer dies upon it, and likewise faith only produces the deserving of praise if its bearer dies upon it. (The answer): The ruling attached to those who die upon disbelief is a collection of matters: among them is the curse if he dies, and among them is abiding in the Fire. And according to us, this collection, namely the curse alone, why do you say that it does not occur except with it?

The sixth issue: Those who say that disbelief (kufr) is among the legal (shar'i) terms, and that what remains upon its original linguistic meaning are the Mu'tazilites, argued with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and die while they are disbelievers﴾. Allah described them at the time of their death as disbelievers. It is known that kufr in the meaning of covering and concealment does not remain in them at the time of death, because concealment only occurs with respect to a living, understanding being.

The seventh issue: The verse indicates the permissibility of specification (takhsis) together with emphasis (tawkid), because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and mankind, all together﴾, although it is specified according to the view of the one who says that what is meant by "mankind" is some of them.

* * *

Page 152

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿abiding therein﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: Khulud (abiding) is long-lasting staying. From it one says: akhlada ila kadha, meaning he remained with it and inclined to it.

The second issue: The governing element of (khalidin, "abiding") is the adverbial phrase from His saying (upon them), because it contains the meaning of the curse being established. So it is a circumstantial state (hal) from the ha' and mim in "'alayhim," like your saying: "upon them is the wealth, humbled."

The third issue: ﴿abiding therein﴾: that is, in the curse. It was said: in the Fire, except that it was made implicit for the sake of magnifying its matter and terrifying. As in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. The first is preferable for several reasons:

The first: When a pronoun has an antecedent mentioned earlier, returning it to that is preferable to returning it to something not mentioned.

The second: Taking this pronoun to refer to the curse is more beneficial than taking it to refer to the Fire, because the curse is distancing from reward through the performance of punishment in the Hereafter and its creation in this world. So the curse includes the Fire and more, and therefore it is preferable to take the wording as referring to it.

The third: His saying, ﴿abiding therein﴾ is a report about the present state, and if the pronoun is taken to refer to the curse, then this would be present now, whereas if it is taken to refer to the Fire, it would not be present now, but would require interpretation. So that is preferable. Know that He, exalted is He, described this punishment with three matters.

The first of them: Khulud, which is long staying according to us, and permanent staying according to the Mu'tazilites, as was discussed earlier in the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81].

The second of them: The absence of lightening, meaning that what reaches them of the punishment of Allah is uniform at all times, and no time becomes less than another. If it is said: This uniformity is impossible for several reasons:

The first: If one imagines the state of another in severe punishment, that would be like a lightening for him.

The second: He, exalted is He, adds to them what was missed of punishment in its time, then that addition ends, so that would be a lightening.

The third: Wherever they are addressed with His saying: ﴿Begone therein, and do not speak to Me﴾, there is no doubt that their grief increases at that time. They answered this: The variation in these minor matters is not noticed by one who is totally overwhelmed by severe punishment, and this small amount of variation is not noticed. They said: Since the verse indicates that this punishment is uniform, it must be permanent, because if they allowed its cessation, that would lighten for them when they imagined it. The explanation of this: One who is in a great affliction in this world, if he is given good news of deliverance after days, he rejoices and is gladdened, and the affliction becomes easier for him to bear. And the greater his affliction, the more the relief and lightening that reaches him by imagining its cessation.

The third attribute of that punishment: His saying: ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾. Reprieve (inzar) is deferment and postponement. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then [let there be] a postponement until a time of ease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 280]. The meaning is that their punishment is not deferred, but is present and continuous with a punishment like it. As if He, exalted is He, informed us that the ruling of the abode of punishment and reward is different from the ruling of this world, for in this world they are given respite until terms that Allah, exalted is He, has decreed, whereas in the Hereafter there is absolutely no respite. When they ask for respite, they are not granted it; when they seek relief, they are not relieved; and when they seek to make amends, they are not allowed to make amends. It is said to them: ﴿Begone therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108]. We seek refuge in Allah from that. The conclusion is that these three attributes which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned for this punishment in this verse indicate the disbeliever's despair of cessation, lightening, and deferment.

[p. 153]

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Your God is One God; there is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾.

Know that the discussion of the word *ilah* (god) has already been given in the commentary on: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Fatiha: 1]. As for *wahid* (one), there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Abu 'Ali said: The expression *wahid* is a term used in two ways in their speech. The first is that it is a noun (*ism*), and the second is that it is a descriptive attribute (*wasf*). The noun that is not an attribute is their saying *wahid*, used in counting, as in *wahid, ithnan, thalatha* (one, two, three). This is a noun, not an attribute, just as all the other number-names are. As for its being an attribute, it is like your saying: *marartu bi-rajulin wahid* (I passed by a single man) and *hadha shay'un wahid* (this is one thing). When this term is applied to the True One, glorified and exalted, it may be that what is used as an attribute is like *'alim* (knowing) and *qadir* (powerful), and it may be that what is used as a noun is like our saying *shay'* (thing). The first is strengthened by His saying: ﴿Your God is One God﴾.

I say: The verification of this discussion by reason is that the things of which it is true to say that they are *wahid* share in the concept of unity (*wahdaniyya*), and differ in the particular realities of their quiddities, namely whether they are a substance (*jawhar*), an accident (*'arad*), a body (*jism*), or an immaterial thing (*mujarrad*). It is also valid for each of the two to be conceived on its own, namely its quiddity and its being one, while being oblivious to the other. Therefore, the substance's being a substance, for example, is one thing, its being one is another thing, and the composite of the two is another thing. So the word *wahid* sometimes conveys only the meaning that it is one, and this is the noun, and sometimes conveys the meaning that it is one at the moment it becomes a description of something else, and this is the meaning of its being a descriptor.

**The second issue:** Is *wahidiyya* (oneness) an attribute added to the essence (*dhat*) or not? They differed concerning it. A group said: It is an attribute added to the essence. They argued for this by saying: When we say, "This substance is one," the concept of its being a substance is other than the concept of its being one, as evidenced by the fact that the substance shares with an accident in being one, but does not share with it in being a substance. Also, it is valid to conceive of its being a substance while oblivious to its being one, and what is known is distinct from what is not known. Also, if its being one were the very same as its being a substance, then our saying "the substance is one" would be like our saying "the substance is a substance." Also, the opposite of substance is accident, and the opposite of one is many. Thus it is established that the concept of its being one is either negative or positive. It cannot be negative, because if it were negative it would be a negation of plurality, and plurality is either negative or positive. If plurality is negative, and unity is the negation of plurality, then unity is the negation of a negation, and the negation of a negation is affirmation; so unity is positive, which is what was sought. If plurality is positive, and there is no meaning to plurality except the collection of unities, then if unity were negative together with plurality, the collection of non-existents would be an existing thing, which is impossible. Thus it is established that unity is an added, positive attribute. Then this added attribute either is said to have no reality except in the mind, or it has a reality outside the mind. The first is false, for otherwise the mental would not correspond to what is outside, and it would follow that the one thing is not one in itself, which is impossible, because we know necessarily that the thing judged to be one was one in itself before it existed mentally, hypothetically, or conventionally. Thus it is established that the being-one of a thing is a positive attribute added to its essence, subsisting in that essence.

Whoever rejected that unity is a positive attribute argued: If unity were an attribute added to the essence, then the unities would be equal in the quiddity of being one and distinct by their specific determinations, so it would follow that unity would have another unity, and this would extend to infinity, which is impossible.

**[p. 154]**

**The third issue:** The one is the thing that is not divisible in respect of that by which it is called one. So a single human being is impossible to divide, insofar as he is a human, into two humans. Rather, it may be divided into parts and components. Of existents, nothing is free of unity, even the number. For one ten, insofar as it is a ten, has unity attached to it. If you say "two tens," then the two tens, once, have unity attached to them from this aspect. So nothing among existents is free of unity. For this reason, unity became confused by some with existence, so they thought that every existent, since it is true of it that it is one, its existence is the very same as its unity. The truth is not so, because existence is divided into the one and the many, and that which is divided into something is other than that by which the division occurs.

**The fourth issue:** The True One, glorified and exalted, is *wahid* in two respects.

The first is that His essence is not composed of the aggregation of many things.

The second is that there is nothing in existence that shares with Him in being necessarily existent, and in being the origin of the existence of all contingent things (*mumkinat*). So the simple substance (*jawhar fard*), according to the one who affirms it, is one in the first sense, and not one in the second sense.

The proof for the establishment of unity in the first sense is that if He were composite, the realization of His existence would depend on the realization of each of His parts, and each of His parts is other than Him. Thus every composite depends on something other than itself, and everything dependent on something other than itself is contingent in its essence and necessary through another. Therefore, what is composite, dependent on something else, and contingent in its essence, is impossible for it to be composite not in the way described. Thus His reality, glorified is He, is a reality that is absolutely one and singular, with no plurality in it in any respect: neither a quantitative plurality, as there is in bodies, nor a conceptual plurality, as there is in a species composed of genus and differentia, or in a person composed of quiddity and individuation. However, this has been difficult for some peoples. That is because He, glorified is He, is Knowing, Powerful, Living, and Willing. The concept of these attributes is either the very concept of His essence, or it is not. The first is false, for several reasons:

The first: We can conceive of His essence while being oblivious to each of these attributes. And if this were not possible, there is no doubt that we can conceive of each of these attributes while being oblivious to conceiving of His particular essence. Indeed, this is necessary according to the one who says that His particular essence is not known, while His attributes are known. And the known is distinct from what is not known. Thus these attributes are matters added to the essence.

The second: If these attributes were the very essence, then our saying of the essence that "it is knowing" or "it is not knowing" would be like our saying "the essence is an essence" or "not an essence." And it would be impossible for that to be a matter in which proof may be offered for its negation or affirmation. For whoever says "the essence is an essence" is known by everyone necessarily to be truthful, and whoever says "the essence is not an essence" is known by everyone necessarily to be lying. And since our saying "the essence is knowing or not knowing" is not equivalent to our saying of an essence "the essence of the essence is not an essence," we know that these attributes are matters added to the essence.

The third: If the reference of these attributes were to His essence alone, and His essence is nothing but one thing, then the reference of these attributes would be to one thing. So establishing the proof that He is Powerful would suffice in place of establishing the proof that He is Knowing and that He is Living. But since this is not the case, and rather we need a specific proof for each attribute, we know that the reference of these attributes is not to the essence. Once it is established that these attributes are matters added to the essence, we say: These attributes are either negative or positive. It is not permissible for them to be negative, because negation is pure negation, and pure negation has no specificity. Also, we have made His being Knowing and Powerful an expression of the negation of ignorance and incapacity. Then ignorance and incapacity either refer to non-existence, meaning that He is not knowing and not powerful, or they refer to something positive: ignorance is an expression of a belief that does not correspond, and incapacity is an expression of a disruption in the state of power. If the first is the case, then knowledge and power are an expression of the negation of negation, so they are positive. If the second is the case, then the negation of ignorance and incapacity in this sense does not necessitate the realization of knowledge and power, for the inanimate object has been stripped of ignorance and incapacity in this sense, while not being described as knowing or powerful. Thus it is established that the attributes of God, exalted is He, are matters added to His essence, subsisting in His essence. And "the God" (*al-ilah*) is an expression for the collection of the essence and the attributes. So the statement returns to the claim that the reality of God, exalted is He, is composed of many matters. Then how is the matter with respect to Him?

**Another problem:** We have shown that unity is an attribute added to the essence subsisting in the essence. So if the reality of the Truth is one, then there are three matters: that reality, that oneness, and the being-described-by-that-oneness of that reality. This makes the third of three. Then where is tawhid?

**A third problem:** Is that reality existent and necessarily existent or not? If it is existent, then by its existence it shares with all other existents, and by its quiddities it is distinguished from all other existents. Thus there is a plurality arising from existence and quiddity. And if it is not existent, then this indicates non-existence. The same applies to necessity. If it is necessarily existent in itself, then the necessity of its existence cannot be the very essence, because necessity is an attribute of the relation of the subject to the predicate by the quality of being described, and a relation is other than each of the two things in itself. So the attribute of that relation being other than the two is even more so. Also, the essence subsists by itself, and it is impossible for the referent of the Necessary to be a thing subsisting by itself. And because we describe the essence by necessity, and describing a thing by itself is impossible, it is established that if a necessarily existent thing is necessary, then the necessity of its existence is added to its essence. So there are two matters: that essence together with that necessity, and the being-described-by-that-necessity. Thus the trinity has returned.

**A fourth problem:** Can this simple reality be reported about, and can it be expressed or not? The first is impossible, because reporting is only of one thing about another thing, so the reported-about is other than the reported-with, and these are two matters, not one. If it cannot be expressed, then it is entirely known neither by negation nor by affirmation, and so it is entirely unattended to. This is the whole of the questions in this context.

**The answer to the first:** He, glorified is He, is an essence described by these attributes. Undoubtedly the whole depends for its realization on the realization of its parts. However, the essence subsists by itself and is necessary in itself. Then after its necessity it is posterior in rank, entailing those qualities and attributes. This is something to which there is no objection according to reason.

As for the second problem, namely that unity is an attribute added to the essence, if you consider it from the aspect of its being one, then there are three matters, not one matter. The answer is that what you have mentioned is true. But a distinction is made between considering it in terms of what it is in itself, and considering it in terms of its being judged to be one. If you consider it in terms of what it is in itself, leaving off attention to its being one, then unity is realized there. And here there is a wondrous state: as long as the intellect is still attending to unity, it has not yet reached the world of unity. But when it leaves off unity, it has reached unity. So consider this state with your subtle mind, perhaps you will reach its secret. This is also the answer to the problem of existence and the problem of necessity.

**The Fourth Problem:** whether it is possible to express Him in words. The truth is that He cannot be expressed, because whenever you describe Him, you have told something about Him, and that which is described is necessarily other than that which is described with. So there is no true oneness. If you say about Him that He cannot be described, then there is a essence together with a particular negation, and so there is no oneness. But if you consider Him in terms of His being Himself, without telling anything about Him, neither by negation nor by affirmation, then you have reached the beginnings of the world of oneness. The turning-away mentioned can be expressed only by the words ﴿He﴾ (*huwa*). For this reason this word carries great weight among those who plunge into the seas of *tawhid* (divine oneness). We will mention a trace of its realities in the commentary on this verse, God willing.

As for oneness in the second sense, namely that there is nothing in existence that shares with Him in necessary existence, this oneness is specific to the essence of the Truth, glorified and exalted is He. The proofs of this are mentioned in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ (21:22).

As for oneness in the first sense, it is not among the special attributes of the essence of the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, because there is no doubt that existent things exist. These existents are either simple or composite. The composite necessarily requires simples, so it is established that simples must be affirmed within the totality of possible things. Thus oneness in the first sense is not among the matters in which the Truth, glorified is He, is unique. As for oneness in the second sense, the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, is singular in it and alone in it, and nothing else shares with Him in that attribute.

This is the summary of the discussion on this point, according to what suits human reason and its limited thought, while acknowledging that He, glorified is He, is far above the fluctuations of thoughts and imaginings, and the bonds of minds and understandings.

* * *

**The Fifth Question:** Al-Jubba'i (the Mu'tazili theologian) said: God, exalted is He, is described as one in four respects: because He has no parts or components; because He alone is eternal; because He alone possesses divinity; and because He alone possesses the attributes of His essence, such as His knowing by Himself and His being powerful by Himself. Abu Hashim (his son) limits himself to three respects: he made His being unique in eternity and in the attributes of the essence a single respect. Al-Qadi (the judge) said: in this verse the intended meaning is His being unique in divinity only, because He attached oneness to that, and for this reason He followed it with His saying ﴿there is no god but Him﴾.

Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: He, glorified and exalted is He, is one in His essence, having no counterpart; one in His attributes, having no likeness; and one in His actions, having no partner.

As for His being one in His essence: that particular essence, which is indicated by our saying "He is the Truth, glorified and exalted," either exists in some other individual apart from Him, or it does not. If the first is the case, then the distinction of His specific essence from the other meaning must be by an additional qualifier, so He would be composite in Himself, of that by which there is commonality and that by which there is distinction. He would then be possible, caused, and dependent, and this is impossible. If the second is the case, then it is established that He, glorified is He, is one in His essence, having no counterpart.

As for His being one in His attributes: His being described by attributes is distinguished from the description of others by attributes in several respects:

First, everything other than Him is perishable, because the attainment of its attributes is not from itself but from another, whereas He, glorified is He, deserves to have His attributes from Himself and not from another.

Second, the attributes of others are specific to one time rather than another, because they are originated, whereas the attributes of the Truth are not like that.

Third, the attributes of the Truth are unlimited in terms of their objects. His knowledge relates to all known things, and His power relates to all capable things. Indeed, for each of the unlimited known things He has unlimited knowledges, because He knows in that indivisible atom how it is and how its state is according to each of the limited spaces and each of the limited attributes. Thus He, glorified is He, is one in His attributes in this respect.

Fourth, the description of His essence by those attributes does not mean that they inhere in His essence or that His essence is a locus for them, nor does it mean that His essence is perfected by them. For we have shown that the essence is like the source of those attributes. If the essence were perfected by the attributes, the source would be deficient in itself and perfected by what is possible in itself, and this is impossible. Rather, His essence perfects itself, and among the necessary consequences of this essential perfection is the realization of the attributes of perfection along with it. Yet the division returns to the perfection itself, and it ends at the point where expression falls short of fulfilling it.

Fifth: there is no knowledge among minds of the reality of His attributes, just as there is no knowledge among them of the reality of His essence. For we know of His knowledge only that it is the matter by which perfection and precision appear in the world of created things. What is known of His knowledge is that it is some matter, and we do not know what it is; but we know of it that this perceptible effect follows from it. The same is said of His being powerful and living. Glory be to Him who, by the light of His majesty, repels the lights of minds and understandings.

As for His being one in His actions, the matter is clear. For the existent is either necessary or possible. The necessary is He Himself, and the possible is everything else. Whatever is possible could fail to exist unless it is connected to the Necessary. This ruling does not differ according to the differing categories of possible things, whether it is dominion or ownership, or an act of the servants, or anything else. Thus it is established that everything other than Him belongs to Him, is owned by Him, and is under His disposal, subjugation, power, and control. At this point you perceive a trace of the fragrances of the secrets of His decree and destiny, and something of the realities of His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created everything in measure﴾ (54:49) becomes apparent to you. And you know that the existent is nothing at all but what it is, and what belongs to it. When the ship of thought enters this deep sea, if it sailed forever it would never stop. For motion is only from one thing to another; the first thing is left behind, the second is sought, and these two are different. So you are still outside the world of singularity and unity. But when you reach the isthmus between the world of origination and eternity, there the movements cease, the signs and indications vanish, and nothing remains in minds and intellects except the bare fact that He is He. So: O He, and O You who is not He except He! Be good to Your weak servant, for Your servant is at Your threshold, and Your poor one is at Your door.

* * *

**The Sixth Question:** If it is asked: what is the meaning of His attributing it with His saying ﴿and your God﴾, and is this attribution valid for all creation, or valid only for the one charged with obligations (*mukallaf*)? We say: since the god (*ilah*, the one deserving worship) is the one who deserves to be worshipped, and what befits him is to be worshipped under this description, this is realized only with respect to those in whom the worship of God, exalted is He, can be conceived. This attribution is valid with respect to all those charged with obligations and to all who can be conceived to become charged with obligations by supposition.

**The Seventh Question:** His saying ﴿and your God﴾ indicates that the meaning of *ilah* is that which can take the attribution. For if the meaning of *ilah* were "the capable," the sense would become "your capable one is one capable," and it is known that this is weak. So this shows that *ilah* means the one worshipped.
