**The Eighth Question:** His saying ﴿and your God is one God﴾ means that He is one in divinity. For the occurrence of the word "one" after the word "god" indicates that this oneness is considered in divinity and not in anything else. It is like describing a man as "one lord" or "one scholar." When He said ﴿and your God is one God,﴾ it was possible that someone might think: "Suppose our god is one; perhaps the god of others differs from ours." Therefore He removed this suspicion by stating absolute oneness, saying ﴿there is no god but Him﴾. For our saying "there is no man" requires the negation of this quiddity (*mahiyya*, the essence or nature), and once this quiddity is negated, all its individuals are negated. For if one individual of that quiddity existed, then whenever that individual existed, the quiddity would exist, and that contradicts what the wording indicates of the negation of the quiddity. Thus it is established that our saying "there is no man" requires a comprehensive general negation. When it is then said "except Zayd," it conveys complete and established oneness.

In this expression there are discussions:

*The first:* a group of grammarians said: the sentence contains an ellipsis and an implied element, and the implied meaning is "there is no god for us," or "there is no god in existence except Allah." Know that this statement does not agree with true oneness. For if you say the implied meaning is "there is no god for us except Allah," this would be oneness of *our* god, not oneness of the god in the absolute sense. Then there would be no difference between His saying ﴿and your God is one God﴾ and His saying ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, and this would be pure repetition, which is not permissible. But if we say the implied meaning is "there is no god in existence," then that problem disappears, though another problem returns from a different direction: for if you say "there is no god in existence but Him," this would be a negation of the existence of a second god. Whereas if this implied element is not supposed, your saying "there is no god but Allah" is a negation of the quiddity of a second god. And it is known that negation of the quiddity is stronger in pure oneness than negation of existence. So it is better to keep the sentence on its apparent sense and to dispense with this implied element.

If it is said: how can the negation of a quiddity be conceived? For when you say "blackness is not black," this would be a judgment that blackness is not black, which is inconceivable. But when you say "blackness is not existent," this is intelligible, coherent, and sound. We reply: negating the quiddity is a necessary matter. For when you say "blackness is not existent," you have negated existence, and existence, as such, is the existence of a quiddity. So when you negate it, you have negated this quiddity called existence. If the negation of this quiddity is conceived in itself, why should the negation of that quiddity not be conceived as well? When this is conceived, it is valid to keep our saying "there is no god but Allah" on its apparent sense, without any need for an implied element.

If you say: when we say "blackness is not existent," we have negated neither the quiddity nor the existence, but we have negated the attribution of existence to the quiddity. We reply: is the attribution of existence to the quiddity a matter separate from the quiddity and from existence or not? If it is separate from them both, then negating it is negating that quiddity, and the quiddity as such can be negated, and then the aforementioned argument returns. If that attribution is not a matter separate from them, then it is impossible to direct the negation to it except by directing the negation either to the quiddity or to existence, and then the aforementioned argument returns. Thus it is established that our saying "there is no god but Him" is true and sound, without any need at all for an implied element.

*The second discussion,* concerning this expression: the conception of negation is posterior to the conception of affirmation. For unless you first conceive existence, it is impossible to conceive non-existence. You conceive of non-existence only as the removal of existence. So the conception of existence is independent of the conception of non-existence, while the conception of non-existence is preceded by the conception of existence. If this is so, what is the reason for reversing this order in this expression, so that we put negation first and affirmation after?

The answer: the matter in the intellect is as you have mentioned, but the placing of negation before affirmation was for the purpose of establishing oneness and negating associates and rivals.

**Third Investigation: On the Word (huwa)**

Know that the linguistic discussions concerning *huwa* have already been covered under ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. As for the subtle meanings, we say: know that expressions are of two kinds, explicit (*muzhara*) and implicit (*mudmara*). The explicit are the terms that signify specific quiddities (*mahiyyat*, essences or whatness) considered in themselves, such as blackness, whiteness, stone, and human. The implicit are the terms that signify something whose quiddity is not specified, such as the speaker, the addressee, and the absent party. They are three: *ana* (I), *anta* (you), and *huwa* (he/it). The most cognizable of them is *ana*, then *anta*, then *huwa*.

The proof for this order is that my conception of myself, insofar as I am "I," is not open to confusion. It is impossible for me to become confused with another, or for another to be confused with me. This is unlike *anta*, for you may be confused with another, and another may be confused with you, in my intellect and my opinion. Moreover, you are more cognizable than *huwa*. The upshot is that the most cognizable of the implicit pronouns is (*ana*), and the most remote from cognition is (*huwa*), while (*anta*) is intermediate between them. Thorough reflection reveals the truth of this claim.

Among the things that indicate that the most cognizable pronoun in speech is my saying "*ana*" is that the speaker, when alone, has a term in which masculine and feminine are alike without distinction. This is because distinction is needed only when there is fear of ambiguity, and here ambiguity is not possible, so there is no need for distinction. As for the dual and the plural, the term remains one. In the attached form, as in your saying *shariba-na* ("we drank"), and in the detached form, as in *nahnu* ("we"), this is so because there is no fear of confusion.

As for the addressee, the feminine and masculine forms are distinguished, and the term has dual and plural forms, because a feminine and a masculine may be present in the presence of the speaker, and he may face both of them and address one of them, and not be known [which one he means] until he specifies it by a sign. The dual and plural of the addressee are good for this reason. As for the fact that the present is more cognizable than the absent, this is a matter akin to what is self-evident.

Having understood this, we say: it has become clear that the cognition of each thing through its own essence is more complete than its cognition through something else, whether it is present or absent. Thus, the complete cognition of God belongs to none but God, because He is the One who says to Himself "*ana*," and the term *ana* is the most cognizable of the three categories. Since no one can reach that Reality through the pronoun that is most cognizable, which is the saying "*ana*," except He, Glorified is He, we know that the complete cognition of Him, Glorified and Exalted is He, belongs to none but Him.

There remains the fact that there are people who permit *ittihad* (union): when human spirits are illumined by the lights of knowledge of that Reality, the intellect becomes united with the intelligible, and at the time of union it is valid for that knower to say: "I am God." However, the doctrine of union is not intelligible, for in the state of union, if both or one of them perish, then that is not union, and if both remain, then they are two, not one. When this path, which is the most perfect of the paths in indication, was closed, the other two paths remained: *anta* (you) and *huwa* (he). As for *anta*, it is for those present in the stations of unveilings and witnessings, for one who has passed away from all human appetites, as God, Exalted is He, related about Jonah, peace be upon him, that after he had passed away from the darkness of the world of origination (*hudut*) and from the traces of origination, he reached the station of witnessing and said: ﴿Then he called out in the darkness: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87]. This alerts you that there is no way to reach the station of contemplation and address except through absence from everything other than Him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I cannot enumerate praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself." As for *huwa*, it is for the absent.

Here there is an investigation: *huwa*, with respect to Him, is the most noble of names, and the following considerations show this:

First: a name is either universal (*kulli*) or particular (*juz'i*). By "universal" I mean that its concept is such that its conception does not prevent the occurrence of sharing (*shirka*). By "particular" I mean that the very conception of it prevents sharing, and this is the term that signifies that specific individual insofar as it is that individual. If it is the first, then what is indicated by that name is not the Real, Glorified is He, for since the concept of that name is something that does not prevent sharing, while His specific essence, Glorified and Exalted is He, prevents sharing, it is necessarily certain that what is indicated by that name is not the Real, Glorified is He. Therefore all derivative names, such as *al-Rahman*, *al-Rahim*, *al-Hakim*, *al-Alim*, and *al-Qadir*, do not encompass His specific essence, nor do they signify it in any way whatsoever. If it is the second, then it is the one named by a proper name (*ism al-'alam*), and the proper name stands in the place of indication, so there is no difference between your saying "O Zayd" and your saying "O you" or "O he." Since the proper name stands in the place of indication, the proper name is a branch, and the demonstrative name is a root, and the root is more noble than the branch. Thus our saying "O you" and "O he" is more noble than all other names entirely. Except that the difference is that *anta* is a term that encompasses the present, and *huwa* encompasses the absent. There is also another secret in it: *huwa* can only be used to refer to something when the form of that thing has arisen in the intellect, and your saying *huwa* encompasses that form while it is present. So the matter returns to the point that *huwa* also encompasses only the present.

Second: we have shown that the reality of the Real is exalted above all modes of composition, and the absolutely single cannot be described, for description requires difference between the described and the description, and when difference occurs, singularity does not remain. Likewise, it is impossible to report about Him, for reporting requires a reported-about and a reporter, and that contradicts singularity. Thus it is established that all derivative names fall short of reaching the essence of the Real. As for the term *huwa*, it reaches the essence of that singular reality, purified of all aspects of multiplicity. Because this term reaches the essence of the reality, it must be more noble than the other terms which cannot reach the essence of that reality.

Third: derivative terms indicate the occurrence of an attribute in the essence. Then the quiddities of the attributes of the Real are also not known except through their manifest traces in the world of origination. Thus we know of His knowledge only that it is the thing by which perfect ordering and mastery are validly issued from Him, and of His power only that it is the thing by which the doing and the leaving undone are validly issued from Him. So these attributes cannot be conceived by us except when we turn to the differing states in the world of origination. Therefore derivative terms do not point to the Real alone, Glorified is He, but point to Him and to the world of origination together. One who looks at two things is not complete in each of them, but rather is deficient and falls short. Thus all derivative names do not yield total immersion in the station of knowing the Real, but rather they become a veil between the servant and total immersion in the knowledge of the Lord. As for *huwa*, it is a term that indicates Him insofar as He is He, not insofar as an relation or attribution to the world of origination has befallen Him. So the term *huwa* connects you to the Real and cuts you off from all else, whereas the other names do not cut you off from all else. Thus with the term *huwa* it is more noble.

Fourth: the previous demonstrations have shown that the source of majesty and might is the Essence, and that His essence is not perfected by attributes; rather His essence, by its perfection, necessitates the attributes of perfection. The term *huwa* connects you to the wellspring of mercy, might, and exaltedness, which is the Essence, while the other terms do not stop you except in the stations of qualities and attributes. Thus the term *huwa* is more noble. This is what came to mind in unveiling the secrets of the term *huwa*. To Him, Glorified is He, we turn in hope that He illumine our breasts and our inner secrets with a pearl from the flashes of its lights, and refresh with it our intellects and our spirits, until we are freed from the narrowness of the world of origination into the expanse of the ascents of eternity, and rise from the low ground of the darkness of humanity to the heavens of lights. That is not difficult for Him.

**Ninth Issue:** The grammarians said, regarding God's saying ﴿There is no god but He﴾, that *huwa* is in the nominative because it is a substitute (*badal*) for the position of *la* together with its noun. Let us speak about your saying: *ma ja'ani rajulun illa Zaydun* ("No man came to me except Zayd"). Here *illa Zaydun* is in the nominative by way of substitution, because substitution is turning away from the first and taking the second. It is as though you said: "Nothing came to me except Zayd." This is intelligible, because it conveys the negation of coming from everyone except Zayd. As for your saying *ja'ani illa Zaydan* ("Creatures came to me except Zayd"), substitution is not possible here, because it becomes in estimation: "Creatures came to me except Zayd," and that requires that everyone came except Zayd, and that is impossible. Thus the difference is clear, and God knows best.

As for ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, the discussion of their interpretation has already preceded, and we explained that mercy with respect to Him, Glorified is He, is blessing, and its agent is the Merciful. When we want to convey multiplicity, we say *Rahim*. When we want the complete intensification that belongs to none but Him, Glorified is He, we say *al-Rahman*.

Know that He, Glorified is He, specifically mentioned these two attributes in this context because the mention of divine singular lordship conveys domination and exaltedness, so He followed them with the mention of this intensification in mercy, as a refreshment for hearts from the awe of divinity and the might of singularity, and as an indication that His mercy has preceded His wrath, and that He created creation only for mercy and beneficence.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 164 (part 1 of 7):

﻿﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ship that runs in the sea with what benefits people, the water that Allah sends down from the sky, giving life thereby to the earth after its death and scattering in it every kind of creature, the turning of the winds, and the clouds subjected between heaven and earth, are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, decreed Oneness and Unity (al-fardaniyya wa'l-wahdaniyya), He mentioned eight kinds of proofs by which His existence may first be established, and by which His Oneness and His freedom from opposites and rivals may be established.

Second: Before entering into the explanation of these proofs, some issues must be clarified.

The first issue: People have disagreed over whether creation (al-khalq) is the created thing (al-makhluq) or something other than it. A group of scholars said: creation is the created thing. They argued for this from the verse and from rational argument. As for the verse, it is this verse, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day﴾ up to His words: ﴿are signs for a people who use their reason﴾. It is known that signs are only in the created thing, because the created thing is what points to the Maker. So this verse shows that creation is the created thing.

As for rational argument, they argued for it with several matters:

The first: Creation is the bringing of a thing from non-existence into existence. If this bringing were something distinct from the power and the effect, then it is either eternal or originated. If it is eternal, then the notion of bringing from non-existence into existence has already occurred in pre-eternity, and bringing from non-existence into existence is preceded by non-existence, while pre-eternity is the negation of being preceded. So if the bringing occurred in pre-eternity, the two contradictories would combine, which is impossible. If it is originated, then it also needs a bringer that brings it from non-existence into existence, so it needs another bringing. The discussion of that is as in the first, and an infinite regress (tasalsul) follows.

The second: He, exalted is He, in pre-eternity was not bringing things from their non-existence into their existence. Then, in pre-eternity, did He originate something or not? If He originated something, that originated thing is the created thing. If He did not originate anything, then Allah, exalted is He, never created anything at all.

The third: Being an agent (al-mu'aththiriyya) is a relation between the essence of the agent and the essence of the effect, and a relation between two things cannot be established without the related thing. So this agency, if it is originated, an infinite regress follows; and if it is eternal, it is one of the necessary attributes of the essence of Allah, exalted is He. The occurrence of the effect, whether in the present or in the future, is then a necessary consequence of this eternal, great attribute, and the necessary consequence of a necessary consequence is necessary. So the effect would be a necessary consequence of the essence of Allah, exalted is He, and then Allah would not be a free, choosing agent, but compelled and forced to that influence, and He would be an essential cause (illa mujiba). And that is disbelief.

Those who held that creation is other than the created thing argued with several points:

The first: They said: There is no dispute that Allah, exalted is He, is described as a Creator before He created things, and the Creator is the one described by creation. So if creation were the created thing, it would follow that He is described by created things, among them devils, Iblis-kind, and filth, and no rational person says that.

The second: When we see something originated that came into being after it was not, we say: if this thing came to exist after it was not, then if it is said to us that Allah, exalted is He, created it and brought it into existence, we accept that and say it is true and correct. But if it were said that it came into existence by itself, we would say that is an error, disbelief and self-contradiction. So since it is valid to explain its origination after non-existence by saying that Allah, exalted is He, created it, and it is not valid to explain its origination by its origination in itself, we know that the creation of it by Allah, exalted is He, is distinct from its existence in itself. So creation is other than the created thing.

The third: We know the actions of servants and we know Allah, exalted is He, and His power, but we do not know whether the agent in the actions of servants is the power of Allah or the power of the servant. What is known is other than what is known. So the agency of the power of the one with power in the occurrence of what is empowered is distinct from that power itself and from that empowered thing itself. Then this distinction cannot be a negative one, because it is the opposite of agency, which is a non-existent (adamiyya) matter. So this agency is a positive attribute (sifa thubutiyya) additional to the essence of the agent and the essence of the effect, and that is what was sought.

The fourth: The grammarians said: when we say "Allah created the world" (khalaqa Allahu al-'alam), the world is not the verbal noun (al-masdar) but the object (al-maf'ul bihi). That shows that the creating of the world is other than the world.

The fifth: It is valid to say "the creation of blackness" and "the creation of whiteness," and "the creation of substance" and "the creation of accident." So the concept of creation is one single matter in all of them, distinct from these differing quiddities (mahiyyat), on the evidence that the division of creatorhood into creatorhood of substance and creatorhood of accident is valid, and the subject of the division is common to the divisions. So it is established that creation is other than the created thing. This is the sum of what is in this issue.

* * *

The second issue: Abu Muslim, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The root of khalq in the language of the Arabs is measuring (al-taqdir). It became a name for the actions of Allah, exalted is He, since all of them are right and proper. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and He created everything and measured it with precise measure﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]. And people say of every well-made matter: "it is made according to a measure" (ma'mul 'ala taqdir).

The third issue: This verse shows that it is necessary to establish the existence of the Maker through rational proofs, and that imitation (taqlid) is not a way to achieve this goal.

* * *

The fourth issue: Ibn Jarir mentioned in the occasion of revelation (sabab nuzul) of the verse: From 'Ata', that when he (peace be upon him) arrived at Medina, there was revealed to him: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163]. The unbelievers of Quraysh in Mecca said: How can one God suffice for people? So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾.

And from Sa'id ibn Masruq, who said: Quraysh asked the Jews, and they said: Tell us about the signs that Moses brought. So they told them about the staff and the white hand. They asked the Christians about that, and they told them about healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead. Then Quraysh said to the Prophet (peace be upon him): Pray to Allah that He make Safa into gold for us, so that we may increase in certainty and in strength against our enemy. So he asked his Lord for that, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him that He would give it to them, but if they denied after that, He would punish them with a punishment that He would not inflict on anyone among the worlds. Then he (peace be upon him) said: «Leave me and my people, I will call them day by day.» Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse, making clear to them that if they wanted Him to make Safa gold for them so that they would increase in certainty, then the creation of the heavens and the earth and all that is mentioned is greater.

* * *

Know that the discussion of these eight kinds of proofs falls into divisions.

The first division: It concerns detailing what is said about each of them. The first kind of proof is reasoning from the conditions of the heavens. We have mentioned a portion of this in the commentary on His words: ﴿He who made the earth for you a bed and the heaven a building﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22]. Let us here mention another pattern of discourse:

It is related that 'Umar ibn al-Husam used to read the book of the Almagest (al-Mijisti) to 'Umar al-Abhari. One day some of the jurists said: What are you reading? He said: I am interpreting a verse of the Qur'an, namely His words: ﴿Have they not looked at the heaven above them, how We built it?﴾ [Qaf: 6], and I am explaining how it was built. Al-Abhari spoke truly in what he said, for everyone who goes deeper into the seas of Allah's created things has more knowledge of the majesty and greatness of Allah, exalted is He. So we say: The discussion of the conditions of the heavens, in the concise manner suitable to this place, is arranged in sections:

* * *

The first section: On the arrangement of the spheres (al-aflak).

They said: The nearest of them to us is the sphere of the Moon, above it the sphere of Mercury, then Venus, then the sphere of the Sun, then the sphere of Mars, then the sphere of Jupiter, then the sphere of Saturn, then the sphere of the fixed stars, then the outermost sphere (al-falak al-a'zam).

Know that on this subject there are investigations:

The first investigation: They mentioned three ways of knowing this order:

The first: Motion. That is, when a lower star passes between our sight and a higher star, the two are seen as one star, and the moving one is distinguished from the hidden one by its dominant color, such as the yellowness of Mercury, the whiteness of Venus, the redness of Mars, the pearl-like hue of Jupiter, and the dusky tint of Saturn. Then the ancients found that the Moon eclipses the six planets and many of the fixed stars along its path in the zodiac, and the planet Mercury eclipses Venus, and Venus eclipses Mars. On this order, this method shows that the Moon is below the Sun, because the Sun is eclipsed by it. But it does not show whether the Sun is above or below the rest of the stars, because the Sun is not eclipsed by any of them, since their lights vanish in the light of the Sun. So this method fails with respect to the Sun.

The second: Difference in parallax (ikhtilaf al-mandhar). It is perceptible for the Moon, Mercury and Venus, and not perceptible for Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. As for the Sun, it is very little. So the Sun must be intermediate between the two groups. This method is quite clear to whoever considers the difference in the parallax of the stars and observes it in the manner we have described. As for one who has not practised it, he is a mere imitator in this matter, especially since Abu al-Rayhan, who is the master of this discipline, mentioned in his summary of the Chapters of al-Farghani that parallax is perceived only in the Moon.

The third: Batlamyus (Ptolemy) said: Saturn, Jupiter and Mars are far from the Sun in all distances, but Mercury and Venus do not get far from the Sun beyond the sextile, let alone other distances. So the Sun must be intermediate between the two groups. But this argument is weak, because it is refuted by the Moon, which is far from the Sun at every distance, although it is beneath all of them.

* * *

The second investigation: On the number of the spheres. They said: They are only nine. The truth is that since observation indicated these nine, we affirmed them. As for what is beyond them, since observation does not indicate it, we neither firmly affirmed its existence nor its non-existence. Ibn Sina mentioned in the Shifa': "It has not become clear to me until now whether the sphere of the fixed stars is one sphere, or spheres one of which is fitted over another." I say: This possibility is real, because what can be used as evidence for the unity of the sphere of the fixed stars is only to say that their motions are uniform, and if that is so, it must be that they are set in one sphere. But both premises are weak.

Page 164

As for the first premise: Although their motions appear similar to our senses, in reality they perhaps are not so. For if we assume that one of them completes the cycle in thirty-six thousand years, and another completes this cycle in the same time but falls short by a tenth, and we distribute that tenth over the days of thirty-six thousand years, there is no doubt that the share of each day, nay, of each year, nay, of each thousand years, is something that does not become perceptible. And if that is so, the certainty of the similarity of the motions of the fixed stars falls away.

The second premise: since their movements are similar, it is necessary that they be fixed in a single sphere. This too is not certain. For things that differ are not far-fetched in sharing one necessary property. Rather, I say: this possibility that Ibn Sina mentioned regarding the sphere of the fixed stars applies to all spheres. For the path to the unity of each sphere is nothing but what we have mentioned and refuted. Therefore it is not possible to be certain of the unity of the daily moving sphere. Perhaps they are many different spheres, differing in the measures of their movements by a very small amount, which our lifetimes are not sufficient to detect. The same holds for all the "imitating" (mumaththalat) and "carrying" (hawamil) spheres.

Some people have affirmed a sphere above the sphere of the fixed stars and beneath the highest sphere (al-falak al-a'zam), and they argued from several aspects:

The first: Observers of the greatest obliquity (al-mayl al-a'zam) found it to vary in magnitude, and whoever's observation was earlier found the greatest obliquity to be larger. Ptolemy found it to be (kj na) [23°51′], then it was found in the time of al-Ma'mun to be (kj lh) [23°35′], then after al-Ma'mun it was found to have decreased by a minute. This implies that it is in the nature of the two poles that their inclination sometimes decreases and sometimes increases. This is only possible if between the sphere of the whole and the sphere of the fixed stars there is another sphere whose two poles revolve around the two poles of the sphere of the whole, and the sphere of the fixed stars also has its two poles revolving around the two poles of that sphere. Thus its pole sometimes comes to be lowered toward the northern side, and sometimes raised toward the southern side. It follows from this that the equator of the day coincides with the zodiac belt and sometimes separates from it toward the south.

Second: Astronomers have greatly disagreed about the measure of the sun's course, as is explained in the extended works. To the extent that Ptolemy reported from Abrikhs (Hipparchus) that he was doubtful whether this course occurs in equal or unequal times.

Then people have mentioned two views regarding the cause of this difference:

One of them is the view of those who make the apogee of the sun (awj al-shams) move. For they claimed that the variation affecting the sun's motion from this aspect differs at the two equinoctial points, due to the difference of their distance from the apogee, so the duration of the sun's course differs because of it.

The second is the view of the people of India, China, and Babylon, and most of the ancient scholars of Rome, Egypt, and Syria: that the cause of it is the movement of the sphere of the zodiac, and the rising and lowering of its poles. It is reported from Abrikhs that he held this view. Barba al-Iskandarani mentioned that the practitioners of talismans (al-tilsamat) also believed this, and that the pole of the zodiac sphere advances from its place and recedes by eight degrees. They said: the beginning of the movement is from (kb) degrees of Pisces to the first point of Aries.

Third: Ptolemy observed the fixed stars and found that they traverse one degree every hundred years, while the later astronomers observed them and found that they traverse one and a half degrees every hundred years. This is a great discrepancy, and it is far-fetched to attribute it to differences in instruments which skilled craftsmen make with careful precision. Therefore it must be attributed to the increase and decrease of obliquity, and this requires affirming the existence of the sphere we have mentioned.

* * *

The third discussion: They argued that the fixed stars are fixed in a sphere above the spheres of these seven planets,
[p. 165]
saying: We have observed for these seven spheres movements faster than the movements of these fixed stars, and it is established that the stars move only by the movement of the sphere. This requires that these fixed stars be fixed in a sphere other than these seven. And it is not permissible that they be fixed in the greatest sphere, because it moves swiftly, revolving in every day and night roughly one full revolution. Then they said: they are fixed in a sphere above the spheres of these seven, because these seven stars sometimes eclipse those fixed stars, and the eclipsing body is beneath the eclipsed one. Therefore the spheres of these seven must be beneath the spheres of the fixed stars.

This route too is weak in several respects:

The first: We do not concede that a star moves only by a celestial motion. They built this on the impossibility of piercing the spheres, and we have already shown the weakness of their proofs for that.

The second: Suppose we grant that these fixed stars must have other spheres. Yet your position is that each of these seven spheres is divided into many parts, whose totality is the imitating sphere (al-falak al-mumaththal), and that this imitating sphere moves slowly in accordance with the motion of the sphere of the fixed stars. So why is it not permissible to say: these fixed stars are fixed in these slow-moving imitating spheres? As for the planets, they are fixed in the carrying spheres (al-hawamil), which are eccentric spheres (aflak kharijat al-markaz). On this supposition, there is no need to establish a sphere of the fixed stars.

The third: Suppose there must be another sphere. Why is it not permissible that there be two spheres, one above the sphere of Saturn and the other beneath the sphere of the Moon? For these planets only pass through the fixed stars that lie in the path of those planets. As for the fixed stars near the two poles, the planets do not pass through any of them nor eclipse them. So the fixed stars that are eclipsed by these planets—suppose we judged them to be fixed in a sphere above the sphere of Saturn—how do we know that those which are not eclipsed by these planets are not beneath the planets? Thus it is established that what they said is not demonstrative, but merely probable.

* * *

The fourth discussion: They claimed that the greatest sphere has the swiftest of motions, for it revolves in a day and night nearly one complete revolution, and that it moves from east to west.

As for the eighth sphere beneath it, it is at extreme slowness, to the point that it moves one degree every hundred years according to Ptolemy, and according to the later astronomers one degree every sixty-six years, and that it moves from west to east, opposite to the first motion. They argued for this by saying: when we observed these fixed stars we found for them a motion contrary to the daily motion.

Know that this too is weak. Why is it not permissible to say: the greatest sphere moves from east to west every day and night in one complete revolution, and the eighth sphere also moves from east to west every day and night in one revolution, except by an amount of about a tenth of a second? Hence we necessarily perceive the motion of the stars in sensation as differing from the first motion by that small quantity in the direction opposite to the first motion. When those amounts accumulate, it appears to the senses as though the fixed star returns with a slow motion in the opposite direction to the daily motion. This possibility is real, and they have not established a proof for its refutation. Then what indicates that it is the truth consists of two aspects:

The first, which is demonstrative: If the motion of the eighth sphere were opposite to the motion of the greatest sphere, then at the moment it moves with the motion of the greatest sphere in one direction, it would either move by its own motion in the opposite direction, or it would not move at that time by the requirement of its own motion. If the first, it follows that one thing simultaneously moves in two directions, and motion in two directions requires being in both directions at once, which is impossible. If the second, it follows that the celestial motions cease, and they do not accept that.

[p. 166]

The second: The limit of motion belongs to the greatest sphere, and the limit of rest belongs to the earth. And what is closer to reason is to say: whatever is nearer to the greatest sphere is swifter in motion, and whatever is farther is slower in motion. The sphere of the fixed stars is the nearest of the spheres to it, so there is no difference between the two motions except by a small amount, which is what results from accumulating the measures of difference in every hundred years of one degree. Next is the sphere of Saturn, for it is slower than the sphere of the fixed stars, so its lag behind the greatest sphere is greater, to the point that when the measures of difference accumulate, they reach a complete revolution in every thirty years. According to this view, whatever is farther from the greatest sphere is slower in motion, so its difference increases until it reaches the sphere of the Moon, which is the slowest of the spheres in motion. It lags behind the greatest sphere by thirteen degrees every day, so it completes its revolution every month. It continues thus until it reaches the earth, which is the farthest of things from the sphere, so it is in the extreme of rest. Thus it is established that their discourse on these principles is corrupt and weak, and that the intellect has no path to reaching them.

* * *

Second section: On knowing the spheres.

The people laid down for themselves two conjectural premises:

One: that the motions of the celestial bodies are uniform and continuous, that they do not slow down at one time and speed up at another, and that they have no reversal from their directions.

The second: that the stars do not move by themselves, but by the motion of the sphere. Then they built upon these two premises another premise, saying: the sphere that carries the stars either has its center at the center of the earth, or does not. If its center is the earth, then either the star is fixed in its thickness, or it is fixed in a body fixed within the thickness of that sphere. If the first, it is impossible for the star's nearness and distance from the earth to differ, and for its traversing of arcs of that sphere to differ, and the accidents of difference in the motion of the sphere or the motion of the star—and we have assumed that these do not occur at all. So the other two divisions remain:

One of them: that the star is fixed in a spherical body moving in a circle, set into the thickness of the sphere surrounding the earth, and we call that body the epicyclic sphere (al-falak al-mudawwar). Then there occurs, by reason of its motion, a variation in the state of the star relative to the earth: sometimes nearness and distance, sometimes retrogression and direct motion, and sometimes smallness and largeness in appearance. The other possibility is that the sphere surrounding the earth does not have its center coinciding with the center of the earth; this is the eccentric sphere (al-falak al-kharij al-markaz). It follows that the carrier, in one half of the zodiac belt of that sphere, is greater than half, and in its other half less than half. Therefore there occurs by means of it nearness and distance from the earth, and it traverses one half of the zodiac in a longer time than it takes to traverse the other half. Thus it is clear that the variation of the states of the stars in their smallness and largeness, their swiftness and slowness, and their nearness and distance from the earth cannot occur except by one of these two things, namely the epicycle and the eccentric sphere.

Having understood this, let us return to the detail: their statement about the spheres. They said: these nine spheres, of which some are a sphere

[p. 167]

**[Commentary of al-Razi, Mafatih al-Ghayb, on Surah 2, verse 164, part 3 of 7]**

...one sphere, which is the outermost sphere (al-falak al-a'zam, the Primum Mobile) and the sphere of the fixed stars (falak al-thawabit). Among them is a sphere that divides into two spheres, which is the sphere of the Sun (falak al-shams). This happens because another sphere separates from it, whose center is not the center of the universe, such that the convex surfaces of the two touch at a point called the apogee (al-awj), which is the farthest distance of the separated sphere. Their concave surfaces touch at a point called the perigee (al-hadid), which is its nearest distance. In reality, they are one sphere, from which another sphere has separated, but it is said "two spheres" loosely. The sphere from which it separated is called the enveloping sphere (al-falak al-mumaththal), and the separated sphere whose center is off-center is called the eccentric sphere of the apogee (falak al-awj). The body of the Sun is immersed in it, such that its surface touches both of their surfaces.

Among them is a sphere that divides into three spheres, which are the spheres of the upper planets (al-kawakib al-ulwiyya) and Venus. Each of these has two spheres like the sphere of the Sun, and another sphere whose position relative to the off-center is like the position of the body of the Sun in its sphere. This is called the epicycle (falak al-tadwir), and the planet is immersed in it such that its surface touches the epicycle's surface. The off-center sphere is called the carrying sphere (al-falak al-hamil).

Among them is a sphere that divides into four spheres, which is the sphere of Mercury and the Moon. As for Mercury, it has two spheres like the two spheres of the Sun, and from the second there separates another sphere in the manner by which the off-center separates from the enveloping, such that its center lies outside the two centers. Its distance from the center of the off-center sphere equals half the distance between the centers of the off-center and the enveloping spheres. The sphere separated from it is called the directing sphere (al-falak al-mudir), and the separated one is the carrying sphere (al-falak al-hamil). From it is the epicycle, and Mercury is in it, as has preceded regarding the four spheres.

As for the Moon, its sphere divides into two parallel spheres: the greater is the enveloping sphere and the lesser is the inclined sphere (al-falak al-mail). The inclined sphere divides into three spheres, as with the four planets. Every sphere from which another sphere separates in the form you have learned in the sphere of the Sun leaves two remaining spheres from the one separated from, of differing thickness, called the complementing spheres (mutammimayn) of that separated sphere. Each of these spheres moves on its own center with a constant, continuous motion until God decrees a matter that is to be done. People have arrived at knowledge of these spheres only on the basis of the premise we established, and there is no doubt that if it is valid, then the statement about these things is valid; the matter is in the premise itself.

* * *

**Chapter Three: On the Magnitudes of the Motions**

The majority said: all the spheres move from west to east, except the outermost sphere, the directing sphere of Mercury, the enveloping sphere, the inclined sphere, and the directing sphere of the Moon. The eastward motion is called motion in the direction of succession (al-harakah ila al-tawali), and the westward motion is called motion against succession. The outermost sphere moves with a rapid motion, completing one revolution every day and night, around two poles called the poles of the universe (qutbay al-'alam). It moves all the spheres and stars. By this motion the rising and setting of the stars occur, and it is called the first motion (al-harakah al-ula). The sphere of the fixed stars moves with a slow motion, one degree every sixty-six years according to the later astronomers, around two poles called the poles of the zodiac sphere (qutbay falak al-buruj). These two revolve around the poles of the universe by the first motion, and all moving spheres move in accordance with this motion. By this motion the apogees shift from their place on the zodiac sphere. It is called the second motion, the motion of the apogee (harakat al-awj), and it is the motion of the fixed stars.

The fixed stars are called "fixed" for several reasons:
First: their motion is slow, since in relation to the planets they resemble the stationary.
[Page 168]
Second: the planets move toward them, while they do not move toward the planets, so it is as if the fixed stars are fixed in waiting for them.
Third: their latitudes are fixed at one measure that does not change.
Fourth: the distances between them are fixed in one state that does not change, so the imagined forms upon them of the forty-eight figures remain.
Fifth: according to most common people of the nations, the times are marked by their rising and setting, such that they differ only over centuries and ages.

As for the off-center spheres, they move each day as follows: Saturn (b), Jupiter (dnt), Mars, by the indication of the Sun (la kr), Venus (nt j), Mercury (nt h), and the Moon (yj yj mw). This is called the motion of the center (harakat al-markaz) and the motion of the mean (harakat al-wasat), and these are the motions of the centers of the epicyclic spheres and the center of the Sun. The epicyclic spheres move by this measure: Saturn (nrh), Jupiter (nd t), Mars (krmb), Venus (lwnt), Mercury (j wkd), and the Moon (yj j nd). This is called the particular motion (al-harakah al-khassa) and the motion of anomaly (harakat al-ikhtilaf), and these are the motions of the centers of the planets. Know that because of these different motions, various conditions befall these planets:

First: the Moon, for example, has various distances which are not fixed in relation to this world. The fixed types among them are four:
The first: the Moon is at the nearest distance of the epicycle, and the center of the epicycle is at the nearest distance from the off-center sphere, which is called the nearest distance. It is approximately thirty-three times half the radius of the Earth.
The second: the Moon is at the farthest distance of the epicycle, and the center of the epicycle is at the nearest distance from the off-center sphere, which is the nearest distance for the farthest. It is forty-three times half the radius of the Earth.
The third: the Moon is at the nearest distance of the epicycle, and the center of the epicycle is at the farthest distance from the off-center sphere, which is the farthest for the nearest. It is fifty-four times half the radius of the Earth.
The fourth: the Moon is at the farthest distance of the epicycle, and the center of the epicycle is at the farthest distance from the off-center sphere, which is the farthest distance. It is sixty-four times half the radius of the Earth. Then, the conditions between these four points differ, as Abu al-Rayhan has explained.

Second: all the planets are linked to the Sun in some way. As for the superior planets, the distance of their centers from the apexes of their epicyclic spheres is always equal to the distance of the Sun's center from the centers of their epicycles. At that time they are burned (muhtarigah, i.e., obscured by the Sun's proximity), and when they are at the perigee they are in opposition, and then they are opposite the Sun. This happens when they are conjoined with the Sun at the midpoint of direct motion, and opposed to it at the midpoint of retrograde motion. It has been said that half the radius of the epicycle of Mars is greater than half the radius of the enveloping sphere of the Sun, so it follows that when it is conjoined with the Sun, the distance of its center from the Sun's center is greater than when it is opposite it. As for the inferior planets, the centers of their epicyclic spheres are always conjoined with the Sun, so it follows that the Sun is conjoined with the apex and the perigee at the midpoints of direct motion, and retrogression is the greatest distance of each of them from the Sun equal to half the radius of their epicycles. For Venus this is (mh) and for Mercury (kh), approximately. As for the Moon, the Sun's center is always intermediate between its farthest distance and the center of its epicycle. Therefore, the distance of the center of its epicycle from the farthest distance is called the doubled distance (al-bu'd al-mudaaf), because it is double the distance of the center of its epicycle from the Sun. It follows that whenever the center of its epicycle is at the farthest distance, it is either opposite the Sun or conjoined with it, and whenever it is at the nearest distance, the Sun is in its quadrature. Therefore, its conjunction and opposition with the Sun occur at the farthest distance, and its quadrature with the Sun at the nearest.

* * *

**Chapter Four: On How These Conditions Are Used as Evidence for the Existence of the Creator**

This is in several aspects:

First: consider the magnitudes of these spheres. Although they share the celestial nature, each of them is specified with a particular magnitude. Yet it is not impossible in reason for them to be other than that magnitude, greater or smaller by an atom. When pure reason decrees that all magnitudes are equally possible, it decrees that their magnitudes require a specifying, directing agent.

Second: consider their locations. Each sphere touches, with its convex side, another sphere above it, and with its concave side another sphere below it. Then that sphere is either uniform in its parts, or it ends ultimately in a uniform body. That uniform body must have the nature of each of its two ends equal to the nature of its other end. So just as it is valid for its convex side to meet a body, it must be valid for its concave side to meet that body. When this is so, it is valid that the higher can become the lower, and the lower can become the higher. When this is so, the specification of each of them to its determined place becomes a permissible matter, which reason decrees requires a determining cause.

Third: each star that is situated in the concavity of a sphere is specified to one side of that sphere rather than the other sides. Then that point of the sphere where the star is situated is equal to its other sides, because the sphere, according to them, is a uniform body. So the specification of that concavity to that star rather than the other sides is a possible and permissible matter, and reason decrees that it requires a specifier.

Fourth: every sphere rotates around two specific poles. If the sphere is uniform in its parts, all the points assumed on it are equal, and all the circles assumed on it are also equal. So the specification of two particular points to be poles rather than the other points, while they are equal in nature, is a permissible matter, and reason decrees that it requires a determining cause. The same applies to the specification of each particular circle among its circles to be the equator.

Fifth: the celestial bodies, although they are alike in celestial nature, each of them is specified with a particular type of motion in slowness and speed. Consider the outermost sphere, with its utmost extent and magnitude: it completes one full revolution in a day and night. The eighth sphere, which is smaller than it, does not complete a full revolution except in thirty-six years according to the majority's view. Then the seventh sphere, which is beneath it, revolves in thirty years. The specification of the greatest with excessive speed and the smallest with excessive slowness is contrary to the judgment of reason, for it would have been fitting that the wider should be slower in motion because of the greatness of its orbit, and the smaller should turn more quickly because of the smallness of its orbit. This is not explained except by a specifier. Reason decrees that each of them is specified with what it is upon, by the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

Sixth: when the off-center sphere separates from the enveloping sphere, two complementing spheres remain: one from the outside and the other from the inside. This is a body of uniform nature. Then one of its sides is specified with extreme thickness, and the other with extreme thinness, in relation to each other. When this is so, the ratio of that thickness and thinness to its nature must be equal, so the specification of one of its sides with thinness and the other with thickness must be through the choosing of a specifying, chooser agent.

Seventh: they differ in the directions of their motions. Some move from east to west, some from west to east, some northward and some southward, although all directions are equal in relation to them. Therefore, there must be a need for a directing agent.

**Eighthly:** We now see the heavenly spheres in motion. It is impossible to say that they were eternally in motion, or that they were not in motion and then began to move. It is impossible to say that they were eternally in motion because the essence of motion (*mahiyyat al-harakah*) requires being preceded by something else, since motion is a transition from one state to another, while eternity (*azal*) excludes being preceded by something else. Therefore, combining motion with eternity is impossible. And if we say that they were not in motion from eternity, whether we say that they existed before that motion and were at rest, or that they did not exist at all before it, then the beginning of motion after the absence of motion requires dependence on an eternal Governor (*mudabbir qadim*), glorified and exalted is He, to set them in motion after they had been non-existent, or after they had been at rest. This line of argument is the best and strongest of arguments.

**Ninthly:** It may be said that their movements are either necessary consequences of their specific corporeality, or not. But we see their specific corporealities separated from each part of that motion. Therefore, each part of their motion is not a necessary consequence of them. Thus the spheres, in their movements, depend on a mover from outside, and that is the Mover of movers, the Governor of the fixed stars and the planets, who is the Truth, glorified and exalted is He.

**Tenthly:** This marvelous order in the composition of these spheres and the harmony of their movements: do you think it is founded on wisdom, or does it occur by chance and without purpose? The second alternative is false and far from reason. If someone allowed that in a lofty building and a towering palace, dust and water came together, then produced bricks, and then these were assembled into a towering palace and a high structure, he would be judged insane. We know that the composition of these spheres, the stars within them, and their movements is no less than that building. Therefore, it is established that there must be the exercise of wisdom in them. Then it is not free of one of two options: either it is said that they are living, rational beings that move by themselves, or it is said that a dominant Governor moves them. The first is false, because their movement is either for the purpose of seeking perfection or not for this purpose. If they move in order to attain some perfection, then they are deficient in their essence, seeking completion, and what is deficient in itself must have a perfecter; so they are dependent and needy. If they do not move to seek perfection, then they are acting in vain. Thus the matter comes down to this: it is unlikely to the intellect that the operation of these vast bodies and constant movements should be founded on vanity and folly. No option remains in the intellect more fitting to be adopted than that a dominant Governor, prevailing over the eternity and time, moves them for hidden secrets and subtle wisdoms, which He alone holds and knows. Our part is only to believe in them in general, as He said: ﴿They reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain."﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 191].

**Eleventhly:** We see them differing in colors: the yellow of Mercury (*Utarid*), the whiteness of Venus (*Zuhrah*), the light of the sun, the redness of Mars (*Mirrikh*), the brilliance of Jupiter (*Mushtari*), the dullness of Saturn (*Zuhal*), and the difference of each of the fixed stars in a particular size, a particular color, and a particular composition. We also see them differing in good and bad fortune. We see the highest of the planets as the most ill-omened, and those below it as more fortunate. We see the lord of the stars (*sultan al-kawakib*) fortunate in some conjunctions and unfortunate in others. We see them differing in faces, cheeks, gums, masculinity and femininity, and in some being diurnal and some nocturnal, some direct and some retrograde, some ascending and some descending, while all of them share transparency, clarity, and purity of substance. The intellect therefore judges that the particular attribute of each of them must come about through the specification of a specifier.

**Twelfthly:** These stars, if they have influence in this world, are either opposing one another, or cooperating, or neither opposing nor cooperating. If they are opposing, then either some of them are stronger than others, or they are equal in strength. If some are stronger than others, the stronger would always prevail and the weaker would always be overcome, and so the conditions of the world would have to continue according to the nature of that star. But this is not the case. If they are equal in strength and yet opposing, then the action of all of them together must be impossible, and the visible effects in the world would have to proceed from something other than them. Thus the governor of the world would not be these stars, but something else. If they are cooperating, then the world would have to remain in one single state without any change whatsoever. If they are sometimes cooperating and sometimes opposing, then their transition from love to hatred and vice versa would be a change in their attributes, and so they would depend, in those changes, on a Maker who dominates them by force and subjugation.

**Thirteenthly:** They are bodies, every body is composite, and every composite depends on each of its parts, and each of its parts is other than it. So every body depends on something other than itself, and is contingent (*mumkin*). Every contingent depends on something other than itself and is contingent in its essence. Every contingent in its essence has an influencer (*mu'aththir*). Every thing that has an influencer, its dependence on its influencer is either during its persistence, or during its coming into being, or during its non-existence. The first is false, because it would require the existence of what already exists, which is impossible. Thus the other two remain, and these two require origination (*huduth*), which indicates the existence of the Maker.

**Fourteenthly:** Bodies are equal in corporeality, because it is valid to divide body into celestial and elemental, dense and subtle, hot and cold, moist and dry. The subject of this division is common to all bodies. So corporeality is a common quality among these attributes. Things equal in quiddity must be equal in receptivity to attributes. Therefore, whatever is valid for one body is valid for another. So the specification of each body with what it is specified with, of extent, position, shape, nature, and quality, must be among the possibilities, and that leads to dependence on the eternal Maker, majestic is His majesty, sanctified are His names, and there is no god but Him.

This is the indication of the foundations of the proofs derived from the bodies of the heavens and the earth for establishing the Maker. ﴿And if all the trees on earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas added to it, were ink, the words of God would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman: 27].

**The second kind of proofs: the conditions of the earth.** It contains two sections.

**The first section: explaining the conditions of the earth.**

Know that the differences in the conditions of the earth have causes.

**The first cause:** The difference in its conditions is due to the rotation of the sphere (*harakat al-falak*). This has several divisions.

**The first division:** Places without latitude (*al-mawadi' al-'adimat al-'ard*), which lie on the equator, where the two poles of the world coincide with it. It intersects the equinoctial circle (*mu'addal al-nahar*) at right angles, and cuts all daily orbits into two halves. The motion of the sphere is like that of a wheel (*dulabiyyah*). There is no difference between the night and the day of any star. No star is imagined to be always visible or always hidden. Rather, every point except the two poles has rising and setting. The zodiac circle (*falak al-buruj*) passes over the zenith twice in the course of its revolution, at the moment it reaches the circle of the horizon. The sun passes over the zenith twice a year, when it reaches the two equinoctial points.

**The second division:** Places that have latitude. The North Pole rises above the horizon in them, and the South Pole sinks below it. The horizon cuts the equinoctial circle into two halves only. As for the rest of the orbits, the horizon cuts them into two unequal parts: the visible part is greater than the hidden in the northern hemisphere, and the reverse in the southern. For this reason the day is longer than the night in the north, and the reverse in the south. The motion here becomes oblique (*hamailiyyah*). No star has the same night and day, except those on the equinoctial circle. The stars near the North Pole become always visible, and those near the South Pole always hidden. The sun passes over the zenith at two points, whose distance from the equinoctial circle to the north equals the latitude of the place.

**The third division:** The place where the elevation of the pole is equal to the greatest declination. Here the rising and setting of the two poles of the zodiac circle disappear, except that they touch the horizon. At that time the zodiac circle passes over the zenith, and the sun passes over the zenith only at the summer solstice.

**The fourth division:** Where the latitude increases beyond that. Here the passage of the zodiac circle and the sun over the zenith ceases. The northern pole of the zodiac becomes always visible, and the other always hidden.

**The fifth division:** Where the latitude becomes equal to the complement of the declination. Here the setting of the summer solstice and the rising of the winter solstice cease, but they touch the horizon. When the vernal equinox reaches the eastern horizon, and the autumnal equinox the western horizon, the summer solstice is in the northern direction and the winter solstice in the southern. At that time the zodiac circle coincides with the horizon. Then there rises from the first of Capricorn to the first of Cancer all at once, and its opposite sets in the same manner. Then the rising signs begin to set and the setting signs to rise, until the previous condition returns. There the night vanishes at the summer solstice, and the day at the winter solstice.

**The sixth division:** Where the latitude increases beyond that. Then an arc of the zodiac circle becomes always visible, near the summer solstice, such that the solstice lies at its middle, and the duration of the sun's passage through it is day. A similar arc near the winter solstice becomes always hidden, and the duration of the sun's passage through it is night. Some signs become inverted there. When Capricorn reaches the middle of the sky from the south, the first of Cancer is on the north side, and the vernal equinox is on the eastern horizon. Thus Cancer has risen before Gemini, Gemini before Taurus, and Taurus before Aries. Then, when the sphere moves, the end and beginning of Pisces necessarily rise beneath the earth, and every part that rises has its counterpart setting. So the signs that rise inverted have their counterparts setting in the same way.

**The seventh division:** Where the elevation of the pole becomes ninety degrees. There the equinoctial circle coincides with the horizon. The motion becomes rotational (*rahawiyyah*), the rising and setting disappear entirely, the northern half of the zodiac circle is always visible, and the southern half always hidden. Half the year becomes night and half of it day.

**The second cause of the difference in the conditions of the earth** is the difference in its conditions due to habitation (*al-'imarah*). Know that the equator cuts

[p. 173]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 164 (part 5 of 7):**

...the earth into two halves, northern and southern. If you posit another great circle intersecting it at right angles, the sphere of the earth is divided by the two into quarters. What has been found inhabited of the earth is one of the two northern quarters, together with its mountains, seas and deserts. It is said, and God knows best, that three-quarters of the earth is water. The place whose length is ninety degrees along the equator is called the Dome of the Earth (*qubbat al-ard*). It is related from the Indians that there is a towering fortress on an island, which is the abode of the devils, and for this reason it is called a dome. Then the length of the inhabited part was found to be about half the circumference, and this is almost agreed upon. They agreed to take its starting point from the west, but they differed on the precise determination. Some take it from the shore of the surrounding sea, which is the Uqyanus Sea (Oceanus). Others take it from islands and remote lands in it called the Islands of the Immortals (*Jaza'ir al-Khalidat*). The ancients claimed that these were inhabited in ancient times, and their distance from the shore is ten parts. It follows from this that there is also disagreement about the endpoint. The latitude of the inhabited area was found only up to a distance of sixty-six degrees from the equator. However, Batlamyus (Ptolemy) claimed that beyond the equator there is inhabited land up to a distance of sixteen degrees, so the latitude of the inhabited area would be about eighty-two degrees. Then they divided this inhabited extent into seven elongated strips parallel to the equator, which are called the climes (*al-aqalim*). Their starting point is the equator. Some take the first clime from a point about thirteen degrees from the equator, and the end of the seventh clime at a distance of fifty degrees, and they do not count what lies beyond it as a clime, because of the scarcity of habitation they found there.

The third cause: the difference in the conditions of the earth. Some of it is land and some sea, some plain and some mountain, some rocky and some sandy, some in a depression and some on a height. Some of these types combine with others, so their conditions differ greatly. What relates to this kind we have examined fully in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Who made the earth a bed for you and the sky a canopy﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 22]. Among what relates to the conditions of the earth is that it is a sphere. You know that the extension of the earth between east and west is called its length, and its extension between north and south is called its breadth. So we say: the length of the earth is either straight, or concave, or convex. The first is false, for otherwise the whole surface of the earth would become illuminated all at once at sunrise, and would become dark all at once at sunset. But this is not the case, because when we observed a single lunar eclipse and noted a precise moment of its four states, which are the beginning and completion of the eclipse and the beginning and completion of its clearing, we did not find this occurring at the same time in lands of different longitudes. The part of the night that had passed was found to be greater in the eastern land than in the western land. The second is also false, for otherwise the part of the night that had passed would have been found greater in the western land than in the eastern land, because in a concave surface the event occurs first in the west and then in the east. Since both alternatives are refuted, it is established that the length of the earth is convex. Then this convexity is either circular or lens-shaped. The second is false, because we find the difference in the times of the same eclipse corresponds to the difference in the arcs of the circle, such that an eclipse that occurs at the far end of the east at the beginning of the night occurs at the far end of the west at the beginning of the day. Thus it is established that it is spherical in length. As for the breadth of the earth, it is either flat, or concave, or convex. The first is false, for otherwise a traveler going south along the direction of the pole would not find the pole's altitude increasing, and the ever-visible stars would not appear to him as they do; but we have shown that their conditions vary with the variation of latitude. The second is also false, for otherwise the ever-visible stars would become hidden from him as he continually penetrated deeper into that depression, and the altitude of the pole would decrease; and the consequences are false, as we stated earlier in explaining the seven levels that arise from the variation of the latitudes of lands. This argument, with the excellence of its formulation, is persuasive rather than demonstrative.

[Page 174]

The second argument: the shadow of the earth is circular, so the earth must be circular.

Explanation of the first premise: the eclipse of the moon is nothing but the shadow of the earth, for there is no meaning to its eclipse except the removal of light from its substance when the earth comes between it and the sun. Then we say: the eclipse of the moon is circular, because we perceive the portion of it that is eclipsed as circular. Once this is established, the earth must be circular, because the extension of the shadow takes the shape of the common boundary between the part illuminated by the sun's rays and the part dark from it. If the shadow is circular, then that common boundary which forms the whole shadow must be circular in its shape. Thus it is established that the earth is spherical. Furthermore, this discourse is not specific to one side of the earth, for the circumstances causing eclipses coincide in all parts of the zodiac, and yet the shape of the eclipse is always circular. Thus the earth is circular in shape from all sides.

The third argument: the earth tends toward distance from the sphere (*falak*), and whenever the condition of all its parts is like this, the earth must be circular, because the extension of the shadow is a sphere.

Those who objected to the sphericity of the earth argued on two grounds:

The first: if the earth were a sphere, its center would coincide with the center of the universe, and if this were so, water would surround it from all sides, because the nature of water demands seeking the center, so water would necessarily surround the whole earth.

The second: what we observe on the earth of hills, great mountains, and very deep depressions.

They answered the first by saying that divine providence required a part of the earth to emerge from the water, like an island in the sea, to be a dwelling place for the animals. Moreover, it is not unlikely that water flows from some sides of the earth into its deep places, and in that case some parts of the earth emerge from the water.

As for the second, they said that these irregularities do not take the earth out of being a sphere. They said: if we make a sphere of wood, with a diameter of one cubit for example, then place upon it things like grains or hairs, and hollow out in it similar depressions, these will not take it out of being spherical. The proportion of the mountains and ravines to the earth is less than the proportion of those fixed features to the small sphere.

**The second section**

On demonstrating the argument from the conditions of the earth for the existence of the Creator (*al-Sani'*)

Know that the argument from the conditions of the earth for the existence of the Creator is easier than the argument from the conditions of the heavens for that. This is because the opponent claims that the attributes of the heavens in their magnitudes, places and positions are necessary in themselves and cannot change, so they are independent of an agent. Therefore, to refute that, one must establish the proof of the similarity of earthly bodies, for we observe their change in all their attributes, I mean their being in their places, and their colors, tastes and natures. We observe that each part of the mountains and of solid rocks can be broken and removed from its place, and the high can be made low and the low high. Since this is so, it is established that the specification of each part of the earth with what it has of place, position, contact, proximity to some bodies and distance from others is subject to change and alteration. And since it is established that the attribution of those bodies with their attributes is a possibility, they necessarily require, for that specification, an eternal, all-knowing Governor, exalted is He above what the wrongdoers say. When you understand the basis of the discussion, the elaboration becomes easy for you.
