**The third type of proofs: the alternation of night and day**

This contains two questions.

**The first question:** They mentioned two explanations of *ikhtilaf* (alternation, difference).

The first: it is a form of *iftiʿal* from their saying *khalafahu yakhlufuhu*, when the first departs and the second comes. So the alternation of night and day is their succession in going and coming. From this one says: "So-and-so *yakhtalifu* to so-and-so," when he goes to him and comes back from him. His departure follows his coming, and his coming follows his departure. Everything that comes after something else is its successor (*khalaf*). It is in this sense that His words, exalted is He, are explained: ﴿And He it is who made night and day to succeed one another﴾ [Al-Furqan: 62].

The second: it means the difference of night and day in length and shortness, in light and darkness, in increase and decrease. Al-Kisa'i said: it is said of any two things that differ that they are *khilfan* (two different things).

I have a third explanation of it, which is that just as night and day differ in length and shortness in times, they also differ in places. For according to one who says the earth is a sphere, whatever hour you specify, that hour is morning in one place on the earth, noon in another place, afternoon in a third, sunset in a fourth, night prayer time in a fifth, and so on. This is when we consider lands that differ in longitude. As for lands that differ in latitude, every land whose northern latitude is greater has longer summer days and shorter summer nights, and its winter days are the opposite of that. These varying conditions of days and nights according to the difference in the longitudes and latitudes of lands are a matter that is diverse and wondrous. God, exalted is He, has mentioned the matter of night and day in His Book in several places. He said, in declaring that He is the Owner of Sovereignty: ﴿He makes the night pass into the day and makes the day pass into the night﴾ [Fatir: 13]. He said in Al-Qasas: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if God made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than God could bring you light? Will you not then listen?﴾ ﴿Say: Have you considered, if God made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than God could bring you a night in which you may rest? Will you not then see?﴾ ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you night and day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty, and that you may be grateful﴾ [Al-Qasas: 71–73]. In Ar-Rum: ﴿And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty. Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾ [Ar-Rum: 23]. In Luqman: ﴿Do you not see that God makes the night pass into the day and makes the day pass into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term?﴾ [Luqman: 29]. In Al-Malaika (Fatir): ﴿He makes the night pass into the day and makes the day pass into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term. That is God, your Lord﴾ [Fatir: 13]. In Ya-Sin: ﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37]. In Az-Zumar: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term﴾ [Az-Zumar: 5]. In Ha-Mim Ghafir: ﴿God it is who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day as something to see by﴾ [Ghafir: 61]. In 'Amma: ﴿And We made the night as a covering﴾ ﴿and We made the day for livelihood﴾ [An-Naba': 10–11]. The verses of this kind are numerous. The exact statement is to say: the variation in the conditions of night and day indicates the Creator in several respects.

**The first:** the variation in the conditions of night and day is linked to the movements of the sun, and these are among the great signs.

**The second:** what results from the length of days at one time and the length of nights at another, from the variation of the seasons, which are spring, summer, autumn and winter. This too is among the great signs.

**The third:** the orderly arrangement of human affairs, through the seeking of livelihood and gain during the days and the seeking of sleep and rest during the nights, is among the great signs.

**The fourth:** that night and day cooperate in achieving

[Page 176]

Al-Razi, *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, commentary on Surah 2, verse 164 (part 6 of 7):

the great signs among the interests of creation, even though the two [opposites] contain opposition and mutual contrariness. For the requirement of opposition between two things is that they should corrupt each other, not that they should cooperate in achieving benefits.

The fifth [sign]: the creatures' turning to sleep at the beginning of the night resembles the death of creatures at the first blast of the Trumpet, and their waking at sunrise resembles the return of life to them at the second blast. This too is among the great signs that point to the great signs.

The sixth [sign]: the splitting of the darkness of the night by the spreading dawn is among the great signs. It is like a stream of clear water flowing into a turbid sea, such that the clear is not discolored by the turbid, nor the turbid by the clear. This is what is meant by the words of the Exalted: ﴿He splits the dawn, and makes the night a repose﴾ [Al-An'am: 96].

The seventh [sign]: the measuring of night and day in a moderate amount that suits the interests [of creatures] is among the great signs. As we have explained, in the place where the pole is directly overhead, the year consists of six months of day and six months of night. There, ripening is not completed, the dwelling is not fit for an animal, and nothing of the means of livelihood can be prepared.

The eighth [sign]: if we say that the appearance of light in the air came about by the power of God Most High from the outset at sunrise, in that He, exalted is He, has established His custom of creating light in the air at sunrise, then there is no dispute. But if we say that the sun causes the light to arise in the body opposite it, then the sun's being singled out for this property, rather than the rest of the bodies, while all bodies are alike, indicates the existence of the Creator, glorified and exalted is He.

If it is said: why could it not be that the mover of the bodies of the heavens is a king of great size and power, and in that case the alternation of night and day would not be a proof that He is the Creator? We reply: as for our position, since the proof has shown that the power of the servant is not fit for bringing things into existence, the objection has been removed. As for the position of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology), Abu Hashim has negated this possibility by revealed testimony (al-sam', scriptural transmission).

The fourth type of proofs: the words of the Exalted: ﴿and the ship that runs in the sea with what benefits mankind﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 164]. Concerning it there are several issues.

The first issue: Al-Wahidi said: the word *falak* originally derives from rotation, and everything circular is a *falak*. The *falak* of the sky is the name for seven orbits in which the stars move. *Falakat al-jariyah* means her breast became round, and the spindle-whorl (*falkat al-mighzal*) derives from this. The ship is called *fulk* because it turns in the water with the easiest turning. He said: *al-fulk* is both singular and plural. When it is intended as singular, it is masculine; when it is intended as plural, it is feminine. An example of this is the saying: *naqah hijan* and *nuq hijan* (a white-colored she-camel, and white-colored she-camels), and *dir' dilas* and *durua dilas* (a smooth coat of mail, and smooth coats of mail). Sibawayh said: when *al-fulk* is intended as singular, the *damma* (vowel-sign u) on its *fa'* is in the position of the *damma* on the *ba'* of *burd* and the *kha'* of *khurj*; when it is intended as plural, the *damma* on its *fa'* is in the position of the *ha'* of *humr* and the *sad* of *sufr*. So the two *dammas*, although they agree in pronunciation, differ in meaning.

The second issue: Al-Layth said: the sea was called *bahr* because of its *istibhar*, which is its expanse and spreading out. It is said: *istabhara fulan fi al-'ilm* when he extended far in knowledge, and *tabahhara fulan fi al-mal* (he spread out in wealth). Others said: the sea was called *bahr* because it is a cleft in the earth; *al-bahr* means a cleft, and from it comes *al-buhayrah* (the small lake).

The third issue: al-Jubba'i and others among the scholars who know the locations of the seas mentioned that the well-known seas are five:

The first: the Sea of India, which is also called the Sea of China.

The second: the Western Sea (the Atlantic).

The third: the Sea of Syria, the Byzantines, and Egypt.

The fourth: the Sea of Nitash.

The fifth: the Sea of Jurjan.

As for the Sea of India, its length extends from the west to the east, from the farthest land of Abyssinia to the farthest land of India and China. Its measure is eight hundred thousand miles, its breadth is two thousand seven hundred miles, and it passes beyond the equator by one thousand seven hundred miles. The gulfs of this sea are:

The first: a gulf near the land of Abyssinia, extending toward the region of the Berbers, called the Berber Gulf. Its length is five hundred miles and its breadth one hundred miles.

The second: the gulf of the Sea of Ayla, which is the Sea of Qulzum (Red Sea), its length one thousand four hundred miles and its breadth seven hundred miles. Its end reaches the sea called the Green Sea, and at its edge is Qulzum, so it was named after it. To its east is the land of Yemen and Aden, and to its west the land of Abyssinia.

The third: the gulf of the Sea of the land of Persia, called the Persian Gulf, which is the Sea of Basra and Persia. To its east are Tiz and Makran, and to its west Oman. Its length is one thousand four hundred miles and its breadth five hundred miles. Between these two gulfs, that is, the Gulf of Ayla and the Gulf of Persia, lie the land of the Hijaz, Yemen, and the rest of the lands of the Arabs, over a distance of between one thousand five hundred miles.

The fourth: from it issues another gulf to the farthest land of India, called the Green Gulf, its length one thousand five hundred miles. They said: among the islands of the Sea of India there are one thousand three hundred and seventy islands, both inhabited and uninhabited. Among them is a large island at the farthest end of the sea opposite the land of India, in the direction of the east near the lands of China, which is Serendib. Three thousand miles surround it. In it are great mountains and many rivers, and from it comes red ruby. Around this island are nineteen inhabited islands, containing flourishing cities and many villages. Among the islands of this sea is the island of Killah, from which lead (*al-raṣāṣ al-qal'i*, tin/lead alloy) is imported, and the island of Sarirah, from which camphor is imported.

As for the Western Sea, it is the one called the Ocean (*al-muhit*), which the Greeks call Oceanus. The Sea of India connects with it. Its end is not known except toward the west and the north, near the lands of the Russians and the Slavs. It takes from the farthest limit in the south, parallel to the land of the Sudan, passing along the borders of the Far Sus, Tangier, and Tahart, then al-Andalus, the Galicians, and the Slavs. Then from there it extends behind the untrodden mountains and the uninhabited lands toward the Eastern Sea. This sea has no ships sailing on it, but ships travel near its shores. In it are six islands opposite the land of Abyssinia called the Islands of the Immortals (*jaza'ir al-Khalidat*). From this sea issues a great gulf in the north of the Slavs, and this gulf extends to the land of the Muslim Bulgars. Its length from east to west is three hundred miles and its breadth one hundred miles.

As for the Sea of the Byzantines, Africa, Egypt, and Syria, its length is about five thousand miles and its breadth six hundred miles. From it issues a gulf toward the north, near the Roman land, its length five hundred miles and its breadth six hundred. From it issues another gulf to the land of Sirrayn, its length two hundred miles. In this sea there are one hundred and sixty-two inhabited islands, of which fifty are large.

As for the Sea of Nitash, it extends from Latakia to behind Constantinople, in the land of the Russians and the Slavs. Its length is one thousand three hundred miles and its breadth three hundred miles.

As for the Sea of Jurjan, its length from west to east is three hundred miles and its breadth six hundred miles. In it are two islands that were inhabited in past times. This sea is known as the Sea of Abuskun, because they are on its edge (*far datihi*). Then it extends to Tabaristan, Daylam, al-Nahrawan, Bab al-Abwab, and the region of Aran. It is not connected to any other sea. These are the great seas. As for the others, they are small lakes and marshes, such as the Lake of Khwarazm and the Lake of Tiberias.

It is related from Aristotle that the Ocean encircles the earth like a belt (*al-mintaqah*) encircles something. This is the brief account concerning the seas.

* * *

The fourth issue: on how the sailing of the ship on the sea is used as evidence for the existence of the Creator, exalted and glorified is He, and it is from several aspects:

The first: although ships are made by human beings, it is God Most High who created the tools by which these ships can be constructed. Had He not created them, this would not have been possible.

The second: had it not been for the winds that help move them, the benefit from them would not have been complete.

The third: had it not been for these winds, and their not being violent, they would not have endured and would not have been safe.

The fourth: had it not been for the strengthening of the hearts of those who board these ships, the purpose would not have been achieved. God Most High made them, from these aspects, a benefit to the servants and a means to their gains and trades.

The fifth: He singled out each region of the world with a specific thing, and made all need one another. This became a motive urging them to plunge into these dangers in these journeys. Had God Most High not singled out each region with something and made all need it, they would not have undertaken these ships. The one who carries goods benefits from it, because he profits, and the one to whom they are carried benefits from what is carried to him.

The sixth: God's subjugation of the sea to bear the ship, along with the great power of the sea when it rages, and the immensity of the terror in it when God sends the winds, so that its waves are agitated and its waters churned.

The seventh: the great rivers, such as the Jayhun and the Sayhun, pour continuously into the Lake of Khwarazm despite its smallness, yet the Lake of Khwarazm never increases at all nor extends. So the Truth, exalted and glorified is He, is the One who knows the condition of these great waters that pour into it.

The eighth: what is in the seas of great animals, and then God Most High rescues the ships from them and brings them to the shores of safety.

The ninth: what is in the seas of this wondrous matter, which is the words of the Exalted: ﴿He has released the two seas, meeting each other, between them a barrier they do not transgress﴾ [Al-Rahman: 19–20], and He said: ﴿This is sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink, and this is salty and bitter﴾ [Fatir: 12]. Then He, by His power, keeps some from mixing with others. All of this guides minds and intellects to their need of a Manager who manages them and a Decreer who preserves them.

The fifth issue: the words in describing the ship, ﴿with what benefits mankind﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 164], indicate the permissibility of riding them, the permissibility of earning and trade, and the permissibility of benefiting from pleasures.

* * *

The fifth type: the words of the Exalted: ﴿and what God sends down from the sky of water, by which He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 164].

Know that its indication of the Creator is from several aspects:

The first: that those bodies and what subsists in them of the qualities of fineness, moisture, and sweetness, no one can create except God Most High. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should sink away, who then will bring you clear water?﴾ [Al-Mulk: 30].

The second: He, Most High, made it a cause of human life and of most of his benefits. The Exalted said: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Did you bring it down from the cloud, or are We the One who brings it down?﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 68–69]. And He said: ﴿And We made from water every living thing. Will they not believe?﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 30].

The third: just as He made it a cause of human life, He made it a cause of his provision. The Exalted said: ﴿And in the sky is your provision and what you are promised﴾ [Al-Dhariyat: 22].

The fourth: the clouds, with the great waters they contain, from which great valleys flow, remain suspended in the atmosphere of the sky, and that is among the great signs.

The fifth: its descent at the time of supplication and the creatures' need for it is measured by the amount of benefit, and that is among the great signs. The Exalted said, recounting Noah: ﴿So I said: Ask forgiveness of your Lord; indeed He is ever Forgiving. He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ [Nuh: 10–11].

[p. 179]

Sixth: He said, ﴿So We drive it to a dead land﴾ [Fatir: 9], and He said, ﴿And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs, swells, and produces every lovely kind of growth﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. If it is said: Do you hold that water descends from the sky in the literal sense, or from the clouds, or do you allow what some have said, that the sun acts upon the earth so that vapours rise from it, and when they reach the cold air they cool and grow heavy, descend from the vast expanse to the narrow centre, and join together, so that from the union of some of those particles with others there form drops, which are the drops of rain?

We say: Rather, we hold that it descends from the sky as God Most High has mentioned, and He is the Truthful in His report. Since He is able to hold water in the clouds, what is the improbability in His holding it in the sky? As for the view of those who say that it comes from the seas of the earth, this is possible in itself, but to assert it with certainty is not possible except after affirming the denial of a free-choosing Agent (al-fa'il al-mukhtar) and the eternity of the world, and that is disbelief. For once we permit a free-choosing Agent capable of creating a body, how can we, while this possibility stands, be certain of what they have said?

As for His saying, ﴿And He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 5], know that this life is of several aspects:

First: the emergence of plants, which are pasture, herbage and what resembles them, without which the earth's animals could not live.

Second: that without it the means of sustenance would not be available to the servants.

Third: that God Most High causes everything to grow in measure to need, because He guaranteed the provision of living creatures in His saying, ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon God﴾ [Hud: 6].

Fourth: that there is found in it colours, tastes, scents, and what is fit for clothing, because all of that is something none can bring about except God.

Fifth: that through plants the earth acquires beauty, freshness, luster and radiance, and that is life.

Know that His describing this as giving life after death is a metaphor, because life is only true of one who perceives and is capable of knowing, and likewise death. But when a body becomes living, various kinds of beauty, freshness, splendour, vitality and growth appear in it, so the term "life" is applied to the occurrence of these things. This is from the eloquent speech which, in its brevity, gathers many meanings.

Know also that the reviving of the earth after its death indicates the Maker in several ways:

First: the growing of the crop itself, for that is not within the power of anyone to produce to the degree in which it emerges.

Second: the variation of its colours in a manner that can hardly be delimited or counted.

Third: the variation of the tastes of what appears on crops and trees.

Fourth: the continuity of customs, with that appearing at its specified times.

* * *

The sixth type of signs: His saying, ﴿And He scattered throughout them every kind of creature﴾. Its counterpart is all the verses indicating the creation of man and the rest of the animals, such as His saying, ﴿And from the two of them He spread forth many men and women﴾ [al-Nisa': 1].

Know that the origination of animals may occur by spontaneous generation (al-tawlid) or by reproduction (al-tawallud), and in either case there must be a wise Maker. So let us clarify this with regard to humans first, then with regard to the rest of the animals.

As for humans, what indicates that their origination requires a Maker are several points:

First: it is related that a man said in the presence of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him: "I marvel at the matter of chess, for its board is a cubit by a cubit, and even if a person played a million times, two games would never coincide in one arrangement." Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Here is something more wondrous than that: the measure of the face is a span by a span, yet the places of the organs in it, such as the two eyebrows, the two eyes, the nose and the mouth, never change at all, and you will not see two persons in East and West who resemble each other. How great is that power and wisdom which has manifested in this small surface these differences which have no limit."

Second: man is generated from a drop of semen, and what shapes and forms the drop is either a power present in the drop or not present in it. If it is a power present in it, then that power either possesses perception, knowledge and wisdom, enabling it to accomplish this wondrous formation, or it does not possess that, but its effect is merely by natural disposition and causal necessity. The first is manifestly false, for a human, when fully developed, has more knowledge and power; yet even at full maturity, if he wished to alter a single hair from its condition, he could not do so. So how could one who was at the extreme of weakness be able to do that?

If, however, that power acts by nature, then this thing is either a body uniform in its parts in itself, or a body with differing parts. If it is uniform in its parts, then a natural power acting upon simple matter must produce a uniform effect, and this would be a sphere; so the human would have to be in the form of a sphere, and all the parts assumed within that sphere would be uniform in nature. This is what they use to argue that simple elements must be spheres. Thus it is established that the drop, in its transformation into flesh, blood and a human being, requires a governing and ordaining agent for its organs, powers and structures; and that is none other than the Maker, glorified and exalted is He.

Third: reasoning from the states of the dissection of animal bodies and the wonders found in their composition and construction. To mention this here would be impractical because of its abundance, and people have thoroughly explained it in books composed on this discipline.

Fourth: what is related from the Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Glory be to Him who gave sight through fat, hearing through bone, and speech through flesh." Among the marvels of this composition is that the natural philosophers said: the highest of the elements must be fire, because it is hot and dry; below it in subtlety is air, then water, and earth must be beneath all because of its heaviness, density and dryness. Then they reversed this principle in the composition of the human body: for the highest of the organs in it is the bone of the skull, which is cold and dry in the nature of earth; beneath it is the brain, which is cold and moist in the nature of water; beneath that is the breath, which is hot and moist in the nature of air; and beneath all is the heart, which is hot and dry in the nature of fire. Glory be to Him in whose hand is the turning of natures: He arranges them as He wills and composes them as He desires.

Among what we have mentioned in this chapter is that every maker who produces a fine engraving protects it from dust, lest it dirty it, from water, lest it erase it, from air, lest it remove its softness and delicacy, and from fire, lest it burn it. Then God, glorified and exalted, placed the design of His creation upon these very things. He said, ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with God is like that of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]; He said, ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30]; He said concerning air, ﴿So We blew into it of Our spirit﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]; He also said, ﴿And when you shaped from clay the likeness of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]; and He said, ﴿And I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]; and He said concerning fire, ﴿And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ [al-Rahman: 15]. This indicates that His making is different from the making of anyone else.

Fifth: look at the infant after its separation from the mother. If you were to place a cloth over its mouth and nose that cuts off its breath, it would die immediately. Yet it remained in the narrow womb for a long period, with breathing there being impossible, and it did not die. Then after separation it is among the weakest of things and the furthest from understanding, such that it cannot distinguish between water and fire, between what harms and what pleases, or between its mother and others. Then, although a human is at first among the furthest of things from understanding, after reaching maturity he becomes the most perfect of animals in understanding, intellect and perception. This shows that this is a gift from the Powerful, the Wise. For if the matter were by nature, then whoever was keenest at the beginning of creation would be most understanding at maturity; but since the matter is not so, and is rather the opposite, we know that all of that is a gift from God, the Creator, the Wise.

Sixth: the variation of languages, the variation of natures, and the variation of temperaments are among the strongest proofs. We see wild and mountain animals strongly resembling one another, while we see humans differing greatly in appearance. Were it not so, livelihood would be disrupted, and each person would be indistinguishable from another, so one could not be distinguished from another, and in that lies the corruption of livelihood. To pursue the discussion of this type fully is not something one can hope for, for it is a sea without a shore.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 165 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, rivals (andad) whom they love as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah. If only those who have wronged could see, when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, established tawhid (the oneness of God) through compelling and decisive proofs, He followed it with a condemnation of what opposes tawhid, because condemning the opposite of a thing reinforces the goodness of that thing. For this reason the poet said:

*And through their opposites things become clear.*

They also said: blessings are unnoticed, and when they are lost they are recognized. People do not know the value of health, but when they fall ill and health returns to them, they recognize its worth. The same applies to all blessings. For this reason, Allah the Exalted followed the verse indicating tawhid with this verse. Here there are several issues.

**The first issue:** As for *nidd* (rival), it is the equal who contends. We have explained its reality in His saying, the Exalted, at the beginning of this surah: ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22]. The scholars differed over what is meant by *andad* (rivals) and gave several views:

First: they are the idols which they took as gods, so that they would bring them near to Allah, and they hoped for benefit and harm from them. They directed their requests to them, made vows to them, and offered sacrifices to them. This is the view of most exegetes. According to this view, the idols are *andad* of one another, meaning equals, not that they are rivals of Allah; or the meaning is that they are rivals of Allah according to their corrupt assumptions.

Second: they are the leaders whom they obeyed, so that because of their obedience they made lawful what Allah had forbidden and forbade what Allah had made lawful. This is from al-Suddi. Those who hold this view preferred it over the first for several reasons:

The first: in His saying ﴿they love them as they love Allah﴾, the *ha'* and *mim* (the pronoun "them") refer to rational beings.

The second: it is far-fetched that they loved idols in the same way they loved Allah, given that they knew idols neither harm nor benefit.

The third: Allah mentioned after this verse: ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166], and this applies only to those who took men as rivals and equals to Allah, binding themselves in exalting them and submitting to them as believers bind themselves in submission to Allah, the Exalted.

Third view on the meaning of *andad*: the view of the Sufis and the gnostics (*arifin*), namely that whatever you occupy your heart with other than Allah, the Exalted, you have made in your heart a rival to Allah, the Exalted. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23].

As for His saying, ﴿they love them as they love Allah﴾, know that what is meant is not love of their essence; therefore there must be an omitted element. The meaning is: they love their custom, or drawing near to them and submitting to them, or all of that. As for His saying ﴿as they love Allah﴾, there are three views on it:

It is said: as their love for Allah; it is said: like the love obligatory upon them toward Allah; and it is said: like the love of the believers for Allah. They differed this way because they disagreed over whether they knew Allah or not. Whoever said that they knew Him, while taking rivals, interpreted it as meaning their love for Allah. Whoever said that they did not know their Lord took the verse as one of the remaining two meanings: either like the obligatory love for them, or like the love of the believers for Allah. The first view is closer, because His saying ﴿they love them as they love Allah﴾ refers to the people previously mentioned, and the apparent sense of ﴿as they love Allah﴾ requires that love for Allah be established within them. It is as if He, the Exalted, had shown in the preceding verse that God is one and drawn attention to His proofs, then related the words of those who associate partners with Him, which requires that they acknowledge Allah, the Exalted.

If it is said: a rational person cannot possibly have love for idols the same as his love for Allah, because by necessity of reason he knows that these idols are stones that neither benefit nor harm, neither hear nor see nor understand; and they acknowledged that this world has a Creator who manages it and is wise. This is why He, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman: 25]. With this belief, how can it be conceived that their love for those idols is like their love for Allah, the Exalted? Furthermore, Allah, the Exalted, related about them that they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. Since this is so, the original aim was seeking the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted; so how can equality in love be conceived with this statement?

We reply: His saying ﴿they love them as they love Allah﴾ means in obedience to them and in exalting them. Equality in love according to this view does not contradict what you have mentioned.

\* \* \*

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** concerning the reality of the servant's love for Allah, the Exalted. Know that there is no dispute among the community (*ummah*) over using this expression, namely that the servant may love Allah, the Exalted. The Qur'an speaks of it, as in this verse, and as in His saying: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]. Likewise the reports: it is related that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said to the Angel of Death, peace be upon him, when he came to take his soul: "Have you seen a beloved (*khalil*) cause his beloved to die?" Then Allah revealed to him: "Have you seen a beloved who dislikes meeting his beloved?" He said: "O Angel of Death, now take it."

"A bedouin came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, when is the Hour?' He said: 'What have you prepared for it?' He said: 'I have not prepared much prayer or fasting, but I love Allah and His Messenger.' The peace and blessings of Allah be upon him said: 'A person is with whom he loves.'" Anas said: "I have never seen the Muslims rejoice at anything after Islam as they rejoiced at that."

It is also related that Isa, peace be upon him, passed by three men whose bodies had become emaciated and whose colors had changed. He said to them: "What has brought you to what I see?" They said: "Fear of the Fire." He said: "It is a right upon Allah to grant security to the one who fears." Then he left them and came upon three others, who were even more emaciated and altered. He said to them: "What has brought you to this station?" They said: "Longing for Paradise." He said: "It is a right upon Allah to give you what you hope for." Then he left them and came upon three others, who were even more emaciated and altered, as if their faces were mirrors of light. He said: "How did you reach this degree?" They said: "By the love of Allah." He said: "You are those brought near to Allah on the Day of Resurrection."

According to al-Suddi, he said: "On the Day of Resurrection the nations will be called by their prophets: 'O community of Musa! O community of Isa! O community of Muhammad!' except those among them who loved; they will be called: 'O friends of Allah (awliya' Allah)!'" In some books: "My servant, by My right, I love you; so by My right upon you, be loving toward Me."

Know that although the community agreed on using this expression, they differed over its meaning. The majority of the theologians (*mutakallimun*) said: love is a kind of will (*iradah*), and will has no connection except with contingent things (*jaizat*); therefore it is impossible for love to be connected to the essence of Allah or His attributes. So when we say "we love Allah," its meaning is "we love obedience to Allah and serving Him," or "we love His reward and His kindness." As for the gnostics, they said: the servant may love Allah, the Exalted, for His own sake, and love of serving Him or love of His reward is a lower rank. They argued by saying: we have found that pleasure is loved for its own sake, and perfection is also loved for its own sake. As for pleasure: if we are asked, "Why do you earn?" we say, "To find wealth." If it is asked, "Why do you seek wealth?" we say, "To find food and drink with it." If they say, "Why do you seek food and drink?" we say, "So that pleasure is attained and pain is removed." If it is said to us, "Why do you seek pleasure and dislike pain?" we say: this is not something that has a cause. For if everything were sought only for the sake of something else, it would necessarily lead either to infinite regress (*tasalsul*) or to circularity (*dawr*), and both are impossible. Therefore one must arrive at what is sought for its own sake. Once this is established, we know that pleasure is sought to be attained for its own sake, and pain is sought to be removed for its own sake, not for another cause.

As for perfection: we love the prophets and the saints simply because they are described by attributes of perfection. When we hear the account of some brave men, such as Rustam and Isfandiyar, and learn how brave they were, our hearts incline toward them, to the point that this inclination may lead us to spend great wealth in establishing their honor, and it may even reach the point of risking life. That pleasure is loved for its own sake does not contradict perfection being loved for its own sake.

Having established this, we say: those who interpreted the love of Allah, the Exalted, as love of His obedience or love of His reward, these are the ones who knew that pleasure is loved for its own sake, but did not know that perfection is loved for its own sake. As for the gnostics who said that He, the Exalted, is loved in His essence and for His own sake, they are the ones for whom it was revealed that perfection is loved for its own sake. This is because the most perfect of the perfect is the Real, glorified and exalted, for by the necessity of His existence He is independent of everything other than Himself, and the perfection of everything is derived from Him. He, glorified and exalted, is the most perfect of the perfect in knowledge and power. If we love a learned man for his perfection in knowledge, and a brave man for his perfection in courage, and an ascetic man for his freedom from what is unbecoming of actions, then how should we not love Allah, when all knowledge is like nothing in comparison to His knowledge, all powers are like nothing in comparison to His power, and all the freedom from imperfections that creatures possess is like nothing in comparison to what the Real possesses of that? Thus it necessarily follows with certainty that the Beloved in truth is Allah, the Exalted, and that He is loved in His essence and for His own sake, whether or not others love Him.

Know that now that you have understood the point on this subject: the servant has no way to know Allah, glorified, directly. Rather, unless he considers His creatures, he cannot reach that station. Therefore, whoever's knowledge of the subtleties of Allah's wisdom and power in creation is more complete, his knowledge of His perfection is more complete, and so his love for Him is more complete. And since there is no limit to the degrees of the servant's understanding of the subtleties of Allah's wisdom, there is consequently no limit to the degrees of the servants' love for the majesty of the presence of Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 165 (part 2 of 2):

Then there arises another state, which is that when the servant frequently contemplates the subtle wisdom of God, the Exalted, his ascent in the station of love for God increases. When this becomes frequent, it becomes a cause for the love of God, the Exalted, to take possession of the servant's heart and penetrate it, in the manner of drops of water falling on a hard rock. Though they are delicate, they pierce solid stones. When the love of God penetrates the heart, the heart takes on its quality and grows intensely attached to it. The stronger this attachment, the stronger the aversion to everything else, because turning toward anything other than Him preoccupies the heart and prevents it from turning toward Him, and whatever prevents the presence of the Beloved is abhorrent. Thus the love of God and the aversion to all else continually alternate in the heart, and each intensifies the other, until the heart becomes averse to everything other than God, the Exalted. Aversion necessitates turning away from everything other than God, and turning away necessitates annihilation (fana', the passing away of the self) from everything other than God, the Exalted. That heart then becomes illumined by the lights of holiness, lit by the radiance of the world of infallibility, annihilated from the portions attached to the world of origination (hudūth). This station is the highest of ranks, and there is no likeness of it in this world except intense passionate love (ʿishq) for whatever it may be. You see merchants who are infatuated with acquiring wealth forget their hunger, their food, and their drink while absorbed in guarding their money. If this can be understood in that base station,
[p. 187]
then how can it be deemed unlikely in the contemplation of the majesty of the Eternal Presence (al-Hadrah al-Samadiyyah)?

* * *

The second issue: on the source of longing (shawq) for God, the Exalted. Know that longing is only conceivable toward something that has been perceived from one aspect and not perceived from another. As for what has not been perceived at all, one does not long for it. If a person has not seen someone and has not heard his description, he cannot conceive of longing for him, and if he were to perceive his perfection, he would not long for him. Longing for the beloved is of two kinds:

The first: when he sees him, then is absent from him, he longs to complete his image through seeing him again.

The second: he sees the face of his beloved but does not see his hair or the rest of his beauties, so he longs for what he has never seen to be revealed to him. Both of these forms are conceivable with regard to God, the Exalted; indeed, they are necessarily present for all the gnostics ('arifun). What has become clear to the gnostics of divine matters, though it is in the utmost clarity, is mixed with the impurities of imaginings, for imaginings do not cease in this world from representation and depiction, and they are the means by which spiritual knowledge is perceived. Complete manifestation (tajalli) is achieved only in the Hereafter. This necessarily entails the occurrence of longing in this world. This is one type of longing, concerning what has become clear in a clear manner.

The second: divine matters have no end, and only some of them are revealed to each servant among the servants, while countless matters remain obscure. When the gnostic knows that what is hidden from his intellect is more than what is present to it, he will continually long to know them. Longing in the first sense ends in the Hereafter in the meaning called seeing, meeting, and witnessing, and it is not conceivable that it be in this world. As for longing in the second sense, it is likely to have no end, since its end would be that the majesty of God, His attributes, and His wisdom in His acts be revealed to the servant in the Hereafter, and these are infinite. Knowing the infinite in detail is impossible. You have now understood the reality of longing for God, the Exalted. Know that this longing is delightful, because when the servant is ascending, through the alternation of finding and deprivation, arrival and separation, he acquires pains mixed with pleasures, and pleasures surrounded by deprivation and loss become stronger. It is likely that this kind of pleasure is something attained only by human beings, for the angels' perfections are present in actuality, and animals are not prepared for them, whereas humans are those who oscillate between the two directions of baseness and elevation.

The third issue: in explaining that those who believe are more intense in their love for God. As for the theologians (mutakallimun), they said: their love for God is of two aspects:

The first: that what proceeds from them of veneration, praise, glorification, and worship is purified from shirk and from whatever belief is unfitting, whereas the love of others is not like this.

The second: their love for God is accompanied by hope in reward, desire for the great station with Him, fear of punishment, and taking the path of escaping it. Whoever worships God and venerates Him to this degree, his love for God will be more intense. As for the gnostics, they said: the believers are those who know God to the extent of human capacity, and we have shown that love is a necessary consequence of knowledge ('irfan). Therefore, the more complete their knowledge, the more intense their love must be. If it is said: how can it be said that the love of believers for God, the Exalted, is more intense, when we see the Hindus performing arduous acts of worship which none of the Muslims perform, and they perform them only for God, the Exalted, and then they kill themselves out of love for God?

The answer has several aspects:

First: those who believe supplicate only to God, unlike the polytheists, who turn to God when they are in need, but when the need passes, they return to rivals (andad). God, the Exalted, says: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 6], to the end of the verse. The believer does not turn away from God in adversity or ease, in hardship or prosperity, whereas the unbeliever may turn away from his Lord. Thus the love of the believer is stronger.

Second: whoever loves another is pleased with his decree and does not act in his dominion without permission. Those ignorant people killed themselves without His permission, whereas believers may kill themselves with His permission, and that is in jihad.

Third: when a person is afflicted with severe torment, he cannot occupy himself with knowing the Lord, so what they did is false.

Fourth: Ibn ʿAbbas said: the polytheists used to worship an idol, and when they saw something better than it, they abandoned it and turned to worshipping the better one.

Fifth: believers affirm the oneness of their Lord, whereas unbelievers worship idols alongside the idol, so the love for the One diminishes, whereas for the one God, the love of all is united toward Him.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if those who have wronged could see when they see the punishment that all power belongs to God entirely﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: know that there are discussions concerning the recitation of this verse.

The first discussion: Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿUmar recited (wa-law tara) with a dotted ta' from above, as an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), as if He said: "If you could see, O Muhammad, those who have wronged..." The rest recited it with a dotted ya' from below, as a report about those who have been mentioned, as if He said: "If those who have wronged themselves by taking rivals could see..." Some said: this reading is preferable, because the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims already know the extent of what the disbelievers witness and behold of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, whereas those threatened in this verse are those who did not know that, so the verb must be attributed to them.

The second discussion: they differed regarding (yarawna). Ibn ʿAmir recited (yurawna) with a dammah on the ya', as a causative form, and his proof is God's saying: ﴿Thus God shows them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167]. The rest recited (yarawna) with a fatha, attributing the seeing to them.

The second discussion (of the grammatical points): they differed regarding (anna). Some reciters read (inna) with a kasra on the alif, as a new sentence. The seven readers read it with a fatha on the alif.

The fourth discussion: since you have learned that (yara alladhina zalamu) was recited sometimes with a dotted ta' from above and other times with a dotted ya' from below, and His saying (anna al-quwwata) was recited sometimes with a fatha on the hamzah of (anna) and other times with a kasra, there arise here four possibilities:

The first possibility: to read (wa-law yara) with a dotted ya' from below and a fatha on the hamzah of (anna). The reasoning is that they applied "yarawna" to "al-quwwah," and the sense is: "If those who have wronged could see that power belongs to God," meaning: if those who have wronged saw the severity and power of God's punishment, they would not have taken rivals besides Him. According to this, the response of (law) is omitted, and this is common in the revelation, such as His saying: ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ [al-Anʿam: 27], ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾ [al-Anʿam: 93], ﴿And if there were a Quran by which mountains could be moved﴾ [al-Raʿd: 31]. People also say: "If you saw so-and-so while the whips were striking him." They said: this omission is more majestic and more awesome, because according to this reading the listener's mind goes to every kind of threat, so that the fear is of whatever threat might have been specified for him.

The second possibility: to read with a dotted ya' from below and a kasra on the hamzah of (inna), and the sense is: "If those who have wronged could see their helplessness at the moment of witnessing God's punishment, they would say: 'Indeed, power belongs to God.'"

The third possibility: to read with a dotted ta' from above and a fatha on the hamzah of (anna), which is the reading of Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir. Al-Farraʾ said: its basis is the repetition of the seeing, and the sense is: "If you could see those who have wronged when they see the punishment, you would see that power belongs to God entirely."

The fourth possibility: to read with a dotted ta' from above and a kasra on the hamzah. Its sense is: "If you could see those who have wronged when they see the punishment, you would say: 'Indeed, power belongs to God entirely.'" This too is a clear and good interpretation.

The second issue: if it is said: how did His saying (wa-law yara alladhina zalamu) come in the future tense together with His saying (idh yarawna al-ʿadhab), where (idh) is for the past? We say: it came in the form of the past because the occurrence of the Hour is near. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or it is nearer﴾ [al-Nahl: 77], and He says: ﴿Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17]. Whatever is near in occurrence is treated as if it had already happened and taken place. On this interpretation God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the companions of Paradise will call out﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 44], and the saying of the one who calls to prayer: "The prayer has been established," which he says before he actually begins the opening takbir of the prayer, because of its nearness. Much of this type appears in the revelation. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And if you could see when they were made to stand﴾ [al-Anʿam: 27], ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anʿam: 93], ﴿And if you could see when they were terrified﴾ [Saba': 51], ﴿And if you could see when the angels take the souls﴾ [al-Anfal: 50].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 166–167:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their means of connection are cut off from them﴾ ﴿And those who followed say, "If only we had another return, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them, and they will not emerge from the Fire﴾.

Know that when He, the Exalted, explained the condition of the one who takes rivals (andad, equals) besides Allah, through His saying, ﴿And if only those who have done wrong could see when they see the punishment﴾, by way of warning, He added to this threat through His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾. So He made clear that those who spent their lives in worshipping them and believed that they were the strongest means of their salvation will disown them when they are in need of them. A parallel to this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Some of you will disbelieve in others and some of you will curse others﴾ [al-Ankabut: 25]. He also said: ﴿Close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67], and He said: ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ [al-A'raf: 38]. And He related of Iblis that he said: ﴿Indeed, I disown what you associated with me before﴾. Here there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning His saying ﴿when [they] disown﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿when they see the punishment﴾.

The second: the governing element (amil al-i'rab) of ﴿idh [when]﴾ is a meaning of ﴿shadid [severe]﴾, as if He said: "He is severe in punishment when [they] disown," meaning at the time of disowning.

The second issue: the meaning of the verse is that those who were followed disown their followers on that Day. Then He, Exalted is He, explained the reason for which they disown them, which is their inability to rescue them from the punishment they see; for His saying ﴿and their means of connection are cut off from them﴾ is included in its meaning, that they found no means to rescue themselves and their followers. One who is hopeless from every direction by which he hopes for deliverance from the affliction that has befallen him and his allies is described as having had his means cut off.

They differed about the intended referents of these "those who were followed" in several ways:

One: they are the leaders and chiefs among the polytheists of mankind; related from Qatadah, al-Rabi' and 'Ata'.

Second: they are the devils among the jinn who became those followed by the disbelievers through whispering; related from al-Suddi.

Third: they are the devils of the jinn and mankind.

Fourth: they are the idols, which they used to call gods.

The closest is the first, because the most apt reading of "those who followed" is that they are those from whom command and prohibition are valid so that they can be followed; this does not befit idols. It is also necessary to interpret them as the leaders of mankind, because they are the ones who can be described, by their greatness, as being loved by their followers as the love of Allah, not the devils. This is confirmed by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they led us astray from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. Mujahid read the first (verb) in the active form and the second in the passive form, meaning: the followers disowned the leaders.

The second issue: they mentioned several interpretations of "disowning" (tabarru'):

One: that it occurs from them by speech.

Two: that the descent of the punishment upon them and their inability to repel it from themselves, let alone from others, leads them to disown.

Three: that regret appeared in them over what they had done of disbelief in Allah and turning away from His prophets and messengers, and that regret was called disowning.

The closest is the first, because it is the literal meaning of the word.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and they see the punishment﴾, the "wa" (waw) is for the circumstantial state (hal), meaning: they disown while seeing the punishment. This is preferable to all other opinions, because in that state terror and fear increase.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and their means of connection are cut off from them﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "disown." They mentioned seven opinions concerning the meaning of al-asbab [the means/connections]:

First: they are the relations through which they used to connect with one another; related from Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Rabi'.

Second: the kinship ties by which they used to show compassion; related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj.

Third: the deeds to which they used to adhere; related from Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi.

Fourth: the covenants and alliances by which they used to show affection among themselves; related from Ibn 'Abbas.

Fifth: what they used to connect through of disbelief, and by which they were cut off; related from al-Asamm.

Sixth: the dwellings they had in this world; related from al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Seventh: the means of salvation were cut off from them. The more evident view is that all of these are included, because this is like a negation, so it encompasses all; it is as if He said: every means by which one could attach himself has vanished from them, and they benefit from no means of whatever kind, whether position, cause, lineage, alliance, contract, or covenant. This is the utmost of despair, and thus there is in it a great emphasis in deterrence.

The second issue: the "ba'" in His saying ﴿by them al-asbab﴾ has the meaning of "'an" (about/from), like His saying: ﴿then ask about Him one who is well informed﴾ [al-Furqan: 59], meaning "about Him." 'Alqamah ibn 'Abdah said:

If you ask me about women, I am indeed
Knowing of the ailments of women, a physician.
That is, "about women."

The third issue: the root meaning of sabab in the language is a rope. They said: a rope is not called sabab unless one descends and ascends by it. From this is His saying: ﴿Let him stretch out a rope to the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]. Then the term was applied to anything by which you reach a place or a need you desire: sabab. It is said: "There is no sabab between me and you," meaning kinship or affection. The road is also called sabab, because by traversing it you reach the place you intend. He said: ﴿then he followed a way﴾ [al-Kahf: 85], meaning a road. And "asbab al-samawat" means its gates, because reaching the sky occurs by entering them. He, Exalted is He, related of Pharaoh: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means﴾ ﴿the means to the heavens﴾ [Ghafir: 36–37]. Zuhayr said:

Whoever shrinks from the means of death, it will reach him,
Even if he tries to climb the means of the sky with a ladder.
Affection among a people is called sabab, because through it they connect with one another.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who followed say: "If only we had another return, we would disown them as they have disowned us"﴾, this is a wish from them that they might be enabled to return to the world and to the state of obligation, so that the choice would be theirs, and they would disown them in the world as they disowned them on the Day of Resurrection. The implication of the statement is that they wished for them, in the world, something approaching the punishment, so that they would disown them and not rescue or help them, just as they did to them on the Day of Resurrection. Its implied sense is: "If only we had another return, and we would disown them, when such a calamity had struck them, just as they disowned us, in this very state," for if they wished for disowning them in a state of safety, there would be no benefit in it.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: concerning His saying ﴿Thus Allah will show them﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: like the disowning of some of them by others, Allah will show them their deeds as regrets, because hope is cut off from everyone.

The second: just as He showed them the punishment, Allah will show them their deeds as regrets, because they became certain of destruction.

The second issue: concerning the intended meaning of "deeds" there are opinions:

The first: the acts of obedience, over which they will regret having wasted them; related from al-Suddi.

The second: the sins and their evil deeds; related from al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd, who will regret having done them.

The third: the reward for their acts of obedience which they performed, but which disbelief nullified; related from al-Asamm.

The fourth: the deeds by which they drew near to their leaders through honoring them and submitting to their commands. The apparent meaning is that the intended deeds are those in which they followed the leaders, namely their disbelief and sins. They become a regret when they see them in their record and become certain of the recompense for them, while it was possible for them to abandon them and turn to acts of obedience. In this view the idafah (attribution) is literal, because they performed them; in the second view it is metaphorical, meaning that it was incumbent upon them and they did not fulfil it.

The third issue: "hasarat" [regrets] is the third object of "ra'a" [to show].

The fourth issue: al-Zajjaj said: al-hasrah is an intense regret, to the point that the regretful one remains like an exhausted beast (hasir) of the animals, which is one that has no benefit in it. It is said: "Fulan hasira yahsaru hasratan and hasran" when his regret over a matter that escaped him became intense. The root of hasr is uncovering; it is said: "He uncovered (hasara) his arms," meaning he bared them. Al-hasrah is the uncovering of the state of regret. Al-husur is exhaustion, because it is the uncovering of the condition caused by a long journey. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain His worship, nor do they grow weary﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19]. Al-mihsarah is the broom, because it uncovers the ground. And birds are "tanhasir," because they are uncovered when their feathers depart.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will not emerge from the Fire﴾, the Companions [i.e., Ash'ari scholars] have argued by it that the people of major sins among the people of the qiblah will emerge from the Fire. They said: His saying ﴿and they﴾ is a specification of them with non-exit by way of restriction (hasr), so it is necessary that non-exit be specific to them. This verse reveals the intended meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, the wicked are in Hellfire, ﴿they will burn in it on the Day of Judgment﴾, ﴿and they will never be absent from it﴾ [al-Infitar: 14–16]. It is established that the intended meaning of "the wicked" here is the disbelievers, by the indication of this verse.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 168–169 (part 1 of 2):

[Page 3]

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality and to say about Allah that which you do not know.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had explained tawhid (the oneness of God) and its proofs, and the reward for those who affirm His oneness, He followed this with mention of shirk (associating partners with God) and of those who take rivals besides Allah and follow the leaders of disbelief. He then followed that with mention of His bounty toward both groups and His kindness to them, and that the disobedience of the one who disobeys Him and the disbelief of the one who disbelieves in Him do not cut off His kindness and blessings from them. So He said: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn Abbas said: the verse was revealed concerning those who forbade for themselves the sawa'ib, the wasa'il and the bahA'ir (types of animals declared forbidden by pre-Islamic Arab custom). They were a people from Thaqif, Banu Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, Khuza'ah and Banu Mudlij.

The second issue: al-halal (the lawful) is what is permissible, the restriction on which has been released. Its root is from al-hall, which is the opposite of al-'aqd (tying or binding). From it comes: halla bil-makan, meaning he alighted in the place, because he untied the fastening of travel for alighting. Also halla al-dayn, meaning the debt became due, because the knot was loosened by the expiry of the term. Also halla min ihramihi, meaning he exited his state of ihram, because he untied the knot of ihram. Also halat 'alayhi al-'uqubah, meaning the punishment became binding upon him, because the knot was loosened by what prevents punishment. Also al-hullah is the izar and the rida' (the lower and upper garments), because it is untied from being folded for wearing. From this comes tahillat al-yamin (the expiation that releases an oath), because it unties the knot of the oath by it. Know that the forbidden may be forbidden because of its impurity, such as carrion, blood and wine, and it may be forbidden without its being impure, such as the property of another when he has not permitted its consumption. Thus the lawful is that which is free of both restrictions.

The third issue: His saying ﴿lawful and good﴾: if you wish, you may put it in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of what is on the earth, and if you wish, you may put it in the accusative as an object (maf'ul).

The fourth issue: al-tayyib (the good) in language may mean the pure, and the lawful is described as good, because the forbidden is described as khabith (foul). Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Say, not equal are the khabith and the tayyib﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100]. Al-tayyib in its origin is what is enjoyed and found pleasant, and it was applied to the pure and the lawful by way of comparison, because the impure is disliked by the soul so it does not take pleasure in it. The forbidden is not enjoyable, because the Law restrains from it.

[Page 4]

Regarding what is meant by al-tayyib in the verse, there are two views:

The first: that it means what is enjoyable, because if we took it to mean the lawful, it would entail repetition. On this view, it is good only if it is of the kind that is desired, because if one consumes what he has no appetite for, it becomes forbidden. However, it is unlikely that a sane person would do that except under a doubt.

The second: what is meant by it is the permissible. As for the claim that it entails repetition, we say: we do not accept that. His saying ﴿lawful﴾ means what its genus is lawful, and His saying ﴿good﴾ means that there is no right of another attached to it. For the consumption of the forbidden, even if the consumer finds it pleasant, insofar as it leads to punishment, it becomes harmful and is not pleasant, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa': 10].

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read (khutuwat) with a damma on the kha' and the ta', and it is one of the two transmissions from Ibn Kathir and from Hafs on the authority of 'Asim. The rest read it with a sukun (no vowel) on the ta'. As for the one who vowels the 'ayn (the second radical), it is because the singular is khutwah, so when you make it plural you vowel the 'ayn for the plural, as is done with nouns of this pattern, such as ghurfah and ghurufat (room, rooms). Vowelling the 'ayn for the plural is done in such plurals to distinguish between the noun and the adjective, because what is a noun is pluralized with a vowel on the 'ayn, such as tamrah and tamarat (date, dates), ghurfah and ghurufat, shahwah and shahawat (desire, desires). What is an adjective is pluralized with a sukun on the 'ayn, such as dakhmah and dakhmat, and 'ablah and 'ablat (a pair of adjectives meaning large and firm). The khutwah is a noun, not an adjective, so it is pluralized with a vowel on the 'ayn. As for the one who lightens the 'ayn, he retains it in its original form and seeks lightness.

The second issue: Ibn al-Sikkit, in what al-Jubba'i related from him, said: khatwah and khutwah have the same meaning. It is reported from al-Farra': khataw tu khatwah, and the khutwah is the distance between the two feet, just as one says hathawtu hathwah (I scooped once), and the hathwah is the name of what one scoops. Likewise ghoraftu ghorfah, and the ghurfah is the name of what one takes in the hand. If this is so, then the khutwah is the place that is stepped over, just as the ghurfah is the thing taken up by the hand. So the meaning is: do not follow his path and do not travel his way, because the khutwah is the name of a place. This is the view of al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutaybah, for they both said: khutuwat al-Shaytan means his paths. If you take the khatwah to mean the khutwah, as al-Jubba'i mentioned, then the sense is: do not take him as your leader and do not follow his trail. The two meanings are close, although the two interpretations differ. This is what concerns the language. As for the meaning, the intent of Allah here is not what concerns language, but rather it is as if it were said to the one who has been permitted to eat in the described manner: beware lest you transgress it toward what Satan calls you to. Restraining the responsible person by this statement from overstepping the lawful into doubtful matters is like restraining him from overstepping it into the forbidden, because Satan only casts into a person what resembles doubt, so he adorns for him what is not lawful for him. Allah, may He be exalted, therefore forbade that. Then He explained the reason for this warning, which is that he is a clear enemy, meaning one who openly displays enmity. This is because Satan has undertaken seven matters in his enmity: four of them are in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and I will mislead them, and I will arouse in them desires, and I will command them so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will command them so they will alter the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 119], and three of them are in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path. Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left, and You will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf: 16–17]. So when Satan undertook these matters, he became an enemy who openly displays enmity, and for this reason Allah, may He be exalted, described him thus.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality and to say about Allah that which you do not know﴾, this is like an explanation of the whole of his enmity, and it comprises three matters:

The first of them: al-su' (evil), which encompasses all sins, whether they are acts of the limbs or acts of the hearts.

[Page 5]

The second of them: al-fahsha' (immorality), which is a kind of evil, because it is the most abominable of its kinds, namely that which is considered grave and shameful among sins.

The third of them: ﴿and to say about Allah that which you do not know﴾, and it seems to be the most abominable kind of immorality, because it is attributing to Allah, may He be exalted, what is not befitting, and it is among the greatest of the major sins. Thus this sentence serves as an explanation of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. It therefore includes that Satan calls to minor sins, major sins, disbelief and ignorance of Allah.

Here there are issues:

The first issue: know that the command and whispering of Satan is an expression for these thoughts that we find within ourselves. People have differed about these thoughts in several respects:

One of them: they differed about their essential nature. Some said: they are letters and hidden sounds. The philosophers said: they are conceptions of letters and sounds and imaginings of them, in the manner of images imprinted in mirrors, for those images resemble those things in some respects, even if they do not resemble them in all respects.

One may say: are the forms of these letters and their imaginings similar to these letters in being letters or not? If the first, then the forms of the letters are letters, and the statement returns to the claim that these thoughts are hidden sounds and letters. If the second, then the conceptions of these letters are not letters. But I find within myself these letters and sounds arranged and ordered according to their order in external reality, and an Arab does not speak in his heart except in Arabic, and likewise a non-Arab. And the conceptions of these letters, their succession and their sequence, can only be in conformity with their succession and sequence in external reality. Thus it is established that in themselves they are letters and hidden sounds.

The second: who is the agent of these thoughts? As for our principle, which is that the Creator of all events is Allah, may He be exalted, the matter is clear. As for the principle of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), they do not hold this view. Moreover, for them the speaker is the one who creates speech. So if the agent of these thoughts were Allah, may He be exalted, and some of them are lies and folly, it would entail that Allah is described by that, exalted is Allah above it. And it cannot be said that the agent of them is the servant, because the servant may dislike the occurrence of those thoughts and may devise ways to repel them from himself, yet they absolutely do not go away; rather, one leads to another in continuous succession. Therefore there must be something else here, which is either the angel or Satan. Perhaps both of them speak with this speech in the far reaches of the brain and in the innermost heart, so that a person, even if he is extremely deaf, hears these letters and sounds. Then, if we say that Satan and the angel are self-subsistent essences, not located in space at all, it is not far-fetched that they are capable of such acts. And if we say that they are subtle bodies, it is also not far-fetched to say that although they do not enter the inner parts of humans, they are able to convey this speech to the inner parts of humans. Nor is it far-fetched to say that, because of their extreme subtlety, they are able to penetrate the narrow passages of the inner human and the openings of his body, and convey speech to the innermost heart and brain. Furthermore, despite their subtlety, they are firmly composed, such that the connection of some of their parts to others is an inseparable connection. Therefore, their penetration into these narrow passages and openings does not necessitate their separation and the dispersion of their parts.

All these possibilities are such that there is no proof of their falsity, and the matter of knowing their realities is with Allah, may He be exalted.

Among what indicates the affirmation of the inspiration of angels toward good is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When your Lord inspired to the angels: "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], meaning: inspire them with steadfastness and encourage them against their enemies. And among the reports that indicate it is the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace: "Indeed, Satan has an influence (lamma) on the son of Adam, and the angel has an influence." And in another hadith also: "When a child is born to the children of Adam, Iblis pairs a devil with him, and Allah pairs an angel with him. The devil squats upon the left ear of his heart, and the angel squats upon the right ear of his heart, and they both call him." Among the Sufi philosophers, some interpreted the angel who calls to good as the rational faculty, and interpreted

[Page 6]

the Satan who calls to evil as the appetitive and irascible faculties.

* * *

The second issue: the verse indicates that Satan commands only ugly things, because Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned it with the word ﴿innama﴾ (only), which is used for restriction. Some of the knowers (al-'arifin) said: Satan may call to good, but for the purpose of drawing the person from it to evil. This indicates several types: either he draws him from the more excellent to the excellent, so that he may be able to bring him out from the excellent to evil; or he draws him from the excellent but easier to the more excellent but harder, so that the increase in hardship becomes a cause for an aversion to obedience altogether.

The third issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and to say about Allah that which you do not know﴾ includes all corrupt doctrines, and indeed it includes even the one who follows the truth by imitation (taqlid), because although he is following the truth by imitation, he says what he does not know, so he deserves blame, by his being included under the blame in this verse.

* * *

Fourth issue: Those who deny analogical reasoning (qiyas) cite His words: ﴿And that you say about God what you do not know﴾. The answer to this is: whenever evidence has been established that acting upon analogical reasoning is obligatory, then acting upon analogical reasoning is saying about God what one knows, not what one does not know.
