Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 170:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾

Know that they differed concerning the pronoun in His saying "lahum" (to them) into three opinions:

The first: that it refers back to "man" (those who) in His saying: ﴿Among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals (to Him)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], and they are the polytheists of the Arabs, whose mention has already preceded.

The second: that it refers to "al-nas" (mankind) in His saying: ﴿O mankind﴾. So He turned away from direct address to third-person reference, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), as an intensification in explaining their misguidance, as if He were saying to the intelligent: "Look at these fools, what are they saying?"

The third: Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited them to Islam, and they said, "We follow what we found our fathers upon, for they were better than us and more knowledgeable than us." According to this, the verse is a new (independent) sentence, and the pronoun in "lahum" returns to something not mentioned, except that a pronoun may return to what is known just as it returns to what has been mentioned. Then Allah, exalted is He, related about them that they said: ﴿Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon.﴾ And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Kisa'i assimilates the lam of "hal" (هَلْ) and "bal" (بَلْ) into eight letters: the taa' as in His saying ﴿Rather, you prefer﴾ [al-A'la: 16]; the nun as in ﴿bal nattabi'u﴾ (here); the tha' as in ﴿hal thuwwiba﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 36]; the sin as in ﴿bal sawwalat﴾ [Yusuf: 18]; the zay as in ﴿bal zuyyina﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33]; the dad as in ﴿bal dallu﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28]; the za' as in ﴿bal zanantum﴾; and the ta' as in ﴿bal taba'a﴾ [al-Nisa': 155]. Most of the readers keep it clear (al-izhar), and some of them agree with him in part, and izhar is the original form.

The second issue: "alfayna" (ﷲ ألفينا) means "wajadna" (we found), as evidenced by His saying in another verse: ﴿Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon﴾ [Luqman: 21]. It is also indicated by His saying: ﴿And they found her master at the door﴾ [Yusuf: 25], and His saying: ﴿Indeed they found their fathers astray﴾ [al-Saffat: 69].

The third issue: The meaning of the verse is that Allah commanded them to follow what Allah has sent down of clear proofs, but they said, "We will not follow that; we only follow our fathers and forefathers." So it is as if they set the proof against imitation (taqlid). Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾ And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: The waw in "awa-law" is the waw of conjunction, preceded by the hamza of interrogation, which is transferred to the meaning of rebuke and censure. The hamza of interrogation has been made for rebuke because it requires an affirmation of something whose affirmation would be a disgrace, just as interrogation requires informing about the one being asked about.

The second issue: The presentation of this answer from several aspects:

The first: It may be said to the imitator: Do you acknowledge that a condition for the permissibility of a person's imitation is that he know that the one imitated is right or not? If you acknowledge that, we do not know the permissibility of his imitation except after you know that he is right; so how did you know that he is right? If you know it by another imitation, a regress (tasalsul) follows; and if you know it by reason, then that is sufficient, and there is no need for imitation. And if you say: It is not a condition for the permissibility of his imitation that it be known that he is right, then you have permitted his imitation even if he is wrong, and then you, in your imitation, do not know whether you are right or wrong.

The second: Suppose that that predecessor was knowledgeable about this matter. Yet if we assume that the predecessor was never knowledgeable about that matter and never chose any position concerning it at all, what would you then do? On the assumption that neither that predecessor nor his position existed, it would have been necessary to turn to reflection; so it is the same here.

The third: When you imitate the one before you, how did you come to know that predecessor? Did you know him through imitation or not through imitation? If you knew him through imitation, then either circularity (dawr) or regress (tasalsul) follows. And if you knew him not through imitation but through proof, then when you make imitation of that predecessor obligatory, you must seek knowledge through proof, not through imitation; for if you sought (knowledge) through imitation and not through proof, while that predecessor sought it through proof and not through imitation, you would be opposing him. Thus it is established that the doctrine of imitation, if it were affirmed, would lead to its own negation, and so it is invalid.

The third issue: Allah mentioned this verse immediately after the prohibition against following the steps of Satan, to alert that there is no difference between following the whisperings of Satan and following imitation. In it is the strongest evidence for the obligation of reflection and inference, and for abandoning reliance on what occurs to the mind without proof, or on what another says without proof.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿understood nothing﴾ is a general expression whose meaning is particular, because they used to understand much of the affairs of the world; so this indicates the permissibility of mentioning the general while the intended meaning is the particular.

The fifth issue: His saying ﴿understood nothing﴾ means that they do not know anything of the religion; and His saying ﴿and were not guided﴾ means that they are not guided to the manner of acquiring it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 171:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the example of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing except a call and an outcry. Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not reason.﴾

Page 8

Know that when He, exalted is He, related about the disbelievers that, when they were called to follow what Allah had sent down, they abandoned reflection and contemplation and clung to imitation, and they said: ﴿Rather, we will follow that upon which we found our fathers﴾, He struck for them this example as an alert to those who hear them that they fell into what they fell into only because of their neglect of listening and their little concern for the religion. Thus He made them, in this respect, like cattle. Such an example increases the listener's knowledge of the states of the disbelievers, and it belittles the disbeliever in his own eyes when he hears it, so it becomes a breaking of his heart and a constriction of his chest, since He has made him like a beast. In this there is the utmost deterrence and repulsion for whoever hears it from treading the path of imitation. Here there are several issues:

The first issue: a shepherd "na'aqa" (called out) to the sheep when he shouted at them; as for the crow, "naghaqa" is with the unpointed ghayn (غ).

The second issue: the scholars among the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) have two approaches regarding this verse:

The first of them: correcting the meaning by means of an implied element (idmar) in the verse.

The second: taking the verse according to its apparent meaning without any implied element.

As for those who posited an implied element, they mentioned several views:

The first, which is the saying of al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutaybah, as if he said: "The example of one who calls the disbelievers to the truth is like the example of one who shouts (to the sheep)." So the shouting one, who is the shepherd, takes the place of the one calling to the truth, namely the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and all other callers to the truth; and the disbelievers take the place of the sheep being shouted at. The point of comparison is that the animal hears the sound but does not understand the intended meaning, and these disbelievers were hearing the voice and words of the Messenger, but they were not benefiting from them or from their meanings. Therefore the point of comparison is established.

The second: the example of the disbelievers in their calling upon their gods, the idols, is like the example of the one who shouts in his calling to what does not hear, such as cattle, and what is similar to that of speech, and animals do not understand. So He likened the idols, in that they do not understand, to these animals. Thus, if there is no doubt that the implied element here is the one called upon, then in the earlier saying the implied element is the caller. And there is an objection to this: that His saying ﴿except a call and an outcry﴾ does not support it, because idols do not hear anything.

The third: Ibn Zayd said: the example of the disbelievers in their calling upon their gods is like the example of one who shouts in his calling at a mountain, for he hears nothing but the echo of his voice. When he says "O Zayd," he hears from the echo, "O Zayd." Likewise these disbelievers, when they call upon these idols, hear nothing but what they themselves utter of calling and outcry.

The second approach to the verse, which is to take it according to its apparent meaning without any implied element, has two views:

The first: that one says: the example of the disbelievers in their lack of intellect in worshipping these idols is like the example of the shepherd when he speaks with the animals. Just as that shepherd is judged to lack intellect, so too here.

The second: the example of the disbelievers in following their fathers and imitating them is like the example of the shepherd when he speaks with the animals. Just as speaking with animals is pointless and of no benefit, so too imitation is pointless and of no benefit.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind﴾, know that when He likened them to animals, He increased their rebuke, saying: ﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind﴾, because they became like the deaf in that what they heard was as if they had not heard it; and like the dumb in that they did not respond to what they were called to; and like the blind in that they turned away from the proofs, so they became as if they had not witnessed them. The grammarians said: ﴿Deaf﴾ means "they are deaf," and it is in the nominative as a form of censure. As for His saying: ﴿so they do not reason﴾, the intended meaning is acquired intellect (al-'aql al-iktisabi), because innate intellect (al-'aql al-matbu') was already present in them. It has been said: intellect is of two kinds, innate and acquired.

Since the path to acquiring acquired intellect is seeking aid through these three faculties, when they turned away from them they lost acquired intellect. For this reason it is said: whoever loses a sense loses a branch of knowledge.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 172:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you, and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him that you worship.﴾

Know that this verse resembles what preceded it in His saying: ﴿Eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168]. Then we say: Allah, glorified is He, spoke from the beginning of the surah until this point about the proofs of Tawhid (Divine Oneness) and Prophethood, and thoroughly refuted the Jews and the Christians. From here He began to explain the rulings. Know that there are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Know that eating may be obligatory, and this is when it is necessary to ward off harm from the self. It may also be recommended (mandub), and this is because a guest may refrain from eating when alone but expands in eating when he is made welcome. This eating is recommended. It may also be permissible (mubah) when it is free of these incidental circumstances. The original state of a thing is that it is free of incidental circumstances, so the very act of eating is permissible. Given that this is the case, His saying ﴿Eat﴾ in this place does not indicate obligation or recommendation, but only permissibility.

* * *

The second issue: The scholars (al-Ashab) argued that provision (rizq) may be unlawful by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿of the good things We have provided for you﴾, for the good (tayyib) is the lawful (halal). So if every provision were lawful, His saying ﴿of the good things We have provided for you﴾ would mean "of the lawful things We have made lawful for you," which would be a repetition, and that contradicts the original principle. They answered this by saying that tayyib in the original language is an expression for what is pleasant and agreeable. Perhaps some people thought that expanding in foods and taking abundantly of their good things was forbidden, so Allah, exalted is He, permitted that by His saying: Eat of the delicious things We have made lawful for you. Thus its specification by mention served this meaning.

The third issue: His saying ﴿and be grateful to Allah﴾ is a command, and not a mere permission. If it is said: Gratitude is either by the heart, or by the tongue, or by the limbs. As for the heart, it is either the knowledge that the blessing proceeds from that Benefactor, or the resolve to exalt Him. As for that knowledge, it is among the necessary requirements of perfect intellect, for the sensible person does not forget it. If that knowledge is necessary, how can it be made obligatory?

As for the resolve to exalt Him by the tongue and the limbs, that resolve of the heart together with acknowledgment by the tongue and action by the limbs, when we have shown that these two do not answer, the resolve that it is not obligatory is more appropriate.

As for gratitude by the tongue, it is either to acknowledge Him as the Benefactor or to praise Him. This is not obligatory by consensus, but rather belongs to the category of the recommended acts.

As for gratitude by the limbs and organs, it is to perform acts indicating His exaltation, and that too is not obligatory. And when this is established, we say: It has become clear that it is not possible to say that gratitude is obligatory. We reply: What is summarized in this chapter is that it is obligatory upon him to believe that He deserves exaltation, and to manifest that by the tongue or by the other acts, if there is any suspicion there.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿if it is Him that you worship﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: In this verse there are several aspects.

One of them: ﴿and be grateful to Allah﴾ if you are those who know Allah and His blessings. He expressed the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, by worshipping Him, applying the name of the effect to the one who causes it.

The second: its meaning is: If you want to worship Allah, then be grateful to Him, for gratitude is the head of the acts of worship.

The third: ﴿and be grateful to Allah﴾, who provided you these blessings, ﴿if it is Him that you worship﴾, that is, if it is valid that you specify Him with worship and acknowledge that He, glorified is He, is the Benefactor and no other. From Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah, exalted is He, says: 'I, and the jinn and mankind, are in a great matter: I create and others are worshipped; I provide and others are thanked.'"

The second issue: Those who said that what is conditioned by the particle (in, "if") does not become nonexistent when that thing is absent have argued with this verse, for He, exalted is He, conditioned the command to be grateful with the word (in, "if") upon the acts of the servants, although whoever does not perform these acts is also obligated to be grateful.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 173 (part 1 of 5):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has forbidden you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than God has been invoked. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, commanded us in the preceding verse to eat of what is lawful, He in this verse detailed the kinds of what is unlawful. The discussion concerning it falls under two types:

The first type: what relates to exegesis (tafsir).

The second type: what relates to the rulings (ahkam) that the scholars deduced from this verse.

The first type contains several issues:

The first issue: know that the word ﴿innama﴾ (only) has two usages:

One of them: that it is a single particle, as in your saying: "Innama dari daruka" (my house is only your house), and "Innama mali malUka" (my wealth is only your wealth).

The second: that ﴿ma﴾ is separate from ﴿inna﴾, and ﴿ma﴾ means "alladhi" (that which), as in your saying: "Inna ma akhadhta maluka" (indeed what you took is your property), and "Inna ma rakibta dabbatuka" (indeed what you rode is your mount). It has come in the revelation in both usages. As for the first, His saying: ﴿Innama Allahu ilahun wahid﴾ [al-Nisa: 171] (God is only one God) and ﴿Innama anta nadhir﴾ [Hud: 12] (you are only a warner).

As for the second, His saying: ﴿Innama sana'u kaydu sahir﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69] (what they have made is only the plot of a magician). Had you put the word "kayda" in the accusative, taking "innama" as a single particle, it would have been correct. And His saying: ﴿Innama ittakhadhtum min duni Allahi awthanan mawaddata baynikum﴾ [al-Ankabut: 25] (you have taken idols besides God only out of affection among you), where "mawadda" may be put in the accusative or the nominative according to these two usages.

They differed regarding its meaning under the first usage. Some of them said that "innama" conveys restriction (hasr, exclusivity), and they argued for this with the Qur'an, poetry, and analogy. As for the Qur'an, His saying: ﴿Innama Allahu ilahun wahid﴾ [al-Nisa: 171], meaning: He is nothing but one God; and He said: ﴿Innama al-sadaqatu lil-fuqara'i wal-masakin﴾ [al-Tawba: 60] (the alms are only for the poor and the needy), meaning: they are for them and not for others; and God said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Qul innama ana basharun mithlukum﴾ [al-Kahf: 110] (say: I am only a human like you), meaning: I am nothing but a human like you. Likewise this verse, for in another verse He said: ﴿Qul la ajidu fi ma uhiya ilayya muharraman ala ta'imin yat'amuhu illa an yakuna maytatan aw damam masfuhan aw lahma khinzir﴾ [al-An'am: 145] (Say: I find in what has been revealed to me nothing forbidden to an eater who eats it, except that it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine). Thus the two verses become one, and His saying ﴿innama harrama alaykumu﴾ in this verse explains His saying ﴿la ajidu fi ma uhiya ilayya muharraman﴾ in that verse, except that such and such is in that verse.

As for poetry, the saying of al-A'sha:
"I am not the most among them in number, but glory belongs only to the multitude"
and the saying of al-Farazdaq:
"I am the defender, the protector of honour, and only one who defends his honour is I or one like me"

As for analogy: the particle "inna" is for affirmation and "ma" is for negation. When they are combined, both must remain on their original bases; so either they establish the existence of what is not mentioned and negate what is mentioned, which is invalid by consensus, or they establish what is mentioned and negate what is not mentioned, which is the objective.

Those who said it does not convey restriction argued with His saying: ﴿Innama anta nadhir﴾ [Hud: 12], whereas others were also warners. The answer: its meaning is "you are nothing but a warner," so it conveys restriction, but it does not negate the existence of another warner.

The second issue: ﴿harrama﴾ is read in the active voice, ﴿hurrima﴾ in the passive, and ﴿harama﴾ on the pattern of ﴿karuma﴾.

* * *

The third issue: al-Wahidi said: carrion (al-maytatu) is that from which the soul has departed without slaughter (dhaka) of what is slaughterable. As for blood, the Arabs used to put blood into intestines, roast them, and then eat them, so God forbade blood. His saying "the flesh of swine" means swine in all its parts, but He specified the flesh because it is the thing intended for eating. As for His saying ﴿wa ma uhilla bihi li-ghayri Allah﴾ (and that over which other than God has been invoked), al-Asma'i said: al-ihlal originally means raising the voice; so every one who raises his voice is a muhill. Ibn Ahmar said:
"The riders of it raise their voices at al-Farqad, as the rider in ihram raises his voice"
This is the meaning of ihlal in the language. Then the one in ihram is called muhill because he raises his voice with the talbiyah at the time of ihram. This is the meaning of ihlal; it is said: "Fulan ahalla bi-hajjatin aw umratin," meaning he entered ihram with it. That is because he raises his voice with the talbiyah at ihram. And the slaughterer is a muhill, because the Arabs used to name the idols at the time of slaughter and raise their voices with their mention. From this comes: "istahalla al-sabiyyu" (the child cried out). So the meaning of His saying ﴿wa ma uhilla bihi li-ghayri Allah﴾ is: what was slaughtered for idols. This is the view of Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Qatadah. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd said: it means what was mentioned over it other than the name of God. This view is preferable, because it is more exactly in accord with the wording. The scholars said: if a Muslim slaughters an animal and intends by its slaughter to draw near to other than God, he becomes an apostate, and his slaughter is the slaughter of an apostate. This ruling applies to other than the slaughter of the People of the Book. As for the slaughter of the People of the Book, it is lawful for us, because of His saying: ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5].

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿fa-man id-tturra﴾ (but whoever is compelled), there are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿famanu id-turra﴾ with a damma on the nun, and the rest with a kasra. The damma is for assimilation (ittiba'), and the kasra is on the original vowel because of the meeting of two sukuns.

The second issue: id-turra means: he is driven and compelled. It is a form of iftu'ala derived from ad-darura (necessity), and its root is from ad-darar, which is constriction.

* * *

The third issue: when God, exalted, forbade those things, He excepted from them the state of necessity. This necessity has two causes:

One of them: severe hunger, when one finds no lawful food with which to keep alive; then he is compelled.

The second: when one is coerced into consuming it by a coercer; then it is lawful for him to consume it.

The fourth issue: compulsion is not an act of the one obligated, so that it could be said "there is no sin upon him, indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful." Therefore, here there must be an implied element, namely eating, and the sense is: "whoever is compelled and eats, there is no sin upon him." The omission here is like the omission in His saying: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], meaning: "then he breaks his fast," the phrase "fa-aftara" being omitted. And His saying: ﴿Whoever among you is ill or has an injury of his head, then a ransom of fasting or charity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], meaning: "then he shaves, then a ransom." The omission is permissible because the addressees know what is omitted and because the context indicates it.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿ghayra baghin﴾ (neither desiring), there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Farra' said: "ghayr" here cannot be taken in the sense of exception (istithna'), because "ghayr" here means negation, which is why "la" is conjoined to it, since it has the meaning of "la." Here it is a circumstantial state (hal) of the one compelled, as if you said: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then it is lawful for him."

The second issue: the root meaning of al-baghy in the language is corruption and exceeding the limit. Al-Laith said: al-baghy in a horse's running is strutting and swaggering, and it is said that it "yabghi" in its running, but one does not say "faras baghin" (a horse that is baghin). Al-baghy is oppression and departure from fairness, and from it comes His saying: ﴿And those who, when wronged, they defend themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 39]. Al-Asma'i said: "baghā al-jurhu yabghi baghyan" when the wound began to fester; "baghati al-sama'" when its rain increased until it exceeded the limit; and "baghā al-jurhu wal-bahru wal-sahabu" when it rose up.

As for His saying: ﴿wa la 'adin﴾ (nor transgressing), al-'adw is transgression in matters and going beyond what one ought to be limited to. It is said: "'adā 'alayhi 'adwan, wa 'udwanan, wa i'tidā'an, wa ta'addiyan" when he wronged him with an injustice exceeding the limit; and "'adā tawrahu" means he exceeded his measure.

* * *

The third issue: the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have two views regarding His saying: ﴿ghayra baghin wa la 'adin﴾:

One of them: that His saying ﴿ghayra baghin wa la 'adin﴾ is restricted to the eating.

The second: that it is general, covering eating and other than eating. As for the first view, there are several interpretations:

The first: ﴿ghayra baghin﴾ means one who finds lawful food that the soul dislikes, and so turns to eating the forbidden food that is delicious; ﴿wa la 'adin﴾ means one who exceeds the measure of the concession.

The second: ghayra baghin li-ladhdhatin, meaning one who seeks pleasure from it; and la 'adin, exceeding what suffices to stave off hunger. This is narrated from al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Rabi', Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The third: ghayra baghin 'ala mudtarrin akhar bil-istila' 'alayhi (not transgressing upon another compelled person by seizing from him), and la 'adin fi sadd al-ju'a (nor exceeding in satisfying hunger).

The second view: that the meaning is "not rebelling against the imam of the Muslims while on a journey, from baghy, and not transgressing by disobedience," i.e., exceeding the path of those who are upright. The discussion concerning the preference of one of these two interpretations over the other will come, God willing.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿fa-la ithma 'alayhi﴾ (there is no sin upon him), there are two questions:

One of them: that eating in that state is obligatory, whereas His saying ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ indicates permissibility.

The second: that the one compelled is like one forced to an act, and one who is forced is not described as "having no sin upon him." We say: we have already explained, in the commentary on His saying ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], that the negation of sin is a common quality shared among the obligatory, the recommended and the permissible. Also, His saying ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ means the lifting of hardship and constriction. Know that this hungry person, if he has the desire for carrion but does not have the intense aversion, then he becomes compelled to consume what sustains his life, just as he becomes compelled to flee from a wild beast when that is possible for him. But if the intense aversion arises, then because of that aversion he is no longer compelled, and he is bound to eat the carrion in the state of aversion he is in; here the meaning of obligation is realized.

* * *

As for His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, there is a difficulty: since He said ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾, how is it fitting that He then says ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, for forgiveness occurs only when a sin has occurred?

The answer has several aspects:

One of them: the cause of prohibition exists in carrion and blood, but the prohibition was lifted because of the presence of a countervailing factor. So when eating it is eating of what contains the cause of prohibition, He expressed it with forgiveness. Then He mentioned after it that He is Merciful, meaning: for the sake of mercy upon you I have permitted that to you.

The second: perhaps the one compelled exceeds eating what is needed, so He, glorified, is Forgiving in that He forgives his sin in consuming the excess, and Merciful in that He permitted eating the measure of need.

The third: when He, exalted, explained these rulings, He followed them with His being Forgiving and Merciful, because He is Forgiving to the disobedient when they repent, and Merciful to the obedient who persist upon the way of His rule, glorified and exalted.

* * *

The second type of discussion concerning this verse: the juristic issues which the scholars deduced from it, arranged in chapters:

The first chapter: concerning what relates to carrion.

The discussion on it is arranged into an introduction and objectives.

As for the introduction: it contains three issues.

The first issue: they differed as to whether prohibition attached to objects (a'yan) implies generality (ijmal). Al-Karkhi said: it implies generality, because objects cannot be described as lawful or unlawful, so the two must be directed to some action of ours upon them; and not all our actions upon them are forbidden, because removing them from oneself or from a place is an action upon them which is not forbidden. Therefore this prohibition must be directed to a specific action, and no one action is preferable to another, so the verse becomes general (mujmal). But most scholars insisted that it is not among the general expressions; rather this word in common usage conveys the prohibition of dealing with these bodies, just as things themselves are not owned, but rather the dispositions over them are owned. So when it is said: "Fulan owns a slave-girl," everyone understands that he owns the right to dispose of her. Likewise here. We have thoroughly examined this discussion in the book al-Mahsul fi 'Ilm al-Usul.

The second issue: since the principle we have mentioned is established, the verse must indicate the prohibition of all dispositions except what the specifying evidence excludes. If it is said: why can the prohibition not be restricted to eating? The answer is based on several points:

One of them: that the customary understanding of the prohibition of carrion is the prohibition of eating it.

The second: that it came right after His saying: ﴿Eat of the good things which We have provided you﴾.

Third, what has been related from the Messenger, peace be upon him (ﷺ), in the report about Maymunah's sheep: "Only its eating is forbidden from carrion."

The answer to the first point: we do not concede that what is commonly understood from the prohibition of carrion is the prohibition of eating it.

As for the second: this verse is self-contained, so it is not necessary to restrict it to what preceded. Rather, it must be applied according to its apparent meaning.

As for the third: the apparent meaning of the Qur'an takes precedence over a solitary report (khabar al-wahid, a report transmitted by a single narrator). This holds only if it is not permissible to specify the Qur'an by a solitary report. It may be answered that the Muslims returned to this verse to learn the grounds of prohibition, and their consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars) shows that it is not specified by the statement of the prohibition of eating. The questioner may, however, deny this consensus.

* * *

**The third issue:** Linguistically, carrion (maytah) is that which has ceased to be alive without being cut by a intentional act. That is why they distinguished between the one killed (maqtul) and the dead (mayyit). In terms of the Sharia, it is what is not properly slaughtered (mudhakka), either because it was not slaughtered at all, or because it was slaughtered but that slaughter was not a valid ritual slaughter (dhakah). We will mention the definition of dhakah in its place. If it is asked: how is this correct, when Allah the Exalted says in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:3], and then mentions after it the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen from a height, which shows that among what is not properly slaughtered some is carrion and some is not? We reply: perhaps at the beginning of the Sharia the matter was according to the original linguistic sense; but after the Sharia became established, carrion is what we have mentioned. And Allah knows best.

As for the objectives (al-maqasid): know that error in the matters derived from this verse occurs in two ways:

One: what they excluded from the verse although it is included in it.

Two: what they included in it although it is outside it.

As for the first category, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, in his most apparent opinion, held that it is forbidden to benefit from the wool, hair and bones of carrion. Malik said: it is forbidden to benefit only from its bones. Most jurists agreed on the prohibition of benefiting from the hair of the pig. Those (who forbid) argued that these things are carrion, so it is necessary that benefiting from them be forbidden. We say they are carrion because of his statement, peace be upon him: "What is cut off from a living thing is dead." This report covers hair, bone and everything. As for what shows that bone specifically is carrion, it is His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:78]. Thus it is established that they were alive, and at death they become carrion. When it is established that they are carrion, it is necessary that benefiting from them be forbidden, by His statement: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾.

The opponent objected that hair and wool have no life in them, because the characteristic of life is perception and feeling, and this is absent in hair. For this reason Malik held that bones are impure, but not hair.

The answer: life is not an expression of the meaning that requires perception and feeling, as shown by the verse and the report. As for the verse, it is His statement: ﴿How will He give life to the earth after its death?﴾ [al-Rum 30:50]. As for the report, it is his statement, peace be upon him: "Whoever revives a dead land, it is his." The basic principle in usage is the literal meaning. So we know that life in the original language is not an expression of what you have mentioned, but rather of an animal or plant being sound in its constitution, balanced in its state, not exposed to decay, corruption and dispersal. When this is established, it becomes clear that it falls under the verse.

Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, argued from the Qur'an, the report, consensus and analogy:

As for the Qur'an: His statement: ﴿And of their wool, their fur and their hair are furnishings and provision for a time﴾ [al-Nahl 16:80]. Here He mentions them in the context of a favour, and favour does not come from something impure which it is not permissible to benefit from.

As for the report: his statement, peace be upon him, concerning Maymunah's sheep: "Only its eating is forbidden from carrion."

As for consensus: they used to wear fox skins and make caps from them. It is related from al-Nakha'i: they did not see any harm in the skins of predators and the skins of carrion when tanned. And they did not distinguish between the state with hair and without. Al-Shafi'i's words "they used to" refer to the Companions. And no one may say: the fox, according to al-Shafi'i, is lawful, so he permits it; because ritual slaughter is a condition by agreement, and it is not present in these foxes.

As for analogy: these hairs and bones are bodies that are beneficial and not exposed to decay and corruption, so it is necessary to rule that they are pure, like tanned hides. As for benefiting from the hair of the pig: among the jurists there are those who deny its impurity, and this is the safer view. Then they said: even granting that the generality of His statement ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ requires the prohibition of benefiting from wool, bone and other things, these proofs produce permission to benefit from them, and the specific takes precedence over the general, so this side is more deserving of consideration.

* * *

**The second issue:** Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: if an animal that has no flowing blood (nafs sa'ilah) dies in water, it does not spoil the water, whether little or much. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, has two opinions regarding little water. Those who argue for al-Shafi'i said: these are living creatures, and when they die they become carrion, so using them is forbidden by the verse, and when using them is forbidden by the verse, it is necessary to rule that they are impure. When their impurity is established, it is necessary to rule that the little water in which they fell is impure. They answered this by saying: it is carrion, and benefiting from it is forbidden; but why do you say that whenever it is like that it is impure? Then its impurity does not necessarily entail that the water becomes impure by it. They argued for the second opinion of al-Shafi'i with his statement, peace be upon him: "If a fly falls into the vessel of one of you, dip it (in the food) and then remove it, for in one of its wings is a disease and in the other is a cure." He commanded dipping it, and perhaps the food was hot, so the fly dies in it. If that were a cause of making it impure, the Prophet, peace be upon him, would not have commanded it.

* * *

**The third issue:** The jurists have seven positions regarding tanning (dibagh). The most lenient of people in this matter is al-Zuhri, for he permits the use of hides in their entirety before tanning. Next is Dawud, who said: all of it becomes pure by tanning. Next is Malik, who said: its outer surface becomes pure, but not its inner surface. Next is Abu Hanifah, who said: all of it becomes pure except the skin of the pig. Next is al-Shafi'i, who said: all of it becomes pure except the skin of the dog and the pig. Next are al-Awza'i and Abu Thawr, who both say: only the skin of what is eaten (meat) becomes pure. Next is Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah be pleased with them all, who said: nothing of them becomes pure by tanning. Ahmad argued from the verse and the report. As for the verse: His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:3], it states the prohibition absolutely, and did not restrict it to one state rather than another.

As for the report: the statement of Abdullah ibn Hakim: "The letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to us before his death: that you should not benefit from carrion by hide or sinew." They answered his reliance on the verse by saying: specifying a general ruling by a solitary report and by analogy is permissible, and here they found the solitary report, which is his statement, peace be upon him: "Whatever hide is tanned has become pure."

As for analogy: tanning returns the hide to what it was in the state of life, and just as its state in life was pure, so also after tanning. This analogy and the report are the basis of al-Shafi'i's position, may Allah have mercy on him.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** They differed as to whether it is permissible to benefit from carrion by feeding it to a falcon (bazi) or an animal. Some of them prohibited this, because when one feeds a falcon that, one has benefited from that carrion, and the verse indicates the prohibition of benefiting from carrion. As for when the falcon of its own accord goes to eat carrion, is it obligatory for us to prevent it or not? On this there are two possibilities.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** They differed as to whether it is permissible to use the fat and grease of carrion for lighting lamps, or not. This must be examined: if that is what life has passed through, or if most of it is in this state, then the apparent meaning requires its prohibition. If it is not so, then it lies outside the general category of carrion, and only other evidence besides the apparent meaning prohibits it. It was related from Ata' ibn Jabir, who said: when the Messenger (ﷺ) came to Makkah, there came to him those who gathered animal fats, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, we gather fats, which are from carrion and other things, and they are for the leather and the ships." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah curse the Jews; fats were forbidden to them, so they sold them and ate their price." So he forbade them from that, and informed them that its absolute prohibition necessitates the prohibition of selling it, just as it necessitates the prohibition of eating it.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** The apparent meaning requires the prohibition of fish and locusts, but these two were specified by a report from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. He, peace be upon him, said: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us. As for the two carrions, they are the locust and the fish (nun); and as for the two bloods, they are the spleen and the liver." And from Jabir, in a long account: the sea cast up to them a whale, and they ate from it for half a month; when they returned, they informed the Prophet, peace be upon him, of that, and he said: "Do you have any of it that you can feed me?" And he, peace be upon him, said in describing the sea: "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful." Also, the permissibility of fish has been established by continuous transmission (tawatur) from the Messenger, peace be upon him. They differed concerning floating fish, which is one that dies in the water of its own accord. Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: there is no harm in it. Abu Hanifah and his companions and al-Hasan ibn Salih said: it is disliked. The Companions differed on this question. From Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "What floats of the sea's game, we do not eat." This is also related from Ibn Abbas and Jabir ibn Abdullah. And it is related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Ayyub, its permissibility. Abu Bakr al-Razi transmitted varying reports from Jabir ibn Abdullah that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "What the sea casts up or what recedes from it, eat it; and what dies in it and floats, do not eat it."

As for al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, he argued from the verse, the report and reason:

As for the verse: His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:96]. This floating fish is part of the food of the sea, so its permissibility is necessary.

As for the report: his statement, peace be upon him: "Two carrions have been made lawful for us: fish and locust." This is absolute. And his statement about the sea: "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful." This is general. And it is related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whatever floats upon the sea."

* * *

**The seventh issue:** Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: there is no harm in eating all locusts, whether you took them or found them. It is related from Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that what is found dead is not lawful; but what is taken alive and then its head is cut off and it is roasted is eaten; and what is taken alive but is neglected until it dies is not eaten.

Malik's proof is the apparent meaning of the verse. The proof of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah is his statement, peace be upon him: "Two carrions have been made lawful for us: fish and locust." So it is necessary to take both on their absolute basis. Thus it becomes clear that if cutting its head is considered a form of ritual slaughter for it, then it is like the sheep that has been ritually slaughtered in that it is not carrion; and so his statement, peace be upon him, "Two carrions have been made lawful for us," would have no benefit. Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa said: "I fought with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in seven campaigns; we ate locusts and ate nothing else; he did not distinguish between carrion and what was killed."

* * *

**Ninth issue**: Whatever is cut off from a living animal is unlawful, since it is carrion. It must therefore be prohibited. We say it is carrion on the basis of both the text and reason. The text is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "What is cut off from a living thing is dead." The reasoning is that this part was alive, since it perceives pain and pleasure; when it was cut off, that quality ceased and it became dead. Therefore it is forbidden, by the words of God Most High: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

* * *

**Tenth issue**: Scholars differ over whether the slaughter of an animal whose meat is not eaten results in the purification of its hide.

According to al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, it does not, because this slaughter does not make the meat lawful to eat, so it should not result in purification, like the slaughter by a Magian. According to Abu Hanifah, it does.

* * *

**The second section: what has entered the verse but is not part of it, and it contains issues.**

**First issue**: Know that the words of God Most High, ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion and blood﴾ and ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾, do not necessitate the prohibition of liquids in which carrion has fallen. They necessitate only the prohibition of the carrion itself. What is adjacent to carrion is not called carrion, so the word "prohibition" does not cover it, like butter into which a mouse has fallen and died, which is not covered by it. This is the apparent view. The discussion of this topic revolves around two points:

One: As for that which becomes impure by contact with carrion, it is forbidden; as for that which does not become impure, it is not forbidden.

Two: How is that which has become impure to be purified?

* * *

**Second issue**: Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak asked Abu Hanifah about a bird that fell into a cooked pot and died. Abu Hanifah said to his companions: "What do you think about it?" They mentioned to him what Ibn Abbas reported: that the meat may be eaten after it is washed and the broth is poured away. Abu Hanifah said: "We say this, on the condition that it fell into it while the pot was still; as in this report. But if it fell in while it was boiling, then neither the meat nor the broth may be eaten." Ibn al-Mubarak said: "Why is that?" He said: "Because if it fell into it while it was boiling and died, then the carrion has mixed into the meat. But if it fell in while the pot was still and died, then the carrion has only seeped into the meat." Ibn al-Mubarak said, counting on his fingers thirty times: "This is zarin," meaning in Persian, the position (madhhab). Ibn al-Mubarak narrated the like of this from al-Hasan.

* * *

**Third issue**: Abu Hanifah said: The milk of a dead sheep and its rennet are both pure. al-Shafi'i and Malik said: This milk and rennet are not lawful. al-Layth said: The egg that comes out of a dead hen may not be eaten.

Know that al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, does not rely in this matter on the apparent meaning of the words ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾, because milk is not described as carrion. Therefore one must return to another proof, both for negation and affirmation. The basis of al-Shafi'i's position is that if milk is collected in a vessel and some carrion falls into it, it becomes impure; so likewise when the animal dies while the milk is still in its udder. The same disagreement applies to rennet.

As for the egg, when it is taken out of the body of the hen, it is pure once washed, and it is lawful to eat, because once the shell hardens it separates what is eaten from the carrion, and so it is lawful. This is also why, if the egg had not formed properly, it would be forbidden.

* * *

We conclude this section with issues common to both divisions.

**First issue**: Theologians differ over whether carrion (maytah) is dead in the sense of death. Some affirm death as a quality opposed to life, as God Most High said: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. Others say it is the absence of life from what is capable of receiving life, and this is closer to the truth.

**Second issue**: Scholars differ over whether the prohibition of carrion necessitates its impurity. The truth is that the prohibition of using it does not necessitate impurity, since it is not impossible in reason that the use of it be forbidden while the use of what is adjacent to it is permitted. However, it has been established by consensus that carrion is impure.

* * *

**The second chapter: on the prohibition of blood, which contains two issues**

**First issue**: al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, prohibited all blood, whether poured forth or not. Abu Hanifah said: the blood of fish is not prohibited. As for al-Shafi'i, he relied on the apparent meaning of this verse, namely the words ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine﴾. This is blood, so it must be prohibited. Abu Hanifah relied on the words of God Most High: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, except that it be carrion or blood poured forth﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. He explicitly stated that he found none of the prohibited things except these. Therefore blood that is not poured forth must not be prohibited by the necessity of this verse. So this verse is specific, and the words ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion and blood﴾ are general, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, replied that the words ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ contain no indication of the permissibility of anything other than the things mentioned in that verse. Rather, it indicates only that God Most High did not make clear to him anything beyond the prohibition of those things. This does not preclude that He later makes clear the prohibition of what lies beyond them. Perhaps the words of God Most High ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion﴾ were revealed afterwards, and that was an explanation of the prohibition of blood, whether poured forth or not. Once this is established, the ruling must be the prohibition of all blood and its impurity, so one must remove blood from meat as far as possible. The same applies to fish. Any blood that falls into water or clothing makes that which it reaches impure.

**Second issue**: Scholars differ over the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood have been made lawful to us: the liver and the spleen." Is the name "blood" applied to these two, making the exception valid, or not? Some deny this, because the liver is treated as meat, and likewise the spleen; they are described as blood only figuratively. Others say it is like congealed blood, and they cite the hadith as evidence for this.

* * *

**The third chapter: on swine, which contains issues**

**First issue**: The community has agreed that swine is forbidden in all its parts. God Most High mentioned its flesh only because most of its use is connected with it. This is like His words: ﴿O you who believe, when the call is made to prayer on the day of Friday, hasten to the remembrance of God and leave off trade﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9]. Trade was singled out for prohibition because it was the greatest of concerns for them. As for the bristles of swine, they are not included in the apparent meaning, although they agreed on their prohibition and impurity. They differed over whether it is permissible to use them for stitching. Abu Hanifah and Muhammad said it is permissible. al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said it is not permissible. Abu Yusuf said: I dislike stitching with them, and a permission from him has also been reported. The proof of Abu Hanifah and Muhammad is that we see Muslims allowing cobblers to use them without any objection appearing from them; and because the need for them is pressing. And if al-Shafi'i said about the blood of fleas that it does not make clothing impure because avoiding it is difficult, why should the same not be permitted for swine bristles when they are used for stitching?

* * *

**Second issue**: Scholars differ over the water-swine. Ibn Abi Layla, Malik, al-Shafi'i and al-Awza'i said: there is no harm in eating anything that lives in the sea. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: it may not be eaten. The proof of al-Shafi'i is the words of God Most High: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 96]. The proof of Abu Hanifah is that this is swine, so it is forbidden by the words of God Most High: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. al-Shafi'i said: When "swine" is used without qualification, the understanding immediately goes to land swine, not sea swine, just as when "meat" is used without qualification, the understanding immediately goes to the meat of non-fish, not fish meat, by general agreement. Also, the water-swine is not called "swine" without qualification, but is called "water-swine."

* * *

**Third issue**: al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, has two opinions on whether a vessel licked by a swine must be washed seven times.

One: Yes, by analogy with the dog.

The second: No, because that strictness was only a means of weaning them from mixing with dogs, and they did not mix with swine. Thus the difference is clear.

* * *

**The fourth chapter: on the prohibition of what has been dedicated to other than God**

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 173 (part 4 of 5):

Among the people is one who claims that what is meant by this is the slaughtered animals of the idol-worshippers, who used to slaughter for their idols, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that which is slaughtered on the stone altars﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. They permitted the slaughter of a Christian when he pronounces over it the name of the Messiah. This is the view of ʿAta', Makhul, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions said: that is not lawful. The proof for this is that if they slaughter in the name of the Messiah, they have then invoked other than God by it, so it must be forbidden.

It is related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "If you hear the Jews and the Christians invoking other than God, then do not eat; and if you do not hear them, then eat, for indeed God, exalted is He, has made their slaughtered animals lawful, and He knows what they say."

The opponent argued with several points:
The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], and this is general.
The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that which is slaughtered on the stone altars﴾, which indicates that what is meant by His saying ﴿that over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾ is the same as what is meant by His saying ﴿that which is slaughtered on the stone altars﴾.
The third: that the Christian, when he mentions God, exalted is He, but intends by it the Messiah; so if his intention in that does not prevent the lawfulness of his slaughter, even though he invokes other than God by it, then likewise his ruling should be the same when he manifests in mentioning God what he conceals, namely his intention of the Messiah.

As for the answer to the first: His saying ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ is general, and His saying ﴿that over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾ is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

As for the second: His saying ﴿that which is slaughtered on the stone altars﴾ does not necessitate the restriction of His saying ﴿that over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾, because they are two distinct verses and there is no equivalence between them. As for the third: we are only obligated to the outward, not to the inward. So if he slaughters it in the name of God, it must be lawful, and we have no way to the inward.

The Fifth Section

Those who hold that the word "innama" (only, indeed) indicates restriction agree that the apparent meaning of the verse requires that nothing other than these things is forbidden. But we know that in the Sharia there are other things besides these that are forbidden, so the word "innama" becomes one whose apparent meaning is abandoned in practice. The Sixth Section: On the one under compulsion, and it contains issues.

The First Issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ means that whoever is compelled and is not described by the attribute of transgression or the attribute of aggression at all, and then eats, there is no sin upon him. Abu Hanifa said: its meaning is: whoever is compelled and eats, neither desiring nor transgressing in the eating, there is no sin upon him. So he restricted the attribute of transgression and aggression to the eating.

It follows from this disagreement whether one who is disobedient by his journey may take the concession or not. al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he may not take the concession, because he is described by aggression, so he does not fall under the verse. Abu Hanifa said: rather he may take the concession, because he is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing in the eating, so he falls under the verse. al-Shafi'i argued for his view with this verse and with reason.

As for the verse: He, glorified and exalted is He, forbade these things to everyone by His saying ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], then permitted them to the compelled one who is described as neither desiring nor transgressing, and the one disobedient by his journey is not described by this attribute; because our saying "so-and-so is not a transgressor" is the contradiction of our saying "so-and-so is a transgressor", and it suffices for its truth that he be transgressing in some matter whatsoever, whether in the journey, or in the eating, or in other than them. And when the name "transgressor" is true of one who transgresses in some matter, whatever matter it is, it must be that our saying "so-and-so is not aggressive" is true only if he is not transgressing in any matter at all. Therefore our saying "neither desiring nor transgressing" is true only if the attribute of transgression is absent from him in every respect. The one disobedient by his journey is transgressing by his journey, so it is not true of him that he is "not aggressive"; and when that is not true of him, it is necessary that he remain under the verse, which is His saying ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾. At most, one might say: this is problematic with regard to the one disobedient in his journey, for he takes the concession although he is described by aggression. But we say: it is a general text which has been specified in this case. The difference between the two cases is that the concession is an aid to the journey; so when the journey is sinful, the concession is an aid to sin. But when the journey is not sinful in itself, the aid to it is not an aid to sin. Thus the difference is clear.

Know that al-Qadi and Abu Bakr al-Razi both transmitted from al-Shafi'i that he said, in explaining His saying ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾: that is, desiring (rebelling) against the imam of the Muslims, nor transgressing by his journey being sinful. Then they both said: the explanation of the verse as "neither desiring nor transgressing in the eating" is better than what al-Shafi'i mentioned. That is because His saying ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ is a condition, and a condition is like an exception in that it does not stand by itself, so it must be linked to something mentioned; and we know that there is nothing mentioned except the eating, because we have shown that the meaning of the verse is: whoever is compelled and eats, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him. Since that is so, it must be linked to the eating, which is in the position of what is mentioned, not to the journey, which is not mentioned at all.

Know that this statement is weak. That is because we have shown that His saying ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ is not true unless the desiring and transgressing are removed from him in all matters, so the negation of aggression by the journey is included implicitly. We do not say that the wording indicates a specific referent. As for restricting it to the eating, that is a restriction without necessity, and so it is contrary to the original principle. Then, what indicates that it is not permissible to turn it to the eating are several points:

One of them: His saying ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ is a circumstantial clause of the compulsion, so the attribute of compulsion must remain together with his remaining neither desiring nor transgressing. If the meaning of his being neither desiring nor transgressing were his being so in the eating, it would be impossible for the attribute of compulsion to remain with it, because the state of eating does not preserve the attribute of compulsion.

The second: that a person by nature recoils from consuming carrion and blood, and what is like that does not need a prohibition against it; so turning this condition to transgression in the eating takes the speech out of its benefit.

The third: that being neither desiring nor transgressing indicates the negation of the quiddity of transgression and the negation of the quiddity of aggression, and this quiddity is negated only when all its instances are negated; aggression in eating is one instance of this quiddity, and likewise aggression in the journey is another instance of it. Therefore the negation of aggression requires the negation of aggression from all these aspects, so restricting it to the eating is not permissible.

As for al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, he does not restrict it by excluding aggression in the journey, but takes it upon its apparent meaning, which is the negation of aggression from all aspects, and this implies the negation of aggression in the journey; and thereby his purpose is achieved.

The fourth: that the possibility we have mentioned is supported by another verse, which is His saying ﴿But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, not inclining toward sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and this is what we have said, that the verse requires that he not be described by transgression and aggression in any matter whatsoever.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, argued with several points:
The first: His saying, exalted is He, in another verse: ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to﴾ [al-An'am: 119]. This person is compelled, so it is necessary that he take the concession.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill yourselves; indeed God is ever Merciful to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], and He said: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]. Refraining from eating is a striving toward killing oneself and casting oneself into destruction, so it must be forbidden.

The third: it is related that he, peace be upon him, granted the concession to the resident for one day and night, and to the traveller for three days and their nights, and he did not differentiate in this between the disobedient and the obedient.

The fourth: that if one disobedient by his journey is asleep and is about to drown or burn, it is obligatory upon one present who is in prayer to cut off his prayer to save him from drowning or burning; so it is even more fitting that it be obligatory upon him in this case to strive to rescue his life.

The fifth: that he should repel the causes of destruction, such as the elephant, the rampaging camel, the snake, and the scorpion; indeed it is obligatory upon him, so likewise here.

The sixth: that the disobedient by his journey, if he is compelled, and if a man were to permit him some of his property, it is lawful for him to take it, indeed it is obligatory upon him; so likewise here, the common factor being the removal of harm from the self.

The seventh: that the burden of repelling harm from people is greater in obligation than every harm that a person repels from himself; so likewise he repels the harm of destruction from himself by this eating, even if he is disobedient.

The eighth: that necessity permits taking the food of another without consent, rather by way of compulsion, and this taking is forbidden were it not for the compulsion; so likewise here.

al-Shafi'i answered the appeal to the general texts by saying that our proof negating the concession is more specific than their proofs permitting it, and the specific takes precedence over the general. As for the analogical arguments, he answered that he can reach the permission of these concessions by repentance, and if he does not repent, then he is the one who has wronged himself. Then he countered these arguments with a strong point, namely that the concession is an aid to the journey; so when the journey is sinful, the concession is an aid to sin, and that is absurd, because sin is forbidden, and aid is striving toward its attainment, and combining the two is contradictory. And God knows best.

* * *

The Second Issue: al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions said: the compelled one may not eat of the carrion except the amount that keeps his soul in his body (his breath).

ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Hasan al-ʿAnbari said: he may eat from it what suppresses his hunger. And from Malik: he eats from it until he is satiated and takes provision; then if he finds independence from it, he discards it. The closer view regarding the indication of the verse is what we mentioned first; because when the cause of the concession is compulsion, then whenever the compulsion is removed the concession is removed, just as if he finds lawful food, it is not permissible for him to consume carrion, because the compulsion to eat it is removed by the existence of the lawful. Likewise, when the compulsion is removed by eating a quantity of it, the excess is forbidden. There is no consideration in this of suppressing the hunger as al-ʿAnbari said, because hunger at the outset does not permit eating carrion if one does not fear harm from abandoning it; so likewise here. What also indicates this is that if he had with him food of an amount which, if he ate it, would keep his soul in his body, it would not be permissible for him to take the carrion; so when he eats that food and the fear of perishing is removed, it is not permissible for him to eat carrion; likewise, when he eats some of the carrion and the fear of harm is removed from him, it is necessary that eating after that be forbidden to him.

* * *

The Third Issue: they differed regarding the compelled one who finds all that is counted among the forbidden things. Most of the scholars gave him the choice among all of them, because carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine are equal in prohibition and in compulsion, so it is necessary that he be given the choice among all. This is the most fitting with the apparent meaning of this verse, and it is preferable to the view of one who obligates that the eating of carrion, rather than the flesh of swine, is of greater gravity in prohibition.

* * *

**Fourth issue:** Scholars differed concerning one who is compelled to drink when he finds only wine, or one who is choking on a morsel and has no water to wash it down but finds wine. Some permitted it by analogy (*qiyas*, analogical reasoning) to the cases already allowed, since Allah, exalted is He, only permitted these prohibited things to preserve the self and to ward off destruction from it. So it is likewise in this case. This is the view closer to the apparent meaning, and it is the opinion of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he should not drink, because it only increases his thirst and hunger and removes his reason. It was answered that his statement, "it only increases thirst and hunger," is an act of obstinacy, and that as for his statement, "it removes reason," our discussion concerns a small amount that does not have that effect.

* * *

**Fifth issue:** Scholars differed where a carrion (*maytah*) is needed for treatment, either on its own or by being mixed into some compound medicines. Some permitted it, on the basis of both the text and the reasoning. As for the text, the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted the people of 'Uraynah to drink the urine and milk of camels for their treatment. As for the reasoning, it is on several grounds:

First: the theriac (*tiryaq*, a compound antidote) into which the flesh of vipers is put is considered wholesome, so it must be permitted, based on His saying: ﴿Lawful for you are the good things﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:4]. The most that can be said is that this generality is restricted, but that does not undermine its being a proof.

Second: Abu Hanifah pardoned an amount the size of a dirham of impurity because of need, and al-Shafi'i pardoned the blood of fleas because of need. So why would they not rule for pardon in this case too, because of need?

Third: Allah permitted eating carrion for the sake of preserving the self, so the same applies here. Some people forbade it, relying on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Verily Allah has not placed the cure of my nation in what He has forbidden to them." The earlier scholars answered that using this report as evidence is valid only if it is established that it is forbidden to take it, and the dispute concerns nothing other than this.

* * *

**Sixth issue:** Scholars differed concerning treating with wine. Know that if the need for such treatment reaches the level of necessity, its ruling has already been given in the fourth issue. If it does not reach the level of necessity, its ruling has already been given in the fifth issue.

[Page 23]

**The Second Ruling**

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book and trade it for a small price — they eat nothing into their bellies except the Fire. God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book and trade it for a small price — they eat nothing into their bellies except the Fire. God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Know that in His statement ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse was revealed concerning the leaders of the Jews: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ka'b ibn Asad, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab. They used to take gifts from their followers. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, they feared the cutting off of those benefits, so they concealed the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the matter of his laws, and this verse was revealed.

* * *

**The second issue:** They differed about what exactly they used to conceal. It was said: they used to conceal the description and attributes of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the good news of him. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Asamm and Abu Muslim. al-Hasan said: they concealed the rulings, and this is supported by His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, many of the rabbis and monks devour people's wealth falsely and turn them away from the way of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34].

**The third issue:** They differed about the manner of the concealment. What is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas is that they were distorters, distorting the Torah and the Gospel.

But according to the theologians (al-mutakallimun, the scholars of kalam, or speculative theology), this is impossible, because these two were books that had reached such fame and mass transmission (tawatur, uninterrupted widespread transmission) that distorting them would be impossible. Rather, they concealed the interpretation (ta'wil, the meaning or explanation of a text), because among them were those who knew the verses indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they would offer false interpretations for them and divert them from their correct meanings, which indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is what is meant by concealment. Thus the meaning becomes: those who conceal the meanings of what God has sent down of the Book.

* * *

As for His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿and trade it for a small price﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The pronoun in "bihi" (with it) may refer to the concealment, since the verb implies the verbal noun; it may also refer to what God has sent down; and it may refer to what is concealed.

**The second issue:** The meaning of His statement ﴿and trade it for a small price﴾ is like His statement: ﴿and do not trade My signs for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41], which has already passed. In sum, their purpose in that concealment was to take wealth by means of it. This is what is meant by their trading it for a small price.

**The third issue:** He called it "small" either because it is small in itself, or because, compared to the great harm it entails, it is small.

[Page 24]

**The fourth issue:** Some people said: their purpose in that concealment was to take wealth from their common folk and followers. Others said: rather, their purpose was to take wealth from their great and wealthy men who supported that religious position. Outwardly, there is nothing more than their trading the concealment for a small price, and there is no clarification of whom they were greedy toward and took from. So the statement is general (mujmal, not specified), and greed in this would only be directed toward one in whom ignorance and little knowledge gather, who is able to give wealth, and who is stingy about what is familiar in religion, so that what he is sought for is granted to them. This is known by custom.

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, mentioned this account about them, He mentioned the threat of punishment for it in several aspects:

First: His statement, ﴿they eat nothing into their bellies except the Fire﴾. On this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** Some said: mentioning "the bellies" here is for added clarification, because one says "so-and-so ate the wealth" when he squandered and ruined it. Others said: rather, there is a benefit in it. His statement ﴿in their bellies﴾ means "filling their bellies." One says "so-and-so ate in his belly" and "so-and-so ate in part of his belly."

**The second issue:** It was said: their eating in this world, although it is pleasant in the present, its outcome is the Fire, so it is described that way, like His statement: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the wealth of orphans unjustly only consume a Fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa': 10]. This is narrated from al-Hasan, al-Rabi' and a group of the people of knowledge. This is because when they ate what necessitates the Fire, it is as if they ate the Fire, as is narrated in another hadith: "One who drinks from vessels of gold and silver only swallows the fire of Hell into his belly." Also His statement: ﴿Indeed, I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36], meaning grapes, so He named it by the name of what it will become. It was also said: in the Hereafter they will eat the Fire because of their eating of the forbidden in this world; this is from al-Asamm.

Third: His statement, ﴿God will not speak to them﴾. Its apparent meaning is that He will not speak to them at all. But since it is placed in the context of a threat, what is understood from it is something that functions as punishment for them. They mentioned three aspects regarding it:

The first: Indications establish that He, glorified and exalted, will speak to them, as in His statement: ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all, concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Hijr: 92-93], and His statement: ﴿We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6]. So we know that He questions each one of the accountable, and questioning cannot be except through speech. They said: therefore the meaning of the verse must be that He will not speak to them with greeting and peace, but He will speak to them with what is greatly distressing to them of grief and remorse, through interrogation and questioning, and by His statement: ﴿Be cast into it, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108].

The second: He will not speak to them at all. As for His statement ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92], the questioning is from the angels by His command, exalted is He. The reason that not being spoken to on the Day of Resurrection is mentioned in the context of threat is that the Day of Resurrection is the day on which God, exalted is He, speaks to all creation directly without an intermediary. At His speech, joy appears in His friends and its opposite in His enemies, and the people of Paradise are distinguished from the people of the Fire by that. Therefore, without doubt, this is among the greatest threats.

The third: His statement ﴿nor will He speak to them﴾ is a metaphor for anger, because it is the custom of kings that when angry they turn away from the one they are angry with and do not speak to him, just as when pleased they turn toward him with their face and conversation.

Fourth: His statement ﴿nor will He purify them﴾. On this there are several aspects:

The first: He will not attribute purification to them nor praise them.

The second: He will not accept their deeds as He accepts the deeds of the pure.

The third: He will not place them in the stations of the pure.

Fifth: His statement ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾. Know that the form fa'il (like *alim*) may mean the active participle (fa'il), as in *sami'* meaning *sami'* (hearing) and *'alim* meaning *'alim* (knowing); it may mean the passive participle (maf'ul), as in *jarih* and *qatil* meaning *majruh* (wounded) and *maqtul* (killed); and it may mean the causative participle (mufil), as in *basir* meaning *mubsir* (seeing) and *alim* (painful) meaning *mu'lim* (causing pain). Know that this verse contains several issues:

[Page 25]

**The first issue:** The scholars of legal theory (ulama' al-usul, the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence) said: punishment ('iqab) is pure harm accompanied by humiliation. So His statement ﴿God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them﴾ is an indication of humiliation and contempt, and His statement ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾ is an indication of harm. He placed humiliation before harm to alert that humiliation is more severe and harder.

**The second issue:** The verse indicates the prohibition of concealing any knowledge in the matter of religion that must be made known.

**The third issue:** What matters is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.
