Although the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, it is general in regard to everyone who conceals anything of the matters of religion that must be made known. Thus it is suitable for those who hold firmly to the threat against the perpetrators of major sins to rely upon it. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 175 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾

Know that when Almighty God described the scholars of the Jews for concealing the truth and magnified the threat concerning it, He described that crime so that it might be known that this punishment was great only because of this great crime.

And know that the act is either considered in its state in this world or in the Hereafter. As for this world, the best of things is guidance and knowledge, and the worst of things is error and ignorance. When they abandoned guidance and knowledge in this world and were content with error and ignorance, there is no doubt that they are in the utmost loss in this world. As for the Hereafter, the best of things is forgiveness and the most losing of things is punishment. When they abandoned forgiveness and were content with punishment, there is no doubt that they are in the utmost loss in the Hereafter.

Since their state is as we have mentioned, they are without doubt the greatest of people in loss, in this world and in the Hereafter. God only judged concerning them that they had bought punishment in exchange for forgiveness, because when they knew what the truth was, and knew that in making it manifest and removing doubt about it lies the greatest reward, and in concealing it and casting doubt upon it lies the greatest punishment, then when they proceeded to conceal that truth, they were, without doubt, those who sold forgiveness for punishment.
* * *
As for His saying: ﴿So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: Know that concerning this expression there are two views:

One of them: that "mā" in this verse is an interrogative of rebuke, meaning: what is it that made them patient, and what thing made them endure the Fire until they abandoned the truth and followed falsehood? This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn Zayd. Ibn al-Anbārī said: "Aṣbara" may mean "ṣabbara" (to make patient), and it is frequent that "afʿala" means "faʿʿala," like "akrama" and "karrama," and "akhbara" and "khabbara."

The second: that it has the sense of wonder (taʿajjub). Its explanation is that one who is content with the cause of a thing must necessarily be content with its effect and its necessary consequence, if he knows that necessity. When they proceeded to do what necessitates the Fire and entails God's punishment, while knowing this, they became like those who are content with God's punishment and patient under it. Therefore He said: ﴿So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾ It is like when you say to someone who exposes himself to what provokes the ruler's anger: how patient you are with the chains and the prison.

Once you know this, it becomes clear that the words ﴿So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾ must be understood in terms of their state in this world, because that is a description of them in the state of being obligated and in the state of their buying error in exchange for guidance.

Al-Aṣamm said: the meaning is that when it is said to them, ﴿Begone therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 108], they fall silent and endure the Fire, out of despair of deliverance. But this is weak for several reasons:

One: God described them with this in the present tense, and turning it to mean that they will become so is contrary to the apparent sense.

Second: the people of the Fire may well express anguish and plead for relief.

The second issue: concerning the reality of wonder (taʿajjub) and the words that indicate it in the language.

Here there are two discussions:

The first discussion: concerning wonder. It is the magnifying of a thing together with the obscurity of the cause of that thing's greatness. So if the two meanings are not found, wonder does not arise. This is the origin. Then the term "wonder" may be used upon mere magnification without obscurity of the cause, or without the greatness having a cause of arising. For this reason Shurayḥ denied the reading of one who read ﴿Nay, you wonder, and they mock﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 12] with a dammah on the tā' from "ʿajibtu," for he saw that the obscurity of anything from God is impossible.

Al-Nakhaʿī said: the meaning of wonder with respect to God, Exalted, is mere magnification, whereas with respect to servants, magnification must be accompanied by obscurity of the cause. Just as it is permissible to attribute mockery, derision and cunning to God, Exalted, not in the sense in which they are attributed to servants.

The second discussion: know that wonder has two forms:

One of them: "mā afʿalahu," as in His saying: ﴿So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾

The second: "afʿil bihi," as in His saying: ﴿How well they hear and see!﴾ [Maryam: 38].

As for the first expression, namely their saying "mā aṣbarahu," there are several positions:

The first view, which is the choice of the Basrans: that "mā" is an indefinite noun that is the subject (mubtadaʾ) of the sentence, "aḥsana" is a verb, and the object is "Zaydan," and its estimate is: a thing made Zayd good, i.e., made him good.

Know that this view is invalid according to the Kufans, and they argued against it with several points:

The first: it is correct to say "mā akrama Allāh," "mā aʿẓamahu," and "mā aʿlamahu," and likewise for all His attributes, but it is impossible to say "a thing made God generous, great, or knowing," because the attributes of God, Glorified and Exalted, are necessary to His essence.

If it is said: when this expression is used of what may be subject to coming into being, its meaning is magnification together with the obscurity of its cause, and when it is applied to God, Exalted, its meaning is only one of its two halves, namely magnification alone.

We reply: when we say "mā aʿẓama Allāh," the word "mā" here does not mean "a thing," so it is not a subject, and "aʿẓama" is not a predicate of it; so it must be turned to another sense. And if that is so, it is established that explaining this verse by these things in the context of wonder is not correct.

The second argument: if the meaning of our saying "mā aḥsana Zaydan" were "a thing made Zayd good," then the sense of wonder would remain when we state this sentence. It is known that when we say "a thing made Zayd good," no sense of wonder remains in it at all, rather it becomes like nonsense. So we know that it is not permissible to explain our saying "mā aḥsana Zaydan" by our saying "a thing made Zayd good."

The third argument: the one who made Zayd good, and the sun, the moon, and the world, is God, Glorified and Exalted, and it is not permissible to refer to Him by "mā." And if that were permissible, then referring to Him, Glorified, by "man" would be more fitting, and so if we said "man aḥsana Zaydan," the sense of wonder should remain; since it does not remain, we know the falsehood of what they said.

The fourth argument: according to the explanation they give, there is no difference between saying "mā aḥsana Zaydan" and saying "Zaydan ḍaraba ʿAmran." Just as the latter is not an expression of wonder, the former must likewise not be.

The fifth argument: every attribute that is established for a thing, its being established for it is either from itself or from another. If the one who effects that attribute is itself or another, then in either case something made it good. Thus the knowledge that something made it good is necessary knowledge, while the knowledge that it is something wondered at is not necessary. Therefore it is not permissible to explain our saying "mā aḥsana Zaydan" by our saying "a thing made Zayd good."

The sixth argument: they said that the subject may not be an indefinite noun, so how did they make the most indefinite of things a subject here? And they said: it is not permissible to say "rajulun kātib" (a man is a writer), because everyone knows that in the world there is a man who is a writer, so this statement would convey nothing. Likewise, everyone knows that some thing is what made Zayd good, so what benefit is there in this report?

The seventh argument: the entry of diminutive formation, which is a feature peculiar to nouns, into your saying "mā aḥsana Zaydan." If it is said: the entry of the diminutive is because this verb has kept to one fixed pattern, so it became similar to a noun and took its property, namely the diminutive, we reply: there is no doubt that the verb has its quiddity and the diminutive has its quiddity. These two quiddities either are mutually exclusive or are not mutually exclusive. If they are mutually exclusive, their combining is impossible in all places; since their combining here shows that this is not a verb. If they are not mutually exclusive, it must be valid for the diminutive to apply to all verbs, and since that is not the case, we know the falsehood of this division.

The eighth argument: the correctness of this word and the invalidity of its being treated as weak (iʿlāl). You say in wonder "mā aqwama Zaydan," with the wāw kept sound, just as you say "Zaydun aqwamu min ʿAmr." Had it been a verb, its wāw would have become an alif because of the fatḥah before it. Do you not see that they say "aqāma yuqīmu"? If it is said: this word, since it has kept one fixed pattern, has become like a noun, and the full statement is that weakening (iʿlāl) in verbs is not for the reason of being a verb, nor is soundness in nouns for the reason of being a noun; rather, weakening in verbs is for seeking lightness when there is a need for much inflection, and non-weakening in nouns is for lack of inflection; and this verb is like a noun in the reason for soundness and for avoiding weakening. We reply: since weakening in verbs is for seeking lightness, it should have been made light and then left in its lightness, for that is closer to reason.

The ninth argument: if your saying "aḥsana" were a verb, and your saying "Zaydan" an object, it would be permissible to separate them by an adverbial phrase, so one would say "mā aḥsana ʿindaka Zaydan" and "mā ajmala al-yawma ʿAbda Allāh." But the apparent transmission is that this is not permissible, so what you have held is refuted.

The tenth argument: if the matter were as you have stated, it should be permissible to express wonder with every transitive verb, whether unaugmented or augmented, triliteral or quadriliteral. Since it is not permissible except from the unaugmented triliteral, this proves the invalidity of this view.

The Basrans argued that "aḥsana" in our saying "mā aḥsana Zaydan" is a verb, with several points:

The first: that "aḥsana" is a verb by agreement, so we hold to its being a verb until there is a proof diverting us from it.

The second: that "aḥsana" ends in a fatḥah, and if it were a noun it would have to take the nominative case when it is the predicate of a subject.

The third: the proof that it is a verb is the attachment of the object pronoun to it, namely your saying "mā aḥsanahu."

As for the answer to the first: just as "aḥsana" may be a verb, it may also be a noun when it is a word of preference. Moreover, we have shown by the many points that it is not permissible for it to be a verb, and you have not asked us for anything but the proof.

As for the answer to the second: we will mention the cause for the obligatory fatḥah at the end of this word.

As for the answer to the third: it is refuted by your saying "laʿallī" and "laytanī." And it is strange that the argument from the diminutive for nominality is stronger than the argument from this pronoun for verbality. So if you abandon that strong proof, then abandoning this weak one is more fitting. This is the sum of what is said regarding this view.

The second view, which is the choice of al-Akhfash, he said: the analogical reading is that what comes after "mā," namely your saying "aḥsana," is made a relative clause (ṣila) for "mā," and the predicate of "mā" is implied. This too is weak, for most of the points mentioned; among them, if you said "alladhī aḥsana Zaydan," it would not be a well-formed sentence, whereas "mā aḥsana Zaydan" is a well-formed sentence. The same applies to the rest of the points.

The third opinion, which is the view preferred by al-Farra', is that the word (ما) is interrogative and أفعل (af'al) is a noun used for comparison (التفضيل, the elative form). It is like your saying: زيد أحسنُ من عمرو (Zayd is better than 'Amr). Its meaning is: "What thing is better than Zayd?" This is an interrogative with an implied denial that anything exists that is better than him. It is like when someone reports about a person's knowledge and another denies it, so the reporter says: "And who is more knowledgeable than so-and-so?" This shows that the opponent's claim is contrary to the truth, that he cannot establish proof for it, and that his inability becomes evident when I demand proof from him. Then your saying أحسنُ, although it should be in the nominative as in your saying ما أحسنُ زيدٍ when you ask about the most beautiful of his limbs, has been put in the accusative so that a distinction is made between that interrogative and this one. For there, the meaning of your saying ما أحسنُ زيدٍ is: "Which of Zayd's limbs is the most beautiful?" Here the meaning is: "Which thing among the existing things in the world is more beautiful than Zayd?" There is a difference between them, as you see. Variation in vowel endings is established to indicate variation in meanings. Our saying زيدًا also (is in the accusative) for the sake of distinction, because there it is in the genitive, since أحسن was made to be in construct with it. Here it is in the accusative for the sake of distinction. Furthermore, in every elative there is the meaning of the verb, and in everything over which something else is preferred there is the meaning of the object. For the meaning of your saying زيدٌ أعلمُ من عمرٍو is that Zayd surpassed 'Amr in knowledge. So this meaning was taken into account when there was need to make the distinction.

The fourth opinion, which is also the view of some of the Kufans, is that (ما) is interrogative and أحسنَ is a verb, as the Basrans say. Its meaning is: "What thing made Zayd beautiful?" It is as if you are inferring the perfection of the one who made this beauty from the perfection of this beauty. Then you say: "My intellect does not encompass the reality of its perfection," so you ask someone else to explain its perfection to you. This is the sum of what has been said on this matter.

As for the detailed discussion of أفعِلْ به, we will mention it, God willing, in His saying: ﴿How well they will hear and see﴾ [Maryam: 38].

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verse 176:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with truth, and indeed those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme dissension.﴾

Know that there are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** Scholars differed over what the word ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (*dhalika*, "that") refers to, and they mentioned two opinions.

The first: It refers to the threat mentioned earlier. When Allah passed the severe threat against those who conceal the clear proofs, He explained that this threat for that concealment was because Allah sent down the Book with truth regarding the description of Muhammad ﷺ, and that these Jews and Christians, out of opposition to the Messenger, conceal it and cast doubt upon it. Therefore they rightly deserved that severe threat. Furthermore, several matters were mentioned in their threat:

First: They have bought punishment in exchange for forgiveness.

Second: They have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance.

Third: For them is a painful punishment.

Fourth: Allah will not purify them.

Fifth: Allah will not speak to them.

So the word ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ may refer to each one of these things individually, and it may refer to all of them together.

The second: ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ refers to what they do of audacity toward Allah in opposing the command of Allah and concealing what Allah has sent down. Allah then explained that this is only because Allah sent down the Book with truth, and in it was revealed that these leaders among the People of the Book do not believe and do not submit, and that from them there will be nothing but persistence in disbelief, as He said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ (al-Baqarah: 6).

**The second issue:** The word ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ may be in the nominative position (*raf'*) or in the accusative position (*nasb*). In the nominative position, it is a *mubtada'* (subject), and it necessarily has a *khabar* (predicate). That predicate has two possibilities:

The first: The meaning is: That threat is known to them because Allah sent down the Book with truth, and in it He made clear the threat against whoever does these things. Thus this threat was necessarily known to them.

The second: The meaning is: That punishment is because Allah sent down the Book and they disbelieved in it. In this case the letter *bā'* (in ﴿بِأنَّ﴾) is in the nominative position as the predicate (i.e., it functions as the predicate's complement). As for the accusative position, the meaning is: We did that because Allah sent down the Book with truth, and they had distorted it.

---

**The third issue:** The intended meaning of "the Book" may be the Torah and the Gospel, which contain the good news of the sending of Muhammad ﷺ. It may also be the Qur'an. If it is the former, the meaning is: Indeed those who differed concerning its interpretation and its distortion are in extreme dissension. If it is the latter, the meaning is: Indeed those who differed concerning its being a true revelation sent down from Allah are in extreme dissension.

**The fourth issue:** The word ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ (*bil-haqq*, "with truth") means "with truthfulness." It was also said to mean "with the clarification of the truth."

---

Regarding Allah's words ﴿And indeed those who differed﴾, there are two issues:

**The first issue:** It was said that "those who differed" are all the disbelievers, who differed concerning the Qur'an. However, the more apt interpretation is that it refers to the Torah and the Gospel, in which the good news of Muhammad ﷺ was mentioned, because these people had recognized that and concealed it, and distorted its interpretation. When Allah mentioned what serves as the cause for sending punishment upon them, the more apt interpretation is that the intended Book is their own scripture, which is the foundation for them, not the Qur'an. If they recognized the Qur'an, it would be by way of following, due to the validity of their own scripture.

As for His words ﴿with truth﴾, it was said: with truthfulness; and it was said: with the clarification of the truth.

As for His words ﴿those who differed concerning the Book﴾, know that even if we say the intended Book is the Qur'an, their difference concerning it was that some of them said it is soothsaying, others said it is sorcery, a third said it is an abomination (*rijz*), a fourth said it is "the fables of the ancients," and a fifth said it is a fabricated transmitted speech.

If we say the intended Book is the Torah and the Gospel, then their difference may refer to several possibilities:

First: They differ regarding the indication of the Torah concerning the prophethood of the Messiah. The Jews said it indicates a denunciation of Jesus, while the Christians said it indicates his prophethood.

Second: The people differed in interpreting the verses that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, and each one of them gave a different, corrupt interpretation. Because when a matter is not true and binding to accept, but is rather forced, each person mentions something different contrary to the saying of his companion. This is what constitutes the difference.

Third: What Abu Muslim mentioned: He said: The word ﴿اخْتَلَفُوا﴾ (*ikhtalafū*) is of the form *if'ala* which is used in place of *fa'ala*, as it is said: *kasaba* and *iktasaba* (to earn), *'amila* and *i'tamala* (to work), *kataba* and *iktataba* (to write), *fa'ala* and *if'ala*. The meaning of His words ﴿those who differed concerning the Book﴾ is: those who succeeded regarding it, i.e., they inherited it and became successors to it, as in His words: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾ (al-A'raf: 169), and His words: ﴿Indeed, in the alternation of the night and the day﴾ (Yunus: 6), meaning each one comes after the other, and His words: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day in succession for whoever wishes to remember﴾ (al-Furqan: 62), meaning each of them succeeds the other.

There is a third interpretation of the verse, which is that the intended meaning of "the Book" is the category of what Allah has sent down, and the intended meaning of "those who differed concerning the Book" is those whose statements about the Book differed, so that they accepted some of the Books of Allah and rejected others. These are the Jews and the Christians, since they accepted some of the Books of Allah, namely the Torah and the Gospel, and rejected the rest, which is the Qur'an.

As for His words ﴿are indeed in extreme dissension﴾, there are several interpretations:

First: These people who differ concerning the manner of distorting the Torah and the Gospel, out of enmity toward you, are among themselves in extreme dissension and fierce contention. Therefore one should not regard their agreement in enmity, for there is no mutual affection or accord among them.

Second: It is as if Allah the Exalted is saying to Muhammad: These people, although they differ among themselves, are as those who agree in enmity toward you and in utmost opposition to you. For this reason Allah singled them out with that threat.

Third: These people agreed on the basic principle of distortion but differed concerning the manner of distortion. Each of them denies his companion, opposes him, and contends with him. If this is the case, then they have admitted their own falsehood through their own statements, so their disparagement of you does not in the least harm you. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 177 (part 1 of 4):**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteous is one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets, and gives wealth, despite love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for freeing captives; and who establishes prayer and gives zakah; and those who fulfill their promise when they promise; and those who are patient in poverty, hardship, and during battle. Those are the ones who have been truthful, and those are the righteous.﴾

Know that this verse contains several issues.

**First issue:** The scholars differed over whether this address is general or specific. Some said that by His words ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ He meant the People of the Book, when they insisted on persisting in facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). So He said: righteousness is not this path; rather, righteousness is the one who believes in Allah. Others said that the intended address is to the believers, when they thought they had attained the goal by facing the Ka'bah, since they loved that, so they were addressed with this statement. Others said that it is an address to everyone, because at the abrogation (naskh) and change of the qiblah, the believers felt elation over this qiblah, and they became excessively strict about that qiblah, until they thought it was the greatest objective in the religion. So Allah, exalted is He, urged them through this address to fulfill all the acts of worship and obedience, and He clarified that righteousness is not in turning your faces east and west, but rather righteousness is such-and-such. This view resembles the apparent meaning more, since there is no specification in it. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: the righteousness that is sought is not the matter of the qiblah; rather, the righteousness sought is these qualities that He enumerated.

**Second issue:** Most scholars hold that (laysa) is a verb (fi'l). Some denied this and claimed that it is a particle that was altered (ḥurrifa).

The argument of those who say it is a verb is that pronouns attach to it, and pronouns attach only to verbs, as in your saying: *lastu*, *lasnā*, *lastum*, and *al-qawmu laysū qā'imīna*. This argument is refuted by *innanī*, *laytanī*, and *la'alla*.

The arguments of those who deny it are as follows:

First: If it were a verb, it would be a past-tense verb, and it cannot be a past-tense verb; therefore, it cannot be a verb. The proof of the implication is that everyone who said it is a verb said it is a past-tense verb. The proof that it cannot be a past-tense verb is the consensus of the majority that it is used to negate the present (*nafy al-ḥāl*). If it were past tense, it would negate the past, not the present.

Second: It enters upon a verb, so we say *laysa yakhruju Zaydun*, and a verb does not enter upon a verb, rationally or by transmitted usage. As for the view of those who say that *laysa* enters upon the pronoun of the matter and the situation, with this sentence explaining that pronoun, it is weak, because if that were permissible, the same would be permissible with *mā*.

Third: The particle *mā* has its meaning appear in other words, and this word is similar, because if you say *laysa Zaydun*, the sentence is not complete; rather, you must say *laysa Zaydun qā'iman*.

Fourth: If *laysa* were a verb, then *mā* would be a verb, and this is false; therefore that (the claim that *laysa* is a verb) is false. The proof of the implication is that if *laysa* were a verb, that would be because it indicates the occurrence of the meaning of negation linked to a specific time, namely the present. This meaning exists in *mā*, so *mā* must be a verb. Since *mā* is not a verb, neither is *laysa*. Or we express this meaning in another way and say: *laysa* is an invariable word that was placed to negate the present, so it resembles *mā* in negating verbhood.

Fifth: You attach *mā* to past-tense verbs, so you say *mā aḥsana Zaydan*, and it is not permissible to attach *mā* to *laysa*, so you do not say *mā laysa Zaydun yadhkuruka*.

Sixth: It is of a form other than the verbal patterns, because *fa'ala* does not exist among the verbal patterns. So to claim that it is a verb is to affirm something that is not among the forms of the verb.

If it is said: its original form is *laysa*, like *ṣayda al-ba'īr*, except that they lightened it and made its lightening obligatory, because it is not inflected, since it has one state only. The verbal patterns differ only according to the differing times they indicate, and they made the pattern specific to it a past tense, because it is the lightest of the patterns.

We reply: all of this is contrary to the basic principle. The basic principle is its absence. Moreover, the basic principle regarding the verb is inflection. When they prevented it from inflection, it was necessary that they leave it in its original pattern, so that deficiencies would not accumulate upon it. As for making the prevention of inflection, which is contrary to the basic principle, a cause for changing the pattern, which is also contrary to the basic principle, that is extremely corrupt.

Seventh: al-Qutaybi mentioned that it is a word composed of letters: the negative *lā*, and *ays*, meaning "existent." He said: therefore they say, "He removed him from *al-laysiyyah* to *al-aysiyyah*," meaning from non-existence to existence, and "*aysatuhu*," meaning "I found him." This is an explicit text on the matter. He said: al-Khalil mentioned that *laysa* is a word of denial whose meaning is *lā ays*, so the hamzah was dropped for lightness because of how much it occurs in speech. The evidence for this is the Arabs' saying: "Bring it to me from where *ays* and *laysa*," meaning: from where it is and where it is not.

Eighth: Induction (*istiqrā'*) shows that the verb is placed only to affirm the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and this (*laysa*) indicates only negation first; therefore it is not a verb. If it is said: your statement is refuted by his saying, *nafā Zaydan wa a'damahu* (he negated Zayd and annihilated him). We reply: your saying *nafā Zaydan* is derived from negation (*nafy*), so your saying *nafā* indicates the occurrence of the meaning of negation, and the verbal form confirms its verbal noun. Therefore the question does not arise.

As for those who hold that *laysa* is a verb, they have strained themselves in answering the first argument, saying that *laysa* may come to negate the past, as in their saying: *jā'anī al-qawmu laysa Zaydan* (the people came to me, not Zayd).

As for the second, it is refuted by their saying: *akhadha yaf'alu kadhā* (he began to do such-and-such).

As for the third, it is refuted by all the other defective verbs (*al-af'āl al-nāqiṣah*).

As for the fourth, resemblance in some respects does not require identity.

As for the fifth, that prohibition arose only because *mā* is for the present and *laysa* is for the past, so they cannot be combined.

As for the sixth, although a change in pattern is contrary to the basic principle, it must be resorted to out of necessity for the working of what we have mentioned as evidence.

As for the seventh: *al-laysiyyah* is a noun, so why do you say that *laysa* is a noun? As for his saying, *min ḥaythu ays wa laysa*, why do you say that the object of the preposition must be a noun? As for the book, it is prohibited from this by the evidence.

As for the eighth: *laysa* is derived from *al-laysiyyah*, so it indicates the establishment of the meaning of *al-laysiyyah*.

This is what can be said on this issue, although these answers differ.

**Third issue:** Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, read ﴿*laysa al-birra*﴾ with a fatḥah on the rāʾ (accusative), and the rest read it with a ḍammah (nominative). Al-Wāḥidī said: both readings are good, because the subject of *laysa* and its predicate are equal in definiteness, so each of them is equally a noun and the other a predicate.

The argument of the one who reads *al-birru* in the nominative is that the subject of *laysa* resembles the agent (*fā'il*), and its predicate resembles the object (*maf'ūl*), and the agent is better placed right after the verb than the object. As for the one who reads *al-birra* in the accusative, he holds that some grammarians said: *anna* with its clause is more appropriate to be the subject of *laysa*, because it resembles the pronoun in that it cannot be described, just as the pronoun cannot be described. So here a pronoun and a noun have come together, and when two come together, the better one to be the subject is the pronoun, since it is more specific than the noun. On this basis, the following is read in the revelation: ﴿So the outcome of both of them was that they were in the Fire﴾ (al-Ḥashr 59:17), and ﴿The answer of his people was only that they said﴾ (al-A'rāf 7:82), and ﴿Their argument was only that they said﴾ (al-Jāthiyah 45:25).

The preferred reading is the nominative *al-birru*, because it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ūd that he read: *laysa al-birru bi-an* (it is not righteousness that...), and the *bā'* enters upon the predicate of *laysa*.

**Fourth issue:** *Al-birr* is a comprehensive term for acts of obedience and good deeds that bring one closer to Allah, exalted is He. From this is *birr al-wālidayn* (kindness to parents). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾ and ﴿Indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire﴾ (al-Infiṭār 82:13–14), so He made *birr* the opposite of wickedness (*fujūr*). And He said: ﴿Cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾ (al-Mā'idah 5:2), so He made *birr* the opposite of sin (*ithm*). This shows that it is a general term for everything for which a person is rewarded. Its root is expansion, and from it comes *al-barr* (land), which is the opposite of the sea, because of its expansiveness.

**Fifth issue:** Al-Qaffāl said: Several views have been stated concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, and what we hold is that it refers to the foolish ones who attacked the Muslims and said: "What turned them away from their qiblah which they were upon?" even though the Jews used to face the west and the Christians used to face the east. So Allah, exalted is He, said: the quality of righteousness is not achieved merely by facing east or west; rather, righteousness is not attained except through a combination of matters:

The first of them: belief in Allah. The People of the Book fell short in this. As for the Jews, it is because of their saying in anthropomorphism (*tajsīm*), and their saying that ʿUzayr is the son of Allah. As for the Christians, their saying is that the Messiah is the son of Allah. Also, the Jews described Allah, exalted is He, as stingy, as Allah related about them in His saying: ﴿They said, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich"﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:181).

[Page 33]

The second: belief in the Last Day. The Jews fell short in this belief when they said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:111), and they said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾. The Christians denied bodily resurrection (*al-maʿād al-jismānī*). All of this is denial of the Last Day.

The third: belief in the angels. The Jews fell short in this when they displayed enmity toward Jibrīl, peace be upon him.

The fourth: belief in the Books of Allah. The Jews and Christians both fell short in this, because despite the presence of evidence that the Qur'an is the Book of Allah, they rejected it and did not accept it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while it is forbidden for you to expel them. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:85).

The fifth: belief in the prophets. The Jews fell short in this when they killed the prophets, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they kill the prophets without right﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:61), and when they criticized the prophethood of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

The sixth: giving wealth in accordance with the command of Allah, glorified is He. The Jews fell short in this, because they cast doubts to seek small amounts of wealth, as He said: ﴿And they sold it for a small price﴾.

The seventh: establishing the prayers and the zakāt. The Jews used to prevent people from them.

The eighth: fulfilling the covenant. The Jews broke the covenant, when He said: ﴿Fulfill My covenant, and I will fulfill your covenant﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:40).

Here there is a question: He, exalted is He, negated that turning toward the qiblah is righteousness, and then ruled that righteousness is a combination of matters, the first of which is prayer, and in it there must be facing the qiblah, which leads to contradiction. Because of this question, the exegetes differed in several views:

The first view: His saying ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ is a negation of the perfection of righteousness, not a negation of its essence. It is as if He said: "Righteousness is not all of this." Righteousness is a name for the combination of praiseworthy qualities, and facing the qiblah is one of them, so it is not the completion of righteousness.

The second view: this is a negation of the very essence of it being righteousness, because their facing east and west was an error at the time of the negation, when Allah, exalted is He, abrogated that. Rather, that was sin and wickedness, because it was acting upon an abrogated ruling which Allah had prohibited, and whatever is like that is not counted as righteousness.

[Page 34]

Third: facing the qiblah does not count as righteousness unless it is accompanied by knowledge of God, and it counts as righteousness only when it is performed together with faith and the other conditions. Likewise, prostration is not among the acts of righteousness unless it is performed together with faith in God and His Messenger. If it is performed without this condition, it is not among the acts of righteousness. It is narrated that when the qiblah was changed, there was much debate over its abrogation (naskh), and it seemed as though nothing was regarded as obedience to God except facing the qiblah. So God revealed this verse, as if He had said: What is this intense dispute over the matter of the qiblah while turning away from all the pillars of the religion?

* * *

Sixth issue: His saying, ﴿But righteousness is [the righteousness of] one who believes in God﴾. There is an omission in it, and regarding how it should be understood there are several views.

The first: "But righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in God." The noun governed (al-mudaf) has been omitted, which is common in speech, as in His saying, ﴿and the calf was made to sink into their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93], meaning the love of the calf. People also say: "Generosity is Hatim, poetry is Zuhayr, and bravery is ʿAntarah." This is the view preferred by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Qutrub. Abu ʿAli said: A similar verse is His saying, ﴿Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims [equal to] one who believes in God?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19], and then He said, ﴿[equal to] one who believes﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19]. Its meaning is: Have you made the people of providing water for the pilgrims like one who believes? Or: Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims like the faith of one who believes? So that the comparison occurs between two verbal nouns (masdars), or between two agents, since a comparison does not occur between a verbal noun and an agent.

The second: Abu ʿUbaydah said: "Al-birr" here means "bi" (with/by), as in His saying, ﴿and the final outcome is for piety﴾ [Taha: 132], meaning for the pious. From the same usage is His saying, ﴿If your water should sink into the earth﴾ [al-Mulk: 30], meaning sunken. And al-Khansa' said:

*"Indeed, it is only coming and going,"*

meaning coming and going at the same time.

The third: Its meaning is: "But the one who possesses righteousness," and so it is omitted, as in their saying, ﴿they are [of] degrees with God﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 163], meaning they are people of degrees. This is from al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: The implied sense is: "But righteousness is attained through faith and such-and-such." This is from al-Mufaddal.

Know that the first view is closer to the intended meaning of the speech, so its meaning is: But the righteousness which is the whole of righteousness, the one that leads to great reward, is the righteousness of one who believes in God. It is reported from al-Mubarrad: "Had I been among those who recite the Qur'an in its (particular) recitation, I would have recited, ‘wa lākinna al-barra’ with a fatha on the ba'." Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir recited "wa lākin" with light (mukhaffafah) and "al-birru" with a damma, while the rest recited "lākinna" with shadda and "al-birra" with a fatha.

* * *

Seventh issue: Know that God, Exalted, has stipulated several matters for the actual realization of the essence of righteousness:

The first: Faith in five matters:

The first of them: Faith in God. Knowledge of God is not attained except through knowledge of His particular essence, and knowledge of what is necessary, permissible and impossible for Him. And these matters are not known except through knowledge of the proof that indicates them. This includes knowledge of the createdness (huduth) of the world, and knowledge of the principles on which the createdness of the world is based. It also includes, within knowledge of what is necessary for Him of attributes, knowledge of His existence, eternity and everlastingness, His being all-knowing of all things known, all-powerful over all possible things, living, willing, all-hearing, all-seeing, and speaking. It includes, within knowledge of what is impossible for Him, knowledge that He is exalted above being in a substrate, being a locus, being spatially confined, and being an accident. It includes, within knowledge of what is permissible regarding Him, His power to create, to bring into existence, and to send the messengers.

The second: Faith in the Last Day. This faith is derived from the first, because as long as we do not know that He is all-knowing of all things known and do not know His power over all possible things, we cannot know the soundness of resurrection and gathering.

The third: Faith in the angels.

The fourth: Faith in the books.

The fifth: Faith in the messengers. Here there are questions:

The first question: We have no way to know the existence of the angels, nor to know the truthfulness of the books, except through the truthfulness of the messengers. So if the word of the messengers is like the foundation for knowing the angels and the books, why did He mention the angels and the books before the messengers?

The answer: Although the matter is as you have stated in our minds and thoughts, the order of existence is the reverse of that. For the angel exists first, then through his conveying the revelation the books are sent down, and then that book reaches the messenger. So what is observed in this verse is the order of external existence, not the order of mental consideration.

The second question: Why were these five matters singled out for faith?

The answer: Because everything that we must affirm enters under them. Under faith in God enters knowing Him in His oneness (tawhid), justice, and wisdom. Under the Last Day enters knowledge of what is required of the rulings on reward, punishment and the return, along with everything connected to that. Under the angels enters what relates to their performance of the mission to the Prophet ﷺ so that he may convey it to us, and other matters that must be known about the state of the angels. Under the books enters the Qur'an and all that God sent down to His prophets. Under the prophets enters faith in their prophethood and the soundness of their laws. Thus it is established that nothing remains that must be believed in except that it enters under this verse.

Another formulation: For the responsible person (mukallaf) there is a beginning, a middle and an end. Knowledge of the beginning and the end is the primary aim, and this is what is meant by faith in God and the Last Day. As for knowing the benefits of the middle, it is not complete except through prophethood, and prophethood is not complete except through three things: the angels who bring the revelation, the revelation itself which is the Book, and the one to whom the revelation is sent, which is the messenger.

The third question: Why was this faith placed before deeds of the limbs, namely giving wealth, prayer and zakat?

The answer: To draw attention to the fact that deeds of the heart are more noble before God than deeds of the limbs.

* * *

The second of the matters that are stipulated for the realization of the reality of righteousness is His saying, ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn﴾. There are issues here:

The first issue: They differed regarding the referent of the pronoun in His saying, ﴿in spite of love for it﴾, and they mentioned several views:

The first, which is the view of the majority: It refers to the wealth. The meaning is: giving wealth out of love for wealth. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud said: That is, that you give it while you are healthy and stingy, hoping for wealth and fearing poverty, and you do not delay until, when it reaches the throat (al-hulqum), you say: "To so-and-so such-and-such, and to so-and-so such-and-such." This interpretation indicates that charity while in good health is better than charity at the approach of death. Reason also indicates this from several aspects:

One: At the time of health there arises the assumption of need for wealth, whereas at the assumption of the approach of death there arises the assumption of having no need for wealth. Giving something when one needs it is a stronger indication of obedience than giving it when one is free of need, as He said: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 92].

Two: Giving while in health is a stronger indication that one is certain of the promise and the threat than giving during illness and at the point of death.

Three: Giving while in health is more difficult, so it carries greater reward, by analogy with what the poor person gives from the effort of one who has little, whose reward exceeds what the rich person gives.

Four: Whoever has wealth on the verge of loss and gives it to someone, knowing that if he did not give it, it would be lost, such a gift is not equal to what is given when one is not afraid of the wealth's loss and then gives it willingly and eagerly. So it is likewise here.

Five: It is supported by His saying, ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾, and His saying, ﴿and they give food in spite of love for it﴾ [al-Insan: 8], that is, in spite of love for the food. It is reported from Abu al-Darda' that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The likeness of one who gives charity at the time of death is the likeness of one who gives a gift after he has become full."

The second view: The pronoun refers to the giving, as if it were said: He gives and loves giving, out of desire for God's reward.

The third view: The pronoun refers back to the name of God, Exalted, meaning they give wealth out of love for God, that is, out of seeking His pleasure.

The second issue: They differed about what is meant by this giving. Some people said it is zakat. This is weak, because He, Exalted, joined zakat to it with His saying, ﴿and established prayer and gave zakat﴾. It is necessary that the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined be different. So it is established that what is meant by it is other than zakat. Then it is either among the voluntary acts or among the obligatory ones. It is not permissible that it be among the voluntary acts, because He said at the end of the verse, ﴿Those are the ones who are truthful, and those are the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾, making righteousness (taqwa) dependent upon it. Had it been recommended, He would not have made righteousness dependent upon it. So it is established that this giving, although it is other than zakat, is among the obligatory duties. Then there are two views about it:

The first view: It is an expression for meeting essential needs, such as feeding the one in distress. What indicates the establishment of this obligation is both the textual evidence and rational argument.

As for the textual evidence, there is His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "One who sleeps satisfied while his neighbor beside him is hungry does not believe in God and the Last Day." It is reported from Fatimah bint Qays that there is a right in wealth besides zakat, and then she recited, ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it﴾. It is related from al-Sha'bi that he was asked about one who has wealth and pays his zakat, whether there is anything upon him besides that. He said: Yes, he joins the kin, gives to the beggar, and then he recited this verse.

As for rational argument, there is no disagreement that when need reaches the level of necessity, people are obliged to give the person the amount that removes the necessity, even if zakat is not obligatory upon them. And if they refuse to give, it is permissible to take it from them by force. This indicates that this giving is obligatory.

Those who objected to this view relied on what is reported from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, that he said: Zakat has abrogated every right.

The answer is in several aspects:

First: It is countered by what is reported that he, peace be upon him, said: "There are rights in wealth besides zakat." And the word of the Messenger takes precedence over the word of ʿAli.

Second: The community has agreed that when a person in distress is present, it is obligatory to give him what averts the harm, even if one has paid zakat in full.

Third: The intended meaning is that zakat abrogated the rights that are prescribed (muqaddar) by measure. As for what is not prescribed by measure, it is not abrogated, as evidenced by the fact that giving charity in cases of necessity is obligatory, and supporting relatives and one's slave is obligatory, and that is not measured. If it is said: Suppose this interpretation is valid, but what is the wisdom in this ordering? We say there are several aspects:

One: He, Exalted, mentioned the more important first and then the next most important. For a poor person who is a relative is more deserving of charity than others, since that combines the bond of kinship with charity. Also, kinship is among the most emphatic reasons for directing wealth to a person, and by it one is entitled to inheritance, and it restricts the owner in bequests, so that he cannot bequeath beyond a third. For this reason, bequests to relatives were obligatory, as He said, ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], although that bequest has become abrogated (mansukhah) except according to some scholars. For these reasons He mentioned the kin first. Then He followed them with orphans, because a poor child who has no father and no earner is cut off from every means in every way. Then He followed them with mention of the needy (masakin), because their need may be severe. Then He mentioned the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil), for his need may become severe when his longing for his family intensifies. Then He mentioned the beggars (al-sa'ilin) and those in bondage (al-riqab), because their need is less than the need of those previously mentioned.

Second, the wisdom in arranging these categories in this order is that a person's awareness of how urgent the need of these groups is grows and diminishes. So God Most High ordered the mention of these categories in this way, because one's knowledge of the urgent need of those who are closest to him is more immediate, then the need of orphans, then the need of the needy (al-masakin), and so on in this sequence.

Third, the near kinsman (dhu al-qurba) is needy and has an additional quality that distinguishes him, because severe need in him distresses him and hurts his heart. Warding off harm from oneself takes precedence over warding off harm from others. For this reason God Most High began with the near kinsman, then the orphans, and placed the needy later, because the distress caused by the helplessness of children in obtaining food and drink is greater than the distress caused by the helplessness of adults in obtaining them. As for the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil), he may be wealthy, and his need may become acute at the moment. The beggar (al-sa'il) may be wealthy while displaying severe need. He placed the slave seeking manumission (al-mukatab) later, because freeing from bondage is not in the place of severe need.

The second opinion: the meaning of "giving wealth" is what is reported from the Prophet ﷺ when he mentioned camels, saying: "Indeed, in them there is a right (haqq)," namely, lending their stallion for breeding and lending their tame (dhaloul) mount. This is far-fetched, because the need for the stallion's services is not something specific to the wayfarer, the beggar, or the slave seeking manumission.

The third opinion: giving wealth to these categories was obligatory, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by zakat (obligatory almsgiving). This also is weak, because God Most High has combined in this verse this giving with zakat.

The second issue: as for the near kinsmen, some people have taken that to refer to those mentioned in the verse on spoils and booty (al-nafl wa al-ghanima). Most exegetes (mufassirun) hold that it refers to the near kinsmen of the givers, and this is the correct view, because they are the most entitled to it. A parallel to this is God Most High's saying: ﴿And let not those of virtue and wealth among you swear not to give to the near kinsmen﴾ [al-Nur: 22].

Know that the near kinsmen are those who are close to him through descent from two parents or from two grandparents. There is no basis for restricting this to those related by a prohibited degree (dhu al-rahim al-muharram), as is reported from some people, because the prohibition of marriage is a legal ruling (hukm shar'i), whereas kinship is a linguistic term established for kinship by lineage, although those who are specifically related vary in closeness and distance.

As for the orphans, some people have taken this to refer to the guardians of orphans. He said: because it is not proper for a giver to hand over wealth to an orphan who cannot discern and does not know the ways of benefiting from it, for if he does so he is mistaken. Rather, if the orphan is an adolescent who knows where his interest lies, and the charity is of the kind that is eaten or worn, and the orphan is not unaware of how to benefit from it, then it is permissible to give it to him. All of this is according to the view of those who say the orphan is one who has no father while still a child. According to our companions (the Shafi'is), this term may apply both to a child and to an adult. The evidence for this is God Most High's saying: ﴿And give the orphans their wealth﴾ [al-Nisa': 2], and it is known that they are not given wealth except when they reach maturity. The Messenger of God ﷺ was called "the orphan of Abu Talib" even after reaching maturity. Accordingly, if the orphan is an adult, the wealth is given to him; otherwise it is given to his guardian (wali).

As for the needy (al-masakin), there is a disagreement that we will mention, God willing, in the chapter of al-Tawba.

What we say here is that the needy are those in need. They are of two types: some refrain from asking, and this is what is meant here; and others ask and are forward about it, and this is what is meant by God's saying: ﴿and the beggars﴾. God Most High distinguished between them in that poverty is apparent on the needy from what shows of his condition, whereas this is not so for the beggar, because by his asking he makes his poverty and need known.

As for the wayfarer, it is reported from Mujahid that he is the traveler, and from Qatada that he is the guest, because he has reached you only through the road (sabil). The first is more apt, because "sabil" is the name for a road, and the traveler is called "son of" it because of his constant attachment to it, just as the water-bird is called "son of the water," and a man who has advanced in years is called "son of the days," and brave warriors are called "sons of war," and people are called "sons of the age." Dhu al-Rumma said:

I came at evening while the Pleiades, as if upon the crown of the head, were a son of water, circling.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and the beggars﴾, it means those who seek. Whoever takes the verse as referring to other than zakat includes in it both the Muslim and the disbeliever. Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, reported that the Prophet, upon him be peace, said: "The beggar has a right, even if he comes on a horse." And God Most High said: ﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 24–25].

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and in the slaves (al-riqab)﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: "al-riqab" is the plural of "raqaba," which is the back part of the base of the neck. Its derivation is from "muraqaba" (watchfulness), because its place in the body is like the place of a watchman overseeing a people. For this meaning it is said: "God freed his raqaba," and it is not said: "God freed his 'unuq (neck)." Because it is called raqaba, as if it watches out for punishment. From this comes the term for a female whose offspring does not survive: "raqub," on account of her watching over the death of her offspring.

The second issue: the meaning of the verse is: and he gives wealth for the freeing of slaves. Al-Qaffal said: People have differed about the "slaves" mentioned in the verse on charities (al-sadaqat). Some said it includes whoever buys a slave and frees him, and whoever is a mukatab, so that one assists him in paying his contract of manumission. These permitted buying slaves from the obligatory zakat. Others said that zakat may only be spent on assisting mukatabs. Whoever interprets this verse as referring to obligatory zakat, then that disagreement remains in it. Whoever takes this verse as referring to other than zakat permits both matters in it with certainty. Some people took the verse to refer to a third meaning, namely ransoming captives.

Know that the complete discussion of the explanation of these categories will come, God willing, in the chapter of al-Tawba, in the explanation of the charities.

* * *

The third matter among the matters that are required for the realization of the reality of righteousness is His saying: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces﴾, and this has already been mentioned.

The fourth matter is God Most High's saying: ﴿and those who fulfill their covenant when they make it﴾, and in this there are two issues.

The first issue: regarding the nominative case of "al-muwfuna" (those who fulfill), there are two opinions.
One: it is coordinated (atf) with the place (mahall) of "man amana" (whoever believes). Its implied sense is: "but righteousness is [for] the believers and those who fulfill," according to al-Farra' and al-Akhfash.
The second: it is nominative by way of praise, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, with the implied sense: "and they are those who fulfill."

The second issue: regarding what is meant by this covenant there are two opinions.
The first: what is meant is what God took from His servants in covenants by their own words, and through the tongues of His messengers to them, to uphold His limits and act in obedience to Him. The servants accepted this insofar as they believed in the prophets and the books. God Most High has informed us about the People of the Book that they broke covenants and pledges, and He commanded them to fulfill them, saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and fulfill My covenant; I will fulfill your covenant﴾ [al-Baqara: 40]. So the meaning of this verse is that righteousness is what has been mentioned of deeds together with fulfilling God's covenant, not like the People of the Book who broke God's pact, did not fulfill His covenants, denied His prophets, killed them, and denied His book. Al-Qadi objected to this opinion and said: God Most High's saying ﴿and those who fulfill their covenant﴾ is explicit in attributing this covenant to them, and then He emphasized that by saying ﴿when they make it﴾, so there is no basis for interpreting it as what its obligation comes from God in the first place.
The answer to this: although He imposed these things on them, they themselves accepted that imposition from their own selves and committed themselves to it, so the attribution of the covenant to them is valid from this aspect.

The second opinion: that this is to be understood as matters that the responsible person commits himself to of his own accord. Know that this covenant is either between the servant and God, or between him and the Messenger of God, or between him and other people. As for the one between him and God, it is what becomes binding on him through vows and oaths. As for the one between him and the Messenger of God, it is what he pledged to the Messenger at the time of allegiance (bay'a), namely to support, aid, strive, befriend whoever the Messenger befriends, and oppose whoever the Messenger opposes. As for the one between him and other people, it may be obligatory, such as what is binding on him in exchange contracts regarding delivery and receipt, and likewise the conditions he commits to in salam (advance sale) and rahn (pledge). It may also be recommended, such as fulfilling promises in spending wealth and sincerity in support. God Most High's saying ﴿and those who fulfill their covenant when they make it﴾ encompasses all these categories, so there is no sense in restricting the verse to some of these categories and not others. This which we have said is what the exegetes (mufassirun) expressed when they said: they are those who, when they promise, fulfill; when they swear or vow, they keep it; when they speak, they tell the truth; and when they are entrusted, they discharge the trust. Some people took it to refer to God Most High's saying: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God: 'If He gives us of His bounty...'﴾ [al-Tawba: 75], and so on.

* * *

The fifth of the matters required for the realization of the reality of righteousness: God Most High's saying ﴿and the patient in misfortune and hardship and in time of violence﴾, and in this there are issues.

The first issue: regarding the accusative case of "al-sabirin" (the patient), there are opinions.
The first: al-Kisa'i said: it is coordinated with ﴿dhawi al-qurba﴾ (near kinsmen), as if He said: "and gave wealth out of love for it to the near kinsmen and the patient." The grammarians said: the sense of the verse becomes thus: "But righteousness is [for] whoever believes in God and gives wealth out of love to the near kinsmen and the patient." According to this, His saying "al-sabirin" is governed by "man" (whoever). The phrase "al-muwfuna" (those who fulfill) comes before "al-sabirin," so it would be coordinated with "man," and in that case you would have coordinated with the relative pronoun before completing its relative clause something, and this is not permissible, because the relative pronoun together with its relative clause is like a single noun, and it is impossible for a noun to be described, emphasized, or coordinated with except after it is complete and finished with all its parts. As for if you make His saying "al-muwfuna" nominative by way of praise, you already know that this interruption is not permissible, and indeed this is more objectionable, because praise is a sentence, so if interruption with a single word is not permissible, then with a sentence it is even less permissible.
If it is said: Is not interruption between the subject and the predicate permitted with a sentence, as when someone says: "Indeed Zayd, understand what I am saying, is a learned man," and as in God Most High's saying: ﴿Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], and then He said: "those" (ula'ika), so He interrupted between the subject and the predicate with His saying "indeed We do not waste"?
We say: the relative pronoun with its relative clause is like one thing, so the connection between them is stronger than the connection between the subject and the predicate, so the permissibility of interruption between subject and predicate does not necessitate its permissibility between the relative pronoun and its relative clause.

The second: the saying of al-Farra': it is accusative by way of praise, even though it is an attribute of "man." He nominated "al-muwfuna" and put "al-sabirin" in the accusative because of the length of the speech by way of praise. The Arabs use the accusative for praise and for blame when the speech is lengthy through coordination in describing a single thing. Al-Farra' recited:

To the sturdy king and the son of the hero, and the lion of the battalion in the throng.

And they said regarding the one who recited ﴿the wood-carrying woman﴾ [al-Masad: 3], and regarding the one who recited with the accusative case on ﴿wood-carrying﴾, that it is in the accusative as a form of censure (dhamm). Abu Ali al-Farisi said: When many descriptive attributes are mentioned in the context of praise or blame, the best course is to vary their grammatical inflection (i'rab), and not to make them all follow the noun they describe. This is because this position is one of the places of elaboration in description and of thoroughness in speech. When the inflection of the attributes is varied, the intended meaning becomes more complete, because when the inflection differs, speech becomes like various kinds of discourse and forms of expression. When the inflection is uniform, it becomes a single aspect and one unified sentence.

Then the Kufans and the Basrans disagreed over whether praise and blame have become causes for the difference in vowel-marking (harakah). Al-Farra' said: The origin of praise and blame lies in the words of the listener. This is because when a man informs another and says to him, "Zayd has stood up," the listener may then praise Zayd and say, "By Allah, you have mentioned the witty one; you have mentioned the intelligent one," meaning, "By Allah, he is the witty one, he is the intelligent one." So the speaker wishes to praise with the same praise that the listener gave him, and the inflection followed that pattern. Al-Khalil said: Praise and blame are put in the accusative with the meaning of "I mean" (a'nī), i.e., "I mean the witty one." Al-Farra' rejected this for two reasons:

The first: "a'nī" is only used as an explanation of an unknown noun, whereas praise comes after a known one.

The second: if what al-Khalil said were correct, it would be correct to say, "Zayd has stood up, your brother," with the meaning "I mean your brother," and this is something the Arabs never said at all.

Know that some people recited (wal-mūfīna) and (wal-ṣābirīna), while others recited (wal-mūfūna) and (wal-ṣābirūna).

[p. 40]

As for His saying ﴿in misfortune﴾ (al-ba's', fī al-ba'sā'), Ibn Abbas said: It means poverty, and it is a noun derived from bu's (hardship). ﴿and adversity﴾ (al-ḍarrā'): he said: It means illness. Both are nouns in the pattern fa'lā' and have no comparative form (af'al), because they are not adjectives. ﴿and at the time of violence﴾ (ḥīn al-ba's): Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: It means fighting in the way of Allah and jihad. The meaning of al-ba's in language is severity, as one says, "There is no ba's upon you in this," meaning there is no severity. ﴿a severe punishment﴾ [al-A'raf: 165], meaning severe. Then war is called ba's because of the severity in it, and punishment is called ba's because of its severity. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 84], ﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾ [al-Anbiya': 12], ﴿Who will then help us against the might of Allah?﴾ [Ghafir: 29].

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the ones who are truthful﴾, meaning: the people possessing these attributes are the ones who were truthful in their faith. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned at the end of this verse a question, which is that he said: These waws connecting the attributes in this verse indicate collection. Among the conditions of righteousness and the completeness of the requirement for the righteous is that these attributes be gathered in him. Whoever possesses only one of them does not merit the description of righteousness. Therefore a person should not suppose that one who fulfils his covenant is among those who embody righteousness, and likewise one who is patient in misfortune. Rather, one is not established in righteousness except when these qualities are combined. For this reason some said: This description is specific to the prophets, peace be upon them, because others do not combine all of these attributes. Others said: This is general to all believers. And my success is only through Allah; upon Him I rely.

﴿O you who believe, retaliation has been prescribed for you concerning the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother in any way, then pursuit should be made in a reasonable manner, and payment should be made to him in a good way. That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 178 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retaliation (qisas) concerning the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother [in any part], then [the pardoned one should be] followed with fairness and [the payment] made to him with good conduct. That is a alleviation from your Lord and a mercy. So whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾

Before beginning the exegesis, it is necessary to mention the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), and concerning it there are three aspects.

The first: the occasion of its revelation was the abolition of rulings that had been in force before the mission of Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is because the Jews used to prescribe only killing, the Christians used to prescribe only pardon, and as for the Arabs, at times they prescribed killing and at other times they prescribed blood-money (diyah), but they would exceed the limits in each of these two rulings. As for killing, when a killing occurred between two tribes, one of which was nobler than the other, the nobles would say: "We will certainly kill for the slave among us the free man among them, for the woman among us the man among them, and for the man among us two men among them." They would make their injuries double the injuries of their adversaries, and perhaps they would exceed even that. It is related that one of them killed a man of the nobles, so the relatives of the killer gathered at the house of the father of the victim and said: "What do you want?" He said: "One of three things." They said: "And what are they?" He said: "Either you bring my son back to life, or you fill my house with the stars of the sky, or you hand over to me all your people so that I may kill them, and then I would not consider that I had taken a substitute."

Page 41

As for the injustice in the matter of blood-money, it is that they would perhaps make the blood-money of the noble many times the blood-money of the base man. So when God the Exalted sent Muhammad (ﷺ), He made the observance of justice obligatory, equalized His servants in the ruling of retaliation, and revealed this verse.

The second narration on this meaning, the saying of al-Suddi, is that Qurayzah and al-Nadir, despite their adherence to the Book, followed the practice of the Arabs in transgression.

The third narration: that it was revealed concerning the event of the killing of Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him.

The fourth narration: what Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari transmitted from some people, and related from Ali ibn Abi Talib and from al-Hasan al-Basri, that the purpose of this verse is to explain that retaliation occurs between two free persons, two slaves, and two males or two females, and that this alone suffices. As for when the killer is free and the victim a slave, or the killer a slave and the victim free, then along with retaliation there is necessarily a mutual compensation (taraju'). As for a free person who kills a slave, the retaliation is his qawad: if the masters of the slave wish to kill the free man, they may kill him on condition that they drop the price of the slave from the blood-money of the free man, and return to the heirs of the free man the remainder of his blood-money. If a slave kills a free man, then retaliation is due against him; if the heirs of the free man wish, they may kill the slave and drop the value of the slave from the blood-money of the free man, and then pay to the heirs of the free man the remainder of his blood-money; and if they wish, they may take the full blood-money and leave off killing the slave. If a man kills a woman, then retaliation is due against him; if the heirs of the woman wish, they may kill him and pay half the blood-money. If a woman kills a man, then retaliation is due against her; if the heirs of the man wish, they may kill her and take half the blood-money, and if they wish, they may be given the full blood-money and leave it. They said: God the Exalted revealed this verse to explain that the sufficiency of retaliation is prescribed between two free persons, two slaves, two females and two males; but when the kinds differ, sufficiency with retaliation is not prescribed in it.

* * *

Having known the occasion of revelation, let us return to the exegesis.

As for His saying, ﴿prescribed for you﴾, its meaning is: "obligated upon you." This word implies obligation in two respects:

The first: His saying ﴿prescribed﴾ conveys obligation in the usage of the Shariah. He, exalted, said: ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183], and He said: ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves behind wealth, is the bequest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and bequest was obligatory. From this also comes "al-salawat al-maktubat," meaning the obligatory prayers. And he (peace be upon him) said: "Three things have been prescribed for me and not prescribed for you."

The second: the phrase ﴿upon you﴾ indicates obligation, as in His saying: ﴿And for Allah upon the people is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. As for retaliation (qisas), it means doing to a person the like of what he did, from your saying: "Fulan followed the trace of Fulan" (iqtassa athara) when he did the like of his deed. He, exalted, said: ﴿So they returned, retracing their footsteps (qasasan)﴾ [al-Kahf: 64], and He said: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up (qussiyhi)"﴾ [al-Qasas: 11], meaning: follow his trace. A narrative is called qissah because through recounting it one equates with what is recounted; and retaliation is called qisas because it reproduces the like of people's accounts. And scissors are called miqass because of the equality of their two sides.

As for His saying ﴿concerning the slain﴾, meaning: because of the killing of the slain; for the word "fi" (in) may be used in the sense of causation, as in his (peace be upon him) saying: "For a believing soul, one hundred camels." Once you know this, the sense of the verse becomes: "O you who have believed, retaliation has become obligatory upon you because of the killing of the slain." So the apparent meaning of the verse indicates the obligation of retaliation upon all believers because of the killing of all the slain. However, they have unanimously agreed that anyone other than the killer is excluded from this generality. As for the killer, the specification (takhsis) has also entered upon him in many cases: when a father kills his child, a master kills his slave, when a Muslim kills a combatant (harbi) or one with a covenant (mu'ahad), and when a Muslim kills a Muslim by mistake. Yet the general ruling that has been specified still remains a proof concerning what lies beyond these.

Page 42

If it is said: your statement that this verse entails the obligation of retaliation involves two problems:

The first: if retaliation were obligatory, it would be obligatory either upon the killer, or upon the guardian of the blood (wali al-dam), or upon a third party, and all three divisions are invalid. We say that it is not obligatory upon the killer, because the killer is not obliged to kill himself; rather it is forbidden for him to do so. And we say that it is not obligatory upon the guardian of the blood, because the guardian of the blood is free to act or to refrain; indeed he is recommended to refrain, by His saying: ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. The third is also invalid, because he would be a stranger to that killing, and a stranger to a thing has no connection to it.

The second problem: once we have established that retaliation is an expression for equalization, the meaning of the verse becomes the obligation of equalization, and on this assumption the verse does not indicate the obligation of killing at all; rather, at most, the verse indicates the obligation of observing equalization in a killing that is legitimate, and on this assumption the verse's indication that killing is legitimate because of killing drops away.

The answer to the first question is in two respects:

The first: the intent is the obligation of carrying out retaliation upon the ruler (imam) or whoever occupies his position, for whenever the conditions for the obligation of qawad are met, it is not lawful for the ruler to abandon qawad, since he is among the believers. The sense is: "O rulers, prescribed for you is the execution of retaliation if the guardian of the blood wishes its execution."

The second: that it is an address to the killers, and the sense is: "O killers, prescribed for you is the surrender of the self when the guardian demands retaliation." This is because the killer does not have the option here to resist or to deny; rather, for the adulterer and the thief there is the option of fleeing from the hadd penalty, and they may also remain veiled by the veil of Allah and not confess. The difference is that this is a right of the human being.

As for the answer to the second question: the apparent meaning of the verse requires the obligation of equalization in killing, and equalization in killing is a quality of the killing, and the obligation of a quality requires the obligation of the essence; so the verse is thereby indicative of the obligation of killing from this aspect. Several issues branch from what we have mentioned:

The first issue: Abu Hanifah held that the requirement for intentional killing is qisas, while al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, held that the requirement for intentional killing is either qisas or blood-money (diyah). Abu Hanifah argued by this verse, but the mode of inference from it is extremely weak; for whether the one addressed by this address is the ruler or the guardian of the blood, it is by consensus conditioned upon the guardian of the blood intending killing specifically. According to us, when the matter is so, qisas becomes determined; the dispute is only whether the guardian of the blood is able to turn to blood-money, and there is no indication in the verse that if he wants blood-money he is not permitted that.

Page 43

The second issue: they differed concerning the manner of the equality which this verse indicates. Al-Shafi'i said: the manner of the first killing is observed; if the first killed him by cutting off a hand, the killer's hand is cut off; if he dies from it on that occasion, well and good, otherwise his neck is struck off. Likewise, if the first was burned with fire, the second is burned; if he dies on that occasion, well and good, otherwise his neck is struck off. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the intent of "equality" is the taking of the self by the most merciful possible means, and on this basis there is no retaliation except by the sword, by striking off the neck. The argument of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that God the Exalted required equality between the two acts, and that requires that equality be achieved in all possible respects; and several things indicate this:
