First: it is permissible to say, "Equality has been prescribed in killings except in the manner of killing," and an exception removes from the statement what would otherwise have entered; so this entering indicates that the manner of killing is included under the text.

Second: if we did not judge by this verse's indication of equality in all matters, the verse would become unclear (mujmal); and if we judged by its generality, the verse would be beneficial, but since it has become specified in some instances, specification is easier than ambiguity.

Third: if the verse did not give more than the requirement of equality in some matter, then any two things are equal in some respect, and in that case nothing at all would be derived from this verse; this third point is close to the second. Thus it is established that this verse indicates the existence of equality in every respect. Then this text is reinforced by the other texts that require the obligation of equivalence, such as His saying: ﴿And the recompense of an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194], ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40]. Then these widely transmitted texts are reinforced by the well-known report from the Messenger (peace be upon him), his saying: "Whoever burns, we burn him; whoever drowns, we drown him." It is also related that a Jew crushed the head of a girl with stones and killed her, so the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that the head of the Jew be crushed with stones. When this is established, the indication of the verse together with the other verses and these hadiths reaches a strong degree in favour of the position of al-Shafi'i.

Abu Hanifah argued by his (peace be upon him) saying: "There is no qawad except by the sword," and by his saying: "None punishes with fire except the Lord of fire."

The answer is that when the hadiths conflict, the indication of the verses remains free of counter-arguments. And Allah knows best.

**[Page 43 continuation]** The third issue: they agreed that if this killer does not repent and persists in refusing repentance, then retaliation (*qisas*, legal retribution in kind) is prescribed against him as a punishment from God Most High. As for the one who repents, they agreed that it cannot be a punishment, because the evidence shows that repentance is accepted. God Most High says: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons misdeeds﴾ [al-Shura: 25]. When repentance is accepted, it is impossible for the penitent to remain deserving of punishment. Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Repentance erases sin (*al-hawbah*)." Thus it is established that the prescription of retaliation against the penitent cannot be a punishment.

Then at this point they differed. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: God does what He wills, and there is no objection to Him in anything. The Mu'tazilah said: it was prescribed to be a kindness (*lutf*, a means of drawing the servant closer to good) toward him. Then they asked themselves: there is no obligation (*taklif*) after killing, so how can this killing be a kindness toward him? They answered that this killing has a benefit for the victim's guardian in terms of satisfaction (*tashaffi*); a benefit for all the morally responsible persons (*mukallafun*) in that it deters the rest of people from killing; and a benefit for the killer himself, in that whenever he knows he must be killed, this becomes a motive for him toward good and toward abandoning persistence and defiance.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾, there are two views:

The first view: this verse requires that retaliation is prescribed only between two free persons, between two slaves, and between two females.

They argued for this with several points:

The first: the definite article (*al-*) in His saying ﴿the free﴾ denotes generality. So His saying ﴿the free for the free﴾ means that every free person is to be killed for a free person. Therefore, if killing a free person for a slave were prescribed, that free person would be killed not for a free person, and this contradicts the requirement that every free person be killed for a free person.

The second: the *ba'* (the preposition "for") is one of the prepositions, so it must be attached to a verb. The sense becomes: "The free is killed for the free." The subject cannot be more general than the predicate; rather it must either be equal to it or more specific than it. In either case, this requires that every free person be killed for a free person, and this contradicts the killing of a free person for a slave.

The third: God made it obligatory at the beginning of the verse to observe equivalence, as in His saying: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you concerning the slain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]. When He then mentioned after it His saying ﴿the free for the free and the slave for the slave﴾, this shows that observing equality in freedom and slavery is required. For His saying ﴿the free for the free and the slave for the slave﴾ comes as an explanation of His saying ﴿retaliation is prescribed for you concerning the slain﴾. Making the free person liable to retaliation for killing a slave neglects the observance of equality in this respect, so it must not be prescribed.

If the opponent argues with His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45], our reply is that the preponderance lies with us for two reasons:

The first: His saying ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ is a law for those before us, whereas the verse we rely on is a law for us. There is no doubt that our law is stronger in its indication than the law of those before us.

The second: the verse we rely on contains rulings on lives in detail and with specification, and there is no doubt that the specific takes precedence over the general.

Then the proponents of this view said: the apparent meaning of this verse requires that a slave is killed only for a slave, and a female is killed only for a female. However, we departed from this apparent meaning because of the consensus (*ijma'*) and because of the meaning derived from the context (*nasaq*) of this verse. That meaning is not present in killing a free person for a slave, so it must remain at the apparent sense of the wording here. As for the consensus, it is evident. As for the derived meaning: since a slave is killed for a slave, then it is all the more fitting that he be killed for a free person, who is above him. But a free person, when killed for a free person, does not necessarily have to be killed for a slave, who is below him. The same applies to killing a female for a male. As for killing a male for a female, there is nothing to support it except consensus. And God knows best.

The second view: His saying Exalted ﴿the free for the free﴾ does not indicate restriction (*hasr*) at all. Rather it indicates the prescription of retaliation between those mentioned, without there being any indication in it regarding the other categories. They argued for this with two points:

The first: His saying ﴿and the female for the female﴾ requires the retaliation of a free woman for an enslaved woman. If His saying ﴿the free for the free and the slave for the slave﴾ prevented this, there would be a contradiction.

The second: His saying Exalted ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you concerning the slain﴾ is a complete sentence, independent in itself. His saying ﴿the free for the free﴾ is a specification of some particular instances of that sentence, mentioned explicitly. When a complete independent sentence has been mentioned first, specifying some particular instances by mention does not prevent the ruling from applying to the other instances. Rather, that specification may be for benefits other than negating the ruling for the other cases. Then they differed about that benefit, and they mentioned two views concerning it:

The first, which is the view of most scholars, is that this benefit is to clarify the abolition of what the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era) used to do, according to what we have related about the occasion of revelation of this verse: they used to kill a free person from the tribe of the killer in retaliation for a slave of the other tribe. So the purpose of the specification is to deter them from that.

Know that the proponents of the first view may say: God's saying ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you concerning the slain﴾ prevents the killing of a free person for a slave, because retaliation (*qisas*) means equivalence, and killing a free person for a slave does not achieve observance of equivalence, since the free person exceeds the slave in nobility, in eligibility for judgeship, leadership and testimony. So it must not be prescribed. At most, this means that the wording of this text was set aside in the case of killing a scholar for an ignorant person and a noble for a lowly person; but it remains, in cases outside the area of consensus, at the original rule. Then, even if we grant that His saying ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you concerning the slain﴾ requires the killing of a free person for a slave, we have shown that His saying ﴿the free for the free and the slave for the slave﴾ prevents the killing of a free person for a slave. This is specific, and what precedes it is general, and the specific takes precedence over the general, especially when the specific is connected to the general in wording, for then it functions as an exception. And there is no doubt about the obligation to give it precedence over the general.

The second point regarding the benefit of the specification: what Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari transmitted from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Hasan al-Basri, that these cases are the ones in which retaliation alone suffices. As for the other cases, namely where retaliation is between a free person and a slave, or between a male and a female, then in those cases retaliation alone does not suffice, and there must be a compensation (*tarajju'*, a return of something in exchange). We have explained this view in the discussion of the occasion of revelation of this verse. However, many verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) claimed that this transmission was not authentically established from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. It is also weak on examination, because it has been established that a group is killed for one person without any compensation (*tarajju'*); likewise a male is killed for a female without any compensation. Furthermore, *qawad* (retaliation in kind) is the ultimate extent of what is due in homicide, so it is not permissible that anything else be obligatory along with it.

* * *

As for His saying Exalted: ﴿But if he is pardoned by his brother in anything, then pursuit should be made in a reasonable manner, and payment should be made to him in a good way﴾. Know that those who said that the obligation for deliberate killing is one of two things, either retaliation or blood money (*diyah*), relied on this verse and said: the verse indicates that in this matter there is one who pardons and one who is pardoned. Here there are only the guardian of the blood and the killer. So the pardoning party is one of them, and it cannot be the killer, because the apparent meaning of pardon (*'afw*) is the waiving of a right, and that is possible only from the guardian who holds the right to retaliation. So the sense of the verse becomes: "If the guardian of the blood pardons something that pertains to the killer, then the killer should follow up that pardon in a reasonable manner." And His saying ﴿anything﴾ is indefinite, so it must be understood in reference to what was mentioned earlier, namely the obligation of retaliation, to remove the ambiguity. So the sense of the verse becomes: "If the pardon of retaliation is granted to the killer, then the killer should follow the pardoning party in a reasonable manner, and pay him money in a good way." By consensus, no payment other than blood money is obligatory, so this obligation must be blood money. This shows that the obligation for deliberate killing is retaliation or wealth. If it were not so, wealth would not be obligatory upon pardoning retaliation. Among what supports this argument is His saying Exalted: ﴿That is a lightening and a mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning that He established for you the choice in taking blood money. And retaliation is a mercy from God upon you, because the ruling for the Jews was the compulsory retaliation, and the ruling for the Christians was the compulsory pardon. So He lightened this for this community and prescribed for them a choice between retaliation and blood money. This is a lightening and a mercy from God toward this community, because the guardian of the blood may find blood money preferable to retaliation if he is in need of wealth, and retaliation may be preferable if he desires satisfaction and to ward off the evil of the killer from himself. So He made the choice for him in what he prefers, as a mercy from God toward him.

If it is said: we do not concede that the pardoning party is the guardian of the blood, and the word "pardon" means the waiving of a right, and this is fitting only for the guardian of the blood.

We reply: we do not concede that pardon means the waiving of a right. Rather, what is meant by His saying ﴿if he is pardoned by his brother in anything﴾ is: "if something is made easy for him by his brother." It is said: "This wealth came to me as an easy gain (*'afwan safwan*)," meaning easily. And it is said: "Take what is easy (*ma 'afa*)," meaning what is easy. God Most High says: ﴿Take what comes easily﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]. So the sense of the verse becomes: "Whoever is among the guardians of the blood, and something of wealth is made easy for him by his brother, who is the killer, then the guardian of the blood should follow up that wealth with the killer in demanding it, and the killer should pay that wealth to the guardian of the blood in a good manner, without delay or evasion." The meaning of the verse on this reading is therefore: God Most High urged the guardians, when they are called to reconciliation over the blood in exchange for the full blood money or part of it, to accept it and to waive retaliation.

Even if we grant that the pardoning party is the guardian of the blood, why not say: the intended meaning is that retaliation is shared between two partners, so one of them pardons, and then the other's share becomes wealth. God Most High then commands the silent partner to follow the killer in a reasonable manner, and commands the killer to pay him in a good way.

Even if we grant that the pardoning party is the guardian of the blood, whether or not he has a partner, why not say: this is conditional on the killer's consent? God Most High did not mention the killer's consent because it is necessarily present; for the apparent state of every person is that he would give up the whole world to avert killing from himself, since if he is killed, neither self nor wealth remains for him. As for giving up wealth, it preserves life. Since this consent is present in the vast majority of cases, He therefore omitted mentioning it, although it is legally relevant in itself.

The answer: interpreting the word "pardon" in this verse as the waiving of the right to retaliation is preferable to interpreting it as the killer sending wealth to the guardian of the blood. Its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: the real meaning of pardon is the waiving of a right, so it should not be a real meaning in anything else, in order to avoid shared meaning (*al-ishtirak*). Interpreting the wording of this verse as the waiving of the right is preferable to interpreting it as you have stated. For since His saying ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you concerning the slain﴾ precedes, it is preferable to interpret His saying ﴿if he is pardoned by his brother in anything﴾ as the waiving of the right of retaliation, because the word ﴿anything﴾ is an indefinite term, and interpreting this indefinite term as the previously mentioned matter is preferable.

**Third part of al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 178**

The second point: if the meaning of "pardon" were what you have mentioned, then His saying ﴿then pursuing it in good manner, and payment to him with good conduct﴾ would be pointless, because once the property reaches him easily and smoothly, there is no need for him to be pursued, and no need for that giver to be commanded to pay that property with good conduct.

As for the second objection, it is answered in two ways.

The first: that statement is only consistent with assuming a specific case, namely where the right of retaliation (qisas) is shared between two persons, one of them pardons, and the other remains silent. But the verse indicates the legitimacy of this ruling in general, so restricting the unrestricted wording to that specific case, which is what the objection requires, goes against the apparent meaning.

The second: the pronoun in His saying ﴿and payment to him with good conduct﴾ refers back to an earlier mention, and the earlier mention is the one who pardons. Therefore the payment of this property is due to the one who pardons. According to your view, its payment is due to someone other than the one who pardons, so your view is invalid.

As for the third objection: the condition of consent (al-rida) is either something that cannot cease, or something that can cease. If it cannot cease, then the entitlement to take the blood money (diyah) must be established for the heir of the blood (wali al-dam) absolutely. If it can cease, then restricting the wording by this condition, which the verse does not indicate as binding, contradicts the apparent meaning and is impermissible.

* * *

Now that this discussion has been summarized, we say: the verse still contains linguistic questions, which we will mention in the form of questions and answers.

**First question:** What is the grammatical structure of His saying ﴿Whoever is pardoned (ʿufiya) by his brother for something﴾?

**Answer:** Its implied sense is: "Whoever has from his brother something of the pardon." It is like the saying: "The journey was taken with Zayd, part of the journey," and "a portion of the journey."

**Second question:** The verb ʿafa (to pardon) is normally followed by ʿan (from), not by the preposition lam (for). So what is the justification for His saying ﴿ʿufiya lahu﴾ ("it was pardoned for him")?

**Answer:** It takes ʿan with the offender and with the offense. One says ʿafawtu ʿan fulanin and ʿan dhanbihi ("I pardoned so-and-so and his offense"). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿May Allah pardon you (ʿafa Allahu ʿanka)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. When it takes the offense as its object, one says: ʿafawtu ʿan fulanin ʿamma jana ("I pardoned so-and-so for what he committed"), just as you say: ʿafawtu lahu ʿan dhanbihi ("I pardoned him for his offense") and tajawaztu lahu ʿanhu ("I overlooked it for him"). This verse is of this type. It is as if it had been said: "Whoever is pardoned, for his crime, by his brother," so the mention of the crime is dispensed with.

* * *

**Third question:** Why was it said "something" (shayʾ) of the pardon?

The answer has two aspects.

The first: this only poses a difficulty if the right is nothing but retaliation (qawad) alone. In that case it is said: retaliation does not divide, so the word ﴿something﴾ serves no purpose. But when the whole of his right is either retaliation or property, the whole of his right is divisible, because he may pardon the retaliation but not the property, and he may pardon all of it. Since this is the case, it is permissible to say ﴿Whoever is pardoned by his brother for something﴾.

The second answer: indefinite wording (tankir) of "something" conveys a great benefit, because it might be supposed that pardon does not remove retaliation unless it is a pardon of the whole. Therefore Allah the Exalted clarified that pardoning part of it is like pardoning all of it in terminating retaliation, and that the pardon of some of the heirs of the blood is like the pardon of all of them regarding their share. Had He defined "something," this meaning would not have been understood from it. When He made it indefinite, this meaning became understood from it. For this reason, the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever is pardoned by his brother for something﴾.

* * *

**Fourth question:** In what sense did Allah affirm the attribute of brotherhood?

**Answer:** It has been said that Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) relied on this verse to establish that the wrongdoer (al-fasiq) remains a believer, in three ways.

The first: He the Exalted called him a believer at the time when retaliation became due against him. Retaliation becomes due against him only when he has committed deliberate, aggressive killing (al-qatl al-ʿamd al-ʿudwan), and that is, by consensus, one of the major sins (al-kaba'ir). This indicates that the perpetrator of a major sin is a believer.

The second: He the Exalted established brotherhood between the killer and the heir of the blood. There is no doubt that this brotherhood is due to religion, as He said: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10]. So, if faith did not remain alongside wrongdoing, the brotherhood that results from faith would not remain.

The third: He the Exalted urged pardoning the killer, and urging pardon is only fitting for a believer.

The Mu'tazilah answered the first aspect by saying: if we say that those addressed by His saying ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ are the rulers (al-a'immah), then the objection falls away. If we say they are the killers themselves, then the answer has two aspects.

The first: the killer, before committing the killing, was a believer, so Allah the Exalted called him a believer under this interpretation.

The second: the killer may repent, and at that point he is a believer. Then He the Exalted included the one who has not repented under the same wording by way of predominance (taghlib).

As for the second aspect, the mention of brotherhood, they answered it in several ways.

The first: the verse was revealed before anyone had killed anyone, and there is no doubt that believers are brothers before committing killing.

The second: the apparent meaning is that the wrongdoer repents, and on this assumption the heir of the slain is his brother.

The third: it is possible that His making him a brother refers to kinship in lineage, as in His saying ﴿And to ʿAd their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf: 65].

The fourth: there arose between the heir of the blood and the killer a connection and closeness, and this degree is sufficient for the use of the name "brother," just as you say to a man: "Tell your companion such-and-such," when there is any slight connection between them.

The fifth: he mentioned it with the word "brother" in order to incline one of them toward the other by reminding him of what is established between them of shared humanity (al-jinsiyyah) in profession and belief.

The answer to these is: all these aspects require restricting brotherhood to a particular time rather than another, and to a particular attribute rather than another, whereas Allah the Exalted established brotherhood absolutely.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Then pursuing it in good manner, and payment to him with good conduct﴾, there are several points.

**First point:** His saying ﴿Then pursuing it in good manner﴾ is in the nominative case (raf'), because it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), and its implied sense is: "So its ruling is pursuit." Or it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and its implied sense is: "So upon him is pursuit in good manner."

**Second point:** It has been said: upon the one who pardons is the pursuit in good manner, and upon the one pardoned is the payment with good conduct. This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Mujahid. It was also said: both are upon the one pardoned, for he follows the pardon of the one who pardons with what is reasonable, and renders that reasonable thing to him with good conduct.

**Third point:** Pursuing in good manner means not pressing the demand, but proceeding in it according to customary practice. If the debtor is in hardship, then there is a respite (nazrah). If he is able to pay the actual property, the creditor should not demand more than the amount of the right. If he is able to pay something other than the property that is due, then there is a postponement until he sells and exchanges. And the pursuit should not prevent him from giving priority to the more important obligations. As for payment with good conduct, it means that he should not claim inability when he is able, should not delay it when he has it, should not advance what is not obligatory upon him, and should pay that property with cheerfulness, openness, and kind speech.

As for His saying ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy﴾, there are several views.

The first: the intended meaning of ﴿That﴾ is the ruling of the legislation of retaliation and blood money, which is an alleviation for you, because pardon and the taking of blood money were forbidden for the People of the Torah (Ahl al-Tawrat), who were absolutely obliged to retaliation. Retaliation and blood money were forbidden for the People of the Gospel (Ahl al-Injil), who were obliged to pardon. This community, however, was given the choice between retaliation, blood money, and pardon, as an expansion and facilitation for them. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: His saying ﴿That﴾ refers back to His saying ﴿then pursuing it in good manner and payment to him with good conduct﴾.

As for His saying ﴿Whoever transgresses after that﴾, the word "transgress" (iʿtada) means going beyond the limit to what is greater than it. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: the intended meaning is that he should not kill after pardon and blood money. This is because the people of the Jahiliyyah, when they pardoned and took blood money, and then afterward got hold of the killer, would kill him. So Allah forbade that. It has also been said that the intended meaning is: that he kill someone other than his killer, or kill more than his killer, or demand more than what was due to him of blood money, or exceed the limit after it was explained to him how retaliation is to be carried out. It must be understood to cover all of these, because of the generality of the wording. ﴿Then for him is a painful punishment (ʿadhab alim)﴾, and regarding this there are two views.

The first, which is the well-known one, is that it is a kind of punishment of severe pain in the Hereafter.

The second: it is reported from Qatadah that the painful punishment is that he be killed without fail, and that he not be pardoned nor have blood money accepted from him, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will not pardon anyone who kills after taking the blood money." This is also reported from al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. This view is weak, for several reasons.

The first: what is understood from "painful punishment" when used absolutely is the punishment of the Hereafter.

The second: we have explained that retaliation is sometimes a punishment and sometimes a test, as in the case of the one who repents. So the name "punishment" cannot be applied to it absolutely, except in one respect and not another.

The third: the killer of one who has been pardoned cannot be singled out in such a way that the heir of the blood is not enabled to pardon him, because that is the right of the heir of the blood, so he has the authority to waive it, by analogy with his entitlement to waive all other rights. And Allah knows best.

[p. 47] [p. 48]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 179:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you, O people of understanding, that you may be God-fearing.﴾

Know that when, in the preceding verse, He, glory be to Him, made retaliation (qisas) obligatory, and retaliation is a matter of inflicting pain, a question arises: how does inflicting pain on a weak servant befit the perfection of His mercy? To remove this question, He mentioned immediately after it the wisdom behind prescribing retaliation, saying: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you.﴾ There are several issues concerning the verse.

The first issue: there are several aspects to the verse.

The first: the meaning of this verse is not that retaliation itself is life, because retaliation is the removal of life, and the removal of a thing cannot be the thing itself. Rather, the meaning is that the prescribing of retaliation leads to life with respect to the one who wishes to become a killer, with respect to the one who is intended to be killed, and with respect to others as well. As for the one who wishes to become a killer, it is because if he knows that were he to kill he would be killed, he abandons killing, so he does not kill and remains alive. As for the one who is intended to be killed, it is because whoever intends to kill him, if he fears retaliation, abandons killing him, so he remains unkilled. As for others, it is because in the prescribing of retaliation there is the survival of the one who has resolved to kill, or who may resolve to do so, and in the survival of these two there is the survival of those who side with them, since strife grows greatly because of killing and leads to war, which ends in the killing of a world of people. And in supposing retaliation to be prescribed is the removal of all that, and in its removal is the life of all.

The second aspect: concerning the interpretation of the verse, its meaning is that retaliation itself is a cause of life. This is because when the shedder of blood is subjected to retaliation, those who were intending to kill are deterred and do not kill; thus retaliation itself is a cause of life in this respect. Know that the aspect we have mentioned is not restricted to retaliation for killing; it includes retaliation for limbs and for wounds to the head. This is because if a man knows that if he wounds his enemy he will be subjected to retaliation, that deters him from advancing, so it becomes a cause of the survival of both. For the wounded person is not safe from death, and likewise the one who inflicts the wound if retaliation is taken from him. Moreover, a wound to the head or a wound for which there is no retaliation falls under the verse, because the one who wounds is not safe from his wound leading to the departure of the soul, in which case retaliation becomes obligatory; so the fear of retaliation is present concerning the soul.

The third aspect: the meaning of retaliation is the imposition of equality, so the meaning is that in the imposition of equality there is life for someone other than the killer, because a non-killer is not killed, unlike what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fourth aspect: Abu al-Jawza' recited ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾, meaning: in what He has related to you of the ruling on killing and retaliation. And it has been said: "al-qisas" is the Qur'an, meaning: for you in the Qur'an there is life for the hearts, like His saying: ﴿a spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52] and ﴿that he who lives may live by clear proof﴾ [al-Anfal: 42]. And God knows best.

* * *

The second issue: the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamaʾ al-bayan) agreed that this verse, in its brevity combined with the comprehensiveness of its meanings in the language, reaches the highest degrees. This is because the Arabs expressed this meaning in many expressions, such as their saying: "The killing of some is life for all," and the saying of others: "Increase killing so that killing may decrease," and the best of the expressions transmitted from them in this domain is their saying: "Killing is more effective in preventing killing." Then the wording of the Qur'an is more eloquent than this, and the difference is shown in several respects:

The first: His saying ﴿And in retaliation there is life﴾ is more concise than all of them, because the phrase "for you" (wa-lakum) does not enter into this domain, since in all of them such an estimation is necessary. For the saying of one who says "the killing of some is life for all" necessarily requires a similar estimation, and likewise in their saying "killing is more effective in preventing killing." So when you reflect, you will know that His saying ﴿fi al-qisas hayah﴾ is more concise than their saying "killing is more effective in preventing killing."

The second: their saying "killing is more effective in preventing killing" apparently implies that a thing is the cause of the negation of itself, which is impossible, whereas His saying ﴿in retaliation there is life﴾ is not like that, because what is mentioned is a type of killing, namely retaliation. Moreover, He did not make it a cause of life in general, since He mentioned "life" indefinitely, but made it a cause of a kind of life.

The third: their saying "killing is more effective in preventing killing" contains a repetition of the word "killing," whereas His saying ﴿in retaliation there is life﴾ is not like that.

The fourth: the saying of one who says "killing is more effective in preventing killing" only conveys deterrence from killing, whereas His saying ﴿in retaliation there is life﴾ conveys deterrence from killing and from wounding and other things, so it is more comprehensive in benefits.

The fifth: the negation of killing is sought secondarily, insofar as it entails the attainment of life, whereas the verse indicates the attainment of life, which is the primary intended aim, so this is more fitting.

The sixth: killing unjustly is also killing, yet it does not negate killing; rather it is a cause of an increase in killing. What negates the occurrence of killing is only the specific killing, namely retaliation. So the apparent meaning of their saying is invalid, whereas the verse is sound both apparently and in its implication. Thus the difference between the verse and the speech of the Arabs becomes evident.

* * *

The third issue: the Mu'tazilah cited this verse as proof against the view of the People of the Sunnah, who say: if the one who is killed had not been killed, he would necessarily have died. They said: if the one who is killed must die were he not killed, then grant that the prescribing of retaliation deters the one who wishes to become a killer from undertaking killing, yet that person will die whether or not this killer kills him, and so the prescribing of retaliation would not lead to the attainment of life.

If it is said: we only say this regarding one who was killed, that had he not been killed he would have died, not regarding one who was intended to be killed but was not killed; so what you have said does not follow. We reply: is it not the case that what is said regarding one who was killed, had he not been killed, is: what would his condition be? So when you say: he would have died, you have judged that for every time in which his killing could validly occur, his death would be like his killing; and this confirms what we have imposed on you, because it must be, according to your known view, that had he not killed him, either a preventer prevented him from killing, or he feared his killing, that he would have died; and in that is the validity of what we have imposed on you. This is all the words of the Qadi.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O people of understanding﴾, what is meant is the intelligent who know the consequences and recognize the causes of fear. When they wish to proceed to kill their enemies, and know that they will be called to account by retaliation, that becomes a deterrent for them; for the intelligent person does not wish to destroy another by destroying himself. So when he fears that, his fear becomes a cause of restraint and abstention. However, this fear arises only from the reflection we have mentioned, in one who has an intellect guiding him to this reflection; whoever has no intellect guiding him to this reflection does not attain this fear. For this reason, God, glory be to Him, specified this address to the people of understanding.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you may be God-fearing﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: the word "la'alla" (perhaps/that) expresses hope, and that is valid only regarding one who does not know all things. Its answer is what has preceded in His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord who created you and those before you, that you may be God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21].

The second issue: al-Jubba'i said: this indicates that He, exalted is He, intended God-fearing from all of them, whether it was known that they would be God-fearing or would not be, unlike the view of the Mujbirah (determinists). Its answer has also preceded in that verse.

The third issue: concerning the interpretation of the verse there are two views:

One of them: the view of al-Hasan and al-Asamm, that what is meant by "that you may be God-fearing" is refraining from killing itself out of fear of retaliation.

The second: that what is meant is God-fearing in every respect, and there is no specification of God-fearing in the verse, so taking it to be general is more fitting. It is known that God, exalted is He, only prescribed for the servants the burdensome matters, including retaliation and other things, in order that they may guard against the Fire by avoiding sins and refraining from them. When this is the primary intended aim, the speech must be understood accordingly.

The fifth ruling

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 180 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches any one of you, if he leaves behind wealth, that he make a bequest to parents and relatives in a fair manner; this is a duty upon the God-conscious.﴾

Know that His saying, ﴿It is prescribed for you﴾, indicates obligation, as we have explained. As for His saying, ﴿when death approaches any one of you﴾, what is meant by it is not the direct witnessing of death, because at that time a person is incapable of making a bequest. Then they (the scholars) gave two interpretations of it
صفحة ٥١
:

The first, which is the choice of the majority, is that what is meant is the appearance of the signs of death, namely a dangerous illness. This is apparent in the language: it is said of someone who is feared to die that death has approached him, just as it is said of someone who has come close to a town that he has arrived.

The second is the statement of al-Asamm: what is meant is that bequest was made obligatory upon you in a state of health, such that you would say: "When death approaches us, do such and such."

Al-Qadi said: The first view is preferable for two reasons:

One of them: that the testator, even if he does not mention death in his bequest, is permitted to do so.

The second: that what we have mentioned is the apparent meaning, and when that is possible, it is not permissible to interpret the speech otherwise.

As for His saying, ﴿if he leaves behind wealth﴾, there is no disagreement that here it means property, and "good" (khayr) is used to mean property in many places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And whatever good you spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272], ﴿And indeed he is intense in his love of wealth﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8], ﴿of good, [I am] in need﴾ [al-Qasas: 24]. Having known this, we say: here there are two views:

One of them: that there is no difference between little and much, and this is the view of al-Zuhri. So the bequest is obligatory in every case. He argued for this with two points:

The first: that God Most High made the bequest obligatory where one leaves behind "good," and a small amount of property is "good," as indicated by the Qur'an and by reason. As for the Qur'an, it is His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ and ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7-8], and also His saying: ﴿of good that You send down to me, [I am] in need﴾ [al-Qasas: 24]. As for reason, good is that from which one benefits, and a small amount of property is likewise, so it is good.

The second argument: that God Most High took into account the rules of inheritance concerning what remains of property, whether little or much, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, whether it is little or much - an obligatory share﴾ [al-Nisa': 7]. So it is necessary that the matter be the same concerning the bequest.

The second view: that the word "good" in this verse is specific to great wealth. They argued for it with several points:

The first: that one who leaves a dirham is not said to have left "good," just as one says: "So-and-so possesses wealth," meaning the magnification of his wealth and its exceeding the limit of those in need. Although the term "wealth" in its literal sense may fall on everything a person owns, whether little or much; and likewise when it is said: "So-and-so is in blessing, and in comfort of life," what is meant is the abundance of blessing, even though no one is free of God's blessing. This is a well-known type of metaphor, namely the negation of a name from a thing because of its deficiency, as has been reported in the saying: "There is no prayer for the neighbor of the mosque except in the mosque," and His saying: "He is not a believer who spends the night satisfied while his neighbor is hungry," and the like.

The third argument: if the bequest were obligatory on everything one leaves, whether little or much, then the restriction by His saying ﴿if he leaves behind good﴾ would not be a meaningful statement, because everyone must leave something behind, whether little or much. As for one who dies naked, with not even a piece of bread remaining with him, nor an amount of cloth with which he covers his nakedness, that is extremely rare. So when it is established that what is meant here by "good" is great wealth, is that wealth determined by a specific fixed quantity or not? On this there are two views:

The first view: that it is determined by a specific quantity. Then those who hold this view differed. It is reported from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he entered upon a freedman of theirs at the time of his death, who had seven hundred dirhams, and he said: "Shall I not make a bequest?" He said: "No, Allah Most High only said: ﴿if he leaves behind good﴾, and you do not have much wealth." And from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that a man said: "I wish to make a bequest," and she said: "How much is your wealth?" He said: "Three thousand." She said: "How many dependents do you have?" He said: "Four." She said: "Allah said ﴿if he leaves behind good﴾, and this is a small amount; leave it for your dependents, which is better." And from Ibn 'Abbas: If he leaves seven hundred dirhams, he should not make a bequest; but if it reaches eight hundred dirhams, he may make a bequest. And from Qatadah: one thousand dirhams. And from al-Nakha'i: one thousand five hundred dirhams.
صفحة ٥٢

The second view: that it is not determined by a specific quantity, but rather it differs according to the condition of men, because with a certain amount of wealth a person is described as wealthy, while with that same amount another is not described as wealthy due to the abundance of dependents and the abundance of expenses. Nor is there any impossibility in obligation being attached to an amount determined by reasoned judgment (ijtihad). So no one may argue that the absence of clarification regarding the amount of wealth is evidence that this bequest was never obligatory, by saying: "If it were obligatory, the obligatory amount of wealth in it would have been specified."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿the bequest﴾, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: He said ﴿prescribed﴾ because He intended by "the bequest" the act of bequeathing, and for this reason He used the pronoun in His saying: ﴿Then whoever alters it after having heard it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 181]. Also, the (feminine) form was mentioned for separation between the verb and "the bequest," since when the speech is long, the separation between the feminine noun and the verb serves as a substitute for the feminine marker (ta' al-ta'nith). The Arabs say: "A woman came to the judge" (hadara al-qadiya imra'ah), using the masculine form, because the judge is between the verb and the woman.

* * *

The second issue: the raising of "the bequest" (al-wasiyyah) is in two ways:

One of them: that it is in the form of the passive voice (ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu).

The second: that it is the subject (mubtada'), and "for the parents" is the predicate (khabar), and the whole sentence is in a position of raising as the object of kutiba (the verb "was prescribed"), just as you say: "It was said: 'Abd Allah is standing." So your saying "'Abd Allah is standing" is a compound sentence of subject and predicate, and the sentence is in a position of raising as the object of qila (it was said).

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿to the parents and the relatives﴾, there are several issues in it:

The first issue: Know that when Allah Most High explained that the bequest is obligatory, He then explained after that that it is obligatory for whom He said: "to the parents and the relatives." In this there are two views:

The first: al-Asamm said: They used to make bequests to distant people seeking pride and honor, and leave relatives in poverty and need. So Allah Most High made the bequest to these obligatory at the beginning of Islam, to prevent the people from what they had become accustomed to, and this is clear.

The second: others said: since the obligation of this bequest was before the verses of inheritance, Allah gave the testator choice regarding his property and obliged him not to exceed, in disposing of his property after his death, beyond the parents and relatives, so that it would reach them by his conveyance and choice. For this reason, when the verses of inheritance were revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has given every rightful person his right, so there is no bequest to an heir." So he explained that what preceded was reaching them by the bequest of the testator; but now Allah Most High has determined for every rightful person his right, and the gift of Allah is more deserving than the gift of the testator. And if that is the case, then there is absolutely no bequest to an heir. On this view, the bequest was previously obligatory for the parents and relatives.

* * *

The second issue: They differed regarding His saying: ﴿and the relatives﴾ — who are they? Some said: they are the children. On this view, Allah Most High commanded the bequest to the parents and the children, and this is the statement of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, from his father.

The second view, which is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, is that what is meant by the relatives is other than the parents.

The third view: they are all kinds of kinship, those who inherit from among them and those who do not inherit. This is the meaning of the statement of those who held that the bequest to relatives was obligatory, and then considered it abrogated.

The fourth view: they are those among a man's relatives who do not inherit from him; as for those who inherit, they are excluded from the wording.

As for His saying: ﴿in a fair manner﴾ (bi'l-ma'ruf), it may mean the amount that is bequeathed, and it may mean the distinguishing of those among the relatives who are bequeathed to from those who are not, since both aspects fall under "fair." It is as if Allah Most High commanded him in the bequest to follow a beautiful path: if he favors some over others, then it is fair; if he equalizes, then it is like-for-like; and if he deprives some, then it is like-for-like too. For if he deprived the poor and bequeathed to the rich, that would not be fair; and if he equalized between the parents, despite the greatness of their right, and the paternal cousins, it would not be fair; and if he bequeathed to the children of a distant grandfather while the brothers were present, what he gives would not be fair. So Allah Most High obliged him in the bequest to a beautiful manner, free of the taints of causing ill feeling, and this is among the matters known by custom. So no one may say: "If the bequest were obligatory, Allah would not have stipulated this condition, which cannot be precisely determined," for the reason we have explained.

* * *

As for His saying Most High: ﴿a duty upon the God-conscious﴾, it is an addition for emphasizing its obligation. His saying "haqqan" (a duty) is an emphatic verbal noun, i.e., "that was due as a duty." If it is said: the apparent meaning of this statement requires restricting this obligation to the God-conscious rather than others.

The answer is in two ways:

The first: that what is meant by His saying ﴿a duty upon the God-conscious﴾ is that it is binding upon one who prefers God-consciousness, seeks it, and makes it his path and creed, so everyone is included in it.

The second: this verse requires the obligation of this meaning upon the God-conscious, and consensus has established that obligations and duties are general with respect to the God-conscious and others, so by this means everyone falls under this obligation. This is the totality of what relates to the interpretation of this verse.

Know that people differed regarding this bequest: some said it was obligatory, and some said it was recommended (nadb). Those who held it obligatory argued by His saying "it is prescribed" (kutiba) and His saying "for you" ('alaykum), and both expressions indicate obligation. Then He emphasized that obligation by His saying ﴿a duty upon the God-conscious﴾. These then differed: some said this verse has become abrogated, and some said it has not become abrogated. This is the view chosen by Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, and the statement of his position is given in several ways:

One: this verse does not contradict the verses of inheritance, and its meaning is: "It is prescribed for you what Allah has commanded of bequeathing to the parents and relatives," from His saying "Allah instructs you concerning your children" [al-Nisa': 11]; or: "it is prescribed upon the one near death that he bequeath to the parents and relatives by completing what Allah has assigned to them, and not diminishing their shares."

Two: there is no contradiction between the heirs' entitlement to inheritance and the bequest being in the form of inheritance as a gift from Allah Most High, since a bequest is a gift from one at the point of death. Thus the heir is given both the bequest and the inheritance, by the ruling of the two verses.

Third: If we suppose that there is a conflict, it would be possible to make the verse of inheritance a specifier (takhsis) of this verse. This is because this verse makes a bequest obligatory for the close relatives. Then the verse of inheritance removes the relative who is an heir, and the relative who is not an heir remains included under this verse. This is because among parents, some inherit and some do not, due to differences in religion, slavery, and killing. Among the relatives, some are never excluded from their share by these blocking causes. Some are excluded in one situation and not in another, depending on whether there is someone with a stronger claim to inheritance in the case. Some are excluded in every situation if they are kin (dhawu rahim). So whoever among these is an heir, a bequest to him is not permitted. Whoever is not an heir, a bequest to him is permitted for the sake of maintaining kinship (silat al-rahim). God Most High has confirmed this with His saying: ﴿And fear God, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ [al-Nisa': 1], and with His saying: ﴿Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct and giving to close relatives﴾ [al-Nahl: 90]. This is the explanation of the position of Abu Muslim on this matter.

* * *

As for those who say that the verse has been abrogated (mansukh), then the following discussions follow from this position:

The first discussion: They differ over what evidence proves that it has been abrogated, and they have mentioned several views.

One of them: It was abrogated only by God Most High giving the heirs each his right. This is far-fetched, because it is not impossible that, alongside a share of right through inheritance, another share becomes obligatory through a bequest. What this would require is specification (takhsis), not abrogation (naskh). For someone might say: it must be that it was abrogated concerning one who leaves only his parents, since then the whole estate becomes their right through inheritance, and nothing remains for the bequest. However, this is specification, not abrogation.

Second: It was abrogated by his saying, peace be upon him: "Verily, there is no bequest to an heir." This is closer to the truth, but the problem with it is that this is a single report (khabar wahid), and it is not permissible to abrogate the Qur'an with it. This objection is answered by saying that although it is a single report, the scholars (a'imma) received it with acceptance, so it has joined the mass-transmitted reports (mutawatir).

One may say: It is claimed that the scholars received it with acceptance in the sense of probable knowledge (zann) or in the sense of certainty (qat'). The first is granted, but that would be a consensus (ijma') among them that it is a single report, and so it is not permissible to abrogate the Qur'an with it. The second is denied, because if they were certain of its authenticity while knowing that it belongs to the category of single reports, then they would have agreed upon an error, and that is not permitted.

Third: It was abrogated by consensus (ijma'). Consensus cannot be the means by which the Qur'an is abrogated, because consensus indicates that the abrogating evidence existed, but they relied on consensus instead of mentioning that evidence.

One may say: Since it is established that among the community there are those who denied that this abrogation occurred, how can it be claimed that a consensus was reached on the occurrence of abrogation?

Fourth: It was abrogated by analogical reasoning (qiyas). The argument is: If this bequest were obligatory, then when this bequest is not made, the rights of these close relatives should not lapse, by analogy with debts that are not established by a bequest. But when no bequest is made for these close relatives, they are not entitled to anything, by the evidence of God Most High's saying in the verse of inheritance: ﴿after any bequest he makes or debt﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. The apparent meaning of the verse requires that if there is no bequest and no debt, then the whole estate is to be given to the heirs. One may say: abrogating the Qur'an by analogy is not permitted. And God knows best.

* * *

The second discussion: Those who say that this verse has been abrogated differ on two positions. Some of them say that it has been abrogated concerning those who inherit and concerning those who do not inherit, and this is the view of most exegetes (mufassirun) and of the respected jurists (fuqaha'). Others say that it is abrogated concerning those who inherit but remains valid concerning those who do not inherit. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan al-Basri, Masruq, Tawus, al-Dahhak, Muslim ibn Yasar, and al-'Ala' ibn Ziyad. al-Dahhak even said: Whoever dies without bequeathing to his relatives has ended his deeds with disobedience. Tawus said: If someone bequeaths to strangers and leaves out his relatives, the bequest is taken from them and returned to the relatives. According to these scholars, this verse remains indicative of the obligation of a bequest to the relative who is not an heir. The proof of these scholars is in two respects:

The first proof: This verse indicates the obligation of a bequest to relatives. Its application has been set aside in the case of the relative who is an heir, either by the verse of inheritance, or by his saying, peace be upon him: "Verily, there is no bequest to an heir," or by consensus that there is no bequest to an heir. Here, however, there is no consensus, since disagreement on it is well known, in the past and in the present. Therefore the verse must remain indicative of the obligation of a bequest to the relative who is not an heir.

The second proof: His saying, peace be upon him: "It is not right for a Muslim man who has property to let two nights pass without his bequest being written and kept with him." We agree that a bequest to non-relatives is not obligatory. Therefore this obligatory bequest must be restricted to relatives, and the Sunnah has become a confirmation of the Qur'an regarding the obligation of this bequest.

As for the majority who say that this verse has been abrogated concerning the relative who is not an heir, the best of their evidence is their reliance on God Most High's saying: ﴿after any bequest he makes or debt﴾, and we have already explained its argument earlier.

* * *

The third discussion: Those who say that this verse has not been abrogated concerning the relative who is not an heir differ on two points:

The first: It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he assigned this bequest to the neediest of the relatives in order of need, while al-Hasan al-Basri said: they and the wealthy are equal.

The second: It is reported from al-Hasan, Khalid ibn Zayd, and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Ya'la that they said concerning one who bequeaths to someone other than his relatives while he has relatives who do not inherit from him: two-thirds of the one-third goes to the relatives, and one-third of the one-third goes to the one to whom the bequest was made. And it is reported from Tawus that if the relatives are in need, the bequest is taken from strangers and returned to the relatives. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 181:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then whoever alters it after he has heard it, the sin is only upon those who alter it. Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the bequest (wasiyyah), its obligation, and the greatness of its matter, He followed it with what serves as a warning concerning altering it.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then whoever alters it﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: Who is this alterer? There are two opinions concerning this.

The first, which is the well-known one, is that he is the executor (wasi), or the witness, or other people. As for the executor, it is that the executor alters the bequest, either in the writing or in the division of the rights. As for the witness, it is that he alters a testimony or conceals it. As for others besides the executor and the witness, it is that they prevent that property from reaching its entitled recipient. All of these are included under His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then whoever alters it﴾.

The second opinion: The one forbidden from altering is the testator. He forbade altering the bequest from the places which Allah, exalted is He, specified for the bequest. This is because we have explained that they, in the Jahiliyyah, used to bequeath to strangers and leave the relatives in hunger and hardship. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded them to bequeath to the nearer relatives, then He rebuked, by His saying: ﴿Then whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾, whoever turned away from this obligation.

* * *

The second issue: The pronoun in His saying: ﴿Then whoever alters it﴾ refers to the bequest, even though the pronoun mentioned is masculine and the bequest (wasiyyah) is feminine. They mentioned several explanations for this:

One of them: The bequest is in the sense of the act of bequeathing (iya') and indicates it, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275], meaning an exhortation. The estimated meaning is: whoever alters what the deceased said, or what he bequeathed, or what he heard from him.

The second: It was said that the pronoun refers to the ruling and the obligation, and the estimated meaning is: whoever alters the matter mentioned previously.

The third: That the pronoun refers to what the deceased bequeathed, and therefore He mentioned it in the masculine, even though the bequest is feminine.

The fourth: That the pronoun returns to the meaning of the bequest, which is a statement or an act.

The fifth: That the feminine gender of the bequest is not real, so it is permissible to refer to it with a masculine pronoun.

As for His saying: ﴿after he has heard it﴾, it indicates that the sin only occurs or becomes great on condition that the alterer knew of it, because there is no meaning to hearing if knowledge of it did not occur. Thus, affirming his hearing is like affirming his knowledge.

As for His saying: ﴿the sin is only upon those who alter it﴾, know that the word (innama) is for restriction (hasr), and the pronoun in His saying (ithmuhu) refers to the alteration. The meaning: the sin of that alteration returns only to the alterer, and the explanation of who the alterer is has already preceded.

Know that the scholars have derived rulings from this verse:

One of them: A child is not punished for the disbelief of his father.

The second: If a person commands the heir to pay his debt, then the heir falls short in it by not paying his debt, the deceased person is not punished because of that heir's negligence, contrary to some ignorant people.

<page 56>

The third: The deceased is not punished for the weeping of others over him. This is because this verse indicates that the sin of alteration returns only to the alterer, for Allah, exalted is He, does not hold anyone accountable for the sin of another. The indication of this verse is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And no soul earns [blame] except against itself, and no bearer bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]; ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self, and whoever does evil, it is against it﴾ [Fussilat: 46]; ﴿It has what it earned, and it bears what it has earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286].

* * *

The third issue: If someone bequeaths to strangers, while among the relatives there is one whose need is pressing, is it permissible for the executor to alter the bequest?

As for one who holds that bequeathing to relatives who do not inherit from the parents and the nearer relatives is obligatory, they differed concerning it. Some of them said: The bequest to the relatives was obligatory upon him, so if he did not do it and diverted the bequest to strangers, that stranger is more entitled to it. Others said: That is annulled and returned to the nearer relatives, and we have already mentioned the detailed position of these people.

As for one who does not make bequeathing to a relative who does not inherit obligatory, then it is either by a third or by more than a third. If it is by a third, it is permissible and it is not permissible to alter it. Then they differed concerning what is recommended. Al-Hasan used to say: What is recommended is less than a third, because he, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "A third, and a third is much." So he urged reduction. Others said: Rather, a third is recommended, because it is his right and the reward in it is greater. Others consider the condition of the deceased, the condition of the heirs, and the amount of the estate, and this is the better view.

As for if the bequest is more than a third, they differed concerning it. Some said: That is not permissible except with the permission of the heirs and seeking their consent. Others said: The words of the heirs have no effect except after death. Then, if he bequeathed more than a third, they differed. Some said: It is permissible if the heir permits it, and it is a gift from the deceased. Others say: Rather, it is like a fresh gift from the heir.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾, its meaning is that He, exalted is He, hears the bequest exactly as it is, and knows it according to its description, so no hidden thing of the alteration that occurs in it is concealed from Him. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 182:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then whoever fears from a testator any deviation (janaf) or sin and makes reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that when Almighty God threatened the one who alters the bequest, He explained that what is meant by that alteration is changing it from the truth to falsehood. As for changing it from falsehood to truth, by way of reform, then he has done well. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Then whoever fears from a testator any deviation or sin and makes reconciliation between them﴾, because reform entails a kind of alteration and change. So God mentioned the distinction between this alteration and that first alteration, by making sin in the first and removing it from the second, after both being alterations and changes, lest it be supposed that their ruling is one in this matter. Here there are several issues.

The first issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, read (muwassin) with shaddah, while the rest read it without shaddah, and both are dialects: wassa and awsa have one meaning.

* * *
The second issue: al-janaf is inclination in affairs, and its root is deviation from straightness. It is said: janifa yajnafu, with kasrah of the nun in the past tense and fathah in the present, janafan, and likewise tajanafa. From it is His saying: ﴿without inclining toward sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. The difference between janaf and ithm is that janaf is error committed without knowing of it, while ithm is deliberate.
Page 57
* * *
The third issue: concerning His saying ﴿whoever fears﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: that what is meant by it is fear and apprehension.

If it is said: fear is only valid regarding something awaited, and the bequest has already occurred, so how can it be connected to fear?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: that what is meant is that this reformer, when he witnesses the testator bequeathing and signs of janaf appear from him, which is inclination away from the path of truth with some kind of ignorance, or with interpretation, or he witnesses from him deliberate action by giving more than what is deserved, or diminishing the rightful share of one who deserves, or turning away from the one who deserves, then upon the appearance of signs of that, and before the bequest is finalized, he begins reform; for reforming a matter when signs of its corruption appear and before its corruption is established is easier. Therefore God connected it to fear rather than to certainty. It is as if the testator, while the executor and the witness are present by way of consultation, says: "I want to bequeath to distant relatives rather than close kin, and to increase so-and-so although he is not entitled to an increase, or to decrease so-and-so although he is entitled to an increase." At that point the listener becomes fearful of wrongdoing and sin, not certain of it. For this reason God said: ﴿whoever fears from a testator deviation﴾, connecting it to fear, which is supposition, and did not connect it to knowledge.

The second aspect of the answer: that if he bequeaths in the manner we have described, it is possible that the testator does not persist in that bequest but rather revokes it, and it is possible that he persists. For the testator, so long as he has not died, has the right to retract the bequest and alter it by increase and decrease. Since this is so, janaf and sin do not become certain, for the permissibility of revoking it prevents it from being definitively established. Therefore He connected it to fear.

The third aspect of the answer: that on the assumption that the bequest becomes settled and the testator dies, it is possible that between the heirs and the beneficiaries a settlement may take place by way of abandoning inclination and error. Since that is awaited, the ruling of janaf and sin is not fixed and established, so it is valid for Him to connect it to fear and the absence of certainty. These aspects may be mentioned regarding the meaning of fear, although the first aspect is the strongest.

The second opinion: concerning the interpretation of His saying ﴿whoever fears﴾, i.e., whoever knows. Fear and apprehension are used in the sense of knowledge, because fear is an expression for a specific state arising from a specific supposition, and between knowledge and supposition there is resemblance in many matters, so it is valid to apply the name of each of them to the other. On this interpretation, the meaning of the verse is that if the deceased errs in his bequest or deliberately acts unjustly in it, there is no blame upon whoever knows of that for changing it and returning it to rectitude after his death. This is the opinion of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Rabiʿ.

The fourth issue: We have mentioned that janaf is error and ithm is deliberate, and it is known that error concerning the rights of others, in that it must be annulled, is equal to deliberate action, so there is no distinction between error and deliberate action in that regard. For this reason Almighty and Majestic God equated the two matters.

* * *
As for His saying ﴿and makes reconciliation between them﴾, there are issues:
The first issue: Who is this reformer? The apparent meaning is that he is the executor, who is indispensable in a bequest, and the witness may also be included. It may also be meant to be whoever takes charge of this after his death, from a ruler, a guardian, or an executor, or one who enjoins good. All of these enter under His saying ﴿whoever fears from a testator﴾ when signs of janaf and sin in the bequest appear to them, or they know of it. There is no basis for restricting this matter, rather the executor and the witness are more entitled to enter under this obligation, because the bequest is established through them, so their connection to it is stronger.

The second issue: One may say: the pronoun in His saying ﴿makes reconciliation between them﴾ must refer to some previously mentioned party, so what is that previously mentioned party?

Its answer: there is no doubt that what is meant is between the people of the bequests, because His saying ﴿from a testator﴾ indicated the one to whom the bequest is made, so it is as if they had been mentioned. Thus it is proper for Him to say ﴿makes reconciliation between them﴾, as if He said: "makes reconciliation between the people of the bequest." Some said: what is meant is "makes reconciliation between the people of the bequest and the inheritance," which is that the testator increases the bequest beyond one third; the reformer then reconciles between the beneficiaries and the heirs in that. This opinion is weak for several reasons:

The first: the word "testator" indicates only the beneficiaries, not the heirs.

The second: janaf and sin do not enter into bequeathing more than one third, because since that is not permissible except with consent, its mention becomes as no mention, and it does not need reconciliation to annul it, since its nullity is evident.

* * *
The third issue: concerning the explanation of how this reconciliation is carried out, and here there are two discussions:
The first discussion: concerning how this reconciliation is carried out before this verse was abrogated. We say: we have explained that this janaf and sin occurred either by increase, by decrease, or by deviation, so its reconciliation is by removing these three matters and returning every right to its rightful owner.

The second discussion: concerning how this reconciliation is carried out after this abrogated verse became so. We say: janaf and sin here occur in several ways:

Among them: that there appears from the sick person what indicates that he intends to prevent the wealth from reaching the heir, either by mentioning an acknowledgment or by binding himself to a contract. In that case he is prevented from it.

Among them: that he bequeaths more than one third.

Among them: that he bequeaths to distant relatives while close kin are in great need.

Among them: that he bequeaths while his wealth is little and his dependents many, and other such aspects.

* * *
As for His saying ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾, there are two issues:
The first issue: One may say: this reformer has performed a great act of obedience in this reconciliation and deserves reward for it, so how is it fitting to say "there is no sin upon him"?

The answer is in several aspects:

The first: when He mentioned the sin of the one who alters at the beginning of the verse, and this too is a kind of alteration, He showed its contrast with the first, and that there is no sin upon him, because he returned the bequest to justice.

The second: since the reformer reduces bequests, and that is difficult for the beneficiary and may give rise to an impression of sin, He removed the doubt and said: ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾.

The third: He explained that by bequeathing and calling witnesses this is not made obligatory, and that whenever he changes it to what is right, even if he opposes the testator's bequest, there is no sin upon him, even if there occurs in it opposition to the testator's bequest and diversion of his wealth from one whom he loved to one whom he disliked; for that may give the impression of ugliness, so God, Mighty and Majestic, explained that this is good by His saying ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾.

The fourth: reconciling among a group requires much speech, and one fears that something unseemly in speech and deed may intrude into it, so God explained that there is no sin upon the reconciler in this kind when his intention in reconciling is beautiful.

The second issue: This verse indicates the permissibility of settlement between disputing parties when the one who wants to settle fears that the dispute will lead to something prohibited in the Shariah.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, there is also a question in it: this statement is fitting only for one who has done something impermissible, whereas this reconciliation is among the acts of obedience, so how does this statement fit it? Its answer has several aspects:

The first: that this is of the nature of alerting the lesser to the greater. It is as if He said: "I am the One who forgives sins, then I show mercy to the sinner. So how much more should I convey My mercy and reward to you, although you have borne many trials in reforming this important matter."

The second: it is possible that what is meant is that this testator who committed janaf and sin, when his bequest is reformed, indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, forgiving him and showing him mercy by His grace.

The third: that the reconciler may, in bringing about reconciliation, need to use words and deeds that it would have been better to avoid. When God knows from him that his aim is nothing but reconciliation, He does not hold him accountable for them, for He is Forgiving and Merciful.

**The Sixth Ruling**

﴿O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may attain taqwa (God-consciousness)﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may attain taqwa﴾.

Know that *al-siyam* (fasting) is a verbal noun from *sama*, like *al-qiyam*. Its original linguistic meaning is abstention from something and leaving it. From this comes the term *sawm* for silence, because it is abstention from speech. God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam: 26]. *Sawm al-nahar* refers to the day when it becomes balanced and the midday heat stands still. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Leave her, and drive away your anxiety about her with a swift she-camel, when the day stands still and grows hot."*

Another poet said:

*"Until, when the day stood still and became balanced..."*

The wind is also said to be *sakitat* (still) when it becomes calm, and a horse is said to be *sa'im* when it stands without grazing. al-Nabigha said:

*"Some horses stand still, and others do not stand still, under the dust, while others chew their bits."*

It is also said: *bakara sa'ima* (a standing camel) when it stands and does not move. The rajiz (poet) said:

*"And the camels, the worst of them is the one that stands still."*

*Masam al-shams* is the place where the sun stands at the middle of the day, and likewise *masam al-najm* (the station of the star). Imru' al-Qays said:

*"As if the Pleiades were hung in their station by cords of flax to a hard boulder."*

This is the meaning of *sawm* in the linguistic sense. In the sacred law (*shari'ah*), it is abstention from the times of dawn until sunset, from things that break the fast, while knowing that one is fasting, together with the accompaniment of intention.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾, there are two issues.

**The first issue:** Regarding this comparison, there are two opinions.

One is that it refers to the basic prescription of fasting. That is, this act of worship was prescribed and obligatory for the prophets and nations from the time of Adam until your time. God did not leave any nation without its obligation upon them. He does not impose it on you alone. The benefit of this statement is that fasting is a difficult act of worship, and a difficult matter becomes easier to bear when it is general.

[Page 60]

The second opinion is that the comparison refers to the time of fasting and its quantity. This is weak, because comparing one thing with another requires that they be equal in some respect. But to say that it requires equality in all respects is not correct. Those who hold this view mentioned several points:

First: God prescribed the fasting of Ramadan for the Jews and the Christians. As for the Jews, they abandoned this month and fasted one day of the year. They claimed it was the day when Pharaoh drowned, but they lied in that too, because that day is the day of 'Ashura according to the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). As for the Christians, they fasted Ramadan, but they encountered intense heat in it, so they moved it to a time that does not change. Then they said at the time of the change: "We will add to it." So they added ten days. Then after some time their king became ill, so he vowed seven days, and they added them. Then after that another king came and said: "What is the matter with these three?" So he completed it to fifty days. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31]. This is narrated from al-Hasan.

Second: They took the precaution for a time, so they fasted a day before the thirty days and a day after them. Then the later generation continued to follow the practice of the generation before it, until they reached fifty days. For this reason, fasting on the day of doubt (*yawm al-shakk*) is disliked. This is narrated from al-Sha'bi.
