Third: The point of comparison is that eating, drinking and intercourse become forbidden after sleep, just as that was forbidden for all the other nations. Those who held this view argued that the community is in consensus that His saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you to go in unto your wives on the night of fasting﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187] indicates the abrogation (*naskh*) of this ruling. So this ruling requires evidence to establish it, and there is no evidence for it except this comparison, His saying: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾. Therefore this comparison must be evidence for the establishment of this meaning.

The proponents of the first view said: We have already explained that comparing one thing with another does not indicate their similarity in every respect. So it does not follow from comparing our fasting with their fasting that their fasting was specific to Ramadan, or that their fasting was fixed at thirty days. Furthermore, this narration is among the things that would repel the Jews and the Christians from accepting Islam if they knew it to be so.

**The second issue:** Regarding the position of *ka-ma* (as), there are three opinions.

The first: al-Zajjaj said: The position of *ka-ma* is in the accusative as an adverbial of manner (*maf'ul mutlaq*), because the meaning is: "It was prescribed for you as a prescription, like that which was prescribed for those before you."

The second: Ibn al-Anbari said: It may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of "fasting," meaning: "Fasting has been prescribed for you, being likened and made similar to that which was prescribed for those before you."

The third: Abu 'Ali said: It is an attribute (*sifah*) of an omitted verbal noun, whose estimate is: "a prescription as that which was prescribed for them." So the verbal noun is omitted, and its adjective is placed in its position. He said: Similar to this in extension and omission is the saying in explicit divorce: "You are one," meaning "You are one who has one pronouncement of divorce." So the qualifier (*mudaf*) and the qualified (*mudaf ilayh*) are omitted, and the attribute of the qualifier is placed in the position of the qualified noun.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿that you may attain taqwa﴾, know that the explanation of *la'alla* (perhaps/so that) regarding God Most High has already been mentioned. As for how this statement fits this context, there are several points:

First: He, glorified is He, showed by this statement that fasting produces taqwa, because it breaks desire and subdues the passions. It restrains from insolence, arrogance and immoral acts, and it makes the pleasures and leadership of this world seem lesser. This is because fasting breaks the desire of the stomach and the private parts. People strive only for these two, as the well-known proverb says: "A man strives for his two enemies, his stomach and his private parts." So whoever fasts much finds these two matters easy and their burden light upon him. This becomes a deterrent for him from committing prohibitions and immoral acts, and it makes the matter of leadership in this world easy for him. This combines the causes of taqwa. So the meaning of the verse is: "I prescribed fasting for you so that you may be among the God-conscious (*muttaqun*) whom I praised in My Book, and I informed you that this Book is guidance for them." Since fasting is particularly distinguished by this quality, it is good for Him to say, when prescribing it: ﴿that you may attain taqwa﴾, indicating by this the obligation of it, because that which prevents the soul from sins must necessarily be obligatory.

[Page 61]

Second: The meaning is: it befits you through fasting that your restraint in taqwa should be strengthened. This is the meaning of *la'alla*.

Third: The meaning is: "so that you may be God-conscious through your fasting and your abstention from desires." For the more desire there is for a thing, the harder it is to refrain from it. The desire for food and for intercourse is stronger than the desire for other things. So when it becomes easy for you to be mindful of God by abstaining from food and intercourse, then being mindful of God by abstaining from other things is easier and lighter.

Fourth: The intention is: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may attain taqwa﴾ means: do not neglect it or fail to maintain it, because of its great ranks and its nobility.

Fifth: "That you may be counted, through this act of worship, among the God-conscious, because fasting is their emblem." And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 184 (part 1 of 4):**

[Page 61]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Fasting for a certain number of days; so whoever among you is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days. And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom: feeding a poor person. And whoever volunteers good, it is better for him. And that you fast is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

Know that in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ayyaman ma'dudat (certain number of days)﴾ there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Concerning the case (i'rab) of *ayyaman* (days), there are several opinions. The first is that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), as if it were said: "Fasting has been prescribed for you on days," and its parallel is your saying: "I intended to go out on Friday."

The second, which is the view of al-Farra' (the grammarian), is that it is the predicate of a passive construction (khabar ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu), like the saying: "Zayd was given wealth."

The third is that it is an explanatory specification (ʿalā al-tafsīr).

The fourth is that it is by an implied verb, meaning: "So fast for days."

**The second issue:** Scholars differed about these days, on two views.

The first view is that they are other than Ramadan. This is the view of Mu'adh, Qatadah and Ata', and it is narrated from Ibn Abbas. Then these scholars differed. It was said: three days of every month, according to Ata'. It was said: three days of every month plus fasting the day of 'Ashura, according to Qatadah. Then they also differed: some said that it was voluntary and then became obligatory, while others said that it was obligatory from the start. These all agreed that it was abrogated (mansukh) by the fasting of Ramadan. Those who held that the intended days are other than the fasting of Ramadan argued with several points:

The first is what has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The fasting of Ramadan has abrogated every fast." This indicates that before Ramadan became obligatory, there was another fast that was obligatory.

The second is that God, Exalted is He, mentioned the ruling for the sick and the traveler in this verse, and then mentioned their ruling again in the verse after this one, which indicates the fasting of Ramadan. So if this fast were the fasting of Ramadan, that would be pure repetition without benefit, and that is not permissible.

The third is that His saying, Exalted is He, in this place: ﴿And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom﴾, indicates that fasting is obligatory on a basis of choice, meaning: if one wishes he fasts, and if one wishes he gives the ransom. As for the fasting of Ramadan, it is obligatory in a fixed manner. Therefore the fasting of these days must be other than the fasting of Ramadan.

The second view, which is the choice of most verifiers (muhaqqiqun), such as Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Abu Muslim, is that the intended "certain number of days" is the month of Ramadan. They said: the explanation is that God first said: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾, and this is open to one day, two days, or several days. Then He specified it by His saying: ﴿certain number of days﴾, so some of the ambiguity was removed. Then He specified it further by His saying: ﴿the month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185]. In this order, it is possible to make the "certain days" themselves the month of Ramadan. And if that is possible, there is no basis for interpreting them as something else and affirming abrogation in them, because all of that is an addition which the wording does not indicate, and so it is not permissible to say it.

As for their first argument, the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The fasting of Ramadan has abrogated every fast."

The answer is: the report does not state that it abrogated, on his behalf and on behalf of his community, every fast. So why would it not be permissible for the meaning to be that it abrogated every obligatory fast in the earlier laws? For just as some parts of his law can abrogate other parts, it is valid that his law abrogates the law of others.

Even if we grant that this report requires that the fasting of Ramadan abrogated a fast that was established in his law, why would it not be permissible that it abrogated a fast that became obligatory by other than this verse? So from where do we know that the intended meaning of this verse is other than the month of Ramadan?

As for their second argument, which is that if these days were the month of Ramadan, the ruling for the sick and the traveler would be repeated:

The answer is: at the beginning, the fasting of the month of Ramadan was not a fixed obligation, but rather choice was established between it and the ransom. When this was so, and the traveler was given the concession to break the fast, it was possible to suppose that what was obligatory for him was the ransom and not the making up. It is also possible that he has neither ransom nor making up, because of the hardship that distinguishes him from the resident. When this was not far-fetched, God, Exalted is He, clarified that the breaking of the fast by the traveler and the sick is, in ruling, different from the choice in the ruling for the resident, for both of them must make up the fast on a number of other days. Then, when God abrogated that for the healthy resident and obligated him to fast definitively, it was possible to suppose that since the ruling on fasting moved from choice to restriction, it is a ruling that covers everyone, so that the sick and the traveler would be in the same position as the healthy resident in terms of the change in God's ruling on fasting. So God, Exalted is He, clarified that the state of the sick and the traveler remains established in the concession to break the fast and the obligation to make up, as it was originally. This is the benefit of repeating the ruling on the traveler and the sick, and not because the "certain days" are other than the month of Ramadan.

As for their third argument, which is their saying that fasting these days is obligatory on a basis of choice, while the fasting of the month of Ramadan is obligatory in a fixed manner:

Its answer is what we have mentioned, that the fasting of the month of Ramadan was obligatory on a basis of choice, and then it became fixed. This is the explanation of this view.

Know that according to both views, there must be an occurrence of abrogation in this verse. As for the first view, it is obvious. As for the second view, this verse requires that the fasting of Ramadan be obligatory on a basis of choice, while the verse after it indicates fixation. So the second verse abrogated the ruling of this verse. There is a difficulty here, which is: how can His saying ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185] be abrogating the choice, when it is connected to what is abrogated? This is not valid.

Its answer: connection in recitation (al-tilawa) does not require connection in revelation (al-nuzul). This is like what the jurists said about the waiting period (ʿidda) of a widow: the one placed first in recitation, which is the abrogating ruling, is in fact later, and the abrogated is earlier. They say this is the opposite of what the state of the abrogating and the abrogated ought to be. They said: that is in recitation, but in revelation, the reckoning by a year was the earlier, and the verse indicating four months and ten days was the later, so it is valid that it is the abrogating one. Likewise, we find in the Qur'an a Meccan verse that is later in recitation than a Medinan verse, and that is common.

[Page 62]

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** Concerning His saying ﴿ma'dudat﴾ (certain), there are two meanings.

One: determined by a known number.

The second: few, as in His saying: ﴿a few dirhams (darahima ma'dudah)﴾ [Yusuf 12:20]. The origin of this is that a small amount of money is measured by counting, and care is taken to know its measure, whereas a large amount is poured out and scooped out in handfuls. The intended meaning of this speech is as if He, glorified is He, says: "I have shown mercy to you and lightened for you, when I did not obligate upon you the fasting of the whole age, nor the fasting of most of it. If I had willed, I would have done that, but I have shown mercy to you, and I did not make fasting obligatory upon you except for a few days."

Some verifiers said: it is possible that His saying ﴿ayyaman ma'dudat﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾, and the similarity between the two obligations occurs in this aspect, which is the tying of fasting to a period that is not prolonged, even if the two periods differ in length and shortness. The intended meaning, by His defining it as "days" that we mentioned, is that the obligation of fasting upon us and upon those before us was only for a short period whose hardship is not severe. This is an explanation that He, Exalted is He, is merciful to all nations, and that He makes the matter of obligations easy for all nations.

\* \* \*

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever among you is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾, the intended meaning is that the obligation of fasting on the certain days applies only to healthy residents. As for whoever is sick or traveling, he may postpone the fast from these days to other days. Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: Look at the wondrous things God has pointed out of the breadth of His grace and mercy in this obligation. God made clear at the beginning of the verse that this community has a model in this obligation in the earlier communities, and the purpose of this is what we mentioned, that when difficult matters become general, they become lighter.

Then, second, He explained the wisdom behind making fasting obligatory, which is that it is a means of attaining God-consciousness (taqwa). If He had not prescribed fasting, this noble purpose would have been lost.

Then, third, He explained that it is restricted to a certain number of days, for if He had made it perpetual or for most of the time, great hardship would have resulted.

Then He explained, fourth, that He specified for it the time of the month in which the Qur'an was sent down, because it is the most noble of the months by virtue of this excellence.

Then He explained, fifth, the removal of hardship in imposing it, so He permitted postponing it for whoever among the travelers and the sick found it difficult, until they return to ease and rest. He, glorified is He, took into account in the obligation of fasting these aspects of mercy. So to Him belongs praise for His many blessings. Having understood this, we say: there are issues in the verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever among you is sick﴾ up to His saying ﴿other﴾ contains the meaning of a condition and its consequence, that is: whoever among you is sick or traveling and breaks the fast, then let him make it up. When you consider the meaning of a condition in it, the intended meaning of His saying "kāna" (is/was) is the future, not the past, as you say: "Whoever comes to me, I will come to him."

\* \* \*

**The second issue:** Sickness (al-maraḍ) is an expression for the lack of the whole of a living being's limbs being in the state that produces its actions in a sound condition, in a manner fitting for it. Scholars differed about the sickness that permits breaking the fast, on three views:

The first: whatever sickness it is, and whatever traveling it is, the person may take the concession, applying his unrestricted wording to its least condition. This is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin. It is related that they came in upon Ibn Sirin in Ramadan while he was eating, and he excused himself by the pain in his finger.

The second: this concession is specific to the sick person who, if he fasted, would fall into hardship and exertion, and to the traveler who is in that state. This is the view of al-Asamm, and its outcome is applying the unrestricted wording to the most complete conditions.

The third, which is the view of most jurists: the sickness that permits breaking the fast is that which leads to harm to the self or an increase in the illness, since there is no difference in the ruling between what one fears from it and what leads to what one fears. Like the feverish person who fears that if he fasts his fever will intensify, and the person with eye pain who fears that if he fasts the pain in his eye will intensify. They said: how is it possible to say that every sickness permits the concession, when we know that among sicknesses there are some that fasting worsens? So the intended meaning is what fasting has an effect on by strengthening it. Then its effect in a slight matter is of no consequence, because that may also occur in someone who is not sick. Therefore, its effect must be what we have mentioned.

\* \* \*

Eighth issue: the third issue: the root of safar (travel) is from kashf (uncovering). It uncovers the conditions and characters of men. The misfarah is the broom, because it uncovers the dust from the ground. The safir is the one who goes between two parties for reconciliation, because he uncovers the harm that has reached them. The musfir is the bright one, because it has become uncovered and manifest, and from it comes asfara al-subh (the morning became bright). The sifr is the book, because it uncovers meanings through its clarification. Asfarat al-mar'ah 'an wajhiha means she unveiled her face when she removed the veil. Al-Azhari said: the traveler (musafir) was so named for uncovering the shelter of the dwelling from his face and emerging onto the open land, and travel (safar) was so named because it unveils the faces and characters of travelers and brings out what was hidden in them.

The jurists differed about the length of travel that permits the concessions (rukhas). Dawud said: the concessions apply to every journey, even if the journey is a farsakh (about three miles). He relied on the argument that since the ruling was made dependent on being a traveler, wherever this meaning is realized the ruling applies. At most, a single report has been transmitted specifying this general statement, but specifying the general text of the Qur'an by a single report (khabar al-wahid) is not permissible. Al-Awza'i said: the permitting journey is the distance of one day, because a shorter distance may happen to one who is resident, and as for the greater, no number is preferable to another, so it is necessary to limit it to the one. The position of al-Shafi'i is that it is determined as sixteen farsakhs, and the distance of return is not counted in it. Each farsakh is three miles by the miles of Hashim, grandfather of the Messenger (ﷺ), who is the one who determined the miles of the desert; each mile is twelve thousand feet, which is four thousand paces, since every three feet is one pace. This is the position of Malik, Ahmad and Ishaq. Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said: the concessions of travel are not obtained except in three stages, twenty-four farsakhs. The proof of al-Shafi'i has two aspects:

The first: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then [an equal number] of other days﴾. Its implication is that the traveler be permitted the concession absolutely; leaving the practice of it in the case where the journey is a single stage would be the case, because the fatigue of one day is easy to bear. But when the fatigue is repeated over two days, it is hard to bear, so the concession is appropriate to obtain this lightening.

The second proof is from the report that al-Shafi'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O people of Makkah, do not shorten [the prayer] for less than four barids from Makkah to 'Usfan." The people of linguistics said: each barid is four farsakhs, so its total is sixteen farsakhs. It is also narrated from al-Shafi'i that 'Ata' said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Shall I shorten [the prayer] to 'Arafah?" He said: "No." He said: "To Marr al-Zahran?" He said: "No. But shorten to Jeddah, 'Usfan and al-Ta'if." Malik said: between Makkah and Jeddah and 'Usfan there are four barids.

The proof of Abu Hanifa is also from two aspects:

The first: the saying: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185] requires the obligation of fasting, from which we have departed in the case of three days by consensus that this amount is a concession, while less than it is disputed, so the obligation of fasting remains.

The second proof is from the report, his words, peace be upon him: "The resident wipes for a day and a night, and the traveler for three days and their nights." The report shows that every traveler may wipe for three days, and this is not so unless the duration of travel is determined as three days, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, made travel the cause of wiping over the two leather socks for three days and their nights, and made this wiping dependent, and the dependent does not exceed its cause.

As for the answer to the first: it is opposed by what we have mentioned of the verse. If they prefer their side on the ground that caution in acts of worship is preferable, we prefer our side on the ground that facilitation in the concessions of travel is what the Law seeks, by the evidence of his saying, peace be upon him: "This is a charity which Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity." The preference of this side is because the evidence indicating that the concessions of travel are sought by the Law is more specific than the evidence indicating the obligation to observe caution.

As for the answer to the second: he, peace be upon him, said: "The resident wipes for a day and a night." This does not indicate that residence is not attained in less than a day and a night, because if one intends to reside in a place of residence for an hour, he becomes a resident. Likewise his saying: "and the traveler three days" does not require that travel is not attained in less than three days.

Fifth issue: "al-'iddah" is a form (fi'lah) from al-'add (counting), and it has the meaning of the counted (ma'dud), like al-tahn (the grinding) with the meaning of the ground (matahun). From this it is said of a counted group of people 'iddah, and the 'iddah of a woman is from this.

If it is said: why did He say (fa-'iddatun) in indefinite form and not say fa-'iddatuha, i.e., the 'iddah of the counted days?

We say: because we have shown that 'iddah means the counted, so He commanded that he fast counted days in its place, and it is evident that he does not come except with the same number, so that sufficed without definition by annexation.

Sixth issue: "'iddatun" has been read in the nominative and the accusative. As for the nominative, it is in the sense of fa-'alayhi sawmu 'iddatin (so upon him is the fasting of a number), so this is from the elision of the modified noun; and as for the implied "'alayhi," the particle fa' indicates it. As for the accusative, it is in the sense of fa-liyasum 'iddatan (so let him fast a number).

Seventh issue: a group of the scholars among the Companions held that it is obligatory upon the sick and the traveler to break the fast and to fast a number of other days. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar. Al-Khattabi in I'lam al-Tanzil reported from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "If he fasts while travelling, he makes it up while resident." This is the choice of Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Isfahani. Most jurists held that breaking the fast is a concession: if he wishes he breaks it, and if he wishes he fasts.

The argument of the first group from the Qur'an and the report: as for the Qur'an, it is from two aspects:

The first: if we read "'iddatan" in the accusative, the estimate is: fa-liyasum 'iddatan min ayyamin ukhar, and this is for obligation. If we read it in the nominative, the estimate is: fa-'alayhi 'iddatun min ayyamin, and the word "'ala" is for obligation. Thus it is established that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an requires the obligation of fasting other days, so it is necessary that breaking the fast on these days be obligatory, since there is no one who says combining is permitted.

The second argument: He, may He be exalted, repeated this verse afterwards, then said after it: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. There must be that this ease and hardship are things previously mentioned. There is no ease there except that the sick and the traveler were permitted to break the fast, and there is no hardship there except their fasting. So His saying ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ means: He intends from you the breaking of the fast and does not intend from you the fasting; this is the confirmation of our saying. As for the report, there are two:

The first: his saying, peace be upon him: "It is not righteousness to fast while travelling." It may not be said: this report came in a particular cause, which is what was reported, that he, peace and blessings be upon him, passed by a man sitting under a shade, and he asked about him, and it was said: this is a fasting man whom thirst has overcome, so he said: "It is not righteousness to fast while travelling." Because we say: the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the cause.

The second: his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The fasting one in travel is like the breaking one in residence."

As for the argument of the majority: it is that there is an implied element in the verse, because the estimate is: fa-aftara fa-'iddatun min ayyamin ukhar. The complete establishment of this statement is that implication in the speech of Allah is permissible in general, and the evidence has indicated its occurrence here. As for the demonstration of permissibility, it is as in His saying, exalted: ﴿We said: strike the rock with your staff, and it burst forth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 60], and the estimate is: so he struck, and it burst forth. Likewise His saying: ﴿And do not shave your heads﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196] up to His saying: ﴿or having an injury of his head, then a ransom﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], i.e., so he shaved, then upon him is a ransom. Thus it is established that implication is permissible. As for the evidence that it has occurred, there are several aspects in its establishment:

The first: al-Qaffal said: His saying, exalted: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185] indicates the obligation of fasting. One may say this is weak, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: if we apply the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ upon generality, it entails implication in His saying: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, and we have shown in the principles of jurisprudence that whenever there is conflict between specification and implication, bearing the specification is preferable.

The second: the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted: "let him fast it" requires the obligation to be individual (ʿayn). Then this obligation is negated with respect to the sick and the traveler, so this verse is specified in their regard on all estimates, whether we apply His saying, exalted, "then upon him is a number of other days" to its apparent meaning or not. Since that is so, it is necessary to apply this verse to its apparent meaning without implication.

The second aspect: what al-Wahidi mentioned in the book al-Basit, saying: the making up is required only by breaking the fast, not by the illness or the journey. When Allah obligated the making up, and making up is preceded by breaking, it shows that breaking must be implied. This is in extreme weakness, because Allah, exalted, did not say: "then upon him is the making up of what passed," but rather said: "then upon him is the fasting of a number of other days," and the obligation of fasting upon him on other days does not require that it be preceded by breaking.

The third aspect: what Abu Dawud narrated in his Sunan from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from 'A'ishah, that Hamzah al-Aslami asked the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I fast while on a journey?" He, peace be upon him, said: "Fast if you wish, and break the fast if you wish." One may say: this implies the abrogation of the Qur'an by a single report, because the apparent meaning of the Qur'an requires the obligation of fasting all the remaining days, so the lifting of this by the report is not permissible if the weakness of these aspects is established. So the reliance in establishing the position is on His saying, exalted, after this verse: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾, and the manner of the inference will come, if Allah the Exalted wills.

Eighth issue: for the position of those who say that fasting is permissible there are two branches:

First branch: they differed as to whether fasting is better or breaking the fast. Anas ibn Malik and 'Uthman ibn Abi Awfa said: fasting is better. This is the position of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Thawri, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. A group said: the better of the two is breaking the fast, and this is the position of Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, al-Awza'i, Ahmad and Ishaq. A third group said: the better of the two is whichever is easier for the person.

The argument of the first group: His saying, exalted: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and His saying, exalted: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾.

The argument of the second group: that shortening the prayer is better, so breaking the fast must be better.

The answer: some of our companions said that completing the prayer is better, but this is weak. The difference is in two respects:

One of them: the obligation remains occupied with the making up of the fast, but not of the prayer, if one shortens it.

The second: the virtue of the time is lost by breaking the fast, but is not lost by shortening the prayer.

The proof of the third group is the saying of Allah, Most High: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185]. This requires that if fasting is easier for him, he fasts, and if breaking the fast is easier, he breaks it.

The second branch: if he breaks the fast, how does he make up (qada', "making up the missed fasts") the days? The position of ʿAlī, Ibn ʿUmar and al-Shaʿbī is that he makes them up consecutively. The rest said: consecutiveness is recommended (mustaḥabb, "encouraged but not required"), and if he separates them, it is permissible.

The proof of the first group has two aspects:
The first: the recitation of Ubayy, "fa-ʿiddatun min ayyāmin mutatābiʿāt" (so a number of days, consecutive).
The second: making up is the counterpart of performing (adāʾ, "performing the fast on its time"). Since performing it is consecutive, so too is making it up.

The proof of the second group: His saying ﴿so a number of other days﴾ is an indefinite noun (nakira) in an affirmative context. Therefore it is a command to fast a number of days equal to those days, without restriction. Restricting it to consecutiveness contradicts this generality.

It is reported from Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ that he said: "Allah did not grant you a concession to break the fast while intending to make it hard for you in making it up. If you wish, make them consecutive, and if you wish, separate them. And Allah knows best."

It is reported that a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I owe days of Ramadan. Would it suffice me to make them up separately?" He said to him: "Tell me, if you had a debt and paid him a dirham and two dirhams, would it not suffice you?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Allah is more worthy to pardon and overlook."

* * *

The ninth issue: ﴿ukhar﴾ (ʾukhar, "other") is not declined (lā yanṣarif, "it does not take nunation and the usual declension"), because two causes are present in it: plurality (jamʿ) and ʿadl (deviation from the regular form). As for plurality, it is the plural of ukhrā. As for ʿadl, it is because ukhrā is the feminine of ākhar, and ākhar follows the pattern afʿal. Whatever follows the pattern afʿal is used either with "min" (from) or with the definite article al-. One says: Zayd is more excellent than ʿAmr (Zaydun afḍalu min ʿAmrin), and Zayd is the most excellent (Zaydun al-afḍalu). By analogy, one should say: "a man other than Zayd" (rajulun ākharu min Zaydin), just as you say "more ancient than ʿAmr" (aqdamu min ʿAmrin). However, they omitted the word "min", because its form implied the meaning of "min", so they dropped "min" relying on the indication of the word. The definite article and "min" are mutually exclusive. Since the word may be used without the article, ukhar, ākhar and ukhrā became deviated from the rule of their counterparts, because the article had been used with them and then deleted.

* * *

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿and for those who are able to do it (wa-ʿalā alladhīna yuṭīqūnahu)﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: the well-known, mutawātir (widely transmitted, "mass-transmitted") recitation is ﴿yuṭīqūnahu﴾. ʿIkrima, Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī and ʿAṭāʾ read ﴿yaṭīqūnahu﴾. Some people said this recitation is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid. Ibn Jinnī said: the middle radical (ʿayn) of ṭāqa is a waw (wāw), as in their saying: "lā ṭāqata lī bihi wa lā ṭawqa lī bihi" (I have no capacity for it). Upon this is the reading ﴿yuṭawwiqūnahu﴾, meaning they do it, like your saying "yujashshimūnahu", meaning they are made to bear it.

* * *

The second issue: they differed about the meaning of ﴿and for those who are able to do it﴾, in three views:

The first: this refers to the traveler and the sick. The traveler and the sick may include one who cannot fast and one who can fast.
[Page 68]
As for the first kind, Allah has stated its ruling in His saying: ﴿And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾.
As for the second kind, the traveler and the sick who are able to fast, the reference is to them in His saying: ﴿and for those who are able to do it, a ransom﴾. It is as if He, Most High, established two states for the sick and the traveler. In one, it is obligatory for him to break the fast and make it up, which is the state of extreme hardship if he were to fast. In the second, he is able to fast without it being heavy on him, and then he is given the choice between fasting and breaking the fast with a ransom.

The second view, which is the view of most exegetes, is that what is meant by ﴿and for those who are able to do it﴾ is the resident who is healthy. Allah gave him the choice between these two first, then this was abrogated (naskh, "abrogation") and fasting was made obligatory upon him in a restricted and fixed way.

The third view: this verse was revealed concerning the decrepit old man. They said: its explanation is in two respects. The first: the capacity (wusʿ) is above ṭāqa. Wusʿ is a term for one who is able to do a thing with ease, whereas ṭāqa is a term for one who is able to do a thing with strain and difficulty. So His saying ﴿and for those who are able to do it﴾ means: for those who are able to fast with strain and difficulty.

The second respect in establishing this view is the irregular (shādhdh, "non-standard") recitation ﴿wa-ʿalā alladhīna yaṭīqūnahu﴾, for its meaning is: for those who are made to bear it and burdened with it. It is known that this is only valid concerning one who is able to do a thing with some kind of hardship.

Having understood this, we say: the proponents of this view differed into two positions:
One of them, which is the view of al-Suddī, is that it refers to the decrepit old man. On this view, the verse is not abrogated. It is reported that Anas, before his death, used to break the fast, being unable to fast, and fed a poor person (miskīn) for each day. Others said: it includes the decrepit old man, the pregnant woman and the nursing mother. Ḥasan al-Baṣrī was asked about a pregnant or nursing woman who fears for herself and for her children. He said: "Which sickness is more severe than pregnancy? She breaks the fast and makes it up."

Know that they agreed that if the decrepit old man breaks the fast, he owes a ransom. As for the pregnant and nursing woman, if they break the fast, is a ransom owed by them? al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: a ransom is owed by them. Abū Ḥanīfa said: it is not obligatory. The proof of al-Shāfiʿī is that His saying ﴿and for those who are able to do it, a ransom﴾ includes the pregnant and nursing woman. Also, the ransom is obligatory on the decrepit old man, so it is obligatory on them too. Abū Ḥanīfa made a distinction, saying: it is not possible to impose making up on the decrepit old man, so the ransom is necessarily obligatory. As for the pregnant and nursing woman, making up is obligatory upon them. If we also imposed a ransom on them, that would be combining two substitutes, and this is impermissible, because making up is a substitute and the ransom is a substitute. This is the explanation of these three views concerning His saying, Most High: ﴿and for those who are able to do it﴾.

As for the first view, which is the view chosen by al-Aṣamm, they argued for its soundness in several respects:

The first: the sickness mentioned in the verse is either the sickness which in the verse is that which cannot be borne, or the intended meaning is every sickness called a sickness, or the intended meaning is what lies between these two degrees. The second is invalid by agreement, and the third is also invalid, because intermediate states have many unrestricted degrees, and each degree is weak relative to what is above it and strong relative to what is below it. So if the wording gives no indication of identifying that degree, while the intention of Allah is that degree, the verse becomes unclear, which goes against the basic principle. Since these two parts are invalid, it is established that the intended meaning is the first part, because it is fixed, and interpreting the verse by it is better, since it does not lead to the verse becoming unclear.
[Page 69]
Having established this, we say: the beginning of the verse indicates the obligation of fasting, which is His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you, a certain number of days﴾. Then He explained the states of those excused. Since those excused are of two kinds, some of whom cannot fast at all, and some of whom can fast with hardship and strain, Allah mentioned the ruling for the first kind, then followed it with the ruling for the second kind.

The second argument in establishing this view: in ordinary usage, one does not say of a strong capable person that he is able (yuṭīqu) to do this act, because this word is only used concerning one who can do it with some kind of hardship.

The third argument: according to your positions, the abrogation must occur in this verse, whereas according to our position it is not required. It is known that abrogation, the less of it there is, the better. So it is impermissible to resort to asserting abrogation without the wording containing something that indicates it.

The fourth argument: those who say this verse is abrogated agree that its abrogator is the verse about witnessing the month, and that is impermissible, because He, Most High, said at the end of that verse: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185]. If the verse were abrogating this, then His saying ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ would not be appropriate in this place, because this assessment made fasting obligatory in a restricted way and lifted its obligation in the way of choice. That would be lifting ease and establishing hardship, so how could He fittingly say: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾?

Al-Qāḍī, may Allah have mercy on him, argued against al-Aṣamm's view, saying: His saying ﴿and for those who are able to do it﴾ is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to the traveler and the sick, and the conjoined must be other than what it is conjoined to. Therefore the view of al-Aṣamm is invalid.

The answer: we have shown that what is meant by the traveler and the sick mentioned in the verse are those who cannot fast at all, while what is meant by His saying ﴿and for those who are able to do it﴾ is the traveler and the sick who are able to fast. So the difference is established. Thus, by what we have shown, the view chosen by al-Aṣamm is not weak. As for if we agree with the majority and accept its invalidity, the other two views remain. Most exegetes and jurists hold the second view, and al-Shāfiʿī chose it, and he argued against the third view, which is the view of those who took it to refer to the decrepit old man and the pregnant and nursing woman, by saying: if the meaning were the decrepit old man, He would not have said at the end of the verse: ﴿and that you fast is better for you﴾, because he is not able to do it. The one who objects may say: this refers to the decrepit old man who is able to fast but it is hard for him. On this assumption, it is not impossible to say to him: if you bear this hardship, that would be better for you, for worship is always greater in reward the more difficult it is.

* * *

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿a ransom, the feeding of a poor person (fidyatun ṭaʿāmu miskīn)﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿fidyatu﴾ without nunation, ﴿ṭaʿāmi﴾ with a kasra, as a genitive complement, and ﴿masākīna﴾ in the plural. The rest read ﴿fidyatun﴾ with nunation, ﴿ṭaʿāmu﴾ with a ḍamma, and ﴿miskīnin﴾ in the genitive. As for the first recitation, there are two discussions:

The first: what is the meaning of annexing ransom to food? We say there are two views:
One of them: ransom has an essence, and its description is that it is food. This is from the type of annexing a described noun to its description, as in their saying: "the masjid of the mosque (masjidu l-jāmiʿi)" and "the herb of the fool (baqlatu l-ḥamqāʾ)".
The second: al-Wāḥidī said: ransom is a term for the required amount, and food is a term that covers ransom and other things. This annexation is of the type that has the meaning of "min" (from), as in your saying: "a garment of silk (thawbu khazzin)" and "a ring of iron (khātamu ḥadīdin)", and the meaning is: a garment of silk and a ring of iron. Likewise here, the implied meaning is: a ransom of food, so ransom is annexed to food, even though you apply the name of food to the ransom.
[Page 70]
The second discussion: in this recitation they made the word "masākīn" plural, because those who are able to do it are a group, and each one of them is liable for one poor person. As for the second recitation, which is ﴿fidyatun﴾ with nunation, they made what follows it an explanation of it, and made "miskīn" singular, because the meaning is: for each one, for each day, the food of one poor person.

The second issue: ransom (fidya) means compensation (jazāʾ), which is an expression for a substitute standing in place of a thing. According to Abū Ḥanīfa, it is half a ṣāʿ of wheat or a ṣāʿ of other food, which is two mudds. According to al-Shāfiʿī, it is one mudd.

* * *

The third issue: al-Jubbāʾī argued from His saying, Most High: ﴿and for those who are able to do it, a ransom﴾ that ability (istiṭāʿa) is prior to the act. He said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿and for those who are able to do it﴾ refers to fasting. So He established the capacity to fast at the time of not fasting, because He made a ransom obligatory on him. A ransom becomes obligatory only if he does not fast. This shows that the capacity to fast exists before the fasting occurs.

If it is said: why can the pronoun not refer to the ransom (fidyah)?

We answer on two grounds.

The first: the ransom has not been mentioned before, so how could the pronoun refer back to it?

The second: the pronoun is masculine, while fidyah is feminine. If it is said: this verse has been abrogated (mansukh), so how is it permissible to use it as evidence? We reply: before it was abrogated, it indicated that the capacity (qudrah) exists before the act, and realities do not change.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾, there are three aspects:

The first: that he feeds one poor person or more.

The second: that he feeds the one poor person more than the required amount.

The third: al-Zuhri said: whoever fasts along with paying the ransom, it is better for him.

As for His words: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: that this is addressed only to those who are able to do it, so the meaning is: "And that you fast, O you who are able, or who are burdened [with difficulty] and bear the hardship, is better for you than the ransom."

The second: that this is addressed to everyone previously mentioned, namely the sick, the traveller, and those who are able to do it. This is more appropriate, because the wording is general, and its being connected to His words ﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾ does not necessitate that its ruling is restricted to them; since the wording is general and there is no contradiction in its applying to all, the ruling is to be given accordingly. At this point it becomes clear that there must be an implied element in His words ﴿So whoever among you is sick or on a journey, then [he shall fast] an equal number of other days﴾, and that the implied meaning is: "So he broke his fast, then [he shall fast] an equal number of other days."

The third: that His words ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾ are coordinated (ʿaṭf) with what comes before them at the beginning of the verse, so the meaning is: "Fasting has been prescribed for you, and that you fast is better for you."

As for His words ﴿if you only knew﴾, that is: since fasting is obligatory for you, know the truth of our statement, and that fasting is better for you.

The second: that the end of the verse is connected to its beginning, and the meaning is: "Fasting has been prescribed for you, and that you fast is better for you, if you only knew," that is, when you reflect you will know what is in fasting of meanings that produce piety and other things that we have mentioned at the start of this verse.

The third: that the one who knows God must have in his heart the fear of God, as He said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28]. So He mentioned knowledge while meaning fear, and the one who has fear observes caution, and caution lies in performing the fast. So it is as if it were said: "If you truly know God, so that you fear Him, fasting would be better for you."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 1 of 4)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down as guidance for mankind, and as clear proofs of guidance and the criterion. So whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it. And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days. Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you, that you may complete the period and glorify Allah for having guided you, and that you may be grateful.﴾ In it are several issues:

**The first issue:** *al-shahr* (the month) is derived from *al-shuhra* (fame). It is said: *shahara al-shay'u yashharu shuhratan wa shahran*, meaning the thing became apparent. The month is called *shahr* because its matter is famous, since people's needs are tied to knowing it, for the timing of their debts and for the performance of their rites of fasting and pilgrimage. *Al-shuhra* is the appearing of a thing, and the crescent is called *shahr* because of its prominence and clarity. Some have said the month was named *shahr* after the crescent (*hilal*).

* * *

**The second issue:** The scholars differed about *Ramadan* in several respects.

First: Mujahid said it is one of the names of Allah, and the meaning of the speaker's saying "the month of Ramadan" is "the month of Allah." It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not say, 'Ramadan has come and Ramadan has gone,' but say, 'The month of Ramadan has come and the month of Ramadan has gone, for Ramadan is one of the names of Allah the Exalted."

The second view: it is the name of a month, like the month of Rajab and Sha'ban. Then they differed about its derivation in several ways.

The first: what is transmitted from al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) is that it derives from *al-ramda'* with the *mim* sukun, which is a rain that comes before autumn and cleanses the face of the earth from dust. The meaning is that just as that rain washes and purifies the face of the earth, so the month of Ramadan washes the bodies of this community from sins and purifies their hearts.

The second: it derives from *al-ramad*, which is the heat of stones from the intensity of the sun's heat, and the name is *al-ramda'*. This month was named thus either because of their being scorched in this month by the heat of hunger or by enduring its severity. Just as they named it *tabi'* (following), because it followed them, i.e., troubled them with its severity upon them. It is also said: when they transferred the names of the months from the ancient language, they named them after the seasons in which they fell, so this month coincided with the days of the scorching heat (*ramad al-harr*). It is also said: it was named thus because it scorches sins, i.e., burns them. It has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Ramadan was named only because it scorches the sins of the servants of Allah."

The third: this name derives from their saying: *ramadtu al-nasl armiduhu ramdan*, when you press the blade between two stones so that it becomes thin; a blade is *rami'* and *marmud*. So this month was named Ramadan because they used to sharpen their weapons in it so that they could fulfill their needs with them. This view is attributed to al-Azhari.

The fourth: even if it is said that Ramadan is a name of Allah and this month is also named by this name, the meaning is that sins dissolve in comparison with the mercy of Allah, until it is as if they were burned, and this month is also Ramadan in the sense that sins are burned in comparison with its blessing.

* * *

**The third issue:** *Shahr* is read with a *raf'* (nominative) and with a *nasb* (accusative). As for the nominative, there are several views:

First: the view of al-Kisa'i, that it is in the nominative as a *badal* (substitute, apposition) of *al-siyam* (the fasting), and the meaning is: "The month of Ramadan has been prescribed for you."

Second: the view of al-Farra' and al-Akhfash, that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, a *badal* of his saying *ayyaman* (days). It is as if it were said: "They are the month of Ramadan," because the words ﴿the month of Ramadan﴾ explain and clarify the ﴿numbered days﴾.

Third: Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: if you wish, you may make it a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted. As when the phrase ﴿fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ preceded, it is as if it were said: "Among what has been prescribed for you of fasting is the month of Ramadan," meaning its fasting.

Fourth: some of them said: it may be that it is a subject and its predicate is *alladhi* (which) with its relative clause, like the saying "Zayd is the one who is in the house." Abu Ali said: the more probable view is that *alladhi* is an attribute (*wasf*), so that the wording of the Qur'an is explicit in the command to fast the month. For if you make it a predicate, the month of Ramadan would not be explicitly stated as obligatory to fast by this wording; it would only be reported as the time in which the Qur'an was sent down. Moreover, when you make *alladhi* an attribute, the proper structure would be that the month be referred to by a pronoun, not stated openly, as in your saying: "The blessed month of Ramadan, whoever witnesses it, let him fast it."

As for the accusative reading, there are several views:

First: the estimate is: "Fast the month of Ramadan."

Second: it is a *badal* of *ayyaman ma'dudat* (numbered days).

Third: it is the object (*maf'ul*) of ﴿and that you fast﴾. This view was mentioned by the author of *al-Kashshaf* (the Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari), and it was objected to, saying: according to this estimate the structure becomes: "And that you fast Ramadan, in which the Qur'an was sent down, is better for you." This requires a separation between the subject and the predicate by this long phrase, which is not permissible, because the subject and predicate function as one thing, and placing a separation between a thing and itself is not permissible.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾: know that when He, exalted is He, specified this month for this worship, He explained the reason for this specification. It is that Allah, glorified is He, singled it out with the greatest of the signs of lordship, which is that the Qur'an was sent down in it. Therefore it is not far-fetched that He also singles it out with a great kind of the signs of servanthood, which is fasting. What confirms this is that the luminous divine lights are always manifest, and it is impossible for them to be hidden or veiled. But human attachments prevent their appearance in human souls, and fasting is the strongest means of removing human attachments. For this reason, the people of unveilings (*ahl al-mukashafat*) have no way to reach them except by fasting. Therefore he, upon whom be blessings and peace, said: "Were it not that the devils hover over the hearts of the children of Adam, they would look upon the realm of the heavens." Thus it is established that there is a great correspondence between fasting and the sending down of the Qur'an. So when this month was specified by the sending down of the Qur'an, it must be specified by fasting. In this place there are many secrets, and the measure we have indicated is sufficient here. Then here are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾. Regarding its interpretation there are two views:

The first, which is the choice of the majority: that Allah, exalted is He, sent down the Qur'an in Ramadan. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "The scrolls of Abraham were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah was sent down after six nights had passed, the Gospel on the thirteenth, and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth." Here there are questions:

**The first question:** The Qur'an was not sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) all at once, but was sent down to him over a period of twenty-three years, in installments and in parts. Just as some of it was sent down in Ramadan, some of it was sent down in other months. So what is the meaning of specifying its sending down to Ramadan?

The answer to this has two aspects:

The first: the Qur'an was sent down on the Night of Decree (*Laylat al-Qadr*) all at once to the lowest heaven, and then it descended to the earth in installments. The matter was arranged in this way because of the benefit that He, exalted is He, knew in this manner. It is not far-fetched that there was a benefit for the angels who dwell in the lowest heaven in sending it down to them; or it was known that there was a benefit for the Messenger (peace be upon him) in expecting the revelation from the nearest directions; or there was a benefit for Jibril (peace be upon him), because he was the one commanded to bring it down and convey it. As for the wisdom of sending the Qur'an down to the Messenger in installments and in parts, we have explained it in *Surat al-Furqan*, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" Thus, that We may strengthen your heart with it﴾ [Al-Furqan: 32].

The second answer to this question: what is meant is that its sending down began on the Night of Decree in the month of Ramadan. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ishaq. This is because the beginnings of religions and dynasties are those by which dating is done, since they are the most noble times, and also because they are fixed and known times.

Know that the first answer does not require bearing any metaphor, whereas here it is required, for according to this answer it is necessary to take the Qur'an as referring to some of its parts and divisions.

**The second question:** How is this verse reconciled, according to this view, with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [Al-Qadr: 1], and with His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down on a blessed night﴾ [Al-Dukhan: 3]?

The answer: it is narrated that Ibn Umar derived from this verse, together with His saying ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾, that the Night of Decree must be in Ramadan. For if the Night of Decree is in Ramadan, then its sending down during the Night of Decree is a sending down in Ramadan. This is like someone who says, "I met so-and-so in this month," and he is asked, "On which day of it?" and he says, "On such-and-such day," so that becomes an explanation of the first statement. Thus it is here.

**The third question:** According to this view, it may be said that Allah, exalted is He, sent down the whole Qur'an from the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*) to the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree, and then sent it down to Muhammad (ﷺ) in installments until the end of his life. It may also be said that He, glorified is He, used to send down from the Preserved Tablet to the lowest heaven of the Qur'an whatever He knew Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his community would need in that year, and then He would send it down to the Messenger in proportion to the need; and so on, forever, for as long as... Which of these two is closer to the truth?

The answer: both are possible. This is because His saying, ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾, may mean a specific individual Ramadan, or it may mean the type. When each of the two is possible and suitable, it is obligatory to suspend judgment.

The second view regarding His saying ﴿in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾: Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: "in which the Qur'an was sent down" means: "in its virtue the Qur'an was sent down." This is the choice of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, who said: a similar usage is to say: "such-and-such a verse was sent down concerning Abu Bakr (al-Siddiq)," meaning concerning his virtue. Ibn al-Anbari said: "the Qur'an was sent down concerning the obligation of its fasting upon creation," just as one says, "Allah sent down such-and-such concerning zakat," meaning concerning its obligation, and "He sent down such-and-such concerning wine," meaning concerning its prohibition.

* * *

**The second issue:** *Al-Qur'an* is the name for the speech of Allah between the two covers, and the scholars differed about its derivation. Al-Wahidi related in *al-Basit* from Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Hakam that al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: "*al-Qur'an* is a proper name and is not hamzated; it was not derived from *qara'tu* (I read). Rather, it is a name for the Book of Allah, like the Torah and the Gospel." He said: "It is pronounced with a hamza when it means recitation (*qira'a*), but the Qur'an itself is not hamzated, as in His saying: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an﴾ [Al-Isra': 45]." Al-Wahidi said: al-Shafi'i's saying that it is a name for the Book of Allah seems to indicate that he held it is not derived. Others held that it is derived. Know that among those who hold this view, some do not hamzate it and some do hamzate it.

[p. 74] As for the first group, they have two derivations:

One of them: it is derived from *qarantu al-shay' bi al-shay'*, when you join one thing to another. So it is derived from *qarana*, and the noun is *quran*, unhamzated. Hence the Qur'an was named *quran*, either because its surahs, verses, and letters are joined one to another, or because its wisdoms and laws are joined one to another, or because its proofs which indicate that it is from Allah are joined one to another, meaning its containing aspects of eloquence, a unique style, reports of unseen matters, and many sciences. On this assumption, it is derived from *qarana*, and the noun is *quran*, unhamzated.

The second: al-Farra' said: "I think the Qur'an was named from *al-qara'in* (the corresponding parts), because its verses confirm one another, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [An-Nisa': 82]. So they are corresponding parts (*qara'in*)." As for those who hamzated it, they have several views:

The first of them: it is the verbal noun (maṣdar) of recitation. One says, "I recited the Qur'an (qara'tu al-Qur'an), so I recite it (af'aluhu) qar'an, qira'atan and Qur'anan," so it is a verbal noun. Among verbal nouns similar to qur'an are al-rujhan (the outweighing), al-nuqsan (the diminishing), al-khusran (the loss) and al-ghufran (the forgiveness). The poet said:

They sacrificed a white-haired old man, whose mark is prostration upon him,
who cuts the night with glorification and Qur'an (recitation).

That is, with recitation. Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isra: 78]. This is the original meaning. Then the thing recited is also called Qur'an, because the object is named by the verbal noun, as they said for the drink, "sharab" (drink), and for the written, "kitab" (book). This name became well known in common usage until they made it the name of the speech of Allah, exalted.

The second: al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ubayda said that it is derived from al-qurʾ, which means gathering. 'Amr said:

A camel of smooth colour, she has not gathered (taqra'') a foetus.

That is, she has not gathered a young one in her womb. From this root comes the qurʾ of a woman, which is the days in which blood gathers in her womb. Thus the Qur'an was called Qur'an, because it gathers the surahs and joins them together.

The third: the view of Qutrub, which is that it was called Qur'an because the reciter (al-qari') collects it, and at the time of recitation he seems to throw it out of his mouth, taking from the saying of the Arabs: "The she-camel never cast (qara'at) a sala' at all," meaning she never threw out a young one, never miscarried a young one, and never discharged it. The menstrual period was called qur' according to this interpretation. So the Qur'an, the reciter pronounces it from his mouth and throws it out, and so it was called Qur'an.

The third issue: We have mentioned in the explanation of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Baqara: 23], that tanzil (sending down) is specific to descent in stages (ʿala sabil al-tadrij), while inzal is specific to that in which the descent occurs in a single instance. For this reason Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3]. Having established this, we say: since what is meant here by His saying, ﴿the month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾, is that it was sent down from the Preserved Tablet to the lowest heaven, he therefore mentioned it with the term inzal and not tanzil. This indicates that this view is preferable over the rest of the views.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: We have explained the meaning of guidance in His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 2].

The question: He, exalted be He, made the Qur'an in that verse a guidance for the God-fearing, and here He made it ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾. So how is the reconciliation? Its answer is what we mentioned there.

The second issue: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: it was sent down as guidance for mankind to the truth, and it is
Page 75
clear, manifest signs that guide to the truth and distinguish between truth and falsehood.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿and clear proofs of guidance and the Criterion﴾, there is a difficulty, namely that it may be asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿and clear proofs of guidance﴾ after His saying "guidance"?

Its answer comes in several ways:

The first: He, exalted be He, mentioned first that it is guidance; then guidance is of two kinds: sometimes its being guidance for mankind is clear and evident, and sometimes it is not so. The first kind is undoubtedly superior, so it is as if it were said: it is guidance, because it is the clear part of guidance and the distinguisher between truth and falsehood. This is from the category in which the genus is mentioned and its species is joined to it, because it is the most noble of its species. The implied sense is as if it were said: this is guidance, this is clear from guidance, and these are clear proofs of guidance. There is no doubt that this is the utmost emphasis.

The second: It may be said that the Qur'an is guidance in itself, and along with being so it is also clear proofs of guidance and the Criterion. What is meant by the guidance and the Criterion is the Torah and the Gospel. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾, ﴿before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3–4]. He said: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, so that you might be guided﴾ [al-Baqara: 53], and He said: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Anbiya: 48]. So He, exalted and sanctified, made clear that the Qur'an, along with being guidance in itself, also contains guidance from the earlier books, which are guidance and criterion.

The third: The first may be taken to refer to the principles of religion, and the second guidance to the branches of religion, and then the repetition disappears. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, related in *al-Basit* from al-Akhfash and al-Mazini that they both said: the fa' in His saying ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ is superfluous (za'ida). They said: this is because the fa' may enter for coordination (al-'atf), or for the consequent (al-jaza'), or it may be superfluous, and it is not for coordination. The consequent here is one possibility. And among the superfluous fa' is His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you; then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 8].

I say: It is possible to say that the fa' here is for the consequent, for when He made clear that Ramadan is distinguished by the great virtue in which no other month shares, He made clear that its distinction in that virtue suits its distinction in this worship. Were it not so, there would be no reason for presenting the statement of that virtue here. It is as if it were said: since it is known that this month is distinguished by this virtue, then you too, single it out for this worship. As for His saying, ﴿for it will surely meet you﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 8], the fa' there is not superfluous; rather this is from the category of contrasting an opposite with its opposite, as if it were said: since they fled from death, their recompense is that death draws near to them, so that they know that caution does not avail against decree.

* * *

The second issue: (shahida) means he was present (hadara), and shuhud means presence. Then here there are two opinions:

One: the object of shahida is omitted, because the meaning is: "whoever of you is present in the town or his house," meaning he was not travelling. The word "the month" (al-shahr) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), and likewise the ha' in His saying "let him fast it" (fal-yasumhu).

The second opinion: the object of shahida is "the month" (al-shahr), and the sense is: whoever witnesses the month with his intellect and knowledge, let him fast it. This is like saying: "I witnessed the era of so-and-so" and "I attained the time of so-and-so." Know that neither of the two opinions is complete except by departing from the apparent meaning. As for the first opinion, it is completed only by supposing an additional matter. As for the second opinion, it entails the entry of specification (takhsis) into the verse, because the witnessing of the month is present for the child, the insane, the sick and the traveller, though none of them is obliged to fast. But we have shown in the principles of jurisprudence that whenever there is a conflict between specification and supposition, specification has priority. Moreover, on the first opinion, since we have accepted supposition, we must also accept specification, because the child, the insane and the sick each witnessed the month though fasting is not obligatory for them; as for the traveller, he does not enter, so this case does not need specification for him. Thus the first opinion works only with accepting supposition and specification, while the second works merely with accepting specification, so the second opinion is preferable. This is my view on it, though most of the verifiers, such as al-Wahidi and the author of *al-Kashshaf*, went to the first opinion.

The third issue: The alif and lam in His saying ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month﴾ are for the previously known referent, which is the month of Ramadan. Its parallel is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it? When they did not bring the witnesses﴾ [al-Nur: 13], that is, when they did not bring the four witnesses.

The fourth issue: Know that there is a difficulty in the verse, namely that His saying ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ is a compound sentence of a condition (shart) and a consequent (jaza'). The condition is witnessing the month and the consequent is the command to fast. As long as the condition is not fulfilled in its entirety, the consequent does not follow from it. The month is a name for the specific period from its beginning to its end, so witnessing the month occurs only at the last part of the month. The apparent meaning of this verse requires that at the witnessing of the last part of the month, fasting the whole month becomes obligatory, and this is impossible, because it leads to performing an act in a time that has passed, which is impossible. Therefore, by this proof we know that it is not possible to apply this verse to its apparent meaning, and that it must be turned to interpretation. Its method is that the word "month" in the condition be taken as a part of the parts of the month, so its formulation becomes: whoever witnesses a part of the parts of the month, let him fast the whole month. On this basis, whoever witnesses the crescent of Ramadan has witnessed a part of the parts of the month, the condition is fulfilled, and the consequent follows from it, which is the command to fast the whole month. On this interpretation the meaning of the verse is sound, and there is nothing in it except taking the word "whole" to mean "part," which is a well-known metaphor.

Know that what is reported from 'Ali is that the intended meaning of this verse is: whoever of you witnesses the first of the month, let him fast all of it. By what we have mentioned as proof, you know that this is the only view that is valid at all. Then two branches follow from this principle:

One: If he witnesses the first of the month, is he obliged to fast the whole month?

The second: If he witnesses the last of the month, is he obliged to fast the whole month?

As for the first: it is reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that whoever the month reaches while he is resident and then travels, it is obligatory for him to fast all of it, because we have shown that the verse indicates that whoever witnesses the first of the month, fasting all of the month becomes obligatory for him. As for the other jurists, they say: His saying, exalted be He, ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, although its meaning is that whoever witnesses the first of the month, let him fast all of it, is general and includes the resident and the traveller. And His saying after that: ﴿But whoever of you is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. Thus it is established that even if he travels after witnessing the month, it is lawful for him to break the fast.

As for the second: that Abu Hanifa held that if the insane person recovers in the course of the month, he is obliged to make up what passed. He said: because we have shown that the implication of this verse is that whoever attains a part of Ramadan is obliged to fast all of Ramadan, and the insane person who recovers in the middle of the month has witnessed a part of Ramadan, so it is obligatory for him to fast all of Ramadan. When fasting what preceded is impossible, making it up is obligatory.

* * *

The fifth issue: Know that His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ calls for two discussions:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 3 of 4):

The first issue: by what does one witness the month? We say: either by sight or by hearing. As for sight, we say: if a person sees the crescent of Ramadan, then either he is alone in that sighting or he is not. If he is alone in it, then either the ruler (al-imam) rejects his testimony or he does not reject it. If he alone sighted it and the ruler rejected his testimony, it is obligatory for him to fast, because Allah Most High made witnessing the month a cause for the obligation of fasting upon him, and witnessing the month has occurred in his case, so it is obligatory upon him to fast. As for when he alone sighted it and the ruler accepted his testimony, or when he was not alone in the sighting, there is no dispute about the obligation to fast. As for hearing, we say: if two just (adl) witnesses testify to the sighting of the crescent, a ruling is made by it for both fasting and breaking the fast. If one just witness testifies to the sighting of the crescent of Shawwal, no ruling is made by it. If he testifies to the crescent of Ramadan, a ruling is made by it out of caution regarding the matter of fasting. The difference between it and the crescent of Shawwal is that the crescent of Ramadan is for entry into worship, and the crescent of Shawwal is for exit from worship. The word of one person is accepted for establishing worship, but for exiting worship it is not accepted except on the word of two. And also, there is no difference between them in reality, because we only accepted the word of one person regarding the crescent of Ramadan so that they may fast and not break the fast, out of caution. Likewise, the word of one person is not accepted regarding the crescent of Shawwal, so that they may fast and not break the fast, out of caution.

The second issue, concerning fasting: we say that fasting is abstaining from the things that break the fast, with knowledge that one is fasting, from the beginning of the true dawn (al-fajr al-sadiq) until the sunset, together with intention (niyyah). In the definition there are conditions:

The first condition: abstention (al-imsak). This is a safeguard against two things:
The first: if a fly flies into his throat, or the dust of the road reaches his stomach, his fast is not invalidated, because avoiding it is difficult, and Allah Most High says in the verse of fasting: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾.
The second: if food or drink is poured into his throat by force, or during sleep, his fast is not invalidated, because what is taken into account is abstention and refraining, and compulsion does not contradict that.

The second condition: our statement "from the things that break the fast." These are three: the entry of something inside, the exit of something outside, and sexual intercourse. The definition of entry is: every substance that reaches from the outside to the inside through an open passage into the interior, either the brain or the stomach and what is in it of the intestines and the bladder. As for the brain, the fast is broken by snuff (al-as'ut). As for the stomach, the fast is broken by an enema (al-huqnah). As for exit, vomiting by choice and masturbation invalidate the fast. As for sexual intercourse, penetration invalidates the fast.

The third condition: our statement "with knowledge that one is fasting." So if one eats or drinks forgetting that he is fasting, his fast is not invalidated according to Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, and according to Malik it is invalidated.

The fourth condition: our statement "from the beginning of the true dawn." The evidence for it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. The word (hatta), "until," indicates the endpoint. Al-A'mash used to say: its beginning is when the sun rises, and he would permit eating and drinking after the dawn and before sunrise, arguing that just as the end of the day is from the time of sunset, so its beginning must be from the time of its rising. This is invalid by the explicit text we have cited. It is narrated from al-A'mash that Abu Hanifa visited him while he was ill, and al-A'mash said to him: "You are a burden on my heart while you are in your house, so how would it be if you visited me!" Abu Hanifa remained silent. When he left, he was asked: "Why did you remain silent?" He said: "And what should I say about a man who has neither fasted nor prayed in his whole life?" He meant by it that he used to eat after the second dawn and before the sun, so he had no fast, and he did not perform ghusl from seminal emission, so he had no prayer.

The fifth condition: our statement "until sunset." The evidence for it is his saying, peace be upon him: "When the night approaches from here and the day departs from here, the fasting person has broken his fast." Some people say that the time of breaking the fast is at the setting of the sun's light, analogizing this end of the day to the first end of the day.

The sixth condition: our statement "together with intention."
