Some people say: there is no need for intention for the fast of Ramadan, because Allah Most High commanded fasting in His saying: (so let him fast), and fasting is abstention, and it has been fulfilled, so he is discharged from the obligation. We say: intention is necessary, because fasting is an act (amal), by the evidence of his saying, peace be upon him: "The best of deeds is fasting." And an act must have intention in it, due to his saying, peace be upon him: "Actions are only by intentions."

The sixth issue: those who hold that the preceding verse indicates that the resident who is healthy has the choice between fasting and breaking the fast with ransom (fidyah). They said: this verse abrogates it (naskh). Abu Muslim al-Isfahani and al-Asamm deny this, and the explanation of this issue has already been given. Then, on the assumption that this view of abrogation is correct, this indicates that abrogating the lighter ruling by a heavier one is permissible, because obligating fasting specifically is heavier than obligating it with the option between it and ransom.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾, the explanation of this verse has already been given, and the reason for the repetition has already been explained.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾, know that this statement is only fittingly mentioned here on the condition that what precedes it is included in it, and the matter here is so. Because Allah Most High obligated fasting in a way of facility and ease, for He only obligated it during a small period of the year, and that small period He did not obligate upon the sick or the traveler, and all of this is in observance of the meaning of ease and facility. Here there are issues:

The first issue: ease (al-yusr) linguistically means facility, and from it comes the word for wealth and abundance, (al-yasar), because affairs become easy by it. And the left hand (al-yad al-yusra) is said to handle actions with ease, and it is said that the matter becomes easier with the help of the right hand.

The second issue: the Mu'tazilah argued with this verse that the imposition of what is beyond one's capacity does not occur. They said: since He, Exalted is He, has explained that He intends for them what is easy and not what is difficult, how then would He impose upon them what they cannot do, such as faith? Its answer: ease and hardship do not indicate generality, because it has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that a singular word to which the definite article (al-) is attached does not indicate generality. Also, even if we concede that, it may refer to a previously known matter, so we restrict it to the previously known matter in this context.

* * *

The third issue: the Mu'tazilah held on to this verse to establish that something may occur from the servant which Allah does not will, because if the sick person forces himself to fast until it exhausts him, then he would have done what Allah does not will from him, since He does not will hardship.

The answer: the wording allows that He does not will to command him with what involves hardship, even if He may will hardship from him, because according to us a command may be established without will.

The fourth issue: they said: this verse indicates His mercy toward His servants. If He willed for them to disbelieve, so that they would go to the Fire, and created that disbelief in them, it would not be fitting for Him to say: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾. The answer: this is countered by knowledge (of Allah).

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you complete the period﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: Abu Bakr, from Asim, read ﴿wa-li-tukmilu al-'iddah﴾ with the letter mim doubled, and the rest read it with the mim light. Both are dialects: aknamtu and kammaltu (both meaning "I completed").

The second issue: someone may ask: ﴿And that you complete the period﴾ is attached to what?

Our answer: they agreed that the verb of causation is omitted. Then there are two views:

One of them is what al-Farra' said, which is that the implied meaning is: "And that you complete the period, and that you glorify Allah for having guided you, and perhaps you will be grateful." The verb refers to the whole of what was mentioned, which is the command to fast the prescribed number of days, the teaching of how to make up the missed days, and the concession to permit breaking the fast. This is because when He mentioned these three matters, He mentioned after them three expressions. So His saying ﴿And that you complete the period﴾ is the reason for the command to observe the prescribed number. ﴿And that you glorify﴾ is the reason for what you have learned of the manner of making up the days. ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾ is the reason for the concession and facilitation. A parallel to what we have mentioned, of omitting a verb that indicates what came before it, is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75], meaning: "We showed him."

The second view is what al-Zajjaj said, which is that what is meant is that the obligation previously imposed upon the resident who is healthy stands, and the concession for the sick and the traveler is only for completing the prescribed number. This is because with capacity it is easy for him to complete the number, and with the concession in illness and travel it is easy to complete the number by making up the days, so it is not hardship. Thus Allah Most High explained that He imposed the obligation on everyone in a way that completing the number is not difficult, but easy and light. The difference between the two views is that in the first there is an implied element that comes after His saying ﴿And that you complete the period﴾, and in the second it comes before it.

The third issue: He said ﴿And that you complete the period﴾ and did not say "And that you complete the month," because when He said "that you complete the period," the number of days of the month entered within it, and the number of days of making up, since both are mentioned. For this reason, the number of days of making up must be equal to the number of days missed. If Allah Most High had said "that you complete the month," it would indicate the ruling of performance (ada') only, and the ruling of making up would not be included.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾, there are two views:

The first: what is meant by it is glorifying (takbir) on the night of Fitr. Ibn Abbas said: it is a duty upon the Muslims, when they see the crescent of Shawwal, to glorify. Al-Shafi'i said: "I love to make the glorification apparent during both festivals." This is also the view of Malik, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. Abu Hanifa said: that is disliked on the morning of Fitr. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, argued by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you complete the period, and that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾, and said: its meaning is: "And that you complete the number of the month of Ramadan, so that you glorify Allah at its conclusion for having guided you to this obedience." Then from this three issues branch out:

The first: his view differed as to which of the two festivals is more emphatic in glorification. In the old view (al-qadim) he said: the night of sacrifice (Nahr) is more emphatic, because the predecessors (salaf) agreed upon it. In the new view (al-jadid) he said: the night of Fitr is more emphatic, because the text (nass) came concerning it.

The second: the time of the glorification is after the sunset of the night of Fitr. Malik said: one does not glorify on the night of Fitr, but glorifies on its day. This is narrated from Ahmad. Ishaq said: when one goes out to the musalla (place of prayer). The argument of al-Shafi'i is that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ indicates that the command to this implies that the glorification occurred as a consequence of achieving this guidance, but after the sunset this guidance is achieved, so the glorification must be from that time.

The third: the view of al-Shafi'i is that the time of this glorification extends until the imam begins the prayer. Two other views have been stated: one is until the imam goes out, and the second is until the imam leaves. The correct one is the first. Abu Hanifa said: when one reaches the nearest musalla, he stops glorifying.

The second opinion: regarding His words ﴿And that you may glorify Allah﴾, it means exalting Allah in gratitude for having been guided to this act of worship. Know that the complete form of this glorification (takbir) is achieved through speech, belief, and action. As for speech: affirming His exalted attributes and His beautiful names, and declaring Him free of whatever is unbefitting for Him, such as rivals, consorts, offspring, and resemblance to created beings. All of this is valid only after the belief of the heart is sound. As for action: devotion through acts of worship such as prayer, fasting, and pilgrimage. Know that the first opinion is closer to the truth, because glorifying Allah in this sense is obligatory at all times and with every act of worship; so singling out this act of worship for this glorification necessitates that this glorification has a special distinction beyond the glorification that is obligatory at all times.

As for His words, ﴿for having guided you﴾, it includes a great favor in this world through the proofs, the making known, the granting of success, and the protection (from error), and according to our companions (the Ash'aris), through the creation of obedience.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾, there are two discussions concerning it:

The first: the word "la'alla" (perhaps, so that) indicates hope (tarajji), and hope is not permissible with respect to Allah.

The second: the discussion of the reality of gratitude (shukr). These two discussions have already been explained.

There remains here a third discussion, which is: what is the benefit of mentioning this expression in this place? We say: when Allah commanded glorification, it cannot be completed unless the servant knows the majesty of Allah, His greatness, His might, His magnificence, and that He is greater than the intellects of the intelligent can reach, the descriptions of those who describe Him, and the mention of those who mention Him. Then the servant knows that He, glorified is He, despite His majesty, His might, and His independence from all created beings, let alone this poor one, has specially favored him with this great guidance. This must lead the servant to occupy himself with thanking Him and to persist in praising Him to the extent of his ability and capacity. For this reason He said: ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 186 (part 1 of 3):

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the one who calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me that they may be guided.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

The first issue: concerning how this verse is connected to what precedes it, there are several views.

The first: when He, exalted is He, said, after the prescription of fasting and the explanation of its rulings: ﴿and so that you may glorify Allah for having guided you, and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], commanding the servant to glorify (takbir), which is remembrance (dhikr), and to give thanks, He clarified that He, glorified is He, by His kindness and mercy, is near to the servant, aware of his remembrance and his thanks, so He hears his call, responds to his supplication, and does not disappoint his hope.

The second: He commanded takbir first and then encouraged supplication second, as an indication that supplication must be preceded by fine praise. Do you not see that the Friend (Khalil, ʿalayhi al-salam) when he wished to supplicate, he put praise before it, so he said first: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 78], up to His saying: ﴿and who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 82]. All of this is praise from him to Allah, the Exalted, then after it he began supplication, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 83]. Likewise here, He commanded takbir first, then began supplication second.

The third: when Allah, the Exalted, prescribed fasting upon them as He had prescribed it upon those before them, and this was such that if they slept, what is forbidden to the fasting person became forbidden to them, this was difficult for some of them, until they disobeyed Allah in that obligation. Then they regretted and asked the Prophet ﷺ about their repentance, so Allah, the Exalted, sent down this verse informing them of the acceptance of their repentance, and abrogated that strictness on account of their supplication and humble entreaty.

* * *

The second issue: they have mentioned several views regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse:

One of them: what is related from Kaʿb, that he said: Musa, peace be upon him, said: "O my Lord, are You near so that I may confide in You, or far so that I may call out to You?" He said: "O Musa, I am the companion of the one who remembers Me." He said: "O my Lord, we are in states in which we would be ashamed to mention You, such as impurity from sexual discharge and defecation." He said: "O Musa, remember Me in every state." When the matter was in this description, Allah, the Exalted, encouraged His servants to remember Him and to turn to Him in all conditions, so Allah, the Exalted, sent down this verse.

Second: "A Bedouin came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: Is our Lord near so that we may confide in Him, or far so that we may call out to Him? So Allah, the Exalted, sent down this verse."

Third: "He, peace be upon him, was on a campaign, and his companions raised their voices with takbir, tahlil and supplication, so he, peace be upon him, said: 'Indeed you do not call upon one who is deaf or absent; rather you call upon One who is All-Hearing and near.'"

Fourth: what is related from Qatadah and others, that its occasion was: "The Companions said: How should we supplicate to our Lord, O Prophet of Allah? So He sent down this verse."

Fifth: "ʿAta' and others said: They asked him: At what hour should we call upon Allah? So Allah, the Exalted, sent down this verse."

Sixth: what Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned: "The Jews of Madinah said: O Muhammad, how does your Lord hear our supplication? So this verse was revealed."

Seventh: al-Hasan said: "The companions of the Prophet ﷺ asked and said: Where is our Lord? So Allah sent down this verse."

Eighth: what we have mentioned, that His saying: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ when it required the prohibition of eating after sleep, then they ate, then they regretted and repented, and asked the Prophet ﷺ whether He, exalted is He, would accept our repentance. So Allah sent down this verse.

Know that His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near﴾ indicates that they asked the Prophet, peace be upon him, about Allah, the Exalted. That question is either a question about the essence of Allah, the Exalted, or about His attributes, or about His acts. As for a question about the essence, it is that the questioner is one who permits anthropomorphism (tashbih), so he asks about nearness and distance in terms of the essence. As for a question about the attributes, it is that the questioner asks whether He, exalted is He, hears our supplication, so the question falls on His being All-Hearing; or the purpose of the question is how He has permitted supplication, whether He has permitted supplication with all names, or has permitted only that we call upon Him with specific names, and whether He has permitted us to call upon Him however we wish, or has not permitted us to call upon Him in a specific manner, as He said: ﴿And do not raise your voice in your prayer nor be silent therein﴾ [al-Isra': 110].

As for a question about the acts, it is that the questioner asks Allah, the Exalted, that when He hears our supplication, will He respond to us with what we seek, and will He do what we ask of Him? So His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me﴾ may encompass all these aspects, except that interpreting it as a question about the essence is more preferable for two reasons:

The first: that the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿about Me﴾ indicates that the question fell upon His essence, not upon His act. The second: that when the question is ambiguous and the answer is detailed, the answer indicates that the intended meaning of that ambiguous thing is that specific thing. So when He said in the answer ﴿indeed I am near﴾, we know that the question was about nearness and distance in terms of the essence. However, the one who says may also say: rather the question was about the act, namely whether He, exalted is He, responds to their supplication and whether their aim is achieved, as evidenced by the fact that when He said ﴿indeed I am near﴾ He said ﴿I respond to the invocation of the one who calls upon Me﴾. This is the explanation of this station.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿indeed I am near﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: know that what is meant by this nearness is not nearness in direction and place, but rather nearness in knowledge and preservation. Here it is necessary to explain two matters:

The first matter: explaining that this nearness is not nearness according to place. There are several proofs for this:

The first: if He were in a place pointed to by the senses, He would be divisible, since it is impossible for something to be as small and insignificant as an indivisible atom. If He were divisible, His quiddity would depend for its realization upon the realization of each of its supposed parts, and a part of a thing is other than it; so if He were in a place, He would depend on something other than Himself, and what depends on something other than itself is contingent in its essence, originated, and dependent upon the Creator; and that is impossible with respect to the eternal Creator. Thus it is established that He, exalted is He, is impossible to be in a place, so His nearness is not nearness by place.

The second: if He were in a place, then either He would be unbounded in all directions, or unbounded in one direction and not another, or He would be bounded from all sides. The first is impossible, because decisive proofs show that supposing an unbounded dimension is impossible. The second is also impossible for this same reason, and also because if one of the two sides were bounded and the other unbounded, the reality of this bounded side would differ in quiddity from the reality of that unbounded side, and it would follow that He is composed of parts of differing natures, and the opponent does not say this. As for the third division, namely that He is bounded from all sides, that is false by agreement between us and our opponents. Thus the view that He is in a direction is refuted.

The third: this verse is among the strongest proofs that the nearness mentioned in this verse is not nearness by direction. For if He were in a place, He would not be near to all things; rather He would be near to the bearers of the Throne and distant from others, and if He were near to Zayd who is in the east, He would be distant from ʿAmr who is in the west. Since the verse indicates that He is near to all, we know that the nearness mentioned in this verse is not nearness according to direction. And since it is refuted that the intended meaning is nearness by direction, it is established that the intended meaning is nearness in the sense that He hears their supplication and sees their humble entreaty, or the intended meaning of this nearness is knowledge and preservation. On this basis He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4], and He said: ﴿And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16], and He said: ﴿There is no secret conversation among three but that He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7]. The Muslims say that He is in every place, and they mean by this management, preservation and guarding. Once you have understood this premise, we say: it is not far-fetched that among those present there was someone who held the view of anthropomorphism, for among the polytheists of the Arabs and among the Jews and others there were those with this outlook. So when they asked him, peace be upon him, saying: "Where is our Lord?", the answer ﴿indeed I am near﴾ was valid. Likewise, if they asked him, peace be upon him, saying: "Does our Lord hear our supplication?", it was valid for him to answer: ﴿indeed I am near﴾, for one who is near to the speaker hears his speech. And if they asked him how we should call upon Him, with raised voice or with lowered voice, the answer ﴿indeed I am near﴾ was valid. And if they asked him whether He will give us what we seek through supplication, this answer was also suitable. And if they asked him: "If we sin and then repent, will Allah accept our repentance?", it was valid for him to answer with the words ﴿indeed I am near﴾, meaning: I am near to them in regard to looking upon them, overlooking their faults, and accepting their repentance. Thus it is established that this answer corresponds to the question under all these possibilities.

* * *

The second issue: the verse indicates that one knows of the occurrence of those things in accordance with the aim of the one who supplicates. It thus indicates that, were there no Governor of this world who hears His servant's supplication and does not disappoint his hope, that aim would not have been achieved at that time.

Know that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿indeed I am near﴾ contains a rational secret. For the attribution of the quiddities of contingent beings to their existences occurs only through the bringing into being by the Maker. So the bringing into being by the Maker is like an intermediary between the quiddities of contingent beings and their existences. Thus the Maker is nearer to the quiddity of every contingent being than the existence of that quiddity is to it. Beyond this there is a more elevated statement: the Maker is the one for whose sake the quiddities of contingent things became existent, and He is also the one for whose sake the substance became a substance, the blackness became blackness, the intellect became intellect, and the soul became soul. Just as through His influence and His creating the quiddities came to exist, likewise through His influence and His creating each quiddity became that quiddity. By analogy with what has preceded, the Maker is nearer to every quiddity than that quiddity is to itself. If it is said: the creating of a quiddity is impossible, for it is not conceivable to make blackness into blackness; we say: likewise it is not possible to make existence into existence, for it is a quiddity, and it is not possible to make the state of being described a sign of the quiddity. Therefore the quiddity is not the agent, and existence is also a quiddity, so it is not the agent; and the describedness of the quiddity by existence is also a quiddity, so it is not by the agent. Therefore nothing at all would come about by the agent, and that is clearly false. Therefore it is necessary to rule that all things are by the agent, and at this point the statement we have established becomes manifest.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I respond to the invocation of the one who calls upon Me when he calls upon Me﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: Abu ʿAmr and Qalun, on the authority of Nafiʿ, read "al-daʿi idha daʿani" with the yāʾ affirmed in both places in pause-free recitation (wasl), and the rest read it with its omission. The first is according to continuous recitation (wasl), and the second according to lightening (takhfif).

**The second issue:** Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: *ad-du'a'* (supplication) is a verbal noun from your saying "da'awtu ash-shay'a ad'uhu du'a'an" (I called upon the thing, I call upon it, calling). Then they used the verbal noun in place of the noun, as you say "sami'tu du'a'an" (I heard a supplication) just as you say "sami'tu sawtan" (I heard a sound). A verbal noun may be placed in the position of a noun, as in their saying "rajulun 'adl" (a just man). The reality of supplication is the servant's seeking of care from his Lord, glorified is His majesty, and his seeking of help from Him.

I say: People have differed about supplication. Some ignorant people said: Supplication is something without benefit, and they argued for this from several aspects:

The first: If what is sought through supplication is known to occur with God, Exalted, then it is necessarily going to occur, and there is no need for supplication. And if it is not known to occur, then it is impossible for it to occur, so there is also no need for supplication.

The second: The occurrence of events in this world must ultimately end, in the final analysis, at the eternal, necessarily existent Originator; otherwise it would necessitate either an infinite regress, or circularity, or an event occurring without an originator, and all of these are impossible. When it is established that they necessarily end, in the final analysis, at the eternal Originator, then whatever that eternal Originator necessitates the existence of with an eternal, everlasting necessitation is necessarily going to occur, and whatever the eternal Originator does not necessitate the existence of with an eternal, everlasting necessitation is impossible to occur. Since these matters were established in eternity, supplication has absolutely no effect. They sometimes expressed this argument by saying: The decrees are preceding and the judgments are prior; supplication does not add to them, and abandoning it does not diminish anything of them, so what is the benefit of supplication? He, peace be upon him, said: "God decreed the decrees before He created creation by so-and-so many years."

It is also narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "The pen has dried by what is to be." And from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Four things have been finished: the lifespan, the provision, the creation, and the character."

The third: He, glorified, is the Knower of unseen things: "He knows the stealthy glances of the eyes and what the breasts conceal" [Ghafir: 19]. So what need does the supplicant have for supplication? For this reason they said that Gabriel, peace be upon him, reached through this statement the highest degrees of sincerity and servitude, and had supplication not been better to abandon, he would not have been so.

The fourth: If what is sought through supplication is of the servant's interests, then the absolutely Generous does not neglect it; and if it is not of his interests, it is not permissible to ask for it.

The fifth: It has been established by the testimonies of reason and authentic hadiths that the most exalted stations of the truthful are contentment with God's decree, Exalted, and supplication contradicts that, because it is occupation with seeking and preference of the self's desire over God's desire, and its request for the portion of humans.

The sixth: Supplication resembles commanding and forbidding, and that from a servant toward the Noble, Merciful Master is bad manners.

The seventh: It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, said, relating from God, glorified and exalted: "Whoever is occupied by remembrance of Me from asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give to those who ask." They said: Thus it is established by these aspects that the better course is to abandon supplication.

The great majority of intellectuals said: Supplication is the most important of the stations of servitude, and this is indicated by several aspects from transmission and reason. As for the transmitted proofs, they are numerous:

The first: God, Exalted, mentioned asking and answering in His Book in several places, some of them fundamental and some of them legal. As for the fundamental ones, His saying: "And they ask you about the Spirit" [al-Isra': 85], "And they ask you about the mountains" [Ta-Ha: 105], "They ask you about the Hour" [an-Nazi'at: 42]. As for the legal ones, among them in al-Baqarah in sequence: "And they ask you what they should spend" [al-Baqarah: 219], "They ask you about the sacred month" [al-Baqarah: 217], "They ask you about wine and gambling" [al-Baqarah: 219], "And they ask you about orphans" [al-Baqarah: 220], "And they ask you about menstruation" [al-Baqarah: 222]. And He also said: "They ask you about the spoils" [al-Anfal: 1], "And they ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn" [al-Kahf: 83], "And they ask you to inform them, 'Is it true?'" [Yunus: 53], "They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah" [an-Nisa': 176].

Knowing this, we say: The answers to these questions came in three types. Most often, when He related the question, He said to Muhammad: "Say"; and in one instance the answer came with His saying "fa-qul" (so say) with the fa' of sequence. The reason for this is that His saying, "And they ask you about the mountains" [Ta-Ha: 105], is a question about their pre-eternity and their origination, and this is a fundamental matter, so God, Exalted, said: "So say: My Lord will blow them away with a blowing" [Ta-Ha: 105], as if He said: O Muhammad, answer this question immediately and do not delay the answer, for doubt in it is disbelief. Then the content of the answer is that blowing away is possible for every part of the mountain, so it is possible for the whole, and the possibility of its non-existence indicates the impossibility of its pre-eternity. As for the rest of the questions, they are legal matters, so the fa' of sequence was not mentioned in them. As for the third type, which is in this verse, He said: "And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near" and did not say "fa-qul inni qarib" (so say, indeed I am near), which indicates the exaltation of the status of supplication in several aspects:

The first: It is as if He, glorified and exalted, says: My servant, you only need an intermediary outside the time of supplication; but at the station of supplication, there is no intermediary between Me and you.

The second: His saying "And when My servants ask you about Me" indicates that the servant belongs to Him, and His saying "indeed I am near" indicates that the Lord is for the servant.

The third: He did not say "so the servant is near to Me," but rather said: "I am near to him," and in this is a precious secret, for the servant is possible of existence, so he, in himself, is at the center of non-existence and the lowest point of annihilation, so he cannot approach the Lord; but the Truth, glorified, is capable of drawing near by His bounty and His mercy to the servant, and the nearness is from the Truth to the servant, not from the servant to the Truth; therefore He said: "indeed I am near."

The fourth: As long as the supplicant's thoughts remain occupied with other than God, he is not a supplicant to Him; but when he passes away from everything and becomes absorbed in knowing the One, the Real, he is prevented from remaining in this station noticing his own right and seeking his portion. So when intermediaries are completely removed, nearness is necessarily attained, for as long as the servant remains turned toward the purpose of his own self, he is not near to God, Exalted, because that purpose veils him from God. Thus it is established that supplication brings nearness to God, so supplication was the best of acts of worship.

The second proof regarding the excellence of supplication: His saying, Exalted: "And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you" [Ghafir: 60].

The third proof: He, Exalted, did not restrict His explanation of the excellence of supplication to commanding it, but explained in another verse that if He is not asked, He becomes angry. He said: "Then why, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts were hardened, and Satan made attractive to them what they used to do" [al-An'am: 43]. He, peace be upon him, also said: "None of you should say: O God, forgive me if You will; rather let him be resolute and say: O God, forgive me." He, peace be upon him, said: "Supplication is the marrow of worship." And it is narrated from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that he, peace be upon him, said: "Supplication is worship," and he recited: "And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you." His saying "Supplication is worship" means that it is the greatest part of worship and its best, like his saying, peace be upon him, "Hajj is 'Arafah," meaning that standing at 'Arafah is the greatest pillar.

The fourth proof: His saying, Exalted: "Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly" [al-A'raf: 55], and He said: "Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication" [al-Furqan: 77]. The verses on this topic are numerous, and whoever nullifies supplication has denied the Qur'an.

As for the answer to the first doubt: it is self-contradictory, because if a person's undertaking of supplication is known to occur, then there is no benefit in your occupying yourselves with nullifying supplication; and if it is known not to occur, there is no need for your denial. Then we say: The manner of God's knowledge and the manner of His decree and destiny is hidden from the intellects, and divine wisdom requires that the servant be suspended between hope and fear, by which servitude is completed. By this path we have validated the doctrine of obligations (taklif) while acknowledging the encompassing of God's knowledge of everything and the operation of His decree and destiny over everything. Regarding this problem, "the Companions asked the Messenger of God ﷺ, saying: Tell us about our deeds: are they something already finished, or a matter He is beginning anew? He said: Rather, something already finished. They said: Then what is the point of action? He said: 'Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for.'" Consider the subtleties of this hadith: he, peace be upon him, linked them between the two matters; he made them fear the preceding decree that is finished, then obligated them to the action which is the path of worship, so he did not nullify the outward action by what the decree implies, nor did he leave one of the two matters for the other. He informed them that the benefit of action is the decreed thing that is finished, saying: "Each is made easy for what he was created for," meaning that he is made easy during the days of his life for the action which destiny had decreed for him before his existence. However, you wish to know here the difference between "muyassar" (made easy) and "musakhkhar" (compelled), so prepare yourself to understand it, for it is on the level of the question of qadar and decree; and likewise is the matter of earning and provision, for it is already finished in origin: effort does not increase it, nor does abandonment diminish it.

As for the answer to the second doubt: The purpose of supplication is not to inform (God), but rather to manifest servitude, humility, brokenness, and returning to God entirely.

As for the third: It is permissible for what is not a benefit to become a benefit according to the precedence of supplication.

As for the fourth: If his aim in supplication is to manifest lowliness and neediness, and afterward he is content with what God has decreed and decided, then that is the greatest of stations. This is the answer to the rest of the doubts on this topic.

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** There is a famous difficult question concerning the verse. He, Exalted, said: "Call upon Me, I will respond to you," and in this verse: "I respond to the call of the caller when he calls Me," and likewise "Or who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him" [an-Naml: 62]. Then we see the supplicant striving greatly in supplication and humility, yet he is not answered.

The answer: Although this verse is absolute, another verse has come restricted, namely His saying, Exalted: "Rather, it is Him you call upon, and He removes what you call upon Him for, if He wills" [al-An'am: 41]. There is no doubt that the absolute is understood in light of the restricted. Then the explanation of the meaning in this has several aspects:

The first: The supplicant must find a return from his supplication, either by the fulfillment of the need for which he called, and this is when it accords with the decree; but if the decree does not assist him, he is given tranquility in his soul, expansion in his chest, and patience by which bearing the present trial becomes easy. In every case he does not lack benefit, and this is a kind of answering.

The second: What al-Qaffal narrated in his tafsir from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The supplication of a Muslim is not rejected except in one of three ways, so long as he does not supplicate for sin or the severing of family ties: either it is hastened for him in this world, or it is stored up for him in the Hereafter, or evil is averted from him to the extent of what he asked."

This report is the complete clarification regarding this question, for He, Exalted, said: "Call upon Me, I will respond to you" [Ghafir: 60], and He did not say "I will respond to you immediately." So when He responds to him, even if in the Hereafter, the promise is true.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 186 (part 3 of 3):**

Third: His saying, ﴿Call upon Me, and I will respond to you﴾, requires that the one who supplicates be one who knows his Lord. Otherwise he would not be calling upon Him, but upon something imagined that has no existence at all. Thus it is established that a condition for the supplicant is that he know his Lord. Among the attributes of the Lord, glorified is He, is that He does only what accords with His decree, His predestination, His knowledge and His wisdom. When the servant knows that the attribute of the Lord is thus, it is impossible for him to say in his heart and mind: "O Lord, I will certainly do such-and-such an act." Rather, he must say: "I will do this act if it accords with Your decree, Your predestination and Your wisdom." At this point the supplication, upon which the verse indicates the ordering of the response, becomes conditioned by these conditions. On this basis, the fourth question disappears. The words "supplication" (du'a') and "response" (ijabah) carry many meanings:

The first: that supplication is an expression for affirming the oneness of God and praising Him, as when the servant says, "O God, there is no god but You." This is called supplication only because you have known God, then declared His oneness and praised Him, so this is called supplication under this interpretation. Since this meaning is called supplication, its acceptance is called response, because of the similarity of the wording, and there are many like this. Ibn al-Anbari (a philologist) said: "Ujib" (I respond) here means "asma'" (I hear), because there is a kind of mutual connection between hearing and responding, and for this reason each of the two is put in place of the other. So when we say "Allah hears whoever praises Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), meaning "Allah responds," likewise here His saying, ﴿I respond to the call of the caller﴾ means "I hear that call." If we take His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Call upon Me, and I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60] in this sense, the difficulty disappears.

Second: that by supplication is meant repentance from sins, because the penitent calls upon God, exalted is He, at the time of repentance. The response to supplication under this interpretation is an expression for the acceptance of repentance. In this sense too there is no difficulty.

Third: that by supplication is meant worship. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Supplication is worship." Among what indicates this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humbled﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. It becomes clear that supplication here is worship. If this is established, then God's response to supplication under this interpretation is an expression for fulfilling what He guaranteed to the obedient of reward, as He said: ﴿and He responds to those who believe and do righteous deeds, and increases them from His bounty﴾ [al-Shura: 26]. Under this sense too the difficulty is removed.

Fourth: that supplication be interpreted as the servant's request of his Lord for his needs. If the question mentioned was directed at this interpretation, it was not directed at the three preceding interpretations, so it is established that the difficulty is removed.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: ﴿I respond to the call of the caller when he calls upon Me﴾ is specific to the believers who have believed and not mixed their faith with wrongdoing. This is because describing a person as one whose supplication God has answered is an attribute of praise and honor. Do you not see that when we want to emphasize the high station of a person in religion, we say that he is one whose supplication is answered? And if this is among the greatest of ranks in religion, while the sinner is deserving of contempt in religion, it is established that this attribute is not established except for one whose faith is not tainted by sin. Rather, the sinner may have God do what he asks, but that is not called the response to supplication.

* * *
*Page 87*

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so let them respond to Me and believe in Me﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The manner of the connection (nazm) is to say: He, exalted is He, said: "I respond to your supplication, although I am entirely independent of you. So you too respond to My call, although you are in need of Me in every respect." How great is this generosity! There is also another subtle point: He, exalted is He, did not say to the servant, "Respond to My call so that I will respond to your supplication," because if He had said that, it would have become a condition for His call. This is a reminder that God's response to His servant is a favor from Him from the outset, that it is not conditioned on the servant's obedience, and that the Lord's response in this matter to the servant precedes the servant's occupation with obedience to the Lord. This indicates the invalidity of what we reported from the Mu'tazila in the fourth issue.

* * *

**The second issue:** al-Wahidi (an exegete) said: "Ajaba" and "istajaba" have one meaning. Ka'b al-Ghanawi said:

*"And a caller who called, 'O You who responds to calls,' but then the Responder did not respond to him."*

The people of meaning said: The servant's response to God is obedience, and God's response to His servant is giving him what he seeks, because the response to each thing is in accordance with what befits it.

**The third issue:** If the servant's response to God is a response by heart and tongue, that is faith itself. In that case His saying, ﴿so let them respond to Me and believe in Me﴾, would be pure repetition. If the servant's response to God is an expression for acts of obedience, then faith precedes acts of obedience, and the arrangement ought to have been: "so let them believe in Me and respond to Me." Why did it come in the reverse order?

The answer: istijabah (responding) is an expression for submission and surrender, while faith is an expression for a quality of the heart. This indicates that the servant does not reach the light of faith and its strength except by first performing acts of obedience and worship.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so that they may be rightly guided﴾, the author of *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari, a Mu'tazili exegete) said: it was read as *yarshudun* and *yarshadun* (with the sh vowelled differently). The meaning of the verse is that if they respond to Me and believe in Me, they will be guided to the interests of their religion and their worldly life, because the *rashid* (rightly guided one) is the one who is like that. It is said: "So-and-so is rashid." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿if you perceive in them maturity of judgment﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], and He said: ﴿those are the rightly guided﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in unto your wives. They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. Allah knows that you used to deceive yourselves, so He turned to you and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you. Eat and drink until﴾
page 88
﴿the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn. Then complete the fast until nightfall. And do not have relations with them while you are staying in the mosques for worship. These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them. Thus does Allah make His verses clear to the people that they may fear Him.﴾

Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: The majority of the exegetes hold that at the beginning of the Sharia of Muhammad (ﷺ), when a fasting person broke his fast, eating, drinking and intercourse were permitted for him on condition that he did not sleep and did not pray the final night prayer (al-ʿIshāʾ al-Ākhira). If he did either of these, these things became forbidden for him. Then Allah, exalted is He, abrogated this with this verse (naskh, abrogation). Abū Muslim al-Isfahani said: this prohibition was never established in our Sharia at all; rather it was established in the Sharia of the Christians, and Allah, exalted is He, abrogated with this verse what was established in their Sharia. He followed here his view that no abrogation has ever occurred in our Sharia at all. The majority argued for their position with several proofs:

The first proof: The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [al-Baqara: 183] requires that our fasting be likened to their fasting. This prohibition was established in their fasting, so by the necessity of this comparison it must also be established in our fasting. And if it is established that the prohibition was established in our Sharia, and this verse abrogates this prohibition, it follows that this verse abrogates a ruling that was established in our Sharia.

The second proof: Holding to the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in unto your wives.﴾ Had this permissibility been established for this community from the very beginning, the saying ﴿It is made lawful for you﴾ would have no benefit.

The third proof: Holding to the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Allah knows that you used to deceive yourselves﴾. Had that been lawful for them, there would have been no need for them to deceive themselves.

The fourth proof: The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿so He turned to you and pardoned you﴾. Had that not been forbidden for them, and had they not committed a sin by engaging in that act, the saying ﴿so He turned to you and pardoned you﴾ would not be valid.

The fifth proof: The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾. Had the permissibility been established before that just as it is now, the saying ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾ would have no benefit.

The sixth proof: The narrations transmitted concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse indicate that this prohibition was established in our Sharia. This is the total of the evidences of those who affirm abrogation.

Abū Muslim responded to these proofs, saying:

As for the first proof: it is weak, because we have shown that likening fasting to fasting is sufficient for its truth through their sharing in the basic obligation.

As for the second proof, it is also weak, because we concede that this prohibition was established in the Sharia of those before us. The saying ﴿It is made lawful for you﴾ means that what was forbidden for others has been made lawful for you.

As for the third proof: it is also weak, because that prohibition was established in the Sharia of ʿIsā (peace be upon him), and Allah, exalted is He, obligated fasting upon us without clarifying in that brevity the removal of that prohibition. So it would occur to them that that prohibition was established in the earlier Sharia, and nothing in our Sharia indicated its removal, so it was necessary to say it remained. Then this illusion was reinforced by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾, for the requirement of the comparison is the occurrence
page 89
of resemblance in all matters. Since this prohibition was established in the earlier Sharia, it must be established in this Sharia as well. Even if this is not a strong proof, it is at least a misleading suspicion. For these reasons they believed that this prohibition remained in our Sharia, so they were inevitably strict and refrained from these matters. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah knows that you used to deceive yourselves﴾, and by this He intended consideration for the believers, with lightening upon them, since had the permission not been made clear, they would have been strict and refrained from these matters, and would have deprived themselves of desire and prevented them from what they wanted. The root of khiyana is deficiency; khāna, ikhtāna and takhawwana have one meaning, like their saying kasaba, iktasaba and takassaba. So the meaning of the verse is: Allah knew that if the permissibility of eating, drinking and intimacy throughout the night had not been made clear to you, you would diminish yourselves in their desires and deprive yourselves of their pleasures and benefits by refraining from that after sleep, like the custom of the Christians.

As for the fourth proof: it is weak, because the repentance of servants is their return to Allah, exalted is He, through worship, and the repentance of Allah is His return to the servant through mercy and kindness. As for pardon (ʿafw), it is overlooking. Allah, exalted is He, thus made clear His bounty upon us by lightening what He had made heavy upon those before us, as in His saying: ﴿and He removes from them their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 157].

As for the fifth proof: it is weak, because they were, due to that suspicion, refraining from intimacy. When Allah, exalted is He, clarified that and removed the suspicion concerning it, He inevitably said: ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾.

As for the sixth proof: it is weak, because our saying that this verse abrogates a ruling that was legislated has no connection to the domain of action, and a single report (khabar al-wahid) is not a proof in it. Also, there is in the verse what indicates the weakness of these narrations, because what is mentioned in those narrations is that the people confessed what they had done before the Messenger, and that contradicts the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Allah knows that you used to deceive yourselves﴾, since its apparent meaning is intimacy, for it is an form (ifti'al) from khiyana. This is the summary of the discussion on this issue.

* * *

The second issue: Those who hold that this prohibition was established in our Sharia and then abrogated mention regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse that at the beginning of the Sharia eating, drinking and intercourse were permitted as long as a man did not sleep or pray the final night prayer; if he did either, these things became forbidden for him until the following night. "A man from the Ansar came in the evening, exhausted by the fast, and they differed about his name. Muʿadh said: his name was Abū Ṣirma; al-Barāʾ said: Qays ibn Ṣirma; al-Kalbi said: Abū Qays ibn Ṣirma; and it was said: Ṣirma ibn Anas. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him about the cause of his weakness, and he said: O Messenger of Allah, I worked in the palm groves all day until evening, then I came to my family that they might feed me something, but they delayed, so I slept, and they woke me up, and eating had become forbidden. Then ʿUmar stood and said: O Messenger of Allah, I apologize to you for the like of this; I returned to my family after I had prayed the final night prayer, and I came to my wife. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: You were not worthy of that, O ʿUmar. Then men stood up and confessed what they had done, and there was revealed the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in unto your wives.﴾"

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: it was read as "Uḥilla lakum laylata al-ṣiyām al-rafath," meaning uḥilla Allāh (Allah made lawful). And ʿAbd Allah read: "al-rufūth."

The fourth issue: Al-Wahidi said: "laylata al-ṣiyām" means "layālī al-ṣiyām" (the nights of the fast), so the singular was used in place of the plural, and from this is the saying of al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās:

"We said: Submit, for we are your brothers; the breasts have been cleansed of grudges."

page 90

I say there is another aspect regarding this: that "laylat al-ṣiyām" does not mean a single night, but rather indicates the night attributed to this reality (the fast).

* * *

The fifth issue: Al-Layth said: al-rafath originally means obscene speech. And al-Zajjaj recited:

"And many a company of pilgrims, restrained from idle talk and the obscene speech of conversation."

It is said: rafatha fi kalamihi yarfuthu and arfatha, when he spoke with ugliness. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity nor wickedness﴾ [al-Baqara: 197]. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he recited while in the state of ihram:

"And they walk with us gently, if the bird speaks truly, we shall mount the lamis."

It was said to him: Do you utter obscenity? He said: Obscenity is only what is said in the presence of women. Thus it is established that the original meaning of rafath is obscene speech, then it became a term for what is said in the presence of women of matters of intimacy, then it became a euphemism for intercourse and for everything that follows it.

If it is said: why did He here use the euphemism for intercourse with the word rafath, which signifies ugliness, unlike His saying: ﴿And some of you have gone in unto others﴾ [al-Nisa: 21], ﴿And when he covered her﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 189], ﴿or you have touched women﴾ [al-Nisa: 43], ﴿you have gone in unto them﴾ [al-Nisa: 23], ﴿before you have touched them﴾ [al-Baqara: 237], ﴿so for what you have enjoyed of them﴾ [al-Nisa: 24], ﴿and do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqara: 222]?

Answer: The reason is the reproach of what they had done before the permission, just as He named it deceiving of themselves; and Allah knows best.

The sixth issue: Al-Akhfash said: He only transitived rafath with ilā because it implies the meaning of ifḍāʾ (going in) in His saying: ﴿And some of you have gone in unto others﴾ [al-Nisa: 21].

* * *

The seventh issue: His saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast, the rafath﴾ requires that the permission occurs throughout the whole night, because "laylata" is put in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf). The night can be a time-frame for the rafath only if the whole night is occupied with the rafath; otherwise the time-frame of that rafath would be part of the night, not all of it. Accordingly, abrogation was achieved by this wording. As for what follows in His saying: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾, that serves as an emphasis of this abrogation. And as for one who says that His saying ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast, the rafath﴾ indicates the permissibility of rafath at night, this amount does not require that abrogation was achieved by it, so the abrogating text is His saying: ﴿Eat and drink﴾.

* * *

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: We have mentioned several aspects regarding the comparison of the spouses to garments:

One: Since the man and the woman embrace, each one presses his body against the body of the other until each becomes for the other like the garment that one wears, each of them was called a garment. Al-Rabiʿ said: "They are a bedding for you, and you are a covering for them." Ibn Zayd said: "They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them" means that each of them conceals the other during intercourse from the eyes of people.

Two: The spouses were called a garment only so that each conceals the other from what is not lawful, as came in the report: "Whoever marries has secured two-thirds of his religion."

Three: He made them a garment for the man in that he particularly belongs to her, as he particularly belongs to his garment, and he regards her as fit for every part of his body to meet every part of hers, as he does with clothing.

Four: It is possible that the meaning is that he is shielded by her from all the harms that would occur in the house if the woman were not present, just as a person shields himself with his clothing from heat, cold and many harms.

Five: al-Asamm mentioned that the meaning is that each of them was like a garment concealing the other in that forbidden act they were committing; but this is weak, because He introduced this description as a favour upon us, so how can it be taken to mean concealing oneself with them in what is forbidden?

The second issue: al-Wahidi said: He made "garment" singular after "them" because it functions as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and fiʿāl is from the verbal nouns of fāʿala, and its interpretation is: they are those who are in contact with you as garments (mulābasāt lakum).

The third question: The author of al-Kashshaf said: If you ask, what is the position of His saying: ﴿They are a garment for you﴾? We say: it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), serving as an explanation of the reason for the permission. That is, when such close association and contact arise between you and them, your patience with them diminishes and it becomes hard for you to abstain from them; therefore He granted you permission to be intimate with them.
* * *
As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾, there are several issues:
The first issue: It is said: khana-hu, yakhunu-hu, khawnan and khiyanatan, when he does not keep faith with him. If a sword fails to strike, it has betrayed you; if fortune turns for the worse, it has betrayed him; if a man does not render a trust, he has betrayed it; and one who breaks a covenant is a traitor (kha'in), because faithfulness was expected of him and he deceived. From this is His saying: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾ [al-Anfal: 58], meaning the breaking of a covenant. A man in debt is also called a traitor, because he has not fulfilled what befits his religion. From this is His saying: ﴿Do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts﴾ [al-Anfal: 27], and He said: ﴿And if they intend to betray you, they have betrayed Allah before﴾ [al-Anfal: 71]. In this verse Allah called disobedience "betrayal." Having understood the meaning of khiyanah, the author of al-Kashshaf said: al-ikhtiyan is from khiyanah, like iktisab from kasb, with an added intensity.
The second issue: Allah, Exalted is He, mentions here that they were betraying themselves, but He does not mention what that betrayal concerned. So this betrayal must be understood as relating to what precedes and what follows. What precedes is the mention of intercourse, and what follows is His saying: ﴿So now, be intimate with them﴾. Therefore the intended betrayal must be intercourse. Here there are two views:
The first: Allah knew that you were secretly committing disobedience in intercourse after the 'atamah (night prayer) and eating after sleep, and you were committing what was forbidden in that. Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has betrayed himself and has betrayed Allah, because he has brought punishment upon himself. According to this view, it must be affirmed that this occurred from some of them, because it cannot be understood as having occurred from all of them. For if His saying "Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves" were taken literally, it would require that all of them were betraying themselves. But we know that the intended meaning is partial, by custom and by report. Once this is established, it must be affirmed that this forbidden intercourse occurred from some of them. From this aspect, it indicates a prior prohibition and that some of them committed it. Abu Muslim may say: we have explained that khiyanah is an expression for failing to fulfil what is obligatory upon one. You have understood it as failing to fulfil obedience to Allah, while we understood it as failing to fulfil what is good for oneself, and this is preferable, because Allah, Exalted is He, did not say "Allah knew that you were betraying Allah," as He said: ﴿Do not betray Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 27], but rather said: ﴿you were betraying yourselves﴾. So if interpreting the wording as we have mentioned is not preferable, it is at least equal, and according to this interpretation abrogation is not established.
The second view: The intended meaning of ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾ is: had that prohibition continued. Its meaning is: Allah knew that if that burdensome obligation continued, they would fall into betrayal. According to this interpretation, betrayal did not actually occur. It may be said: the first interpretation is preferable, because it does not require supposing a condition. And it may be said: rather, the second is preferable, because according to the first interpretation their committing disobedience would become a cause for abrogating the obligation, whereas according to the second: Allah knew that if that obligation continued, betrayal would occur, so that becomes a cause for abrogating the obligation out of Allah's mercy toward His servants, so that they would not fall into betrayal.
As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He turned to you in forgiveness﴾, its meaning according to Abu Muslim is: He returned to you by permitting this act and granting you latitude. According to those who affirm abrogation, it necessarily requires an implied element, its supposed meaning being: "you repented, so He turned to you in forgiveness."
As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and pardoned you﴾, according to Abu Muslim its meaning is: He widened things for you by permitting you to eat, drink and be intimate throughout the night. The word 'afw is sometimes used for widening and easing. He, peace be upon him, said: "I have excused you from the charity of horses and slaves," and he said: "The beginning of the time is Allah's pleasure, and its end is Allah's pardon," meaning the easing of delaying the prayer until the end of its time. It is said: this wealth came to me 'afwan, that is, easily. Thus it is established that the word 'afw does not imply a prior prohibition. As for those who affirm abrogation, His saying "He pardoned you" must be understood as implying: "He pardoned your sins." This also strengthens Abu Muslim's view, because his interpretation does not need an implied element, whereas the interpretation of those who affirm abrogation does.
* * *
As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So now, be intimate with them﴾, there are two issues:
The first issue: This is a command coming after a prohibition. Those who said that a command coming after a prohibition is only for permissibility have a clear argument. As for those who said that a command in its unrestricted form indicates obligation, they said: we have set aside the apparent meaning and know that this command is for permissibility by consensus.
* * *
The second issue: Regarding mubashara (intimacy) there are two views:
The first, which is the view of the majority: it means intercourse. It was so named because the two skins touch and join. Among the reports is that he, peace be upon him, "forbade a man to be intimate with a man, or a woman with a woman."
The second, which is the view of al-Asamm: it means intercourse and what is less than it. On this basis, the commentators differed about the meaning of His saying: ﴿And do not be intimate with them while you are in retreat in the mosques﴾. Some understood it as covering all forms of intimacy and did not restrict it to intercourse. The closer view is that since the word mubashara is derived from the touching of the two skins, it is not restricted to intercourse, but includes intercourse short of the private part, and likewise embracing and touching. However, they agreed in this verse that what is meant is intercourse, because the cause of this concession was that intercourse had occurred among the people, and because the earlier-mentioned rafath can only mean intercourse. But since permission for intercourse entails permission for what is less than it, its permission indicates the permissibility of other things. So it is correct here to understand the speech as referring to intercourse alone. And since prohibition of intercourse during i'tikaf does not indicate prohibition of what is less than it, the commentators' disagreement about it is acceptable. This is what must be relied upon, as summarized by al-Qadi.
* * *
As for His saying: ﴿and seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾, there are several issues:
The first issue: The commentators mentioned several interpretations of the verse:
One: "And seek what Allah has decreed for you" means offspring through intimacy; that is, do not engage in intimacy merely to satisfy desire, but to seek what marriage was established by Allah for, namely procreation. He, peace be upon him, said: "Marry, multiply, so that you increase in number."
Two: It forbids coitus interruptus ('azl), and reports have been transmitted disliking it. Al-Shafi'i said: a man should not practise 'azl with a free woman except with her permission, and there is no harm in practising it with a slave woman. 'Asim transmitted from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he disliked 'azl. And from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ "forbade practising 'azl with a free woman except with her permission."
Three: The meaning is: seek the place that Allah has decreed and made lawful for you, not the forbidden place. A parallel is His saying: ﴿So come to them as Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222].
Four: This emphasis means: "So now, be intimate with them, and seek this intimacy which He has prescribed for you after it had been forbidden to you."
Five: According to Abu Muslim: "So now, be intimate with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you," meaning this intimacy which Allah had decreed for you, even though you thought it forbidden to you.
Six: Intimacy with a wife may be forbidden at certain times due to menstruation, postpartum bleeding, the waiting period, or apostasy. So His saying "and seek what Allah has decreed for you" means: do not be intimate with them except in the states and times in which you have been permitted to be intimate with them.
Seven: His saying "So now, be intimate with them" is permission for intimacy, and His saying "and seek what Allah has decreed for you" means: do not seek this intimacy except with a wife or a slave-woman, because that is what Allah has decreed for you by His saying: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 30].
Eight: Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Abu al-Jawza', said: it means seek Laylat al-Qadr and the reward that Allah has decreed for you in it, if you find it. Most of the verifiers considered this view unlikely, but in my view there is no harm in it. That is: as long as a person's heart is occupied with seeking desire and pleasure, he cannot then devote himself to obedience, servanthood and presence. But when he has fulfilled his need and becomes free from seeking desire, he can then devote himself to servanthood. So the meaning of the verse is: "So now, be intimate with them" until you are freed from those thoughts that prevent sincerity in servanthood; and when you have been freed from them, "seek what Allah has decreed" of sincerity in servanthood, in prayer, remembrance, glorification, declaring God's oneness, and seeking Laylat al-Qadr. Undoubtedly, this report on this interpretation is not unlikely.
* * *
The second issue: Regarding "kataba" (decreed), there are several meanings:
One: "kataba" here means "ja'ala" (made), like His saying: ﴿He has written faith in their hearts﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22], i.e., made; and His saying: ﴿So write us among the witnesses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 53], and ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], i.e., I will make it.
Two: It means "qada" (decreed), like His saying: ﴿Say: Nothing will afflict us except what Allah has decreed for us﴾ [al-Tawbah: 51], i.e., decreed it; and His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: I and My messengers will surely prevail﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21]; and His saying: ﴿Those for whom death was decreed would have gone forth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154], i.e., decreed.
Three: Its origin is what Allah has written in the Preserved Tablet of what is to exist, and every ruling He has issued upon His servants He has recorded in the Preserved Tablet.
Four: It is what Allah has written in the Qur'an of the permissibility of these acts.
The third issue: Ibn 'Abbas recited "wabtaghu" and al-A'mash recited "wabghu."

As for His saying: ﴿And eat and drink﴾, the benefit of mentioning them is that since the prohibition of both and of intercourse at night after sleep had preceded, each of them needed a specific proof by which the prohibition would be lifted. Had Exalted Allah confined Himself to His saying "So now, be intimate with them," it would not have been known from that that the prohibition on eating and drinking had been lifted. So He added His saying "And eat and drink" to complete the indication of permissibility.
* * *
As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn﴾, there are issues:
The first issue: "It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, 'Adi ibn Hatim said: I took two cords, one white and one black,"

[Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verse 187 (part 3 of 4)]

I placed them under my pillow, and I would get up during the night and look at them, but the white did not become distinct to me from the black. When I awoke in the morning, I went early to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and he laughed and said: "Indeed you have a broad nape. That is only the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him, "Indeed you have a broad nape," because that is among the things by which a man's dullness is inferred. We say: this clearly indicates that He, the Exalted, used these words as a metaphor for the whiteness of the beginning of the day and the blackness of the end of the night.

There is a difficulty here. The whiteness of dawn likened to a black thread is the "false dawn" (al-subh al-kadhib), because it is an elongated whiteness resembling a thread. As for the "true dawn" (al-subh al-sadiq), it is a whiteness spreading round on the horizon. So, by the implication of this verse, the beginning of the day would have to be from the rising of the false dawn, and by consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars) this is not the case.

Its answer: had it not been for the words of His, the Exalted, at the end of this verse, ﴿from the dawn﴾, the question would be unavoidable. This is because dawn (al-fajr) is only called "fajr" because light bursts forth from it (yanfajiru minhu al-nur), and this happens only at the second dawn, not at the first dawn. So when the verse indicates that the white thread must be "from the dawn," we know that what is meant is not the false dawn but the true dawn. If it is said: how is the true dawn likened to a thread, when the true dawn is not elongated and the thread is elongated?

Its answer: the amount of whiteness that becomes forbidden is the beginning of the true dawn, and the beginning of the true dawn is not spread out but is small and fine. Indeed, the difference between it and the false dawn is that the false dawn rises fine and thin, while the true dawn appears fine and then rises elongated. Thus the question is resolved. As for what is related from ʿAdiyy ibn Hatim, it is far-fetched, because it is unlikely that such a metaphor would be hidden from someone like him, together with His words, the Exalted: ﴿from the dawn﴾.

Second issue: there is no doubt that the word "ḥattā" (until) indicates the endpoint of a limit. This verse indicates that the permissibility of intimate relations, eating and drinking ends at the rising of dawn. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani claimed that none of the things that break the fast are other than one of these three. As for the matters the jurists mention, such as deliberately inducing vomiting, enema, and snuff (nasal medication), none of them breaks the fast. He said: because all of these things were permitted, then this verse made these three forbidden to the fasting person after dawn, so everything other than them remains in its original permissibility, and none of them breaks the fast. The jurists said that Allah, the Exalted, singled out these three things for mention because the soul inclines toward them, whereas the soul dislikes vomiting and enemas, and snuff is rare, which is why it was not mentioned.

* * *

Third issue: the position of Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy is that if a person in a state of major impurity (junub) reaches the morning before performing ghusl, he has no valid fast. This verse refutes their view, because if intimate relations were permitted until the breaking of dawn, it would not have been possible for him to perform ghusl except after the breaking of dawn.

* * *

Fourth issue: al-A'mash claimed that eating, drinking and intercourse are permitted after the breaking of dawn and before the sunrise, by analogy of the beginning of the day to its end. Just as the end of the day is by the sinking of the disc (of the sun), the beginning of it must be by the rising of the disc. He said regarding the verse that what is meant by the white thread and the black thread is the day and the night, and the point of resemblance is only in whiteness and blackness. If the resemblance in shape were intended, this is impermissible, because the darkness of the horizon at the time of dawn cannot be likened to a black thread in shape at all. So it is established that what is meant by the white thread and the black thread is the day and the night. Then, when we investigated the reality of "night" in His words, ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾, we found it to mean the period of the sun's absence, as evidenced by the fact that Allah, the Exalted, called what comes after sunset "night" even though light remains in it. It is thus established that the matter at the first end of the day is similar, so that before the sunrise it is night, and the day only exists at the rising of the disc. This is the formulation of al-A'mash's view. Among people, some accepted that the beginning of the day is from the rising of dawn, and by analogy applied this to the end of the day. Some said: breaking the fast is not permitted until the redness has disappeared. Others went further and said: breaking the fast is not permitted except at the appearance of the stars. These positions have died out, and the jurists have unanimously agreed on their invalidity, so there is no benefit in extended discussion of them.

Fifth issue: "al-fajr" is the verbal noun of your saying: "fajartu al-maʾ (I split the water), afjuruhu fajran," and "fajjartuhu tafjiran." Al-Azhari said: the root of "fajr" is splitting. Based on this, the fajr at the end of the night is the splitting of the darkness of the night by the light of dawn.

* * *

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿from the dawn﴾, it has been said that "min" here is for partition (lil-tab'id), because what is considered is part of the dawn and not all of it. It has also been said that it is for explanation (lil-tabyin), as if it were said: "the white thread which is the dawn."

Sixth issue: when Allah, the Exalted, made intercourse, eating and drinking permissible up to the limit of the clear appearance of dawn, it became necessary to know what the clear appearance of dawn is. We say: the way to knowing the clear appearance of dawn is either definitive (qat'i) or presumptive (zanni). As for the definitive, it is that one sees the dawn rise, or one is certain that a period of time has passed in which dawn must rise. As for the presumptive, we say: either a presumption arises that dawn has risen, in which case eating, drinking and intercourse become forbidden; or a presumption arises that it has not risen, in which case eating, drinking and intercourse remain permissible. If he eats and then it becomes clear that this presumption was mistaken and that dawn had risen at the time of that eating, the scholars have disagreed. Likewise if he presumed the sun had set, broke the fast, and then it became clear that it had not set. Al-Hasan said: there is no expiation (qada') in either case, by analogy with the case of one who eats forgetfully. Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in the narration of al-Muzani from him said: expiation is obligatory, because he was commanded to fast from dawn until sunset and did not do so. As for the forgetful person, according to Malik, expiation is obligatory for him. As for the rest, who accepted that there is no expiation, they said: the requirement of the evidence is that expiation be obligatory for him as well, but we dropped it for him on the basis of a textual proof, which is what Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man said: 'I ate and drank while I was fasting.' Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'May Allah feed you and give you drink, for you are the guest of Allah; complete your fast.'"

The third position: if he errs regarding the rising of dawn, there is no expiation; if he errs regarding the sinking of the sun, expiation is required. The difference is that the basic principle regarding anything established is that it remains as it was. What is established at night is the permissibility of eating, and during the day its prohibition. As for when the person has not come to a firm presumption either that night persists or that dawn has risen, but remains uncertain about both, then in this case eating, drinking and intercourse are disliked for him. If he does them, it is permissible, because the original state is that night persists. And Allah knows best.

* * *
