As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: the word ﴿until﴾ (ila) indicates the endpoint of a limit. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the fast ends upon the entry of the night. This is because the limit (ghayah) of a thing is its termination and endpoint, and it is only a termination and endpoint if nothing remains after it. This word may also come not for ending, as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿to the elbows﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], but this is contrary to the evidence. The difference between the two cases is that the night is not of the same kind as the day, so the night lies outside the ruling of the day, whereas the elbows are of the same kind as the hand, so they are included in it. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: it is a matter of inclusion and exclusion, and both are permissible. You say: "I ate the fish up to its head," and it is permissible that the head is included in the eating and also excluded from it. However, no person of sound intellect doubts that the night is outside the fast, for if it were included in it the hardship would be great, and the elbows would have been included in the washing out of caution. Then, whether we say it is ambiguous (mujmal) or not ambiguous, the sound hadith concerning it has been transmitted, which is what ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the night approaches from here, and the day turns its back from here, and the sun has set, the fasting person has broken his fast." This hadith indicates that the fast ends at this time. As for whether it is obligatory for the responsible person to take something at this time, the evidence for it is what al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated with his chain from Ibn ʿUmar: that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade continuous fasting (wisal). It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, you practise continuous fasting?" That is: how can you forbid us from a matter you yourself do? He said: "I am not like you. I spend the night with my Lord; He feeds me and gives me drink." Several meanings have been stated regarding this:

One: he was fed and given drink from the food of Paradise.

Second: he, peace be upon him, said: "I am certain that if I needed food, He would feed me while I continue fasting." Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari related from Ibn al-Zubayr that he used to fast continuously for seven days; when he grew old, he made it five; when he grew very old, he made it three. The apparent words of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) indicate that this prohibition is a prohibition of prohibition (tahrim). It has also been said that it is a prohibition of disapproval (tanzih), because it is the abandonment of what is permissible, and on this interpretation the action of Ibn al-Zubayr is valid. Having understood this, we say: if one consumes something small, even a drop of water, then he has the choice to continue fasting, unless one fears that he will fall short in the fast that follows or in other acts of worship, in which case he must then take from the food an amount that removes this fear.

* * *

Second issue: they differed regarding what the night is. Some people said: it is the end of the day upon its beginning. They considered the disappearance of the traces of the sun as the criterion for the arrival of night, just as the disappearance of the night is taken as the criterion for the appearance of the traces of the sun. Then among these some were satisfied with the disappearance of the redness, and some required the appearance of complete darkness and the appearance of the stars. However, the hadith narrated by ʿUmar refutes that, and it is the position on which the jurists act.

* * *

Third issue: the Hanafiyyah (the followers of Abu Hanifa) held onto this verse for the view that intention (tabyit) and specification (ta'yin) are not conditions for the validity of the fast. They said: fasting (al-sawm) in the language is abstention (al-imsak), and this exists here, so he is fasting, and it is obligatory for him to complete it, based on His words, the Exalted: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾. Therefore it is necessary to say that it is valid, because abstention involves hardship, difficulty and strain, which are negated by His words, the Exalted: ﴿He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and His words: ﴿Allah does not intend hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Its application was abandoned in a valid fast, so the invalid fast remains on the original basis. Then we say: the requirement of this evidence is that an obligatory fast be valid with an intention made after midday (al-zawal). However, we said: the lesser follows the greater, so we invalidated a fast with an intention after midday and validated its intention before midday.

* * *

Fourth issue: the Hanafiyyah held onto this verse for the view that a voluntary fast must be completed. They said: because His words, the Exalted: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾ is a command, and a command is for obligation, and it encompasses all fasts. The Shafi'iyyah said: this was revealed only to explain the rulings of the obligatory fast, so what is meant by it is the obligatory fast.

The seventh ruling

* * *

Among the rulings mentioned in this surah is i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque for worship).

His words, the Exalted: ﴿And do not have intimate relations with them while you are devoting yourselves to worship in the mosques.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, explained the fast and explained that among its rulings is the prohibition of intimate relations, it could have been thought that in

[Page 97]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 4 of 4):

…al-i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque) that its state is like the state of fasting in that intercourse is forbidden in it during the day but not at night. So God, exalted is He, clarified the prohibition of physical contact in it both by day and by night, and said: ﴿And do not have intimate contact with them while you are devoted to retreat in the mosques﴾. Then, in the verse there are issues:

The first issue: al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: The linguistic meaning of i'tikaf (devotion, adhering) is a person's constant attachment to something and confining himself to it, whether for good or for evil. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They cling to idols they worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. The legal meaning of i'tikaf is staying in the House of God seeking nearness to Him. Its essence returns to restricting the general term to a specific type by way of custom, and it is one of the earlier laws. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Purify My House for those who circumambulate it and those who devote themselves to worship there﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not have intimate contact with them while you are devoted to retreat in the mosques﴾.

The second issue: If a man touches a woman without desire, it is permitted, "because A'isha, may God be pleased with her, used to comb the hair of the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was in i'tikaf." As for if he touches her with desire, or kisses her, or has physical contact with her short of the private part, this is forbidden for the one in i'tikaf. Does his i'tikaf become void by it? Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, has two opinions on this. The more correct view is that it becomes void. Abu Hanifa said: The i'tikaf is not invalidated if he does not ejaculate.

Those who say it is invalidated argue that the original meaning of the word mubashara (intimate contact) is the meeting of two skins. So His saying ﴿do not have intimate contact with them﴾ prohibits this literal meaning, and therefore intercourse and all these other matters enter into it, because the meaning of mubashara is present in all of them.

If it is said: Why did you interpret mubashara in the earlier verse as intercourse?

We say: Because what precedes the verse indicates that it is intercourse, namely His saying ﴿It has been made lawful for you on the night of fasting to go in to your wives (al-rafath)﴾, and the occasion of revelation of that verse indicates that it is intercourse. Then, when He permitted intercourse, that was by a stronger inference a permission for what is less than intercourse. Here, however, none of these indicators exists, so the word mubashara must be kept in its original place. The argument of those who say it does not invalidate the i'tikaf: We agree that this contact does not invalidate fasting or the pilgrimage, so it must not invalidate i'tikaf, because i'tikaf is not of a higher rank than these two. The answer: The text takes precedence over analogy.

* * *

The third issue: They agreed that the condition of i'tikaf is not sitting in the mosque, because the mosque is distinguished from the rest of the places in that it was built for the performance of acts of worship in it. Then they differed concerning it. It is reported from Ali, may God be pleased with him, that it is not permissible except in the Sacred Mosque. The proof for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you purify My House for those who circumambulate and those who devote themselves to worship there﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125], so He specified that House for all who devote themselves to worship. If i'tikaf were permissible in another place, that generality would not be valid. Ata said: It is not permissible except in the Sacred Mosque and the Mosque of Medina, because of what Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr reported, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers in any other mosque except the Sacred Mosque, and a prayer in the Sacred Mosque is better than a hundred prayers in my mosque." Hudhayfa said: It is permissible in these two mosques and in the mosque of Jerusalem, because of his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "Journeys are not undertaken except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, the Farthest Mosque, and this mosque of mine." Al-Zuhri said: It is not valid except in the congregational mosque. Abu Hanifa said: It is not valid except in a mosque that has a regular imam and a regular muezzin. Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: It is permissible in all mosques, except that the congregational mosque is more excellent, so that one does not need to leave for the Friday prayer. Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, argued by this verse, because His saying ﴿and do not have intimate contact with them while you are devoted to retreat in the mosques﴾ is general and encompasses all mosques.

* * *

Page 98

The fourth issue: It is permissible to perform i'tikaf without fasting, and it is better to fast with it. Abu Hanifa said: It is not permissible except with fasting. The argument of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, is this verse, because one who is without fasting is still devoted (a'if), and God, exalted is He, prohibited the one devoted from intimate contact with women. If his i'tikaf were void, it would not be prohibited. Leaving off acting on the apparent wording when he abandons the intention is what is left, and in other cases it stays on the original basis. Al-Muzani argued for the soundness of al-Shafi'i's view, may God be pleased with him, with three matters:

The first: If i'tikaf required fasting, it would not be valid in Ramadan, because the fasting that it requires is either the fasting of Ramadan, which is void because it is obligatory by reason of the month and not by reason of i'tikaf, or another fast besides the fast of Ramadan, which is impossible. Since they agreed that it is valid in Ramadan, we know that fasting is not required by i'tikaf.

The second: If i'tikaf were not permissible except combined with fasting, the one fasting would leave i'tikaf at night because he would be leaving fasting during it. Since the matter is not like that, we know that i'tikaf is permissible alone at all times without fasting.

The third: What Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with him, reported: He said: "O Messenger of God, I vowed in the Jahiliyya that I would perform i'tikaf for God for one night." He, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "Fulfil your vow." It is well known that fasting at night is not permissible.

* * *

The fifth issue: Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: There is no set duration for i'tikaf. If he vows to perform i'tikaf for an hour, it is valid. If he vows to perform i'tikaf without specifying, he fulfils his vow by performing an hour of i'tikaf, just as if he vowed to give charity without specifying, he gives whatever he wishes, little or much. Then al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: "I prefer that he perform i'tikaf for a day," and he said this only to leave the disagreement, for Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, does not permit i'tikaf of less than a day, on condition that he enters before the break of dawn and leaves after sunset. The argument of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, is that fixing i'tikaf to a specific measure of time is no better than any other, so the fixing must be abandoned and one must return to the least that is necessary. The argument of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, is that i'tikaf is confining oneself to it, and that does not occur in a single moment; and also, on this reckoning, the one in i'tikaf would not be distinguished from one who is waiting for the prayer.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the limits of God﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿these﴾ cannot be a reference to the ruling on i'tikaf, because "limits" is plural, and God did not mention in i'tikaf except one limit, which is the prohibition of intimate contact. Rather, it is a reference to everything that preceded from the beginning of the verse on fasting up to here, according to what its issues were explained in detail earlier.

The second issue: Al-Layth said: The limit of a thing is its end and its termination. Al-Azhari said: From this it is said of one deprived that he is mahdud (restricted), because he is prevented from provision, and the gatekeeper is called haddad (blocker), because he prevents people from entering. The boundary of a house is what prevents others from entering it, and the limits of God are what prevent one from violating them. The speakers of kalam call a comprehensive and restrictive statement a definition (hadd), and iron is called hadid because of the restriction in it, and likewise the mourning of a woman (ihdad), because she is prevented from adornment. Having known the derivation, we say: What is meant by the limits of God is His limited things, that is, His decreed matters which He determined with specific measures and fixed attributes.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not approach them﴾, there are two difficulties:

The first: His saying ﴿these are the limits of God﴾ refers to everything preceding, and some of the preceding matters are permissions and some are prohibitions, so how did He say of all of them ﴿do not approach them﴾?

The second: He, exalted is He, said in another verse: ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], and in the verse of inheritance: ﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger and transgresses His limits﴾ [al-Nisa: 14], and here He said: ﴿So do not approach them﴾. How is the combining of these?

The answer to the two questions is in several ways:

The first, which is the best and strongest: whoever is in obedience to God and acting by His laws is acting within the sphere of truth, so he is forbidden to overstep it, because whoever oversteps it falls into the sphere of error. Then it is intensified in this, so he is forbidden to approach the limit which is the barrier between the sphere of truth and falsehood, lest he come near to falsehood, and that he be far from the edge, let alone that he cross over it, as the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "Every king has a protected preserve, and God's protected preserve is His prohibitions; whoever grazes around the preserve is about to fall into it."

The second: what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned: "Do not approach them" means do not interfere with them by altering them, like His saying: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾ [al-An'am: 152].

The third: Although the rulings mentioned before are many, the closest of them to this verse is only His saying: ﴿And do not have intimate contact with them while you are devoted to retreat in the mosques﴾, and before this verse is His saying: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾, which requires the prohibition of eating and drinking during the day. And before this verse is His saying: ﴿And seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, which requires the prohibition of intercourse with other than wife and slave-woman, and the prohibition of intercourse with them in a forbidden manner, and the prohibition of intercourse with them during menstruation, postpartum bleeding, the waiting period, and apostasy. There is nothing in it except the permission of drinking, eating, and intercourse at night. So since most of the earlier rulings were prohibitions, the side of prohibition was naturally predominant, and He said: ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not approach them﴾, meaning: those things from which you have been prevented are prevented only by God's prohibition and His forbidding of them, so do not approach them.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus God makes clear His signs to mankind﴾, there are several interpretations:

One of them: The meaning is that just as He made clear what He commanded you and forbade you in this place, so He makes clear all His other proofs for His religion and His law.

The second: Abu Muslim said: The signs here mean the obligations which He made clear, as He said: ﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and in which We have sent down clear signs﴾ [al-Nur: 1]. Then He explained the signs with His saying: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer﴾ [al-Nur: 2], up to the rest of what He clarified of the rulings on fornication. So it is as if He said: Thus God makes clear to mankind what He has prescribed for them, so that they may be mindful of Him by acting upon what is incumbent.

The third: It may be that the meaning is that when He, glorified is He, clarified the rulings of fasting in full detail in this verse with few words, in a complete and sufficient clarification, He said after it: ﴿Thus God makes clear His signs to mankind﴾, meaning: such a complete, sufficient, clear and perfect clarification is what is mentioned to mankind. The purpose of this is to exalt the status of clarification and to exalt His mercy upon creation in mentioning such a clarification.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that they may be mindful of God﴾, its explanation has passed more than once.

The Eighth Ruling

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 188:

Among the rulings mentioned in this surah is the ruling on property.

﴿And do not consume one another's property unjustly, or send it [as bribes] to the rulers so that you may consume a portion of the property of people sinfully while you know [it to be wrong].﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not consume one another's property unjustly, or send it [as bribes] to the rulers so that you may consume a portion of the property of people sinfully while you know [it to be wrong].﴾

Page 100

Know that they have compared His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And do not consume your property among yourselves﴾ with His saying: ﴿And do not defame one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11]. This is different from it, because one's consuming of his own property unjustly is valid just as his consuming of another's property is valid. Shaykh Abu Hamid al-Ghazali said in the Kitab al-Ihya': Property is only forbidden either because of a meaning inherent in itself, or because of a condition in the manner of its acquisition.

The first category: that which is forbidden because of a quality inherent in itself.

Know that property is either from minerals, or from plants, or from animals. As for minerals, which are the parts of the earth, nothing from them is forbidden except insofar as it harms when consumed, such as that which acts as poison. As for plants, nothing from them is forbidden except that which removes life, health, or reason: poisons remove life, medicines taken out of their proper time remove health, and intoxicants such as wine, henbane, and all other intoxicants remove reason.

As for animals, they are divided into what is eaten and what is not eaten. That which is lawful is lawful only when it is slaughtered in the legal manner. Then, once it is slaughtered, it is not lawful in all of its parts; rather, the dung (farth) and the blood are forbidden from it, and all of that is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

The second category: that which is forbidden due to a defect in the manner of taking possession of it. We say: taking property is either by the choice of the one who owns it, or without his choice, such as inheritance. That which is by his choice is either taken from a non-owner, such as taking minerals, or taken from an owner. That [taking from an owner] is either taken by compulsion or by mutual consent. That which is taken by compulsion is either taken because the ownership's protection has lapsed, such as spoils of war, or because taking is merited, such as the zakat of those who refuse and the obligatory maintenance owed by them. That which is taken by mutual consent is either taken in exchange for a consideration, such as sale, dower, and wages, or taken without consideration, such as gift and bequest. From this division there arise six categories:

The first: what is taken from a non-owner, such as obtaining minerals, reviving dead land, hunting, gathering firewood, drawing water from rivers, and cutting grass. This is lawful on condition that the thing taken is not exclusively the property of a person with protected rights among human beings.

The second: what is taken by compulsion from one who has no protected status, namely the fay', the ghanimah (spoils), and all the property of warring unbelievers. This is lawful for the Muslims if they set aside the one-fifth from it and divide it justly among its rightful recipients, and if they do not take it from an unbeliever who has protected status, a safe-conduct, or a covenant.

The third: what is taken by compulsion through entitlement when the obligated party refuses, so it is taken without his consent. This is lawful when the cause of entitlement is complete, the description of the one entitled is complete, and it is limited to the entitled amount.

The fourth: what is taken by mutual consent in an exchange. This is lawful when the conditions of the two exchanged items, the conditions of the two contracting parties, and the conditions of the two formulations, i.e., the offer and acceptance, are observed in ways the Shari'ah recognizes as valid, avoiding any corrupting condition.

The fifth: what is taken by consent without consideration, as in gift, bequest, and charity, when the conditions of the thing given, the conditions of the two parties, and the conditions of the contract are observed, and it does not lead to harm to an heir or others.

The sixth: what is obtained without one's choice, such as inheritance. This is lawful if the deceased acquired the property from some of the five sources in a lawful manner, and then this is after the payment of debts, the execution of bequests, the equalizing of distribution among the heirs, and the payment of zakat, hajj, and expiation if they were obligatory. These are the sum total of the entrances of what is lawful, and the books of jurisprudence contain their details. So whatever is like this is lawful property, and whatever is contrary to it is unlawful. Having understood this, we say: property is either the property of another or of oneself. If it is another's, its prohibition is due to the six aspects mentioned. If it is one's own, then consuming it unlawfully is by spending it on drinking wine, fornication, sodomy, gambling, or on forbidden extravagance. All these categories fall under His saying: ﴿And do not consume your property among yourselves unjustly﴾. Know that He, glorified is He, repeated this prohibition in several places in His Book

Page 101

so He said: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume one another's property unjustly, except that it be trade﴾ [an-Nisa': 29], and He said: ﴿Those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ [an-Nisa': 10], and He said: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest, if you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 278], then He said: ﴿But if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279], then He said: ﴿But if you repent, you will have your principal﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279], then He said: ﴿And whoever returns, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]. He made the one who consumes interest, at the beginning of the matter, one announcing war against Allah, and at its end, one exposed to the Fire.

The second issue: His saying ﴿And do not consume﴾ does not mean specifically consuming (eating), because other dispositions of property, like consuming, fall under this same ruling. But since the greatest purpose of property is in fact consumption, it became customary to say of one who spends his wealth that he "consumed" it. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, expressed it by "consuming."

The third issue: "al-batil" (the unjust, the false) in lexical usage means that which is vanished and gone. It is said: "batala al-shay'" (the thing became void) "butulan," so it is "batil"; the plural of batil is bawatil, and abatil is the plural of ubtulah. It is also said: "batala al-ajir yabtulu batalah" when a hired worker becomes idle and follows frivolity.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and send it to the rulers﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: al-idla' (sending down) is derived from the idla' of the bucket (dalw), which is sending it into the well to draw water. It is said: "adlaytu dalwi udlīha idlā'an"; when you pull it out, you say: "dalawtuha." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he lowered his bucket﴾ [Yusuf: 19]. Then every casting of a statement or an act was termed idla'. From this one says of a person presenting his argument: "adla bi hujjatihi" (he put forth his proof), as if he sends it out so that it reaches his aim, like the drawer of water lowering the bucket to reach what he seeks of water. And so-and-so "yudli ila al-mayyit" by kinship or blood ties, when he is connected to the deceased, so he seeks the inheritance by that connection, just as one seeking water seeks it with the bucket. Having understood this, we say: it falls under the ruling of the prohibition, and the sense is: "do not consume your property among yourselves unjustly, and do not send [it] to the rulers," i.e., do not bribe them with it so that you may consume a portion of people's property unjustly. Regarding the comparison of bribery to idla', there are two aspects:

One: bribery is the rope of need; just as a bucket full of water reaches from afar to near by means of the rope, the meaning is that the distant becomes near through the bribe.

The second: the ruler, because of taking a bribe, proceeds with that judgment without verification, like the bucket proceeding as it is lowered. Then the exegetes mentioned several views:

One: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatadah said: it refers to deposits and what has no evidence to establish it.

Second: that it refers to the property of an orphan in the hands of guardians, who give part of it to the judge so that the rest remains with them.

Third: that by "the rulers" is meant false testimony; this is the view of al-Kalbi.

Fourth: al-Hasan said: it means swearing an oath in order to take away his right.

Fifth: it is giving a bribe to the ruler, and this is closest to the apparent meaning. It is also not far-fetched to take the wording in its full generality, because all of these are consuming unjustly.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while you know﴾, the meaning is: while you know that you are wrongdoers. There is no doubt that proceeding with an ugly act while knowing its ugliness is worse, and its doer is more deserving of reproach. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Two men brought a dispute before the Prophet ﷺ: one knowledgeable in disputation and one ignorant of it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ judged for the knowledgeable one. The one against whom judgment was given said: 'O Messenger of Allah, by Him besides whom there is no god, I am in the right.' He said: 'If you wish, I will repeat it to him.' He repeated it, and he judged for the knowledgeable one. The one against whom judgment was given said the same as he said at first. Then he repeated it a third time. Then he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Whoever takes the right of a Muslim man through his dispute has merely taken a piece of the Fire.' The knowledgeable one for whom judgment was given said: 'O Messenger of Allah, indeed the right is his right.' He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Whoever takes by his dispute and his argument the right of another, let him take his seat in the Fire.'"

The Ninth Ruling
﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are times marked out for people and for the Hajj. And it is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah. So enter houses through their doors and fear Allah that you may succeed.﴾

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are times marked out for people and for the Hajj. And it is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah. So enter houses through their doors and fear Allah that you may succeed.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "No people asked fewer questions than the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). They asked about fourteen matters, and they were answered."

I say: Eight of them are in Sūrat al-Baqara:

The first of them: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ [al-Baqara 2:186].

The second: this verse, and then the six remaining after it in Sūrat al-Baqara. So the total of those from this sūra is eight.

The ninth: the words of the Exalted in Sūrat al-Māʾida: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Māʾida 5:4].

The tenth: in Sūrat al-Anfāl: ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ [al-Anfāl 8:1].

The eleventh: in Banī Isrāʾīl: ﴿And they ask you about the soul﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:85].

The twelfth: in al-Kahf: ﴿And they ask you about Dhū al-Qarnayn﴾ [al-Kahf 18:83].

The thirteenth: in Ṭāhā: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains﴾ [Ṭāhā 20:105].

The fourteenth: in al-Nāziʿāt: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time?﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt 79:42].

These questions have a wondrous arrangement: two of them are at the beginning, concerning the explanation of the origin (al-mabdaʾ):

The first is His words: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me﴾ [al-Baqara 2:186], and this is a question about the Essence (al-dhāt).

The second is His words: ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾, and this is a question about the attribute of the wisdom of creation (al-khalāqiyya) and the wisdom in making the crescent in this form. Two of them are at the end, concerning the explanation of the return (al-maʿād):

One of them is His words: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains﴾ [Ṭāhā 20:105].

The second is His words: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time?﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt 79:42]. A parallel to this is that there occur in the Qur'an two sūras:

The first: "O people" (yā ayyuhā al-nās). One of them is in the first half, and it is the fourth sūra of the first half, for its first is al-Fātiḥa, its second is al-Baqara, its third is Āl ʿImrān, and its fourth is al-Nisāʾ. The second is in the second half of the Qur'an, and it is also the fourth sūra of the second half: its first is Maryam, its second is Ṭāhā, its third is al-Anbiyāʾ, and its fourth is al-Ḥajj. Then the "O people" in the first half includes the explanation of the origin, as He said: ﴿O people, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:1]. And the "O people" in the second half includes the explanation of the return, as He said: ﴿O people, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ [al-Ḥajj 22:1]. So glory be to Him, in whose Qur'an are hidden secrets and folded wisdoms that none knows except His chosen servants.

The second issue: It is reported that Muʿādh ibn Jabal and Thaʿlaba ibn Ghanm, each of whom was from the Anṣār (the Helpers), said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the matter with the crescent? It appears thin like a thread, then it increases until it becomes full and complete, then it continues to decrease until it returns as it began. It is not in one state, like the sun." So this verse was revealed. And it is also narrated from Muʿādh that the Jews asked about the new moons.

Know that the words of the Exalted ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾ do not state about what they asked; but the answer indicates the place of the question, because His words ﴿Say: They are times marked out for people and for the Hajj﴾ show that their question was about the benefit and wisdom in the change of the state of the new moons in waning and waxing. Thus the Qur'an and the report agree that the question was about this meaning.

* * *

The third issue: al-ahilla is the plural of hilāl (the crescent), which is the first state of the moon when people see it. It is called "the hilāl of two nights" from the beginning of the month, and then after that it becomes a qamar (moon). Abū al-Haytham said: the moon is called hilāl for the two nights at the beginning of the month, and likewise for the two nights at the end of the month; then what lies between them is called qamar. Al-Zajjāj said: fiʿāl is pluralized, for the smallest number, as afʿila, like mithāl and amthila, and ḥimār and aḥmira; and for the larger number it is pluralized as fuʿul, like ḥumur, because they disliked fuʿal in doubled forms, like hulal and khulal, so they limited themselves to the plural of the smaller number.

* * *

As for His words ﴿Say: They are times marked out for people and for the Hajj﴾, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: al-mawāqīt is the plural of al-mīqāt in the sense of al-waqt (time), like al-mīʿād in the sense of al-waʿd (promise). Some of them said: al-mīqāt is the limit of a time. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So the term of his Lord was completed﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:142]. The crescent is the appointed time of the month, and the places of ihrām (the sacred state) are the appointed times of the Hajj, because they are places reached at which one stops. Mawāqīt is not made to take tanwīn (nunation) because it is the ultimate of the plurals, so it is as if the plural pattern is repeated in it. If it is said: why are qawārīr given tanwīn? It is said: because it is a rhyme-ending (fāṣila) that falls at the end of a verse, so it takes nunation to follow the pattern of the verses, just as qawāfī (rhymes in poetry) take nunation, like His words in the poem:

"Lessen your blame, O censurer, and your reproach."

* * *

The second issue: Know that He, glorified and exalted, made time measured in four ways: the year, the month, the day, and the hour. As for the year, it is an expression of the time resulting from the motion of the sun from a specific point of the sphere, through its motion which results from the opposition to the motion of the sphere, until it returns to that very same point. However, the people (the astronomers) agreed that this point is the vernal equinox point, which is the first degree of Aries (awwal al-ḥamal). As for the month, it is an expression of the motion of the moon from a specific point of its own sphere until it returns to that point. Since the most well-known of the moon's states is its conjunction with the sun, and the most well-known of its positions relative to the sun is the Arabic crescent, and since at this time the moon resembles what exists after non-existence and what is born emerging from darkness, they therefore made this time the end of the month. As for the day with its night, it is an expression of the separation of a point of the equator's circle (dāʾirat muʿaddal al-nahār) from a point of the horizon circle, or a point of the meridian circle and its return to it. So the measured time is an expression of the day with its night. Then the astrologers agreed to fix the meridian circle as the beginning of the day with its night. As for most nations, they made the beginnings of days with their nights from the sun's separation from the horizon of the east and its return to it in the morning. The one who supported their doctrine argued that the sun at its rising is like what exists after non-existence, so making that the beginning is more appropriate. So the time of the day is an expression of the duration of the sun being above the earth, and the time of the night is an expression of its being beneath the earth. In the Islamic law, they begin the day from the first time of the dawn (fajr) in the obligation of the prayer, the fast, and other rulings. According to the astrologers, the duration of fasting in the Sharīʿa is the whole time of the day along with an addition of a known amount of the night's time with a defined beginning. As for the hour, it is of two kinds: equal, which is one part of twenty-four of a day and night.

So this is a brief statement on defining the year, the month, the day, and the hour. Now we say: as for the year, it is an expression of the sun's cycle, by which the four seasons come about. This is because when the sun is in Aries, and then it leaves this position toward the northern side, the air on the northern side takes some heat because it is near the zenith of the heads (musāmatat al-ruʾūs), and the heating continues until it reaches the beginning of Cancer. The heat intensifies and the warmth increases as long as it is in Cancer and Leo, because it is near the zenith of the heads, and the heating is continuous. Then it reverses until it reaches Libra; at that time the air becomes pleasant and moderate. Then the heat begins to decrease and the cold to increase, and the cold continues to increase until the sun reaches the beginning of Capricorn; the cold then becomes severe because it is far from the zenith of the heads, and the cold is continuous. Then the sun begins to ascend towards the northern side, and as long as it is in Capricorn and Aquarius the cold is at its strongest, until it reaches Aries. Then the air becomes pleasant and moderate, the sun returns to the beginning of its motion, the time of the year reaches its end, and the four seasons occur, which are spring, summer, autumn, and winter. The benefits of the four seasons and their alternation are apparent and well known in the books.

As for the month, it is an expression of the cycle of the moon in its own sphere. They claimed that its light is derived from the sun, and that always one of its two halves is fully illuminated, except that at conjunction the illuminated half is the upper half, so we indeed see none of its light. At opposition, its illuminated half faces us, so we indeed see it fully illuminated. The closer the moon is to the sun, the less of its illuminated half is seen, and the farther it is, the more of its illuminated half is seen. Then from the time of conjunction until the time of separation, each night it is farther from the sun, and each night its light is seen more than from the time of opposition until the time of conjunction, when each night it is closer to the sun, so each night its light is seen less, and it keeps decreasing and decreasing: ﴿until it returned like an old date-stalk﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:39]. This is what the natural philosophers and astrologers said.

As for what the theologians (uṣūliyyūn, those who work on the foundations of belief) say: the moon is a body, and all bodies are equal in bodiliness, and things equal in the completeness of their quiddity cannot differ in their necessary attributes. This is a certain premise. Therefore, the occurrence of light in the bodies of the sun and the moon is something that is possible to occur, and whatever is like this, the preponderance of its existence over its non-existence is impossible except by means of a chooser agent. Whatever is the act of a chooser agent, that agent is able to bring it into being and to annihilate it. On this assumption, the attribution of these variations occurring in the moon's light to its nearness to and distance from the sun is not necessary. Rather, according to us, the occurrence of light in the body of the sun was only through the bringing into being by the powerful chooser, and likewise what is in the body of the moon.

* * *

It remains here to be said: why did the chooser agent specify the moon, and not the sun, with these variations? We say that the scholars of Islam have two answers in this regard:

One of them: It is said that the agency of Allah the Exalted cannot be explained by a purpose and a benefit. This is shown by several points:

The first: whoever does an act for a purpose, if he is able to achieve that purpose without that intermediary, then the act of that intermediary is in vain; and if he is not able, then he is incapable.

The second: whoever does an act for a purpose, if the existence of that purpose is better for him than its non-existence, then he is deficient in himself and perfected by another; and if it is not better for him, then it is not a purpose.

The third: if it were an act caused by a purpose, then that purpose, if it is originated, would require that its origination be due to another purpose, and if it is eternal, then its eternity would necessitate the eternity of the act, which is impossible. Therefore they said: everything is His creation and there is no cause for His creating it, and it is absolutely not permissible to explain His acts and rulings by causes: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:23].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 189 (part 2 of 3):

The second answer is the statement of those who said: In the acts and rulings of God there must be regard for interests (maslahah) and wisdoms (hikam). The proponents of this view concede that human intellects are, in most matters, too limited to reach the secrets of God's wisdom in His dominion and kingdom. We have shown that the people asked only about the wisdom in the variation of the moon's phases, and God, exalted is He, mentioned the aspects of wisdom in it, which is His saying: ﴿Say: They are times for people and for the Hajj﴾. He mentioned this same meaning in another verse, His saying: ﴿And He determined for it stations, that you may know the number of years and the calculation﴾ [Yunus: 5], and He said in a third verse: ﴿So We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day visible, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the calculation﴾ [al-Isra': 12]. The detailed explanation is that measuring time by months has benefits, some of which are connected to religion and some to worldly affairs. As for what is connected to religion, there are many, among them fasting. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

Second: the Hajj. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197].

Third: the waiting period (iddah) of a woman whose husband has died. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They shall wait by themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234].

Fourth: vows that are tied to times, and the merits of fasting on days that cannot be known except through the crescent moons.

As for what is connected to worldly affairs, it includes debts, contracts of hire, appointed terms, and the period of pregnancy and nursing, as He said: ﴿And his carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15], and other matters. All of these are such that the timing cannot easily be fixed except when the variation in the moon's shape occurs.

If it is said: We do not concede that we need the appearance of the month in determining periods of time, because it is possible to determine them by the year, which is the cycle of the sun, and by its divisions. For example, one may say: "He obligated you to such-and-such act of worship at the beginning of the year, or at its sixth, or its half," and similarly for the other parts. It is also possible to determine them by days, for example: "You were obligated to such-and-such act of worship on the first day of the year, and after fifty days from the beginning of the year." Moreover, even granting that it is necessary, alongside determining time by the year and the day, to determine it by the moon, the month is a cycle from its conjunction with the sun until it again conjoins with it. This determination is achieved whether or not a variation occurs in the forms of its light. Do you not see that determining the year by the motion of the sun is achieved even though no variation occurs in the light of the sun? Likewise it is possible to determine [the year] by the motion of the moon, even if no variation occurs in the light of the moon. And if the light of the moon has no variation whatsoever and no effect in this matter, it is not permissible to determine time by it.

The answer to the first question: Although what you mentioned is possible, counting the crescents is easier than counting the days, because the crescents are twelve months while the days are many. It is known that dividing the total of time into years, then dividing each year into months, then dividing the months into days, then dividing each day into hours, then dividing each hour into breaths, is closer to precision and further from confusion. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with God is twelve﴾ [p. 106] ﴿months﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. This is like an author who observes good arrangement, dividing his composition into books, then each book into chapters, then each chapter into sections, then each section into issues. Likewise is the answer here.

As for the second question, its answer is what you mentioned, except that whenever the moon is varied in shape, knowing the beginnings of the months, their midpoints and their ends is easier than when it is not so. He, majestic is His majesty, informed that He arranged the crescents in this wondrous arrangement for the benefits of His servants in the sustenance of their worldly life, together with what they derive from these varying states as evidence for the oneness of God, exalted is He, and the perfection of His power, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 190], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations and placed therein a lamp and a moon giving light﴾ [al-Furqan: 61]. Furthermore, had this variation not occurred in the body of the moon, the doubts of the philosophers would have been reinforced in their claim that celestial bodies cannot admit change in their states. So He, exalted is He, in His overpowering wisdom, kept the sun in one state and manifested variation in the states of the moon, so that it becomes clear to the intelligent person that the sun's remaining in its states is nothing but by God's preservation, and the moon's change in its forms is nothing but by God's alteration. Thus all of it, by this means, becomes a witness to their need for a wise, powerful, overpowering Manager, as He said: ﴿And there is not a thing except that it exalts Him with His praise, but you do not understand their exalting﴾ [al-Isra': 44].

Having understood this whole matter, we say: When it became clear that the variation in the states of the moon is a great aid in determining times from the aspects we have mentioned, God, exalted is He, by His saying ﴿Say: They are times for people and for the Hajj﴾, alluded to all these benefits. For enumerating all these matters would lead to prolixity, while limiting [the answer] to some and not others would be preference without a preferrer. So nothing remained but to limit it to the fact that it is a timekeeper (miqat), and this limiting is evidence of great eloquence.

As for His saying ﴿and the Hajj﴾, there is an implied element, its estimate being "and for the Hajj," like His saying: ﴿And if you wish to have your children nursed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233], meaning "for your children." Know that we have explained that the crescents are timekeepers for many acts of worship, so singling out the Hajj for mention must have a benefit. It cannot be said that this benefit is that the times of the Hajj are known only through the crescents, as He said: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], because the time of fasting is likewise known only through the crescents, as He said: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "Fast when you see it and break your fast when you see it." The best aspect in this matter is what al-Qaffal (may God have mercy on him) mentioned, namely that singling out the Hajj for mention was only to clarify that the Hajj is restricted to the months which God designated for its obligation, and that it is not permissible to shift the Hajj from those months to other months, as the Arabs used to do in the practice of al-Nasi' (intercalation). And God knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: They mentioned several views regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse:

One of them: al-Hasan and al-Asamm said: In the pre-Islamic era, when a man intended something and his objective was difficult for him, he would not enter his house by its door, but would come to it from behind, and he would remain in this state for a full year. So God forbade them from this, because they used to do it as a form of tatayyur (taking omens, from the root meaning to be inauspicious). Accordingly, the interpretation of the verse is: "Righteousness is not that you come to houses from their backs out of tatayyur. Rather, righteousness is that one fears God, does not fear anything else, and is not afraid of anything through which he would take omens, but relies upon God and fears Him alone." Then He said: ﴿And fear God that you may be successful﴾, meaning, so that you may win good in religion and in the world, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out﴾ and ﴿and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2–3] and ﴿And whoever fears God, He will make for him ease in his affair﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. The complete verification of the verse is that one who returns unsuccessful is described as: "He did not succeed and did not prosper." So it is possible that the success mentioned in the verse means that it is obligatory upon you to fear God so that you become successful and prosperous. Reports have come from the Prophet (ﷺ) forbidding tatayyur, and he said: "There is no contagion and no tiyarah (omen)." He also said: "Whoever is turned back from his journey by an omen has committed shirk," or as he said. He also used to dislike tiyarah and love a good fa'l (optimistic sign). God, exalted is He, censured a people who took omens from Moses and those with him: ﴿They said: We have taken an omen from you and from those with you. He said: Your omen is with God﴾ [al-Naml: 47].

The second occasion of revelation: It is related that at the beginning of Islam, when a man among them entered the state of ihram, if he was a townsman, he would breach the back of his house and enter and exit through it, or he would make a ladder by which he climbed onto the roof of his house and then descended. If he was a dweller of the wabar (tents of hair or wool), he would exit from behind the tent. So it was said to them: "Righteousness is not in your scrupulousness about entering through the door, but righteousness is in him who fears God."

The third occasion: When one of the people of the pre-Islamic era entered ihram, he would breach a hole behind his house or tent, through which he would enter and exit, except for the Hums (ḥumus, the strict ones). They are Quraysh, Kinanah, Khuza'ah, Thaqif, Khaytham, the Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, and the Banu Nasr ibn Mu'awiyah. They were called Hums because of their strictness in their religion; al-hamasah means severity. When these people entered ihram, they would never enter their houses at all, nor would they seek shade in a tent of wool, nor eat ghee or aqit (dried curd). Then: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in ihram, and another man was also in ihram. The Messenger of God (ﷺ), while in ihram, entered through the door of a garden that had fallen into ruin. That man who was in ihram saw him and followed him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Step away from me.' He said: 'Why, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'You entered through the door while you are in ihram.' That man stopped and said: 'I am content with your sunnah and your guidance. I have seen you enter, so I entered.' Then God revealed this verse." He informed them that their severity regarding the matter of ihram is not righteousness, but righteousness is in one who avoids disobedience to God, and He commanded them to abandon the custom of the pre-Islamic era, so He said: ﴿And come to houses through their doors﴾. This is what has been said regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse.

The second issue: They mentioned three aspects regarding the interpretation of the verse:

The first: This is the view of most exegetes, that the verse is applied to these circumstances which we related in the occasions of revelation. However, on this reading, the wording of the verse becomes difficult, for the people asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the wisdom in the change of the moon's light, and God mentioned the wisdom in that, which is His saying: ﴿Say: They are times for people and for the Hajj﴾. So what connection is there between explaining the wisdom in the variation of the moon's light and this story? Then the proponents of this view answered this question in several ways:

One: When God mentioned that the wisdom in the variation of the states of the crescents is that they are timekeepers for people and for the Hajj, and this matter is among the things that are taken into account in the Hajj, God therefore spoke about it.

Two: He, exalted is He, connected His saying ﴿And it is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾ with His saying ﴿They ask you about the crescents﴾, because the two incidents happened to occur at one time, so the verse was revealed concerning both together at one time, and He joined one matter to the other.

Three: It is as if they asked about the wisdom in the variation of the states of the crescents, and it was said to them: "Leave off asking about this matter, which does not concern you, and turn to what is more important for you to investigate. For you think that entering houses from their backs is righteousness, and the matter is not so."

The second view regarding the interpretation of the verse: that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And it is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾ is a parable which God struck for them, and its outward meaning is not intended. Its explanation: the straight path that is known is that one derives the unknown from the known, upon

al-Mazhnun ("the conjectural"), fa-amma an yastadilla bil-mazhnun ʿala al-maʿlum fa-dhaka ʿaksu al-wajib wa-didd al-haqq. Terms: tafsir, wajib... Glosses only first time technical term appears. al-maẓnūn (the conjectural). As for inferring the known from the conjectural, that is the reverse of what is obligatory and the opposite of the truth. Now, having understood this, we say: It has been established by proofs that the Knower has a Creator who chooses and is wise, and it has been established that the Wise does not act except rightly, free from futility and folly. When we know this, and we know that the variation in the moon's light is from His doing, we know that there is in it wisdom and benefit. This is because our knowledge of this Wise One, who does not act except with wisdom, gives us certainty that there is wisdom in it, since this is inference from the known to the unknown. As for inferring from our lack of knowledge of the wisdom in it that its Agent is not wise, this inference is invalid, because it is inferring from the unknown to discredit the known. Having understood this, the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾ is that, since you did not know His wisdom in the variation of the moonlight, you became doubtful about the wisdom of the Creator. Thus you have come to the matter neither from righteousness nor from perfection of intellect. Rather, righteousness is to enter houses by their doors, so that you infer from the known and certain, namely the wisdom of its Creator, to this unknown, and thus you are certain that in it there is profound wisdom, even if you do not know it. So entering houses from their backs is made a metaphor for deviating from the correct path, and entering them by their doors a metaphor for adhering to the straight path. This is a well-known mode of metaphor: whoever guides another to the correct course says to him, "You should come to the matter by its door." In its opposite it is said: "He went to the thing not by its door." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾ [Ali ʿImran 3:187], and He said: ﴿And you have taken it behind your backs﴾ [Hud 11:92]. Since this is a well-known and customary path in metaphors, God, exalted is He, mentioned it here. This is the interpretation of the theologians (mutakallimun), and the interpretation of this verse in its first sense is not sound, for interpreting it that way brings to the verse a defect of disorder, and the speech of God is exalted above that.

The third opinion regarding the interpretation of the verse is what Abu Muslim mentioned: that the intended meaning of this verse is what they knew of the nasi' (the intercalation of months). They would move the pilgrimage away from its appointed time that God had fixed for it, so they would forbid what is lawful and make lawful what is forbidden. Thus the mention of entering houses from their backs is an example of violating what is obligatory regarding the pilgrimage and its months.

The third matter: His words, exalted is He: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who fears God﴾. Its estimate is: "But the righteousness of righteousness is that of one who fears God," so it is like His words: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in God﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:177], and its explanation has already been given.

The fourth matter: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, and Qalun from Nafi' read "al-buyut" with a kasra on the ba' (bi-kasri al-ba'), because they found it burdensome to move from a damma on the ba' to a ya'. The rest read it with a damma, according to the original form. The readers have various views and differences concerning this word and its analogues, such as buyut, ʿuyun, and juyub, whose detailed explanation would be lengthy.

As for His words: ﴿And fear God﴾, we have already shown that it includes the performance of every obligation and the avoidance of every prohibition beneath it. ﴿So that you may prosper﴾: that is, in order that you may succeed. Success (al-falah) is attaining the desired goal. The Mu'tazila said: This indicates that God wills the success of all of them, since there is no specification in the verse. And God knows best.

**The Tenth Ruling: Concerning Fighting**

﴿And fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love the transgressors.﴾

Page 109

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love the transgressors.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**First issue:** In the preceding verse, He commanded uprightness (istiqamah) in the path of knowing God, exalted is He, saying: ﴿It is not righteousness to enter houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears God. So enter houses through their doors﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189]. He commanded piety (taqwa) in the path of obeying God, which is an expression for abstaining from what is forbidden and performing what is obligatory. Thus uprightness is knowledge, and piety is action, and obligation lies only in these two. Then, when He commanded in this verse the most severe and difficult kind of piety upon the self, which is killing the enemies of God, He said: ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾.

**Second issue:** Regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), there are two opinions.

The first: al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd said: this verse is the first verse revealed about fighting. When it was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would fight whoever fought him and refrain from fighting whoever left him alone. He remained in this state until the saying of God, exalted is He, was revealed: ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

The second opinion: he (upon him be blessings and peace) set out with his companions intending to perform the Hajj, and he alighted at al-Hudaybiyyah, a place abounding in trees and water. The polytheists prevented them from entering the House, so he stayed for a month unable to do so. Then they made a treaty with him that he would return that year and come back to them the following year, and they would leave Makkah to him for three days so that he could circumambulate, sacrifice the offering, and do whatever he wished. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) accepted this and concluded the treaty on those terms. Then he returned to Madinah and prepared for the following year. Afterward, his companions feared that the Quraysh would not fulfill the promise, would bar them from the Sacred Mosque, and would fight them. They disliked fighting them in the sacred month and in the Sanctuary. So God, exalted is He, revealed these verses, and He explained to them how to fight if they needed to, saying: ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾.

* * *

**Third issue:** ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾ means in obedience to Him and in seeking His good pleasure. Abu Musa narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the one who fights in the way of God, and he said: "It is the one who fights so that the word of God may be supreme, and he does not fight for show or for reputation."

**Fourth issue:** Scholars differed concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿those who fight you﴾, in several ways.

The first, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas: the meaning is, fight those who fight you, either by way of repelling them from the Hajj or by way of initiating combat. This view agrees with what we narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse.

The second: fight everyone who has the capability and the capacity for fighting.

The third: fight everyone who has the capability and similarly the capacity, except those who incline to peace. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [al-Anfal: 61]. Know that the first view is closer to the apparent meaning, because the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those who fight you﴾ requires that they be the ones who actually engage in fighting. As for one who prepares for fighting and is qualified for it before he undertakes it, he is not described as a fighter except in a metaphorical sense.

* * *

**Fifth issue:** Some people said: this verse is abrogated (mansukh, i.e., its ruling has been cancelled by a later revelation). This is because this verse indicates that God, exalted is He, obligated the fighting of those who fight, and forbade fighting those who do not fight, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of God those who fight you﴾, and then after it: ﴿but do not transgress﴾, meaning: do not fight those who do not fight you. Thus it is established that this verse prohibits fighting those who do not fight. Then He, exalted is He, said after that: ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191]. This requires the fighting of those who do not fight, and so it indicates that this verse is abrogated.

The response may be: we accept that this verse indicates the command to fight those who do not fight us, but this ruling has not become abrogated. As for the claim that it indicates a prohibition on fighting those who do not fight us, this is not accepted. As for His saying: ﴿but do not transgress﴾, this admits of other meanings besides what you have mentioned. Among them: the meaning is, do not initiate fighting within the Sanctuary. Among them: the meaning is, do not transgress by fighting those whom you have been forbidden to fight from among those with whom you have a covenant; or by trickery; or by surprise attack without prior summons; or by killing women, children, and the aged infirm. Under all these interpretations, the verse is not abrogated.

If it is said: suppose there is no abrogation in the verse, but what is the reason that God, exalted is He, first commanded the fighting of those who fight, and then at the end of the matter permitted fighting them whether they fight or not?

We say: because at the beginning the Muslims were few, so the proper course was to use gentleness, softness, and courtesy. When Islam grew strong and the community multiplied, and those among them who remained upon polytheism did so after the manifest miracles had appeared and repeatedly came to them, situation after situation, despair of their becoming Muslim arose. Therefore God, exalted is He, commanded fighting them without restriction.

**Sixth issue:** The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) argued with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God does not love the transgressors.﴾ They said: if transgression were by the will of God and by His creating it, this statement would not be valid. Its answer has already been given, and God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 191–192:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them, and expel them from where they expelled you, for persecution is worse than killing. And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein. But if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Concerning it are several issues:

The first issue: al-thaqf (ثقف) means finding something by way of seizing and overpowering, and from it comes the phrase rajul thaqif (رجل ثقيف), a man quick to seize his opponents. He said:

"If you capture me, then kill me; for whoever is captured, there is no immortality."

Then we say: His saying, ﴿And kill them﴾, the address in it is directed at the Prophet ﷺ and those who emigrated with him, although the intent of it applies to every believer. The pronoun in His saying ﴿And kill them﴾ refers to those whom He commanded to be killed in the first verse, and they are the disbelievers of the people of Makkah. So Allah the Exalted commanded their killing wherever they were, in the sacred territory (al-Haram) and in the sacred month. The clarification of the matter is that He, the Exalted, commanded jihad in the first verse on the condition that the disbelievers initiate fighting; in this one He added to the obligation and commanded jihad against them whether or not they fought, and He made an exception to it: fighting at the Sacred Mosque.

The second issue: It is reported from Muqatil that he said: the verse preceding this one, namely His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190], is abrogated (mansukhah) by His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾, and then that verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no persecution﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193]. And this statement is weak.

As for his claim that His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾ is abrogated by this verse, its refutation has already passed. As for his claim that this verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾, this is from the category of specification (takhsis), not from the category of abrogation (naskh). As for his claim that ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾ is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no persecution﴾, this is also an error, because it is not permissible to initiate fighting within the Sacred Precinct, and this ruling has not been abrogated but remains in force. Thus it is established that his statement is weak; and moreover, it is far from the Wise One to combine consecutive verses in such a way that each one abrogates the other.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The word "expulsion" (al-ikhraj) may bear two meanings:

One: that they compelled them to leave by force.

The second: that they exaggerated in intimidating them and in making the matter severe for them, until they became compelled to leave.

The second discussion: The form of the word "ḥaythu" (حيث) may bear two meanings:

One: expel them from the place from which they expelled you, which is Makkah.

The second: expel them from their dwellings. Having understood this, we say: Allah the Exalted commanded the believers to expel those disbelievers from Makkah if they persisted in their polytheism, if they were able to do so. But it was known that they would be able to do so afterward; for this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ expelled every polytheist from the Sacred Precinct, and then he expelled them also from Madinah, and he ﷺ said: "Two religions shall not coexist in the Arabian Peninsula."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And persecution is worse than killing﴾, there are several interpretations:

One of them, and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the intended meaning of "persecution" (fitnah) is disbelief in Allah the Exalted. Disbelief was called "fitnah" because it is corruption on the earth which leads to injustice and chaos (al-harj), and in it is fitnah. Disbelief was made greater than killing because disbelief is a sin for which its doer deserves everlasting punishment, whereas killing is not like that; and disbelief takes its doer out of the community (ummah), whereas killing is not like that. So disbelief is greater than killing. It is also reported concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse that some of the Companions had killed a man of the disbelievers in the sacred month, and the believers reproached them for that, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. The meaning is: you have no right to consider it a grave matter to take the initiative in killing in the sacred month, for the disbelievers' initiative in disbelief during the sacred month is far greater than that.

Second: The root of "fitnah" is placing gold over fire to extract it from impurities; then it became a term for everything that is a cause of testing, by analogy with this root. The meaning is: the disbelievers' initiative in disbelief, and in intimidating the believers, and in making the matter so severe for them that they became forced to abandon family and homeland, fleeing from their misguidance in religion and seeking to save themselves from what they fear and dread, is a severe fitnah; indeed it is worse than killing, which entails deliverance from the calamities and afflictions of this world. Some of the wise said: What is worse than this killing which He has obligated upon you as a recompense, other than that fitnah.

The third aspect: the intended meaning of fitnah is the everlasting punishment that befalls them because of their disbelief. It is as if it were said: kill them wherever you overtake them, and know that behind that is a punishment from Allah greater than it, as in His saying: ﴿And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52]. The application of the name "fitnah" to punishment is permissible, and that is from the category of applying the name of the cause to the effect. The Exalted said: ﴿On the Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13], then He said after it: ﴿Taste your fitnah﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 14], meaning your punishment. And He said: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted (fatanu) the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], meaning they tortured them. And He said: ﴿So when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the fitnah of people as the punishment of Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10], meaning their punishment as His punishment.

The fourth aspect: the intended meaning is their fitnah of you by barring you from the Sacred Mosque is worse than your killing of them in the Sacred Precinct, because they strive to prevent the worship and obedience for which jinn and mankind were created only.

The fifth aspect: the apostasy of a believer is more grievous to him than being killed while in the right. The meaning is: expel them from where they expelled you, even if that falls upon your own selves; for if you are killed while upon the truth, that is better for you and easier for you than that you apostatize from your religion or grow lax in obedience to your Lord.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: This explains that this condition remains in force for fighting them in this particular sacred ground, whereas previously it had been a condition for all fighting and in the sacred months.

The second issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited: (وَلَا تَقْتُلُوهُمْ حَتَّى يَقْتُلُوكُمْ فَإِنْ قَتَلُوكُمْ), all of it without an alif, while the rest recited all of that with an alif. It is written in the Mushaf without an alif, and it was written that way for brevity, just as "al-Rahman" is written without an alif, and likewise "Salih," and similar letters of madd and layn. The judge, may Allah have mercy on him, said: When the two well-known recitations do not conflict in practice, it is obligatory to act upon both, just as two verses are acted upon when their practice does not conflict; and what these two well-known recitations require does not conflict, so it is obligatory to act upon both as long as abrogation does not occur in it. It is narrated that al-A'mash said to Hamzah: What do you say about your recitation: when a man is killed, how can he afterward become a killer of others? Hamzah said: When a man of the Arabs is killed, they say "we were killed," and when a man of them is struck, they say "we were struck."

* * *

The third issue: The Hanafis held to this verse in the matter of one who seeks refuge in the Sacred Precinct, and they said: since killing at the Sacred Mosque was not permitted on account of the crime of disbelief, then it is more fitting that killing in the Sacred Mosque is not permitted on account of a sin that is less than disbelief. The full discussion of this is in the books of disagreement (kutub al-khilaf).

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, know that He, the Exalted, made fighting obligatory upon them as previously mentioned, and it was possible to assume that this fighting would continue even if they desisted and repented, as has been established in many of the hudud that repentance does not remove them. So He, the Exalted, said after making killing obligatory upon them: ﴿But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, thereby clarifying that whenever they desist from that, the obligation of killing falls from them. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal: 38].

* * *

Concerning the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: "But if they desist" means from fighting. Al-Hasan said: "But if they desist" means from polytheism (shirk).

The argument of the first opinion: the intended purpose of permission to fight is to prevent the disbelievers from fighting, so His saying "But if they desist" is to be understood as ceasing to fight.

The argument of the second opinion: the disbeliever does not attain Allah's forgiveness and mercy by ceasing to fight, but only by ceasing to disbelieve.

The second issue: Desisting from disbelief in reality is not achieved except by two things: one of them is repentance, and the other is adherence to Islam. Although it may be said outwardly of one who has professed the two testimonies that he has desisted from disbelief, that only has effect in preserving blood alone. As for what has effect in entitlement to reward, forgiveness and sanctity, it is nothing other than what we have mentioned.

The third issue: The verse indicates that repentance from every sin is accepted. The statement of one who says that repentance from deliberate killing is not accepted is an error, because if Allah accepts the repentance of a disbeliever, then accepting the repentance of a killer is more fitting. Moreover, a disbeliever may be one who combined, along with being a disbeliever, being a killer; so when the verse indicates the acceptance of the repentance of every disbeliever, it indicates that his repentance is accepted even if he was a killer. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 191–192:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them, and expel them from where they expelled you, for persecution is worse than killing.
