Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Concerning it are several issues:

The first issue: al-thaqf (ثقف) means finding something by way of seizing and overpowering, and from it comes the phrase rajul thaqif (رجل ثقيف), a man quick to seize his opponents. He said:

"If you capture me, then kill me; for whoever is captured, there is no immortality."

Then we say: His saying, ﴿And kill them﴾, the address in it is directed at the Prophet ﷺ and those who emigrated with him, although the intent of it applies to every believer. The pronoun in His saying ﴿And kill them﴾ refers to those whom He commanded to be killed in the first verse, and they are the disbelievers of the people of Makkah. So Allah the Exalted commanded their killing wherever they were, in the sacred territory (al-Haram) and in the sacred month. The clarification of the matter is that He, the Exalted, commanded jihad in the first verse on the condition that the disbelievers initiate fighting; in this one He added to the obligation and commanded jihad against them whether or not they fought, and He made an exception to it: fighting at the Sacred Mosque.

The second issue: It is reported from Muqatil that he said: the verse preceding this one, namely His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190], is abrogated (mansukhah) by His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾, and then that verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no persecution﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193]. As for his claim that His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾ is abrogated by this verse, its refutation has already passed. As for his claim that ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾ is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no persecution﴾, this is also an error, because it is not permissible to initiate fighting within the Sacred Precinct, and this ruling has not been abrogated but remains in force. Thus it is established that his statement is weak; and moreover, it is far from the Wise One to combine consecutive verses in such a way that each one abrogates the other.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The word "expulsion" (al-ikhraj) may bear two meanings:

One: that they compelled them to leave by force.

The second: that they exaggerated in intimidating them and in making the matter severe for them, until they became compelled to leave.

The second discussion: The form of the word "ḥaythu" (حيث) may bear two meanings:

One: expel them from the place from which they expelled you, which is Makkah.

The second: expel them from their dwellings. Having understood this, we say: Allah the Exalted commanded the believers to expel those disbelievers from Makkah if they persisted in their polytheism, if they were able to do so. But it was known that they would be able to do so afterward; for this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ expelled every polytheist from the Sacred Precinct, and then he expelled them also from Madinah, and he ﷺ said: "Two religions shall not coexist in the Arabian Peninsula."

* * *

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verse 193:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah (persecution/disbelief) and the religion is for Allah. But if they cease, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers.﴾

There are several issues here.

**The first issue:** The people said: this verse abrogates (*naskh*, the cancelling of one ruling by a later one) His words: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you there﴾ [2:191]. The correct view is that it does not, because the initiation of fighting at al-Masjid al-Haram removed its sanctity. At most, this description is general, but the position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and the correct view, is that a general ruling, whether it precedes the specifying text or comes after it, becomes specified by it. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The second issue:** Regarding the meaning of *fitnah* here, there are several views.

The first: it means shirk (association of partners with Allah) and kufr (disbelief). They said: their *fitnah* was that they would strike and harm the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah until they went to Abyssinia. Then they persisted in that harm until they went to Madinah. Their aim in stirring up that *fitnah* was that the believers would abandon their religion and return to disbelief. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. The meaning is: fight them until you prevail over them, so that they do not tempt you away from your religion and you do not fall into shirk.

The second: Abu Muslim said: the meaning of *fitnah* here is *jurm* (transgression/crime). He said: Allah the Exalted commanded fighting them so that there would no longer be the fighting which, when they initiated it, was a *fitnah* upon the believers, because of the various kinds of harm they feared in it. If it is said: how can it be said, ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾, when we know that fighting them does not remove kufr, and it does not follow from this that the report of Allah is not true?

We say: the answer is from two angles.

The first: this is to be understood as the usual case, because usually when they are fought, kufr and shirk cease. For whoever is killed, his kufr has ended, and whoever is not killed is feared to remain steadfast in disbelief. So when this is the usual outcome, it is permissible to say this.

The second answer: the meaning is, fight them with the intention of ending kufr. For it is obligatory on one who fights the disbelievers that this be his aim. Therefore, whenever he thinks that the one he is fighting will give up disbelief without fighting, it becomes obligatory for him to turn away from fighting.

As for His words, ﴿and the religion is for Allah﴾, this indicates that *fitnah* is to be understood as shirk, because there is no intermediary between shirk and the whole religion being for Allah. The meaning of this is that He, the Exalted, is the one worshipped and obeyed, not the rest of what is worshipped and obeyed besides Him. So the sense becomes as if He, the Exalted, said: fight them until kufr disappears and Islam is established, and until what leads to punishment disappears and what leads to reward is attained. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿You fight them, or they submit﴾ [48:16]. In this is clarification that He, the Exalted, only commanded fighting for this purpose.

As for His words, ﴿But if they cease﴾, the meaning is: if they cease from the matter for which fighting them became obligatory, which is either their kufr or their fighting. At that point, it is not permissible to fight them. This is like His words: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven for them﴾ [8:38].

* * *

As for His words, ﴿then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾, there are two views on it.

The first: if they cease, then there is no aggression, meaning there is no killing except against those who do not cease in disbelief, for they, by persisting in their disbelief, are wrongdoers against themselves, as He said: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great wrong﴾ [31:13].

If it is said: why was that killing called aggression when in itself it is right and correct?

We say: because that killing is the recompense for aggression, so it is correct to apply the name of aggression to it, as in His words: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [42:40], and His words: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [2:194], and ﴿They schemed and Allah schemed﴾ [3:54], and ﴿They mock them, so Allah mocks them﴾ [9:79].

The second: if you confront them after they have ceased from shirk and fighting, you would be the wrongdoers, and We would then give power over you to those who would commit aggression against you.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 194:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and sacred things are subject to retaliation. So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is with those who are mindful of Him.﴾

Know that when Allah permitted fighting, and that was objectionable among them, He mentioned in this verse what removes that objection, saying: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾. On it there are several aspects:

The first: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out in the year of al-Hudaybiyah for the 'umrah, and that was in Dhu al-Qa'dah in the sixth year after the Hijrah. The people of Makkah prevented him from that, then they made a treaty with him that he would turn back and return in the following year, and they would leave Makkah to him for three days. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned in the following year, in Dhu al-Qa'dah of the seventh year, entered Makkah and performed 'umrah, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse." Meaning: you entered the Sacred Precinct in a sacred month, and those people had prevented you in the previous year in this same month, so this month is for that month.

The second: What is narrated from al-Hasan, that the disbelievers heard that Allah, exalted is He, had forbidden the Messenger (ﷺ) from fighting them in the sacred months, so they wanted to fight him, thinking that he would not fight them. This is His saying: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting in it is grave, but averting from the way of Allah, disbelief in Him, and (barring access to) the Sacred Mosque...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse to explain the ruling in this incident, saying: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾, meaning: whoever among the polytheists makes your blood lawful in a sacred month, then make theirs lawful in it.

The third: What some of the theologians mentioned, namely that since the sacred month did not prevent you from disbelief in Allah, how should it prevent us from fighting you? So the sacred month on our side is matched by the sacred month on your side. The sum of the three aspects is that since the sanctity of the sacred month did not prevent them from disbelief and ugly deeds, how should they make it a cause for preventing fighting against their evil and corruption?

As for His saying: ﴿and sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾, "sacred things" is the plural of "sanctity" (ḥurmah), and ḥurmah is that which is forbidden to violate, and qiṣāṣ (retaliation) is equality. Knowing this, those aspects return in this verse.

As for the first aspect: the meaning of "sacred things" is the sacred month, the sacred land, and the sanctity of the state of ihram. So His saying: ﴿and sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾ means: since they violated these sanctities in the sixth year, you were granted success until you exacted it from them by their own claim in the seventh year.

As for the second aspect: the meaning is that if they proceed to fight you, then you fight them as well. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah, exalted is He, made known through this verse that it is not permitted for the Muslims to violate these sanctities by way of initiation, but only by way of retaliation. This view is more fitting with what precedes this verse, namely His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], and with what follows it, namely His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you.﴾

As for the third view: His saying: ﴿and sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾ means the sanctity of each of the two months is like the sanctity of the other, so they are equal, and retaliation is equality. Since the sanctity of the month did not prevent you from disbelief, sedition and fighting, how should it prevent us from fighting?

As for His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾, what is meant is the command to return the requital that corresponds to the transgression. The implied meaning: whoever transgresses against you, then respond to him. The reason for calling it "transgression" has already been mentioned. Then He said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, and the meaning of God-consciousness has already been mentioned. Then He said: ﴿And know that Allah is with those who are mindful of Him﴾, meaning with aid, support, protection and knowledge. This is among the strongest proofs that He is not a body and not in a place, for if He were a body He would be in a specific place, and then either He would be with one of them and not with the other, or with each of the believers there would be a part of His parts and a portion of His portions, exalted is Allah above that by a great exaltation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 195:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah, and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction, and do good; indeed, Allah loves the good-doers.﴾

Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is in two respects.

The first: when He, may He be exalted, commanded fighting, and engaging in fighting cannot be accomplished except with weapons and equipment, which require wealth, and it may be that the wealthy person is incapable of fighting while the brave man capable of fighting is poor and has no wealth, therefore Allah, may He be exalted, commanded the rich to spend on the poor who are able to fight.

The second: it is related that "when the saying of Allah, may He be exalted, was revealed: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and violations are subject to retribution﴾, a man among those present said: 'By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, we have no provisions, and there is no one to feed us.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that they spend in the way of Allah and give charity, and that they not withhold their hands from charity, even with half a date that is carried in the way of Allah, lest they perish. So this verse was revealed" in accordance with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Page 116

Know that spending (infaq) is the disbursement of wealth toward the ways of benefit; therefore one does not say of a wasteful person that he is a spender (munfiq). When spending is restricted by mention of "the way of Allah," the meaning is "in the path of religion," not that "sabil" means "path" in general; the way of Allah is His religion. Thus everything that Allah has commanded in His religion of spending is included in the verse, whether it is spending on pilgrimage (hajj) or lesser pilgrimage (umrah), or it is striving with the self, or equipping another, or spending on maintaining family ties, or on charities, or on dependents, or on zakat and expiations, or building a road, and other than that. However, the closer meaning in this verse, since jihad has been mentioned, is that it refers to spending in jihad. Indeed He said: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾ for two reasons:

The first: this is like an indication of the cause for the obligation of this spending, because wealth is Allah's wealth, so it is obligatory to spend it in the way of Allah; and because when the believer hears the mention of Allah, he is stirred and becomes active, so spending wealth becomes easy for him.

The second: this verse was revealed at the time the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went to Makkah to perform the umrah, and that umrah had to lead to fighting if the polytheists prevented them, so it was an umrah and a jihad, and both meanings were combined in it. When the matter was thus, He, may He be exalted, said without doubt: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾ and did not say: "spend in jihad and umrah."

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾, in it there are several issues:

The first issue: Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj said: "al-tahluka" is destruction; one says halaka yahlaku halakan, and halakan, and tahlukatan. Al-Kharazanji said: "I do not know in the speech of the Arabs a verbal noun on the pattern taf'ula with a damma on the 'ain except this one." Abu 'Ali said: "Sibawayh has transmitted al-tanusra and al-tastura, and this pattern has come as a noun other than a verbal noun." He said: "We do not know of it coming as an adjective." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "It is permissible to say that its origin is al-tahlika, like al-tajriba and al-tabsira, on the basis that it is a verbal noun in this form, then the damma was replaced by a kasra, as al-juwar came for al-jiwar."

I say: I am greatly astonished at the far-fetched explanations of these grammarians in such places, for if they found an unattributed line of poetry that supports what they wanted, they would rejoice in it and take it as a strong proof. The occurrence of this word in the speech of Allah, may He be exalted, which is agreed upon by both those who agree and those who disagree as eloquent, is more deserving of indicating the soundness and correctness of this word.

The second issue: They agreed that the particle "bi" in His saying ﴿with your own hands﴾ requires either an addition or an omission. Some people said: the "bi" is extra, and the meaning is: "and do not throw your hands into destruction." It is like His saying: "I pulled the garment by the garment," and "I took the pen by the pen," so these are two commonly used and well-known dialects. Or the intended meaning of "hands" is the selves, like His saying: ﴿for what your two hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Hajj: 10] or ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30]; so the meaning is: "and do not throw yourselves into destruction." Others said: rather, there is an ellipsis here, and the meaning is: "and do not throw yourselves with your hands into destruction."

The third issue: His saying: ﴿and do not throw with your own hands into destruction﴾. The exegetes differed about it. Some of them said it refers to the spending itself, and some said it refers to something other than it. As for the first group, they mentioned several meanings:

The first: that they should not spend their wealth on the important matters of jihad, so that the enemy overpowers them and destroys them. It is as if it were said: "If you are among the men of religion, spend your wealth in the way of Allah and seeking His pleasure; and if you are among the men of this world, spend your wealth to repel destruction and harm from yourself."

The second meaning: when He commanded them to spend, He forbade them from spending all their wealth, for spending all the wealth leads to destruction when there is severe need for food, drink, and clothing. Therefore the intended meaning is what He mentioned in His saying:

Page 117

﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither wasteful nor stingy, but are ever between that being a balance﴾ [al-Furqan: 67], and in His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29]. As for those who said that what is meant is other than spending, they mentioned several meanings:

One of them: that they neglect jihad and thereby expose themselves to destruction, which is the punishment of the Fire; so He urged them by this to adhere to jihad, and it is like His saying: ﴿that whoever perishes might perish upon clear evidence﴾ [al-Anfal: 42].

The second: what is meant by His saying: ﴿and do not throw with your own hands into destruction﴾ is: do not rush into war in a manner where you do not hope for benefit, and there is nothing for you in it except killing yourselves, for that is not permissible. Rather, one is obliged to rush in only when he hopes to inflict damage on the enemy, even if he fears being killed. But if he is hopeless of inflicting damage and it is most likely that he will be killed, then he is not permitted to advance into it. This meaning is transmitted from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib. It is also related from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said regarding this verse: it is the man who charges alone between the two lines. Some people criticized this interpretation and said: "This killing is not forbidden," and argued against it with several points:

The first: it is related that a man from the emigrants (muhajirun) charged at the enemy line, and the people shouted at him, but he threw himself with his hand into destruction. Then Abu Ayyub al-Ansari said: "We know best about this verse, and it was revealed concerning us: we accompanied the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), helped him, and witnessed the battles with him. When Islam became strong and its adherents increased, we returned to our families, our wealth, and our affairs. So the destruction was staying with family and wealth and abandoning jihad."

The second: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, related that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned Paradise, and a man from the Ansar said to him: 'What do you think, O Messenger of Allah, if I am killed while patient and seeking reward?' He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'For you is Paradise.' So he plunged into the group of the enemy and they killed him in front of the Messenger of Allah." And that a man from the Ansar threw away a shield he had on him when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, mentioned Paradise, then plunged into the enemy and they killed him.

The third: it is related that a man from the Ansar lagged behind from the Banu Mu'awiya, and he saw the birds hovering over those among his companions who had been killed. He said to some of those with him: "I will advance toward the enemy and they will kill me, and I will not lag behind from a battlefield where my companions were killed." He did so, and they mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said a good word about him.

The fourth: it is related that some people besieged a fortress, and a man fought until he was killed. It was said: "He threw his hand into destruction." This reached 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "They lied. Does not Allah, may He be exalted, say: ﴿And among the people is he who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207]?" And for the one who supports that interpretation there is an answer to these points, which is to say: "We only forbade throwing oneself into the ranks of the enemy when no damage from them is expected. But when damage is expected, we permit that. So why do you claim that this meaning exists in these incidents?"

The third meaning regarding the interpretation of the verse is that it is connected to His saying: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and violations are subject to retribution﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. That is: if they fight you in the sacred month, then fight them in it, for violations are subject to retribution; so repay their aggression against you. And do not let the sanctity of the month lead you to surrender to the one who fights you, so that you perish by abandoning fighting, for by that you would be "throwing your own hands into destruction."

The fourth meaning of the interpretation: the meaning is: spend in the way of Allah, and do not say, "We fear poverty if we spend, so we will perish and nothing will remain with us." They were forbidden to make themselves doomed by spending. The intended meaning of this "making" and "throwing" is the judgment of that, as one says: "So-and-so made so-and-so doomed and threw him into destruction" when he judges him to be so.

The fifth meaning: ﴿and do not throw with your own hands into destruction﴾ refers to the man who commits a sin and believes that no deed will benefit him with it; that is the throwing of oneself into destruction. The summary is that its meaning is the prohibition of despairing of the mercy of Allah, because that leads a person to abandon worship and persist in sin.

The sixth meaning: it is possible that the intended meaning is: "And spend in the way of Allah, and do not throw that spending into destruction and nullification." That is, by doing after that spending an action that nullifies its reward, either by reminding of favor or by mentioning acts of showing off and seeking reputation. Its parallel is His saying:

Page 118

﴿and do not nullify your deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 33].

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do good; indeed Allah loves the good-doers﴾, in it there are several issues:

The first issue: they differed as to what the word "muhsin" (good-doer) is derived from, and there are several opinions:

The first: that it is derived from the act of goodness (husn), and its use became common for one who benefits another with a good benefit, since goodness (ihsan) is good in itself. According to this, if beating and killing are good, the one who does them is a muhsin.

The second: that it is derived from ihsan, so the doer of goodness is not described as a muhsin unless his act is both good and ihsan together. Thus the derivation arises only from both matters combined.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿and do good﴾ has several meanings:

One of them: al-Asamm said: "Do good in the obligations of Allah."

The second: "Do good in spending on those whose maintenance and provision are obligatory upon you, and the intent of this is that that spending should be moderate, so do not be wasteful nor stingy." This is the closer meaning because of its connection to what precedes it, and it is possible to carry the verse on all these meanings.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿indeed Allah loves the good-doers﴾, it is clear, and its explanation has been mentioned many times before.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 1 of 6):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah. But if you are prevented, then [make an offering of] what is feasible of the sacrificial animal. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of sacrifice.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-ḥajj (pilgrimage) linguistically denotes intending something, and it is said: "Fulan ḥajja the thing" when he intends it repeatedly and keeps frequenting it. Al-ḥijjah, with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, means a year, and it is so called because people perform the pilgrimage in every year. In the Sharia, however, it is a term for specific acts, among which are pillars (arkān), among which are essentials (abʿāḍ), and among which are recommended forms (hayʾāt). The pillars are those things without which one does not exit the state of ihram (taḥallul) until one performs them; the essentials are the obligatory acts, such that if one is omitted, it is compensated by a sacrifice (dam); and the forms are those for whose omission no sacrifice is required. According to us, the pillars are five: the ihram, standing at ʿArafah, the circumambulation of the House (ṭawāf), the running between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah (saʿy), and, regarding the shaving or shortening of the head, there are two opinions: the more sound of them is that it is a rite (nusuk) without which taḥallul is not attained.

As for the essentials, they are: the ihram from the miqat; remaining at ʿArafah until sunset according to one opinion; spending the night at Muzdalifah on the night of sacrifice according to one opinion; throwing at Jamrat al-ʿAqabah; and spending the nights at Mina during the days of tashriq according to one opinion, and throwing on its days.

As for the rest of the acts of Hajj, they are sunnah.

As for the pillars of ʿUmrah, they are four: the ihram, the ṭawāf, the saʿy, and regarding shaving there are two opinions. Then the one performing ʿUmrah, after finishing the saʿy, if he has a sacrificial animal with him, slaughters it and then shaves or shortens [his hair]; and exiting the state of ihram does not depend on slaughtering the offering.

* * *

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And complete﴾ is a command to completion. Is this command absolute, or is it conditional upon entering into it? Our companions held that it is absolute, and the meaning is: perform the Hajj and the ʿUmrah in the manner of perfection and completeness.

The second view, which is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, is that this command is conditional, and the meaning is that whoever begins it should complete it. They said: it is permissible that entering into something is not obligatory, but after entering into it, completing it becomes obligatory. The benefit of this disagreement is that ʿUmrah is obligatory according to our companions, and not obligatory according to Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him.

The arguments of our companions are from several aspects:

The first argument: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah.﴾ The basis of the inference from it is that completion may mean performing an act fully and completely, and it may be understood as: if you begin the act, then complete it. When the possibility is established, the meaning of this expression must be that. As for demonstrating the possibility, it is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with commands, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], i.e., performed them in the manner of completeness and perfection; and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then complete the fast until night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], i.e., perform the fast completely until night. Taking the expression in this sense is preferable to the view of one who says: the meaning is "begin the fast then complete it," because on that reading an ellipsis is needed, whereas on the reading we have mentioned no ellipsis is needed. Thus it is established that His saying: ﴿And complete the Hajj﴾ may mean performing it in the manner of completeness and perfection, so it is necessary to interpret it thus. At most, it is possible that it also means: when you begin it, then complete it; but interpreting the expression in the first sense is preferable, and the following points indicate this:

The first: interpreting the verse in the second sense requires that this command be conditional, and the sense would be: complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah if you have begun them. On the first interpretation, which we have supported, there is no need to supply this condition, so it is preferable.

The second: the people of tafsir mentioned that this verse is the first verse revealed concerning the Hajj, so interpreting it as the obligation of Hajj is preferable to interpreting it as completion conditional upon beginning.

The third: some reciters read (And establish the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah). Although this is an irregular reading (qirāʾah shādhdhah), functioning as a report of a single transmitter, it is by consensus suitable for preferring one interpretation over another.

The fourth: the aspect we have supported indicates the obligation of Hajj and ʿUmrah, and the obligation of completing both after beginning them, whereas the interpretation you mentioned indicates only the basic obligation. Therefore what we have supported has greater benefit, so interpreting the word of Allah in that way is preferable.

The fifth: the matter is one of worship (ʿibadah), so caution in it is preferable, and the view that Hajj and ʿUmrah are both obligatory is closer to caution; therefore the expression must be interpreted accordingly.

The sixth: suppose we interpret the expression as the obligation of completion; we still say: the expression definitively indicates the obligation of completion, and the apparent sense of a command is obligation. So completion is definitively obligatory, and completion is preceded by beginning; and what the obligation cannot be fulfilled without, and what is within the power of the responsible person, is itself obligatory. Thus it follows that beginning is obligatory in Hajj and in ʿUmrah.

The seventh: it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, it is indeed its companion in the Book of Allah," meaning that ʿUmrah is the companion of Hajj in the command in the Book of Allah, i.e., in this verse. So it is like His saying: ﴿Establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾ [al-Hajj: 41]. This is the full elaboration of this argument.

If it is said: ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, and al-Shaʿbi read "wa-l-ʿumrata lillah" with the nominative (rafʿ), and this indicates that they intended to remove ʿUmrah from the ruling of Hajj regarding obligation.

We say: this is refuted in several ways:

The first: this is an irregular reading, so it does not oppose the widely transmitted (mutawatir) reading.

The second: it contains weakness in Arabic grammar (ʿarabiyyah), because it requires conjoining a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah) to a verbal sentence (jumlah fiʿliyyah).

The third: His saying: ﴿and ʿUmrah is for Allah﴾ means that ʿUmrah is the worship of Allah, and the mere fact that it is worship of Allah does not negate its obligation; otherwise a contradiction would arise between the meanings of the two readings, and that is impermissible.

The fourth: since His saying: ﴿and ʿUmrah is for Allah﴾ means: "and ʿUmrah is the worship of Allah," ʿUmrah must be something commanded, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5], and the command indicates obligation; and thus the purpose is achieved.

The second argument concerning the obligation of ʿUmrah: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿on the day of the greater pilgrimage﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3] indicates the existence of a lesser pilgrimage, according to the literal sense of the elative form (afʿal); and that is none other than ʿUmrah by consensus. Since it is established that ʿUmrah is a pilgrimage, it must be obligatory, by His saying: ﴿And complete the Hajj﴾, and by His saying: ﴿And for Allah is the pilgrimage to the House, incumbent upon mankind﴾ [Aal ʿImran: 97].

The third argument: concerning this issue there are hadiths, among them what Ibn al-Jawzi cited in al-Muttafaq bayna al-Sahihayn: "Jibril, peace be upon him, asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about Islam, and he said: 'That you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, that you establish the prayer, pay the zakat, fast Ramadan, and perform Hajj and ʿUmrah.'" And al-Nuʿman ibn Salim narrated from ʿUmar ibn Aws, "from Abu Razin that he asked the Prophet, peace be upon him, and said: 'My father is an elderly man who reached Islam, and he is unable to perform Hajj and ʿUmrah nor to travel,' so he, peace be upon him, said: 'Perform Hajj on behalf of your father and perform ʿUmrah,'" and he commanded both, and the command is for obligation. Among them is what Ibn Sirin narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, that he, peace be upon him, said: "Hajj and ʿUmrah are two obligations; it does not harm you with which of them you begin." Among them is what ʿAʾishah bint Talhah narrated, may Allah be pleased with her, "from ʿAʾishah, the Mother of the Believers, who said: I said, O Messenger of Allah, is there jihad upon women? He, peace be upon him, said: Upon them is a jihad without fighting in it: Hajj and ʿUmrah."

The fourth argument: concerning the obligation of ʿUmrah, al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Prophet ﷺ performed ʿUmrah before Hajj; and if ʿUmrah were not obligatory, it would have been more fitting for him to hasten to Hajj, which is obligatory.

The argument of the one who says ʿUmrah is not obligatory consists of several points:

The first argument: "The Bedouin who asked the Messenger, peace be upon him, about the pillars of Islam, and he taught him the prayer, zakat, Hajj, and fasting. The Bedouin said: 'Is there anything upon me besides this?' He said: 'No, unless you do something voluntarily.' The Bedouin said: 'I will not add to this nor reduce from it.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'The Bedouin has succeeded, if he is truthful.'" And he, peace be upon him, said: "Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, giving zakat, fasting Ramadan, and pilgrimage to the House." And he, peace be upon him, said: "Pray your five prayers, give zakat on your wealth, and make pilgrimage to your House, you will enter the Garden of your Lord." These are well-known reports, almost mutawatir, so it is not permissible to add to them or to reject them. From Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah: "The Prophet ﷺ was asked about ʿUmrah: is it obligatory or not? He said: 'No, but if you perform it, it is good for you.'" And from Muʿawiyah al-Darir, from Abu Salih al-Hanafi, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Hajj is jihad and ʿUmrah is voluntary."

The answer consists of several points:

One: what you have mentioned are solitary reports (akhbar ahad), so they do not oppose the Qur'an.

Second: perhaps ʿUmrah was not obligatory at the time the Messenger, peace be upon him, mentioned those hadiths, and afterward His saying was revealed: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah﴾. This is the closer view, because this verse was revealed in the seventh year after the Hijrah.

Third: the story of the Bedouin includes mention of Hajj, but it does not contain a detailed explanation of Hajj; and we have shown that ʿUmrah is a Hajj, since it is the lesser Hajj, so it is not contrary to the obligation of ʿUmrah. As for the hadith of Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, they said: its narration is through Hajjaj ibn Artah, who is weak.

* * *

The third issue: know that Hajj has three types: ifrad, qiran, and tamattuʿ. Ifrad is that one performs Hajj and then, after finishing it, performs ʿUmrah from the nearest area of the Haram (adna al-hill), or performs ʿUmrah before the months [of Hajj], then performs Hajj in that same year. Qiran is that one enters ihram with both Hajj and ʿUmrah together in the months of Hajj, by intending both in the heart; and likewise if one enters ihram with ʿUmrah in the months of Hajj, then before the ṭawāf adds Hajj to it, it becomes qiran. Tamattuʿ is that one enters ihram with ʿUmrah in the months of Hajj, performs its acts, then performs Hajj in that same year. It is called tamattuʿ because one enjoys the prohibitions of ihram after exiting the state of ihram from ʿUmrah, before entering ihram for Hajj.

Having known this, we say: people differed about which of these three is best. Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the best of them is ifrad, then tamattuʿ, then qiran; and in his work Ikhtilaf al-Hadith he said: tamattuʿ is better than ifrad, and Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, held this view. Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: qiran is best, then ifrad, then tamattuʿ, and this is the view of al-Muzani, Abu Ishaq, and al-Marwazi among our companions. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: qiran is best, then tamattuʿ, then ifrad.

The arguments of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, that ifrad is better are from several aspects:

The first: adhering to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah﴾, and the inference from it is in three aspects:

The first: the verse requires the conjunction of ʿUmrah to Hajj, and conjunction requires distinction between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined; and distinction is achieved only in ifrad. As for qiran, what exists is one thing, namely Hajj and ʿUmrah together, and that prevents the validity of the conjunction.

صفحة ١٢١

The second point: His saying, ﴿Complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾, requires ifrad (performing Hajj alone, without combining it with 'Umrah), by the evidence that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if you are prevented, then [sacrifice] what is feasible of the offering﴾. The qarin (one who performs qiran, combining Hajj and 'Umrah) is obligated to two offerings when prevented. Also, He obligated the creatures to one expiation (fidyah) when performing [the rites], whereas the qarin is obligated to two expiations when prevented.

The third point: This verse indicates the obligation of completion, and completion is only achieved through ifrad. This is supported by two aspects:

The first: Travel is intended in Hajj, as evidence that whoever bequeaths that Hajj be performed on his behalf, it is performed from his homeland. Were travel not intended in Hajj, it would be performed on his behalf from the nearest of the miqat (ritual boundary points). It is also indicated by the scholars' statement that if someone vows to perform Hajj on foot and performs it riding, he incurs a sacrifice (dam). Thus it is established that travel is intended, and qiran requires reducing travel, because through it the two journeys become one journey. So it is established that completion is only achieved through ifrad.

The second: Hajj has no meaning except visiting sanctified places and honored sites, and the pilgrim is the visitor of Allah, while Allah is the one visited. There is no doubt that whenever the visit and service are more numerous, their standing before the one served is greater. Through qiran, the two visits turn into one visit. Indeed, the truth is that all kinds of acts of worship in Hajj and 'Umrah are repeated under ifrad and become one under qiran. Thus it is established that ifrad is closer to completion. So if ifrad is not obligatory upon you by the ruling of this verse, it is at least more excellent.

The second argument in demonstrating that ifrad is more excellent: ifrad requires that one performs Hajj first, then 'Umrah afterward, so the arduous acts are greater in ifrad, and therefore it must be more excellent, due to his (peace be upon him) saying: "The most excellent of deeds is the most arduous of them," i.e., the most difficult.

The third argument: He (peace be upon him) performed ifrad, so ifrad must be more excellent. As for our statement that he performed ifrad, know that the Companions' narrations differed on this matter. Muslim narrated in his Sahih from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed ifrad for Hajj. Jabir and Ibn 'Umar narrated that he performed ifrad. As for Anas, it was narrated from him that he said: "I was standing by the chest of the she-camel of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and her saliva was dripping onto my shoulder, and I heard him saying: 'Labbayka bi-Hajjin wa 'Umrah ma'an' (Here I am for Hajj and 'Umrah together)." Then al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) preferred the narration of 'A'ishah, Jabir and Ibn 'Umar over the narration of Anas on several grounds.

The first of them concerns the status of the narrators. As for 'A'ishah, she was learned, and despite her knowledge, she was the most closely attached of people to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the most aware of his conditions. As for Jabir, he had been a companion of the Messenger (ﷺ) longer than Anas, and Anas was young at that time, before he had knowledge. As for Ibn 'Umar, despite his jurisprudence, he was closer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) than others, because his sister Hafsah was a wife of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: the absence of qiran is firmly established by continuity (istishab, the presumption of continuity of the original state).

The third: ifrad requires increasing worship, while qiran requires reducing it. So it is more fitting to attribute ifrad to the Prophet (peace be upon him). When it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed ifrad, it must be that ifrad is more excellent, because he (peace be upon him) chose the more excellent for himself, and because he said: "Take from me your rites (manasik)," i.e., learn from me.

The fourth argument: ifrad requires increasing worship, while qiran requires reducing it, so the former is more fitting, because the purpose of creating jinn and humankind is worship, and whatever leads more to increasing worship is more excellent.

The arguments of Abu Hanifah (may Allah be pleased with him) are from several aspects:

The first argument: holding to His saying, ﴿Complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾. This wording may mean that the intention is the obligation of each of them, or that the intention is the obligation of combining both of them in full completion. If we interpret it as the first, it does not yield the second. If we interpret it as the second, it yields the first as well, so the second is more beneficial, and therefore the wording must be interpreted as such, because it is preferable to interpret the speech of Allah as what is more beneficial.

The second argument: qiran is a combination of the two rites, so it must be more excellent than performing a single rite.

The third argument: in qiran there is hastening toward both rites, while in ifrad there is failure to hasten toward one of the two rites, so qiran must be more excellent, due to His saying: ﴿And hasten toward forgiveness﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133].

As for the answer to the first: we have shown that this verse indicates ifrad in three aspects, indicating what is more beneficial. As for what you have mentioned, it is merely good assumption, since you said: interpreting the wording as what is more beneficial is preferable. If this is so, the preference lies with our position.

As for the answer to the second and third: everything the qarin does, the mufrid also does, except that qiran was a stratagem for dropping an act of worship, so its status ends at being permitted, but as for being more excellent, no. In sum, al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) does not say that a Hajj performed alone without 'Umrah is more excellent than a combined Hajj. Rather, he says: whoever performs Hajj in its time, then 'Umrah in its time, the combination of these two matters is more excellent than performing the combined pilgrimage.

* * *

The fourth issue: the interpretation of completion (al-itmam) in His saying: ﴿Complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾, and there are several views.

The first: it was narrated from 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud that completing them means entering the state of ihram (consecration) from the dwelling of one's family.

The second: Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that whoever intends Hajj and 'Umrah for Allah, completion becomes obligatory upon him. He said: evidence for the soundness of this interpretation is that this verse was revealed after the disbelievers prevented the Prophet (ﷺ) from Hajj and 'Umrah the previous year. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger in this verse not to return [page 123] until he completes this obligation. A jurisprudential benefit arises from this interpretation, namely that voluntary Hajj and 'Umrah are like their obligatory counterparts in the obligation of completion.

The third: al-Asamm said: Allah, exalted is He, prescribed Hajj and 'Umrah, then commanded His servants to complete the recognized etiquette. Shaykh al-Imam Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned in his book Ihya' what relates to this subject. He said: the matters to be observed before setting out for ihram are eight:

The first: concerning wealth. One should begin with repentance, returning wrongful takings, settling debts, and preparing provision for everyone whose maintenance is obligatory upon him until the time of return. He should return any deposits he holds, and take along lawful, good wealth sufficient for his going and returning, without stinginess, but in a manner enabling him to be generous with provisions and kind to the poor. He should give some charity before his departure, and buy for himself a mount strong enough for carrying, or hire one. If he hires it, he should make clear to the renter everything that will bring the renter's contentment.

The second: concerning companions. One should seek a righteous companion who loves goodness and helps him toward it: if he forgets, he reminds him; if he remembers, he assists him; if he is fearful, he encourages him; if he is weak, he strengthens him; and if his chest is constricted, he gives him patience. As for brothers and companions who remain at home, he bids them farewell and seeks their supplications, for Allah, exalted is He, has placed goodness in their supplication. The Sunnah in farewell is to say: "I entrust to Allah your religion, your trust, and the conclusions of your deeds."

The third: concerning leaving the home. When he resolves to depart, he prays two rak'ahs, reciting in the first, after al-Fatihah, ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1], and in the second, al-Ikhlas, and after finishing he humbles himself before Allah with sincerity.

The fourth: when he reaches the door of the house, he says: "In the name of Allah, I have placed my trust in Allah; there is no power nor strength except through Allah." And the more supplications, the better.

The fifth: concerning mounting. When he mounts the riding animal, he says: "In the name of Allah, and by Allah, and Allah is greatest. I place my trust in Allah. There is no power nor strength except through Allah, the Most High, the Most Great. What Allah wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. Glory be to Allah who has subjected this to us, and we were not able to control it, and indeed to our Lord we will return."

The sixth: concerning dismounting. The Sunnah is that most of his travel be by night, and he should not dismount until the day heats up. When he dismounts, he prays two rak'ahs and calls upon Allah much.

The seventh: if an enemy or a predatory beast approaches him, by night or day, he should recite Ayat al-Kursi, Shahida Allah, al-Ikhlas, and the two Mu'awwidhatayn, and say: "I have sought refuge in Allah, the Mighty, and sought help from the Living who does not die."

The eighth: whenever he ascends a high place of land on the road, it is recommended that he say "Allahu Akbar" three times.

The ninth: that this journey not be mixed with any trace of immediate aims, such as trade or others.

The tenth: that a person guard his tongue against obscenity, wickedness, and disputation. Then, after bringing these preliminaries, he performs all the pillars of Hajj in the most correct manner, closest to conforming with the Book and the Sunnah, and his aim in all these matters is seeking the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He. So His saying: ﴿Complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah﴾ is a word comprehensive and inclusive of these meanings. When the servant performs Hajj in this manner, he is following the religion of Ibrahim, since Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The fourth aspect: concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾, that the intended meaning is: perform each of them with a separate journey. This is the interpretation of those who say ifrad, and we have already demonstrated it with evidence. This interpretation is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), and it has also been narrated as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report from Abu Hurayrah. 'Umar used to abandon qiran and tamattu', and would mention that this is more complete for Hajj and 'Umrah, and that one should perform 'Umrah outside the months of Hajj, since Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Hajj is in well-known months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "Separate your Hajj and your 'Umrah."

* * *

The fifth issue: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "al-Hajj" with a fatha on the ha' throughout the Qur'an, and this is the dialect of the Hijaz. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, from 'Asim, read it with a kasra in Al 'Imran. [page 124] Al-Kisa'i said: both are two dialects with the same meaning, like ratl and rittl (two units of weight). It was said: with the fatha it is the verbal noun (masdar), and with the kasra it is the noun (ism).

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you are prevented (uhsirtum)﴾. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: the root of al-hasr and al-ihsar is confinement (habs). From it one says of the person who does not divulge his secret: hasara, because he confined himself from disclosure. Al-hasr is the retention of excrement. Al-hasir means the king, because he is like one confined between the chamberlains. In the poetry of Labid:

Jinn at the door of al-Hasir standing

Al-hasir (the mat) is known, named so because some of its parts are joined to others, by analogy with a thing being confined with something else.

Having known this, we say: they agreed that the word hasr is specific to the enemy's prevention when he prevents someone from his purpose and constrains him. As for the word ihsar, they differed concerning it on three views.

The first, which is the choice of Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn al-Sikkit, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutaybah, and most of the lexicographers, is that it is specific to illness. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said "ahsarahu al-marad" (illness prevented him) when it prevents him from travel. Tha'lab said in Fasih al-Kalam: "uhsira" is used for illness, and "husira" for the enemy.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 3 of 6):

The second opinion: the word ihsar (ihsār) denotes confinement and prevention, whether it is caused by an enemy or by illness. This is the view of al-Farra'. The third opinion: it is specific to the prevention that comes from an enemy. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, for they both said: "There is no ihsar except the ihsar of an enemy." Most of the people of linguistic knowledge (ahl al-lughah) reject this view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. The benefit of this inquiry appears in a legal question (mas'alah fiqhiyyah), namely: they agreed that the ruling on ihsar is established when there is confinement by an enemy. Is it also established by illness and other impediments? Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is established. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not established. The argument of Abu Hanifa is evident according to the view of the people of linguistic knowledge, because the people of linguistic knowledge are of two kinds:

One of them: those who said that ihsar is specific to confinement caused by illness only. According to this view, this verse is an explicit text that ihsar by illness produces this ruling.

The second: those who said that ihsar is a name for confinement in general, whether it is caused by illness or by an enemy. According to this view too, the argument of Abu Hanifa is evident, because Allah the Exalted attached the ruling to the designation of ihsar, so the ruling must be established whenever ihsar occurs, whether it is caused by an enemy or by illness. As for the third view, that ihsar is a name for the prevention caused by an enemy, this view is invalid by the consensus of the people of linguistic knowledge. Even assuming it is established, we analogize illness to the enemy by the common factor of removing hardship, and this is a clear and evident analogy (qiyas jali). This is the formulation of Abu Hanifa's view, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is evident and strong. As for the formulation of al-Shafi'i's view, may Allah be pleased with him, we claim that what is meant by ihsar in this verse is only the prevention by an enemy, and the reports transmitted from the people of linguistic knowledge are countered by the reports transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar. There is no doubt that their statement is preferable, because they precede those lesser people in knowledge of the language and in knowledge of the interpretation of the Qur'an. Then, after this, we reinforce this view with several proofs.

The first proof: ihsar is an form (if'al) derived from hasr, and the form (al-if'al) sometimes comes to mean transitivity, as in: dhahaba Zayd and adhhabtuhu ana (Zayd went, and I made him go); and it comes to mean "became possessed of such-and-such," as in: aghadda al-ba'ir, when it became possessed of a swelling (ghuddah), and ajraba al-rajul, when he became possessed of camels afflicted with mange (jarba); and it comes to mean "found him with such-and-such a quality," as in: ahmadtu al-rajul, meaning I found him praiseworthy. And ihsar cannot be for transitivity, so it must be taken either as becoming or as finding. The meaning is: they became confined or they were found confined. Then the people of linguistic knowledge agreed that the one confined (al-mahsur) is the one prevented by an enemy, not by illness. So the meaning of ihsar must be that they became prevented by an enemy, or were found prevented by an enemy, and this reinforces our view.

The second proof: hasr is an expression for prevention, and one is said to be prevented from his action and restrained from his aim only when he is capable of that action and able to do it, and then an obstacle prevents him from it. Capability is an expression for the condition that results from the balance of temperament and soundness of the limbs, and this is absent in the case of the sick person, so he is not capable at all of the action. Therefore it is impossible to rule that he is prevented, because attributing the ruling to an impediment requires the presence of the cause. But when one is prevented by an enemy, capability for the action is present, except that the action is impossible due to repelling the enemy, so it is correct here to say that he is prevented from the action. Thus it is established that the word ihsar is literal in the case of the enemy, and it cannot be literal in the case of illness.

The third proof: the meaning of His saying: ﴿uhsirtum﴾ ("if you are prevented"), i.e., you were confined and prevented, and confinement necessarily has a confiner, and prevention necessarily has a preventer. It is impossible to describe illness as being a confiner and a preventer, because confining and preventing are acts, and attributing an act to illness is rationally impossible, since illness is an accident (ard) that does not persist for two moments, so how could it be an agent, confiner and preventer? As for describing the enemy as confiner and preventer, this is a real description, and bearing the speech on its literal meaning is preferable to bearing it on its figurative meaning.

The fourth proof: ihsar is derived from hasr, and the word hasr carries no indication of illness, so the word ihsar must be free of any indication of illness, by analogy with all derived words.

The fifth proof: after this verse Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever among you is ill, or has an ailment of his head﴾, and here He conjoined the sick person. So if the one prevented were the sick person, or one whom illness encompasses, this would be conjoining a thing to itself.

If it is said: He specified this illness by mention because it has a particular ruling, namely shaving the head, so the sense of the verse becomes: if you are prevented by illness, you are released by a sacrifice; and if your head is harmed by illness, you shave and expiate.

We say: although this is good for this purpose, it still entails conjoining a thing to itself. But if the one prevented is not defined as the sick person, conjoining a thing to itself does not follow, and so reading the one prevented as other than the sick person avoids this objection, and that is preferable.

The sixth proof: He, the Exalted, said at the end of the verse: ﴿Then when you are secure, whoever enjoys ʿumrah until ḥajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. The word amn (security) is used only regarding fear of an enemy, not regarding illness, for one says of the sick person: he was healed and recovered, and one does not say: he became secure.

If it is said: We do not concede that the word amn is used only for fear, for one says: the sick man became secure from death. Also, the specificity of the end of the verse does not undermine the generality of its beginning.

We say: the word amn, when unrestricted, conveys only security from the enemy.

As for his saying: the specificity of the latter part of the verse does not prevent the generality of its beginning.

We say: rather, it necessitates it, because His saying: ﴿then when you are secure﴾ does not indicate from what security was obtained, so it is necessary

[page 126]

that the intended meaning be security from something previously mentioned, and what was previously mentioned is ihsar. So the sense becomes: then when you are secure from that ihsar. Since it is established that the word amn is applied only with respect to an enemy, the intended ihsar must be prevention by an enemy. Thus by these proofs it is established that the ihsar mentioned in the verse is only prevention by an enemy, and as for the statement of one who says it is the prevention caused by illness alone, it is invalid by these proofs.

There is also another proof: the exegetes unanimously agreed that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that the unbelievers prevented the Prophet ﷺ at al-Hudaybiyah. And although people differed as to whether a verse revealed concerning a specific cause includes other than that cause, they agreed that the cause itself may not lie outside it. So if ihsar were a name for the prevention of illness, the occasion of revelation of the verse would lie outside it, and that is invalid by consensus. Thus it is established from what we have mentioned that ihsar in this verse is an expression for prevention by an enemy. Once this is established, we say: it is not possible to analogize the prevention of illness to it, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: the word "in" (in) is a conditional particle according to the people of linguistic knowledge, and the ruling of a condition is that the conditioned falls away when its condition falls away, apparently. This requires that the ruling not be established except for the ihsar that the verse indicates. So if we established this ruling for something else by analogy, that would be abrogation of the text by analogy, and this is impermissible.

The second aspect: ihram is a binding legal obligation that does not admit abrogation intentionally. Do you not see that if one has intercourse with his wife so that his hajj is invalidated, he does not exit his ihram; and likewise if the hajj is missed so that making up (qada') becomes obligatory? And illness is not like the enemy; for the sick person does not gain security from his illness by releasing himself and returning. But the one prevented by an enemy, if he stays, fears being killed; so if he returns, he has freed himself from fear of death. This is what I have on this question, in a manner befitting the tafsir.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿So what is easy of the offering﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the sense is: "then release yourselves, so what is easy [is due]," like His saying: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], meaning "then he breaks his fast, then a number." And within it there is another ellipsis, because His saying: ﴿so what is easy of the offering﴾ is an incomplete statement which must have an ellipsis. Then there are two possibilities:

One: that the position of "mā" is nominative, and the sense is: "then what is easy is incumbent upon you."

The second: al-Farra' said: if you put it in the accusative, meaning "offer what is easy," it would be correct; but most of what came in the Qur'an of its kind is nominative.

Second issue: "istaysara" means "tayassara," and similar to it are "ista'ẓama" meaning "ta'ẓẓama" (became great), "istakbara" meaning "takabbara" (became proud), and "istaṣʿaba" meaning "taṣʿʿaba" (became difficult).

Third issue: "al-hadyu" is the plural of "hadyah," as you say: "tamr" and "tamrah." Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā said: the people of the Ḥijāz pronounce "al-hadya" lightly, while Tamīm pronounce it heavily, so they say: "hadiyyah" and "hadiyy," and "maṭiyyah" and "maṭiyy." The poet said:

"I swore by the Lord of Makkah and the place of prayer, and by the necks of the offerings, garlanded."

The meaning of "al-hady" is what is brought as a gift to the House of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, seeking nearness to Him, like the gift that a person gives to another seeking nearness to him. Then ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said: the best of the offering is a camel (badanah), its middle is a cow, and its least is a sheep; so what is easy of these kinds is incumbent.

* * *

[page 127]

Fourth issue: If the one prevented is able to offer the hady, is there a substitute to which he may move? For al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, there are two opinions:

One: there is no substitute for him, and the hady remains in his obligation forever. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him. The argument is that Allah the Exalted made the offering obligatory upon the one prevented specifically, and did not establish a substitute for it.

The second: that he has a substitute to which he moves. This is the view of Ahmad. If we adopt the first view, is it permissible for him to release himself immediately, or should he remain in his ihram? There are two opinions:

One: that he remains in his ihram until he finds it. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, and the apparent meaning of the verse supports it.

The second: that he releases himself immediately, because of hardship, and this is the more correct. If we adopt the second view, there are many differences of opinion, and the nearest of them is that it is said: the offering is valued in dirhams, and with them food is bought and given in charity; and we said this only because it is closest to the hady.

* * *

Fifth issue: If the one prevented wishes to release himself and slaughters, he must intend release at the time of slaughter, and he may not release himself at all before the slaughter.

* * *

Sixth issue: Scholars differed regarding the ʿumrah. Most jurists said its ruling regarding ihsar is like the ruling of hajj. Ibn Sirin reported that there is no ihsar in it because it is not time-bound; but this is invalid, because the saying of the Exalted: ﴿But if you are prevented﴾ is mentioned after hajj and ʿumrah, so it refers back to both.

* * *

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: there is an omission in the verse, because a man is not released by the offering reaching its place of sacrifice; release occurs only by slaughtering. So the sense of the verse is: until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice and is slaughtered; and when it is slaughtered, then shave.

**Second issue:** Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: it is permissible to slaughter the sacrificial animal of ihsar (being prevented from completing the pilgrimage) outside the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), wherever one is detained. Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) said: this is permissible only within the Sacred Precinct. The source of the disagreement is the interpretation of this verse. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) held that *al-mahall* (the place or time of reaching the destination) in this verse is a term for the time at which the release from the state of ihram takes place. Abu Hanifa said it is a term for the place.

The proofs of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) are of several kinds.

The first: the Prophet (ﷺ) was prevented at al-Hudaybiyyah and slaughtered there, and al-Hudaybiyyah is not within the Sacred Precinct. The companions of Abu Hanifa said that he was prevented only at the edge of al-Hudaybiyyah that is nearest to Makkah, and that this is within the Sacred Precinct.

Al-Waqidi said: al-Hudaybiyyah lies on the edge of the Sacred Precinct, nine miles from Makkah. Al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) answered this question in his *Tafsir*, saying: the evidence that the slaughter of that sacrificial animal did not take place within the Sacred Precinct is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They are those who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram, and the sacrificial animals detained from reaching their place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. Allah the Exalted thus made clear that the disbelievers prevented the Prophet (ﷺ) from bringing the sacrificial animal to the place of sacrifice that he intended. This shows that they slaughtered that animal outside the Sacred Precinct.

The second proof: whether the muhsar is in the open area (al-hill) or in the Sacred Precinct, he is commanded to slaughter the sacrificial animal. Therefore he must be able to slaughter it both in the open area and in the Sacred Precinct.

The explanation of the first premise: the words ﴿If you are prevented﴾ cover every person who is prevented, whether he is in the open area or in the Sacred Precinct. His words after that, ﴿then what is easy of the sacrificial animal﴾, mean either: "then whatever sacrificial animal is easy is obligatory," or they mean:
*[p. 128]*
"then slaughter what is easy of the sacrificial animal." Under either reading, it is established that this verse indicates that slaughtering the sacrificial animal is obligatory upon the muhsar, whether he is prevented in the open area or in the Sacred Precinct. Once this is established, it must be that he may slaughter in both the open area and the Sacred Precinct, because the first level of a person charged with an obligation is that it is permissible for him to perform what is commanded. If this is so, it must be that the muhsar is able to shed the blood wherever he is prevented.

The third proof: Allah, glorified is He, granted the muhsar release from the state of ihram through slaughter only so that he could free himself from fear of the enemy at the present time. If slaughter were not permitted except within the Sacred Precinct, and release does not occur until the slaughter takes place (by the indication of the verse), then release would not take place at the present time. That contradicts the purpose of this ruling. Moreover, if the one who brings the animal to the Sacred Precinct is himself, then the fear has been removed, and how can one be secure in this act while fear persists? And if it is someone else, then he may not find such a person, so what will he do?

The proofs of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) are of several kinds:

The first: the word *mahall*, with the vowel of the middle letter of the verb, is an expression for a place, like *al-masjid* (mosque) and *al-majlis* (assembly). Thus the words ﴿until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of sacrifice﴾ indicate that it has not yet reached the place of release at present, whereas according to you it has reached its *mahall* at present.

The answer to this: *mahall* is an expression for a time, and it is well known that the *mahall* of a debt is the time at which it becomes due.

The second: suppose that the word *mahall* admits both place and time. Allah nonetheless removed this possibility by His words ﴿Then its place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj: 33], and in His words ﴿as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. There is no doubt that what is meant is the Sacred Precinct, since the House itself is not a place where blood is shed.

The answer to this: al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: whatever is obligatory upon the muhrim from his property, such as a camel or a compensatory offering, may be given only within the Sacred Precinct, to its poor, except in two cases:
One of them: whoever drives an offering animal and, on the way, it becomes lame, he may slaughter it and leave it to the poor.
The second: the blood-offering of one prevented by an enemy, for he slaughters where he is detained. So the verses you cited concerning all other blood-offerings, why do you say that they cover this case?

The third: they said: the offering is called *hadyu* (sacrificial animal) because it is like the gift (*hadiyyah*) that a servant sends to his Lord, and a gift is not a gift unless the giver sends it to the house of the one to whom it is given. This meaning cannot be conceived except by making the place of the offering the Sacred Precinct.

The answer to this: this is an argument based on the name. Moreover, it is to be understood as the preferred course when one is able.

The fourth: all blood-offerings of the Hajj, whether voluntary or expiatory, are valid only within the Sacred Precinct, so this one is too.

The answer to this: this blood-offering was obligatory only to remove fear, and the removal of fear takes place only if one is able to slaughter where one is prevented. But if it were required to send it to the Sacred Precinct, this purpose would not be achieved. This meaning does not exist in the other blood-offerings, so the difference is evident.

The third issue: this verse indicates that they should not release themselves from ihram and shave their heads until after offering what is easy of the sacrificial animal, just as He commanded them not to consult the Messenger except after offering a charity.

* * *

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So whoever among you is ill, or has an injury of his head, then an expiation by fasting or charity or sacrifice (nusuk). And when you are secure, whoever combines Umrah with Hajj [tamattu'] must offer what is easy of the sacrificial animal. And whoever cannot find one, then fasting three days during Hajj and seven when you return, that is ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Haram. And fear Allah and know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾. In this verse there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn Abbas said: this verse was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah. Ka'b said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by me during al-Hudaybiyyah, and there was much lice and nits in my hair, and they were falling onto my face. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do the vermin of your head harm you?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Shave your head." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. The purpose of it is that when the muhrim is harmed by an illness or by vermin of his head, he is permitted treatment and shaving, on condition of paying the expiation (fidyah). And Allah knows best.

The second issue: ﴿fidyah﴾ is in the nominative because it is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is omitted. The implied sense is: "then upon him is an expiation." There is also another omission in it, the sense being: "so he shaved, and upon him is an expiation."

The third issue: some said: this verse concerns only the muhsar, because before the sacrificial animal reaches its place of sacrifice, he may be afflicted by an illness or an injury to his head. If he endures it, Allah permitted him to do so on condition of giving the expiation. Others said: rather, the statement is a new one, applying to every muhrim who is afflicted in his body by illness and needs treatment, or is harmed in his head and needs to shave. Allah the Exalted made clear that he has this allowance and explained what expiation is obligatory upon him.

Having understood this, we say: illness may necessitate wearing clothing, so the concession regarding clothing is like the concession regarding shaving. This may also happen without illness, from extreme cold and the like, so he is permitted it on condition of the expiation. He may also need to use perfume for many illnesses, and the ruling there is the same. As for one who has an injury of his head, this may be due to lice and nits, may be due to headache, or may be from fear of an illness or pain arising. In sum, this ruling is general to all the prohibitions of the Hajj.

* * *

The fourth issue: they differed over whether one offers the expiation first and then takes the concession, or delays the expiation until after taking the concession. What the apparent meaning requires is that one delays the expiation until after taking the concession, because undertaking the concession is like the cause for the obligation of the expiation, so it precedes it. Also, we have already explained that the implied sense of the verse is: "so he shaved, and upon him is an expiation," and the speech is not coherent except in this form. Therefore the expiation must be delayed.

*[p. 130]*

As for the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿by fasting or charity or sacrifice (nusuk)﴾, the meaning is that this expiation is one of these three things. In this verse there are issues:

The first issue: the root of *nusuk* is worship. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *nusuk* means ingots of silver, each ingot of which is a *nasikah*. Then the one who worships was called *nasik*, because he purified himself from the filth of sins and cleansed it, like the ingot purified of impurity. This is the root meaning of *nusuk*. Then the sacrificial animal was called *nusuk*, because it is among the most noble acts of worship by which one draws near to Allah.

The second issue: they agreed that regarding *nusuk*, its minimum is a sheep, because *nusuk* is not fulfilled except by one of three things: the camel, the cow, or the sheep. Since the least of them is the sheep, the least obligatory amount in *nusuk* is a sheep. As for fasting and feeding, there is nothing in the verse indicating their quantity and manner. On what their explanation depends, there are two views:

One of them: that it came from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, namely what Abu Dawud related in his *Sunan*, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah and saw the abundance of vermin in his head, he said to him: "Shave, then slaughter a sheep as nusuk, or fast three days, or feed three sa' of dates to six poor people."

The second view: what is related from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan, that they both said: fasting for the one who combines is ten days, and feeding is similar in number. Their argument is that since fasting and feeding are general in this place, they must be interpreted by what is explained afterwards, namely what is required of the one combining when he does not find the sacrificial animal. The first view is what most jurists hold.

The third issue: the verse indicates the ruling for one who commits any of the prohibitions of the Hajj out of necessity. As for one who shaves his head deliberately without excuse, according to al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) and Abu Hanifa, what is obligatory upon him is a blood-offering (dam). Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) said: his ruling is the ruling of one who does this out of necessity. The verse is an argument against him, because the words ﴿So whoever among you is ill, or has an injury of his head, then an expiation by fasting﴾ indicate that this ruling is conditioned on these excuses, and what is conditioned on something is absent when the condition is absent.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when you are secure﴾. Know that its implied sense is: "And when you are secure from the prevention."

His words: ﴿whoever combines Umrah with Hajj﴾. In this there are issues:

The first issue: the meaning of *tamatta'* is enjoyment. It is said: "he enjoyed (tamatta'a) the thing," meaning he took pleasure in it. *Mata'* is everything that one enjoys. Its root is from their saying: "a long rope" (*hablun mati'*), meaning long. Whoever's companionship with a thing is prolonged is one who enjoys it.
