The one who combines Umrah with Hajj is one who comes to Makkah, performs Umrah in the months of Hajj, then remains in Makkah in the state of release, from which he sets out for Hajj, and performs Hajj in that same year. He was called *mutamatti'* because he enjoys the prohibitions of ihram in the interval between his release from Umrah and his entering ihram for Hajj. Combining on this basis is valid and carries no disapprobation. There is another kind of combining that is disliked, which Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) warned against when he said: "There were two enjoyments (*mut'atan*) in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I forbid them and punish for them: the enjoyment of women and the enjoyment of Hajj." What is meant by this enjoyment is that one combines the two ihrams, then changes the Hajj into Umrah and enjoys it up to the Hajj. It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted his companions to do this, and then it was abrogated (*nusikha*, abrogated by later ruling).

It is related from Abu Dharr that he said: "The enjoyment of Hajj was only for me alone." The reason for this was that they did not regard Umrah during the months of Hajj as valid, and considered it among the most wicked of wickedness. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to overturn this belief among them, he went to great lengths, by moving them during the months of Hajj from Hajj to Umrah. This is a reason in which others do not share with them, and for this meaning the changing of Hajj was specific to them.

*[p. 131]*

Second issue: His saying, exalted is He: "So whoever enjoys (tamattu') by the 'umrah..." means: whoever enjoys by means of the 'umrah. It is as if he does not enjoy the 'umrah itself, but he enjoys the prohibited things of ihram by means of his performing the 'umrah. This is the meaning of tamattu' by the 'umrah until the hajj.
* * *
As for His saying, exalted is He: "then what is feasible of the offering (hady)", there are several issues:
The first issue: Our companions (the Shafi'is) said: the obligation of the tamattu' sacrifice (dam al-tamattu') has five conditions:
The first: that he puts the 'umrah before the hajj.
The second: that he enters ihram for the 'umrah during the months of the hajj. If he enters ihram for it before the months of the hajj and performs some of the tawaf, even one circuit, then completes the rest during the months of the hajj, and performs the hajj in this same year, no sacrifice is obligatory upon him, because he has not combined the two rites within the months of the hajj. If he enters ihram for the 'umrah before the months of the hajj and performs its acts during the months of the hajj, there are two opinions. He said in al-Umm, and this is the more correct view: no tamattu' sacrifice is obligatory upon him, because he performed a pillar of the 'umrah before the months of the hajj, just as if he had performed tawaf before them. He said in al-Qadim and al-Imla': it is obligatory upon him, and he treats the continuation of ihram during the months of the hajj like its initiation. Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) said: if he performs part of the tawaf before the months of the hajj, he is a mutamatti' provided he has not performed most of it.
The third condition: that he performs the hajj in this same year. If he performs the hajj in another year, the sacrifice is not obligatory upon him, because the combining of hajj and 'umrah in a single year did not occur.
The fourth condition: that he is not one of the residents of al-Masjid al-Haram, based on His saying, exalted is He: "That is for the one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Haram." The resident of al-Masjid al-Haram is one whose family is at a distance less than the distance of shortening the prayer (masafat al-qasr). If they are at the distance of shortening the prayer, he is not among the residents. This distance is reckoned from Makkah or from the Haram, and on this there are two views.
The fifth condition: that he enters ihram for the hajj from within Makkah after finishing the 'umrah. If he returns to the miqat and enters ihram for the hajj from there, the tamattu' sacrifice is not obligatory upon him, because the obligation of the sacrifice is for abandoning ihram from the miqat, and that did not occur. These are the conditions regarded as necessary for the obligation of the tamattu' sacrifice.
* * *
The second issue: al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the tamattu' sacrifice is a sacrifice of compensation (dam jubran) for a fault, so it is not permissible for him to eat from it. Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) said: it is a sacrifice of rite (dam nusuk), and he may eat from it. Al-Shafi'i's proof is in several respects:
The first proof: the tamattu' has a defect in it, so the sacrifice must be a sacrifice of compensation.
The demonstration that a defect occurs in it is in three respects:
The first: it was narrated that Uthman used to forbid the mut'ah, and 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said to him: you have resorted to a concession born of need and estrangement, and that indicates there is a deficiency in it.
The second: He, exalted is He, named it tamattu', and tamattu' is an expression for pleasure and gratification, whereas the foundation of worship is hardship. So this indicates that in its being an act of worship there is some kind of defect.
The third, which is the explanation of the defect in detail: in tamattu' the journey became for the 'umrah, whereas it should rightly have been for the hajj, since the greater pilgrimage is the hajj. Also, a state of ease occurred at the time of release (ihlal) between the two, and that is a defect. Also, it was proper to make the miqat for the hajj, since it is greater, so when the miqat was made for the 'umrah, that was a kind of defect. And when it is established that there is a defect in this hajj, it becomes necessary to make the sacrifice a sacrifice of compensation and not a sacrifice of rite.
The second proof: the sacrifice is not one of the original rites (nusuk asliyy) of the hajj or the 'umrah, as it would not be if one performed them separately, and as it is in the case of the Makkan. Combining the two acts of worship also does not make the sacrifice obligatory, by the evidence that whoever combines prayer, fasting and i'tikaf is not obliged to a sacrifice. Thus it is established that this sacrifice is not a sacrifice of rite, so it must be a sacrifice of compensation.
The third proof: Allah, exalted is He, made the offering obligatory upon the tamattu' without a fixed time, and that it is not fixed in time is evidence that it is a sacrifice of compensation, because all the rites are fixed in time.
<br>
The fourth proof: fasting has a share in it, and a sacrifice of rite is not replaced by fasting. Once you know the soundness of what we have mentioned, we say: Allah, exalted is He, obligated the one who is responsible to complete the hajj in His saying: "And complete the hajj and the 'umrah for Allah." We have shown that the hajj of tamattu' is not complete, and therefore He, exalted is He, said: "Whoever enjoys by the 'umrah until the hajj, then what is feasible of the offering." That is because your tamattu' brings about a deficiency in your hajj, so compensate it with the offering so that your hajj may be completed by it. This is a fine meaning understood from the context of the verse, and it is established only according to the madhhab of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him).
* * *
The third issue: the sacrifice obligatory through tamattu' is a sheep of a six-month-old (jadhaʿa) lamb of the sheep, or a thaniyya of the goats; and if six people share in a cow or a camel (badana), it is permissible. Its time of obligation is after one has entered ihram for the hajj, because the fa' in His saying: "then what is feasible of the offering" indicates that it is obligatory immediately after the tamattu'. It is recommended to slaughter it on the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). If he slaughters it after entering ihram for the hajj, it is permissible, because the tamattu' has already been realized. According to Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) it is not permissible. The root of this is that the tamattu' sacrifice, according to us, is a sacrifice of compensation like all the sacrifices of compensation, and according to him it is a sacrifice of rite like the sacrifice of the udhiyya, so it is restricted to the Day of Sacrifice.
As for His saying, exalted is He: "Then whoever does not find (the offering), then a fast of three days" the meaning is that if the tamattu' finds the offering, there is no discussion; and if he does not find it, Allah, exalted is He, has clarified its substitute, which is fasting. So is this offering better or fasting? The apparent view is that the replaced thing, which is the original, is better. However, He, exalted is He, made clear in this substitute that in perfection and reward it is like the offering. It is like His saying: "Those are ten complete." In the verse there are issues:
The first issue: the verse is an explicit text for when one does not find the offering. The jurists analogized upon it the case where one finds the offering but does not find its price, or whose wealth is absent, or where it is sold at a high price; here too he turns to fasting.
The second issue: His saying: "a fast of three days in the hajj" means: upon him are three days during the time he is occupied with the hajj. A jurisprudential issue branches from this: that the mutamatti' who does not find the offering, his fasting is not valid after entering ihram for the 'umrah and before entering ihram for the hajj. Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) said: it is valid.
The proof of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) is in several respects:
The first: he fasted before its time, so it is not permissible, like one who fasts Ramadan before it, and like one who fasts the seven days before returning. We say he fasted before its time because Allah, exalted is He, said: "a fast of three days in the hajj," and by it He intended the ihram of the hajj, because the other acts of the hajj are not suitable as a boundary for fasting, whereas the ihram is suitable; so it is necessary to interpret it as such.
The second: what precedes the ihram for the hajj is not a time for the offering, which is the superior, so likewise it is not a time for fasting, which is its substitute, by analogy with all the originals and their substitutes. To verify this: the substitute in the absence of the original stands in its place, so it becomes in ruling as if it were the original, and therefore it is not permissible that it occur at a time when, had the original been found, it would not be permissible.
Having known this, we say: they agreed that it is permissible after beginning the hajj up to the Day of Sacrifice; the more correct view is that it is not permissible on the Day of Sacrifice nor on the days of tashriq, because of the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Do not fast on these days." The recommended practice is to fast on the days of the hajj, such that on the Day of 'Arafah he is not fasting.
* * *
The third issue: they differed regarding the meaning of "returning" in His saying: "when you return." Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said in al-Jadid: it is the return to the family and homeland. Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the intended return is the completion of
Page 133
the acts of the hajj and the beginning of the return journey. It follows from this that if he fasts the seven days after returning from the hajj and before arriving at his house, it does not suffice according to al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him), and it suffices according to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him). The proofs of al-Shafi'i are several:
The first: His saying: "when you return" means to the homeland, for Allah, exalted is He, made the return to the homeland a condition, and what the condition is not present for, the conditioned is not present. The return to the homeland is not attained except upon arriving at the homeland, so before it the condition was not present; therefore the conditioned must not be present. What we have said is strengthened by the fact that if he dies before reaching the homeland, nothing is incumbent upon him.
The second: what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When we came to Makkah, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Make your ihlal for the hajj an 'umrah, except for one who has garlanded the offering." So we circumambulated the House and (performed the sa'y between) al-Safa and al-Marwah, and we had relations with the women and wore garments. Then on the evening of the Tarwiyah he commanded us to make ihlal for the hajj. When we finished, he said: "Upon you is the offering; if you do not find it, then a fast of three days in the hajj and seven when you return to your cities."
The third: Allah, exalted is He, removed the obligation of fasting from the traveler in Ramadan; so the fasting of tamattu' is lighter in status than it.
The fourth issue: Ibn Abi 'Abla read "sab'atan" in the accusative, as a conjunction upon the place of "three days," as if it were said: "a fast of three days," like His saying: "or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan" (al-Balad: 14).
* * *
As for His saying, exalted is He: "Those are ten complete," the atheists, may Allah curse them, have attacked it in two respects:
One of them: it is known by necessity that three and seven are ten, so mentioning it is an explanation of the evident.
The second: His saying "complete" suggests the existence of ten that are not complete in being ten, and that is impossible. The scholars have mentioned kinds of benefit in this statement:
The first: the waw in His saying "and seven when you return" is not a definitive text for conjunction; rather it may mean "or," as in His saying: "two, three, or four" (al-Nisa: 3), and as in the saying: "sit with al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin," meaning sit with this one or that one. So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned "ten complete" to remove this suspicion.
The second kind: it is customary that the substitute is weaker in status than what it replaces, as in tayammum with water. Allah, exalted is He, explained that this substitute is not like that; rather it is complete in standing in the place of what it replaces, so that the one lacking the offering, bearing the hardship of fasting, may be at peace with what he has obtained of the complete reward from Allah. The mention of "ten" is only for the correctness of the connection to His saying "complete," as if He had said: "those are complete," it would allow that by it is meant the three separated from the seven, or the seven separated from the three; so it is necessary to mention "ten" in this. Then know that His saying "complete" admits of explaining completeness in three respects:
One: that they are complete as a substitute for the offering, standing in its place.
Second: that the reward of its doer is complete, like the reward of one who brings the offering from among those able to do so.
Third: that the hajj of the mutamatti', if he performs this fasting, is complete, like the hajj of one who did not perform this tamattu'.
The third kind: when Allah, exalted is He, says: "I have obligated upon you fasting ten days," it is not far-fetched that there be some indication requiring the exclusion of some of these days from this wording, for the specification of the general (takhsis al-'amm) is frequent in the Shari'ah and in custom. So if He had said: "three days in the hajj and seven when you return," there would remain the possibility that it is specified according to some specifying indications. But when He says after it: "Those are ten complete," this is an explicit statement that this specifier does not exist at all, so its indication is stronger and its susceptibility to specification and abrogation is more remote.

The Fourth Type: The levels of numbers are four: units, tens, hundreds, and thousands. Beyond that, a number is either compound or fractional. That ten is a number described with perfection by this explanation requires clarification, so the sense of the speech becomes:
[Page 134]
"I have only made this number obligatory because it is a number described with the attribute of perfection, free of fraction and composition."

The Fifth Type: Emphasis (tawkid) is a well-known method in Arabic speech, as in His saying: ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that grow blind﴾ [al-Hajj: 46], and He said: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. Its benefit is that a statement expressed in many phrases and known through many attributes is further from forgetting and oblivion than a statement expressed in a single phrase. Expression through many phrases indicates that the matter itself contains many benefits, and it is not permissible to neglect them. As for what is expressed in a single phrase, it is not known from it that it is a significant benefit that may not be neglected. Since emphasis includes this wisdom, its mention in this place indicates that observing the number in this fast is among the important matters that may by no means be neglected.

The Sixth Type: Concerning the explanation of the benefit of this statement: this address is to the Arabs, and they were not people of calculation. So Allah, exalted is He, clarified this with a decisive explanation that removes doubt and uncertainty. This is like what is narrated: he (ﷺ) said about the month, "It is like this and like this," and he gestured with his hands three times, and gestured a second time and folded his thumb at the third, indicating by the first gesture thirty, and by the second twenty-nine.

The Seventh Type: This statement removes the ambiguity arising from a misreading of the script, because seven and nine are similar in writing. When He says after it, "That is ten complete," this confusion is removed.

The Eighth Type: His saying ﴿a fast of three days during the Hajj and seven when you return﴾ may mean that what is obligatory after returning is to complete seven days, counting from these seven those three earlier days, so that the remainder owed after the Hajj is four in addition to the three earlier. It may also mean that what is obligatory after returning is seven in addition to those three earlier. This statement is thus open to these two interpretations. When He says after it, "That is ten complete," this problem is removed, and it clarifies that what is obligatory after returning is seven in addition to the three earlier.

The Ninth Type: Although the wording is a report, its meaning is a command. The sense is: let those fasts be complete fasts, because the Hajj commanded is a complete Hajj, as He said: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'umrah for Allah﴾. These fasts are a compensation (jubran) for the deficiency occurring in that Hajj, so these fasts must be complete fasts so that they compensate for the deficiency in that Hajj, which must be complete and whole. What is meant by these fasts being complete is what we mentioned in explaining the Hajj being complete. The wording was shifted from command to report because when an obligation is extremely emphasized, it is apparent that the obligated act will come into existence. For this reason, it is permissible to make the report of a matter as occurring a metaphor (kinayah) for the strong emphasis on it and the Law's emphasis on making it obligatory.

The Tenth Type: When He, glorified and exalted is He, commanded a fast of three days during the Hajj and seven after returning from the Hajj, this measure alone does not show that it is a great and complete act of obedience with Allah, glorified and exalted is He. When He said after it, "That is ten complete," this indicates that this act of obedience is in the utmost perfection. This is because fasting is ascribed to Allah, exalted is He, with the lam of exclusivity, as He said: "Fasting is for Me." The Hajj is also ascribed to Allah, exalted is He, with the lam of exclusivity, as He said: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'umrah for Allah﴾. Just as the text indicates a greater exclusivity of these two acts of worship to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, reason also indicates this. As for fasting, it is an act of worship whose wisdom the intellect never fully grasps, and it is, moreover, very hard on the self. Therefore it is performed only purely for the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He. The Hajj is also an act of worship whose wisdom the intellect never fully grasps, and it is, moreover, very hard, because it requires leaving family and homeland and distancing oneself from most pleasures. Therefore it is performed only for the pure pleasure of Allah. Furthermore, some of these ten days fall during the time of the Hajj, so it combines two very hard acts; and some fall after completing the Hajj, which is a transition from one hardship to another. It is well known that this is a cause for greater reward and elevated rank. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, made obligatory the fasting of these ten days, and testified that it is an act of worship in the utmost perfection and elevation, saying: ﴿That is ten complete﴾. The indefinite form in this place indicates the magnification of the matter; it is as if He said: "Ten, and what a ten: ten complete." Thus it has become clear through these ten aspects that this phrase contains these precious benefits, and by this explanation the criticism of the heretics regarding this verse has been refuted. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is for one whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾, there are several issues:

The First Issue: His saying ﴿That﴾ refers to what has preceded. The nearest of the mentioned matters is the mention of what the one performing tamattu' must offer as a sacrifice (hady) and its substitute, and the furthest is the mention of their tamattu'. For this reason they differed. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it refers to the nearest, namely the obligation of the sacrifice and its substitute on the one performing tamattu', meaning that it applies only if the one performing tamattu' is not from those present at the Sacred Mosque. If he is from the people of the Haram, he is not obligated to offer a sacrifice or its substitute. This is because, according to al-Shafi'i, this sacrifice is obligatory only upon the one coming from afar (afaqi), since it was obligatory upon him to enter the state of ihram for Hajj from the miqat. When he entered ihram from the miqat for 'umrah and then entered ihram for Hajj not from the miqat, a deficiency occurred, so it was made compensated by this sacrifice. The Meccan is not obligated to enter ihram from the miqat, so his undertaking tamattu' does not cause a deficiency in his Hajj, and therefore he is not obligated to a sacrifice or a substitute. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: His saying ﴿That﴾ refers to the furthest, which is the mention of tamattu'. According to him, there is no tamattu' or qiran for the people of the Sacred Mosque, and whoever performs tamattu' or qiran among them must offer a sacrifice which is a sacrifice of penalty (dam jinayah), from which he may not eat. The proofs of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, are of several kinds:

The First Proof: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then whoever performs tamattu' by 'umrah until Hajj﴾ is general and includes the people of the Haram.

The Second Proof: His saying ﴿That﴾ is a pronoun (kinayah), so it must return to the nearest thing mentioned, which is the obligation of the sacrifice. If the obligation of the sacrifice is restricted to the one performing tamattu' who is from afar, it is certain that someone not from afar may also be one performing tamattu'.

The Third Proof: Allah, exalted is He, legislated qiran and tamattu' to make clear the abrogation of what the people of the Jahiliyyah had done in forbidding 'umrah during the months of Hajj, and abrogation applies to all people.

The Fourth Proof: Whoever is of the people of ifrad is of the people of tamattu' by analogy to the Medinan, except that a Meccan performing tamattu' has no sacrifice upon him, for the reason we have mentioned.

The proof of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is that His saying ﴿That﴾ is a pronoun, so it must return to everything previously mentioned, because one part is not preferable over another.

The answer to this: Why is it not permissible to say that its return to the nearest is preferable? Because nearness is a cause of preference. Is it not the case that his own school holds that an exception stated after a series of sentences applies only to the last sentence, and that this sentence was distinguished from the other sentences only because of its nearness? So likewise here.

* * *

The Second Issue: They differed regarding the meaning of "those present at the Sacred Mosque." Malik said: they are the people of Mecca and the people of Dhi Tuwa. He said: If the people of Mina entered ihram for 'umrah from where it is permitted for them, and then remained in Mecca until they performed Hajj, they would be performers of tamattu'. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked about the people of the Haram: is what is obligatory on the performer of tamattu' obligatory on them? He said: Yes, but they are not like the people of Mecca. It was said to him: What about the people of Mina? He said: I do not consider it applicable except to the people of Mecca specifically. Tawus said: Those present at the Sacred Mosque are the people of the Haram. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: They are those who are at a distance from Mecca of less than the distance for shortening prayer (qasr). If they are at the distance for qasr, they are not among those present. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Those present at the Sacred Mosque are the people of the miqats, which are Dhu'l-Hulayfah, al-Juhfah, Qarn, Yalamlam, and Dhat 'Irq. So whoever is from the people of one of these places, or from the people of what lies beyond them up to Mecca, is one of those present at the Sacred Mosque. This is the detailed account of people's positions.

The wording of the verse agrees with the school of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, because the people of Mecca are those who witness the Sacred Mosque and are present at it, so the wording of the verse indicates only them. However, al-Shafi'i said: Allah often mentions the Sacred Mosque and means by it the Haram. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1], and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken by night from the Haram, not from the Sacred Mosque itself. And He said: ﴿Then its place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj: 33], and what is meant is the Haram, because blood is not spilled inside the House or the Mosque.

Having established this, we say: what is meant by the Sacred Mosque here is what we have mentioned, and two things indicate this:

The first: "present" (hadir) is the opposite of "traveler" (musafir). Everyone who is not a traveler is present. Since the rule of travel applies only at the distance of qasr, everyone who is less than the distance of qasr is not a traveler and is present.

The second: The Arabs call the people of settled places "present" (hadirah and hadirin), and the people of the open desert "bedouin" (badiyah and badin). The common expression among people is: "the people of the desert and the settled," meaning the people of the tents and the people of the villages.

* * *

The Third Issue: Al-Farra' said: the lam in His saying ﴿for one whose﴾ means "upon," meaning: that obligation, which is the sacrifice or the fast, is incumbent upon the one who is not from the people of Mecca, like the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Stipulate for them the wala' (patronage)," meaning upon them.

The Fourth Issue: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the presence of the family, but what is meant is the presence of the one in ihram, not the presence of the family, because the usual case for a man is that he lives where his family lives.

The Fifth Issue: The Sacred Mosque is described with this description because the root of "haram" (sacred/forbidden) is what is prohibited and deprived, namely what is forbidden from gains, and anything prohibited is haram because it is forbidden to approach. The Sacred Mosque is forbidden from having done in it what is prohibited from being done. Al-Farra' said: It is said "haram" and "haram" like "zaman" and "zaman."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: He means in what has been made obligatory upon you. ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever neglects His limits. Abu Muslim said: "al-'iqab" and "al-mu'aqabah" are the same, and it is the requital of the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing. It is derived from "al-'aqibah" (outcome), as if it means the outcome of the wrongdoer's act, like the saying of the speaker: "You will surely taste the outcome of your action."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 197 (part 1 of 3):

Page 137
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months. So whoever undertakes the Hajj in them, there shall be no obscenity, no transgression, and no disputing during the Hajj. And whatever good you do, Allah knows it. And take provision, for the best provision is piety. And fear Me, O people of understanding.﴾ Concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: It is known necessarily that the Hajj is not the months themselves, so an interpretation (ta'wil) is necessary here, and there are several views on it:

The first: the estimate is "the months of the Hajj are well-known months," so the genitive construction (mudaf) is omitted. This is like their saying: "The cold is two months," meaning the time of the cold is two months.

The second: the estimate is "the Hajj is well-known months," meaning there is no Hajj except in these months, and it is not permissible in other than them, as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to permit it in other months. So the verbal noun (masdar) that is added to the months is omitted.

The third: the verse can be made sound without any omission, namely that He made the months themselves the Hajj, since the Hajj takes place in them, like their saying: "a standing night" and "a fasting day."

* * *

The second issue: The exegetes agreed that Shawwal and Dhu al-Qa'dah are among the months of the Hajj, and they differed concerning Dhu al-Hijjah. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: it is entirely among the months of the Hajj, and this is the view of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah are among the months of the Hajj, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid and al-Hasan. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the first nine days of Dhu al-Hijjah, from the night of the sacrifice (laylat al-nahr), are among the months of the Hajj.

The arguments of Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, are of several kinds:

The first: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the months with the plural form, and its minimum is three.

The second argument: the days of sacrifice (ayyam al-nahr) include some of what is connected to the Hajj, namely stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimar), and a menstruating woman may delay the obligatory tawaf until after some days beyond the ten. The view of 'Urwah is that it is permissible to delay the tawaf of visitation (tawaf al-ziyarah) until the end of the month.

The answer to the first: from two aspects:
One of them: the plural form is shared by whatever is beyond one, as is evident from His saying: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].
The second: He gave a part of the month the status of all of it, as one says: "I saw you in such-and-such a year," when he saw him only in an hour of it.

The answer to the second: stoning the pillars is performed by a person who has already completed the Hajj through shaving, tawaf and sacrifice from his ihram, so it is as if it is not among the actions of the Hajj. And a menstruating woman who performs tawaf after it is, as it were, in the ruling of qada' (making up) and not in the ruling of ada' (performance on time). As for those who said that the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah are among the months of the Hajj, they relied on two aspects:
The first: some exegetes claimed that the Greater Day of Hajj is the day of sacrifice.
The second: the day of sacrifice is the time for a pillar of the Hajj, namely the tawaf of visitation. As for al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, he argued for his view that the Hajj is lost by the dawn of the day of sacrifice, and worship is not lost while its time remains. This is the exposition of these views.

Two problems remain here:
The first: He, exalted is He, said earlier: ﴿They ask you about the crescents. Say: they are times (mawaqit) for people and for the Hajj﴾, so He made all the crescents times for the Hajj.
The second: it is well known from the leading Companions that they said: "Among the completion of the Hajj is that a person enters ihram from the dwelling of his family (duwayrat ahlihi)." Whoever's home is very far away may not enter ihram for Hajj from the dwelling of his family except before the months of the Hajj, and this indicates that the months of the Hajj are not restricted to a specific time.

The answer to the first: that verse is general, while this verse, namely His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾, is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. The answer to the second: the text is not opposed by a report transmitted from the Companions.

* * *

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿well-known﴾ has several aspects:
The first: the Hajj occurs only once a year
Page 138
in well-known months of its months, unlike the 'umrah, which is performed many times in the year. He referred them, for knowing those months, to what they had known before the revelation of this law. According to this view, the Shari'ah did not come contrary to what they knew, but came confirming it.
The second: what is meant is that they are well-known through the explanation of the Messenger (ﷺ).
The third: what is meant is that they are fixed at specific times, which may not be brought forward or delayed, unlike what those did who were described in His saying: ﴿The postponement is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37].

* * *

The fourth issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: no one may begin the Hajj (ihlal bil-hajj) before the months of the Hajj. This was also the view of Ahmad and Ishaq. Malik, al-Thawri and Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with them, said: it is not permissible at any time of the year.

The argument of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾. "Ashhur" is a plural of paucity (jam' qillah) used in an indefinite manner, so it does not encompass the whole, and its maximum is ten, its minimum is three. When it is indefinite, it refers to the minimum. So it is established that the intended meaning is that the months of the Hajj are three. The exegetes agreed that these three are: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and part of Dhu al-Hijjah. If this is established, we say: it is necessary that it is not permissible to enter ihram for Hajj before its time. This is shown by three aspects:
The first: entering ihram for an act of worship before the time of performance is not valid, by analogy with prayer.
The second: the khutbah in the Friday prayer is not permissible before its time, because it was established in place of two rak'ahs of the Zuhr prayer in ruling, so entering ihram, which is the beginning of worship, is even less valid.
The third: ihram does not remain valid for performing the Hajj if the time of the Hajj passes before performance; so it is even less likely to be validly concluded for performing the Hajj before its time, because continuation is easier than initiation.

The argument of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, consists of two aspects:
The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the crescents. Say: they are times for people and for the Hajj﴾, so He made all the crescents times for the Hajj, while they are not times for the Hajj itself. It is therefore established that they are times for the validity of entering ihram, and it is permissible to call ihram "Hajj" metaphorically, just as the time was called "Hajj" in His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾. Indeed this is more appropriate, because ihram is closer to the Hajj than the time is.
The second argument: ihram is a commitment to the Hajj, so it is permissible to advance it before the time, like a vow (nadhr).

The answer to the first: the verse we cited is more specific than the verse you relied upon.
The answer to the second: the difference between a vow and ihram is that the time is considered for performance, and the connection of a vow is to performance, as is shown by the fact that performance is not conceivable except through a fresh contract. As for ihram, although it is a commitment, it is also a beginning of performance and a contract upon it, so it necessarily requires a time.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever undertakes the Hajj in them﴾; concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: the meaning of "farada" (undertook/made obligatory) in the language is to oblige and make binding, one says: "I imposed such-and-such upon you," meaning I made it obligatory. The original meaning of fard in the language is cutting and notching. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-fard is a notch in a bowl, in a peg, and in other things, and fursat al-qaws is the notch in which the bowstring sits, and fursat al-watad is the notch in it. From this comes the fard of prayer and others, because they are binding on the servant, like the binding of the notch to the bowl. So "farada" here means "awjaba" (made obligatory). It has also come in the Qur'an with the meaning of "distinguishing (abana)," namely His saying: ﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory (faradna)﴾ [al-Nur: 1] with the light form, and His saying: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [al-Tahrim: 2]. This also returns to the meaning of cutting, because whoever cuts something has separated it from others, and when Allah ordains something He separates it from others. So "farada" means both "awjaba" and "abana," and both return to a single root.

* * *

The second issue: know that in this verse there is an ellipsis (hadhf), and the estimate is: "whoever binds himself to the Hajj in them." The intended meaning of this obligation is that by which the one entering ihram becomes a muhrim, since there is no disagreement that he does not become a pilgrim except by an act that he performs, whereby he leaves the state of being lawful. Hunting, wearing sewn clothes, perfume, women, covering the head, and other things become forbidden to him. It is because of the prohibition of these matters upon him that he is called a muhrim, since he has done what made these things forbidden upon himself. For this same reason the sacred territory was called haram, since it makes forbidden what is within it that would not otherwise be forbidden. So His saying: ﴿whoever undertakes the Hajj in them﴾ indicates that the muhrim must perform an act by which he becomes a pilgrim and a muhrim. Then the jurists differed as to what that act is. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: ihram is concluded by intention alone, without need of talbiyah. Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the beginning of ihram by intention alone is not valid until talbiyah or driving the sacrificial animal (sawq al-hady) is added to it. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir: it is reported from a group that whoever marks his sacrificial animal (ash'ara hadyahu) or garlands it has entered ihram. Nafi' reported from Ibn 'Umar that he said: if he garlands or marks it, he has entered ihram. And from Ibn 'Abbas: if he garlands the sacrificial animal and accompanies it, intending 'umrah and Hajj, he has entered ihram.

The arguments of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, are several:

The first argument: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever undertakes the Hajj in them, there shall be no obscenity, no transgression, and no disputing during the Hajj﴾. The undertaking of the Hajj cannot mean talbiyah or driving the sacrificial animal, for there is absolutely no indication in talbiyah that one is a muhrim, neither literally nor metaphorically. So it remains only that the undertaking of the Hajj means intention, and the undertaking of the Hajj necessitates the conclusion of the Hajj, as shown by His saying: ﴿there shall be no obscenity﴾. Therefore intention must be sufficient for concluding the Hajj.

The second argument: the apparent meaning of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended."

The third argument: analogy, namely that the beginning of Hajj is a restraint from prohibited things, so it is valid to begin it by intention, like fasting.

The arguments of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, are two:
The first: what Abu Mansur al-Maturidi reported in his tafsir from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "None enters ihram except one who utters the talbiyah or declares it."
The second: the Hajj is an act of worship that has permitted and forbidden elements, so one does not begin it except by intention alone, like prayer.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿there shall be no obscenity, no transgression, and no disputing during the Hajj﴾, concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "fala rafathun wa la fusuqun" with nunation and raising, and "wa la jidal" with the accusative, while the rest read all of them in the accusative.

Know that the discussion of the difference between the two readings in meaning must be preceded by two premises. The first: everything that has a name, the substance of the name is an indication of the substance of the named, and the vowels of the name and its other states are an indication of the states of the named. Your saying "rajul" (a man) conveys the specific quiddity, and the vowels of this word, I mean its being in the accusative, nominative, or genitive, indicate the states of that quiddity, namely being object, subject, or genitive-related. This is the rational order, so that the principal corresponds to the principal and the attribute to the attribute. On this basis, names that indicate quiddities should be pronounced with the final letter quiescent, so one says: rajul, jidar, hajar. This is because those vowels were set to define different states in the named thing, so when the named thing is to be defined without reference to any of its states, the word must be left free of vowels; and if at some point it is to be vocalized, it should be said with the accusative, since it is the lightest vowel and the closest to quiescence.

Page 140

**The second premise:** If you say "lā rajula" (there is no man) with a fathah on the final word, you have negated the quiddity (māhiyya, the essential nature of the thing), and the negation of the quiddity necessarily entails the negation of all its instances. But if you say "lā rajulun" with a damma and tanwin, you have negated an indefinite, unspecified man, and by its very form this does not entail the negation of all instances of that quiddity except through a separate indicator (dalīl munfaṣil). Thus it is established that your saying "lā rajula" with a fathah is more indicative of the generality of the negation than your saying "lā rajulun" with a damma and tanwin.

Having understood these two premises, let us return to the difference between the readings. As for those who read *thalāthatan* with a fathah, there is no difficulty. As for those who read the first two words with a damma and tanwin, and the third with a fathah, this indicates that the concern with negating disputation (jidāl) is greater than the concern with negating obscenity (rafath) and wickedness (fusūq). This is because rafath is an expression for the satisfaction of desire, and disputation includes that, since the disputant desires to have his words prevail. Fusūq is an expression for opposition to the command of God, and the disputant does not submit to the truth, and often proceeds to harm and alienate, which leads to enmity and hatred. Since disputation includes all kinds of ugliness, God, in this reading, specifically subjected it to additional admonition and emphasis in negation. As for the exegetes, they said: whoever reads the first two with a damma and the third with a fathah has taken the first two to carry the meaning of a prohibition, as if it were said: "there shall be no obscenity and no wickedness," and has taken the third to be a report of the negation of disputation. This is what they have said, but it does not explain why the first two were singled out for prohibition and the third for negation.

* * *

**The second issue:** As for rafath, we have explained it in His saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives﴾ [al-Baqara 187]. The intended meaning is intercourse. Al-Ḥasan said: what is intended by it is everything connected with intercourse. Thus, rafath by the tongue is mentioning intercourse and what relates to it; rafath by the hand is touching and squeezing; and rafath by the private parts is intercourse. These scholars said: uttering it in the absence of women is not rafath. They argued that Ibn ʿAbbās used to urge on his camel while in the state of iḥrām and say:

*"And they walk with us in gentle murmurs; if the bird speaks truly, we shall have intercourse with a soft-skinned one."*

Abū al-ʿĀliya said to him: "Do you utter rafath while you are in iḥrām?" He replied: "Rafath is only what is said in the presence of women."

Others said: rafath is the speech of indecency and vulgarity. These scholars argued from both the report (khabar) and the lexicon. As for the report, it is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: «When it is the day of one of you fasting, let him not commit rafath nor act ignorantly; if someone reviles him, let him say: "I am fasting."» It is known that rafath here cannot bear any meaning except the speech of vulgarity and indecency. As for the lexicon, it is narrated from Abū ʿUbayd that he said: rafath is indecency in speech; it is said: *arfatha al-rajulu irfāthan* (the man uttered rafath). Abū ʿUbayda said: rafath is idle talk.

As for fusūq, know that *fisq* and *fusūq* are the same, and both are verbal nouns of *fasaqa yafsuqu*. We have mentioned earlier that fusūq is departure from obedience. The exegetes differed. Many of the scholarly verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) took it to mean all sins. They said: because the word is apt for all of them and encompasses them, and prohibition of a thing necessitates abstention from all its kinds; so restricting the word to some kinds of fusūq is arbitrary without any evidence. This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿So he transgressed against the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 50], and His saying: ﴿But God has made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to you﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt 7].

Some said that what is intended is some of the kinds, and then they mentioned several views:

*First:* what is intended is reviling (sibāb). They argued for this from the Qur'an and the report. As for the Qur'an, His saying: ﴿And do not insult one another by nicknames; wretched is the name of wickedness after faith﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt 11]. As for the report, his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: «Reviling a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief.»

*Second:* what is intended is harm and vulgar abuse. God said: ﴿Let no scribe or witness be harmed; and if you do, it is indeed wickedness in you﴾ [al-Baqara 282].

*Third:* Ibn Zayd said: it is slaughtering for idols, for they, in their pilgrimage, would slaughter for the sake of the pilgrimage and for the sake of the idols. God said: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for it is indeed wickedness﴾ [al-Anʿām 121]; and His saying: ﴿or a wickedness over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾ [al-Anʿām 145].

*Fourth:* Ibn ʿUmar said: it is the sinner in killing game and other things that are forbidden to the one in iḥrām.

*Fifth:* rafath is intercourse and its preliminaries with one's spouse, and fusūq is intercourse and its preliminaries in the manner of fornication.

*Sixth:* Muḥammad ibn al-Ṭabarī said: fusūq is the resolve to perform the pilgrimage when one does not resolve to abstain from its prohibited acts.

As for disputation (jidāl), it is a form (fiʿāl) from *mujādala*, and its root is from *jadal*, which is from twisting (qatl): one says *zimām majdūl* and *jadīl*, meaning twisted. The *jadīl* is the name of the halter, for it is only made twisted. Disputation between two parties is called *mujādala* because each of the two adversaries wishes to twist the other away from his opinion. The exegetes mentioned several views concerning this disputation.

*First:* al-Ḥasan said: it is the disputation which leads to fear of going out to reviling, accusation of lying, and ignorance-attribution.

*Second:* Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said: when the Quraysh gathered at Minā, some would say: "Our pilgrimage is more complete," and others would say: "Rather, our pilgrimage is more complete." So God forbade them from that.

*Third:* Mālik said in *al-Muwaṭṭaʾ*: the disputation concerning the pilgrimage was that the Quraysh would stand at the Sacred Landmark (al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām) in Muzdalifa, at Quzaḥ, while others would stand at ʿArafāt. They would dispute: these would say, "We are more correct," and those would say, "We are more correct." God said: ﴿For every community We have appointed rites which they perform; so let them not dispute with you concerning the matter, but call to your Lord, for you are indeed upon right guidance. And if they dispute with you, say: God knows best what you do﴾ [al-Ḥajj 67]. Mālik said: this is the disputation, as it is transmitted, and God knows best.

*Fourth:* al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad said: the disputation concerning the pilgrimage is that some would say: "The pilgrimage is today," and others would say: "Rather, it is tomorrow." This was because they were commanded to base the reckoning of months on the sighting of the crescents, while others used to base it on counting. For this reason they differed: some would say, "This day is the day of the festival," and others would say, "Rather, it is tomorrow." So God forbade them from that. It is as if it were said to them: "We have made clear to you that the crescents are timings for people and for the pilgrimage; so keep to that, and do not dispute about it from any other standpoint."

*Fifth:* al-Qaffāl, may God have mercy on him, said: this prohibition includes what they disputed with the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, when he commanded them to change the pilgrimage into ʿumra; this was hard on them, and they said: "Shall we set out for Minā with our private parts dripping with semen?" The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «If I had known from my affair what I have come to know later, I would not have brought the offering, and I would have made it an ʿumra.» Then they abandoned the disputation at that time.

*Sixth:* ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd said: their disputation concerning the pilgrimage was due to their differing over which of them was correct about the pilgrimage at the time of Abraham, peace be upon him.

*Seventh:* they differed about the years, so it was said to them: "There is no disputation concerning the pilgrimage, for time has revolved and returned to what the pilgrimage was in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him." This is what is intended by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, in the Farewell Pilgrimage: «Indeed time has returned to its form on the day God created the heavens and the earth.» This is the totality of what the exegetes have said on this subject.

[p. 142]

Al-Qāḍī (ʿAbd al-Jabbār) mentioned a fine statement on this point. He said: His saying, ﴿So there shall be no rafath, nor fusūq, nor jidāl in the pilgrimage﴾, may be a report (khabar) or a prohibition (nahy), like His saying: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 9], meaning: do not doubt in it. The apparent meaning of the wording is that it is a report. If we take it as a report, its meaning is that the pilgrimage does not hold together with any one of these qualities, but rather becomes void, because it is like their opposite, and they prevent its validity. On this understanding the meaning does not stand, unless rafath is taken to mean intercourse that invalidates the pilgrimage, fusūq is taken to mean fornication, since it invalidates the pilgrimage, and jidāl is taken to mean doubt concerning the pilgrimage and its obligation, since that would be disbelief, and no pilgrimage is valid along with it. We have taken these three words in these senses only so that God's report—that these things do not occur together with the pilgrimage—may be true. If it is said: Is it not the case that with these things the pilgrimage becomes void, and its performer must proceed with it? And if the pilgrimage remains along with them, the report that these things do not occur together with the pilgrimage is not true. We reply: what is intended by the verse is the incompatibility between these things and the pilgrimage that God first commanded, and that valid pilgrimage does not remain along with these things, as evidenced by the fact that it must be made up (qaḍāʾ). The invalid pilgrimage that he must continue is something other than the pilgrimage God first commanded. As for disputation arising from doubt about the obligation of the pilgrimage, it is clear that the work of the pilgrimage does not remain with it, because that is disbelief, and the work of the pilgrimage is conditioned upon Islam. Thus it is established that if we take the wording as a report, we must take rafath, fusūq and jidāl in the sense we have described. But if we take it as a prohibition, which is in reality a departure from the apparent wording, then rafath may be taken to mean intercourse, its preliminaries, and speech of indecency; fusūq may be taken to mean all its kinds; and jidāl may be taken to mean all its kinds, since the word is unrestricted and encompasses all these categories. Thus the prohibition of them is a prohibition of all their categories. On this understanding, this verse is like an exhortation to beautiful character, adherence to good manners, and caution against what nullifies the reward of acts of obedience.

**The third issue:** The wisdom in God's mentioning these three words—no more and no fewer—in His saying: ﴿So there shall be no rafath, nor fusūq, nor jidāl in the pilgrimage﴾, is that it has been established in the rational sciences that a human being has four faculties: a appetitive bestial faculty (shahwāniyya bahīmiyya), an irascible predatory faculty (ghaḍabiyya sabuʿiyya), an imaginative satanic faculty (wahmiyya shayṭāniyya), and a rational angelic faculty (ʿaqliyya malakiyya). The purpose of all acts of worship is to subdue the three faculties, namely the appetitive, the irascible, and the imaginative. Thus His saying, ﴿So there shall be no rafath﴾, is an allusion to subduing the appetitive faculty; His saying, ﴿nor fusūq﴾, is an allusion to subduing the irascible faculty which produces defiance and anger; and His saying, ﴿nor jidāl﴾, is an allusion to the imaginative faculty which drives a person to dispute about the essence of God, His attributes, His acts, His rulings, and His names. It is also what impels a person to contend with people, to argue with them, and to quarrel with them about everything. Since the source of evil is confined to these three matters, He said: ﴿So there shall be no rafath, nor fusūq, nor jidāl in the pilgrimage﴾; that is, whoever intends to know God, to love Him, to become acquainted with the light of His majesty, and to enter into the company of His elect servants, will not have these matters present in him. These are precious secrets, which are the ultimate aim of these verses, and a sensible person should not be heedless of them. Success in all matters is from God.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Among people there are those who found fault with inference (istidlāl), inquiry (baḥth), reflection (naẓar), and disputation (jidāl), and they argued with several points.

The first of them: God said: ﴿nor jidāl in the pilgrimage﴾, and this requires the negation of all kinds of disputation. Had disputation in religion been an act of obedience and a means to knowing God, He would not have prohibited it during the pilgrimage. Rather, on that assumption, occupation with disputation during the pilgrimage would have been the joining of one act of obedience to another, and it would have been more deserving of encouragement.

Second, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They did not strike it for you except as a dispute. Rather, they are a quarrelsome people﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 58]. He faulted them for being people of contention, and this indicates that contention (jadal) is blameworthy.

Third, His saying: ﴿And do not dispute, lest you lose courage and your strength depart﴾ [al-Anfal: 46]. This is a prohibition of disputation (munazi'ah).

As for the majority of the scholars of kalam (mutakallimun), they said: disputation concerning religion is a great act of obedience. They argued for this with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition, and argue with them in the best manner﴾ [an-Nahl: 125], and with His saying, may He be exalted, relating the words of the disbelievers to Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿They said, "O Noah, you have disputed with us and multiplied our disputation"﴾ [Hud: 32]. It is known that that disputation was only for establishing the fundamentals of religion.

Having established this, we say: it is necessary to reconcile these texts. So we interpret the blameworthy disputation as disputation in upholding falsehood and in seeking wealth and status, and the praiseworthy disputation as disputation in upholding the truth, calling people to the path of God, and defending the religion of God, may He be exalted.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whatever good you do, God knows it. And take provision, for the best provision is piety﴾. Know that God, may He be exalted, before this verse commanded what is good and obedience, saying: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for God﴾, and He said: ﴿Then whoever makes obligatory upon himself the Hajj therein﴾, and He forbade what is evil and disobedience, saying: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no disputing during the Hajj﴾. Then He followed all of this with His saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, God knows it﴾. Outwardly it would have been more fitting to say: "And whatever you do, God knows it," so that it would encompass all that preceded of good and evil. However, He, may He be exalted, singled out good by saying that God knows it, for several benefits and subtleties:

First: when I know good from you, I mention it and make it known; and when I know evil from you, I conceal it and hide it. So that you may know that if My mercy toward you in this world is like this, then how will it be in the Hereafter.

Second: some of the exegetes said, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I am about to conceal it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15], that its meaning is: "If I could conceal it even from Myself, I would do so." So likewise this verse: it is as if it were said to the servant: "As for the good you do, I know it; as for the evil you do, if it were possible for Me to conceal it even from Myself, I would do so."

Third: when a great sovereign says to his obedient servant: "Whatever kinds of hardship and service you bear for My sake, I know it and am aware of it," this is a promise to him of great reward. If he said that to his sinful, rebellious servant, it would be a threat of severe punishment. Since the Truth, glorified is He, is the most generous of the generous, He mentioned what indicates the promise of reward and did not mention what indicates the threat of punishment.

Fourth: when Gabriel, peace be upon him, asked, "What is ihsan?", the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Ihsan is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." Here he made clear to the servant that He sees him and knows all the good deeds he does, so that the servant's obedience to the Lord would be of the ihsan which is the highest rank of worship. For when the servant knows that his master is watching him and is not heedless of his conditions, he is more eager in work, takes more pleasure in it, and is less averse to it.

Fifth: when the servant knows that the master is aware of all his conditions and what he does, his diligence and effort in performing acts of obedience and in guarding against forbidden things become greater than if he did not know this. For these reasons, God, may He be exalted, followed the command to Hajj and the prohibition of obscenity, wickedness, and disputing with His saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, God knows it﴾.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is piety﴾, there are two views concerning it:

One of them: the meaning is "And take provision of piety," and the evidence for this is His saying after it: ﴿for the best provision is piety﴾. The precise explanation is that a person has two journeys: a journey in this world and a journey from this world. The journey in this world necessarily requires provision, which is food, drink, mount, and wealth. The journey from this world also necessarily requires provision, which is knowledge of God, love of Him, and turning away from all else. This provision is better than the first provision for several reasons:

The first: the provision of this world delivers you from a suspected punishment, while the provision of the Hereafter delivers you from a certain punishment.

Second: the provision of this world delivers you from a punishment that ends, while the provision of the Hereafter delivers you from a punishment that is everlasting.

Third: the provision of this world brings you to a pleasure mixed with pains, sicknesses, and afflictions, while the provision of the Hereafter brings you to lasting pleasures, pure, free from the taints of harm, and safe from cessation and decline.

Fourth: the provision of this world, which is every hour in retreat and passing away, while the provision of the Hereafter brings you to the Hereafter, which is every hour in advance, nearness, and arrival.

Fifth: the provision of this world brings you to the pedestal of desire and the self, while the provision of the Hereafter brings you to the threshold of majesty and holiness. Thus it is established from the totality of what we have mentioned that the best provision is piety.

Having known this, let us return to the interpretation of the verse. It is as if He, may He be exalted, said: Since it has been established that the best provision is piety, then occupy yourselves with My piety, O people of understanding. That is, if you are among the people of understanding who know the realities of matters, it is obligatory upon you by the judgment of your intellect and your reason to occupy yourselves with acquiring this provision, because of its many benefits. Al-A'sha said, explaining this meaning:

If you do not set out with a provision of piety, and you meet after death one who has provided himself,
You will regret that you were not like him, and that you did not prepare as he prepared.

The second view: this verse was revealed concerning some people from Yemen who used to perform Hajj without provision, saying, "We are reliant upon God (mutawakkilun)," and then they would beg from people, and perhaps they wronged people and seized their property. So God, may He be exalted, commanded them to take provision, saying: "And take provision of what will carry you through, for the best provision is that by which you restrain your faces from begging and your souls from wronging." It is related from Ibn Zayd that some tribes of the Arabs used to forbid provision in Hajj and 'Umrah, and so this was revealed. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "They, when they entered the state of ihram and had with them provisions, would throw them away, so they were forbidden from that by this verse."

The qadi said: This is far-fetched, because His saying: ﴿for the best provision is piety﴾ refers back to His saying: ﴿And take provision﴾, so its implied meaning is: "And take provision of piety," and piety in the usage of the Shari'ah and the Qur'an is an expression for performing the obligations and abstaining from forbidden things. He said: If we want to validate this view, there are two aspects:

One: whoever is able to take provision with him on the journey, and does not take it, has disobeyed God in that. According to this approach, its inclusion under the verse is valid.

The second: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the meaning is: "And take provision for your immediate journey and for the deferred one, for the best provision is piety."

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fear Me﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: His saying ﴿And fear Me﴾ contains an alert to the perfection of God's greatness and majesty, and it is like the saying of the poet:

I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry.

Second issue: Abu 'Amr affirmed the ya' in His saying ﴿And fear Me﴾ according to the original form, while others omitted it for lightness and because the kasra indicates it.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾, know that the lubab (kernel) of a thing and its lubb is its pure essence. Then they differed after that. Some said: it is a term for the intellect, because it is the most noble thing in man, and that by which man is distinguished from the beasts and comes close to the rank of the angels, and by which he is prepared to distinguish between the better of two goods and the worse of two evils. Others said: it is originally a term for the heart, which is the locus of the intellect, and the heart may be used as a metonymy for the intellect. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while he is a witness﴾ [Qaf: 37]. So likewise here the lubb is used as a metonymy for the intellect, and His saying ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ means: "O people of intellects." And the use of the name of the locus for the state is a well-known metaphor, for it is said of one who has jealousy and zeal: "So-and-so has a nafs (spirit)," and of one who has no zeal: "So-and-so has no nafs," likewise here.

If it is said: since only the address to the rational can be valid, what is the benefit of His saying ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾?

We say: its meaning is that since you are people of understanding, you are able to know these things and act upon them, so their obligation upon you is more established and your turning away from them is uglier. For this reason the poet said:

I have not seen among the faults of people anything like the deficiency of those who are able to complete.

For this reason God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿They are like cattle; rather, they are more astray﴾ [al-A'raf: 179]. That is, cattle are excused because of incapacity, but as for these who are able, their turning away is more shameful, and so they are indeed more astray.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 198 (part 1 of 3):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord. And when you depart from Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram (the sacred monument), and remember Him as He has guided you, though before it you were certainly among the astray.﴾ On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** There is an ellipsis in the verse. The estimated meaning is: "There is no blame upon you in seeking bounty," and Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** Know that doubt existed regarding the prohibition of trade during the Hajj, for several reasons:

First: He, exalted is He, forbade disputation in what precedes this verse, and trade very often leads to dispute because of disagreement over the price, whether it is low or high. So it was necessary that trade be prohibited at the time of Hajj.

Second: Trade was prohibited at the time of Hajj in the religion of the people of ignorance (jahiliyyah). The apparent meaning of this is something commendable, because the one engaged in Hajj is engaged in the service of Allah, exalted is He, so this act should not be tainted by worldly desires.

Third: When the Muslims knew that many permissible things had become forbidden to them at the time of Hajj, such as wearing (ordinary) clothing, perfume, hunting, and intimacy with their spouses, it prevailed upon their assumption that since Hajj had become a cause for the prohibition of wearing clothing, even though there is a strong need for it, then it would be even more fitting that it become a cause for the prohibition of trade, even though the need for it is less.

Fourth: During the performance of prayer, engaging in all other acts of worship is forbidden, let alone permissible things. So it was necessary that the matter be the same in Hajj. These considerations are fit to become a doubt concerning the prohibition of engaging in trade while engaged in Hajj. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, clarified here that trade is permissible and not forbidden. Now that you know this, we say:

[p. 146]

The exegetes mentioned two interpretations of His saying: ﴿to seek bounty from your Lord﴾:

The first: that what is meant is trade. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And others travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and His saying: ﴿He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73]. Then, what indicates the soundness of this interpretation are two things:

The first: what 'Ata' narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Zubayr, that they both recited: "that you seek bounty from your Lord during the seasons of Hajj."

The second: the narrations mentioned concerning the occasion of revelation.

As for the first narration, Ibn 'Abbas said: Some people among the Arabs used to refrain from trade during the days of Hajj. When the ten days began, they went to great lengths in abandoning buying and selling entirely. They used to call the trader during Hajj the *dāj*, and they would say: "These are *dāj*s, not *hājj*s (pilgrims)." The meaning of *dāj* is one who earns and gathers, and it is derived from *dajājah* (hen/poultry). They went to extremes in avoiding activities, to the point that they refrained from rescuing the one in distress, aiding the weak, and feeding the hungry. So Allah, exalted is He, removed this misconception and clarified that there is no blame in trade. Then, since what precedes this verse concerns the rulings of Hajj, and what follows it is also about Hajj, namely His saying: ﴿And when you depart from Arafat﴾, this indicates that this ruling applies during the time of Hajj. For this reason, it was dispensed with mentioning it.

The second narration: It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that a man said to him: "We are a people who hire out (camels), and a people claim that there is no Hajj for us." He said: "A man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) what you have asked, and he did not answer him until the verse ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ was revealed. So he called him and said: 'You are pilgrims.'" In summary, this verse was revealed in refutation of those who say there is no Hajj for merchants, laborers, and camel-drivers.

The third narration: That 'Ukaz, Majannah, and Dhu al-Majaz used to engage in trade during the seasons there, and their livelihoods came from them. When Islam came, they disliked trading during Hajj without permission, so they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed.

The fourth narration: Mujahid said: They used not to trade during the pre-Islamic period at 'Arafat or Mina, so this verse was revealed.

Once the soundness of this view is established, we say: Most of those who adopted this view interpreted the verse as referring to trade during the days of Hajj. As for Abu Muslim, he interpreted the verse as referring to what comes after Hajj. He said: The estimated meaning is: "Fear Me in all the acts of Hajj, then after that, ﴿there is no blame upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord.﴾" A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10].

Know that this view is weak for several reasons:

First: The *fa'* (then) in His saying: ﴿And when you depart from Arafat﴾ indicates that this departure occurred after seeking bounty, and that indicates that trade took place during the time of Hajj.

Second: Interpreting the verse in terms of the point of doubt is better than interpreting it in a way that does not address the point of doubt. It is known that the locus of doubt is trade during the time of Hajj. As for after the completion of Hajj, everyone knows the permissibility of trade.

As for what Abu Muslim mentioned, analogizing Hajj to prayer, his response is: The acts of prayer are continuous, so it is not valid to engage in something else during them. As for the acts of Hajj, they are separated from one another, so in between them a person remains under the original ruling, since he is not in a state of Hajj. It cannot be said: "Rather, the ruling of Hajj remains in all those times, as evidenced by the fact that the prohibition of perfume, clothing, and the like remains." For we say: This is an analogy opposed to a text, so it is invalid.

[p. 147]

**The third view:** What is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to seek bounty from your Lord﴾ is that a person, while in the state of Hajj, performs other acts that bring about deserving Allah's bounty and mercy, such as aiding the weak, rescuing the one in distress, and feeding the hungry. This view is attributed to Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, peace be upon them. The Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) objected to it, saying: "This is either obligatory or recommended, and one does not say in such a case, 'There is no blame upon you in it.' This expression is used only for permissible matters."

The response: We do not concede that this expression is used only for permissible matters. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you shorten (your prayer)﴾ [al-Nisa': 101], and shortening the prayer is by consensus among the recommended acts. Moreover, the people of ignorance believed that combining other acts of worship with Hajj would cause a defect and deficiency in Hajj, so Allah, exalted is He, clarified that the matter is not so, by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236].

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** The scholars agreed that if trade causes a deficiency in obedience, it is not permissible. But if it causes no deficiency whatsoever, then it is among the permissible matters that it is better to leave, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5]. Sincerity (ikhlas) means that there is no motive for the act other than that it is an act of worship. The Prophet, peace be upon him, related from Allah, exalted is He: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners; whoever does an action in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his association." The summary is that the permission for this trade is in the category of concessions.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you depart from Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram﴾, there are issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** *Ifadah* (departure) means rushing forward in movement in great numbers. From it one says: *afada al-ba'ir bi-jarratih* (the camel poured forth its cud) when it sets down its cud and throws it out scattered. Likewise, *afada al-aqdah fi al-maysir* (he cast the arrows in gambling) means he gathered them and then threw them scattered. The pouring out of water derives from this, because when it is poured it scatters. And *ifadah* in speech is only rushing into it with abundance and manipulating its aspects. In this sense is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when you plunge into it﴾ [Yunus: 61]. From it one says of people: *fawd*, and also their gathering is *fawda* (disorder). One also says: *afadat al-'ayn dam'aha* (the eye poured forth its tears). So the root of this word is pushing something until it scatters. Thus His saying, exalted is He: ﴿afadtum﴾ means you pushed forcefully, and its original sense is *afadtum anfusakum* (you poured yourselves out), but the object was omitted, as it is omitted in their saying: "They pushed from such-and-such a place and poured out." In the hadith of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "He descended in the valley of Qayrawan, while he was scratching his camel with his staff."

**The second issue:** *'Arafat* is the plural of *'Arafah*. A single place was named by it, like their saying: *thawb akhlaq* (a worn-out garment), *burmah a'shar* (a pot in pieces), and *ard sabasib* (a vast land). The estimate is: as if each piece of that land were 'Arafah, so the collection of those pieces was named 'Arafat. If it is asked: "Why is it not made diptote (not taking tanwin), since it has two reasons: definiteness and femininity?" We say: This word originally was a name for many pieces of land, each one of which was called 'Arafah. On this estimate, it was not a proper noun. Then it was made a proper noun for the collection of those pieces, and after that they left it on its original state of not taking tanwin.

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** Know that the eighth day of Dhu al-Hijjah is called *Yawm al-Tarwiyah* (the Day of Tarwiyah), and the ninth day of it is called *Yawm 'Arafah* (the Day of 'Arafah), and that specific place was named 'Arafat. The scholars mentioned several explanations for these names. As for the Day of Tarwiyah, there are two views:

One: from *rawa, yarwi tarwiyah*, when one reflects and exercises his thought and deliberation.

Two: from *rawahu min al-ma', yarwihi*, when one gives him water to quench thirst.

As for the first: there are three views on it:

[p. 148]

One: that Adam, peace be upon him, was commanded to build the House. When he had built it, he reflected and said: "My Lord, for every worker there is a reward; what is my reward for this work?" He said: "When you circumambulate it, I will forgive your sins with the first round of your circumambulation." He said: "My Lord, increase it for me." He said: "I will forgive your descendants when they circumambulate it." He said: "Increase it for me."
