He said: "I will forgive everyone for whom those circumambulating seek forgiveness from among your monotheistic descendants." He said: "Enough, my Lord, enough."

Two: that Abraham, peace be upon him, saw in his dream on the night of Tarwiyah as if he were slaughtering his son. He woke in the morning reflecting whether this was from Allah, exalted is He, or from Satan. When he saw it again on the night of 'Arafah, being commanded to do it, he woke in the morning and said: "I have recognized, my Lord, that it is from You."

Three: that the people of Makkah used to go out on the Day of Tarwiyah to Mina, and they would ponder (yarwun) the supplications they wished to mention on the next day at 'Arafat.

As for the second view, which derives it from the watering of water, there are three views:

One: that the people of Makkah used to conceal water from the pilgrims who came to them from the horizons. The pilgrims would rest on this day from the hardships of travel, and they would have ample water, and they would water their animals after suffering the scarcity of water on their path.

Two: that they would take water with them to 'Arafah.

Three: that the sinners are like the thirsty who came to the seas of Allah's mercy and drank from them until they were quenched.

As for the excellence of this day, it is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾ [al-Fajr: 3]. From Ibn 'Abbas: the even is the Day of Tarwiyah and 'Arafah, and the odd is the Day of Sacrifice (al-Nahr). From 'Ubadah: the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The fasting of the ten days of al-Adha, each day of which is like a month, and for one who fasts the Day of Tarwiyah there is a year's reward, and for one who fasts the Day of 'Arafah there are two years." Anas reported that he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever fasts the Day of Tarwiyah, Allah will give him the like of the reward of Job for his trial, and whoever fasts the Day of 'Arafah, Allah, exalted is He, will give him the like of the reward of Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon him."

As for the Day of 'Arafah, it has ten names: five of them are specific to it, and five are shared between it and others.

As for the first five:

One of them is 'Arafah. Regarding its derivation there are three views:

One: that it is derived from *ma'rifah* (knowledge), and in this there are eight views:

The first: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas that Adam and Eve met at 'Arafah, and one of them recognized the other, so the day was named 'Arafah and the place 'Arafat. That is because when they were sent down from Paradise, Adam landed in Sarandib, Eve in Jeddah, Iblis in Nisan, and the serpent in Isfahan. When Allah, exalted is He, commanded Adam to perform Hajj, he met Eve at 'Arafat, and they recognized each other (ta'arafa).

Eighth, that He, may He be exalted, makes Himself known (yataʿarrafu) to the pilgrim there through forgiveness and mercy.

The second opinion concerns the derivation of ʿArafah: that it comes from iʿtiraf (acknowledgment). The reason is that when the pilgrims stand at ʿArafah, they acknowledge the Truth's lordship, majesty, self-sufficiency and independence (al-samadiyyah), and they acknowledge their own poverty, lowliness, neediness and need. It is also said that when Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, stood at ʿArafat, they said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves" (Qur'an 7:23), and Allah, glorified and exalted, said: "Now you have recognized yourselves."

[Page 149]

The third opinion is that the name comes from al-ʿarf, which means a pleasant fragrance. He, may He be exalted, said: "And He will admit them into the Garden, which He has made known to them" (Qur'an 47:6), meaning, He has perfumed it for them. The meaning of this is that when sinners repent at ʿArafat, they are purified of the filth of sins and acquire a pleasant fragrance with Allah, exalted is He. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The odour from the mouth of one who fasts is more fragrant to Allah than the scent of musk."

The second name: the day on which the disbelievers despaired of the religion of Islam.

The third: the day on which the religion was perfected.

The fourth: the day on which the blessing was completed.

The fifth: the day of good pleasure (al-ridwan).

Allah, exalted is He, has gathered these things into four verses, in His saying: "Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion" (Qur'an 5:3), up to the end of the verse. ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas said: this verse was revealed on the evening of ʿArafah, and it was a Friday, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was standing at ʿArafah in the place of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, during the Farewell Pilgrimage, when disbelief had been crushed and the structure of the Jahiliyyah had been demolished. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "If people knew what they have in this verse, their eyes would be delighted." A Jew said to ʿUmar: "If this verse had been revealed to us, we would have taken that day as a festival." ʿUmar said: "As for us, we have made it two festivals: the day of ʿArafah and the day of Friday."

As for the meaning of the despair of the polytheists: they despaired that the people of Muhammad, peace be upon him, would revert and return to their religion. As for the meaning of the perfection of the religion: He, exalted is He, did not command them with any legislative rule after that. As for the completion of the blessing: the greatest of blessings is the blessing of religion, because by it one deserves success with Paradise and deliverance from the Fire, and it was completed on that day. Likewise He said in the verse of ablution: "And that He may complete His blessing upon you, so that you may be grateful" (Qur'an 5:6). When the bearer of good news came and reached Jacob, he said: "On what religion did you leave Joseph?" He said: "On the religion of Islam." He said: "Now the blessing is complete."

As for the meaning of good pleasure: He, exalted is He, was pleased with their religion to which they adhered, which is Islam. This is good news that He gave them on that day, so there is no day more complete than the day on which He gave them the good news of the perfection of the religion. It has been said: this day is the day of the joining of those who join (ṣilah), "Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My blessing upon you" (Qur'an 5:3), and the day of the severing of those who sever, "That Allah is free of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger" (Qur'an 9:3), and the day of the pardon of the stumbling of the regretful and the acceptance of the repentance of the repentant, "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves" (Qur'an 7:23). Just as He accepted Adam's repentance on it by His mercy, so He accepts the repentance of his descendants: "And He is the One who accepts repentance from His servants" (Qur'an 42:25). It is also the day of the delegation of those who come: "And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot" (Qur'an 22:27). In a report: "The pilgrim is the delegation of Allah, and the pilgrims are the visitors of Allah, and it is due upon the Generous One who is visited that He honour His visitor."

As for the other five names of the day of ʿArafah:

The first of them: the Greater Day of Pilgrimage. Allah, exalted is He, said: "And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage" (Qur'an 9:3). This name is shared between ʿArafah and the day of sacrifice (al-Nahr). The earliest generation of the Companions and the Successors differed concerning it. Some of them said that it is ʿArafah, and it was so named because standing at ʿArafat takes place on it, and the Hajj is ʿArafah: if one catches it, and all the other rites of Hajj escape him, the sacrifice (dam) suffices for them. For this reason it was called the Greater Hajj. Al-Hasan said: it was called so because the disbelievers and the Muslims gathered on it, and it was proclaimed on it that no polytheist should perform Hajj after that. Ibn Sirin said: it was called so only because on it the festivals of all the religious communities gathered, the Jews and the Christians, and the Muslims performed Hajj, and this did not happen before it or after it. Others said: it is the day of sacrifice, because most of the rites of Hajj take place on it, whereas standing (wuquf) is not obligatory on the day but suffices at night. Both opinions were narrated from ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

The second: the even (al-shafʿ). The third: the odd (al-witr). The fourth: the witness (al-shahid). The fifth: the witnessed (al-mashhud), in His saying: "By the witness and the witnessed" (Qur'an 85:3). These names we have explained in the commentary on this verse.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, singled out the day of ʿArafah from among all the days of the Hajj with virtues. Among them: He, exalted is He, has specified its fasting for abundant reward. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The fasting of the Day of Tarwiyah is an expiation for one year, and the fasting of the Day of ʿArafah is an expiation for two years." It is reported from Anas that it used to be said of the days of the ten: each day is worth a thousand, and the Day of ʿArafah is worth ten thousand. Moreover, it is recommended for the pilgrim standing at ʿArafat to break his fast, so that at the time of supplication he is strong of heart and present of soul.

* * *

The fourth issue: Know that it is necessary for us to give a true indication of the order of the actions of the Hajj, so that the meaning of the verse becomes easy to grasp. Whoever enters Makkah in the state of ihram (the sacred state of pilgrimage) in Dhu al-Hijjah, or before it, if he is performing Hajj alone (ifrad) or combining Hajj and ʿUmrah (qiran), performs the tawaf of arrival (tawaf al-qudum) and remains in his ihram until he goes out to ʿArafat. If he is performing tamattuʿ (the pilgrim who completes ʿUmrah first and then performs Hajj), he performs tawaf, sayʿ (the walking between Safa and Marwah), shaves or cuts his hair, and comes out of ihram from his ʿUmrah, and remains until the time of his departure to ʿArafat. At that time he enters ihram for Hajj from within Makkah and sets out. The same applies to a Makkan who wishes to perform Hajj. The Sunnah for the imam is to deliver a sermon in Makkah on the seventh day of Dhu al-Hijjah, after he has prayed the noon prayer, a single sermon in which he commands the people to set out tomorrow after they have prayed the dawn prayer to Mina, and teaches them those rites. Then the people go on the Day of Tarwiyah to Mina, so as to reach it at the time of the noon prayer, and they pray there with the imam: the noon, the afternoon, the sunset, the night and the dawn prayers of the Day of ʿArafah. Then, when the sun rises over Thabir, they set out for ʿArafat. When they approach it, the Sunnah is that they do not enter it, but the imam pitches his tent at Namirah, which is near ʿArafah, and they stop there until the sun declines. Then the imam delivers two sermons, explaining to them the rites of Hajj and encouraging them to increase supplication and the tahlil (saying "La ilaha illa Allah") at the standing place. When he finishes the first sermon he sits down, then stands and begins the second sermon, while the muezzins begin the call to prayer with him. He keeps it brief, so that his finishing coincides with the muezzins' finishing the call to prayer. Then he descends, the muezzins give the iqamah, and he leads them in the noon prayer; then they give the iqamah immediately and he leads them in the afternoon prayer. This combining (of the two prayers) is agreed upon. Then, after finishing the prayer, they set out for ʿArafat and stop at the rocks (al-sakhrat), because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, stood there. When they stand, they face the qiblah, remembering Allah, exalted is He, and supplicating Him until the sun sets.

Know that standing (al-wuquf) at ʿArafat is a pillar (rukn) without which Hajj is not attained. Whoever misses standing at its time and in its place has missed the Hajj. The time of standing begins with the decline of the sun on the Day of ʿArafah, and extends until the break of dawn on the Day of Sacrifice. That is half a day and a full night. If the pilgrim is present there at this time for a single moment of the night or the day, it suffices. Ahmad said: the time of standing is from the break of dawn on the Day of ʿArafah, and extends until the break of dawn on the Day of Sacrifice. When the sun sets, the imam departs from ʿArafat and delays the sunset prayer until he combines it with the night prayer at Muzdalifah.

Concerning the naming of Muzdalifah there are several opinions:

The first: that they draw near (yaqrubuna) to Mina there, and al-izdilaf means nearness.

The second: that the people gather there, and al-ijtimaʿ (gathering) is al-izdilaf.

The third: that they draw near (yazdalifuna) to Allah, the Exalted, that is, they seek nearness through standing. Muzdalifah is also called Jamʿ, because the sunset and night prayers are combined there. This is the opinion of Qatadah. It has also been said that Adam, peace be upon him, gathered there with Eve, and drew near to her (izdalafa ilayha), that is, approached her.

Then, when the imam reaches Muzdalifah, he combines the sunset and night prayers with two iqamahs. Then they spend the night there. If one does not spend the night there, he owes a sheep as expiation. When the dawn breaks, they pray the dawn prayer in the dim light (bi-ghalas), and hastening the dawn prayer here is more strongly recommended than elsewhere, and this is agreed upon. When they have prayed the dawn prayer, they take pebbles from there for the stoning (al-ramy), each person taking seventy pebbles. Then they go to al-Mashʿar al-Haram, which is a mountain called Quzah, and it is what is meant by His saying, "So when you pour forth from ʿArafat, remember Allah at al-Mashʿar al-Haram" (Qur'an 2:198). This mountain is the furthest part of Muzdalifah on the side nearest Mina. He climbs up to its top if he is able, or stands near it if he is unable, praising Allah, glorifying Him (tahlil and takbir), and he continues thus until it becomes fully light. Then he departs before the sunrise, and passing through suffices, as at ʿArafah. Then they go from there to the Valley of Muhassir. When they reach the bottom of Muhassir, it is recommended for one who is riding to urge his mount forward, and for one who is walking to hasten vigorously for a distance equal to a stone's throw. When they come to Mina, they stone Jamrat al-ʿAqabah from the bottom of the valley with seven pebbles, and he stops the talbiyah (the chant "Here I am, O Allah") when he begins the stoning. When he has stoned Jamrat al-ʿAqabah, he sacrifices the offering (hady) if he has one with him. This is a Sunnah; if he leaves it, there is nothing on him, because perhaps he does not have an offering with him. Then, after sacrificing the offering, he shaves his head or trims it, and trimming means cutting the ends of his hair. Then, after the shaving, he comes to Makkah and performs the tawaf of ifadah (the tawaf of return), prays the two rakʿahs of the tawaf, and performs sayʿ between Safa and Marwah. After that they return to Mina for the rest of the Day of Sacrifice, and it is obligatory for them to spend the nights at Mina during the days of tashriq for the sake of the stoning. They agreed that whenever the stoning, the shaving and the tawaf have been done, release (tahallul) has been achieved, and by release is meant the lifting of the prohibitions of wearing sewn clothing, of trimming (nails and hair), and of intercourse. This is what there is to say about the actions of the Hajj, and Allah knows best.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** Know that the people of the Jahiliyyah had altered the rites of Hajj from the Sunnah of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Quraysh and some other tribes called themselves the Hums (al-Hums), meaning those who are strict in their religion. Al-hamasah means severity, and it is said: a man is *ahmas* and a people are *hums*. These people would not stand at Arafat, and they would say: "We do not leave the Haram, nor do we abandon it at a time of worship." Others would stand at Arafat, and those who stood at Arafat would depart before the sun set. Those who stood at Muzdalifah would depart when the sun rose, and they would say: "Shine, O Thabir, so that we may rush forth." Its meaning is: "Shine, O Thabir, with the sun, so that we may press on from Muzdalifah." They would then enter a *ghawr* (a low depression) of the land, which is its lowest part, because they had passed Muzdalifah and found themselves in a *ghawr* of the land. So God, exalted is He, commanded Muhammad (peace be upon him) to oppose the people in both departures: He commanded him to depart from Arafat after the sun had set, and to depart from Muzdalifah before the sunrise. The verse contains no indication of this, but the Sunnah indicates these rulings.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** The correct view is that the verse indicates that presence at Arafat is obligatory in Hajj. This is because the verse indicates the obligation of remembering God at the Mash'ar al-Haram (the sacred landmark, al-Mash'ar al-Haram) when departing from Arafat. Departing from Arafat is conditional upon being present at Arafat, and whatever an obligation cannot be completed without, and which is within the capacity of the responsible person, is itself obligatory. Thus it is established that the verse indicates that presence at Arafat is obligatory in Hajj. If one does not do it, then one has not performed the Hajj that was commanded, and so one is not released from the obligation. This necessitates that standing at Arafat be a condition (*shart*). At most, the matter is that Hajj is still valid when some of the commanded acts are omitted; but the basic principle is what we have mentioned, and one departs from it only by a separate proof. Many scholars held that the verse does not indicate that standing is a condition. It is transmitted from al-Hasan that standing at Arafat is obligatory, but if one misses it, standing anywhere in the entire Haram takes its place. The rest of the jurists rejected this, and they agreed that Hajj is not achieved except by standing at Arafat.

* * *

**The seventh issue:** His words, ﴿So remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾, indicate that presence at the Sacred Landmark is obligatory, and passing through it suffices, as is the case at Arafat. As for standing there, it is recommended (*masnun*). It is related from Alqamah and al-Nakha'i that they both said: standing at Muzdalifah is a pillar (*rukn*), on the same level as standing at Arafat. Their evidence is His words: ﴿Then when you depart from Arafat, remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾. This is because the standing at Arafat has no explicit mention of remembrance in the Book, and it was made obligatory only by an allusion of the verse or by the Sunnah, whereas the Sacred Landmark has a clear command. Most jurists said: it is not a pillar. They argued with His, peace be upon him, saying: "Hajj is Arafah; whoever stands at Arafah has completed his Hajj." And with his saying: "Whoever reaches Arafah has reached Hajj, and whoever misses Arafah has missed Hajj." They said: in the verse there is an indication of what we have said, because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then when you depart from Arafat, remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾. He commanded remembrance, not standing. So it is known that standing at the Sacred Landmark follows the remembrance and is not a principle. As for standing at Arafat, it is the principle, because He said: ﴿When you depart from Arafat﴾, and He did not say "the remembrance at Arafat."

**The eighth issue:** *Al-Mash'ar* means the landmark (*al-ma'lam*). Its root is from your saying: "I *shi'rtu* with the thing" when you know it, and "*layta shi'ri*" (would that I knew) what so-and-so did, meaning my knowledge has not reached him or encompassed him. The *shi'ar* of a thing is its signs. God, exalted is He, named that place "the Sacred Landmark" because it is one of the landmarks of Hajj. Then they differed. Some said: the Sacred Landmark is Muzdalifah, and God named it so because prayer, staying, spending the night there, and supplication occur there. Thus al-Wahidi said in *al-Basit*. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: the more correct view is that it is Quzah, which is the last boundary of Muzdalifah. The first view is closer, because the *fa'* in His words, ﴿So remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾, indicates that the remembrance at the Sacred Landmark occurs immediately after departing from Arafat, and that is only by spending the night at Muzdalifah.

* * *

**The ninth issue:** They differed about the remembrance commanded at the Sacred Landmark. Some said: what is intended by it is the combining of the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers there, and prayer is called remembrance. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]. The evidence for this is that His words, ﴿So remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾, are a command, and a command indicates obligation, and there is no remembrance there that is obligatory except this. As for the majority, they said: what is intended is the remembrance of God by glorifying (*tasbih*), praising (*tahmid*), and declaring His oneness (*tahlil*). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he looked at the people on that night and said: when the people reached this night, they did not sleep.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, there are questions about it:

**The first question:** When He said, ﴿So remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾, why did He say again, ﴿and remember Him﴾? What is the benefit of this repetition?

The answer has several aspects:

First: our school holds that the names of God, exalted is He, are *tawqifiyyah* (established by revelation), not *qiyasiyyah* (derived by analogy). So His first words, ﴿Remember God﴾, are a command to remember, and His second words, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, are a command to us to remember Him, glorified is He, by the names and attributes that He has explained to us and commanded us to remember Him by, not by names we derive by opinion and analogy.

Second: He commanded remembrance first, then said second, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, meaning: do what We have commanded you of remembrance, just as God has guided you to the religion of Islam. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "I commanded you with this remembrance only so that you would be thankful for that blessing." A parallel is what He commanded them regarding the *takbir* when they complete the month of Ramadan. He said: ﴿and that you complete the period, and that you magnify God for guiding you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. And He said regarding the sacrificial animals: ﴿He subjected them to you that you may magnify God for guiding you﴾ [al-Hajj: 37].

Third: His first words, ﴿So remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾, command remembrance by the tongue, and His second words, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, command remembrance by the heart. The explanation is that remembrance in the speech of the Arabs has two kinds: one is remembrance that is the opposite of forgetting, and the other is remembrance by speech. What is the opposite of forgetting is His saying: ﴿And none made me forget to mention it except Satan﴾ [al-Kahf: 63]. As for remembrance that is speech, it is like His saying: ﴿So remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200], and ﴿And remember God during the appointed days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203]. Thus it is established that remembrance comes with both meanings. The first is to be understood as remembrance by the tongue, and the second as remembrance by the heart, for by both is complete servitude achieved.

Fourth: Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of His words, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, is: remember Him by His unity, just as He has mentioned you by His guidance.

Fifth: It is possible that what is intended by remembrance is the continuation of remembrance, as if it were said to them: "Remember God, and remember Him", meaning: remember Him with remembrance after remembrance, just as He has guided you with guidance after guidance. Its sum returns to His words: ﴿O you who believe, remember God with much remembrance﴾ [al-Ahzab: 41].

Sixth: He, exalted is He, commanded remembrance at the Sacred Landmark, and that is an indication of performing the duties of the Sharia. Then He said after it, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾. The meaning is that restricting remembrance to the Sacred Landmark contains the establishment of the duties of the Sharia. When you know this, you have come close to the stations of Truth, which is that your heart is severed from the Sacred Landmark, and indeed from everything other than Him, so that it becomes absorbed in the light of His majesty and His self-sufficiency, and it remembers Him, because He is the one deserving of this remembrance. This remembrance also gives you a noble relation to Him, since in this state you are in the station of ascent, remembering Him and occupied with praising Him. He began with the first and followed with the second because the servant in this state is in the station of ascent, so he climbs from the lower to the higher. This is a noble station that speech cannot describe and imagination cannot express. Whoever wishes to reach it, let him be among those who arrive at the essence, not among those who merely hear the report.

Seventh: the first remembrance may be intended as the mention of God's names and His beautiful attributes, and the second remembrance as occupation with thanking Him for His blessings. Thanksgiving also includes remembrance, so it is correct to call thanksgiving remembrance. The evidence that the second remembrance is thanksgiving is that He linked it to guidance, saying: ﴿as He has guided you﴾, and remembrance that is consequent upon a blessing is nothing but thanksgiving.

Eighth: when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿So remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾, it might be supposed that remembrance is restricted to this place and this act of worship, namely Hajj. So God, exalted is He, removed this doubt by saying: ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, meaning: remember Him in every state and in every place. This remembrance is obligatory as thanks for His guidance, and since the blessing of guidance is continuous and uninterrupted, thanksgiving likewise must be continuous and uninterrupted.

Ninth: His words, ﴿So remember God at the Sacred Landmark﴾, are intended to mean combining the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers there, and then His words, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, are intended to mean declaring His oneness (*tahlil*) and glorification (*tasbih*).

**The second question:** What is meant by guidance in His words, ﴿as He has guided you﴾?

The answer: some said it is specific, and what is meant is: as He has guided you by returning you in your rites of Hajj to the Sunnah of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Others said: no, it is general, encompassing every kind of guidance in knowing God, exalted is He, His angels, His books, His messengers, and His laws.

**The third question:** To what does the pronoun in His words, ﴿from before it﴾, refer?

The answer: it may refer to "guidance," and the implied meaning is: "And indeed you were, before He guided you, among those who went astray." Some said it refers to the Qur'an, and the implied meaning is: "And remember Him as He has guided you by His Book, which has explained to you the landmarks of His religion, and indeed you were, before its revelation to you, among those who went astray."

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed you were before it among the astray﴾, al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: in it there are two aspects. One: "And you were not before it except among the astray." The second: "Indeed you were before it among the astray." It is like His saying: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4], and His saying: ﴿And indeed We think you are among the liars﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 186].

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 199:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness from God. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

On this there are two opinions.

The first: it refers to departing from ʿArafat. Those who hold this view differ. Most of them maintain that this verse is a command to the Quraysh and their allies, who were the *Hums* (the Hums were a group of tribes who claimed a special sanctity and exempted themselves from some rites). They did not go beyond Muzdalifah, and they argued with several points:

First: the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) is superior to other places, so standing there is more fitting.

Second: they held themselves above the people and said, "We are the People of God, so we do not leave the Sacred Precinct of God."

Third: if they conceded that the place of standing is ʿArafat and not the Haram, that would imply a deficiency in the Haram, and that deficiency would return upon them. For this reason the Hums did not stand anywhere except Muzdalifah. So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse as a command to them to stand at ʿArafat and to depart from it as all other people do. It has been narrated that when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, appointed Abu Bakr as leader of the pilgrimage, he ordered him to bring the people out to ʿArafat. When Abu Bakr set out, he passed by the Hums and left them, and they said to him, "Where are you going? This is the station of your fathers and your people, so do not go." He paid them no heed and proceeded by God's command to ʿArafat, stood there, and ordered the rest of the people to stand there.

According to this interpretation, His saying ﴿from where the people depart﴾ means: let your departure be from the place from which all the other people depart, those who are standing at ʿArafat.

Among those who hold that this verse refers to departing from ʿArafat is one who says: His saying ﴿Then depart﴾ is a general command to all people, and His saying ﴿from where the people depart﴾ refers to Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them both, for their practice was to depart from ʿArafat. It has been narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to stand at ʿArafat in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period) along with the rest of the people, and opposed the Hums.

Using a collective noun for a single person is permissible when that person is a leader who is followed. This is like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom the people said﴾ [Al ʿImran: 173], meaning Nuʿaym ibn Masʿud, ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al ʿImran: 173], meaning Abu Sufyan. Using a collective noun for a single, honoured person is a well-known figurative usage. Among its examples is His statement: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1].

There is a third view on this verse, mentioned by al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him: that His saying ﴿from where the people depart﴾ is an expression for the longstanding practice of departing from ʿArafat, and that this is the ancient ordinance, while anything other than it is an innovation and a newly introduced matter, just as one says, "This is something the people have done since antiquity." This is the sum of the arguments in establishing the position of those who say that this departure refers to departing from ʿArafat.

The second opinion, which is the choice of al-Dahhak: that this departure refers to departing from Muzdalifah to Mina on the Day of Sacrifice, before sunrise, for the stoning and the sacrifice. His saying ﴿from where he departed﴾ refers to people meaning Abraham, Ishmael, and their followers. This is because their practice was to depart from Muzdalifah before sunrise, as the Messenger, peace be upon him, brought. The Arabs who were standing at Muzdalifah used to depart after sunrise, so God, exalted is He, commanded them that their departure from Muzdalifah should take place at the time when the departure of Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them both, used to occur.

Know that each of the two opinions faces a difficulty.

As for the difficulty for the first opinion: its apparent meaning, His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾, implies that this departure is other than what is indicated by His statement ﴿So when you depart from ʿArafat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198], because of the particle ﴿then﴾ (thumma), which necessitates sequence. And if the intended meaning of this verse were departing from ʿArafat, while it is coordinated with His statement ﴿So when you depart from ʿArafat﴾, this would be coordinating a thing with itself, which is not permissible. Moreover, the sense of the verse would become: "So when you depart from ʿArafat, then depart from ʿArafat," and this is not permissible.

If it is said: why is it not permissible to say that this verse precedes what comes before it, and the sense is: ﴿So fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], then ﴿depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness from God. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, ﴿there is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198], then ﴿when you depart from ʿArafat, remember God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198]? In this order, it is valid that this departure be the very same one.

We reply: although this is possible, the original principle is that it is not so. And when it is possible to carry the speech according to the second opinion without committing to what you have mentioned, what need do we have to commit to it?

As for the difficulty for the second opinion: it is that the view cannot be sustained unless we take the word ﴿from where﴾ in His statement ﴿from where the people depart﴾ to mean time, and that is not permissible, since it is specific to place and not to time.

Those who hold the first opinion answered this question by saying that the particle ﴿then﴾ here is like what occurs in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is? It is freeing a slave﴾ [al-Balad: 12–13], up to His statement ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17], meaning: he was, along with this, among the believers. And a man may say to another, "I gave you such-and-such today, and then I gave you such-and-such yesterday." The benefit of the word "then" here is the delay of one of the two reports relative to the other, not the delay of this subject relative to that subject.

Those who hold the second opinion answered: the designation of time and place are very similar, so it is not far-fetched to use a word employed for one of them in the sense of the other, by way of figurative usage.

As for His statement ﴿from where the people depart﴾: we have mentioned that the intended meaning of "the people" is either those standing at ʿArafat, or Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them both, and their followers. There is a third view on this, which is the view of al-Zuhri: that the intended meaning of "the people" in this verse is Adam, peace be upon him. He relied on the recitation of Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "Then depart from where the people depart," and said: it is Adam, who forgot what he had been enjoined. It is also narrated that he recited "an-nāsi" with a kasra on the sin, being satisfied with the kasra in place of the yāʾ, and the meaning is: the departure from ʿArafat is an ancient legislated practice, so do not abandon it.

As for His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and seek forgiveness from God﴾: what is meant by it is seeking forgiveness with the tongue together with repentance in the heart. That is, one regrets every shortcoming in obedience to God, and resolves not to fall short in the future, and one's aim in this is to attain the pleasure of God, exalted is He, not for his immediate worldly benefits. Just as the recitation of the two testimonies (of faith) does not benefit unless the heart is present and firmly settled upon their meaning. As for seeking forgiveness with the tongue without the occurrence of repentance in the heart, it is closer to harm.

If it is said: how can He command seeking forgiveness without qualification, when perhaps some of them have not sinned, and so for them there is no need to seek forgiveness?

The answer: if he has sinned, seeking forgiveness is obligatory. And if he has not sinned, yet it is possible that some shortcoming has occurred from him in the performance of obligations and in guarding against prohibited things, then seeking forgiveness is also obligatory for him, to make up for that possible lapse. And if he is certain that no lapse has occurred from him at all in any act of obedience, this is almost impossible for a human being. How could he be certain of this in a single act, let alone in the acts of his whole life? Nevertheless, even if this were possible, seeking forgiveness is still obligatory, because the obedience of a creature is not fitting before the presence of the Creator. For this reason the angels said: "Glory be to You, we have not worshipped You as You deserve to be worshipped." So seeking forgiveness is required from this aspect. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, there is a veil over my heart, and indeed I seek forgiveness from God a hundred times a day" (seventy times).

\* \* \*

As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. You know that *Ghafūr* (Forgiving) conveys intensity, and likewise *Raḥīm* (Merciful). Then in this verse there are two issues.

The first issue: this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, accepts the repentance of the penitent. For when He, exalted is He, commanded the sinner to seek forgiveness, and then described Himself as abundant in forgiveness and abundant in mercy, this indicates with certainty that He, exalted is He, will forgive the one who seeks forgiveness, and will show mercy to the one who has held fast to the rope of His mercy and generosity.

The second issue: the scholars differed about the forgiveness promised in this verse. Some said that it occurs at the departure from ʿArafat to Muzdalifah, and others said that it occurs at the departure from Muzdalifah to Mina. This disagreement is based on what we mentioned: on which of the two matters the statement ﴿Then depart﴾ is to be understood?

Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: The second opinion is reinforced by what Nafiʿ narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, addressed us on the evening of the Day of ʿArafat and said: 'O people, indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, looks upon you in this station of yours. He accepted from your good-doers, and He forgave your evil-doers for the sake of your good-doers, and the claims of people (for wrongs) are compensated by Him from His own. Depart in the name of God.'" His companions said: "O Messenger of God, you departed with us yesterday sorrowful and grieved, and you depart with us today joyful and happy." He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, I asked my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, yesterday for something He did not grant me: I asked Him for the claims of people, and He refused me. Then today, Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to me and said: 'Your Lord sends you greetings of peace and says to you: I have guaranteed compensation for the claims of people from Myself.'" O God, make us among its people by Your grace, O Most Generous of the generous.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 200–202 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah's words: ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

**The First Issue:** Ibn 'Abbas narrated that when the Arabs had finished their pilgrimage, after the days of Tashriq (the days of Tashriq, the three days after Eid al-Adha), they would stand between the mosque of Mina and the mountain. Each one of them would mention the virtues of his fathers in generosity, valour and kinship ties. They would recite poetry to one another on these themes and speak in prose, and each one of them, through this act, wanted to gain fame and to raise himself up by the glorious deeds of his forefathers. When Allah blessed them with Islam, He commanded them that their remembrance should be of their Lord in the same way that they had remembered their fathers.

Al-Qaffal narrated in his *Tafsir*, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) circumambulated the Ka'bah on his she-camel on the day of the Conquest, touching the corner with his staff. Then he praised Allah and extolled Him, and then said: 'To proceed, O people, Allah has removed from you the arrogance of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) and its boasting. O people, people are of two kinds: one who is righteous and god-fearing and noble before Allah, and one who is wicked and miserable and worthless before Allah.' Then he recited: ﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], and said: 'I say this statement of mine, and I ask Allah's forgiveness for myself and for you.'"

And from al-Suddi: the Arabs at Mina, after finishing the Hajj, would each say: "O Allah, indeed my father had a great bowl (for hospitality), was of great standing, and had abundant wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him." So Allah revealed this verse.

* * *
[Page 157]

**The Second Issue:** Know that when *qada'* (completion, decree, judgement) is connected to the action of the self, it means completion and finishing. When it is connected to the action of another, it means obligating. An example of the first is His words: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 12]; ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded﴾; and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whatever you missed, complete it." It is also said of a judge, when he settles a dispute: "He judged between them." An example of the second is His words: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. When it is used to mean informing, the meaning is also this, as in His words: ﴿And We made known to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isra': 4], meaning, "We informed them."

Having established this, we say: His words ﴿When you have completed your rites﴾ admit only of the completion of the whole thereof, especially since the remembrance of much of it has already been mentioned earlier. Some have said that it may mean: remember Allah at the rites, and the remembrance here would be what they were commanded to do: supplication at 'Arafat and al-Mash'ar al-Haram, the tawaf, and the sa'y. The words ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah﴾ would then be like someone saying: "When you perform Hajj, make tawaf and stand at 'Arafat," where he does not mean the completion of the Hajj but the entering into it. But this view is weak, because we have explained that His words ﴿When you have completed your rites﴾ indicate completion and finishing of all of it. This differs from the statement "When you perform Hajj, stand at 'Arafat," because the intent there is entering into Hajj, not completing it. As for this verse, it cannot mean anything other than completing the Hajj.

* * *
**The Third Issue:** *Al-manasik* is the plural of *mansak*. The *mansak*, which is the verbal noun, is equivalent to *nusk* (worship), meaning: when you have completed your acts of worship which you were commanded to perform in the Hajj. If you take it as the plural of *mansak*, which is the place of worship, then the sense is: "When you have completed the actions of your places of worship," and this would be an instance of omitting a word (the *mudaf*, or the governing noun).

Having understood this, we say: some commentators have said that the meaning of *al-manasik* here is what Allah commanded people to do in the Hajj of acts of worship. It is reported from Mujahid that the completion of the rites is the shedding of blood (sacrifice).

**The Fourth Issue:** The *fa'* in His words ﴿then remember Allah﴾ indicates that completion of the rites necessitates this remembrance. Therefore they differed about what kind of remembrance this is. Some interpreted it as remembrance by the sacrifice (the slaughter of the animal). Others interpreted it as the remembrance which is the takbirat (repeated proclamations of "Allahu akbar") after the prayer on the day of sacrifice and the days of Tashriq, according to their disagreement on its beginning and end, because after completing the Hajj there is no specific remembrance except these takbirat. Others said: rather, what is meant is turning the people away from what they had become accustomed to after the Hajj, namely the remembrance that boasts of the deeds of their fathers. For if He had not forbidden that by revealing this verse, they would not have deviated from this blameworthy practice. It is as if He said: "When you have completed and finished the obligations of the Hajj and have exited the state of ihram, then devote yourselves to the remembrance of Allah rather than the remembrance of your fathers." Others said: rather, what is meant is that completion of the Hajj necessitates turning to supplication and seeking forgiveness, because whoever has borne separation from family and homeland, spent wealth, and undertaken hardships on the journey of Hajj, is deserving, after finishing it, to turn to supplication, humble entreaty, abundant seeking of forgiveness, and devotion to Allah, the Exalted. On this basis, the practice has continued after the prayer with many supplications.

There is also a fifth aspect: the purpose of engaging in this worship is the subjugation of the self and the erasing of the traces of the ego and the natural disposition. This resolve is not sought for its own sake; rather, what is intended by it is that the false imprints be removed from the tablet of the spirit, so that the light of Allah's majesty may be manifested in it. The sense is: "When you have completed your rites and removed the traces of humanity, and cleared the obstacles from the path of spiritual journeying, then busy yourselves after that with illuminating the heart through the remembrance of Allah." The first is negation, and the second is affirmation; the first is the removal of whatever is other than the Truth from the ways of traces, and the second is the illumination of the heart through the remembrance of the Sovereign, the Almighty.

* * *
[Page 158]

As for His words ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾, there are several views:

*First*, and this is the view of the majority of commentators: we have mentioned that after completing the Hajj the people would exaggerate in praising their fathers, recounting their merits and virtues. So Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿then remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾, meaning: "Devote yourselves to the remembrance of Allah as you were devoting yourselves to the remembrance of your fathers, and exert your utmost effort in praising Allah and describing His favours and blessings, just as you exerted your utmost effort in praising your fathers. For this is more fitting and closer to reason than praising the fathers. If the recounting of the fathers' glories is false, it leads to baseness in this world and punishment in the Hereafter; and if it is true, it leads to self-admiration, arrogance and excessive pride, and all of these are among the chief destroyers. Thus it is established that your occupation with the remembrance of Allah is better than your occupation with your fathers' glories. And if this is not superiority, then at least it is equality."

*Second*: al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: "Remember Allah as you remember your fathers and your mothers," and mention of the fathers is sufficient in place of the mothers, as in His words: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81] (where the cold is omitted). They said: this is the speech of the child when he first begins to speak clearly: "Abbah, abbah" and "Ammah, ammah" (i.e., "Father, father" and "Mother, mother"). That is, be constant in the remembrance of Allah just as a child in his youth is constant in remembering his father and mother.

*Third*: Abu Muslim said: the mention of the fathers came as an example of constancy in remembrance. The meaning is that just as a man does not forget the remembrance of his father, so likewise he must not neglect the remembrance of Allah.

*Fourth*: Ibn al-Anbari said regarding this verse: the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah most often swore by their fathers, as in their saying: "By my father," "By your father," "By my grandfather," "By your grandfather." So He, the Exalted, said: "Glorify Allah as you glorify your fathers."

*Fifth*: Some of those mentioned said: the meaning is: "Remember Allah with His oneness, as you remember your fathers with their oneness." For if one of them were attributed to his parents, he would be offended and disdain it; and then he would set up gods for himself. So it was said to them: "Remember Allah with His oneness as you remember your fathers with their oneness." Rather, the emphasis on monotheism here is more fitting than there. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾.

*Sixth*: a child returns to his father for all his important needs and remembers him with reverence; so you too should be like that in the remembrance of Allah.

*Seventh*: It is possible that they used to mention their fathers in order to seek intercession through their remembrance for the answering of supplication with Allah. So Allah, the Exalted, informed them that their fathers were not in that rank, since their good deeds had become of no account because of their polytheism. They were commanded instead to enumerate Allah's blessings and favours and to increase praise of Him, so that this would be a means to the continual succession of blessings in the future. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade them from swearing by their fathers, saying: "Whoever is going to swear, let him swear by Allah or remain silent." If whatever is other than Allah is only for Allah and by Allah, then the more fitting course is to glorify Allah, the Exalted, and there is no god but Him.

*Eighth*: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding the interpretation of this verse: it means that you become angrier for Allah when He is disobeyed than your anger for your father when he is mentioned with evil.

Know that although these aspects are all possible, the first aspect is the one that is definite. All the aspects share one thing: it is obligatory upon the servant to be constantly mindful of his Lord, constantly glorifying Him, constantly returning to Him for the seeking of his needs, and constantly detached from all others. O Allah, make us people of this description, O Most Generous of the generous.

* * *
As for His words ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾, there are two issues:

**The First Issue:** The grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of ﴿أشد﴾ (*ashadda*, "greater"): it has been said that its governing element is the *kaf* (the particle "like" in *kadhikrikum*), so its position is in the genitive. It has also been said that its governing element is *udhkuru* ("remember"), so its position is in the accusative. The sense would be: "Remember Allah in the like of your remembrance of your fathers, and remember Him *ashadda dhikran* (with greater remembrance) than your fathers."

**The Second Issue:** His words ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾ mean: "rather, with greater remembrance." This is because the glories of their fathers were few, whereas the attributes of perfection of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are without limit. Therefore their occupation with the remembrance of the attributes of perfection of Allah, the Exalted, must be greater than their occupation with the glories of their fathers. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the figurative usage of the language in such a case is well known. A man says to another: "Do this by a month or sooner than that," and he does not mean to create doubt; he means only to shift from the first to something closer to it.

* *
Allah's words: ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter. And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in account.﴾ There are issues in this verse:

**The First Issue:** Know that Allah first explained the details of the rites of Hajj, then after them commanded remembrance, saying: ﴿So when you depart from 'Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and remember Him as He has guided you﴾. Then He explained that it is better to leave aside the remembrance of others and to restrict oneself to the remembrance of Him, saying: ﴿So remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾. Then after this remembrance He explained the manner of supplication, saying: ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾. How excellent is this order! For it is necessary to first precede with worship to break the self and remove its darkness; then after worship it is necessary to occupy oneself with the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, to illuminate the heart and manifest the light of His majesty; then after that remembrance a man busies himself with supplication, for supplication is only perfected when it is preceded by remembrance. Thus it is related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he began with remembrance, saying: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 78], then said: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 83]. So he put remembrance before supplication.

[Page 159 continued]

When you have understood this, we say: Allah, exalted is He, has made clear that those who call upon Allah are of two groups. One of them is those whose supplication is confined to seeking this world. The second is those who combine in their supplication the seeking of this world and the seeking of the Hereafter. The division also contained a third category, which is one whose supplication is confined to seeking the Hereafter. The scholars differed as to whether this category is prescribed or not. Most of them held that it is not prescribed. This is because man was created needy and weak, with no capacity for the pains of this world nor for the hardships of the Hereafter. Therefore, it is better for him to seek refuge with his Lord from all the evils of this world and the Hereafter. Al-Qaffal (d. c. 417 AH), in his *Tafsir*, related from Anas that the Prophet (peace be upon him) "entered upon a man who was visiting him, and the illness had worn him out. He said: What were you supplicating to Allah with before this? He said: I used to say, 'O Allah, whatever punishment You would inflict upon me in the Hereafter, hasten it for me in this world.' The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Glory be to Allah! Indeed you cannot bear that. Why did you not say: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾?' He said: So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) supplicated for him, and he was cured."

Know that if He, glorified is He, were to inflict pain upon a single vein in the body, or upon the root of a single hair, it would disturb the matter
[Page 160]
for the human being, and because of it he would be deprived of obedience to Allah, exalted is He, and of occupying himself with His remembrance. So who is it that is independent of the outpouring of Allah's mercy in his first life and his final end? Thus it is established that restricting supplication to seeking the Hereafter alone is impermissible. In the verse there is an indication to this, in that He mentioned the two categories and omitted this third category.

* * *

The second issue: The scholars differed concerning those whom Allah reported as confining their supplication to seeking this world, who they are. Some said: They are the disbelievers. It was related from Ibn Abbas that the polytheists used to say when they stood in prayer: "O Allah, provide us with camels, cattle, sheep, male slaves and female slaves," and they did not seek repentance or forgiveness, because they denied resurrection and the return. And from Anas: They used to say, "Give us rain and grant us victory over our enemy." So Allah informed that whoever is of this group, "there is no share (khalaq) for him in the Hereafter," meaning there is no portion for him in it of honour, bliss, or reward. It is related from Shaykh Abu 'Ali al-Daqqaq, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: The people of the Fire will cry for help, then they will say, "Pour upon us water, or some of what Allah has provided you in this world," seeking food and drink. When their desires overcame them, they were disgraced in this world and the Hereafter. Others said: These may be believers, but they ask Allah for their worldly affairs, not for their otherworldly affairs. Their request is among the sins, since they asked Allah, in the greatest of standing places and the most noble of assemblies, for the debris of this world and its fleeting goods, turning away from asking for lasting bliss in the Hereafter. It may be said of one who does this that he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter, even if the doer is a Muslim. This is like what was related concerning the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, those who trade away the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price — those will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77]. It was said that it was revealed concerning one who took property by a perjurious oath. It was related from the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Indeed Allah supports this religion through people who have no share (in the Hereafter)." Then the meaning of that is in several aspects:

The first: he has no share in the Hereafter unless he repents.

The second: he has no share in the Hereafter unless Allah pardons him.

The third: he has no share in the Hereafter like the share of one who asked Allah for his Hereafter. Likewise, one who took property by a perjurious oath has no share like the share of one who abstained from that. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾. The object of "give us" (ātinā) has been omitted from the speech because it is understood. Know that the levels of felicity are three: spiritual, bodily, and external. As for the spiritual, they are two: perfecting the theoretical faculty through knowledge, and perfecting the practical faculty through virtuous character. As for the bodily, they are two: health and beauty. As for the external, they are two: wealth and standing. So His saying: ﴿give us in this world﴾ encompasses all these categories. For knowledge, if it is desired for adornment in this world and for elevating oneself above one's peers, it is of this world. Virtuous character, if it is desired for leadership in this world and for controlling its interests, is of this world. Everyone who does not believe in resurrection and the return seeks no virtue, neither spiritual nor physical, except for the sake of this world. Then Allah, exalted is He, said concerning this group: ﴿and he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾, meaning he has no portion in the bliss of the Hereafter. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him from it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20]. Then He, exalted is He, did not mention in this verse whether what he asked for in this world was granted to him or not. Some said: Such a person is not fit for being answered, because being one whose supplication is answered is a quality of praise, and it is not established except for one who is a friend (wali) of Allah, exalted is He, deserving of honour. However, it is not obligatory. As long as he is a living, accountable person, Allah, exalted is He, gives him his provision, as He said: ﴿There is no creature on earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud: 6]. Others said: Such a person may indeed be answered, but that answer may be a deception and a gradual drawing-on (istidraj).

* * *

[Page 161]

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them is one who says: Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, the exegetes have mentioned several aspects concerning it:

The first: that "good" in this world is an expression for health, security, sufficiency, a righteous child, a righteous wife, and victory over enemies. Allah, exalted is He, has called abundance and expansion in provision, and what resembles it, "good," as He said: ﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them﴾ [al-Tawba: 50]. And concerning His saying: ﴿Say: Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes?﴾ [al-Tawba: 52] it was said that the two are victory, triumph, and martyrdom. As for "good" in the Hereafter, it is success in reward and deliverance from punishment. In sum, His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter﴾ is a comprehensive word encompassing all the aims of this world and the Hereafter. Hammad ibn Salama related from Thabit that they said to Anas: "Pray for us." He said: "O Allah, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." They said: "Add more for us." So he repeated it. They said: "Add more for us." He said: "What do you want? I have asked for you the good of this world and the Hereafter." Anas spoke truly, for a servant has no abode other than this world and the Hereafter. When he asks for the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter, nothing remains beyond it.

The second: that what is meant by "good" in this world is useful action, which is faith and obedience, and "good" in the Hereafter is lasting delight, honour, and enjoyment in the remembrance of Allah, in intimacy with Him, in His love, and in beholding Him. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn Abbas that "a man supplicated to his Lord and said in his supplication: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'I do not know that this man asked Allah for anything of the affairs of this world.' Some of the Companions said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, he said: "Our Lord, give us good in this world."' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'He is saying: give us in this world righteous action.'" This is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who say: Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and our offspring the coolness of the eyes﴾ [al-Furqan: 74]. That coolness is for them to see their children and spouses obedient, faithful, and constant in servitude.

The third: Qatada said: "Good" in this world and in the Hereafter is seeking well-being in both abodes. And from al-Hasan: "Good" in this world is understanding the Book of Allah, exalted is He, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. And know that the origin of the discussion in the verse is that if it were said, "Give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter," that would encompass all goods. But He said: ﴿in this world good, and in the Hereafter good﴾, and this is an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, so it does not encompass more than one good. Therefore the earlier exegetes differed, and each of them interpreted the expression according to what he saw as the best kind of good.

If it is said: Is it not the case that if it were said, "Give us the good in this world and the good in the Hereafter," that would encompass all the categories? Why was that omitted and it was mentioned in the indefinite form?

I say: What I think on this point, and knowledge is with Allah, is that we have already explained earlier that it is not proper for the supplicant to say, "O Allah, give me such and such," but rather he must say, "O Allah, if such and such is a benefit for me and is in accord with Your decree and destiny, then give me that." So if he said, "O Allah, give me the good in this world and the Hereafter," that would be an absolute assertion, and we have already explained that this is impermissible. But since it is mentioned in the indefinite form, when he says, "Give me good in this world," what is meant is one good, namely the good that accords with His decree, destiny, pleasure, judgment, and wisdom. That is closer to observing courtesy and preserving the foundations of certainty.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those﴾. There are two opinions concerning it:

One of them: It refers only to the second group, those who
[Page 162]
asked for this world and the Hereafter. The evidence for this is that He mentioned the ruling of the first group when He said: ﴿and he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾.

The second opinion: That it refers to both groups, meaning that each of these has a share of his work according to what he intended. Whoever denies resurrection and performs pilgrimage seeking the reward of this world, that is disbelief and polytheism from him, and Allah will repay him. Or what is meant is that whoever works for this world is given a share like it in his worldly life, as He said: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him from it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20].

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for them there is a share of what they have earned﴾, there are questions concerning it:

The first question: His saying, ﴿for them there is a share of what they have earned﴾, runs in the manner of belittling and diminishing, so what is meant by it?

The answer: What is meant is: for them there is a share of this world and of the Hereafter by means of their earning and their action. So the word "min" (of) in His saying ﴿of what they have earned﴾ is for the beginning of the extent, not for partition.

The second question: Does this verse indicate that the recompense is for the deed?

The answer: Yes, but according to the promise, not according to inherent entitlement.

The third question: What is kasb (acquisition, earning)?

The answer: Kasb is applied to what a person attains by his action, so it is his earning and what he has acquired, on condition that this brings a benefit or repels a harm. On this basis it is said of profits that they are the earnings of so-and-so, and that he has much earnings or little earnings, because only gain is intended. As for what our companions say, that kasb is an intermediate position between determinism (jabr) and creation (khalq), it is mentioned in the earlier books on theology.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, there are issues concerning it.

The first issue: sarī' (swift) is an active participle from speed. Ibn al-Sikkit said: sariʿa yasraʿu sarʿan and surʿatan, so he is sarīʿ. "Al-ḥisāb" (reckoning) is a verbal noun like "al-muḥāsaba." The meaning of ḥisāb in the lexicon is counting. It is said: ḥasiba yaḥsubu ḥisāban, ḥisbatan and ḥasaban, when he counted. Al-Layth and Ibn al-Sikkit mentioned it. Al-ḥasb is what is counted, and from it comes ḥasab (lineage) of a man, which is what is counted of his distinguished deeds and glories. Al-iḥtisāb is taking account of a thing. Al-Zajjaj said: ḥisāb in the lexicon is derived from their saying, "ḥasbuka kadhā," meaning, "what is sufficient for you is such-and-such." So the reckoning in transactions was called ḥisāb, because by it one knows what is sufficient, with neither excess nor deficiency in the measure.

**The second issue:** People have differed over the meaning of God, may He be exalted, being the one who calls His creation to account (*muhasib*), and there are several views:

First: The meaning of *hisab* (reckoning) is that God informs them of what is for them and what is against them. That is, God creates in their hearts *darury* (necessary, self-evident) knowledge in proportion to their deeds, their quantity and their qualities, and in proportion to what they receive of reward and punishment. They said: the basis of this *majaz* (figurative usage) is that reckoning is a cause of a person's knowing what is for him and against him, so applying the name of reckoning to this informing is applying the name of the cause to the effect, and this is a well-known *majaz*. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "There is no reckoning for the creation. Rather, they stand before God, may He be exalted, and are given their books in their right hands. In them are their evil deeds, and it is said to them: 'These are your evil deeds, and I have overlooked them.' Then they are given their good deeds, and it is said: 'These are your good deeds, and I have multiplied them for you.'"

[Page 163]

The second view: *muhasabah* (reckoning) is an expression for requital. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And how many a city that defied the command of its Lord and His messengers—We reckoned with it with a severe reckoning﴾ [al-Talaq, 65:8]. The basis of the *majaz* here is that reckoning is a cause of taking and giving, and applying the name of the cause to the effect is permissible, so the word "reckoning" is rightly applied to requital.

The third view: God speaks to His servants about the states of their deeds and the manner of the reward and punishment that belong to them. Whoever says that His speech is neither a letter nor a sound says that God creates in the ear of the one under obligation (*mukallaf*) a hearing by which he hears His eternal speech, just as He creates in his eye a sight by which he sees His eternal essence. Whoever says that it is a sound says that God creates a speech that every *mukallaf* hears, either by creating that speech in the ear of each one of them, or in a body near his ear, such that the force of that sound does not prevent others from understanding what they are obligated to. This is the meaning of God being the one who reckons with His creation.

**The third issue:** They have mentioned several meanings for God being *sari' al-hisab* (swift in reckoning):

First: His reckoning amounts either to His creating necessary knowledge in the heart of every *mukallaf* in proportion to his deeds and the measure of his reward and punishment; or to His delivering to every *mukallaf* what is his due of reward; or to His creating a hearing in the ear of every *mukallaf* by which he hears the eternal speech; or to His creating in the ear of every *mukallaf* a sound indicating the measures of reward and punishment and the four aspects mentioned. So the upshot of God being the reckoner returns to His creating something. Since God's power relates to all possible things, and His creating and bringing into being does not depend on the prior existence of a material, nor a duration, nor an instrument, and no affair distracts Him from another affair, He is therefore certainly able to create all of creation in less than the blink of an eye. This is a clear statement. For this reason it is reported in a *khabar* (report) that God reckons with creation in the time it takes to milk a she-camel.

Second: The meaning of His being *sari' al-hisab* is that He is swift to accept the supplications of His servants and to respond to them. This is because at one and the same time, each of the petitioners asks Him for different things concerning the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, and He gives each one what he seeks without anything becoming confused for Him. If it were a matter with one of the creatures, the counting would be long and the reckoning would be prolonged. So God informs that He is *sari' al-hisab*, that is, He knows all the requests of those who ask, because God does not need to count on fingers nor to think and deliberate. This is the meaning of the transmitted supplication: "O You whom one affair does not distract from another." The upshot of this view is that the meaning of God being swift in reckoning is that He knows all the states and deeds of creation. The basis of the *majaz* here is that one who is reckoned is only reckoned so that he may gain knowledge of that matter; so reckoning is a cause of gaining knowledge, and the name of the cause is applied to the effect.

Third: God's reckoning is swift in the sense that it is coming without doubt.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 200–202 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah's words: ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

**The First Issue:** Ibn 'Abbas narrated that when the Arabs had finished their pilgrimage, after the days of Tashriq (the days of Tashriq, the three days after Eid al-Adha), they would stand between the mosque of Mina and the mountain. Each one of them would mention the virtues of his fathers in generosity, valour and kinship ties. They would recite poetry to one another on these themes and speak in prose, and each one of them, through this act, wanted to gain fame and to raise himself up by the glorious deeds of his forefathers. When Allah blessed them with Islam, He commanded them that their remembrance should be of their Lord in the same way that they had remembered their fathers.

Al-Qaffal narrated in his *Tafsir*, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) circumambulated the Ka'bah on his she-camel on the day of the Conquest, touching the corner with his staff. Then he praised Allah and extolled Him, and then said: 'To proceed, O people, Allah has removed from you the arrogance of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) and its boasting. O people, people are of two kinds: one who is righteous and god-fearing and noble before Allah, and one who is wicked and miserable and worthless before Allah.' Then he recited: ﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], and said: 'I say this statement of mine, and I ask Allah's forgiveness for myself and for you.'"

And from al-Suddi: the Arabs at Mina, after finishing the Hajj, would each say: "O Allah, indeed my father had a great bowl (for hospitality), was of great standing, and had abundant wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him." So Allah revealed this verse.

* * *
[Page 157]

**The Second Issue:** Know that when *qada'* (completion, decree, judgement) is connected to the action of the self, it means completion and finishing. When it is connected to the action of another, it means obligating. An example of the first is His words: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 12]; ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded﴾; and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whatever you missed, complete it." It is also said of a judge, when he settles a dispute: "He judged between them." An example of the second is His words: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. When it is used to mean informing, the meaning is also this, as in His words: ﴿And We made known to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isra': 4], meaning, "We informed them."

Having established this, we say: His words ﴿When you have completed your rites﴾ admit only of the completion of the whole thereof, especially since the remembrance of much of it has already been mentioned earlier. Some have said that it may mean: remember Allah at the rites, and the remembrance here would be what they were commanded to do: supplication at 'Arafat and al-Mash'ar al-Haram, the tawaf, and the sa'y. The words ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah﴾ would then be like someone saying: "When you perform Hajj, make tawaf and stand at 'Arafat," where he does not mean the completion of the Hajj but the entering into it. But this view is weak, because we have explained that His words ﴿When you have completed your rites﴾ indicate completion and finishing of all of it. This differs from the statement "When you perform Hajj, stand at 'Arafat," because the intent there is entering into Hajj, not completing it. As for this verse, it cannot mean anything other than completing the Hajj.

* * *
**The Third Issue:** *Al-manasik* is the plural of *mansak*. The *mansak*, which is the verbal noun, is equivalent to *nusk* (worship), meaning: when you have completed your acts of worship which you were commanded to perform in the Hajj. If you take it as the plural of *mansak*, which is the place of worship, then the sense is: "When you have completed the actions of your places of worship," and this would be an instance of omitting a word (the *mudaf*, or the governing noun).

Having understood this, we say: some commentators have said that the meaning of *al-manasik* here is what Allah commanded people to do in the Hajj of acts of worship. It is reported from Mujahid that the completion of the rites is the shedding of blood (sacrifice).

**The Fourth Issue:** The *fa'* in His words ﴿then remember Allah﴾ indicates that completion of the rites necessitates this remembrance. Therefore they differed about what kind of remembrance this is. Some interpreted it as remembrance by the sacrifice (the slaughter of the animal). Others interpreted it as the remembrance which is the takbirat (repeated proclamations of "Allahu akbar") after the prayer on the day of sacrifice and the days of Tashriq, according to their disagreement on its beginning and end, because after completing the Hajj there is no specific remembrance except these takbirat. Others said: rather, what is meant is turning the people away from what they had become accustomed to after the Hajj, namely the remembrance that boasts of the deeds of their fathers. For if He had not forbidden that by revealing this verse, they would not have deviated from this blameworthy practice. It is as if He said: "When you have completed and finished the obligations of the Hajj and have exited the state of ihram, then devote yourselves to the remembrance of Allah rather than the remembrance of your fathers." Others said: rather, what is meant is that completion of the Hajj necessitates turning to supplication and seeking forgiveness, because whoever has borne separation from family and homeland, spent wealth, and undertaken hardships on the journey of Hajj, is deserving, after finishing it, to turn to supplication, humble entreaty, abundant seeking of forgiveness, and devotion to Allah, the Exalted. On this basis, the practice has continued after the prayer with many supplications.

There is also a fifth aspect: the purpose of engaging in this worship is the subjugation of the self and the erasing of the traces of the ego and the natural disposition. This resolve is not sought for its own sake; rather, what is intended by it is that the false imprints be removed from the tablet of the spirit, so that the light of Allah's majesty may be manifested in it.
