The sense is: "When you have completed your rites and removed the traces of humanity, and cleared the obstacles from the path of spiritual journeying, then busy yourselves after that with illuminating the heart through the remembrance of Allah." The first is negation, and the second is affirmation; the first is the removal of whatever is other than the Truth from the ways of traces, and the second is the illumination of the heart through the remembrance of the Sovereign, the Almighty.

* * *
[Page 158]

As for His words ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾, there are several views:

*First*, and this is the view of the majority of commentators: we have mentioned that after completing the Hajj the people would exaggerate in praising their fathers, recounting their merits and virtues. So Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿then remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾, meaning: "Devote yourselves to the remembrance of Allah as you were devoting yourselves to the remembrance of your fathers, and exert your utmost effort in praising Allah and describing His favours and blessings, just as you exerted your utmost effort in praising your fathers. For this is more fitting and closer to reason than praising the fathers. If the recounting of the fathers' glories is false, it leads to baseness in this world and punishment in the Hereafter; and if it is true, it leads to self-admiration, arrogance and excessive pride, and all of these are among the chief destroyers. Thus it is established that your occupation with the remembrance of Allah is better than your occupation with your fathers' glories. And if this is not superiority, then at least it is equality."

*Second*: al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: "Remember Allah as you remember your fathers and your mothers," and mention of the fathers is sufficient in place of the mothers, as in His words: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81] (where the cold is omitted). They said: this is the speech of the child when he first begins to speak clearly: "Abbah, abbah" and "Ammah, ammah" (i.e., "Father, father" and "Mother, mother"). That is, be constant in the remembrance of Allah just as a child in his youth is constant in remembering his father and mother.

*Third*: Abu Muslim said: the mention of the fathers came as an example of constancy in remembrance. The meaning is that just as a man does not forget the remembrance of his father, so likewise he must not neglect the remembrance of Allah.

*Fourth*: Ibn al-Anbari said regarding this verse: the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah most often swore by their fathers, as in their saying: "By my father," "By your father," "By my grandfather," "By your grandfather." So He, the Exalted, said: "Glorify Allah as you glorify your fathers."

*Fifth*: Some of those mentioned said: the meaning is: "Remember Allah with His oneness, as you remember your fathers with their oneness." For if one of them were attributed to his parents, he would be offended and disdain it; and then he would set up gods for himself. So it was said to them: "Remember Allah with His oneness as you remember your fathers with their oneness." Rather, the emphasis on monotheism here is more fitting than there. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾.

*Sixth*: a child returns to his father for all his important needs and remembers him with reverence; so you too should be like that in the remembrance of Allah.

*Seventh*: It is possible that they used to mention their fathers in order to seek intercession through their remembrance for the answering of supplication with Allah. So Allah, the Exalted, informed them that their fathers were not in that rank, since their good deeds had become of no account because of their polytheism. They were commanded instead to enumerate Allah's blessings and favours and to increase praise of Him, so that this would be a means to the continual succession of blessings in the future. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade them from swearing by their fathers, saying: "Whoever is going to swear, let him swear by Allah or remain silent." If whatever is other than Allah is only for Allah and by Allah, then the more fitting course is to glorify Allah, the Exalted, and there is no god but Him.

*Eighth*: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding the interpretation of this verse: it means that you become angrier for Allah when He is disobeyed than your anger for your father when he is mentioned with evil.

Know that although these aspects are all possible, the first aspect is the one that is definite. All the aspects share one thing: it is obligatory upon the servant to be constantly mindful of his Lord, constantly glorifying Him, constantly returning to Him for the seeking of his needs, and constantly detached from all others. O Allah, make us people of this description, O Most Generous of the generous.

* * *
As for His words ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾, there are two issues:

**The First Issue:** The grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of ﴿أشد﴾ (*ashadda*, "greater"): it has been said that its governing element is the *kaf* (the particle "like" in *kadhikrikum*), so its position is in the genitive. It has also been said that its governing element is *udhkuru* ("remember"), so its position is in the accusative. The sense would be: "Remember Allah in the like of your remembrance of your fathers, and remember Him *ashadda dhikran* (with greater remembrance) than your fathers."

**The Second Issue:** His words ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾ mean: "rather, with greater remembrance." This is because the glories of their fathers were few, whereas the attributes of perfection of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are without limit. Therefore their occupation with the remembrance of the attributes of perfection of Allah, the Exalted, must be greater than their occupation with the glories of their fathers. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the figurative usage of the language in such a case is well known. A man says to another: "Do this by a month or sooner than that," and he does not mean to create doubt; he means only to shift from the first to something closer to it.

* *
Allah's words: ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter. And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in account.﴾ There are issues in this verse:

**The First Issue:** Know that Allah first explained the details of the rites of Hajj, then after them commanded remembrance, saying: ﴿So when you depart from 'Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and remember Him as He has guided you﴾. Then He explained that it is better to leave aside the remembrance of others and to restrict oneself to the remembrance of Him, saying: ﴿So remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾. Then after this remembrance He explained the manner of supplication, saying: ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾. How excellent is this order! For it is necessary to first precede with worship to break the self and remove its darkness; then after worship it is necessary to occupy oneself with the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, to illuminate the heart and manifest the light of His majesty; then after that remembrance a man busies himself with supplication, for supplication is only perfected when it is preceded by remembrance. Thus it is related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he began with remembrance, saying: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 78], then said: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 83]. So he put remembrance before supplication.

[Page 159 continued]

When you have understood this, we say: Allah, exalted is He, has made clear that those who call upon Allah are of two groups. One of them is those whose supplication is confined to seeking this world. The second is those who combine in their supplication the seeking of this world and the seeking of the Hereafter. The division also contained a third category, which is one whose supplication is confined to seeking the Hereafter. The scholars differed as to whether this category is prescribed or not. Most of them held that it is not prescribed. This is because man was created needy and weak, with no capacity for the pains of this world nor for the hardships of the Hereafter. Therefore, it is better for him to seek refuge with his Lord from all the evils of this world and the Hereafter. Al-Qaffal (d. c. 417 AH), in his *Tafsir*, related from Anas that the Prophet (peace be upon him) "entered upon a man who was visiting him, and the illness had worn him out. He said: What were you supplicating to Allah with before this? He said: I used to say, 'O Allah, whatever punishment You would inflict upon me in the Hereafter, hasten it for me in this world.' The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Glory be to Allah! Indeed you cannot bear that. Why did you not say: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾?' He said: So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) supplicated for him, and he was cured."

Know that if He, glorified is He, were to inflict pain upon a single vein in the body, or upon the root of a single hair, it would disturb the matter
[Page 160]
for the human being, and because of it he would be deprived of obedience to Allah, exalted is He, and of occupying himself with His remembrance. So who is it that is independent of the outpouring of Allah's mercy in his first life and his final end? Thus it is established that restricting supplication to seeking the Hereafter alone is impermissible. In the verse there is an indication to this, in that He mentioned the two categories and omitted this third category.

* * *

The second issue: The scholars differed concerning those whom Allah reported as confining their supplication to seeking this world, who they are. Some said: They are the disbelievers. It was related from Ibn Abbas that the polytheists used to say when they stood in prayer: "O Allah, provide us with camels, cattle, sheep, male slaves and female slaves," and they did not seek repentance or forgiveness, because they denied resurrection and the return. And from Anas: They used to say, "Give us rain and grant us victory over our enemy." So Allah informed that whoever is of this group, "there is no share (khalaq) for him in the Hereafter," meaning there is no portion for him in it of honour, bliss, or reward. It is related from Shaykh Abu 'Ali al-Daqqaq, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: The people of the Fire will cry for help, then they will say, "Pour upon us water, or some of what Allah has provided you in this world," seeking food and drink. When their desires overcame them, they were disgraced in this world and the Hereafter. Others said: These may be believers, but they ask Allah for their worldly affairs, not for their otherworldly affairs. Their request is among the sins, since they asked Allah, in the greatest of standing places and the most noble of assemblies, for the debris of this world and its fleeting goods, turning away from asking for lasting bliss in the Hereafter. It may be said of one who does this that he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter, even if the doer is a Muslim. This is like what was related concerning the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, those who trade away the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price — those will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77]. It was said that it was revealed concerning one who took property by a perjurious oath. It was related from the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Indeed Allah supports this religion through people who have no share (in the Hereafter)." Then the meaning of that is in several aspects:

The first: he has no share in the Hereafter unless he repents.

The second: he has no share in the Hereafter unless Allah pardons him.

The third: he has no share in the Hereafter like the share of one who asked Allah for his Hereafter. Likewise, one who took property by a perjurious oath has no share like the share of one who abstained from that. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾. The object of "give us" (ātinā) has been omitted from the speech because it is understood. Know that the levels of felicity are three: spiritual, bodily, and external. As for the spiritual, they are two: perfecting the theoretical faculty through knowledge, and perfecting the practical faculty through virtuous character. As for the bodily, they are two: health and beauty. As for the external, they are two: wealth and standing. So His saying: ﴿give us in this world﴾ encompasses all these categories. For knowledge, if it is desired for adornment in this world and for elevating oneself above one's peers, it is of this world. Virtuous character, if it is desired for leadership in this world and for controlling its interests, is of this world. Everyone who does not believe in resurrection and the return seeks no virtue, neither spiritual nor physical, except for the sake of this world. Then Allah, exalted is He, said concerning this group: ﴿and he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾, meaning he has no portion in the bliss of the Hereafter. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him from it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20]. Then He, exalted is He, did not mention in this verse whether what he asked for in this world was granted to him or not. Some said: Such a person is not fit for being answered, because being one whose supplication is answered is a quality of praise, and it is not established except for one who is a friend (wali) of Allah, exalted is He, deserving of honour. However, it is not obligatory. As long as he is a living, accountable person, Allah, exalted is He, gives him his provision, as He said: ﴿There is no creature on earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud: 6]. Others said: Such a person may indeed be answered, but that answer may be a deception and a gradual drawing-on (istidraj).

* * *

[Page 161]

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them is one who says: Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, the exegetes have mentioned several aspects concerning it:

The first: that "good" in this world is an expression for health, security, sufficiency, a righteous child, a righteous wife, and victory over enemies. Allah, exalted is He, has called abundance and expansion in provision, and what resembles it, "good," as He said: ﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them﴾ [al-Tawba: 50]. And concerning His saying: ﴿Say: Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes?﴾ [al-Tawba: 52] it was said that the two are victory, triumph, and martyrdom. As for "good" in the Hereafter, it is success in reward and deliverance from punishment. In sum, His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter﴾ is a comprehensive word encompassing all the aims of this world and the Hereafter. Hammad ibn Salama related from Thabit that they said to Anas: "Pray for us." He said: "O Allah, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." They said: "Add more for us." So he repeated it. They said: "Add more for us." He said: "What do you want? I have asked for you the good of this world and the Hereafter." Anas spoke truly, for a servant has no abode other than this world and the Hereafter. When he asks for the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter, nothing remains beyond it.

The second: that what is meant by "good" in this world is useful action, which is faith and obedience, and "good" in the Hereafter is lasting delight, honour, and enjoyment in the remembrance of Allah, in intimacy with Him, in His love, and in beholding Him. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn Abbas that "a man supplicated to his Lord and said in his supplication: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'I do not know that this man asked Allah for anything of the affairs of this world.' Some of the Companions said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, he said: "Our Lord, give us good in this world."' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'He is saying: give us in this world righteous action.'" This is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who say: Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and our offspring the coolness of the eyes﴾ [al-Furqan: 74]. That coolness is for them to see their children and spouses obedient, faithful, and constant in servitude.

The third: Qatada said: "Good" in this world and in the Hereafter is seeking well-being in both abodes. And from al-Hasan: "Good" in this world is understanding the Book of Allah, exalted is He, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. And know that the origin of the discussion in the verse is that if it were said, "Give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter," that would encompass all goods. But He said: ﴿in this world good, and in the Hereafter good﴾, and this is an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, so it does not encompass more than one good. Therefore the earlier exegetes differed, and each of them interpreted the expression according to what he saw as the best kind of good.

If it is said: Is it not the case that if it were said, "Give us the good in this world and the good in the Hereafter," that would encompass all the categories? Why was that omitted and it was mentioned in the indefinite form?

I say: What I think on this point, and knowledge is with Allah, is that we have already explained earlier that it is not proper for the supplicant to say, "O Allah, give me such and such," but rather he must say, "O Allah, if such and such is a benefit for me and is in accord with Your decree and destiny, then give me that." So if he said, "O Allah, give me the good in this world and the Hereafter," that would be an absolute assertion, and we have already explained that this is impermissible. But since it is mentioned in the indefinite form, when he says, "Give me good in this world," what is meant is one good, namely the good that accords with His decree, destiny, pleasure, judgment, and wisdom. That is closer to observing courtesy and preserving the foundations of certainty.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those﴾. There are two opinions concerning it:

One of them: It refers only to the second group, those who
[Page 162]
asked for this world and the Hereafter. The evidence for this is that He mentioned the ruling of the first group when He said: ﴿and he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾.

The second opinion: That it refers to both groups, meaning that each of these has a share of his work according to what he intended. Whoever denies resurrection and performs pilgrimage seeking the reward of this world, that is disbelief and polytheism from him, and Allah will repay him. Or what is meant is that whoever works for this world is given a share like it in his worldly life, as He said: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him from it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20].

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for them there is a share of what they have earned﴾, there are questions concerning it:

The first question: His saying, ﴿for them there is a share of what they have earned﴾, runs in the manner of belittling and diminishing, so what is meant by it?

The answer: What is meant is: for them there is a share of this world and of the Hereafter by means of their earning and their action. So the word "min" (of) in His saying ﴿of what they have earned﴾ is for the beginning of the extent, not for partition.

The second question: Does this verse indicate that the recompense is for the deed?

The answer: Yes, but according to the promise, not according to inherent entitlement.

The third question: What is kasb (acquisition, earning)?

The answer: Kasb is applied to what a person attains by his action, so it is his earning and what he has acquired, on condition that this brings a benefit or repels a harm. On this basis it is said of profits that they are the earnings of so-and-so, and that he has much earnings or little earnings, because only gain is intended. As for what our companions say, that kasb is an intermediate position between determinism (jabr) and creation (khalq), it is mentioned in the earlier books on theology.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, there are issues concerning it.

The first issue: sarī' (swift) is an active participle from speed. Ibn al-Sikkit said: sariʿa yasraʿu sarʿan and surʿatan, so he is sarīʿ. "Al-ḥisāb" (reckoning) is a verbal noun like "al-muḥāsaba." The meaning of ḥisāb in the lexicon is counting. It is said: ḥasiba yaḥsubu ḥisāban, ḥisbatan and ḥasaban, when he counted. Al-Layth and Ibn al-Sikkit mentioned it. Al-ḥasb is what is counted, and from it comes ḥasab (lineage) of a man, which is what is counted of his distinguished deeds and glories. Al-iḥtisāb is taking account of a thing. Al-Zajjaj said: ḥisāb in the lexicon is derived from their saying, "ḥasbuka kadhā," meaning, "what is sufficient for you is such-and-such." So the reckoning in transactions was called ḥisāb, because by it one knows what is sufficient, with neither excess nor deficiency in the measure.

**The second issue:** People have differed over the meaning of God, may He be exalted, being the one who calls His creation to account (*muhasib*), and there are several views:

First: The meaning of *hisab* (reckoning) is that God informs them of what is for them and what is against them. That is, God creates in their hearts *darury* (necessary, self-evident) knowledge in proportion to their deeds, their quantity and their qualities, and in proportion to what they receive of reward and punishment. They said: the basis of this *majaz* (figurative usage) is that reckoning is a cause of a person's knowing what is for him and against him, so applying the name of reckoning to this informing is applying the name of the cause to the effect, and this is a well-known *majaz*. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "There is no reckoning for the creation. Rather, they stand before God, may He be exalted, and are given their books in their right hands. In them are their evil deeds, and it is said to them: 'These are your evil deeds, and I have overlooked them.' Then they are given their good deeds, and it is said: 'These are your good deeds, and I have multiplied them for you.'"

[Page 163]

The second view: *muhasabah* (reckoning) is an expression for requital. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And how many a city that defied the command of its Lord and His messengers—We reckoned with it with a severe reckoning﴾ [al-Talaq, 65:8]. The basis of the *majaz* here is that reckoning is a cause of taking and giving, and applying the name of the cause to the effect is permissible, so the word "reckoning" is rightly applied to requital.

The third view: God speaks to His servants about the states of their deeds and the manner of the reward and punishment that belong to them. Whoever says that His speech is neither a letter nor a sound says that God creates in the ear of the one under obligation (*mukallaf*) a hearing by which he hears His eternal speech, just as He creates in his eye a sight by which he sees His eternal essence. Whoever says that it is a sound says that God creates a speech that every *mukallaf* hears, either by creating that speech in the ear of each one of them, or in a body near his ear, such that the force of that sound does not prevent others from understanding what they are obligated to. This is the meaning of God being the one who reckons with His creation.

**The third issue:** They have mentioned several meanings for God being *sari' al-hisab* (swift in reckoning):

First: His reckoning amounts either to His creating necessary knowledge in the heart of every *mukallaf* in proportion to his deeds and the measure of his reward and punishment; or to His delivering to every *mukallaf* what is his due of reward; or to His creating a hearing in the ear of every *mukallaf* by which he hears the eternal speech; or to His creating in the ear of every *mukallaf* a sound indicating the measures of reward and punishment and the four aspects mentioned. So the upshot of God being the reckoner returns to His creating something. Since God's power relates to all possible things, and His creating and bringing into being does not depend on the prior existence of a material, nor a duration, nor an instrument, and no affair distracts Him from another affair, He is therefore certainly able to create all of creation in less than the blink of an eye. This is a clear statement. For this reason it is reported in a *khabar* (report) that God reckons with creation in the time it takes to milk a she-camel.

Second: The meaning of His being *sari' al-hisab* is that He is swift to accept the supplications of His servants and to respond to them. This is because at one and the same time, each of the petitioners asks Him for different things concerning the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, and He gives each one what he seeks without anything becoming confused for Him. If it were a matter with one of the creatures, the counting would be long and the reckoning would be prolonged. So God informs that He is *sari' al-hisab*, that is, He knows all the requests of those who ask, because God does not need to count on fingers nor to think and deliberate. This is the meaning of the transmitted supplication: "O You whom one affair does not distract from another." The upshot of this view is that the meaning of God being swift in reckoning is that He knows all the states and deeds of creation. The basis of the *majaz* here is that one who is reckoned is only reckoned so that he may gain knowledge of that matter; so reckoning is a cause of gaining knowledge, and the name of the cause is applied to the effect.

Third: God's reckoning is swift in the sense that it is coming without doubt.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 200–202 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah's words: ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

**The First Issue:** Ibn 'Abbas narrated that when the Arabs had finished their pilgrimage, after the days of Tashriq (the days of Tashriq, the three days after Eid al-Adha), they would stand between the mosque of Mina and the mountain. Each one of them would mention the virtues of his fathers in generosity, valour and kinship ties. They would recite poetry to one another on these themes and speak in prose, and each one of them, through this act, wanted to gain fame and to raise himself up by the glorious deeds of his forefathers. When Allah blessed them with Islam, He commanded them that their remembrance should be of their Lord in the same way that they had remembered their fathers.

Al-Qaffal narrated in his *Tafsir*, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) circumambulated the Ka'bah on his she-camel on the day of the Conquest, touching the corner with his staff. Then he praised Allah and extolled Him, and then said: 'To proceed, O people, Allah has removed from you the arrogance of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) and its boasting. O people, people are of two kinds: one who is righteous and god-fearing and noble before Allah, and one who is wicked and miserable and worthless before Allah.' Then he recited: ﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], and said: 'I say this statement of mine, and I ask Allah's forgiveness for myself and for you.'"

And from al-Suddi: the Arabs at Mina, after finishing the Hajj, would each say: "O Allah, indeed my father had a great bowl (for hospitality), was of great standing, and had abundant wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him." So Allah revealed this verse.

* * *
[Page 157]

**The Second Issue:** Know that when *qada'* (completion, decree, judgement) is connected to the action of the self, it means completion and finishing. When it is connected to the action of another, it means obligating. An example of the first is His words: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 12]; ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded﴾; and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whatever you missed, complete it." It is also said of a judge, when he settles a dispute: "He judged between them." An example of the second is His words: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. When it is used to mean informing, the meaning is also this, as in His words: ﴿And We made known to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isra': 4], meaning, "We informed them."

Having established this, we say: His words ﴿When you have completed your rites﴾ admit only of the completion of the whole thereof, especially since the remembrance of much of it has already been mentioned earlier. Some have said that it may mean: remember Allah at the rites, and the remembrance here would be what they were commanded to do: supplication at 'Arafat and al-Mash'ar al-Haram, the tawaf, and the sa'y. The words ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah﴾ would then be like someone saying: "When you perform Hajj, make tawaf and stand at 'Arafat," where he does not mean the completion of the Hajj but the entering into it. But this view is weak, because we have explained that His words ﴿When you have completed your rites﴾ indicate completion and finishing of all of it. This differs from the statement "When you perform Hajj, stand at 'Arafat," because the intent there is entering into Hajj, not completing it. As for this verse, it cannot mean anything other than completing the Hajj.

* * *
**The Third Issue:** *Al-manasik* is the plural of *mansak*. The *mansak*, which is the verbal noun, is equivalent to *nusk* (worship), meaning: when you have completed your acts of worship which you were commanded to perform in the Hajj. If you take it as the plural of *mansak*, which is the place of worship, then the sense is: "When you have completed the actions of your places of worship," and this would be an instance of omitting a word (the *mudaf*, or the governing noun).

Having understood this, we say: some commentators have said that the meaning of *al-manasik* here is what Allah commanded people to do in the Hajj of acts of worship. It is reported from Mujahid that the completion of the rites is the shedding of blood (sacrifice).

**The Fourth Issue:** The *fa'* in His words ﴿then remember Allah﴾ indicates that completion of the rites necessitates this remembrance. Therefore they differed about what kind of remembrance this is. Some interpreted it as remembrance by the sacrifice (the slaughter of the animal). Others interpreted it as the remembrance which is the takbirat (repeated proclamations of "Allahu akbar") after the prayer on the day of sacrifice and the days of Tashriq, according to their disagreement on its beginning and end, because after completing the Hajj there is no specific remembrance except these takbirat. Others said: rather, what is meant is turning the people away from what they had become accustomed to after the Hajj, namely the remembrance that boasts of the deeds of their fathers. For if He had not forbidden that by revealing this verse, they would not have deviated from this blameworthy practice. It is as if He said: "When you have completed and finished the obligations of the Hajj and have exited the state of ihram, then devote yourselves to the remembrance of Allah rather than the remembrance of your fathers." Others said: rather, what is meant is that completion of the Hajj necessitates turning to supplication and seeking forgiveness, because whoever has borne separation from family and homeland, spent wealth, and undertaken hardships on the journey of Hajj, is deserving, after finishing it, to turn to supplication, humble entreaty, abundant seeking of forgiveness, and devotion to Allah, the Exalted. On this basis, the practice has continued after the prayer with many supplications.

There is also a fifth aspect: the purpose of engaging in this worship is the subjugation of the self and the erasing of the traces of the ego and the natural disposition. This resolve is not sought for its own sake; rather, what is intended by it is that the false imprints be removed from the tablet of the spirit, so that the light of Allah's majesty may be manifested in it. The sense is: "When you have completed your rites and removed the traces of humanity, and cleared the obstacles from the path of spiritual journeying, then busy yourselves after that with illuminating the heart through the remembrance of Allah." The first is negation, and the second is affirmation; the first is the removal of whatever is other than the Truth from the ways of traces, and the second is the illumination of the heart through the remembrance of the Sovereign, the Almighty.

* * *
[Page 158]

As for His words ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾, there are several views:

*First*, and this is the view of the majority of commentators: we have mentioned that after completing the Hajj the people would exaggerate in praising their fathers, recounting their merits and virtues. So Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿then remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾, meaning: "Devote yourselves to the remembrance of Allah as you were devoting yourselves to the remembrance of your fathers, and exert your utmost effort in praising Allah and describing His favours and blessings, just as you exerted your utmost effort in praising your fathers. For this is more fitting and closer to reason than praising the fathers. If the recounting of the fathers' glories is false, it leads to baseness in this world and punishment in the Hereafter; and if it is true, it leads to self-admiration, arrogance and excessive pride, and all of these are among the chief destroyers. Thus it is established that your occupation with the remembrance of Allah is better than your occupation with your fathers' glories. And if this is not superiority, then at least it is equality."

*Second*: al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: "Remember Allah as you remember your fathers and your mothers," and mention of the fathers is sufficient in place of the mothers, as in His words: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81] (where the cold is omitted). They said: this is the speech of the child when he first begins to speak clearly: "Abbah, abbah" and "Ammah, ammah" (i.e., "Father, father" and "Mother, mother"). That is, be constant in the remembrance of Allah just as a child in his youth is constant in remembering his father and mother.

*Third*: Abu Muslim said: the mention of the fathers came as an example of constancy in remembrance. The meaning is that just as a man does not forget the remembrance of his father, so likewise he must not neglect the remembrance of Allah.

*Fourth*: Ibn al-Anbari said regarding this verse: the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah most often swore by their fathers, as in their saying: "By my father," "By your father," "By my grandfather," "By your grandfather." So He, the Exalted, said: "Glorify Allah as you glorify your fathers."

*Fifth*: Some of those mentioned said: the meaning is: "Remember Allah with His oneness, as you remember your fathers with their oneness." For if one of them were attributed to his parents, he would be offended and disdain it; and then he would set up gods for himself. So it was said to them: "Remember Allah with His oneness as you remember your fathers with their oneness." Rather, the emphasis on monotheism here is more fitting than there. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾.

*Sixth*: a child returns to his father for all his important needs and remembers him with reverence; so you too should be like that in the remembrance of Allah.

*Seventh*: It is possible that they used to mention their fathers in order to seek intercession through their remembrance for the answering of supplication with Allah. So Allah, the Exalted, informed them that their fathers were not in that rank, since their good deeds had become of no account because of their polytheism. They were commanded instead to enumerate Allah's blessings and favours and to increase praise of Him, so that this would be a means to the continual succession of blessings in the future. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade them from swearing by their fathers, saying: "Whoever is going to swear, let him swear by Allah or remain silent." If whatever is other than Allah is only for Allah and by Allah, then the more fitting course is to glorify Allah, the Exalted, and there is no god but Him.

*Eighth*: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding the interpretation of this verse: it means that you become angrier for Allah when He is disobeyed than your anger for your father when he is mentioned with evil.

Know that although these aspects are all possible, the first aspect is the one that is definite. All the aspects share one thing: it is obligatory upon the servant to be constantly mindful of his Lord, constantly glorifying Him, constantly returning to Him for the seeking of his needs, and constantly detached from all others. O Allah, make us people of this description, O Most Generous of the generous.

* * *
As for His words ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾, there are two issues:

**The First Issue:** The grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of ﴿أشد﴾ (*ashadda*, "greater"): it has been said that its governing element is the *kaf* (the particle "like" in *kadhikrikum*), so its position is in the genitive. It has also been said that its governing element is *udhkuru* ("remember"), so its position is in the accusative. The sense would be: "Remember Allah in the like of your remembrance of your fathers, and remember Him *ashadda dhikran* (with greater remembrance) than your fathers."

**The Second Issue:** His words ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾ mean: "rather, with greater remembrance." This is because the glories of their fathers were few, whereas the attributes of perfection of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are without limit. Therefore their occupation with the remembrance of the attributes of perfection of Allah, the Exalted, must be greater than their occupation with the glories of their fathers. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the figurative usage of the language in such a case is well known. A man says to another: "Do this by a month or sooner than that," and he does not mean to create doubt; he means only to shift from the first to something closer to it.

* *
Allah's words: ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter. And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in account.﴾ There are issues in this verse:

**The First Issue:** Know that Allah first explained the details of the rites of Hajj, then after them commanded remembrance, saying: ﴿So when you depart from 'Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and remember Him as He has guided you﴾. Then He explained that it is better to leave aside the remembrance of others and to restrict oneself to the remembrance of Him, saying: ﴿So remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾. Then after this remembrance He explained the manner of supplication, saying: ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾. How excellent is this order! For it is necessary to first precede with worship to break the self and remove its darkness; then after worship it is necessary to occupy oneself with the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, to illuminate the heart and manifest the light of His majesty; then after that remembrance a man busies himself with supplication, for supplication is only perfected when it is preceded by remembrance. Thus it is related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he began with remembrance, saying: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 78], then said: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 83]. So he put remembrance before supplication.

[Page 159 continued]

When you have understood this, we say: Allah, exalted is He, has made clear that those who call upon Allah are of two groups. One of them is those whose supplication is confined to seeking this world. The second is those who combine in their supplication the seeking of this world and the seeking of the Hereafter. The division also contained a third category, which is one whose supplication is confined to seeking the Hereafter. The scholars differed as to whether this category is prescribed or not. Most of them held that it is not prescribed. This is because man was created needy and weak, with no capacity for the pains of this world nor for the hardships of the Hereafter. Therefore, it is better for him to seek refuge with his Lord from all the evils of this world and the Hereafter. Al-Qaffal (d. c. 417 AH), in his *Tafsir*, related from Anas that the Prophet (peace be upon him) "entered upon a man who was visiting him, and the illness had worn him out. He said: What were you supplicating to Allah with before this? He said: I used to say, 'O Allah, whatever punishment You would inflict upon me in the Hereafter, hasten it for me in this world.' The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Glory be to Allah! Indeed you cannot bear that. Why did you not say: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾?' He said: So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) supplicated for him, and he was cured."

Know that if He, glorified is He, were to inflict pain upon a single vein in the body, or upon the root of a single hair, it would disturb the matter
[Page 160]
for the human being, and because of it he would be deprived of obedience to Allah, exalted is He, and of occupying himself with His remembrance. So who is it that is independent of the outpouring of Allah's mercy in his first life and his final end? Thus it is established that restricting supplication to seeking the Hereafter alone is impermissible. In the verse there is an indication to this, in that He mentioned the two categories and omitted this third category.

* * *

The second issue: The scholars differed concerning those whom Allah reported as confining their supplication to seeking this world, who they are. Some said: They are the disbelievers. It was related from Ibn Abbas that the polytheists used to say when they stood in prayer: "O Allah, provide us with camels, cattle, sheep, male slaves and female slaves," and they did not seek repentance or forgiveness, because they denied resurrection and the return. And from Anas: They used to say, "Give us rain and grant us victory over our enemy." So Allah informed that whoever is of this group, "there is no share (khalaq) for him in the Hereafter," meaning there is no portion for him in it of honour, bliss, or reward. It is related from Shaykh Abu 'Ali al-Daqqaq, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: The people of the Fire will cry for help, then they will say, "Pour upon us water, or some of what Allah has provided you in this world," seeking food and drink. When their desires overcame them, they were disgraced in this world and the Hereafter. Others said: These may be believers, but they ask Allah for their worldly affairs, not for their otherworldly affairs. Their request is among the sins, since they asked Allah, in the greatest of standing places and the most noble of assemblies, for the debris of this world and its fleeting goods, turning away from asking for lasting bliss in the Hereafter. It may be said of one who does this that he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter, even if the doer is a Muslim. This is like what was related concerning the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, those who trade away the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price — those will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77]. It was said that it was revealed concerning one who took property by a perjurious oath. It was related from the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Indeed Allah supports this religion through people who have no share (in the Hereafter)." Then the meaning of that is in several aspects:

The first: he has no share in the Hereafter unless he repents.

The second: he has no share in the Hereafter unless Allah pardons him.

The third: he has no share in the Hereafter like the share of one who asked Allah for his Hereafter. Likewise, one who took property by a perjurious oath has no share like the share of one who abstained from that. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾. The object of "give us" (ātinā) has been omitted from the speech because it is understood. Know that the levels of felicity are three: spiritual, bodily, and external. As for the spiritual, they are two: perfecting the theoretical faculty through knowledge, and perfecting the practical faculty through virtuous character. As for the bodily, they are two: health and beauty. As for the external, they are two: wealth and standing. So His saying: ﴿give us in this world﴾ encompasses all these categories. For knowledge, if it is desired for adornment in this world and for elevating oneself above one's peers, it is of this world. Virtuous character, if it is desired for leadership in this world and for controlling its interests, is of this world. Everyone who does not believe in resurrection and the return seeks no virtue, neither spiritual nor physical, except for the sake of this world. Then Allah, exalted is He, said concerning this group: ﴿and he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾, meaning he has no portion in the bliss of the Hereafter. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him from it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20]. Then He, exalted is He, did not mention in this verse whether what he asked for in this world was granted to him or not. Some said: Such a person is not fit for being answered, because being one whose supplication is answered is a quality of praise, and it is not established except for one who is a friend (wali) of Allah, exalted is He, deserving of honour. However, it is not obligatory. As long as he is a living, accountable person, Allah, exalted is He, gives him his provision, as He said: ﴿There is no creature on earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud: 6]. Others said: Such a person may indeed be answered, but that answer may be a deception and a gradual drawing-on (istidraj).

* * *

[Page 161]

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them is one who says: Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, the exegetes have mentioned several aspects concerning it:

The first: that "good" in this world is an expression for health, security, sufficiency, a righteous child, a righteous wife, and victory over enemies. Allah, exalted is He, has called abundance and expansion in provision, and what resembles it, "good," as He said: ﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them﴾ [al-Tawba: 50]. And concerning His saying: ﴿Say: Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes?﴾ [al-Tawba: 52] it was said that the two are victory, triumph, and martyrdom. As for "good" in the Hereafter, it is success in reward and deliverance from punishment. In sum, His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter﴾ is a comprehensive word encompassing all the aims of this world and the Hereafter. Hammad ibn Salama related from Thabit that they said to Anas: "Pray for us." He said: "O Allah, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." They said: "Add more for us." So he repeated it. They said: "Add more for us." He said: "What do you want? I have asked for you the good of this world and the Hereafter." Anas spoke truly, for a servant has no abode other than this world and the Hereafter. When he asks for the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter, nothing remains beyond it.

The second: that what is meant by "good" in this world is useful action, which is faith and obedience, and "good" in the Hereafter is lasting delight, honour, and enjoyment in the remembrance of Allah, in intimacy with Him, in His love, and in beholding Him. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn Abbas that "a man supplicated to his Lord and said in his supplication: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'I do not know that this man asked Allah for anything of the affairs of this world.' Some of the Companions said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, he said: "Our Lord, give us good in this world."' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'He is saying: give us in this world righteous action.'" This is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who say: Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and our offspring the coolness of the eyes﴾ [al-Furqan: 74]. That coolness is for them to see their children and spouses obedient, faithful, and constant in servitude.

The third: Qatada said: "Good" in this world and in the Hereafter is seeking well-being in both abodes. And from al-Hasan: "Good" in this world is understanding the Book of Allah, exalted is He, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. And know that the origin of the discussion in the verse is that if it were said, "Give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter," that would encompass all goods. But He said: ﴿in this world good, and in the Hereafter good﴾, and this is an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, so it does not encompass more than one good. Therefore the earlier exegetes differed, and each of them interpreted the expression according to what he saw as the best kind of good.

If it is said: Is it not the case that if it were said, "Give us the good in this world and the good in the Hereafter," that would encompass all the categories? Why was that omitted and it was mentioned in the indefinite form?

I say: What I think on this point, and knowledge is with Allah, is that we have already explained earlier that it is not proper for the supplicant to say, "O Allah, give me such and such," but rather he must say, "O Allah, if such and such is a benefit for me and is in accord with Your decree and destiny, then give me that." So if he said, "O Allah, give me the good in this world and the Hereafter," that would be an absolute assertion, and we have already explained that this is impermissible. But since it is mentioned in the indefinite form, when he says, "Give me good in this world," what is meant is one good, namely the good that accords with His decree, destiny, pleasure, judgment, and wisdom. That is closer to observing courtesy and preserving the foundations of certainty.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those﴾. There are two opinions concerning it:

One of them: It refers only to the second group, those who
[Page 162]
asked for this world and the Hereafter. The evidence for this is that He mentioned the ruling of the first group when He said: ﴿and he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾.

The second opinion: That it refers to both groups, meaning that each of these has a share of his work according to what he intended. Whoever denies resurrection and performs pilgrimage seeking the reward of this world, that is disbelief and polytheism from him, and Allah will repay him. Or what is meant is that whoever works for this world is given a share like it in his worldly life, as He said: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him from it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20].

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for them there is a share of what they have earned﴾, there are questions concerning it:

The first question: His saying, ﴿for them there is a share of what they have earned﴾, runs in the manner of belittling and diminishing, so what is meant by it?

The answer: What is meant is: for them there is a share of this world and of the Hereafter by means of their earning and their action. So the word "min" (of) in His saying ﴿of what they have earned﴾ is for the beginning of the extent, not for partition.

The second question: Does this verse indicate that the recompense is for the deed?

The answer: Yes, but according to the promise, not according to inherent entitlement.

The third question: What is kasb (acquisition, earning)?

The answer: Kasb is applied to what a person attains by his action, so it is his earning and what he has acquired, on condition that this brings a benefit or repels a harm. On this basis it is said of profits that they are the earnings of so-and-so, and that he has much earnings or little earnings, because only gain is intended. As for what our companions say, that kasb is an intermediate position between determinism (jabr) and creation (khalq), it is mentioned in the earlier books on theology.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, there are issues concerning it.

The first issue: sarī' (swift) is an active participle from speed. Ibn al-Sikkit said: sariʿa yasraʿu sarʿan and surʿatan, so he is sarīʿ. "Al-ḥisāb" (reckoning) is a verbal noun like "al-muḥāsaba." The meaning of ḥisāb in the lexicon is counting. It is said: ḥasiba yaḥsubu ḥisāban, ḥisbatan and ḥasaban, when he counted. Al-Layth and Ibn al-Sikkit mentioned it. Al-ḥasb is what is counted, and from it comes ḥasab (lineage) of a man, which is what is counted of his distinguished deeds and glories. Al-iḥtisāb is taking account of a thing. Al-Zajjaj said: ḥisāb in the lexicon is derived from their saying, "ḥasbuka kadhā," meaning, "what is sufficient for you is such-and-such." So the reckoning in transactions was called ḥisāb, because by it one knows what is sufficient, with neither excess nor deficiency in the measure.

**The second issue:** People have differed over the meaning of God, may He be exalted, being the one who calls His creation to account (*muhasib*), and there are several views:

First: The meaning of *hisab* (reckoning) is that God informs them of what is for them and what is against them. That is, God creates in their hearts *darury* (necessary, self-evident) knowledge in proportion to their deeds, their quantity and their qualities, and in proportion to what they receive of reward and punishment. They said: the basis of this *majaz* (figurative usage) is that reckoning is a cause of a person's knowing what is for him and against him, so applying the name of reckoning to this informing is applying the name of the cause to the effect, and this is a well-known *majaz*. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "There is no reckoning for the creation. Rather, they stand before God, may He be exalted, and are given their books in their right hands. In them are their evil deeds, and it is said to them: 'These are your evil deeds, and I have overlooked them.' Then they are given their good deeds, and it is said: 'These are your good deeds, and I have multiplied them for you.'"

[Page 163]

The second view: *muhasabah* (reckoning) is an expression for requital. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And how many a city that defied the command of its Lord and His messengers—We reckoned with it with a severe reckoning﴾ [al-Talaq, 65:8]. The basis of the *majaz* here is that reckoning is a cause of taking and giving, and applying the name of the cause to the effect is permissible, so the word "reckoning" is rightly applied to requital.

The third view: God speaks to His servants about the states of their deeds and the manner of the reward and punishment that belong to them. Whoever says that His speech is neither a letter nor a sound says that God creates in the ear of the one under obligation (*mukallaf*) a hearing by which he hears His eternal speech, just as He creates in his eye a sight by which he sees His eternal essence. Whoever says that it is a sound says that God creates a speech that every *mukallaf* hears, either by creating that speech in the ear of each one of them, or in a body near his ear, such that the force of that sound does not prevent others from understanding what they are obligated to. This is the meaning of God being the one who reckons with His creation.

**The third issue:** They have mentioned several meanings for God being *sari' al-hisab* (swift in reckoning):

First: His reckoning amounts either to His creating necessary knowledge in the heart of every *mukallaf* in proportion to his deeds and the measure of his reward and punishment; or to His delivering to every *mukallaf* what is his due of reward; or to His creating a hearing in the ear of every *mukallaf* by which he hears the eternal speech; or to His creating in the ear of every *mukallaf* a sound indicating the measures of reward and punishment and the four aspects mentioned. So the upshot of God being the reckoner returns to His creating something. Since God's power relates to all possible things, and His creating and bringing into being does not depend on the prior existence of a material, nor a duration, nor an instrument, and no affair distracts Him from another affair, He is therefore certainly able to create all of creation in less than the blink of an eye. This is a clear statement. For this reason it is reported in a *khabar* (report) that God reckons with creation in the time it takes to milk a she-camel.

Second: The meaning of His being *sari' al-hisab* is that He is swift to accept the supplications of His servants and to respond to them. This is because at one and the same time, each of the petitioners asks Him for different things concerning the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, and He gives each one what he seeks without anything becoming confused for Him. If it were a matter with one of the creatures, the counting would be long and the reckoning would be prolonged. So God informs that He is *sari' al-hisab*, that is, He knows all the requests of those who ask, because God does not need to count on fingers nor to think and deliberate. This is the meaning of the transmitted supplication: "O You whom one affair does not distract from another." The upshot of this view is that the meaning of God being swift in reckoning is that He knows all the states and deeds of creation. The basis of the *majaz* here is that one who is reckoned is only reckoned so that he may gain knowledge of that matter; so reckoning is a cause of gaining knowledge, and the name of the cause is applied to the effect.

Third: God's reckoning is swift in the sense that it is coming without doubt.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 203 (part 1 of 2):

God the Exalted says: ﴿And remember God during the counted days. Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, for him who fears God. And fear God, and know that you will be gathered to Him.﴾

Know that when He mentioned what relates to the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), He did not mention the stoning (al-Ramy) for two reasons:

The first: that this was a well-known matter among them, and they did not deny it. However, God mentioned the remembrance of God that is in it, because they were not performing that.

The second: perhaps He did not mention the stoning because the command to remember God during these days is an indication of it, since it was part of its practice to say "Allahu Akbar" with every pebble
[Page 164]
from it. Then He said: ﴿And remember God during the counted days.﴾ On this there are several issues.

**First issue:** God the Exalted mentioned in the rites of the Hajj "the counted days" and "the known days." Here He said: ﴿And remember God during the counted days,﴾ and in Surat al-Hajj He said: ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of God during known days﴾ [al-Hajj: 28]. The position of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, is that "the known days" are the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, the last of which is the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). As for "the counted days," they are three days after the Day of Sacrifice, which are the Days of Tashriq (Ayyam al-Tashriq, the days of drying meat). He argued that the counted days are the Days of Tashriq by saying that God mentioned "the counted days," and "days" is a plural noun, so its least number is three. Then He said after it: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him,﴾ and this requires that what is meant by ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ is from these counted days. The community has agreed that this ruling applies only in the days of Mina, which are the Days of Tashriq. So we know that the counted days are the Days of Tashriq. Al-Qaffal confirmed this by what he narrated in his *Tafsir* from Abd al-Rahman ibn Nu'man al-Daylami, that the Messenger of God ﷺ commanded a herald, and he called out: "The Hajj is Arafah. Whoever comes on the night of Jam' before the rising of dawn has attained the Hajj. The days of Mina are three days; whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him." This indicates that the counted days are the Days of Tashriq. Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The Days of Tashriq are three days after the Day of Sacrifice. The first of them is the Day of Departure (Yawm al-Nafr), which is the eleventh day of Dhu al-Hijjah, when people depart from Mina. The second is the first Day of Departure, because some people depart from Mina on this day. The third is the second Day of Departure. These three days together with the Day of Sacrifice are all the Days of Sacrifice (Ayyam al-Nahr). The days of stoning the pillars (Jamarat) during these four days, together with the Day of Arafah, are the days of takbir after the prayers, according to the positions of the people on it which we will explain.

* * *

**Second issue:** The remembrance meant during these days is the remembrance at the Jamarat, where one says takbir with every pebble, and the remembrance after the prayers. The people have agreed on this, but they differed on several points.

**The first point:** The community has agreed that the takbirs tied to the end of the prayers (adbar al-salawat) are specific to the Festival of Sacrifice (Eid al-Adha). Then there is disagreement about when they begin and end.

The first view: They begin from the noon prayer (Zuhr) on the Day of Sacrifice until after the dawn prayer on the last of the Days of Tashriq. On this view, the takbirs are said after fifteen prayers. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, and Malik and al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with them both, in one of his opinions. The evidence for it is that the command to these takbirs came specifically concerning the pilgrim. God said: ﴿Then remember God as you remember your fathers﴾, then He said: ﴿And remember God during the counted days. Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him,﴾ and this applies only to the pilgrim. So it indicates that the command to these takbirs came concerning the pilgrim, and the rest of the people follow them in that. Moreover, the noon prayer is the first prayer in which the pilgrim says takbir at Mina, since they recite the talbiyah before that, and the last prayer they pray at Mina is the dawn prayer on the last of the Days of Tashriq. Therefore, these takbirs for non-pilgrims must be limited to this period.

The second view: For al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, it begins with the sunset prayer (Maghrib) on the night of the Day of Sacrifice, until the dawn prayer on the last of the Days of Tashriq. On this view, the takbirs are said after eighteen prayers.

The third view of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him: It begins with the dawn prayer on the Day of Arafah and ends after the afternoon prayer (Asr) on the Day of Sacrifice. The takbirs are then said after eight prayers. This is the view of Alqamah, al-Aswad, al-Nakha'i and Abu Hanifah.

The fourth view: It begins with the dawn prayer on the Day of Arafah and ends after the afternoon prayer on the last of the Days of Tashriq, so the takbirs are said after twenty-three prayers. This is the view of the senior Companions, such as Ali, Umar, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. Among the jurists, it is the view of al-Thawri, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Muzani and Ibn Shurayh, and the practice of the people in the cities is according to it. The following points indicate it:

The first: what Jabir narrated, that "the Prophet ﷺ prayed the dawn prayer on the Day of Arafah, then he turned to us and said: 'God is greatest,' and he extended the takbir until the afternoon prayer on the last of the Days of Tashriq."

The second: What Abu Hanifah said takes the lesser, while this view takes the greater, and increasing the takbir is better, because of His saying: ﴿Remember God with much remembrance﴾ [al-Ahzab: 41].

The third: This is the more cautious, because if one adds to the takbirs, that is better than reducing them.

The fourth: These takbirs are attributed to the Days of Tashriq, so they must be performed until the end of the Days of Tashriq.

If it is said: These takbirs are attached to the counted days, which are the Days of Tashriq, so they must not be prescribed on the Day of Arafah.

We say: That would require that one not say takbir on the Day of Sacrifice, and that is invalid by consensus. Also, since most of this period consists of the Days of Tashriq, it is correct to attribute the takbir to them.

**The second point:** Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: It is recommended that the takbirs be three times in succession, meaning consecutively. This is also the view of Malik. Abu Hanifah and Ahmad said: One says takbir twice. The evidence of al-Shafi'i is what Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr ibn Amr ibn Hazm narrated, who said: "I saw the leaders saying takbir during the Days of Tashriq after the prayer three times." Also, it is an increase in takbir, so it is better, because of God's saying: ﴿Remember God with much remembrance.﴾ Then al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: After the three, one says: "There is no god but God, God is greatest, and to God belongs praise." Then he said: Whatever is added of the remembrance of God is good. He said regarding the talbiyah: I like not to exceed the talbiyah of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The difference is that the talbiyah is by nature repeated, so repeating it is better than adding something to it, whereas here one says takbir once, so adding something is better than silence. As for the takbir at the Jamarat, it has been narrated that "the Prophet, peace be upon him, used to say takbir with every pebble," so it is appropriate that this be done.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, for him who fears God﴾, there are several questions:

**First question:** Why did He say "fa-man ta'ajjala" (whoever hastens) and not "fa-man ajjala"?

Answer: The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *ta'ajjala* and *is'tajjala* come as intransitive forms (mutawi'ayn) of *ajjala*, meaning "to hurry." One says *ta'ajjala fi al-amr* and *is'tajjala*. They also come as transitive verbs, one says *ta'ajjala al-dhahab* and *is'tajjala-hu*.

**Second question:** His saying: ﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ presents a difficulty. For if he has completed everything that is required of him for the completion of the Hajj, what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾? This expression is used only regarding one who fell short, and is not used regarding one who has completed the act.

The answer has several aspects:

First: When God permitted hastening as a concession (rukhsah), it was possible that some people might think that whoever does not act according to the requirement of this concession is sinful. Do you not see that Abu Hanifah, may God be pleased with him, says: shortening the prayer (qasr) is obligatory, and completing it is not permissible? Since this possibility existed, God the Exalted removed this doubt and made clear that there is no sin in either of the two matters. If one wishes to hasten and act according to the requirement of the concession, he may do so, and if one wishes not to hasten and not to act according to the requirement of the concession, there is no sin upon him in either matter together.

Second: Some exegetes said: Among them were those who hastened and those who delayed, and each of the two groups criticized the action of the other. The one who delayed thought that hastening opposed the sunnah of the Hajj, and the one who hastened thought that delaying opposed the sunnah of the Hajj. So God the Exalted made clear that there is no fault or sin in either of the two categories. If one wishes to hasten, he may, and if one wishes not to hasten, he need not.

Third: The meaning of removing sin from the one who delays is only for one who stays beyond the three days. It is as if it was said: The days of Mina during which it is appropriate to remain are three. Whoever falls short of them by hastening on the second day, there is no sin upon him, and whoever stays beyond them by delaying past the third to the fourth and does not depart with the general people, there is nothing upon him.

Fourth: This statement was mentioned as an exaggeration in explaining that the Hajj is a cause for the removal of sins and the expiation of wrongdoings. This is like when a person takes theriac (tiryaq, an antidote). The physician says to him: Now, if you take poison, there is no harm, and if you do not take it, there is no harm. His purpose by this is to explain that theriac is a complete remedy for averting harms, not to explain that taking poison and not taking it are the same. Likewise here, the purpose of this statement is to explain the extent to which the Hajj expiates all sins, not to explain that hastening and not hastening are equal. Among what indicates that the Hajj is a strong cause for the expiation of sins is his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever performs the Hajj without indecency or wickedness will return from his sins as on the day his mother bore him."

Fifth: Many scholars said: Residing near the Sacred Precinct (al-jiwar) is disliked, because if one stays near the Haram and the House, its awe diminishes in his eyes, and when he is away, his longing for it increases. If that is the case, it is possible that someone may think, on this basis, that whoever hastens in two days is in a better state than whoever does not hasten, since he has chosen to remain at Mina and has left off hastening in the circumambulation. For this reason, a doubt remains in the mind as to whether the one who hastens is better or the one who delays. So God the Exalted made clear that there is no sin and no fault in either of them.

Sixth: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: He only said ﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ so that the first expression would agree with the second, as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. We know that the recompense for an evil and for transgression is neither an evil nor a transgression. So if what does not hold true in meaning is brought into agreement with the wording, then it is more fitting that what holds true in meaning be brought into agreement with the wording, since for the one whose Hajj is accepted and rewarded, it is correct in meaning to negate sin from him.

**Third question:** Is there in the verse an indication of the obligation of residing at Mina after departing from Muzdalifah?

Answer: Yes, just as His saying: ﴿When you depart from Arafat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198] is an indication of their standing there.

**[Page 167]**

Know that the jurists said: the hastening (ta'ajjul) in the two days is permitted only for one who hastens before the sun sets on the second day. If the sun sets on the second day before he departs (nafr), then he may not depart except on the third day, because when the sun sets the day has gone, and the permission to hasten was granted for the two days only, not for the third. This is the position of al-Shafi'i and the view of many of the jurists of the Successors (al-Tabi'un). Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he may depart as long as dawn has not risen, because the time of the stoning (al-ramy) has not yet entered.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾, there are several aspects to it:

The first: the pilgrim returns forgiven on the condition that he fears Allah in the rest of his life and does not commit what would make him deserving of punishment. Its meaning is a warning against relying on the good deeds of the Hajj that have already passed. So Allah, exalted is He, made clear that, alongside that, they must persist in God-consciousness (taqwa) and avoid being deceived by the Hajj they performed before.

The second: this forgiveness is attained only by one who was God-conscious before his Hajj, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah only accepts from the God-conscious﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 27]. The reality of this is that one who persists in sin does not benefit from his Hajj, even if he has fulfilled the obligation outwardly.

The third: this forgiveness is attained only by one who was God-conscious, refraining from all prohibited things, while engaged in the Hajj, as is reported in the hadith of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ): "Whoever performs Hajj and does not engage in obscenity (rafath) or transgression (fusuq)..." Know that the first of these aspects that we have mentioned points to its being considered in the present, and the verification is that all of them are necessary.

Some of the exegetes said: what is meant by His saying ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾ is what he is obliged to guard against during the Hajj, such as killing game and other things, because if he does not avoid these he becomes sinful, and perhaps his deed becomes nullified. This view is weak for two reasons:

The first: it is a restriction of an unrestricted word without any evidence.

The second: this would be valid only if it were applied to the period before these days, because on the Day of Sacrifice, if he has stoned, circumambulated and shaved, he has already exited the state of ihram before stoning the pillars (al-jimar), so he is not obliged to avoid game except within the Sacred Precinct (al-haram). But that is not for the state of ihram. Yet the wording indicates that this avoidance is required during these days, so this aspect falls.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and fear Allah﴾, it is a command in the future tense, and it differs from His saying ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾, which is meant in the past tense, so it is not a repetition. You have learned that God-consciousness (taqwa) is an expression for performing the obligatory acts and abandoning the forbidden ones.

As for His saying: ﴿and know that you will be gathered to Him﴾, it is an emphasis on the command to God-consciousness and an incitement to be strict in it, because whoever imagines that there must be a gathering, a reckoning and an accounting, and that after death there is no abode except Paradise or Hellfire, this becomes among the strongest motives for him toward God-consciousness. As for the gathering (al-hashr), it is a term that applies from the beginning of their emergence from the graves until the end of the standing place, because their being there is not complete except with all these matters. The meaning of His saying ﴿to Him﴾ is that there is no owner besides Him, no refuge except Him, and no one can repel anything from himself, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day when no soul will have power over any soul in anything, and the command that Day belongs to Allah﴾ [al-Infitar: 19].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 204–206 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart, yet he is the most stubborn of opponents.﴾ ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock; but Allah does not love corruption.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him; so Hell is sufficient for him, and what an evil resting place.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, explained that those who witness the rites of the Hajj are of two groups: a disbeliever, who says, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾, and a believer, who says, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201], the hypocrite remained, so He mentioned him in this verse and described his attributes and actions. This is what relates to the arrangement of the verse. The purpose of all of this is to urge the servants toward the good way in matters concerning the actions of the hearts and limbs, and that they should know that the One worshipped cannot be kept ignorant of affairs. Then the exegetes differed into two opinions. Some of them said: this verse is specific to particular people. Others said: it is general in regard to everyone who is described by this attribute mentioned in this verse. As for the first group, they differed in several ways:

The first narration: it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, an ally of Banu Zuhrah, who came to the Prophet ﷺ and displayed Islam, and claimed that he loved him and swore by Allah to that effect. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾. However, he was a hypocrite, pleasant in outward appearance and wicked within.
