Then he left from the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, passed by a field of crops belonging to some Muslims, burned the crops and killed the donkeys. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock﴾. Others said: what is meant by His saying: ﴿whose speech pleases you﴾ is that al-Akhnas advised Banu Zuhrah on the day of Badr to return, and said to them: "Muhammad is the son of your sister; if he is a liar, all the people will suffice you against him, and if he is truthful, you will be the happiest of people with him." They said: "What an excellent opinion you have expressed." He said: "When the people are called to depart, I will withdraw with you, so follow me." Then he withdrew with three hundred men of Banu Zuhrah from fighting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He was therefore named al-Akhnas for this reason, and his name was Ubayy ibn Shariq. This reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and pleased him. In my view, however, this statement is weak, because by this action he does not deserve blame, whereas His saying: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾ is mentioned in the context of censure, so it cannot be applied to it. Rather, the first opinion is the most correct.

The second narration: concerning the cause of revelation of this verse, what is reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak: that the disbelievers of Quraysh sent to the Prophet ﷺ saying, "We have accepted Islam, so send us some scholars from your companions." He sent to them a group, and they alighted at Batn al-Raji'. The news reached the disbelievers, so seventy riders of them set out, surrounded them, killed them and crucified them. It was concerning them that this verse was revealed. For this reason, He follows it afterward with mention of the one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, thereby drawing attention to the state of these martyrs.

The second opinion concerning the verse, which is the choice of most of the careful exegetes, is that this verse is general regarding everyone who is described by these mentioned attributes. It is reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that a discussion took place between him and another concerning this verse, and he said: "Although it was revealed concerning the one mentioned, it is not impossible that the verse was revealed about a man and yet is general regarding everyone who is described by those attributes." The verification of the matter is that His saying: ﴿And among the people﴾ indicates some of them; it may refer to one or to many. His saying: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness﴾ does not indicate that the intended one is a single person among the people, since it is possible that this refers to the wording rather than the meaning, which is plural. As for its being revealed concerning the cause we have described, this does not prevent generality. Rather, we say: there is in it that which indicates generality, from several aspects:

First: that the ruling being attached to a fitting attribute indicates causation. When Allah censured a people and described them with attributes that necessitate deserving censure, we know that what necessitates that blame is those attributes, and so it follows that everyone described by those attributes deserves blame.

Second: that applying the verse to generality is more beneficial, because it serves as a deterrent for all the responsible persons from that blameworthy path.

Third: that this is closer to caution, for if we take the verse in its generality, that person is included in it; whereas if we restrict it to that person alone, the ruling would not be established for others. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that applying the verse to generality is preferable. Having understood this, we say: they differed as to whether the verse indicates that the one described by these attributes is a hypocrite or not. The correct view is that it does not indicate that, because Allah the Exalted described this mentioned person with five attributes, none of which indicates hypocrisy. The first of them is His saying: ﴿whose speech about the life of this world pleases you﴾, and this has no indication of a blameworthy attribute except by way of the implication conveyed by His saying: ﴿about the life of this world﴾, because when it is said of a person that his speech is sweet concerning worldly matters, it suggests a kind of blame.

Second: His saying: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾. This has no indication of a reprehensible state, for if we assume in it a hidden meaning, that he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart while his heart is otherwise, then the statement with this hidden meaning does not indicate hypocrisy, because the verse does not say that what he shows the Messenger of the matters of Islam and monotheism is what he conceals contrary to it, so that he must be a hypocrite. Rather, perhaps the meaning is that he conceals corruption and displays its opposite, so that he is a show-off.

Third: His saying: ﴿yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾. This also does not necessitate hypocrisy.

Fourth: His saying: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein﴾. A Muslim who is a corrupter may also be like that.

Fifth: His saying: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him﴾. This too does not necessitate hypocrisy. Thus we know that all these attributes mentioned in the verse, just as they may be found in a hypocrite, may be found in a show-off. Therefore there is no indication in the verse that this mentioned person must be a hypocrite, except that the hypocrite is included in the verse, because every hypocrite is described by these five attributes, though one who is described by these five attributes may not be a hypocrite. It is established that whenever we apply the verse to the one described by these five attributes, the hypocrite and the show-off are included in it. Having understood this summary, we say: Allah the Exalted described this mentioned person with five attributes:

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿whose speech about the life of this world pleases you﴾. The meaning: it pleases you and becomes great in your heart; from it comes the word "ajib" (wonderful), which is something that greatly impresses the soul.

As for His saying: ﴿about the life of this world﴾, there are several aspects:

One: it is like the saying of one who says: "I am impressed by so-and-so's speech on this matter," meaning: his speech and talk pleases you when he speaks seeking the benefits of this world.

The second: the intended meaning may be: his speech and talk about the life of this world pleases you, even if his speech about the Hereafter does not please you, because as long as he is in this world he is bold of tongue and sweet of speech; but in the Hereafter he is seized by inarticulateness and stammering out of fear of Allah's awe and the subjugation of His majesty.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾. The meaning: he affirms the truthfulness of his speech and claim by calling Allah to witness. This witnessing may be by oath and swearing, or it may be by saying: "Allah bears witness that the matter is as I have said," and this is calling Allah as witness without being an oath. The majority of readers read ﴿wayushhidu Allah﴾ with a dammah on the ya', meaning: this speaker calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his inner self. Ibn Muhaysin read "yashhadu Allahu 'ala ma fi qalbihi" with a fathah on the ya', and the meaning is: Allah knows the one whose heart is contrary to what he displays.

The first reading indicates that he is a show-off and that he calls Allah to witness falsely about his hypocrisy and his display. As for the second reading, it indicates only that he is a liar; as for his calling Allah as witness deliberately in falsehood, it does not indicate that. Therefore, the first reading is more indicative of blame.

The third attribute: His saying the Exalted: ﴿yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

First issue: "al-Alladd" means the one who is most intense in dispute. It is said: a man "alladd," and people "ludd," and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and you may warn thereby a people most stubborn﴾ [Maryam: 97]. It is like His saying: ﴿Rather they are a contentious people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58]. It is said of it: "ladda yaladdu," with a fathah on the lam in its imperfect; so he is "alladd" when he is contentious. And "laddadtu al-rajul" with a dammah on the lam, "aluddu," when you overcome him by dispute. Al-Zajjaj said: its derivation is from "ladidatay al-unuq," which are its two sides, and "ladidayay al-wadi," which are its two banks; and its interpretation is that whichever direction his opponent takes from right and left in the gates of dispute, he overcomes the one who disputes with him.

As for "al-khisam," there are two opinions. One of them, which is the opinion of al-Khalil, is that it is a verbal noun meaning "mukhasamah" (disputing), like "qital" and "tia'n" meaning "muqatalah" and "mutaana"; so the meaning is: he is most intense in disputing. Then in this idafah there are two aspects: one is that it means "fi" (in), so the sense is: most stubborn in disputing. The second is that he made the disputing itself the most stubborn, by way of emphasis.

The second opinion is that "al-khisam" is the plural of "khasm," like "si'ab" and "sa'b," and "dikhamun" and "dakhm," and the meaning is: he is the most intense of opponents in disputing. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. The exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, as we have explained. Concerning him was also revealed His saying: ﴿Woe to every backbiter and slanderer﴾ [al-Humazah: 1], and His saying: ﴿And do not obey every vile swearer, backbiter, going about with slander﴾ [al-Qalam: 10–11]. Then the exegetes have various expressions in interpreting this word. Mujahid said: "alladd al-khisam" means: one who seeks what is not straight. Al-Suddi said: crooked in dispute. Qatadah said: "alladd al-khisam" means that he is contentious with falsehood, intensely hard in disobedience to Allah, learned in tongue and ignorant in action.

* * *

Second issue: Those who deny speculation and disputation have held to this verse. They said: Allah censured that person for being intense in dispute, and if this attribute were not one of the attributes of blame, it would not be permissible. Its answer is what has preceded in His saying: ﴿nor is there any disputing in the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197].

The fourth attribute: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock; and Allah does not love corruption.﴾ Know that when He, the Exalted, explained concerning that person that he is sweet of speech, that he affirms the truthfulness of his words by calling Allah to witness, and that he is the most stubborn of opponents, He then explained that all that he mentions by tongue, his heart conceals its opposite. So He said: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein.﴾ Then in the verse there are issues:

First issue: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when he turns away﴾, concerning which there are two opinions:

One of them: its meaning is: "And when he departs from you, he strives in the land with corruption." Then this corruption may have two aspects:

One of them: what is the destruction of wealth

[p. 170 continues from the previous part]

...by destruction, burning, and plunder. On this interpretation they have transmitted reports, among them what we have already mentioned: that al-Akhnas, when he showed the Messenger (ﷺ) that he loved him and was resolved to become a believer, then, once he left his presence, passed by a field of crops belonging to the Muslims, burned the crops, and slaughtered the donkeys. Another report says that when he returned from Badr, he passed by Banu Zuhra, between whom and Thaqif there was enmity. He attacked them by night, destroyed their livestock, and burned their crops.

The second interpretation of *fasad* (corruption) is that after leaving the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), he would busy himself with planting doubts in the hearts of the Muslims and devising stratagems to strengthen disbelief. This meaning is called *fasad*. God, the Exalted, said, relating the words of Pharaoh's people when they said to him: ﴿Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land?﴾ [al-A'raf 7:127], meaning: to turn your people away from their religion and to corrupt their law for them. He also said: ﴿I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾ [Ghafir 40:26]. We have already mentioned, in the commentary on His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption in the land"﴾ [al-Baqara 2:11], something close to this meaning. This meaning is called corruption in the land because it produces discord among people, divides their word, and leads some of them to disavow others, so that kinship ties are severed and blood is shed. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So would you, if you were to turn away, do corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Muhammad 47:22]. Thus He informed that if they turned away from His religion, they would achieve nothing but corruption in the land and the severing of kinship ties, and this is in the sense we have described, which is frequent in the Qur'an.

Know that interpreting *fasad* in this way is preferable to interpreting it as destruction and plunder, because God said: ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾, and the conjoined term is necessarily different from the term it is conjoined to.

The second view concerns the interpretation of His words: ﴿And when he turns away﴾, meaning: when he becomes a ruler, he does what the wicked rulers do of corruption in the land by destroying crops and offspring. It has also been said: he displays injustice to the extent that God, because of the wickedness of his oppression, withholds rain, so that crops and offspring perish. The first view is closer to the structure of the verse, because the aim is to explain his hypocrisy: in his presence he speaks fine words and displays love, but in his absence he strives to stir up strife and corruption.

The second issue: His words ﴿He strives in the land﴾ mean: he exerted himself in provoking fighting. The root meaning of *sa'y* (striving) is walking swiftly, but it is used figuratively for stirring up strife and sowing destruction among people. From this one says: "So-and-so strives with tale-bearing (*namima*)." God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have added nothing to you but confusion, and they would have hurried about among you seeking to stir up sedition for you﴾ [al-Tawba 9:47].

The third issue: whoever interprets *fasad* as destruction says that God mentioned it first in general terms, which is His words: ﴿to cause corruption therein﴾, and then mentioned it again in detail, saying: ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾. Whoever interprets corruption as casting doubt says: just as true religion has two components, first knowledge and second action, so false religion has two components, first doubts and second the commission of wrongs. Here God mentioned first from this man his occupation with doubts, which is what is meant by His words: ﴿to cause corruption therein﴾, and then mentioned his undertaking of wrongs, which is what is meant by His words: ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾. There is no doubt that this interpretation is preferable.

Then whoever says that the occasion of revelation of the verse was that al-Akhnas passed by a field of crops belonging to the Muslims, burned the crops and slaughtered the donkeys, says: the *harth* (crops) means the produce, and the *nasl* (offspring) means those donkeys. *Harth* is that from which crops come. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow?﴾ [al-Waqi'a 56:63–64]. It applies to every kind of plant that is ploughed and sown. It has also been said that *harth* is the tilling of the earth, and that the instrument used for it is called *mihrath*. As for *nasl* on this interpretation, it is the offspring of animals. *Nasl* in the language means offspring. Its derivation may be from the saying *nasala yansilu*, when something comes out and falls: thus one says of the feathers of a bird, the wool of a camel, or the hair of a donkey, that it *nasala* when it comes out and falls, and a piece that falls off is called *nusala*. From this is His words: ﴿They will hasten to their Lord﴾ [Ya Sin 36:51], meaning: they will hurry, because he rushes out with vigour. *Nasl* means offspring because it comes out from the father's back and the mother's womb and falls. Mankind is the offspring of Adam. The root of the word is from *nusul*, which means coming out.

As for whoever says that the occasion of revelation is that al-Akhnas attacked the people of Thaqif by night and killed a number of them, then *harth* means either the women, in accordance with His words: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqara 2:223], or the men, which is the view of some exegetes who interpreted *harth* as tilling the earth, since men are those who till the soil of procreation. As for *nasl*, it means the children.

Know that on all these interpretations, the intent is to show that this corruption is a great corruption, and there is no greater. For on the first interpretation, what is meant is the destruction of plants and animals, and on the second interpretation, the destruction of animals in their origin and offspring. On both views, there is no greater corruption than this. Therefore His words ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾ are extremely eloquent expressions which, despite their brevity, convey great emphasis. A parallel in brevity is what He said in describing Paradise: ﴿therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:71], and He said: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:31].

[p. 171]

If it is asked: does the verse indicate that he destroys the crops and the offspring, or does it indicate that he intended that?

We answer: His words ﴿He strives in the land to cause corruption therein﴾ indicate that his aim was to strive toward that. Then, His words ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾, if we take them as conjoined to the first clause, the verse does not indicate that this actually occurred, for the sense of the verse is as follows: he strives in the land to cause corruption therein, and he strives to destroy the crops and the offspring. If, however, we take it as an independent sentence separate from the first, it indicates that this has occurred. The first reading is preferable, although the reports mentioned concerning the occasion of revelation indicate that these things did occur and came into existence.

The fourth issue: some reciters read *wa-yahlaku al-harthu wa-al-naslu* (with the verb being intransitive, the crops and offspring being the subject), meaning that the act belongs to the crops and offspring. Al-Hasan read *yahlaka* with a fatha on the lam, a dialect form similar to *aba ya'ba* (from *abā yaʼbā*). It is also reported from him as *wa-yuhlaku* in the passive voice.

* * *

The fifth issue: the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) used God's words ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ to establish that God does not will ugly acts. They said: love is an expression for will, and the proof of this is His words: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾ [al-Nur 24:19], meaning that they desire it. Also, it is related from the Messenger (ﷺ) that he said: "God loves three things for you and dislikes three things for you. He loves that you worship Him and associate nothing with Him, that you give sincere counsel to those in authority over you, and He dislikes for you gossip, the squandering of wealth, and excessive questioning." He made dislike the opposite of love. Had love not been an expression for will, dislike would be the opposite of will. Furthermore, if love were other than will, it would be possible to love an act while disliking it, because on this view dislike opposes only will and not love. They said: since it is established that love is itself will, His words ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ are like His words "God does not will corruption," as in His words: ﴿And God does not desire injustice for His servants﴾ [Ghafir 40:31]. Indeed, the indication of this verse is even stronger, because God mentioned the corruption that occurred from this hypocrite and then said: ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾, as an allusion to it. This indicates that what happened occurred not by the will of God, the Exalted. And if it is established that He does not will corruption, it follows that He is not its creator, since creation is not possible without will. Thus this verse becomes an indication of the question of will and the question of the creation of acts.

The Ash'aris (al-Ashab) answered this in two ways.

The first: love is other than will. Rather, love is an expression for praising a thing and mentioning its magnificence.

The second: even if we grant that love is itself will, His words ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ do not imply generality, because the definite article *al-* (alif and lam) in the wording does not imply generality. Then, what undermines the force of this argument are two considerations:

The first: the servant's power and motive are capable of both righteousness and corruption. So if corruption is preponderant over righteousness, then if it occurs without a cause, the existence of the Creator is negated; and if it occurs due to a determining factor, that determining factor must be from God, otherwise an infinite regress would follow. It is therefore established that God, glorified be He, is the one who makes corruption preponderant over righteousness. How, then, can it be conceived that it is said that He does not will it?

The second: He knows that corruption will occur. If He wills that corruption not occur, it would follow that He wills to turn His knowledge of Himself into ignorance, and that is impossible.

The fifth attribute: His words: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride in sin takes hold of him.﴾ On this there are several issues.

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: His words ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes hold of him﴾ mean that the Messenger of God invited him to abandon these acts, but arrogance and haughtiness led him to injustice.

Know that this interpretation is weak, because His words ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes hold of him﴾ contain no indication except that whenever this statement is made to him, pride takes hold of him. Whether this statement was actually made or not, there is nothing in the verse indicating it. If that is established by a report, it must be accepted; yet we know that he (peace be upon him) used to invite everyone to piety without specification.

The second issue: God, the Exalted, related from this hypocrite a number of blameworthy acts:
First: his busying himself with fine speech in pursuit of worldly gain.
Second: his swearing by God falsely and deceitfully.
Third: his obstinacy in nullifying the truth and establishing falsehood.
Fourth: his striving in corruption.
Fifth: his striving to destroy the crops and the offspring.
All of these are reprehensible, ugly acts. The apparent sense of His words ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God"﴾ does not favour one of these acts over another, so it must be understood as applying to all of them. It is as if it were said: "Fear God in destroying the crops and the offspring, and in striving toward corruption, and in obstinate falsehood, and in swearing by God in this manner, and in greed for worldly gain." For there is no reason to restrict the admonition to some of these over others.

* * *

The third issue: His words ﴿pride in sin takes hold of him﴾ have several possible meanings.

One: this is derived from the expression "such-and-such took so-and-so to do something," meaning it compelled him to it and decided it for him. Thus the sense of the verse is: pride took him to commit sin, and that sin is his neglect of this admonisher and his refusal to listen to him.

Two: ﴿pride took hold of him﴾ means it stuck to him, as one says "fever took him" meaning it clung to him, or "old age took him" meaning it overcame him. So the meaning of the verse is: when he is told "Fear God," the pride that arises from the sin in his heart clings to him. This pride arose only because of what was in his heart of disbelief, ignorance, and failure to reflect upon the proofs. A parallel is His words: ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition﴾ [Sad 38:2]. Here the particle *bi-* (with) has the meaning of *li-* (for), as when a man says: "I did this because of you and for your sake," or "I punished him for his crime and because of his crime."

Concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Hasbuhu Jahannam (Sufficient for him is Hell)﴾. The exegetes said: its sufficiency is Hell as his recompense and punishment. It is said: "Hasbuka dirham" meaning "a dirham suffices you," and "Hasbuna Allah" meaning "Allah is sufficient for us." As for Jahannam (Hell), Yunus and most of the grammarians said: it is a name for the Fire with which Allah punishes in the Hereafter, and it is non-Arabic (a'jamiyyah). Others said: Jahannam is an Arabic name, and the Fire of the Hereafter was named by it because of the depth of its bottom (qa'r). It is reported from Ru'bah that he said:

"A well of Jihnam, far in its depth."

Concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿wa-labi'sa al-mihad (and how wretched is the resting-place)﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: that al-mihad and al-tamhid mean preparation and making ready (al-tawti'ah). Its root is from al-mahd (the cradle). Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the earth—We spread it out, and how excellent are the Spreaders (al-ma"hidun)﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 48], meaning those who prepare and establish, that is, We made it still and firmly settled, not swaying with its inhabitants and not throwing them off. And Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So for themselves they prepare (yamhidun)﴾ [al-Rum: 44], meaning they spread out and make ready.

The second: that His words ﴿wa-labi'sa al-mihad﴾ mean "and how wretched is the place of settling," like His words: ﴿Hell, they will burn therein, and how wretched is the abode (al-qarar)﴾ [Ibrahim: 29]. Some scholars said: al-mihad is the bedding for sleep. Since the one punished in the Fire is cast upon the fire of Hell, He made that a mihad (bedding) and firash (couch) for him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 204–206 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart, yet he is the most stubborn of opponents.﴾ ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock; but Allah does not love corruption.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him; so Hell is sufficient for him, and what an evil resting place.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, explained that those who witness the rites of the Hajj are of two groups: a disbeliever, who says, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾, and a believer, who says, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201], the hypocrite remained, so He mentioned him in this verse and described his attributes and actions. This is what relates to the arrangement of the verse. The purpose of all of this is to urge the servants toward the good way in matters concerning the actions of the hearts and limbs, and that they should know that the One worshipped cannot be kept ignorant of affairs. Then the exegetes differed into two opinions. Some of them said: this verse is specific to particular people. Others said: it is general in regard to everyone who is described by this attribute mentioned in this verse. As for the first group, they differed in several ways:

The first narration: it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, an ally of Banu Zuhrah, who came to the Prophet ﷺ and displayed Islam, and claimed that he loved him and swore by Allah to that effect. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾. However, he was a hypocrite, pleasant in outward appearance and wicked within. Then he left from the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, passed by a field of crops belonging to some Muslims, burned the crops and killed the donkeys. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock﴾. Others said: what is meant by His saying: ﴿whose speech pleases you﴾ is that al-Akhnas advised Banu Zuhrah on the day of Badr to return, and said to them: "Muhammad is the son of your sister; if he is a liar, all the people will suffice you against him, and if he is truthful, you will be the happiest of people with him." They said: "What an excellent opinion you have expressed." He said: "When the people are called to depart, I will withdraw with you, so follow me." Then he withdrew with three hundred men of Banu Zuhrah from fighting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He was therefore named al-Akhnas for this reason, and his name was Ubayy ibn Shariq. This reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and pleased him. In my view, however, this statement is weak, because by this action he does not deserve blame, whereas His saying: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾ is mentioned in the context of censure, so it cannot be applied to it. Rather, the first opinion is the most correct.

The second narration: concerning the cause of revelation of this verse, what is reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak: that the disbelievers of Quraysh sent to the Prophet ﷺ saying, "We have accepted Islam, so send us some scholars from your companions." He sent to them a group, and they alighted at Batn al-Raji'. The news reached the disbelievers, so seventy riders of them set out, surrounded them, killed them and crucified them. It was concerning them that this verse was revealed. For this reason, He follows it afterward with mention of the one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, thereby drawing attention to the state of these martyrs.

The second opinion concerning the verse, which is the choice of most of the careful exegetes, is that this verse is general regarding everyone who is described by these mentioned attributes. It is reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that a discussion took place between him and another concerning this verse, and he said: "Although it was revealed concerning the one mentioned, it is not impossible that the verse was revealed about a man and yet is general regarding everyone who is described by those attributes." The verification of the matter is that His saying: ﴿And among the people﴾ indicates some of them; it may refer to one or to many. His saying: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness﴾ does not indicate that the intended one is a single person among the people, since it is possible that this refers to the wording rather than the meaning, which is plural. As for its being revealed concerning the cause we have described, this does not prevent generality. Rather, we say: there is in it that which indicates generality, from several aspects:

First: that the ruling being attached to a fitting attribute indicates causation. When Allah censured a people and described them with attributes that necessitate deserving censure, we know that what necessitates that blame is those attributes, and so it follows that everyone described by those attributes deserves blame.

Second: that applying the verse to generality is more beneficial, because it serves as a deterrent for all the responsible persons from that blameworthy path.

Third: that this is closer to caution, for if we take the verse in its generality, that person is included in it; whereas if we restrict it to that person alone, the ruling would not be established for others. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that applying the verse to generality is preferable. Having understood this, we say: they differed as to whether the verse indicates that the one described by these attributes is a hypocrite or not. The correct view is that it does not indicate that, because Allah the Exalted described this mentioned person with five attributes, none of which indicates hypocrisy. The first of them is His saying: ﴿whose speech about the life of this world pleases you﴾, and this has no indication of a blameworthy attribute except by way of the implication conveyed by His saying: ﴿about the life of this world﴾, because when it is said of a person that his speech is sweet concerning worldly matters, it suggests a kind of blame.

Second: His saying: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾. This has no indication of a reprehensible state, for if we assume in it a hidden meaning, that he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart while his heart is otherwise, then the statement with this hidden meaning does not indicate hypocrisy, because the verse does not say that what he shows the Messenger of the matters of Islam and monotheism is what he conceals contrary to it, so that he must be a hypocrite. Rather, perhaps the meaning is that he conceals corruption and displays its opposite, so that he is a show-off.

Third: His saying: ﴿yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾. This also does not necessitate hypocrisy.

Fourth: His saying: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein﴾. A Muslim who is a corrupter may also be like that.

Fifth: His saying: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him﴾. This too does not necessitate hypocrisy. Thus we know that all these attributes mentioned in the verse, just as they may be found in a hypocrite, may be found in a show-off. Therefore there is no indication in the verse that this mentioned person must be a hypocrite, except that the hypocrite is included in the verse, because every hypocrite is described by these five attributes, though one who is described by these five attributes may not be a hypocrite. It is established that whenever we apply the verse to the one described by these five attributes, the hypocrite and the show-off are included in it. Having understood this summary, we say: Allah the Exalted described this mentioned person with five attributes:

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿whose speech about the life of this world pleases you﴾. The meaning: it pleases you and becomes great in your heart; from it comes the word "ajib" (wonderful), which is something that greatly impresses the soul.

As for His saying: ﴿about the life of this world﴾, there are several aspects:

One: it is like the saying of one who says: "I am impressed by so-and-so's speech on this matter," meaning: his speech and talk pleases you when he speaks seeking the benefits of this world.

The second: the intended meaning may be: his speech and talk about the life of this world pleases you, even if his speech about the Hereafter does not please you, because as long as he is in this world he is bold of tongue and sweet of speech; but in the Hereafter he is seized by inarticulateness and stammering out of fear of Allah's awe and the subjugation of His majesty.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾. The meaning: he affirms the truthfulness of his speech and claim by calling Allah to witness. This witnessing may be by oath and swearing, or it may be by saying: "Allah bears witness that the matter is as I have said," and this is calling Allah as witness without being an oath. The majority of readers read ﴿wayushhidu Allah﴾ with a dammah on the ya', meaning: this speaker calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his inner self. Ibn Muhaysin read "yashhadu Allahu 'ala ma fi qalbihi" with a fathah on the ya', and the meaning is: Allah knows the one whose heart is contrary to what he displays.

The first reading indicates that he is a show-off and that he calls Allah to witness falsely about his hypocrisy and his display. As for the second reading, it indicates only that he is a liar; as for his calling Allah as witness deliberately in falsehood, it does not indicate that. Therefore, the first reading is more indicative of blame.

The third attribute: His saying the Exalted: ﴿yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

First issue: "al-Alladd" means the one who is most intense in dispute. It is said: a man "alladd," and people "ludd," and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and you may warn thereby a people most stubborn﴾ [Maryam: 97]. It is like His saying: ﴿Rather they are a contentious people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58]. It is said of it: "ladda yaladdu," with a fathah on the lam in its imperfect; so he is "alladd" when he is contentious. And "laddadtu al-rajul" with a dammah on the lam, "aluddu," when you overcome him by dispute. Al-Zajjaj said: its derivation is from "ladidatay al-unuq," which are its two sides, and "ladidayay al-wadi," which are its two banks; and its interpretation is that whichever direction his opponent takes from right and left in the gates of dispute, he overcomes the one who disputes with him.

As for "al-khisam," there are two opinions. One of them, which is the opinion of al-Khalil, is that it is a verbal noun meaning "mukhasamah" (disputing), like "qital" and "tia'n" meaning "muqatalah" and "mutaana"; so the meaning is: he is most intense in disputing. Then in this idafah there are two aspects: one is that it means "fi" (in), so the sense is: most stubborn in disputing. The second is that he made the disputing itself the most stubborn, by way of emphasis.

The second opinion is that "al-khisam" is the plural of "khasm," like "si'ab" and "sa'b," and "dikhamun" and "dakhm," and the meaning is: he is the most intense of opponents in disputing. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. The exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, as we have explained. Concerning him was also revealed His saying: ﴿Woe to every backbiter and slanderer﴾ [al-Humazah: 1], and His saying: ﴿And do not obey every vile swearer, backbiter, going about with slander﴾ [al-Qalam: 10–11]. Then the exegetes have various expressions in interpreting this word. Mujahid said: "alladd al-khisam" means: one who seeks what is not straight. Al-Suddi said: crooked in dispute. Qatadah said: "alladd al-khisam" means that he is contentious with falsehood, intensely hard in disobedience to Allah, learned in tongue and ignorant in action.

* * *

Second issue: Those who deny speculation and disputation have held to this verse. They said: Allah censured that person for being intense in dispute, and if this attribute were not one of the attributes of blame, it would not be permissible. Its answer is what has preceded in His saying: ﴿nor is there any disputing in the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197].

The fourth attribute: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock; and Allah does not love corruption.﴾ Know that when He, the Exalted, explained concerning that person that he is sweet of speech, that he affirms the truthfulness of his words by calling Allah to witness, and that he is the most stubborn of opponents, He then explained that all that he mentions by tongue, his heart conceals its opposite. So He said: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein.﴾ Then in the verse there are issues:

First issue: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when he turns away﴾, concerning which there are two opinions:

One of them: its meaning is: "And when he departs from you, he strives in the land with corruption." Then this corruption may have two aspects:

One of them: what is the destruction of wealth

[p. 170 continues from the previous part]

...by destruction, burning, and plunder. On this interpretation they have transmitted reports, among them what we have already mentioned: that al-Akhnas, when he showed the Messenger (ﷺ) that he loved him and was resolved to become a believer, then, once he left his presence, passed by a field of crops belonging to the Muslims, burned the crops, and slaughtered the donkeys. Another report says that when he returned from Badr, he passed by Banu Zuhra, between whom and Thaqif there was enmity. He attacked them by night, destroyed their livestock, and burned their crops.

The second interpretation of *fasad* (corruption) is that after leaving the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), he would busy himself with planting doubts in the hearts of the Muslims and devising stratagems to strengthen disbelief. This meaning is called *fasad*. God, the Exalted, said, relating the words of Pharaoh's people when they said to him: ﴿Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land?﴾ [al-A'raf 7:127], meaning: to turn your people away from their religion and to corrupt their law for them. He also said: ﴿I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾ [Ghafir 40:26]. We have already mentioned, in the commentary on His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption in the land"﴾ [al-Baqara 2:11], something close to this meaning. This meaning is called corruption in the land because it produces discord among people, divides their word, and leads some of them to disavow others, so that kinship ties are severed and blood is shed. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So would you, if you were to turn away, do corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Muhammad 47:22]. Thus He informed that if they turned away from His religion, they would achieve nothing but corruption in the land and the severing of kinship ties, and this is in the sense we have described, which is frequent in the Qur'an.

Know that interpreting *fasad* in this way is preferable to interpreting it as destruction and plunder, because God said: ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾, and the conjoined term is necessarily different from the term it is conjoined to.

The second view concerns the interpretation of His words: ﴿And when he turns away﴾, meaning: when he becomes a ruler, he does what the wicked rulers do of corruption in the land by destroying crops and offspring. It has also been said: he displays injustice to the extent that God, because of the wickedness of his oppression, withholds rain, so that crops and offspring perish. The first view is closer to the structure of the verse, because the aim is to explain his hypocrisy: in his presence he speaks fine words and displays love, but in his absence he strives to stir up strife and corruption.

The second issue: His words ﴿He strives in the land﴾ mean: he exerted himself in provoking fighting. The root meaning of *sa'y* (striving) is walking swiftly, but it is used figuratively for stirring up strife and sowing destruction among people. From this one says: "So-and-so strives with tale-bearing (*namima*)." God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have added nothing to you but confusion, and they would have hurried about among you seeking to stir up sedition for you﴾ [al-Tawba 9:47].

The third issue: whoever interprets *fasad* as destruction says that God mentioned it first in general terms, which is His words: ﴿to cause corruption therein﴾, and then mentioned it again in detail, saying: ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾. Whoever interprets corruption as casting doubt says: just as true religion has two components, first knowledge and second action, so false religion has two components, first doubts and second the commission of wrongs. Here God mentioned first from this man his occupation with doubts, which is what is meant by His words: ﴿to cause corruption therein﴾, and then mentioned his undertaking of wrongs, which is what is meant by His words: ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾. There is no doubt that this interpretation is preferable.

Then whoever says that the occasion of revelation of the verse was that al-Akhnas passed by a field of crops belonging to the Muslims, burned the crops and slaughtered the donkeys, says: the *harth* (crops) means the produce, and the *nasl* (offspring) means those donkeys. *Harth* is that from which crops come. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow?﴾ [al-Waqi'a 56:63–64]. It applies to every kind of plant that is ploughed and sown. It has also been said that *harth* is the tilling of the earth, and that the instrument used for it is called *mihrath*. As for *nasl* on this interpretation, it is the offspring of animals. *Nasl* in the language means offspring. Its derivation may be from the saying *nasala yansilu*, when something comes out and falls: thus one says of the feathers of a bird, the wool of a camel, or the hair of a donkey, that it *nasala* when it comes out and falls, and a piece that falls off is called *nusala*. From this is His words: ﴿They will hasten to their Lord﴾ [Ya Sin 36:51], meaning: they will hurry, because he rushes out with vigour. *Nasl* means offspring because it comes out from the father's back and the mother's womb and falls. Mankind is the offspring of Adam. The root of the word is from *nusul*, which means coming out.

As for whoever says that the occasion of revelation is that al-Akhnas attacked the people of Thaqif by night and killed a number of them, then *harth* means either the women, in accordance with His words: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqara 2:223], or the men, which is the view of some exegetes who interpreted *harth* as tilling the earth, since men are those who till the soil of procreation. As for *nasl*, it means the children.

Know that on all these interpretations, the intent is to show that this corruption is a great corruption, and there is no greater. For on the first interpretation, what is meant is the destruction of plants and animals, and on the second interpretation, the destruction of animals in their origin and offspring. On both views, there is no greater corruption than this. Therefore His words ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾ are extremely eloquent expressions which, despite their brevity, convey great emphasis. A parallel in brevity is what He said in describing Paradise: ﴿therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:71], and He said: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:31].

[p. 171]

If it is asked: does the verse indicate that he destroys the crops and the offspring, or does it indicate that he intended that?

We answer: His words ﴿He strives in the land to cause corruption therein﴾ indicate that his aim was to strive toward that. Then, His words ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾, if we take them as conjoined to the first clause, the verse does not indicate that this actually occurred, for the sense of the verse is as follows: he strives in the land to cause corruption therein, and he strives to destroy the crops and the offspring. If, however, we take it as an independent sentence separate from the first, it indicates that this has occurred. The first reading is preferable, although the reports mentioned concerning the occasion of revelation indicate that these things did occur and came into existence.

The fourth issue: some reciters read *wa-yahlaku al-harthu wa-al-naslu* (with the verb being intransitive, the crops and offspring being the subject), meaning that the act belongs to the crops and offspring. Al-Hasan read *yahlaka* with a fatha on the lam, a dialect form similar to *aba ya'ba* (from *abā yaʼbā*). It is also reported from him as *wa-yuhlaku* in the passive voice.

* * *

The fifth issue: the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) used God's words ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ to establish that God does not will ugly acts. They said: love is an expression for will, and the proof of this is His words: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾ [al-Nur 24:19], meaning that they desire it. Also, it is related from the Messenger (ﷺ) that he said: "God loves three things for you and dislikes three things for you. He loves that you worship Him and associate nothing with Him, that you give sincere counsel to those in authority over you, and He dislikes for you gossip, the squandering of wealth, and excessive questioning." He made dislike the opposite of love. Had love not been an expression for will, dislike would be the opposite of will. Furthermore, if love were other than will, it would be possible to love an act while disliking it, because on this view dislike opposes only will and not love. They said: since it is established that love is itself will, His words ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ are like His words "God does not will corruption," as in His words: ﴿And God does not desire injustice for His servants﴾ [Ghafir 40:31]. Indeed, the indication of this verse is even stronger, because God mentioned the corruption that occurred from this hypocrite and then said: ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾, as an allusion to it. This indicates that what happened occurred not by the will of God, the Exalted. And if it is established that He does not will corruption, it follows that He is not its creator, since creation is not possible without will. Thus this verse becomes an indication of the question of will and the question of the creation of acts.

The Ash'aris (al-Ashab) answered this in two ways.

The first: love is other than will. Rather, love is an expression for praising a thing and mentioning its magnificence.

The second: even if we grant that love is itself will, His words ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ do not imply generality, because the definite article *al-* (alif and lam) in the wording does not imply generality. Then, what undermines the force of this argument are two considerations:

The first: the servant's power and motive are capable of both righteousness and corruption. So if corruption is preponderant over righteousness, then if it occurs without a cause, the existence of the Creator is negated; and if it occurs due to a determining factor, that determining factor must be from God, otherwise an infinite regress would follow. It is therefore established that God, glorified be He, is the one who makes corruption preponderant over righteousness. How, then, can it be conceived that it is said that He does not will it?

The second: He knows that corruption will occur. If He wills that corruption not occur, it would follow that He wills to turn His knowledge of Himself into ignorance, and that is impossible.

The fifth attribute: His words: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride in sin takes hold of him.﴾ On this there are several issues.

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: His words ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes hold of him﴾ mean that the Messenger of God invited him to abandon these acts, but arrogance and haughtiness led him to injustice.

Know that this interpretation is weak, because His words ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes hold of him﴾ contain no indication except that whenever this statement is made to him, pride takes hold of him. Whether this statement was actually made or not, there is nothing in the verse indicating it. If that is established by a report, it must be accepted; yet we know that he (peace be upon him) used to invite everyone to piety without specification.

The second issue: God, the Exalted, related from this hypocrite a number of blameworthy acts:
First: his busying himself with fine speech in pursuit of worldly gain.
Second: his swearing by God falsely and deceitfully.
Third: his obstinacy in nullifying the truth and establishing falsehood.
Fourth: his striving in corruption.
Fifth: his striving to destroy the crops and the offspring.
All of these are reprehensible, ugly acts. The apparent sense of His words ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God"﴾ does not favour one of these acts over another, so it must be understood as applying to all of them. It is as if it were said: "Fear God in destroying the crops and the offspring, and in striving toward corruption, and in obstinate falsehood, and in swearing by God in this manner, and in greed for worldly gain." For there is no reason to restrict the admonition to some of these over others.

* * *

The third issue: His words ﴿pride in sin takes hold of him﴾ have several possible meanings.

One: this is derived from the expression "such-and-such took so-and-so to do something," meaning it compelled him to it and decided it for him. Thus the sense of the verse is: pride took him to commit sin, and that sin is his neglect of this admonisher and his refusal to listen to him.

Two: ﴿pride took hold of him﴾ means it stuck to him, as one says "fever took him" meaning it clung to him, or "old age took him" meaning it overcame him. So the meaning of the verse is: when he is told "Fear God," the pride that arises from the sin in his heart clings to him. This pride arose only because of what was in his heart of disbelief, ignorance, and failure to reflect upon the proofs. A parallel is His words: ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition﴾ [Sad 38:2]. Here the particle *bi-* (with) has the meaning of *li-* (for), as when a man says: "I did this because of you and for your sake," or "I punished him for his crime and because of his crime."

Concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Hasbuhu Jahannam (Sufficient for him is Hell)﴾. The exegetes said: its sufficiency is Hell as his recompense and punishment. It is said: "Hasbuka dirham" meaning "a dirham suffices you," and "Hasbuna Allah" meaning "Allah is sufficient for us." As for Jahannam (Hell), Yunus and most of the grammarians said: it is a name for the Fire with which Allah punishes in the Hereafter, and it is non-Arabic (a'jamiyyah). Others said: Jahannam is an Arabic name, and the Fire of the Hereafter was named by it because of the depth of its bottom (qa'r). It is reported from Ru'bah that he said:

"A well of Jihnam, far in its depth."

Concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿wa-labi'sa al-mihad (and how wretched is the resting-place)﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: that al-mihad and al-tamhid mean preparation and making ready (al-tawti'ah). Its root is from al-mahd (the cradle). Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the earth—We spread it out, and how excellent are the Spreaders (al-ma"hidun)﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 48], meaning those who prepare and establish, that is, We made it still and firmly settled, not swaying with its inhabitants and not throwing them off. And Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So for themselves they prepare (yamhidun)﴾ [al-Rum: 44], meaning they spread out and make ready.

The second: that His words ﴿wa-labi'sa al-mihad﴾ mean "and how wretched is the place of settling," like His words: ﴿Hell, they will burn therein, and how wretched is the abode (al-qarar)﴾ [Ibrahim: 29]. Some scholars said: al-mihad is the bedding for sleep. Since the one punished in the Fire is cast upon the fire of Hell, He made that a mihad (bedding) and firash (couch) for him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 204–206 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart, yet he is the most stubborn of opponents.﴾ ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock; but Allah does not love corruption.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him; so Hell is sufficient for him, and what an evil resting place.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, explained that those who witness the rites of the Hajj are of two groups: a disbeliever, who says, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾, and a believer, who says, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201], the hypocrite remained, so He mentioned him in this verse and described his attributes and actions. This is what relates to the arrangement of the verse. The purpose of all of this is to urge the servants toward the good way in matters concerning the actions of the hearts and limbs, and that they should know that the One worshipped cannot be kept ignorant of affairs. Then the exegetes differed into two opinions. Some of them said: this verse is specific to particular people. Others said: it is general in regard to everyone who is described by this attribute mentioned in this verse. As for the first group, they differed in several ways:

The first narration: it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, an ally of Banu Zuhrah, who came to the Prophet ﷺ and displayed Islam, and claimed that he loved him and swore by Allah to that effect. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾. However, he was a hypocrite, pleasant in outward appearance and wicked within. Then he left from the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, passed by a field of crops belonging to some Muslims, burned the crops and killed the donkeys. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock﴾. Others said: what is meant by His saying: ﴿whose speech pleases you﴾ is that al-Akhnas advised Banu Zuhrah on the day of Badr to return, and said to them: "Muhammad is the son of your sister; if he is a liar, all the people will suffice you against him, and if he is truthful, you will be the happiest of people with him." They said: "What an excellent opinion you have expressed." He said: "When the people are called to depart, I will withdraw with you, so follow me." Then he withdrew with three hundred men of Banu Zuhrah from fighting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He was therefore named al-Akhnas for this reason, and his name was Ubayy ibn Shariq. This reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and pleased him. In my view, however, this statement is weak, because by this action he does not deserve blame, whereas His saying: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾ is mentioned in the context of censure, so it cannot be applied to it. Rather, the first opinion is the most correct.

The second narration: concerning the cause of revelation of this verse, what is reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak: that the disbelievers of Quraysh sent to the Prophet ﷺ saying, "We have accepted Islam, so send us some scholars from your companions." He sent to them a group, and they alighted at Batn al-Raji'. The news reached the disbelievers, so seventy riders of them set out, surrounded them, killed them and crucified them. It was concerning them that this verse was revealed. For this reason, He follows it afterward with mention of the one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, thereby drawing attention to the state of these martyrs.

The second opinion concerning the verse, which is the choice of most of the careful exegetes, is that this verse is general regarding everyone who is described by these mentioned attributes. It is reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that a discussion took place between him and another concerning this verse, and he said: "Although it was revealed concerning the one mentioned, it is not impossible that the verse was revealed about a man and yet is general regarding everyone who is described by those attributes." The verification of the matter is that His saying: ﴿And among the people﴾ indicates some of them; it may refer to one or to many. His saying: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness﴾ does not indicate that the intended one is a single person among the people, since it is possible that this refers to the wording rather than the meaning, which is plural. As for its being revealed concerning the cause we have described, this does not prevent generality. Rather, we say: there is in it that which indicates generality, from several aspects:

First: that the ruling being attached to a fitting attribute indicates causation. When Allah censured a people and described them with attributes that necessitate deserving censure, we know that what necessitates that blame is those attributes, and so it follows that everyone described by those attributes deserves blame.

Second: that applying the verse to generality is more beneficial, because it serves as a deterrent for all the responsible persons from that blameworthy path.

Third: that this is closer to caution, for if we take the verse in its generality, that person is included in it; whereas if we restrict it to that person alone, the ruling would not be established for others. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that applying the verse to generality is preferable. Having understood this, we say: they differed as to whether the verse indicates that the one described by these attributes is a hypocrite or not. The correct view is that it does not indicate that, because Allah the Exalted described this mentioned person with five attributes, none of which indicates hypocrisy. The first of them is His saying: ﴿whose speech about the life of this world pleases you﴾, and this has no indication of a blameworthy attribute except by way of the implication conveyed by His saying: ﴿about the life of this world﴾, because when it is said of a person that his speech is sweet concerning worldly matters, it suggests a kind of blame.

Second: His saying: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾. This has no indication of a reprehensible state, for if we assume in it a hidden meaning, that he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart while his heart is otherwise, then the statement with this hidden meaning does not indicate hypocrisy, because the verse does not say that what he shows the Messenger of the matters of Islam and monotheism is what he conceals contrary to it, so that he must be a hypocrite. Rather, perhaps the meaning is that he conceals corruption and displays its opposite, so that he is a show-off.

Third: His saying: ﴿yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾. This also does not necessitate hypocrisy.

Fourth: His saying: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein﴾. A Muslim who is a corrupter may also be like that.

Fifth: His saying: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him﴾. This too does not necessitate hypocrisy. Thus we know that all these attributes mentioned in the verse, just as they may be found in a hypocrite, may be found in a show-off. Therefore there is no indication in the verse that this mentioned person must be a hypocrite, except that the hypocrite is included in the verse, because every hypocrite is described by these five attributes, though one who is described by these five attributes may not be a hypocrite. It is established that whenever we apply the verse to the one described by these five attributes, the hypocrite and the show-off are included in it. Having understood this summary, we say: Allah the Exalted described this mentioned person with five attributes:

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿whose speech about the life of this world pleases you﴾. The meaning: it pleases you and becomes great in your heart; from it comes the word "ajib" (wonderful), which is something that greatly impresses the soul.

As for His saying: ﴿about the life of this world﴾, there are several aspects:

One: it is like the saying of one who says: "I am impressed by so-and-so's speech on this matter," meaning: his speech and talk pleases you when he speaks seeking the benefits of this world.

The second: the intended meaning may be: his speech and talk about the life of this world pleases you, even if his speech about the Hereafter does not please you, because as long as he is in this world he is bold of tongue and sweet of speech; but in the Hereafter he is seized by inarticulateness and stammering out of fear of Allah's awe and the subjugation of His majesty.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his heart﴾. The meaning: he affirms the truthfulness of his speech and claim by calling Allah to witness. This witnessing may be by oath and swearing, or it may be by saying: "Allah bears witness that the matter is as I have said," and this is calling Allah as witness without being an oath. The majority of readers read ﴿wayushhidu Allah﴾ with a dammah on the ya', meaning: this speaker calls Allah to witness regarding what is in his inner self. Ibn Muhaysin read "yashhadu Allahu 'ala ma fi qalbihi" with a fathah on the ya', and the meaning is: Allah knows the one whose heart is contrary to what he displays.

The first reading indicates that he is a show-off and that he calls Allah to witness falsely about his hypocrisy and his display. As for the second reading, it indicates only that he is a liar; as for his calling Allah as witness deliberately in falsehood, it does not indicate that. Therefore, the first reading is more indicative of blame.

The third attribute: His saying the Exalted: ﴿yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

First issue: "al-Alladd" means the one who is most intense in dispute. It is said: a man "alladd," and people "ludd," and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and you may warn thereby a people most stubborn﴾ [Maryam: 97]. It is like His saying: ﴿Rather they are a contentious people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58]. It is said of it: "ladda yaladdu," with a fathah on the lam in its imperfect; so he is "alladd" when he is contentious. And "laddadtu al-rajul" with a dammah on the lam, "aluddu," when you overcome him by dispute. Al-Zajjaj said: its derivation is from "ladidatay al-unuq," which are its two sides, and "ladidayay al-wadi," which are its two banks; and its interpretation is that whichever direction his opponent takes from right and left in the gates of dispute, he overcomes the one who disputes with him.

As for "al-khisam," there are two opinions. One of them, which is the opinion of al-Khalil, is that it is a verbal noun meaning "mukhasamah" (disputing), like "qital" and "tia'n" meaning "muqatalah" and "mutaana"; so the meaning is: he is most intense in disputing. Then in this idafah there are two aspects: one is that it means "fi" (in), so the sense is: most stubborn in disputing. The second is that he made the disputing itself the most stubborn, by way of emphasis.

The second opinion is that "al-khisam" is the plural of "khasm," like "si'ab" and "sa'b," and "dikhamun" and "dakhm," and the meaning is: he is the most intense of opponents in disputing. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. The exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, as we have explained. Concerning him was also revealed His saying: ﴿Woe to every backbiter and slanderer﴾ [al-Humazah: 1], and His saying: ﴿And do not obey every vile swearer, backbiter, going about with slander﴾ [al-Qalam: 10–11]. Then the exegetes have various expressions in interpreting this word. Mujahid said: "alladd al-khisam" means: one who seeks what is not straight. Al-Suddi said: crooked in dispute. Qatadah said: "alladd al-khisam" means that he is contentious with falsehood, intensely hard in disobedience to Allah, learned in tongue and ignorant in action.

* * *

Second issue: Those who deny speculation and disputation have held to this verse. They said: Allah censured that person for being intense in dispute, and if this attribute were not one of the attributes of blame, it would not be permissible. Its answer is what has preceded in His saying: ﴿nor is there any disputing in the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197].

The fourth attribute: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock; and Allah does not love corruption.﴾ Know that when He, the Exalted, explained concerning that person that he is sweet of speech, that he affirms the truthfulness of his words by calling Allah to witness, and that he is the most stubborn of opponents, He then explained that all that he mentions by tongue, his heart conceals its opposite. So He said: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein.﴾ Then in the verse there are issues:

First issue: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when he turns away﴾, concerning which there are two opinions:

One of them: its meaning is: "And when he departs from you, he strives in the land with corruption." Then this corruption may have two aspects:

One of them: what is the destruction of wealth

[p. 170 continues from the previous part]

...by destruction, burning, and plunder. On this interpretation they have transmitted reports, among them what we have already mentioned: that al-Akhnas, when he showed the Messenger (ﷺ) that he loved him and was resolved to become a believer, then, once he left his presence, passed by a field of crops belonging to the Muslims, burned the crops, and slaughtered the donkeys. Another report says that when he returned from Badr, he passed by Banu Zuhra, between whom and Thaqif there was enmity. He attacked them by night, destroyed their livestock, and burned their crops.

The second interpretation of *fasad* (corruption) is that after leaving the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), he would busy himself with planting doubts in the hearts of the Muslims and devising stratagems to strengthen disbelief. This meaning is called *fasad*. God, the Exalted, said, relating the words of Pharaoh's people when they said to him: ﴿Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land?﴾ [al-A'raf 7:127], meaning: to turn your people away from their religion and to corrupt their law for them. He also said: ﴿I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾ [Ghafir 40:26]. We have already mentioned, in the commentary on His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption in the land"﴾ [al-Baqara 2:11], something close to this meaning. This meaning is called corruption in the land because it produces discord among people, divides their word, and leads some of them to disavow others, so that kinship ties are severed and blood is shed. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So would you, if you were to turn away, do corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Muhammad 47:22]. Thus He informed that if they turned away from His religion, they would achieve nothing but corruption in the land and the severing of kinship ties, and this is in the sense we have described, which is frequent in the Qur'an.

Know that interpreting *fasad* in this way is preferable to interpreting it as destruction and plunder, because God said: ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾, and the conjoined term is necessarily different from the term it is conjoined to.

The second view concerns the interpretation of His words: ﴿And when he turns away﴾, meaning: when he becomes a ruler, he does what the wicked rulers do of corruption in the land by destroying crops and offspring. It has also been said: he displays injustice to the extent that God, because of the wickedness of his oppression, withholds rain, so that crops and offspring perish. The first view is closer to the structure of the verse, because the aim is to explain his hypocrisy: in his presence he speaks fine words and displays love, but in his absence he strives to stir up strife and corruption.

The second issue: His words ﴿He strives in the land﴾ mean: he exerted himself in provoking fighting. The root meaning of *sa'y* (striving) is walking swiftly, but it is used figuratively for stirring up strife and sowing destruction among people. From this one says: "So-and-so strives with tale-bearing (*namima*)." God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have added nothing to you but confusion, and they would have hurried about among you seeking to stir up sedition for you﴾ [al-Tawba 9:47].

The third issue: whoever interprets *fasad* as destruction says that God mentioned it first in general terms, which is His words: ﴿to cause corruption therein﴾, and then mentioned it again in detail, saying: ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾. Whoever interprets corruption as casting doubt says: just as true religion has two components, first knowledge and second action, so false religion has two components, first doubts and second the commission of wrongs. Here God mentioned first from this man his occupation with doubts, which is what is meant by His words: ﴿to cause corruption therein﴾, and then mentioned his undertaking of wrongs, which is what is meant by His words: ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾. There is no doubt that this interpretation is preferable.

Then whoever says that the occasion of revelation of the verse was that al-Akhnas passed by a field of crops belonging to the Muslims, burned the crops and slaughtered the donkeys, says: the *harth* (crops) means the produce, and the *nasl* (offspring) means those donkeys. *Harth* is that from which crops come. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow?﴾ [al-Waqi'a 56:63–64]. It applies to every kind of plant that is ploughed and sown. It has also been said that *harth* is the tilling of the earth, and that the instrument used for it is called *mihrath*. As for *nasl* on this interpretation, it is the offspring of animals. *Nasl* in the language means offspring. Its derivation may be from the saying *nasala yansilu*, when something comes out and falls: thus one says of the feathers of a bird, the wool of a camel, or the hair of a donkey, that it *nasala* when it comes out and falls, and a piece that falls off is called *nusala*. From this is His words: ﴿They will hasten to their Lord﴾ [Ya Sin 36:51], meaning: they will hurry, because he rushes out with vigour. *Nasl* means offspring because it comes out from the father's back and the mother's womb and falls. Mankind is the offspring of Adam. The root of the word is from *nusul*, which means coming out.

As for whoever says that the occasion of revelation is that al-Akhnas attacked the people of Thaqif by night and killed a number of them, then *harth* means either the women, in accordance with His words: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqara 2:223], or the men, which is the view of some exegetes who interpreted *harth* as tilling the earth, since men are those who till the soil of procreation. As for *nasl*, it means the children.

Know that on all these interpretations, the intent is to show that this corruption is a great corruption, and there is no greater. For on the first interpretation, what is meant is the destruction of plants and animals, and on the second interpretation, the destruction of animals in their origin and offspring. On both views, there is no greater corruption than this. Therefore His words ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾ are extremely eloquent expressions which, despite their brevity, convey great emphasis. A parallel in brevity is what He said in describing Paradise: ﴿therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:71], and He said: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:31].

[p. 171]

If it is asked: does the verse indicate that he destroys the crops and the offspring, or does it indicate that he intended that?

We answer: His words ﴿He strives in the land to cause corruption therein﴾ indicate that his aim was to strive toward that. Then, His words ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾, if we take them as conjoined to the first clause, the verse does not indicate that this actually occurred, for the sense of the verse is as follows: he strives in the land to cause corruption therein, and he strives to destroy the crops and the offspring. If, however, we take it as an independent sentence separate from the first, it indicates that this has occurred. The first reading is preferable, although the reports mentioned concerning the occasion of revelation indicate that these things did occur and came into existence.

The fourth issue: some reciters read *wa-yahlaku al-harthu wa-al-naslu* (with the verb being intransitive, the crops and offspring being the subject), meaning that the act belongs to the crops and offspring. Al-Hasan read *yahlaka* with a fatha on the lam, a dialect form similar to *aba ya'ba* (from *abā yaʼbā*). It is also reported from him as *wa-yuhlaku* in the passive voice.

* * *

The fifth issue: the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) used God's words ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ to establish that God does not will ugly acts. They said: love is an expression for will, and the proof of this is His words: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾ [al-Nur 24:19], meaning that they desire it. Also, it is related from the Messenger (ﷺ) that he said: "God loves three things for you and dislikes three things for you. He loves that you worship Him and associate nothing with Him, that you give sincere counsel to those in authority over you, and He dislikes for you gossip, the squandering of wealth, and excessive questioning." He made dislike the opposite of love. Had love not been an expression for will, dislike would be the opposite of will. Furthermore, if love were other than will, it would be possible to love an act while disliking it, because on this view dislike opposes only will and not love. They said: since it is established that love is itself will, His words ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ are like His words "God does not will corruption," as in His words: ﴿And God does not desire injustice for His servants﴾ [Ghafir 40:31]. Indeed, the indication of this verse is even stronger, because God mentioned the corruption that occurred from this hypocrite and then said: ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾, as an allusion to it. This indicates that what happened occurred not by the will of God, the Exalted. And if it is established that He does not will corruption, it follows that He is not its creator, since creation is not possible without will. Thus this verse becomes an indication of the question of will and the question of the creation of acts.

The Ash'aris (al-Ashab) answered this in two ways.

The first: love is other than will. Rather, love is an expression for praising a thing and mentioning its magnificence.
