The second: even if we grant that love is itself will, His words ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ do not imply generality, because the definite article *al-* (alif and lam) in the wording does not imply generality. Then, what undermines the force of this argument are two considerations:

The first: the servant's power and motive are capable of both righteousness and corruption. So if corruption is preponderant over righteousness, then if it occurs without a cause, the existence of the Creator is negated; and if it occurs due to a determining factor, that determining factor must be from God, otherwise an infinite regress would follow. It is therefore established that God, glorified be He, is the one who makes corruption preponderant over righteousness. How, then, can it be conceived that it is said that He does not will it?

The second: He knows that corruption will occur. If He wills that corruption not occur, it would follow that He wills to turn His knowledge of Himself into ignorance, and that is impossible.

The fifth attribute: His words: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride in sin takes hold of him.﴾ On this there are several issues.

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: His words ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes hold of him﴾ mean that the Messenger of God invited him to abandon these acts, but arrogance and haughtiness led him to injustice.

Know that this interpretation is weak, because His words ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes hold of him﴾ contain no indication except that whenever this statement is made to him, pride takes hold of him. Whether this statement was actually made or not, there is nothing in the verse indicating it. If that is established by a report, it must be accepted; yet we know that he (peace be upon him) used to invite everyone to piety without specification.

The second issue: God, the Exalted, related from this hypocrite a number of blameworthy acts:
First: his busying himself with fine speech in pursuit of worldly gain.
Second: his swearing by God falsely and deceitfully.
Third: his obstinacy in nullifying the truth and establishing falsehood.
Fourth: his striving in corruption.
Fifth: his striving to destroy the crops and the offspring.
All of these are reprehensible, ugly acts. The apparent sense of His words ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God"﴾ does not favour one of these acts over another, so it must be understood as applying to all of them. It is as if it were said: "Fear God in destroying the crops and the offspring, and in striving toward corruption, and in obstinate falsehood, and in swearing by God in this manner, and in greed for worldly gain." For there is no reason to restrict the admonition to some of these over others.

* * *

The third issue: His words ﴿pride in sin takes hold of him﴾ have several possible meanings.

One: this is derived from the expression "such-and-such took so-and-so to do something," meaning it compelled him to it and decided it for him. Thus the sense of the verse is: pride took him to commit sin, and that sin is his neglect of this admonisher and his refusal to listen to him.

Two: ﴿pride took hold of him﴾ means it stuck to him, as one says "fever took him" meaning it clung to him, or "old age took him" meaning it overcame him. So the meaning of the verse is: when he is told "Fear God," the pride that arises from the sin in his heart clings to him. This pride arose only because of what was in his heart of disbelief, ignorance, and failure to reflect upon the proofs. A parallel is His words: ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition﴾ [Sad 38:2]. Here the particle *bi-* (with) has the meaning of *li-* (for), as when a man says: "I did this because of you and for your sake," or "I punished him for his crime and because of his crime."

Concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Hasbuhu Jahannam (Sufficient for him is Hell)﴾. The exegetes said: its sufficiency is Hell as his recompense and punishment. It is said: "Hasbuka dirham" meaning "a dirham suffices you," and "Hasbuna Allah" meaning "Allah is sufficient for us." As for Jahannam (Hell), Yunus and most of the grammarians said: it is a name for the Fire with which Allah punishes in the Hereafter, and it is non-Arabic (a'jamiyyah). Others said: Jahannam is an Arabic name, and the Fire of the Hereafter was named by it because of the depth of its bottom (qa'r). It is reported from Ru'bah that he said:

"A well of Jihnam, far in its depth."

Concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿wa-labi'sa al-mihad (and how wretched is the resting-place)﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: that al-mihad and al-tamhid mean preparation and making ready (al-tawti'ah). Its root is from al-mahd (the cradle). Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the earth—We spread it out, and how excellent are the Spreaders (al-ma"hidun)﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 48], meaning those who prepare and establish, that is, We made it still and firmly settled, not swaying with its inhabitants and not throwing them off. And Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So for themselves they prepare (yamhidun)﴾ [al-Rum: 44], meaning they spread out and make ready.

The second: that His words ﴿wa-labi'sa al-mihad﴾ mean "and how wretched is the place of settling," like His words: ﴿Hell, they will burn therein, and how wretched is the abode (al-qarar)﴾ [Ibrahim: 29]. Some scholars said: al-mihad is the bedding for sleep. Since the one punished in the Fire is cast upon the fire of Hell, He made that a mihad (bedding) and firash (couch) for him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 207:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among mankind is he who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is Kind to the servants.﴾

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, described in the preceding verse the state of the one who gives up his religion in pursuit of worldly life, He mentioned in this verse the state of the one who gives up his worldly life, his self and his wealth in pursuit of the religion. So He said: ﴿And among mankind is he who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah.﴾ Then, there are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), there are several narrations.

One of them: Ibn 'Abbas narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Suhayb ibn Sinan, the client (mawla) of 'Abd Allah ibn Jud'an, and concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and concerning Sumayya his mother, and Yasir his father, and Bilal, the client of Abu Bakr, and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, and 'Abis, the client of Huwaytib, whom the polytheists seized and tortured. As for Suhayb, he said to the people of Makkah: "I am an old man, and I have wealth and property, and it will not harm you whether I was with you or with your enemy. I have spoken a word, and I dislike to abandon it. I will give you my wealth and my property, and I will buy my religion from you." So they accepted this from him and let him go, and he set off returning to Madinah, and the verse was revealed. And when Suhayb entered Madinah, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, met him and said to him: "Your sale has been profitable." Suhayb said to him: "And yours too; so what is this?" He said: "Allah revealed concerning you such and such," and he recited the verse to him. As for Khabbab ibn al-Aratt and Abu Dhar, they fled and came to Madinah. As for Sumayya, she was tied between two camels and then killed, and Yasir was killed. As for the rest, they gave to the torturers some of what the polytheists wanted, and so they were left alone. And concerning them was revealed the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged﴾ [al-Nahl: 41], referring to the torment of the people of Makkah, ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾ [al-Nahl: 41], through victory and booty, ﴿but the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾. And concerning them was revealed: ﴿except one who has been forced while his heart is at rest with faith﴾.

The second narration: it was revealed concerning a man who enjoined what is right and forbade what is wrong, related from 'Umar, 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The third narration: it was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who slept on the bed of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of his departure to the cave. It is related that when he slept on his bed, Jibril, peace be upon him, stood at his head, and Mika'il at his feet, and Jibril was calling out: "Bakh, bakh! Who is like you, O son of Abu Talib! Allah boasts of you to the angels." And the verse was revealed.

* * *

The second issue: most exegetes hold that what is meant by this "purchase" is "sale." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they sold him for a meager price﴾ [Yusuf: 20], meaning they sold him. The reality of this is that the responsible person sells his self for the reward of the Hereafter, and this sale is that he expends it in obedience to Allah, through prayer, fasting, pilgrimage and jihad, and then through that he attains the reward of Allah. What he expends of himself is like a commodity, the one who expends it is like the seller, and Allah is like the buyer, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties in exchange for that they will have Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111]. Allah the Exalted has also named that a trade, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment? You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives﴾ [al-Saff: 10–11].

In my view, it is possible to keep the word "purchase" (shira') on its apparent meaning. That is because whoever proceeds to disbelief, polytheism, indulgence in the pleasures of this world and turning away from the Hereafter, falls into everlasting punishment, so in effect it is as if his self had been his own; but through disbelief and corruption it leaves his possession and becomes a right of the Fire and of punishment. When he abandons disbelief and corruption and proceeds to faith and obedience, it is as if he has bought back his self from punishment and the Fire. Thus the state of the believer is like that of a mukatab (a slave who has contracted to buy his freedom) who gives countable dirhams and buys his self with them. Likewise, the believer gives countable breaths and buys his self with them forever. But the mukatab remains a slave as long as he owes a single dirham; likewise the responsible person is not freed from the bondage of servitude as long as he has a single breath in this world. For this reason 'Isa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿and He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I remain alive﴾ [Maryam: 31], and Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet, peace be upon him: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr: 99].

If it is said: Allah the Exalted made Himself the buyer when He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their selves and their properties﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], and this prevents the believer from being a buyer.

We say: there is no contradiction between the two matters. It is like one who buys a garment with a slave: each of them is a seller and each of them is a buyer. Likewise here. And according to this interpretation, there is no need to abandon the apparent meaning or to take the word "purchase" to mean "sale."

Having understood this, we say: every hardship that a person bears in seeking the religion falls under this verse. It includes the one who strives (mujahid), and the one who sacrifices his life and endures being killed, as Abu 'Ammar and his mother did; and it includes the runaway from the disbelievers to the Muslims; and it includes the one who buys his self from the disbelievers with his wealth, as Suhayb did; and it includes the one who manifests the religion and the truth in the presence of an oppressive ruler.

It is related that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, sent an army, and they besieged a fortress. One of them advanced, fought until he was killed. Some of the people said: "He threw himself into destruction (al-tahlukah)." 'Umar said: "You have lied. May Allah have mercy on so-and-so," and he recited: ﴿And among mankind is he who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah.﴾

Then know that the hardship that a person bears must necessarily be in accordance with the Shari'ah, so that by means of it he enters under the verse. As for what is contrary to the Shari'ah, it is not included in it; rather that is counted as casting oneself into destruction, like the case of one who fears death from bathing after major impurity (janabah) and does so anyway. Qatadah said: "By Allah, they were not the people of Harura, the Kharijites who passed through the religion; rather they were companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Muhajirun and the Ansar. When they saw the polytheists claiming another god alongside Allah, they fought for the religion of Allah, and they sold themselves out of zeal for Allah and jihad in His cause."

The second issue (as numbered in the text): ﴿yashri nafsahu ibtigha'a marḍati Allah﴾ means "for the sake of seeking the pleasure of Allah," and "yashri" means "yashtari" (buys).

As for the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Kind to the servants﴾, among His kindness is that He made everlasting bliss a reward for a small, finite deed. Among His kindness is that He permitted them the word of disbelief to preserve the self. Among His kindness is that He does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Among His kindness and mercy is that one who persists in disbelief for a hundred years, if he repents even for a moment, Allah drops all that punishment, and gives him everlasting reward. Among His kindness is that the self and the wealth belong to Him, and yet He buys His own possession with His possession, out of grace, mercy and benevolence.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 208:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, enter into submission (al-silm) completely, and do not follow the steps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related about the hypocrite that he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and progeny, He commanded the believers with what opposes that, namely agreement in Islam and in its laws. So He said: ﴿O you who have believed, enter into submission completely﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "*al-silm*" with a fatha on the sin, and likewise in His saying ﴿and if they incline to peace (lil-silm)﴾ [al-Anfal: 61] and His saying ﴿and call to peace (al-silm)﴾ [Muhammad: 35]. Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash, read "*al-silam*" with a kasra on the sin in all of these. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the sin in this verse, in the one in al-Baqarah, and in the one in surah Muhammad in His saying "and call to peace (al-silm)". Ibn Amir read it with a kasra on the sin in this verse in al-Baqarah alone, and with a fatha on the sin in al-Anfal and in surah Muhammad. Some scholars went to the view that both are dialectal forms, with fatha and kasra, like *ratl* and *ritl* (a unit of weight), and *jasr* and *jisr* (bridge). Al-A'mash read it with a fatha on both the sin and the lam.

**The second issue:** The origin of this word is from submission (*al-inqiyad*). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. Islam (*al-Islam*) was called Islam only for this meaning. The name *al-silm* came to be applied to reconciliation and the abandonment of war, and this too goes back to this meaning, because at reconciliation each one submits to his counterpart and does not contend with him over it. Abu Ubayda said: in it there are three dialectal forms: *al-silm*, *al-salm*, and *al-salam*.

**The third issue:** There is a difficulty in the verse, which is that many exegetes understood *al-silm* to mean Islam, so that the sense of the verse becomes: "O you who have believed, enter into Islam." But faith is Islam, and it is known that this is not permissible. Because of this question, the exegetes mentioned several interpretations of this verse:

*The first:* The intended meaning of the verse is the hypocrites, and the sense is: "O you who have believed with your tongues, enter with your whole selves into Islam, and do not follow the steps of Satan," meaning the traces of his adornment and deception in persisting in hypocrisy. Whoever holds this interpretation argues for its soundness by the fact that this verse came directly after the mention of the hypocrites, namely His saying ﴿And among the people is one whose speech impresses you﴾ and so on. When He described the hypocrite with what was mentioned, He called in this verse to faith in the heart and to the abandonment of hypocrisy.

*The second:* This verse was revealed concerning a group of Muslims from the People of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions. When they believed in the Prophet, peace be upon him, they continued after him in venerating the laws of Musa (Moses). They venerated the Sabbath, disliked the flesh and milk of camels, and they used to say: "Abandoning these things is permitted in Islam, and obligatory in the Torah, so we abandon them out of caution." God, exalted is He, disliked that from them and commanded them to enter into *al-silm* completely, that is, into the laws of Islam completely, and not to cling to anything of the rulings of the Torah, either by believing in it or by acting upon it, because it had become abrogated (*mansukha*). ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ by clinging to the rulings of the Torah after you have come to know that they have become abrogated. Those who hold this view made His saying ﴿completely (kaffah)﴾ a qualifier of *al-silm*, as if it were said: "Enter into all the laws of Islam, in belief and in action."

*The third:* This address may be directed at the People of the Book who had not believed in the Prophet, peace be upon him. So His saying ﴿O you who have believed﴾ means: in the earlier Scripture. ﴿Enter into al-silm completely﴾ means: complete your obedience in faith, and that is by believing in all of His prophets and books. So enter, by your faith in Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his Book, into *al-silm* in its entirety. ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ in adorning for you the restriction to the religion of the Torah, on the grounds that it is a religion on which they all agree is true, on the grounds that it was stated in the Torah: "Hold to the Sabbath as long as the heavens and the earth endure." In sum, the intended meaning of "the steps of Satan" is the doubts by which they cling to the persistence of that law.

*The fourth:* This address is directed at the Muslims. ﴿O you who have believed﴾ with their tongues. ﴿Enter into al-silm completely﴾, that is, persist in Islam in what you undertake of your lifetime, and do not depart from it or from any of its laws. ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾, that is, do not turn toward the doubts that the people of error and misguidance cast upon you. Whoever holds this interpretation says: this view is reinforced by what precedes this verse and by what follows it. As for what precedes it, it is what God mentioned in the description of that hypocrite in His saying ﴿He strives in the land to cause corruption therein﴾, and what we mentioned there, that it means casting doubts upon the Muslims. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Persist in your Islam, and do not follow those doubts that the hypocrites mention." As for what follows this verse, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210], meaning: these disbelievers are obstinate and insist upon disbelief, their excuses have been removed, and they will not stop their words by this true religion except upon false matters, such as that God should come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels.

If it is said: One who is already standing in something is told "persist in it," but he is not told "enter into it," and what is mentioned in the verse is His saying ﴿enter﴾.

We reply: One who is inside a house, if he knows that in the future he will leave it, it is not impossible that he be commanded to enter it in the future, moment by moment, even though he is inside it at present, because his state of being in it is other than the state in which he is commanded to enter it. When, at a second time, he may leave it, it is correct that he be commanded to enter it. It is known that believers may depart from the qualities of faith through sleep, forgetfulness, and other states, so there is nothing impossible in God, exalted is He, commanding them to enter into Islam in the future.

*The fifth:* The *silm* mentioned in the verse means reconciliation, the abandonment of fighting and of contention. The sense is: "O you who have believed, enter into *al-silm* completely," that is, be in agreement and united in supporting the religion and bearing the trial within it. ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ by his moving you to seek this world and to contend with people. This is like His saying ﴿And do not dispute, lest you lose courage and your strength depart﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103]. He also said ﴿O you who have believed, be patient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 200], and He said ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of God, and do not divide﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103]. And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The believer wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself." Most exegetes mentioned these interpretations, but I have other interpretations of it:

*The first:* His saying ﴿O you who have believed﴾ is an indication of knowledge and assent in the heart. His saying ﴿enter into al-silm completely﴾ is an indication of abandoning sins and acts of disobedience, because disobedience is opposition to God and His Messenger, so it is correct to call abandoning it *silm*. Or the intended meaning may be: "Be submissive to God in performing acts of obedience and in abstaining from what is forbidden." This is because our school holds that faith remains alongside the occupation with sins. This is an apparent interpretation.

*The second:* The intended meaning of *silm* is the servant being content and his heart not being agitated, as is related in the hadith: "Contentment with the decree is the greatest door of God."

*The third:* The intended meaning is abandoning retaliation, as in His saying ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72], and in His saying ﴿Take forgiveness, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]. This is the discussion of the interpretations of this verse.

**The fourth issue:** Al-Qaffal said: "*kaffah*" may refer back to those addressed by the command to enter, i.e., "Enter all of you into *al-silm*, and do not separate or differ." Qutrub said: the Arabs say "I saw the people *kaffatan* and *kaffin*, and I saw the women *kaffat*." It may also refer back to Islam, i.e., "Enter into Islam entirely," that is, into all its laws. Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: this is closest to the apparent meaning of the exegesis, because they were commanded to undertake all of it. The meaning of *kaffah* in the language is "that which restrains and prevents." One says "I restrained so-and-so from evil," meaning I prevented him. One says "*kaff al-qamis*" (the cuff of the shirt) because it holds back the garment from spreading; and the extremity of the hand is called *kaff* because by it one is restrained from the rest of the body; and a man who is *makfuf* is one whose sight is restrained from seeing. So *kaffah* means "restraining," and then it became a name for the comprehensive whole, because gathering prevents separation and deviation. So His saying ﴿enter into al-silm completely﴾ means: enter into the laws of Islam up to where the laws of Islam end, so that you restrain yourselves from abandoning any part of its laws. Or the meaning may be: "Enter, all of you, so that you prevent any one of you from not entering it."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and do not follow the steps of Satan﴾, the meaning is: do not obey him. It is well known in speech to say of one who follows a person's custom that he "followed his footsteps," and there is no difference between that and saying "I followed his steps." *Khutuwat* is the plural of *khutwah*, and this has already been discussed.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: "*mubin*" is a quality of the eloquent one who expresses what is in his heart. I say: What indicates the soundness of this meaning is His saying ﴿Ha Mim. By the Clear Book﴾ [al-Dukhan: 1-2], and by His saying *mubinan* He means nothing but that.

If it is said: How is it possible to describe Satan as "clear," when we do not see his essence nor hear his speech?

We reply: When God, exalted is He, made clear his enmity toward Adam and his progeny, on account of that matter it is correct to describe him as "a clear enemy," even if he is not seen. An example: one who openly shows enmity toward a man in a distant land may correctly be said to be "a clear enemy to you," even though he is not present with him at the moment. I have another way of understanding this: the basic meaning of *ibanah* (making clear) is cutting off, and *bayan* (clarity) is called that for this reason, since it cuts off some possibilities from others. So describing Satan as "clear" means that he cuts off the responsible person, by his whispering, from obedience to God, from His reward, and from His good pleasure.

If it is said: Satan's being an enemy to us is either because he intends to inflict pains and hardships upon us at present, or because by his whispering he prevents us from the religion and from reward. The first is false, for if it were so he would have caused us illnesses, pains and calamities, and it is known that this is not the case. And if it is the second, it is also false, because whoever accepts that whispering does so from his own self, as He said: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. If this is established, how can it be said that he is "a clear enemy" in enmity, when the situation is as we have described?

The answer: He is an enemy in both respects together. As for the fact that he seeks to inflict harm upon us, he is indeed so, except that God, exalted is He, prevented him from that. And it does not follow from his being intent upon inflicting harm upon us that he is able to do so. As for the fact that he proceeds to whispering, it is known that adorning sins and casting doubts are all a cause for a person's falling into falsehood, and by it he becomes deprived of reward. So this is among the greatest aspects of enmity.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 209:**

[Page 179]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that God is Mighty, Wise﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Abu al-Sammal read *zaliltum* (زَلِلْتُمْ) with a kasra on the first lam. Both are dialects (*lughatan*), like *dalaltu* and *daliltu*.

**The second issue:** It is said *zalla yazillu zululan wa-zilzalan* when his foot slipped and he slid in mud. It is also said of one who slips out of a state he was in: "the situation slipped away from him." A sin is called a *zallah* (slip), meaning a slip that moves a person away from what is obligatory. So His saying ﴿if you slip﴾ means: you err from the truth and transgress it.

As for the occasion of revelation of this verse, they differed concerning *al-silm* (peace) in His saying *kaffah* (entirely). Whoever said that the first (address) concerns the hypocrites, then the second is likewise; whoever said that it concerns the People of the Book, then the second is likewise. Apply the rest accordingly.

It is related from Ibn Abbas: ﴿if you slip﴾ regarding the prohibition of the Sabbath and the flesh of camels, ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ) and his laws, ﴿then know that God is Mighty﴾ in retribution, ﴿Wise﴾ in all His acts. Upon this they said: "If you wish, O Messenger of God, we will abandon every book except your book." So God, exalted, revealed: ﴿O you who believe, believe in God and His Messenger﴾ (An-Nisa 4:136).

**The third issue:** Concerning His saying ﴿if you slip﴾, there is a question: a conditional ruling is only appropriate with regard to one who does not know the outcomes of affairs. Qatada answered this, saying: "He knew that they would slip, but He, exalted, mentioned that and threatened over it so that it would be a proof for Him against His creation."

**The fourth issue:** His saying, exalted, ﴿if you slip﴾ means: if you deviate from the path you were commanded to follow. On this interpretation, both major and minor sins fall under it, for deviation occurs through the great as well as through the small. He, exalted, threatened for all of that as a deterrent from departing from the path, so that the believer would guard against both the little and the much of it. For whatever is among the major sins, there is no doubt about the obligation to avoid it. And whatever is not known to be a major sin, one cannot be sure that punishment is not deserved for it, and in that case avoiding it is obligatory.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted, ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾ encompasses all the proofs, both rational (*ʿaqliyyah*) and transmitted (*samʿiyyah*). The rational proofs are the evidences for matters which establish the validity of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and which cannot be established except after they are established: such as knowledge of the origination of the world and its need of a Creator who knows all things, is capable of all possibilities, and is free from all needs; and such as the knowledge of the distinction between a miracle and magic, and the knowledge of a miracle's indication of truthfulness. All of these are rational clear proofs. As for the transmitted clear proofs, they are the clarification that comes through the Qur'an and the clarification that comes through the Sunnah. All of these clear proofs are included in the verse, inasmuch as the excuse of the responsible person does not cease when all these clear proofs have come.

**The sixth issue:** The Qadi said: The verse indicates that taking someone to account for a sin does not occur except after clarification and the removal of the cause. So when He makes the threat conditional upon the coming and occurrence of the clear proofs, it is more fitting that the threat should not apply to one who has no ability at all to act. Also, indication is only benefited by those who have capacity, and capacity may benefit even when indication is absent. He also said: The verse indicates that what is considered is the arrival of the clear proofs, not the certainty of the responsible person. From this aspect, the verse indicates that one who is able to reflect and reason is subject to the threat just as one who knows is. Thus the view of whoever claimed that God has no proof against one who knows and recognizes is invalidated.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted, ﴿then know that God is Mighty, Wise﴾, there are issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** One may say: His saying ﴿if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you﴾ points to their sin and offense, so how does His saying ﴿that God is Mighty, Wise﴾ indicate warning and threat?

The answer: The Mighty (*al-ʿAziz*) is one who cannot be prevented from His will, and this is only achieved through complete power. It has been established that He, glorified and exalted, is capable of all possibilities, so He is Mighty in an absolute sense. Thus the meaning of the verse becomes: "If you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that God is capable over you, and no preventer prevents Him from you, so what He wills from you does not escape Him." This is the utmost in threat, because it combines kinds of fear that the threat by mentioning punishment does not combine. A father may say to his son: "If you disobey me, you know who I am, and you know my power over you and the severity of my might." This speech is more forceful in deterrence than mentioning beating or other things.

If it is asked: Does this verse include promise just as it includes threat? We say: Yes, inasmuch as He followed it with His saying ﴿Wise﴾, for it is fitting for wisdom to distinguish between the one who does good and the one who does evil. Just as it is becoming for the Wise to bring punishment upon the evildoer, so it is becoming for Him to bring reward to the doer of good. Indeed, this is more fitting to wisdom and closer to mercy.

**The second issue:** Whoever argued that nothing is obligatory before the Revealed Law (*shar*') used this verse. He said: Because He, exalted, established the threat and warning conditional upon the coming of the clear proofs, and the word "clear proofs" (*al-bayyinat*) is a plural word encompassing all of them. This indicates that the threat is conditional upon the coming of all the clear proofs. Before the Law, not all the clear proofs had come, so the threat must not occur, and therefore obligation must not be established before the Law.

**The third issue:** Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i said: If the matter were as the Mujbira (those who hold that human acts are compelled) say, that He, exalted, wills from the foolish and the unbelievers foolishness and unbelief, it would not be permissible to describe Him as Wise, because whoever does foolishness and wills it is foolish, and the foolish is not wise. The Ashab (our companions, the Ash'arites) answered: The Wise is the one who knows the outcomes of affairs. Thus the meaning of His being Wise returns to His being knowing of all known things, and that does not contradict His being the Creator of all things and willing them. Rather, it necessitates that, for as we have explained, if He willed what He knew not to exist, He would have willed to make Himself ignorant. They said: If that were necessary, then whenever He commanded something whose non-existence He knew, He would have commanded the making of Himself ignorant.

We say: This would only follow if commanding something were commanding what cannot be completed except through it, and this we reject. If they say: If it were not so, it would follow that He imposes what cannot be borne, we say: This is permissible according to us. And God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** It is related that a reciter recited ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ and a Bedouin heard him and rejected it, saying: "If this is the speech of God, He would not say so. The Wise does not mention forgiveness at the time of slipping, for that is an incitement to it."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 210 (part 1 of 2):

God the Exalted said: ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels, and the matter be decided? And to God all matters are returned.﴾

Know that there are several issues concerning this verse.

The first issue: The thorough discussion of the word "nazar" (looking/awaiting) has been mentioned in the commentary on His saying: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23]. The scholars agree that it comes with the meaning of "waiting" (intizar). God the Exalted said: ﴿So the messengers will wait to see what the reply will be﴾ [al-Naml: 35]. Therefore what is meant by His saying ﴿Do they await﴾ is waiting.

* * *

The second issue: The rational scholars agree that He, glorified and exalted, is exempt from coming and going, and this is demonstrated by several considerations:

The first of them: It is established in the science of principles (usul) that whatever can be described as coming and going cannot be separated from motion and rest, and both of these are originated (muhdath). What cannot be separated from the originated is itself originated. It follows that everything to which coming and going can apply must be originated and created, while the eternal God is impossible to be so.

The second: Whatever can be described as moving from one place to another is either so small and insignificant, like the indivisible part (al-juz' alladhi la yatajazza'), which is invalid by the agreement of rational people; or it is not so, but is something large, such that one of its sides differs from the other, and so it is composed of parts and portions. Every composite depends for its existence on the existence of each of its parts, and each of its parts is other than it; so every composite is dependent on something other than itself. Everything dependent on something other than itself is contingent in its essence (mumkin li-dhatihi), and everything contingent in its essence needs, for its existence, a determiner (murajjih) and a bringer-into-being (muwjid). So whatever is like this is originated, created, preceded by non-existence, and the eternal God is precluded from being like this.

The third: Whatever can be described as moving from one place to another is bounded and finite, and so it is specified with a determined quantity, although it was possible in the intellect for it to be upon a greater or lesser quantity. Its being specified with that determined quantity must be due to the preference of a preferrer and the specification of a specifier. Whatever is like this is the act of a free-choosing agent, and whatever is like this is originated and created. Therefore the eternal, pre-eternal God is precluded from being like this.

The fourth: If we permit that the thing to which coming and going can apply be an eternal, pre-eternal god, then we cannot judge the negation of divinity of the sun and the moon. Some of our intelligent companions used to say: "There is no defect in the sun and the moon that prevents saying they are divine, except that they are bodies that can be subject to absence and presence. So whoever permits coming and going upon God the Exalted, why does he not judge the sun to be divine? And what obliges him to affirm another existent that he claims to be a god?"

The fifth: God the Exalted related of the Friend (Khalil), upon him be peace, that he disputed the divinity of the stars, the moon and the sun by his saying: ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ [al-An'am: 76]. And there is no meaning to "setting" except absence and presence. So whoever permits absence and presence upon God the Exalted has disputed the proof of the Friend, upon him be peace, and has declared God a liar in confirming the Friend upon him be peace in that.

The sixth: When Pharaoh, may the curse of God be upon him, asked Moses, upon him be peace, saying: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 23], and sought from him the quiddity, the genus and the substance, then if God, the Exalted, were a body described by shapes and measures, the answer to this question would be nothing but mentioning the form, the shape and the measure. So Moses' answer, upon him be peace, by his saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 24], ﴿your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones﴾ [al-Dukhan: 8], ﴿Lord of the East and the West﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 28], would have been an error and falsehood. This would necessitate faulting Moses, upon him be peace, in what he mentioned as the answer, and endorsing Pharaoh in his saying: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad!﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 27]. Since all of that is false, we know that He, the Exalted, is exempt from being a body, from being in a place, and from being such that coming and going can apply to Him.

The seventh: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: He is God, One (Ahad)﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. Ahad is the one perfect in oneness, and every body is divisible, by reference to the intention and by pointing, into two parts. Since He, the Exalted, is Ahad, it is impossible for Him to be a body or something occupying a space. Since He is neither a body nor occupying a space, coming and going are impossible for Him. Also, He said: ﴿Do you know anyone worthy of His name?﴾ [Maryam: 65], meaning a likeness. If He were a body occupying space, He would be like bodies in corporeality; difference only arises beyond corporeality, and that is either in magnitude or in attributes and qualities, and that does not prevent the likeness in essence. Also, He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Nothing is like Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]; had He been a body, He would have been a likeness to bodies.

The eighth: If He were a body occupying space, He would share with all other bodies in the general quality of corporeality. At that point, either He differs from them in the specific nature of His particular essence, or He does not. If the first, then what makes Him share is other than what makes Him distinct; so the general quality of being a body is other than the specific nature of His particular essence. This is impossible, because when we describe that particular essence by the concept of being a body, we have made body an attribute, and this is impossible, because body is the bearer of the attribute. And if we say that this particular essence, which is other than the concept of being a body, is not described as a body, then the essence of God, the Exalted, is a thing other than the concept of body and not described by it, and that negates His being a body. And if it is said: His essence, having been a body, does not differ from the rest of bodies in any particularity, then He is an absolute likeness to them, and whatever applies to them applies to Him; so if these bodies are originated, it is necessary that His essence be likewise. All of that is impossible. Thus it is established that He, the Exalted, is neither a body nor occupying a space, and that coming and going do not apply to Him.

* * *

Having known this, we say: The people of kalam (theology) differed concerning His saying: ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them﴾, and they mentioned several interpretations:

The first interpretation: This is the doctrine of the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih): since it has been established by decisive proofs that coming and going upon God the Exalted is impossible, we know with certainty that God's intended meaning in this verse is not coming and going, and that His intended meaning is something else. If we specify that intended meaning, we are not safe from error; so it is better to refrain from interpretation (ta'wil) and to commit the meaning of the verse in detail to God, the Exalted. This is what is meant by what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Qur'an was revealed in four aspects: an aspect that no one knows because of its obscurity; an aspect that the scholars know and explain; an aspect that we know only through the Arabic language; and an aspect that none knows but God. We have thoroughly discussed this saying in the commentary on His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾.

The third interpretation: This is the saying of the majority of the mutakallimun: that interpretation in detail is necessary. Then they mentioned several interpretations:

The first: What is meant by ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them﴾ is that the signs of God should come to them. Thus the coming of the signs is made a coming of Him, in magnification of the matter of the signs, as one says: "The king has come" when a great army has come from his side. What indicates the soundness of this interpretation is that He, the Exalted, said in the preceding verse: ﴿But if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that God is Mighty and Wise﴾, mentioning that in the context of warning and threat. Then He, the Exalted, emphasized that with His saying: ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them﴾. It is well known that, on the supposition that coming upon God were valid, mere presence would not be a cause for threat and warning, because at the presence He would both rebuke the disbelievers and punish them, and reward the believers and bring them near. Thus it is established that mere presence is not a cause for threat and warning. Since the intent of the verse is nothing but warning and threat, it is necessary that the coming of awe, subjugation and threat be understood in the verse; and when we understand that, the doubt is removed entirely. This is a fine interpretation that accords with the composition of the verse.

The second interpretation: What is meant by ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them﴾ is that the command of God should come, i.e., the command of God. The principle in this matter is that when He, the Exalted, mentions an act and attributes it to something, if that is impossible, then it must be diverted to interpretation, as the scholars said concerning His saying: ﴿Those who wage war against God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33], where what is meant is "those who wage war against His allies"; and He said: ﴿Ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], where what is meant is "ask the people of the town." So likewise His saying: ﴿God comes to them﴾ means that the command of God comes to them; and His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr: 22] means that the command of your Lord comes. There is nothing in this but the omission of the modified noun and the placing of the modified-to noun in its place, and this is a well-known metaphor: one says "the emir struck so-and-so," "crucified him," "gave him," and what is meant is that he ordered that, not that he personally performed that act. Then two things confirm the soundness of this interpretation:

The first: His saying here: ﴿God comes to them﴾ and His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ are reports about the state of the Resurrection. Then He mentioned this very event in Surah al-Nahl, saying: ﴿Do they await only that the angels should come to them, or that the command of your Lord should come?﴾ [al-Nahl: 33]. So this ruling becomes an explanation of that ambiguous text, since all these verses came concerning one single event, and it is not far-fetched to interpret some of them by others.

The second: He, the Exalted, said after it: ﴿And the matter is decided﴾, and there is no doubt that the alif and lam are for a previously known referent, so there must have been a mention of a matter before that, so that the alif and lam point to it; and that is none other than what we supposed: that His saying ﴿God comes to them﴾ means that the command of God comes to them.

If it is said: The command of God, according to you, is an eternal attribute, so coming upon it is impossible; and according to the Mu'tazilah it is sounds, so they are accidents, and coming upon them is likewise impossible.

We reply: The word "amr" in the language has two meanings:

One of them is the act, the affair and the way, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a blink of the eye﴾ [al-Qamar: 50], and ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [Hud: 97]. And in the proverb: "For some matter Qasir split his nose," and "For some matter he who rules, rules." So "amr" here is understood as the act, which is what befits those situations of terrors and the manifestation of the clear signs; and this is the first interpretation we mentioned. As for our understanding of "amr" as the command that is the opposite of prohibition, there are two possibilities:

One of them: that the sense is that a herald will proclaim on the Day of Resurrection: "Behold, God commands you with such and such," and that is the coming of the command. His saying ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ means "together with canopies," and the sense is that the hearing of that proclamation and the arrival of those canopies will occur at one time.

The second: that what is meant by the coming of the command of God in canopies of clouds is the occurrence of specific articulated sounds in those clouds indicating God's ruling upon each person according to what befits him of happiness and wretchedness; or that what is meant is that He created patterns arranged in canopies of clouds, owing to their intense whiteness, and the blackness of that writing makes known by it the state of the people of the place of standing regarding promise, threat and other things; and the benefit of the canopies of clouds is that He made them a sign of what He intends to send down upon the people, so that by it they know that the matter has come and drawn near.

The sixth [interpretation]: and it is, in my view, the clearest of all that has preceded it. We have mentioned that the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿O you who believe, enter into submission (al-silm) completely﴾ were revealed concerning the Jews. On this basis, His words ﴿But if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ are addressed to the Jews. In that case, His words, exalted is He, ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them within canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾ are a report about the Jews. The meaning is: they will not accept your religion unless Allah comes to them within canopies of clouds and the angels. Do you not see that they did the same with Moses, saying: ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55]? When this is a report about the state of the Jews, and it does not prevent the verse from being applied to its apparent meaning, then this is because the Jews held the doctrine of anthropomorphism (tashbih), and they permitted coming and going upon Allah, and they used to say that He, exalted is He, manifested Himself to Moses, peace be upon him, on the mountain within canopies of clouds, and they sought the like of that in the time of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. On this basis, this statement is a report of the belief of the Jews who held anthropomorphism, so there is no need then for ta'wil (interpretation), nor for carrying the wording upon majaz (figurative usage). In sum, the verse indicates that a people await that Allah should come to them, and there is nothing in the verse indicating that they are right in that expectation or that they are wrong. On this basis, the difficulty falls away.

If it is said: On this interpretation, how does His statement ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ relate to it?

We say: The reasoning is that when He, exalted is He, related their obstinacy and their hesitation in accepting the religion on this corrupt condition, He then mentioned after it something that serves as a threat, saying: ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned.﴾ This interpretation is, in my view, more evident than all that has preceded it, and Allah knows best the reality of His speech.

The seventh [interpretation]: what al-Qaffal related in his Tafsir from Abu al-'Aliyah, which is that the coming within the canopies is attributed to the angels; as for what is attributed to Allah, may His majesty be exalted, it is the coming alone. So the speech is taken with inversion and reordering (al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir), and he cites in support of its soundness the reading of one who recited: "Do they await only that Allah should come to them, and the angels, within canopies of clouds." Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This interpretation is objectionable.

* * *

As for His statement ﴿within canopies of clouds﴾: know that "al-zulal" (canopies) is the plural of zullah, which is that by which Allah shades you. And the "ghamam" (clouds) is not like that except when it is gathered and piled up. So "canopies of clouds" is an expression for separate pieces, each piece of which is at the utmost density and magnitude; thus each piece is a zullah, and the plural is zulal. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when a wave covers them like canopies﴾ [Luqman: 32]. And some of them recited: "illa an ya'tiyahumu Allahu fi zilalin mina al-ghamam" (in shadows [zilal] of clouds). This may be that zilal is the plural of zullah, like qilal and qullah, and it may be the plural of zill.

Page 185

Having known this, we say: the meaning is: they await only that the subjugation of Allah and His punishment should come to them within canopies of clouds.

If it is said: Why would the punishment come to them in the clouds?

We say: For several reasons:

The first: clouds are the place where mercy is expected, so when punishment descends from them, the matter is more dreadful, because evil that comes from where one does not expect it is more terrifying and more frightful, just as good that comes from where one does not expect it has greater effect in gladness. How much more so when evil comes from where one expects good. From this, the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned﴾ [al-Zumar: 47] weighed heavily upon those who reflect on the Book of Allah.

The second: the descent of the clouds is a sign of the manifestation of what will be among the greatest terrors on the Day of Resurrection. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the day the sky will split open with clouds and the angels will be sent down in descent﴾ ﴿The sovereignty that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Furqan: 25–26].

The third: from the clouds descend many drops, not limited or restricted; likewise this cloud descends with drops of punishment, descending without limit.

As for His statement, ﴿and the angels﴾, it is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon what preceded it, and the sense is: "and the angels will come to them." The coming of the angels can be taken in its literal sense, so it is obligatory to take it so, and the meaning becomes: the command of Allah and His signs will come, and the angels together with that will come to carry out what they have been commanded with of humiliation or punishment or other matters of the judgments of the Day of Resurrection.

* * *

As for His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and the matter is decided﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: the meaning is that what they were promised has been completed, so at that time no excuse will be accepted from them, no punishment will be averted from them, and no stratagem will avail in repelling what has befallen them.

The second issue: His statement ﴿and the matter is decided﴾ means: "and He decides the matter." The sense is: "unless Allah comes and decides the matter." So the past tense is placed in the position of the future, and this is frequent in the Qur'an, especially concerning the affairs of the Hereafter, for reports about them often occur in the past tense. Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. The reasons for choosing this figurative usage (majaz) are two:

One of them: to alert to the nearness of the matter of the Hereafter, as though the Hour has already come and what Allah wills to bring about has occurred.

The second: to emphasize strongly that it must come to pass, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has striven; thus, by the certainty and definiteness of its occurrence, it is as though it has already occurred and taken place.

The third issue: the matter mentioned here is the decisive judgment among the creatures, the taking of rights for their owners, and the placing of every responsible person in his station in Paradise or Hell. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter is decided: "Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth"﴾ [Ibrahim: 22].

Having known this, we say: His statement ﴿and the matter is decided﴾ indicates that the states of the Resurrection come into being all at once without delay, for He, exalted is He, has no repeller of His decree and no preventer of His judgment.

The fourth issue: Mu'adh ibn Jabal recited "wa qada'u al-amr" (and the decree of the matter), as a nominative verbal noun (masdar marfu') coordinated upon "the angels."

* * *

As for His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: among the anthropomorphists (mujassimah) is one who said: the word "ila" (to) denotes the endpoint of a goal, and that requires that Allah, exalted is He, be in a place that is reached on the Day of Resurrection. The people of tawhid (monotheism) answered him in two ways:

The first: He, exalted is He, has given His servants authority in the world over many of the affairs of His creation. So when they reach the Hereafter, there is no possessor of judgment over the servants other than Him, as He said: ﴿And the command that Day belongs to Allah﴾ [al-Infitar: 19]. This is like the saying: "Our affair has returned to the amir," when he is the one who specifically deals with it. A parallel to it is His statement: ﴿And to Allah is the final destination﴾ [al-Nur: 42], even though the creatures at that hour are in His dominion and authority.

The second: Abu Muslim said: He, exalted is He, has given everyone authority in the abode of testing and trial over matters as a test. So when the affairs of this abode end and we arrive at the abode of reward and punishment, the entire command will belong to Allah alone. If that is so, then He is worthy to be feared and obeyed, to be entered into submission as He commanded, and to be guarded against the footsteps of Satan as He forbade.

The second issue: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim recited "turja'u" (are returned) with a dammah on the ta', in the sense of "tarid" (come back/are brought back), as one says: "raja'tuhu," meaning "radadtuhu" (I returned him). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾ [Fussilat: 50], and in another place: ﴿And if I am sent back to my Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 36], and in another place: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am: 62]. And He said: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ ﴿that I may do righteousness﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], meaning "return me." Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "tarji'u" (return) with a fatha on the ta', meaning "tasir" (become/arrive), like His statement: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah all matters will arrive﴾ [al-Shura: 53], and His statement: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 25], and ﴿To Allah is your return﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48].

Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The meaning in the two readings is close, because things return to Him, glorified and exalted, and He returns them to Himself by annihilating the world and establishing the Resurrection. Then he said: In His statement ﴿turja'u al-umur﴾ with a dammah on the ta', there are three meanings:

One of them: this which we have mentioned, namely that He, glorified and exalted, returns them, as He said in this verse: ﴿and the matter is decided﴾, and He is the one who decides it.

The second: that it is according to the manner of the Arabs in their saying: "So-and-so is pleased with himself" (yu'jabu bi-nafsihi), and a man says to another: "Where is he taking you?" even though no one is taking him.

The third: that the very natures and attributes of people, since they bear witness against them that they are created, originated, and held to account, and since they refer their affairs back to their Creator, His statement ﴿turja'u al-umur﴾ means that the servants return their affairs to Him and to His judgment by the testimony of their own selves. This is like His statement: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 1], for this glorification is according to the testimony of the state, not according to utterance by the tongue. And upon this is also understood His statement: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15]. It has been said: the meaning is that the believers prostrate to Him willingly, and the disbelievers prostrate to Him unwillingly, by the testimony of their own selves that they are servants of Allah. Thus it is likewise permissible to say that the servants return their affairs to Allah and acknowledge their return to Him: as for the believers, by speech; as for the disbelievers, by the testimony of their state.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 211:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them. And whoever substitutes the favour of Allah after it has come to him—indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿Sal﴾ (ask). Originally it was isal (ask), and the hamza, which is the middle radical of the verb, was dropped for lightness because of its frequent occurrence in speech, and its vowel was transferred to the consonant preceding it. With this inflection, the alif of connection (alif al-wasl) was dispensed with. Qutrub said: it is said saala yas'alu, like za'ara al-asadu yaz'aru (the lion roared), and sala yasalu, like khafa yakhafu (to fear). The imperative in it is sal, like khaf. On this reckoning, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (sala sa'il) on the pattern of qala and kala. As for His saying ﴿kam﴾ (how many), it is an indeclinable noun (ism mabni) built on quiescence, used for number. It is said that it is composed of the particle of comparison kaf with ﴿ma﴾, then ma was shortened and its mim was made quiescent, and it was built on quiescence because it contains the interrogative particle. It is sometimes used in statements and sometimes in questions. The most common usage of Arabic is to put it in the genitive in statements and in the accusative in questions, while some Arabs put it in the accusative in statements and in the genitive in questions. Here it may be interrogative and it may be declarative.

The second issue: Know that the intended meaning of "Ask the Children of Israel" is not that they should inform you of those signs so that you come to know them, because the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, already knew those circumstances through Allah's informing him. Rather, the intended meaning is to emphasize the rebuke against turning away from the proofs of Allah, exalted is He. The explanation of this statement is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who believe, enter into submission completely and do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 208], commanding Islam and forbidding disbelief. Then He said: ﴿But if you slip after clear proofs have come to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209], meaning, if you turn away from this obligation you become deserving of threat by His saying: ﴿then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209]. Then He clarified that threat by His saying: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them within canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210]. Then He reinforced that threat by His saying: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾, meaning: ask these present ones that We, when We gave their forefathers clear signs, they denied them, so they deserved punishment from Allah, exalted is He. This is an admonition to these present ones that if they slipped away from the signs of Allah, they would fall into punishment just as those earlier ones fell into it. The purpose of mentioning this narrative is that they should take lessons from others, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So take warning, O you with vision﴾ [al-Hashr: 2], and He said: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf: 111]. This is the explanation of the connection of the discourse.

The third issue: Abu 'Amr distinguished in ﴿sal﴾ between its connection by waw or fa' and its beginning as a fresh start. He read (salhum) and ﴿sal Bani Isra'il﴾ without a hamza, while ﴿wa-s'al al-qaryah﴾ [Yusuf: 82], ﴿fa-s'al alladhina yaqra'una al-kitab﴾ [Yunus: 94], and ﴿wa-s'alu Allaha min fadlihi﴾ [al-Nisa': 32] he read with the hamza. Al-Kisa'i equalized all of them and read all without a hamza. The reason for the distinction is that the lightening in the fresh start leads to dropping the initial hamza, which is independent, and this is not so in connection. Al-Kisa'i followed the Mushaf, since the alif is dropped in all of them.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿a clear sign﴾ (min ayatin bayyinatin) has two opinions:

One: What is meant is the miracles of Musa, upon him be peace, such as splitting the sea, shading by clouds, sending down manna and quails, lifting the mountain, Allah's speaking to Musa, upon him be peace, from the cloud, sending down the Torah upon them, and making clear to them the guidance from disbelief. All of that are clear signs.

The second opinion: the meaning is: how many proofs We gave them, clear proofs for Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, by which his truthfulness and the soundness of his law are known.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever substitutes the favour of Allah﴾, in it there are issues:

The first issue: It is read (wa-man yubdil) with lightening.

The second issue: Abu Muslim said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the estimate is: how many clear signs We gave them and they disbelieved in them; but His saying ﴿and whoever substitutes the favour of Allah﴾ does not indicate this implied elision.

The third issue: Concerning (the favour of Allah) here there are two opinions:

The first opinion: What is meant is His signs and proofs, which are among the greatest kinds of Allah's favours, because they are the means of guidance and salvation from misguidance. Then according to this opinion, regarding their substituting them there are two views. Whoever says that the clear sign means the miracles of Musa, upon him be peace, says: what is meant by substituting them is that Allah, exalted is He, manifested them so that they would be means of their guidance, but they made them means of their misguidance, like His saying: ﴿So it increased them in filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125]. Whoever says that the clear sign means what is in the Torah and the Gospel of the proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad, upon him be peace, says: what is meant by substituting them is distorting them and introducing doubt into them.

The second opinion: What is meant by the favour of Allah is what Allah gave them of the means of health, security and sufficiency, and Allah, exalted is He, is the One who replaced the favour with retribution when they disbelieved. But He attributed the substitution to them, because it was a cause from their side, namely their abandoning the upholding of what was obligatory upon them of acting by those clear signs.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after it has come to him﴾, if we interpret the favour as the giving of signs and proofs, then the meaning of His saying ﴿after it has come to him﴾ is: after he became able to know them, or after he knew them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they distort it after they had understood it, while they know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75]; because when he is not able to know them, or does not know them, they are as if absent from him. If we interpret the favour as what pertains to the worldly life, of health, security and sufficiency, then there is no doubt that when these means are obtained, gratitude becomes more obligatory, so disbelief becomes more ugly. Therefore He said: ﴿indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: in it there is an ellipsis, and the meaning is "severe in punishment to him."

[Continued on page 5]
I say: 'Abd al-Qahir al-Nahwi explained in his book "Dala'il al-I'jaz" that leaving out this ellipsis is preferable, because the purpose of the verse is to instill fear by describing Him, in His essence, as severe in punishment, without regard to His being severe in punishment for this or for that. Then al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: al-'iqab is a punishment that follows a crime.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 212 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they mock those who believe. But those who fear God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. God provides for whomever He wills without reckoning.﴾

Know that when God, may He be exalted, mentioned earlier the condition of those who exchange God's blessing after it has come to them, namely the disbelievers who denied the proofs and the prophets and turned away from them, He followed it with mention of the cause for which this was their way. So He said: ﴿The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve.﴾ The essence of this statement is to make known the weakness of the intellects of the disbelievers and polytheists in preferring the transient adornments of this world over the lasting ranks of the Hereafter.

Regarding the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: Why did He not say "زُيِّنَتْ" (zuyyinat, feminine) instead of "زُيِّنَ" (zuyyina, masculine)?

There are several reasons:

First, which is the view of al-Farra': "life" and "living" are one and the same. If it is feminine, then it is according to the wording; if it is masculine, then it is according to the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:275], and ﴿The cry seized those who did wrong﴾ [Hud 11:67].

Second, which is the view of al-Zajjaj: the feminine of "life" is not real (ḥaqīqī), because it is not an animal that has a male counterpart, like "woman and man" or "she-camel and male camel." Rather, the meaning of "life," "livelihood," and "survival" is one. So it is as if He said: "The worldly life and survival have been made attractive to those who disbelieve."

Third, which is the view of Ibn al-Anbari: He did not say "زُيِّنَتْ" because there was a separation between "زُيِّنَ" and "the worldly life" by His saying: ﴿to those who disbelieve.﴾ When a separation by a intervening element occurs between a feminine verb and its noun, it is good to use the masculine form of the verb, because the intervening element does the job of the feminine marker (the tā' of feminine).

* * *

The second issue: They mentioned several views regarding the cause of revelation (sabab al-nuzul):

The first narration: Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and the leaders of Quraysh, who used to mock the poor Muslims, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, 'Ammar, Khabbab, Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, 'Amir ibn Fuhayra, and Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, because of the poverty and hardship they were in, and their patience with various kinds of trials, while the disbelievers were in luxury and ease.

The second narration: It was revealed concerning the leaders and scholars of the Jews from the tribes of Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir, and Banu Qaynuqa', who mocked the poor Muslim emigrants (muhajirun), since they had been expelled from their homes and their properties.

The third narration: Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, who used to mock the weak Muslims and the poor emigrants. Know that there is no obstacle to its being revealed concerning all of them.

[Page 6]

* * *

The third issue: The scholars differed about the manner of this making-attractive (tazyin). As for the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that holds that humans create their own actions), they mentioned several views:

One of them: al-Jubba'i said: The one who makes it attractive is the misguided ones among the jinn and humans. They made the greed for this world attractive to the disbelievers, and made the matter of the Hereafter repulsive in their eyes, and they gave the impression that there is no truth to what is said about the matter of the Hereafter, so do not spoil your life in this world. He said: As for what the Mujbira (the determinists, who hold that God compels human actions) say, that God made it attractive, it is false. This is because the one who makes something attractive is the one who informs about its goodness. If the one making it attractive is God, exalted is He, then either He is truthful in that making-attractive or He is lying. If He is truthful, then what He made attractive must be good, and then the one who finds it good is correct; and this entails that the disbeliever is correct in his disbelief and disobedience, and this view is disbelief. If He is lying in that making-attractive, this leads to the conclusion that there is no trust in anything He says or reports, and this too is disbelief. He said: So it is established that the meaning of the verse is that the one who makes it attractive is Satan. This is the complete statement of Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i in his tafsir.

I say: This is weak. This is because God's saying ﴿made attractive to those who disbelieve﴾ encompasses all disbelievers. This requires that all the disbelievers have someone who makes it attractive to them, and the one who makes it attractive to all the disbelievers must necessarily be other than them. Unless it is said that each of them used to make it attractive to the others, but then it becomes circular. So it is established that the one who makes disbelief attractive to all the disbelievers must necessarily be other than them. Thus the claim that the ones who make it attractive are the misguided among the jinn and humans is void, because these misguided ones are also included among the disbelievers, and we have shown that the one who makes it attractive must necessarily be other than them. So this interpretation is established as weak. As for his saying: "The one who makes something attractive is the one who informs about its goodness," this is disputed. Rather, the one who makes something attractive is the one who causes the thing to be described with adornment, and these are attributes subsisting in the thing by virtue of which the thing becomes adorned. On this assumption, his argument collapses. Furthermore, even if we concede that the one who makes something attractive is the one who informs about its goodness, why can it not be said that God, exalted is He, informed about its goodness, and what is meant is that He informed about the pleasures, good things, and comforts it contains? Informing about these is not a lie, and affirming them is not disbelief. So al-Jubba'i's argument in this matter collapses entirely.

Second interpretation: Abu Muslim said: It is possible that in ﴿made attractive to those who disbelieve﴾ they made it attractive to themselves. The Arabs say to someone who strays far from them: "Where is he taking you?" They do not mean that some other traveler took him, and this is the meaning of His saying in many verses: ﴿How are they turned away?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:75], ﴿How are they diverted?﴾ [Ghafir 40:69], and so on. He reinforced this with His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not let your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:9]. So He attributed the diversion to them, since they are like the cause. And since Satan cannot force a person to act, the person is in reality the one who made it attractive to himself. Know that this is weak, because His saying "زُيِّنَ" requires that there be an adorner who adorned it, and turning from the literal to the figurative is not permissible.

Third interpretation: This one who makes it attractive is God, exalted is He. Two things indicate the soundness of this interpretation:

One of them: the reading of the one who reads ("زَيَّنَ لِلَّذِينِ كَفَرُوا الحَياةَ الدُّنْيا") in the active voice.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, so that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf 18:7].

Then those who hold this interpretation mentioned several points:

The first: It is impossible that God is the one who adorns by what He manifested in this world of freshness, radiance, goodness, and pleasure, for He did that only as a trial for His servants. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Adorned for people is the love of desires﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:14], up to His saying: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who fear God, with their Lord are gardens﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:15]. And He also said: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life, but the lasting good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope﴾ [al-Kahf 18:46]. They said: These verses are consistent, and the meaning in all of them is that God, majestic is His majesty, made this world a place of trial and testing. So He placed in human natures an inclination toward pleasures and love of desires, not in the sense of a compulsion that cannot be avoided, but in the sense of an attraction toward which the soul inclines while it is still possible to turn it away, so that the test may be completed, and so that the believer may struggle against his desire, restricting himself to what is permissible and restraining himself from what is forbidden.

The second: The meaning of the adornment is that God gave them respite in this world and did not prevent them from turning toward it and their intense greed in seeking it. This respite is what is called "adornment."

Know that all of these views which we have transmitted from the Mu'tazila face one single question: The occurrence of this adornment in the hearts of the disbelievers must have a cause that brings it about; otherwise, a thing would have come into existence without an influence, and that is impossible. Then, does this adornment in the hearts of the disbelievers tip the balance toward disbelief and disobedience over belief and obedience, or does it not tip the balance? If it does not tip the balance at all, but the person with this adornment in his heart is the same as without it, then this prevents it from being an adornment in his heart, while the text indicates that this adornment did occur. If we say that the occurrence of this adornment in his heart tips the balance toward disbelief and disobedience over belief and obedience, then free choice (ikhtiyar) has been removed. For when the state of equilibrium is impossible to tip, then the state in which one of the two sides has become inclined is even more impossible to occur. And when the tipping factor has become impossible to occur, the preponderant side becomes necessary to occur, because there is no escape from the two contradictories. This is the formulation of the question. It is well known that it is not resolved by the views which these Mu'tazila have mentioned.

The third view on establishing this interpretation: the meaning is that God, exalted is He, made attractive from the worldly life only what was among the permissible things, not the forbidden. On this view the problem disappears. But this too is weak, because God specified the disbelievers for this adornment, and making permissible things attractive is not specific to the disbelievers. So it is impossible that what is meant by this adornment is the making attractive of permissible things. Furthermore, when a believer enjoys the permissible good things of this world, his enjoyment of them is accompanied by fear and anxiety about the reckoning in the Hereafter. So even if his wealth and standing are abundant, his life is troubled and clouded, and his main aim is the reward of the Hereafter, regarding this world merely as a means to it. The disbeliever is not like this. Even if his means are few, his joy in them is dominant in his opinion, because he believes that they are the complete goal and nothing else.
