Given that this is his condition, it is valid that the verse does not mean the making attractive of permissible things. Also, God followed that verse with His saying: ﴿and they mock those who believe﴾, which indicates that they used to mock them for abandoning forbidden pleasures and for bearing obligatory hardships. This shows that the adornment did not occur in permissible things, but rather in forbidden ones.

As for our companions (the Ash'ari scholars), they understood the adornment to mean that God created in his heart the desire for things and the power over those things; indeed, He created those actions and states themselves. This is based on the principle that the only creator of the actions of servants is God, glory be to Him. On this understanding the meaning of the verse becomes clear.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they mock those who believe﴾, we have transmitted several narrations about the manner of that mockery. Al-Wahidi said: His saying "﴿and they mock﴾" is a new sentence (mustaʾnaf), not conjoined to "زُيِّنَ" (was made attractive). It is not far-fetched to begin a present/future-tense verb after a past-tense one, because God informed about them with "زُيِّنَ" (past), then informed about them with an action that they continually perform, saying: ﴿and they mock those who believe﴾. The meaning of this mockery is that they used to say: "These poor people have abandoned the pleasures, good things, and desires of this world, and bear hardships and toils in seeking the Hereafter, even though the claim of the Hereafter is false." Without doubt, if the claim of resurrection were false, this mockery would be justified. But if the claim of the Hereafter is established as true, then the mockery turns back upon them. For whoever turns away from eternal dominion because of base pleasures in a few countable breaths, no one among creation is more deserving of mockery than him. Indeed, some researchers said: turning away from this world and turning toward the Hereafter is the prudent choice under all possibilities. For if the claim of the Hereafter is false, what is lost is only base pleasures and a few countable breaths; and if the claim of the Hereafter is true, turning away from this world and turning toward the Hereafter becomes a definite necessity. Thus it is established that that mockery was baseless, and that its turning back upon them is more fitting.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But those who fear God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, there are questions about it:

The first question: Why did He say ﴿from those who believe﴾ and then say ﴿those who fear God﴾?

The answer: To show that the supreme happiness is attained only by the believer who fears God, and to serve as a motivation for the believers toward piety (taqwa).

Second question: What is meant by this "above-ness"?
The answer: There are several views.
One: that "above-ness" means above-ness in place, since the believers will be in ʿIlliyyin in the heaven, and the disbelievers will be in Sijjin in the earth.
Two: it may be that "above-ness" means above-ness in honour and rank.
If it is said: one says "so-and-so is above so-and-so in honour" only when each of them has honour and then one of them is higher in state than the other in that honour; and the disbeliever has no share of honour at all, so how can it be said that the believer is above him in honour?
We say: the meaning is that they were above them in the worldly felicities; then in the Hereafter the matter is reversed, for God Most High gives the believer of the felicities of the Hereafter that which is above the worldly felicities that the disbelievers had.
Three: the meaning may be that they are above them in proof on the Day of Resurrection. This is because the doubts of the disbelievers would sometimes fall upon the hearts of the believers, and then they would repel them from their hearts by the aid of God Most High's success; but on the Day of Resurrection nothing of that remains, rather doubts vanish, and the whisperings of Satan have no effect, as God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ up to His saying: ﴿So today those who believed [laugh at the disbelievers]﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29] etc.
Four: the mockery of the believers at the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection is greater than the mockery of the disbelievers at the believers in this world; for the mockery of the disbeliever at the believer is false, and along with its falsehood it is finite; while the mockery of the believer at the disbeliever in the Hereafter is true, and along with its truth it is lasting and enduring.
Third question: Does the verse indicate with certainty the threat of corruption (wa'id al-fasad)? For one may say: He, Exalted is He, specified those who have taqwa with this above-ness; so those who are not described with taqwa must not attain this above-ness, and if they do not attain this above-ness, they are among the people of the Fire.
The answer: This is an argument from the implication (mafhum), so it is not stronger in indication than the general statements which we have explained are specified by the indications of pardon.
Page 9
As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾, it may be that what is meant by it is what God gives the pious in the Hereafter of reward, and it may be that what is meant is what He gives in this world to the various kinds of His servants, believers and disbelievers. If we take it to mean the provision of the Hereafter, it admits several meanings:
One: that He provides for whom He wills in the Hereafter, namely the believers, without reckoning, i.e. with a wide, abundant provision that has no end and no cessation; and it is like His saying: ﴿Those enter the Garden, being provided therein without reckoning﴾ [Ghafir: 40]. For everything that enters under reckoning, limitation and measure is finite; so what is not finite is necessarily outside reckoning.
Two: that the benefits reaching them in the Garden are partly reward and partly bounty, as He said: ﴿So He will pay them their wages and increase them of His bounty﴾ [an-Nisa: 173]. So the bounty from Him is without reckoning.
Three: that He does not fear its exhaustion with Him, so He has no need to reckon what goes out from Him; for the giver only reckons in order to know the measure of what he gives and what remains, so that he does not exceed in his gifts to the point of ruin; and God does not need reckoning, because He is knowing and rich, and His capacities have no limit.
Four: that by this He intended the provision of the people of Paradise; this is because reckoning is only needed when, if one gives something, the due amount is diminished from what it was; but reward is not like that, for after the passing of ages and eras the reward due by the decree of the promise and bounty remains; accordingly, reckoning does not apply to reward at all.
Five: He meant that what is given has no ratio to what is in the treasury; for what is given at every time is necessarily finite, while what is in the treasury of God's power is infinite, and the finite has no ratio to the infinite. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿without reckoning﴾, and it is an indication that God's capacities have no end.
Six: ﴿without reckoning﴾, i.e. without entitlement; it is said: "So-and-so has a reckoning against so-and-so" when he has a right against him; and this indicates that no one can claim anything from Him, and no one has a reckoning with Him; rather, everything He gives He gives by mere bounty and kindness, not by way of entitlement.
Seven: ﴿without reckoning﴾, i.e. He increases beyond the measure of sufficiency; it is said: "So-and-so spends by reckoning" when he does not exceed the measure of sufficiency; but if he exceeds it, it is said: "He spends without reckoning."
Eight: ﴿without reckoning﴾, i.e. He gives abundantly; for what enters reckoning is little.
Know that all these meanings are admissible, and God's gifts accommodate them all; so it is permissible that all of them are meant, and God knows best.
As for if we take the verse to mean what He gives in this world to the various kinds of His servants, believers and disbelievers, then there are several meanings:
One: and it is most fitting to the composition of the verse, that the disbelievers used only to mock the poor Muslims, because they would infer from the attainment of worldly felicities that they were upon the truth, and they would deprive the poor Muslims of those felicities as evidence that they were upon falsehood. So God Most High refuted this premise by His saying: ﴿And God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾, meaning: He gives in this world to whom He wills without that being indicative of whether the recipient is right or wrong, good or evil; this depends purely on His will. He widened the world for Qarun and constricted it for Job, peace be upon him. So it is not permissible for you, O disbelievers, to infer from your attainment of worldly goods and the poor Muslims' lack of them that you are right and they are wrong; rather, the disbeliever may be widened upon as an increase in respite, and the believer may be constricted upon as an increase in trial and testing. For this reason He Exalted said: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 33].
Two: the meaning is: that God provides in this world for whom He wills, of disbeliever and believer, without reckoning that would be owed to anyone upon Him,

nor any demand, nor any consequence, nor any question of a questioner; and the purpose of this is that the disbeliever should not say: "If the believer is upon the truth, why was he not widened upon in this world?" and that the believer should not say: "If the disbeliever is a wrongdoer, why is he widened upon in this world?" Rather, the objection is void, the command is His command and the judgment is His judgment: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya: 23].
Three: His saying: ﴿without reckoning﴾, i.e. from where one does not reckon, as a man says when there comes to him what was not in his estimation: "This was not in my reckoning." According to this aspect, the meaning of the verse is: that these disbelievers, although they mock those who believed because of their poverty, God Most High may provide for whom He wills from where they do not reckon, and perhaps He will do so for the believers. Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: He has indeed done so for them, enriching them with what He granted them of the wealth of the chieftains of Quraysh and the leaders of the Jews, and with what He opened to His Messenger ﷺ after his death through the hands of his Companions, until they possessed the treasures of Kisra and Caesar.
If it is said: God Most High has said regarding the description of the pious and what reaches them: ﴿a reward reckoned﴾ [an-Naba: 36]; is that not like a contradiction to what is in this verse?
We say: As for one who takes His saying ﴿without reckoning﴾ to mean bounty, and takes His saying ﴿a reward reckoned﴾ to mean what is due by the promise, according to our view, or by entitlement according to the view of the Mu'tazilah, then the objection falls. As for one who takes His saying ﴿without reckoning﴾ to mean the other aspects, he may say: that this reward, if it is similar and uniform across times, it is correct in this respect to describe it as "a reward reckoned", and what we have mentioned regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿without reckoning﴾ does not contradict it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community; then God sent the prophets as bringers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between people concerning that over which they differed. And none differed over it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of animosity among themselves. So God guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they had differed, by His permission. And God guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾
Know that when He, Exalted, explained in the preceding verse that the cause of these disbelievers' persistence in their disbelief is love of the world, He explained in this verse that this meaning is not specific to this time, but was present in earlier ages; for mankind was one community standing upon the truth, then they differed, and their difference was only due to transgression, envy and dispute over seeking the world. This is the discussion regarding the arrangement of the composition.
Concerning the verse there are issues:
Page 11
The first issue: al-Qaffal said: the ummah is a people gathered upon one thing, following one another, and it is derived from the ta'tim (following/taking as a leader).
The second issue: The verse indicates that mankind was one community, but it does not indicate whether they were one community in truth or in falsehood, and the exegetes differed on this in three opinions:
The first opinion: that they were upon one religion, which is faith and truth; this is the view of most of the researchers, and the following considerations indicate it:
The first: what al-Qaffal mentioned, saying: the evidence for it is His saying after this verse: ﴿then God sent the prophets as bringers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾; this indicates that the prophets, peace be upon them, were sent only at the time of difference. This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿And mankind was not but one community, then they differed﴾ [Yunus: 19], and it is further reinforced by what is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited: ﴿Mankind was one community, then God sent the prophets﴾ up to His saying: ﴿to judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾.
Having known this, we say: the fa' in His saying ﴿then God sent the prophets﴾ requires that their sending be after the difference; and if they had been one community in disbelief before that, the sending of the messengers before this difference would have been more fitting; for since they were sent when some of them were right and some wrong, then their being sent when they were all wrongdoers, persisting in disbelief, would be all the more fitting. This consideration which al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, mentioned is good on this subject.
Second: that He, Exalted, judged that mankind was one community, then the difference occurred after it, according to the indication of the evidence and according to the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. Then He said: ﴿And none differed over it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of animosity among themselves.﴾ The apparent meaning is that this difference is the difference arising after that agreement referred to by His saying: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾. Then He judged this difference as having arisen only because of transgression, and this description is fitting only to false doctrines. So the verse indicates that false doctrines arose only because of transgression, and this shows that the agreement that existed before this difference was upon the truth, not upon falsehood. Thus it is established that mankind was one community in the true religion, not in the false religion.

The third view: Abu Muslim and al-Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) chose that people were one community in adhering to the rational laws (al-sharaʾiʿ al-ʿaqliyya), namely acknowledging the existence of the Creator and His attributes, occupying oneself with His worship and thanking His blessings, and abstaining from rationally ugly acts such as injustice, lying, ignorance, and futility, and the like.

Al-Qadi argued for the soundness of his view by saying that the word "the prophets" (al-nabiyyin) conveys generality and totality, and the letter fa' (fa) conveys sequence, so that His saying ﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ النَّبِيِّينَ﴾ ("Then God sent the prophets") indicates that the sending of all the prophets came after the people were one community. Therefore that unity preceding the sending of all the laws must be a unity in a law not derived from the prophets, and so it must be in a law derived from reason, which is what we have explained. Also, knowledge of the goodness of thanking the Benefactor, obedience to the Creator, beneficence to creation, and justice is shared among all, and knowledge of the ugliness of lying, injustice, ignorance, and futility is shared among all. Thus it is most apparent that people were, at the beginning of the matter, upon this, and then they differed afterward for separate causes. Then he asked himself: Is not the first of mankind Adam, peace be upon him, and was he not a prophet? How then is it valid to affirm that people were accountable before the sending of the messengers? He answered that it is possible that he, peace be upon him, together with his offspring, were united in adhering to the rational laws first; then God sent him to his offspring after that. It is also possible that after that his law became effaced, so the people returned to adhering to the rational laws. Know that this view is valid only with the affirmation of the rational goodness and ugliness of acts (tahsin al-ʿaql wa taqbihih), and the discussion of this is well known in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

The fourth view: the verse indicates that people were one community, but it does not say whether they were upon faith or upon disbelief; that is contingent upon evidence.

The fifth view: that by "the people" here is meant the People of the Book who believed in Musa, peace be upon him. This is because we have shown that this verse is connected to what preceded it, His saying ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا ادْخُلُوا فِي السِّلْمِ كَافَّةً﴾ ("O you who have believed, enter into Islam completely," 2:208), and we mentioned that many exegetes claimed that verse was revealed concerning the Jews. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿كَانَ النَّاسُ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾ means: those who believed in Musa were one community, upon one religion and one creed. Then they differed because of rebellion and envy, so God sent the prophets, who are those who came after Musa, peace be upon him, and He sent down with them the Book, just as He sent the Psalms to Dawud, the Torah to Musa, the Gospel to ʿIsa, and the Furqan to Muhammad, peace be upon him, so that those books would judge between them in those matters over which they differed. This view agrees with the composition of the verse and accords with what comes before and after it, and there is no difficulty in it, except that restricting the word "the people" in His saying ﴿كَانَ النَّاسُ﴾ to specific people is contrary to the apparent meaning. Yet you know that the alif and lam (al-alif wa al-lam) may be for totality (al-istighraq) and may also be for a specific referent (al-ʿahd). This is what relates to this verse.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ النَّبِيِّينَ مُبَشِّرِينَ وَمُنْذِرِينَ﴾ ("God sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners"): know that we have mentioned that an implied element (al-idmar) is necessary here, and the estimate is: "The people were one community, then they differed, so God sent the prophets." Know also that God, exalted is He, described the prophets with three attributes:

The first attribute: that they are bearers of good tidings (mubashshirin).

The second attribute: that they are warners (mundhirin). Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿رُسُلًا مُبَشِّرِينَ وَمُنْذِرِينَ﴾ ("messengers as bearers of good tidings and warners," 4:165). He placed good tidings before warning because good tidings operate in the manner of preserving health, while warning operates in the manner of removing sickness; and there is no doubt that the primary aim is the former rather than the latter, so it is necessarily mentioned first.

The third attribute: His saying ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ مَعَهُمُ الْكِتَابَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ ("and sent down with them the Book with truth"). If it is said: the sending down of the Book occurs before the command and prohibition reach the accountable persons, and the reaching of command and prohibition to them occurs before good tidings and warning; why then did He mention good tidings and warning before the sending down of the Books? Al-Qadi answered this, saying: because promise and threat from them before the explanation of the law is possible in what relates to rational matters, such as knowledge of God and abstention from injustice and other things. But in my view there is another aspect, which is that the accountable person only undertakes to examine the evidence of the miracle's truthfulness, and the distinction between the miracle, when he fears that if he does not examine, he might abandon the truth and thereby become deserving of punishment. Fear only grows and becomes complete at the time of good tidings and warning, so necessarily the good tidings and warning were placed before the sending down of the Book in mention. Then al-Qadi said: the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that there is no prophet except that with him is a Book sent down containing the explanation of the truth, whether that Book was long or short, written down or not written down, and whether that Book was a miracle or not; because the Book's being sent down with them does not entail any of that.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿لِيَحْكُمَ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ﴾ ("that he might judge between the people"): know that His saying ﴿لِيَحْكُمَ﴾ is a verb, so it must be attributed to something previously mentioned. Three things have been mentioned previously: the closest to this expression is the Book, then the prophets, then God. Therefore the supposition of each of them is valid, so the meaning is: that God might judge, or the prophet to whom it was sent down, or the Book. Then each of these possibilities has a ground of preference. As for the Book, it is because it is the closest of the things mentioned; as for God, it is because He, glorified is He, is the real Judge, not the Book; and as for the prophet, it is because he is the one who manifests it. It is not far-fetched to say that attributing it to the Book is preferable. At most one may say: the Judge is God, so attributing judgment to the Book is a metaphor (majaz). But we may say this metaphor is acceptable for two reasons:

The first: that it is a well-known metaphor; one says: "The Book has judged by such-and-such," "The Book of God has decreed such-and-such," and "We are content with the Book of God." And since it is permissible for it to be guidance and healing, it is permissible for it to be a judge. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ وَيُبَشِّرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright and gives good tidings to the believers," 17:9).

The second: that it conveys the magnification of the Quran's status and the exalting of its condition.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 212 (part 4 of 4):

As for His saying, ﴿concerning that about which they differed﴾, know that the pronoun in His saying ﴿concerning that about which they differed﴾ must refer either to the Book or to the Truth, since both have already been mentioned. However, its reference to the Truth is preferable, because the verse indicates that God only sent down the Book so that it would be the judge concerning that about which they differed. Thus the Book is the judge, the matter in dispute is the thing judged, and the judge must be distinct from the thing judged.

As for His saying, ﴿And none differed concerning it except those who were given it﴾, the first pronoun refers to the Truth and the second to the Book. The meaning is: none differed concerning the Truth except those who were given the Book. Then most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: by "these" is meant the Jews and the Christians, and God frequently mentions them in the Qur'an with this expression, as in His saying, ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:5), and ﴿Say, O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:64). Then their difference may be understood as each of them declaring the other to be in disbelief, as in His saying, ﴿The Jews say, "The Christians are not founded upon anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not founded upon anything," while they recite the Scripture﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:113). It may also be understood as their distortion and alteration (of the Scripture). So His saying, ﴿And none differed concerning it except those who were given it﴾ means: none differed concerning the Truth except those who were given the Scripture, even though the purpose of sending down the Book was that they should not differ and that they should put an end to dispute in religion. Know that this indicates that difference concerning the Truth did not arise except after the sending of the prophets and the revelation of the Books. This necessarily implies that before their sending there was no difference concerning the Truth; rather, agreement concerning the Truth prevailed. This indicates that His saying, ﴿Mankind was one community﴾, means one community in the religion of Truth.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 213:

As for His saying, ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, it requires that God's giving them the Book happened after the coming of the clear proofs, so these clear proofs are necessarily distinct from the giving of the Book. These clear proofs can only be understood as the rational proofs that God established for proving the foundations, without which prophethood cannot be affirmed. This is because the theologians (mutakallimun) say: whatever the affirmation of prophethood depends upon being established first, that thing cannot be proven by transmitted (sam'i) proofs, otherwise circularity (dawr) would occur; rather, it must be proven by rational proofs. So these proofs are the clear proofs that preceded God's giving them the Books.

As for His saying, ﴿out of rivalry among themselves﴾, the meaning is that proofs are either transmitted (sam'iyyah) or rational ('aqliyyah). The transmitted proofs were achieved through the giving of the Book, and the rational proofs were achieved through the clear proofs that preceded the giving of the Book. At that point the clear proofs were complete, and there remained no excuse or pretext for deviation. So if turning away and deviation occurred, it could only have been due to envy, rebellion, and greed for worldly pursuits. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 4].

As for His saying, ﴿So God guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed, by His permission﴾, know that when He described the condition of the People of the Book, that after the clear proofs were complete they persisted in disbelief and ignorance because of rebellion and envy, He explained that the condition of this Ummah is different from the condition of those; God protected them from error and guided them to the truth in the matters over which the People of the Book differed. It is related that he (ﷺ) said: "We are the last but the first on the Day of Resurrection, and we are the first of people to enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection, except that they were given the Book before us and we were given it after them. Then God guided us to the truth concerning what they differed over, by His permission. This is the day He guided us to, and people follow us in it: tomorrow is for the Jews, and the day after for the Christians." Ibn Zayd said: They differed over the qibla, so the Jews prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis and the Christians toward the east, and God guided us to the Ka'bah. They differed over fasting, and God guided us to the month of Ramadan. They differed over Ibrahim: the Jews said he was a Jew, and the Christians said he was a Christian, and we said he was a hanif, a Muslim. They differed over 'Isa: the Jews were remiss, the Christians went to excess, and we said the just word.

Some matters remain concerning the verse:

First matter: Some of our companions (al-Ash'ariyyah) cited this verse to show that faith is created by God Most High. They said: guidance is knowledge and recognition, and His saying ﴿God guided﴾ is explicit that guidance was achieved by the act of God Most High, so this shows that faith is created by God Most High.

Know that this argument is weak, because we have shown that guidance (hidayah) is one thing and being guided (ihtida') is another. What indicates here that guidance cannot be a term for faith are two points:

The first: guidance to faith is other than faith, just as enabling (tawfiq) for faith is other than faith.

The second: He said at the end of the verse, ﴿by His permission﴾, and this permission cannot be attributed to His saying ﴿God guided﴾, since it is not permissible for Him to give permission to Himself. So an ellipsis is necessary here to direct this permission to it, and the estimate is: "God guided those who believed to the truth concerning what they differed over, so they were guided by His permission." If that is so, guidance is distinct from being guided.

* * *

Second matter: The companions (al-Ash'ariyyah) argued by this verse that God Most High may particularly bestow upon the believer guidances which He does not bestow upon the disbeliever. The Mu'tazilah answered this from several aspects:

One: they were singled out for being guided, so He made guidance specific to them, as in His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], then He said: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

Second: the intended meaning is guidance to reward and the path to Paradise.

Third: He guided them to the truth through favours (alutf).

* * *

Third matter: His saying ﴿concerning that over which they differed﴾ means "to that over which they differed," as in His saying: ﴿they go back on what they said﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3], i.e., to what they said. It is said: "I guided him the road," "to the road," and "to the road" (all used).

If it is asked: why did He say "He guided them to the truth concerning that over which they differed, by His permission," and not say "He guided them to the truth concerning what they differed over," and place the difference first?

The answer is in two respects:

The first: since the concern was with mentioning their difference, He began with it, then explained it with those whom He guided.

The second: al-Farra' said: this is an inversion (maqlub), meaning: "He guided them to that over which they differed."

* * *

Fourth matter: His saying ﴿by His permission﴾ has two meanings:
One: al-Zajjaj said: "by His knowledge."

The second: He guided them by His command, i.e., guidance was achieved through the cause of the command, as one says "I cut with the knife," because the truth was not distinguished from falsehood, and by the command the distinction was achieved, so guidance was made dependent on His permission.

The third: some said: there must be an ellipsis here, the estimate being: "He guided them, so they were guided by His permission."

As for His saying: ﴿And God guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾, the companions' use of it as evidence is well known, and the Mu'tazilah answered from three aspects:

One: the intended guidance is clarification (bayan), so God Most High specified it for the accountable.

The second: the intended guidance is the path to Paradise.

The third: the intended meaning is favour (lutf), so it is specific to whomever He knows is suited to it, and this is the view of Abu Bakr al-Razi.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 214 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come to you the like of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken, until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?" Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾

In the arrangement (nazm) of the verse there are two aspects:

The first: In the preceding verse He said, ﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path,﴾ and the meaning is that He guides whom He wills to the truth and to seeking Paradise. Then in this verse He explains that this seeking is not completed or perfected except by enduring hardships in the obligations, so He said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come to you the like of those who passed away before you?⦆ and so on.

The second: In the preceding verse, when He explained that He guided them to what they differed about of the truth by His permission, He explained in this verse that after that guidance they endured hardships in upholding the truth and were patient in trials. Likewise, you, O companions of Muhammad, do not deserve excellence in religion except by bearing these tribulations.

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: We have thoroughly discussed the particle (am) in the commentary on His saying:
﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. What we intend here is to say: (am) is an intermediate interrogative (istifham mutawassit), just as (hal) is an initial interrogative (istifham sabiq). It is permissible to say: hal 'indaka rajul? a'indaka rajul? at the beginning, but it is not permissible to say: am 'indaka rajul? As for when it is intermediate, it is permissible whether it is preceded by another interrogative or not. When it is preceded by another interrogative, it is like your saying: "You are a man who does not act justly; do you do this out of ignorance, or do you have authority?" As for the one not preceded by an interrogative, it is like His saying: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 3]. This type is in the sense of the first type, and the meaning is: "Do they believe in this, or do they say he has invented it?" Thus the sense of this verse is: "So Allah guided those who believed to what they differed about of the truth by His permission, and they were patient over the mockery of their people toward them. Will you then follow their path, or do you suppose that you will enter Paradise without following their path?" This is what al-Qaffal summarized, may Allah have mercy on him, and Allah knows best.

* * *

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and there has not yet come to you the like of those who passed away before you﴾, i.e., "and there has not come to you the like of those who passed away." The Kufan grammarians mentioned that (lamma) is actually (lam) with (ma) added as a supplement, but Sibawayh said: (ma) is not superfluous, because (lamma) occurs in places where (lam) does not occur. A man says to his companion: "Has so-and-so arrived?" and he answers: "Lamma," and does not say "lam" alone. Al-Mubarrad said: When one says: "Zayd has not come to me (lam yati-ni Zayd)," it is a negation of your saying: "Zayd has come to you." And when he says: "Lamma ya'ti-ni (not yet come to me)," its meaning is that he has not come to me yet, and I am expecting him. The poet al-Nabighah said:

"The departure has drawn near, except that our camels have not yet stood at our saddles, and as if they had."

Accordingly, His saying: ﴿and there has not yet come to you the like of those who passed away before you﴾ indicates that the coming of that is expected and awaited.

* * *

The third issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered Madinah, the harm upon them intensified, because they had left without wealth, and had left their homes and property in the hands of the polytheists, and the Jews openly showed enmity toward the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So Allah the Exalted revealed, to console their hearts: ﴿Or did you think...﴾. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: It was revealed concerning the Battle of the Trench, when there befell the Muslims what befell them of hardship and grief, and it was as He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10]. It was also said: It was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud, when 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said to the companions of Muhammad ﷺ: "How long will you kill yourselves and hope for falsehood? If Muhammad were a prophet, Allah would not have let captivity and killing overtake you?" Then Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Know that the implied sense of the verse is: "Or did you think, O believers, that you would enter Paradise merely by faith in Me and belief in My Messenger, without worshipping Allah in all that He has commanded you to worship, and being tested with patience upon it, and that there would not befall you harm from the disbelievers, and enduring poverty and need, and bearing hardship and distress in livelihood, and confronting terrors in striving against the enemy, just as it was so for those who were before you among the believers?" This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and there has not come to you the like of those who passed away before you﴾. The (mathal) is the (mithl), meaning the likeness or resemblance, and they are two dialects: mathal, mithl, shabah, and shibh. However, (mathal) is used metaphorically for a strange state or a wondrous story that has importance, and from it is His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description (al-mathal al-a'la)﴾ [al-Nahl: 60], i.e., the attribute that has great importance.

Know that in the speech there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: "the likeness of the trial of those before you." His saying ﴿touched them﴾ is an explanation of (mathal), and it is a resumption (isti'naf), as if someone said: "How was that likeness?" So He said: ﴿Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken.﴾

As for ﴿al-ba'sa'﴾, it is a noun from (al-bu's), meaning hardship, and it is poverty and destitution, and from it one says: "So-and-so is in distress and hardship."

[Page 18]

As for ﴿al-darra'﴾, the closest view concerning it is that it is the arrival of harms upon a person, such as pains, aches, and kinds of fear. In my view, al-ba'sa' is an expression for the constriction of the avenues of good and benefit upon him, and al-darra' is an expression for the opening of the avenues of evil, calamity, and pain upon him.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿wa-zulzilu﴾, i.e., they were moved by various kinds of afflictions and calamities. Al-Zajjaj said: The origin of zalzalah in the language is from "azala al-shay' 'an makanihi" (he removed the thing from its place). When you say "zalzaltuhu," its interpretation is that you repeated that removal, so its wording was doubled by doubling its meaning. Every word in which there is repetition has the first radical of the verb repeated, such as sarra and sarsara, salla and salsala, kaffa and kafkafa. And "aqalla al-shay'" means he lifted it from its place; when it is repeated one says "qalqala." Some commentators explained ﴿wa-zulzilu﴾ here as "they were frightened," but its real meaning is other than what we have mentioned. That is because one who is afraid does not remain still; rather his heart is agitated, and for this reason that is not said except of a lasting, paralyzing fear, since it removes calm. Therefore zulzilu here must be metaphorical, and the intended meaning is "they were frightened." It is also possible that they were agitated and could not settle, because of the anxiety and fear in their hearts. Then, after mentioning these things, He, exalted is He, mentioned something else, which is the utmost in indicating the completeness of harm, hardship, and trial, so He said: ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ This is because the messengers, peace be upon them, are at the height of steadfastness, patience, and self-control when affliction descends. So when they no longer had patience, until they cried out, that was the ultimate extreme of severity. When their hardship reached this great degree, it was said to them: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near,﴾ answering their request. So the sense of the verse is: "Thus was their condition until the help of Allah came to them, and the prolonged affliction did not change them from their religion. And you, O assembly of Muslims, be upon that, and bear harm and hardship in seeking the truth, for the help of Allah is near, because it is coming, and everything that is coming is near." This verse is like His saying: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. Do people think they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ ﴿And We certainly tested those before them, and Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful...﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1-2]. And He said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and known the patient?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142]. The purpose of this verse is what we have mentioned: that the companions of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, were struck by great hardship and harm from the polytheists, the hypocrites, and the Jews; and when they were permitted to fight, they suffered wounds, loss of property, and loss of lives, which is not hidden. So Allah consoled them in that and explained that the condition of those before them in seeking the religion was like that, and that a calamity, when it is general, becomes easier to bear. Allah also mentioned the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his being thrown into the fire, and the matter of Ayyub, peace be upon him, and what Allah tested him with, and the matter of all the other prophets, peace be upon them, in their perseverance under various trials, which became a consolation for the believers.

Qays ibn Abi Hazim narrated from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who said: "We complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about what we suffered from the polytheists, and he said: 'Those nations before you were tortured with kinds of trials, yet that did not turn them from their religion. A man would have a saw placed upon his head and be split in two, and a man would be combed with iron combs down to the flesh and sinew and bone, and that would not turn him from his religion. By Allah, Allah will surely complete this matter, until a rider travels between San'a' and Hadramawt fearing none but Allah and the wolf concerning his sheep, but you are hasty.'"

* * *

The fourth issue: Nafi' read: (hatta yaqula) with a raised lam (damma), and the rest read it with a fatha (naṣb). Its basis is that when (hatta) puts the present tense into the subjunctive, it is of two kinds:

One is that it means "ila" (until/up to). In this kind, the action that occurred before (hatta) and the action that occurred after it have both occurred and passed, as you say: "I traveled until I entered it," meaning "up to the point that I entered it." The traveling and the entering both occurred and passed. The naṣb in this verse is upon this sense, because the sense is: "they were shaken up to the point that the Messenger said..." and the shaking and the saying both occurred.

The second is that it means "kay" (in order that), as in His saying: "I obeyed Allah until I enter Paradise," meaning "in order that I enter Paradise." The obedience has occurred, but the entering has not occurred. The naṣb of this verse cannot be upon this sense.

As for the raising (raf'), know that the verb after (hatta) must be in the sense of a narrated present state (al-hal al-mahkiyyah) that has occurred, just as the state is narrated in His saying: ﴿This is of his party, and this is of his enemy﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], and in His saying: ﴿And their dog stretching forth his forelegs at the threshold﴾ [al-Kahf: 18], because this is valid only on the basis that at that time this speech was being said. And it is said: "The camels drank until a camel comes dragging its belly," meaning: they drank to the point that whoever was present there would say, "A camel comes dragging its belly." Then this may be true when only the cause has ended, without the effect, as when you say: "I traveled until I enter the town." It is possible that the traveling and the entering both occurred and took place, and it is possible that the traveling occurred but the entering had not yet occurred. This is the discussion on establishing the sense of the naṣb and the sense of the raf'. Know that most scholars preferred the naṣb, because the reading with raf' is valid only if we take the speech as a narration from one who reports the state at the moment of its occurrence, whereas the reading with naṣb does not require this assumption; therefore the reading with naṣb is more preferable.

* * *

The fifth issue: There is a difficulty in the verse, namely: how is it fitting for the Messenger, who is certain of the truth of Allah's promise and threat, to say, in a manner of impatience: ﴿When is the help of Allah?﴾

The answer to it is from several aspects:

**The first:** That he is a messenger does not prevent him from being distressed by the schemes of the enemies. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿We know that your breast is constrained by what they say﴾ [al-Hijr: 97]. And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3]. And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been denied, Our help came to them, and whom We willed was delivered﴾ [Yusuf: 110]. Based on this, when his heart is constrained and his resources are few, and he has heard from Allah the Exalted that He will help him but He has not specified the time for that, he says in the constraint of his heart: ﴿When is the help of Allah?﴾ Thus, if he knows the time is near, his worry and grief depart and his heart is at ease. What indicates the soundness of this is that He said in the reply: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾ Since the answer mentions nearness, this shows that the question was about nearness. Had the question been about whether help would occur or not, this answer would not correspond to that question. This is the relied-upon answer.

**The second answer:** Allah the Exalted informed about the Messenger and those who believed that they said a statement, then mentioned two sayings:
The first: ﴿When is the help of Allah?﴾
The second: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾
So it is necessary to attribute each of these two sayings to one of those two mentioned. The believers said: ﴿When is the help of Allah?﴾ and the Messenger ﷺ said: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾

They said: For this there is a parallel in the Qur'an and in poetry.
As for the Qur'an, it is His saying: ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73]. The meaning is: that you may rest at night and seek His bounty during the day.
As for poetry, it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:
*As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry, beside their nests are the 'unnab and the decayed dried date-pulp.*
Here the comparison with the 'unnab applies to the moist, and with the decayed dried date-pulp to the dry. This is an answer mentioned by a group, and it is very far-fetched (mutakallaf jiddan).

**The sixth issue:** ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ may be a reply from Allah the Exalted to them, when they said: ﴿When﴾
[Page 20]
﴿the help of Allah?﴾ Then their speech ends at His saying: ﴿When is the help of Allah?﴾ and Allah then says: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾ It is also possible that this is a statement from a group among them, as if, when they said: ﴿When is the help of Allah?﴾ they returned to themselves and knew that Allah would not let their enemy prevail over them, so they said: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾ So we have endured, O our Lord, trusting in Your promise.

If it is said: His saying ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ requires that whoever is afflicted with hardship should know that he will soon triumph over its removal, and that is not established.

We say: It is not impossible that this is among the special qualities of the prophets, peace be upon them. It is also possible that this is general for everyone, since whoever is in a trial must have one of two outcomes: either he is freed from it, or he dies. And if he dies, he has reached One who does not neglect his affair and does not waste his right, and that is among the greatest help. He made it near only because death is near.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 215:**

**[Page 20]**

The Exalted and Glorified said: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents and relatives, orphans, the needy and the wayfarer. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾

Know that when He, glory be to Him and exalted, had emphasized that every person who is accountable must turn away from seeking the immediate (al-'ajil), must devote himself to seeking the deferred (al-ajil), and must be ready to spend his self and his wealth in that cause, He then began to explain the rulings (al-ahkam). This runs from this verse to His saying: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243]. This is because it is the custom of the Qur'an to mix together the explanation of monotheism (al-tawhid), the explanation of admonition and counsel, and the explanation of rulings, so that each of them strengthens and reinforces the others.

**The First Ruling**

Concerning spending (al-nafaqah), there is this verse, and in it are several issues.

**The first issue:** 'Ata' reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse was revealed concerning "a man who came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and said: I have a dinar. He said: Spend it on yourself. He said: I have two dinars. He said: Spend them on your family. He said: I have three. He said: Spend them on your servant. He said: I have four. He said: Spend them on your parents. He said: I have five. He said: Spend them on your relatives. He said: I have six. He said: Spend them in the way of Allah, and that is the best of them." Al-Kalbi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was a very old, decrepit man, and he is the one who was killed on the day of Uhud while possessing great wealth. He said: "What should we spend of our wealth, and where should we place it?" Then this verse was revealed.

* * *

**The second issue:** The grammarians have two opinions regarding (madha):

The first: that one takes (ma) together with (dha) as a single noun, and the position is in the accusative governed by "﴿they spend﴾". The evidence for this is that the Arabs say: "'ammadha tas'al?" (about what do you ask?) with the alif retained in (ma). Had (ma) with (dha) not been a single noun, they would have said: "'ammadha tas'al?" with the alif deleted, as they deleted it in His saying: ﴿About what do they ask one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1] and His saying: ﴿In what are you [concerned] to mention it?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 43]. Since they did not delete the alif from the end of (ma), you know that it is with (dha) a single noun, and they did not delete the alif from it because it was not the end of the noun. Deletion affects it when it is at the end, except in poetry, as in the saying:

*"Ala ma qama yashtumuni la'imun*
*ka-khinzirin tamarraga fi ramadi"*

The second opinion: that one takes (dha) to mean (alladhi, "the one which"), and (ma) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), with (dha) as its predicate. The Arabs sometimes use (dha) with the meaning of (alladhi), saying: "man dha yaqulu dhaka?" meaning "who is the one who says that?" According to this, the construction of the verse would be: "they ask you what is it that they spend."

* * *

**The third issue:** In the verse there is a question: the people asked about what they should spend, not about to whom the expenditure should be directed. So how did He answer them with this?

The answer to this is given in several ways.

First: the verse contains what serves as an answer to the question, and He added to it an extra element by which that purpose is completed. This is because His saying: ﴿Whatever good you spend﴾ is an answer to the question. Then, that spending is not complete unless it is directed to a category of those who are entitled to it. Therefore, when God, exalted is He, mentioned the answer, He followed it with mention of the recipients, to complete the explanation.

Second: al-Qaffal said: Although the question came in the form of (ma), the intended meaning was a question about the manner. This is because they knew that what they were commanded to do was to spend wealth that would be an act of drawing near to God, exalted is He. Since this was known, the mind would not turn to the question of what that wealth is. And when this is excluded from being intended, it becomes determined that what was sought by the question was: what is its recipient? Then the answer corresponds to the question. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is, for the cows have become confused for us, and we, if Allah wills, will be guided." He said: "He says it is a cow neither worn by labor..."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 70]. This answer corresponded to that question because it was known that the cow is the animal whose nature and attributes are such-and-such. So His saying: ﴿what is it﴾ cannot be taken to seek the quiddity (al-mahiyyah), so it is determined that what is meant by it is seeking the attribute by which that cow is distinguished from others. By this path we say that this answer corresponds to that question. Likewise here: when we know that they knew what it was they were commanded to spend, it must be concluded that their intention in saying ﴿What should they spend?﴾ was not to seek the quiddity, but to seek the recipient. Therefore the answer is fitting.

Third: it is possible that what is meant is that they asked this question, so it was as if they were told: "This is a flawed question. Spend whatever you like, but on condition that it is lawful wealth, and on condition that it is directed to its proper recipients." This is like a person who is in good health, to whom eating any food does no harm, who says to the physician: "What should I eat?" and the physician says: "Eat twice a day." The meaning was: "Eat whatever you wish, but on this condition." Likewise here, the meaning is: "Spend whatever you wish, on condition that the recipient is that."

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Know that He, exalted is He, observed the order in spending: He put the parents first. This is because they are like the cause that brought him from non-existence into existence in the world of causes, and then they raised him in the state in which he was in extreme weakness. Their benefaction to the child is therefore greater than the benefaction of anyone else to him. For this reason He said: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents be good﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. In this is an indication that after observing the right of Allah, exalted is He, there is nothing more obligatory than observing the right of the parents, because Allah, exalted is He, is the One who truly brought the human being from non-existence into existence, while the two parents are the ones who brought him into existence in the world of visible causes. Thus it is established that their right is greater than the right of anyone else. Therefore He made it obligatory to give them precedence over others in observing rights.

Then He mentioned, after the parents, the relatives (al-aqrabun). The reason for this is that a person cannot be responsible for the welfare of all the poor; rather, he must give preference to some over others, and preference must have a basis for preferring. Kinship is suitable to be a cause for preference, in several respects:

First: kinship is a likely cause of close association, and association is a cause for each of them to know the state of the other. So when one of them is rich and the other poor, the poor person's knowledge of the rich one is more complete, and the rich person's knowledge of the poor one is more complete, and that is among the strongest motives for spending.

Second: if he did not take into account the side of the poor person, the poor person would need to turn to someone else, and that is a shame and a defect for him. So it is better that he take responsibility for their welfare, to repel harm from the self.

Third: a person's relative is like a part of him, and spending on oneself takes precedence over spending on others. For this reason, spending on a relative takes precedence over spending on a stranger. Then, God, exalted is He, mentioned after the relatives the orphans. This is because, due to their youth, they cannot earn, and because they are orphans, there is no one who earns for them. The child whose father has died has lost both earning and the one who earns, and is on the verge of being lost. Then He mentioned after them the needy (al-masakin). Their need is less than that of the orphans, because their ability to obtain is greater than the ability of orphans. Then He mentioned after them the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil), for he, because of being cut off from his land, may fall into need and poverty. This is the correct order which God, exalted is He, arranged in the manner of spending. Then, after He had explained this excellent and complete detail, He followed it with a summary, saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾ That is: every good thing you have done, whether to these mentioned persons or with others, out of seeking the pleasure of Allah, desiring His abundant reward and fleeing from His painful punishment, indeed Allah is Knowing of it. (al-'Alim) is an intensive form of being knowing: nothing escapes His knowledge, not even the weight of an atom on earth or in heaven, so He will reward you with the best of rewards for it, as He said: ﴿Indeed I do not allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], and He said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7].

* * *

**The fifth issue:** The intended meaning of "good" (al-khayr) is wealth, as in His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8], and He said: ﴿If he leaves behind wealth, [the bequest]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180]. So the meaning is: "whatever you spend of wealth, whether little or much." There is another opinion, that His saying: ﴿whatever good you do﴾ encompasses this spending and all other aspects of righteousness and obedience, and this is preferable.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** Some have said that this verse is abrogated (mansukhah, i.e., subject to naskh, abrogation) by the verse of inheritance. This is weak, because it is possible to interpret this verse in ways in which abrogation does not apply:

First: Abu Muslim said: spending on parents is obligatory when they are unable to earn and own property, and what is meant by "relatives" is the child and the child's child, whose maintenance may be obligatory when there is no property. When we interpret the verse in this way, the view of the one who said it is abrogated by the verse of inheritance has no basis. This is because this expenditure is obligatory during life, whereas inheritance arrives after death. Also, what arrives after death is not described as expenditure.

Second: the meaning may be whoever wishes to draw near to Allah, exalted is He, in the matter of spending; it is better for him to spend it on these categories, giving precedence to the more deserving and then the more deserving, so the meaning is voluntary charity (al-tatawwu').

**[Page 21]**

Third: the meaning may be that obligation applies regarding what concerns parents and relatives in terms of sufficiency, and regarding what concerns orphans and the needy in what is zakah.

Fourth: it is possible that by spending on parents and relatives He means what serves as an incitement to maintaining kinship ties, and in what he gives to orphans and the needy, what is purely for charity. So the apparent meaning of the verse admits all these aspects without abrogation.

The second ruling concerning fighting:

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is disliked by you. But perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.ﴩ

The statement of Him, exalted is He: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is disliked by you. But perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that the Prophet ﷺ was not permitted to fight during the period of his residence in Makkah. When he migrated, he was permitted to fight those among the polytheists who fought against him. Then he was permitted to fight the polytheists in general. Then Allah made jihad obligatory. The scholars differed concerning this verse. A group said: it requires that fighting be obligatory upon everyone. It is reported from Makhul that he used to swear by Allah beside the House that military campaign (ghazw) is obligatory. And it is reported from Ibn 'Umar and 'Ata' that this verse requires that fighting be obligatory only upon the Companions of the Messenger ﷺ at that time.

The argument of the first group is that His saying ﴿prescribed﴾ requires obligation, and His saying ﴿for you﴾ requires it as well. The address with the second person plural in ﴿for you﴾ does not prevent the obligation from applying to those present and to those who will exist after them, as in His saying ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178] and ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183].

If it is said: does the apparent meaning of the verse require that it be obligatory upon each individual (fard 'ayn) or upon the community as a whole (fard kifayah, a collective obligation)?

We say: rather, it requires that it be obligatory upon each individual, because His saying ﴿for you﴾ means: upon each one of you individually, as in His saying ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you﴾ and ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾.

The argument of 'Ata' is that His saying ﴿prescribed﴾ requires the imposition, and performing it once suffices, while His saying ﴿for you﴾ restricts this address to those present at that time. However, we say: His saying ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178] and ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183], the state of those present in it is like the state of those who will exist after that, by a separate indication, which is the consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars). That indication is absent here, so it must remain on its original wording.

They said: among what indicates the soundness of this view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. Had the one who stays behind neglected an obligation, he would not have been promised the best. Except that it may be said: the obligation was established and then abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation). However, the commitment of the people to abrogation without any proof indicating it is not permissible. It is also indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. And the claim of abrogation is not permissible, as we have explained. And the consensus today is established that it is among the collective obligations, except that if the polytheists enter the lands of the Muslims, then jihad becomes obligatory upon everyone at that time. And Allah knows best.

[p. 24]

* * *

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿and it is disliked by you﴾ presents a difficulty. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿prescribed for you﴾ is that this address is to the believers, and reason also indicates this, because a disbeliever is not commanded to fight a disbeliever. If that is so, how does He say ﴿and it is disliked by you﴾? This implies that the believer dislikes the command and imposition of Allah, and that is impermissible, because a believer is not displeased with the commands of Allah, exalted is He, and His impositions. Rather, he is content with them, loves them, holds fast to them, and knows that they are his benefit and that neglecting them is his corruption.

The answer is in two parts:

The first: the intended meaning of dislike is that it is burdensome to the self. Although the one who is obligated knows that what Allah commanded him is his benefit, he does not thereby cease to find it heavy and burdensome to the self, because obligation is the imposition of something whose performance involves hardship and difficulty. It is known that what the nature inclines to most is life, so fighting is among the hardest things for the self.

The second: the intended meaning is their dislike of fighting before it was prescribed, because of the fear involved in it and the large number of enemies. Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear that what you dislike of fighting is good for you rather than leaving it, so that you do not dislike it after it has been prescribed for you.

* * *

**The third issue:** Al-kurh (with a dammah on the kaf) means dislike (al-karahah). The evidence is His saying ﴿and perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾. Then there are two possibilities:

One of them: the meaning is that a verbal noun (masdar) is placed in the position of an adjective for emphasis, like the saying of al-Khansa':

*For it is only advance and retreat*

As if it were in itself dislike, because of the extreme dislike they had for it.

The second: it is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), like the report in the sense of the reported (al-makhbur), meaning: and it is disliked for you. Al-Sulami read it with a fatha (al-kaṛh), and both are dialects, like al-da'f and al-da'af. It may also mean compulsion (al-ikrah) in a metaphorical sense, as if they were compelled to it because of their intense dislike of it and the hardship it caused them. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿His mother bore him with difficulty and gave birth to him with difficulty﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. And Allah knows best. Some have said: al-kurh, with a dammah, is what you dislike of what you were not compelled to; and when it is by compulsion, it is with a fatha.

As for His saying ﴿And perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** ﴿'asa﴾ (perhaps) is a verb whose present tense has been discontinued while its past tense remains. It is said from it: 'asayta and 'asaytum. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So would you perhaps...﴾ [Muhammad: 22]. The noun after it is in the nominative case, as it is after the verb, so you say: 'asa Zayd (perhaps Zayd), just as you say: qama Zayd (Zayd stood). Its meaning is: it is near. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: perhaps it has drawn close to you﴾ [al-Naml: 72], meaning: it has drawn near. So your saying 'asa Zayd an yaqum, its estimation is: 'asa qiyam Zayd, meaning: the standing of Zayd has drawn near.

[p. 25]

**The second issue:** The meaning of the verse is that a thing may sometimes be burdensome to you in the present, yet it is a cause of great benefits in the future, and conversely. For this reason it is good to drink a bitter medicine in the present, in anticipation of attaining health in the future. It is good to bear the dangers of travel in anticipation of gaining profit in the future. It is good to bear hardships in seeking knowledge for the sake of attaining great happiness in this world and in the Hereafter. Here it is similar. Leaving jihad, although it preserves the self from the danger of being killed and preserves wealth from being spent, in the present, nevertheless it involves kinds of harm. Among them: when the enemy knows that you are inclined to ease and inaction, he targets your lands and seeks to kill you. Then either he will seize you and make your blood and wealth lawful to himself, or you will be forced to fight them without having prepared weapons and arms. This is like leaving the treatment of a disease at its first appearance because of the soul's aversion to bearing the bitterness of the medicine. Then in the end a person becomes compelled to bear many times that aversion and hardship.

The conclusion is that fighting is a cause of attaining security, and that is better than benefiting from the safety of the moment. Among its benefits is the acquisition of spoils, and among them is the great joy of prevailing over the enemies.

As for what relates to religion, these are many. Among them is the great reward that the mujahid obtains when he performs jihad seeking nearness to Allah and as worship, and follows the path of uprightness, so that he does not spoil what he has done. Among them is that your enemy fears that he may overpower you, and you do not endure the trial, so you turn away from the religion. Among them is that when your enemy sees your earnestness in your religion and your giving of your selves and wealth in seeking it, he inclines because of that toward your religion. Then if he embraces Islam at your hands, you thereby become deserving of the great reward with Allah. Among them is that whoever advances to fighting seeking the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, has borne the pain of being killed for the sake of seeking the good pleasure of Allah. And as long as a man is not certain of the grace and mercy of Allah, and that He does not waste the reward of the good-doers, and that the pleasures of this world are vain matters, he does not accept being killed. When this is so, a person departs this world loving Allah and hating the world, and that is among the greatest felicities of a human being.

So it has been established by what we have mentioned that the nature, even if it dislikes fighting the enemies of Allah, contains much good, and conversely. It is known that when two matters conflict, the one that is more beneficial is the preferred one. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾.

**The third issue:** Al-sharr (evil) is harm (al-su'). Its origin is from sharartu al-shay' when I spread it out: it is said, sharartu al-lahm wa al-thawb when I spread them out to dry. From this is His saying:

*Until the pages of the Qur'an were spread out by the palms*

And al-sharar is the flame, because of its spreading out. Accordingly, al-sharr is the spreading out of harmful things.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** ﴿'Asa﴾ suggests doubt, like ﴿la'alla﴾ (perhaps), but from Allah, exalted is He, it is certainty. Some have said: it is a word expressing hope, so it does not indicate that doubt occurs in the speaker, but it indicates that doubt occurs in the listener. On this assumption there is no need for interpretation (ta'wil, figurative explanation). But if we say that it has the meaning of ﴿la'alla﴾, then the interpretation of it is among the explanations mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. Al-Khalil said: ﴿'asa﴾ from Allah is obligatory in the Qur'an. He said: ﴿So perhaps Allah will bring the victory﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52], and it has occurred. And ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾ [Yusuf: 83], and it has happened. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows, while you know not﴾, its purpose is a great encouragement to jihad. This is because when a person believes in the deficiency of his own knowledge and the perfection of the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and then knows that He, glorified is He, commands the servant only with what contains his good and his welfare, he knows with certainty that what Allah, exalted is He, has commanded him is obligatory for him to comply with, whether it is disliked by his nature or not. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: O servant, know that My knowledge is more perfect than yours, so be occupied with My obedience and do not turn to the demands of your nature. Thus this verse in this context follows the course of His saying, exalted is He, in reply to the angels: ﴿Indeed I know what you do not know﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 217 (part 1 of 3):

God's words: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin), but barring from the way of God, disbelief in Him, barring (people) from the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is greater in the sight of God; and persecution is greater than killing. They will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. Whoever of you apostatizes from his religion and dies while a disbeliever, those—their deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire, wherein they will abide forever.﴾

There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: scholars differ over whether the questioner was a Muslim or a disbeliever. Those who say he was a Muslim are of two groups.

The first group: They said that when God prescribed fighting for them, and the people held the sacred month and the Sacred Mosque in the greatest sanctity regarding the prohibition of fighting, it was not far-fetched in their minds that the command to fight was restricted to other times and other places. This led them to ask the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "Is it lawful for us to fight them in this month and in this place?" Then the verse was revealed. According to this view, the apparent meaning is that the question came from Muslims.

The second group, who are the majority of the exegetes, related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent ʿAbdullah ibn Jahsh al-Asadi, who was his cousin on his father's side, two months before the battle of Badr, and seventeen months after his arrival in Medina, with eight men. He wrote him a letter and a covenant and handed it to him, and commanded him to open it after two stages and read it to his companions and act upon what was in it. When he opened it, it said: 'To proceed: march in the blessing of God, Exalted, with those who follow you until you reach Batn Nakhla, and lie in wait there for the caravan of Quraysh, perhaps you will bring us some good from it.' ʿAbdullah said: 'I hear and obey his command.' Then he said to his companions: 'Whoever among you loves martyrdom, let him come with me, for I am proceeding in obedience to his command; and whoever loves to stay behind, let him stay behind.' He proceeded until he reached Batn Nakhla between Mecca and al-Taif. ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami and three men with him passed by them. When they saw the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), they shaved the head of one of them, giving the impression that they were pilgrims (ʿummar). Then Waqid ibn ʿAbdullah al-Handhali, who was one of those with ʿAbdullah ibn Jahsh, came and shot ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami and killed him. They captured two men and drove the caravan with what was in it until they arrived before the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Quraysh cried out and said: 'Muhammad has made lawful the sacred month, a month in which the frightened man is safe, yet he sheds blood in it.' The Muslims too were troubled by this. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I did not command you to fight in the sacred month.' ʿAbdullah ibn Jahsh said: 'O Messenger of God, we killed Ibn al-Hadrami, then we entered the evening and looked at the crescent of Rajab, and we do not know whether we struck him in Rajab or in Jumada.' Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) held back the caravan and the captives, and this verse was revealed. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) then took the spoils.'" On this interpretation, the most evident view is that this question came from Muslims, for several reasons.

The first: most of those present with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were Muslims.

The second: what comes before this verse and what comes after it is addressed to the Muslims. What comes before it is God's words: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:214], which is addressed to the Muslims. And (what comes after it is) His words: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:219], and ﴿They ask you about orphans﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:220].

The third: Saʿid ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "I have never seen a people better than the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They asked him only about thirteen questions until he passed away, all of which are in the Qur'an, among them: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾."

The second view is that this question came from the disbelievers. They said: they asked the Messenger (ﷺ) about fighting in the sacred month, so that if he informed them that it was permitted, they would ambush him and make lawful fighting him in it. So God revealed this verse: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾, meaning: they ask you about fighting in the sacred month. ﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin)﴾, but barring from the way of God, from the Sacred Mosque, and disbelief in Him, is greater than that fighting. ﴿They will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion﴾. Thus God made clear that their purpose in this question was to fight the Muslims. Then God revealed after it His words: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and violations are subject to retribution. So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:194]. In this verse He thus stated explicitly that fighting by way of defence is permissible.

The second issue: God's words ﴿fighting in it﴾ are in the genitive case as a substitute (badal) for ﴿the sacred month﴾. This is called badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), like your saying: "Zayd's knowledge impressed me, Zayd's speech benefited me, Zayd's wealth was stolen, Zayd's reward was taken." God said: ﴿Killed were the companions of the trench, the fire full of fuel﴾ [al-Buruj 85:4–5]. Some said: the genitive in ﴿fighting﴾ is by repetition of the governing word, and the implied meaning is: they ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. This is also how it is read in the recitation of Ibn Masʿud and al-Rabiʿ. A parallel is God's words: ﴿to those who were oppressed among them, to those of them who believed﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:75]. ʿIkrimah read it as (qatlin fihi) [with the word "killing" in the genitive].

As for God's words ﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin)﴾, there are two issues in it.

The first issue: ﴿fighting in it﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿a great (sin)﴾ is its predicate. Although ﴿fighting﴾ is indefinite, it has been specified by ﴿in it﴾, so it was good to make it the subject. The meaning of ﴿great﴾ is: grave and reprehensible, just as a grave sin is called a major sin (kabirah). God said: ﴿How grave a word it is that issues from their mouths﴾ [al-Kahf 18:5].
