If it is asked: why was ﴿fighting﴾ made indefinite in God's words ﴿fighting in it﴾? For the rule is that when an indefinite noun is repeated, the second must come with the definite article so that the second mention is the same as the first; for otherwise the second mention would be other than the first, as in God's words: ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ [al-Sharh 94:6].

We say: Yes, what you mention is true, that when a word is repeated and both are indefinite, the second is intended as other than the first. But the people meant by their words ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾ that particular fighting which ʿAbdullah ibn Jahsh had undertaken. So God said: ﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin)﴾. This contains an indication that the fighting which is truly great is not this fighting about which you asked; rather it is another fighting. For this fighting had the aim of supporting Islam and humbling disbelief, so how could this be among the major sins? The truly great fighting is that whose aim is the destruction of Islam and the strengthening of disbelief. Thus the choice of indefiniteness in both expressions was for the sake of this subtle point. However, God did not state this explicitly, lest their hearts be constricted. Rather, He left the statement ambiguous, such that its outward form resembles what they intended, while its inner meaning agrees with the truth. This was achieved by mentioning these two expressions in the indefinite form. Had either of them, or both, been expressed in the definite form, this noble benefit would have been lost. Glory be to Him, beneath every word of this Book is a subtle secret, which none can grasp except people of understanding.

The second issue: the majority agree that the ruling of this verse is the prohibition of fighting in the sacred month. Then they differed over whether this ruling remains in force or has been abrogated (naskh). It is related from Ibn Jurayj that he said: "ʿAta' swore to me by God that it is not lawful for people to make war in the Sanctuary or in the sacred months, except by way of defence." Jabir related: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not make war in the sacred month unless he was attacked." Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab was asked: "Is it proper for the Muslims to fight the disbelievers in the sacred month?" He said: "Yes." Abu ʿUbayd said: "Today, people on the frontiers, all of them, hold this view and consider raiding permissible in all the months, and I have not seen any scholar of Syria or Iraq object to them in this, according to the view of the people of the Hijaz."

The evidence for its permissibility is God's words: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:5], and this verse abrogates the prohibition of fighting in the sacred month. But in my view, God's words ﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin)﴾ are an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, so it refers to a single instance and not to all instances. Therefore this verse contains no proof of the absolute prohibition of fighting in the sacred month, and there is no need to posit abrogation (naskh) here.

As for God's words ﴿and barring from the way of God, disbelief in Him, (barring from) the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is greater in the sight of God﴾, there are two issues in it.

The first issue: the grammarians have several interpretations of this verse.

The first is the view of the Basrans, which al-Zajjaj chose: that God's words ﴿barring from the way of God, disbelief in Him, the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it﴾ are all in the nominative case by way of the inceptive (mubtada'), and their predicate is ﴿is greater in the sight of God﴾. The meaning is: the fighting you asked about, although it is great, these things are greater than it. So if you do not refrain from these in the sacred month, how can you blame ʿAbdullah ibn Jahsh for that fighting, when he had a clear excuse for it? For it was possible that that killing took place in Jumada al-Akhirah. A parallel is God's words to the Children of Israel: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:44], and ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff 61:2]. This is a clear view. However, they differed over the genitive in God's words ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾, and mentioned two possibilities:

One: it is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿in it﴾ (bihi).

The second, which is the view of most, is that it is conjoined to ﴿the way of God﴾. They said: this is reinforced by God's words: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar (people) from the way of God and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Hajj 22:25].

They raised objections against the first view, that it is not permissible to conjoin to a pronoun, since one does not say: "I passed by him and ʿAmr." And against the second, that on this view the sense of the verse would be: "barring from the way of God and barring from the Sacred Mosque," so the phrase "from the Sacred Mosque" would be a complement of "barring," and a complement and its relative clause are regarded as one thing, so inserting a foreign element between them is not permissible.

The answer to the first: why is it not permissible to posit an implied preposition there, so that the sense is: "and disbelief in Him and in the Sacred Mosque"? Implication in God's speech is not strange. This is further confirmed by the recitation of Hamzah (tasa'aluna bihi wal-arham) [al-Nisa' 4:1] in the genitive. If Hamzah had transmitted this dialect, it would be accepted by consensus; and if he recited it in the Book of God, it is all the more likely to be accepted.

As for the majority who chose the second view, they said: there is no doubt that it entails a foreign element coming between the complement and its relative clause, and the rule is that this is not permitted; but we have accepted it here for two reasons:

The first: barring from the way of God and disbelief in Him are like a single thing in meaning, so it is as though there is no separation.

The second: the position of God's words ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾ should be right after ﴿the Sacred Mosque﴾, but it was placed before it because of the great concern (for it), as in God's words: ﴿and none is equal to Him, anyone﴾ [al-Ikhlas 112:4]. The sentence should have been: "and none is equal to Him," but the great concern required placing it first; so likewise here.

The second view on this verse, which is the choice of al-Farra' and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, is that God's words ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾ are conjoined by the conjunction "and" to ﴿the sacred month﴾, and the meaning is: they ask you about fighting in the sacred month and the Sacred Mosque. After this there are two ways.

[Page 27]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 217 (part 2 of 3):

The first way: His saying ﴿fighting in it﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and His saying ﴿is a grave matter, and barring from the way of God and disbelief in Him﴾ is a predicate after a predicate (khabar ba'da khabar). The implied meaning is: fighting in it is judged to be grave, judged to be a barring from the way of God, and judged to be disbelief in God.

The second way: His saying ﴿fighting in it is grave﴾ is a complete subject-predicate sentence (jumlat mubtada' wa khabar). As for His saying ﴿and barring from the way of God﴾, it is in the nominative by virtue of being a subject, and likewise His saying ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾. The predicate is omitted because what precedes it indicates it. The implied meaning is: Say, "Fighting in it is grave, and barring from the way of God is grave, and disbelief in Him is grave." A parallel is your saying, "Zayd is departing, and 'Amr," whose implied meaning is "and 'Amr is departing."

The Basrans criticised this answer. They said: As for your claim that the implied wording of the verse is "They ask you about fighting in the Sacred Mosque," this is weak, because the question was actually about fighting in the Sacred Month, not about fighting in the Sacred Mosque. They also criticised the first way, saying that it requires fighting in the Sacred Month to be disbelief in God, and this is an error by consensus (ijma'). They criticised the second way by saying that when He said afterwards ﴿and expelling its people from it is greater﴾, meaning greater than everything mentioned before, it follows that expelling the people of the Mosque from the Mosque is greater before God than disbelief, and this too is an error by consensus.

I say: al-Farra' (the grammarian) may answer the first objection by asking: Who told you that the question did not concern fighting in the Sacred Mosque? Rather, the apparent meaning is that it did, because the people regarded fighting in the Sacred Month and in the Sacred Land as grave, and in their view each was as ugly as the other. So it is apparent that they combined the two in the question. And their claim on the first way entails that fighting in the Sacred Month is disbelief.

We reply: It follows that fighting in the Sacred Month is disbelief, and we affirm this, because an indefinite noun in an affirmative sentence does not indicate generality. In our view, a single fighting in the Sacred Mosque is disbelief, but it does not follow that every fighting is like that. Their claim on the second way entails that expelling the people of the Mosque from it is greater than disbelief. We reply: By "the people of the Mosque" is meant the Messenger (peace be upon him) and the Companions. Expelling the Messenger from the Mosque in a humiliating manner is, without doubt, disbelief, and together with being disbelief it is also injustice, because it is harming a person without a prior offence or any subsequent cause. And there is no doubt that a thing which is both injustice and disbelief is greater and uglier before God than something which is disbelief alone. This is the summary of the explanation of al-Farra's view.

The third view concerning the verse is His saying ﴿Say: fighting in it is grave, and barring from the way of God, and disbelief in Him﴾. Its meaning is clear: fighting in it is described by these attributes. As for the genitive case in His saying ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾, it is the particle of oath (waw al-qasam), except that the majority of scholars gave this view no weight.

* * *

Second issue: As for barring from the way of God, there are several interpretations:

First: It is a barring from faith in God and in Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Second: It is a barring of the Muslims from emigrating to the Messenger (peace be upon him).

Third: It is the barring of the Muslims, in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, from performing the 'umrah to the House.

Someone might object: The report indicates that this verse was revealed before the battle of Badr, in the story of 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, while the incident of al-Hudaybiyya took place a long time after the battle of Badr. It may be answered that what is in the foreknowledge of God, exalted is He, is as if it had occurred. As for disbelief in God, it is disbelief in His being the sender of the Messengers, deserving worship, and able to resurrect. As for His saying ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾: if we attach it to the pronoun in ﴿in it﴾, the meaning is "and disbelief in the Sacred Mosque." Disbelief in the Sacred Mosque means preventing people from praying in it and circumambulating it, and so they have disbelieved in that which is the cause of its excellence by which it is distinguished from the rest of the sacred places. But whoever holds that it is conjoined to "the way of God" means: "and barring from the Sacred Mosque," because they barred from the Sacred Mosque those who circumambulate it, those who remain in it for worship, and those who bow and prostrate.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and expelling its people from it﴾, the meaning is that they expelled the Muslims from the Mosque, indeed from Mecca. He called them its people because they were the ones who upheld the rights of the House, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He made them hold to the word of piety, and they were more deserving of it and worthy of it﴾ [al-Fath 48:26]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And what is wrong with them that God should not punish them, while they bar from the Sacred Mosque, and they were not its guardians? Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾ [al-Anfal 8:34]. Thus God informed us that the polytheists, by their polytheism, had removed themselves from being the guardians of the Mosque. Then, after He mentioned these things, He judged them to be greater, meaning that each of them is greater than fighting in the Sacred Month. This is a deduction from the view of al-Zajjaj.

We say that each of these things is greater than fighting in the Sacred Month for two reasons:

First: Each of these things is disbelief, and disbelief is greater than fighting.

Second: We claim that each of these things is greater than fighting in the Sacred Month, namely the fighting that proceeded from 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, which was certain to have occurred in the Sacred Month. These disbelievers are certain that these things were done by them in the Sacred Month, so it follows that the occurrence of these things is greater.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and persecution is greater than killing﴾, scholars have mentioned two views concerning persecution (fitna):

First: It is disbelief. This is the view of most exegetes, but in my opinion it is weak, because on al-Zajjaj's view this has already been mentioned, since He, exalted is He, said ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾, and then ﴿is greater﴾. So interpreting persecution as disbelief would be a repetition. Rather, this interpretation is sound on the view of al-Farra'.

Second: Persecution is that by which they tested the Muslims concerning their religion, sometimes by casting doubts into their hearts and sometimes by torture, as they did to Bilal, Suhayb and 'Ammar ibn Yasir. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ishaq. We have already mentioned that persecution (fitna) is an expression for testing (imtihan). It is said: "I subjected the gold to fire" when you put it into the fire to remove the impurity from it. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial (fitna)﴾ [al-Taghabun 64:15], meaning a test for you, because when a man is required to spend his wealth in the way of God, he thinks about his child, and this becomes a barrier preventing him from spending. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. Do people think that they will be left to say "We believe" and they will not be tested (yuftanun)?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:1-2], meaning they will not be examined concerning their religion through various kinds of affliction. He said: ﴿And We tested you with trials (futunan)﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:40], and it is nothing but examination through affliction. He said: ﴿And among people is one who says, "We believe in God," but when he is harmed for God's sake, he regards the persecution of people as the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:10], and what is meant is the trial which befalls him from the direction of religion at the hands of the disbelievers. He said: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted (fatanu) the believing men and believing women and did not repent﴾ [al-Buruj 85:10], meaning they harmed them and subjected them to torture in order to test their steadfastness in their religion. He said: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieved will persecute you (yaftinakum)﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:101]. He said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot tempt [anyone] to it, except one who is destined for Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat 37:161-163]. He said: ﴿So they follow that which is unclear of it, seeking persecution (fitna)﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:7], meaning trial in religion. He said: ﴿And beware of them, lest they tempt you (yaftinuka) away from some of what God has revealed to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:49]. He said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial (fitna) for those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:5]. He said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾ [Yunus 10:85], and the meaning is that they should be tempted away from their religion, so that what they are in of disbelief and wrongdoing becomes beautiful in their eyes. He said: ﴿So you will see and they will see, which of you is the afflicted (maftun)﴾ [al-Qalam 68:5-6]. It was said that "the afflicted" means "the insane," and madness is a fitna, since it is an affliction and a departure from the path of those who are sound in intellect.

Thus these verses establish that fitna is examination. We have said that persecution is greater than killing because persecution from religion leads to much killing in this world and to the deserving of everlasting punishment in the Hereafter. So it is correct that persecution is greater than killing, let alone that killing about which the question was asked, which was the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami.

It is reported that when this verse was revealed, 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, the commander of this expedition (sariyya), wrote to the believers in Mecca: "When the polytheists reproach you for fighting in the Sacred Month, reproach them in turn for disbelief, for expelling the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) from Mecca, and for preventing the believers from the Sacred House." He said: ﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able﴾. The meaning is clear. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Neither the Jews nor the Christians will be pleased with you until you follow their religion﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:120].

* * *

In this there are some issues:

First issue: "He has ceased doing such-and-such" (ma zala yafa'lu kadha) and "he does not cease doing such-and-such" (la yazal yafa'lu kadha). al-Wahidi said: This is a verb that has no verbal noun (masdar), and no active or passive participle is derived from it. Examples of such verbs are numerous, like 'asa (perhaps), which has neither a verbal noun nor a present tense form; and likewise dhu, ma fati'a, halumma, haka, hat, and ta'al. The meaning of ﴿they will not cease﴾ is that they persist in that action, because cessation (zawal) implies negation, so when you add ma to it, it becomes a negation of a negation, which indicates continuous affirmation.

Second issue: His saying ﴿until they turn you back from your religion﴾ means "until they turn you back"; it was also said that the meaning is "so that they may turn you back."

Third issue: His saying ﴿if they are able﴾ is a suggestion that their ability is unlikely, like a man saying to his enemy, "If you overcome me, then do not spare me," while he is confident that the enemy will not overcome him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾. On this there are issues:

First issue: al-Wahidi said: His saying ﴿and whoever reverts﴾ manifests the doubling of the consonant with a jussive form, because the second radical is vowelless. This is more common in the language than assimilation (idgham). His saying ﴿and dies﴾ is in the jussive by conjunction with ﴿reverts﴾, and its answer is ﴿those, their deeds have become void﴾.

Second issue: When He, exalted is He, made clear that their aim in that fighting was that the Muslims should revert from their religion, He mentioned after it a severe threat against apostasy (ridda), saying: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those, their deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter﴾, and he deserves everlasting punishment in the Fire.

* * *

Third issue: The apparent meaning of the verse requires that the rulings mentioned follow from apostasy only if the apostate dies upon disbelief. But if he embraces Islam again after apostasy, none of these rulings applies. From this point arise a legal-theoretical discussion (usuli) and a positive-law discussion (furu'i).

As for the legal-theoretical discussion, a group of theologians (mutakallimun) claimed that a condition for the validity of faith and disbelief is the attainment of the end (al-muwafah), so faith is not faith unless the believer dies upon it, and disbelief is not disbelief unless the disbeliever dies upon it. They said: Because whoever was a believer and then reverted, God forbid, if that outward faith were faith in reality, he would have deserved everlasting reward, and then after his disbelief he deserves everlasting punishment. Then either both entitlements remain, which is impossible, or it is said that the later removes the earlier, and this is impossible for several reasons:

First: The contrariness exists between the earlier and the later, so the later removing the earlier is no more likely than the earlier repelling the later. Rather the second is more likely, because repelling is easier than removing.

Second: If the contrariness exists from both sides, then the condition for the later to arise is the cessation of the earlier. So if we explained the cessation of the earlier by the arising of the later, it would lead to circular reasoning (dawr), which is impossible.

**Third point:** The reward of earlier faith and the punishment of later disbelief are either equal, or one exceeds the other. If they are equal, each must cancel the other entirely, and then the person is neither among the people of reward nor among the people of punishment. This is invalid by *ijma'* (scholarly consensus). If one exceeds the other, let us suppose the earlier is greater. When the later arrives, it removes only what is equal to it, so some of the entitlements are removed and others are not, even though they are alike in their essence. That would be a preponderance without a preponderant cause, which is impossible. Let us suppose instead that the earlier is less. Then either the entirety of the later, as the greater, has an effect in removing the earlier, in which case independent causes converge on a single effect, which is impossible. Or only some parts of the later have the effect in removing the earlier, and the specification of that part with this effect is a preponderance of like over like without a preponderant cause, which is impossible. Therefore, from what we have mentioned, it is established that if a person was a believer and then disbelieved, that earlier faith, although we used to think it was faith, was not faith in God's sight. It thus becomes clear that *muwafah* (dying in a state of faith or disbelief) is a condition for faith to be faith and for disbelief to be disbelief. This is what the verse indicates, for it shows that the condition for apostasy to bring about those rulings is that the apostate dies in that apostasy.

* * *

**The legal question:** If a Muslim prays, then apostatizes, then reverts to Islam within the prayer time, al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) said: there is no obligation to repeat it. Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him) said: he must make up what he performed, and likewise the Hajj. The proof of al-Shafi'i (may God be pleased with him) is the words of God, Exalted: ﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become void.﴾ This is a condition for the voiding of deeds: that one dies while a disbeliever. This person did not meet this condition, so his deed must not be voided. If it is objected that this is contradicted by His words: ﴿Had they associated others with God, what they used to do would have been lost from them﴾ [al-An'am: 88], and His words: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become void﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], the reply is that one cannot say that the absolute must be understood in light of the restricted, for this is not a case of the absolute and the restricted (*mutlaq* and *muqayyad*). Scholars have agreed that if a ruling is linked to two conditions, and it is linked to the condition that the ruling takes effect when either of them is met, as when a man says to his slave: "You are free when Thursday comes," and then: "You are free when Thursday or Friday comes," neither statement is nullified. Rather, when Thursday comes, he is freed. If he sold the slave, and then Thursday came while the slave was not in his possession, then he bought him back, and then Friday came while the slave was in his possession, the slave is freed by the first conditional.

The second question concerns the use of this verse as evidence: this verse indicates that dying in apostasy is a condition for the whole set of rulings mentioned in it, and we affirm this. Among these rulings is eternal abiding in the Fire, which is established only with this condition. The dispute is only about the voiding of deeds, and the verse contains no indication that dying in apostasy is a condition for it.

The reply is that this is a case of the absolute and the restricted, not a case of linking a ruling to one condition versus two conditions. Linking to one condition or to two conditions is valid only if linking to each of them does not prevent linking to the other. In our issue, if we make mere apostasy the cause of voiding, then dying in apostasy would have no effect on voiding at any time at all. Therefore we know that this is not a case of linking to one condition versus two, but a case of the absolute and the restricted.

As for the second question, its answer is that the verse indicates that apostasy causes voiding only on the condition of dying in apostasy, and that it causes eternal abiding in the Fire only on the condition of dying in apostasy. On this basis, that question falls away.

* * *

**On God's words:** ﴿Then those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ On this there are several issues.

**First issue:** The people of language said: the root of *habat* (ihbat, "voiding," from *habat*, to be spoiled) is that camels eat something that harms them, so their bellies swell and they perish. In the hadith: "Indeed, among what spring's growth produces is that which kills by bloating or brings near death." So the nullification of deeds was named after this, because it is like the spoiling of a thing through the entry of a corrupting agent upon it.

* * *

**Second issue:** The meaning of the voiding of a deed is not the annihilation of the deed itself, for a deed is a thing which, whenever it comes into existence, passes away and ceases, and annihilating what is already non-existent is impossible. Then the theologians differed about it. Those who affirm *ihbat* (voiding) and *takfir* (the cancellation of merit) said: its meaning is that the punishment for the apostasy that has occurred cancels the reward of the earlier faith. This is either on the condition of equivalence, according to the view of Abu Hashim and the majority of the later Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist theological school), or without the condition of equivalence, according to the view of Abu 'Ali (al-Jubba'i). Those who deny *ihbat* in this sense said: the meaning of voiding mentioned in God's Book is that when the apostate commits apostasy, that apostasy is a voiding deed, because the one who commits apostasy could have performed instead of it a deed that merits reward. When he does not perform that good deed, and instead performs in its place this bad deed from which he gains no benefit, but rather gains the greatest harm, it is said: he voided his deed, that is, he performed a false deed that has no benefit but has harm. Then those who deny *ihbat* said: this which we have mentioned as the interpretation of *ihbat* either is the literal meaning of the word *ihbat*, or it is not. If it is the literal meaning, it must be adopted. If it is a figurative meaning, it must also be adopted, because we have mentioned the decisive proofs in the issue that *muwafah* is a condition for the validity of faith. Moreover, the claim that the effect of a later act removes the effect of an earlier act is impossible.

**Third issue:** As for the voiding of deeds in this world, it means that he is killed when he is captured, and fought until he is captured. He does not deserve loyalty, support, or good praise from the believers. His wife is separated from him, and he does not inherit from the Muslims. It is also possible that the meaning of God's words ﴿their deeds have become void in this world﴾ is that whatever they intend after apostasy of harming the Muslims and plotting against them by leaving their religion is all void, so they gain nothing from it, because God exalts Islam through His helpers. On this interpretation, "deeds" means what they do after apostasy. As for the voiding of their deeds in the Hereafter, according to those who affirm *ihbat*, it means that this apostasy nullifies their entitlement to the reward they had earned by their earlier deeds. According to those who deny this, it means that they gain from that apostasy no reward or benefit in the Hereafter, but rather gain from it the greatest harms. Then He explained the manner of that harm, saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 218:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated and striven in the way of Allah - those expect the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Page 34

There are two issues concerning the verse.

The first issue: concerning the connection of this verse with what precedes it, there are two views.

The first: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh said: 'O Messenger of Allah, suppose there is no punishment for what we have done; do we then hope for a reward and recompense from it?' So this verse was revealed." This is because ʿAbd Allah was a believer, was an emigrant (muhajir), and, because of this fighting, was a fighter in struggle (mujahid).

The second: when the Exalted had made jihad obligatory earlier by His saying, ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216], and explained that abandoning it is a cause of threat, He followed that with mention of those who undertake it, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated and striven in the way of Allah﴾. And a threat is hardly ever found without a promise following it.

* * *

The second issue: ﴿emigrated﴾ means they left their homelands and their kin. Its origin is from hajr, which is the opposite of wasl (union). From it comes the term hujr for ugly speech, because it is something that ought to be shunned; and al-Hajirah is the time at which work is abandoned (the midday heat). Al-muhajarah is a form of mufa'alah from hijrah. It is permissible that what is meant is that loved ones and relatives shunned them because of this religion, and they too shunned those people for this same reason, so that was a mutual forsaking (muhajarah). As for al-mujahadah, its origin is from jahd, which is hardship. It is also permissible that the meaning of mujahadah is that one adds his effort to another effort in supporting the religion of Allah, just as al-musa'adah (assistance) is an expression for a man joining his arm to another arm so that support and strength are obtained. It is also permissible that what is meant by mujahadah is exerting effort in fighting the enemy, and when the enemy does the same, it becomes a mutual act (mufa'alah).

Then the Exalted said: ﴿those expect the mercy of Allah﴾, and concerning this there are two views:

The first: that what is meant by it is hope (raja'), which is an expression for the supposition of benefits one anticipates. The Exalted intends in this place that they hope for the reward of Allah; this is because ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh was not certain of success and reward in his deed, but rather he anticipated and hoped for it.

If it is asked: why was the promise made absolutely by way of hope, and not stated definitively as in the other verses?

We say: the answer has several aspects.

First: our school holds that reward for faith and deed is not obligatory by reason, but only by the ruling of the promise; therefore He attached it to hope.

Second: suppose it is obligatory by reason through the ruling of the promise; nevertheless it is conditioned on not disbelieving after that, and this condition is doubtful, not certain; therefore what is attained is indeed hope, not certainty.

Third: what is mentioned here is faith, emigration, and striving in the way of Allah, and beyond these a person necessarily needs all other deeds, and that he hope Allah will grant him success in them, just as He granted him success in these three; therefore He attached it to hope.

Fourth: the meaning of the verse is not that Allah made the servant doubtful about this forgiveness; rather the meaning is describing them as departing this world with emigration and striving, considering themselves deficient in regard to the right of Allah the Exalted, seeing that they have not worshipped Him as He deserves and have not fulfilled what is incumbent upon them in supporting His religion; so they come before Allah in fear and hope, as He said: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

The second view: that what is meant by hope is certainty and conviction regarding the very principle of reward, while supposition entered only into its quantity and its timing. Concerning this there are aspects which we established in the explanation of His saying: ﴿those who assume that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46].

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: Allah the Exalted will fulfill their hope for them if they die upon faith and righteous deeds, and that He is Forgiving and Merciful; He forgave ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions what they did not know, and showed mercy to them.

Page 35

The third ruling: on wine.

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾

Know that His saying: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾ does not state what they asked about. It is possible that they asked about its reality and essence; it is possible that they asked about the permissibility of benefiting from it; and it is possible that they asked about the lawfulness or prohibition of drinking it. However, when He, exalted is He, answered by mentioning prohibition, the specificity of the answer indicates that the question was about lawfulness and prohibition.

On the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: They said: Four verses were revealed concerning wine. In Mecca was revealed His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapes you take intoxicant and good provision﴾ [al-Nahl: 67]. The Muslims drank it, and it was lawful for them. Then "Umar, Mu'adh and a group of the Companions said: O Messenger of Allah, give us a ruling on wine, for it removes the intellect and plunders wealth. So there was revealed concerning it His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: In them is great sin and some benefit for people﴾. Some drank it and others abstained. Then 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf invited some of them, and they drank and became intoxicated. Some of them stood to pray and recited: "Say: O disbelievers, I worship what you worship." So there was revealed: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]. Few then drank it. Then a group of the Ansar gathered, among them Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. When they became intoxicated they boasted and recited poetry to one another, until Sa'd recited a poem containing satire of the Ansar. An Ansari struck him with a jawbone of a camel, wounding him with a severe wound, and he complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). 'Umar said: O Allah, make clear to us a healing explanation concerning wine. So there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90] up to His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. 'Umar said: We have desisted, O Lord."

Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The wisdom in the prohibition occurring in this order is that Allah, exalted is He, knew that the people had become accustomed to drinking wine and derived much benefit from it. So He knew that if He prohibited it all at once, that would be difficult for them. Therefore He employed this gradualness and gentleness in the prohibition. Some people said that Allah prohibited wine and gambling by this verse. Then there was revealed His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], which required the prohibition of drinking wine at the time of prayer, because a wine drinker cannot pray except while intoxicated; so the prohibition of that was an implicit prohibition of drinking. Then the verse of al-Ma'idah was revealed, and it was in the utmost strength in prohibition. It is related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that this verse was revealed after the prohibition of wine.

* * *

The second issue: Know that according to us this verse indicates the prohibition of wine, so we need to explain what wine is, and then to explain that this verse indicates the prohibition of drinking wine.

Page 36

As for the first stage: in explaining what wine is. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Every intoxicating drink is wine. Abu Hanifa said: Wine is the name for strong grape juice that has frothed.

The proofs of al-Shafi'i for his view are several:

The first: What Abu Dawud related in his Sunan, from al-Sha'bi, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The prohibition of wine was revealed on the day it was revealed, and it was from five: from grapes, dates, wheat, barley, and millet; and wine is that which covers the intellect. The mode of inference from it is in three aspects:

The first: that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, informed that wine was prohibited on the day it was prohibited while it was made from wheat and barley, just as it was made from grapes and dates; and this indicates that they called all of them wine.

The second: that he said: Wine was prohibited on the day it was prohibited, while it was made from these things, the wine; and this is as an explicit statement that the prohibition of wine encompasses the prohibition of these five kinds.

The third: that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, added to them every drink that covers the intellect, and there is no doubt that 'Umar was knowledgeable in the language, and his report that wine is the name for everything that covers the intellect is a changing of it.

The second proof: Abu Dawud related from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, from grapes is wine, and from dates is wine, and from honey is wine, and from wheat is wine, and from barley is wine." The inference from it is in two respects:

One: that this is explicit that these things fall under the name of wine, and so they fall under the verse indicating the prohibition of wine.

The second: that it is not the intent of the Lawgiver to teach languages, so his purpose must be to show that the ruling established for wine is established for these, or that the well-known ruling specific to wine is the prohibition of drinking, so it must be established for these drinks. Al-Khattabi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The specification of wine with these five things is not because wine cannot be made except from these five specifically, but their mention came specifically because they were known in that time. So whatever is in their meaning, of millet, sorghum, or the juice of a tree, its ruling is the ruling of these five, just as the specifying of the six items in the report on usury does not prevent the ruling of usury from applying to others.

The third proof: Abu Dawud also related from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is wine, and every intoxicant is forbidden." Al-Khattabi said: His saying, peace be upon him: "Every intoxicant is wine" indicates two things:

One: that wine is the name for everything from which intoxication is found among all drinks. The purpose is that since the verse indicated the prohibition of wine, and the name "wine" was unknown to the people, it was fitting for the Lawgiver to say: the intent of Allah, exalted is He, by this term is this, either in the sense that this is its name in the Arabic language, or in the sense that he established a legal name by way of innovation, as in prayer, fasting, and others.

The other aspect: that its meaning is that it is like wine in prohibition; because his saying "this is wine" means that the literal meaning of this expression indicates that it is itself wine. If there is evidence that this is impossible, it becomes necessary to take it figuratively as similarity in the ruling, which is the distinctive property of that thing.

The fourth proof: Abu Dawud related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about bit', so he said: 'Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden.'" Al-Khattabi said: Bit' is a drink made from honey. In this is the refutation of every interpretation mentioned by those who permit nabidh, and the refutation of the one who says that a small amount of an intoxicant is permissible; for he, peace be upon him, was asked about one type of nabidh and answered by prohibiting the category, so it includes its little and its much. Had there been a distinction in some of its types or quantities, he would have mentioned it and not left it unexplained.

The fifth proof: Abu Dawud related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What its large quantity intoxicates, its small quantity is forbidden."

The sixth proof: It is also related from al-Qasim, from 'A'isha, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Every intoxicant is forbidden, and what the faraq intoxicates, a handful of it is forbidden." Al-Khattabi said: The "faraq" is a measure that holds sixteen ratls. In it is the clearest explanation that the prohibition encompasses all parts of the drink.

The seventh proof: Abu Dawud related from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Umm Salamah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade every intoxicant and every narcotic." Al-Khattabi said: The "mufattir" is every drink that produces lassitude and numbness in the limbs, and there is no doubt that this encompasses all kinds of drinks. Thus all these hadiths indicate that every intoxicant is wine, and it is forbidden.

* * *

The second type of evidence that every intoxicant is wine: adhering to etymological derivations. The people of language said: The root of this letter-sequence is covering. The khimar (veil) was named khimar because it covers the head of the woman; and khamr is what conceals you of trees and other things, of a hollow or a hill; and "I covered the head of the vessel" means I covered it; and the khamir is one who conceals his testimony. Ibn al-Anbari said: It was named khamr because it "ukhamir" the intellect, i.e., mixes with it; it is said: the disease "khamarahu" when it mixed with him; and he recited for Kuthayyir:

"Wholesome, pleasant, free of any mixing ailment."

And it is said: the sickness "khamara" his liver. What he mentioned goes back to the first, because when one thing mixes with another, it becomes like a veil for it. So these derivations indicate that khamr is that which veils the intellect, just as it is called intoxicant (muskir) because it intoxicates the intellect, i.e., restrains it. It seems that it was named by the verbal noun from "khammarahu khamran" when he covered it, for emphasis. Its outcome returns to the point that khamr is intoxication; for intoxication covers the intellect and prevents its light from reaching the limbs. These derivations are among the strongest evidences that the referent of khamr is the intoxicant. How much more so when the numerous hadiths are added to it. It may not be said: This is establishing a language by analogy, which is impermissible; for we say: This is not establishing a language by analogy, but rather determining the referent through these derivations, just as the companions of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on them, say that the referent of nikah is intercourse and they establish it by derivations, and the referent of sawm is abstention and they establish it by derivations.

* * *

The third type of evidence that khamr is the intoxicant: the Ummah is in consensus that the verses revealed concerning wine are three, and two of them came with the word khamr: one is this verse, and the second is the verse of al-Ma'idah; and the third came concerning intoxication, which is His saying: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]. This indicates that what is meant by khamr is the intoxicant.

* * *

The fourth type of proof: that the cause of the prohibition of wine was that "'Umar and Mu'adh said: O Messenger of Allah, indeed wine removes the intellect and plunders wealth, so make clear to us concerning it." They sought the ruling from Allah and His Messenger only because wine removes the intellect; so it is necessary that whatever is equal to wine in this meaning is either wine or equal to wine in this ruling.

* * *

The fifth type of proof: Allah gave as the reason for prohibiting wine His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. There is no doubt that these acts are caused by intoxication, and this causal link is certain. Accordingly, this verse is an explicit text that the prohibition of wine is caused by its being intoxicating. Therefore it must be certain that every intoxicant is wine, and if not, then this ruling must necessarily be established for every intoxicant. Whoever is fair and abandons obstinacy knows that these aspects are manifest and clear in establishing this claim.

The proofs of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, are of several aspects:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapes you take intoxicant and good provision﴾ [al-Nahl: 67]. Allah, exalted is He, bestowed upon us the taking of an intoxicant and good provision; and what we are discussing is an intoxicant and good provision; so it must be permissible, for a favour is only by what is permissible.

**[Page 38 continues]**

The second proof: what Ibn Abbas narrated, that "he (ﷺ) came to the water-station (al-siqaya) in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, leaned against it and said, 'Give me water to drink.' Al-Abbas said, 'Shall I give you a drink of what we steep in our houses?' He said, 'What do you give people to drink?' So he brought him a cup of nabidh (steeped drink). He smelled it, frowned and pushed it away. Al-Abbas said, 'O Messenger of Allah, you have ruined the drink of the people of Makkah!' He said, 'Return the cup to me.' They returned it to him. He asked for water from Zamzam, poured it over the drink, drank it, and said: 'When these drinks become sharp (ightalamat) upon you, cut off their rankness with water.'"

The manner of deriving the proof from it: frowning occurs only at something strong. Also, mixing it with water was to cut its strength, according to the text. And ightilam (sharpness) of a drink means its intensity, like the ightilam of a camel, which means its rage.

The third proof: adhering to the reports of the Companions.

As for the answer to the first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾ (An-Nahl: 67), is indefinite (nakira) in affirmation. So why do you say that this intoxicant and good provision is this nabidh? Then the exegetes agreed that that verse was revealed before these three verses which indicate the prohibition of wine. So these three are either abrogating it (nasikha, i.e., naskh: abrogation) or specifying it (mukhassisa).

As for the hadith, perhaps that nabidh was water in which dates had been steeped so that the saltiness would go away, so the taste of the water changed slightly toward sourness. His nature (peace be upon him) was of extreme delicacy, so his noble nature could not bear that taste, and for this reason he frowned. Also, the purpose of pouring water into it was to remove that amount of sourness or smell. In sum, every intelligent person knows that turning away from those proofs we have mentioned, on the basis of this weak kind of inference, is not permissible.

As for the reports of the Companions, they are contradictory and conflicting, so it is obligatory to set them aside and to return to the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger, peace be upon him. This is the discussion on the reality of wine.

The second position: explaining that this verse indicates the prohibition of wine. Its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: the verse indicates that wine contains sin (ithm), and sin is forbidden, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden, and sin and oppression﴾ (Al-A'raf: 33). The combination of these two verses is therefore evidence for the prohibition of wine.

The second: sin may be meant as punishment, and it may be meant as the sins that deserve punishment. Whichever is meant, it cannot be described by it except what is forbidden.

The third: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit﴾. He declared the preponderance of sin and punishment, and that requires prohibition.

[Page 39]

If it is said: the verse does not indicate that drinking wine is sinful, but only that there is sin in it. Grant that this sin is forbidden, so why do you say that drinking wine, since that sin occurs in it, must be forbidden?

We say: because the question was concerning wine in general. When He, exalted is He, explained that there is sin in it, the meaning was that this sin is inseparable from it under all circumstances. So drinking wine entails this forbidden inseparability, and what entails the forbidden is forbidden. Therefore drinking must be forbidden.

Some said: this verse does not indicate the prohibition of wine, and they argued for this with several points:

One: He, exalted is He, affirmed in it benefits for people, and the forbidden contains no benefit.

The second: If this verse indicated its prohibition, why did they not content themselves with it until the verse of al-Ma'idah and the verse prohibiting prayer while intoxicated were revealed?

The third: He, exalted is He, informed that in both of them there is a great sin. Its implication is that this great sin is present so long as both exist. So if that great sin were the cause of their prohibition, it would be necessary to affirm that their prohibition holds in all the laws.

The answer to the first: obtaining an immediate benefit from it in this world does not prevent it from being forbidden. And when that is so, the presence of benefit in both does not prevent their prohibition, because the truth of the particular entails the truth of the general.

The answer to the second: we have related from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning the prohibition of wine. The hesitation you mentioned is not transmitted from them. It is possible that the senior Companions wished for the revelation of something more emphatic than this verse regarding prohibition, just as Ibrahim, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, asked to witness the giving of life to the dead, so that he might have greater tranquility and assurance.

The answer to the third: His saying, ﴿In both there is a great sin﴾, is a report about the present state, not about the past. In our view, Allah, exalted is He, knew that drinking wine was corrupting for them in that time, and He knew that it was not corrupting for those who were before this nation. This is the complete discussion on this subject.

* * *

The third issue: the reality of maysir (gambling). We say: maysir is gambling (qimar). It is a verbal noun from yasara, like al-mawid and al-marji' from their verbs. It is said: "yasartuhu" when I gambled against him. The scholars differed on its derivation in several ways:

First: Muqatil said: it derives from al-yusr (ease), because it is taking a man's wealth with ease and facility, without toil or hardship. They used to say: "Yassiru lana thaman al-jazur" (provide us with the price of the slaughtered camel). Or it derives from al-yasar (wealth), because it is the cause of his becoming wealthy. And from Ibn Abbas: in the Jahiliyyah a man would risk his family and his property.

Second: Ibn Qutaybah said: maysir comes from division and apportioning. It is said: "yasaru al-shay'" meaning they divided it. So the slaughtered camel itself is called muyassar, because it is divided into parts; it is as if it were the place of division. The yasir is the one who butchers, because he divides the camel's meat. Then those who cast arrows and gambled for the camel are called yasiroon, because by that act they divide the camel's meat.

Third: al-Wahidi said: it is from their saying: "yassara li hadha al-shay'" (this thing became obligatory for me) — "yuyassiru, yusran, wa maysiran," when it became due. The yasir is the one obligated by means of the arrows.

This is the discussion on the derivation of this word.

As for the description of maysir, the author of al-Kashshaf said: they had ten arrows, which are the azlam and aqlam: al-Fadh, al-Tawam, al-Raqib, al-Halis (with a fatha on the ha and kasra on the lam; it is also said with a kasra on the ha and sukun on the lam), al-Musbil, al-Mu'alla, al-Nafis, al-Manih, al-Safih, and al-Wagh. For each of them there was a specified share of a slaughtered camel, which they slaughtered and divided into ten parts. It is also said: twenty-eight parts minus three, and these three are al-Manih, al-Safih, and al-Wagh. For one of them there is a verse on this meaning:

"In this world I have arrows, none of them is a winner;
their names are al-Wagh, al-Safih, and al-Manih."

So al-Fadh has one share, al-Tawam has two, al-Raqib has three, al-Halis has four, al-Nafis has five, al-Musbil has six, and al-Mu'alla has seven. They would place them in the rababa, which is the bag, and place it in the hand of a trustworthy man. Then he shakes it and puts his hand in and brings out an arrow for each man by name. Whoever drew an arrow bearing a share took the share marked by that arrow. Whoever drew an arrow with no share got nothing and had to pay the price of the whole camel. They would give those shares to the poor and would not eat from them, and they took pride in this and would blame whoever did not take part in it, calling him al-baram (the stingy one).

* * *

The fourth issue: they differed on whether maysir is the name of that specific gambling or the name of all kinds of gambling. It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware of these two knucklebones (al-ka'batayn), for they are of the maysir of the non-Arabs (al-'ajam)." And from Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, and Ata': everything in which there is a stake (khatar) is of maysir, even children's play with walnuts. As for chess (al-shatranj), it is related from Ali, peace be upon him, that he said: backgammon (al-nard) and chess are of maysir. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: if chess is free of wagering, and the tongue free of transgression, and the prayer free of forgetfulness, it is not forbidden, and it lies outside maysir, because maysir is that which requires giving up property or taking property, and this is not so. So it is not qimar or maysir. And Allah knows best. As for racing with horses or camels, it is by agreement not of maysir, and its explanation is mentioned in the Book of Races and Archery in the books of jurisprudence.

* * *

The fifth issue: the great sin (al-ithm al-kabir). In it are several matters:

One: the intellect is the noblest of a person's attributes, and wine is the enemy of the intellect, and whatever is the enemy of the noblest is the basest. So it follows that drinking wine is among the basest matters. Its explanation: the intellect is called "aql" only because it functions like the tether (iqal) of a she-camel. When a person's nature calls him to a vile act, his intellect prevents him from undertaking it. When he drinks wine, the nature that calls to vile acts remains free of the intellect that restrains it. The consequence after that is well known. Ibn Abi al-Dunya related that he passed by a drunkard who was urinating into his hand and wiping his face with it, as one performing ablution, saying: "Praise be to Allah who made Islam a light and water a purifier." And from al-Abbas ibn Mirdas: it was said to him in the Jahiliyyah: "Why do you not drink wine, for it increases your boldness?" He said: "I am not one who takes my ignorance in my hand and puts it into my belly, nor am I content to become the chief of a people and in the evening be their fool."

Two: what Allah, exalted is He, mentioned of causing enmity and hatred and turning people away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer.

Three: among the peculiar features of this sin is that the more a person busies himself with it and the more persistently he commits it, the greater his inclination to it and the stronger his soul's craving for it becomes. This differs from other sins. For example, an adulterer, once he has done it once, his desire for that act wanes, and the more he does it, the more his aversion grows and his revulsion becomes complete. But with drinking, the more he undertakes it, the more his vigor increases and his desire for it becomes complete. When a person persists in it, he becomes immersed in bodily pleasures, turning away from remembering the Hereafter and the Return, until he becomes among those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. In sum, wine removes the intellect, and when the intellect is removed, all vices arise. For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Wine is the mother of all vices" (umm al-khaba'ith).

As for maysir, its sin is that it leads to enmity, and also because of the insults and disputes that occur between them, and because it is the consumption of wealth falsely (bil-batil). That too breeds enmity, for when the one who has lost sees his property taken for nothing, he hates the winner intensely. It also distracts from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer.

As for the benefits mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and benefits for people﴾, the benefits of wine are that they used to get high prices for it when they brought it from distant regions, and when the buyer abandoned haggling over the price, they regarded that as a virtue and nobility, so their profits increased through this cause. Among its benefits is that it strengthens the weak, aids digestion, helps with sexual potency, consoles the grieving, emboldens the coward, makes the stingy generous, clears the complexion, revives natural heat, and increases ambition and loftiness.

Among the benefits of maysir is providing relief to those in need, because whoever won did not eat from the camel, but used to distribute it to the needy. Al-Waqidi mentioned that one of them might win a hundred camels in a single session, and so he obtained wealth without toil or hardship, then he spent it on the needy, and thereby earned praise and commendation.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (kathir) with a *tha'* dotted above (*kathirun*, "much"), while the rest read it with a *ba'* dotted below (*kabir*, "great"). The argument of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i is that God described many kinds of sin in wine and gambling, as in His words: ﴿Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. Thus He mentioned multiple sins in them. Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) cursed ten people because of wine, which indicates the abundance of sin in them. Moreover, the sin mentioned in this verse is like the opposite of the benefits, for He said: "In both there is great sin and benefits." Just as the benefits are many, so too is the sin. The meaning becomes as if He said: "In both there are many harms and many benefits."

The argument of the others is that the intensification of the gravity of a sin comes through its greatness, not through its being many. This is indicated by God's words: ﴿the major sins﴾ [al-Shura: 37], ﴿the major things you are forbidden﴾ [al-Nisa': 31], and ﴿it was a great sin﴾ [al-Nisa': 2]. Also, the readers agreed on His words ﴿and their sin is greater﴾ being with the *ba'* dotted below, and this supports what we have said.

* * *

**The fourth ruling: on spending**

﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus. Thus God makes the verses clear to you, so that you may reflect﴾ ﴿on this world and the Hereafter﴾.

God the Exalted said: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus. Thus God makes the verses clear to you, so that you may reflect﴾ ﴿on this world and the Hereafter﴾.

Know that this question has already been mentioned earlier, and it was answered by mentioning the recipients. Here it is repeated, and it is answered by mentioning the quantity. Al-Qaffal said: A man may ask another about the religion and character of a certain person, and he says: "This person is such that his religion is such-and-such, and his character is such-and-such." Having understood this, we say: When the people saw God and His Messenger encouraging spending and indicating its great reward, they asked about the measure of what they were obligated to give, whether it is all their wealth or part of it. So God informed them that the surplus is acceptable. There are several issues in this verse:

**The first issue:** Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The original meaning of *al-'afw* in the language is "excess." God said: ﴿Take the surplus﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], meaning the excess. He also said: ﴿until they grew in number﴾ [al-A'raf: 95], meaning they increased beyond what they had been in number. Al-Qaffal said: *al-'afw* is what is easy and readily available of what is more than sufficiency. It is said: "Take what is 'afa for you," meaning what is easy. The pardon for a sin seems to return to the sense of ease and facilitation. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have exempted you from the zakat on horses and slaves, so bring a quarter of a tenth of your wealth." Its meaning is lightening by dropping the zakat on horses and slaves. It is also said: "So-and-so *a'fa* so-and-so his right," when he delivered it to him without insistence in demanding it, and this also returns to lightening. It is said: "He gave him such-and-such *'afwan wa safwan*," when he did not spoil it for him with harm. It is also said: "Take from people what is 'afa for you," meaning what is easy. From this is His saying: ﴿Take the surplus﴾, meaning what is easy for you from people. It is also said of easy land: *al-'afw*. Since *al-'afw* is ease, what is generally meant is that which exceeds a person's own need, the needs of his dependents, and those whose maintenance is obligatory upon him. So the statement of one who said that *al-'afw* means excess returns to the explanation we mentioned.

The summary of the interpretation is that God the Exalted disciplined people in spending. He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Give the near of kin his right, and the needy and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully﴾ ﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾ [al-Isra': 26-27]. He said: ﴿Do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29]. He said: ﴿Those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾ [al-Furqan: 67]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If one of you has something, let him begin with himself, then with those he supports, and so on and so forth." He (peace be upon him) also said: "The best charity is that which leaves one wealthy, and one is not blamed for what is sufficient." It is narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah who said: "While we were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), a man came to him with something the size of an egg of gold and said: 'O Messenger of God, take it as charity, for by God I have no other.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned away from him. Then he came to him from in front of him and said: 'Bring it,' angrily. He took it from him and then threw it at him in such a way that if it had hit him it would have hurt him. Then he said: 'One of you comes to me with his wealth, having no other, then sits begging from people. Charity is only from a surplus of wealth. Take it, for we have no need of it.'" And it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would store for his family the provision of a year.

The wise have said: Virtue lies between the two extremes of excess and deficiency. Lavish spending is squandering, and extreme scarcity is stinginess, while justice is virtue, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Say: the surplus﴾. The basis of the law of Muhammad (ﷺ) rests upon observing this subtle point. The law of the Jews is founded on complete harshness, and the law of the Christians on complete leniency, while the law of Muhammad (ﷺ) is moderate in all these matters. Therefore it is more perfect than all of them.

**The second issue:** Abu 'Amr read (*al-'afwu*) with a *damma* on the *waw*, while the rest read it in the accusative (*al-'afwa*). Whoever reads it in the nominative makes *dha* mean *alladhi* ("that which"), and *yunfiqun* is its relative clause, as if he said: "What is it that they spend?" And the answer is: "It is the surplus." Whoever reads it in the accusative, the implied meaning is: "What do they spend?" And its answer is: "They spend the surplus."

* * *

**The third issue:** They differed over whether the spending meant here is obligatory spending or voluntary. As for those who say it is obligatory, they have two views:

[Page 43]

The first: the view of Abu Muslim, that the surplus may be zakat, and its mention here came in summary, while its details are mentioned in the Sunnah.

The second: that this was before the revelation of the verse on charities. People were commanded to take from their earnings what would suffice them for their year, and then to spend the remainder. Then this was abrogated (*mansukh*, i.e., replaced by a later ruling) by the verse of zakat. On this assumption, the verse is abrogated.

The second view: the spending meant here is voluntary giving, which is charity. The one who holds this argues that if it were obligatory, God the Exalted would have specified its amount. Since He did not specify it, but left it to the judgment of the addressee, we know it is not an obligation.

The answer to this: It is not unlikely that God obligates something in general terms and then mentions its detail and explanation by another means.

As for His saying: ﴿Thus God makes the verses clear to you﴾, its meaning is: I have explained to you the matter concerning what you asked about, the aspects and recipients of spending. Likewise I will explain to you, in the future of your days, all that you need.

And His saying: ﴿so that you may reflect﴾ ﴿on this world and the Hereafter﴾ has several aspects:

**The first:** Al-Hasan said: There is inversion in it, and the meaning is: "Thus God makes the verses clear to you, in this world and the Hereafter, so that you may reflect."

**The second:** ﴿Thus God makes the verses clear to you﴾, so that He informs you that wine and gambling have benefits in this world and harms in the Hereafter. When you reflect on the conditions of this world and the Hereafter, you will know that it is necessary to prefer the Hereafter over this world.

**The third:** He informs you that spending wealth on good causes is for the sake of the Hereafter, and withholding it is for the sake of this world. So you reflect on the matter of this world and the Hereafter, and you know that it is necessary to prefer the Hereafter over this world.

Know that since the speech can be taken according to its apparent meaning, as we have established in these two aspects, then positing inversion, as al-Hasan said, would be a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence, and that is not permissible.

**The Fifth Ruling: Concerning Orphans**

﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is good. And if you mix with them, they are your brothers. Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. Had Allah willed, He would have burdened you. Indeed Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is good. And if you mix with them, they are your brothers. Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. Had Allah willed, He would have burdened you. Indeed Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**First issue:** The people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) had become accustomed to profiting from orphans' property. Sometimes they married an orphan girl out of greed for her wealth, or they married her to one of their sons so that her property would not leave their hands. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa', 10]. He also revealed in the verses: ﴿If you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, then marry from among women what seems good to you﴾ [al-Nisa', 3], and His saying: ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, yet you desire to marry them﴾ [al-Nisa', 127], and His saying: ﴿and concerning the oppressed among the children, and that you should stand up for orphans with justice. Whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it﴾ [al-Nisa', 127], and His saying: ﴿Do not approach the property of an orphan except in the best way﴾ [al-An'am, 152]. At that point the people abandoned mixing with orphans, approaching their property, and attending to their affairs. Consequently the orphans' welfare was disrupted and their livelihood deteriorated. This weighed heavily on the people, and they remained perplexed: if they mixed with the orphans and took charge of their property, they feared the severe threat; and if they left them and turned away, the orphans' livelihood was ruined. The people were thus bewildered.

Then, here, it is possible that they asked the Messenger (ﷺ) about this matter. It is also possible that the question was in their hearts, and that they wished Allah would explain to them the correct state of affairs in this matter. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse. It is also reported that when those verses were revealed, they withdrew from the property of orphans and avoided mixing with them in every respect, to the point that food would be set out for an orphan, some of it would be left over, and they would leave it without eating it until it spoiled. A guardian would set aside for the orphan a separate dwelling, food, and drink. This weighed heavily on the weaker Muslims. 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah said: "O Messenger of Allah, not all of us have houses where orphans can live, nor does everyone have food and drink to set aside for an orphan." So this verse was revealed.

***

**Second issue:** His saying: ﴿Setting things right for them is good﴾ has several interpretations.

The first: al-Qadi said: "This statement encompasses attention to the orphan's interests through correction, discipline, and other means, so that he grows up with knowledge, good manners, and virtue. This is because such care has a greater effect on him than improving his material circumstances through trade. It also includes setting right his property, so that it is not consumed by expenses, by means of trade. It further includes the meaning of His saying: ﴿Give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ [al-Nisa', 2]. The word ﴿good﴾ applies to the state of the guardian: that is, this action is better for him than being negligent regarding the orphan's rights. It also applies to the state of the orphan: that is, this action is better for the orphan, in that it includes the well-being of his self and the well-being of his property. Thus this expression comprises all the interests of both the orphan and the guardian."

If it is said: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Setting things right for them is good﴾ covers only the management of their persons, not their property.

We reply: This is not so, because what leads to setting right his property by growing and increasing it is itself a setting right for him. Therefore there is no barrier to its falling under the apparent meaning. This view is the best of the views mentioned on this point.

The second: the view of one who said: the word "good" refers to the guardian. That is, setting right their property without compensation or wage is better for the guardian and brings him greater reward.

The third: that the word "good" refers to the orphan, and the meaning is that mixing with them in a way that sets things right is better for them than standing apart from them and turning away from mixing with them.

The first view is preferable, because the wording is unrestricted, and restricting it to some aspects but not others is preference without a basis, which is impermissible. Therefore it is necessary to interpret it as referring to the benefits returning to the guardian, and to the orphan in the correction of both self and property. In sum, the meaning of the verse is that the aspects of welfare are varied and not fixed, so the guardian of the orphan's interests should aim, for himself, at obtaining good in this world and the Hereafter, and for the orphan, at good in his property and in his self. Thus this expression comprehensively covers all these aspects.

As for His saying: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Mixing (al-mukhalatah) is a union in which distinction becomes difficult. From it comes the word for sexual intercourse, al-khilat. It is also said: "the man was khulit," meaning he went mad, and khilat means madness, because affairs become confused for the one afflicted, through the loss of his reason.

***

**Second issue:** Regarding the interpretation of the verse, there are several views.

The first: the meaning is: if you mix with them in food, drink, dwelling, and servants, then they are your brothers. The meaning is that the people had separated the orphan's food from their own food, his drink from their drink, and his dwelling from theirs. So Allah permitted them to combine the two foods and the two drinks, and to live together in one dwelling, just as a man does with his child's property, for this is more conducive to good companionship and mutual affection. The meaning is: if you mix with them in a way that does not involve corrupting their property, then that is permissible.

The second: that this mixing means that they may benefit from the orphans' property to the extent that the reward for their labor would be equal to that benefit. Among those who held this view, some permitted it whether the guardian was rich or poor. Others said: if the guardian is rich, he should not eat from the orphan's property, because that is an obligation upon him, and taking a wage for an obligatory act is not permitted. They argued for this from His saying: ﴿Whoever is rich, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [al-Nisa', 6]. As for a poor guardian, they said: he may eat according to his need and repay it when he becomes well-off; if he never becomes well-off, he may be absolved of it by the orphan. It is reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I have placed myself with regard to Allah's property in the position of the orphan's guardian: if I am wealthy, I abstain; if I am in need, I eat as a loan in a reasonable manner, and then I repay it." And it is reported from Mujahid that if the guardian is poor and eats in a reasonable manner, there is no obligation of repayment upon him.

The third view: the meaning of the verse is that they should mix the orphans' property with their own property on the basis of partnership, under the condition of observing what is in the interest and benefit of the child.

The fourth view, which is the choice of Abu Muslim, is that the intended meaning of mixing is marriage through in-law relations, in the manner of His saying: ﴿If you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, then marry﴾ [al-Nisa', 3], and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women﴾ [al-Nisa', 127]. He said: This view is preferred over the others for several reasons:

First: this view is a mixing with the orphan himself, whereas partnership is a mixing with his property.

Second: partnership is included in His saying: ﴿Setting things right for them is good﴾, whereas mixing through marriage was not included in that; therefore, interpreting the statement as referring to this kind of mixing is closer to the context.

Third: His saying ﴿they are your brothers﴾ indicates that the intended mixing is this kind, because if the orphan were not one of the children of the Muslims, it would be obligatory to seek the welfare of his property just as one would if he were Muslim. Therefore the reference in His saying ﴿they are your brothers﴾ must be to another kind of mixing.

Fourth: after this verse, He said: ﴿Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah, 221]. So the meaning is that the mixing that is recommended is only with orphans who are your brothers in Islam. They are the ones with whom you should intermarry to strengthen affection. If the orphan is of polytheistic women, then do not do that.

**Third issue:** His saying ﴿they are your brothers﴾ means: they are your brothers. Al-Farra' said: "Had you put it in the accusative, it would have been correct, and the meaning would be: you mix with your brothers."

As for His saying: ﴿Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾, it has been said: the corrupter of their property from the reformer of it. It has also been said: He knows the inner intentions of one who intends corruption and covets their property through marriage, from the one who intends reform. That is, if you show outwardly an intention to set things right while in your hearts you do not intend it, but rather your aim is another purpose, then Allah is aware of your inner selves and knows what is in your hearts. This is a severe warning. The reason is that the orphan cannot secure his own welfare, and there is no one else who attends to it. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: Since there is no one to take charge of his interests, I am the one who takes charge, and I hold his guardian accountable. It has also been said: Allah knows the reformer who acts on behalf of the orphan in a way that makes it lawful for him to benefit from the orphan's property, and He knows the corrupter who does not act to set right the orphan's affairs in a way that makes it lawful for him to benefit from the orphan's property. So beware of taking anything from the orphan's property without setting right his property yourselves.
