As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have burdened you﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Al-i'nat (burdening) means imposing a hardship that cannot be borne. It is said: "So-and-so burdened so-and-so" when he placed him in a situation from which he cannot escape. And "ta'annata" means he confused him in his questioning. And "'anata al-'azm al-majbur" means the bone that was set was broken again after setting. The root of 'anat is hardship; and "akamah 'anut" means a hill that is difficult and steep. From this is His saying: ﴿It grieves him what you suffer﴾ [al-Tawbah, 128], meaning: it is severe for him, what burdens you. It is also said: "a'natani fi al-su'al," meaning he pressed me hard and sought to harm me, and 'anat is harm. As for the commentators, Ibn 'Abbas said: "Had Allah willed, He would have made what you have taken from the orphans' property a cause of destruction." 'Ata' said: "Had Allah willed, He would have brought hardship upon you, just as you brought it upon yourselves, and He would have made the matter narrow for you in mixing with them." Al-Zajjaj said: "Had Allah willed, He would have obligated you with what would be difficult for you."

***

**Second issue:** Al-Jubba'i used this verse as evidence, saying: It indicates that Allah does not burden the servant with what he cannot bear, because His saying ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have burdened you﴾ indicates that Allah did not impose burdening and straitness in the obligations. Had He obligated the servant with what the servant cannot bear, He would have exceeded the limit of burdening and the limit of straitness.

Know that the basis of this argument is that the word "law" (lau) indicates the non-existence of one thing because of the non-existence of another. Then they raised an objection to themselves: this verse was revealed concerning the orphan. They answered that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. Furthermore, the guardian of this orphan may not, by Allah's act, be given the power to set things right, because this is their own position regarding one who chooses what is contrary to reform. If that is so, how can it be permissible for Allah to say specifically concerning him: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have burdened you﴾, when He has obligated him with what he cannot bear and has no way to do? Moreover, burdening is valid only regarding one who has the ability to do a thing, so that it becomes hard and straitened for him; but one who has no ability at all, burdening does not apply to him. According to the opponent, when the guardian chooses reform, it is not possible for him to commit corruption; and if he cannot commit corruption, it is not valid to say concerning him: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have burdened you﴾.

The answer to this is: a counter-argument based on the issue of knowledge and the one who has the ability to act. And Allah knows best.

Third issue: al-Ka'bi (ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad al-Ka'bi, a Mu'tazili theologian) argued from this verse that God is able to act contrary to justice. His reasoning: if it were impossible to describe Him as capable of causing hardship (al-i'nat), then it would not be permissible for Him to say, ﴿And if God had willed, He would have caused you hardship﴾. In response, al-Nazzam (Ibrahim ibn Sayyar al-Nazzam, another Mu'tazili theologian) could answer that this statement is conditional upon the will to cause hardship. Then ask: why do you say that this will is possible to be established in relation to God, Exalted is He? And God knows best.

**[Page 47]**

**The Sixth Ruling: Concerning Marriage**

﴿Do not marry idolatresses until they believe. A believing slave woman is better than an idolatress, even though she may please you. And do not marry idolaters until they believe. A believing slave is better than an idolater, even though he may please you. Those invite to the Fire, but Allah invites to Paradise and forgiveness, by His permission, and He makes His verses clear to the people that they may remember.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not marry idolatresses until they believe. A believing slave woman is better than an idolatress, even though she may please you. And do not marry idolaters until they believe. A believing slave is better than an idolater, even though he may please you. Those invite to the Fire, but Allah invites to Paradise and forgiveness, by His permission, and He makes His verses clear to the people that they may remember.﴾

Know that this verse is similar to His saying: ﴿And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]. It has been read with a *damm* on the *tā'* (*tunkihū*, i.e., "do not let them marry"), meaning: do not give them in marriage. According to this reading, they (the believers) would not marry them off.

Know also that the exegetes differed over whether this verse is the beginning of a ruling and a legal prescription, or whether it is connected to what came before. Most of them hold that it is the beginning of a legal prescription, explaining what is lawful and what is unlawful. Abu Muslim said: rather, it is connected to the story of the orphans. When Almighty Allah said: ﴿And if you mix your affairs with them, they are your brothers﴾ and He intended the mixing of marriage, He followed it with what stirs the desire for orphans, and that this is better than what they used to pursue, namely the desire for idolatresses. He clarified that a believing slave woman is better than an idolatress, even if the latter reaches the utmost in what calls for desire toward her, so that this would indicate what moves one to marry orphans, and to marry off orphans when they reach puberty, so that this becomes a motive for what He commanded regarding looking after their welfare and the welfare of their property. In either of the two interpretations the ruling of the verse does not differ.

Then, there are several issues concerning the verse:

**The first issue:** It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) sent Marthad ibn Abi Marthad, an ally of the Banu Hashim, to Makkah to bring out some Muslims there secretly. Upon his arrival, a woman came to him named ʿAnaq, who had been his female companion in the Jahiliyyah. She had turned away from him at the time of Islam, so she sought seclusion with him. He informed her that Islam prohibits that. Then he promised her that he would seek the permission of the Messenger (ﷺ) and then marry her. When he returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he informed him of what had happened regarding ʿAnaq, and asked him whether it was lawful for him to marry her. Then Allah revealed this verse.

* * *

**The second issue:** People differed over the word *nikāh* (marriage). Most of the companions of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is literally used for the contract (ʿaqd). They argued for this with several points:

First: His saying (peace be upon him): "There is no marriage except with a guardian and two witnesses." He restricted the marriage to the guardian and the witnesses, and what depends on the guardian and the witnesses is the contract, not sexual intercourse.

Second: His saying (peace be upon him): "I was born of a marriage and not of fornication (*siḥāḥ*)." The hadith indicates that marriage is set in contrast to fornication, and it is known that fornication involves sexual intercourse. So if *nikāh* were a term for intercourse, marriage could not be the counterpart of fornication.

Third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And marry off the single among you and the righteous of your male and female slaves﴾ [al-Nur: 32]. There is no doubt that the word *ankiḥū* (marry off) can only be understood as the contract.

Fourth: the saying of al-Aʿsha, which al-Wahidi recited in *al-Basit*:

*So do not approach a neighbouring woman, for her secret is forbidden to you; so marry, or else remain single.*

His saying "so marry" (*fa-ankiḥan*) can only mean the command to contract. For he said: "do not approach a neighbouring woman," meaning: do not approach her in the way that is forbidden. So contract and marry; otherwise, remain single and avoid women.

The majority of the companions of Abu Hanifa said: it is literally used for intercourse (*waṭʾ*), and they argued for this with several points:

First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. The prohibition on lawfulness extends until the limit of marriage, and the marriage by which this prohibition ends is not the contract, as evidenced by his saying (peace be upon him): "No, until you taste his *ʿusaylah* (honey, i.e., sexual intercourse) and he tastes yours." Therefore it must be that what is meant by it is intercourse.

Second: His saying (peace be upon him): "The one who marries by hand is cursed, and the one who marries an animal is cursed." Here he affirmed marriage in the absence of a contract.

Third: In language, *nikāh* is an expression for joining and intercourse. It is said: "The rain *nakaḥa* the earth," when it reached it; "sleep *nakaḥa* his eye." In a proverb: "We married off the wild ass, and we shall see." A poet said:

*Those who abandon their women in a state of purity, and those who have intercourse with them by the banks of the Tigris, the cows.*

And al-Mutanabbi said:

*I wed the deaf stones of its pebbles, a hoof of a swift camel, which stumbled with me, towards you, over the plain and the mountain.*

It is known that the meaning of joining and intercourse in actual contact is more complete than in the contract, so it must be understood as that. Some people said: *nikāh* is an expression for joining, and the meaning of joining exists in both the contract and intercourse, so it is proper to use this word for both together. Ibn Jinni said: I asked Abu ʿAli (al-Farisi) about the expression "he *nakaḥa* the woman," and he said: the Arabs have made a subtle distinction in usage so that there is no confusion. When they say "so-and-so *nakaḥa* so-and-so (a woman)," they mean that he married her and contracted with her. When they say "he *nakaḥa* his wife" or "his spouse," they mean nothing other than cohabitation, because when he mentions that he *nakaḥa* his wife or spouse, he has already dispensed with mentioning the contract, so the word does not admit anything other than cohabitation. This is the complete discussion of this word.

The exegetes agreed that what is meant by His saying ﴿Do not marry (*tankiḥū*)﴾ in this verse is: do not contract marriage with them.

* * *

**The third issue:** They differed over whether the word *mushrik* (idolater) includes disbelievers from among the People of the Book (*ahl al-kitāb*, i.e., Jews and Christians). Some denied this, but most scholars hold that the word *mushrik* includes disbelieving People of the Book, and this is the preferred view. The following points indicate this:

First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Jews say, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." ... Exalted is He above what they associate (with Him)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30–31]. In this verse, He said at its end: "Exalted is He above what they associate," and this verse is explicit that the Jew and the Christian are idolaters.

Second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa: 48]. This verse indicates that Allah may forgive what is other than *shirk* in general. So if the disbelief of the Jew and the Christian were not *shirk*, then by the implication of this verse Allah would have to forgive it in general; since that is false, we know that their disbelief is *shirk*.

Third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who said, "Indeed Allah is the third of three," have certainly disbelieved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73]. This "trinity" is either because they believed in three attributes or because they believed in three essences. The first is false, because what is understood from His being Knowing is other than what is understood from His being Powerful and from His being Living. If these three concepts must be acknowledged, then affirming three attributes is one of the necessities of the religion of Islam, so how could the Christians be condemned for that? When this is shown to be false, we know that He condemned them only because they affirmed three eternal, independent essences. For this reason, they permitted that the "Word" (*uqnūm al-kalimah*) could be incarnate in ʿIsa, and they permitted that the "Life" (*uqnūm al-ḥayah*) could be incarnate in Maryam. Had these things, which they call "hypostases" (*aqānīm*), not been self-subsisting essences, they would not have permitted them to pass from one essence to another. Thus it is established that they hold to the affirmation of self-subsisting, eternal, beginningless essences, and this is *shirk*, a claim that there are gods. So they are idolaters. And when it is established that they fall under the name of *mushrik*, it must be that the Jew is likewise, since there is no one who makes a distinction.

Fourth: what is narrated: that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) appointed a commander and said: "When you encounter a group of idolaters, invite them to Islam. If they respond to you, accept from them; and if they refuse, invite them to pay the *jizyah* (poll tax) and to the covenant of protection (*ʿaqd al-dhimmah*). If they respond to you, accept from them and refrain from them." He called those from whom the *jizyah* and the covenant of protection are accepted "idolaters." This indicates that the *dhimmi* (protected non-Muslim subject) is called an idolater.

Fifth: what Abu Bakr al-Asamm argued: every one who denies his (the Prophet's) prophethood is an idolater, because those miracles that appeared at his hand were beyond human power, and they denied that they came from Allah, exalted is He. Rather, they attributed them to the jinn and the devils, for they used to say concerning them that they were magic and that they came from the jinn and devils. So these people have associated a partner with Allah, glorified is He, in the creation of these things that are beyond human power, and so it is necessary to conclude that they are idolaters, because there is no meaning to deity except for one who is capable of creating these things.

Al-Qadi raised an objection and said: this follows only if the Jew concedes that what appeared at the hand of Muhammad (ﷺ) was among the matters beyond human power. In that case, when he ascribes it to other than Allah, exalted is He, he is an idolater. But if he denies this and claims that what appeared at the hand of Muhammad (ﷺ) is of the kind that servants are capable of, it does not follow that he is an idolater by attributing it to other than Allah, exalted is He.

The answer: the acknowledgement or non-acknowledgement of his (the Jew's) claim that those miracles are beyond human capacity is of no consequence. What matters is that this miracle is indeed beyond human power. Whoever attributes it to other than Allah, exalted is He, is an idolater. Just as if a person were to say that the creation of a body and life is of the kind of what humans are capable of, and then attributed the creation of animals and plants to the spheres and the stars, he would be an idolater, so it is here. This is the total of what indicates that the Jew and the Christian fall under the name of *mushrik*.

Those who deny this argued that Allah, exalted is He, separated the People of the Book from the idolaters in mention, and this indicates that the People of the Book do not fall under the name of *mushrik*. We say that He did separate them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated (*ashrakū*)...﴾ [al-Hajj: 17]. He also said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the idolaters do not wish that any good be sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105]. And He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the idolaters were not going to leave (their religion)﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1]. In these verses He separated the two categories and joined one to the other, and this requires that they be different.

The answer: this is problematic in light of His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7], and His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mikail﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. If they say: "He singled them out for mention to alert to the perfection of the degree in that stated attribute," we say: here too He singled out the worshippers of idols in these verses with this name, to alert to the perfection of their rank in this disbelief. This is the total of what is in this issue.

[Page 50]

Then know that those who hold that the Jews and Christians fall under the term *mushrik* (polytheist) have differed on two views. One group said: the application of this term to them is linguistic, because we have explained that the Jews and Christians do hold to *shirk* (association of partners with God). Al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi said: this term is among the *shar'i* (legal-technical) terms. They argued for this by saying that it has been transmitted by mass transmission (*tawatur*) from the Messenger (ﷺ) that he would call every disbeliever a *mushrik*. Among the disbelievers were those who did not affirm any god at all, or who doubted his existence, or who doubted the existence of a partner. Among them were some who, at the time of the mission, denied resurrection and the Last Day, and therefore denied prophethood and religious obligation. Not all of them worshipped idols. Among those who did worship idols, some said that the idols were God's partners in creation and in the governance of the world. Rather, some would say: "These are our intercessors with God." Thus it is established that most of them acknowledged that the God of the world is one, and that He has no associate or equal in divinity, in creating or governing the world. Once this is established, it becomes clear that the application of the term *mushrik* to the disbeliever is not a linguistic term but a *shar'i* term, like *salah* (prayer) and *zakah* (almsgiving) and others. And if this is so, it is obligatory that every disbeliever falls under this term. This is the summary of the discussion on this question, and success is from God.

* * *

[Page 50, continued]

The Fourth Issue (*masʾala*): Those who said that the term *mushrik* applies only to idol-worshippers said: God's words, ﴿And do not marry polytheist women﴾, are a prohibition on marrying idolatresses. As for those who said that the term *mushrik* covers all disbelievers, they said: the apparent meaning of God's words, ﴿And do not marry polytheist women﴾, indicates that it is not permissible at all to marry a disbelieving woman, whether she is from the People of the Book or not. Then, those who hold this view differed. The majority of the imams said that it is permissible for a man to marry a woman from the People of the Book. But Ibn 'Umar, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, and al-Hadi (one of the imams of the Zaydiyya) are reported to have said that this is forbidden. The majority's proof is God's words in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5]. And Surat al-Ma'idah in its entirety is firmly established, and nothing in it has ever been abrogated.

If it is said: why can it not be that what is meant is: those who believed after having been People of the Book?

We reply: this is not correct, because God first made lawful "the chaste women from among the believers," and this includes those among them who believed after disbelief and those who were believers from the outset. Also, God's words ﴿from among those who were given the Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5] indicate that this attribute holds at the time of permissibility. Among what indicates the permissibility of this is what is related: that the Companions used to marry women from the People of the Book, and no one among them is known to have objected to this. So this constitutes a consensus (*ijma'*) on permissibility.

It is related that Hudhayfa married a Jewish or Christian woman, and 'Umar wrote to him: "Divorce her." He wrote back: "Do you claim that she is forbidden?" 'Umar said: "No, but I fear (that the people will follow you)."

And on the authority of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We marry the women of the People of the Book, but they do not marry our women." It is also indicated by the well-known report that 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, related: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the Magians: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book, except that you may not marry their women nor eat their slaughtered animals." Had marrying their women not been permissible, this exception would have been pointless.

Those who held that it is not permissible argued on several grounds:

The first: the word *mushrik* includes the women of the People of the Book, as we have explained. So God's words, ﴿And do not marry polytheist women until they believe﴾, are explicit in forbidding marriage to women of the People of the Book. And specification (*takhsis*) and abrogation (*naskh*) go against the apparent meaning, so it is necessary to adopt the apparent meaning. Then they said: there is in the verse something that confirms what we have mentioned. That is because God said at the end of the verse: ﴿They invite to the Fire﴾. When a descriptive attribute is mentioned right after a ruling, and that attribute is appropriate to the ruling, the apparent meaning is that the attribute is the *'illah* (effective cause) of that ruling. So it is as if God said: "I have forbidden you to marry polytheist women because they invite to the Fire." This cause is present in the women of the People of the Book, so it is necessary to affirm with certainty that they are forbidden.

The second argument for them: Ibn 'Umar was asked about this question and recited the verse of prohibition and the verse of permission. The point of the argument is that the basic principle regarding sexual relations (*al-abda'*) is prohibition. When the evidence for prohibition conflicts with the evidence for permission, they cancel each other out, so the original ruling must remain. By this same method, when 'Uthman was asked about combining two sisters in ownership by right of possession (*milk al-yamin*), he said: "One verse permitted them, and another verse forbade them." So you judged, at that point, that it was prohibited, for the reason we have mentioned. So it is the same here.

The third argument for them: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari related in his *Tafsir* from Ibn 'Abbas the prohibition of all types of women except believing women, and he argued from God's words: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have become void﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5]. And if this is so, she is like an apostate woman in that it is not permissible to contract a marriage with her.

The fourth argument: holding to the report from 'Umar. It is related that Talha married a Jewish woman and Hudhayfa a Christian woman, and 'Umar became extremely angry with them. They said: "We will divorce them, O Commander of the Faithful, so do not be angry." He said: "If their divorce is lawful, then their marriage is lawful. But I will take them away from you."

[Page 51]

The earlier scholars answered the first argument as follows: whoever says that a Jew or a Christian does not fall under the term *mushrik* has no problem with this objection. And whoever accepts that they do fall under it says: God's words ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5] are more specific than this verse. If the report is sound that this prohibition was established and then removed, we make His words "and chaste women" abrogating (*nasikh*). If it is not established, we make it specifying (*mukhassis*). At most, abrogation and specification go against the basic principle. But since there is no way to reconcile the two verses except by this method, it is necessary to adopt it.

As for their second point, that God's words in the verse of the Ma'idah are an exception to the general prohibition, it is said: the difference between them is that the polytheist woman openly displays opposition and hostility, so perhaps the husband may love her, and then she may drive him to fight alongside the polytheists against the Muslims. This meaning does not exist in the *dhimmiyya* (a non-Muslim protected by a covenant), because she is subdued, content with humiliation and lowliness, so the occurrence of that marriage does not lead to fighting.

As for their third point, that the verses of prohibition and permission conflict, we say: but the verse of permission is more specific and, by consensus, later in revelation. So it must be considered to precede the verse of prohibition. This differs from the two verses regarding combining two sisters in ownership by right of possession, because each of those two verses is more specific than the other in one respect and more general in another respect, so there was no cause for preference.

As for their point here: God's words ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5] are more specific than His words ﴿And do not marry polytheist women until they believe﴾ in an unqualified sense. So preference is required.

As for their reliance on God's words ﴿his deeds have become void﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5]:

The answer: since we have distinguished between the woman from the People of the Book and the apostate woman in many rulings, why should it not be permissible to distinguish between them in this ruling as well?

As for their reliance on the report from 'Umar: we have already related from him that he said: "It is not forbidden." And when there is conflict, the argument from it falls away. And God knows best.

* * *

The Fifth Issue: All agree that what is meant by God's words ﴿until they believe﴾ is affirmation of the testimony of faith and commitment to the rulings of Islam. At this point, the Karramiyya used this verse to argue that faith (*iman*) is merely a verbal affirmation. They said: God has made faith here the limit of the prohibition, and what is the limit of the prohibition here is verbal affirmation. So it is established that faith, in the terminology of the Shari'ah, means verbal affirmation.

Our companions argued against this doctrine with several points:

The first: we have demonstrated with many proofs, in our explanation of God's words ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah 3], that faith means assent (*tasdiq*) in the heart.

The second: God's words ﴿And among people are those who say: "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah 8]. If faith were merely verbal affirmation, God's words ﴿but they are not believers﴾ would be false.

The third: God's words ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed"﴾ [al-Hujurat 14]. If faith were merely verbal affirmation, God's words ﴿Say, "You have not believed"﴾ would be false.

Then they answered their reliance on this verse by saying: the assent that is in the heart cannot be known by others, so verbal affirmation has been placed in the position of assent in the heart.

* * *

The Sixth Issue: It is reported from al-Hasan that he said: this verse abrogates what they used to do regarding marrying polytheist women. Al-Qadi said: their being, before the revelation of this verse, inclined to marry polytheist women, if it was by way of custom and not by way of the Shari'ah, makes it impossible to describe this verse as abrogating, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) that the abrogating and the abrogated must both be legal rulings. But if the permissibility of marrying a polytheist woman before the revelation of this verse was established by the Shari'ah, then this verse is abrogating.

As for God's words ﴿And a believing slave woman is better than a polytheist, even though she might please you﴾, there are several issues here:

The First Issue: Abu Muslim said: the lam in His words "and a believing slave woman" (*wa la-amatun*) is in function of emphasis, resembling the lam of oath.

The Second Issue: *Al-khayr* (good) is beneficial goodness. The meaning is: if the polytheist woman possesses wealth, beauty, and lineage, then a believing slave woman is better than her, because faith is connected to religion, while wealth, beauty, and lineage are connected to this world, and religion is better than this world. Also, religion is the most noble thing for everyone, so when there is agreement in religion, love is perfected, and so the benefits of this world are perfected, such as health, obedience, and the preservation of wealth and children. But when there is disagreement in religion, love is not attained, so none of the benefits of this world are gained from that woman. Some have said that the meaning is: "a believing slave woman is better than a free polytheist woman."

Know that there is no need for this restriction, for two reasons:

One: the wording is unrestricted.

Two: God's words ﴿even though she might please you﴾ indicate the attribute of freedom, because the implied meaning is: "even though she might please you with her beauty, her wealth, her freedom, or her lineage." All of these fall under God's words ﴿even though she might please you﴾.

* * *

The Third Issue: Al-Jubba'i said: the verse indicates that one who is able to afford a free woman (*tawl al-hurra*) may marry a slave woman, according to the position of Abu Hanifa. That is because the verse indicates that one who lacks the means to marry a free polytheist woman may marry a slave woman. But one who lacks the means to marry a free polytheist woman will necessarily be one who lacks the means to marry a free Muslim woman, because the cause of difference in disbelief and faith does not vary by the amount of wealth needed for the expenses of marriage. So it necessarily follows, with certainty, that one who lacks the means to marry a free Muslim woman may marry a slave woman. This is a subtle argument on this question.

* * *

The Fourth Issue: There is a difficulty in the verse. God's words ﴿And do not marry polytheist women﴾ require the prohibition of marrying a polytheist woman. Then His words ﴿And a believing slave woman is better than a polytheist﴾ require the permissibility of marrying a polytheist woman, because the form *af'al* (comparative) implies sharing in the attribute while one of the two has a superiority.

We said: marrying a polytheist woman involves worldly benefits, and marrying a believing woman involves benefits of the Hereafter. The two benefits share the basic quality of being benefits, but the benefit of the Hereafter has the greatest excellence. Thus the objection is dispelled. And God knows best.

As for His saying, ﴿And do not marry [your women to] polytheists until they believe﴾, there is no disagreement here that it applies to all of them, and that a believing woman may never be married to a disbeliever, regardless of the different kinds of disbelievers.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾, the discussion of it follows the same approach as what preceded.

As for His saying, ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: this verse is similar to His saying, ﴿What is [the matter] with me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir: 41].

[Page 53]

If it is asked: how can they invite to the Fire when they may not believe in the Fire at all? How can they invite to it?

The answer: the scholars have mentioned several interpretations (ta'wil) of this verse:

The first: they invite to what leads to the Fire. Apparently, marriage is a cause of affection, love and mutual attachment, and all of this requires agreement in aims and purposes. This may lead a Muslim to abandon Islam for the sake of agreeing with his beloved.

If it is objected: the possibility of love exists on both sides. Just as a Muslim may become a disbeliever because of affection and love, a disbeliever may also become a Muslim because of affection and love. When the two possibilities conflict, they must cancel each other out, and the original permissibility remains.

We reply: the preference lies with this side, because if the disbeliever abandons his disbelief, the Muslim thereby earns greater reward and rank, whereas if the Muslim abandons his Islam, he incurs a great punishment. Undertaking this action lies between gaining greater benefit and suffering great harm. In such a case, one must guard against harm. For this reason God, exalted is He, gave preference to the side of prohibition over the side of permission.

The second interpretation: some people understood His saying, ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾, to mean that they invite to abandoning fighting and combat. Abandoning these entails deserving the Fire and punishment. The purpose of this interpreter in this interpretation is to make this a distinction between the dhimmi woman (a non-Muslim under the protection of a Muslim state) and others, since a dhimmi wife does not urge her husband to fight. Thus the distinction becomes clear.

The third interpretation: the child who is born may be called by the disbelieving parent to disbelief, so the child becomes one of the people of the Fire. This is the invitation to the Fire. ﴿But God invites to Paradise﴾, since He commanded us to marry a Muslim woman so that the child may be a Muslim and one of the people of Paradise.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And God invites to Paradise and forgiveness by His permission﴾, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: the meaning is that the friends of God invite to Paradise. It is as if it were said: the enemies of God invite to the Fire, and the friends of God invite to Paradise and forgiveness. Therefore it is necessary for a sensible person not to frequent the polytheist women, who are the enemies of God, exalted is He, and to marry believing women, for they invite to Paradise and forgiveness.

The second: when He, glorified is He, explained these rulings, permitting some and prohibiting others, He said: ﴿And God invites to Paradise and forgiveness﴾, because whoever adheres to them deserves Paradise and forgiveness.

As for His saying, (by His permission), the meaning is: by God's facilitating and enabling the action by which one deserves Paradise and forgiveness. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿And it was not for a soul to believe except by the permission of God﴾ [Yunus: 100], and His saying: ﴿And it was not for a soul to die except by the permission of God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145], and His saying: ﴿And they could not harm anyone thereby except by the permission of God﴾ [Al-Baqara: 102]. Al-Hasan read "wal-maghfiratu bi-idhnihi" (and forgiveness [is] by His permission) with the nominative case (ar-raf'), meaning: and forgiveness is attained by His facilitation.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He makes His signs clear to the people so that they may remember﴾, its meaning is apparent.

[p. 54]

**The Seventh Ruling: Concerning Menstruation**

﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: "It is an harm, so withdraw from women during menstruation, and do not approach them until they are purified. When they have purified themselves, come to them as God has commanded you. Indeed God loves those who turn often (to Him) and loves those who purify themselves."﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: "It is an harm, so withdraw from women during menstruation, and do not approach them until they are purified. When they have purified themselves, come to them as God has commanded you. Indeed God loves those who turn often (to Him) and loves those who purify themselves."﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The First Issue:** Know that He, exalted is He, gathered six questions in this passage. He mentioned the first three without the conjunction *wa* ("and"), and mentioned the last three with *wa*. The reason is that their questions about those first incidents occurred at different times, so no conjunction was used, because each of those questions was a separate, independent question. They asked about the last three issues at one time, so the conjunction of gathering was used for that, as if it were said: "They gather together for you the question about wine and gambling, the question about such-and-such, and the question about such-and-such."

* * *

**The Second Issue:** It is reported that the Jews and the Magians (Majus) were excessive in keeping away from a woman during her menstruation, while the Christians would have intercourse with them and did not care about menstruation. It is also reported that the people of the pre-Islamic period (*Jahiliyyah*), when a woman menstruated, would not eat with her, drink with her, sit with her on the same bedding, or live with her in the same house, in the manner of the Jews and Magians. When this verse was revealed, the Muslims took the apparent meaning of the verse and expelled women from their houses. Some of the Bedouin (*a'rab*) said: "O Messenger of God, the cold is severe and the clothes are few. If we give the women the clothes, the rest of the household will perish, and if we keep them for ourselves, the menstruating women will perish." The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I only commanded you to refrain from having intercourse with them when they menstruate. I did not command you to expel them from the houses in the manner of the non-Arabs (*a'ajim*)." When the Jews heard this, they said: "This man wants to leave nothing of our affairs without opposing us in it." Then 'Abbad ibn Bishr and Usayd ibn Hudayr came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him of this, and they said: "O Messenger of God, should we not marry them during menstruation?" The face of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) changed until we thought that he was angry with them both. So they stood up, and a gift of milk came to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent for them both and gave them to drink, and we knew that he was not angry with them.

* * *

**The Third Issue:** The original meaning of *hayd* (menstruation) in the language is flowing, as it is said: "The flood (*sayl*) menstruated and overflowed (*hāḍa wa fāḍa*)." Al-Azhari said: From this is derived the word *hawd* (basin/pond), because water *yahīḍu* (flows) into it, meaning it flows into it. The Arabs substitute *waw* for *ya'* and *ya'* for *waw*, because they are of the same kind.

Having known this, we say: This pattern (*binā'*) may come to denote a place, as in *mabīt* (a place of spending the night), *maqīl* (a place of siesta), and *maghīb* (a place of disappearance). It may also come as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*); it is said: "She menstruated a menstruation (*ḥāḍat maḥīḍan*)," "He came a coming (*jā'a majī'an*)," and "He spent the night a spending of the night (*bāta mabītan*)." Al-Wahidi in *al-Basit* related from Ibn al-Sikkit: When the verb is from the three-letter roots, such as *kāla yakīlu* (he measured) and *ḥāḍa yaḥīḍu* (he menstruated) and similar, the noun form (*ism*) of it is with a kasra, and the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) is with a fatḥa. From this: *māla mamālan* (he inclined, an inclination). Its causative *mumīl* leads, with kasra, to the noun, and with fatḥa to the verbal noun.

*[p. 55]*

And if one were to put a fatḥa on both, or a kasra on both in the verbal noun and the noun, it would be permissible. The Arabs say: *al-ma'āsh* and *al-ma'īsh* (livelihood), *al-maghāb* and *al-maghīb* (place of setting/disappearance), and *al-masār* and *al-masīr* (journey). Thus it is established that the word *maḥīḍ* is literally used for the place of menstruation, and it is also a noun for menstruation itself. Having established this, know that most of the exegetes among the scholars (*udabā'*) claimed that the intended meaning of *maḥīḍ* here is menstruation. But in my view this is not so. For if the intended meaning of *maḥīḍ* here were menstruation, then His saying ﴿withdraw from women during menstruation﴾ would mean: "withdraw from women during menstruation," and the intended meaning would be "withdraw from women during the time of menstruation." Its apparent meaning would then forbid enjoyment of her from above the navel to below the knee. Since this prohibition is not established, it would follow that the verse must be subject to abrogation (*naskh*) or specification (*takhṣīṣ*), and it is known that this is contrary to the original principle.

As for when we take *maḥīḍ* to mean the place of menstruation, the meaning of the verse becomes: "withdraw from women in the place of menstruation," that is, "withdraw from the place of menstruation of women." On this reading, neither abrogation nor specification enters the verse. It is known that when a word is shared between two meanings (*mushtarak*), and applying it to one of them entails an undesirable consequence while applying it to the other does not, then applying the word to the meaning that does not entail that undesirable consequence is preferable. This holds if we grant that the word *maḥīḍ* is shared between the place and the verbal noun, although we know that its use for the place is more common and more famous than its use for the verbal noun.

If it is said: The evidence that the intended meaning of *maḥīḍ* is menstruation is that He said: ﴿It is an harm (*huwa adhan*)﴾, that is, "menstruation is a harm," and if the intended meaning of *maḥīḍ* were the place, this attribute would not be valid.

We reply: Granting that *maḥīḍ* is an expression for menstruation, menstruation in itself is not a harm, because menstruation is an expression for a specific blood, and harm (*adhan*) is a specific quality, and it is an accident (*'arad*), and a body cannot be the very accident. So they must say: The intended meaning is that menstruation is described as being a harm. And if that is permissible, then it is also permissible for us to say: The intended meaning is that that place is possessed of harm. Furthermore, why could it not be that the intended meaning of the first *maḥīḍ* is menstruation, and the intended meaning of the second *maḥīḍ* is the place of menstruation? On this reading, the difficulty you have mentioned disappears. This is what I hold on this matter, and success is from God.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "It is an harm"﴾, 'Aṭā', Qatadah, and al-Suddi said: that is, filth (*qadhar*). Know that *adhan* in the language is whatever is disliked in anything. As for His saying ﴿so withdraw from women during menstruation﴾: *i'tizāl* means withdrawing from a thing. He mentioned the cause, which is harm, first, and then ordered the ruling upon it, which is the obligation of withdrawal.

If it is said: Harm is nothing but blood, and it exists during *istiḥāḍah* (irregular bleeding), yet withdrawing from a woman during *istiḥāḍah* is not obligatory. So this cause has been invalidated.

We reply: The cause is not invalidated, because menstrual blood is corrupt blood that is generated from a surplus which the woman's nature expels through the womb. If that surplus were retained, the woman would fall ill. That blood is like urine and excrement, so it is harm and filth. As for the blood of *istiḥāḍah*, it is not like that; rather it is sound blood flowing from veins that burst in the depth of the womb, so it is not harm. This is what I hold on this subject, and it is a medical principle; by establishing it, the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is freed from criticism. And God knows best what He intends.

* * *

**The Fourth Issue:** Know that menstrual blood is described by real attributes, and legal rulings branch from it. As for the real attributes, there are two:

The first is its source. Menstrual blood is blood that comes out of the womb. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:228]. It was said in its interpretation that it refers to menstruation and pregnancy. As for the blood of *istiḥāḍah*, it does not come out of the womb, but from veins that open at the mouth of the womb. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said concerning the blood of *istiḥāḍah*: "It is the blood of a vein that burst." This statement supports what we mentioned in answering the objection to the Qur'anic reasoning.

The second kind of attributes of menstrual blood are those by which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) described menstrual blood:

First: that it is black.
Second: that it is thick.
Third: that it is *muhtadim*, meaning burnt from the intensity of its heat.
Fourth: that it comes out gently and does not flow with a gush.
Fifth: that it has a foul smell, unlike the rest of the bloods, because it is one of the excretions which nature expels.
Sixth: that it is *baḥrānī* (like sea water), which is intensely red. It was also said: it is that in which turbidity arises, likening it to sea water.

These attributes are the real attributes.

Then some people said: Menstrual blood is distinguished from the blood of *istiḥāḍah*. So every blood that has these attributes is menstrual blood, and what does not have them is not menstrual blood. Where the matter is uncertain, the original state of the legal obligations remains, and their removal occurs only due to the occurrence of menstruation. So when its existence is not known, the obligations that were binding remain as they were.

Others said: These attributes may be confused for the one who is legally responsible (*mukallaf*). Requiring careful examination of those bloods and those attributes entails difficulty and hardship. Therefore the Lawgiver fixed a definite period: whenever blood occurs within it, its ruling is the ruling of menstruation, however that blood may be. Whenever blood occurs outside that period, its ruling is not the ruling of menstruation, whatever the description of that blood. The purpose of this is to remove difficulty and hardship from the one who is legally responsible.

Furthermore, the legal rulings for menstruation are: prohibition of prayer and fasting, avoiding entry into the mosque, touching the *muṣḥaf* (the written Qur'an), and reciting the Qur'an. The woman becomes (ritually) *bāligh* (mature/of legal age) by it. The ruling established for menstruation by the explicit text of the Qur'an is only the prohibition of intercourse, as we have explained the manner in which the verse indicates it.

* * *

**The Fifth Issue:** People differed concerning the duration of menstruation. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: its minimum is one day and one night, and its maximum is fifteen days. This is also the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Aṭā' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Awza'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq, may God be pleased with them all.

Abu Hanifah and al-Thawri said: its minimum is three days and their nights, and if it is less than that, it is corrupt blood. Its maximum is ten days. Abu Bakr al-Razi said in *Aḥkām al-Qur'ān*: Abu Hanifah used to say the view of 'Aṭā': that the minimum of menstruation is a day and a night, and its maximum is fifteen days, but then he abandoned it.

Malik said: there is no fixed limit for its minimum or maximum. If it is found for an hour, it is menstruation, and if it is found for days, it is likewise.

Abu Bakr al-Razi argued in *Aḥkām al-Qur'ān* against the invalidity of Malik's view, saying: If the measure were dropped for both little and much, then menstruation would have to be all the blood found in a woman, and it would follow that there would be no *mustaḥāḍah* (woman with irregular bleeding) in the world, since all that blood would be menstruation according to this view. That is false by the consensus of the community. Also, it is reported that Fatimah bint Abi Ḥubaysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have *istiḥāḍah* and I do not become pure." Also, it is reported that Hamnah suffered *istiḥāḍah* for seven years, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not tell her or them that all of that was menstruation; rather he informed them that some of it was menstruation and some of it was *istiḥāḍah*. Thus this view is invalid. And God knows best.

Know that this argument is weak, because one may say: menstrual blood is distinguished from the blood of *istiḥāḍah* only by the attributes which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) mentioned for menstrual blood. When we know that these are established, we rule that it is menstruation; when we know that they are absent, we rule that it is not menstruation; and when we are in doubt about both, the occurrence of menstruation is unknown, while the continuation of the obligation, which is the original state, is known. The doubtful does not oppose the known. Therefore it is ruled that the original obligations remain. By this method menstruation is distinguished from *istiḥāḍah*, even if no fixed period is established for menstruation.

Malik's argument is from two aspects:

The first: The Prophet (ﷺ) explained the sign and description of menstrual blood by saying: "Menstrual blood is the black, burning blood." So whenever the blood has this description, menstruation is present, and it falls under His saying, exalted is He: ﴿withdraw from women during menstruation﴾, and under the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, to Fatimah bint Abi Ḥubaysh: "When the menstrual period comes, leave off prayer."

**The second argument:** God, exalted is He, said concerning menstrual blood: ﴿It is a harm, so keep away from women during menstruation﴾. He mentioned its being a harm in the context of explaining the reason for the obligation to keep away. It is a harm because of the repugnant smell in it, its corrupt color, and the strong sharpness that is in it. Since the obligation to keep away is caused by these meanings, then whenever these meanings are present, avoidance is obligatory, in accordance with the cause mentioned in the Book of God explicitly. In my view, Malik's position is very strong.

As for al-Shafi'i, he argued against Abu Hanifa with two arguments:

**The first argument:** Menstrual blood is found within a day and night, and also beyond ten days. The proof is that the Prophet (ﷺ) described menstrual blood as black and thick. When that is found, menstruation has occurred, and so it falls under the general wording of God's words: ﴿so keep away from women during menstruation﴾. We have set aside this evidence for less than a day and night, and for more than fifteen days, by agreement between me and Abu Hanifa. Therefore it must remain acted upon within this period.

**The second argument:** For al-Shafi'i, on the side of the excess, there is what has been related: that when the Prophet (ﷺ) described women as deficient in religion, he explained that by saying: "One of them remains for half her life without praying." This indicates that menstruation may last fifteen days, because on this assumption the purity period would also be fifteen days, so menstruation would be half her life. If menstruation were less than that, no woman would be found who does not pray for half her life.

Abu Bakr al-Razi (al-Razi) answered this in two ways:

The first: the word *shatr* does not mean half; it means a portion.

The second: there is no woman in the world who is menstruating for half her life, because what has passed of her life before puberty is still part of her life.

The answer to the first: *shatr* means half. One says, "I divided the thing (*shatartu al-shay'*)," meaning I made it into two halves. And it is said in a proverb: "Milk for yourself, its half (*ajlib halaban laka shatruhu*)," meaning its half.

As to the second: his words (ﷺ): "One of them remains for half her life without praying," refer only to the time in which she would be praying, and that only applies to the period after puberty.

Abu Bakr al-Razi argued in favour of Abu Hanifa's position from several angles:

**The first argument:** What has been related from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The least of menstruation is three days, and its most is ten days." Abu Bakr said: If this hadith is sound, then no one may deviate from it.

**The second argument:** What has been related from Anas ibn Malik and Uthman ibn Abi al-As al-Thaqafi, that they both said: "Menstruation is three days, and four days up to ten days; whatever exceeds that is irregular bleeding (*istihadah*)." The reasoning from this has two aspects:

One: when a statement is reported from a Companion and no one opposes it, it is a consensus (*ijma'*).

Two: the measure (of menstruation) is something the intellect cannot reach by reasoning, so whenever it is reported from a Companion, the apparent meaning is that he heard it from the Messenger (ﷺ).

**The third argument:** His (ﷺ) words to Hamnah bint Jahsh: "Menstruate for six or seven days in God's knowledge, as women menstruate every month." Its implication is that the menstruation of all women every month is this amount. We have departed from this apparent meaning for the range from three to ten days, so what lies beyond remains on the original basis.

**The fourth argument:** His (ﷺ) words concerning women: "I have not seen anyone more overpowering to the intellects of those endowed with understanding than women deficient in intellect and religion." It was asked: "What is the deficiency of their religion?" He said: "One of them remains for days and nights without praying." This report indicates that the period of menstruation is what falls under the term "days and nights," and its least is three, and its most is ten, because one does not say the word "days" for one or two, nor is the word "days" said for more than ten days; rather one says "eleven days." As for three to ten, the word "days" is used for them. Also, he (ﷺ) said to Fatimah bint Abi Hubaysh: "Leave off prayer for the days of your menstrual cycles (*aqra'*)." The word "days" is specific to the range from three to ten. And in the hadith of Umm Salamah concerning the woman who asked him that she was bleeding profusely, he said: "Let her look at the number of nights and days in which she used to menstruate each month, then let her leave off prayer for that amount of the month, then let her perform ghusl and pray."

If it is said: Perhaps that woman's menstruation was fixed at that amount.

We reply: He (ﷺ) did not ask her about the amount of her menstruation; rather he ruled upon her with this ruling without qualification. This indicates that menstruation in general is determined by what the word "days" applies to. Also, he said in the hadith of Adi ibn Thabit: "The woman with irregular bleeding leaves off prayer for the days of her menstruation," and this is general concerning all women.

**The fifth argument:** This is an argument mentioned by al-Jubba'i, one of the shaykhs of the Mu'tazilah, in his *Tafsir*. He said: The obligation of fasting and prayer is binding, and the general texts indicating their obligation are specified. The application of those texts was set aside for the range from three to ten days, so it is necessary that they remain on the original basis for what is less than three and more than ten. That is because for what is less than three there is disagreement among the scholars, which produces doubt, so we did not make it menstruation. And what exceeds ten days also involves disagreement among the scholars, which produces doubt, so we did not make it menstruation. But from three to ten there is agreement, so we made it menstruation. This is the essence of the jurists' discussion on this issue. And success is from God.

* * *

**Sixth issue:** The Muslims agree on the prohibition of intercourse during menstruation. They agree on the permissibility of enjoying a woman from above the navel to below the knee. They disagree on whether it is permissible to enjoy what is below the navel and above the knee. We say: If we interpret *al-mahid* (the place of menstruation) as the place of menstruation, as we have chosen, then the verse indicates the prohibition of intercourse alone, so there is no indication in it of the prohibition of what lies beyond it. Rather, whoever says that singling out a thing by mention indicates that its ruling is contrary for what is other than it, says that this verse indicates the permissibility of everything other than intercourse. As for whoever interprets *al-mahid* as *al-hayd* (menstruation), the meaning of the verse according to him is: "Keep away from women during the time of menstruation." Then he says: The application of this verse was set aside for what is above the navel and below the knee, so the remainder must remain prohibited. And success is from God.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach them until they become pure. And when they have purified themselves, then come to them from where God has commanded you﴾. Know that His words ﴿do not approach them﴾ mean: do not have intercourse with them. It is said: "The man approached (*qaraba*) his wife" when he had intercourse with her. This is like an emphasis on His words: ﴿keep away from women during menstruation﴾. It is also possible to take it as conveying a great new benefit, namely that His words ﴿keep away from women during menstruation﴾ are a prohibition against sexual contact with the place of blood, and His words ﴿do not approach them﴾ are a prohibition against deriving pleasure from what is near that place.

[Page 59]

**Issues concerning the verse:**

**First issue:** Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub al-Hadrami, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read ﴿hatta yatharna﴾ with a light pronunciation, from *tahara* (to be pure). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *yattahharna* with the doubled consonant, and so did Hafs from 'Asim. The one who reads it lightly means the cessation of the blood, because *yathurna* is from "the woman became pure from her menstruation," and that happens when the menstruation stops. So the meaning is: "Do not approach them until the blood has ceased from them." The one who reads *yattahharna* with the doubled consonant means *yatatahharna* (they purify themselves), and it was assimilated, as in His words: ﴿O you wrapped up (*al-muzzammil*)﴾ and ﴿O you wrapped up (*al-muddaththir*)﴾, meaning *al-mutazammil* and *al-mutadaththir*. And success is from God.

* * *

**Second issue:** Most of the jurists of the major cities hold that when a woman's menstruation stops, it is not permissible for her husband to have intercourse with her until she performs ghusl from menstruation. This is the position of Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, and al-Thawri. The well-known position of Abu Hanifa is that if she sees purity for less than ten days, her husband may not approach her, and if she sees it for ten days, it is permissible for him to approach her before ghusl.

Al-Shafi'i's argument has two aspects:

**The first argument:** The mutawatir recitation (a recitation transmitted by so many chains that its authenticity is beyond doubt) is a proof by consensus. When two mutawatir recitations exist and it is possible to combine them, it is obligatory to combine them.

Having established this, we say: ﴿hatta yatharna﴾ has been recited with the light form and with the doubled form. *Yathurna* with the light form expresses the cessation of the blood, and with the doubled form it expresses purification by water. Combining the two matters is possible, so this verse indicates the obligation of both matters. And since this prohibition must not end except when both matters have occurred.

**The second argument:** His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when they have purified themselves, then come to them﴾ make the coming to them conditional upon purification by the particle *idha* (when/if). In the Arabic language, *idha* is a conditional particle, and what is conditional upon a condition is absent when the condition is absent. Therefore it is not permissible to come to them when purification has not occurred.

The argument of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach them until they become pure﴾. He forbade approaching them, and made the end of that prohibition that they become pure, meaning that their menstruation stops. And if the cessation of menstruation is the end of this prohibition, then this prohibition must not remain when menstruation has stopped.

The judge (al-Qadi) answered this by saying: If He had limited Himself to His words ﴿until they become pure﴾, then what you have mentioned would be necessary. But since His words ﴿when they have purified themselves﴾ were added to it, the whole combination has become the end point. This is like a man saying: "Do not speak to so-and-so until he enters the house, and when his heart is content after entering, then speak to him." It is necessary that the permissibility of speaking to him depend on both matters together. And since it has been established that after the cessation of menstruation there must be purification, the jurists have disagreed about the nature of that purification. Al-Shafi'i and most jurists said: it is ghusl. Some said: it is washing the place. 'Ata' and Tawus said: it is washing the place and performing wudu'. The correct view is the first, for two reasons:

**The first:** The apparent meaning of His words ﴿when they have purified themselves﴾ is a ruling that returns to the woman herself. Therefore this purification must occur in her whole body, not in a part of her body.

**The second:** Interpreting it as the purification that menstruation specifically requires is better than the purification that applies also in irregular bleeding, as it applies in menstruation. This entails that what is meant is ghusl. If it is possible with water, but water is unavailable, then the scholars who require ghusl agree that tayammum (dry ablution with earth or dust) stands in its place. We have established tayammum as a substitute for ghusl only by the evidence of consensus. Otherwise, the apparent meaning requires that intercourse with her is not permissible except after ghusl with water.

[Page 60]

* * *

**Third issue:** The scholars have disagreed about what is meant by His words, exalted is He: ﴿then come to them from where God has commanded you﴾. There are several views:

**The first:** This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibrahim, Qatadah, and 'Ikrimah: "Come to them in the place of coming, for that is what God has commanded, and do not come to them in other than the place of coming." His words ﴿from where God has commanded you﴾ mean: "in the place where God has commanded you," like His words: ﴿when the call is made to prayer on the day of Friday﴾ (62:9), meaning "on the day of Friday."

**The second:** Al-Asamm and al-Zajjaj said: this means "come to them from where it is lawful for you to approach them," which is that they are not fasting, nor in seclusion (*i'tikaf*), nor in the state of ihram.

**The third:** This is the view of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah: "Come to them from what is lawful, not from wickedness."

The closest of these is the first view, because the word *haythu* (where) is literally about place and only metaphorically about other things.

As for His words: ﴿God loves those who turn often (in repentance) and loves those who purify themselves﴾. The discussion concerns the explanation of God's love, exalted is He, and the explanation of repentance has already been given earlier, so we do not repeat it. Except that we say: *al-tawwab* (one who turns often) is the one who frequently performs what is called repentance. And it may be said: this is from the right of God, exalted is He, in that He frequently accepts repentance.

"If it is said: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He loves the repentance of [people] absolutely, while reason indicates that repentance is only fitting for the sinner; so whoever is not a sinner, repentance from him should not be valid.

The answer is in two respects:

The first: the responsible person (al-mukallaf) is never safe from shortcoming, so repentance is obligatory upon him to avert that possible shortcoming.

The second: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: "Repentance (tawbah) in the language is an expression for return, and the servant's return to God Most High in all circumstances is praiseworthy." Al-Qadi (al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar) objected to this, saying: although tawbah is, in its original linguistic sense, an expression for return, in the usage of the Shari'ah (ʿurf al-shar') it is an expression for remorse over what was done in the past, abandoning [the sin] in the present, and resolving not to do the like of it in the future; therefore it is necessary to interpret it according to this Shari'i meaning rather than the linguistic concept. Abu Muslim may answer him: "My intention in this answer is that if it is possible to interpret the expression as the Shari'i repentance, then the expression is sound and is free from the objection; and if that is impossible, I interpret it according to the original linguistic meaning, so that criticism and objection do not arise."

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And He loves those who purify themselves﴾, there are several views concerning it:

The first: what is meant by it is purity from sins and disobedience. This is because the penitent (al-tawwab) is one who committed [a sin] and then abandoned it, while the one who purifies himself (al-mutatahhir) is one who did not commit it, keeping himself pure from it, and there is no third category apart from these two. The expression allows for this, because sin is a spiritual impurity, and for this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure (najas)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. Thus abandoning it is spiritual purity, and in this sense God Most High is described as "Pure and Purifying" (tahir mutahhar) in that He is exalted above defects and vices; and it is said: "So-and-so is pure of skirt (tahir al-dhayl)."

The second view: what is meant is: he does not approach [his wife] during the time of menstruation, and does not approach her in other than the place of approach, as in His saying: ﴿So come to them from where God has commanded you﴾. Whoever holds this view says: this is more apt, because it fits better with what precedes the verse; and because He, Most High, said, relating about the people of Lot: ﴿Expel them from your town; indeed, they are people who purify themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 82], so His saying ﴿And He loves those who purify themselves﴾ means abstaining from intercourse in the posteriors.

The third view: since He, Most High, commanded us to purify ourselves in His saying ﴿when they have purified themselves﴾, He therefore praised the one who purifies himself, saying ﴿And He loves those who purify themselves﴾, and what is meant by it is purification with water. God Most High has said: ﴿There are men who love to purify themselves, and God loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108]; and it was said in the exegesis that they used to cleanse themselves with water, so God praised them."

The Eighth Ruling

﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish, and send ahead for yourselves, and fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish, and send ahead for yourselves, and fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾

There are several issues concerning the verse.

The first issue: They have mentioned several accounts regarding the occasion of revelation:

One: "It is narrated that the Jews said: whoever has intercourse with his wife from her rear in her front, the child will be cross-eyed and insane. They claimed that this was in the Torah. This was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: 'The Jews have lied.' And this verse was revealed."

Second: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "'Umar came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have been ruined,'" and he related that this had occurred from him, and so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Third: The Ansar used to deny that a man could approach his wife from her rear in her front. They had taken this from the Jews, while the Quraysh used to do it. The Ansar denounced this practice of theirs, and so the verse was revealed.

* * *

The second issue: ﴿A tilth for you﴾ means a field and a place of growth for the child. This is by way of comparison: the womb of the woman is like the earth, the drop of semen is like the seed, and the child is like the plant that emerges. "Tilth" (ḥarth) is a verbal noun, and for this reason it is stated in the singular. The meaning is: your wives are possessors of tilth for you, in whom you sow for the child. Thus the modifier is omitted. Also, the place of a thing is sometimes named by the name of the thing, for emphasis, as in the saying of the poet:

"For indeed she is advance and retreat."

And it is said: "This is the command of Allah," meaning its object; and "This is the desire of so-and-so," meaning its object of desire. Likewise, a man's tilth is the place of his tilling.

* * *

The third issue: Most of the scholars held that the meaning of the verse is that the man is free to approach her from her front in her front, or to approach her from her rear in her front. So His saying, "however you wish," is taken to refer to this. Nafi' transmitted from Ibn 'Umar that he used to say: the meaning of the verse is the permission to approach women in their rear. The rest of the people denied Nafi' this narration. This is the view of Malik, and the choice of al-Sayyid al-Murtada from the Shi'a, and al-Murtada transmitted it from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

The proofs of those who said that it is not permissible to approach women in their rear are several:

The first proof: Allah, exalted is He, said in the verse about menstruation: ﴿Say: it is a harm, so keep away from women during menstruation﴾. He made the existence of harm the cause for the prohibition of approaching the place of harm. The word "harm" has no meaning except that by which a person is harmed, and here a person is harmed by the foul odor of that blood. The presence of this cause in the place in dispute is more evident, and so if that cause exists here, the prohibition must be established.

The second proof: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾. The apparent sense of a command is obligation, and it cannot be said that it indicates the obligation of approaching them, because that is not obligatory. So it must be taken to mean that whoever approaches a woman must do so in the place that Allah, exalted is He, has commanded. Then this is not to be understood as referring to the rear, because that is by consensus not obligatory. Therefore it is determined that it refers to the front, and that is what was sought.

The third proof: Khuzaymah ibn Thabit transmitted that "a man asked the Prophet ﷺ about approaching women in their rear, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'It is permitted.' When the man turned away, he called him back and said: 'How did you put it: in which of the two ruins, or in which of the two holes, or in which of the two slits? Whether from her front in her front, yes; whether from her rear in her front, yes; whether from her rear in her rear, no. Indeed Allah is not shy of the truth: "Do not approach women in their rear.""' By "ruin" (kharbah) he meant her passage, and the origin of kharbah is the handle of a water-skin, and he likened the perforation to it. The kharaza is that with which the leather-worker pierces, and he used it as an allusion to the place of intercourse. Likewise khasfah derives from their saying: "I stitched the hide" when I pierced it.

The argument of those who held permissibility consists of several points:

The first argument: They hold to this verse on two grounds:

The first: He, exalted is He, made "tilth" a name for the woman, saying: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾. This indicates that "tilth" is a name for the woman and not for a specific place. Then when He said after it: ﴿so go to your tilth however you wish﴾, the meaning is: go to your wives however you wish. This is therefore a general permission to approach them in all manners, and so the disputed case is included in it.

The second: The word "however" (anna) means "where." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Where did this come to you? She said: it is from Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], and the sense is: "From where did this come to you?" So the sense of the verse becomes: "go to your tilth wherever you wish." The phrase "wherever you wish" indicates a multiplicity of places, as when you say: "sit wherever you wish." This is an option among places.

Having established this, we say: it becomes clear that the verse cannot be taken to mean approaching from her front in her front, or from her rear in her front, because on that reading the place is one, and the variation falls only in the manner of approach. The fitting wording for that would be: "go to her however you wish." Since the word used here is not "how" but "where" (anna), and it is established that "anna" implies a choice among places, it is established that the meaning is not what you have stated, but what we have stated.

The second argument for them: holding to the general sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6]. Its application was set aside with respect to males by consensus, so it must remain operative with respect to women.

The third argument: We agree that if a man says to a woman, "your rear is forbidden to me," intending divorce, it is a divorce. This requires that her rear be lawful to him. This is the sum of what these people said in this chapter.

The earlier scholars answered: The indications that the verse cannot mean intercourse with women in other than the place of tilth are several:

The first: "Tilth" is a name for the place of tilling, and it is known that the whole of her body is not a place of tilling. Therefore it is impossible to apply the name "tilth" to the woman's whole person. This argument would require that the word "tilth" be applied to the woman's person, but we have abandoned this argument regarding His saying: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾, because Allah, exalted is He, here explicitly applied the word "tilth" to the woman's person, so we take that to be the well-known metaphor of naming the whole by the name of its part. This case is absent in His saying: ﴿so go to your tilth﴾. So it is obligatory to take "tilth" here to mean the place of tilling specifically. Thus it is established that the verse has no indication except for approaching women in the proper place.

The second: To show that this verse cannot indicate what they claimed: we have shown that what precedes this verse indicates the prohibition of what they mentioned, in two respects:

One of them: His saying: ﴿Say: it is a harm﴾.

The second: His saying: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾. If this verse indicated permissibility, that would be combining in one place what indicates prohibition with what indicates permission, and the principle is that this is not permissible.

The third: The well-known reports that the occasion of revelation of this verse was their disagreement over whether it is permissible to approach a woman from her rear in her front. The occasion of revelation cannot lie outside the verse, so the verse must include this case. And when we take the verse to refer to this case, we have no need to take it to refer to the other case. Thus by these points it is established that the meaning of the verse is not what they stated. At this point we examine in detail the points on which they relied:

As for the first argument: we have shown that His saying, ﴿so go to your tilth﴾, means: go to the place of tilth.

As for the second: since "tilth" in His saying ﴿so go to your tilth﴾ refers to that specific place, "however you wish" cannot be taken as a choice of place. At this point one must supply an addition, namely that "however you wish" means "whoever you wish," supplying the word "man." It may be objected that this does not keep the word "tilth" in its literal sense, but the adoption of this supplying is preferable to taking "tilth" as a metaphor for the woman, so that this supplying does not bind us; rather, this is preferable, because the default regarding private parts is prohibition.

As for the third: its answer is that His saying: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ is general, while our proofs are specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

As for the fourth: its answer is that His saying "your rear is forbidden to me" is only suitable as a metaphor for divorce, because it is the place of enjoyment of touching and lying together, so this is like his saying "your hand is divorced." And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: The exegetes differed in interpreting His saying: "however you wish." The well-known view is what we have mentioned, that it is permissible for the husband to approach her from her front in her front and from her rear in her front.

The second view: the meaning is: at whatever time you wish of the times of lawfulness; that is, when she is not a non-Muslim woman, or forbidden to you, or fasting, or menstruating.

The third view: it is permissible for a man to have intercourse with her standing, or kneeling, or lying down, provided it is in the vagina.

The fourth: Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is, if he wishes he may withdraw, and if he wishes he may not withdraw. This is also transmitted from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

The fifth: whenever you wish, by night or by day.

If it is said: what is the preferred view among these sayings?

We say: it has become clear from the exegetes that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that the Jews used to say: whoever approaches a woman from her rear in her front, the child will come out cross-eyed. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this to refute their saying, and so it is preferable to take the wording as referring to it. As for the times, they have no place in this matter, because "anna" can mean "when" and can mean "how." As for withdrawal and its opposite, these do not fall under "anna," because the state of intercourse does not differ by that. So there is no way to take the speech except as we have said.

As for His saying: ﴿And send ahead for yourselves﴾, its meaning is: do the deeds by which you deserve Paradise and honor. A parallel is when a man says to another: "send ahead a righteous deed for yourself." This is like His saying: ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. A parallel to the word "send ahead" is what Allah, exalted is He, related of a group of the people of the Fire, His saying: ﴿They will say: rather, you, no welcome to you! You have brought it upon us, so what an evil abode﴾ [Sad: 60].

If it is said: how does this statement connect to what precedes it?

I say: It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said its meaning is "saying the basmalah (tasmiyah) during intercourse," but this is extremely far-fetched.
