What I hold regarding it is that His words ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ serve as an indication of the reason for the permissibility of intercourse, as if it were said: "These women, the Law has only ruled that you may have intercourse with them because they are a tilth for you"; that is, because offspring come into being from them. Then He said after it: ﴿So come to your tilth however you wish﴾, meaning: since the cause of the permissibility of intercourse with them for you is the occurrence of tilling, then come to your tilth, and do not come to other than the place of tilling. So His words ﴿So come to your tilth﴾ are evidence of permission for that place and prohibition of other than that place. Since the verse contains permission for one of the two places and prohibition of the other, necessarily He said: ﴿And put forward for yourselves﴾, meaning: do not be bound by the fetter of satisfying desire, but be bound by the fetter of putting forward obedience. Then God, exalted is He, emphasized this by His words: "And fear God," then emphasized it a third time by His words: ﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾. These three successive warnings are not fitting to mention except when they are preceded by a prohibition of something pleasurable and desired. Thus it is established that what precedes this verse indicates the prohibition of this act, and what follows it also indicates its prohibition. It becomes clear that the correct view in interpreting this verse is that held by the majority of the mujtahids (jumhur al-mujtahidin).

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿And fear God and know that you will meet Him﴾, know that the discussion of taqwa (God-consciousness) has already preceded, and the discussion of the meaning of meeting God, exalted is He, has already preceded in His words: ﴿Those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46]. Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned these three matters:
First: ﴿And put forward for yourselves﴾, and what is meant by it is the performance of acts of obedience.
Second: His words "And fear God," and what is meant by it is abandoning forbidden matters.
Third: His words ﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾, and in it is an indication that I only obligated you to bear hardship in performing acts of obedience and abandoning forbidden matters for the sake of the Day of Resurrection, the rising, and the reckoning. Were it not for that Day, bearing hardship in performing acts of obedience and abandoning forbidden matters would be pointless. How excellent this arrangement is! Then He said: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, and what is meant by it is observing the arrangement regarded in the Qur'an, which is that He pairs every threat with a promise. The meaning is: give good tidings specifically to the believers of reward and honour, and He omitted mention of them because they are as if known. So it is like His words: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them from God is great bounty﴾ [al-Ahzab: 47].

THE NINTH RULING

On Oaths

﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths, [against] your being righteous and mindful of Allah and making peace among the people. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

The statement of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths, [against] your being righteous and mindful of Allah and making peace among the people. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

The exegetes have said much regarding this verse, and the best of what they have mentioned are two interpretations:

The first: this is what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani (Abu Muslim al-Isfahani) mentioned, and it is the best view, that His saying: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾ forbids audacity toward Allah through excessive swearing by Him. For whoever frequently mentions a thing in any sense has made it an obstacle to himself. A man says: "You have made me a target for your blame" (qad ja'altani 'urdatan li-lawmika), and the poet said:

"And do not make me a target for the blamers."

Allah, exalted is He, has dispraised the one who swears excessively, saying: ﴿And do not obey every constant swearer, contemptible﴾ [al-Qalam: 10], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And guard your oaths﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. The Arabs used to praise a person for swearing rarely, as Kuthayyir said:

"Few in oaths, guarding his oath, and if an oath slips from him, he is righteous."

The wisdom in the command to reduce oaths is that whoever swears in every small and great matter by Allah, his tongue becomes accustomed to it, and the oath no longer has any weight in his heart; thus his readiness to swear a false oath cannot be relied upon, and the essential purpose of the oath is thereby defeated. Furthermore, the more a person magnifies Allah, exalted is He, the more perfect he is in servitude, and among the perfection of magnification is that the mention of Allah, exalted is He, be greater and higher in his sight than to call Him as a witness for some worldly aim.

As for His saying after that: (an tabarru), it is the reason for this prohibition. So His saying (an tabarru) means "for the sake of your being righteous." The meaning is: I have only forbidden you from this because avoiding it is part of righteousness, piety and reform, so that you, O assembly of believers, will be righteous, pious, and reformers in the earth, not corrupters.

If it is said: How does refraining from swearing necessarily result in righteousness, piety and reform among people?

We say: Because whoever refrains from swearing, believing that Allah, exalted and great is He, is too great to be called upon by His mighty name for the aims of this world and the base aims of oaths, there is no doubt that this is among the greatest gates of righteousness. As for the meaning of piety, it is evident that he guards himself against anything that would violate the glorification of Allah. As for reconciliation among people, whenever they believe in the truthfulness of his speech and his distance from corrupt aims, they will accept his word, and reconciliation is achieved through his mediation.

The second interpretation: They said: "al-'urdah" is an expression for an obstacle (al-mani'), and the evidence for the soundness of this usage is that one says: "I wanted to do such-and-such, then such-and-such a matter 'arada (presented itself) to me and i'tarada (intervened)," meaning he avoided that and it prevented me from it. Its derivation is from a thing placed across the road so that it becomes a barrier preventing people from passing and traversing. One also says: "So-and-so raised an objection (i'tarada) to the speech of so-and-so," and made his speech opposed (mu'aridan) to another speech, meaning he mentioned what prevents him from affirming his speech. Once you know the origin of the derivation, "al-'urdah" is on the pattern fu'lah in the sense of maf'ul, like "al-qubdah" and "al-ghurfah," so it is the name of what is placed across in front of a thing and serves as a barrier to it. Thus it is established that "al-'urdah" is an expression for an obstacle. As for the lam in His saying (li-aymanikum), it is for causation (li-l-ta'lil).

Having known this, we say: The construction of the verse is: "Do not make the mention of Allah an obstacle, by reason of your oaths, from your being righteous, or regarding your being righteous." The preposition was dropped because it is unnecessary given its clarity.

They said: The occasion of revelation of the verse is that a man would swear to abandon good deeds such as maintaining family ties, reconciling between people, or doing good to one of his dependents, and then say: "I fear Allah that I might break my oath." Thus he would forsake righteousness, intending to keep his oath. So it was said: Do not make the mention of Allah an obstacle, by reason of these oaths, to doing righteousness and piety. This is the best of what the exegetes have mentioned, and they have elaborated in other words, but there is no benefit in them, so we have left them.

Then he said at the end of the verse: ﴿And Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾, meaning: if you swear, He hears; and if you abandon swearing, out of glorifying Allah and exalting Him above being called upon by His noble name for fleeting aims, then He is Knowing, Aware of what is in your hearts and your intentions.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 225:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle [oaths] in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned. And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾

In the verse there are two issues:

**The first issue:** *al-laghw* (idle, meaningless speech) is that which falls away and is not counted, whether it is speech or something else. That this word is used in speech is shown by the verse, the report, and the transmitted usage. From the verse, there is His saying: ﴿When they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ (28:55); His saying: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk or sinful speech﴾ (56:25); His saying: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾ (41:26); and His saying: ﴿Elevated, in which you hear no idle talk﴾ (88:10–11). As for His saying: ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ (25:72), it may mean that they pass by speech that is idle, or that they pass by an action that is idle.

From the report, there is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever says to his companion on Friday, 'Be silent (ṣah),' while the imam is delivering the khutbah, has indeed engaged in *laghā*."

From the usage of the language: it is said, "the bird *laghā yalghū laghwan*," when it makes a sound, and the *laghw* of a bird is its sound. The word is also used for things that are not counted among the young of camels; it is said that these are *laghw*. Jarir said:

*The genealogists count the houses of glory of Banu Tamim as four, being great,*
*And they exclude from them the one who is seen as laghw, just as you disregarded the young camel in the blood-money.*

Al-Ajjaj said:

*And many a company of pilgrims, restrained*
*From al-laghā and obscene talk.*

Al-Farra' said: *al-laghā* is the verbal noun of *laghaytu*, and *al-laghw* is the verbal noun of *laghawtu*. This is what relates to the language.

As for the exegetes, they have mentioned several views:

**The first:** al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the Arabs' saying, "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah," which they use to emphasise their speech, and the notion of swearing does not occur to their minds. If one of them were told, "I heard you swear a thousand times today in al-Masjid al-Haram," he would deny it, and perhaps he had said, "No, by Allah," a thousand times.

**The second:** this is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him: *al-laghw* is that a person swears about something he believes existed, then it becomes clear that it did not exist. This is *al-laghw*. The benefit of this disagreement is that al-Shafi'i does not require expiation (*kaffārah*) for a man's saying, "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah," but he does require it when someone swears about something he believes existed and then it becomes clear that it did not. Abu Hanifa rules the opposite of this. The school of al-Shafi'i is the view of Aisha, al-Sha'bi and Ikrimah. The view of Abu Hanifa is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Qatada, al-Suddi and Makhul.

The proofs for al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, for his view are several:

The first: what Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, related from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "*Laghw* in oaths is a man's saying in his speech, 'Indeed, no, by Allah,' 'Yes, by Allah,' and 'No, by Allah.'" It is also related that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a group of people shooting arrows, and with him was a man from among his companions. A man from the group shot, and said, "By Allah, I hit it!" Then he missed, and the companion who was with the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "The man has broken his oath, O Messenger of Allah!" He (ﷺ) said: "All the oaths of archers are *laghw*; there is no expiation for them and no punishment." It is also related from Aisha that she said: "The oaths of *laghw* are those made in jest, in dispute, and in quarrels, by which the heart is not bound." And the report of a Companion in the interpretation of the speech of Allah is a proof.

The second proof: His saying, ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle [oaths] in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾ indicates that *laghw* of oaths is like the opposite of what results from the earning of the heart. What is meant by His saying, ﴿what your hearts have earned﴾, is that which a person intends seriously and binds his heart to. If this is so, then *laghw*, which is its opposite, must mean what a person does not intend seriously and does not bind his heart to. This is the saying of people by way of habit in speech: "No, by Allah," "Yes, by Allah." As for when a person swears seriously about something that he believed was present, and then it became clear that it was not, he intended by that oath to affirm the truth of his own statement and to bind his heart to it, so it was not *laghw* at all, but was something earned by the heart.

The third proof: He, glorified is He, mentioned before this verse: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾ (2:224). We have explained that its meaning is a prohibition against frequent swearing and oaths. Those who say, by habit, "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah," undoubtedly swear frequently. So, after His saying, ﴿do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾, He mentioned the condition of those who swear frequently by habit in speech, not with the intention of swearing, and He made clear that there is no accountability upon them and no expiation; because imposing accountability and expiation upon them would lead either to their refraining from speech, or to an expiation being due upon them at every moment, and both of these are a hardship in religion. Thus it became clear that interpreting *laghw* as we have mentioned is the one that fits what comes before the verse. As for what Abu Hanifa said, it does not fit what comes before the verse. Therefore, al-Shafi'i's interpretation is more appropriate.

The proofs of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, are from several aspects:

The first proof: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else as better than it, let him do what is better and then make expiation for his oath." The hadith indicates that expiation is obligatory upon the one who breaks an oath, absolutely, without distinction between the serious and the joking.

The second proof: an oath is a matter that cannot be cancelled, so intention is not a condition for it, like divorce and manumission. These two proofs require expiation in the saying of people, "No, by Allah," "Yes, by Allah," when the breaking of the oath occurs. Then, what indicates that *laghw* cannot be explained by what al-Shafi'i said, and that it must be explained by what Abu Hanifa said, is that the oath in language is an expression for strength. The poet said:

*When a banner is raised for glory,*
*'Arabah receives it with the right hand.*

That is, with strength.

The purpose of an oath is to strengthen the side of truthfulness over the side of breaking the oath by means of the oath. This is done only in a case that is capable of being strengthened, and this happens only when the oath is sworn about a future action. As for when the oath is sworn about the past, that does not admit of strengthening at all. Thus, an oath about the past is empty of the benefit sought from it, and what is empty of the sought benefit is *laghw*. So it is established that *laghw* is the oath about the past. As for the oath about the future, it is capable of strengthening, so this oath is not empty of the intended purpose, and therefore it is not *laghw*.

*[p. 68]*

**The third view** on the interpretation of the oath of *laghw*: it is that if a person swears to abandon an act of obedience or to commit an act of disobedience, this is the oath of *laghw*, and it is disobedience. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿When they hear idle talk, they turn away from it﴾ (28:55). Thus He made clear that He does not hold accountable for abandoning these oaths. Then He said: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾, that is, for persisting in that which you swore to, of abandoning obedience and committing disobedience. They said: this interpretation contradicts His (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else as better than it, let him do what is better and then make expiation," and this interpretation is weak on two grounds:

The first: the accountability mentioned in this verse is explained in the verse of al-Ma'idah by His saying: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what you have bound by oaths, so its expiation is…﴾ (5:89). Since the meaning of accountability is the requirement of expiation, and here expiation is obligatory, we know that the meaning of the verse is not this case.

The second: He, exalted is He, made the opposite of *laghw* to be the earning of the heart, and it is not possible to interpret it as what he mentioned about persisting in what they swore to, because the earning of the heart indicates the beginning of a new action. As for continuing in what was already the case, that is not called the earning of the heart.

**The fourth view** on the interpretation of the oath of *laghw*: it is the oath that is expiated; it was called *laghw* because the expiation removed the sin, so it is as if it was said: "Allah will not hold you accountable for *laghw* when you make expiation." This is the view of al-Dahhak.

**The fifth view**, which is the view of al-Qadi: what is meant by it is what occurs by inadvertence, not intended. The evidence for this is His saying after that: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾, that is, He will hold you accountable if you do it deliberately. It is known that the opposite of deliberateness is inadvertence.

\* \* \*

**The second issue:** al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, used this verse as evidence for the obligation of expiation in the *yamin al-ghamus* (the oath of deception, sworn falsely about the past knowingly). He said: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned here ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾, and He said in the verse of al-Ma'idah: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what you have bound by oaths﴾ (5:89). The binding of an oath is open to two possibilities: that it means binding the heart to it, and that it means a binding that is the opposite of untying. When He said here, ﴿what your hearts have earned﴾, we know that what is meant by that binding is the binding of the heart. Also, He mentioned accountability here without making clear what that accountability is, and He made it clear in the verse of al-Ma'idah by His saying: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what you have bound by oaths, so its expiation is…﴾ (5:89), making clear that accountability is expiation. Thus each of these two verses is general in one respect and explained in another respect, so each of them explains the other in one respect. From each of them it results that every oath mentioned in a serious manner and with the binding of the heart requires expiation; the oath of deception is also like this, so expiation is obligatory for it.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾, you know that *al-Ghafur* (the Forgiving) is an intensive form meaning covering over sins and removing their punishment. As for *al-Halim* (the Forbearing), know that *al-hilm* in the speech of the Arabs means deliberation and calmness. It is said: "Place the howdah on the most deliberate of the camels," that is, the one most steady in its pace. From this comes *al-hulm* (dream), because it is seen in a state of stillness; and *halamat al-thadi* (the nipple). The meaning of *al-Halim* as an attribute of Allah is the One who does not hasten punishment, but delays the punishment of disbelievers and wrongdoers.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 226–227 (part 1 of 2):

Page 69
"The tenth ruling, concerning ila' (vowing abstinence from marital relations) and divorce"
﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. If they go back, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if they are determined upon divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. If they go back, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. And if they are determined upon divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾
In the verse there are several issues:
The first issue: "Ala yu'li" (to swear) — ila' (an oath of abstinence), ta'alla yata'allā ta'allīyan, and i'tala ya'tali i'tilā'an. The noun from it is ulliyyah and ulluwwah, both with shaddah. Abu 'Ubaydah reported three dialectal forms: alwah, ulwah, and ilwah. In summary, ulliyyah, qasam (oath), yamin (oath) and hilf (swearing) are all expressions for one meaning. In a hadith, related as a saying of Allah, the Exalted: "I have sworn that I will act contrary to those who measure (i.e., who try to limit Me)." Kuthayyir said:
Few are his oaths, guarding his oath; if an oath slips from him, he fulfils it.
This is the meaning of the word according to the original linguistic usage. As for its usage in the sharia, it is an oath to abstain from intercourse, such as when one says: "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with you, nor will I approach you." Some exegetes said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, its estimate being: "For those who swear to separate from their wives," but it was omitted because the remainder indicates it. I say: this supposition is only needed if we take the word ila' in its lexical sense; but if we take it in its sharia-established sense, we dispense with this supposition.
* * *
The second issue: It is narrated that ila' in the pre-Islamic period was a form of divorce. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: A man would not want a woman, nor would he like another man to marry her, so he would swear that he would not approach her. He would leave her thus, neither a widow nor a married woman, and the purpose of this was to harm the woman. Then the people of Islam also used to do this, so Allah, exalted is He, removed that and granted the husband a period so that he might reflect and consider. If he saw benefit in abandoning this harm, he would do so; and if he saw benefit in separating from the woman, he would separate from her.
The third issue: 'Abdullah recited: "those who swear off (aluw) from their wives," and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited: "those who swear (yuqsimuna) from their wives."
As for His saying "min nisa'ihim" (from their wives), there is a question: it is said that the customary usage is "halafa fulan 'ala kadha" or "ala 'ala kadha," so why has the word "'ala" been replaced here with "min"?
The answer has two aspects:
The first: that it is meant: "for them, from their wives, is a waiting period of four months," as one says: "li minka kadha" (I have from you such-and-such).
The second: that in this oath the meaning of distance has been implied, so it is as if it were said: "they keep away from their wives, swearing off or swearing."
As for His exalted saying "a waiting period of four months": know that tarabbus is delay and waiting. One says: "I waited for the thing"
Page 70
tarabbus, and one says: "ma li 'ala hadha al-amr rubsah," meaning I have no delay in this matter. The attribution of tarabbus to four months is the attribution of the verbal noun to a time-expression, like His saying: "between them is a day's journey," meaning a journey during a day, and there are many like it.
As for His saying "fa in fa'u" (if they go back), its meaning is: if they return. Fay' in the language is the return of a thing to what it was before. For this reason, the shadow that the sun has removed and then returns is called fay'. The grammarians distinguished between fay' and zill: they said fay' is what is in the evening, because it is what the sun has removed; and zill is what is in the morning, because the sun has not removed it. In Paradise there is zill and there is no fay', because there is no sun in it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and shade extended﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30], and they recited:
Neither the shade can endure the coolness of forenoon, nor the fay' the coolness of evening.
It is said: "Fulan is quick to fay' and fay'ah," both reported by al-Farra' from the Arabs, meaning quick to return from anger to the earlier state. It is also said that what Allah returned to the Muslims from the property of the polytheists is called fay', as if it had belonged to them and then returned to them. So His saying "fa in fa'u" means: if they return from what they swore about, namely abstaining from intercourse with them, ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ toward the husband when he repents of harming his wife, just as He is Forgiving and Merciful to all who repent.
As for His exalted saying ﴿And if they are determined upon divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾: know that 'azm is the firm resolve of the heart upon a thing. One says: "'azama 'ala al-shay' ya'zimu 'azman wa 'azimah," and "'azamtu 'alayka lataf'alanna," meaning I swore. Talaq is the verbal noun of "tallaqtu al-mar'ah, utallliqu talaqan." Al-Layth said: "talluqat" with a damma on the lam; Ibn al-A'rabi said: "tulluqat" with a damma on the lam from talaq is better. The meaning of talaq is the dissolution of the marriage bond by what is lawful in the sharia, and its root is from infilaq, which is departure, so talaq is an expression for the woman's release. This is what relates to the explanation of the wording of the verse.
* * *
As for the rulings, they are many, and we mention here some of what the verse indicates, in several issues:
The first issue: every husband who is capable of intercourse, and whose disposition is valid in the sharia, may validly make ila'. This condition is considered both by inclusion and by exclusion. As for inclusion: everyone who is so qualified has a valid ila', and from this certain rulings follow. First: the ila' of a dhimmi is valid; this is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: his ila' by Allah is not valid, but it is valid by divorce and manumission. Our proof is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months﴾, and this generality includes the disbeliever and the Muslim.
Second ruling: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the period of ila' does not differ by slavery or freedom; it is four months whether the spouses are both free, both slaves, or one free and the other a slave. According to Abu Hanifah and Malik, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is halved by slavery, except that according to Abu Hanifah it is halved by the slavery of the woman, and according to Malik by the slavery of the man, just as they both said regarding divorce. Our proof is that the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾ includes all, and specification is contrary to the apparent meaning; for the setting of this period was for a reason relating to natural disposition and temperament, namely the scarcity of patience at being separated from the husband, so free and slave are equal in it, like menstruation, the period of nursing, and the waiting period of 'iddah.
Third ruling: ila' is valid both in a state of contentment and in a state of anger. Malik said: it is valid only in a state of anger. Our proof is the apparent meaning of this verse.
Page 71
Fourth ruling: ila' is valid from the wife whether she is in the marriage bond or is one divorced by a revocable divorce, on the basis that a revocably divorced woman is correctly described as among his wives, as evidenced by the fact that if he said, "my wives are divorced," divorce would fall upon her. And since it is established that she is among his wives, she enters under the verse by the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾.
As for the converse of this matter, namely that one from whom intercourse cannot be imagined has no valid ila', there are two rulings concerning it:
First ruling: the ila' of a eunuch (khasi) is valid, because he has intercourse just as a stallion does; what is lacking in his case is ejaculation, and that has no effect; and because he falls under the generality of the verse.
Second ruling: if a castrated man (majbub) retains what enables him to have intercourse, his ila' is valid; if nothing remains, there are two opinions. One is that his ila' is not valid; this is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him. The second is that it is valid, by the generality of this verse, since the intention of harm through the oath has occurred from him.
The second condition: that he be a husband. If he said to a non-related woman, "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with you," and then married her, he is not a mu'li (one who makes ila'), because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months﴾ indicates that this ruling belongs to them and not to others, like His saying: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6], meaning for you, not for others.
* * *
The second issue: the thing sworn by and the oath are either by Allah or by other than Allah. If it is by Allah, he is a mu'li. Then if he has intercourse with her during the period of ila', he leaves the state of ila'. Is the expiation of oath (kaffarat al-yamin) obligatory? On this there are two opinions: the new (jadid) opinion, which is the more correct, and the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the expiation of oath is obligatory; and the old (qadim) opinion, that if he returns after the period has passed or during the period, there is no expiation upon him. (The argument of the first view: "By Allah, I will not approach you," then he approaches her; and between saying "By Allah, I will not speak to you," then he speaks to her.) The argument of the old view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If they go back, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, and the inference from it is in two respects:
One: if expiation were obligatory, Allah would have mentioned it here, because the need to know it is pressing here, and delaying clarification beyond the time of need is not permitted.
The second: just as He did not mention the obligation of expiation, He indicated its removal by His saying: ﴿If they go back, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, and forgiveness entails the absence of blame. The proponents of the first view may reply: Allah left out expiation here only because He explained it in the Qur'an and upon the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in other places.
As for His saying "Forgiving and Merciful", it indicates the absence of punishment; but the absence of punishment does not negate the obligation of the act, just as the one who repents of fornication or killing is not punished, yet hadd and qisas are still obligatory on him. As for if the oath in ila' is by other than Allah, as when he says: "If I have intercourse with you, then my slave is free," or "you are divorced," or "your co-wife is divorced," or he binds himself to something upon his obligation, saying: "If I have intercourse with you, then for Allah upon me is the freeing of a slave, or charity, or fasting, or pilgrimage, or prayer," is he then a mu'li? Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, has two opinions on this. In the old opinion he said: he is not a mu'li, and this is the view of Ahmad in the apparent narration. The evidence is that ila' was known in the pre-Islamic period, and it is established that what was known in the pre-Islamic period in this matter was swearing by Allah. Also it is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever swears, let him swear by Allah," so absolute swearing is understood to mean swearing by Allah. In the new opinion, which is the view of Abu Hanifah, Malik and the majority of scholars, may Allah have mercy on them: he is a mu'li, because the word ila' includes all of these; and the two opinions are linked, so his oath is binding. If he has attached to it a manumission or a divorce, then when he has intercourse, that attached thing takes effect; and if what is attached to it is an obligation of an act of worship upon himself, then he is subject to the rulings of the vow of heated dispute (nadhr al-lajaj). There are opinions on this:
The most correct: he owes the expiation of oath.
The second: he must fulfil what he named.
The third: he has the choice between the expiation of oath and fulfilling what he named. The benefit of these two opinions: if we say he is a mu'li, then after four months have passed, the matter becomes binding upon him until he returns or divorces; and if we say he is not a mu'li, the matter does not become binding upon him.
* * *
The third issue: they differed on the length of the period of ila' according to several opinions:
The first: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas that he is not a mu'li until he swears that he will never have intercourse with her.
The second: the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri and Ishaq: whatever period he swears upon, he is a mu'li, even if it is a single day; these two positions are at extreme distance.
The third: the saying of Abu Hanifah and al-Thawri that he is not a mu'li until he swears that he will not have intercourse with her for four months or more.
The fourth: the saying of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Malik, may Allah be pleased with them: he is not a mu'li until the period exceeds four months.
The benefit of the disagreement between Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that if he makes ila' from her for more than four months, he is granted four months; this period is a right of the husband, and when it passes, the wife demands from the husband either a return or divorce; if the husband refuses both, the judge divorces her against him. It is reported from Abu Hanifah: when four months pass, the divorce takes effect by itself. The proof of al-Shafi'i is from several aspects:

The first argument: the fa' (فاء, "then/so") in His words, ﴿And if they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ ﴿and if they resolve on divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾, requires that these two rulings be legislated as following after the expiry of the four months, with a delay.

If it is said: What you have mentioned is disputed, because His words ﴿if they return﴾ and ﴿if they resolve on divorce﴾ are an elaboration (tafsil) of His words ﴿for those who swear off their wives﴾, and an elaboration follows what it elaborates. As you say: "I will stay with you this month; if you honour me, I will remain with you, and if not, I will depart from you."

We say: This is weak, because His words ﴿for those who swear off their wives a waiting period﴾ indicate both matters for this period, and the fa' in His words ﴿if they return﴾ comes right after the mention of both of them. Thus this ruling is legislated right after the swearing off (iyla') and right after the completion of the waiting in this period. This differs from the example he gave, "I will stay with you; if you honour me, I will remain, and if not, I will depart," because there the fa' comes after that staying. Here, however, the fa' is mentioned right after the mention of the swearing off and the mention of the waiting, so what the fa' is attached to must occur right after these two matters. This is a clear statement.

The second argument of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: His words ﴿and if they resolve on divorce﴾ are explicit that divorce occurs only by the husband's pronouncement, whereas according to the opinion of Abu Hanifah, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him, divorce occurs by the passing of the period, not by the husband's pronouncement.

If it is said: The iyla' itself is a divorce. So what is meant by His words ﴿and if they resolve on divorce﴾ is the earlier iyla'.

We say: This is far-fetched, because His words ﴿and if they resolve on divorce﴾ must mean: "and if those who swear off resolve on divorce." So He made the one who swears off the one resolving, and this requires that the iyla' and the resolve have come together. As for divorce, it is the object of the resolve, and the object of the resolve comes after the resolve, so divorce is necessarily after the resolve. The iyla' is either concurrent with the resolve or precedes it. This indicates with certainty that the divorce in this verse is different from that iyla'. This is a clear statement.

The third argument: His words, exalted is He, ﴿and if they resolve on divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ require that something audible proceed from the husband. That can only mean that we take the verse's meaning to be: "and if they resolve on divorce and pronounce divorce, then indeed Allah hears their speech and knows what is in their hearts."

صفحة ٧٣

If it is said: Why can it not be that what is meant is: "Indeed Allah hears that iyla'"?

We say: This is unlikely, because this threat does not fall upon the iyla' itself, but only upon something that occurs after the iyla', which is speech other than it, so that ﴿then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ would be a threat upon it.

The fourth argument: His words, exalted is He, ﴿if they return﴾ and ﴿if they resolve﴾ apparently offer a choice between the two matters, and this requires that the time of their establishment be one and the same. According to the opinion of Abu Hanifah, the matter is not so.

The fifth argument: The iyla' in itself is not a divorce; rather it is an oath to abstain from intercourse for a specific period. However, the Law set a known measure of time, because a man may abandon intercourse with his wife for a period of time not out of harm (darar). This occurs only when the period is short. As for abandoning intercourse for a long time, it happens only with the intention of harm. Since length and brevity in this matter are not precisely fixed, God the Exalted specified a dividing limit between the short and the long. When this limit is reached, the intention of harm becomes manifest, and this does not necessarily entail the occurrence of divorce. Rather, what is fitting to the wisdom of the Law, when the intention of harm becomes evident, is that he be commanded either to cease the harm or to free her from the bond of the iyla'. This principle is recognized in the Law, as we said regarding setting a term in the case of the impotent man (al-'innin) and others.

The proof of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him: that Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recited: "fa-in fa'u fihinna" (then if they return to them in it).

The correct answer: An irregular recitation (qira'ah shadhdhah) is rejected, because everything that is Qur'an must be established by mass transmission (tawatur). Where it is not established by tawatur, we are certain that it is not Qur'an. The person most entitled to this principle is Abu Hanifah himself, for he relied on this variant to hold that the basmala is not part of the Qur'an. Moreover, we have already shown that the verse contains three matters which indicate that this return does not occur within the period. Since the irregular recitation contradicts them, its invalidity must be certain.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 226–227 (part 1 of 2):

Page 69
"The tenth ruling, concerning ila' (vowing abstinence from marital relations) and divorce"
﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. If they go back, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if they are determined upon divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. If they go back, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. And if they are determined upon divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾
In the verse there are several issues:
The first issue: "Ala yu'li" (to swear) — ila' (an oath of abstinence), ta'alla yata'allā ta'allīyan, and i'tala ya'tali i'tilā'an. The noun from it is ulliyyah and ulluwwah, both with shaddah. Abu 'Ubaydah reported three dialectal forms: alwah, ulwah, and ilwah. In summary, ulliyyah, qasam (oath), yamin (oath) and hilf (swearing) are all expressions for one meaning. In a hadith, related as a saying of Allah, the Exalted: "I have sworn that I will act contrary to those who measure (i.e., who try to limit Me)." Kuthayyir said:
Few are his oaths, guarding his oath; if an oath slips from him, he fulfils it.
This is the meaning of the word according to the original linguistic usage. As for its usage in the sharia, it is an oath to abstain from intercourse, such as when one says: "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with you, nor will I approach you." Some exegetes said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, its estimate being: "For those who swear to separate from their wives," but it was omitted because the remainder indicates it. I say: this supposition is only needed if we take the word ila' in its lexical sense; but if we take it in its sharia-established sense, we dispense with this supposition.
* * *
The second issue: It is narrated that ila' in the pre-Islamic period was a form of divorce. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: A man would not want a woman, nor would he like another man to marry her, so he would swear that he would not approach her. He would leave her thus, neither a widow nor a married woman, and the purpose of this was to harm the woman. Then the people of Islam also used to do this, so Allah, exalted is He, removed that and granted the husband a period so that he might reflect and consider. If he saw benefit in abandoning this harm, he would do so; and if he saw benefit in separating from the woman, he would separate from her.
The third issue: 'Abdullah recited: "those who swear off (aluw) from their wives," and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited: "those who swear (yuqsimuna) from their wives."
As for His saying "min nisa'ihim" (from their wives), there is a question: it is said that the customary usage is "halafa fulan 'ala kadha" or "ala 'ala kadha," so why has the word "'ala" been replaced here with "min"?
The answer has two aspects:
The first: that it is meant: "for them, from their wives, is a waiting period of four months," as one says: "li minka kadha" (I have from you such-and-such).
The second: that in this oath the meaning of distance has been implied, so it is as if it were said: "they keep away from their wives, swearing off or swearing."
As for His exalted saying "a waiting period of four months": know that tarabbus is delay and waiting. One says: "I waited for the thing"

tarabbus, and one says: "ma li 'ala hadha al-amr rubsah," meaning I have no delay in this matter. The attribution of tarabbus to four months is the attribution of the verbal noun to a time-expression, like His saying: "between them is a day's journey," meaning a journey during a day, and there are many like it.
As for His saying "fa in fa'u" (if they go back), its meaning is: if they return. Fay' in the language is the return of a thing to what it was before. For this reason, the shadow that the sun has removed and then returns is called fay'. The grammarians distinguished between fay' and zill: they said fay' is what is in the evening, because it is what the sun has removed; and zill is what is in the morning, because the sun has not removed it. In Paradise there is zill and there is no fay', because there is no sun in it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and shade extended﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30], and they recited:
Neither the shade can endure the coolness of forenoon, nor the fay' the coolness of evening.
It is said: "Fulan is quick to fay' and fay'ah," both reported by al-Farra' from the Arabs, meaning quick to return from anger to the earlier state. It is also said that what Allah returned to the Muslims from the property of the polytheists is called fay', as if it had belonged to them and then returned to them. So His saying "fa in fa'u" means: if they return from what they swore about, namely abstaining from intercourse with them, ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ toward the husband when he repents of harming his wife, just as He is Forgiving and Merciful to all who repent.
As for His exalted saying ﴿And if they are determined upon divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾: know that 'azm is the firm resolve of the heart upon a thing. One says: "'azama 'ala al-shay' ya'zimu 'azman wa 'azimah," and "'azamtu 'alayka lataf'alanna," meaning I swore. Talaq is the verbal noun of "tallaqtu al-mar'ah, utallliqu talaqan." Al-Layth said: "talluqat" with a damma on the lam; Ibn al-A'rabi said: "tulluqat" with a damma on the lam from talaq is better. The meaning of talaq is the dissolution of the marriage bond by what is lawful in the sharia, and its root is from infilaq, which is departure, so talaq is an expression for the woman's release. This is what relates to the explanation of the wording of the verse.

As for the rulings, they are many, and we mention here some of what the verse indicates, in several issues:
The first issue: every husband who is capable of intercourse, and whose disposition is valid in the sharia, may validly make ila'. This condition is considered both by inclusion and by exclusion. As for inclusion: everyone who is so qualified has a valid ila', and from this certain rulings follow. First: the ila' of a dhimmi is valid; this is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: his ila' by Allah is not valid, but it is valid by divorce and manumission. Our proof is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months﴾, and this generality includes the disbeliever and the Muslim.
Second ruling: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the period of ila' does not differ by slavery or freedom; it is four months whether the spouses are both free, both slaves, or one free and the other a slave. According to Abu Hanifah and Malik, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is halved by slavery, except that according to Abu Hanifah it is halved by the slavery of the woman, and according to Malik by the slavery of the man, just as they both said regarding divorce. Our proof is that the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾ includes all, and specification is contrary to the apparent meaning; for the setting of this period was for a reason relating to natural disposition and temperament, namely the scarcity of patience at being separated from the husband, so free and slave are equal in it, like menstruation, the period of nursing, and the waiting period of 'iddah.
Third ruling: ila' is valid both in a state of contentment and in a state of anger. Malik said: it is valid only in a state of anger. Our proof is the apparent meaning of this verse.

Fourth ruling: ila' is valid from the wife whether she is in the marriage bond or is one divorced by a revocable divorce, on the basis that a revocably divorced woman is correctly described as among his wives, as evidenced by the fact that if he said, "my wives are divorced," divorce would fall upon her. And since it is established that she is among his wives, she enters under the verse by the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾.
As for the converse of this matter, namely that one from whom intercourse cannot be imagined has no valid ila', there are two rulings concerning it:
First ruling: the ila' of a eunuch (khasi) is valid, because he has intercourse just as a stallion does; what is lacking in his case is ejaculation, and that has no effect; and because he falls under the generality of the verse.
Second ruling: if a castrated man (majbub) retains what enables him to have intercourse, his ila' is valid; if nothing remains, there are two opinions. One is that his ila' is not valid; this is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him. The second is that it is valid, by the generality of this verse, since the intention of harm through the oath has occurred from him.
The second condition: that he be a husband. If he said to a non-related woman, "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with you," and then married her, he is not a mu'li (one who makes ila'), because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months﴾ indicates that this ruling belongs to them and not to others, like His saying: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6], meaning for you, not for others.

The second issue: the thing sworn by and the oath are either by Allah or by other than Allah. If it is by Allah, he is a mu'li. Also it is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever swears, let him swear by Allah," so absolute swearing is understood to mean swearing by Allah. **The Eleventh Ruling: Concerning Divorce**

﴿The divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods (qurū'), and it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day.﴾

The Exalted said: ﴿The divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods, and it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day.﴾

Know that He, the Exalted, mentioned in this place many rulings concerning divorce.

The first ruling concerning divorce is the obligation of the waiting period ('iddah). Know that the divorced woman (al-muṭallaqah) is the woman upon whom divorce has been pronounced. She is either a stranger (ajnabiyyah) or a married woman (mankūḥah). If she is a stranger, then when divorce is pronounced upon her she is "divorced" according to the linguistic usage, but she is not "divorced" according to the usage of the Sharia. A waiting period is not obligatory for her by consensus (ijmā'). As for the married woman, she is either one who has been consummated with (madkhūlan bihā) or one who has not. If she has not been consummated with, a waiting period is not obligatory for her. The Exalted said:

﴿When you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no waiting period for them to count.﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 49]

As for the one who has been consummated with, she is either non-pregnant (ḥā'il) or pregnant (ḥāmil). If she is pregnant, her waiting period is by the delivery of the child, not by the qurū'. The Exalted said:

﴿And for those with children, their term is until they give birth to their burden.﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 4]

As for the non-pregnant one, either menstruation is possible for her or it is not. If menstruation is impossible for her, either because of extreme youth or extreme old age, her waiting period is by months, not by the qurū'. The Exalted said:

﴿And those who have despaired of menstruation among your women...﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 4]

If menstruation is possible for her, then either she is a slave (raqīqah) or a free woman (ḥurrah). If she is a slave, her waiting period is two qurū', not three. As for when the woman is married, is divorced after consummation, is non-pregnant, is one of those who menstruate, and is free, then when these attributes are combined her waiting period is the three qurū' as Allah has specified its ruling in this verse.

* * *

Among the questions regarding the verse:

The first question: The general (al-'āmm) may only be specified (takhṣīṣ) when what remains after the specification is greater in number. This is because it is customary to apply the word "all" to the majority. One says of a garment that it is black if black predominates over it, or if there is a small amount of white in it. But if white predominates over it and black is little, then applying the word "black" to it is false. Thus it is established that the condition for a general term to be specified is that what remains after the specification be the greater part. This verse is not like that, for you have excluded five categories from its generality and left only one category. Applying the general term in such a place does not befit the wisdom of Allah, the Exalted.

The answer: As for the stranger, she is outside the wording, for it is not said of a stranger that she is "divorced." As for the one who has not been consummated with, the context excludes her, because the purpose of the waiting period is the clearing of the womb (barā'at al-raḥm), and the need for clearing arises only when there was prior occupation (sabq al-shughl). As for the pregnant one and the one who has despaired, they are both outside the wording, because the obligation of waiting by qurū' applies only where qurū' occur, and in the case of these two categories the qurū' do not occur. As for the slave, her marriage is like something rare. Thus it is established that the greater and more prevalent category remains under this generality.

* * *

The second question: The phrase ﴿yatarabbaṣna (they shall wait)﴾ is undoubtedly in the form of a report (khabar), while what is meant is a command (amr). So what is the benefit of expressing a command with the wording of a report?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: If He had mentioned it in the wording of a command, that would have given the impression that the purpose is achieved only if she undertakes it with intention and choice. On this basis, if the husband died and the woman did not know of it until the waiting period ended, it would follow that this would not be sufficient for the purpose, since she was commanded to do it and would not be released from the obligation unless she intended to perform the obligation. But when Allah mentioned this obligation in the wording of a report, that impression is removed, and it becomes known that whenever this waiting period ends, the purpose is achieved, whether she knew or did not know, and whether she began the waiting period willingly or unwillingly.

The second: The author of al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī) said: Expressing a command in the form of a report conveys the emphasis of the command, indicating that it is something whose fulfilment must be hastened. It is as if they had already complied with the command to wait, so He reports it as existing. A parallel is the people's saying in supplication, "May Allah have mercy on you," which is expressed in the form of a report out of confidence in its being answered, as though the mercy had already come about, so He reports it.

* * *

The third question: If He had said ﴿yatarabbaṣu al-muṭallaqāt﴾ (the divorced women shall wait), that would have been a verbal sentence of verb and subject. So what is the wisdom in leaving that, and making "the divorced women" the subject (mubtada'), then saying ﴿yatarabbaṣna﴾ with the verb ascribed to the agent, and then making this sentence the predicate (khabar) of that subject?

The answer: Shaykh 'Abd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī said in the book Dalā'il al-I'jāz: When you put the noun first and say "Zayd did it," this conveys emphasis and strength that the saying "did Zayd" does not convey. That is because your saying "Zayd did it" is used for two matters. One: that it is to specify that agent with that action, as in your saying "I write to the sultan about such-and-such important matter," where what is meant is the speaker's claim to exclusivity. Two: that the intention is not that, but rather that mentioning the subject of the statement first is to establish that action, as in their saying, "He gives abundantly," where they do not mean restriction, but rather to establish for the hearer that giving abundantly is his habit. A similar example is the Exalted's saying:

﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are created.﴾ [al-Naḥl: 20]

It is not meant to restrict createdness (to them). And His saying:

﴿When they come to you they say, "We believe," but they had entered with disbelief and they had left with it.﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 61]

And the saying of the poet:

They both wear glory in the finest wearing,
Two brave men, each of them as able as the other.

The reason this meaning is produced when the subject is mentioned first is that when you say "'Abd Allāh," you have indicated that you intend to report about him, so a longing arises in the intellect to know that. When you then mention that predicate, the intellect accepts it as the lover accepts his beloved, and this is more forceful in establishing the matter and removing doubt.

* * *

The fourth question: Why was it not said ﴿yatarabbaṣna thalāthata qurū'\﴾ as it was said ﴿tarabbuṣu arba'ati ashhur (a waiting of four months)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226]? And what is the benefit of mentioning "the selves" (anfus)?

The answer: Mentioning "the selves" stirs them up to wait and adds to the incitement, because it contains something that they would find repugnant, which drives them to wait. This is because women's selves are inclined toward men, so He wanted them to restrain their selves, overcome their longing, and compel them to wait.

* * *

The fifth question: The word "anfus" is a plural of paucity (jam' qillah), although they are many selves, while qurū' is a plural of abundance (jam' kathrah). So why did He mention the plural of abundance when what is meant is these three qurū', which are few?

The answer: They take liberties in this, using each of the two plurals in place of the other because both share the sense of plurality. Or perhaps qurū' was more commonly used as the plural of qur' than aqrā' was.

* * *

The sixth question: Why was it not said "thalātha qurū'," as one says "thalāthatu ḥiyaḍ"?

The answer: Because it followed the masculine grammatical gender of the word, and the word qur' is masculine.

This is what relates to the questions on this verse. One matter remains from the discussion of this verse, concerning the reality of the qurū'. We say: qurū' is the plural of qar' and qur'. There is no disagreement that the term qur' applies to both menstruation (ḥayḍ) and purity (ṭuhr). Abū 'Ubayd said: al-aqrā' is among the antonyms (al-aḍdād) in the speech of the Arabs. The well-known view is that it is literally applied to both, like al-shafaq, which is the name for both redness and whiteness together. Others said: it is literal for menstruation and metaphorical for purity, and some reversed this. Still others said: it is established with a single common meaning shared between menstruation and purity. Those who held this view disagreed on three opinions:

The first: that the qar' is gathering (al-ijtimā'). At the time of menstruation, blood gathers in the womb, and at the time of purity, blood gathers in the body. This is the view of al-Aṣma'ī, al-Akhfash, al-Farrā', and al-Kisā'ī.

The second view, which is the view of Abū 'Ubayd: it is an expression for the transition from one state to another.

The third view, which is the view of Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā': the qar' is the time. It is said: "Aqra'at al-nujūm" when the stars rose, and "aqra'at" when they set. It is also said: "This is the qāri' of the winds," meaning the time when they blow. They recited the line of al-Hudhalī:

When the winds blow for their qāri' (appointed time)

When it is established that the qar' is the time, both menstruation and purity enter into it, because each of them has a specific time. Know that the Exalted commanded the divorced woman to observe a waiting period of three qurū'. The apparent meaning requires that if she observes a waiting period of three things that are called three qurū', she is released from the obligation. However, the scholars unanimously agreed that this is not sufficient. Rather, she must observe three qurū' of one of the two kinds, and they differed about which. The school of al-Shāfi'ī, may Allah be pleased with him, holds that they are the periods of purity. This is reported from Ibn 'Umar, Zayd, 'Ā'ishah, the seven jurists of Madinah, Mālik, Rabī'ah, and Aḥmad, may Allah be pleased with them all, in one narration. 'Alī, 'Umar, and Ibn Mas'ūd said they are the menstrual periods, and this is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā'ī, Ibn Abī Layla, Ibn Shubrumah, and Isḥāq, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The benefit of the disagreement is that the duration of the waiting period is shorter according to al-Shāfi'ī and longer according to them. So if he divorces her during a period of purity, the remainder of that purity counts as one qur', and if she menstruates immediately after it, then when she enters the third menstrual period her waiting period is complete. According to Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah be pleased with him, if the divorce was during a period of purity, the waiting period is not judged complete until she is purified from the third menstrual period, and if the divorce was during menstruation, until she is purified from the fourth menstrual period. He then said: if she becomes pure for the majority of menstruation, her waiting period ends before the ghusl. But if she becomes pure for the minimum of menstruation, her waiting period does not end until she performs ghusl, or performs tayammum when water is unavailable, or until the time of a prayer passes over her.

The arguments of al-Shāfi'ī are from several aspects:

The first argument: the saying of the Exalted:

﴿So divorce them at the commencement of their waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 1]

Its meaning is at the time of their waiting period. But divorce during the time of menstruation is forbidden, so it is necessary that the time of the waiting period be other than the time of menstruation. The author of al-Kashshāf answered this by saying: it means "those who are to be facing their waiting period," as one says "for three remaining in the month," meaning "facing three." I say: this statement strengthens al-Shāfi'ī's argument, because the speaker's saying "for three remaining in the month" means "for a time at which the beginning of the three occurs immediately afterward." Likewise here, the saying "So divorce them at the commencement of their waiting period" means: divorce them in such a way that the beginning of the waiting period occurs immediately after it. Since the command is fulfilled by divorcing during the entire time of purity, it is necessary that the purity which occurs immediately after the time of divorce be part of the waiting period, and that is what is sought.

The second argument: what is reported from 'Ā'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "Do you know what the aqrā' are? The aqrā' are the periods of purity." Then al-Shāfi'ī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Women have the most knowledge of this, because this is what women experience."

The third argument: "qur'" is an expression for gathering. It is said: "The she-camel never qara'at offspring," meaning she never gathered a young one in her womb. From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthūm:

Pure-coloured, she had never gathered a foetus (lam taqra' janīnan)

[Page 77]

Al-Akhfash said: It is said, "ma qara'at ḥayḍatan," meaning she did not gather her womb over a menstrual period (ḥayḍah). The pool was called *maqra'ah* because water gathers in it. "Aqra'at al-nujūm" means the stars gathered at sunset. The Qur'an was called *Qur'ān* because its letters and words are gathered together and because many sciences are gathered in it. "Qara'a al-qāri'" means he gathered the letters, some of them to others.

[Page 77 continued]

Having established this, we say: the time of the gathering of blood is the period of purity (ṭuhr), because blood gathers in the body during that period.

If it is said: why can this name not be applied to the period of menstruation (ḥayḍ), since blood gathers in the womb during that period?

We reply: blood does not gather in the womb at all, but separates drop by drop. In the period of purity, however, everything is gathered within the body, so the meaning of gathering is more complete in the period of purity. The full explanation is this: since the name *qur'* (lit. gathering, a cycle of purity and menstruation) indicates gathering, the state in which the womb is most gathered and enveloped in blood is the end of the period of purity. For if it were not filled with that outflow, it would not flow out. So from the beginning of the purity period it begins to gather and increase until its end, and the end is the state of complete gathering. Therefore the end of the purity period is in reality the *qur'*. This is a clear argument.

The third argument: the principle is that no sane, legally responsible person has a right over another to restrain him or prevent him from his dispositions. We have abandoned this principle when the evidence for an exception exists. The least that is called "three *aqrā'*" is the three periods of purity, because reckoning by purity periods takes less time than reckoning by menstrual periods. Since this is so, we affirm the lesser (as required by the application of this verse) and discard the greater, in fulfilment of the evidences showing that the principle is that no one has the power to restrain or prevent another.

The fourth argument: the apparent meaning of the words of the Exalted, "And the divorced women shall wait by themselves for three *qurū'*" (2:228), requires that when she observes a waiting period of three things called *aqrā'*, she is released from the obligation. Each of purity and menstruation is called by this name, so it is necessary that the woman be released from the obligation by either of them, as an option. But we have shown that the waiting period by purity periods is shorter than the waiting period by menstrual periods. Accordingly, the woman is free to observe either the shorter period or the longer period. Since this is so, she is able to abandon the additional portion without any substitute, and whatever is of this nature is not obligatory. Therefore observing the portion beyond the purity periods is not obligatory. This entails that observing the period of menstruation is not obligatory, which is what was to be proven.

The argument of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, from several aspects:

The first: although *aqrā'* in the lexical sense is shared between purity periods and menstrual periods, in the Shari'ah its use for menstruation has become predominant, because of what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Abstain from prayer during your days of *aqrā'*." Once this is established, it is better to interpret the *aqrā'* mentioned in the Qur'an as referring to menstruation.

The second argument: the view that *aqrā'* are menstrual periods allows the completion of three full *aqrā'*, because this speaker says that the divorced woman must observe three menstrual periods, and she is released from the obligation only by the cessation of the third menstrual period. But the one who says they are purity periods makes her released from the waiting period after two *qurū'* and part of the third, because in his view, if he divorces her at the end of a purity period, she counts that as a *qur'*. So since in one of the two opinions she completes the three *aqrā'*, and in the other opinion she does not, the first opinion is more consistent with the apparent meaning.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, answered this by saying that Allah said, "The Hajj is in well-known months" (2:197), and "months" (ashhur) is a plural whose minimum is three. Then we interpreted the verse as referring to two months and part of a third, and that is Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and part of Dhu al-Hijjah. Likewise here, these three may be interpreted as two purity periods and part of a purity period.

Al-Jubba'i, one of the shaykhs of the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that emphasized divine justice and human free will and rational reasoning), answered this response in two ways:

The first: we abandoned the apparent meaning in that verse on account of an evidence, so it does not follow that we must abandon the apparent meaning here without evidence.

The second: in the waiting period there is a continuous waiting, so the three must be completed. This is not the case with the months of Hajj, because there is no continuous action in them. It is as if it were said: these months are the time of Hajj, not in the sense of continuity throughout.

Later scholars of our school answered this argument in two ways:

The first: just as interpreting *aqrā'* as purity periods entails a deficiency below three, interpreting them as menstrual periods entails an excess. For if she divorces her in the middle of a purity period, the remainder of that purity period is not counted as part of the waiting period, so an excess results. Their excuse for this is that this must be borne out of necessity: for if divorce during menstruation were permitted, we would order him to divorce her at the end of menstruation so that she observes complete purity periods. Since divorce is specific to the state of purity, that excess becomes tolerated out of necessity. We also say: since *aqrā'* have been explained as purity periods, and Allah has commanded us to divorce during purity, the meaning of the verse becomes: "they shall wait by themselves for three purity periods, the purity in which the divorce occurs being one of them."

The second answer: we have shown that *qur'* is a name for gathering, and the complete gathering occurs only at the end of the purity period as a complete *qur'*. On this reckoning, no deficiency enters into any part of the *qur'*.

The third argument for them: Allah transferred to months when menstruation is absent, saying, "And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months" (65:4). So He placed months in the position of menstruation, not of purity periods. Also, since months were legislated as a substitute for *aqrā'*, and a substitute is measured by its completeness (for months must be completed), it is also necessary that completeness be considered in what is replaced. Therefore the complete *aqrā'* must be menstruation, whereas for purity periods the obligation is two *qurū'* and a part.

The fourth argument for them: the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), "The divorce of a slave-woman is two pronouncements, and her waiting period is two menstruations." They all agreed that the waiting period of a slave-woman is half the waiting period of a free woman, so the waiting period of a free woman must be menstruation.

The fifth argument: we all agreed that the *istibrā'* (the period of establishing that a womb is clear) in the purchase of slave-girls is by one menstruation. Likewise the waiting period is by one menstruation, because the purpose of *istibrā'* and of the waiting period is one and the same thing.

The sixth argument for them: the primary purpose of the waiting period is to establish that the womb is clear, and it is menstruation, not purity, by which wombs are cleared. Therefore what is considered must be menstruation, not purity.

The seventh argument for them: the view that *qurū'* are menstrual periods is caution and giving precedence to the side of prohibition. For if the divorced woman has passed the remainder of a purity period and has entered the third menstruation, then if we take *qur'* to mean menstruation, it becomes prohibited for another man to marry her; and if we take *qur'* to mean purity, it becomes permitted for another to marry her. The side of prohibition is more deserving of consideration, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whenever the lawful and the unlawful are mixed, the unlawful prevails over the lawful." Also, the original ruling concerning intimate relations is prohibition, and this view is closer to caution, so it is preferable, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt."

This is the sum of the arguments in this matter.

Know that when these arguments conflict, the preponderance of the preferences weakens, and the ruling of Allah with respect to all is what his ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) leads him to.

As for the words of the Exalted, "And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs" (2:228): know that since the completion of the waiting period is based on the completion of a *qur'* for those who have *aqrā'*, and on the delivery of the child for the pregnant woman, and since it was impossible for men to know this, the woman was made trustworthy regarding the waiting period, and her word was accepted when she claims the completion of her *qur'* within a period in which that is possible. According to the school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, this period is thirty-two days and an hour. For her case is taken to mean that she was divorced while pure, and then menstruated after an hour, then menstruated for one day and one night, which is the minimum of menstruation, then was pure for fifteen days, which is the minimum of purity, then menstruated again for one day and one night, then was pure for fifteen days, then saw blood. Then her waiting period is complete with the occurrence of three purity periods. Whenever she claims this or more than this, her word is accepted. Likewise, if she is pregnant and claims that she miscarried, her word is accepted, because she is on the basis of her trustworthiness.

* * *

Know that the commentators have three opinions regarding the words, "what Allah has created in their wombs" (2:228):

The first: it refers to both pregnancy and menstruation together. This is because a woman has many motives for concealing both. As for concealing pregnancy, her aim in it is that the completion of her waiting period by *qurū'* is a shorter time than the completion of her waiting period by delivery of the child. If she conceals the pregnancy, the period of her waiting is shortened, so she may marry quickly. Perhaps she dislikes returning to her first husband, or perhaps she loves to marry another husband, or she loves that her child should be attributed to the second husband. For these aims she conceals the pregnancy. As for concealing menstruation, her aim in it is that if her husband divorces her while she is among those with *aqrā'*, she may love to prolong her waiting period so that her first husband may take her back, or she may love to shorten her waiting period in order to nullify his right of return. This cannot be fully accomplished for her except by concealing some of the menstruation at some times. For if she menstruates first and conceals it, then at the second menstruation she shows that this is the first of her menstruations, she has prolonged the waiting period. And if she conceals that the third menstruation has occurred, it is similar. And if she conceals that her menstruation is still continuing, she has cut off her husband's right of return. Thus it is established that just as she has a motive for concealing pregnancy, she has a motive for concealing menstruation. Therefore the prohibition must be understood as covering both matters together.

The second opinion: the intended meaning is the prohibition against concealing pregnancy only. They argued for this with several aspects:

The first: the words of the Exalted, "It is He who forms you in the wombs as He wills" (3:6).

The second: menstruation is outside the womb, not something created within the womb.

The third: interpreting the words, "what Allah has created in their wombs," as referring to the child, which is a noble substance, is better than interpreting it as referring to menstruation, which is something of utmost baseness and filth.

Know that these aspects are weak, because the aim was to prevent them from concealing these conditions which no one else can know, and by which the matters of prohibition and permissibility in marriage vary. Therefore the wording must be understood as covering all of them.

The third opinion: the intended meaning is the prohibition against concealing menstruation only, because this verse came immediately after the mention of *aqrā'*, and the pregnancy had not been mentioned earlier. This too is weak, because the words, "And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs," are a new, independent statement that does not depend on what came before. Therefore it must be understood as referring to everything that is created in the womb.

As for the words of the Exalted, "if you truly believe in Allah and the Last Day" (2:228): the intended meaning is not that this prohibition is conditioned upon her being a believer. Rather, it is like when you say to a man who is oppressing: "If you are a believer, do not oppress." You mean: if you are a believer, then your faith should keep you from oppressing me. There is no doubt that this is a severe warning to women, and it is like what He said regarding testimony: "And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful" (2:283), and He said: "But if one of you entrusts another, let the one who is entrusted fulfil his trust and fear Allah, his Lord" (2:283). The verse indicates that whoever is made trustworthy in something and betrays it, his matter before Allah is grave.

* * *

[Page 80]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 228 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period], if they desire reconciliation. And women have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable. But men have a degree over them. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾

The Exalted said: ﴿Their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period], if they desire reconciliation. And women have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable. But men have a degree over them. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾

Know that this is the second ruling concerning divorce, namely the revocable divorce (al-raj'iyyah). Regarding *al-bu'ulah* (husbands) there are two opinions. The first is that it is the plural of *ba'l*, like *al-fuhulah*, *al-dhukurah*, *al-jududah* and *al-'umumah*, and this *ha'* is an added letter that emphasizes the feminine form of the plural. It is not permissible to add it to every plural, but only to those attested by the lexicographers from the Arabs. So one does not say *ka'b* → *ku'ubah*, nor *kalb* → *kilabah*.

Know also that the term *al-ba'l* is one that both spouses share. The wife is called *ba'lah*, just as she is called *zawjah*, in many dialects, and the husband is called *zawj* in the most eloquent usage. Thus they are both *ba'l* just as they are both *zawj*. The root meaning of *al-ba'l* is said to be "lord" or "owner," as one says, "Who is the *ba'l* of this she-camel?" just as one says, "Who is its *rabb* (master)?" *Ba'l* is also the name of an idol which they used to take as a lord. Women used to call their husbands by the title of nobility (*al-su'dud*).

The second opinion is that *al-bu'ulah* is a verbal noun (*masdar*). One says, "*ba'ala al-rajul yab'alu bu'ulah*" when he becomes a *ba'l*, and "*ba'ala al-rajul imra'atahu*" when he has intercourse with her. In a hadith, the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the days of Tashriq: "Indeed they are days of eating, drinking and *ba'al*."
