One of them: what conforms to the Shari'ah, namely a lawful contract, a permissible dower, and upright witnesses.

The second: that what is meant by it is the opposite of what we mentioned in His saying: ﴿and do not keep them to harm them, so that you transgress﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:231]. So the meaning of the verse is that each of the two is content with what has been incumbent upon him in this contract toward his companion, until a fine companionship is achieved and affection endures.

**The second issue:** Some of them said: agreement in a reasonable manner is the mahr al-mithl (the customary dower of women of her standing), and they derived from this a legal question: if she marries herself and her dower falls short of the customary dower by a grossly excessive amount, then according to Abu Hanifa the marriage is valid, but the guardian has the right to object to her on account of the shortfall in the dower. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: the guardian does not have that right.

Abu Hanifa's argument (may Allah have mercy on him) regarding this verse is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿when they agree among themselves in a reasonable manner﴾. Also, by this reduction [in the dower], she intends to bring disgrace upon the guardians, because the guardians are harmed by it: they are reproached for the smallness of dowers and they boast of their largeness. For this reason they conceal a small dower out of shame and display a large dower out of ostentation. Also, the women of the clan are harmed by it, because there may arise a need to make the mahr al-mithl (the customary dower) obligatory for some of them, and they would then measure it by this small dower. Therefore it is only right that the guardians prevent her from this and act on behalf of the women of the clan. Then, when He, Exalted, explained the wisdom of the obligation, He coupled it with a warning, saying: ﴿This is admonished to whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾. That is because it is part of the nature of admonition that it includes a warning against disobedience just as it includes an encouragement toward compliance, so the verse is a threat from this aspect.

There are two questions regarding the verse:

The first question: Why did He use the singular kaf in His saying ﴿dhalika﴾ ("this"), although He is addressing a group?

The answer: This is permissible in the language, and the dual is also permissible, and the Qur'an was revealed in all of the [various] forms of speech. Exalted is He said: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾ [Yusuf: 37], and He said: ﴿So that is the one about whom you blamed me﴾ [Yusuf: 32], and He said: ﴿by which he is admonished﴾, and He said: ﴿Did I not forbid you from that tree?﴾ [al-A'raf: 22].

Page 99

The second question: Why did He restrict this admonition to the believers and not others?

The answer: For several reasons:

The first: Since the believer is the one who benefits from it, it is fitting to restrict it to him, as in His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], although it is guidance for all, as He said: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and He said: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], and ﴿You warn only those who follow the Reminder﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11], although he was a warner to all, as He said: ﴿that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1].

The second: Some have argued from this verse that disbelievers are not addressed by the branches of the religion. They said: the evidence for this is that His saying ﴿dhalika﴾ refers to what has preceded of the explanation of the rulings; so when He restricted that to the believers, it indicates that the obligation of the branches of the laws applies only to believers. This is weak, because it is established that this obligation is general, as Exalted is He said: ﴿And for Allah, of mankind, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97].

The third: Although the explanation of the rulings is general with respect to those who are accountable, the fact that this explanation is an admonition is specific to the believers. This is because these obligations are imposed upon disbelievers by way of establishing them through the compelling, binding, and miraculous proof, whereas for the believer who acknowledges their truth, they are mentioned and explained to him by way of reminder and warning. Then He said: ﴿That is purer for you and more purifying﴾. It is said: "zakā al-zar'" means the crop grew. So His saying ﴿azka lakum﴾ indicates the deserving of lasting reward, and His saying ﴿wa-aṭhar﴾ indicates the removal of sins and disobediences whose occurrence would be a cause for punishment. Then He said: ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾. The meaning is that the accountable person, although he knows the wisdom of these obligations in general, the details of these matters are not known to him, whereas Allah, Exalted, knows in every matter He commanded and forbade, both in quantity and quality, according to what is actual and according to what is hypothetical, because He, Exalted, knows what has no limit of known things. Given that this is so, it is correct to say: ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾. It is also possible that what is intended is: Allah knows who acts in accordance with these obligations and who does not act by them. In all these aspects, the purpose of the verses is to establish the method of promise and threat.

**The twelfth ruling: on breastfeeding**

﴿And mothers shall breastfeed their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. And upon the father of the child is their provision and clothing in a reasonable manner. No soul is burdened except according to its capacity. No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child. And upon the heir is the like of that. But if the two of them desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them both.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And mothers shall breastfeed their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. And upon the father of the child is their provision and clothing in a reasonable manner. No soul is burdened except according to its capacity. No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child. And upon the heir is the like of that. But if the two of them desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them both.﴾.

Know that in His saying, ﴿And mothers﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: what is meant is what the apparent wording indicates, namely all mothers, whether they are married or divorced. The evidence for this is that the wording is general, and no evidence for specification has been established, so it must be left on its general sense.

[Page 100]

The second opinion: what is meant is divorced mothers. They said: what indicates that this is the meaning is two considerations.

The first of them: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this verse immediately after the verses on divorce, so this verse is, apparently, a completion of those verses. The reason for the connection between this verse and what precedes it is that when separation occurs, hostility and enmity arise, and that impels the woman to harm the child in two ways:

One of them: harming the child includes harming the divorcing husband.

The second: she may desire to marry another husband, and that requires her to neglect the affair of the infant. Since this possibility exists, Allah therefore urged divorced mothers to attend to the welfare of the children and to concern themselves with their affairs. So He said: ﴿And mothers shall breastfeed their children﴾, and what is meant is divorced mothers.

The second argument for them: what al-Suddi mentioned. He said: what is meant by ﴿mothers﴾ is divorced mothers, because Allah, exalted is He, said after this verse: ﴿And upon the father of the child is their provision and clothing﴾. Had the marital bond still existed, this would have been obligatory upon the husband by virtue of the marriage itself, not on account of nursing.

Know that the first argument can be answered by saying that this verse contains an independent ruling in itself, so it is not necessary that it be connected to what precedes it. As for the second argument, it is not far-fetched that a woman may deserve a certain amount of property because of the marriage and another amount because of nursing, for there is no contradiction between the two matters.

The third opinion: al-Wahidi said in *al-Basit*: it is preferable to understand it as referring to wives while the marriage continues, because a divorced woman is not entitled to clothing but is entitled to payment.

If it is said: when the marital bond still exists, she is entitled to maintenance and clothing by virtue of the marriage, whether or not she nurses the child, so what is the reason for making this entitlement conditional upon nursing?

We say: maintenance and clothing are owed in return for her availability (to the husband). When she is occupied with custody and nursing, she is not free to serve the husband, so someone might suppose that her maintenance and clothing fall away because of the lapse in her service to the husband. Allah therefore dispelled that supposition by making provision and clothing obligatory, even if the woman is occupied with nursing. This is all the words of al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿they breastfeed their children﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: although this statement is in form a report, in meaning it is a command. This is permissible for two reasons:

The first: the verse is to be understood as "And mothers shall breastfeed their children according to the ruling of Allah that He has made obligatory," but this was omitted because the context indicates it.

The second: that the meaning of ﴿they breastfeed﴾ is "let them breastfeed," but this was omitted for the sake of varying the expression while removing ambiguity.

The second issue: this command is not a command of obligation. Two things indicate this:

The first: His saying: ﴿And if they breastfeed for you, give them their wages﴾ [al-Talaq: 6]. Had nursing been obligatory upon her, she would not have been entitled to a wage.

The second: He, exalted is He, said after that: ﴿And if you disagree, then another woman shall nurse for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 6], and this is an explicit text. Some of them relied, in denying that it is obligatory upon her, on His saying: ﴿And upon the father of the child is their provision and clothing﴾. A mother may be divorced, so the obligation of her provision upon the father is only because of nursing. Had nursing been obligatory upon her, this would not have been required. Regarding this there is the discussion we have already presented. Once it is established that nursing is not obligatory upon the mother, this command is to be understood as recommendation, inasmuch as raising a child on its mother's milk is better for it than other milks, and inasmuch as a mother's compassion for it is more complete than the compassion of others. This applies when the situation regarding the child does not reach the point of necessity, namely when no one else is available other than the mother, or when the child will not nurse except from her. In that case it becomes obligatory upon her to nurse him, just as it is obligatory upon everyone to assist the one in dire need with food.

[Page 101]

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿two complete years﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: the root of *al-hawl* (year) is from *hala al-shay'* (the thing changed), meaning it turned over; so the year is a passage from one time to another. The word "complete" was mentioned to remove the supposition that it is like the common expression: "So-and-so stayed in such-and-such a place for two years or two months," when he actually stayed one year and part of the other. And they say: "It has been two days since I last saw him," when they mean one day and part of another day.

* * *

The second issue: know that the limitation to two years is not a limitation of obligation. Two things indicate this:

The first: He, exalted is He, said after that: ﴿For whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾. Since He made this completion dependent upon our wish, it is established that this completion is not obligatory.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if the two of them desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them both﴾. Thus it is established that the purpose of mentioning this limitation is not to make obligatory this specific duration. Rather, there are several aspects to it:

The first, and it is the most correct: the purpose of it is to end disputes between the spouses when they argue about the duration of nursing. Allah set it at two years so that they may return to it when a dispute arises between them. If the father wishes to wean him before the two years and the mother does not agree, he has no right to do so; and likewise if the situation is reversed. But if both of them agree to wean the child before the completion of the two years, then they may do so.

The second aspect regarding the purpose of this limitation: for nursing there is a specific ruling in the Shari'ah, namely His (ﷺ) saying: "What is forbidden by blood relationship is forbidden by nursing." The purpose of mentioning this limitation is to explain that nursing that does not occur within this period does not establish this ruling. This is the position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is the view of 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, 'Alqamah, al-Sha'bi, and al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with them all. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the period of nursing is thirty months.

The proofs of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, are from several aspects:

The first proof: the intent of His saying ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ is not completion according to the child's need for it. It is known that a child, just as it becomes independent of milk at the completion of two years, may still need it afterwards because of weakness in its constitution, since children differ in this. If the meaning of completion cannot be this, then it must be that the intended meaning is the specific ruling connected to nursing. On this reading, the verse indicates that the ruling of nursing is established only if nursing occurs within this period.

The second proof: it has been related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no nursing after weaning." And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and his weaning is in two years﴾ [Luqman: 14].

The third proof: what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Nothing is forbidden by nursing except what occurs within the two years."

The third aspect regarding the purpose of this limitation: what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said to a woman who gave birth after six months: she nurses for two complete years; but if she gave birth after seven months, she nurses for twenty-three months. Others said: these two years are the limit for the nursing of every infant. The argument of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿His carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. This verse indicates that the period of these two states is this amount of time; so just as the duration of one of the two states increases, the duration of the other decreases.

* * *

The third issue: it has been related that a man came to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "I married a virgin slave-girl and saw no suspicion in her, then she gave birth after six months." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Allah says: ﴿His carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15], and He says: ﴿And mothers shall breastfeed their children for two complete years﴾. So the carrying is six months, and the child is yours. It has also been related from 'Umar that a woman was brought to him who had given birth after six months, and he consulted about stoning her. Ibn 'Abbas said: "If I dispute with you by the Book of Allah, I will defeat you," and then he cited these two verses and derived from them that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read: "for whoever wishes that he completes the nursing" (*yukmila*). And it was also read: *al-ri'ada* (with a kasra on the *ra'*).

The second issue: regarding how this verse connects to what precedes it, there are two views:

The first: the meaning of the verse is: this ruling applies to whoever wishes to complete the nursing. It is related from Qatadah: Allah sent down "two complete years," then He sent down ease and relief, saying: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, permitted a shortfall by means of this verse.

The second: the lam is connected to His saying ﴿they breastfeed﴾, as you would say: "So-and-so breastfed for so-and-so his child," meaning: they breastfeed for two years for whoever among the fathers wishes to complete the nursing, because the father is obligated to nurse the child rather than the mother, for the reason we have explained.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And upon the father of the child is their provision and clothing in a reasonable manner﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿the father of the child﴾ (*al-mawlud lahu*) is the father. He expressed him by this term for several reasons:

The first: the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: the reason for it is to make known that mothers only gave birth to the children for the fathers, which is why children are attributed to them and not to the mothers. He recited, for al-Ma'mun, son of Harun al-Rashid:

*Indeed, the mothers of people are but vessels, entrusted repositories; and for the fathers are the sons.*

The second: this is an indication that the child is joined to the father because he was born upon his bed, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The child belongs to the bed." It is as if He said: when a woman gives birth to a child for a man, upon his bed, it becomes obligatory for him to care for its interests. So this is an indication that the cause of lineage and attachment is merely this much.

The third: it has been said in explaining His saying, ﴿He said: O son of my mother﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94], that what is meant is that the mother is compassionate toward the child, so the purpose of mentioning the mother was to call attention to compassion. Likewise here He mentioned the father with the expression "the father of the child," to point out that this child was born for the sake of the father, so his deficiency returns to him, and caring for his interests is binding upon him, as it is said: "A word for you, and a word against you."

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 233 (part 2 of 3):

The second issue: Just as He, exalted is He, enjoined upon the mother the care of the child's interests in His saying, ﴿And mothers suckle their children for two complete years﴾, He enjoined upon the father the care of the mother's interests, so that she may be able to look after the child's welfare. Thus He commanded him to provide for her food and clothing ﴿in a fair manner﴾. In this matter, what is "fair" (al-ma'ruf) may be limited by a condition and a contract, or it may be unlimited except by custom. For if he provides what suffices her for her food and clothing, he is excused from fixing a wage. But if that is less than what is sufficient, she will suffer hunger and nakedness, and her harm will extend to the child.
[Page 103]
* * *
The third issue: He, exalted is He, enjoined upon the mother the care of the child first, and then enjoined upon the father the care of him second. This indicates that the child's need for the mother's care is greater than his need for the father's care, because there is absolutely no intermediary between the child and the mother's care. As for the father's care, it reaches the child only through an intermediary, for he hires a woman to nurse and nurture him in exchange for maintenance and clothing. This indicates that the mother's right is greater than the father's right. The reports that agree with this meaning are numerous and well known.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾. On this there are several issues:
The first issue: Taklif (imposition, obligation) means to require. It is said: "He imposed the matter upon him (kallafahu al-amr), so he undertook it (takallafa) and was burdened with it (kullifa)." It is also said that its root is from kalf, which is a mark of blackness on a surface. So the meaning of "takallafa al-amr" is that he strove to show its trace in it, and "kallafahu" means that he obliged him to do what would show its trace in it. The wus' (capacity) is what a person can contain so that he is able to take it on, from the expression "sa'at al-mulk," meaning its breadth. If it were narrow, he would be unable to bear it. Capacity is equivalent to power, which is why it is said: "wus' is above ṭāqah (ability)."
The second issue: The meaning of the verse is that the father of this child is not obliged to spend on him and on his mother except within what his means can bear, because wus' in the language is what one's power can contain without exhausting it. He made clear that the father is bound only to this. It is similar to His saying in Surat al-Talaq: ﴿If they suckle for you, give them their wages﴾ [al-Talaq: 6], then He said: ﴿But if you disagree, then another woman shall suckle for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 6]. Then He clarified regarding maintenance that it is according to the man's ability, by His saying: ﴿Let the one of wealth spend from his wealth, and whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him. Allah does not burden a soul except with what He has given it﴾ [al-Talaq: 7].
* * *
The third issue: The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) held fast to this verse to prove that Allah, exalted is He, does not burden His servants except with what they are able to do. For He informed that He does not burden anyone except within what their power can contain, and wus' is above ṭāqah. So if Allah does not burden someone with what their power cannot contain, then it is even more fitting that He does not burden them with what they have no power over.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿No mother shall be harmed because of her child﴾. On this there are several issues:
The first issue: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Qutaybah from al-Kisa'i read lā tuḍārru with a raised final consonant (ḍammah), and the rest read it with fatḥah. As for the ḍammah, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said that it is a coordination (nasaq) with His saying ﴿is not burdened﴾. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: This is an error, because coordination with "lā" only introduces the second item as excluded from what the first included, as in: "I struck Zayd, not 'Amr." But to say "Zayd stands, not 'Amr sits" is not permissible by coordination. Rather, the correct view is that it is raised as a resumption (isti'naf) in the prohibition, as one says: "Zayd does not strike; do not kill 'Amr." As for the fatḥah, it is on the basis of prohibition, and the original is lā tuḍāraru, then the first rā' was assimilated into the second (idgham) and the second was given a fatḥah because of the meeting of two sukūns. It is said: "Rajul yuḍārir Zayd." This is because the root of the word is doubling (taḍ'īf), so one of the two rā's was assimilated into the other, becoming lā tuḍārr, just as you say: "lā taruddu," then you assimilate and say: "lā tarredd" with fatḥah. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, whoever of you reverts from his religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]. Al-Hasan read lā tuḍārr with kasrah, which is permissible in the language. Aban from 'Asim read lā tuḍārir, with the rā' expressed and kasrah, on the basis that the verb belongs to her.
* * *
The second issue: The phrase ﴿lā tuḍārr﴾ may bear two meanings, both permissible in the language. The two meanings arise only because of the assimilation that occurs in tuḍārr.
One of them: its original form is lā tuḍārir, with the first rā' kasrah. On this view the mother is the agent of harm.
The second: its original form is lā tuḍārar, with the first rā' fatḥah, so the mother is the one upon whom harm is inflicted.
On the first view the meaning is: the mother should not do harm to the father by causing harm to the child, namely by refusing to nurse him while the father has not withheld from her maintenance of food and clothing, so she leaves the child upon him. On the second view the meaning is: she should not be harmed, i.e., the father should not do harm to the mother by taking the child from her while she desires to keep him and has intense love for him. His saying ﴿nor shall the father be harmed because of his child﴾ means: nor should the mother do harm to the father by leaving the child upon him. Both meanings return to one thing, namely that one of them enrages the other because of the child.
If it is asked: Why did He say "tuḍārr" while the verb is for one party?
We say: For several reasons:
One: its meaning is intensification, for harming one who harms you is stronger than harming one who does not harm you.
Two: neither the mother nor the father should be harmed by the mother not nursing or by the father forbidding her and taking the child from her.
Three: what is intended by each of them in harming the child is the harm of the other, so this in reality is mutual harm.
* * *
The third issue: His saying ﴿No mother shall be harmed because of her child﴾, though it is apparently a report, its intended meaning is a prohibition, and it covers her harming the child by refusing to nurse and by neglecting care and protection.
His saying ﴿nor shall the father be harmed because of his child﴾ covers all forms of harm: that he prevents the mother from nursing him while she is more compassionate toward him; or that he restricts her maintenance and clothing; or that he treats her badly, which leads her to harm the child. All of this falls within this prohibition. And Allah knows best.
As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾, know that since the mention of the child, the father, and the mothers preceded, the "heir" could be linked to any of these. The scholars did not leave any possible view without someone holding it.
The first view, which is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: the intended meaning is the heir of the father. This is because His saying ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿And upon the one to whom the child belongs is their provision and clothing in a fair manner﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ) to clarify what is fair. The meaning is that if the father of the child dies, then upon his heir is the like of what was obligatory upon him of provision and clothing; that is, if the father dies, his heir must take his place in providing for and clothing them according to the stated condition, which is observing what is fair and avoiding harm. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: This view is weak, because if we take the wording to refer to the heir of the child, and the child is also an heir of his father, it would lead to the obligation of his maintenance upon others while he has property from which he could spend. And this is not permissible. It can be answered that when a child inherits property from his father, he needs someone to take care of him and spend that property on him in a fair manner, and to protect him from harm, and these matters can be imposed upon the heir of the father.
The second view: the intended meaning is the heir of the father, upon whom at the father's death is obligatory everything that was obligatory upon the father. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Muslim, and al-Qadi. Then those who hold this view differed as to what kind of heir he is. It is said: he is the 'asabah (agnatic male relatives) to the exclusion of the mother and the maternal siblings. This is the view of 'Umar, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ata, Sufyan, and Ibrahim. It is also said: he is the heir of the child, whether men or women, in proportion to their share of the inheritance. This is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Abi Layla, who said: maintenance is according to the share of inheritance. It is also said: the heir is among those who are related by a forbidden kinship (dhū raḥim muḥarram) to the exclusion of others such as the paternal cousin and the client (mawla). This is the view of Abu Hanifah and his companions.
Know that the apparent meaning of the speech requires that there be no preference between one heir and another, because He, exalted is He, used the word without qualification. So the one without kinship is equal to the one with kinship, just as the distant is equal to the near, and women are equal to men. And were it not that the mother has been excluded from this by the fact that her entitlement has already been mentioned, it would also be valid for her to be included in the speech, because she may be an heir just like others.
The third view: the intended meaning of "heir" is the surviving one of the two parents. It came in the well-known supplication: "and make him the heir among us," meaning the survivor. This is the view of Sufyan and a group.
The fourth view: by "the heir" is meant the child himself, who is the heir of his deceased father. For if he has property, the wage for nursing is due from his property, and if he has no property, his mother is compelled to nurse him. Only the parents are compelled to maintain a child, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i.
As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the like of that﴾, it is said: it refers to maintenance and clothing, from Ibrahim. It is said: it refers to refraining from harm, from al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri, and al-Dahhak. And it is said: it refers to both, from most scholars.
* * *
As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them both﴾, know that there are several issues in this verse:
The first issue: Regarding al-fiṣāl (weaning) there are two views. The first is that it is weaning (al-fiṭām), based on His saying: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. Weaning is called fiṣāl because the child is separated (yanfaṣilu) from feeding on his mother's milk to other foods. Al-Mubarrad said: It is said: "the child was separated from the mother," faṣlan and fiṣālan, and both are read in His saying: ﴿And his carrying and his fiṣāl﴾. Al-fiṣāl is better, because when he separates from his mother, she has also separated from him, so between them there is fiṣāl, like qitāl and ḍirāb. The young camel is called faṣīl because it is separated from its mother. It is said: "faṣala min al-balad" when he went out of it and left it, as He said: ﴿So when Talut set out with the armies﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249]. And know that interpreting fiṣāl here as weaning is the view of most exegetes.
Know that when He made clear that the two full years is the complete period of nursing, it became necessary to interpret this verse as other than that, so that there is no repetition. Then they differed. Some said: the intended meaning of this verse is that weaning before the two years is permissible. Others said: it indicates that weaning before the two years is permissible, and after it is also permissible. This view is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.
The argument of the first view is that since what precedes the verse indicated the permissibility of weaning at the completion of the two years, it also indicates the permissibility of exceeding the two years. And if that is so, this verse remains indicating only the permissibility of weaning before the completion of the two years.
The argument of the second view is that the child may be weak and need nursing, and weaning him may harm him just as it would before the two years. The first group answered that harm arising from weaning after the two years is rare, and the speech must be understood according to what is customary. And Allah knows best.
The second view regarding the interpretation of fiṣāl: when Abu Muslim mentioned the first view, he said: "It may also have another meaning, namely that what is intended by fiṣāl is the bringing about of separation between the mother and the child when mutual consent and consultation occur in this matter, and no harm returns to the child because of it."
* * *
[Page 106]

**The second issue (al-mas'alah al-thaniyah):** Linguistically, *al-tashawur* (consultation) means gathering opinion (*istijma' al-ra'y*). Likewise *al-mashurah* (consultation). *Al-mashurah* is a *maf'alah* form derived from it, like *al-ma'unah*. One says *shurtu al-'asal* ("I extracted the honey"). Abu Zayd said: *shurtu al-dabbah* and *ashartuha*, meaning I made the animal run in order to draw out its running. *Al-shiwar* means household goods, because they are visible to the onlooker. They also said *shawwartuhu fa-tashawwar*, meaning I embarrassed him, so he was embarrassed. *Al-sharah* is a man's appearance, because it is what shows of his dress and what appears of his adornment. *Al-isharah* is bringing out what is in one's self and making it manifest to the addressee, by speech or otherwise.

* * *

**The third issue (al-mas'alah al-thalithah):** The verse shows that weaning before two years is not permitted except with the consent of both parents and after consulting people of experience. This is because the mother may tire of nursing and so seek weaning, and the father may also tire of paying the wage for nursing, so he may seek weaning to relieve himself of it. Yet the two rarely agree on harming the child for the sake of their own desires. Then, even if they agree, consultation with others is required. At that point it is unlikely that everyone would agree to something harmful to the child. So when all agree, this indicates that weaning before two years does not harm him at all. Consider God's beneficence toward this small infant: how many conditions He stipulated for the permissibility of weaning him, to repel harms from him. Then, when all these conditions are met, He did not state the permission explicitly but said ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾. This indicates that the more weak a person is, the greater is God's mercy toward him and the stronger His care for him.

* *

**His saying, exalted is He:** ﴿And if you wish to seek wet-nurses for your children, there is no blame upon you, provided you hand over what you gave in accordance with what is customary. And fear God, and know that God is Seeing of what you do.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained the ruling for the mother and that she has the better right to nursing, He explained that it is permissible to depart in this matter from the mother to someone else.

* * *

Then in the verse there are issues:

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *istarda'a* is derived from *ard'a*. One says: the woman *arda'at* the child, and the child *istard'aha*. It takes two objects, as you say: *anjaha al-hajah* and *istanjahathu al-hajah*. The meaning is that you seek wet-nurses to nurse your children. One of the two objects is omitted because it is understood, as you say *istanjahtu al-hajah* without mentioning whom you made it succeed. The same rule applies to every pair of objects where the last is not a representation of the first. Al-Wahidi said: ﴿an tastarda'u awladakum﴾ means for your children. The preposition *li* ("for") was dropped, relying on the indication of *istirda'*, because it is only for children. It is not permitted to say *da'awtu Zaydan* while meaning *li-Zayd*, because that would be confusing here, unlike what we said about *istirda'*. A parallel to the dropping of *li* is His saying: ﴿And when they measure for them or weigh for them﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 3], meaning they measure for them or weigh for them.

* * *

**The second issue:** Know that we have explained that the mother has the better right to nursing. But if an obstacle to that arises, it is permissible to depart from her to someone else. Among these obstacles: if she marries another man, since attending to that husband's rights prevents her from nursing. Another: if her first husband divorces her, she may dislike nursing until another husband marries her. Another: the woman may refuse to accept the child, to harm the divorcing husband and to upset him. Another: she may fall ill or her milk may dry up. So when one of these circumstances obtains, and we find another wet-nurse, and the child accepts her milk, it is permissible to depart from the mother to another. But if we do not find another wet-nurse, or we find one but the child does not accept her milk, then nursing is obligatory upon the mother.

As for His saying: ﴿when you hand over what you gave in accordance with what is customary﴾, there are two issues in it:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir alone recited *"ma ataytum"* with the alif shortened, while the rest read ﴿ma ataytum﴾ with the alif lengthened. As for the lengthened reading, its underlying form is *ma ataytumuhu al-mar'ah*, meaning what you intended to give her. As for the shortened reading, its underlying form is *ma ataytum bihi*, so the two objects were omitted in the first, and the word *bihi* was omitted in the second because the meaning is known. Shayban transmitted from 'Asim *"ma ut'itum"*, meaning what God gave you and enabled you to provide of wages. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7].

**The second issue:** Handing over is not a condition for validity or permissibility. It is only a recommendation of the better course. Its purpose is that the wage be handed to the wet-nurse hand to hand, so that she is content and willing. That causes the child's condition to improve and brings care for his interests. Then God, exalted is He, concluded the verse with a warning, saying: ﴿And fear God, and know that God is Seeing of what you do.﴾

[Page 107]

[p. 108]

**The Thirteenth Ruling: The Waiting Period (ʿiddah) for the Death of a Husband**

﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days. When they have reached their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in an honorable manner. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days. When they have reached their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in an honorable manner. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ In it are several issues:

**The first issue:** *yutawaffawna* means they die and are taken (*yuqbaḍūn*). Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]. The root meaning of *tawaffī* is taking a thing in full and complete. So whoever dies has had his lifespan taken in full and complete. It is said: *tuwuffiya fulān* and *tawaffā*, meaning he died. Whoever says *tuwuffiya* means he was taken and seized. Whoever says *tawaffā* means he fulfilled his term and fulfilled his lifespan. Upon this is the reading of ʿAlī, peace be upon him: *yatawaffawna* with a fatḥah on the yāʾ.

***

As for His saying ﴿yadharūna﴾, it means they leave. The past tense and the verbal noun are not used from it, being dispensed with by *taraka tarkan*. Similarly *yadaʿu* is used in place of its verbal noun and past tense. These two verbs, the transitive and its imperative, exist, and it is said: *fulān yadaʿu kadhā wa yadharu*, and *duʿhu* and *dhurhu*. As for the past tense and the verbal noun, neither of these exists from them. The word *azwāj* here means wives. The Arabs call a man a *zawj* and his wife a *zawj* to him, and sometimes they add the *hāʾ* to it.

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿alladhīna﴾ is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and it must have a predicate (*khabar*). The scholars differed about its predicate in several opinions:

The first: the noun being added to is omitted, and the estimate is: *wa-azwāju alladhīna yutawaffawna minkum yatarabbaṣna*, "and the wives of those among you who die shall wait."

The second, which is the view of al-Akhfash: the estimate is *yatarabbaṣna baʿdahum*, "they shall wait after them," except that it was dropped because it is evident, like the saying: "Ghee is two *manns* for a dirham," and His saying, may He be exalted: [p. 108 continues]
﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, that is indeed of the matters requiring resolve﴾ [al-Shura: 43].

The third, which is the view of al-Mubarrad: "Those of you who die and leave wives behind, their wives shall wait." He said: omitting a subject is not strange. Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire﴾ [al-Hajj: 72], meaning "it is the Fire." And His saying: ﴿So patience is fitting﴾ [Yusuf: 18].

If it is said: you have here supposed an omitted subject that is an added noun, and that is not one thing but two things, whereas the examples you mentioned involve an omitted single thing.

We say: just as the omission of a single subject has occurred, so too has the omission of an added subject occurred. Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you﴾ ﴿A brief enjoyment﴾ [Al ʿImran: 197], and the meaning is: "their movement is a brief enjoyment."

The fourth, which is the view of al-Kisaʾi and al-Farraʾ: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Those of you who die﴾ is a subject, but the purpose here is not connected with explaining a ruling that returns to them, but with explaining a ruling that returns to their wives. Therefore no predicate was mentioned for that subject. Al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj rejected this, because a subject coming without a predicate is impossible.

***

**The third issue:** We have already explained earlier the meaning of *tarabbuṣ* (waiting), and we explained the benefit in His saying ﴿by themselves﴾. We also explained that although this is a statement in form, its intended meaning is a command, and we explained the benefit of shifting from the wording of a command to the wording of a statement.

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿and ten﴾ is stated in the feminine form, although what is meant is ten days. The scholars gave several explanations for this:

The first: the nights are given precedence over the days, because the beginning of the month is from the night. Since the nights are the first, they were given precedence, because the first is stronger than the second. Ibn al-Sikkit said: they say, "We fasted five of the month," giving precedence to the nights over the days, since they did not mention the days. But when they make the days explicit, they say, "We fasted five days."

The second: these days are days of grief and hardship, and days of this kind are called by nights in a figurative sense, as in their saying: "We went out during the nights of the trial," and "We came during the nights of al-Hajjaj's governorship."

The third, mentioned by al-Mubarrad: the feminine form of *ʿashr* is used because what is meant is a period, meaning "and ten periods," and each period of that is a day and a night.

The fourth: some jurists adhered to the apparent meaning of the verse and said: when four months and ten nights have passed for her, she is lawfully free for marriage. So they interpret the ten as nights. This was the view of al-Awzaʿi and Abu Bakr al-Asamm.

***

**The fifth issue:** It is narrated from Abu al-ʿĀliyah that Allah, glorified is He, set the waiting period at this amount because the spirit is breathed into the fetus in the ten days after the four months. This is also reported from al-Hasan al-Basri.

**The sixth issue:** Know that this waiting period is obligatory for every woman whose husband has died, except in two cases:

The first: that she is a slave woman. According to most jurists, she observes half the waiting period of a free woman. Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: her waiting period is the waiting period of free women, and he held to the apparent meaning of the verse. Also, Allah, may He be exalted, made the delivery of the child, for a pregnant woman, a substitute for this period. Then the delivery of the child is shared between the free woman and the slave woman, so likewise the observing of this period should be shared between them. But the rest of the jurists said: halving this period is possible, whereas halving the delivery of a child is not possible, so the difference is clear.

The second case: the meaning is that if she is pregnant, her waiting period ends with the delivery of the child. When she gives birth, she is free, even if that is an hour after the death of the husband. It is narrated from ʿAlī, peace be upon him: she waits for the longer of the two terms. The evidence for this is the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

[p. 109]

As for the Qur'an, it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for those with children, their term is that they deliver their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. Some people made this verse specify the general wording of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾. Al-Shafiʿi did not hold this view, for two reasons:

The first: each of these two verses is more general than the other in one respect and more specific than it in another respect, because a pregnant woman may or may not have a husband who died, and a woman whose husband died may or may not be pregnant. Since the matter is like this, it is impossible to make one of the two verses specify the other.

The second: His saying ﴿And for those with children, their term is that they deliver their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4] came right after the mention of divorced women, so someone might say: it refers to a divorced woman, not to a woman whose husband has died. For these two reasons, al-Shafiʿi did not rely on the Qur'an in this matter, but relied on the Sunnah, which is what Abu Dawud narrated with his chain: that Subayʿah bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyyah was married to Saʿd ibn Khawlah, and he died leaving her during the Farewell Pilgrimage while she was pregnant. She gave birth half a month after her husband's death. When she was purified from her bleeding, she adorned herself for suitors. Some people said to her: "You will not marry until four months and ten days have passed over you." Subayʿah said: I asked the Prophet ﷺ about that, and he gave me a ruling that I had become lawfully free when I delivered my child, and he commanded me to marry if I wished.

Having understood this principle, here are some branches:

The first: there is no difference in the waiting period for death between a young girl and a mature woman. Ibn ʿAbbas said: there is no waiting period for her before consummation. This is a rejected view, because the verse is general concerning all of them.

The second ruling: when four months and ten days are complete, her waiting period has ended, even if she has not seen her customary menstruation during them. Malik said: her waiting period does not end until she sees her customary menstruation during those days. For example, if her custom is to menstruate once every month, then in the waiting period for death she must have four menstrual periods. If her custom is to menstruate once every two months, she must have two. If her custom is to menstruate once every four months, she must have one menstrual period. If her custom is to menstruate once every five months, then in this case the months suffice for her. The proof of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, is that this verse shows that Allah, may He be exalted, commanded the woman whose husband has died to observe this period, and did not add to this amount. Therefore this amount must be sufficient. Then al-Shafiʿi said: if she has doubts, she must clear herself of doubt, just as a woman with menstrual cycles (*dhāt al-aqrāʾ*), if she has doubts, must be cautious.

The third ruling: when the husband dies, if more than ten days of the month of death remain, then the second, third and fourth months are counted by the crescent moons, whether they come out complete or incomplete. Then she completes the first month with the fifth, thirty days, and then adds ten days to it. If he dies when fewer than ten days of the month remain, then four months after that are counted by the crescent moons, and the ten days are completed from the sixth month.

***

**The seventh issue:** The jurists agreed that this verse abrogates (*nāsikh*, abrogation) what comes after it concerning the waiting period of a year, even though it comes earlier in the recitation. The exception is Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, who refused to accept its abrogation. We will mention his statement later, if Allah, may He be exalted, wills.

Coming earlier in the recitation does not prevent coming later in revelation, since the arrangement of the *muṣḥaf* is not according to the order of revelation. The arrangement of the recitation in the codices is the arrangement of Gabriel by the command of Allah, may He be exalted.

***

**The eighth issue:** The scholars differed as to whether the cause of this waiting period is the death or the knowledge of the death. Some of them said: as long as she does not know of her husband's death, the days do not count toward the waiting period. They argued that He, may He be exalted, said ﴿they shall wait by themselves﴾, and this does not occur unless she intends this waiting, and the intention to wait does not occur except with knowledge of it. Most of them said: the cause is the death itself. [p. 110] So if the period passes, or most of it passes, and then news of the husband's death reaches her, she must count what has passed. They said: the evidence for this is that a young girl who has no knowledge is still considered to have completed her waiting period when this period has passed.

***

**The ninth issue:** What is meant by her waiting by herself is abstaining from marriage, abstaining from leaving the house in which her husband died, and abstaining from adornment. This wording is almost general (*mujmal*), because it does not state what she waits in. However, we say: abstaining from marriage is agreed upon. As for abstaining from leaving the house, it is obligatory except in case of necessity or need. As for giving up adornment, it is obligatory, because of what is narrated from ʿĀʾishah and Ḥafṣah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn (*tuḥidd*) for a dead person for more than three nights, except for a husband, for four months and ten days." Al-Hasan and al-Shaʿbi said: it is not obligatory, because the hadith implies the permissibility of mourning, not its obligation. And Allah knows best.

They also argued with what is narrated from Asma' bint ʿUmays, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Wait three days, then do whatever you wish."

***

**The tenth issue:** Those who said that disbelievers are not addressed by the particular rulings of the sacred law argued with His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Those of you who die﴾. His saying ﴿of you﴾ is an address to the believers, which indicates that the address concerning these particular rulings is restricted to the believers alone.

The answer to this is: since the believers are the ones who act upon it, He specified them by mention, as in His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 45], even though he was a warner to all, as His saying shows: ﴿that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1].

***

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 234 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿When they have reached their term﴾, the meaning is: when this period, which is the term of the ʿiddah (waiting period), has ended, ﴿then there is no blame upon you﴾. It has been said: the address is to the guardians (awliya'), because they are the ones who conduct the marriage contract. And it has been said: the address is to the rulers (hukkam) and the righteous among the Muslims. That is because if they (the women) marry during the period of the ʿiddah, it becomes obligatory upon each one (of the Muslims) to prevent them from that, if he is able to prevent it; and if he is unable, it becomes obligatory upon him to seek the help of the authority (al-sultan). That is because the purpose of this ʿiddah is that the womb of the woman not be assumed to contain the water of her former husband. There is a third view regarding the verse: that ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ is to be understood as: there is no blame upon the women and upon you. Then He said: ﴿concerning what they do with themselves in a fair manner﴾, i.e., what is good by reason and by the Law; for it is the opposite of the reprehensible (munkar), which is not good. That is the lawful marriage when it fulfills the conditions of validity. Then He concluded the verse with a warning, saying: ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾.
* * *
Some issues remain concerning the verse:

The first issue: Some scholars have used His saying, ﴿concerning what they do with themselves﴾, as evidence for the obligation of mourning (ihdad) upon the woman. Its apparent meaning requires that what is meant is what the woman performs alone, and marriage is not like that, for it is not completed except with another. Therefore it must be understood as referring to what is completed by the woman alone, such as adornment, perfuming and other things.
* * *
The second issue: The companions of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of marriage without a guardian (wali). They said: if she marries herself, it must be permissible, because of His saying, ﴿there is no blame upon you concerning what they do with themselves﴾. The attribution of the act to its doer is taken to mean direct performance, because this is the literal meaning of the word. The companions of al-Shafiʿi (may Allah be pleased with him) have used it to argue that this marriage is not valid except through the guardian; because His saying, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, is an address to the guardians, and if this contract were not valid except through the guardian, he would not have been addressed with His saying, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾. And success is with Allah.

**The Fourteenth Ruling: On Proposing Marriage to Women**

{Allah the Exalted said:} ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply in proposing to women, or what you conceal within yourselves. Allah knows that you will remember them. But do not make promises to them in secret, unless you speak in an acceptable manner.﴾

This is the Exalted's saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply in proposing to women, or what you conceal within yourselves. Allah knows that you will remember them. But do not make promises to them in secret, unless you speak in an acceptable manner.﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue: Ta'rid (allusion).** Linguistically, *ta'rid* is the opposite of *tasrih* (explicit statement). Its meaning is that a speaker includes in his words something that can indicate his intended meaning and can also indicate something other than his intended meaning, though its indication of the intended meaning is more complete and more likely. It derives from *ard al-shay'*, meaning its side, as if the speaker circles around the matter without openly showing it. An example of this is when a person in need says to the one from whom he needs something: "I came to greet you and to look upon your noble face." That is why they said:

*"And let my greeting to you be enough as a demand (for what is due)."*

Ta'rid is sometimes called *talwih* (hinting), because what he wants gleams through it. The difference between *kinaya* (metonymy or indirect reference) and *ta'rid* is that *kinaya* is to mention a thing by mentioning its necessary attributes, as in your saying: "So-and-so has long neck-straps and much ashes," whereas *ta'rid* is to mention a statement that may bear your intended meaning and may bear something other than it, but the circumstantial indicators of your situation confirm that it is to be understood as your intended meaning.

As for *khitba* (proposal of marriage), al-Farra' said: *al-khitba* is a verbal noun in the position of *al-khatb*, like your saying: "He has a good sitting and seating (*al-qa'da* and *al-jilsa*)," meaning sitting and sitting down. There are two views on its derivation:

First: *al-khatb* means matter or affair, as in the saying: "What is your *khatb*?" meaning, "What is your affair?" So the saying "Fulan proposed to Fulana (*khataba fulan fulana*)" means he sought from her an affair or matter concerning herself.

Second: The origin of *khitba* is from *khitab*, which is speech. It is said: "He proposed to the woman with a proposal (*khataba al-mar'a khitba*)," because he addresses her guardian in the marriage contract. And "he delivered a sermon (*khataba khutba*)," meaning he addressed with rebuke and admonition. And *al-khatb* means a great matter, because much address (*khitab*) is needed in it.

\* \* \*

**The second issue: The categories of women regarding proposals.** Women are of three categories with respect to proposals:

The first: those whose proposal is permissible both by allusion and by explicit statement. These are the women who are free from marriages and waiting periods. Since marrying them is permitted in this state, how could proposing to them not be permitted? Rather, one exception is excluded from this, based on what al-Shafi'i narrated from Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "None of you should propose upon the proposal of his brother." This hadith, although it is stated in general terms, has three situations:

The first situation: If a man proposes to a woman and she accepts him explicitly, then in this case it is not lawful for another to propose to her, because of this hadith.

The second situation: If he finds clear refusal to accept, then in this case it is lawful for another to propose to her.

The third situation: If there is neither clear acceptance nor clear rejection, al-Shafi'i has two opinions here:

One of them: It is permissible for another to propose to her, because silence does not indicate consent.

The second, which is the older opinion (*al-qadim*) and the view of Malik: Although silence does not indicate consent, it also does not indicate aversion, for perhaps there is desire present in some respect. So this second proposal removes that measure of desire.

The second category: those whose proposal is not permissible, neither explicitly nor by allusion. These are women who are married to another man. This is because his proposing to her may become a cause of disturbing the matter for her husband, since if she knows the suitor's desire, it may move her to refrain from fulfilling the rights of her husband. Causing this is forbidden. The same applies to the revocably divorced woman (*al-raj'iyya*), for she is in the status of a married woman, as evidenced by the fact that her divorce, her *zihar* (a form of divorce oath), and her *li'an* (mutual oath of accusation) are valid, she observes the waiting period of widowhood from him, and they inherit from each other.

The third category: those whose proposal is to be distinguished in terms of allusion and explicit statement, namely a woman observing a waiting period other than a revocable one. She too is of three types:

The first type: The woman who is in the waiting period of widowhood. It is permissible to propose to her by allusion but not explicitly. As for the permissibility of allusion, it is based on the Exalted's saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply in proposing to women﴾, and its apparent meaning is that it refers to the woman whose husband has died, since this verse is mentioned right after that verse. As for the impermissibility of explicit statement, al-Shafi'i said: When He restricted allusion by the absence of blame, it became necessary that explicit statement be the opposite of that. Then the meaning confirms this, namely that explicit statement does not admit of anything other than marriage, so there is no assurance that desire for marriage would not move her to report the end of the waiting period before its time. By contrast, allusion admits of something other than that, so it does not lead her to lie.

The second type: The woman observing the waiting period after three divorces. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said in *al-Umm*: "I do not like allusion to propose to her." He said in *al-Qadim* and *al-Imla'*: "It is permissible, because she is not in a marriage, so she resembles the woman observing the waiting period of widowhood." The reason for prohibition is that with the widow, there is assurance against betrayal concerning the waiting period through the proposal, since her waiting period ends by months. But here, her waiting period ends by menstrual cycles (*aqra'*), so there is no assurance against betrayal because of her desire for this suitor. The form of betrayal is that she would announce the end of her waiting period before it actually ends.

The third type: The irrevocably divorced woman (*al-ba'in*) whose husband may lawfully remarry her during her waiting period. This includes the woman divorced by *khul'* (divorce at the wife's request), and the woman whose marriage was annulled due to a defect, or impotence, or the husband's inability to provide maintenance. In this case, her husband may use both allusion and explicit statement, because since he has the right to remarry her during the waiting period, explicit statement is more appropriate for him. As for a man other than the husband, there is no doubt that it is not lawful for him to make an explicit statement. Regarding allusion, there are two opinions:

One of them: It is lawful, as with the widow and the woman divorced three times.

The second, which is more sound: It is not lawful, because she is a woman in a waiting period in which her husband may lawfully remarry her, so allusion is not lawful for her, like the revocably divorced woman.

\* \* \*

**The third issue: Examples of allusion.** Al-Shafi'i said: Allusion is common, and it is like saying: "Many a man desires you," or "Who would find someone like you?" or "You are not unmarried," or "When you are free, inform me." All the other exegetes mentioned from the forms of allusion: "Indeed you are beautiful," "Indeed you are righteous," "Indeed you are beneficial," "Indeed it is my intention to marry," and "Indeed I am desirous of you."

As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿or what you conceal within yourselves﴾. Know that *al-iknan* means concealment and hiding. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs have two usages for "*akkanna al-shay'*," meaning he concealed it: *kanantuhu* and *akkantuhu*, both used for "in the shelter" and "in the self" with the same meaning. From it is the verse: ﴿what their breasts conceal﴾ [al-Qasas 28:69] and ﴿like hidden eggs﴾ [al-Saffat 37:49]. Some people distinguished between them, saying: *kanantu al-shay'* means when you protect it so that no harm reaches it, even if it is not hidden. It is said: "a hidden pearl" (*durr maknun*), "a hidden girl" (*jariya maknuna*), and "hidden eggs" (*bayd maknun*), meaning protected from rolling about. As for *akkantu*, it means I concealed, and this is used for the thing a person conceals and hides from others. It is the opposite of *a'lantu* and *azhartu* (I made known and I revealed). The intended meaning of the verse is that there is no sin in alluding to a woman in her waiting period of widowhood, nor in what a man conceals within himself of desire for her.

If it is said: Allusion to a proposal is a greater matter than that his heart inclines toward her without his mentioning anything. So when He first permitted allusion to proposal, His saying afterward: ﴿or what you conceal within yourselves﴾ would be like explaining what is already clear.

We say: That is not the intended meaning. Rather, the intended meaning is that He permitted allusion and forbade explicit statement in the present. Then He said: ﴿or what you conceal within yourselves﴾, meaning that he resolves in his heart that he will state it explicitly in the future. So the first verse permits allusion in the present and forbids explicit statement in the present, while the second verse permits resolving in the heart that he will state it explicitly after the waiting period has passed. Then He mentioned the reason for which He permitted this, saying: ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them﴾, because when the desire of the self arises in the matter of marriage, the one who desires it can hardly be free of resolve and wishing. So when repelling this thought seems like a difficult thing, the Exalted dropped this burden from him and permitted it.

\* \* \*

Then the Exalted said: ﴿But do not make promises to them in secret﴾. On this there are two questions:

**The first question:** Where is the thing implied by the Exalted's saying: ﴿But do not make promises to them in secret﴾?

**Answer:** It is omitted, because the statement ﴿you will remember them﴾ indicates it. Its estimated meaning is: ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them﴾, so remember them, ﴿but do not make promises to them﴾.

**The second question:** What is the meaning of *sirr* (secret)?

**Answer:** *Sirr* is the opposite of *jahr* (openness) and *i'lan* (public declaration). So it may be that *sirr* here describes the act of promising something, meaning: do not promise them a secret promise. It may also describe what is promised, in the sense: do not promise them a thing that has the attribute of being secret. As for the first estimate, which is the more apparent of the two, then intimacy between a man and a woman in a secret manner is inevitably, apparently, a promise of something among the forbidden matters. Here there are several possibilities:

The first: That he promises her in secret marriage, so the meaning would be that the beginning of the verse grants permission for allusion to proposal, and the end of the verse prohibits explicit proposal.

The second: That he promises her with mention of intercourse and sexual talk, since mentioning such matters between a non-related man and woman is not permitted. The Exalted said to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿so do not be soft in speech﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:32], meaning: do not say anything about sexual talk ﴿lest he in whose heart is a disease should be inclined﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:32].

The third: Al-Hasan said: ﴿But do not make promises to them in secret﴾ means regarding fornication. Al-Qadi criticized this view and said: Making promises is forbidden absolutely, so interpreting the statement as referring to what is specific to the suitor during the waiting period is more appropriate.

The answer: Al-Hasan narrated that a man would enter upon a woman while he was alluding to marriage, and he would say to her: "Let me have intercourse with you, and when you complete your waiting period I will declare your marriage." So Allah the Exalted forbade that.

The fourth: That this is a prohibition against a man speaking privately with a non-related woman, because that produces a kind of suspicion about her.

The fifth: That he pledges to her that he will not marry anyone other than her.

As for if we interpret *sirr* as referring to what is promised, then there are several views:

The first: *Sirr* means intercourse. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"And that such as I should not witness the secret."*

Al-Farazdaq said:

*"They guard their secrets, except from their own people, and they defeat what the jealous and infatuated one suspects."*

That is, the one whom love for them has consumed. He means that they are chaste women who refuse intercourse except with their husbands.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: The meaning is that he should not describe himself to her by saying: "I will come to you four or five times."

The second: The meaning of *sirr* is marriage, because intercourse is called *sirr*, and marriage is its cause, and naming a thing after its cause is permissible.

As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿unless you speak in an acceptable manner﴾, there is a question about it, namely: upon what did He make this exception dependent?

Its answer: When the Exalted granted permission at the beginning of the verse for allusion, and then forbade private conversation with her in order to avert suspicion and backbiting, He made an exception from it: that he may speak privately to her with an acceptable word. That is, he promises her in secret of kindness toward her, concern for her affairs, and taking charge of her welfare, so that mention of these good things would reinforce that allusion. And Allah knows best.

\* \*

The Exalted said: ﴿And do not determine the tie of marriage until the prescribed term reaches its end. And know that Allah knows what is in your selves, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾

Know that the word *'azm* (resolve) has several meanings:

The first view: it is an expression for the heart's resolve upon some action, as God Most High says: ﴿So when you have resolved, then rely upon God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. Know that resolve (al-'azm) is only a resolve upon an action, so the verse necessarily implies a verb, and this word is only transitive to the action by the particle "upon" (ʿalā), as one says: "So-and-so resolved upon such-and-such." If this is established, the sense of the verse is: "And do not resolve upon the tie of marriage." Sibawayh said: "Omission in these matters is not to be analogized." So the sense of the verse is: "And do not resolve the tie of marriage, that you should determine it, until the Book reaches its term." The purpose of this is to emphasize the prohibition of marriage during the period of waiting ('idda), for resolve precedes the object of resolve; so when the prohibition on resolving is given, the prohibition on proceeding with the object of resolve is all the more emphatic and fitting.

The second view: that resolve (al-'azm) is an expression for obligation. One says: "I resolved upon you," meaning, "I obligated you," and it is said: "This is of the category of 'ʿazāʾim' (obligatory acts), not of the category of 'rukhas' (concessions)." The Prophet ﷺ said: "It is a resolve from the resolves of our Lord," and he said: "Indeed God loves that His concessions be accepted, just as He loves that His obligations be fulfilled." Therefore resolve in this sense is permissible to attribute to God Most High, whereas in the first sense it is not permissible.

Having understood this, we say: obligation is the apparent cause of existence, so it is not far-fetched that the word "resolve" be used for existence. On this basis, His saying: ﴿and do not resolve the tie of marriage﴾ means: do not establish that, do not initiate it, and do not complete it in action ﴿until the Book reaches its term﴾. This view is the choice of most of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun).

The third view: al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: He did not say "do not resolve upon the tie of marriage" because the meaning is: "Do not resolve upon them the tie of marriage," that is, do not resolve upon them that they conclude the marriage contract, just as you say: "I resolved upon you that you do such-and-such."

As for His saying ﴿the tie of marriage﴾, know that the origin of 'aqd (tie/contract) is binding, and covenants and marriages are called 'uqud because they are tied just as a rope is tied.

As for His saying ﴿until the Book reaches its term﴾, there are two views concerning "the Book":
First: What is meant by it is the written decree, and the sense is: the prescribed waiting period reaches its end and is concluded.
Second: That "the Book" itself carries the meaning of obligation, as in His saying: ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 183]. The meaning then is: until this obligation reaches its last limit and its end. The expression of the meaning "obligated" by the word "kataba" (prescribed) is fitting because what is written falls upon souls as more firm and more emphatic. His saying ﴿until﴾ denotes a limit, so it must indicate the lifting of the preceding prohibition, because it is the right of a limit set for a prohibition that it entails its removal.

Then God Most High concluded the verse with a warning, saying: ﴿And know that God knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him﴾. This is an admonition that since God Most High knows the secret and the open, it is obligatory to be wary in everything a person does, in secret and in public. Then after the warning He mentioned the promise, saying: ﴿And know that God is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 236 (part 1 of 2):

The Fifteenth Ruling
The ruling concerning the divorced woman before consummation

﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligation. But provide for them, the wealthy according to his capacity and the poor according to his capacity, a provision according to what is reasonable, an obligation upon the doers of good.﴾

God Most High says: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligation. But provide for them, the wealthy according to his capacity and the poor according to his capacity, a provision according to what is reasonable, an obligation upon the doers of good.﴾

Know that the categories of divorced women are four:

The first: the divorced woman who has been assigned a dower (mafrud laha) and has been consummated (madkhul biha). God Most High mentioned the rulings of this category earlier, namely that nothing is to be taken from them in exchange for separation as an injustice, and then He informed that they are owed the full dower and that their waiting period (iddah) is three periods (quru').

The second category of divorced women: the one who has not been assigned a dower and has not been consummated. This is the one God Most High mentioned in this verse, and He stated that she has no dower and that she is entitled to a provision (mut'ah) according to what is reasonable.

The third category of divorced women: the one who has been assigned a dower but has not been consummated. She is the one mentioned in the verse after this verse, which is His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them and you have specified for them an obligation, then half of what you specified﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. Know that He, Most High, explained the ruling on the waiting period of the unconsummated woman, and in Surat al-Ahzab He mentioned that she has no waiting period at all, when He said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, then you have no waiting period for them to count; so provide for them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49].

The fourth category of divorced women: the one who has been consummated but has not been assigned a dower. The ruling of this category is mentioned in His saying: ﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them, give them their compensation﴾ [an-Nisa': 24]. Also, clear analogy (al-qiyas al-jali) indicates it, because the community (ummah) is in agreement that a woman who has been cohabited with by way of a doubtful union (wat' bi-al-shubhah) is owed a dower equivalent (mahr al-mithl). So the woman who has been consummated through a valid marriage is more deserving of this ruling. This division is an alert to the purpose of this verse. This division can also be expressed in another way: it is said that the contract of marriage necessitates a compensation (badal) in every case; then that compensation is either stated or unstated. If the compensation is stated and consummation occurs, it is fully established; this is the ruling of the divorced women whom God Most High mentioned before this verse. If consummation does not occur, half of what was stated falls away by the divorce; this is the ruling of the divorced women whom God Most High mentioned in the verse that comes after this verse.

If the compensation is not stated: if consummation does not occur, this is the divorced woman whose ruling God Most High mentioned in this verse, and her ruling is that she has no dower and no waiting period is upon her, and a provision (mut'ah) is obligatory for her from him. If consummation occurs, her ruling is not mentioned in these verses, except that they agreed that what is obligatory for her is the dower equivalent (mahr al-mithl). Since we have alerted to this division, let us return to the exegesis.

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women﴾, this is a clear text that divorce is permissible. Know that many of our companions (the Shafi'is) hold fast to this verse in demonstrating that combining three divorces at once is not forbidden. They said: because His saying, ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women﴾ encompasses all types of divorces, as evidenced by the fact that it is valid to make an exception of three from it. It is said: "There is no blame upon you if you divorce women, except if you divorce them three divorces," for there the blame is established. They said: the function of an exception is to remove what would have been included had it not been there. So it is established that His saying, ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women﴾ encompasses all types of divorces, meaning the case of singleness and the case of combining. This argument, in my view, is weak. That is because the verse indicates permission for bringing this reality into existence, and it suffices in acting upon it to bring it into existence once. For this reason we say that an absolute command does not imply repetition. For this reason we say that if a man says to his wife, "If you enter the house, then you are divorced," the oath is concluded upon one occurrence only. Thus it is established that this wording does not encompass the case of combining. As for the exception they mentioned, we say: this is problematic in the case of the command, for it does not imply repetition by the agreement of the verifiers, although it is valid to say: "Pray except at such-and-such time," and "Fast except on such-and-such day." And God knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿as long as you have not touched them﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿tumasshuhunna﴾ with an alif, in the form of mufa'alah, and likewise in al-Ahzab. The rest read ﴿tamassuhunna﴾ without an alif. The argument of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i is that the body of each one touches the body of the other, and they both touch each other; and also His saying, Most High, ﴿before they touch one another﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3] indicates this, and it is agreed upon. The argument of the others is their consensus upon His saying: ﴿no man has touched me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 47].
