Also, most of the expressions with this meaning came in the form of a verb without a subject, as in His saying: ﴿no man or jinn has touched them before them﴾ [ar-Rahman: 56], and as in His saying: ﴿so marry them with the permission of their families﴾ [an-Nisa': 25]. Also, the intended meaning of this touching is intercourse, and that is the act of the man. The second verse also indicates that the intended meaning of this touching is intercourse. As for what came in the context of zihar in His saying, Most High: ﴿before they touch one another﴾, the intended meaning there is touching which is other than intercourse, and it is forbidden in zihar. Some who read ﴿tumassuhunna﴾ said that it has the meaning of ﴿tamassuhunna﴾, because the form faa'ala may be used with the meaning of fa'ala, as in the saying: "I followed the sandal" (taraqtu al-na'l), and "I punished the thief" ('aqabtu al-lis), and this is common.

* * *

The second issue: One might say: the apparent meaning of the verse suggests that the removal of blame from the divorcer is conditional upon the absence of touching, and this is not so, for there is also no blame upon him after touching.

Its answer is from several aspects:

The first: the verse indicates the permissibility of divorce before touching absolutely, and this absoluteness is not established after touching; for divorce is not lawful after touching during menstruation, nor in the purity in which he had intercourse with her. So when what is mentioned in the verse is the lawfulness of divorce in an absolute sense, and the lawfulness of divorce in an absolute sense is not established except with the condition of the absence of touching, the apparent wording is correct.

The second aspect in the answer: some said that (ma) in His saying ﴿as long as you have not touched them﴾ has the meaning of (alladhi), and the sense is: "There is no blame upon you if you divorce the women who you have not touched." However, (ma) is an invariable noun that does not take inflection, and in it neither the i'rab (grammatical case) nor the number is made clear, and on this assumption the word (ma) is not a conditional particle, so the question falls away.

The third aspect in the answer is what al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, revolves around, and its essence returns to what I say, which is that the intended meaning of the blame (junah) in this verse is the obligation of the dower. So the sense of the verse is: "There is no dower upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligation," meaning: the dower is not obligatory except by one of these two matters; if both are absent, the dower is not obligatory. This is a clear statement, but we need to show that His saying ﴿no blame (junah)﴾ means no dower. So we say: the application of the word junah to the dower is probable, and the evidence indicates it, so it is necessary to turn to it. As for demonstrating the probability, the root meaning of junah in the language is heaviness. It is said: "The ship inclined (ajnahat al-safinah)" when it leaned because of its heaviness, and the sin is called a junah because of the heaviness in it. God Most High said: ﴿and they will bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13]. Once it is established that junah is heaviness, and the obligation to pay wealth is a heaviness, it is a junah. Thus it is established that the word is probable for this meaning. We said that the evidence indicates that this is the intended meaning for two reasons:

The first: He, Most High, said: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligation﴾; He negated the blame, limited to an end point, which is either the touching or the specification. The sense is: it is necessary that this blame be established upon the occurrence of one of these two matters. Then, the blame that is established upon one of these two matters is the obligation of the dower. So it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the blame negated at the beginning of the verse is the obligation of the dower.

The second: the divorce of women before touching is of two kinds:
One: that which occurs before touching and before the specification of the dower; this is the one mentioned in this verse.
The second: that which occurs before touching and after the specification of the dower; this is the one mentioned in the verse after this verse, which is His saying: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them and you have specified for them an obligation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. Then in this kind He made obligatory half of what was specified, and this kind is like the counterpart to that kind. So it follows that the blame negated there is the same as that affirmed here. Since what is affirmed here is the obligation of the dower, it must be said that the blame negated there is the obligation of the dower. And God knows best.

Know that we mentioned at the beginning of the exegesis of this verse that the categories of divorced women are four, and this verse includes the explanation of the ruling for three of these categories. For when the sense of the verse becomes: "There is no dower except upon touching or upon specification," it is known from it that the one who is neither touched nor assigned a dower is not owed a dower; and it is known that the one who is touched but not assigned a dower, and the one who is assigned a dower but not touched, are each owed the dower. So this verse includes the explanation of the ruling for these three categories.

As for the fourth category, the one who is touched and assigned a dower, the explanation of its ruling is mentioned in the preceding verse. On this basis, these verses include the explanation of the ruling for all four categories completely, and this is among the subtleties of the wording. Praise be to God for that.

* * *

The third issue: Abu Bakr al-Asamm and al-Zajjaj said: this verse indicates that the contract of marriage without a dower is permissible. Al-Qadi said: it does not indicate permissibility, but it indicates validity. As for the explanation of its indication of validity: if it were not valid, divorce would not be lawful, and the provision would not be binding. As for its not indicating permissibility: because validity does not necessarily imply permissibility, as evidenced by the fact that divorce during menstruation is forbidden, yet it takes effect and is valid.

* * *

The fourth issue: They agreed that the intended meaning of touching (masis) in this verse is entry (dukhul). Abu Muslim said: God Most High only used the expression ﴿tamassuhunna﴾ as a euphemism for intercourse, to discipline the servants in choosing the best words in what they address one another with. And God knows best.

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿or specify for them an obligation﴾, the meaning is: he estimates for her a quantity of dower which he makes obligatory upon himself; for specification (al-fard) in the language is estimation (al-taqdir). Many of the exegetes mentioned that "aw" here has the meaning of "wa" (and), and the intended sense is: "as long as you have not touched them and have not specified for them an obligation," as in His saying: ﴿or they increase﴾ [as-Saffat: 147]. But if you reflect on what we have summarized, you will know that this interpretation is forced, indeed certainly erroneous. And God knows best.

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿But provide for them﴾, know that when He, Most High, explained that there is no dower in the absence of touching and specification, He explained that a provision (mut'ah) is obligatory for her. The explanation of the word mut'ah has already passed in His saying: ﴿So whoever enjoys the 'Umrah until the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

* * *

Within the verse there are issues:

Mafatih al-Ghayb (al-Razi) on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 236 (part 2 of 2):

The first issue: divorced women are of two kinds: a woman divorced before consummation (al-dukhul) and a woman divorced after consummation. As for the woman divorced before consummation, one looks: if no dowry (mahr) has been fixed for her, then she is entitled to a provision (mut'ah) by this verse which we are discussing; and if a dowry has been fixed for her, then there is no mut'ah, because God Exalted made half the dowry obligatory for her and did not mention mut'ah. Had mut'ah been obligatory, He would have mentioned it.

Ibn 'Umar said: every divorced woman has a mut'ah, except the one for whom a dowry has been fixed and who has not been consummated with; for her, half the dowry suffices.

As for the woman divorced after consummation, whether a dowry was fixed for her or not, is she entitled to mut'ah? On this there are two opinions. He said in al-Qadim (the Old view), and Abu Hanifah agreed: she has no mut'ah, because she is entitled to the dowry, like the woman divorced after a fixing of the dowry but before consummation. And he said in al-Jadid (the New view): rather, she has mut'ah. This is the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, and Ibn 'Umar. The evidence for it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for divorced women is a provision according to what is reasonable﴾ [al-Baqarah: 241], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So come, I will provide for you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 28], and that was said concerning women with whom the Prophet ﷺ had consummated [the marriage]. And she is not like the woman divorced after fixing [the dowry] but before touching, because she became entitled to the dowry not in exchange for the permission of an exchange [of intimacy], so she is not entitled to mut'ah. Whereas the woman divorced after consummation became entitled to the dowry in exchange for the permission of intimacy, so mut'ah is obligatory for her on account of the distress of separation.

* * *

The second issue: the view of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah is that mut'ah is obligatory. This is also the view of Shurayh, al-Sha'bi and al-Zuhri. It is narrated from the Seven Jurists of Madinah that they did not regard it as obligatory, and this is the view of Malik. Our evidence is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And provide for them﴾, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. And He said: ﴿And for divorced women is a provision﴾ [al-Baqarah: 241], so He made it a possession for them, or in the sense of a possession. The argument of Malik is that He, Exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿a duty upon the doers of good﴾. So He made this a matter of goodness, and it is only said of an act that it is goodness when it is not obligatory; if one is obligated to pay a debt and pays it, one is not said to have done good. Also, He, Exalted is He, said:
Page 119
﴿There is no blame upon the doers of good﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91], and this indicates non-obligation. The answer to this is that the verse you have cited supports our view, because He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿a duty upon the doers of good﴾, mentioning it with the word "upon" (ʿala), which indicates obligation. And because when it is said, "This is a duty upon so-and-so," it is not understood from it as recommendation but as obligation.

The third issue: the root of mut'ah and mata' is what is benefited from in a way that does not remain, but ends soon. For this reason it is said: "The world is mata' (a passing enjoyment)," and enjoyment is called tamatto' (taking pleasure) because it ends quickly and has little duration.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿According to the wealthy his capacity, and according to the straitened his capacity﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: (al-muwsi'): the rich one who is in ease through his wealth. It is said: awsa'a al-rajul, when a man's wealth multiplies and his condition becomes broad; and it is said: awsa'ahu kadha, meaning he widened it for him. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, We are expanding it﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47]. His saying "qadaruhu" means the measure of his ability and capacity, so the noun is elided. Al-muqtir is one who is in constraint because of his poverty, that is, the needy poor man; and aqtara means: when he became poor.

The second issue: Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (qadruhu) with a sukun on the dal, and the rest read ﴿qadarahu﴾ with a fatha on the dal. Both are dialectal forms for all the meanings of qadar. It is said: qaddara al-qawm amrahum yuqaddiruhu qadran (the people measured their affair); and hadha qadru hadha (this is the measure of that); and ihmil 'ala ra'sika qadra ma tuti (carry on your head the amount you can bear). And qaddara Allah al-rizq yuqaddiruhu wa yaqduruhu qadran (God decreed the provision). And qaddartu al-shay' bi al-shay' uqaddiruhu qadran (I measured one thing against another), and qadirtu 'ala al-amr aqdiru 'alayhi qudratan (I was able to do the matter). All of this permits both vocalisation with a fatha and with a sukun. It is said: they dispute about the qadr and the qadar; and I served him with the qadr of such-and-such and with the qadar of such-and-such. God Exalted said: ﴿So the valleys flowed with their measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17], and He said: ﴿And they did not measure God with the true measure of Him﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. Had it been vocalised with a fatha, it would have been permissible. Likewise: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything with measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49]; had it been lightened (with sukun), it would also be permissible.

* * *

The third issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿According to the wealthy his capacity, and according to the straitened his capacity﴾ indicates that the determination of mut'ah is entrusted to ijtihad, and because it is like the maintenance (nafaqah) which God Exalted obligated for wives, and He explained that the wealthy differs from the straitened. Al-Shafi'i said: the recommended amount for the wealthy is a servant; for the middling, thirty dirhams; and for the straitened, a headscarf (miqna'ah). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that he said: the most of mut'ah is a servant, and the least is a headscarf; and whatever amount one pays is permissible, whether at the higher or the lower end. Abu Hanifah said: mut'ah is not to exceed half the mahr al-mithl (the customary dowry). He said: because the condition of a woman for whom a dowry has been named is better than that of one for whom none was named. Then, since no more than half the named dowry becomes due to her if he divorces her before consummation, it is all the more so that no more than half the mahr al-mithl should become due. And God knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a provision according to what is reasonable﴾, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: the meaning of the verse is that it must be according to the husband's situation in wealth and poverty. Then they differed: some take into account the situation of both of them, and this is the view of the qadi; and some take into account only the situation of the husband. Abu Bakr al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, said regarding mut'ah: the man's condition is considered, and regarding the mahr al-mithl, her condition is considered; and likewise regarding maintenance. Abu Bakr argued with His saying: ﴿According to the wealthy his capacity﴾. The qadi argued with His saying: ﴿according to what is reasonable﴾, for that indicates both of their conditions, since it is not reasonable to equate the noble woman with the lowly one.

* * *

The second issue: ﴿a provision﴾ is an emphasis on "provide for them"; meaning: provide for them with a reasonable provision. And ﴿a duty﴾ is an attribute of "a provision," that is:
Page 120
a provision obligatory upon them; or it is a duty that this be a duty upon the doers of good. It was said: it is accusative as a state (hal) of "qadaruhu," because it is definite, and its governing element is the adverbial phrase; and it was said: it is accusative as an absolute (qat').

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿upon the doers of good﴾, regarding the reason for singling them out for mention there are several views:

The first: the doer of good is the one who benefits from this explanation, like His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45]. The second: Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that whoever wishes to be among the doers of good, this is his way and his path, and the doer of good is the believer, so the meaning is that acting upon what I have mentioned is the way of the believers. The third: ﴿a duty upon the doers of good﴾ means toward themselves, in hastening to obey God Exalted.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 237 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already appointed for them a bridal gift, then half of what you have appointed (is due), unless they forgo, or he in whose hand is the marriage tie forgoes. And that you forgo is nearer to piety. And do not forget graciousness between you. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the ruling concerning a divorced woman who has not been touched, for whom no dower has been appointed, He spoke next about a divorced woman who has not been touched, for whom a dower has been appointed. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: The position of al-Shafi'i (the founder of the Shafi'i school) is that seclusion (khalwah) does not establish the full dower. Abu Hanifa said: valid seclusion establishes the dower. By valid seclusion (al-khalwah al-sahihah) he means that he is alone with her while there is no sensory impediment or legal impediment. A sensory impediment is such as blockage (al-rataq), a bone-like obstruction (al-qarn), or illness; or there is a third person with them even if he is asleep. A legal impediment is such as menstruation, postnatal bleeding, obligatory fasting, obligatory prayer, and the state of ihram whether it is obligatory or voluntary.

The argument of al-Shafi'i is that divorce before touching (al-masis) requires the falling away of half the dower, and here divorce occurred before touching, so it is necessary to say that half the dower falls away.

Explanation of the first premise: His saying, ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already appointed for them a bridal gift, then half of what you have appointed﴾. His saying ﴿then half of what you have appointed﴾ is not a complete sentence; rather, another element must be supplied to complete the meaning. Either one supplies: "then half of what you have appointed falls away," or one supplies: "then half of what you have appointed is established." The first is the intended meaning, and the second is weaker, for several reasons:

One: What is conditioned by the particle "in" (if) is, apparently, absent when the condition is not met. If we take the phrase to mean obligation, we abandon the implication of the conditional, since the half is not negated before it. But if we take it to mean falling away, we act according to the implication of the conditional, since it is negated before it.

Two: His saying, ﴿and you have already appointed for them a bridal gift﴾, requires the obligation of the whole dower upon him, since when he has committed himself, the whole is binding upon him by His saying: ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾. Thus there was no need to explain the establishment of the half, because what requires the obligation of the whole also requires the obligation of the half. What needs explaining is the falling away of the half, because when the cause for the obligation of the whole is present, the apparent meaning is the obligation of the whole; so the falling away of part in this context is what needs explanation. Therefore it is better to read the verse as explaining the falling away rather than explaining the obligation.

Three: The verse establishing the obligation to give the whole dower has already come before, as in His saying: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. Therefore reading the verse as the falling away of half is better than reading it as the obligation of half.

Four: The matter mentioned in the verse is divorce before touching, and that divorce occurs before touching suits the falling away of half the dower; it does not suit the obligation of anything. Since what is mentioned in the verse suits falling away and not obligation, it is better to supply falling away. We have examined these points at length because some say that the meaning of the verse is: "then half of what you have appointed is obligatory," and specifying the half for obligation does not indicate the falling away of the other half, except by way of the argument from the mention (dalil al-khitab), which according to Abu Hanifa is not a valid proof. So our purpose in this thorough examination is to repel this objection.

Explanation of the second premise, that here divorce occurred before touching: the meaning of touching (al-masis) is either the literal touching by hand, or it is used as a metaphor for intercourse, and in either case divorce occurred before it. The argument of Abu Hanifa is His saying: ﴿And if you desire to exchange a wife in place of a wife, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, then take not from it anything. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin? And how could you take it when you have gone in unto one another?﴾ [al-Nisa': 20–21]. The way of relying on it is in two ways:

The first: He forbade taking the dower and did not distinguish between divorce and non-divorce, unless we agree that He specified divorce before seclusion; and whoever claims specification here must provide the proof.

The second: Allah forbade taking the dower and gave as the reason the cause of "going in" (al-ifda'), which is seclusion. The word ifda' is derived from al-fada', which is an empty place. So we know that seclusion establishes the dower.

Our answer to this is that the verse they relied upon is general (amm), and the verse we relied upon is specific (khass), and the specific takes precedence over the general. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿and you have already appointed for them a bridal gift﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of ﴿you divorce them﴾, and the sense is: "you divorce them while you have appointed for them a bridal gift."

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿unless they forgo﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: The nun was not dropped from ﴿yaʻfuna﴾ even though the particle ﴿an﴾ (which governs verbs in the subjunctive) entered upon it, because ﴿yaʻfuna﴾ is a verb of feminine plurals, so the nominative, accusative and jussive forms are the same in it. The nun in ﴿yaʻfuna﴾, when the verb is attributed to women, is the pronoun of feminine plural, and when the verb is attributed to men, the nun is the sign of the nominative. Therefore the nun, which is the pronoun of feminine plural, was not dropped, just as the waw, which is the pronoun of masculine plural, was not dropped. The element that is dropped in ﴿yaʻfuna﴾ when it refers to men is the waw that is the lam of the verb in ﴿yaʻfuna﴾, not the waw that is the plural pronoun. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: The meaning: "unless the divorced women forgo their husbands, so that they do not demand from them half the dower." The woman says: "He has not seen me, nor has he served me, nor has he enjoyed me. So how can I take anything from him?"

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or he in whose hand is the marriage tie forgoes﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: In the verse there are two opinions. The first is that it is the husband. This is the view of ʻAli ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and many of the Companions and Successors, and it is the view of Abu Hanifa.

Page 122

The second opinion is that it is the guardian (wali). This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid and ʻAlqamah, and it is the view of the companions of al-Shafi'i.

The arguments of the first opinion are several:

The first: It is not permissible for the guardian to forgo the dower of the woman under his guardianship, whether she is a minor or an adult, so the verse cannot be read as referring to the guardian.

The second: What is in the hand of the guardian is the contract of marriage. When it is concluded, the knot (ʻuqdah) comes into being, because the pattern fu'lah indicates the object, as in al-ukhlah (the morsel eaten) and al-luqmah (the mouthful). As for the verbal noun, al-ʻaqd (the contracting) is like al-akl (the eating) and al-laqm (the swallowing). Then it is known that the knot that comes into being after the contract is in the hand of the husband, not in the hand of the guardian.

The third: His saying, ﴿he in whose hand is the marriage knot﴾ means: he in whose hand is a knot of marriage that is established for him, not for another, just as His saying: ﴿And he restrained the self from desire. Surely the Garden will be the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 40–41] means: he restrained the self from the desire that belongs to him, not to another; the Garden was established for him, so it is his refuge.

The fourth: What is reported from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, that he married a woman and divorced her before he had consummated the marriage, and he completed the dower and said: "I am more entitled to forgo." This shows that the Companions understood from the verse the forgoing that proceeds from the husband.

The arguments of those who say the intended one is the guardian are several:

The first: What proceeds from the husband is that he gives her the whole dower, and that is a gift, and a gift is not called a forgoing. The earlier scholars answered this in several ways:

One: It was usual among them that a man would send the dower to the woman at the time of marriage; so when he divorced her, he was entitled to demand from her half of what he had sent to her. If he left off the demand, he had forgone it from her.

Two: He called it a forgoing by way of parallelism (al-mushakalah).

Three: The forgoing may mean facilitation. It is said: "So-and-so found the wealth a forgoing and a clear gain." We have already explained the sense of this view in the exegesis of His saying: ﴿And whoever is forgiven anything by his brother﴾. On this basis, the man's forgoing is that he sends her the whole dower with ease.

Those who say the intended one is the guardian answered the first question: the forgoing from the husband in that manner occurs only under some of the assumed conditions, whereas God commended forgoing without restriction, and restricting the unrestricted to the restricted is contrary to the original principle. They answered the second question: the forgoing that proceeds from the woman is the release (al-ibra'), and this is forgoing in the true sense; but what proceeds from the man is pure gift, so how can it be called forgoing?

They answered the third question: if forgoing meant facilitation, then everyone who facilitates something for a person would be said to have forgone it from him, and it is known that this is not so.

The second argument of those who say the intended one is the guardian: the mention of the husband has already come in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾. So if the intended meaning of ﴿or he in whose hand is the marriage knot forgoes﴾ were the husband, He would have said "or you forgo" in the form of address. Since He did not do that, but expressed it with the third-person form, we know that what is meant is other than the husband.

The earlier scholars answered that the reason for shifting from address to the third person is to draw attention to the meaning that moves the husband to forgo: the sense is "unless they forgo, or the husband forgoes, the one who has restrained her by holding the knot of her marriage from other husbands, and then there was no cause on her part for the separation; rather, the husband himself separated from her. Therefore it is fitting that he should not diminish her dower from her and should complete her bridal gift for her."

The third argument of those who say it is the guardian: the husband does not at all have in his hand the knot of marriage. Before marriage the husband was a stranger to the woman and had no power to dispose of her in any way, so he has no power to conclude the marriage with her at all. After marriage the marriage has come into being, and he has no power to bring into existence what already exists; rather, he has power only to dissolve the marriage. And Allah, exalted is He, established forgoing for the one who has in his hand and in his power the knot of marriage. Since it is established that the husband has no hand or power to conclude the marriage, it is established that the husband is not the one meant. The guardian, however, has power to give her in marriage, so the one meant in the verse is the guardian, not the husband.

Then those who held this view answered the arguments of those who say the husband is meant.

As for the first argument, a verb may be attributed to the doer sometimes when he performs it directly, and other times when he is the cause. It is said: "The governor built a house," and "He minted a dinar." Apparently women refer their important affairs and the knowledge of their interests to the opinions of guardians, and apparently in all matters related to marriage the woman does not engage herself but entrusts it entirely to the guardian's judgment. On this assumption, the occurrence of forgoing is by the guardian's choice and effort, and for this reason the forgoing is attributed to the guardians.

As for the second argument, which is their saying: what is in the hand of the guardian is the contract of marriage, not the knot of marriage, we reply: the knot may be used to mean the contract, as He said: ﴿And do not determine the knot of marriage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235]. Granting that the knot is the thing contracted, that contracted thing came into being and was formed through the contract, and the contract of marriage was initially in the hand of the guardian; so the knot of marriage was also in the hand of the guardian, by way of being one of its results and effects.

As for the third argument, which is their saying: the verse means the one in whose hand is the knot of marriage for himself, the reply is that this restriction is not required by the wording. When it is said: "So-and-so has in his hand the command and the prohibition, the raising and the lowering," it is not meant that he has the command of himself and the prohibition of himself; rather, it is meant that he has in his hand the command and prohibition of others. So it is likewise here.

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 237 (part 2 of 2):

The second issue: Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) may cite this verse to show that marriage is not valid except with a guardian (wali). This is because the majority of exegetes agreed that what is meant by His words, ﴿or the one in whose hand is the marriage tie﴾, is either the husband or the guardian. Its interpretation as the husband has been ruled out, because we have explained that the husband has absolutely no power over the marriage tie. Therefore it must be interpreted as the guardian.

Given this, we say: His words, ﴿in whose hand is the marriage tie﴾, convey restriction (hasr), since when it is said, "the command and the prohibition are in his hand," the meaning is that they are in his hand and not in the hand of another. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To you is your religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6], meaning, not to others. Likewise here: the marriage tie is in the hand of the guardian and not in the hand of another. And if that is so, then the marriage tie must be in the hand of the woman, and that is what was sought. And Allah knows best.

* * *

His exalted words, ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to righteousness﴾. On this there are several issues.

The first issue: This is an address to men and women alike, but the masculine form prevails when they are combined with females. The reason for this prevalence is that the masculine is the root and the feminine is a branch, both in wording and in meaning. As for wording, you say "qa'im" (standing, masc.), then if you want the feminine you say "qa'ima." So the word indicating the masculine is the root, and the word indicating the feminine is derived from it. As for meaning, perfection belongs to males and deficiency to females. For this reason, whenever the masculine and feminine are combined, the masculine side is given precedence.

The second issue: The position of "an" (that) is a nominative subject (raf' bi'l-ibtida'), and the sense is: "and pardoning is nearer to righteousness." The lam here carries the meaning of "ila" (to).

The third issue: The meaning of the verse is that one party's pardoning of another is nearer to attaining the sense of righteousness. The matter is so for two reasons:

The first: whoever is generous in forgoing his right is a doer of good (muhsin), and whoever is a doer of good has earned reward, and whoever has earned reward thereby cancels out and removes whatever punishment is lesser than it.

The second: this conduct calls him to abandon injustice, which is righteousness in reality, because whoever is generous with his right, while he has the means to claim it, seeking nearness to his Lord, is further from wronging another by taking what is not rightfully his. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾. The intent of this is not a prohibition against forgetting, since that is not within one's capacity; rather the intent is abandoning. So He, exalted is He, said: Do not abandon graciousness and bounty among yourselves. This is because when a man marries a woman, her heart becomes attached to him; so if he divorces her before consummation, that becomes a cause of her being hurt by him. Also, if a man is obliged to give her a dowry without having benefited from her at all, that becomes a cause of his being hurt by her. So He, exalted is He, urged each of them to an act that removes that hurt from the heart of the other: He urged the husband to console her heart by handing over the dowry to her in full, and He urged the woman to forgo the dowry entirely. Then He, exalted is He, concluded the verse with what functions as a warning, according to the familiar custom, saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾.

**The Sixteenth Ruling: Guarding the Prayers and the Middle Prayer**

﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before God in devotion.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before God in devotion.﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, had explained to the responsible people what He explained of the landmarks of His religion, and made clear to them some of the laws of His legislation, He then commanded them to guard the prayers strictly. This is for several reasons.

The first: the prayer, by virtue of its recitation, standing, bowing, prostration, submissiveness and humility, produces a heart broken from awe of God, removes the rebelliousness of the natural disposition, brings about submission to God's commands, and restraint from His prohibitions, as He said: ﴿Indeed, the prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45].

The second: the prayer reminds the servant of the majesty of Lordship, the humility of servanthood, and the matter of reward and punishment. At that point, submission to obedience becomes easy for him. For this reason He said: ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45].

The third: all that preceded of the explanation of marriage, divorce and the waiting period is occupation with the interests of this world, so He followed that with mention of the prayer, which is the interest of the Hereafter.

* * *

**Issues concerning the verse**

**First issue:** The Muslims have agreed that the obligatory prayers are five. This verse which we are explaining indicates this, because His saying ﴿the prayers﴾ indicates three, since the least of the plural is three. Then His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the middle prayer﴾ indicates something more than three; otherwise repetition would result, and the default is its absence. Then that additional number cannot be four, for otherwise there would be no middle for them. So another number must be added to those three by which a middle is produced for the whole, and the least of that is five. Thus this verse indicates the obligation of the five prayers by this route. Know that this argument is complete only if we establish that what is meant by "middle" is what is middle in number, not what is middle because of its excellence. We will demonstrate that with evidence, God willing. However, although this verse indicates the obligation of the five prayers, it does not indicate their times. The verses which indicate the detailed times are four:

*The first verse:* His saying: ﴿So glorify God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17]. This verse is the clearest of the verses on the prescribed times. His saying "so glorify God" means: pray to God. Its meaning is: pray to God when you enter the evening, meaning by it the prayer of Maghrib and 'Isha', (and when you enter the morning) meaning the dawn prayer, (and in the late afternoon) meaning the 'Asr prayer, (and when you enter midday) the Zuhr prayer.

[Page 125]

*The second verse:* His saying: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. By "decline" he meant its passing the zenith, so the Zuhr, 'Asr, Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers are included in it. Then He said: "Establish the prayer," meaning the dawn prayer.

*The third verse:* His saying: ﴿And glorify with the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130]. Some people said: this verse indicates the five prayers, because the time is either before the rising of the sun or before its setting, so the night and the day are included in these two expressions.

*The fourth verse:* His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in parts of the night﴾ [Hud: 114]. What is meant by "the two ends of the day" is the dawn and the 'Asr prayers, and His saying ﴿and in parts of the night﴾ refers to Maghrib and 'Isha'. Some of them held to this for the obligation of the witr prayer, because the word "zulafan" (parts) is plural, and the least of the plural is three.

* * *

**Second issue:** Know that the command to guard the prayer is a command to guard all its conditions, namely: the purity of the body, the garment and the place; guarding the covering of the private parts; facing the qiblah; guarding all the pillars of the prayer; and guarding against all things that invalidate the prayer, whether they are actions of the heart, of the tongue, or of the limbs. The most important matter in the prayer is observing the intention, for it is the primary objective of the prayer. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And establish the prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]. Whoever performs the prayer in this manner is one who guards the prayer; otherwise he is not.

If it is said: guarding is only between two parties, as in litigation or fighting. How then is the meaning here?

The answer is in two respects:

First: this guarding is between the servant and the Lord. It is as if it were said to him: Guard the prayer so that the God who commanded you to pray will guard you. This is like His saying: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152]. And in a hadith: "Guard God, He will guard you."

Second: the guarding is between the worshipper and the prayer. It is as if it were said: Guard the prayer so that the prayer guards you. Know that the prayer's guarding of the worshipper takes three forms:

The first: the prayer guards him from sins. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45]. Whoever guards the prayer, the prayer guards him from indecency.

The second: the prayer guards him from trials and tribulations. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153]. And God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God said: Indeed I am with you, if you establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12]. Its meaning: I am with you through support and protection, if you have established the prayer and given the zakah.

The third: the prayer guards its owner and intercedes for those who pray. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And establish the prayer and give zakah, and whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110]. Also, because the prayer contains recitation, and the Qur'an intercedes for its reciter, and it is the intercessor that is granted intercession. In a report: "The Surah al-Baqarah and Surah Al 'Imran will come as though they were two clouds, and they will testify and intercede." And also in a report: "Surah al-Mulk averts from the one who recites it at night the punishment of the grave, and argues on his behalf on the Day of Gathering, and stands at the Sirat by his feet, and says to the Fire: there is no path for you against him." And God knows best.

* * *

**Third issue:** Scholars differed concerning the middle prayer, in seven positions.

The first view: God commanded us to guard it, but did not specify for us which prayer it is. We say that He did not specify, because if He had specified it, it would either be said that He specified it by a definitive means or by a speculative means. The first is invalid, for the clarification would be either by this verse, or by another definitive route, or by a mutawatir report (one transmitted by so many chains that its agreement on falsehood is impossible). It is not possible that the clarification is present in this verse, because the number of prayers is five, and there is no mention in the verse of the first or the last of them. And if this is so, it is possible for each of those prayers to be called the middle one. Or it is said: the clarification came in another verse or a mutawatir report, and that is absent. As for clarifying it by a speculative route, namely a solitary report (khabar al-wahid) or qiyas (analogical reasoning), this is impermissible, because a route that yields only probability is valid in practical matters, while this matter is not of that kind. So it is established that God, exalted is He, did not clarify which prayer is the middle one. Then they said: the wisdom in this is that when He singled it out for special emphasis, though He did not specify it, a person may think that every prayer he performs could be the middle one, and this becomes a motive to perform all of them in the fullest and most complete manner. For this reason God concealed the Night of Destiny in Ramadan, concealed the hour of answered supplication on Friday, concealed His greatest Name among all the names, and concealed the time of death among the times, so that the responsible person would fear death at all times, and therefore would be turning to repentance at all times. This view was chosen by a group of scholars.

Muhammad ibn Sirin said: A man asked Zayd ibn Thabit about the middle prayer, and he said: Guard all the prayers and you will hit it. And from al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham: someone asked him about it, and he said: O cousin, the middle is one of them, so guard all of them and you will be guarding the middle. Then al-Rabi' said: If you knew it precisely, you would be guarding it and neglecting the rest. The questioner said: No. Al-Rabi' said: If you guard them all, you have guarded the middle.

The second view: it is the whole of the five prayers. This is because these five are the middle of the acts of obedience. Its explanation: faith has seventy-some degrees, the highest of which is the testimony that there is no god but God, and the lowest of which is removing harm from the road. The obligatory prayers are below faith and above removing harm, so they are an intermediary between the two extremes.

The third view: it is the dawn prayer. This view is from the Companions: the view of 'Ali, peace be upon him, 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Abu Umamah al-Bahili. From the Successors: the view of Tawus, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah and Mujahid, and it is the school of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him. What indicates the soundness of this view are several aspects:

The first: this prayer is performed in the ghalas (the darkness before dawn light), so its beginning falls in darkness, and it resembles the night prayer, and its end falls in light, so it resembles the day prayer.

The second: this prayer is performed after the dawn breaks and before the sun rises, and in this span of time the darkness is not complete, nor is the light complete, so it is as though it is neither night nor day, and it is intermediate between them.

The third: in full daytime there are two prayers, Zuhr and 'Asr, and in the night there are two prayers, Maghrib and 'Isha', and the dawn prayer is like the intermediary between the night prayers and the day prayers.

If it is said: these meanings are also present in the Maghrib prayer, we say: we prefer the dawn prayer over Maghrib because of the abundance of the virtues of the dawn prayer, as will be explained later, God willing.

The fourth: Zuhr and 'Asr are combined at 'Arafah by consensus, and during travel according to al-Shafi'i; likewise Maghrib and 'Isha'. As for the dawn prayer, it stands alone in its own time. So the time of Zuhr and 'Asr is one time, and the time of Maghrib and 'Isha' is one time, and the time of Fajr is intermediate between them. Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: The realization of this argument returns to the fact that people say: So-and-so is "wasat" (middle) when he does not lean toward either of the two disputants, so he stands separate from both. And God knows best.

The fifth: the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the recitation of the dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. It has been established by tawatur that what is meant by it is the dawn prayer, and He made it "witnessed" because it is performed in the presence of the angels of the night and the angels of the day.

Having known this, the way of deriving evidence from this verse is in two respects:

The first: God, exalted is He, singled out the dawn prayer with mention, and this indicates its additional excellence. Then He, exalted is He, singled out the middle prayer for additional emphasis, so it is strongly supposed that since it has been established by that verse that the dawn prayer is more excellent, it must be the one meant by the emphasis mentioned in this verse.

The second: the angels alternate by night and day, so the angels of the night and the angels of the day do not gather at one time except at the dawn prayer. Thus it is established that the dawn prayer has taken hold of both ends of the night and the day in this respect, so it is like the intermediate thing.

The sixth: He, exalted is He, said after mentioning the middle prayer: ﴿and stand before God in devotion﴾. He joined this prayer with the mention of qunut (standing in devout prolonged supplication). There is no prayer in the Shari'ah for which qunut has been established by sound reports except the dawn prayer. So this indicates that what is meant by the middle prayer is the dawn prayer.

**Seventh:** There is no doubt that Allah, exalted is He, singled it out for mention in order to emphasise it. And there is no doubt that the Dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-ṣubḥ) is the prayer most in need of emphasis, since no prayer is more burdensome than it. It is obligatory upon people at the most pleasant time of sleep, so much so that the Arabs used to call the sleep of dawn *al-ʿusaylah* (the little sweet one) because of its delight. And there is no doubt that abandoning pleasant, sweet sleep at that time, turning to the use of cold water, going out to the mosque and preparing for prayer is difficult and arduous for the soul. Therefore it must be the one intended by "the middle prayer", since it is the prayer most in need of emphasis.

**Eighth:** The Dawn prayer is the most excellent of the prayers. If that is so, then the middle prayer must be the Dawn prayer. We say that it is the most excellent of the prayers for several reasons:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the patient, the truthful … and those who seek forgiveness before dawn﴾ [Al ʿImrān: 17]. He concluded their noble acts of obedience and their complete worship by mentioning that they seek forgiveness at the hours before dawn. Then the greatest kind of seeking forgiveness must be the performance of the obligation, because of the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, relating from his Lord, exalted is He: "The ones who draw near to Me will never draw nearer to Me than by performing what I have made obligatory upon them." And this implies that the most excellent act of worship after faith is the Dawn prayer.

The second: What has been related concerning it, that the first takbīr (opening takbīr) of it, performed with the congregation, is better than this world and all that is in it.

The third: It has been established by sound reports that the Dawn prayer is singled out for an adhān (call to prayer) twice: once before the break of dawn, and once after it. This is because the purpose of the first is to wake people so that they rise and hasten to perform ablution.

The fourth: Allah, exalted is He, named it by several names. He said concerning the Children of Israel: ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 78], and He said in al-Nūr: ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾ [al-Nūr: 58], and He said in al-Rūm: ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rūm: 17]. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: the intended meaning of His saying: ﴿and the receding of the stars﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 49] is the Dawn prayer.

The fifth: He, exalted is He, swore by it, saying: ﴿By the dawn﴾ ﴿and ten nights﴾ [al-Fajr: 1–2]. This is not contradicted by His saying: ﴿By the time (al-ʿaṣr)﴾ ﴿indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 1–2], for even if we grant that what is meant by it is an oath by the ʿAṣr prayer, there is still emphasis upon the Dawn prayer in His saying: ﴿and establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hūd: 114]. We have already explained that this emphasis is not found in the ʿAṣr.

The sixth: The tathwīb (the phrase added in the dawn adhān) is prescribed in the adhān for Dawn prayer. It consists of saying, after completing the two ḥayʿalas: "The prayer is better than sleep," twice. Such emphasis is not present in the other prayers.

The seventh: When a person rises from his sleep, it is as if he had been non-existent and then came into existence, or had been dead and then became alive. Indeed, it is as if all creation had been dead throughout the night, and then they became living. When they rise from their sleep and witness this great matter, the perfection of Allah's power and mercy, in that He removed from them the darkness of the night, the darkness of sleep and heedlessness, and the darkness of incapacity and bewilderment, and replaced all of that with goodness; and He filled the world with light, and the bodies with the strength of life, intellect, understanding and knowledge — then there is no doubt that this time is the most fitting of times for the servant to occupy himself with performing servitude, and manifesting humility, lowliness and neediness. Thus it has been established by the totality of these explanations that the Dawn prayer is the most excellent of the prayers, and so it is more fitting to interpret the "middle" as referring to it.

The ninth: What has been related from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, peace be upon him, that he was asked about the middle prayer and said: "We used to consider it to be the Dawn prayer." And from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he prayed the Dawn prayer and then said: "This is the middle prayer."

The tenth: The Sunnah prayers of Dawn are more emphasised than the other Sunnah prayers. Therefore its obligatory form must be stronger than the other obligatory prayers, so directing the emphasis towards it is more fitting. This is the sum of what is used as evidence that the middle prayer is the Dawn prayer.

**The fourth opinion:** the view of those who said that it is the Ẓuhr (noon) prayer. This view is related from ʿUmar, Zayd, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and Usāmah ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them, and it is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions. They argued for it with several points:

The first: The Ẓuhr was difficult for them because it falls at the time of midday rest and intense heat, so directing the emphasis toward it is more fitting. It is related from Zayd ibn Thābit that "the Prophet ﷺ used to pray at the hottest part of the day (al-hājirah), and it was the heaviest of prayers upon his companions, and sometimes behind him there were only one or two rows. So the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: 'I had intended to burn the houses of people who do not attend the prayer.' Then this verse was revealed."

The second: The Ẓuhr prayer falls in the middle of the day, and among the obligatory prayers there is no other prayer that falls in the middle of the night or the day.

The third: It is between two daytime prayers: the Dawn and the ʿAṣr.

The fourth: It is a prayer between the two coolnesses: the coolness of the morning and the coolness of the evening.

The fifth: Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: "I prayed the Ẓuhr with the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and when they had finished I asked them about the middle prayer, and they said: 'It is the one you have just prayed.'"

The sixth: It was related from ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she used to recite: "Maintain the prayers, and the middle prayer, and the ʿAṣr prayer." The basis of the argument is that she conjoined the ʿAṣr prayer to the middle prayer, and the thing conjoined to (the middle prayer) comes before the thing conjoined (the ʿAṣr), and the prayer that comes before the ʿAṣr is the Ẓuhr.

The seventh: It was related that a group of people were with Zayd ibn Thābit, and they sent to Usāmah ibn Zayd and asked him about the middle prayer. He said: "It is the Ẓuhr prayer, which used to be established at the hottest part of the day."

The eighth: It has been related in sound reports "that the first occasion on which Jibrīl led the Prophet ﷺ in prayer was in the Ẓuhr prayer." This indicates that it is the most noble of the prayers, so directing the emphasis toward it is more fitting.

The ninth: The Friday prayer (ṣalāt al-jumuʿah) is the most noble of the prayers, and it is the Ẓuhr prayer, so directing the emphasis toward it is more fitting.

**The fifth opinion:** the view of those who said that it is the ʿAṣr prayer. This is related from the Companions: from ʿAlī, peace be upon him, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah; and from the jurists: al-Nakhaʿī, Qatādah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk; and it is related from Abū Ḥanīfah. They argued for it with several points:

The first: What has been related from ʿAlī, peace be upon him, that the Prophet ﷺ said on the day of the Trench: "They have kept us busy from the middle prayer; may Allah fill their houses and their graves with fire." This ḥadīth was related by al-Bukhārī, Muslim and all the (other) imams, and it has a great impact on this question. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim it reads: "They have kept us busy from the middle prayer, the ʿAṣr prayer." Some jurists answered this by saying: "The ʿAṣr is a middle prayer, but it is not the one mentioned in the Qur'an. There are two middle prayers: the Dawn and the ʿAṣr. One of them is established by the Qur'an and the other by the Sunnah, just as there are two sanctuaries: the sanctuary of Makkah by the Qur'an, and the sanctuary of Madinah by the Sunnah." This answer is extremely far-fetched (mutakallif jiddan).

The second: They said: "What has been related concerning the ʿAṣr prayer of emphasis is not related concerning any other. The Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: 'Whoever misses the ʿAṣr prayer, it is as if he has lost his family and his wealth.'" Also, Allah, exalted is He, swore by it, saying: ﴿By the time (al-ʿaṣr)﴾ ﴿indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 1–2]. This indicates that it is the most beloved of the times to Allah, exalted is He.

The third: The ʿAṣr is more deserving of emphasis in that
