The second: knowledge and capability are perfections attained by the very essence of the human being, while wealth and status are matters external to the human's essence.

The third: knowledge and capability cannot be removed from a human, while wealth and status can be removed from a human.

The fourth: knowledge of the affairs of war, and one who is strong and powerful in fighting, the benefit from him in preserving the welfare of the land and in repelling the evil of enemies is more complete than the benefit from a man of noble lineage and wealth who has no knowledge of managing interests and no capacity to repel enemies. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that ascribing kingship to one who is knowledgeable and capable is more fitting than ascribing it to one of noble lineage and wealth.

* * *

Then here are issues:

The first issue: Our scholars, in the matter of the creation of actions, argued with His saying: ﴿and increased him broadly in knowledge and physique﴾. This indicates that the knowledge that is acquired by creatures is only acquired through the creation and origination of Allah, exalted is He. The Mu'tazilah said: this attribution is only because He, exalted is He, is the One who gives reason and establishes the proofs. Our companions answered that the original meaning of attribution is direct causation, not indirect causation.

* * *

The second issue: Some of them said: The intended meaning of expansiveness in physique is tallness of stature; he surpassed people by his head and shoulder, and he was named Ṭālūt because of his height. It was said: the intended meaning of expansiveness in physique is beauty, and he was the most handsome of the Children of Israel. It was also said: the intended meaning is strength, and this view is more sound in my opinion, because what is beneficial in repelling enemies is strength and power, not height and beauty.

The third issue: He, exalted is He, put expansiveness in knowledge before expansiveness in physique, and this from Him, exalted is He, is an alert that the soul's virtues are higher, nobler, and more complete than the bodily virtues.

The third aspect in answering the doubt is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills﴾. Its explanation is that kingship belongs to Allah and the servants belong to Allah, so He, glorified is He, gives His kingship to whom He wills, and no one has any objection to Him in His action, because when the owner disposes of his property, no one has any objection to his action.

The fourth aspect in answering: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is all-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. In it there are three opinions. The first: He, exalted is He, is all-Encompassing in bounty, provision, and mercy; His mercy encompasses everything. The meaning is: You criticized Ṭālūt for being poor, while Allah, exalted is He, is all-Encompassing in bounty and mercy. So when He entrusts kingship to him, if He knows that kingship cannot function without wealth, Allah, exalted is He, will open to him the door of provision and abundance in wealth.

The second opinion: that He is all-Encompassing, in the sense of making expansive (muwassi'), meaning He expands upon whom He wills of His blessings, and its connection to what precedes it is as we have mentioned.

The third: that He is all-Encompassing in the sense of possessing expansiveness (dhu sa'ah), and the pattern fā'il comes with the meaning of "possessing such-and-such," as in His saying: ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 21], meaning a life possessing pleasure, and "a weary worry possessing fatigue." Then by His saying "All-Knowing" He explained that He, exalted is He, with His power to enrich the poor, is knowing of the measures of what he needs in managing the kingship, and knowing of the state of that kingship in the present and the future, so He chooses, by His knowledge of all consequences, what is his welfare in carrying out the affair of kingship.

[Page 150]

The Exalted said: ﴿And their Prophet said to them: "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you, in which is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind, carried by the angels. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers."﴾ ﴿So when Talut set out with the armies, he said: "Indeed, Allah is going to test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who scoops up a handful with his hand." But they drank from it, except for a few of them. Then when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his armies." Those who were certain that they would meet Allah said: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by the permission of Allah! And Allah is with the patient."﴾

Know that the apparent meaning of the preceding verse indicates that those people acknowledged the prophethood of the prophet who was among them, because the words of the Exalted, relating about them, ﴿When they said to a prophet of theirs: "Raise up for us a king"﴾, are nearly explicit that they were acknowledging the prophethood of that prophet and affirming that he had been sent by Allah the Exalted. Then, when that prophet said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has raised up Talut as a king for you﴾, this was a decisive proof that Talut was king. Then, out of the perfection of His mercy toward creation, the Exalted added to that proof another proof, which indicates that the prophet was truthful in that statement, and also indicates that Allah the Exalted had appointed Talut to kingship. And multiplying proofs from Allah the Exalted is permissible; for this reason the miracles of Moses, peace be upon him, and of Muhammad, may blessings and peace be upon him, were many. Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿And their Prophet said to them: "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you"﴾. And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: the coming of that Ark must occur in a manner that is contrary to habit, so that it may be valid as a sign from Allah, indicating the truth of that claim. Then the scholars of reports (Ashab al-Akhbar) said: Allah the Exalted sent down to Adam, peace be upon him, an ark in which were the images of the prophets from his descendants. Adam's descendants inherited it until it reached Jacob. Then it remained in the hands of the Children of Israel. Whenever they disagreed about something, it would speak and judge between them. When they attended battle, they would place it before them, seeking victory over their enemy by means of it. The angels would carry it above the army while they fought the enemy. When they heard a cry from the Ark, they were certain of victory. But when they disobeyed and became corrupt, Allah gave power over them to the Amalekites, who overcame them, took the Ark from them and plundered it. When they asked their prophet for proof of Talut's kingship, that prophet said: "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that you will find the Ark in his house." Then the unbelievers who had plundered that Ark had placed it in a place of urine and excrement. The prophet supplicated against them at that time, so Allah sent affliction upon those unbelievers, such that everyone who urinated or defecated there was afflicted by Allah with hemorrhoids. The unbelievers knew that this was because of their contempt for the Ark, so they brought it out and placed it on two oxen. The two oxen set off walking, and Allah appointed four angels to drive them, until they reached the dwelling of Talut. Then the people of that prophet saw the Ark with Talut, and they knew that this was a proof that he was their king. This is the meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And their Prophet said: "Indeed, the sign of his kingship"﴾. The coming in this sense is a metaphor, because it was brought, while it did not come by itself; so it was attributed to it by extension, as one says: "The dirhams profited" and "The trade lost."

The second report: the Ark was a chest in which Moses, peace be upon him, used to place the Torah. It was made of wood, and they knew it. Then Allah the Exalted lifted it up after Moses, peace be upon him, had died, because of His wrath against the Children of Israel. Then the prophet of that people said: "Indeed, the sign of Talut's kingship is that the Ark will come to you from the sky." The Ark was not carried by the angels or by the oxen; rather, it descended from the sky to the earth, and the angels were guarding it, while the people were looking at it, until it came down at the dwelling of Talut. This is the statement of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. In this view, the coming is literal with respect to the Ark, and the carrying is attributed to the angels in both opinions, because whoever guards something along the way may be described as having carried that thing, even if he did not carry it himself, as one says: "I carried the goods to Zayd" when he guarded them on the road, even if the one who physically carried them was someone else.

Know that the Exalted made the coming of the Ark a miracle. Then there are two possibilities:

One: that the coming of the Ark itself is the miracle, and this is what we have established.

The second: that the Ark is not itself the miracle, but what is in it is the miracle. This would be by their witnessing the Ark empty, then that prophet placing it in a room in the presence of the people and they locking the room. Then the prophet claims that Allah the Exalted has created in it something that indicates our situation. When they open the door of the room and look at the Ark, they find in it a writing indicating that their king is Talut, and that Allah will give them victory over their enemies. This would be a decisive miracle, indicating that it is from Allah the Exalted. The wording of the Qur'an allows for this, because the words ﴿the Ark will come to you in which is tranquility from your Lord﴾ may mean that they would find in the Ark this miracle, which is the cause of the settling of their hearts and the tranquility of their souls. So this is a possibility.

* * *

The second issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: The measure of "al-tabut" (التّابُوتُ) is either فَعْلُوتًا (fa'lut) or فاعُولًا (fa'ul). The second is less likely, because in the speech of the Arabs there is little word in which the first and last radicals are of the same kind, like سَلَسٌ (salas, "smooth") and قَلَقٌ (qalaq, "restless"). So one does not say تابُوتٌ from تَبَتَ (tabata) by analogy with what has been transmitted. When this possibility is invalid, the first is determined, namely that it is فَعْلُوتٌ from التَّوْبِ (al-tawb), meaning "return," because it is a container into which things are placed and deposited, and what comes out of it keeps returning to it, and its owner returns to it for what he needs of his deposits.

The third issue: all read "al-tabut" with the tā' (التّابُوتُ). Ubayy and Zayd ibn Thabit read "al-tabuh" (التّابُوهُ) with the hā', and this is the dialect of the Ansar.

* * *

The fourth issue: some people said that Talut was a prophet, because Allah the Exalted manifested the miracle through him, and whoever is like that is a prophet. It cannot be said that this was one of the karamat (marvels) of the saints, because the difference between a karama and a miracle is that a karama does not occur as a challenge, whereas this occurred as a challenge, so it must not be of the type of karamat.
The answer: it is not far-fetched that this was a miracle for the prophet of that time, and although it was a miracle for him, it was also a decisive sign of the establishment of his kingship.

As for the words of the Exalted ﴿in it is tranquility from your Lord﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: al-sakina (السَّكِينَةُ) is on the pattern فَعِيلَةٌ (fa'ila) from al-sukun (السُّكُونِ), which is the opposite of motion. It is a verbal noun that has taken the place of a noun, like القَضِيَّةُ (al-qadiyya), البَقِيَّةُ (al-baqiyya), and العَزِيمَةُ (al-'azima).

* * *

The second issue: they differed about al-sakina. The summary of the views on it is that we say: by al-sakina, either it is said that it was something present in the Ark, or it was not so.

The second division is the statement of Abu Bakr al-Asamm, who said: the words ﴿the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you, in which is tranquility from your Lord﴾ mean: you will be at rest upon its arrival, you will acknowledge his kingship, and your aversion to him will disappear, because when the Ark came to them from the sky and they witnessed that state, their hearts necessarily became settled toward him and their aversion disappeared completely.

As for the first division: that by al-sakina is meant something placed in the Ark, then on this there are several views:

The first, which is the statement of Abu Muslim: in the Ark were good tidings from the books of Allah the Exalted revealed to Moses, Aaron, and the prophets after them, peace be upon them, that Allah would give victory to Talut and his army and remove the fear of the enemy from them.

The second, which is the statement of Ali, peace be upon him: it had a face like a human face, and it had a light, gentle breeze.

The third, which is the statement of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: it was a figure of emerald or ruby, with a head like the head of a cat and a tail like its tail. When it meowed like the meowing of a cat, the Ark would go toward the enemy while they walked with it, and when it stopped, they stopped, and victory descended.

The fourth view: the statement of Amr ibn Ubayd: the tranquility that was in the Ark is a thing that is not known.

Know that sakina is an expression for steadfastness and security, and it is like His words in the story of the cave: ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. Likewise the words of the Exalted ﴿in it is tranquility from your Lord﴾ mean security and calm.

Those who argue that something came to be in the Ark argue with two points:

The first: that His words ﴿in it is tranquility﴾ indicate that the Ark is a container for the tranquility.

The second: that He conjoined to it His words ﴿and a remnant of what the family of Moses left behind﴾. So just as the Ark was a container for the remnant, it must also be a container for the tranquility.

The answer to the first: the particle فِي (fi, "in") may be used for location, but it may also be used for causation. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "For a believing soul, one hundred camels," and he said: "For five camels, a sheep," meaning: because of it. So His words in this verse ﴿in it is tranquility﴾ mean: because of it, tranquility is attained.

The answer to the second: it is not far-fetched that the intended meaning of "a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind" is the religion and the law, and the meaning is that because of this Ark, the affairs of what remained of their religion and their law are put in order.

As for those who say that the intended meaning of "remnant" is something placed in the Ark, they said: the remnant is the fragments of the tablets, the staff of Moses, his garments, a portion of the Torah, and a qafiz (measure) of the manna that used to descend upon them.

As for His words ﴿the family of Moses and the family of Aaron﴾, there are two views:

The first: some of the exegetes said: it is possible that by "the family of Moses and the family of Aaron" is meant Moses and Aaron themselves. The evidence for this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: "He has been given a flute from the flutes of the family of David," meaning David himself, because no one of the family of David had a beautiful voice like that of David, peace be upon him.

The second view: al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this was attributed to the family of Moses and the family of Aaron because that Ark was passed down through generations after them until the time of Talut, and what was in the Ark were things inherited by the scholars among the followers of Moses and Aaron. So "the family" means the followers, as the Exalted said: ﴿Cause the family of Pharaoh to enter the severest punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 46].

* * *

As for His words ﴿carried by the angels﴾, its discussion has already preceded.

* * *

As for His words ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾, the meaning is that this sign is a dazzling miracle, if you are among those who believe through the indication of a miracle for the truthfulness of the one who claims.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 249 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Saul set out with the troops﴾. Concerning it there are issues.

The first issue: Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it becomes clear by positing an omitted element that the rest of the discourse indicates. The meaning is: when he brought them the sign of the Ark, they submitted to him and agreed to march under his banner. ﴿When he set out with them﴾, i.e., he departed with them beyond the boundary of his city and left it behind. The meaning of *fasl* (separation) is cutting off. One says *qawl faṣl* (a decisive word) when it cuts between truth and falsehood. One says *faṣaltu al-laḥma ʿan al-ʿaẓm faṣlan* (I separated the meat from the bone). *Fāṣala al-rajulu sharīkahu wa-imra'atahu fiṣālan* (a man separated from his partner or his wife). Weaning is called *fiṣāl*, because it cuts one off from nursing. *Faṣala ʿan al-makān* means he cut himself off from the place by leaving it. From this is His saying: ﴿When the caravan set out﴾ [Yusuf: 94]. The author of *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's commentary) said: the saying *faṣala ʿan mawḍiʿ kadhā* originally was *faṣala nafsahu* (he separated himself), then, because of its frequent use, they omitted the object until it took on the status of an intransitive verb, as one says *infaṣala* (he separated himself). *Junūd* is the plural of *jund*, and every kind of creation is a distinct *jund*. It is said of large swarms of locusts that they are "the soldiers of Allah." From this is his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "Souls are armies mobilized" (*al-arwāḥu junūdun mujannadah*).

The second issue: It is narrated that Saul said to his people: "No man should march with me who is building a structure he has not finished, nor a merchant occupied with trade, nor a man who has married a woman and not yet consummated the marriage. I want only the young, energetic, and free of obligations." Thereupon there gathered to him, from those who had chosen (to go), eighty thousand.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Indeed Allah is going to test you with a river﴾, concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: They differed about who this speaker was. Most said: he is Saul, and this is the more apparent view, because his saying "must" must be attributed to a previously mentioned person, and the previously mentioned person is Saul. Then, on this view, it is possible that the saying was from Saul himself, but he received it from the prophet of the time, and on this assumption it does not follow that Saul was a prophet. It is also possible that it was from his own initiative, but then there must have been a revelation that came to him from his Lord, and that requires that he was a prophet alongside being a king.

The second view: the speaker of this saying is the prophet mentioned at the beginning of the verse, and the meaning is: when Saul set out with the troops, their prophet said to them: ﴿Indeed Allah is going to test you with a river﴾. The prophet of that time was Samuel (Ishmawil), upon him be peace.

* * *

The second issue: Regarding the wisdom of this test there are two views:

The first: al-Qadi (the judge) said: It was well known among the Children of Israel that they opposed the prophets and the kings even when clear signs appeared. So Allah, exalted is He, willed to display a sign before meeting the enemy, by which those who would endure the battle would be distinguished from those who would not endure. This is because turning back before meeting the enemy does not have the same effect as turning back during the encounter with the enemy. Since this was the proper course before fighting the enemy, he therefore said: ﴿Indeed Allah is going to test you with a river﴾.

The second: that He, exalted is He, tested them so that they would become accustomed to patience in hardships.

* * *

The third issue: Regarding the river there are several views:

One of them, which is the view of Qatadah and al-Rabi', is that it is a river between the Jordan and Palestine.

[Page 153]

The second, which is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi, is that it is the river of Palestine. The Qadi said: The reconciliation between the two views is that a river flowing from one land may be attributed to either of the two lands.

The third view, which al-Kashshaf transmitted: the weather was summer heat, so they took a desert track and asked Allah to make a river flow for them. So He said: ﴿Indeed Allah is going to test you with what you have proposed of the river﴾.

* * *

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿tested you with a river﴾ means: He will examine you with the examination of a servant, as He said: ﴿Indeed We created man from a drop of mingled fluid, [so] We may try him﴾ [al-Insan: 2]. Since testing among people occurs only for the manifestation of a matter, and since it is established that Allah, exalted is He, does not reward or punish on the basis of His knowledge alone, but rather acts that way only upon the manifestation of deeds among people, and this does not occur except through obligation, therefore obligation is called *ibtila'* (testing). It has two forms: *balā yablū* and *ibtalā yabtalī*. The poet said:

*And indeed I tested you, and I tried my successor, and indeed my affection has sufficed you with its good conduct.*

Thus he used both forms.

The fifth issue: *nahr* and *nahar*, with the letter *hā'* vowelled or unvowelled, are two dialectal forms. Every triliteral word whose middle radical is one of the throat letters comes in both patterns, as in your saying: *ṣakhr* and *ṣakhar*, *shaʿr* and *shaʿar*. They also said *baḥr* and *baḥar*. The poet said:

*As if his two palms were made of stone, so that between his hands and generosity there is no deed.*

*He sees tayammum (dry ablution) on land and on sea, for fear that the dampness on his palm be seen.*

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me﴾, concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿is not of me﴾ is in the manner of a rebuke, meaning: he is not of the people of My religion and obedience. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿The believing men and believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71], and before it He said: ﴿The hypocrite men and hypocrite women are of one another; they enjoin what is wrong and forbid what is right﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67]. Also its parallel is his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "He is not of us who does not show mercy to our young and does not respect our elders" (*laysa minnā man lam yarḥam ṣaghīranā wa-lam yuwaqqir kabīranā*), meaning: he is not upon our religion and our way. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: The lexicographers said: ﴿does not taste it﴾ means does not sip it, and it derives from *ṭaʿm* (taste), which applies to food and drink. This is what the lexicographers said. In my view, this term was chosen for two benefits:

One of them: when a person is extremely thirsty and then drinks water, and wishes to describe that water as pleasant and delicious, he says: "This water is as if it were rose-water, and as if it were honey," describing it with delicious tastes. So His saying ﴿and whoever does not taste it﴾ means: even if thirst drives him to the point where that water is in his mouth as though it were described by these pleasant tastes, he is obliged to refrain from it and not to drink it.

The second: whoever puts water in his mouth and rinses with it and then expels it from the mouth is said truly to have tasted it and eaten it, but it is not truly said of him that he drank it. So if He had said "whoever does not drink it is of me," the prohibition would be restricted to drinking. But since He said ﴿and whoever does not taste it﴾, the prohibition applied to both drinking and rinsing. It is well known that this obligation is more difficult, and that one who is forbidden to drink water, when he rinses with it, finds a kind of lightness and relief.

The third issue: In the beginning of the verse He said ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾, then He said after it ﴿and whoever does not taste it﴾. It would have been expected to say "and whoever does not taste *from it*," so that the end of the verse would match its beginning, but He abandoned that wording, and this wording was chosen for a benefit. The jurists differed about this: if someone swears that he will not drink from this river, how does he break his oath? Abu Hanifa said: He breaks it only if he drinks by bending down directly to the river (*karaʿa min al-nahr*), so that even if he scoops water from that river with a cup and drinks it, he does not break it, because drinking "from" something means that the beginning of the drinking is directly connected to that thing, and this does not occur except by drinking from the river itself. The rest said: if he scoops water with a cup from that river and drinks it, he breaks the oath, because that, though it is metaphorical, is a well-known and familiar metaphor.

Having understood this, we say: His saying ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾ apparently means that the prohibition is restricted to drinking directly from the river, so that if he took it with a cup and drank, he would not fall under the prohibition. Since this possibility existed in the first wording, He mentioned in the second wording what removes this ambiguity, saying ﴿and whoever does not taste it is of me﴾. He attributed both tasting and drinking to the water, not to the river, to remove that ambiguity.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Except one who scoops a handful with his hand﴾, concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu Amr read *ghurfatan* with a fatha on the *ghayn*. Likewise Ya'qub and Khalaf. Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma. The lexicographers said: *al-ghurfah* with a damma is the small amount that is held in the palm, and *al-ghurfah* with a fatha is the act, namely scooping once. Similar to it are *al-ukla* and *al-akla* (a meal). One says: "So-and-so eats once during the day," *akla wāḥida* (one meal), and "I did not eat with them except *ukla*," with a damma, meaning a little, like a morsel. One also says: *al-ḥuzzah* from meat with a damma for a small piece of it, and *ḥazaztu al-laḥma ḥazzatan*, meaning I cut the meat once. Similar to it: *al-khuṭwah* and *al-khaṭwah*: with a damma it is the distance between the two feet, and with a fatha it is taking a step once. Al-Mubarrad said: *ghurfah* with a fatha is a verbal noun that applies to a little or a lot of what is in the hand, and *al-ghurfah* with a damma is the name for the amount that fills the palm, or what is scooped with it.

* * *

The second issue: His saying ﴿Except one who scoops﴾ is an exception from His saying ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾. This sentence is in the status of an exception connected to what precedes it, except that it was placed first in mention for emphasis.

The third issue: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The *ghurfah* was that from which he himself, his animals, and his servants would drink, and from which he would carry water.

I say: this statement may bear two meanings:

One of them: he was permitted to take from the water whatever he wished in one scoop, such that what was taken in that one scoop would suffice him, his animals, and his servants, and that he could carry it along with himself.

The second: he took only a little, but Allah, exalted is He, placed blessing in it so that it sufficed all of them. This was a miracle for the prophet of that age, just as He, exalted is He, satisfied a great multitude from a small amount of water in the time of Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they drank from it, except a few of them﴾, concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: Ubayy and al-A'mash read *illā qalīlun* (with a nominative *qalīlun*). The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: This is because of their inclination toward the meaning and their turning away from the wording, since His saying ﴿they drank from it﴾ means: "they did not obey him," so they treated it accordingly, as if it were said: "none of them obeyed him except a few of them."

The second issue: We have mentioned that the purpose of this test is that the truthful be distinguished from the heretic, and the one in agreement from the one in opposition. When Allah, exalted is He, stated that those fit for this fighting are those who do not drink from this river, and that whoever drinks from it is not permitted in this fighting, and there was in their hearts a strong aversion to that fighting, they therefore went ahead and drank, so the one in agreement was distinguished from the one in opposition, and the truthful from the enemy. It is related that when the companions of Saul rushed to the river after severe thirst, most of them fell into the river and drank heavily, but a small group obeyed the command of Allah, exalted is He, and did not exceed scooping. As for those who drank and opposed the command of Allah, their lips blackened, thirst overcame them, they were not satisfied, and they remained on the bank of the river and were cowardly in facing the enemy. As for those who obeyed the command of Allah, exalted is He, their hearts grew strong, their faith was sound, and they crossed the river safely.

The third issue: The few who did not drink are said to have been four thousand. The well-known view, which is the view of al-Hasan, is that they were the number of the people of Badr, three hundred and some ten, and they were the believers. The evidence for this is that the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, said to his companions on the day of Badr: "Today you are on the number of the companions of Saul when they crossed the river, and no one crossed with him except a believer." Al-Bara' ibn Azib said: "On that day we were three hundred and thirteen men."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Then when he and those who believed with him had crossed it, they said: We have no power today against Jalut and his troops﴾, concerning it there are two issues: [Page 155]

**First issue:** There is no disagreement among the exegetes (mufassirun) that those who disobeyed God and drank from the river returned to their homeland, and that only the one who obeyed God in the matter of drinking from the river went with him to meet the enemy. They differ only on whether their return to their homeland happened before crossing the river or after it, and on this there are two opinions.

**The first opinion:** Only the obedient crossed with him. This speaker argued from several points:

**The first argument:** God says, ﴿So when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him﴾. The phrase ﴿those who believed with him﴾ refers to those who agreed with him in that obedience. When God mentioned the whole army and then singled out the obedient as the ones who crossed the river, we know that no one crossed the river except the obedient.

**The second argument:** The preceding verse, God's words quoted from Talut, ﴿whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾, meaning, is not one of my companions on this journey, is like a man who tells another, "You are not one of us in this matter." He said: the meaning of ﴿so they drank from it﴾ is that they made drinking the means of their turning back, because of the corruption of their religion and their hearts.

**The third argument:** The purpose of this trial was to distinguish the obedient from the disobedient and the rebellious, so that he could remove them from himself and send them back before they apostatized when the enemy appeared. If the purpose of this trial was only this, then the apparent meaning is that he removed them from himself at that time and did not permit them to cross the river.

**The second opinion:** He took all his soldiers with him, and all of them crossed the river. Proponents of this view rely on God's words quoting the people of Talut, ﴿They said, "We have no power today against Goliath and his soldiers"﴾. It is well known that this statement does not befit a believer who submits to his Lord's command. Rather, it could only come from a hypocrite or a sinner. This argument is weak, and its weakness can be shown in several ways:

First: It may be said that when Talut resolved to cross the river and most of them held back, those who held back gave as their excuse that they had no power today against Goliath and his soldiers, so they were excused for this holding back. The most that can be said against this is that the particle ﴿fa﴾ in His words ﴿when he crossed it﴾ requires that their statement ﴿we have no power today against Goliath﴾ came only after the crossing. But we say: it may be that when Talut and the believers crossed the river and saw the people who had held back and not crossed, he asked them about the reason for their holding back, and they mentioned this. The river was not so large as to prevent conversation. It may also be that the meaning of "crossing" is "being close to crossing," and on this interpretation the problem also disappears.

The second answer: It may be said that the believers who crossed the river were of two groups. Some of them loved life and disliked death, and fear and anxiety predominated in their nature. Others were brave and strong of heart, and did not care about death in the cause of God the Exalted.

The first group are those who said, ﴿We have no power today﴾.
The second group are those who replied with their words, ﴿How often has a small company overcome a large company﴾.

The third answer: It may be said that the first group of believers, when they saw how small their army was, said, ﴿We have no power today against Goliath and his soldiers﴾. So they had to prepare themselves for death, since there is no escape from God's command.
The second group said: "We will not prepare ourselves for death; rather, we hope from God for victory and triumph." So the aim of the first group was to encourage seeking martyrdom and winning Paradise, and the aim of the second group was to encourage seeking victory and support. On this interpretation, neither of the two statements contradicts the other.

**Second issue:** The word *taqah* (power, capacity) is a verbal noun equivalent to *ițaqah*. One says *aṭaqtu al-shay'a iṭaqatan wa ṭaqatan* (I was able to do the thing). Similarly, *aṭāʿa yuṭīʿu iṭāʿatan*, and the noun is *al-ṭāʿah* (obedience). And *aghāra yughīru ighāratan*, and the noun is *al-ghārah* (raid). And *ajāba yujību ijābatan*, and the noun is *al-jābah*. In the proverb: *asāʾa samʿan fa-asāʾa jābatan*, meaning he heard badly and so answered badly, that is, gave a bad answer.

* * *

As for God's words, ﴿Those who thought that they would meet God said﴾, there is a question here: why did He make them people who thought (yaẓunnūn) and not people who were certain (ḥāzimūn)?

The answer to this involves several matters:

**The first:** This is the view of Qatada, that by "meeting God" is meant death. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him, and whoever dislikes to meet God, God dislikes to meet him." Since these believers had prepared themselves for being killed, and the conviction that they would not escape death had come to dominate their thoughts, they were therefore described as those who think they will meet God.

**The second:** ﴿Those who think they will meet God﴾ means that they will meet God's reward for this obedience. This is because no one knows the outcome of his affair, so a person must be one who thinks and hopes, even if he reaches the utmost degree of obedience, except for one whom God informs of the outcome of his affair. This is the view of Abu Muslim, and it is a good one.

**The third aspect:** The meaning may be: "those who think they will meet the obedience of God." This is because a person cannot be certain that the deed he performed is an act of obedience, since he may have mixed into it some showing off and seeking reputation, and it may not have been done with sincere intention. In that case the act would not be obedience. What is possible is that he thinks he performed it in the manner of obedience and sincerity.

**The fourth:** We mentioned, in explaining God's words, ﴿that there will come to you the ark, in which is tranquility from your Lord﴾, that according to some exegetes the "tranquility" meant that the ark contained divine books sent down to earlier prophets, indicating that victory and triumph would come to Talut and his soldiers. But these books did not state whether victory would come on the first occasion or later. So His words, ﴿those who think they will meet God﴾, mean those who think they will meet God's promise of victory. He described it as a thought and not a certainty because its occurrence in general, though certain, was not certain to occur on the first occasion, which was only by way of good assumption.

**The fifth:** Many exegetes said: by His words, ﴿who think they will meet God﴾, is meant that they know and are certain. But the word "thought" (ẓann) was applied to certainty figuratively, because of the resemblance between thought and certainty in the firmness of belief.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿How often has a small company overcome a large company by God's permission﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Its purpose is to strengthen the hearts of those who said, ﴿We have no power today against Goliath and his soldiers﴾. The meaning is that numbers carry no weight; what carries weight is divine support and heavenly help. When good fortune comes, there is no harm in small numbers and weakness; when trial comes, there is no benefit in great numbers and equipment.

**The second issue:** *Fi'ah* means a group, because some of them have gone back (*fā'a*) to others, so they became a group. Al-Zajjaj said: the origin of *fi'ah* is from their saying, *fa'autu ra'sahu bi'l-sayf* (I cut his head with the sword) and *fa'aytu* when you cut. So *fi'ah* is a band of people, as if it were a piece of them.

**The third issue:** Al-Farra' said: if *min* (from) were removed here, then *fi'ah* could be read in the nominative, the accusative, or the genitive. As for the accusative, it is because *kam* (how many) functions like a number, so the noun after it is in the accusative, as in *ʿishrīna rajulan* (twenty men). As for the genitive, it is by assuming that the particle *min* enters before it. As for the nominative, it is by intending to place the verb first, as if it were said: *kam ghalabat fi'atun* (how many a group has overcome).

* * *

As for His words, ﴿And God is with the steadfast﴾, there is no doubt that what is meant is assistance and support. It may be that this is a statement from those who said, ﴿How often has a small company﴾, and it may be a statement from God the Exalted, though the first is more apparent.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, verse 250:**

[p. 158]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When they came out against Jalut and his troops, they said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make our feet firm, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾

On this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** *al-mubarazah* (single combat) in warfare means that each of the two sides comes forward to his opponent at the time of fighting. The root meaning is that open, unobstructed ground with no screen is called *al-biraz*. So *al-buruz* refers to each of the two being in the open ground called *al-biraz*, that is, each being in a position where he can see his opponent.

**The second issue:** When the scholars and the strong among Talut's army agreed with the common people and the weak that "many a small company has overcome a large company by God's permission," and made clear that victory and support come only through God's help, then when Talut's army came out against Jalut's army and saw the few on their side and the many on the side of their enemy, they turned without doubt to supplication and humble entreaty, and said: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience.﴾ A parallel to this is what God related of other people, who said when they met the polytheists: ﴿And how many a prophet fought, and with him many devoted followers. They did not weaken for what befell them in God's way, nor did they falter, nor did they submit. God loves the steadfast.﴾ (Qur'an 3:146) up to His saying: ﴿And their only words were: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, make our feet firm, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ (Qur'an 3:147). And this is what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did in all his encounters. It is related of him, concerning the story of Badr, that he (peace be upon him) continued to pray and to demand from God the fulfilment of His promise. And whenever he met an enemy he would say: "O God, I seek refuge in You from their evils, and I place You against their throats." He also used to say: "O God, by You I attack, and by You I retreat."

**The third issue:** *al-ifraγ* (pouring) is to pour out, as one says: "I emptied the vessel" (*afraghtu al-inaʾ*) when you poured out what was in it. Its root is from *al-faragh* (emptiness). One says: "So-and-so is free" (*farigh*), meaning he is clear of what occupies him. *Al-ifraγ* is the emptying of the vessel of what is in it, and a vessel is emptied only by pouring out all that is in it.

Given this, we say: His saying ﴿pour upon us patience﴾ indicates an intensification in asking for patience in two respects:

The first: when a thing is poured into another thing, it has been fixed in it so that it does not leave it, and this indicates emphasis.

The second: the emptying of a vessel (*ifraγ al-inaʾ*) is its being made empty, and this happens by pouring out everything that is in it. So the meaning of ﴿pour upon us patience﴾ is: pour upon us the most complete and thorough pouring.

**The fourth issue:** Know that the qualities required in combat are three together:

The first is that a person be patient in facing fears and terrifying matters, and this is the supreme pillar for a fighter, for if he is a coward, nothing of the intended aim is achieved from him at all.

The second is that he possess, from the instruments, tools and favourable circumstances, what enables him to stand firm and hold his position, and not be compelled to flee.

The third is that his strength increase beyond the strength of his enemy, so that he can overcome the enemy.

Given this, we say: the first level is what is meant by His saying ﴿pour upon us patience﴾.

The second is what is meant by His saying ﴿and make our feet firm﴾.

The third is what is meant by His saying ﴿and help us against the disbelieving people﴾.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** The companions (*al-Ashab*, i.e., the Ashʿarī theologians) argued that the acts of servants are created by God, Exalted, from His saying ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾. This is because there is no meaning of patience except the resolve to remain steady, and no meaning of steadiness except stillness and stability. This verse indicates that this resolve called patience is from God, Exalted, namely His saying ﴿pour upon us patience﴾, and that the steadiness and stillness that occur with this resolve are also by the act of God, Exalted, namely His saying ﴿and make our feet firm﴾. This is explicit that the volition is from the act of the servant and by the creation of God, Exalted.

The Qadi (al-Qadi) answered this by saying that what is meant by patience and making the feet firm is the securing of the means of patience and the means of firmness of the feet, and these means are several things:

First: that He place in their enemies' hearts terror and cowardice toward them, so that disorder befalls the enemy because of this, and this becomes a cause for the boldness of the Muslims against them, and a motive for them to be patient in fighting and to avoid flight.

Second: that He show kindness to some of their enemies regarding the knowledge of the falsehood of what they hold, so that discord and dispersion arise among them, and this becomes a cause for the boldness of the believers against them.

Third: that God, Exalted, bring upon them and upon their lands and families afflictions such as death and plague, and whatever causes them to be preoccupied with themselves, so that they are then not free for fighting, and this becomes a cause for the boldness of the Muslims against them.

Fourth: that He afflict them with a sickness and weakness that encompasses them all or most of them, or that their leader and the one who manages their affairs die, so that the believers know this, and it becomes a cause for the strengthening of their hearts, and a reason for them to attain patience and firmness. This is the Qadi's statement.

The reply to this is in two respects:

The first: we have shown that patience is an expression for the resolve toward steadiness, and firmness is an expression for stillness. Thus this verse indicates that the volition of the servant and his intention are from God, Exalted. This refutes your statement, since you divert the speech from its apparent meaning and interpret it as the means of patience and firmness of the feet. It is known that abandoning the apparent meaning without evidence is not permissible.

[p. 159]

The second reply: these means which you accept as acts of God, Exalted, when they occur and come into existence, either they have an effect on the preponderance of the motive or they have no effect on it. If they have no effect on it, then asking God for them has no benefit. If they have an effect on the preponderance, then when these preponderating causes proceed from God, preponderance occurs, and when preponderance occurs, the disfavoured side becomes impossible, so the favoured side must come into being, because there is no exit from the two sides of a contradiction. This is what was sought. And God knows best.

**The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 251 (part 1 of 2)**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah, and David killed Goliath, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom, and taught him of what He willed. And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted; but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.﴾

The meaning: Allah the Exalted answered their supplication, poured patience upon them, made their feet firm, and gave them victory over the disbelieving people, Goliath (Jalut) and his soldiers. By His grace and mercy He fulfilled the expectation of the one who said: ﴿How many a small company has overcome a large company by the permission of Allah!﴾ ﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah.﴾

The root of *hazm* (routing, breaking) in the language is "breaking." It is said: *siqa'un munhazim* ("a water-skin that is broken") when it cracks while dry. One says: *hazamtu al-'azma aw al-qasabah hazman* ("I broke the bone or the reed"). The *hazmah* is a hollow in a mountain or in a rock. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said of Zamzam: "It is the *hazmat Jibril*," meaning that Jibril struck it with his foot and the water emerged. It is also said: "I heard the *hazmat* of thunder," as if it were a sound containing a cracking. The cloud is called *hazim*, because it cracks open with rain. And one says: *hazama al-darʻa* (he broke the udder), and its *hazm* is what is broken from it.

Then Allah the Exalted informed that this routing was by the permission of Allah, by His aid, His granting of success, and His facilitation. And that had His aid and facilitation not been there, it would never have occurred at all.

Then He said: ﴿and David killed Goliath.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: David, peace be upon him, was a shepherd, and he had seven brothers serving with Talut (Saul). When news of his brothers was delayed to their father, Iyashi (Jesse), he sent his son David to them to bring him word of them. So he came to them while they were in the battle lines, and Jalut the tyrant, who was of the people of 'Ad, came forward to single combat, but no one came out to meet him. He said: "O children of Israel, if you were upon the truth, one of you would have come out to fight me." David said to his brothers: "Is there none among you who will go out to this uncircumcised one?" They were silent. So he went to a part of the line where his brothers were not, and Talut passed by him while he was urging the people on. David said to him: "What will you do for the one who kills this uncircumcised one?" Talut said: "I will marry him to my daughter and give him half my kingdom." David said: "Then I will go out to him." It was his habit to fight wolves and lions while herding with a sling (*miqla'*). Talut knew of his stout courage. When David resolved to go out, Goliath threw at him and struck him in the chest, and the stone pierced him, and he killed many people after him. Allah routed the armies of Jalut. ﴿And David killed Goliath.﴾ Then Talut envied him, expelled him from his kingdom, and did not fulfil his promise to him. Then he regretted it and went seeking him until he was killed. David became king, and prophethood was granted to him. And kingship and prophethood were not combined among the children of Israel except in him.

Know that His words, ﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah, and David killed Goliath﴾, indicate that the routing of Goliath's army was by Talut, although the killing of Goliath was only by David. There is no indication in the apparent sense as to whether the rout of the army occurred before or after the killing of Goliath, because the *wa* (conjunction "and") does not indicate sequence.

* * *

Page 160

As for His words, ﴿and Allah gave him the kingdom and the wisdom﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: Some said: Allah gave him the kingdom and prophethood as a reward for the great obedience he performed and for giving up his life in the way of Allah. Yet Allah was aware that he was fit to bear the matter of prophethood, and it is not impossible to make prophethood a reward for acts of obedience, as He said: ﴿And We chose them with knowledge above the worlds﴾ and ﴿We gave them of the signs that contained a clear trial﴾ [al-Dukhan: 32, 33]. And He said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. The apparent sense of this verse also indicates this, because when He related that David killed Goliath, He said after it: ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom.﴾ When a ruler bestows favour upon one of his servants who has carried out a hard service, it is strongly presumed that this favour is because of that service. But most scholars said: It is not permissible to make prophethood a reward for deeds; rather, it is pure bounty and grace. He said: ﴿Allah chooses messengers from the angels and from mankind﴾ [al-Hajj: 75].

The second issue: Some said: The apparent sense of the verse indicates that when David killed Goliath, Allah gave him the kingdom and prophethood. That is because He mentioned the giving of kingship and prophethood directly after His mention of David killing Goliath, and the placing of a judgment upon a fitting attribute suggests that this attribute is the cause of that judgment. The explanation of the suitability is that when he, peace be upon him, killed such a great opponent with the sling and the stone, that was a miracle, especially since the stones clung to him and said: "Take us, for you will kill Goliath with us." So the manifestation of a miracle indicates prophethood. As for kingship, when the people witnessed from him the subduing of that great, awe-inspiring enemy by that small deed, there is no doubt that souls inclined towards him, and this requires that kingship be attained by him openly.

But most scholars said: The attainment of kingship and prophethood by him was delayed from that time by seven years, according to what al-Dahhak said. They said: The reports came with this. They said: Because Allah had already appointed Talut to kingship, it is unlikely that He would remove him from kingship while he was alive. The well-known account regarding the affairs of the children of Israel is that the prophet of that time was Ishmuwil (Samuel), and the king of that time was Talut. When Ishmuwil died, Allah gave prophethood to David, and when Talut died, Allah gave kingship to David, so kingship and prophethood were combined in him.

The third issue: *Al-hikmah* (wisdom) is placing matters in their proper places, in accordance with what is right and good. The perfection of this meaning is only attained through prophethood. So it is not far-fetched that the intended meaning of *al-hikmah* here is prophethood. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? We had given the family of Abraham the Book and the wisdom, and We had given them a great kingdom﴾ [al-Nisa': 54]. And He said regarding what He sent His Prophet, peace be upon him, with: ﴿and teaches them the Book and the wisdom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164].

If it is said: If the intended meaning of wisdom is prophethood, why did He place kingship before wisdom, when kingship is of lower rank than prophethood?

We say: Because Allah, the Exalted, explained in this verse the manner of David's ascent, peace be upon him, to the lofty ranks. When a speaker discusses the manner of ascent, whatever is mentioned later is of higher status and greater rank.

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿and taught him of what He willed﴾, there are several aspects to it:

The first: The intended meaning is what He mentioned in His words: ﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you, to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Anbiya': 80], and He said: ﴿And We made iron soft for him, [saying]: Make full coats of mail and measure well the links﴾ [Saba': 10, 11].

The second: The intended meaning is the speech of birds and ants. He, the Exalted, said, relating about him: ﴿We have been taught the speech of birds﴾ [al-Naml: 16].

Page 161

The third: The intended meaning is what concerns the interests of this world and the governing of kingship, for he did not inherit kingship from his fathers, because they were not kings but shepherds.

The fourth: The knowledge of religion. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We gave David the Zabur (Psalms)﴾ [al-Nisa': 163]. This is because he was a judge among the people, so Allah the Exalted must have taught him the manner of judgment and adjudication.

The fifth: Beautiful melodies. It is not far-fetched to take the word in its entirety.

If it is said: When He mentioned that He gave him wisdom, and the intended meaning of wisdom is prophethood, then knowledge has entered into that. Why then did He mention after it: ﴿and taught him of what He willed﴾?

We say: The purpose of it is to alert that a servant never reaches a state in which he is free from needing to learn, whether he is a prophet or not. For this reason He said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114].

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, clarified that the corruption that befell Goliath and his soldiers was removed by what came from Talut and his soldiers, and by what came from David in killing Goliath, He then clarified, after that, a comprehensive statement that encompasses every detail in this domain, which is that He repels people by means of one another so that the earth will not be corrupted. He said: ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted.﴾ Here there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited ﴿wa-lawla daf'u Allah﴾ without an *alif*, and likewise in surah al-Hajj: ﴿wa-lawla daf'u Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]. They both also recited (*inna Allaha yadfa'u 'ani alladhina amanu*, "Indeed Allah repels from those who believed") without an *alif*. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir al-Yahsubi agreed with the two of them on *daf'u Allah* without an *alif*, except that they recited ﴿Indeed Allah repels (*yudafi'u*) from those who believed﴾ with an *alif*. Nafi' recited (*wa-lawla difa'u Allah*, "and had the defence of Allah not...") and ﴿Indeed Allah repels (*yudafi'u*)﴾ with an *alif*.

Having known these transmissions, we say: As for the one who recites *wa-lawla daf'u Allah* and *yadfa'u*, its reasoning is clear. As for the one who recites *wa-lawla difa'u Allah* and ﴿yudafi'u 'ani alladhina amanu﴾, the difficulty in it is that *mudafa'ah* is a form of *mufa'alah* (reciprocal action), which means that each of the two who repel is repelling the other and preventing him from his action. For a servant with respect to Allah, the Exalted, this is impossible. The answer to this is that the people of the language have two views regarding the word *difa'*:

The first: It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *dafaʻa* (he repelled). One says: *daftuhu daf'an wa-difa'an* ("I repelled him, a repelling and a defence"), just as one says: *katabtuhu katban wa-kitaban* ("I wrote it, a writing and a book"). They said: *fi'al* very often comes as a verbal noun of the triliteral verbs *fa'ala* and *fa'ila*. One says: *jamaha jimahan*, and *tamaha timahan*; and one says: *laqitahu liqa'an*, and *qumtu qiyaman*. According to this interpretation, His words *wa-lawla difa'u Allah* mean *wa-lawla daf'u Allah* ("and had the repelling of Allah not...").

The second view: the view of those who made *difa'* from *dafa'a* (to contend or defend). The meaning then is that He, glorified is He, only restrains the oppressors and the disobedient from oppressing the believers through the hands of His prophets, messengers, and the imams of His religion. There occurred between those upright ones and those deviant ones *mudafa'at* (contentions) and *mukafahat* (struggles). Thus it was fine to describe this with the word *mudafa'ah*, just as He said: ﴿They wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33], ﴿They oppose Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 13], and just as He said: ﴿Allah fights them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], and its like. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: Know that He, the Exalted, mentioned in this verse the one repelled and the means by which he is repelled. His words, ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others﴾, point to the one repelled, and His words *bi-ba'd* ("by means of others") point to the means of repelling. As for the one from whom they are repelled, it is not mentioned in the verse. So it is possible that the one from whom they are repelled is the evils in religion, and it is possible that it is the evils of this world, and it is possible that it is both together.

Page 162

As for the first division, that the one from whom they are repelled is the evils in religion: those evils either return to disbelief, or to wickedness (*fisq*), or to both. Let us mention these possibilities.

The first possibility: the meaning is: And had Allah not repelled some people from disbelief by means of others. In this case, those who repel are the prophets and the leaders of guidance, for they are the ones who prevent people from falling into disbelief by manifesting the proofs, evidences and clear signs. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you, that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light﴾ [Ibrahim: 1].

The second possibility: the intended meaning is: And had Allah not repelled some people from sins and evil deeds by means of others. In this case, those who repel are those who enjoin the good and forbid the evil, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind; you enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. Within this category enter the imams appointed by Allah, the Exalted, for the purpose of establishing the prescribed punishments (*hudud*) and manifesting the symbols of Islam. A parallel to this is His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Repel with that which is better the evil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 96], and in another place: ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾ [al-Ra'd: 22].

The third possibility: "Had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, from chaos and turmoil and the stirring up of strife in this world because of some of them." Know that the repellers in this reading are the prophets, peace be upon them, and then the imams and the kings who defend their laws. The argument is this: a single human being cannot live alone, for unless this one bakes for that one, and that one grinds for this one, and this one builds for that one, and that one weaves for this one, the welfare of a single human being is not complete. It is complete only when a group gathers in one place. Hence it was said: man is civil by nature (madani bi'l-tab'). Then, gathering leads to rivalry, which leads first to disputes and then to fighting. Therefore, in divine wisdom, there must be a law (shari'a) set among creation, so that the law may put an end to disputes and contentions. The prophets, peace be upon them, who were given these laws from Allah, are those by means of whom, and by means of whose law, Allah repelled calamities from creation. For as long as people remain adhering to the laws, no dispute or strife occurs among them. Thus, whenever kings and imams hold fast to these laws, strife disappears and benefits are secured. It thus becomes clear that Allah, exalted is He, repels from the believers all kinds of worldly evils by means of the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them.

Know that just as the law is necessary to end disputes and contentions, so too is government (mulk) necessary to enforce the law. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Islam and authority (sultan) are twin brothers." He also said: "Islam is a commander, and authority is a guardian; what has no commander is defeated, and what has no guardian is lost." For this reason Allah, exalted is He, repels from the Muslims all kinds of worldly evils by means of the establishing of laws and by means of appointing kings and strengthening them. Whoever holds this view, in interpreting His saying ﴿the earth would have been corrupted﴾, means: the killing and sins would have prevailed over the people of the earth, and that is called corruption (fasad). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He destroys the crops and the offspring, and Allah does not like corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205]. He said: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You intend only to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not intend to be among the reformers﴾ [al-Qasas: 19]. He said: ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾ [Ghafir: 26]. He said: ﴿Will you leave Musa and his people to cause corruption in the land?﴾ [al-A'raf: 127]. He said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum: 41]. This interpretation is supported by His saying in Surat al-Hajj: ﴿And had Allah not repelled people, some by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques would have been demolished﴾ [al-Hajj: 40].

The fourth possibility: "Had Allah not repelled by means of the believers and the righteous the disbelievers and the wicked, the earth would have been corrupted and its inhabitants destroyed because of those among them." What confirms this is what has been related: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By those among my community who pray, harm is repelled from those who do not pray; by those who give zakat, from those who do not give zakat; by those who fast, from those who do not fast; by those who perform Hajj, from those who do not perform Hajj; by those who strive (jihad), from those who do not strive. And if they all came together to abandon these things, Allah would not grant them respite for the blink of an eye." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse. As Qur'anic support for the soundness of this view is His saying: ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure for them, and their father had been righteous﴾ [al-Kahf: 82]. He said: ﴿Had there not been believing men and believing women [whom you did not know]... [that] had they been separated, We would have punished those who disbelieved among them with a painful punishment﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. He said: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. Whoever holds this view, in interpreting His saying ﴿the earth would have been corrupted﴾, means: Allah would have destroyed its people because of the multitude of disbelievers and sinners.

The fifth possibility: that the expression be taken as applying to all of these, because among these categories there is a common element, namely the repelling of harm (mafsada). When we take the expression in this sense, all the categories enter into it together.

The Third Issue: The judge (al-Qadi) said: This verse is among the strongest proofs against the doctrine of compulsion (al-jabr), because if corruption comes from His creation, how could God, may He be exalted, say: ﴿Had God not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted﴾? And it must be that, according to their view, the repelling of some people by others has no effect in removing corruption, because—according to their view—corruption only fails to occur due to God, may He be exalted, not doing it and not creating it, not due to a matter that returns to people.

The answer: God, may He be exalted, when He knew that corruption would occur, if it were valid alongside that knowledge that He not do the corruption, the meaning would be that it is valid for the servant to combine the absence of corruption with knowledge of the existence of corruption, and it would follow that he is able to combine negation and affirmation, which is impossible.

As for His words: ﴿But God is full of bounty toward the worlds﴾, the intention is that the repelling of corruption by this means is a favour encompassing all people. Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued by this verse that everything occurs by the decree of God, may He be exalted. They said: If the act of the servant were not a creation of God, may He be exalted, the repelling of the righteous from the evil of the wrongdoers would not be a bounty from God upon the people of this world, because the one who undertakes that repelling would be the servant from his own self and by his own choice, and not God. Yet His words ﴿But God is full of bounty toward the worlds﴾, following His words ﴿Had God not repelled some people by means of others﴾, indicate that He, may He be exalted, is full of bounty toward the worlds because of that repelling. This shows that that repelling, which is their act, is from God's creation and His decree.

If they say: This should be understood as clarification, guidance and command.

We say: All of that applies to unbelievers and sinners as well, and the repelling did not result from it. So we know that God's bounty and grace upon us was only because of the repelling itself, and that requires our position. And God knows best.

﴿Those are the signs of God; We recite them to you in truth, and you are indeed among the messengers﴾

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the signs of God; We recite them to you in truth, and you are indeed among the messengers﴾

Know that His words "Those" (tilka) refer to the stories He mentioned: the account of the thousands and their death and revival, the making of Talut as king, the manifestation of the sign which is the descent of the ark (al-tabut) from heaven, and the defeat of the tyrants at the hand of Dawud while he was a poor youth. There is no doubt that these circumstances are striking signs indicating the perfection of God's power, wisdom and mercy.

If it is said: Why did He say "tilka" and not "hadhihi," given that "tilka" is used for an absent thing and not a present one?

We say: We have already explained in the commentary on His words ﴿That is the Book, in which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] that "tilka" and "dhalika" return to the meaning of "hadhihi" and "hadha." Also, these stories, once mentioned, became like a thing that has passed and gone, so they were in the status of the absent, and for this interpretation He said "tilka."

As for His words, may He be exalted, "We recite them" (natluha): it means Jibril, peace be upon him, recites them to you; but He, may He be exalted, made Jibril's recitation His own recitation, and this is a great honour to Jibril, peace be upon him. It is like His words: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you pledge allegiance only to God﴾ [al-Fath: 10].

As for His words "in truth" (bil-haqq), there are several aspects:

First: The purpose of mentioning these stories is that Muhammad ﷺ should take lessons from them, and his community should take lessons from them in enduring hardships in jihad, just as the believers endured them in earlier nations.

Second: "In truth" means with certainty, about which the People of the Book have no doubt, because it is in their books, in the same way, without any discrepancy at all.

Third: We sent down these verses in a way that they indicate your prophethood, because of the eloquence and rhetorical excellence in them.

Fourth: ﴿Those are the signs of God; We recite them to you in truth﴾, meaning it must be known that the descent of these verses upon you is from God, may He be exalted, and not because of the casting of the devils, nor because of the distortion of soothsayers and sorcerers.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And you are indeed among the messengers﴾. He mentioned this following what preceded it for several reasons. First: You reported these narratives without having learned them or studied them, and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, mentioned and knew them only through revelation from God, may He be exalted. Second: Through these verses you came to know what befell the prophets, peace be upon them, among the Children of Israel, of fear on their behalf and rejection of their words. So let not the unbelief of those who disbelieve in you, or the opposition of those who oppose you, weigh heavily upon you, for you are like them. Every one of them was sent only to convey the message and to carry out the command by way of choice and voluntary submission, not by way of compulsion. So there is no blame upon you for their opposition and unbelief, and the burden of that returns upon them. This is a consolation to the Messenger ﷺ regarding what appears from the unbelievers and hypocrites, and His words ﴿And you are indeed among the messengers﴾ serve as an alert to that.

[Page 165]

﴿Those messengers — some of them We preferred over others. Among them are those to whom God spoke, and some of them He raised in degrees. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear signs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear signs had come to them, but they differed: some of them believed and some of them disbelieved. Had God willed, they would not have fought one another, but God does what He wills.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The First Issue: ﴿Tilka﴾ ("those") is the subject (mubtada'). He said ﴿tilka﴾ and not ﴿ula'ika﴾ ("those") with ﴿al-rusul﴾ ("the messengers"), because he took the reference to be to a group, as if it were said: "Those, the group of messengers," in the nominative, because it is a description of ﴿tilka﴾. The predicate of the subject is ﴿fadalna ba'dahum 'ala ba'd﴾ ("We preferred some of them over others").

The Second Issue: Concerning His words ﴿those messengers﴾ there are several opinions:

First: That what is meant is those prophets previously mentioned in the Qur'an, such as Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Moses and others, may God's blessings be upon them.

Second: That what is meant is those mentioned in this verse, such as Samuel, David and Saul, according to the opinion of those who regard him (Saul) as a prophet.

Third: And this is the view of al-Asamm: "those messengers" are those whom God sent to repel corruption, to whom the indication refers in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Had God not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted﴾.

The Third Issue: The connection of this verse with what precedes it is what Abu Muslim mentioned, namely that He, exalted is He, informed Muhammad (ﷺ) of the reports about earlier peoples with their nations, such as the request of the people of Moses: ﴿Show us God plainly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], and their saying: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]; and like the people of Jesus, after they had witnessed from him the raising of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper by God's permission, yet they denied him and sought to kill him. Then a group persisted in disbelief in him, and they are the Jews; and a group claimed that they were his followers, and they claimed against the Jews that they had killed him and crucified him, which God did not refute them concerning. Likewise the chiefs of the Children of Israel envied Saul and repelled his kingship after the request, and likewise what happened concerning the river. So God consoled His Messenger for what he saw from his people of denial and envy, and said: These are the messengers, whom God spoke to some of, and raised others in degrees, and strengthened Jesus with the Holy Spirit; they encountered from their peoples what we have mentioned, after witnessing the miracles. And you are a messenger like them, so do not grieve over what you see from your people. Had God willed, you and they would not have differed; but what God has decreed comes to pass, and what He has determined occurs. In sum, the purpose of this discourse is to console the Messenger (ﷺ) for the harm his people caused him.

* * *

The Fourth Issue: The Ummah (community) has agreed (ijma', consensus) that some prophets are superior to others, and that Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to all of them. This is indicated by several points:

First: His words, exalted is He: ﴿We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]. Since he is a mercy to all the worlds, it necessarily follows that he is superior to all the worlds.

The Second Argument: His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We have raised your mention﴾ [al-Sharh: 4]. It was said concerning it that He joined the mention of Muhammad with His own mention in the testimony of faith (shahada), in the call to prayer (adhan), and in the tashahhud, and the mention of the other prophets was not so.

The Third Argument: He, exalted is He, joined obedience to him with obedience to Himself, saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾ [al-Nisa': 80]; and joined pledging allegiance to him with pledging allegiance to Himself, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are actually pledging allegiance to God; the hand of God is over their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10]; and joined His might with his might, saying: ﴿And to God belongs honor, and to His Messenger﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]; and joined His pleasure with his pleasure, saying: ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62]; and joined responding to him with responding to Himself, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to God and to the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 24].

The Fourth Argument: God commanded Muhammad to challenge them with every surah of the Qur'an, saying: ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]. The shortest surah is Surat al-Kawthar, which has three verses, and God challenged them with every three verses of the Qur'an. Since the whole Qur'an is six thousand verses, and it is so many verses, it follows that the Qur'an's miraculous character is not a single miracle but two thousand miracles or more.

[Page 166]

Given that this is established, we say: God, exalted is He, mentioned the honouring of Moses with nine clear signs; so the honouring of Muhammad with these many signs is more fitting.

The Fifth Argument: The miracle of our Messenger (ﷺ) is superior to the miracles of all other prophets, so our Messenger must be superior to all other prophets.

The explanation of the first point is his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "The Qur'an among speech is like Adam among created beings."

The explanation of the second point is that the more noble a robe of honour is, the more honoured its wearer is with the king.

The Sixth Argument: His miracle, peace be upon him, is the Qur'an, which is of the kind of letters and sounds, and these are accidents that do not endure; whereas the miracles of all other prophets are of the kind of enduring things. Then He, exalted is He, made the miracle of Muhammad (ﷺ) lasting until the end of time, while the miracles of the other prophets passed away and ended.

The Seventh Argument: After He, exalted is He, related the conditions of the prophets, peace be upon them, He said: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to follow those before him. Either it is said that he was commanded to follow them in the foundations of religion (usul al-din), and this is not permissible because it would be imitation (taqlid); or in its subsidiary rulings (furu' al-din), and this is also not permissible, because his law abrogated all other laws. So nothing remains except that what is meant is the noble qualities of character. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "We have informed you of their conditions and their ways; choose from them the best and the finest, and be an imitator of them in all of them." This indicates that there were gathered in him the praiseworthy qualities that were scattered among them, and so it is necessary that he be superior to them.

The Eighth Argument: He, peace be upon him, was sent to all creation, and this requires that his hardship be greater, so it is necessary that he be superior. As for his being sent to all creation, this is by His words: ﴿We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind﴾ [Saba': 28]. As for the claim that this requires his hardship to be greater, it is because he was a single human being without wealth, helpers or supporters. When he said to all the worlds, "O you disbelievers," they all became his enemies, and then he became fearful of everyone, so the hardship was great. Likewise, when Moses, peace be upon him, was sent to the Children of Israel, he feared no one except Pharaoh and his people; whereas Muhammad, peace be upon him, had everyone as his enemy.
