This is clarified by the following: if a person were told: "This land is empty of friend or companion, except that there is one man in it, powerful and armed; go to him today alone and convey to him news that will distress and harm him," he would hardly allow his soul to do so, even though it is a single person. And if he were told: "Go to a distant desert where there is no companion or friend, and convey to the chief of that desert such and such distressing news," that would be difficult for a human being. As for the Prophet (ﷺ), he was commanded to go throughout his night and day, throughout his whole life, to the jinn and humans with whom he had no prior acquaintance; indeed, the usual response from them was that they were hostile to him, harmed him and treated him with contempt. Then he, peace be upon him, did not tire of this condition, nor did he hesitate, but hastened to it, listening and obeying. This indicates that he bore in the establishment of God's religion the greatest hardships. For this reason, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the victory﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. It is known that this trial fell upon the Messenger (ﷺ). So if the virtue of the Companions is magnified because of that hardship, what then is to be thought of the Messenger? And since it is established that his hardship was greater than the hardship of others, it is necessary that his virtue be greater than the virtue of others, due to his (ﷺ) saying: "The best acts of worship are the most arduous."

[Page 167]

The Ninth Argument: The religion of Muhammad, peace be upon him, is the best of religions, so it follows that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of the prophets.

The explanation of the first point: He, exalted is He, made Islam abrogating all other religions, and the abrogating must be superior, by His (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever establishes a good practice, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." Since this religion is superior and greater in reward, its founder is greater in reward than the founders of all other religions, so it follows that Muhammad, peace be upon him, is superior to all other prophets.

The Tenth Argument: The Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of nations, so it is necessary that Muhammad be the best of the prophets.

The explanation of the first point is His words: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

The explanation of the second point: this community attained this virtue only by following Muhammad (ﷺ). He said: ﴿Say: If you love God, then follow me; God will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31]. The virtue of the follower necessitates the virtue of the one followed. Also, Muhammad (ﷺ) has greater reward because he was sent to jinn and humans, so his reward must be greater, for the multitude of those who respond has an effect on the elevation of the one followed.

The Eleventh Argument: He, peace be upon him, is the Seal of the Messengers, so it is necessary that he be the best, because abrogating the superior by the inferior is considered ugly by reason.

The Twelfth Argument: The preference of some prophets over others is due to several matters:

Among them: the abundance of miracles, which indicate their truthfulness and necessitate their honouring. And there has occurred for our Prophet, peace be upon him, what exceeds three thousand. These are, in sum, of several kinds: some relate to power, such as feeding a large number of people with little food and giving them drink from little water; some relate to knowledge, such as informing about the unseen and the eloquence of the Qur'an; and some relate to his personal excellences, such as that he was of the most noble lineage among the nobles of the Arabs. He was also in the utmost bravery, as is related that after the combat of Ali, may God be pleased with him, with Amr ibn Wudd, he (ﷺ) said: "How did you find yourself, O Ali?" He said: "I found myself such that if all the people of Medina were on one side and I on the other, I would have prevailed over them." He said: "Prepare yourself, for a youth will come out of this valley to fight you," and the report continues to its end, and it is well known. Among them is his character, his forbearance, his fidelity, his eloquence and his generosity; and the books of hadith are full of the details of these subjects.

The Thirteenth Argument: His words, peace be upon him: "Adam and whoever is below him will be under my banner on the Day of Resurrection." This indicates that he is superior to Adam and to all of Adam's descendants. He, peace be upon him, also said: "I am the master of the sons of Adam, and there is no boast." And he, peace be upon him, said: "None of the prophets will enter Paradise until I enter it, and none of the nations will enter it until my nation enters it." Anas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am the first of people to come out when they are raised, and I am their speaker when they come in delegations, and I am their bringer of good news when they despair, the banner of praise is in my hand, and I am the most honoured of the sons of Adam before my Lord, and there is no boast." And from Ibn Abbas, who said: Some of the Companions sat discussing, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard their conversation. Some of them said: "How strange! God took Abraham as a close friend." Another said: "What is more wonderful than that God spoke to Moses directly?" Another said: "Jesus is the Word of God and His Spirit." Another said: "Adam was chosen by God." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came out and said: "I have heard your speech and your argument: that Abraham is the close friend of God, and he is so; Moses is the one who conversed with God, and he is so; Jesus is the Spirit of God, and he is so; Adam was chosen by God the Exalted, and he is so. Behold, I am the beloved of God, and there is no boast. I carry the banner of praise on the Day of Resurrection, and there is no boast. I am the first intercessor, and I am the first whose intercession is accepted on the Day of Resurrection, and there is no boast. I am the first to move the ring of Paradise, and it will be opened for me, and I will enter it, and with me will be the poor among the believers, and there is no boast. I am the most honoured of the first and the last, and there is no boast."

[Page 168]

The Fourteenth Argument: al-Bayhaqi narrated in *Fada'il al-Sahabah* that "Ali ibn Abi Talib appeared from afar, and he (peace be upon him) said: 'This is the master of the Arabs.' Aisha said: 'Are you not the master of the Arabs?' He said: 'I am the master of all the worlds, and he is the master of the Arabs.'" This indicates that he is the most excellent of the Prophets (peace be upon them).

The Fifteenth Argument: Mujahid narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been given five things that no one before me was given, and I say this without boasting: I was sent to the red and the black (all of mankind). Every prophet before me was sent only to his own people. The earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a purifier. I have been aided with terror striking (my enemies) a distance of a month's journey. Spoils of war have been made lawful for me, though they were not lawful for anyone before me. And I have been given intercession, which I have saved for my community, and it will be attained, God willing, by whoever does not associate anything with Allah." The point of inference is that this is explicit that Allah has favored him over others with these virtues.

The Sixteenth Argument: Muhammad ibn Isa al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, in explaining this meaning, said: Every ruler's maintenance (ma'unah, the resources he needs) is in proportion to his subjects. The ruler whose rule is over a village requires resources according to that village. Whoever rules the East and the West needs wealth and treasures greater than the wealth of the ruler of that village. Likewise, every messenger sent to his people is given from the treasures of monotheism (tawhid) and the jewels of knowledge in proportion to the message he carries. The messenger sent to his people in a particular region of the earth is given from these spiritual treasures only according to the extent of that place. The messenger sent to all the people of the East and the West, both mankind and jinn, must necessarily be given knowledge in proportion to what enables him to undertake the affairs of the people of the East and the West. Since this is so, the relation of Muhammad's prophethood to the prophethood of all the other prophets is like the relation of all the East and West to the dominion of some specific lands. Since this is so, it is inevitable that he was given treasures of wisdom and knowledge that no one before him was given, and so he attained in knowledge a level that no human being attained. Allah the Exalted said concerning him: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10]. And in eloquence, he said: "I have been given the comprehensive words (jawami' al-kalim)." His book became a guardian over the (previous) books, and his community became the best of communities.

The Seventeenth Argument: Muhammad ibn Isa al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated in the book *al-Nawadir*, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Allah took Ibrahim as a close friend (khalil), and Musa as one who conversed with Him (najiy), and He took me as a beloved (habib). Then He said: 'By My might and My majesty, I will certainly prefer My beloved over My close friend and My confidant.'"

The Eighteenth Argument: In the *Two Sahihs*, from Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My example and the example of the prophets before me is like a man who built a house, making it excellent, beautiful and complete, except for the place of one brick in one of its corners. The people began to walk around it, admiring the building, and they said: 'Why did you not place this brick, so that your building would be complete?' Muhammad said: 'I was that brick.'"

The Nineteenth Argument: Whenever Allah the Exalted called a prophet in the Qur'an, He called him by his name: ﴿O Adam, dwell﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]; ﴿And We called him: O Ibrahim﴾ [al-Saffat: 104]; ﴿O Musa﴾, ﴿Indeed I am your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 11-12]. As for the Prophet (peace be upon him), He addressed him with the words: ﴿O Prophet﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], ﴿O Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]. This indicates excellence.

* * *

The opponent argued with several points:

First: The miracles of the prophets were greater than his miracles. Adam (peace be upon him) was prostrated to by the angels, and Muhammad (peace be upon him) was not like that. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was thrown into great fires, which turned into coolness and peace for him. Musa (peace be upon him) was given those great miracles, and Muhammad did not have their like. Dawud had iron made soft in his hand. Sulayman had the jinn, mankind, birds, wild beasts and winds subjected to him, and none of that was granted to Muhammad (ﷺ). Isa was enabled by Allah to speak in infancy, and empowered to raise the dead and to heal the blind and the leper, and none of that was granted to Muhammad (ﷺ).

Second: He, the Exalted, named Ibrahim in His book a close friend (khalil), saying: ﴿And Allah took Ibrahim as a close friend﴾ [al-Nisa: 125]. He said of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa directly﴾ [al-Nisa: 164]. He said of Isa (peace be upon him): ﴿So We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. Some of this was not said concerning Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Third: His (peace be upon him) saying: "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta." And his (ﷺ) saying: "Do not make distinctions among the prophets."

Fourth: It is narrated "from Ibn Abbas, who said: We were in the mosque discussing the excellence of the prophets. We mentioned Nuh for the length of his worship, Ibrahim for his close friendship, Musa for Allah's speaking to him, and Isa for his being raised to heaven. We said: The Messenger of Allah is more excellent than them, for he was sent to all people, his past and future sins were forgiven, and he is the seal of the prophets. The Messenger of Allah entered and said: 'What are you discussing?' We told him, and he said: 'It is not fitting for anyone to be better than Yahya ibn Zakariyya,' because he never committed a sin nor even intended one."

The answer: That Adam (peace be upon him) was prostrated to by the angels does not necessitate that he is more excellent than Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is shown by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Adam and whoever is below him will be under my banner on the Day of Resurrection," and his saying: "I was a prophet while Adam was between water and clay." It is also reported that Jibril (peace be upon him) took hold of the stirrup of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the night of the Mi'raj, and this is greater than prostration. Furthermore, Allah Himself sent blessings upon Muhammad (ﷺ), and He commanded the angels and the believers to send blessings upon him, and that is more excellent than the prostration of the angels. This is indicated by several points:

First: He commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam as a discipline (ta'dib), and He commanded them to send blessings upon Muhammad (ﷺ) as a means of drawing near (taqrib).

Second: The sending of blessings upon Muhammad (peace be upon him) continues until the Day of Resurrection, whereas the prostration of the angels to Adam (peace be upon him) occurred only once.

Third: The prostration to Adam was undertaken by the angels alone, whereas the blessing upon Muhammad (ﷺ) was undertaken by the Lord of the worlds Himself, and then He commanded the angels and the believers to do it.

Fourth: The angels were commanded to prostrate to Adam because the light of Muhammad (peace be upon him) was in Adam's forehead.

If it is said: He, the Exalted, singled out Adam with knowledge, saying: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. As for Muhammad (peace be upon him), He said concerning him: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [al-Shura: 52], and He said: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Duha: 7]. Furthermore, the one who taught Adam was Allah the Exalted, as He said: ﴿And He taught Adam the names﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], whereas the teacher of Muhammad (peace be upon him) was Jibril (peace be upon him), by His saying: ﴿One mighty in power taught him﴾ [al-Najm: 5].

The answer: He, the Exalted, said concerning the knowledge of Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And He taught you what you did not know, and the bounty of Allah upon you has been great﴾ [al-Nisa: 113]. He (peace be upon him) said: "My Lord disciplined me, and He disciplined me well." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Most Merciful, taught the Qur'an﴾ [al-Rahman: 1-2]. He (peace be upon him) used to say: ("Show us things as they really are"). Allah the Exalted said to Muhammad (peace be upon him): ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. As for reconciling this with His saying: ﴿One mighty in power taught him﴾ [al-Najm: 5], this refers to instruction by way of inspiration (talqin), whereas the actual teaching is from Allah the Exalted, just as He said: ﴿Say: The angel of death will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11], and then He said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42].

[Page 170]

If it is said: Nuh (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And I am not one to drive away the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 114], and Allah the Exalted said to Muhammad (peace be upon him): ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 52]. This indicates that the character of Nuh is better.

We say: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We sent Nuh to his people, that warn your people before a painful punishment comes to them﴾ [Nuh: 1]. So his first command was about punishment. As for Muhammad (peace be upon him), it was said concerning him: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 107], and ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128] up to His saying: ﴿Kind and merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. The end result for Nuh was that he said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26], whereas the end result for Muhammad (peace be upon him) is intercession: ﴿Perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra: 79]. As for the rest of the miracles, it has been mentioned in books on the proofs of prophethood that for each one of them there is a miracle of Muhammad (ﷺ) that is more excellent than it. This book cannot bear more than what we have mentioned, and Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Among them is one to whom Allah spoke﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: What is meant is the one to whom Allah the Exalted spoke, and the pronoun (ha) is often omitted, as in His saying: ﴿And therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71].

The second issue: It has been read as (kallama Allaha) with the accusative (nasb). The first reading is more indicative of excellence, because every believer speaks to Allah, as he (peace be upon him) said: "The one who prays is conversing with his Lord." The honor lies only in Allah the Exalted speaking to him. Al-Yamani read (kalama Allah), from the verb of mutual speech (mukalamah), and this is supported by the saying "Kalim Allah," meaning one who converses with Him.

The third issue: They differed concerning what is heard from the one to whom Allah spoke. Is it the eternal, pre-eternal speech, which is neither a letter nor a sound, or something else? Al-Ash'ari (the founder of the Ash'ari school of theology) and his followers said: What is heard is that (eternal speech), for since it is not impossible to see what is not qualified (by modality), likewise it is not unlikely to hear what is not qualified. Al-Maturidi (the founder of the Maturidi school) said: Hearing that speech is impossible, and what is heard is only the letter and the sound.

The fourth issue: They agreed that Musa (peace be upon him) is meant by His saying: ﴿Among them is one to whom Allah spoke﴾. They said: The seventy chosen men of the people of Musa heard it, and they are the ones whom Allah meant by His saying: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. Did Muhammad (ﷺ) hear it on the night of the Mi'raj? They differed on this. Some of them said: Yes, based on His saying: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10].

If it is said: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Among them is one to whom Allah spoke﴾ aims to show the highest degree of virtue of those prophets to whom Allah the Exalted spoke. For this reason, when He exalted Musa (peace be upon him), He said: ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa directly﴾ [al-Nisa: 164]. Then in the Qur'an there is a conversation between Allah and Iblis, where He said: ﴿He said: Give me respite until the day they are resurrected﴾ ﴿He said: Indeed, you are of those given respite﴾ ﴿Until the day of the time made known﴾ [al-Hijr: 36-38], up to the end of these verses. The apparent meaning of these verses indicates much conversation between Allah and Iblis. If that necessitates the highest honor, how did Iblis come to be blamed? And if it does not necessitate honor, how did He mention it in the context of honoring Musa (peace be upon him), saying: ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa directly﴾ [al-Nisa: 164]?

The answer: The story of Iblis contains nothing indicating that He Himself spoke those replies to him without an intermediary, so perhaps there was an intermediary present.

[Page 171]

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He raised some of them in rank by degrees﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 253 (part 3 of 4):**

The first view: the purpose of the verse is to show that the ranks of the Messengers differ. God took Abraham as a close friend (khalil), and He did not grant anyone else this same virtue. He combined kingship and prophethood for David, which was not given to anyone else. He subjected to Solomon humans, jinn, birds and the wind, and this was not given to his father David, peace be upon them both. Muhammad, peace be upon him, is distinguished by being sent to both jinn and humans, and by his law (shar') abrogating (nasikh) all previous laws. This applies if we understand "degrees" as positions and ranks. If we understand them as miracles (mu'jizat), there is also a point here: each of the prophets was given a type of miracle suited to his time. The miracles of Moses, peace be upon him, namely the transformation of the staff into a serpent, the white hand, and the splitting of the sea, were like what the people of that age excelled in, which was magic. The miracles of Jesus, peace be upon him, namely healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead, were like what the people of that age excelled in, which was medicine. The miracle of Muhammad, peace be upon him, which is the Qur'an, was of the kind of eloquence, rhetoric, sermons and poetry. In sum, miracles differ in number and quantity, in lasting and not lasting, and in strength and lack of strength. There is a third view, which is that the intended meaning of the differing degrees is what concerns this world, namely the number of the community and companions and the strength of the state. If you reflect on these three aspects, you will know that Muhammad ﷺ combined all of them: his position is the highest, his miracles are the most enduring and the strongest, his people are the most numerous, and his dominion is the greatest and most abundant.

The second view: the verse intends Muhammad, peace be upon him, because he is the one preferred over all. God said ﴿and raised some of them in degrees﴾ in the manner of an indication and an allusion, like someone who has done a great deed and is asked, "Who did this?" and he replies, "One of you," or "Some of you," meaning himself. This is more majestic than stating it openly. Al-Hutay'ah was asked about the best poets, and he mentioned Zuhayr and al-Nabighah, then said, "If I wished, I would mention the third," meaning himself. If he had said, "If I wished, I would mention myself," it would have lost its grandeur.

If it is objected: the meaning of "and raised some of them in degrees" is the same as the meaning of "Those messengers: We preferred some of them over others," so what is the benefit of the repetition? Also, "Those messengers: We preferred some of them over others" is a general statement, and his saying after it "Among them are those to whom God spoke" begins the detailing of that general statement, and his saying after that "and raised some of them in degrees" is a restatement of that general point. It is known that restating a statement after beginning to detail its particulars is superfluous.

The answer: His saying "Those messengers: We preferred some of them over others" establishes that some were preferred over others. But it does not indicate whether that preference was achieved through many degrees or few degrees. So His saying "and raised some of them in degrees" carries an additional benefit, and therefore it is not a repetition.

As for God's saying ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book and We caused to follow﴾, there are questions about it.

The first question: God said at the beginning of the verse ﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾, then He shifted from this kind of speech to the third person (ghaybah), saying ﴿Among them are those to whom God spoke, and He raised some of them in degrees﴾, then He shifted from the third person back to the first kind of speech, saying ﴿And We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs﴾. So what is the benefit of shifting from direct address to the third person, and then from that back to direct address again?

The answer: His saying ﴿Among them are those to whom God spoke﴾ is more awe-inspiring and has greater impact than saying "Among them are those to whom We spoke." For this reason He said ﴿And God spoke to Moses directly﴾ [al-Nisa': 164]. For this purpose He chose the third-person form.

*  *  *

As for His saying ﴿And We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs﴾, He chose the direct-address form because the pronoun in His saying "And We gave" is the pronoun of magnification, and the magnification of the one who is given indicates the greatness of the giving.

The second question: Why did He single out Moses and Jesus from among the prophets for mention? Does this indicate that they are superior to others?

The answer: The reason for singling them out is that their miracles were more manifest and stronger than the miracles of others. Also, their communities are present and existing in this time, whereas the communities of the other prophets do not exist. So singling them out for mention is an indication of disparagement of their communities, as if it were said: these two Messengers, despite their high rank and the abundance of their miracles, did not win the obedience of their communities. Rather, they disputed and opposed, and they turned away from the duty of obeying them.

The third question: Singling out Jesus son of Mary for the giving of clear proofs indicates, or implies, that the giving of clear proofs did not occur with anyone else. It is known that this is impermissible. If you say: He singled them out for mention because those proofs were stronger, we say: the proofs of Moses, peace be upon him, were stronger than the proofs of Jesus, peace be upon him. And if they were not stronger, then they were at least equal.

The answer: The intent of this is to draw attention to the ugliness of the deeds of the Jews, in that they denied the prophethood of Jesus, peace be upon him, despite the manifest clear proofs that appeared at his hands.

The fourth question: "al-bayyinat" (the clear proofs) is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah), and that is not suitable for this context.

We say: We do not concede that it is the plural of paucity. And God knows best.

*  *  *

As for His saying ﴿And We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: the word al-qudus is pronounced with a heavy "dammah" (ḍamma) on the "dal" (al-qudus) by the people of the Hijaz, and lightened (al-qudus) by the Banu Tamim.

The second issue: there are several views on its interpretation.

The first: al-Hasan said: "al-Qudus" is God the Exalted, and "His spirit" is Gabriel, peace be upon him. The idafah (possessive construction) is for honour. The meaning is that He aided him with Gabriel, peace be upon him, at the beginning of his affair, in its middle, and at its end. At the beginning, this is based on His saying ﴿Then We breathed into him of Our spirit﴾. In the middle, Gabriel, peace be upon him, taught him the sciences and protected him from enemies. At the end, when the Jews wanted to kill him, Gabriel, peace be upon him, aided him and raised him to heaven. What indicates that the Holy Spirit is Gabriel, peace be upon him, is God's saying ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Nahl: 102].

The second view, which is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, is that the Holy Spirit is the Name by which Jesus, peace be upon him, used to revive the dead.

The third view, which is the view of Abu Muslim, is that the Holy Spirit with which he was strengthened may be the pure spirit which God breathed into him, and by which He distinguished him from others who were created from the union of the two drops of male and female.

*  *  *

Then God the Exalted said ﴿Had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, and there are issues concerning it.

The first issue: the connection of this with what precedes it is that after the Messengers had received the clear proofs, and the evidences and demonstrations had become manifest to them, their peoples differed. Some of them believed and some of them disbelieved, and because of that difference they fought and waged war.

The second issue: Those who hold that all events occur by God's decree and destiny argued from this verse, saying: The sense of the verse is: "Had God willed that they not fight, they would not have fought." The meaning is that the absence of fighting is necessarily connected with the will of the absence of fighting, and the absence of what is necessarily connected indicates the absence of what necessitates it. So, since fighting exists, we know that the will for the absence of fighting is not present, but rather what occurred was the will for fighting. There is no doubt that this fighting is a sin, and this indicates that disbelief and belief, obedience and disobedience, occur by God's decree, destiny and will, and that the killing and fighting of the disbelievers against the believers occurs by God the Exalted's will.

As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), they answered the argument and said: The purpose of the verse is to explain that if the disbelievers kill, that is not by overpowering God the Exalted. This purpose is achieved by saying that if He had willed, He would have destroyed them and annihilated them; or it is said: if He had willed, He would have stripped them of strength and power; or it is said: if He had willed, He would have prevented them from fighting by compulsion and force. Since this is so, His saying ﴿Had God willed﴾ means these kinds of will. This is like saying: "If the imam had willed, the Magians would not have worshipped fire in his kingdom, and the Christians would not have drunk wine," and what is meant is the will we have mentioned. Likewise here. Then al-Qadi (the judge) reinforced these answers and said: If will occurs in several ways and is negated in several ways, there is no indication in the apparent wording of the specific way intended, especially since these kinds of will are distinct and mutually contradictory.

The answer: Although the kinds of will differ and are distinct, they share the general fact of being will. What is mentioned in the verse, in the context of a condition, is will insofar as it is will, not insofar as it is a specific will. So this general concept must be realized. Restricting will to a particular will, whether the will of destruction, or the will of stripping strength and power, or the will of compulsion and force, is a restriction of the unrestricted, which is impermissible. Just as this specification contradicts the apparent sense of the wording, it also contradicts a decisive proof. This is because God the Exalted, being knowing of the occurrence of fighting, and knowledge of the occurrence of fighting at the time when fighting does not occur, is a combination of negation and affirmation, and of negation and assertion. So if at the moment of the knowledge of the existence of fighting He willed the absence of fighting, He would have willed the combination of negation and affirmation, and that is impossible. Thus it is established that the apparent sense of the verse is contrary to their view, and that the decisive proof is contrary to their view. And success is with God.

*  *  *

Then He said ﴿But they differed: some of them believed and some of them disbelieved﴾. We have already mentioned at the beginning of the verse that the meaning is: "Had He willed, they would not have differed." If they had not differed, they would not have fought. And since they differed, they inevitably fought. This verse indicates that an act does not occur except after the motive has come into existence, because He explained that difference necessitates fighting. The meaning is that their difference in religion motivates them to fight. This indicates that fighting occurs only for this motive, and that whenever this motive comes into being, fighting occurs. From this aspect it indicates that the act is impossible to occur in the absence of a motive, and necessary when the motive is present. And once this is established, it becomes clear that everything is by God's decree and destiny, because motives inevitably rest upon a motive which God creates in the servant, to avoid an infinite regress (tasalsul). Thus the verse also indicates, from this aspect, the soundness of our doctrine.

*  *  *

Then He said ﴿Had God willed, they would not have fought﴾. If it is said: What is the benefit of the repetition?

We say: al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: He repeated it for emphasis of the statement, and to refute those who claim that they did this of their own accord, and that no decree or destiny from God the Exalted had been involved in it.

Then He said: ﴿But Allah does what He intends﴾, so He grants success to whom He wills and forsakes whom He wills, and there is no objection to Him in His action. The Companions (al-Ashab, i.e., the Ash'arite scholars) used this verse as evidence that He, may He be exalted, is the Creator of the faith of believers. They said: since the opponent agrees that He, may He be exalted, wills faith from the believer, and the verse indicates that He does whatever He wills, it follows that the one who creates the faith of the believer is Allah, may He be exalted. Also, since it indicates that He does whatever He wills, then if He willed faith from the disbelievers, He would have created faith in them and they would be believers. Since that is not the case, it indicates that He, may He be exalted, does not will faith from them. So this verse indicates the issue of the creation of actions and the issue of the will of created beings.

The Mu'tazilah restrict the unrestricted and say: the meaning is "He does whatever He wills of His own actions." This is weak, for several reasons:

First: it is a restriction of the unrestricted (taqyid al-mutlaq).

Second: on this restriction, the verse becomes an explanation of the obvious, for the meaning of the verse becomes "He does what He does."

Third: every person is like this, so describing Allah, may He be exalted, with this does not serve as evidence of the perfection of His power and the loftiness of His rank. And Allah knows best.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿يا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَنْفِقُوا مِمَّا رَزَقْناكُمْ مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ يَوْمٌ لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ وَلا خُلَّةٌ وَلا شَفاعَةٌ وَالكافِرُونَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾

اعْلَمْ أنَّ أصْعَبَ الأشْياءِ عَلى الإنْسانِ بَذْلُ النَّفْسِ في القِتالِ، وبَذْلُ المالِ في الإنْفاقِ، فَلَمّا قَدَّمَ الأمْرَ بِالقِتالِ أعْقَبَهُ بِالأمْرِ بِالإنْفاقِ. وأيْضًا فِيهِ وجْهٌ آخَرُ، وهو أنَّهُ تَعالى أمَرَ بِالقِتالِ فِيما سَبَقَ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وَقاتِلُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ [البقرة: ١٩٠]، ثُمَّ أعْقَبَهُ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿مَنْ ذا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا﴾ [البقرة: ٢٤٥]، والمَقْصُودُ مِنهُ إنْفاقُ المالِ في الجِهادِ. ثُمَّ إنَّهُ مَرَّةً ثانِيَةً أكَّدَ الأمْرَ بِالقِتالِ وذَكَرَ فِيهِ قِصَّةَ طالُوتَ، ثُمَّ أعْقَبَهُ بِالأمْرِ بِالإنْفاقِ في الجِهادِ، وهو قَوْلُهُ: ﴿يا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَنْفِقُوا﴾.

إذا عَرَفْتَ وجْهَ النَّظْمِ فَنَقُولُ: في الآيَةِ مَسائِلُ:

المَسْألَةُ الأُولى: احْتَجَّ المُعْتَزِلَةُ (Mu'tazilah، وهم أهل الاعتزال) عَلى أنَّ الرِّزْقَ لا يَكُونُ إلّا حَلالًا بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿أَنْفِقُوا مِمَّا رَزَقْناكُمْ﴾. فَنَقُولُ: اللَّهُ تَعالى أمَرَ بِالإنْفاقِ مِنْ كُلِّ ما كانَ رِزْقًا بِالإجْماعِ، أمّا ما كانَ حَرامًا فَإنَّهُ لا يَجُوزُ إنْفاقُهُ، وهَذا يُفِيدُ القَطْعَ بِأنَّ الرِّزْقَ لا يَكُونُ حَرامًا. والأصْحابُ قالُوا: ظاهِرُ الآيَةِ وإنْ كانَ يَدُلُّ عَلى الأمْرِ بِإنْفاقِ كُلِّ ما كانَ رِزْقًا، إلّا أنّا نُخَصِّصُ هَذا الأمْرَ بِإنْفاقِ كُلِّ ما كانَ رِزْقًا حَلالًا.

المَسْألَةُ الثّانِيَةُ: اخْتَلَفُوا في أنَّ قَوْلَهُ: (أَنْفِقُوا) مُخْتَصٌّ بِالإنْفاقِ الواجِبِ كالزَّكاةِ، أمْ هو عامٌّ في كُلِّ الإنْفاقاتِ، سَواءٌ كانَتْ واجِبَةً أوْ مَنْدُوبَةً؟ فَقالَ الحَسَنُ (يعني الحسن البصري): هَذا الأمْرُ مُخْتَصٌّ بِالزَّكاةِ، قالَ: لِأنَّ قَوْلَهُ: ﴿مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ يَوْمٌ لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ وَلا خُلَّةٌ﴾ كالوَعْدِ والوَعِيدِ لا يَتَوَجَّهُ إلّا عَلى الواجِبِ. وقالَ الأكْثَرُونَ: هَذا الأمْرُ يَتَناوَلُ الواجِبَ والمَنْدُوبَ، ولَيْسَ في الآيَةِ وعِيدٌ، فَكَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: حَصِّلُوا مَنافِعَ الآخِرَةِ حِينَ تَكُونُونَ في الدُّنْيا، فَإنَّكُمْ

[صفحة ١٧٥]
إذا خَرَجْتُمْ مِنَ الدُّنْيا لا يُمْكِنُكُمْ تَحْصِيلُها واكْتِسابُها في الآخِرَةِ.
والقَوْلُ الثّالِثُ: أنَّ المُرادَ مِنهُ الإنْفاقُ في الجِهادِ، والدَّلِيلُ عَلَيْهِ أنَّهُ مَذْكُورٌ بَعْدَ الأمْرِ بِالجِهادِ، فَكانَ المُرادُ مِنهُ الإنْفاقَ في الجِهادِ، وهَذا قَوْلُ الأصَمِّ.

المَسْألَةُ الثّالِثَةُ: قَرَأ ابْنُ كَثِيرٍ وأبُو عَمْرٍو (لا بَيْعَ ولا خُلَّةَ ولا شَفاعَةَ) بِالنَّصْبِ، وفي سُورَةِ إبْراهِيمَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ ﴿لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ ولا خِلالٌ﴾ [إبراهيم: ٣١]، وفي الطُّورِ ﴿لا لَغْوٌ فِيها ولا تَأْثِيمٌ﴾ [الطور: ٢٣]. والباقُونَ جَمِيعًا بِالرَّفْعِ. والفَرْقُ بَيْنَ النَّصْبِ والرَّفْعِ قَدْ ذَكَرْناهُ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَلا رَفَثَ ولا فُسُوقَ ولا جِدالَ﴾ [البقرة: ١٩٧].

* * *

المَسْألَةُ الرّابِعَةُ: المَقْصُودُ مِنَ الآيَةِ أنَّ الإنْسانَ يَجِيءُ وحْدَهُ، ولا يَكُونُ مَعَهُ شَيْءٌ مِمّا حَصَّلَهُ في الدُّنْيا، قالَ تَعالى: ﴿وَلَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونا فُرادى كَما خَلَقْناكُمْ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ وَتَرَكْتُمْ ما خَوَّلْناكُمْ وَراءَ ظُهُورِكُمْ﴾ [الأنعام: ٩٤]، وقالَ: ﴿وَنَرِثُهُ ما يَقُولُ وَيَأْتِينا فَرْدًا﴾ [مريم: ٨٠].
أمّا قَوْلُهُ: ﴿لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ﴾ فَفِيهِ وجْهانِ:

الأوَّلُ: أنَّ البَيْعَ هَهُنا بِمَعْنى الفِدْيَةِ، كَما قالَ: ﴿فَالْيَوْمَ لا يُؤْخَذُ مِنْكُمْ فِدْيَةٌ﴾ [الحديد: ١٥]، وقالَ: ﴿وَلا يُقْبَلُ مِنْها عَدْلٌ﴾ [البقرة: ١٢٣]، وقالَ: ﴿وَإِنْ تَعْدِلْ كُلَّ عَدْلٍ لا يُؤْخَذْ مِنْها﴾ [الأنعام: ٧٠]. فَكَأنَّهُ قالَ: مِنْ قَبْلِ أنْ يَأْتِيَ يَوْمٌ لا تِجارَةَ فِيهِ فَتَكْتَسِبَ ما تَفْتَدِي بِهِ مِنَ العَذابِ.

والثّانِي: أنْ يَكُونَ المَعْنى: قَدِّمُوا لِأنْفُسِكُمْ مِنَ المالِ الَّذِي هو في مِلْكِكُمْ قَبْلَ أنْ يَأْتِيَ اليَوْمُ الَّذِي لا يَكُونُ فِيهِ تِجارَةٌ ولا مُبايَعَةٌ حَتّى يُكْتَسَبَ شَيْءٌ مِنَ المالِ.

أمّا قَوْلُهُ: ﴿وَلا خُلَّةٌ﴾ فالمُرادُ المَوَدَّةُ، ونَظِيرُهُ مِنَ الآياتِ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿الْأَخِلّاءُ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَعْضُهُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ إلّا الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [الزخرف: ٦٧]، وقالَ: ﴿وَتَقَطَّعَتْ بِهِمُ الْأَسْبابُ﴾ [البقرة: ١٦٦]، وقالَ: ﴿ثُمَّ يَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ يَكْفُرُ بَعْضُكُمْ بِبَعْضٍ وَيَلْعَنُ بَعْضُكُمْ بَعْضًا﴾ [العنكبوت: ٢٥]، وقالَ حِكايَةً عَنِ الكُفّارِ: ﴿فَما لَنا مِنْ شافِعِينَ﴾ ﴿وَلا صَدِيقٍ حَمِيمٍ﴾ [الشعراء: ١٠٠-١٠١]، وقالَ: ﴿وَما لِلظّالِمِينَ مِنْ أَنْصارٍ﴾ [البقرة: ٢٧٠]. وأمّا قَوْلُهُ: ﴿وَلا شَفاعَةٌ﴾ فَيَقْتَضِي نَفْيَ كُلِّ الشَّفاعاتِ.

واعْلَمْ أنَّ قَوْلَهُ: ﴿وَلا خُلَّةٌ وَلا شَفاعَةٌ﴾ عامٌّ في الكُلِّ، إلّا أنَّ سائِرَ الدَّلائِلِ دَلَّتْ عَلى ثُبُوتِ المَوَدَّةِ والمَحَبَّةِ بَيْنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ، وعَلى ثُبُوتِ الشَّفاعَةِ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ، وقَدْ بَيَّنّاهُ في تَفْسِيرِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وَاتَّقُوا يَوْمًا تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إلَى اللَّهِ﴾ [البقرة: ٢٨١]، و﴿لا تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَنْ نَفْسٍ شَيْئًا وَلا يُقْبَلُ مِنْها شَفاعَةٌ﴾ [البقرة: ٤٨].

واعْلَمْ أنَّ السَّبَبَ في عَدَمِ الخُلَّةِ والشَّفاعَةِ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ أُمُورٌ:

أحَدُها: أنَّ كُلَّ أحَدٍ يَكُونُ مَشْغُولًا بِنَفْسِهِ، عَلى ما قالَ تَعالى: ﴿لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مِنْهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ شَأْنٌ يُغْنِيهِ﴾ [عبس: ٣٧].

والثّانِي: أنَّ الخَوْفَ الشَّدِيدَ غالِبٌ عَلى كُلِّ أحَدٍ، عَلى ما قالَ: ﴿يَوْمَ تَرَوْنَها تَذْهَلُ كُلُّ مُرْضِعَةٍ عَمّا أَرْضَعَتْ وَتَضَعُ كُلُّ ذاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَها وَتَرَى النّاسَ سُكارى وَما هُمْ بِسُكارى﴾ [الحج: ٢].

والثّالِثُ: أنَّهُ إذا نَزَلَ العَذابُ بِسَبَبِ الكُفْرِ والفِسْقِ صارَ مُبَغِّضًا لِهَذَيْنِ الأمْرَيْنِ، وإذا صارَ مُبَغِّضًا لَهُما صارَ مُبَغِّضًا لِمَنْ كانَ مَوْصُوفًا بِهِما.

أمّا قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَالْكافِرُونَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾ فَنُقِلَ عَنْ عَطاءِ بْنِ يَسارٍ أنَّهُ كانَ يَقُولُ: الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي قالَ: ﴿وَالْكافِرُونَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾ ولَمْ يَقُلِ: الظّالِمُونَ هُمُ الكافِرُونَ. ثُمَّ ذَكَرُوا في تَأْوِيلِ هَذِهِ الآيَةِ وُجُوهًا:

أحَدُها: أنَّهُ تَعالى لَمّا قالَ: ﴿وَلا خُلَّةٌ وَلا شَفاعَةٌ﴾ أوْهَمَ ذَلِكَ نَفْيَ الخُلَّةِ والشَّفاعَةِ مُطْلَقًا، فَذَكَرَ تَعالى عَقِيبَهُ: ﴿وَالْكافِرُونَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾ لِيَدُلَّ عَلى أنَّ ذَلِكَ النَّفْيَ مُخْتَصٌّ بِالكافِرِينَ، وعَلى هَذا التَّقْدِيرِ تَصِيرُ الآيَةُ دالَّةً

[صفحة ١٧٦]
عَلى إثْباتِ الشَّفاعَةِ في حَقِّ الفُسّاقِ. قالَ القاضِي: هَذا التَّأْوِيلُ غَيْرُ صَحِيحٍ؛ لِأنَّ قَوْلَهُ: ﴿وَالْكافِرُونَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾ كَلامٌ مُبْتَدَأٌ فَلَمْ يَجِبْ تَعْلِيقُهُ بِما تَقَدَّمَ.
والجَوابُ: أنّا لَوْ جَعَلْنا هَذا الكَلامَ مُبْتَدَأً تَطَرَّقَ الخُلْفُ إلى كَلامِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، لِأنَّ غَيْرَ الكافِرِينَ قَدْ يَكُونُ ظالِمًا. أمّا إذا عَلَّقْناهُ بِما تَقَدَّمَ زالَ الإشْكالُ، فَوَجَبَ المَصِيرُ إلى تَعْلِيقِهِ بِما قَبْلَهُ.

التَّأْوِيلُ الثّانِي: أنَّ الكافِرِينَ إذا دَخَلُوا النّارَ عَجَزُوا عَنِ التَّخَلُّصِ عَنْ ذَلِكَ العَذابِ، فاللَّهُ تَعالى لَمْ يَظْلِمْهُمْ بِذَلِكَ العَذابِ، بَلْ هُمُ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا أنْفُسَهُمْ حَيْثُ اخْتارُوا الكُفْرَ والفِسْقَ حَتّى صارُوا مُسْتَحِقِّينَ لِهَذا العَذابِ، ونَظِيرُهُ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَوَجَدُوا ما عَمِلُوا حاضِرًا وَلا يَظْلِمُ رَبُّكَ أَحَدًا﴾ [الكهف: ٤٩].

والتَّأْوِيلُ الثّالِثُ: أنَّ الكافِرِينَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ حَيْثُ تَرَكُوا تَقْدِيمَ الخَيْراتِ لِيَوْمِ فاقَتِهِمْ وحاجَتِهِمْ، وأنْتُمْ أيُّها الحاضِرُونَ لا تَقْتَدُوا بِهِمْ في هَذا الِاخْتِيارِ الرَّدِيءِ، ولَكِنْ قَدِّمُوا لِأنْفُسِكُمْ ما تَجْعَلُونَهُ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ فِدْيَةً لِأنْفُسِكُمْ مِنْ عَذابِ اللَّهِ.

والتَّأْوِيلُ الرّابِعُ: الكافِرُونَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ لِأنْفُسِهِمْ بِوَضْعِ الأُمُورِ في غَيْرِ مَواضِعِها، لِتَوَقُّعِهِمُ الشَّفاعَةَ مِمَّنْ لا يَشْفَعُ لَهُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ، فَإنَّهُمْ كانُوا يَقُولُونَ في الأوْثانِ: هَؤُلاءِ شُفَعاؤُنا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ، وقالُوا أيْضًا: ما نَعْبُدُهُمْ إلّا لِيُقَرِّبُونا إلى اللَّهِ زُلْفى. فَمَنْ عَبَدَ جَمادًا وتَوَقَّعَ أنْ يَكُونَ شَفِيعًا لَهُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ فَقَدْ ظَلَمَ نَفْسَهُ حَيْثُ تَوَقَّعَ الخَيْرَ مِمَّنْ لا يَجُوزُ التَّوَقُّعُ مِنْهُ.

والتَّأْوِيلُ الخامِسُ: المُرادُ مِنَ الظُّلْمِ تَرْكُ الإنْفاقِ، قالَ تَعالى: ﴿آتَتْ أُكُلَها وَلَمْ تَظْلِمْ مِنْهُ شَيْئًا﴾ [الكهف: ٣٣]، أيْ: أعْطَتْ ولَمْ تَمْنَعْ. فَيَكُونُ مَعْنى الآيَةِ: والكافِرُونَ التّارِكُونَ لِلْإنْفاقِ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ، وأمّا المُسْلِمُ فَلا بُدَّ وأنْ يُنْفِقَ مِنْهُ شَيْئًا قَلَّ أوْ كَثُرَ.

والتَّأْوِيلُ السّادِسُ: ﴿وَالْكافِرُونَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾ أيْ: هُمُ الكامِلُونَ في الظُّلْمِ البالِغُونَ المَبْلَغَ العَظِيمَ فِيهِ، كَما يُقالُ: العُلَماءُ هُمُ المُتَكَلِّمُونَ، أيْ هُمُ الكامِلُونَ في العِلْمِ، فَكَذا هَهُنا. وأكْثَرُ هَذِهِ الوُجُوهِ قَدْ ذَكَرَها القَفّالُ رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ. واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah! There is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Seat extends over the heavens and the earth, and He feels no burden in preserving them, and He is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

Know that it is among the practice of Him, glorified and exalted, in this noble Book, that He mixes these three types with one another: I mean the science of tawhid (the science of God's oneness), the science of rulings (ahkam), and the science of narratives (qasas). The purpose of mentioning the narratives is either to establish the proofs of tawhid, or to emphasize the binding of the rulings and obligations. This method is the best method, since keeping a person in a single type would cause weariness. When a person moves from one type of knowledge to another type, it opens his breast and gladdens his heart. It is as if he has traveled from one land to another and moved from one garden to another garden, and moved from eating one delicious food to eating another kind. There is no doubt that it becomes more delightful and more appetizing. And since He mentioned previously, from the science of rulings and the science of narratives, what He saw as beneficial, He now mentions what relates to the science of tawhid, and said: ﴿Allah! There is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ And in the verse there are issues:

The first issue: concerning the virtues of this verse. It has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "No house in which this verse is recited is entered by the devils for thirty days, and no sorcerer or sorceress enters it for forty nights." And from Ali that he said: I heard your Prophet on the pulpit steps saying: "Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne after every obligatory prayer, nothing will prevent him from entering Paradise except death, and none persists in it except a truthful one (siddiq) or a worshipper. And whoever recites it when he takes his bed, Allah will grant him safety for himself, his neighbor, his neighbor's neighbor, and the households around him." And the Companions discussed the best of what is in the Qur'an, and Ali said to them: Where are you from the Verse of the Throne? Then he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "O Ali, the lord of mankind is Adam, the lord of the Arabs is Muhammad, without boasting, the lord of speech is the Qur'an, the lord of the Qur'an is al-Baqarah, and the lord of al-Baqarah is the Verse of the Throne." And from Ali that he said: On the day of Badr I fought, then I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to see what he was doing. He said: I came while he was prostrating and saying: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting," and he did not add anything to that. Then I returned to the fighting, then I came and he was saying that, and I kept going back and forth and looking at him, and he did not add more to that until Allah granted him victory.

Know that remembrance and knowledge follow what is remembered and known. So whenever what is remembered and known is more noble, the remembrance and knowledge are more noble. The most noble of what is remembered and known is Allah, glorified is He. Indeed, He is exalted above being said to be more noble than other than Him, because that would imply a kind of similarity and resemblance, and He is sanctified above the similarity of anything other than Him. For this reason, every speech that includes the attributes of His majesty and the qualities of His greatness is in the highest degree of majesty and nobility. And since this verse is like that, it is inevitable that this verse reaches the utmost of nobility and the most eloquent of ends.

* * *

The second issue: know that the explanation of the word "Allah" has preceded at the beginning of the book, and the explanation of His saying ﴿there is no god but He﴾ has preceded in His saying: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no god but He﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163]. What remains here is that we speak about the explanation of His saying ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to say: the greatest of the names of Allah is ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. And what we have related, that he, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, did not add to His remembrance during prostration on the day of Badr, indicates the greatness of this name. The rational proofs also indicate its soundness. Its establishment, and from Allah is success, is as follows: There is no doubt in the existence of existent things. They are either all possible, or all necessary, or some of them possible and some necessary. It is impossible that they are all possible, because every aggregate depends on each one of its parts, and each one of the parts of this aggregate is possible, and what depends on the possible is more entitled to possibility. So this aggregate is possible in itself. And each one of its parts is possible, for its existence is not preferred over its non-existence except by a determining cause other than itself. So this aggregate depends, by virtue of being an aggregate and by virtue of each of its parts, on a determining cause other than itself. And whatever is other than all possible things is not possible, so there exists an existent that is not possible. Thus the claim that every existent is possible is invalidated.

As for the second division, namely that it is said: all existents are necessary, this is also invalid. For if there were two existences, each of which is necessary in itself, they would share in necessity by essence and differ in being distinct. What makes them share is other than what makes them distinct. So each of them would be composed, in its necessity, of that by which they share and that by which they are distinguished. Every composite depends on each of its parts and on the part of another, and every composite depends on something other than itself, and everything that depends on something other than itself is possible in itself. So if the Necessary Existent were more than one, none of them would be Necessary Existent, and that is impossible. Since these two divisions are invalidated, it is established that among the aggregate of existents there is one existent that is necessary in itself, and that everything other than it is possible in itself and exists through the bringing into existence of that existent which is necessary in itself. Since these two are invalidated, the Necessary in itself exists in and through itself, and is independent in its existence of everything other than itself. As for everything other than it, it depends in its existence and quiddity on the bringing into being by the Necessary in itself. So the Necessary in itself subsists by itself, and is the cause of the subsistence of everything other than it in its quiddity and in its existence. He is the Living, the Self-Subsisting with respect to all existents. Al-Qayyum is the one who subsists by Himself, who sustains everything other than Himself in its quiddity and existence. And since He is Necessary in Himself, He is the true Self-Subsisting with respect to all. Then, since the agent in other things is either an agent by way of causation and necessitation, or an agent by way of choice and will, he therefore removed the illusion of His being an agent by causation and necessitation by His saying ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. For the Living is the Perceiver, the Doer. By His saying "the Living" He indicated that He is Knowing and Powerful, and by His saying "the Self-Subsisting" He indicated that He subsists by His essence and sustains everything other than Himself. From these two principles branch out all the issues considered in the science of tawhid.

The first of them: the Necessary Existent is one, in the sense that its quiddity is not composed of parts. Its proof is that every composite depends for its realization on the realization of each of its parts, and its part is other than it, and every composite is sustained by other than itself, and what is sustained by other than itself is not self-subsisting, so it is not Self-Subsisting. We have already shown by proof that He is Self-Subsisting. And when it is established that He, exalted is He, is one in His essence, this principle has two corollaries. One of them: the Necessary Existent is one, in the sense that there are not in existence two things each of which is necessary in itself. For if that were assumed, they would share in necessity and differ in determination, and what makes them share is other than what makes them differ, so each of them would be composed of two parts, and we have shown that this is impossible.

The second corollary: since it is impossible in His reality that He be composed of two parts, it is impossible that He be spatially located, for every spatially located thing is divisible, and it has been established that composition is impossible for Him. And when it is established that He is not spatially located, it is impossible that He be in a direction, for there is no meaning to "spatially located" except that which can be pointed to by a sensory indication. And when it is established that He is neither spatially located nor in a direction, it is impossible that He have limbs, movement, or rest.

Second: since He is Self-Subsisting, He subsists by His essence, and His subsisting by His essence requires several matters:

The first corollary: He is not an accident in a subject, nor a form in matter, nor a state in a locus at all, for the state depends on a locus, and what depends on other than itself is not self-subsisting by essence.

The second corollary: some scholars said: there is no meaning to knowledge except the presence of the reality of the known to the knower. So when He is Self-Subsisting in the sense that He subsists by His own self and not by other than Himself, His reality is present to His essence. And since there is no meaning to knowledge except this presence, it must be that His reality is known to His essence. Thus His essence is known to His essence. And everything other than Him comes into being only through His influence. And since we have shown that He is Self-Subsisting in the sense that He sustains others, that influence, if it is by choice, then the choosing agent must have awareness of his act; and if it is by necessitation, it also necessarily follows that He knows everything other than Himself, because His essence necessitates everything other than Himself. And we have shown that from His subsisting by His own self it follows that He knows His essence, and knowledge of the cause is a cause of knowledge of the effect. So in all the scenarios it follows from His being Self-Subsisting that He knows all the known things.

Third: since He is Self-Subsisting for everything other than Himself, everything other than Himself is originated, because His influence in sustaining that other cannot be while that other is remaining, for the realization of what is already realized is impossible. So it is either in the state of its non-existence or in the state of its coming into being, and in either case everything must be originated.

Fourth: since He is Self-Subsisting for all possible things, all possible things are traced back to Him, either through an intermediary or without an intermediary, and in either case the doctrine of qada' and qadar (divine decree and measure) is true. We have explained and clarified this in this book in many verses. So if success assists you and you reflect on these foundations that we have mentioned, you will know that there is no way to comprehend any of the issues related to the divine knowledge except through His, exalted is He, being Living and Self-Subsisting. Therefore it is not far-fetched that the Greatest Name is this one. As for the rest of the divine verses, such as His saying: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no god but He﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163], and His saying ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 18], it contains an explanation of tawhid in the sense of negating any counterpart and equal. As for His saying ﴿Say: He is Allah, One﴾, it contains an explanation of tawhid in the sense of negating any counterpart and equal, and in the sense that His reality is not composed of parts. As for His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], it contains an explanation of the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah), and there is in it no explanation of the unity of reality. As for His saying ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, it indicates all of that, because His being Self-Subsisting requires that He subsist by His own self and that He sustain others. His subsisting by His own self requires oneness in the sense of negating multiplicity in His reality, and that requires oneness in the sense of negating counterpart and equal, and it requires negating spatial location, and through that it requires negating direction. Also, His being Self-Subsisting in the sense of sustaining others requires the origination of everything other than Him, whether body or spirit, intellect or soul, and it requires that everything be traced back to Him, and that the whole chain of causes and effects terminate in Him, and this necessitates the doctrine of qada' and qadar. Thus it becomes clear that these two words are like encompassing all the topics of the divine science. Therefore this verse has reached the furthest goal in nobility, and it is fitting that it be the Greatest Name among the names of Allah, exalted is He.

Then, when He, may He be exalted, had shown that He is the Living, the Self-Subsisting, He affirmed this by His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾. The meaning is that He is not heedless of the governance of creation, for the one in charge of a child, if he were heedless of him for a moment, the child's affairs would fall into disorder. He, glorified is He, is the Sustainer of all originated things and the Self-Subsisting of all contingent things, so it is impossible that He should be heedless of their governance. His saying ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ is thus like an emphasis clarifying that He is Self-Standing. It is like what is said to one who neglects and is negligent: "Indeed you are drowsy and asleep."

Then, when He, may He be exalted, had shown that His being Self-Subsisting means His standing by His own essence and sustaining others, He established a ruling upon it, which is His saying: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. For since everything other than Him has its quiddity sustained, and its existence obtained only through His sustaining, bringing into being and creating, it follows that everything other than Him is His dominion and His possession. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. Then, when it has been established that He is the King and the Owner of everything other than Him, it is established that His judgment executes over all, and that no other has any ruling over anything except by His permission and command. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾

Then, when He had shown that it follows from His being the Owner of all that no other may have any disposal in His dominion in any way, He also showed that it follows from His being Knowing of all, and others not being Knowing of all, that no other may have any disposal in His dominion in any way except by His permission. This is His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, which indicates His, glorified is He, being Knowing of all. Then He said: ﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾, which indicates that others are not knowing of all the knowables. Then, when He had shown the perfection of His dominion and judgment in the heavens and the earth, He showed that His dominion beyond the heavens and the earth is greater and more majestic, and that this is something to which the imaginings of the imaginers cannot reach, and which the fancies of the fanciful cannot attain even to the lowest of its degrees. So He said: ﴿His Footstool encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾. Then He showed that the execution of His judgment and dominion over all is in one manner and one form, so He said: ﴿And the preserving of them does not weary Him﴾. Then, when He had shown His being Self-Subsisting in the sense of sustaining originated, contingent and created things, He showed His being Self-Subsisting in the sense of standing by His own self and essence, free from need of another in any matter. So He is exalted above being spatially delimited such that He would need a place, or changing such that He would need a time. Thus He said: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾. What is meant by it is loftiness and greatness, in the sense that He does not need another in any matter, and is not attributed to another in any quality or any description. So He said: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾, as an indication of what He began with in the verse, namely His being Self-Subsisting in the sense of standing by His own essence and sustaining others. Whoever's intellect has encompassed what we have mentioned knows that there is no more perfect speech about divine matters among the human intellects, nor a clearer proof, than what these verses contain.

Now that you have known these secrets, let us return to the apparent exegesis.

As for His saying: ﴿Allah — there is no god but Him﴾, there are two issues in it.

The first issue: (Allah) is in the nominative by being the subject (mubtada'), and what follows it is its predicate (khabar).

The second issue: Some said: al-Ilah is the one worshipped (al-ma'bud). This is an error for two reasons:

The first: He, exalted is He, was a god (Ilah) in eternity, and was not worshipped.

The second: He, exalted is He, affirmed in the Qur'an a worshipped other than Him by His saying: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98]. Rather, al-Ilah is the One Who is capable of that which, if He does it, He deserves to be worshipped.

As for His saying: (al-Hayy), there are issues in it:

The first issue: al-Hayy originally is hayiy, like hadhir and tama', so the yā' was assimilated into the yā' when they came together. Ibn al-Anbari said: its origin is al-hayw; when the yā' and the wāw came together, and the earlier of them was sukūn, they were both made into a shaddah yā'.

The second issue: The theologians said: al-Hayy is every essence that is valid to know and to be able. They differed over whether this concept is an existent attribute or not. Some said: it is an expression of the thing's being such that it is not impossible that it knows and is able, and the non-impossibility is not an existent attribute. The verifiers said: Since life is an expression of non-impossibility, and it has been established that impossibility is a negative matter, for if it were an existent attribute, the thing described by it would be existent, so that which is impossible to exist would be existent, which is absurd; and it has been established that impossibility is a non-existence, and that life is the non-existence of this impossibility, and that the non-existence of a non-existence is an existence, it follows that the concept of life is an existent attribute, which is what was sought.

The third issue: Someone may say: since the meaning of al-Hayy is that He is the One who is valid to know and be able, and this measure is present in all living beings, how is it fitting that God praise Himself with an attribute in which the basest of living beings shares with Him?

What I hold in this regard is that al-Hayy in the origin of the language is not an expression of this validity; rather, everything that is perfect in its kind is called living. Do you not see that the cultivating of a ruined land is called "reviving the dead"? And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Look then at the traces of the mercy of Allah, how He revives the earth after its death﴾ [al-Rum: 50], and He said: ﴿to a dead land, and We revived by it the earth﴾ [Fatir: 9]. The attribute named in the usage of the theologians was named "life" only because the perfect state of a body is to be described by that attribute, so that attribute was necessarily called life. The perfect state of trees is to be green and leafy, so that state was necessarily called life. The perfect state of the earth is to be inhabited, so that state was necessarily called life. Thus it is established that the original concept of the word al-Hayy is its being applied to the most perfect of its states and attributes. When this is so, the difficulty disappears, because the concept of al-Hayy is the Perfect. And since it is not restricted by being perfect in this respect rather than that, this indicates that He is perfect absolutely. So His saying al-Hayy conveys that He is perfect absolutely, and the perfect is one that is not receptive to non-existence, neither in His essence, nor in His real attributes, nor in His relational and additional attributes. Then, on this basis, if we restrict al-Qayyum to being the cause of the standing of others, the difficulty disappears, because His being the cause of the standing of others indicates His being self-standing, and His being al-Qayyum indicates His sustaining others. And if we make al-Qayyum a name that indicates that it includes both the self-standing and the sustainer of others, then the word al-Qayyum conveys the benefit of the word al-Hayy with an addition. This is what I hold in this regard, and Allah knows best.

Page 8

As for His, exalted is He, saying: (al-Qayyum), there are issues in it:

The first issue: al-Qayyum in the language is an intensive form of al-Qa'im (the one standing). When the yā' and the wāw came together, and the earlier was sukūn, they were both made into a shaddah yā'. It cannot be on the pattern fa'ul, for if it were so it would be qawwum. In it there are three dialects: qayyum, qayyam, and qayyim. It is narrated from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited: al-Hayy al-Qayyam. Some people said: this word is Hebrew, not Arabic, because they say: hayyan qayyuman. This is not so, for we have shown that it has a sound linguistic basis. Similar to it is: ma fi al-dar dayyar, and dayyur, and dayyir, and it is from al-dawaran, i.e., there is no creature in it that turns, meaning one who comes and goes. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"The Overseer, the Self-Subsisting, has decreed it."

The second issue: The expressions of the exegetes differed in this matter. Mujahid said: al-Qayyum is the one standing over every thing, and its interpretation is that He stands in directing the affairs of creation in their bringing into being and in their provisions. Its parallel among the verses is His saying: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33], and He said: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], up to His saying ﴿standing in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], and He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, no one could hold them after Him﴾ [Fatir: 41]. This saying's ultimate meaning returns to His being the sustainer of others. Qatada... [sic] al-Dahhak said: al-Qayyum is the One whose existence is lasting, who is impossible to change. I say: this saying's meaning returns to His being self-standing in His essence and His existence. Some said: al-Qayyum is the One who does not sleep, in Syriac; and this saying is far-fetched, because it would make His saying ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [a repetition].

* * *

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: "al-Sinah" is the preliminary languor that precedes sleep, called drowsiness.

If it is said: if al-sinah is an expression for the precursor of sleep, then when He says ﴿Neither drowsiness overtakes Him﴾, it indicates that sleep does not overtake Him by a fortiori, and mentioning sleep would be repetition.

We say: the sense of the verse is: drowsiness does not overtake Him, let alone sleep overtake Him.

The second issue: Rational proof has shown that sleep, inattention and heedlessness are impossible for Allah, exalted is He; for these things are either expressions of lack of knowledge, or of opposites of knowledge. Under either assumption, the possibility of their occurrence entails the possibility of the cessation of Allah's knowledge, exalted is He. If that were so, His essence would be such that it is valid for Him to be knowing and valid for Him not to be knowing. Then the acquisition of the attribute of knowledge by Him would require an agent, and the discussion of that is as in the first, and infinite regress is impossible, so it must terminate at One whose knowledge is an attribute necessary to be established and impossible to cease. If that is so, then sleep, heedlessness and inattention are impossible for Him.

The third issue: It is narrated from the Messenger ﷺ that he related from Musa, peace be upon him, that there occurred to his soul: does Allah, exalted is He, sleep or not? So Allah sent to him an angel who kept him awake for three nights, then gave him two flasks, one in each hand, and ordered him to keep them safe. He was guarding them with all his effort until, in the end, he fell asleep, and his hands shook and the two flasks broke. So Allah, exalted is He, struck this as a parable for him, to show that if He were to sleep He would not be able to preserve the heavens and the earth.

Page 9

Know that such a thing cannot be attributed to Musa, peace be upon him, for whoever permits sleep upon Allah, or is doubtful about its permissibility, is a disbeliever. How then is it permissible to attribute this to Musa? Rather, if the narration is sound, the obligation is to attribute this question to the ignorant of his people.

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, the intended sense of this idafah (attribution) is the attribution of creation and ownership. Its explanation is what we have mentioned: since the Necessarily Existent is One, whatever is other than Him is possible in existence by its essence, and every possible thing has an effecter, and everything that has an effecter is originated. Therefore everything other than Him is originated by His origination and brought into being by His innovation, so this idafah is the idafah of dominion and bringing into existence.

If it is said: why did He say ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ and not say "whoever is in the heavens"?

We say: since the intended sense is the attribution of what is other than Him to Him by createdness, and what predominates among them is what does not reason, He applied the predominant to the whole and expressed it by the word "what" (ma). Also, these things were attributed to Him only insofar as they are created, and insofar as they are created they are non-rational, so He expressed them by the word "what" to alert that the intended attribution to Him is the attribution from this aspect.

Know that the Companions (the Ash'ari theologians) have used this verse to argue that the actions of servants are created by Allah, the Exalted. They said: His saying, ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, encompasses everything in the heavens and the earth, and the actions of servants are among what is in the heavens and the earth. Therefore they must be attributed to Allah, the Exalted, in the sense of ownership and creation. Just as the wording indicates this meaning, reason affirms it. This is because everything other than Him is possible in its essence, and what is possible in its essence is not preferred over another possibility except through the influence of the One whose existence is necessary in His essence. Otherwise, the preponderance of the possible without a preponderant cause would follow, and that is impossible.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿Who is it that...﴾, is an interrogative whose meaning is denial and negation, i.e., no one intercedes with Him except by His command. This is because the polytheists used to claim that the idols would intercede for them. Allah, the Exalted, has informed about them that they say: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [az-Zumar: 3], and their saying: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18]. Then the Exalted explained that they do not find this sought-after thing, so He said: ﴿They worship besides Allah that which neither harms them nor benefits them﴾ [Yunus: 18]. Thus Allah, the Exalted, informed that there is no intercession with Him for anyone except the one whom Allah, the Exalted, excepts by His saying: ﴿except by His permission﴾. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and who says what is correct﴾ [an-Naba': 38].

The second issue: al-Qaffal (the exegete) said: He, the Exalted, does not permit intercession for other than the obedient, since it is not permissible in His wisdom to equate the people of obedience with the people of disobedience. He elaborated at length in establishing this.

I say: This al-Qaffal had a great inclination towards the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) and a good opinion of their statements. Nevertheless, he had little comprehensive knowledge of their principles. This is because among the doctrines of the Basrans (the scholars of Basra) of them is that pardoning the perpetrator of a major sin is good according to reason, but revelation has indicated that this does not occur. If that is so, then rational argumentation for prohibiting intercession on behalf of the sinners is an error according to their own view. Rather, according to the doctrine of al-Ka'bi, pardoning sins is ugly by reason. So if al-Qaffal was upon the doctrine of al-Ka'bi, then this argument would be sound. However, the response to it refutes that in several aspects:

First: The punishment is the right of Allah, the Exalted, and the one who is entitled to it may waive his own right. This is unlike the reward, which is the right of the servant, so it is not for Allah, the Exalted, to waive it. This distinction was mentioned by the Basrans in answering the doubt of al-Ka'bi.

Second: As for his saying that it is not permissible to equate the obedient and the disobedient, if he meant that it is not permissible to equate them in any matter, then this is ignorance, because He, the Exalted, has equated them in creation, life, provision, feeding on good things, and enabling them to attain their desires. And if he meant that it is not permissible to equate them in all matters, then we say in accordance with it. How could he not say so, when the obedient person has no anguish and is not fearful of punishment, whereas the sinner is in extreme fear, and perhaps enters the Fire and suffers for a period, then Allah, the Exalted, rescues him from that punishment through the intercession of the Messenger (ﷺ).

Know that al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) had good speech in tafsir and a keen insight into the interpretations of words, but he was greatly exaggerating in establishing the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, while he had little share of the science of kalam (dialectical theology) and little portion of knowing the speech of the Mu'tazilah.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (az-Zamakhshari) said: The pronoun refers to what is in the heavens and the earth, because among them are the rational beings, or to what is indicated by "who" (man dha), namely the angels and the prophets.

The second issue: There are several aspects concerning the verse:

The first: Mujahid, 'Ata', and as-Suddi said: ﴿What is before them﴾ is what was before them of worldly affairs, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ is what will be after them of matters of the Hereafter.

The second: ad-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: ﴿He knows what is before them﴾ means the Hereafter, because they will go forward to it, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ means the world, because they will leave it behind their backs.

The third: 'Ata' reported from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿He knows what is before them﴾ from the heaven to the earth, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ means what is in the heavens.

The fourth: ﴿He knows what is before them﴾ after the expiry of their terms, and ﴿what is behind them﴾, i.e., what was before He created them.

The fifth: What they did of good and evil, and what they will do after that.

Know that the purpose of this statement is that He, glorified is He, knows the circumstances of the intercessor and the one for whom intercession is made, with regard to what relates to deserving punishment and reward, because He knows all knowable things, nothing is hidden from Him. And the intercessors do not know about themselves whether they have the obedience that makes them deserving of this great station with Allah, the Exalted, nor do they know whether Allah, the Exalted, has permitted them for that intercession, and whether they deserve censure and rebuke for it. This indicates that none of the creatures may undertake intercession except by the permission of Allah, the Exalted.

The third issue: Those mentioned in this verse may be the angels, and all others who intercede on the Day of Resurrection from among the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, and the righteous.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: What is meant by "knowledge" here is the known, as one says: "O Allah, forgive us Your knowledge of us," i.e., Your known. And when a great sign appears, it is said: "This is the power of Allah," i.e., His power-object. The meaning is that no one encompasses the known things of Allah, the Exalted.

[Page 11]

The second issue: Some of the Companions (the Ash'ari scholars) argued with this verse to establish the attribute of knowledge for Allah, the Exalted, and it is weak for several reasons:

The first: The word "min" (of) is for partitiveness, and it enters here upon "knowledge." So if what is meant by knowledge were the attribute itself, it would follow that partitiveness enters the attribute of Allah, the Exalted, and that is impossible.

The second: His saying ﴿except what He wills﴾ does not apply to knowledge; it applies only to the known.

The third: The discourse here concerns only the known things, and what is meant is that He, the Exalted, knows all known things, while creatures do not know all known things; rather they know only a little of them.

The third issue: Al-Layth said: It is said of anyone who has acquired something, or whose knowledge has reached its extent, "He has encompassed it," because when he knows the beginning of a thing and its end in its entirety, knowledge becomes like one who encompasses it.

As for His saying: ﴿except what He wills﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

One of them: They do not know anything of His known things except what He wills to teach them, as He related about them when they said: ﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32].

The second: They do not know the unseen except when Allah informs some of His prophets about some of the unseen, as He said: ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except a messenger whom He has approved﴾ [al-Jinn: 26–27].

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾, know that it is said: "The thing encompassed (wasi'a) him, encompassing him in extent" when it bears him, is able for him, and it is possible for him to carry it. "This does not encompass you," i.e., you cannot bear it and cannot tolerate it. From this is His saying, peace be upon him: "If Musa were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me," i.e., he could not bear other than that. As for al-Kursi, its root in the language is from the composition of one thing upon another. The "kirs" are the urine and dung of animals, some of which pile up upon others. "Akrasat al-dar" means that the house became full of dung and urine, and some of it piled up upon others. "Takarrasa al-shay'" means that the thing became composed. From this comes "al-kurrasa" (the notebook), because some of its pages are composed upon others. And "al-Kursi" is this well-known thing, because its wooden pieces are composed upon one another.

The exegetes differed in four opinions:
