The first: It is a great body that encompasses the heavens and the earth. Then they differed concerning it. al-Hasan said: "al-Kursi" is the very Throne ('arsh), because a throne is sometimes described as an 'arsh and sometimes as a kursi, since each of them is such that sitting upon it is valid. Others said: Rather, the Kursi is other than the Throne. Then they differed: Some of them said: It is below the Throne and above the seventh heaven. Others said: It is beneath the earth, and this is reported from as-Suddi.

Know that the word "al-Kursi" occurs in the verse, and sound reports have come that it is a great body beneath the Throne and above the seventh heaven. There is no impossibility in saying so, so it is obligatory to follow it. As for what has been reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that he said: "It is the place of the two feet," it is far-fetched that Ibn 'Abbas would say: "It is the place of the feet of Allah," exalted is He above limbs and members. We have already mentioned many proofs for negating corporeality in many places in this book. Therefore this report must be rejected, or interpreted to mean that the Kursi is the place of the two feet of the Greatest Spirit or of another angel of great rank with Allah, the Exalted.

The second opinion: What is meant by "al-Kursi" is authority, power, and dominion. Sometimes it is said: Divinity is not attained except through power, creation, and origination; and the Arabs call the origin of everything "al-Kursi." Sometimes dominion is called "al-Kursi," because the king sits upon the kursi, so the king is named by the name of the place of dominion.

[Page 12]

The third opinion: "al-Kursi" is knowledge, because knowledge is the place of the knower, and that is the Kursi. So the attribute of a thing is named by the name of the place of that thing, figuratively, because knowledge is the matter relied upon, and the kursi is that upon which one relies. From this, scholars are called "karasi," because they are those upon whom one relies, just as they are called "the pegs of the earth."

The fourth opinion: That which al-Qaffal chose, which is that the purpose of this statement is to depict the greatness and majesty of Allah. Its explanation is that He, the Exalted, addressed the creation in describing His essence and attributes using what they were accustomed to with their kings and great ones. Among that: He made the Ka'bah His house, which people circumambulate, just as they circumambulate the houses of their kings, and He commanded people to visit it, just as people visit the houses of their kings. He mentioned about the Black Stone that it is the right hand of Allah on His earth, then made it a place for kissing, just as people kiss the hands of their kings. Likewise what He mentioned about the reckoning of servants on the Day of Resurrection: the presence of the angels, prophets, and martyrs, and the placing of the scales. On this analogy, He affirmed for Himself a throne, saying: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]; then He described His throne, saying: ﴿And His Throne was over the water﴾ [Hud: 7]; then He said: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, exalting their Lord with praise﴾ [az-Zumar: 75]; and He said: ﴿And above them that Day, eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17]; and He said: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. Then He affirmed for Himself a kursi, saying: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾.

Having understood this, we say: Every expression that comes in the case of the Throne and the Kursi that gives rise to the notion of anthropomorphism has similar expressions, indeed even stronger ones, concerning the Ka'bah, circumambulation, and kissing the Black Stone. Since we agree here that the purpose is to describe the greatness and majesty of Allah, while being certain that He is exalted above the Ka'bah, the same applies to the Throne and the Kursi. This is a clear response. However, the one relied upon is the first opinion, because abandoning the apparent meaning without evidence is not permissible. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 4 of 4):

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And their preservation tires Him not﴾, know that it is said: "ada yaʾudu-hu" (to burden, to weigh down), meaning when something makes him heavy and exhausts him. And "udtu al-ʿūda awdan" (I bent the stick), which is when you lean on it with weight until you bend it. The meaning is: their preservation does not weigh upon Him and does not burden Him, namely the preservation of the heavens and the earth.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾. Know that it is not permissible that what is meant by it is highness in terms of direction (ʿuluww bi-l-jihah). We have demonstrated this with many proofs, and we add here two further proofs:
The first: If His highness were due to place, then He would either be finite in the upward direction, or infinite in that direction. The first is false, because if He were finite in the upward direction, then a hypothetical part above Him would be higher than Him, and He would not be higher than everything else; rather something else would be higher than Him. If He were infinite, this is impossible, because the claim of a dimension without limit is refuted by certain demonstrations. Also, if we assume a dimension without limit, then in that dimension there would be hypothesized points without limit. Either one point in them would exist with no other point hypothesized above it, or none would exist. If the first, then that point is the end of that dimension, and so that dimension is finite, while we assumed it infinite; this is a contradiction. If no point exists without another point above it, then each of those hypothesized points in that dimension is a lowest point, and there is no point in it that is absolutely above. Then none of the hypothesized points in that dimension has absolute highness at all, and that negates the attribute of being high.
Page 13
The second proof: The world is a sphere. Whenever this is so, every side that is hypothesized as high relative to one face of the earth is low relative to the other face, so the extreme of highness becomes the extreme of lowness.
The third proof: Every attribute whose existence belongs to one of two things essentially, and to the other by following the first, that judgment is more complete and perfect in the essential, and weaker and less complete in the accidental. So if God's highness were due to place, then the highness of the place through which this highness is attained would be an essential attribute, and the attainment of this highness by God Exalted would be a following of His attainment of place. Then the highness of place would be more complete and perfect than the highness of God's essence, so God's highness would be deficient and the highness of other than Him complete, and that is impossible. These proofs are decisive that God's highness cannot be by direction.
How excellent is what Abu Muslim ibn Bahr al-Isfahani said in interpreting His saying: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God﴾ [al-An'am 6:12]. He said: This indicates that place and all that is in place belong entirely to God Exalted, His dominion. Then He said: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day﴾ [al-An'am 6:13]. This indicates that time and all that is in time belong entirely to God Exalted, His dominion. Exalted and sanctified is He above His highness being due to place. As for His greatness, it is also through awe, power, and majesty, and it is impossible for it to be due to magnitude and size. For if He were infinite in all directions or in some directions, this is impossible, since the decisive proofs establish that infinite dimensions cannot be affirmed. And if He were finite in all directions, the spaces surrounding that finite thing would be greater than it, so such a thing would not be great in an absolute sense. The truth is that He, glorified and exalted, is higher and greater than being of the kind of substances and bodies, exalted far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clear from error. So whoever disbelieves in the false deities and believes in Allah has grasped the firmest handle, which will never break. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ On it are two issues:

The first issue: the *lam* in "*al-dīn*" (religion) has two views. One is that it is the *lam al-ʿahd* (the *lam* of prior reference). The other is that it is a substitute for the possessive pronoun (*badal min al-iḍāfa*), as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 41], meaning "its refuge." The intended meaning is "the religion of Allah."

The second issue: there are several interpretations of the verse.

The first, which is the view of Abū Muslim and al-Qaffāl, and is the most fitting to the principles of the Muʿtazila (*uṣūl al-Muʿtazila*), is that its meaning is that He did not base the matter of faith on coercion and compulsion, but based it on capacity and choice. Al-Qaffāl then argued that this is the intended meaning, saying: when He, may He be exalted, clarified the proofs of monotheism with a complete clarity that cut off any excuse, He said after that, "There remains, after the clarification of these proofs, no excuse for the unbeliever to persist in disbelief, except that he be forced and compelled to faith. That is not permissible in the abode of this world, which is the abode of trial, for in coercion and compulsion regarding religion the meaning of trial and testing is nullified. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. And in another sûrah He said, ﴿And if your Lord had willed, all those on earth would have believed together. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yūnus: 99]. And in sûrat al-Shuʿarāʾ He said, ﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself with grief that they do not believe. If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the sky, and their necks would remain bowed before it﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 3–4]."

[p. 14]

"And what strengthens this view is that He, may He be exalted, said after this verse, ﴿The right course has become clear from error﴾, meaning: the proofs have become manifest and the clear signs have become evident, and after them there remains only the path of forcing, compelling and coercion. That is not permissible, because it contradicts the imposition of obligation (*al-taklīf*). This is the explanation of this interpretation."

The second interpretation: coercion means that a Muslim says to a disbeliever, "If you do not believe, I will kill you." Then He said, ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ As for the People of the Book and the Magians, when they accept the *jizya* (poll tax), killing is lifted from them. As for the other unbelievers, if they become Jews or Christians, the jurists have differed concerning them. Some of them said: he is allowed to remain upon it, and according to this assumption, killing is lifted from him if he accepts the *jizya*. According to the view of these scholars, His saying, ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, is general, applying to all unbelievers. But as for those jurists who say that the other unbelievers, if they become Jews or Christians, are not allowed to remain upon it, then according to their view, compulsion is valid with regard to them, and His saying, ﴿There is no compulsion﴾, is specific to the People of the Book.

The third view: do not say of one who entered the religion after the war that he entered it under compulsion, because if he is content after the war and his Islam is valid, then he is not under compulsion. The meaning is: do not attribute to them compulsion. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 94].

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿The right course has become clear from error﴾, on it are two issues:

The first issue: it is said *bāna al-shayʾ*, *istabāna* and *tabayyana* when a thing becomes apparent and clear. From this is the proverb, "The dawn has become clear to the one who has two eyes." In my view, clarification and explanation are called *bayān* only because it creates separation and distinction (*bayʹūna*) between the intended matter and other than it. *Al-rushd* in the language means attaining good. It has two forms: *rushd* and *rashad*, and *al-rashād* is also a verbal noun like *al-rushd*. *Al-ghayy* is the opposite of *al-rushd*. It is said: *ghawā yaghwī ghayyan wa-ghawāyatan*, when one takes a path other than the path of right guidance.

The second issue: ﴿The right course has become clear from error﴾, that is, the truth has been distinguished from falsehood, faith from disbelief, and guidance from misguidance, through the abundance of the proofs and the indicative signs. Al-Qāḍī said: the meaning of "the right course has become clear" is that it has become plain and evident through the evidences, not that every person under obligation has become alert, since that is known. I say: we have mentioned that the meaning of *tabayyana* is "separated and distinguished," so the intended meaning is that separation came about between the right course and error because of the strength of the proofs and the confirmation of the demonstrations. On this basis the expression remains on its apparent meaning.

As for His saying, ﴿So whoever disbelieves in the *ṭāghūt*﴾: the grammarians said: the *ṭāghūt* is of the pattern *faʿlūt*, like *jabarūt*, and the *tāʾ* is extra, and it is derived from *ṭaghā* (to transgress). Its original form is *ṭaghawūt*, but the *lām* of the verb was moved to the position of the *ʿayn*, as is their custom in metathesis, as in *al-ṣāqiʿa* and *al-ṣāʿiqa*. Then the *wāw* was changed to an *alif* because it fell in a position with a vowel and an open letter before it. Al-Mubarrad said about *al-ṭāghūt*: "In my view the more correct is that it is a plural." Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: "The matter is not so according to us, because *al-ṭāghūt* is a verbal noun like *al-rahabūt*, *al-rahbūt* and *al-malakūt*. Just as these nouns are singular, so this noun is singular and not a plural. What indicates that it is a singular verbal noun is His saying, ﴿Their protectors are the *ṭāghūt*﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], where it is used in the singular in place of the plural, as one says, 'they are consent' (*riḍan*), 'they are justice' (*ʿadlun*)." They said: this word applies to the singular and to the plural. As for the singular, it is as in His saying, ﴿They wish to take their disputes to the *ṭāghūt*, though they were commanded to reject it﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 60]. As for the plural, it is as in His saying, ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their protectors are the *ṭāghūt*﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. They said: the original form of it is masculine. As for His saying, ﴿And those who avoided the *ṭāghūt*, not worshipping it﴾ [al-Zumar: 17], it was made feminine because the intended meaning is the false deities.

Having understood this, we say: the commentators mentioned five views concerning it:

The first: ʿUmar, Mujāhid and Qatādah said: it is Satan.

The second: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: it is the soothsayer.

The third: Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: it is the sorcerer.

The fourth: some said: it is the idols.

The fifth: that it is the rebellious ones among the jinn and mankind, and everything that transgresses.

The verification is that when transgression occurred through contact with these things, these things were made causes of transgression, as in His saying, ﴿My Lord, they have led many people astray﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 36].

As for His saying, ﴿and believes in Allah﴾, it contains an indication that the disbeliever must first repent of disbelief, and then believe after that.

As for His saying, ﴿then he has grasped the firmest handle﴾, know that it is said: *istamsaka bi-l-shayʾ* when one holds fast to a thing. The *ʿurwa* (handle), its plural is *ʿurā*, as in the handle of the bucket or the jug. It was called so because the *ʿurwa* is an expression for the thing one clings to. *Al-wuthqā* is the feminine of *al-awthaq* (most firm). This is from the metaphorical use of the sensible for the intelligible, because whoever wants to hold a thing by its handle, likewise here, whoever wants to hold fast to this religion clings to the proofs that indicate it. And since the proofs of Islam are the strongest and clearest proofs, for this reason it was described as "the firmest handle."

As for His saying, ﴿which will never break﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: *al-faṣm* is breaking a thing without separating it, and *al-infiṣām* is the reflexive of *al-faṣm*: "I broke it and it broke." The intent of this expression is emphasis, because if it has no breaking, then it has no severing is more fitting.

The second issue: the grammarians said: the structure of the verse is: "by the firmest handle which has no breaking," and the Arabs omit *allatī* (which/that), *alladhī* and *man* and suffice with their relative clauses. Salāmah ibn Jandal said:

"And the swift horses are names for the blood, with them, as if their necks were the stone pillars of Tarḥīb."

He means: "the swift horses which." Allah said, ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 164], meaning: "none of us but he who has a known station."

* * *

Then He said, ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾. Concerning it there are two views:

The first view: He, may He be exalted, hears the speech of one who utters the two testimonies and the speech of one who utters disbelief, and He knows what is in the heart of the believer of pure belief and what is in the heart of the disbeliever of corrupt belief.

The second view: ʿAṭāʾ narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved the conversion to Islam of the People of the Book among the Jews who were around Madinah, and he used to ask Allah, may He be exalted, for that secretly and openly. So the meaning of His saying, ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, is: He hears your supplication, O Muhammad, with your eagerness for it and your striving.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 257:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Protector (walī) of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the false deities (ṭāghūt); they bring them out of light into darkness. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

In this there are two issues.

The first issue: al-walī is a form (fa‘īl) in the sense of the active participle (fā‘il), from their saying: falān waliya al-shay' yalīhi wilāyatan, so he is wālin and waliyy. Its root is from al-waly, which is nearness. Al-Hudhalī said:

"Enemies ran past, short of your nearness, cutting across."

From this one says: "my house is adjacent (talī) to her house," meaning it is near to it. From this one calls a loving helper a walī, because he draws near to you through love and support and does not part from you. From this comes al-wālī (the governor), because he governs (yalī) the people by management, command and prohibition. From this comes al-mawlā. Hence, regarding the opposite of wilāyah, they said: al-‘adāwah (enmity), from ‘adā al-shay' when he passes beyond it. For this reason wilāyah is the opposite of ‘adāwah.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash‘aris) argued by this verse that God's favours (alṭāf) toward the believer in matters of religion are greater than His favours toward the disbeliever, saying: the verse indicates that He is specifically the walī of those who believe. It is known that the walī of a thing is the one who takes charge of what causes a person's welfare and the rectitude of his affair toward the desired aim. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They bar from the Sacred Mosque, though they were not its protectors. Its protectors are only the God-fearing﴾ [al-Anfal: 34], so He made the one who maintains the mosque its walī and denied that the disbelievers were its protectors. Since the meaning of walī is one who undertakes welfare, and He, exalted is He, made Himself the walī of the believers specifically, we know that He undertakes their welfare beyond what He undertakes for the disbelievers. According to the Mu‘tazilah, God made no distinction between disbelievers and believers in guidance, success and favours, so this verse refutes their position. The Mu‘tazilah said: this specification is to be understood in one of several ways:

The first: this is to be understood as an increase in favours, as He mentioned in His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17]. Its rational explanation is that good and obedience call to one another, because when the believer attends a gathering in which admonition takes place, humility, submission and brokenness settle upon his heart, and his state differs from the state of one whose heart has been hardened by disbelief and sins. This indicates that favours which are valid for the believer are not valid for others, so the specification of the believers as having Him as their walī is to be understood in this sense.

The second way: He rewards them in the Hereafter and singles them out with lasting bliss and great honour, so the specification is to be understood as this.

The third way: although He is the walī of all in the sense that He undertakes the welfare of all equally, the one who benefits from that wilāyah is the believer, so it is correct to specify him by this verse, as in His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

Page 17

The fourth way: He is the walī of the believers in the sense that He loves them, and what is meant is that He loves to exalt them.

The companions answered the first by saying: an increase in favours, whenever it is possible, is obligatory according to you, and God has in regard to the believer nothing but the performance of what is obligatory. This meaning is fully present regarding the disbeliever as well; rather, the believer did what made him deserve that extra favour from God.

As for the second question, namely that He rewards him in the Hereafter, this too is far-fetched, because that reward is obligatory upon God, so the walī of the believer is the one who made him deserve that reward from God, and thus his walī is himself, and God is not his walī.

As for the third question, namely that the one who benefits from God's wilāyah is the believer, we say: this matter by which the believer is distinguished from the disbeliever in the domain of wilāyah proceeds from the servant, not from God, exalted is He, so on this view the walī of the servant is the servant himself and no other.

As for the fourth question, namely that wilāyah here means love: (the answer is) that love means bestowing reward, and that is the second question, which we have already answered.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He brings them out of darkness into light﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: The exegetes agreed that what is meant here by darkness and light is disbelief and faith. Thus the verse is explicit that God is the One who brings a person out of disbelief and enters him into faith, so it follows that faith is by the creation of God; for if it came about by the creation of the servant, then he would be the one who brought himself out of disbelief into faith, and that contradicts the explicit text of the verse.

The Mu‘tazilah answered this from two aspects:

The first: bringing out from darkness into light is to be understood as setting up proofs, sending prophets, sending down books, encouraging faith in the most eloquent ways and warning against disbelief in the strongest ways. The Qadi said: God has attributed misguidance to the idols in His saying: ﴿My Lord, they have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], because idols are in some way a cause of their misguidance. So it is more fitting that the bringing out from darkness into light be attributed to God, given the strength of the causes He has established for the one who believes.

The second aspect: bringing out from darkness into light is to be understood as God transferring them from the Fire to Paradise. The Qadi said: this is closer to the reality, because what occurs of this in the Hereafter is an act of His, so it is as if He did it.

The answer to the first is in two parts:

One: this attribution is literal regarding the act, and figurative regarding exhortation and encouragement, and the principle is to keep the wording to its literal sense.

Two: if these encouragements have an effect in tipping the motive, then the preponderant becomes necessary and the non-preponderant impossible, and then the Mu‘tazilite position is refuted; and if they have no effect in tipping, it is not correct to call them "bringing out."

As for the second question, namely interpreting the wording as transferring them from the Fire to Paradise, this too is rebutted from two aspects:

The first: al-Waqidi said: every instance in the Qur'an of "from darkness into light" means disbelief and faith, except His saying in Surat al-An‘am: ﴿and He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An‘am: 1], where He means night and day. And he said: He made disbelief a darkness, because it is like darkness in preventing perception, and He made faith light, because it is like the cause of attaining perception.

The second answer: transferring the believer from the Fire to Paradise is, according to the Mu‘tazilah, something obligatory upon God, so it is not permissible to interpret the wording as referring to it.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿He brings them out of darkness into light﴾ apparently implies that they were in disbelief and then God brought them out of that disbelief into faith. Here there are two views:

The first view: the wording is left to its apparent sense, namely that this verse specifically concerns one who was a disbeliever and then embraced Islam. Those who hold this view have mentioned narrations regarding the occasion of revelation:

The first: Mujahid said: this verse was revealed concerning a people who believed in ‘Isa, peace be upon him, and a people who disbelieved in him. When God sent Muhammad ﷺ, whoever had disbelieved in ‘Isa believed in him, and whoever had believed in ‘Isa disbelieved in him.

The second: the verse was revealed concerning a people who believed in ‘Isa, peace be upon him, according to the way of the Christians, and then after him believed in Muhammad ﷺ. Their faith in ‘Isa, at the time they believed in him, was darkness and disbelief, because the doctrine of incarnation (ittihād) is disbelief, and God brought them out of those darknesses into the light of Islam.

The third: the verse was revealed concerning every disbeliever who embraced Islam through Muhammad ﷺ.

The second view: the wording is to be understood as applying to everyone who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, whether that faith came after disbelief or not. Its explanation: it is not far-fetched to say: "He brings them out of light into darkness" even if they were never in darkness at all. What indicates its permissibility is the Qur'an, the Hadith and common usage. As for the Qur'an, His saying: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He rescued you from it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], and it is known that they were never in the Fire. And He said: ﴿When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace﴾ [Yunus: 98], and no punishment had ever befallen them. And in the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿I have forsaken the religion of a people who do not believe in God﴾ [Yusuf: 37], and he had never been in it. And He said: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾ [al-Nahl: 70], and they had never been in it. As for the Hadith, it is narrated that he ﷺ heard a man say: "I bear witness that there is no god but God," and he said: "upon the fitrah," and when the man said: "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," he said: "He has come out of the Fire." And it is known that he was never in it. It is also narrated that he ﷺ turned to his companions and said: "You are plunging into the Fire like the plunging of locusts, and here I am taking hold of your waistbands," and it is known that they were never plunging into the Fire. As for common usage, if a father has spent all his wealth, the son may say to him: "You have taken me out of your wealth," meaning you did not leave anything of it for me, not that I was in it and then was taken out of it. The realization of this is that if the servant were left without God's success, he would fall into darknesses, so God's success becomes the cause of averting those darknesses from him, and there is a resemblance between averting and removing, so by this way it is permissible to use "bringing out" and "removing far" in the sense of averting and lifting. And God knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the false deities (ṭāghūt)﴾, know that al-Hasan read "awliyā'uhumu al-ṭawāghīt" (plural), and argued by His saying after it: "they bring them out" (yukhrijūnahum, plural). However, this is anomalous and contrary to the codex (al-muṣḥaf). Also, we have already explained in the derivation of this word that it is singular, not plural.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they bring them out of light into darkness﴾, the Mu‘tazilah have used this verse to argue that disbelief is not from God, exalted is He. They said: because He attributed it to the false deities figuratively by agreement, since what is meant by the ṭāghūt according to the most apparent of the views is the idol,

Page 19

and this is reinforced by His saying: ﴿My Lord, they have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], where He attributed the misguidance to the idol. And if this attribution is figurative by agreement between us and you, it falls out of being a proof for you.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ It may be that this refers to the disbelievers alone, and it may be that it refers to the disbelievers and the false deities together, so that it is a rebuke and warning for all. For the word "those" (ulā'ika), when it is plural and it is correct that it refers to both of the mentioned parties, it must refer to both together. And God knows best the correct matter.

[Page 20 marker omitted; see note below]

The Exalted said: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because God had given him dominion? When Abraham said, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death." Abraham said, "Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." So the one who disbelieved was overwhelmed. And God does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿Or [consider] like the one who passed by a town that was fallen down on its roofs. He said, "How will God bring this to life after its death?" So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then resurrected him. He said, "How long have you remained?" He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you have remained a hundred years. But look at your food and your drink; they have not spoiled. And look at your donkey. [We will do this] that We may make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh." And when it became clear to him, he said, "I know that God is over all things competent."﴾

Here God mentions three stories. The first of them is for establishing the knowledge of the Creator. The second and third are for establishing the Gathering, the Spreading out and the Resurrection. The first story is the debate of Abraham (ﷺ) with the king of his time, and it is this verse that we are explaining. So we say:

As for the Exalted's words, ﴿Have you not considered﴾, it is a phrase by which the one addressed is made to stop and wonder at something. Its wording is that of a question, and it is as one says: "Have you not considered how so-and-so acts?" Its meaning is: "Have you not seen, like so-and-so, in his action, such-and-such?"

As for His words, ﴿the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾, Mujahid said: he is Nimrod ibn Canaan, and he was the first to be tyrannical and to claim lordship (rububiyya). They differed about the time of this argument. It was said that it was at the breaking of the idols, before being thrown into the fire, according to Muqatil. And it was said: after he was thrown into the fire. Al-muhajja (argument) is contention, one says: "I argued with him and I overcame him," meaning I contended with him and I prevailed over him. The pronoun in His words ﴿about his Lord﴾ may refer back to Abraham, and it may refer back to the opponent. The first is more evident, as He said: ﴿And his people argued with him. He said, "Do you argue with me about God?"﴾ [al-An'am: 80]. The meaning is: his people argued with him about his Lord.

As for His words, ﴿because God had given him dominion﴾, know that there are two opinions concerning the verse:

The first: the pronoun in "given him" (ataahu) refers back to Abraham, meaning that God gave Abraham (ﷺ) dominion. Those who hold this view argued with several proofs:

The first: the Exalted's words, ﴿We had already given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great dominion﴾ [an-Nisa': 54], meaning sovereignty through prophethood and upholding the religion of God, the Exalted.

The second: it is not permissible for God, the Exalted, to give dominion to a disbeliever who claims lordship for himself.

The third: returning a pronoun to the nearest of those mentioned is obligatory, and Abraham is the nearest of those mentioned to this pronoun, so this pronoun must refer to him.

The second opinion, which is the view of the majority of the commentators, is that the pronoun refers back to that man who argued with Abraham.

They answered the first proof by saying that this verse indicates that dominion was given to the family of Abraham, and there is no indication in it that dominion was given to Abraham, peace be upon him.

As for the second proof, they said that what is meant by dominion here is capability, power and expansiveness in this world. Experience shows that God may give this meaning to a disbeliever. Moreover, why is it not permissible to say that He gave him dominion while he was a believer, and then after that he disbelieved in God, the Exalted?

As for the third proof, they said that although Abraham is the nearest of those mentioned, numerous reports state that the one who argued with Abraham was the king. Therefore, returning the pronoun to him is preferable from this aspect. Then those who hold this view argued for their position with several proofs:

The first: the Exalted's words, ﴿because God had given him dominion﴾, may bear three interpretations, and each one of them is valid only if we say that the pronoun refers to dominion and not to Abraham. One of these interpretations is that the meaning is: he argued with Abraham about his Lord because God had given him dominion, in the sense that the giving of dominion made him insolent and brought him arrogance and haughtiness, so he argued for this reason. It is known that this is fitting only for a haughty king. The second interpretation is that the meaning is that he made his argument concerning his Lord a thanks for the fact that his Lord had given him dominion, as one says: "So-and-so turned hostile to me because I did him a kindness," meaning that he reversed what he owed him of loyalty in return for the kindness. A parallel to this is the Exalted's words: ﴿And you make your provision [the denial of it] that you deny﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 82]. This interpretation too is not fitting for a prophet, for it is obligatory on him to manifest the argument before the attainment of dominion and after it. But as for a haughty king, it is not fitting for him to display this severe haughtiness except after great dominion has been attained for him. Thus it is established that no meaning or interpretation is consistent with His words ﴿because God had given him dominion﴾ unless we take it as referring to the haughty king.

The second proof: the purpose of this verse is to show the complete state of Abraham (ﷺ) in manifesting the call to the true religion. When the disbeliever is a dignified and awe-inspiring ruler, and Abraham was not a king, this meaning is more complete than if Abraham had been a king. And since the disbeliever was a king, it is necessary to go to what we have mentioned.

The third proof: what Abu Bakr al-Asamm mentioned, namely that if Abraham (ﷺ) had been the king, the disbeliever would not have been able to kill one of the two men and spare the other. Rather, Abraham (ﷺ) would have prevented him from it with the strongest prevention, and he would have been obliged to be a refuge so that he would not do that. Al-Qadi (the judge) said: this argument is weak, because it is possible to say that Abraham (ﷺ) was a king and a ruler in religion, and had the capacity to manifest miracles, while that disbeliever was a king empowered and capable of injustice. For this reason he was able to kill one of the two men. Moreover, it is possible to say that he killed one of the two men by way of retaliation (qawd), and the choice was up to him, and he spared the other, either because there was no killing obligation upon him, or because he paid the blood money (diya) and spared him.

Also, His words ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ are a statement and a promise, and there is no proof in the Qur'an that he actually did it. This is what relates to this question.

* * *

As for the Exalted's words, ﴿When Abraham said, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death"﴾, there are several issues in it:

The first issue: the apparent meaning is that this is the answer to a previous question that is not mentioned. This is because it is known that the prophets, peace be upon them, were sent to call people, and it is evident that whenever a prophet claims prophethood, the denier demands of him proof that the world has a god. Do you not see that when Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 16], Pharaoh said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 23]. Moses, peace be upon him, argued for establishing divinity by his words: ﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 24]. Likewise here, the apparent meaning is that Abraham claimed prophethood, and Nimrod said: "Who is your Lord?" Abraham said: "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death." However, that premise was omitted because the event indicates it.

The second issue: Abraham's proof was in the utmost soundness. This is because there is no way to know God, the Exalted, except through His acts in which none of the capable ones shares with Him. Giving life and causing death are like this, because creatures are incapable of them. And knowledge after choice is necessary. So there must be another influencer besides these capable ones whom you see. That influencer is either an efficient cause acting by necessity or a chooser. The first is false, because if it is constant, its effect would be constant too, so the giving of life would not be replaced by causing death, nor would causing death be replaced by giving life. The second: we see in animals organs that differ in shape, quality, nature and property, and the influence of an efficient cause acting by necessity does not vary like this. So we know that for giving life and causing death there must be another existence that influences by way of power and choice in giving life to these animals and in causing them to die, and that is God, glorified and exalted be He. This is a strong and firm proof, which God, glorified and exalted be He, mentioned in several places in His Book, such as His words: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12], to the end of it, and His words: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature. Then We return him to the lowest of the low﴾ [at-Tin: 4-5], and the Exalted said: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

The third issue: one may say that the Exalted mentioned death before life in several verses, among them His words: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28], and He said: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. And it is reported about Abraham that in his praise of God, the Exalted, he said: ﴿And He who causes me to die and then gives me life﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 81]. So for what reason is the mention of life given precedence over death in this verse, where he said: ﴿My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]?

The answer: because the purpose of mentioning the proof is calling people to God, the Exalted, it is necessary that the proof be in utmost clarity. Without doubt, the wonders of creation are greater during life, and a person's awareness of them is more complete. Therefore, it is inevitable that life be mentioned first here.

* * *

As for the Exalted's words, ﴿He said, "I give life and cause death"﴾, there are several issues in it:

The first issue: it is reported that when Abraham (ﷺ) made that argument, that disbelieving king summoned two persons, killed one of them, and spared the other, and said: "I also give life and cause death." This is what is related in the commentary, but in my view it is far-fetched. This is because the apparent state of Abraham is that he explained the reality of giving life and the reality of causing death in the manner we have summarized in the argument. Once he explained it in that manner, it is impossible that giving life and causing death in that manner could be confused by an intelligent person with killing and sparing as a matter of giving life and causing death. And it is far-fetched that a great multitude would be so foolish that they could not recognize this degree of difference. The meaning of the verse, and God knows best, is something else: when Abraham (ﷺ) argued with giving life and causing death from God, the denier said: "You claim giving life and causing death from God directly, without an intermediary of earthly causes or heavenly causes; or you claim that giving life and causing death proceed from God, the Exalted, through the intermediary of earthly causes and heavenly causes." As for the first, there is no way to it. As for the second, it does not indicate the intended point, because each of us is able to give life and cause death through the intermediary of other causes. Sexual intercourse may lead to a living child through earthly and heavenly causes, and taking poison may lead to death. When Nimrod raised this question in this manner, Abraham (ﷺ) answered by saying: "Suppose that giving life and causing death occurred from God, the Exalted, through the celestial connections. Yet those celestial connections and movements must have a governing agent. If the one governing those celestial movements is God, the Exalted, then the giving of life and causing of death accomplished through those celestial movements are also from God, the Exalted. But the giving of life and causing of death that proceed among men through earthly and celestial causes are not like that, because men have no power over the celestial connections. Thus the difference is evident."

وإذا عَرَفْتَ هَذا، فَقَوْلُهُ: ﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْتِي بِالشَّمْسِ مِنَ الْمَشْرِقِ﴾ ليس دليلًا آخَرَ، بل تمامُ الدليل الأول. ومعناه: أنه وإن كان الإحياءُ والإماتةُ من الله بواسطة حركات الأفلاك، إلا أنّ حركات الأفلاك من الله، فكان الإحياءُ والإماتةُ أيضًا من الله تعالى. وأما البشرُ، فإنه وإن صدر منه الإحياءُ والإماتةُ بواسطة الاستعانة بالأسباب السماوية والأرضية، إلا أنّ الأسبابَ ليست واقعةً بقدرته، فثبت أنّ الإحياءَ والإماتةَ الصادرين عن البشر ليسا على ذلك الوجه، وأنه لا يصلح نقضًا عليه. فهذا هو الذي أعتقده في كيفية جريان هذه المناظرة، لا ما هو المشهورُ عند الكل، والله أعلم بحقيقة الحال.

المسألة الثانية: أجمع القرّاء على إسقاط ألف ﴿أنا﴾ في الوصل في جميع القرآن، إلا ما رُوي عن نافع من إثباتها عند استقبال الهمزة. والصحيحُ ما عليه الجمهور، لأنّ ضمير المتكلم هو ﴿أنَ﴾ وهو الهمزة والنون، فأما الألف فإنما تلحقها في الوقف كما تلحق الهاءَ في سكتِه للوقف، وكما أنّ هذه الهاء تسقط عند الوصل، فكذا هذه الألف تسقط عند الوصل؛ لأنّ ما يتصل به يقوم مقامه. ألا ترى أنّ همزة الوصل (hamzat al-wasl، أي الهمزة التي تُنطق عند الابتداء وتسقط في الدرج) إذا اتصلت الكلمة التي هي فيها بشيء سقطت ولم تثبت؛ لأنّ ما يتصل به يُتوصَّل به إلى النطق بما بعد الهمزة، فلا تثبت الهمزة. فكذا الألف في ﴿أنا﴾، والهاءُ التي في الوقف يجب سقوطها عند الوصل كما يجب سقوط الهمزة عند الوصل.

[صفحة ٢٣]

أما قوله تعالى: ﴿قالَ إبراهيمُ فإنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْتِي بِالشَّمْسِ مِنَ الْمَشْرِقِ فَأْتِ بِها مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ﴾، فاعلم أنّ للناس في هذا المقام طريقين:

الأول: وهو طريقةُ أكثر المفسّرين (tafsir: التفسير، أي شرح معاني القرآن)، أنّ إبراهيم عليه السلام لمّا رأى من نمرود أنه ألقى تلك الشبهة عدل عن ذلك إلى دليل آخر أوضح منه، فقال: ﴿فإنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْتِي بِالشَّمْسِ مِنَ الْمَشْرِقِ فَأْتِ بِها مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ﴾، فزعم أنّ الانتقال من دليل إلى دليل آخر أوضح منه جائزٌ للمستدِلّ.

فإن قيل: هلّا قال نمرود: ﴿فَلْيَأْتِ رَبُّكَ بِها مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ﴾؟

قلنا: الجواب من وجهين:

أحدهما: أنّ هذه المحاجّة كانت مع إبراهيم بعد إلقائه في النار وخروجه منها سالمًا، فعلم أنّ من قدر على حفظ إبراهيم في تلك النار العظيمة من الاحتراق يقدر على أن يأتي بالشمس من المغرب.

والثاني: أنّ الله خذله وأنساه إيرادَ هذه الشبهة نصرةً لنبيّه عليه السلام.

والطريق الثاني، وهو الذي قال به المحققون: أنّ هذا ما كان انتقالًا من دليل إلى دليل آخر، بل الدليل واحدٌ في الموضعين، وهو أنّا نرى حدوثَ أشياءَ لا يقدر الخلق على إحداثها، فلا بدّ من قادرٍ آخر يتولّى إحداثها، وهو الله سبحانه وتعالى. ثم إنّ قولنا: نرى حدوثَ أشياءَ لا يقدر الخلق على إحداثها، له أمثلةٌ منها: الإحياء والإماتة، ومنها السحاب والرعد والبرق، ومنها حركاتُ الأفلاك والكواكب. والمستدِلُّ لا يجوز له أن ينتقل من دليل إلى دليل آخر، لكن إذا ذكر لإيضاح كلامٍ مثالًا فله أن ينتقل من ذلك المثال إلى مثالٍ آخر، فكان ما فعله إبراهيمُ من باب ما يكون الدليلُ واحدًا، إلا أنه يقع الانتقالُ عند إيضاحه من مثالٍ إلى مثالٍ آخر، وليس من باب ما يقع الانتقالُ من دليلٍ إلى دليلٍ آخر. وهذا الوجه أحسنُ من الأول وألْيَقُ بكلام أهل التحقيق منه. والإشكالُ عليهما من وجوه:

الإشكال الأول: أنّ صاحب الشبهة إذا ذكر الشبهة ووقعت تلك الشبهة في الأسماع، وجب على المحِقّ القادرِ على الجواب أن يذكر الجوابَ في الحال، إزالةً لذلك التلبيس والجهلِ عن العقول. فلمّا طعن الملكُ الكافرُ في الدليل الأول، أو في المثال الأول، بتلك الشبهة، كان الاشتغالُ بإزالة تلك الشبهة واجبًا مضيِّقًا، فكيف يليق بالمعصوم (أي المنزَّه عن الخطأ) أن يترك ذلك الواجب؟

والإشكال الثاني: أنه لمّا أورد المبطلُ ذلك السؤال، فإذا ترك المحِقُّ الكلامَ الأول وانتقل إلى كلامٍ آخر، أوهم أنّ كلامه الأول كان ضعيفًا ساقطًا، وأنه ما كان عالمًا بضعفه، وأنّ ذلك المبطلَ علم وجهَ ضعفه وكونه ساقطًا، وأنه كان عالمًا بضعفه فنبّه عليه. وهذا ربما يوجب سقوطَ وقع الرسول وحقارةَ شأنه، وإنه غيرُ جائز.

والإشكال الثالث: وهو أنه وإن كان يُحسن الانتقالَ من دليلٍ إلى دليل، أو من مثالٍ إلى مثال، لكنه يجب أن يكون المنتقَلُ إليه أوضحَ وأقربَ، وهاهنا ليس الأمرُ كذلك، لأنّ جنسَ الإحياء لا قدرةَ للخلق عليه، وأما جنسُ تحريك الأجسام فللخلق قدرةٌ عليه، ولا يبعد في العقل وجودُ ملكٍ عظيمٍ في الجثّة أعظمَ من السماوات، وأنه هو الذي يكون محرِّكًا للسماوات. وعلى هذا التقدير: الاستدلالُ بالإحياء والإماتة على وجود الصانع أظهرُ وأقوى من الاستدلال بطلوع الشمس على وجود الصانع، فكيف يليق بالنبي المعصوم أن ينتقل من الدليل الأوضح الأظهر إلى الدليل الخفيّ الذي لا يكون في نفس الأمر قويًّا؟

[صفحة ٢٤]

والإشكال الرابع: أنّ دلالةَ الإحياء والإماتة على وجود الصانع أقوى من دلالة طلوع الشمس عليه، وذلك لأنّا نرى في ذات الإنسان وصفاتِه تبديلاتٍ واختلافاتٍ، والتبدّلُ قويُّ الدلالة على الحاجة إلى المؤثِّر القادر. أمّا الشمسُ فلا نرى في ذاتها تبدُّلًا، ولا في صفاتها تبدُّلًا، ولا في منهج حركاتها تبدُّلًا البتّةَ، فكانت دلالةُ الإحياء والإماتة على الصانع أقوى، فكان العدولُ منه إلى طلوع الشمس انتقالًا من الأقوى الأجلى إلى الأخفى الأضعف، وإنه لا يجوز.

الإشكال الخامس: أنّ نمرود لمّا لم يستحِ من معارضة الإحياء والإماتة الصادرين عن الله تعالى بالقتل والتخلية، فكيف يُؤمَن منه عند استدلال إبراهيم بطلوع الشمس أن يقول: طلوعُ الشمس من المشرق مني، فإن كان لك إلهٌ فقُلْ له حتى يُطلعها من المغرب؟ وعند ذلك التزم المحقّقون من المفسّرين ذلك فقالوا: إنه لو أورد هذا السؤال لكان من الواجب أن تطلع الشمس من المغرب، ومن المعلوم أنّ الاشتغال بإظهار فساد سؤاله في الإحياء والإماتة أسهلُ بكثيرٍ من التزام إطلاع الشمس من المغرب. فبتقدير أن يحصل طلوعُ الشمس من المغرب، إلا أنه يكون الدليلُ على وجود الصانع هو طلوعَ الشمس من المغرب، ولا يكون طلوعُ الشمس من المشرق دليلًا على وجود الصانع، وحينئذٍ يصير دليلُه الثاني ضائعًا كما صار دليلُه الأول ضائعًا. وأيضًا فما الدليل الذي حمل إبراهيمَ عليه السلام على أن ترك الجوابَ عن ذلك السؤال الرَّكيك، والتزم الانقطاعَ، واعترف بالحاجة إلى الانتقال إلى تمسّكٍ بدليلٍ لا يمكنه تمشيتُه إلا بالتزام طلوعِ الشمس من المغرب؟ وبتقدير أن يأتي بإطلاع الشمس من المغرب، فإنه يضيع دليلُه الثاني كما ضاع الأول. ومن المعلوم أنّ التزامَ هذه المحذورات لا يليق بأقلِّ الناس علمًا، فضلًا عن أفضل العقلاء وأعلم العلماء. فظهر بهذا أنّ هذا التفسيرَ الذي أجمع المفسّرون عليه ضعيفٌ. وأما الوجهُ الذي ذكرناه فلا يتوجّه عليه شيءٌ من هذه الإشكالات، لأنّا نقول: لمّا احتجّ إبراهيمُ عليه السلام بالإحياء والإماتة أورد الخصمُ عليه سؤالًا لا يليق بالعقلاء، وهو أنك إذا ادّعيتَ الإحياءَ والإماتةَ لا بواسطة، فذلك لا تجد إلى إثباته سبيلًا، وإن ادّعيتَ حصولَهما بواسطة حركات الأفلاك فنظيرُه أو ما يقرب منه حاصلٌ للبشر. فأجاب إبراهيمُ عليه السلام بأنّ الإحياء والإماتة وإن حصلا بواسطة حركات الأفلاك، لكنّ تلك الحركات حصلت من الله تعالى، وذلك لا يقدح في كون الإحياء والإماتة من الله تعالى، بخلاف الخلق، فإنه لا قدرةَ لهم على تحريكات الأفلاك، فلا جرم لا يكون الإحياءُ والإماتةُ صادرين منهم. ومتى حملنا الكلام على هذا الوجه لم يكن شيءٌ من المحذورات المذكورة لازمًا عليه، والله أعلم بحقيقة كلامه.

أما قوله تعالى: ﴿فَبُهِتَ الَّذِي كَفَرَ﴾، فالمعنى: فبقي مغلوبًا لا يجد مقالًا، ولا للمسألة جوابًا، وهو كقوله: ﴿بَلْ تَأْتِيهِمْ بَغْتَةً فَتَبْهَتُهُمْ فَلا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ رَدَّها﴾ [الأنبياء: ٤٠]. قال الواحدي: وفيه ثلاث لغات: بُهِتَ الرجلُ فهو مَبْهوت، وبَهَتَ، وبَهِتَ. قال عروةُ العُذْريّ:

فَما هو إلّا أنْ أُراها فُجاءَةً فَأُبْهَتُ حَتّى ما أكادُ أُجِيبُ

أي: أتحيّر وأسكت.

* * *

ثم قال: ﴿وَاللَّهُ لا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾، وتأويلُه على قولنا ظاهرٌ. أمّا المعتزلة (Mu'tazilah، أهل الاعتزال) فقال القاضي (أي القاضي عبد الجبار): يحتمل

[صفحة ٢٥]

وجوهًا:

منها: أنه لا يهديهم لظلمهم وكفرهم للحجاج وللحقّ كما يهدي المؤمن، فإنه لا بدّ في الكافر من أن يعجز وينقطع.

وأقول: هذا ضعيف، لأنّ قوله ﴿لا يهديهم للحجاج﴾ إنما يصح حيث يكون الحجاجُ موجودًا، ولا حجاجَ على الكفر، فكيف يصح أن يُقال: إنّ الله تعالى لا يهديه إليه؟ قال القاضي: ومنها أن يريد أنه لا يهديهم لزيادات الألطاف (lutf: الألطاف الإلهية التي تقرّب العبد إلى الطاعة)، من حيث إنهم بالكفر والظلم سدّوا على أنفسهم طريقَ الانتفاع به.

وأقول: هذا أيضًا ضعيف، لأنّ تلك الزيادات إذا كانت في حقهم ممتنعةً عقلًا لم يصح أن يُقال: إنه تعالى لا يهديهم، كما لا يُقال: إنه تعالى يجمع بين الضدّين فلا يجمع بين الوجود والعدم. قال القاضي: ومنها أنه تعالى لا يهديهم إلى الثواب في الآخرة، ولا يهديهم إلى الجنة.

وأقول: هذا أيضًا ضعيف، لأنّ المذكورَ هاهنا أمرُ الاستدلال وتحصيلُ المعرفة، ولم يجرِ للجنة ذكرٌ، فيبعُد صرفُ اللفظ إلى الجنة. بل أقول: اللائقُ بسياق الآية أن يُقال: إنه تعالى لمّا بيّن أنّ الدليل كان قد بلغ في الظهور والحجة إلى حيث صار المبطلُ كالمبهوت عند سماعه، إلا أنّ الله تعالى لمّا لم يُقدِّر له الاهتداءَ لم ينفعه ذلك الدليلُ الظاهر. ونظيرُ هذا التفسير قولُه: ﴿وَلَوْ أَنَّنا نَزَّلْنا إلَيْهِمُ الْمَلائِكَةَ وَكَلَّمَهُمُ الْمَوْتَى وَحَشَرْنا عَلَيْهِمْ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ قُبُلًا ما كانُوا لِيُؤْمِنُوا إلّا أنْ يَشاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ [الأنعام: ١١١].

* * *

القصة الثانية:

والمقصودُ منها إثباتُ المعاد، وقولُه تعالى: ﴿أَوْ كَالَّذِي مَرَّ عَلَى قَرْيَةٍ وَهِيَ خاوِيَةٌ عَلَى عُرُوشِها﴾.

وفي الآية مسائل:

المسألة الأولى: اختلف النحويون (grammarians) في إدخال الكاف في قوله: ﴿أَوْ كَالَّذِي﴾، وذكروا فيه ثلاثةَ أوجه:

الأول: أن يكون قولُه: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ إلَى الَّذِي حاجَّ إبْراهِيمَ﴾ في معنى ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ كَالَّذِي حاجَّ إبْراهِيمَ﴾، وتكون هذه الآيةُ معطوفةً عليه، والتقديرُ: أرأيتَ كالذي حاجّ إبراهيمَ، أو كالذي مرّ على قرية؟ فيكون هذا عطفًا على المعنى، وهو قولُ الكسائي والفرّاء وأبي علي الفارسي وأكثرِ النحويين. قالوا: ونظيرُه من القرآن قولُه تعالى: ﴿قُلْ لِمَنِ الْأَرْضُ وَمَن فِيها إنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ﴿سَيَقُولُونَ لِلَّهِ﴾ [المؤمنون: ٨٤ - ٨٥]، ثم قال: ﴿مَن رَبُّ السَّماواتِ السَّبْعِ وَرَبُّ الْعَرْشِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾ ﴿سَيَقُولُونَ لِلَّهِ﴾ [المؤمنون: ٨٦، ٨٧]، فهذا عطفٌ على المعنى؛ لأنّ معناه: لمن السماواتُ؟ فقيل: لله. قال الشاعر:

مُعاوِيَ إنَّنا بَشَرٌ فَأسْجِحْ فَلَسْنا بِالْجِبالِ وَلا الْحَدِيدا

فحُمل على المعنى وتُرك اللفظ.

The second opinion, which is the view chosen by al-Akhfash, is that the kaf (ك) is extra (za'ida), and the intended meaning is: "Have you not considered the one who disputed with Abraham, and the one who passed by a town?"

The third opinion, which is the view chosen by al-Mubarrad, is that we supply an additional element in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "Have you not considered the one who disputed with Abraham, and have you not considered one who was like the one who passed by a town?"
Page 26

The second issue: the scholars differed concerning the one who passed by the town. Some said he was a disbelieving man who doubted the resurrection; this is the view of Mujahid and most of the exegetes among the Mu'tazilah. Others said he was a Muslim. Then Qatadah, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: he was 'Uzayr. 'Ata' reported from Ibn 'Abbas: he was Armiya. Among these, some said that Armiya is al-Khidr, peace be upon him, and that he was a man from the tribe of Harun ibn 'Imran, peace be upon them both; this is the view of Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Armiya is the prophet whom God sent when Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar) destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and burned the Torah.

The argument of those who said that this passer-by was a disbeliever consists of several points:

The first: God related of him that he said: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾ This is the speech of one who considers it far-fetched that God would bring life after death, and that is disbelief.

If it is said: it is possible that this occurred from him before puberty.

We reply: if that were so, it would not be permissible for God to have His Messenger marvel at him, since one does not marvel at the doubt of a child regarding such a matter. This argument is weak, because it is possible that this improbability did not arise from doubt about God's power to do that, but rather from the regular course of customs, that such a desolate place is rarely made populated by God. This is like when one of us points to a mountain and says: "When will God turn it into gold or rubies?" His intention is not doubt in God's power, but rather that this does not happen or occur in the regular course of customs. So it is here too.

The second point: they said that God said concerning him: ﴿When it became clear to him﴾. This indicates that before that, this clarity had not been obtained by him. This too is weak, because the clarity of resurrection through direct witnessing had not been obtained by him before that; but as for whether clarity of it through inference had been obtained, that is disputed.

The third point: he said: ﴿I know that God is over all things competent﴾. This indicates that this knowledge came to him only at that time, and that he had been devoid of such knowledge before that time. This too is weak, because that witnessing undoubtedly produced a kind of confirmation, tranquility and assurance, and that degree of confirmation came about only at that time; this does not indicate that the very root of knowledge had not been present before that.

The fourth point for them: this passer-by was a disbeliever because he was grouped together with Nimrod in one thread. This is also weak, because although before him is the story of Nimrod, after him is the story of Abraham's questioning, so it is necessary that he be a prophet of the kind of Abraham.

The argument of those who said he was a believer and a prophet consists of several points:

The first: his saying ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾ indicates that he was knowing of God, and that he was knowing that God is able to bring life in general. For singling out this matter for astonishment at revival is valid only if acknowledgment of the power to bring life in general has been obtained; but for one who believes that the power to bring life is impossible, this singling out has no point.

The second argument: his saying ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ necessarily has a speaker, and the previously mentioned one is God, the Exalted; so the sense becomes: God the Exalted said: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ and that person said: ﴿I remained a day or part of a day﴾; then God the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, you remained a hundred years﴾. What confirms that the speaker of this statement is God the Exalted is His saying: ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾; and it is known that the one capable of making him a sign for the people is God the Exalted. Then He said: ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh﴾; and there is no doubt that the speaker of this statement is God the Exalted. Thus it is established that this verse indicates, by these many aspects, that God spoke with him; and it is known that this does not befit the state of this disbeliever.

If it is said: perhaps God sent to him a messenger or an angel so that he said this statement to him on behalf of God the Exalted.

We reply: the apparent meaning of this speech indicates that the speaker of these statements with him is God the Exalted; so diverting the wording from this apparent meaning to a figurative meaning without a proof requiring it is not permissible.

The third argument: his restoration to life, and the preservation of the food and drink in their state, and the restoration of the donkey to life after it had become decayed bones, while he was witnessing the reassembly of the donkey's parts into composition and life, is a great honor and a noble distinction; and that does not befit the state of a disbeliever.

If it is said: why is it not permissible to say that all these things were brought into existence by God only as an honor to another man who was a prophet in that time?

We reply: no mention of this prophet has occurred in this verse, and there is no circumstance in this story suggesting the existence of a prophet at all. If the purpose of displaying these things were to honor that prophet and to confirm his mission by a miracle, then leaving out mention of that messenger would be neglect of the principal aim of the speech, and that is not permissible.

If it is said: if that person were such, then it would be said either that he claimed prophethood before the death and revival, or after them. The first is false, because the sending of a prophet from God is for a benefit that returns to the community, and that is not accomplished after death. And if he claimed prophethood after the revival, then the miracle preceded the claim, and that is not permissible.

We reply: the manifestation of extraordinary events at the hand of one whom God knows will become a messenger is permissible in our view, and by this path the objection is removed.

The fourth argument: God said concerning this person: ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾, and this wording is used only concerning prophets and messengers. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. So this was a promise from God, the Exalted, that He would make him a prophet. Furthermore, even if this statement does not indicate prophethood by its explicit wording, there is no doubt that it conveys a great honor, and that does not befit the state of one who died in disbelief and in doubt about God's power, the Exalted.

If it is said: why is it not permissible that the meaning of making him a sign is that whoever among the people knew him as a complete young man, when they see him after a hundred years still in his youth while they have grown old or decrepit, or they hear the report that he had died long ago and has returned young, it is valid to say on account of that that he is a sign for the people, because they take lesson from it and know through it the power of God the Exalted and the prophethood of the prophet of that time?

The answer comes in two respects:

The first: His saying ﴿And that We may make you a sign﴾ is a report that God, the Exalted, will make him a sign; and this report occurred only after God had revived him and spoken with him, and what is made is not made a second time. So it is necessary to interpret His saying ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾ as referring to a matter additional to this revival; whereas you interpret it as referring to this very revival itself, and so it is invalid.

The second: the basis of the argument is that His saying ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾ indicates a great honor, and that does not befit the state of one who died in disbelief and in doubt about God's power, the Exalted.

Page 28

The fifth argument: what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, concerning the occasion of the revelation of the verse. He said: Bukhtansar raided the Children of Israel and took captive many of them, and among them was 'Uzayr, who was one of their scholars. He brought them to Babylon. One day 'Uzayr entered that town, and alighted beneath a tree while he was on a donkey. He tied up his donkey and went around the town, but did not see anyone in it. He marvelled at that and said: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾ not by way of doubt concerning power, but by way of considering it far-fetched according to habit. The trees were fruit-bearing, so he took some of the fruit, figs and grapes, and drank some grape juice, and slept. God caused him to die in his sleep for a hundred years while he was young. Then God also made the humans, the beasts and the birds unaware of his death. Then God revived him after the hundred years, and he was called from heaven: "O 'Uzayr, how long have you remained [after death]?" He said: "A day," then he saw some remaining of the sun and said: ﴿Or part of a day.﴾ God the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, you remained a hundred years.﴾ Look at your food and drink: ﴿of the figs and grapes﴾ and ﴿your drink﴾ from the juice, their taste had not changed. So he looked, and behold, the figs and grapes were as he had witnessed them. Then He said: ﴿And look at your donkey.﴾ So he looked, and behold, it was white bones glistening, its joints scattered, and he heard a voice: "O decayed bones, I am placing a spirit in you," so the bones came together, one with another, then each limb attached to what suited it: the rib to the rib, and the forearm to its place; then the head came to its place, then the sinews and the veins; then He caused the flesh to grow over it, then the skin spread over it, then the hair emerged from the skin, then the spirit was blown into it, and behold, it stood up braying. 'Uzayr fell down prostrate and said: ﴿I know that God is over all things competent.﴾ Then he entered Bayt al-Maqdis, and the people said: "Our fathers told us that 'Uzayr ibn Sharkhiya' died in Babylon, and Bukhtansar had killed in Bayt al-Maqdis forty thousand of those who had read the Torah, and 'Uzayr was among them, and the people did not know that he was reading the Torah." When he came to them after a hundred years, he renewed the Torah for them and dictated it to them from memory, not omitting a single letter from it. The Torah had been buried in a place and was brought out, and it was compared with what he had dictated, and they did not differ in a single letter. At that they said: "'Uzayr is the son of God." This report is well known among people, and that indicates that that passer-by was a prophet.

The third issue: the scholars differed concerning that town. Wahb, Qatadah, Ikrimah and al-Rabi' said: it is Iliya', which is Bayt al-Maqdis. Ibn Zayd said: it is the town from which thousands went out fearing death.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and it was fallen upon its roofs﴾, al-Asma'i said: the house became khawiya, khawa'an (with a long vowel), when it was empty of its people; and al-khawa is the emptiness of the belly of food. In a hadith: "When the Prophet ﷺ prostrated, he would spread out (khawwa)," meaning he separated what was between his upper arms and his sides, and his belly and thighs. And "the horse spread out what was between its legs." Then the house when it collapses is called khawa, because by its collapse it becomes empty of its people; likewise "the stars went down (khawat) and fell (akhwat)" when they fell without rain, because they were empty of rain. The 'arsh is the roof of a house, and the 'urush are the buildings, and the roofs of wood; it is said: "'arasha al-rajul ya'rishu and ya'rushu" when he built and roofed with wood. So His saying ﴿and it was fallen upon its roofs﴾ means: collapsed, fallen, in ruins, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Concerning it there are several aspects:

One of them: its walls were standing while its roofs had collapsed, then the walls were uprooted from their foundations and fell upon the collapsed roofs. The meaning of khawiya is "uprooted," and it is uprooted from its roots; the evidence is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿as if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees (a'jaz nakhlin khawiya)﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7], and in another place: ﴿trunks of palm trees uprooted (munqa'ir)﴾ [al-Qamar: 20]. This description of the ruin of dwellings is among the best that can be used to describe it.

The second: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿khawiya 'ala 'urushiha﴾ means: empty of its roofs; ''ala'' is taken in the sense of ''an'', like His saying: ﴿when they take measure from people ('ala al-nas)﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 2], meaning: from them.

The third: that what is meant is that the town was empty

Page 29

with the trees being trellised (ma'rushah), so the astonishment was greater. For it is generally the case that in a deserted, ruined town, the trellises of its fruit trees collapse; so when the town was ruined while its trellises remained, the astonishment was greater.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"﴾ we have mentioned that whoever said the passerby was a disbeliever understood it as doubt about the power of Allah, Exalted is He; and whoever said he was a prophet understood it as a matter of regarding it as improbable according to the customary course of affairs and habit, or the purpose of it was to seek additional proofs for the sake of confirmation, just as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. His saying "how" (anna) means "from where," as in His saying: ﴿How is this (come) to you?﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 37]. The intended meaning of bringing this town to life is its resettlement, i.e., when will Allah, Exalted is He, do that? In the sense that He would not do it. So Allah wished to show him within himself, and in the bringing to life of the town there is a sign. ﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years﴾, and we have mentioned the story.

If it is said: What is the benefit of Allah causing him to die for a hundred years, given that the proof by revival after a day or after part of a day is already attained?

We say: Because revival after a long lapse of time is more remote to the intellects than revival after a short period; and also because, after a long lapse of time, what is witnessed from him and what he witnesses from others is more wondrous.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He resurrected him﴾, the meaning is: then He brought him to life. The Day of Resurrection is called the Day of Resurrection (yawm al-ba'th) because people are raised (yub'athun) from their graves; its root is from "ba'athtu al-naqah" (I made the she-camel rise) when I raised her from her place. And He said "then He resurrected him" and did not say "then He brought him to life," because His saying "then He resurrected him" indicates that he returned as he was at first: alive, rational, understanding, and prepared for reflection and inference regarding the divine knowledge; whereas had He said "then He brought him to life," these benefits would not have been attained.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 1 of 2):

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He said, "How long have you remained?"﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: there are two readings of it. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with idgham (assimilation, merging of the two similar letters), while the rest read it with izhar (clear articulation). Whoever reads with idgham does so because the two places of articulation are close, and whoever reads with izhar does so because the two places of articulation are distinct, even though they are close.

The second issue: they are agreed that the speaker of this statement is Allah, exalted is He. It is known that this address was from Allah, exalted is He, because that address was accompanied by a miracle, and because after the revival he witnessed, regarding his donkey and the appearance of decay in its bones, what made him know that those extraordinary events had come only from Allah, exalted is He.

The third issue: there is a difficulty in the verse, namely that Allah, exalted is He, knew that he had been dead, and knew that a dead person, once he has become alive, cannot know whether the duration of his death was long or short. So despite that, for what wisdom did He ask him about the amount of that duration?

The answer to it: the purpose of this question was to draw attention to the occurrence of the extraordinary events that took place.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"I have remained a day or part of a day."﴾, there are questions concerning it.

The first question: why did he mention this uncertainty?

The answer: whether the dead person's duration of death was long or short, the state is one and the same with respect to him, so he answered with the least that could be considered as being dead, since that is the certainty. It is said in the tafsir that his death took place at the beginning of the day, so he said, "a day." Then, when he looked at the sunlight remaining on the tops of the walls, he said, ﴿"or part of a day."﴾

The second question: since the duration of his stay was one hundred years, and then he said, ﴿"I have remained a day or part of a day,"﴾ would this not be a lie?

The answer: he said that according to his assumption, and he would not be held accountable for this falsehood. A parallel to it is that Allah, exalted is He, related about the People of the Cave that they said, ﴿"We have remained a day or part of a day"﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], according to what they supposed and what occurred to them. Also, the brothers of Joseph, peace be upon him, said, ﴿"O our father, indeed your son has stolen, and we did not testify except to what we knew"﴾ [Yusuf: 81], and they only said that based on the indication of the drinking cup being removed from his baggage.

The third question: did he know that this stay was due to death, or did he not know that, but rather believed that this stay was due to death?

The answer: the more apparent view is that he knew that this stay was due to death. That is because the primary purpose of causing him to die and then reviving him after one hundred years was that he would witness revival after death, and that is not achieved unless he knew that this stay was due to death. He had also witnessed, either in himself or in his donkey, states indicating that this stay was due to death.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"He said, 'Rather, you have remained one hundred years.'"﴾, its meaning is clear. It is said: the word "'am" (year) is originally from al-'awm, which is swimming, because in it there is a long swimming that does not allow one to control oneself in it.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"Look at your food and your drink; they have not spoiled"﴾, there are issues concerning it.

The first issue: the reciters differed over affirming the haa' in pause-connection in His saying ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ and in (iqtadih) [al-An'am: 90], (maliyah) [al-Haqqah: 28], (sultaniyah) [al-Haqqah: 29] and (mahiyah) [al-Qari'ah: 10], after they had agreed on affirming them in pause. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read all these letters with affirming the haa' in connection. Hamzah used to delete them in connection, and al-Kisa'i used to delete the haa' in connection in His saying ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ and (iqtadih) [al-An'am: 90], and affirm it in connection in the rest. They did not differ over His saying ﴿"I was not given my record, and I did not know what my account is"﴾ [al-Haqqah: 25, 26] that it has the haa' in both connection and pause.

Having understood this, we say: as for the deletion, there are several aspects:

The first: the derivation of the word (yatasannah) is from the word "sanah" (year). Many people claim that the original of "sanah" is "sanawah." They said: the evidence for this is that they say in deriving from it, "asanna'l-qawm" when a year of drought struck them, and the poet said:

"And the men of Makkah are famished, emaciated."

They say in its plural: "sanawat," and in its verb: "sanaytu'r-rajula musanat-an" when he dealt with him year by year, and in diminutive: "sunayyah." If this is established, then the haa' in His saying ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ is for pausal (sakt), not for the root.

The second: al-Wahidi related from al-Farra' that he said: it is possible that the original of "sanah" is "sananah," because they said in its diminutive "sunaynah," although that is rare. On this basis, it is possible that ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ originally was lam yatasannan, then the final nun was dropped, then the haa' of pause was added to it when pausing on it, just as the original of lam yatqaddi al-baz'i (the falcon's talons did not...) was lam yatqaddad al-bazi, then the final dal was dropped, then the haa' of pause was added to it when pausing, so it is said: lam yatqaddah.

The third: that ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ is derived from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from black mud, moulded﴾ [al-Hijr: 26], and "sinn" in the language means pouring. This is what Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said. So His saying, lam yatasannan, means the drink remained in its state and did not decrease, though one hundred years had passed over it. Then the final nun was dropped and replaced by the haa' of pause when pausing, according to what we established in the second aspect. These three aspects explain the deletion. As for the explanation of the affirmation, it is that ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ is derived from "sanah," and the root of "sanah" is "sanhah," as evidenced by the fact that its diminutive is said to be "sunayhah," and it is said: "sanahat al-nakhlah," meaning it bore fruit in alternate years, and "a'jartu'd-dar musanahah" (I rented out the house yearly). If that is so, then the haa' in ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ is a radical letter of the verb, and therefore it was not deleted at all, neither in connection nor in pause.

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ means: it did not change. The original meaning of ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ is: the years did not pass over it, because when the passing of years does not produce any change, it is as if they had not passed over it. We have related from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi: lam yatasannan, meaning the drink did not decrease. Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿"Rather, you have remained one hundred years,"﴾ it was incumbent that He mention after it something that indicates that. His saying, ﴿"Look at your food and your drink; they have not spoiled,"﴾ does not indicate that he remained one hundred years, but rather apparently indicates what he had said, that he remained a day or part of a day.

The answer: whenever the doubt is stronger while the person knows in general that it is a doubt, the hearing of the proof that removes that doubt is more emphatic and its occurrence in action is more complete. So when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿"Rather, you have remained one hundred years,"﴾ He said, ﴿"Look at your food and your drink; they have not spoiled,"﴾ for this confirms your saying, ﴿"I have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ Then your longing for the proof that uncovers this doubt intensifies. Then He said after it, ﴿"And look at your donkey,"﴾ so he saw that the donkey had become dust and decayed bones, and his amazement at the power of Allah, exalted is He, greatly increased. For food and drink quickly change, while a donkey may remain for a long age and a great time. So he saw what does not remain remaining, namely food and drink, and what remains not remaining, namely bones. Thus his amazement at the power of Allah, exalted is He, greatly increased, and this proof took firm hold in his mind and in his heart.

The second question: He, exalted is He, mentioned the food and the drink, and His saying, ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ refers to the drink, not to the food.

The answer: just as the drink is described as not having changed, so too the food is described as not having changed, especially if the food is delicate, for corruption swiftly reaches it. It is narrated that his food was figs and grapes, and his drink was grape juice and milk. And in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "Look at your food and this your drink; they have not spoiled" (lam yatasannan).

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"And look at your donkey,"﴾ the meaning is that he came to know the length of the duration of his death by witnessing his donkey's bones decayed and crumbled. In reality, this does not indicate by itself, because when he witnessed the decayed bones turning back to life immediately, he knew that the One capable of that is capable of causing the donkey to die immediately and making its bones crumbled and decayed immediately. In that case, the donkey's bones cannot be used as evidence for the length of the duration of death. Rather, the return of the donkey's bones to life is a miracle indicating the truth of what he had heard in His saying, ﴿"Rather, you have remained one hundred years."﴾ Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of His saying is that when he was brought back to life after death, it was a proof of the validity of resurrection. Others said: it was a sign, because Allah, exalted is He, revived him as a young man with black hair, while his grandsons were old men with white beards and white hair.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"And that We may make you a sign for the people,"﴾ we have already explained that what is meant by it is honour, exaltation, and the promise of a high rank in religion and in this world, and that is not fitting for one who died in disbelief and doubt about the power of Allah, exalted is He.

If it is said: what is the benefit of the waw in His saying, ﴿"and that We may make you"﴾?
