We say: al-Farra' said: the waw entered because after it there is a hidden verb, for if He had said, "Look at your donkey that We may make you a sign," the looking at the donkey would have been a condition and making him a sign would have been a consequence, and this meaning is not what is intended by this discourse. But since He said, ﴿"and that We may make you a sign,"﴾ the meaning is: and that We may make you a sign, We did what We did of causing death and reviving. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"Thus do We vary the verses, and that they may say, 'You have studied'"﴾ [al-An'am: 105], meaning: and that they may say, "You have studied," We varied the verses. And ﴿"Thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain"﴾ [al-An'am: 75], meaning: and We showed him the dominion.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"And look at the bones"﴾, most of the exegetes hold that what is meant by the bones is the bones of his donkey, for the definite article in it is a substitute for the pronoun. Others said that they meant by it the bones of this man himself. They said: Allah, exalted is He, revived his head and his eyes, while the rest of his body was decayed bones, so he would look at the parts of the bones of his own self and saw them gathering and some parts joining with others, and he would see his donkey standing as he had tied it when it was alive, not having eaten or drunk for one hundred years. The sense of the statement on this view is: "And look at your bones." This is the view of Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd, and in my opinion it is weak, for several reasons:

The first: His saying, ﴿"I have remained a day or part of a day,"﴾ is only fitting for one who does not see the effect of change on himself, so he thinks he was asleep for part of a day. But one who witnessed the scattered parts of his body and the decayed, crumbled bones of his body, that statement is not fitting for him.

The second: He, exalted is He, related of him that he addressed and answered, so the one who answered must be the one whom Allah caused to die, and if the death was related to his whole self, then the one who answered, whom Allah resurrected, must also be the whole person.

The third: His saying, ﴿"So Allah caused him to die for one hundred years, then resurrected him,"﴾ indicates that He revived that whole body and resurrected it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, (كَيْفَ نُنْشِرُها) ("how We raise them"), the meaning is "how We bring them to life." It is said: anshara Allahu al-mayyita wa-nasharahu (God revived the dead person, and He revived him), and the Exalted said: ﴿Then, when He wills, He will raise him again﴾ [Abasa: 22]. God has also described the bones as being brought to life in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" ﴾ ﴿Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time."﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78-79]

It has been read as "nunshiruha" with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the shin. Al-Farra' said: "It is as if he went to the meaning of spreading out after folding, because with life comes the expansion of movement; so the dead one is as if folded for as long as he is dead, and when he returns he is as if spread out after being folded."

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "nunshizuha" with a zay marked with a dot above, and the meaning is that We raise some of them up to others. Inshaz al-shay' (raising a thing) means lifting it; it is said: ansha'tuhu fa-nashaza, meaning: I raised it and it rose. What rises up from the ground is called nashaz, and from this comes nushuz of the woman, which is that she rises above the limit of the husband's contentment. The meaning of the verse according to this reading is: how do We raise them from the earth, return them to their places in the body, and assemble some of them upon others.

It is related from al-Nakha'i that he used to read "nanshuzuha" with a fatha on the nun, a damma on the shin and a zay, and its basis is what al-Akhfash said: it is said nashaztuhu and anshaztuhu, meaning: I raised him. The meaning from all the readings is that the Exalted assembled the bones upon one another until they were joined in an arrangement, then spread the flesh over them, and spread the veins, sinews, flesh and skins over them, and raised some of it beside the other part; so all the readings are included in that.
* * *
Then the Exalted said: ﴿Then when it became clear to him﴾. This refers back to what was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿How will God give life to this after its death?﴾
Page 33
The meaning: when it became clear to him the occurrence of what he had been deeming unlikely to occur. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the subject of "tabayyana lahu" is a concealed pronoun whose estimate is "when it became clear to him that God is powerful over everything," and he said: ﴿I know that God is powerful over everything﴾, so the first was omitted because the second indicates it. This, in my view, involves strain (ta'assuf); rather, the correct view is that when the matter of causing death and giving life became clear to him by way of direct observation, he said: ﴿I know that God is powerful over everything﴾, and its interpretation is: I have now come to know by direct observation what I used to know before that inference.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "qala i'lam" in the form of a command, and there are two possibilities regarding it:
One: that when it became clear, he commanded himself with that, as al-A'sha said:
"Bid farewell to Umamah, for the caravan has departed"
The second: that God the Exalted said: ﴿I know that God is powerful over everything﴾. What supports the soundness of this interpretation is the reading of ʿAbd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) and al-A'mash: "qila a'lamu anna Allaha ʿala kulli shay'in qadir" (It was said: "I know that God is powerful over everything"). It is reinforced by His saying in the story of Abraham: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾, then He said at its end: ﴿And know that God is Mighty and Wise﴾. The judge (al-Qadi) said: the first reading is preferable, because a command to do something is only appropriate when the thing commanded is absent; here the knowledge is already present, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Then when it became clear to him﴾, so commanding the acquisition of knowledge after that is not permissible, whereas reporting that it has been acquired is permissible.

The third story: it too indicates the possibility of resurrection.

﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but [I ask] that my heart may be assured." He said, "Take four birds and incline them toward yourself. Then put on every mountain a portion of them; then call them, and they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise."﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but [I ask] that my heart may be assured." He said, "Take four birds and incline them toward yourself. Then put on every mountain a portion of them; then call them, and they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise."﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding the governing element of "idh" (when), there are two opinions. Al-Zajjaj said: the estimate is "Remember when Abraham said..." Others said it is coordinated with His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham﴾, meaning: "Have you not considered when he argued with Abraham concerning his Lord, and when Abraham said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead'?"

The second issue: He, may He be exalted, did not name Uzair when He said: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾, but here He named Abraham, although the purpose of the discussion in both stories is one and the same. The reason is that Uzair did not observe proper manners, but rather said: ﴿How will Allah give life to this after its death?﴾, whereas Abraham observed proper manners, for he first praised Allah by saying "My Lord" and then made his request when he said "show me." Also, when Abraham observed proper manners, he attributed the giving and taking of life to birds, whereas Uzair, when he did not observe proper manners, attributed the giving and taking of life to himself.

Page 34

The third issue: They mentioned several reasons for Abraham's question:

The first: Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ata' and Ibn Jurayj said: He saw a carcass thrown on the bank of the sea. When the sea rose, the sea creatures ate from it; when the sea receded, the beasts came and ate; when the beasts left, the birds came, ate and flew away. So Abraham said: "My Lord, show me how You gather the parts of the living creature from the bellies of beasts, birds and sea creatures." It was said to him: "Have you not believed?" He said: "Yes, but what is sought from the question is that knowledge through inference become necessary knowledge."

The second: Muhammad ibn Ishaq and al-Qadi said: The reason for the question is that, when he debated with Nimrod and Nimrod said, "My lord is He who gives life and causes death," [Nimrod] said, "I give life and cause death," and he released a prisoner and killed a man, Abraham said, "This is not giving life and causing death." At that point he said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead," so that this matter would be made clear before Nimrod and his followers. It is reported from Nimrod that he said: "Tell your Lord to give life, or else I will kill you," so he asked Allah for this. His saying, "that my heart may be assured," [means] by my deliverance from being killed, or that my heart may be assured by the strength of my proof and evidence; and his shifting from it to another [argument] was not because of the weakness of that proof, but because of the ignorance of the listener.

The third: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi, may Allah be pleased with them, said: Allah revealed to him, "I am going to take a human being as a close friend (khalil)." Abraham found this greatly significant and said, "My God, what are the signs of that?" He said, "Its sign is that he will give life to the dead by his supplication." When Abraham's station was greatly exalted in the degrees of servitude and the performance of the message, it occurred to him, "Perhaps I am that friend," so he asked for the reviving of the dead. Allah said: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ He said, "Yes, but that my heart may be assured," [that You have chosen me] as Your friend.

The fourth: He, peace be upon him, asked this only for his people, because the followers of the prophets used to demand from them things sometimes false and sometimes true, like their saying to Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. So Abraham asked for this, and the aim was that they would witness it and doubt would vanish from their hearts.

The fifth: What occurred to my mind, and I say: There is no doubt that just as the community needs, in order to know that the Messenger is truthful in his claim to prophethood, a miracle that appears at his hand, so too the Messenger, upon the arrival of the angel to him and the angel's informing him that Allah has sent him as a messenger, needs a miracle that appears at the hand of that angel, so that the Messenger may know that the one who has come is a noble angel and not an accursed devil. Likewise, when the angel hears the speech of Allah, he needs a miracle indicating that this speech is the speech of Allah, Exalted, and not the speech of another. Given this, it is not far-fetched to say: when the angel came to Abraham and informed him that Allah, Exalted, had sent him as a messenger to creation, he sought a miracle, saying: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but that my heart may be assured,"﴾ [so that it may be known] that the one who comes is a noble angel and not an accursed devil.

The sixth, which is in the words of the people of Sufism: The intended meaning of "the dead" is the hearts veiled from the lights of unveilings and manifestation, and "giving life" is an expression for the occurrence of that manifestation and the divine lights. So His saying, "show me how You give life to the dead," is a request for that manifestation and unveilings. He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, I believe in it with the faith of the unseen, but I seek its occurrence so that my heart may be assured through the occurrence of that manifestation." According to the view of the theologians: inferential knowledge is something to which doubts and suspicions can penetrate, so he sought a necessary knowledge with which the heart would settle in a firm settlement that nothing of doubts and suspicions could stir.

The seventh: Perhaps he had read in the scrolls that Allah sent down to him that He would honor his son Jesus by having him give life to the dead through his supplication, so he asked for that. It was said to him: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ He said, "Yes, but that my heart may be assured," [meaning]: "I am not of lower rank in Your presence than my son Jesus."

The eighth: Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to sacrifice his son, so he hastened to it. Then he said: "You commanded me to make a being with a soul into one without a soul, and I did so; and I ask You to make what has no soul into one with a spirit." He said: "Have you not believed?" He said: "Yes, but that my heart may be assured, [and that] You have taken me as a friend."

The ninth: Abraham, peace be upon him, looked into his heart and saw it dead through love of his son, so he felt shame before Allah and said: "Show me how You give life to the dead," i.e., the heart when it has died through heedlessness, how its reviving occurs through the remembrance of Allah, Exalted.

The tenth: The estimate of the verse is that all of creation witnesses the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, so show me that in this world. He said: "Have you not believed?" He said: "Yes, but that my heart may be assured, [by Your] having singled me out in this world with more of this honor."

The eleventh: Abraham's intention was not the giving of life to the dead, but rather his intention was to hear speech without an intermediary.

The twelfth: What some ignorant people said, namely that Abraham, peace be upon him, was in doubt about knowledge of the origin and knowledge of the return. As for his doubt about knowledge of the origin, it is his saying: (﴿This is my Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 78]) and his saying: ﴿If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾ [al-An'am: 77]. As for his doubt about the return, it is in this verse. This view is foolish, rather it is disbelief; for whoever is ignorant of Allah's power to give life to the dead is a disbeliever, so whoever attributes that to the infallible Prophet has declared the infallible Prophet a disbeliever, and disbelief is more fitting for this. Among what proves the corruption of this are several points:

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ He said, "Yes, but that my heart may be assured." Had he been in doubt, this would not have been correct.

The second: His saying, ﴿but that my heart may be assured﴾, which is the speech of one who knows and seeks greater certainty. Also, doubt about Allah's power entails doubt about prophethood, so how would he know the prophethood of himself?

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾, there are two aspects to it, the first of which is:

That it is an interrogative with the meaning of affirmation, as the poet said:
"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts, and the most generous of all people in the giving of wine?"

The second: The intended purpose of this question is that he would answer with what he answered, so that the listeners would know that he, peace be upon him, was a believer in that, knowing it, and that the intended purpose of this question was something else.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Yes, but that my heart may be assured."﴾ know that the lam in "li-yatma'inna" is connected to an omitted element, and the estimate is: "I asked that for the purpose of the heart's assurance." They said: what is meant by it is that the thoughts that occur to the one reasoning should be removed from it; otherwise certainty is present in both states.

Here is a rational inquiry, namely that the exegesis is based on the view that knowledges may be such that some of them are stronger than others, and there is a difficult question in this: a person at the moment of acquiring knowledge either allows its opposite in some respect, or does not. If he allows its opposite in some respect, then that is strong supposition, not firm belief; and if he does not allow its opposite in any respect, then variation in knowledges is impossible.

Know that this difficulty arises only if we say the aim is the attainment of tranquility in belief in Allah's power to give life; but if we say the intended purpose is something else, the question disappears.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Take four birds﴾, Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: he took a peacock, a vulture, a crow and a rooster. In the view of Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them both: a dove in place of the vulture. Here there are discussions:

The first discussion: Since He specified birds from among the animals for this condition, they mentioned two reasons:

The first: flying is in the sky and rising in the air, and the Friend's aspiration was elevation and reaching the realm of dominion, so his miracle was made to correspond to his aspiration.

The second reason: when the Friend, peace be upon him, slaughtered the birds and made them into pieces, and placed mixed pieces on top of every mountain, then called them, each part flew to its like. It was said to him: just as each part flew to its like, so on the Day of Resurrection each part flies to its like, until the bodies are assembled and the spirits are connected to them. This is confirmed by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7].

The second discussion: The purpose of giving and taking life was achieved by a single animal, so why was he commanded to take four animals? There are two aspects:

The first: the meaning is that you asked for one according to the measure of servitude, and I give four according to the measure of lordship.

The second: the four birds are an indication of the four elements from which the bodies of animals and plants are composed. The implication is that unless you separate these four birds, the bird of the spirit cannot rise to the air of lordship and the purity of the world of holiness.

The third discussion: He specified these animals because the peacock is an indication of what is in man of love of adornment, status and self-exaltation; He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14]. The vulture is an indication of intense craving for food, the rooster is an indication of intense craving for satisfying desire from the private parts, and the crow is an indication of intense greed for accumulation and seeking, for among the greed of the crow is that it flies at night and goes out by day in the utmost cold to seek. The implication is that a person, unless he strives to kill the desire of the self and of the private parts, and to nullify greed and nullify adorning himself for creation, will not find in his heart rest and relief from the light of the majesty of Allah.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then incline them toward yourself﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: Hamzah recited "faṣirhunna ilayka" with a kasra on the ṣād, and the rest read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād. As for the ḍammah, there are two opinions:

[p. 37]

The first view: it derives from *ṣirtu al-shay'a asūruhu*, meaning "I inclined the thing towards myself." A man described as *aṣwar* has a leaning neck. It is also said, "So-and-so *ṣāra ilā kadhā*," meaning he adopted that view and inclined to it. On this interpretation, an omission occurs in the speech, as if it were said: "Incline them towards yourself and cut them up, then place on every mountain a portion of them." The clause "cut them up" is omitted because the context indicates it, as in His saying: ﴿Strike with your staff the sea, and it split﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:63], meaning: "he struck, and it split," because His saying, "then place on every mountain a portion of them," indicates the cutting.

If it is asked: what is the benefit of His command to bring them back to himself after he has taken them?

We say: the benefit is that he should contemplate them, know their forms and features, so that they are not confused for him after the revival, and so that he does not imagine that they are other than those.

The second view, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Mujahid, is that ﴿then incline them to yourself﴾ means "cut them up." It is said: *ṣāra al-shay'a yaṣūruhu ṣawran*, when he cut it. Ru'bah, describing a stubborn adversary, said: "We cut him down by judgment," meaning we cut him. On this view, there is no need for any supposed omission. As for the recitation of Hamzah with a kasra on the ṣād, this word has also been explained at times as "inclining" and at other times as "cutting." As for "inclining," al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of Hudhayl and Sulaym: *ṣārahu yaṣīruhu*, when he made it incline. Al-Akhfash and others said: "ṣirhunna" with a kasra on the ṣād means "cut them up"; it is said *ṣārahu yaṣīruhu* when he cut it. Al-Farra' said: I think that this is a metathesis of *ṣarā yaṣrī*, when he cut, so its yā' was moved forward, just as they said *'athā* and *'ā'a*. Al-Mubarrad said: this is not sound, because each of these two words is an independent root in itself, so it is not permissible to make one of them a derivative of the other.

The second issue: the people of tafsir (exegesis) agreed that the meaning of the verse is "cut them up," and that Ibrahim cut their limbs, flesh, feathers and blood, and mixed some of them with others, except Abu Muslim, who denied this. He said: when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) asked God to revive the dead, God showed him an example that brought the matter near to him. The meaning of "incline them to yourself" is to accustom them to the call, i.e., train the four birds so that when you call them they respond and come to you. When they are like that, place on every mountain one of them while alive, then call them and they will come to you running. The purpose of this is to give a tangible example of the return of souls to bodies in an easy manner. He denied the view that the meaning is "so cut them up," and argued for it with several points:

First: the well-known meaning in the language of His saying ﴿so incline them﴾ is "bring them to you." As for cutting and slaughtering, nothing in the verse indicates it. So adding it to the verse is attaching an addition to the verse for which no evidence exists, and this is not permissible.

Second: if the meaning of "incline them" were "cut them," He would not have said "to you," since that verb does not take *ilā* as its object. It takes this particle only when it means "to incline."

If it is asked: why is it not permissible to say that there is inversion and transposition in the speech, the intended meaning being: "So take four birds to yourself and incline them"?

We say: committing to inversion and transposition without a compelling proof is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Third: the pronoun in His saying ﴿then call them﴾ refers to the birds themselves, not to their parts. If the parts were scattered and separated, and what was placed on each mountain was some of those parts, the pronoun would necessarily refer to those parts and not to the birds, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. Also, the pronoun in His saying ﴿they will come to you running﴾ refers to the birds, not to their parts. According to your view, if some parts were to run to other parts, the pronoun in ﴿they will come to you﴾ would refer to the parts and not to the birds.

Those who held the well-known view argued with several points:

First: all the exegetes who preceded Abu Muslim agreed that the slaughter of those birds and the cutting of their parts took place. Therefore denying this amounts to denying the consensus (ijma').

Second: what he mentioned is not specific to Ibrahim (ﷺ), so there would be no distinction for him over others in it.

Third: Ibrahim wanted God to show him how He gives life to the dead, and the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that he was answered in that. According to Abu Muslim's view, the answer does not actually take place.

Fourth: His saying ﴿then place on every mountain of them a portion﴾ indicates that those birds were made into portions, portion by portion. Abu Muslim responded to this point by saying: since He attributed the portion to the four, the intended meaning of "portion" must be one of those four.

The reply: what you have mentioned, although it is possible, the interpretation of "portion" as what we have stated is more apparent. The estimated meaning is: "then place on every mountain from each one of them a portion or a part."

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then place on every mountain of them a portion﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿on every mountain﴾ is all the mountains of the world. Mujahid and al-Dahhak held to generality according to what is possible, as if it were said: "Distribute them over every mountain on which you are able to distribute them." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: four mountains, according to the number of the four birds and also according to the four directions, namely east, west, north and south. Al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj said: seven mountains, because the intended meaning is every mountain that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) could see, so that calling the birds would be valid, since that cannot be completed except by visibility. The mountains that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) could see were seven.

The second issue: it is narrated that he (ﷺ) was commanded to slaughter them, pluck their feathers, cut them up portion by portion, mix their blood and flesh, and hold their heads. Then he was commanded to place their parts on the mountains, on every mountain a quarter of each bird. Then he would call out to them: "Come, by God's permission." Then each part would fly towards the other until the bodies were complete, and then each body would come to its head, and each head would join its body, and all would be alive by God's permission, exalted is He.

The third issue: Abu Bakr and al-Fadl, in the transmission of 'Asim, read "juz'an" with a heavy pronunciation and hamza wherever it occurs, while the rest read it with hamza and light pronunciation. They are two dialects with one meaning.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then call them, they will come to you running﴾, it was said: running, or walking on their feet, because that is more forceful as proof. It was also said: flying, but this is not correct, because it is not said of a bird when it flies: "it ran." Some answered this by saying that running (*sa'y*) is intensifying in movement; if the movement is flying, then running in it is intensifying in that movement.

Our companions (the Ash'aris) have argued with this verse that bodily structure is not a condition for the validity of life, because He, exalted is He, made each one of those parts and fragments alive, understanding the call, able to run and to sprint. This indicates that structure is not a condition for the validity of life.

The judge (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: the verse indicates that structure is necessary, since cutting entails the invalidity of their life.

The reply: this is weak, because the occurrence of concomitance does not indicate the necessity of concomitance. As for separation from it in some states, it indicates that concomitance, wherever it occurs, was not necessary. Since the verse indicates the existence of comprehension of the call and the ability to run in those parts while they are separated, this is a decisive proof that structure is not a condition for life.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and know that God is Mighty and Wise﴾, the meaning is that He is dominant over all possible things, and "Wise" means: knowing the ends of matters and the final purposes of things.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 261:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears; in every ear there are a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies for whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, mentioned the foundations of knowledge of the Origin and the Return, and some of the proofs of their soundness, He wished to follow that with the explanation of the laws, rulings and obligations.

So the first ruling concerns the explanation of the obligations regarding the spending of wealth, and in the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: concerning the manner of the arrangement (naẓm), there are several aspects.

The first: Al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: When He, exalted is He, stated in general terms His saying: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a good loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], He then detailed those multiples after that in this verse. He mentioned between the two verses the proofs of His power through giving life and causing death, because without that it would not be fitting to impose the obligation of spending; for if there were no God who rewards and punishes, spending in the other acts of obedience would be pointless. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said to the one whom He encouraged to spend: You know that I created you and perfected My blessing upon you through giving life and enabling you, and you know My power to recompense and reward. Let your knowledge of these conditions be a motive to spend wealth, for He repays the little with the much. Then He gave an example of that abundance: that whoever sows one grain which yields seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains, the one becomes seven hundred.

The second aspect concerning the arrangement: what al-Asamm mentioned, namely that He, exalted is He, gave this example after He had argued against all of them with what necessitates the confirmation of the Prophet ﷺ, so that they would be eager to strive with their selves and their wealth in supporting him and raising up his law.

The third aspect: when He, exalted is He, clarified that He is the Guardian of the believers, and that the disbelievers have as their guardians the Taghut, He explained the likeness of what the believer spends in the way of Allah and what the disbeliever spends in the way of the Taghut.

The second issue: there is an elision in the verse, and the implied meaning is: the likeness of the charities of those who spend their wealth is like the likeness of a grain. It was also said: the likeness of those who spend their wealth is like the likeness of a sower of a grain.

The third issue: the meaning of ﴿spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾ is, namely, in His religion. It was said: it refers specifically to spending in jihad. It was also said: it encompasses all the doors of righteousness, and it includes obligatory and voluntary spending in emigration with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, spending in jihad on oneself and on others, directing wealth to charities, and spending it on public welfare; for all of this is counted within the path, which is the religion of Allah and His way, since all of this is "spending in the way of Allah."

If it is said: Have you ever seen an ear in which there are a hundred grains, so that the example is struck with it?

We say: the answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: the purpose of the verse is that if a person seeking increase and profit knew that when he sows one grain it yields for him seven hundred grains, it would not be fitting for him to abandon that or to be negligent in it. Likewise, it is fitting for one who seeks the reward in the Hereafter with Allah not to abandon it when he knows that he will obtain for one ten, a hundred and seven hundred. And when this meaning is intelligible, whether or not an ear with this description exists in this world, the meaning is achieved and sound. This is the saying of al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is very good.

The second answer: it has been witnessed in the ear of the millet (al-jawars), but this answer is in extreme weakness.

The fourth issue: Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i used to assimilate the (ت) into the (س) in His saying ﴿anbatat sab'a sanabil﴾, because they are two unvoiced letters, while the rest pronounced it clearly according to the original form.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾, and there is no statement in it of the quantity of that multiplication, nor a statement of whom Allah honours with this multiplication. Rather, it must be permissible that He, exalted is He, multiplies for all the God-fearing, and it is permissible that He multiplies for some of them, in cases where their spending is more sincere, or because He, out of His grace and kindness, makes their obedience accompanied by greater acceptance and reward.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, meaning: All-Encompassing in power to recompense them for their generosity and bounty, according to the measures of the expenditures and the manner in which they deserve reward for them. And when the matter is so, the work of the worker does not become lost before Allah, exalted is He.

The Exalted said: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah, then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury, theirs is their reward with their Lord; no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾

Know that when the Exalted magnified the matter of spending in the way of Allah, He followed it with an explanation of the matters that must be achieved so that this reward remains, among them: abandoning reminders of generosity (al-mann) and injury (al-adha). Then, in the verse, there are issues:

The first issue: The verse was revealed concerning ʿUthman and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf. As for ʿUthman, he equipped the army of hardship (jaysh al-ʿusrah) in the Battle of Tabuk with a thousand camels with their saddles and a thousand dinars, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his hands saying: "O Lord, ʿUthman, I am pleased with him, so be pleased with him." As for ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, he gave in charity half his wealth, four thousand dinars, so the verse was revealed.

The second issue: Some exegetes said: the preceding verse is specific to one who spends on himself, and this verse is about one who spends on others, so the Exalted clarified that spending on others produces the great reward mentioned in the verse only if it is not followed by reminder of generosity or injury.

Al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is possible that this condition is also considered for one who spends on himself, namely that he spends on himself and attends jihad with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims seeking the pleasure of Allah, and does not remind the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers of it, nor harm any of the believers, such as saying: "Had I not attended, this matter would not have been accomplished," and saying to another: "You are weak and idle, there is no benefit from you in jihad."

The third issue: "al-mann" (المَنُّ) in the language has several meanings:

One of them: it means bestowing favour. It is said: "Allah has favoured (manna) so-and-so" if He bestowed a favour, or "so-and-so has a favour (minnah) upon me." Ibn al-Anbari recited:

"So favour us with greeting, for your speech is rubies and strung pearls."

From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Among people there is none who has favoured us more in his companionship and his wealth than Ibn Abi Quhafah." He means one who bestowed more favour with his wealth. Also, Allah the Exalted is described as Mannan, meaning Bestower of favours.

The second meaning in interpretation: "al-mann" is diminishing of what is due and withholding it. The Exalted said: ﴿And indeed for you is a reward never cut off﴾ [al-Qalam: 3], meaning uncut and unwithheld. From it death is called "manun" because it diminishes lifespans and cuts off excuses. From this category is the blameworthy reminder (al-minnah), because it diminishes the blessing and clouds it. The Arabs praise abandoning reminders of a favour, and one of them said:

"Your kindness increased in my sight in greatness, that it is hidden and small with me.
You forget it as if you had not given it, though in the world it is famous and abundant."

Having known this, we say: al-mann is displaying the act of benefaction toward them, and al-adha is complaining about them because of what one has given them. The reminder was blameworthy for several reasons:

The first: The poor man who takes charity is broken-hearted because of his need for charity and is not acknowledging the upper hand of the giver. When the giver adds to that the display of the favour, his heart's brokenness increases, so it becomes in the status of harm after benefit, and in the status of one who wrongs him after having done him good.

The second: Displaying reminders keeps the needy away from desiring his charity when it becomes known from his conduct.

The third: The giver must believe that this blessing is from Allah the Exalted upon him, and believe that Allah has great blessings upon him in that He enabled him to this deed, and fear whether he has attached to this bestowal something that removes him from Allah's acceptance of it. When this is the case, it is impossible for him to regard it as a favour upon others.

The fourth, which is the original secret: If he knows that this giving became easy only because Allah the Exalted prepared for him the means of giving and removed the means of withholding, then the giver in reality is Allah, not the servant. When the servant is at this level, his heart is illuminated by the light of Allah the Exalted. But if he is not like this, rather he is preoccupied with the apparent physical causes and deprived of contemplating the true divine causes, then he is in the rank of the beasts whose sight does not rise from the sensible to the intelligible, nor from effects to the Effector.

As for injury (adha), they differed about it. Some took it in its general sense as harm to believers, and that is not the same as reminder; rather it must be restricted to what was mentioned earlier, such as saying to the poor man: "You always come to me with pain, and Allah has relieved me of you and distanced between me and you." So the Exalted clarified that whoever spends his wealth and then does not follow it with reminder or injury, for him is the great reward and the abundant recompense.

If it is said: The apparent wording indicates that both together nullify the reward, so it follows that if only one of them is present without the other, the reward is not nullified.

We say: Rather the condition is that neither of them be present, because His saying: ﴿they do not follow what they have spent with reminder or injury﴾ requires that neither this nor that occur from them.

The fourth issue: The Mu'tazilah said: the verse indicates that major sins nullify the reward of their doer, because He the Exalted clarified that this reward remains only if reminder and injury are absent; for if it stood with their absence and with their presence, this condition would have no benefit.

Our companions answered that the meaning of the verse is that the occurrence of reminder and injury removes the spending from having any reward or recompense at all, because they indicate that he spent in order to remind, and did not spend seeking the pleasure of Allah, nor in the manner of nearness and worship; therefore the reward was necessarily nullified.

Al-Qadi criticized this answer, saying: He the Exalted clarified that this spending has been validated, which is why He said: ﴿they do not follow what they have spent﴾, and the word "thumma" (then) indicates sequence, and what comes after the spending necessitates reward, because the condition of the affected thing must be present at the time the effecting cause occurs, not after it.

Our companions answered him in several ways:

The first: Although the mention of reminder and injury comes after the spending, this later mention apparently indicates that at the time he spent, his spending was not for the sake of Allah, but for the sake of exalting himself over people and seeking show and reputation. When this is the case, his spending does not necessitate reward.

The second: Grant that this condition is later, yet it is not permissible to say that the effect of the effecting cause depends on there being nothing opposing it after it, according to the position of the adherents of "al-muwafah" (the final outcome), and its establishment is known in theology (ʿilm al-kalam).

The fifth issue: The verse indicates that reminder and injury are among the major sins, since this great act of obedience is, because of each of them, removed from producing that abundant reward.

As for His saying: ﴿for them is their reward﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that deeds necessitate reward from Allah the Exalted. Our companions say: the attainment of reward is by way of the promise, not by the deed itself, because the deed is obligatory upon the servant, and performing an obligation does not necessitate reward.

The second issue: Our companions used this verse to refute nullification (al-ihbat), because it indicates that the reward is attained for them absolutely, so the reward must be attained for them after committing major sins, and that nullifies the doctrine of nullification.

The third issue: The community agreed that His saying: ﴿for them is their reward with their Lord﴾ is conditional upon there being no disbelief from them, and that indicates that it is permissible to speak in general terms while intending the specific. Once that is permissible in general, the indication of a general expression toward comprehensiveness is not a definitive indication, and that necessitates the collapse of the Mu'tazilah's proofs from general expressions for certainty regarding the threat.

As for His saying: ﴿no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: Their spending in the way of Allah is not lost; rather its reward is fully preserved for them on the Day of Resurrection. They do not fear that it will not be found, nor do they grieve because it might not be found. This is like His saying: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, he will not fear injustice or diminishment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 112].

The second: The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection they will not fear punishment at all, as He said: ﴿And they will be secure from terror that Day﴾ [al-Naml: 89], and He said: ﴿The great terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 263–265 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His example is like the example of a smooth rock upon which is dust, and then a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the approval of Allah and for the strengthening of their souls is like an garden on a hill: a heavy rain strikes it and it yields its produce twofold. And if it is not struck by a heavy rain, then a light rain. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

As for "kind speech" (qawl ma'ruf), it is the speech that hearts accept and do not reject. What is meant here is that one should turn away the beggar in a good and pleasant manner. ʿAtaʾ said: "This is a good deed." As for "forgiveness" (maghfirah), there are several interpretations:

First: When the poor man is turned away without obtaining his purpose, this distresses him, and this may lead him to abusive speech. So he is commanded to pardon the poor man's abuse and to overlook his wrongdoing.

Second: What is meant is obtaining forgiveness from Allah through the kind refusal.

Third: What is meant by forgiveness is that one should conceal the poor man's need and not expose his concealment, and what is meant by kind speech is turning him away in the best manner; and by forgiveness, not exposing his concealment by mentioning his condition to someone whom the poor man dislikes to know of his state.

Fourth: His saying, ﴿Kind speech﴾, is an address to the one asked, that he should turn the beggar away in the best manner, and His saying, ﴿and forgiveness﴾, is an address to the beggar, that he should excuse the one asked for that refusal, since he may not have been able to give that thing at that time. Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that the man's doing of these two matters is better for him than charity followed by injury. The reason for this preference is that when he gives and then follows the giving with injury, there is a combination of benefit and harm, and the reward of the benefit may not outweigh the punishment for the harm. As for kind speech, there is benefit in it, in that it includes bringing joy to the heart of a Muslim, and no harm accompanies it, so this is better than the former.

Page 44

Know that some people have said: the verse concerns voluntary charity, because the obligatory (zakat) may not be withheld, nor may the beggar be turned away from it. It is possible that what is meant is the obligatory, and it may be that one shifts from one beggar to another and from one poor man to another.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is Free of need﴾ from the charity of the servants; so He commanded you to give only so that He may reward you for it. ﴿Forbearing﴾, in that He did not hasten the punishment against the one who reminds and injures with his charity. This is a expression of His displeasure and a threat to him. Then He, exalted is He, described these two types of spending: one of them is that which is followed by reminder and injury; and the second is that which is not followed by reminder and injury. He explained the state of each of them and gave an example for each of them.

He said regarding the first category, that which is followed by reminder and injury: ﴿O you who have believed, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day.﴾ In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: The judge (al-Qadi) said: He, exalted is He, emphasized the prohibition against nullifying charity by reminder and injury, and removed every doubt of the Murji'ah by making clear that what is meant is that reminder and injury nullify the charity. It is known that the charity has already occurred and passed, so it is not valid that it be nullified; therefore what is meant is the nullifying of its reward and recompense, because the reward has not yet come about and is in the future, so its nullification by what comes after it of reminder and injury is valid.

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned two examples for the manner in which the reward of charity is nullified by reminder and injury. He first gave the example of one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people, and who is, moreover, a disbeliever who does not believe in Allah and the Last Day, because the nullification of the reward of the spending of this showy disbeliever is more evident than the nullification of the reward of the charity of one who follows it with reminder and injury. Then He gave the second example: the smooth rock upon which there is dust and earth, then a strong rain strikes it, which removes that dust from it until it becomes as though there was never any dust or earth upon it at all. So the disbeliever is like the smooth rock, the dust is like that spending, and the heavy rain is like the disbelief which nullifies the deed of the disbeliever, and like the reminder and injury which nullify the deed of this spender. He said: Just as the heavy rain removed the dust that had settled on the smooth rock, likewise reminder and injury necessitate that they nullify the reward of the spending after it has occurred; and this is an explicit statement in favor of the doctrine of nullification (ihbat) and expiation (takfir).

Al-Jubba'i said: Just as this text proves the validity of our view, reason also proves it, because whoever obeys and disobeys, if he were to deserve the reward for his obedience and the punishment for his disobedience, it would necessarily follow that he deserves two opposites; for the condition of reward is that it be pure, lasting benefit joined with honor, and the condition of punishment is that it be pure, lasting harm joined with humiliation. So if nullification did not occur, the deserving of two opposites would result, and that is impossible. Moreover, when He punishes him, He has withheld the reward from him, and withholding the reward is injustice, while this punishment is justice; so it would follow that this punishment is just insofar as it is his due, and unjust insofar as it withholds the reward, so He would be unjust by the very act in which He is just, and that is impossible. Thus our view of nullification and expiation is established by this text and by the proof of reason. This is the statement of the Mu'tazilah.

As for our companions (the Ash'arites), they said: What is meant by His saying ﴿do not nullify﴾ is not the prohibition against removing this reward after it has been established, but rather that one should perform this deed as void from the beginning, because when one intends by it other than the face of Allah, he has performed it from the start in the state of nullity. Our companions argued against the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah with several proofs:

The first: If the preventing and the subsequent do not have any opposition between them, then the coming of the subsequent does not necessitate the removal of the preventing; and if there is opposition between them, then the dispelling of the subsequent is not more apt than the removal of the preventing, but rather this may be more apt, because prevention is easier than removal.

Second: If the subsequent were to nullify, it would either nullify what has entered existence in the past, which is impossible because the past has ended and does not remain in the present, and annihilating what is non-existent is impossible; or it would nullify what exists in the present, which is also impossible, because if it annihilated what exists in the present at the present, it would necessitate the combination of non-existence and existence, which is impossible; or it would nullify what will exist in the future, which is impossible, because what will exist in the future is non-existent at present, and annihilating what has not yet existed is impossible.

Third: The condition for the coming of the subsequent is the removal of the preventing; so if we made the removal of the preventing caused by the coming of the subsequent, it would necessitate circularity, which is impossible.

Fourth: When the subsequent comes and annihilates the prior reward, the prior reward either loses something from this subsequent or it loses nothing from it. The first is the equivalence (muwazanah), the view of Abu Hashim, and it is false, because the cause of the non-existence of each of them is the existence of the other; so if the two non-existences occur together, which are caused, it would necessitate the occurrence of the two existences which are the causes, so that each of them would be existent while each of them is non-existent, which is impossible. As for the second, the view of Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, it is also false, because when the subsequent punishment removed the prior reward, and that prior reward has no effect whatsoever in removing anything from this subsequent punishment, then the deed which necessitated the prior reward yields no benefit at all, neither in bringing reward nor in averting punishment; and this contradicts the explicit text: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7]. Moreover, it is contrary to justice, since the servant bears the hardship of obedience while no effect of it appears for him, neither in bringing benefit nor in averting harm.

Fifth: You say that a minor sin nullifies some parts of the reward and not others, and that is an absurd statement, because the parts of the deserved merits are equal in essence; so if the effect of the subsequent minor sin is directed to some of those merits and not others, while all are equal in essence, that would be preferring the possible without a preponderant, which is impossible. Therefore there remains only that it be said that the subsequent minor sin removes all of those merits, which is false by consensus, or that it removes none of them, which is what was sought.

Sixth: If the punishment for a major sin is greater than the reward of the earlier deed, then either it is said that the influence in nullifying the reward is some parts of the subsequent punishment or all of it. The first is false, because the specification of some of those parts with influence and not others, while all are equal in essence, is preponderance of the possible without a preponderant, which is impossible. The second is also false, because then two parts of the punishment would combine to nullify one part of the reward, while each of those two parts is independently sufficient to nullify that reward; so two independent influences would converge on one effect, which is impossible, because one would then be independent of each of them while being in need of both together, which is impossible.

Seventh: There is no opposition between these two deservings, because if a master says to his slave: guard the goods lest the thief steal them, and then at that time an enemy comes intending to kill the master, and the slave busies himself fighting that enemy and killing him, then that act of the slave necessitates his deserving praise and honor, since he repelled death from his master, and it necessitates his deserving blame, since he exposed his property to theft; and each of the two deservings is established. Reasonable people, in such an event, resort to preponderance or to a rotation of duties; but to judge that one of the two deservings is negated and removed is rejected by the self-evident judgment of reason.

Page 45

Eighth: The cause of the occurrence of this deserving is the prior act. So this subsequent matter either has an effect on the aspect of that act's necessitating that deserving or it does not. The first is impossible, because that act exists only in past time; so if this subsequent matter had an effect on that past act, this would be bringing about an effect in past time, which is impossible. And if the subsequent matter has no effect on the prior act's necessitating that deserving, then that necessitation must remain as it was and must not be removed.

It may not be said: why could this subsequent matter not be a barrier preventing the manifestation of the effect upon that prior act? For we say: if this subsequent matter cannot act at all, in any way, upon the aspect of that act's necessitation, since bringing about an effect in the past is impossible, and the cancellation of this subsequent matter's effect is possible in general, then the past, on this assumption, is stronger than this new occurrence, so the past's repelling this occurrence is more fitting than the reverse.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 263–265 (part 2 of 3):

Ninth: These Mu'tazilites say that drinking a single sip of wine nullifies (yuhbitu) the reward of faith and of seventy years of obedience performed sincerely, and this is impossible. For we know by necessity that the reward of these acts of obedience is greater than the punishment for this one act of disobedience, and the greater does not encompass the lesser. Al-Jubba'i said: It is not impossible that one major sin be greater than every act of obedience, because disobedience to God increases in proportion to the abundance of His blessings and bounty, just as the obligation of gratitude owed to one who has raised a person, bestowed possessions upon him and brought him to a great state is greater than the gratitude owed for the abundance of his favours. Thus, when God's blessings upon His servants are such that they cannot be measured in greatness or abundance, it is not impossible that the single act of disobedience deserve a great punishment that equals the reward of all acts of obedience together. Know that this excuse is weak, because when a king's favours upon his servant are great, and that servant then fulfils the duty of servitude for fifty years, and then deliberately breaks the tip of that king's pen, if the king were to nullify all of his obedience because of that amount of offence, everyone would blame him and attribute to him a lack of fairness and harshness. It is well known that all sins, in relation to the majesty of God the Exalted, are less than breaking the tip of a pen. Thus it is clear that what they have said runs contrary to the measure of reason.

Tenth: The faith of an hour demolishes the disbelief of seventy years. So how can the faith of seventy years be demolished by the immorality of an hour?! This is something reason does not accept. And God knows best.

These, then, are the bulk of the rational proofs against the doctrine of nullification (al-muhabatah, the cancelling of good deeds by sins) in the Mu'tazilites' reliance on this verse. We say: God's words, "O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reproach and injury" (2:264), admit of two meanings:

The first: do not bring them into being as void. That is, that one intends by the charity show-off (riya') and reputation-seeking, so this charity, at the moment it exists, has come into being void. This interpretation does not harm us at all.

The second meaning: that the nullification is meant to be that it is performed in a manner that would earn reward, and then, after that, when it is followed by reproach and injury, the punishment of the reproach and injury becomes a remover of the reward of that charity. On this reading, the Mu'tazilites benefit from invoking the verse. So why is it that carrying the wording to this second meaning is preferable to carrying it to the first?

Know that God the Exalted mentioned two similitudes for this. One of them corresponds to the first possibility, namely His words: "like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in God" (2:264). For it is well known that what is meant by his deed being void is that it came into existence void, not that it came into existence valid and then ceased, because the obstacle to the validity of this deed is disbelief, and disbelief is concomitant with it, so its coming into existence validly is impossible. Thus this similitude supports what we have adopted as the interpretation. As for the second similitude, the smooth rock on which dust and earth have settled and then a heavy rain strikes it, this supports their interpretation, because God made the heavy rain a remover of that dust after the dust had settled on the rock. So here, the reproach and injury must likewise remove the reward and recompense after the entitlement to reward has occurred. However, we may say: we do not concede that what is likened to the dust settling on the rock is the attainment of reward by the disbeliever. Rather, what is likened to that is the performance of this act, which, were it not joined to a corrupt intention, would have been entailing the attainment of reward and recompense. So what is likened to the dust lying on the smooth rock is that act performed by him. And reading the speech according to what we have mentioned is preferable, because when dust falls on a smooth rock it is not really attached to it or embedded in it at all; rather, that contact is like separation. It appears to the eye as connected, but in reality it is not connected. Likewise, charity accompanied by reproach and injury appears outwardly to be an act of righteousness, but in reality it is not so. Thus it is clear that their reliance on this verse is weak. As for the rational argument they relied upon, we have shown that there is no contradiction in combining the two entitlements, and that the consequence of such combining is either weighting (tarjih) or alternation (muhaya'ah).

Second issue: Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him both, said: "Do not nullify your charities by reproach toward God on account of your charity, and by injury toward that beggar." Others said: "by reproach toward the poor man, and by injury toward the poor man." Ibn 'Abbas's view is plausible, because when a person spends boastfully over his deed, and does not follow the path of humility, of turning to God, and of acknowledging that this is from His grace, His guidance and His kindness, he becomes like one who reproaches God the Exalted, even though the second view is more apparent.

* * *

As for His words, "like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people" (2:264), in it there are two issues:

First issue: The kaf in His words "like one who" has two views:

The first: it is connected to an implied element, and the sense is: "do not nullify your charities with reproach and injury, as the nullification of one who spends his wealth to be seen by people." God thus clarifies that reproach and injury nullify charity, just as hypocrisy and show-off nullify it. The explanation of this is that the hypocrite and the show-off give charity not for the sake of God the Exalted, and whoever joins charity with reproach and injury has also given that charity not for the sake of God, for if his purpose in that charity were to seek God's pleasure, he would not have reproached the poor man or harmed him. Thus the two cases are established as sharing the fact that the charity was not given for the sake of God the Exalted. This confirms what we said, that the intended nullification is bringing the act into being void, not that the act was brought into being valid and then removed and nullified by reproach and injury.

The second view: the kaf is in the accusative position as a circumstantial element (hal), meaning: "do not nullify your charities while being like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people."

Second issue: riya' is a verbal noun, like muraa'at; it is said: "ra'aytuhu riya'an wa muraa'atan," like "ra'aytuhu mura'atan wa ri'an," and it means that you show your deed to another. The full discussion of riya' has already been given above. Then, when God mentioned this similitude, He followed it with a second similitude, saying: "fa-mathaluhu" (its likeness). In this pronoun there are two views:

One: it refers to the hypocrite, so the meaning is that God likened the one who reproaches and injures to the hypocrite, then likened the hypocrite to a rock, then said: "like a smooth rock (safwan)," which is the smooth stone. Abu 'Ubayd related from al-Asma'i that safwan, safa and safwa are one and the same, all of them with a short final vowel (maqsur). Some said: safwan is the plural of safwanah, like marjan and marjanah, and sa'dan and sa'danah. Then He said: "a heavy rain (wabil) struck it," wabil being intense rain; it is said: "the sky rained heavily (wabalat al-sama' tabil wabilan)," and "a land that has been rained upon heavily (mawbulah)," meaning a heavy rain struck it. Then He said: "and left it bare (saldan)." Saldan is smooth and dry; it is said: "a hard rock (hajarsald) and a hard mountain (jabal sald)" when it is glistening and smooth, and "a barren land (ardh saldah)," meaning it produces nothing, like hard rock; and "the tinder became saldah" when it does not produce fire.

Know that this is a similitude God has struck for the deed of the one who reproaches and injures, and for the deed of the hypocrite, for people see outwardly that these have deeds, just as the dust is seen on this smooth rock. When the Day of Resurrection comes, all of it is dissolved and vanishes, because it becomes clear that those deeds were not for God the Exalted, just as the heavy rain removed the dust that was on the rock. As for the Mu'tazilites, they said: the meaning is that this charity had required the reward and recompense, then reproach and injury removed that reward, just as the heavy rain removes the dust from the face of the rock.

Know that there are two views regarding how this comparison works:

The first: what we mentioned, that the outward deed is like the dust, and the one who reproaches, injures and is a hypocrite is like the smooth rock on the Day of Resurrection. This is according to our view. As for the view of the Mu'tazilites, reproach and injury are like the heavy rain.

The second view on the comparison: al-Qaffal, may God the Exalted have mercy on him, said: There is another possibility, namely that the deeds of servants are stored treasures for them on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever acts sincerely is like one who casts a seed into the earth, and it is multiplied for him and grows until he harvests it at its time and finds it at the time of his need. The smooth rock is the place of the hypocrite's seed, and it is well known that nothing grows in it and there is no receptivity in it for the seed. The meaning is that the deed of the one who reproaches, injures and is a hypocrite resembles, when one casts a seed onto a hard smooth rock on which there is little dust, that when a generous rain strikes it, it remains with its seed deposited, empty, with nothing in it. Do you not see that God struck the parable of the sincere one with a garden on a height, and a garden is that in which there are trees and palms? So whoever is sincere for God the Exalted is like one who planted an orchard on a raised piece of land; he gathers the fruit of its plantings at times of need, and it yields its produce every season by the permission of its Lord, multiplied and increased. As for the deed of the one who reproaches, injures and is a hypocrite, it is like one who sowed in the smooth rock over which there is dust, so that when he needs to sow he finds nothing in it.

Some of the heretics (mulhidah) criticized the comparison, saying: when the heavy rain strikes the smooth rock, it makes it pure, clean and free of dust and earth, so how can God liken the hypocrite's deed to it?

The answer: the point of the comparison is what we have mentioned, so it should not be judged by their differing in what lies beyond it.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: Moreover, the settling of dust on the smooth rock yields several benefits: first, it is more suitable for a seed to settle on it; second, benefit from it in tayammum (dry ablution); third, benefit from it in matters connected with vegetation. This last point mentioned by the judge is good, but reliance is on the first.

As for God's words, "They have no power over anything of what they have earned" (2:264), know that the pronoun in His words "they have no power" (la yaqdiruna): to what does it refer? There are two views:

The first: it refers to something known but not mentioned, meaning: no one among creatures has power over that seed cast into that dust which was on that smooth rock, because that dust has been removed and what was in it, so no one has any ability to benefit from that seed. This strengthens the second view of the comparison mentioned by al-Qaffal, may God the Exalted have mercy on him. Likewise, none of those who reproach, injure and are hypocrites will benefit from their deed on the Day of Resurrection.

The second: it refers back to His words "like one who spends his wealth" and this is taken on this meaning, because His words "like one who spends his wealth" are directed at the category, and the category is in the ruling of the general.

Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: There is also a third view, namely that this is a return to the words "do not nullify" (la) "your charities with reproach and injury," for if you do that, you will have no power over anything of what you have earned. So the address shifts from direct address to the absent third person, like His words: "until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them" (Yunus 10:22).

Then He said: "And God does not guide the disbelieving people" (2:264). Its meaning according to their view is the withdrawal of faith, and according to the Mu'tazilites' view, that God leads them astray from reward and the path to Paradise by their own wrong choice.

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: "And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and for the firming of their own souls is like a garden on a height which a heavy rain strikes, so it yields its produce twofold; and if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain; and God is seer of what you do" (2:265).

Know that when God the Exalted mentioned the likeness of the spender who is reproaching and injuring, He mentioned the likeness of the spender who is not like that, which is this verse, and God made clear that the aim of these spenders in this spending is two things:

First: seeking the pleasure of God the Exalted. Ibtigha' is an ifti'al form from baghaytu, meaning I sought; and "baghaytu" and "ibtaghaytu" are equivalent.

The second aim: the firming of the self, and on this there are several views:

**[Part 3 of 3]**

First: they settle their souls upon preserving this act of obedience and abandoning whatever corrupts it. Among that is abandoning the following of it with reproach and harm. This is the view of al-Qadi.

Second: it is a strengthening from themselves, for the believers, that they are truthful in faith and sincere in it. This is supported by the reading of Mujahid, "and a strengthening from some of their souls" (*wa-tathbitan min ba'di anfusihim*).

Third: the soul has no steadfastness in the station of servitude unless it has been subdued through striving (*mujahadah*). What it loves are two things: the hastening life and wealth. When it is charged with spending wealth, it has been subdued in some respect. When it is charged with giving up its life, it has been subdued in some respect. Therefore some steadfastness is indeed achieved, and for this reason the particle *min*, which denotes partiality, is used. The meaning is that whoever spends his wealth for the sake of Allah has strengthened part of his soul, and whoever spends both his wealth and his life together has strengthened it entirely. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives﴾ [al-Saff: 11]. This aspect was mentioned by the author of *al-Kashshaf*, and it is a good statement and a subtle interpretation.

Fourth, and this is what occurred to my mind at the time of writing this section: the steadfastness of the heart is achieved only through the remembrance of Allah, as He said: ﴿Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. Whoever spends his wealth in the way of Allah does not attain tranquility of heart in the station of manifestation (*tajalli*) unless his spending is purely for the aim of servitude. For this reason it is related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said regarding his spending: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah; we desire no reward from you, nor thanks﴾ [al-Insan: 9]. And he described the spending of Abu Bakr, saying: ﴿And none has a favor upon him to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High. And he is going to be pleased﴾ [al-Layl: 19–21]. So when a servant's spending is for the sake of the servitude of the Real, not for the sake of the soul's aim and the seeking of its desire, then his heart is at rest there, his soul settles, and no conflict arises between his soul and his heart. For this reason He first said of this spending that it was for seeking the good pleasure of Allah, and then followed that with His saying: ﴿and a strengthening from their own souls﴾.

Fifth: it is established in the rational sciences that the repetition of acts is a cause for the acquisition of stable dispositions (*malakat*).

Having known this, we say: whoever persists in spending again and again, seeking the good pleasure of Allah, gains two things from that persistence:

First: the attainment of this meaning.

Second: that this seeking and aspiring becomes a firmly established disposition in the soul, so that the heart reaches a state where, if an act issues from it through heedlessness or by chance, the heart immediately returns to the sanctuary of holiness. This is because that worship becomes like a habit and a natural disposition of the spirit. Thus the servant's performance of obedience to Allah, seeking the good pleasure of Allah, produces this firmly established disposition, which the Qur'an expresses as the steadying of the soul. This is also what is meant by His saying: ﴿Allah makes firm those who believe﴾. [Page 50] When this steadiness is attained, the spirit in this world becomes of the substance of the spiritual angels and the holy essences. So the servant becomes, as one of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) said, "absent yet present, traveling yet resident."

Sixth: al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the steadiness is that they spend it while certain that Allah, the Exalted, will not waste their deed nor disappoint their hope, because it is coupled with reward, punishment, and resurrection. This is unlike the hypocrite, for when he spends, that spending is considered lost, because he does not believe in reward. So this certainty is what is meant by steadiness.

Seventh: al-Hasan, Mujahid, and 'Ata' said: the meaning is that the one who gives charity exercises care (*tathabbut*) in giving it, placing it with the righteous and the chaste. Al-Hasan said: when a man intended to give charity, he would take care; if it was for Allah, he would give, and if it was mixed with something else, he would withhold. Al-Wahidi said: it is permissible for steadiness to mean carefulness, because they made their souls steadfast in seeking the one deserving and in directing the wealth to its proper destination.

Then, after He explained that their aim in spending was these two matters, He set forth a parable for their spending, saying: ﴿Like a garden on a height, struck by a heavy rain﴾. There are issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read *bi-rabwatin* with a *fatha* on the *ra'*, and in al-Mu'minun *ila rabwatin*, which is the dialect of Tamim. The rest read it with a *damma* on the *ra'* in both places, and this is the most well-known dialect and the dialect of Quraysh. There are seven forms: *rabwah* with the three vowels on the *ra'*, *rabawah* with an *alif* with the three vowels on the *ra'*, and *rabw*. *Al-rabwah* is an elevated place. Al-Akhfash said: what I choose is *rubwah* with a *damma*, because its plural is *ruba*. Its root is from their saying *raba al-shay'* (the thing grew), which means it increased and rose. From it comes *al-rabiyah* (the elevated mound), because its parts have risen. From it comes *al-rabw*, when a person has extra breath in his chest. From it comes *al-riba* (usury), because it takes the excess.

Know that the commentators said: a garden on an elevated piece of land is better and yields more.

I have a difficulty with this: when a garden is on a raised area of land, it is above the water, rivers do not rise up to it, and the winds strike it heavily, so its yield is not good. When it is in a depression of the land, the waters of the rivers pour into it, and the stirring of the winds does not reach it, so its yield is also not good. Therefore a garden's yield is good only when it is on level ground that is neither elevated nor depressed. Thus the meaning of this *rabwah* is not what they mentioned. Rather, the meaning is that the land is soft, fertile earth, such that when rain falls upon it, it swells, grows, and increases. When land has this quality, its yield abounds and its trees become perfect. This interpretation that I have mentioned is confirmed by two proofs:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. The meaning of its swelling is what we have mentioned, so likewise here.

The second: He, exalted is He, mentioned this parable in contrast to the first parable. The first parable was the smooth rock upon which rain has no effect, and which does not swell or grow by the descent of rain upon it. Therefore the meaning of *rabwah* in this parable is the land being in a state where it swells and grows. This is what occurred to my mind, and Allah knows best what He intends.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿struck by a heavy rain, it yielded its produce twofold﴾. There are issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read *ukulaha* with the lightened form, and the rest with the emphatic form, which is the original. *Al-ukul* with a *damma* means food, because it is of its nature to be eaten. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It gives its produce every season by the permission of its Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 25], meaning its fruit and what is eaten from it. So *al-akl* in meaning is like *al-tu'mah* (food). Al-Akhfash recited:

*"So a meal, if you obtain it, is not a gain, nor is hunger, if you go hungry, with a shabby garment."*

[Page 51] Abu Zayd said: it is said, "He is possessed of food (*la-dhu akl*)" when he has a share of this world.

**The second issue:** al-Zajjaj said: ﴿yielded its produce twofold﴾ means double. For the double of a thing is its like plus added to it. It was also said that the double of a thing is its two like amounts. 'Ata' said: it bore in one season what other gardens bear in two years. Al-Asamm said: twice what it would ordinarily produce in other circumstances. Abu Muslim said: twice what was customary from it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain (*tall*)﴾. The *tall* is a rain of small drops. Then in meaning there are several aspects:

First: the meaning is that if a heavy rain does not strike this garden, then a rain less than heavy strikes it, yet its fruit remains in its condition under both circumstances, not diminished because of the lessening of the rain. This is due to the nobility of the soil.
