Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿so it is struck by a whirlwind containing fire, so it is burned﴾. Al-i'sar is a wind that rises and spirals toward the sky like a column, and it is what people call the zawba'ah. It is a wind of the utmost severity, and from it is the poet's saying:

If you are a wind, then you have met a whirlwind.
The purpose of this parable is to show that there arises in the heart of this person such grief, distress, regret and bewilderment as no one knows but Allah. Likewise, whoever performs good deeds but does not intend thereby the face of Allah, rather attaches to them matters that remove them from being a cause of reward, when he comes on the Day of Resurrection in the utmost need and the extreme of inability to earn, his regret becomes great and his bewilderment extreme. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned﴾ [az-Zumar: 47], and His saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23].
* * *
Then He said: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾, i.e., just as Allah has made clear to you His signs and proofs in this matter, by way of encouragement and warning, thus Allah makes clear to you His signs and proofs in all the other matters of the religion.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿that you might give thought﴾. There are two issues here:
The first issue: that "la'alla" is for expectation (tarajji), and that does not befit Allah, exalted is He.

The second issue: the Mu'tazilah held fast to it, saying that it indicates that He, exalted is He, intended faith from all. The explanation of these two verses has been given before, many times.

[Page 53]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth, and do not aim at the defective therefrom to spend from it, while you would not take it yourselves except by overlooking [its defects] in it. And know that Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, encouraged spending, then explained that spending is of two kinds: one kind that is followed by reminding of one's favour and by harm, and another kind that is not followed by that.

Then He, exalted is He, explained what pertains to each of these two kinds, and He presented for each of them an example that reveals the meaning and clarifies the intended purpose in the most eloquent manner.

[Page 54]

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse how the wealth that He commanded to be spent in the way of Allah ought to be. So He said: ﴿Spend from the good things you have earned.﴾ The scholars differed about what is meant by His saying "spend" (anfiqu). Al-Hasan said: it means the obligatory zakat. Some people said: it means voluntary charity (tatawwu'). A third group said: it includes both the obligatory and the voluntary.

The argument of those who said it means obligatory zakat: His saying "spend" is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, and obligatory spending is nothing other than zakat and the other obligatory expenditures.

The argument of those who said it means voluntary charity: what is reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah ennoble his face, al-Hasan and Mujahid, that they used to give charity from the worst of their fruits and the inferior of their wealth, so Allah revealed this verse. And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "A man came one day with a cluster of dry, spoiled dates (ʿidhq ḥashaf) and placed it in the charity, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Evil is what this one's owner has done.'" Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

The argument of those who said that both the obligatory and the voluntary are included in this verse: what is understood from a command is the preference of the act over its omission, without any indication of whether omission is permitted or not, and this understood meaning is a common element between the obligatory and the voluntary, so both must fall under the command.

Having understood this, we say: As for the first view, namely that it is for obligation, certain issues branch from it:

The first issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the obligation of zakat on every wealth that a person acquires, so it includes trade zakat, zakat on gold and silver, and zakat on livestock, since all of that is described as acquired. It also indicates the obligation of zakat on everything that the earth produces, according to the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, and his argument from this verse is very clear. However, his opponents restricted this generality by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There is no charity on vegetables." Also, the school of Abu Hanifa holds that paying zakat on everything the earth produces is obligatory, whether little or much, and the apparent meaning of the verse supports his view. However, his opponents restricted this generality by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There is no charity on what is less than five wasq."

The second issue: The scholars differed about what is meant by "good" (ṭayyib) in this verse, in two views:

The first view: it means the superior of the wealth, not the inferior. So the word "good" is applied to the superior by way of metaphor (istiʿāra). According to this interpretation, what is meant by "the defective" (al-khabīth) mentioned in this verse is the inferior.

The second view, which is the view of Ibn Masʿud and Mujahid: "the good" is the lawful (ḥalāl), and "the defective" is the unlawful (ḥarām).

The arguments of the first view are several:

The first argument: We mentioned in the occasion of revelation that they used to give charity from their inferior wealth, so the verse was revealed, and this indicates that what is meant by "the good" is the superior.

The second argument: What is unlawful may not be taken, neither by overlooking nor without overlooking, whereas the verse indicates that the defective may be taken by overlooking. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It can be answered that what is meant by "overlooking" is tolerance and leaving off scrutiny, so the meaning becomes: "And you would not take it while you know it is unlawful, unless you permit yourselves to take what is unlawful, and do not care from what source you have taken the wealth, whether from its lawful or its unlawful part."

The third argument: This view is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 92], and this indicates that what is meant by "the good things" are the precious things whose ownership is desired, not the base things which everyone must push away from himself and remove from his house.

[Page 55]

Al-Qadi argued for the second view, saying: We agree that what is meant by "the good" in this verse is either the superior or the lawful. So if the first is invalid, the second is determined. And we say the first is invalid because if what is meant were the superior, that would be a command to spend the superior in general, whether it were unlawful or lawful, and that is not permissible, and taking a restriction is contrary to the original principle. Therefore it is established that what is meant is not the superior but the lawful. It is possible to mention a third view here, namely that what is meant by "the good" in this place is what is good from every aspect, so it is good in the sense of lawful and it is good in the sense of excellence. There is no objection that the shared word cannot be carried on both its meanings, because we say: The lawful is called good only because the intellect and religion find it good, and the superior is called good only because inclination and appetite find it good, so the meaning of "finding good" is one concept shared between the two categories, and the word is therefore carried upon it, when it is established that what is meant by it is the superior lawful wealth. So we say: Zakatable wealth is either entirely noble, or entirely base, or intermediate, or mixed. If all of it is noble, what is taken by the calculation of zakat is likewise noble. If all of it is base, the zakat is also from that base wealth, and this does not contradict the verse, because what is taken in this case is not base from that wealth; rather, if the wealth contains both superior and inferior, then it is said to the person: Do not make the zakat from your inferior wealth. As for when the wealth is mixed, the obligation is the middling. The Prophet ﷺ said to Muʿadh ibn Jabal when he sent him to Yemen: "Inform them that upon them is a charity, taken from their rich and returned to their poor, and beware of the choicest of their wealth." All of this applies if we say that what is meant by His saying: ﴿Spend from the good things you have earned﴾ is obligatory zakat. As for the second view, namely that what is meant by it is voluntary charity, or we say that what is meant is obligatory and voluntary spending together, we say: Allah, exalted is He, urged them to draw near to Him with the best of what they possess, like one who draws near to a great king with a gift and a present; it is necessary that this gift be the best and most noble of what is in his kingdom, and so it is here.

One question remains in the verse, namely: what is the benefit of the word "min" (from) in His saying: ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾?

Its answer: The implied structure of the verse is: "Spend from the good things you have earned, and spend from the good things We have produced for you from the earth." However, since mention of "the good things" occurred once, it is omitted the second time because the first mention indicates it.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not aim at the defective﴾ (wa lā tayammamū al-khabītha), there are two issues:

The first issue: It is said: amamtuhu, yammamtuhu, and ta'ammamtuhu, all of which mean "I intended him." Al-A'sha said:

"I aimed at Qays, and between me and him are many lands, a waste with a noble ridge."

The second issue: Ibn Kathir alone read "wa lā tayyammamū" with a doubled tā', because originally there were two tā's: the tā' of address and the tā' of the verb, so one of them was assimilated into the other. The rest read it with a single, light tā' (fatha). On this basis, the same disagreement applies to its counterparts, which are twenty-three places: "lā tafarraqū," "tawaffāhum," "taʿāwanū," "fatafarraqa bikum," "talqafu," "tawallaw," "tanāzaʿū," "tarabbaṣūn," "fa-in tawallaw," "lā tukallamu," "talaqqawnahu," "tabarrajna," "tabaddala," "tanāṣarūn," "tajassasū," "tanābazū," "li-taʿārafū," "tamayyaz," "takhayyarūn," "talahhā," "talaẓẓā," "tanazzalu al-malāʾika." And here there are two investigations:

The first investigation: Abu ʿAli said: This assimilation is not permissible, because the assimilated letter is made quiescent, and when it is made quiescent it is necessary to introduce the hamzat al-wasl when beginning with it, as it was introduced in past-tense forms such as "iddāraʾtum," "irtabtum," and "iṭṭayyarnā." But they agreed that the hamzat al-wasl does not enter upon the imperfect.

[Page 56]

The second investigation: They differed about the omitted tā' according to the reading of the majority. Some said it is the first tā', but Sibawayh does not drop anything except the second, while al-Farra' says: whichever of them is dropped is permissible, because the remaining one substitutes for it.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from it you spend.﴾

Know that there are two ways of arranging the structure of the verse:

The first: The sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿and do not aim at the defective﴾, then He begins: ﴿from it you spend, while you would not take it yourselves except by overlooking [its defects] in it.﴾ So His saying "from it you spend" is an interrogative in the sense of denunciation, and the meaning is: "Do you spend from it, while you would not take it yourselves except with overlooking?"

The second: The sentence is only complete at His saying: ﴿except by overlooking [its defects] in it﴾, and "the one" (alladhī) is implied, and the estimate is: "and do not aim at the defective from it, the one you spend, while you would not take it except with overlooking in it." Its parallel is the implied "alladhī" in His saying: ﴿Whoever has grasped the most reliable handhold, which will never break﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256], and the meaning is "the most reliable handhold which has no breaking."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while you would not take it yourselves except by overlooking [its defects] in it﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: Al-ighmāḍ (overlooking) in the language means lowering the gaze and closing one eyelid over another, and its origin is from ghumūḍ, which is obscurity, and it is said: "this speech is ghāmiḍ," meaning hard to grasp. And al-ghamḍ is the low, hidden part of the land.

The second issue: As for the meaning of overlooking in this verse, there are several views:

The first: What is meant by overlooking here is leniency, because when a person sees what he dislikes, he closes his eyes so as not to see it, and then this became so common that every concession and leniency in sale or otherwise was called overlooking. So His saying: ﴿while you would not take it yourselves except by overlooking [its defects] in it﴾ means: "If such things were presented to you as a gift, you would not accept them except with embarrassment and overlooking, so how do you accept for Me what you would not accept for yourselves?!"

The second: Overlooking may be taken in its transitive sense, as you say: "I closed the eyes of the dead" (aghmaḍtu baṣara al-mayyit wa ghammaḍtuhu). The meaning is: "you would not take it except if you closed the seller's eyes," that is, you asked him to overlook and reduce the price.

Then He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿And know that Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾ The meaning is that He is free of need of your charities, and the meaning of "Praiseworthy" is praised for what He has bestowed through explanation. There is another view in it, namely that His saying "Free of need" is like a warning against giving inferior things in charity, and "Praiseworthy" is in the sense of "one who praises," meaning: "I praise you for the good deeds you do," as in His saying: ﴿Those whose effort was appreciated﴾ [al-Isrā': 19].

[Page 57]

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾**

Know that when Allah the Exalted had encouraged man to spend from the best of what he possesses, He afterwards warned him against the whispering of Satan, saying:

[Page 57]
**﴿The Satan threatens you with poverty﴾**, meaning: it is said to you, "If you spend the best, you will become poor, so pay no attention to what he says, for the Most Merciful ﴿promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾." There are several issues concerning this verse:

**First issue:** Scholars differ regarding "the Satan." It has been said that it refers to Iblis, and it has been said that it refers to all the devils, and it has been said that it refers to the devils of the jinn and of mankind, and it has been said that it refers to the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara bi'l-su').

**Second issue:** The word *al-wa'd* (promise) is used for both good and evil. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Fire Allah has promised to those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Hajj: 72]. It is possible that this is meant ironically, as in His saying: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21].

**Third issue:** *Al-faqr* and *al-fuqr* are two dialectal forms (lughatan), and they mean weakness due to lack of wealth. The original meaning of *al-faqr* in the language is breaking of the spine (kasr al-fiqar). It is said: "a man is *faqir* and *fiqar* when his spine is broken." Tarafa said:

*Verily I am not one pledged to poverty (fiqr).*

The author of *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's exegesis) said: *al-fuqr* has been recited with a *damma* and *al-faqar* with two *fathas*.

**Fourth issue:** As for the discussion of the reality of *al-waswasa* (whispering), we have mentioned it at the beginning of the book in the commentary on "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan." It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed, Satan has a *lamma* (an impulse or visitation), and the angel has a *lamma*. The *lamma* of Satan is the threat of evil, and the *lamma* of the angel is the promise of good. Whoever finds that, let him know that it is from Allah, and whoever finds the first, let him seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan." Then he recited this verse. Al-Hasan narrated that some of the Emigrants (muhajirun) said: "Whoever would like to know where Satan is in him, let him reflect on the place from which he finds the desire to commit the evil deed."

As for His saying: **﴿and commands you to indecency﴾**, there are several interpretations:

**The first:** *Al-fahsha'* is stinginess (al-bukhl). **﴿And commands you to indecency﴾** means: he urges you to stinginess, like the urging of one who commands to one who is commanded. In the language of the Arabs, *al-fahish* is the stingy person. Tarafa said:

*I see death choosing the noble and taking the best of the wealth of the stingy, tight-fisted one.*

*Ya'tam* is derived from the expression "'āma fulan ila al-laban" when he craved milk, and by *al-fahish* he meant the stingy person. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed he is intensely fond of wealth﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8]. In this verse Allah the Exalted has pointed to a subtle matter: that Satan first frightens him with poverty, and then through this frightening he reaches the point of commanding him to indecency and urging him to stinginess. This is because stinginess is a blameworthy quality in the sight of everyone, so Satan cannot make stinginess appealing in his eyes except by first presenting that preliminary step, which is the fear of poverty.

**The second interpretation of *al-fahsha'*:** Satan says: "Do not spend the good part of your wealth in obedience to Allah, lest you become poor." If a man obeys Satan in this, Satan increases his demands, and prevents him from spending altogether, so that he gives neither the good nor the bad, and even withholds the obligatory rights. So he does not pay zakat, does not maintain the ties of kinship, and does not return a deposit. When he becomes like this, the weight of sins falls away from his heart and he becomes unconcerned about committing them. At that point the breach widens and he becomes bold in committing all sins, and that is *al-fahsha'*. The reality of this is that every disposition has two extremes and a middle. The complete extreme is that a person spends everything he owns in the way of Allah, both the good and the bad. The extreme of indecency, which is deficient, is that he spends nothing in the way of Allah, neither the good nor the bad. The intermediate matter is that he withholds the good and spends the bad. So when Satan wants to move him from the virtuous extreme to the indecent extreme, he cannot do so except by first drawing him to the middle. If a person disobeys Satan at this stage, Satan's hope of him is cut off, and if he obeys him in this, Satan hopes to draw him from the middle to the indecent extreme. So the middle is His saying: **﴿threatens you with poverty﴾**, and the indecent extreme is His saying: **﴿and commands you to indecency﴾**.

Then, after the Glorified and Exalted mentioned the levels of Satan's whispering, He followed it with the mention of the inspirations of the Most Merciful, saying: **﴿while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾**. So *al-maghfira* (forgiveness) indicates the benefits of the Hereafter, and *al-fadl* (bounty) indicates what is obtained in this world from creation. It is narrated from him (ﷺ) that an angel calls out every night: "O Allah, give every spender a replacement, and every withholder destruction."

In this verse there is a subtle point: Satan threatens you with poverty in the tomorrow of your worldly life, while the Most Merciful promises you forgiveness in the tomorrow of your final outcome. The promise of the Most Merciful regarding the tomorrow of the final outcome is more worthy of acceptance for several reasons:

**One:** The attainment of the tomorrow of this world is doubtful, while the attainment of the tomorrow of the final outcome is certain and definite.

**Second:** Even if one attains the tomorrow of this world, the wealth withheld may remain or may not remain. But at the attainment of the tomorrow of the final outcome, there must be the attainment of the forgiveness promised by Allah the Exalted, because He is the Truthful, in whose speech falsehood is impossible.

**Third:** Even if the withheld wealth remains into the tomorrow of this world, a person may or may not be able to benefit from it, either because of fear, illness, or preoccupation with another important matter. But at the attainment of the tomorrow of the final outcome, the benefit is secured through Allah's forgiveness, bounty, and kindness.

**Fourth:** Even if one benefits from the withheld wealth in the tomorrow of this world, there is no doubt that this benefit comes to an end and does not endure. But the benefit of Allah's forgiveness, bounty, and kindness is the enduring one that does not cease or vanish.

**Fifth:** The enjoyment of worldly pleasures is mixed with harms. You do not see any of the pleasures except that it becomes a cause of trial in a thousand ways, unlike the benefits of the Hereafter, which are pure and free from impurities. Whoever reflects on what we have mentioned will know that submitting to the promise of the Most Merciful of bounty and forgiveness is more worthy than submitting to the promise of Satan.

Having known this, we say: The intended meaning of *al-maghfira* is the expiation of sins, as He said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cleanse them﴾ [al-Tawba: 103]. In the verse there are two expressions that indicate the perfection of this forgiveness:

**One:** The indefiniteness in the word *maghfira*, meaning a forgiveness of what magnitude!

**The second:** His saying: **﴿forgiveness from Him﴾**. His saying "from Him" indicates the perfect state of this forgiveness, because the perfection of His generosity and the extremity of His bounty is known to all intelligent beings, and that forgiveness is from Him is also known to everyone. So when He specified this forgiveness by saying it is from Him, it is known that the intention is to magnify the status of this forgiveness, because the greatness of the giver indicates the greatness of the gift. The perfection of this forgiveness may mean what He said in another verse: ﴿Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ [al-Furqan: 70]. It may also mean that He makes him an intercessor for the forgiveness of the sins of other sinners. It may also be that the perfection of that forgiveness is a matter that our intellect cannot reach while we are in the abode of this world, for most details of the affairs of the Hereafter are hidden from us while we are in this world.

As for the meaning of *al-fadl* (bounty), it is the hastened replacement in this world. In my view, this bounty may have several meanings:

**One:** The intended meaning of this bounty is the virtue attained by the soul, namely the virtue of generosity and liberality. This is because the levels of happiness are three: psychological (nafsaniyya), bodily, and external. Ownership of wealth is among the external virtues, and the acquisition of the disposition of generosity and liberality is among the psychological virtues.

They agreed that the most noble of these three levels is the psychological happiness, and the lowest is the external happiness. So when spending wealth does not occur, the external happiness is present while its psychological opposite is present with it. When spending occurs, the psychological perfection and the external deficiency are attained. There is no doubt that this state is more perfect. Thus it is established that mere spending necessitates the attainment of what Allah promised, namely the attainment of bounty.

**The second:** When the faculty of spending is acquired, the state of being preoccupied with worldly pleasures and greedily pursuing its objectives is removed from the spirit. Nothing prevents the spirit from being illuminated by the light of Allah's majesty except the love of this world. For this reason, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "Were it not that the devils whisper to the hearts of the sons of Adam, they would look upon the dominion of the heavens." When the dust of love of this world is removed from the face of the heart, it becomes illuminated with the lights of the world of holiness, becomes like a brilliant star, and joins the spirits of the angels. This is the bounty and nothing else.

**The third, which is the best of the interpretations:** Whenever a person is known to spend his wealth on the ways of good, hearts incline toward him, and they do not hinder him in his pursuits. Then the doors of this world open for him, and because those on whom he spent his wealth help him with prayer and resolve, Allah opens for him the doors of good.

Then He concluded the verse with His saying: **﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾**, meaning: He is vast in forgiveness, able to make you wealthy and to replace what you spend. He is All-Knowing, nothing of what you spend is hidden from Him, so He will replace it for you.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, Verse 269**

**His words, may He be exalted:** ﴿He gives wisdom (*hikmah*) to whomever He wills. And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good. And none will be mindful except the people of understanding.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned in the preceding verse that Satan promises poverty and orders immorality, while the Most Merciful promises forgiveness and bounty, He drew attention to the matter for which it became necessary to prefer the promise of the Most Merciful over the promise of Satan. It is that the promise of the Most Merciful is favoured by wisdom and reason, while the promise of Satan is favoured by desire and the self (*nafs*), inasmuch as these two command the pursuit of immediate pleasure and the following of the judgements of imagination and illusion. There is no doubt that the judgement of wisdom and reason is the true judge, free from deviation and defect, whereas the judgement of the senses, desire and the self casts a person into trial and affliction. So the judgement of wisdom and reason is more deserving of acceptance. This is the indication of the connection (*wajh al-nazm*) of the verse. There remain some issues concerning the verse:

**First issue:** By *hikmah* is meant either knowledge or doing what is right. It is narrated from Muqatil that he said: the explanation of *hikmah* in the Qur'an has four aspects.

The first: the admonitions of the Qur'an. He said in al-Baqarah: ﴿And what has been sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, with which He admonishes you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:231], meaning the admonitions of the Qur'an. And in al-Nisa': ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:113], meaning the admonitions. The same applies in Al 'Imran.

The second: *hikmah* in the sense of understanding and knowledge. From this is His saying: ﴿And We gave him judgement while he was a child﴾ [Maryam 19:12]. And in Luqman: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman 31:12], meaning understanding and knowledge. In al-An'am: ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book and judgement and prophethood﴾ [al-An'am 6:89], meaning prophethood. In Sad: ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾ [Sad 38:20], meaning prophethood. In al-Baqarah: ﴿And Allah gave him kingship and wisdom﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:251].

The fourth: the Qur'an with what it contains of wondrous secrets. In al-Nahl: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾ [al-Nahl 16:125].

And in this verse: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good.﴾ All these aspects, upon careful examination, return to knowledge. Then consider, O poor one, that He has given only a little of knowledge. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra' 17:85]. He called the whole of this world "little" when He said: ﴿Say: the enjoyment of this world is little﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:77]. Look at how small this little is, so that you may know the greatness of that abundance. The rational proof also agrees with this, since this world is limited in extent and limited in duration, whereas the levels of knowledge, their number, the duration of their survival, and the happiness that results from them have no limit. This indicates the excellence of knowledge. The full discussion of this matter has already passed in the explanation of His saying: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:31].

As for *hikmah* in the sense of doing what is right, it has been said in defining it: it is to take on the character of Allah according to human capacity. The basis of this meaning is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Take on the character of Allah, the Exalted." Know that *hikmah* cannot be taken outside these two meanings. This is because human perfection lies in two things: that one knows the truth for its own sake, and the good for the sake of acting upon it. The first returns to knowledge and correct perception, and the second returns to doing justice and what is right. Thus it is related of Abraham (ﷺ) that he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me judgement﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:83], which is theoretical wisdom, ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:83], which is practical wisdom. Moses (ﷺ) was called and said: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:14], which is theoretical wisdom. Then He said: ﴿So worship Me﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:14], which is practical wisdom. Concerning Jesus (ﷺ) He said that he said: ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾ [Maryam 19:30], to the end of the verse, and all of that belongs to theoretical wisdom. Then He said: ﴿And He has enjoined on me prayer and zakat as long as I remain alive﴾ [Maryam 19:31], which is practical wisdom. About Muhammad (ﷺ) He said: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾ [Muhammad 47:19], which is theoretical wisdom. Then He said: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Muhammad 47:19], which is practical wisdom. And about all the prophets He said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the revelation of His command upon whom He wills of His servants, [saying]: warn that there is no deity except Me﴾ [al-Nahl 16:2], which is theoretical wisdom. Then He said: ﴿So fear Me﴾ [al-Nahl 16:2], which is practical wisdom. The Qur'an is among the verses that indicate that the perfection of the human condition lies in nothing but these two powers.

Abu Muslim said: *hikmah* is a noun of the form *fi'lah* from *hukm* (judgement), like *nahlah* from *nahl* (bee). A man is *hakim* when he possesses intellect, sound reason and correctness of opinion, and in this context it has the sense of the active participle. It is also said: *amr hakim*, meaning *muhkam* (firm, established), and this is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*. Allah says: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:4]. What Abu Muslim said regarding the derivation in the language agrees with the meaning we have mentioned.

**Second issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has been read as ﴿wa-man yu'ti al-hikmah﴾ (with *yu'ti* in the active), meaning: "and whoever Allah gives wisdom to." This is how al-A'mash read it.

**Third issue:** Our companions (the Ash'arites) have used this verse as evidence that the act of the servant is created by Allah, the Exalted. This is because if we explain *hikmah* as knowledge, it cannot be explained as necessary knowledge (*al-'ulum al-darurIyyah*), since that is possessed by animals, the insane and children, and these things are not described as possessing wisdom. So it is explained as theoretical knowledge. And if we explain it as sensible actions, the matter is clear. On either interpretation, it follows that the acquisition of theoretical knowledge and sensible actions is established by Allah's giving and by His enabling, and that the one who gives is none other than Allah, the Exalted, by general agreement. This indicates that the act of the servant is a creation of Allah, the Exalted.

If it is said: why could it not be that what is meant by *hikmah* is prophethood and the Qur'an, or the power of understanding and sensible perception, as al-Rabi' ibn Anas holds?

We reply: the argument we have mentioned repels these possibilities, because by continuous transmission it is established that the word *hakim* is used for other than the prophets. So *hikmah* is different from prophethood and the Qur'an. Rather, it is explained either as knowing the realities of things, or as undertaking correct good actions. On either interpretation the purpose is achieved. If the Mu'tazilah try to take the giving (*ita'*) to mean granting success (*tawfiq*), help (*i'anah*) and kindnesses (*altaf*), we reply: whatever He does of this kind for the believers He has also done for the unbelievers, and yet this great praise mentioned in this verse does not include them. So we know that the *hikmah* mentioned in this verse is something other than the performing of kindnesses. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And none will be mindful except the people of understanding.﴾ What is meant by it, in my view, and Allah knows best, is that when a person sees wisdom and knowledge present in his heart, then reflects and contemplates and knows that they were not obtained except by the giving and facilitation of Allah, the Exalted, he is among the people of understanding (*ulu al-albab*). This is because he has not stopped at the effects, but has ascended from them to their causes. This movement from the effect to the cause is the remembrance (*tadhakkur*) which is attained only by the people of understanding. As for the one who attributes these states to himself, and believes that he is the cause of their coming about and their acquisition, he is among the apparent-minded (*zahiriyyun*) who are unable to move from effects to causes.

As for the Mu'tazilah, when they explained *hikmah* as strength of understanding and the laying down of proofs, they said: this wisdom does not subsist by itself; a person benefits from it only by reflecting and meditating, so that he knows what is for him and what is against him, and at that point he advances or refrains.

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿Whatever you spend or whatever vow you make, indeed Allah knows it. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that spending must be from the best of wealth, He then urged it first by saying ﴿And do not aim at the bad [to spend from]﴾, second by saying ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty﴾, and third, He urged it by saying ﴿Whatever you spend or whatever vow you make, indeed Allah knows it.﴾ There are several issues concerning the verse:

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾, despite its brevity, conveys a great promise to the obedient and a severe warning to the rebellious. Its explanation is in several aspects:

First: He, exalted is He, knows what is in the heart of the one who gives charity, whether the intention of sincerity and servitude, or the intention of showing off and seeking reputation.

Second: His knowledge of the manner of the giver's intention necessitates the acceptance of those acts of obedience, as He said: ﴿Allah only accepts from the God-fearing﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 27], and His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7, 8].

Third: He, exalted is He, knows the amount deserved of reward and punishment for those motives and intentions, so He neglects none of them, and nothing about them is obscure to Him.

**The second issue:** Why He said ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ and did not say "knows them" (in the plural), there are two reasons:

The first: the pronoun refers to the nearer noun (the last mentioned), as in His saying: ﴿And whoever earns a fault or a sin and then throws it onto an innocent person﴾ [al-Nisa': 112]. This is the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat, a grammarian).

The second: the pronoun refers to what is in His saying ﴿whatever you spend of expenditure﴾, because it is a noun (in the singular collective sense), as in His saying: ﴿And what Allah has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom by which He instructs you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231].

**[Page 62]**

**The third issue:** The *nadhr* (vow) is what a person obligates upon himself by making it incumbent on himself. It is said: *nadhara yandhuru*. Its root is from fear, because a person only binds himself out of fear of falling short in an important matter for him. And *andhartu al-qawm indharan* means I warned the people by frightening them. In the Shari'ah, it is of two types: specified (*mufassar*) and unspecified (*ghayr mufassar*). The specified is that one says: "For Allah upon me is the freeing of a slave," or "For Allah upon me is Hajj." In this case, it is obligatory to fulfill it, and nothing else can substitute for it. The unspecified is that one says: "I have vowed to Allah that I will not do such-and-such," and then does it; or one says: "For Allah upon me is a vow," without specifying. In this case, the expiation of an oath (*kaffarat yamin*) is obligatory, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever makes a vow and specifies it, then what he specified is binding upon him, and whoever makes a vow and does not specify, then the expiation of an oath is binding upon him."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the wrongdoers will have no helpers﴾, there are two issues:

**The first issue:** It is a severe warning to the wrongdoers. Wrongdoing is of two kinds. As for wronging oneself, that is present in every sin. As for wronging others, it is by not spending, or by diverting the spending away from the one deserving it to someone else, or by having the intention in spending on the deserving one be showing off and seeking reputation, or by corrupting it with sins. These last two kinds are not a matter of wronging others, but rather a matter of wronging oneself.

**The second issue:** The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school) relied on this verse to negate intercession (*shafa'ah*) for the people of major sins. They said: "Because a person's helper is one who repels harm from him. So if punishment were averted from them by the intercession of intercessors, those would be helpers for them, and that would contradict His saying: ﴿And the wrongdoers will have no helpers.﴾"

Know that common usage does not call the intercessor a helper, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48]. So He distinguished between the intercessor and the helper, and therefore the negation of helpers does not necessitate the negation of intercessors.

The second answer: There are no helpers for the collective of the wrongdoers. So why do you say there are no helpers for some of the wrongdoers?

If it is said: The word "wrongdoers" and the word "helpers" are both plural, and when a plural is set against a plural, the individual is distributed over the individual, so the meaning would be: none of the wrongdoers has any one of the helpers.

We say: We do not concede that setting a plural against a plural necessitates the distribution of the individual over the individual, since it is possible that what is meant is only the setting of plural against plural, not the setting of individual against individual.

The third answer: This evidence negating intercession is general concerning all people and at all times, while the evidence affirming intercession is specific concerning some people and at some times, and the specific takes precedence over the general. And Allah knows best.

The fourth answer: We have explained that a general term is not decisive in its comprehensiveness, but only apparent with strong probability. Therefore the evidence becomes probabilistic (*zanni*), while the matter is not probabilistic, so relying on it is invalid.

**The third issue:** *Al-ansar* is the plural of *nasir*, like *ashraf* is the plural of *sharif*, and *ahbab* is the plural of *habib*.

[p. 64]

The Exalted said: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you, and He will expiate from you some of your misdeeds. And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, first explained that spending includes what is followed by reminder and harm, and what is not like that, and mentioned the ruling for each of the two categories. Secondly, He mentioned that spending may come from good wealth and from bad wealth, and mentioned the ruling for each of the two categories. In this verse He mentioned that spending may be open and may be secret, and mentioned each of the two categories, saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent.﴾ There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: "They asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Is secret charity better, or open charity? So this verse was revealed."

The second issue: The word *ṣadaqah* (charity) is applied to both the obligatory and the voluntary. The Exalted said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity that purifies them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103], and He said: ﴿The charities are only for the poor﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60], and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man's spending on his dependants is a charity." Yet *zakāh* (obligatory almsgiving) is applied only to the obligatory. The lexicographers said: the root *ṣ-d-q* is, in this order, established for soundness and perfection. From it come the expressions: "a man of truthful gaze" (*ṣidq al-naẓar*), "truthful meeting" (*ṣidq al-liqā'*), "they were truthful with them in fighting" (*ṣadaqūhum al-qitāl*), "so-and-so is sincere in affection" (*ṣādiq al-mawaddah*), "this vinegar is pure in its sourness" (*ṣādiq al-ḥumūḍah*), and "something is pure in its sweetness" (*ṣādiq al-ḥalāwah*). Also, "so-and-so spoke truthfully in his report" when he reported it in the way it actually was, sound and complete. The *ṣadīq* (friend) is called *ṣadīq* for the truthfulness of his affection. The *ṣadāq* (bridal gift) is called *ṣadāq* because the marriage contract is completed and perfected by it. And Allah the Exalted called *zakāh* a *ṣadaqah* because wealth is made sound and complete by it. So it is a cause either for the completeness and preservation of wealth, or because through it the servant's truthfulness in his faith and its perfection is evidenced.

The third issue: The original form of the word in ﴿*fa-ni'immā*﴾ is *ni'ma mā*, but one of the two *mīms* was assimilated into the other. There are then three recitations:

Abu 'Amr, Qalun, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited *fa-ni'mā* with a kasrah on the *nūn* and sukun on the *'ayn*. This is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd, who said: "Because it is the dialect of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said to 'Amr ibn al-'As: 'Excellent is good wealth for a righteous man.'" This is how it is narrated in the hadith, with the *'ayn* sukun. The grammarians said: this requires joining two sukuns, which is not permissible except where the first of the two letters is a long vowel letter, as in *dābbatin* and *shābbatin*, because the length in that letter becomes a substitute for the vowel. As for the hadith, since the senses indicate that it is not possible to join these two sukuns, we know that when the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke it, he produced a slight vowel in the *'ayn* by way of *ikhtilās* (a very brief, almost imperceptible vowel).

The second recitation: Ibn Kathir and Nafi' (through the transmission of Warsh), and 'Asim (through the transmission of Hafs), recited *fa-ni'immā hiya* with a kasrah on both the *nūn* and the *'ayn*. In its explanation there are two possibilities:
One: when they needed to move the *'ayn*, they moved it with the same vowel as the letter before it.
Two: this is according to the dialect of those who say *ni'im* with a kasrah on the *nūn* and the *'ayn*. Sibawayh said: this is the dialect of Hudhayl.

The third recitation, which is the recitation of the rest of the reciters: *fa-na'immā hiya*, with a fatḥah on the *nūn* and a kasrah on the *'ayn*. Whoever recites this recitation has pronounced this word according to its original form, which is *ni'ma*. Tarafa said:
*"They strove in a noble matter, and excellent were they in striving"* (nami'a al-sā'ūna fī al-amri al-mubarri)

The fourth issue: al-Zajjaj said: *mā* here is in the sense of *shay'* (thing), i.e., "excellent is the thing it is." Abu 'Ali said: the better way to illustrate this is to say that *mā* is in the sense of *shay'* (something), because *mā* here is indefinite, and illustrating it with an indefinite is clearer. The proof that *mā* is indefinite here is that if it were definite, it would need a relative clause (ṣilah), and there is nothing here for it to be connected to, since what follows *mā* is *hiya*, and the word *hiya* is a single pronoun, and a single word cannot be a relative clause for *mā*. When this view is refuted, we say: *mā* is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*), and the meaning is: "excellent is a thing: it is the disclosure of charities." The governed noun has been omitted because the context indicates it.

* * *

The fifth issue: They differed about whether the charity mentioned in this verse means voluntary charity, or obligatory charity, or both together.

The first view, which is the view of most scholars, is that it means voluntary charity. They said: because concealment is more excellent in voluntary charity, and disclosure is more excellent in *zakāh*. On this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: whether it is more excellent in giving voluntary charity to conceal it or to disclose it. First, let us mention the considerations indicating that concealing it is more excellent:

The first: it is further from showing off (*riyā'*) and seeking reputation (*sum'ah*). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah does not accept from one who seeks to be heard, nor from one who shows off, nor from one who reminds." The one who speaks of his charity undoubtedly seeks reputation, and the giver before a crowd of people seeks to show off. Concealment and silence are what free one from both. Some people went to great lengths in seeking concealment and tried hard that the recipient would not know them. Some of them would place it in the hand of a blind man, some would put it on the path of the poor, or in the place where he sits, where he sees it but does not see the giver; some would tie it into the clothes of a poor man while he was sleeping; and some would convey it to the poor man's hand through another's hand. The aim of all of this is to guard against showing off, reputation, and obligation, because if the poor man knows the giver, then both showing off and obligation have occurred together, whereas knowing an intermediary does not involve showing off.

The second: if he conceals his charity, he does not gain fame, praise, and honour among people, and this is hard on the soul, so it must carry greater reward.

The third: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best charity is the utmost effort of one with little, given to the poor in secret." He also said: "A servant may do a deed in secret, which Allah records for him as secret. If he discloses it, it is transferred from the secret and recorded as open. If he speaks of it, it is transferred from both the secret and the open and recorded as showing off." And in the well-known hadith: "Allah the Exalted will shade seven people under His shade on the Day of Resurrection, on a day when there is no shade but His shade: one of them is a man who gave a charity and his left hand did not know what his right hand had given." And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Secret charity extinguishes the wrath of the Lord."

The fourth: disclosure entails harm to the recipient in several ways, while concealment does not involve that, so concealment must be preferable. The harms of disclosure are of several kinds:
First: disclosure exposes the poor man's honour and reveals his poverty, and the poor man may not be content with that.
Second: disclosure removes the poor man from the state of self-restraint and not asking. Allah the Exalted praised this in the verse that comes after this verse, which is His saying: ﴿The ignorant man thinks them wealthy because of their self-restraint; you recognise them by their mark; they do not ask people persistently﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273].
Third: people may disapprove of the poor man taking that charity, thinking that he took it while not needing it, so the poor man falls into blame and the people fall into backbiting.
Fourth: disclosing the giving humiliates and degrades the recipient, and causing a believer to slip is not permissible.
Fifth: charity is like a gift, and the Prophet (ﷺ), upon whom be blessings and peace, said: "Whoever is given a gift while he has a group of people with him, they are his partners in it." The poor man may not give any of that charity to his present companions, and thus through the disclosure of that charity he falls into doing what is not fitting.

These are the principal considerations indicating that concealing voluntary charity is preferable.

As for the reason for the permissibility of disclosing charity: when a person knows that by disclosing it he will become a cause for people to follow him in giving charity, and the poor benefit from it, then disclosure may not be disallowed in this case and may be more excellent. Ibn 'Umar narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Secret is better than open, but open is better for one who wishes to be emulated." Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said: when a person performs a deed while concealing it from the creation, but within himself there is a desire that people see him doing it, and he suppresses that desire, then here Satan brings to him the thought of people seeing him, while the heart rejects that and repels it. This person is in struggle with Satan, so his deed is multiplied seventy times over the open deed. Then there are servants of Allah who have trained their souls until Allah bestowed upon them various kinds of His guidance, so the lights of knowledge accumulated upon their hearts, and the whisperings of the soul departed from them, because their desires have died in them and their hearts have fallen into the seas of the greatness of Allah the Exalted. So when such a person does a deed openly, he does not need to struggle, because the desire of the soul has been annulled and its contention has dissolved. When he makes it known, he intends only that others should follow him in it. This is a servant whose essence has been perfected, so he strives to perfect others so that he may be complete and beyond completeness. Do you not see that Allah the Exalted praised a people in His revelation, called them the servants of the Most Merciful, and granted them the highest ranks in Paradise, saying: ﴿These will be rewarded with the lofty chamber﴾ [al-Furqan: 75]? Then He mentioned among the qualities they asked for in supplication that they said: ﴿And make us leaders for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Furqan: 74]. He praised the community of Moses (peace be upon him), saying: ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and act justly by it﴾ [al-A'raf: 159]. He praised the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. Then He spoke of an unspecified community, saying: ﴿And among those whom We created is a community who guide by the truth and act justly by it﴾ [al-A'raf: 181]. These are the leaders of guidance, the standard-bearers of the religion, and the masters of creation, by whom people are guided in their journey to Allah.

If it is said: if the matter is as you have stated, then why did He prefer concealment over disclosure in His saying: ﴿But if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾?

The answer has two parts. First: we do not concede that His saying ﴿it is better for you﴾ indicates preference, for it may mean that giving charity while concealing it is good among good deeds and an act of obedience among the acts of obedience. So what is intended is to explain that it is good and obedient in itself, not that the purpose is to indicate preference.

The second part: even if we grant that what is intended is preference, the meaning of the verse is that when the situation is the same in disclosure and concealment, then concealment is more excellent. But when there is some other factor in disclosure, it is not far-fetched to prefer disclosure over concealment.

* * *

The second discussion: disclosure in giving obligatory *zakāh* is more excellent, and the following considerations indicate this:

The first: the Exalted commanded the leaders to dispatch collectors (*al-su'āt*) to seek *zakāh*, and in handing it over to the collectors there is disclosure of it.

The second: in disclosure there is the removal of suspicion. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray most of his prayers at home, except the obligatory prayers. So when the ruling on the obligatory prayer and the voluntary prayer differ regarding disclosure and concealment in order to remove suspicion, then likewise for *zakāh*.

The third: disclosure of it involves hastening to the command and obligation of Allah the Exalted, whereas concealing it suggests neglect of attention to performing the obligation. So disclosure is preferable.

This is all in explanation of the view of those who said that the charities mentioned in this verse refer to voluntary charity only.

The second view, which is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, is that the wording encompasses both obligatory and recommended charity. He answered the claim of those who said that disclosure is preferable in the obligatory with several points:

The first: disclosing the *zakāh* of wealth necessitates disclosing the amount of wealth, and this may be a cause of harm, such that it tempts oppressors toward his wealth or increases his envious rivals. And if it is best for him to conceal his wealth, it necessarily follows that concealing the *zakāh* is preferable.

The second point: this verse was revealed in the days of the Messenger (ﷺ), and the Companions were not suspected of withholding zakat. Therefore concealing zakat was better for them, since it is further from showing off (riya') and seeking reputation (sum'ah). Now, however, since suspicion has arisen, making it public is better because of the occurrence of suspicion.

The third point: we do not accept that His saying ﴿so it is better﴾ indicates preference (tarjih), and its explanation has already preceded.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾, concealment (al-ikhfa') is the opposite of showing (al-izhar). His saying "fa-huwa" (it) is a reference (kinayah) to concealment, because the verb indicates the verbal noun, i.e., "concealment is better for you." We have mentioned that His saying ﴿better for you﴾ may mean that it is in itself one of the good things, as one says "the thareed (broth-soaked bread) is good," and it may mean preference (tarjih). God, exalted is He, only stipulated that concealment be superior on condition that you give them to the poor, because when concealing, the most likely outcome is that one may divert zakat away from the poor toward beloved ones and friends who are not entitled to zakat. For this reason He stipulated that the giving to the poor occur together with concealment. The aim is to motivate the giver to seek out the place of charity, so that he becomes knowledgeable about the poor and distinguishes them from others. When this earlier scrutiny has occurred from him, and then he conceals it, the virtue is attained.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: takfir (expiation) in the language means covering and concealing. A man is called "mukaffar" when he is covered in armor (al-silah), and from this one says "kaffara 'an yaminihi" (he expiated his oath), meaning he covered the sin of breaking the oath by what he gave in charity. Expiation (kaffarah) is a covering for the sin that has occurred.

The second issue: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read "nukaffiru" with the nun and a raised ra', and in this there are several possibilities:
One of them: that it is a conjunction (atf) upon the position (mahall) of what follows the fa'.
The second: that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "and We expiate."
The third: that it is a clause of a verb and subject, a new independent sentence not connected to what precedes it.

The second reading is that of Hamzah, Nafi', and al-Kisa'i with the nun and the jazm (apocope), and its basis is that the statement is understood as referring to the position of His saying ﴿so it is better for you﴾, for its position is jazm. Do you not see that if he had said, "And if you conceal them, it will be greater for your reward," it would be jussed, so it becomes clear that His saying ﴿better for you﴾ is in a position of jazm. Similar to this in taking account of the position of jazm is the reading of one who reads (whoever Allah leaves astray, there is none to guide him, and He leaves them) [al-A'raf: 186] with jazm.

The third reading is that of Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim, "yukaffiru" with the ya' and kasrah on the fa' and raised ra', and the meaning: Allah expiates, or the concealment expiates. Their argument is that what follows it is in the singular form, which is His saying ﴿and Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, so His saying "yukaffiru" would be more akin to what follows it. The former answered and said: there is no harm in mentioning the plural form first and then the singular form second, just as He used the singular first and the plural second in His saying ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1], then He said ﴿and We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-Isra': 2].

The author of al-Kashshaf transmitted a fourth reading, "wa-tukaffiru" with the ta' in the raised and jussed forms, with the subject being "the charities."

And a fifth reading, which is the reading of al-Hasan, with the ta' and the nasb (accusative) by the implied "an": and its meaning: "If you conceal them, it will be good for you, and that We expiate for you some of your misdeeds, it is good for you."

Page 67

The third issue: concerning the entry of "min" in His saying ﴿from your misdeeds﴾, there are several views:
One of them: the meaning is "and We expiate for you some of your misdeeds," because not all misdeeds are expiated by this, but only some of them are expiated. Then the statement is left vague regarding that portion, because clarifying it would be like an incitement to commit them if he knew they were expiated. Rather, the servant must in all his states be between fear and hope, and that occurs only with vagueness.
The second: that "min" means "min ajli" (because of), and the meaning: "and We expiate for you because of your sins," as you say, "I struck you because of the badness of your character," meaning because of that.
The third: that it is an extra (za'idah) particle, like His saying ﴿therein of every kind of fruit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 266], and the implication: "and We expiate for you all of your misdeeds." The first is more preferable and is the most correct.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, and this is an indication of the preference of secret charity over public charity. The meaning is that Allah knows the secret and the public, and you only intend by charity the seeking of His good pleasure, so your aim is achieved in secrecy; so what is the meaning of disclosure? Thus they were urged by this statement toward concealment, so that it would be further from showing off.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 272:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is not your responsibility to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills. Whatever good you spend is for yourselves, and you spend only seeking the Face of Allah. Whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged.﴾

This is the fourth of the rulings concerning spending (infaq), and it explains who it is permissible to spend upon. Then, in the verse, there are issues:

**The first issue: on the occasion of revelation, there are several reports.**

The first: this verse was revealed when Nutaylah, the mother of Asma' bint Abi Bakr, came to her seeking help, and so did her grandmother, and both were polytheists. They came to Asma' asking her for something, and she said: "I will not give you anything until I consult the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for you are not upon my religion." So she consulted him about that, and Allah revealed this verse, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded her to give charity to them both.

The second report: some of the Ansar had relatives from Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and they used to not give charity to them, saying: "Until you become Muslims, we will not give you anything." So this verse was revealed.

The third report: the Prophet ﷺ used not to give charity to the polytheists, until this verse was revealed, and he then gave charity to them.

The meaning according to all the reports is: "It is not your responsibility to guide those who oppose you, such that you withhold charity from them in order that they enter Islam. Rather, give charity to them for the sake of Allah, and do not make that conditional upon their Islam." A parallel to this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 8]. Thus He granted permission to maintain ties with this category of polytheists.

[Page 68]

**The second issue:** The Prophet ﷺ was extremely eager for their faith, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over them, if they do not believe in this discourse﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]; ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself because they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3]; and He said: ﴿Would you compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99]; and He said: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is your suffering, anxious over you, to the believers kind and merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. So Allah informed him that He sent him as a bringer of good news, a warner, one who calls to Allah by His permission, a illuminating lamp, and a clarifier of proofs. As for their being guided, that is not from you, nor by you. Thus "guidance" here means "being guided." Whether they are guided or not, do not cut off your support, your kindness, and your charity from them. There is also another meaning: it is not incumbent upon you to compel them to guidance by withholding your charity from them until they believe, for such faith does not benefit them. Rather, the faith required of them is faith through voluntary choice.

**The third issue:** The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿It is not your responsibility to guide them﴾ is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, but what is intended is him and his community. Do you not see that He said: ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271], which is a general address? Then He said: ﴿It is not your responsibility to guide them,﴾ which is apparently specific. Then He said after it: ﴿Whatever good you spend is for yourselves,﴾ which is general, and it is understood from the generality of what precedes the verse, and the generality of what follows it is also general.

As for His saying: ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills,﴾ the Ashab (the Ash'ari theologians) have used it to argue that Allah's guidance is not universal, but is specific to the believers. They said: because His saying ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ is an affirmation of the guidance which He negated by His saying ﴿It is not your responsibility to guide them.﴾ However, what is negated by His saying ﴿It is not your responsibility to guide them﴾ is the attainment of guidance through voluntary choice. Therefore His saying ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ is an expression of the attainment of guidance through voluntary choice, and this requires that the guidance attained through choice occurs by Allah's decree, creation, and bringing into being, and that is what is required.

The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theologians) said: ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ admits of several meanings:

First: He guides, by reward and recompense, whom He wills of those who deserve that.

Second: He guides, by favors (lutf) and increases in guidance, whom He wills.

Third: But Allah guides by compulsion whom He wills, in the sense that He is able to do that even if He does not do it.

Fourth: He guides by the name and the ruling whom He wills; so whoever is guided deserves to be praised for that.

The Ashab answered all these meanings together: the affirmed element in His saying ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ is the same as the negated element first mentioned in His saying ﴿It is not your responsibility to guide them.﴾ What is intended by that negated element in His saying first ﴿It is not your responsibility to guide them﴾ is guidance through voluntary choice. Therefore what is affirmed by His saying ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ must be guidance through voluntary choice. On this interpretation, it negates all the meanings above.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Whatever good you spend is for yourselves.﴾ The meaning is: every expenditure of good that you spend is for yourselves, that is, so that its reward accrues to yourselves; therefore their disbelief does not harm you.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you spend only seeking the Face of Allah.﴾ On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** There are several interpretations of this verse:

The first: the meaning is: "When you give charity to your relatives among the polytheists, you do not intend anything except the Face of Allah. Allah knows this from your hearts. So spend on them, if you are only seeking by that the Face of Allah, in maintaining ties of kinship and relieving the need of one in distress. It is not incumbent upon you that they be guided, so that this should prevent you from spending on them."

[Page 69]

The second: although its apparent form is a report, its meaning is a prohibition, that is: "And do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah." Reports that carry the meaning of commands and prohibitions occur frequently. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Mothers shall breastfeed their children﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]; ﴿Divorced women shall wait﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228].

The third: His saying ﴿And you spend﴾ means: "And do not be spenders deserving this name, which conveys praise, until you seek by that the Face of Allah."

**The second issue:** Regarding the phrase ﴿seeking the Face of Allah,﴾ two views are mentioned. One of them: when you say, "I did it for the face of Zayd," it is more eloquent in expression than your saying, "I did it for him," because the face of a thing is its noblest part; then the usage became widespread until this expression was used to denote nobility. The second: when you say, "I did this act for him," it may be understood that you did it for him and also for others. But when you say, "I did this act for his face," this indicates that you did the act for him alone, and no one else shares in it.

**The third issue:** The scholars agreed that zakat may not be given to a non-Muslim, so this verse is specific to voluntary charity. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, permitted giving zakat al-fitr (the charity of fast-breaking at the end of Ramadan) to the dhimmis (non-Muslim subjects living under Muslim protection), but others rejected this. It is reported from some scholars: "Even if he were the worst of Allah's creation, you would still have the reward of your expenditure."

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full,﴾ that is, its recompense will be paid to you in full in the Hereafter. The phrase "to you" (ilaykum) is appropriate with "repaid in full" because it includes the meaning of "delivered."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And you will not be wronged,﴾ that is, you will not be diminished in the reward of your deeds by anything, according to His saying: ﴿Each of its gardens gave its produce and did not fall short in anything﴾ [al-Kahf: 33]; meaning, it did not diminish.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 273 (part 1 of 2):**

[Page 70]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For the poor who have been confined in the way of Allah, who cannot move about upon the earth. The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their modesty; you will recognize them by their mark. They do not ask people persistently. And whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained in the first verse that it is permissible to give charity to any poor person, He explained in this verse who among people is most deserving of receiving charity. So He said: ﴿For the poor who have been confined in the way of Allah.﴾ There are several issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** To what does the lam in His saying ﴿for the poor﴾ relate? There are several views on this:

The first: Since many verses urging spending had preceded it, He said after them, ﴿for the poor﴾, meaning: that spending which has been urged is for the poor. This is like when a man has been mentioned and you say, "He is intelligent and sagacious," meaning that the one whose description has passed is intelligent and sagacious. Similarly, people write on the bag in which they place gold and dirhams: "Two thousand and two hundred," meaning that what is in the bag is two thousand and two hundred. This is the best of the views.

The second: The sense of the verse is: "Direct yourselves to the poor, and make what you spend for the poor."

The third: It is possible that the predicate of the subject is omitted, and the sense is: "And your charities are for the poor."

[* * *]

**The second issue:** The verse was revealed concerning the poor among the Muhajirun (emigrants), who numbered about four hundred. They were the People of the Suffa (Ahl al-Suffa, the companions who lived in a sheltered area of the mosque). They had no dwelling and no tribes in Medina. They stayed constantly in the mosque, learned the Qur'an, fasted, and went out on every military expedition. On the authority of Ibn Abbas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once stood among the People of the Suffa, saw their poverty and their striving, and comforted their hearts. He said: 'Rejoice, O People of the Suffa, for whoever of my community meets me in the state you are in, content with what it contains, he is among my companions.'"

Know that Allah, exalted is He, described these poor people with five attributes:

**The first attribute:** His saying: ﴿who have been confined in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273]. We say: In the language, ihsar (confinement, being prevented) means that something arises for a man that prevents him from his journey, whether illness, old age, an enemy, the loss of provisions, or what is similar to these things. It is said: "The man was confined (uhsira), so he is confined (muhsar)." The discussion of the meaning of ihsar was given at His saying: ﴿But if you are prevented﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], sufficiently so as not to need repetition.

As for the interpretation, this verse has been explained by all the possible meanings of ihsar:

The first: The meaning is that they confined themselves and devoted themselves to jihad. His saying ﴿in the way of Allah﴾ is, in the usage of the Qur'an, specific to jihad. Jihad was obligatory in that era, and there was great need for those who would restrict themselves to striving alongside the Messenger (ﷺ), so that they would be ready for it whenever the need arose. Thus Allah, exalted is He, stated that these poor people were of this description. For one whose situation is this, giving charity to them yields several benefits. One: removing their need. Two: strengthening their hearts in what they have devoted themselves to. Three: strengthening Islam by strengthening the mujahidin. Four: they were in great need, yet they did not display their need, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They cannot move about upon the earth. The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their modesty.﴾

The second view, which is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd: they restrained themselves from engaging in trade for their livelihood out of fear of the enemy, the unbelievers, because the unbelievers were gathered around Medina, and whenever they found them they would kill them.

The third view, which is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and the preference of al-Kisa'i: these people had received wounds alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and became disabled, so illness and disability confined them from traveling on the earth.

The fourth view: Ibn Abbas said: These are a group of the Muhajirun whom poverty prevented from striving in the way of Allah, so Allah excused them.

The fifth view: These were a people occupied with the remembrance of Allah, obedience to Him, and worship of Him, and their intense absorption in that obedience confined them from occupying themselves with other pressing matters.

**The second attribute** of these poor people: His saying: ﴿who cannot move about upon the earth.﴾ It is said: "I struck upon the earth (darabtu fi al-ardi darban)" when you traveled in it. Then their inability may be either because their occupation with the welfare of the religion and the matter of jihad prevents them from earning and trade, or because their fear of enemies prevents them from traveling, or because their illness and weakness prevent them from it. In all these cases there is no doubt about the intensity of their need for someone to assist them in their affairs.

[Page 71]

**The third attribute** of theirs: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their modesty.﴾ On this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Asim, Ibn Amir and Hamza read yahsabuhum with a fatha on the sin (yahsabu), while the rest read it with a kasra. The two are of one meaning. The Qur'anic words of this root have been recited in both dialects, fatha and kasra. Among the linguists the fatha is more analogical, because when the past tense is on fa'ila, such as hasiba, the present tense is on yaf'alu, like fariqa yafraqu and shariba yashrabu. Hasiba yahsibu is anomalous, and came on yaf'ilu together with other words. The kasra is good because it is transmitted by report, though it is irregular with respect to analogy.

**The second issue:** Al-husban is opinion (zann). His saying ﴿the ignorant one﴾ does not mean ignorance which is the opposite of intellect, but rather ignorance which is the opposite of testing. The meaning is: whoever has not tested their condition thinks them wealthy because of their modesty. This is from the form tafa'ul of al-iffah (chastity), and the meaning of iffah in the language is leaving a thing and refraining from it. He intended "because of their modesty" as abstaining from asking, so they abstain from it out of knowledge. They appear wealthy to the ignorant only because they display self-sufficiency and refrain from asking.

**The fourth attribute** of these poor people: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you will recognize them by their mark.﴾ Al-sima and al-simiya are the sign by which a thing is recognized, and its origin is from al-simah, which is the sign. The waw was changed to the place of the ayn. Al-Wahidi said: its pattern is ʿifl, as they said: "He has standing (jah) among people," that is, face (wajh). Some said: al-sima means elevation, because it is a sign set up for visibility. Mujahid said: "Their mark" is humility and modesty. Al-Rabi' and al-Suddi said: the trace of hardship from poverty and need. Al-Dahhak said: the yellowing of their complexions from hunger. Ibn Zayd said: the shabbiness of their clothing, while hunger is hidden. In my view, all of this is open to scrutiny, because everything they mentioned consists of signs indicating the existence of poverty, and that contradicts His saying: ﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their modesty.﴾ Rather, the intended meaning is something else: that the sincere servants of Allah have a awe and a weight in the hearts of creation, so that whoever sees them is affected by them and humbles himself before them. That is a spiritual perception, not a physical symptom. Do you not see that when a lion passes, the rest of the beasts of prey fear it by their nature, not through experience, since it is apparent that no such experience has occurred? And when the falcon flies, weak birds flee from it. All of this is spiritual perception, not physical. So it is here as well. From this category are the traces of humility in prayer, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. Also, the appearance of the traces of contemplation. It is related that they would stand in the night for tahajjud (night prayer), and gather firewood during the day for the sake of chastity.

**The fifth attribute** of these poor people: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They do not ask people persistently.﴾ On the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "Allah loves the chaste one who refrains, and hates the vile and obscene one, the beggar who insists, who if he is given much, exaggerates in praise, and if he is given little, exaggerates in blame." And on the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever opens a door of asking, Allah will open for him a door of poverty. Whoever seeks independence, Allah will make him independent. Whoever seeks to be chaste, Allah will make him chaste. Indeed, for one of you to take a rope, gather firewood, and sell it for a mudd of dates is better for him than to ask people."

Know that this verse is problematic, and they mentioned several interpretations of it:

**The first:** That ilhaf is ilhah (insistence), and the meaning is that they asked gently and did not insist. This is the view chosen by the author of al-Kashshaf, and it is weak, because Allah, exalted is He, had described them before this as abstaining from asking when He said: ﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their modesty﴾, and that contradicts the occurrence of asking from them.

**The second**, which occurred to me when writing this topic: The purpose of His saying ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾ is not to describe them as not asking people persistently.
