That is because He had already described them before that as being chaste regarding asking. When it is known that they do not ask at all, it is also known that they do not ask persistently. Rather, the intention is to alert to the bad manner of one who asks people persistently. An example: if two men are present with you, one of them wise, dignified, and steady, and the other frivolous, babbling, and foolish, and you want to praise one of them and indirectly disparage the other, you say: "So-and-so is a wise, dignified man, few in speech, who does not wade into trivialities and does not engage in foolishness." Your purpose in saying "he does not wade into trivialities and foolishness" is not to describe him with that, since the good attributes already mentioned suffice for that. Rather, your purpose is to alert to the blameworthiness of the second. Likewise here: His saying ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾ after His saying ﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their modesty﴾ is intended to alert to the one who asks people persistently, and to show the difference between the two kinds in deserving praise and honor.

**The third:** The persistent, insistent asker is one who extracts wealth through the abundance of his gentle coaxing. So His saying ﴿they cannot move about upon the earth﴾ [implies that they do not ask] with gentleness and coaxing. If asking is not found in this manner, then it is more fitting that it not be found in the manner of harshness. If both kinds are negated, then the occurrence of asking has been negated. On this view, His saying ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾ acts as an implication for the absence of asking from them altogether.

**The fourth**, which also occurred to me at this time: He, exalted is He, showed earlier the intensity of the need of these poor people, and whoever's need is intense cannot refrain from asking except through strong insistence upon himself. They did not ask people, but they could refrain from asking only when they insisted upon the self and restrained it by severe obligation from that asking. From this is the saying of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him:

*I have a self that, when it disputes with me, I say to it: "Perhaps, or maybe."*

**The fifth:** Everyone who asks must, at some times, insist, because when he asks he has spilled the water of his face and bears the humiliation of showing that request. He says: "Since I have borne these hardships, I will not return without my aim." This thought drives him to persistence and insistence. So it is established that everyone who asks must at some times resort to insistence. Therefore, the absolute negation of insistence from them entails the absolute negation of asking from them.

The sixth aspect: this also occurred to me at this time. Whoever shows outward signs of poverty, humiliation and need, and then refrains from asking, is in effect making a pressing, importunate request. The visible signs of need indicate the need, and his silence indicates that he has nothing with which to meet it. When a person conceives of this, his heart softens greatly and drives him to give him something. So displaying this state amounts to asking in the manner of importunity. Therefore, His saying ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾ means that they keep silent about asking, but they do not add to that silence any shabbiness of condition or display of brokenness that would take the place of asking in the manner of importunity. Rather, they make themselves appear dignified before people, they adorn themselves with this character, and they conceal their poverty and need so that none perceives it except the Creator. This aspect too is fitting and rationally sound.

[Page 73]

This verse is one of the difficult ones, and people have said many things about it. These three aspects occurred to me, by God's grace, at the time this tafsir of this verse was being written, and God knows best what He intends.

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned the attributes of these poor people and then said after it: ﴿Whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾ This is the parallel of what He mentioned before this verse, His saying: ﴿Whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged.﴾ This is not mere repetition, and in it there are two aspects.

The first: when He said ﴿Whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full﴾, and it is known that full repayment of the reward without diminution or deficiency is not possible except with knowledge of the measure of the deed and the manner of its aspects that affect the deserving of reward, He therefore established in this verse that He is knowing of the measures of deeds and their modes.

The second: when He encouraged giving charity to the Muslim and the dhimmi (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection), He said ﴿Whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full﴾, showing that its reward will certainly reach them. Then, when He encouraged in this verse giving charity to the poor who are described by these complete attributes, and this giving being the greatest forms of spending, He therefore followed it with what indicates the greatness of its reward, saying ﴿Whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾ This is like what a great sovereign would say to a servant whose service he approves of: "Let it suffice you that My knowledge witnesses the manner of your obedience and the excellence of your service," for this has a greater effect than if he said to him: "Your reward will certainly reach you."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 274:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, they shall have their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾

Regarding the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the arrangement (naẓm) of the verse, there are several views. The first: when, in the preceding verse, He explained who is the most deserving recipient of expenditure, He explained in this verse what the most perfect manner of spending is, so He said: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, theirs is [the reward]﴾.

The second: God mentioned this verse to reinforce what preceded, His saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good⁠﻿﻿ [2:271]. The third: this verse is the last of the verses mentioned concerning the rulings on spending, so, without doubt, He guided creatures to the most perfect ways of spending.

The second issue: concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), there are several reports:

The first: when the verse ﴿for the poor who have been confined in the way of God﴾ was revealed, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf sent dinars to the People of the Ṣuffa, and ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, sent a wasq of dates at night. So the most beloved of the two charities to God, exalted is He, was his charity, and then this verse was revealed. Thus night charity was the most perfect.

The second: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "ʿAlī, peace be upon him, possessed nothing but four dirhams. He gave one dirham at night, one by day, one secretly, and one openly. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'What moved you to this?' He said: 'To deserve what my Lord has promised me.' He said: 'For you is that.'"

God then revealed this verse.

The third: the author of al-Kashshaf said: it was revealed concerning Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, when he gave forty thousand dinars in charity: ten at night, ten by day, ten secretly, and ten openly.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning the fodder of horses and their tethering in the way of God. Abū Hurayra, whenever he passed a fat horse, would recite this verse.

The fifth: the verse is general, concerning those who encompass all times and states with charity, urging them toward good. So whenever the need of one in need arises, they hasten to meet it, and do not delay it, nor tie it to a time or a state. This is the best of the views, because this is the last of the verses mentioned in explaining the ruling on expenditure, so without doubt He mentioned in it the most perfect ways of spending. And God knows best.

The third issue: al-Zajjāj said: "alladhīna" is in the nominative by being the subject (mubtadaʾ), and it is permissible that the fāʾ in His saying "falahum" (then for them) be the response (jawāb) to "alladhīna," because it comes with the meaning of a conditional and a consequent. The sense would be: "whoever spends, his reward will not be lost." Its illustration: if one says, "The one who honored me, for him is a dirham," it does not indicate that the dirham is due to the honoring; but if one says, "The one who honored me, then for him is a dirham," it indicates that the dirham is due to the honoring. Here the fāʾ indicates that the attainment of the reward is only because of the spending. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: in the verse there is an indication that the charity given secretly is better than the charity given openly, because He placed the night before the day, and the secret before the open in mention.

Then He said at the close of the verse: ﴿then they shall have their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾, and the meaning is known. Concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: it indicates that the people of reward have no fear upon them on the Day of Resurrection, and this is confirmed by His saying: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [21:103].

The second issue: this is conditioned, according to all, on not being followed by disbelief, and according to the Muʿtazila, on not being followed by a major sin that nullifies (muḥbiṭa). We have already settled this issue, and here is the end of the verses mentioned in explaining the rulings on spending.

**The Second Ruling**

Among the legal rulings mentioned in this part of this surah is the ruling on *ribā* (usury, interest):

﴿Those who consume usury will not rise [on the Day of Resurrection] except as one rises whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch. That is because they say, "Trade is only like usury," while Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury. So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, he may keep what is past, and his affair is with Allah. But whoever returns [to it], those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

The verse: ﴿Those who consume usury will not rise [on the Day of Resurrection] except as one rises whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch. That is because they say, "Trade is only like usury," while Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury. So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, he may keep what is past, and his affair is with Allah. But whoever returns [to it], those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

Know that there is a connection between usury and charity by way of opposition. Charity is a diminishing of wealth [for the sake of Allah] by reason of Allah's command to do so, whereas usury is seeking an increase on wealth together with Allah's prohibition of it. Thus they are opposites. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah destroys usury and makes charities grow.﴾ Since there is this kind of connection between these two rulings, he mentioned the ruling on usury right after the ruling on charities.

As for His saying ﴿those who consume usury﴾, what is meant is those who deal in it. He specified "consuming" because it is the main aspect of the matter, as in His saying: ﴿Those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ (An-Nisa 4:10). Just as it is not permissible to consume an orphan's property, it is also not permissible to destroy it; but He mentioned "consuming" as an indication of other uses. Similarly, His saying: ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:188). Also, because the usury itself, which is the increase in wealth as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, is not eaten; rather, it is spent on food, and so it is eaten. What is meant is its disposal. Allah therefore forbade the disposal of usury by the threat mentioned. Also, it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah has cursed the one who consumes usury, the one who pays it, its witness, its scribe, and the one who makes it lawful." So we know that the prohibition is not restricted to the one who consumes it. Also, it is established by the evidence of concomitance and reciprocity that what is forbidden is not restricted in its prohibition to consumption alone, to the exclusion of other dispositions. Thus, by these four considerations, it is established that what is meant by "consuming usury" in this verse is disposing of usury.

As for usury itself, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** In the language, *ribā* means an increase. It is said: *rabā al-shay'u yarbū* ("the thing increased"). From this is His saying: ﴿it stirs and swells﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:5), meaning it increased. *Arbā al-rajulu* means a man dealt in usury. From this is the hadith: "Whoever practices *ijbā'* has practiced *ribā*," meaning he dealt in usury. *Ijbā'* is selling the crop before its maturity. This is the meaning of *ribā* in the language.

**The second issue:** Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read *al-ribā* with *imālah* (fronting of the vowel) because of the kasrah on the *rā'*, while the others read it with *tafkhīm* (velarization) with a fatḥah on the *bā'*. In the codices it is written with a *wāw*, and you may write it with an *alif*, a *wāw*, or a *yā'*. The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: *al-ribā* was written with a *wāw* according to the dialect of those who velarize, just as *al-ṣalāh* and *al-zakāh* were written, and an *alif* was added after it by analogy with the *wāw* of the plural.

* * *

**The third issue:** Know that *ribā* is of two kinds: *ribā al-nasī'ah* (usury of deferment) and *ribā al-faḍl* (usury of excess).

As for *ribā al-nasī'ah*, it is the well-known practice that was current in the Jahiliyyah: they would give money on condition that they take a specified amount every month while the principal remained intact. Then, when the debt came due, they demanded the principal from the debtor. If he could not pay, they increased the amount owed and extended the term. This is the *ribā* they used to practice in the Jahiliyyah.

As for *ribā al-naqd* (usury of cash exchange), it is selling a *mann* of wheat for two *mann*s of it, and similar cases.

Having understood this, we say: It is reported from Ibn 'Abbās that he did not prohibit anything except the first kind. He used to say: "There is no *ribā* except in deferment," and he permitted cash exchange. Abū Sa'īd al-Khudrī said to him: "You witnessed what you did not witness, or you heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) what you did not hear." Then it is reported that he retracted it. Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn said: "We were in a house, and with us was 'Ikrimah. A man said: 'O 'Ikrimah, do you not remember, when we were in the house of so-and-so with Ibn 'Abbās?' He said: 'I had only permitted the disposal by my own opinion; then it reached me that the Prophet (ﷺ) prohibited it. So bear witness that I have forbidden it and I have disavowed it before Allah.'"

Ibn 'Abbās's argument was that His saying ﴿and Allah has permitted trade﴾ includes the exchange of one dirham for two dirhams in cash, and His saying ﴿and forbidden usury﴾ does not include it, because *ribā* means an increase, and not every increase is forbidden. Rather, His saying ﴿and forbidden usury﴾ only refers to the specific contract that was known among them as *ribā*, and that is *ribā al-nasī'ah*. So His saying ﴿and forbidden usury﴾ is specific to deferment. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿and Allah has permitted trade﴾ includes *ribā al-naqd*, and His saying ﴿and forbidden usury﴾ does not include it, so it must remain permissible. It cannot be said that it is forbidden by a hadith, because that would require specifying the apparent meaning of the Qur'an by a solitary report (*khabar al-wāḥid*), and that is not permissible. This is the position of Ibn 'Abbās, and its real substance comes down to this question: is it permissible to specify the Qur'an by a solitary report or not?

As for the majority of the mujtahids, they agreed on the prohibition of *ribā* in both kinds. The first kind is forbidden by the Qur'an, and *ribā al-naqd* by the report. Then the report indicated the prohibition of *ribā al-naqd* in six items. Then they differed. The majority of jurists said: the prohibition of excess is not restricted to these six, but is established in other items as well. The opponents of analogical reasoning (*qiyās*) said: rather, the prohibition is restricted to these. Their arguments are of several kinds:

**The first argument:** The Lawgiver singled out four items from among the measured, edible, and staple goods. If the ruling applied to all measured goods or to all edible goods, he would have said: "Do not sell a measured good for a measured good in excess," or "Do not sell an edible good for an edible good in excess," for that expression would be more concise and more beneficial. Since he did not say that, but enumerated the four, we know that the ruling of prohibition is restricted to them alone.

**The second argument:** We have shown that His saying the Exalted ﴿and Allah has permitted trade﴾ requires the permissibility of cash *ribā*. You have removed cash *ribā* from under this general statement by a solitary report concerning the six items, and then you established the prohibition in other items by analogy with them. This is therefore a specification of the general text of the Qur'an concerning the six items by a solitary report, and concerning other items by analogy with the six items for which the ruling was established by a solitary report. Such an analogy is far weaker than a solitary report, and a solitary report is weaker than the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. So this is preferring the weaker over the stronger, and that is not permissible.

**The third argument:** Extending a ruling from the place of the text to other than the place of the text is only possible through the *'illah* (effective cause) of the ruling in the place of the text. That is not permissible. First, because it would require giving a reason for the ruling of Allah, and that is impossible according to what is established in the principles of jurisprudence. Second, because the ruling in the place of the text is known, while the language is conjectural, and tying what is known to what is conjectural is not permissible. The majority of jurists agreed that the prohibition of cash *ribā* is not restricted to these six items, but is established in others. Then it is well known that the ruling cannot be extended from the place of the text to other than the place of the text except by giving the ruling established in the place of the text an *'illah* found in other than the place of the text. Therefore, on this basis they differed about the *'illah*, according to several positions.

The first position is that of al-Shāfi'ī, may Allah be pleased with him: the *'illah* for the prohibition of *ribā* is food (*ṭu'm*) in the four items, together with the requirement of the unity of kind; and for gold and silver it is their being currency (*naqdiyyah*).

The second position is the position of Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah be pleased with him: whatever is measured (*muqaddar*) is subject to *ribā*. The *'illah* for dirhams and dinars is weight, and for the four items it is measure (*kayl*) together with the unity of kind.

The third position is that of Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him: the *'illah* is staple food (*qūt*) or what staple food is made with, which is salt.

The fourth position is that of 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn: whatever is useful in any way is subject to *ribā*. This is the summary of the positions of people regarding the ruling on *ribā*. A discussion of the details of these issues is not appropriate for tafsir.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** They mentioned several reasons for the prohibition of *ribā*:

First: *ribā* requires taking a person's property without any compensation, because whoever sells one dirham for two dirhams, in cash or on deferment, gains an extra dirham without compensation. A person's property is the object of his need and has great sanctity. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The sanctity of a person's property is like the sanctity of his blood." Therefore taking his property without compensation must be forbidden.

If it is said: why can the retention of the principal in his hand for a long period not be the compensation for the extra dirham? Because if the principal remained in his hand for this period, the owner could have engaged in trade with it and gained profit through that trade. When he left it in the debtor's hand and the debtor benefited from it, it is not unlikely that the debtor should pay the owner that extra dirham as compensation for his benefit from the owner's property.

We say: this benefit you mention is a presumed matter, which may or may not occur, whereas taking the extra dirham is a certain matter. Sacrificing the certain for the sake of the presumed does not avoid some kind of harm.

Second: Some said: Allah prohibited *ribā* because it prevents people from engaging in earning. For when the owner of a dirham is able, through a *ribā* contract, to obtain an extra dirham, whether in cash or on deferment, earning a livelihood becomes easy for him, and he hardly bears the hardship of work, trade, and difficult crafts. That leads to the cessation of people's benefits. It is well known that the interests of the world are not organized except by trade, crafts, professions, and construction.

Third: It was said: the reason for prohibiting the *ribā* contract is that it leads to the disappearance of the goodness among people in lending. For if people are content to lend a dirham and get back its equivalent, but *ribā* were permitted, the need of the one in want would drive him to take one dirham for two, and that would lead to the cessation of mutual help, goodness, and kindness.

Fourth: It is that the usual case is that the lender is rich and the borrower is poor. So permitting the *ribā* contract enables the rich to take extra wealth from the poor and weak, and that is not permissible by the mercy of the Merciful.

Fifth: The prohibition of *ribā* has been established by the text, and it is not necessary that the wisdom behind all obligations be known to people. Therefore we must hold for certain the prohibition of the *ribā* contract, even if we do not know the reason for it.

As for His saying the Exalted ﴿they will not rise﴾, most exegetes said: what is meant is rising on the Day of Resurrection. Others said: what is meant is rising from the grave. Know that there is no contradiction between the two interpretations, so the wording must be understood as including both.

* * *

As for His saying the Exalted ﴿except as one rises whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch﴾, there are several issues:

[p. 78]

**The first issue:** *al-takhabbut* (تَخَبُّط) means striking without balance or direction. It is said of a man who acts in a matter without guidance: "he gropes like a blind camel" (*yakhbitu khabṭa ʿashwāʾ*). It is also said that a camel *khabaṭa* the ground with its hooves. *Takhabbatahu al-shaytān* means that Satan touched him with madness or insanity, because this is like striking without balance, in bewilderment. The affliction of madness or insanity caused by Satan is called *khabṭa*, and one says: "He has a *khabṭa* of madness." *Al-mass* means madness, and one says: "The man was *massa*, so he is *mamsūs*, and he has *mass*." Its root is touching with the hand, as if Satan touches the person and drives him mad. Then madness was called *mass*, just as Satan *yatakhabbatuhu* (strikes him) and tramples him with his foot, so that he is deranged, and madness was called *khabṭa*. Thus *takhabbut* is with the foot and *mass* is with the hand. Then there are two questions.

*The first question:* *Takhabbut* is of the *tafaʿʿul* form, so how can it be transitive?

*The answer:* *Tafaʿʿala* can mean *faʿala* in the sense of intensity, as in *taqassamahu* meaning *qasamahu* (he divided it), and *taqaṭṭaʿahu* meaning *qaṭaʿahu* (he cut it).

*The second question:* With what is the phrase *min al-mass* (﴿from the touch﴾) connected?

[p. 78 continued] We say: there are two possibilities. The first is that it is connected to *lā yaqūmūn* (﴿they will not stand﴾). The meaning is: they will not stand up from the touch that they have, except as one stands whom Satan has struck. The second is that it is connected to *yaqūmu* (stand), and the meaning is: they will not stand except as one who is struck stands because of the touch.

**The second issue:** Al-Jubbāʾī (al-Jubbāʾī) said: People say that the one who is overcome (*al-maṣrūʿ*) only had that condition because Satan touches him and throws him down. This is false, because Satan is weak and cannot overpower people or kill them. This is shown by several points.

First, God's words, relating what Satan says: ﴿I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me﴾ (Ibrahim 14:22). This is clear that Satan has no power to overthrow, kill, or harm.

Second: Satan is either said to be a dense body or a subtle body. If he is the first, he must be seen and observed, for if it were possible for him to be dense, present, and yet unseen, then it would be possible that there are suns, thunders, lightnings, and mountains in our presence that we do not see, and that is great ignorance. Furthermore, if he were a dense body, how could he enter the inside of a human body? If he is a subtle body like air, then such a thing cannot have firmness and strength, and so it is impossible for it to be able to overthrow a person and kill him.

Third: If Satan could overthrow and kill, it would be possible for him to perform the miracles of the prophets, peace be upon them, and that would lead to undermining prophethood.

Fourth: If Satan were able to do that, why does he not overthrow all the believers? Why does he not strike them, despite his intense enmity toward the people of faith? Why does he not seize their wealth, corrupt their conditions, reveal their secrets, and remove their minds? All of this is evidently corrupt.

Those who argue that Satan has the power to do these things rely on two points. The first:

It is reported that in the time of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both, the devils performed heavy labors, as God related about them, that they worked for him whatever he wished: sanctuaries, statues, basins like cisterns, and firmly set cooking pots.

The answer to this is that God obligated them in the time of Sulayman, and at that time they were able to do these acts, and that was among the miracles of Sulayman, peace be upon him. The second point is that this verse, His words ﴿the one whom Satan strikes﴾, is clear that Satan strikes because of his touch.

The answer to this is that Satan touches him with his harmful whispering, by which the overthrow occurs. This is like the words of Ayyub, peace be upon him: ﴿Satan has touched me with hardship and torment﴾ (Sad 38:41). The overthrow occurs at that whispering because God created him (the afflicted person) with weakness of temperament and dominance of black bile (*al-sawdāʾ*, melancholy), such that he fears at the whispering and does not dare, so he is overthrown at that whispering, just as the coward is thrown down from an empty place. For this reason, this striking is not found in the excellent, the perfect, and the people of firmness and intellect; it is found only in one who has a defect in temperament and a disorder in the brain. This is the whole of al-Jubbāʾī's speech on this subject.

Al-Qaffāl mentioned another view on this, which is that people attribute the overthrow to Satan and the jinn, so they were addressed according to what they were accustomed to. Also, it is a habit of people that when they wish to disparage something, they attribute it to Satan, as in God's words: ﴿its shoots are as if they were the heads of devils﴾ (al-Saffat 37:65).

**The third issue:** The commentators have several views on the verse.

The first: The one who consumes usury will be raised on the Day of Resurrection insane, and this is like a special sign of the one who consumes usury. The people of the place of standing recognize him by that sign as one who consumed usury in the world. According to this, the meaning of the verse is: they will rise as madmen, like one whom Satan has afflicted with madness.

The second view: Ibn Munabbih said: It means that when people are raised from their graves, they come out quickly, according to His words: ﴿they will come out from the graves hastening﴾ (al-Maʿarij 70:43), except the consumers of usury, who will rise and fall, as one rises whom Satan strikes from touch. This is because they consumed usury in the world, so God made it grow in their bellies on the Day of Resurrection until it weighed them down, so they rise, fall, want to hasten, and cannot. This view is different from the first, because it means that the consumers of usury cannot walk quickly because of the weight of the belly, and this has nothing to do with madness. This view is supported by what is reported in the story of the Night Journey: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was taken by Gabriel to men, each one of whom was like a large house. One of them would rise, and his belly would tilt him and he would be thrown down. I said: O Gabriel, who are these? He said: ﴿Those who consume usury will not rise except as one rises whom Satan strikes from touch.﴾"

The third view: It is taken from God's words: ﴿Indeed, those who fear God, when a visitation from Satan touches them, remember, and then they see clearly﴾ (al-Aʿraf 7:201). This is because Satan calls to the pursuit of pleasures and desires and to occupation with other than God. This is what is meant by the touch of Satan. Whoever is like this is confused in worldly affairs: at one time Satan drags him to the self and desire, and at another time the angel drags him to religion and piety, so there arise agitated movements and divergent actions. This is the striking that results from Satan's action. The consumer of usury, there is no doubt, is excessive in love of the world and infatuated with it. If he dies in that love, that love becomes a veil between him and God, the Exalted. So the striking that existed in the world because of love of wealth caused him to be struck in the Hereafter and placed him in the humiliation of the veil. This interpretation is closer to me than the two views we have quoted from those whom we quoted.

* * *

As for God's words: ﴿That is because they said: trade is only like usury﴾, there are several issues.

**The first issue:** The people were justifying usury with this doubt: that whoever buys a garment for ten and sells it for eleven, this is lawful. So if one sells ten for eleven, it must also be lawful, because there is no difference by reason between the two matters. This is regarding cash usury (*ribā al-naqd*). As for credit usury (*ribā al-nasīʾa*), it is also the same: if one sells a garment worth ten now for eleven at a month's deferment, it is permitted. So if one gives ten for eleven at a month's deferment, it must also be permitted, because there is no difference by reason between the two cases. This is because that was permitted there since mutual consent occurred on both sides, so here too, since mutual consent occurred on both sides, it must be permitted. Trade was legislated to meet needs. Perhaps a person is empty-handed now and in great need, but will have much wealth in the future. If usury is not permitted, the owner of the money will not give him anything, and the person will remain in hardship and need. Either by the permission of usury, the owner of money gives him out of hope for increase, and the debtor repays it when he finds money, and giving that increase when he finds money is easier for him than remaining in need before finding money. This requires the permissibility of usury, as we judged all other trades permissible for the sake of meeting need. This is the doubt of the people.

God answered it with one word: ﴿God has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:275). The answer is that what you mentioned is a counter-argument against a textual ruling (*naṣṣ*) by analogy (*qiyās*, reasoning by analogy), and this is the work of Iblis. When God commanded him to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, he opposed the textual command with analogy, saying: ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ (Sad 38:76). Know that those who deny analogy hold fast to this word and say: If religion were by analogy, this doubt would be binding; since it was rejected, we know that religion is by textual evidence, not by analogy.

Al-Qaffāl, may God have mercy on him, mentioned the difference between the two categories: whoever sells a garment worth ten for twenty has made the garment itself equivalent to twenty. When mutual consent on this equivalence occurred, each of the two became equivalent to the other in value according to both of them, so he did not take anything from his companion without return. But if he sells ten for ten, he has taken the extra ten without any return. It cannot be said that his purpose was delay during the term, because delay is not wealth or a thing pointed to, so that he could make it a return for the extra ten. Thus the difference between the two cases is clear.

**The second issue:** The apparent meaning of God's words ﴿That is because they said: trade is only like usury﴾ indicates that the threat only applies to their declaring usury permissible, not to engaging in it and consuming it while knowing it is forbidden. According to this interpretation, this verse does not establish that usury is one of the major sins.

If it is said: The introduction of the verse indicates that their rising on the Day of Resurrection in a state of staggering was because they consumed usury.

We say: His words ﴿That is because they said: trade is only like usury﴾ are clear that the cause of that staggering is only this statement and belief. At this point, the introduction of the verse must be interpreted. We have already shown that the intended meaning of "consuming" is not consuming itself, and we mentioned several proofs for that. You have taken it to mean dealing in usury, while we take it to mean declaring usury lawful and finding it pleasant. This is because "consuming" is sometimes used to express considering something lawful, as one says: "So-and-so eats God's wealth greedily and voraciously," meaning he considers its disposal lawful. When we take "consuming" to mean considering it lawful, the introduction of the verse corresponds to its conclusion. This is what the wording of the verse indicates. However, the majority of commentators took the verse as a threat against one who deals in usury money, not against one who considers this contract lawful.

**The third issue:** There is a question in the verse: Why did it not say: "Usury is only like trade"? This is because the permissibility of trade is agreed upon, so they wanted to analogize usury to it, and it is proper in analogy to compare the disputed case to the agreed case. So the wording of the verse should have been: "Usury is only like trade." What is the wisdom in reversing this proposition, saying ﴿trade is only like usury﴾?

The answer: The intention of the people was not to adhere to the form of analogy. Rather, their aim was that usury and trade are equal in all the relevant respects, so how is it permissible to make one of the two equals lawful and the other forbidden? According to this, whichever of the two is put first or last is permissible.

* * *

As for God's words: ﴿God has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾, there are several issues:

Subject: Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 275 (part 3 of 3):

The first issue: It is possible that this statement is part of the speech of the disbelievers, and the meaning is that they said: "Trade is just like usury (riba)." Then you say, ﴿Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾. How can this be understood? That is, since the two are alike, if one were permitted and the other forbidden, that would be making a distinction between two like things, and that is not fitting for the wisdom of the All-Wise. So His saying, ﴿Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾, was mentioned by the disbelievers by way of denial. However, most of the exegetes (mufassirun) agree that the speech of the disbelievers ended at His saying, ﴿Trade is only like usury﴾, and that His saying, ﴿Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾, is the speech of Allah the Exalted, and its explicit statement of this distinction is mentioned as a refutation of the saying of the disbelievers, "Trade is only like usury." The proofs for the soundness of this view are several:
Page 81
The first proof: The view of the one who says, "This is the speech of the disbelievers," cannot be sustained except by supplying additional elements, by taking it as an interrogative of denial, or by taking it as a report from the speech of the Muslims. It is well known that supplying what is not stated goes against the original principle. But if we take it as the speech of Allah from the outset, no such supplying is needed, and so this is preferable.
The second proof: The Muslims have always relied upon this verse in all matters concerning trade. Had they not known that it is the speech of Allah and not the speech of the disbelievers, it would not have been permissible for them to cite it as evidence. There is a discussion of this proof that will come in the second issue.
The third proof: He the Exalted mentioned right after this statement His saying: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists, he may keep what is past, and his affair is up to Allah; but whoever returns to it — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾. The apparent meaning of this indicates that when they adhered to that doubt, which is their saying, ﴿Trade is only like usury﴾, Allah the Exalted exposed the corruption and weakness of that doubt. Had His saying, ﴿Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾, not been the speech of Allah, the answer to that doubt would not have been mentioned, and His saying, ﴿There has come to him an admonition from his Lord﴾, would not have been fitting in this place.

The second issue: The school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, holds that His saying, ﴿Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾, is among the general (mujmal) statements that may not be used as evidence for particular rulings. This is the view I prefer, and it is supported by several considerations:
The first: We have shown in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that the singular noun prefixed with the definite article (al-) does not at all indicate generality; rather, it indicates only the definition of the quiddity (ma'huwiyyah), and when it is so, acting upon it suffices for establishing its ruling in a single instance.
The second consideration: Even if we grant that it indicates generality, we have no doubt that its indication of generality is weaker than the indication of plural forms for generality. For example, His saying, ﴿Allah has permitted trade﴾, although it indicates comprehensiveness, His saying "Allah has permitted the trades" is stronger in indicating comprehensiveness. Thus it is established that His saying, ﴿Allah has permitted trade﴾, indicates comprehensiveness only with weak indication. Then, the generality must inevitably be subject to numerous specifications beyond counting and control, and such a generality is not fitting for the speech of Allah the Exalted or the speech of His Messenger (ﷺ), because it would be a falsehood, and lying upon Allah the Exalted is impossible. As for a general statement in which the scope of specification is very small, that is permissible, because applying the term of comprehensiveness to the majority is a well-known usage in the speech of the Arabs. Thus it is established that taking this to be general is not permissible.
The third consideration: What has been narrated from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) departed from this world and we did not ask him about usury." Had this wording indicated generality, he would not have said that. So we know that this verse is among the general statements.
The fourth consideration: His saying, ﴿Allah has permitted trade﴾, requires that every trade be lawful, and His saying, ﴿and forbidden usury﴾, requires that every usury be unlawful, because usury is an increase, and there is no trade except that increase is intended in it. So the beginning of the verse permits all trades, and its end forbids all of them, and thus the lawful is not distinguished from the unlawful by this verse. Therefore it is a general statement, and it is obligatory to return, regarding what is lawful and unlawful, to the explanation of the Messenger (ﷺ).

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord﴾: know that He made the verb of admonition masculine because its feminine marking is not real, and because it has the meaning of exhortation (wa'z). Ubayy and al-Hasan read, "So whoever has received an admonition," then He said, ﴿and desists﴾, that is, refrains, then He said, ﴿he may keep what is past﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:
Page 82
The first issue: Regarding the interpretation there are two views. The first: al-Zajjaj said: that is, He pardoned him for what was past of his sin before the revelation of this verse, as in His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. This interpretation is weak, because before the revelation of the verse concerning the prohibition, that was not unlawful nor a sin, so how can it be said that the meaning of the verse is pardon for that sin when there was no sin there? A later prohibition does not affect an earlier act. Also, He the Exalted attributed that to him with the particle of possession, in His saying, ﴿he may keep what is past﴾, so how could that be a sin? The second: al-Suddi said: "he may keep what is past" means: he may keep what he consumed of usury, and he is not obliged to return what has already passed; but as for one who has not yet taken it, it is not lawful for him to take it, and he is entitled only to his capital, as He explained after that in His saying, ﴿And if you repent, you shall have your capital﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279].
The second issue: al-Wahidi said: "salaf" means what has preceded; and everything you have sent ahead of you is a salaf. From this comes "the past nations" (al-ummah al-salifah), and "al-salifah" is the neck, because of its being raised in the direction of height; and "al-sulfah" is what is served before food, and "sulafat al-khamr" is its essence, because it is the first thing that comes out of its pressing.

As for His saying the Exalted, ﴿and his affair is up to Allah﴾, there are several views among the exegetes. However, what I say is that this verse is specific to one who has abandoned considering usury lawful, without stating whether he has abandoned consuming usury or not. The evidence for this is the beginning and the end of the verse.
As for the beginning of the verse: His saying, ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists﴾ does not state what he desisted from, so that mentioned thing must be directed to what precedes; and the nearest of the things mentioned in this statement is what Allah related, that they said, "Trade is only like usury." So His saying, ﴿and desists﴾ refers to it, meaning: he desisted from this saying.
As for the end of the verse: His saying, ﴿but whoever returns — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾, its meaning being: whoever returns to the earlier statement, which is considering usury lawful, ﴿and his affair is up to Allah﴾. Then this person: either it is said that just as he desisted from considering usury lawful, he also desisted from consuming usury, or it is not so. If it is the first, this person is one who acknowledges the religion of Allah and knows Allah's obligation, and then he deserves praise, honor and esteem; but His saying, ﴿and his affair is up to Allah﴾ does not fit that, because it indicates that if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him. Thus it is established that this verse does not suit the disbeliever nor the obedient believer, and so it remains that it is specific to one who acknowledged the prohibition of usury and then consumed usury. In this case his affair is up to Allah: if He wills He punishes him, and if He wills He forgives him, like His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa: 48]. This is therefore clear evidence for the soundness of our view that pardon from Allah is hoped for.

As for His saying, ﴿and whoever returns — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾, its meaning is: whoever returns to considering usury lawful, to the point of becoming a disbeliever.

Know that His saying, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ is a decisive proof that eternal abiding is only for the disbeliever, because His saying, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire﴾ indicates restriction regarding one who returns to the saying of the disbeliever, and likewise His saying, ﴿they will abide therein eternally﴾ indicates restriction. This indicates that being a companion of the Fire and abiding eternally in the Fire does not occur except for disbelievers. At most, we have departed from this apparent meaning and included the rest of the disbelievers in it, but it remains on its apparent meaning regarding the one guilty of a major sin. So reflect on these points. Our position is that one guilty of a major sin, if he is a believer in Allah and His Messenger, it is permissible regarding him that Allah pardon him, and it is permissible that Allah punish him, and his affair in both cases is entrusted to Allah. Then, supposing Allah punishes him, he will not abide eternally in the Fire, but He will bring him out of it. Allah the Exalted has shown the soundness of this doctrine in these verses by His saying, ﴿and his affair is up to Allah﴾, indicating the permissibility of pardon for one guilty of a major sin, as we have explained.

Then His saying, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ indicates that, supposing Allah causes him to enter the Fire, He does not make him abide in it eternally, because eternal abiding is specific to the disbelievers and not to the people of faith. This is a noble explanation and a good interpretation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 276:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah deprives usury of blessing and gives increase for charities. And Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had emphasized the prohibition of usury, and had emphasized in the preceding verses the command to give charity, He mentioned here what amounts to a call to abandon charities and to engage in usury, and He exposed its corruption. This is because the motive for engaging in usury is obtaining more of the goods, while what diverts one from charities is guarding against the loss of goods. Thus God, may He be exalted, made clear that usury, although it is an increase in appearance, is in reality a loss, and that charity, although it is a loss in appearance, is an increase in meaning. Since the matter is so, it is fitting for the intelligent person not to turn to what the nature and the senses dictate of motives and deterrents, but to rely upon what the Law has urged him toward of motives and deterrents. This is the aspect of the arrangement (of the verse). In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-mahq (deprivation) is the diminution of a thing gradually, step by step, and from it comes al-mahaq in the moon (its waning). It is said: Allah mahaqahu, so it was diminished and vanished (infamaqa wa-mtahaqa). It is also said: hajirun mahiq, when it diminishes everything by its heat.

The second issue: Know that the deprivation of usury and the increase of charities may be in this world and may be in the Hereafter. As for this world, we say: the deprivation of usury in this world is from several aspects:

The first of them: that the usual outcome for the usurer, even if his wealth increases, is that his end leads to poverty, and blessing is removed from his wealth. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Usury, however much it increases, ends in little."

The second: if his wealth does not diminish, its consequence is blame, deficiency, loss of uprightness, loss of trustworthiness, and acquiring the name of wickedness, harshness and coarseness.

The third: that the poor who see that he took their wealth by means of usury curse him, hate him, and invoke (God) against him, and that is a cause for the removal of good and blessing from him in his person and his wealth.

The fourth: that when it becomes known among people that he gathered his wealth from usury, greed is directed toward him, and every oppressor, rebel and greedy person targets him, and they say: that wealth is not truly his, so it is not left in his hand. As for usury being a cause of deprivation in the Hereafter, it is for several reasons:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: the meaning of this deprivation is that Allah, may He be exalted, does not accept from him charity, nor jihad, nor hajj, nor maintaining ties of kinship.

The second: the wealth of this world does not remain at death, while the consequence and the punishment remain, and that is the greatest loss.

The third: it is established in a hadith that the rich enter Paradise five hundred years after the poor. If the rich man from lawful sources is like this, then what do you think of the rich man from unlawful sources, whose prohibition is certain? How will it be? That is the deprivation and the loss.

As for the increase of charities, it may be that what is meant is in this world, and it may be that what is meant is in the Hereafter.

Page 84
As for in this world, it is from several aspects:

The first: whoever is for Allah, Allah is for him. When a person, despite his poverty and need, does good to the servants of Allah, Allah, may He be exalted, will not leave him lost in this world. In the hadith we narrated earlier, the angel calls out every day: "O Allah, grant every spender a replacement, and every withholder a loss."

The second: he increases every day in his standing, his good remembrance, the inclination of hearts toward him and people's tranquility in him, and that is better than wealth with the opposites of these conditions.

The third: the poor support him with righteous supplications.

The fourth: greed is cut off from him, for when it becomes known that he exerts himself to set right the affairs of the poor and the weak, every person guards against disputing with him, and every oppressor and every greedy person is unable to take anything of his wealth, except rarely. This is what is meant by the increase of charities in this world.

As for their increase in the Hereafter, Abu Hurayrah narrated that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, may He be exalted, accepts charities and accepts from them only what is good, and He takes them with His right hand and nurtures them as one of you nurtures his foal or his colt, until the morsel becomes like Uhud." The confirmation of this is clear in the Book of Allah: ﴿Do they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charities?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 104], and: ﴿Allah deprives usury and gives increase for charities.﴾ Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The likeness of His saying ﴿Allah deprives usury﴾ is the parable He gave earlier of a smooth rock upon which is dust, then a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. The likeness of His saying ﴿and gives increase for charities﴾ is the parable Allah gave of a grain that grew seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains.

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾, know that kaffar is an intensive form (fa''al) from disbelief (kufr), and its meaning is one for whom that is a habit. The Arabs describe a person persistent in something this way, so they say: so-and-so is constantly doing good and enjoining it. Athim is (fa'il in the form of fa'il), meaning the sinner, and it is also an intensive expression of persistence in acquiring sins and continuing in them. This is not fitting except for one who denies the prohibition of usury, so he would be a rejecter. There is another aspect: that kaffar refers to one who considers it lawful, and athim refers to one who does it while believing it is forbidden, so the verse includes both groups.

[Page 85]

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, and establish the prayer (ṣalāh, the ritual prayer) and give the zakāt (obligatory almsgiving), for them is their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾

Know that God's custom in the Qur'an is consistent: whenever He mentions a threat (waʿīd), He follows it with a promise (waʿd). When He had gone to the utmost in threatening the one who practises usury (ribā), He followed it with this promise. The interpretation of this verse has already passed in more than one place. It contains several issues.

The first issue: Those who hold that righteous deeds are outside the designation of faith (īmān) argue from this verse, for He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, so He conjoined "doing righteous deeds" to faith, and the conjoined element is different from the element it is conjoined to. Some people have answered this: Did He not say in this same verse, ﴿and do righteous deeds, and establish the prayer, and give the zakāt﴾, although there is no dispute that establishing the prayer and giving zakāt are included under ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾? So the same applies to what you have mentioned. Also, He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the way of God﴾ [An-Nahl: 88], and He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 39].

The first arguer may answer this objection by saying that the basic principle is to interpret every word as conveying a new meaning, which is set aside only when it is impossible; so it remains in the places where it is not impossible, according to the basic principle.

The second issue: His saying ﴿for them is their reward with their Lord﴾ is stronger than saying "their reward is upon their Lord," because the first is like the case of a sale for cash, where the price is present there and the seller takes it whenever he wishes; whereas "their reward is upon their Lord" is like the case of a sale on credit (nasīʾah), in which the price is a debt. There is no doubt that the first is better.

The third issue: Scholars differ concerning His saying ﴿and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "There will be no fear for them concerning what awaits them of the states of the Resurrection, and they will not grieve because of what they left behind in the world, for one who moves from one state to another higher than it may sometimes grieve over some of what he has missed of the earlier states, even though he rejoices in the second because of his familiarity with it and his habit. So He made clear that this degree of sorrow does not befall the people of reward and honour." Al-Aṣamm said: "There will be no fear for them of the punishment of that Day, and they will not grieve because the abundant bliss that has been granted to others among the blessed has escaped them, since there is no rivalry in the Hereafter. They will also not grieve because no greater obedience proceeded from us in the world, so that we might have deserved a greater reward than what we have found. This is because such thoughts do not occur in the Hereafter."

The fourth issue: Concerning His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, and establish the prayer and give the zakāt, for them is their reward with their Lord﴾, there is a difficulty: a woman who reaches maturity knowing God, and as soon as she reaches it she menstruates and then dies when her menstruation ceases; or a man who reaches maturity knowing God and dies before the prayer and zakāt become obligatory upon him. Both of these, by consensus, are among the people of reward. This shows that the entitlement to reward does not depend on the occurrence of deeds. Also, it is part of our school's doctrine that God may reward a believing sinner who is devoid of all deeds. If that is so, how did God here make the attainment of reward contingent upon the occurrence of deeds?

The answer: He, the Exalted, mentioned these attributes not because entitlement to reward is conditional upon them, but because each of them has an effect in bringing about reward. As He said of the opposite of this: ﴿And those who do not call upon any other god along with God﴾ [Al-Furqan: 68], then He said: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty (āthām)﴾ [Al-Furqan: 68]. It is known that one who invokes another god along with God does not need, for his deserving of punishment, another deed. Rather, God combined fornication and the killing of a soul, in the manner of treating them as lawful, with calling upon other than God as a god, to show that each of these attributes necessitates punishment.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verses 278–279:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains [due] of interest, if you should be believers.﴾ ﴿And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger. But if you repent, you may have your principal. [So] do not wrong, and you will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And if someone is in hardship, then [let there be] postponement until [a time of] ease. But if you give [from your right as] charity, it is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah. Then every soul will be functionally compensated what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾

Regarding the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, explained in the preceding verse that whoever desists from interest, for him is what has passed, one might have supposed that there is no difference between what has been received from it and what remains in the debtors' obligation. So He, exalted is He, said in this verse: ﴿and give up what remains [due] of interest﴾, and by this He made clear that if it is owed to them and has not been received, then the excess is forbidden, and they are not entitled to take anything except their principal. He emphasized this because whoever has waited a long time for the term to fall due, and then the time arrives and he imagines that this excess has been obtained for him, will need a great effort to be restrained from it. So He said: ﴿fear Allah﴾, and fearing Him means refraining from what He has forbidden, ﴿and give up what remains of interest﴾, meaning: if you have already received something, let it be forgiven; and if you have not received it, or have not received part of it, then what you have not received, whether all or part, it is forbidden to receive.

Know that this verse is a major principle regarding the rulings for disbelievers when they embrace Islam. This is because what took place during the time of disbelief remains and is not annulled or dissolved, and whatever did not occur in any part during the state of disbelief is ruled according to Islam. So if they contracted marriages according to what is permissible in their view but not permissible in Islam, it is a pardoned matter that is not pursued. If the marriage took place with a prohibited term and the woman has received it, it stands; and if she has not received it, then she is entitled to the customary bride-price (mahr al-mithl) rather than the stipulated bride-price. This is the school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him.

If it is said: How did He say: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾ and then say at its end: ﴿if you should be believers﴾?

The answer: from several aspects:

The first: this is like saying: "If you are a brother, then honor me," meaning: whoever is a brother should honor his brother.

The second: it has been said: its meaning is "if you were believers before this."

The third: "if you want the continuation of the ruling for you by faith."

The fourth: "O you who have believed with their tongues, give up what remains of interest, if you are believers in your hearts."

The second issue: concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse, there are narrations:

The first narration: it is an address to the people of Makkah who used to practice interest. When they embraced Islam at the conquest of Makkah, Allah the Exalted commanded them to take only their principal without the excess.

The second narration: Muqatil said: the verse was revealed concerning four brothers from Thaqif: Mas'ud, 'Abd Yalil, Habib and Rabi'ah, the sons of 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi, who used to lend to the Banu al-Mughirah. When the Prophet ﷺ prevailed over Ta'if, the brothers embraced Islam, then they demanded their interest from the Banu al-Mughirah, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

The third narration: it was revealed concerning al-'Abbas and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who had advanced payment for dates. When the time of harvesting came, they received part, and added to the remainder, so the verse was revealed. This is the statement of 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah.

The fourth narration: it was revealed concerning al-'Abbas and Khalid ibn al-Walid, who used to lend at interest. This is the statement of al-Suddi.

The third issue: al-Qadi said: His saying ﴿if you should be believers﴾ is like an indication that faith is not complete if a person persists in a major sin, and that he only becomes a believer absolutely if he avoids all major sins.

The answer: since the numerous proofs mentioned in the explanation of His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ indicate that action lies outside the designation of faith, this verse is understood as referring to the perfection of faith and its obligations, so the intended meaning is: "if you are acting in accordance with the requirements of the obligations of faith." Although this departs from the apparent meaning, we have adopted it because of those proofs.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

The first issue: Asim and Hamzah read (fa-ādhanū) with an initial alif, extended, with a kasrah on the dhal, on the pattern of (fa-āminū), while the rest read ﴿fa-adhanū﴾ with a sukun on the hamzah, a fatha on the dhal, and short. It is also narrated from the Prophet ﷺ and from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that they both read it in that manner (fa-ādhinū), extended, meaning "then inform," from His saying: ﴿Say: I have informed you upon equal terms﴾ [al-Anbiya': 109]. The object of the informing is omitted in this verse, and the sense is: "then inform those who have not desisted from interest of a war from Allah and His Messenger." Since they are commanded to inform others, they themselves also know this, but there is nothing in their knowledge that indicates informing others; therefore this reading is more emphatic in rhetoric. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: the common reading is from the idhn, meaning "be upon knowledge and notice." Al-Hasan read (fa-ayqinū), and this is a proof for the common reading.

The second issue: they differed as to whether the address in His saying ﴿then if you do not do it, then be informed of a war from Allah﴾ is addressed to believers persisting in dealing in interest, or whether it is addressed to disbelievers who consider interest lawful, those who said: "trade is only like interest." Al-Qadi said: the first possibility is preferable, because His saying ﴿fa-adhanū﴾ is an address to a people whose mention has preceded, namely those addressed in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest﴾, and this indicates that the address is to believers.

If it is said: how did He command warfare against Muslims?

We say: this expression is sometimes applied to one who disobeys Allah without considering it lawful, as in the report: "Whoever humiliates a friend of Mine has declared war upon Me." And from Jabir, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever does not abandon muhabarah, let him be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger." Many exegetes and jurists have taken His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33] as originally concerning highway robbery among Muslims. Thus it is established that this kind of threat in regard to Muslims occurs in the Book of Allah and in the Sunnah of His Messenger.

Having known this, we say: concerning the answer to the question mentioned, there are two views. The first: the intention is the emphasis of the threat, not war itself. The second: the intention is war itself, and in this there is detail. We say: if persistence in practicing interest comes from a person and the ruler is able over him, he seizes him and applies to him the ruling of Allah, namely discretionary punishment (ta'zir) and imprisonment, until repentance from him becomes apparent. If it comes from a group that has an army and power, the ruler fights them as he fights a rebellious faction, just as Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, fought those who withheld zakat. Likewise, if a people agree to abandon the call to prayer or the burial of the dead, he does to them what we have mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: whoever deals in interest is asked to repent; if he repents, well, otherwise his neck is struck.

The second view concerning this verse is that His saying ﴿then if you do not do it, then be informed﴾ is addressed to disbelievers, and that the meaning of the verse, ﴿give up what remains of interest, if you are believers﴾, is "acknowledging the prohibition of interest," and ﴿then if you do not do it﴾ means "if you do not acknowledge its prohibition," ﴿then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger.﴾ Those who adopt this view say that it contains proof that whoever disbelieves in one of the legal rulings of Islam is a disbeliever, just as if he disbelieved in all of its rulings.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you repent﴾, and the meaning according to the first view is: you repent from dealing in interest; and according to the second view: from considering interest lawful. ﴿Then you have your principal. Do not wrong, and you will not be wronged﴾, that is: do not wrong the debtor by demanding an excess over the principal, and you will not be wronged, that is, by a reduction of the principal.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you repent﴾, and the meaning according to the first view is: you repent from dealing in interest; and according to the second view: from considering interest lawful. ﴿Then you have your principal. Do not wrong, and you will not be wronged﴾, that is: do not wrong the debtor by demanding an excess over the principal, and you will not be wronged, that is, by a reduction of the principal.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship, then let there be postponement until a time of ease.﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first issue: The grammarians said: "kāna" (was) is a word used in several ways.

The first: that it is equivalent to ḥadatha and waqa'a (occurred, came to be), as in your saying: qad kāna al-amr (the matter has occurred), meaning it came into existence. In this sense it does not require a predicate (khabar).

The second: that the meaning of occurrence is stripped from it, so that the word remains bare of meaning other than time. In this sense it requires a predicate, as in your saying: kāna Zayd dhāhiban (Zayd was going).

Know that when I was residing in Khwarazm, and there was there a group of the leading men of letters, I raised a difficulty for them concerning this topic. I said: "You say that kāna, when it is incomplete (nāqiṣa), is a verb. This is impossible, because a verb is that which indicates the conjunction of an event with a time. Your saying kāna indicates the occurrence of the meaning of existence in past time. And when it conveys this meaning, it is complete (tāmma), not incomplete. So this argument requires that if it is a verb, it is complete and not incomplete; and if it is not complete, it is not a verb at all but a particle (ḥarf). And you deny that." They remained in this difficulty for a long time, and they composed books in answer to it, but they did not succeed. Then there was revealed to me a secret in it, which I will mention here: that kāna has no meaning except ḥadatha, waqa'a and wujida (occurred, happened, came into being). However, your saying wujida and ḥadatha is of two kinds. One: that the meaning is: the thing came into being and occurred, as in your saying: the substance came into being, the accident occurred. The second: that the meaning is: the attribute of the thing by something came into being and occurred, so when you say: kāna Zayd ʿāliman (Zayd was knowing), its meaning is: the attribution of knowledge to Zayd occurred in past time. The first kind is what is called complete kāna, and the second kind is what is called incomplete kāna. In reality, what is understood from kāna in both places is occurrence and happening; but in the first kind, what is intended is the occurrence of the thing in itself, so the single noun is sufficient. In the second kind, what is intended is the occurrence of the attribution of one of the two matters to the other, so the single noun is not sufficient, but it is necessary to mention two nouns, so that it is possible to indicate the attribution of one of them to the other. This is among the subtleties of inquiry. As for if we say that it is a verb, kāna indicates the occurrence of the verbal noun in past time, and then it is complete, not incomplete. And if we say it is not a verb but a particle, how can past, future and imperative, and all the properties of verbs, enter into it? When the imperative is understood as we have said, it becomes clear that it is a verb, and the difficulty is removed entirely.

The third meaning of kāna: it is used with the meaning of ṣāra (became). They cited:

In a barren wilderness, where the mounts are like sandgrouse of the sand-dune, whose eggs have become fledglings.

In my view, this word here is to be understood in terms of what we have mentioned, for the meaning of ṣāra is that the attribution of the essence with this quality came into being after it was not attributed with that. So it here means ḥadatha and waqa'a, but it is a particular occurrence: the attribution of the essence with this quality came into being after what had been established was the attribution of the essence with another quality.

The fourth meaning: that it is superfluous (zā'ida). They cited:

The nobles of the sons of Abu Bakr have excelled over the ... of the marked fine horses.

When you have understood this rule, let us return to the exegesis and say: In (kāna) in this verse there are two possibilities. The first: that it means waqa'a and ḥadatha, and the meaning is: "And if a debtor in hardship came into being." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿except that it be a present trade﴾ [al-Baqara: 282] in the nominative, meaning: "if a present trade occurs." The intended meaning of the verse is correct on this reading, because if it were said: "And if he is (kāna) one in hardship," the meaning would be: "And if the buyer is in hardship, then postponement," so the postponement would be restricted to him; but the matter is not so, because the buyer and others, if they are in hardship, have the right to postponement until ease. The second: that it is incomplete, with the predicate omitted, its estimate being: "And if a debtor in hardship is a creditor of yours." ʿUthmān read (dhā ʿusratin), and the estimate is: "If the debtor is in hardship." It was also read: "wa-man kāna dhā ʿusratin."

The second issue: ʿUsrah (hardship) is a noun from iʿsār (straitness), which is the inability to obtain existing wealth. It is said: aʿsara al-rajul (the man became straitened) when he came to a state of hardship (ʿusrah), which is the state in which the existence of wealth becomes difficult.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease﴾ and in this there are several issues.

The first issue: There is an omission in the verse, and the estimate is: "So the ruling is," or "So the matter is postponement," or "So what you deal in is postponement."

The second issue: naẓira (postponement) means delay, and nazira is the noun from inẓār, which is granting respite. You say: I sold him the thing on credit (bi-naẓira) and on postponement (bi-inẓār). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said: Grant me respite until the day they are raised.﴾ ﴿He said: Indeed you are among those granted respite.﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 14–15] ﴿until the day of the appointed time.﴾

The third issue: It was read: "fa-naẓrah" with the ẓāʾ sukūn. ʿAṭāʾ read: "fa-nāẓirhu," meaning: so the possessor of the right, that is, one who awaits him, or the possessor of his respite, by way of relation (nisba), as in their saying: makān ʿāshib and bāqil, meaning: a place having herbage and having green vegetation. It is also reported from him: "fa-nāẓirhu" in the imperative, meaning: so grant him respite with postponement until ease.

The fourth issue: al-maysarah is a form of maf'alah from yusr and yasar, which is the opposite of iʿsār, and is the facility of existing wealth. From it it is said: aysara al-rajul, so he is mūsir, meaning he came to ease. So al-maysarah, al-yusr and al-maysur mean wealth.

The fifth issue: Nafiʿ read (maysurah) with a ḍammah on the sīn, and the rest read it with a fatḥah. These are two well-known dialects, like al-maqbarah, al-mashrafah, al-mashrabah and al-masrabah. The fatḥah is the more famous of the two dialects, because it occurs in their speech much.

The sixth issue: They differed as to whether the ruling of granting respite is specific to usury (ribā) or general to all. Ibn ʿAbbas, Shurayh, al-Ḍaḥḥak, al-Suddi and Ibrahim said: the verse concerns usury. It is reported from Shurayh that he ordered the detention of one of the two disputants, and it was said: "He is in hardship." Shurayh said: "That applies only to usury, and God, exalted is He, said in His Book: ﴿Indeed God commands you to render the trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa: 58]." The commentators mentioned, regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, that when His saying was revealed: ﴿then be warned of war from God and His Messenger﴾, the four brothers who used to deal in usury said: "Rather we repent to God, for we have no power for war with God and His Messenger." They agreed to the principal, but sought from the sons of al-Mughira that matter, and the sons of al-Mughira complained of hardship and said: "Delay us until the harvests come in." They refused to delay them, so God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And if a debtor is in hardship, then let there be postponement until a time of ease.﴾

The second view, which is the view of Mujahid and a group of commentators: it is general to every debt. They argued with what we have mentioned, that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if there is one in hardship﴾ and did not say: "if he is one in hardship" (dhā), so that the ruling would be general to all cases. The judge (al-Qadi) said: The first view is more preferred, because He, exalted is He, said in the preceding verse: ﴿but if you repent, you shall have your principal sums﴾ without loss or diminution. Then He said in this verse: if the one owing the wealth is in hardship, it is obligatory to grant him respite until the time of ability. For postponement is intended by it, so there must be a right previously mentioned for postponement to apply. Rather, since the obligation of granting respite in this case was established by the text, its obligation in the other cases is established by necessity, because of the shared meaning, namely that one unable to pay wealth may not be obligated to it. This is the view of most jurists, such as Abu Hanifa, Malik and al-Shafiʿi, may God be pleased with them.

The seventh issue: Know that it is necessary to explain iʿsār. We say: iʿsār is that one does not find in his possession what would discharge it in kind, and he has no property which, if he sold it, would enable him to pay the debt from its price. For this reason we say: whoever has a house and clothes is not counted among those in hardship, if it is possible for him to sell them and pay their price. It is not permitted to withhold anything except the food of a day for himself and his dependents, and what they must have of clothing for their prayers and for protection from cold and heat.

They differed concerning one who is strong: is he obligated to hire himself out to the creditor or to another? Some said: he is obligated to that, just as he is obligated when he needs it for himself and his dependents. Others said: he is not obligated to that. They also differed concerning one who is in hardship when another offers to pay on his behalf: is he obligated to accept and allow the payment, or is he not obligated to that? As for one who has merchandise that has become unsaleable to him, it is obligatory on him to sell it at a loss if there is no other way, and pay the debt with it.

The eighth issue: If a person knows that his debtor is in hardship, it is forbidden for him to imprison him or to demand from him what is owed to him, and granting respite until the time of ease becomes obligatory. But if he has doubt about his hardship, it is permitted for him to detain him until the hardship becomes evident. Know that when he claims hardship and the creditor denies it, this debt that is binding on him is either from a consideration he received, such as sale or loan, or it is not so. In the first kind, there must be two just witnesses that this consideration has perished. In the second kind, where the debt is established without a consideration, such as destruction of property, dowry or guarantee, his word is accepted and the creditors must provide proof, because the original state is poverty.
