Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And that you give charity is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ In this there are several issues.

The first issue: ʿĀṣim read "taṣaddaqū" with the ṣād lightened, and the rest with it doubled. The original form is: an tataṣaddaqū with two tāʾs. Whoever lightens it omits one of the two tāʾs for lightness, and whoever doubles it assimilates one tāʾ into the other.

The second issue: Regarding taṣaddaq there are two views. The first: its meaning is: "And that you give charity to the one in hardship with what he owes you as debt," since it is not valid to give it in charity to anyone else. This omission is permitted because it is known, since the one in hardship and the principal have been mentioned, so it is understood that the charity refers to both. It is like His saying: ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Baqara: 237]. The second: that what is meant by taṣaddaq is granting respite, based on His, upon him be peace, saying: "The debt of a Muslim man is not lawful to be delayed by him except that for every day there is a charity for him." This view is weak, because granting respite has been established as obligatory by the first verse, so this verse must be read as conveying a new benefit. Also, His saying: ﴿is better for you﴾ does not suit what is obligatory, but what is recommended.

The third issue: What is meant by the good (khayr) is the attainment of fine praise in this world and great reward in the Hereafter.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿if you only knew﴾, and in this there are several possibilities:

The first: its meaning is: "if you know that this charity is better for you if you do it," making action a necessary consequence of knowledge, and in this there is a severe threat to the disobedient. The second: "if you know the excellence of charity over granting respite and receiving." The third: "if you know that what your Lord commands you is more beneficial for you."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And fear a Day in which you will be returned to God, then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾ Know that this verse concerns the great men who used to deal in usury, who possessed wealth, majesty, supporters and helpers, and from them there was often domination over people by reason of their wealth. So they needed further restraint, warning and threat, so that they would refrain from usury and from taking people's wealth unjustly. Therefore God threatened them with this verse and frightened them in the strongest way. In it there are several issues:

**Issue One:** Ibn ʿAbbas said: This verse was the last verse revealed to the Messenger (ﷺ). When he performed the Ḥajj, ﴿They ask you for a ruling﴾ [An-Nisa: 127] was revealed, which is the verse of *al-kalalah* (a person who leaves neither ascendants nor descendants). Then he (ﷺ) was revealed ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 3] while standing at ʿArafah. Then ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 281] was revealed. Jibril (peace be upon him) then said: "O Muhammad, place it at the head of eighty-two verses of al-Baqarah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lived after it eighty-one days. It is also said twenty-one days, and it is said seven days, and it is said three hours.

**Issue Two:** Abu ʿAmr read *turjaʿūna* with a fatḥah on the *tāʾ*, while the others read it with a ḍammah on the *tāʾ*. Know that *al-rujūʿ* (returning) is intransitive, while *al-rajʿ* (returning something) is transitive, and both readings are derived from this.

**Issue Three:** *Yawman* (a day) is in the accusative as a direct object (*maf'ūl bihi*), not as an adverbial of time (*ẓarf*). This is because the meaning is not "fear Allah on this day," but rather "prepare yourselves to meet it by sending forward righteous deeds." A similar example is His saying: ﴿How will you guard yourselves, if you disbelieve, against a Day that will make children grey-haired?﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 17], meaning: how will you guard yourselves against this day, whose description is this, while you disbelieve in Allah?

**Issue Four:** Al-Qadi said: "Yawm" is an expression for a specific period of time, and that cannot be guarded against. Rather, what is guarded against is what occurs in it of hardship and terrors, and guarding against those terrors is only possible in this worldly abode, by avoiding sins and performing obligations. Thus His saying ﴿and fear a day﴾ includes the command to comply with all categories of obligations.

**Issue Five:** The return to Allah Most High does not mean what relates to place and direction, for that is impossible for Allah Most High. Nor does it mean returning to His knowledge and protection, for He is with them wherever they are. Rather, every instance in the Qur'an of His saying ﴿you will be returned to Allah in it﴾ has two meanings. The first: a person has three states in sequence:

The first state is their being in the bellies of their mothers, during which they do not possess benefit or harm for themselves, and the only one who disposes of them is Allah, glorified and exalted.

The second state is their being after emerging from their mothers' bellies. In this state, the one who initially takes charge of their welfare is the two parents, and after that some of them dispose of others in the outward judgment.

The third state is after death. In it, the one who truly disposes of them in reality is none but Allah, glorified be He. So it is as if, after leaving this world, they return to the state they were in before entering this world. This is the meaning of the return to Allah. The second meaning: the intended sense is that they return to what Allah has prepared for them of reward or punishment. Both interpretations are good and agree with the wording.

Then He said: ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged﴾. There are two issues in this:

**Issue One:** The meaning is that every responsible person, upon returning to Allah, will necessarily receive the full recompense of their deeds, as He said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [Al-Zalzalah: 7–8]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, if it should be the weight of a mustard seed and should be within a rock or within the heavens or within the earth, Allah will bring it forth﴾ [Luqman: 16]. And He said: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And if there is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 47]. Regarding His saying ﴿what it earned﴾ there are two interpretations: The first: there is an ellipsis, and the estimated meaning is "the recompense of what it earned." The second: what is earned is that recompense itself, because what a man acquires through his trade of wealth is described in the language as "his earnings." So His saying ﴿every soul will be paid what it earned﴾ means every soul will be paid its earnings. This interpretation is preferable, because whenever a statement can be explained without needing to supply anything, it is better.

**Issue Two:** The Waʿīdiyya (Mu'tazila and Khawarij, who hold that the threat of punishment is absolute for sinners) use this verse to affirm with certainty the threat against the sinners. Our companions (the Ashʿarī school) use it to affirm with certainty the non-eternity of punishment, because when someone has believed, the reward of faith must necessarily reach them, and this is not possible except by their leaving the Fire and entering Paradise.

Then He said: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾. There is a question here: His saying ﴿every soul will be paid what it earned﴾ has no meaning except that they will not be wronged, so this would be a repetition.

The answer: When He Most High said ﴿every soul will be paid what it earned﴾, this was an indication of the delivery of punishment to the sinners and disbelievers. So someone might say: "How is it fitting for the generosity of the most generous of the generous to punish His servants?" He answered this with His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾. The meaning is that the servant is the one who put himself into that predicament, because Allah Most High empowered him, removed his excuse, facilitated for him the path of reasoning, and granted him respite. So whoever fell short is the one who wronged himself. This answer holds only according to the principles of the Mu'tazila. As for according to the principles of our companions, it is that He, glorified be He, is the Owner of creation, and an owner who acts with his property as he wishes and wills does not commit injustice. Thus His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ after mentioning the threat is an allusion to what we have mentioned.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship, then let there be postponement until a time of ease.﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first issue: The grammarians said: "kāna" (was) is a word used in several ways.

The first: that it is equivalent to ḥadatha and waqa'a (occurred, came to be), as in your saying: qad kāna al-amr (the matter has occurred), meaning it came into existence. In this sense it does not require a predicate (khabar).

The second: that the meaning of occurrence is stripped from it, so that the word remains bare of meaning other than time. In this sense it requires a predicate, as in your saying: kāna Zayd dhāhiban (Zayd was going).

Know that when I was residing in Khwarazm, and there was there a group of the leading men of letters, I raised a difficulty for them concerning this topic. I said: "You say that kāna, when it is incomplete (nāqiṣa), is a verb. This is impossible, because a verb is that which indicates the conjunction of an event with a time. Your saying kāna indicates the occurrence of the meaning of existence in past time. And when it conveys this meaning, it is complete (tāmma), not incomplete. So this argument requires that if it is a verb, it is complete and not incomplete; and if it is not complete, it is not a verb at all but a particle (ḥarf). And you deny that." They remained in this difficulty for a long time, and they composed books in answer to it, but they did not succeed. Then there was revealed to me a secret in it, which I will mention here: that kāna has no meaning except ḥadatha, waqa'a and wujida (occurred, happened, came into being). However, your saying wujida and ḥadatha is of two kinds. One: that the meaning is: the thing came into being and occurred, as in your saying: the substance came into being, the accident occurred. The second: that the meaning is: the attribute of the thing by something came into being and occurred, so when you say: kāna Zayd ʿāliman (Zayd was knowing), its meaning is: the attribution of knowledge to Zayd occurred in past time. The first kind is what is called complete kāna, and the second kind is what is called incomplete kāna. In reality, what is understood from kāna in both places is occurrence and happening; but in the first kind, what is intended is the occurrence of the thing in itself, so the single noun is sufficient. In the second kind, what is intended is the occurrence of the attribution of one of the two matters to the other, so the single noun is not sufficient, but it is necessary to mention two nouns, so that it is possible to indicate the attribution of one of them to the other. This is among the subtleties of inquiry. As for if we say that it is a verb, kāna indicates the occurrence of the verbal noun in past time, and then it is complete, not incomplete. And if we say it is not a verb but a particle, how can past, future and imperative, and all the properties of verbs, enter into it? When the imperative is understood as we have said, it becomes clear that it is a verb, and the difficulty is removed entirely.

The third meaning of kāna: it is used with the meaning of ṣāra (became). They cited:

In a barren wilderness, where the mounts are like sandgrouse of the sand-dune, whose eggs have become fledglings.

In my view, this word here is to be understood in terms of what we have mentioned, for the meaning of ṣāra is that the attribution of the essence with this quality came into being after it was not attributed with that. So it here means ḥadatha and waqa'a, but it is a particular occurrence: the attribution of the essence with this quality came into being after what had been established was the attribution of the essence with another quality.

The fourth meaning: that it is superfluous (zā'ida). They cited:

The nobles of the sons of Abu Bakr have excelled over the ... of the marked fine horses.

When you have understood this rule, let us return to the exegesis and say: In (kāna) in this verse there are two possibilities. The first: that it means waqa'a and ḥadatha, and the meaning is: "And if a debtor in hardship came into being." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿except that it be a present trade﴾ [al-Baqara: 282] in the nominative, meaning: "if a present trade occurs." The intended meaning of the verse is correct on this reading, because if it were said: "And if he is (kāna) one in hardship," the meaning would be: "And if the buyer is in hardship, then postponement," so the postponement would be restricted to him; but the matter is not so, because the buyer and others, if they are in hardship, have the right to postponement until ease. The second: that it is incomplete, with the predicate omitted, its estimate being: "And if a debtor in hardship is a creditor of yours." ʿUthmān read (dhā ʿusratin), and the estimate is: "If the debtor is in hardship." It was also read: "wa-man kāna dhā ʿusratin."

The second issue: ʿUsrah (hardship) is a noun from iʿsār (straitness), which is the inability to obtain existing wealth. It is said: aʿsara al-rajul (the man became straitened) when he came to a state of hardship (ʿusrah), which is the state in which the existence of wealth becomes difficult.

**Issue One:** The meaning is that every responsible person, upon returning to Allah, will necessarily receive the full recompense of their deeds, as He said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [Al-Zalzalah: 7–8]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, if it should be the weight of a mustard seed and should be within a rock or within the heavens or within the earth, Allah will bring it forth﴾ [Luqman: 16]. And He said: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And if there is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 47]. Regarding His saying ﴿what it earned﴾ there are two interpretations: The first: there is an ellipsis, and the estimated meaning is "the recompense of what it earned." The second: what is earned is that recompense itself, because what a man acquires through his trade of wealth is described in the language as "his earnings." So His saying ﴿every soul will be paid what it earned﴾ means every soul will be paid its earnings. This interpretation is preferable, because whenever a statement can be explained without needing to supply anything, it is better.

**Issue Two:** The Waʿīdiyya (Mu'tazila and Khawarij, who hold that the threat of punishment is absolute for sinners) use this verse to affirm with certainty the threat against the sinners. Our companions (the Ashʿarī school) use it to affirm with certainty the non-eternity of punishment, because when someone has believed, the reward of faith must necessarily reach them, and this is not possible except by their leaving the Fire and entering Paradise.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾. There is a question here: His saying ﴿every soul will be paid what it earned﴾ has no meaning except that they will not be wronged, so this would be a repetition.

The answer: When He Most High said ﴿every soul will be paid what it earned﴾, this was an indication of the delivery of punishment to the sinners and disbelievers. So someone might say: "How is it fitting for the generosity of the most generous of the generous to punish His servants?" He answered this with His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾. The meaning is that the servant is the one who put himself into that predicament, because Allah Most High empowered him, removed his excuse, facilitated for him the path of reasoning, and granted him respite. So whoever fell short is the one who wronged himself. This answer holds only according to the principles of the Mu'tazila. As for according to the principles of our companions, it is that He, glorified be He, is the Owner of creation, and an owner who acts with his property as he wishes and wills does not commit injustice. Thus His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ after mentioning the threat is an allusion to what we have mentioned.

**The third ruling**
Among the legal rulings mentioned in this part of this surah is the verse of debt-contracting (ayat al-mudayana).
﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. And let a scribe write [it] between you in justice. Let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him, so let him write. And let the one who has the obligation dictate, and let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not leave anything out of it. But if the one who has the obligation is of limited understanding or weak or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate in justice. And bring to witness two witnesses from among your men. And if there are not two men, then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses - so that if one of the two errs, the other can remind her. And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called upon. And do not be unwilling to write it, whether it is small or large, for its term. That is more just in the sight of Allah and more suitable as evidence and closer to avoiding doubt - except when it is a present trade which you conduct among yourselves; then there is no blame upon you that you not write it. And take witnesses when you conclude a sale. And let no scribe or witness be harmed. And if you do so, indeed it is deviation in you. And fear Allah; and Allah teaches you. And Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

Know that in the verse there are several issues:

**Issue One: On the manner of its arrangement (nazm), there are two aspects:**

The first: When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned before this ruling two types of rulings: the first being spending in the way of Allah, which entails diminishing wealth, and the second being abandoning riba, which is also a cause of diminishing wealth. Then He, exalted is He, concluded those two rulings with a great warning, saying: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾. Piety closes off for a person most of the doors of gain and benefit. He then followed this by urging him toward the manner of preserving lawful wealth and guarding it from corruption and ruin; for the ability to spend in the way of Allah, to abandon riba, and to persist in piety is not complete and does not perfect except upon the existence of wealth. Then, for the sake of this subtle point, He emphasized strongly the preservation of lawful wealth from the ways of loss and destruction. A similar statement occurs in Surat an-Nisa: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property which Allah has made for you a means of sustenance﴾ [An-Nisa: 5], urging caution regarding wealth because it is a cause of the benefits of livelihood and the Hereafter.

Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What indicates this is that the words of the Qur'an generally proceed by brevity, but in this verse there is great elaboration. Do you not see that He said: ﴿When you contract a debt for a specified term, write it﴾, then He said secondly: ﴿And let a scribe write between you in justice﴾, then He said thirdly: ﴿Let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him﴾, so this was like a repetition of His saying ﴿let a scribe write between you in justice﴾, because justice is what Allah has taught. Then He said fourthly: (so let him write), which is a repetition of the first command. Then He said fifthly: ﴿And let the one who has the obligation dictate﴾, and in His saying ﴿let a scribe write between you in justice﴾ there is sufficiency from His saying ﴿let the one who has the obligation dictate﴾, because the scribe who writes in justice only writes what is dictated to him. Then He said sixthly: ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾, which is emphasis. Then He said seventhly: ﴿and not leave anything out of it﴾, which is like what is derived from His saying ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾. Then He said eighthly: ﴿And do not be unwilling to write it, whether small or large, for its term﴾, which is also emphasis of what preceded. Then He said ninthly: ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah and more suitable as evidence and closer to avoiding doubt﴾, thus mentioning these three benefits for those prior emphases. All of this indicates that when He urged what runs in the course of the cause of diminishing wealth in the first two rulings, He emphasized in this ruling the preservation of lawful wealth and guarding it from destruction and ruin, so that a person may through it be enabled to spend in the way of Allah, to turn away from what displeases Allah such as riba and others, and to persevere in the piety of Allah. This is the first aspect of the arrangement, and it is fine and subtle.

The second aspect: Some of the exegetes said: the intended meaning of mudayana is salam (advance sale). So when Allah, glorified and exalted is He, forbade riba in the preceding verse, He permitted salam in all of this verse, although all the benefits sought from riba are achieved in salam. For this reason some scholars said: No pleasure or benefit that is reached through the forbidden way except that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has placed for obtaining the like of that pleasure a lawful way and a legislated path. This is what pertains to the aspect of the arrangement.

**Issue Two:** Tadayantum is a reciprocal form from ad-dayn (debt); its meaning is "some of you contracted debt with one another," and tadayantum means "you conducted a sale on credit." The lexicographers said: qard (loan) is other than dayn, because qard is that a person lends dirhams, or dinars, or grain, or dates, or the like, and a term (ajal) is not permitted in it, whereas dayn permits a term. It is said from dayn: "adana" when he sold his goods for a price to a term; "dana yadinu" when he lent; and "dana" when he borrowed. Al-Ahmar recited:
"We lend and God settles for us, though we see the downfall of a people who do not lend, straitened."

Having known this, we say: concerning the intended meaning of this mudayana there are several views. Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning salam, because the Prophet ﷺ came to Medina and they were making advance sales in dates for two or three years, and he ﷺ said: "Whoever makes an advance sale, let him make it in a known measure and a known weight to a known term." Then Allah, exalted is He, made known to the obligated the manner of precaution in measure, weight and term, saying: ﴿When you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down﴾.

The second view: that it is qard (loan), and this is weak, because of what we have explained, that a term cannot be stipulated in a loan, whereas the debt mentioned in the verse has had a term stipulated in it.

The third view, which is the view of most exegetes: sales are of four kinds. The first: exchange of specific for specific, which is not mudayana at all. The second: exchange of debt for debt, which is void, so it does not fall under this verse. There remain two categories: exchange of specific for debt, which is when one sells something for a deferred price, and exchange of debt for specific, which is called salam; both of these fall under this verse. And in the verse there are questions:

**First question:** Mudayana is a form of mufa'ala, and its reality is that from each of the two there arises a debt, and that is the exchange of debt for debt, which is void by consensus.

Answer: The intended meaning of "you contract" (tadayantum) is "you deal," and the implication is: when you deal in what involves a debt.

**Second question:** His saying "tadayantum" indicates debt, so what is the benefit of His saying "bi-dayn"?

Answer, in several respects:
First: Ibn al-Anbari said: tadayun occurs in two senses: one, tadayun in terms of wealth; and the other, tadayun in the sense of recompense, from their saying: "as you owe, so you are owed," and dayn means recompense. So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned dayn to specify one of the two meanings.
Second: The author of al-Kashshaf said: He mentioned dayn so that the pronoun would refer to it in His saying ﴿fa-uktubuhu﴾ (so write it), for if He had not mentioned it, it would have been necessary to say: "write the debt," and the arrangement would not have been as fine.
Third: He, exalted is He, mentioned it for emphasis, like His saying: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾ [Al-Hijr: 30], and ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [Al-An'am: 38].
Fourth: "So when you contract a debt, whatever debt it is, small or large, in whatever manner it is, whether a loan or salam or sale of a specific thing, for a term."
Fifth: What occurred to my mind is that we have stated that mudayana is mufa'ala, and that applies only to the exchange of debt for debt, which is void. If He had said "if you contract," the text would have been restricted to the exchange of debt for debt, which is void. But since He said ﴿when you contract a debt for a specified term﴾, the meaning is: when you conduct a dealing in which one debt arises. In that case, the exchange of debt for debt is excluded from the text, and the exchange of specific for debt, or debt for specific, remains, since in each of these only one debt arises.

**Third question:** The meaning of the verse is: whenever you contract a debt, write it. The word "idha" (when) does not imply generality, so why did He say "tadayantum" and not "kullama tadayantum" (whenever you contract)?

Answer: Although the word "idha" does not necessitate generality, it does not prevent generality, and here evidence has established that the intended meaning is generality, because He, exalted is He, stated the reason for the command to write at the end of the verse, which is His saying: ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah and more suitable as evidence and closer to avoiding doubt﴾. The meaning is: if a transaction involving debt takes place and it is not written down, then it is apparent that the details are forgotten, so one may imagine an increase and demand an increase, which is injustice, or one may imagine a decrease and abandon one's right without praise or reward. But when one writes down the details of the event, one is safe from these dangers. Since the text indicates that this is the reason, and this reason exists in all cases, the ruling is also obtained in all cases.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿to a specified term﴾, there are two questions:

**First question:** What is the ajal (term)?

Answer: Ajal in the language is the time set for the end of a period. The ajal of a person is the time of the end of his life, and the ajal of a debt is a specific time in the future. Its root is delay; it is said: "ajila al-shay'u ya'jilu ujulan" when a thing was delayed, and al-ajil is the opposite of al-'ajil (the immediate).

**Second question:** Mudayana is only deferred, so what is the benefit of mentioning the term after mentioning mudayana?

Answer: He mentioned the term so that it could be described by His saying "musamma" (specified). The benefit of His saying "musamma" is to make known that it is a requirement of the term that it be known, such as fixing it by year, month or days. If He had said "until the harvest," or "until the threshing," or "until the arrival of the pilgrims," it would not be permitted, due to the lack of specification.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-uktubuhu﴾ (so write it): know that He, exalted is He, commanded in debt two things. The first: writing, which is His saying here ﴿fa-uktubuhu﴾. The second: calling witnesses, which is His saying: ﴿and bring to witness two witnesses from among your men﴾. On this there are two issues:

**First issue:** The benefit of writing and of calling witnesses is that in what involves a term, the demand is delayed, forgetfulness intervenes, and denial enters. Thus writing becomes like a means of preserving wealth from both sides. For when the creditor knows that his right has been bound by writing and witnessing, he is cautious of demanding an increase and of making demands before the term arrives. And the debtor, when he knows this, is cautious of denial, and takes steps before the term arrives to acquire wealth so that he may be able to pay at the time the debt falls due. Since writing and witnessing achieve these benefits, Allah has indeed commanded it, and Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** Those who hold that the apparent sense of a command is recommendation (nadb) face no difficulty here. As for those who hold that its apparent sense is obligation (wujub), they have disagreed about it. Some said it is obligatory. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Nakhaʿī, and the view chosen by Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī. al-Nakhaʿī said: "One should call witnesses even over a bundle of herbs." Others said: this command is to be understood as recommendation, and this is the view of the majority of the qualified jurists (mujtahidūn). The evidence for this is that we see the majority of Muslims in all the lands of Islam selling on deferred payment without writing or witnessing, and this is a consensus (ijmāʿ) that neither is obligatory. Moreover, to make them obligatory would be the greatest hardship upon the Muslims, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was sent with the easy, tolerant monotheism (al-ḥanīfiyyah al-samḥah)."

Others said: rather, it was obligatory, but this was abrogated (mansūkh, i.e. superseded by naskh) by His saying: ﴿But if one of you trusts another, let the one who is trusted fulfil his trust﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 283]. This is the view of al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥakam, and Ibn ʿUyaynah. al-Taymī said: "I asked al-Ḥasan about it, and he said: 'If he wishes he may call witnesses, and if he wishes he need not call witnesses. Do you not hear His saying: ﴿But if one of you trusts another﴾?'"

Know that when He commanded the writing of this debt contract, He stipulated two conditions in that writing.

**The first condition:** that the scribe be just (ʿadl). This is His saying: ﴿Let a scribe write it down between you justly﴾. Know that His saying, "fa-uktubūhu" (so write it down), apparently implies that it is obligatory upon every person to write. But that is not possible, for that person may not be a scribe. So the meaning of His saying "fa-uktubūhu" is: this writing must come about. This is like His saying: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands as a recompense﴾ [Al-Māʾidah: 38]. Its apparent sense implies addressing everyone with this act, but we know that what is intended is that the cutting of the hand must occur by one person, either the imam, his deputy, or the owner. So likewise here. Then what we have said is confirmed by His saying: ﴿Let a scribe write it down between you justly﴾, for this indicates that the intended purpose is that this writing occur by whichever person it may be.

As for His saying "bil-ʿadl" (justly), there are several aspects:

First: that he writes in such a way that it neither adds to the debt nor subtracts from it, and writes it in such a way that it is fit to serve as evidence for him when he needs it.

Second: if he is a jurist, he must write in such a way that he does not favour one of the two parties with precaution over the other. Rather, he must write it in such a way that each of the two adversaries is secure from the other's ability to nullify his right.

Third: some jurists said: justice is that what he writes should be agreed upon among the scholars, and not be such that a judge of the Muslims finds a way to nullify it according to the view of some of the mujtahids.

Fourth: that he avoid ambiguous terms about which disputes arise concerning what they mean. These matters we have mentioned cannot be observed except when the scribe is a jurist who knows the views of the mujtahids, and is a man of letters who distinguishes between similar words.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him﴾. On this there are issues.

**The first issue:** The apparent sense of this statement is a prohibition upon everyone who is a scribe from refusing to write, and an obligation to write upon everyone who is a scribe. On this there are several views.

First: this is by way of guidance toward what is better, not by way of obligation. The meaning is that since Allah has taught him writing and honoured him with knowledge of the legal rulings, it is better that he write to accomplish the need of his Muslim brother, as thanks for that blessing. This is like His saying: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ [Al-Qaṣaṣ: 77]. People benefit from his writing just as Allah benefited him by teaching him it.

The second view, which is the view of al-Shaʿbī: it is a collective obligation (farḍ kifāyah). If he finds no one to write other than that one person, it is obligatory upon him to write. If he finds several people, then it is obligatory upon one of them to write.

The third view: this was obligatory upon the scribe, then it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾.

The fourth view: the object of the obligation is that he write as Allah has taught him. That is, on the assumption that he writes, what is obligatory is that he write according to what Allah has taught him, that he not neglect any of the conditions, and that he not insert any restriction that defeats the purpose of the person. This is because if he writes without observing these conditions, the person's purpose is defeated and his wealth is lost. So it is as if it were said to him: if you are going to write, then write it justly, taking into account all the conditions that Allah has prescribed.

**The second issue:** His saying "kamā ʿallamahu Allāh" (as Allah has taught him) has two possibilities. The first: that it is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: "let no scribe refuse writing that Allah has taught him, and it is not proper for him to write anything other than the writing that Allah has taught him." Then He said after that: "let him write that writing which Allah has taught him."

The second possibility: that it is connected to what follows it, and the meaning is: "let no scribe refuse to write," and here the sentence is complete. Then He said after it: "as Allah has taught him, let him write." The first then is a command to write in general, and then it is followed by a command to write that writing which Allah has taught him. Both possibilities were mentioned by al-Zajjāj.

* * *

**The second condition regarding the writing:** His saying: ﴿And let the one who owes the debt dictate﴾. On this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** Although the writing must be entrusted to one who knows how to write conditions and registers, this cannot be completed without the dictation of the one who owes the debt. So he must include in his dictation his acknowledgement of what he owes, its amount, its kind, its attributes, its term, and so on. For this reason He said: ﴿And let the one who owes the debt dictate﴾.

**The second issue:** "al-imlāl" and "al-imlāʾ" are two dialectal forms. al-Farrāʾ said: "amlaltu ʿalayhi al-kitāb" is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz and Banū Asad, and "amlaytu" is the dialect of Tamīm and Qays. The Qur'an was revealed in both dialects. He said, in the second dialect: ﴿and it is dictated to him morning and evening﴾ [Al-Furqān: 5].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not diminish anything from it﴾. This is a command to this dictator who owes the debt, that he acknowledge the amount of wealth that he owes and not diminish any of it.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But if the one who owes the debt is feeble-minded, or weak, or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate justly﴾. The meaning is that whoever owes a debt, if his acknowledgement is not valid, then the valid acknowledgement is that of his guardian.

Then in the verse there are issues:

**The first issue:** The insertion of the particle "aw" (or) between these three terms, namely the feeble-minded (safīh), the weak (ḍaʿīf), and the one unable to dictate (man lā yastaṭīʿu an yumilla), requires that they be distinct categories. Its meaning is that if the one who owes the debt is characterized by one of these three attributes, then his guardian must dictate justly. Thus the three must be distinct. Given this, the safīh must be understood as one of weak judgement and deficient intellect among the adults, and the ḍaʿīf as a child, a madman, or a senile old man, that is, those who have wholly lost reason. And the one who cannot dictate is one whose tongue is too weak for dictation due to muteness, or due to his ignorance of his property and what he owes. All of these cannot validly dictate or acknowledge, so someone else must stand in their place. Hence He said: ﴿then let his guardian dictate justly﴾. The intended meaning is the guardian of each of these three, because the guardian of the one under restraint who is feeble-minded, and the guardian of the child, is the one who acknowledges the debt on his behalf, just as he acknowledges his other affairs. This is the correct view. Ibn ʿAbbās, Muqātil, and al-Rabīʿ said: the intended meaning of "his guardian" is the guardian of the debt, meaning that the creditor dictates. But this is far-fetched, because how could the claim of the claimant be accepted, even if his statement is valid? Then what need would there be for writing and witnessing?

* * *

**The second kind of matter that Allah prescribed in the debt contract:** witnessing, which is His saying: ﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾. Know that the purpose of writing is witnessing, so that when there is denial, the witnesses enable one to attain the recovery of the right. In the verse there are issues.

**The first issue:** "istashhidū" means "ashhidū" (call to witness). It is said: "ashhadtu al-rajul" and "istashhadtuhu" with the same meaning. And "al-shahīdān" means "al-shāhidān" (the two witnesses), with "faʿīl" in the sense of "fāʿil."

**The second issue:** The genitive construction in His saying "min rijālikum" (from among your men) has several aspects:

First: that is, from among the people of your religion, who are the Muslims.

Second: some said: that is, the free.

Third: "from among your men" means those whom you consider fit to testify because of their justice.

**The third issue:** The conditions of testimony are numerous and mentioned in the books of jurisprudence. Here we mention one issue only: according to Shurayḥ, Ibn Sīrīn, and Aḥmad, the testimony of a slave is permissible, while according to al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah be pleased with them both) it is not permissible. The argument of Shurayḥ is that His saying: ﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾ is general, encompassing slaves and others. The meaning drawn from the text also indicates this, because a person's intellect, religion, and justice prevent him from lying. When he testifies with these conditions combined, his claim is strengthened, and that becomes a cause for the reviving of his right. Intellect, religion, and justice do not differ due to freedom or slavery, so the testimony of slaves must be accepted. The argument of al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah be pleased with them both) is His saying: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are summoned﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 282]. This requires that every person who is a witness must go to the place where testimony is given, and it is forbidden for him not to go to give testimony. Since the verse indicates that every witness is obligated to go, and consensus indicates that a slave is not obligated to go, it follows that a slave is not a witness. This argument is sound.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾, we have shown that some said: "call upon two witnesses from among your men whom you consider fit to give testimony." On this reading, why do you say that slaves are likewise?

* * *

Then He said: ﴿But if there are not two men, then a man and two women﴾. In the nominative of "a man and two women" there are four possibilities: first, "let there be a man and two women"; second, "let a man and two women testify"; third, "the witness is a man and two women"; fourth, "a man and two women who testify." All these estimates are permissible and sound. ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned them.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿of those whom you accept as witnesses﴾. This is like His saying concerning divorce: ﴿and call to witness two just persons from among you﴾ [Al-Ṭalāq: 2]. Know that this verse indicates that not everyone is fit for testimony. The jurists said: the conditions for the acceptance of testimony are ten: that he be free, adult, Muslim, just, knowing of what he testifies to, that he not draw benefit to himself through that testimony nor ward off harm from himself by it, that he not be known for frequent error, nor for abandoning manliness (murūwah), and that there be no enmity between him and the person against whom he testifies.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other may remind her﴾. The meaning is that forgetfulness is the predominant trait of women's natures, because of the abundance of coldness and moisture in their temperaments. And for two women to both be forgetful is less likely, by reason, than forgetfulness occurring in a single woman. So the two women were placed in the position of one man, such that if one of them forgot, the other would remind her. This is the purpose of the verse. Then in it there are issues:

**[Page 100]**

**The first issue:** Hamzah read ﴿إن تضل﴾ with a kasra on *in*, and ﴿فتذكر﴾ with a *raf'* (nominative) and *tashdid* (doubling of the *dhal*). Its meaning is the conditional (*jaza'*, the apodosis). The position of ﴿تضل﴾ is jussive (*jazm*), but this is not visible because of the doubled letter. ﴿فتذكر﴾ is in the nominative because what follows the conditional is an independent subject (*mubtada'*). All the other readers (*qurra'*) read *an* in the accusative, and there are two possible explanations for this. The first is that the original was *li-an tadilla*, "so that she should err," with the preposition deleted. The second is that it is the object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), meaning "out of the desire that she should err."

If it is asked: how can this statement be valid when the purpose of the testimony is to cause remembrance, not to cause error?

We say: there are two aims here. The first is that the testimony is established, and this cannot happen except by reminding the second of the two women. The second is to show the superiority of the man over the woman, so that it becomes clear that placing two women in the position of one man is the justice in this matter. This cannot happen except through the error of one of the two women. Since each of these two matters, namely the establishment of testimony and the demonstration of the man's superiority over the woman, is intended, and there is no way to achieve them except through the error of one of them and the reminder of the other, these two matters are necessarily sought. This is what came to my mind as the answer to this question at the time of writing this section. The grammarians have other answers which I did not find satisfactory, and the books contain them. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** The "error" in His saying ﴿أن تضل إحداهما﴾ has two possible meanings. The first is that it means forgetting, as He says: ﴿وضل عنهم ما كانوا يفترون﴾ (Al-Nahl 16:87), meaning "what they used to invent went away from them." The second is that it derives from "one strays on the road" when one does not find the way. The two meanings are close. Abu 'Amr said: the root meaning of *dalal* (error) in the language is concealment (*al-ghaybubah*).

**The third issue:** Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read ﴿فتذكر﴾ with doubling and the accusative. Hamzah read it with doubling and the nominative. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it without doubling and with the accusative. Both *dhakkara* and *adhkara* are dialectal forms, like *nazzala* and *anzala*, and the doubled form is more commonly used. He says: ﴿فذكر إنما أنت مذكر﴾ (Al-Ghashiyah 88:21). Whoever reads without doubling has made the verb transitive through the *hamzah* of causation.

Most commentators hold that this reminding and causing to remember is from forgetting. An exception is what is reported from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, who said about His saying ﴿فتذكر إحداهما الأخرى﴾ that it means that you make her a male (*dhakar*), meaning that the combined testimony of the two women is like the testimony of one man. This view is also reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', who said: "If a woman testifies, and then the other comes and testifies with her, she makes her a male, because the two of them stand in the position of one man." This view is invalid by the agreement of the commentators in general. Two points show its weakness.

The first is that if women, however many they were, were not accompanied by a man, their testimony would not be valid. Given that this is the case, the second woman has not made the first male.

The second is that His saying ﴿فتذكر﴾ corresponds to what precedes it, His saying ﴿أن تضل إحداهما﴾. Since the error was explained as forgetting, the reminding must be explained as what is opposed to forgetting.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿ولا يأب الشهداء إذا ما دعوا﴾ and in this there are issues.

**The first issue:** In this verse there are several views.

The first, which is the most correct, is that He forbade the witness from refusing to give testimony when the rightful owner needs it.

The second is that what is meant is bearing testimony in general. This is the view of Qatadah and the choice of al-Qaffal, who said: just as He commanded the scribe not to refuse to write, so He commanded the witness not to refuse to bear testimony, because each of the two depends on the other, and without both there is loss of rights.

The third is that what is meant is bearing testimony when no one else is available.

The fourth, which is the view of al-Zajjaj, is that what is meant by the combination of the two matters is bearing testimony first and giving it afterward.

Those who held the first view argued from several points.

The first is that His saying ﴿ولا يأب الشهداء إذا ما دعوا﴾ requires that they be already witnesses, and this cannot be true except at the time of giving testimony. As for the time of bearing testimony, they were not yet witnesses before that time.

If it is said: this is problematic in light of His saying ﴿واستشهدوا شهيدين من رجالكم﴾, and likewise He called the scribe a scribe before he had written.

We say: the argument we mentioned has become abandoned by necessity in this verse, so we may not abandon it because of a necessity in that verse.

The second is that the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿ولا يأب الشهداء إذا ما دعوا﴾ is a prohibition against refusing and a command to act. This is obligatory for everyone. It is known that bearing testimony is not obligatory on everyone, so it is not permissible to interpret it that way. As for giving testimony after bearing it, this is obligatory on everyone and is emphasized by His saying: ﴿ولا تكتموا الشهادة﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:283), so this is more appropriate.

The third is that the command to call for witnesses implies the command to the witness to bear testimony in some respects. So the command to bear testimony becomes included in His saying ﴿واستشهدوا شهيدين من رجالكم﴾. Therefore, directing His saying ﴿ولا يأب الشهداء إذا ما دعوا﴾ toward the command to give testimony, so that it has a new benefit, is better. It has thus become clear from what we have mentioned that the verse indicates that the witness must not refuse to establish testimony when he is called to it.

[Page 101]

Know that the witness is either specified, or there is a large number of them. If he is specified, it is obligatory for him to give testimony. If there is a large number of them, it becomes a collective obligation (*fard 'ala al-kifayah*).

**The second issue:** We have already explained the indication of this verse that a slave may not be a witness, so we will not repeat it.

**The third issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: judgment may be given on the basis of one witness and an oath. Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is not permissible. Abu Hanifah argued from this verse, saying: Allah, exalted is He, made obligatory, in the absence of the testimony of two men, the testimony of one man and two women, specifically. So if we permitted relying on one witness and an oath, that specification would be nullified. The argument of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is that the Prophet (ﷺ) judged by one witness and an oath. The full discussion of this is mentioned in the books of disputed jurisprudence (*khilafiyyat al-fiqh*).

* * *

Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded writing first in the case of a debt, and then commanded calling for witnesses second, He repeated this again by way of emphasis. So He commanded writing, saying: ﴿ولا تسأموا أن تكتبوه صغيرا أو كبيرا إلى أجله﴾ and in this there are issues.

**The first issue:** *al-sa'amah* means weariness and boredom. One says: *sa'imtu al-shay'* (I became weary of the thing), with the verbal noun *sa'aman* and *sa'amah*. The purpose of the verse is to urge writing, whether the amount of money is small or large, because even a small amount of money, in such precaution, is like a large amount, since disputes arising from a small amount of money may lead to great corruption and severe obstinacy. So He, exalted is He, commanded writing for both large and small amounts, saying ﴿ولا تسأموا﴾, meaning, "Do not become weary, so that you abandon it and then regret it."

If it is asked: does the grain or the carat fall under this command?

We say: no, because this is understood in terms of custom, and it is not the custom to write down trivial amounts.

**The second issue:** *an* is in the accusative position for two reasons. If you wish, you may make it, together with the verb, a verbal noun, so the sense is "do not become weary of its writing." If you wish, you may take it with the removal of the preposition, so the sense is "do not become weary of writing it down until its term."

**The third issue:** The pronoun in His saying ﴿أن تكتبوه﴾ must refer to what was mentioned previously, and here it is either the debt or the right.

**The fourth issue:** It has been read as ﴿ولا يسأموا أن يكتبوه﴾ with the *ya'* in both places.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿ذلكم أقسط عند الله وأقوم للشهادة وأدنى ألا ترتابوا﴾ Know that Allah, exalted is He, explained that writing includes these three benefits.

The first benefit is His saying ﴿ذلكم أقسط عند الله﴾. In His saying *dhalikum* there are two possibilities. The first is that it refers to His saying ﴿أن تكتبوه﴾, because it has the sense of a verbal noun, meaning "that writing is more just." The second: al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "That which I commanded you with, of writing and calling for witnesses, is for the sake of those who are satisfied (with it)." The meaning of ﴿أقسط عند الله﴾ is "more just in the sight of Allah." *al-qist* is a noun, and *al-iqsat* is a verbal noun. One says *aqsata fulan fi al-hukm yuqsitu iqsatan* when he acts justly, so he is *muqsit*. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿إن الله يحب المقسطين﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:42). One also says he is *qasit* when he acts unjustly. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿وأما القاسطون فكانوا لجهنم حطبا﴾ (Al-Jinn 72:15). This was more just in the sight of Allah because when it is written, it is closer to certainty and truthfulness, and farther from ignorance and lying, so it is more just in the sight of Allah. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ادعوهم لآبائهم هو أقسط عند الله﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:5), meaning "more just in the sight of Allah, and closer to the truth than that you attribute them to other than their fathers."

[Page 102]

The second benefit is His saying ﴿وأقوم للشهادة﴾. The meaning of *aqwam* is more emphatic in uprightness, which is the opposite of crookedness, because the one who stands erect is the opposite of the bent and crooked.

If it is asked: from what is the superlative *af'al* formed, namely *aqsat* and *aqwam*?

We say: according to the view of Sibawayh, both may be formed from *aqsata* and *aqama*. It is also possible that *aqsat* is formed from *qasit*, and *aqwam* from *qawim*.

Know that writing was more upright for testimony because it is a cause of preservation and remembrance, so it was closer to uprightness. The difference between the first and second benefits is that the first relates to attaining the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, while the second relates to attaining the worldly benefit. The first was placed before the second to indicate that religion must be given precedence over the world.

The third benefit is His saying ﴿وأدنى ألا ترتابوا﴾, meaning it is closer to removing doubt and suspicion from the hearts of the contracting parties. The difference between the first two benefits and this third one is that the first two point to the attainment of benefit: the first refers to attaining the benefit of religion, and the second refers to attaining the benefit of this world. This third refers to averting harm from oneself and from others. As for averting harm from oneself, it is because no doubt remains in the mind about how the matter was, or whether what was said was true or false. As for averting harm from others, it is because that other person may attribute lying or negligence to him, and he would then fall into the punishment of backbiting and slander. How excellent these benefits are, and how well they fit justice, and how excellent the order among them.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿إلا أن تكون تجارة حاضرة تديرونها بينكم﴾ and in this there are issues.

**The first issue:** The word *illa* (except) here has two possibilities. One is that it is a contiguous exception (*istithna' muttasil*), and the other is that it is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*). As for the first, there are two possibilities. The first is that it refers back to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إذا تداينتم بدين إلى أجل مسمى فاكتبوه﴾ ("When you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down"). This is because a sale on credit may be for a near term or a distant term. Since He commanded writing at the time of incurring debt, He excepted from this the case where the term is near, and the sense is: "When you incur a debt for a specified term, write it down, except if the term is near," and this is what is meant by "present commerce." The second is that this is an exception from His saying ﴿ولا يأب كاتب أن يكتب كما علمه﴾ ("Let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him").

As for the second possibility, namely that this is a disconnected exception, the sense would be: "But when it is present commerce that you conduct among yourselves, there is no blame on you if you do not write it down." This is a new statement. Allah, exalted is He, permitted leaving writing and calling witnesses in this kind of commerce because of how frequently it takes place among people. If writing and calling witnesses were required for it, the matter would become difficult for people. Moreover, when each of the two parties to the dealing takes his right from the other at that meeting, there is no fear of denial, and so there is no need for writing or calling witnesses.

Second issue: as for His saying, "that it be" (an takūna), there are two views. The first is that it derives from kawn in the sense of occurring and taking place, as we mentioned in His saying, ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾. The second: al-Farrā' said, "If you wish, you may make kāna (was/be) here a defective verb (nāqisa), with the subject being 'a present trade' and the predicate 'you circulate it,' and the sense being: 'unless there is a present trade circulating among you.'"

Third issue: 'Āṣim read "tijāratan" (trade) in the accusative, while the rest read it in the nominative. As for the accusative reading, it is because it is the predicate of kāna, and the subject must necessarily be supplied. There are several interpretations of this:

First: the sense is, "unless the trade is a present trade, [i.e., involving] the writing of the document." From this is the saying of the poet:

Page 103

Banī Asad, do you know our trial,
when there was a day with bright stars, grey-white?

That is, when the day was (such).

Second: the sense is, "unless the matter and affair is a trade."

Third: al-Zajjāj said, "The sense is: unless the debt-transaction (mudāyana) is a present trade." Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī said, "This is not permissible, because a debt-transaction cannot be a present trade." It may be answered that when the debt-transaction is for a deferred term of an hour, it is valid to call it a present trade, for whoever sells a garment for a dirham owed, on condition that the dirham be paid within this hour, that is a debt-transaction and a present trade. As for the nominative reading, its justification is what we mentioned in the second issue. And God knows best.

Fourth issue: "Trade" (tijāra) is an expression for disposing of wealth, whether it is present or in the liability (dhimma), in seeking profit. It is said: tajara al-rajul yatjuru tijāratan, fa-huwa tājir. Know that whether the exchange is by credit or by a present item, it is a present trade. Thus His saying, ﴿unless it is a present trade﴾, cannot be taken in its apparent sense; rather, what is meant by trade is what is traded in of exchanges, and the meaning of "circulating it among you" is that you deal in it hand to hand. Then He said, ﴿there is no blame upon you that you not write it﴾, meaning: there is no harm upon you in leaving off writing. He did not intend sin upon you, for if He had intended sin, the writing mentioned would be obligatory upon them, and the creditor would sin by leaving it; but the opposite has been established, and the proof that there is no harm upon them in leaving it is what we have previously presented.

* * *

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿And take witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the meaning is that although writing is lifted from them in trade, witnessing is not lifted from them, because witnessing without writing is less burdensome, and because when the need arises for it, forgetfulness is not feared in it.

Know that there is no doubt that the purpose of this command is guidance toward the path of caution.

* * *

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿And let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾. Know that it is possible that this is a prohibition to the scribe and the witness against harming the one who holds the right: as for the scribe, by adding, subtracting, or abandoning caution; and as for the witness, by not testifying or testifying in a manner from which no benefit results. It is also possible that it is a prohibition to the one holding the right against harming the scribe and the witness, by harming them or preventing them from their duties. The first is the view of most exegetes, al-Ḥasan, Ṭāwūs and Qatāda; the second is the view of Ibn Mas'ūd, 'Aṭā' and Mujāhid.

Know that both views are permissible in the language, and the two possibilities arise because of the assimilation (idghām) occurring in "lā yuḍārr" (let not be harmed). One possibility: its original form is lā yuḍārir, with the first rā' kasra, so the scribe and the witness are the ones doing the harming. The second: its original form is lā yuḍārar, with the first rā' fatḥa, so they are the ones harmed. A parallel to this verse is the one that preceded in this sura: His saying, ﴿let no mother be harmed through her child﴾, and we have fully explained this wording there. The evidence for the two possibilities we mentioned is the reading of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, "wa-lā yuḍārir" with clear pronunciation and kasra, and the reading of Ibn 'Abbās, "wa-lā yuḍārar" with clear pronunciation and fatḥa. Al-Zajjāj preferred the first view, and argued for it with His saying, Exalted be He, after this: ﴿And if you do it, then it is an act of transgression in you﴾, saying: this is because the name of transgression (fisq) applies to one who distorts the writing and to one who refrains from testifying until he entirely nullifies the right, more fittingly than to one who harms the scribe and the witness. Also, He, Exalted, said concerning one who refrains from giving testimony, ﴿and whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], and "sinful" (āthim) and "transgressor" (fāsiq) are close in meaning. Those who supported the second view argued that if this were addressed to the scribe and the witness, it would have said: "and if you two do it, then it is an act of transgression in you." And since this is addressed to those who enter into debt-transactions, those prohibited from harm are them. And God knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And if you do it, then it is an act of transgression in you﴾. There are two views on this. The first: it may be understood as specific to this place, and the meaning is: if you do what I have forbidden you of harm. The second: it is general over all obligations, and the meaning is: if you do something of what I have forbidden you, or leave something of what I have commanded you, then it is an act of transgression in you, that is, a departure from God's command and obedience to Him.

* * *

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿And fear God﴾, meaning in what He has warned against here, which is harm; or it may be general, and the meaning is: fear God in all His commands and prohibitions.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And God teaches you﴾. The meaning: He teaches you what is guidance and caution in worldly matters, just as He teaches you what is guidance in religious matters. ﴿And God is Knowing of all things﴾ is an indication that He, glorified and exalted, is knowing of all the interests of this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 283:

[Allah the Exalted says]: ﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken in hand. But if one of you trusts another, let the one who is trusted fulfil his trust and let him fear Allah, his Lord. And do not conceal testimony, for whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

Know that He, the Exalted, in this verse divided transactions (bi'a, pl. bi'at) into three categories: a transaction with a written document and witnesses, a transaction with a pledge taken in hand, and a transaction of trust (bay' al-amanah). When He had commanded, at the end of the preceding verse, writing and calling witnesses, and you should know that this may be impossible on a journey, either because no scribe is found or because, though one is found, the writing instruments are not available, He mentioned another kind of securing a right, namely taking a pledge (rahn). This is the connection of the verse's arrangement. This is more emphatic in precaution than writing and witnesses. Then, in the verse, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** We have mentioned the derivation of the word safar (journey) in His words: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then [he should fast] an equal number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], and we repeat it here. The lexicographers said: the root of these letters denotes manifestation and disclosure. So safar is "the book" (al-kitab), because it makes a thing clear and plain. The journey was named safar because it unveils the characters of men, i.e., it reveals them. Or because when one leaves the shelter (kinn) for the open desert, one is exposed to people. Or because when one goes out into the desert, the home's ground becomes uncovered and empty. One says asfara al-subh (the dawn became bright) when it appears, asfarat al-mar'ah 'an wajhiha (the woman unveiled her face), meaning she uncovered it. Safartu 'an al-qawm usfiru sifarah when you uncover what is in their hearts. Safartu usfiru when you sweep, and al-safr is sweeping, because when you sweep you reveal what was under the dust. Al-safr also means the leaves that the wind carries away. The remaining whiteness of the day after sunset is called safar for its clarity. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The second issue:** The original meaning of rahn (pledge) is from permanence. One says rahana al-shay' when it lasts and remains firm, and ni'mah rahinah means a lasting, enduring blessing.

Once you know the original meaning, we say: the root of rahn is a verbal noun (masdar). One says rahantu 'inda al-rajul arhanuhu rahnan when you place (a thing) with him as a pledge. The poet said:

*He stakes me, and I stake him with his sons, and I stake him with my sons over what I say.*

Knowing this, we say: verbal nouns may be transferred and made into nouns, and the action of the verb departs from them. So when one says rahantu 'inda Zaid rahnan, its accusative case is not that of a verbal noun but that of the direct object, as when you say rahantu 'inda Zaid thawban (I pledged a garment with Zaid). Since it was made a noun in this way, it takes plurals as nouns do. It has two plurals: ruhun and rihan. Among what came on the pattern ruhun is the saying of al-A'sha:

*I swore I would not give him from our sons a pledge, so that he corrupts them, like one who has corrupted (them).*

And Bu'ayth said:

*Su'ad has departed, and 'Adan has become beyond her, and before you the pledges were closed to her.*

Its parallel is our saying: rahn and ruhun, saqf and suqaf, nashr and nushur, khalq and khuluq. Al-Zajjaj said: fa'l and fu'ul is rare. Al-Farra' claimed that the plural of rahn is rihan, and then the plural of rihan is ruhun, so ruhun is a plural of a plural, like their saying thimar and thumur. Some people reversed this and said: ruhun is the plural of rahn, and rahn is the plural of rihan. Know that when these two conflict, they cancel each other out, especially since Sibawayh does not regard the plural of a plural as regular, so it must not be asserted except where there is agreement. As for rihan being the plural of rahn, it is a plain analogy, like na'l and ni'al, kabsh and kibash, ka'b and ki'ab, kalb and kilab.

**The third issue:** Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (fa-rud̲ubun) with a damma on the ra' and the ha', and it was also transmitted from them (fa-ruhnun) with a raising of the ra' and sukun on the ha'. The rest read (fa-rihan). Abu 'Amr said: I do not know rihan except for horses, so I read (furuhun) to distinguish between rihan for horses and the plural of rahn. As for Abu 'Amr's reading with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the ha', al-Akhfash said it is ugly, because fa'l is not pluralized as fu'ul except rarely and irregularly, as one says suqf and suqf sometimes with a damma on the qaf and sometimes with sukun, and qulb and qulub for palm trees, and luhd and luhud, busut and busut, and furs and wurd, and khayl and wurud (horses).

**The fourth issue:** There is an ellipsis in the verse. If we wish, we make it a subject (mubtada') and supply the predicate, and the implied sense is: then a pledge taken in hand is in place of the two witnesses or what stands in their place, or upon him is a pledge taken in hand. And if we wish, we make it a predicate and supply the subject, and the implied sense is: so the securing is a pledge taken in hand.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** The jurists today agree that the pledge is valid on a journey and at home alike, whether or not a scribe is present. Mujahid held that the pledge is permissible only on a journey, taking the apparent wording of the verse. His view is not acted upon today. The verse was restricted by mention of the journey as a matter of what is usual, as in His words: ﴿There is no fault upon you if you shorten the prayer, if you fear﴾ [al-Nisa': 101], and fear is not a condition for the permissibility of shortening.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** The rulings on pledges are numerous. Those who argued that pledging an undivided share (musha') is not permissible said: the verse indicates that the pledge must be taken in hand, and reason also indicates it, because the purpose of the pledge is securing the side of the creditor by preventing denial, and that is not achieved except by taking possession, and an undivided share cannot be taken in hand, so the pledge of an undivided share must not be valid.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿But if one of you trusts another, let the one who is trusted fulfil his trust.﴾ Know that this is the third category of the transactions mentioned in the verse, namely the transaction of trust, meaning that in which there is neither writing nor witnesses nor pledge. It has several issues:

**The first issue:** Fulan amina ghayrah means he was not afraid of him. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother?﴾ [Yusuf: 64]. So His words ﴿But if one of you trusts another﴾ mean: does not fear his betrayal or denial. ﴿Let the one who is trusted fulfil his trust﴾ means: let the debtor, who was trustworthy and entrusted in the creditor's opinion, not disappoint his opinion in discharging his trust and his right owed to him. One says amintuhu and ta'mantuhu, so he is ma'mun and mu'taman.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord.﴾ That is, this debtor must fear Allah and not deny (the debt). Because the creditor treated him kindly, in that he relied on his trustworthiness and did not demand from him the securities of writing, witnessing, or pledge, it is fitting for this debtor to fear Allah and deal with him kindly, by not denying that right, and by paying it to him when the term falls due. There is another view regarding the verse: that it is addressed to the pledgee (murtahin), that he must return the pledge when he collects the money, for it is a trust in his hand. The first view is the correct one.

**The second issue:** Some people said: this verse abrogates (naskh) the preceding verses that indicate the obligation of writing, witnessing, and taking a pledge. Know that claiming the occurrence of abrogation without evidence compelling it is an error. Rather, those commands are understood as guidance and as taking precaution, and this verse is understood as a concession. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: there is no abrogation in the verse of debt. Then He said: ﴿And do not conceal testimony.﴾ On its interpretation there are several views:

**The first view:** Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: when He permitted abandoning writing, witnessing, and the pledge upon the belief that the debtor is trustworthy, it was possible that this debtor might disappoint that opinion and turn out to be a treacherous one who denies the right. Yet it is possible that some people are aware of their circumstances. Here Allah urged that person to strive to revive that right and to testify on behalf of the rightful owner to his right, and forbade him from concealing that testimony, whether or not the rightful owner knew of that testimony, and He emphasized it by making him sinful in heart if he left it. There is a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that supports this interpretation, namely his saying: "The best of witnesses is the one who testifies before he is asked to testify."

**The second view:** Concealment of testimony may mean denying knowledge of that event. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes were Jews or Christians? Say: Are you more knowing or is Allah? And who is more unjust?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140]. The intended meaning there is denial and rejection of knowledge.

**The third view:** Concealment of testimony means withholding it and refusing to discharge it when there is need to establish it. This has already been mentioned in His words: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. Because whenever he refrains from establishing testimony, his right is nullified, and by refusing to testify he becomes like one who nullifies his own right. The sanctity of a Muslim's property is like the sanctity of his blood. So this is severe in threat.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful.﴾ On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *Al-athim* means the wicked sinner. It is related that 'Umar was teaching a Bedouin ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ ﴿is the food of the sinner﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43-44], and he was saying: "the food of the orphan (yatim)." 'Umar said to him: "the food of the wicked one (fajir)." This shows that *ithm* means wickedness.

**The second issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *athimun* is the predicate of *inna*, and *qalbuhu* is in the nominative by *athimun* as the agent, as if it were said: "indeed he sins, his heart." It is read *qalbahu* with a fatha, like His words: ﴿He has made a fool of himself﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130]. Ibn Abi 'Abla read (athtama qalbahu), meaning he made it sinful.

**The third issue:** Know that many of the theologians (mutakallimun) said: the doer, the knower, the one commanded, and the one forbidden is the heart. We have fully investigated this question in the commentary on surah al-Shu'ara', in His words: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193-194], and we mentioned part of it in the commentary on His words: ﴿Say: whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, indeed he has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]. These people hold fast to this verse and say: He attributed sinfulness to the heart, so if the heart were not the agent, it would not be sinful.

Those who disagreed with this view replied that attributing an act to a part of the body occurs because the greatest means of assistance toward that act arises from that organ. One says: "This is what my eye saw, my ear heard, and my heart knew," and one says: "So-and-so has a corrupt private part." It is well known that the actions of the limbs follow the actions of the hearts and arise from the motives and deterrents occurring in the hearts. Since this is so, for this reason the sinfulness is attributed here to the heart.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾ This is a warning against proceeding to conceal. For the responsible person, when he knows that nothing in the inward thought of his heart escapes the knowledge of Allah, he is fearful and cautious of opposing the command of Allah, the Exalted, for he knows that He will hold him accountable for all those actions and will repay him for them: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

[Page 108]

**The statement of God, Exalted is He: ﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and God is over all things competent.﴾**

**There are several issues concerning this verse.**

**The first issue: concerning the manner of the arrangement (nazm) of the verse, there are several aspects.**

**The first:** al-Asamm said: When God, in this surah, gathered many matters of the foundations of the religion (ʿilm al-usul), which is the proof of tawhid (the oneness of God) and prophethood, and many matters of the rulings of the sacred law (al-shara'i') and obligations (al-takalif), namely prayer, zakat, retaliation (al-qisas), fasting, pilgrimage, jihad, menstruation, divorce, the waiting period (ʿiddah), dowry, khul' (divorce initiated by the wife), ila' (a husband's oath to abstain from intercourse), breastfeeding, sale, usury (riba), and the manner of contracting debts, God concluded this surah with this verse by way of warning.

I say: It has been established that the attributes which are genuine perfections are nothing other than power (qudrah) and knowledge (ʿilm). Thus He, glory be to Him, expressed the perfection of power by His saying ﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, in both sovereignty (mulkan) and ownership (milkan). And He expressed the perfection of all-encompassing knowledge of universals and particulars by His saying ﴿And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it﴾. When the perfection of power and knowledge is established, and everyone in the heavens and the earth is a servant and a created being who came into existence by His creation and formation, this constitutes the ultimate promise to the obedient and the final threat to the sinners. For this reason God concluded this surah with this verse.

**The second aspect concerning the arrangement:** Abu Muslim said: When God said at the end of the preceding verse ﴿And God knows what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], He followed it with something that works as a rational proof, saying ﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The meaning of this ownership is that these things, since they are originated, came into existence by His creation, formation, and origination. Whoever is the agent of these precisely wrought, perfected, wondrous and strange acts, which contain many wisdoms and great benefits, must necessarily have knowledge of them, for it is impossible that a precise and perfected act proceed from one who is ignorant of it. Thus God argued, through His creating the heavens and the earth together with the aspects of their precision and perfection, that He knows them and encompasses their parts and particulars.

**The third aspect concerning the arrangement:** al-Qadi said: When God commanded these documentary measures, namely writing, calling witnesses, and pledging collateral, and the purpose of commanding them was the safeguarding of wealth and caution in preserving it, God made clear that the purpose is a benefit that returns to the creatures, not a benefit that returns to Him, glory be to Him, for to Him belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth.

**The fourth aspect:** al-Shaʿbi, ʿIkrimah and Mujahid said: When God forbade concealing testimony and threatened for it, He made clear that to Him belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth, so He will requite both concealing and disclosing.

* * *

**The second issue:** The companions (al-Ashab, i.e., the Ashʿari theologians) argued from His saying ﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ that the act of the servant is the creation of God, Exalted is He, because it is among what is in the heavens and the earth, as evidenced by the validity of the exception.
