The lam in His saying "for God" (li-llah) is not the lam of purpose (lam al-gharad), since the purpose of the wrongdoer in his wickedness is not obedience to God. Therefore the intended meaning must be the lam of ownership and creation.

* * *

**The third issue:** The companions argued from this verse that the non-existent is not a thing, because among what is in the heavens and the earth are the realities of things (haqaʾiq al-ashya') and their quiddities (mahiyyat). These must necessarily be under the power of God, glory be to Him and exalted. The realities and quiddities could only be under His power if He were capable of actualizing those realities and bringing those quiddities into being. If that is the case, then the power of God is what creates the essences and actualizes the realities. Therefore the claim that the non-existent is a thing is false.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it﴾. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: When this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, Muʿadh and some people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, we have been charged with deeds we cannot bear. One of us speaks to himself about things he does not wish to take root in his heart, and he has the world (i.e., the worldly things of life)." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Perhaps you are saying what the Children of Israel said: 'We hear and we disobey.' Say: 'We hear and we obey.'" They said: "We hear and we obey." This weighed heavily upon them, and they remained in that state for a year. Then God revealed ﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], which abrogated (nasakha) this verse. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: "God has overlooked for my community what they speak to themselves about, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it."

Know that the point of inquiry in this verse is that His saying ﴿And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it﴾ seems to encompass the inner talk of the soul (hadith al-nafs) and the corrupt thoughts that come to the heart, which one cannot repel, so holding one accountable for them would be like imposing what cannot be borne. The scholars answered this from several aspects:

**The first aspect:** The thoughts arising in the heart are of two kinds. Some are those which a person prepares himself for and resolves to bring into existence. Others are not like that, but are matters that pass through the mind although the person dislikes them, and he cannot drive them away from the soul. The first kind is one for which he is held accountable. The second is not one for which he is held accountable. Do you not see His saying: ﴿God will not hold you accountable for the slips in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 225]? And He said at the end of this surah ﴿It has what it earned and it bears what it has merited﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, those who love that immorality should spread among those who believe﴾ [al-Nur: 19]. This is the relied-upon answer.

**The second aspect:** Whatever is in the heart that does not enter into action falls under the category of pardon. His saying ﴿And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it﴾ means that He brings that action into existence, either openly or secretly. As for what exists in the heart of resolutions and intentions that have not been connected to action, all of that falls under pardon. This answer is weak, because most accountabilities concern actions of the heart. Do you not see that holding the beliefs of disbelief and innovation is nothing but an action of the heart, and the greatest kinds of punishment are consequent upon it? Also, bodily actions, when devoid of actions of the heart, do not entail punishment, like the actions of the sleeper and the heedless. Thus the weakness of this answer is established.

**The third aspect of the answer:** God will hold him accountable for them, but the accountability for them is the sorrows and worries of this world. Al-Dahhak reported from ʿAisha, may God be pleased with her, that she said: "Whatever evil a servant speaks to himself about, God's reckoning for it is a grief with which He tests him in this world, or sorrow, or harm. When the Hereafter comes, he will not be questioned about it nor punished for it." And she related that she asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this verse, and he answered her with something of this meaning.

If it is said: How can accountability occur in this world, given His saying ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17]?

We say: That is specific, and the specific takes precedence over that general.

**The fourth aspect of the answer:** He said ﴿God will call you to account for it﴾ and did not say "God will hold you accountable for it." We have mentioned in the meaning of His being Ḥasib (the Reckoner) and Muḥasib (the one who calls to account) many aspects, and we have mentioned that among the interpretations of it is that He, exalted, knows them. Thus the meaning of this verse returns to His being knowing of everything in the inner thoughts and secret places. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, that he said: "When God gathers the creatures, He will inform them of what was in their souls. The believer will be informed of it and then He will pardon him, while the people of sins He will inform of what they concealed of denial and sin."

**The fifth aspect of the answer:** After this verse He said ﴿Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾. So forgiveness is the portion of one who was averse to the arrival of those thoughts, and punishment is the portion of one who persists in those thoughts and takes pleasure in them.

**The sixth aspect:** Some said: The intended meaning of this verse is the concealing of testimony. This is weak, because the wording is general, and even if it was revealed following that particular case, it does not require restricting it to that.

**The seventh aspect of the answer:** What we have related from some of the exegetes, that this verse was abrogated by His saying ﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. This too is weak, for several reasons:

The first: This abrogation would only be valid if we said that they were, before this abrogation, commanded to guard against those thoughts which they were unable to repel. But that is false, because obligation has never been imposed except within what is within one's capacity. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "I was sent with the easy, tolerant monotheism (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah)."

The second: Abrogation is only needed if the verse indicated that punishment would result from those thoughts, and we have already shown that the verse does not indicate that.

The third: The abrogation of a report (khabar) is not permissible; what is permissible is the abrogation of commands and prohibitions.

Know that people differ over whether a report can be abrogated or not, and we have discussed this in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). And God knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** The companions (the Ashʿaris) have argued from this verse that it is permissible for God to forgive the sins of the major sinners. This is because the obedient believer is certainly rewarded and not punished, and the disbeliever is certainly punished and not rewarded. His saying ﴿Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ removes the certainty of either of the two matters. Thus nothing remains except that this is a portion of the believer, which the sinner inherits through his deeds.

**The second issue:** ʿAsim and Ibn ʿAmir read (fa-yaghfiru, wa-yuʿadhdhibu) with a raised (rafʿ) ra' and ba', while the rest read them in the jussive (jazm). The raised form is on the basis of a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf), the meaning being: "so He forgives." The jussive form is by coordination (ʿatf) with "He will call you to account" (yuḥāsibkum). It is transmitted from Abu ʿAmr that he assimilated the ra' into the lam in His saying "He forgives whom He wills" (yaghfiru li-man yashaʾ). The author of al-Kashshaf said: This is a grammatical error (lahn), and attributing it to Abu ʿAmr is a lie, for how could such an error befit one of the most learned of people in Arabic?

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾. He has made clear by His saying ﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ that He possesses complete dominion and sovereignty (al-mulk wal-malakut). He has made clear by His saying ﴿And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it﴾ that He possesses complete knowledge and encompassment. Then He made clear by His saying ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾ that He possesses complete power, prevailing over all possibilities (al-mumkinat) through subjugation, power, creation and annihilation. There is no higher or greater perfection than the attainment of perfection in these attributes. The one described by these perfections must, according to every rational person, be a servant submitting to Him, subject to His commands and prohibitions, guarding against His wrath and His prohibitions. And success is from God.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 285 (part 1 of 4):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. Each one believes in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers. "We make no distinction between any of His messengers." And they say: "We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return."﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The First Issue:** Regarding the manner of the arrangement (nazm, the composition and order of the verses), there are several aspects.

The first: When God, exalted is He, explained in the preceding verse the perfection of sovereignty, the perfection of knowledge, and the perfection of power belonging to God, and these require the perfection of the attributes of lordship (rububiyyah), He followed this by explaining that the believers are in the utmost state of submission, obedience, and humility before God, exalted is He, and that is the perfection of servanthood (ubudiyyah). When the perfection of lordship has become manifest to us, and the perfection of servanthood has appeared from us, then what is hoped for from His abundant grace and beneficence is that on the Day of Resurrection He will manifest toward us the perfection of care, mercy, and kindness. O God, make this hope come true.

The second aspect of the arrangement: When God said, ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it﴾, He explained that nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him of our secret or open affairs, our inward or outward. Then, after this, He mentioned what amounts to praise of us and commendation of us, saying: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. Each one...﴾ It is as though, by His grace, He is saying: "My servant, though I know all your conditions, I will not reveal from your conditions, nor mention from them, except what constitutes praise of you and commendation of you, until you know that just as I am perfect in sovereignty, knowledge, and power, I am also perfect in generosity and mercy, in displaying good deeds, and in veiling misdeeds."

The third aspect: He began the surah by praising the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer, and spend from what We have provided them. At the end of the surah He explained that those whom He praised at the beginning of the surah are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). So He said: ﴿And the believers, each one believes in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers. We make no distinction between any of His messengers.﴾ This is what is meant by His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3].

Then He said here: ﴿and they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾, which is what is meant by His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿and who establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3].

Then He said here: ﴿"Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return"﴾, which is what is meant by His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4]. Then He related here their manner of humble supplication to their Lord in their saying: ﴿"Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], to the end of the surah. This is what is meant by His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. So observe how the harmony between the beginning of the surah and its end has been achieved.

The fourth aspect: When an angel comes to the Messenger from God and says to him: "God has sent you as a messenger to creation," the Messenger here cannot know the truthfulness of that angel except by a miracle (mu'jizah) that God displays as confirmation of the truthfulness of that angel in his claim. Were it not for that miracle, the Messenger might suppose that the one informing him is a misguided, misleading devil. And that angel too, when he hears the speech of God, exalted is He, needs a miracle that indicates that what he heard is the speech of God and nothing else. These ranks are to be taken into account. The first of them: the presence of a miracle showing that what is heard is the speech of God and not another, so that through that miracle the angel knows that he has heard the speech of God, exalted is He. The second: the presence of a miracle with the Prophet (ﷺ) showing that this angel is truthful in his claim, and that he is an angel sent by God, exalted is He, and not a devil. The third: that a miracle be established at the hand of the Messenger in the sight of the community, so that the community may take it as evidence that the Messenger is truthful in his claim. Therefore, since the Messenger does not know that he is a messenger from God, the community cannot come to know that. When God, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah the kinds of laws and categories of rulings, He said: ﴿The Messenger believes﴾, and so He made clear that the Messenger knew that this was revelation from God, exalted is He, which had been conveyed to him, and that the one who informed him of it was an angel sent from God, exalted is He, protected from distortion, and not a misleading devil. Then He mentioned the Prophet's (ﷺ) belief in this, which is the earlier rank, and mentioned after it the belief of the believers in it, which is the later rank. So He said: ﴿And the believers, each one believes in God﴾.

Whoever reflects on the subtleties of the arrangement of this surah and the marvels of its ordering will know that the Qur'an is, just as it is miraculous in terms of the eloquence of its words and the nobility of its meanings, also miraculous in terms of its ordering and the arrangement of its verses. Perhaps those who said that it is miraculous in terms of its style meant this. However, I have seen that most of the exegetes turn away from these subtleties and are not attentive to these matters. The matter in this domain is not as someone has said:

*The star: the eyes consider its sight small,*
*yet the tail, for the glance, not the star, is small.*

We ask God, exalted is He, to benefit us through what He has taught us, and to teach us what will benefit us, by His grace and mercy.

\* \* \*

**The Second Issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers﴾. The meaning is that he knew, through compelling proofs and dazzling miracles, that this Qur'an and all that it contains of laws and rulings came down from God, exalted is He, and that it is not of the kind of the casting of devils, nor of the nature of sorcery, soothsaying, or trickery. The Messenger (ﷺ) knew this only through the compelling miracles that appeared at the hand of Jibril (peace be upon him).

As for His saying: (and the believers), there are two possibilities. The first: that the sentence is complete at His saying: (and the believers), so the meaning is: "The Messenger and the believers believe in what has been sent down to him from his Lord," and then He begins after that with His saying ﴿each one believes in God﴾, the meaning being: each one of those mentioned earlier, namely the Messenger and the believers, believes in God.

The second possibility: that the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿in what has been sent down to him from his Lord﴾, then it begins from His saying: ﴿and the believers, each one believes in God﴾, and the meaning is that the Messenger believed in all that was sent down to him from his Lord, while as for the believers, they believed in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers. The first aspect suggests that he, peace be upon him, was not a believer in his Lord and then became a believer in Him, and it is possible that he lacked belief at the time of reasoning. On the second aspect, the wording suggests that what came about was his belief in the laws that were sent down to him, as He said: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. As for belief in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers in general, it had been present since God created him at the very beginning. And how is that to be deemed unlikely, when Jesus (peace be upon him), when he emerged from his mother, said: "I am the servant of God; He has given me the Book" [Maryam: 30]? If it is not unlikely that Jesus (peace be upon him) was a messenger from God while he was still a child, how then is it deemed unlikely to say that Muhammad (ﷺ) was knowing of his Lord from the very beginning of his creation, with complete intellect?

\[Page 113\]

**The Third Issue:** The verse indicates that the Messenger believed in what was sent down to him from his Lord, and the believers believed in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers. The Messenger was singled out for this because what was sent down to him from his Lord may be a recited speech that others hear, know, and are able to believe in, and it may be a revelation that no one else knows. In that case he (ﷺ) is singled out in believing in it, and no one else can attain belief in it. For this reason the Messenger was singled out in the domain of belief in what cannot be attained by others.

\* \* \*

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the believers, each one believes in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

**The First Issue:** Know that this verse indicates that knowledge of these four ranks is among the necessities of faith.

The first rank: belief in God, glorified and exalted is He. This is because, unless it is established that the world has a Creator, able over all that can be done, knowing all that can be known, free of all needs, it is impossible to know the truthfulness of the prophets, peace be upon them. Thus knowledge of God, exalted is He, is the foundation, and for this reason God, exalted is He, mentioned this rank first.

The second rank: God, glorified and exalted is He, reveals to the prophets, peace be upon them, only through the angels. So He said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Nahl: 2]. He said: ﴿It is not for any human that God should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or that He send a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 51]. He said: ﴿Indeed, it is He who has sent it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]. He said: ﴿The trustworthy Spirit brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193-194]. He said: ﴿Taught him by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5]. Since it has been established that the revelation of God, exalted is He, reaches mankind only through the angels, the angels are like an intermediary between God, exalted is He, and mankind. For this reason He placed the mention of the angels in the second rank. And for this secret He also said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18].

The third rank: the books, which is the revelation that the angel receives from God, exalted is He, and conveys to mankind. This, by way of illustration, is like the illumination of the surface of the moon from the light of the sun. The essence of the angel is like the moon, and the essence of revelation is like the illumination of the moon. Just as the essence of the moon is prior in rank to its illumination, so too the essence of the angel is prior to the occurrence of that revelation which is expressed by these books. For this reason the books are later in rank than the angels, and so God, exalted is He, necessarily delayed the mention of the books after the mention of the angels.

The fourth rank: the messengers, who draw the lights of revelation from the angels, and so they are later in rank than the books. For this reason God, exalted is He, placed the mention of the messengers in the fourth rank. Know that in the arrangement of these four ranks in this manner there are profound secrets and great wisdoms, which it would not be fitting to deposit in books. The portion we have mentioned is sufficient for honor.

\* \* \*

**The Second Issue:** The meaning of belief in God is an expression for belief in His existence, His attributes, His actions, His rulings, and His names.

As for belief in His existence: it is that one knows that beyond the spatially-bounded things (al-mutahayyizat) there is an existent who created them. On this basis, the anthropomorphist (al-mujassim) is not one who affirms the existence of God, exalted is He, because he does not affirm anything beyond the spatially-bounded things, so his disagreement with us is over affirming the essence of God, exalted is He. As for the philosophers and the Mu'tazilah, they affirm an existent other than the spatially-bounded things that brings them into being, so the disagreement with them is not over the essence but over the attributes.

As for belief in His attributes: attributes are either negative (salbiyyah) or affirmative (thubutiyyah).

As for the negative attributes: it is that one knows that He is one, transcendent above all aspects of composition. For every composite is dependent on each of its parts, and each of its parts is other than it, so it is composite, and so it is dependent on something other than itself and possible in its essence. Therefore, every composite is possible in its essence. And whatever is not possible in its essence, but is necessary in its essence, is impossible for it to be composite in any respect, but rather it is absolutely one. And if it is one in its essence, it necessarily follows that it is not spatially-bounded, nor a body, nor a substance, nor in a place, nor inhering, nor in a substrate, nor changing, nor in need in any respect whatsoever.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 285 (part 2 of 4):

As for the positive attributes (*al-sifat al-thubutiyyah*), one should know that the Necessary Existent, who acts by His essence, stands in the same relation to some of the possible beings as He does to the rest. When we see that these created things have come into being in a manner that could have been otherwise, we know that their Originator is a Powerful Chooser (*qadir mukhtar*), not one who acts by essential necessity (*mujib bil-dhat*). Then one infers, from the wisdom and perfection in His acts, the perfection of His knowledge. At that point one recognizes Him as Powerful, Knowing, Living, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, described and characterized by majesty and the attributes of perfection. We have examined this thoroughly in our commentary on His words: ﴿Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence﴾ [2:255].

As for belief in His acts, it consists in knowing that everything other than Him is possible and originated. By the immediate judgment of your intellect, you know that a possible, originated thing does not exist by itself, but must have an originator who brings it into being, and that originator is the Eternal. This proof compels you to affirm that everything other than Him has come into being through His creating, bringing into existence and fashioning. However, there is a knot in between: the events, which are the voluntary acts of living beings. The first judgment, that these are possible and originated, requires that they too be ascribed to the Necessarily Existent, and this applies to them without exception.

If you say: "I find within myself that if I wish to move, I move, and if I wish not to move, I do not move. So my movements and stillnesses come from me, not from another."

We say: You have made your movement dependent on your will to move, and your stillness dependent on your will to be still. Before the will to move arises, you do not move; before the will to be still arises, you do not become still; and when the will to move arises, you necessarily move.

Having established this, we say: how did this will come into being? Its coming into being is either without any originator at all, or it has an originator. If that originator is the servant himself or Allah, the Exalted. If it came into being without an originator, then the denial of the Creator follows. If its originator is the servant, then bringing it into being would require another will, and this leads to an infinite regress (*tasalsul*). Thus it is established that its originator is Allah, glorified and exalted.

Having established this, we say: a human has no choice in the coming into being of that will. And after it has come into being, he has no choice regarding the act's following upon it, except through the will that accompanies it. The act does not come about after the will except by that will. So the human being is compelled in the form of one who chooses. This is a forceful and powerful argument. Yet in opposing it there are two difficulties. The first: how is it fitting, given the perfect wisdom of Allah, the Exalted, that He should bring into being these abominations and immoralities, such as disbelief and wickedness? The second: if everything is by His creation, how can commands and prohibitions, praise and blame, reward and punishment be directed at the servant? This is the crux on which the opponent relies. However, it also applies against them in the matter of knowledge, as we have established in several places.

As for the fourth rank in belief in Allah: it is knowledge of His rulings (*ahkam*). In regard to His rulings, one must know four things. The first: they are not caused by any cause at all, because whatever is caused by a cause has an essentially deficient possessor, complete only through another, and that is impossible for the Truth, glorified be He. The second: one must know that the purpose of their legislation is a benefit returning to the servant, not to the Truth, for He is exalted above seeking benefits or repelling harms. The third: one must know that He has the authority to impose obligation and judgment in this world as He wills and intends. The fourth: one must know that no one has any claim upon the Truth, by reason of his deeds and actions, to anything; that in the Hereafter He forgives whom He wills by His grace and punishes whom He wills by His justice; that nothing is unjust (*yuqabbah*) from Him, and nothing is obligatory upon Him, because everything belongs to Him and is under His dominion. A ruled servant has no right against the ruling master, so how much less the true servant against the true Master.

As for the fifth rank in belief in Allah: it is knowledge of His names. He says in al-A'raf: ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ [7:180]. He says in Bani Isra'il: ﴿Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [17:110]. He says in Ta-Ha: ﴿Allah — there is no deity except Him; to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [20:8]. He says at the end of al-Hashr: ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names; whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him﴾ [59:24]. The most beautiful names are the names mentioned in the books of Allah, revealed upon the tongues of His infallible prophets. This indicates the central points of belief in Allah.

As for belief in the angels, it has four aspects. The first: belief in their existence, and the investigation of whether they are purely spiritual, or corporeal, or composed of both. If they are corporeal, then they are either subtle or dense bodies. If they are subtle, then they are luminous or airy bodies. And if they are such, how can they, despite the subtlety of their bodies, be extremely powerful to the utmost degree? That is the station of the scholars firmly grounded in the sciences of Qur'anic and demonstrative wisdom.

The second rank in belief in the angels: knowledge that they are infallible and purified: ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and do what they are commanded﴾ [16:50]; ﴿They do not disdain His worship, nor do they tire﴾ [21:19]. Their delight is in the remembrance of Allah, and their intimacy is in worshipping Allah. Just as the life of each of us is by his breath, which is the inhaling of air, so their life is by the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, and by knowing Him and obeying Him.

The third rank: they are intermediaries between Allah and mankind. Each category of them is entrusted with a category of this world, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿By those ranged in ranks﴾ ﴿and those who drive with a driving﴾ [37:1, 2]; and He said: ﴿By those who scatter, scattering﴾ ﴿and those who carry a burden﴾ [51:1, 2]; and He said: ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾ ﴿and those that blow with violence﴾ [77:1, 2]; and He said: ﴿By those who drag forth with violence﴾ ﴿and those who glide with ease﴾ [79:1, 2]. We have mentioned in the commentary on these verses hidden secrets which, when those firmly grounded in knowledge examine them, they will comprehend.

The fourth rank: the revealed books of Allah reached the prophets only through the angels. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne, obeyed and trustworthy﴾ [81:19–21]. These ranks are necessary for attaining belief in the angels. Whenever the intellect delves more deeply into these ranks, its belief in the angels becomes more complete.

[p. 116]

As for belief in the books, four matters are necessary. The first: one must know that these books are revelation from Allah, the Exalted, to His messenger, and that they are not a matter of soothsaying, nor of sorcery, nor of the satanic and evil spirits' throwing (*ilqa' al-shayatin*). The second: one must know that although the revelation of these books came through the purified angels, Allah, the Exalted, did not enable any of the devils to insert anything of their misguidance into the midst of this pure revelation. At this point it is known that whoever says that Satan cast his words, "Those are the exalted cranes" (*tilka al-gharaniq al-ula*), into the midst of the revelation, has uttered a grave statement and has opened the way for accusation and suspicion against the Qur'an. The third rank: this Qur'an has not been altered or distorted. The corruption of the view of those who say that the arrangement of the Qur'an in this order was something done by Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, has entered into it, for whoever says that has removed the Qur'an from being a proof. The fourth rank: one must know that the Qur'an comprises the clear (*muhkam*) and the ambiguous (*mutashabih*), and that its clear verses elucidate its ambiguous ones.

As for belief in the messengers, four matters are necessary:

The first rank: one must know that they are preserved from sins. We have settled this question in our commentary on His words: ﴿Satan caused them to slip from it and removed them from that in which they had been﴾ [2:36]. And all the verses which those who oppose this view cling to, we have mentioned how they are to be interpreted in this commentary, by the help of Allah, glorified and exalted.

The second rank in belief in them: one must know that the prophet is more excellent than one who is not a prophet. Some Sufis dispute this matter.

The third rank: some have said that they (the prophets) are more excellent than the angels, while many scholars have said that the heavenly angels are more excellent than them, and they are more excellent than the earthly angels. We have mentioned this question in our commentary on His words: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ [2:34]. And the people of unveiling (*arbab al-mukashafat*) have subtle discussions on this question.

The fourth rank: one must know that some of them are more excellent than others. We have explained this in our commentary on His words, exalted be He: ﴿Those messengers — some of them We have preferred over others﴾ [2:253]. Some of them have denied this and have clung to His words in this verse: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾.

The scholars answered this by saying that the purpose of this statement is something else: that the path to establishing the prophethood of the prophets, peace be upon them, when they are present, is the manifestation of a miracle in accordance with their claims. If this is the path, then it is necessary that whoever has a miracle manifested in accordance with his claim must be truthful. And if this path is not valid, then it must not indicate the validity of the message of any of them. As for indicating the message of some but not others, that is a corrupt and self-contradictory view. The aim of this statement is to refute the method of the Jews and Christians, who acknowledge the prophethood of Moses and Jesus but deny the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. This is the intended meaning of His words: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾, not what you have mentioned, that it is not permissible for some of them to be more excellent than others. This is the indication of the fundamentals of belief in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers.

* * *

The third issue: Hamzah read (*wa-kitabihi*) in the singular, while the rest read (*kutubihi*) in the plural. As for the first, there are two aspects:

[p. 117]

One of them: the intended meaning is the Qur'an, and belief in it includes belief in all the books and messengers. The second: it is in the sense of a genus (*jins*), so it agrees with the meaning of the plural. Its parallel is His words: ﴿So Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth﴾ [2:213].

If it is said: a generic noun conveys generality only when it is preceded by the definite article (*al-*), and this one is in the construct state (*idafah*).

We reply: construct nouns have come to express plurality, as we mean by them multiplicity. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [14:34]. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿It has been made lawful for you the night of fasting to go to your wives﴾ [2:187], and this permissibility is common throughout all fasting. The scholars said: the reading in the plural is superior, for it matches the plural forms before and after it, and because most of the recitation is in that form.

Know that the readers agreed on the vowelling of (*wa-rusulihi*) with a *damma* on the sin, while according to Abu 'Amr it is with sukun, and according to Nafi' (*wa-kutbihi wa-rusbihi*) are read with light (*mukhaffafayn*) pronunciation. The argument of the majority is that the original form of the word is *fu'ul* with a *damma* on the middle letter. The argument of Abu 'Amr is that four consecutive moving letters should not occur, because they disliked that, and for this reason such successive vowels do not occur in poetry except in a deviated form (*muzahaf*). The first group answered that this is disliked within a single word, but not within two words, as evidenced by the fact that assimilation (*idgham*) is not obligatory in (*wa-ja'ala*), even though five moving letters occur there, and that when a pronoun is attached to a word, it is then two words, not one word.

The fourth issue: His words, ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾, contain an ellipsis. The estimated meaning is: they say, "We make no distinction between any of His messengers," like His words: ﴿And the angels extend their hands, [saying], "Bring forth your souls"﴾ [6:93], meaning they say, "Bring forth." And He said: ﴿And those who have taken protectors other than Him [say], "We worship them only that they may bring us nearer to Allah"﴾ [39:3], meaning they said this.

The fifth issue: Abu 'Amr read (*yufarriqu*) with the *ya'* , on the basis that the verb refers to each one. And 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read (*la yufarriquna*).

The Third Issue: "Ahad" is used in the sense of the plural, as in His saying: ﴿So there is none of you who could withhold Him from it⦘ [al-Haqqah: 47]. The implied meaning is: "We do not differentiate between all of His messengers." This is what they (the commentators) have said. However, in my view, it is not permissible for "ahad" to be here in the sense of the plural, because the meaning would then become: "We do not differentiate between all of His messengers," and this does not contradict their differentiating between some of the messengers, whereas the intended purpose of the negation is precisely this. For the Jews and the Christians did not differentiate between all the messengers; rather, they differentiated between some of them, namely Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus it is established that the interpretation they mentioned is invalid. Rather, the meaning of the verse is: "We do not differentiate between any one of the messengers and another in prophethood." When we interpret it in this way, the intended purpose of the speech is achieved, and God knows best.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And they said, "We hear and we obey. [We seek] Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the destination."⦘

In the verse there are several issues:

The First Issue: Discussion of the composition of this verse from several aspects:

The first: The perfection of a human being lies in knowing the truth for its own sake, and the good for the sake of acting upon it; perfecting the theoretical faculty through knowledge, and perfecting the practical faculty through performing good deeds. The theoretical faculty is nobler than the practical faculty, and the Qur'an is full of mention of both, on condition that the theoretical faculty precedes the practical. He said, concerning Abraham: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous⦘ [ash-Shu'ara': 83]. So "wisdom" is the perfection of the theoretical faculty, and "join me with the righteous" is the perfection of the practical faculty. We have elaborated on evidences of this meaning from the Qur'an earlier in this book.

Page 118

Having known this, we say: The matter in this verse is likewise. His saying: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and [so do] the believers. All of them believe in God and His angels and His books and His messengers. We make no distinction between any of His messengers⦘ is an indication of the perfection of the theoretical faculty through these noble cognitions. And His saying: ﴿And they said, "We hear and we obey"⦘ is an indication of the perfection of the practical human faculty through these virtuous and complete deeds. Whoever comprehends this subtle point will know that the Qur'an contains wondrous secrets which most people have overlooked.

The second aspect of the composition in this verse is that a human being has three days: The past, and the inquiry into it is called knowledge of the origin (ma'rifat al-mabda'); the present day, and the inquiry into it is called knowledge of the middle (ilm al-wasat); and the future, and the inquiry into it is called knowledge of the return (ilm al-ma'ad). The Qur'an encompasses the observance of these three levels. He said at the end of Surah Hud: ﴿And to God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him the whole matter is returned⦘ [Hud: 123]. This is an indication of knowledge of the origin. Since the true perfections are nothing but knowledge and power, He necessarily mentioned them in this verse. His saying ﴿To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth⦘ is an indication of the perfection of knowledge, and His saying ﴿and to Him the whole matter is returned⦘ is an indication of the perfection of power. This is the indication of the knowledge of the origin. As for the knowledge of the middle, which is the knowledge of what must be occupied with today, it also has two stages: the beginning and the end. The beginning is occupation with servitude ('ubudiyyah), and the end is severing regard from means and entrusting all affairs to the Causer of causes; this is what is called tawakkul (trust in God). So He mentioned these two stations, saying: ﴿So worship Him and put your trust in Him⦘ [Hud: 123].

As for the knowledge of the return, it is His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do⦘ [al-An'am: 132], meaning: your day tomorrow will bring the results of your deeds to you. Thus this verse has encompassed the perfection of what is investigated in these three levels. A parallel to it is also His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe⦘ [as-Saffat: 180], which is an indication of the knowledge of the origin. Then He said: ﴿And peace be upon the messengers⦘ [as-Saffat: 181], which is an indication of the knowledge of the middle. Then He said: ﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds⦘ [as-Saffat: 182], which is an indication of the knowledge of the return, in accordance with what He said describing the people of Paradise: ﴿Their call therein will be, "Glory be to You, O God," and their greeting therein will be, "Peace"⦘ [Yunus: 100].

Having known this, we say: The description of these three levels is mentioned at the end of Surah al-Baqarah. His saying ﴿The Messenger believes…⦘ up to His saying ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers⦘ is an indication of the knowledge of the origin. His saying ﴿And they said, "We hear and we obey"⦘ is an indication of the knowledge of the middle, which is knowing the states that a person must know and be occupied with for as long as he remains in this worldly life. His saying ﴿[We seek] Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the destination⦘ is an indication of the knowledge of the return. Contemplation of these secrets illuminates the heart and draws it from the narrowness of the world of bodies to the expanse of the world of the spheres and the lights of the splendor of the heavens.

The third aspect of the composition: The subjects of inquiry are of two kinds. One is the investigation of the realities of existent things. The second is the investigation of the rulings on actions in terms of obligation, permissibility, and prohibition. The first kind is derived from reason, and the second is derived from revelation (sam'). The first kind is what is meant by His saying ﴿And the believers, all of them believe in God⦘, and the second kind is what is meant by His saying ﴿And they said, "We hear and we obey"⦘.

The Second Issue: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: His saying ﴿We hear and we obey⦘ means: we hear His word and obey His command, except that the object has been omitted, because the context contains an indication of it in that they are praised for it.

I say: This is among the cases which 'Abd al-Qahir al-Nahwi, may God have mercy on him, mentioned, that omitting the object is preferable both outwardly and in implication. For if you take the implied meaning to be "we hear His word and obey His command," then there would be another word apart from His word, and another command that is obeyed apart from His command. But when that object is not implied, it conveys that there is no speech in existence that must be heard except His speech, and no command in existence which is set against "we obey" except His command. Thus omitting the object, both in form and in meaning, is preferable in this place.

The Third Issue: Know that when He, Most High, described the faith of these believers, He afterwards described them as saying: "We hear and we obey." His saying "We hear" does not mean outward hearing, for that would not convey praise. Rather, it means that we heard it with the ears of our intellects, that is, we understood it and knew its soundness, and we were certain that every obligation that came upon the tongues of the angels and prophets, peace be upon them, to us is true, sound, and must be accepted. The word "hearing" in the sense of acceptance and understanding occurs in the Qur'an. God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while he is present⦘ [Qaf: 37]. The meaning: for whoever hears the reminder with present understanding. The opposite of this is His saying: ﴿As if he had not heard it, as if in his ears was deafness⦘ [Luqman: 7]. Then He said after that, "and we obey." This indicates that just as their belief in these obligations is sound, they have not neglected any of them. Thus God Most High, by these two expressions, gathered everything relating to the chapters of obligation, in knowledge and in practice.

* * *

Then He related of them afterwards that they said: ﴿[We seek] Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the destination.⦘ In this are issues:

The First Issue: In this verse there is a question: Since these people accepted the obligations and acted upon them, what need do they have to ask for forgiveness?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: Although they exerted their utmost effort in fulfilling these obligations, they were fearful of a shortcoming that might proceed from them. When they admitted that possibility, they said: ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord⦘, meaning that they seek forgiveness from Him for whatever they fear of shortcoming in what they do and what they leave undone.

The second: It has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, there is a veil over my heart, and I seek God's forgiveness seventy times in a day and a night." So they have offered interpretations of this hadith, among which: that he, peace be upon him, was in the ascent through the stations of servitude, and whenever he ascended from one station to a higher station than the previous one, he saw the previous one as small, so he would seek God's forgiveness from it. Therefore, understanding the seeking of forgiveness in the Qur'an in this verse in this way is also not far-fetched.

The third: All acts of obedience, in comparison with the rights of His divinity, are faults, and all kinds of knowledge present in creatures, in comparison with the lights of His majesty, are shortcoming, deficiency, and ignorance. For this reason He said: ﴿And they did not measure God with His true measure⦘ [al-An'am: 91]. Since this is so, the servant, whatever station of servitude he is in, and however knowledgeable he may be, when it is compared with the splendor of God's majesty, becomes the very shortcoming from which he must seek forgiveness. This is the secret of His saying to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿So know that there is no deity except God, and ask forgiveness for your sin⦘ [Muhammad: 19]. For although the stations of his servitude were lofty, it was revealed to him, in the degrees of his unveilings, that they were, relative to what befits the Eternal Presence, a shortcoming, so he sought forgiveness from them. Likewise, God related the speech of the people of Paradise, saying: ﴿Their call therein will be, "Glory be to You, O God"⦘ [Yunus: 10]. So "Glory be to You, O God" is an indication of transcendence.

Then He said: ﴿Their call therein will be, "Glory be to You, O God," and their greeting therein will be, "Peace"⦘ [Yunus: 10], meaning that all praise belongs to God, even though we cannot grasp that praise with our intellects nor mention it with our tongues.

The Second Issue: His saying "[We seek] Your forgiveness" has the implied form "Forgive us Your forgiveness," and the verbal noun is used in place of the verb in supplication, as in the phrase *suqyan* and *ra'yan* (may you be watered, may you be pastured). Al-Farra' said: It is a verbal noun that has taken the place of the imperative, so it is put in the accusative, and similar to it are *as-salata as-salata* and *al-asada al-asada*. This is preferable to the view of those who say: "We ask You for Your forgiveness," because this form, being originally established for this meaning, is more indicative of it. A parallel to it is your saying: *hamdan hamdan* and *shukran shukran*, meaning: I praise (God) with praise, and I thank (Him) with thanks.

The Third Issue: The request for this forgiveness is attached to two things. One is its attribution to Him, which is His saying "[Your] forgiveness." The second is that He followed it with "our Lord." These two qualifiers contain several benefits:

The first: You are perfect in this attribute. You are the One who forgives sins, You are the Forgiving: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving⦘ [al-Kahf: 58], ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving⦘ [al-Buruj: 14], and You are the Oft-Forgiving: ﴿Seek forgiveness from your Lord; indeed, He is ever Oft-Forgiving⦘ [Nuh: 10]. This means that His being Oft-Forgiving is not from this time; rather, before this time He was the Forgiver of sins. This forgiving quality is like a craft proper to Him. So His saying here "[Your] forgiveness" means: I seek forgiveness from You, and You are perfect in this attribute. What is expected from one perfect in an attribute is that he gives a perfect gift. So "[Your] forgiveness" is a request for complete forgiveness, and that is nothing but forgiving all sins through His grace and mercy, and replacing them with good deeds, as He said: ﴿As for those, God will replace their evil deeds with good deeds⦘ [al-Furqan: 70].

The second: It has been reported in the sound hadith: "Indeed, God has a hundred parts of mercy. He sent down one part of it among the jinn, mankind, and all living creatures, and by it they show mercy to one another, and He has stored away ninety-nine parts for the Day of Resurrection." I think that what is meant by His saying "[Your] forgiveness" is that great forgiveness. The servant says: Suppose my offence is great, but Your forgiveness is greater than my offence.

The third: As if the servant says: Every attribute of Your majesty and divinity has its effect appearing in a specific locus. Had there not been existence after non-existence, the effects of Your power would not have appeared; and had there not been the wondrous arrangement and the elegant composition, the effects of Your knowledge would not have appeared. Likewise, had it not been for the servant's sin and his transgression, his weakness and his need, the effects of Your forgiveness would not have appeared. So His saying "[Your] forgiveness" means a request for that forgiveness whose effect cannot manifest except in my case and in the case of those like me among the sinners.

As for the second attached qualifier, which is His saying "our Lord" (*rabbana*), it contains benefits:

The first: You nurtured me when I did not mention Your Oneness. How, then, does it befit Your generosity that You would not nurture me when I have spent my life in Your Oneness?

The second: You nurtured me when I was non-existent. Had You not nurtured me at that time, I would not have been harmed by it, for I would have remained in non-existence. But now, if You do not nurture me, I would fall into severe harm. So I ask You not to neglect me.

The third: You nurtured me in the past, so make my past a intercessor for me with You that You nurture me in the future.

The fourth: You nurtured me in the past, and the completion of a kindness is better than its beginning. So complete this nurturing by Your bounty and Your mercy.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to You is the final return﴾. In this there are two benefits.

The first: a clarification that, just as they affirmed the origin (al-mabda', the beginning of creation), they likewise affirmed the return (al-ma'ad, the Resurrection). This is because belief in the origin is the foundation of belief in the Resurrection, for whoever affirms that Allah knows particulars and is capable of all possibilities must necessarily affirm the Resurrection.

The second: a clarification that when a servant knows that he must inevitably go back to Him, and to a place where there is no judgment except Allah's judgment, and no one can intercede except by Allah's permission, his sincerity in acts of obedience becomes more complete and his avoidance of misdeeds becomes more perfect. And here ends what Allah the Exalted has explained of the faith of the believers.

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 2, Verse 286 (Part 1 of 4)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. It has what it earned, and it bears what it has earned. Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make mistakes.﴾

Know that there are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾, may be the beginning of a report from God, or it may be a quotation from the Messenger and the believers in the sequence (nasaq) of the discourse, as in His saying: ﴿And they said, "We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return."﴾ and they said: ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.﴾ What supports this is what follows it, His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not hold us accountable.﴾ It is as if God, may He be exalted, related their manner of adhering to faith and righteous deeds, and related, as part of that, that they described their Lord as one who does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.

**The second issue:** Regarding the composition (nazm) of the verse: If we say that this is the speech of the believers, the connection is that when they said, ﴿We hear and we obey,﴾ it is as if they said: How could we not hear and obey, when He, may He be exalted, does not burden us except with what is within our capacity and power? And since He, by the judgment of divine mercy, does not demand of us except what is easy and light, so likewise we, by the judgment of servanthood, must be hearing and obeying. If we say that this is the speech of God, may He be exalted, the connection is that when they said, ﴿We hear and we obey,﴾ and then said after it, ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord,﴾ this indicates that their saying "Your forgiveness" is a request for forgiveness for the shortcomings that proceed from them deliberately. Since their saying "Your forgiveness" was a request for forgiveness for that shortcoming, God, may He be exalted, therefore lightened that burden for them and said: ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.﴾ The meaning is: When you hear and obey, and you do not deliberately fall short, then if some kind of shortcoming occurs from you through forgetfulness and heedlessness, do not be fearful of it, for God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. In sum, this is an answer to them in their supplication in their saying: ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord.﴾

**The third issue:** It is said: "He burdened him with the thing, so he took it upon himself (takallafa)." The noun from it is *kalaf*. *Wus'* (capacity) is what a person can bear, which does not constrain him, nor cause him hardship. Al-Farra' said: It is a noun like *wujd* and *juhd*. Some said: *Wus'* is less than *majhud* (exertion) in hardship; it is what a person's power can encompass.

**The fourth issue:** The Mu'tazilah relied on this verse to establish that God does not burden the servant with what he cannot bear or has no power over. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and His saying: ﴿God wishes to lighten for you﴾ [al-Nisa: 28], and His saying: ﴿God wishes ease for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. They said: This verse is explicit in negating the imposition of what cannot be borne. They said: And once this is established, there are two principles here:

The first: The servant is the originator (mujid) of his own actions. For if God were the originator of them, then imposing the act upon the servant would be imposing what cannot be borne. For when God creates the act, it necessarily occurs, and the servant has absolutely no power over that act, nor over abandoning it. Either he has no power to perform it, because that act has come into being by the power of God, and what exists is not brought into being a second time; or he has no power to repel it, because his power is weaker than the power of God, so how could his power prevail over the power of God? And if God does not create the act, it is impossible for the servant to have power over acquiring it. Thus it is established that if the originator of the servant's act were God, may He be exalted, then imposing the act upon the servant would be imposing what cannot be borne.

The second: The capacity (istita'ah) must precede the act; otherwise the disbeliever commanded to believe would not be able to believe, and that imposition would be the imposition of what cannot be borne. This is the complete argument of the Mu'tazilah on this point.

* * *

As for the Ash'ari scholars (al-Ashab), they said: The rational proofs have established the occurrence of imposition in this manner, so it is necessary to resort to interpreting this verse.

**The first argument:** Whoever dies in disbelief, his death in disbelief indicates that God had knowledge from eternity that he would die in disbelief and never believe. So the knowledge of his non-belief existed, and knowledge of his non-belief contradicts the existence of belief, as we have established in several places. This is also a self-evident premise. So imposing belief upon him, while there is knowledge of his non-belief, is an imposition of the combining of two contradictories. This argument applies to knowledge just as it applies to predestination (jabr).

**The second argument:** The act's proceeding from the servant depends on a motive (da'i), and that motive is created by God, may He be exalted. When this is the case, the imposition of what cannot be borne becomes necessary. We say that the act's proceeding from the servant depends on a motive because the servant's power, since it is capable of doing and of abandoning, if one of the two sides were preferred over the other without a preponderating factor, it would necessitate that a possible thing occurs without a preponderating factor, which is the negation of the Creator. And we say that this motive is from God, because if it were from the servant, its bringing into being would require another motive, and this would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul). And we say that when this is the case, predestination is necessary: because when the preponderating motive for one of the two sides is present, the other side becomes less probable, and what is less probable is impossible to occur. And when the less probable is impossible, the more probable is necessary, for there is no exit from the two contradictories. Therefore, the proceeding of belief from the disbeliever is impossible, while he is commanded to it. So the imposition is an imposition of what cannot be borne.

**The third argument:** The imposition either falls upon the servant in the state of equal motives, or in the state of one motive's preponderance. If it is the first, then it is the imposition of what cannot be borne, because equality contradicts preponderance. So if he is commanded in the state of equality to prefer one side, he has been commanded to combine two contradictories. If it is the second, then the preponderant is necessary and the less probable is impossible. If the imposition was with the preponderant, then it was with the necessary; if it was with the less probable, then it was with the impossible.

**The fourth argument:** God commanded Abu Lahab to believe, and faith is affirming as true everything God has reported. Among what He has reported is that he will not believe. So Abu Lahab has become commanded to believe that he will not believe, and that is the imposition of what cannot be borne.

**The fifth argument:** The servant does not have knowledge of the details of his act. For whoever moves his finger does not know the number of moments in which he moved his finger, because slow movement, according to the theologians (mutakallimun), is a composite of movements mixed with stillnesses. The servant has never thought that he moves at some moments and rests at others, or where he moved and where he rested. And when he does not have knowledge of the details of his act, he is not its originator, because he did not intend to bring into being that specific number of acts. So if he performed that number and not more or less, then a possible thing has been preferred without a preponderating factor, which is impossible. Thus it is established that the servant is not the originator. And when he is not the originator, the imposition of what cannot be borne is necessary according to what you have stated. These are rational arguments that are decisive and certain in this matter. So we know that
