the verse necessarily requires interpretation (ta'wil), and there are several ways to do so:

**The first, and the most correct:** It has been established that when there is a conflict between a rational certainty and an apparent scriptural text, one must either affirm both, which is impossible because it combines two contradictories; or deny both, which is impossible because it negates two contradictories; or deny the rational certainty and prefer the apparent scriptural text, which would open the door to attacking rational proofs, and if that were so, tawhid, prophethood, and the Qur'an would all be invalidated. And preferring the scriptural proof leads to undermining both the rational proof and the scriptural proof together. So there remains only that one must affirm the soundness of the rational proofs and take the apparent scriptural text to be interpreted. This is the very argument on which the Mu'tazilah always rely in repelling the apparent texts that the anthropomorphists (ahl al-tashbih) cite. By this method we know that this verse has an interpretation in general, whether we know it or not. In that case, there is no need to go into it in detail.

**The second answer:** The meaning of imposition (taklif) in command and prohibition is nothing but informing that whoever does such-and-such will be rewarded, and whoever does not will be punished. So when the apparent form of a command exists, if the commanded act is possible, it is a command and an imposition in reality; otherwise it is not an imposition in reality, but rather an announcement that punishment for it will descend in the Hereafter, and an indication that he was only created for the Fire.

**The third answer:** A person, as long as he has not died, and we do not know whether God knew of him that he would die in disbelief or not, we are in doubt about the existence of an impediment. Therefore we command him to believe and urge him toward it. If he dies in disbelief, we learn after his death that the impediment was present in his case. So it becomes clear that the condition of imposition had been absent from him during his life. This is the view of a group of the early predestinarians.

**The fourth answer:** We have explained that His saying, ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity,﴾ is not the saying of God, may He be exalted, but rather the saying of the believers, and therefore it is not a proof. However, this is weak, because when God related it from them in the context of praising them and commending them, it is necessary that they were truthful in this statement, for if they were lying in it, their being honored on account of it would not be permissible. This is the furthest that can be said on this point. We ask the Mighty God to have mercy on our incapacity and the shortcoming of our understanding, and to pardon our errors, for we seek only the truth and aim only at sincerity.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It has what it earned, and it bears what it has earned,﴾ there are several issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** They differed over whether there is a distinction in the language between *kasb* (earning) and *iktisab* (acquiring). Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The correct view among the people of language is that *kasb* and *iktisab* are one and the same, with no difference between them. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*He found his father in that earning, acquiring.*

The Qur'an also speaks to this, as God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38], and He says: ﴿No soul earns anything except against itself﴾ [al-An'am: 164], and He says: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil and his sin surrounds him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81], and He says: ﴿And those who harm believing men and believing women for what they have not acquired﴾ [al-Ahzab: 58]. This indicates that each of these two terms may stand in the place of the other. Some people have accepted that there is a distinction, and then there are two views on it:

*One:* That *iktisab* is more specific than *kasb*, because *kasb* is divided into earning for oneself and earning for others, whereas *iktisab* applies only to what a person acquires for himself. It is said: "So-and-so is a *kasib* (earner) for his family," but it is not said: "*muktasib* (acquirer) for his family."

*The second:* The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: Good is specified with *kasb*, and evil with *iktisab*, because *iktisab* implies exertion (i'timal). Since evil is something the soul desires, and the soul is drawn toward it and commands it, it is more active and diligent in attaining it. So for this meaning, it is described as *iktisab* in it. And since that is not the case in the matter of good, it is described with what does not indicate exertion. And God knows best.

**The second issue:** The Mu'tazilah argued with this verse that the servant's act is by his origination and bringing into being. They said: Because the verse is explicit in attributing its good and evil to him. And if that were by God's creation, this attribution would be void, and the servant's acts proceeding from him would be like his color, his height, his shape, and all the other matters over which he has absolutely no power. The discussion of this is well known, and success is from God.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 286 (part 2 of 4):

The judge (al-Qadi) said: If He created their acts, what is the benefit of imposing obligations (taklif)? As for the reason they ask Him not to burden them: for them, the heavy and the light are alike in that He creates it in them, and no fatigue (nasab) or weariness (lughub) befalls them from it.

* * *

Third question: Our companions (the Ash'arites) used this verse to refute the doctrine of cancellation (muhabata), which holds that sins cancel out good deeds. They said: Because He affirmed both matters together. He stated that it has the reward of what it earned and bears the punishment of what it earned. This is explicit that these two entitlements can coexist, and that the arrival of one does not necessarily entail the cessation of the other. Al-Jubba'i said: The apparent meaning of the verse, although it indicates an unconditional sense, is conditional, and the implied meaning is: it has the reward of good deeds, provided it does not nullify them, and it bears the punishment for what it earned, provided it does not expiate it through repentance. We resorted to supplying this condition because we have explained that reward must be a pure and lasting benefit, and that punishment must be a pure and lasting harm, and combining the two is impossible according to reason. Therefore combining the entitlement to both is also impossible.

Know that the discussion of this question has already been pursued thoroughly in the commentary on His words: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264], so we will not repeat it.

* * *

Fourth question: Many of the theologians (mutakallimun) used this verse to show that God does not punish children for the sins of their fathers. The basis of this inference is evident in it. Its parallel is His words: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164].

* * *

Fifth question: The jurists (fuqaha') relied on this verse to establish that the default in retention (imsak) is continuation and persistence, because the lam in His words ﴿it shall have what it earned﴾ indicates the establishment of this exclusive right. This is reinforced by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every person has more right to his earnings than his father, his child, and all other people." When this principle is established, a great many questions of jurisprudence (fiqh) follow from it.

Among them: guaranteed property is not owned merely by paying its compensation (daman), because the factor requiring the continuation of ownership is present, namely His words ﴿it shall have what it earned﴾, while the incidental factor, whether usurpation (ghasb) or guarantee (daman), does not require the cessation of ownership, as shown by the umm walad (a slave woman who bore her master's child) and the mudabbar (a slave freed upon his master's death).

Among them: if one usurps a plot of land and incorporates it into his building, or usurps wheat and grinds it, ownership does not cease, by His words ﴿it shall have what it earned﴾.

Among them: there is no pre-emption (shufah) for a neighbour, because the factor requiring the continuation of ownership is present, namely His words ﴿it shall have what it earned﴾. The distinction between a partner and a neighbour is evident, as shown by the fact that a neighbour is not given precedence over a partner, and that prevents equality from being achieved. Also, harm from mingling with a neighbour is less, and also, in partnership one needs to bear the cost of division (qismah), and this meaning is absent in the case of a neighbour.

Among them: amputation (qat') does not prevent the obligation of compensation, because the factor requiring the continuation of ownership is present, namely His words ﴿it shall have what it earned﴾, and amputation does not require the cessation of ownership, as shown by the fact that a stolen item, whenever it remains existing, must be returned to its owner, and amputation does not make the cessation of his ownership necessary.

Among them: those who deny the obligation of zakat have argued with it. Its answer is that the proofs requiring zakat are more specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. In sum, this verse is a great foundation for the derivative rulings of jurisprudence. And God knows best.

* * *

Then know that He related the supplication (du'a') of the believers. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Supplication is the marrow of worship." This is because the supplicant witnesses himself in a state of poverty, need, humility, and destitution, and witnesses the majesty of God, His generosity, His might, and His greatness, through the attributes of self-sufficiency and exaltation. This is the aim of all acts of worship and obedience. For this reason, He concluded this noble surah, which contains these great sciences, with supplication and humble entreaty to God. The discussion of the realities of supplication has been mentioned in the commentary on His words: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186]. He said: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make mistakes﴾. In the verse there are questions:

First question: Know that He related four kinds of supplication from the believers, and at the beginning of each of them He mentioned the words "Our Lord" (rabbana), except in the fourth kind of supplication, where He omitted this word, which is His words: ﴿And pardon us and forgive us﴾.

As for the first kind, it is His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make mistakes﴾. And in it are questions:

First question: "Do not take us to task" means do not punish us. He used the form of mufa'alah (reciprocal form), although the act is one, because the one who forgets has given himself the opportunity and opened the way to it by his own act, so whoever punishes him for his sin is like one who helps him harm himself. I have another view on this, which is that God takes the sinner to account through punishment, and so the sinner seems to take his Lord to account by demanding pardon and generosity, for he finds no one to deliver him from His punishment except Him. For this reason, the servant clings to Him when he fears Him. Since each of them takes the other to account, it was expressed with the term mu'akhadhah (taking to account).

Second question: Regarding forgetting, there are two views.

The first: its meaning is forgetting itself, which is the opposite of remembrance.

If it is said: Is not the act of the forgetful person in the domain of pardon, by the judgment of reason, since it is impossible to impose what cannot be borne, and by the judgment of revelation, namely the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Error and forgetfulness are lifted from my community, and what they are coerced into"? If forgetfulness is definitely within the domain of pardon, then what is the meaning of asking for pardon for it in supplication?

The answer to this is in several respects.

The first: forgetfulness is of two kinds: some of it is excusable for its doer, and some of it is not excusable. Do you not see that whoever sees blood on his garment, then delays removing it until he forgets and prays while it is on his garment, is considered negligent, since it was incumbent upon him to hasten to remove it? But if he did not see it on his garment, he is excused. And whoever shoots at game in a place and hits a person, the shooter may be in a situation where he does not know whether he is hitting that game or someone else. If he shoots and does not take precaution, he is blameworthy. But if there were no clear signs of error, and then he shoots and hits a person, he is excused here. Likewise, a person who neglects study and repetition until he forgets the Qur'an is blameworthy. But if he persisted in recitation, yet afterward forgot, he is excused here. Thus it is established that forgetfulness is of two kinds: some of it is excusable, and some is not excusable. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he wanted to recall a need, would tie a thread on his finger. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the forgetful person may not be excused, and that is when he abandons caution and turns away from the causes of remembrance. And when this is so, asking for his forgiveness through supplication is valid.

The second answer: that this is a supplication on the basis of supposition. This is because these believers who related this supplication were mindful of God with the mindfulness due to Him, so nothing unbecoming came from them except by way of forgetfulness and error. Therefore, describing them as supplicating in this way was an indication of the innocence of their conduct from what they might be taken to account for, as if it were said: If forgetfulness is something for which one may be taken to account, then do not take us to account for it.

The third answer: the purpose of supplication is to show humble entreaty to God, not to demand the act. For this reason, the supplicant often prays for something he is certain God will do whether he supplicates or not. God the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 112], and He said: ﴿Our Lord, give us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al 'Imran: 194]. The angels also said in their supplication: ﴿So forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. Likewise in this verse, the knowledge that forgetfulness is forgiven does not prevent the goodness of asking for it in supplication.

The fourth answer: taking the forgetful person to account is not rationally impossible. This is because when a person knows that after forgetting he will be taken to account, then out of fear of being taken to account he perpetuates remembrance. In that case, nothing proceeds from him except that the perpetuation of that remembrance is an act burdensome to the self. Since that is permissible according to reason, it is indeed proper to ask for forgiveness from it through supplication.

The fifth answer: our companions who permit imposing what cannot be borne cling to this verse, saying: The forgetful person is not able to guard against the act. So, were it not rationally permissible for God the Exalted to punish him for it, He would not have asked, through supplication, for the abandonment of being taken to account for it.

The second view on the meaning of forgetfulness: that it be understood as abandonment. God the Exalted said: ﴿He forgot, and We found in him no determination﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115], and He said: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], that is, they abandoned acting for God, so He abandoned them. And a man says to his companion, "Do not forget me from your gift," that is, do not abandon me. So what is meant by this forgetfulness is that one abandons the act due to a corrupt interpretation, and what is meant by error is that one performs the act due to a corrupt interpretation.

Third question: It is known that the forgetfulness and error mentioned in this verse are either both explained by an explanation in which the intention to do what is unbecoming is involved, or one of them is such and the other is not. As for the first possibility, it indicates the granting of pardon to the perpetrators of major sins, because intention toward disobedience being present in forgetfulness and in error, and then God commanded the Muslims to supplicate to Him with their words: ﴿Do not take us to task if we forget or make mistakes﴾, this was a command from God the Exalted to them to ask God not to punish them for their sins. And since He commanded them to ask for that, it shows that He will give them what they ask for, and this indicates the granting of pardon to the perpetrators of major sins.

As for the second and third possibilities, they are both invalid, because taking to account for that is ugly according to the opponent, and what is ugly in its doing from God cannot be requested through supplication.

If it is said: The forgetful person may be taken to account for failing to guard, intentionally and deliberately, according to what you established in the previous question.

We say: He is in reality taken to account for failing to guard deliberately and intentionally, so the taking to account only occurred for what he deliberately abandoned. And the apparent meaning of what we have mentioned is that this verse indicates the hope of pardon for the people of major sins.

* *

His words, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden (isr) like that which You laid upon those before us﴾.

Know that this is the second kind of supplication, and in it are questions.

First question: Isr, in the language, means heaviness and hardship. Al-Nabigha said:

"O preventer of oppression from overtaking their chiefs, and the lifter of the burden from them after they had known it"

Then the covenant was called isr because it is heavy. God the Exalted said: ﴿And you have taken upon that My covenant (isri)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81], that is, My covenant and My pledge. And isr also means inclination (atf). It is said: "What binds me to him is a kinship (ifrah)," that is, kinship and relationship. Inclination was called isr because your inclination toward it weighs heavily on your heart with every hardship that reaches it.

Second question: The people of exegesis (ahl al-tafsir) mentioned two views regarding it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 286 (part 3 of 4):

The first view: "Do not burden us with obligations as You burdened those before us, the Jews." The exegetes said: God the Exalted imposed fifty prayers on them, and commanded them to give a quarter of their wealth in zakat (obligatory almsgiving). Whoever got impurity on his garment was commanded to cut that part off. When they forgot something, punishment was hastened for them in this world. When they committed a sin, some of the foods that had been lawful to them were made unlawful for them. God the Exalted said: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them [certain good things]﴾ [An-Nisa: 160]. He also said: ﴿And if We had decreed for them, "Kill yourselves or leave your homes," they would not have done it, except a few of them﴾ [An-Nisa: 66]. The people of Talut (Saul) were forbidden to drink from the river while traveling, and their punishment was hastened in this world, as He said: ﴿Before We obliterate faces﴾ [An-Nisa: 47]. They were transformed into apes and swine. Al-Qaffal said: Whoever looks into the Fifth Book of the Torah, which these Jews claim to hold, will find what covenants and pledges of severe strictness were taken from them, and will see many wonders. So the believers asked their Lord to protect them from the likes of these harsh restrictions, and He, in His grace and mercy, has removed that from them. God the Exalted said, describing this community: ﴿And He relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [Al-A'raf: 157]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Transformation (al-maskh), engulfment (al-khasf) and drowning have been lifted from my community." God the Exalted said: ﴿And God would not punish them while you are among them, nor would God punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was sent with the easy, tolerant hanifiyyah (the upright monotheistic religion)."

The believers only sought this lightening because severity is a cause of shortcoming, shortcoming necessitates punishment, and they have no capacity for the punishment of God the Exalted. Therefore, they naturally sought ease in the obligations.

The second view: "Do not place upon us a covenant and pledge resembling the pledge of those before us in harshness and severity." This view returns in reality to the first, but with the addition of something beyond what is expressed, so the first view is preferable.

The third issue: Someone may say: The rational and revealed proofs indicate that He is the Most Generous of the generous and the Most Merciful of the merciful. So what is the reason that He made the obligations severe for the Jews, to the point that this led them to fall into transgressions and rebellion?

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) said: It is permissible that a thing be a benefit for one person and a harm for another. The Jews had harshness and coarseness predominant in their natures, so they were only corrected by heavy obligations and severity. This community had gentleness and nobility of character predominant in their natures, so their benefit lay in lightness and the avoidance of harshness.

The Ash'aris (al-Ashab, the scholars of the Ash'ari school) answered: The question we raised in the first position we transfer to the second position. We say: Why did He single out the Jews with coarseness of nature, hardness of heart and meanness of aspiration, so that they needed enormous severities in the obligations? And why did He single out this community with delicacy of nature, nobility of character and loftiness of aspiration, so that easy obligations suffice them in attaining their benefits?

Whoever reflects and is fair will know that these explanations are flawed, for the majesty of the Divine Majesty is too exalted to be weighed by the scale of Mu'tazilism. He, glory be to Him, does what He wills and decrees what He desires: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾.

* * *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with that which we have no capacity to bear﴾.

Know that this is the third type of the supplication of the believers, and it contains issues:

The first issue: "Taqah" (capacity) is a noun derived from "ittaqah" (to be able), like "ta'ah" from "i'ta'ah" (obedience) and "jabah" from "ijabah" (response). It is used in place of the verbal noun.

The second issue: Some of the Ash'aris held to this verse as evidence that imposing what cannot be borne is permissible, for if it were not permissible, asking for it in supplication to God the Exalted would not be good.

The Mu'tazilah answered this with several points:

First: His saying ﴿that which we have no capacity to bear﴾ means: its performance would be an enormous hardship, just as a man says: "I cannot look at so-and-so, when he is burdensome to me." The poet said:

"If I burden you with what I cannot bear, you will be displeased with what pleases you of my character."

And in a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the slave: "He is to be given his food and clothing, and he is not to be burdened with work that he cannot bear," meaning what is hard for him.

'Imran ibn Husayn narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The sick person prays sitting, and if he cannot, then lying on his side." His saying "if he cannot" does not mean lacking the strength to sit; rather, all the jurists say that what is meant is when sitting would cause him a great and severe hardship. God the Exalted also said, describing the disbelievers: ﴿They were not able to hear﴾ [Hud: 20], meaning it was hard for them.

Second: He, may He be exalted, did not say: "Do not impose upon us that which we have no capacity to bear." Rather He said: ﴿And do not burden us with that which we have no capacity to bear﴾. "Tahmil" (burdening) is to place upon someone what he has no capacity for by making him bear it, so what is meant is punishment, and the meaning is: "Do not burden us with Your punishment, which we cannot endure." If we interpret the verse this way, then His saying "do not burden us" is literal in that sense; but if we interpret it as obligation, then His saying "do not burden us" is metaphorical. So the first is preferable.

Third: Suppose they asked God the Exalted that He not impose on them what they have no power over; still, that does not indicate that it is permissible for Him to do the opposite. For if it indicated that, then His saying ﴿My Lord, judge with truth﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 112] would indicate that He may judge falsely. Likewise, Abraham's saying, peace be upon him: ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 87] would indicate that He may disgrace the prophets. And God the Exalted said to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 48], yet this does not indicate that the Messenger may obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. The same applies to His saying: ﴿If you associate partners with Him, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [Az-Zumar: 65]. This is the sum of the Mu'tazilah's answers.

The Ash'aris answered and said:

As for the first point: it is refuted in two ways:

First: If His saying ﴿And do not burden us with that which we have no capacity to bear﴾ were understood to mean that He should not make the obligations severe for them, then its meaning and the meaning of the preceding verse, which is His saying ﴿And do not place upon us a burden like that which You placed upon those before us﴾, would be one and the same, and this verse would be pure repetition, which is impermissible.

Second: We have explained that "taqah" is "ittaqah" and power. So His saying ﴿that which we have no capacity to bear﴾ apparently means: "do not burden us with what we have no power over." At most, this expression has come, in some usages, with the meaning of the future by way of metaphor, but the original principle is to take the expression literally.

As for the second point: its answer is that "tahammul" (bearing) in the usage of the Qur'an is specific to obligation. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 72], down to His saying ﴿and man undertook it﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 72]. Even if this usage did not exist, His saying ﴿that which we have no capacity to bear﴾ is general in regard to punishment and to obligation, so it must be applied to its apparent meaning. Restricting it without evidence is impermissible.

As for the third point: its answer is that if performing a thing is impossible, it is not permissible to ask, by way of supplication and humble entreaty, that it be prevented. That would be like one who says in his supplication and entreaty: "Our Lord, do not combine two opposites, and do not turn the eternal into the originated," for just as that is impermissible, so is what you mentioned.

Having established this, we say: This is the original principle. When it is set aside in some cases by a detailed proof, it does not become obligatory to set it aside in all other cases without evidence. And success is from God.

* * *

The third issue: Know that there remain in the verse some questions.

The first question: Why did He say in the first verse ﴿And do not place upon us a burden [isr]﴾, and in this verse ﴿And do not burden us﴾? He specified the first with "placing" (haml) and this with "burdening" (tahmil).

The answer: What is difficult can be carried, but what is not within one's capacity cannot be carried. So in what is beyond capacity, only "tahmil" (causing to bear) occurs, but "haml" (carrying) is impossible. In what is difficult, both carrying and causing to bear are possible. For this reason, He specified the last verse with "tahmil."

The second question: When they asked, with the words ﴿do not place upon us a burden﴾, that He not impose upon them difficult acts, it follows that He would not impose upon them what they cannot bear. Given this, the reverse of this order would be preferable.

The answer: What I imagine regarding it, and God knows best, is that the servant has two stations. The first is his adherence to the outward Shari'ah. The second is his beginning of the unveilings (al-mukashafat), which is that he occupies himself with knowing God, serving Him, obeying Him and thanking Him for His blessings. In the first station, he asked that the severity not be imposed. In the second station, he said: "Do not demand from me praise worthy of Your majesty, nor thanks worthy of Your bounties and favors, nor knowledge worthy of the sanctity of Your greatness, for that is not worthy of my remembrance, gratitude and contemplation, and I have no capacity for it." And since the Shari'ah precedes the Reality (al-haqiqah), it is inevitable that His saying ﴿And do not place upon us a burden﴾ is mentioned before His saying ﴿And do not burden us with that which we have no capacity to bear﴾.

The third question: He, may He be exalted, related these supplications of the believers in the plural form, that they said: ﴿Do not take us to task if we forget or err﴾, ﴿And do not place upon us a burden as You placed upon those before us﴾, ﴿And do not burden us with that which we have no capacity to bear﴾. So what is the benefit of this collective form at the time of supplication?

The answer: The purpose of it is to show that the acceptance of supplication is more perfect when made collectively. This is because aspirations have effects, so when souls and motivations unite upon one thing, its attainment is more perfect.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And pardon us, and forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾.

Know that those three kinds of supplication were all about asking for removal (of burden), and they were joined with the word "Our Lord" (rabbana). As for this fourth supplication, the word "Our Lord" has been omitted from it, and its apparent meaning indicates a request for an action. So there are two questions about it:

The first question: Why is the word "Our Lord" not mentioned here?

The answer: Calling out (nida') is only needed when there is distance. When there is closeness, it is not needed. The address was omitted to indicate that when the servant persists in humble supplication, he attains nearness to God the Exalted. This is a great secret, from which one perceives other secrets.

The second question: What is the difference between pardon (al-'afw), forgiveness (al-maghfirah) and mercy (al-rahmah)?

The answer: Pardon is that He drops the punishment from him. Forgiveness is that He covers his sin, protecting him from the torment of shame and disgrace. It is as if the servant says: "I ask You for pardon, and if You pardon me, then cover it over for me, for deliverance from the torment of the grave is only sweet when it is followed by deliverance from the torment of disgrace." The first is physical torment, and the second is spiritual torment. When he is delivered from both, he turns to seeking reward. This reward is also of two kinds: physical reward, which is the bliss of Paradise, its pleasures and its good things; and spiritual reward, whose ultimate goal is that the light of God the Exalted's majesty be manifested to him, and that the sublimity of God's greatness be revealed to him to the extent of his capacity, by his becoming absent from everything other than God the Exalted, wholly absorbed in the light of the presence of God's majesty, may He be exalted. So His saying "and have mercy on us" is a request for physical reward, and His saying after that ﴿You are our Protector﴾ is a request for spiritual reward. And so that the servant may turn wholly toward God the Exalted, because His saying ﴿You are our Protector﴾ is an address to those present, and perhaps many of

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 2, verse 286 (part 4 of 4):

The theologians (mutakallimun, scholars of kalam, rational theology) find these words far-fetched and say: they are of the category of acts of obedience (ta'at). They have spoken truly in what they say, for that is the extent of their knowledge: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾ [an-Najm: 30].

In His saying ﴿You are our Mawla (Master/Guardian)﴾ there is another benefit. This word indicates the utmost submission, humility, and acknowledgment that He, glory be to Him, is the one who grants every blessing they attain and the giver of every honour they win. Therefore, when they made supplication, they showed that in their being obligated to His grace and kindness they are like a child whose welfare is not complete except through the management of his guardian, and like a servant whose affairs are not ordered except through the rectification of his master. He, glory be to Him, is the Qayyum (Sustainer) of the heavens and the earth, the one who rectifies the affairs of all, and in reality He is the Mawla of all, as He said: ﴿An excellent Mawla and an excellent Helper﴾ [al-Anfal: 40]. Similar to this verse is ﴿Allah is the Wali (Protector) of those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], meaning His Naseer (Helper). And His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is His Mawla﴾ [at-Tahrim: 4], meaning His Helper. And His saying ﴿That is because Allah is the Mawla of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no Mawla﴾ [Muhammad: 11].
* * *
Then He said: ﴿So help us against the disbelieving people﴾, meaning: help us against them in our fighting with them, in our argument with them through proof, and in raising the dominion of Islam above their dominion, as He said: ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [at-Tawbah: 33]. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: ﴿So help us against the disbelieving people﴾ means Allah's aid through the spiritual, angelic power against the bodily faculties that call to other than Allah. This is the end of the surah.

Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated from Muqatil ibn Sulayman that when the Prophet ﷺ was taken by night to the heaven, he was given the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah. The angels said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has honoured you with excellent praise of you in His saying ﴿The Messenger believes﴾. So ask Him and seek His favour." Jibril, peace be upon them both, taught him how to supplicate. Muhammad ﷺ said: ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return﴾. Allah the Exalted said: "I have forgiven you." He said: ﴿Do not take us to task﴾. Allah said: "I will not take you to task." He said: ﴿And do not burden us with a burden as You burdened those before us﴾. He said: "I will not make it heavy upon you." Muhammad said: ﴿And do not burden us with that which we have no ability to bear﴾. He said: "I will not burden you with that." Muhammad said: ﴿And pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy upon us﴾. Allah the Exalted said: "I have pardoned you, forgiven you, shown mercy to you, and I will help you against the disbelieving people." In some narrations, Muhammad ﷺ used to recite these supplications, and the angels would say: Amin.

And this poor, wretched, needy one, the compiler of these words, says: My God and my Master, everything I sought and wrote, I intended by it only Your Face and Your pleasure. If I am correct, it is by Your guidance that I am correct, so accept it from this beggar by Your grace. And if I have erred, then pass over me by Your grace and mercy, O You whom the insistence of the insistent does not weary, and whom the request of the askers does not occupy. This is the end of the discourse on the tafsir of this surah, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad, the Prophet, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
